generated_summary: Voters in 11 states are choosing governors, and Republicans look poised to make net gains, potentially extending their control to over two-thirds of U.S. governorships. Of the seats up, eight are held by Democrats and three by Republicans; currently Republicans hold 29 governors, Democrats 20, and one is independent. Only three races—Montana, New Hampshire and Washington—are highly competitive as incumbents step down. Republicans are expected to pick up North Carolina and hold Utah, North Dakota and Indiana; Democrats are likely to retain Vermont, Delaware, Missouri and West Virginia. Political scientists note governors will be influential on health care after a Supreme Court ruling allowing states to opt out of Medicaid expansion, giving governors significant leverage over implementation. Outcomes could be further amplified by a Republican presidential victory, which would empower Republican governors on federal-state policy choices.

This update clarifies facts around the “Hey Facebook what’s SO wrong with a pic of two men kissing?” controversy tied to a London “kiss-in” protest. The image used in the original post was a promotional still from the British soap EastEnders showing Christian Clarke (actor John Partridge) kissing another man; that storyline previously sparked UK complaints when aired pre-watershed, though the character has since had additional gay storylines. The photo was chosen because it was relatively mild compared with other considered images. Contrary to some reports, Facebook did not remove the John Snow Kiss-In event page; organizer Paul Shetler made the event private after it finished due to trolls posting abusive comments. Media misreporting also wrongly suggested Richard Metzger organized the event; he did not. Separately, Facebook acknowledged removing a kiss photo from a Dangerous Minds promotional page in error, apologizing and noting it did not violate site rules. The erroneous removal prompted many people to post same-sex kissing photos in protest.

Siskiyou County supervisors voted 4-1 to pursue seceding from California and join a proposed new state of Jefferson comprising rural Northern California and Southern Oregon counties. More than 100 residents attended the meeting, almost all supporting the move; speakers cited lack of representation in Sacramento, burdensome regulations, water-rights disputes and a rural fire prevention fee. Advocates, led locally by rancher Mark Baird, want more local control and restoration of limited government; opponents note the constitutional and practical hurdles. Board chair Ed Valenzuela was the lone dissent, saying he took an oath to uphold California’s constitution and prefers working within the system. Neighboring counties, including Humboldt, are considering similar measures, though some supervisors warned about Jefferson’s economic viability given small tax bases, state roads and federal lands. Any new state would require approval by California’s Legislature and Congress.

Microsoft's acquisition of most of Nokia represents a decisive push to transform Microsoft from a primarily software-and-services firm into a vertically integrated devices-and-services company. The deal is intended to reconnect Microsoft to hardware as desktops give way to smartphones and tablets, preserving Windows’ influence as users shift to mobile platforms and preventing Apple or Google from locking down app innovation, distribution and economics. Analysts view the move as inevitable given dwindling investment from other Windows Phone licensees and Nokia’s alignment with Microsoft after losing ground to iOS and Android. Forrester’s Charles Golvin warns Microsoft must still harmonize many brands and services — Windows, Nokia, Live, Surface, Xbox, Bing — into a cohesive customer experience, a task that should influence CEO selection.

The acquisition buys Microsoft deeper integration, patents, carrier relationships and stronger presence in emerging markets. Nokia gains R&D and marketing scale, while Microsoft receives Nokia’s device expertise and access to low-cost and entry-level segments via Asha devices — useful as growth shifts to emerging markets. Analysts caution, however, that Windows Phone’s modest market share limits developer reach, and competition from low-cost Android manufacturers is fierce. Microsoft risks straining relations with PC and device partners by moving into hardware (Surface, potential Nokia tablets), complicating Windows 8’s ecosystem.

Nokia’s collapse over the prior decade — from dominant handset maker to struggling partner — stemmed from missed smartphone opportunities, platform missteps (Symbian, delayed MeeGo) and inability to compete with Apple’s integrated experience and Android’s ecosystem growth. Stephen Elop’s “burning platform” memo framed Nokia’s urgency and explained the strategic shift toward partnering with Microsoft; his return to Microsoft cements the earlier alignment. While the deal is bold and arguably necessary to avoid terminal decline, success hinges on tight integration, consumer appeal in mature markets, and a clear strategy for emerging markets and enterprise mobility.

As the Supreme Court begins its new term, conservatives may score major wins after a year of liberal successes, with several high-stakes cases poised to reshape labor, higher education, voting representation, religious exemptions and abortion rights. At the forefront is Friedrichs v. California Teachers Association, in which public-school teachers challenge a 38-year precedent allowing unions to collect fees from nonmembers for collective bargaining. A decision limiting or overruling Abood could sharply weaken public-sector unions by reducing dues and membership, altering political influence built on organized labor.

The Court will also revisit affirmative action in Fisher v. University of Texas at Austin. Abigail Fisher contends UT’s race-conscious admissions unfairly disadvantaged her; the justices previously demanded strict scrutiny of such programs and now must decide whether that standard will force many public universities to abandon race-based measures to foster diversity. Justice Kennedy’s vote is pivotal, and Justice Kagan is recused.

Evenwel v. Abbott raises whether states may apportion legislative districts based on eligible voters rather than total population. A ruling allowing voter-based counts could shift power from diverse urban areas—including many Latino communities—to whiter suburban and rural regions, with potential partisan consequences.

Religious non-profits have pressed challenges to Obamacare’s contraception mandate and the administrative accommodation process. Following Hobby Lobby, these cases ask whether religiously affiliated institutions must comply with opt-out paperwork that they say violates their beliefs; multiple petitions await the Court’s choice.

Finally, the justices are likely to take up abortion-clinic regulations—laws requiring doctors to have hospital admitting privileges and clinics to meet surgical-center standards. The Texas law at issue could drastically reduce clinics and prompt the most consequential abortion ruling since Planned Parenthood v. Casey. Several capital-punishment and other high-profile cases also populate the term, setting up a June 2016 decision season that could influence the presidential race and the Court’s future composition.

A preservationist’s basement inspection at 50 Bowery in Manhattan uncovered structural elements he believes belong to the 18th‑century Bull’s Head Tavern, a site tied to George Washington’s 1783 return to the city. Photographer and preservationist Adam Woodward found apparent Colonial‑era hand‑hewn and hand‑planed joists, wide floorboards and a brick‑and‑stone foundation beneath later 19th‑ and 20th‑century additions. If confirmed, the remains could make the site Manhattan’s oldest surviving building fabric and offer a rare archaeological record of a Revolutionary‑era tavern that later became home to the famed Atlantic Garden beer hall (1858–1911). Historians including David Freeland and Kerri Culhane emphasized the location’s layered history — from a mid‑18th‑century tavern on the Bowery’s butchers’ route to a German immigrant beer garden and a Tin Pan Alley watering hole — and the significance of preserving any original fabric. The property’s owner plans to demolish the existing structure for a hotel, prompting calls from preservationists for an immediate, proper archaeological exploration. The Landmarks Preservation Commission is aware but lacks authority to compel the owner to perform archaeology, limiting action to advising and providing archaeologist referrals; local elected officials are pressing the issue but must negotiate with the owner. The site’s fate hinges on whether demolition can be paused for professional investigation.

An unmanned aircraft that entered southern Israeli airspace was shot down on Saturday, highlighting regional tensions and prompting accusations about Israeli air defenses. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps deputy coordinator Jamaluddin Aberoumand told Fars the incident exposed weaknesses in Israel’s Iron Dome, though that system is designed for short-range rockets rather than slow drones. Israel released a short video clip showing a fighter jet missile destroying the small aircraft after it was first seen over the Mediterranean near Gaza and later shot down above a West Bank forest. Israeli MP Miri Regev suggested on Twitter the drone was Iranian and launched by Hezbollah; Israeli officials did not confirm this and Tehran called such claims a psychological operation. Separately, Israel struck targets in Gaza after militants fired rockets at southern Israel in retaliation for an earlier strike that killed a militant linked to a Sinai attack. Hamas and Islamic Jihad said they participated in the rocket salvo; Gaza medics reported casualties and damage from Israeli tank fire and air raids. The incidents underscore persistent hostilities around Gaza, Israeli concerns about Iranian-backed actors, and risks of escalation.

The Pompidou Centre in Paris is preparing to display a long-missing Picasso painting after U.S. customs recovered it in December. The cubist 1911 canvas "La Coiffeuse" ("The Hairdresser"), valued at more than $2.5 million, vanished from a Pompidou storeroom in 2001 after being bequeathed to France’s National Museums. The painting had been last exhibited in Munich in 1998 and was declared stolen when a 2001 loan request prompted staffers to find it missing. Federal agents intercepted the work in a FedEx shipment from Belgium to a climate-controlled storage facility in Long Island City; shipping paperwork deceitfully described the piece as a $37 “art craft/toy” marked “Joyeux Noel.” Seized at the Port of Newark, the canvas was examined by French museum officials who confirmed it as the stolen Picasso. U.S. Attorney Loretta E. Lynch filed a civil forfeiture complaint to return the painting to France. Pompidou director Alain Seban said the recovery is a welcome relief amid broader cultural losses and hopes the work will be publicly exhibited again in May. No arrests have been announced; court documents identified the shipper only as “Robert” and did not disclose the intended recipient. Authorities say the seizure reflects shrinking markets for stolen antiquities in the United States.

Beginning in 1996, Alexa Internet began donating its web crawl data to the Internet Archive; those ongoing daily data transfers are incorporated into the Wayback Machine after an embargo period, enriching the Archive’s historical web collections.

Local food, drink, and culture highlights from the Twin Cities region include a group of personal and curated picks: St. Paul’s top three dive bars are celebrated for atmosphere and standout menu items—one notably touted for having “the best burger in town” and a compact, intimate setting. In northeast Minneapolis, Que Viet earned WCCO viewers’ choice recognition for the best egg roll in Minnesota, marking it as a neighborhood favorite. The Sunshine Factory, opened in 1976 in New Hope, retains a strong 1970s vibe and long-running local appeal. A data-driven roundup identifies five top Minneapolis distilleries under the “Minneapolis Moonshine” banner to help readers find the best distilling spots. Arts-focused offers in St. Paul highlight three accessible “artsy deals” for those wanting to deepen their appreciation of local art. Finally, a cocktail feature from “Mike’s Mix” showcases Crooked Water Spirits and presents the “BB Boulevardier,” a bourbon-forward riff on the classic Boulevardier (itself a bourbon variant of the Negroni).

A Dallas police officer, Rogelio Santander, died Wednesday morning at Texas Health Presbyterian Dallas after being shot Tuesday at a North Dallas Home Depot. Two others shot in the same incident—Officer Crystal Almeida, 26, and Home Depot loss-prevention officer Scott Painter—underwent surgery and remained hospitalized in critical condition but were described by Dallas Police Chief U. Renee Hall as making “remarkable recoveries.” The suspect, 29-year-old Armando Luis Juarez, was arrested late Tuesday after a police chase that ended near Love Field; he was initially charged with aggravated assault and felony theft and, after Santander’s death, was charged with capital murder. Authorities say Juarez was detained earlier by an off-duty officer at the store when officers Santander and Almeida responded; a witness inside the loss-prevention office reported seeing Juarez shoot all three. A large search, aided by surveillance video, led police to Juarez’s white work truck and a pursuit that culminated in his capture. The Dallas district attorney has assigned a prosecutorial team; community and departmental leaders have called for prayers and expressed grief.

The U.S. Coast Guard is seeking a man suspected of making 28 false distress calls from the Annapolis, Maryland, area since July 2014, a campaign of hoaxes that has cost the service roughly $500,000. The calls, all on an emergency radio channel and using the same male voice repeatedly saying “mayday,” most recently occurred during the night of July 21 and early July 22. Investigators located the calls’ origin between Loretta Heights and Admiral Drive. The Coast Guard released an audio clip of the caller and warned that bogus distress alerts endanger both the public and responders by diverting resources from real emergencies. Making false distress calls is a felony that can carry up to six years in prison, hefty fines — including up to $250,000 criminal and $10,000 civil penalties — and an obligation to reimburse response costs. Anyone with information should contact the regional command center or CGIS-Baltimore investigators.

High-profile donors from entertainment, sports, business and politics have made last-minute, large contributions to both Barack Obama and Mitt Romney as the election reaches its final stretch. Federal campaign finance filings show a string of four-figure gifts in recent days to Obama from actors Jake Gyllenhaal, Zach Galifianakis, Renée Zellweger, Susan Saint James Ebersol and Amanda Seyfried. Other notable Obama backers include author Anne Rice, Disney TV Animation executive producer Dan Povenmire and comedy writer Ian Maxtone-Graham.

Romney’s late supporters include actor Kelsey Grammer, former NFL star and Denver Broncos executive John Elway, and former game show host Bob Barker, all making four-figure donations. Sarah Palin’s political action committee, SARAH PAC, donated $5,000 last week. Additional Romney donors at the $1,000-or-more level include Heritage Foundation executive Becky Dunlop, American Beverage Association CEO Susan Neely, former Mike’s Hard Lemonade president Philip W. O’Neil, the political action committee of the Consumer Electronics Association and the congressional campaign committee of Rep. Frank Wolf (R‑Va.).

In parallel with these fundraising pushes, the Obama campaign has rolled out a humorous, internet-savvy get-out-the-vote mailer targeted at the crucial battleground state of Ohio. Modeled after popular online cat memes, the flyer features a cat peeking from behind a laptop adorned with Ohio-themed Obama stickers and urges recipients: “STOP LOOKING AT CATS ONLINE AND GO VOTE.” A Reddit user, MollyBloom11, posted a photo of the mailer and praised the campaign’s grasp of internet culture; the Obama campaign confirmed the mailer was authentic and deployed in Ohio, though it did not immediately say whether similar imagery has been used online or in other states. The late donations and creative outreach underscore both campaigns’ intensified efforts to mobilize supporters and secure votes in competitive areas.

Two brothers, Benjamin Ullestad, 25, and Brandon Ullestad, 22, were found dead from gunshot wounds Sunday, Nov. 19, in the Huntington Beach apartment they shared, authorities said. Officers responded to a call at about 2:45–3:00 p.m. to an apartment on the 15700 block of Taft Lane, near Marina High School, the Marina Park baseball fields and Helen Murphy Branch Library, and discovered both men deceased. A handgun was recovered at the scene. Huntington Beach police and the Orange County Coroner’s Office are investigating the incident but have released few details. Investigators have not identified any outstanding suspects and said they are not ruling out murder-suicide or an accidental suicide as possible explanations. Police spokeswoman Officer Angela Bennett and Lt. David Dereszynski emphasized there is no known threat to the community. It remains unclear who made the distress call that brought officers to the apartment. A building owner at the scene, who declined to give his name, was observed handling trash during the police response. The case remains under investigation as authorities work to piece together the events that led to the brothers’ deaths.

Behind the political confrontation over the deadly U.S. consulate attack in Benghazi, Libya, lies a tightly edited 94-word intelligence summary that has come to be known as the "talking points." Those words were the product of a daylong email debate among more than two dozen intelligence officials who contested, pared down and anonymized the available evidence. The final product was a bland, cautious assessment that omitted any direct reference to al Qaeda, an omission the administration later acknowledged was inaccurate. The talking points were distributed within the government and wound up being used by U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Susan Rice during Sunday television interviews in the days after the assault. Rice’s appearances and reliance on the talking points transformed that short passage into a focal point for partisan scrutiny and broader questions about the administration’s handling and public presentation of intelligence. Critics seized on the lack of mention of al Qaeda and on how the language appeared to downplay the possibility of a coordinated terrorist attack. Supporters argued the talking points reflected the best available intelligence at the time and represented appropriate caution given competing, incomplete reports. The episode highlighted internal tensions between intelligence professionals, who debated language and caveats, and political officials, who had to explain events to the public under intense pressure. Ultimately, the controversy revealed the difficulties of quickly distilling fragmentary, evolving intelligence into concise public statements—and how those editorial choices can become lightning rods in a highly charged political environment.

A volcanic eruption northwest of Tonga’s capital has produced a sizable new island, though scientists say it may be short-lived. The submarine volcano, about 65 kilometers (40 miles) from Nukuʻalofa, began erupting in late December after roughly five years of quiet and has been active for about a month. New Zealand volcanologist Nico Fournier of GNS Science visited by boat and reported the new landform is primarily loose scoria, roughly 1.8 by 1.5 kilometers (1.1 by 0.9 miles) in dimensions and rising about 100 meters (109 yards) above sea level. He described the scene as visually spectacular but eerily quiet, with the volcano mainly emitting steam and limited ash, the latter reaching no more than about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) high — a relief for commercial aviation since ash clouds pose the main hazard to aircraft. Government ministry observers noted eruptions from two vents, one depositing wet ash and rock onto the uninhabited Hunga Haʻapai and another venting underwater about 100 meters offshore. Eruptive bursts have reached roughly 400 meters, throwing large rocks nearby, and vegetation close to the volcano appears to be dying from ash and gases. Because the new island is made of loose material rather than solid lava, Fournier predicted ocean erosion could wash it away within months unless it becomes capped by more durable lava. Tonga’s king is expected to determine an official name for the new island.

The U.S. Census Bureau’s 2014 Families and Living Arrangements data show that 16 million children—about one in five—received Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits in 2014, a sharp rise from roughly 9 million, or one in eight, in 2007 before the Great Recession. The increase includes a doubling in the rate of children living with married parents who receive food stamps since 2007, signaling that economic recovery has been uneven and many lower-income families continue to struggle. Overall participation in food stamps peaked near 48 million people in 2013 and dipped only slightly to about 46 million in 2014. The numbers have become a political flashpoint: Republicans argue that improving economic conditions justify cuts to SNAP as part of deficit reduction, while Democrats contend that high participation shows the program remains necessary during recovery. Legislative debates produced substantial proposed reductions—around $39–40 billion over ten years in early GOP plans—but the final farm bill signed by President Obama trimmed roughly $8.6–8.7 billion over a decade, estimated to eliminate benefits for about 850,000 people and reduce benefits for affected households by about $90 per month. The Census release also highlights broader family changes: 27 percent of the nation’s 73.7 million children lived in single-parent homes in 2014 (up from 9 percent in 1960), less than half of households are married couples, and median ages at first marriage have risen to 29 for men and 27 for women.

A viral video out of St. Augustine, Florida, highlights a simple but powerful accessibility innovation at a new Starbucks drive-thru that made ordering possible and easy for a deaf customer. Rebecca King, 28, posted footage of her visit in which she pulls up to the drive-thru speaker and, after the usual audio greeting, waits silently. A barista then appears on a two-way video screen; King signs her order and the barista, Katie Wyble, signs back. The exchange, which included ordering two coffees, was completed smoothly using sign language via the monitor. King’s post—celebrating the interaction and urging viewers to “share it away” to help change the world—quickly went viral, garnering millions of views and tens of thousands of shares. Wyble, who says she has loved sign language since preschool, called the technology a way to move customer service to “a whole new level” and hopes more businesses will adopt similar measures. Local ASL professor Tiri Fellows, who is deaf, praised the device as giving the deaf community an effective way to use drive-thrus; she and friends around the country reposted the video and expressed that such a tool addresses a long-standing hassle for hearing-impaired patrons. The positive public reaction underscores both immediate practical benefits—allowing independent, respectful transactions—and a broader push for accessible customer service. Advocates hope the visibility of this successful use case will encourage other restaurants and retailers to install two-way video or comparable technology so more people with disabilities can access everyday services without barriers.

A Texas tourist, Diana Fiscal-Gonzalez of Dallas, was sentenced after collecting 40 queen conch shells from waters around Key West, Florida. A Florida judge ordered her to serve 15 days in jail, six months of probation, pay a $500 fine and $268 in court costs after she pleaded guilty. Fiscal-Gonzalez told authorities she did not realize removing the shells was illegal and said she intended to give the state-protected mollusks away as gifts. While recreational collection of empty seashells is allowed in Florida, it is illegal to take a living queen conch or to kill, mutilate, or remove a living conch from its shell, according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. The arrest followed an anonymous tip to the agency on July 13, 2017; Officer John Martino reported finding three containers of queen conches soaking in bleach and water when he met with Fiscal-Gonzalez. Queen conch shells hold cultural significance in the Florida Keys—residents born there are nicknamed Conchs, and the area is sometimes called the Conch Republic—and empty conch shells have long been used as signaling devices. The case underscores legal protections for marine life and the importance of knowing local wildlife regulations.

Suzanne Shaw, the second ex-wife of Peter Cook, has issued a public apology to his first wife, supermodel Christie Brinkley, acknowledging she was wrong to blame Brinkley for the collapse of her marriage. In a letter obtained by The Post, Shaw said she had privately apologized and felt a public apology was “appropriate and deserved” given the high-profile divorce and custody battles. Shaw regretted her 2012 remark that it was “the black cloud of Christie Brinkley’s hate” that tainted her marriage, acknowledging instead that Cook continued to pursue other women. Shaw wrote that Brinkley had been unfairly vilified and had every right to publicly confront Cook to protect their children and reveal the truth amid his behavior and the custody fight. Brinkley’s six-year marriage to Cook ended in 2007 after she discovered his affair with a much younger office clerk; Cook later married Shaw, who initially defended him during Brinkley’s legal battles. Shaw recalled a 2012 courthouse exchange in which Brinkley warned her that Cook was cheating; Shaw dismissed the warning at the time. Shaw says she fell under Cook’s spell but now regrets her involvement, praises Brinkley as a devoted mother and community member, and thanks her for forgiveness. Shaw and Cook have filed for divorce; Shaw said she wants to move on quietly. Reports and unnamed sources allege Cook’s repeated infidelities led to the separation, though Cook’s lawyer denies allegations of cheating.

With under two months until the Iowa caucuses, the 2012 Republican primary has shifted from introductions to survival. The CNBC debate in Michigan will test candidates’ ability to avoid fatal missteps as voters form firmer impressions. Except for front-runner Mitt Romney—and perhaps perennial libertarian favorite Ron Paul—most contenders are precariously close to political extinction. Herman Cain faces the gravest immediate threat: sexual-harassment allegations have stalled his momentum and could end his viability unless he shifts the conversation back to policy. Other once-promising candidates like Rick Perry and Michele Bachmann cannot afford another weak forum performance, while Newt Gingrich and Rick Santorum must seize this chaotic moment or risk missing a last chance to break through. Jon Huntsman’s maverick message is also running out of time to resonate.

Debate dynamics include whether rivals will confront Cain directly or ignore the controversy to focus on economics, and whether the “anybody-but-Mitt” movement can dent Romney’s lead—Huntsman is attempting to capitalize on that sentiment. Gingrich could rise into the top tier if he tempers his polarizing style; Perry and Bachmann must revitalize fading campaigns. Finally, observers will watch for substantive economic plans on taxation, jobs, and the deficit amid the spectacle and high stakes of the elimination phase.

The piece profiles Duck Dynasty patriarch Phil Robertson during a Louisiana outing that captures his outdoorsman persona, blunt religiosity, and controversial views. Riding in an ATV with loaded weapons, Robertson frames hunting as a God-given activity and describes an ideal “pristine earth” without cities or sinners. Comfortable and affable, he nonetheless expresses raw, unapologetic opinions off-camera—most notably about homosexuality and race—that sparked public outrage. The article recounts Robertson’s upbringing in poverty, athletic promise at Louisiana Tech, descent into booze and drugs, conversion to Christianity, and founding of Duck Commander in 1972. That company and his family’s personality-driven storytelling led to Duck Dynasty’s huge cable success, spin-off books, merchandise, and massive cultural reach. The show’s charm rests on the family’s humor, revealed personal struggles, and overt faith—three “no-compromise” rules they insisted on with A&E. After Robertson’s GQ remarks, civil-rights leaders including Jesse Jackson, GLAAD, and others demanded meetings with A&E and retailers; A&E suspended him. Robertson defended his comments as Biblical quotations and refused to back down, deepening the debate over free expression, platform responsibility, and the cost of celebrity faith-based authenticity.

Eight of 14 critically endangered black rhinos moved to a newly created sanctuary in Tsavo East National Park, Kenya, have died, authorities and conservationists reported. The Ministry of Tourism and Wildlife said preliminary investigations point to salt poisoning: the animals may have become dehydrated, increased intake of saltier water at the release site, and entered a fatal cycle. The ministry suspended further translocations and said surviving rhinos are being closely monitored. The operation, announced by the tourism minister and carried out with WWF Kenya, aimed to establish a new population in line with national conservation strategy; Kenya hopes to raise its black rhino population to 2,000 by creating suitable habitats. Conservationists described the loss as unprecedented and catastrophic. Paula Kahumbu of WildlifeDirect called it “a complete disaster” and demanded transparency; Cathy Dean of Save the Rhino urged external experts and full publication of the investigation, noting the death toll from this translocation exceeds recent poaching losses. Translocation — the process of sedating and transporting wildlife — carries risks, but such mortality is highly unusual. The ministry invited an external expert from South Africa and warned of disciplinary action if negligence is found; results will be made public. The incident compounds wider rhino conservation challenges including historic population collapse, ongoing poaching, habitat loss, and the recent death of the last male northern white rhino.

A North Korean soldier defected to South Korea across the heavily fortified Demilitarized Zone on Saturday, claiming he shot dead his platoon and squad commanders while on guard duty before crossing the western section around noon. South Korean troops heard six gunshots, confirmed his intent to defect by loudspeaker, and escorted him to a guard post; he is in protective custody and being interrogated. There has been no independent confirmation of North Korean casualties or unusual activity on the northern side. Defections across the land border are rare—the last known soldier defection was in 2010—and most North Koreans who flee go via China and Southeast Asia. Analysts caution this appears to be an isolated case, noting border troops are typically vetted for loyalty. South Korea has increased DMZ surveillance and activated its crisis-management facility.

Weeks of heavy rain and storm runoff across Northern California have stirred a renewed gold rush, with experts and local prospectors predicting one of the best summers for finding gold in about 20 years. Flooding and erosion have scoured riverbanks, uprooted trees, washed out old dig sites and liberated gold from abandoned mines, sending it downstream into rivers like the Feather, American, Mokelumne and Yuba. Local miner “Gary” Thomas and a Bureau of Land Management official say the floods “concentrate” gold by removing lighter material, making fine flakes and small nuggets easier to find in newly exposed streambeds. Prospecting shops from Oroville to Sacramento report booming interest: customers are buying pans, sluice boxes, metal detectors and wet suits, and groups like the Mother Lode Goldhounds are planning outings. Enthusiasts describe panning as a rewarding outdoor hobby—even when finds are modest—and champions demonstrate fast panning skills at competitions. Some hope the Oroville spillway area or diversion pool may reveal rich deposits, but access is restricted and authorities will enforce closures. Prospects are promising once waters recede, though dredging and motorized suction equipment remain illegal; many say the season will be about adventure, history and fresh air more than striking it rich.

A North Carolina couple, Deena Murphy and Timothy Sullivan, have sued Big Coat TV (producer of HGTV’s Love It or List It) and a listed contractor, alleging the show’s renovation left their home damaged and that the production company engaged in unfair business practices. The suit claims the couple paid $140,000 into a fund Big Coat controlled for renovations, but only about $85,780.50 was paid to the contractor. Murphy and Sullivan allege the remainder was used for production costs and that Big Coat’s incentives favored television-making over homeowners’ interests.

The complaint questions Big Coat’s role as an unlicensed general contractor, asserts the program relied on television personalities rather than professionals who actually managed the renovation, and says no licensed architect developed plans. The couple also alleges they were not shown genuine North Carolina listings by licensed brokers during the “list it” portion of the show, and that much of the work performed duplicated plans they had previously arranged with another firm. They describe the renovation results as “disastrous,” citing open duct work that allowed vermin entry, low-grade carpeting, unpainted surfaces, and windows painted shut, and say parts of the home were irreparably damaged.

Big Coat TV disputes the allegations and says it will defend itself vigorously. The contractor named in the suit did not respond to requests for comment. Legal analysts note the lawsuit could expose more of the behind-the-scenes realities of home renovation reality TV, arguing production incentives may not align with homeowners’ best interests. The case raises broader questions about transparency, licensing, and financial handling on televised renovation projects.

Anissa Weier will change her plea to not guilty by reason of mental disease or defect (NGI) in the Slender Man stabbing case, her attorney Maura McMahon said; a hearing on the plea change is set for Sept. 9. Weier, now 14, and co-defendant Morgan Geyser — who already entered an NGI plea and has been diagnosed with early-onset schizophrenia — were 12 when prosecutors say they plotted and stabbed classmate Payton Leutner 19 times in May 2014. Leutner survived after crawling to a nearby path and being found by a bicyclist. Both girls told police they believed the fictional internet character Slender Man would harm them or their families if they did not kill their friend. Their attorneys have sought transfer to juvenile court and moves for jurors from outside Waukesha County due to pretrial publicity; the appeals court denied transfer, so they remain charged as adults with attempted first-degree intentional homicide. NGI pleas require court-appointed psychiatric evaluations; someone found NGI is typically committed to a state mental hospital for treatment. No trial date has been set.

A male University of Chicago student, identified in court papers as “John Doe,” has filed a federal suit alleging the school created a gender‑biased, hostile environment against men and violated Title IX in its handling of two sexual‑assault complaints filed against him. The complaint, seeking about $175,000, contends that both allegations—one decided in Doe’s favor in 2014 and another filed in 2016 about an encounter in 2013—were either false or improperly pursued, and that the university treated him unfairly throughout investigations and afterwards.

Doe says two women, labeled “Jane Roe” and “Jane Doe” in the suit, falsely accused him; he claims their relationships with him were consensual and cites blog posts and social media as evidence. The complaint accuses the university of selective enforcement, retaliation, and applying pro‑female, anti‑male assumptions—arguing administrators adopted such a stance in response to criticism that the school had previously ignored female complainants. Doe alleges the school allowed one accuser to spread public statements and include his name on the unofficial “Hyde Park List,” prompting campus protests, flyers urging boycotts of a student production he directed, and his removal from shared classes despite being cleared in a disciplinary hearing.

The suit also asserts the university refused to file a Title IX complaint on his behalf for harassment and initially sought to adjudicate a later claim under a stricter 2015 consent standard rather than the 2013 manual in effect when the encounter occurred. Claims include defamation, emotional distress, and Title IX violations; proceedings will continue with pseudonyms, and the next hearing was scheduled for mid‑September. The case mirrors a broader wave of male students litigating perceived gender bias in campus sexual‑misconduct processes.

Five years ago, White House senior adviser David Plouffe publicly criticized Republican presidential candidates Rick Santorum and Newt Gingrich for their responses to President Barack Obama’s remarks about the Trayvon Martin shooting. Obama had expressed empathy with the Martin family and noted that, if he had a son, he might look like Trayvon. Santorum accused the president of politicizing the tragedy and using it to divide the country, while Gingrich dismissed Obama’s comments as “nonsense.” Plouffe called their reactions “reprehensible,” “irresponsible” and “hard to stomach,” characterizing the GOP primary as a “circus” and suggesting the comments appealed to voters’ worst instincts. He also acknowledged Mitt Romney’s delegate lead and predicted a competitive fall campaign.

Separately that weekend, Plouffe expressed confidence that the Supreme Court would uphold the Affordable Care Act, arguing the individual mandate originated with conservative thinkers and noting that much opposition was driven by costly attacks; he predicted public opinion would improve as benefits took effect. A body believed to be that of 21-year-old Savannah Gold, who vanished after heading to work at Bonefish Grill in Jacksonville, was found late Saturday in a pond off Club Duclay Road near Blanding Boulevard, the Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office (JSO) said. Surveillance footage showed Gold getting into a car driven by 28-year-old Bonefish Grill manager Lee Rodarte; JSO said a possible struggle occurred in the vehicle. Gold’s car remained in the restaurant parking lot with a slashed tire and her purse, ID, credit cards and money inside, prompting concern when she failed to report for her shift. About 30 minutes after she was due at work, her father received a suspiciously worded text from her phone claiming she was running away with a “great guy.” Investigators believe Rodarte sent the message.

Rodarte, who had an off-and-on relationship with Gold and earlier lived on the same street where the body was found, became a suspect after inconsistencies in his account. He was arrested Saturday night at a Mandarin restaurant, admitted to killing Gold and led police to the pond where remains were recovered, according to JSO. He faces charges of murder and tampering with evidence and is being held without bond; an autopsy and formal identification by the medical examiner are pending. Bonefish Grill’s owner expressed sorrow and the local restaurant closed briefly; Gold’s family has launched a GoFundMe for funeral expenses as the community mourns.

Rihanna has been making headlines in New York for provocative daytime appearances and high-profile public moments that highlight ongoing tensions between her and parts of her management. She was photographed shopping in SoHo wearing a revealing pink, see-through strapless bra and pleated skirt, paired with Converse, sunglasses and bright yellow talon nails, then dining with friends and family. She recently canceled a UK trip to spend time with her ailing grandmother, Dolly, and was seen at Jay-Z’s 40/40 club watching the Miami Heat with family; Chris Brown later joined the group, and the two were also in proximity that night at Meatpacking hotspot SL. Reports that Jay-Z ordered her to “go to rehab” were disputed by Page Six sources, who instead describe a management struggle at Roc Nation over how to handle Rihanna’s rebellious public behavior and her refusal to distance herself from Brown. Insiders say Rihanna feels entitled to enjoy her success, taking more vacations, posting freely on Twitter, wearing bold outfits and asserting her artistic autonomy. Meanwhile, a huge Times Square billboard for her fragrance Rebelle — a nude image of Rihanna covering herself with her arms — drew attention and underscored her embrace of sensual promotion. She also publicly lashed out at The Sun after it suggested a body double was used in parts of her Armani Jeans commercial. Industry insiders worry the controversy and her closeness with Brown could delay new music releases amid fears of public backlash.

Multiple outlets report Maroon 5 will perform the Super Bowl LIII halftime show in Atlanta on February 3, 2019. Sources say the band has accepted an offer and their touring schedule leaves them available between a Las Vegas New Year’s Eve date and the Australian leg beginning February 19. Frontman Adam Levine has long expressed interest in playing the Super Bowl, telling Howard Stern in 2015 the group was on a “short list.” The NFL and sponsor Pepsi declined to confirm plans, calling speculation a tradition. Maroon 5’s recent work includes hits like “Girls Like You” with Cardi B and a collaboration with Kendrick Lamar, leaving open the possibility of surprise guest appearances. The announcement follows Justin Timberlake’s 2018 halftime performance.

The FBI’s Rocky Mountain Safe Streets Task Force is seeking help identifying a man who used a taxi to commit a bank robbery in Centennial in the Denver Tech Center. Surveillance shows the suspect entering a cab near the Bellco Theater, directing the driver to wait while he robbed the Public Service Credit Union at 6850 S. Yosemite St., then instructing the cabbie to drive him to Denver International Airport. It is unknown whether he boarded a plane. Bank images show the suspect wearing what appears to be a white dust mask and displaying a small handgun to a teller before leaving with an undisclosed amount of money. He is described as a white male, late 20s–early 30s, about 6 feet tall, thin to medium build, wearing a black beanie, dark gray jacket, dark jeans, dark sunglasses and a black shirt with white letters. Anyone with information should contact Metro Denver Crime Stoppers at 720-913-7867 or text 274637 with the keyword DMCS.

Rome’s Christmas tree this year — a 70–72-foot Norway spruce installed in Piazza Venezia — quickly became an embarrassing symbol for the city. Nicknamed Spelacchio, or “Mangy,” the fir began to gray and shed needles within days of being erected, leaving it looking thin and nearly transparent. Transported from the Trentino region near the Austrian border, the tree cost taxpayers about €48,000 (roughly $57,000) once moving and decoration expenses were included. Observers and experts debated the cause of its rapid decline: some suggested the stress of transit or preexisting illness, while a tree historian pointed to concrete poured around its roots to stabilize it as a likely killer. With little time, money, or political appetite to replace it, Spelacchio remains in place for the holidays, but it has already become a potent metaphor for Rome’s broader troubles. Residents and social media users mocked the tree, and Italians used the spectacle to criticize chronic civic problems — traffic congestion, unreliable public transport, and inconsistent trash collection — and to lament the disillusionment with Mayor Virginia Raggi, elected the previous year on an anti-establishment platform but soon mired in accusations of corruption and nepotism. The uproar prompted a consumer-rights group to ask an administrative court to investigate the expenditure and to demand the tree’s removal, calling it a “shameful spectacle for citizens and tourists.” The sorry spruce therefore stands as seasonal satire on civic mismanagement and unmet expectations.

Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh faced a fourth day of public scrutiny in his Senate Judiciary Committee confirmation hearings after two long days of questioning. Kavanaugh, a judge on the D.C. Circuit, is widely expected to be confirmed if Republican unity holds. Much of Thursday’s session centered on his past work in the George W. Bush White House, his writings on presidential power, and newly public emails that Democrats argued had been improperly kept from the public.

Tensions erupted over “committee confidential” documents. Sen. Cory Booker dramatically threatened—and briefly acted on—releasing emails he said showed Kavanaugh’s positions on race-conscious policies and Roe v. Wade. Republicans countered that the documents had been cleared for release overnight, and White House and Bush administration representatives later confirmed they had approved public disclosure of the material. The episode underscored partisan distrust over access to tens of thousands of pages from Kavanaugh’s record.

Kavanaugh repeatedly avoided definitive positions on politically charged questions. He declined to say whether Obergefell (same-sex marriage) or Roe v. Wade were correctly decided, instead calling such precedents “precedent” or attributing views to “legal scholars.” He emphasized judicial independence, saying courts—not presidents—are “the final word” when court orders bind the executive, and he resisted calls to commit to recusal from cases tied to the Mueller probe, arguing such pledges could undermine perceived judicial independence. He denied having “inappropriate” discussions about the Mueller investigation and said he did not recall talking about it with figures at the Kasowitz firm.

Senators pressed him on contraception rulings, religious objections, affirmative action, and his past involvement in controversial judicial confirmations. Protesters intermittently disrupted proceedings. At adjournment, committee chairman Chuck Grassley praised Kavanaugh’s testimony as “compelling and credible.” The hearing’s final public day will include witness statements as the Senate moves toward a confirmation vote.

Cartoon Wars Part I: In this episode, Cartman and Kyle clash over Family Guy. The show's creators plan to depict the prophet Muhammad, prompting the network to consider banning the episode. Seeing an opportunity to eliminate Family Guy permanently, Cartman races Kyle across the country. Their frantic competition becomes a high-stakes chase to Hollywood, where the network’s decision—and the show’s fate—will be determined by whichever boy arrives first. The episode explores themes of censorship, free expression, and the volatile consequences of provocative content.

President Obama has significantly expanded his network of high-value fundraisers as he prepares for a costly re-election campaign: at least 41 bundlers have raised $500,000 or more for him, up from 27 previously. These well-connected bundlers—including former Goldman Sachs executive Jon Corzine and DreamWorks CEO Jeffrey Katzenberg—have helped Obama pull in large sums despite a weak economy, slipping approval ratings and criticism from some liberals. The campaign and the Democratic National Committee have together raised over $150 million, with Obama reporting $43 million for the quarter; bundlers account for roughly a third of his funds. At the same time, about 40 percent of contributions last quarter came from small donors giving $200 or less, and the campaign says about 600,000 people donated in the third quarter. Meanwhile, Republicans Mitt Romney and Rick Perry raised $14 million and $17 million respectively for the quarter, leaving them with similar cash-on-hand positions for primary contests. Notably, Wall Street giving has shifted: Romney has far outpaced Obama this year among many financial firms and employees, reflecting strained relations between Obama and parts of the finance industry even as the president leverages public anger over Wall Street excesses.

A wedding at Penn Park in Whittier turned tragic Saturday afternoon when a roughly 100-foot eucalyptus tree unexpectedly toppled onto a group taking photos, killing one woman and injuring multiple others. Authorities received 911 calls around 4:30 p.m.; firefighters used chainsaws to free people trapped beneath the tree’s limbs. Reports vary slightly on injury counts, but five to seven people were hurt, including a young child taken to a trauma center and others treated for minor to moderate injuries—most are expected to recover. Witnesses described chaotic scenes, with the bride distraught over her unresponsive mother. A search dog was used to check for additional victims. City officials closed Penn Park indefinitely and preserved the scene for investigation; arborists will inspect the fallen tree to determine cause. Officials said recent heavy rains and years of drought may have stressed vegetation but stressed they will not speculate until the arborist’s review. The community and city leaders offered support and counseling to the grieving family.

Authorities in South Carolina searched Wednesday for inmate Jimmy Causey, who is believed to have escaped from the maximum-security Lieber Correctional Institution, about 90 miles southeast of Columbia. The search began just before 2 p.m., officials said; no further details were released. Causey, 46, has now escaped from two different state prisons over roughly a dozen years. In 2005 he and convicted murderer Johnny Brewer escaped from Broad River Correctional Institution in Columbia by hiding in a trash truck. The pair evaded capture for three days before being found at a motel near Interstate 95; a pizza delivery driver recognized one of the escapees and alerted authorities. Both men were returned to custody, but Brewer was found dead in his cell two years later, hanging from a bedsheet. At the time of the 2005 escape, then-prisons director Jon Ozmint attributed the breach in part to budget cuts that eliminated roughly 800 security positions, leaving areas such as the trash compactor and loading dock unmonitored; the escapees also reportedly used toilet-paper “heads” to fool an early-morning count. Causey received a life sentence in 2004 for holding Columbia attorney Jack Swerling and his family at gunpoint; his earliest state incarceration began in 1992 on charges including grand larceny. The report also notes a December escape from McCormick Correctional Institution in which inmate Michael Allen Williamson, serving life, stabbed a police officer during his breakout. Authorities continue to investigate and search for Causey.

Lois Lerner, head of the IRS division overseeing tax-exempt organizations, was placed on paid administrative leave amid fallout from revelations that the agency gave extra scrutiny to conservative groups seeking 501(c)(4) status. The Treasury inspector general found Lerner knew as early as June 2011 that staff were using political criteria—searching for names like “Tea Party” and “patriots”—and ordered the criteria changed, though inappropriate screening later recurred in a Cincinnati office. Lerner disclosed the scrutiny nearly two weeks earlier by answering a planted question at an American Bar Association conference, a rollout now criticized as suspicious. She invoked her Fifth Amendment right at a House Oversight hearing after previously insisting she had done nothing wrong. Acting Commissioner Danny Werfel asked for her resignation; she declined and was placed on leave. Ken Corbin was named acting director of the exempt-organizations division, and Joseph Grant will retire. Lawmakers from both parties have called for further action.

Surgeons at Johns Hopkins performed what they call the world’s most extensive genital transplant: a 14-hour operation transplanting a penis, scrotum and part of the abdominal wall from a deceased donor into a U.S. military veteran injured by an IED in Afghanistan. The patient, who remains anonymous, is recovering well and is expected to regain urinary function before discharge and sexual sensation within months as nerves regenerate. The scrotum transplant excluded donor testicles to avoid ethical and reproductive complications associated with transferring another person’s sperm.

The procedure connected multiple arteries, veins and nerves and included a large skin graft; surgeons also infused donor bone marrow to reduce rejection risk and allow the recipient to take a single low-dose immunosuppressant rather than multiple drugs. Rejection and lifelong immunosuppression remain significant concerns. Johns Hopkins covered the cost and is screening other veterans; the hospital does not plan to use the technique for gender reassignment. Earlier, more limited penis transplants were done in South Africa and at Massachusetts General Hospital, where the patient’s sexual function has not fully returned. Experts note such injuries inflict deep psychological harm, and successful transplants can restore identity and relationships much like hand transplants aided amputees. Challenges include finding willing donors—separate consent is required in the U.S.—long-term immune management, funding and ethical questions, particularly regarding fertility when donor reproductive tissue is involved. The team hopes this case encourages other injured veterans to seek care.

A 12-year-old boy, Melquan Kwame Robinson, was fatally electrocuted Monday at Fleming Athletic Complex near the Bernie Ward Community Center in Augusta while at football practice. Richmond County Coroner Mark Bowen said Melquan climbed a chain-link fence to retrieve a football; when he came back over the fence he contacted a live wire that had energized the fence and was electrocuted. He was taken to the Children’s Hospital of Georgia and pronounced dead at 9:56 p.m. His body will be sent to the Georgia Bureau of Investigation lab for autopsy. Three others were injured — two juveniles and one adult — after attempting to help him; two boys who tried to pull Melquan from the fence were hospitalized. A deputy on scene performed chest compressions and emergency crews transported the victims. Investigations will be conducted by the coroner’s office, the sheriff’s office and the city; Bowen will focus on the death while the city examines how the live wire energized the fence. Georgia Power said it will cooperate with investigators and noted its preliminary review indicates it does not control or maintain the voltage that energized the fences. Melquan, a seventh-grader at Morgan Road Middle School and a member of the Trinity Elite Titans football team, was remembered by friends and coach Don Clark as energetic, athletic and protective of his siblings; the family is grieving. The city canceled football activities at Fleming Park for the week. A community vigil is planned for Thursday at 6 p.m. at the Bernie Ward Community Center.

Same-sex marriage became legal in Hawaii, and officials and businesses are positioning the islands as a new wedding-tourism destination. Wedding planners such as Keane Akao, who launched Perfectly Planned Hawaii as the debate unfolded, are marketing secluded beaches and full-service packages to same-sex couples. Couples from states that don’t recognize their unions, like Cira Abiseid and Cyrilla Owle from Arkansas, plan ceremonies in Hawaii both for legal recognition and for a honeymoon in the islands’ famed scenery and aloha spirit.

Economist Sumner La Croix projects about a $217 million boost to Hawaii tourism over three years from marriage equality. The state’s already robust tourism infrastructure—hotels, photographers, caterers and venues experienced with weddings—gives it an advantage over other markets. Local hospitality groups, from boutique chains to large resorts such as the Sheraton Waikiki (which can provide on-site marriage licenses), are rolling out LGBT-focused packages and advertising to mainland gay and lesbian travelers.

When the law took effect, six couples married shortly after midnight and resorts hosted mass ceremonies. Hawaii’s process allows same-day licensing, including online pre-registration and statewide verification, making spontaneous or short-stay tourist weddings feasible. Advocates recall Hawaii’s historical role in the national same-sex marriage conversation and view the new law as both a civil-rights milestone and an economic opportunity embraced by many in the business community.

A technical malfunction shut down trading in all Nasdaq-listed stocks and options for about three hours, halting market activity and prompting Nasdaq OMX to notify investors of problems with "quote submissions." At Nasdaq’s request, the NYSE also suspended trading in Nasdaq securities and canceled orders back to customers. The Nasdaq Composite was halted at 3,631.17. Nasdaq officials worked to diagnose the issue, provided few details during the outage, and reopened trading only late in the session once they were confident systems and banks could resume transactions.

Motus markets ergonomic D- and T-grip attachments for shovels, scoops, pushers and roof rakes intended to reduce arthritis, back pain, blisters and repetitive strain injuries like carpal tunnel and tendinitis. The D-grip mounts mid-shaft to add lifting leverage; the T-grip mounts at the top for pushing and pulling control. A 1992 case-study biomechanical assessment by Dean Kriellaars (University of Manitoba) used static equilibrium modeling to evaluate the straight (T) grip during shoveling. Key findings: the grip keeps the wrist near neutral—reducing ulnar deviation from about 35° to under 10°—which protects wrist tissues; it orients the forearm into pronation, altering muscle recruitment away from biceps toward forearm extensors and larger trunk/lower-limb muscles; it increases shoulder abduction slightly, potentially engaging larger deltoid muscles and lowering risk of shoulder tendinitis; and it reduces trunk flexion by ~5°, bringing loads about 5 cm closer to the body. Combined effects lower the mechanical load by roughly 10%, which could meaningfully decrease fatigue and cumulative trauma and aid low-back injury prevention and rehabilitation. The grips also reduce skin shear and blister risk and fit a wide range of implement shafts.

Idina Menzel and Taye Diggs have announced they are separating after 10 years of marriage. Representatives for both actors said the decision was mutual and that their primary focus is the well-being and privacy of their four-year-old son, Walker. The couple, both 42, met as costars in the original Broadway production of Rent in the mid-1990s, married in 2003 and welcomed Walker in September 2009. Earlier this year Menzel acknowledged their relationship had challenges but emphasized they worked at it and tried to stay together as much as possible despite busy careers and past rumors.

New scientific tests and a recent restoration of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre’s inner shrine, the Holy Edicule, provide strong evidence that the tomb enshrined there dates to the early fourth century A.D., around the time Constantine’s delegation identified the site as holy. Conservators from the National Technical University of Athens opened the small tomb for about 60 hours during a nine-month restoration in 2016, sampling mortar between the original limestone burial surface and marble coverings. Using ground-penetrating radar, laser scanning and optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating of quartz sediments in mortar, teams dated various mortars to roughly A.D. 325–345 as well as to later known repair phases (11th-, 16th-, and 1570-era work). The mid-fourth-century dates align with historical accounts that Constantine’s team tore down a Roman temple built over a rock-hewn cave and built a shrine and church around the cave where they believed Jesus had been buried. While archaeology cannot prove the identity of an individual buried there in the 1st century, the new results push the structural evidence for the current tomb complex back 1,700 years—earlier than previously confirmed Crusader-era remains—and corroborate the sequence of construction and restorations recorded in texts. The Greek restoration team that worked on the Acropolis led the Edicule conservation. Researchers say the collected data hold more insights yet to be analyzed and will be published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports.

Billionaire collector Steve Wynn’s planned Christie’s sale was disrupted after a Picasso was damaged during pre-auction preparations, forcing its withdrawal. The damaged work, Picasso’s 1943 self-portrait Le Marin, valued at about $70 million and measuring just over 4 by 2½ feet, was pulled Friday and will not appear at the May 17 sale; Christie’s declined to describe the damage. Another Picasso from Wynn, the 1964 Femme au chat assise dans un fauteuil (estimated $25–35 million), was also withdrawn by mutual agreement. Both works had been guaranteed by Christie’s and supported by third‑party guarantees; Christie’s says withdrawal voids guarantees and that consignment contracts include insurance for damage and contingencies. The remaining Wynn lot, Andy Warhol’s 1963 Double Elvis [Ferus Type] (est. $30M+), will still be offered. The incident recalls Wynn’s 2006 accident in which he elbowed Picasso’s Le Rêve, leaving a silver-dollar-sized hole; after restoration its value was disputed in litigation and the painting later sold to Steve Cohen. Wynn resigned as CEO of Wynn Resorts amid sexual‑misconduct allegations, which he denies.

When the Camp Fire devastated Butte County in November 2018—killing at least 85 people, destroying thousands of homes and displacing many in the Chico area—Sierra Nevada Brewing Co. mobilized a massive relief effort centered on a beer. The brewery created Resilience Butte County Proud IPA and pledged 100% of proceeds to the Sierra Nevada Camp Fire Relief Fund, seeded with a $100,000 donation from founder Ken Grossman. Sierra Nevada invited breweries nationwide to brew the recipe and donate all sales; malt, hop and yeast suppliers agreed to donate ingredients; wholesalers and retailers agreed to carry and donate proceeds; and competitors volunteered time and labor. The industry response was historic: more than 1,200–1,400 breweries signed up to brew Resilience, producing millions of pints across cans and draft. Sierra Nevada canned and will distribute some Resilience starting in mid–late December (with larger releases and draft availability into January), while many participating breweries will serve draft-only versions. The beer is a classic West Coast IPA—Centennial and Cascade hops, piney, citrusy and fresh—created to taste like home. Sierra Nevada promoted a Resilience Night on December 20 to coordinate sales and partnered with Untappd to offer a limited badge for check-ins to any participating brewery’s Resilience IPA. The campaign aims to raise more than $10 million for long-term rebuilding. Sierra Nevada emphasized sustained commitment to the community, working with partner organizations to distribute funds for rebuilding. The project drew praise across the brewing community as perhaps the largest-ever collaborative industry charity, exemplifying craft brewers’ tradition of mutual support.

Former political consultant W. Samuel (Sam) Patten, a onetime associate of Paul Manafort, pleaded guilty to failing to register as a foreign agent and agreed to cooperate with U.S. prosecutors. Patten admitted he lobbied in the United States on behalf of a Ukrainian political party and a prominent Ukrainian oligarch—details that align with previously identified figure Sergei Lyovochkin—while receiving over $1 million through a company he co-owned with a Russian national. That company, Begemot Ventures International Ltd., was formed in 2015 with Konstantin Kilimnik, a former International Republican Institute (IRI) employee who later worked closely with Manafort and has been accused of ties to Russian military intelligence (GRU). Kilimnik has been indicted in absentia alongside Manafort on obstruction charges.

Patten’s cooperation could give prosecutors inside perspective on international lobbying tied to Manafort’s network, though the precise scope of his assistance was not disclosed. Mueller’s team referred the case to the U.S. Attorney’s Office in D.C., where the matter was handled; the referral’s reasons—routine jurisdiction, resources, or case size—were not specified. At Patten’s plea hearing, notable prosecutors connected to the Manafort prosecutions, including Andrew Weissmann, attended.

Court filings also suggest Patten arranged a straw donation allowing a foreign national to attend President Trump’s inauguration, raising questions about improper foreign funding to the Trump Inaugural Committee. Patten previously worked on Ukrainian campaigns and reportedly collaborated with Cambridge Analytica during the 2014 cycle. No sentencing date has been set. The Senate Intelligence Committee also made a criminal referral based on material Patten provided.

South Korea’s presidency has been engulfed in scandal after authorities found about 360 pills of Viagra and similar generics in President Park Geun-hye’s offices while investigating corruption allegations. The Blue House says the drugs were purchased in December to prevent altitude sickness for aides on official trips to high-altitude African capitals (Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya) and that the pills were never used. Medical commentators note Viagra (sildenafil) was discovered during trials for a heart drug and can help prevent pulmonary hypertension that can afflict climbers, so some Korean doctors prescribe it for altitude-related problems.  

The discovery has fed public unease, adding to perceptions that Park is remote and out of touch, and has coincided with raids on Samsung and the National Pension Service as prosecutors probe whether Park and her confidante Choi Soon-sil pressured institutions—possibly including the pension fund—to back a controversial Samsung merger. Opposition parties and some within Park’s own party are preparing an impeachment push amid allegations that Choi, the daughter of a shadowy quasi-religious leader, wielded improper influence and profited from her access. Tens of thousands of protesters have demanded Park’s resignation for weeks; prosecutors say they believe Park was collusively involved in criminal activities including coercing companies to donate to foundations and businesses controlled by Choi.

Search teams scouring a vast area of the southern Indian Ocean have been unable to relocate faint underwater sounds first detected late Saturday and early Sunday that were consistent with the locator beacons on a plane’s black boxes, officials said. Angus Houston, head of the Australian-coordinated search for Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370, said the Ocean Shield’s towed pinger locator recorded two separate signals—one lasting about 2 hours 20 minutes and a later pair of “pinger returns” for about 13 minutes—but subsequent sweeps have found no further transmissions. With the beacons’ batteries expected to last roughly 30 days, Tuesday marked a critical deadline: if the signals halt, finding the recorders on the ocean floor—about 2.8 miles deep—becomes extremely difficult. Up to 14 ships and 14 aircraft continue surface and underwater searches across a roughly 30,000-square-mile zone about 1,400 miles northwest of Perth. An autonomous sub, Bluefin-21, remains on the Ocean Shield but officials say they must narrow the search area with more ping data before deploying it; the AUV searches slowly along the seabed and would require many days to cover the possible locations. So far aerial searches have completed 133 missions without recovering debris from MH370.

Kate Downing, a Palo Alto Planning and Transportation Commissioner and co-founder of Palo Alto Forward, resigned publicly, announcing she and her husband are moving to Santa Cruz because they can no longer afford to raise a family in Palo Alto. Despite both being well-paid professionals—Downing a corporate attorney and her husband a software engineer—they rent a four-bedroom home with another couple for $6,200 a month. Buying that same home would cost roughly $2.7 million, producing monthly payments around $12,177 (mortgage, taxes, insurance), or about $146,127 annually—effectively an entire professional’s pre-tax income—making ownership unattainable even for high earners. Downing frames her departure as symptomatic of a broader crisis: the Bay Area’s jobs-housing imbalance is pricing out teachers, first responders, service workers and many middle-class residents, forcing long-time neighbors to leave and deterring new talent from accepting local jobs.

In her letter she criticized the City Council for pursuing slow-growth policies that prioritize office space over housing, ignoring petitions from over 1,000 residents and repeated public pleas to make housing a top priority. She outlined practical, modest policy changes she’d advocated—allowing additional housing floors in mixed-use developments, enforcing minimum density so developers build apartments rather than penthouses, legalizing duplexes and easing granny-unit restrictions, permitting housing above single-use commercial areas, and using parking policy experiments to support car-free housing. Downing warned that without action Palo Alto risks becoming a hollowed-out museum of its former community life: streets and storefronts may remain but the social fabric—young families, volunteers, neighborhood cohesion—will erode as the city becomes accessible mainly to wealthy long-time owners and high-net-worth newcomers. She pledged her housing and transportation organization will continue advocating for more inclusive housing despite her departure.

Prince William and Duchess Kate have adopted a male cocker spaniel puppy, a few months old and bred from a litter produced by Kate’s mother, Carole Middleton’s dog. The couple acquired him in early December and are settling him into their North Wales farmhouse and Kensington Palace. Palace aides say the pup is a private pet and his name will not be revealed. The new dog replaces William’s late labrador Widgeon and will keep Kate company while William is deployed to the Falkland Islands.

AMC Theatres abandoned a controversial plan to allow texting during films after a swift and negative public backlash. CEO Adam Aron had floated the idea—suggesting some auditoriums could be made “texting friendly” to attract millennials—during an interview with Variety as part of broader efforts to modernize AMC and boost attendance. Aron argued younger patrons view constant cellphone use as normal and suggested segregating different viewer preferences so those who want to use phones wouldn’t disturb others. He framed experimentation as part of a broader strategy that includes upgraded food, loyalty programs, marketing, and major moves such as the planned acquisition of Carmike Cinemas and possible technology partnerships like Screening Room.

Reaction on social media was overwhelmingly hostile, with many moviegoers threatening to boycott AMC. Citing audience sentiment and survey data—Pew Research found 95% of Americans view phone use at movies as inappropriate—AMC quickly reversed course. The company tweeted, “NO TEXTING AT AMC. Won’t happen. You spoke. We listened. Quickly, that idea has been sent to the cutting room floor,” and pledged there will be no texting in auditoriums “not today, not tomorrow, and not in the foreseeable future.”

Aron, a newcomer to exhibition with a background at Starwood and other companies, emphasized innovation and testing within AMC’s theaters while also affirming the importance of preserving the moviegoing experience. The texting episode highlighted tensions between adapting to new consumer habits and protecting traditional cinema etiquette.

A Nevada parole board unanimously voted to grant O.J. Simpson parole after he apologized for his role in a 2007 armed robbery and kidnapping, described himself as a model prisoner, and outlined stable post-release plans. Simpson, 70, has served nine years of a nine-to-33-year sentence at Lovelock Correctional Center and could be released as early as October to his Florida home. His July parole hearing attracted extensive TV coverage that recalled the nationwide fascination of his 1995 murder trial, when he was acquitted in the deaths of ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman — a case that continues to resonate for its themes of race, policing, celebrity and domestic violence.

At the hearing Simpson portrayed himself as contrite about the Las Vegas incident but stopped short of full responsibility, saying he was misled by associates. He called the episode “stupid,” insisted he had no intent to harm anyone, and claimed he had lived a “conflict-free life,” a comment that drew attention given his past. Associates paint a different picture: Tom Riccio, one co-defendant, told CNN that Simpson orchestrated the robbery and gathered armed men, and accused others of blaming Simpson to avoid punishment.

Mitigating factors cited included Simpson’s disciplinary record, participation in violence-prevention classes, family and community support, and a victim’s forgiveness—Bruce Fromong, one of the robbery victims, testified in favor of release. Parole board member Tony Corda labeled Simpson a “low risk to reoffend.” Simpson has long maintained his innocence in the 1994 murders; a civil jury later held him liable in a wrongful-death judgment. His legal team has argued the 2008 sentence was excessive and possibly retaliatory for the 1995 acquittal. The hearing revived wide public interest, fueled by recent portrayals like the documentary “O.J.: Made in America” and the FX dramatization of his murder trial.

Actor Scott Baio has filed a police report alleging he was physically attacked by Nancy Mack, wife of Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer Chad Smith, over his visible support for Donald Trump. The alleged incident occurred at a Thousand Oaks elementary school event where both families were present. Baio told authorities Mack confronted him, angrily berating and cursing him while repeatedly mimicking Trump’s infamous “grab ’em by the pussy” remark. Baio says he asked her to stop because children were present; when she didn’t, he claims Mack grabbed him under the arms, shook and pushed him. Sources close to Mack say she was only demonstrating “how Donald Trump hugs women” and did not intend to harm anyone. The Ventura County Sheriff’s Department is investigating and has listed Mack as a battery suspect. The confrontation reflects the intense, often personal clashes tied to the 2016 election: Baio was a prominent Hollywood supporter of Trump who spoke at the Republican National Convention, while Chad Smith publicly criticized Trump’s supporters as “uneducated” and defended victims of Trump’s controversial comments. Neither Baio nor Mack provided public statements beyond the police report and internal sources.

Former Ohio State wrestlers have publicly contradicted Rep. Jim Jordan’s repeated denials that he knew about alleged sexual abuse by team physician Dr. Richard Strauss during Jordan’s tenure as assistant wrestling coach (1986–1994). Shawn Dailey told NBC News he was groped multiple times by Strauss in the mid-1990s and said locker-room talk made Strauss’ conduct widely known among athletes, including conversations with Jordan. Dailey said he was too embarrassed to report the incidents directly at the time but recalled teammates, including Dunyasha Yetts, bringing complaints to Jordan and head coach Russ Hellickson. Yetts has said he told Jordan after Strauss tried to pull down his shorts during a visit for a thumb injury; Hellickson has admitted in a video submitted to investigators that he warned Strauss to stop being “hands on.”

Mark Coleman, a former teammate and UFC champion, also told The Wall Street Journal he believes Jordan must remember the abuse and that Jordan took no action. Several other former wrestlers, interviewed over recent weeks, described Strauss showering with athletes, inappropriately touching them during exams, and being the subject of pervasive locker-room jokes and concern. Mike DiSabato’s allegations prompted Ohio State to open an independent probe in April; the Perkins Coie team has interviewed more than 150 former students and witnesses and received reports from athletes across 14 varsity sports. Ohio State has said it has shared information with investigators and law enforcement.

Jordan and his spokesman deny any knowledge; Jordan has said he would have acted had he known, and President Trump publicly voiced support. Perkins Coie has sought to interview Jordan; the university continues to investigate whether administrators or coaches knew about Strauss’ misconduct and whether appropriate responses were taken. Strauss, who died by suicide in 2005, served as an OSU physician from the late 1970s into the 1990s. Several former athletes now urge more victims to come forward so the scope of abuse and institutional response can be fully examined.

A Johnston County 911 supervisor’s quick thinking helped rescue a woman who had been locked in the trunk of a moving car on Jan. 14. Around 4 a.m., Shift Supervisor Tim Medlin answered a frantic call from a woman who managed to say she was trapped in a car trunk before the call dropped and she stopped answering callbacks. Realizing voice contact was failing, Medlin used an office emergency cell phone to text her; she replied and confirmed she needed help, gave the vehicle’s make and color (a red Mustang) and said she believed they were headed to Fayetteville. Medlin contacted Cumberland County authorities, who worked with Verizon to locate the phone. Fayetteville police intercepted the vehicle, found the woman unharmed in the trunk and arrested her boyfriend, 32-year-old Nicholas Mattevi, on a false imprisonment charge; he was later released on $10,000 bond. Johnston County 911 Director Jason Barbour praised Medlin’s actions and highlighted a limitation: 911 centers can receive texts but cannot initiate them from their systems. Medlin’s use of a flip phone in the dispatch center underscored the need for updated equipment; Barbour said centers should be enabled to send texts directly and that staff will be outfitted with better phones to ensure they can respond similarly in future emergencies.
