U.S. credit and debit cards are moving to EMV chip technology (Europay, MasterCard, Visa), adding a tiny metallic microchip on the card face that must be inserted ("dipped") into updated card readers instead of being swiped. The chip stores payment data and generates a unique cryptographic code for each purchase, making counterfeit cards far harder to produce and reducing fraud substantially in countries that adopted EMV. Visa reports jurisdictions that moved quickly saw counterfeit fraud fall 60–70 percent. Experts say even if a unique transaction code were intercepted it would be useless for subsequent charges. Consumers will still be asked to sign for many chip transactions. A downside is slower processing: dip transactions take about five to ten seconds versus three to five seconds for swipes, which could lengthen checkout lines at busy times like Black Friday.

A liability shift tied to major card networks’ deadlines transfers responsibility for card-present fraud to merchants who haven’t upgraded terminals by the cutoffs (Oct. 1 for Mastercard and Visa; Oct. 16 for American Express). Federal law continues to protect consumers—banks must reimburse victims of many fraud types—but banks may pursue retailers that failed to implement chip-capable terminals. Not all customers will have chip cards by the deadlines; large banks aim to issue most cards by year’s end, with some replacements delayed until 2016 or until existing cards expire. Old magnetic-stripe cards will continue to work until they expire or until a consumer activates a new card, and swipe-compatible terminals will still accept them though updated machines will prompt users to dip chip-enabled cards. Consumer groups advise always using the chip reader when available.

The documents examine the persistent dangers of modern U.S. fraternity life, focusing on alcohol-fueled deaths, severe injuries, hazing, and the political and legal power of national fraternity organizations. A Bloomberg investigation recounts how California Polytechnic State University imposed a deferred freshman recruitment ban after Sigma Alpha Epsilon initiation led to Carson Starkey’s 2008 death from alcohol poisoning. The North-American Interfraternity Conference (NIC) aggressively opposed the ban—providing research, lobbying administrators and students, and pressing legal threats—helping Cal Poly reverse course and restore immediate recruitment in exchange for new oversight measures. Critics, including former Princeton president Shirley Tilghman, argue that delaying recruitment could protect vulnerable freshmen; statistics show freshmen account for a disproportionate share of fraternity-related deaths. Fraternities counter that deferred recruitment is a superficial fix, and that national organizations promote alcohol-education policies and other reforms.

A longer magazine piece broadens the portrait of fraternity hazards through grisly anecdotes—from bottle-rocket and rectal-injury episodes to multiple falls from windows and porches—showing these events are regular rather than freakish. It traces fraternities’ historical roots, cultural resurgence, and the evolution of risk management and self-insurance (FIPG, national trusts) designed to shield chapters and nationals from liability. The article details crisis-management playbooks that often serve to protect the organization’s interests and limit institutional exposure, and explains how strict alcohol policies can be weaponized to deny coverage to individual members—leaving students and families financially vulnerable. It contrasts defenders like NIC chief Peter Smithhisler, who emphasize leadership and charity benefits, with plaintiff attorneys who portray fraternities as profit‑and‑image-driven industries tolerating systemic risk. Both pieces highlight colleges’ dependency on Greek life for housing, recruitment appeal, and alumni giving, which complicates efforts to rein in dangerous behavior. Overall, the reporting argues fraternities remain potent cultural and institutional forces that produce substantial benefits for members yet repeatedly yield preventable harm, prompting difficult questions about accountability, prevention, and the limits of campus authority.

Hurricane Irene barreled northward toward the U.S. East Coast, prompting widespread emergency declarations, mass evacuations and major event cancellations as officials prepared for a slow-moving, potentially devastating storm. With winds reported around 115 mph while passing the Bahamas and forecasts calling for landfall near North Carolina’s Outer Banks, governors in Virginia, Maryland, New Jersey, New York, Connecticut and North Carolina declared states of emergency. Authorities warned that the storm could bring destructive storm surge, prolonged high winds, torrential rain and extensive power outages from the Carolinas into New England, endangering as many as tens of millions of residents.

Local and regional responses were broad: mandatory evacuations were ordered for barrier islands and resort towns such as Ocean City and areas of the Outer Banks; New York City officials planned possible mass-transit shutdowns and urged low-lying hospitals and nursing homes to evacuate; Amtrak suspended some service; airports and airlines prepared for delays and allowed rebooking; and utility companies prepositioned crews for post-storm restoration. Colleges adjusted move-in schedules and the federal government staged FEMA supply depots. Sandbagging and Metro precautions were implemented in Washington, where storm track shifts led organizers to postpone the Martin Luther King Jr. memorial dedication originally set for Aug. 28 — a decision aimed at protecting attendees and allowing travel adjustments.

Officials emphasized the storm’s severity and unpredictability, noting potential economic losses in the billions and comparing the projected path to past powerful storms. Residents scrambled to evacuate or prepare, with coastal traffic jams, shortages at gas stations and stores, and some choosing to remain despite warnings. Authorities repeatedly urged people to heed evacuation orders and prepare for extended disruptions to power, transit and daily life.

Researchers have developed a way to make distilled spirits from spent coffee grounds, turning a waste product into a 40% ethanol liquor comparable to vodka or tequila. In the study, scientists collected used grounds from a Portuguese roaster, dried them, and heated the powder in water at 163°C for 45 minutes. They separated the liquid, added sugar, inoculated with yeast to ferment, then concentrated the fermented mash to raise alcohol content—steps similar to whiskey or rum production. Eight trained tasters evaluated the resulting “Spent Coffee Ground” spirit, reporting coffee-like aromas and bitter, pungent flavors; researchers suggested aging could improve taste and judged the product fit for consumption. Unlike caffeinated alcoholic beverages, most caffeine is lost during brewing, avoiding the stimulant-alcohol mix linked to safety concerns. The work responds to distillers’ interest in novel flavor sources and highlights a sustainable route to create distinctive spirits from coffee industry byproducts.

A mother in Santa Rosa, Delia Garcia-Bratcher, 30, was arrested after allegedly grabbing a 12-year-old boy by the throat at Olivet Charter Elementary School while confronting him about bullying her daughter. The incident occurred at lunchtime when Garcia-Bratcher reportedly came onto campus without signing in, asked her son to point out the suspected bully, approached the boy in front of other students, and physically accosted him. The boy ran to a classroom and reported the assault; school staff photographed red marks and apparent fingerprints on his neck. Deputies arrested Garcia-Bratcher on suspicion of felony child abuse/inflicting injury on a child; she was released on $30,000 bail and is due in court. Authorities and the school district are investigating possible bullying but so far have not substantiated claims linking the boy to harassment of the girl. School officials stressed visitor sign-in policies and student safety; the district plans to notify parents and pursue its own inquiry. Garcia-Bratcher has disputed the accusations on social media, saying she was hurt by them.

Researchers studying African elephants in Kenya report that elephants can distinguish between human languages and between voices of men, women, and boys, using these cues to assess threat and adjust behavior. In experiments at Amboseli National Park, scientists played recordings of the same phrase—“Look, look over there, a group of elephants is coming”—spoken by Maasai men (who sometimes clash with and occasionally kill elephants), Kamba men (generally less threatening), Maasai women, and boys. Elephants across 47 family groups responded defensively—bunching together, smelling, and moving away—more often when they heard adult Maasai male voices than when they heard female, boy, or Kamba male voices. Older matriarchs improved group threat assessment, supporting the role of learning and memory. Altering voice pitch did not fool elephants: they still treated altered male voices as threatening and altered female voices as nonthreatening, suggesting sensitivity to cues beyond simple pitch. Authors argue this discrimination reflects sophisticated cognition and socially learned knowledge of people sharing their habitat. The work, published in PNAS, underscores growing human–elephant conflict: elephants now regard humans as a species to monitor, reinforcing concerns about conservation as interactions intensify.

Russell Crowe stormed out of a BBC Radio 4 Front Row interview after host Mark Lawson suggested his Robin Hood accent had “hints” of Irish. Discussing Ridley Scott’s new prequel, Crowe—New Zealand–born and Australia–based—reacted angrily, calling Lawson’s ears “dead” and insisting there was nothing Irish in the portrayal. The exchange grew heated, with Crowe swearing, refusing to answer some questions, and ultimately waving a cigarette and walking out. Voice coaches reportedly aimed for a Rutland/East Midlands tone; critics have variously described his accent as inconsistent or odd. Crowe said he’d studied Michael Parkinson’s tapes to shape the voice and referenced historical claims tying Robin Hood to Yorkshire or Nottinghamshire. The confrontation followed a pattern of Crowe’s past public tempers, including a 2005 assault charge in New York. The interview aired on Front Row on BBC Radio 4.

A Brooklyn grand jury has indicted rookie NYPD officer Peter Liang on second-degree manslaughter and related charges over the Nov. 20 shooting death of 28-year-old Akai Gurley in an unlit stairwell of the Pink Houses in East New York. Liang, 27, a probationary officer with less than 18 months on the force, allegedly fired a single shot while conducting a vertical patrol; the bullet struck Gurley, who was unarmed and standing on a landing below with his girlfriend. Liang also faces reckless endangerment, second-degree assault and official misconduct counts and could face up to 15 years in prison. The panel began hearing evidence in early February; Liang did not testify. Gurley’s partner and family, civil attorneys and activists, including Rev. Al Sharpton, welcomed the indictment as a step toward accountability, while police union leaders called for due process and characterized the shooting as an accident in a dangerous housing project. Mayor de Blasio urged respect for the judicial process. The case follows national scrutiny of police killings and contrasts with recent grand juries that declined to indict officers in Ferguson and Staten Island.

Ron and Mary Tarnowski, an elderly Duluth couple who had been missing since July 29, were found dead Aug. 5 in a remote, swampy area off Highway 2 near Brookston, Minnesota. U.S. Customs and Border Protection air crews located their Chevy Tahoe about 150 yards off the road on what appeared to be an overgrown, seasonal trail. Mary, 78, was inside the vehicle and Ron, 82, was found outside about 50 feet from the road. Authorities believe the SUV became stuck in mud and that Ron left to seek help. Autopsy results are pending, but investigators and the family suspect the couple died of exposure, dehydration and heat on a warm day; no foul play is suspected.

The Tarnowskis, married 59 years, had largely been homebound because Mary suffered right-side paralysis from a decades-old stroke and Ron had early-stage dementia. Their sons reported the couple left unexpectedly without phones, medications, Mary’s wheelchair or her purse; their OnStar system was not active. Surveillance footage captured the couple slowly walking into a Brookston restaurant earlier that day. Evidence shows they stopped at a bank and a restaurant before heading northwest on Highway 2 toward family hunting property about 30 miles from their Duluth home.

Their disappearance spurred a week-long, community-wide search involving family, law enforcement, retired and active firefighters and hundreds of volunteers. A “Find Ron and Mary Tarnowski” Facebook group exceeded 7,000 followers; residents tied purple ribbons for Alzheimer’s awareness. The family and officials praised the broad search efforts and urged caregivers of vulnerable adults to ensure they carry tracking devices or phones. The tragic outcome highlighted risks faced by vulnerable seniors and prompted an outpouring of condolences for the devoted couple and their grieving family.

Pakistani TV has sparked outrage by giving away abandoned newborns live on a Ramadan-era game show hosted by Aamir Liaquat Hussain. During marathon seven-hour broadcasts of Aman Ramazan, Hussain presented two infant girls—rescued by the Chhipa Welfare Association—to childless couples on air, and announced a baby boy would be handed over soon. The show, described as a religious-entertainment mix and compared to The Price Is Right, awards household appliances and motorbikes to audience members who answer Quran questions; it also features cooking, hymns, children’s segments and animals. Chhipa says it recovers up to 15 abandoned babies monthly and vetted the adopting families, but paperwork and formal adoption procedures were not completed before live presentation. Adoption lacks clear legal recognition in Pakistan, so new parents must apply for guardianship in family court. Supporters say rescuing infants from dangerous abandonment gives them a chance at life; critics call the stunt a ratings-driven publicity ploy that treats babies like trophies. Hussain insists the giveaways promote social unity and deter child abandonment and extremism. The episodes have broken ratings records, attracted intense debate, and highlighted broader concerns about media sensationalism, poverty-driven child abandonment, and weak adoption laws.

At the court-martial of Sgt. Adam Holcomb, testimony detailed persistent hazing and racial taunts that prosecutors say drove Pvt. Danny Chen, a 19-year-old Chinese American soldier, to suicide at an Afghan combat outpost on Oct. 3. Holcomb, 30, is the first of eight soldiers to be tried in connection with Chen’s death; others, including an officer, face later courts-martial. Military witnesses painted a picture of repeated abuse: Holcomb allegedly used racial slurs, physically abused Chen by dragging him across sharp, baseball-sized rocks—leaving bloodied abrasions on Chen’s back—and otherwise “hounded” him for infractions such as failing to turn off power to a water heater. Army Pvt. Marcus Merritt, an African American soldier, testified that Holcomb directed a racial slur at him and threatened to “kill me and put me in a body bag and send me home,” and said the sergeant’s conduct left him suicidal. Merritt later acknowledged under cross-examination that he did not believe Holcomb was literally going to kill him, but stated he feared the sergeant and once told a military psychiatrist he wanted to kill Holcomb. Holcomb’s immediate superior, Staff Sgt. Darren Holt, told the panel he confronted Holcomb after learning Holcomb had dragged Chen across rocks and that Holt reported and counseled Holcomb that physical abuse was unacceptable. Defense lawyers argue Chen’s suicide stemmed from family pressures—his parents allegedly disowned him for enlisting instead of going to college—and depict Chen as a struggling, at times negligent, soldier who required corrective training. They also contended nicknames and brusque language, including racially tinged nicknames, were used as terms of camaraderie in the platoon. Some witnesses said most of Holcomb’s discipline was justified, and the platoon medic testified Chen denied suicidal thoughts when asked. The proceedings have heightened scrutiny of hazing and racism in the Army and drawn attention from Chinese American communities and international media.

Earlier this week Instagram updated its privacy policy and terms of service, triggering widespread user alarm about advertising, data sharing with Facebook, and whether users’ photos could be used in ads without compensation. Critics pointed to language suggesting Instagram might display users’ names, likenesses and photos in paid content, and that Facebook could use personal data to target ads. After intense backlash—including defections to rival apps and high-profile accounts leaving—co-founder Kevin Systrom apologized for unclear communication and announced Instagram would revert the advertising clause to the original terms from October 2010. He insisted Instagram never intended to sell users’ photos and does not own them, and said the company will finish its advertising plans before returning to users with clear explanations. Instagram will also tweak its privacy policy to clarify how photos are shared. The episode sent users to competitors like Pheed and Flickr, which saw spikes in sign-ups and downloads, underscoring both Instagram’s massive user base and the fragility of its public trust as it faces pressure to monetize.

New Jersey lawmakers are debating a broad distracted-driving bill that would penalize motorists for any activity that “interferes with the safe operation” of a vehicle — from using electronic devices to eating, drinking, grooming or reading. Sponsors, led by Assemblyman John Wisniewski, say the measure is meant to curb dangerously common multitasking on the road and save lives. Federal data cited by supporters show about 400,000 distraction-involved crashes in 2014, including roughly 3,000 deaths, underscoring calls for stronger deterrents.

Under the proposal, fines would range from $200–$400 for a first offense and $400–$600 for a second. A third or subsequent violation could carry a $600–$800 fine, motor-vehicle points and up to a 90-day license suspension. Lawmakers describe the bill as modeled on Maine’s law and intended more to educate drivers than to unduly punish them, arguing that broad language avoids constant rewrites as new technologies emerge.

The proposal has provoked controversy and widespread public reaction. Critics — including the National Motorists Association and AAA — say the bill is vague, could criminalize commonplace adjustments like changing a radio station or talking to a passenger, and would be hard for police to enforce without observing unsafe maneuvers. Supporters counter that a cultural shift, similar to seat-belt adoption, could follow from clearer legal norms and public education, reducing preventable deaths. Wisniewski notes the bill does not single out coffee or eating, despite media portrayals, and he doubts officers would ticket drivers solely for sipping a beverage. The measure has been introduced multiple times but has yet to reach a committee vote.

North Korean pair Ryom Tae-Ok and Kim Ju-Sik earned one of the last available Olympic figure-skating berths at September’s Nebelhorn Trophy in Oberstdorf, Germany, securing North Korea’s presence at the PyeongChang 2018 Winter Games. Their short program, set to the Beatles, and an improved free skate to “Je suis qu’une chanson” won them one of five qualifying spots and the International Skating Union confirmed their qualification. Russia and Germany had already qualified. The duo, who trained in Montreal over the summer with coach Bruno Marcotte and finished 15th at last season’s World Championships, celebrated emotionally after their routine. The final decision on whether they will actually compete rests with the North Korean Olympic Committee.

Their qualification is seen as a potentially positive diplomatic development amid heightened tensions on the Korean peninsula, where recent exchanges of aggressive rhetoric between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and U.S. President Donald Trump have raised fears. South Korean President Moon Jae-in has urged North Korea to decide up until the last minute whether to participate, arguing that participation could aid inter-Korean peace and reconciliation. North Korea has sent teams to some South Korean events this year, including women’s hockey and taekwondo contingents, but historically geopolitics have affected Olympic involvement—Pyongyang boycotted the 1988 Seoul Games and did not attend Sochi in 2014.

The International Olympic Committee has been actively supporting North Korean athletes’ efforts to qualify, offering equipment, travel and accommodation assistance. Other North Korean winter athletes, such as speed skaters and Nordic skiers, still have upcoming qualification opportunities. While Ryom and Kim appeared composed after the event, their coach and officials emphasized that decisions about Olympic participation are ultimately political and beyond the skaters’ control.

Adrianne Haslet-Davis, a professional ballroom dancer who lost her left leg below the knee in the Boston Marathon bombing, announced she’s training for the 120th Boston Marathon this April. Forming team “#AdrianneStrong” about five weeks ago, she will raise funds for Limbs for Life. Though never a runner, she’s reached 10-mile training runs using a prosthetic blade and plans to dedicate her April 18 race to supporters and fellow survivors. Haslet-Davis previously vowed to dance again and returned to the marathon finish line to perform last April, symbolizing resilience as she continues physical and emotional recovery alongside her husband.

This document explains the Federal Trade Commission’s (FTC) guidance and enforcement policy for “Made in USA” claims, clarifying what manufacturers and marketers must prove to make unqualified or qualified U.S.-origin assertions. The FTC enforces an “all or virtually all” standard for unqualified claims: all significant parts and processing must be from the United States (including territories and D.C.), meaning negligible foreign content. Companies making such claims must have a reasonable, documented basis—competent, reliable evidence—showing final assembly or processing occurs in the U.S. and that U.S. parts and costs predominate. The FTC evaluates total manufacturing costs, proximity of foreign content to the finished product, and whether foreign inputs are significant. Qualified claims (e.g., “Made in USA of U.S. and imported parts,” or percentage statements) are permitted when accurate, clearly limited, and substantiated; vague terms like “created” or “produced” can imply broader origin and risk deception. “Assembled in USA” is acceptable only when principal assembly and the last substantial transformation happened domestically. The document distinguishes FTC authority from U.S. Customs, which determines country of origin for imports using “substantial transformation” and enforces marking requirements; products may meet Customs rules but still fail the FTC’s advertising standard. It also cites related statutes (textile, fur, automobile labeling, Buy American) and outlines how to report suspected violations to FTC, Customs, state attorneys general, NAD, or via private Lanham Act suits. The piece includes a case study: watchdog Truth in Advertising found over 100 alleged “Made in USA” labeling errors on Walmart’s website, prompting removal of labels and highlighting the importance of accurate, substantiated origin claims.

Nancy Motes, the 37-year-old half-sister of Julia Roberts, was found dead in a bathtub in Los Angeles on Feb. 9 in an apparent overdose. The Los Angeles County Coroner reported prescription and non-prescription pills and multiple notes at the scene; toxicology results are pending and could take weeks. Initial reports indicate at least one multi-page suicide note in which Motes reportedly wrote about her fraught relationship with Roberts and other family members.

Motes, a former production assistant on Glee, had a long history of conflict with her famous sister and struggled with weight and prescription drug problems. She publicly criticized Roberts in interviews and on Twitter in recent months, accusing her of cruelty and saying family rejection contributed to her depression. Sources say Roberts privately tried for years to get Motes into rehab; Motes reportedly agreed once but backed out. Roberts canceled public appearances following the death and has not publicly commented.

A sharp dispute has emerged between Motes’ fiancé, John Dilbeck, and surviving family members. Dilbeck’s brother, Conner, claimed the suicide was timed to damage Roberts’ Oscar chances and said the note contained “dark secrets” about the actress; Conner and other friends have publicly blamed Roberts and the family for driving Motes to despair. Conversely, other sources noted longstanding concerns that Dilbeck was a bad influence and warned he might control or monetize Motes’ personal effects and writings as estate beneficiary.

Authorities continue to investigate. The reports include warnings about suicide resources for anyone in crisis.

Anthony Scaramucci, newly named White House communications director, responded angrily this week after Politico published his government financial disclosure, threatening on Twitter to involve the FBI and Justice Department over what he called a “felony” leak. He initially tagged Chief of Staff Reince Priebus, later deleting the tweet and saying Priebus was helping crack down on leaks. The disclosure shows Scaramucci’s substantial wealth and continued financial ties to his investment firm, SkyBridge Capital: he reported $4.9 million from his SkyBridge stake and over $5 million in salary between January 1, 2016, and late June. His filings value SkyBridge at more than $50 million and list him as owning nearly 44 percent. A sale of SkyBridge to RON Transatlantic and China’s HNA Group was announced in January and was valued by Bloomberg at $200–230 million; when the sale closes, Scaramucci stands to receive the agreed proceeds for his share. The deal has attracted regulatory scrutiny from the interagency Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States amid broader concern over China-linked transactions. Scaramucci said his official White House start would be delayed until August so his finances could be “100 percent totally cleansed.” He has assets worth up to $85 million, including a minority stake in the New York Mets, real estate, and other investments, and has been on unpaid leave from Export-Import Bank since June.

A Democratic source told CNN that Hillary Clinton is not considering Bernie Sanders for vice president. Sanders, who has not yet formally conceded the Democratic primary to Clinton, was not expecting to be offered the VP slot and does not take Clinton’s decision personally, according to someone close to him. Instead of seeking to join Clinton’s ticket, Sanders remains focused on reshaping the Democratic Party from within and continuing his independent political momentum rather than "becoming her partner." Those close to him say joining the ticket could damage his standing with devoted supporters who might view such a move as a sell-out, so Clinton’s decision is not a surprise. The Vermont senator did not raise the vice-presidential topic during a private, roughly 90-minute meeting with Clinton on Tuesday night. Observers and aides familiar with both campaigns have signaled that a Sanders vice-presidential role was unlikely given ideological differences, Sanders’ base’s expectations, and the political risks to his future influence if he were perceived to have capitulated. The development underscores Sanders’ intention to maintain an active, independent role in Democratic politics and continue advocating for the policy changes that energized his campaign, rather than subsuming that agenda into a Clinton administration. The piece also includes an unrelated note about Alexa Internet’s long-standing practice, since 1996, of donating crawl data to the Internet Archive for inclusion in the Wayback Machine after an embargo period.

A large analysis of U.S. cancer registry data indicates colorectal cancer is increasingly affecting adults under 50, prompting questions about current screening practices that generally start at age 50. Researchers led by Dr. Samantha Hendren examined nearly 258,000 colorectal cancer cases diagnosed from 1998–2011 and found about 37,847 (nearly 15%) occurred in patients younger than 50. The study and accompanying expert commentary highlight several key findings and implications.

Younger patients were more likely than older ones to present with advanced disease: they were approximately 30% more likely to have tumors that spread to lymph nodes and 50% more likely to have metastatic disease. Consequently, younger patients with advanced disease more often received aggressive treatments—72% underwent surgery versus 63% of older patients, and 53% received radiation versus 48% of older patients. Despite being diagnosed at later stages, younger patients had somewhat better outcomes by stage: five-year survival for localized disease was 95.1% versus 91.9%; regional disease 76% versus 70.3%; and distant disease 21.3% versus 14.1%.

Authors caution the analysis lacked information on family history and other risk factors, and selection bias could influence treatment and survival patterns. Experts urge increased clinical vigilance: symptoms such as anemia, changes in bowel habits, dark or mixed blood in stool, and unexplained pain should prompt diagnostic workups regardless of age. While some high-risk individuals already receive earlier screening, whether population-wide screening should begin before 50 remains unresolved; the yield would be lower and the balance of benefits and harms uncertain. The study serves as a “wake-up call” for the medical community to reassess risk assessment, symptom recognition, and follow-up for younger adults.

The Wisconsin Air National Guard’s 115th Fighter Wing will conduct nighttime training flights Monday through Thursday, with F-16s taking off and landing until about 10 p.m., officials said. While such exercises typically occur during daytime, pilots and maintenance crews must practice night operations for readiness. Flight paths will be chosen to minimize noise for nearby residents, and personnel have the option to delete Tweet location history if they share location-tagged posts. Separately, freezing temperatures Tuesday night likely produced a “frostquake” — a cryoseism — in parts of southern Wisconsin between Columbus, Fox Lake, Johnson Creek and Oconomowoc, the National Weather Service in Sullivan reported. Witnesses described a loud boom and brief rumble that shook houses but caused no known damage. Meteorologist Justin Schultz explained frostquakes occur when groundwater or subsurface moisture freezes, expands, and fractures soil and rock; Wisconsin is among states that have experienced such events.

Engineers raced to restore power and cooling at the tsunami-damaged Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear plant after the March 11 quake and tsunami crippled backup systems, causing fires, explosions and partial meltdowns at several units. Workers laid external cables to restart pumps for four reactors while spraying seawater from fire trucks and, briefly, military helicopters to cool overheated cores and spent-fuel pools. Authorities warned some spent-fuel pools — notably at Unit 3, which uses mixed-oxide fuel containing plutonium — were low or nearly dry, raising the risk of worsening radiation releases. Japan raised the incident to level 5 on the INES scale, comparable to Three Mile Island, though experts differ on severity; Chernobyl was level 7. Thousands died or were missing after the quake and tsunami, and hundreds of thousands were displaced amid shortages of food, water, medicine and heating. International concern prompted U.S. advisories, aircraft monitoring and joint financial interventions to stabilize markets; the U.S. recommended a wider evacuation radius and pledged technical help as efforts to cool reactors continued, possibly taking days or weeks.

A multi-year scheme to steal and cash U.S. Postal Service money orders led to multiple convictions and prison terms for several participants, while the alleged organizer—a former postal employee—avoided prison. Eugene Bowen, 35, of Knoxville, Tennessee, pleaded guilty to transmitting and presenting unlawfully issued USPS money orders and was sentenced in Camden federal court to 20 months in prison, three years of supervised release, and $18,470 in restitution. Bowen admitted recruiting individuals, including residents of homeless shelters in Knoxville, to cash stolen money orders; he paid them small fees and kept the remainder for himself and Marc Saunders, a former New Lisbon USPS employee who supplied the forged orders.

Saunders, 40, of Sicklerville, admitted producing the fraudulent money orders using a stolen imprinting machine and giving them to others to cash. He pleaded guilty in December 2017; his sentencing was scheduled for July 24, 2018. Despite his central role, Saunders received five years probation with eight months home confinement and was ordered to pay nearly $100,000 in restitution. Other participants also received prison time: Anthony Bell, 39, of Philadelphia, was sentenced to a year and a day; Andre Sutton received nine months. Restitution totals for the middlemen were roughly $22,400 (Bell), $18,500 (Bowen), and $4,700 (Sutton).

An affidavit detailed postal mismanagement that enabled the theft: an older money-order imprinting machine and loose money orders were left unsecured after new equipment was introduced in 2013. Investigators traced cashed money orders by serial numbers and ZIP-code imprints to multiple offices nationwide. Cellphone records, Facebook links, and family and childhood ties connected lower-level participants to Saunders and Bowen. The investigation was conducted by USPS Office of Inspector General special agents; the government was represented by Assistant U.S. Attorney Alyson M. Oswald. Defense counsel for Bowen was John Brennan. Judge Joseph H. Rodriguez imposed the sentences.

The author argues that the popular “sober January” or “dry January” trend is misguided, rooted in guilt rather than evidence, and can be actively harmful for people with alcohol problems. Speaking from personal experience as someone who repeatedly used month-long abstentions as a form of denial before finally acknowledging alcoholism and quitting permanently, the author explains how a temporary detox appeals to the addict’s all-or-nothing mentality: binge over the holidays, then “white-knuckle” sobriety for a month, and resume drinking afterwards. That cycle enabled self-deception—if one could manage a month off, one could not be an alcoholic. The author is troubled that major charities promote the challenge; even with small-print warnings that dependent drinkers should not attempt it, such campaigns attract exactly the people at risk, while “normal” social drinkers typically ignore it. Rather than treating a month off as a corrective, the author recommends assessing whether drinking is a real problem by testing controlled drinking. Citing Alcoholics Anonymous cofounder Bill Wilson, who advised that suspected alcoholics try drinking in a controlled way to see if they can stop, the piece suggests that attempting regulated consumption—like limiting yourself to a single pint nightly—will more honestly reveal whether cravings override control. In short, the author advises against using sober January as a badge of virtue or proof of moderation; it’s easy and can mask addiction. If you’re concerned about your drinking, the right approach is honest evaluation, not a guilt-driven 31-day challenge.

The University of Winnipeg Library, together with the University of Manitoba Libraries, the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, and Library and Archives Canada, has assembled an expanding web-archive documenting Manitoba’s engagement with the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. The curated selection captures webpages, blogs, news reports and PDFs related to survivors’ stories, apologies, institutional responses, cultural events and other facets of reconciliation and healing across the province. The project is ongoing and will grow as new initiatives and community work emerge; funding support was provided by Manitoba Tourism, Culture, Heritage, Sport and Consumer Protection and the Government of Canada.

Separately, a rare World War II Enigma machine bought for 100 euros at a Bucharest flea market sold at auction for 45,000 euros (about $51,500). The collector who purchased the device—reported to be a cryptography professor—recognized its significance and consigned it to Artmark auction house, where it was purchased by an anonymous online bidder. Made in Germany in 1941 and described as being in near-perfect condition, this Enigma I is part of the family of cipher machines used by Nazi forces to encrypt military communications. Although Enigma codes were believed secure, Alan Turing and codebreakers at Bletchley Park cracked them, a breakthrough that historians say helped shorten the war by around two years. Romania’s wartime history as a German ally means more such machines might surface there; recent high-profile Enigma sales have fetched far higher prices at international auctions.

Scientists led by Shoukhrat Mitalipov at Oregon Health & Science University have for the first time reliably derived embryonic stem cell (ESC) lines from cloned human embryos using somatic-cell nuclear transfer (SCNT). After years of attempts and prior failures—including a notorious fraud in South Korea—Mitalipov’s team reported stable ESC lines from six embryos created with donated eggs, using technical refinements such as inactivated Sendai virus for fusion, an electrical activation pulse, and caffeine to prevent premature egg activation. Lines were produced from fetal skin cells and from a child with Leigh syndrome, and were shown capable of differentiating into cell types including contracting heart cells. The work rekindles debate over therapeutic cloning: it could permit creation of patient-matched tissues that avoid immune rejection and, uniquely, replace defective mitochondrial genes via the egg’s mitochondria. Critics cite ethical concerns about creating and destroying embryos and potential exploitation of egg donors; U.S. federal funding restrictions complicate research. Many researchers favor the simpler induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell reprogramming approach, which avoids eggs and embryos, but differences between iPS and embryo-derived cells mean direct comparisons are essential to evaluate clinical utility of SCNT-derived cells.

A high-profile theft at a Feltham, West London, warehouse on the night of January 29–30 has left rare-book dealers and the antiquarian trade reeling after thieves targeted containers holding hundreds of valuable volumes bound for the California International Antiquarian Book Fair. Owners report losses ranging from around £1 million (one dealer, Alessandro Meda Riquier, said 51 books including Galileo and rare Dante editions were taken) to media claims of more than £2 million and 160-plus titles. Stolen works reportedly include landmark scientific and literary texts: a 1566 Copernicus De Revolutionibus, early Galileo volumes, Newton’s Principia, a 1506 Dante Divine Comedy and other Renaissance and scientific rarities.

CCTV apparently captured a dramatic roof entry: thieves cut reinforced skylights, abseiled into the building, targeted specific containers, packed holdalls, hauled them to the roof and escaped by van. Sources say the gang ignored other goods and may have worked from lists, suggesting an organized, possibly inside-informed operation. Police (Metropolitan) are investigating commercial burglary—crime ref 0502127/17—and appeal for info via 101 or Crimestoppers; the SCD6 Art and Antiques Unit and antiquarian bodies have circulated detailed stolen-book lists and contact points for sightings or offers.

Experts warn stolen rare books are hard to fence publicly; publicity and databases can deter sale but also push items underground or prompt dismantling of works. Recovery and recording losses promptly are crucial to make the volumes unsellable and aid investigation.

Donald Trump accused Amazon founder Jeff Bezos of using The Washington Post to shield Amazon from taxes and antitrust scrutiny, saying on Fox’s Sean Hannity that Bezos treats the paper “like a toy” to influence politicians and protect his company. Trump complained that Post reporters call “every hour” with “ridiculous” questions and predicted the newspaper would compile inaccurate stories and a book about him. His comments followed Post associate editor Bob Woodward’s disclosure that the paper had assigned about 20 reporters to investigate Trump’s life and real estate dealings; Woodward said the Post planned extensive multi-part reporting on presidential candidates so voters would be well informed. Trump framed Bezos as having a “huge antitrust problem,” arguing Amazon controls too much of the market and is avoiding proper taxation, and claimed Bezos uses the Post politically to prevent antitrust action and higher taxes. The story notes Bezos bought the Post in 2013 and has donated to both parties, and that neither Bezos nor Amazon immediately responded to Trump’s accusations. Woodward added Bezos encouraged broad coverage of all candidates rather than targeting any single campaign.

Avengers: Infinity War remained dominant in its third weekend, earning an estimated $61.8 million domestically and bringing its U.S. total to $547.8 million. Bolstered by a near-record $200 million opening in China, the film grossed $343.1 million worldwide that weekend and passed $1.6 billion globally, becoming the fifth-highest grossing film ever. It also became the second-fastest film to reach $500 million domestically. Mother's Day weekend saw two female-led releases: Melissa McCarthy’s Life of the Party opened second with $18.5 million from 3,656 locations, one of her lower openings and currently averaging 41% on Rotten Tomatoes and a B CinemaScore. Gabrielle Union’s low-budget thriller Breaking In debuted third with $16.5 million from 2,537 sites and a 27% Rotten Tomatoes rating. Lionsgate’s Overboard held fourth with $10 million, while A Quiet Place stayed strong at No. 5 with $6.3 million, totaling $169 million domestically. Year-to-date box office is up 4.9% from 2017, with Deadpool 2 and Solo on the horizon.

France has seen a string of shocking infanticides in recent decades, highlighted by cases like Véronique Courjault, Céline Lesage and Dominique Cottrez, who admitted hiding pregnancies and killing multiple newborns. Investigations revealed fathers often were unaware of the pregnancies. Experts point to pregnancy denial — a severe psychological state in which women do not recognize or accept pregnancy — as a common explanation. Clinicians describe denial that can blunt physical signs and render the newborn psychologically nonexistent, prompting some women to kill newborns as if disposing of trash. Causes suggested include prior trauma, identity issues, or broader social shifts devaluing parenting. Some specialists urge medical and legal recognition and better detection and treatment rather than only punishment.

Former Nixon lawyer John Dean likens the Trump White House to “a nightmare,” emphasizing the anxiety among aides uncertain if they’re implicated in unfolding investigations. Amid that turmoil, public attention has zeroed in on First Lady Melania Trump’s apparent unhappiness and awkward public interactions with President Trump. Multiple viral moments—Melania flinching when Trump touched her during a Florida rally, failing to grasp his hand on the Tel Aviv tarmac, and generally distancing herself during appearances—have fueled speculation about her marriage and well-being. Social media responded with concern, accusations of abuse, and a wave of schadenfreude from critics who relish any sign of discord. Reporters and commentators point to a pattern: stiff public behavior at the inauguration, minimal affectionate contact, and Ivanka Trump filling many traditional first‑lady roles. Melania’s team briefly managed a social‑media like that mocked her changeable expressions, later attributing it to account access. Critics note she chose this life and could leave, but others say her visible rebuffs offer a rare, lighthearted public counterpoint to a presidency that many find alarming. Overall, the narrative combines legal peril inside the administration with persistent, highly publicized signs of strain in the first couple’s relationship.

Pantone 448 C—a drab, greenish-brown shade dubbed “opaque couché” and widely called the “world’s ugliest colour”—was deliberately chosen to curb smoking by making cigarette packs visually repellent. In 2012 the Australian government commissioned marketing research firm GfK Bluemoon to identify a color that would generate the most negative associations; over three months and seven studies involving more than 1,000 smokers, respondents described the hue with words like “dirty,” “tar,” and “death.” Australia adopted the color on plain cigarette packaging alongside graphic health warnings, and early evidence suggests standardized, unbranded packs may reduce smoking prevalence and increase quit attempts. A Cochrane Review summarized multiple studies and concluded the available evidence supports a beneficial effect of plain packaging on attitudes and behavior. Following Australia’s lead, the United Kingdom, Ireland and France passed plain-packaging laws using the same murky color, and other countries have shown interest. The strategy forms part of Australia’s broader tobacco-control program that spans decades: mandatory health warnings since 1973, advertising bans, public smoking prohibitions, higher excise taxes, point-of-sale restrictions, and multiple excise increases through the 2010s. National surveys show steady declines in smoking—adult daily smoking fell from mid-20s percentages in the 1990s to around 13–16% by the early 2010s, with further reductions reported in subsequent years; youth smoking and uptake have declined sharply as well. Nevertheless, disparities remain: higher smoking rates persist in remote areas, lower socioeconomic groups, unemployed people, and within Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations. Public-health goals include reducing adult daily smoking to 10% by 2018 and halving Indigenous smoking rates. The use of Pantone 448 C also reflects a longer history of leveraging color psychology to influence behavior—examples range from workplace design to branding—though perceptions of color can vary among individuals.

Cleveland’s Game 2 World Series win by the Chicago Cubs spotlighted an improbable comeback: Kyle Schwarber, who missed six months after tearing two knee ligaments April 7, returned without any regular-season at-bats and has become a postseason sensation. With the Series tied 1-1 after the Cubs’ 5-1 victory, Schwarber’s unexpected production — a double off Corey Kluber in Game 1 and a 2-for-4 performance with two RBIs and a walk in Game 2 — has teammates and media calling it “The Legend of Kyle Schwarber.” At 23, he’s hitting .429 in the Series, reaching base five times in nine plate appearances, and has drawn raves for his plate discipline and professional at-bats. Teammates praise his relentless work ethic: watching film, rehabbing obsessively, and staying integrated with the club despite being sidelined.

Cubs management, including Theo Epstein and Jed Hoyer, fast-tracked his return when medical reports showed he was ahead of schedule; a private plane brought him in for Game 1. Doctors initially cleared him to hit and run bases as a DH, but with the Series shifting to National League rules at Wrigley Field, the big question is whether he’ll play left field. The club plans to consult medical staff and protect him from undue risk, perhaps using defensive replacements or limiting him to pinch-hit roles if needed. Beyond baseball, Schwarber’s emotional connection to a young fan with mitochondrial disease adds poignancy to his story. Whether he plays the field or not, his comeback has transformed the World Series narrative and energized Cubs fans heading into Game 3 at Wrigley.

Cassie Young, a 31-year-old digital director for The Bert Show who has worked through long-standing issues with body image, recently confronted unsolicited fat-shaming from a personal trainer on Twitter after announcing her engagement. The trainer messaged congratulations but immediately offered to help her “get in shape” for the wedding. When Young politely declined—explaining she felt healthy and happy with her body—the trainer persisted, arguing she should hire someone so her wedding photos wouldn’t reflect a body he deemed unacceptable. He insisted that people who promote “big body acceptance” must be lying about their happiness with their appearance.

Young posted screenshots of the exchange to Facebook to illustrate a common, predatory tactic: professionals who try to acquire clients by preying on insecurities. In her responses she explained that it took years to reach self-acceptance after childhood teasing and dieting, and that she’d worked to stop letting body folds or clothing sizes define her worth. She called out the trainer for tying his self-worth to looks and for perpetuating shame rather than supporting genuine health. Although the encounter upset her, Young declined to name the trainer publicly, saying she wanted the episode to be a learning opportunity rather than an exercise in vilification.

The post went viral and drew widespread support in the comments, with many readers condemning the trainer’s approach and celebrating body positivity. Young closed her message with an urging: life is too short to be spent worrying about a belly roll—go be happy and live fully. The exchange highlights ongoing cultural tensions around appearance, professional ethics, and the right to embrace diverse body types without shame.

This document combines two unrelated items: a description of a large web-archiving crawl and coverage of a niche Disney-focused dating site called Mouse Mingle. The crawl, labeled "Survey 7," began Feb. 24, 2018 and used Heritrix with maxHops=0 to capture listed URLs and their embeds. Its seed list contained 339,249,218 URLs derived from Wayback Machine records that returned HTTP 200 during 2017 (query run Feb. 1, 2018). The resulting WARC files are not publicly available. The crawl is part of the Internet Archive’s “No More 404” effort to archive pages as they are created and their referenced pages, so links remain resolvable even if original content changes or disappears—intended to reduce broken links by preserving the live versions authors referenced.

The second part describes MouseMingle.com, launched by Dave Tavres, a former Disneyland Railroad engineer, as the first all-Disney dating site. Profiles are public but messaging costs $12.55/month. The site matches users through Disney-specific questions (songs, characters, parks, memories) and aims to connect passionate Disney fans worldwide, including those far from Disney parks. It joins other niche dating platforms.

Moses Malone, the three-time NBA MVP and dominant rebounder who led the Philadelphia 76ers to their 1983 NBA championship, died in his sleep at 60 in Norfolk, Va. The Sixers announced his passing without immediate cause. Acquired in the summer of 1982, Malone provided the physical presence coach Billy Cunningham said the team needed, averaging 24.5 points and 15.3 rebounds in the regular season and 26 and 15.8 in the 13 playoff games that year, earning Finals MVP. Known for a fierce on-court scowl and a warm off-court laugh, Malone quickly bonded with teammates and fans. He began his pro career out of high school in the ABA, played 19 NBA seasons, was a 12-time All-Star, three-time MVP, led the league in rebounding multiple times, and was a Hall of Famer (2001) and member of the NBA’s 50th anniversary team. The Sixers lauded him as an icon and pillar of their storied era.

FBI agents joined Cass County investigators searching a remote, wooded area south of Belton after a mushroom hunter found human bones Monday and a second skull was discovered nearby Tuesday. The remains were located near E. 233rd and State Route Y; authorities closed about 6.5 miles of S. State Route Y while searching, and the closure could last into Wednesday. The recovered remains have been sent to the Jackson County medical examiner; age, sex and race have not yet been determined and no identifications have been confirmed.

Families of two long-missing Kansas City–area women — Kara Kopetsky, last seen leaving Belton High School in May 2007, and Jessica Runions, last seen at a Sept. 2016 party — were notified that investigators had contacted them but officials would not say whether the remains belong to either woman. The mothers, Rhonda Beckford (Kopetsky) and Jamie Runions, who have become close through their shared grief, expressed hope for answers and urged the investigation continue so they can have closure.

The article notes that Kylr Yust, who had ties to both women, was the last person reportedly seen with Runions and had a restraining order filed against him by Kopetsky and her mother before her disappearance. Yust has faced charges including burning Runions’ vehicle and earlier convictions for violent offenses and animal abuse. Searches in the area will continue pending weather and daylight.

Former reality star Kate Gosselin has taken a non-TV job as a coupon blogger for CouponCabin.com. Announced by multiple outlets, she’ll write weekly posts offering money-saving advice—starting Nov. 22 with tips on navigating Black Friday—and cover budgeting for large families, holiday shopping, and gift ideas. CouponCabin praised her long-time couponing experience; Kate called coupons “like free money in your pocket.” Writers noted the move keeps her children off TV for now, could generate publicity and fodder for snarky blog commentary, and reflects practical flexibility amid unemployment and changing career plans.

The Patriots launched wellsreportcontext.com to publish a 20,000-word rebuttal to the Wells Report on “Deflategate,” arguing the investigation was flawed, selective, and scientifically unsound. Patriots lawyer Daniel L. Goldberg disputes key findings: he says texts and witness statements were misinterpreted, contends Jim McNally’s “deflator” nickname referred to weight loss, and asserts no evidence shows Tom Brady preferred footballs below the 12.5-PSI minimum. The rebuttal highlights timing, gauge, wetness, and temperature issues—invoking the Ideal Gas Law and a Nobel laureate’s critique—to argue measured pressure drops at the AFC title game were explainable without misconduct. It criticizes the NFL for leaked, inaccurate PSI data, opaque procedures, withheld interview notes, and alleged prejudgment. Meanwhile Brady has appealed his four-game suspension; the team was fined $1 million and lost two draft picks.

Six women attending a wedding in Sydney unexpectedly arrived wearing the same A$160 Forever New dress, creating a lighthearted scene rather than embarrassment. The group, none of whom were bridesmaids, discovered their matching outfits on arrival and decided to embrace the coincidence by lining up for photos with the bride, Julia Mammone. Debbie Speranza, one of the women, posted the image on Facebook calling themselves “#backupbridesmaids,” and shared it with the retailer, joking that shops should warn customers if others have bought the same dress. The picture quickly went viral—tens of thousands of people viewed, liked, commented and reshared it—prompting amused recollections of similar fashion mishaps. Responses ranged from delight, with some saying it was a great conversation starter, to horror at the thought of matching someone else at a special event. Another guest, Chantel Lopez-Rubio, later posted about the mortifying moment of matching her dress to curtains. Overall, what began as an awkward coincidence turned into camaraderie for the six women, who bonded, posed for photos with the bride, and enjoyed the wedding despite the unexpected sartorial synchronicity.

In a CBS Evening News interview, Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney said his stance on abortion is narrower than the GOP platform adopted at the national convention. Romney said he supports allowing abortion in cases of rape, incest and when the mother’s life or health is at risk. That position contrasts with language in the party platform calling for a constitutional amendment to ban abortion without exceptions for rape, incest or the mother’s health. Democrats have amplified attacks on Republican reproductive-rights positions, pointing to Romney’s running mate Rep. Paul Ryan’s strong anti‑abortion views and controversial comments by GOP Senate candidate Todd Akin. President Obama warned Romney would not block congressional attempts to curtail reproductive rights. Romney downplayed the political debate, saying abortion law is ultimately a matter for the Supreme Court and that Democrats politicize it every four years. The campaign notes Romney’s position has evolved: he once supported abortion rights while running for Senate in Massachusetts but as presidential nominee opposes them except in the stated exceptions. Campaign spokeswoman Andrea Saul reiterated his exceptions-based stance.

Rafe Esquith, a once-celebrated Los Angeles elementary-school teacher and the only K–12 educator to receive the National Medal of the Arts, has been accused of long‑standing sexual misconduct in documents released by Los Angeles Unified School District. Esquith, 61, taught fifth grade at Hobart Elementary for over 30 years and led the famed Hobart Shakespeareans program that drew national attention, a PBS documentary, and numerous awards—including honors from Oprah, Disney, and the Dalai Lama. He was removed from the classroom this spring after allegations surfaced and was fired in October, prompting public debate and defenses framing his dismissal as part of wider, possibly overzealous district actions.

The newly released 66‑page file outlines multiple troubling incidents and communications. Colleagues reported inappropriate jokes such as suggesting students might perform nude if fundraising failed; separate allegations describe a 2015 comment urging a student to “surf the net for porn” and suggestions that performers could appear “in a fig leaf.” The documents detail accusations of spanking, fondling, tickling female students, and showing sexually inappropriate movies to fifth‑graders after school. A trove of emails to students—some as young as 14—contain sexually suggestive language and nicknames (e.g., “Supermodel,” “Your Favorite ATM,” “How is my favorite Hottie?”) and praises like “Beautiful...Sexy...Gorgeous,” along with messages encouraging partying and drug use.

Esquith has not been criminally charged; his lawyer denounced the district’s narrative as fraudulent. In October he filed a $1 billion class-action suit on behalf of roughly 2,000 LAUSD teachers removed from classrooms, alleging age‑discrimination and coerced retirements. The release of the documents has shifted public perception, complicating earlier portrayals of Esquith solely as an inspirational educator.

More than 400 people have reported falling ill after eating at the Chipotle on 9733 Sawmill Parkway in Powell, Ohio, according to crowdsourced reports on iwaspoisoned.com. The site’s founder, Patrick Quade, said 228 reports describe 418 customers becoming sick since Friday; Business Insider noted a surge in reports after its article about the restaurant’s temporary closure. The Delaware General Health District is investigating and reported receiving 518 inquiries — 95 emails and 423 calls — about the possible outbreak. Health inspectors visited the restaurant, delivered 33 stool-sample kits to symptomatic patrons, and found no immediate reason to prevent reopening based on observed food-protection procedures. Chipotle voluntarily closed the Powell location on Monday for deep cleaning and disposal of exposed foods and single-use items; the company said it planned to reopen Tuesday while cooperating with health officials and investigating a few illness complaints. Chipotle also reported that two to five employees called out sick over the weekend. Previous local inspection records showed two corrected critical violations (temperature control for beans and improper cooling of cut lettuce). Iwaspoisoned.com — which screens consumer reports and helped identify Chipotle’s 2015 outbreak — continues to collect complaints; Chipotle’s stock dipped in after-hours trading following the news. No confirmed foodborne pathogen has been announced.

Houston Tex-Mex chain El Tiempo Cantina deactivated its Facebook, Instagram and Twitter pages after posting and then removing a photo of Attorney General Jeff Sessions dining at one of its locations. The image, originally posted by owner Roland Laurenzo’s social media manager with a caption calling it an “honor” to serve Sessions, sparked immediate backlash and boycott calls because of Sessions’ role in the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement and family separations. Laurenzo issued a statement saying the post “does not represent us supporting (Sessions’) positions,” explaining the Secret Service notified the restaurant that a government official would arrive but his identity was unknown until he entered. He said staff were focused on catering to the security detail and serving customers, and that the photo was posted without ownership review. Despite the clarification and insistence that El Tiempo opposes family separation and does not endorse Sessions’ policies, criticism persisted from both opponents who felt the damage was done and supporters who objected to the retraction. Laurenzo reported harassment and even death threats, prompting temporary account takedowns; he expressed hope patrons would remember the family’s long-standing service to Houston’s Hispanic community.

A 25-year-old woman riding a Divvy bike in Chicago was killed after colliding with a flatbed truck on July 1, 2016, in what industry officials and observers said appears to be the first fatality in the United States involving a bike-share bicycle. The crash occurred at about 9 a.m. in the Avondale neighborhood near Sacramento and Belmont avenues when both the truck and bicyclist, traveling north on Sacramento, turned east at Belmont and struck one another. The rider, later identified as Virginia Murray, was taken to Advocate Illinois Masonic Medical Center in critical condition and pronounced dead. The Chicago Police Department’s Major Accident Investigation Unit launched an investigation, and the city and Divvy issued condolences to the victim’s family.

Bike-share systems—where users rent bikes from automated stations by paying per ride or using membership tokens—have expanded rapidly across the U.S. since the first program in Tulsa in 2007. By 2016 there were tens of thousands of shared bikes in dozens of cities, and Chicago’s Divvy alone logged nearly 8 million rides since its 2013 launch. Despite that growth, officials noted few comparable fatalities domestically; previous bike-share deaths had been reported in Canada and Mexico.

The incident prompted calls to accelerate street-safety improvements. Advocates and city planners pointed to initiatives such as Chicago’s forthcoming Vision Zero plan, aimed at eliminating traffic deaths. At the same time, researchers have reported that bike-share riders generally experience lower collision and injury rates than regular bicyclists. A March study from the Mineta Transportation Institute and related research suggest factors such as the heavier, more stable bike-share bicycle design, reduced speeds, greater visibility, and a user base that may ride more cautiously contribute to relatively lower risk. Still, low helmet use among bike-share riders and the prevalence of irregular cyclists unfamiliar with local conditions remain safety concerns as programs continue to grow nationally.

A 12-year-old Mulberry Middle School student brought a 100 mg Green Hornet THC gummy pack to school and shared it during gym class, sending six seventh-graders to the hospital Thursday after they consumed most of it. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said the gummies—ten 10 mg pieces—are illegal in Florida without a medical card and are not sold in-state dispensaries. Five students were taken by ambulance and one by a parent; symptoms included stomach pain, dizziness, nausea and near-fainting. Detectives are investigating how the child obtained the edibles; the student told investigators he did not eat any himself. The 12-year-old faces seven felony charges (six counts of distribution within 1,000 feet of a school and one for possession of cannabis resin) and a misdemeanor for possession of paraphernalia. School officials praised staff response, urged parental vigilance over children’s purchases and online activity, and said all students are expected to recover.

At the Iowa State Fair, Hillary Clinton sought to counter criticisms from her 2008 campaign by engaging directly and warmly with voters: shaking hands, taking selfies, hugging, listening to personal stories, and even sampling fair food. Endorsed recently by former Sen. Tom Harkin, she avoided rope lines and spent about 90 minutes moving slowly through dense crowds so voters could approach her. Supporters noted a marked difference from her previous, more distant image; she posed for dozens of photos and chatted informally with fairgoers and acquaintances. Clinton declined to speak on the fair’s traditional soapbox—an absence noticed when rival Bernie Sanders drew a larger soapbox crowd—yet she took time to hear constituent pleas, including a harrowing medical-marijuana appeal from a mother of a terminally ill child. Reporters pressed her on the ongoing private-email controversy; she reiterated that she never knowingly sent or received marked classified material and downplayed how often locals raised the issue.

Separately, FBI counterintelligence agents in Washington are investigating how classified information ended up on Clinton’s private email account and whether State Department employees forwarded such material onto unclassified systems. The probe seeks access to many State Department accounts and Clinton’s server, recovered from her email provider, to trace information flow and to determine if foreign actors breached the account. Inspector General findings flagged several emails containing highly classified material, possibly from sensitive surveillance programs. Clinton maintains she handled classified information appropriately and has cooperated by turning over work emails; no evidence has yet proven illegal conduct or that her account was hacked, though investigators continue forensic and cybersecurity inquiries.

An elderly Massachusetts man, identified as 90-year-old Nicholas Salerno, reported being the victim of a theft after paying a woman he says was roughly half his age $100 for a sexual act in his home earlier this summer. According to police, the woman, 48-year-old Karen Proia, left his residence and Salerno later noticed a necklace missing. The stolen necklace was subsequently located at a South Yarmouth pawn shop and recovered by police. When Salerno went to Orleans police to report the theft, an officer informed him he would be charged with soliciting a prostitute. Salerno reacted bluntly, telling the Cape Cod Times he did not care about the potential charge, adding, “I don’t give a [expletive]. I’m 90 years old….” Both Proia and Salerno were arraigned Tuesday and each pleaded not guilty to the charges. The case highlights the intersection of alleged theft and sex-work solicitation enforcement; despite Salerno’s role as the reported victim of the jewelry theft, police moved to charge him for soliciting prostitution. Further legal proceedings will determine the outcomes for both individuals.

Michael Schumacher’s manager, Sabine Kehm, announced that medical files believed to be his have been stolen from Grenoble hospital and offered to media outlets for roughly €50,000. The documents reportedly include details of surgical procedures; Kehm said the theft has been reported and authorities are involved. She warned that buying or publishing such private medical data is forbidden and vowed to pursue criminal charges and damages against anyone who publishes or references the files. Schumacher, the seven-time Formula One champion, has been hospitalized since a December 29 off‑piste skiing accident in Meribel that caused severe head trauma; he spent months in a medically induced coma and was recently transferred to a Swiss rehabilitation facility. Grenoble hospital has said it will sue for theft and breach of medical confidentiality.

A meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials examined whether influenza vaccination reduces cardiovascular events in high-risk patients. Researchers searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register through August 2013 and identified six RCTs (five published, one unpublished) including 6,735 participants (mean age 67; 51% women; 36% with prior cardiac disease) with mean follow-up of 7.9 months. Using random-effects Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios, vaccination was associated with a lower risk of composite cardiovascular events: 2.9% of vaccinated versus 4.7% of controls experienced an event (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.48–0.86, P = .003). A significant interaction showed the benefit concentrated among patients with recent acute coronary syndrome (ACS): vaccinated patients with recent ACS had RR 0.45 (95% CI 0.32–0.63), whereas those without recent ACS showed no clear benefit (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.55–1.61; P for interaction = .02). Cardiovascular mortality alone did not differ significantly between groups. Authors conclude influenza vaccination is associated with fewer major adverse cardiovascular events, particularly in patients with active coronary disease, and recommend a large, adequately powered multicenter trial to confirm these findings and evaluate individual cardiovascular endpoints.

At least nine people died after a Walmart employee’s call led authorities to discover dozens of undocumented migrants crammed and severely injured in the back of a tractor-trailer in San Antonio early Sunday. Initial survivor interviews suggest more than 100 people may have been inside the 18-wheeler during the journey, ICE acting Director Thomas Homan said. A man trapped inside asked a Walmart worker for water; the worker then called police for a welfare check. Officers found eight bodies at the scene and 31 people with various injuries; a ninth victim later died at a hospital. The truck’s refrigeration was not functioning while temperatures near 100°F (38°C) likely caused heatstroke and irreversible organ damage for some victims. Two hospitalized individuals are 15 years old. Surveillance footage showed multiple vehicles arriving and picking up survivors, and some people fled into nearby woods. The driver, James Matthew Bradley Jr., 60, of Clearwater, Florida, was detained and federal prosecutors planned a criminal complaint. Officials described the incident as human smuggling and trafficking; Homeland Security Investigations and local authorities are jointly investigating. Walmart is cooperating with law enforcement but declined to release footage.

KFC’s much-hyped Double Down—a bunless sandwich using two Original Recipe chicken filets as the “bread”—arrived to mixed reviews. It includes two filets, two bacon strips, two slices of Monterey Jack and pepper jack (or a merged cheese/sauce-like spread), and Colonel’s Sauce. Nutritionally heavy (about 540 calories, 32 g fat, 1,380 mg sodium), reviewers noted an overwhelming saltiness, likely from the chicken breading, though the filets were moist and crispy. Bacon was real but minimal and often lost between the large filets; the cheese was thick, gummy, jalapeño-flecked, and sometimes clashed with the chicken’s flavor. The sauce was described as an indistinct ketchup-mustard-mayo mix. Portions look small in their packaging, and the sandwich is filling enough to replace sides, yet many found it underwhelming—novel and satisfying in a single salty, indulgent sitting but unlikely to become a repeat favorite. Overall ratings ranged low, calling it a guilty, borderline gimmick.

The International Criminal Court has opened a preliminary investigation into allegations that Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte and other officials committed crimes against humanity during the government’s anti-drug campaign. ICC prosecutor Fatou Bensouda said her office will examine events since July 1, 2016, to determine whether there is sufficient evidence to proceed. She emphasized the ICC’s independence and called for engagement from Philippine authorities. The inquiry is the ICC’s first preliminary examination in Southeast Asia.

The probe follows complaints and a 77-page report accusing Duterte of overseeing extrajudicial killings and mass murder dating back to his time as Davao mayor in 1988. Official police figures cite about 4,000 deaths in anti-drug operations since Duterte became president in 2016, while complainants claim the toll exceeds 8,000. Opposition figures, including Gary Alejano, welcomed the ICC decision as validation for victims who lack recourse domestically, arguing police, prosecutors, and legislators have failed to provide impartial investigations.

Duterte’s spokesman Harry Roque criticized the ICC move as a waste of resources, asserting many allegations predate the Philippines’ ICC accession and that domestic courts can address any wrongdoing. He insisted the crackdown was legitimate police work and said Duterte is prepared to defend himself. Duterte dismisses the ICC and has repeatedly threatened withdrawal. Human Rights Watch supported the ICC’s initiative, noting a lack of credible domestic probes. The ICC defines crimes against humanity as serious, large-scale attacks on civilians; since 2002 it has received over 12,000 communications, with nine cases reaching trial.

Orexigen Therapeutics’ investigational weight-loss pill Contrave—a combination of bupropion and naltrexone—won a favorable FDA advisory panel vote, boosting the company’s stock and reviving hopes for new prescription obesity treatments. Advisers judged Contrave’s modest weight-loss benefit worth the risks of increased pulse and blood pressure, and allowed a large cardiovascular outcomes study to occur post-approval. The decision followed earlier advisory rejections of rival drugs from Arena (lorcaserin) and Vivus (Qnexa), whose setbacks helped Orexigen refine safety commitments. Contrave’s phase III trials showed more patients achieved ≥5% weight loss versus placebo, but the mean treatment-placebo weight-loss difference (about 3.3–4.8%) missed the FDA’s 5% benchmark. Safety concerns included higher blood pressure, heart rate, and rare seizures; some panelists dissented, urging pre-approval cardiovascular data. The FDA must decide by Jan. 31. Physicians expressed cautious optimism that another therapeutic option could aid patients when paired with lifestyle changes, though long-term risks remain to be clarified.

A family rushing to their loved one’s funeral received an extraordinary act of compassion from two Delta/Endeavor Air pilots who turned a plane back so they could board. Jay W. Short, 56, died of lung cancer on December 16 and wished to be buried with family in Bolivar, Tennessee. His wife Marcia booked flights from Phoenix so she and their three children could reach Memphis; Jay’s body was flown ahead on December 19. Their initial flight from Phoenix was delayed on the tarmac due to damaged cargo doors, leaving only seven minutes to make a crucial connection in Minneapolis to the last flight to Memphis that day. They sprinted to the gate, but the jetway door had been closed and the plane was taxiing away. Desperate, Marcia, her son and daughters waved and pleaded with ground staff and pilots, fearing they would miss the funeral scheduled for the next morning. Though attendants told them there was nothing to be done and suggested routing through Atlanta, the pilots ultimately pulled back to the gate and allowed the family to board. The family later identified the crew as Pilots Adams and Anderson on flight DL 3955; other reports named Capt. Adam Cohen of Endeavor Air, a Delta regional carrier, as the pilot who returned. Marcia and relatives expressed profound gratitude, calling the decision an almost unheard-of kindness in the airline industry. Delta praised the human touch, while analysts noted the pilot risked company censure by delaying departure, since on-time records are tightly enforced. The family made the funeral, thanking the crew for a gift they’ll never forget.

Berkshire Hathaway’s audit committee concluded that former executive David Sokol misled Warren Buffett and violated company policies by buying nearly $10 million of Lubrizol stock while promoting Berkshire’s acquisition of the company. The report accuses Sokol of “misleadingly incomplete” disclosures and suggests some answers were “intended to deceive,” saying his conduct breached the duty of candor under Delaware law. Sokol made roughly $3 million in trading profits that the board may seek to recover and said it will cooperate with any SEC or government probe. Sokol’s attorney disputes the findings, calling him scrupulous. The report aims to shield Buffett from blame, addresses shareholder pressure ahead of Berkshire’s annual meeting, and signals possible civil action against Sokol.

Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov’s 35th birthday on Oct. 5 was marked by an extravagant, Kremlin-financed celebration in Grozny that drew international entertainers and sharp criticism from human rights groups. Photos and video show Hilary Swank, Jean-Claude Van Damme and violinist Vanessa-Mae on a floating stage as fireworks, acrobats and large portraits of Kadyrov filled the city. Talent reps say performers at such events often receive six-figure fees and luxury perks. Human Rights Watch and the Human Rights Foundation condemned the appearance of Western celebrities, calling it inappropriate and saying paid attendance bolsters and legitimizes a leader accused of ordering abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. The Foundation said Swank had been warned about Kadyrov’s record and that her manager initially denied plans to attend; Human Rights Foundation president Thor Halvorssen called the participation “disheartening and shameful.” Kadyrov—who framed the festivities as marking Grozny’s founding anniversary—offered vague comments when asked who funded the party.
