Authorities and artist representatives have not provided substantive responses.

Rep. Michele Bachmann’s recent accusations that Huma Abedin and Rep. Keith Ellison are tied to the Muslim Brotherhood drew swift bipartisan condemnation in Washington, but in her Minnesota district the reaction was the opposite: her core supporters rallied behind her. Locals at parades and fairs praised Bachmann, with some embracing broader conspiratorial views and trusting her assertions. Bachmann has long warned of Muslim Brotherhood infiltration, even before her intelligence committee role, and former aides say she’s been exposed to briefings that solidified those concerns. Nationally, however, Republican leaders and figures across the spectrum — including John Boehner, John McCain and Marco Rubio — criticized her claims as over the line. Bachmann and four other Republicans cited a controversial Center for Security Policy video series alleging figures like Grover Norquist helped the Brotherhood gain influence; that report fueled a call for inspector general probes into Abedin’s ties. The allegations sparked threats against Abedin, prompting security scrutiny, and have revived Democratic efforts to oust Bachmann, with Democrat Jim Graves positioning himself as a moderate alternative. Bachmann insists her inquiries were national-security driven, not distorted.

When gunfire erupted at the Las Vegas music festival, many people dropped to their stomachs—often a sensible response—but that choice may have increased their vulnerability because the shooter, Stephen Paddock, was firing from an elevated hotel room. His vantage point over obstacles and the crowd meant shots that would normally fly harmlessly overhead or strike the ground could instead penetrate areas where people were huddled. Audio from the attack suggests at least one of Paddock’s weapons discharged in bursts typical of automatic fire, raising questions about whether he used fully automatic firearms, semiautomatic weapons modified to fire more rapidly, or bump/slide-fire techniques that harness recoil to increase rate of fire. Federal law long regulates fully automatic weapons more strictly than semiautomatics, which are regulated differently by state. Authorities recovered at least 16 rifles—ranging from .308 to .223 caliber—and a handgun from Paddock’s Mandalay Bay room; officials said AR-15–style rifles were among them but have not specified which guns were fired. Some weapons were purchased in Arizona, according to a gun seller. Videos and images emerging from the scene capture the chaos: crowds fleeing, people lying still, and at least one man taunting the shooter amid gunfire—an extreme, bewildering reaction against a backdrop of panic. The attack left 59 dead and 527 injured, and the disturbing footage underlines the human terror and confusion during mass shootings.

Lou Ferrigno, the 67-year-old actor best known as The Incredible Hulk, was briefly hospitalized after receiving a pneumonia vaccination that allegedly went wrong. Ferrigno posted a photo of himself in a green hospital gown to Instagram and Twitter, saying he “went in for a pneumonia shot and landed up here with fluid in my bicep.” He warned followers to watch who administers injections, ensure the site is swabbed properly, and to watch the needle come out of its package. Fans responded with well wishes; Ferrigno later reported he was feeling better. After his release, he attended a Smash Global MMA event in Los Angeles and socialized with friends including Dolph Lundgren. Representatives had not immediately commented. The report noted two types of pneumococcal vaccines—PCV13 and PPSV23—are recommended for adults 65 and older; PCV13 has been associated with injection-site swelling. The CDC emphasizes the U.S. vaccine supply is safe and effective despite occasional local reactions. Beyond the incident, Ferrigno’s recent acting credits include The Avengers (2012) and Enter the Fire (2018), with projects planned for 2019; he also co-founded Ferrigno Fit with his daughter Shanna and previously trained Michael Jackson for his comeback tour.

David Stockman, Reagan’s former budget chief, urges Republicans to “bring it on” and briefly shut the government to force deep spending cuts, arguing the Obama White House would quickly yield and deliver $60 billion in reductions. Speaking to Lloyd Grove, Stockman denounced Beltway leaders as fools, criticized Paul Ryan’s long-term budget proposals as irrelevant to today’s fiscal crisis, and faulted both parties for failing to address massive public and private indebtedness. He downplayed short-term economic harms from a temporary shutdown, calling warnings exaggerated, and warned that persistently low interest rates will eventually climb—raising federal costs dramatically and exposing fiscal unsustainability. Though he applauded Tea Party fiscal demands, Stockman opposed mixing social policy riders into budget fights. He conceded political risks for Republicans if the public reacts negatively, but maintained a shutdown could be a rude wake-up call to confront America’s debt.

The Iran Human Rights Documentation Center (IHRDC) has published the first full English translation of Book Five of Iran’s Islamic Penal Code, the only permanently adopted portion of the Penal Code. Enacted in 1996 and incorporating amendments through January 2012, Book Five governs ta’zir (discretionary) and deterrent punishments across a wide range of offenses including crimes against state security, property and persons, forgery, bribery, public morality, family law violations, and traffic offenses. The translation presents the chapter-by-chapter structure and full-text articles that specify definitions, criminal elements, and punishments—often phrased as ranges of imprisonment, lashes, fines, confiscation, or restitution—and includes special rules for mitigating or aggravating circumstances, accomplices, and officials’ misconduct.

Notable provisions include severe penalties for organizing or joining groups deemed to threaten national security, espionage, propaganda against the state, and cooperation with foreign powers; laws criminalizing insults to sacred figures and the Supreme Leader; extensive forgery and counterfeiting rules (including for official stamps, court verdicts, currencies, and academic certificates); protections for cultural heritage and strict controls on excavation and export of artifacts; and comprehensive rules on bribery, usury, and public officials’ offenses. The text also addresses juvenile and family matters, perjury and secrecy, theft and banditry, arson and environmental harms, trespass and property disputes, public morality (including penalties for alcohol, prostitution and indecency), and traffic-related manslaughter. For certain offenses the code conditions prosecution on a private complainant; in others judges may apply discretionary mitigation, retrial, or alternative punishments.

The release provides an authoritative resource for researchers, lawyers, and human-rights advocates seeking to understand the operative criminal law in Iran, and highlights areas—such as juvenile capital punishment and discretionary ta’zir sentencing—where international human-rights concerns persist.

A group of 31 senior international scientists and clinicians have published an editorial in the Journal of Alzheimer’s Disease arguing that microbes—particularly herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV1), Chlamydia pneumoniae and various spirochaetes—may be primary drivers of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). They summarize decades of human, animal and cellular studies showing microbial presence in elderly brains, colocalization of pathogen signatures with AD pathology, and experimental induction of amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau changes after infection. The authors note that microbes can remain latent and reactivate with age, stress or immunosuppression, potentially damaging limbic regions linked to memory and personality. They highlight APOE ε4, a known genetic AD risk factor, which also increases susceptibility to infections, and point to genome-wide links between immune-related genes and AD risk. Mechanistically, they argue Aβ may be an antimicrobial peptide produced in response to infection, and that antiviral or antibiotic treatments can block pathogen-induced Aβ and tau changes in vitro and in animals. Given repeated clinical trial failures targeting amyloid and tau (hundreds of trials with no clear disease-modifying success), the authors call for urgent re-evaluation of infectious hypotheses and prospective antimicrobial clinical trials. Dementia charities and many researchers welcome further study but caution that current evidence is insufficient to conclude microbes cause most AD cases or that AD is contagious. Critics stress this remains a minority view requiring rigorous testing; proponents compare the situation to early resistance faced by microbial causes of other diseases that were later validated.

Chinese authorities confirmed a woman, Feng Jianmei, was forcibly made to abort at seven months, sparking outrage after images of the baby’s corpse circulated online. Rights groups and activists say Feng was compelled to terminate the pregnancy because she could not pay a large fine for breaching China’s one‑child policy. A Shaanxi provincial probe called the case “basically true,” said it violated national family planning regulations (which ban late‑term abortions since 2001), and recommended punishing those responsible. The statement did not name perpetrators but pledged steps to prevent recurrence. Internet users reacted with anger and comparisons to historical atrocities; Feng and her husband reportedly opposed the termination and say she was restrained and taken to hospital. The incident intensified criticism of China’s decades‑long family planning program, which allows most urban families one child and rural families limited exceptions, imposing fines for violations. Rights groups note many coerced abortions historically; prominent activist Chen Guangcheng previously exposed forced terminations. The U.S. has publicly opposed coercive birth‑limitation practices and raised concerns with Chinese authorities.

Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach, a close immigration adviser to President-elect Donald Trump and possible candidate for a senior administration post, brought a written plan to a meeting with Trump that outlines aggressive changes to the Department of Homeland Security. Photographs captured Kobach clutching a partly visible document titled his “Department of Homeland Security Kobach Strategic Plan for First 365 Days.” The visible items call for reinstating and updating the National Security Entry-Exit Registration System (NSEERS) to track “all aliens from high-risk areas,” a program Kobach helped design after 9/11 and that was largely suspended in 2011 amid civil-rights criticism for profiling mostly Muslim nationals. The plan also proposes “extreme vetting questions” for high-risk entrants, asking about support for Sharia law, jihad, gender equality and the U.S. Constitution, and seeks to halt Syrian refugee resettlement entirely. Other partly obscured references appear to include mass arrests and removals of illegal immigrants, construction of “386 miles” of actual wall, PATRIOT Act measures and changes to voter rolls. Civil-liberties groups and Muslim advocacy organizations criticized the proposals as discriminatory, unconstitutional and “inquisition-style.” Kobach, long a hard-liner on immigration and voting rules, has defended stricter measures since 9/11 and is advising Trump’s transition. The Trump team said the meeting addressed border security, terrorism and federal reform; Kobach’s visible plan signals the kind of stringent immigration policies he and some Trump allies favor implementing.

French authorities temporarily closed embassies, consulates, cultural centers and French schools in about 20 countries on a Friday prayer day after satirical weekly Charlie Hebdo published caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad. Officials feared the images would intensify unrest already sparked by an anti-Islam film produced in the United States. The issue’s cover mocked the film and referenced the popular movie Intouchables, while inside pages included graphic depictions that many Muslims found offensive. The French government denounced the publication as provocative but defended freedom of expression; Prime Minister Jean‑Marc Ayrault reiterated that those offended can seek legal redress and said a planned Paris march against the US film would be banned to avoid importing foreign conflicts. Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius ordered heightened security at French diplomatic posts in vulnerable countries and urged restraint, calling the timing of the cartoons “not intelligent.” Charlie Hebdo, which has previously published provocative material about Islam and was firebombed last year, said it was exercising press freedom and denied deliberate provocation. Muslim leaders and organizations in France and abroad condemned the caricatures and appealed for calm, urging protests, if any, to be peaceful and legal to avoid escalating tensions amid already widespread violent demonstrations tied to the film.

Oklahoma-born country superstar Carrie Underwood created a memorable moment at her Louisville, Ky., concert when she invited 12-year-old fan Chase onstage after he held up a sign reading “Carrie be my first kiss.” After jokingly noting her husband, NHL player Mike Fisher, was in the audience, Underwood asked how to proceed; Chase bravely replied “Lip to lip,” and Underwood kissed him on the lips. She later tweeted a photo thanking Chase and Louisville, captioning it “#liptolip.” The incident occurred during her Blown Away Tour, which will play Oklahoma City (Oct. 25) and Tulsa (Nov. 21).

After a stressful year caring for husband Michael Douglas during his throat cancer treatment and coping with family and legal turmoil, Catherine Zeta-Jones checked into a mental health facility for a brief stay to treat Bipolar II disorder, her publicist confirmed. Sources say she struggled to cope amid her stepson’s incarceration and Douglas’ legal battles, though her rep did not link the stay to substance use. Bipolar II involves mood shifts less severe than bipolar I but still includes depressive episodes. Her rep added she’s feeling great and is set to begin work on two upcoming films, and the couple say the ordeal drew them closer.

Three adults have died and four children were rescued after seven people got into difficulty in the sea off Mawgan Porth, near Newquay, Cornwall. Multiple 999 calls were received at about 13:15 BST when the group is believed to have been caught in a rip current. A major sea and air rescue involving Newquay and Padstow Coastguard teams, RNLI lifeboats, a Royal Navy helicopter from RNAS Culdrose and air ambulances recovered the casualties. The three adults—two Cornish residents in their 40s (a man and a woman) and a man in his 50s from outside the Devon and Cornwall area—were brought ashore unconscious, given treatment on the beach, airlifted to Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro and later pronounced dead. The four children, described as teenagers, were uninjured and taken to the hospital as a precaution; they were sheltered at a nearby pub during the response. Emergency services are investigating the circumstances and supporting families. Locals and surf operators said conditions had bigger waves and stronger currents than usual, warning rip currents can quickly overwhelm inexperienced swimmers or rescuers who fight the flow.

Vanderbilt University announced it will pay $1.2 million to the Tennessee chapter of the United Daughters of the Confederacy to relinquish naming rights to Confederate Memorial Hall, a residence building whose stone inscription has read “Confederate Memorial Hall” since it opened in 1935. The decision, announced by Chancellor Nicholas S. Zeppos, concludes a 14-year effort to remove the Confederate designation. The original $50,000 donation from the United Daughters in 1933 funded the hall and secured its name; a 2005 Tennessee appeals court ruling required Vanderbilt to return the gift’s present value before altering the inscription. Anonymous donors provided the funds needed to meet that legal requirement, and crews began covering the word “Confederate” on the facade immediately after the Board of Trust authorized the payment. Zeppos, who has supported changing the name for years, called the Confederate reference “a symbol and a reminder of racism, slavery and a very, very bloody Civil War,” and said maintaining the word on a student residence was unacceptable. The move drew criticism from the attorney who represented the United Daughters, who called it an erasure of history, while student leaders and others praised it as responsiveness to concerns about inclusion and campus climate. Vanderbilt’s action is part of a broader national re-evaluation of Confederate symbols on campuses and in public spaces, a debate intensified after racially motivated violence such as the 2015 Charleston church shooting and shaped locally by recent state laws affecting removal of historic markers.

The estate of late artist Dash Snow is suing McDonald’s, alleging the fast-food chain copied his distinctive graffiti tag “SACE” and used it as part of faux “graffiti” décor in numerous restaurants worldwide. Jade Berreau, Snow’s former girlfriend, mother of his child, and administrator of his estate, first asked McDonald’s in June 2016 to remove the likeness from redesigned locations but says the request was ignored. The October federal complaint accuses McDonald’s of copyright and trademark infringement, unfair competition, falsifying copyright management information under the DMCA, and negligence. It argues McDonald’s prominently displayed a SACE-like mark — the most visible, media-highlighted element of the graffiti-themed interiors — in a way that implied Snow had authorized or created the work, potentially harming the market and value of his originals, which have fetched high prices at auction. Snow, who began as a 1990s street artist with the IRAK crew and died in 2009 at 27, deliberately avoided corporate associations; his estate contends he never made his art available online, in retail, or in restaurants. Public backlash over a graffiti-styled Brixton McDonald’s in 2016 amplified the dispute; the suit says the chain “arrogantly refused” earlier removal requests and is improperly trading on Snow’s reputation.

Congress and the White House raced to salvage negotiations to avert the "fiscal cliff" after talks collapsed publicly when House Republicans scuttled Speaker John Boehner’s fallback “Plan B.” According to the Wall Street Journal reconstruction, a crucial breakdown occurred in Boehner’s Capitol office as he struggled to keep his conference united behind a deal that would raise taxes on high earners. Key GOP leaders—Ways and Means Chair Dave Camp and Budget Chair Paul Ryan—rejected the broader package for different reasons, prompting Boehner to pivot to Plan B, which later failed to muster support and was withdrawn.

The stalemate reflected deeper tensions: Republicans viewed the White House as unwilling to concede significant entitlement or structural spending changes, while Democrats, bolstered by the election and a Senate bill to let Bush-era rates expire for incomes above $250,000, believed they could secure roughly $700–800 billion in revenue without trading away concessions. In several face-to-face and staff-level sessions, negotiators clashed over immediate tax-rate increases, spending cuts, and inclusion of the debt ceiling. Mr. Obama warned he would portray Republicans as responsible if no deal emerged and insisted on protecting middle-class tax levels.

As support for Boehner’s backup plan evaporated, prospects narrowed to a smaller short-term package that might forestall parts of the cliff but defer a larger deficit showdown into the next year—potentially increasing pressure around the debt ceiling and future negotiations.

At a routine 20-week anatomy scan, Kristine Barry and her husband Christopher learned their unborn son, Sebastian, had severe complete transposition of the great arteries (TGA): his aorta and pulmonary artery were reversed. Complicating matters, the walls inside his heart were closed, so once separated from the placenta he wouldn’t be able to mix oxygenated and deoxygenated blood—risking rapid brain damage or death. Normally surgeons would perform an open-heart arterial switch after birth, but Sebastian’s anatomy left only minutes to act at delivery.

A multidisciplinary team from Mount Sinai Hospital and the Hospital for Sick Children devised a different plan: an ultrasound-guided in utero balloon atrial septoplasty (BAS). On May 18, with about 30 clinicians standing by and neonatal teams prepared for an emergency C-section, doctors inserted a needle through Barry’s abdomen into Sebastian’s heart, passed a catheter and inflated a tiny balloon to create a roughly 3.5 mm hole between the atria. The goal was to allow mixing of blood and oxygenation until definitive surgery after birth. The procedure, believed to be the world’s first BAS for fetal TGA, took about 20 minutes and succeeded.

Barry was induced five days later and delivered a pink, crying baby. Sebastian had a repeat BAS after birth and, a week later, underwent the required open-heart arterial switch at SickKids. Now at home and meeting developmental milestones, Sebastian is expected to lead a largely normal life, though the family will attend neurodevelopmental follow-ups. His parents express deep gratitude for the innovative, life-saving care.

Baltimore Ravens cornerback Tray Walker, 23, died Friday from injuries sustained in a motorcycle crash Thursday night in Miami. Miami-Dade police said Walker was riding a Honda dirt bike without lights and wearing dark clothing and no helmet when he collided with a Ford Escape around 8 p.m. Authorities do not suspect alcohol, drugs or racing. Walker, a Miami native drafted in the fourth round in 2015 from Texas Southern, played mainly on special teams last season. Ravens coaches and teammates mourned him, praising his smile, promise and character; John Harbaugh urged players to value choices, safety and brotherhood in a letter to the team.

Grim LeRogue, a 33-year-old Brooklyn man who legally changed his name from Joe Rogan, was arrested after running onto the field during Game 3 of the American League Championship Series at Yankee Stadium intending to confront Yankees star Alex Rodriguez over his relationship with actress Cameron Diaz. Police say LeRogue carried five photos, including one of Rodriguez marked with an X and a written threat accusing him of ruining “too many of our white queens.” He also had a photo of Diaz annotated “We will be together soon.” Other images included Osama bin Laden labeled with “I will serve you,” a picture of Whitney Houston captioned “Whitney Bin Laden,” and a photo of Bobby Brown with “You need to be terminated.” Tackled by security without weapons found on him, LeRogue — who has past arrests for assault and burglary and is a known graffiti vandal — was charged with assault and interfering with a sporting event and taken to Lincoln Hospital for psychiatric evaluation. His mother described him as troubled but denied he was dangerous, saying he sought publicity for a self-published novel.

New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, on CNN’s Piers Morgan Tonight, bluntly dismissed repeated attention on Warren Buffett’s calls for higher taxes on the wealthy. Christie told Morgan that Buffett “should just write a check and shut up,” saying he was tired of hearing about the billionaire’s appeals for government action. When pressed, Christie noted Buffett doesn’t live in New Jersey but ultimately said his role is to serve all residents, not to engage in class-warfare arguments that elevate some citizens above others. Christie emphasized government should respond to everyone’s needs, especially the most vulnerable, and rejected singling out wealthy individuals for special attention. The exchange came amid national debate over the so-called “Buffett Rule,” which proposes that those earning over $1 million pay at least the same tax rates as middle-class households. Buffett’s high-profile complaint—that he pays a lower effective tax rate than his secretary—has fueled discussions about income inequality and tax fairness, linked to movements like Occupy Wall Street.

A San Francisco Victorian made famous in the 1993 film Mrs. Doubtfire was the target of a suspected arson attack Monday night. Authorities responded around 8 p.m. to the Pacific Heights home at Broadway and Steiner after small fires were set at the garage and front door; investigators believe an accelerant such as gasoline may have been used. Police remained on scene until after 11 p.m., and no suspect has been identified. The residence, long a fan landmark and a makeshift memorial site after Robin Williams’ death, is owned by Dr. Douglas Ousterhout, a plastic surgeon known for facial feminization procedures. Ousterhout told police he has had problems with a former client but said he did not know who might be responsible. A police official indicated the incident did not appear to be a hate crime as the investigation continued. Local media covered the scene and the home’s cultural significance.

The Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery unveiled the official portraits of former President Barack Obama and former First Lady Michelle Obama, an event that drew attention for both the subjects and the artists chosen. Barack Obama’s portrait was painted by Kehinde Wiley, a Yale-trained artist celebrated for placing African-American subjects in poses and settings reminiscent of Old Master paintings. Wiley’s portrait shows Obama seated against dense green foliage interwoven with symbolic flowers—chrysanthemums for Chicago, jasmine for Hawaii and African blue lilies referencing his heritage—elements Wiley said chart the subject’s path on Earth. Obama joked about negotiating his appearance and praised Wiley’s challenge to traditional ideas of power and privilege; he also noted personal commonalities with the artist, including family backgrounds. Kehinde Wiley is the first African-American artist to paint an official presidential portrait for the National Portrait Gallery. Michelle Obama’s portrait was created by Baltimore-based Amy Sherald, winner of the Portrait Gallery’s 2016 Outwin Boochever competition. Sherald, known for painting black skin tones in grayscale and emphasizing shape and color over realism, portrayed Michelle in a patterned halter dress with a thoughtful pose. Michelle highlighted the importance of the image for girls and girls of color seeing someone who looks like them in a major American institution. Both portraits, selected from long artist shortlists, will be publicly displayed at the museum.

Richard Carpenter has sued Universal Music Group and A&M Records in Los Angeles Superior Court, alleging the labels underpaid digital royalties owed to him and the estate of his late sister, Karen Carpenter. The suit claims the companies paid only a “miniscule fraction” of what the Carpenters are owed from iTunes and other online distributors. Accountants hired by Richard reportedly found multiple errors in the labels’ accounting: digital downloads were allegedly misclassified as record sales rather than licensing of master recordings (which would carry a higher royalty rate), downloads were undercounted, and an incorrect base price was applied to CD sales. Richard seeks at least $2 million in compensatory damages and alleges breach of contract and breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. He cites precedent in litigation over Eminem’s recordings, where the 9th Circuit held that digital downloads constitute licensing of master recordings rather than sales. Carpenter said he tried to resolve the dispute amicably but will now prove the claims in court. The Carpenters recorded 11 albums, released 31 singles, won three Grammys, and Karen Carpenter died in 1983. A UMG spokeswoman had not responded to requests for comment.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn, 62, managing director of the International Monetary Fund since 2007, was charged in New York with attempted rape, a criminal sexual act and unlawful imprisonment after a 32-year-old Sofitel hotel maid accused him of attacking her in his $3,000-a-night suite. A prominent economist, former French finance minister (1997–1999), ex-legislator and possible French presidential contender, Strauss-Kahn had led the IMF through the 2007–09 financial crisis and played a central role in managing European debt rescues. Police say he emerged naked from the bathroom, assaulted the maid, tried to lock her in the room and later fled, only to be removed from an Air France plane bound for Paris and arrested. He denies wrongdoing and will plead not guilty; his U.S. attorney Benjamin Brafman is defending him. The allegations stunned French politics, likely ending his presidential prospects, and triggered an IMF leadership crisis with John Lipsky named acting managing director. Strauss-Kahn’s wife Anne Sinclair defended him. The case raises questions about prior complaints and the IMF’s handling of earlier misconduct allegations against him.

A Malaysia Airlines Boeing 777 flying from Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur was shot down over eastern Ukraine, killing all 298 on board. Among the victims were many delegates en route to the 20th International AIDS Conference in Melbourne, including prominent HIV researchers, WHO staff and long-time activists. The International AIDS Society and UNAIDS confirmed that colleagues and friends were aboard and expressed deep sorrow; later reports determined six conference delegates were among the dead and other counts indicated as many as 100+ AIDS community members were affected. Notable losses reported included Dutch HIV researcher Joep Lange, described by peers as a humanitarian and a giant of the field, and WHO media adviser Glenn Thomas. Global health figures and conference organizers said the Melbourne meeting would be sombre and offered condolences.

The crash intensified international outrage and diplomatic fallout. The U.S. and EU said evidence points to the jet being downed by a Russian-made surface-to-air missile fired from separatist-held territory; the U.S. prepared declassified intelligence to support its claim. EU foreign ministers discussed expanded sanctions on Russia — targeting individuals, finance, defence and energy technology — while debates continued about measures such as an arms embargo. Recovery and investigation efforts were hampered by security concerns at the crash site; remains were transported via train to Kharkiv and then flown to the Netherlands for forensic identification. Calls grew for full access for international investigators, stricter aviation safety guidance, and justice for victims as nations mourned and pressed for accountability.

U.S. federal air marshals have been quietly conducting targeted surveillance of American travelers on domestic flights under a little-known program called "Quiet Skies," The Boston Globe reported. Internal documents show that since March small teams of armed, undercover marshals have followed thousands of unsuspecting passengers, observing roughly 35 targets per day and recording behaviors such as fidgeting, laptop or smartphone use, sweating, or sleeping. The Transportation Security Administration, which oversees the Federal Air Marshal Service, confirmed the program exists in some form since 2010 but declined to say how targets are chosen or whether the surveillance has produced arrests. TSA spokesman James Gregory likened the presence to a cop stationed where incidents are more likely, and said observed behavior that concludes with a safe flight will be noted without confrontation. Civil liberties groups, notably the ACLU, criticized the program as opaque, wasteful, constitutionally suspect and prone to unreliable, unscientific screening. Even some air marshals expressed concern about legality and resource use.

In Egypt, archaeologists opened a nearly 30-ton black granite sarcophagus unearthed in Alexandria and found three badly decomposed mummies and reddish sewage-contaminated water, not the hoped-for famed ruler or curse. The sarcophagus, from the early Ptolemaic period, likely contained soldiers; one skull shows arrow trauma. The tomb was sealed for millennia and excavators used military engineers to lift the heavy lid; specialists will analyze the remains to determine identity and cause of death. Authorities ruled out curses, though concerns over fumes and preservation remain.

A DC customer reports being refused service at Chinatown Coffee Co. after ordering three shots of espresso poured over ice. The barista insisted they “don’t do that” because ice would “shock” and ruin their espresso, offered an Americano instead, then walked away and insulted the patron. The incident echoes a past controversy: in 2008 a blogger at Murky Coffee was similarly denied and publicly defied the rule by pouring espresso over ice himself, sparking a viral debate and prompting Murky to publish strict house policies (no espresso over ice, no espresso in to-go cups, etc.). The episode has reignited discussion in Washington about whether cafes can or should refuse customer requests on aesthetic or quality grounds, and where customer rights end and barista/café standards begin. The story asks readers whether customers have a right to “bad taste.”

A global e-mail malware campaign surfaced Thursday under the subject line "Here you have," prompting widespread inbox floods that disrupted corporate and government e-mail systems, including NASA, Comcast, Disney and others. Initially labeled a worm by some, researchers clarified it is a Trojan relying on users to click a malicious link disguised as a PDF; once executed it can spread via a victim’s contacts, shared drives and USBs and attempts to disable security tools. Variants used subjects like "Just For you" and echoed tactics from the 2001 "Anna Kournikova" virus. Security firms McAfee and Symantec and US-CERT investigated, noting links to prior August activity and possible ties to hacktivist groups; DHS and federal agencies analyzed samples and issued mitigation advice. Users were urged not to click unknown links and to keep antivirus updated.

A recently published 2006 letter from then-Archbishop Leonardo Sandri confirms that the Vatican was informed in 2000 about allegations of sexual misconduct involving Cardinal Theodore McCarrick, lending weight to claims of a high-level cover-up. Catholic News Service released the letter, which Sandri — who was the No. 3 official in the Secretariat of State at the time and is now a cardinal — sent in October 2006 to Father Boniface Ramsey, a New York priest who had reported complaints from seminarians at Seton Hall’s Immaculate Conception Seminary in November 2000. Ramsey says he wrote the nuncio because seminarians complained McCarrick invited them to his beach house and into his bed. Sandri’s 2006 note explicitly referenced Ramsey’s 2000 confidential communication to the then-U.S. apostolic nuncio, indicating the allegation reached senior Vatican offices well before McCarrick was made a cardinal in 2001.

The letter corroborates elements of Archbishop Carlo Maria Viganò’s recent accusations that multiple Vatican officials knew about McCarrick’s behavior and that Pope Francis may have rehabilitated McCarrick despite prior sanctions reportedly imposed under Pope Benedict XVI. Ramsey never received a formal reply to his 2000 letter but regards Sandri’s later acknowledgement as proof the concerns were received and considered. McCarrick resigned as a cardinal in July after a U.S. investigation found a 1970s allegation of groping a teenage altar boy credible; additional former seminarians have since accused him of repeatedly bedding or harassing them. McCarrick’s lawyer says he intends to seek due process and maintains his client’s rights.

Two students were shot outside Frederick High School on Wednesday night while a junior varsity basketball game against Gov. Thomas Johnson High was underway. The shooting occurred about 8:10 p.m.; officers locked down the building, moved roughly 200 people into the cafeteria, interviewed witnesses and later released students to parents from a nearby bowling alley parking lot. The victims, both Frederick County public school students who did not attend Frederick High, were flown to a Baltimore hospital with non–life‑threatening injuries and initially reported in stable condition; later reports indicated one may have been in critical condition. One victim was shot in the leg and the other in the back.

Frederick police have not made any arrests and had not identified suspects or a definitive motive. Investigators are probing multiple leads, including student reports that four to five males in heavy coats entered the gym during the game and left shortly before the shooting, and suggestions the incident could be gang-related or tied to school rivalry. Officers searched the high school and nearby West Frederick Middle School; both were closed to students the following day while staff worked and investigators continued collecting evidence. School and county officials arranged crisis counseling, reviewed security practices, and said additional campus security would be provided. Authorities asked anyone with information to contact police as the search for suspects and motive continued.

Steven Spielberg’s Bridge of Spies recasts a true Cold War episode as a measured, craft-driven drama that places moral steadiness above breathless action. Tom Hanks stars as James B. Donovan, a Brooklyn insurance lawyer who, in 1957, is asked to defend Rudolf Abel (Mark Rylance), a quiet Soviet spy. Donovan accepts to prove the fairness of the American legal system, and his conscientious defense—despite public scorn, threats to his family, and a hostile climate of McCarthy-era paranoia—becomes the hinge for a later mission: negotiating a prisoner swap in East Berlin after U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers is shot down.

The film is less a high-octane thriller than a slow-burning moral drama and elegant procedural. Spielberg, longtime cinematographer Janusz Kaminski, and production designer Adam Stockhausen luxuriate in period detail and visual atmosphere—muted blues, grays, mist—crafting a film that often feels carved from granite. The Coen brothers, with Matt Charman, sharpen Charman’s script with a spiky humor and subversive wit that at times sits uneasily alongside the movie’s more traditional themes of patriotism and American exceptionalism. Still, the screenplay rewards patience: disparate bits of dialogue and incident cohere in the third act, revealing a precise dramatic design.

Mark Rylance is the film’s revelation—his taciturn, disciplined Abel immediately commands the screen, making even moments of inaction riveting. Hanks’s Donovan is portrayed as an everyman of rectitude, more James Stewart than cinematic superhero—doubtful, domestic, stubbornly principled. Spielberg avoids hagiography; Donovan isn’t sentimentalized but presented as a real, fallible man whose faith in due process and decency informs the film’s moral core.

The Berlin sequences provide the most overt suspense and geopolitical texture—recreating the Wall’s rise and the fraught crossings—though some critics find those scenes talky and less compelling without Abel’s presence. Ultimately, Bridge of Spies is a handcrafted, thoughtful spy picture: a moral tale driven by an insurance lawyer that works largely because of Spielberg’s steady hand, meticulous craftsmanship, and standout performances, especially Rylance’s quietly magnetic turn.

Netflix has officially cleared production on a Gilmore Girls revival: four 90-minute films that together serve as a farewell season for the beloved WB series. After protracted negotiations, Alexis Bledel and Lauren Graham have signed on to reprise Rory and Lorelai Gilmore, and the core quartet returns intact with Scott Patterson (Luke) and Kelly Bishop (Emily). Sean Gunn (Kirk) and Keiko Agena (Lane) also rejoin the cast. Amy Sherman-Palladino, who stepped away before the original series’ final season, is back as creator and executive producer; she and her husband Daniel Palladino will write and direct all four films. Each movie is set in the present and will cover a different season over the course of a year. Produced by Dorothy Parker Drank Here in association with Warner Bros. Television, the revival’s exact title and premiere date remain TBD; Netflix confirmed the project with a celebratory tweet. The cast has already conducted a table read for the first film. Notable absences from initial returns include Liza Weil (Paris) and Yanic Truesdale (Michel); Melissa McCarthy’s participation is also unclear. Fans hope the revival will provide closure Sherman-Palladino was unable to deliver previously and resolve lingering questions—particularly Rory’s romantic future and how Lorelai and Luke’s story concludes.

U.S. and Mexican authorities this week uncovered two elaborate drug-smuggling tunnels linking warehouses in Tijuana and the Otay Mesa industrial park in San Diego — the sixth and seventh "super tunnels" found between the cities since 2010. Neither tunnel contained drugs or contraband when discovered. The first, located under a San Diego warehouse selling children’s toys and electronics, stretched roughly 600 yards, sat about 70 feet underground, and featured wooden trusses, lighting, a crude rail and a pulley hoist to lift packages to the surface. The second, found by Mexican investigators nearby, was roughly 700 yards long and more sophisticated, with ventilation and a multi-tiered electric rail system. Authorities say the tunnels cost millions to build. On Wednesday ICE arrested 73-year-old Glennys Rodriguez of Chula Vista, accusing her of managing logistics for one passage and charging her with conspiring to maintain a drug-involved premises; other suspects were named in her complaint. Officials emphasized that careful observation and detective work led to the discoveries. Since 2006, more than 80 cross-border tunnels have been found from California to Arizona, including an 1,800-foot tunnel in Otay Mesa in 2010.

At the G-20 summit in Toronto, leaders agreed—with caveats—to halve annual budget deficits by 2013 and stabilize debt-to-GDP ratios by 2016, reflecting a shift from crisis stimulus toward fiscal consolidation. President Obama warned the recovery remains fragile and urged measured deficit cuts paired with growth-supporting policies to avoid triggering a double-dip recession. The communiqué stressed nation-specific pacing, calibration to protect growth, and complementary reforms; the IMF and some economists warned against oversimplified targets. The group also backed tougher bank capital standards and left a global bank tax to national choice. Emerging markets, notably China, were urged to rebalance by boosting domestic demand, infrastructure investment and social safety nets, while advanced surplus countries pledged to narrow trade imbalances.

A review of Ivanka Trump’s emails found she used a private email account throughout much of 2017 to send hundreds of messages about White House business, contacting aides, Cabinet officials and personal staff. The practice came to light after the watchdog group American Oversight’s records requests prompted agencies to gather emails; White House ethics officials then discovered the volume of private correspondence. Her lawyer and spokesman said she sometimes used the private account, largely for logistics, scheduling and family matters, and that she stopped after being briefed on rules. They insist no classified information was transmitted, no private server was created, no emails were deleted, and relevant government-related messages were turned over for preservation.

Critics, including Austin Evers of American Oversight, called for congressional inquiry, noting the potential violation of the Presidential Records Act and Federal Records Act, which require officials to preserve official correspondence and prohibit sharing classified or privileged material on private systems. The episode drew comparisons to Hillary Clinton’s email controversy — a frequent 2016 target of Donald Trump — though aides and lawyers emphasize differences, such as Clinton’s exclusive use of a private home server and FBI findings that some Clinton emails contained classified material. White House officials say much of Ivanka Trump’s private correspondence was logistical; others inside the administration were alarmed by both the frequency and by her apparent unfamiliarity with rules governing private email use. The discovery underscores risks that private accounts can place official records beyond public or congressional reach and raises questions about compliance and oversight.

Federal prosecutors in Manhattan granted longtime Trump Organization chief financial officer Allen Weisselberg immunity and he testified before a grand jury in the Michael Cohen investigation, sources tell NBC News and The Wall Street Journal. Identified as “Executive 1” in the criminal information in the Cohen case, Weisselberg is implicated in documents showing Cohen sent an invoice to him for “Payment for services rendered for the month of January and February, 2017,” a reimbursement tied to a payment to Stormy Daniels. Weisselberg then emailed another Trump Organization executive instructing the payment be made “from the Trust” and posted as legal expenses with a “retainer” description. Prosecutors declined comment.

Weisselberg, 70, has worked at the Trump Organization since the 1970s and served as treasurer of the Donald J. Trump Foundation, which faced a New York attorney general lawsuit. His name also appears on a recorded call seized in the FBI raid of Cohen’s office and residence, in which Cohen tells President Trump he discussed with Weisselberg setting up a corporation to handle a payment related to a story about Karen McDougal. Weisselberg’s immunity marks him as the third longstanding Trump confidant to cooperate in the federal hush-money probe that has touched associates of President Trump.

Thai authorities have mobilized inspectors to prevent price gouging on black and white mourning clothes after the death of King Bhumibol Adulyadej prompted a year-long national mourning. The Commerce Ministry directed provincial offices to survey supplies and prices of black garments and decorative fabrics, asking vendors to clearly label prices, avoid hoarding and refrain from unreasonable mark-ups. Violators face up to seven years in jail and fines up to 140,000 baht. Commerce Minister Apiradi Tantraporn said teams will coordinate with distributors to ensure sufficient stocks nationwide. In Bangkok, surging demand has brought shoppers to wholesale markets such as Bo Bae and Pratunam, causing traffic congestion. Street and market traders report brisk sales but deny exploiting the situation. One stallholder said she buys shirts at about 90 baht wholesale and sells them for 120–130 baht, having sold hundreds over two days. Consumers, while noting slight price rises, say cost is secondary to observance: many are buying new black shirts for themselves and family members to wear throughout the mourning year and to comply with the government’s call to wear black or white and suspend festivities.

After a brutal fighting season, many Afghan army units face a severe logistics crisis: critical equipment—especially armored Humvees and spare parts—is broken and can’t be repaired or replaced. Battalions in volatile regions reported large percentages of armored vehicles out of service, forcing soldiers to walk long distances or cram into the few remaining vehicles. The U.S. military, which had previously handled repairs and parts distribution, reduced that role during the transition, leaving an underdeveloped Afghan supply chain and a Defense Ministry hampered by corruption to fill the gap. Units report Humvees destroyed by roadside bombs and RPGs, mechanics lacking parts (even engine oil), and replacement requests delayed for years by bureaucratic procedures. The shortage constrains operations—EOD teams have far fewer vehicles, patrols shrink, and even special forces suffer nonreplacement of lost Humvees. Beyond vehicles, procurement failures have denied tens of thousands of soldiers proper boots and ammunition for rocket launchers; fuel deliveries are incomplete and suspected of being siphoned. NATO and U.S. officials acknowledge the problems and pledge to improve supply chains and training, but advisers are being pulled to higher levels as U.S. forces withdraw, reducing hands-on help at battalion level. Meanwhile, U.S. drawdown produces vast amounts of damaged surplus: billions in equipment left behind or destroyed before sale to prevent militant reuse, creating massive scrap yards around bases like Bagram. Afghans who hoped to repurpose or buy usable gear are frustrated that much is rendered unusable, leaving questions about whether the Afghan army will be ready before the next fighting season.

Sen. Marco Rubio is publicly undecided about running for reelection after the Orlando nightclub massacre prompted reflection on where he can best serve. Rubio told reporters a decision wouldn’t come until later in the week; the June 24 filing deadline looms. Close friend and 20-year ally Florida Lt. Gov. Carlos Lopez-Cantera—who has been campaigning in a crowded GOP primary for Rubio’s seat with Rubio’s prior encouragement—unexpectedly urged Rubio to reconsider running while they witnessed the massacre’s aftermath together. Lopez-Cantera emphasized the stakes for the country and said he remained committed to his own campaign, adding that “nothing has changed” and “I’m still running. Marco isn’t.” That interchange removed a key obstacle Rubio feared: damaging a longstanding friendship by entering the race. Friends and insiders are divided—many expect Rubio to forego another Senate term for family time and higher private-sector earnings, while others say only Rubio truly knows. Polling shows Rubio would be the strongest Republican against Democrat Patrick Murphy, and leaders and donors have pressured him to run, freezing fundraising and dampening enthusiasm among GOP candidates. Rumors of backroom deals and orchestrated plans—some suggesting Rubio would win then resign to open the seat—are widespread but denied by both men. Rubio has been lining up private-sector opportunities and may seek a national role in future cycles; supporters counter that as a senator he retains influence on foreign policy and classified briefings he would miss if he leaves.

The writer recalls first falling for Melissa McCarthy in Bridesmaids, praising her wildly original, scene-stealing comic performance, and contrasts that affection with outrage at Rex Reed’s vitriolic New York Observer review of McCarthy’s new film Identity Thief. Reed’s critique is excerpted at length and savaged as gratuitously attacking McCarthy’s weight and reducing film criticism to cruelty. Reed’s review calls Identity Thief a “chunk of junk,” assigns one star, and criticizes the screenplay by Craig Mazin and Jerry Eeten and Seth Gordon’s direction. The plot summary Reed provides frames Jason Bateman as Sandy Patterson, a Denver accountant whose identity is stolen by Diana (McCarthy), a loud, aggressive Florida con woman who runs up bills and destroys his credit. When authorities fail to help, Sandy travels to Florida to force Diana to return to Colorado and clear his name. Reed rails that the premise is flimsy and that the film stretches a thin idea into a long string of contrived set pieces—car chases, bar fights, a grotesque motel sequence, slapstick mishaps, kidnappings and improbable thugs—often veering into vulgarity and implausibility. He argues that identity theft is a serious subject better suited to drama than comedy, and that the script’s attempts to convert the premise into a road-buddy movie like Midnight Run fail; characters don’t genuinely bond and the sentiment feels forced. Reed concedes McCarthy can coax a laugh and Bateman tries to keep dignity, but finds the movie mostly unfunny, mean-spirited, and sentimental in a manipulative way. He also objects to the film’s treatment of weight and crude humor, calling much of it obnoxious and a squandered opportunity given McCarthy’s comedic gifts.

A Jefferson County judge dismissed the capital murder charge against Gabe Watson in the 2003 drowning death of his wife, Tina, during their Australian honeymoon, ruling prosecutors failed to prove he intentionally killed her for financial gain. Judge Tommy Nail said the state’s evidence was “sorely lacking,” noting the only eyewitness believed Watson was trying to save his wife and that motive evidence was speculative. The ruling came after the prosecution rested and before the defense presented its case; the courtroom cheered as Watson left with his wife. Watson had pleaded guilty in Australia in 2009 to negligent manslaughter and served 18 months. Prosecutors had argued the killing occurred for insurance money, but the judge found no proof a reasonable person could regard as beyond a reasonable doubt, and barred some contested testimony about alleged insurance motives.

The Democratic National Convention’s second night centers on Bill Clinton, who will formally place President Obama’s name in nomination and give a high-profile endorsement. Clinton’s appearance is a calculated risk for Obama: his popularity and economic credibility could bolster the president—especially with white, middle-class and undecided voters—but there’s concern Clinton might outshine or invite comparisons to the 1990s boom. The campaign says they’ve spoken with Clinton frequently and expect a pro-Obama speech, though they had not fully vetted the text publicly; campaign officials dismissed worries as overblown. Clinton’s complex relationship with Obama stems from the bruising 2008 primary and differing styles, yet political necessity has united them for 2012. Clinton will speak late Wednesday, likely after 10:30 p.m. ET, and may set the stage for the roll call that formally nominates Obama and Biden. The convention spotlights several themes: a slate of female speakers, including Elizabeth Warren and Sandra Fluke, aiming to cement Obama’s advantage with women voters; and business leaders framed as supporters of Obama’s economic plans. Elizabeth Warren, a Harvard law professor and former architect of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, is highlighted as a marquee speaker and Democratic challenger in the high-stakes Massachusetts Senate race against Republican Scott Brown. That contest is the nation’s most-watched and most expensive Senate contest to date, polarized and polling nearly tied; both candidates emphasize differing appeals—Brown’s bipartisan, working-class image versus Warren’s middle-class and consumer-protection message. The campaign atmosphere in Charlotte is lively, with extensive local engagement, debate plans for Senate contenders, and a constant media presence as the convention unfolds.

A study from Indiana University investigated how media (email vs. voicemail) and task type (romantic vs. utilitarian) affect senders’ physiological arousal and message content. Using psychophysiological measures on 72 college-age participants, researchers Alan R. Dennis and Taylor M. Wells found that composing emails produced greater arousal than leaving voicemails across both task types. Participants showed more muscular activity associated with emotion and higher arousal when writing emails, suggesting deeper cognitive and emotional engagement during composition. The medium also shaped message content: for romantic tasks, emails contained more positive and stronger emotional language than voicemails, while for utilitarian tasks the reverse occurred—voicemails were relatively more positive than utilitarian emails. The authors propose that email’s editability and the extra time spend composing messages encourage careful word choice and greater processing, which can increase arousal and lead senders to add positive content—perhaps compensating for lack of vocal tone—whereas voicemails are typically recorded in a single take and less edited. Contrary to media naturalness theory, which predicts decreasing effectiveness as communication diverges from face-to-face interaction, the findings suggest that millennials may have adapted to text-based media so they can convey emotion effectively via email. Gender did not affect outcomes, and emoticon use was minimal. The researchers caution that these results don’t diminish the value of synchronous, cue-rich channels (phone, face-to-face, video) for clarifying meaning, but they highlight how the choice of medium influences how senders feel and what they say.

In a surprising discovery recounted by KARE 11, two Minnesota women, Denice Juneski and Linda Jourdeans, learned at age 72 that they had been switched at birth in 1945. The revelation began when Denice, an ancestry enthusiast from Eagan, submitted a DNA sample to 23andMe to learn more about her health and family history. When her reported DNA relatives didn’t include any familiar names, she retested and reached the same baffling result—prompting the suspicion she’d been raised in the wrong family. The missing puzzle piece arrived when Linda’s niece saw Denice listed among her DNA matches; Linda then took a test and the results confirmed they had been switched as newborns at Bethesda Hospital in St. Paul on December 19, 1945. For seven decades each woman had lived the other’s life—Denice grew up as a lone blonde among brunettes and redheads in a family of athletes, while Linda, a redhead, fit into a different household and played softball into her 50s. Family photos and anecdotes supported the DNA findings. Since connecting in April, Denice and Linda have met multiple times and have begun meeting biological relatives, including visits to Marianne Mayer, 99, who raised Denice and gave birth to Linda; Marianne enjoys visits from both women. The discovery has been emotional—especially for Linda, whose birth mother died young—but both women say learning the truth is a gift, and they’re embracing new relationships and an unexpected bond they call “new friends.”

Hackers briefly hijacked Taylor Swift’s social accounts on January 27, 2015, tweeting links to members of the Lizard Squad and claiming to possess nude photos of the singer. Twitter removed the malicious posts, suspended the implicated accounts, and locked Swift’s account while passwords were reset. Swift reassured fans via Tumblr and later tweeted wryly that there were no nude pictures and taunted hackers trying to Photoshop something that “got NOTHING.” She also thanked a friend who alerted her to the breach and continued engaging lightheartedly online. The incident followed wider disruptions attributed to the Lizard Squad, who had been tied to attacks on PlayStation and Xbox networks and other service outages. Separately, the article touches on lighter Swift-related items: fans noting storm and natural-disaster imagery in her album reputation, playful commentary about Swift revealing her belly button in a Maui bikini snapshot with the Haim sisters, and Swift’s supportive Tumblr message to a bullied fan named Caillou about embracing what makes you different. Swift was on a Hawaiian trip with friends when the hacking occurred.

On the night of May 27 into the morning of May 28, 2017, a shooting spree in Lincoln County, Mississippi, left eight people dead, including Lincoln County Deputy William Durr. Suspect Willie Corey (Cory) Godbolt, 35, was arrested after about seven hours on the run and has been charged with one count of capital murder and seven counts of first-degree murder. Godbolt told The Clarion-Ledger he had intended to commit “suicide by cop” after an argument with his estranged wife over their children and said, “I ain't fit to live, not after what I done.”

The violence began around 11:30 p.m. Saturday at a residence on Lee Drive in Bogue Chitto, where Godbolt had gone to discuss custody of his children. Neighbors called police; when Deputy Durr arrived trying to calm the situation, Godbolt reportedly pulled a gun from his back pocket and opened fire. Four bodies were recovered at that scene: three women and Deputy Durr, a two-year Lincoln County deputy and former Brookhaven officer described as a community favorite who worked with children. At a second scene on Coopertown Road in Brookhaven, the bodies of two boys were found; those killings occurred between midnight and 5 a.m. A man and a woman were later found dead at a Brookhaven residence on East Lincoln Road where officers found Godbolt as he attempted to flee.

Family members identified several victims; authorities withheld full names pending next-of-kin notification. Witnesses said most victims were relatives of Godbolt. Godbolt claimed he’d been shot inside a home and was treated at a Jackson hospital; it was unclear who shot him. The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation and numerous local and state agencies responded. Officials and community leaders expressed shock and grief at what authorities called the largest crime spree in Lincoln County’s memory. Governor Phil Bryant urged prayers and praised law enforcement response.

Tesla provided a detailed account of the March 23 fatal Model X crash that killed 38-year-old Walter Huang in Mountain View, saying Autopilot was engaged and adaptive cruise control follow-distance was set to minimum. Vehicle logs show the driver had received several visual and one audible hands-on warning earlier in the drive and that his hands were not detected on the wheel for six seconds before impact. The car had about five seconds and 150 meters of unobstructed view of a concrete divider with a crushed crash attenuator, but no evasive action was recorded. Tesla stressed the crash’s severity resulted largely from the attenuator having been crushed in a prior crash and not replaced; the company said it had never seen similar damage to a Model X. Tesla cited safety data showing Autopilot has historically reduced crash rates and that vehicles with Autopilot hardware have a lower fatality rate compared with overall U.S. vehicle fatalities. The company urged that while Autopilot cannot prevent every accident, it improves safety and could save many lives if widely adopted. Huang’s family reported he had complained multiple times that Autopilot veered toward that barrier and had taken the car to a dealer; investigators and agencies including NTSB, CHP and CalTrans continue probing the incident. Tesla expressed condolences and reiterated commitment to working with investigators.

Police arrested a man after a confrontation and shooting inside the Excalibur Hotel and Casino on March 18, 2014. The suspect, seen backstage wearing a SWAT hat, firefighter shirt and mismatched shoes, was found with stolen costumes and props from performers in the all-male revue Thunder From Down Under. When confronted by dancers and the show director, he claimed he had bought the items, then pulled a .44 Magnum, threatened to shoot, and a round discharged into a wall as performers pushed the weapon away. The performers overpowered and detained him until security and Metro officers arrived. He was treated at University Medical Center for injuries and sedated for violent behavior, then booked on attempted murder, attempted robbery and burglary charges with a deadly weapon. MGM said the show remained on schedule.

Two researchers announced a potentially paradigm-shifting claim: they say they have located Fort Caroline, the 1564 French fortified settlement long sought by scholars, and that it lies not in northeast Florida near Jacksonville but on Rhetts Island at the mouth of Georgia’s Altamaha River, two miles southeast of Darien. Presenting at Florida State University’s “La Floride Française” conference, historian Fletcher Crowe and anthropologist Anita Spring argued their conclusion from extensive archival research in the Bibliothèque Nationale de France, comparisons of 16th–18th century French maps with modern NOAA and USGS charts, linguistic evidence identifying the local Native speakers as Guale (associated with the Georgia coast), and trade-route links to regional gold deposits. If confirmed, Fort Caroline would be the oldest fortified European settlement in what is now the United States, predating St. Augustine, Roanoke, Jamestown and Plymouth. The pair say the longstanding belief that the fort sat east of Jacksonville resulted from mistranslations and map misreadings dating back centuries. Their proposed site is currently protected by Georgia authorities and they hold a special-use permit to excavate soon; however, no archaeological proof has yet been produced. The claim provoked skepticism from some archaeologists who have long searched in Jacksonville and who stress the need for physical evidence and for reconciling historical accounts of Spanish troops marching from a St. Augustine camp to attack the fort in 1565. Crowe and Spring welcome scrutiny and plan further fieldwork to test their provocative, contested hypothesis.

In July 2014, after serving 29 years of a life sentence for spying for Israel, Jonathan J. Pollard was denied parole, but that hearing prompted an intensive legal campaign by his attorneys to secure his release when he reached the 30-year eligibility mark. Lawyers working pro bono for Pollard compiled letters, statistics and evidence showing he met legal parole standards: good behavior in prison and a low risk of returning to espionage. On Tuesday the United States Parole Commission concluded Pollard met those standards and granted parole; he is scheduled to leave federal prison in Butner, N.C., on Nov. 20 (reported elsewhere as Nov. 21). Pollard’s release comes exactly 30 years after his arrest and has been a recurring issue in U.S.-Israel relations, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu long advocating his freedom. The White House stated the Parole Commission acted under standard procedures and denied any link between the decision and foreign policy matters such as the Iran nuclear deal. The Justice Department and Pollard’s lawyers confirmed the release date.

The Sochi Winter Olympics opened amid excitement over new events and persistent concerns about safety and logistics. Organizers added a dozen events since Vancouver 2010, including slopestyle snowboarding and freestyle skiing, to attract younger viewers; snowboarding and freestyle together account for 20 of Sochi’s 98 events. Slopestyle, debuting as the first medal competition, instantly became emblematic of both the appeal and risks of pushing extreme sports into the Olympic program.

High-profile withdrawals and injuries underscored those risks. Shaun White abruptly pulled out of the inaugural Olympic slopestyle competition the day before qualifying, citing an ongoing wrist issue and the “potential risk of injury” that could jeopardize his primary goal: winning a third straight halfpipe gold. White’s decision followed crashes during early practice on Rosa Khutor Extreme Park’s slopestyle course that left Norway’s Torstein Horgmo with a broken collarbone and Finland’s Merike Enne with an ankle injury; White himself jammed a wrist. Riders described the course—first ridden only after rain cancelled earlier tests—as intimidating, with jump heights that surprised even seasoned X Games athletes. After appeals, organizers smoothed the tops and bottoms of several jumps; some competitors said the changes helped make the course safer while preserving the ability to perform big tricks.

The debate about course safety fed broader worries about serious injuries — and whether Olympic organizers pushed the “no-limits” extreme-sports ethos too far in pursuit of youth appeal. Supporters of athlete caution applauded White, arguing obstacle builders should redesign unsafe elements or remove them.

Security and political issues also dominated the prelude to the Games. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Kozak downplayed terrorism fears and defended Sochi’s security preparations, despite intelligence alerts and previous regional attacks. A U.S. Homeland Security advisory warned airlines of possible explosives hidden in toothpaste tubes on flights to Russia. Human-rights concerns around Russia’s “gay propaganda” law surfaced when U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon criticized arrests and discriminatory restrictions; Kozak and other officials insisted visitors would not be targeted.

Competition began 32 hours before the opening ceremony to accommodate the expanded schedule, with men’s and women’s slopestyle and women’s moguls among the early events. As Sochi set out to blend spectacle, new disciplines and political theater, safety — both on the slopes and off — remained at the forefront.

President Donald Trump spent part of his first morning in office focused on criticizing turnout at his inauguration, calling acting National Park Service (NPS) director Michael T. Reynolds to demand additional aerial photos after the agency’s official Twitter account retweeted a side-by-side comparison showing far larger crowds for Barack Obama’s 2009 inauguration. White House deputy press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders framed the call as evidence of Trump’s hands-on management style. According to multiple sources, Trump believed new photos might disprove media reports that attendance was below past inaugurations and accused news outlets of lying; he repeatedly told audiences the crowd was “massive,” claims experts say are unsupported. Reynolds, a long-time NPS official who had been acting director only briefly, obtained and forwarded more aerial images through Interior Department channels, but they did not validate Trump’s contention of turnout near one million. The episode unfolded amid wider tensions between the administration and career agency employees after the NPS account also retweeted a post noting policy changes on the White House website; Interior temporarily ordered agency Twitter platforms shut down and later apologized for the retweets. Separate incidents, such as the Badlands National Park account briefly posting climate-related tweets by a former employee, further heightened scrutiny. White House press secretary Sean Spicer publicly rebuked media coverage of the inauguration, and Trump continued pressing the narrative that media images were unfair or angled to minimize attendance.

Scott Weiland’s ex-wife Mary Forsberg has filed to be named executor of his estate, submitting a copy of a will signed by Weiland dated April 2007. Forsberg, his second wife and mother of his two children, claims Scott named her executor; the will comes from a period when their marriage was failing and Weiland was struggling with addiction. Reports indicate his probate estate is about $2 million, and he also established a trust with undisclosed assets. Forsberg, who wrote a memoir about their life and his substance abuse and penned a public letter after his death, could face a challenge: Weiland’s widow, Jamie Wachtel, who was married to him at the time he died in December 2015, may contest the filing. Weiland died at 48 from a drug-and-alcohol-related cause; a hearing on the executor matter is scheduled for Feb. 5.

Republicans in the House pushed two abortion-related bills through the chamber amid a contentious fight over Planned Parenthood funding and an impending Sept. 30 government funding deadline. In near party-line votes, the House approved a one-year ban on most federal funding to Planned Parenthood (241-187) and the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act, which would impose criminal penalties on medical personnel who fail to care for infants born alive after attempted abortions (248-177). The votes followed the release of undercover videos by anti-abortion activists alleging improper fetal tissue practices by Planned Parenthood; the organization denies wrongdoing and says the videos are deceptively edited.

GOP leaders sought to placate conservative members demanding a showdown with President Obama while avoiding a government shutdown. Many Republicans, including Speaker John Boehner and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, warned that attaching defunding language to a must-pass spending bill would provoke a veto in the White House and fail in the Democratic-controlled Senate, risking voter backlash. Internal GOP polling presented to House members suggested most voters would oppose a shutdown over the issue.

Democrats argued the measures attack women’s health care and noted federal funds already are barred from paying for abortions; they also stressed that community health centers could not readily absorb Planned Parenthood’s patients. Senate Democrats signaled they would block the measures, and the White House threatened vetoes, making their enactment unlikely. The dispute heightened intra-GOP tensions, with hard-liners threatening leadership and talk of a possible motion to vacate the speakership if leaders back down. As the fiscal deadline nears, leaders in both parties continued negotiating for a short-term “clean” continuing resolution to avert a shutdown while broader spending talks proceed.

The White House released recipes for two home-brewed beers — the White House Honey Brown Ale and a Honey Porter — marking what the White House says is the first beer brewed on the White House grounds. The announcement came while President Barack Obama campaigned in Iowa after weeks of public curiosity, petitions and questions about the brew. White House chef Sam Kass, who brews the beer in the White House kitchen, and staff developed the recipes after Obama bought a home-brewing kit and they received help from local home-brew shops and colleagues. Both brews use honey harvested from the first White House South Lawn beehive, giving the beers aroma and finish without added sweetness. The administration posted detailed ingredient lists and step-by-step directions, plus a video of the brewing process, noting the president purchased the materials himself. The Honey Ale’s components include light malt extract, amber crystal malt, honey, gypsum, yeast and corn sugar; the Porter recipe uses a mix of malts, hops, honey and Nottingham yeast. Kass praises the results but says production is limited.

President Trump tweeted that he declined Time magazine’s offer to be named Person of the Year again because he would have had to agree to an interview and major photo shoot, and he rejected the “probably” wording. Time quickly tweeted that his account was incorrect. Trump, who praised being Time’s 2016 Person of the Year as a “tremendous honor,” often touts magazine covers and was previously found to display fake Time issues at several golf clubs. Time’s Person of the Year—originally “Man of the Year” from 1928 and changed to “Person of the Year” in 1999—is not always celebratory but denotes the individual(s) who most influenced the year’s news, for better or worse; past selections have included figures like Adolf Hitler and Joseph Stalin. The announcement for the 2017 Person of the Year was scheduled for December 6. The report also summarizes Trump’s other Friday activities: condemning a deadly mosque attack in Egypt, calling for tougher anti-terror measures and immigration restrictions, and discussing Syria and Kurdish arms with Turkey’s Erdogan.

Four-year-old Jillian Massey of Coopersburg, Pa., a brain cancer patient who spent six months at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, wanted to bring gifts to the friends she left behind when she went home for the holidays. What began as a hope for 50 presents grew to more than 3,000 after her family created an Amazon wish list and her mother’s coworkers helped promote it. Jillian’s mother, Janelle, says they will deliver the toys on Monday, and Jillian is excited to spread cheer.

A 24-year-old North Korean soldier identified only as Oh was shot multiple times as he fled across the Demilitarized Zone into South Korea on Nov. 13 and has since become the focus of intense medical, military and public attention. Trauma surgeon John Cook-Jong Lee at Ajou University Hospital has led several major surgeries to remove bullet fragments, repair shredded organs and treat severe pre-existing infections. Oh arrived near death by helicopter after U.S. flight medics treated a collapsed lung en route; hospital teams pumped as much as 12 liters (about 40 units) of type O blood into him—roughly two to three times a normal human blood volume—to stop massive internal bleeding. Surgeons repaired his colon in seven places and removed at least four bullets; he also suffered from tuberculosis, hepatitis B and a severe parasitic infestation including a long intestinal worm and undigested corn kernels, conditions rare in contemporary South Korea. Physically fragile—about 5'5" and 130 pounds—Oh is now conscious, able to eat clear liquids, smile and speak, but he remains guarded by South Korean special forces and intelligence officers and shows signs of psychological trauma, including nightmares of being repatriated. Lee has tried to shield him from stressful questioning and media coverage, delaying intelligence interviews until he recovers. To comfort him, medical staff have played South Korean pop and Western movies and shows—Oh reportedly enjoys K-pop, Bruce Almighty, Transporter 3 and CSI—and hung a South Korean flag in his room. The dramatic CCTV and UN Command footage of his escape showed South Korean and U.S. soldiers hauling him to safety under fire; several rescuers received commendations. In response to the defection, North Korea reportedly replaced border guards and fortified the crossing area with trenches and trees. Lee cautions that although Oh is expected to survive, some injuries, especially to his colon, may cause lifelong complications, and his psychological recovery will require careful attention before any formal debriefing.

New NRDC research finds about 10% of U.S. coastal and lakefront beaches fail to meet EPA water-safety standards, exposing swimmers to illnesses like gastroenteritis, conjunctivitis, respiratory problems, and potentially worse. Trouble spots include New England, the Gulf Coast, the Great Lakes, and many California beaches. The main cause is polluted stormwater runoff—garbage, oil, and human and animal waste—compounded by hundreds of billions of gallons of untreated sewage annually, which contributes to 3.5 million American illnesses each year. Federal law requires bacterial testing and closures; for example, nearly 2,000 New York and New Jersey beach closures occurred in 2012. In California, 9% of 2013 samples exceeded EPA’s protective Beach Action Value; some sites failed much of the time. Solutions include green infrastructure (rain gardens, curb cuts, rain barrels, porous pavement), stronger protections for streams and wetlands under the Clean Water Act, and public awareness—check local water quality before swimming. Despite problems, some California beaches remain clean, showing improvement is possible.

World of Beer (WOB), a Tampa-based tavern chain with 77 locations, is offering a unique paid summer internship: three candidates will spend four months traveling to breweries and WOB taverns nationwide and overseas to taste beer, attend festivals, and document their experiences.
