The internship pays $12,000 and covers travel, meals, and lodging. Applicants must be at least 21; strong writing and social media skills are preferred because the role is social-media focused and successful interns will have work published in Draft Magazine. WOB launched the program as a first-time “Drink It Intern” initiative to provide a global experience and share stories with customers. Interested candidates could apply by submitting an online video or by interviewing at one of multiple in-tavern live judging events; some live interview dates already occurred, with additional sessions scheduled in Orlando, Tempe (AZ), College Station (TX), and Tampa (FL). The top ten applicants will be chosen in early April for Skype interviews with corporate, which will select the final three. Applications were due March 26.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948, established for the first time a universal set of fundamental rights to be protected for all people and nations. Drafted by representatives from diverse legal and cultural backgrounds, it has been translated into over 500 languages and framed as a common standard of achievement. Its preamble stresses inherent human dignity, freedom, justice, the rule of law, and international cooperation to prevent tyranny and promote peace. The Declaration’s articles enumerate civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights: equality and non‑discrimination; rights to life, liberty and security; prohibition of slavery and torture; legal recognition, due process, and protection from arbitrary arrest; privacy; freedom of movement and asylum; nationality; marriage and family protections; property rights; freedoms of thought, religion, opinion, expression, assembly and association; political participation and fair public service; social security, work, rest, adequate living standards, health care and education; cultural participation and protection of authors’ rights; and the duty of individuals to respect the rights of others within lawful limits. The UDHR insists no provision may be used to destroy its rights and calls on all organs of society to promote and secure their universal observance. Its text is now memorialized in public spaces, including the new WTC Cortlandt subway station in Lower Manhattan, whose walls display excerpts alongside other national documents.

A Pew Research Center study finds U.S. mothers are older and more educated than two decades ago. Between 1990 and 2008 births to women 35+ rose from 368,000 to 603,000, so one in seven babies was born to a mother 35 or older in 2008; births to teenagers fell. The average age for a first child is 25. Most newborn mothers (54%) had some college in 2008, up from 41% in 1990; 71% of mothers 35+ had some college. Medical advances and fertility treatments, delayed marriage, longer education and career-building contribute to these shifts. Unwed births also rose to a record 41% in 2008. Multiple births increased, linked to older maternal age and fertility treatments. A survey found 87% cite “the joy of having children,” yet nearly half said parenthood “just happened,” indicating mixed intentions.

Israel’s 2013 election saw record turnout and surprising shifts that reshaped its political landscape. By 8 p.m. some 3.6 million Israelis—63.7% of eligible voters—had cast ballots, surpassing comparable mid-election figures from recent campaigns, with voting continuing until 10 p.m. Polling stations nationwide reported heavy, sustained flows of voters; election officials credited a turnout campaign, and police described the day as a “celebration of democracy,” noting only isolated incidents. High-profile figures, including President Shimon Peres, urged citizens to vote.

Media attention abroad was muted, partly because the vote coincided with the U.S. presidential inauguration and because coverage emphasized the election’s lackluster, non-confrontational campaign—few debates on major foreign-policy issues like Iran and Syria and no clear shifts in Israel’s external posture.

Domestically the biggest story was the rise of Yair Lapid’s new centrist Yesh Atid, which captured 19 seats and surprised many by focusing on middle-class “kitchen-table” concerns such as education and housing, while avoiding polarizing security rhetoric. Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud-Beiteinu led but lost seats (31), weakening his mandate. With blocs nearly evenly split—right-wing/religious parties and center/left/Arab factions each holding about 60 Knesset seats—the coming coalition-building promises complex negotiations and potential paralysis, as Lapid emerges as a decisive kingmaker open to partnering yet insisting on a strong centrist agenda.

Disney and Lucasfilm announced the cast for Star Wars Episode IX, revealing that the late Carrie Fisher will appear as Leia Organa using previously unreleased footage from The Force Awakens. Director J.J. Abrams said the filmmakers refused to recast or use a CGI Leia, and with the blessing of Fisher’s daughter Billie Lourd, they found a way to honor Fisher’s legacy. Fisher died in December 2016 at 60 after a cardiac event. Returning cast includes Daisy Ridley, Adam Driver, John Boyega, Oscar Isaac, Lupita Nyong’o, Kelly Marie Tran, Mark Hamill, Billy Dee Williams, and others; Naomi Ackie and Richard E. Grant join in new roles. John Williams will compose the score; production was slated to begin August 1, with a December 20, 2019 release date.

Less than a week after Washington had praised North Korea for apparent restraint, Pyongyang dramatically escalated tensions by firing a ballistic missile that flew over northern Japan and landed in the Pacific. The launch, which followed other shorter-range tests, punctured diplomatic patience and increased momentum for tougher measures against North Korea, including potential new sanctions on its remaining export sectors and financial links. Analysts said the strike — timed during U.S.-South Korea military exercises and apparently calibrated to threaten but avoid provoking full military retaliation — will bolster U.S. and allied calls to “squeeze” Pyongyang economically and to target firms and banks that enable its trade.

Sanctions adopted by the U.N. Security Council on Aug. 5 aimed to cut about $1 billion in North Korean exports by curbing coal, iron ore and seafood shipments, but left textiles and apparel as major remaining export categories. Reports suggest Chinese firms may be using North Korean factories to produce clothes labeled “Made in China,” making textiles a likely next target. Crude oil supplies, which China no longer reports in customs data, are another sensitive lever both for sanctions and for clandestine support; opaque reporting makes it hard to track and regulate these flows. U.S. authorities have already sanctioned some Chinese and Russian entities and blocked a regional Chinese bank for alleged illicit ties, but experts argue tougher penalties against major Chinese banks could be required—though such moves risk provoking Beijing.

Beyond economics, the missile underscored a core strategic reality: North Korea appears intent on developing nuclear-capable missiles to deter U.S. retaliation, potentially changing the calculus of any U.S. military option. Deterrence experts warn that if Pyongyang can credibly threaten U.S. cities, Washington’s willingness to carry out decisive strikes could be constrained. Kim Jong Un’s strategy seems to aim at holding U.S. or allied targets at risk to blunt the prospect of regime-ending retaliation, while building a diversified, survivable missile force.

International reactions were pointed: the U.S. sought an emergency U.N. Security Council meeting; Tokyo decried an “unprecedented, grave and serious threat”; and Washington and Tokyo pledged coordinated pressure. China and Russia urged restraint and warned sanctions alone cannot resolve the crisis, while also criticizing U.S. military drills as provocative. In Japan, the launch triggered warning alerts, halted trains, briefly disrupted daily life in Hokkaido and revived debate over bolstering Japan’s defense. Markets initially dipped on fears of escalation but recovered as no immediate retaliation followed. Overall, the overflight deepened regional alarm, reinforced calls for tougher enforcement of sanctions and underscored the precarious balance between deterrence and escalation on the Korean Peninsula.

Former U.S. Rep. Corrine Brown was convicted on 18 of 22 federal counts for using a sham charity, One Door for Education, to siphon donor funds intended for disadvantaged students. Prosecutors say Brown and associates raised about $833,000 between 2012 and 2016 but distributed only $1,200 in scholarships. Convictions include seven counts of wire fraud, five of mail fraud, one conspiracy count and three counts of falsifying tax returns; jurors acquitted her on two mail and two wire fraud charges. Authorities presented bank records, emails, checks and other documents to show Brown directed deposits of One Door cash into her personal account and helped plan nine costly events that used roughly $330,000 of charity funds, including a golf tournament and luxury entertainment. Prosecutors portrayed Brown as living beyond her means and inflating charitable deductions while hiding income. Brown blamed former chief of staff Elias “Ronnie” Simmons, who pleaded guilty and testified against her; One Door president Carla Wiley also testified for prosecutors. Brown, who lost re-election after her indictment, maintains her innocence; her attorney plans motions for a new trial and will seek to delay sentencing, which Judge Timothy Corrigan could schedule within about three months if motions fail. Federal officials condemned the abuse of public trust.

A Seminole County mother, Sarah Anne Markham, was arrested in June on a child neglect charge after Casselberry police say she refused medical care for her newborn, who doctors said was dehydrated and losing weight. A pediatrician had advised immediate hospital admission, but Markham allegedly went home instead, declined to answer officers’ knocks, and preferred to seek a “second opinion” from a self-described vegan or natural practitioner whose details she could not provide. According to police, she also refused prescribed formula/medicine because it contained animal-derived ingredients and instead bought organic soy formula from Whole Foods, believing it safe without medical confirmation. Officers and Child Protective Services forced entry after an hour and the infant was taken to Florida Hospital South for treatment and placed in state custody; Markham was jailed but later bonded out. Police described her as uncooperative and unconcerned about the newborn’s well-being; she maintained she pursued religious-based or natural treatments and claimed bowel movements showed the baby was fine. Months later, a Seminole County judge returned custody to Markham on condition she provide a nutritionist’s report within 10 days. The judge dismissed child protective claims that she was unfit; family and defense attorneys say they expect the criminal case may be dropped. The baby, Caleb, remains on soy formula and has reportedly regained weight and is healthy with grandparents.

A lightning strike at the T-Bois Blues Festival in Larose, Louisiana, on Friday night, March 18, killed a 28-year-old New Orleans woman and injured two others who had sought shelter in a small personal tent during severe weather. Lafourche Parish Sheriff Craig Webre identified the deceased as Jacqui Stavis, a massage therapist and recent New Orleans transplant, who was found unresponsive after the strike around 10:05 p.m. and pronounced dead the next day at a local hospital. Two other New Orleans women in the same tent, ages 24 and 30, suffered injuries consistent with electric shock; the 24-year-old was transferred to University Medical Center in New Orleans, while the 30-year-old remained hospitalized in Larose. A large Labrador that had been inside the tent also died.

Responders including deputies, volunteer firefighters and EMTs transported the three victims to hospitals. Investigators learned the women had retreated into the small tent as a storm brought heavy wind, rain, thunder and lightning across the festival grounds. No specific cause of death has been released; National Weather Service data note that lightning strikes can cause cardiac arrest or severe brain injury and account for about 49 U.S. fatalities per year on average.

The low-key, three-day T-Bois festival—held on an alligator and crawfish farm and sometimes called the “Cajun Burning Man”—features blues and other music, camping and an arts-focused Burning Village. Friends and family mourned Stavis as a joyful, culturally immersed member of the New Orleans community whose sudden loss left a wide circle of loved ones devastated.

A viral New York magazine profile claiming 17-year-old Stuyvesant senior Mohammed Islam had made $72 million trading stocks has been revealed as fabricated. Islam and a friend, Damir Tulemaganbetov, told the New York Observer they had been swept up in attention and exaggerated or invented details. A public relations firm for Islam called the millions “about as real as monopoly money,” saying he runs a school investment club that conducts simulated trades, not real-money investing. Islam admitted he misled a reporter and now regrets the consequences for his family, who were embarrassed and angry.

The original New York piece described Islam as a wunderkind with “high eight figures,” featured him in the magazine’s “Reasons to Love New York” issue, and led other outlets to amplify the claim. After publication, readers and commenters questioned the plausibility; the magazine later amended its headline and acknowledged shortcomings in fact-checking, saying it had been duped and apologizing. Islam had even produced a document that appeared to be a Chase statement during fact-checking, but sources later said the documents were falsified.

Islam and Tulemaganbetov recounted how the rumor escalated—from a conversation with a reporter (connected via a friend’s parent) to media appearances and even a planned CNBC spot they ultimately canceled. They described sleepless nights as messages and coverage flooded in and expressed remorse, particularly toward their families. Critics noted the story’s implausibility—turning small sums into $72 million in a few years would require unreal returns—and blamed both the teens and the publications for failing to verify claims. The episode highlights the power of rumor, especially in tight communities, and lapses in journalistic fact-checking.

Authorities in Fargo, North Dakota, say 22-year-old Savanna Greywind, who was eight months pregnant when she disappeared Aug. 19, was the victim of homicidal violence; her body was found wrapped in plastic and duct tape in the Red River after extensive searches. A newborn believed to be Greywind’s daughter was discovered days earlier in an apartment in the same building where Greywind lived; the infant is now in social services custody. Prosecutors have charged neighbors Brooke Crews, 38, and William Hoehn, 32, with conspiracy to commit murder, conspiracy to commit kidnapping and giving false information to police. Both were detained with bond set at $2 million each and did not enter pleas at their initial court appearance. Court documents present conflicting accounts from the suspects. Crews reportedly told police she had arranged for Greywind to come to her apartment, advised her how to induce labor, and later admitted taking advantage of Greywind to obtain the baby and possibly keep it. Hoehn gave a different statement, claiming he returned to find Crews cleaning blood from their bathroom and that Crews presented him with the infant, saying, “This is our baby. This is our family.” He also said he discarded bloody shoes and towels away from the complex. Authorities found a farmstead on the Minnesota side of the river being searched for possible evidence, and said suspicious items there suggested it might be a crime scene. Officials are conducting DNA tests to confirm the infant’s parentage. Family members and the Native American community have reacted with anger and sorrow; a memorial with flowers and candles was placed at Greywind’s apartment building. Authorities have not released further autopsy details.

The remains of Brazilian football legend Manuel Francisco dos Santos, known as Garrincha, are missing, his family and local authorities say. Garrincha, who died in 1983 aged 49 and helped Brazil win World Cups in 1958 and 1962, was buried in Raiz da Serra cemetery in Magé, in Rio de Janeiro’s Baixada Fluminense. Relatives and cemetery staff now believe his body may have been removed during an exhumation about a decade ago to make space for another family burial and placed in a niche, but there is no documentation to confirm the move. The cemetery has two plots bearing Garrincha’s name—his original 1983 grave and a second tomb with an obelisk built in 1985—but administrators say there is uncertainty whether his remains are actually in either location.

Garrincha’s daughter, Rosangela Santos, expressed distress at not knowing where her father lies, while a cousin, Joao Rogoginsky, said the family was not present for the alleged exhumation and received no paperwork. Magé’s mayor, Rafael Tubarão, has proposed re-exhuming the graves, with the family’s consent, to perform DNA testing on any remains found and to possibly provide Garrincha with a proper mausoleum ahead of his birthday commemoration. Garrincha, celebrated as one of football’s greatest dribblers despite lifelong physical deformities and struggles with alcoholism, remains an iconic figure in Brazil; the uncertainty over his final resting place has prompted public concern and a push for official verification.

NASA has announced a broad suspension of bilateral engagements with Russia in response to Moscow’s actions in Ukraine, though cooperation on the operational International Space Station (ISS) is explicitly exempted. Michael O’Brien, NASA’s associate administrator for international and interagency relations, directed staff to halt travel, visits, meetings, emails and calls with Russian government representatives unless specifically excepted; multilateral meetings outside Russia that include Russian participants are allowed. The agency framed the move as part of U.S. diplomatic pressure and reiterated a push to restore U.S. human spaceflight launches from American soil via commercial partners—SpaceX, Sierra Nevada and Boeing—after reliance on Russian Soyuz flights since the shuttle’s retirement. Commercial crew flights, originally targeted for 2015, face funding delays and are now expected around 2017; each Soyuz seat costs roughly $71 million. Russian officials warned the freeze could harm international projects but said Russia can adapt. Observers note the ISS remains a shared and vulnerable symbol of cooperation: the partners have the greatest financial stake and, for the next few years, depend on Russia to transport crews, making the station a potential pressure point in the crisis.

A masked assailant carried out a deadly stabbing at the Kronan school in Trollhättan, Sweden, on a Thursday morning, killing a male teacher and a 17-year-old pupil and wounding two others before police shot him; the attacker later died in hospital. The 21-year-old local suspect entered school premises around 10:10 a.m., clad in black and wearing a mask, carrying several knife-like weapons—reports described a long sword among them. He reportedly knocked on two classroom doors and stabbed the students who opened them and struck at staff in a cafe area used by pupils, including younger children who had visited the library earlier. Some students initially thought his appearance was a prank or Halloween stunt; at least one pupil said classmates posed for photos with him before the violence began. Police fired two shots when the attacker attempted to assault officers; one round struck him. Authorities searched his home and said they found “interesting” material, and were investigating possible links to far-right extremism after media and social accounts reportedly showed Nazi-era imagery and references. Officials have identified the suspect but did not immediately release his name; they said they do not believe others were involved. Two victims—another pupil (around 15) and a teacher—were seriously injured and underwent surgery and remained in critical condition. The incident shook the community of about 400 students across age groups and drew national attention: Prime Minister Stefan Löfven and King Carl XVI Gustaf condemned the attack, calling it a dark, shocking day for Sweden and promising support for victims, families, and the school community. School attacks are rare in Sweden, making the event particularly traumatic.

Itzcoatl “Izzy” Ocampo, a 25-year-old former Marine accused of killing six people — four homeless men and a woman and her son — died after ingesting Ajax while jailed awaiting trial, his attorney said. Deputies found Ocampo vomiting and shaking in his single-person cell Wednesday evening; he was hospitalized and pronounced dead Thursday afternoon. Authorities will perform an autopsy and the Orange County district attorney’s office is conducting the routine investigation into the in-custody death. Ocampo’s lawyer said the cleaning product was apparently accumulated over time and that his client, who exhibited severe and obvious mental-health problems, should have been more closely supervised. Jail officials noted deputies are generally required to check cells at least hourly. Prosecutors had alleged Ocampo embarked on a “serial thrill-kill” rampage in late 2011 and early 2012, stabbing four homeless men — some more than 40 times — with a single-edged blade, and also killing a school friend’s mother and brother. He was charged in 2012 and faced possible death-penalty prosecution; his scheduled pretrial appearance was in January. Victims’ relatives expressed relief that the suspect would no longer stand trial, while officials said his death denies the families the opportunity for judicial closure.

When Google announced its corporate restructuring and new parent name, Alphabet, the move immediately ran into naming conflicts. German automaker BMW already owns the valuable alphabet.com domain for its fleet services unit and told The New York Times it does not intend to sell; BMW is reviewing whether Google’s use of the Alphabet name infringes its trademark but has not pursued legal action. Alphabet instead launched abc.xyz as its web address, and shortly afterward Google also registered the long alphabet string domain (abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz.com), though its purpose is unclear. The shift prompted confusion because many entities use “alphabet”: over 100 U.S. trademark registrations incorporate the word, and an Ohio company named Alphabet, Inc. has existed since 1965. Social handles were likewise unavailable—@Alphabet on Twitter is owned by an individual, Chris Andrikanich, who drew attention after the announcement. Critics pointed out the strategic importance of owning a .com, echoing Paul Graham’s advice that lacking it “signals weakness,” but Google co-founder Larry Page said Alphabet will not be a consumer-facing brand and won’t introduce products under that name. Alphabet will serve as a holding company for Google and unrelated “moonshot” ventures, aiming to improve management, transparency, and focus.

A Food and Drug Administration (FDA) study has found that most dark chocolate bars tested contain milk, posing a risk for people with milk allergies. Of 94 unique dark chocolate bars sampled from across the U.S., 61% tested positive for milk or milk-derived components, even though only six listed milk as an ingredient. The contamination arises partly because milk ingredients and powdered milk are widely used in chocolate production and because equipment and facilities are often shared between milk and non-milk products, allowing cross-contact.

Advisory label statements such as “may contain milk,” “made on equipment shared with milk,” or “manufactured in a facility that uses milk” frequently indicate actual milk presence: the FDA found milk in 75% of bars carrying such warnings. Labels claiming “dairy-free,” “lactose-free,” or “vegan” were also sometimes misleading—15% of dairy-free/lactose-free bars and 25% of vegan-labeled bars contained milk. Even bars with no mention of milk on the label showed contamination in 33% of cases. Because milk proteins (not just lactose) can trigger serious allergic reactions, these findings are especially concerning; “may” often functions as “likely” for milk presence in dark chocolate.

The FDA and industry groups advise that people with severe milk allergies avoid dark chocolate unless the manufacturer explicitly confirms production in a milk-free facility using dedicated equipment. The FDA is evaluating regulatory responses and cites the forthcoming Preventive Controls for Human Food rule under FSMA, which would require firms to implement allergen controls and reduce cross-contact risks. Until labeling and manufacturing practices improve, consumers who must avoid milk should treat most dark chocolate as a high-risk food and seek trusted, dedicated allergen-free sources.

President Donald Trump spent the weekend at his Mar-a-Lago resort — his third straight there — and played a full round of golf Sunday, reversing an earlier White House statement that he had only played a few holes. White House spokesperson Sarah Sanders clarified that Trump “intended to play a few holes and decided to play longer” while also conducting meetings and interviews. Professional golfer Rory McIlroy revealed on his site that he played 18 holes with Trump at Trump International, Florida, and estimated the president “probably shot around 80,” calling him “a decent player for a guy in his 70s.” A photo of Trump with McIlroy, Clear Sports CEO Garry Singer and former Yankees player Paul O’Neill circulated widely; the actual four-ball included McIlroy, Trump, ISM agent Nick Mullen and friend Rich Levine. McIlroy said he accepted the impromptu invitation despite a rib injury. Trump has hosted other golf partners, including Tiger Woods, Ernie Els and Lexi Thompson, and has used golf for informal diplomacy, previously playing with Japanese PM Shinzo Abe. McIlroy’s round with Trump drew notable social media backlash, with critics calling his decision politicized; defenders like Piers Morgan denounced the online vitriol.

President Trump, frustrated that Congress allocated only $1.6 billion for border barriers in the recent $1.3 trillion spending bill, has privately suggested using Pentagon funds to finance construction of the U.S.-Mexico wall. He raised the idea with advisers, Defense Secretary Jim Mattis and House Speaker Paul D. Ryan, framing the project as a national-security priority and noting the Pentagon’s roughly $700 billion allocation in the omnibus package. Trump lamented signing the spending bill and has publicly and privately sought ways to deliver on his campaign promise that Mexico would pay for the wall. 

Administration officials and advisers described the proposal as unlikely to succeed. Reprogramming current defense appropriations or moving funds from the 2019 defense budget would require congressional approval—likely a 60-vote threshold in the Senate for a budget amendment—and could provoke resistance from Democrats and defense-focused Republicans who oppose diverting money intended for aircraft, weapons and readiness. The $1.6 billion that was approved is tightly restricted, largely limited to levees and operational fencing, and excludes most of the prototype designs Trump favors except near San Diego. 

White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders declined to discuss specifics but said construction would continue. Critics, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, called redirecting military funds a misuse of resources that could be legally challenged and would harm troops. The idea emerged amid collapsed talks to secure $25 billion for the wall in exchange for protections for young immigrants, and reflects Trump’s urgency to show progress to supporters before midterm elections.

Charlottesville police continued an intensive search for 18-year-old University of Virginia student Hannah Graham, nearly two weeks after she was last seen Sept. 13. Authorities have combed most of the college town and expanded searches into surrounding Albemarle County farms and woodlands, asking property owners, real estate agents and neighbors to check vacant buildings, lawns and rural roads for anything unusual — tire tracks, clothing, an iPhone 5S in a pink case reportedly missing with Graham, or other evidence. Police emphasized the urgency as more time passes, while maintaining hope her parents share.

Jesse L. “LJ” Matthew Jr., 32, is the last person known to have been with Graham and has been charged with abduction with intent to sexually assault her. Investigators collected evidence from his car and apartment and say forensic lab work contributed to the decision to charge him, though officials have not publicly detailed the specific evidence. Matthew was captured Wednesday on the Bolivar Peninsula in Galveston County, Texas, after a woman on a Gilchrist beach reported a suspicious man. A deputy found him camping in a tent; he initially gave a false name and was arrested after his plates matched a Virginia warrant. He waived extradition in a Texas court, declined a court-appointed attorney and is to be returned to Charlottesville. Charlottesville police have not interviewed him since his arrest because he has invoked his right to counsel.

Eye-witness accounts differ about whether Graham entered the Tempo restaurant where she was last seen: the owner says she waited outside while Matthew bought drinks and left with him; police say they have at least one witness placing her inside. Surveillance captured Graham walking with Matthew on the Downtown Mall shortly after 1 a.m., and her friends received a last text at 1:06 a.m. Investigators are asking people who know Matthew to identify locations he frequented — places he might fish or visit — and a $100,000 reward is being offered for information leading to her safe return.

Matthew, described by acquaintances as a “gentle giant” who worked at UVA hospital and volunteered as a youth coach, grew up locally and attended regional universities but has unclear ties to Texas. Galveston officials have searched his car and nearby dunes and plan to widen searches, though they say there is no indication of Graham’s location. Residents of the remote Bolivar Peninsula, where Matthew was arrested, said its sparse beaches and transient campers could allow someone to remain unnoticed, underscoring the challenge authorities face in locating Graham.

Chelsea Clinton, raised in Arkansas and shaped by elite education and varied early careers, has settled into a defining role as vice chair of the Bill, Hillary & Chelsea Clinton Foundation. After exploring international relations at Oxford, consulting at McKinsey, hedge funds, media, and public health studies, Chelsea returned to the family enterprise with a data-driven, managerial focus. She aims to modernize the sprawling charity—consolidating offices, building a database to track projects, pushing impact audits for the Clinton Global Initiative’s 2,800 commitments, and recruiting younger, tech-savvy members. Chelsea champions measurable results over anecdote, drives initiatives on childhood diarrhea treatment and juvenile-detention nutrition, and leverages her profile to convene partners and speed commitments. Her role sits uneasily within a powerful family machine: Bill remains the fundraising, celebrity force and Hillary a likely 2016 candidate, so Chelsea must balance visibility with organizational stewardship and campaign law constraints. Though she resists a fixed political path, she no longer reflexively rules out office and may serve as a senior adviser or eventually run for Congress—using the foundation as a platform to shape policy and public service.

A Los Angeles entertainment executive who says she was sexually assaulted by a man she met on Match.com has filed suit asking the dating site to screen members against sex-offender registries. Identified only as Jane Doe in the complaint, the plaintiff is represented by attorney Mark L. Webb, who plans to ask a Los Angeles County Superior Court judge for a temporary injunction to halt new Match.com sign-ups until the company implements such checks. The woman, described as an Ivy League graduate working in film and television, met the alleged assailant at a West Hollywood café. After a second date he allegedly followed her home and assaulted her; she later discovered online that he had prior convictions for sexual battery. Charges stemming from the incident are pending, Webb said. Match.com did not comment to reporters, though the company previously told KABC-TV that it posts safety tips and emphasizes members’ responsibility to vet people they meet, calling incidents “extremely rare” but nonetheless horrifying. Webb argues registry checks are not foolproof but would be a meaningful safety measure.

As Israel’s Operation Protective Edge entered its fourth week, Israel’s security cabinet ordered continued offensive operations in Gaza with a stated focus on destroying Hamas’ cross-border tunnel network. Heavy fighting and airstrikes have driven high casualties and displacement: Palestinian health officials report well over 1,300 dead and thousands wounded, while Israel has lost dozens of soldiers and several civilians. Israel called up additional reservists and vowed to complete tunnel destruction “with or without a cease-fire.” Diplomatic efforts, including Egyptian-brokered talks and U.S.–UN appeals, pushed a 72-hour ceasefire starting Friday, with both sides indicating conditional agreement. Humanitarian concerns mounted as UN agencies reported schools sheltering displaced people were struck, provoking international condemnation and accusations of possible war crimes against both sides.

A grizzly bear that had been linked by DNA to the scene of a fatal mauling in Yellowstone was euthanized after investigators connected the sow to the area where a second hiker’s body was found, park officials said. The 250-pound female was associated with the killing of John Wallace of Michigan in August after hair and scat recovered near his body matched the bear. Wallace had been hiking alone in Hayden Valley, a backcountry area frequented by bears, and there were no witnesses. By the time other hikers found him a day later, one or more bears had fed on his body. Park Superintendent Dan Wenk said the decision to kill the bear was made to protect visitors and staff, though the inquiry remains open and may never definitively prove whether the same sow also killed California hiker Brian Matayoshi in July. After Matayoshi’s death park officials had allowed the bear to remain free because it appeared to be defending cubs and showed no predatory behavior. Investigators now suspect cub tracks at Wallace’s scene may have been washed away by rain. Wildlife officials captured at least seven bears in Hayden Valley after the mauling; DNA, tracks and other evidence indicated at least nine bears were in the area, attracted by two nearby bison carcasses. Two cubs were captured and relocated to the Grizzly and Wolf Discovery Center. The greater Yellowstone ecosystem hosts roughly 600 grizzlies, and human-bear conflicts have reached record levels, with many incidents driven by bears seeking human-related foods.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention postponed a planned Public Health Grand Rounds session on the public health response to a nuclear detonation after strong media interest and amid heightened U.S.–North Korea rhetoric. The webinar, scheduled for Tuesday and organized months in advance, would have included U.S. experts discussing radiation, preparedness and a presentation titled “Preparing for the Unthinkable.” The initial announcement featured a mushroom-cloud image, drawing attention as it came shortly after public exchanges between President Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un about nuclear capabilities and “nuclear buttons.” About three dozen media outlets sought to attend the Atlanta-based broadcast. On Friday, the CDC substituted the topic with one focused on influenza, citing a nationwide spike in flu cases. The agency said the Grand Rounds would instead provide timely guidance for public health professionals on reducing seasonal flu spread and managing antiviral shortages in hard-hit areas, noting the season’s heavy burden largely stems from influenza A H3N2 and poses particular risk to young children and those 65 and older. The CDC said the nuclear preparedness session would be rescheduled and emphasized that Grand Rounds aim to deliver up-to-date, science-based information to clinicians and public health workers.

Republican tax proposals in Congress would greatly reduce or eliminate the federal estate tax, a change Iowa lawmakers, including Sen. Chuck Grassley and Reps. Steve King, David Young and Rod Blum, have endorsed as protecting family farms and small businesses. They argue the tax — a 40 percent levy on assets above $5.5 million for individuals ($11 million for couples) — can force heirs to liquidate farms or businesses and penalizes savers by effectively taxing earnings twice. The House bill would double exemptions and then repeal the tax in 2024; the Senate bill raises exemptions to $11 million/$22 million, cutting projected revenues by tens of billions over a decade.

But federal data and nonpartisan research suggest the practical impact on family farms and small businesses is very limited. Nationwide only about 5,000 estates a year owe estate tax; IRS data show just 682 of those filers in 2016 reported any farm assets, and a Congressional Research Service study estimated only about 65 farm estates annually owe estate tax. USDA analysis places farm estates owing tax higher in 2016 (roughly 160), but the vast majority are larger, diversified operations often with nonfarm assets. In Iowa, IRS records show only dozens of taxpayers annually file estate returns that result in tax owed; experts at Iowa State say they know of no Iowa families forced to sell land to pay estate taxes since the exemption rose in 2012.

Critics highlight that while a few farms and small businesses could be affected, most estate-tax revenues come from the very wealthy (72 percent from the top 1 percent). Supporters counter that even the planning burden — expensive legal and accounting work to avoid liability — is harmful. Grassley also drew public criticism for a remark contrasting “investors” with people who spend on “booze or women or movies,” a comment he later defended as emphasizing fairness and the protection of savings. Lawmakers must reconcile House and Senate differences before a final bill reaches the president.

Reports claim Robert Pattinson and Riley Keough—Elvis Presley’s 24-year-old granddaughter—are romantically linked after being seen together in his truck and spending time during late June. Sources say the pair, who met through mutual connections including Kristen Stewart and Dior events, are “having fun” and may spend the Fourth of July together before Pattinson leaves for filming. Insiders suggest Pattinson values Keough’s perceived trustworthiness and “lady-like” manner following the fallout from Stewart’s widely publicized affair with director Rupert Sanders. Friends describe the relationship as early and possibly short-term. The situation reportedly upset Stewart, who introduced Keough to the circle while mentoring her on The Runaways. Coverage also notes Pattinson’s recent social life, past struggles with fame, and Keough’s modeling and acting background.

A New York City real estate agent’s remark to China’s CCTV about an extravagant purchase has gone global: an anonymous Chinese mother reportedly bought a $6.5 million condominium in Manhattan’s luxury One57 building for her two‑year‑old daughter. Sotheby’s senior VP Kevin Brown recounted that the buyer insisted her child needed to be near top universities like Columbia, NYU or Harvard, prompting the surprising revelation of the daughter’s age. One57, a 90‑story tower designed by a Pritzker Prize–winning architect, features lavish amenities including a library with a pool table and large aquarium, a private concert hall and a pet washroom. The purchase has provoked debate: some view it as extreme spoiling, while others note it may be a shrewd investment—Brown said the condo’s value rose to about $8.9 million less than two years later. In China, social media speculation tied the buyer’s wealth to possible connections with corrupt officials, a sensitive topic amid widening income inequality and President Xi Jinping’s anti‑corruption campaign.

Theresa May and Andrea Leadsom emerged as the final two contenders to succeed David Cameron after MPs eliminated Michael Gove. May topped the parliamentary ballots with 199 votes to Leadsom’s 84; Conservative members will decide the winner by 9 September. May, a long-serving home secretary and former Remain supporter, presents herself as an experienced unifier able to negotiate Brexit; Leadsom, a junior energy minister and prominent Leave campaigner, emphasizes business experience and swift action on leaving the EU despite limited cabinet experience. The contest highlights deep party divides over Brexit, leadership style and priorities, as rank-and-file Conservatives—mostly older, middle-class members—cast the deciding votes.

A concerning form of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) carrying OXA-48-like carbapenemase enzymes is increasing in the United States, the CDC reports. CRE are dangerous because they resist many antibiotics and can cause health-care–associated infections with high mortality. What distinguishes these OXA-48–producing strains is that the carbapenemase gene is plasmid-borne—a mobile piece of DNA that can transfer between bacteria—raising the risk of rapid spread and of other normally susceptible bacteria acquiring resistance. Although OXA-48 producers often show lower-level carbapenem resistance and can remain susceptible to some cephalosporins, that atypical susceptibility profile has hindered detection in routine U.S. lab testing, earning the strains the nickname “the phantom menace.” Between June 2010 and August 2015, CDC confirmed CRE with OXA-48-like enzymes from 43 patients across 19 states; case counts rose from one in 2010 to 11 annually in 2013–2015, and small U.S. clusters indicate in-country transmission. Many affected patients had recent international travel or hospitalization—especially in India—suggesting importation as a major source. The report also notes parallel global alarms, including a plasmid-mediated colistin-resistance gene first found in China and subsequently detected in Denmark, underscoring how mobile resistance genes can spread worldwide via people, animals, and food. CDC has broadened surveillance definitions to improve detection and urges screening and transmission-based precautions for patients recently hospitalized abroad. Experts emphasize prudent antibiotic use, enhanced detection, and infection-control measures to limit further dissemination.

Royalty Exchange has launched a new vehicle, Royalty Flow, and signed a letter of intent to buy at least 15 percent of an income stream from Eminem’s recordings, with an option to acquire 25 percent. The stream originates from FBT Productions, the Bass brothers’ company that invested in Eminem early and retains royalties from his studio albums released between 1999 and 2013. Royalty Flow plans a Regulation A+ offering to raise $11 million–$50 million; if it reaches a minimum funding target it will pursue a NASDAQ listing. If proceeds are under $25 million Royalty Flow will pay $9.75 million for 15 percent; above $25 million it will pay $18.75 million for 25 percent. FBT’s earnings from Eminem rose 43 percent to $5.07 million last year, and historically FBT has received $47.2 million since 2011, though revenues vary year to year. The offering’s minimum investment will be $2,250 for 150 shares, and Royalty Flow intends to pay dividends from royalties while reinvesting to buy additional catalogs. The Bass brothers and Royalty Flow emphasize this as a new model letting fans and smaller investors buy into superstar music assets—assets they see as uncorrelated with public markets and benefiting from streaming growth. Eminem is not involved in the deal; his representative says he was not consulted and has no connection to the company. The plan follows legal precedents—FBT won a 2012 ruling affirming its share of digital revenues—and historical precedents in music securitization like Bowie Bonds. Royalty Flow will remain a passive investor, aiming to acquire and hold royalty streams and potentially set a template for future securitizations of major artists’ catalogs if the model proves successful.

Fidel Ángel Castro Díaz-Balart, the 68-year-old eldest son of former Cuban leader Fidel Castro and widely known as “Fidelito,” has died by suicide in Havana after months of treatment for deep depression, Cuban state media reported. A nuclear physicist trained in the Soviet Union, Fidelito headed Cuba’s nuclear program from 1980 until its suspension in 1992 following the USSR’s collapse. In later years he served as a scientific adviser to the Council of State and as vice president of Cuba’s Academy of Sciences, though colleagues said his role had become largely ceremonial and his proposals—particularly on renewable energy—were not adopted by the government. Born in 1949 during his father’s first marriage to Mirta Díaz-Balart, Fidelito spent part of his childhood in the United States before being brought back to Cuba after the 1959 revolution; through his mother he was related to critics in the Cuban-American exile community, including U.S. Congressman Mario Díaz-Balart. The son’s personal struggles were little known publicly until the announcement of his death, which came just over a year after Fidel Castro’s own death in November 2016. State outlets said he had been hospitalized and then treated as an outpatient; funeral arrangements will be handled by his family. Colleagues recall him as multilingual, curious, and increasingly weary of living in his father’s shadow.

A flurry of developments has intensified the federal investigation into possible coordination between Russia and the 2016 Trump campaign, bringing scrutiny into the West Wing itself. The probe — which began last July to explore whether campaign associates coordinated with Russian operatives — has moved into a more active phase with interviews, grand-jury subpoenas and the recent appointment of former FBI director Robert S. Mueller III as special counsel. Investigators have identified a current senior White House adviser, described as close to the president, as a “significant person of interest,” signaling reach into top levels of government; officials declined to name the individual. Authorities remain focused on former campaign and administration figures such as Michael Flynn and Paul Manafort, while also examining potential financial crimes and influence operations tied to Russia.

Controversy erupted after President Trump, a day after firing FBI Director James Comey, disparaged Comey during an Oval Office meeting with Russia’s foreign minister Sergey Lavrov and Ambassador Sergey Kislyak. White House notes and officials’ accounts describe Trump complaining about pressure from the investigation; the administration defended the remarks as diplomatic tactics and blamed leaks for harming national security. The president has denied collusion. Separately, investigators have subpoenaed records related to Flynn’s Flynn Intel Group, which received foreign payments, and continue probes into contacts by Jared Kushner, Jeff Sessions, Rex Tillerson and others. The inquiry aims to determine contacts with Kremlin operatives, business ties to Russia, and any role in hacking and email disclosures during the campaign; its course under Mueller is unfolding.

Jayme Closs, a 13-year-old from Barron, Wisconsin, has been missing since Monday, Oct. 15, after her parents, James (56) and Denise Closs (46), were found shot to death in their home following a 911 call. Deputies arrived within minutes, found the parents deceased from gunshot wounds, and discovered Jayme was gone. Investigators believe she was in the house during the killings and consider her endangered; authorities do not believe she ran away and have not identified a suspect or motive. The phone that placed the 911 call was recovered and traced, but officials declined to name its owner. Over 800 tips have poured in, more than 100 local and state FBI agents are involved, and the FBI expanded the search nationwide, adding Jayme to a top missing-persons list and distributing digital posters. Sheriff Chris Fitzgerald organized a 100-person volunteer search of areas near Highway 8; nothing of evidentiary value was found. The community is shaken; schools received support from a Wausau school resource officer and therapy dog, and the state will send counselors and trauma-informed training funded by an emergency grant. Jayme is described as 5 feet tall, 100 pounds, with green eyes and blonde or strawberry-blonde hair. Tips: 1-855-744-3879.

The piece foregrounds the transactional, often adversarial nature of celebrity interviews while centering on Kate McKinnon, the Emmy-winning S.N.L. performer whose comic gifts—mimicry, slapstick, elastic physicality—have made her a standout of her generation. The writer opens with a wry thesis: interviews masquerade as friendly chats but are really mutual hustles—stars want exposure, journalists want revelations. Against that cynical frame, McKinnon emerges as unusually likable, disarmingly unpretentious, and vividly talented. In a sweaty East Village lunch the author observes her casual, unglamorous attire and striking, feline features; her alert, sensitive demeanor that can be spooked by recorder pens or other intrusions; and the paradox of someone both un-vanity and photogenic. Much of McKinnon’s recent renown derives from her S.N.L. work—above all her Hillary Clinton, an impression that combines sharp satire with surprising empathy. Her Hillary is neither merely vicious nor purely comic: she’s a steadier, plaintive figure—“half schoolmarm, half princess”—whose pathos makes audiences laugh and feel. McKinnon’s approach depends on close imaginative identification with real figures; impersonation requires staying open and emotionally raw, which can be psychologically risky. The article situates McKinnon among S.N.L. traditions—invoking Jan Hooks, Amy Poehler, Molly Shannon, Tina Fey, and Catherine O’Hara—and credits her collaborative chemistry with writers Chris Kelly and Sarah Schneider. It notes her film roles (Ghostbusters, Rough Night) but suggests her political theater on S.N.L. is culturally essential, especially during a hyperpoliticized era when the show has become a cathartic national ritual. The piece also reflects on Alec Baldwin’s Trump and S.N.L.’s odd symbiosis with the White House, underscoring how satire can reshape public perception. Overall, McKinnon is presented as a rare comic who makes characters lovable through generosity and empathy while navigating the complicated public-business of modern fame.

Multiple outlets report that 20-year-old Kylie Jenner is pregnant with her first child, a girl, with 25-year-old rapper Travis Scott, and is reportedly due in February. Sources tell PEOPLE that Jenner and Scott began sharing the news with friends in recent weeks, though Scott reportedly started telling friends as early as July. Insiders describe the pregnancy as unexpected but joyous; they say both are excited, with Scott said to be affectionate and eager to become a father. Jenner, who has been dating Scott since April after splitting from longtime boyfriend Tyga, was reportedly careful about concealing the pregnancy early on — posting older photos that showed a flat stomach — because she feared the news would leak before she was ready to announce it publicly.

Family members are said to be thrilled and supportive of the relationship; sources note there are currently no wedding plans. The announcement arrives as other KarJenner family additions are expected: Kim Kardashian West is reported to be expecting a child via surrogate, and Jenner is already aunt to several nieces and nephews. Tabloid reports also reference social-media reactions from ex Tyga, who briefly posted and deleted a Snapchat that implied paternity dispute. Representatives for Jenner and Scott did not immediately comment.

Former Penn State assistant coach Jerry Sandusky, interviewed at length after his indictment on numerous child sexual abuse charges, denied sexually abusing any child while insisting his decades of work with disadvantaged youngsters had been misconstrued. He acknowledged, however, that his household and professional life blurred conventional boundaries: his State College home became, he said, an “extended family” and second home for many Second Mile charity kids, with wrestling, sleepovers, showers and travel together. Sandusky described physical affection—hugging, wrestling, even blowing on stomachs—as spontaneous and benign, and defended gifts, jobs at camps and bank accounts he set up for youths as acts of benevolence. He admitted some of these behaviors and supports matched elements prosecutors cite as manipulative tools to build trust. Sandusky said Penn State legend Joe Paterno never confronted him about alleged incidents, including a 2002 shower episode, and maintained that charity supervisors did not restrict his access until 2008; Second Mile’s executive director later resigned after the indictment. Sandusky’s wife had raised concerns about neglecting their own children amid the chaotic household. Throughout the interview he oscillated between subdued reflection, awkward humor and sorrow over his ruined reputation, emphasizing he misses coaching, the Second Mile, and ordinary relationships now threatened by the charges.

A large prospective analysis from the Nurses’ Health Study II suggests higher pre-pregnancy potato intake is associated with an increased risk of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). The study followed 15,632 women across 21,693 singleton pregnancies between 1991 and 2001, documenting 854 GDM cases. Dietary information, captured every four years, distinguished baked/boiled/mashed potatoes, French fries, and chips. After adjusting for age, parity, family history, lifestyle and overall diet quality, consuming two to four 100 g servings of potatoes weekly was linked to a 27% higher GDM risk; five or more servings weekly raised risk by about 50%. Associations remained significant after additional adjustment for BMI, though the French-fries link was attenuated by BMI adjustment. Substituting two weekly potato servings with other vegetables, legumes, or whole grains was associated with a 9–12% lower GDM risk. Investigators propose high-glycaemic starch in potatoes causes sharp postprandial glucose spikes that may stress pancreatic β cells; fried potatoes may add harmful fats and advanced glycation products. Strengths include prospective design, repeated dietary measures and numerous cases; limitations include primarily white, health-professional participants, self-reported diet and GDM, lack of gestational weight-gain data, and observational design that precludes causal inference. UK experts and public-health authorities caution that this single observational study does not prove causation and underline that starchy foods, including potatoes, are important sources of energy and fiber within balanced diets; guidance emphasizes variety and wholegrain choices. Authors call for intervention trials to confirm findings. Meanwhile, moderate consumption and swapping some potato servings for lower-GI vegetables, legumes or whole grains could be a prudent approach for women planning pregnancy.

In 2012 Harvard Divinity School’s Karen King announced a Coptic papyrus fragment—the so-called “Gospel of Jesus’s Wife”—containing the phrase “Jesus said to them, ‘My wife…’ ” This provoked wide interest because, if authentic, it might suggest beliefs that Jesus was married. The fragment’s anonymous owner and provenance raised early questions, and subsequent investigation has increasingly suggested the piece is a modern forgery.

Live Science traced documents claiming the owner bought the papyrus from Hans‑Ulrich Laukamp in Potsdam in 1963, but inquiries found Laukamp did not collect antiquities, and could not plausibly have acquired the item across the Berlin Wall. Berlin export records show no matching paperwork. Christian Askeland, a Coptic specialist, analyzed a second papyrus from the same owner—a double‑sided fragment containing Gospel of John text—and demonstrated it copied line breaks from a 1924 publication, a telltale sign of forgery. That John fragment shares handwriting and ink characteristics with the Jesus’s‑wife fragment; radiocarbon dating places the John piece in the 7th–9th centuries, but its Lycopolitan dialect had fallen out of use earlier, reinforcing doubts.

Scholars argue that the matching suspicious features across multiple items from the same cache make repeated “lottery wins” implausible and point to fabrication. Some experts urge retraction; others are reviewing Askeland’s findings. Harvard has not publicly responded to the mounting evidence. Meanwhile, a Smithsonian Channel documentary planned to air despite the controversy.

At a tense House Intelligence Committee hearing following disclosures about National Security Agency programs, NSA Director Keith Alexander said communications surveillance helped thwart more than 50 “potential terrorist events” worldwide since Sept. 11, 2001. He said about 10 of those plots had a U.S. nexus; most were disrupted overseas. Alexander and other senior officials emphasized that two distinct authorities played central roles: Section 702 of the Patriot Act, which permits targeting foreigners’ Internet communications (commonly associated with the PRISM program), and Section 215, which authorizes bulk collection of U.S. phone metadata. Alexander estimated roughly 90 percent of the disrupted plots involved the Internet-surveillance program; a smaller portion relied on call-tracking records. Deputy FBI Director Sean Joyce detailed four cases publicly: the 2009 Najibullah Zazi subway bombing plot, a disrupted scheme targeting the New York Stock Exchange, a plot against a Danish newspaper tied to the 2006 cartoons, and a reopened post-9/11 investigation that produced new leads. Officials argued these tools “connect the dots” and are vital to prevention, while noting oversight mechanisms—FISA court approvals, internal auditing, and limited access—govern their use. Deputy Attorney General James Cole defended the legal basis, saying Congress twice reauthorized the relevant Patriot Act provision and asserting Fourth Amendment protections don’t apply to the metadata collected under Section 215. Lawmakers pressed on what could be disclosed without harming methods; Alexander said classified briefings would provide more detail. Officials warned leaks have done “irreversible” damage and could hinder capabilities, while acknowledging uncertainty about whether some plots might have been stopped by other means. Public opinion remained divided, and the hearing underscored the ongoing tension between national security, secrecy, and civil liberties.

EMILY's List launched "Sarah Doesn't Speak for Me," an online campaign backing 32 pro-choice female candidates and challenging Sarah Palin's "Mama Grizzlies" endorsements. President Stephanie Schriock called Palin's allies "backwards-looking" and highlighted key races against Palin-endorsed women. Susan B. Anthony List countered, praising Palin and promoting pro-life female candidates via a bus tour. Both groups tout long records electing women—EMILY's List pro-choice victors and Susan B. Anthony List pro-life winners—escalating partisan competition over women candidates.

At the National Museum of African American History and Culture dedication, a warm, widely shared moment captured increasing public camaraderie between former President George W. Bush and First Lady Michelle Obama. Bush, who signed the legislation creating the museum in 2003, was a featured speaker at the Smithsonian event. Photographers including David Hume Kennerly captured Michelle Obama reaching over to hug Bush as their spouses applauded. The image quickly sparked strong reactions online, with many praising the display of respect and bipartisanship amid a politically polarized climate; some users called it a symbol of unity during fraught times. Others mocked the moment or used it for partisan commentary. Reddit users also turned the photo into a playful editing meme, reimagining Bush in humorous roles while presidential contenders appeared in altered versions. The embrace resonated broadly because it showed leaders from different parties sharing a candid, human moment at a ceremony honoring African American history.

Health officials reported 279 pregnant women in the United States and its territories with laboratory evidence of possible Zika virus infection as of May 12, 2016—157 in U.S. states and DC, and 122 in territories. The CDC’s new weekly surveillance counts both symptomatic and asymptomatic infections to better track outcomes. Fewer than a dozen adverse fetal or infant outcomes have been reported so far, but most pregnancies remain ongoing, so risks could rise. Most U.S. mainland cases are travel-related; there have been no confirmed mosquito-borne transmissions in the continental U.S., though local spread is occurring in Puerto Rico. President Obama urged Congress to approve robust funding—White House requests $1.9 billion—to support vaccine research, mosquito control, surveillance, and care for affected families.

United Parcel Service (UPS) said it will begin applying surcharges for residential deliveries after costs surged during a disappointing holiday season that left fourth-quarter profit down from a year earlier. UPS mobilized more workers and equipment to handle an anticipated holiday peak that failed to materialize, driving up operating expenses—especially in its domestic ground package unit—and prompting the new pricing move. CEO David Abney said surcharges will be phased in over several years as contracts with major customers are renegotiated, aiming to ensure UPS is compensated for the higher cost of one-off home deliveries, which the company says can cost roughly three times more than business deliveries. Despite spending $500 million on network improvements and adding seasonal staff after 2013’s delivery failures, forecasting e-commerce volumes proved difficult. For the quarter, UPS reported net profit of $1.15 billion and earnings per share of $1.25, with revenue up 6% to $15.9 billion; operating expenses rose over 20%, severely eroding domestic ground unit profits. UPS forecast 2015 EPS of $5.05–$5.30, near analyst estimates.

A Detroit teenager was detained Monday after attempting to rob a Chase Bank on West Seven Mile. The 15- or 16-year-old entered about 2–2:30 p.m., handed a teller a note and threatened a bomb to demand cash. The teller complied, but as the suspect tried to leave, she activated the bank’s “man-trap” — a two-set automatic door system that locked him between doors, trapping him until police arrived. Officers took the teen into custody and transported him to a juvenile facility. Authorities said it’s unclear whether he had a weapon and whether he’ll be prosecuted in juvenile or adult court. The teller’s quick action prevented his escape.

Kelly Preston told TODAY host Natalie Morales that Scientology’s “silent birth” method shaped the birth of her new son Benjamin and influenced her parenting. She described the practice as keeping spoken words to a minimum during delivery—allowing only natural sounds like moaning—so the baby is brought into the world “as peaceful and gentle a way as possible.” Preston credited this approach with contributing to her children’s calm, happy demeanors and said Benjamin’s arrival has helped renew purpose and healing in her family after the 2009 death of their 16-year-old son Jett. Conceiving Benjamin took three years and, at age 48, Preston said she didn’t dwell on the medical risks of a later-in-life pregnancy, only on the challenges. She called the baby “wonderfully healing” and noted the couple has received many touching messages from the public. Preston was also promoting her film Casino Jack and praised co-star Kevin Spacey for making her laugh and easing her return to work during a difficult time. The interview included further explanation of silent birth and its ideology.

Dash cam footage shows a 34-year-old Oklahoma woman, Luz Avilla of Chickasha, leading police on a dangerous high-speed chase after initially being observed traveling about 5–10 mph over the limit. When an officer attempted to stop her, Avilla accelerated to roughly 90–100 mph and began weaving across lanes, creating significant hazard to other drivers. Chickasha Police Sgt. Shannon McClain warned that at those speeds even small movements by surrounding vehicles could cause a catastrophe. The pursuit continued toward the county line; a few miles shy of it Avilla finally pulled over and explained to officers that she had refused to stop because she preferred to be jailed in neighboring Caddo County rather than Grady County. After stopping, she initially refused to exit the vehicle, prompting an officer to draw his firearm. Backup arrived, and occupants were ordered out; several people were subsequently taken into custody. Avilla faces multiple charges, including driving under the influence and eluding police. The incident, captured on dash cam, highlights risks posed by impaired drivers and those who evade law enforcement at excessive speeds.

Ramon C. Estrada, a 62-year-old inmate at Utah State Prison who was due to be paroled in less than three weeks, died Sunday night after missing scheduled dialysis treatments when a contracted dialysis technician failed to appear on both Friday and Saturday. Prison officials and medics were preparing to transport him to the hospital around 10:30 p.m. Sunday when he suffered an apparent cardiac arrest related to renal failure; the Utah State Medical Examiner will perform an autopsy to determine the exact cause of death. Six other inmates also missed scheduled dialysis and were taken to University Hospital for evaluation: two returned to the prison after assessment, three were admitted and later released back to the facility, and one remained hospitalized as of Tuesday. The dialysis services are provided by a University of Utah Health Care clinic (South Valley Dialysis); the hospital acknowledged a scheduling miscommunication and said it will conduct a thorough review and improve communications and procedures. The Utah Department of Corrections has launched an internal investigation and placed the department’s Clinical Services Bureau director on administrative leave while reviewing the response of prison medical leadership, staff actions, and the contractor’s performance. Immediate corrective steps at the prison include creating a dialysis schedule calendar with technician contact numbers, requiring nurses to obtain post-treatment reports and better chart notes, and mandating prompt notification to charge nurses when schedules change or technicians miss appointments. The Unified Police Department is also investigating; no signs of foul play have been found.

The Court of Master Sommeliers (CMS) has voided the tasting results from the 2018 Master Sommelier Diploma Examination after discovering that a member disclosed confidential information about the blind-tasting flight in advance. The CMS board said legal counsel reported that a Master breached exam confidentiality by releasing “detailed information concerning wines in the tasting flight,” prompting the unanimous decision to invalidate the tasting portion for all candidates. As a result, 23 of the 24 people announced in September as new Masters will temporarily lose their MS title; one candidate, Morgan Harris, retains his credential because he had already passed the tasting portion in 2017 and only completed the service segment this year.

The tasting section—25 minutes to identify six blind wines including grape variety, region and vintage—is widely considered the exam’s most difficult component and central to the credential’s prestige. The board has barred the implicated Master from CMS events and initiated membership termination proceedings. CMS is refunding tasting fees and will offer the affected candidates two expedited opportunities to retake the tasting exam (one in late 2018 and another in spring/summer 2019), with assistance for travel expenses.

The decision has shocked the tight-knit sommelier community; candidates invest years, large sums, and intense study to earn the MS title, which substantially affects career prospects and earnings. CMS chairman Devon Broglie said protecting the exam’s integrity and the Master Sommelier credential’s reputation required the action, despite the personal and professional blow to those who passed fairly.

Sixteen-year-old Phylicia Simone Barnes, a straight-A honor student from Monroe, N.C., disappeared in Baltimore after visiting her 27-year-old half-sister. Last seen and heard from on Dec. 28 via Facebook, Phylicia has been missing since; her cell phone and social accounts went dark. Baltimore police and the FBI are investigating, treating several visitors to the sister’s apartment as persons of interest and pursuing abduction or homicide scenarios. Searches, security video reviews, interviews, and items sent to the FBI lab have produced no definitive leads. Authorities have deployed helicopters, investigators, and billboards along I-95; Crime Stoppers offered a $2,000 reward. Family, schoolmates, and nearly 9,000 online supporters continue to appeal for help as officials urge national media attention and public tips to aid the search.

Details have emerged about alleged prolonged animal abuse by 24-year-old Michigan State University medical student Andrew David Thompson. Prosecutors say Thompson bought multiple dogs over months and killed, mutilated or tortured them in his Berry Tree apartment in Meridian Township. He originally faced 11 charges and was later charged with three additional counts, bringing total counts to at least 14 plus an abandonment/cruelty charge; more charges may follow. Thompson was arrested after a search warrant, jailed in Ingham County with bail set at $600,000, and suspended by MSU’s College of Osteopathic Medicine.

New research suggests that feeling younger than your chronological age is linked to lower mortality in older adults. A study published in JAMA Internal Medicine analyzed data from 6,489 participants in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (2004–2005). Researchers asked participants, “How old do you feel you are?” The average chronological age was 65.8 years, while average self-perceived age was 56.8 years. Participants were grouped as feeling close to their actual age (25.6%), feeling more than one year older (4.8%), or feeling three or more years younger (69.6%). Over an average follow-up of 8.25 years through March 2013, mortality was 14.3% among those who felt younger, 18.0% for those who felt about their age, and 24.6% for those who felt older. The association was particularly strong for cardiovascular deaths but not for cancer deaths. After adjusting for baseline health, physical disability, and health behaviors, those who felt older still had a 41% higher mortality hazard than those who felt younger. The authors ruled out reverse causality by excluding deaths within the first year. They note the relatively small proportion who felt older may limit conclusions and call for further study into mechanisms. Possible explanations include greater resilience, empowerment, will to live, and better adherence to health behaviors among those who feel younger. Because self-perceived age can change, the researchers suggest interventions and targeted health messaging to promote positive attitudes and behaviors toward aging.

PNC Wealth Management’s annual Christmas Price Index finds that buying every gift in “The Twelve Days of Christmas” repeated through the song would cost $107,300 this year, a 6.1% increase from last year. PNC attributes much of the rise to higher bird prices after the 2011 drought pushed up feed costs: geese jumped 29.6% to $210 for six, and swans rose 11% to $1,000 each (seven swans = $7,000). Five gold rings increased 16.3% to $750, three French hens rose to $165, and a pear tree climbed to $189.99. No gift fell in price; six items remained unchanged, including the partridge ($15), two turtle doves ($125), four calling birds ($519.96), eight maids-a-milking ($58), nine ladies dancing ($6,294), ten lords a-leaping ($4,767), eleven pipers ($2,562) and twelve drummers ($2,776). Buying one set of each core item costs $24,431 in stores but $40,440 online, partly due to shipping live birds. PNC compiles prices from retailers, performance companies and institutions such as the National Aviary and Pennsylvania Ballet.

Episode 7 of the UFC Unfiltered podcast features UFC Women’s Bantamweight champion Miesha Tate and Game of Thrones creators David Benioff and D.B. Weiss alongside hosts Matt Serra and Jim Norton. The episode covers varied topics: Benioff and Weiss discuss translating George R.R. Martin’s books to TV, decisions about character deaths, fan and network reactions, how many episodes remain, potential prequels, and why season seven will be delayed into later 2017 to capture winter weather for locations like King’s Landing and Highgarden. They confirm the series will have two shortened final seasons. Tate talks about her upcoming title defense against Amanda Nunes at UFC 200, Amanda’s strengths and weaknesses, whether the five-round title format helps her, the possibility of a third fight with Ronda Rousey, her post-victory actions, mindset inside the Octagon, and how she rebounded from past losses. The show also includes lighter segments and UFC history bits.

Actor Charlie Sheen publicly announced he is HIV positive in a televised TODAY interview, saying the diagnosis—made about four years ago—was difficult to accept and that he’s going public to stop extortion and smear campaigns. Sheen claimed he paid more than $10 million to people in his inner circle to keep the diagnosis secret and called those payouts “shakedowns,” saying he wanted to end the financial and emotional toll on his family. He said he doesn’t know how he contracted HIV, described early symptoms as severe headaches, and insisted he never knowingly infected anyone. He acknowledged having unprotected sex with two partners after his diagnosis but said both were informed and under medical care. Sheen takes four antiretroviral pills daily and his physician emphasized that the main risk is relapse into substance abuse or depression, which could disrupt treatment adherence. Sheen said he hopes his disclosure will reduce stigma and lead to philanthropic work; he’s told ex-wives and his eldest daughter. Separately, a UNAIDS report celebrated reaching 15 million people on HIV treatment ahead of schedule, noting huge global progress but warning of persistent stigma, legal barriers, regional disparities, and the need for sustained funding. California law criminalizes willful exposure to HIV; no complaints against Sheen had been reported at the time.

Max Spiers, a 39-year-old British conspiracy theorist known for investigating UFOs and alleged government cover-ups, was found dead on a sofa in a Warsaw apartment on July 16 after traveling to Poland for talks. His mother, Vanessa Bates, says he was in “incredibly good health” and had warned her two days earlier, “If anything happens to me, investigate.” Polish authorities initially ruled the death natural without performing a post-mortem there; Bates says she has only a death certificate and was denied paperwork because she lacks her son’s written permission. Friends reported he had vomited a black liquid and suffered migraines in the days before his death, fueling suspicions of foul play among his followers. Online conspiracy figures and blogs urged an autopsy and speculated that UFO researchers might be targeted; Scott C. Waring suggested researchers are being silenced, while Craig Hewlett hinted at poisoning. Nick Pope, who ran the UK government’s UFO project in the 1990s, dismissed claims of an organized campaign to kill investigators. Spiers’s body was repatriated and buried in Canterbury; a post-mortem was later carried out in Kent and the North East Kent coroner said an investigation was at an early stage, but Bates had not received toxicology results months later and pressed for transparency. Spiers had recently expanded his investigations to include politicians and celebrities and propagated fringe theories—ranging from the “Fourth Reich” and alliances of Nazis and Zionists to secret underground bases and alleged child exploitation—leading followers to question whether his work made him enemies.

Iran’s new president, Hassan Rouhani, and U.S. President Barack Obama exchanged unusually direct, cordial letters after Rouhani’s election, sparking cautious optimism about a diplomatic opening between Tehran and Washington. Rouhani’s team, and apparently Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, received Obama’s outreach positively; Tehran prefers face-to-face talks to prolonged multilateral negotiations. Rouhani answered with a similarly toned letter urging gestures of good faith, while U.S. officials stressed that any talks must be verified by concrete steps and that direct meetings might not necessarily be leader-to-leader. Rouhani’s broader charm offensive — op-eds, planned U.N. and media appearances, domestic liberalizations, and sidelining of hard-line rivals — aims to revive Iran’s economy and end punishing sanctions, especially banking restrictions like SWIFT exclusion. Western analysts warn that goodwill alone won’t secure major sanctions relief: Iran would need to accept meaningful nuclear constraints. Both sides see a limited window to reach progress before Iranian parliamentary election campaigning begins, and there’s recognition in Tehran that failure could quickly erode internal consensus for engagement. While cautious optimism pervades Washington and Tehran, significant mistrust and difficult concessions remain before a durable diplomatic breakthrough can be achieved.

Pop star Britney Spears recently wrapped a tightly controlled radio tour to promote her Las Vegas residency, new single “Work Bitch,” and album “Britney Jean,” with handlers instructing stations to limit five-minute interviews to those topics and avoid personal questions. Stations were told the guidance was to keep interviews smooth, but radio insiders say the restrictions produced awkward, one-sided segments that some stations chose not to air.
