Examples include taped interviews in Houston deemed unentertaining and a live phoner where Spears sounded detached and had to be asked twice about her fragrance. Meanwhile, rumors persist that she’ll lip-sync in Vegas—claims she has denied—and visual-effects images from the “Work Bitch” video suggest digital slimming in post-production; Team Britney declined to comment.

Other celebrity items: Martha Stewart spoke about cleanliness and dating; Beyoncé posted a face-free Instagram with daughter Blue Ivy while touring; Charlie Hunnam avoided public appearances amid backlash over leaving 50 Shades of Grey; Arnold Schwarzenegger and co-stars dined after an Escape Plan screening; Elvis Duran and Eric Trump will walk the Brooklyn Bridge for St. Jude; and Bayside! The Musical extended its Off-Broadway run. Separately, conservatorship court filings reveal Britney’s father, Jamie Spears, seeks continued pay ($16,000 monthly) and higher office expense reimbursement, extending his control and income from her estate for years to come.

Archaeologists have recovered 39 metal ingots identified as orichalcum from a shipwreck off the coast of Gela, Sicily, dating to the first half of the 6th century BCE (about 2,600 years ago). The hoard was found in shallow water near contrada Bulala, an area that previously yielded remains of three Archaic ships. Volunteers from the Mare Nostrum association initially spotted the find; divers from the Coast Guard, Guardia di Finanza and the Soprintendenza del Mare recovered the lumps. X‑ray fluorescence analysis by Dario Panetta (TQ, Genoa) shows the ingots are a copper‑zinc alloy—roughly 75–80% copper and 15–20% zinc, with traces of nickel, lead and iron—akin to brass and consistent with ancient descriptions of orichalcum. The material was likely produced with advanced metallurgical techniques possibly transmitted by Phoenicians and destined for high‑quality local workshops in Gela, underscoring the city’s wealth and specialized craftsmanship about a century after its 689 BCE foundation. The cargo probably originated in Greece or Asia Minor and sank en route to Gela, perhaps in a storm. The find sheds new light on Mediterranean metal supply routes and ancient economies; authorities plan a full excavation of the wreck to recover the rest of the cargo and refine understanding of orichalcum’s production and trade.

Sky's comedy Sick Note has cast Lindsay Lohan in its newly announced second season, joining Rupert Grint, Nick Frost and Don Johnson. The series centers on Daniel Glass (Grint), a compulsive liar trapped in a failing relationship and a dead-end insurance job, whose life spirals when an incompetent doctor (Frost) wrongly diagnoses him as terminal and urges him to hide the misdiagnosis. Lohan will play the daughter of Johnson’s character when season two, currently shooting in the U.K., airs after the first season debuts this fall on Sky 1. Produced by King Bert and created by Nat Saunders and James Serafinowicz, Sick Note is directed by Matt Lipsey and is part of Sky 1’s push for edgier late‑night comedies. Executive producer Jo Sargent praised Lohan’s addition to the cast.

Investigators reviewing the crash of UPS Flight 1354 near Birmingham-Shuttlesworth International Airport found cockpit recordings showing descent-rate warnings seconds before impact. NTSB member Robert Sumwalt said the first of two audible alerts occurred 16 seconds before the sound of impact with trees or terrain; the warnings indicated the Airbus A300 was descending faster than normal for its altitude. Authorities have not determined a cause and have ruled nothing in or out. The twin-engine A300 went down less than a mile from the end of Runway 18 during an early-morning first landing attempt, killing Capt. Cerea Beal Jr., 58, and First Officer Shanda Fanning, 37. Sumwalt noted the captain had 8,600 flight hours, including about 3,200 in the A300, but it’s unclear whether either pilot had previously landed on Runway 18. Investigators will analyze aircraft weight, approach procedures and runway equipment; Runway 18 lacks precision vertical guidance and was the only available runway because the longer main runway was closed for maintenance. Weather showed overcast ceilings with clouds near 1,100 feet. The plane struck trees about a mile from the runway end, shearing parts off before hitting a hillside; debris damaged nearby homes. Pilots and experts said Runway 18’s terrain makes approaches more challenging and some crews avoid it when possible.

The published transcripts of President Donald Trump’s January phone calls with Mexican President Enrique Peña Nieto and Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull, obtained and released by The Washington Post, expose both the content of those exchanges and deeper dysfunction inside the U.S. administration. The Turnbull call centers on an Obama-era deal for the U.S. to vet and admit up to 1,250 refugees Australia had detained after they arrived by boat. Australia’s policy is to refuse resettlement of boat arrivals to deter people-smuggling and prevent drownings; Turnbull repeatedly explains these refugees are not detained because they are criminals or dangerous but because Australia applies a categorical bar to boat arrivals.

Throughout the 24-minute call, Trump repeatedly fails to grasp these points. He inflates the refugee number to “2,000” or more, insists the detainees are “prisoners” and “bad” people, and repeatedly asks why Australia “discriminates against boats” — indicating he doesn’t absorb that the policy targets the method of arrival rather than the refugees’ origin or moral worth. Trump worries aloud about political optics, fretting that honoring the agreement will make him look weak in his first week and that one might become “the Boston bomber.” He boasts of being “the world’s greatest person that does not want to let people into the country,” laments “stupid deals,” and ends the call in frustration, remarking Putin was a “pleasant call” by comparison.

In the Peña Nieto call, Trump pressures the Mexican president to stop publicly denying that Mexico will pay for the border wall. He urges both leaders to say vaguely “we will work it out,” even as Peña Nieto firmly rejects paying. Trump reveals the wall’s political importance to him—“the least important thing… but politically this might be the most important”—and makes repeated self-promotional and inflammatory remarks, including describing New Hampshire as a “drug-infested den” and portraying Mexican drug trafficking as a catastrophe for U.S. cities.

Beyond the substance, the leaks themselves are consequential. The transcripts’ release — drawn from White House note-takers’ read-outs circulated internally — signals a breakdown of norms inside the executive branch. The reporting suggests the leak was carefully chosen: the conversations had already been publicly reported, the transcripts make allied leaders appear reasonable, and they depict Trump as ill-informed, narcissistic, and often incoherent without exposing classified national-security secrets. That leaves the U.S. government’s internal workings damaged: trust and confidentiality have been eroded, internal discord is more visible, and normal diplomatic channels are undermined.

Commentators argue the leaks may have come from national-security professionals alarmed by Trump’s conduct, a “cry for help” reflecting anxiety about erratic leadership. The episode reveals how Trump’s fixation on image and politics can supersede alliance management and long-term strategy, and how his behavior has pushed others inside government toward countervailing irregular actions—deepening institutional instability that could outlast his presidency.

Republican Congressman Ron Paul was excluded from a Republican Jewish Coalition forum, a move the RJC justified by calling his views “misguided and extreme.” Critics argued the exclusion was driven by Paul’s noninterventionist stance on Israel, but the deeper controversy stems from decades-old newsletters published under his name that promoted racist assertions, conspiracy theories, and praise for antigovernment militias. Investigations uncovered newsletters—Ron Paul’s Freedom Report, Political Report, Survival Report, and Investment Letter—containing passages that described Black men as largely criminal, derided Martin Luther King Jr., spread false AIDS claims, and encouraged militia secrecy and preparedness. Paul has variously denied authorship, accepted moral responsibility for using his name, and said he did not know who wrote the offensive pieces; aides maintain he “did not write, edit or authorize” the language. The newsletters also generated substantial income, raising questions about Paul’s oversight. Supporters contend much of the material reflected ghostwriters or a past political strategy of courting fringe activists, while critics worry it reveals tolerance for extremists and poor judgment. As Paul gains electoral traction, renewed scrutiny of the newsletters raises persistent questions about his leadership, staffing, and the movement he inspires.

A 45-year-old man wanted for questioning in the deaths of a North Royalton woman and her two adult daughters was taken into custody after an overnight standoff in Brunswick. Officers located the suspect at a home on Valley Forge Drive around 9 p.m. and negotiated through a loudspeaker beginning about 2:30 a.m.; residents were ordered to stay indoors and a street section was blocked. Shortly before 5:30 a.m., tactical officers entered through an unlocked front door, subdued the armed suspect with a Taser, and led him out; the home’s female owner exited earlier unharmed. Police say the suspect is connected to the deaths of 45-year-old Suzanne Taylor and her daughters, 21-year-old Taylor Pifer and 18-year-old Kylie Pifer, whose bodies were discovered Sunday evening at their North Royalton residence. Investigators described the killings as targeted rather than random. Officials reported the victims were found under covers in the mother’s bed; Suzanne Taylor had an apparent knife wound, while the daughters’ causes of death remain under investigation. A family friend and the daughter’s boyfriend were involved in the 911 reports. Forensic and autopsy work is ongoing as detectives and the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation continue probing the case.

A routine pre-dawn traffic stop in South Seattle turned into an unexpected childbirth when officers helped deliver a baby in the couple’s car. Around 3:45 a.m., Officer Anthony Reynolds pulled over a speeding vehicle on Martin Luther King Jr. Way S.; the driver, Abdul Abdashiek, leapt out saying his wife, Maly Yusuf, was in labor. Reynolds called for an ambulance, but the baby arrived before medics. Officers Lorissa Johnson, Nicholas Kartes and Jason Alvord joined Reynolds as Yusuf gave birth inside the car. The newborn girl cried but then struggled to breathe; Officer Reynolds, aided by the mother, cleared the infant’s airway and restored breathing. Paramedics soon arrived and transported mother and daughter to a nearby hospital, where both were reported in stable condition. The family named the child Hadaya, meaning “gift” in Arabic, and later left a heartfelt note for the officers: “You have helped deliver a precious gift. We are so grateful.” The father hugged the officers as the ambulance departed.

A devastating magnitude-7 earthquake struck Haiti, flattening much of Port-au-Prince and overwhelming the country’s limited response capacity. Survivors spent days digging through rubble with bare hands and basic tools, pulling out the injured and dead; bodies lay in streets, hospitals were overwhelmed, and makeshift triage centers operated in parking lots. Communications were hampered as phone networks failed, and looting and prison escapes were reported amid security strains. International aid began to arrive slowly: planes from China, France, Belgium and others delivered search-and-rescue teams, medics, food, and mobile hospitals, while Cuba’s doctors and Doctors Without Borders set up field clinics. The U.S. pledged a major humanitarian effort, deploying military assets including the USS Carl Vinson and ordering Marines aboard the USS Bataan, and evacuated critically injured personnel to regional hospitals. Estimates of casualties varied wildly, from thousands to tens of thousands, and the Red Cross warned up to three million people might need emergency help. With government institutions damaged and relief distribution scarcely visible, survivors improvised shelters, scavenged supplies, and waited as the international community mobilized to respond.

Moe’s Southwest Grill has overtaken Chipotle as America’s favorite Mexican-inspired fast-casual chain in the latest Harris Poll, ending Chipotle’s three-year run as the category’s top brand. Harris surveyed more than 97,000 U.S. consumers about over 3,800 brands; Moe’s outperformed rivals on familiarity, perceived quality and purchase consideration. With roughly 600–650 locations versus Chipotle’s about 1,900, Moe’s achieved the largest brand equity gain (13 percent) of any restaurant measured and one of the biggest increases across all brands—notable because brand equity typically moves slowly.

Chipotle’s collapse in the rankings follows a tumultuous year marked by multiple foodborne illness outbreaks, including norovirus, salmonella and E. coli across several states. Those incidents precipitated a tumble in sales—same-store sales down nearly 30% in the first quarter—and a sharp drop in its stock price. Critics and analysts say Chipotle has struggled to restore consumer confidence despite new food-safety protocols and promotional efforts such as free-burrito offers; some observers argue the chain hasn’t done enough to visibly communicate safety improvements in stores.

Moe’s rise has been aided both by its expansion—around 70 new restaurants last year—and by opportunistic marketing, such as a full-page USA Today ad when Chipotle temporarily closed locations for safety checks. Placed data show Moe’s has seen a roughly 5 percent increase in foot traffic, though Chipotle still commands far greater visitation and sales ($4.5 billion in 2015 vs. nearly $640 million for Moe’s last year). Other chains outranking Chipotle in the poll were Taco Bell (No. 2), Qdoba (No. 3) and Baja Fresh (No. 4). Industry watchers say Moe’s now has a chance to convert improved brand perception into more visits and narrow the gap with Chipotle as consumers reconsider where to get Mexican-inspired fast-casual meals.

The dispute over Kurt Cobain’s iconic Martin D-18E — the left-handed guitar he played during Nirvana’s 1993 “MTV Unplugged” performance — has escalated into an imminent multimillion-dollar court fight. Frances Bean Cobain, Cobain’s daughter with Courtney Love, says the guitar is a family heirloom and denies ever gifting it to her estranged husband, musician Isaiah Silva. Silva, formerly of the Eeries, contends Frances secretly gave him the instrument as a wedding present after they married in 2014. Once insured for $1 million, experts believe the guitar is now worth several times that, intensifying the stakes. Court sources say negotiations collapsed and Frances intends to litigate after what her side describes as Silva taking “extreme and unsupportable positions.” In an interim development, a judge ordered Frances to pay Silva $15,000 per month in spousal support while mediation over the guitar continued. Separately, Silva has filed for substantive spousal support—seeking $25,000 monthly—claiming he left steady work when they married and that Frances promised to cover various expenses, including private school and housing for his child from a prior relationship. Silva also alleges Frances has access to substantial funds tied to her father’s estate and seeks a share of earnings from business deals made during their two-year marriage; Frances says the Cobain-related money is hers but remains open to some support. Representatives for Silva did not respond to requests for comment.

Scarlett Johansson and Ryan Reynolds’ surprise split stunned even their friends, who say the couple kept their brief marriage intensely private. Few people had any inkling it was coming, and insiders doubt the reasons will ever be publicly revealed. The pair rarely appeared together and avoided discussing their relationship; Reynolds told GQ he’d grown more guarded since marrying to avoid a “soap opera.” Friends expect neither will give interviews about the breakup, despite Reynolds’ upcoming promotional obligations for Green Lantern, and press on that tour may be asked to refrain from personal questions. The couple issued a joint statement saying they ended their marriage with love and kindness and asking for privacy.

A Delaware family vacationing at the Sirenusa Condominium Resort in Cruz Bay, St. John, fell gravely ill after methyl bromide fumigation in a neighboring unit, federal officials say. On March 20 paramedics were called after Steve Esmond, his wife Theresa Devine, and their two teenage sons experienced seizures; all were airlifted to U.S. hospitals. Devine was released after treatment; Esmond is improving, but both sons remain in critical condition and comatose weeks later. Preliminary EPA testing confirmed methyl bromide — an odorless, colorless neurotoxic fumigant banned for indoor residential use since 1984 — was present in the family’s unit. The EPA found the chemical had been applied by a certified applicator from Terminix targeting wood-consuming beetles; methyl bromide had also been used in the complex previously, including units treated months earlier. The Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation into Terminix and possible violations of environmental laws. Sea Glass Vacations, which rents units at Sirenusa, has terminated its contract with Terminix and says the treated home is unoccupied. Federal agencies, including the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, are interviewing guests and staff to determine exposure scope. Authorities emphasize public-health protection and holding responsible parties accountable if wrongdoing is found.

A federal appeals court has upheld major parts of Texas’s strict 2013 abortion law, allowing hospital-like structural requirements to take effect and likely forcing most clinics to close. The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that mandated features — specified room and doorway sizes, air sterilization systems, backup generators and on-site blood supplies — along with prior requirements that physicians hold admitting privileges at nearby hospitals and tighter rules on abortion-inducing drugs, do not constitute an “undue burden” on a “large fraction” of women. Before the law passed there were about 40 clinics in Texas; today roughly 17 remain and only seven currently meet the new building standards. The court exempted one McAllen clinic from some requirements, but even that exception may not keep it viable. Supporters, including Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott, argue the rules protect women’s health; opponents, led by the Center for Reproductive Rights, contend the measures are designed to restrict access and vowed to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court. The ruling could be enforced in about three weeks unless the high court intervenes; if upheld, many women — especially outside major cities — would face long travel distances or crossing state lines to obtain abortions.

Russia has named actor Steven Seagal a "special representative" for US-Russian humanitarian ties, the Russian Foreign Ministry announced on its official Facebook page. The unpaid role, likened to a United Nations goodwill ambassadorship, will involve promoting cultural, public and youth exchanges to bolster relations between the two countries. Seagal, who became a Russian citizen in 2016 and is a well-known friend of President Vladimir Putin, attended Putin’s May inauguration. He has publicly defended Putin and dismissed allegations of Russian election meddling in the US, calling such claims “stupid” and “propaganda” in a televised interview with Piers Morgan, where he also praised Putin as “a great world leader” and “a brilliant tactician.” In 2013, BuzzFeed reported Putin had suggested to President Obama that Seagal serve as an honorary envoy to improve bilateral ties, and that same year Rep. Dana Rohrabacher credited Seagal with facilitating meetings for a congressional delegation to Russia following the Boston Marathon bombings. CNN has contacted Seagal’s spokesperson for comment. The document also includes unrelated Russian-language remarks summarizing a Tunisian visit focused on expanding trade, investment, infrastructure and technical cooperation, urging faster agreement on bilateral programs and projects.

A 59-year-old Kansas man, James Zordel of Russell, died Friday night after his 1992 Suzuki motorcycle struck a cow on a rural paved road about six miles south of Interstate 70 near Russell. Kansas Highway Patrol trooper Brant Birney said the collision occurred on a dark stretch of 189th Street with no witnesses, and investigators do not know whether Zordel was speeding or the cow suddenly entered the roadway. The animal was described as black, and Birney noted the combination of darkness and road conditions may mean the exact cause is never known. Zordel was not wearing a helmet and was pronounced dead at the scene; no one else was injured.

Bill Bresnan of Toms River has spent nearly 40 years doing one simple, relentless thing: writing a note to his wife, Kirsten, every single day since they met in 1974. What began as flirtatious napkin scribbles passed between them on Long Island Railroad commutes grew into a disciplined, daily ritual of cards, postcards and letters — more than 10,000 messages now stored in 25 boxes, chronologically filed as a living “love diary” that documents their life together. The notes range from romantic and tender to funny and playful, and each ends with the same signature line: “I love you madly++, my Darling,” followed by an infinity sign.

Their relationship blends small daily rituals with occasional grand gestures: candlelit dinners every night, no TV in the bedroom, nightly kisses, games together at breakfast, and memorable trips such as a Mediterranean reenactment of the film Summertime in Venice. Bill even had a ring engraved with Egyptian hieroglyphs he translated from a temple inscription expressing a pharaoh’s love — a sentiment he says is deeply personal and meaningful. Kris began organizing his notes by date early on, creating folders that the couple can open to revisit a specific day, meal, cruise or moment in their life.

They credit communication, shared fun and daily effort for their lasting bond. They say they’ve essentially never had a major fight, always resolving issues before the night’s goodnight kiss. They supported each other through illnesses — “we have cancer,” Bill recalls, reflecting their solidarity. As they review which letters to keep for their children, Bill worries only about the day he might forget to write one. Their advice to younger couples: put phones down, focus on each other, and work at love every day.

Amanda Longacre, who was stripped of her Miss Delaware crown two weeks into her reign after officials said she was too old under Miss America rules, has sued state pageant officials and the Miss America Organization in Delaware’s Court of Chancery. The complaint seeks reinstatement as Miss Delaware, restoration of her Miss Pike Creek title and scholarships, an age waiver to compete at Miss America in September, and $500,000 in damages for Longacre plus $2.5 million for a class of contestants she says were recruited and later disqualified — a total of $3 million. The suit alleges officials knowingly recruited ineligible contestants to boost participation and fundraising, then disqualified them, and recounts Longacre’s extensive commitments and expenses made while serving her brief reign. It also claims other 2014 contestants were too old. Pageant officials have called the lawsuit meritless and said they will defend it; some scholarships were later offered to Longacre after she publicized her removal. The suit asks for clearer age disclosures on pageant materials.

The Arcade Fire’s “We Used to Wait” isn’t just a music video—it’s an interactive web experience called The Wilderness Downtown. Built with HTML5 in collaboration with Google and directed by Chris Milk, the site asks you to enter the address of the home where you grew up and then weaves personalized Google Maps and Street View imagery into a multi-window “film.” As the song plays, video clips, vector animations, satellite shots and prompts—like writing a postcard to your younger self—open in your browser, creating a nostalgic, emotional ride through familiar streets and memories. Optimized for Chrome (works in Safari; other browsers are hit-or-miss), the project demonstrates how music videos can evolve into immersive, web-native experiences. It’s part video, part interactive project and part art piece—sometimes sentimental or corny, but an exciting glimpse of where digital music visuals might go next.

Autopsies and investigator statements released in late April detail the brutal, apparently premeditated slayings of eight members of the Rhoden family in rural Pike County, Ohio. The Hamilton County coroner reported the victims—three women, four men and a 16-year-old boy—died of gunshot wounds; seven were shot multiple times (one as many as nine), and some showed soft-tissue bruising consistent with a struggle. Bodies were found across four nearby properties in Piketon, and officials described the attacks as carefully planned, execution-style killings. Investigators uncovered indoor marijuana grow operations at three of the scenes—one reportedly containing more than 100 plants and possibly hundreds overall—suggesting production beyond personal use. Evidence of birds in small cages raised the possibility of cockfighting at one site, though relevance to the murders remains unclear. Authorities have received hundreds of tips, served multiple search warrants and submitted dozens of items to a state crime lab for DNA, fingerprint and other testing; more than 200 law enforcement personnel and many agencies, including the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation, FBI and DEA, are involved. Officials have not announced suspects or a motive; Attorney General Mike DeWine cautioned investigators are pursuing many leads, including previous threats via Facebook. The community mourns eight dead while three young children found unharmed recover; a $25,000 reward has been offered for information.

Google has launched a new wedding-focused site just in time for Valentine’s Day, positioning itself as an unlikely wedding planner. The offering lets couples create wedding websites, edit photos and plan their events using wedding-specific templates across Google Sites, Google Docs and Picnik. Google partnered with noted wedding planner Michelle Rago to design the templates and provide planning tips for diverse settings, from beach destinations to backyard ceremonies. To promote the service, Google is running a wedding sweepstakes with a $25,000 prize and the opportunity to have Rago assist with planning. This initiative is part of Google’s broader effort to weave its tools into consumers’ everyday lives, following services like Google Health. That expansion raises privacy considerations, as past moves—such as Google Health’s partnership with CVS to share prescription histories—prompted concerns about access to sensitive personal information.

MasterCard announced at Mobile World Congress that it will let customers replace passwords with biometric checks—selfies or fingerprints—for online payment authentication. Trials in the U.S. and the Netherlands showed strong user preference, with MasterCard reporting 92% of participants favored the system over passwords. The rollout planned for summer covers multiple countries including the UK, US, Canada and much of Europe. Users download an app to their device; during a purchase they still enter card details but, when additional authentication is required, they can verify identity via their phone’s camera or fingerprint sensor. Selfie users must blink into the camera to prove they are live and not a photo. MasterCard argues biometrics are more secure and user-friendly than passwords, which are often weak or reused across sites. The firm says biometric data won’t be transmitted in a form usable by scammers and that other security mechanisms will help detect suspicious behavior. Critics note facial scans and fingerprint sensors can be spoofed, but proponents see biometrics as a path to reduce fraud associated with card-not-present transactions and possibly lower costs for merchants and consumers. Other companies, like Alibaba, Microsoft and platform wallet providers, are also exploring similar biometric authentication.

At a New Hampshire town hall, Donald Trump faced immediate backlash after failing to challenge a questioner who asked when the U.S. could "get rid" of Muslims and asserted President Barack Obama is Muslim. The questioner warned of training camps; Trump responded vaguely—"We're going to be looking at a lot of different things"—and did not correct the false claim about Obama. Critics across parties condemned the exchange: White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest, Democrats including Hillary Clinton, Bernie Sanders, Martin O’Malley, Rep. Keith Ellison and DNC Chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz denounced the rhetoric as hateful and racist. Trump’s campaign manager later said Trump didn’t hear the Obama comment, framing concerns as about "waging a war on Christianity." New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie said leaders must correct falsehoods at events. The episode revived long-standing falsehoods about Obama’s faith and citizenship, reflected in polls showing lingering misbeliefs about his background.

Ricky Gervais delivered a deliberately provocative opening monologue when he returned to host the 73rd Golden Globes, living up to a pre-broadcast promise to “offend Hollywood.” The British comedian targeted a long list of celebrities and industry foibles with blunt sarcasm and dark humor, drawing laughs and gasps as he skewered stars, awards, studios and the Hollywood Foreign Press.

Gervais began by mock-offending Sean Penn and swiftly moved through barbs at the rich and famous, noting many attendees “just married well.” He ribbed NBC for having no nominations, quipped about Caitlyn Jenner’s transformative year while joking about women drivers, and mocked Jennifer Lawrence’s high pay with a line on public outrage at her $52 million earnings. Gervais insisted he’d been given free rein by Globe organizers and warned he wouldn’t break any laws even as he promised to be offensive.

Religion and scandal were frequent targets. He praised Spotlight while mocking the Catholic Church and cited a Roman Polanski quip. He attacked film categorization and tastes, calling The Martian a comedy and comparing its humor to that of Schindler’s List in an intentionally shocking gag. He lampooned Hollywood’s trend of all-female remakes as a cheap box-office ploy and dismissed the awards themselves as “a bit of metal” that mostly matters to winners.

Gervais also made pointed jabs at fellow celebrities: Matt Damon as “the only person Ben Affleck hasn’t been unfaithful to,” and quips at Eva Longoria and America Ferrera framed as lines about deportation under Donald Trump. He revisited the Mel Gibson controversy—introducing Gibson awkwardly, then asking an expletive-filled question about Gibson’s prior remarks that NBC bleeped entirely. He referenced Jeffrey Tambor, Roman Polanski, and others in quick, caustic lines and closed with a crude joke about his own Golden Globes trophies.

Context in the piece outlines Gervais’s Golden Globes history—this was his fourth time hosting—and background on his career: creator/star of The Office (UK), former pop duo member, and past Globe winner. The report concludes by noting ancillary coverage available—live blogs, photos and winners lists—and includes an unrelated appendix compiling Mel Gibson’s prior offensive quotes, underscoring why Gibson remains a controversial figure.

A Pembroke Pines Arby’s sparked local outrage after Sgt. Jennifer Martin reported she was initially refused service at the drive‑thru because she was a police officer. According to the officer’s report, clerk Kenneth Davenport took her card but the manager, Angel Mirabal, approached the window and told her “he doesn’t want to serve you because you are a police officer,” then laughed and said the clerk could refuse service. Martin accepted a refund and left her food, uncomfortable eating it. The Pembroke Pines chief, Dan Giustino, called Arby’s corporate; CEO Paul Brown and a senior operations executive apologized, saying the employee’s behavior was unacceptable and not representative of company values. The chief accepted the apology and considered the matter closed. Locally, the incident prompted protests by officers’ wives, widespread social media criticism, and calls from police unions for a national boycott and for the employees to be fired. Arby’s later fired the manager and suspended Davenport; the company offered free meals to uniformed officers in Miami‑Dade and Broward counties and its CEO met with PBA leaders at the Pembroke Pines location. Competing businesses and residents delivered food to the police department in support. Davenport and his grandfather say the remark was a poorly timed joke and taken out of context; Davenport insisted he does not hate cops. Union leaders linked the episode to broader concerns about hostility toward law enforcement and demanded stronger corrective action, though officials labeled the incident isolated.

House Speaker John Boehner reiterated that any agreement to raise the U.S. debt ceiling must include entitlement reforms and cannot include tax increases, setting a hardline as GOP and Democratic leaders met the president to avert a possible default. Boehner said his private talks with President Obama didn’t include tax hikes and emphasized Republicans will oppose raising taxes on “job creators.” He proposed simplifying and lowering tax rates to spur growth and claimed that would increase revenue, but acknowledged opposition from conservative Republicans ended those negotiations. Boehner pressed for deeper cuts to Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security, real restraints on future spending, and a balanced-budget amendment. He accused the White House of insisting on tax increases while not being serious enough about entitlement overhaul.

At a House Science, Space, and Technology Committee hearing, Republican Rep. Mo Brooks (R‑Ala.) challenged climate scientist Philip Duffy of the Woods Hole Research Center about causes of observed sea level rise—about 3.3 millimeters per year on average. Brooks suggested that erosion and river-borne silt depositing on the ocean floor, and cliff collapses such as the White Cliffs of Dover or California shorelines, displace water and therefore raise sea levels. Duffy replied that such geological inputs and local ground subsidence (which can worsen relative sea level rise in sinking cities like New Orleans) are, on human timescales, “miniscule” contributors compared with melting ice and thermal expansion. Duffy emphasized that the recent century-scale rise is largely attributable to human-driven warming: melting land ice (glaciers and ice sheets) and warming seas expanding. The article quantifies how small Brooks’s proposed mechanism is by showing the enormous volume of material—roughly 1.2 trillion cubic meters, or a stone sphere over eight miles across—required to produce an annual 3.3 mm global rise, underscoring the implausibility of erosion as a primary driver today. Brooks also disputed evidence on Antarctic ice loss, saying some studies show growth; Duffy countered that satellite records show Antarctic mass loss and accelerating shrinkage. The exchange reflects broader congressional skepticism about climate science, with Brooks attributing alarm and projections to flawed models, politics and money, while Duffy reiterated that sea level rise is primarily caused by climate change.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid and GOP Leader Mitch McConnell, working with the White House, moved negotiations late Saturday into Sunday to avert a looming U.S. debt default. Reid delayed a cloture vote on his $2.2 trillion debt-ceiling bill after progress in talks between McConnell and Vice President Biden, and leaders signaled relief that default seemed less likely though many details remained unresolved. The main sticking points were Republicans’ demand for dollar-for-dollar deficit reductions without new revenue and an enforcement “trigger” to compel a joint congressional committee to find roughly $1.6 trillion in savings. Speaker John Boehner emerged as a critical holdout; sources said he had not fully signed off, in part because the framework could force deep defense cuts—politically difficult for veteran Republicans Boehner needs to win House support. Democrats feared their priorities—new revenues and protections for Medicare—might be sacrificed. Options under discussion included an across-the-board sequester to create pressure to meet targets. Meanwhile, the House pre-emptively voted on a related measure amid tense debate as the Treasury’s deadline loomed.

New Zealand’s Health Ministry has considered drastic cigarette price rises to reach a smoke-free goal by 2025, including scenarios that would push packs toward NZ$100 via immediate “shock” increases followed by steep annual hikes. Other models propose steady 10% yearly rises or a shock increase then smaller rises, potentially reaching about $60–$100 per pack by 2024–2025. Officials note taxation is the most effective tool to reduce smoking, but the paper is an internal discussion, not government policy. Prime Minister John Key warned such big hikes could spur a black market, while Associate Health Minister Tariana Turia said she supports “whatever it takes.”

Giant hogweed (Heracleum mantegazzianum) is a large invasive plant that poses serious health and ecological risks. Its sap contains photosensitizing furanocoumarins that, when combined with sunlight, can cause phytophotodermatitis—painful blisters, long-lasting dark pigmentation, scars that may persist for years, long-term heightened sunlight sensitivity, and in severe cases, blindness if sap enters the eyes. Sap is present throughout the plant but concentrates in the lower hollow stem, petioles, hollow hairs, foliage, flowers, fruit and seeds. Because the sap can splash several feet, do not use weed whackers or brush cutters; handling requires strict protective measures including waterproof gloves, long sleeves and pants, eye protection, and avoiding sunlight exposure for 48 hours after contact. If exposed, wash immediately with soap and cold water, keep the area out of sunlight, and seek medical advice for reactions.

Giant hogweed spreads almost entirely by seed; a single plant can produce thousands of viable seeds that may persist in soil for up to 15 years. Control is most effective when multiple methods are used over several years and when reinfestation is prevented. Manual and mechanical control options include root cutting (cut taproot 6–10 inches deep and remove tops), flower/seed head removal with sealed-bag solarization and disposal, repeated cutting/mowing (must be done multiple times per season and never when plants bear seed), and cut-and-cover with black plastic or fabric followed by revegetation. Systemic herbicides—glyphosate and triclopyr—are effective when applied to actively growing leaves (March–June), often requiring follow-up treatments; triclopyr is selective for broadleaf plants and allows faster grass recolonization. Licensed applicators may use specific FIFRA 2(ee)‑recommended products.

After removal, re-establishing native or non-invasive vegetation is essential to prevent erosion and suppress seedlings. Long-term monitoring of treated sites for several years is crucial to detect and eradicate emerging plants from the seed bank. Report sightings to local extension agents or authorities.

PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), the accounting firm responsible for counting and delivering the Oscars winners’ envelopes, publicly accepted full responsibility for the catastrophic Best Picture mistake at the 89th Academy Awards, acknowledging they did not act “quickly enough” to correct it. PwC said partner Brian Cullinan accidentally handed presenters Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway the Best Actress envelope — Emma Stone’s — instead of the Best Picture envelope. Beatty, confused onstage, read the actress name and passed the card to Dunaway, who announced La La Land as Best Picture before the mistake was discovered; the true winner was Moonlight. PwC apologized for the error and for the delayed implementation of protocols to fix it, expressing remorse to Beatty, Dunaway, host Jimmy Kimmel, and the casts affected. Tim Ryan, PwC’s U.S. chairman, called the incident a firm-wide failure and said Cullinan felt “very, very terrible.” Reports note Cullinan had earlier publicly described PwC’s multiple-check system as robust and boasted the firm’s long, trusted relationship with the Academy — a relationship that Academy officials later said would be reviewed. Questions intensified after it emerged Cullinan tweeted a backstage photo of Emma Stone minutes before the Best Picture announcement, despite being told not to use social media during the show; the tweet was later deleted. PwC partners Cullinan and Martha Ruiz had stood on opposite sides of the stage with duplicate briefcases of envelopes, a convenience-based system that may be reconsidered. The Academy launched a full review, considering measures such as placing two auditors at each stage entrance as a fail-safe. The mishap was ultimately blamed on a sequence of failures: the wrong envelope handed over, delayed corrective action, and no immediate production halt, producing one of the most embarrassing moments in Oscars history.

A music fan has launched a tongue-in-cheek crowdfunding campaign aimed at keeping Nickelback out of London. Craig Mandell, inspired by a successful Tilt campaign that persuaded the Foo Fighters to play an unscheduled U.S. gig, created a page called “Don’t Let Nickel Back” hoping to raise $1,000 (£626) to discourage the Canadian band, led by Chad Kroeger, from scheduling any London shows. Mandell’s tactic is to generate a flood of emails to Nickelback’s management on contributors’ behalf: each $1 donated equals one email, $5 yields a “slightly more forceful” message, and a $50 donation triggers an email with an attached Nickelback MP3—humorously intended to make the band “likely retire immediately.” The page promises proceeds will go to charity or, facetiously, to therapy for those “affected by the band.” Mandell set a deadline of November 3 to meet the target; at the time of reporting he had not received any funding. The campaign explicitly references the viral nature of recent fan-led Tilt efforts — notably one that reached its £150,000 goal to bring Foo Fighters to Cornwall in two days, although that campaign still needed the band’s agreement to perform. A correction appended to the story clarifies the crowdfunding platform as Tilt. The Nickelback campaign blends satire and protest, aiming to mobilize anti-Nickelback sentiment into an organized, if playful, blockade of potential London dates.

The document contains two film reviews. First, the Coen brothers’ remake of True Grit, faithfully adapted from Charles Portis’s 1968 novel, centers on 14-year-old Mattie Ross (Hailee Steinfeld) who hires one-eyed marshal Rooster Cogburn (Jeff Bridges) to avenge her father’s murder. The Coens preserve the novel’s darkly comic, revenge-driven American gothic tone, with Roger Deakins’s pale, atmospheric cinematography, memorable dialogue, and strong performances from Bridges, Steinfield and Matt Damon as a swaggering Texas Ranger. The film is praised as a beautiful, haunting Western that balances humor, grit and character. Second, Tony Kaye’s Detachment, a polarizing, ambitious high-school drama, features Adrien Brody as a detached substitute teacher; despite uneven elements and Kaye’s volatile persona, the film’s visual daring and emotional intensity—and standout performances—make it compelling, if imperfect.

About a dozen motorcycle riders spent a weekend crawling through the median on U.S. 61 in St. Paul searching for a gold wedding band lost when Randy Thill crashed and died on June 25. Randy, 47, a Medtronic technician, lost control of his Harley-Davidson and struck the median about a half-mile south of Warner Road. His wife Rhonda, who has three children with Randy and wore his band for nearly 19 years, did not receive the ring among his belongings. Desperate for closure but unable to return to the crash site herself, Rhonda enlisted friends and family to look. A state trooper and family members with a metal detector came up empty, and an initial planned search was postponed by weather.

Tim Allen, a high school friend and vice president of the Los Valientes motorcycle club, mobilized fellow riders after Rhonda’s plea. He contacted Rapid Recovery, the towing company that retrieved Randy’s bike; Jay Stevens, the company contact and vice president of the Sober Soldiers motorcycle club, organized a tow truck to mark the scene and brought club members to assist. About a dozen bikers searched a 100-foot stretch, some using metal detectors and others combing the grass. They found paramedics’ rubber gloves and, nearby, Stevens discovered the ring pushed into soil behind a weed. The group returned to Rhonda’s home to present the ring; she was overwhelmed with gratitude for the strangers and friends who helped her regain a cherished memento. A benefit ride and poker run, “Riding with Randy,” is planned for Sept. 5.

Ralph and Marcella Bracamonte hired 64-year-old Diane Stretton in March as a live-in nanny via Craigslist to care for their three children in exchange for room and board. Initially satisfactory, the Bracamontes say Stretton’s performance declined after a few weeks: she allegedly stopped contributing to household duties and limited her activity to staying in her room. The family fired her on June 6 and asked her to leave; Stretton refused, telling them she would not move out and later threatening legal action for alleged elder abuse and wrongful termination. Because she was given a room as part of the arrangement, local authorities explain she has tenant rights and the Bracamontes must pursue civil eviction proceedings if she won’t leave—processes that can take months and could involve deputies removing her after a court order.

After national media attention, Stretton stopped returning to the house but continued to have belongings there and was spotted driving past the property and later sitting in her car near a police station. She has declined media interviews. In communications with the family’s attorney, she said she planned to vacate by July 4 but set conditions: the media must leave, she needs to avoid a coming heat wave, and she requested permission to stay for a few more nights and to use the family’s shower. The Bracamontes suspect the delay may be a tactic—Marcella fears Stretton might try to lock them out while they are briefly away for a family wedding.

Reporting also uncovered Stretton’s extensive litigious history: court records show she appears in numerous cases across Southern California since 2002, both as plaintiff and defendant, and she is listed as a vexatious litigant in California for abusive legal filings.

A federal judge temporarily blocked the deportation of Pablo Villavicencio, a 35-year-old Ecuadorean pizza delivery worker and father of two U.S.-born daughters, after he was detained June 1 while making a delivery to Fort Hamilton in Brooklyn. Military police called Immigration and Customs Enforcement after a background check—triggered when Villavicencio sought a daily pass and presented a city ID—revealed a 2010 final order for removal following a failure to depart after voluntary departure was granted. The Legal Aid Society filed an emergency habeas petition and won a stay of removal until July 20; Villavicencio remains in ICE custody in New Jersey pending further proceedings. His attorneys say he has no criminal record, had a pending green card application filed in February, and has made deliveries to the base many times before. Legal Aid called the stay a win for due process; they will pursue adjustment of status on his behalf. New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo urged an investigation and requested Villavicencio’s release, arguing expedited removal served no public safety purpose, risked violating rights, and would be inhumane given his long New York residency and role as primary provider for a family that includes a child with serious medical needs.

The Big C centers on Cathy, a Minneapolis high-school teacher (Laura Linney) diagnosed with Stage IV melanoma who chooses secrecy and irreverence over treatment and confession. The series frames her terminal diagnosis as liberation: she flirts with her doctor, smokes, indulges in desserts, digs a pool, plays pranks and lashes out at family and students rather than disclose her prognosis. Reviews praise Linney’s talent and some darkly comic, honest moments of truth-telling, and Oliver Platt brings believable depth as her childish, conflicted husband, Paul. Yet critics argue the show misjudges tone—too jaunty and populated with exaggerated, attention-grabbing eccentric characters—so Cathy's daring choices read forced and superficially zany rather than organically moving. Supporting roles (including John Benjamin Hickey as Cathy’s homeless brother, Gabourey Sidibe as a defiant student and Phyllis Somerville as a cantankerous neighbor) are unevenly used. While the premise—how one would live knowing the end date—offers rich possibilities and occasional grace, many feel the series overcompensates for cancer’s weight with manic gags and cliché, undermining its emotional truth.

President Obama, frustrated by stalled budget talks, demanded House Speaker John Boehner and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid either reach an agreement or return to the White House daily until they do. In a surprise briefing he said his team, including Vice President Biden, was prepared to meet “for as long as possible” to avert a government shutdown when funding expires Friday. Boehner and Reid met later Tuesday; Boehner’s office said the leaders remained far apart and disputed White House claims Republicans had agreed to $33 billion in cuts. Obama allowed only a very short extension to keep negotiations going, not a long-term delay. Republicans pushed deeper cuts and policy riders, while House conservatives unveiled a sweeping budget blueprint to cut trillions and restructure Medicare and Medicaid. The White House began contingency planning for a possible shutdown.

President Donald Trump drew sharp rebukes from British officials after tweeting that the suspects in the Parsons Green Tube bombing were “in the sights of Scotland Yard” and urging authorities to be “proactive.” The early-morning tweets — calling the attackers “loser terrorists,” urging tougher measures, cutting off terrorists’ internet access, and boasting U.S. gains against ISIS — provoked immediate pushback. Prime Minister Theresa May said speculation was unhelpful while police and security services continued an active investigation; a Metropolitan Police spokesperson called Trump’s remark “speculation” and noted that suspects had not even been identified. London Mayor Sadiq Khan said he was focused on response efforts rather than Twitter.

National Security Adviser H.R. McMaster sought to soften the fallout, saying Trump’s comment was intended as a general compliment to UK law enforcement rather than a claim based on classified information. A White House official noted Chief of Staff John Kelly was not with the president when the tweets were sent; it was unclear whether Kelly had discussed them with Trump. The White House later said Trump spoke privately with May, offering condolences and pledging continued U.S.-U.K. cooperation against terrorism; a readout said they also discussed North Korea.

The incident again strained the “special relationship,” recalling earlier tensions after leaked Manchester attack images published in U.S. media led Britain to temporarily halt intelligence sharing. Critics called Trump’s public speculation “unhelpful” for an ally and intelligence partner; former May aide Nick Timothy echoed that sentiment.

New Federal Reserve survey data underscore widespread retirement insecurity and uneven recovery years after the Great Recession. Surveying about 4,100 adults in September–October 2013, the Fed found roughly 31% of respondents had no retirement savings or pension; that rises to 19% for people aged 55–64 and 54% among those earning under $25,000. Nearly 40% of adults 45+ who were not yet retired have postponed retirement plans; overall, 36% plan to retire later than they had before 2008 while only 5% now expect to retire sooner. Among 55–64 year olds still working, only 18% expect a traditional full-time-until-a-date retirement; many anticipate working as long as possible (24%), taking part-time work (18%), or becoming self-employed (9%). The shift from defined-benefit pensions to defined-contribution plans places more responsibility on individuals, yet only about one-quarter actively plan for retirement and about one-quarter of all respondents (14% of those 45+) say they don’t know how they’ll pay expenses in retirement. Access to workplace plans is uneven—around three-quarters of full-time private-sector workers have access, versus 37% of part-time workers—contributing to low savings. The survey also found mixed post-crisis financial outcomes: 34% reported being worse off than in 2008, another 34% the same, and 30% better, with retirement, education, and jobs as top concerns.

Ariel Winter, the 19-year-old Modern Family star, continues to dominate social media and court controversy with her bold outfits and unapologetic attitude. Known for posting revealing photos on Instagram and Snapchat, Winter embraces a “zero-fucks-given” approach that many find empowering; in an Elite Daily interview she emphasized self-relationship over pleasing critics, saying if people don’t like her posts they can unfollow. Her confidence was on display at an ABC screening event where she wore a gilded, embellished mini dress with mesh cutouts and gold stilettos—an outfit that stood out beside more casual choices from male co-stars and prompted both admiration and harsh online backlash. Some tweets labeled her look “slutty” and attacked her character, prompting Winter to clap back on Instagram: why should she have to dress like everyone else, and why can’t people let others feel good about themselves? She urged people to “WEAR WHATEVER YOU WANT” and not let others stifle self-expression. Separately, a Conan interview clip of Winter using a high-pitched “baby voice” drew ridicule online, with some calling it cringeworthy. Despite criticism, Winter remains outspoken about owning her image and defending her choices.

Japanese novelist Haruki Murakami, often a perennial Nobel candidate and famed for surreal, introspective fiction, will briefly open an unusual channel to readers: answering questions directly on his publisher Shinchosha’s website. The initiative, called “Murakami’s Place” (“Murakami‑san no tokoro”), runs with questions accepted from January 15–31 (or until the end of January in some reports) and Murakami’s replies posted through the end of March. The 65‑year‑old author, who has long cultivated a reclusive public persona and splits his time between Japan and the United States, told his publisher he wants after so long to exchange emails with readers; the scheme echoes a similar project he ran in 2006. Shinchosha stressed Murakami will receive questions “of any kind,” in multiple languages, and that he will choose which queries to answer, so readers’ submissions may meet varying fates. Expected topics include his recurring personal interests—running, cats, and his devotion to the Yakult Swallows baseball team—alongside literature, life’s big questions and the surreal themes that mark his novels. Born in Kyoto to schoolteacher parents, Murakami’s work—translated into more than 50 languages—often explores loneliness, pain, and the ambiguity between reality and dream; his 2013 bestseller Colorless Tsukuru Tazaki and His Years of Pilgrimage sold out at midnight releases in Japan. Shinchosha framed the project as a way to smooth interaction with his vast, global readership and warned of some “rather strange questions” while leaving response selection to Murakami himself. Details such as the site’s URL or submission email were not provided at announcement.

President Obama’s recent pledge to use force “wherever” Islamic State (IS) operates—explicitly naming Syria—has already translated into a swifter and more robust military move than many anticipated. Monday night’s airstrikes in Syria targeted IS strongholds and the Khorasan Group, an Al Qaeda offshoot believed to be plotting attacks on Americans. Conducted with a few Arab partners, the strikes raise the prospect of a prolonged U.S.-led air campaign in a nation whose government did not invite intervention.

This shift represents a notable reversal for Obama, who had carefully avoided deeper entanglement in Syria’s civil war. The conflict pits President Bashar Assad, a brutal but secular ruler, against a fragmented opposition that mixes moderates and extremists in ways that defy easy categorization. Obama’s reluctance to intervene was rooted in the complexity and risks of such involvement.

Two developments altered his calculus: the rapid advances of IS in Iraq—where its fighters routed Iraqi forces, terrorized minorities and threatened Baghdad—and the gruesome beheadings of two American journalists. Those events persuaded Obama to commit to a long-term campaign aimed at “degrading and ultimately destroying” IS. He insists that this can be done without deploying U.S. combat troops, but the boundary between airpower and boots-on-the-ground is porous. Gen. Martin Dempsey has indicated he might recommend sending U.S. military “advisors” to accompany Iraqi forces if necessary.

The administration has also secured congressional funds to train what it deems moderate Syrian rebels, further signaling a more active U.S. role. While IS is undeniably a brutal threat to regional stability and U.S. interests abroad, it is less clear that it poses a direct homeland threat or that the United States has a coherent, achievable strategy for escalation. The case for expanding military involvement in Syria and Iraq remains to be convincingly made.

The Supreme Court declined to review the conviction and death sentence of Dr. Ronald Mikos, who was convicted in 2005 of killing a former patient, Joyce Brannon, to prevent her testimony in a Medicare fraud case; Mikos’s lawyers argued prosecutors improperly emphasized his decision not to testify as evidence of lack of remorse. The 7th U.S. Circuit upheld the sentence.

Separately, federal prosecutors announced they will seek the death penalty against former University of Illinois graduate student Brendt Christensen, accused of kidnapping, torturing, and killing visiting scholar Yingying Zhang in June; her body has not been found and she is presumed dead. The decision, approved by Attorney General Jeff Sessions, follows allegations that Christensen previously choked and sexually assaulted another victim in 2013 and sought notoriety as a killer. Evidence cited includes surveillance video, cleaned areas of Christensen’s car, web searches about kidnapping fantasies, and audio from a wired girlfriend in which he discussed an “ideal victim” and admitted to the abduction. The death-penalty move will likely delay trial.

The article details a U.S. Justice Department criminal probe into allegations that Wal‑Mart’s Mexican unit paid more than $24 million in bribes to local officials to speed store openings, potentially violating the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA). A New York Times report said company investigators learned of the misconduct in 2005 after a whistleblower found evidence, but Wal‑Mart then halted the inquiry and did not inform authorities. The revelations have damaged Wal‑Mart’s carefully cultivated image and prompted a near 5% slide in its U.S. shares and a sharper drop for its Mexican unit. Wal‑Mart says it takes FCPA compliance seriously, is conducting an “aggressive investigation,” has met voluntarily with the Justice Department and SEC, and is strengthening controls. Congressional Democrats have requested a meeting with CEO Mike Duke and signaled oversight action. Governance experts warn of possible executive departures and heavy penalties if senior managers failed to act; settlements can equal sizable percentages of sales, and FCPA probes often last years. The episode also spotlights the U.S. Chamber’s push to limit the FCPA and raises questions about earlier disclosure to investors.

Sparkle, a 2012 remake of the 1976 musical, arrives freighted with expectations and the haunting context of Whitney Houston’s death during post-production. Set in 1968 Detroit amid Motown’s rise, the film follows three sisters — Sparkle (Jordin Sparks), Sister (Carmen Ejogo) and Dee (Tika Sumpter) — who form a girl group while navigating family tensions, fame’s lure, and personal demons. Houston plays their stern, churchgoing mother Emma, a former singer who warns against the industry’s pitfalls; her final on-screen moment — a gospel rendition of “His Eye Is on the Sparrow” — stands as a powerful, emotionally raw highlight and an unintentional elegy, drawing strong audience reaction despite a noticeably huskier voice.

Director Salim Akil and writer Mara Brock Akil evoke Motown’s retro visuals and stage energy, and several performances, especially Ejogo’s and Sparks’s big number “One Wing,” register with vitality. Yet the film often sinks into formula: cardboard dialogue, predictable “behind-the-music” beats, and melodramatic plot turns involving abuse, addiction, and betrayal that sometimes feel like Lifetime material. Mike Epps and Derek Luke add color, while Tika Sumpter’s limited screen time is a missed chance. Ultimately, Sparkle is uneven — intermittently spirited and stylish but weighed down by clichés — remembered most for Houston’s poignant swan song rather than as a triumphant remake.

U.S. Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, a leading conservative voice on the high court, was found dead at age 79 on Feb. 13 at Cibolo Creek Ranch near Marfa, Texas. He had been staying at the 30,000-acre resort for a private gathering, retired to his room after dinner Friday, and was discovered unresponsive the next morning; a priest administered last rites. Officials, including the U.S. Marshals Service, Presidio County authorities and the FBI, found no signs of foul play and described his death as natural; local officials later listed a heart attack as the cause. Scalia, appointed by President Ronald Reagan in 1986 and the court’s most prominent originalist and textualist, transformed legal debate with sharp, often acerbic opinions and vigorous courtroom questioning. His notable majority opinion in District of Columbia v. Heller affirmed an individual Second Amendment right; he authored forceful dissents in same-sex marriage and other cases. Scalia’s passing immediately reshaped the Supreme Court’s docket and U.S. politics: pending 5-4 cases could deadlock 4-4, leaving lower-court rulings intact, and his vacancy sparked a partisan battle over whether President Barack Obama should nominate a successor during an election year. Leaders across the political spectrum—Chief Justice John Roberts, former presidents, governors and presidential candidates—offered condolences and underscored Scalia’s lasting impact on American jurisprudence.

A Philippine Catholic priest was suspended and ordered to reflect after riding a hoverboard down the nave and singing during Christmas Eve Mass, an episode captured on cell phone video that went viral. In the footage the unidentified cleric cruises up and down the church aisle with a microphone, singing "May the Good Lord Bless and Keep You," and receives applause from parishioners when he dismounts to give the final blessing. The Diocese of San Pablo, however, publicly rebuked the act as inappropriate for the liturgy and announced the priest would be removed from his parish for a period of reflection. The diocese stressed that Mass is the church’s highest form of worship and "is not a personal celebration where one can capriciously introduce something to get the attention of people." According to the diocese’s statement, the priest acknowledged his mistake, apologized, and described the suspension as a "wake-up call," promising the behavior would not be repeated. The episode drew widespread attention in late December 2015, coinciding with the holiday season when hoverboards were a popular but sometimes controversial gift due to safety concerns. News outlets reported the suspension without naming the priest. The viral clip and diocesan reaction highlight tensions between informal, attention-grabbing gestures and expectations for reverence and liturgical propriety during Catholic worship.

A 14-year-old girl from Greenwood, Delaware, fell approximately 25 feet from a stopped gondola on the Sky Ride at Six Flags in Queensbury, New York, Saturday night and tumbled into a crowd gathered below attempting to catch her. The ride had been stopped by an operator after personnel were alerted that a rider was in distress. The teenager struck a tree before landing amid park guests and employees; she was initially treated by on-site emergency medical staff, transported by ambulance to Glens Falls Hospital, and then flown by helicopter to Albany Medical Center. Authorities reported late Saturday that she was in stable condition with no serious injuries. A 47-year-old male guest from Schenectady who tried to catch the girl was treated and released from a hospital for a back injury. The Warren County Sheriff’s Office and park officials said the attraction was inspected and appeared to be in proper working order; the park emphasized guest safety as a top priority and closed the ride pending a thorough review. No additional details were immediately available. The report appeared alongside an explanatory note about archived web crawls intended to preserve pages and links as they originally appeared to prevent broken references, part of a broader effort by the Internet Archive to maintain access to cited materials.

Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney released his 2010 tax returns and 2011 estimates after pressure from rivals, revealing that most of his income comes from investments—capital gains, dividends and interest—rather than wages. The Romneys reported $42.5 million in income across 2010–2011 and an estimated $6.2 million in federal taxes, yielding effective tax rates of 13.9% for 2010 and 15.4% for 2011. Those rates are well below the top wage tax rate of 35% because capital gains and certain private equity earnings are taxed at a lower 15% rate. Romney earned roughly $12.5 million in capital gains in 2010 and an estimated $10.7 million in 2011, and reported about $13 million over two years from “carried interest,” a controversial private-equity compensation taxed as investment income. The returns include nearly 550 pages of documentation—three blind trust returns, foreign holdings in places like the Cayman Islands and Luxembourg, and a now-closed Swiss bank account—with campaign advisers stressing compliance with tax laws. The couple donated about $7 million to charity over two years, much to the Mormon Church. Release of the returns aimed to blunt attacks from GOP rival Newt Gingrich after South Carolina losses, but also intensified debate over tax fairness and income inequality, themes President Obama planned to highlight in the State of the Union and in support of measures like the “Buffett rule.” Critics pressed for older returns to illuminate Romney’s Bain Capital years; the campaign declined to release records from the 1980s and 1990s.

SpaceX successfully launched a classified National Reconnaissance Office mission, NROL-76, from Kennedy Space Center at 7:15 a.m. ET on May 1, 2017 despite high-altitude wind shear nearly forcing a scrub. CEO Elon Musk confirmed the satellite’s deployment and praised the landing of the Falcon 9 first stage, which returned to Landing Zone 1 after flip maneuvers, engine burns, grid fin stabilization and a single-engine touchdown — marking SpaceX’s tenth first-stage recovery and the company’s fourth land landing. A sensor issue delayed the launch from Sunday by one day; coverage of the mission was cut early to protect secrecy. Analysts and hobbyist trackers suggested the payload may be an imaging satellite from Ball Aerospace headed to a low-Earth orbit inclined about 50–60 degrees. The flight continues SpaceX’s push toward reusable boosters and competition with legacy government launch providers.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet donated crawl data to the Internet Archive, which are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo. In the wake of Josh Duggar’s Ashley Madison revelation, internet sleuths traced his reported Ashley Madison login—joesmithsonnwa@gmail.com—to a lone OkCupid result using the username joesmithsonnwa. That OkCupid profile used a photo belonging to model and DJ Matthew James McCarthy, who says his image was hijacked and appears on multiple Duggar-linked accounts, including Ashley Madison, OkCupid and Twitter. McCarthy, raised in a devout Catholic family, says the association has humiliated him, cost him work, and led to harassment labeling him “Duggar’s boy toy.” He is suing Duggar for wrongful use of his likeness and damages. The OkCupid profile (now deleted) claimed a 27-year-old politics worker near Alexandria, VA, sought “casual sex” while claiming to be “strictly monogamous,” and listed answers inconsistent with Duggar’s real biography. No definitive proof links the profile to Duggar; Duggar has not responded.

The University of California, Irvine tightened its admissions enforcement this year, withdrawing 499 freshman offers after more students accepted spots than the campus had planned to enroll. Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs Thomas Parham acknowledged the university “took a harder line on the terms and conditions” and apologized to applicants who felt mistreated, promising to correct errors swiftly and empathetically. UCI’s stricter approach targeted missing or discrepant final transcripts and unacceptable final grades—standard provisions that make admission provisional until official records are verified. Of the 499 rescinded offers, 299 were related to transcript issues (185 appealed) and 209 were grade-related (110 appealed). By the most recent update, 63 students who appealed had been reinstated. UCI officials said they were less lenient on missed deadlines and documentation this year because of enrollment pressures: the campus received more than 104,000 applications for 2017–18, offered admission to 31,103 freshmen, about 7,100 accepted, and planned for a freshman class of roughly 6,250. Students and campus leaders accused UCI of over-enrolling and then using technicalities to reduce numbers; the student government demanded apologies, reimbursement for affected students, and guaranteed admission after two years at community college for those whose offers were revoked. Many applicants say errors by their schools or the university caused the rescissions and great distress—examples include lost certified transcripts, misclassified course names, and clerical issues. UCI has increased staffing for appeals to expedite decisions—initially expected to take four to six weeks—with pending appeals prioritized and anticipated to be resolved quickly. Some students, unwilling to wait, have accepted other schools or alternate plans. Parham stressed that any student meeting the offer terms will be welcomed and that no acceptance will be withdrawn simply to address over-enrollment.

In November 2012 the scandal that forced CIA Director David Petraeus to resign widened as the FBI’s probe into harassing emails revealed potentially inappropriate communications involving Marine Gen. John Allen, then the U.S. commander in Afghanistan and nominee for NATO commander. The FBI traced harassing messages Jill Kelley complained about to Paula Broadwell, Petraeus’s biographer and alleged mistress. In the course of that inquiry agents discovered thousands of emails exchanged between Kelley, a Tampa social volunteer well connected to military circles, and Gen. Allen. President Obama and Defense Secretary Leon Panetta put Allen’s NATO nomination on hold while investigators reviewed the material.

Officials said investigators found no classified material in the Allen–Kelley messages and no evidence yet of criminal wrongdoing or security lapses by Allen. Allen has denied any affair with Kelley, denied sharing classified information, and said he was never alone with her. Some officials portray Kelley as flirtatious in military social settings and say Allen may have used affectionate terms innocently; others view the messages as potentially inappropriate. The Pentagon received the information from the FBI and stressed Allen is entitled to due process and could remain ISAF commander while the review proceeds.

The probe began when Kelley complained of harassing emails traced to Broadwell. That complaint eventually led to discovery of Broadwell’s relationship with Petraeus, classified documents on Broadwell’s computer, and Petraeus’s resignation. Broadwell also sent pseudonymous emails disparaging Kelley; Allen reportedly forwarded one such message from Broadwell to Kelley.

Further reporting painted Kelley as an “honorary consul” for South Korea—an unpaid, symbolic role—whom she sometimes invoked during a 911 call, though the title carries no legal diplomatic protections. Media accounts also detailed the Kelleys’ lavish social life hosting senior officers at their Tampa home amid long-running financial troubles including foreclosure and multiple lawsuits. The unfolding revelations touched multiple institutions—the CIA, FBI and U.S. military—and left Allen’s high-profile nomination and reputations of those involved under intense scrutiny.

Tony Curtis’s last will, written five months before his death at 85, disinherits all five of his children, including Jamie Lee Curtis, stating he “acknowledge[s] the existence of my children...and have intentionally and with full knowledge chosen not to provide for them.” Instead, the estate was left to his fifth wife, Jill Vandenberg Curtis, who was named representative of the estate in Nevada filings. Inside Edition obtained the document; one child (not Jamie Lee) unsuccessfully contested it in court. Jill called the will and Tony’s wishes private family matters. Tony Curtis, born Bernard Schwartz, starred in Some Like It Hot and Spartacus and had children with three previous wives.

Austin Tice, a 34-year-old former U.S. Marine turned journalist who reported for outlets including McClatchy and The Washington Post, was abducted in Syria on Aug. 12, 2012. Apart from an early video showing him in custody of unknown gunmen, there has been no confirmed sighting since. His parents, Marc and Debra Tice, have endured years without answers, and this anniversary marks their fourth Christmas without him. In a joint open letter to President Obama, the families of four American hostages killed while held by the Islamic State—journalists James Foley and Steven Sotloff and aid workers Abdul-Rahman Peter Kassig and Kayla Mueller—implored the administration to “use all appropriate means” to find and return Austin Tice. The slain hostages’ parents, who united previously to press for hostage-policy reforms, urged bold diplomatic action and criticized Obama for not mentioning Tice at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner. State Department spokesman John Kirby said officials are working through the Czech government, which serves as U.S. protecting power in Syria, to determine Tice’s welfare and whereabouts and that his case has high-level attention. The letter emphasized families’ pain and pleaded that the government not repeat past missed opportunities; they asked the president to set aside political concerns and pursue every appropriate avenue to bring Tice home.

A controversial PC game called Active Shooter, marketed by Revived Games/ACID as a “dynamic SWAT simulator” that also let players assume the role of the shooter, provoked widespread outrage for simulating a school massacre. Survivors and relatives of the Parkland shooting, advocates and politicians condemned the title as exploitative; Sen. Bill Nelson called it “inexcusable.” The developer’s chaotic forum replies and apparent intent to keep a shooter mode made matters worse. After investigating, Valve removed the game and banned the developer/publisher, identifying them as a repeat offender using aliases (Ata Berdiyev) with a record of customer abuse, copyright violations and review manipulation. Steam said it won’t work with such actors and will revisit content policies. Critics noted prior precedents of similar games being pulled amid public backlash.

House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi said she would not trade with President Donald Trump for funding of a border wall, calling it a “manhood issue” for him and making clear Democrats won’t barter core immigration principles for the project. Speaking at Harvard’s Institute of Politics, Pelosi reiterated that Democrats support border security but prefer strengthening existing measures as part of comprehensive immigration reform rather than building the wall, which she characterized as “probably the worst way to protect the border.” Trump and GOP leaders have signaled they will press for roughly $5 billion in wall funding during December appropriations talks; seven of the 12 annual spending bills, including the Homeland Security bill where wall money would appear, are on a continuing resolution that expires Dec. 7. Pelosi acknowledged that during the lame-duck House session Republicans likely have enough votes to pass wall funding, and that Senate Democrats will be the main barrier—though Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has not ruled out negotiating. If appropriations stretch into the next Congress and Democrats win the House, Pelosi said she would have more leverage. She expressed confidence about potentially reclaiming the speakership while expecting intra-party leadership challenges. Pelosi outlined Democratic priorities if they take the majority—lowering health-care costs, boosting paychecks, green infrastructure, campaign finance reform as HR1, gun control, and protection for Dreamers—and said impeachment is divisive and not her preferred path, though robust, targeted oversight of the Trump administration will proceed.

The 2014 All-Star Game in Minneapolis became a sentimental sendoff for Derek Jeter, but an offhand comment by National League starter Adam Wainwright turned him into a lightning rod. Wainwright visibly honored Jeter by stepping off the mound and joining the applause before the at-bat.
