After Jeter ripped an opposite-field double, Wainwright later admitted he had planned to throw "a couple of pipe shots" to give Jeter a moment, saying he “probably should have pitched him a little bit better.” That candid remark sparked criticism, with many accusing Wainwright of undermining Jeter’s moment and the All-Star Game’s integrity. Wainwright quickly apologized, calling himself a “knucklehead” and insisting he didn’t intend to gift the hit, but acknowledged his poor choice of words. The episode spotlighted broader tensions about the All-Star Game’s role since MLB began awarding World Series home-field advantage to the winning league—an experiment meant to increase stakes but which has produced awkward incentives. Critics argue the current fan-driven lineup selection, player votes, and manager choices dilute competitive purity: fan favorites and farewell appearances like Jeter’s may not reflect the best matchup-focused roster. The controversy revived debate about whether the “This One Counts” policy should be retired and whether MLB should redefine the All-Star Game’s balance between showmanship, respect, and true competition.

On June 14, 2016, a Chinese national was fined $1,000 plus a $30 court processing fee after leaving the boardwalk at Mammoth Hot Springs in Yellowstone National Park, walking on fragile travertine formations near Liberty Cap and collecting thermal water. A visitor witnessed the incident, photographed it, and reported the man breaking through the crust; park rangers took the witness’s statement, photos and location. During the law enforcement interview the individual admitted collecting the hot springs water and said he had not read the safety information provided at park entry; park officials said he sought the water for medicinal purposes. He received a federal violation notice requiring a mandatory appearance in Yellowstone Justice Center Court. Park spokespeople stressed that regulations requiring visitors to stay on designated trails and boardwalks protect both visitor safety and irreplaceable natural resources, and noted that collecting park resources is a federal violation. The fine was partly justified by the “irreplaceable nature of the thermal feature.” The incident follows a string of recent park accidents and violations, including a fatal fall into a hot spring and other off-boardwalk and wildlife-related infractions.

Betel nut, the seed of the Areca palm widely chewed across South and Southeast Asia and the Pacific, is a deeply rooted cultural habit and a powerful stimulant—often called “Taiwan’s chewing gum.” Chewed fresh, dried, or as a betel quid (wrapped in a betel leaf and mixed with slaked lime, spices and often tobacco), it produces an energizing buzz comparable to several cups of coffee. Around 600 million people worldwide use some form of betel nut, making it one of the most common psychoactive substances after nicotine, alcohol and caffeine. It is associated with social rituals, perceived health benefits and workplace customs—especially among manual laborers who chew to stay alert.

However, extensive research and public-health agencies classify betel nut as carcinogenic. The quid’s ingredients—slaked lime and tobacco in particular—cause small oral abrasions and expose tissues to carcinogens; this contributes to very high rates of oral cancers and precancerous conditions such as oral submucous fibrosis. In Taiwan, where the habit is common and awareness has been low, oral cancer incidence and mortality rank among the world’s highest. About 5,400 Taiwanese men annually are diagnosed with oral cancer or precancerous lesions, and 80–90% of those affected chew betel nut. Symptoms can progress from white or red mouth lesions to disfiguring, flesh-eating tumours that devastate speech, eating and facial expression.

Responding to the crisis, Taiwan and other countries have launched screening, education and cessation programs, offered free oral checks, and subsidized cutting down betel palms in favor of alternative crops. Measures reduced male use significantly since 2013, but cultural acceptance, industry resistance and the long latency of cancer mean many current sufferers will not benefit from recent changes. Global public-health efforts—including WHO action plans—advocate policy, community outreach and awareness campaigns to curb use and prevent further disease.

U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, on a nearly two-week Asia-Pacific tour, firmly ruled out presidential bids in 2012 and 2016 during interviews in New Zealand, saying she is “very pleased” with her role as secretary of state. Asked whether the United States was ready for a female president, she said it should be, though “not me,” adding that other countries’ histories of electing women—like New Zealand’s former prime ministers Helen Clark and Jenny Shipley, and Australia’s Julia Gillard—are encouraging examples. Clinton also defended President Barack Obama amid Democrats’ heavy losses in the midterm elections, calling the setbacks “big” but within historical patterns and arguing that the administration’s economic actions, though unpopular to some, helped avert worse outcomes. Reports noted a light moment when New Zealand Prime Minister John Key mistakenly called her “President Clinton” during remarks.

Newly released internal emails show the Obama administration pushed aggressively to approve and later restructure a $535 million Department of Energy loan guarantee to solar-panel maker Solyndra, despite internal warnings about the company’s viability and the legality of a restructuring that favored private investors over taxpayers. Solyndra, the first recipient of a federal loan guarantee for clean-energy projects, later declared bankruptcy, laid off 1,100 workers and became the subject of FBI and Congressional investigations over its finances and the loan’s oversight.

The emails reveal high-level cheerleading: senior White House officials discussed presidential and vice-presidential involvement in announcing the loan, and advisers promoted Solyndra as a stimulus success. Energy Department adviser Steven Spinner—who had disclosed that his wife’s law firm represented Solyndra and agreed to recuse himself—repeatedly pressed OMB and other officials for faster action, communicated with Solyndra executives, and helped coordinate public announcements, drawing scrutiny over a potential conflict of interest.

Treasury and OMB officials raised legal objections to an August 2011 restructuring that would let private investors be repaid ahead of the government; Treasury’s general counsel said the deal likely violated statute and DOE regulations and recommended Justice Department review, which officials say did not occur. Energy Department career lawyers later approved the restructuring, and Secretary Steven Chu signed off in February. Critics say the restructuring now means taxpayers will likely shoulder most of the loss. Republicans on the House committee argue the correspondence shows improper closeness among the White House, campaign donors and investors. Energy Department spokesmen maintain decisions were made by career staff and that ethics arrangements permitted Spinner to monitor but not decide loan terms.

The document collects varied Democratic reactions and commentary on President Obama’s Afghanistan speech, debating his decision to escalate troop levels and set a July 2011 withdrawal start. Many writers note Obama’s centrist, pragmatic tone—less Wilsonian idealism, more Kissingerian realism—framing the mission in national-interest terms rather than democracy promotion. Some commentators commend his sober articulation of how the U.S. became involved and his effort to present a coherent exit plan; others find the logic flawed, questioning why an arbitrary date was chosen and whether a troop buildup can produce victory. Critics argue Obama glossed over Afghan governance failures, corruption, Karzai’s shaky legitimacy, and whether a promised “civilian surge” can work amid dysfunctional institutions. Several pieces wrestle with the political fallout: disappointed progressives feel betrayed though some concede Obama has long governed as a centrist. The writings also place Afghanistan in a broader context—linking policy choices to past wars and concerns about leadership in wartime—and reflect skepticism that more troops will yield lasting success without broader political and social change in Afghanistan and Pakistan. Overall, the responses mix cautious respect for Obama’s resolve with deep doubts about the strategy’s feasibility and political consequences.

Alvin Cross Jr., an Albany, Georgia man on probation, accidentally texted his probation officer “you have some weed?” when he intended to contact a dealer. The probation officer notified police, who obtained a search warrant and raided Cross’s home, where they found a bag of cocaine. Cross pleaded guilty to cocaine possession and to violating probation; he was sentenced to one year in jail for possession and another year for the probation violation. Reports do not specify the original offense that put him on probation, the exact amount of cocaine seized, or other case details. The incident has been widely mocked in media coverage as a spectacularly ill-advised mistake — a cautionary tale about the perils of hitting “send” without double-checking recipients, especially when under legal supervision. Coverage noted the broader theme that instant communication can have immediate and severe consequences, and urged people on probation to be especially careful. The story was reported by local outlet WALB and picked up by multiple outlets, which highlighted both the absurdity of the misdirected message and the serious legal outcome that followed: two years total behind bars. Observers used the case to remind readers that small lapses in judgment with a phone can lead to major, lifelong repercussions when the justice system is involved.

A bipartisan Commission on Wartime Contracting reports massive waste, fraud and abuse in Iraq and Afghanistan contracting, estimating tens of billions squandered of roughly $200 billion spent since 2002. The commission blames excessive reliance on contractors—about 200,000 hired for logistics, security, construction and translation—poor government planning and oversight, contractor misconduct and corruption. Contractors have even been used to monitor other contractors, creating conflicts and weak accountability; past violators can be rehired due to legal and procedural barriers. The report documents heavy human cost—over 2,200 contractor deaths and nearly 49,800 injuries between 2001 and 2010—and spotlights failures in performance reporting systems. Recommended reforms include restricting routine contractor use, ending contractor oversight of contractors, embedding federal personnel to command, control and monitor private security, creating deployable federal oversight teams, and strengthening interagency standards and contractor debarment procedures. The commission urged Congress and the Defense Department to act and held hearings to press its findings.

Lucinda (Lucy) Smith, a 43-year-old mother of two from Billericay, Essex, died from sepsis after a minor gardening scratch led to a rapidly worsening infection. A few days after she scratched the back of her hand, she developed shoulder pain and visited her GP. The doctor diagnosed a trapped nerve, prescribed anti‑depressants to relax her, and advised physiotherapy. Her condition deteriorated over the next three days: her hand and arm became swollen and blotchy, she began vomiting and experienced increasing pain. A subsequent doctor suspected a blood clot and sent her to Basildon Hospital, where a blood test quickly revealed sepsis. Despite immediate intravenous antibiotics and transfer to a critical care unit, Smith suffered multi‑organ failure and died two days later; an inquest recorded toxic shock from sepsis as the cause of death.

Her family believe earlier recognition and basic checks—such as blood tests and blood pressure measurement at the initial GP visit—might have identified sepsis in time to save her. The case underscores sepsis’ danger: it can arise from common infections, progress rapidly, and lead to septic shock and organ failure. Health experts emphasize early treatment with antibiotics and fluids improves survival, and public awareness of sepsis signs is vital. Symptoms warranting urgent care include fever or chills, severe pain, clammy skin, confusion, shortness of breath, and fast heart rate. Authorities urge patients and clinicians to consider “Could this be sepsis?” as a potentially life‑saving question.

A 60-year-old man was found dead on a roadside near Windidda Station in Western Australia’s remote Wiluna region after his vehicle broke down and he walked for help. The pair had been traveling between Wonganoo and Windidda stations when their car failed on January 4. They camped overnight waiting for assistance; when none arrived, the man left early Monday with only a “small container of water” intending to walk about 48 kilometres to Windidda. Temperatures in the area were extreme, reaching over 39–41.5°C during the period. The woman remained with the vehicle but later set out herself when the man did not return; she spent a night on the roadside and was located by workers from Wongawol Station, who took her to Windidda and raised the alarm. Station residents and police searched the area and discovered the man’s body late Wednesday, only two kilometres from Windidda. Police said there were no suspicious circumstances and a report will be prepared for the coroner. Authorities used the case to reiterate safety advice for remote travel: stay with your vehicle if it breaks down because it is easier to spot from the air, carry at least three days’ food and water per person, ensure the vehicle is suitable and fueled for the route, carry an emergency beacon, satellite phone or CB radio, check current maps and road conditions, and inform contacts of your plans and expected arrival times.

Egyptian authorities handed heavy sentences to nearly two dozen women and girls for protesting in support of ousted President Mohamed Morsi, in a decision that followed a wider, escalating crackdown on dissent. In Alexandria, 14 women—most aged 18–22—were sentenced to 11 years, and seven teenagers (15–16) were given juvenile detention until they turn 18; six other Brotherhood members received 15-year terms. The convictions stemmed from an Oct. 31 demonstration demanding Morsi’s reinstatement. The harsh penalties and recent images of police beating, humiliating and desert-dropping detained female activists recalled tactics from the Hosni Mubarak era and signaled growing boldness by the military-backed government in silencing opposition. Authorities cited a new restrictive protest law banning gatherings over ten people without a permit, framing enforcement as necessary to combat terrorism and preserve order ahead of a referendum on constitutional amendments. The crackdown has increasingly targeted secular youth activists as well as Islamists, risking reuniting disparate opposition groups. Prominent activists, defense lawyers (including Ahmed El-Hamrawy) and organizers like Alaa Abdel-Fattah and Ahmed Maher have been detained or questioned, prompting domestic and international criticism that the judiciary and security forces are politicizing prosecutions to stifle dissent.

An illegally constructed residential building collapsed in Thane, a Mumbai suburb, on Thursday evening, killing at least 45 people — including many children — and injuring around 70, with dozens feared trapped beneath the seven- to eight-storey wreck. Witnesses said the structure tilted and fell “like a pack of cards” within seconds while construction of additional floors was under way and several completed floors were already occupied. Rescue teams used bulldozers, cutting tools, hydraulic jacks and dogs in a prolonged search for survivors; dozens were rescued but several floors of rubble remain to be cleared. Police say the builder lacked required clearances and likely used substandard materials; authorities have registered a case and are seeking to arrest those responsible, and are probing officials who supervised the work. The collapse highlights a wider, chronic problem in India: rapid, often illegal vertical expansion to meet housing demand, poor construction practices, and alleged collusion or bribery enabling unsafe, unauthorized buildings that repeatedly lead to deadly failures.

A rookie South Pasadena police officer, Chris Perez, prevented a 12-year-old girl from jumping off the York Bridge after she fled a Los Angeles group home. Responding to a “possible jumper” call, Perez—only an hour into his shift and with a year on the force—found the sobbing child perched on a six-inch ledge about 80 feet above asphalt, hanging by one hand. He approached slowly and calmly, deliberately waiting until he reached the sidewalk before beginning conversation so as not to frighten her into letting go. The girl told him she had run away because she felt mistreated at the group home and wanted to live with her only relative, an aunt.

Perez built rapport through patient, steady dialogue, asking permission to get closer and to help her into a safer position. After back-and-forth conversation, she allowed him to lean over, he hugged her, pulled her over the railing and dragged her to safety. He then sat with her, offered water, and called paramedics when she complained of an ankle injury. The girl was taken into protective police custody for medical evaluation.

Officials praised Perez’s calm, professional actions for saving the child’s life. Perez downplayed hero labels, saying he was simply doing the right thing and was relieved his parents—his father is also an officer—approved. The incident left him shaken; he now feels fear when he looks at the bridge, but remains grateful the girl is safe.

Camp John Waters is a three-day adult summer camp celebrating the cult filmmaker behind Pink Flamingos and Polyester, set for September 22–24, 2017, at Camp Getaway in Kent, Connecticut. Limited to 300 campers, the event blends traditional outdoors activities—ziplining, canoeing, hiking—with John Waters–themed amusements: film screenings, Blood Mary Bingo, Hairspray karaoke, burlesque lessons, a Scotch-and-cigars session, and a costume contest judged by the “Prince of Puke.” Waters will headline with a one-man show, readings from his new book Make Trouble, and a Q&A; every attendee receives a signed copy of the book. Alcohol is available for an extra fee; cabin availability and pricing details were provided by organizers. Make Trouble, adapted from Waters’s 2015 RISD commencement speech, has earned warm praise: critics call it witty, inspirational, and provocatively personal, enhanced by Eric Hanson’s playful sketches. Reviews from the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, Tufts Daily, Johns Hopkins News-Letter, and San Francisco Book Review highlight its mix of humor, subversion, and genuine advice for outsiders and creators, describing the book as funny, thought-provoking, and a rallying manifesto to “make trouble” in the face of social change.

A late-night house fire in Youngstown, Ohio, on Sunday around 11:30 p.m. killed five children and severely injured their mother. The blaze at 434 Parkcliffe Ave., a two-story wood home built in 1924, began on the first floor, where firefighters found flames upon arrival. Neighbors reported hearing a loud boom and seeing flames shooting from first-floor windows; a neighbor called 911. The mother, 26-year-old America Negron Acevedo, reportedly jumped from a second-floor window and alerted firefighters that five children remained inside. Rescuers pulled three children from the house and performed CPR; those children later died at St. Elizabeth Hospital. The Mahoning County Coroner identified the victims as Aleysha Rosario, 9; Charles Gunn, 3; Ly’Asia Gunn, 2; and 1-year-old twins Brianna and Arianna Negron. Acevedo was transferred to MetroHealth’s Burn Center in Cleveland in stable but critical condition, sedated and unaware, according to family. Two firefighters were treated for injuries and released. Investigators from the Youngstown Fire Arson Unit and the state fire marshal are examining the cause; officials say there is currently no indication the fire was suspicious. The tragedy has prompted community mourning and offers of support, with memorials and donations appearing outside the home as neighbors and city leaders mobilize assistance for the family.

Microsoft officially renamed its long-rumored motion-control system Project Natal to Kinect, unveiling it at a theatrical Cirque du Soleil event ahead of E3. Kinect for Xbox 360 uses cameras and voice recognition to let players control games and media without a handheld controller; Microsoft positions it as a major push into the living room and a direct challenge to Nintendo’s Wii and Sony’s upcoming Move. The performance showcased family-oriented demos—rafting, racing, sword-fighting in a Star Wars segment, yoga/Tai chi, multi-sport competitions (sprints, hurdles, javelin, bowling, volleyball, soccer), dancing, and creature-interaction titles like Kinectimals. Revealed games included Kinect Sports, Kinectimals, Kinect Adventures, Joyride, Dance Central, and others featuring Disney and Star Wars characters. Microsoft also demonstrated non-game uses: gesture-based Netflix navigation, photo browsing, and live video chat. Pricing and ship date weren’t announced; Microsoft planned to reveal further details at its Monday E3 press conference. Observers saw strong potential but expected more specifics to judge whether Kinect truly reshapes motion gaming.

Lawyers for Boston Marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev have asked for a new trial and appealed his death sentence, arguing Boston’s pervasive publicity made an impartial jury impossible and that capital punishment may be unconstitutional. Defense filings say jurors were exposed to relentless coverage and social-media posts about the 2013 bombings, victims and the family, noting Boston even created a holiday while jurors deliberated. They also cite a Supreme Court discussion questioning the death penalty and challenge the use of the “crime of violence” label. Tsarnaev was convicted on 30 federal counts for the blasts that killed three and wounded hundreds; his execution, like most federal death sentences, could take years amid lengthy appeals.

Sen. Bernie Sanders will introduce the "Justice Is Not For Sale" Act seeking to end for-profit prisons and reshape U.S. incarceration policy. Co-sponsored by Reps. Raúl Grijalva, Keith Ellison and Bobby Rush, the bill would bar federal, state and local governments from contracting with private prison companies within two to three years, eliminate ICE’s 34,000-detainee daily quota, reinstate the federal parole system abolished in 1984, and curb high fees for inmate services like phone calls and banking. Sanders and supporters argue private prisons create a “perverse incentive” to keep people imprisoned, lobbying for harsher sentencing and immigration policies that benefit industry revenues. The private prison sector houses significant shares of federal and immigration detainees and is dominated by firms like GEO Group and Corrections Corporation of America; it constitutes a multibillion-dollar industry. Studies cited by reformers indicate private prison inmates may serve longer sentences and show similar recidivism to those in public facilities, undermining cost-saving claims—especially where contracts guarantee minimum populations. Sanders frames the effort as part of broader criminal justice reform and racial-justice concerns, aiming to reduce mass incarceration and appeal to African-American and Latino voters. While facing uphill congressional odds, the proposal adds a concrete plan to a national debate and could dovetail with bipartisan reforms gaining traction.

Miami doctor Arturo Carvajal has filed a negligence lawsuit against Hillstone Restaurant Group, owner of Houston’s, after he says grilled artichoke leaves he ate at a North Miami Beach location became lodged in his small bowel. Carvajal, who says he had never seen or heard of the dish before dining there in May 2009, claims the server failed to explain that the tough outer leaf portions are indigestible and that only the inner portions should be eaten. He reportedly suffered severe abdominal pain and underwent an exploratory laparotomy; the complaint alleges artichoke leaves were found in his bowel. Carvajal seeks unspecified damages for bodily injury, pain and suffering, disability, disfigurement, mental anguish, and related losses, arguing the restaurant and its manager were negligent in not training servers to instruct patrons on proper consumption. Hillstone’s general counsel called the claim “a silly notion,” questioning whether restaurants must warn customers not to eat bones in ribs, and said the company will defend the suit vigorously.

Des Moines police issued an Amber Alert after a complicated alleged abduction that involved family members and acquaintances. On Tuesday, 2-year-old Ronnie Tran and his 40-year-old mother were reportedly taken by force from a Des Moines home. Authorities say two women known to the mother — later identified as the boy’s 65-year-old paternal grandmother, Vien Nguyen, and the father’s girlfriend, Alyssa Chang, 46 — arrived, stunned the mother with an electrical device, bound her with plastic ties, and transported her and the child to a house in Fife. At the Fife residence the mother was tied in a garage cupboard while the child was taken inside. The mother escaped Tuesday afternoon and sought help from a relative rather than immediately calling police; officers were notified later that night, and the Amber Alert was issued Wednesday morning.

A key break came when Chang purportedly brought the toddler to her brother John Truong to babysit. Truong saw the Amber Alert the next morning, recognized the child, and contacted police. Officers recovered the unharmed boy in Renton and reunited him with his parents. Chang was arrested and charged with kidnapping, felony assault and unlawful imprisonment; Nguyen turned herself in later and faces the same charges, though police said Nguyen was fingerprinted and released for medical reasons. One woman was initially taken into custody and investigators located the Hyundai Sonata used in the alleged abduction. Police say the case involves complex family dynamics and multiple interviews; the child’s father cooperated with detectives and was not charged. Authorities continue investigating the motives and relationships involved.

The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 2 continued to dominate the box office, topping ticket sales for the fourth consecutive weekend with $11.3 million, bringing its total to $244.5 million. New wide release In the Heart of the Sea, directed by Ron Howard and starring Chris Hemsworth, opened poorly with about $11 million over the weekend against a roughly $100 million production budget. Critics were lukewarm (43% on RottenTomatoes) though audiences gave it a B+ CinemaScore; analysts blamed weak reviews, lack of buzz and a crowded holiday slate led by the imminent Star Wars: The Force Awakens. Pixar’s The Good Dinosaur held third with $10.5 million (total $89.7M), Creed added $10.1 million (total $79.3M) and Krampus took fifth with $8 million (total $28.2M). Meanwhile, The Big Short posted an impressive limited opening: $720,000 from eight theaters for a $90,000 per-theater average, buoyed by strong reviews (86% RT), A CinemaScore and Golden Globe and SAG nominations. Warner Bros., after a difficult year with several flops, is hoping future tentpoles like Batman v Superman can reverse fortunes as the season pivots to Star Wars’ massive release.

Scientists from the U.S. and Denmark are launching a novel airborne survey this November to map the hidden hydrothermal “plumbing” beneath Yellowstone National Park, aiming to reveal where and how hot water travels to feed geysers such as Old Faithful and to better understand rare, sometimes massive hydrothermal explosions. The interdisciplinary team—led by U.S. Geological Survey scientist Carol Finn and including researchers from Aarhus University (Denmark) and the University of Wyoming, in partnership with Yellowstone National Park—will fly a helicopter towing a hoop-shaped electromagnetic (EM) sensor developed in Denmark. The EM system acts like an underground “X-ray,” distinguishing water from rock and altered (“rotten”) sulfuric materials to roughly 1,500 feet (about 500 meters) depth by recording tiny voltage signals. Similar EM techniques have revealed subsurface volcanic hazards elsewhere in the U.S. and will for the first time provide a large-scale view of groundwater flow paths beneath Yellowstone’s thermal areas. Key scientific questions include whether geothermal waters travel vertically down and back up, move laterally, or follow other pathways—information currently unknown. The survey could also shed light on the mechanics of hydrothermal explosions, which occur when pressurized, superheated groundwater suddenly flashes to steam; one event (or a series) around 13,800 years ago produced a roughly 1.5-mile-wide crater beneath Yellowstone Lake, possibly the world’s largest of its kind. Beyond science, mapping subsurface conditions will help park managers plan development, protect fragile thermal features, and identify unstable ground, enhancing visitor safety. Flights will follow the Mammoth–Norris corridor and take about four weeks to complete.

Thirty-three years ago, Peter Brosnan heard a wild claim: buried in the sand dunes of California’s Central Coast were the remains of an enormous Egyptian movie set from Cecil B. DeMille’s 1923 The Ten Commandments. Initially skeptical, Brosnan later pursued the story, learning the set—built for the film’s City of the Pharaoh—had been a vast, costly spectacle: a 120-foot-tall, 800-foot-long temple, plaster sphinxes, massive statues, and a tent city housing thousands of extras. DeMille’s production pushed budgets skyward; he defied Paramount’s demands to stop, financed parts personally, and allegedly destroyed and buried the set to prevent rivals from using it. In 1983 Brosnan located a plaster fragment poking from a dune and publicized the find, attracting media attention, archaeologists’ interest, and tentative institutional support. He hoped to document and excavate the site—arguing early Hollywood set design deserves preservation as cultural history—but funding, environmental permitting, and protected wildlife (the western snowy plover) repeatedly stalled efforts. Ground-penetrating radar in 1990 suggested much remained intact, but a full dig was too costly. Decades later, renewed interest and a private donor allowed excavation of a sphinx and filming of the recovery; parts are now displayed at the Dunes Center in Guadalupe. The dunes’ mineral-rich sand acted as a desiccant preserving the plaster, but recent storms have exposed and eroded more of the ruins, accelerating decay. Applied Earthworks and archaeologists now use aerial photography to locate the long-buried production camp before more artifacts are lost, planning further flyovers and ground investigations to recover and conserve Hollywood’s buried monument.

The Deepwater Horizon disaster prompted a contentious federal six-month moratorium on deepwater drilling that Transocean, which owned the rig, and industry groups sharply criticized as unnecessary and economically damaging. The April 20 explosion killed 11 workers and caused the largest U.S. offshore oil spill; efforts to stop the leak continue with relief wells expected by August. At a New Orleans hearing, a judge considered lifting the ban after plaintiffs argued the shutdown was arbitrary and harmful to jobs and local economies; the government defended the pause as needed to reassess deepwater safety. Interior Secretary Ken Salazar said a new moratorium order would be issued with supporting evidence. BP has spent about $2 billion responding and compensating victims; Kenneth Feinberg will oversee a $20 billion claims fund to accelerate payments. Cleanup progress varied along the Gulf coast while environmental and industry stakeholders clashed over risks and responses.

A Trigana Air ATR 42-300 carrying 54 people crashed in Indonesia’s remote Bintang Mountains in Papua after losing contact on a short flight from Jayapura to Oksibil. Officials and villagers reported wreckage and smoke near Tangok mountain; bad weather, rugged terrain and failing light hampered search and rescue, and it was unclear if there were survivors. The aircraft, built 27 years ago, carried 44 adults, five children/infants and five crew, plus bags of cash for remote villagers. Trigana, on the EU banned list since 2007, has a history of safety incidents; Indonesia has seen multiple recent deadly air disasters.

The Thomas Jefferson Memorial’s once-brilliant white dome has developed a conspicuous black coating of biofilm—complex communities of algae, bacteria and fungi—that has gradually darkened the stone since about 2006. National Park Service (NPS) staff and outside specialists have been studying the phenomenon since 2014 to understand its causes, effects on the Vermont marble, and safe treatment options. Biofilm is widespread on monuments worldwide and on other D.C. sites (Lincoln Memorial, Washington Monument, Arlington amphitheater, Congressional Cemetery); it was treated successfully at the D.C. War Memorial in 2011. Experts suspect factors such as reduced air pollution, local microclimate (humidity from the Tidal Basin), and especially weathering-roughened, pitted marble surfaces that provide nutrients and places to grow help explain the memorial’s pronounced colonization. Scientists are uncertain whether the organisms accelerate stone deterioration or sometimes protect surfaces; research is ongoing. Because the marble is relatively soft, treatments must eliminate or reduce biofilm without damaging the stone or encouraging regrowth. NPS conservators, architects and molecular biologists are testing ten chemical biocides on small patches and exploring nontraditional methods including ozonated water, laser irradiation, and other cleaning approaches. Some cleaners temporarily discolor the stone; abrasive scrubbing is prohibitive. There is no timeline for full dome restoration: NPS emphasizes a deliberate, evidence-based selection of a method that balances effectiveness, stone preservation, environmental safety, visitor protection, cost and scheduling. Any chosen treatment will determine restoration cost and when larger repairs—planned for future maintenance —can proceed.

Talia Jane, a 25-year-old customer service representative for Eat24 (a Yelp-owned food-delivery service), published a widely read Medium post titled “An Open Letter To My CEO” describing severe financial hardship while working in San Francisco. Hired in August after earning an English literature degree, she said she took the support role as a pathway into media but was told transfers wouldn’t occur for at least a year. Living roughly 30 miles from the office, Jane reported earning $12.25/hour (about $8.15 after taxes), spending roughly 80% of her income on rent, paying over $200 monthly for commuting, and surviving on a 10-pound bag of rice. She described coworkers struggling similarly—some taking side jobs, living at home, starting GoFundMes, or becoming homeless—and detailed how benefits’ copays and transit costs still made basic care inaccessible.

After tweeting directly at Yelp CEO Jeremy Stoppelman and publishing the Medium piece, Jane’s company email was shut off within two hours; she announced she had been fired. Yelp and Stoppelman publicly acknowledged the Bay Area’s high cost of living and said they agreed with many points in her narrative. Stoppelman denied personal involvement in her termination and urged restraint online; Yelp declined to comment on personnel matters but later said it was expanding Eat24 support hiring to Phoenix to address cost issues. The letter went viral, sparking debate about fair pay, employee conduct, and corporate responsibility in expensive urban centers. Commentators and readers were divided: some defended Yelp’s decision as a predictable response to a public attack on leadership, while others saw Jane’s post as a legitimate plea highlighting systemic problems in the gig economy and an opportunity for employers to address livable wages and housing-cost pressures in tech hubs.

Severe storms and historic rainfall have unleashed deadly flooding and widespread damage across Texas and neighboring states, leaving communities scrambling for rescues, recovery and renewed warnings of more rain. In Central Texas, the Blanco River violently surged through homes in Wimberley and San Marcos, ripping doors off frames and sweeping furniture away; dramatic boat rescues saved some families, but many others were not so fortunate. At least 37 people have died over the prior five days from tornadoes and floodwaters—17 in Texas, 14 in northern Mexico and six in Oklahoma—with multiple people still missing in Hays and other counties. Crews recovered the body of a boy near the Blanco and identified other victims; family members remain unaccounted for. Houston and other cities endured heavy damage: about 1,400 structures in Houston were hit, dozens of vehicles stranded, and neighborhoods evacuated as rivers and bayous rose. Dallas saw nearly 7 inches of rain, prompting more than 200 rescues of motorists trapped in cars and large-scale road closures; power outages affected thousands of customers. Officials across the state issued voluntary evacuations where the Colorado and Brazos rivers were expected to crest above flood stage, and flash flood watches extended from south of San Antonio to Oklahoma and into Kansas. State climatologists reported May as the wettest month on record for Texas. Emergency responders continue search-and-rescue operations while warning that additional storms over several days could produce more runoff, shift debris, and hamper recovery. Federal support was pledged as communities brace for more rain and significant rebuilding.

Charlie Sheen’s recent public admission that he is HIV-positive has reignited discussion about his career prospects, including hopes for another primetime sitcom. Before the revelation—prompted by a National Enquirer report—Sheen had been meeting with producers, including Eric Tannenbaum of CBS TV Studios and executives at Sony Pictures TV, about a new half-hour vehicle; no series is currently set up. On the Today show, Sheen said he has major projects and several films lined up, and insisted his diagnosis won’t hurt his career, noting Sony chairman Steve Mosko was “excited” to work with him and that “thus far, there’s been no resistance.” Legal exposure from possible lawsuits by former sexual partners who say he concealed his status could alter that outlook.

Sheen says he was diagnosed in 2011 and was HIV-positive throughout his run on Anger Management (2012–2014). It’s unclear if producers and FX were informed; many cast and crew reportedly learned only after health-related shutdowns. A leaked 2014 Sony email joking about Sheen’s condition indicates some industry insiders knew earlier, though the information didn’t become public until now. Despite past public meltdown, substance abuse, and being fired from Two and a Half Men, Sheen completed 100 episodes of Anger Management and is seeking a fourth sitcom.

Two months after their daughter Casey Anthony was acquitted in the death of her daughter Caylee, George and Cindy Anthony spoke publicly for the first time in an interview with Dr. Phil McGraw. Excerpts aired on NBC’s Today show reveal Cindy’s explanation for a July 3 MySpace message that began “My Caylee is missing,” written about 12 days before Caylee was officially reported missing. Cindy says the child was “missing in my heart” that day—emotionally absent to her—though she believed she physically knew where Caylee was and wrote the message to convey her pain and to pressure Casey. Both parents were also questioned about a smell detected in the trunk of Casey’s car; Cindy says she still does not know its cause, while George says he prefers not to believe Caylee was in the trunk, relying on what investigators told him and acknowledging only that Caylee is gone. Cindy defends George against suggestions he knew of Caylee’s disappearance, saying she saw him distressed and frantic throughout the six months they did not know Caylee’s whereabouts. The full interview is scheduled to air across two Dr. Phil episodes; McGraw’s production reportedly paid a fee to Caylee’s Fund related to the interview.

A predawn accident on Interstate 10 near Blythe, Calif., on May 21, 2014, left four bus passengers dead and many others injured after a tractor-trailer spilled dozens of long steel pipes across the dark highway. The pipes tumbled from a jackknifed flatbed truck that drifted off the roadway while attempting to pass slower traffic in a 70 mph zone; some pipes were as long as 50 feet and blocked lanes in both directions. Minutes after two eastbound vehicles struck the debris, a passenger bus carrying about 32–33 people from El Paso to Los Angeles—having changed drivers in Phoenix—hit the pipes, slid down an embankment and overturned about 50 feet off the freeway. Among the survivors was a mother who cradled her 12-day-old baby through the rollover and escaped through a roof emergency exit; the infant was uninjured. Seven passengers were seriously hurt and airlifted or taken to hospitals; 14 others were treated for minor injuries. The truck driver was unhurt. Authorities closed the interstate for hours and investigated the truck company’s records; federal inspections had previously noted issues such as an expired medical certificate and missed periodic inspections for the carrier. Traffic was diverted and lengthy backups formed around the crash site.

Jeddah’s historic Al-Balad district, a UNESCO Cultural Heritage Site since 2014, faces ongoing threats from fire and decay despite its centuries-old prominence as a center of trade and Hijazi architecture. Over time, modernization and oil-driven development prompted many residents to leave, leaving ornate coral-stone buildings and intricately carved rawashin windows vulnerable. FalconViz, a Saudi 3D surveying and mapping firm, is using drones, laser-scanning, photogrammetry and Autodesk software to document and preserve Al-Balad’s fragile fabric. Their aerial and terrestrial scans produce dense point clouds and hundreds of images that, unlike lossy mesh methods, can be directly imported into AutoCAD and other Autodesk tools (ReCap, Revit, 3ds Max). This workflow yields highly accurate 3D models and as-built plans with measurements accurate to about 1 cm, enabling detailed drawings, structural analysis and simulations—such as fire-safety assessments and evacuation planning—through Building Information Modeling. FalconViz’s approach reduces time and cost dramatically: tasks that once required many teams and weeks can now be completed in a day, improving restoration efficiency and providing authorities with precise references for reconstruction after damage. The firm’s mission to “digitally document the world” supports both heritage preservation and contemporary urban planning, offering dual-use technology that helps restore Al-Balad’s cultural treasures and informs future infrastructure development.

New Mexico and Vermont authorities say a foiled murder-for-hire plot may have targeted pop star Justin Bieber and his bodyguard. The scheme emerged after convicted killer Dana Martin, 45, told investigators he had recruited former cellmate Mark Staake, 41, and Staake’s nephew Tanner Ruane, 23, to carry out four killings in two states. Martin — serving nearly 989 years for prior murders — allegedly became obsessed with a famous individual identified in police documents only as “J.B.”; investigators say that referred to Bieber. Martin claimed he wanted notoriety after feeling ignored by the singer, had a tattoo of Bieber on his leg, and wrote him letters. According to an arrest-warrant affidavit, Martin instructed Staake and Ruane to strangle two initial victims with a paisley tie (the same method Martin used previously) and then castrate them with garden shears, allegedly offering $2,500 per testicle. The affidavit does not indicate castration was planned for the celebrity target. Martin said the plan called for killing the celebrity’s bodyguard first. The plot unraveled when Staake was arrested Nov. 19 on a probation violation after missing an exit near the Canadian border; recorded calls between Ruane and Martin further exposed intentions. New Mexico police arrested Staake and Ruane in late November and are seeking extradition; no murders were committed. Bieber’s management issued a brief statement saying they take every precaution to protect his safety and that of his fans. Investigations continue.

Iran has set bail at $500,000 each for Americans Shane Bauer and Josh Fattal, arrested with Sarah Shourd along the Iran‑Iraq border in July 2009 on espionage-related charges, their lawyer Masoud Shafiei said. Shafiei told the Swiss Embassy—representing U.S. interests—that payment would secure their release; Shourd was freed in September 2010 after posting the same bond. President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad told The Washington Post he intends to grant a “unilateral pardon” and expected the two to return home in days, though clerical review is required. Bauer and Fattal were recently sentenced to eight years; the case remains open to appeal. The announcement arrives ahead of Ahmadinejad’s U.N. visit and amid other diplomatic outreach, including offers of talks on Iran’s nuclear program.

Lake Superior State University released its 38th annual “Banished Words” list, a tongue‑in‑cheek roundup of terms voters want retired for misuse and overuse. Top nominees included “selfie,” “twerk,” “hashtag,” “fiscal cliff,” and “spoiler alert,” alongside entries like “YOLO,” “job creators,” “passion/passionate,” “superfood,” “guru,” “boneless wings,” and “double down.” Submissions from the U.S., Canada and beyond criticize social‑media driven buzzwords and worn metaphors. LSSU, which has “banished” about 900 terms over decades, invites annual nominations and notes the list is a playful commentary rather than a linguistic decree.

A landlocked country has no coastline or direct sea access; there are 43 such countries worldwide, the largest being Kazakhstan. Being landlocked brings both benefits—protection from ocean-driven disasters like tsunamis and hurricanes, and easier border monitoring—and significant challenges, especially for developing nations. Without ports they depend on neighbouring coastal states for imports and exports, incurring higher transport costs, customs duties and political pressure to maintain good relations for transit access.

The document lists the world’s ten largest landlocked countries by area: 10) Central African Republic (752,612 km²; ~4.4M people); 9) Afghanistan (647,500 km²; ~29.1M); 8) Zambia (752,612 km²; ~12.9M); 7) Bolivia (1,098,581 km²; ~10.9M); 6) Ethiopia (1,104,300 km²; ~85.2M); 5) Mali (1,240,192 km²; ~14.5M); 4) Niger (1,267,000 km²; ~15.3M); 3) Chad (1,284,000 km²; ~10.3M); 2) Mongolia (1,566,500 km²; ~3M); 1) Kazakhstan (2,724,900 km²; ~16.37M). Kazakhstan, the world’s largest landlocked state, is spotlighted for its capital Astana (Nur-Sultan), noted for ambitious, futuristic architecture by Norman Foster, including the Bayterek Tower, Palace of Peace and Reconciliation, and Khan Shatyr. Astana rose in prominence hosting Expo 2017 on “Future Energy,” showcasing Nur Alem pavilion and prompting major hotel investments. The city blends Soviet-era character and modern skyline, offers cultural sites, and serves as a gateway to Kazakhstan’s vast landscapes—Charyn Canyon, alpine skiing, and mountain lakes—positioning it as an emerging, adventurous travel destination.

Henri Bendel, the iconic luxury retailer founded in 1895, will close all 23 stores and its e-commerce site in January 2019 after 123 years. Parent company L Brands, which bought Bendel in 1985, said the move—driven by declining sales (about $85 million in 2018) and the need to focus on higher-growth brands like Victoria’s Secret and Bath & Body Works—aims to improve profitability. The Fifth Avenue flagship will remain open through mid-January and receive holiday merchandise; future use of the space is unknown.

Kayla Mueller, a 26-year-old American aid worker abducted in Aleppo in August 2013, has been confirmed dead while in the custody of the Islamic State (ISIS). Her family, who had publicly pleaded for proof and privately communicated with her captors, received photographic evidence over a weekend that U.S. intelligence authenticated as showing Mueller’s corpse with facial bruising. The family earlier released a letter Kayla wrote from captivity describing herself as “in a safe location, completely unharmed [and] healthy,” and saying she had been treated with “utmost respect [and] kindness.” Still, officials and the family have not been able to determine when or how she died, and questions remain about the cause and circumstances of her death.

ISIS claimed Mueller had been killed in a coalition airstrike—specifically a Jordanian strike—but U.S. officials rejected that account. Pentagon and State Department spokespeople said there was no evidence of civilians at the targeted site and that the injuries in the photographs were inconsistent with an airstrike. The White House and intelligence community, while confirming her death, cautioned that published accounts of her time in captivity remain speculative and uncorroborated. A National Security Council statement urged readers to consult Mueller’s own letter for a firsthand perspective.

Intelligence indicates that Mueller was sometimes held with or passed into the care of an ISIS commander—possibly through forced marriage—and was not treated merely as a bargaining chip. She was rarely seen in ISIS propaganda or execution videos; her last proven contact was in May, and U.S. agencies had a credible visual sighting of her in the fall, though that provided no current location. U.S. forces mounted at least one rescue attempt in July 2014— a raid in Raqqa that missed her by days—and officials stressed they never stopped efforts to recover hostages. Special operations previously tried to free hostages at an oil facility but found the captives had been moved.

Mueller’s family, friends, and community remembered her long history of volunteer work helping refugees and vulnerable populations—from India to Turkey and Syria—and her deep compassion. President Obama and other officials expressed condolences and emphasized the U.S. commitment to freeing hostages. The family’s disclosure of Kayla’s letters and their confirmation of her death have re-centered attention on her humanitarian work and the plight of Syrian refugees she sought to help.

On April 15, North Korea attempted to launch an intermediate-range ballistic missile—likely a Musudan—from its east coast to mark Kim Il Sung’s birthday, but U.S. and South Korean officials say the launch failed. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs reported the missile deviated from a normal trajectory and presumed failure; U.S. Strategic Command also tracked the event and assessed it did not succeed. The Musudan, road-mobile and theoretically able to reach Guam, has not been flight-tested before; it shares engine technology with an earlier failed submarine-launched missile test. Experts say the setback undermines North Korean claims of advancing missile capabilities but also yields learning for the regime, raising the prospect of future successful tests. The failed launch occurred amid intensified North Korean weapons activity since a January nuclear test and a February long-range rocket launch, prompting U.N. sanctions and regional concern. Analysts warn the failure could increase the likelihood of further provocations, including a possible fifth nuclear test. China criticized the launch as counterproductive and urged adherence to U.N. resolutions, while the U.S. and South Korea remain on high alert as Pyongyang prepares for a major party congress.

A widely published photograph of nine-year-old Lakhan Kale tied by the ankle to a bus-stop pole in Mumbai sparked outrage and prompted authorities and charities to act. Lakhan, who is deaf, non-verbal and has cerebral palsy and epilepsy, had been raised on the pavement by his 66-year-old grandmother, Sakkubai, after his father died and his mother left. Fearing he would wander into traffic while she and Lakhan’s 12-year-old sister worked selling toys and garlands, Sakkubai tethered him during the day and tied his leg to hers at night. She said shelters previously refused to admit him. After the photo ran in local papers, Marine Drive police and social worker Meena Mutha intervened; with medical records, a guardian NOC and Mutha’s Manav Foundation support, Lakhan was admitted to The Children’s Aid Society, a state-run shelter in Dongri, where he will receive care and treatment. Activists say the case highlights systemic gaps: residential homes and specialized services are scarce, non-government organisations often lack space, and state support is limited. Campaigners call for stronger government provision and effective legislation to protect and support India’s estimated 40–60 million people with disabilities.

When celebrity chef Mario Batali stepped away from his restaurant empire after multiple accusations of sexual misconduct, many former employees at The Spotted Pig — co-owned by Ken Friedman and chef April Bloomfield, where Batali was an investor and frequent guest — said the move was unsurprising. Dozens who worked there described a workplace culture of intimidation, harassment and sexual assault in which abuses by powerful men were normalized and complaints went nowhere. Servers, managers and wine executives recounted repeated incidents: Batali allegedly made unwanted advances, groped women, and was seen on surveillance reaching between the legs of an apparently unconscious woman in a third-floor party room. Multiple staffers said Friedman minimized or ignored complaints; several women accused him of sexual assault or unwanted sexual advances and of sending coercive messages afterward. Victims described feeling powerless, fearing job loss or blackballing if they spoke up. Human-resources infrastructure was minimal until 2017, and staff said Bloomfield failed to protect them; she has said she is severing ties with Friedman and regrets not doing more. One woman who says she was assaulted in 2005 reported waking up injured on The Spotted Pig’s third floor with what she believed was semen on her clothing; she sought medical help but did not file a police report. The New York Police Department confirmed ongoing criminal investigations into Batali, including additional reported incidents dating to the mid-2000s. Batali has issued a statement expressing remorse for inappropriate past behavior but has denied specific assault allegations. Friedman has denied non-consensual activity while apologizing for mistakes. The accounts highlight a broader, pervasive problem of harassment and abuse in the restaurant industry.

White House national security adviser Gen. James Jones warned Americans will feel “a certain shock” when a declassified report details missed clues that might have prevented the Christmas Day attempted bombing. President Obama is “legitimately and correctly alarmed” that available information and behavioral patterns were not acted upon; Jones stressed fixes will be tweaks—like hiring more intelligence analysts—not a full post‑9/11 overhaul. Umar Farouk Abdulmutallab, indicted on multiple counts including attempted murder and using a weapon of mass destruction, is accused of being trained in Yemen by an al-Qaeda affiliate and reportedly met radical cleric Anwar al‑Awlaki there after recruitment in London. Abdulmutallab’s father warned the U.S. embassy but his visa wasn’t revoked and he wasn’t placed on the no‑fly list. Senate Intelligence Chairman Dianne Feinstein urged expanding the no‑fly list to those under “reasonable suspicion.”

Yahoo faced intense backlash after instituting a companywide ban on remote work, prompting it to clarify the move was specific to its own needs, not a commentary on broader workplace trends. In a statement to The New York Times, the company said, “This isn’t a broad industry view on working from home. This is about what is right for Yahoo right now.” The policy, rolled out under CEO Marissa Mayer, aims to boost camaraderie, intensity, creativity, and accountability by having employees physically together, and to shed underperformers who had effectively checked out. The announcement upset employees who joined for flexible arrangements and ignited a global debate about work-life balance, with critics warning it could set back flexible-work progress, particularly for women. Supporters inside Yahoo argued the company needs renewed commitment to regain competitiveness and morale, and many saw Mayer’s decision as a decisive leadership move after years of decline. Reporting cited employees who said remote work had been abused by some, even enabling outside startups while on payroll. Analysts noted poor remote arrangements often reflect management failures, but also warned the policy risks losing talented staff. The memo’s tone—discouraging even occasional home days—was criticized as insensitive to legitimate personal needs.

Recent documents show Louisiana prison officials sought to obtain pentobarbital from an Oklahoma compounding pharmacy, The Apothecary Shoppe, for the Feb. 5 execution of Christopher Sepulvado. That pharmacy is not licensed to supply drugs in Louisiana, making such a sale potentially illegal. The Apothecary Shoppe asked Louisiana to sign a non‑disclosure agreement; the state acknowledged it was “in the process of procuring” pentobarbital but initially provided incomplete, heavily redacted records to defense lawyers. The pharmacy is also suspected of supplying pentobarbital for recent executions in Oklahoma and Missouri, and compounding outlets like it are lightly regulated, raising concerns about potency and sterility. These procurement problems reflect a wider national crisis: European and pharmaceutical company boycotts have starved U.S. prisons of traditional execution drugs, prompting states to use compounded or experimental protocols. Studies and eyewitness reports show executions using single‑drug pentobarbital or novel two‑drug mixes have taken longer and sometimes produced apparent suffering, prompting legal challenges over cruel and unusual punishment. With drug shortages, some lawmakers have proposed reviving older methods—firing squads, electrocution, gas chambers—stoking legal, ethical and public‑opinion controversy over capital punishment.

A Manhattan judge has ruled that several personal items belonging to Madonna, including a 1995 breakup letter from Tupac Shakur, may be sold by New York auction house Gotta Have Rock and Roll. The items had been scheduled for auction last year, prompting Madonna to file a temporary restraining order to halt the sale after media reports revealed she no longer possessed many of the objects. Plaintiffs and the auction house said they had performed due diligence before listing the items; the auction house co-owners said the judge’s decision validated that confidence. 

Judge Gerald Lebovits found Madonna had pursued the wrong target by suing Darlene Lutz, an art collector who says she acquired the items while frequently in Madonna’s orbit in the 1990s. Lutz and her lawyer argued any disputes were resolved by a 2004 agreement; the judge questioned why Madonna had not sued her own assistants, whom she had alleged gave the possessions to Lutz. Lutz’s attorney described the ruling as a total victory, freeing her to dispose of the property as she sees fit. Madonna has not publicly commented since the decision. 

Among the 22 items cleared for sale are a lock of hair, a pair of panties, an old checkbook, a hairbrush, personal photos and two letters: the widely reported handwritten letter from Tupac, dated Jan. 15, 1995, written from Clinton Correctional Facility in which he explains why their relationship was problematic for his image; and an unsent Madonna draft to a former boyfriend criticizing Whitney Houston and Sharon Stone as “horribly mediocre.” The auction house says the items will be relisted in July. Madonna’s lawyers previously argued her celebrity does not negate her privacy rights; the court’s ruling, however, allows the collector to proceed with the sale after rejecting Madonna’s chosen legal approach.

Ben Carson is traveling to Jordan on Friday to visit Syrian refugees at the Azraq camp, aiming to gain firsthand knowledge of the crisis and bolster his presidential candidacy amid rising scrutiny of his foreign policy credentials. Departing late on Thanksgiving Day on a charter aircraft, the retired neurosurgeon said he believes direct exposure makes a stronger impression than secondhand information. At Azraq he plans to tour a clinic and hospital and distribute soccer balls and Beanie Babies to children.

Carson’s trip comes as his standing in national and Iowa polls has weakened since the Paris terror attacks heightened voters’ security concerns. Once leading in some surveys, he has lost ground to Donald Trump—now ahead in Iowa after advocating policies like a registry for Muslims—and to Senator Ted Cruz, who has criticized President Obama over the rise of the Islamic State. A Quinnipiac University poll cited shows Carson’s Iowa support fell by 10 points since October, pushing him behind Trump and Cruz in a state the campaign views as crucial.

The visit follows persistent criticism of Carson’s positions on refugees and his foreign-policy grasp. He has opposed accepting Syrian refugees into the United States and urged Congress to defund refugee programs, drawing fire for comparing refugee-related security worries to “a rabid dog” and saying screening must identify “mad dogs.” Carson has also faced questions about factual accuracy and depth on international issues after suggesting, then attempting to clarify, that China was involved in Syria during a Republican debate. The Jordan trip appears intended to address those critiques by showing on-the-ground engagement.

In the weeks before his sudden death at 43, conservative provocateur Andrew Breitbart told a CPAC crowd he possessed college-era videos of President Obama he planned to release in 2012, claiming they would expose racial and class-based motives behind Obama’s political message. Breitbart’s unexpected collapse and death in Los Angeles sparked immediate, unfounded assassination theories across right-wing sites and Twitter, where users speculated wildly—from allegations of Obama’s supposed gay lovers and cocaine use to elaborate Obama-Clinton-Bush conspiracies and comparisons to Stalin. The piece highlights how conspiracy thinking thrives without evidence, with social media amplifying sensational claims and hashtags about a supposed “hit job.” It also recounts Breitbart’s last public exchange: a jocular Twitter spat in which he called 29-year-old law student Lamar White Jr. a “putz.” White, who admired Breitbart’s panache despite political differences, called the feud a fluke and rejected the conspiracy theories, expressing sympathy for Breitbart’s family while acknowledging Breitbart’s polarizing but influential legacy.

Elon Musk announced he is considering taking Tesla private at $420 per share, a roughly 20% premium to the prevailing share price when he informed the board on August 2. He proposed a structure allowing existing investors to remain shareholders in a private Tesla, with the $420 buyout applying only to those who chose to exit. After initial board discussions, Musk was asked to consult major long-term investors about their willingness to stay invested; he says he publicly disclosed his intention so all shareholders would have equal information. Musk described a long-standing interest from the Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund, which recently bought almost 5% of Tesla stock and, in a July 31 meeting, expressed readiness to fund a going-private deal subject to due diligence and internal approvals—prompting Musk’s “funding secured” tweet. He emphasizes most financing would be equity, not heavy debt, and estimates about two-thirds of current shares might roll over, reducing the cash needed. Advisors and investor conversations continue; a special board committee and legal counsel will evaluate any formal proposal, followed by regulatory approvals and a shareholder vote. The tweet triggered regulatory scrutiny and criticism for its abrupt public airing.

Shots fired at a Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Park gathering in Liberty City disrupted MLK Day events Monday, wounding eight people, five of them juveniles, Miami-Dade police say. The crowd had assembled after the annual MLK Day parade when gunfire erupted; officers blocked off NW 32nd Avenue from NW 62nd Street and several blocks south as they responded. Detective Daniel Ferrin, a department spokesman, said two suspects are being questioned, two firearms were recovered, and the investigation is ongoing. Victims’ ages range from 11 to 30. Five were listed in stable condition and one remained in critical condition; two juveniles who were grazed by bullets received on-scene treatment and were released. Authorities have not released additional details about the suspects or a possible motive. The incident marred a holiday observance in the northwest Miami-Dade neighborhood and prompted an active police presence and continued inquiries into the shooting.

A three-year Vanderbilt University study in metropolitan Nashville found that offering individual teacher bonuses—up to $15,000 annually—based on student gains on Tennessee standardized math exams produced no measurable improvement in student test scores. About 300 fifth- to eighth-grade math teachers were studied from 2007–2009; roughly half were eligible for bonuses, and only ~40 teachers received awards each year. Scores rose modestly for both groups, suggesting pay incentives alone didn’t change outcomes. Lead researcher Matthew Springer said pay can’t be the sole solution. The Department of Education criticized the study as narrowly focused, while the American Federation of Teachers and others argued the results underscore the need for better training, support, and broader reforms beyond merit pay.

Apple’s new $5 billion “spaceship” campus in Cupertino has produced multiple injuries from employees walking into its nearly invisible glass walls. Public records obtained by the San Francisco Chronicle reveal three January 2018 911 calls documenting separate incidents in which workers struck glass panes at Apple Park’s transit center, suffering head cuts and temporary disorientation. Two calls on January 2 described men who hit their heads—one bleeding and slightly disoriented, another with a cut over his eyebrow likely needing stitches—while a third call on January 4 captured a 23-year-old who called the mishap “very silly” and reported no serious bleeding. In each case dispatchers instructed on bleeding control and told staff not to move patients or let them eat or drink until paramedics arrived. Cupertino building officials say they warned Apple beforehand that the glass could be hazardous—Albert Salvador noted cleaned windows can become essentially invisible, and he and a fire official once watched a contractor walk into glass during a site visit. The design ethos at Apple Park prioritized seamless, distraction-free movement and minimalist aesthetics, eliminating visual cues that normally warn people of doorways and thresholds. Bloomberg reported Apple discouraged ad hoc fixes like Post-it markers, raising concern that new or distracted employees may continue to collide with glass. A search of OSHA records found no related results.

Thousands of European dairy farmers, joined by hundreds of tractors, descended on Brussels for a two-day protest over collapsing milk prices and perceived unjust EU policies. Coordinated by the European Milk Board, demonstrators blocked roads around the European Commission and Parliament, sprayed thousands of litres of milk at the parliament and police, burned hay and tyres, and erected symbolic props to highlight their plight. Farmers demand price increases of up to 25% to cover rising production costs; the EMB says wholesale milk prices often fall below production costs (Belgium cited €0.26/litre wholesale vs. €0.40 cost). Protesters warned that small and medium producers are being driven out of business, blaming falling international demand, excess quotas and increased competition. The EU, the world’s largest milk producer, spends a large share of its budget on farm subsidies and plans to phase out milk quotas by 2015—moves farmers say risk further harm. Organizers said the next day’s actions would be more symbolic and calmer.

Venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers is seeking about $973,000 in legal costs from former partner Ellen Pao after a jury cleared the firm of her gender-discrimination and retaliation claims. In a court filing, Kleiner said the bulk of the amount—roughly $865,000—covers expert witness fees and offered to waive the request if Pao agrees not to appeal. The firm also disclosed it had earlier proposed a nearly $965,000 settlement based on projected case costs, an offer it says Pao did not respond to. Kleiner framed its stance as a wish to move beyond litigation and focus on improving gender diversity in tech. Pao, now interim CEO of Reddit, and her lawyers are reportedly considering the firm’s offer. Observers note defendants commonly seek costs after prevailing in employment suits; appellate data show California’s First District often affirms employer wins. Some commentators called Kleiner’s move punitive, while the firm maintains it is a standard post-trial action.

Astronomers using NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope have produced a new, highly precise measurement of the universe’s expansion rate—the Hubble constant—that is about 73.2 km/s per megaparsec, roughly 5–9 percent higher than values inferred from observations of the early universe (WMAP and Planck). The SH0ES team led by Nobel laureate Adam Riess reduced uncertainty to 2.4 percent by measuring ~2,400 Cepheid variable stars in 19 galaxies and calibrating Type Ia supernovae as “standard candles,” then applying that calibration to about 300 more distant supernovae. The result tightens the local expansion rate but does not match the lower rate predicted from the cosmic microwave background, creating a statistically significant tension between local and early-universe measurements. Researchers caution that further scrutiny is required, but if the discrepancy persists it may signal new physics. Possible explanations include evolving or stronger-than-expected dark energy, unexpected properties of dark matter, additional relativistic particles (“dark radiation,” e.g., an extra neutrino-like species) present in the early universe, or shortcomings in our understanding of gravity. Some outside scientists urge caution and note the most likely resolution could be unrecognized systematic errors, but the SH0ES team continues to refine measurements aiming for 1 percent accuracy using Hubble and future missions (Gaia, JWST, WFIRST). The disagreement, if confirmed, would have profound implications for cosmology by pointing to missing ingredients in the standard model of the universe.

Senior House Judiciary Committee staffers quietly assisted Trump aides in drafting the executive order that curbed immigration from seven majority-Muslim countries, sources say, but committee Chairman Bob Goodlatte and GOP leadership were not informed. The aides worked during the transition and reportedly signed nondisclosure agreements; the White House ultimately made the final policy choices. That limited consultation helps explain why most Capitol Hill Republicans and relevant committee members — including full Homeland Security panels and key senators — saw the final text only hours before or after it was signed. Leadership and rank-and-file Republicans scrambled over the weekend to understand and respond as detentions and confusions unfolded at airports, notably involving lawful permanent residents. Critics on the Hill and some administration allies said the rollout was poorly coordinated and unnecessarily chaotic. The order was largely driven inside the West Wing by Stephen Miller and Steve Bannon, who kept key officials and agencies at arm’s length; even some Cabinet members, such as John Kelly and James Mattis, learned details late. The White House defended its actions, saying relevant committee staff had been involved, while Senate and House leaders pushed back that they were not briefed. The botched implementation prompted public protests, bipartisan alarm, and internal White House infighting over blame and management style. Some Republicans urged better vetting and consultation in future to avoid legal, operational, and political fallout; the episode intensified mistrust between the White House and congressional Republicans as the administration’s chaotic early weeks continued.

A new Department of Labor rule, finalized now, tightens standards for retirement advisers by requiring them to act in clients’ best interests and giving savers the right to sue or arbitrate when advisers fail to disclose conflicts or meet ethical duties. Historically, retirement advisers have fallen into two camps: registered investment advisers, who are fiduciaries paid directly by clients and held to a duty to act in clients’ best interests, and broker-dealers, who typically earn commissions and revenue-sharing payments that can bias recommendations and are held only to a looser “suitability” standard. The Labor Department’s move follows efforts since 2008 to better protect middle-class savers; a White House CEA report estimated conflicted advice reduces saver returns by about 1% annually—roughly $17 billion nationwide—and can cost individuals large chunks of retirement balances when they roll 401(k)s into higher-fee IRAs. Industry groups argue most brokers already behave responsibly and warn the rule could spur lawsuits, force extra disclosures, or drive many brokers away from middle-class clients. Both critics and supporters expect significant industry changes: brokers may comply and earn lower commissions, shift to flat fees like registered advisers, or stop advising. The U.K.’s similar reforms reduced adviser numbers modestly but shifted income from commissions to fees. Some fear an “advice gap” for less-wealthy savers, though proponents note robo-advisers and plain guidance on basic saving—save regularly, favor low-cost index funds, and avoid early withdrawals—can suffice for many. Former SEC chair Arthur Levitt Jr. argues Congress should not delay the rule; further study often kills reform and leaves investors exposed to costly conflicted advice.

Police in Santa Cruz, California, recovered the body of 8-year-old Madyson “Maddy” Middleton Monday evening in a recycling bin at the Tannery Arts Center, a housing complex where she and a 15-year-old neighbor lived. Authorities say the teen lured Maddy to his apartment, killed her there, then concealed and dumped her body in the bin; detectives found her during a detailed second search. The boy, who had helped search for her and was present near the bin when the body was discovered, was arrested early Tuesday and remains in juvenile detention; the district attorney said he could be charged as an adult. Police have not released cause of death or said whether a sexual assault occurred; autopsy results are pending. Maddy was last seen on surveillance video Sunday at 5:07 p.m. riding her scooter; a missing-person call came about an hour later. The community has mourned with flowers and vigils, and officials described the case as heartbreaking as investigators continue to collect evidence and interview witnesses.

MSNBC hosts Joe Scarborough and Mika Brzezinski say senior White House aides tried to use a National Enquirer exposé about their relationship as leverage to extract an apology for their increasingly critical coverage of President Donald Trump. In an op-ed and on Morning Joe, they recounted that multiple top administration officials warned them the Enquirer, whose publisher David Pecker is a longtime Trump friend, planned a negative story and suggested calling Trump to have him “pick up the phone” to quash it — but only if they apologized. Scarborough says he refused; the Enquirer ran a June cover headlined a “sleazy cheating scandal.” Trump tweeted that Scarborough had called him to stop the piece; Scarborough called that a lie and said he has texts and phone records to prove it. The Enquirer denied involvement in any White House conversations and defended its reporting as accurate. The episode follows months of escalating public attacks between the hosts and Trump, including tweets insulting Brzezinski’s appearance and accusing the hosts of dishonesty. Media analysts say the spat reflects a troubling pattern of the president undermining the press and leveraging allies like tabloid publishers. Reporting on David Pecker’s National Enquirer shows a history of pro‑Trump, sensational coverage, paid “catch-and-kill” arrangements, and close personal ties to Trump and his circle. Pecker’s tabloids have repeatedly protected Trump while publishing damaging pieces about his rivals, raising concerns about use of media influence to help the president and punish critics.

When President Obama posted the first message from the official @POTUS Twitter account from the Oval Office, the White House presented it as a new, personal channel for the president to engage directly with the public. A photograph showing him at his desk with an iPhone underscored the moment. The administration emphasized that tweets would come exclusively from the president, and the account was framed as a milestone in presidential communication.

Almost immediately, the account drew a torrent of abusive, racist and sexually explicit replies. Some messages used racial slurs and dehumanizing imagery — including a depiction of the president with a noose — reflecting longstanding online racial hostility toward the nation’s first Black president. Other replies were crude sexual solicitations and explicit commands that, while vulgar, were nevertheless public replies aimed directly at the president.

Because the White House archives tweets, mentions and direct messages involving official accounts to comply with the Presidential Records Act, these abusive public replies become part of the official record. The White House’s online privacy policy confirms that tweets and mentions of official accounts are automatically archived. As a result, grotesque or offensive user messages — from racist epithets to lewd sexual demands — are preserved in White House files and, ultimately, accessible for inclusion in the Library of Congress collections.
