The episode highlights two tensions of modern presidential communication: the democratic transparency of direct social-media engagement, and the way that openness also broadcasts and preserves the worst elements of online discourse.

Republican presidential candidate Rick Santorum released federal tax returns for 2007–2010 showing a rapid rise in post‑Senate income tied to consulting and media work. The Santorums’ joint adjusted gross income climbed from about $659,000 in 2007 to $1.1 million in 2009, then dipped to $923,000 in 2010. Federal taxes paid were roughly $167,000 (2007), $262,000 (2008), $310,000 (2009) and $263,000 (2010), implying effective rates near 25–29 percent in high‑earning years. Much income flowed through Excelsior LLC: over $820,000 in fees in 2008 and more than $550,000 in 2010 from consulting and media appearances. Returns show stock sales, depreciation on condo and rental properties, mortgage deductions, modest charitable giving, and the purchase of an Audi claimed as a business expense. Santorum’s financial picture—consulting fees, board compensation from Universal Health Services, and rental holdings—contrasts with his outsider image and is modest compared with Romney’s and Gingrich’s reported incomes.

Los Angeles officials arrested a “person of interest” early Monday in connection with more than 50 deliberate fires that have caused about $2 million in damage. No new arsons have been reported since the detention, but authorities said the investigation is ongoing and an arson task force is reviewing roughly 100 leads. Police found materials in the suspect’s minivan that could have been used to start fires; the vehicle had Canadian plates and the man is reportedly a native of Germany. Sources said he may have been in a dispute with federal immigration officials over a relative’s status, and LAPD is coordinating with federal authorities, though any motive remains unclear. Witnesses said he was taken near Fairfax and Sunset; surveillance images apparently match the detainee. Booking on arson charges was expected later Monday.

Polls taken immediately after the 2010 midterms showed Republican primary voters coalescing around familiar names, but those early numbers mean little for the 2012 nomination fight. A Rasmussen national survey of likely GOP primary voters found a three-way dead heat: Mitt Romney 20%, Mike Huckabee 19% and Sarah Palin 19%, followed by Newt Gingrich (13%), Tim Pawlenty (6%), Ron Paul (5%) and Mitch Daniels (3%); 7% preferred someone else and 8% were undecided. Such national snapshots mostly reflect name recognition rather than electability or campaign strength. State polls in early-voting states matter far more; a CNN summary showed varying leaders by state—Romney and Huckabee tied in Iowa, Romney strong in New Hampshire, and Palin leading in South Carolina—illustrating the fluidity of early support. Historical parallels, like Rudy Giuliani’s early lead in 2008, underscore the unreliability of early polls. Commentary suggests Romney is the likely frontrunner with Palin his main challenger, Huckabee a persistent spoiler, and Gingrich hampered by baggage. Observers hope a less prominent governor or a fresh figure such as Marco Rubio might emerge, but early fundraising demands and a fast-starting race make late entries difficult. Overall, these polls are a starting point, not a prediction.

General Mills is answering fans’ long-running request with a limited run of Marshmallow Only Lucky Charms boxes. To celebrate marshmallow devotees, the company will give away just 10 special boxes via a social-media sweepstakes. From October 14–18, U.S. residents 18+ can enter by posting a photo of themselves holding an imaginary Lucky Charms box on Facebook, Twitter or Instagram and tagging it #Lucky10Sweepstakes; three entries max per person (one per platform). Winners will be notified around October 20. The promotion, which includes videos featuring Biz Markie, rewards fans who obsess over the cereal’s marshmallows.

The Senate narrowly advanced President Obama’s trade agenda Tuesday, voting 60–37 to end debate on Trade Promotion Authority (TPA), or “fast-track,” clearing the way for a final Senate vote Wednesday and likely eventual enactment. TPA would let the president negotiate major pacts—most immediately the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP)—and send deals to Congress for an up-or-down vote without amendment. Thirteen Democrats joined Republicans to reach the 60-vote threshold, despite objections that TPA was separated from Trade Adjustment Assistance (TAA), a worker aid program Democrats demanded. Leaders split TPA and TAA to overcome House opposition; senators pledged separate votes on TAA and on a package including African trade preferences (AGOA). Supporters, including Sen. Ron Wyden and Sen. Orrin Hatch, argued TPA is needed to compete with growing markets abroad and set high standards on labor and environment. Opponents—labor unions, Sen. Sherrod Brown, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and others—warned TPA would cost jobs and favor corporations. Republican maneuvering, late lobbying, and political calculations produced the slender victory, while Ex-Im Bank renewal and intra-party dissent added last-minute drama.

I, Tonya is a darkly comic biopic that revisits the life and scandal of American figure skater Tonya Harding, focusing as much on her upbringing and relationships as on the infamous 1994 attack on rival Nancy Kerrigan. Directed by Craig Gillespie from a screenplay by Steven Rogers and released in late 2017, the film blends faux-documentary techniques—talking-head confessionals, fourth-wall asides, unreliable narrators—and stylized flashbacks to present a chaotic, sympathetic portrait of a woman vilified by the media and skating establishment.

Margot Robbie stars as Harding, delivering a career-highlight performance that captures Tonya’s raw athleticism, defiant swagger and the deep vulnerability born of lifelong abuse. Allison Janney is unforgettable as LaVona Golden, Tonya’s profane, chain-smoking mother whose physical and verbal cruelty both forges Tonya’s drive and damages her self-worth. Sebastian Stan plays Jeff Gillooly, Tonya’s volatile husband whose involvement with a hapless conspiracy to attack Nancy Kerrigan—engineered largely by an unqualified “bodyguard,” Shawn Eckhardt (Paul Walter Hauser)—becomes the scandal that ruins Harding’s career and public reputation.

The film emphasizes class and image politics in figure skating: Tonya’s exceptional technical feats (she was one of the first American women to land a triple axel in competition) never translated into acceptance by judges or elites who preferred a polished, conventional ice-queen archetype. Gillespie’s tone oscillates between satire and genuine emotional weight, mining humor from the era’s pop-culture excess while refusing to reduce Tonya to a one-dimensional punchline. The result humanizes her—showing how poverty, abuse, and loyalty trapped her in destructive relationships—and questions the audience’s own appetite for scandal.

Critics praised Robbie and Janney’s performances and the movie’s inventive approach; some notes found the soundtrack needle-drops and stylistic devices occasionally on-the-nose, but most regarded those as minor flaws in an otherwise powerful film. With a runtime near two hours, an R rating, and distribution by NEON, I, Tonya was both a critical success and a provocative reassessment of a tabloid-era tragedy that remains relevant for its themes of class, gender, exploitation, and the distortions of media-driven public memory.

Nineteen-year-old Yaasmeen Castanada, a Cal State L.A. sophomore and mother of a 4-month-old, is critically ill in the burn unit at UC Irvine after a severe drug-induced allergic reaction. What began as a sore throat on Thanksgiving turned life-threatening when she took an antibiotic given by a friend. Within 24 hours she developed burning of her lips, throat and eyes, severe blistering and large open wounds; she was rushed to the ER, intubated and later transferred to the burn center. Physicians diagnosed Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS), which progressed to Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) as the reaction affected an estimated 65% of her skin and mucous membranes. Dermatologists and burn specialists describe the condition as essentially “burning from the inside out,” because layers of skin and mucosa separate and slough off, producing painful lesions, risk of infection and complications affecting taste, swallowing and vision. Yaasmeen has undergone surgeries, received multiple blood transfusions and been treated with specialized adherent dressings to allow skin healing without repeatedly removing bandages. Doctors are particularly concerned about eye involvement that could scar corneas and cause permanent blindness; reconstructive airway surgery and a tracheotomy were also required during her prolonged course. While mortality for SJS/TEN can be high, clinicians say early treatment improves outcomes and her overall prognosis is hopeful, though recovery will be long and include extensive rehabilitation and possible future procedures such as cornea transplant. Her distraught family urges people not to share medications and to know drug allergies in advance. A GoFundMe has been set up to help cover her care as loved ones seek support while she fights to recover and return to her studies and daughter.

On May 22, 2010, Bitcoin enthusiast Laszlo Hanyecz arranged to pay 10,000 bitcoins for two Papa John’s pizzas, believing his mined coins were worth roughly 0.003 cents each. Bitcoin is created through mining, where computers solve complex mathematical problems and miners are rewarded with new coins. What was a $30 pizza purchase then would be worth about $22.5 million at later prices, and a $100 investment at that 0.003-cent price would have grown to roughly $75 million. Bitcoin’s price has seen dramatic swings: it first surpassed $1,000 in late 2013, fell to around $280 in early 2014, was near $900 at the end of 2016, and later rose above $2,100 with a month of gains exceeding 65%. Several factors have driven recent rallies, including new Japanese legislation allowing retailers to accept bitcoin as legal currency—boosting yen-denominated trading to over 40% of volume—global political uncertainty increasing demand as a perceived safe haven, and community debates over blockchain upgrades that once threatened a split but have since eased. The surge has encouraged many rival cryptocurrencies (now comprising a growing share of trading), prompting concerns from some commentators about a potential unsustainable bubble.

Every year Ben Kinsey, a U.S. military veteran, stands on a South Carolina I-20 overpass waving an American flag for 11 hours to honor those killed on Sept. 11. This year he appeared two months early to pay tribute to four U.S. Marines killed in a Chattanooga, Tenn., attack. Noah Smith, who spotted Kinsey while driving, photographed him and posted the image on Facebook where it went viral. Smith asked Kinsey why he was there; Kinsey said he planned to stand four hours—one for each slain Marine—and noted that veterans can survive combat only to be killed at home. Kinsey told a local CBS affiliate he has observed the bridge vigil each 9/11 for the past three years, intending to continue annually. Dozens of social media users recognized Kinsey from prior vigils; Whitney Degnan recalled encountering him last Sept. 11 and praised his dedication despite extreme heat and advanced age. Hundreds offered to join him next year, and Degnan said she will visit again, calling Kinsey a reminder of national resilience.

Federal authorities charged 107 medical professionals — doctors, nurses, social workers and others — in a nationwide Medicare fraud sweep that targeted roughly $452 million in bogus claims, the largest single takedown by the Justice Department’s strike force. Arrests were made across seven cities, including Los Angeles, Miami, Baton Rouge, Houston, Detroit, Chicago and Tampa, with 87 detained immediately. Cases ranged from billing for ambulance rides, power wheelchairs and feeding tubes never provided to false home health, mental health, HIV infusion and physical therapy claims, and schemes involving kickbacks and altered paperwork. Baton Rouge cases alone involved about $225.6 million in fraudulent claims from two community mental health centers. Officials said the government sought to recover at least $59.5 million from initial complaints and indictments. The Obama administration highlighted intensified anti-fraud efforts, including data-analytic tools from the Affordable Care Act that prompted suspension of payments to 52 providers. The FBI is investigating thousands of healthcare fraud leads as prosecutions and provider exclusions multiply.

President Obama has ordered a significant increase in U.S. support for the hunt for Joseph Kony and his Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA), deploying additional Special Operations forces and aircraft to Uganda. At least four CV-22 Osprey tilt-rotor aircraft, refueling planes, and roughly 150 Air Force Special Operations personnel are arriving to enhance rapid troop transport and sustainment; total U.S. personnel in-country will be about 300 under a War Powers Act notification. U.S. forces remain in an advisory, information-sharing role to an African Union (AU) task force operating across Uganda, the Central African Republic, South Sudan and Congo, and are barred from offensive action except in self-defense. The move addresses AU leaders’ need for greater air mobility to respond to intelligence and defections that generate leads on Kony’s whereabouts. Kony, indicted by the International Criminal Court for atrocities including mutilations and child abductions, now commands only a few hundred fighters and has largely evaded capture in remote jungle regions. U.S. officials say LRA violence has fallen sharply since 2010, but the administration frames the deployment as both a humanitarian effort and a cost-effective demonstration of engagement in a region facing other security threats. The U.S. also links the mission to broader human-rights priorities in its relations with Uganda.

Idaho State University (ISU) has been fined $8,500 by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) after discovering it could not account for a small sample of plutonium-239 used in research. The missing material, about one gram—roughly a 30th of an ounce and the size of a U.S. quarter—was last documented in 2003. University officials, who realized the discrepancy during a routine inventory and notified the NRC on Oct. 13, say the loss stemmed from partially completed disposal paperwork when the item was taken out of service. ISU believes the sample was likely transferred to a licensed disposal facility, but no records exist to confirm that transfer, so the source has been officially listed as missing. The university emphasized the quantity is too small to construct a nuclear weapon, and ISU’s vice president for research, Dr. Cornelis Van der Schyf, said the source poses no direct health or public safety risk. The plutonium had been used in experiments to test nuclear waste container integrity and to develop methods to detect illicit radioactive materials entering the U.S. after 9/11. After discovering the missing item, ISU reviewed historical paperwork from 2003–2004, inspected waste barrels on and off campus, and physically searched the site, but could not locate the sample. The NRC noted ISU generally has a good compliance record; senior ISU officials planned to return remaining plutonium holdings to the Department of Energy as part of inventory reduction. The university has 30 days to dispute the proposed fine. The case underlines NRC’s rigorous controls and record-keeping expectations for radioactive materials.

A Reddit user, BlackPanther2016, is threatening to sue Warner Bros./DC Entertainment over what he calls false advertising for Suicide Squad. He likens movie trailers to menus: if a preview shows specific scenes, the audience should get those scenes in the theatrical cut. He says several Joker moments heavily featured in trailers—banging his head on a car window, “let me show you my toys,” punching a car roof, and dropping a bomb while saying “BYE BYE!”—were not in the film. He also cites two Katana shots shown in ads—her eyes going black and a slow-motion soul-taking sequence—that were missing. The user claims he drove 300 miles to London specifically to see those scenes, paid for tickets, and left disappointed; when he asked for a refund at the theater he says staff laughed and ejected him. He plans legal action to recover his ticket and travel costs, compensation for embarrassment, and to protest what he calls a growing habit of studios showcasing deleted or non-existent footage in trailers. The post rallied other disgruntled fans and criticized studios’ reliance on promises of extended or “director’s” cuts. Meanwhile, reports confirm Jared Leto’s Joker already had several cut scenes, though studios often omit such footage from final releases.

Taylor Swift pledged $1 million to Louisiana’s disaster relief fund after catastrophic flooding killed at least 11 people and damaged roughly 40,000 homes. In a statement to the Associated Press, Swift said she felt welcomed when she launched her 1989 World Tour in Louisiana and called it “heartbreaking” that so many residents have been forced from their homes. The floods—among the worst in the state’s history—prompted over 60,000 people to seek aid from FEMA and more than 30,000 rescues since the event began. Swift encouraged others who can to help, sending “love and prayers” to those affected. The donation continues a pattern of charitable giving by the singer, who is estimated to be worth about $250 million; past gifts include $50,000 donations to a young fan with cancer and to the nephew of a backup dancer, $50,000 to the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia in 2014, and $100,000 to the Red Cross in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, after flooding in 2008. Her contribution aims to support immediate relief and recovery for Louisiana communities.

A 5-year-old Florida boy, Billy Nolin, phoned 911 while playing with an old cellphone and invited deputies to his family’s Thanksgiving dinner. The call, which simply asked, “Will you come over cause we’re eating Thanksgiving,” amused Walton County dispatchers amid their usual difficult calls. Billy’s mother, Landi McCormick, first scolded him for misusing 911, and he cried. Deputies Dannon Byrd and Aaron Ethridge soon arrived; instead of punishing him they thanked him for the kind invitation, reminded him 911 is for emergencies, gave him a sheriff’s badge, let him sit in a patrol car and use the lights and siren, and asked about his future—he said he wants to be a cop. Photos of the visit went viral and highlighted deputies’ community role.

A Pew Research Center analysis, reviewed by 24/7 Wall St., ranks U.S. states by religiosity using four measures: weekly worship attendance, daily prayer, absolute belief in God, and saying religion is very important. “Highly religious” adults report at least two of these high-observance behaviors (or three high and one low). Southern states like Mississippi and Alabama top the list, with 77% classified as highly religious; both report 82% who are certain God exists and high rates of daily prayer and importance of religion. New England states — New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Vermont and Maine — are least religious (about 33–34% highly religious), with low weekly attendance and fewer certain of God’s existence. Overall, 70% of Americans identify as Christian, though the unaffiliated is the fastest-growing group.

Canadian freestyle ski star Sarah Burke, 28, suffered severe head injuries while training in Park City, Utah’s Eagle Superpipe and was flown to the University of Utah hospital in critical condition, sedated and in a medically induced coma. The fall occurred near the bottom of the pipe after a routine trick; she landed on her feet but then hit her head. Burke, a dominant superpipe competitor with four Winter X Games golds and world titles, had been instrumental in promoting the discipline and lobbying for its inclusion in the 2014 Olympics. Family, including husband Rory Bushfield, traveled to be with her; friends planned a statement. Doctors said inducing a coma and cooling are standard for serious brain injuries to reduce swelling. The accident revived concerns about halfpipe danger—echoing Kevin Pearce’s 2009 crash—and reinforced calls for safety measures, though officials maintained that inherent risks are acceptable and the trick was not extreme.

Photojournalist Michael Forster Rothbart spent years documenting life around Chernobyl and Fukushima to counter sensationalized images of deformity and abandonment. His book Would You Stay? shows that daily life continues amid lingering health problems, economic decline, and long-term uncertainty: older residents often stay despite cancer and poverty while younger people leave. After Chernobyl in 1986 authorities established concentric zones: a sealed Exclusion Zone with a few illegal “self-settlers,” plus three wider zones with encouraged evacuations that still host millions. Up to 3,800 workers remain at the defunct plant to manage slow, underfunded decommissioning. Radiation’s unseen, probabilistic threat—“how much, how dangerous, how soon”—haunts residents decades later; Fukushima evacuees face similar limbo, despite daily monitoring.

Ukraine is exploring a pragmatic reuse of the exclusion zone: solar arrays. Officials cite cheap land, existing high-voltage lines and trained personnel; investors from the U.S. and Canada have expressed interest and a small 4 MW pilot is planned. The plan could advance renewables, cut reliance on Russian gas, and signal European-style modernization amid conflict in Donbass. Meanwhile, Chernobyl’s physical legacy remains daunting: a brittle radioactive mass in Reactor 4, an interim sarcophagus expected to last 100 years, and unresolved needs for century- to millennia-scale containment. Locals like Alexandr Sirota straddle nostalgia and risk—living with Geiger counters, guiding tourists, and accepting compromises as the region’s environmental, social, and technical problems endure.

Comedian and broadcaster Stephen Fry sparked controversy after comments attributed to him in an interview with Attitude magazine suggested women do not enjoy casual sex the way men do and only have sex with men as “the price they are willing to pay for a relationship.” The Observer quoted Fry’s remarks and called them an uncharacteristic tonal shift; Fry responded on Twitter, saying he had been misquoted and posting “I give up” and later “Bye bye,” prompting widespread reaction among his nearly two million followers. The remarks — including a claim that if women enjoyed sex like men there would be straight cruising areas — drew sharp criticism from feminists and commentators. Germaine Greer dismissed his conclusions as “madness,” arguing women seek intimacy and passion differently, not that they lack sexual interest. Rosie Boycott called the assertions “rubbish,” and others questioned Fry’s authority to generalize about female sexuality. Attitude’s editor Matthew Todd said Fry was pondering reasons rather than passing judgment. Fry’s interview also touched on his past interest in the cottaging subculture. The episode reignited debate about gender, casual sex, and public misquotation.

Two and a half weeks after Defense Secretary Leon Panetta launched an inquiry, Pentagon investigators are poring over e-mail exchanges between Marine Gen. John R. Allen, then NATO commander in Afghanistan, and Tampa socialite Jill Kelley. About 15 investigators working full-time have identified roughly 60–70 messages that warrant close review from among hundreds of e-mails spanning about two and a half years beginning in 2010, when Allen served as deputy commander of U.S. Central Command in Tampa. The correspondence was uncovered during an FBI probe into anonymous threatening messages Kelley received asking her to stay away from then–CIA director David Petraeus; the FBI traced those notes to Paula Broadwell, Petraeus’s biographer, whose affair with Petraeus led to his resignation.

Officials have called the Allen–Kelley exchanges potentially “inappropriate,” though content descriptions vary: some law enforcement sources labeled a few messages sexually explicit, Pentagon briefers termed several “embarrassing,” and Allen’s allies insisted the e-mails were benign and affectionate rather than sexual. Investigators are assessing whether the messages violated Defense Department policy, government regulations or military law, including possible misconduct, misuse of government resources, or security breaches; so far no security violations have been found. The inquiry, handled by an unusually large and expedited team, may delay or derail Allen’s expected nomination as NATO supreme allied commander in Europe and is unlikely to conclude before year’s end. Allen, married with two children and stationed in Kabul overseeing the Afghan drawdown, is cooperating and denies adultery; interviews with him or Kelley had not progressed as of the report.

Kelley, who had social ties to Petraeus and Allen and once served informally as a local “social ambassador” and honorary consul for South Korea, has retained attorney Abbe Lowell. Lowell has demanded answers from prosecutors about leaks that publicized Kelley’s and her husband’s names and has sought to rebut claims that she exploited connections. Kelley lost her honorary consul role amid questions about misusing the title. Her lawyer also disputed public statements by two men who criticized her business dealings and past attorney-client conversations, threatening legal action for defamation and breaches of privilege. The episode has thrust Kelley and several military figures into national scrutiny and complicated senior leadership transitions in the military.

Fairfax County police are seeking a woman who reportedly impersonated a Target employee and stole more than $40,000 worth of iPhones from the Richmond Highway Target in Alexandria, Virginia. The incident occurred March 15, when the suspect, dressed as a Target worker, gained access to the store’s stockroom, placed multiple iPhones into a box, and left. Surveillance footage released by police shows her exiting the store and getting into a Volvo station wagon. Investigators say she appeared familiar with Target procedures, employee schedules and the precise location of iPhones in the stockroom, though she is not an employee. Authorities are asking anyone with information to contact Fairfax County police at 703-691-2131.

Apple premiered its iPad commercial during the 2010 Oscars, generating immediate buzz on Twitter and tech blogs. The ad follows Apple’s familiar creative style and doesn’t reveal new features ahead of the iPad’s April 3 release. CEO Steve Jobs’ red carpet appearance at the Kodak Theatre, where Pixar’s Up won animation honors, fueled speculation about Apple’s presence and future surprises.

Officials in New York and New Jersey scrambled to ensure storm-affected residents could vote, but long lines, poor lighting, organizational failures and confusion marked Election Day in areas hit by Superstorm Sandy. Despite measures—shuttle buses, consolidated polling locations and Gov. Andrew Cuomo’s executive order allowing displaced voters to cast ballots outside their districts—many polling sites opened unprepared. In Rockaway Park, a consolidated tent site lacked generators, heaters and lights; pollworkers and voters struggled to see ballots. In Hoboken, the Multi Service Center opened late, keys and voting machines were hard to locate, and signage directing voters by district was absent, creating disorganization and long waits. Even parts of New York City with power experienced disruption: Park Slope voters were redirected from a high school shelter to a more distant elementary school, producing long lines; some displaced voters received separate, shorter lines. Midtown sites at times ran out of affidavit ballot envelopes or had voters submit ballots without envelopes, risking disqualification. In Teterboro and some unaffected neighborhoods, voting ran smoothly, and shuttles helped displaced residents vote. Electronic absentee voters in New Jersey faced uncertainty—applications were acknowledged but ballots not received—prompting fears their votes would not count. Many displaced voters had trouble finding clear instructions; some gave up when new locations were too far. Across the region, voters voiced frustration but generally remained patient and civil. The piece highlights how last-minute fixes helped some but could not entirely overcome logistical hurdles created by the storm, leaving many intent voters anxious about whether their ballots would be properly cast and counted.

Senator John McCain, speaking on CBS' The Early Show, urged caution amid Republican optimism about winning the House and possibly the Senate, warning that Democrats’ strong get-out-the-vote efforts and late results in California and Washington could decide control. He lamented the surge in campaign spending enabled by the Citizens United decision, expressing concern about large anonymous or union-funded expenditures and recalling his own heavy primary spending. On expiring Bush-era tax cuts, McCain favored a temporary extension for all taxpayers for a couple of years rather than immediately raising taxes on the wealthy, arguing spending — not taxes — is the real problem. He praised former running mate Sarah Palin as an “outstanding candidate” for 2012 but said it’s too early to endorse her or pick winners.

The Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Gill v. Whitford, a high-stakes challenge to Wisconsin’s 2011 legislative map that Democrats say was engineered to entrench Republican control. A three-judge panel previously found the map an extreme partisan gerrymander that violated voters’ rights; the Supreme Court must now decide whether courts can police such maps and, if so, by what standard. Justices were sharply divided. Liberals—joined potentially by Justice Anthony Kennedy—expressed concern that maps which “stack” legislatures preordain outcomes and erode the right to vote. Conservatives, led by Chief Justice John Roberts and Justices Alito and Gorsuch, warned that courts lack workable, nonpartisan standards, that social-science metrics like the “efficiency gap” are new or unreliable, and that judicial intervention could damage the Court’s legitimacy and flood it with challenges. Several justices, including Breyer and Kagan, sketched or supported manageable tests using statistical and comparative tools; Breyer proposed a multifactored inquiry into one-party control, persistent partisan asymmetry, and extreme outlier maps. The case raises procedural questions about plaintiffs’ standing to challenge whole maps. If the Court rules for the plaintiffs, it could force new redistricting rules nationwide; if it declines, partisan mapmaking will likely continue. A decision is expected by summer.

At the Rio 2016 Olympics, a moment of true sportsmanship briefly eclipsed medal counts and world records: in the women’s 5,000m heat New Zealander Nikki Hamblin and American Abbey D’Agostino collided and fell. D’Agostino quickly helped Hamblin to her feet and encouraged her to finish; she herself suffered serious injury—later revealed as a ruptured ACL—and was eventually unable to walk. The two embraced at the finish line, with D’Agostino taken away in a wheelchair. Their selfless actions captured global attention and embodied Olympic values. In recognition, the International Olympic Committee awarded both athletes the rare Pierre de Coubertin medal, given only 17 times in history for exemplifying the Olympic spirit. Separately, the International Fair Play Committee, backed by the IOC, honored Hamblin and D’Agostino and also awarded the Norwegian men’s handball team for accepting an adverse result rather than lodging a protest after a controversial late goal allowed Germany to qualify for the Olympics. Presenters praised these acts as reminders that the Games celebrate excellence, friendship, respect and fair play as much as athletic achievement.

Eric Hites, a 40-year-old man from Danville who once weighed more than 560 pounds, embarked on an extraordinary cross-country bicycle journey to reclaim his health and his marriage. Motivated by a promise to his estranged wife and inspired by The Proclaimers’ “500 Miles,” Hites set off in June with a modest, heavily loaded bike and a trailer carrying roughly 300 pounds of gear. He hoped to lose hundreds of pounds, target a healthier weight near 300 pounds, and rebuild his life—documenting the trip through blogs and video posts on his site, FatGuyAcrossAmerica.

The trip has been grueling from the start. Hites battled unsuitable equipment, including the wrong suspension and gearing that wasted energy, and his rims warped under the strain. He slept wherever he could—on bike paths, in hostels, in tents—and faced repeated doubts and loneliness. Despite setbacks, by his early days on the road he had already lost significant weight (reports vary between 60 and 80 pounds) and covered dozens of miles. His persistence began to attract attention: local communities rallied to help when his rim failed in Tiverton, Rhode Island. Newport Bicycle donated a sturdier bike built for his size; the Tiverton Police Department and local people supplied other necessities; and a growing online audience contributed to his crowdfunding and offered moral support.

As word spread, offers poured in—dozens of bike offers, donations, and an emerging national interest. Fitness networks signaled intent to amplify his story and leverage his journey to encourage others to get active. Hites’s aim expanded beyond personal redemption: his transparency and determination resonated with many who felt stuck and alone, turning his solo quest into a broader movement about resilience, community, and transformation.

Medically supervised with training and therapy, Hites continues to work on his health and plans to resume his ride when cleared. He intends to keep chronicling the trip, interview people along the way, and ultimately write a book about the experience. What began as a personal pledge has become a public mission: he’s not just riding for himself anymore, but carrying hope for others trying to change their lives.

Kansas City Chiefs safety Husain Abdullah was mistakenly penalized for unsportsmanlike conduct after he dropped to his knees in prayer following a 39-yard interception return for a touchdown against the New England Patriots. The NFL later acknowledged the flag should not have been thrown, saying officials are not to penalize a player who goes to the ground as part of a religious expression. The initial call drew criticism on social media and prompted the Council on American-Islamic Relations to urge the league to clarify its prayer policy to avoid a double standard. Abdullah, a devout Muslim who took a year off to complete the pilgrimage to Mecca, said he knew he would prostrate in the end zone after intercepting Tom Brady and believes the flag likely resulted from his slide into the prayer rather than the prostration itself. Chiefs coach Andy Reid said officials told him the slide, not the prayer, prompted the penalty and joked that “when you go to Mecca … you should have the privilege to slide anywhere you want to slide.” Abdullah, thankful for the play and the ball, said the interception will have a place of honor in his home.

Amanda Knox, who went to Italy to study writing and later became the subject of an international murder case, has resumed writing as a freelance journalist in Seattle nearly a year after an Italian court reconvicted her. She’s been working for the small West Seattle Herald, which offered her the role to help her reclaim a normal life rather than capitalize on her notoriety. Initially writing under a pen name for privacy, Knox later published under her own name after showing strong writing and photography skills. The Herald’s Web Editor Patrick Robinson emphasized that hiring her was about giving a local resident and talented young writer an opportunity, not about the ongoing legal controversy or Italy’s extradition request. Knox covers human-interest pieces and local arts, including a high-school production of Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead. Despite awareness of potential outside attention, the paper manages interactions privately and focuses on providing her a chance to be treated as a regular member of the community.

In 2015 Oxford Dictionaries broke with tradition by naming not a written word but an emoji—“Face With Tears of Joy”—as its Word of the Year, reflecting how pictographs have become central to digital communication. Partnering with keyboard app SwiftKey, Oxford found that the laughing-crying emoji accounted for nearly 20% of emoji use in the U.S. and U.K., making it the most-used emoji globally and the clear choice to represent the year. Oxford’s president, Caspar Grathwohl, said the selection signals how pictographic communication fills gaps left by alphabetic scripts, offering immediacy, tone and cross-linguistic expressiveness. Though emoji have been included conceptually—the word “emoji” has appeared in Oxford resources since 2013—Oxford has not added emoji definitions into its main dictionaries. The piece recalls emoji’s origins with Japanese designer Shigetaka Kurita in 1999 and notes growing scholarly interest in treating emoji as serious communicative tools. Oxford’s 2015 shortlist also included contemporary terms such as ad blocker, Brexit, Dark Web, lumbersexual, on fleek, refugee, sharing economy and singular they. The choice underscores broader cultural trends—digital immediacy, visual expression and changing social vocabularies—and highlights that modern language selection can encompass symbols as well as words when they capture a year’s collective mood.

The Wilpon family, longtime owners of the New York Mets, reached a mediated settlement with Irving Picard, the trustee for Bernard Madoff’s victims, resolving claims that the Wilpons received fictitious profits from Madoff accounts. Publicly announced terms require them to return $162 million in so-called fictitious gains from 2002–2008, which includes a prior $83 million judgment. In practice, the Wilpons may pay far less: they can apply to offset $178 million in losses from other Madoff accounts, receiving a pro rata reimbursement based on overall recoveries Picard secures. If recoveries average about 50 percent, their net obligation could fall substantially, with only a guaranteed maximum additional payment of about $29 million if Picard’s recoveries fall short after three years. The settlement, brokered by former governor Mario Cuomo, ended years of contentious litigation and removed a major financial threat, allowing the owners to focus on the Mets amid ongoing team losses and heavy debt. Legal observers viewed Picard’s concession as weakening aggressive trustee claims against other defendants, though Picard defended the deal as maximizing returns for victims while avoiding trial risks.

Matthew Hickey, a recently retired Marietta, Ohio, K-9 officer, is fighting to keep his police dog Ajax after city policy and state law classify the dog as municipal property that must be auctioned if no other handler is available. Hickey retired last month because of an injury and said he was initially told he could keep Ajax by paying the dog’s assessed value, which he understood to be about $3,500–$4,000. He and his family regard Ajax as a member of the family. Under Ohio law, however, a police dog remains city property and must be sold at auction when its handler leaves the force unless another handler takes the dog. The Marietta Police Department noted Ajax could remain an active working dog for another five to six years. To resolve the situation, Marietta’s city council will consider options during a Thursday meeting; Mayor Joe Matthews said the council will officially offer Hickey an auxiliary officer position that would allow him to retain Ajax. Meanwhile, a GoFundMe supporting Hickey has raised over $70,000 and the platform has verified the funds will go to the intended recipient.

Langley, on Whidbey Island, is grappling with an overflowing population of wild rabbits that are damaging property, posing health concerns and frustrating residents. Thought to be descendants of a few European hares that escaped the Island County Fairgrounds decades ago, the rabbits have multiplied and found refuge in town where people feed them and buildings provide burrow sites, sheltering them from predators. The proliferation has caused extensive digging—leaving playgrounds and the middle school football field, recently restored at a cost of $80,000, riddled with holes that reappear after being filled. School officials report feces everywhere and worry about disease transmission; the district is considering spending $60,000 on fencing to protect campus grounds.

Homeowners report landscaped yards and young plants eaten or destroyed; one resident estimated about $300 in damage. Responses among locals vary: some feed and shelter the animals, while others push for control. The mayor ruled out city-sponsored trapping or killing because it would be unpopular. Possible solutions under discussion include relocation, introducing raptors, and encouraging residents to deter nesting by installing pavers and chicken wire and stopping feeding so rabbits return to forests where predators control them. Legal options are complex—some rabbit species are game and regulated, while domestic-type rabbits may be trapped or killed under certain rules—but enforcement and public sentiment complicate lethal measures. A community meeting is scheduled for October 7 to decide how to proceed.

Google reported a strong third quarter, with net income of $2.73 billion on $9.72 billion in revenue, beating expectations and sending shares up about 6% in after-hours trading. CEO Larry Page called it “a great quarter,” noting rapid growth in Google+ (over 40 million users) and continued expansion in mobile, including the planned $12.5 billion Motorola Mobility acquisition. Headcount rose to 31,353 worldwide by September. However, Google faces intensified tax scrutiny: the IRS is auditing how it shifted profits and intellectual property to low-tax subsidiaries after acquisitions like YouTube, examining transfer-pricing and valuations that have helped reduce its U.S. tax rate. France has opened a related probe. The company’s tax strategies—such as routing royalties through Ireland, the Netherlands and Bermuda—have cut its tax bill by roughly $1 billion annually and drawn regulatory and SEC attention.

NASA reported that one of the International Space Station’s two external ammonia cooling loops (Loop-A) shut down after hitting a preset temperature limit, forcing coolant to be routed to Loop-B and prompting shutdowns of some noncritical systems. Life support, power and scientific freezers were prioritized, and the six-person crew was never in danger. Engineers suspect a malfunctioning flow-control valve and are evaluating whether a software fix will work or if a contingency spacewalk is needed. Decision could take days to weeks; planning for major repairs typically requires about two weeks.

Shermain Miles, a 52-year-old Chicago woman with 396 arrests over 35 years for offenses from disorderly conduct and theft to assaulting an alderman, says she’s determined to change after her latest release. A judge sentenced her to time served in June after she agreed to enter mental health and substance-abuse treatment. Released from Logan Correctional Center, she rode home by train, read her Bible, vowed to give up drugs, alcohol and old associates, and headed to a residential program for former inmates in Humboldt Park. Officials and advocates say she behaved well in prison and express guarded optimism that she can break the cycle, though some locals remain skeptical about her long-term prospects.

Nicholas Kristof’s interview with Iran’s President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad in New York (Sept. 20, 2011) reveals a contradictory, conciliatory yet combative leader. Ahmadinejad began warmly, later defended Iran’s record on democracy and human rights, and disputed Western accusations of deception over its nuclear program. He renewed an offer: if the West supplied 20 percent enriched uranium for medical use, Iran would halt domestic enrichment to that level—insisting this material is for cancer-treatment reactors and not weapons. He claimed Iran had been transparent with the IAEA and denied wrongdoing, blaming political pressure on the agency. On detainees, he urged that the two jailed American hikers had trespassed and noted judicial independence in Iran. He criticized Western hypocrisy, contrasted U.S. problems with Iran’s resilience under sanctions, and urged respectful dialogue rather than coercion. On Syria, he urged dialogue and warned foreign intervention would worsen matters, while defending Iran’s own post-election actions as different. The interview oscillates between openness to negotiation and dismissive rebuttals of external criticism, concluding with Ahmadinejad expressing affection for the American people.

A suspected car bomb exploded Tuesday in Ankara’s central Kizilay district near government buildings, killing three people and wounding 15, Interior Minister Naim Sahin said. The blast, which occurred on a busy street less than a kilometer from the prime minister’s office and other ministries, came from a parked vehicle and set off secondary explosions as nearby cars—many running on liquefied petroleum gas—caught fire. Ambulances and fire crews rushed to the scene; bomb disposal teams searched for further devices. President Abdullah Gul, visiting Germany, condemned the attack as terrorism. No group immediately claimed responsibility; authorities noted Kurdish separatists, Islamist and leftist militants have previously carried out urban bombings. Several of the wounded were in critical condition, some reportedly losing limbs. The explosion damaged shops opposite a primary school and prompted a security cordon while investigations continued.

A Minnesota couple identified as John and Jane Doe has filed a federal lawsuit challenging state and federal adoption rules that require tribes be notified when an American Indian child is placed for adoption. The couple, who secretly carried their pregnancy and chose a white adoptive family, argue the notification requirement violates their due process and equal protection rights. They fear that informing the child’s tribe could trigger tribal intervention and re-placement with Indian parents under laws designed to keep Indian children in Indian families.

The suit targets the Minnesota Department of Human Services, the state attorney general and a Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe official. Their attorney, Mark Fiddler—a member of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa—contends only Native birth parents must surrender confidential adoption information to tribes and says birth parents should choose adoptive homes, even if non-Native. He warns that failing to notify could lead to fraud charges or voided adoptions. The couple declined interviews; the baby, born in April in Minneapolis, is currently living with the prospective adoptive white family.

Supporters of the notification requirement, including tribal advocates and attorneys, say the law protects the child’s cultural identity and ties to tribal community, which non-Native families cannot provide. They point to historic policies that separated Indian children from their families and to studies linking loss of cultural identity with increased mental-health risks. Critics of how the Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) is applied say enforcement can sometimes disrupt stable non-Native placements months or years later, citing cases like Baby Veronica and other contested adoptions. The Bureau of Indian Affairs has proposed rules to strengthen ICWA enforcement; tribes such as the Cherokee Nation support clearer guidance. Minnesota and tribal officials had not commented publicly at the time of reporting.

Twelve years ago, ecology student James Russell learned how hard it can be to catch a single invasive rat when a radio-collared animal called Razza escaped during an island study in New Zealand. The episode highlighted a key challenge in eradication efforts: removing the first or last individuals, a problem critical to achieving true pest-free status. Today, Russell coordinates R&D for New Zealand’s bold 2050 goal to eliminate invasive vertebrate predators — rats, possums, stoats and more — to protect native species. The plan builds on New Zealand’s global leadership in island eradications (over 200 projects) and broader “mega eradications” worldwide, but faces daunting scale: New Zealand’s 268,000 km2 and populated areas greatly complicate efforts that have worked on much smaller islands.

Current tools—poison baits (1080, brodifacoum), traps, helicopters and intensive planning—have proven effective on islands, but scaling up demands innovation. Researchers are developing new species-specific baits and traps, wireless biosensors, drone delivery, and genetic biocontrols. Gene drives via CRISPR could spread harmful traits through populations, and the Trojan Female Technique exploits mitochondrial mutations to produce sterile males without rapid selection against the trait. These methods remain largely experimental and controversial, raising ecological and ethical concerns, including risks if modified traits spread beyond New Zealand.

Public support and cooperation are essential because eradication needs near-perfect coverage; New Zealand benefits from strong volunteer networks and conservation culture, yet skepticism about genetic engineering and funding shortfalls persist. The government and philanthropists have pledged NZ$3 billion toward an estimated NZ$9 billion need; officials hope scientific advances will reduce costs. Successes such as the recent Antipodes Islands project — where a NZ$4 million “Million Dollar Mouse” campaign used helicopter-broadcast brodifacoum baiting, detection dogs and monitoring to eradicate about 200,000 mice — demonstrate progress and inform future strategies. Researchers stress a mixed, adaptable approach over time, combining conventional methods with new technologies to realistically pursue the ambitious 2050 target.

As the Sochi Winter Olympics approach, U.S. officials and teams are grappling with heightened terror concerns and complex evacuation logistics should a catastrophic attack occur. Russia, spending billions and erecting an extensive “ring of steel,” insists on primary control of security within its borders, making unilateral U.S. rescue operations unlikely without Kremlin approval. The State Department and FBI will have officers in Sochi, and U.S. military assets — including Black Sea warships and aircraft on standby in Europe — have been discussed for contingency support, but their deployment would depend on Russian cooperation. Rising threats include claims by Islamist militants and recent suicide bombings in Volgograd; analysts warn lone-wolf attackers remain a risk despite heavy defenses. Some U.S. teams have hired private firm Global Rescue for communications, rally points and potential air extraction, though details and feasibility in Russia remain unclear. Athletes express mixed feelings: some are worried and taking extra precautions, while others stay focused on competition. International delegations largely rely on Russian security, with a few nations adding discreet protections. Overall, despite unprecedented security measures, officials caution the risk level is higher than at past Games and that any large-scale crisis would pose severe diplomatic and logistical challenges.

New research from UBC’s Okanagan campus finds that while men are initially stronger, women exhibit markedly greater muscle endurance during dynamic, practical movements. Assistant Professor Brian Dalton and collaborators tested eight men and nine women of similar fitness, having them perform 200 rapid foot flexes while capturing speed, power, torque and muscle electrical activity. Men produced higher initial speed and power but fatigued far faster; women remained considerably less exhausted. Though the study focused on calf muscles, Dalton expects similar sex differences in other muscle groups and notes consistency with prior findings—women show lower fatigue in isometric tests and even in ultra-distance events, where men may be faster overall but women finish significantly less tired. Practical applications include tailoring exercise programs and workplace loads to reduce fatigue and improve productivity, perhaps by lowering initial male loads to better match female endurance.

Separately, a commentary by Oiselle founder Sally Bergesen argues that women’s sports lack celebrated, easy-to-name milestones comparable to men’s—like the four-minute mile or marquee male champions—so female achievements and traditions remain less visible. While landmark moments and policies such as Title IX expanded participation, they haven’t created equally resonant cultural narratives for women’s sport. Bergesen highlights the push to popularize the sub-4:30 mile as a clear, celebrated benchmark for American women—only 71 have achieved it—urging the community to build and broadcast traditions that create heroes, inspire athletes, and give fans definitive milestones to admire.

Florida county commissioners have approved zoning changes for American Dream Miami, a 6.2‑million‑square‑foot retail and entertainment complex proposed by Canadian developer Triple Five Worldwide. At an estimated $4 billion, the project would be the largest and most expensive mall in U.S. history, roughly twice the size of the current largest, King of Prussia. Planned for undeveloped land off the Florida Turnpike on a 174‑acre site, the complex is designed more like an indoor amusement park than a conventional mall. Proposed attractions include a giant indoor water park and pool, an indoor ice rink, an artificial ski slope, “submarine” rides, dozens of restaurants, up to 1,200 stores, and hotel rooms. Triple Five, known for Mall of America and West Edmonton Mall, projects about 30 million annual visitors and says the destination model—mixing entertainment with retail—can attract regional tourists and keep patrons on site longer, subsidizing stores.

Despite city approval, the project still needs permits, financing, and stormwater infrastructure plans. It has faced pushback from local malls worried about market saturation and from residents and environmentalists citing concerns about water and energy use, stormwater runoff, and flooding risk in Miami’s low‑lying areas. The approval comes as U.S. malls and many stores continue to close amid online shopping and shifting habits; analysts predict further attrition in the next decade. Proponents suggest American Dream Miami could model a future for struggling malls by emphasizing experiential, “destination” attractions. Critics question the wisdom of building a massive new mall in an over‑stored retail landscape, pointing to slow, troubled histories of other mega‑malls, including Triple Five’s long‑delayed American Dream Meadowlands project.

A 37-year-old Newman man has been charged with an offence likely to endanger life, health or safety after allegedly taxiing a propeller-driven Beechcraft two-seater down the main street and parking it outside the Newman Hotel (the Purple Pub) on Friday at about 2:10pm. Witnesses reported the aircraft, which had its propeller running, had been moved along Newman Drive after the owner bought it elsewhere in town and was taking it home but decided to stop for a drink. The plane had no wings, no steering wheel, and was reportedly being steered with foot pedals; police later found a fuel line connected to a jerry can in the cabin and the ignition left on. The empty aircraft attracted a crowd, emergency crews, and a tow truck which removed it. Police treated the incident seriously because children were walking home from school and traffic was heavy; CCTV and witness statements were being used in the investigation. The man, who does not hold a pilot’s licence, had the aircraft impounded and is due to appear in Newman Magistrates Court on November 18. Witnesses have been asked to contact police.

Disney has been granted a patent for a shoe- and foot-recognition system designed to track guests throughout its theme parks to collect movement and behavioral data. Filed in April 2015 and issued in July, the patent outlines a network of low-level, easily concealed cameras and depth sensors — including a mobile “robot” at park entrances — that would capture detailed images of visitors’ shoes and feet. The system would record characteristics such as shoe color, tread patterns, wear, stains, and even gum residue, and could supplement shoe data with lower-leg measurements when needed to distinguish between similar footwear.

According to the patent, this approach is intended to be less invasive and more reliable than other biometric methods like retinal, fingerprint, or facial recognition, and superior to clothing-based tracking which can be visible, changeable, or common across guests. Disney frames the technology as a tool for operational improvement: aggregating guest paths and dwell times could reveal the most popular rides, busiest walkways, and high-traffic retail areas, enabling better staffing, layout adjustments, and tailored experiences (for example, personalized media outputs at attractions).

The company emphasizes that the system would be unobtrusive, with sensors positioned “out of a person’s line of sight,” though the patent also notes the potential to recognize individual guests or allow registration at specific attractions. As with many filings, the patent represents a proposal rather than an imminent rollout; nonetheless, it signals Disney’s continued interest in gathering detailed visitor data to refine park operations and enhance guest experiences, with implications for visitation and regional tourism economics.

A 13-year-old Rocklin girl, identified as Ashley Wood, was found dead in her home on Monument Springs Drive Tuesday morning, prompting a homicide investigation that has left neighbors stunned and searching for answers. Ashley’s mother discovered her body in a bedroom just before 11 a.m.; police say she suffered blunt-force trauma. A 14-year-old boy who lived in the house fled into a nearby field and was arrested about a half-mile to a mile away after a multi-agency search; he is being held in the Placer County juvenile detention facility pending arraignment. Authorities have not released whether the teens were siblings, though multiple reports describe them as relatives. Investigators collected extensive evidence from the home under a search warrant and the California Department of Justice is assisting to provide additional transparency. Public records show the residence is co-owned by Jeffrey and Sonya Wood; a Jeffrey Wood listed at the same address is a senior prosecutor with the Placer County District Attorney’s Office, and the DA’s office declined further comment. Ashley was a former Sierra Elementary student and competitive gymnast remembered fondly online and by teammates; community members and officials have expressed deep sorrow for her family.

Reader’s Digest, the 91-year-old publisher, filed Chapter 11 to shed roughly $465 million in remaining senior notes as it restructures amid the shift from print to digital and heavy debt from its 2007 leveraged buyout by Ripplewood Holdings. RDA Holding listed over $1 billion in assets and debt; under a restructuring supported by Wells Fargo, $465 million of senior notes will convert to equity, leaving about $100 million in debt — an ~80% reduction. CEO Robert Guth says the company is simplifying operations, licensing international markets, selling properties like Allrecipes, and focusing on strong North American brands and digital editions, while seeking up to $45 million in debtor-in-possession financing. The FTC and Luxor Capital rank among creditors; Canada and other international operations are outside the filing. Management asserts the iconic brand can thrive post-restructuring.

President Trump used Thanksgiving messages and appearances to tout his administration’s achievements and praise the military. Speaking by video from Mar-a-Lago, he told members of the 1st Brigade Combat Team, 82nd Airborne, in Kandahar that U.S. forces are “fighting to win,” criticizing the Obama administration for limiting troops’ actions. He also claimed the military is delivering “defeat after defeat” to ISIS. In tweets and prepared remarks he highlighted economic gains—jobs returning, record stock market, low unemployment—promised border wall construction, veterans’ care reforms, a strong Supreme Court pick, regulatory cuts, and upcoming tax cuts. Trump additionally asserted credit for securing the release of three U.S. basketball players from China and emphasized national unity, gratitude, and God’s blessings.

Authorities announced the largest gun bust in New York City history after a 10-month undercover operation that dismantled two loosely organized smuggling rings funneling weapons from the Carolinas to New York for resale. Nineteen people were arrested and 254 firearms recovered. The rings were run by Walter Walker (Sanford, NC) and Earl Campbell (Rock Hill, SC), who trafficked guns via discount Chinatown buses to a Brooklyn broker, Omole Adedji. Guns often sold in New York for roughly three times their original price; officials say at least $160,000 profit was made on some sales.

The sting, dubbed “Up on the Hill,” grew out of an unrelated narcotics probe after Instagram and YouTube posts by aspiring rapper Mathew Best—who used a Brooklyn recording studio and posted images boasting about guns—led detectives to the traffickers. Wiretap and undercover buys documented frequent trips to New York, use of straw purchasers and black-market sources, and crude methods like transporting disassembled assault rifles in luggage (one girlfriend struggled to assemble parts using a YouTube video). Tape captured Campbell worrying about stop-and-frisk; sellers called bullets “cop killers.” Authorities said the seizures likely saved lives. The Manhattan DA, ATF and the Office of the Special Narcotics Prosecutor are involved in the ongoing investigation.

India has rejected NSA leaker Edward Snowden’s request for political asylum, the External Affairs Ministry said, after the Indian embassy in Moscow received his application. Spokesman Syed Akbaruddin and External Affairs Minister Salman Khurshid emphasized India’s cautious, restrictive asylum policy and said there was no reason to accede to Snowden’s request; India has not ratified the 1951 UN refugee convention and lacks routine asylum procedures. WikiLeaks said Snowden had applied to 21 countries, including Russia, China, Ecuador, Venezuela and several European states, though many European nations said asylum must be sought on their territory and thus deemed overseas petitions invalid. Russia initially signaled willingness to shelter Snowden only if he ceased “anti-American” activity; Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov later said Snowden withdrew his Russian application after learning Moscow’s conditions. Snowden, who exposed broad NSA surveillance programs, has been stranded in Moscow’s Sheremetyevo airport transit zone since flying from Hong Kong on June 23. The US revoked his passport and pressed other governments to deny his requests, according to Snowden and WikiLeaks. Ecuador’s president said Quito would only consider asylum if Snowden reached Ecuadorian territory and disavowed an unauthorized travel document issued by an Ecuadorian consul in London. Snowden calls himself stateless and argues his right to seek asylum has been obstructed.

A 21-year-old Baltimore-area man, Tawon Boyd, died in hospital days after a struggle with Baltimore County police and medics who responded to a late-night disturbance call. Accounts differ on who placed the 911 call: Boyd’s family and his attorney say Boyd called himself seeking an ambulance because he felt disoriented; police initially reported Boyd’s girlfriend as the caller but later said dispatch information made them think a woman was on the line. Dispatch records show two related calls and a timeline: police dispatched at 3:09 a.m., arrived about 3:18, requested EMS at 3:28, and medics left with Boyd at 3:58, arriving at the hospital at 4:10.

Officers described Boyd as confused, paranoid, sweating, and possibly under the influence. He reportedly asked police to enter his home, attempted to get into patrol cars, then ran to a neighbor seeking help. The incident report portrays minor, largely accidental contact—scratching a reporter’s neck, an accidental kick, and grabbing an officer’s face—while saying officers used body weight to restrain him. One officer, Bowman, admitted to delivering two closed-fist strikes to Boyd’s face. Witnesses, including Boyd’s grandmother and his girlfriend per family statements, say Boyd cried “Stop, I can’t breathe,” was struck repeatedly, choked while pinned face-down, and later went limp.

Medics reportedly administered haloperidol to calm Boyd; police noted that he became very calm and a medic checked his pulse before transport. Boyd subsequently developed brain swelling and kidney failure, family attorney A. Dwight Pettit said; an autopsy is pending and could take weeks. Authorities are investigating; family members dispute police characterizations and are pursuing answers as they prepare for his funeral.

President-elect Donald Trump publicly rebuked President Obama on Dec. 28, accusing him of creating “roadblocks” to a smooth transition despite previously praising Obama’s efforts. Trump tweeted he was “doing my best to disregard the many inflammatory President O statements and roadblocks. Thought it was going to be a smooth transition — NOT!” The comments followed a string of exchanges and apparent friction after initially cordial post-election interactions. Tensions escalated after Obama, in a podcast, said he believed he could have beaten Trump, prompting Trump to counter on Twitter and criticize Obama’s campaign efforts for Hillary Clinton. Trump also attacked outgoing administration decisions on Middle East policy—especially Secretary of State John Kerry’s planned speech and the administration’s refusal to veto a U.N. resolution condemning Israeli settlements—calling the Iran deal “horrible” and urging Israel to “stay strong,” while reminding that his inauguration was “fast approaching.” Transition spokesman Sean Spicer said the tweets “speak for themselves” but later noted the Obama team had been helpful on logistical matters. Trump later said he’d had a “very nice conversation” with Obama and described their call as constructive. The White House declined to comment on Trump’s tweets; Obama continues to pledge a peaceful handover and to attend the inauguration.

President Obama issued a new Executive Order expanding U.S. sanctions under the national emergency on Ukraine, citing Russian actions — including deployment of military forces in Crimea — as undermining Ukrainian democracy, security, sovereignty and contributing to asset misappropriation. Building on E.O. 13660, the order authorizes the Treasury, with State, to sanction named Russian officials, anyone in the Russian arms industry, and those acting for or supporting senior Russian officials. Seven Russian officials were designated and had U.S. assets frozen: Vladislav Surkov, Sergey Glazyev, Leonid Slutsky, Andrei Klishas, Valentina Matviyenko, Dmitry Rogozin, and Yelena Mizulina. The U.S. will also target individuals who support senior Russian figures even if they hold no official post, focusing on personal assets rather than state-run companies. Additionally, under E.O. 13660 the Treasury sanctioned four others: Crimea separatist leaders Sergey Aksyonov and Vladimir Konstantinov, former Ukrainian chief of staff Viktor Medvedchuk, and ex-President Viktor Yanukovych. The White House warned further measures will follow if Russia does not withdraw forces and respect Ukraine’s territorial integrity; the EU has announced parallel measures.

Experts say modern cars don’t need extended idling to warm up, while local ordinances and safety concerns still lead to tickets and debate. Chris Lague, a veteran service writer in Vermont, explains that fuel-injected, computer-controlled engines reach operating condition quickly—about 30 seconds to a minute is typically enough for oil to circulate—so driving gently shortly after startup warms the car faster than prolonged idling. Vermont’s anti-idling law (2014) limits idling to five minutes per hour, reflecting environmental concerns even as emissions fall. Some drivers remain “old school,” convinced that long warm-ups protect engines in very cold weather; that practice traces to carbureted vehicles of decades past. Mechanics note that vintage carbureted cars are an exception, but most modern vehicles don’t need long idling periods.

A Michigan case highlights another angle: a Roseville man, Nick Taylor, was ticketed after leaving his 1997 Chrysler running and unattended in his driveway with the keys inside. Police cited a “motor vehicle unattended” ordinance, citing public safety—cars left running with keys inside are easily stolen—while officials say remote starters (where keys aren’t inside) avoid this issue. The ticket prompted widespread online backlash, but authorities emphasize the rule’s safety rationale. Taylor faces a court appearance to contest the citation. Overall, while warming a car briefly for comfort causes little harm, leaving an unattended, keyed, running vehicle risks legal trouble and theft.

Stanford University has instituted an immediate policy banning hard liquor and shots at all undergraduate on‑campus parties, while still allowing beer and wine. High‑volume liquor containers (750 mL or larger) are also prohibited in undergraduate housing; graduate residences and registered graduate‑hosted events may permit liquor under restrictions. Administrators describe the change as a targeted effort to curb high‑risk binge drinking, limit rapid consumption of hard alcohol, and “meaningfully change the campus culture around alcohol.” The policy grew from a working group including the Office of Alcohol Policy and Education, Vaden Health Center and Residential Education, and followed consultations with students, resident fellows and RAs. Violations can lead to referral to residence deans, the Office of Community Standards, or removal from university housing. The move comes amid heightened scrutiny after the widely publicized Brock Turner sexual‑assault case, though officials say the rule was not a direct response. Critics argue the ban is tone‑deaf and could push drinking into private settings, increasing risks of bingeing, alcohol poisoning and sexual assault, and contend the university should instead focus on consent education and accountability. Administrators counter the measures are evidence‑based attempts to reduce availability and high‑risk behavior.

A study published in Neuropsychopharmacology found that the taste of beer alone can trigger dopamine release in the brain’s reward centers, even without intoxicating alcohol levels. Researchers at Indiana University gave 49 men tiny sips (15 ml) of their preferred beer, plus comparisons of a sports drink and water, while scanning brains with positron emission tomography. Beer taste produced greater dopamine increases and stronger self-reported cravings than the nonalcoholic beverages. Men with a family history of alcoholism showed an amplified dopamine response, suggesting a possible heritable risk factor for alcohol misuse. Experts note the results confirm that sensory cues like flavor can drive desire and relapse risk, though interpreting the family-history effect and completely ruling out any pharmacological influence remains challenging.

The Gardiner Water and Sewer Treatment District in Montana has sued the National Park Service over persistent arsenic contamination in wastewater that originates from Yellowstone National Park and is treated by the district. Facing a roughly $2 million required replacement of sludge treatment pond liners and state pressure to complete the work, the district says it has repeatedly tried to get the Park Service to address infiltration of arsenic-laden water into its sewer system but received insufficient and untimely responses. An engineer’s 2015 report found elevated arsenic in sewage coming from Mammoth—inside Yellowstone—observing that Yellowstone effluent accounted for about 95 percent of arsenic reaching the treatment plant and that the contamination appeared to be entering via manholes or breaks in underground pipes. The engineer advised resolving the infiltration first to prevent arsenic levels from rebounding after sludge removal. The district sent letters in March and December 2015 and again in August 2016; the Park Service eventually acknowledged ongoing infiltration and indicated it might contribute substantially to the cleanup costs but offered no timetable to repair pipelines and said funds likely would not be available until 2020. The lawsuit alleges breach of an oral contract, trespass, public and private nuisance, and negligence, and seeks a court order compelling the Park Service to repair and monitor its sewer lines quarterly, provide reports, address the arsenic problem, and help fund the sludge removal project to safeguard public safety.

Three inmates escaped early Saturday from the Choctaw County jail in Butler, Alabama, prompting a multi-agency manhunt. Authorities identified the escapees as 23-year-old Demarcus Woodard and 32-year-old Germayel (Gemayel) Culbert—both held on capital murder charges—and 23-year-old Justin (Terrell) Gordon, charged with armed robbery. The men, locked together in one cell, allegedly lured a jailer to open the door by claiming one was sick; when he did, they overpowered and choked him, stole his keys and cell phone, and fled. Tracking dogs followed their trail about a quarter-mile down State Highway 17, where officials believe a vehicle picked them up. The jailer was treated and released from a local hospital. The FBI, Alabama Bureau of Investigation, U.S. Marshals and local law enforcement are searching the area and beyond. Authorities ask anyone with information to contact the Choctaw County Sheriff’s Department. The report will be updated as new details emerge.

Robert Zemeckis’s Flight opens with a harrowing, technically brilliant plane crash that instantly captivates: a rain-slashed commercial flight suffers cascading mechanical failures, and Denzel Washington’s Captain Whip Whitaker performs an extraordinary inverted landing that saves most passengers. The film then pivots into a moral and psychological drama about addiction, culpability, and hero worship. Whip is both savior and suspect—hailed for his flying skill yet revealed by toxicology to have been intoxicated with alcohol and cocaine. The script follows the aftermath: investigations by the NTSB, maneuvering by the airline and pilots’ union, and legal spin from Don Cheadle’s lawyer. Rather than sustaining the aeronautical tension, the movie detours into familiar addiction tropes—Whip oscillates between charm and self-destruction, aided and enabled by John Goodman’s flamboyant dealer and glimpses of redemption offered by Kelly Reilly’s recovering addict, Nicole. Critics praise Washington’s raw, complex performance as the film’s anchor; his haunted, unvarnished portrayal renders Whip’s moral crisis compelling. Zemeckis, returning to live-action, balances spectacular technical filmmaking with intimate human drama, though some find the screenplay uneven and sentimental. Ultimately Flight soars in its opening and in Washington’s performance, but stumbles when it shifts toward a conventional morality play.

The University of Virginia has issued four-year trespass warnings banning Richard Spencer and nine others for their roles in the August 2017 white-supremacist torchlight march and the subsequent Unite the Right events in Charlottesville. Spencer, a U-Va. alumnus who organized the Aug. 11 torchlight procession and spoke at the Thomas Jefferson statue, was cited for taking credit for “defeating” counterprotesters and for statements indicating his group surrounded and prevented anti-racist demonstrators from leaving. The next day’s rally descended into violent clashes that left dozens injured and counterprotester Heather Heyer dead after being struck by a vehicle. 

The no-trespass orders follow a year-long investigation by U-Va. police working with state and federal authorities, which concluded the 10 identified individuals either committed or conspired to commit violence or other conduct that threatened community safety. University leaders emphasized the distinction between protected speech and actionable conduct aimed at intimidating or promoting violence; violations of the bans are criminal trespass offenses. U-Va. counsel Timothy Heaphy said the bans address policy violations, not expression, and the university may add more individuals identified as having violated campus rules. 

Other banned individuals include Benjamin Daley, Antonio Foreman, Thomas Gillen, Elliott Kline, Michael Miselis, Vasillious Pistolis, Robert Ray, Wil Smith and Cole White. Four were recently federally charged with rioting; one was dismissed from the Marines after a court-martial. Spencer has said ideas cannot be censored and has no immediate plans to engage in campus activism; separate divorce filings have also surfaced allegations of abuse against him.

Authorities investigating Todd Kohlhepp’s property near Woodruff, South Carolina, have recovered a third body, bringing to light a case tying the 45-year-old real estate agent and registered sex offender to multiple killings and a kidnapping. The remains were found Monday close to another body unearthed the day before; identifications, sex and causes of death remain pending pending anthropological and forensic analysis. Investigators had earlier rescued Kala Brown, a 30-year-old woman discovered chained by neck and ankle inside a metal storage container on Kohlhepp’s 95-acre parcel. Her boyfriend, 32-year-old Charles Carver, was found dead in a shallow grave and identified as a victim; Kohlhepp has not been charged in Carver’s death yet. After his arrest, Kohlhepp confessed to a 2003 quadruple slaying at Superbike Motorsports in Chesnee, for which he faces four murder counts; he has been linked to as many as seven deaths and authorities are searching other properties he owned, including sites outside South Carolina. Kohlhepp, who previously served time for a 1987 kidnapping and rape of a 14-year-old in Arizona, has chosen to represent himself and reportedly cooperated at times—granting investigators access, speaking with them and asking to contact his mother. Searches continue and officials say they believe they have located all graves on the Woodruff property, though further excavations and examinations are ongoing.
