Zack Snyder is singled out as Hollywood’s go-to director whenever studios demand a reboot with one instruction: “Make it grittier.” Known for draining levity and warmth from established heroes, Snyder’s hallmark is a hyper-serious, hyper-muscular aesthetic—think glossy, rippling bodies and somber, slow-motion brooding. The piece criticizes his tendency to transform traditionally optimistic characters into dour, destructive figures who shrug off collateral damage and moral clarity in favor of mood and muscle. Superman, emblematic of that shift, is described as being stripped of his role as a moral beacon and recast as “Superbro,” a bleak, uncompassionate enforcer who demolishes surroundings without concern. Snyder’s visual signature is summed up bluntly: take a cheerful hero, douse them in gloom, then compel them to brood as if the story depends on it. This profile appears as part of GQ’s third annual list targeting people who have overstayed their spotlight and used their fame poorly; Snyder is among the top twenty-five. The editorial challenge was narrowing the list, and the package also includes a short “retirement” mini-list for figures judged to have been ineffectual or irrelevant for so long that their cultural cachet is considered permanently diminished. Overall, the piece frames Snyder as the embodiment of a tired, pervasive Hollywood impulse to equate grit and visual severity with maturity, often at the cost of character and joy.

Two Afghan trainees assigned to Moody Air Force Base in south Georgia have been reported missing after failing to return to aircraft maintenance training on Monday. The men, identified in initial reporting as Mirwais Kohistani and Shirzad Rohullah, had been at Moody since February 2015 as part of a U.S. program to train Afghan personnel to operate and maintain A-29 Super Tucano aircraft; they were scheduled to graduate Dec. 18. The base last had contact with them Friday, and trainees are permitted off base on weekends. Federal, state and local agencies, along with base security, are tracing their movements over the past five days; Valdosta Regional Airport confirmed law enforcement seized hours of surveillance video related to the investigation. Base and local officials emphasized that both men were vetted before entering the United States—screened by Afghan authorities, the U.S. Naval Air Training Command, and the State Department—and that there is no evidence they pose a threat. Valdosta Police Chief Brian Childress and Air Force spokesmen stressed the trainees were cleared and had not previously caused problems. Officials also noted concerns about potential risks to the men and their families if their affiliation with the Afghan air force became known, given that some adversaries might want to harm them. The incident echoes past cases of Afghan military personnel absconding during U.S. training, but authorities are focused on locating the two men and determining why they left.

Archaeologists unveiled a nearly 1,500-year-old carved limestone altar from the Maya site La Corona in northern Petén, Guatemala, shedding new light on the rise of the Kaanul (Snake) dynasty and its long campaign against Tikal. Discovered in 2017 encased in tree roots within a collapsed temple, the one-ton altar was painstakingly excavated and moved to Guatemala City’s National Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology for study and display. Dated to May 12, A.D. 544, the slab depicts a previously unknown La Corona ruler, Chak Took Ich’aak, holding a double-headed serpent effigy and conjuring local patron gods. Inscriptions and later evidence show the same ruler became a vassal of the Kaanul dynasty and governed the larger nearby city of El Peru–Waka two decades later, indicating shifting political alignments. Researchers led by Marcello Canuto of Tulane and co-director Tomás Barrientos interpret the altar as evidence that the Snake Kings expanded not only by warfare but by decades of diplomacy, marriage alliances, cultural appropriation, and forming allied city networks that gradually encircled and strangled Tikal. A royal marriage between a Kaanul princess and La Corona’s dynasty two decades earlier underscores this strategic entanglement. Colleagues liken the subtle, behind‑the‑scenes maneuvering to a “Game of Thrones”‑style power play rather than a sudden military blitz. The team—using LiDAR mapping and long-term excavation—says the altar fills crucial gaps in Classic‑period Maya history, illustrating early Kaanul strategies that presaged their regional dominance for centuries amid challenges like looting and environmental threats to the Petén archaeological landscape.

President-elect Donald Trump’s transition team sent the Energy Department a detailed questionnaire seeking names of employees and contractors who worked on climate-related meetings, publications, and policies, prompting alarm among department staff, unions and Democrats. The memo — containing 74 questions and asking for lists of attendees at UN climate talks, work on the social cost of carbon, and publications from the department’s 17 national labs — left many career scientists and contractors “unsettled,” officials said. Energy spokesman Eben Burnham-Snyder announced the department will not provide individual names, stressing it will share only publicly available information and will “respect the professional and scientific integrity and independence” of its workforce. Union leaders and congressional Democrats called the request intimidating and potentially punitive. Rep. Steny Hoyer and Rep. Elijah Cummings warned it could chill scientific work or constitute retribution for following Obama-era policies; union heads compared it to political “witch hunts.” Civil service experts noted that while firing career staff outright is unlikely due to protections, employees could be marginalized or contractors have contracts not renewed based on political judgments. Outside analysts and the Union of Concerned Scientists applauded the department’s refusal, calling the request dangerous. The episode underscored potential friction in the transition: Trump has previously called global warming a hoax and criticized the Paris climate agreement, though he later said he was keeping an open mind and met with Al Gore. Transition officials did not comment; Reuters reported Rick Perry was expected to be nominated to lead the Energy Department. The episode has heightened fears among federal scientists about politicization of climate work under the incoming administration.

Sen. Marco Rubio, a principal architect and public face of the Gang of Eight comprehensive immigration reform bill, told radio host Hugh Hewitt he will not vote for the version emerging from the Judiciary Committee unless its border-security provisions are substantially strengthened and made less discretionary for the Department of Homeland Security. Rubio said he’s working with colleagues on amendments that would specify measures—such as targeted fencing, manpower, and clear sector-by-sector requirements—based on input from border patrol agents, and include measurable effectiveness standards (for example, high apprehension rates). Central to his demands is replacing vague DHS-crafted plans with specific, congressionally mandated actions whose completion would trigger legalization pathways; if those triggers aren’t met, the green-card process would remain paused. Rubio emphasized the goal is to prevent another wave of illegal immigration and argued many senators support reform only if enforcement guarantees exist. He said if the amendments fail, he won’t back the bill, believing it wouldn’t become law as is. Rubio also stressed an open, deliberative Senate process rather than rushed action and acknowledged some conservatives will remain opposed regardless, but he hopes clear, enforceable border-security language can win broader support.

On a recent episode of The Colbert Report, host Stephen Colbert—usually dominant in interview segments with his in-character improvisation—met his match in members of Pussy Riot. The punk collective, known for being imprisoned and later released after protesting Russian President Vladimir Putin, appeared via a translator, which could have slowed the exchange but instead heightened its impact. Band members Nadya Tolokonnikova and Masha Alyokhina delivered sharp, witty, and sometimes poignant answers that played off Colbert’s style while asserting their own voice. They recounted their experiences of imprisonment and release, took jabs at Putin and even dared him to re-incarcerate them, and offered commentary that alternated between hilarious and sobering—particularly regarding Russia’s anti-gay laws. The translator’s presence made viewers hang on every word, demonstrating that humor can survive—and even be amplified—through translation. Comedy Central posted the interview in two parts. The article also notes a contact tip line for Mediaite and includes an unrelated fact about Alexa Internet donating crawl data to the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine since 1996.

Operators at Japan’s crippled Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant have begun removing massive protective covers from one reactor, marking a key step in the long, complex decommissioning process that began after the March 2011 earthquake and tsunami. That disaster caused meltdowns in three of the plant’s six reactors, killed about 16,000 people, displaced roughly 300,000 residents and rendered large areas unusable for years. In October 2011 TEPCO installed six 136-foot covers over Unit 1 to limit radioactive releases; removal of the first cover started in July 2015 and work to take down wall panels is expected around September 2016. The covers must be cleared so crews can access and ultimately extract 292 spent fuel rods inside—rod removal is targeted to start in 2020 after all covers have been removed by the end of the following year. Separately, the government approved raising compensation for the disaster to 7.07 trillion yen ($57.2 billion), adding 950 billion yen to earlier commitments, as many evacuees still live in temporary housing more than four years on. TEPCO, which was bailed out by taxpayers in 2012, faces lawsuits and huge cleanup costs; revoking most evacuation orders within two years is planned to cap payouts and accelerate reconstruction.

The prosecution team for the woman who accused former IMF chief Dominique Strauss-Kahn of sexual assault has enlisted French lawyer Thibault de Montbrial to help locate any of Strauss-Kahn’s alleged past victims. New York attorneys Kenneth Thompson and Douglas Wigdor sought a visible, independent French attorney fluent in English; De Montbrial—known for work on major political and financial cases like Clearstream and the Karachi bombing suits, though not for sexual-assault cases—confirmed he was hired to contact potential victims. The move could aim to find witnesses to testify or serve as a public-relations tactic to show the accuser’s team is aggressive. Strauss-Kahn, under New York house arrest, has pleaded not guilty to multiple charges including attempted rape and faces up to 25 years if convicted. His defense has asked whether prosecutors will raise prior allegations at trial.

President-elect Hassan Rouhani has called for significant social and media reforms in Iran, urging the government and clergy to stop interfering in citizens’ private lives, loosen internet restrictions, and allow state media to report more openly on domestic problems. Speaking to clerics and in media interviews two weeks after his surprise election, Rouhani emphasized that a strong government earns trust by providing services and enabling development, not by limiting freedoms. He criticized widespread internet filtering as ineffective and politically motivated, arguing social networks are a positive force and that online restrictions only increase public distrust. Rouhani condemned state broadcaster IRIB for ignoring pressing domestic issues—citing its coverage of trivial events while failing to report on unpaid workers’ protests—and said freer expression would restore audiences’ faith in national media. He pledged to reduce censorship of arts and culture, oppose gender segregation in society and universities, and criticized crackdowns by morality police, saying noncompliance with dress codes does not prove a lack of virtue. Backed by moderates and reformers, Rouhani still faces potential resistance from hardliners who control parliament, the Revolutionary Guards, security agencies, and state media. He urged patience, noting severe economic and political challenges compounded by international sanctions, and stressed that meaningful change will require the support of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei and time to implement.

The authors appreciate the power of online activism but warn that hashtag campaigns like #BringBackOurGirls have limits and risks. Social media can quickly raise awareness and pressure leaders, as seen when celebrities and politicians acknowledged the abductions of over 200 Nigerian schoolgirls by Boko Haram. That visibility helped prompt offers of international assistance and political responses. Yet the piece argues that awareness alone can create a false sense of accomplishment, obscuring deeper policy and structural issues and failing to produce concrete results for those suffering on the ground. By the time widespread attention arrived, weeks had passed and U.S. coverage had already begun to wane. The writers caution that tweeting or reposting can substitute for sustained, strategic action—researching the context, supporting targeted advocacy, and holding authorities accountable—rather than actually helping victims. They note past disappointments where public outrage did not translate into justice, citing cases like Joseph Kony and George Zimmerman. The authors also critique how newsworthiness and audience interest shape media coverage; atrocities in regions perceived as distant or familiar receive less attention, and sensational or relatable narratives dominate. Hashtag activism can also spread misinformation rapidly, illustrated by viral but misattributed images circulated under #BringBackOurGirls. Nonetheless, the essays conclude that hashtag campaigns have real influence: they mobilize public sentiment, draw media and political attention, and even catch the notice of extremist groups. Therefore, while imperfect and sometimes hypocritical, social media activism is growing in power and should be used thoughtfully alongside informed, sustained action.

Europe's GOCE gravity-mapping satellite re-entered and burned up over the southern Atlantic after losing contact late Sunday while flying about 75 miles above Antarctica, the European Space Agency and tracking agencies reported. Ground stations last received a signal at 22:42 GMT; models indicate breakup began around 00:16 GMT near the Falkland Islands with debris likely falling into the South Atlantic east of Tierra del Fuego. About a quarter of the one-tonne, car-sized probe — launched in 2009 — was expected to survive re-entry, though no damage has been reported. GOCE, nicknamed the "Ferrari of space" for its sleek shape, operated at an unusually low 224 km orbit and required continuous ion-thrusting; it fell once its xenon fuel ran out on Oct. 21. Its precise gravity maps improved understanding of the crust–mantle boundary, aided ocean circulation and height measurements, and will remain a valuable resource despite the mission’s uncontrolled end.

The document combines two different items: a brief institutional description of Brigham Young University’s L. Tom Perry Special Collections Web Archive and a human-interest news account about a lost engagement ring recovered from Loose Park Pond.

The BYU L. Tom Perry Special Collections Web Archive, a partner of Archive-It since February 2013, aims to advance scholarship and learning by documenting, providing access to, and preserving online material that reflects the state of Mormonism in all its variations. Its primary emphasis is on the Mormon experience as expressed through culture, history, philosophy, theology, ideology, society and the arts. The archive also collects material related to secondary topics connected to Mormon life and interests, such as business, education, politics, activism, and philanthropy. The organization’s web presence is hosted at lib.byu.edu.

The second piece is a feature about a Kansas City couple, Seth Dixon and Ruth Salas, whose engagement proposal took an unexpected turn when Dixon’s engagement ring fell through a bridge into the murky waters of Loose Park Pond. A local Good Samaritan, Michael Long, heard about the mishap and volunteered to help retrieve the ring using a metal detector. Over two days and hours spent in the water—braving murky conditions, poking through debris with a bucket of rocks to hold himself down—Long found numerous small objects (about 25 nails and a toy car) before finally locating the ring after roughly three hours on his final search. He verified the ring belonged to Seth and Ruth and handed it to a friend of the couple. The story gained wider attention: the couple shared the episode publicly before flying back to Kansas City from California, appeared on Jimmy Kimmel Live!, and received a new ring from Kimmel. The report closes by noting there was no immediate word on the fate of the recovered original ring.

The National Library of Medicine collects and preserves biomedical information and has archived web content documenting health histories. Explorer and UC San Diego scientist Albert Lin launched the Valley of the Khans Project to locate Genghis Khan’s lost tombs across Mongolia’s vast terrain using crowdsourced image analysis. Through Field Expedition Mongolia, developed with National Geographic, more than 7,000 volunteers tag 85,000 high-resolution satellite images for roads, rivers, modern and ancient structures, or “other” anomalies humans spot better than computers. Volunteers’ clustered tags guide on-the-ground inspections, yielding discoveries like Bronze Age tombs and ancient city remnants. The project exemplifies modern citizen science—engaging, game-like web platforms motivating unpaid contributors. Similar initiatives include EteRNA (RNA design), Galaxy Zoo (galaxy classification), and USGS bird-data digitization, all harnessing public participation to accelerate research and produce valuable scientific datasets.

President Donald Trump spoke with Texas Governor Greg Abbott as Hurricane Harvey approached the Texas coast, promising federal support for preparation, rescue and recovery. Abbott had already declared a State of Disaster in 30 counties and coordinated with federal officials including Acting DHS Secretary Elaine Duke and FEMA Director Brock Long. The White House considered and moved toward disaster declarations while federal agencies readied resources; the governor activated 700 members of the Texas Army, Air and State Guards.

Harvey was forecast to make landfall as a major hurricane—initially projected as Category 3 and later reported by some outlets as Category 4—bringing life-threatening storm surge, destructive winds and catastrophic rainfall. Meteorologists warned Harvey combined several worst-case features: very warm and deep Gulf water, weak upper-level winds, a projected path that could keep part of the storm over water, and a slow forward speed likely to make it stall near the coast. Those ingredients supported rapid intensification and prolonged heavy rain. Forecasts suggested storm surge of 6–13 feet in places, sustained winds well over 100 mph in the eyewall, and rainfall totals of 15–35 inches across a broad area with isolated amounts higher—predictions that prompted comparisons to Katrina, Ike and other historic storms.

Emergency officials urged evacuation for vulnerable coastal communities. Large-scale evacuations from the Corpus Christi area produced long traffic backups, as families fled with pets and possessions. Local anecdotes highlighted the difficult choices residents faced: some left for inland shelters or hotels with pets, while others boarded up and decided to stay. Officials warned that those remaining should prepare for severe roof and structural damage, widespread downed trees and power lines, and days to weeks without water or electricity.

The U.S. National Weather Service and meteorologists emphasized that Harvey’s slow movement could turn it into a prolonged flooding disaster, especially for low-lying and urbanized regions including the Texas Coastal Bend, Houston and inland corridors toward Austin and San Antonio. Emergency managers advised stocking nonperishable food, water, medications, batteries and flashlights, securing homes and following evacuation orders. Local stores saw surges in supply purchases; while water and essentials were prioritized, media coverage noted a notable spike in alcohol sales in Houston as some residents stocked up on beer and wine.

FEMA and state authorities warned the public that the primary threats were storm surge and prolonged inland flooding; they urged heeding local officials’ directives to protect life, as Harvey’s impacts were expected to unfold over several days and create long-lasting damage and displacement across affected communities.

Most psychologists hold that basic personality—traits like introversion or extraversion—remains fundamentally consistent across life, with apparent changes often reflecting reactions to life events (new job, marriage, parenthood). Research, however, shows personality stability itself changes with age: it generally increases from young adulthood into middle age and then declines in later life. A New Zealand study of about 4,000 participants aged 20–80 who completed a personality inventory twice across a two‑year interval measured honesty‑humility plus the Big Five traits (extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, openness). Overall, personalities were fairly stable, but trait stability followed a bell‑shaped curve across the lifespan—peaking in middle age and waning among the oldest participants. For some traits (conscientiousness, openness, honesty‑humility), stability in the oldest group resembled that of the youngest. The study also found domain‑specific shifts linked to life stage: people in their 30s exhibited relatively high neuroticism, which tended to diminish by their 50s, when conscientiousness, openness and honesty‑humility became more prominent. These findings suggest personality becomes more fixed through middle age but can loosen again in later years, with certain traits shifting according to life circumstances.

Attorneys for Adel Daoud, a 19-year-old charged with attempting to detonate a car bomb outside a downtown Chicago bar in September 2012, accuse prosecutors of deliberately concealing whether evidence against him came from surveillance under Section 702 of the FISA Amendments Act (FAA). Daoud’s lawyers say the government is denying a simple yes-or-no answer to avoid creating standing for a constitutional challenge to the program, which allows warrantless interception of foreigners’ communications that may include contacts with Americans. Senate Intelligence Committee chair Dianne Feinstein had previously cited the Chicago case as an example of the law’s success. The Supreme Court earlier rejected a separate challenge to Section 702 for lack of standing, but said defendants must be notified if Section 702-derived evidence will be used so they can contest its lawfulness. U.S. Attorney Gary S. Shapiro’s office told the court the evidence came from a traditional FISA court order rather than Section 702; Daoud’s lawyers dispute that, suggesting Section 702 likely led to the probe and that the FBI later obtained a conventional order for the sting. Civil liberties advocates warn that without disclosure courts will never publicly review Section 702’s sweeping, warrantless reach. Daoud has pleaded not guilty; trial is set for February.

A new study of the Peach Spring Tuff (PST) — the product of an 18.8-million-year-old supereruption from the Silver Creek caldera — integrates field mapping, lithic measurements and laboratory experiments to infer the nature and speed of long-runout pyroclastic flows. Researchers mapped 20 key outcrops across ~30–150 km from the caldera, documenting abundant locally derived substrate blocks (10 cm to >1 m) within the ignimbrite. The presence of large clasts far from their source would be incompatible with fully dilute, turbulent pyroclastic surges, which would require unrealistically high velocities (>100–600 m/s) to entrain such blocks. Instead, field evidence and experiments support a dense, fluid-like basal flow with sustained pore-gas pressure that can entrain and transport substrate particles via an uplift mechanism at the flow-substrate interface. Lab analogs using fines and coarse beads show that uplift onset scales with the square of flow-front velocity; entrained particles follow mixed uplift/settling trajectories and are ultimately frozen into aggrading basal deposits. Applying a theoretical relation between block size and front velocity to measured PST block sizes yields realistic flow speeds of roughly 5–20 m/s (about 10–45 mph) across the runout, implying flow durations of several hours (minimum ~2.5–10 h) over distances up to ~170 km. Such sustained, pressurized, dense currents require prolonged high eruption rates but suggest that some supereruptions can produce devastating yet comparatively slow-moving pyroclastic flows, potentially allowing hours for evacuation at distal distances — though proximal zones would remain unsurvivable.

Charlotte-Mecklenburg police released portions of a dashcam and a body-worn camera video showing the fatal Sept. 20 shooting of Keith Lamont Scott, a 43-year-old Black man, after days of protests in Charlotte demanding transparency. The footage shows Scott exiting an SUV, stepping backward with his hands at his sides, and then collapsing after four shots ring out. Neither video clearly shows whether Scott was holding a gun or depicts the officer firing; the officer who shot Scott, Brentley Vinson, was not wearing a body camera. Police also released photos of a loaded handgun, an ankle holster and a marijuana “blunt” recovered at the scene and said Scott’s DNA and fingerprints were on the gun. Chief Kerr Putney said the tapes, together with forensics and witness interviews, support the department’s account that Scott held a weapon and did not follow commands to drop it; he said no officers would be charged at this time and the State Bureau of Investigation is probing the case. Scott’s family disputes the gun claim and said the released footage raises more questions. Protesters and community leaders continue to call for full transparency; city officials and the DOJ have monitored tensions as investigations proceed.

Hidekichi Miyazaki, a sprightly 105-year-old from Kyoto, reclaimed the title of world’s oldest competitive sprinter by completing a 100-meter dash in 42.22 seconds at the Kyoto Masters Athletics Autumn Competition. Born on September 22, 1910, Miyazaki—nicknamed the “Golden Bolt” for mimicking Usain Bolt’s signature pose—turned heads as he trotted across the finish to cheers and flowers from his great-grandchildren. Guinness World Records authenticated the mark in the over-105 category, for which no previous time existed. A perfectionist, Miyazaki said he aimed for 35 seconds and was disappointed with his performance, but proud to finish. He only began running in his early 90s after losing friends and seeking a solo hobby; since then he has repeatedly set age-group records, including earlier 100m times at ages 103 and 104. Standing 1.53 meters tall and weighing 42 kg, he trains by walking with a weighted rucksack and maintains regular medical checkups; doctors report he is remarkably fit. Always upbeat, Miyazaki dreams of racing Usain Bolt someday, plans to continue competing for several more years, and sees his persistence as a testament to willpower and good health.

As Hurricane Irma struck southern Florida, White House social media director Dan Scavino posted a video he identified as a waterlogged Miami International Airport, saying he was sharing Hurricane Irma updates hourly with President Donald Trump and Vice President Mike Pence. Miami International Airport quickly corrected him on Twitter, stating the clip was not from the airport, and Scavino deleted the tweet and acknowledged the mistake. The clip had circulated online earlier, labeled as footage from another location—apparently Mexico City—and predated Irma’s arrival, having appeared while Hurricane Harvey impacted the Gulf region. The incident highlighted how quickly unverified content spreads during fast-moving crises and raised questions about the White House’s process for vetting and sharing such material with top officials overseeing the federal response. Scavino said the post was “among 100s of videos/pix I am receiving” and that he shared it while trying “to notify all,” but he did not clarify how he verifies content before passing it to the president and vice president or whether they relied on those specific posts. Miami International Airport and others spent time correcting the misattributed footage as it was reshared across social media. The White House did not respond to questions about Scavino’s verification practices.

Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) publicly named a man it alleges is the CIA station chief in Islamabad and demanded his arrest over a 21 November drone strike that killed five militants, including Haqqani Network commanders. The party also listed CIA director John Brennan as an “accused person” for murder and “waging war against Pakistan.” The U.S. embassy and CIA declined to confirm the identity; AP withheld the name because it could not be verified. If confirmed, it would echo 2010 when another station chief was exposed and forced out. PTI spokeswoman Shireen Mazari argued the station chief lacks diplomatic immunity and sought interrogation to identify drone pilots. The disclosure intensifies debate over U.S. drone strikes, which critics—led politically by Khan—blame for fueling domestic terrorism and violating sovereignty, while U.S. officials dispute high civilian casualty counts. PTI has staged protests and attempted to block NATO supply trucks to press for an end to strikes.

A Politico/Morning Consult poll finds growing public support for the Affordable Care Act even as President Trump and congressional Republicans push repeal-and-replace efforts. Among 2,013 registered voters surveyed, 45 percent approve of Obamacare and 45 percent oppose it; opposition has fallen seven points since early January while approval rose four points. Voters are divided on whether to fully repeal, partially repeal, keep, or expand the law: 24 percent favor complete repeal, 27 percent partial repeal, 12 percent keeping it as is, and 26 percent expanding it. However, when asked about nine specific ACA provisions, voters favored keeping eight. Strong majorities support protections for pre-existing conditions (65%), subsidies for low-income people (61%), coverage for young adults up to age 26 (63%), employer coverage requirements (about 60%), and contraceptive coverage (55%). The lone provision a majority wants removed is the individual mandate (57% want repeal). Separately, Republican lawmakers are privately consulting governors—especially Scott Walker, John Kasich, Bill Haslam, and Brian Sandoval—to craft a compromise on Medicaid expansion affecting 31 states. GOP leaders face internal divisions between conservatives seeking deep cuts and others wary of leaving millions uninsured; proposals include per-capita federal funding formulas, tax credits, and Health Savings Account changes.

On Thursday afternoon May 29, 2014, 17-year-old Omotayo Adeoye, a junior at the High School for Math, Science and Engineering at City College in Harlem, walked out of school and into the Hudson River near West 165th Street after being confronted for allegedly using a cellphone during a German exam. Classmates said a teacher seized her phone, accused students of cheating, and Adeoye apologized before leaving the classroom. She reportedly wrote a suicide note on her exam that read, “I just want to go away forever on the bottom of the river,” placed her identification and belongings on a rock at the river’s edge, and entered the water fully clothed. Witnesses pleaded with her to come out; a fisherman and others tried to intervene, but she sank beneath the surface and disappeared. Rescue teams searched the area over the following days but had not recovered a body by Saturday evening. Adeoye, described by friends and family as an excellent, ambitious student who hoped to become a doctor, had been selected for a research fellowship at City College’s Grove School of Engineering and played basketball and soccer. Her death prompted grief among classmates and tributes online. The Department of Education opened an investigation into the incident, and city school leaders said they would reexamine student mental-health awareness in response to the tragedy.

Former NSA contractor Edward Snowden continued to elude U.S. authorities as he moved from Hong Kong to Moscow and sought a route to asylum in Latin America. After revealing thousands of classified documents to The Guardian and The Washington Post about expansive U.S. surveillance programs, Snowden left Hong Kong—where U.S. extradition efforts were rebuffed—and arrived in Moscow. He reportedly sought asylum in Ecuador; Ecuador’s foreign minister confirmed receiving an asylum request and said Quito was in contact with Russian authorities. WikiLeaks said it assisted Snowden, and Julian Assange claimed Snowden traveled with WikiLeaks associate Sarah Harrison and had been given travel documentation facilitating his trip after his U.S. passport was revoked.

U.S. officials pressed Russia to detain and return Snowden to face espionage charges, with Secretary of State John Kerry warning that allowing Snowden to travel would have consequences for bilateral relations. The National Security Council criticized Hong Kong for permitting Snowden’s departure despite a U.S. provisional arrest request under the U.S.–Hong Kong surrender agreement; the Justice Department said its request complied with treaty requirements, while Hong Kong officials said the U.S. submission lacked legal sufficiency. The U.S. did not seek an Interpol red notice, saying that is most useful when a fugitive’s location is unknown.

Snowden was reported to have registered for an Aeroflot flight from Moscow to Havana but then did not board, leaving journalists and officials uncertain of his whereabouts. Reports indicated possible onward travel to Cuba, Venezuela, and ultimately Ecuador—countries with varying degrees of legal cooperation with the United States. The U.S. has no extradition treaty with Russia, and although it does with Cuba, Venezuela and Ecuador, any government could grant a political exemption. U.S. officials privately criticized Snowden’s apparent reliance on authoritarian states and argued his actions harmed U.S. national security.

China and Hong Kong’s handling of Snowden reflected competing pressures: popular sentiment favored protection after disclosures highlighted U.S. surveillance, but Beijing prioritized stable relations with Washington. Intelligence sources suggested China may have copied data from Snowden’s devices, reducing its incentive to shelter him. Meanwhile, U.S. political and legal responses intensified as Snowden’s disclosures continued to reverberate globally, straining diplomacy and provoking debate over surveillance, civil liberties and international law.

The FBI is weighing domestic terrorism charges against the man accused of shooting a guard at the conservative Family Research Council. Under the bureau’s definition, domestic terrorism involves Americans attacking other Americans motivated by U.S.-based extremist ideologies. This consideration signals authorities may view the shooting as ideologically driven rather than solely criminal. The report also notes the FBI is currently pursuing seven people charged with domestic terrorism-related crimes, and that five of those suspects are women—an unusual demographic detail given typical profiles in such cases. The focus on this particular incident and the broader group of suspects reflects heightened attention to homegrown extremism and how the bureau classifies and prosecutes ideologically motivated violence. Determining domestic terrorism charges can affect investigative resources, legal strategy and public messaging, and may influence how similar acts are tracked and prevented in the future. Authorities continue to investigate motives and gather evidence to support any potential terrorism prosecution.

During the World Cup in Samara, local utilities asked residents to share showers to conserve water for visiting fans. Samarskiye Kommunalniye Systemy said they had increased supplies in recent days to cope with higher demand driven by the tournament and an accompanying heat wave. The utility noted that thousands of visitors also use water, straining the system, and urged conservation measures to ensure sufficient supply for everyone. The appeal framed the request as part of hospitality toward guests, asking locals to alter usual habits briefly so available water can meet both resident and visitor needs.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has published the first photographs of a small, egg-sized seer stone long associated with founder Joseph Smith’s translation of the Book of Mormon, part of a broader effort to increase transparency about its origins. Unveiled alongside images of the printer’s manuscript in the new volume of the Joseph Smith Papers, the pictures show the smooth, dark-brown stone with lighter swirls and a weathered leather pouch believed to have been made by Emma Smith. Church historians say publishing images helps those who favor visuals better connect to the religion’s early history; the stone itself will remain in the church vault.

The release fits a recent institutional push to open archives and address sensitive topics—such as polygamy and the past priesthood ban for black men—aimed at providing accurate information online for both members and nonmembers as curiosity has grown with church membership expansion. Historians and scholars say transparency helps prevent shock or disillusionment among faithful who might otherwise discover difficult information online.

Latter-day Saint accounts describe two instruments used in translation: the interpreters or Urim and Thummim—clear stones in a metal frame found with the gold plates—and a separate seer stone Joseph had used earlier for folk practices like treasure seeking. Witnesses reported Joseph placing the instrument in a hat, blocking light, and reading English words that appeared, which he then dictated to scribes such as Oliver Cowdery and Emma Smith. Most of the original manuscript was lost or water-damaged; Cowdery’s printer’s manuscript survived with the Community of Christ, which collaborated with the LDS Church on its publication, signaling improved relations.

Church materials emphasize that Smith translated “by the gift and power of God,” a phrase repeated by Joseph and his witnesses. While some particulars remain sparse by design, historians study recollections and surviving pages—whose features suggest dictation from another language—to understand the process that produced the Book of Mormon, first published in 1830 and now translated into many languages worldwide.

A photo from an off‑campus College at Brockport party showing a black Labrador named Mya being held upside down over a beer keg went viral, prompting an investigation and arrests. The image was posted by an unaffiliated Twitter account that shares SUNY party photos. Brockport police say student Shane Oliver held the dog while student Robert Yates photographed and posted it; both, age 20, were charged with misdemeanor animal torture and issued court appearance tickets. Authorities believe the dog had been taken from its owner; the animal is now in protective custody and reportedly in good condition. SUNY Brockport officials announced an inquiry and possible disciplinary action, while the photo sparked widespread outrage online and debate among students about intent versus cruelty.

A judge ordered Dr. Conrad Murray jailed minutes after a jury found him guilty of involuntary manslaughter in Michael Jackson’s 2009 death. The verdict followed about nine hours of deliberation by a 12-member jury after a four-week trial in which prosecutors portrayed Murray as deceptive and incompetent. Witnesses described multiple severe medical failures: administering propofol in an unmonitored, non-surgical setting, poor resuscitation efforts, lack of records, distractions with phone calls and texts, delays in seeking help, and lying to paramedics and emergency physicians. Central to the case was Murray’s own 2½-hour police interview admitting he gave Jackson propofol and other drugs, saying he caved to Jackson’s repeated requests. Expert testimony, notably from anesthesiologist Dr. Steven Shafer, concluded that drug levels found at autopsy contradicted Murray’s account and suggested a continuous infusion was left running even after Jackson stopped breathing. Murray, 58, faces up to four years in state prison, possible probation, and likely loss of his medical license. Jail officials labeled him a “keep away” inmate, assigning a single cell and constant escort for his protection.

This document presents findings from two studies that together characterize catastrophic and noncatastrophic injuries in pole vaulting and identify prevention targets. The first is a retrospective review (1982–1998) of 32 catastrophic pole-vault injuries reported to the National Center for Catastrophic Sports Injury Research. All cases involved male athletes averaging 17.5 years old. Thirty-one were catastrophic head injuries and one was a thoracic spine fracture leading to paraplegia. Three main accident mechanisms accounted for most events: landing with the body on the landing pad but the head on adjacent hard ground (17 cases, 53%); falling into the vault box after becoming stranded at peak height (8 cases, 25%); and completely missing the landing pad (5 cases, 16%). Two mechanisms were unknown. Outcomes were severe: 16 athletes (50%) died and 6 (19%) sustained permanent disability. The primary prevention recommendations were enlarging minimum landing pad dimensions and enforcing rules requiring soft surfaces around pads; additional rule and equipment changes were discussed as possible risk mitigations.

The second study is a prospective cohort investigation of collegiate pole vaulters over a single track season, enrolling 135 athletes from 15 universities. Across 8,823 athlete-exposures there were 70 injury events: 41% of vaulters were injured and the overall rate was 7.9 injuries per 1,000 exposures. Most injuries involved the lower body (60%), especially the low back (16.7%), hamstrings, and lower leg (13.9% each); no head or neck injuries occurred in this sample. Strains (39.2%) and overuse injuries (25.5%) predominated. Thirty percent of injuries, and 83% of low back injuries, occurred during the plant/takeoff phase; one-third of lumbar injuries were spondylolysis and 75% of those ended the athlete’s season. Having multiple prior injuries increased injury odds 2.7-fold (95% CI, 1.1–7.1). Together, these studies highlight distinct risk profiles: rare but devastating catastrophic head injuries linked to landing-area failures, and more common musculoskeletal and overuse injuries tied to technique, prior injury history, and takeoff mechanics—pointing to equipment, surface, rule enforcement, and training/conditioning interventions.

An 18-year-old Wimauma man, Austin Lane Hatfield, is recovering at Tampa General Hospital after being bitten on the lip by a cottonmouth (water moccasin) he had captured and was keeping illegally. The snake escaped from a pillowcase around 11:45 p.m., slithered across his chest, and bit him when he tried to recapture it. Hatfield required antivenin, was ventilated due to swelling, and was initially in critical condition but later upgraded to good; his family requested privacy. Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) officials said possession of venomous snakes requires a state permit, and they are investigating; Hatfield could face charges. The cottonmouth was captured and euthanized to allow proper identification and to assist treatment. FWC and emergency officials warn people to keep a wide berth from cottonmouths—venomous pit vipers 2–4 feet long with triangular heads, heat-sensing pits, and a white interior mouth that gives them their name. Officials stressed that inexperienced people should not handle venomous reptiles because of the risk to themselves and others.

Facing a Supreme Court order to demolish 30 illegally built apartments in the West Bank outpost of Ulpana, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu proposed an extraordinary plan: slice the five evacuated three-story buildings into sections, transport them to nearby land, and reassemble them so the homes survive instead of being razed. The government began evacuations, with many settlers complying peacefully under rabbinic counsel, even as critics call the relocation costly, impractical and an attempt to sidestep the court. Construction experts say cutting concrete buildings with massive circular blades, moving parts by crane and truck, and reconstructing disrupted electrical, plumbing and structural systems would be far more expensive—estimates range up to $25 million—than rebuilding at roughly $150,000 per apartment. Israel requested a demolition deadline extension until November, arguing work can’t finish by the July 1 court date. Palestinians and rights lawyers argue the plan defies the court, while settlers fear the evictions set a precedent for other removals. Netanyahu pledged 300 replacement homes in Beit El; displaced families received temporary state housing and vowed resistance to further expulsions.

After a contest with more than 140,000 entries, 1-year-old Lucas Warren of Dalton, Georgia, was named Gerber’s 2018 Spokesbaby — the first child with Down syndrome to win the title since the online contest began in 2010. His mom, Cortney, entered a cheerful photo of Lucas showing his signature smile and outgoing personality; Gerber CEO Bill Partyka said that smile captured the team. The Warrens received a $50,000 prize to support Lucas’s education and a year of exposure on Gerber’s social channels. Parents hope his selection boosts acceptance and representation for children with special needs.

Guy Scott, Zambia’s vice-president, rose to prominence after the Patriotic Front’s 2011 victory and made headlines as Africa’s most prominent white senior official since independence. Born in Livingstone to British parents, Cambridge-trained and an academic turned politician, Scott became deputy to Michael Sata — the populist “King Cobra” — a symbolic appointment that underlined Sata’s claim not to be a tribalist. Scott’s easy rapport with voters belies occasional legal challenges to his Zambian nationality and a constitutional clause that may bar him from running for president because his parents were foreign-born.

Scott has offered an unexpectedly sympathetic, nuanced view of Zimbabwe’s Robert Mugabe, praising aspects of his rhetoric while condemning violent policies. Central to Scott’s agenda is managing Zambia’s fraught relationship with China: massive Chinese investment and labour have fueled economic ties but provoked local resentment over business dominance, poor management and labor clashes. Elected on anti-Chinese rhetoric, Scott says the campaign’s tone was shock politics and calls for recalibration — standing up to exploitative practices while preserving beneficial cooperation. Following Sata’s death, Scott briefly served as acting leader amid constitutional and political uncertainty.

American humanitarian worker Kayla Mueller, 25, endured 18 months of captivity under ISIS after being abducted from near Aleppo in August 2013. ABC News’ 20/20 special, “The Girl Left Behind,” draws on first-time on-camera testimony from four former hostages who shared cells with Mueller and describe prolonged physical and psychological abuse: torture, forced labor, isolation, sensory deprivation, verbal degradation and repeated sexual assault. Mueller was held in a rotating series of makeshift prisons overseen by a quartet of British captors dubbed “The Beatles,” led by Mohammed Emwazi (“Jihadi John”), and later was handed to Abu Sayyaf and his wife, who enslaved her and several Yazidi girls in ISIS leader Abu Bakr al‑Baghdadi’s household. Witnesses recount Mueller’s resolute faith, empathy and courage — she comforted fellow prisoners, defended her Christian belief against threats, and refused to escape with Yazidi teens to increase their chance of freedom. She smuggled handwritten letters to family via other hostages and appeared briefly in a proof-of-life video. Negotiations involving emails between her family and ISIS proceeded amid international pressure and U.S. airstrikes, which coincided with ISIS executions of Western captives. Mueller’s death was confirmed in 2015 after conflicting claims; ISIS had earlier asserted she died in a Jordanian airstrike, a claim the U.S. denied. Former cellmates remember her as selfless, kind and spiritually steadfast despite relentless abuse.

Author Zinzi Clemmons announced she will no longer contribute to Lena Dunham and Jenni Konner’s Lenny Letter, citing longstanding concerns about Dunham’s and her circle’s racism and Dunham’s recent public response to an assault allegation. Clemmons, who has known Dunham since college and has overlapping social circles with her, said she long avoided those friends because of what she calls “hipster racism” — a sarcastic, provocative behavior that dismisses objections as overreactions or “just a joke.” Clemmons recalls peers who used racial slurs for shock value and then gaslit critics, and says this pattern persisted even after they gained influence in arts and media.

The immediate catalyst for Clemmons’s decision was Dunham and Konner’s initial statement defending Murray Miller, a writer and executive producer on Girls, after actress Aurora Perrineau accused him of sexual assault. Dunham and Konner characterized Perrineau’s claim as among the small percentage of assault reports they consider misreports, prompting backlash and a later apology. Clemmons says Dunham’s first response mirrored how powerful people in that circle dismissed survivors, and it echoed an assault a friend of hers experienced involving another member of Dunham’s network. Feeling complicit if she stayed, Clemmons concluded, “She cannot have our words if she cannot respect us,” urging other writers—especially women of color—to reconsider their association with Dunham.

Writing from a literary festival in Nigeria, Clemmons also framed her departure within broader concerns about violence against women worldwide, contrasting local privilege and power dynamics with the dangers women face elsewhere. Her public resignation amplifies criticism of Dunham’s behavior and raises questions about who should be platforms for women’s voices.

Microscope Gallery presented two provocative projects: James Fotopoulos’s Dreamful Slumbers (Jan 7–Feb 6, 2012), a New York solo debut of over 80 charcoal, pastel and conté drawings (2008–2011) alongside new short videos; and Marni Kotak’s long-term performance The Birth of Baby X, a public home-birth staged in the gallery as living art.

Fotopoulos, known for more than 100 films and past shows at the Whitney and MoMA, returned to drawing after a period of artistic introspection. Dreamful Slumbers traces his progression in charcoal works—animals, bodies, childhood symbols, coded words—moving from black-and-white to red and then blue. Drawings connected to films like Thick Comb, Chimera and Alice in Wonderland illuminate his relationship between static and moving image; new short video Wellness uses his drawings in distinctive animation, and a Blue series pairs drawings with 15–30 second silent color videos.

Kotak’s project transforms Microscope into a home-birth center where she plans to labor and deliver before an audience, aided by a midwife and doula, documenting the child’s life thereafter. Framing birth as the “highest form of art,” she staged a domestic installation—bed, rocking chair, birthing pool, projections—and invited viewers to witness an unrepeatable, authentic performance rooted in lived experience.

Jorge Mario Bergoglio, elected this week as the first Latin American pope, reportedly traced his path to the priesthood back to childhood. Amalia Damonte, his 76-year-old former neighbor and childhood sweetheart from Flores, Buenos Aires, recounted that a young Bergoglio told her, "If I can't marry you, I'll become a priest," after she rejected him at age 12. Damonte said their parents kept them apart; she recalled being punished for having written him a note. Speaking from a home four doors from where Bergoglio grew up, she joked that her refusal turned out to be "lucky" for him. Bergoglio’s sister, María Elena Bergoglio, expressed mixed emotions about his elevation: pride that he is the first non-European, Latin American pope, and worry he will face "infinite loneliness" in the demanding role. Despite reportedly jokingly resisting the idea, the 76-year-old was elected to succeed 85-year-old Benedict XVI, who resigned last month. Pope Francis now inherits a church confronting deep challenges, including competition from evangelical movements, a priest shortage, and the ongoing sexual abuse crisis.

Anne Hathaway, who long admired Valentino and even had a custom gown for her wedding by him, originally planned to wear a pale pink embroidered tulle Valentino gown to the Oscars on Feb. 24, where she won Best Supporting Actress. Valentino’s team even issued a press release hours before the red carpet announcing Hathaway would wear that design and that Jennifer Aniston would wear a nude embroidered silk tulle Valentino dress. Neither woman wore those announced gowns. Hathaway switched at the last minute to a Prada column dress that ignited debate over its design details; a source tells Us Weekly the change followed Hathaway learning that co-star Amanda Seyfried would be wearing an Alexander McQueen dress strikingly similar to the Valentino she intended to wear. After Seyfried sent a photo, Hathaway decided to avoid a duplicate look. Industry insiders said Hathaway “really should have worn Valentino,” praising the originally planned gown. Aniston appeared in a bright red strapless Valentino instead of the announced nude tulle; some speculate Hathaway’s camp may have influenced that decision to prevent two actresses arriving in pale tulle. Hathaway expressed regret about the last-minute switch and disappointment it caused.

On July 7, pop star Taylor Swift surprised 7-year-old Naomi, who is battling acute myelogenous leukemia, by donating $50,000 to her GoFundMe campaign. Naomi’s diagnosis came after bruising led her parents to seek medical care; doctors confirmed AML, an aggressive form of leukemia requiring 6–9 months of intensive treatment. Her family—described by relatives as loving and faith-filled—faced immediate bills and mounting medical expenses, prompting Naomi’s aunt to start the GoFundMe with a $30,000 goal to help cover care and related costs. Swift’s large gift exceeded GoFundMe’s prior single-transaction limit of $15,000; the company’s CEO, Rob Solomon, said the platform increased its donation cap to $50,000 as a result. Solomon noted that Swift has given more across campaigns than any other donor in GoFundMe history and called her actions an inspiration for future charitable giving. Naomi and her family expressed deep gratitude and posted a video thanking Swift for the life-changing support. The campaign link and family updates remain available online for those who want to help.

After the conventions, Obama appears to have a clearer path to victory while Romney’s prospects dim, GOP advisers privately concede. Romney’s campaign was disappointed the expected post-convention bounce failed to materialize, and internal state-level polling — notably in Ohio — favors Obama by several points, making a Romney path to 270 electoral votes much harder. Both campaigns expect little national movement before the Oct. 3 debate, which they see as pivotal; Romney’s strategy centers on portraying the economy as failing and blaming Obama, relying heavily on negative advertising. Democrats worry the small pool of undecided voters (6–8 percent) skews toward white, middle-aged, economically stressed voters who voted for Obama in 2008, but Obama’s team argues that there aren’t enough undecideds for Romney to flip decisively.

Post-convention tracking polls show Obama gaining several points, suggesting his bounce could grow when fully captured, potentially giving him a substantive lead. Analysts see Obama as the favorite unless his gains quickly evaporate; Romney would likely need late economic or foreign-policy shifts to reverse course.

Pink is PEOPLE’s cover star for the 2018 Beautiful Issue, posing with her children Jameson Moon, 15 months, and Willow Sage, 6½. On The Ellen DeGeneres Show she joked about feeling especially beautiful, quipping that no one should look her in the eyes while the issue is out, and laughed aloud when told she’d made the cover. Pink—real name Alecia Moore—said her kids likely sealed the deal and playfully wondered whether Jameson will be embarrassed by his first magazine cover in the future.

Willow’s reaction to the cover and to Pink’s viral MTV VMAs speech about body image was candid: she told her mother she still feels “the ugliest girl I know,” prompting a lighthearted exchange in which Pink acknowledged that everyone sometimes feels insecure. The singer reflected on changing definitions of beauty, praising a broader acceptance of different sizes, shades, and kinds of beauty and celebrating humor as one of her best attributes.

In PEOPLE’s profile, Pink discusses parenting candidly, admitting that she takes it “day by day” and often worries if she’s doing things right. Raised in a free-range Pennsylvania childhood, she practices attachment parenting: showing affection, meeting needs, and teaching rules so her children can know when to break them. She aims for a label-free, gender-neutral home where fairness and freedom are emphasized—boys can ride dirt bikes or wear dresses; girls can do anything. Pink and husband Carey Hart focus on family, humor, and providing emotional security amid worries about the wider world. The Beautiful Issue hits newsstands Friday.

U.S. Ambassador Robert Ford visited Hama to signal U.S. support for Syrians demanding change, meeting residents and wounded at a hospital amid intense unrest. State Department spokeswoman Victoria Nuland said Ford’s presence underscored U.S. backing for peaceful expression; Syria’s government accused him of interfering, saying he entered without permission. Hama has seen repeated large anti-government demonstrations, including reports of hundreds of thousands marching and protesters carrying olive branches, followed by fierce crackdowns with arrests and dozens killed according to activists and rights groups. Tensions eased slightly after the provincial governor was dismissed and tanks pulled back, but many fled fearing further operations; rights monitors reported at least dozens killed across multiple cities. French diplomats also showed solidarity. Damascus blamed “armed gangs” and denounced foreign involvement, while the U.S. summoned Syria’s ambassador over reported filming of U.S. protests. Hama’s volatile history—especially the brutal 1982 massacre—heightens fears as nationwide protests continue.

In 2017, actor Mark Hamill — best known as Luke Skywalker — waded into a heated online debate about the Federal Communications Commission’s decision to roll back net neutrality protections. The FCC’s vote, driven by chairman Ajit Pai, repealed rules that had prevented internet service providers from throttling traffic or charging for preferential access. Critics warned the move would benefit large corporations at the expense of consumers, independent creators, artists, and smaller businesses that depend on open internet access. In the midst of that controversy, a Twitter exchange between Hamill and Republican Senator Ted Cruz drew attention: Hamill mockingly corrected Cruz’s misspelling of his name and jabbed at the senator’s credibility, delivering a signature sharp, celebrity-backed response that resonated with many online. The incident underscored how public figures and entertainers were mobilizing against the repeal and amplifying concerns that eliminating net neutrality could harm creative industries. That same week, excitement around the release of Star Wars: The Last Jedi added to Hamill’s visibility; his active, irreverent presence on Twitter — and occasional criticism of President Trump — meant his reactions quickly gained traction. The episode illustrated the intersection of pop culture, politics, and tech policy in 2017: a high-profile repeal prompted legal challenges and public outcry, with celebrities like Hamill joining a broader chorus warning that deregulation could stifle innovation and unfairly advantage powerful internet companies.

Seth Owen, an 18-year-old from Jacksonville, Fla., overcame family rejection, “conversion therapy,” and homelessness to earn acceptance to Georgetown University and become co-valedictorian of his high school. After his parents discovered he was gay, they sent him to Christian counseling aimed at changing his sexual orientation. When Owen refused to continue attending his parents’ church and challenged their anti-LGBTQ views, they gave him an ultimatum: attend their church or move out. He left home in February of his senior year and couch-surfed with friends and mentors while maintaining an exceptional academic record—reported GPAs range from 4.16 to 4.61—and participating in extracurriculars like swimming and dual enrollment courses.

Georgetown offered Owen admission but based his financial aid package on an assumption of parental support, leaving a roughly $20,000–$22,000 gap for the first year after scholarships and aid. Appeals to the university, supported by letters from mental-health professionals, teachers, and community advocates, did not change the initial package. Owen’s former biology teacher and mentor, Jane Martin, launched a GoFundMe to cover the shortfall. The campaign drew hundreds of donors and rapidly exceeded its $20,000 goal—raising well over $30,000 and later reports of $50,000—ensuring Owen can attend Georgetown. Both Owen and his supporters hope that if Georgetown revises his aid, surplus donations could seed a scholarship for other youths in similar circumstances.

Owen says he wants to become a defense attorney for teens, inspired by his own experiences, and hopes his story encourages others facing family rejection to seek support. Georgetown stated it works with students whose financial circumstances change, though it would not comment on individual cases. Owen will begin classes with Georgetown’s Class of 2022, grateful for community support and focused on paying forward the help he received.

Jake Perry, an 85-year-old retired plumber from Austin, Texas, is best known as a devoted "cat man" whose household produced two Guinness World Record holders for oldest cat: Granpa Rexs Allen (34 years) and Creme Puff (38 years). Since the 1980s Perry has adopted and rehomed hundreds of cats, at times caring for dozens concurrently in a home he adapted into an elaborate feline environment—tracks along walls, a jungle-gym interior, and a garage converted into a movie theater where he screens nature documentaries (and even 3-D films with plastic glasses) for his pets. He prepared home-cooked breakfasts (eggs, turkey bacon, broccoli, coffee with cream) and occasionally purportedly gave small amounts of red wine and coffee, which veterinarians stress is unsafe. Perry also celebrated his cats with themed holidays, birthday parties that attracted media attention, and elaborate funerals—47 of his cats are buried in fiberglass caskets in his backyard pet cemetery, marked by a headstone for Granpa and a Virgin Mary statue.

Local veterinarian Bruce Hardesty, who treated many of Perry’s cats over 15 years, corroborates that an unusual number lived into their late 20s and 30s, though exact ages are sometimes uncertain. Experts emphasize one concrete contributor to longevity: sterilization. Spaying and neutering reduces roaming and disease risks and may, via hormonal changes, be linked to longer lifespan across species. Still, most specialists reject Perry’s caffeine- and alcohol-inclusive diet as harmful. Researchers note genetic factors, indoor living, regular vet care, and sterilization all boost survival, but even these usually don’t explain cats living to 30-plus years.

Perry’s intense focus on feline companions made him a local legend—pet calendars, T-shirts, and media-covered birthday parties—and he established a trust funded partly by lottery winnings to care for his cats after he’s gone. Now recovering from cancer, he contemplates his final years and hopes to open a pet cemetery that might eventually include himself beside the animals he called his children. The story underscores a mix of devotion, ritual, and a few verifiable practices (sterilization, indoor care) that plausibly contributed to exceptional feline longevity, even as some of Perry’s claimed methods remain dubious.

Deputy Defense Secretary Robert Work warned that China is mounting a serious challenge to U.S. air and space military superiority, prompting the Pentagon to pursue new technologies and systems to maintain its edge. Speaking to aerospace experts at the inaugural China Aerospace Studies Initiative conference, Work said China is “quickly closing the technological gaps,” fielding radar‑evading aircraft, advanced reconnaissance platforms, sophisticated missiles and strong electronic‑warfare systems. While the U.S. seeks constructive ties, Work emphasized the need to acknowledge competitive dynamics and to “hedge” against the risk that rising-power interactions can escalate into conflict. For 25 years the United States has relied on technological superiority, he noted, but that margin is eroding; the Defense Department is therefore accelerating development of capabilities—such as directed‑energy weapons—that could provide cost‑effective defenses against expensive enemy systems. The conference, a U.S. Air Force–RAND partnership to boost research on China’s aerospace ambitions, coincided with the U.S.‑China Strategic and Economic Dialogue in Washington. Complementing U.S. concerns, Chinese senior leader Xu Qiliang, vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, called for faster innovation and a shift from catch‑up research to independent advances in national defense technology. Xu urged prioritizing basic and cutting‑edge research, converting discoveries into production and combat capability, and mobilizing societal support—talent, funds and integrated backing—to strengthen China’s military modernization.

China has indefinitely suspended imports of shellfish from Washington, Oregon, Alaska and Northern California after its inspectors found high arsenic and paralytic shellfish poisoning (PSP) toxin in recent geoduck shipments. The unprecedented ban cuts off a roughly $270 million Northwest export market—about 90% of U.S. geoduck exports go to China—and has effectively halted the geoduck industry, idling divers and forcing firms to curtail operations. Washington and federal agencies say their testing shows PSP levels well below international safety limits where the shipments originated, and U.S. officials argue Chinese inspectors may have applied stricter standards. Communication from China has been limited; NOAA stopped certifying shellfish exports while negotiations are sought. Meanwhile tribes and companies are pursuing alternative domestic and U.S. markets, asking federal officials and politicians to press China for details and to reopen trade, but the closure could last months and risks domestic oversupply and layoffs.

Tom Hiddleston earned his first Emmy nomination on July 14, 2016, for Lead Actor in a Limited Series or Movie for his role as Jonathan Pine in AMC’s six-part adaptation of John le Carré’s The Night Manager. Filming Thor: Ragnarok in Australia at the time, Hiddleston told MTV News he was “delighted,” calling the series “a huge undertaking and an enormous labor of love” and one of his proudest career achievements. Co-stars Hugh Laurie and Olivia Colman, director Susanne Bier, and the series itself also received nominations. Though better known for film and theater, Hiddleston said transitioning to television felt natural after reading just 60 pages of the first episode script. He celebrated the nomination with a modest “shake of happiness” between shoots.

The summer also put Hiddleston and Taylor Swift in the tabloids: they were seen together since mid-June, including on Australia’s Gold Coast, and Hiddleston confirmed to The Hollywood Reporter that they were “together” and “very happy,” denying claims their relationship was a publicity stunt. His appearance with Swift followed a series of public spats connected to Swift’s exes. Calvin Harris publicly criticized Swift after her role in co-writing “This Is What You Came For” was revealed; he asserted he produced and arranged the song and accused Swift and her team of trying to make him look bad. Harris’s tweets referenced past disputes and mentioned other celebrities like Katy Perry, who appeared pleased by Harris’s commentary because it seemed to vindicate her own long-running tensions with Swift. Media and celebrity outlets covered the overlapping stories of Hiddleston’s Emmy nod, his relationship with Swift, and the broader social-media fallout among pop stars, creating a media-saturated summer for all involved.

Analysis of ancient DNA from submerged sediments at Bouldnor Cliff, off the Isle of Wight, indicates that people living there used wheat about 8,000 years ago—around 2,000 years before agriculture appears in Britain. Researchers led by Dr. Robin Allaby of the University of Warwick extracted DNA fragments from 8,000-year-old cores taken 11–11.5 metres below the Solent surface from a site identified as a Mesolithic settlement and probable boat-building locus. The wheat DNA matched cultivated strains known from southern Europe, yet there was no wheat pollen or other evidence of local cultivation, implying the cereal was brought in from elsewhere. At that time Britain was still connected to mainland Europe or separated by a much narrower Channel, facilitating contact. Alongside wheat DNA, analyses recovered plant and animal signals including oak, poplar, beech, dogs/wolves, deer, grouse and aurochs. The findings, published in Science, suggest sustained contact—trade, exchange, gifting or raiding—between Mesolithic hunter-gatherers in Britain and Neolithic farming communities in continental Europe well before the local adoption of farming. The discovery challenges the conventional model of isolated, inward-looking hunter-gatherers who only adopted agriculture after direct cultural replacement, and supports growing evidence for early networks linking foragers and farmers across Europe. Authors caution further research is needed to clarify mechanisms and the scale of these interactions.

Former President Barack Obama and Michelle Obama have purchased the Kalorama mansion they’d been renting since leaving the White House. Property records show the Obamas bought the eight-bedroom, 8,200-square-foot, nine-and-a-half-bath home for $8.1 million from Joe Lockhart; the deed was recorded Wednesday. The couple said buying made sense because they’ll remain in Washington while their younger daughter Sasha finishes high school at Sidwell Friends. The house, renovated in 2011, is the neighborhood’s second-most expensive sale after Jeff Bezos’s purchase, and the Obamas still own a home in Chicago.

A McAfee Labs–cited investigation into Dark Web marketplaces has found that stolen or illicitly obtained subscriptions to mainstream streaming services—like Netflix, Spotify, HBO NOW and HBO GO—are being sold for extremely low prices. Accessible through anonymizing browsers such as TOR, these hidden marketplaces list “lifetime” access to Netflix for as little as $0.50 and Spotify for $1.95, with other services ranging up to about $15 for premium sports offerings. Intel Security CTO Raj Samani told Tech Insider sellers operate in a highly competitive environment and even offer guarantees and help-desk–style support to reduce buyer risk; when purchased credentials are shut down, sellers may replace them. McAfee and Samani believe many listings are derived from stolen account credentials and compromised credit-card data. The availability of cheap, seemingly reliable accounts is striking given how inexpensive regular subscriptions already are, and the existence of replacement guarantees suggests an organized underground economy. Samani warns that having your own account appear on these markets can cause major headaches—suspension, fraud investigations, and time-consuming recovery—and recommends protective measures: unique strong passwords, two-factor authentication, and credit monitoring. The findings and the broader implications of the Dark Web are explored further in Tech Insider’s reporting and the Codebreaker podcast, which features commentary on the risks from former Homeland Security official Michael Chertoff.

Manhattan prosecutors cleared Fox 5 co‑host Greg Kelly of rape after a sex‑crimes unit review found the facts did not meet New York’s legal definitions of sexual assault. The accuser, a paralegal who had said she was too intoxicated to consent after a South Street Seaport night out, reported the alleged incident in January; investigators reviewed interviews, bar receipts, security logs, texts and phone records and interviewed both parties. Sex‑crimes chief Martha Bashford told Kelly’s lawyer no criminal charges were warranted. Kelly, who had been off the air, thanked supporters and said he looks forward to returning to Good Day New York; the DA will not pursue false‑reporting charges.

Nearly two years after predictions that Hillary Clinton’s and Sarah Palin’s candidacies would spur a surge of female candidates across parties, the momentum has favored Republicans. Recent primaries produced several high-profile GOP women Senate nominees, bringing Republican Senate nominees to five this cycle versus four non-incumbent Democratic nominees (one already defeated). Democratic strategists acknowledge a palpable shift: Republican women—energized by Palin’s endorsements and Tea Party activism—are emerging as fresh faces and credible challengers, especially in gubernatorial contests where both parties nominated five women but Republicans appear better positioned in several states. Despite Democrats still holding more women in office overall (notably in the Senate and House), Republicans have fielded more female challengers to incumbents this year. Critics note some GOP nominees are ideological outliers and less likely to win general elections, and Emily’s List warns many successful primary candidates are ultra-conservative and unappealing to moderates. Media focus on personalities like O’Donnell and Haley may exaggerate trends, but Palin’s active recruitment and Clinton’s unavailability to counterbalance her have contributed to a shifting landscape in which the Democratic two-decade dominance on electing women could erode.

A woman fleeing police through a pasture was corralled by a herd of cows and arrested after officers waited on the other side of a fence, according to Sanford Police. Seminole County Sheriff’s Office helicopter footage captured 46-year-old Jennifer Anne Kaufman running through the field as more than a dozen cows chased and followed her toward the perimeter, where law enforcement took her into custody. The incident followed a pursuit of a stolen Subaru reportedly taken from Brevard County; officers deployed stop sticks and the vehicle crashed near the pasture. Two occupants fled the scene: Kaufman and another 46-year-old, Jamie Michael Young, who was later caught by a K9 unit; a third occupant, 38-year-old Erin Thomas, remained with the car. A search of the Subaru turned up over a gram of cocaine, a crack pipe, syringes and a metal spoon. Kaufman faces multiple charges including petit theft, cocaine possession, drug paraphernalia possession, trespassing, resisting arrest and violation of probation, and is held in Seminole County Jail. The report noted the story is developing.

Two weeks after the March 11 magnitude-9 earthquake and tsunami, Japan faced a cascading national crisis: the official death toll topped 10,000 with more than 17,000 still missing, hundreds of thousands homeless in temporary shelters, and damages possibly reaching $310 billion. The quake also severely damaged the Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear plant, compromising cooling systems and releasing radioactive materials into air, water and parts of the food chain. Tests found iodine-131 and cesium-137 in seawater and radioactive iodine in tap water and various vegetables near the plant. Infants were especially at risk; Tokyo distributed bottled water to households with babies while some neighboring prefectures warned against giving tap water to infants. International import restrictions and safety checks were imposed by several countries. Workers at the plant suffered radiation exposure during recovery efforts as crews struggled to restore cooling and electricity and investigated possible damage to reactor No. 3, which uses MOX fuel. Farmers faced contaminated crops, uncertain livelihoods and long-term land recovery challenges, while authorities and aid groups mobilized relief and financial support.

Amazon’s annual letter to shareholders from CEO Jeff Bezos highlights several employee-focused programs at its fulfillment centers, notably “Pay to Quit” and “Career Choice.” Pay to Quit, originated at Zappos and adopted at Amazon, offers yearly cash incentives for fulfillment-center associates to voluntarily leave if they’re unhappy—$2,000 in the first eligible year, rising by $1,000 each year to a $5,000 maximum by year four. Bezos says the offer’s message, “Please Don’t Take This Offer,” reflects the company’s hope that workers stay, while prompting employees to reflect on whether the job fits them; only a small percentage accept it. Career Choice pre-pays 95% of tuition for hourly employees pursuing in-demand fields—such as aviation mechanics or nursing—whether or not the training directly relates to Amazon work, aiming to give workers options for career development. The letter frames both initiatives as enabling choice: some employees will make long-term careers at Amazon, others will use Amazon as a stepping stone. The Pay to Quit program applies to full-time fulfillment-center staff; temporary workers are generally ineligible.
