Bezos situates these programs within broader Amazon efforts to empower employees—like virtual contact centers and veteran hiring—and to continually improve fulfillment operations. The article notes Amazon’s Tennessee facilities benefited from significant tax breaks and state grants, and mentions ongoing legal and labor discussions around warehouse working conditions.

A Minnesota judge narrowed the pool of potential heirs to Prince’s estate, excluding nearly 30 claimants and ordering genetic testing for six individuals. Carver County Judge Kevin Eide’s ruling accepted that six people—Prince’s sister Tyka Nelson and five half-siblings named in a petition—are the primary potential heirs, and he directed DNA tests for Tyka plus three half-siblings who claim the same father (John L. Nelson): Sharon, Norrine and John Nelson. Testing was also ordered for Brianna Nelson, who says she is Prince’s niece, and Victoria Nelson, a claimed grand-niece. Two other half-brothers, Alfred Jackson and Omar Baker, who claim relation through Prince’s mother Mattie Shaw, were not ordered tested. The judge dismissed a wide range of other claims, including those of five people asserting Prince was their father, a woman alleging a secret classified marriage, and several others asserting descent from more distant relatives. With no known will or children, Prince’s roughly estimated $300 million–$500 million estate would, under Minnesota law, be divided among siblings and descendants of deceased siblings. Bremer Trust, the special administrator, is valuing the estate as probate proceeds.

Egypt erupted into violent street clashes after President Mohamed Mursi’s decree granting himself wide powers and an Islamist-dominated assembly pushed through a contested draft constitution. The Muslim Brotherhood called supporters to the presidential palace, where they fought opposition protesters—throwing stones and petrol bombs—and riot police struggled to separate the sides. Dozens were wounded, including some with gunshot wounds; reports described assaults and severe injuries. Vice President Mahmoud Mekky proposed negotiating amendments to disputed articles and submitting a written agreement to the next parliament after a Dec. 15 referendum, urging consensus and warning that street mobilization posed a “real danger.” Opposition leaders, including Mohamed ElBaradei, said they would only dialogue if Mursi rescinded his Nov. 22 decree and postponed the referendum. International figures, notably U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and Britain’s William Hague, called for urgent inclusive dialogue and restraint. The crisis underlined deep polarization as Egypt’s transition and economy suffer continued instability.

Steve Silverman argues that Tiger Woods’ decline from all-time great to uneven, often poor performer is now undeniable. After posting an 80 in the U.S. Open’s opening round at Chambers Bay and following with a 76, Woods missed the cut and finished 16-over. Silverman likens Woods’ errors to amateur mishits, noting a 15-year-old amateur outscored him in the first round and recalling Woods’ recent disastrous Memorial showing. Once arguably the best golfer of his generation—compared favorably to Nicklaus, Hogan and Palmer—Woods hasn’t regained sustained elite form since his 2008 personal scandal and subsequent injury troubles. Though he had a resurgence in 2013 with five wins, he hasn’t added to his 14 majors in years. Silverman concedes that, despite supporters’ hopes, Woods appears past his peak; his recent missed cuts and poor rounds suggest his major-chasing days are likely over. Woods plans to play the Greenbrier Classic and the British Open next, but for many observers the evidence is clear: Tiger’s best competitive years are behind him.

A federal judge in Mississippi on May 15, 2017, sentenced Joshua Vallum to 49 years in prison for the 2015 killing of 17-year-old Mercedes Williamson, marking the first-ever conviction under the federal Hate Crimes Prevention Act for a victim targeted because of gender identity. Vallum had pleaded guilty in December to federal hate crime charges and previously pleaded guilty to a state murder charge that resulted in life without parole. Prosecutors said Vallum, a member of the Latin Kings gang, tortured and murdered Williamson because he feared fellow gang members would discover they had been sexually involved and that gang rules outlawed homosexual activity, punishable by death. According to prosecutors, Vallum lured Williamson into a car, drove her from Alabama to Mississippi, stunned her with a stun gun, stabbed her with a pocketknife, and ultimately struck her head with a hammer when she tried to flee. U.S. District Judge Louis Guirola Jr. could have imposed life in prison but accepted a lesser sentence recommended in a plea agreement, citing Vallum’s abusive, neglected childhood and other mitigating factors presented by defense counsel. Vallum apologized in court, expressing remorse and asking forgiveness, though Williamson’s family was not present. The case drew national attention amid concerns about violence against transgender people and prompted comments from then-Attorney General Jeff Sessions emphasizing accountability for bias-motivated crimes. LGBT advocates hailed the landmark prosecution while noting the case originated under the Obama administration and expressing concern about subsequent policy shifts affecting transgender rights under the Trump administration.

Donald Trump did not invent lying, but his relationship to truth is unprecedented and dangerous for American democracy. Lies have long been part of politics, yet the United States depends on a civic commitment to verifiable truth as a foundation for justice and liberty. Past presidents have lied while typically understanding the truth; Trump’s apparent indifference to distinguishing fact from fiction sets him apart. He instinctively exploits fears, resentments and conspiracy-minded audiences, elevating fringe claims—birtherism, falsehoods about terrorism, and inflated inauguration crowd sizes—into national debate. When a falsehood fails, he doubles down, dismisses evidence, or redefines terms rather than conceding error.

Trump’s method—frequent, impulsive tweets and public repetition of unverified claims—suggests both a willingness to weaponize falsehoods and a troubling gullibility. He repackages fringe content from bloggers, conspiracy peddlers, and foreign actors, apparently unfamiliar with verification standards that undergird science, law and journalism. The presence of “alternative facts” at the White House marks a cultural shift: verifiable truth is being treated as optional, even replaceable by popularity or ideology.

Beyond rhetoric, Trump’s presidency has already produced policy moves with real harms—threatening healthcare coverage, environmental protections and education—while expanding the Pentagon and weakening regulations. But the most alarming threat is his unpredictability, disregard for institutions and sustained attacks on truth. He disparages judges, intelligence agencies, journalists and other pillars of democratic accountability, encouraging public distrust of essential institutions.

Defending democracy requires citizens and institutions to insist on facts: investigate, read, listen and demand verification. Opposition must be active—protests, voting, congressional courage, judicial safeguards and state protections—to counteract reckless policies and preserve the rule of law. The civics of truth must be defended to prevent further erosion by demagoguery.

Students and teachers returned to Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, two weeks after a former student opened fire, killing 17. The district emphasized emotional recovery over academics: Principal Ty Thomas asked students to leave backpacks at home and focus on comfort and healing. The campus was tightly controlled, with only students, parents and staff admitted through a security cordon; about 50 armed officers were present, and police guided long lines of cars amid heavy media presence. Memorials—flowers and photos—lined the walkway to the campus, and many students planned small tributes in maroon, the school color, to honor classmates like Luke Hoyer. Some students said they felt nervous and expected to replay the shooting in their heads but wanted to return to routine and support one another.

In the wider aftermath, student activists, notably David Hogg, continued pressing for gun reforms and described the sight of armed officers as “education in fear.” Relatives of victims testified at a legislative hearing in Tallahassee urging changes including raising the minimum age to buy long guns from 18 to 21. The proposed bill also would allow certain trained, deputized teachers to carry concealed weapons if approved locally—a measure the district superintendent opposes. Retail responses included Dick’s Sporting Goods announcing an immediate end to assault-style rifle sales and a policy barring gun sales to anyone under 21. The community’s return to school was framed as the start of a long healing process and renewed public debate on gun policy.

A massive 30-mile ice jam on the Yukon River caused severe flooding in Galena, Alaska, forcing most of the 500-person town to evacuate and threatening downstream communities. By Wednesday, aerial surveys showed chunks breaking off the jam’s front, signaling it could move and allow Galena’s waters to begin receding; however, when the jam finally releases, a surge will endanger Koyukuk, about 14 miles downriver. The flood lifted homes from foundations, washed out roads, submerged vehicles, breached sewage lagoons, and left sheens of spilled fuel on the water. An airport dike formed a temporary dry island where about 30–40 people sheltered in former Air Force barracks or camped with dogs, eating MREs. Power, fresh water, and cell service were lost, and most homes were damaged; there were no reported injuries or fatalities. The National Guard and state troopers evacuated more than 300 residents and numerous pets to Fairbanks and other locations. Officials warned conditions could change rapidly as the jam shifts; the Weather Service expected the surge to reach Koyukuk within hours of a break and issued flood warnings. State officials, including Gov. Sean Parnell, assessed damage and considered a disaster declaration to unlock relief funds and supplies.

Stephanie Smith, owner of Bubba Likes Tortillas and a self-described large-scale cannabis real estate developer, sued the city of San Bernardino seeking to overturn a new ordinance she says would effectively bar her and her tenants from the legal marijuana market. The suit, filed in San Bernardino County Superior Court, contends the city’s rules create monopolies by limiting the number and types of commercial cannabis licenses and unlawfully disqualify operators without due process.

The dispute stems from December raids on three San Bernardino buildings Smith owns, where police and federal agents seized tens of thousands of marijuana plants — reports cite roughly 35,000 seized at one location and about 18,000 pounds across properties — and detained several workers. Authorities described one converted warehouse as a fortified multi-level grow operation with high electric bills and sophisticated irrigation, lighting and security; Smith was not arrested. Her attorney, Ben Eilenberg, says the tenants were in the process of applying for city licenses and had approval letters after the shutdowns, but the new ordinance appears to render them ineligible by disqualifying anyone who allegedly violated cannabis laws or failed to report income, even absent convictions or hearings.

Smith argues the ordinance is a “backdoor ban” contrary to voters who approved legalization and to Prop. 64, that it violates constitutional due process by disqualifying people without administrative or criminal proceedings, and that it could concentrate certain license types among a few operators. San Bernardino’s ordinance allows only 17 commercial businesses in the first year while state law recognizes 19 license categories, a gap Smith’s suit says could produce monopolies. The city has not yet commented; municipal officials note complex ongoing litigation around Measure O and temporary moratoria as courts and the council address the local regulatory framework.

At a Florida GOP dinner, Congressman Allen West delivered a blistering attack on Democrats — naming President Obama, Harry Reid, Nancy Pelosi and Debbie Wasserman-Schultz — declaring Florida a “battlefield” where voters must reject Democratic policies. He denounced what he called messages of “equality of achievement,” “economic dependency,” and the “enslav[ing]” of entrepreneurial spirit, urging Democrats to take those ideas elsewhere and vowing to do everything to stop Obama from “destroying” the country. West invited electoral challengers with a defiant “Bring it on!” Shortly after, controversy erupted within Florida Republicans over redistricting that could imperil West’s re-election. Reports said preliminary maps significantly weakened his district and that House leaders, including Mitt Romney spokesman Will Weatherford, had effectively finalized maps in coordination with other GOP leaders. Supporters created SaveAllenWest, but insiders warned it might be too late. West later disputed legal excuses for the maps, claiming alternatives preserving his district were submitted.

The Buffalo Bills have hired Kathryn Smith as a quality control-special teams coach, making her the first full-time female assistant coach in NFL history. Smith, who will report to special teams coordinator Danny Crossman and work with Eric Smith, has been with Rex Ryan’s staff for seven years and will enter her 14th NFL season next year. She joined the Bills in 2015 as an administrative assistant to the head coach after a 12-year stint with the New York Jets, where she progressed from gameday/special events intern in 2003 to player personnel assistant and assistant to the head coach.

Bills head coach Rex Ryan praised Smith’s knowledge, commitment and readiness for the promotion, noting he consulted Bruce Arians—who previously hired a female assistant during training camp—about the move. Smith’s hiring follows other milestones for women in pro football, including Jen Welter’s temporary assistant role in 2015 and Sarah Thomas becoming the NFL’s first full-time female referee last year. The move is seen as a major step for gender progress in the NFL, joining similar advances across other leagues like the NBA and MLB, while the NHL has yet to make comparable strides.

Richland County Senior Deputy Ben Fields, a school resource officer at Spring Valley High School, was fired after videos showed him forcefully removing and flipping a Black female student during a classroom incident. Sheriff Leon Lott said an internal review found Fields’ tactics unacceptable and contrary to training — deputies should use tactical communication or limited pain-compliance, not throw or push a nonthreatening seated student. Fields had been suspended after footage went viral; he and his lawyer maintain his actions were lawful and professional. The student’s attorney says she sustained arm, neck and back injuries. A second student who protested was also arrested; both faced charges of disturbing schools. The Department of Justice and FBI opened civil rights probes, and Lott asked for federal assistance while promising improved training and certification for school officers. Civil rights groups praised the termination. Officials acknowledged the student’s disruption but stressed it did not justify the use of force, and the school district pledged to review police roles and strengthen officer training.

American leaders and public figures across the political spectrum reacted with relief and praise after President Obama announced that U.S. forces killed Osama bin Laden in a targeted operation in Pakistan. Former President George W. Bush called it a “momentous achievement,” congratulating the military and intelligence personnel and saying the act sent a clear message that justice will be done. Bill Clinton echoed congratulations to the president, national security team and armed forces for bringing bin Laden to justice after years of murderous al-Qaida attacks. Congressional leaders—Senators Schumer, McCain and Reid, Speaker Boehner, Representative Pelosi and others—hailed the operation as a significant victory in the fight against al-Qaida while stressing the broader campaign against terrorism must continue. Family members of 9/11 victims and advocates, including the Families of Flight 93, expressed that the news brings some comfort though it cannot undo the losses. Republican figures such as Mitt Romney, Sarah Palin, Reince Priebus and others commended the courage and perseverance of U.S. service members and intelligence professionals. Many emphasized gratitude to those who devoted years to the mission and warned vigilance remains essential.

Hours before Los Angeles woke on New Year’s Day, someone draped white and black tarps over the final two O’s of the Hollywood sign, turning it into “Hollyweed.” The Hollywood Sign Trust, which maintains the landmark, called the act a trespass and said it will add technology to tighten surveillance after the rare, high-profile prank exposed weaknesses in the system. Chair Chris Baumgart said the existing camera network — first installed in 1994 and periodically updated and monitored by LAPD — is “constantly evolving,” but the incident revealed opportunities for improvement; the trust will identify and fix the weakest link to deter future trespassers and protect public safety on the treacherous hillside.

Photos showed a peace sign and heart on the tarps and a partial message referencing California’s marijuana legalization vote; the sign was restored by mid-morning with no lasting damage. No arrests or suspects have been publicly identified, and artists and observers speculated about motives and execution. The stunt echoed a famous 1976 alteration by Cal State Northridge student Daniel Finegood, who turned the sign into “Hollyweed” as an art statement; his son noted the careful planning involved in that earlier act. Contemporary street artist Plastic Jesus praised the anonymity and focus on message, while figures like Steve-O expressed admiration for the execution. The incident remains unsolved and has prompted renewed focus on improving security around the iconic landmark.

The Secret Service is investigating and said it is taking "appropriate action" after revelations that Kerry O’Grady, a senior agent who heads the Denver district, posted partisan and critical remarks about Donald Trump on Facebook. In an October post obtained by The Washington Examiner, O’Grady wrote she would rather "take jail time" than "take a bullet" for what she called a "disaster" for the country, a statement that implicitly referenced then-candidate Trump and explicitly endorsed Hillary Clinton. The comments, later deleted, acknowledged potential Hatch Act violations; that law restricts political activity by most executive-branch employees, including Secret Service staff. O’Grady told the Examiner she removed the posts after a few days, saying they reflected an emotional reaction—prompted in part by the release of a lewd Access Hollywood tape—and that she would not shirk her duty to protect the president despite personal opposition. She also used social media to mark the Women’s March and posted imagery aligning with "the resistance." Screenshots of her posts spurred complaints to the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of the Inspector General and to Secret Service supervisors; critics on social media and some colleagues called for her firing. The agency declined to comment on personnel specifics but confirmed awareness and review of the matter, while O’Grady issued a statement emphasizing her commitment to the mission, pride in service, and belief in free expression.

JPMorgan Chase posted a strong year overall—reporting a record fourth-quarter profit of $5.7 billion (up 53% year-over-year) and full-year earnings of $21.3 billion—driven by broad strength across lending, deposits, investment banking, commercial banking, asset management and a mortgage refinancing surge. Revenue improvements and reduced loan-loss reserves boosted results, and mortgage banking swung to a large quarterly profit. However, the year was marred by a multibillion-dollar “London Whale” derivatives loss (about $6.2 billion through Q3) that the bank continued to unwind and which produced regulatory enforcement actions citing risk-management failures and inadequate board oversight. In response, JPMorgan’s board cut CEO Jamie Dimon’s 2012 pay to $11.5 million from $23 million, delayed vesting on stock sales, and highlighted his ultimate responsibility while also praising the firm’s overall performance. Internal and board investigations blamed senior managers—most notably Ina Drew and others—for execution, oversight and control weaknesses; several executives resigned or were criticized. JPMorgan faces ongoing legal and regulatory challenges, will curb near-term buybacks to build capital under Basel III, and expects the trading issue to wind down soon.

A Savannah-based film crew shooting the Gregg Allman biopic Midnight Rider was struck by a CSX freight train on a railroad trestle over the Altamaha River in Wayne County, Georgia, on Thursday, killing 27-year-old Sarah Elizabeth Jones of Atlanta and injuring seven others. The crew, from Meddin Studios and working on property owned by Rayonier, had permission to be on Rayonier’s land but not, authorities say, on the CSX-owned tracks or trestle. Sheriff’s investigators and CSX are cooperating in an ongoing probe; investigators initially treated the death as suspicious pending further inquiry. It remained unclear whether crew members were on the trestle or at the track edge, whether they were awaiting a train or were unaware of one, and whether some injuries resulted from flying debris as equipment was struck. Among items found on the tracks was what appeared to be a mattress. Production sources said Open Road Films still plans a U.S. release, though no date is set. The film, based on Allman’s memoir My Cross to Bear, stars William Hurt and Tyson Ritter; Meddin Studios and the production issued statements expressing devastation and condolences while cooperating with authorities.

Johnny Cash’s boyhood home in Dyess, Ark., has been added to the National Register of Historic Places. The five-room farmhouse, built in 1934 as part of the Federal Emergency Relief Administration’s Dyess Resettlement Colony, was nominated last December. A National Register historian returned the nomination in January, asking for stronger emphasis on how Dyess shaped Cash’s development as an artist rather than focusing mainly on architectural claims. The nomination was revised, retitled “Farm No. 266, Johnny Cash Boyhood Home,” and refiled in April under Criterion B for association with the life of a significant person. The Arkansas Historic Preservation Program announced the listing in May; Arkansas State University, which owns the restored property, spent $575,000 to purchase, restore, furnish and landscape it. Supporters say the site vividly links Cash’s formative years in Dyess to songs such as “Five Feet High and Rising” and “Pickin’ Time.” Cash lived in the house from age 3 through high school; he and others have credited his Dyess upbringing with helping shape his music and career. The broader Dyess colony was listed in 1976, but the Cash house fell outside the original boundary.

A 17-year-old Turpin daughter’s trembling 911 call, played at a Riverside, California, preliminary hearing, laid out years of severe abuse and neglect suffered by her and 12 siblings in a Perris home. In the recording she begged a dispatcher to “help my sisters,” saying two younger sisters and a brother were chained to their beds; she described being routinely choked, beaten and left unbathed so long the house reeked of human waste. The parents, David and Louise Turpin, have pleaded not guilty to charges including torture and child abuse and are held on $12 million bail each.

Authorities say the January call triggered the rescue of three children shackled to beds and the arrest of their parents. Officers found a home hidden behind a neat exterior that showed signs of extreme deprivation: filth so severe the girl said she sometimes woke unable to breathe, dirt caked on her skin, and signs of starvation—one adult child weighed just 82 pounds. The children ranged in age from 2 to 29 and reportedly lived in isolation, with some not understanding what police were when officers arrived.

The girl told investigators she had planned an escape for two years and was terrified as she climbed out a window to run for help, unable at first even to dial 911 because of fear. She read the family address from a scrap of paper at the dispatcher’s prompting and said she hadn’t finished first grade, spoke in a childlike way, and referred to her parents as “Mother” and “Father,” invoking a strict religious atmosphere. She described long periods confined to rooms, allowed out only to eat, use the bathroom or brush teeth, with meals often limited to a single combined lunch-dinner of sandwiches or frozen items. Punishments included slapping and hair-pulling; she also recounted a sexual incident when she was 12, and an episode in which her mother choked her for watching a Justin Bieber video and told her she “wanted to die” and would “go to hell.” The children kept journals that may corroborate their accounts, and the case has drawn international attention for its extreme neglect and abuse.

Central Texas teen Macie Martinez, a junior at Lake Travis High School and a trainer for the school’s softball team, is recovering with humor and resilience after being struck by lightning in her Dripping Springs home on Memorial Day. The strike happened when Macie opened the refrigerator to get applesauce; her mother, Misty Villarreal, described a surreal explosion, sudden blackout and a terrifying, deep scream from her daughter. Macie was rushed to the hospital where doctors documented a fern-shaped skin pattern—commonly seen in lightning strikes—and discovered she had been temporarily paralyzed in her legs for about 45 minutes. She also sustained nerve damage in her arms and hands, and continues to experience fatigue, numbness, and occasional confusion and forgetfulness. Physicians are monitoring her liver and kidneys as part of her follow-up care.

Despite the severity of the event, Macie has kept a light-hearted online presence, jokingly posting “call me Sparky” and sharing photos with lightning bolt motifs. Her family likewise uses humor—nicknaming her “Sparky” or “Bolt”—to cope with the trauma. Physical losses were limited to household items: gaming systems, wood flooring, appliances and sensors were damaged or destroyed, while the family counts themselves fortunate that the only human injuries were survivable. Macie is following doctors’ orders to rest and complete final exams. Her mother remains worried about potential long-term nerve effects but grateful their outcomes weren’t worse. The family’s mixture of worry, gratitude and levity reflects their effort to stay positive during recovery.

Barry Byron Mills, known as “Baron,” the long-time leader of the Aryan Brotherhood prison gang, was found dead on July 8 in his single-person cell at the federal supermax in Florence, Colorado, a day after turning 70. Mills was serving multiple life-without-parole sentences for murders tied to his leadership of the white supremacist gang; an autopsy is underway but authorities say his death does not appear suspicious. A native of the San Francisco Bay Area, Mills joined the Aryan Brotherhood in San Quentin in the mid-1970s and transformed what had been a small prison clique into a nationwide criminal organization. His influence was particularly strong in Northern California, and he aggressively recruited members and ran operations from behind bars. Mills was notorious for brutal violence, including a savage attempted decapitation while in federal custody, and for orchestrating crimes via couriers that stretched from coast to coast. Prosecutors say his orders helped spark a race war among prison gangs and included an infamous protection deal with mob boss John Gotti. Federal authorities mounted a major RICO case in the early 2000s charging Mills and dozens of co-conspirators in multiple killings and attempted hits; Mills was convicted in 2006. Facing possible death, jurors split 9–3, so he received life terms and spent decades in near-total lockdown at ADX Florence. Supporters and associates described him as feared and admired; his longtime attorney said Mills refused to seek leniency at sentencing, insisting on “no sniveling.”

On Sept. 11, 2012, the U.S. Consulate in Benghazi, Libya, was attacked, killing Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens and three other Americans. The assault involved gunfire, rocket-propelled grenades and arson; victims appear to have died from smoke inhalation while trying to escape a burning building. U.S. officials said the attack was a planned, military-style operation that may have used protests over an anti-Islam film—"Innocence of Muslims"—as a diversion; investigators and analysts suggested militant groups, possibly linked to al-Qaida, could have been responsible. The film’s cast disavowed the project, saying they were misled. The U.S. deployed Marines and discussed surveillance drone flights over eastern Libya to locate suspects; the FBI and other agencies were mobilized for the investigation. World leaders, the U.N. Security Council and Libyan officials condemned the attack; Libya apologized and pledged to pursue the culprits. President Obama ordered flags lowered and vowed justice; Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and other U.S. officials praised Stevens’ service and stressed that the assault would not alter U.S. support for Libya’s transition. The incident intensified debate in the U.S. over diplomatic security and became a flashpoint in the 2012 presidential campaign.

At the East Asia Summit in Phnom Penh, President Barack Obama stepped into a fraught regional dispute over the South China Sea, where China and five neighbors contest strategic, resource-rich waters. The territorial row—most vocally between China and the Philippines, but also involving Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei—again dominated talks and undermined ASEAN unity. Cambodia, a China ally and summit host, tried to keep focus on economics and free-trade initiatives, but its move to block discussion of maritime disputes provoked a blunt protest from Philippine President Benigno Aquino III and objection from Vietnam and Singapore. ASEAN’s consensus-based decisionmaking left any agreement vulnerable to a single veto, exposing the bloc’s divisions and past failures to issue joint communiqués. Washington insists it takes no side territorially but opposes use of force and urges a binding “code of conduct” to prevent clashes—an idea backed by Japan and Australia but resisted by China, which prefers bilateral talks. The summit also advanced trade talks, including RCEP and trilateral China-Japan-South Korea discussions, even as security tensions cloud the region.

Speaking in Malmö, Sweden, the Dalai Lama said Europe is "morally responsible" to help refugees genuinely facing life-threatening danger but insisted "Europe belongs to the Europeans" and that migrants should ultimately return to rebuild their home countries. He urged receiving, educating and assisting refugees temporarily, while emphasizing reconstruction of their nations as the long-term goal. The remarks, made after Sweden’s election gains by the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, echoed his past comments about Germany and reflect concerns in Sweden over rising violent crime linked by some to recent migrant inflows. The exiled Tibetan leader fled China in 1959.

Zsa Zsa Gabor, the glamorous Hungarian-American socialite and actress who helped define celebrity culture, died at 99. Renowned for her effortless wit, unabashed charm and talent for staying in the spotlight, she was often described as the first person to be famous largely for being famous. Gabor’s public persona was built on quips about love, marriage and luxury, many of which have become classic one-liners. She famously said, “I’m a great housekeeper. Every time I get a divorce, I keep the house,” and joked about age and image: “You can say I’m full of s—t — but don’t say I’m old.” A serial bride who married nine times, she quipped, “Husbands are like fires. They go out when unattended,” and wryly noted, “A man in love is incomplete until he has married. Then he’s finished.” Gabor loved paradox and self-mythology—“Personally, I know nothing about sex because I have always been married”—and rarely missed an opportunity for theatrical flourish, as when she delayed reporters to ensure they saw “the famous Zsa Zsa face” after a jail release. Her sharp humor, glamour and unapologetic persona left a lasting mark on Hollywood and celebrity culture.

Kathy and Brandon, who met and married in Kalamazoo, revealed a touching nine-year story behind a wedding gift from Kathy’s Great Aunt Alison. The plain white box came with a single instruction: “Do not open until your 1st disagreement.” Over nearly a decade and through many arguments, slammed doors, and even moments when both considered giving up, the couple avoided opening it. They feared that using the box would symbolize failure or that if they opened it after a relatively small fight, they might be without it for a worse one later. The box sat on high shelves through three moves, quietly reminding them of commitment without ever being used.

Rather than being a secret solution, the unopened box became a lesson: its very presence encouraged tolerance, compromise, patience and reflection. The couple learned to reassess conflicts, lean on each other, and grow as friends and teammates—realizing that the tools for a healthy marriage were within themselves, not inside a package. When they finally opened the box, it contained simple, loving items: wine glasses and personal notes. Brandon’s note included cash and instructions to buy flowers and a bottle of wine; Kathy’s included cash and suggested buying a pizza or shrimp and preparing a bath. In the end, the gift fulfilled its purpose not by rescuing them from conflict, but by prompting the growth that made those rescue tools unnecessary.

President Donald Trump stirred controversy by publicly calling for Russia’s reinstatement into the G-7 as he departed for the summit in Quebec, arguing Moscow should be “at the negotiating table.” His remarks — made amid growing tensions with allies over newly imposed U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum — drew bipartisan criticism at home and skepticism from many partners. Trump’s suggestion revived debate over Russia’s 2014 expulsion from the then-G8 following its annexation of Crimea and support for separatists in eastern Ukraine. Critics including Sen. Chuck Schumer, Sen. Ben Sasse, Sen. John McCain and former Vice President Joe Biden condemned the idea, citing Russian election interference, aggressions in Ukraine and other malign actions. Britain and several European leaders warned against readmission; yet Italy’s new prime minister, Giuseppe Conte, voiced support. The president defended his broader Russia posture by highlighting administration actions such as sanctions and diplomat expulsions, and by asserting he had been tough on Moscow when necessary. The comments came amid an acrimonious run-up to the summit, marked by sharp exchanges with French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau over trade. Western leaders largely remain committed to maintaining pressure on Russia until its behavior changes, despite Trump’s outreach.

Eight-year-old Jack Russell Knuckles became a YouTube hit after howling whenever the Law & Order theme plays, prompting dozens of similar videos of dogs “singing” along. Owners and bloggers have posted clips showing dogs of various sizes whining, lifting their heads, or approaching screens when the theme begins. Experts say the reaction likely stems from the theme’s high-register, staccato notes and sharp timbre, which can irritate or trigger dogs’ auditory nerves—similar to responses to sirens—whereas lower, simpler tones tend to calm dogs. Composer Mike Post was amused and surprised that his tune inspires such canine performances.

This document appears to be a collage of short reviews, notices, and holiday hours for a local English eatery, emphasizing its straightforward, traditional cooking and friendly, unpretentious service. Multiple reviewers praise the food—calling it “great” and “simple down-to-earth good English food”—and many express eagerness to try the widely recommended Sunday roast. Comments imply a warm, familiar atmosphere run by people who may lack formal business training but have plenty of hands-on experience and heart, which customers appreciate.

Interspersed with the reviews are holiday opening details. The establishment will be closed for several days around late December: Boxing Day, December 27–30, New Year’s Eve, and New Year’s Day. It reopens on January 2 with normal hours from 7:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. There are also specific Christmas Eve hours listed as 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., and a note about Christmas Day bookings (though that line is incomplete). A festive greeting—“Merry Christmas Everyone & Happy New Year!”—is included, reinforcing the seasonal context.

Overall, the material conveys a positive community sentiment toward a modest, well-loved local restaurant known for traditional English fare, attentive regulars, and clear holiday scheduling. The combination of enthusiastic food recommendations and practical opening-hour notices makes this useful both as an endorsement and as a service update for patrons planning visits over the holiday period.

Jessica Hayes, a 38-year-old high school theology teacher from Fort Wayne, Indiana, became the Fort Wayne-South Bend Diocese’s first consecrated virgin in 25 years during a public ceremony at the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception. Hundreds attended as she symbolically “married” Jesus Christ, making a lifelong, public commitment to serve the Church while remaining a layperson — a key difference from becoming a nun. Consecrated virgins are rare: roughly 3,000 worldwide and about 200 in the United States, and Hayes is currently the only one in her diocese.

Hayes described the decision as the result of years of prayer and discernment, choosing the path that brought her the most joy and allowed her to continue teaching and participating in parish life while dedicating herself more fully to Christ. She discussed practical details of the ceremony, including selecting an appropriate dress and lying prostrate before the altar, and clarified she will still be addressed as Ms. Hayes. Hayes hopes her visible vocation will encourage other women to consider consecrated life, especially younger women who rarely encounter contemporary examples of this calling.

LeBron James married longtime girlfriend Savannah Brinson in a private ceremony Saturday at the upscale Grand Del Mar Hotel in San Diego, attended by about 200 guests. The three-day celebration, ending with a Sunday brunch, featured intense security and strict no-phone rules; guests were escorted under tents and umbrellas to conceal arrivals. Notable attendees included Heat owner Micky Arison, coach Erik Spoelstra and teammates like Dwyane Wade and Chris Bosh. James and Brinson, together since high school with two sons, became engaged Jan. 1, 2012. The wedding followed Miami’s recent NBA championship.

First Lady Melania Trump told ABC News in an interview that she has warned her husband there are people in his administration she doesn’t trust and that governing is harder when “you always need to watch your back.” Her remarks come amid turmoil after an anonymous New York Times op-ed from a senior administration official who claimed some aides are actively frustrating parts of the president’s agenda; President Trump called the essay “gutless” and tweeted “TREASON?” The interview, filmed during Melania’s solo Africa trip to promote her “Be Best” anti-bullying campaign, also featured her saying she could be “the most bullied person in the world,” later clarifying she is “one of them” given what people say about her. She linked her personal experience with harassment to the motivation for focusing Be Best on social media and online behavior, noting concerns about how bullying can affect children, including her son Barron. ABC’s special “Being Melania — The First Lady” will air more of the wide-ranging interview.

In 2002 professional criminal Octave Durham and an accomplice executed a brisk heist at Amsterdam’s Van Gogh Museum, stealing two little-known but inestimably valuable works: View of the Sea at Scheveningen (1882) and Congregation Leaving the Reformed Church in Nuenen (1882–84). In a recent documentary and press interviews, Durham for the first time offers extensive, brash details of the theft after years of publicly denying involvement. He describes entering through a small broken window, stuffing the two smallest canvases—chosen not for artistic interest but because they were easiest to remove—into a bag, and escaping down a rope; the whole operation lasted about 3 minutes and 40 seconds. He recounts sliding into his getaway car, lowering the window, removing his ski mask and listening over his police scanner as officers investigated, unaware he was nearby. Durham admits he damaged the seascape during the landing, chipping paint, and left a black baseball cap at the scene; a guard called police but was not permitted to use force to stop them. He boasts of other criminal exploits—bank and safety-deposit robberies—and insists he targeted the museum simply because he could.

The paintings are historically significant and never before auctioned; comparable van Gogh landscapes sell for roughly $10–70 million. Durham and his partner initially hoped to steal more famous works but were thwarted by security or size. After the theft they tried to sell the paintings in the Netherlands, including to underworld figures who were subsequently assassinated, and ultimately sold them to the Italian mafia. Durham was convicted in 2005 and received 3.5 years; he still owes substantial damages to the museum. He spent recent time attempting to recover the works to repay the debt; Italian police found and seized the canvases last year. After serving as evidence in a mafia probe, an Italian court cleared their release and they are now being returned to Amsterdam.

CBS abruptly overhauled The Early Show, replacing longtime co-hosts Harry Smith and Maggie Rodriguez and weather forecaster Dave Price. Beginning Jan. 3, weekday anchors will be Saturday team Chris Wragge and Erica Hill, joined by Jeff Glor as news reader and Marysol Castro from ABC’s Good Morning America as weather forecaster. Executive producer David Friedman said the change aims to improve energy and chemistry to boost ratings, where CBS trails Today and GMA. Smith will remain at CBS as a reporter and primary substitute on Evening News, Face the Nation and Sunday Morning; new roles for Rodriguez and Price are undecided. Critics called the swift shakeup startling.

The Chicago Cubs' 2016 season ended a century-long championship drought and capped a dramatic end to the long-rumored “Curse of the Billy Goat.” The curse allegedly began in 1945 when tavern owner William Sianis was ejected from Game 4 of the World Series with his goat Murphy and purportedly declared the Cubs would never win another World Series. After losing that Series, the Cubs endured decades of near-misses and infamous incidents—black cats, blown postseason leads, Leon Durham’s error in 1984, the Steve Bartman episode in 2003, and multiple postseason collapses—that fans and media tied to the curse. Numerous theatrical and sincere attempts to lift the curse unfolded over the years: goats paraded to Wrigley, symbolic rituals, priests’ blessings, and grassroots “Reverse the Curse” campaigns. Many former Cubs later won titles elsewhere, fueling the narrative. In 2016, with a 103–58 record, the Cubs won the National League pennant—breaking the curse on the 46th anniversary of Sianis’s death—and then defeated the Cleveland Indians in a seven-game World Series thriller, winning Game 7 in 10 innings to claim their first championship since 1908. Celebrities and lifelong fans celebrated at Wrigley Field throughout the run.

Syrian opposition activists report that Islamic State fighters have seized several strategic towns and villages near the Turkey border after deadly clashes with other rebel groups. Activists said IS captured Akhtarin and Turkmanbareh in Aleppo countryside, along with three nearby areas, displacing rebel factions that had been fighting to overthrow President Bashar al-Assad. The takeover was reported by multiple activist sources, jihadists affiliated with IS on social media, and the Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights. These gains add to IS’s expanding self-styled caliphate across large parts of eastern Syria and northern and western Iraq.

Meanwhile, concern over the rapid IS advance in Iraq prompted international responses. France, calling the situation in Iraqi Kurdistan “catastrophic,” announced it would begin supplying arms to Kurdish forces battling IS militants. The move, described as urgent, came amid broader international adjustments: U.S. officials acknowledged that American intelligence agencies were directly arming Kurdish fighters—marking a shift from the prior policy of working exclusively through Baghdad—and about 130 U.S. troops were sent to Irbil on a temporary mission to coordinate efforts to help trapped Yazidi civilians on Mount Sinjar. France said its arms shipment, details of which it did not disclose, was coordinated with the Iraqi government.

European Union diplomats held high-level talks and agreed to consider Kurdish requests for urgent military assistance in close coordination with Iraqi authorities. France also pledged a 20-ton humanitarian shipment—medicine, tents, and water treatment equipment—to Irbil. The international alarm follows IS’s swift offensive in June that captured Mosul, routed Iraqi forces in parts of the country, and produced widespread killing and displacement: thousands dead and more than 1.5 million people uprooted by the violence.

Aimee Copeland, a 24-year-old Georgia graduate student who developed necrotizing fasciitis after cutting her leg in a May 1 zip-line fall, has spoken for the first time since being hospitalized. Her father, Andy Copeland, called May 27 “Aimee Day” and announced she can talk. Aimee, who has had multiple amputations and recently began breathing on her own and sitting up, remains unaware of the national attention but has been moved by widespread blood donations.

Beneath Yellowstone National Park lies a massive supervolcano capable of ejecting over 1,000 cubic kilometers of rock and ash—enough to blanket large parts of North America and induce global climate effects. Its last supereruption occurred about 631,000 years ago, and geological evidence shows Yellowstone has produced three such eruptions in roughly the past 2.1 million years. Researchers have long assumed that supereruption systems require centuries or millennia to mature after being drained by a prior blast. New studies, however, challenge that view.

Work presented by Arizona State University geologists Hannah Shamloo and Christy Till examined phenocryst crystals in the Lava Creek Tuff deposit from Yellowstone’s most recent supereruption. The crystals’ outer rims record abrupt changes in temperature and chemistry—most notably increased barium—occurring over mere decades. Their interpretation is that two injections of new, hotter magma from deeper reservoirs mixed into the shallow chamber shortly before eruption, rapidly priming the system. This suggests supervolcanoes can evolve from quiescent to eruptible on far shorter timescales than previously thought.

Parallel modeling by the USGS using the Ash3D program shows a modern Yellowstone supereruption would generate an expansive umbrella ash cloud, producing a “bull’s-eye” ash deposit centered on the park and depositing meters of ash nearby and measurable layers across the continent. Despite these findings, Yellowstone is closely monitored and currently shows no signs of imminent eruption; the USGS estimates the annual chance of another massive blast as about 1 in 730,000. Scientists emphasize more work is needed to translate crystal-based histories into reliable early-warning indicators.

Damascus, long Assad’s secure stronghold, is losing its bubble of normalcy as the Syrian civil war creeps into daily life. What were once routine 25-minute drives now become perilous ordeals as fighting in suburbs halts traffic, checkpoints multiply, and soldiers and shabiha forces search vehicles. Residents fear greater destruction and tightening rebel pressure; suicide bombings and kidnappings have increased, gasoline and heating oil are scarce, and streets or bridges can be closed without warning. Social life has frayed—nightlife and embassy events have vanished, children are increasingly traumatized, and many families are homeschooling children to avoid dangerous commutes. Wealthy neighborhoods experience high-profile kidnappings and ransom demands, and people are cautious about assigning blame amid a swirl of rebel, extremist, and regime-linked perpetrators.

Beyond Damascus, tensions within the Alawite community—on which Assad heavily relies—are emerging as a new vulnerability for the regime. Long a pillar of regime support, Alawites increasingly voice unease as their sons fill coffins arriving from front lines. Reports from the Alawite coastal heartland include a shootout among Assad relatives in Qardaha and the detention of an Alawite dissident, hinting at clan rivalries and political strains. While a broad defection of Alawites to the opposition remains unlikely—fears of reprisals and survival instincts bind many to Assad—analysts warn that growing frustration and high casualty rates undermine cohesion and could have long-term consequences.

The conflict’s economic fallout further erodes stability. Factories have been damaged or burned, sanctions and disrupted banking hinder trade and investment, inflation and currency collapse bite, and fuel shortages multiply. Many business owners have fled or struggle to keep operations afloat; some resent Assad yet fear the uncertainty a collapse would bring. The regime survives with external support and a pared-down economy to sustain the military, but whether that is sustainable remains doubtful as the humanitarian, social, sectarian, and economic pressures mount.

A shooting at Delaware Valley Charter High School in north Philadelphia wounded two students in the gym on a Friday afternoon. A bullet first struck an 18-year-old girl’s arm, exited, and then hit a 17-year-old boy, who remained hospitalized in stable condition; the girl was treated and released. Surveillance footage and interviews led police to identify suspects; a 17-year-old later surrendered and was charged with two counts of aggravated assault, while a 16-year-old questioned was released without charges. The school, which uses metal detectors and security, was locked down; officials and parents expressed concern about how a gun entered the building.

In his first extended interview since announcing a split with Gwyneth Paltrow, Coldplay frontman Chris Martin took responsibility for the collapse of his decade-long marriage and explained how those personal struggles shaped the band’s new album, Ghost Stories. Speaking to BBC Radio 1’s Zane Lowe, Martin rejected the term “breakdown,” calling the separation a wake-up moment and a push to “grow up.” He said that for about two years he had been “a mess,” unable to enjoy his work or the positive things around him because he was burdened by internal issues. He stressed that blaming others was no longer an option and that he needed to make changes in himself.

Martin repeatedly framed the split as a consequence of his own inability to be fully vulnerable. “If you can’t open yourself up, you can’t appreciate the wonder inside,” he said, noting that one can be with someone wonderful yet fail to celebrate that relationship because of personal barriers. He emphasized that letting love in requires risk—pain and rejection are possible, but openness ultimately allows love to be reciprocated. Martin described life as full of “colorful challenges” — love, money, children, illness — and said Ghost Stories is an honest reflection of navigating those hardships rather than running away from them. The album, he explained, provided a way to confront and express what had been happening in his life.

He also discussed creative choices around the album’s promotion, including hiding handwritten lyric sheets in libraries worldwide and releasing the single “Magic,” which explores nuanced feelings between people amid life’s complications like travel, illness, and addiction. Martin revealed he’s taking practical steps to improve himself, mentioning boxing and working with a personal trainer to get in better physical shape.

Beyond the separation and music, the interview touched on Martin’s admiration for other artists—he praised One Direction and defended Kanye West as often misunderstood. While Martin acknowledged it may be too late to save his marriage, his candidness portrayed someone intent on self-improvement and on channeling personal upheaval into honest art.

For years the U.S. has relied on exporting its recyclable plastics—especially mixed, low-grade items—to China rather than building domestic recycling capacity. China has been the largest buyer of U.S. scrap and trash, but a recent crackdown called Operation Green Fence bans many contaminated or mixed plastic imports. Chinese inspectors are rejecting shipments that contain unwashed plastics or contaminants; even a single syringe can trigger refusal. As a result, truckloads of plastic are piling up at U.S. recycling depots—Oregon recyclers report canceled orders and dozens of trucks waiting—and companies face scrambling to re-sort materials into specific resin types that China will still accept. The restrictions mainly affect miscellaneous rigid plastics (numbers 3, 6, 7) like coffee cup lids, PVC pipe, clamshells and garden planters, not common curbside items such as milk jugs or soda bottles. The crisis exposes how U.S. recycling rested on foreign markets rather than investing in domestic sorting, labor, and technology; expanding U.S. capacity would be costly, and cities now confront mounting piles of material and uncertain buyers.

When Princeton graduate student Joshua Vandiver married Henry Velandia on Aug. 29, 2010, they did not expect to face deportation threats. Velandia, a Venezuelan who emigrated in 2002, founded the HotSalsaHot dance school, taught salsa at Whitman College and appeared on Univision’s Mira Quien Baila. His work-visa application was denied and his current visa expired; because the 1996 Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) bars federal recognition of same-sex marriages, Vandiver cannot sponsor Velandia for a green card. Velandia is scheduled to appear before an immigration judge in Newark on Nov. 17. The couple is campaigning for repeal of DOMA, urging Congress and DHS to halt deportation hearings for foreign-born spouses of U.S. citizens, and have drawn online and campus support. They say they would consider leaving the U.S. together rather than be separated, though legal experts view their prospects as slim.

Rep. Darrell Issa intensified the confrontation over the Justice Department’s failed ATF “Fast and Furious” gun-tracking operation by directly accusing President Obama in a letter of either participating in managing the operation’s aftermath or improperly invoking executive privilege to obstruct Congress. Issa, chairman of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, framed Obama’s assertion of privilege as evidence that the White House may have been involved in Justice Department deliberations — an allegation the White House rejected as baseless and defended the privilege as consistent with longstanding executive-branch practice.

The move escalates tensions ahead of a planned House vote on whether to hold Attorney General Eric Holder in contempt for refusing to produce more than 100,000 subpoenaed documents. Issa’s committee already recommended a contempt finding along party lines. Republicans argue the Justice Department is stonewalling and insist they seek internal documents not shielded by deliberative-process protections. Democrats counter that the contempt push is politically motivated and could undermine Holder’s ability to protect minority voting rights.

Prominent civil-rights leaders, including Al Sharpton, warned that a contempt vote would hamper the Justice Department’s defense of black and Hispanic voters and other civil-rights protections; Sharpton has characterized Republican tactics as having a racial effect. House Democratic leaders, including Nancy Pelosi, tied the timing of the contempt effort to the DOJ’s opposition to state voter-ID laws and called the initiative partisan. Some Democrats previously urged transparency on Fast and Furious, but many oppose holding Holder in contempt. If the House votes to hold Holder in contempt, the matter could be referred to the DOJ — which legal experts expect would decline prosecution — leaving Republicans to consider litigation in federal court. Calls for Holder’s resignation have been voiced by some Republicans but lack broad bipartisan support.

Florida International University has suspended its Pi Kappa Alpha (Pike) chapter after an anonymous email revealed screenshots from a supposedly private Facebook group that became public. The screenshots—about 70 posts—allege drug sales, hazing, misogyny and homophobic slurs. Examples include members asking for “coke,” offering to sell Adderall with a posted phone number, advertising an on‑campus “Pike Pharmacy,” and sharing photos of topless women—one allegedly 17. Posts bragged about hazing, mocked overweight women, denigrated rival fraternities and sororities, and celebrated unsporting conduct in intramural soccer. FIU ordered the chapter to cease meetings and events while campus police and university conduct investigators probe the allegations. Pike’s national office said it had not known about the private group until notified and is cooperating with the temporary suspension and investigation.

This is the latest in a history of disciplinary problems for the chapter: prior probation for serving alcohol to a pledge, and earlier incidents since 2006 including underage drinking, drinking games, egging a rival house, vandalism and fines or community service. The story also references a separate, severe national incident at the University of Tennessee where a student was hospitalized after “butt‑chugging” alcohol via rectal tubing at a Pike event—highlighting dangerous fringe behaviors tied to Greek life. Psychologist Susan Lipkins warned these posts reflect broader cultural issues in fraternities: universities may overlook misconduct because Greek organizations aid recruitment, alumni donations and housing, and problematic behavior can be widespread rather than exceptional.

An experimental Phase I drug trial in Rennes, France, has left one volunteer brain-dead and five others hospitalized after 90 people were given oral doses. The trial was run by French contract-research clinic Biotrial for Portuguese company Bial; regulators have suspended the study and recalled all participants while the Paris prosecutor has opened an investigation. Volunteers began regular dosing on 7 January and developed severe symptoms within days. Rennes neurosurgeon Pierre‑Gilles Edan reported that among the six men hospitalized (aged 28–49), one is brain-dead, three face possible irreversible neurological damage, a fifth has neurological problems, and a sixth is being monitored but is not critical. Health Minister Marisol Touraine said the compound was a FAAH inhibitor acting on the endocannabinoid system to affect pain, and denied media reports that the drug contained cannabis or cannabinoids. Testing on animals, including primates, had preceded human dosing. Biotrial said it followed regulations and procedures and notified authorities after “serious adverse events.” Phase I trials, which test safety and tolerance in healthy volunteers, always carry risk despite extensive preclinical work; experts note safeguards reduce but do not eliminate risk. The incident is rare but serious, prompting government scrutiny and renewed attention to trial oversight as authorities work to determine the cause and ensure participant welfare.

A newborn in Chongqing, China, described by local media as a “miracle baby” or “chopstick girl,” has survived her first week after being born at just 23 weeks’ gestation. The baby, now eight days old, arrived following an emergency operation to correct a problem with her mother’s cervix; doctors had warned the parents that the infant would be severely premature with a very low chance of survival. Despite those bleak expectations, the baby — weighing about 660 grams and measuring roughly 28 cm, about the length of a chopstick — survived the delivery and was immediately placed in an incubator for intensive, round-the-clock neonatal care. Medical staff report that her organs and blood vessels are still underdeveloped, complicating the administration of medications and nutrients. Hospital paediatric leaders called survival after such a “spontaneous abortion” extremely rare. The infant remains in critical but surviving condition as clinicians manage the significant risks associated with extreme prematurity. The case has drawn attention for its rarity and the challenges of caring for babies born at the edge of viability.

Researchers from the Max Planck Institute report that the interjection “Huh?” — a brief, questioning syllable used to request clarification — appears in strikingly similar form and function across unrelated languages, suggesting it is essentially universal. Examining nearly 200 natural conversational tokens from ten languages on five continents (including Cha'palaa, Dutch, Icelandic, Lao, Mandarin, Murrinh-Patha, Russian, Siwu, Spanish, and Italian), the team found the repair-initiator to be a monosyllable with an unrounded low-front central vowel, optional glottal/H onset, and questioning intonation. Crucially, each language’s form is calibrated to its phonology and prosody, showing the item is learned and integrated into linguistic systems rather than an innate grunt. The authors argue the cross-linguistic similarity arises from convergent cultural evolution: conversational pressures — tight turn-taking, need for rapid, low-effort signals that prompt a repeat or reformulation — favor a minimal, easily produced interrogative token. This “conversational infrastructure” imposes selective pressures that constrain variation, producing analogous forms across languages while allowing language-specific tuning. The finding reframes “huh?” as a bona fide word with evolutionary and communicative significance and suggests similar mechanisms may explain cross-linguistic uniformity in other discourse-regulatory tokens (e.g., mm-hm, uh/um, oh).

Oyster, the New York startup that launched a Netflix-style e-book subscription in 2013, is shutting down its service and moving on to new opportunities, the founders announced in a company blog post. They said they plan to “sunset” the current product within months and encouraged subscribers to request refunds; they also reiterated a belief that smartphones will be the primary reading device globally and hinted their future work will better realize their e-book vision. Google confirmed it has hired “a portion of the Oyster team” to work on Google Play Books; reports say CEO Eric Stromberg and co-founders Andrew Brown and Willem Van Lancker are among those joining Google in what appears to be an “acqhire,” with investors reportedly compensated for the hire rights. Oyster raised about $17 million and initially offered an all-you-can-read plan for $9.95/month, later expanding in April to include an e-book store selling individual titles to compete more directly with Amazon, which launched Kindle Unlimited. Despite building a library of over 1 million titles and signing three of the five largest U.S. publishers, Oyster struggled to change reading habits—subscribers tended not to binge-read as with video or music services—and publishers often delayed new releases on subscription platforms. Oyster’s app worked across phones, tablets and computers but not on Kindle devices.

Last week’s chemical spill into the Elk River left more than 300,000 West Virginians without safe tap water and exposed long-standing regulatory gaps in a state heavily tied to coal and chemical industries. A ruptured 40,000-gallon tank at a Freedom Industries storage site released an estimated 7,500 gallons of 4-methylcyclohexane methanol (MCHM), used in coal washing, contaminating the water supply and prompting a do-not-use order across nine counties. Residents queued for bottled water and many businesses and schools closed; 169 people sought medical care for exposure symptoms, with ten hospital admissions not life-threatening. The site had not been inspected by state or federal authorities since 1991 because West Virginia requires inspections only for chemical production, not storage facilities. Critics say the state’s industry-friendly regulatory culture and resistance to federal oversight have undermined enforcement. State officials and federal agencies, including the U.S. Chemical Safety Board and the U.S. attorney, opened investigations. Testing showed encouraging declines in contamination; officials began phased zone-by-zone testing to lift the ban, prioritizing hospitals and high-use areas. Governor Tomblin pledged regulatory review and tighter oversight of chemical storage, even as industry representatives urged that coal companies not be blamed for this chemical-company accident.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn, the former IMF chief, said his sexual encounter with a New York hotel maid was an "error" and a moral failing but denied any violence, constraint or aggression. In his first TV interview since his May arrest, he expressed deep regret that the episode cost him the chance to run in France’s 2012 presidential race and said he would no longer seek the Socialist nomination. Strauss-Kahn insisted the maid, Nafissatou Diallo, had lied; criminal charges in New York were dropped when prosecutors questioned her credibility, though she still pursues a civil suit. He also dismissed as "imaginary" a separate 2003 allegation by writer Tristane Banon, who accuses him of attempted rape; he is suing her for defamation and was recently interviewed by police in France. Strauss-Kahn said he felt frightened and humiliated by the US justice system and will "take time to reflect" before deciding whether to return to public life, stressing his lifelong commitment to public service.

Starbucks is expanding its grocery and healthier-food push by partnering with Danone to introduce Greek yogurt parfaits and related products. Branded “Evolution Fresh, Inspired by Dannon,” the yogurt will debut in U.S. Starbucks cafes next year and reach supermarket shelves in 2015, with possible international rollouts. Danone will manufacture and distribute the products; financial terms were not disclosed. The move aligns with CEO Howard Schultz’s strategy to offer healthier fare and grow Starbucks’ packaged-goods footprint—a strategy accelerated after Starbucks reclaimed control of its supermarket business from Kraft in 2011 and acquired Evolution Fresh and Teavana. Starbucks’ retail-packaged revenue surged 50 percent to $1.29 billion in the year ended September, outpacing overall revenue growth. The U.S. Greek yogurt market is booming—Nielsen reported a 48 percent rise for Greek-style yogurt—and is highly competitive, with Chobani, Yoplait and Fage among leading players. Observers warn brand diversification carries risk: too many disparate products can blur Starbucks’ identity. Starbucks expects Danone’s distribution to limit capital costs and sees the partnership as a strategic step in its health-and-wellness evolution.

Albert Mehrabian’s Baby Name Report Card argues that names strongly influence how people are perceived and treated across life. Drawing on more than a decade of large-scale surveys and multiple publications, Mehrabian maps name impressions along key dimensions—Ethical-Caring (trustworthy, warm), Popular-Fun (playful, outgoing), Successful (ambitious, intelligent), Masculine–Feminine, and Overall Attractiveness (a composite of the first three). Names are rated on 0–100 scales (50 average), producing clear differences: for example, “John” scores extremely high for Success while “Knut” rates very low. The book offers practical guidance: general naming guidelines, how to change an unfavorable name, issues like nicknames and unconventional spellings, and alphabetical listings of girls’ and boys’ names with their connoted impressions. It is intended to help parents choose names that will be lifelong assets rather than liabilities and to aid adults wishing to assume new names.

The accompanying human-interest piece shows how powerful and personal naming choices are today. Some grandparents attempt to influence or even buy naming rights—offering money, businesses, or weddings—reflecting tensions between tradition and parents’ desires for unique, personality-reflective names. Naming consultants and large baby-name databases are becoming part of the process; parents negotiate compromises such as using family names as middle names, blending names, or using different names privately versus officially. Financial dependence or cohabitation with older relatives can increase pressure to honor family naming traditions. Ultimately, many couples strive to balance honoring relatives with choosing a name they both love—like the Hudocks, who chose Max to honor a deceased grandfather rather than accept a monetary inducement to use a different traditional name.

A controversial obituary for Cornelia June Rogers Miller, who died in February, sparked outrage after the Cherokee Scout of Murphy, North Carolina, published a caustic notice nearly four months later that said her “presence will not be missed by many” and accused her of a life consumed by drugs, hatred and destruction of family ties. Miller, who lived in Florida and kept a summer home in Murphy, was 82 and had been in an assisted living facility with her husband before she died. Her son Robert called the obituary untrue, tragic and sad, and said he wants his mother remembered as loving and generous; he submitted a replacement obituary to run the following week. The paper’s publisher, David Brown, said the family’s will overrode the editor and that the paper reviews obituaries but edits only for very compelling reasons; he would not disclose who submitted the original notice.

Family members and community readers were shocked. Robert blamed his sisters for writing the notice, but at least one sister denied authoring it. Observers labeled the obituary disturbing, and the family is trying to learn who wrote and submitted the piece. A viewer alerted WTVC that parts of the obituary appear to be plagiarized from a 2008 obituary for Dolores Aguilar in the Vallejo Times Herald, prompting further criticism that the author “didn’t even have the integrity to write something for herself — just goes out and steals something.” The paper has not named the submitter, leaving questions about authorship, motive and editorial responsibility unresolved while the family searches for answers and seeks to restore a more respectful remembrance of Cornelia Miller.

For more than half a century the “Bermuda Triangle” — an area roughly bounded by Miami, Puerto Rico and Bermuda — has been linked in popular culture to mysterious disappearances of ships and planes. Skeptics note the Triangle was popularized by a 1964 pulp article and that investigations by the U.S. Navy, Lloyd’s of London and others find no unusual loss rate there. Many attributed vanishings have prosaic explanations (e.g., navigation errors, fuel exhaustion, storms) or were misreported. Still, a persistent physical hypothesis has long suggested sudden releases of methane from the seafloor could generate giant rising bubble plumes that momentarily reduce water density and buoyancy, potentially swamping vessels.

Recent geological discoveries have renewed interest in that idea. Scientists mapping the seabed off Norway’s coast found enormous craters, up to hundreds of meters across and tens of meters deep, interpreted as sites of past violent methane blowouts from buried gas hydrates. Similar explosive methane releases have been proposed to explain enigmatic sinkholes found in Siberian permafrost. Gas hydrates — icy compounds that trap methane under high pressure — can dissociate and produce large gas bubbles that rise through the water column, possibly creating a trough that could threaten a ship if the vessel is positioned in the critical zone between the bubble’s stagnation point and the trough edge.

Laboratory work modeling a single large bubble beneath a small hull showed that, in principle, such a mechanism can cause loss of buoyancy and sinking under specific geometric conditions. However, no documented modern case definitively links a methane eruption to a real ship loss; the largest documented seafloor venting in the North Atlantic occurred millennia ago following the last ice age. Many researchers therefore view methane blowouts as an intriguing but unproven contribution to some disappearances, not a general explanation for the Bermuda Triangle, which likely remains a mixture of myth, heavy traffic, and ordinary hazards.

After his fiancée Crystal Harris abruptly left Hugh Hefner and moved out of the Playboy Mansion, Hefner quickly filled the void: his former Playboy playmates, identical twins Karissa and Kristina Shannon, have reportedly moved back into the mansion. The sisters, who had left the estate about a year and a half earlier, returned just days after Harris’s departure. Sources suggest Karissa ended a relationship with actor Sam Jones III to return to Hefner alongside her twin, a move presented as part of supporting Hefner through the breakup. The coverage frames the twins’ return as a swift shift in the mansion’s domestic dynamics and a sign that Hefner is being surrounded by familiar company to help him recover from the split. The reports emphasize the speed of the roster change and the interpersonal choices involved—Karissa’s breakup and the twins’ decision to move back—as central elements of the story, underscoring the sensational aspects of relationships and living arrangements at the Playboy Mansion following the engagement’s collapse. (Image credit: WENN.)

During the high-profile Senate Judiciary Committee hearings for Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh, three Republican senators—Lindsey Graham, Mike Lee and Orrin Hatch—had private information including home addresses and phone numbers posted on their Wikipedia pages. The edits, which appeared while Christine Blasey Ford and Kavanaugh testified, were traced to an IP address on Capitol Hill and were quickly removed after aides and authorities were alerted. A Twitter bot that monitors Congressional Wikipedia edits first flagged the changes; the bot deleted posts that exposed the personal data.

On Wednesday, U.S. Capitol Police arrested Jackson A. Cosko, 27, a former Senate Democratic staffer who had worked for Sen. Maggie Hassan and previously for Sen. Barbara Boxer, after he was found inside Hassan’s Capitol Hill office. Cosko, who had been working as an intern in Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee’s office and was subsequently fired, faces multiple federal counts including making public restricted personal information (doxing), witness tampering, threats in interstate communications, identity theft and unauthorized access of a government computer, as well as District charges of second-degree burglary and unlawful entry. He remained in custody pending a court appearance, and investigators indicated additional charges could follow as the probe continues.

Republican presidential hopeful Jon Huntsman, though lagging in polls, released a parody video mocking Herman Cain’s controversial “smoking man” ad. Posted to YouTube on October 28, 2011, by user Jon2012Girls, the spot stars Huntsman’s three daughters wearing horn-rimmed glasses and false mustaches. The sisters deliver tongue-in-cheek lines—“Tomorrow is Friday, one day closer to the weekend,” and a dry endorsement of their father’s “experience and proven track record to revive America’s economy and create jobs,” followed by the quip, “Even if we didn’t believe that, we’d still have to be here.” They acknowledge aggressively promoting their dad, and the ad closes with a playful counter to Cain’s cigarette moment: instead of smoking, all three daughters blow soap bubbles in unison. The video plays on political parody and family-friendly satire to lampoon Cain’s style and present Huntsman with a humorous, self-aware campaign touch.

A jewelry store robbery at Rolling Oaks Mall on the northeast side of San Antonio turned deadly Sunday afternoon. Two armed suspects fled Kay Jewelers and encountered at least two shoppers who tried to intervene. One “good Samaritan” was fatally shot by a suspect; a second citizen with a concealed-carry license shot and wounded one of the robbers. The other robber ran through the mall firing, injuring multiple people; some victims suffered gunshot wounds while others had non-shooting injuries. Police locked down and swept the mall, treated and transported several victims, and later arrested both suspects, who face preliminary charges including capital murder and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Investigations and witness interviews are ongoing.

Audi is rolling out an industry-first feature that shows drivers how long until a red traffic light turns green by linking cars wirelessly to city traffic-management systems. The countdown appears in the instrument cluster and stops a few seconds before the light changes so drivers look up; if the car predicts the driver won’t clear the intersection, it will count down as if the light remains red. The system debuts on 2017 Q7 SUVs and A4 sedans built after June 1 and will be enabled city by city, with five to seven cities expected by year-end though Audi hasn’t named them. Audi frames the feature as a comfort and safety enhancement and a building block for vehicle-to-infrastructure communications relevant to autonomous driving. The service requires the paid Connect Prime subscription ($199 for six months, about $25–$33 monthly) and is integrated directly into the car, not a smartphone app.

Miley Cyrus is defending her shift from Disney teen star to a more mature pop artist with the release of her new album, Can't Be Tamed.
