At 17, Cyrus says she's embracing a more grown-up image and creative control over her music and wardrobe, rejecting suggestions she's trying to be "slutty" or merely provocative. She argues her style reflects personal comfort and fitness—favoring shorts and hot pants—and that her current look and sound are consistent with who she is now, not who she was five years ago. With her Hannah Montana series ending, Cyrus expects to shed the blonde wig and pursue solo stardom while emphasizing she wants listeners to buy her record for its music rather than sexual appeal. Can't Be Tamed is due out Monday. Separate reports note Heather Locklear is moving from a psychiatric ward to a long-term facility for continued mental health and substance-abuse care after a recent hospitalization.

West Virginia Governor Jim Justice announced at a Huntington rally with President Donald Trump that he will change his party registration from Democrat to Republican, saying he could no longer serve effectively as a Democrat. Trump had teased a “very big announcement” before the event. Justice’s switch underscores West Virginia’s strong rightward shift since 2016, where Trump won overwhelmingly, and follows Justice’s visible ties to Trump and his family. The move surprised many Democrats who worked for Justice’s 2016 run; the Democratic Governors Association and unions had helped his campaign. Prominent West Virginia Democrat Sen. Joe Manchin expressed disappointment but reiterated his commitment to the party and to working across lines. Reactions ranged from pragmatic acceptance—some hope the GOP alignment will attract federal attention and jobs—to anger among Democrats who feel betrayed after investing in Justice’s election. Justice’s past donations to Republican causes and friendships with GOP leaders ease his transition. Political observers note the switch complicates Manchin’s 2018 reelection bid and reflects broader state trends: economic hardship, population decline, high opioid death rates, and nostalgia for coal. Trump’s pro-coal rhetoric and promises to restore mining jobs remain popular in the state, despite policy moves affecting Medicaid and mixed economic results touted by the White House.

In the Dodgers’ 5-0 win over the Tampa Bay Rays, Juan Uribe learned a baserunning lesson the hard way. After reaching third on a sacrifice fly with one out remaining in the fourth inning, Uribe looked down while dusting himself off; Rays players covertly relayed the ball to Evan Longoria, who tagged Uribe out the moment he stepped off the bag. Teammate Yasiel Puig subsequently posted a video clip with a caption in Spanish advising to keep a foot on the base to avoid being tagged out, underscoring the basic but crucial baserunning rule.

The UN and Western officials warned of escalating Syrian violence, fearing government forces may be preparing a massacre in Haffa, Latakia province, where UN military observers have been denied access. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and envoy Kofi Annan urged unimpeded UNSMIS entry, citing reports of heavy shelling, helicopter gunship attacks, and civilians trapped in Homs and Haffa. The observers are monitoring a largely collapsed Annan-brokered ceasefire. US State Department spokeswoman Victoria Nuland noted conflicting claims from Syrian media and stressed political and economic pressure over foreign intervention. Fighting was also reported in Rastan, Talbisa, Idlib and Deir al-Zour, where a car bomb killed 10. Separately, the UN’s annual report on children and armed conflict listed Syrian government forces and allied shabiha militias among 52 perpetrators of grave violations against children, documenting killings, torture, sexual violence, and use of children as human shields, while highlighting global child casualties and some positive delistings.

The Project on Student Debt and other analyses show student borrowing climbed for the Class of 2012, with 71 percent of 2011–12 bachelor’s graduates holding loans and the average borrower owing about $29,400—up from $26,600 for 2011 graduates. The Institute for College Access and Success (TICAS) derived its figures from an annual survey of over 1,000 colleges plus a federal quadrennial survey, and notes the rise reflects rising tuition combined with stagnant family incomes after the recession. Fewer parental resources mean students borrow more; parents covered 27 percent of college costs in a recent Sallie Mae study, down from 37 percent in 2010. The weak job market also makes repayment harder for new graduates.

For-profit colleges, which award roughly 6 percent of bachelor’s degrees, skew the averages upward because their students borrow more and at higher rates; excluding those schools lowers the share with debt and the average balance. TICAS published college-by-college data online: some private schools (e.g., Anna Maria and Wheelock Colleges) reported over 80 percent of graduates with loans and average debts near $49,000; other small colleges showed over 90 percent borrowing. State variation is notable—Delaware graduates had the highest average debt (~$33,649), while South Dakota had the highest incidence of indebted graduates (78%).

Policy attention is increasing: the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau will extend oversight to large loan servicers, addressing problems borrowers face when seeking repayment changes. About one-fifth of students hold private loans, which are often harder to manage and less flexible than federal loans.

Robin Lee, a 45-year-old Islington artist, was arrested on 10 July after being challenged for plugging his iPhone into a socket on a London Overground train. A police community support officer (PCSO) confronted him between Hackney Wick and Camden Road, accusing him of “abstracting electricity,” an offence under section 13 of the Theft Act 1968 that can carry up to five years’ custody. Lee says he was incredulous, calling the intervention “overzealous” and “ridiculous.” He was handcuffed, taken to a British Transport Police (BTP) station on Caledonian Road, then de-arrested for abstracting electricity but later re-arrested for “unacceptable behaviour” after allegedly becoming aggressive when objecting to his initial arrest. BTP said a decision on further action would follow and that he has been reported for the unacceptable behaviour offence. Overground sockets are labelled “cleaners use only,” and forum users note they’re intended for depot cleaning equipment; plugging consumer devices risks power surges and potential damage. The small amount of electricity involved would cost under £1 a year to charge a phone, and the custody photos Lee posted on Twitter were later deleted.

University of Virginia second-year student Hannah Graham, 18, has been missing since late Friday/early Saturday morning, September 13. Charlottesville police released surveillance video showing Graham on the downtown mall around 1:06–1:08 a.m., with an unidentified white male following her and, according to that man, a second man intervening. Investigators are now seeking a person of interest described as a Black male, about 5'10"–5'11", 250–285 pounds, late 20s–early 30s, close-shaved head, goatee, slight “beer belly,” wearing black jeans and a white T-shirt. Police canvassed downtown businesses and banks for more video, expanded searches east toward the Rivanna River and north on East High Street, and found no phone, shoes, or other items. A $50,000 reward is offered. Authorities and agencies will coordinate community searches Sept. 20–21; volunteers must sign up. A candlelight vigil is planned at the UVA Amphitheater. Anyone with information should call the tip line at 434-295-3851.

The U.S.-China Internet Industry Forum at Microsoft’s Redmond campus brought together an unprecedented constellation of tech power: Apple’s Tim Cook, Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Facebook’s Mark Zuckerberg, Alibaba’s Jack Ma, and dozens more—including leading executives from Baidu, Tencent, LinkedIn, Intel, IBM, Airbnb, Qualcomm and others—met Chinese President Xi Jinping and his delegation, including internet regulator Lu Wei. The visit concluded a broader Seattle-area itinerary in which Xi toured Boeing and Microsoft and later planned to meet President Obama in Washington, D.C.

Xi toured Microsoft’s executive building, saw demos of HoloLens and data-visualization tools, and then greeted CEOs for a staged group photo and brief remarks. In a short six-minute address he emphasized mutual respect, cooperation on cybersecurity, and balancing national policies with global internet development: China offers the largest internet market, while the U.S. has leading internet technologies. Xi framed cooperation as a way to ensure cyberspace benefits people in both countries and worldwide.

Mark Zuckerberg highlighted his brief conversation with Xi—speaking in Mandarin—as a personal milestone and posted about the encounter, which drew debate given Facebook’s block in China and past gestures perceived as courting Beijing. Observers noted the symbolism: the gathering illustrated the enormous commercial and diplomatic allure of China’s market and the willingness of major Western tech leaders to engage directly with Beijing despite tensions over censorship, intellectual property and cybersecurity. The meeting underscored both opportunity and friction in U.S.-China tech relations.

The United States has ordered the closure of three Russian diplomatic facilities — the Consulate General in San Francisco, a chancery annex in Washington, D.C., and a consular annex in New York City — in response to Russia’s earlier forced reductions of U.S. diplomatic staff in Moscow. The State Department framed the move as restoring “parity” after Moscow compelled the U.S. to cut 755 personnel this year as retaliation for American sanctions. Spokesperson Heather Nauert and Secretary of State Rex Tillerson signaled the closures are a measured reciprocal step; the Russian sites must shut by September 2.

U.S. officials say they fully implemented Russia’s demand to downsize the U.S. mission in Russia but view Moscow’s action as unwarranted and harmful to bilateral relations. By requiring the three Russian facilities to close while allowing some annexes to remain, the United States intends to mirror the number of consulates each country maintains — three apiece — even though a disparity in annexes will persist. The State Department emphasized the closure decision aims to halt further deterioration in ties and leave room for improved relations and cooperation where possible, reflecting stated goals of both presidents. At the same time, Washington warned it remains prepared to take additional measures if necessary. The step marks a further tightening of diplomatic relations between the two countries amid ongoing sanctions and mutual retaliatory actions.

At the G20 in Hamburg, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin held their first in-person meeting, a highly anticipated encounter overshadowed by tensions over Syria, Ukraine and allegations of Russian interference in the 2016 US election. The private, extended meeting—attended only by the two presidents, their foreign ministers and translators—limited leaks and excluded skeptical advisers, a dynamic the Guardian’s Shaun Walker suggests favored Putin. While election hacking was raised, neither side made it central; Tillerson said Trump focused on “how do we move forward,” and Lavrov claimed Trump accepted Putin’s denials. A working group on non-interference was reportedly agreed but may offer little reassurance in Washington. The talks coincided with a US-Russia ceasefire announcement in southwestern Syria. Trump’s preparation and stance were scrutinized amid ongoing US investigations into Russia, congressional concerns about returning seized diplomatic properties, and broader strategic priorities including North Korea.

Belinda Stuckey, a 35-year-old primary school teacher from Sydney, has become an unlikely emblem of online dating frustration: since joining eHarmony in December 2013 she’s accumulated about 4,700 matches and gone on roughly 136 first dates across about two years, yet has never been asked for—or offered—a second date. One of the site’s most contacted members in Australia, Stuckey receives around ten matches a day but declines about 80% of them, choosing to meet only those she finds promising. She credits her popularity to an honest profile that clearly states who she is and what she’s looking for, saying there’s no point pretending to be someone else. Despite the long string of one-offs, Stuckey remains upbeat and resilient: she questions what she might have done wrong after no follow-up contact, but keeps a “thick skin,” takes rejection with a grain of salt, and maintains hope that the right partner is out there. Having entered online dating after leaving a four-year relationship, she frames her standards as confidence in her own worth—she won’t compromise on someone “worthy of my time and attention.” Though baffling to some, her experience highlights the odd, often impersonal nature of modern dating and her determined refusal to give up on finding a meaningful match.

Warren Buffett’s latest annual letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders emphasizes both optimism about America and a renewed push to deploy the conglomerate’s cash. A year after the $26 billion Burlington Northern Santa Fe purchase, Buffett says Berkshire is hunting for more large acquisitions — “Our elephant gun has been reloaded, and my trigger finger is itchy.” He praises U.S. opportunity, reports $13 billion net income (up 61% from 2009) and a 13% book-value rise, and notes substantial U.S. capital spending. Buffett highlights Berkshire’s thrift, the strategic shift toward wholly owned businesses, and the growing importance of operating companies alongside its investment portfolio. Burlington Northern boosted Berkshire’s earnings power by over 30% and exemplifies deals that let Berkshire absorb large sums at once; yet the firm still holds about $38 billion in cash. Succession details remain vague, though he lauds executives Ajit Jain and new hire Todd Combs. Buffett also critiques hedge funds’ compensation and reiterates Berkshire’s readiness to spend on infrastructure and acquisitions when the right opportunities arise.

Solar Impulse 2, a solar-powered aircraft, completed a record-setting trans-Pacific leg when Swiss pilot André Borschberg landed in Hawaii after an arduous nearly five-day nonstop flight from Nagoya, Japan. The 4,000-mile (about 5,079-mile/8,200 km) crossing was the eighth leg of the plane’s round-the-world campaign and set new records for the longest solo flight by time and the longest flight solely powered by solar energy. Borschberg departed Japan at 3am and spent roughly 4 days, 21 hours and 51 minutes in the cramped cockpit, resting only in short 20-minute naps and enduring temperatures near 37°C. To conserve energy, the single-seater climbs to about 9,000 meters by day to recharge its batteries via 17,000 photovoltaic cells and then glides lower and slower at night. The mission, shared with co-pilot Bertrand Piccard who will next pilot the aircraft to Phoenix on a planned 100-hour leg, faced multiple delays from bad weather and the constant challenge of finding clear skies to replenish solar charge. Beyond breaking records, the Solar Impulse team emphasizes demonstrating renewable technologies’ potential to reduce CO2 emissions while advancing aviation endurance and energy management techniques. The flight continued the project’s wider educational and environmental goals.

Authorities responded to a workplace shooting at about 9:06 a.m. Thursday at the Rite Aid distribution campus on Perryman Road in Harford County, Maryland. Deputies and allied agencies arrived within five minutes; the FBI, DEA, ATF and state and local police assisted. Officials said a lone suspect, reportedly a woman, was taken into custody and transported to a hospital in critical condition. Law enforcement confirmed a single handgun was used and that no officers fired. Preliminary reports indicate multiple fatalities and wounded—AP said three killed—with fewer than 10 victims overall. Several wounded were taken to Johns Hopkins Bayview and one to Christiana Hospital; families were being notified and a reunification center was established in Havre de Grace. Schools were placed on modified lockdown and roads closed; residents were urged to avoid the area. Harford leaders praised first responders, asked anyone still inside the facility to call 911, and cautioned that details remain preliminary as the investigation continues.

Kristine Bunch, imprisoned since 1996 for allegedly setting a fire that killed her 3-year-old son Tony, was released in 2012 after the Indiana Court of Appeals granted her a new trial based on new evidence. Bunch, convicted at 22 and sentenced to 60 years, always maintained her innocence. The Northwestern University Center on Wrongful Convictions (CWC) and pro bono counsel uncovered advances in fire science and raw laboratory data suggesting investigators’ original conclusions were flawed. Attorneys argued that tests showed Tony died of carbon monoxide poisoning rather than burns from an accelerant-fueled blaze as prosecutors maintained; had an accelerant been used as alleged, death would likely have been from burns. The team also identified possible alterations or misinterpretations in ATF lab results that had supported the arson finding. Based on these revelations, a three-judge panel reversed her conviction and the state ultimately declined to retry her. Bunch walked free after more than 16 years behind bars, reuniting with family and her teenage son Trenton for the first time outside prison.

Her case illustrates broader patterns the CWC’s Women’s Project has identified: wrongfully convicted women often face different challenges than men. Women are more frequently accused of harming those in their care; DNA rarely exonerates them because domestic crimes seldom leave useful genetic evidence. Many convictions of women involve accidental deaths misclassified as homicides or rely on flawed forensic science (arson indicators, shaken-baby diagnoses). Gendered stereotypes about motives and maternal behavior also influence prosecutions and jury perceptions. Recognizing these patterns, Northwestern’s Women’s Project targets cases requiring complex technical expertise and challenges to forensic evidence, acknowledging that exonerating women often demands different tools and long, resource-intensive investigations. Bunch, now engaged with the project and pursuing education and advocacy, hopes to help others who suffered similar injustices while coping with the lasting emotional scars of wrongful conviction.

Zimbabwe’s 93-year-old President Robert Mugabe has been repeatedly photographed with his eyes closed during public events, prompting speculation about his fitness ahead of next year’s elections. His spokesman, George Charamba, insists Mugabe is merely resting because he is sensitive to bright lights and is receiving specialised eye treatment in Singapore. Charamba compared Mugabe’s condition to Nelson Mandela’s documented light sensitivity and said reports that the president is asleep make him “very, very pained.” Critics point to a long history of similar images dating back more than a decade and cite concerns over Mugabe’s ability to govern as Zimbabwe’s economy struggles and citizens face bank crises. Mugabe rejects claims Zimbabwe is fragile, calling it “one of the most highly developed countries in Africa.”

Multiple companies are racing to turn Elon Musk’s Hyperloop idea—pods traveling in low-pressure tubes at near-supersonic speeds—into reality, but progress mixes promising technical demos with major practical concerns. Hyperloop Transportation Technologies (HTT) announced it will license a passive magnetic-levitation system from Lawrence Livermore, which levitates pods via magnets interacting with coils in the tube, eliminating powered track infrastructure and allowing pods to remain levitated during power loss until low speeds. HTT argues this reduces cost and improves safety. Rival Hyperloop One (formerly Hyperloop Technologies/HTI) successfully demonstrated a linear induction propulsion sled in Nevada, reaching roughly 115 mph and showing 2.4 g acceleration; future tests aim for higher speeds and full pod capabilities. Teams including MIT, SkyTran, and crowd-sourced groups like rLoop (which made a Break-a-Pod game) are also developing pods and prototypes. Yet skepticism abounds: critics cite passenger comfort (high accelerations and turns could induce nausea), safety, regulatory hurdles, enormous infrastructure and land-rights challenges, environmental reviews, and high cost estimates (billions for long routes). While technical building blocks—maglev principles, propulsion, regenerative braking—are advancing, analysts stress that bureaucratic, physiological, and funding obstacles may be the largest barriers before Hyperloop becomes a practical transport option.

Militants claiming to have abducted a British aid worker in Kunar province, Afghanistan, say they will demand the release of Pakistani neuroscientist Aafia Siddiqui in exchange. The unnamed Scottish woman, in her 30s and thought to work for U.S. charity Development Alternatives International on a USAID-funded agricultural project, was travelling with three Afghan colleagues when gunmen stopped their convoy en route to a canal opening near Jalalabad. A local commander, Mohammed Osman, claimed responsibility, linking the abduction to outrage over Siddiqui’s recent 86-year U.S. prison sentence for the attempted murder of U.S. agents. Afghan police, tribal elders and international agencies are conducting searches; the British embassy declined comment. The incident follows the fatal ambush of British doctor Karen Woo last month and echoes earlier kidnappings in Taliban-held areas. Siddiqui’s case has provoked protests in Pakistan, where politicians and many citizens have called for her repatriation.

Puerto Rico senator Roberto Arango, a prominent GOP supporter who once vice-chaired George W. Bush’s 2004 Puerto Rico campaign, was recently implicated in a social-media scandal after images allegedly from his Grindr profile surfaced. When a Puerto Rican TV program pressed him about the photos, Arango offered an evasive, flippant response that neither confirmed nor denied authorship: he claimed to be losing weight, taking many photos, and not recalling whether he had taken the specific picture in question. His remarks were laced with absurdist humor and self-parody—mock explanations about mistaking Grindr for a fitness community and exaggerated commentary about toning intimate areas—rather than a straightforward denial or apology. The exchange drew attention because it combined a public official’s apparent involvement with a gay hook-up app and a deflective, unserious reaction to being confronted on camera. The episode quickly circulated in Puerto Rican media and online, prompting scrutiny of Arango’s conduct and public image. Observers noted the contrast between his political standing and the incongruous, awkward nature of his response to the allegations.

As 2016 ended, timekeepers announced an extra leap second would be added to compensate for the gradual, irregular slowing of Earth’s rotation. The International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (IERS) declared that Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) would include an extra tick at 23:59:60 on 31 December 2016 so astronomical time (UT1), based on Earth’s rotation, stays within 0.9 seconds of atomic time (UTC). Atomic time (TAI) is maintained by nearly 400 cesium clocks worldwide and is currently dozens of seconds ahead of UTC; the gap grows as leap seconds are added. Leap seconds have been implemented since 1972 and typically occur at the end of June or December when IERS measures UTC leading UT1 by about 0.4 seconds or more.

While leap seconds preserve alignment between clock time and celestial motion, they can disrupt computer systems, data logging, telecommunications, and time-distribution services because many systems cannot represent a 61st second. To reduce risk, several large internet and cloud providers apply a “leap smear”—gradually adjusting their clocks around the event so the extra second is spread over hours instead of inserted instantaneously. Google, for example, used a 20-hour smear (10 hours before and after) running clocks 0.0014% slower; others like Amazon and Akamai have used 24-hour smears. Google offered its public NTP servers to help enterprises synchronize to its smeared time and has advocated for a standardized approach.

Debate continues about the long-term future of leap seconds; proposals include switching to less frequent larger corrections (leap hours) or stopping corrections altogether and publishing UT1 offsets for those who need precise astronomical time.

Bradley Cooper directs, co-wrote, and stars in a new remake of A Star Is Born, opening October 5, which pairs him opposite Lady Gaga in her feature-film debut. He plays Jackson Maine, a washed-up country singer battling alcoholism who discovers and falls for shy, self-doubting singer Ally (Gaga). The trailer follows their meeting, his encouragement of her talent, and the strain as her star rises while his life unravels. Cooper performs live on camera, and much of the soundtrack is original music co-written by Cooper and Gaga with collaborators such as Lukas Nelson, Jason Isbell, and Mark Ronson, recorded live. The supporting cast includes Sam Elliott, Dave Chappelle, and Andrew Dice Clay.

A newly discovered bug can permanently disable certain iPhones and iPads if their system date is manually set to January 1, 1970. Reports and demonstrations show devices with 64-bit processors — including iPhone 5S and later, iPad Air, iPad mini 2 and later, and newer iPod Touch models — become unbootable after being set to that date. Affected units power on to the Apple logo but never complete startup; attempts to restore or update via iTunes fail, and connecting to a computer does not revive the device. Accounts surfaced on forums and social sites after a 4chan post, and a video from 9to5Mac illustrated the problem. One user reported trying shutdown, restart, restore and update with no success. The bug appears tied to Unix time: January 1, 1970 is the zero point for Unix timestamp systems, and forcing that value on iOS seems to create a conflict that “bricks” affected hardware. Apple had not commented on the issue at the time of reporting; fixes reportedly require an Apple Store visit and are likely to result in replacement devices. The incident echoes prior time-related glitches seen on other platforms and highlights risks from tinkering with low-level system settings.

Volkswagen’s US CEO Michael Horn publicly admitted the company “totally screwed up,” acknowledging VW had been dishonest with regulators and the public after US authorities found software that cheated diesel emissions tests. The Environmental Protection Agency says the “defeat device” allowed affected Audi and VW models — including the A3, Jetta, Beetle, Golf and Passat — to show low nitrogen oxide (NOx) output during lab tests while emitting up to 40 times more pollution on the road. The US ordered a recall of about 482,000 vehicles and potential fines could reach $18 billion; criminal probes and shareholder and consumer litigation are also possible. Shares plunged, wiping billions from VW’s market value.

Governments and regulators reacted swiftly: France’s finance minister urged a Europe-wide investigation to reassure the public, and South Korea launched probes of recent Golf, Jetta, Beetle and Audi A3 imports, warning of fines and expanded checks if problems are found. US Congress and the Department of Justice have opened inquiries. VW’s CEO Martin Winterkorn apologized and ordered an external investigation. Experts warn the issue could extend beyond VW, other manufacturers, and diesel to broader emissions and testing practices. Critics say European testing regimes are more vulnerable to manipulation than US independent testing, and industry representatives concede current tests are outdated and need reform to reflect real-world conditions.

Rapper Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson filed court papers in Connecticut revealing detailed finances after declaring bankruptcy following a $7 million jury judgment ordering him to pay Lastonia Leviston over an allegedly posted sex tape. His filing lists $25 million in assets—including an $8 million Connecticut mansion, a $572,000 Long Island home, an Atlanta property, roughly $10 million in cash and about $500,000 in vehicles (three Chevy Suburbans and a 2010 Rolls‑Royce)—but $33 million in liabilities, leaving him reportedly underwater. Major debts include the $7 million judgment and an $18 million claim from electronics company Sleek Audio stemming from a failed headphone deal. The documents show monthly income of about $185,000–$3 million annually from music, plus additional earnings: roughly $370,000 from his boxing promotions company SMS Promotions and about $771,000 from books, films, touring and G‑Unit enterprises. Monthly expenses are listed near $108,000, covering $72,000 to maintain his suburban Hartford mansion, $5,000 for gardening, a $5,745 Bentley lease, $12,000 in child support, and payments to a stylist, barber and fitness coach. The filing also notes significant recent credit card and stylist payments. Jackson is due back in bankruptcy court soon; his representatives did not respond to requests for comment.

House Budget Chairman Paul Ryan, long criticized for proposing to privatize Medicare, unveiled a revised approach developed with Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden that preserves traditional, government-run Medicare as an option for future retirees while adding competing private plans. Like Ryan’s earlier “premium support” idea, the plan would give beneficiaries a government subsidy to buy coverage, but unlike his original proposal the subsidy would track actual policy costs and rise modestly with the economy—offering more protection for seniors though likely reducing projected federal savings. The blueprint, influenced by Alice Rivlin and Pete Domenici, would take effect for new retirees in 2022, add catastrophic coverage with out-of-pocket caps, and rely on insurer competition to control costs. Ryan and Wyden stress the proposal maintains the Medicare guarantee and seek bipartisan consensus, though they won’t draft legislation before the next Congress.

A joint investigation by the Boulder Daily Camera and KUSA/9News has reexamined the DNA evidence that former Boulder District Attorney Mary Lacy relied on when she publicly exonerated JonBenet Ramsey’s family in 2008. Independent forensic experts who reviewed laboratory reports and raw test results obtained by the news organizations conclude those DNA findings do not convincingly support Lacy’s declaration. Key points: the male DNA profile long cited as “Unknown Male 1”—initially developed from trace material on JonBenet’s underwear—may be a composite mixture rather than a single individual’s profile. Tests on two areas of JonBenet’s long johns returned mixtures indicating DNA from JonBenet, the previously identified male profile, and at least one additional unidentified contributor; Bode Technology analysts warned the mixtures “should not be considered a single-source profile.” Those caveats were omitted from Lacy’s exoneration letter, which claimed the crotch DNA matched material on the long johns and insisted “there is no innocent explanation” for its presence. Independent experts dispute that, noting the samples were minute and potentially transferable through innocuous contact or secondary transfer, and that the profile’s complexity and low quantity undermine reproducibility and CODIS matching. The revelation that a third person’s markers may be present has not been publicly disclosed before and raises questions about using that profile to clear dozens of suspects. Critics say Lacy displayed confirmation bias, failing to pursue additional testing or legal steps such as a John Doe warrant. Authorities acknowledge DNA technology has advanced since 2008—Y-STR testing could help isolate male contributors—and some officials urge renewed testing and review. Overall, experts call the DNA evidence indeterminate: it neither proves an intruder theory nor definitively exonerates family members, and should be treated as one investigative thread among many rather than a “silver bullet.”

The discovery of Laci and her unborn son Conner’s bodies in April 2003 marked a pivotal shift in the investigation of Laci’s disappearance and intensified scrutiny on her husband, Scott Peterson. He was arrested days after the bodies were found, convicted in 2004, and sentenced to death—though he continues to appeal. The case’s narrative remains sharply contested, a divide explored in two television specials: A&E’s The Murder of Laci Peterson and ABC’s Truth and Lies: The Murder of Laci Peterson.

An exclusive clip from the A&E series highlights conflicting recollections of Scott’s reaction when detectives told him the bodies had been recovered. Retired Modesto detective Jon Buehler recalls that Scott showed “very little reaction,” portraying him as emotionally flat in a way Buehler found consistent with guilt. Buehler has previously described Scott’s response as almost contrived—asking, “Is that my wife and son?” and then offering what Buehler mimicked as “fake sniffles.” Scott, speaking from death row in audio included in the episode, disputes that account, saying he experienced a “terrible physical reaction” but stifled it in front of detectives because he didn’t want them to see his emotion.

ABC’s special focuses more on the family’s perspective, especially Laci’s mother, Sharon Rocha, who describes the agonizing doubt about suspecting a family member. She recounts her last memory of Laci — sitting together watching TV when Laci mentioned the baby had kicked and confided that Scott rarely wanted to touch her pregnant stomach — a remark that later haunted Rocha. The ABC program includes new interviews, never-before-seen home video, and archival interviews with Scott and his parents.

Prosecutors’ largely circumstantial case emphasized Scott’s affair with Amber Frey, his behavior and movements around the disappearance, and physical evidence linking the bodies’ recovery location and condition to his alleged actions. Laci’s family maintains he is guilty; Scott and his supporters maintain his innocence. His legal team continues to seek a new trial, alleging defense failures and juror misconduct, while the California Attorney General defends the conviction as supported by overwhelming evidence. The two specials air in September, revisiting the case’s unresolved questions and enduring controversies.

European Union foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton met late Monday with deposed Egyptian president Mohamed Morsi, marking the first contact Morsi has had with an independent official since his July 3 removal and nearly a month of military custody. Ashton spent about two hours with Morsi at an undisclosed location and afterward told reporters he was well, had access to television and newspapers, and that she had ensured his family knew he was in good condition. She declined to discuss details of their “friendly and open” conversation and denied offering him a “safe exit.” The visit came two days after violent clashes that left about 80 pro‑Morsi demonstrators and a police officer dead and amid prosecutors’ investigations into Morsi on espionage and murder allegations that his supporters call politically motivated. Ashton also met Egypt’s interim Vice President Mohamed ElBaradei, military chief Gen. Abdel Fattah al‑Sisi, liberal politicians, hard‑line Islamists, and Muslim Brotherhood representatives. ElBaradei said the Brotherhood should be included in a political roadmap despite viewing Morsi’s year in power as a failure. Ashton said the EU seeks to help Egyptians find a democratic path and urged inclusive dialogue, while U.S. officials called for restraint and reconciliation.

A 22-year-old Salvadoran woman known as Beatriz, who suffers from lupus and kidney failure, underwent a Caesarean section at 27 weeks after being denied a medical abortion under El Salvador’s strict laws that ban abortion in all cases. Ultrasounds showed the fetus had anencephaly—developing only a brain stem and with little chance of survival. El Salvador’s Supreme Court had rejected her lawyers’ appeal, saying her conditions were controlled, while the Inter-American Court on Human Rights urged action to protect her life. The Health Ministry authorized the C-section to save the mother without formally performing an abortion; the baby was born without a brain and died several hours later. Officials said Beatriz was stable and recovering. The case drew international attention and intensified debate over El Salvador’s absolute abortion ban.

Russian and Chinese naval drills in the Baltic this year were deliberately modest, officials and analysts say, reflecting limited strategic aims rather than a major escalation. Maxim Shepovalenko, a former Russian navy captain and analyst at CAST, described the Russian contribution as “merely symbolic,” arguing Moscow saw no need for a large-scale Baltic exercise and that China used the event to gain experience operating at greater distances. The week-long Joint Sea maneuvers, commanded by Russian Vice Admiral Alexander Fedotenkov and Chinese Vice-Admiral Tian Zhong, include anti-submarine, anti-aircraft and anti-ship drills, plus anti-piracy and search-and-rescue training; the Baltic Fleet’s press service said the exercises are conducted in Russian. China’s naval expansion—including a new overseas base in Djibouti—and recent joint drills by the U.S. with India and Japan in the Indian Ocean have framed the Baltic exercises as a Chinese show of growing reach. Meanwhile, concern persists in eastern Europe about Russia’s much larger planned Zapad 2017 war games in Belarus. U.S. Army Lt. Gen. Ben Hodges warned allies worry the exercises could become a “Trojan horse” for leaving equipment in Belarus, and urged greater Russian transparency. Moscow rejected such accusations, calling Western alarmism politically motivated. NATO remains wary because past Russian drills have featured tactics later used in Crimea, eastern Ukraine and Syria; allies are watching troop numbers, adherence to Vienna Document observer rules and whether exercises involve long-range systems or nuclear training.

Gracelyn Mae Violet Griffin’s arrival was anything but ordinary: her birth certificate even lists her location as “Born in Chick-fil-A,” and her father, Robert Griffin, who is not a doctor, is recorded as the attending physician. The unexpected delivery occurred late one Tuesday night when Robert and his wife, Falon—38 weeks pregnant—were driving to University Hospital and stopped at the Stone Ridge Chick-fil-A in far north San Antonio because Falon needed a restroom. The restaurant was closed, but employees finishing up for the night let them inside.

What began as a hurried bathroom break turned urgent when Falon began screaming as labor progressed. With an ambulance too slow to arrive, Robert rushed in and found their daughter crowning. He coached Falon through the delivery, who was straddling the toilet and essentially standing while giving birth. As the baby’s shoulders emerged, Robert discovered the umbilical cord wrapped twice around the newborn’s neck; he carefully unwound it so Gracelyn could breathe. The entire ordeal took about six minutes. Robert wrapped the newborn in his “Trump 2020” T-shirt before paramedics arrived, a detail he later noted with pride on social media.

Chick-fil-A employees, some in their early twenties, acted quickly—calling 911, assisting until help arrived and providing emotional support. The franchise owner later announced Gracelyn will receive free Chick-fil-A for life and a guaranteed job at 16, and staff are planning a chicken-nugget-themed first birthday. The Griffins, who already liked the restaurant, had bought their daughter a “Little Nugget” onesie before her birth. Robert’s viral Facebook post has drawn tens of thousands of reactions and comments, and the family says the episode forged a lasting friendship with the employees who helped deliver their baby.

Adam Seger, formerly director of restaurants at Louisville’s Seelbach Hotel, has admitted that the widely told origin of the Seelbach Cocktail was a fabrication he created as a promotional stunt. Long touted as a rescued pre-Prohibition bourbon-and-champagne signature from the storied hotel—linked to F. Scott Fitzgerald and The Great Gatsby—the drink became widely accepted after Seger, who took over the hotel bar in 1995, claimed he’d discovered the old recipe and restored it to the menu. He said an Irish hotel school intern had found the recipe and that a tale about a Rathskeller bartender catching overflowing champagne with a Manhattan explained its invention. That narrative was repeated in a 1997 Courier-Journal piece and later included in cocktail books such as New Classic Cocktails and Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails, helping the Seelbach Cocktail spread onto menus worldwide. In a recent New York Times piece, Seger acknowledged he made up the backstory and crafted the drink himself to give the hotel a signature cocktail and boost his profile. Authors and journalists who published the story—some admitting suspicion but accepting the account—never requested verification like seeing an old menu. Despite Seger’s confession, the Seelbach Hilton plans to keep the Seelbach Cocktail on its menu, with hotel officials calling it a tradition that will remain part of the hotel’s identity. The recipe commonly attributed to the hotel combines Old Forester bourbon, triple sec, bitters and Korbel Brut.

This text promotes fast, short-term cash loans—commonly called payday or emergency loans—arguing they can quickly cover unexpected expenses like medical bills, utilities, car repairs, rent, or small celebrations. It emphasizes speedy, often paperless, online application processes with minimal documentation and sometimes no credit check, reassuring applicants that past credit problems won’t block approval. Typical loan amounts mentioned range from roughly 80 to 1,500 (currency unspecified) with very short terms—often one to four weeks—or longer installment options repaid via monthly payments with added interest. The piece warns that emergency borrowing carries costs: fees and rapidly accruing interest that can worsen future finances, and it recommends savings as a cheaper alternative when possible. It also lists basic UK lender requirements—being 18+, a permanent resident, employed with a recent bank account—and encourages prompt application through lender websites.

Dennis Prager argues that saying "Merry Christmas" is appropriate for all Americans, including religious Jews like himself. He notes that nine in ten Americans celebrate Christmas and asserts the holiday functions as both a Christian holy day and a national American holiday—comparable to Thanksgiving or the Fourth of July. Prager highlights Jewish contributions to Christmas culture—famous songs and traditions written by Jewish composers—and recounts his Orthodox family's practice of enjoying the season, including watching the Vatican Mass. He criticizes efforts to remove Christmas from public life, attributing them to left-wing multiculturalism and secularization from the 1960s and ’70s, and sees the replacement of "Merry Christmas" with "Happy Holidays" and altered school performances as symptomatic of an anti-Christmas trend. Prager also states that many who push to exclude Christmas are non-religious Jews motivated by leftism or resentment toward Christianity.

Complementing Prager’s piece, a lighter essay defends Jewish participation in Christmas festivities. It argues cultural Christmas elements—trees, Santa, songs—are largely secular and widely embraced by American Jews. The essay cites Pew data showing many Jewish households have Christmas trees and highlights Jewish creators of Christmas entertainment. It acknowledges boundaries: celebrating Christ’s divinity would cross a line for Jews, but enjoying seasonal customs does not. It concludes by encouraging Jews who feel inclined to join in seasonal cheer and wishes everyone a Merry Christmas.

Rescue teams searched the Java Sea after AirAsia Indonesia Flight 8501 vanished Sunday en route from Surabaya to Singapore with 162 people aboard. The Airbus A320 disappeared from radar about halfway into the flight between Belitung and Borneo; last contact was at 06:12 local time when the pilot requested to turn left and climb to 38,000 feet to avoid clouds. Radar contact was lost minutes later without a distress call. Authorities said weather—heavy thunderstorms in the area—was likely a factor and hampered search efforts with large waves and cloud cover.

Search-and-rescue operations led by Indonesia expanded to 13 zones across roughly 156,000 square kilometers. More than 1,100 personnel from Indonesia, Australia, Singapore, Malaysia, South Korea, Japan, New Zealand and others joined the effort; ships, aircraft and helicopters scoured the sea for debris. Multiple possible leads—an oil slick, faint pings, objects in the water, and smoke spotted on an island—were investigated but not yet confirmed as linked to the plane. Officials said the plane likely lies on the sea bottom based on its last known track, and teams hope to recover flight data and cockpit voice recorders, whose homing beacons assist locating wreckage.

Investigators are considering several explanations: severe weather and turbulence, potential pilot error, catastrophic structural failure or rare metal fatigue (though the six-year-old aircraft’s age makes that less likely), and remote possibilities like deliberate action—none proven. Questions arose about whether the crew climbed without ATC permission after a denied altitude increase due to traffic. AirAsia—operated by an Indonesian affiliate of the Malaysian carrier—has had a good safety record until now. The disappearance comes months after Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 and the downing of MH17, but authorities stress the incidents are unrelated; the region’s rapid aviation growth and busy airspace complicate operations and heighten public concern. Families of victims received briefings and will be flown over the search area; identification preparations are underway.

Morley Safer, the Canadian-born journalist who became a defining voice of 60 Minutes, died at 84. Hired by CBS in 1964, he reported from Saigon, filmed the controversial 1965 Cam Ne report showing Marines burning huts, and helped shape broadcast journalism. Safer joined 60 Minutes in 1970 and spent 46 years there, producing more than 900 pieces that ranged from tough investigations—such as the Lenell Geter segment that overturned a wrongful conviction—to cultural profiles and quirky travel features. Renowned for his elegant writing, wit and storytelling, he won numerous awards, including Emmys, Peabodys and duPont-Columbia honors. He is survived by his wife Jane, their daughter Sarah, three grandchildren, and siblings. Funeral arrangements are private; a memorial will be announced later.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture has approved J.R. Simplot Co.’s genetically modified “Innate” potato for commercial planting, but major buyer McDonald’s says it will not source GMO potatoes. Simplot engineered the Innate potato to produce less acrylamide—a chemical formed when potatoes are cooked at high temperatures and suspected to be carcinogenic—and to resist bruising. Simplot, a longtime supplier of fries and other potato products to restaurants, planted 400 test acres this fall and says wider production won’t scale up until after the 2015 harvest. The company predicts the fresh potato market and consumers will welcome reduced sugars and fewer potential carcinogens, but it has not confirmed plans to sell to fast-food or dehydrated potato industries, which have cautioned growers against planting GMO varieties. Some growers, like Rupert farmer Duane Grant, hope to find buyers attracted by higher yields from reduced bruising, but acknowledge food industry buyers fear consumer backlash and value brand equity. Food & Water Watch praised McDonald’s decision as a victory for consumers and urged other chains to follow suit, noting strong public opposition reflected in more than 90,000 petitions asking McDonald’s to reject GMO potatoes.

A rapidly expanding sinkhole in Land O’ Lakes, Florida, swallowed a boat, destroyed two homes and forced voluntary evacuations of 10 neighboring residences on July 14, 2017. Emergency crews responded shortly after 7:30 a.m. to a report of a “depression” beneath a backyard boat in Lake Padgett Estates; within minutes the ground gave way. Dramatic video showed one house collapsing into the chasm as the hole quickly grew to roughly 200 feet (60 meters) across—about two-thirds of a football field—and about 50 feet (15 meters) deep. Firefighters rescued two dogs and retrieved some belongings before the first house fell, and by early afternoon the adjacent home had also been destroyed. No injuries were reported.

Pasco County officials noted the property where the first house was lost had experienced a sinkhole in 2012 that was reportedly stabilized; the house sold in 2015. County procedure for stabilizing sinkholes can include boring into the ground and injecting concrete. Ten nearby homes were declared unsafe and residents were asked to leave voluntarily; firefighters and deputies assisted occupants in recovering items. Duke Energy shut power to about 100 homes in the area, and the American Red Cross is aiding displaced residents. Pasco County Fire Chief Shawn Whited and assistant county administrator Kevin Guthrie described the scene as frightening for those evacuated, emphasizing the sudden, destructive power of natural ground collapse. Authorities continue to monitor the site and support affected families.

About two months after Hurricane Harvey struck Texas, 31-year-old Josue Zurita died from necrotizing fasciitis, a rare but rapidly progressing flesh-eating bacterial infection, the Galveston County Health District announced. Zurita, a carpenter who had emigrated from Oaxaca, Mexico, to support his family, was helping repair homes damaged by Harvey when he sought hospital care on October 10 for a severely infected wound on his upper left arm. He died six days later. Local reports and his obituary describe him as a devoted father and hardworking man who remained to assist with post-Harvey rebuilding efforts.

Health officials believe the infection likely entered Zurita’s body through a cut or wound exposed to floodwater or hurricane debris. Galveston County health authority Dr. Philip Keiser noted the infection’s danger: it can spread over hours, traveling between skin and muscle, destroying tissue, nerves and blood vessels. Necrotizing fasciitis is uncommon—CDC estimates about 700–1,100 U.S. cases annually—but the post-storm environment, with widespread wounds, debris and water exposure, can increase risk. Zurita’s death follows at least two other Harvey-related cases: a 77-year-old woman, Nancy Reed, who died in September, and J.R. Atkins, a former first responder who survived after contracting a similar infection while checking on neighbors.

Officials emphasize prevention through prompt and proper wound care: keep open wounds clean and covered, avoid contact with natural bodies of water when injured, treat minor wounds promptly, wash hands, stay current on tetanus vaccines, and seek immediate medical attention for redness, swelling or fever.

Ford announced a $1 billion, five-year majority investment in Argo AI, a previously secret Pittsburgh-based startup founded by former Google self-driving lead Bryan Salesky and ex-Uber engineer Peter Rander. Ford frames the deal as an investment rather than an outright acquisition, but will treat Argo AI as a subsidiary while granting it operational independence and the ability to offer equity to attract talent. Argo AI will focus exclusively on developing Ford’s “virtual driver” autonomous system, aiming to help Ford deploy a production-ready, SAE Level 4 self-driving vehicle by 2021 and potentially license the software to other automakers or pursue an IPO later. The arrangement transfers some Ford software employees to Argo AI while Ford retains vehicle hardware and systems integration expertise. Ford’s move reflects an industry-wide arms race for scarce talent in machine learning, computer vision, robotics, and related fields, as tech firms and automakers like Waymo, Tesla, GM (Cruise), Uber, and others compete to commercialize self-driving fleets. Argo AI plans offices in Pittsburgh, Michigan, and Silicon Valley and expects roughly 200 staff by year’s end. Ford sees the investment as essential to evolving into a broader mobility company and avoiding disruption by Silicon Valley competitors.

When the wedding of Carol and Willie Fowler’s daughter was cancelled about 40 days before the reception, the Atlanta couple chose an extraordinary response: rather than abandon the nonrefundable venue, catering and entertainment, they donated the entire event to homeless women, children and families. The Fowlers contacted Hosea Feed the Hungry — where their daughter had once volunteered — and partnered with other local shelters to bring 200 guests to Villa Christina for a formal afternoon celebration on Sept. 15.

Organizers initially feared the offer was a prank because the venue and menu were so upscale. But the Fowlers were sincere. Buses transported guests from multiple shelters; children had their own room with face painting, juggling, a clown and crowns, while adults were treated to passed hors d’oeuvres and a four-course plated meal (children ate chicken fingers, fries and fruit; adults had salmon and chicken). Volunteers taught table etiquette — which forks to use and how to behave at a formal setting — turning the event into both a festive and educational experience. An inspirational speaker reminded attendees that “your beginning does not determine your destiny.”

The family renamed the event the “First Annual Fowler Family Celebration of Love,” noting that it coincided with Willie Fowler’s 70th birthday and served as a larger commitment to community service. The couple hopes to make it an annual, multi-day affair with sponsors and added programming. They urge others with cancelled events to consider donating them to charities rather than letting opportunities go to waste, emphasizing the profound emotional impact and lasting memories the gift created for the guests.

At a private GOP donors’ retreat in Park City, Utah, Senate candidate Mitt Romney predicted President Donald Trump will easily secure the 2020 Republican nomination and win reelection, citing a strong economy with rising wages and the prospect that Democrats might nominate an “out of the mainstream” candidate. Romney’s remarks mark a notable softening from his 2016 “con man” indictment of Trump; since launching his Utah Senate bid he has both praised some of Trump’s early actions and criticized his style and truthfulness. Speaking at his annual E2 Summit—attended by major figures like Paul Ryan, Michael Bloomberg and others—Romney also expressed confidence Republicans will retain both chambers in the 2018 midterms. He is the frontrunner for Utah’s Senate seat and faces a June 26 GOP runoff against state Rep. Mike Kennedy.

Schlitterbahn Waterparks said its 168-foot Verrückt waterslide at the Kansas City park will be permanently removed once the ongoing investigations are complete and the court grants permission. The slide, billed as the world’s tallest, has been closed since Aug. 7, 2016, when 10-year-old Caleb Schwab — son of Kansas state Rep. Scott Schwab — died during a run; a police report cited a fatal neck injury. Two women who rode with him were also injured. Schlitterbahn’s family owners expressed deep sorrow, stressing that guest and staff safety is their top priority and calling decommissioning the only proper response. They said they are cooperating with investigative teams, working with the victims’ families and attorneys, and will announce future plans for the site later.

The criminal inquiry remains open but investigators are nearing completion; the homicide detective has retained rafts, netting and metal frames for evidence. Attorneys for the Schwab family have coordinated with Schlitterbahn on tearing down the slide, though demolition must await conclusion of investigations and any potential litigation. Independent investigations by attorneys and experts for the victims have been conducted; private engineering and technical reviews are expected given the complexity of the ride. The tragedy has intensified scrutiny of state oversight: Kansas allows private inspectors for annual amusement-ride checks, and Schlitterbahn had passed private inspections in June. No criminal charges or civil lawsuits had been filed at the time of the statements; potential civil limits on damages in Kansas and possible jurisdictional choices for litigation were noted as unresolved issues.

Marie Joseph, 36, of Fall River, was found floating in the deep end of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Pool at Lafayette Park on Tuesday night after swimming there with neighborhood friends on Sunday. Police responded to reports from teenagers who discovered the body around 10 p.m. The pool had been closed and locked, and investigators are probing how the teens accessed the area. Authorities identified Joseph and say friends hadn’t seen her since Sunday; park staff later reported finding clothing, a cell phone and her ID left behind when they closed. A nine-year-old boy Joseph was supervising told detectives she unexpectedly went down a slide with him, colliding and then not resurfacing; the slide’s landing area is 12 feet deep. Officials await an autopsy to determine cause of death. The state Department of Conservation and Recreation closed all 30 of its deep-water pools for 24–48 hours for an operational review and placed the Lafayette Park pool staff on administrative leave while the investigation continues.

Operation Card Shop was an FBI two-year undercover sting that created and ran the online “carding” forum Carder Profit to expose an international credit-card fraud ecosystem. Authorities arrested 24 men aged 18–25 across 13 countries, including 11 in the United States, charging them with trafficking stolen card data, selling malware and remote-access tools, creating counterfeit cards, and arranging shipping or drop services for stolen goods. The probe notified banks of over 411,000 compromised cards and is said to have prevented about $205 million in potential losses. High-profile arrests included Mir Islam (aka JoshTheGod) accused of trafficking 50,000 cards. Officials said the operation disrupted organized cybercriminal networks and highlighted growing sophistication in card fraud.

Nebraska executed convicted killer Carey Dean Moore Tuesday morning at the Nebraska State Penitentiary in Lincoln by lethal injection. Four media witnesses were escorted into the viewing room; the execution chamber is soundproof and separated from witnesses by partitions. At 10:24 a.m. a curtain was lifted to reveal Moore on a gurney, covered by a white sheet with an arm connected to an IV. Department director Scott Frakes and acting Warden Robert Madsen were present. The first drug, diazepam (37 cc), was started; Moore appeared to speak to family and a spiritual adviser seated behind a partition. A saline flush followed and Moore closed his eyes, looked toward witnesses, and began to breathe more visibly. At 10:29 Madsen conducted a consciousness check. At 10:30 fentanyl (46 cc) was administered; Moore coughed and his diaphragm and abdomen heaved. Saline was then run and his chest ceased moving; his face reddened then darkened. At 10:32 cisatracurium besylate (15 cc) was given, followed by saline, and at 10:33 potassium chloride (120 cc) was delivered. By 10:39 Frakes communicated by radio and the curtain was lowered; Moore was pronounced dead at 10:47 by Lancaster County Coroner Pat Condon, out of sight of witnesses. The curtain was raised again at 10:53 to show Moore’s body, and custody was later transferred to the Nebraska State Patrol for autopsy.

House Majority Leader Eric Cantor announced he will step down from his leadership post effective July 31 after his shocking primary defeat to Tea Party-backed economist Dave Brat. Cantor, who will remain in Congress until his term ends in January, declared he would not mount a write-in campaign and voiced optimism about the GOP’s future while endorsing Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy as a strong successor. His departure set off an immediate leadership scramble: McCarthy is preparing a bid for majority leader but faces competition from conservatives including Rep. Pete Sessions and Jeb Hensarling, among others. Sessions and other Texas Republicans quickly mobilized, arguing for a more conservative, southern presence in leadership, while establishment figures urged a swift, orderly transition to avoid a divisive, protracted fight. The majority-whip contest also warmed up, with Peter Roskam and Steve Scalise among those positioning for the role if McCarthy moves up. Speaker John Boehner praised Cantor privately and publicly; he remains neutral in the leadership race. The unexpected upset intensified long-standing tensions between establishment Republicans and the party’s conservative flank over ideology, geographic representation, and strategy heading into the next Congress.

President Trump announced he will nominate Robert Wilkie, the acting secretary of Veterans Affairs, to become the department’s permanent leader. The surprise announcement came during a White House event; Wilkie, who has led the VA since March and was previously confirmed to a Pentagon post, was present when Trump praised his recent stewardship. Wilkie’s nomination follows the withdrawal of Ronny Jackson, the president’s former physician whose candidacy collapsed amid allegations of misconduct and other controversies. Congressional veterans affairs leaders offered cautious support: Senate Veterans’ Affairs Chairman Johnny Isakson congratulated Wilkie and looked forward to the confirmation process and implementation plans for the VA MISSION Act, while House panel chair Rep. Phil Roe called Wilkie accessible and knowledgeable. Advocates said Wilkie could bring needed stability after high-profile departures and ethics scandals that have roiled the agency. However, Wilkie’s nomination may face scrutiny because of his role as a congressional aide involved in a 2016 Republican platform debate over a Russia provision that special counsel Robert Mueller has reportedly examined.

Lawmakers from both parties weighed in this week on several federal controversies and the 2012 presidential contest, offering reactions that ranged from calls for institutional change to pledges of restraint.

Sen. Susan Collins (R‑Maine) and Rep. Carolyn Maloney (D‑N.Y.) both suggested the Secret Service’s problems might stem in part from its lack of female agents. Speaking on ABC’s “This Week,” Collins wondered whether incidents such as the prostitution scandal in Cartagena, Colombia, would have occurred if more women had been on the protective detail. Maloney, noting that the Secret Service is only about 11 percent female, urged greater diversity — more women and minorities — in the agency as a possible corrective.

On the Republican side of the presidential race, Sen. Marco Rubio (R‑Fla.) said he would no longer publicly discuss the vice‑presidential selection process and vowed to “be respectful of the process” that nominee Mitt Romney has established. On CNN’s “State of the Union,” Rubio said it would be wise to let Romney’s vetting play out, praised Romney’s judgment, and expressed a preference that Jeb Bush accept the slot if asked.

Independent Sen. Joe Lieberman (Conn.) — who has a history of crossing partisan lines — said on “Fox News Sunday” that he intends to stay out of the 2012 campaign cycle, enjoying his decision not to seek reelection and preferring to cast a private vote like most Americans.

Meanwhile, the Obama administration faced criticism over lavish GSA spending. David Axelrod told NBC’s “Meet the Press” that President Obama was “apoplectic” about waste uncovered at the General Services Administration and praised the swift administrative response. Conservative Sen. Tom Coburn (R‑Okla.) said on “Face the Nation” he was not critical of the White House handling of the Secret Service scandal, calling the misconduct an aberration and expressing confidence in Secret Service Director Mark Sullivan.

Hillary Clinton’s team clarified that every email on her private account was read individually before either being turned over to the State Department or deleted, addressing controversy over the roughly 30,490 messages labeled work-related and the nearly 31,830 labeled personal and discarded. Clinton spokesman Nick Merrill said a previously released fact sheet should have explicitly stated that reading every message was the “most important, fundamental and exhaustive” step; other multi-step searches detailed in the fact sheet were performed in addition to that review. Clinton has defended her use of a private account as convenient and said she deleted personal messages she saw no reason to keep, citing topics like family matters and travel. Critics, including Rep. Trey Gowdy, questioned who decides what is personal versus public—especially for mixed-use messages—and urged greater access. The controversy deepened when the State Department acknowledged that automatic archiving of senior officials’ emails was not routine until recently, undermining Clinton’s claim that many work-related messages sent to .gov addresses would have been preserved. Some messages may nonetheless survive through other officials’ records, printed copies, or special preservation actions, but historians and transparency advocates warned that lax archiving risks losing historically important communications. The revelations prompted calls for further investigation from House Republicans and renewed scrutiny of records practices.

A University of Toulouse team led by Young-Ho Eom used link-analysis methods inspired by Google’s PageRank to identify the most “important” people on Wikipedia. They examined 24 major language editions and ranked individuals by how articles link to and from their pages. Using PageRank alone produced some odd results: in the English-language network Frank Sinatra emerged as top, followed by Michael Jackson and Pope Pius XII, while across all 24 editions Adolf Hitler topped the list, with Michael Jackson and Madonna following. A striking anomaly occurred when PageRank across languages put Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus first—an artifact of Wikipedia’s near-complete collection of species pages that repeatedly link to Linnaeus because he established scientific naming conventions. To correct such distortions, the researchers combined PageRank (importance by incoming links) with CheiRank (connectivity by outgoing links) into a 2DRank metric that balances being referred to and referring to others; this blend produced the final top-100 lists and placed Sinatra at number one in English. The study’s broader aim was to reveal biases in Wikipedia’s attention by gender, era, and geography. The authors found a concentration of notable figures born in Western countries after the 17th century and a male dominance, although each language edition emphasizes local figures tied to its culture. The work highlights both the usefulness and limits of link-based measures: they capture network centrality but can be skewed by domain-specific linking patterns, as Linnaeus’s case illustrates. The study joins other efforts to quantify historical influence using citation and link networks.

President Trump’s April strike on a Syrian airfield prompted sharply divided reactions across Congress and in the media, cutting across partisan lines. Congressional leaders in both parties offered cautious support while insisting any wider escalation should involve Congress. House Speaker Paul Ryan called the strikes “appropriate and just.” Top Democrats including Nancy Pelosi and Dick Durbin termed the strikes a proportional response to Assad’s chemical attacks but said further action must be scrutinized and authorized by Congress. Chuck Schumer echoed that the administration must present a strategy and consult lawmakers.

A coalition of libertarian-leaning Republicans (Rand Paul, Mike Lee) and liberal Democrats (Brian Schatz, Ted Lieu, Barbara Lee, Tim Kaine) condemned the strikes as unconstitutional without congressional authorization, with Lee calling it an “act of war.” Defense hawks including John McCain, Lindsey Graham and Marco Rubio praised Trump’s decisive action, arguing it sent a message that war crimes would not go unpunished. The debate highlighted longstanding tensions over presidential war powers: past conflicts sometimes had congressional authorizations (Iraq, Afghanistan), while interventions like Libya in 2011 proceeded without them. The CRS noted presidents have frequently committed forces without specific authorization, raising constitutional controversies.

The strikes were the first direct U.S. military action against the Assad regime and were justified by the administration as necessary to deter chemical weapon use. Media reaction also drew scrutiny: MSNBC anchor Brian Williams was criticized after calling the Pentagon footage of Tomahawk missiles “beautiful” and quoting Leonard Cohen; critics accused him of glamorizing war and questioned his judgment given past credibility issues.

Last month Rolling Stone published a dramatic account alleging a 2012 gang rape of a University of Virginia freshman, “Jackie,” at a Phi Kappa Psi fraternity party and criticized UVA’s alleged history of minimizing sexual assault. The piece spurred campus outrage, student protests and calls for administrative reform. Rolling Stone says it honored Jackie’s request not to contact accused students, but subsequent reporting revealed discrepancies in her account and raised questions about key details; the magazine later acknowledged mistakes in its reporting process and apologized for not seeking the other side. The article also recounts Jackie’s trauma, the social pressures that discouraged reporting, and a campus culture of heavy drinking, entrenched Greek life and victim-blaming that survivors say silences them. It situates Jackie’s story amid other allegations and past UVA failures to hold perpetrators accountable, noting federal Title IX scrutiny of the university. In response, UVA President Teresa Sullivan suspended all Greek social activity through January, called for investigations, urged witnesses to come forward, and pledged policy review and community dialogue. The episode intensified debate about campus sexual violence, institutional responsibility, and how universities investigate and prevent assaults.

Baby-name trends in 2013 showed strong TV and celebrity influence, according to BabyCentre and BabyCenter surveys. Breaking Bad boosted Jesse (+13%) and Skyler (+70%), while Homeland raised Brody, Carrie and Dana. Duck Dynasty names like Korie (+89%), Silas and Sadie climbed, and royal baby George spurred rises in George (including feminine use), Giorgio and Georgia. Kanye and North West increased Kanye (+38%) and West (+22%). HBO’s Girls lifted Marnie and Shoshanna, and creator Lena Dunham’s name rose too. Sophia remained the top girls’ name (several years running), with Jackson leading boys; other top-ten names included Aiden, Liam, Noah, Olivia and Emma. Celebrity scandals dented some names—Reese, Paula and Lindsay fell—while anchors Al and Hoda gained. BabyCenter’s list draws on hundreds of thousands of parent submissions and groups variant spellings to reflect true popularity.

A threatening email claiming coordinated jihadi attacks on schools prompted very different responses in Los Angeles and New York. Both districts received similar messages describing bombs, nerve gas and armed assailants; investigators later judged both threats to be hoaxes. Los Angeles Unified—serving over 640,000 students—closed all campuses for a day after the email, traced to an IP in Frankfurt and sent from a pornographic “Cockmail” address affiliated with 8chan. The LA message contained telltale signs of fakery (offensive domains, lowercase “allah,” and an author claiming to be bullied), but officials shut schools out of caution, citing recent mass shootings and the apparent specificity of the warning. LA leaders, including Superintendent Ramon Cortines, Mayor Eric Garcetti and Police Chief Charlie Beck, defended the closure as prudent given what decision-makers knew before dawn; they conducted campus sweeps with LAPD, county sheriff and school police and reopened schools the next day after deeming them safe. New York officials, seeing the same email, kept schools open, calling the threat noncredible. Critics argued the LA shutdown showed how easily fear can be sown by an absurd, low-cost hoax designed to create disruption rather than physical harm.

Reporters uncovered an internal December email from Tennessee Virtual Academy (TNVA), a for-profit online public school run by K12 Inc., instructing teachers to delete September and October progress reports so only November progress would show. Critics, including Rep. Gloria Johnson and TEA interim director Mitchell Johnson, called the directive grade-fixing and questioned whether leaders were trying to hide failing student performance. TNVA principal Josh Williams defended the practice as reflecting students’ most recent progress and paralleling traditional make-up and extra credit opportunities, saying it helped identify who needed remediation. The email also advised removing widely failed assignments and prioritizing reading and math over history and science. TNVA has poor standardized test results, prompting Gov. Bill Haslam to propose limiting virtual school enrollment; legislation is pending that could cap new virtual schools at 1,500 students and allow closure or caps for schools with two years of below-standard performance. A House subcommittee debated but did not repeal the 2011 law permitting for-profit virtual schools; proponents argued TNVA serves some students well, while critics highlighted K12’s state funding (about $4,700 per student claimed by K12) and questioned transparency about expenditures and outcomes.

Houston Texans defensive end J.J. Watt will miss the rest of the season after sustaining a tibial plateau fracture during the Texans’ 42-34 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs, head coach Bill O’Brien confirmed. Watt went down while engaged in a block on the Chiefs’ opening drive, received sideline treatment, was carted off and transported to a hospital. O’Brien also announced that outside linebacker Whitney Mercilus requires surgery for a torn pectoral muscle and will be out for the season as well. O’Brien stressed the team must move on and that replacing players of Watt’s and Mercilus’s caliber will require multiple contributors rather than a single replacement. Watt, 28, who had returned from September 2016 back surgery and had missed most of that season, apologized to teammates and the city on Twitter, saying he was devastated and wanted to be on the field for them. In four games this season he recorded 13 tackles but no sacks. When healthy, Watt has been among the NFL’s most dominant defenders—accumulating 372 tackles and 74.5 sacks from 2011–2015, earning multiple Defensive Player of the Year and All-Pro honors. With Watt sidelined, depth players such as Brandon Dunn, Joel Heath and Carlos Watkins are expected to see increased snaps.

Detectives investigating the March poisoning of former Russian double agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia say the highest concentration of the nerve agent was found on the front door of Skripal’s Salisbury home, leading them to conclude the pair first came into contact with the toxin there. The father, 66, and daughter, 33, were discovered unconscious on a park bench in Salisbury and remain critically ill; medical teams have warned they may never fully recover. About 250 counterterrorism detectives are working the case, examining over 5,000 hours of CCTV, more than 1,350 seized items and hundreds of witness statements. Traces of the nerve agent have been detected at other locations but at lower concentrations than at the home, prompting focused searches of the neighbourhood; police say the public risk is low and searches are precautionary. The UK government attributes the attack to the Russian state. In response, more than 150 Russian officials have been expelled from over 25 countries; Moscow has denied involvement and retaliated by expelling British diplomats. British ministers are considering further measures, including financial restrictions. Public health experts continue to assess any long-term risk to Salisbury residents; the town will receive a £1m government support package. Authorities say the investigation is complex and likely to continue for weeks or months as the manhunt for the perpetrators and forensic inquiries proceed.

This document compiles multiple reports and studies about Millennials’ demographics, labor patterns, life choices and consumer preferences, as well as related generational context. Key findings challenge several common assumptions about Millennials and sketch how this cohort differs from earlier generations.

Labor tenure and job mobility
Government data from the Current Population Survey show Millennials (born 1981–1998) are as likely to remain with an employer as Generation X was at the same ages. In January 2016, 63.4% of employed 18–35-year-old Millennials reported tenure of at least 13 months, compared with 59.9% of 18–35-year-olds in February 2000 (mostly Gen X). Long-tenure shares (five years or more) were also similar: about 22% for Millennials versus 21.8% for Gen X. Education helps explain part of this stability: college attainment among 25–35-year-old Millennials (38% of men, 46% of women) exceeded that of Gen X at the same age in 2000. Among college-educated 25–35-year-olds, roughly 75% of Millennials had at least 13 months with their employer versus 70–72% of Gen X then. The increase in tenure among college-educated workers aligns with a broader, decades-long decline in job switching across working-age adults, though causes remain poorly understood. The report notes longer tenure does not necessarily equal higher wages or better job prospects; fewer job moves might reflect limited opportunities rather than preference. Less-educated young adults show similar tenure patterns to their Gen X counterparts.

Demographics and generational size
Census Bureau estimates indicate Millennials (defined here as ages 18–34 in 2015) became the largest living generation, numbering about 75.4 million and surpassing Baby Boomers. Immigration is a key contributor to Millennial growth. Projections show the Millennial cohort peaking around 2036 and gradually shrinking thereafter, while Gen X will briefly outnumber Boomers by 2028. Boomers remain historically large but are declining due to aging and mortality.
