Social and economic behavior
Census analysis of 25–34-year-olds from 1976–2016 highlights major shifts: young adults prioritize education and economic stability over early marriage and homemaking. The share of young women working rose sharply (from 50% to 70%), while homemaking as a primary role fell from 43% to 14%. Cohabitation has risen noticeably; many young adults still live with parents rather than spouses. Income patterns show gains for women but also rising low-income shares among young men.

Consumer preferences
A Conde Nast/Goldman Sachs survey of 13–34-year-olds ranks brands Millennials and Gen Z favor most: Victoria’s Secret, Sephora and Nike top retail/beauty/fashion lists, while Amazon dominates overall and as a shopping app. The study underscores younger consumers’ digital-first expectations and the importance of robust e-commerce and mobile experiences for brands courting this demographic.

Overall, the assembled findings portray Millennials as a large, increasingly educated cohort showing greater labor stability than stereotypes suggest, shifting life-course priorities toward education and economic security, and holding strong digital-driven consumer preferences.

A large Northwestern Medicine study following more than 10,000 men from adolescence into their early 30s found that becoming a father is associated with modest but measurable weight gain. Over roughly 20 years, researchers tracked participants’ BMI at four time points and classified them as non-fathers, resident fathers (living with their child), or non-resident fathers. After controlling for age, race, education, income, activity, screen time and marriage, the typical 6-foot-tall resident father gained about 4.4 pounds (a 2.6% BMI rise) after becoming a first-time dad; a comparable non-resident father gained about 3.3 pounds (a 2% BMI rise). By contrast, men who remained child-free lost an average of 1.4 pounds over the same span. The analysis, one of the first to link fatherhood specifically to changes in a major health biomarker, appears in the American Journal of Men’s Health.

Investigators suggest lifestyle shifts tied to parenting—reduced time for exercise, disrupted sleep, and greater exposure to child-friendly, calorie-dense foods and leftovers—likely drive the “fatherhood effect.” Lead author Dr. Craig Garfield notes these gains add to weight increases already associated with marriage and raise long-term risks for heart disease, diabetes and cancer. Because many new fathers do not have their own physicians, pediatric visits offer a practical opportunity to counsel fathers on nutrition, mental health and self-care; earlier work by Garfield also found increased depressive symptoms among new dads. The study highlights the transition to fatherhood as an important life stage and potential social determinant of men’s health, calling for medical engagement and preventive guidance for men of child-rearing age. The research was supported by an NIH institute grant.

The Treasury Inspector General’s report on the IRS review of 501(c)(4) applications found serious procedural failures but did not establish clear partisan intent. Investigators concluded the IRS used “inappropriate criteria” — including names and policy positions like “Tea Party,” “9/12” and “patriots” — to flag applications, creating the appearance of bias. Management repeatedly told staff to shift to neutral, activity-focused criteria, but the Cincinnati team reverted to the prior test without authorization; supervisors later tightened approval rules. The IG found delays and poor case management: many organizations waited more than a year (some over 1,000 days) for decisions, requests for information came after long inactivity with short response deadlines, and many cases remained open across election cycles. The report criticizes unnecessary, burdensome requests for donor lists and reading materials; the IRS acknowledged overreach and destroyed improperly collected donor lists. About 69 percent of fully documented flagged cases did show potential violations, but the process still imposed real costs on applicants. The report doesn’t resolve whether senior officials misled Congress about what they knew and when; that issue remains for congressional hearings. The IG made nine recommendations; the IRS agreed to seven and proposed alternatives for two, signaling reforms but leaving questions about accountability.

A CDC analysis of 2001–2015 emergency department (ED) data found marked increases in nonfatal self-inflicted injuries among U.S. youth aged 10–24, driven largely by rising rates in females, especially girls aged 10–14. Using the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System—All Injury Program, researchers identified 43,138 ED visits for first-time, intentional self-harm during the study period and calculated nationally weighted, age-adjusted rates by sex, age group, and method. Overall rates were stable through about 2008, then rose 5.7% annually through 2015, reaching 303.7 per 100,000. Male rates remained stable across ages. Female rates showed no significant trend until 2009, then increased 8.4% per year; girls 10–14 experienced the steepest rise—an 18.8% annual increase from 2009 to 2015, with rates climbing from ~110 to ~318 per 100,000. Females 15–19 and 20–24 also rose (7.2% and 2.0% annually, respectively). Poisoning was the most common method for females, increasing after 2007; cutting with sharp objects also rose for females throughout 2001–2015. The study likely underestimates incidence because it captures only ED-treated cases. Trends align with rising youth suicide and depression rates, particularly among young girls. Authors recommend implementing evidence-based prevention across health systems and communities—improving access to care, creating protective environments, fostering connectedness, teaching coping skills, and identifying at-risk youth for support.

Protests erupted in Madison after a white police officer fatally shot 19-year-old Tony Robinson, an unarmed black man, late Friday following a confrontation in Robinson’s apartment. Demonstrators chanting “Black Lives Matter” gathered outside the police department and later near the scene, calling for answers and accountability; police and city leaders urged peaceful demonstrations. Madison Police Chief Mike Koval acknowledged community anger, pledged to protect First Amendment rights during protests, and asked for nondestructive actions in line with the family’s wishes. Koval said Officer Matt Kenny, a 12‑plus‑year veteran placed on administrative leave, forced entry into the apartment after responding to disturbance calls and fired after being assaulted, though investigators have not released the number of shots. Kenny was injured; Robinson was taken to a hospital where he died. The officer had been involved in a prior fatal shooting in 2007 that authorities deemed justified. The state Division of Criminal Investigation will probe the case, as required by a 2014 Wisconsin law mandating outside review of officer-involved deaths. Robinson’s family, who attended community meetings and some protests, said they have not been allowed to see his body and expressed deep grief. Robinson’s mother read a statement saying she could not comprehend what happened. Neighbors described Robinson as known in the neighborhood; court records show a 2014 guilty plea to felony armed robbery followed by probation. Mayor Paul Soglin promised transparency as questions mount. The shooting — coming days after federal closure of the Darren Wilson case in Ferguson and amid national scrutiny over other high-profile deaths of black people in police encounters — intensified local tensions and renewed calls for answers about policing and racial justice.

Three days after a gunman killed nine people at Umpqua Community College in Oregon, Republican presidential frontrunner Donald Trump used a rally in suburban Nashville to deliver one of his most emphatic defenses of gun rights since launching his campaign. Trump said he holds a New York concealed-carry permit and suggested that armed instructors or teachers could have limited the slaughter at the community college, condemning "gun-free zones" and arguing the attacks stem from "sick people" rather than firearms. Evoking 1970s vigilante icon Charles Bronson and the film Death Wish, he joked that any attacker would be “shocked” if they tried to assault him, framing the debate as one of self-defense. Trump also called for stronger attention to mental-health care, blaming the closure of facilities and lack of funding for exacerbating the problem. He dismissed proposals for tighter gun laws as ineffective, saying jurisdictions with the strictest rules are often the worst off, and criticized President Obama’s response to the shooting as divisive. In media appearances, Trump reiterated that mass shootings are inevitable to some degree because "sick" but sometimes intelligent perpetrators can "break the system," and said mental illness, not guns, should be the focus. Outside of the shooting debate, he defended his tax and cost-cutting claims, and brushed off poll comparisons to Democratic figures, asserting his record of winning even as he faces scrutiny over evolving positions on gun control.

Former U.S. Rep. Anthony Weiner’s long-running sexting scandals ended in a guilty plea and prison sentence that closed a tumultuous chapter in his public life and reverberated through national politics. Elected to Congress in 1998, Weiner resigned in 2011 after admitting he sent explicit images from his Twitter account and repeatedly lied about it. He attempted a political comeback with a 2013 New York mayoral run, but that effort collapsed when additional sexually explicit exchanges surfaced, including high-profile messages with a woman who called him “Carlos Danger.” The episode was documented in the film “Weiner,” which highlighted the strain on his marriage to Huma Abedin, a longtime aide to Hillary Clinton.

Weiner resurfaced in scandal again in 2016 when a “40-something” woman published photos he had sent—one showing his toddler beside him—and later when a 15-year-old girl told media outlets she had months-long sexually explicit online communications with him. Federal investigators in New York and North Carolina pursued a probe into his online interactions with the minor. Agents seized Weiner’s laptop and other devices; material found there included emails involving Huma Abedin that prompted FBI Director James Comey to announce a brief, late-October review of previously closed Clinton email matters. Comey later said the newly discovered Clinton-related emails didn’t change the conclusion that no charges were warranted, but his disclosure days before the 2016 election drew criticism and was cited by Clinton as a factor in her loss.

In May 2017 Weiner pleaded guilty to transmitting obscene material to a minor, admitting he exchanged explicit images and encouraged sexual conduct with a girl he believed to be 15. He apologized in court, acknowledged a compulsive pattern of seeking attention via social media, and said he had entered treatment. The charge required registration as a sex offender; Weiner signed a plea agreement limiting appeals and faced up to 10 years, but agreed to a recommended sentence range. In September he was sentenced to 21 months in prison, bringing legal finality to misconduct that wrecked his career, his marriage, and had unexpected political consequences well beyond his personal downfall.

Arizona State University permanently revoked recognition of the local Tau Kappa Epsilon (TKE) chapter after photos surfaced of a Martin Luther King Jr. holiday weekend party that depicted racial stereotypes and encouraged underage drinking. The unregistered off-campus event showed attendees in stereotypical hip-hop attire, posing with hollowed-out watermelon cups and using the hashtag #blackoutformlk, prompting swift condemnation from civil-rights leaders. ASU said TKE violated four student‑conduct provisions: discriminatory activity, alcohol rules, breach of prior sanctions, and risky off‑campus behavior. The 65‑year‑old chapter can no longer recruit, meet on campus, or be listed as an ASU organization. The action follows prior incidents: in November 2012 about 20 TKE members assaulted an African‑American fraternity member, leading to probation and party bans; two members later pleaded guilty to aggravated assault. National TKE officials said they are reviewing ASU’s findings and will complete their own investigation. Civil-rights advocates demanded student discipline and broader campus reforms, threatening athletic and fundraising boycotts if further steps aren’t taken.

The article juxtaposes two threads: the brutal reality of North Korea’s human-rights abuses and how Western media and entertainment often reduce the regime and Asians to caricature. It opens by describing North Korea’s multigenerational prison camps where whole families—labeled “bad class”—were interned for decades; many never left, some died of starvation, and survivors who escape offer fragmented, dated testimony that’s hard for outsiders to process. Despite horrific, sustained abuses, outrage has often been muted compared with sensational stories like the Sony hack over The Interview. The piece then shifts to how Hollywood perpetuates the “Asian goofball” stereotype—clownish, harmless, sexless Asian men—from historic caricatures to viral figures like William Hung and Psy’s comic reception. That lens leads media to favor bizarre, laughable North Korean stories (unicorn lairs, absurd propaganda), which make Kim Jong Un seem ridiculous rather than monstrous. The author argues The Interview, while flawed, avoids pure clowning by giving Randall Park’s Kim some agency and menace, and notes emerging Asian-American media like Fresh Off the Boat may help move beyond tired stereotypes toward fuller representation.

Daniel Ramirez Medina, a 23-year-old Mexican national brought to the U.S. as a child, was arrested by ICE agents in Washington last week despite having been granted and twice renewed Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) work authorization. Agents went to his father’s home to arrest the father; Ramirez was taken into custody during that operation and is being held at the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma. His attorneys contend he has no criminal record, denies any gang affiliation, and that ICE pressured him to admit gang membership. ICE says Ramirez “self‑admitted” gang ties and was encountered during the arrest of a previously deported felon, asserting he poses a public‑safety risk and has been placed in removal proceedings. Lawyers filed a federal petition challenging his detention, arguing the government violated his due‑process rights because DACA conferred lawful presence and work authorization that should preclude such action. A U.S. magistrate ordered the government to explain Ramirez’s custody status and set a hearing; a bond hearing was later scheduled. The case has drawn local political attention—Seattle officials reiterated sanctuary protections—and raised broader concerns that the Trump administration may expand enforcement to include DACA recipients, unsettling roughly 750,000 Dreamers.

Oregon lawmakers have seen a flurry of proposals as the Legislature prepares to address a roughly $1.8 billion budget shortfall for the 2017–2019 biennium. One controversial but unlikely idea, House Bill 2875, would levy a five-cent-per-pound tax on wholesale coffee to create an “Alternative Education Sustainability Fund.” Revenue would be split evenly between the Oregon Military Department for the Oregon National Guard Youth Challenge Program and grants administered by the Oregon Department of Education to support alternative high school programs and primary school reading programs, covering operations and capital costs. The bill lacks an estimated revenue projection, would take effect July 1, 2018, and requires a three-fifths legislative majority. House Democrats’ spokesman and the Revenue Committee chair indicated the bill is unlikely to advance amid hundreds of proposals. The broader budget debate includes Governor Kate Brown’s mix of targeted cuts and revenue adjustments—closing tax loopholes, raising tobacco taxes, and trimming planned higher education increases—to close the gap without deep service cuts. Other major session topics are repealing the statewide ban on local rent control, rural economic concerns, criminal justice reforms, and ethics rules for revolving-door state employment.

Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz remains confident about the company’s long-term prospects in China despite the country’s slowest economic growth in 25 years. Speaking from Shanghai, Schultz said Starbucks will continue an aggressive expansion there, planning to open more than one new store per day on average over the next five years and aiming to reach nearly 5,000 stores by 2021. He framed the strategy as part of a long-term play: Starbucks has invested “ahead of the growth curve” in people and systems and has focused on building the coffee habit among Chinese consumers since opening its first China store 17 years ago. Early on the business struggled and relied heavily on expats and tourists, but Schultz said the customer base has shifted to predominantly Chinese patrons and recent results in China have been among the strongest the company has seen.

Schultz anticipates China will eventually surpass the U.S. as Starbucks’ largest market, though he would not specify a timeline. He contrasted Starbucks’ progress with several prominent U.S. tech and ride-hailing companies that have failed or retreated from China, noting that selling coffee is less politically or technologically sensitive than those industries. Schultz also distinguished Starbucks from other American food-and-drink chains now rethinking China strategies—such as KFC and McDonald’s—saying Starbucks intends to keep stores operated by company employees rather than local partners. He concluded that China’s market remains in its early stages for Starbucks, and the company’s patience and local investment strategy have set it up for continued growth there.

A Daily Caller piece criticizing 11-year-old Barron Trump’s casual attire while boarding Air Force One—khaki shorts, suede loafers and a bright red J.Crew T‑shirt—sparked widespread backlash and renewed calls to shield the president’s son from media scrutiny. The article argued Barron should “dress the part” alongside his impeccably attired parents, President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump, after the family returned to Washington from New Jersey. Many on social media and public figures condemned the focus on a minor, calling the story “mean‑spirited,” intrusive and irrelevant.

The White House formally requested privacy for Barron, with spokeswoman Stephanie Grisham urging the media to allow him a private childhood. Chelsea Clinton publicly defended Barron, tweeting that the media and others should leave him alone and calling attacks on a child “for shame.” Clinton cited past incidents—such as criticism following his father’s inauguration and a controversial “Saturday Night Live” writer’s tweet—that prompted similar defenses. Melania Trump thanked Clinton and reinforced an anti‑bullying message.

Responses varied: some mocked the Daily Caller’s emphasis, others complimented Barron’s relaxed look, and several noted the T‑shirt’s retail origin and swift sellout. The episode intensified debate over whether presidential children should be off-limits in public discourse, with critics arguing minors deserve protection from partisan or personal attacks regardless of their family’s prominence. A correction clarified Barron returned from New Jersey, not Arizona.

NASCAR and 30 major tracks urged fans to refrain from displaying the Confederate flag at events, issuing a joint statement asking for an “all-inclusive, even more welcoming atmosphere.” The appeal, signed by venues owned by International Speedway Corporation and Speedway Motorsports Inc., follows NASCAR Chairman Brian France’s comments that the sanctioning body would try “as far as we can” to eliminate the flag from its events and its support for removing the flag from South Carolina’s capitol grounds. Daytona International Speedway announced a voluntary flag exchange for the Coke Zero 400 weekend allowing fans to trade Confederate flags for American flags; track president Joie Chitwood said Confederate flags in the infield would not be banned outright. NASCAR clarified the request targets overt, boisterous displays—such as very large flags—that could lead to removal from premises. The sport already prohibits Confederate imagery on licensed merchandise and frames the move as promoting mutual respect and a welcoming environment for all attendees.

Three children — an 8-year-old girl and two boys, ages 5 and 3 — were removed from a Salinas, California, home on March 14 after a welfare check revealed severe neglect and abuse, Monterey County authorities said. Deputies found the residence cluttered and filthy with little food; the children showed signs of malnourishment, bruises and emotional trauma. The girl appeared the worst affected: investigators say she had been chained at times to prevent her from getting food, sometimes shackled at the ankle or by a collar and possibly confined in a closet. She was hospitalized for several days and described by sheriff’s officials as traumatized and emaciated. The children, who were home-schooled, were placed in foster care; the older girl and the 5-year-old were adopted, and the 3-year-old is the biological son of one of the adults. Eraca Dawn Craig, 31, and Christian Jessica Deanda, 44 — domestic partners who were arrested at the scene — face felony child cruelty, false imprisonment and related charges and remain in custody awaiting a preliminary hearing.

Federal Court Justice Robin Camp has resigned after the Canadian Judicial Council (CJC) recommended his removal for his handling of a 2014 sexual-assault trial. Transcripts showed Camp, then a provincial judge, asking the 19-year-old, homeless complainant why she didn’t “keep her knees together,” saying “pain and sex sometimes go together,” and repeatedly referring to her as “the accused.” The complainant told the disciplinary hearing the comments made her hate herself and contemplate suicide. The Alberta Court of Appeal had earlier overturned Camp’s ruling, criticizing his reliance on myths and stereotypes; the accused, Alexander Wagar, was later acquitted again.

Camp apologized publicly, undertook counselling and training, and sought to address the CJC in person to argue he acted from “ignorance, not animus.” The CJC declined his request and, by 19–4, concluded his conduct “profoundly destructive” to judicial impartiality and public confidence, rendering him incapable of continuing on the bench. Four dissenting members—male judges from Atlantic Canada—found misconduct but opposed dismissal, citing rehabilitation. Camp announced his resignation and apologized; Justice Minister Jody Wilson-Raybould had been preparing a parliamentary motion to support the CJC recommendation.

The case sparked debate on judicial treatment of sexual-assault complainants and renewed calls for mandatory judicial training on gendered violence. Observers called the decision a watershed moment signaling that gender bias in court will no longer be tolerated.

Three new adaptations—Gone Girl, The Two Faces of January and The Blue Room—rework popular novels into films about marriages beginning to crack, dissatisfied women, and the violent impulses that creep out of domestic fissures. The most attention here falls on David Fincher’s Gone Girl, adapted by Gillian Flynn from her own bestseller, a film that alternates dark satire of media spectacle with a cat-and-mouse marriage thriller.

Gone Girl opens with Nick Dunne (Ben Affleck), a melancholic, Midwestern-born former New Yorker who now runs a bar with his twin sister Margo (Carrie Coon). On his fifth anniversary he returns home to find his house ransacked and his wife Amy (Rosamund Pike) missing. The discovery launches a police investigation led by Detective Boney (Kim Dickens) and a voracious media circus that quickly narrows suspicion on Nick. Fincher frames the story through shifting points of view—present-day procedural scenes and Amy’s diary backstory—so the audience constantly reassesses what is true. The film foregrounds how narrative and perception are manipulated: Amy’s parents wrote the “Amazing Amy” books that fictionalize and polish her life, and TV pundits and tabloids incessantly reconstruct the Dunnes’ private pain.

Fincher’s strengths—meticulous detail, a cool palette, precise control—serve the material well; Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross’s score amplifies its unease, and a major violent set piece lands with unnerving sound design. Yet some critics find the movie uneven at its core. Nick is presented as a relatively dull, sometimes lunkheaded figure, while Amy, though brilliantly played by Pike, can feel contrived onscreen—her extreme cunning occasionally reads as cartoonish against Fincher’s sober realism. The film revels in its portraits of peripheral characters—Tyler Perry’s media-savvy lawyer Tanner Bolt, Kim Dickens’s detective, and Carrie Coon’s grounded, wounded sister—and in its satire of cable news’ appetite for spectacle. Neil Patrick Harris turns up as an unsettling ex, inserting a Gothic subplot faithful to the novel but, for some reviewers, tonally jarring.

Praise centers on the film’s savage wit, performances (especially Pike’s), and its smart interrogation of marriage, class and media culture; criticism focuses on a loss of narrative logic in the final stretch and on the difficulty of translating certain novelistic devices to screen. Overall, Gone Girl proves thrilling and provocative for much of its running time—an assured, often wickedly funny thriller that prompts uneasy conversations about truth, storytelling and the public consumption of private catastrophe.

Scientists in East Africa are expanding an innovative tuberculosis (TB) screening program using African Giant Pouched Rats trained by the Belgian NGO APOPO. Known for detecting landmines, these "HeroRATS" are now used to sniff sputum samples for TB in high-risk, hard-to-reach populations—initially targeting crowded prisons in Tanzania and Mozambique with USAID support. TB remains a leading infectious killer after HIV, with around 9 million new global cases and 2 million deaths annually. Existing diagnostic systems are often slow, costly, and insufficiently scalable, leaving many cases undetected, particularly in underserved communities and institutions where people live in close quarters.

APOPO begins training rats at four weeks old; socialization and scent recognition are reinforced until the animals are ready to work at about nine months. In practice, a rat inspects rows of 10 sputum samples and signals detection by hovering for three seconds. APOPO reports near-100% detection accuracy for TB presence (though rats cannot differentiate drug-resistant strains), and much faster throughput: a rat can screen about 100 samples in 20 minutes versus four days for a lab technician. Operating near capacity, screening costs per sample can be as low as $0.20. APOPO’s programs have screened over 340,000 samples, interrupting more than 36,000 potential infections and boosting detection rates by over 40% in partner clinics.

Health experts in Tanzania praise the rats’ sensitivity to volatile molecules in sputum, which can reveal even low-parasite samples, offering a potentially low-cost, rapid mass-screening tool adaptable to prisons, slums, factories, and high-risk groups such as people living with HIV/AIDS. The WHO cautions lab technicians should not exceed testing more than 20 patients daily to avoid misdiagnosis, underscoring the need for scalable alternatives like the rat detection system. The rats receive regular health checks and may retire when no longer enthusiastic, living out comfortable lives post-service.

An Indonesian Trigana Air Service ATR 42-300 twin-turboprop flying from Jayapura to Oksibil crashed into a mountain in Papua province, killing all 54 people aboard. The aircraft lost contact with air traffic control on Sunday about half an hour into the short flight; villagers reported seeing it strike terrain amid heavy rain, strong winds and fog. Rescuers reached the remote, forested crash site two days later after being hindered by bad weather and rugged, mountainous terrain; more than 70 personnel on foot and by helicopter finally accessed the wreckage at about 2,600 meters altitude. The plane was “totally destroyed,” bodies were burned and difficult to identify, and all remains were recovered for transport to Jayapura. Search teams recovered the flight data and cockpit voice recorders in good condition, which investigators hope will clarify the cause. Among the passengers were Indonesian officials, postal workers escorting roughly $470,000 in government aid, and several local legislators. Trigana Air, banned from Europe for safety concerns, has a history of incidents. Indonesia’s transport safety committee has opened an investigation; officials noted poor weather and the treacherous terrain as possible factors amid the country’s broader aviation safety challenges.

Journalists and social-media metrics agreed: the Democratic National Convention’s Tuesday night was far more energetic than many had expected. Commentators from CNN, POLITICO, The Atlantic, NBC and others repeatedly contrasted the DNC’s palpable enthusiasm with the comparatively muted Republican convention in Tampa. Observers said the crowd’s vitality made even non-primetime speakers feel strong and gave the event a confident, lively tone. While most reactions praised the atmosphere—calling it “hot” versus Tampa’s “cool” and noting delegates genuinely wanted to be there—some dissenters like Laura Ingraham saw low energy and a lack of 2008-style youth appeal. Michelle Obama’s primetime address amplified the momentum, generating a peak of 28,003 tweets per minute, nearly double the peak during Mitt Romney’s RNC acceptance. Her speech, filled with quotable, Twitter-friendly lines—most notably “Being president doesn't change who you are. It reveals who you are.”—drove widespread engagement and helped push DNC-related tweets past 3 million by night’s end, approaching the Republican convention’s total. Reactions on Twitter ranged from admiration to ridicule, reflecting broad public interest.

The weekend box office crowned The Angry Birds Movie as the top new release, opening at an estimated $39 million. The family comedy based on the popular mobile game earned the third-best animated debut of the year behind Zootopia and Kung Fu Panda 3, displacing Captain America: Civil War to second place. With a $73 million budget and voices including Jason Sudeikis, Sean Penn and Maya Rudolph, Angry Birds drew audiences despite mixed reviews (42% on RottenTomatoes) and a warmer audience reception (61%). Analyst Paul Dergarabedian noted the brand’s built-in fanbase and the strong draw of PG-rated family fare, even as overall box office was about 25% lower than last year. Civil War added $33.1 million in week three, nearing $347.4 million domestically and passing $1 billion worldwide. Other openings: Neighbors 2 debuted with $21.8 million, The Nice Guys earned $11.3 million, and Disney’s live-action The Jungle Book continued strong with $11 million. Final box office figures were pending.

Apple’s 2012 iPad (branded simply “iPad”) is an evolutionary, not revolutionary, upgrade that nonetheless reasserts Apple’s lead in tablets by dramatically improving two core elements: display and cellular speed. The centerpiece is a 9.7-inch “Retina” screen with 2048x1536 resolution—four times the pixels of the iPad 2—which renders text and images far sharper and more vivid. The new display boosts color saturation and makes reading and media consumption noticeably better, though glossy LCD limitations in sunlight remain. Apple also upgraded the processor (A5X with quad‑core graphics), added a much improved 5‑megapixel rear camera capable of 1080p video with stabilization, and introduced dictation (a Siri subset) and optional 4G LTE on cellular models. Despite these additions, battery life stays near the prior model’s nine–ten hours thanks to a larger battery and power efficiencies, at the cost of a slightly thicker and heavier device. Prices match the iPad 2’s launch levels: Wi‑Fi 16GB from $499; 4G models carry higher SKUs; iPad 2 remains available at $399. Downsides include no expandable storage or Flash, no camera flash, partial Siri functionality, and larger Retina-ready apps consuming much more storage. For new buyers wanting the best general-purpose tablet, the new iPad is the top choice; owners of very recent iPad 2s may find the upgrade less urgent unless they need the Retina display or LTE.

A.K. Verma, an assistant executive engineer who joined the Central Public Works Department (CPWD) in 1980, has been dismissed after remaining absent from duty since December 1990. Verma went on earned leave that month and continued to seek extensions, which were not sanctioned; he repeatedly defied orders to report back. An inquiry into wilful absence was initiated in September 1992, but Verma’s non-cooperation delayed proceedings. A fresh charge sheet was issued in 2005, and an inquiry report finding him guilty was submitted in July 2007 and accepted by the then Urban Development Minister in August 2007; nonetheless, no further action was taken for years. Upon assuming office, Urban Development Minister M. Venkaiah Naidu reviewed pending vigilance and disciplinary cases and ordered Verma’s dismissal for unauthorised absence, also directing officials to fix responsibility for the prolonged inaction. The case underscores long-standing problems with absenteeism and slow disciplinary processes in India’s bureaucracy, a system often criticized for rigid labour protections that make dismissals difficult. The episode occurred amid wider efforts—highlighted by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s push for stricter attendance measures—to improve accountability, including biometric attendance tracking and high-level scrutiny of civil servant conduct.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un used his New Year’s speech to combine stark nuclear posturing with a surprising outreach to the South. Kim declared that a “nuclear button” is always on his desk and claimed the entire United States is within reach of North Korea’s nuclear forces, insisting this was “reality, not a threat.” He reiterated plans to mass-produce nuclear warheads and ballistic missiles and speed their deployment, while saying Pyongyang would use its weapons only if its security or sovereignty were threatened. These boasts follow a year of accelerated testing, including a powerful nuclear test in September and an advanced ICBM launch in November, prompting new UN sanctions and continued international skepticism about North Korea’s true operational delivery capability.

At the same time, Kim signaled openness to dialogue with South Korea and suggested Pyongyang might send a delegation to the PyeongChang Winter Olympics in February. He urged “melting the frozen North-South relations,” offering talks and possible urgent meetings between officials; Seoul welcomed discussion and has proposed delaying joint U.S.-South Korean military drills until after the Games to reduce tensions. Analysts see Kim’s dual message as aimed at strengthening deterrence while seeking economic and diplomatic relief, potentially driving a wedge between Seoul and Washington. U.S. President Donald Trump responded tersely, “We’ll see,” reflecting continued uncertainty about how to engage Pyongyang. Observers say the Olympics provide a timely opening for de-escalation and dialogue.

Environmental groups criticize bottled water for waste, often citing the roughly 50 billion mostly plastic bottles discarded annually. In response, the International Bottled Water Association (IBWA) commissioned its first study of water input per liter of bottled water. The study found North American companies use about 1.39 liters of water to produce one liter of bottled water. The IBWA contrasts that favorably with other beverages: a liter of soda averages 2.02 liters of water, beer 4 liters, wine 4.74 liters and distilled spirits a striking 34.55 liters per liter. The industry uses these figures to argue bottled water is comparatively efficient. Critics and water-footprint experts say the IBWA study understates true water impacts because it omits broader supply-chain and packaging water use. Ertug Ercin of the Water Footprint Network argues a full water footprint must include all freshwater consumed across production, including water for packaging materials and processes; for example, making a half-liter plastic bottle might consume around three liters of water, meaning packaging can multiply the footprint many times over. Ercin notes plastic production and paper manufacturing also consume substantial water, though he acknowledges bottled-water packaging still uses less water than soda when factoring in sugar cultivation and dye production. The IBWA contends defining boundaries is difficult and that companies are seeking efficiencies, saying water is central to their business.

Jennifer Westfeldt is beginning performances of the new play The Power of Duff with Greg Kinnear at Vassar’s Powerhouse Theater, a campus venue that feels like summer camp. Westfeldt joked about being kicked out of camp at 13 for going out for pizza with a boyfriend and quipped that longtime partner Jon Hamm has visited the campus “but without incident” because she’s “of age now.”

Much of the rest of the document focuses on Madonna and controversies surrounding her MDNA tour. In Warsaw, Poland, a Catholic youth group called Youth Crusade is petitioning local authorities to cancel Madonna’s August 1 concert because it coincides with the annual Warsaw Uprising remembrance day. Activists argue her show would desecrate the memorial day and protest her stage imagery, which they say attacks Catholic faith and promotes homosexuality and pornography, citing past onstage acts such as burning crosses and wearing a crown of thorns.

Madonna’s tour has provoked varied reactions across Europe. Performances included explicit moments—she flashed her breast in Turkey and France, exposed her bottom in Rome, and performed a striptease at London’s Hyde Park, revealing a sheer bra and black thong. The Hyde Park show drew mixed responses: some fans and critics called it one of her worst gigs, blaming sound problems, rain, curfew constraints, high ticket prices, and a limited number of classic hits; others praised the spectacle. The tour has also faced political backlash for imagery like an overlaid swastika and logistical issues, including the cancellation of planned Australian dates amid concerns about market viability and ticket sales.

U.S. and South Korean militaries said initial equipment for the Terminal High-Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system has arrived in South Korea, coming a day after North Korea test-fired four ballistic missiles toward waters near Japan. THAAD, intended to intercept short- and medium-range ballistic missiles in their terminal phase using hit-to-kill interceptors and powerful X-band radar, is to be deployed this year to bolster defense against North Korean threats; some South Korean reports say it could be operational as early as April. Washington and Seoul insist the system is defensive, but China and Russia strongly oppose deployment, arguing THAAD’s radar could undermine their strategic deterrents. China warned it will take “necessary measures” and said the U.S. and South Korea will bear consequences; Beijing’s criticism has coincided with apparent economic and popular pressure—such as protests and restrictions affecting Lotte, which offered a site for THAAD, and reported curbs on Chinese tour groups to South Korea. North Korea framed its missile launches as retaliation for U.S.-South Korean military exercises and its state media emphasized readiness to strike perceived U.S. and South Korean “aggressors.” The launches, described by Seoul as upgraded Scud-type missiles reaching about 1,000 km, prompted regional concern and emergency diplomatic consultations; U.S. Pacific Command called the launches proof of the prudence of deploying THAAD. Domestic opposition in South Korea also persists over safety and the system becoming a target.

A large study of more than 91,000 women in the Nurses’ Health Study II found that drinking alcohol between a girl’s first menstrual period and her first pregnancy is linked to higher risks of proliferative benign breast disease (BBD) and breast cancer later in life. Researchers reported an 11% increase in breast cancer risk for every 10 grams of alcohol per day (about six drinks per week) compared with nondrinkers; about one drink daily raised BBD risk by roughly 16%. The risk rose with greater consumption and was independent of drinking after the first pregnancy. Longer intervals between menarche and first pregnancy showed stronger associations. Investigators caution the results show association, not causation, but suggest breast tissue is especially vulnerable before first pregnancy. Authors recommend moderation—reducing intake to less than one drink daily, especially before first pregnancy, to help lower breast cancer risk.

President Trump used a North Dakota rally to cast Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy’s retirement as a pivotal reason for Republicans to hold the Senate this fall. Speaking in Fargo while campaigning for Republican Kevin Cramer against Democratic Sen. Heidi Heitkamp, Trump framed Senate control as “one of the vital issues of our time,” stressing that a GOP majority is essential to confirm a conservative Kennedy successor who could shape the court for decades. He praised Kennedy as a “very special guy,” said he was honored Kennedy retired during his term, and vowed to pick a nominee with “intellect” who might serve 40-plus years.

Trump accused Heitkamp of opposing his future court selections, asserting she would vote “no” on any pick despite her earlier vote to confirm Neil Gorsuch. He portrayed Heitkamp as aligned with national Democratic leaders like Chuck Schumer and Nancy Pelosi and suggested that her occasional bipartisan votes were exceptions rather than a pattern. Heitkamp responded that she answers to North Dakotans, not party leaders or the president, and emphasized her willingness to work across the aisle.

Kennedy’s departure gives the White House an opportunity to shift the Supreme Court’s balance and places pressure on vulnerable red-state Democrats—Heitkamp, Joe Manchin and Joe Donnelly—whose prior Gorsuch votes mark them as potential swing votes on a new nominee. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell signaled he wants a confirmation vote before the midterms, heightening stakes for control of the Senate, currently 51–49 for Republicans with a slim working majority given Sen. John McCain’s absence.

The Democratic National Committee contacted the FBI after detecting what it believed was a sophisticated attempt to breach its voter database, alerting federal authorities amid heightened concerns about election-related cyber threats. Early Tuesday the DNC was notified by a cloud provider and a security research firm that a fake login page had been created to capture usernames and passwords for Votebuilder, the widely used service that houses the party’s voter file. The DNC, the companies that detected the operation, and officials said the activity was blocked and believed to be a thwarted attempt to harvest credentials. The DNC called its voter file “the party’s most sensitive information,” and chief security officer Bob Lord warned the episode illustrated ongoing threats as the nation approaches midterm elections. The incident sits alongside broader patterns of interference: Microsoft reported hackers linked to Russian intelligence targeted the Senate and conservative think tanks with fake websites, and Facebook recently disclosed a political influence operation aimed at disrupting elections while uncovering additional global disinformation efforts. Cybersecurity experts note a shift in tactics from stealing secrets to using cyber tools to project national power and manipulate political systems. The episode, plus repeated influence operations and attempted breaches of institutions, underlines how vulnerable many election-related systems are—from state voter-registration databases to party infrastructure—creating plentiful opportunities for foreign and domestic manipulation.

A tourist ferry carrying roughly 170 people capsized Sunday on the Guatape reservoir near Medellín, Colombia, killing nine and leaving about 28 people unaccounted for, officials said. The four‑story vessel, named El Almirante, sank rapidly—survivors and bystanders said it went under in about four minutes—prompting firefighters, air force crews and local recreational boaters and jet ski operators to rush in and pull people from the water. Dramatic videos showed passengers crawling from the roof as lower decks flooded; a survivor reported those on the first and second floors were submerged immediately. Authorities reported 99 people rescued and another 40 who reached shore on their own and were in good condition. Early accounts suggested the boat may have been overloaded and that passengers were not wearing life vests, but investigators had not determined the exact cause. Rescue teams set up a shore center and called for scuba divers to aid searches; officials struggled to confirm the exact passenger count and asked relatives to report. The reservoir, famous for the rocky El Peñol outcrop, was crowded for a holiday weekend. Reports included heartbreaking scenes at hospitals, such as a rescued infant whose mother remained missing. AP reporters Christine Armario and Joshua Goodman contributed to the coverage.

A day of largely peaceful Occupy Oakland protests, including a mass march that shut down the Port of Oakland, devolved into violent confrontations after midnight when a smaller group occupied a vacant building, smashed windows, set fires and erected barricades. Police, responding after attempts to contain vandalism, used tear gas and flash-bang grenades and arrested dozens. At least four protesters were hospitalized and several officers suffered minor injuries. Organizers hailed the daytime general strike and port shutdown—about 7,000 people participated—as a significant statement against economic inequality, drawing solidarity demonstrations nationwide. But attendees were divided over late-night tactics: some condemned the vandalism and tried to extinguish fires, while masked militants defended drastic actions to draw attention. Officials warned the port closure harmed workers and urged a return to operations. The unrest intensified debates over crowd control, police tactics, protesters’ goals and the movement’s direction.

Angel Gonzalez, 41, walked free after nearly 20 years imprisoned for a 1994 Waukegan rape and abduction that new DNA testing showed he did not commit. Lake County prosecutors moved to vacate his 55‑year conviction after recent analyses detected genetic profiles from two other unidentified men, contradicting the victim’s “show‑up” identification and discrediting a videotaped confession Gonzalez gave after lengthy questioning. The Innocence Project and the Illinois Innocence Project pursued re‑examination of the case; attorneys say investigative flaws, unreliable identification procedures, and inconsistencies in the confession contributed to the wrongful conviction.

Although a judge vacated the rape and kidnapping conviction, Gonzalez remained incarcerated until a separate 1990s conviction for damaging a sink in solitary — a three‑year sentence to run after the rape term — was dismissed in Livingston County. His attorneys argued that conviction arose while he was serving a wrongful sentence and that Gonzalez, who speaks limited English, pleaded guilty without an interpreter. With the property‑damage charge voided and an ICE detainer lifted, Gonzalez was released from Dixon Correctional Center and reunited with family.

Family members described emotional scenes of celebration and practical preparations as they welcomed him home; Gonzalez said he felt alive again and looked forward to painting and learning to adjust to life outside. He had used prison time to earn a diploma, mentor inmates, and develop skills. Prosecutors and Innocence Project lawyers praised the DNA work; Lake County’s state’s attorney Mike Nerheim apologized and acted swiftly, marking a shift from earlier office practices that resisted DNA evidence. Gonzalez’s immigration status and future citizenship prospects remain under review by federal agencies.

Investigators from open-source outlet Bellingcat and partner The Insider say the man named by UK authorities as Ruslan Boshirov — one of two suspects in the March Salisbury Novichok poisoning — is actually Colonel Anatoliy Vladimirovich Chepiga, a decorated GRU (Russian military intelligence) officer awarded the Hero of the Russian Federation in December 2014. Bellingcat’s multi-part probe traced Chepiga from the Far-Eastern Military Command Academy and service with the GRU’s 14th Spetsnaz Brigade in Khabarovsk, where he accrued more than 20 military awards and deployments to Chechnya. Leaked databases and passport extracts tied an Anatoliy Chepiga (born 5 April 1979) to Military Unit 20662 and produced a 2003 passport photo that strongly matches the image released by UK police of “Boshirov.” Investigators conclude Chepiga was relocated to Moscow under the false identity Ruslan Boshirov and worked undercover for years. Bellingcat argues the secretive 2014 state award, given without public decree, likely recognizes clandestine operations — plausibly in eastern Ukraine — and that sending a colonel on such a field mission implies orders from very high levels. Russia’s Kremlin and state media maintain Boshirov is a civilian tourist; Boshirov and his companion “Alexander Petrov” appeared on Russian television denying involvement. UK authorities link the two men to the Skripal attack and a later Amesbury exposure that killed Dawn Sturgess; European arrest warrants and Interpol notices have been issued, while Russia refuses to extradite its nationals. The BBC says there is no dispute over the identification.

The Fourth Kind, written and directed by Olatunde Osunsanmi and starring Milla Jovovich, Elias Koteas and Will Patton, presents itself as a re-enactment of “real” alien abductions in Nome, Alaska. Jovovich plays Dr. Abigail Tyler, an Alaska psychologist whose hypnotized patients report nocturnal terrors: a smiling owl omen, levitations, memory gaps and invasive procedures by off-world beings. The film intercuts dramatized scenes with supposedly archived, grainy footage of contorting patients and interview segments with a hollow-eyed “real” Tyler, while Bulgaria doubles for Alaska. Borrowing heavily from found-footage hits like The Blair Witch Project and Paranormal Activity, it delivers occasional effective scares and a strong, deadpan performance from Jovovich. Yet the faux-documentary conceit, obvious fake footage and awkward hybrid structure often pull viewers out of the story. Will Patton’s over-the-top sheriff and other flourishes can’t fully compensate, leaving the movie an uneven, sometimes compelling but ultimately unconvincing horror entry.

Heather McGill, wife of Alabama State Sen. Shadrack McGill (R-Woodville), posted an outspoken message on her husband’s official Facebook page accusing multiple women—some possibly fake—of repeatedly soliciting him online and sending explicit photos while their children might see. Declaring she had remained silent too long, she vowed to protect her family, warned the women they would be publicly named before being “unfriended,” and framed her actions as a moral, faith-driven duty to strengthen marriages and families. The post gained traction and support online.

Sen. McGill told AL.com the post reflected frustrations dating back to his 2010 campaign, when two strippers reportedly arrived at his home late at night and other incidents occurred—women handing out strip-club business cards and strangers allegedly hijacking his Facebook to send half-naked photos and false messages claiming intimacy. He said Heather and a secretary typically manage his account and praised his wife’s boldness, acknowledging concern that such behavior could worsen during campaign season. McGill said he might delete his Facebook if the platform’s moral problems continue. Heather’s post had drawn hundreds of likes and supportive comments by midday Tuesday.

Ohio State and the NCAA announced suspensions for six players after an investigation found they accepted discounted tattoo services and sold team memorabilia to a local tattoo-parlor owner beginning in 2009. Star quarterback Terrelle Pryor, receiver DeVier Posey, running back Dan Herron, left tackle Mike Adams and defensive end Solomon Thomas each will miss the first five games of 2011 and must repay charities between $1,000 and $2,500 for rings, awards and discounts; linebacker Jordan Whiting will miss one game and pay $150. All six are allowed to play in the Jan. 4 Sugar Bowl. OSU plans to appeal the suspensions; the school acknowledged shortcomings in educating players about rules.

Three months after Amanda Berry forced open a door and freed herself and two other captives, former school bus driver Ariel Castro was sentenced in Cleveland for abducting, imprisoning and repeatedly raping three women over roughly a decade. Castro pleaded guilty to 937 counts, including kidnapping, rape and aggravated murder related to forced miscarriages, in a deal that removed the death penalty. Judge Michael Russo imposed life without parole plus an additional 1,000 years, ordered forfeiture of property and fined Castro $100,000.

Prosecutors and law-enforcement witnesses described a makeshift prison in Castro’s 1,400-square-foot house on Seymour Avenue: rooms reconfigured to hide victims, windows boarded from the inside, removed doorknobs and multiple locks, an alarm on the back door, chains bolted to walls and poles, plastic toilets rarely emptied and severe deprivation of food. FBI and local detectives recounted diaries kept by the women that documented years of forced sexual conduct, beatings, confinement in dark rooms, and hope for escape. Detectives testified each woman was lured by Castro—who used the names of his children or family acquaintances to gain trust—then chained within hours of abduction and assaulted vaginally, orally and anally.

The victims—Michelle Knight (abducted 2002 at age 20), Amanda Berry (2003, age 16) and Gina DeJesus (2004, age 14)—endured repeated pregnancies; one victim suffered five forced miscarriages after Castro beat her. He fathered a daughter with Berry, who was born in 2006; prosecutors asked that Castro never see the child. Authorities also described episodes in which Castro forced the women to play Russian roulette, paid them after rapes only to demand money back, and attended vigils held for missing women while his captives were hidden under his roof.

At sentencing Knight directly addressed Castro, telling him he had taken 11 years of her life and that she would live on while he would “die a little every day.” Mental-health experts described the survivors’ resilience amid severe, prolonged trauma and concluded Castro showed no psychiatric disorder that excused his crimes. Castro attempted to minimize his conduct in a disjointed statement—calling himself “sick,” insisting he had not tortured them and begging for forgiveness—comments the judge and prosecutors rejected. Castro was immediately remanded; he was later found dead in his cell in September. The three survivors have begun rebuilding their lives and publicly thanked the community for support.

Average American weights have climbed sharply since 1960. CDC data show the average U.S. woman now weighs 166.2 pounds—roughly the same as the average American man did in the early 1960s—and the average man has risen from about 166.3 pounds then to 195.5 pounds today, a gain of nearly 30 pounds. Both sexes are also about an inch taller than in 1960, which explains a portion of the increase, but overall weight gain has been substantial: women’s average weight rose about 18.5 percent and men’s about 17.6 percent. Today’s average man roughly equals the mass of 1.5 1960s women; with a mean weight of 195.5 pounds and an average waist near 39.7 inches, male girth has grown noticeably. Women average a 37.5-inch waist and about 166 pounds, up from roughly 140 pounds in 1960.

Obesity is widespread: more than one-third (35.1 percent) of U.S. adults over 20 are classified as obese, and 69 percent are either overweight or obese. Childhood obesity is also a concern, with over 20 percent of 12–19-year-olds and 17.7 percent of 6–11-year-olds considered obese.

Researchers link the trend primarily to poorer diets, increased caloric intake, and reduced physical activity. A 2012 BMC Public Health analysis ranked Americans as the world’s third-heaviest people after Tonga and Micronesia; the average U.S. adult is about 33 pounds heavier than the average French adult and 70 pounds heavier than someone from Bangladesh. That study estimated global adult biomass at 287 million tons in 2005 and suggested that if every country matched U.S. weight distributions, the world would carry roughly 58 million extra tons—highlighting implications for food security and ecological sustainability.

Pulaski County authorities continued a constrained, fact-focused investigation after the body of five-year-old Noah Terry Thomas was recovered from a septic tank on his family’s property in Dublin, Va. The medical examiner has completed the autopsy, but the official cause of death remains pending; authorities say that determination will be crucial to understanding what happened. No arrests, suspects or charges have been announced, and officials have repeatedly urged the public to provide any information or tips. 

Noah was reported missing Sunday after his mother told investigators she last saw him watching cartoons before taking a two-hour nap. A multi-day search covered nearly a 10-mile radius around the home, but a more detailed and “aggressive” search of the property led to the discovery of his body Thursday afternoon. The FBI is assisting with forensic support. Local officials have been guarded in public comments, declining to answer many specific questions about how the septic tank was accessed or whether the death was accidental. Family members have expressed suspicion of foul play; an uncle told the Roanoke Times, “You don’t get in a septic tank by accident. Somebody’s going to pay.” 

The sheriff’s office thanked residents, search teams and media for cooperation and stressed the family is fully cooperating with investigators. A candlelight vigil for Noah was scheduled Friday evening in Pearisburg, and a previously offered $5,000 reward had been publicized during the search. Authorities reiterated they will rely on physical evidence and the autopsy findings rather than speculation as the probe continues.

A Tesco demonstration iPhone 4S startled shoppers when Siri responded to 12-year-old Charlie Le Quesne’s question, “How many people are there in the world?” with a profane insult. Charlie’s mother heard the expletive and, after repeating the question, received the same abusive reply. Store staff suggested the phone had been tampered with: a prankster may have entered the rude phrase as the device owner’s name during setup, causing Siri to speak it. Tesco launched an investigation and sent the handset back to Apple for diagnosis. The incident highlights both Siri’s occasionally cheeky or unsettling responses—documented widely online—and the fragility of demo devices in stores. Previous quirks have included darkly literal replies to requests like “I need to bury a body” and troubling search-result biases, prompting Apple to adjust Siri as it moved from beta to full release. The episode raises questions about where and when the phone was modified: in-store mischief or earlier in the supply chain.

Muqtada al-Sadr’s Shiite movement unexpectedly backed Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki after months of electoral deadlock, potentially breaking the stalemate but alarming the U.S. and other Iraqi factions. The March vote produced no clear majority: secular Shiite Ayad Allawi’s Iraqiya won 91 seats, Maliki 89, and Sadrists 39. Sadrist support could give Maliki a path to reappointment but risks splitting Shiite ranks and alienating Sunnis and secularists. Sadrists demand key ministries and posts, seeking to expand influence and possibly vie for the premiership after U.S. withdrawal. Washington opposes empowering the Iran-aligned Sadrists, worried about security and democratic prospects, while Kurdish blocs remain kingmakers. Negotiations continue.

President Trump sent a personal $25,000 check to the family of Army Cpl. Dillon Baldridge the same day The Washington Post reported Trump had promised the soldier’s father a donation during a June condolence call but had not immediately followed through. The White House confirmed the payment to CNN, with spokeswoman Lindsay Walters calling media scrutiny “disgusting” and asserting the gesture was private and sincere. Press secretary Sarah Sanders also confirmed it was a personal check from Trump. The timing prompted questions because a White House official initially declined to comment but later said the check had been sent and been “in the pipeline” since the president’s conversation with Baldridge’s father. A spokesperson explained that transmitting personal funds when the president interacts with the public can involve a substantial process and multiple agencies; they did not specify which agencies or detail the steps involved. Baldridge, 22, was killed in June by an Afghan police officer. The episode unfolded amid broader controversy over how presidents handle condolence calls: Trump’s exchange with the widow of Sgt. La David Johnson in Niger drew public attention after Rep. Frederica Wilson recounted Trump’s characterization of the fallen soldier, which Trump denied. Separately, Trump has claimed President Obama did not call all families of fallen service members, suggesting reporters ask Chief of Staff John Kelly—who lost his son Robert in Afghanistan in 2010—whether Obama had called him.

The document defends the documentary The Hunting Ground against critics who challenge its portrayal of campus sexual assault and specific cases, asserting the filmmakers’ facts are sound. It details Kamilah Willingham’s account of a January 2011 assault at Harvard Law and the school’s subsequent processes: an independent Fact Finder found the accused, Brandon Winston, not credible and concluded Willingham had not consented; the Harvard Law Administrative Board found sexual misconduct and dismissed Winston. A controversial appeal followed in which faculty overturned those findings amid procedural violations of Title IX guidelines; the U.S. Department of Education later required Harvard Law to change its appeal process. Criminal proceedings in Massachusetts produced indictments and a later conviction on a non-sexual assault charge. The document also summarizes Erica Kinsman’s December 2012 accusation against Jameis Winston at Florida State University, outlining a flawed, delayed investigation by police and FSU, eventual DNA matches, a closed police case, and protracted university proceedings. It cites national studies showing roughly 20–27% of female college students experience unwanted sexual contact. The latter portion covers the public controversy over the film’s airing on CNN, including legal threats from Winston’s attorneys alleging defamation and factual omissions, filmmakers’ rebuttals defending survivors’ accounts, and debate over the film’s accuracy and impact on public discussion of campus sexual assault.

Meteorologist Kyle Hunter, a certified AMS meteorologist with over 20 years’ experience, has sued CBS and Los Angeles stations KCBS and KCAL for age and gender discrimination. Represented by Gloria Allred, Hunter alleges his applications for two prime-time weather positions were ignored or rejected in favor of young, attractive women, despite his qualifications. The suit claims the stations sought to boost male viewership by hiring “sexy newscasters,” even dropping certification requirements to hire less-qualified women. Hunter seeks unspecified and punitive damages plus attorneys’ fees. CBS called the complaint frivolous and based on factual misstatements, saying it will vigorously defend itself. The case may be notable as one of the first male plaintiffs alleging gender discrimination in California broadcast hiring.

Scottish distilleries were stunned when Japan’s Yamazaki Single Malt Sherry Cask 2013 was named the world’s best whisky in Jim Murray’s 2015 World Whisky Bible. Murray awarded the bottling 97.5/100, calling it “near incredible genius” with an “exquisite bold” nose and a finish of “light, teasing spice.” The result marks the first time in the 12-year history of the Whisky Bible that no Scottish malt made the top five and the first time a Japanese whisky took the top spot—an outcome Murray described as a “wake up call” and urged Scots to show “a little dose of humility,” warning many Scottish malts risk being “drab or mediocre.” The best European whisky went to England’s Chapter 14 Not Peated. Only 18,000 bottles of Yamazaki 2013 were produced, available in a few specialist UK shops at about £100, so enthusiasts may need to act fast.

Lois Lowry’s 1993 novel The Giver—an influential, classroom-favorite YA dystopia about a controlled, colorless community—finally reached the screen in Phillip Noyce’s film, but reviewers agree the movie arrives late to a genre it helped inspire. The plot follows Jonas (Brenton Thwaites), a boy in a future society that enforces “Sameness”: no art, no strong emotion, assigned family units and life-long jobs chosen by elders. Jonas is appointed Receiver of Memory, apprenticed to the Giver (Jeff Bridges), who transmits vivid memories of color, love, war and suffering. Those memories awaken Jonas’s conscience and propel him toward choices that challenge the community’s euphemistic cruelties—like the “release” of the old and unwanted infants—and eventually to an escape that shifts the story toward action.

Critics praise certain elements: Bridges’s world-weary gravitas, the striking visual motif of black-and-white shifting into color as Jonas learns, and Noyce’s restraint in avoiding nonstop blockbuster spectacle. The film also introduces young viewers to historical touchstones via the memories—Mandela, Tiananmen—that broaden its moral landscape. Yet many find the adaptation undercooked and familiar amid a glut of YA dystopias (Hunger Games, Divergent, Ender’s Game, Maze Runner). Performances are often muted or underwritten—Meryl Streep’s Chief Elder is wasted, Katie Holmes plays a rigid mother with little nuance, Taylor Swift’s cameo is unnecessary—and the screenplay compresses complex ideas into blunt, heavy-handed imagery. Some sequences with memory-transfers feel rushed, while a late third-act chase trades ambiguity for conventional action. Overall, reviewers describe The Giver as earnest and often visually appealing but ultimately bland and less resonant than its source: a talented cast and crucial themes weighed down by predictability and a failure to fully realize the novel’s subtle moral ambiguity.

Jacksonville International Airport was closed for nearly five hours Tuesday evening after police discovered two suspicious packages, one described as having a “destructive nature” that required offsite deactivation by a bomb squad. The terminal and adjacent parking garage were evacuated shortly after 6 p.m.; officials would not say which package was the dangerous one or confirm media reports of arrests. Incoming aircraft were held on the tarmac, stranding passengers until buses could take them to offsite hotels. At least one plane preparing to depart was grounded and no flights were allowed to take off during the closure. After the airport reopened around 11 p.m., individual airlines began work to resume operations and reunite passengers with their luggage. Passengers reported confusion and delays but said they remained calm; one bus reportedly arrived around 9:30 p.m. to transport disembarking travelers. Associated Press writers in Miami and Atlanta contributed.

In early May, Sadiya in Upper Assam was beset by an unexpected outbreak of aggressive spiders that descended on villagers during a Bihu festival, biting scores and causing panic. Two people—a resident, Purnakanta Buragohain, and a schoolboy—died after alleged bites, while many others sought hospital care; accounts mention victims first consulting witch doctors, possibly worsening outcomes. Hospital staff lacked antivenom, equipment and power reliability. Scientists from Dibrugarh and Gauhati universities collected specimens; preliminary assessments describe a theraphosid-like spider, possibly similar to tarantulas (genera such as Selenocosmia or Lyrognathus) or related to funnel-webs or the black wishbone, but identification and venom toxicity tests remain pending. Experts note the species is unusually aggressive and nocturnal, and the swarm behavior is puzzling—potentially tied to environmental anomalies or accidental introduction and hybridization. Specimens were sent to the Indian Society of Arachnology; without definitive identification or a visiting arachnologist, officials’ responses have been criticized as inadequate, leaving residents anxious and questions unresolved.

French air strikes and the deployment of French troops have forced Islamist militants to withdraw from several northern Malian towns, but the insurgents struck back by seizing the western town of Diabaly, underscoring the scale and complexity of the campaign to restore state control. Over nearly ten months the Islamist groups—Ansar Dine, MUJAO and affiliates of al‑Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM)—had imposed harsh Islamic law across northern Mali, committing atrocities and destroying cultural heritage. French Rafale and Mirage jets, supported by helicopters and roughly 650 French soldiers on the ground (with more troops en route), launched strikes on militant strongholds including Timbuktu, Gao and Douentza; residents reported militants had withdrawn ahead of bombardments, calling it a “tactical retreat.” Local and French sources reported dozens to over a hundred militants killed in the initial days of operations.

Despite those setbacks for the insurgents, they mounted counter‑attacks in areas beyond immediate French control. Diabaly, about 400 km north of the capital Bamako and home to a key army base, fell to Islamist forces after heavy fighting and amid reports of Malian army shortages and defections. France’s defense minister described the western front as “difficult,” with militants well‑armed and mobile. The clashes have produced civilian displacement and casualties; Médecins Sans Frontières reported wounded unable to reach care and hundreds fleeing toward Mauritania.

Paris secured broad international and regional backing for the intervention. The UN Security Council expressed unanimous support; France sought to accelerate deployment of a UN‑mandated West African force of 3,300, to be led by Nigeria with contributions pledged by several African states. The US, UK, Canada and others offered logistical, intelligence and transport assistance. Algeria closed its long desert border to curb militant movement. France framed the operation as urgent to prevent a terrorist safe haven at Europe’s doorstep and said its involvement would be limited in duration, though analysts cautioned that freeing towns would be only the start: militants could shift to insurgency tactics, use child soldiers and create urban traps, making a drawn‑out counterinsurgency likely. The crisis followed a March coup that weakened Mali’s army and enabled militants—some battle‑hardened returnees from Libya—to seize the north, exposing limits of prior Western training and regional containment plans.

Researchers at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute are describing a newly recognized, irresistibly cute deep‑sea octopus in the genus Opisthoteuthis. Collected from Monterey Bay as far back as 1990, the gelatinous, roughly seven‑inch umbrella‑shaped animal has distinctive webbed arms, large “puppy‑dog” eyes, and steers by spreading its web and using mantle fins. Initially lumped with the pink flapjack octopus (Opisthoteuthis californiana), careful study revealed key differences. Postdoc Stephanie Bush hopes to formally name it—she’s proposed Opisthoteuthis adorabilis—though the formal taxonomic process will take years of analysis, publication and specimen deposition.

At the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia, Hillary Clinton accepted the nomination as the first female major-party presidential candidate, emphasizing community, cooperation, and “Stronger Together” while sharply criticizing Donald Trump’s temperament, business record, and nationalist rhetoric. Her hour-long speech contrasted collective responsibility with Trump’s “I alone can fix it” claim, outlined policy proposals—debt-free college, immigration and campaign finance reform, and a stronger safety net—and sought to unite Democrats, progressives, veterans, and disaffected Republicans into a broad coalition.

Three law enforcement agencies searched for 19‑year‑old Aftab M. Aslam of Johns Creek after his family reported him missing on April 27. Aslam, described as 5'10", 165 pounds with medium-length black hair, was reported missing from his parents’ Morton Crossing home after they received an early‑morning text claiming he had been kidnapped. Johns Creek Police responded and, with assistance from the FBI and the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, traced the phone that sent the message and determined Aslam had purchased the device and that no one else had handled it. Investigators concluded the text likely originated from Aslam himself. Authorities asked the public to contact Det. James Harris with any information. On Sunday evening around 9 p.m., Aslam returned home unharmed and told investigators he left voluntarily for personal reasons. Investigators are verifying his account; no charges have been filed. The case remains under review as officials confirm details surrounding his disappearance and the circumstances of the text message.

Search teams found a metal object on Australia’s southwest coast but detailed photos convinced investigators it was not from Malaysia Airlines Flight 370. The piece, found near Augusta about 1,000 miles from the suspected crash zone, had been treated as an “object of interest” but was ruled not a lead after examination. The underwater hunt in the southern Indian Ocean has been painstaking and often frustrating: the Bluefin-21 autonomous sub has scanned more than 90% of the designated seabed area and began its 12th mission, but nothing identifiable has been found. Searchers regularly encounter debris, garbage, jellyfish and fishing gear, complicating efforts. Bad weather and false leads have hampered air and sea searches; up to 11 military aircraft and 11 ships continue operations. Authorities say they will not abandon the search and are planning longer-term strategies, possibly expanding the search corridor and deploying deeper, longer-range sonar like deep-towed systems used to find Titanic. If flight recorders are recovered, Australia has the technical ability to decode them, but Malaysia leads the official investigation.

Researchers reexamining Liang Bua cave on Flores, Indonesia, have revised the timeline for Homo floresiensis, the diminutive hominin nicknamed "hobbits." Discovered in 2003, these individuals stood about 1.1 meters tall, weighed roughly 35 kg, made stone tools, and coexisted with fauna such as pygmy elephants and Komodo dragons. Early analyses suggested they survived until about 12,000 years ago, raising the possibility of encounters with modern humans. New, more extensive excavations and five independent dating methods (including uranium-series and luminescence dating) show the skeletal remains are far older—likely between 100,000 and 60,000 years old—while stone-tool use at the site extends from around 190,000 to 50,000 years ago. The discrepancy arose because erosion created a sloped surface filled by younger sediments near the cave entrance, misleading initial stratigraphic interpretations.

The revised chronology implies H. floresiensis probably disappeared before or shortly after Homo sapiens arrived in the region (~50,000 years ago), making direct interaction possible but not certain. Explanations for their extinction include competition or impact from modern humans, environmental upheaval (climate shifts, volcanic activity), or collapse of key prey populations such as pygmy Stegodon. Debates remain about the species’ origins—whether island dwarfing from Homo erectus or descent from an earlier hominin—and about alternative diagnoses (pathological modern humans). Unique wrist anatomy and other traits support recognition as a distinct species. Continued excavation on Flores is expected to clarify their evolution, behavior, and the causes of their extinction.

The NFL broke with decades of tradition for Super Bowl 50, announcing it will use the Arabic numeral "50" in its main logo instead of the Roman numeral "L." League VP of brand and creative Jaime Weston said the change is a one-year exception driven by design concerns—the standalone "L" did not work visually—after 73 logo iterations since design work began in April 2013. Two official logos were produced for the Feb. 7, 2016 game at Levi's Stadium: a national and a regional version. Both feature the gold "50" to highlight the game’s golden anniversary and California’s nickname, and both include the Lombardi Trophy, part of the Super Bowl identity since 2010. The regional mark also depicts Levi’s Stadium and San Francisco landmarks. The NFL tested the design in situ on Wilson footballs and a painted field. The league stressed Roman numerals will return for Super Bowl LI in Houston in 2017.

Former Massachusetts state senator Brian A. Joyce was arrested and federally indicted on more than 100 counts alleging he used his legislative office for private gain. The 102-page indictment accuses the 55-year-old Democrat of racketeering, wire fraud, extortion, money laundering and related offenses tied to schemes dating back to about 2010. Prosecutors say Joyce accepted a “stream of concealed bribes and kickbacks” — allegedly including up to $1 million in payments, a Jeep, hundreds of pounds of Dunkin’ Donuts coffee and other benefits — in exchange for official actions, pressuring local officials and promoting legislation favorable to benefactors. Authorities allege he laundered illicit proceeds through his Canton law practice and a shell company, mischaracterizing payments as legal or consulting fees and using sham retirement accounts to hide stock purchases and evade taxes. The indictment details schemes involving an energy brokerage, a Dunkin’ franchisee and developers, among others.
