Joyce pleaded not guilty in federal court and was released on a $250,000 secured bond with travel restrictions and surrender of his passport. His lawyer criticized prosecutorial overreach and noted other public-official prosecutions have failed; Joyce maintains his innocence. State leaders said law enforcement acted appropriately and expressed confidence in the judicial process as the investigation continues.

A Portland mother has filed an $8.6 million wrongful-death lawsuit against Portland Adventist Medical Center, alleging hospital negligence led to the accidental smothering death of her newborn son. Monica Thompson says her son Jacob, born by C-section on Aug. 2, 2012, was healthy and unimpaired when he was taken to the nursery three days later so she could continue recovering. The suit contends that around midnight the hospital gave Thompson a combination of narcotic painkillers (Vicodin) and a sleep aid (Ambien). At about 3 a.m. a nurse returned Jacob to Thompson so she could breastfeed; the nurse then left, leaving the medicated, drowsy mother unsupervised. Approximately an hour later Thompson awoke to find Jacob unresponsive in her arms. Staff performed emergency procedures and Jacob was transferred to Randall Children’s Hospital at Legacy Emanuel Medical Center. He remained on life support and died at ten days old after being withdrawn from life support when brain damage proved irreversible. The complaint alleges the hospital was negligent in medicating a breastfeeding mother, placing the infant in her bed without supervision, and failing to maintain or enforce clear policies about the dangers of bed-sharing when parents are sedated. It seeks compensation for emotional distress, counseling for Thompson’s depression and PTSD, and other damages totaling $8.6 million. The suit was filed by the Conde Law Group of Lake Oswego; the hospital declined to comment pending review. The case highlights concerns about mother–infant bed-sharing and hospital policies after sedating medications.

New research challenges the long‑held idea that yawning supplies oxygen to the brain; instead, studies indicate yawning regulates brain temperature to boost alertness and cognitive efficiency. Austrian researchers from the University of Vienna tested the “thermoregulatory” hypothesis by inducing contagious yawning in pedestrians during summer and winter and comparing results with an earlier Arizona study. Participants viewed images of people yawning and self‑reported whether they yawned. Findings show contagious yawning peaks within a thermal window around 20°C and falls off at temperature extremes: it decreased when ambient temperature neared body temperature (about 37°C in Arizona summer) and also when air was freezing (Vienna winter). That pattern held across climates—Vienna subjects yawned more in summer, Arizonans more in winter—implying ambient temperature, not season or other factors, predicts yawning likelihood. Authors conclude yawning cools the brain via inhalation and heat exchange, improving arousal; when air is too hot or too cold the behavior is unnecessary or potentially harmful. This supports a thermoregulatory function for both spontaneous and contagious yawning and suggests group vigilance may benefit.

The Women’s Convention, organized by the Women’s March and set for Oct. 27–29 in Detroit, aims to convert the energy of the January Women’s March into sustained political action, training and coalition-building. Branded “Reclaiming Our Time” — inspired by Rep. Maxine Waters’ viral rebuke — the three-day event will host more than 60 speakers and expects around 3,000 attendees for workshops, strategy sessions and activist training focused on collective liberation across race, gender identity, ability, immigration status and economic background.

Controversy erupted after organizers announced Senator Bernie Sanders would speak on opening night. Critics argued that having a man open the first national women’s convention in decades undercuts the event’s purpose and optics, asserting that a woman should occupy that marquee role. Emily’s List president Stephanie Schriock and many social media users voiced disappointment; a petition called for a female opener. Organizers, including co-chair Tamika D. Mallory, defended the choice, noting Sanders’ ability to mobilize younger activists and emphasizing that only two men are among the many speakers. Mallory clarified that Rep. Maxine Waters is the event headliner and stressed the convention is led largely by women of color.

Besides Sanders and Waters, announced participants include Piper Perabo, Sally Kohn, Nomiki Konst, Leah Greenberg, Stacey Abrams, Ai-jen Poo, Nina Turner, Gretchen Whitmer and numerous grassroots leaders. Organizers say the convention will combine political focus—building power for the 2018 elections—with educational components to equip new activists. Ticket prices and registration details are available on the convention website. Despite the backlash over the opener, organizers emphasize a broad, woman-led program intended to empower survivors and organizers to tell their stories and organize locally.

In Fort Dodge, Iowa, Rachel and Ben Kohnen were held at gunpoint after refusing to pull over while speeding to the hospital early Tuesday morning. Around 4 a.m., Rachel, in active labor, and her husband were driving at about 85 mph in a 55-mph zone when a Manson officer attempted to stop them. The couple didn’t pull over because the birth was imminent; Rachel later said she feared delivering in the car and was screaming that the baby was coming. They attempted to call 911, but dispatchers reportedly could not understand Rachel amid contractions. The officer called for backup and tire spikes were placed on Highway 7; the couple said all four tires were blown out, forcing them to stop. Officers ordered them to the ground and held them at gunpoint until realizing the situation was a medical emergency. Police then rushed Rachel to a nearby hospital, and about an hour later she delivered their fourth child, Hazel, a nearly 10-pound baby who is doing well. No charges have been filed yet; the county attorney will decide whether any will be pursued. The police chief advised calling ahead when possible to avoid similar incidents.

The Vatican reiterated its opposition to gay adoption and same-sex marriage after Italy’s Court of Cassation ruled it was “mere prejudice” to assume children fare worse with homosexual parents. L’Osservatore Romano published an editorial asserting the ideal child-rearing environment is a monogamous union of masculine and feminine parenthood, arguing no one has a “right” to children as claimed by gay couples. The stance came amid wider protests: in St. Peter’s Square four topless Femen activists painted with slogans like “In Gay We Trust” disrupted Pope Benedict’s Angelus, provoking angry reactions and swift police removal. The demonstration coincided with massive protests in Paris against French plans to legalize same-sex marriage and adoption, where Catholic leaders oppose the reforms and the Vatican has voiced support for that opposition.

The State Department’s travel arm sparked backlash after a poorly phrased Twitter warning intended to caution Americans about overseas scams. The @TravelGov account posted a tweet reading, “Not a ‘10’ in the US? Then not a 10 overseas,” implying travelers shouldn’t be flattered into buying expensive drinks or falling victim to robbery. Many users called the message sexist, objectifying and patronizing. Travel Bureau staff initially defended the post, saying the warning applied to anyone and that the intent wasn’t to “neg” people but to alert travelers to scam artists. The tweet drew ridicule and parody accounts mocking its tone. Facing mounting criticism, the department deleted the tweet and issued a two-part apology, saying it regretted offending people and reiterating that it aims to warn Americans to be careful while traveling. The incident followed other @TravelGov advisories during spring break, including a previous warning about contests offering “free luggage” that was actually filled with cocaine. The episode underscored sensitivity around government social-media messaging and the risks of ill-judged attempts at humor.

A top-secret presidential directive signed by President Barack Obama, revealed by the Guardian, orders senior national security and intelligence officials to prepare a list of potential overseas targets for Offensive Cyber Effects Operations (OCEO). The 18-page Presidential Policy Directive 20, issued in October, frames cyber operations as tools that can achieve U.S. national objectives with effects ranging from subtle to severely damaging, and mandates agencies to identify systems and infrastructure against which the U.S. should establish and maintain offensive cyber capabilities. While stressing compliance with U.S. and international law and requiring presidential approval for actions likely to have significant consequences, the directive allows emergency domestic operations without prior presidential sign-off and authorizes nonconsensual strikes abroad when U.S. national interests require anticipatory action. The document urges weighing impacts such as loss of life, retaliation, damage to property, intelligence implications, and threats to internet stability. Its publication coincides with diplomatic talks between Obama and China’s Xi Jinping, intensifying debate as China denies hypocrisy and accuses the U.S. of similar hacking. The directive follows prior U.S. cyber initiatives including Stuxnet and Pentagon expansion of Cyber Command under Gen. Keith Alexander. Administration spokespeople emphasize restraint, prioritizing defense and law enforcement, while privacy advocates and researchers warn offensive cyber operations risk escalation into kinetic conflict.

In an exclusive ABC News interview, President Obama downplayed Arizona Gov. Jan Brewer’s account of a tense tarmac encounter, joking he’s often accused of being “too relaxed.” Brewer had called him “thin-skinned” and “a little tense,” and in her book criticized his manner and White House staff. Obama described the meeting as a minor matter blown out of proportion and said he agreed to meet after receiving her letter.

Turning to his re-election stance, Obama signaled an aggressive campaign posture, saying he will “fight with every fiber” to win because the country needs his leadership. He criticized GOP contenders—Mitt Romney, Newt Gingrich and Rick Santorum—arguing their policies of lower taxes and lighter regulation contributed to the financial crash and job losses, and rejecting rhetoric like Gingrich’s “food stamp president” label. Obama defended expanding safety-net programs amid economic crisis and advocated higher taxes on the wealthy to fund investments and deficit reduction rather than cutting benefits for seniors or students.

He said Michelle Obama is eager to campaign; their daughters remain focused on normal childhood concerns. On Iran, Obama reiterated sanctions and diplomacy remain priorities while keeping military options available but declined to discuss classified matters.

Actor Mark Wahlberg has formally petitioned the Massachusetts Board of Pardons to erase a decades-old assault conviction stemming from a violent 1988 incident in Dorchester, when he was 16. In a Nov. 26 application, Wahlberg admits he tried to steal two cases of alcohol outside a convenience store on April 8, 1988, struck a man, Thanh Lam, over the head with a wooden stick and, while fleeing police, punched another man. He acknowledges being under the influence of alcohol and narcotics that night and having a small amount of marijuana when detained. Tried as an adult, he was convicted of assault after facing more severe charges, served 45 days of a 90-day sentence, and the attack left Lam blind in one eye; reports also documented racial slurs used during the assault.

Wahlberg expresses deep remorse in the petition and frames the pardon as recognition that he has changed. He details more than two decades of public acknowledgment of his past, steady church attendance, and extensive charitable work: founding the Mark Wahlberg Youth Foundation, supporting the Dorchester Boys and Girls Club, renovating a local gym, and funding programs for children with cancer through One Mission. He stresses his philanthropy is not meant to erase his history but to show redemption is possible and to serve as an example to his children and at-risk youth. Practically, a pardon would facilitate business plans—such as obtaining concessionaire’s licenses for Wahlburgers expansions—and enable him to better partner with law enforcement and youth programs.

The Board of Pardons must investigate and may hold a public hearing before recommending action to the governor and governor’s council; any decision could take time and a change in the governor’s office. Observers note Wahlberg’s sustained public service and say a pardon would formally recognize his rehabilitation.

Nestle has failed to persuade the European Court of Justice that the four‑finger shape of its KitKat bar should be registrable as a trademark in the UK. The EU court held that Nestle must prove consumers identify the product by shape alone, not by the shape together with other branding such as the KitKat name. Judges noted trademark protection is inappropriate where a shape “contains three essential features, one of which results from the nature of the goods and two necessary to obtain a technical result.” That makes it difficult to show distinctiveness if other marks are used on the product.

The ruling stems from Nestle’s 2010 UK application and a broader legal battle with Cadbury that has lasted more than a decade. Cadbury opposed the application, arguing the shape is not distinctive; it welcomed the EU decision. Nestle also faces a separate challenge to a 2006 EU trademark for the same shape. The case will return to the UK High Court for a final ruling. Both parties described themselves as pleased with the outcome.

Analysts expect Nestle to press on with its arguments—its history includes prolonged efforts to register hard‑fought marks, such as the “Have a Break” slogan, registered after more than 40 years. A successful Nestle registration would have barred rivals from producing similar four‑finger bars; similar products like Norway’s Kvikk Lunsj, marketed in parts of the UK, underscore competitive concerns. The dispute highlights limits on protecting product shapes under European trademark law.

At a Nuclear Security Summit in Washington on April 1, 2016, President Barack Obama warned world leaders that nuclear terrorism remains a grave, evolving threat and urged stronger measures to secure vulnerable nuclear materials and facilities. Citing recent attacks by Islamic State and the discovery that attackers had videotaped a Belgian nuclear plant manager, Obama warned that if extremist “madmen” obtained fissile material or a bomb, they would use it to kill large numbers and “change our world.” More than 50 leaders attended his fourth and final summit on the issue, where participants reviewed progress — including the ratification by 102 countries of a treaty amendment tightening protections against theft and smuggling and the removal by the U.S. and Japan of highly enriched uranium and separated plutonium from a Japanese reactor. Leaders agreed to bolster protections against cyberattacks, a growing vulnerability, but outcomes were largely technical rather than transformative, in part because Russia boycotted the U.S.-hosted gathering amid tensions over Ukraine and Syria. Obama defended the Iran nuclear deal as a major diplomatic success and convened P5+1 talks to review its implementation. He also pressed allies to increase pressure on North Korea after recent tests. With his presidency ending soon, Obama acknowledged the summit’s achievements but warned that momentum could slow under his successor, and he criticized presidential candidate Donald Trump’s suggestion that allies should develop nuclear arsenals.

Katie Couric appeared on Watch What Happens Live with Andy Cohen on May 1 to address the resurfacing of earlier comments about her former Today show co-anchor Matt Lauer after his 2017 firing for alleged inappropriate sexual behavior. A 2012 clip of Couric joking on the show that Lauer “pinches me on the ass a lot” trended when the scandal broke; Couric told Cohen the remark was a joke she now regrets because it was misconstrued. On The Wendy Williams Show the same day, Couric described the episode as painful for people who worked with and cared about Lauer, noting she personally was always treated “respectfully and appropriately.” She said she does not know the full extent of the allegations and suggested the scope may be larger than publicly known, while also criticizing some reporting as blown out of proportion. Couric disputed sensational claims—like reports of a button under Lauer’s desk used for locking a door—calling such perks a common executive convenience rather than a nefarious setup. She acknowledged her past jokes about Lauer’s behavior, apologized for them, and observed that any potential comeback for him would be challenging; Lauer has denied coercive or abusive actions.

Michael Bay’s Pain & Gain is vintage Bay—loud, muscular and aggressive—yet comparatively modest: no cities blown to bits, but still a grisly true-crime tale pumped with steroid-fueled bravado. Based on Pete Collins’s Miami New Times articles and scripted by Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely, the film opens with a chaotic police chase that flashes back into two hours of sweat, blood, crude humor and voice-over musings on Jesus, fitness and the American dream. Mark Wahlberg stars as Daniel Lugo, a personal trainer and ex-con with a brittle mix of entitlement and self-pity who believes the universe owes him wealth, women and status. Influenced by a self-help guru (Ken Jeong), Daniel recruits fellow gym rats Adrian (Anthony Mackie) and Paul (Dwayne Johnson) after identifying wealthy client Victor Kershaw (Tony Shalhoub) as a ticket out of “palookaville.” Rather than a straightforward ransom, they choose torture to force Victor to sign over his assets. The plot compresses events but stays close to the absurd, idiotic criminality and sloppy police work chronicled by Collins, leaving viewers unsure whether they are watching a monumentally stupid film or a sharp portrait of stupidity itself. Mackie brings frantic nuttiness tempered with reason to Adrian, while Johnson balances hulking menace and surprising vulnerability, finding both humor and soul even amid grotesque moments—like roasting severed hands on a grill. The film’s moral ambiguity and dark comedy hinge on its characters’ delusions of grandeur and Bay’s relentless, pumped-up style.

Sombra, a six-year-old German shepherd with Colombia’s National Police counter-narcotics unit, has been relocated and given extra protection after intelligence revealed a substantial bounty placed on her by the Urabeños (also called the Úsuga or Gulf Clan). The gang reportedly offered between 20 million and 200 million Colombian pesos (about $7,000–$70,000) for her capture or death after she sniffed out roughly nine to ten tonnes of their cocaine across multiple high-profile seizures. Sombra’s finds have included 5.3 tonnes in Turbo and several multi-ton shipments concealed in exports and auto parts, culminating in at least 245 arrests and more than 300 operations. Her successes have made her a public face of Colombia’s drug-fighting effort—honored with medals, featured on television, and a magnet for selfies—but that visibility has also made her a target. Because the Urabeños dominate trafficking along the northwest coast and remain led by fugitive boss Dairo Antonio Úsuga (“Otoniel”), police moved Sombra from the Urabá/Turbo region to El Dorado International Airport in Bogotá, outside the gang’s main area of control. In Bogotá she continues to work alongside her handler but now is accompanied by additional officers to improve security. Authorities say the bounty underscores the financial damage her detections have inflicted on traffickers; police stress she remains calm and friendly with the public while being relentless in detecting illicit drugs.

Nine-year-old Zianna Oliphant moved a national audience when she spoke tearfully at a Charlotte City Council forum about racism and policing after the police shooting of Keith Lamont Scott. Zianna, a fourth-grader, said her decision to speak was spontaneous: she was nervous but felt compelled to “tell them how I feel.” Watching news coverage of the shooting and subsequent protests with her mother, Precious Oliphant, the child said she cried because her words felt powerful and true to her experience.

At the meeting, Zianna and her brother Marquis joined other members of Charlotte’s black community calling for changes in how police treat African Americans. Zianna told council members that black people “shouldn’t have to feel like this” and stressed that protests arise from a need to assert rights in the face of mistreatment. She clarified the group’s stance: “It’s not hate. We don’t hate the police. We hate how we are treated by the police, how we are targeted by the police.” Her remarks included a heartbreaking recognition of loss and fear: she lamented that families must bury fathers and mothers and that children shouldn’t have to shed such tears.

Precious Oliphant said she was proud but saddened to have to educate her children about discrimination. She noted that despite involvement in a police youth league—where officers serve as positive role models—her family has experienced what she views as discriminatory stops for trivial reasons like hairstyle. The forum took place amid protests sparked by Scott’s death and questions about whether deadly force was warranted; some attendees demanded the police chief’s and mayor’s resignations. Zianna, who aspires to be a doctor, said she isn’t shy about speaking up and wanted to make her feelings known to city leaders. Her speech drew applause and chants of “No justice, no peace.”

On a muggy Fourth of July outside Austin, Rep. Beto O’Rourke appeared at Willie Nelson’s long-running Fourth of July Picnic, drawing both loud cheers and boos. O’Rourke used the stage to stress that America need not fear immigrants, Muslims or those who seem different, praising Texas’ strength and invoking Nelson and fellow musician Ray Benson as sources of joy during dark times. After speaking, O’Rourke removed his button-down, picked up a guitar and joined Nelson and his band for spirited renditions of “Roll Me Up and Smoke Me When I Die” and “Will the Circle Be Unbroken.” The appearance underscored Nelson’s decades-long willingness to take liberal stances uncommon in country music—supporting causes from environmentalism to same-sex marriage and marijuana legalization—and his past endorsements of figures including Barack Obama, Bernie Sanders and Hillary Clinton.

Nelson later announced he would headline a Sept. 29 concert and rally for O’Rourke in Austin’s Auditorium Shores, joined by artists including Joe Ely, Carrie Rodriguez, Tameca Jones and Nelson’s sons Lukas and Micah; Leon Bridges was later confirmed. The free event requires RSVP through O’Rourke’s site. Nelson’s press release said he and his wife Annie have met O’Rourke and share concerns about the country’s direction, praising his energy and integrity. The announcement prompted backlash from some fans on social media who called Nelson’s alignment with O’Rourke “socialist” and vowed to boycott shows; others defended Nelson’s right to speak and act politically. The story corrects an earlier line: this is not Nelson’s first public concert for a political candidate. Nelson also has a new album, My Way, releasing on Legacy Recordings, and the July Picnic encore where O’Rourke joined him remains a noted moment in the heated Senate race between O’Rourke and incumbent Ted Cruz.

Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar’s Nobel Peace Prize laureate, began a 17-day European visit — her first to the continent in nearly 25 years — urging foreign governments to withhold their companies from joint ventures with Myanmar’s state oil and gas enterprise until it improves transparency and accountability. Speaking at the ILO in Geneva, she called for adoption of internationally recognized fiscal transparency standards and urged investors to be responsible, linking sound investment to the country’s democratic transition. Suu Kyi praised some firms like Total as sensitive to human rights and environmental concerns and said she would not press Western companies such as Chevron and Total to withdraw. Her trip, which includes Norway, Britain, Ireland and France and will culminate in formally accepting her Nobel Prize, was briefly disrupted when she fell ill and left a Bern press conference after vomiting; an official dinner was canceled though she later attended a reception. She welcomed foreign direct investment that creates jobs but stressed it must support democratisation and prudent energy policy.

A 54-year-old Florida man, David Edward Benes, has been arrested after allegedly restraining his 80-year-old live-in girlfriend and attempting to perform an exorcism to “get the devil out of her.” The Pasco County Sheriff’s Office says the incident began during a fight at their home outside Tampa; the woman reported he held her down, caused bruises and scratches to her arms, removed batteries from the home phones, took her car keys, and sabotaged the garage door to prevent her from leaving or calling for help. Deputies found Benes intoxicated and passed out on a couch; he later claimed he was too drunk to remember events and accused the woman of starting the fight. He faces charges including battery on a person 65 or older, false imprisonment, and tampering with a witness, and is jailed without bail. Records show prior battery convictions and a domestic violence injunction violation.

Arizona’s new abortion restriction, House Bill 2036, takes effect this week and bans most abortions at 20 weeks’ gestation, but defines gestational age from the last menstrual period—effectively prohibiting abortions beginning around 18 weeks, the time many fetal anomalies are first seen on ultrasound. Arizona joins nine other states with 20-week limits, but is unique in pushing the practical cutoff back to 18 weeks. State records show about 100 abortions after 20 weeks annually in Arizona; how many are for fetal anomalies is unclear.

The law also requires doctors to inform women who consider abortion because of fatal fetal defects about perinatal hospice services and requires the state to list organizations that provide support. Two Arizona nonprofits, MISS Foundation and Embrace, offer counseling, birth planning, hands-on support at delivery, mementos, funeral help and extended family services. They rely on volunteers and private donations; the Legislature provided no funding. Leaders fear being overwhelmed by increased demand when abortions for severe anomalies become legally unavailable.

Embrace assists roughly 20 families, offering medical explanation, emotional support, appointment accompaniment, birth-plan coordination, and bereavement care. The article profiles Julia Gonzales, whose baby Carmen was diagnosed at 18 weeks with anencephaly; Gonzales declined abortion for religious reasons and is supported by Embrace in preparing for a likely brief life. Another family whose son had DiGeorge syndrome benefited from Embrace and now has a thriving infant.

A federal judge recently upheld the law as constitutional, citing evidence that fetuses can feel pain by 20 weeks; the Center for Reproductive Rights is appealing. The ruling shifts Arizona’s prior viability-based limit (about 24 weeks) earlier in pregnancy, raising legal and practical questions about access to abortion and the capacity of nonprofits to meet new needs.

Bitcoin briefly climbed back above $9,000 after G-20 finance ministers and central bank governors held “productive” private discussions on cryptocurrency regulation in Buenos Aires, signaling that sweeping crackdowns were unlikely in the short term. At the meeting officials agreed to gather more information and aim for harmonized proposals by July, which helped lift bitcoin more than 4.5% to around $9,000, recovering from a weekend low near $7,336 amid recent ad bans by major tech platforms.

Separately, German researchers from RWTH Aachen and Goethe University published findings that raise a serious legal and ethical challenge for Bitcoin and other immutable blockchains: they identified roughly 1,600 instances of non-financial data embedded in bitcoin’s ledger, including at least eight items of sexual content, one believed to be child sexual abuse imagery, and 274 links to abusive material (142 pointing to dark web services). Because the blockchain is replicated and persistently stored by nodes worldwide, possession of such illegal content could expose users — miners, full-node operators, and others who download the ledger — to criminal liability in jurisdictions where mere possession of child abuse material is punishable. The researchers warn that immutable illegal content could jeopardize blockchain-based systems and major cryptocurrency markets.

The discovery revives earlier warnings (e.g., Interpol in 2015) about malware or illicit material being permanently hosted on blockchains. It also compounds compliance and data-protection tensions, since many countries require deletion rights or criminalize certain content, and because altering or forking a blockchain to remove content is practically and politically fraught. The issue deepens legal uncertainty for global participants in bitcoin’s ecosystem even as markets respond to regulatory developments.

Lois Riess, 56, wanted in Minnesota for the March killing of her husband, David Riess, is now charged in the murder of Pamela Hutchinson, 59, in Fort Myers Beach, Florida. Investigators say Riess targeted Hutchinson because they resembled each other, shot her, and stole her cash, credit cards, ID and white 2005 Acura TL (Florida plate Y37TAA) — a vehicle later spotted in Louisiana and Corpus Christi, Texas. Riess’s own white Cadillac Escalade was found abandoned in a Florida park. Authorities believe Riess befriended women who looked like her to assume their identities; she is considered armed and dangerous. Warrants for murder, grand theft auto and identity theft have been issued in Florida, and Dodge County, Minnesota, has charged her with second-degree murder in her husband’s death. Anyone with information is urged to contact law enforcement.

Despite speculation that Al Gore might enter the 2016 presidential race amid Hillary Clinton’s troubles, advisers say he is not considering a bid. Gore spokeswoman Betsy McManus said he’s “laser-focused on solving the climate crisis.” Reports that supporters were quietly discussing a run were dismissed by close aides and former staffers, who called the chatter Democrats talking among themselves. Gore, who won the 2000 popular vote, has focused on environmental work and business ventures since then. Though some see him as a potential fallback candidate, insiders say a campaign is unlikely.

A 15-year UK study of more than 530,000 women found that having an appendix or tonsils removed was associated with higher pregnancy rates and a shorter time to first pregnancy. Using the Clinical Practice Research Datalink, researchers compared women who underwent appendectomy (54,675), tonsillectomy (112,607), or both (10,340) between 1987 and 2012 with 355,244 matched comparators. During a mean follow-up of about 14.7 years, 54.4% of women after appendectomy, 53.4% after tonsillectomy, and 59.7% after both had pregnancies, compared with 43.7% in the comparator group. Adjusted hazard ratios for subsequent births were 1.34 after appendectomy, 1.49 after tonsillectomy, and 1.43 after both, indicating a cumulative effect when both organs were removed. Time to pregnancy was shortest in women who had both procedures, then appendectomy alone, then tonsillectomy alone. Authors propose two possible explanations: a biological mechanism in which chronically inflamed tonsils or appendix raise systemic inflammation that impairs reproductive function, and a behavioral explanation linking lifestyle or sexual activity to both higher infection rates and pregnancy likelihood. Experts regard the findings as intriguing and potentially informative for future research into fertility mechanisms or treatments but caution against interpreting the association as causal. They emphasize that women should not seek these surgeries to boost fertility, nor should necessary removals be avoided out of fear of harming future fertility. Further research is needed to identify underlying mechanisms and confirm causality before clinical recommendations change.

Bryson DeChambeau dominated the opening FedEx Cup playoff event, The Northern Trust at Ridgewood Country Club, cruising to a four-shot victory and moving atop the FedEx Cup standings. Staked to a four-shot lead in the final round, he never let anyone get closer than two shots, closed with a 2-under 69 and finished at 18-under 266. A critical up-and-down chip from just short of the reachable par-4 12th halted Aaron Wise’s surge and effectively sealed the win. DeChambeau’s victory was his second this year, both against strong fields, and it strengthens his case for a Ryder Cup captain’s pick after narrowly missing automatic qualification; he said he’s “a man on a mission” for both the Ryder Cup and FedEx Cup.

Tony Finau also made a Ryder Cup statement, closing with a 68 to finish solo second and cracking the top 20 in the world at No. 18. Other notable performances: Billy Horschel and Cameron Smith tied for third; Ryan Palmer surged from No. 100 to No. 50 in the standings after a final-round 65; Dustin Johnson birdied the final four holes to preserve his No. 1 world ranking; and six players, including Nick Watney, moved into the top 100 to advance to the next playoff stage.

Tiger Woods struggled for birdies, shot 70 to tie for 40th and declined to engage in political controversy, saying the office of the president deserves respect after briefly discussing his acquaintance with Donald Trump.

President Obama said that recent events—specifically the incidents in Ferguson, Missouri, and the chokehold death of Eric Garner in New York—have heightened public awareness that law enforcement is not always applied in a “colorblind fashion.” He suggested these high-profile cases have prompted a broader national conversation about racial disparities in policing and the criminal justice system. Obama’s remarks acknowledged growing concern among Americans that people of color frequently experience different treatment by police, sparking calls for reform and greater accountability.

The president addressed how these incidents fit into a pattern that many see as systemic rather than isolated, noting that outrage and debate across communities reflect a deeper recognition of unequal application of justice. He emphasized the importance of confronting uncomfortable truths, arguing that acknowledging the problem is a necessary first step toward meaningful change. Obama also indicated that this awareness has catalyzed policy discussions and efforts at multiple levels—local, state, and federal—aimed at improving police practices, increasing transparency, and strengthening community trust.

In highlighting Ferguson and Eric Garner, the president connected public protests and grassroots activism with a broader movement demanding reform. He recognized the pain and frustration expressed by communities affected by police violence and urged constructive engagement between law enforcement and the communities they serve. Obama called for practical reforms such as better training, body cameras, clearer use-of-force standards, and improved data collection to identify and address bias.

Overall, the president framed recent tragedies as a wake-up call that has made Americans more aware of racial inequities in policing, creating momentum for policy changes intended to make law enforcement fairer and more accountable to all citizens.

Over the weekend filmmaker and explorer James Cameron became the first person to make a solo descent to Challenger Deep, the deepest known point in the Mariana Trench, roughly 35,800 feet (nearly 7 miles) beneath the Pacific surface. Piloting his 12-ton, vertical “Deepsea Challenger” submersible, outfitted with 3D cameras and powerful LEDs, Cameron reached the seafloor after a 156-minute descent and intended to spend six hours collecting samples and footage. He surfaced three hours earlier than planned when he noticed hydraulic fluid leaking, losing thrusters and much of the starboard side, and deciding the mission’s diminishing returns and equipment damage warranted an early ascent. The ascent took 70 minutes; he was recovered by helicopter and the support vessel Mermaid Sapphire. Cameron described the seafloor as bleak and moonlike, seeing only a few amphipods and finding limited obvious biology or geological features during the shortened visit. The dive was dangerous—risks included implosion under extreme pressure, hypothermia if stranded, onboard fire from elevated oxygen, contact with superheated hydrothermal vents, and entanglement in seabed cables—but the mission succeeded without catastrophe. National Geographic will document the expedition in 3D, and Cameron suggested future dives may follow.

The Pentagon’s official Twitter account briefly reposted a tweet urging President Donald Trump to resign, then swiftly deleted it and disavowed the action. The retweet came from an account called @proudresister, which criticized several politicians accused of sexual misconduct — including Roy Moore, Al Franken and Trump — and linked to an anti-Trump merchandise site. Pentagon spokesman Col. Rob Manning and press secretary Dana White said an “authorized operator” had “erroneously re-tweeted content that would not be endorsed by the Department of Defense,” and that the operator caught the mistake and removed the post immediately. The incident highlighted social-media risks for official accounts and arrived amid renewed scrutiny of sexual-harassment allegations involving public figures, including prior accusations against Trump that the White House has repeatedly dismissed.

Mary Agnes “Pink” Mullaney, a Milwaukee woman born in 1927, is being remembered for a life wholly devoted to kindness. She died this week at 85 and is survived by six children and 17 grandchildren. Rather than a conventional obituary, her family published a colorful, lesson-filled death notice that captured her spirit: practical, humorous, and deeply compassionate. Excerpts encourage everyday generosity—carrying a chicken sandwich to give a homeless friend after Mass, inviting strangers to Thanksgiving, bringing magazines to waiting rooms without removing the mailing label so readers can contact the donor, and simple acts like letting the homeless warm up in your car. Pink famously greeted everyone equally, from doctors to the houseless, stopped to kiss babies, wrote thousands of letters, and found joy in small, quirky solutions (like using old pantyhose for household fixes or coaxing a possum out with a brush). Friends and family say her life should be an example: assume the best of people and perform small acts of care. Newsline 9 says Pink inspired a return of its “Someone You Should Know” series and invites nominations of similarly noteworthy neighbors. Link to obituary included.

We live in an age where readily available photo filters and editing apps have reshaped notions of beauty and, experts warn, fueled harmful self-perception. Snapchat, Instagram, Facetune and similar tools let anyone instantly smooth skin, whiten teeth, enlarge eyes, slim faces and otherwise create polished, often unrealistic versions of themselves. Researchers and clinicians are increasingly concerned that these altered images are driving a rise in body dissatisfaction, body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), and requests for cosmetic procedures to match filtered selfies — a phenomenon dubbed “Snapchat dysmorphia.” Surgeons report a notable uptick in patients bringing edited self-photos as templates for surgery; the American Academy of Facial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery found 55% of surgeons saw selfie-driven requests in 2017, up from 42% the year before.

Boston University authors, writing in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery, argue that filter-enabled perfection is blurring fantasy and reality, normalizing unattainable standards that were once limited to celebrity retouching. BDD is a debilitating condition marked by obsessive preoccupation with perceived appearance flaws, compulsive checking or camouflage, social withdrawal, and high comorbidity with depression and substance use. Empirical evidence indicates alarmingly high suicidality in BDD — lifetime suicidal ideation around 80% and attempts in 24–28% — and even elevated completed suicide rates in some prospective data. Effective treatments include high-dose serotonin reuptake inhibitors and cognitive-behavioral therapy; cosmetic interventions generally do not resolve underlying BDD. Clinicians urge better recognition, screening, and treatment of BDD and public awareness that edited images create unrealistic expectations that can harm mental health.

The Baltic Sea is a rich repository of shipwrecks, many from the two World Wars, and continues to yield maritime finds both dangerous and historically valuable. Thomas Dehling, head of hydrographic surveying at Germany’s Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency (BSH), says German waters alone—under 10% of the Baltic—contain roughly 1,000 known objects. Most wrecks date to the early 20th century, though occasional much older finds turn up: a Finnish wreck over 400 years old and a 15th–16th-century wooden ship in German waters with cargo including copper disks. The BSH regularly surveys wrecks—more often when they threaten shipping lanes—and still discovers 10–15 previously unknown objects yearly thanks to improved seafloor mapping. The agency shares navigationally critical information with maritime authorities but restricts precise locations of historically interesting wrecks to qualified parties because of diving risks and entanglement hazards from fishing nets.

One remarkable discovery in 2010 illustrates the Baltic’s archaeological and scientific value: divers found 168 bottles of 19th-century champagne aboard a sunken trade schooner off Finland, preserved 160 feet down in cold, dark conditions. Scientists led by Philippe Jeandet analyzed a sample, identifying vintners via cork markings, including Veuve Clicquot. Chemical and sensory analyses revealed lower alcohol but very high sugar (at least 140 g/L versus 6–8 g/L in modern champagne), elevated iron, copper, sodium and chlorine, and wood-derived compounds—signs of older production practices, metal- and wood-contact vessels, vineyard treatments like copper sulfate, and salt added for stabilization. The sugar level suggests a likely Germanic market destination rather than the extremely sweet Russian preference. Taste panels described complex, evolving aromas—initially “animal” or “cheesy,” then smoky, spicy, leathery, with fruity and floral notes after aeration. Some bottles have fetched high auction prices and inspired interest in deep-sea aging as a potential enological technique.

Under pressure from changing public attitudes and internal surveys, the Boy Scouts of America proposed lifting its ban on gay youth members while continuing to prohibit gay adults from serving as leaders. The proposal, to be voted on by the National Council in May, would bar denying youth membership solely for sexual orientation, but require adult members to meet existing standards that exclude openly gay leaders. Reactions split: gay-rights groups welcomed the move for youths but condemned continued adult exclusions; many religious and conservative backers opposed any change. Major supporters like AT&T’s CEO backed the youth change; the Mormon Church said it would review the proposal. The compromise reflects deep tensions within scouting and broader US debates over gay rights.

Late summer marks more than back-to-school season for many sports fans: it’s fantasy football draft time. Fantasy sports have become a major industry, with roughly 36 million participants across the U.S. and Canada, and the pastime is evolving beyond casual, once-a-season play. The story of Drew Dinkmeyer illustrates that shift: he left a career as an investment analyst to pursue fantasy sports full-time. Dinkmeyer told NPR that his decision was possible because he now gambles multiple daily contests with stakes around $500 per game, rather than the occasional, modest entry fees typical of many players. Over several years of consistent play, he says his earnings reached levels comparable to his previous financial-sector salary, making full-time play feasible. He frames daily fantasy sports as analogous to day trading: participants receive assigned prices for individual athletes and must identify players whose expected point production exceeds their costs, thereby assembling the most valuable lineup within salary constraints. That approach — combining analytics, market pricing, and rapid decision-making — mirrors finding undervalued stocks. Dinkmeyer supplements contest winnings with income from writing for fantasy sports websites and hosting a satellite radio show, creating a diversified revenue stream tied to the sport. Confident in the sustainability of his model, he describes this blend of competition, analysis and media work as a long-term vocation he expects to continue for the foreseeable future.

Saturday Night Live opened with Taran Killam as Rush Limbaugh mocking the backlash over his attacks on Georgetown student Sandra Fluke, lampooning lost sponsors with absurd fake ads. The sketch repeated the same gag and felt long despite Killam’s committed delivery, ending with a sign-off line about calling "cockroaches sluts." Separately, Radio-Info.com reported 98 advertisers told Premiere Radio Networks they want to avoid buying time on shows deemed offensive, including Limbaugh, Levin, Beck and others. Major brands—from automakers to insurers and restaurants—have pulled ads from Limbaugh after his misogynistic comments, and his WABC online feed has aired public service announcements in place of commercials.

Engadget reports Barnes & Noble is quietly phasing out the 3G Nook, allegedly encouraging partners not to place bulk orders because supply won’t meet demand; sales would continue only until existing stock is exhausted. The tip’s credibility is mixed—Engadget has been wrong before, though this piece is by a veteran reporter—and B&N won’t comment on its roadmap. Many customers favor cheaper Wi‑Fi only readers, and industry observers think B&N may refresh its e‑ink line to cut costs, while likely keeping a sub‑$200 3G option if Amazon does.

Kris Humphries plans to respond to Kim Kardashian’s divorce filing by seeking a legal separation rather than an immediate divorce, sources tell PEOPLE. Humphries is expected to file within days and ultimately hopes to obtain an annulment to erase the marriage entirely — a shift from earlier reports that he intended simply to move on and sign divorce papers. Kardashian, 31, filed for divorce from the 26-year-old NBA player on Oct. 31 after a 72-day marriage, citing irreconcilable differences; their difficulties surfaced almost immediately and were depicted in the season premiere of Kourtney & Kim Take Manhattan.

Separately, Daniel Craig sharply criticized the Kardashian family in a GQ interview, calling them “f***ing idiots” for monetizing their private lives on reality TV. Craig argued people who “sell” their private moments can’t reclaim their privacy and mocked the idea of seeking solitude after exposing intimate details on camera. He contrasted that exposure with his own secret wedding to Rachel Weisz, which he described as deliberately private to avoid public intrusion. Craig also reflected on his career, saying he remains persistently unsatisfied and always striving to “get it right.” The interview appears in British GQ’s January issue.

Additionally, Kourtney Kardashian and Scott Disick are expecting their second child, Us Weekly reports. Kourtney is nine weeks along; the couple already shares son Mason, nearly two, and say this pregnancy was planned.

A 25-year-old man, Sidney Bouvier Gilstrap-Portley, was arrested after allegedly posing as a Hurricane Harvey evacuee and enrolling at Dallas ISD’s Hillcrest High School under the name Rashun Richardson. Claiming displacement by the storm allowed him to bypass standard documentation requirements; he may have provided only immunization records and a physical. Gilstrap-Portley, who graduated from North Mesquite High in 2011 and has a young child, also briefly played on Hillcrest’s basketball team and previously enrolled at Skyline High School. The ruse was uncovered when a former coach recognized him playing for a high school team, prompting a detective’s investigation and his arrest on tampering-with-government-records charges; he has since been released. Hillcrest and district officials said they immediately notified authorities upon learning a student had enrolled under false pretenses and emphasized the need to improve safeguards when admitting displaced students. Victims and community members expressed anger and concern.

The Bank of England will unveil its first polymer banknote, a Winston Churchill £5, at Blenheim Palace as part of a switch from paper to plastic notes that ends 320 years of paper currency. The Churchill note, entering circulation in September, begins a series that includes a Jane Austen £10 next year and a J. M. W. Turner £20 by 2020. Polymer notes are made from a transparent plastic film with an ink coating, enabling clear “windows” to deter counterfeiting; they are cleaner, more durable and more secure than paper. The Bank says polymer notes last up to 2.5 times longer, offsetting higher production costs and saving about £100m. Tests indicate polymer notes withstand temperatures up to 120°C and should survive washing-machine cycles but can be damaged by hot irons. Adopting plastic will cost retailers and banks up to an estimated £236m to recalibrate or replace ATMs, vending machines and self-service devices because the new notes are 15% smaller. More than 30 countries, beginning with Australia in 1988, already use polymer currency. The Churchill design shows him with Westminster and Big Ben at about 3pm on 13 May 1940.

Amazon Flex is Amazon’s app-driven “last-mile” delivery program that uses independent contractors to deliver packages in dozens of cities. Marketed as flexible work—“be your own boss,” choose blocks of time, and earn roughly $18–$25/hour—Flex recruits drivers with minimal requirements (age 21+, background check, smartphone, vehicle) and light onboarding (videos, optional short trainings). Drivers pick up timed “blocks” through the app, collect pre-sorted packages at fulfillment centers, and follow Amazon’s suggested routes. Pay varies by location and block type (Prime Now vs. Logistics); many drivers treat Flex as supplemental income rather than full-time work.

Reporting from interviews with 15 current or former drivers and several courier-company sources highlights persistent problems: unpredictable and sometimes insufficient work; misaligned block lengths and package counts; unpaid overtime when blocks run long; alleged caps on hours; scant training on safety; and arbitrary deactivations following vague performance complaints. Drivers face poor support channels, inconsistent FC rules, competition and “botting” to snag shifts, and a culture where small mistakes can lead to termination. Third-party courier companies contracted for larger routes operate under similar controls, creating a tiered contractor system that can leave drivers without traditional employee protections.

Labor experts argue Flex’s tight operational control, integration into Amazon’s services, and prolonged, regular engagement may constitute employee—not contractor—work, raising misclassification concerns. Arbitration clauses in Flex contracts further hinder class actions, limiting drivers’ legal recourse. Regulators appear largely unaware or unequipped to oversee Flex, and advocates warn that Amazon’s model exemplifies broader trends toward precarious, poorly protected gig work that existing laws and enforcement have not yet adequately addressed.

A Florida man who had survived Hurricane Irma was fatally shot on Jan. 3 by a young FEMA contractor he had befriended months earlier while the contractor was assessing storm damage, authorities say. Victim William Reiss, 68, had shown the contractor, 18-year-old Gerjuan Jackson, his firearm collection and sold him two handguns after they met during post‑Irma inspections in Polk County. Jackson, who lives in Mobile, Ala., allegedly returned to Polk County with two accomplices, Kenley Campbell and Darril Rankin Jr., both 22, to steal more guns. Investigators say Jackson entered Reiss’s home, shot him four times and also shot Reiss’s roommate, 57‑year‑old Kenneth Maier, who staggered out and flagged down passing motorists. Good Samaritans found Reiss dead inside; Maier later died of his wounds. The suspects reportedly loaded up to 25 firearms and a TV into vehicles, torched Reiss’s truck after returning to Alabama, and sold most of the stolen guns and the TV on the street. Police recovered three remaining firearms and Jackson’s FEMA ID when they arrested the trio. All three face first‑degree murder charges and multiple counts related to robbery, burglary and grand theft; additional murder charges are pending in Maier’s death. FEMA said the agency is investigating the matter and coordinating with law enforcement, noting Jackson worked for a private contractor. Neighbors expressed shock that someone who had passed a background check had been inside their homes.

Adam Peterson, 29, the son of Milwaukee County Chief Medical Examiner Dr. Brian Peterson, died Monday in what investigators believe was a drug overdose. Found face down on the floor of a friend's apartment on West Clybourn Street, he was unresponsive to Narcan and was pronounced dead about 7:30 p.m. A medical examiner’s report noted a history of drug use and that Peterson was believed to be homeless. Investigators found medications including topiramate and citalopram in his bag, along with a razor blade and cotton balls at the scene.

His death comes amid an unprecedented surge in drug fatalities in Milwaukee County. Dr. Peterson recently told an opioid round-table that overdoses have outpaced other major causes of death when combined, and his office announced that 70 people died of probable overdoses in a seven-week span. As of July 27, there were 168 confirmed drug-related deaths in 2016, already exceeding totals from some prior years and forcing the medical examiner’s office to abandon earlier projections; the office had estimated 288 total drug deaths for 2016 before the spike. Last year saw a record 254 drug-related deaths. Officials and community groups, including IMPACT, continue outreach and support for those struggling with addiction. Dr. Peterson has asked for privacy as his office describes the current death toll as “unprecedented.”

An Egyptian court in Minya has provoked international outcry after sentencing 528 supporters of deposed President Mohammed Morsi to death following a rapidly conducted trial over an August attack on a police station. The UN human rights office called the mass sentences “unprecedented” and a breach of international law, while human rights groups and foreign governments criticized the proceedings as marred by grave procedural irregularities: most defendants were absent, defence lawyers were barred or boycotted the hearings, and prosecutors reportedly presented no individualized evidence. A separate mass trial of 683 alleged Islamists, including Muslim Brotherhood leader Mohammed Badie and other senior figures, opened amid a lawyers’ boycott; the judge adjourned until 28 April to deliver verdicts. Security forces clashed with protesting Minya University students, using tear gas and rubber bullets. Egyptian authorities defend the rulings and note death sentences must be ratified by the grand mufti and can be appealed; legal experts expect higher courts may order retrials or reduce sentences. The cases are part of a broader crackdown that has seen some 16,000 arrests since Morsi’s ouster.

Actor Mandy Patinkin, famed for playing Inigo Montoya in the 1987 film The Princess Bride, has recently found his image and lines repurposed online with Texas Senator Ted Cruz’s face Photoshopped onto Patinkin’s character. Patinkin told reporters he received many emails and videos of Cruz reciting lines from the film on the campaign trail and wondered how to stop the digital appropriation. Cruz, who lists The Princess Bride as his favorite movie and reportedly memorized much of it while at Princeton, has been quoting and performing its lines at public events — including an Iowa Central Community College appearance and a taped “Candidate Cafe” segment — delighting some audiences and puzzling others.

Patinkin expressed bemusement and concern that Cruz uses the movie’s iconic dialogue without embracing what Patinkin sees as its core message. He singled out a lesser-quoted, more reflective Inigo line — delivered after the climactic duel — about being unsure what to do with life once revenge is over, urging Cruz to also recite that line if he invokes the character. Patinkin contrasted the movie’s themes of love, hope and redemption with what he described as Cruz’s political rhetoric he perceives as fearmongering — citing Cruz’s hawkish comments on ISIS and stances on immigration — and urged more compassion toward refugees.

Cruz’s campaign spokeswoman called him “a huge fan of the film and the actors in it,” framing his performances as harmless fun. Separate profiles and interviews sketch Cruz as a multifaceted, ambitious first-term senator who led opposition to Obamacare, is considered a 2016 presidential contender, and enjoys games, movies, and a surprising food dislike: avocados. Media pieces note his dramatic recitations of The Princess Bride have become a recurring, attention-getting quirk on the campaign trail, drawing both laughter and raised eyebrows.

First Lady Michelle Obama appeared on The Tonight Show with Jay Leno to promote her Let’s Move! initiative and encourage healthy eating. She teased Leno—who had joked he hadn’t eaten a vegetable in decades—into tasting apples dipped in White House honey, sweet potato fries, and a whole-wheat crust pizza topped with eggplant, peppers and zucchini. The lighthearted segment included banter about the White House and politics; Obama deflected partisan commentary, calling “America the Beautiful” a song for every American after Leno asked about Mitt Romney’s recent sing-along. She also discussed President Barack Obama’s surprise soulful rendition of Al Green at a fundraiser, praising his “beautiful” voice and noting he sings classics like Al Green, Marvin Gaye and Stevie Wonder at home. On a two-day California swing to back Let’s Move! and help raise funds for Democrats, she said there’s no way to mentally prepare for a tough re-election campaign—“you take each day as it comes.”

Rapper Kevin Gates was convicted of misdemeanor battery by a six-woman jury and sentenced Wednesday to 180 days in Polk County Jail, plus fines, court costs and credit for time served, stemming from an August 29, 2015 Lakeland concert incident. Cellphone video that went viral showed Gates kick fan Miranda Dixon at Rumors Nightclub; prosecutors sought 60 days’ jail, one year probation and anger management, but the judge imposed a longer jail term. Gates acknowledged in earlier hearings that he kicked the fan after she and others grabbed his pants multiple times; he argued the act was self-defense under Florida’s Stand Your Ground law. Defense attorney Jose Baez contended Dixon either was not struck or was exaggerating to support an upcoming civil suit and attacked her credibility. Witnesses included the club’s head of security, who said ample security and stage space were available, and Dixon’s friend, Termeral Redding, who admitted encouraging Dixon to grab Gates to get his attention and said the front row was grabbing at him. Dixon said she blacked out and later underwent a CT scan; thousands signed a petition seeking to ban Gates from Florida venues.

Since 1996, Alexa Internet has regularly donated its web crawl data to the Internet Archive, where the captures are integrated into the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. These continuous daily inflows of crawl data are intended to preserve web pages as they are created and to capture the pages those newly created pages reference. By archiving both primary content and its linked resources, the Archive aims to preserve the exact versions that were live when an author wrote or cited them. This approach helps address the common problem of link rot—when referenced web pages change or disappear—by providing stable archived versions that can replace broken links or serve as companion links so readers can see the original context and intent of authors.

The effort is framed as a drive to “fix all broken links on the web.” To that end, the Internet Archive focuses on crawling supported sites participating in initiatives like “No More 404,” ensuring systematic coverage and preservation of content most likely to be cited or referenced. The Archive also notes user-facing features such as adding location data to Tweets via web or third-party apps and giving users the ability to delete Tweet location histories, although this is tangential to the crawling work. Overall, the partnership with Alexa and ongoing crawls strengthen the Wayback Machine’s mission of maintaining a reliable historical record of the web and mitigating the impact of disappearing or altered online content.

Three years after Casey Anthony’s 2011 trial, Orlando defense attorney J. Cheney Mason — who joined Anthony’s legal team pro bono — reflects on the case and his new book arguing the nation misjudged her. Anthony was tried for the 2008 death of her 2-year-old daughter, Caylee, after the child disappeared and was later found skeletal near the Anthony home. The widely publicized, two-month trial ended July 5, 2011, with Anthony acquitted of first-degree murder, aggravated manslaughter and aggravated child abuse, though convicted on four misdemeanors for lying to law enforcement.

Mason, a veteran death-penalty-qualified lawyer who began advising Jose Baez and later joined the defense, recounts meeting the small, frightened-seeming Anthony in jail and committing extensive unpaid time and money to the case. Baez shocked the courtroom by alleging sexual abuse by Casey’s father in opening statements, a claim Mason says they could not prove without George Anthony testifying; George denied the accusations when called by prosecutors. The defense argued Caylee accidentally drowned and that a cover-up followed, while prosecutors presented a largely circumstantial case.

Mason describes Anthony’s life since acquittal as constrained by public hatred and death threats: she lives in a hidden Florida location, does clerical work from home, avoids public places and has little contact with her parents. Mason’s forthcoming book, Justice in America, critiques media bias, prosecutorial conduct and public rushes to judgment, promising behind-the-scenes details and legal documents from the case. Mason and his wife remain among Anthony’s closest ties.

Cate Blanchett is attached to play Lucille Ball in an authorized biopic being produced by Ball’s children, Lucie Arnaz and Desi Arnaz Jr., with Escape Artists and oversight from Jenna Block. Aaron Sorkin is the studio’s top choice to write the script, though he has not officially committed or begun work. The film will focus on Ball’s life and her 20-year marriage to Desi Arnaz, highlighting her TV career on I Love Lucy and other shows and her multiple Emmy wins and a Cecil B. DeMille Award. Blanchett’s recent and upcoming projects include Carol, Cinderella, Truth and Knight of Cups.

A Politico investigation alleges the Obama administration’s 2016 prisoner swap with Iran — tied to the nuclear deal — released not just seven U.S.-held Iranian-born detainees framed publicly as nonviolent “sanctions violators,” but also effectively cleared charges or removed Interpol red notices for 14 additional Iranian fugitives accused of serious national-security offenses. The report says several released individuals were linked to procurement networks supplying Tehran with U.S.-origin microelectronics used in surface-to-air and cruise missiles, satellite hardware, and other dual-use components critical to enrichment centrifuges and missile programs. One high-value figure, Seyed Abolfazl Shahab Jamili, had allegedly advanced Iran’s centrifuge development by sourcing pressure transducers; another had helped supply U.S. military antennas used in IEDs that killed American troops. Justice Department prosecutors and counterproliferation agents were reportedly shocked and angry, claiming investigations were slowed or frozen as the White House and State Department prioritized diplomacy to secure the deal and the return of Americans. Officials describe an informal “embargo” on Iran prosecutions from 2014 onward, including delayed extradition or “lure” operations and vacated cases that undermined the National Counterproliferation Initiative’s momentum. Administration defenders argue secrecy and diplomatic necessity guided decisions and that dismissed cases could restart if illegal activity resumes. Critics say the swap sacrificed long-term enforcement and intelligence leads for a short-term foreign-policy win, erasing years of investigative work, weakening deterrence, and allowing key operatives to avoid accountability. The Trump administration’s review of the deal and renewed emphasis on Iran may spotlight these unresolved counterproliferation harms.

Scientists have described a small, crow-sized, birdlike dinosaur from northeastern China, Caihong juji — Mandarin for “rainbow with a big crest” — dating to about 161 million years ago in the Late Jurassic. The nearly complete fossil, found in Hebei Province and reported in Nature Communications, preserves extensive plumage and microscopic pigment-bearing organelles (melanosomes) indicating iridescent feathers, especially concentrated on the head, neck and chest. Those feather nanostructures are pancake- or platelet-shaped and organized in sheets, closely resembling melanosomes seen in modern iridescent hummingbirds and swifts, suggesting shimmering, angle-dependent colors. Discriminant analyses predict most of the body was dark while the head and chest were iridescent, likely serving display or sexual signaling functions; a prominent bony lacrimal crest would have enhanced visual display.

Anatomically, Caihong blends birdlike and raptor-like traits. It had a shallow, elongated skull with sharp teeth, a short bony tail but a broad frond-like array of large pennaceous tail feathers, extensive leg and toe feathering, and forelimbs with long remiges and possible alula-like feathers. Notably, Caihong preserves the earliest-documented asymmetrical tail feathers—features linked to aerodynamic steering in birds—though its short forelimbs suggest it probably could not sustain powered flight; gliding remains possible. Phylogenetically it sits among basal paravians closely related to early birds like Archaeopteryx. The discovery expands evidence that Jurassic ecosystems included vividly colored, structurally iridescent dinosaurs and underscores the complexity of early feather evolution, including display, insulation and emerging aerodynamic roles.

Juan Salaz, a Texas inmate who escaped nearly 16 years ago, was captured in Mexico last week and is awaiting extradition to finish serving his sentence, authorities said. Salaz fled the Garza East Unit in Beeville on March 22, 1997 by scaling three 16-foot, razor wire–topped fences. He had been serving three concurrent 35-year terms for aggravated kidnapping with a deadly weapon and two counts of attempted capital murder of police stemming from a 1995 incident in which he and an accomplice opened fire on undercover Houston officers during a staged ransom exchange. Salaz was wounded in the shootout, later pleaded guilty, and now faces an additional felony escape charge. U.S. Marshals, Texas prison investigators and Mexican law enforcement had long sought him, with previous leads placing him near Monterrey and possibly moving across the border with family assistance. His capture reduces Texas’s list of prison fugitives to one remaining escapee believed to be in Mexico.

A 25-year-old German man developed seizures triggered specifically by solving Sudoku after suffering oxygen deprivation in an avalanche, researchers report in JAMA Neurology. The man was buried and unconscious for about 15 minutes during a November 2008 skiing accident; he sustained a ruptured spleen, hip fracture and hypoxic brain injury. Soon afterward he developed myoclonic jerks—sudden muscle twitches—when speaking and walking, and tonic-clonic seizures in his left arm while hospitalized. Weeks later, during rehabilitation, attempting Sudoku reliably provoked clonic seizures in his left arm; stopping the mental strategy immediately halted the fits.

Doctors determined his Sudoku strategy involved an intense three-dimensional visualization of numbers. Hypoxia had damaged inhibitory fibers in the right centro-parietal brain region that normally temper activation during 3D imagination. With reduced inhibition, engaging that spatial processing produced overactivation and focal motor seizures in his left arm. The seizures did not occur with other math tasks or reading, but the patient later reported similar triggers from crosswords, spreadsheets and other tasks combining visual grids, focused calculation and hand movements.

He manages seizures with anti-epileptic medication and avoiding such puzzles; he has been seizure-free for over five years, and myoclonic symptoms have improved with therapy. Clinicians describe this as reflex epilepsy—seizures provoked by specific external stimuli—and the case illustrates how localized loss of inhibition can create task-specific seizure triggers.

The Dallas Morning News broke a 75-year tradition by endorsing Democrat Hillary Clinton over Republican Donald Trump, calling her the only "serious candidate" on the ballot. Long aligned with conservative values—favoring free markets, individual liberty and a strong national defense—the paper emphasized that its decision was not made lightly. While acknowledging concerns about Clinton’s judgment, notably the private email server and the need for greater transparency around the Clinton Foundation, the editors argued these shortcomings pale beside Trump’s behavior and temperament.

The editorial excoriated Trump for exploiting fear and latent prejudices—xenophobia, racism and misogyny—portraying him as unprepared, erratic and reckless. His frequent policy reversals, improvisational insults and impulsive late-night tweets were cited as signs of dangerously poor judgment and lack of impulse control. By contrast, Clinton was described as a “known quantity” with extensive experience: eight years in the Senate with bipartisan reach, service as secretary of state making tough foreign-policy decisions, and endorsements from numerous Republican foreign-policy figures and former GOP officials. The paper concluded Clinton was more likely to preserve national security, protect American ideals and govern competently.

The endorsement signals how disruptive Trump’s candidacy has been, even to traditional Republican institutions. Though skeptics note declining newspaper influence and growing political polarization—which may limit the impact of such endorsements—research suggests cross-partisan endorsements can sway readers, especially when they break predictable patterns. Given the Dallas Morning News’ long Republican streak, its choice to back Clinton is both symbolically striking and potentially influential. The paper urged voters to reject the politics of personal destruction and support Clinton as the more qualified, steady choice in a consequential election.

Researchers have developed a topical drug that induces true tanning in human skin samples without ultraviolet (UV) exposure, representing an early step toward a lotion or cream that could lower skin cancer risk for fair-skinned people. Unlike conventional self-tanners that merely stain skin and offer minimal UV protection, this compound stimulates production of eumelanin—the dark form of melanin that absorbs UV radiation and reduces cellular damage. The technique builds on prior work with the plant extract forskolin in genetically engineered mice modeling red-haired, fair-skinned humans who normally cannot tan because of a nonfunctional receptor on pigment cells.

Published June 13 in Cell Reports, the study shows the small molecules penetrate live human skin samples and trigger real melanin synthesis in a UV-independent manner. Microscopic analysis confirmed authentic melanin production, and tests indicated the pigment could block harmful UV rays. Researchers envision combining the agent with sunscreen to maximize protection; they emphasize it would supplement, not replace, sunscreen use. The approach may enable tanning even in individuals with red hair, though it’s unclear whether hair color would be affected—the drug likely cannot reach deep hair follicles.

Scientists stress more safety testing is needed before human use, and so far no adverse signals have emerged. Experts call the strategy a novel, promising avenue for primary skin cancer prevention and possibly for reducing photoaging. Next steps include establishing safety and initial trials in high-risk individuals. The team may also seek a more user-friendly name than “SIK-inhibitor” before commercialization.

Stephon Alonzo Clark, a 22-year-old father of two, was shot and killed by Sacramento police in his grandparents’ backyard on the night of March 18. Officers responding to reports of someone breaking car windows encountered Clark after deputies in a helicopter tracked a man matching the description. Police say Clark fled into the backyard, then turned and advanced toward officers while holding an object; fearing for their safety, two officers fired a total of 20 rounds, striking him multiple times. Authorities later said the only item recovered near Clark’s body was a cellphone; items possibly linked to earlier property damage — a cinder block and a piece of aluminum — were found near a broken sliding door at a neighbor’s home. Clark’s family maintain he was trying to enter his grandmother’s home, where he lived, and his grandmother said she heard no police commands before gunfire and first learned of the shooting when she saw his body outside. Both officers involved have been placed on paid administrative leave.

The shooting has prompted public outcry, protests and calls for justice from community activists and family members. An oversight committee, multiple investigations by the district attorney, city attorney, internal affairs and homicide detectives were announced; police said body-camera and aerial footage will be shown to Clark’s family within days and released publicly within a week, ahead of the 30-day policy requirement. Friends set up a memorial fund and GoFundMe for funeral costs. Family and supporters describe Clark as a changed man, devoted to his children Aiden and Cairo, and mourn his loss while demanding transparency and accountability.

A powerful winter storm swept across the Midwest and Northeast, dumping heavy snow, driving winds and dangerously cold temperatures that disrupted travel, closed schools and prompted emergency measures. Parts of New England saw up to 20–21 inches of snow, with Boxford, Mass., reporting 21 inches and some Massachusetts areas near two feet. Major cities recorded varied accumulations—New York City about 7 inches, Boston up to 14 inches, Hartford 6–10 inches, Philadelphia roughly 5 inches and Baltimore 3–6 inches. The storm brought sub-zero temperatures and wind chills as low as minus-30 in spots, with forecasts of brutally cold highs only in the teens for New York City and evening lows near single digits, feeling well below zero with wind chill.

Air travel was severely affected: thousands of flights were canceled—about 2,000 on Thursday and roughly 1,600 more on Friday—creating national scheduling knock-on effects that grounded planes and marooned passengers in airports, including dozens of flights delayed at LAX. Major airports like JFK and Boston Logan temporarily shut down, and highway closures included New York’s Thruway sections, the Long Island Expressway and parts of I-84. Governors in New York, New Jersey and Massachusetts declared states of emergency; New York urged residents to avoid travel and stay indoors. Schools across the Northeast, including all New York City public schools, were closed.

Officials warned of life-threatening cold, frostbite and hypothermia risk and urged people to limit outside exposure. Outreach teams and shelters, such as Boston’s Pine Street Inn, prepared for increased demand and promised not to turn anyone away. The storm also led to hazardous road conditions as salt loses effectiveness below about 10–20 degrees, complicating clearing efforts. Authorities prepared for a second, severe Arctic blast expected to move from the Plains and Midwest into the East later in the weekend, bringing record-shattering lows and extending the severe cold threat across a broad swath of the country.

A woman employed temporarily at a CEVA Logistics facility in Redford Township, Michigan, gave birth in a restroom stall at work and later concealed the newborn in a bag under her cubicle, where coworkers subsequently found the deceased infant. The discovery followed employees hearing moaning from the women’s restroom around mid-morning and finding blood in a stall. When staff checked on colleagues, one 25–26-year-old woman from Wyandotte initially reported feeling lightheaded but did not disclose she had delivered a baby; she later returned to her desk. Concerned coworkers called police; officers found the infant in the woman’s bag beneath her desk and transported both mother and baby to a local hospital. Paramedics’ resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful and the newborn was pronounced dead. The mother, who reportedly had told coworkers she was not pregnant, is recovering at the hospital and is under investigation while police determine whether the baby was born alive and whether any criminal charges are warranted. The Wayne County Medical Examiner performed an autopsy; results are pending and expected in about two weeks. CEVA Logistics, which employs roughly 150–240 people at the site, and the temporary staffing agency Level Professional Services are providing grief counseling and cooperating with authorities. Company representatives declined further comment while law enforcement continues its open investigation. The family of the woman declined to comment.
