An eighth-grade history assignment at Great Hearts Monte Vista charter school in San Antonio sparked outrage after students were asked to list "positive" and "negative" aspects of slavery. A parent posted a photograph of the worksheet, titled "The Life of Slaves: A Balanced View," after his son brought it home upset; the student wrote "not applicable" under positive aspects and listed many negatives. Parents, teachers and local leaders—including U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro and state Rep. Diego Bernal—criticized the worksheet as inappropriate and insensitive.

Great Hearts Texas Superintendent Aaron Kindel responded quickly, calling the assignment “very inappropriate and entirely inconsistent” with the school’s values and stressing “there is no debate about slavery. It is immoral and a crime against humanity.” The district said the incident was limited to one teacher at the Monte Vista North campus, placed that teacher on leave while investigating, and removed the specific history textbook, Prentice Hall Classics: A History of the United States, from classrooms pending an audit. The school pledged to meet with impacted students to explain the mistake, provide more thoughtful instruction on the period, and take steps to prevent future incidents, promising a follow-up communication by May 9.

The school initially said the worksheet came from the textbook, but Pearson, the textbook publisher, denied creating or endorsing the worksheet and condemned any implication that slavery had positive aspects. The episode has prompted demands for accountability, textbook review, and clearer oversight of classroom materials, and parents have met with school officials to press for outcomes, including whether the teacher will be retained.

Dunkin' is officially dropping "Donuts" from its name, becoming simply "Dunkin'" starting in January. The 68-year-old chain will roll out the new name on napkins, boxes, signage and social media in the U.S., then internationally, while keeping doughnuts on the menu. The move reflects a shift to a beverage-led strategy—coffee and other drinks account for about 60% of U.S. sales—and aims to attract younger customers. The refreshed branding retains the familiar rounded font and orange-and-pink colors. Dunkin' is also simplifying its menu, adding mobile-order lanes, digital kiosks, expanded Grab & Go options, and plans to open 1,000 new U.S. stores by the end of 2020.

Oracle Team USA completed one of sport’s greatest comebacks, winning the 34th America’s Cup after trailing Emirates Team New Zealand 8-1. Skipper Jimmy Spithill guided Oracle’s high-speed 72-foot foiling catamaran to an 11-9 series victory, capping an eight-race winning streak with a winner-take-all triumph on San Francisco Bay. Penalized two points earlier for illegal modifications, Oracle overcame adversity as the boat found greater foil time and superior speed. The dramatic final saw New Zealand briefly lead, but Oracle’s pace and strategy prevailed. Owner Larry Ellison celebrated aboard as the crew sprayed champagne.

The document compiles brief, unrelated political and media items and commentary. It begins by noting a retraction request after the Telegraph magazine’s January 19 cover story “The mystery of Melania” contained several false statements; the publisher accepts these should not have been printed and clarifies that Mrs. Trump’s father was not the intimidating figure the piece suggested. Next, it highlights singer Mary J. Blige’s public support for President Obama: she appears in a Planned Parenthood ad titled “Yes We Plan,” alongside Q-Tip and Julianne Moore, urging voters to re-elect Obama and praising Planned Parenthood’s role in women’s health throughout her life. Finally, the document describes a provocative, Michael Moore-produced ad associated with MoveOn.org that claims to voice the “Greatest Generation” warning Republicans and Mitt Romney about voter suppression; the spot contains aggressive, explicit threats and crass language, prompting the note that it’s more Michael Moore than authentic elder-statesperson testimony and advising viewer discretion.

Russian ex-spy Anna Chapman has posed provocatively in Russia’s Maxim, appearing in nylon and lace and posing with a handgun, with the magazine lauding her for stoking patriotism. Chapman was among ten alleged sleeper agents deported from the United States in July and exchanged for four Russians imprisoned for allegedly trading secrets with the West. Although the Kremlin and media celebrated the group and President Dmitry Medvedev awarded them the nation’s highest honors, reports indicate the spy ring failed to secure major intelligence before their arrests. The Maxim feature includes photos and an interview, and Chapman is listed among Russia’s 100 sexiest women.

This morning former reality star Tila Tequila resurfaced online with a shocking, photoshopped Facebook image showing herself in front of Auschwitz wearing an SS cap and a red swastika armband while holding a pistol. The post’s caption proclaimed her alter ego “Tilisis the GODDESS of LOVE & WAR,” and she has since linked to a blog post titled “Why I Sympathize With Hitler Part 1,” defending Adolf Hitler and suggesting modern governments might learn from him. The image originally bore libertarian cartoonist Ben Garrison’s signature; he denies involvement.

Over the past week Tequila also shared a Daily Mail article about the murder of James Marcus Howe and posted celebratory, explicitly anti-Semitic commentary, including slurs and apocalyptic-sounding claims about being “returned as his messenger.” She released a low-fi track called “It’s Going Down!” in which she calls out “Jewluminati” and raps under the moniker “Hitila,” mixing Holocaust denialish sympathy with conspiracy rhetoric. Her blog and social feeds are peppered with standard anti-Semitic tropes about Jews controlling banks and media, but also dive into extreme conspiracy content—claims of battles with reptilian Illuminati agents, angelic portals, and violent, delusional fantasies. This represents a disturbing escalation from prior years, only two years after she publicly said she intended to convert to Judaism, and follows a history of substance-related health struggles and erratic public behavior.

In Florida, legacy litigation from the state Supreme Court’s 2006 Engle decision continues to drive thousands of smoking-related suits, with more than 7,000 claims pending in state and federal courts. Engle bound juries to certain findings—such as that cigarettes were “defective” and “unreasonably dangerous”—giving plaintiffs a significant advantage and producing over $250 million in damages in progeny cases. In Bronson, a jury awarded $80 million to the daughter of James Cayce Horner, who died of lung cancer in 1996 after smoking two packs a day; $72 million were punitive damages. The jury apportioned 90% fault to R.J. Reynolds and 10% to Horner. Plaintiffs’ lawyer David Sales emphasized tobacco’s human cost; R.J. Reynolds declined comment. The verdict halts a recent tobacco defense streak, which included eight straight wins for defendants, most recently a Miami win for Philip Morris USA. Also noted: since 1996, Alexa Internet has donated crawl data to the Internet Archive, added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo.

California has agreed to end its practice of unlimited isolation for imprisoned gang leaders, significantly restricting a policy that kept hundreds of inmates in long-term segregation units for a decade or more. The change stems from a class-action federal lawsuit brought by the Center for Constitutional Rights on behalf of nearly 3,000 inmates held in segregation statewide. California’s correctional system had stood out nationally for the large number of inmates subjected to prolonged solitary confinement in soundproofed, windowless cells—conditions that prompted large-scale hunger strikes and criticism from figures including President Obama and Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy.

Under the settlement, inmates will be segregated primarily for new crimes committed inside prisons rather than solely to prevent them from directing gang activity from cells. Time in isolation will be limited: inmates may be held for up to five years for in-prison offenses, with gang members eligible for an additional two years. The state will create restrictive custody units that offer more personal contact and privileges for high-security inmates who refuse rehabilitation or repeatedly break rules, and will house those who would be endangered by general population placement.

Previously, criteria used to validate and isolate prisoners included tattoos, possession of gang-symbolic artwork, and informant statements. Until recently, the only path out of solitary was to become an informant—an incentive critics said endangered inmates. The settlement aims to bring California closer to how other states manage high-risk prisoners while retaining tools to handle problematic inmates. Officials note reforms and prior policy changes cut segregated populations from over 4,100 in January 2012 to about 2,858. Advocates hail the settlement as a major step toward ending extreme solitary confinement and a model for nationwide reform; corrections officials acknowledge past overuse of long-term segregation and pledge to address staff safety concerns during implementation.

On Fox & Friends, co-hosts defended President Donald Trump’s border enforcement while sparring with critics over his family-separation policy and broader immigration stance. Ainsley Earhardt framed Trump’s approach as necessary vetting — “in case it’s MS-13 or drugs” — arguing the policy is designed to screen who crosses the border. Brian Kilmeade expanded that defense, saying someone must address immigration and portraying Trump as open to alternative proposals rather than mere criticism. Kilmeade described the administration’s actions as sending a message to other countries that U.S. laws and rules must be respected and insisted the United States cannot admit everyone who wishes to enter. He further contended that the migrants are “not our kids” and suggested compassion is appropriate but that care and priority should lie with U.S. taxpayers and residents, a remark he later clarified.

The on-air discussion followed Trump’s signing of an executive order he claimed would end the policy that had led to thousands of children being separated from their parents at the U.S.–Mexico border. Critics note, however, that the executive order also seeks to bolster the government’s capacity to detain families together indefinitely — a change that raises its own human-rights and legal concerns. MSNBC’s Stephanie Ruhle publicly rebuked Kilmeade’s remarks, signaling partisan dispute over both the administration’s rhetoric and the policy’s consequences. The exchange highlights ongoing national debate over immigration enforcement, deterrence messaging to migrant-sending countries, and how to reconcile border security with humanitarian obligations to families and children seeking asylum.

Western nations signalled a cautious shift in policy toward Syria, pledging non-lethal aid to opposition forces while stopping short of providing weapons. In Rome, US Secretary of State John Kerry announced Washington would for the first time deliver medical supplies and Meals Ready-to-Eat directly to vetted rebel units and seek an additional $60 million to help the Syrian National Coalition govern rebel-held areas — doubling US civilian opposition support. The EU amended its embargo to permit armoured vehicles, non-lethal military equipment and technical aid intended to protect civilians. Leaders framed the move as pressure on President Bashar al-Assad, whom Kerry said “is out of time,” but the package disappointed many opposition figures and commanders who seek anti-tank and anti-aircraft weapons. Fighting, especially around Aleppo where rebels claimed the Umayyad Mosque and other sites, has intensified; the UN estimates over 70,000 killed and nearly a million refugees. Allies warned non-lethal aid is only a first step amid concerns weapons could empower extremists or escalate bloodshed.

A federal judge has allowed a lawsuit by the District of Columbia and Maryland alleging President Trump violated the Constitution’s emoluments clauses to proceed, marking the first time such a suit has cleared the standing hurdle. U.S. District Judge Peter J. Messitte ruled the jurisdictions plausibly showed injury because Trump’s continued financial interest in the Trump International Hotel in Washington could give it an unfair competitive advantage and divert business from local hotels and convention centers. Messitte cited examples of foreign governments, including Kuwait and Bahrain, patronizing the Trump hotel and noted local officials granted tax breaks and concessions to Trump-related properties, creating dilemmas for state and local governments weighing revenue against potential presidential repercussions. The judge narrowed the case’s scope primarily to the D.C. hotel, rejecting arguments that only Congress can enforce the emoluments clauses and finding courts can review presidential compliance with the law absent congressional action. If the ruling stands, D.C. and Maryland may seek Trump Organization documents and financial records to quantify payments from state and foreign entities. The Justice Department, defending the president, said it would continue to seek dismissal; the Trump Organization emphasized remaining legal arguments it believes warrant complete dismissal. Attorneys general Racine and Frosh said they will pursue the president’s financial documents and tax returns as the case proceeds.

On June 30, 2013 — the one-year anniversary of Mohamed Morsi’s inauguration — massive, nationwide protests in Egypt demanded his ouster. Hundreds of thousands rallied in Cairo’s Tahrir Square and at the presidential palace, as well as in Alexandria and dozens of other cities. Organizers backed by the Tamarod (Rebel) campaign claimed more than 22 million signatures calling for Morsi to step down; the figure could not be independently verified. Opposition crowds of secularists, liberals, Christians and moderate Muslims accused Morsi and Islamist allies, notably the Muslim Brotherhood, of monopolizing power, imposing a constitution skewed toward Islamists, failing to manage the economy and tolerating repression. Morsi’s supporters, tens of thousands camped in east Cairo, defended his election legitimacy and vowed to protect the presidency; some took defensive measures with helmets, shields and makeshift armor. Clashes in the preceding week and on the day left at least seven dead and hundreds injured, with reports of firearms, explosives and attacks on Brotherhood offices. The military, under Defense Minister Gen. Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi, warned of intervention if no compromise emerged; army deployments and helicopter patrols heightened tensions. Morsi refused calls for early elections, insisting on constitutional legitimacy, while both sides braced for a pivotal showdown.

Leslie Gibson, a Republican who had been the only declared candidate for Maine’s 57th District state House seat, withdrew from the race after intense backlash over offensive social-media attacks on two teen survivors of the Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School shooting in Parkland, Florida. Gibson had called Emma González a “skinhead lesbian” and dismissed her survivor status, and labeled David Hogg “a bald-faced liar” after Hogg criticized NRA spokeswoman Dana Loesch on CNN. The remarks drew condemnation from across the political spectrum, including Maine Republican lawmakers, and prompted Hogg to urge followers to find someone to challenge Gibson.

Gibson apologized on Twitter, then made his accounts private as the controversy escalated. He said his decision to exit followed discussions with family, friends and colleagues, including Republican Thomas Martin Jr., who entered the race this week, and that stepping aside was “the best thing for everybody.” Gibson, a Navy retiree and lifetime NRA member who has frequently used social media to defend conservative positions, framed his comments as coming from a desire to protect constitutional rights while acknowledging he should not have singled out the Parkland students.

The uproar spurred two challengers to file: Republican Thomas Martin Jr., a former state senator, and Democrat Eryn Gilchrist, a 28-year-old Bates College graduate who said she was “horrified and embarrassed” at the idea Gibson might represent her. González publicly thanked Gilchrist. Gibson said he hopes his withdrawal will restore normalcy and allow his family some peace after the controversy.

A large crack appeared in a 36th-floor window of San Francisco’s sinking and tilting Millennium Tower over the Labor Day weekend, alarming residents and city officials. Residents reported hearing creaking and a loud pop around 2:30 a.m. before discovering the damage. The 58-story tower, which has sunk roughly 17–18 inches and tilted about 14–18 inches since construction, has been the subject of lawsuits and ongoing safety concerns. San Francisco’s Department of Building Inspection issued a correction notice requiring building engineers to assess the cracked glass, the adjacent curtain wall system, and necessary repairs within 72 hours; inspectors initially could not access the unit. Supervisor Aaron Peskin emphasized the danger if a high-rise window failed, noting the curtain wall was designed for hurricane-force winds and urging possible sidewalk closures beneath the affected area. Management placed a protective barrier along Mission Street and said experts would evaluate the incident, acknowledging it might be related to broader settlement issues. The city continues to monitor potential façade separation and public safety implications as follow-up inspections proceed.

Ten volunteer firefighters from the Fairmont and Orrum fire departments were arrested after a year-long Robeson County investigation into a nearly two-year spree of intentionally set fires to woods and abandoned structures. Authorities say the probe — sparked by a tip and involving the Robeson County Sheriff’s Office, SBI, ATF and NC Forestry Service — resulted in about 90 arson-related charges with more expected. The arrested include former Maxton police officer Melquan Williams and a Department of Corrections employee, Austin Seth Hunt, along with eight others aged 17 to 42 from Fairmont, Rowland and Orrum. Charges range from felony arson, setting fire to grass/brush/woods, conspiracy counts, and one misdemeanor larceny; bonds were set between $100,000 and $200,000. Sheriff Kenneth Sealey and State officials stressed the arrests involve individuals, not the departments, and noted the misconduct has cost taxpayers thousands. Investigators said all county fire departments remain fully functional. Anyone with information is asked to contact Lt. Kevin Graham of the Robeson County Sheriff’s Office.

A recent study from the University of York shows that environmentally realistic exposure to the antidepressant fluoxetine (Prozac) can alter courtship behaviour in wild-caught starlings. Fluoxetine and other pharmaceuticals enter waterways via sewage and concentrate in invertebrates at treatment plants, where foraging birds can ingest them. Researchers measured typical residue levels in invertebrates, dosed worms accordingly (less than 10% of a human therapeutic dose), and fed them to starlings in outdoor aviaries. During breeding-season pairings, males paired with fluoxetine-exposed females sang half as often and for half the duration compared with males paired with control females—singing being a key courtship signal. Males also exhibited increased aggression toward treated females (chasing, pecking, feather-tugging). Treated females were initially aggressive and became less so by the second day, whereas control females maintained intermediate aggression; female courtship behaviours, body condition, and circulating testosterone and estradiol did not differ by treatment and did not explain male preferences. The authors interpret these results as evidence that low, environmentally relevant concentrations of an antidepressant can reduce female attractiveness and disrupt mating interactions, potentially affecting breeding success and population dynamics. The study raises broader concerns because wild birds may encounter mixtures of pharmaceuticals in sewage-contaminated food sources. The researchers urge better wastewater treatment to remove pharmaceuticals and further field studies to determine whether these experimental effects translate into population-level impacts in the wild.

Researchers report that modern sperm whales globally trace their mitochondrial DNA back to a single maternal ancestor living within the last ~80,000 years. A Molecular Ecology study analyzed mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) from 1,633 individuals (combining 1,091 published samples with 542 new profiles, including previously unsampled Indian Ocean whales) and found very low worldwide mtDNA diversity (π = 0.430%), consistent with a past expansion event. Despite low overall diversity, mtDNA is strongly structured by ocean basin, by regions within some oceans, and among social groups. That structure contrasts with low differentiation at nuclear microsatellite markers, which likely reflects male-mediated gene flow as roaming males breed across groups. The pattern arises from female philopatry—females remain in stable, matrilineal social groups and tend to stay within regional and oceanic areas—so female lineages remain localized and distinct even after a global expansion. Hierarchical analyses indicate the relative importance of geographic versus social philopatry varies by ocean and sex: regions help explain mtDNA variance in the Indian Ocean but less so in the Pacific, and social groups partition mtDNA and microsatellite variance in multiple oceans. The authors suggest sperm whales underwent a worldwide population expansion followed by rapid local assortment driven by female social organization. Low mitochondrial diversity makes populations more vulnerable to environmental changes (e.g., climate-driven habitat shifts) because philopatry limits the mixing that would restore diversity. Though all living sperm whales may share an “Eve,” contemporary females’ tendency to stay local could hinder future recovery of genetic variation, posing conservation concerns.

Peterson Air Force Base disclosed that about 150,000 gallons of water contaminated with perfluorinated compounds (PFCs) from a firefighter training holding tank was released into the Colorado Springs Utilities sewer system and flowed through the Las Vegas Street wastewater plant into Fountain Creek. The discharge was discovered Oct. 12 during a routine inspection; the cause is under investigation and base officials noted the tank requires multiple valves to be opened to discharge, leaving intentional release a possibility. The tank held outflow from training exercises dating back to 2013, and the water reportedly wasn’t tested for PFC levels before release. Utilities say there was no immediate risk to finished drinking water in Colorado Springs because the waste went to the wastewater system, but the treatment plant cannot remove PFCs and the chemical entered the creek that feeds downstream aquifers. PFCs—components of firefighting foam linked to cancers and other health problems—have already contaminated wells in Security, Widefield and Fountain at concentrations far above the EPA’s 70 parts-per-trillion advisory (some tests found up to 2,000 ppt). Local agencies and residents are relying on alternative supplies; the Air Force has banned nonemergency foam use, plans to replace it at Peterson, contributed funds to affected communities, and opened an investigation while state health officials coordinate monitoring.

Former President George W. Bush returned to the public stage in Dallas to break ground on the $300 million George W. Bush Presidential Center at Southern Methodist University, joined by an array of former aides and allies including Vice President Dick Cheney, Condoleezza Rice and Laura Bush. The ceremony marked a highly orchestrated reemergence after two years of relative seclusion and coincided with Bush’s new memoir, Decision Points. Bush pledged to defend his administration’s priorities without criticizing his successor and outlined plans for a policy institute at the center to advance human freedom, global health, economic growth and education reform. Cheney, appearing frail after recent heart problems, praised Bush and suggested public judgment was becoming more measured. The pair publicly reaffirmed their longstanding friendship despite past disputes recounted in the memoir, with Bush reiterating that Cheney was the right running mate in 2000 and a valued vice president and friend. Laura Bush emphasized global women’s rights at the event.

SkyMall’s parent company, Xhibit Corp., filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, blaming shifts in traveler behavior, rising costs and fierce e-commerce competition for its decline. Once a cultural fixture in airplane seat pockets, the SkyMall catalog—known for novelty items from garden gnomes to $1,000 “Serenity Pods” for pets—saw sales tumble as passengers increasingly used smartphones, laptops and in-flight Wi‑Fi instead of browsing printed catalogs. Xhibit said catalogs were no longer the sole in-flight shopping option and that airlines found the printing and carriage costs less attractive; Delta ended its contract Nov. 30 and Southwest planned to stop carrying SkyMall by April, a blow that threatened roughly 7 percent of merchandise sales. Xhibit listed assets of $1–10 million and liabilities of $10–50 million, with creditor claims around $12 million; major carriers including Delta, American and US Airways are among creditors. SkyMall generated $33.7 million in revenue in 2013 but only $15.8 million in the first nine months of 2014. Acting CEO Scott Wiley said the company hopes to sell the online retail business and other assets in a court-supervised process and possibly preserve the SkyMall brand, though 47 of 150 employees were laid off after retail catalog operations were suspended. Analysts pointed to the broader mail-order industry’s decline—driven by Amazon and other e-retailers offering convenience, competitive pricing and targeted digital marketing—and said survival requires embracing online and mobile strategies to reach niche audiences. The filing underscores how quickly a once-ubiquitous, captive-audience business was displaced by digital habits.

Rescuers found all 12 boys, aged 11–16, and their 25-year-old football coach alive deep inside Thailand’s Tham Luang cave complex on the 10th day after they became trapped by sudden monsoon flooding. The group was discovered on a rock ledge about 4 km from the cave mouth by two British divers who had joined the multinational search. Video from the initial contact shows the boys answering by torchlight that all 13 were there and very hungry. Seven divers, including a doctor and nurse, have since reached them and provided the first food and medical attention in ten days; officials say most are in stable condition with only minor injuries.

Authorities stressed that any extraction will prioritize safety above speed. Many of the boys cannot swim, complicating possible evacuation through submerged, narrow, zero-visibility passages. Options under consideration include teaching them to dive with full-face scuba masks, pumping water from the caves, searching for alternative entrances, or keeping the navy doctors with the group for up to four months until waters recede. Rain forecast in coming days and rising water levels threaten the air pocket where they shelter, increasing urgency. Thai officials have requested small full-face masks to reduce risks during an underwater transit and are installing a phone line so the boys can speak with families. International experts cautioned that escorting inexperienced divers through flooded cave corridors is extremely risky and that supplying the group in place may be safest depending on dive difficulty. The discovery prompted nationwide relief and praise for local and foreign rescuers involved in the operation.

A large, government-funded study published in the New England Journal of Medicine found no clear link between antidepressant use in the first trimester and congenital heart defects. The research, led by Krista Huybrechts at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, re-examined earlier studies that had prompted a 2005 FDA warning about paroxetine (Paxil) and heart malformations. Investigators used Medicaid Analytic eXtract data from 46 states and D.C. spanning 2000–2007 to assemble a cohort of nearly one million women aged 12–55 who delivered liveborn infants and lacked supplementary private insurance. Women exposed to known teratogens or whose infants had chromosomal abnormalities were excluded.

Exposure was defined by pharmacy dispensing records overlapping the first trimester, and antidepressant categories included SSRIs (paroxetine, sertraline, fluoxetine), SNRIs, tricyclics, bupropion, and others. Cardiac malformations were identified from ICD-9 diagnostic codes in maternal and infant records within 90 days after delivery, with validation showing reasonable predictive values. The study adjusted for many potential confounders—sociodemographic factors, chronic illnesses, other medications, depression severity proxies—and used propensity-score methods including high-dimensional algorithms.

Analyses included unadjusted, depression-restricted, and propensity-score–adjusted models, plus subgroup, dose-response, and sensitivity checks to address exposure/outcome misclassification. Overall, after extensive adjustment for confounding, first-trimester antidepressant use, including SSRIs, was not associated with a meaningful increase in heart malformation risk, challenging prior findings and informing risk–benefit considerations for treating depression in pregnancy.

Howard Stern said Wednesday he wishes Donald Trump had never run for president, arguing the office will be harmful to Trump’s mental health because he craves approval and admiration. Stern, who has known Trump for years and hosted him repeatedly on his shock-jock show, said Trump “wants to be liked, he wants to be loved” and that the hostility now coming at him—especially from Hollywood and the press—will be unhealthy. Although Stern calls Trump a friend and said he likes him personally, he strongly opposes Trump’s politics and was “shocked” when Trump ran and people took the campaign seriously. Stern recalled Trump once supported Hillary Clinton and held more liberal views, including pro-choice positions, and suggested Trump’s current stances are performative appeals to the religious-right base rather than genuine belief. Stern also speculated that Trump’s initial candidacy may have been a bid to boost his negotiating leverage with NBC over The Apprentice and criticized Trump’s calls for voter-fraud probes as stemming from anger over the election outcome. Stern warned the toll of the presidency is visible—“there’s a reason every president who leaves the office has gray hair.”

Richardson police are investigating the disappearance of 3-year-old Sherin Mathews, last seen early Saturday near her family’s backyard. According to the father, 37-year-old Wesley Mathews, he directed Sherin to stand by a large tree about 100 feet from the home at roughly 3 a.m. as punishment for refusing to drink her milk; he returned about 15 minutes later and found her gone. He searched, then waited inside and did laundry, and did not notify police for about five hours — a delay investigators find “certainly concerning.” Sherin, who was adopted from an Indian orphanage two years ago, is described as 3 feet tall, 22 pounds, with black hair and brown eyes; she has developmental issues and limited verbal skills.

Wesley Mathews was arrested Saturday on a child endangerment/abandonment charge and released Sunday on $250,000 bond. Authorities say the mother, Sini Mathews, was asleep during the incident and is not charged. She has retained attorney Kent Starr and another lawyer; Starr says she is distraught, has cooperated with police, and “all she wants is for her daughter to be returned.” Richardson police, however, told reporters the parents stopped cooperating over the weekend.

Investigators widened the search, involving an FBI Evidence Response Team that processed the home and seized three vehicles (a Lexus has been returned; an Audi and a minivan remain), cellphones and laptops, and reviewed neighborhood surveillance. Child Protective Services removed the couple’s 4-year-old daughter into protective custody. The Amber Alert was discontinued due to lack of new leads but could be reactivated. Police say there’s no evidence of forcible abduction and continue to follow multiple investigative avenues; anyone with information is asked to contact Richardson Police.

Los Angeles City Council voted 14–1 to direct the city attorney to draft an ordinance raising the city’s minimum wage to $15 an hour, with incremental increases beginning July 2016 and reaching $15 by July 2020 (small businesses of 25 or fewer employees would follow a delayed schedule reaching $15 by July 2021). The measure, which still requires final council approval after the city attorney drafts the ordinance, makes L.A. the largest U.S. city to adopt a $15 minimum, joining Seattle and San Francisco and adding momentum to a national Fight for $15 movement backed by unions and progressive groups.

Supporters argue the phased increase is a major anti-poverty victory that will boost incomes for hundreds of thousands of workers, spur similar actions nationwide, and help low-wage families afford basics like housing and transit. Labor leaders, migrant workers and activists hailed the passage as transformative, citing studies projecting sizeable earnings gains for affected workers and increased local spending by those who receive raises.

Opponents—principally business groups and some council members—warn of negative consequences: higher operating costs could force layoffs, reduced hours, price increases, or businesses relocating outside city limits. Critics also questioned the independence of impact studies and expressed concern about the scale of effects in a city of nearly four million. The lone dissenting vote came from Republican Councilman Mitchell Englander, who warned the policy could create competitive disadvantages for L.A. industries. City leaders characterized the policy as consistent with California’s broader progressive turn and a potential catalyst for regional and national wage reforms.

The document covers the final weekend of an NFL regular season marked by emotional farewells, record-setting performances and big postseason implications — but centers on the Indianapolis Colts, Peyton Manning’s uncertain future, and the likely arrival of Stanford quarterback Andrew Luck.

In Jacksonville, the Jaguars beat the Colts 19-13, handing Indianapolis a league-worst 2-14 finish and securing the No. 1 overall pick. That outcome intensifies the central dilemma for Colts owner Jim Irsay and the franchise: whether to use that top selection on Andrew Luck, a prospect widely expected to be the first pick, potentially ushering in a transition away from Peyton Manning. Manning, sidelined all season after two neck surgeries, watched from the sideline, expressed frustration at being unable to play, and stressed his priority is getting healthy. He noted he hasn’t speculated about the draft, saying personnel decisions are management’s purview, but acknowledged coexistence with a young QB wouldn’t be new for him. Teammates like long-time center Jeff Saturday praised Manning’s professionalism but recognized the team is in transition; Saturday and coach Jim Caldwell declined to speculate on personnel or coaching futures.

Beyond Indianapolis, the roundup highlights week’s major games and milestones: New England rallied from a three-touchdown deficit to beat Buffalo 49-21, clinching AFC home-field advantage; Drew Brees exploded for 389 yards and five TDs as the Saints set multiple team and NFL offensive season records in a 45-17 win over Carolina; Maurice Jones-Drew led Jacksonville with 169 rushing yards and took the rushing title; the Packers rested starters while Matt Flynn threw for 480 yards and six TDs in a 45-41 win over Detroit; Tennessee’s 23-22 victory over Houston kept Titans’ playoff hopes alive; Miami eliminated the Jets with a 19-17 upset; Chicago beat Minnesota 17-13; Philadelphia closed 8-8 with a 34-10 win; and San Francisco secured a No. 2 seed with a 34-27 win over St. Louis.

The piece frames Indianapolis’s loss as the catalyst for franchise-defining choices: hold to their veteran, injured Hall of Famer or pivot decisively to a potential long-term successor. The stakes are framed as more than roster moves — a possible turning point for a franchise built around Manning for 14 seasons.

Seven high school students and a teacher died and more than 40 people were injured after an avalanche struck near the Nasu Onsen ski area in Tochigi prefecture, about 120–150 km north of Tokyo. The group comprised 52 students and 11 teachers from seven high schools taking part in a three‑day mountaineering training trip when the avalanche hit at about 9:20 a.m. on Monday. Rescue teams, supported by Japan’s Self‑Defense Forces, recovered the victims and transported dozens to hospitals; two students were reported in serious condition. Heavy snowfall overnight—over 30 cm in the Nasu highlands—with strong winds and rising temperatures had prompted official avalanche advisories. Organizers had canceled an ascent because of bad weather and the students were practicing walking in deep snow when the slide occurred about 500 meters from their hotel at 1,300 meters altitude. Authorities opened a police inquiry and are examining whether the exercise proceeded despite hazardous conditions, with potential professional negligence probes. Local officials and organizers expressed sorrow and said crisis management and safety assessments would be reviewed after the tragedy.

At a House Oversight Committee hearing, Michael Botticelli, deputy director of the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy, acknowledged that marijuana is much less likely to cause death than alcohol or prescription drugs, calling fatal overdoses from pot “very rare.” Pressed by Rep. Gerry Connolly, Botticelli conceded there is “nothing comparable” between marijuana and the higher death tolls tied to alcohol and prescription medication. Despite that admission, he emphasized the administration still views marijuana as harmful, arguing its “totality of harm” warrants caution and reiterating the Justice Department’s duty to enforce the Controlled Substances Act. 

Botticelli maintained the administration’s stance opposing state-level legalization efforts, even as President Obama had recently suggested allowing legalization experiments in Colorado and Washington and likened marijuana’s dangers to alcohol. Republicans, notably subpanel chairman Rep. John Mica, warned the president’s comments may lower perceived risk among youth and criticized the federal government’s inconsistent policy. Democrats countered with concerns about racial disparities in enforcement; Rep. Elijah Cummings defended Obama’s remarks, noting that minorities and poor youth are disproportionately punished for marijuana offenses while others avoid enforcement. 

The hearing occurred amid shifting state and D.C. laws—two states have legalized recreational use, 20 states and D.C. permit medical marijuana, and D.C. voted to decriminalize possession—placing Congress in a complicated position over federal preemption and potential intervention.

Engineers have created a sperm-shaped micro-robot, dubbed “MagnetoSperm,” that can be propelled and steered using a modest oscillating magnetic field. The devices are fabricated from a flexible polymer body with a thin metal (cobalt‑nickel) coating on the head applied by electron-beam evaporation. When placed in a moving magnetic field produced by electromagnet coils, the magnetic head orients and oscillates, causing the flexible tail to whip and generate forward thrust—mimicking biological flagellar propulsion. The robots, roughly six times longer than human sperm, swim at up to about 0.5 body lengths per second and can be navigated toward fixed targets by programming the magnetic field. Researchers see potential applications in targeted drug delivery, precision positioning and assembly in nanomanufacturing, and even assisted reproduction techniques, though they caution that performance must be tested in more complex environments. The design outsources power and control to the external magnetic field, enabling a very small footprint. Future work aims to make the devices smaller and faster and to explore magnetic nanofibers for tails and operation in realistic biological settings.

Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez has turned to Serbian practitioner Marijana Kovacevic as he battles an injury crisis, sending Glen Johnson and Fabio Aurelio to Belgrade for her controversial placenta-based treatments. Kovacevic, who gained notoriety after Arsenal’s Robin van Persie sought her help for ruptured ankle ligaments, uses fluids derived from placentas (reportedly horse, possibly human), electrolysis and lengthy, candlelit sessions; she charges up to €3,000 for a three-day course. Several Premier League players—including Liverpool’s Yossi Benayoun and Albert Riera, and overseas Manchester City players—have visited her, and clubs generally tolerate players’ trips despite scepticism. Serbia’s FA has considered bringing her in-house to monitor her influence. Liverpool face multiple fitness concerns (Torres, Gerrard, Aquilani, Riera, Skrtel) amid poor form, making alternative remedies more attractive despite limited scientific support.

Two lunchboxes containing 12 gold bars each were found hidden in aircraft toilets on a Jet Airways plane at Kolkata’s international airport, first prompting a bomb scare and then a smuggling probe, officials said. The 1 kg bars—about the size of a smartphone—are believed from Dubai and worth 73.68 million rupees ($1.18 million). Smuggling into India has risen after import duty and restrictions reduced domestic supply. Investigators are questioning airline and airport staff, screening passenger profiles and training crews to watch for people loitering in lavatories. Officials say detected seizures may be under 10 percent of actual smuggling.

A 19-year-old woman, Shana Grice, complained repeatedly to Sussex Police about stalking and harassment by her ex-boyfriend, Michael Lane, but at one point was penalised for wasting police time before she was found murdered. Miss Grice was discovered with her throat slit in a smoke-filled bedroom set alight at her Portslade home in August. Lane, 27, denies murder.

The prosecution outlined months of contacts between Miss Grice and police. In February she reported being stalked: Lane allegedly hid outside her home, sent unwanted flowers and left a threatening note on her new boyfriend’s car. In March Lane denied an alleged assault and presented messages from Miss Grice indicating she wanted to be with him. Police issued Miss Grice a fixed penalty notice for failing to disclose she had been in a relationship with Lane and for making a false report, with no further action taken against him.

On 9 July Lane was cautioned and ordered to stay away after admitting he stole a key and let himself into her house to watch her sleep. The next day Miss Grice reported repeated calls from a withheld number including heavy breathing; police considered there were no further lines of inquiry. On 12 July she reported being followed but the matter was treated as low risk.

In his defence, Lane denied killing Miss Grice. He admitted entering her home to discover why their relationship ended, leaving the note on the car and fitting a tracker to her vehicle, and said he had sex with her two days before her death. He claimed to have found her body, panicked, did not call 999, and later disposed of clothing and hid trainers after noticing blood. He denied setting the fire and said he had bought petrol intending to commit suicide. Lane admitted lying in police interviews. The trial was adjourned.

Oklahoma Republican Rep. Frank Lucas easily won his primary with about 82.8% of the vote, while challenger Timothy Ray Murray received roughly 5.2%. Rather than concede, Murray has announced he will contest the results, claiming Lucas is dead and has been replaced by a look‑alike or “robot” impersonator. Murray’s campaign website and a press release assert that “it is widely known Rep. Frank D. Lucas is no longer alive and has been displayed by a look alike,” even alleging Lucas’s double was “depicted as sentenced on a white stage in southern Ukraine on or about Jan. 11, 2011.” Lucas’s office and spokeswoman Stacy Buck refute the claims: Lucas is alive and has never been to Ukraine. The Oklahoma State Election Board said Murray had not filed a formal petition to challenge the outcome as of reporting; he had a deadline to decide and the window to contest a candidate’s qualifications had passed. Observers and commentators treated Murray’s accusations as bizarre; University of Oklahoma political scientist Keith Gaddie called them among the more outlandish developments in state politics. Murray has a history of fringe assertions on his website, including vows not to use artificial intelligence or look‑alikes. Lucas, a 20‑year incumbent who faced Murray previously, dismissed the allegation as the first time he’d been accused of being a body double or robot. The episode drew comparisons to fictional plots about doubles, such as the film Dave.

Herman Cain’s campaign released a 56-second web video centered on Mark Block, Cain’s chief of staff, that quickly became a viral puzzle. Most of the spot features Block delivering broad, patriotic platitudes about Cain and urging supporters to “take this country back.” In the ad’s final seconds, an anthemic song (“I Am America”) crescendos as Block takes a slow drag from a cigarette and exhales toward the camera, then Cain offers a slow, sidelong smile. The smoking moment—unusual and controversial in a campaign ad—drowned out Block’s earlier remarks and sparked immediate online parody (including a @FakeMarkBlock Twitter account) and debate. Commentators advanced theories: a nod to Cain’s past industry ties to tobacco, a deliberate anti-establishment image, an appeal to working‑class voters, a stunt to guarantee viral attention, or simply an uncalculated choice. Block later told Fox News there was no hidden meaning: he’s a smoker and staffers told producers “let Block be Block,” adding that smoking can resonate in certain voter settings. Observers noted the ad’s amateurish tone could reinforce doubts about Cain’s seriousness as a national candidate even as it succeeded in drawing massive attention.

AllOut.org launched a petition defending Electronic Arts (EA) and BioWare for including LGBT characters in their games, aiming to push back against anti-gay boycott groups like the Family Research Council. The petition drew wide support from AllOut’s near-900,000 membership and from gamers opposing homophobia, but the campaign page was hit by a massive spambot attack that added roughly 3,000–5,000 duplicate comments and signatures—many with odd names and varied country tags such as “Fred from Pakistan.” AllOut temporarily disabled the page, is removing spam entries, and says the majority of signatures are legitimate. Community Manager Tile Wolfe and co-founder Andre Banks stressed AllOut acted independently of EA, launched the campaign to show corporate support for LGBT inclusion, and had no contact with the publisher. Widespread online speculation quickly accused EA of orchestrating the inflated support—fuelled by past incidents like a staged protest for Dante’s Inferno—but there’s no evidence implicating EA; the spam originated from anonymous IPs and the source remains unknown. Meanwhile, conservative groups such as the Florida Family Association continue to attack BioWare/EA over plans to add same-sex romance options in titles like Star Wars: The Old Republic, often misrepresenting how the games function and the player demographics. Investigations and cleanup are ongoing.

Sarah Catherine Long, 41, was found dead in her Davidson, North Carolina, townhouse on July 23 with a single gunshot wound to the left side of her head and a .357 revolver in her left hand. Her death was initially ruled a suicide, but investigators soon identified a number of inconsistencies that prompted a reclassification as a suspicious death or potential homicide. Long was right-handed, yet the gun was in her left hand; the medical examiner could not definitively link the fatal wound to her death and found no blood on the hand she allegedly used to fire the weapon. Neighbors reported seeing Long with a man, later identified as William Becker, on July 18–19, and one neighbor heard a loud bang on the 19th, the day police suspect she may have died. Becker, who told police he had been in a seven-month secret affair with Long, notified authorities after not seeing her for days and soon produced documents indicating Long had named him sole beneficiary of her estate—valued at roughly $1–1.5 million. He told investigators Long was depressed and recently diagnosed with cervical cancer, but her physician later said she only had abnormal cervical cells treatable with a minor outpatient procedure. Becker’s wife allegedly reported an earlier incident in which a smoothie he gave her “tasted funny,” and Becker reportedly admitted adding a sleep aid to it to help her rest. Police have seized Long’s electronics, mail and financial records and obtained her Yahoo! account and router data to reconstruct her final days and identify any other person present that night. Forensic tests—including toxicology and gunpowder residue analysis—are pending. Authorities say they have identified a person of interest but have not made any arrests and are continuing an active investigation.

Saudi media mistakenly reported a satirical column as real news when US humorist Andy Borowitz jokingly wrote that President Barack Obama would tell Congress he is Muslim to reach a compromise with Republicans. Al-Hayat and Sabq.org ran straight accounts of Borowitz’s piece, with headlines like “Obama doesn’t mind coming out as a Muslim” and “Obama: ‘I'm ready to announce that I am a Muslim,’” and quoted mock lines about his birthplace being “negotiable.” Borowitz’s parody—published on the Huffington Post and The Borowitz Report—mocked the persistent rumors about Obama’s faith and birthplace, satirically suggesting he might even claim to be born in the Atlantic Ocean. The incident highlighted how satire can be misunderstood and picked up as fact.

A hoax circulated online claiming iOS 8 included a “Wave” feature that lets iPhones be wirelessly recharged in a microwave. The fake ads spread on Twitter and Reddit after the iOS 8 release, and users on Reddit traced the prank back to a 4chan thread. The post urged people to microwave their phones for about 60–70 seconds, which is false and dangerous. This stunt echoes earlier 4chan hoaxes, such as last year’s spoof that iOS 7 would make phones waterproof, and follows longstanding YouTube videos promoting similar microwave-recharge myths. While it’s unclear how many people believed the claim, some tweets showed fried iPhones and damaged microwaves—though those posts may have been jokes. The article emphasizes that iOS 8 does not enable microwave charging and warns users not to attempt it, noting that Twitter stores tweet locations (which users can toggle or delete) and pointing readers toward more information about iOS 8’s legitimate features like app extensions and improved keyboards.

The World Health Organization has declared Cuba the first country to eliminate mother-to-child transmission of both HIV and syphilis. An international WHO and Pan American Health Organization team found Cuba met validation criteria after 2013 data showed only two infants born with HIV and five with syphilis. WHO and PAHO credited Cuba’s achievements to universal prenatal care, early testing and timely treatment for infected mothers and newborns. Antiretroviral therapy before and after birth and for newborns can reduce HIV transmission risk to under 1 percent, and antibiotics can prevent congenital syphilis when given to infected pregnant women. Globally, about 1.4 million HIV-positive women become pregnant annually and, without treatment, transmission risk can be as high as 45 percent; worldwide access to prophylactic drugs reached 67 percent in low- and middle-income countries by 2013. WHO and UNAIDS hailed Cuba’s success as proof that ending pediatric HIV is possible and urged donors and governments to scale up services to replicate these results.

A search warrant made public this week identifies Dr. Michael Todd Schulenberg as a Minnesota physician who treated Prince twice in April, including on April 20 — the day before the musician was found dead at Paisley Park on April 21. The warrant, later sealed after being inadvertently left unsealed, says Schulenberg prescribed medications for Prince and delivered test results to Paisley Park the morning Prince’s body was discovered. Investigators executed the warrant at North Memorial Medical Center, where Schulenberg had worked in Minnetonka but no longer is employed; hospital officials declined to give details. Schulenberg told detectives he had seen Prince on April 7 — the day Prince canceled Atlanta shows citing illness — and again on April 20, and that the prescription was to be filled at a Walgreens. He is not on the federal list of buprenorphine prescribers. Separately, Prince’s representatives contacted California addiction specialist Dr. Howard Kornfeld on April 20; Kornfeld sent his son and another doctor to Minnesota, and Kornfeld arranged for a Minnesota physician to evaluate Prince on April 21, an appointment that did not occur. The affidavit notes others present at the death scene and that Prince had sought prior treatment for unspecified illness and reportedly for opioid withdrawal. Authorities are examining prescription data and possible opioid involvement; the Midwest Medical Examiner’s Office continues investigating, with results pending.

When Robert Wang lost his software job in 2008, he channeled his spare time into solving a common family problem: making healthy, quick dinners. The result was the Instant Pot, an electric “smart cooker” that combines pressure cooking with functions like slow cooking, steaming, rice cooking, yogurt making, sautéing and sterilizing. Launched in 2010 as a five-in-one device, the Instant Pot evolved into a 10-in-one appliance and found enormous consumer traction after engineers added digital controls, sensors and safety features—including a burn-detection mechanism—to make pressure cooking accessible to novices.

The device’s popularity surged through word of mouth, social media and blogger endorsements rather than traditional advertising. An active official Facebook community of over 750,000 members shares recipes and troubleshooting tips, fueling cult-like devotion among users who often replace many other kitchen tools with the Instant Pot. Strong endorsements from food writers and TV segments helped, and the pot became a top seller on Amazon — moving about 250,000 units on Prime Day and prompting Wang to prepare for even larger orders during Black Friday. Double Insight, the Ottawa-based company Wang leads, reached profitability in 2012 and has reported rapid revenue growth since.

Cooks praise the Instant Pot for drastically cutting time for dishes that traditionally take hours—dried beans, braised meats, risotto and even octopus can be made far more quickly—while its limitations (delicate fish and some pasta) are acknowledged. A growing multi-cooker market and competing models from established brands suggest the trend will persist. Wang’s goal remains ambitious: an Instant Pot in every kitchen, backed by ongoing product development and responsiveness to customer needs.

Authorities in Nicaragua and New York say Orlando Tercero has been arrested in connection with the homicide of 22-year-old Haley Anderson, a nursing student at SUNY Binghamton from Westbury, Long Island. Nicaragua’s National Police confirmed Tercero was detained Tuesday and is being transferred to El Chipote prison near Managua. Binghamton police had identified Tercero, Anderson’s ex-boyfriend and a fellow student, as a person of interest after Anderson’s body was discovered Friday during a welfare check at an off-campus home about a mile from campus. Her death was ruled a homicide following autopsy. Investigators say Tercero flew from JFK to Nicaragua before Anderson’s body was found; authorities believe he may have dual citizenship and traveled there because he has family. Broome County prosecutors are preparing a warrant and expect to present evidence to a grand jury; if indicted they will seek expedited extradition. Friends, classmates and coworkers described Anderson as outgoing and close to graduation; the university and community have expressed condolences. Details about the circumstances of the killing have not been released.

Over the Memorial Day weekend in Dallas, someone tampered with three portable Texas Department of Transportation electronic construction signs, replacing routine traffic warnings with prank and political messages. Drivers on westbound Interstate 30 and nearby Westmoreland Road awoke to displays reading “Donald Trump is a … shape shifting lizard!,” “Bernie for president,” and “Work is canceled. Go back home.” TxDOT crews discovered the alterations early Tuesday and restored normal messages shortly before 6 a.m. Officials say the signs belong to a contractor working along I-30 and were believed to have been powered down and locked for the holiday, so the vandal(s) had to physically access the control panels, cut locks, and reset passwords to change the displays. TxDOT spokesman Ryan LaFontaine stressed the seriousness of the incident, noting the tampering could endanger motorists who rely on the signs for construction warnings and that altering roadway message boards is a third-degree felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison. Authorities urged the public to report suspicious activity around portable signs, especially when no work is ongoing. The Associated Press and local outlets sought further comment from TxDOT but noted the agency called the hack no laughing matter.

A massive mudslide near Oso, Washington, devastated roughly one square mile Saturday, killing at least eight people, destroying about 30 homes and burying a mile-long stretch of Highway 530 under up to 20 feet of mud. Rescue teams searched through soupy, tree-strewn debris Sunday and into the night but heard no signs of life after initial cries for help late Saturday; shifting debris and darkness forced them to pause operations. Authorities worked from a “soft list” of more than 100 unaccounted-for people, though officials cautioned the true number would likely be lower as some residents may have been away. Several people were hospitalized, including critically injured infants and elderly patients. The slide, in an area that partially collapsed in 2006, likely resulted from saturated ground after heavy rain. The mud formed a dam across the North Fork Stillaguamish River; water began seeping through the blockage Sunday, easing but not eliminating flooding concerns. Governor Jay Inslee described the scene as “total devastation” and praised rescuers amid grim expectations as search continued.

A deadly collapse at the Big Four Ice Caves in Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest left one hiker dead and several others injured on Monday as visitors sought shelter from a heat wave. Eighteen-year-old Chloe Jakubowski and friends were inside the popular cave near Granite Falls when a loud crack signaled a sudden avalanche of ice and rock. Jakubowski crouched behind a large ice block; when she emerged she found people with cuts, broken bones and one unconscious woman. Jakubowski and others assisted victims until help arrived.

Snohomish County officials said one person was killed and five others — three adults and two juveniles — were transported to hospitals. Three adults were airlifted to Harborview Medical Center in Seattle: a 25-year-old man initially critical but later upgraded to serious in intensive care, a 35-year-old man whose condition improved from serious to satisfactory, and a 35-year-old woman treated and released. Two girls with minor injuries were taken to Providence Regional Medical Center and released. The deceased remained at the scene while rescue teams assessed hazardous, unstable ice before recovery.

Rescue response was delayed because of cell reception limits and the caller’s need to drive out to reach a payphone, costing about 45 minutes. More than 100 rescuers ultimately responded. Authorities warned that a recent heat wave had weakened the caves, describing them as frozen-over avalanche chutes vulnerable to collapse. The U.S. Forest Service had previously warned visitors to avoid standing on or near the caves; signs already cautioned of danger after prior incidents, including the 2010 death of 11-year-old Grace Tam. Trail reports and visitor videos had recently shown melting and ice calving from cave mouths. Officials said the area would be closed indefinitely while recovery and safety assessments continue.

Point Loma Nazarene University (PLNU) students, staff, professors and alumni launched the Beauty for Ashes Fund to provide college education for survivors of human trafficking. The campaign seeks to seed the fund with $40,000 to cover tuition, room and board for survivors admitted to PLNU, with smaller amounts allocated for vocational discernment and student administrative support. Organizers emphasize that survivors consistently express a desire for higher education as a crucial step in long-term rehabilitation — moving from victim to survivor to thriver — and that a Christian university setting can provide loving, academically rigorous mentorship to support that transformation.

Human trafficking — defined as recruiting, harboring, transporting, providing or obtaining a person for compelled labor or commercial sex through force, fraud or coercion — is presented as a pervasive local and national problem that affects U.S. teens and children as young as 12–14. The campaign situates PLNU’s efforts within a broader movement of increased rescues, prosecutions and services aimed at ending modern-day slavery. PLNU frames the initiative as rooted in its mission and Nazarene heritage of serving the marginalized, extending the university’s educational mission to those most vulnerable as well as those who want to help.

The campaign encourages donations (tax deductible) and outreach, noting that even if the $40,000 target isn’t reached, all funds raised will go to the Beauty for Ashes Fund. Rather than relying on traditional crowdfund “perks,” most campaign incentives are donated by supporters; donors may claim them, though perk value is deducted from tax-deductible amounts. New perks include a Rising Lotus soap created by a PLNU alum and donated art pieces from events. The campaign has received local and national media coverage (KPBS, Fox San Diego, Fox News, The Examiner, USA TODAY College). Organizers invite sharing on social media and direct inquiries to BeautyforAshes@pointloma.edu.

U.S. forces carried out targeted airstrikes and humanitarian airdrops in northern Iraq as ISIS advanced across the region in August 2014. Two F/A-18s and later additional jets and drones struck ISIS artillery, mortar positions and a seven-vehicle convoy near Irbil after President Obama authorized action to protect U.S. personnel and vulnerable civilians. The strikes marked the first direct U.S. attacks on the Islamic State in Iraq and were launched amid warnings that ISIS fighters, who had seized Mosul earlier, were approaching Irbil and had captured the Mosul Dam—raising fears of catastrophic flooding. U.S. cargo planes also airdropped 72 bundles of food and water onto Mount Sinjar, where tens of thousands of Yazidis—fleeing ISIS ultimatums to convert, pay a tax, flee or die—were trapped; officials said most supplies reached the refugees. The U.S. committed not to send combat troops back to Iraq but said airstrikes could continue to protect civilians and American personnel. International partners including Britain and France pledged support, the U.N. prepared humanitarian corridors, and Iraqi and Kurdish forces reportedly coordinated more closely. Critics urged broader intervention, while some U.S. senators called for expanded strikes against ISIS in Iraq and Syria.

Buffalo Bills receiver Stevie Johnson sparked controversy after joking about North Korea’s nuclear threats on Twitter. Responding to escalating rhetoric, Johnson wrote that if North Korea were to “bomb 1st,” they should “Bomb Foxboro, Mass.” — home of the New England Patriots and a place the Bills hadn’t beaten since 2000. Patriots fans reacted angrily to the remark, calling it in poor taste and uncomfortable given the subject. The piece mocks the idea of imagining Gillette Stadium destroyed and quips about the absurdity of radiation-enhanced Bill Belichick. The story argues Johnson’s comment was a tasteless joke, but notes many Americans aren’t taking North Korea seriously and that the comment was unlikely to be heeded by the regime. After backlash, Johnson softened his stance, tweeting that some people took it too seriously and expressing “Much Respect for The Pats along with Every other NFL Team,” predicting a great NFL 2013 season. The article frames the episode as a social-media misstep rather than a serious provocation.

A ForbesWoman/NEFE Harris Interactive poll of 2,019 U.S. adults found financial infidelity is common: 31% of people who combine finances admitted lying to a spouse, and another third said they’d been deceived. Common deceptions include hiding cash (58%), minor purchases (54%), bills (30%), major purchases (16%), secret accounts (15%), and lying about debt or income (11% each). Consequences are serious: 67% reported arguments, 42% less trust, 16% said lies led to divorce and 11% to separation. Therapists and lawyers describe motives such as pragmatism, control, guilt, and fear; deception cuts across income levels and can involve extreme schemes. Experts recommend early money talks, transparent budgeting, and investigating the depth of lies if discovered. Many affected couples plan better communication and shared budgets going forward.

When Houston restaurants first embraced Twitter in 2008, social media quickly became essential for engaging customers, sharing reviews and photos, and shaping reputations. But tweeting can also have immediate, real-world consequences. In August 2011, Allison Hiromi Matsu was asked to leave Down House in the Heights after she posted a now-deleted Tweet calling a bartender a “twerp” and using derogatory hashtags. General manager Forrest DeSpain, who monitors the restaurant’s Twitter, read the comment, called the bar, spoke with Matsu by phone and asked her to leave; Matsu later posted that she left in tears and said the staff had blocked her online. The incident—one of the first high-profile cases of a patron being ejected for online remarks made while dining—sparked debate about whether establishments should prioritize the in-person experience or their broader social-media audience. Some criticized Down House’s handling, while PR professionals noted that the controversy still increases the restaurant’s visibility.

A new social media prank known as "Put ’Em in a Coffin" has caused real-world damage in Houston after teens imitated viral videos and jumped onto car hoods. The trend began in May when a member of the rap group ThotBoyz posted a clip of himself falling backwards across a car hood with his arms crossed like a body in a coffin; that original Vine drew millions of views and spawned numerous copycat videos. In Houston, homeowner James McHugh discovered that a group of seven young men filmed by his home security camera had approached his driveway and sequentially flopped onto the hoods of his white BMW and his wife’s car, leaving a deep dent and significant damage. McHugh says repairs will run about $4,000, a cost he finds infuriating given the short-lived amusement the prank provides its perpetrators. Reporters note the stunt has also expanded beyond cars to include jumps onto fast-food counters, store displays, bins and even other people, raising concerns about property damage and safety. McHugh called the behavior senseless and frustrating, lamenting that hard-earned money was “washed away” for ten seconds of laughter.

James Joseph “Joe” Dresnok, the last known American defector who lived in North Korea, died in November at age 74, his sons announced in a state-posted video. Dresnok deserted the U.S. Army in 1962, reportedly crossing a minefield through the demilitarized zone after a divorce and the prospect of court-martial. He spent the rest of his life in North Korea, becoming part of state propaganda efforts and appearing in North Korean films and interviews, consistently expressing loyalty to the regime. 

In the video carried on the Uriminzokkiri website, sons Ted (Hong Soon-chol) and James (Hong Chol), both born and raised in North Korea and speaking Korean with northern accents, said their father “was in the arms of the republic” and “received only the love and care of the party until his passing.” They wore Korean People’s Army uniforms with badges showing the portraits of Kim Il-sung and Kim Jong-il while delivering scripted praise and pledging devoted service to Kim Jong-un, reflecting the tightly controlled language typically used by foreign residents on state media. This appearance followed an earlier televised interview in May 2016 in which they also praised the country.

The brothers used the platform to criticize the United States, accusing “US imperialists” of fomenting “war hysteria” amid heightened tensions following North Korea’s recent intercontinental ballistic missile tests. They warned that if war broke out North Korea would “wipe the land of the US from the earth,” and reaffirmed confidence in Kim Jong-un as the guarantor of victory. Dresnok had previously told Western journalists he was satisfied with his life in Pyongyang and would not leave the country even for vast riches. His life was the subject of the 2006 British documentary Crossing the Line, which chronicled his unusual defection and decades-long stay in the isolated state.

A first-of-its-kind pilot study reports microplastics in human stools from participants across eight countries, suggesting pervasive human exposure through the modern plastic-dominated environment. Researchers at the Medical University of Vienna and Environment Agency Austria analyzed stool samples from eight healthy volunteers in Finland, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Poland, Russia, the U.K. and Austria using a newly developed analytical procedure (micro FT-IR). Every sample contained microplastic particles sized 50–500 micrometres; up to nine different polymer types were identified, most commonly polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene terephthalate (PET). On average, researchers detected about 20 microplastic particles per 10 grams of stool. Participants’ food diaries indicated universal exposure to plastic-wrapped foods or plastic bottles and frequent seafood consumption by most, though the precise sources remain unknown.

Authors caution the study’s small sample size and emphasize the need for larger studies to confirm prevalence, quantify exposure pathways, and probe health effects. Animal studies indicate microplastics can cross intestinal barriers, enter the bloodstream and lymphatic system, accumulate in organs such as the liver, impair gut structure and nutrient absorption, and possibly carry toxins or pathogens—raising concerns for gastrointestinal and systemic health. The findings reinforce growing evidence that plastics have infiltrated food chains and environments worldwide (oceans, tap water, bottled water, salt, seafood) and bolster calls to reduce plastic use, improve waste management and expand monitoring. Policymakers are responding with bans on microbeads and single-use items, producer-responsibility measures and targets for bottle collection, but critics say current action may be insufficient. Further research is urgently needed to determine health implications for humans.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman returned to Pyongyang, traveling from Beijing as a private citizen and saying his goal is to "open the door" and bring sports to North Korea. Rodman, who befriended leader Kim Jong-un during visits in 2013 and 2014 and has called him a "friend for life," spoke briefly to reporters wearing branded clothing for a marijuana-focused digital currency sponsor. The U.S. State Department said it was aware of his visit and reiterated travel warnings advising Americans not to travel to North Korea for safety reasons. Rodman suggested President Donald Trump would support his efforts, noting their past association on Celebrity Apprentice and Trump’s earlier comments that Rodman might be "better than what we have" in handling delicate situations. Rodman’s entourage includes a previous travel companion, professor Joseph Terwilliger; North Korean officials said he would remain until Saturday. He said detained Americans in North Korea were not his present focus. His trips—dubbed "basketball diplomacy"—have drawn criticism from rights groups and observers who argue he fails to press Pyongyang on human rights or detainee cases, though he has previously tried to raise awareness about prisoners like Kenneth Bae. Past visits included sponsored events and a 2014 game where Rodman performed for Kim; critics warn such visits are politically fraught amid heightened U.S.–North Korea tensions.

In late February and early March 2015, rising tensions over Iran’s nuclear negotiations exposed sharp divisions within U.S. foreign policy and strained U.S.-Israeli relations. The Obama administration, focused on securing a diplomatic agreement with Iran and other world powers by an end-of-March framework deadline, warned it would veto U.S. legislation—sponsored by a bipartisan group including Republican Senator Bob Corker—that would require any final Iran deal to be submitted to Congress within five days and bar the president from suspending sanctions for 60 days. The White House argued such measures would complicate negotiators’ work and jeopardize the best chance to curb Iran’s nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, openly challenged that approach. He accepted an invitation to address a joint session of the U.S. Congress—arranged without White House consultation—warning that a prospective deal would imperil Israel’s survival by leaving Iran with the capacity to build nuclear weapons. His decision infuriated the Obama administration and split U.S. political opinion: many congressional Republicans embraced Netanyahu’s message, while dozens of Democrats planned to boycott his speech. Netanyahu framed the visit as a moral, nonpartisan warning to avert a “bad deal,” even as critics accused him of undermining U.S. diplomacy for electoral gain ahead of Israel’s March 17 election.

U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and other administration officials sought to dampen rhetoric, reaffirming close security ties with Israel while insisting negotiations offered a better way to prevent a nuclear-armed Iran than military action. Kerry continued intensive diplomacy with Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Javad Zarif, and coordinated with other international partners. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), meanwhile, reported slow Iranian cooperation on unresolved questions about possible past weapons-related activities and said its inquiry could not continue indefinitely; the IAEA expected to play a monitoring role if an agreement were reached.

The episode highlighted broader regional anxieties: Saudi and Arab allies worried a deal might embolden Iran, while analysts noted the potential legacy importance of any accord for the Obama administration. The dispute over strategy and tone underscored a rare deep rift between Washington and Jerusalem even as both sides maintained that long-term security cooperation would continue.

President Enrique Peña Nieto unveiled a sweeping anti-crime initiative after nationwide outrage over the disappearance of 43 trainee teachers in Iguala, Guerrero, allegedly seized by municipal police and handed to a drug gang. Acknowledging the “cruelty” of the case, Peña Nieto proposed constitutional reforms to curb rampant local corruption by placing municipal police under state control, allowing Congress to dissolve local governments infiltrated by organized crime, and replacing roughly 1,800 municipal forces with state-level units beginning in four violence-plagued states: Guerrero, Michoacán, Jalisco and Tamaulipas. The plan would also simplify jurisdictional divisions among federal, state and local authorities, introduce a single national emergency number (potentially 911), and establish a national identity document. More federal police and security forces would be deployed to the most troubled regions, especially the “hot land” overlapping Guerrero and Michoacán. Critics note similar federal initiatives in 2004 and 2008 produced modest gains but failed to prevent entire municipal forces from being co-opted by gangs, leaving public skepticism. The announcement follows gruesome violence in Guerrero — including 11 decapitated bodies found near Chilapa — underscoring the depth of insecurity. Peña Nieto’s speech marks his first major public pivot to tackling organized crime and local corruption since taking office in 2012.

Former model Christina Estrada has been awarded about £75 million (reported roughly $68m) in a High Court divorce settlement from Saudi businessman Sheikh Walid Juffali, marking one of the largest “needs” awards in English family law. Estrada, 54, and Juffali, 61, were married for 12 years and share a daughter. Juffali divorced her in Saudi Arabia in 2014 under Islamic law without her knowledge and later married a younger woman. Unable to seek relief in Saudi courts, Estrada applied in England under the Matrimonial and Family Proceedings Act.

Estrada had sought far more—estimates of up to £196.5m or £238m appeared in filings—arguing she required a lavish lifestyle to meet “reasonable needs,” including expensive homes in London and Beverly Hills, five cars, and large annual allowances for clothing, travel (including private jet charters), and luxury goods. The court accepted that she had lived an “extraordinary and exorbitant” life but awarded less than she demanded: about £53m in cash plus assets valued at roughly £22m. Juffali’s team argued he had offered substantial alternatives (cash, property use, and other provisions) and disputed claims about his net worth—his lawyers put it far lower than Estrada’s estimate.
