Juffali, who is undergoing treatment in Switzerland for advanced lung cancer, could not attend. Both sides framed the ruling as resolving the question of appropriate support: Estrada stressed her aim to secure her daughter’s future, while Juffali indicated he intended to leave most wealth to his children. The case reinforces London’s role as a forum for high-value divorce claims.

At the 2012 European Individual Women’s Chess Championship in Gaziantep, ECU General Secretary Sava Stoisavljevic explained the new dress code, created after observers noticed players arriving in overly casual or revealing attire. The regulations adopt business-casual standards: men should wear trousers or neat jeans and shirts; women may wear blouses, trousers, skirts or dresses but cleavage is limited (up to the second button) and clothing must be clean, undamaged and appropriate. Caps and hats are banned except for religious reasons, partly to prevent cheating. Prize-giving demands more formal dress. Officials may warn, write up, or deny access or ceremony participation to those who repeatedly breach the code. Stoisavljevic acknowledged the balance between maintaining chess’s image and spectator appeal, and noted ongoing discussion about limits like skirt length.

House Oversight Committee leaders say classified documents show former national security adviser Michael Flynn failed to disclose significant foreign payments and may have broken the law. After a private review of Pentagon and other records, Chairman Jason Chaffetz (R-Utah) and Ranking Member Elijah Cummings (D-Md.) concluded Flynn did not report fees from Russian-linked entities — including a $45,000 RT-paid speech in Moscow in December 2015 — nor obtain required permission for such foreign income when renewing his security clearance via an SF-86 in January 2016. They also noted large payments tied to lobbying for Turkey. Both lawmakers warned that knowingly falsifying or concealing material facts on clearance forms is a felony and said Flynn could face penalties, including repayment of funds or criminal investigation, though proving “knowingly and willfully” is challenging. Flynn resigned in February after misleading the vice president about conversations with the Russian ambassador and later amended financial disclosures to list some foreign payments. The White House has declined to turn over pre-inauguration documents, saying they are not in its possession and that post-inauguration materials requested involve sensitive information. Flynn has offered to testify to congressional intelligence panels in exchange for immunity; committees have not accepted. The FBI and congressional inquiries into Russia’s 2016 interference continue.

This July, Zhangjiajie in Hunan province, China, will debut the world’s longest and highest glass-bottom bridge, a dramatic skywalk spanning about 430 meters (more than 1,400 feet) and hovering roughly 300 meters (nearly 1,000 feet) above the Zhangjiajie Grand Canyon. Designed by Israeli architect Haim Dotan, the 20-foot-wide structure can reportedly hold up to 800 people at once and offers transparent views over the sides and through the bottom, framing sandstone and quartz peaks, forests, and waterfalls that inspired the movie Avatar. Operators plan additional attractions, including a bungee jump that would be the world’s highest of its kind, and even using the span as a fashion runway.

Safety questions have followed other high-profile incidents with glass skywalks in China, notably cracking reported on a Yuntai Mountain walkway after a tourist dropped a thermos. To reassure the public, Zhangjiajie organizers invited BBC reporter Dan Simmons to test a bridge panel by striking it with a sledgehammer. The panel’s top layer cracked visibly after initial blows, but the multilayered glass remained intact and did not shatter through, demonstrating layered redundancy in the design. Ahead of its opening, the bridge has already drawn global attention and record claims, and officials emphasize its structural robustness even as they prepare to welcome thrill-seeking visitors.

A powerful magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck in the Caribbean Sea off the northern coast of Honduras late Tuesday night, one of the strongest quakes to hit the region in modern times. The U.S. Geological Survey located the shallow temblor about 202 km (125 miles) north-northeast of Barra Patuca, Honduras, roughly 44 km east of the sparsely populated Swan Islands, and about 303 km southwest of George Town, Cayman Islands. The quake occurred at a depth of roughly 10 km (6.2 miles), which amplified shaking felt widely across northern Central America and the Caribbean. Shaking was reported across much of Honduras, in Tegucigalpa and coastal provinces, and as far afield as Mexico’s Quintana Roo and Belize; residents described strong, brief jolts and swaying utility poles. Authorities reported some minor damage such as cracks in homes in Colon, Atlantida and Olancho provinces, but no immediate reports of serious injuries or major structural collapse. Tsunami centers initially issued warnings and advisories for multiple Caribbean islands and Central American coasts, cautioning sea level rises of 0.3–1 meter, but alerts were canceled about an hour later and no damaging tsunami materialized. Several aftershocks of magnitude 4+ followed. Officials kept emergency systems active and urged coastal residents to remain alert.

Search teams in the southern Indian Ocean pursued multiple acoustic leads Sunday in the hunt for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, which vanished with 239 people aboard nearly a month earlier. A Chinese patrol ship, Haixun 01, reported detecting brief electronic signals at 37.5 kHz — the frequency used by black box beacons — on Friday and again on Saturday; a British Royal Navy vessel was en route to investigate. Separately, Australia’s naval ship Ocean Shield, equipped with a U.S. towed pinger locator, tracked an acoustic noise in another area. Authorities called the detections “an important and encouraging lead” but warned they were unverified and possibly fleeting. Up to 10 military planes, two civilian aircraft and 13 ships were assigned to search three zones totaling roughly 216,000 sq km about 2,000 km northwest of Perth. Teams also reported white objects nearby. Searchers face a race against time as black box battery life approaches 30 days, and investigators urged caution until signals are confirmed.

MainStreet pushes back on the narrative that iconic American brands are gone, noting many beloved products still carry U.S. manufacturing ties even as globalization has shifted production. Surveys show strong consumer preference for "Made in America"—61% overall and far higher for older groups—with many willing to pay premiums, especially after safety scares tied to Chinese-made toys and food. Yet branding often masks global supply chains: familiar names frequently rely on foreign ownership, parts, or factories. Examples include Budweiser and Coors, now part of multinational brewing giants (InBev, MolsonCoors/SABMiller) despite patriotic marketing; Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra, which have substantial Mexican assembly; and the Ford F-150, assembled in the U.S. but with only about 60% domestic parts. Rawlings baseballs, Levi’s jeans, American Girl dolls, Craftsman tools and Schwinn bicycles all shifted much production overseas, while some lines remain partially or wholly U.S.-made. One standout is KitchenAid mixers, still produced in Greenville, Ohio. The piece stresses that patriotic packaging doesn’t guarantee American origin and urges consumers to look beyond marketing to determine true domestic content.

A newly released FBI profile of Adam Lanza finds he planned the Dec. 14, 2012, Sandy Hook massacre methodically, possibly contemplating it as early as March 2011. Interviews, neighbor canvasses and an hour-long interview with an unidentified woman who corresponded with Lanza online for years portray him as isolated, socially awkward, obsessed with mass shootings and meticulous about a spreadsheet cataloging killers. Agents noted deteriorating relations with his mother, rigid thinking, possible pedophilic interest (no evidence of acting on it), nightmares about shootings, and knowledge of guns.

In a dramatic end to three days of terror around Paris, French security forces killed the two brothers suspected of murdering 12 people at Charlie Hebdo and an accomplice who seized hostages at a kosher supermarket. The Kouachi brothers, Chérif and Saïd, were cornered at a printing plant in Dammartin-en-Goële after the January 7 attack on the satirical weekly. A 26-year-old graphic designer hiding inside the building—reported as Lilian Lepere—sent text messages to police with tactical details and his location while sheltering under a sink, providing crucial intelligence that helped time the assault. The brothers briefly held and later released a manager; another hidden employee was rescued when police accessed the upper floor with an armored vehicle.

Simultaneously in Paris, Amedy Coulibaly burst into a kosher market, killed four hostages and held others for several hours, claiming allegiance to Islamic State and coordinating with the Kouachis. Police tracked some hostages via a relative’s phone number and stormed the store after hearing Coulibaly on a call; explosions and heavy gunfire ended both sieges at dusk. In total three gunmen and four hostages were killed; 16 hostages were freed. Authorities linked the attackers to al-Qaida in Yemen and long-standing extremist networks; one brother had prior terrorism convictions and both were on U.S. no-fly lists. President François Hollande urged unity and vigilance as investigations and charges against associates continued.

Jahi McMath, a California teenager declared brain dead after complications from a 2013 tonsillectomy, remains the focus of ongoing family advocacy and public interest. In a March Facebook post—the first substantive update in over three months—Jahi’s mother, Nailah Winkfield, shared a photo and emotional message saying her daughter appears “as healthy and beautiful as ever,” calling Jahi “a fighter, a warrior, a blessed child” and urging supporters to keep praying. Winkfield thanked those who helped move Jahi to another facility and those whose public commentary, positive or negative, raised awareness of her case. The family raised nearly $50,000 in private donations and eventually transferred Jahi in 2014 to a long-term care facility in New Jersey, where state law offers a religious exemption allowing continued life support despite a brain-death diagnosis. The move followed an intense legal battle with Children’s Hospital Oakland, where doctors declared Jahi brain dead after she suffered massive, irreversible brain injuries during a December 2013 procedure to treat sleep apnea. Hospital officials sought to withdraw life support, but the family obtained a restraining order and later sued the hospital, alleging a botched surgery and claiming staff pressured them to donate Jahi’s organs. Winkfield also filed a federal suit seeking to have her daughter’s death certificate voided. Medical experts generally hold that brain death is legal death; Dr. Paul Vespa of UCLA described apparent consciousness in brain-dead patients as an illusion sustained by medical technology. Still, Jahi’s case has provoked debate about definitions of death, religious and legal protections, and the role of public attention in medical disputes.

The holiday’s must-have toy, Hatchimals, has spawned a federal class-action lawsuit after many purchased eggs failed to “hatch.” Plaintiff Jodie Hejduk of Bakersfield filed the complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California, alleging she bought a retail Hatchimal for about $50 as a birthday gift; despite following the package instructions, the toy did not emerge from its shell. The suit, brought on behalf of state and national classes, accuses Spin Master of deceptive business practices, false advertising, breach of warranty and unjust enrichment, and seeks compensatory, statutory and punitive damages, restitution, a recall and class certification.

Hatchimals—interactive, mystery-creature toys marketed to hatch after rubbing, tapping and warming the egg—launched in October 2016 and quickly sold out, fueling resale prices well above retail. The lawsuit contends Spin Master knew “hatching” was the product’s chief appeal and that many toys malfunctioned, replacing children’s excitement with disappointment. Plaintiffs cite numerous online complaints and claim Spin Master failed to adequately address malfunction reports, leaving some consumers on hold for hours or without timely resolution.

Spin Master disputes the allegations. Executive vice president and general counsel Christopher Harrs says the company provided troubleshooting support, increased consumer-care staffing and issued replacement products where needed, and maintains the lawsuit’s claims are inaccurate. Attorneys for the plaintiffs, including Mark Geragos and Ben Meiselas, counter that Spin Master sold a defective product and did not do enough to remedy issues during peak holiday demand, saying the case could send a message to companies that market unready products. The suit remains pending.

A large die-off of bottlenose dolphins along the U.S. Mid-Atlantic coast is now being attributed largely to morbillivirus, a measles-like pathogen that suppresses immune systems. Since July 1, 333 dolphins have stranded from New York to North Carolina, with the greatest concentration in Virginia (174). NOAA tested 33 fresh carcasses and found 32 with confirmed or suspected morbillivirus; genetic sequencing identified the cetacean form in 11 animals. The outbreak resembles a devastating 1987–88 event and may continue through spring 2014 if it follows similar patterns. Morbillivirus weakens dolphins, producing lesions in skin, lymph nodes, brain and lungs and leaving animals vulnerable to secondary infections; Brucella bacteria have also been detected in a few samples. Researchers note populations may have lost herd-level immunity since the last outbreak, creating a largely susceptible host pool. Many carcasses are too decomposed for conclusive testing, complicating the investigation, and scientists have no practical way to vaccinate wild dolphins. NOAA advises caution around stranded animals—avoid contact and keep pets away—especially if you have open wounds, though the risk of direct transmission to humans is considered extremely low because morbillivirus strains are species-specific. The die-off will likely end only as surviving animals develop immunity and susceptible numbers diminish.

NASA has released an early concept for a one-ton robotic submarine designed to explore Kraken Mare, the largest hydrocarbon sea on Saturn’s moon Titan. The Titan Submarine Phase I Conceptual Design envisions a nuclear-powered drone that would probe the frigid methane-ethane seas, sampling chemistry, imaging the seafloor, and studying tides, currents, shorelines and any exotic chemistry-based life possibilities. Titan is an unusually Earth-like moon in some ways—larger than Mercury with a dense, nitrogen-methane atmosphere and surface lakes—yet its surface temperature of about −179 °C and hydrocarbon seas make human exploration impractical and highly hazardous, so a robotic craft is appropriate.

The proposed sub would weigh roughly one metric ton, use electrically driven turbines for propulsion, and rely on a radiothermal Stirling generator to produce about 1 kW of power; solar panels are ineffective so far from the Sun and under the surface. It could travel at ~1 m/s and would surface about 16 hours per day to transmit data using a dorsal fin housing a planar phased-array antenna, avoiding the need for a dedicated relay orbiter. Ballast tanks would handle diving and surfacing, though methane/ethane behavior and condensed nitrogen present engineering challenges. Delivering the craft to Titan is nontrivial—standard lander shapes won’t fit it—and concepts include deployment from a spaceplane or parachute-assisted splashdown. The idea is preliminary; a descendant mission might arrive in the 2040s, with substantial development still required.

Because of renewed investigation tied to John Wayne Gacy, a long-unidentified homicide victim known as John Doe No. 89 now has a name: Andy (Andre) Drath. Drath, a ward of Illinois’ Department of Children and Family Services, disappeared at age 16 in late 1978 or early 1979 after traveling west to San Francisco to seek transfer of his guardianship. In June 1979 a male body with multiple gunshot wounds was found in San Francisco and remained unidentified for decades.

After Gacy’s December 1978 arrest and subsequent conviction for raping and murdering 33 young men and boys, many victims remained unnamed. In 2011 the Cook County Sheriff’s Office launched a DNA-driven effort to identify eight of Gacy’s unidentified victims; over time that wider review and public outreach produced 12 case closures related to leads from Gacy-era tips. Investigators encouraged relatives of missing people to submit DNA, and Drath’s maternal half-sister, Dr. Willia Wertheimer, submitted a sample believing he fit the profile of Gacy’s victims. Although Drath was not linked to Gacy’s remains, Drath’s tissue DNA uploaded in late 2014 matched Wertheimer in May 2015. Dental records and a tattoo reading “Andy” further confirmed his identity. San Francisco police are now pursuing the investigation into who killed Andre Drath so he can be returned home and buried with dignity. Cook County Sheriff Thomas Dart hailed the outcome as proof never to give up on cold cases.

Charlo Greene, who quit on live Alaska TV in 2014 with the now-famous line “Fuck it, I quit,” faces a high-stakes criminal case that highlights tensions in the evolving legal landscape around marijuana. Greene (legal name Charlene Egbe) left her KTVA reporting job to run the Alaska Cannabis Club and became a prominent advocate after Alaska voters approved recreational legalization in November 2014. Despite the voter initiative, state regulators had not completed licensing rules, leaving a legal gray area for early operators. Greene’s club sold memberships and accepted donations that patrons could use to obtain marijuana, a model critics and officials say skirted emerging regulations. Anchorage police conducted multiple undercover purchases and two armed raids on the club, producing charges that prosecutors say stem from Greene’s status as the club’s registered owner.

Initially indicted on eight counts of “misconduct involving a controlled substance” carrying up to 24 years in prison, Greene later learned the charges were expanded to 14 counts with a potential 54-year sentence. She has pleaded not guilty and calls the prosecution a “modern day lynching,” criticizing law enforcement tactics during raids and alleging prosecutorial misrepresentation about the club’s structure. Support from the broader cannabis community has been limited, and some legalization advocates argue a fine or administrative penalty would have been more appropriate than felony prosecution. Legal experts note Alaska’s patchwork laws and delayed regulatory framework created confusion, and Greene’s case may carry broader implications as more states legalize and seek to regulate cannabis — raising questions about enforcement discretion, racial disparities in drug prosecutions, and how early entrants into newly legal markets will be treated.

Twinsburg police say they arrested John H. Ford, 35, of Cleveland, suspected in a Streetsboro bank robbery after dashcam video showed him apparently eating a piece of paper while handcuffed and leaning over the hood of a cruiser. Investigators feared the consumed paper might have been the robbery note handed to a FirstMerit teller demanding cash; the robber displayed no gun inside the bank and fled in a dark Ford Escort. Officers found a .38-caliber pistol on Ford’s driver-side floor and a wad of red-ink-stained cash on the passenger side. Ford is also suspected in Stow and Akron robberies.

Sotheby’s is staging a high-profile rock memorabilia auction titled “A Rock & Roll History: Presley to Punk,” offering up to $5 million in items from music icons. The top lot is Bob Dylan’s original, heavily revised handwritten lyrics to “Like a Rolling Stone,” penned on hotel stationery and pared down from 20 pages to four; they’re expected to fetch $1–2 million and are hailed as the “holy grail of lyrics.” Also featured is an elaborately bejeweled white jumpsuit worn by Elvis Presley in Las Vegas—complete with preserved sweat stains—estimated at $100,000–$200,000. John Lennon’s piano, later played by Elton John and David Bowie, is another highlight, with a $100,000–$200,000 estimate, alongside Lennon drawings and Jim Morrison’s “Love Her Madly” lyrics. The sale underscores collectors’ appetite for tangible links to music history and the market’s strong valuations for iconic artifacts.

A California man filmed a dramatic encounter off Mexico’s Guadalupe Island when a great white shark breached a dive cage, broke a metal rail and entered briefly with a diver inside. Posted to YouTube, the video shows the shark lunging at a tuna bait, striking the cage and momentarily ending up inside the top; the single diver, identified as Ming Chan, emerged shaken but uninjured. The videographer and crew explain that when great whites bite bait they can be temporarily blinded and cannot swim backward, which likely caused the accidental collision. Crew members quickly lifted the cage top and helped resolve the situation; observers credit the diver’s calm response, the crew’s actions and luck for preventing serious harm. The shark sustained only minor injury and is reportedly fine. The operators said they work with authorities and scientists, and are reviewing cage design and baiting techniques to improve safety for both divers and sharks. Despite the frightening incident, those involved say they will return to shark diving in the future.

Seasonal monsoon rains have caused catastrophic flooding across northern India, southern Nepal and northern Bangladesh, killing hundreds and affecting tens of millions. Officials report more than 950 deaths in the region—680 in India’s hardest-hit states (Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Assam), 146 in Nepal and 132 in Bangladesh—with some reports placing total deaths nearer 1,400. Around 40 million people are impacted; millions were evacuated and hundreds of thousands shelter in relief camps. Floods washed away homes, crops and infrastructure, destroying vast agricultural areas and raising urgent fears of food insecurity, disease outbreaks and long-term humanitarian needs.

A California man’s viral claim that he was served a deep‑fried rat at a KFC has been discredited after an independent DNA test confirmed the item was chicken, the company says. The controversy began on June 12 when 25‑year‑old Devorise Dixon posted photos on Facebook of a breaded, rodent‑shaped object with what looked like a long tail. His post described biting into a “very hard/touch and rubbery” piece he believed to be a cooked rat, and he said a store manager allegedly admitted the item was a rat and apologized. The image quickly spread online, drawing both shock and skepticism. KFC responded publicly almost immediately, noting that their hand‑breaded tenders vary in size and shape and that other photos Dixon posted “clearly” showed white meat consistent with chicken. Dixon’s attorney later turned the item over to an independent lab for testing. KFC released the lab results and said the DNA confirmed the product was chicken, not a rat. Company spokesperson Rodrigo Coronel said KFC conducted an internal investigation and spoke with employees, calling Dixon’s statement false. The chain has asked Dixon to apologize and to stop making the false claim. ABC News sought comment from Dixon but had not received a response. The episode highlights how quickly sensational social media posts can spread and the role of independent testing and corporate statements in resolving such disputes.

A Swedish psychologist, Carl-Johan Forssen Ehrlin, has published a self‑help children’s picture book, The Rabbit Who Wants to Fall Asleep, which claims to use psychological techniques to help children fall asleep quickly. Since its release the book has topped Amazon’s Best Sellers list, outselling major titles. Written originally in Swedish (2011) and translated into English in 2014, it is now available in multiple languages. The 26‑page tale follows Roger the Rabbit as he, with help from characters such as Uncle Yawn, Sleepy Snail and a Heavy‑Eyed Owl, learns to relax and drift off. The story is intentionally structured: Ehrlin uses specific language patterns, sentence structures, complementary images and embedded cues for the reader—such as instructions to read slowly, yawn at certain moments, and even insert the child’s name—to induce relaxation and a sleep response in the listener. Parents and some sleep experts liken the approach to gentle hypnosis or guided meditation because it repeatedly focuses attention on sleep and models the desired sleepy behavior. The book includes prompts and coaching for parents to maximize effectiveness and has prompted many positive anecdotal reviews claiming rapid results at bedtime. Psychologists and therapists are reported to recommend it, and reviewers have compared its effect to rocking a child to sleep verbally. Ehrlin, who previously authored adult psychology and leadership books, says the method gives suggestions to the child’s unconscious to facilitate calmer, faster sleep. He has received feedback from families and hints that future books may apply similar techniques to other childhood challenges such as potty training. Overall the title’s commercial success highlights strong parental demand for practical, science‑informed bedtime solutions.

Archaeologists have uncovered a 32-foot escape tunnel five feet below ground at the site of the Sobibor extermination camp in German-occupied Poland, offering the first physical evidence that prisoners attempted to dig out of the death camp. The passage, found beneath the area of the sonderkommando barracks and extending under barbed wire, was about as wide as a person; researchers are 99 percent certain it was intended for escape. The sonderkommando—prisoners forced to shepherd victims to gas chambers and dispose of bodies—would have had the relative time and access to excavate, but investigators found no sign the tunnel was ever used. Experts believe the tunnel was likely discovered during the war, its builders executed, and the shaft filled in. Sobibor operated from 1942–43, where an estimated 167,000–250,000 people, mostly Jews, were murdered; after a 600-prisoner uprising in October 1943 the camp was leveled and camouflaged on Himmler’s orders. Long-term excavations have also revealed a crematorium, human remains, and personal artifacts shedding new light on a site that Nazis tried to erase.

Princeton University posted documents from John F. Nash Jr.’s academic file after his and his wife Alicia’s fatal car crash. Among them is a brief Feb. 11, 1948 recommendation from Richard J. Duffin calling Nash “a mathematical genius,” which helped secure his admission to Princeton’s graduate program. Nash completed a 27‑page 1950 Princeton dissertation, “Non‑cooperative games,” introducing the Nash equilibrium, a foundational concept in game theory and the subject of widespread citation and use. He later won the 1994 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences and was recently awarded the Abel Prize. Princeton’s release of these materials accompanies renewed attention to Nash’s life and work, popularized by the film A Beautiful Mind and influential across economics, mathematics, and social sciences.

The author, who lived through Israel’s 1982 invasion of Lebanon, recounts the devastation in besieged West Beirut and criticizes the celebratory media treatment of Ariel Sharon after his death. They describe murderous bombardments around Beirut’s Arab University, the destruction of a refugee building in Sanayeh, and the use of a car bomb to target rescuers. Sharon, as defense minister, is held chiefly responsible for launching the Lebanon war, which produced tens of thousands of casualties, prolonged Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon until 2000, intensified the Lebanese civil war, and cost many combatant lives. The author argues Sharon’s legacy extends to the near-impossibility of a viable Palestinian state: from agriculture minister onward he promoted settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, personally scouting sites and facilitating land seizure, and later engineered Gaza’s unilateral withdrawal while maintaining strict external control. Citing a 1982 meeting transcript during the Sabra and Shatila massacre, the author portrays Sharon as callous and culpable, repeatedly labeling Palestinians “terrorists” and obstructing evacuation or protection. They condemn U.S. and Israeli media praise and suggest Sharon should have faced international justice. The piece contrasts this view with another account praising Sharon’s late-career move toward withdrawal and peace, noting the complexity but insisting his record of atrocities cannot be ignored.

New Orleans federal Judge Kurt Engelhardt sentenced 73-year-old real-estate heir Robert Durst to 85 months (seven years, one month) in prison after Durst pleaded guilty in February to being a felon in possession of a firearm following a March 2015 search of his New Orleans hotel room. Durst, thin and frail in court, renewed his insistence that he is innocent of the 2000 Los Angeles murder of friend Susan Berman and asked to be transferred promptly to California to face that charge. The plea deal resolves related state and federal matters in New York, Texas and Louisiana and includes forfeiture of items seized in the search. Prosecutors say Durst killed Berman to silence her about his first wife’s 1982 disappearance; Durst denies this. The judge agreed to recommend he serve his federal sentence in a low-security California facility, likely enabling transfer within weeks; Durst is expected to be arraigned in Los Angeles in mid-August. Durst has prior convictions and a high-profile history highlighted by the HBO series The Jinx.

Will Gibb, a 31-year-old from Red Deer, Alberta, fought off a cougar that attacked his female husky, Sasha, outside a Tim Hortons in Whitecourt on Dec. 26. Gibb had briefly let his two dogs, Sasha and Mongo, out in the parking lot when he heard Sasha yelp. He found the cougar wrapped around her and instinctively punched the animal in the head, only then realizing it was a big cat. The cougar retreated briefly, but re-emerged and charged again while Sasha, injured and panicked, bit Gibb’s left hand—likely mistaking him for the cougar. Gibb swung, screamed, and called for help from his brother and a friend, grabbed a large stick, and ran into the trees to confront the animal. He managed to get both dogs back into his truck and drive them to safety. Sasha had bite wounds to her neck, belly and under her legs and required sewing for muscle tears; she was treated at a nearby veterinary clinic and released several days later. Gibb sustained deep claw marks but no life-threatening injuries. Local RCMP and wildlife officials located and killed the cougar after consulting about the threat it posed to other pets and people. Whitecourt officials noted cougar sightings are not uncommon in the forested area surrounding town, and Sgt. Jack Poitras advised caution when visiting mountain or wilderness-adjacent areas with pets, warning that dogs can be easy prey. Poitras also said Gibb’s quick action likely saved Sasha’s life, though he did not recommend others wrestle with cougars.

House and Senate leaders and members weighed in Sunday on multiple urgent national issues: the fight against the Islamic State, the looming “fiscal cliff,” the expiring farm bill and renewed calls for gun-control reforms after the Newtown shooting.

Back from a trip to Iraq, Rep. Darrell Issa criticized the Baghdad government as “delusional” about its readiness to fight ISIL, saying Iraqi forces are still focused on long-term training rather than immediate combat. Issa expressed willingness to vote to authorize U.S. military action, argued that Iraqis — notably the Kurds — should conduct ground operations with U.S. air support and technical assistance, and emphasized that American forces are already engaged.

On the fiscal cliff, Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham congratulated President Obama for securing what Graham called a political victory on tax-rate increases for higher earners, while stopping short of endorsing the president’s approach. Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer put the odds of a last-minute fiscal deal at better than 50/50, noting his experience that big agreements often happen at the eleventh hour. Sen. John Barrasso reported no deal yet and criticized Obama’s leadership, accusing him of “outsourcing” the resolution to Congress; Rep. Donna Edwards countered that Democrats are united and blamed Republican obstruction.

Agriculture Secretary Tom Vilsack warned that failure to extend the farm bill by Jan. 1 would devastate agriculture, spike food prices, harm biofuels, exports and conservation programs, and pointed out that most SNAP recipients are seniors, disabled people or children in working families — arguing cuts to the program are misguided.

Following the Sandy Hook massacre, Sen. Dianne Feinstein urged the nation to “bite the bullet” on gun reform and plans to introduce legislation tightening background checks and registration, arguing stronger controls are needed after the slaughter of young children.

In 2008 Robert McCoy was convicted and sentenced to death for the murders of his estranged wife’s son, mother and stepfather. At trial his court-appointed lawyer, Larry English, repeatedly told the jury McCoy was guilty and urged a lesser charge to avoid the death penalty—even though McCoy vehemently protested, insisted on his innocence, sought to fire English, and testified in his own defense. The trial judge denied McCoy’s requests to replace counsel or to represent himself. Louisiana courts upheld English’s tactic, finding his concession a reasonable strategy given the “overwhelming” evidence, a conclusion grounded in precedent allowing concessions when defendants don’t object. McCoy appealed, arguing that counsel’s admission of guilt over his express objection violated the Sixth Amendment right to control the defense. The U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear McCoy v. Louisiana, spotlighting whether a lawyer may concede guilt against a client’s wishes—an issue that pits strategies to save a defendant’s life against the defendant’s autonomy to decide his defense. The case has drawn briefs from national legal groups, state officials, academics and ethics scholars, many arguing counsel’s conduct was unconstitutional and ethically improper.

The Dutch Safety Board concluded that Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 was brought down on 17 July 2014 by a warhead from a Russian-made Buk surface-to-air missile detonating above the left front of the cockpit. The final report, presented after reconstruction of wreckage, found the explosion caused structural failure that led the Boeing 777 to break up in flight, killing all 298 people aboard, most of them Dutch. Investigators identified the warhead as a 9N314M model carried on the 9M38M1 missile, based on characteristic bow-tie and cube-shaped fragments found in wreckage and in crew remains; paint on fragments inside the aircraft matched missile debris recovered on the ground. The board ruled out alternative causes such as meteor strike, internal explosion, or air-to-air missile. It delineated a 320 km2 area in eastern Ukraine from which the missile must have been launched and noted that pro-Russian separatists controlled that territory at the time, though the technical investigation did not assign responsibility for firing the missile. The report also criticised Ukraine for not closing airspace over the conflict zone; around 160 commercial flights used the corridor that day. A separate Dutch criminal probe continues and has identified “persons of interest.” Reactions were sharply divided: Western nations and Ukraine pushed for accountability and cited the report as evidence implicating separatists or Russian involvement, while Russia and Buk manufacturer Almaz-Antey disputed the findings, offering alternative simulations and arguing older missile variants in Ukrainian hands could have produced such fragments. The Safety Board issued 11 safety recommendations urging timely airspace closures during conflicts and stronger international aviation rules.

The George Washington Bridge has long been a suicide hotspot, and 2012 set grim records: 18 people died by jumping from the 212-foot span and there were 43 attempted suicides, both all-time highs for the 81-year-old crossing, Port Authority records show. Authorities say the jump totals from the bridge usually exceed those from all other local bridges combined, and a veteran Port Authority police official suggested the increase may be linked to hard economic times. After several suicides in early May 2012, police acting Chief John Ryan ordered intensified foot and vehicle patrols, and the police union has urged upgrades to the bridge’s closed-circuit television system.

Against this backdrop, Port Authority Police Officer Jesse Turano made a dramatic rescue one night when a 40-year-old Queens man ignored a security guard and ran onto the bridge’s north walkway, appearing intent on jumping. Patroling near the walkway around 10 p.m., Turano pursued the man, turned on his cruiser’s emergency light, then physically grabbed and pulled him back as the man attempted to fling himself over the railing. Turano handcuffed the man for safety, rode with him to Bergen Regional Medical Center, and said the man told him he had been unemployed for three years and wanted to die. Turano, a seven-year veteran assigned to the bridge since 2010, has saved at least four would-be jumpers this year and downplays his heroism, while colleagues praise his dedication.

Aretha Franklin is suing satirical website The News Nerd for $10 million over a fictional story that claimed she and Patti LaBelle fought at a March 20 concert in Atlanta. The article alleged LaBelle attacked Franklin, was arrested for assault and battery, and described a cinematic Mayweather-style beating following a supposed snub at a PBS "In Performance at the White House: Women of Soul" taping. Franklin’s publicist, Gwendolyn Quinn, said the piece “was not presented as satire or humor” and portrayed Franklin in a “slanderous and derogatory way,” asserting defamation of character. Franklin denied the incident in a public statement, calling the story “crazy,” confirming she and LaBelle are “cool,” noting she was in New York preparing for a birthday party that day, and pointing out the PBS program actually showed Franklin hugging LaBelle.

The News Nerd’s site carries a footer disclaimer stating its content is purely satirical, and the contested article originally ran under the byline “Kato Leonard” but has since been credited to “The News Nerd Staff” and appears edited. Despite the disclaimer, the fabricated story went viral, being widely shared on social media and prompting many readers to take it seriously. Commenters on the story and elsewhere showed confusion about its satirical intent, which Franklin’s legal team is now addressing. Observers note that while satire offers some legal protection, Franklin’s high-profile response may nonetheless amplify the truth and highlight potential harms when parody is mistaken for real news.

A landmark High Court ruling rejected Marie Fleming’s challenge to Ireland’s absolute ban on assisted suicide. Fleming, a 59-year-old former lecturer now severely disabled by advanced multiple sclerosis, had sought a declaration that the Criminal Law (Suicide) Act’s prohibition breached her constitutional and ECHR rights by preventing her partner from lawfully assisting her death. The three-judge panel found the ban justified to protect vulnerable people — the aged, disabled, poor, lonely or emotionally compromised — from pressure to end their lives. The court said it could not tailor an individualized exception without risking wider harm and held that only the Oireachtas can change the law; the Director of Public Prosecutions may not issue guidelines that would effectively nullify the statute. Judges praised Fleming’s courage and noted the difficulty of the decision; the State will pay her costs. Fleming said she was “very disappointed and saddened” and is expected to appeal the 120–121 page judgment to the Supreme Court.

Mack Wolford, a 44-year-old Pentecostal pastor from West Virginia known across Appalachia for handling venomous snakes as an expression of faith, died after being bitten by a rattlesnake at an outdoor service he organized at Panther Wildlife Management Area. Profiled last year in The Washington Post Magazine for his outspoken, media-friendly evangelism, Wolford believed the Bible—citing Mark 16:17-18—requires true believers to “take up serpents” and trust God to heal them if bitten. The gathering, meant as a homecoming-style revival and birthday celebration, drew family members, some of whom had abandoned serpent handling. About 30 minutes in, Wolford placed a yellow timber rattlesnake on the ground after passing it to congregants; the snake bit him on the thigh. Initially taken to a relative’s home as with prior bites, his condition worsened, and he later died at Bluefield Regional Medical Center. Witnesses reported he was bitten around 1:30 p.m. and died late that night, echoing the death of his father, who died of a similar bite when Wolford was a teenager. Wolford kept several venomous snakes at home, taught others the practice—even in states where it’s illegal—and aimed to preserve the tradition. His funeral will be held Saturday at House of the Lord Jesus in Matoaka.

Italian health authorities have launched an investigation after a 4-year-old girl died of cerebral malaria despite never having traveled to a malaria-risk country. The child, identified as Sofia (also reported as Sonia) Zago, developed a high fever after a holiday in Bibione and was admitted to a Trento hospital, where she fell into a coma and was diagnosed with malaria. She was transferred to a tropical diseases hospital in Brescia but died soon after. Italy has been considered malaria-free since the mid-20th century and does not host the Anopheles mosquito species typically responsible for transmitting Plasmodium parasites locally, making the case highly unusual.

Officials sent an expert team to Trento to determine how the infection occurred. Suspicion briefly focused on the Trento hospital because two other children treated there had malaria contracted in Burkina Faso; however, hospital managers said the malaria patients were isolated in separate rooms, single-use equipment was used, and Sofia did not receive blood transfusions, which makes direct patient-to-patient transmission unlikely. Clinicians noted the incubation period might align with her recent seaside trip, and investigators are considering the “mosquito-in-luggage” scenario—infected mosquitoes inadvertently transported from endemic areas in travelers’ baggage—which the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control has linked to several Western European cases over recent decades.

Experts also noted that an unusually hot summer and climate change could increase the chance that vector species survive or adapt, though linking climate shifts directly to single events is complex. The World Health Organization and European agencies monitor such incidents closely to preserve Europe’s malaria-free status and examine possible routes of local transmission.

President Trump’s legal team views the Justice Department and FBI — more than special counsel Robert Mueller — as responsible for what they call a “witch hunt,” and some allies want a new special counsel to probe the investigators. Mueller’s team, staffed with a dozen-plus lawyers and investigators, has aggressively pursued leads, securing voluminous documents and interviewing close Trump associates; some Trump loyalists describe Mueller’s deputies as “killers.” Trump’s defense is led by John Dowd, Ty Cobb (a White House lawyer), and Jay Sekulow. They act as lawyers, strategists, advisers and sometimes public spokesmen, providing Mueller’s team requested documents, calming the president, and telling him the investigation is nearing its end. Critics in legal circles call them error-prone, indiscreet, and under-resourced compared with the large teams typically assembled in major probes. Cobb, paid by the government and representing the presidency, lacks attorney-client privilege; Dowd and Sekulow represent Trump personally. The lawyers reassure Trump he has done nothing wrong and downplay obstruction concerns, despite detailed questioning by Mueller’s team about Comey’s firing and potentially damaging public statements and tweets. Separately, Fox News reported that Justice Department official Bruce Ohr had secret contacts with Fusion GPS figures and that his wife, Nellie Ohr, worked for Fusion GPS in 2016, fueling Republican inquiries into whether the dossier influenced FISA applications; DOJ has not publicly explained Ohr’s demotion.

In 2013 Med Express, a seller of refurbished medical equipment, sued two eBay buyers over negative feedback, claiming the comments and lowered seller ratings harmed the company. One buyer, Amy Nicholls, had paid $175 plus $12 shipping for a microscope light and later was charged $1.44 postage due; she posted a complaint on eBay noting the unexpected charge and lack of seller communication. Med Express founder Richard Radey said the detailed seller ratings and resulting loss of “Top Rated Seller Plus” status prompted the suit; the company later apologized and withdrew the lawsuits after public backlash. Nicholls retained pro bono help from Public Citizen attorney Paul Levy and Ohio lawyers Jeffrey Nye and Thomas Haren, who took the matter seriously and filed counterclaims alleging frivolous, malicious litigation and a pattern of suing out-of-state buyers who would be hard-pressed to defend themselves. After a lengthy sanctions process—including an initial 2014 hearing with an oral fee agreement that Med Express failed to honor, followed by a second trial where the judge found Radey’s testimony inconsistent and not credible—the court ruled that Med Express and Radey must pay $19,250 to cover Nye’s and Haren’s attorneys’ fees. Levy worked pro bono and sought no fees. The judge also observed that much of Nicholls’s feedback was protected opinion and that any factual statements were true and unreasonably disputed by Med Express. The attorneys noted the decision defends consumer speech and urged Ohio to adopt anti‑SLAPP protections to deter suit‑to‑silence tactics.

India’s government abruptly invalidated its 500 and 1,000 rupee notes in a surprise November announcement aimed at combating corruption, tax evasion, counterfeit currency and the informal “black money” economy. Prime Minister Narendra Modi framed the move as a necessary hardship that would expose undeclared cash, help stamp out corruption and terrorism financing, and nudge the country toward greater use of banks and digital payments. The demonetised notes—about 85% of cash in circulation—ceased to be legal tender at midnight, and citizens were given 50 days to exchange or deposit them at banks and post offices; airports, railways and hospitals will accept them only until 11 November. New 500 and 2,000 rupee notes were introduced and slated for phased release over weeks. The shock decision triggered long ATM queues, temporary bank and ATM closures, and concern for small traders, vendors, laborers and the upcoming wedding season. Officials said large or suspicious exchanges would be scrutinised for tax liabilities; no explicit upper limit was imposed on deposits, though cash withdrawals would be restricted. The move drew mixed public reaction—praise on social media as bold and necessary, along with jokes and anxieties about short-term disruption. The new Mahatma Gandhi series notes include enhanced security features and designs highlighting national achievements and sanitation campaigns.

Mitt Romney’s early two-day visit to Britain as the Republican presidential nominee has been marked by gaffes and awkwardness that undercut his bid to appear informed and presidential. Purported as a foreign-policy trip, Romney largely offered vague oppositions to Obama without concrete alternatives, and his public comments—questioning London’s readiness for the Olympics, calling some preparations “disconcerting,” and awkwardly describing views from “the backside of 10 Downing Street”—provoked ridicule and a sharp, public put-down from Prime Minister David Cameron. Romney’s mentions of meeting the head of MI6 and seeming disinterest in his wife’s expensive dressage horse reinforced perceptions of elite detachment. British media and politicians lampooned him, and comparators to Obama’s more charismatic European visits amplified the contrast. Behind the missteps, campaign aides’ remarks about shared Anglo-Saxon heritage have further fed concerns that Romney’s campaign is framing Obama as an outsider. Overall, the trip has been a comedy of errors that threatens to tarnish Romney’s image and highlight his lack of substantive foreign-policy proposals.

A week-long survey led by Nancy Rabalais of the Louisiana Universities Marine Consortium found this year’s Gulf of Mexico low-oxygen “dead zone” covered 5,052 square miles—about the size of Connecticut and roughly 800 square miles smaller than in 2013. That measurement matched late-June predictions based on May nutrient loads in the Mississippi and Atchafalaya rivers. Excessive nitrogen runoff from Midwest agriculture is identified as the primary driver: rainwater carries fertilizer into streams, which reach the rivers and flow into the Gulf, where lighter freshwater and nutrients fuel algal blooms. When algae die and decompose, oxygen is consumed at the bottom, creating hypoxia (under 2 parts per million) that kills or displaces bottom-dwelling organisms like shrimp and benthic species.

The five-year average hypoxic area is 5,543 square miles—nearly three times larger than the 1,991-square-mile reduction goal set by a 2001 federal/state task force and reaffirmed in 2008. Scientists warn nutrient loads, including rising nitrate concentrations, remain high; some nitrogen also accumulates in sediments and can be released later. Rabalais noted that recent heavy rains and near-record nitrate levels could have produced an even larger zone had they coincided with the survey.

Environmental groups have reacted strongly, pressing the EPA for numeric water-quality standards for nitrogen and phosphorus and suing to force regulatory action. Critics say voluntary state actions have failed and call for stronger federal enforcement; others note federal farm policy and increased row-crop acreage since the 1960s have intensified pollution. Research funded by NOAA, EPA and NSF underscores that reducing hypoxia will require land-use changes and agricultural practices that cut nutrient runoff without hurting yields.

General Motors is preparing to release findings from its internal probe into why it waited more than a decade to recall 2.6 million small cars with a defective ignition switch tied to at least 13 deaths. Families of some victims have received settlement payments, often confidential and reportedly modest; several described the legal process as painful and humiliating. One grieving mother said attorneys “dragged my son through the mud” after he was killed in Texas in 2004. G.M. has publicly contested direct responsibility in some cases, noting many crashes occurred off-road at high speeds and that factors like not wearing seatbelts and alcohol use sometimes played a role. The Times’ reporting, however, found alcohol cited in only four of the ten accidents it identified, including one crash caused when a drunken driver in another vehicle struck a defective G.M. car, killing the occupants of the G.M. vehicle and leaving a toddler paralyzed.

G.M. has not yet outlined how it will compensate the families of the 13 fatalities or other potential victims; federal regulators have suggested more than 13 lives may have been lost. Kenneth R. Feinberg, the victim-compensation expert retained by G.M., is expected to reveal a claims plan in the coming weeks.

One detailed case involves Mikale Erickson, who died in November 2004 when a Saturn Ion driven by his fiancée, Candice Anderson, went off a rural Texas road and hit a tree. Neither wore seatbelts; the airbags did not deploy. Anderson survived, later pleaded guilty to criminal negligent homicide, and has carried lifelong consequences. In late May she learned Erickson’s death was among those linked to the ignition defect. Erickson’s mother says G.M. has not contacted the family and wants an apology and answers from the automaker’s internal investigation, including whether Anderson’s conviction should be reconsidered in light of the defect.

Comcast faced public embarrassment after a Spokane, Washington customer, Ricardo Brown, discovered his billing name had been changed to “Asshole Brown” following his wife Lisa’s attempt to cancel their cable service. Lisa, a missions volunteer, says she was polite but was routed to a retention specialist who tried to keep her as a customer and offer a new two‑year contract; when she declined, someone allegedly altered the account name. The incident was first reported by consumer advocate Christopher Elliott, who verified the bill and contacted Comcast. Comcast spokesperson Steve Kipp (vice president of communications for the Washington region) apologized, called the name change “completely unacceptable and inappropriate,” and said the company has zero tolerance for such behavior. Comcast opened a thorough investigation, promised to make things right, and initially offered to waive the $60 cancellation fee. Senior Comcast officials later contacted the Browns and corrected the billing name; a general manager and a senior director of government affairs made additional reassurances. Lisa Brown requested a larger remedy — a full refund for past service — arguing the offense warranted more than an apology and a cancellation fee waiver. Comcast ultimately refunded two years of charges, though conflicting reports briefly suggested it had offered two free years; the company clarified it issued only the refund. The episode joined other highly publicized Comcast customer-service failures and underscored criticisms of aggressive retention tactics and the potential for frontline employees to act unprofessionally, prompting calls for better oversight and accountability.

Recent research challenges the widespread belief that relational aggression—harming peers by damaging or manipulating relationships through rumors, exclusion, or turning others against someone—is primarily a female behavior. Pamela Orpinas and colleagues followed 620 students from sixth through twelfth grade, asking how often in the past 30 days they engaged in behaviors like spreading false rumors or ostracizing peers. Overall relational aggression declined with age, but in the earlier years significantly more boys exhibited a persistent pattern of high relational aggression: two-thirds (66.7 percent) of the high-aggression group were male. Orpinas argues this undermines the common narrative that boys are mainly physically aggressive while girls monopolize social nastiness. Other work aligns with this reassessment: a 2012 cross-national study found no consistent sex differences in relational aggression, and Rosalind Wiseman—author of Queen Bees and Wannabes—shifted attention in Masterminds and Wingmen to boys’ social lives, noting boys often lack the language and cultural permission to express worries and relational struggles. Both researchers urge that schools and parents recognize relational aggression as not single-gendered, incorporate both boys and girls into prevention programs, and model nonaggressive behavior. They also emphasize promoting positive social conduct among children and changing adult discourse, which tends to highlight conflict over cooperation; adults should spotlight and reinforce examples of kids helping and speaking well of one another to make caring and kindness socially valued.

The document summarizes major Pulitzer Prize winners and recounts the Bell, California corruption scandal uncovered by the Los Angeles Times. The Times won the Public Service prize for exposing how Bell’s officials, led by City Manager Robert Rizzo, secretly enriched themselves with extravagant salaries and benefits while illegally increasing taxes on a poor community. That investigation — driven by a team of reporters including Jeff Gottlieb and Ruben Vives — led to felony charges against Rizzo and others, tax rebates to residents, stricter disclosure laws, recalls of council members and broader scrutiny of pension practices. Photographer Barbara Davidson won for feature photography depicting victims of gang violence. Other Pulitzer winners included ProPublica (national reporting), the New York Times (international reporting and commentary), and finalists across newsrooms. The entry lists book and arts winners (Jennifer Egan, Siddhartha Mukherjee, Ron Chernow, Eric Foner, Kay Ryan, Bruce Norris, Zhou Long). The Bell follow-ups detail legal maneuvers over inflated pensions, audits revealing illegal taxes and fees, missing funds, aggressive towing and code fines, and investigations into election and civil-rights issues, showing widespread municipal malfeasance and systemic oversight failures.

Mickey Rooney’s will, signed weeks before his death at 93, left his modest estate to stepson Mark (the actor’s caretaker) and excluded his wife Jan Rooney and most biological children. Jan has filed objections, with her lawyer arguing the will misstates settlement agreements and does not strip her surviving-spouse rights. The court-appointed conservator and executor, Michael Augustine, calls Jan’s challenge “totally without merit,” saying Rooney was competent when he signed the March 11, 2014 will and that the estate’s value is small. Separately, Rooney’s eight biological children filed a contest alleging undue influence: they accuse Mark Aber and the conservator of manipulating an elderly, vulnerable Rooney during a period of alleged elder abuse to draft and execute the will in Aber’s favor. The children seek to nullify the will and recover legal fees. A probate hearing is scheduled to begin the process of validating the will, launching what promises to be a contentious estate dispute.

Kellyanne Conway, a counselor to President Trump, sparked widespread ethics controversy after using her White House platform on Fox & Friends to urge viewers to “go buy Ivanka’s stuff,” promoting the clothing and accessories line of the president’s daughter. Her comments came a day after President Trump publicly criticized Nordstrom for dropping Ivanka’s brand. Federal rules bar executive-branch employees from using public office to endorse products or benefit relatives’ businesses, and ethics experts, watchdog groups and lawmakers quickly called Conway’s remark a likely violation.

House Oversight Chairman Jason Chaffetz (R-Utah) and ranking member Elijah Cummings (D-Md.) jointly asked the Office of Government Ethics (OGE) to review the matter and recommend any appropriate disciplinary action, noting a conflict of interest because Conway’s “agency head” is the president. Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington filed a complaint with OGE and the White House counsel. The White House said Conway had been “counseled” and Conway later said the president supported her “100%.” OGE reported an extraordinary surge of public contacts in response to recent events.

Observers warned that while OGE can advise and recommend discipline, enforcement rests with the White House; OGE itself lacks investigative power. Some legal analysts suggested a single statement might prompt only a warning, but a repeated pattern could lead to significant consequences. The episode underscored continuing tensions over the Trump family’s business ties and the administration’s handling of established ethics norms.

Graphic crime scene photographs from Stephen Paddock’s Mandalay Bay hotel room have been widely circulated online, prompting Las Vegas Metropolitan Police to open an internal investigation into how the images leaked. Undersheriff Kevin McMahill confirmed the photos are authentic and showed Paddock’s body, numerous high-powered weapons, dozens of shell casings, guns mounted on tripods, and other items including electrical tape and what appears to be paper and a pen. Police recovered 23 guns from room 32135 and believe Paddock used ten suitcases to bring them up. Some images suggest he died from a self-inflicted head wound before SWAT entered. Media outlets, beginning with MailOnline, published the photos; officials worry leaks could compromise the probe and have appealed for patience as forensic processing neared completion.

The report notes prior examples of law-enforcement leaks: an LAPD officer who leaked Rihanna photos lost her job in 2009, and sensitive Manchester attack images in 2016 triggered U.S.-U.K. tensions and potential investigations into sources. While Nevada law may lack explicit penalties, internal affairs can impose suspension or termination, and federal investigations into leaks have led to prosecutions in other cases. Authorities hope Paddock’s girlfriend, Marilou Danley, may soon provide information to clarify motive. External photos also show a camera mounted inside the room and another in the door peephole, possibly placed to monitor or film events.

Documents from Edward Snowden reveal that New Zealand’s signals intelligence agency, the Government Communications Security Bureau (GCSB), worked with the U.S. NSA in 2012–2013 to build a mass metadata surveillance program dubbed “Speargun,” despite repeated public assurances by Prime Minister John Key that no such mass surveillance was planned or legally permitted. Snowden and reporting in The Intercept show Phase I involved covert “cable access” to the Southern Cross undersea cable; Phase II planned insertion of “metadata probes” to capture dates, times, senders and recipients of communications. NSA files note Speargun awaited passage of a new GCSB Act—enacted in 2013—that extended domestic surveillance powers the government publicly denied would allow wholesale metadata collection. Snowden says New Zealanders’ communications were routinely visible in the shared XKEYSCORE system and that GCSB provided data and algorithms to the NSA. Key has denied an operational program, calling proposals a rejected “cyber protection” business case, and released declassified papers; he also promised to declassify more. The revelations have fueled political controversy ahead of a national election, intensified scrutiny over GCSB’s past illegal spying (notably the Kim Dotcom case), and raised broader concerns about secrecy, oversight, and civil liberties in New Zealand.

Three Los Angeles-area women — Monica Kenyon, Marla Saltzer and Sonia Ulrich — are being praised after they intervened to stop a woman from being drugged during a date at FIG, the restaurant inside the Fairmont Miramar hotel in Santa Monica. The women were at happy hour when Kenyon noticed a man acting strangely at a nearby table: fumbling with his date’s glass, producing a small black vial and dropping something into her drink. Monica alerted her friends, and Ulrich found the woman in the restroom to warn her. The warned woman, stunned, told them the man was “one of my best friends,” having worked together for more than a year, and returned to the table while trying to act normal.

The trio told restaurant staff; the manager notified security and checked surveillance footage, which confirmed the man had placed an unknown substance into the woman’s glass. Staff offered the woman a sparkling water while the situation unfolded. The man repeatedly prodded her to drink by clinking his glass with hers. Police arrived before the couple left; the man was detained without protest. Authorities later said they found multiple vials of a clear substance on him; identification is pending.

Ulrich’s viral Facebook post, shared tens of thousands of times, thanks the FIG staff and urges people to speak up if they suspect something. After the incident, many patrons thanked the women and shared similar stories of being targeted or knowing someone who was. The episode highlights the importance of bystander intervention and vigilance in preventing drugging and sexual assault.

Nancy Mace, the first woman to graduate from The Citadel, and state Sen. Lee Bright plan to challenge Sen. Lindsey Graham in the 2014 GOP primary, joining businessman Richard Cash. Mace will formally announce her campaign Saturday in Goose Creek; Bright will enter in the coming weeks. They and Tea Party groups criticize Graham for compromising with Democrats on issues like immigration, NSA surveillance, and spending. Political scientists warn multiple challengers could split conservative voters and actually help Graham, who has $6.3 million cash on hand and an active super PAC backing him. Bright emphasizes his conservative voting record; Mace leverages a high-profile personal story and grassroots appeal. Analysts note Graham has shifted rightward ahead of the primary and say a contested primary could push him further conservative even if he wins. Fundraising from outside groups could play a decisive role.

An heiress to the Seagram fortune, Clare Bronfman, and three associates were arrested in connection with the investigation of NXIVM, a self-improvement organization prosecutors allege operated as a sex‑trafficking and criminal enterprise. Bronfman, 39, surrendered to the FBI, pleaded not guilty to racketeering conspiracy charges, and was released under house arrest after pledging a $100 million bond. Authorities say she belonged to an “inner circle” that helped NXIVM leader Keith Raniere exert control over members through identity theft, interception of communications, money laundering, and other illegal acts. Prosecutors allege NXIVM ran a secret sub‑society that branded female recruits with a symbol resembling Raniere’s initials and pressured them into sexual servitude; actress Allison Mack has been charged with recruiting for that subgroup. Raniere was arrested in Mexico earlier this year and faces sex‑trafficking and forced labor charges. Also arrested were NXIVM cofounder Nancy Salzman, her daughter Lauren Salzman, and bookkeeper Kathy Russell; all were released on bail without entering pleas. Bronfman’s lawyer contends the charges reflect government overreach and insists she will be exonerated. Prosecutors maintain the investigation reveals a broad array of crimes—identity theft, extortion, forced labor, money laundering, wire fraud and obstruction—allegedly committed to promote and protect Raniere and NXIVM.

A Sony Electronics and Nielsen survey ranked the most impactful TV events of the past 50 years by asking viewers whether they watched, remembered where they were, who they were with, and whether they discussed them. Top moments were the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks (by far), Hurricane Katrina (2005), the O.J. Simpson verdict (1995), the Challenger explosion (1986) and Osama bin Laden’s death (2011). News events dominated over entertainment; age and gender shaped memories—older viewers recalled JFK’s assassination more, while younger people ranked Obama’s 2008 victory and bin Laden’s death higher. The online study polled 1,077 adults.

Katie Couric has officially announced she will step down as anchor of the CBS Evening News. Couric told People she’s excited about the future and is exploring formats that allow more “multi-dimensional storytelling,” though details — including her next network — remain under discussion. Her CBS contract runs through June, and she likely will remain until it expires. Internal negotiations have included an offer for Couric to remain at CBS in a daytime syndicated talk show plus a role on 60 Minutes, but sources say ABC has made a stronger bid: a talk show with broader exposure across ABC’s news platforms, involvement in 2012 presidential coverage, and prime-time specials. NBC reportedly is no longer pursuing her. CBS insiders, weary of prolonged negotiations, appear ready to let her go. Scott Pelley, a 60 Minutes correspondent, is expected to be named her successor on the evening newscast, possibly announced around May 6. Couric, who became CBS Evening News anchor in September 2006, was unable to lift the program from third place in the ratings; CBS has not yet set an official exit date.

This document stitches together several related threads: an Internet Archive effort to crawl and preserve web pages to prevent link rot; a celebrity engagement announcement; and extensive excerpts from Glennon Doyle Melton’s personal writings about marriage, divorce, faith, and LGBTQ+ acceptance.

First, the Archive’s “No More 404” crawls aim to archive pages as created and their referenced links so future readers can access the exact versions authors relied on, reducing broken links and preserving context.

Then, in lighter media news, Abby Wambach and Glennon Doyle Melton announced their engagement via social posts celebrating their relationship after both had recently ended marriages. Melton publicly shared her journey from divorce to new love, emphasizing hope and visibility for her children.

The bulk of the text is Melton’s heartfelt reflections: announcing her separation from Craig, describing trauma, healing, and how personal transformation made her incompatible with her marriage despite deep love. She explains choosing honesty over career concerns, committing to truth and showing up vulnerably on tour. Melton urges compassionate responses from others, defends her ex-husband, and requests support rather than judgment. She also recounts wrestling with Christian teachings on homosexuality, concluding that love and empathy must guide faith. She rejects shame, champions inclusive love, and asks readers to stay close as she navigates new life, asserting that love—messy, brutal, holy—endures.

The Labor Department reported that U.S. payrolls increased by just 74,000 in December, the smallest monthly gain in three years, leaving 2013 with modest job growth overall. Revisions raised October and November employment by a combined 38,000, with November’s gain revised up to 241,000. The unemployment rate fell to 6.7% from 7.0% in November, but that decline reflected a drop in labor force participation rather than a surge in hiring; the civilian participation rate slipped to 62.8% from 63.6% a year earlier. Employers averaged roughly 182,000 new jobs per month in 2013, similar to 2012’s pace. Short-term trends cooled: three-month and six-month averages were near 172,000 per month, below midyear gains that approached 195,000. Sector-wise, retail added 55,000 jobs in December, professional and business services 19,000, and wholesale trade 15,000. Construction lost 16,000 jobs—the largest decline in 20 months—possibly affected by cold weather, while federal employment fell by 7,000. Private-sector average weekly hours edged down to 34.4 and hourly earnings rose two cents to $24.17, up 42 cents year-over-year.

Aubrey Jayce Carroll, a Georgia teen who disappeared from Spalding High School in May 2016 at about age 15, has been found safe and returned to his mother after nearly two years. The Spalding County Sheriff’s Office announced in a Tuesday press release and Facebook post that the 17-year-old is “safe, healthy and unharmed.” In a video shared by authorities, Aubrey greets viewers, thanks them for their prayers, and says he is okay and smiling.

Investigators from the Spalding County Sheriff’s Office, the FBI and the Griffin Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office briefed Aubrey’s parents in April 2018, showing photos and a Facebook account he had created under an assumed name. Sheriff Darrell Dix said the probe revealed Aubrey had at least five contacts with law enforcement across states from Alabama to Arizona and that he traveled extensively on the West Coast and Midwest. Authorities found he joined a nomadic group living by bartering, using cash only, and moving from state to state—described by Dix as resembling Woodstock-era lifestyles. Officials believed he was not in danger and, since he was now 17, had the right to stay away; they and the family agreed not to contact him directly to avoid driving him off again.

After a family member reached out, Aubrey responded, called his mother, and agreed to return under certain conditions. He came home Monday night and met with Lt. Mike Morris and Sheriff Dix the following morning, telling them he left voluntarily and was not abducted or harmed. Authorities rebuilt the investigation after his disappearance and had even listed him on the FBI missing persons site; a $5,000 reward had been offered. Sheriff Dix emphasized that credit is irrelevant—what matters is that Aubrey is safe, urging others with missing loved ones to keep faith and keep searching.

At the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, revelers found confetti strips that were not commercial confetti but inadequately shredded Nassau County Police Department documents containing highly sensitive personal and investigative information. Paradegoer Ethan Finkelstein and friends picked up pieces showing Social Security numbers, dates of birth, bank details, phone numbers, addresses, license plates, incident reports, and even details linked to Mitt Romney’s motorcade. Some strips named detectives — reportedly including undercover officers — and described specific incidents such as a pipe-bombing report. Nassau County police said they are “very concerned” and will investigate and review disposal procedures; Macy’s said it uses commercially manufactured confetti, not shredded paper. The episode highlights how shredded documents can sometimes be reconstructed: technicians scan shreds, assign IDs, and use software to match pieces, though success depends on shred type. Strip shredders are easiest to reassemble, cross-cut is better, and pulverizing makes reconstruction essentially impossible. Authorities are probing the source of the leaked shredded files.

Three days after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake devastated Port-au-Prince, Haiti, relief efforts struggled to meet overwhelming needs as survivors clamored for food, water, medical care and rescue. Many cries for help went unanswered; tens of thousands may be dead, with PAHO estimating 50,000–100,000 fatalities and UN reports of thousands buried in mass graves. Streets and hospitals overflowed with corpses, and people were paid to collect bodies. Looting and rising tensions threatened security as hunger and desperation mounted; aid distribution was slow and chaotic, prompting the U.S. to assume airport control and the FAA to restrict flights. Washington sent thousands of troops, the aircraft carrier Carl Vinson with helicopters, water purification and surgical facilities, and Secretary Clinton prepared to visit. The UN launched a $550 million flash appeal. Rescue workers and relatives, lacking heavy equipment, frantically dug by hand for survivors trapped under rubble. Observers warned that without accelerated, better-coordinated aid and security, conditions and violence could worsen.

A 20-second video filmed at the Rőszke border camp in Hungary showed an N1TV camerawoman, Petra László, deliberately tripping a fleeing man carrying a child and kicking two other refugee children as they ran from police. The footage, posted on Twitter by RTL reporter Stephan Richter and shared widely, also appeared on Hungarian sites including Index and 444.hu and prompted the Facebook page “The Petra László Wall of Shame.” Outrage flooded social media; commenters called the act “horrific” and demanded accountability. N1TV—linked to the far-right Jobbik party and known for anti-immigrant content—immediately fired László, with editor-in-chief Szabolcs Kisberk calling her behavior “unacceptable.” Opposition parties Együtt-PM and the Democratic Coalition said they would press charges of violence against a community member, a crime punishable by up to five years’ imprisonment. The episode came amid heightened tensions at the overcrowded camp near the Hungarian-Serbian border, where hundreds of refugees were trying to continue on to Germany and Austria while clashing with local police. The incident intensified debate over Hungary’s media and political stance on migrants.

CBS announced the Celebrity Big Brother cast ahead of the 2018 Grammys, and the reveal sparked immediate reaction online. The lineup includes Omarosa Manigault, Brandi Glanville, Metta World Peace (Ron Artest), Marisa Jaret Winokur, Keisha Knight Pulliam, Chuck Liddell, Shannon Elizabeth, Ross Matthews, Mark McGrath, Adriana Gutierrez and James Maslow. Fans and celebrities weighed in on Twitter within hours, with polarized responses focused largely on Omarosa’s participation after her recent departure from the Trump White House. Watch What Happens Live host Andy Cohen mocked the move and predicted Brandi would outshine Omarosa, while former NSYNC member Lance Bass named Ross Mathews, Shannon Elizabeth and Marisa Winokur as his top three to win. Some users criticized Omarosa’s career turn from political aide to reality TV contestant as a sign of decline; one called it “a fall from grace” and another said her presence might cost the show viewers. Others anticipated dramatic television, saying Omarosa and Brandi would provide major conflict and entertainment. The range of reactions included disappointment, amusement and excitement, with many people citing the pairing as both controversial and ratings-worthy. Us Weekly invited readers to follow further coverage and sign up for its newsletter.

Russian special forces stormed the Liberian-flagged oil tanker Moscow University after Somali pirates seized it off the Somali coast, freeing all 23 crew members and detaining several pirates during a dawn helicopter-backed raid. The crippled tanker, carrying about 86,000 tons of crude worth roughly $50–52 million, had its crew sheltered in a secure safe room. EU Naval Force officials said shots were fired but no crew were injured; Russian sources reported one pirate possibly killed while others were captured. The Marshal Shaposhnikov delivered the assault team and coordinated tactically with EU personnel. The incident, about 500 miles east of Somalia, reflects a trend of more aggressive international naval actions against piracy, raising both praise and controversy over rescue operations.

Jerusalem’s largest soccer club, Beitar Jerusalem, announced it had permanently added “Trump” to its name in praise of President Donald Trump’s recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital and the U.S. embassy move from Tel Aviv. The club lauded Trump on Facebook for “courage” and “true love” of Israel; owners Eli Tabib and executive manager Eli Ohana announced the name change ahead of the embassy opening.
