Beitar, a top Israeli club currently second in the premier league, has long been associated with anti-Arab and anti-Muslim sentiment and remains the only Israeli league club never to have had an Arab Muslim player; its ultras, including the La-Familia faction, have been tied to violent incidents and charges. The announcement coincided with the U.S. embassy inauguration in Jerusalem, attended by senior Trump advisers and family members. The embassy move — timed with Israel’s 70th anniversary and Palestinians’ Nakba commemoration — sparked large protests along the Gaza border, where Israeli fire killed dozens of Palestinians and wounded thousands in the deadliest day since 2014. The violence drew international condemnation, Palestinian leaders’ fury, and U.S. accusations blaming Hamas, while the embassy opening underscored deep divisions over Jerusalem’s contested status.

Last week federal marshals raided Gibson Guitar’s Tennessee facilities—evacuating employees, seizing wood and shutting production—as part of an investigation into possible trafficking in illegally obtained timber under the Lacey Act, which was amended in 2008 to cover plants. Gibson’s CEO Henry Juszkiewicz says the company has been damaged without being charged or told specifically how it violated the law. A June court motion alleges Gibson’s Madagascar ebony was contraband and quotes emails suggesting awareness of risky supply chains. The Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) contends that end users must verify legality back to the tree and that Gibson knowingly imported tainted wood; EIA’s Andrea Johnson later clarified wording about verification and a Madagascar inspection. Gibson denies wrongdoing, says its Madagascar purchases complied with laws, provided documentation, and stopped importing from Madagascar in 2009; it also says the raid seized legally obtained Indian wood. The dispute highlights wider industry concerns: some builders support the Lacey Act to curb illegal logging, while others fear its retroactivity and burdens—potentially forcing provenance proof for decades-old instruments and complicating international movement of vintage guitars. The legal definition of “responsible” sourcing awaits court resolution.

Jonah Hill returned to SNL for a strong third turn as host, showing real growth even if he’s not yet in the same hosting tier as Justin Timberlake or Jon Hamm. The episode’s highlights included a sharp monologue with surprise Leonardo DiCaprio cameo, a funny “Lamborghini” sketch from Vanessa Bayer and Cecily Strong, and an inventive Spike Jonze/Her parody with Michael Cera. Weekend Update remained solid under Seth Meyers and Strong, though the looming handoff to Colin Jost raises concerns about timing and chemistry. Overall problems persist: the cast has ballooned to 17, making it hard to build familiar faces or memorable characters, and several sketches (notably “Ranch,” “Benihana,” and “Boss Dinner”) fell flat. The episode averages out as uneven but enjoyable, showcasing Hill’s comic strengths amid a muddled ensemble.

Lebanon has banned Lady Gaga’s album Born This Way, impounding shipments for lyrics deemed offensive to Christianity; her single “Judas” was already banned on Lebanese radio. Malaysia likewise barred the title track, calling it promotion of homosexuality. Despite the bans, Born This Way went platinum in its first week in the U.S., selling 1.1 million copies, and some Lebanese access it digitally. Gaga has criticized institutional religion’s influence on government and society.

News Corp. will close its 168-year-old Sunday tabloid News of the World after revelations that reporters allegedly hacked voicemails, including those of a murdered 13-year-old and other victims. James Murdoch said the paper’s conduct was “inhuman” and had sullied its reputation; the final edition will publish Sunday. The closure aims to contain mounting criminal probes, civil suits and political fallout that also threaten News Corp.’s broader U.K. interests and leadership, including calls for resignations.

Nine-year-old James Savage of Los Banos completed a grueling open-water swim from San Francisco’s Aquatic Park to Alcatraz Island and back on Tuesday, becoming the youngest swimmer on record to make the round trip. The fourth-grader — just 4-foot-6 and 57 pounds — started at 7:00 a.m. and spent a little over two hours in the chilly, choppy waters, covering more than two miles. About 30 minutes into the swim strong waves and a powerful current battered him and made him consider quitting. A fleet of paddlers, his coach Josh Weinberger and vocal encouragement from his support team kept him going. Weinberger credited James’s training and technique, saying they “pushed each other” and eventually found a rhythm that carried him through. James also received a financial incentive from his father — originally $100, raised to $200 during the swim — which helped motivate him to continue. James recounted supporters yelling, “I believe you can do it,” which bolstered his resolve. Reporters greeted him afterward as he walked ashore smiling and cheered; his achievement broke the previous record held by a 10-year-old. After this milestone, James said his next goal is to swim the length of the Golden Gate Bridge, a roughly 8,981-foot (2,737.4-meter) challenge.

Andrew Young, a longtime aide to former U.S. senator and presidential candidate John Edwards, testified in Edwards’ federal trial about the 2007–2008 effort to conceal Edwards’ affair with campaign videographer Rielle Hunter and the birth of their child. Young described receiving a late-night call from a distraught Hunter reporting her pregnancy, Edwards’ initial dismissal of paternity (“a crazy slut” and “1-in-3 chance”), and the subsequent plan to hide the relationship as Edwards campaigned for president. Young recounted how Edwards used a secret cellphone—nicknamed the “bat phone”—and often called through staffers’ phones to avoid detection by his wife, Elizabeth.

Prosecutors contend that nearly $1 million in payments from heiress Rachel “Bunny” Mellon and Texas lawyer Fred Baron were concealed and used to support Hunter, constituting illegal campaign contributions. Young testified Mellon wrote roughly $750,000 in checks made out to an interior decorator and later routed to Young and his wife, who deposited them. He said Edwards directed him to begin paying Hunter monthly allowances and to move her out of North Carolina when press attention grew. Young and his family housed Hunter for weeks and later traveled with her to luxury hotels and Baron’s Aspen mansion while arranging further support; prosecutors showed photos and played voicemails illustrating frequent contact among Edwards, Baron and Young.

Young acknowledged missteps and inconsistencies on the stand and admitted he agreed to claim paternity partly out of self-interest—hoping benefits if Edwards won office—though he also cited belief in Edwards’ political goals. The defense argues Young masterminded the scheme and diverted funds for personal use, while Edwards denies knowing about Mellon’s checks. If convicted on six counts of campaign-finance violations, Edwards faces up to 30 years in prison and $1.5 million in fines. Young’s testimony continued as the trial proceeded.

Justin Bieber told L.A.’s Power 106 he was “retiring” after his next album, joking that he might quit music. The 19-year-old’s comment came while promoting his new collection Journals, a set of previously released Music Mondays tracks plus five unreleased songs, videos and the Believe trailer. Sources and his camp said the retirement claim wasn’t serious; Bieber plans to evolve and mature as an artist.

A viral video showing a man punching a kangaroo in the face during a confrontation over the weekend has stirred debate and revealed a more complex backstory. Originally posted on Facebook by user Steven Stubenraugh, the clip has amassed millions of views and shows a man running toward a kangaroo that has a dog in a headlock. After a struggle the kangaroo releases the dog, and one of the men suddenly delivers a punch to the animal’s face. Viewers questioned whether the footage was staged and argued about the ethics and legality of striking an animal in apparent self-defence.

Local reporting has since shed light on the circumstances. The outing was not a random street encounter but part of a wild pig-hunting trip organized as a “final” excursion for a young man named Kailem, who reportedly died of cancer last week. Organizer Mathew Amor told news.com.au that friends gathered to give Kailem one last boar-hunting experience; another friend filmed over an hour of footage to compile a DVD for Kailem and his family. According to Amor, the man who struck the kangaroo—referred to as “Goo”—stunned the animal rather than delivering a severe blow, and his hand was uninjured. The dog involved was protected by a breastplate designed to shield it from boar tusks and was reported to be fine.

The identity of the puncher remains partly disputed. Amor said the man kept quiet because he holds a “good government job,” while the Daily Mail claims to have identified him as a zookeeper who works in the elephant enclosure at Taronga Western Plains Zoo—an assertion that, if accurate, adds another layer of oddity to the episode. Observers noted the irony of a typically placid friend delivering what others teased as a weak punch, underscoring the bizarre, uniquely Australian feel of the incident.

With Timothy Geithner under fire for the slow recovery, high unemployment and fiscal concerns, New York Post sources say JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon is being discussed as a possible replacement. Dimon has higher visibility in Washington, penned a recent Washington Post op-ed, and is seen as capable after navigating JPMorgan through the crisis. Yet he diverges from the Obama administration on key reforms: he opposes a consumer-protection agency overseeing credit cards and mortgages—arguing it raises costs—and rejects capping big banks, advocating instead for a regulatory framework allowing large firms to fail without taxpayer bailouts. Critics warn his Wall Street ties would provoke political backlash and accusations of self-interest. Dimon reportedly plans to stay at JPMorgan and has downplayed interest in the Treasury post.

At the Sochi Olympics, the U.S. speedskating team decided to abandon the newly introduced, high-tech Under Armour “Mach 39” skinsuits and revert to the previously approved Under Armour World Cup suits after disappointing results and mounting athlete concerns. US Speedskating president Mike Plant announced the switch following poor performances—no U.S. skater had medaled through six long-track events, a surprising outcome for a program with 67 Winter Olympic medals historically. The Mach 39, developed with Lockheed Martin and billed as the fastest suit, had been used only after the team was selected and never in actual competition before the Games. Athletes complained vents designed to release heat may have let air in, affecting form; Heather Richardson even patched a vent but still finished off the podium. Team leaders filed appeals with the ISU and IOC to allow the change, which is permitted if every team member can use the approved alternative. Officials stressed they were also evaluating training, blades, tactics and preparation. Some skaters defended the Mach 39, but others favored the familiar World Cup suits for confidence and proven results as they seek to salvage the remainder of the Games.

Reality Leigh Winner, a 25-year-old former Air Force cryptologic language analyst turned contractor, was arrested and charged by the Justice Department for allegedly leaking a classified NSA report about Russian military cyberoperations targeting U.S. electoral systems to The Intercept. Winner, who had Top Secret clearance and worked for Pluribus International at a government facility in Georgia, is accused of printing, removing, and mailing the May 5 document; she allegedly confessed to an FBI agent on June 3. Her detention hearing is pending and she has not entered a plea.

Her case highlights two tensions within U.S. intelligence: the routine presence of very young personnel with high clearances—many NSA front-line analysts are recently enlisted—and a growing pattern of employees who leak secrets out of perceived public duty rather than for money or insider score-settling. Observers link this trend in part to political polarization after Donald Trump’s election. Winner’s social media activity under handles like Sara Winners and @Reezlie showed outspoken anti-Trump views, follows of figures such as Edward Snowden and WikiLeaks, and interest in “alt” government accounts. Family and acquaintances describe her as passionate, not previously political, and surprised by her alleged action; her attorney calls her a low-level worker caught in a political whirlwind.

Josh Sanchez-Maldonado, a 24-year-old American financial trader based in San Francisco, has been missing in London since Oct. 22, when he was last seen leaving the St. Giles Hotel in Feltham just after noon. He flew into the U.K. from Japan the previous day for what his family says was a potential job interview; investigators have been unable to confirm details of the appointment. Sanchez-Maldonado was due to return to San Francisco via Dublin on Oct. 23 but did not board the flight. His family say this was his first solo trip outside the United States and that he had been in daily contact with his father until Oct. 21.

London’s Metropolitan Police describe him as white, about 5 ft 8 in, slim, with short dark hair. When last seen he wore a dark flat cap, brown/grey T-shirt, white shorts and black trainers. He reportedly had no access to money while in London. Officers are increasingly concerned for his welfare and have focused inquiries on financial districts such as the City and Canary Wharf, places his family believe he would have wanted to visit. The family, who have traveled to the U.K. to appeal for help, describe Josh as goal-oriented, organized, kind and sociable, and urge him to make contact. The U.S. Embassy in London is aware of the case and is cooperating with police and the family. Anyone with information is asked to contact Hounslow CID on 020 8247 6653/6246 or via 101.

Anne Hathaway and husband Adam Shulman have welcomed their first child, a son named Jonathan Rosebanks Shulman, born March 24, the couple’s rep confirmed. The Oscar winner, 33, and the actor-producer had publicly confirmed the pregnancy last November; Hathaway first hinted at it in a January bikini Instagram post and later shared a photo of her baby bump ahead of the 88th Academy Awards. Fans on social media praised the couple for choosing a traditional name. Sources told E! News the newborn is “extremely healthy” and surrounded by friends and family in Los Angeles, and that Hathaway and Shulman are “ecstatic” to be parents. The birth followed a relaxed baby shower the actress enjoyed in March with close friends, including Camila Alves; guests described a joyful, laughter-filled gathering. Hathaway and Shulman married in Big Sur in September 2012 after getting engaged in November 2011, and Hathaway has spoken previously about wanting to start a family and have children for many years.

Kenai leaders have proposed adding cats to the city code requirement that pets be restrained—by leash, fence or building—after increased complaints about roaming cats and a rise in shelter intake. Mayor Pat Porter and Councilman Tim Navarre introduced the ordinance citing residents’ reports of cats defecating on property and disturbing neighbors, and shelter staff say demand for loaner live traps has surged. The council postponed a vote to Oct. 5 so City Manager Rick Koch can gather complaint data and examples from other Alaska cities. Residents warned enforcement could burden the Kenai Animal Shelter and questioned compliance and fiscal impacts; shelter officials say current capacity and budget appear sufficient.

Supporters of former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick rallied outside NFL headquarters in midtown Manhattan demanding he be signed before the regular season begins. More than 1,000 people turned out, many wearing Kaepernick jerseys, chanting “Boycott!” and listening to speeches, poems and prayers over about an hour and a half. Kaepernick, who opted out of his contract in March and remains unsigned, drew national attention last season when he refused to stand for the national anthem to protest police brutality against Black people. Supporters argue he is being blackballed for his activism; critics say his absence from rosters reflects on-field performance—he posted a 3-16 record over the past two seasons—or object to his protest. Speakers at the rally linked his treatment to broader racial and player-health concerns: the Rev. Jamal Bryant charged the league tolerates harm to Black players but not their conscience, and NAACP leaders called for a meeting with Commissioner Roger Goodell, saying it is “no sheer coincidence” Kaepernick remains unsigned and that punishing a player for free speech violates rights and league rules. Some current players continue similar protests; the topic has drawn polarized public and political responses.

Hawaii reclaimed the top spot in Gallup-Healthways’ 2015 Well-Being Index, which surveyed over 175,000 U.S. adults by phone to measure purpose, social, financial, community and physical well-being. Alaska slipped to second, followed by Montana, Colorado and Wyoming; the West dominated the top ranks while Southern states populated the bottom. West Virginia and Kentucky again ranked last and second-last. National well-being was unchanged from 2014, but financial well-being and life ratings improved, and food and health-care insecurity and smoking declined to multi-year lows. Negative trends persisted: obesity reached a new high and more part-time workers sought full-time roles. Alabama showed the biggest improvement, while Vermont fell most.

Since 9/11, the Pentagon’s Joint Special Operations Command (JSOC) has grown from a little-known hostage-rescue unit into a highly secretive, powerful counterterrorism force eclipsing the CIA in some lethal and detention capacities. JSOC—home to Delta Force, SEAL Team 6, the 24th Special Tactics Squadron and specialized aviation and ranger units—expanded from about 1,800 personnel before 9/11 to tens of thousands, acquiring its own intelligence apparatus, drones, reconnaissance aircraft, satellites and cyber teams. Operating under direct presidential and defense-department authority, JSOC has conducted intelligence gathering, raids and targeted killings across Iraq, Afghanistan and numerous countries where the U.S. was not at war. Its kill-list authority and opaque operations have drawn criticism and legal controversy over assassination-like practices and limited congressional oversight. Under leaders like Stanley McChrystal, JSOC centralized targeting, fused intelligence from the NSA, CIA and other agencies, and harnessed technologies—phone-locating sensors, massive bandwidth and media-exploitation teams—to find and dismantle networks, producing high body counts and the death of figures like Abu Musab al-Zarqawi. Yet JSOC also suffered mistakes and abuses—errant strikes, harsh detention practices and incidents that fueled local grievances. Today JSOC’s remit includes psychological and financial operations and domestic-facing task forces, reflecting its influence but raising questions about secrecy, oversight and the long-term costs of a kill-centric approach.

Two Wisconsin middle-school girls charged with attempted first-degree intentional homicide in the May stabbing of a classmate, allegedly to gain favor with the fictional online figure Slender Man, were ruled competent Thursday to face prosecution. Waukesha County Circuit Judge Michael Bohren held back-to-back hearings after mental health evaluations produced differing opinions.

For 13-year-old Anissa E. Weier, three experts testified: two defense psychologists argued she was not competent because emotional immaturity and limited decision-making—rather than mental illness—prevented her from understanding procedural nuances like plea bargaining. They described her as intelligent but prone to ignoring relevant factors and lacking a meaningful grasp of long timeframes. A court-appointed psychiatrist countered that Weier was bright, articulate and capable of rational participation in proceedings. Bohren sided with the psychiatrist, finding age and maturity issues did not override competency.

Co-defendant Morgan Geyser, 12, had previously been deemed incompetent in August but underwent treatment at Winnebago Mental Health Institute. Her attorney disclosed that psychiatrist Kenneth Casimir diagnosed her with schizophrenia but did not challenge Casimir’s November finding that she had been restored to competency. Bohren agreed to keep Geyser at Winnebago for continued treatment and monitoring rather than return her to juvenile detention.

A joint preliminary hearing is set for February, when the judge must decide whether probable cause exists to proceed to trial. If tried as adults, they face up to 60 years; in juvenile court, confinement could extend only to age 25. The victim, Payton Leutner, survived and has returned to school.

Shaniece Luke, whose 33-year-old brother Rasheen Rose died in 2012 while under care at the Bernard Fineson Developmental Center in Queens, has been sent an $11.67 million bill from the state Office for People With Developmental Disabilities (OPWDD). The notarized claim, issued to Rose’s estate, seeks reimbursement for Medicaid assistance provided to him from August 6, 2002, until his death on August 6, 2012. Luke and her attorneys say the demand is retaliatory, coming after she filed a federal wrongful-death suit alleging that staff fatally restrained Rose, who had severe autism and was nonverbal. The city medical examiner ruled Rose’s death a homicide, citing injuries sustained while he was physically restrained; investigators say he was held prone for up to 30 minutes by multiple staff, including a heavier worker who sat on him, and became unresponsive as others stood by. OPWDD says it must seek reimbursement to comply with federal Medicaid rules. Luke’s lawyers and advocates call the move punitive and unprecedented; other families who sued after deaths in state care reportedly received similar notices. The Queens district attorney found no criminal charges but left the case open. In court, seven staff deny wrongdoing; the state attorney general and private counsel defend them. The case highlights broader scrutiny of New York’s residential developmental centers amid plans to close facilities like Fineson.

Salma Hayek announced on Instagram that her dog, Mozart, was found fatally shot last week at her Washington State ranch. The 49-year-old actress, who said she personally delivered Mozart from his mother, revealed she’d been mourning and urged authorities to seek justice for the nine-year-old dog, describing him as loving, loyal and never aggressive. She condemned his “slow and painful death.” Hayek frequently shares photos with animals, recently posting on set with a canine co-star, and previously joined public outrage over Cecil the lion’s killing.

The first day of Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh’s Senate Judiciary Committee hearings opened amid rancor, protests and partisan theatrics, even as Republicans largely signaled confidence he will be confirmed. The four-day hearing began with Democrats demanding a delay after the committee received some 42,000 pages of Kavanaugh-related documents late Monday and accusing the White House of withholding more than 100,000 additional pages under executive privilege. Democratic senators — including several with 2020 presidential ambitions such as Kamala Harris, Cory Booker and Amy Klobuchar — repeatedly interrupted Chairman Chuck Grassley and moved to adjourn; Grassley refused, and the session proceeded after repeated clashes.

Protesters inside the hearing room repeatedly shouted objections to Kavanaugh and were escorted out; Capitol Police charged more than 70 people with disorderly conduct or obstruction. Democrats framed their opposition in terms of transparency and high stakes: Kavanaugh once served in the George W. Bush White House and now would likely shift the Supreme Court rightward, potentially affecting abortion rights, the Affordable Care Act and executive-power cases, including issues that could touch President Trump amid ongoing investigations. Republicans countered that Democrats were politicizing the process, re-litigating the 2016 election, and engaged in a show for the cameras. Senate Republicans pointed to a solid majority that can confirm Kavanaugh without Democratic votes, bolstered by Arizona’s appointment of Jon Kyl to fill John McCain’s seat.

After sitting impassively through hours of opening statements, Kavanaugh addressed senators for under 20 minutes, stressing judicial independence and promising to be “a team player on the Team of Nine.” He described his judicial philosophy as neutral and text- and tradition-informed: “A judge must be independent and must interpret the law, not make the law.” He invoked mentors across the ideological spectrum, praised Chief Judge Merrick Garland and emphasized hiring and mentoring women and coaching his daughters’ sports teams — an apparent effort to blunt concerns about his impact on women’s rights.

Democrats signaled they will press Kavanaugh on abortion, executive authority, past work on counterterrorism policies and whether Roe v. Wade is correctly decided. Republicans warned against asking how he would rule on future cases. With committee debate expected to continue and a likely party-line committee vote looming, the proceedings set the tone for a bruising confirmation fight that could be decided in the full Senate before the Supreme Court’s Oct. 1 term start.

Westminster on Wednesday saw a surprising scene: BBC political editor Nick Robinson, noted for his trademark spectacles and TV presence, was filmed angrily ripping and stamping on an anti-war placard reading "Cut the war not the poor" after repeated interruptions during a live broadcast. Initially unapologetic—telling a protester he was "not remotely ashamed"—Robinson later admitted on his blog that he had "lost my temper and I regret that." Separately, former minister Ed Balls reflected on his recent electoral defeat, describing a "sense of loss" but urging focus on achievements rather than what was missed. He highlighted contributions over two decades: keeping Britain out of the euro, securing Bank of England independence, raising the education leaving age to 18, Sure Start, the national minimum wage, and health service reforms.

U.S. stocks fell after weaker-than-expected earnings from blue-chip firms and disappointing economic data heightened concerns about a strong dollar weighing on profits. Microsoft and Caterpillar drove significant Dow losses—Microsoft plunged after lowering its fiscal forecast due to the dollar, Caterpillar cut guidance amid weak commodity prices—and Procter & Gamble warned currency volatility would hit sales and profit. Durable-goods orders dropped 3.4% in December. Investors favored small-cap and haven assets as markets reacted.

Steve Simoff, 61, makes an extraordinary daily commute from his basement apartment in Davis City to an overnight janitorial job at Lakeside Casino in Osceola—about 35 miles each way. To save scarce gas money and ensure he keeps his job supporting his wife Renee (disabled after a stroke and heart surgeries) and their adopted grandson Steven III, Simoff often begins walking at 3:30 p.m. for an 11 p.m. shift. Some days he walks only parts of the route; on average he walks nearly four hours a day and gets rides about three of five workdays. He times a longer but busier route along I-35 to increase chances of motorists stopping; over a decade he’s built a network of “road friends” including local officials, casino coworkers and neighbors who routinely give him lifts. Local sheriff Herbert Muir and coworkers praise Simoff’s reliability and character; casino coworkers pick him up when they can. Though he owns a 2002 minivan, gas is a luxury, and the couple’s biggest monthly bill is $400 rent. Simoff suffers from osteoarthritis in his knee but takes no regular medication beyond occasional aspirin and keeps working—standing through eight-hour shifts with just short breaks. His grit drew comparisons to James Robertson, the Detroit man who walked 21 miles daily and later received wide public support. Simoff, however, has remained largely private and local despite being well-known in the county. He says he walks to keep the job and pay bills: “If I don’t get to work, bills don’t get paid. As long as my two feet are good and my health is good, I don’t think I’ll change.” His story highlights the lengths low-wage workers go to preserve housing and stability amid tight finances.

Michael Vaudreuil, a 54-year-old who worked second-shift as a custodian at Worcester Polytechnic Institute while pursuing a mechanical engineering degree, has accepted an engineering position with Pratt & Whitney in Connecticut. Vaudreuil’s journey—from earning an associate’s in aeronautical technology in 1982, to running a plastering business that collapsed in the 2008 recession, to cleaning classrooms and bathrooms while studying at WPI—resonated worldwide after his graduation went viral. His commencement video garnered millions of views and drew attention from major outlets including NBC Nightly News, the UK’s Independent, and other international media, which Vaudreuil says helped his networking and job prospects. Following his television segment, four Pratt & Whitney employees contacted him independently, and the company offered him a role on its Production Integrated Product Team (PIPT) in Hot Section Engineering, working with jet engine combustion chambers, turbine and exhaust systems—a strong fit given his earlier aeronautical training. He starts July 11 and will relocate from Auburn to Connecticut with his wife Joyce, who supported him through the years-long effort to complete his degree. Vaudreuil expects to continue custodial duties at WPI through June. He describes the job offer as one he “couldn’t refuse” and says it represents the payoff of persistent, goal-focused effort. Beyond personal triumph, he hopes his story challenges stereotypes about older graduates and job candidates, showing that life experience, work ethic and energy should not be underestimated. Vaudreuil sees the outcome as mission complete: graduation was emotional, but landing the job provided the full satisfaction he’d worked for.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Wednesday escalated his long-standing campaign questioning vaccine safety by announcing a $100,000 “World Mercury Project Challenge” and pressing for a Trump administration vaccine safety commission. At a National Press Club event that included actor Robert De Niro, Kennedy urged public debate and offered the prize to anyone who could produce a scientific study proving the safety of thimerosal-containing vaccines for children and pregnant women. Kennedy, who has promoted the debunked theory that thimerosal—a mercury-based preservative used in some flu vaccines—causes autism, said he has spoken with White House aides multiple times since a January meeting with President Trump and believes a commission is still being planned, though he acknowledged uncertainty about its formation.

Kennedy’s claims and motivations drew swift criticism from scientists and medical organizations. The American Academy of Pediatrics led 350 groups in a letter to President Trump affirming unequivocal support for vaccine safety, and the CDC states there is no link between vaccines and autism. Peter Hotez, a vaccine scientist, called Kennedy’s assertions implausible and warned such attention distracts from important public health work. Kennedy accused the CDC and journalists of colluding with pharmaceutical interests, labeling the agency corrupt and insufficiently transparent. De Niro, who has a son with autism and previously faced backlash for supporting an anti-vaccine film, voiced strong support for Kennedy’s comments but distanced himself from politics, saying he only cares about the issue. The episode has renewed concerns among experts that political attention could lend credibility to debunked anti-vaccine claims and undermine public health efforts.

Aaron Schock, a youthful Republican congressman from Illinois, mixes media-savvy charisma with a serious policy agenda centered on long-term planning and personal responsibility—especially in health. Born in the 1980s and elected at 19 to a school board, Schock emphasizes leading by example: he promotes fitness with his Fit for Summer, Fit for Life challenge and follows an intense regimen (P90X, heavy weights, or high-rep calisthenics plus cardio). He frames obesity and rising health-care costs as generational issues, praising Michelle Obama’s Let's Move while noting many Americans feel intimidated by gyms. Politically a deficit hawk, he champions energy independence, better water management, and smarter education spending to boost competitiveness. Comfortable with media attention and active on committees, Schock serves as deputy whip and pursues a disciplined, strategic approach—urging young Americans to plan for their futures and urging Washington to adopt long-term solutions rather than short-term fixes.

Three Hawaii-based Marines — Sgt. Benjamin E. Johns, Lance Cpl. Jacob D. Jacoby and Lance Cpl. Carlos Orozco III — will be tried at a general court-martial on charges stemming from alleged hazing of 21-year-old Lance Cpl. Harry Lew, who died by suicide in Afghanistan on April 3. Brig. Gen. Frederick Padilla referred the case for trial after an Article 32 hearing in Hawaii that examined testimony about repeated incidents in which Lew, who fell asleep on watch multiple times at a remote patrol base, was reportedly punched, kicked, forced to do exercise in combat gear and humiliated; commanders later suggested Lew might have been depressed or medically unwell. Jacoby and Orozco face additional assault charges; Orozco also faces cruelty and maltreatment counts. The Marine Corps emphasized it does not tolerate hazing and reminded that the accused are presumed innocent. Lew, from Santa Clara and a nephew of Rep. Judy Chu, had written a farewell note before his death; no trial date has been set.

Joan Rivers received the flamboyant, star-studded farewell she’d long imagined when mourners gathered Sunday at Temple Emanu-El on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. Celebrities from Howard Stern—who joked Rivers was “chasing Johnny Carson with a baseball bat”—to David Letterman, Kathy Griffin, Whoopi Goldberg, Sarah Jessica Parker, Hugh Jackman (who sang), Barbara Walters and many others attended. Rivers’ daughter Melissa read a light-hearted letter and later greeted fans outside, sharing cupcakes and gratitude. The program echoed Rivers’ irreverent wishes from her book for a showbiz-style service—wind machine, Meryl Streep in multiple accents—and featured jokes about her plastic surgery, sex life and career. Fans dressed in designer tributes, and tributes noted Rivers as a trailblazer for comedians, especially women. Authorities continue investigating her death after a throat procedure and cardiac arrest on Aug. 28. Donations were suggested in lieu of flowers.

Seth Rogen and collaborator Evan Goldberg reflected on the failures behind The Green Hornet and another ill-received film, mixing self-deprecation with insight about filmmaking missteps. Rogen joked about the absurd on-set direction to "talk loud because the engine will be roaring," referencing moments early in flights where dialogue would be drowned out, and used that anecdote to poke fun at the movie’s problems. He called The Green Hornet the "perfect storm of bad s--t happening," while Goldberg noted they tried to make the picture appeal simultaneously to American and Chinese audiences, a compromise that complicated creative choices. Rogen added that they learned not to build expensive films that constrain their comedic instincts, quipping that their strength is simple, crude humor—"a million dick jokes"—and that they should focus on what they do best rather than overreaching with costly, multi-market tentpoles.

A young man from Sewell, New Jersey, Kenneth Bachman, unintentionally took an Uber more than 300 miles from Morgantown, West Virginia, back to his Gloucester County home after a night of heavy drinking near West Virginia University. Bachman says he blacked out after partying and woke up in the passenger seat of a 2011 Toyota Sienna minivan with an older driver an hour from New Jersey. He realized he’d been taken all the way home rather than to his friends’ place in West Virginia. The trip cost a staggering $1,635.93. The fare breakdown included a $3.94 base fare, a $2.35 booking fee, roughly $696.95 for distance, and $115.90 for time; Bachman says he accidentally ordered an UberXL, which is much more expensive than a standard UberX, and surge pricing doubled most charges—had he ordered a regular Uber, he estimates the ride would have been about $819.14. He said he couldn’t simply get out of the car when he woke because he didn’t want to be stranded on the roadside. He also reports the driver lacked cash for tolls and used Bachman’s phone to arrange payments; Bachman says the driver even answered a FaceTime call while he slept. Uber confirmed the trip occurred and that the driver took the passenger to the requested destination, later contacting Bachman; the company says the matter was resolved and Bachman agreed to pay the fare. Despite the episode, Bachman gave the driver five stars, called the situation embarrassing, and plans to return to West Virginia to collect his belongings.

An 11-year-old boy, identified as Anthony Perez McClean, died after plunging into a frozen pond in Forest Park, Queens, while trying to rescue a 12-year-old friend who had fallen through thin ice. The boys were playing near the pond around 4 p.m. when the older boy walked onto the ice and broke through. Anthony went out to help and was able to push his friend back toward safety, but then the ice gave way beneath him and he fell in. The friend ran home for help.

Responders arrived and waded into chest-deep, frigid water, breaking through thin ice by hand to reach the child. Some rescuers themselves fell through the ice during the effort; two firefighters were treated for hypothermia and minor injuries. Anthony was pulled from the pond unconscious, given CPR on the scene and en route, and taken to Jamaica Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Neighbors described Anthony as kind, helpful and well-liked, calling him a hero for his attempt to save his friend. Residents also expressed sorrow and frustration about the pond’s presence in what used to be a baseball field. FDNY Deputy Chief George Healy urged parents to warn children about the dangers of playing on frozen bodies of water, noting that days with temperatures just above freezing are particularly hazardous because ice can appear solid but will not support weight. Authorities emphasized visible warning signs around city lakes and ponds, and reiterated the tragic consequences that can occur when ice fails.

Ozzy Osbourne has condemned Kansas-based Westboro Baptist Church for using his 1980 hit "Crazy Train" during protests on the steps of the U.S. Supreme Court. The controversial congregation, known for picketing funerals of U.S. soldiers and anti-gay demonstrations, altered the song’s lyrics into a taunt—“You’re going straight to hell on your crazy train”—while protesting as the Court prepared to review a $5 million judgment awarded to the family of Lance Cpl. Matthew Snyder, who sued the group for emotional distress. Ozzy called the church’s actions “sickening and disgusting,” stressing that “Crazy Train” is actually a plea for tolerance and understanding, not hatred. The protest and its use of his music have sparked renewed attention and criticism of Westboro’s tactics.

A powerful winter storm swept from the Midwest to the Northeast, disrupting life for more than 120 million people with heavy snow, freezing rain, ice and frigid temperatures. Nearly a million customers lost power across several states—more than 595,000 in the Philadelphia area alone and huge outages in Pennsylvania and New Jersey—forcing utility crews to mobilize from out of state and prompting emergency declarations in New York and New Jersey. Travel was crippled: between roughly 2,700 and over 3,000 flights were canceled nationwide, with major impacts at New York, Boston, Philadelphia and Chicago airports; many rail and bus services were delayed or suspended. The storm caused traffic accidents, infrastructure damage from downed trees and lines, and at least three storm-related deaths in Kansas. Boston and other New England communities saw heavy snow and blowing conditions, while High Plains temperatures plunged up to 40 degrees below normal. Forecasters warned another potential, possibly intense storm could strike the East Coast over the weekend into Monday, threatening more coastal snow, strong winds, coastal flooding and further travel disruption.

On Dec. 25, 2015, an Associated Press report covered George Lucas’s controversial remarks about Disney’s handling of Star Wars and his subsequent apology. In a Charlie Rose interview that aired Dec. 24, Lucas, who sold Lucasfilm to Disney for about $4 billion in 2012, expressed frustration about being sidelined from the new trilogy and criticized Disney’s “fan-centric” approach to The Force Awakens. He said Disney chose to make the sequel “for the fans” rather than using his story ideas, and acknowledged that he stepped back because he no longer had control and feared he would “muck everything up.” Lucas described letting go of the franchise—and other properties like Indiana Jones—as emotionally wrenching, calling the films his “kids.” During the interview he used an offensive analogy, saying he had “sold them to the white slavers,” a remark he later apologized for in a statement, calling it “very inappropriate” and saying he misspoke. The report notes that Lucas had previously seemed supportive of The Force Awakens and may have attended its premiere, but his comments underscored that the remake/“remakequel” direction taken by Disney was not the path he would have followed. Lucas explained his decision to sell Lucasfilm partly by citing time: he had ideas for three more episodes and believed doing them “right” would take a decade, and at his age he wanted to pursue other films rather than commit to another long saga. The article also includes unrelated interview excerpts with actor Leonardo DiCaprio on early career anecdotes, near-misses with roles like Robin, Anakin Skywalker and Spider-Man, and his admiration for director Christopher Nolan and films such as Inception, illustrating separate reflections on career choices and cinematic influences.

Ohio State coach Urban Meyer responded to reports that he or the University of Florida covered up problems involving former Gators and Patriots tight end Aaron Hernandez. After Hernandez was arrested in June in the June slaying of semi-pro player Odin Lloyd, media accounts and a Rolling Stone preview alleged Hernandez abused PCP, carried a gun, joined a violent cohort, and that Meyer may have concealed failed drug tests and violent incidents while Hernandez played at Florida. Meyer texted The Columbus Dispatch denying cover-up claims, saying Hernandez was held to the same drug-testing policy as other players and that he and his staff worked to mentor him. The Rolling Stone piece also alleges family turmoil and that Patriots coach Bill Belichick had considered cutting Hernandez for missed practices and problematic behavior.

Former Alaska Governor and 2008 vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin obtained a 20-day protective order against 18-year-old Shawn R. Christy of McAdoo, Pennsylvania, after Anchorage Magistrate Colleen Ray found probable cause that he had stalked and threatened her. Palin and friend Kristan Cole, who also received a protective order, said Christy began contacting them in mid-2009 by phone, email and lengthy letters, claiming a relationship with Palin, professing religious turmoil, and threatening violence. Christy allegedly sent a gun purchase receipt, said he was buying a one-way ticket to Alaska, called to claim he had arrived, and told Cole she was “evil” and must be punished. Palin testified by phone she feared for her life and her family’s safety and disputed Christy’s claim of a sexual relationship with her. The orders bar Christy from contacting Palin, Cole, their families, or approaching within a mile of Palin’s home and a Wasilla-area high school; violation could lead to arrest. A hearing on a possible six-month protective order is set for October. Law enforcement and the Secret Service were notified; Palin’s attorney said Christy is among the most persistent of numerous past threats.

Alan Thicke’s two eldest sons, Robin and Brennan Thicke, have filed court papers in Los Angeles County to protect their father’s estate from what they describe as overreaching demands by his widow, Tanya Callau. The brothers—co-trustees of Alan Thicke’s living trust—say they were forced to seek court intervention to enforce the trust and a 2005 prenuptial agreement Callau signed when she married the actor. Alan Thicke died suddenly at 69 in December after an aortic rupture.

According to the petition, Thicke’s trust and will allocated property and assets among his three children and his wife: each child shares equally in a Carpinteria ranch, 75 percent of personal effects and 60 percent of the residual estate; Callau received the ranch furnishings, 25 percent of personal effects, a $500,000 life insurance policy, death benefits from pensions and unions, 40 percent of the remaining estate, and the right to live at the ranch provided she pays expenses and maintains it. The sons emphasize that Thicke acquired most of his wealth before meeting Callau.

In filings and statements, the brothers assert Callau now claims the prenup is invalid, argues she has substantial community property and reimbursement rights, and contends she sacrificed career opportunities to support Thicke and raise their youngest son, Carter. The sons’ attorney, Alex Weingarten, also alleges Callau threatened to expose disputes to tabloids unless the co-trustees agreed to mediation and her demands.

The Thicke brothers seek judicial clarification that the trust assets are separate property and that Callau waived community property rights via the prenup. Tanya Callau’s lawyer, Adam Streisand, denies his client threatened publicity and calls the sons’ action a “distasteful public smear,” saying she prefers to resolve matters privately while grieving.

Author and filmmaker Amy Krouse Rosenthal captured global attention in March 2017 when, just 10 days before she died of ovarian cancer, she published a tender, witty New York Times essay titled “You May Want to Marry My Husband.” The piece, a heartfelt personal ad for her husband Jason, described him as thoughtful, handy, handsome and an “absolutely wonderful father” to their three grown children. In a candid TED Talk and subsequent interviews, Jason Rosenthal has opened up about the pain of Amy’s final weeks and how he is learning to live with loss while honoring her wish that he “go on.”

Jason recounted the haunting memory of carrying Amy’s lifeless body from their bedroom to a waiting gurney and the emotional fog that followed her death and, months later, his father’s passing. He described assisting her through everyday tasks as she became frail and how those intimate moments remain etched in him. Despite enduring deep grief, he finds solace in small pleasures—music, nature, time with his children—and takes strength from Amy’s public permission to seek joy again. The essay also prompted outreach from readers, including humorous and sincere marriage proposals, which provided moments of levity. The Rosenthal family has relaunched the Amy Krouse Rosenthal Foundation to support ovarian cancer research and children’s literacy, continuing Amy’s legacy of creativity and compassion.

President Trump’s first budget blueprint, titled “America First: A Budget Blueprint to Make America Great Again,” lays out a stark reordering of federal priorities: a $54 billion boost to defense spending paired with deep cuts across many domestic and international programs. The proposal focuses on discretionary spending for fiscal 2018 and would shift roughly $54 billion from more than 18 agencies to the Pentagon, Veterans Affairs, Homeland Security and law enforcement priorities while eliminating funding for numerous smaller federal programs and independent agencies.

Major increases and priorities
- Defense: a roughly 10% increase (about $52–54 billion), described as the largest since the Reagan buildup, intended for readiness, procurement (including F-35s), munitions and nuclear forces. Details on precise allocations and operational use against threats like ISIS were sparse.
- Homeland Security and immigration enforcement: increases to hire border agents and immigration judges, plus an initial $1.5 billion this year and $2.6 billion in 2018 to begin construction of a border wall.
- Veterans Affairs, FBI, drug enforcement and school-choice initiatives also receive additional funding.

Cuts, eliminations and affected agencies
- EPA: targeted for a roughly 31% cut—about $2.6 billion—eliminating roughly 50 programs and 3,200 positions, and wiping out climate-related research and programs like the Clean Power Plan; some core state drinking-water grants would be preserved.
- State Dept./USAID: nearly a 29% reduction (about $10 billion), cutting foreign aid, multilateral contributions and diplomacy budgets.
- Health and Human Services/NIH: a $12.6 billion cut overall with $5.8 billion (near 20%) shaved off NIH funding, despite presidential rhetoric on curing disease.
- Agriculture, Labor, Transportation, Commerce and HUD face double-digit reductions; Amtrak long-distance routes, HUD community development grants and Low-Income Home Energy Assistance are among programs proposed for elimination.
- Independent bodies proposed to be zeroed out include the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, National Endowments for the Arts and Humanities, AmeriCorps and others.

Scope, politics and process
The 53-page “skinny” budget is intentionally brief and vague on many specifics, notably job cuts and account-level detail. White House OMB Director Mick Mulvaney framed the plan as delivering campaign promises and warned of reductions in the federal workforce. Congressional action is required to enact the plan; many Republicans and Democrats have already signaled resistance to key cuts (especially foreign aid, NIH, EPA grants and programs benefiting rural and local constituencies). The proposal does not address mandatory entitlements (Social Security, Medicare) or tax changes; a fuller budget with ten-year projections is expected in May. Short-term deadlines—including a temporary funding bill expiring in late April and the debt-ceiling negotiations—could intensify the political standoff and raise shutdown risks if agreement with Congress cannot be reached.

A 61-year-old sound mixer, James M. Emswiller of Pittsburgh’s Lincoln Place, died after falling from a balcony while working on the film You Are My Friend, a biographical movie about Fred Rogers starring Tom Hanks. The incident occurred around 7:30 p.m. in Mt. Lebanon during a break in filming; police said Emswiller fell about two stories from an apartment building’s balcony on Shady Drive East. Colleagues and a set medic attempted life-saving measures before medics transported him to UPMC Mercy, where he died roughly an hour later. Authorities suspect he may have suffered a medical event prior to the fall. The Allegheny County Medical Examiner determined the cause of death was blunt impact injuries to the head and torso and ruled the manner of death an accident. Sony’s TriStar Pictures said the studio is investigating and expressed condolences; filming was paused for the evening and Tom Hanks, who was on set, left after the incident. Emswiller, an Emmy-winning sound professional credited on Pittsburgh-shot films including Jack Reacher, Abduction and Concussion, was listed on IMDb as a sound mixer for the Mr. Rogers/Tom Hanks project. The new film explores journalist Tom Junod’s 1998 profile of Rogers and the bond that developed between them.

A 1-year-old Chinese boy named Hanhang suffered a serious injury when a chopstick punctured his brain after he tripped while holding the utensil, Central European News reported. His parents removed the visible portion and took him to a hospital, where initial examinations failed to detect remaining fragments lodged inside his head. Back home, the family broke and discarded their chopsticks out of fear, unaware a piece remained. Over the following days Hanhang developed vomiting and lethargy, prompting a second hospital visit. An X-ray then revealed a six-centimeter fragment penetrating his brain; surgeons removed it, and his condition improved immediately. However, he developed a brain infection and remained hospitalized for further treatment. Medical staff described the outcome as fortunately not severely affecting him. The report underscores risks when children handle chopsticks; similar incidents cited include previous cases of youngsters with chopsticks penetrating the brain or neck, requiring extended surgeries. Authorities and commentators advised that chopsticks should be used only by children while seated at the dinner table to reduce the risk of such dangerous accidents.

A 25-year-old volunteer for Ben Carson’s Republican presidential campaign, Braden Joplin of Midland, Texas and a student at Texas Tech University, died Tuesday after suffering injuries in a crash on an icy road in Cass County, Iowa. A campaign van carrying three volunteers—Joplin, Aaron Ohnemus and Ryan Patrick Shellooe—and a paid staffer, field director Drew McCall, hit a patch of ice, flipped onto its side and was struck by another vehicle. The three others were treated and released from a local hospital; Joplin was airlifted to the University of Nebraska Medical Center in Omaha, where he died late Tuesday afternoon. Carson, who was campaigning in South Carolina at the time, suspended campaign events for at least two days, flew to Omaha, and called Joplin “an amazing young man.” He posted a photo and condolences on Twitter and said he hoped Joplin’s death would prompt reflection on compassion and the value of life. The campaign said it would cover travel expenses for Joplin’s family and had chartered a private jet to bring them to Omaha. Texas Tech and representatives from across the 2016 presidential field—Republicans including Ted Cruz, Marco Rubio and Jeb Bush, and Democrats such as Hillary Clinton and Bernie Sanders—offered condolences and praised the commitment of young political volunteers. The crash occurred as candidates and campaigns were intensifying efforts ahead of the Iowa caucuses.

The author recounts discovering breast cancer after two friends’ diagnoses prompted her first mammogram. Initially dismissing a strange stiffness as anxiety, she schedules a screening at a welcoming clinic she found online. She narrates the everyday digital sharing that steadies her—tweeting through the wait—and the kindness of clinic staff who make the experience human. Ultrasound reveals a troubling “crater” and an enlarged lymph node; Dr. Kristi Funk, a forthright physician, explains the likelihood of cancer and arranges an immediate biopsy. The invasive procedure and the diagnosis flood her with shock, shaking, and disbelief, even as clinicians and loved ones mobilize around her. Confronted with medical terms—treatable, curable, chemo, surgery—the author absorbs a new reality: uncertainty, altered priorities, and a changed relationship to time, body, and loved ones. Fellow survivors advise accepting not knowing and finding balance amid this altered “gravity.” She ends by acknowledging the recurring waves of fear that isolate her and the sustaining power of love that brings her back.

A British couple returned from a Caribbean cruise with identical, intensely itchy rashes on their buttocks after sunbathing on a Martinique beach. The wife first felt a burning sensation that developed within a day into a red, pinprick-marked, winding rash; her husband developed a similar lesion after sitting with her on the sand. Shipboard medical staff prescribed antibiotics, antifungals and a steroid cream, but the lesions persisted. Ten days after the beach exposure they sought care at Addenbrooke’s Hospital in Cambridge, where clinicians diagnosed cutaneous larva migrans, a skin condition caused by hookworm larvae—commonly Ancylostoma braziliense in the Caribbean—usually deposited in sand or moist soil via feces of infected dogs or cats. Larvae penetrate skin and burrow, producing “creeping eruption” tracks; heavy exposure can allow larvae to enter the bloodstream and reach the lungs. After anti-parasitic medication was started, the woman developed chest symptoms—shortness of breath, dry cough and chest pain—and both showed lung involvement on imaging, prompting a second dose of treatment that rapidly resolved skin and pulmonary signs.

The case was written up for BMJ Case Reports with photos of the affected areas; although patient consent was obtained, subsequent tabloid coverage and identifiable contextual details led the couple to fear community recognition. The BMJ voluntarily removed the article at the patient’s request—without retracting its findings—citing the distress caused. Public-health authorities advise protective measures on beaches—wearing shoes and using mats—to avoid direct skin contact with sand potentially contaminated by animal feces. Hookworm infections remain a widespread global health issue but are treatable with antiparasitic drugs.

U.S. and NATO officials have warned that Russian influence with the Afghan Taliban appears to be growing and may even include material support. At a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing, Army Gen. Curtis Scaparrotti, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, said he had observed increased Russian association with—and “perhaps even supply to”—the Taliban, though he gave no details about the nature or timing of any deliveries. Earlier testimony from Gen. John Nicholson, commander of U.S. forces in Afghanistan, similarly accused Moscow of encouraging the Taliban, providing diplomatic cover, and meeting the group in Moscow without inviting the Afghan government. U.S. commanders argue Russia frames its contacts as targeting ISIS in Afghanistan, but that this lends undeserved legitimacy to the Taliban and undermines U.S. and Afghan efforts.

Moscow denies supplying the insurgents and calls allegations “fabrications,” saying such claims are used to justify U.S. failures in Afghanistan; Russian envoys assert contacts aim to bring the Taliban to talks. Russia has also said it exchanges limited information with the Taliban to combat ISIS, while officially designating the Taliban a banned terrorist organization. The warnings come amid a deteriorating security picture in Afghanistan: Taliban fighters recently seized Sangin district in Helmand province, reflecting expanded insurgent control and prompting U.S. commanders to warn the conflict is at a stalemate and to request more international troops to bolster Afghan forces.

The Internet Archive’s Political TV Ad Archive collects 2016 primary political TV ads and related social media, exposing metadata to help journalists, researchers, civic groups, and the public understand who is trying to influence voters. Meanwhile, the FCC has released a final draft to roll back nearly all 2015 net neutrality protections, leaving only a transparency requirement that ISPs disclose practices like blocking, throttling, and paid prioritization. The commission labels the 2015 rules legally flawed and claims removing them will spur broadband investment, relying on the FTC and antitrust enforcement rather than telecom-specific rules. It also seeks to bar states from enacting their own net neutrality laws. The order is expected to be voted on December 14.

McDonald’s is phasing out plastic straws across its 1,361 restaurants in the United Kingdom and Ireland, beginning a rollout in September with completion slated for 2019. The decision followed successful trials and customer feedback favoring a switch to paper straws, which will be sourced from certified sustainable suppliers in the UK and Ireland. The chain uses about 1.8 million straws daily in those markets; plastic straws are a common litter item globally and are rarely recycled because of mixed plastics. The move aligns with broader efforts to curb single-use plastics: the EU recently proposed banning several disposable items by 2030, the UK government has signaled similar action, and many restaurant chains and companies have pledged reductions in plastic use. McDonald’s said plastic straws will remain available on request for those who need them, kept behind the counter. Trials of alternatives and request-only policies will extend to other countries. Officials and environmental advocates praised the step, while disability groups warn some plastic straw users require them for safe drinking.

Chinese artist and government critic Ai Weiwei was allowed his first family visit more than 40 days after his detention on April 3. His wife, Lu Qing, met him briefly at an undisclosed location after being summoned by police; she said Ai appeared healthy but tense and emotionally constrained, with redness in his eyes. The meeting lasted about 20 minutes, was closely supervised by at least two officials—one taking notes—and focused only on his health and family. Authorities warned the family not to discuss the visit with media. Chinese officials say Ai is under investigation for suspected “economic crimes,” but have not provided details. He has been held largely incommunicado without lawyer access, prompting international criticism from governments, human rights groups, and the art world. Observers suspect he may be subject to residential surveillance, a measure that can be imposed for months and often allows detention outside formal facilities. Ai, a former co-designer of Beijing’s “Bird’s Nest” stadium turned outspoken dissident, gained prominence advocating for victims of the 2008 Sichuan earthquake and criticizing government corruption and censorship. His detention has sparked global calls for clarity and his release, with museums, artists, and international officials urging China to uphold human rights and due process.

The CIA has spotlighted a selection of once-classified UFO files from its FOIA collection, primarily dating to the late 1940s and 1950s, to help the public navigate hundreds of declassified reports released in 1978. Framing the release with a pop-culture nod to The X-Files, the agency picked five “Mulder” documents that seem to support extraterrestrial interpretations and five “Scully” documents that favor scientific explanations. Highlighted Mulder-worthy cases include 1952 reports of a huge “frying pan” craft seen in East Germany, fiery disks above uranium mines in the then-Belgian Congo, and sightings over Spain and North Africa that left smoke trails or emitted pale green light. The German account describes a roughly 49-foot object with two men and a glowing chest protrusion; the Congo report recounts discs seen by a pilot, sketched by the CIA, that maneuvered at high speed and appeared enveloped in flame. The agency also posted photos of unexplained sightings above Minneapolis (1960) and Sheffield, U.K. (1962), plus an image of a Socorro, N.M., investigation. Complementary documents include memos from 1949–1953, a 1953 scientific advisory panel review, and minutes from an Office of Scientific Intelligence advisory group. While many cases remain mysterious, agency analyses and the 1953 panel often found weak data or terrestrial explanations for most sightings. The curated release invites the public to explore the records and weigh evidence for itself.

The partial U.S. government shutdown has sharply curtailed many science, public health, and park services, producing immediate and potentially serious consequences. At the National Institutes of Health (NIH), Director Francis Collins called the closure of the NIH Clinical Center to new patients “the most painful consequence.” The Clinical Center halted enrollment in new trials and the start of planned studies; four protocols scheduled to begin this week were postponed. Of 1,437 trials underway, roughly 500 study new drugs or devices and 255 focus on cancer treatments for adults and children. Reduced staff will continue to care for current inpatients, but new admissions are allowed only if deemed medically necessary by the center’s director. NIH basic research activities largely stopped, though staff continue minimal animal care. NIH furloughed about 75 percent (14,700) of its employees; officials estimate roughly 200 patients weekly will be delayed from clinical trial enrollment, including about 10 children with cancer.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) furloughed about 9,000 employees, leaving only about 4,000 of 13,000 staff working. The CDC suspended multi-state outbreak investigations and significantly reduced surveillance: seasonal influenza tracking was halted, H7N9 and MERS monitoring became less robust, though some urgent investigations (e.g., Naegleria cases) continue and PulseNet remains operational. The Food and Drug Administration furloughed roughly 45 percent of its staff, curtailing most food safety, nutrition, and cosmetics activities while maintaining select critical functions such as high-risk recalls and import reviews.

NASA scaled back operations—mission control for the ISS stayed staffed, but most employees were furloughed, the agency website was offline, and some missions (e.g., MAVEN) risk missing critical launch windows if delays persist. The U.S. Geological Survey kept only 43 of 8,600 employees on duty, preserving minimal earthquake, volcano, and Landsat data monitoring; satellite data collection continues but analysis and distribution are delayed. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration maintained weather forecasting and the National Weather Service functions as essential to protect life and property. The Environmental Protection Agency furloughed roughly 95 percent of staff, delaying many cleanup, review, and monitoring programs though emergency responses remain.

Other impacts include reduced staffing for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission after a week, curtailed Forest Service operations except essential fire and land protection, and closures of national parks and attractions that also disrupt search-and-rescue efforts at sites such as Craters of the Moon where a missing hiker’s search was hampered. Broadly, the shutdown disrupts regulatory oversight, research, public-health surveillance, clinical care access, and federal employee incomes, with many effects escalating the longer the shutdown continues.

Finland’s state-owned postal service Posti is expanding beyond deliveries this summer by offering a paid lawn-mowing service delivered alongside mail routes. Available nationwide from mid-May until the end of August, the pilot runs on Tuesdays—chosen because mail volumes are typically lower—and customers buy one-month packages. Two options are offered: 30 minutes weekly for €65 or 60 minutes weekly for €130. Customers must supply their own lawnmower; Posti staff perform mowing within the time the customer estimates, and services are rescheduled if it rains. Orders are placed through Posti’s online shop and are tax-deductible as domestic services. The initiative emerged from postal employees themselves, says Posti director Anu Punola; staff have volunteered and planners will incorporate orders into mail delivery routes. The move forms part of a broader strategic shift as traditional mail volumes decline: Posti already delivers meals, runs pilots with security provider Securitas, and partners with municipal health and social care provider Eksote to support home care and disabled clients by assisting with daily chores and meal help. That municipal cooperation aims to increase flexibility and presence in clients’ homes, particularly for elderly and disabled people, while Eksote retains responsibility for medical and specialized care. Posti argues its dense nationwide network—reaching some 2.8 million households on weekdays—can cost-effectively provide diverse home services. However, industry group Real Estate Employers has raised concerns about competence and safety when using power-driven equipment, warning that lawn care requires expertise that not all postal workers may possess.

The Carolina Panthers deactivated defensive end Greg Hardy for their Sunday home game after a Mecklenburg County judge found him guilty in July of assaulting and threatening his ex-girlfriend. Coach Ron Rivera said he made the decision “in the best interest of the Carolina Panthers” after discussions within the organization, and stressed letting the legal process play out; Hardy is appealing and a jury trial is tentatively scheduled. The move follows public outrage over domestic violence cases around the NFL, including the Ray Rice video, and intensified scrutiny after Hardy missed practice to meet his attorney. Teammates publicly supported Hardy and hoped for his return, while reserve Mario Addison started in his place. Hardy, franchised for the season, will still be paid his salary. The team cited difficult broader league issues and ongoing internal deliberations.

A 2-year-old boy, Braydon Barnes, died of hyperthermia after being left alone in his room for roughly 38 hours with a space heater that never turned off, authorities in St. Charles, Missouri, say. Braydon’s mother, 22-year-old Kathleen M. Peacock, discovered him dead on Sunday, December 20, and alerted neighbors in the Elm Point Mobile Home Village. A neighbor who entered the child’s room reported it felt like more than 100 degrees. An autopsy determined hyperthermia was the cause of death. Police later revealed that both parents were using and manufacturing methamphetamine; they reportedly ignored the child’s cries during a weekend drug binge. Peacock and the father, 25-year-old Lucas R. Barnes, face charges including child abuse and neglect and manufacturing meth. Police also noted Peacock is pregnant.

Relatives and neighbors expressed devastation and said they had distanced themselves from the couple because of drug problems; one relative said Braydon had appeared malnourished recently. Neighbors who attempted to help described extreme heat in the room. Community advocates urged greater awareness and use of local resources such as the St. Louis Crisis Nursery, suggesting more families might seek help if they knew services were available and stigma-free. Family members warned there could be other children in similar situations and called for intervention to prevent further tragedies.

Researchers are narrowing estimates of how often Zika infection during pregnancy causes severe birth defects, especially microcephaly, and are documenting new related problems such as previously unreported eye abnormalities. A large CDC analysis focused on roughly 400 microcephaly diagnoses in Bahia, Brazil, estimated that infection during the first trimester carries a substantial risk of microcephaly — broadly ranging from about 1% to nearly 14% depending on how widespread infection was in the population. The wide range reflects uncertainties: not all microcephaly cases were confirmed, maternal infection status was often unknown, and overall attack rates in the population were imprecisely measured. The risk for infections occurring later in pregnancy was far lower (well below 1%), though other studies have found additional fetal harms from second- and third-trimester infections. Earlier, much smaller studies (e.g., French Polynesia) estimated about a 1% first-trimester risk; a Rio de Janeiro study suggested nearly 30% risk for all Zika-related fetal abnormalities and fetal death, which need not conflict with the new findings because they measured broader outcomes. CDC and other experts warn even a low percentage can overwhelm health systems where many women become infected.

Separately, ophthalmology teams from Brazil and Stanford examined three Brazilian infants with Zika-associated microcephaly and identified retinal hemorrhages, abnormal retinal blood vessels, torpedo maculopathy, pigmentary maculopathy and chorioretinal atrophy — findings that could cause severe visual impairment. It’s not yet clear whether eye lesions stem directly from infection or secondarily from microcephaly, but authors and the CDC advise retinal screening for all newborns with microcephaly in Zika-affected areas to guide care and improve understanding of the virus’s effects.

A 17-year-old senior at Escambia Academy in Atmore, Alabama, Chelsey Ramer of the Poarch Creek Band of Indians, was denied her diploma after wearing an eagle feather on her graduation cap May 23. The private school had issued a contract forbidding “extraneous items” at graduation and threatened disciplinary action and a $1,000 fine for violations; students had to sign it to participate. Ramer says she never signed the paper and, after seeing other Native students wear feathers in prior years, chose to display the eagle feather as an expression of her heritage. During the ceremony staff appeared upset but did not stop her; she received applause but was not handed her diploma afterward. When she later sought to speak with Headmaster Betty Warren, she learned Warren was no longer at the school; an interim headmaster, basketball coach David Walker, said he would like to give Ramer her diploma but must obtain board approval. Tribal members and parents reportedly sought meetings with the school board without success. Supporters note potential conflicts with protections for Native religious expression; the school did not respond to requests for comment. Ramer still lacks her diploma.

The two pieces critique President Obama’s American Jobs Act and depict a shift in his political strategy after midterm losses and stalled bipartisan deals. A Washington Times columnist argues Obama misled Congress and the public by claiming bipartisan support and reliable financing for the plan; Democrats, facing re-election pressure and tax-hike resistance, are unlikely to back the bill, and Senate leaders appear to prioritize other measures. The Newsweek analysis traces Obama’s post-Labor Day populist turn — targeting tax breaks for millionaires and corporations — as a reaction to failure to deliver jobs and difficult negotiations with Republicans and business. Advisors urged a bolder stance; Obama embraced a message focused on middle-class jobs and taxing the wealthy rather than appeasing House Republicans. Critics say his approach risks alienating business donors and may not solve unemployment, leaving Democrats and the president politically exposed heading into 2012.

A car drove into a group of children outside a primary school in Huludao, Liaoning province, killing five and injuring 18, local officials said. The driver was detained after the midday incident in Jianchang county; authorities described it as a “major traffic accident” and are investigating whether it was deliberate or an evasive maneuver. Security camera footage showed the vehicle change lanes and swerve into a line of pupils crossing the street. The attack echoes a string of recent and past assaults on public gatherings and schools in China, including vehicle-ramming and knife attacks that have killed and injured dozens. Authorities have linked many such attackers to mental illness, social alienation, or personal grievances, prompting renewed concern and occasional tightened school security.

A CDC analysis of 2012 data from 17 states examined 12,312 suicides to compare rates across occupational groups. Overall, suicide was the nation’s 10th leading cause of death and rates rose 21% from 2000–2012. The highest suicide rates were in farming, fishing, and forestry (about 85 per 100,000), followed by construction and extraction (53) and installation/maintenance/repair (48). Men accounted for most suicides and had higher rates across all groups; male farming, fishing, and forestry workers had the highest male rate (≈91). Among women, protective service, legal, and healthcare practitioner groups had the highest rates. Lowest rates were in education, training, and library occupations (≈8). Researchers could only analyze broad occupational categories and did not determine causes; they recommended prevention efforts emphasizing social support, connectedness, access to services, and reduced stigma.

Universal’s reboot The Mummy, directed by Alex Kurtzman and starring Tom Cruise, Sofia Boutella, Annabelle Wallis and Russell Crowe, attempts to launch a shared “Dark Universe” of monster reboots but largely collapses under its own ambitions. The film casts Cruise as Nick Morton, a mercenary tomb raider who unwittingly frees Ahmanet (Boutella), an ancient Egyptian princess cursed and entombed for murdering her family and bargaining with the god Set. Once revived, Ahmanet pursues Nick with eroticized hallucinations and a campaign of life-draining kisses that reanimate victims into a zombie army. Jenny Halsey (Wallis), an Egyptologist and Nick’s on-again companion, and her boss Dr. Henry Jekyll (Crowe) attempt to contain the threat, with Jekyll shoehorned into a dual role that mixes mad scientist, franchise architect and combustible alter ego.

Critics argue the movie feels like a Frankenstein of genres—action, horror, comedy and superhero-style worldbuilding—driven more by CGI spectacle than coherent storytelling. Reviewers find the tone confused, the plotting convoluted, and the screenplay’s injections of humor and one-liners often dopey. The film leans heavily on set pieces—an early subway-tunnel discovery, a dramatic plane-crash sequence, and an underwater chase—some of which deliver thrills, but these moments are undermined by weak character chemistry, especially between Cruise and Wallis, and by old-fashioned sexism in the depiction of female characters: Ahmanet as an embodiment of evil and Jenny largely relegated to a rescue plotline.

The Mummy borrows blatantly from many earlier horror and sci-fi films—nods to Quatermass, An American Werewolf in London, Lifeforce, Evil Dead and more—producing a pastiche that many find shameless rather than affectionate. While Cruise and Crowe bring star power, the film’s rushed franchise-signaling and tonal inconsistency leave it feeling bloated and undercooked, a disappointing and often clumsy start to Universal’s planned monster universe.

The California Supreme Court has added a civility pledge to the oath required of new lawyers, effective May 23.
