Until now, California attorneys swore only to support the U.S. and state constitutions and to “faithfully discharge the duties of an attorney.” The new wording requires newly admitted lawyers also to promise: “As an officer of the court, I will strive to conduct myself at all times with dignity, courtesy, and integrity.” The change was urged by the American Board of Trial Advocates and backed by former State Bar president Patrick Kelly, who argued that incivility—shouting, personal attacks in filings, refusal to accommodate routine scheduling requests and attempts to intimidate judges—has become more common during his 45 years of practice. Supporters call the revision a historic, positive reminder of professional responsibilities; critics and some legal ethics experts question whether a vow will curb bad behavior and worry about vague terms like “dignity” being used for discipline. Court officials, however, say the civility pledge is an admonition intended to encourage professionalism, not a new basis for disciplinary action.

Actress Sally Struthers was arrested early Wednesday in Ogunquit, Maine, and charged with operating under the influence after being pulled over on U.S. Route 1. The 65-year-old, known for All in the Family and charity work, posted $160 bail and was released. She’s performing in the Ogunquit Playhouse production of 9 to 5. Her publicist says she denies the charges and is fine.

The document compiles several 2015 political news items highlighting fundraising, candidacies, and controversies shaping the early 2016 presidential campaign. It opens with a profile of Bernie Sanders’s insurgent Democratic fundraising model: he rejects super PAC money and relies heavily on small donors, with an average contribution of $31.30 and roughly $11.4 million (about 75% of his haul) coming through ActBlue. Sanders had raised $15.2 million by July filings and reported $12.1 million cash on hand, having spent conservatively—about $3 million—compared with Hillary Clinton’s much larger fundraising and spending operation ($47.5 million raised that spring quarter, $18.7 million spent, $28.9 million on hand). Sanders and aides argue a grass-roots, low-cost strategy can remain competitive even while being outspent, and the candidate has rebuffed offers to form a super PAC.

The document then shifts to controversial endorsements and reactions: white supremacist David Duke praised Donald Trump for his immigration stances, calling Trump “the best of the lot” despite mistrust, and making anti-Semitic remarks about media and tech-company leadership. Separately, Donald Trump’s combative media behavior is recounted—most notably his public clash with Univision reporter Jorge Ramos and repeated Twitter attacks on Fox’s Megyn Kelly—illustrating his confrontational media strategy.

Joe Biden’s possible candidacy receives in-depth treatment: still grieving his son Beau’s death, Biden is portrayed as subdued and deliberative, accelerating outreach to donors and allies while not yet committed to run. Family concerns—especially Jill Biden’s hesitation—loom large. Though Biden polls well and remains a potential contender, officials including Obama and Clinton’s camp are monitoring developments closely.

Finally, the piece notes donor attrition for repeat Republican candidates Rick Perry and Rick Santorum: many 2012 donors shifted support to other 2016 contenders, notably Ted Cruz, exacerbating fundraising struggles for their comeback bids. Overall, the collection underscores fundraising dynamics, personal and political pressures, and polarizing rhetoric shaping the early nomination contests.

Police in New Delhi have arrested Abu Jundal (also known as Syed Zabiuddin, Abu Hamza, or Abu Jindal), a key Lashkar-e-Taiba operative alleged to have been a primary handler of the 2008 Mumbai attacks. Tracked for over three years and reportedly deported from Saudi Arabia, the 30-year-old was taken into custody after arriving in India from the Gulf. Authorities say he trained the 10 attackers in Hindi, provided weapon training, and directed operations from a Karachi control room during the 60-hour siege that killed 165 people. Intercepted tapes and testimony by surviving attacker Ajmal Kasab identify his voice; investigators say he urged killers to hide Pakistani identity and instructed them at Nariman House that hostages would protect them and to shoot if pressured. Jundal is linked to earlier attacks and arms seizures; police will obtain voice samples and continue probing his Pakistan- and Gulf-based activities.

BrandZ’s 2017 Global Top 100 values rose 8% year‑on‑year to $3.6 trillion, and 152% over 12 years, driven largely by technology brands. Technology (including telecom and e‑commerce) now makes up 54% of the Top 100 value with 37 brands; tech brand value grew 16% versus 4% for others. The US dominates with 54 brands and 71% of total value, rising 181% over 12 years, while Chinese brands jumped 937% and now account for 11% of value. Amazon vaulted into the top 10 with 41% growth; Apple and Google remain Nos. 2 and 1. Retail surged 14% led by e‑commerce. Newcomers are mostly tech firms; average Top 100 brand age is falling.

Joan Lee, wife of Marvel Comics legend Stan Lee, died Thursday in Los Angeles at age 93 (some reports gave 95). She had been hospitalized after suffering a stroke earlier in the week. A family spokesperson said she passed away quietly, surrounded by family, and asked for privacy as they grieve. Born Joan Clayton in England, she was a former hat model who met Stan when he visited a shop where she worked; they married on Dec. 5, 1947, and remained devoted for 69 years. The couple had two children: Joan Celia (J.C.) and Jan, who died three days after birth. Before meeting Stan, Joan experienced an unhappy wartime marriage that ended with a quick Reno divorce; Stan famously traveled to Reno to marry her soon after. Joan is credited by Stan as an inspiration for his work, urging him to write a comic he could be proud of—a push that helped spark the Fantastic Four and Marvel’s creative revival with Jack Kirby in 1961. The Lees moved to California in 1981 for Stan’s TV and film projects. Joan did voice work on 1990s animated Marvel shows and cameoed in 2016’s X-Men: Apocalypse; she also authored the 1987 novel The Pleasure Palace and had other unpublished manuscripts. Marvel and Stan’s POW! Entertainment acknowledged condolences and appreciated the outpouring of love.

Amanda Knox, the Seattle woman accused in the 2007 murder of her British flatmate Meredith Kercher, said she will not return to Italy and would become “a fugitive” if an appeals court upholds her reconviction. Knox, 26, remains in the US during the Florence appeal of the 2009 guilty verdicts against her and former boyfriend Raffaele Sollecito; their 2011 acquittals were overturned by Italy’s supreme court, which ordered a retrial. Sollecito has attended the hearings and his lawyer argued prosecutors grabbed at convenient suspects to calm public fear. Knox has not attended, citing fear of wrongful conviction and imprisonment; she told La Repubblica she would continue fighting her innocence rather than submit to what she called injustice. Legal experts note any Florentine guilty ruling must still be confirmed by Italy’s highest court before extradition could be requested, and U.S. authorities would consider contesting such a request partly on double-jeopardy grounds. Kercher’s family lawyers oppose Knox’s public remarks and continue to seek confirmation of the conviction, while another suspect, Rudy Guede, already serves a reduced sentence.

Producers confirmed that former New Life Church pastor Ted Haggard and his wife Gayle will appear on ABC’s Celebrity Wife Swap, trading partners with actor Gary Busey and his reported partner Steffanie Sampson. Filming is set to take place at the GLBT Pride Center in Colorado Springs. Haggard, who rose to national prominence as president of the National Association of Evangelicals, became infamous in 2006 after admitting to paying a male escort for sex and using crystal meth; the scandal led to his resignation. He has since returned to ministry as pastor of St. James, a nondenominational church, and has publicly denounced homosexuality while later acknowledging he might identify as bisexual if younger. Busey, a born-again Christian and Promise Keepers participant, has prior reality-TV experience on shows like Celebrity Rehab and Celebrity Apprentice. Celebrity Wife Swap follows the original Wife Swap format: couples switch partners, with men setting rules initially, then the women taking charge, promising cultural clashes and conflict—particularly between Haggard and Sampson, who reportedly is spiritual but skeptical of organized religion. Haggard declined to comment.

A 150-year-old chestnut tree that Anne Frank mentioned in her wartime diary toppled in Amsterdam after heavy wind and rain, damaging fences, a brick wall and sheds but missing the nearby Anne Frank House museum and causing no injuries. The tree, one of the few natural sights visible from the hidden attic where Frank and her family hid, had been infected by fungus and moths and more than half its trunk had rotted. City officials planned to fell it in 2007 for visitor safety, but conservationists and a support campaign secured a reprieve and a steel frame was later installed to stabilize the trunk. Horticulturalists had estimated the tree could live for decades with support, but the frame failed and the trunk snapped about one metre above ground. Clones and saplings from the original had been planted in Amsterdam and internationally; it is unclear whether a replacement will be planted at the original site, which is on private property. Portions of the fallen tree were later offered for sale online. Supporters said the tree’s long life had now ended.

After more than five years in Hamas captivity, Israeli Sgt. Gilad Schalit was released Oct. 18, 2011, in a swap that freed roughly 1,000 Palestinian prisoners. Schalit, thin, dazed and showing signs of malnutrition and shrapnel wounds from his 2006 capture, was handed to Egyptian mediators at Rafah after a contentious Egyptian TV interview and flown to Israel, where he reunited with family, met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and military leaders, and was taken for medical exams. His father, Noam Schalit, said Gilad faces a long recovery from physical and psychological wounds inflicted by prolonged isolation and lack of sunlight and human contact, but the family hopes he can lead a normal life. In Gaza and the West Bank, tens of thousands celebrated the prisoner releases with mass rallies that bolstered Hamas politically and alarmed many Israelis. Netanyahu warned released militants against returning to violence; critics and victims’ families contested the deal as excessively one-sided but the government proceeded, citing the duty to bring soldiers home.

Bernie Sanders endorses President Obama’s approach to gun violence: acknowledging no solution is absolute but urging stronger measures to reduce killings. He backs significantly expanded instant background checks, closing the gun-show loophole and ending straw purchases, along with bolstering mental-health services to help those who are suicidal or homicidal.

Separately, New York City is retiring its long-familiar subway token. The Metropolitan Transportation Authority stopped token sales April 12; on May 4, when fares rise to $2, tokens will cease to be accepted for subway rides (buses accept them with a surcharge until year-end). Tokens linger briefly on the Roosevelt Island Tram. Introduced in 1953 because turnstiles couldn’t handle mixed coins, successive token designs marked fare hikes through 1995. Tokens became iconic and nostalgic, appearing in souvenirs and civic honors, but technological and cost reasons—MetroCards are cheaper, programmable, and save about $6 million annually—led to the phase-out. Many tokens are held in vaults or by collectors; unused stock may be scrapped. Riders and officials wonder what to call former token booths—officially “station service booths,” though old habits may keep the “token booth” name alive. Finally, Alexa Internet has donated crawl data to the Internet Archive for the Wayback Machine since 1996.

Gunmen attacked the luxury Corinthia Hotel in Tripoli, Libya, in a brazen assault that included a car bombing in the parking lot and an hourslong shootout, killing at least 10 people, including an American and several Europeans, and wounding others. The facility, a seaside landmark that houses foreign visitors, businesses and diplomatic offices, was largely empty when the assault began; many foreigners had already fled Libya amid the ongoing turmoil. Witnesses described five masked attackers in bulletproof vests storming the lobby, firing randomly, and forcing guests and staff to flee out the back. A car explosion occurred in the parking area as protection forces engaged the assailants. Security officials later said at least two attackers were killed and that at least one attacker apparently killed himself with a grenade or suicide vest.

A group calling itself “Islamic State in Tripoli Province” claimed responsibility, naming two fighters said to be Tunisian and Sudanese, and framed the attack as retaliation for the recent death in U.S. custody of Abu Anas al-Libi, accused in the 1998 U.S. embassy bombings. The claim echoed previous local IS-linked operations, including embassy and embassy-guard attacks and kidnappings. Libya’s fractured politics complicated responses: the Tripoli-based Libya Dawn coalition denied IS responsibility and blamed Qaddafi loyalists or rivals, while the eastern Tobruk-based government accused Libya Dawn of allying with extremists. The assault underscored Libya’s post‑2011 collapse into competing militias and rival governments, and highlighted growing IS presence and threats to foreign and diplomatic targets in Tripoli.

Five Southern California high school students died in a fiery single-car crash in Newport Beach while heading to the beach on Memorial Day. The victims — three girls and two boys from Irvine Unified School District — were identified as 17-year-old driver Abdulrahman Alyahyan, 17-year-old seniors Robin Cabrera and Cecilia Zamora, 16-year-old sophomore Aurora Cabrera, and 17-year-old junior Nozad Al Hamawendi. The Infiniti sedan reportedly veered off Jamboree Road around 5:20 p.m., struck a tree with such force the car split and caught fire; four occupants were thrown from the vehicle and died at the scene, the fifth died at a hospital. Investigators believe speed was a factor; the posted limit on that stretch is 55 mph. The crash was described by local authorities as one of the worst solo-vehicle accidents in recent Newport Beach memory, with severe vehicle fragmentation requiring fingerprints for identification. Friends and classmates mourned at Irvine High, recalling the victims’ talents, close friendships and immigrant backgrounds. The Cabrera sisters were dedicated dancers; Alyahyan and Al Hamawendi were close friends, part of a group of first- and second-generation Middle Eastern teens. School officials said counselors would be available as the community copes with the sudden loss.

A woman confesses feeling guilty when assigning stories, influenced by a desire to please others and by Janet Malcolm’s view that journalism can be “morally indefensible.” The document then summarizes Bristol Palin’s memoir Not Afraid of Life, which offers an intimate look at her life beyond headlines: growing up in Alaska, sudden national scrutiny when her mother became the 2008 Republican VP candidate, teen pregnancy and single motherhood, public relationship struggles, and her stint on Dancing with the Stars. Palin emphasizes faith, future aspirations, and down‑to‑earth reflections while adjusting to life in Arizona with her son Tripp and revealing personal developments such as a new relationship and a canceled college talk.

Three-term Arizona Sen. Jon Kyl announced he will retire from the Senate when his term ends in January 2013, saying it’s "time to end my public service." The No. 2 Senate Republican, 68, pledged to focus on his duties over the remaining 22 months and help other Republicans win office, though he said only the vice presidency would tempt him as a post-Senate role. A four-term former House member and respected voice on finance and defense, Kyl’s departure creates a competitive open seat and drew praise from GOP colleagues and opportunistic interest from Democrats.

Google changed some autocomplete suggestions after being alerted that queries like “are Jews…”, “are women…”, and “are Muslims…” returned hateful prompts and search results. Reporters found autocomplete offering “are Jews evil,” “are women evil,” and “are Muslims bad,” with the resulting pages dominated by rightwing, antisemitic and extremist sites—often ranking nine of the top ten links to hate sites, Holocaust denial pages or misogynistic content. Google said it acted within hours of notification and reiterated that autocomplete is algorithmically generated from web content and user activity; it acknowledged offensive outputs can arise and said it works to prevent porn and hate speech but that the system is imperfect.

Academics and commentators condemned the episode as evidence that search engines have become manipulable editorial agents. Researchers described a coordinated network of fake-news and extremist sites that game Google’s PageRank by interlinking and amplifying one another, creating a “satellite” propaganda ecosystem. Experts warned this feedback loop—searches driving clicks, clicks boosting rankings—can normalize hateful narratives and influence opinions and politics. Calls followed for algorithmic accountability, human oversight or editorial responsibility; critics argued Google’s ad-hoc tweaks and PR responses are insufficient and opaque.

The controversy raises broader concerns about how dominant tech platforms shape information, the opacity of their algorithms, targeted political influence using data firms, and the democratic risks of leaving content curation to manipulable automated systems. Observers urged societal, regulatory and corporate reforms to reclaim the internet from propaganda and protect civic discourse.

A Jackson Pollock painting long thought lost has resurfaced in a Sun City, Arizona retirement community and will be auctioned June 20 by J. Levine Auction & Appraisal in Scottsdale after nearly 18 months of intensive research and authentication. The untitled abstract gouache, 22½ x 32 inches, emerged when auctioneer Josh Levine was asked to evaluate Lakers memorabilia; what he discovered instead was a trove of mid-20th-century modern works, including pieces attributed to Kenneth Noland, Jules Olitski, Cora Kelley Ward and Jackson Pollock. The collection came from the estate of Jenifer Gordon (Cosgriff), who lived in New York and was a close friend of influential critic Clement Greenberg and socialite-collector Peggy Guggenheim; Gordon bequeathed the works to her half-brother, now a Sun City resident. Levine traced provenance, hired private investigators and commissioned forensic testing by Peter Paul Biro. The forensic report found no pigments or binding media introduced after Pollock’s death, dating the work to the mid-20th century and aligning materials and technique with Pollock’s working methods. Complementary witness statements—including an artist who knew Gordon—supported the painting’s pedigree. Levine says he is confident enough to label it an original Pollock and expects it to fetch between $10 million and $15 million; he previously sold the Noland, “Replace!,” for $110,000 in 2016. Levine acknowledges ongoing debates over Pollock authentication and that the Pollock-Krasner Foundation does not authenticate works, but maintains the combined forensic, provenance and investigative evidence justifies the attribution. Online and live bidding will be available at the auction house.

A baby boy born five months ago to Jordanian parents is the world’s first confirmed child conceived using a mitochondrial replacement technique sometimes called “three-parent” IVF. The procedure, performed in Mexico by John Zhang’s team from New Hope Fertility Center, aimed to prevent transmission of mitochondrial mutations that caused Leigh syndrome — a fatal neurological disorder that had killed the couple’s two earlier children. Because the parents objected on religious grounds to discarding embryos, the team used spindle nuclear transfer: the mother’s egg nucleus was removed and placed into a donor egg whose nucleus had been removed, and that reconstructed egg was fertilized with the father’s sperm. Five embryos were created, one developed normally and was implanted; tests show under 1% of the child’s mitochondria carry the disease mutation, well below levels generally thought to cause disease, though experts say long-term monitoring is needed in case mutant mitochondria expand over time.

Mitochondrial replacement has been controversial. Critics warn it could open a path to germline modification and “designer babies,” while proponents stress mitochondria contribute only a tiny fraction of total DNA and do not determine personal traits. The UK approved a related technique, pronuclear transfer, in 2015; that method fertilizes both eggs and swaps pronuclei, but it involves discarding embryos. Supporters argue mitochondrial replacement can prevent devastating inherited diseases and point to extensive safety reviews and animal studies, although past attempts in the 1990s raised safety concerns and led to regulatory bans.

Leigh syndrome arises from mutations affecting mitochondrial energy production — often disruptions of oxidative phosphorylation complexes I or IV or mutations in mtDNA such as MT-ATP6 — which disproportionately damage high-energy tissues like brain and muscle. Advocates emphasize the technique’s potential to spare families repeated loss and severe disease, while opponents call for caution and further study before wider clinical use. The team will present full findings at an upcoming scientific congress.

A large, nationally representative study published in JAMA Internal Medicine found that dementia prevalence among U.S. adults age 65 and older fell from 11.6% in 2000 to 8.8% in 2012, a relative decline of about 24%. Using data from the Health and Retirement Study covering more than 21,000 people, researchers led by Dr. Kenneth Langa linked part of this decline to increased educational attainment: average years of schooling rose from 11.8 to 12.7, and more education was associated with lower dementia odds. The team suggests education may build “cognitive reserve,” improve health behaviors, and afford better medical care, all of which could reduce dementia risk. Despite rising rates of cardiovascular risk factors—obesity, diabetes, and hypertension—improved treatment intensity for these conditions (for example, greater diabetes medication use) may have produced spillover benefits, lowering vascular-related dementia risk. Regression models showed that education, higher net worth, and improved cardiovascular care together explained a meaningful portion of the decline, though much remains unexplained. The study validated cognitive classifications against clinical measures but noted limitations including reliance on brief cognitive tests, shifts in interview modes and proxy use between waves, and potential self-report inaccuracies. Although age-specific dementia risk appears to be decreasing, the absolute number of people with dementia is still expected to grow as the population ages, underscoring the need for continued monitoring and investigation of social, behavioral, and medical contributors to dementia trends.

Facebook is marking Data Privacy Day by rolling out two new security features to help users protect their accounts. First, it’s offering full-site HTTPS so all traffic to Facebook can be encrypted—not just password submissions—reducing the risk of credential theft on public or insecure networks. The HTTPS option will be available under Account Settings → Account Security and is being rolled out over several weeks; Facebook notes encrypted pages may load slower and some third-party apps may not yet work. Second, Facebook is testing “social authentication”: when suspicious activity is detected, instead of a traditional captcha it may show photos of your friends and ask you to identify them to verify your identity. Facebook will continue testing and gathering feedback. Commentary notes the HTTPS rollout is overdue, should be default, and doesn’t yet cover mobile apps.

A pregnant waitress in Delaware helped bring two missing Maine teenage girls safely home after trusting her instincts and using Facebook. On Nov. 2, Lisa Stephenson, 26, who works at the Blue Crab Grill in Newark, became uneasy when two teens applied for jobs during school hours. The girls looked young, weren’t in school, gave no addresses or phone numbers on applications, and claimed their phones and money had been stolen in New York. Concerned they might be runaways and vulnerable near nearby truck stops and motels, Stephenson wrote down their names and later searched Facebook. She found a missing-persons post from a Brunswick, Maine, mother reporting her 16-year-old daughter and a 14-year-old friend from Bath had disappeared on Oct. 25 after failing to show up for a babysitting job and that the Bath teen’s Toyota Camry was missing.

Stephenson sent the mother a friend request, told her what she’d observed, and notified local police and her cousins, who are county deputies. On Nov. 3 deputies in Maryland located the girls panhandling outside a strip mall in Waldorf; an officer took them to a station until a social worker arrived. Both teens were reunited with their mothers — the younger mother flew to Maryland and the older rented a car overnight to retrieve them. The older girl’s mother later described the girls’ “Thelma and Louise” journey south through Boston, New York and other risky areas, saying they were dangerously close to regions known for human trafficking.

The teens returned to Maine, grounded and, in the older girl’s case, barred from social media. Families praised Stephenson online and called her a hero. She demurred, saying she simply followed her gut and hoped others will speak up when something seems off. No charges were filed against the girls.

Prince Harry and American actress Meghan Markle announced their engagement and will marry in May at St. George’s Chapel, Windsor Castle, Kensington Palace said. Windsor, a royal residence west of London, is an intimate 15th-century chapel chosen over Westminster Abbey; the queen will attend and the royal family will pay for the wedding. Markle will be baptized into the Church of England and begin the process of becoming a British citizen, though retaining U.S. citizenship and dual nationality remain uncertain and the process could take years. The couple dated for about 18 months after meeting on a mutual friend’s blind date, keeping a largely private, long-distance relationship; Harry proposed during a cozy night at Nottingham Cottage, presenting a ring he designed with a Botswana stone and two diamonds from Princess Diana’s collection. They will live at Nottingham Cottage, Markle will join The Royal Foundation as a patron, and their first joint engagement is in Nottingham. Media and newspapers celebrated the couple as a modernizing influence on the monarchy; no special public holiday has been planned for the wedding.

Kristina Chesterman, a 21-year-old nursing student at Chico State, was struck by an alleged drunk driver last September and declared brain dead days later. Though her life was cut short, her decision to be an organ donor has profoundly affected many: five Northern Californians received her organs. A portion of her liver saved infant Jayden Kirby of Fremont, who likely would have died without the transplant; Jayden’s family tracked down Kristina’s relatives after news reports and has formed a close bond with them. Sakariah “Zak” Pappachan received a kidney and is recovering from renal failure, becoming an advocate for donation and forming a friendship with the Chestermans. A 42-year-old man received her kidney and pancreas, the remainder of her liver went to a San Francisco man, and Kristina’s heart beats in a 63-year-old South Bay woman, Susan Vieira, who has met Kristina’s mother, Sandra, and shares how many items on Kristina’s bucket list she already completed.

Kristina had written a bucket list in high school—things like flying a plane, skydiving and saving a life—and her family and friends have adopted many of those goals in her memory. Fellow students have raised funds for a nursing scholarship and plan a medical clinic in Nigeria; friends have skydived and flown first-class carrying her photo. The Chestermans find comfort and community with the recipient families as legal cases related to Kristina’s death and a prior assault on her brother proceed. Sandra Chesterman feels her daughter’s spirit guiding them and believes Kristina’s legacy will continue to inspire good works.

A recent Allegro Christmas advert, which has been viewed by over 2.5 million people, aims to capture the emotional reality of Polish families separated by migration. A spokesperson for the e-commerce platform told BuzzFeed News that the company wanted the ad to reflect the lives of millions of Poles who left the country—nearly one million have emigrated, many to the United Kingdom—in search of work. The advert follows a grandfather who learns English via an “English for beginners” set, plastering Post-It notes around his home as he prepares to reconnect with relatives abroad. Allegro says the story—about overcoming obstacles to reunite with loved ones—resonates broadly, especially at Christmas when family ties can feel strained, and ties it to the campaign slogan, “what are you looking for,” which blends everyday reality with personal feelings.

Separately, a viral Facebook video from designer Ji Lee highlights a different intergenerational effort to bridge distance: his 75-year-old Korean father in Brazil learned to draw daily Instagram pictures for grandchildren after they moved back to Korea. Initially resistant to technology, the grandfather began posting drawings—with Lee’s mother adding stories—to keep the family connected and teach heritage and life lessons. The project rejuvenated family communication across languages and countries and sparked wide online admiration; the grandfather’s account jumped from about 1,000 to over 63,000 followers within days. Viewers reported being inspired to reconnect aging parents with technology. Both stories underscore how simple, heartfelt efforts—whether a polished advert or a grandfather’s sketches—can powerfully reconnect distant families.

President Obama urged Congress to pass a short-term package of spending cuts and tax changes to delay the sequester’s automatic across-the-board domestic and defense spending reductions, set to begin March 1, until lawmakers can reach a “smarter solution.” He did not present a detailed plan but reiterated his preference for a broader deficit-reduction deal that would cut spending, reform mandatory programs, and close tax loopholes that benefit the wealthy and certain industries. Any delay would require tens of billions in offsetting savings from targeted cuts or revenue increases. Republicans, including House Speaker John Boehner, opposed new tax hikes and have warmed to letting the sequester proceed because it guarantees large spending cuts; they argue replacing it should focus on spending reforms without tax increases. Democrats in the Senate, led by Sen. Patty Murray, backed a balanced short-term replacement. The sequester — conceived in 2011 to force deficit reduction — would cut $1.2 trillion over a decade. Looming deadlines also include a late-March funding expiration and a summer debt-limit showdown. The nonpartisan CBO projects deficits will fall under $1 trillion in 2013, partly due to recent tax increases and the pending sequester.

Martin Shkreli, 32, CEO of Turing Pharmaceuticals, became a lightning rod for public outrage after his company acquired Daraprim, a 62-year-old drug essential for treating toxoplasmosis in immunocompromised patients, and raised the price from about $13.50 to $750 per pill—a more than 5,000% increase. His combative, unapologetic public stance and brash online persona intensified backlash from patients’ groups, politicians and social media, prompting death threats and widespread vilification. Shkreli, a former hedge-fund manager from Brooklyn who founded firms including MSMB and biotech company Retrophin (from which he was ousted amid legal disputes), launched Turing in 2015 with the stated goal of focusing on treatments for rare diseases. He defended the hike by arguing that Daraprim was underpriced and likened its prior cost to selling an Aston Martin as a bicycle; he claimed the profits would fund improvements. Amid the uproar—and extensive media coverage—Shkreli later agreed to lower the price to a level he described as “affordable” while allowing a “very small profit.” The episode highlighted a broader problem: steep price hikes for niche generics when a single company corners the market, deterring new entrants due to limited demand. Policy responses remain contested; proposals range from forcing drugmakers to reinvest profits to speeding FDA approval for generic competitors. Many observers argue sustainable reform will require regulatory change and sustained public pressure, not just castigating individual executives.

Sacha Baron Cohen has offered to pay fines for six Czech tourists arrested in Kazakhstan after wearing the actor’s signature “mankini” on a visit to Astana. The men were detained and fined 22,500 tenge (about $67) each for “minor hooliganism” and posing for photos in freezing temperatures while dressed in the revealing one-piece made famous by Cohen’s Borat character. Baron Cohen posted on Facebook, asking the Czechs to send proof and their details to an email he set up — arrestedforwearingyourmankini@gmail.com — and pledging to cover the penalties. The incident drew mixed reactions from Kazakh social media: some demanded harsher punishment, while others praised Cohen for promoting Kazakhstan’s profile and boosting tourism, a role that even led a Kazakh minister to thank him in 2012 despite the government’s earlier ban and threats over the controversial film. The story also recalls past local bans on mankinis as “inappropriate” clothing in places like Newquay.

Sen. Ted Cruz plans to formally launch his 2016 presidential campaign Monday at Liberty University, forgoing an exploratory committee and immediately entering the Republican field as its first major entrant. Advisors expect him to raise $40–50 million and aim to consolidate tea party, libertarian and social conservative voters—seeking to be the second choice across these groups to build a winning coalition against the Republican establishment’s preferred candidate. The outspoken Texas senator built his national profile by confronting both parties, leading a 2013 government shutdown effort to oppose the Affordable Care Act and cultivating conservative activists. Supporters praise his principled conservatism; critics doubt his ability to win establishment donors, endorsements or broad general-election appeal, noting early polls where he trails likely Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton. Cruz, 44, will continue to hold his Senate seat if unsuccessful and would be the first Hispanic president if elected.

Greece’s parliament moved toward approving a deeply unpopular austerity package as lawmakers debated measures including wage cuts, tax hikes and privatizations required by foreign lenders. Prime Minister George Papandreou, commanding a slim five-seat majority, worked to secure party support; at least one Socialist MP reversed course after talks with new Finance Minister Evangelos Venizelos. The EU, ECB and IMF have pledged a €12 billion tranche contingent on passage, officials warned this was essential to avoid an imminent default. Opposition leader Antonis Samaras and parts of the Socialist rank-and-file criticized the plan, while EU officials sought cross-party backing. The debate coincided with a nationwide 48-hour general strike—the longest since 1974—uniting unions and youthful demonstrators in mass protests around Syntagma Square and elsewhere. Demonstrations began peacefully but devolved into clashes: hooded youths threw stones and firebombs, police used tear gas and stun grenades, dozens were detained and scores of officers hurt. Greeks, facing soaring unemployment and deeper cuts, expressed despair and anger, lamenting being forced to pay for a crisis many blame on political elites.

Starting in 1996 Alexa Internet donated daily web crawl data to the Internet Archive; after an embargo these captures populate the Wayback Machine. A curated archive collects websites, blogs and materials tied to 17 Russian political and cultural figures who have opposed aspects of Vladimir Putin’s policies. Captured individuals include prominent bloggers, activists, journalists and opposition politicians such as Aleksei Navalny, Boris Nemtsov, Oleg Kashin, Andrei Makarevich and others, plus émigrés and dissidents. The archive also preserves eight sites reflecting contemporary political and human-rights debates: Civil Platform, Human Rights in Russia, Nashi, Politkom.ru, Putin.Itogi, Solidarnost’, Bolotnaya Square Case and Traitor.net. Separately, a viral YouTube clip filmed in New York shows birds forming a face some Russian viewers say resembles Putin; the footage drew widespread attention and speculation after Russian state-owned Zvezda aired it, though authenticity remains disputed.

After the 1986 Chernobyl reactor disaster and the evacuation of over 100,000 people, researchers report that large mammals have rebounded strongly in the exclusion zone, transforming it into a de facto wildlife preserve. An international team led by Tatiana Deryabina and Jim Smith used long-term aerial surveys (1987–1997) and winter track censuses (2008–2010) across the Belarusian Polessye State Radioecological Reserve (PSRER) and compared results with four nearby uncontaminated reserves. Contrary to expectations, densities of elk (moose), roe deer, red deer, and wild boar in the exclusion zone are now comparable to those in the uncontaminated parks. Wolves are especially abundant—more than seven times the density found in the comparison reserves—likely reflecting the near absence of hunting. Helicopter data also show rising trends in elk, roe deer, and wild boar within a decade after the accident; a later wild boar decline was linked to disease (African swine fever) and increased wolf predation, not radiation.

The authors conclude that, despite decades of chronic radiation exposure, the exclusion zone supports an abundant mammal community. They emphasize this does not mean radiation benefits wildlife; rather, it highlights how human activities—hunting, farming, forestry—can be more detrimental than contamination for population sizes. Critics and other researchers note the study addresses population abundance of large mammals but does not assess individual-level effects of radiation on health, reproduction, longevity, or smaller taxa (birds, insects, small mammals), where documented negative impacts exist. Nevertheless, the findings illustrate wildlife resilience and suggest that reduced human presence can allow many large mammal populations to recover, even in contaminated landscapes—underscoring complex trade-offs between contamination risks and pressures from human land use.

An elderly South Texas couple, William “W.T.” Steele and his wife Myrtle, died and their son Richard was injured after a swarm of bees attacked them while they cleaned a remote hunting cabin near Hebbronville. The 95-year-old William (reported elsewhere as 90 or 95) collapsed and died at the scene after being stung hundreds of times; Myrtle, 92, was airlifted to a Corpus Christi hospital and died there. Their 67-year-old son drove about 15 miles to reach a road and summon help; he was treated for many stings to his head and face and later released. Jim Hogg County investigators said the bees—likely aggressive Africanized honey bees common in south Texas—were disturbed when the family exposed a hive while moving a wood stove or spraying inside the fireplace. Deputies who responded were themselves swarmed but avoided serious injury. Authorities cautioned against untrained attempts to remove swarms; fatal attacks remain rare.

Iris Zink, an MSN, RN and rheumatology-certified nurse practitioner in Lansing, Michigan, donated a kidney to her longtime patient and friend, Ginny Holcomb, after Holcomb was diagnosed with kidney cancer. Zink had treated Holcomb for more than 15 years and the two had become close; when Holcomb’s kidney function began to fail, Zink said she “didn’t hesitate” to offer a kidney because she couldn’t “watch her die.” After about a year of testing, the pair learned they were a perfect match and underwent the transplant in July. Both women describe the moment the match was confirmed as profound — Holcomb called it a “God moment” and initially cried when Zink told her. The surgery was successful: Zink reports she has fully recovered and is “back to 100 percent,” while Holcomb’s condition is improving. The women remain close, speak daily, and wear kidney-shaped necklaces to symbolize their bond. They call their relationship lifelong—“she’s got part of me in her”—and hope sharing their story will encourage others to consider organ donation. For those seeking more information on donating, resources such as the National Kidney Foundation’s transplant donor guidance are recommended.

Research In Motion (RIM) faces deepening trouble as it readies fiscal first-quarter results expected to show a net loss and sharply lower revenue—analysts forecast a 3-cent-per-share loss on $3.1 billion in revenue versus a prior-year profit of $1.33 on nearly $5 billion. Shares have plunged about 68–70% over the past year, shrinking market value below $5 billion. Analysts warn guidance could be worse and predict continued declines in units, revenue and subscriber additions, possibly forcing a sale in 2013. Internal missteps contributed: a split leadership under co-CEOs Mike Lazaridis and Jim Balsillie created competing strategies and poor coordination, blunting response to the touchscreen smartphone shift. RIM bet on its email and keyboard strengths, missed market warnings, and produced several catch-up devices that failed to compete with Apple and Android rivals. New CEO Thorsten Heins is cutting costs, exploring strategic options with bankers, and betting on BlackBerry 10’s rollout to restore value or make the firm more sale- or partner-ready.

More than $1 million in jewelry was stolen from Diva Diamonds & Jewels on Santa Fe’s historic Plaza during the city’s crowded post‑Thanksgiving holiday tree‑lighting event. Santa Fe police say two men and a woman entered the busy store between 5:15 and 5:30 p.m., removed 11 items from an unlocked display case while employees attended customers, and left undetected; missing pieces were noticed around 6 p.m. Investigators believe the trio had scoped the shop in the weeks beforehand, asking questions about values, and distributed security images seeking help identifying them. Police call the dollar amount unusual for the area despite frequent downtown thefts. Detectives Abe Maes and Matthew Champlin can be reached with tips at 505-231-6497 and 505-469-5707.

North Carolina’s Republican-led legislature has passed a broad gun bill that stiffens penalties for firearms violations and expands where concealed handgun permit holders may carry. The compromise, approved by the House 73-41 and Senate 32-14, keeps the state’s existing handgun purchase-permit system but restricts sheriffs’ discretion: they can no longer limit how many permits an individual may obtain per year and must document and justify denials. The bill permits concealed-carry holders to bring firearms into bars and restaurants that serve alcohol (provided the carrier does not consume alcohol), to carry in funeral processions, and to keep locked firearms in cars parked on public school and college campuses. It also allows guns in greenways, playgrounds and other public recreation areas, removes permit-holder information from public records, increases background-check data such as mental health information, and strengthens penalties for violations. Supporters argue permit holders receive extra training and vetting; opponents, including campus representatives, warn of safety concerns as the bill goes to Gov. Pat McCrory.

Bethany Townsend, a 23-year-old makeup artist from Worcester who has battled Crohn’s disease since age three, has reclaimed her confidence and modeling ambitions after publicly posing in a bikini that revealed her two colostomy bags. Townsend received the bags in 2010 after a life-threatening bowel rupture and initially stopped modeling, devastated by the surgery’s physical and emotional impact. Encouraged by her husband Ian, she wore a bikini on a Mexico holiday and later shared a photo with Crohn’s and Colitis UK’s Facebook page. The image resonated widely, going viral with millions of views, hundreds of thousands of likes, and thousands of supportive comments. The overwhelmingly positive response helped Townsend accept her body and inspired her to pursue modeling again; she has since booked work, including for a lingerie brand that designs for people with colostomy bags. Townsend continues to struggle with active Crohn’s—having undergone further treatments and facing possible bowel transplant options—but remains hopeful. Her openness has raised awareness about Crohn’s, challenged narrow beauty standards, and offered encouragement to others living with chronic illness or visible medical devices, promoting body positivity and resilience.

A Ku Klux Klan rally in Charlottesville to protest the city council’s decision to remove the Robert E. Lee statue drew roughly 30 Klan members to Justice Park and about 1,000 counterprotesters, creating a tense, heavily policed scene. Klan demonstrators chanted “white power,” some wore robes and a few carried sidearms; their speeches were repeatedly drowned out by boos and chants. Police in riot gear escorted Klan members, declared the remaining crowd an unlawful assembly near the park, used gas canisters, and arrested 22 people. Three people were hospitalized for heat- or alcohol-related issues. City leaders organized alternative events and warned against direct confrontation, while local residents and activists stressed confronting racist ideology and debating the statue’s removal. Legal challenges have delayed the council’s removal decision, and further protests by white nationalist groups are already planned.

Hannah Upp, a 32-year-old Montessori teacher with a rare form of dissociative amnesia known as dissociative fugue, disappeared from her St. Thomas apartment on September 14 as the U.S. Virgin Islands braced for Hurricane Maria. Her car was located at Sapphire Beach and her sandals, sarong and dress were found on the sand, prompting fears she might have drowned, been the victim of a crime, or entered another fugue state. The search has been hampered by hurricane damage, chaotic recovery efforts after Hurricane Irma, limited cellphone service, and federal search resources diverted to storm response.

Upp has a history of similar disappearances. In 2008 she vanished while running in Manhattan and reappeared nearly three weeks later, found afloat off an island, with no recollection of the intervening time. In 2013 she disappeared for about two days in Maryland and again reported complete amnesia for that period. Friends and colleagues describe her as energetic, loving, bilingual with young children, and deeply committed to Montessori education; she had taught in New York, at a Quaker retreat outside Philadelphia, in Maryland, and most recently at the Virgin Islands Montessori School.

Those close to her—school head Michael Bornn, fellow teacher Maggie Guzman, and volunteer searchers including EMT Jake Bradley—have circulated flyers, canvassed beaches, checked shelters and hospitals, and monitored tips. Bornn emphasizes that a person in a fugue state may appear functional and should still be approached with concern. Upp’s family released a statement expressing hope for her safe return but acknowledged uncertainty. Friends hold out hope that, if disoriented rather than harmed, she may recognize posters or be found wandering confused; meanwhile, the community continues to search amid the region’s ongoing hurricane recovery.

After the 2012 election, many Democrats set aside earlier qualms about the impact of big money and embraced super PACs and nonprofit spending as essential to compete with a better-funded conservative movement. Senior Democrats and liberal outside groups met privately with major donors at the Democracy Alliance winter conference to plan expanded, long-term efforts — including state-level work, policy fights, and primary influence — and to re-solicit 2012 contributors. New Democratic megadonors have emerged, and groups like Priorities USA Action, American Bridge 21st Century, House Majority PAC, America Votes and EMILY’s List aim to build a permanent network of independent organizations to counter Republican shadow-party spending. At the same time, tax-exempt advocacy groups that funneled large, often opaque sums into politics face intensified scrutiny from state regulators. With federal oversight gridlocked — the FEC deadlocked and Congress failing to act — several states have required disclosure of nonprofit donors or launched investigations into routed donations, calling some transfers “campaign money laundering.” High-profile probes have exposed donors behind groups such as Americans for Job Security and Education Voters of Idaho, prompting possible fines and new state disclosure laws. The clashes highlight tensions between federal ambiguity, state enforcement, and ongoing legal fights over the boundaries of political activity by nonprofits.

A 22-year-old Middletown man, Tony Moreno, jumped from the Arrigoni Bridge into the Connecticut River around 11:45 p.m. Sunday after calling someone and threatening suicide; that caller reported hearing Moreno’s 7-month-old son, Aaden, crying in the background. Responding officers witnessed Moreno jump; firefighters pulled him from the water and he was airlifted to a hospital where he was listed in serious condition but later conscious and alert. Police and rescuers searched the river for nearly 24 hours using boats, paddleboards and jet skis but did not locate the infant and later classified the effort as a recovery mission. State police issued a Silver Alert for Aaden, though officials said chances of finding him alive are slim. Authorities continue to investigate and expect to file charges; it was unclear whether Moreno has provided information about the child’s whereabouts. The community held a candlelight vigil and organized online support. Family and advocates noted the case echoes domestic violence patterns, referencing a denied restraining-order application involving Aaden’s mother. Middletown police ask anyone with information to call 860-638-4000.

A decomposing body was discovered inside a brick entrance column at the WinCo Foods in Lancaster after a store manager reported a strong foul odor on Saturday afternoon. A plumber and the store handyman broke away bricks and found a leg and shoe, prompting the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department homicide unit to respond. Investigators believe the remains may be those of a 35-year-old man, later identified by the coroner as Raymundo Rivera. Authorities think Rivera could be the suspect who fled from deputies earlier in the week after a traffic stop for a fake license plate. According to deputies, the driver crashed, ran into the store, climbed to the roof and disappeared; there is rooftop access to the store’s fascia and to internal crawl spaces around the column. Detectives theorize the man may have entered the roof or crawl space to hide, slipped or became trapped inside the pillar and was unable to escape. The coroner will determine the exact cause of death and whether he fell or succumbed inside the confined, heat-exposed space; deputies noted temperatures exceeding 100 degrees and described the discovery as a shocking, grim scenario. The store remained closed during recovery and investigation, and authorities asked anyone with information to contact the LASD Homicide Bureau or Crime Stoppers.

A mother humpback and her calf became stranded on a sandbar off North Stradbroke Island, east of Brisbane, before managing to free themselves. Queensland Parks and Wildlife (QPWS) first received reports Thursday night that the pair were stuck at Dunwich; they may have been stranded nearby overnight and then became stuck again. Early on Wednesday morning footage showed the distressed calf swimming close and apparently nudging or pushing the mother as she splashed in attempts to dislodge herself. About 40 minutes after getting stuck the mother managed to free herself, aided by the incoming tide and the calf’s efforts. QPWS personnel were dispatched and planned to stabilise the pair until a Sea World team could arrive, but the whales got free before that team reached them. A QPWS boat trailed and helped herd them through shallow water to the open sea to reduce the risk of re‑stranding; the mother was described as tired and distressed. Whales are common off Queensland this season as many give birth and rear calves before returning south.

Three months ago “fake news” meant outright fabrications—made-up stories about Trump’s health or papal endorsements—but conservatives, led by President Trump, have broadened the term to include any unfavorable reporting. Trump tweeted that “any negative polls are fake news” and amplified a Federalist list claiming 16 fake stories since his election. Many of those items were errors or sloppy sourcing, not intentional fabrications. Examples include a debunked tweet alleging a photoshopped hand in Trump’s inauguration photo, a parody Twitter account that mimicked Reuters and misreported a Quebec shooting, an uncorroborated immigration-related claim on a Detroit Fox affiliate, and Time’s erroneous but honest account of a Martin Luther King Jr. bust’s visibility in the Oval Office. Some conservative objections targeted tone or mockery—such as coverage of Betsy DeVos—rather than factual falsehoods. CNN’s Chris Cuomo likened “fake news” accusations to a deeply insulting slur against journalists and later apologized for the remark.

A late-game interruption at Busch Stadium turned into an unexpected turning point in the Cardinals-Royals interleague matchup. With the Royals holding a 5-4 lead in the bottom of the sixth and two outs, Royals reliever Peter Moylan faced the bases-loaded Yadier Molina. As Moylan threw a ball, a small cat dashed onto the field, first wandering over to Cardinals center fielder Lorenzo Cain and creating a brief, chaotic distraction. Manager Mike Matheny admitted he initially thought a streaker had appeared, but was relieved it was only an animal. Stadium staff eventually chased and caught the feisty feline, which scratched and bit an employee resisting removal. The playful interruption was followed immediately by a dramatic swing: on the very next pitch, Molina crushed a grand slam that flipped the game and gave the Cardinals an 8-5 lead that held for the win. The victory had standings implications, as the Cardinals leapfrogged the Brewers into second place in the NL Central, closing to 1.5 games behind the Cubs. Players and staff made light of the moment afterward; Matheny joked he liked the cat despite not being a pet person, and Molina referenced past animal superstitions like the 2011 “Rally Squirrel.” With Molina’s nickname “Yadi” in mind, some fans and commentators quickly dubbed the intruding animal “Yadi the Rally Cat.” The episode offered a mix of levity and baseball drama, turning a bizarre interruption into the catalyst for a pivotal postseason-style moment.

Univision located Yaneisi Fernandez, a 21-year-old Dominican woman named in records alleging she was hired as a prostitute by associates of Florida eye doctor Salomon Melgen, who has ties to Sen. Bob Menendez (D-N.J.). Fernandez and her family deny any involvement in prostitution; she said she never met Menendez and has never been to Casa de Campo. The allegations surfaced after an FBI raid on Melgen’s office amid a Medicare fraud probe and reports that Menendez reimbursed Melgen for private-jet flights to the Dominican Republic. Earlier reports from the Daily Caller accused Menendez of patronizing prostitutes, including minors, at Melgen’s estate. Menendez has denied wrongdoing. The Senate Ethics Committee and federal investigators are reviewing the matter; top Democrats, including Majority Leader Harry Reid, have expressed confidence pending investigation. Menendez repaid $58,500 for two 2010 flights and faces scrutiny over possible intervention on behalf of a Melgen-owned company seeking a Dominican port-security contract.

Three Cleveland women rescued after being held captive for about a decade—Amanda Berry, Gina DeJesus and Michelle Knight—say they are “happy and safe” as they continue healing, according to a letter released by their attorneys thanking the public for support and respect for their privacy. The attorneys said media presence has eased, allowing the women space to reconnect with family and recover. A Cleveland charity, the Cleveland Courage Fund, has collected substantial donations—reported between $650,000 and $825,000—from across the U.S. and abroad; funds are being distributed to the four survivors (including Berry’s young daughter) and will be placed into trusts so 100% of future donations benefit them. Officials and volunteers have also offered services such as medical and dental care and housing. The abductions—Knight disappeared in 2002, Berry in 2003, and DeJesus in 2004—sparked scrutiny of local police and renewed attention to missing-persons cases. Ariel Castro, charged with multiple counts including kidnapping and rape, is jailed. Local leaders are exploring further support measures, including a proposed state bill to provide financial, medical and educational aid to long-term abduction survivors.

The U.N. Security Council unanimously called for a cease-fire in the Gaza-centered Israeli-Palestinian conflict, urging de-escalation, restoration of calm, and resumption of direct Israeli-Palestinian talks aimed at a two-state solution. The statement, nonbinding and approved by all 15 members, specifically called for "the reinstitution of the November 2012 cease-fire" but set no start date; Palestinian envoy Riyad Mansour said Palestinians expect an immediate halt and warned the council would be pressed further if Israel did not comply. International pressure grew as Britain’s foreign secretary and other Western officials sought emergency consultations in Vienna, while Arab foreign ministers planned talks. The U.S. reiterated support for Israel’s right to defend itself against Hamas rocket attacks but expressed concern about further escalation and said it stood ready to help facilitate a cease-fire. The council text avoided naming Hamas or Israel’s military response, instead stressing protection of civilians and respect for international humanitarian law. Palestinians had drafted a more strongly worded, legally binding resolution condemning violence and calling for an immediate durable cease-fire; that draft, which omitted mention of Hamas rockets, risked a U.S. veto. On the ground, five days of Israeli airstrikes and a first known ground raid wounded four Israeli soldiers, prompted mass civilian displacement warnings in northern Gaza, and left heavy Palestinian casualties amid fears the offensive could intensify.

On May 2 in Wellington, Florida, landscaper Jason Scott Falbo, 24, allegedly used his riding lawnmower to kill nine of 11 newly hatched Muscovy ducklings belonging to Boyd Jentzsch and his family. The family had been feeding the mother and her ducklings outside their home when Falbo drove his mower toward them; witnesses say he lowered the blades and the machine struck the ducklings, sending feathers and small bones into the air. The distraught family — Boyd, his wife Laura Gontchar and their 7-year-old son Kai — rushed outside as Falbo reportedly backed up and ran over the ducklings a second time, smiling and laughing. Four ducklings initially escaped but two drowned; only two survived. The boy was traumatized, asking afterward whether “everybody out there” was capable of such cruelty. Police and Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control responded, recovered the remains, and charged Falbo with nine counts of animal cruelty; officers’ reports say the ducklings died “cruelly and viciously with extreme intent.” Falbo, who had a March arrest for domestic battery and aggravated child abuse against a girlfriend, was booked at Palm Beach County Jail on $27,000 bail. The Jentzsches remain emotionally shaken and are trying to help Kai process the incident, using it to teach about the value of life and how to respond to cruelty. The case highlights the family’s distress and community concern over a shocking, seemingly intentional act against defenseless animals.

A California appeals court ruled that a 2006 state law banning handheld cellphone use while driving, which targets conversations without a hands-free device, does not prohibit consulting map apps. The 5th District Court of Appeal overturned a $165 ticket issued to Fresno driver Steven Spriggs, who was stopped in freeway traffic in January 2012 while checking an iPhone map for an alternate route. Lower courts had upheld the citation, but the appellate panel said the statute’s language and legislative history show its focus was on hands-on talking, not all handheld uses. Justice Herbert Levy noted the Legislature later enacted a separate ban on texting while driving, which supports the narrower interpretation. Spriggs, who uses hands-free devices and whose family was personally affected by distracted driving, argued the law should be clarified so officers can enforce dangerous behavior appropriately; he will recoup his fine. The state attorney general’s office is reviewing whether to appeal to the California Supreme Court. The ruling could have statewide effect unless overturned or changed by new legislation.

The Cook Political Report certified all 50 states and D.C., showing Hillary Clinton received 65,844,610 votes (48.2%) to Donald Trump’s 62,979,636 (46.1%), a near 3 million popular-vote margin for Clinton. Other candidates totaled 7,804,213 votes (5.7%). Despite Clinton’s substantial raw-vote lead—the largest for a losing candidate—Trump won the presidency via the Electoral College, taking 306 electoral votes on Election Day and receiving 304 electors’ votes after the college convened; Clinton secured 232 electoral votes and 227 electors’ votes due to seven defections. The outcome has renewed debate over the Electoral College’s fairness.

On his late-night show, Jimmy Kimmel responded to the news that Toys “R” Us will close all 735 stores, quipping that shoppers now buy toys online and joking Amazon will turn other retailers into “abandoned warehouses.” The show featured an appearance by Geoffrey the Giraffe, who tearfully lamented the chain’s bankruptcy and blamed customers for buying from Amazon, admitting he was drunk. Geoffrey sang the old “I’m a Toys’R’Us Kid” jingle as Kimmel called the scene “the saddest thing” he’d seen and had security escort the crestfallen mascot out, suggesting they get him another drink. The segment aired March 16, 2018.

Summary:

Following the racially motivated mass shooting at Emanuel AME Church in Charleston, South Carolina, former Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney called for the immediate removal of the Confederate battle flag from the South Carolina Statehouse grounds, calling it “a symbol of racial hatred” and urging its removal to honor the victims. His statement intensified a national debate and pressured Republican presidential hopefuls to state positions on a divisive cultural symbol tied to the state that hosts an important early primary.

Responses among GOP figures were mixed. Some candidates and prominent Republicans supported removal or noted prior action in their states: Jeb Bush cited his 2001 decision in Florida to move the Confederate flag from the Capitol to a museum. Mitt Romney had previously criticized the flag during his campaigns and repeated opposition. Ohio Gov. John Kasich said the decision belongs to South Carolinians but personally would favor taking it down. Several Democrats, including President Obama and many civil-rights leaders, also called for the flag’s removal.

Many Republican contenders, however, urged deference to South Carolina officials and warned against outsiders dictating the outcome. Ted Cruz and Marco Rubio emphasized that South Carolinians should lead the decision; Cruz framed the debate as balancing historical remembrance and recognition of slavery’s legacy. Scott Walker declined to take a firm stand immediately, calling instead for sensitivity while families mourned. Lindsey Graham resisted making the flag central, insisting the shooter’s motives and actions—not the flag—were the core issue. Carly Fiorina labeled the flag a symbol of racial hatred personally but deferred to state decision-makers. Several other candidates either avoided comment or had campaign spokesmen decline to comment.

Political calculations complicated responses: the Confederate flag is a potent symbol among some conservative South Carolina voters, and the state’s early role in the GOP primary calendar makes the issue electorally sensitive. Romney’s intervention, backed by his national stature, intensified pressure on the field. The broader coverage recounted varied Republican stances, noted the flag’s relocation history in South Carolina (removed from the Capitol dome in 2000 and flown at a nearby memorial), and situated the debate within the national reckoning over race and public symbols after the Charleston killings.

Casey Johnson, a 30-year-old Johnson & Johnson heiress, spent her final months in severe decline, sources say. Once an heir to a multibillion-dollar fortune, she lived in a squalid rented Los Angeles home without electricity, gas, or water, amid vermin and a revolving cast of questionable acquaintances. Johnson battled brittle diabetes—reportedly requiring an insulin pump—and was hospitalized multiple times over the past year; accounts differ on whether missed insulin doses contributed to her crises. Her behavior grew increasingly erratic: she faced arrest for alleged grand theft after being accused of breaking into friends’ homes, lost custody of her adopted daughter, and had prior suicide attempts, including a November overdose that led to intensive care. Friends and family say she self-medicated with prescription medications (OxyContin, Klonopin, Adderall) and illegal drugs (marijuana, ecstasy, cocaine), briefly entered rehab but left early, and resisted further treatment despite being cut off financially by relatives. In recent months she became publicly involved with reality figure Tila Tequila; the pair announced an engagement in a video that friends said showed Johnson incapacitated. Her body was discovered days after her final public tweet; an initial autopsy was inconclusive with no obvious trauma, and toxicology results were pending. Her family arranged for a private funeral, established a memorial fund with the Juvenile Diabetes Foundation, and asked for donations in her honor.

Disney and J.J. Abrams have unveiled the cast and title for Star Wars: Episode VII, now officially named Star Wars: The Force Awakens, which wrapped principal photography and is set for release on Dec. 18, 2015. The film reunites original trilogy icons Harrison Ford, Carrie Fisher and Mark Hamill as Han Solo, Leia and Luke Skywalker, alongside returning favorites Kenny Baker (R2-D2), Anthony Daniels (C-3PO) and Peter Mayhew (Chewbacca). Abrams balanced veteran stars with fresh faces, echoing George Lucas’s original casting approach: established actors lend gravitas while newcomers carry the next-generation storyline.

Notable additions include Lupita Nyong’o, Gwendoline Christie, Andy Serkis, Max von Sydow, Adam Driver, Oscar Isaac, John Boyega, Domhnall Gleeson and newcomer Daisy Ridley. The mix drew praise for combining demonstrated talent and relative unknowns who won’t distract audiences through prior high-profile roles. Fans speculated about parts—Ridley is rumored to be related to Han Solo—but specific character assignments were not released. Billy Dee Williams’s absence as Lando was noted as a surprise, though a cameo remained possible.

The title, The Force Awakens, nods to the franchise’s mythic element and suggests the Force’s resurgence through new characters, provoking fan debate about its implications. Production had its challenges, including on-set injuries to Ford and widespread leaks, but filming covered diverse locations from Abu Dhabi deserts to English forests. Produced by Kathleen Kennedy and Bryan Burke, the film aims to honor the legacy of the original trilogy while passing the torch to a younger ensemble, with expectations high and speculation rampant in the months leading to its 2015 premiere.

Three space travelers returned safely to Earth Sept. 2–3 when their Soyuz MS-04 capsule touched down on the Kazakh steppes, concluding a mission notable mainly for NASA astronaut Peggy Whitson’s record-breaking stay. Whitson spent 288 days on this flight and now holds the U.S. cumulative space endurance record with 665 days total, surpassing previous American marks and setting the longest single spaceflight by a woman. Her crewmates, NASA’s Jack Fischer and Roscosmos’ Fyodor Yurchikhin, spent 136 days on this mission; Yurchikhin’s career total is now 673 days, placing him seventh on the all-time endurance list while Whitson is eighth.

The Soyuz undocked from the station’s Poisk module and completed a 3-hour, 24-minute descent. During reentry the capsule experienced exterior temperatures up to about 2,500°F (1,400°C) while a heat shield protected the crew. Parachutes and six soft-landing engines slowed and cushioned touchdown near Dzhezkazgan. The capsule tipped onto its side, a common occurrence, and recovery teams reached the site by helicopter to assist the crew and move them to a medical tent. From there Whitson and Fischer will fly via an ESA aircraft to Cologne, then on to Houston, because Hurricane Harvey disrupted NASA’s usual direct return flight; Yurchikhin will return to Russia.

Back at Johnson Space Center, Whitson and Fischer will undergo about 45 days of rehabilitation and postflight research and debriefs. On station, Randy Bresnik, Paolo Nespoli and Sergey Ryazansky will remain until the next Soyuz arrives Sept. 12 carrying Joe Acaba, Mark Vande Hei and Alexander Misurkin. Whitson’s mission featured multiple firsts—oldest woman in space, most female spacewalks (10), and the first woman to command the ISS twice—and she emphasized the hard work of teams supporting the station during adverse conditions.

A Portland resident, Henry Kraemer, launched the "Trump Has Tiny Hands PAC" to poke fun at Republican front-runner Donald Trump after a campaign spat about the size of his hands. The controversy began when Senator Marco Rubio quipped that men with small hands can’t be trusted, prompting Trump to defensively display his hands at a debate and insist his are large. Kraemer said he formed the PAC when Trump began denying he has “tiny baby hands,” joking that voters should know if Trump could even lift a 3 a.m. phone. Yelp joined the mockery by joking about app usability for small hands. The episode echoes past taunts — including Graydon Carter’s long-running “short-fingered vulgarian” barbs — which Trump reportedly reacts to by sending photos trying to prove otherwise. The piece also notes unrelated content collected about Hillary Clinton’s email controversy.

Two Vermont lawmakers, Reps. Jean O’Sullivan and Chris Pearson, filed a provocative bill that would effectively reinstate alcohol prohibition in the state — a move intended not to pass but to jolt lawmakers into legalizing marijuana. House Bill 502 would criminalize alcohol possession with penalties mirroring current marijuana laws: fines up to $500 for small possession and potential prison terms up to 30 years and $1 million in penalties for sale and distribution. O’Sullivan admits she doesn’t actually support banning alcohol; the bill is a rhetorical gambit to highlight what they view as the inconsistency of keeping marijuana illegal while allowing a far more dangerous substance. Citing studies showing marijuana’s lower mortality risk compared with alcohol and tobacco, the sponsors argue legalization could bring substantial tax revenue — a Rand estimate projects $20–70 million annually from a regulated market — and help close Vermont’s budget shortfall. Companion bills proposing regulated marijuana sales are also pending in the legislature.

Supporters in Ferguson, Mo., quickly rebuilt a roadside memorial to Michael Brown on Dec. 26 after a vehicle drove through and scattered flowers, signs and mementos left at the Canfield Drive shrine. The memorial, erected near the Canfield Green apartments where the 18-year-old was shot and killed by Officer Darren Wilson on Aug. 9, had become a focal point of protests and national debate over race and policing. Social media accounts and local activists reported the destruction was intentional; volunteers gathered overnight after seeing photos and video to restore the tribute, and by morning the shrine had been rebuilt. 

Ferguson Police Department public information officer Timothy Zoll initially told a Washington Post reporter that no crime had been reported and questioned whether the matter warranted attention, calling the site “a pile of trash in the middle of the street.” After city officials said Zoll misled his superiors about his comments, he was placed on unpaid administrative leave as the department opened an internal inquiry. The city stressed Zoll’s remarks did not reflect department views and noted officials have been working to relocate the memorial to a safer location. The suspension comes amid broader efforts by Ferguson officials to repair trust with the community in the wake of Brown’s shooting.

A collection of odd tourist “massage” attractions is described with a mix of disbelief and dark humor. One involves live snakes slithering over people’s bodies: larger snakes reportedly concentrate on the belly or back and produce a kneading sensation, while smaller ones wander to sensitive areas like the face—an unnerving sight captured in a referenced video. Although the snakes are nonvenomous, the experience is portrayed as more terrifying than soothing, and the writer quips that many other animals would make better masseurs. Another attraction at Thailand’s Maesa Elephant Camp features trained elephants stepping on tourists’ backs to “ease stress.” The piece highlights the danger and absurdity: the sight of a massive animal potentially crushing you overshadows any supposed relaxation, and tourists are sometimes tricked into expecting a calf only to get an adult instead. Overall, the tone is skeptical and bemused, framing these offerings as questionable, stressful tourist spectacles rather than legitimate wellness treatments.

President Obama mounted an intense public and behind-the-scenes campaign to secure support for the Iran nuclear agreement as Congress prepared for a potentially decisive fall vote. Acknowledging heavy lobbying and ad campaigns led by opponents like Aipac and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the White House urged Democrats to declare backing before leaving Washington. Obama planned a major speech at American University—evoking JFK’s 1963 test-ban address—followed by media interviews and a nationwide push featuring senior officials, including nuclear physicist Energy Secretary Ernest Moniz, to explain the deal’s technical terms.

Obama framed the vote as the most consequential foreign policy debate since the Iraq War, arguing that many critics who now oppose the deal earlier supported the 2003 invasion. He warned that rejecting the agreement risks isolating the U.S., undermining diplomacy’s credibility, and making war the remaining option to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. He defended the deal as the strongest nonproliferation arrangement, with extensive IAEA inspections and sanctions relief tied to limits on Iran’s program.

The administration sought to persuade undecided Democrats and prepare to veto congressional rejection; leaders including Barbara Boxer, Tim Kaine, Bill Nelson, Chris Murphy, and Angus King publicly backed the pact. Critics, including Republicans and some Jewish groups, called Obama’s rhetoric partisan and overstated, asserting alternatives to war remain. Nonetheless, the White House intensified outreach to counter mounting opposition.

Wayne Flynt, Auburn University professor emeritus and longtime friend of Harper Lee, has published Mockingbird Songs: My Friendship With Harper Lee, drawing on decades of correspondence and visits that continued until Lee’s death in 2016. Flynt first met Lee in 1983 and remained one of the few people she allowed regular contact with after she moved into a nursing home. The book, timed for broad release, offers an intimate portrait of the famously private author of To Kill a Mockingbird and addresses long-debated aspects of her life and relationships.

Flynt says Lee asked only that he not write about her while she lived; he believes the new book lets her “speak beyond the grave” without threatening her privacy. He recounts Lee’s deep discomfort with fame—stemming in part from an experience with a stalker—and her fear of obsessive fans, even to the point of worrying about assassination. Lee also suffered intense pre-interview anxiety, Flynt reports, sometimes becoming physically ill before public appearances.

A substantial thread in Flynt’s narrative revisits Lee’s complex relationship with Truman Capote. Childhood friends in Monroeville and creative collaborators—Lee helped research and edit portions of Capote’s In Cold Blood—their friendship frayed, Flynt says, over Capote’s resentment after Lee’s novel succeeded. In a March 2006 letter included in the book Lee called Capote a “compulsive liar” and suggested his envy lingered for decades. Flynt also contends Lee “may not have fully participated” in the 2015 publication of her early, flawed manuscript Go Set a Watchman because of age and health, although she had welcomed its release at the time. Mockingbird Songs promises both personal memories and clarifying details about Lee’s life and choices.

Jamie Tull, a 33-year-old former elementary school teacher from Modesto, Calif., was found alive after nearly three weeks missing following a July 17 crash near Le Grand in Merced County.
