Family and friends, joined by searchers, located her on Aug. 4 about half a mile to a mile from the vehicle’s ditch crash site in desolate grazing land on the outskirts of Planada. Emaciated, badly sunburned and weak, she was lying in tall grass near a cattle water trough; her phone was discovered nearby. Rescuers said she was able to speak and initially asked only for food and water, and reportedly insisted she did not want to be found. Authorities said she had essentially sheltered beside a water tank that provided shade and survived a scorching heatwave by drinking from the dirty trough and eating insects — reportedly two grasshoppers and a fly. Sheriff Vern Warnke said Tull had been struggling with emotional issues and had stopped taking prescription medication months earlier. Her father says she has bipolar disorder and had not taken medication for about six months after influences from a pastor and his wife. When found, she told searchers she was trying to get to Yosemite, though Le Grand is over 60 miles from the park. Airlifted by helicopter to a Fresno hospital for treatment, she was to be returned to relatives for further care. Search organizers noted that if she had not been located that day, volunteer efforts would have been scaled back. Attempts to reach her husband and mother for comment were not successful.

A veteran collapsed in the cafeteria at the Raymond G. Murphy VA Medical Center in Albuquerque and died after a prolonged delay getting to the hospital’s emergency room, about 500 yards away. Hospital officials said staff followed a local policy requiring 911 be called for emergencies occurring outside the main hospital; an ambulance was dispatched roughly 11 minutes after the collapse and arrived at the cafeteria several minutes later, with estimates that 14 to 30 minutes elapsed from collapse to ER arrival. Kirtland Air Force Medical Group personnel performed CPR until emergency responders arrived. VA spokeswoman Sonja Brown said the local policy is under expedited review; it dates to 2010 and limits the internal Code Blue response area, directing staff to call Albuquerque EMS for incidents elsewhere on the campus. Family members and visiting veterans criticized the delay, saying the man could have been moved more quickly within the complex. Questions remain about the presence of an AED and whether VA vehicles or onsite medical staff could have transported him. The death adds to broader scrutiny of the Department of Veterans Affairs amid reports of systemic failures, long appointment delays and a recent scathing review calling for fundamental restructuring.

Fernando Benitez, a Tijuana-based attorney, is representing 18-year-old Ethan Couch in Mexico as Mexican judges consider his detention and possible deportation. Couch, who gained notoriety after his "affluenza" defense following a 2013 drunk-driving crash that killed four people, was detained with his mother, Tonya, in Puerto Vallarta after authorities traced a pizza delivery. Tonya Couch was deported to the U.S. and faces a Texas charge of hindering apprehension; she is held on $1 million bond. Ethan, who was 16 at the time of the crash and was sentenced to 10 years’ probation after pleading guilty to multiple counts of intoxication manslaughter and assault, missed a probation meeting in December and fled to Mexico, according to Tarrant County officials.

Benitez argues the matter is an international law case focused on protecting Couch’s constitutional rights under Mexican law and ensuring due process; he says there is no formal U.S. extradition request and opposes a rushed deportation that could violate Mexican constitutional standards. He denies reports Couch had a gun when detained. A Mexican judge granted a temporary injunction delaying deportation; an evidentiary hearing may be weeks away and a ruling could take up to 90 days, with potential appeals thereafter. Legal analysts say asylum is unlikely, and Texas prosecutors intend to seek transfer of Couch’s case to adult court, where harsher penalties could follow if his probation is violated. A probation-violation hearing is set for Jan. 19.

The Daily Caller launched a weekly gun giveaway through Election Day 2012, offering an FMK9C1 9mm engraved with the Bill of Rights to new email subscribers on its NRA-backed "Guns and Gear" page. The firearm’s manufacturer, FMK founder Jim Pontillo, has published extreme right-wing commentary attacking progressives, praising secessionists, and framing liberalism as antithetical to American values. The promotion requires winners to be 21+, US residents where transfers are legal, pass NICS background checks, and handle FFL transfer procedures and fees. Rules limit liability and specify Delaware law for disputes.

Clarissa Dickson Wright, best known as one half of the BBC’s cult cookery duo Two Fat Ladies, has died in Edinburgh at 66. A formidable and outspoken personality, she combined deep knowledge of food history with unabashed eccentricity, a sharp intellect, and a taste for traditional, high-fat British cooking that often flouted contemporary health trends. Discovered while running a culinary bookshop, she was paired with Jennifer Paterson in 1996; the pair toured Britain by motorcycle and sidecar, celebrating roast meats, lard and other rich ingredients with brash humour and unapologetic relish. The show made her a television star and led to books and further series after Paterson’s death in 1999. 

Born in 1947 into a privileged but troubled family, Dickson Wright trained as a barrister at 21 but succumbed to alcoholism, later quitting law. She recovered at 40, reinventing herself as a cook, caterer, bookseller and writer. Her life included spells as a private cook, running Books for Cooks, serving hundreds at a luncheon club, and becoming one of England’s few female guild butchers. She published a respected history of English food in 2011 and a memoir, Spilling the Beans.

A fierce countryside campaigner, she supported hunting rights, was convicted in 2009 for attending hare coursing, and controversially suggested using meat from culled badgers. Loved by many for wit and learning, she could also be confrontational and politically non‑PC. She lived in Edinburgh, never married, and is survived by two sisters. Her agents and peers remember her fun, laughter, and uncompromising intelligence.

Health authorities are investigating and tracing contacts after a woman with extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR‑TB) traveled to the United States from India in April through Chicago O’Hare and then spent time in Missouri and Tennessee before seeking care seven weeks later. She was initially isolated at a Chicago‑area hospital and has since been transferred to the National Institutes of Health Clinical Center in Bethesda, where she is housed in a specialized isolation room and receiving care under an existing NIAID protocol for treating TB, including XDR cases. Her condition is reported stable, but XDR‑TB requires prolonged, complex treatment and carries far lower cure rates than ordinary TB.

XDR‑TB resists isoniazid and rifampin plus any fluoroquinolone and at least one injectable second‑line drug, leaving few effective therapies; globally outcomes are often poor and only about 30–50% of cases can be cured depending on resistance extent, disease severity and patient immunity. Treatment is considerably more expensive—averaging far above typical TB care—and may take months to years, sometimes requiring surgery. CDC and NIH laboratories are conducting drug‑susceptibility testing to guide therapy.

Because TB bacteria spread via airborne particles when an infected person coughs, sings or sneezes, public health officials are conducting contact investigations, including obtaining the airplane manifest to notify passengers who may have had prolonged close exposure. While the overall risk to the general public and air travelers is considered low, officials emphasize caution given the severity of XDR‑TB. People with weakened immunity, such as those with HIV, face higher risk of progression to active disease. CDC and WHO recommend rapid diagnosis, strict treatment adherence, robust infection control in high‑risk settings, and strengthened TB programs worldwide to prevent emergence and spread of drug‑resistant TB.

A Los Angeles Times investigation revealed that nearly 10,000 U.S. soldiers — many in the California National Guard — have been ordered to repay signing bonuses and student loan repayments that were granted during the height of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. The Pentagon and National Guard Bureau say federal law requires reclaiming overpayments identified after audits, even when the payments were made a decade earlier amid fast-paced enlistment and retention efforts. Critics say the military’s aggressive clawbacks punish service members for mistakes and fraud committed by others higher in the chain of command.

The incentives, part of expanded retention programs between 2000 and 2008, ballooned defense spending on selective reenlistment bonuses from $891 million to $1.4 billion. Auditors later determined that rules limiting large payments to certain specialties were often ignored. California is a focal point because of its large guard force and a 2010 scandal in which the guard’s incentive program misused as much as $100 million; a former program leader was jailed for false claims. After 42 auditors reviewed California cases, many veterans received repayment notices and, in some cases, tax liens and wage garnishments.

Affected veterans report severe financial and emotional strain. Some, like former Army Capt. Christopher Van Meter, refinanced mortgages to repay tens of thousands; others, such as former Master Sgt. Susan Haley, now make monthly payments on large sums. Many insist they fulfilled their contractual obligations and are appealing; some have launched petitions calling on Congress or the Army to waive debts. California Guard leaders say they lack authority to cancel debts but have helped some soldiers retain $37 million of original payments and are assisting appeals. They urge congressional relief, while also asserting they must follow the law. The situation has ignited anger among veterans and the public, who argue institutional failures — not individual soldiers — should bear responsibility.

An Alaska Airlines Boeing 737 bound for Seattle from JFK made an unscheduled landing at Minneapolis–St. Paul Airport Monday morning after a passenger tried to open a rear cabin door in mid-flight. Alaska spokeswoman Halley Knigge and crew members emphasized that it is physically impossible to open an aircraft door while the cabin is pressurized, and the attempted action prompted crew intervention. Flight 7 had originated at JFK at 7:15 a.m. Eastern and took off toward Seattle at 11:08 a.m. Central with 180 passengers aboard; it landed in Minneapolis about 9:45 a.m. Central and subsequently arrived at Sea-Tac just before 1 p.m. Pacific.

Passengers described the man as acting oddly from boarding through the flight. One seatmate, Shoshana Godwin, said he repeatedly reached into his bag, took a pill, appeared drowsy, and later spoke incoherently and asked to cancel his trip. Flight attendants and air marshals quickly surrounded him; crew radioed that they were “dropping off one of our passengers early” and told passengers the diversion was a medical emergency. Minneapolis-St. Paul police arrested the man after landing, determined he posed a danger to himself, and he was taken to Fairview Southdale Hospital in Edina. Passengers praised the calm, effective response of the cabin crew. It remained unclear whether the man would face criminal charges.

Chicago has won the competition to host filmmaker George Lucas’s new Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, beating Los Angeles and San Francisco. Announced after Mayor Rahm Emanuel’s aggressive bid, the decision follows the Presidio board’s rejection of Lucas’s preferred San Francisco site. The museum will be built on a 17-acre lakefront site on parking lots between Soldier Field and McCormick Place, opening in 2018, and will reportedly cost $1 billion. Lucas — who praised Chicago while affirming personal ties to the Bay Area — and his team cited the larger site, transit access, and proximity to the Museum Campus as deciding factors. The self-funded museum will house Lucas’s extensive collection of artwork, magazine illustrations, movie posters, special effects artifacts from Industrial Light & Magic, Norman Rockwell paintings and memorabilia like the Darth Vader costume, all organized around the theme of storytelling. Lucas intends to place parking underground and create green space; the project would lease Park District land for $1 and cover construction and a planned $400 million endowment without taxpayer operating subsidies. Supporters tout jobs, tourism and educational partnerships with city schools; opponents, including Friends of the Parks, vow legal challenges citing lakefront protection policies. Architectural renderings will be presented to city officials in the fall, and the museum board may formalize a name change.

Nathaniel Marston, best known for his role as Michael McBain on One Life to Live (2001–07), died on November 11, 2015, after suffering catastrophic injuries in a car crash. His mother, Elizabeth Jackson, announced that Nathaniel “put up the good fight” but his injuries failed to respond to treatment; he passed peacefully in Reno, Nevada, at 3:15 p.m., surrounded by family and close friends. Doctors had indicated that, had he survived, he would likely have required a ventilator and faced life as a quadriplegic—an outcome his family believed he would not have wanted. Jackson expressed gratitude for the outpouring of support during the traumatic two weeks following the October 30 single-vehicle accident on SR447. According to the Nevada Highway Patrol, Marston’s 1985 Ford F-150 drifted, overturned multiple times, and he was ejected; he was reportedly not wearing a seatbelt. Initial reports described a broken and fractured neck, broken shoulder and ribs, and a collapsed lung; doctors warned he might be paralyzed and ventilator-dependent. Family planned memorial services in New York City, Kauai, and Gerlach, NV, with details to be posted later.

Saturday Night Live’s recent episode delivered a mixed bag: a slow start overall, but standout sketches and a controversial monologue made the night memorable. Aidy Bryant’s portrayal of Sarah Huckabee Sanders was the episode’s highlight — her shift from a formal setting into a high-energy musical number performing Demi Lovato’s “Confident” won big laughs. Bryant’s impression evolved from a southern-accented joke to a fuller embodiment of Sanders’ blithe obliviousness, and the sketch smartly pushed beyond tired Trump caricatures by embracing a surreal, nightmare-logic approach similar to SNL’s strongest political bits like “Through Donald Trump’s Eyes” and “Kellywise.” Meanwhile, Larry David’s opening monologue divided viewers. The Curb Your Enthusiasm star attempted darkly self-deprecating jokes about flirting under extreme historical circumstances, including imagined pickup lines in a concentration camp. Many viewers found the material cringeworthy and offensive, though some defended David’s right as a Jewish comedian to tackle such topics. The episode also featured Alec Baldwin’s return as Donald Trump in a bizarre sketch where Trump showers with Paul Manafort (Alex Moffat) to ensure he isn’t wearing a wire, joined by Kate McKinnon’s Jeff Sessions and Beck Bennett’s Mike Pence. The sketch culminated in absurd plans to pardon or accidentally eat Manafort, blending political satire with grotesque humor.

Transformers: Age of Extinction (2014), directed by Michael Bay and starring Mark Wahlberg, Kelsey Grammer, Stanley Tucci, Nicola Peltz and voices including Peter Cullen and John Goodman, is a 165-minute, PG-13 continuation of the blockbuster franchise. Set five years after Dark of the Moon, humans have nearly eradicated Transformers under a CIA-led purge spearheaded by Harold Attinger (Grammer), who collaborates with the bounty-hunting Decepticon Lockdown to track down Optimus Prime. Billionaire inventor Joshua Joyce (Tucci) unveils Galvatron, a Megatron-like creation, while four surviving Autobots—Bumblebee, Hound, Crosshairs and Drift—team with Texas mechanic Cade Yeager (Wahlberg), his daughter Tessa (Peltz) and her boyfriend Shane to find and revive Optimus and evade capture.

Critics characterize the film as a long, loud, soulless spectacle: nearly three hours of relentless CGI, explosions and destruction—most memorably in Chicago and Hong Kong—drowning out whatever plot exists. Bay’s visual effects are praised for technical prowess and occasional breathtaking tableaux, but the story and characters are widely derided as bland, repetitive and underwritten. Wahlberg is considered an improvement over the franchise’s earlier human lead but largely inert; Tucci provides moments of comic relief and one memorable line, while Peltz’s performance as Tessa draws ire for being grating and poorly conceived. Reviewers conclude the film is cynical blockbuster moviemaking—visually impressive yet creatively bankrupt—an exhausting experience that nevertheless will likely guarantee another sequel due to box-office returns.

President Donald Trump and U.S. lawmakers signaled that new measures are needed to curb North Korea’s accelerating nuclear program even after a unanimous 15-0 U.N. Security Council vote imposing additional sanctions. Trump downplayed the resolution as “just another very small step,” saying tougher actions “ultimately will have to happen.” State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert called the resolution the strongest yet and said the international community is not “at the ceiling” of options. North Korea condemned the sanctions as a “heinous provocation,” threatening severe retaliation.

On Capitol Hill, bipartisan frustration focused on China’s perceived inaction; lawmakers and Treasury and State officials urged tougher pressure on Chinese banks and firms that enable Pyongyang’s illicit revenue flows. Treasury official Marshall Billingslea accused China and Russia of allowing DPRK evasion through banks, front companies and ship transfers—ships with lights off moving coal through Russia to disguise origins. Administration officials said they are pushing China to do more while exploring additional tools, including targeted economic sanctions and maritime enforcement, though cutting trade with China would carry serious consequences. Officials stressed readiness to use military force if necessary while pursuing diplomatic isolation to bring North Korea to talks.

Meanwhile, South Korea announced formation of a “decapitation” special forces brigade—dubbed Spartan 3000—to target North Korean leadership if needed. Seoul is accelerating defense measures, including missile upgrades, THAAD deployments, and contingency war plans (Kill Chain; Korea Air and Missile Defense; Korea Massive Punishment and Retaliation). The moves reflect mounting regional anxiety as Pyongyang increases missile tests and recently conducted its most powerful nuclear detonation.

President Trump ousted Chief of Staff Reince Priebus after 189 turbulent days, replacing him with Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly. Priebus said he had privately offered his resignation Thursday and framed Trump’s move as a “reset,” while aides disputed timing and motives. Trump announced Kelly’s appointment via Twitter after returning to Joint Base Andrews; Kelly will start Monday. The change follows months of criticism of Priebus for failing to control leaks, manage White House chaos, and help pass key legislation like the Obamacare repeal effort. Infighting intensified this week after new communications director Anthony Scaramucci’s vulgar attack on Priebus. Priebus, a former RNC chair brought in for his Washington ties, lacked support from Trump’s inner circle, including Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner.

Trenton Lewis, a 21-year-old UPS loader in Little Rock, has been walking roughly five to 5.5 miles each way for months so he could make his 4 a.m. shifts. A new father, Lewis said providing for his daughter gave him the motivation to endure pre-dawn treks through rain, cold and rough parts of town without missing a single shift or being late. He described walking for two-and-a-half to three hours with music in his head and a focus on working to improve his life after having been unemployed when his daughter was born. Coworkers Patricia and Kenneth Bryant learned of his daily struggle and organized a quiet effort among UPS staff to help. They collected donations from colleagues—about $1,900 to $2,000—and purchased a reliable used Saturn, overcoming a few false starts with earlier cars that fell through. The Bryants even fixed a cosmetic nick to make the surprise special. They staged a fake union meeting in the parking lot and presented Lewis with the keys; he was stunned, initially thinking the keys weren’t for him. Now, with his first car, Lewis leaves home around 3:30 a.m., gets more rest and no longer has to walk miles each day. The gesture strengthened workplace bonds and highlighted both Lewis’s dedication as a father and the willingness of his coworkers to come together to support someone committed to doing whatever it takes to succeed.

A powerful blizzard threatened the U.S. Northeast, with forecasts warning of up to 2–3 feet of snow from Boston down through parts of New York and New Jersey beginning Friday. Meteorologists said two storm systems would merge offshore, producing heavy snowfall, hurricane-force gusts in places (up to 70–75 mph), coastal flooding, and widespread power outages—especially worrying for areas still recovering from Superstorm Sandy. Cities and states mobilized: Boston, Providence, Hartford and others canceled schools; governors urged nonessential workers to stay home; Amtrak and numerous airlines suspended service, canceling thousands of flights; municipal crews readied plows, salt and sand; utilities staged extra crews. Forecasters compared the threat to the historic 1978 blizzard and said southern New England could see one of its top-ten snowstorms, possibly breaking Boston’s snowfall records. Residents flocked to supermarkets and gas stations for supplies, and hardware stores sold shovels and snow gear as panic-buying spread. Officials warned of near-zero visibility, dangerous travel, and the potential for prolonged outages that could leave people without heat. Emergency managers prepared debris removal, supply distribution and rescues, urging the public to avoid travel and take the storm seriously.

Former President George H.W. Bush’s casket was transported from Houston to Washington, where he lay in state in the U.S. Capitol Rotunda ahead of an invitation-only funeral Wednesday at the National Cathedral and burial in Texas. A military plane, renamed Special Air Mission 41, carried the flag-draped coffin after ceremonies and a 21-gun salute at Ellington Field. Family members including former President George W. Bush accompanied the remains; Secret Service agents and military personnel served as pallbearers. Lawmakers and leaders including Paul Ryan, Mitch McConnell and Mike Pence delivered eulogies in the Rotunda. President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump paid respects in the evening and plan to attend the funeral. Houston held a public tribute, urging attendees to wear Bush’s trademark colorful socks; his service dog Sully accompanied the casket on part of the journey. Bush died Friday at 94.

The Warren County community is grieving the sudden death of Evan Murray, a Warren Hills Regional High School senior and three-year starting quarterback who also starred in basketball and baseball. Murray was injured during a home varsity football game Friday night against Summit and died; school officials have not released specific details about the circumstances. By Saturday morning classmates, faculty and family gathered at the stadium to mourn, leaving flowers and cards — one marked with a Superman emblem — as students remembered him as a leader, dedicated athlete and a dependable, levelheaded young man. Coaches and peers described Murray’s character and work ethic, saying he inspired teammates and was “one of the greatest kids” in the community. Interim Superintendent Gary Bowen said grief counselors would be available to students, and coaches urged players to stay together as the school copes. The loss follows other recent tragedies affecting Warren Hills, deepening the community’s sorrow. Administrators and coaches emphasized support services and the need for unity as students and staff process the shock and grief.

Iran hosted the 16th Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) summit in late August 2012, using the gathering of about 120 developing-nation leaders to push back against Western attempts to isolate it over its disputed nuclear program and to showcase diplomatic outreach. Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei asserted Iran’s position—“nuclear energy for all and nuclear weapons for none”—insisting Tehran seeks peaceful nuclear energy while denouncing the U.N. Security Council and U.S. behavior. U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon attended, voiced “serious concerns” about Iran’s human rights record, urged greater cooperation with U.N. bodies and inspectors to demonstrate the peaceful nature of Iran’s program, and pressed Iran to influence Syria’s leadership to end violence. Ban also criticized threats to destroy states and attempts to deny historical facts such as the Holocaust, comments that were subject to altered translations on Iranian state TV.

The summit was quickly overshadowed by sharp divisions over Syria. Egyptian President Mohamed Mursi — the first Egyptian head of state to visit Iran since 1979 — called for NAM solidarity with Syrians seeking to overthrow Bashar al-Assad, prompting the Syrian delegation to walk out and reflecting deep regional fractures: Egypt’s new assertive foreign policy clashed with Iran’s steadfast support for Assad. Iran proposed a troika and a three-month reconciliation mechanism including Egypt, Iran and Venezuela plus Iraq and Lebanon; Assad reportedly welcomed it, but rebels and Western governments doubted Iran’s impartiality.

The event also highlighted wider concerns: resumed scrutiny of Iran’s nuclear efforts (including reports about scientist Mohsen Fakhrizadeh), stalled negotiations with world powers, and divergent international views on Iran’s role in regional conflicts. Tehran aimed to show it retained broad support among developing countries even as tensions with the West persisted.

CBS producer Robert “Joe” Halderman, accused of attempting to extort $2 million from David Letterman, faces his first Manhattan court hearing Tuesday. Indicted Oct. 2 on attempted grand larceny charges that carry up to 15 years, Halderman has raised about $100,000 for his defense and appears unlikely to accept a plea, with attorney Gerry Shargel and supporters signaling a readiness to try the case. Tuesday’s session will mainly set schedules and address evidentiary issues, though observers expect possible theatrics from the defense. Separately, Levi Johnston received a Fleshbot “Crossover Star Award” and hinted at an SNL appearance.

San Vitaliano, a town of about 6,000 north of Naples in Campania, has temporarily outlawed wood-burning stoves in pizzerias, bakeries and other businesses as a precaution against severe air pollution. The mayor, Antonio Falcone, issued the ordinance after the town recorded 114 days in 2015 with particulate (PM10) levels above safe limits—worse than Milan’s 86 exceedances—though environmental agency tests have not conclusively identified the cause. The measure, effective from December 17 and initially scheduled to run through March or until June 30 in some reports, bans burning solid biomass such as wood, woodchips, coal and charcoal unless establishments install filtration systems capable of removing at least 80% of PM10 particulates. The ban is to be enforced by police checks; violators face fines from €200 to €1,032.

Local pizzeria owners and residents protested, arguing the restriction unfairly singles out pizza-makers and artisanal bakers. Business owners say typical output—one cited owner makes about 34 pizzas a day—cannot account for the town’s chronic smog, and they note that Naples, with far more pizzerias, does not suffer the same pollution levels. Critics say the ordinance could force costly fuel changes or expensive filter installations and accuse authorities of failing to identify the real sources of pollution. Officials framed the move as a necessary precaution while winter pollution worsens and further analysis continues; the rule may be reintroduced in October if filters prove insufficient. The dispute highlights tensions between public health measures and small-business livelihoods in communities grappling with persistent air-quality problems.

South Korea’s main opposition staged an unprecedented nine-day filibuster to block a government-backed anti-terrorism bill, producing what appears to be the world’s longest combined filibuster: 192 hours and 25 minutes. Beginning Feb. 23 and ending the evening of March 2, 39 opposition lawmakers took turns speaking around the clock to delay a parliamentary vote, arguing the bill would grant the National Intelligence Service intrusive powers to collect private communications, travel and financial data and could be misused to monitor civilians and political opponents.

Minjoo Party floor leader Lee Jong-kul delivered the final, emotion-charged address, speaking for 12 hours and 31 minutes (751 minutes), breaking a domestic record set earlier in the week. Reported totals vary slightly, but roughly 38–49 MPs participated at different points, using tactics such as reading academic papers, news stories and long passages from George Orwell’s 1984—the most-cited book during the speeches—to underscore fears of state surveillance. More than 5,000 citizens visited the National Assembly to witness the marathon.

Despite the filibuster’s length and public spectacle—speakers wore trainers, avoided water to minimize breaks, and even prompted moments of criticism for delaying other legislation—the ruling Saenuri Party’s majority made passage likely. After the filibuster ended, lawmakers prepared to vote on the anti-terror bill, as well as bipartisan measures on electoral redistricting and a North Korean human rights bill. Supporters, including President Park Geun-hye, argued the law was needed for security; opponents warned it would erode privacy and civil liberties.

Capitol Hill buzzed about possible Republican theatrics during President Obama's State of the Union, recalling Rep. Joe Wilson’s “You lie” outburst last September. House Minority Whip Eric Cantor said he hoped for no interruptions, though he previously urged Republicans to be “attentive.” Wilson pledged to be a “gentleman” and instead planned a live Facebook response after the address, drawing a DCCC challenge and jokes about fundraising. Republicans criticized the president beforehand: Cantor said Obama should have “listened and learned,” Rep. Jeb Hensarling said he agreed with some rhetoric but not actions and dismissed the spending freeze as headline-focused, while Grover Norquist’s group mocked the speech with a satirical “Bingo” card.

Since launching her 2012 presidential bid, Michele Bachmann’s campaign has become notable not only for loud Elvis music and promises to make Barack Obama a one-term president, but increasingly for physical confrontations between her staff and reporters. In under two months the campaign was tied to at least five hostile encounters involving pushing, shoving and at least one allegation of a threatened injury. Incidents ranged from ABC’s Brian Ross and CNN’s Don Lemon being jostled by Bachmann aides (including her husband) to a Fox correspondent warning a bodyguard not to touch him and a Norwegian reporter alleging an aide threatened to break his arm — a charge the campaign denies. The campaign defends the conduct as necessary security for a popular, controversial candidate, noting a retired Secret Service agent among its staff who, they say, knows how to protect principals. Critics contrast Bachmann’s aggressive media management with other high-profile campaigns that have given reporters broader access, and note the conduct has been unusually intense for the open, access-driven Iowa campaign trail.

Captain Francesco Schettino returned to the wreck of the Costa Concordia off Giglio in February 2014 as part of his manslaughter and abandoning-ship trial. The 2012 disaster, when the cruise liner struck a reef and capsized, killed 32 people. Schettino, who denies abandoning ship and faces up to 20 years, toured the righted but stranded 290m vessel after a safety briefing and was escorted by court-appointed experts; the judge stressed he was there as a defendant. He has acknowledged some responsibility and sought forgiveness but says he steered the ship closer to shore to avoid greater loss. His lawyers claim Costa Crociere shifted blame onto him. Local reactions were mixed, salvage and dismantling bids continue, and five others were previously convicted after plea bargains.

Researchers at Oxford used diffusion-weighted and resting-state fMRI to map the human ventrolateral frontal cortex (vlFC), a region tied to high-level cognition and language, and compared it with scans from 25 macaques. They divided the human vlFC into 12 consistent subregions, each with a distinct “neural fingerprint” of connections to the rest of the brain. When the team compared these areas to macaque prefrontal organization, 11 of the 12 matched closely in location and connectivity. One area, however—the lateral frontal pole—appeared to be uniquely human. This small, ball‑shaped region, present bilaterally above and behind the eyebrows, is implicated in strategic planning, decision making, multitasking and in evaluating choices not taken—essentially gauging “how green the grass is on the other side.” The study also found stronger connections between auditory regions and the human vlFC than in macaques, a difference that may underlie human speech and language capacities. The findings, published in Neuron, highlight a mostly conserved prefrontal architecture with a few critical human specializations and may inform understanding of psychiatric disorders and the neural basis of uniquely human cognitive abilities.

Jillian Rose Jacobson, a 31-year-old photography teacher at El Dorado High School in Placentia, was found dead by students in her locked classroom on the morning of March 2. Students arriving for first period noticed the door locked — unusual for that hour — and after getting another teacher to unlock it, discovered Jacobson hanging from the ceiling. Colleagues removed her and set her on the floor; emergency responders performed CPR but she was in cardiac arrest and was declared dead at the scene. Police and fire officials said investigators suspect suicide; no note was found and there was no sign of foul play. The coroner estimated her time of death at about 7 a.m., with an autopsy pending.

Jacobson, who had taught photography at El Dorado for about a decade, was remembered by students and staff as upbeat, friendly and passionate about teaching, especially outdoor photography and working with film cameras. Many students and teachers were stunned and distraught; eyewitness accounts described running teachers, locked classrooms, and students gathered in the gym as staff broke the news. Several students who discovered her were immediately offered crisis counseling and grief counselors were made available to the broader school community. A candlelight vigil was planned that evening.

The campus has experienced other recent tragedies: a student was killed by a vehicle last year and a teacher died of a heart attack in 2009. School officials expected classes to resume the next day to help restore normalcy, while recognizing some students who found Jacobson might not return immediately. Local officials and colleagues expressed condolences and offered support to students and staff.

Twenty years after the Ms. Foundation launched Take Our Daughters to Work Day to demystify careers, that goal has largely been achieved; women now comprise half the workforce. The new challenge is cultivating women leaders. Jennifer Allyn argues we should evolve the tradition into “Take Our Daughters to the C‑Suite,” exposing girls to top executives, explaining daily leadership responsibilities, and sustaining support year-round. Girls report wanting role models but rarely meet senior women; many lack confidence about leading. Princeton’s targeted encouragement of female students resulted in more winners of top honors, illustrating how sponsorship—advocates who use influence to create opportunities—drives advancement better than mentorship alone. Formal corporate sponsorship programs and proactive efforts to identify and groom female talent can narrow leadership gaps. Bringing girls into the halls of power, not just offices, will help ensure they lead in the future.

At the G20 summit in St. Petersburg, President Obama sought international backing to strengthen his case to Congress for limited military strikes against Syria after an alleged Aug. 21 chemical-weapons attack that U.S. intelligence says killed more than 1,400 people. Despite two days of intense diplomacy, he left with only a cautious joint statement from 10 countries saying evidence points to the Assad government and calling for a strong response; it stopped short of endorsing military action or pledging participation. Russia, Syria’s chief ally, and other leaders declined to back strikes, and Putin said he would keep supplying Assad with weapons. Obama and Putin held a candid 20-minute discussion but remained unconvinced by each other. Back home, Obama prepared a White House address and an unprecedented lobbying effort to win congressional approval for “limited, not open-ended” strikes aimed at deterring further chemical attacks. Public and many lawmakers remained skeptical: polls showed majority opposition, Britain’s parliament rejected participation, and even some U.S. lawmakers urged nonmilitary measures. The administration argued limited force could strengthen diplomacy and uphold norms against chemical warfare, while acknowledging the political and moral risks if Americans are not persuaded.

Multiple sources tell PEOPLE that President Donald Trump and former vice-presidential nominee Sarah Palin were not invited to Senator John McCain’s memorial services following his death at 81 from brain cancer. Carla Eudy, a longtime McCain family friend and fundraiser involved in planning, confirmed invitations were not extended to the two figures. Sources say Eudy removed several longtime McCain staffers from the guest list in recent days as well. While those close to the family would not specify who ordered the exclusions, Capitol Hill speculation points to the family—likely Cindy McCain—wishing to protect John’s memory during a difficult time. Insiders emphasize Trump and Palin were not given formal legal bans; rather, stay-away messages were relayed through intermediaries and were received. Trump’s public, acrimonious history with McCain during the 2008 primary makes his exclusion unsurprising to some, while others lament Palin’s exclusion given her past friendship with McCain. Palin had publicly mourned McCain, calling him “an American original” and recalling their friendship despite past reports that McCain had later expressed regret over selecting her. Separately, attention in Washington has already turned to McCain’s Senate replacement. Rumors that Cindy McCain might be a candidate reportedly originated with her, sources say, and officials expect a decision soon. The Arizona governor is scheduled to meet in Washington, and insiders predict an announcement as early as next week, making the replacement a fast-moving and highly scrutinized topic among lawmakers.

After teasing fans with cryptic videos and a social-media purge, Taylor Swift announced her sixth studio album, Reputation, due Nov. 10, and revealed its cover and that a lead single would drop the following night. The black-and-white cover shows Swift in wet hair, dark lipstick and a chain choker against a backdrop of repeated “Taylor Swift” newspaper headlines; the release follows a series of three snake-themed videos, reclaiming an animal long used by critics against her. The rollout reignited past drama with pop producer Harris — who briefly blamed Swift for a post-breakup song and launched a Twitter rant invoking Katy Perry; supporters spammed Swift’s Instagram with snake emojis. Harris has since expressed regret for his tweets.

Gambian President Yahya Jammeh announced that all inmates on death row will be executed by mid-September, breaking a roughly three-decade de facto moratorium. Speaking on state television during Eid-al-Fitr, Jammeh vowed to enforce capital punishment for serious crimes—citing murder, treason, drug offenses, terrorism, banditry and homosexuality—and said security forces and the judiciary would be empowered to carry out sentences. Reports vary on how many are affected: human rights groups noted about 44 by year-end, AFP tallied up to 47, while local judicial sources suggested higher numbers. International rights organizations and governments—including Amnesty International, Reprieve and France—condemned the move, warning that Gambian trials often fail to meet fair-trial standards and that death sentences have been used against political opponents. Jammeh, who seized power in a 1994 coup and has dominated politics since, previously threatened to resume executions in 2009 but did not act; critics say the announcement risks a major human rights setback.

At Paris Fashion Week Karl Lagerfeld transformed Chanel’s Grand Palais into a full-scale spoof supermarket for his Fall/Winter 2014-15 ready-to-wear show, mixing high spectacle with everyday life. Shelves were stocked with over 100,000 Chanel-branded items—Tweed cola, Chateau Gabrielle wine, “Chanel crémeuh” milk—complete with trolleys, yellow discount signs and supermarket announcements. Models pushed brightly colored carts and carried metallic Chanel baskets while walking to pop music through aisles arranged like a Carrefour. The collection itself fused youthful energy and classic Chanel codes: oversized tweed jackets, rounded shoulders, cinched or exposed midriffs, shiny slim pants, jogging suits, fluorescent leggings and standout single pieces such as a fluid black coat. Lagerfeld defended the concept as “pop art of today,” saying luxury should be worn like you’re going to the supermarket. Celebrities including Keira Knightley and Rihanna watched from the front row, but the exuberant set ended chaotically when attendees began stripping the shelves—security searched bags afterward and some items were later given to charity. Other Paris shows included Iris van Herpen’s body-focused, provocative designs, Alexander McQueen’s gothic-inflected romantics, and Valentino’s 1960s-tinged, couture-infused looks.

Iran has released American hikers Shane Bauer and Joshua Fattal, jailed since their 2009 arrest with Sarah Shourd for allegedly crossing from Iraq into Iran. Their eight-year sentences were commuted to bail—reportedly $1 million, paid by Oman—and they were flown to Oman to reunite with family; Shourd had been freed on bail in 2010. Convicted of illegal entry and espionage amid disputed claims they crossed the border accidentally, their release followed international diplomacy and came just before President Ahmadinejad’s U.N. visit.

Over four months ending last October, a national survey asked Americans their impressions of each state. Overall, most states are viewed favorably; only five have net-negative ratings led by California (27% favorable, 44% unfavorable), Illinois, New Jersey, Mississippi, and Utah. Hawaii is the most liked (54% favorable, 10% unfavorable), followed by Colorado, Tennessee, South Dakota, Virginia, Montana, Alaska, Oregon, North Carolina, and Pennsylvania. Ten states have strong positive margins; one (Louisiana) breaks even. Opinions vary by demographics: women view several Northeastern states far more positively than men, while men favor many Plains and Southern states. Democrats most like Hawaii, Washington, and Massachusetts and dislike Texas, Alabama, and Mississippi; Republicans favor Alaska and Texas and strongly dislike California. Black voters dislike most Deep South states, favoring North Carolina and Virginia, with Alabama and Mississippi least liked. Texas ranks 38th, with distinct high familiarity and polarized views.

Thomas Balmès’s documentary Babies follows four infants—Ponijao (Namibia), Bayarjargal (Mongolia), Mari (Tokyo) and Hattie (San Francisco)—through roughly their first year, using observational footage without narration, subtitles, or overt commentary. Shot over 400 days, the film emphasizes visual storytelling, lush photography and Bruno Coulais’ score to highlight both universal milestones (cooing, crawling, discovering feet) and striking cultural contrasts: Ponijao’s communal, rustic Himba upbringing, Bayar’s freedom among cattle, Mari’s toy-filled urban life, and Hattie’s pampered American routine. Critics praise its immediacy, charm and moments of cross-cultural insight but note its limitation: with no narrative or hardship, the 79-minute runtime can feel repetitive—essentially “life with the dull bits intact”—making the movie delightful but slight as a study of parenting.

Two Gwinnett County, Georgia, police officers were fired after videos surfaced showing them using excessive force during a traffic stop and arrest of 21-year-old Demetrius Bryan Hollins. The incident occurred about 4 p.m. on a Wednesday in Lawrenceville. One video shows Sgt. Michael Bongiovanni punching Hollins in the face as Hollins stepped from his vehicle with his hands raised. A second video, filmed from a different angle, shows Master Police Officer Robert McDonald running up to a handcuffed Hollins lying face-down in a lane and appearing to stomp on his head. Hollins’s booking photo shows blood on his nose and lip. Hollins told NBC News he had been trying to open his phone to record when officers shoved him, and that he was attacked despite having his hands up and later while handcuffed. He faces multiple charges including traffic offenses, obstruction and possession of less than an ounce of marijuana, and was released on bond. Gwinnett police say they launched immediate internal and criminal investigations; findings will be shared with the county district attorney for potential prosecution. Chief Butch Ayers called the actions “uncalled for,” said one officer “got tunnel vision,” and emphasized the department’s commitment to standards and swift action. The department plans to outfit uniformed officers with body cameras by year’s end. The videos went viral and drew condemnation from community activists including Black Lives Matter of Greater Atlanta, whose leaders demanded criminal charges and termination. The firings and released personnel files followed discovery of the footage that contradicted officers’ initial reports.

The document outlines two main topics. First, it describes the “open edge cloud,” a software layer that leverages standard compute and storage resources massively distributed in service providers’ last‑mile networks. By exposing Open APIs for rapid resource allocation, the edge cloud enables high‑performance content and application delivery tailored to next‑generation demands. This architecture promises service providers more control, flexibility and differentiation through new services that exploit unique last‑mile reach and scale.

Second, it reports that Google’s YouTube reached a preliminary all‑cash deal to acquire videogame‑streaming company Twitch for over $1 billion, a move expected to be announced imminently. The acquisition would be YouTube’s largest since Google bought it in 2006. Twitch, founded in 2011 by Justin Kan and Emmett Shear, has some 45 million monthly users, a paid subscription model, and partnerships with gaming outlets. YouTube anticipates regulatory scrutiny from U.S. authorities over potential anticompetitive concerns. Twitch has raised about $35 million, employs roughly 130 people, and plays a leading role in game streaming and e‑sports, accounting for a notable share of broadband downstream traffic.

Calcific myonecrosis is a rare, slowly enlarging, often painless mass that develops when muscle necrosis follows severe trauma or ischemia, frequently after compartment syndrome and sometimes decades later. It typically affects the anterior or lateral leg compartments and appears on X-ray as a fusiform cavity with peripheral, plaque-like calcification and central liquefaction; MRI shows central fluid signal with peripheral low signal calcification. Biopsy risks infection, so asymptomatic cases are observed; symptomatic lesions require complete excision with flap coverage or careful closure and prolonged drainage, plus extended antibiotics. A reported Thai woman developed a large calcified leg mass more than 50 years after a Malayan pit viper bite that likely caused untreated compartment syndrome; surgical removal healed her wound.

United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon visited Pope Francis at the Vatican in May 2014 with senior UN agency leaders to discuss poverty; in a private exchange the pope emphasized how environmental degradation falls most heavily on the poor. That theme culminated in Francis’s first major environmental encyclical, Laudato Si’, released in June 2015 and aimed at a global audience far beyond Catholic faithful. The pope frames ecological destruction and climate change as moral and ethical crises tied to inequality and an economic system driven by profit and consumption. He warns that humanity’s “tyrannical” exploitation of nature risks catastrophic consequences and calls for an ethical and economic revolution—a change of heart—as well as stewardship of creation to protect the vulnerable.

Scientists welcomed the encyclical as potentially more influential than diplomatic negotiations because it speaks to values and reaches over a billion Catholics; many hope it will galvanize public will ahead of the crucial UN climate talks in Paris. The Vatican intentionally broadened the launch: a cardinal, an Orthodox theologian and an atheist climate scientist unveiled the document to emphasize its universal intent. The pope, who trained as a chemist, has declared that science largely affirms human-driven climate change. His stance has provoked pushback from conservative politicians and some religious critics, but it resonated strongly in the developing world and among climate researchers who see moral leadership as essential to overcome ideological resistance and stimulate policy action.

At the Toronto International Film Festival, Madonna premiered her second film W.E. and faced mixed critical reaction and a minor controversy. The Globe and Mail reported that backstage volunteers said Madonna instructed them to turn their backs to her as she moved through the venue; her camp immediately issued a press release denying the claim, saying neither she nor her security ever gave such instructions, praising volunteers publicly from the stage, and calling the allegation inexplicable. At a press conference, Madonna emphasized she welcomes criticism of her filmmaking when it concerns the work and not her personally, noting she had to earn her reputation as a musician and expects to do the same as a director. W.E., which juxtaposes the 1930s romance of King Edward VIII and Wallis Simpson with a contemporary storyline, premiered in Venice and drew split reviews—praised for visuals but criticized for focus and performances. Madonna described Edward VIII as “very punk rock” and defended creative choices like using the Sex Pistols on the soundtrack. Composer Abel Korzeniowski recounted artistic exchanges with Madonna. With a roughly $15 million budget, W.E. opens widely in the U.S. in December amid Madonna’s modest Oscar hopes.

Evie, also known as Turdi, is a 66-year-old Indonesian who was born male but identifies as a woman and who once cared for a young Barack Obama while he lived in Jakarta. She remembers meeting Ann Dunham in 1969 after working in high-ranking households; Dunham hired her for cooking and childcare, and Evie became the boy’s nanny for roughly two years. Neighbors confirm her presence in the Menteng neighborhood and recall her kindness and patience with the child. Evie says she never showed Obama her feminine dress in front of him, though he sometimes laughed when she tried on his mother’s lipstick.

Evie’s life chronicles the precarious position of transgender Indonesians. After childhood abuse and repeated harassment—soldiers shaving her hair and burning her—Evie turned away from public expression of gender after finding a transgender friend’s brutalized body in a canal in the 1980s. She then lived as a man to survive, later resorting to sex work when other jobs were unavailable. Today she ekes out a living in a tiny Jakarta slum washing laundry, prays at the mosque, and lives with fear and little hope.

Indonesia’s stance toward transgender people is conflicted: visible in pageants, salons and some entertainment yet stigmatized culturally and religiously. The Indonesian Ulema Council says transgender people must live by their birth gender; hard-line attacks and routine ridicule persist. Many trans people face violence, discrimination, joblessness, and health risks; rights groups document frequent abuses and murders. Some activists are pushing back, seeking leadership roles and visibility. Evie hopes Obama’s historic election and the appointment of an openly transgender U.S. official might inspire change, taking personal pride in having once been the nanny of the U.S. president.

Texas education officials recently revised parts of the state’s social studies curriculum, prompting debate over which historical figures and themes should be taught to millions of students. A work group of teachers evaluated hundreds of figures and suggested simplifications; members said they aimed for objective decisions and tried to avoid political controversy. Their recommendations included dropping some names from grade-level lists — for example, removing Helen Keller from a third-grade lesson on “characteristics of good citizenship,” with the group noting that Keller “does not best represent the concept of citizenship” and suggesting military personnel and first responders as better examples. Bill Clinton was also recommended for removal from a grade-level listing (though students are still required to learn about his impeachment), but no explanatory note accompanied that suggestion. Two teachers involved stressed they were not part of the subgroup that made the Keller and Clinton decisions.

The State Board of Education, composed of elected members and long a flashpoint for cultural skirmishes, considered the work group’s proposals amid broader controversies over teaching evolution, math standards, and ethnic studies. Some of the group’s recommendations — notably removal of references to the nation’s “Judeo-Christian” heritage — were rejected by the board after pushback from conservative activists. Texas Values, a Christian advocacy group, praised the board for restoring references to Christian heritage and protecting symbols such as the Alamo. Democratic lawmakers were critical; House Democratic Caucus Chair Chris Turner urged the reinstatement of Keller and Clinton, arguing Keller’s historical significance remains and noting Hillary Clinton’s place in history as a major-party female presidential nominee.

Among approved changes, the board replaced San Jacinto Day with Constitution Day in a section on community and national customs and removed Helen Keller from the citizenship unit, while other adjustments reshuffled which figures are emphasized across third, fourth and eighth grade standards.

The Internet Archive’s crawls aim to preserve web pages as they are created and the pages they reference, so that when referenced pages change or disappear, a link to the version that existed when the referencing page was written remains available. By storing these snapshots, the Archive hopes site owners and authors will replace or supplement broken links with links to the archived versions, preserving the original context and intent of citations. This effort is part of a broader ambition — described as “No More 404” — to reduce broken links across the web. Since 1996, Alexa Internet has been contributing crawl data to the Internet Archive; this incoming data is added to the Wayback Machine following an embargo period. (Notice: you must log in to continue.) In other news, Westchester County, N.Y., authorities and local partners concluded a large-scale search in Panama after the body of 23-year-old Catherine Johannet of Scarsdale was found Sunday on a trail on Bastimento Island. Johannet, last seen around 10 a.m. Thursday on Isla Colón, had been staying in Bocas del Toro and was reportedly heading to Red Frog Beach with plans to return in the afternoon. Her friends, who had posted flyers locally, reported her missing after finding her belongings at the hostel where she stayed. The search involved volunteers along with the National Police, the National Civil Protection Agency, and the Bocas del Toro Fire Department. A cause of death has not yet been released, and Johannet’s family is reportedly en route to Panama. Check back for updates.

Sen. John Kerry’s daughter, Alexandra Kerry, 36, was arrested in Los Angeles early Thursday in a DUI investigation after being stopped for expired registration. She posted $5,000 bail and was released at 5:25 a.m. after a breathalyzer at the station registered below California’s .08 legal limit, according to Kerry’s spokeswoman. Kerry voiced support and declined further comment. Police say she failed a field sobriety test; prosecutors are unlikely to file charges. A Dec. 10 court date is scheduled.

During the LOTOJA bike race Saturday, Robert (Rob) Verhaaren, 42, of Mesa, Arizona, died after crashing on a bridge over the Snake River south of Jackson Hole, Wyoming. Race and sheriff’s officials say Verhaaren encountered a roadway hazard—believed to be a pothole—swerved, over-corrected, hit a guardrail and was catapulted about 30–40 feet into the river. Fellow racers rendered aid and he was taken to St. John’s Hospital, where he was later pronounced dead. The Teton County coroner noted a possible cervical fracture; deputies reported only minor external injuries. Verhaaren, who would have turned 43 next week, leaves his wife Bridget and three children, Ansel, Helena and Karl. He was a BYU accounting graduate (magna cum laude), held a J.D. from NYU School of Law and was Managing Director at Universal Equity Group Funds Arizona. Neighbors and friends remembered him as a devoted family man and scoutmaster. Race organizers reported additional serious crashes and many flat tires; this is the first fatality in LOTOJA’s 30-year history. LOTOJA is a roughly 206-mile, single-day race sanctioned by USA Cycling.

A series of three small earthquakes struck north of Phoenix near Black Canyon City on Sunday night, centered along the Agua Fria River a few miles north of the town. The sequence included a 3.2 foreshock around 8:59 p.m., then a 4.1-magnitude event at 11:29 p.m., and a 4.0 aftershock at 11:49 p.m. The largest temblor occurred about 6.5 km (4 miles) beneath the surface, which likely made it more noticeable even though magnitudes were modest. Residents across metro Phoenix—from Black Canyon City and Camp Verde to Queen Creek and Scottsdale—reported being startled but there were no injuries or significant damage. Scientists had not yet identified the specific fault; because the quake didn’t rupture the ground and was relatively small, locating the source is difficult. Officials expected aftershocks in the coming days.

Across many regions, older “fat” PlayStation 3 consoles began failing with error 8001050F, preventing PSN sign-ins, trophy access, dynamic themes, and even some offline single-player games. Affected systems sometimes reset to Jan 1, 2000, displayed copyright or trophy-install failures, rebooted, or looped on debug units, disrupting development work. Initially blamed on PSN changes, community reports and developer accounts pointed to a system-level fault; Sony later confirmed a clock-functionality bug causing the error and advised owners of non‑Slim models not to use their consoles to avoid data/trophy loss. Sony worked to fix the issue within 24 hours, provided status updates via PlayStation channels, and reported consoles were returning to normal about a day after the outage.

Professor David Shambaugh is a leading scholar of contemporary China and Asian international relations, with notable interests in the European Union and transatlantic affairs. Before his long tenure at George Washington University, he held positions including Reader in Chinese Politics at SOAS and Editor of The China Quarterly, and served as an analyst for the U.S. National Security Council and State Department in the late 1970s. Shambaugh’s career spans roles at major think tanks and institutions—nonresident Senior Fellow at Brookings, director of the Asia Program at the Wilson Center, board member of the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations—and memberships in elite bodies like the International Institute for Strategic Studies and the Council on Foreign Relations. He has received grants from foundations including Ford and Rockefeller, held fellowships and visiting appointments across China, Europe, and Asia, and authored more than 30 books and over 300 articles. He is also active in media commentary, editorial boards, and consulting for governments and corporations.

A separate, contemporaneous development in Chinese propaganda practice has drawn attention: state media have reportedly been instructed to stop using the affectionate nickname “Xi Dada” (Big Daddy or Uncle Xi) for President Xi Jinping. The moniker emerged after Xi’s rise to power in 2012 and became central to a campaign portraying him as an approachable, paternal leader through songs, videos, poems, and state-backed performances. Supporters and some grassroots artists produced a wide array of tributes—pop songs, poetry, and televised spectacles—while official outlets promoted images of a leader who was both supremely authoritative and personable.

However, the proliferation of “Xi Dada” has provoked unease at home and abroad, stirring fears of a Mao-style personality cult. Propaganda chiefs appear to have scaled back the nickname’s use in outlets such as Xinhua and the 21st Century Business Herald, reportedly via verbal directives. Analysts suggest the tactic overplayed Xi’s familiarity and risked making him seem either ridiculous or autocratic; authorities seem to prefer an image that is imposing and awe-inspiring rather than overly intimate. Observers caution that while the nickname’s suppression signals a recalibration of publicity tactics, it does not indicate substantive changes in Xi’s consolidation of power or political principles.

Sacha Baron Cohen was effectively barred from attending the 84th Academy Awards red carpet amid fears he would appear in full costume as the title character from his upcoming comedy The Dictator. Though invited as a cast member of Best Picture nominee Hugo, the Academy contacted his representatives demanding assurances he would not use the red carpet for a publicity stunt; without that promise, they said they would withhold his tickets. The move followed concerns that Cohen—known for disruptive in-character appearances as Borat and Bruno—would promote the film live during interviews. Deadline and other outlets reported the ban, prompting debate about the Academy’s strict decorum versus publicity-driven antics. Past unsanctioned stunts (Trey Parker and Matt Stone in gowns, Ben Stiller in Avatar makeup) and sanctioned stage gags show mixed precedent, but AMPAS officials stressed the red carpet is not for unpredictable stunts. Paramount and Cohen’s camp were engaging with the Academy as the situation unfolded.

Researchers have long thought that great apes—chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans—could infer others’ goals, intentions and desires but lacked the ability to attribute false beliefs to others, a cognitive milestone seen as central to human social cognition. A PLOS ONE study by David Buttelmann and colleagues challenges that view. Using an interactive helping task adapted from tests given to 18-month-old human infants, the team tested 34 apes at the Leipzig Zoo to see whether the animals would use another’s belief (true or false) to decide how to help.

In the experiment an experimenter (E) placed a novel object into one of two transparent-front boxes and then left. An assistant either moved the object to the other box while E was absent (false-belief condition) or moved it while E watched (true-belief condition). E then returned, tried unsuccessfully to open the original box (displaying effort and a helpless gesture), and pushed both boxes into the ape’s reach. The apes had previously been trained to unlock the boxes and retrieve rewards. Researchers recorded which box each ape first touched (the locking mechanism).

Results showed that in the false-belief condition apes chose the box containing the object significantly more often than chance and were more likely to help find the object when the human held a false belief. This pattern mirrors findings in human infants and indicates that great apes can attribute false beliefs and use that understanding in social interactions. The study was carefully controlled, included multiple training and test rounds, and achieved perfect inter-rater reliability. If replicated and extended, these findings suggest the qualitative gap between human and great ape social cognition may lie not in basic mindreading capacity but elsewhere, prompting further research into the evolutionary development of belief understanding.

Maverick County officials confirmed the death of 69-year-old Lucila Robles, who was killed when a truck hauling a flatbed trailer loaded with airbag cartridges exploded near Quemado, Texas, on Aug. 22. Forensic testing, including dental analysis by the Laredo medical examiner, identified Robles’ remains found in the smoldering rubble of her home; Justice of the Peace June Smith pronounced her dead on Aug. 24. Robles, who lived alone near U.S. Highway 277 and FM 1666, was apparently inside her home when the truck left the road, caught fire and detonated in front of the property, destroying the house. The truck had been traveling from Del Rio to a Takata plant in Eagle Pass. The driver, Mario Alberto Rodriguez, 20, and a passenger fled the vehicle before the blast and were injured, along with an older couple in a passing SUV; all four were hospitalized and later airlifted to San Antonio. The explosion damaged about ten nearby homes, scattered debris up to a mile away, cratered the roadway and led to intermittent closures of U.S. 277 for roughly 30 hours. Takata said the cargo included propellant and newly manufactured inflators and that safety procedures and regulations were followed; the truck was operated by an unnamed subcontractor. Federal and local investigators, including the Department of Transportation, are probing packaging, handling, placarding, routing, driver certification and compliance with hazardous-materials rules, noting ammonium nitrate propellant can explode on its own. Takata’s history includes a 2006 ammonium nitrate–related series of blasts at its Monclova plant.

Sony Pictures’ controversial comedy The Interview, about a fictional plot to kill North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, opened on Christmas Day in more than 300 independently owned U.S. theaters and via online platforms after an earlier cancellation prompted by hackers. Major chains initially pulled the film following threats from the Guardians of Peace and a destructive cyberattack on Sony blamed by U.S. officials on North Korea. Public backlash, including criticism from President Obama and others about self-censorship, pushed Sony to seek alternative distribution: Google Play, YouTube Movies, Microsoft’s Xbox Video, a Sony site, and select theaters. Early screenings drew sellouts and patriotic crowds who framed attendance as support for free expression; co-directors Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg made surprise appearances. Most showings were uneventful, though some online services and gaming networks reported connectivity issues, and pirated copies proliferated on foreign sites. Reviews called the film uneven and often not serious political commentary, but controversy turned it into an event and a symbol against intimidation. Sony declined to release immediate sales or box office figures; theaters reported strong demand and the release illustrated a novel, same-day digital-and-limited-theatrical strategy born of extraordinary circumstances.

In September 1977 a blonde, brown‑eyed toddler was found abandoned at the Amarillo Terminal Airport by security guard Vickey Vanderford. The child, estimated at 16–18 months, sat between sliding glass doors in an oversized T‑shirt clutching a bottle of soured juice and wearing a makeshift diaper. Treated at Northwest Texas Hospital for minor bruises, she entered custody of Potter‑Randall County Child Welfare as “Jane Doe 927.” The story drew public attention; she was described as alert and friendly, and more than 100 people applied to adopt her. Parental rights were terminated in January 1978 and she was adopted soon after.

Years later a possible match surfaced 1,000 miles away. Rosalee Webster of Long Beach returned home in 1981 after a mysterious absence during which her daughter Bonnie, born May 1976, did not return with her. Rosalee gave inconsistent accounts—claiming Bonnie had died, been taken by authorities, or abandoned at a bus terminal or airport while Rosalee battled substance abuse. Family members never filed a missing persons report; Rosalee died in 2008. In 1998 Rosalee’s sister petitioned online for help finding Bonnie. Genealogist Ronda Randall later connected that plea to the Globe‑News file about Jane Doe 927 and noted a striking resemblance between the newspaper photo and Rosalee’s daughter.

The woman who believes she might be Jane Doe 927 is Shelley Schooley, adopted as an infant by an Odessa family and raised with newspaper clippings of her abandonment. Now 41 and living in Newfoundland, Schooley has two sons and a stable family life; she prizes gratitude for having been adopted. After Randall discovered a video of Schooley recounting her origin story, Schooley and the Websters have spoken. Schooley says she would take DNA testing only if it would provide closure for the Websters, but currently cannot justify the expense. Thus the possible identification of Jane Doe 927 as Bonnie Lee Webster remains unresolved.

U.S. National Security Adviser Michael Flynn sharply warned Iran after Tehran test-fired a ballistic missile, saying the administration was “officially putting Iran on notice.” Flynn called the launch part of a pattern of “destabilizing” behavior — including support for Houthi rebels — and criticized the prior U.S. response as inadequate. He did not specify actions, and officials said options under deliberation range from financial measures and sanctions to potential military responses, though they stressed missile activity would be treated separately from the Iran nuclear deal. Iran insists the test was defensive and not in breach of U.N. Resolution 2231, which “calls upon” Tehran to refrain from work on missiles capable of carrying nuclear warheads; Tehran says it has no nuclear weapons program. The Security Council reviewed the test and Nikki Haley called it unacceptable. Regional tensions are high: multinational naval exercises are underway in the Persian Gulf, Iran has warned foreign ships to stay out of territorial waters, and critics warn that U.S. rhetoric risks escalation.

Chuck Pfarrer’s new book SEAL Target Geronimo revisits the raid that killed Osama bin Laden, disputing several widely repeated accounts. Pfarrer, a former SEAL Team Six commander, says the SEALs landed on the Abbottabad compound roof, entered within seconds, and bin Laden was shot almost immediately—three of four suppressed rounds struck him after he allegedly shoved his youngest wife toward the assaulters. There was no prolonged 45-minute gun battle; Pfarrer reports the whole operation lasted 38 minutes and only 12 rounds were fired. He alleges the White House overruled Navy plans for F-18 fighter cover and newer “ghost hawk” helicopters, forcing use of older craft, one of which crashed and was destroyed onsite. Pfarrer criticizes the CIA’s public portrayal while also downplaying its role in locating bin Laden, and suggests the president’s quick announcement of the kill may have foreclosed follow-up raids on al Qaeda leaders. U.S. officials have called portions of the book inaccurate; the manuscript faced government review and legal worries before publication.

Kuki Gallmann, the 73-year-old Italian-born conservationist and author of I Dreamed of Africa, was ambushed and shot in the stomach while surveying her Laikipia Nature Conservancy in central Kenya. She was with Kenya Wildlife Service rangers assessing arson damage after suspected cattle herders burned her Mukutan Retreat lodge the previous month. Airlifted to Nairobi after initial treatment, Gallmann underwent surgery and was reported in stable but seriously injured condition. Ownership of roughly 360 sq km, home to rare wildlife and community projects, has placed Gallmann at the center of intensifying conflict in drought-stricken Laikipia. Extended drought has driven nomadic herders—largely from Pokot and Samburu communities—onto private ranches seeking pasture, bringing thousands of cattle, escalating clashes with landowners, and prompting forceful police and military operations that sometimes killed livestock. Violence has included burned lodges, tens of thousands of cattle driven onto private land, and at least a dozen deaths; British rancher Tristan Voorspuy was killed while inspecting his property in March. Local farmers’ associations and some landowners blame politicians for inciting invasions ahead of national elections, a claim officials deny. Authorities have not confirmed who carried out the attack on Gallmann; suspicions fall on invading herders after repeated incursions. The situation reflects a volatile mix of environmental stress, alleged political manipulation, and rising insecurity across parts of Laikipia.

Tensions in Cairo exploded into some of the worst street violence since Egypt’s 2011 revolution as rival political camps fought outside the presidential palace. Islamist supporters of President Mohamed Morsi—mobilized by the Muslim Brotherhood’s Freedom and Justice Party and allied Salafis—moved to evict a sit‑in of anti‑Morsi protesters, tearing down tents and forcing pitched battles along boulevards in the upscale Heliopolis area. Rocks, sticks, firebombs and alleged gunshots were reported; medics gave injury figures ranging from about 125 to over 600 and officials later reported several dead. Police and, subsequently, army units and Republican Guard tanks were deployed to separate crowds and secure the palace. The clashes follow Morsi’s Nov. 22 decree expanding his powers and shielding an Islamist‑dominated constitutional assembly from judicial review; opponents say the rushed draft constitution curtails civil rights and favors Islamic law. Opposition leaders including Mohamed ElBaradei vowed no dialogue unless the decree is rescinded and the referendum postponed; Brotherhood figures urged mass defense of “legitimacy.” The crisis prompted resignations of several presidential advisers and spread unrest and attacks on Brotherhood offices across other cities, raising fears of deeper national polarization and further bloodshed.

A life-size foam sculpture of Donald Trump, titled "The Emperor Has No Balls," created by guerrilla art collective INDECLINE, will be auctioned by Julien’s Auctions in Los Angeles on Oct. 22 with an estimated price of $10,000–$20,000. The orange-tinted, exaggerated likeness—portraying Trump nude with a protruding belly and small fingers—first appeared without warning in five U.S. cities (New York, San Francisco, Seattle, Cleveland and Los Angeles) in August, drawing crowds and photos before officials in most locations confiscated or destroyed the pieces. Julien’s says the Los Angeles version, rescued by gallery owner Matt Kennedy of La Luz de Jesus, is the only surviving statue. Kennedy drew criticism for refusing police requests to obscure or remove the nude depiction. Julien’s plans to display the work Oct. 17–22 at its Westside gallery and calls it part of a street and contemporary art sale that includes pieces by Banksy, Keith Haring, Jean-Michel Basquiat, Andy Warhol and Shepard Fairey. A portion of the auction proceeds will benefit the National Immigration Forum, an immigrant advocacy organization, and the sale also features politically themed works by other artists.

University of California officials announced they will pay medical expenses for students pepper-sprayed during an Occupy Davis protest and dropped charges against 10 arrested. UC President Mark Yudof created an independent advisory panel led by former police chief Bill Bratton to investigate the incident. Chancellor Linda Katehi said campus police defied orders to act peacefully, placed officers on leave, and called for policy changes. The pepper-spray video sparked protests, calls for resignations, campus encampments and statewide review.

Twelve-year-old Shamera Harris died after a parked Ford Explorer rolled backward and dragged her into a tree on Schenley Manor Drive late Sunday. Her mother, Carla Harris, 52, said she had warned the vehicle’s driver, 53-year-old Richard Benton of Wilkinsburg and Shamera’s father, not to drink; she did not realize he had been drinking when he offered to drive. After picking up Shamera and a friend from the Waterworks Mall, Benton stopped so Shamera could step out while he took a photo and, according to Carla, fidgeted with the gearshift. The SUV “just took off at full speed,” killing Shamera, who died at the scene about 8:30 p.m. Carla Harris attempted CPR and tried to stop the vehicle but said her daughter was already gone. Police reported Benton smelled of alcohol, slurred his speech, appeared unsteady and refused field sobriety and breath tests; he was handcuffed, taken for medical treatment, charged with driving under the influence and released on nonmonetary bond with court conditions. The Allegheny County medical examiner ruled Shamera’s death an accidental blunt-force-trauma fatality; the investigation continues and collision investigators will inspect the vehicle. Shamera was described by family and school staff as a pleasant, rule-following honor-roll student who enjoyed swimming and socializing; the family mourns another young death after an earlier fatality in the family. Funeral arrangements were pending.
