One example of content being preserved involves a video of Helmetta, New Jersey Special Police Officer Richard Recine criticizing President Barack Obama and asserting officers need not follow the Constitution if the president does not. The video, recorded by residents campaigning for animal shelter reform, shows an exchange at a municipal building between Recine and resident Steve Wronko, who had been photographing inside the building and insisted he had a constitutional right to record in a public place. Recine, a retired Franklin cop collecting a $79,000 annual pension and working part time, repeatedly told Wronko that “Obama has decimated the friggin’ constitution, so I don’t give a damn,” prompting an internal affairs investigation after Police Director Robert Manney called the remarks “uncalled for and unprofessional” and “an embarrassment.” The Wronkos had been seeking accountability for an animal shelter that allegedly provided them a sick underage puppy and had previously been told to stop recording at the shelter. Manney said police may ask visitors to identify themselves in municipal buildings and that the investigation should be swift because video evidence exists.

Steven Spielberg’s Lincoln led early nominations for the EE British Academy Film Awards, earning ten nods including Best Film and acting nominations for Daniel Day-Lewis, Tommy Lee Jones and Sally Field. Tom Hooper’s Les Miserables and Ang Lee’s Life of Pi followed closely with nine nominations each, while Skyfall received eight. The BAFTA Best Film field also includes Argo, Zero Dark Thirty and the three leaders. Alongside Day-Lewis, Best Actor nominees include Ben Affleck (Argo), Bradley Cooper (Silver Linings Playbook), Hugh Jackman (Les Miserables) and Joaquin Phoenix (The Master). Best Actress nominees are Emmanuelle Riva (Amour), Helen Mirren (Hitchcock), Jennifer Lawrence (Silver Linings Playbook), Jessica Chastain (Zero Dark Thirty) and Marion Cotillard (Rust and Bone).

Separately, the Razzie nominations again targeted the Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 2 led with 11 nominations across every category, including Worst Picture and acting categories; Kristen Stewart received two Worst Actress nominations for Breaking Dawn Part 2 and Snow White and the Huntsman.

The Directors Guild of America announced its motion picture nominees, giving Ben Affleck his first DGA nomination for Argo. Competing directors are Kathryn Bigelow (Zero Dark Thirty), Tom Hooper, Ang Lee and Steven Spielberg. Notable omissions included Quentin Tarantino, David O. Russell, Paul Thomas Anderson and Wes Anderson. The 65th DGA Awards, hosted by Kelsey Grammer, will be held Feb. 2; the DGA winner is historically a strong indicator for the Academy Award for Best Director.

Airbus plans to test a prototype self-piloted “flying car” by year-end through its Urban Air Mobility division, CEO Tom Enders said in Munich. The program explores single-person vehicles and multi-rider, helicopter-style VTOLs bookable via an app, aiming to relieve urban gridlock and cut infrastructure costs. Airbus emphasizes experimentation, autonomous systems, AI and clean propulsion to avoid worsening city pollution, and warns that ignoring such tech risks losing business. Skeptics note the long, unrealized history of flying-car promises and caution that prototypes—like A3’s Project Vahana—face major hurdles: sense-and-avoid safety systems, regulation, airspace management, noise, cost, maintenance, and the need for landing infrastructure. Many startups and investors are pursuing similar ideas, but these aircraft more closely resemble compact helicopters than cars. While Airbus’s scale gives it an advantage, practical, economic and regulatory obstacles mean widespread urban airborne taxis remain uncertain despite active development and publicity.

A Seminole County man, George Jolicoeur, pleaded no contest to five charges after repeatedly scamming restaurants and convenience stores for refunds, including falsely claiming $50 of beef jerky from a 7-Eleven was moldy. The piece then shifts to a tongue-in-cheek Florida hurricane-season list explaining why residents stay despite risks: stocking generators and supplies, unpaid gambling losses, underwater mortgages, tarpaulin-topped roofs, poor football seasons, neighborly bonds, coupon use, ocean access, avoiding California quakes, and escaping Iowa’s lack of coastline.

Axios AM’s debut newsletter previews the incoming Trump administration and spotlights Jared Kushner’s growing influence. Transition teams have staged intensive “murder board” rehearsals for confirmation hearings, coaching nominees to deflect and avoid criticizing Trump. Republicans are rushing hearings; Democrats plan to slow-floor votes. Early impressions of Transition Trump mix unpredictability and surprising effectiveness, with some GOP insiders betting on substantial legislative success.

Kushner is poised to join the West Wing as senior adviser with significant staffing authority. Axios and New York Magazine portray him as a central, unusually powerful figure—trusted by Trump, close to Steve Bannon, and instrumental in recruitment and strategy. Kushner’s evolution from Manhattan real-estate scion and Observer publisher into the campaign’s managerial brain involved leveraging tech-style direct marketing, digital tactics, and a willingness to disrupt conventional political playbooks. He cultivated relationships with business leaders, promoted a centrist economic team heavy on Goldman alumni, and helped steer transition personnel decisions, often exercising influence behind the scenes.

Profiles trace Kushner’s family background—from Holocaust-survivor grandparents and his father Charlie’s legal fall—to his aggressive real-estate deals (notably 666 Fifth Avenue), media ownership, and political networking. His devotion to family loyalty, market-minded pragmatism, and appetite for dealmaking shape his approach. While some hope he will temper Trump’s impulses, the reporting suggests his loyalties and alignment with insurgent populists like Bannon make him a defining architect of “Trump Nationalism,” likely reshaping GOP politics and Washington’s power dynamics.

Tiffany Johnson, a mother of three from Concord, N.C., survived a shark attack while snorkeling on the final stop of a Bahamas cruise. She says she felt a bump, turned, and found a shark with her arm in its mouth. After struggling for several minutes, the shark severed part of her arm; her husband James heard her screams, jumped in to help, and she credits a “tangible” sense of peace and what she calls supernatural strength for keeping her calm. Local Bahamian doctors stopped the bleeding, but passport and customs complications delayed evacuation. A Medevac flight to Carolinas Medical Center would have cost $16,000; the company ultimately agreed to cover the cost. Tiffany has undergone surgeries, will have another procedure to prepare for a prosthetic, and has met with a prosthetics team. She expresses gratitude for being alive, hopes her story will inspire others, and encourages prayers and financial support to help with ongoing medical expenses.

Human Rights Watch concluded that four Israeli strikes on journalists and media facilities in Gaza during the November 2012 fighting violated the laws of war because they targeted civilians and civilian objects that were not shown to be making an effective contribution to military operations. The incidents killed two al-Aqsa TV cameramen—Mahmoud al-Kumi and Hussam Salama—wounded at least ten media workers, badly damaged multiple media offices and private businesses, and killed a two-year-old child by shrapnel. Israeli officials asserted each target was linked to Hamas military activity—calling the cameramen “Hamas operatives” and describing rooftop antennas and media offices as “operational communications” or “command centers”—but provided no specific evidence. Human Rights Watch’s site inspections and interviews found no indication the individuals or facilities were directly participating in hostilities; broadcasts praising attacks or expressing support do not constitute direct participation. The report urges impartial investigations, accountability for unlawful attacks, and compensation for victims, while noting unlawful attacks occurred on both sides during the conflict. Israeli authorities say they are reviewing the incidents.

On March 18, 2015, gunmen attacked Tunisia’s National Bardo Museum in central Tunis, killing 23 people and wounding nearly 50, in one of the deadliest civilian assaults the country has seen since 2002. Authorities said 18 of the dead were foreign tourists and five were Tunisians, including a police officer; some counts initially varied and several victims remained unidentified. The victims included nationals from Japan, Italy, Colombia, Spain, the UK, Australia, France and Poland; reports also mentioned potential South African victims. Among those killed were groups of cruise-ship passengers visiting Tunis for the day. The two shooters, named by officials as Yassine Laabidi and Hatem Khachnaoui, were Tunisian and were killed by security forces after holding hostages for hours inside the museum; authorities searched for two or three possible accomplices and arrested multiple suspects in the days following the attack. Tunisia’s prime minister said Laabidi had been known to security services but without any specific, actionable intelligence.

The assault began at midday as the gunmen opened fire near tourist buses outside the museum, then entered the galleries—home to famed Roman mosaics—and took hostages. Security forces stormed the building after a prolonged siege. About 40–47 people were treated for gunshot wounds in hospitals; harrowing survivor accounts described people hiding in galleries and remaining concealed overnight, including two Spanish tourists who emerged only after dawn. A police officer died in the rescue operation.

Islamic State later claimed responsibility through propaganda channels, praising the attackers, though analysts cautioned that IS has no formal territorial foothold in Tunisia; jihadist or extremist links to Libya and returning Tunisian fighters were cited as context for rising security concerns. The attack struck at Tunisia’s fragile democracy and its crucial tourism sector—tourism accounts for a significant portion of GDP—and prompted immediate repercussions: major cities saw increased military deployment, arrests, and stepped-up security at tourist sites and hotels; some cruise lines suspended Tunis calls.

Domestically, thousands protested in Tunis in a show of unity against terrorism, lighting candles and waving national flags. President Beji Caid Essebsi and other world leaders condemned the attack; the UN Security Council offered condolences and urged that perpetrators be brought to justice. Tunisian officials vowed to pursue militants while grappling with how to preserve democratic freedoms amid heightened counterterrorism measures.

Researchers analyzing about 3.4 million leaked numeric passwords found striking nonrandom patterns in 4-digit codes, suggesting many online password choices mirror ATM PIN behavior. The top three codes—1234, 1111, and 0000—account for nearly 20% of entries; 1234 alone appears in ~11%. Codes beginning with "19" (birth years) and MMDD birthday-style patterns are disproportionately common, boosting guessability. Simple patterns (repeated digits like 1111, sequential runs like 4321, keypad paths like 2580) and even-number preferences (2468 over 1357) dominate. Half of all PINs are among the 426 most popular combinations; roughly one-third of accounts could be cracked by trying just 61 guesses. Conversely, rare codes like 8068 occur under 0.001%. The findings underscore poor human randomness and urge users to avoid obvious patterns and developers to stop storing passwords in plaintext to protect users from trivial guessing attacks.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Chris Dodd announced he will introduce a revised, likely non‑bipartisan, bank reform bill after months of talks with Sen. Bob Corker and other Republicans failed to produce consensus. Dodd said time is short to pass reform in 2010 and plans a committee vote the week of March 22, with possible Senate floor consideration in spring. Corker, disappointed, said negotiators were “on the five‑yard line” and blamed White House pressure to finish quickly so Congress could focus on health care. Key negotiated elements reportedly included a powerful consumer financial protection unit, oversight by a five‑agency council with veto authority over its rules, regulator enforcement of those rules, heightened liability for credit raters, payday‑lender oversight, and derivatives clearing rules. Major disagreements remain over shareholder‑empowerment provisions, proxy access, executive pay votes, and exemptions for derivatives end users, leaving passage uncertain.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) at the Port of Charleston seized two shipments totaling 2,380 counterfeit hoverboards manufactured in China. Valued at about $1.66 million if genuine, the items violated trademark protections and posed safety risks due to potentially substandard lithium-ion batteries that have been linked to fires. CBP emphasized enforcing product safety and intellectual property rights to protect consumers and legitimate businesses from dangerous, unfairly competing goods. The Charleston seizure adds to nationwide efforts: Chicago officers recently seized over 16,000 hoverboards, and more than 50,000 potentially unsafe boards—approaching $20 million MSRP—have been confiscated across the U.S. Suspected trade violations can be reported to CBP’s e-Allegations system or 1-800-BE-ALERT.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) released updated 2016 guidance to reduce sleep-related infant deaths, including sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS), urging clear, simple safe-sleep practices. The AAP recommends that infants sleep on their backs on a firm, separate sleep surface—such as a crib or bassinet—with a tight-fitting sheet and no soft bedding, bumper pads, pillows or soft toys. Room-sharing is advised: infants should sleep in the parents’ bedroom, but on a separate surface, preferably for the first year and at minimum for six months; this can cut SIDS risk by as much as 50 percent. Parents are cautioned never to place infants to sleep on sofas, armchairs or other soft surfaces, alone or with another person, as these are especially hazardous.

The updated policy, the first since 2011, incorporates new evidence supporting immediate post-birth skin-to-skin care for at least an hour when the mother is awake and medically stable, and reaffirms breastfeeding as protective against SIDS. After feeding, caregivers should return the infant to a separate sleep space. If a caregiver fears they might fall asleep while feeding, they should avoid feeding on sofas or cushioned chairs; if they do fall asleep, they must move the baby to a separate bed upon waking. The AAP also advises offering a pacifier at naps and bedtime, ensuring infants receive all recommended vaccinations, and providing daily supervised tummy time while awake to aid development. The statement warns against use of commercial devices or home monitors marketed to reduce SIDS risk, and stresses avoiding exposure to smoke, alcohol and illicit drugs.

The guidance encourages clinicians to discuss sleep practices openly and nonjudgmentally with families and asks media and advertisers to model safe-sleep images. The release follows tragic individual cases—such as a 2017 infant death linked to crib blankets—that underscore the danger of loose bedding and the importance of “bare” crib environments. Approximately 3,500 U.S. infants die annually from sleep-related causes, and the AAP emphasizes that simple precautions can significantly improve safety.

The University of Virginia adopted strict new safety rules for fraternities and sororities after a high-profile Rolling Stone article alleged a 2012 gang rape at a fraternity—claims that later came under scrutiny and led the magazine to acknowledge reporting failures. UVA had suspended Greek social activities in November; President Teresa A. Sullivan announced Tuesday that the suspension would be lifted immediately if chapters sign on to the new measures by Jan. 16.

Key provisions apply to 31 Inter-Fraternity Council chapters (28 with houses) and to other Greek councils: at least three “sober and lucid” monitors must staff every party, with one posted at the staircase leading to bedrooms and carrying immediate key access to each room. Monitors must wear standardized identification; at least one must supervise alcohol distribution. Entry management requires guest lists checked by a hired security agent at large events or by a chapter member at smaller ones.

Alcohol rules aim to reduce shared, easily drugged sources: beer only in unopened cans, wine served visibly by a sober member, and an explicit ban on pre-mixed drinks, punch, kegs, and other common alcohol sources. Hard liquor is allowed only with licensed bartenders at large events or bottles behind a sober-supervised bar at smaller gatherings. The addendum for all Greek groups also emphasizes bystander-intervention training and alcohol-education programs.

University officials and Greek leaders framed the changes as student-driven safety improvements, though some provisions—like sober monitors—had been informal practice already. The new rules reflect a pragmatic stance that underage drinking will occur and that harm-reduction protocols are needed to make parties safer and to help prevent sexual violence on campus.

Republican Tim Pawlenty announced he will not sign the Family Leader’s Marriage Vow, a pledge by a conservative Iowa group that asks presidential hopefuls to denounce same-sex marriage, pornography and certain forms of Islamic law. Though Pawlenty said he agrees with the vow’s principles, he prefers to “choose my own words,” emphasizing a desire to show compassion to people in broken families who may not be at fault. He becomes the second prominent Republican to decline the pledge, following Mitt Romney’s decision the previous day; two other Republicans, Rep. Michele Bachmann and former Sen. Rick Santorum, have signed it. Pawlenty’s refusal coincided with the launch of a new radio ad and web video in which he and his wife discuss their faith, underscoring his approach to addressing religious and family issues on his own terms rather than through a formal pledge.

Country star Chely Wright married girlfriend and LGBT activist Lauren Blitzer in Connecticut just over a year after publicly coming out as a lesbian. Wright, who posted wedding photos on Twitter, revealed in May 2010 that the admission had been painful for her career and personal life; she told the Los Angeles Times that country music tolerates many scandals but not being gay. Sales have dipped and she’s shifted toward Americana, yet fans flooded her Twitter with congratulations as she celebrated the wedding and honeymoon.

U.S. naval commanders in the Mediterranean kept a destroyer from making a scheduled port call in Naples so it would remain alongside a second destroyer within striking distance of Syria; both ships carried Tomahawk cruise missiles that Pentagon officials said would likely be among the first weapons used if the president ordered military action. Pentagon officials characterized the decision as a local commander’s move, not a direct order from Washington. Russia urged Syrian President Bashar al-Assad to allow U.N. investigators into areas east of Damascus where a chemical attack occurred, but diplomats said Moscow’s statement did not signal a change in its support for Assad or its opposition to punitive Security Council measures. Russia’s foreign ministry shifted blame toward Syrian opposition forces, suggesting the incident was a rebel provocation and citing internet reports that appeared to criticize government troops posted hours before the attack. A ministry spokesman, Aleksandr Lukashevich, implied the timing suggested a planned provocation, though timestamping practices on YouTube could explain apparent timing anomalies. He also noted Syria welcomed U.N. commissioner Carla del Ponte, who has suggested rebels used chemical weapons. Separately, CBS News reported U.S. intelligence detected activity at known chemical weapons sites before the attack, possibly indicating preparations.

The article criticizes sexist media coverage that shamed Chelsea Clinton for missing her daughter Charlotte’s first day of preschool while campaigning for her mother, Hillary Clinton. A Daily Mail piece framed the moment as scandalous — noting Charlotte, nearly two, was pushed to her Manhattan school by a nanny while father Marc Mezvinsky was on his phone — and questioned why Hillary, recovering from pneumonia, wasn’t babysitting. The tone and headlines implied Chelsea had failed motherhood duties by prioritizing political work, reinforcing a double standard: working mothers are judged for family absences that would rarely attract the same scrutiny if they were men.

The author deconstructs the Mail’s “It takes a village!” framing, pointing out Marc is Charlotte’s father and fully responsible for parenting duties, and ridicules the implication that grandmothers should drop everything to provide childcare — a demand never leveled at male politicians. The piece highlights how outlets like Fox 32 Chicago amplified the shaming by asking viewers whether Chelsea should have been there, a question later removed. It argues this kind of coverage perpetuates the message that women’s professional roles are always subordinate to motherhood, and that mothers must be omnipresent or be deemed failures.

Context includes trivial tabloid details about Marc’s recent career troubles and lifestyle, which underline the story’s voyeuristic nature. The author rejects the notion that such a routine childcare arrangement is newsworthy and calls out the persistent cultural expectation that women must choose family over public service. The piece concludes by condemning mom-shaming and celebrating progress toward female political leadership.

More than 350 volunteers and later nearly 1,000 people joined searches after 8-year-old Elizabeth Collins and her 10-year-old cousin Lyric Cook-Morrissey vanished Friday after leaving to ride bicycles in Evansdale, Iowa. Their bikes, Elizabeth’s purse and cellphone were found near Meyers Lake a few hours after they were reported missing; about 40 percent of the lake had been searched. Authorities, assisted by FBI and state agents, interviewed family, friends and local registered sex offenders and checked tips but said they had no new clues and suspended the large volunteer effort. Families remained hopeful but anguished: relatives described the girls as outgoing and sweet while admitting they’re “bracing for the worst, but hoping for the best.” Parents speculated about swimming or being lured; investigators said there was no sign so far that the girls had left Evansdale or of confirmed foul play. The case remains an active missing-persons investigation.

Baltimore’s Department of Public Works has discovered a large “fatberg” — a congealed mass of fats, oils and grease (FOG) mixed with non‑biodegradable items like wet wipes — blocking a 100‑year‑old, 24‑inch sewer main between Penn Station and the 1700 block of Charles Street. Engineers found up to about 85% of the pipe’s interior coated with FOG when they inspected the line after repeated dry‑weather sanitary overflows. The fatberg is blamed for at least two recent overflows, including a September 21 incident that released nearly 1.2 million gallons of sewage into the Jones Falls at North Charles and West Lanvale Streets. While much of the mass has been scraped away and sent to landfill, smaller fatbergs exist elsewhere in the system. The blockage slowed sewage flow and triggered an engineered overflow that diverts sewer backups into the stormwater system and local waterways. DPW is assessing whether pipe repairs or replacements are needed once FOG removal is complete; long‑term upgrades to the sewer collection and treatment systems are planned under a consent decree. Officials stress prevention: restaurants must follow FOG program rules and homeowners should avoid pouring grease down drains and should not flush wipes.

The Supreme Court heard arguments in American Broadcasting Companies, Inc. v. Aereo, a case that pits broadcasters’ copyright claims against a startup that rents tiny remote antennas and DVRs to let subscribers stream and record over-the-air TV over the Internet. At issue is whether Aereo’s user-initiated transmissions constitute private performances (permissible under Sony’s Betamax fair-use precedent) or public performances that require broadcaster licenses. The technical details of Aereo’s design—individual antennas and user-controlled recordings—are central to its defense, but the justices repeatedly struggled to grasp or accept those distinctions.

Aereo’s counsel emphasized that each recording and stream is initiated and controlled by the user, mirroring what consumers can do at home with an antenna and DVR. He relied on the Second Circuit’s Cartoon Network v. Cablevision ruling, which held that user-controlled, individual cloud DVR copies did not create public performances. That decision is Aereo’s strongest precedent: if user control determines privacy, Aereo’s model should be lawful.

Broadcasters countered that when a service provider transmits programming from its facilities to subscribers, the performance becomes public, likening Aereo to a cable company rather than a mere hardware vendor. They warned that allowing Aereo to avoid licensing would undercut retransmission revenue and threaten free over-the-air broadcasting. Their counsel argued that Aereo’s remote operations and repeated, separate copies effectively serve the public, and suggested the company is trying to engineer around copyright obligations.

Justices voiced concerns in both directions. Several worried a pro-broadcaster ruling could chill cloud services and storage providers—Dropbox, iCloud, and other “cloud locker” businesses—by turning routine user-initiated cloud access into public performances. Others, notably Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Scalia, expressed skepticism about Aereo’s use of many tiny antennas as a possible circumvention of copyright law. Analogies—between car dealers and valet services, or buying an antenna versus renting one remotely—failed to settle the core legal question: whether location and ownership of equipment or user control define the line between private and public performances.

The Court’s decision will shape the balance between copyright protection and cloud-based innovation. A ruling for the broadcasters could force services like Aereo to obtain licenses or cease operations; a ruling for Aereo could validate user-specific cloud DVR models and reassure the wider cloud computing industry that user-initiated, private access remains legally distinct from public retransmission. The justices appeared deeply divided and cautious about unintended consequences, signaling a careful, consequential ruling ahead.

Maria von Trapp, the last surviving member of the original Trapp Family Singers who inspired The Sound of Music, has died at age 99 at her home in Stowe, Vermont, her brother Johannes von Trapp said. Remembered by him as “one of the few truly good people,” Maria was the third child and second-oldest daughter of Austrian naval captain Georg von Trapp and his first wife, Agathe Whitehead. The seven von Trapp children’s musical talents and family story were dramatized in the 1949 book by Maria’s stepmother (also named Maria), the 1959 Broadway musical and the 1965 Oscar-winning film. In 1938 the family fled Nazi-occupied Austria, toured Europe and completed a three-month U.S. tour before settling in Vermont in the early 1940s, where they opened the Trapp Family Lodge in Stowe. Maria played accordion and, with her sister Rosmarie, taught Austrian dance at the lodge. Her personal biography notes she was born in the Alps after her family fled World War I fighting and grew up immersed in music—her father played violin, accordion and mandolin and her mother piano and violin. She also served as a lay missionary in Papua New Guinea. Surviving siblings include Rosmarie, Johannes and Eleonore von Trapp Campbell. The Trapp Family Lodge remains a Vermont resort celebrating their Austrian heritage.

Two major polls taken around the killing of Osama bin Laden find his death improved President Obama’s standing on terrorism and national security but produced mixed or limited changes in overall approval and no durable boost on the economy. The Washington Post–Pew poll showed Obama’s overall approval rose nine points to 56 percent, with career highs on terrorism (69%) and Afghanistan (60%), and independents driving the gain. Most Americans credit the president and overwhelmingly credit U.S. military and intelligence. The Newsweek/Daily Beast poll, conducted immediately before and after the announcement, found no change in overall approval (48/49) or reelection support; many respondents praised his leadership on terrorism (63%) but continued to rate the economy poorly, keeping broad dissatisfaction about the country’s direction. Partisan views differ on who deserves credit—Obama or George W. Bush—but both polls underscore that success on one front did not erase economic concerns or guarantee lasting political gains.

A Los Angeles judge reversed a prior order requiring artificial feeding and hydration for radio legend Casey Kasem and reaffirmed eldest daughter Kerri Kasem’s conservatorship, allowing her to continue making medical decisions as the ailing 82-year-old enters his final days. The reversal followed new medical records from St. Anthony’s Hospital near Seattle indicating that artificial nutrition and fluids were causing painful complications and that Kasem was not tolerating them; doctors advised against restoring them. Judge Daniel S. Murphy said reinstating nutrition and hydration would be “acutely harmful.” Kerri’s attorney said earlier attempts at hydration nearly caused Kasem to “drown” and that he is now receiving morphine drips for comfort. 

The hearing grew emotional and contentious. Jean Kasem, Casey’s wife of 34 years, denounced the decision, accusing the court and Kerri of imposing a “death sentence” and storming out, with her lawyer echoing the charge. Jean testified under penalty of perjury that a brief hospital interaction showed Casey signaling a desire to live via eye and eyebrow movements and accused Kerri of stopping medication to hasten his death—claims Kerri’s lawyer denied. Jean also said she and daughter Liberty had been terrorized by Kerri. 

Casey Kasem, famed voice actor and host of American Top 40, is in late-stage Lewy body disease and was recently admitted to intensive care with an infection linked to a severe bedsore. The judge found Jean acted against Casey’s best interests when she removed him from a California skilled nursing facility in May and transported him to Washington. The WARC files for this report are not publicly available.

UC Berkeley researchers have taken a significant step toward decoding visual experience by reconstructing dynamic video from brain activity. In the study, subjects (the researchers themselves) watched YouTube clips while lying in an fMRI scanner; the team used blood-flow signals in visual cortex to train a model that associates neural patterns with visual features by comparing them against millions of seconds of YouTube content. When run in reverse, the model generated continuous, dream-like, blurry reconstructions of the original trailers. Unlike prior work on static images, this demonstrates decoding of dynamic visual input and suggests future potential to reveal internally generated imagery such as dreams, memories, or imagined actions. The authors stress current limits—only part of the visual system was sampled, resolution is low, and massive data and computation are needed—but anticipate improving models and modules to enhance fidelity and explore practical applications, from assistive technologies to basic neuroscience.

North Korea has detained Otto Frederick Warmbier, a 21-year-old University of Virginia student from Cincinnati, accusing him of committing a “hostile act” aimed at “destroying the country’s unity.” Warmbier, an Echols Scholar majoring in economics, was traveling with China-based Young Pioneer Tours on a five-day New Year trip and was arrested at Pyongyang airport on Jan. 2 while about to depart for China. North Korea’s KCNA news agency said the act was “tolerated and manipulated by the U.S. government” and that Warmbier is under investigation; it gave no further details. Young Pioneer Tours and Warmbier’s family have been informed and are in contact with U.S. officials and the Swedish Embassy in Pyongyang, which represents U.S. interests in North Korea. The U.S. State Department acknowledged media reports of a detained citizen but cited privacy concerns and offered no specifics. Warmbier’s detention comes amid heightened tensions after North Korea’s fourth nuclear test and claims of a hydrogen bomb, prompting calls for tougher UN sanctions and regional warnings. North Korea has a history of detaining foreigners—sometimes using them to extract concessions—and the U.S. and Canadian governments advise against travel there. Warmbier is the third known Westerner currently held by Pyongyang.

Late last year President Obama asked his speechwriter to insert a quote from Pope Francis into a speech on economic inequality, citing the pope’s line about how an elderly homeless person’s death gets less attention than the stock market losing two points. That citation signals a shift: unlike his treatment of Pope Benedict XVI—whom Obama referred to chiefly as the head of a state—Obama is treating Francis as a moral authority whose views bolster temporal policy. Francis’s moral influence stems from presenting himself as nonpolitical: modest, plain-spoken, and willing to confess personal sin, he rejected papal trappings (living simply, wearing plain vestments, driving an ordinary car) and embraced a “people’s pope” persona. Elected amid crises—church scandals, declining attendance in many regions, and global poverty—Francis has navigated division and won extraordinary popular approval, reportedly outstripping Obama’s. Both men were media favorites and historic firsts in their arenas, yet Francis’s apparent humility and refusal to wield power ostentatiously have made him arguably the world’s most politically influential religious leader and a model contemporary politicians might study.

President Donald Trump intensified public criticism of Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, accusing his own appointee of impeding economic growth by raising interest rates too quickly. In a Wall Street Journal interview, Trump said Powell “almost looks like he’s happy raising interest rates” and suggested he “maybe” regretted nominating him, arguing that rate hikes undercut the momentum from the administration’s tax cuts and fiscal measures. Trump framed the Fed’s actions as the biggest economic risk—greater even than tariffs, trade tensions, or geopolitics—and contrasted Powell’s approach with the low-rate environment under President Barack Obama, asking rhetorically how one competes with “zero interest” rates. 

The Fed has raised rates by a quarter-point three times this year, with another increase likely in December as policymakers try to temper credit demand and prevent overheating. Powell has acknowledged the Fed’s difficult balance: move too fast and risk shortening the expansion, or move too slowly and risk destabilizing overheating. Trump’s remarks follow a string of public attacks in recent weeks—calling the Fed “going loco” and “out of control”—although he has publicly said he does not intend to fire Powell; removal would be unprecedented and legally fraught, requiring cause under the Federal Reserve Act. 

Economists and former Fed officials generally defend Powell’s gradual normalization of policy as prudent after the 2008 crisis and the tax-fueled stimulus, noting the need to rebuild policy space before the next downturn. Former Fed Chair Janet Yellen and ex-adviser Gary Cohn have warned that presidential commentary risks politicizing the Fed and undermining its independent credibility.

These crawls are part of an effort to archive pages as they are created and to capture the pages they reference, preserving the versions that were live when a page was written. The Internet Archive hopes archived links will replace broken links or serve as companion links so readers can see what the original authors intended, with the broader goal of fixing broken links across the web. The document also includes a news excerpt about Taylor Swift from Dec 7, 2018: her online profiles were wiped clean, prompting fan speculation that she would announce a new album—referred to as #TS6IsComing—on the three-year anniversary of her single "Shake It Off." Fans flooded social media with excited reactions and memes; Swift’s representatives did not immediately comment.

Late Monday night, someone with access to Senator Ted Cruz’s official Twitter account “liked” a tweet containing a pornographic video, briefly linking the Texas Republican to explicit content and sending his name trending worldwide. Cruz’s communications director said staff removed the offensive like and reported it to Twitter around 1 a.m. The senator told reporters the action was inadvertent, blaming a staffer with access to the account and calling it a mistake that is being handled internally; he declined to identify or say whether the person would be disciplined. Pornhub’s vice president cheekily announced the video would be made widely available, and the clip—originally published by Reality Kings in 2016—circulated broadly online. The episode revived past moments when Cruz intersected with pornography in the public record: he recounted viewing explicit material with Supreme Court justices in the 1990s while clerking, and as Texas solicitor general once defended a law banning sale of sex toys. The incident produced widespread online mockery and media attention, including jokes that the unwanted attention might have helped him during his presidential primary, and comments from the porn actress featured in the clip noting her surprise at the sudden trend.

Apple is launching an in-store iPhone trade-in program this month, working with distributor Brightstar to encourage upgrades to the iPhone 5 and funnel older models into refurbished channels. The program will let customers get instant credit for used devices, lowering out-of-pocket costs and potentially enabling some to buy an iPhone 5 with no money down. Apple aims to boost sales amid slowing growth and Samsung’s rising smartphone share by keeping users in its ecosystem and reselling collected phones in emerging markets where demand for cheaper iPhones is strong. Brightstar handles trade-ins for carriers and expects to resell millions globally.

Patton Oswalt paid tribute on Twitter to his wife, crime writer Michelle McNamara, who died unexpectedly at home in Los Angeles at age 46. He praised her writing—“She wrote lines that stung & hummed”—and called his 13 years with her “happily humbling.” The couple, married in 2005, share a daughter, Alice, born in 2009. Oswalt also shared a poignant remark from seven‑year‑old Alice: “When your mom dies you’re the best memory of her. Everything you do is a memory of her.” No cause of death was given. Oswalt retweeted a link to 826LA, a youth writing organization accepting donations in McNamara’s honor to continue her creative legacy; she had been working on a book about the “Golden State Killer.”

A deadly weekend of bull-related events in Spain saw a professional matador and a participant in a village bull-run killed, with several others injured during the famed San Fermin festivities in Pamplona. Victor Barrio, a 29-year-old bullfighter who began as an apprentice at Madrid’s Las Ventas in 2010, was fatally gored while fighting a 1,166-pound bull in Teruel, Aragon. Television captured the attack: Barrio was first struck in the thigh and flipped, then gored again in the chest as he lay on the ground. The horn penetrated a lung and the aorta; medics attempted to save him but he was pronounced dead by a surgeon at the ring. Las Ventas confirmed his death, and Spanish leaders and fellow bullfighters expressed condolences—Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy tweeted his sympathies, and prominent matador Enrique Ponce lamented the loss. Festivities in Teruel were suspended, and runners at San Fermin wore improvised black armbands in tribute. Barrio is the first professional matador to die in a Spanish bullring since 1985; earlier ring deaths since then involved assistants killed in 1992. Separately, in Pedreguer near Valencia, a 28-year-old man was killed during a local bull-run after a horn pierced his lung and heart as he attempted to help another runner. At Pamplona’s San Fermin run on the same day, a 33-year-old Japanese man was gored in the chest and a 24-year-old Spaniard injured in the arm; another 12 people sustained minor injuries. Such bull festivals, held across Spain in summer, routinely attract thousands and carry significant risks, with occasional fatalities and injuries each year.

Republican leaders got a late boost in their bid to pass the American Health Care Act when Reps. Fred Upton (Mich.) and Billy Long (Mo.) reversed earlier opposition after a White House meeting and secured an amendment adding $8 billion to help cover people with pre-existing conditions. Their switches eased immediate concerns about losing critical votes; leaders said the change could attract more moderates without alienating conservatives. House Freedom Caucus chair Mark Meadows and others signaled openness to the amendment, and lawmakers like Rep. Mike Coffman said tightened protections might win their support.

The White House pushed for a quick vote—possibly as soon as Thursday—with Trump personally calling lawmakers and administration officials pressing leadership to act before recess. Speaker Paul Ryan declined to commit to a floor date but said they were close to sufficient support; Republicans can afford only about 22 defections. Critics, including Protect Our Care’s Leslie Dach, called the amendment insufficient, arguing it fails to prevent waivers that could let insurers charge higher premiums or reduce coverage for those with pre-existing conditions. Polling showed public skepticism about waiving coverage requirements and a preference to wait for a Congressional Budget Office review, which previously predicted millions more uninsured under earlier AHCA versions.

South Korea announced it will withdraw about 175–180 of its nationals from the Kaesong Industrial Complex after North Korea rejected Seoul’s demand for talks to resolve a standoff that began when Pyongyang blocked South Korean access and recalled the 53,000 North Korean workers in early April. Unification Minister Ryoo Kihl-jae described the withdrawal as “inevitable” to protect workers who are running low on food and medicine; he urged North Korea to safeguard South Korean property and ensure managers’ safety during the pullout but did not give a timetable.

Pyongyang dismissed Seoul’s offer as insincere, citing ongoing U.S.–South Korea military drills and leaflet drops as proof, and warned it might take “final and decisive” measures if the South escalates. The military exercises continue, with air and amphibious drills that North Korea calls war preparations. Analysts say the decision is a high-stakes gamble that could leave Kaesong shuttered long-term and raise the risk that North Korea might seize South Korean assets, as it did with a resort in 2010.

Established in 2004, Kaesong has been the last major cooperative venture between the Koreas—pairing South Korean investment and technology with cheap Northern labor—but its future now looks uncertain amid heightened tensions over North Korea’s nuclear test and subsequent U.N. sanctions. Businesses with facilities there expressed shock at Seoul’s move.

Thomas “Tom” McDonald, a 58-year-old Queens native and retired NYC Transit worker, has spent the last seven to eight years carrying out an unconventional tribute to his lifelong friend Roy Riegel: flushing small portions of Riegel’s cremated remains down toilets at Major League Baseball parks and other meaningful sites. The two grew up together near Shea Stadium and bonded over the Mets; Riegel, a master plumber and passionate music fan, died April 8, 2008, the day of Shea’s last season home opener. With Riegel’s family’s blessing, McDonald kept some ashes and began discreetly scattering them at ballparks nationwide. After a windy failed attempt to sprinkle ashes outdoors, an impromptu flush in a Minnesota bar restroom inspired McDonald’s signature ritual — fitting for a plumber. He wraps tiny plastic bottles of ashes in old Mets ticket stubs and follows rules: a game must be in progress when he performs the act. To date he’s visited at least 16 stadiums, including stops in Chicago (White Sox only), Pittsburgh, Cleveland (both Progressive Field and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame for Riegel’s love of rock), Cincinnati, Detroit, Baltimore, Toronto’s Rogers Centre, and more. He’s also scattered ashes at sentimental local sites tied to their youth— a schoolyard, Shea’s original home plate marker, and a Broadway Mets parade marker — and even at Ireland’s Cliffs of Moher. Friends and family say Roy would have approved. McDonald has enough left for one final stop: Durham Athletic Park, famed as the filming site of Bull Durham.

In January, Choteau, Montana beekeeper Lloyd Cunniff reported 488 hives stolen from a California site where he’d placed them for almond pollination. Fresno County agricultural crime investigators, aided by tips from the beekeeping community, located much of the stolen equipment at three sites—a rented bee nursery, a cow pasture where the suspects had trespassed, and hidden in a freeway drainage. Detectives recovered about $170,000 of roughly $224,000 reported stolen and arrested two Ukrainian-Russian suspects on possession of stolen property charges; further charges and arrests are possible as the probe continues and federal interest grows because of the scale and possible organized-crime links. Many recovered hives were mixed, damaged or potentially infected, so Cunniff quarantined them away from his new colonies and won’t know their viability until fall. Insurance helped him replace lost stock earlier, and he’s preparing new colonies for the coming season while hoping for convictions and a full recovery of his business losses.

Elliott Broidy, a Los Angeles investor and prominent GOP fundraiser who served as a deputy national finance chairman for the RNC and a major Trump backer, resigned Friday after reports that he paid $1.6 million to settle with a former Playboy model he had a consensual affair with. Broidy acknowledged the relationship, apologized to his wife and family, and said the woman became pregnant and chose to end the pregnancy; he said he offered financial help. He retained Michael Cohen—President Trump’s personal lawyer—after Cohen told him the woman’s attorney had contacted him. The Wall Street Journal first reported Cohen’s role; Cohen’s office, home and hotel were raided by the FBI days earlier as part of a criminal probe into his business dealings and efforts to suppress stories damaging to Trump during the 2016 campaign. Federal prosecutors have empaneled a grand jury in the Southern District of New York; the case was referred by Special Counsel Robert Mueller. Terms of the settlement barred the woman from discussing the relationship while allowing her to keep the baby (if she chose), determine paternity and seek child support later. The episode links Cohen to other hush-money arrangements—he negotiated a $130,000 agreement with Stormy Daniels in 2016—and involves figures tied to AMI’s “catch-and-kill” deal for Karen McDougal. RNC Chair Ronna McDaniel said she accepted Broidy’s resignation and will review Cohen’s role; Cohen and his lawyer did not comment.

Ashley Judd responded forcefully to a wave of media speculation about her appearance, using an op-ed in The Daily Beast to challenge the misogynistic culture that produced it. After observers widely suggested the 43-year-old actress had cosmetic procedures when she appeared with a puffier face and had gained weight, Judd explained the changes: steroid treatment for a sinus infection and “a lazy six months of not exercising.” Rather than offer a perfunctory denial, she reframed the discussion, arguing that the episode reveals how conversations about women’s bodies operate to objectify, police, and degrade women.

Judd outlines how multiple outlets reached contradictory conclusions about the same appearance—claiming surgical work when she looked flawless, and mocking her when she showed any sign of aging or weight fluctuation—often without contacting her. She stresses that the scrutiny is gendered, ageist, and frequently fueled by other women, which she links to the broader system of patriarchy that encourages mutual policing of women’s bodies. The piece critiques media practices that treat female celebrities as public property and reduce personhood to physical appearance, noting the spillover effects on self-image, relationships, workplace treatment, and girls’ and women’s autonomy.

While some commentators argue that actresses accept heightened focus on their looks as part of their profession, Judd insists the cultural habit of speculation and ridicule must stop and calls for a feminist reframing of such conversations. She urges personal, familial, and social reflection to shed internalized beliefs that perpetuate meanness, and advocates stronger female-to-female solidarity to change how society talks about and treats bodies—celebrity or otherwise.

Workers opened a 113-year-old time capsule removed from inside the golden lion atop Boston’s Old State House and discovered papers in remarkably good condition — and an unexpected mystery: a small red hardcover book. The copper box, about the size of a shoebox and weighing 5–10 pounds, had been sealed in the lion’s head in 1901 during repairs overseen by Samuel D. Rogers and then forgotten. Its existence was known from Rogers’s family letters and a 1901 Boston Globe article that listed photographs, autographs, newspapers, a population map, campaign buttons and family histories as likely contents. When conservators at Skylight Studios in Woburn carefully removed the crown and freed the capsule, archivists found no mold or water damage. Because the items are fragile and tightly packed, Bostonian Society archivist Elizabeth Roscio chose not to unpack them at the press event; the box will be examined later in an environmentally controlled setting and the materials eventually displayed. Rogers’s great-great-granddaughter, Heidi Rogers Grundhauser, had long sought confirmation of the capsule and hopes it will shed light on family history. The Society plans to create a new, more accessible titanium time capsule to return to the lion and is soliciting public suggestions of modern items to include — already considering a 2013 Boston Marathon medal and images or artifacts representing today’s Boston. The discovery drew public interest and promises further study once conservators safely remove and document the contents.

In May, a Richmond Police Department (RPD) officer anonymously told CBS 6 that during President Obama’s VCU visit colleagues made threats and lewd remarks about the president and First Lady Michelle Obama—allegedly a supervisor told a sharpshooter to “take a couple of shots,” another suggested planting a bomb under the stage, and others made sexual comments about Michelle Obama. The Secret Service later found no criminal wrongdoing, though two officers were fired amid the controversy. The whistleblower was terminated this February for violating department policy by speaking to the media. Employment attorneys say he may have First Amendment protection for speaking on a public concern and warned the firing could chill other whistleblowers. The fired officers deny the allegations and seek reinstatement, alleging their careers were unfairly ended; their attorney accused city officials of rushing to fire them. The whistleblower is considering legal action; RPD says it conferred with the Secret Service and has investigated administratively.

Hawaii Gov. Neil Abercrombie appointed Lt. Gov. Brian Schatz to fill the U.S. Senate seat left vacant by the Dec. 17 death of Sen. Daniel Inouye. Abercrombie chose Schatz from a three-person list submitted by the state Democratic Party that also included U.S. Rep. Colleen Hanabusa and Esther Kiaaina. Inouye had expressed a wish that Hanabusa succeed him, and her supporters expressed disappointment that the governor did not honor that request, though Hanabusa congratulated Schatz and said she respected the process. Schatz, 40, a former state representative and party chairman who led Obama’s 2008 Hawaii campaign, will be sworn in quickly to participate in looming Senate votes on fiscal and budget issues; he could be sworn in as soon as Thursday and flew to Washington on Air Force One. Schatz will serve until a 2014 election to fill the remainder of Inouye’s term and plans to run in both 2014 and 2016. His appointment makes him Hawaii’s senior senator, with Mazie Hirono as junior.

A New York Times/CBS News poll taken April 24–28 finds most Americans willing to accept expanded surveillance and tougher prevention measures after the Boston Marathon bombings. Seventy-eight percent favor public video cameras; 66 percent want restrictions on online explosive-making instructions. Nine in ten say terrorism is an enduring risk, and 66 percent now think another attack is at least somewhat likely—up sharply from last year. Confidence in federal and local law enforcement is high: 84 percent approve of the response to the bombings, and 68 percent approve of President Obama’s handling of the incident; 56 percent approve of his terrorism policy overall. Views are mixed on prevention: 41 percent say intelligence agencies had information that might have prevented the attack, while 45 percent disagree. Fifty-three percent believe the suspects had links to a larger group; 32 percent say they acted alone. Most respondents (72 percent) do not plan to avoid large public events, and 49 percent think the balance between security and civil liberties is about right, though opinions vary on surveillance limits.

This mixed document contains two main stories: a description of the Game of Thrones opening-title astrolabe design and a detailed report on the discovery and analysis of the earliest known marine astrolabe recovered from a 1503 shipwreck.

The first part explains the concept behind the Game of Thrones title sequence created by Elastic, led creatively by Angus Wall. Inspired by the maps that open the novels, designers placed a map of Westeros on the inside of a sphere centered on an astrolabe-like sun. The sequence’s camera travels over the map while relief-sculpted bands on the astrolabe recount backstory in miniature: dragons attacking Westeros, rival houses uniting to defeat them, and the houses’ animal sigils bowing to the Baratheon stag. The sequence’s rotating gears and cogs echo Leonardo da Vinci’s inventions; close-up bands on the astrolabe contain sculpted historical detail, enhancing the title sequence’s narrative economy and visual richness.

The second, longer account describes an archaeological find from the Esmeralda, a ship in Vasco da Gama’s fleet that sank off Oman in 1503. In 2014 divers recovered a thin bronze disc—later identified as a mariner’s astrolabe—among nearly 2,800 artifacts. Initially the navigational markings were invisible, but 3D laser scanning and pioneering imaging by Professor Mark Williams at the University of Warwick revealed etches around the edge separated by five-degree increments, confirming its function. The disc, 17.5 cm across and engraved with the Portuguese coat of arms and King Manuel I’s emblem, dates to about 1495–1500, making it the earliest confirmed marine astrolabe by several decades and only the 108th cataloged. Excavation leader David Mearns hailed it as a rare, historically important find that fills gaps in maritime history; the high-resolution scans allowed precise modeling to 0.1 mm and opened research opportunities into early navigational technology.

A Florida jury’s acquittal of George Zimmerman in the 2012 shooting death of Trayvon Martin reignited national debate over race, justice and gun laws, prompting emotional responses, protests and calls for further investigation. Zimmerman, a neighborhood-watch volunteer, was found not guilty by a six-woman jury, a verdict that divided public opinion: some saw a lawful self-defense claim, others perceived a miscarriage of justice rooted in racial bias. With no living eyewitnesses aside from Zimmerman, prosecutors faced difficulty meeting the criminal standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt; defense attorneys stressed the jury carefully weighed limited evidence and defended Zimmerman’s actions.

President Barack Obama, who had earlier called Martin’s death an “American tragedy” and empathized with the family, urged calm and respect for the jury’s decision while asking Americans to widen compassion, address gun violence, and reflect on community safety. Republicans such as Rep. Steve King criticized the administration, saying Obama politicized the case and alleging Justice Department overreach. Civil-rights leaders and activists, including NAACP President Ben Jealous, called on Attorney General Eric Holder and the Justice Department to pursue a civil-rights investigation; the DOJ confirmed its probe remained open as officials evaluated whether federal charges were warranted.

Across the country, rallies, vigils and church services expressed grief and anger, with protestors decrying the verdict as evidence of systemic racial injustice and urging changes including challenges to “stand your ground” laws. Trayvon Martin’s family, mourning and stunned, leaned on faith and considered civil lawsuits and continued advocacy, establishing a foundation to fight gun violence. Supporters of Zimmerman celebrated the legal vindication, while the nation remained sharply divided over the larger issues the case laid bare.

Bob Dylan’s Nobel Prize lecture has sparked accusations that he lifted substantial phrasing about Moby-Dick from SparkNotes rather than Herman Melville’s novel. In a June 4 recorded talk required to claim his prize, Dylan discussed three formative works—Moby-Dick, All Quiet on the Western Front, and the Odyssey—recounting scenes and character sketches. Journalist Andrea Pitzer compared Dylan’s Moby-Dick passages to SparkNotes and found numerous near-matches: for example, Dylan’s “There’s a crazy prophet, Gabriel, on one of the vessels, and he predicts Ahab’s doom” echoes SparkNotes’ “One of the ships ... carries Gabriel, a crazed prophet who predicts doom.” Dylan also quoted an aphorism to Flask—“Some men who receive injuries are led to God, others are led to bitterness”—which does not appear in Melville but resembles SparkNotes’ character summary language. Pitzer identified about a dozen or more sentences among 78 describing Moby-Dick that closely resemble the study-guide text.

The piece situates this episode within Dylan’s long history of borrowing, appropriation, and collage—practices he has openly embraced and defended as folk tradition and artistic method. Critics note that using SparkNotes differs from folk quotations, yet some scholars call the lecture a postmodern collage in which such borrowing is permissible and not disqualifying. Dylan did not respond to inquiries; commentators largely doubt the Swedish Academy would rescind the prize, viewing the episode as another chapter in Dylan’s ambivalent relationship with source material and originality.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) used a Senate floor speech Thursday to forcefully oppose President Obama’s attorney general nominee, Loretta Lynch, arguing she would continue what he called the “lawlessness” of outgoing AG Eric Holder, particularly on immigration and executive overreach. Cruz urged Republicans to block her confirmation, saying no senator could in good conscience vote for her after her hearing responses. He voted against cloture on the nomination — a key procedural attempt to end debate — but the motion passed 66-34, clearing the way for a final confirmation vote. When the Senate later approved Lynch 56-43, Cruz was the only senator absent. His staff gave varying explanations: spokesmen said his cloture vote was “the vote that mattered” and that, once invoked, confirmation was inevitable; others said he left for a Texas fundraiser and travel. Critics noted Cruz’s recent pattern of missed votes, including on a unanimous human-trafficking bill and other matters. Cruz’s aides emphasized he led the opposition through speeches, interviews and op-eds, blaming Republican colleagues who supported cloture for enabling Lynch’s confirmation.

Flint remains under a boil-water advisory after a major transmission line break Tuesday that caused a Dupont water main failure and pressure drops, potentially allowing bacterial contamination. Officials contained and isolated the leak, restored normal pressures, and are assessing and repairing the damaged main. Bacteria testing results expected Thursday will determine when the precautionary notice can be lifted. Until then, residents using filters should boil filtered water for one minute and cool it; unfiltered users should flush taps for at least seven minutes before boiling. Officials warn against flushing systems through filters. The disruption comes amid Flint’s ongoing lead crisis from the 2014 switch to Flint River water; Mayor Karen Weaver seeks $55 million to replace lead pipes. State budget proposals include funds for Flint infrastructure, health, and relief. Contact: (810) 766-7202.

Google apologized after its new Photos app automatically labeled pictures of two Black men as “gorillas,” highlighting the limits and risks of automated image recognition. New York–based web developer Jacky Alcine posted the error on Twitter, prompting rapid responses from Google executives and an apology from the company. Yonatan Zunger, Google’s chief architect of social, acknowledged the severity of the bug and said engineers were removing problematic linguistic tags and improving image-recognition for darker skin tones and varied lighting. Google said it was “appalled” and committed to immediate and longer-term fixes.

The incident echoes earlier failures by other platforms: Flickr drew criticism when its auto-tagging labeled Black people as “ape” or “animal,” and Google Maps previously returned racist search results linking slurs to the White House. Companies emphasize that tagging systems learn from user corrections, but these errors expose how machine-learning systems can reproduce harmful biases present in training data or arise from technical limitations like contrast and occlusion. Alcine questioned what images and people had been used to train the models and urged broader, sustained efforts to address diversity in development and testing. The episode underscores the need for more careful oversight, diverse datasets, and sensitivity when deploying AI that classifies people.

A forensic bloodstain-pattern analysis of the Shroud of Turin concludes the stains are inconsistent with a single, supine or crucified body and instead point to staged or multiple separate applications—supporting the view the cloth is not an authentic burial shroud. Forensic anthropologist Matteo Borrini and chemist Luigi Garlaschelli tested blood flow behavior using donated human blood and synthetic blood on live volunteers and mannequins, simulating wounds shown on the shroud: the left hand, forearms, a spear (lance) wound in the torso, and a band-like stain across the lower back. They compared the angles and shapes of rivulets produced in different body positions (standing, supine, arms at various angles) to the patterns visible on the linen.

Their experiments found key inconsistencies. Forearm rivulets matched an arm held roughly 90° from the body, while hand trickles matched an arm at about 45°; some hand stains differed from each other by up to 10°. The chest/spear-wound flow resembled blood from an upright, hanging body in direction but produced discrete rivulets in tests rather than the continuous stain seen on the cloth. Crucially, the characteristic “blood belt” across the lumbar region could not be replicated in any realistic bleeding scenario, whether from a supine body or a body laid down after standing. A wood-contact test was inconclusive.

The authors argue these contradictions cannot be reconciled by undocumented postmortem movements or cleaning and suggest the stains reflect an artistic or didactic fabrication—consistent with radiocarbon dating placing the linen in the 1260–1390 CE medieval period. Published in the Journal of Forensic Sciences, the study does not settle how the shroud’s image was formed, but it adds forensic weight to skepticism about its authenticity and calls for further scientific inquiry.

In December, after Australia redefined its marriage laws, Jo Grant and Jill Kindt became the country’s first legally married same-sex couple — a revelation disclosed in Queensland’s parliament by Attorney-General Yvette D’Ath. The couple, together for eight years and who had held a commitment “promise day” in 2013, were granted an exemption from the mandatory waiting period because Ms Grant was terminally ill with a rare cancer and receiving palliative care. Their private garden ceremony on the Sunshine Coast on 15 December was approved, performed and registered within 24 hours after officials ruled the circumstances exceptional. Staff from Queensland Births, Deaths and Marriages went to extraordinary lengths to make the wedding possible, including driving about 100 km to hand-deliver paperwork to the marriage celebrant at a roadside meeting en route to the ceremony. Ms Grant died on 30 January, less than seven weeks after the wedding; the couple were legally married for 48 days. Ms Kindt said they had considered themselves married since 2013 but were grateful to have the legal recognition they both wanted. Ms D’Ath described the episode as inspiring and emblematic of Queensland’s embrace of equal rights, noting other same-sex couples also received exemptions to bypass the waiting period, and some well-publicized midnight weddings occurred. The story was revealed in parliament with the family’s permission and highlights both the human urgency behind some early same-sex marriages and the efforts by officials and staff who expedited approvals so terminally ill partners could marry before death intervened.

Workers replacing century-old water mains beneath Washington Square Park in Greenwich Village uncovered two buried brick vaults dating to the late 18th or early 19th century, revealing the remains of more than a dozen people. The vaults, about 15 by 18 feet each and roughly 8 feet deep in one report, were found just 3½ feet beneath the street amid utility cables. Archaeologists from Chrysalis, already on site because the adjacent park had served as a potter’s field during early-1800s yellow fever outbreaks, documented skulls and skeletons in one disturbed crypt and stacked wooden coffins in the other. City Department of Design and Construction officials said contractors first exposed the vaults while excavating for a multiyear, $9 million water main replacement project; engineers are considering rerouting the work to preserve the burial grounds, consistent with city policy to avoid disturbing graves when possible. Specialists — archaeologists and anthropologists — will continue excavation, photographing coffin plates with zoom cameras and searching church archives, death records and newspapers to try to identify the interred. The discovery underscores how routine infrastructure projects in New York can unearth forgotten historic remains and artifacts, prompting careful archaeological study and coordination with the Landmarks Preservation Commission. Access near the site has been restricted during the investigation.

New York Gov. David Paterson appeared on Larry King Live to confront persistent, sensational rumors—spurred by talk of an unpublished New York Times story—about alleged sexual and drug misconduct. Paterson repeatedly denied the rumors, calling them "flat-out lie[s]" and lamented that speculation has flourished because the Times has not published or clarified its reporting. He urged the media to investigate the sources spreading the allegations rather than amplify them, and suggested the public’s sensitivity after Eliot Spitzer’s scandal has made such stories stick. Paterson refused to rebut each charge individually, saying detailed denials might only fuel gossip, and insisted addressing rumors hasn’t clarified anything; he even hinted someone might be targeting him. Mixing sober defense with gallows humor, he begged the Times to "clear the air" or publish so the ordeal could end, while dismissing talk of resignation.

Former Army Capt. William D. Swenson received the Medal of Honor for risking his life during the 2009 Battle of Ganjgal in Afghanistan, where he repeatedly braved intense fire to recover bodies and assist wounded comrades. Awarded by President Obama, the ceremony followed years of controversy after Swenson’s nomination was reportedly misplaced, prompting investigations and congressional intervention; two commanders later received reprimands. Swenson, who left the Army in 2011 and also holds a Purple Heart and Bronze Star, has formally requested to return to active duty — a rare move for a living Medal of Honor recipient. Officials say he must complete routine reviews and are optimistic his reenlistment can proceed.

A deadly bus crash in North Hwanghae province, North Korea, killed 32 Chinese tourists and four North Koreans when the tour bus plunged off a bridge on Sunday night. Two Chinese were seriously injured. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited a hospital treating the victims, met Chinese Ambassador Li Jinjun at the embassy, and expressed “bitter sorrow” and condolences, an unusually public acknowledgement. China sent medical staff and diplomats to assist. Chinese tourists make up the vast majority of visitors to North Korea and are an important source of hard currency; the accident was shown in state media amid scenes of wreckage and poor road conditions.

An apparent international crime syndicate stole more than 1.4 billion yen (about US$12.7m) from Japanese ATMs in under three hours on the morning of May 15, police say. Around 100 people allegedly used forged credit cards—data believed to have been illegally obtained from a South African bank—to make 14,000 coordinated withdrawals of 100,000 yen each at roughly 1,400 convenience-store machines across Tokyo and 16 prefectures. Withdrawals began just after 5am and ended before 8am, and no suspects have been arrested; authorities suspect many perpetrators may have already left Japan. Transaction records point to roughly 1,600 compromised card accounts. Japanese police have asked South African authorities, via Interpol, to investigate how the card data were leaked. The bank implicated called the incident a sophisticated coordinated fraud, said customers did not lose money, and moved quickly to contain the breach. Japan has been targeted before in similar global ATM frauds.

The Porsche and Piëch clans, who control a 52% voting stake in Volkswagen through Porsche SE, have largely stayed out of public view as VW reels from its diesel-emissions scandal, creating a leadership void that labor and management struggles have had to fill. Wolfgang Porsche, the family’s understated patriarch, largely avoided public comment during the crisis until December, when he addressed 20,000 Wolfsburg workers to pledge job preservation and express confidence in VW’s ability to recover, but offered little about the fraudulent emissions cheating that affected 11 million vehicles and has cost VW billions. The episode has cut the family’s paper wealth and forced VW to post record losses and set aside large reserves to cover scandal costs, squeezing dividends from the holding company.

The extended family—about 80 members with varied careers—has long prioritized consensus and discretion, and succession has been slow: older patriarchs remain in control while the next generation shows mixed interest in running the car business. A few younger members, like Mark Philipp Porsche and Peter Daniell Porsche, have taken limited board roles or advisory posts, but the family’s governing structures and rules around share sales aim to maintain unity rather than active stewardship. Ferdinand Piëch, the sharp-edged former SVB chairman who steered VW to global prominence, was forced out last year after clashes with management; his absence removed a dominant voice and left Wolfgang more isolated.

With the family largely disengaged, VW’s strong unions—holding significant supervisory-board representation—have asserted themselves, led by union boss Bernd Osterloh, insisting workers won’t bear the scandal’s costs. Meanwhile, disputes over the company’s handling of its wartime past and the departure of corporate historian Manfred Grieger have prompted criticism that VW remains cautious and opaque in confronting sensitive history, echoing concerns about its transparency during the emissions controversy. Overall, the crisis has exposed governance gaps in the family-controlled conglomerate and raised questions about succession, oversight, and corporate accountability.

Jon Stewart announced he will step down as host of Comedy Central’s The Daily Show later this year, ending a nearly 17-year run that transformed the program into a major force in political satire and late-night television. Stewart, 52, revealed the news during a taping, saying he’s still working out timing — “I’m up in September, might be December or July” — and that the show “doesn’t deserve an even slightly restless host.” He said he had “a lot of ideas” but no specific plans, and looked forward to spending more time with family.

Stewart took over the show in January 1999 from Craig Kilborn and under his stewardship it won numerous Emmys and launched the careers of many comedians, including Stephen Colbert, John Oliver and Samantha Bee. He became a prominent political satirist and influential interviewer, famously challenging cable news and advocating causes like benefits for 9/11 first responders and supporting international satirists such as Bassem Youssef. Stewart also directed the film Rosewater during a recent hiatus. Comedy Central president Michele Ganeless praised his impact and said the show will endure beyond his departure. The network has not named a successor.

A dining dispute at Restaurant Marc Forgione in TriBeCa turned into a public kicking-out after diner Ron Lieber confronted the chef for loudly berating staff in full view of patrons. Lieber, disturbed by the chef’s sustained yelling and the visible distress of a server, walked into the open kitchen to ask the chef to stop. The chef responded that the kitchen is a sacred space and that his corrections were about maintaining quality; after a tense exchange, he asked Lieber and his party to leave. Lieber defends speaking up despite acknowledging he might have handled it better. A former waitress’s response condemns Lieber’s intrusion into the kitchen as entitled, arguing customers should respect restaurant choreography and staff and offering etiquette tips: make eye contact, respect pacing, avoid making a mess, complain promptly if something’s wrong, handle the check efficiently, tip at least 20 percent in fine dining, and never enter the kitchen. The incident highlights tensions between diners’ expectations of civility and chefs’ intense backstage standards; Forgione refused to serve Lieber thereafter.

Cambodian authorities confirmed they will not extradite French architect Patrick Henri Devillers, detained in Phnom Penh amid an investigation tied to China’s biggest recent political scandal. Cambodia’s foreign minister said Devillers, whose exact location and the charges against him remain undisclosed, will stay in custody for further local investigation rather than being sent to France or China. Devillers, 52, has lived in Cambodia for years and was closely connected to the circle of disgraced Chinese politician Bo Xilai and Bo’s wife, Gu Kailai, a chief suspect in the November murder of British businessman Neil Heywood. Chinese authorities reportedly sought Devillers over alleged involvement in moving Gu’s undeclared funds overseas. Chinese probes into Gu have alleged bribe-taking, large cross-border remittances (possibly billions), and elicited a reported confession; investigators have detained numerous Bo associates as the case unfolds.

This document compiles several distinct materials about presidential powers, historical impeachment articles, recent U.S. politics, and a breaking aid decision, together illustrating tensions over executive authority, accountability, and foreign policy.

It begins with a near-complete recitation of Article II of the U.S. Constitution, outlining the presidency: a four-year term with a vice president; the Electoral College mechanics; qualifications (natural-born citizen, 35 years old, 14 years’ residency); succession and temporary disability procedures; fixed presidential compensation; the oath of office; commander-in-chief status; powers to seek written opinions from executive department heads; grant reprieves and pardons (except in impeachment); make treaties and appoint senior officers with Senate advice and consent; fill Senate recess appointments; report the state of the union and convene Congress; ensure faithful execution of laws; and impeachment grounds for treason, bribery, and other high crimes and misdemeanors.

The text then reproduces Articles of Impeachment adopted by the House Judiciary Committee against President Richard Nixon in July 1974 (which never reached a full House vote). The two detailed articles accuse Nixon of obstructing justice—covering up the Watergate break-in, misleading investigators, misusing executive agencies, secret payments, and impeding inquiries—and of violating citizens’ constitutional rights by abusing IRS, FBI, CIA, and other institutions. The committee framed these actions as contrary to his oath and warranting impeachment and removal.

Interwoven are contemporary items: reporting that the Trump administration held up $125 million in U.S. aid to UNRWA pending a review, with potential further cuts up to $180 million—moves that could worsen humanitarian conditions in Gaza and other refugee areas and concern Israeli and U.N. officials. Also included is commentary from John Dowd, a Trump lawyer, asserting that a president cannot obstruct justice under Article II—echoing past defenses of executive prerogative—and defending a Trump tweet about Michael Flynn, while critics see such assertions as echoing Nixon-era claims about unchecked presidential power.
