Overall, the collection highlights recurring debates over the scope of executive authority, oversight, and the political consequences of using or withholding presidential powers.

Rookie began as Tavi Gevinson’s teenage passion project and grew into an influential online magazine and yearbook series for girls. Launched when she was 15, Rookie combined thoughtful cultural criticism, personal essays, music and fashion coverage, and visual art, curated around monthly themes. Gevinson—part teen wunderkind, part savvy editor—built a staff of contributors, attracted established voices, and expanded into events and print anthologies featuring interviews and pieces by big names alongside teen writers. The site fostered inclusion, aimed to validate young women’s tastes and intelligence, and amassed millions of monthly pageviews and a devoted readership.

A recurring concern in Rookie’s voice is the condescending treatment young women and their interests receive from older male critics. The magazine’s writers push back against cultural gatekeeping that dismisses teen tastes as trivial, argues that grown men often misread or belittle girls’ media consumption, and highlights how adult commentators misrepresent young women and female artists. Pieces defend teen fandoms, challenge biased music and film coverage, and call for listening to girls rather than speaking over them.

Rookie also published candid first-person essays about representation and body image, praising nuanced portrayals like Rae in My Mad Fat Diary while critiquing reductive Hollywood caricatures of fat women. The site showcased a wide range of pop culture appreciations—from Lorde’s breakout to classic TV and movies—rooted in a desire to give teenage voices respect, complexity, and a platform.

Keith Olbermann, the former MSNBC anchor, will return to television with a prime-time, one-hour nightly show on Current TV beginning in the spring, and he will also serve as the network’s chief news officer. Current TV, a lower-rated cable channel co-founded by Al Gore and Joel Hyatt, hopes Olbermann’s high-profile move will boost its visibility; the channel targets younger viewers and mixes user-generated content with traditional programming. Olbermann reportedly will take an equity stake in Current and gain greater editorial independence than at corporate-owned networks. His departure from MSNBC in January followed tensions with management and a contractual waiting period, which his Current start will respect. Current is available in fewer homes than MSNBC and often on digital tiers, so Olbermann’s audience may shrink, but his presence promises heightened attention. He has also hinted at pursuing additional ventures, including online projects. In announcing the move, Olbermann praised Current’s independent model and its dedication to editorial content, framing the partnership as an exciting new chapter in his career.

Emma Paulsen, a Langley, B.C., dog walker, has been charged following the deaths of six dogs left in her care last May. The animals died of heatstroke after being left in the back of her truck on a day that reached about 25 C. Paulsen initially reported the dogs stolen from her vehicle at a Langley dog park; their bodies were found in a ditch in the Fraser Valley a week later during a community search. The B.C. SPCA and Crown approved multiple charges under the Criminal Code and the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, including killing or injuring an animal, causing unnecessary pain or suffering, failing to provide necessities, reporting an offence when it did not occur, and two counts of causing animals to remain in distress — a precedent-setting application of a preventative duty-of-care provision. The charges carry potential prison terms, hefty fines, and possible lifetime bans on animal ownership; the date of Paulsen’s first court appearance is not yet known. Owners say they seek justice for their pets.

On May 13 in South Carolina, AP reports 18-year-old inmate Ezekiel Stevenson tried to escape during a hospital visit by carjacking a nearby vehicle. The plan failed because the car’s driver still had the key fob on him. When Stevenson pulled the driver from the car and attempted to drive off, the owner used the proximity key to shut the vehicle down remotely, leaving it immobile. Stevenson tried to lock the doors from inside, but the owner repeatedly unlocked them with the fob until police could enter. Stevenson fled into nearby woods but was captured within an hour. The incident highlights a rare win for proximity key technology: instead of the simpler vulnerability of a conventional physical key, the fob allowed the owner to disable and regain control of the car, prompting the writer to grudgingly apologize for previously resenting proximity keys.

“If I Stay,” adapted by R.J. Cutler and Shauna Cross from Gayle Forman’s young-adult novel, is a sentimental, visually polished melodrama in the vein of “The Fault in Our Stars.” Chloe Grace Moretz stars as Mia Hall, a 17-year-old cello prodigy who survives a catastrophic snowy highway crash that kills much of her family. The film alternates between Mia’s out-of-body presence at the hospital — where she watches over her coma-bound body and the loved ones she may never see again — and flashbacks to the comfortable, music-soaked life she cherished in Portland. Jamie Blackley plays Adam, her earnest guitarist boyfriend, and Mireille Enos and Joshua Leonard are warmly understated as her effortlessly cool, music-quoting parents. Stacy Keach provides a moving turn as Mia’s grandfather.

Cutler’s direction bathes the film in a soft amber glow and a slightly dreamy, out-of-focus look, reinforcing the story’s aestheticized wish-fulfillment. Cross’s screenplay keeps dialogue simple and emotionally direct, occasionally leaning toward maudlin or saccharine moments. The movie’s supernatural premise—Mia as an active, busybody wraith—can feel implausible and diminishes some dramatic tension, as her hospital wanderings and repeated flashbacks prolong the anguished vigil. Moretz, known for edgier roles, plays Mia with restraint but is sometimes subsumed by the character’s bland, earnest center; Blackley fares better, particularly in scenes that showcase the urgency of young love. Musical interludes, including a backyard jam, inject welcome energy into otherwise talky, tear-driven sequences.

Despite its clumsier elements and overt emotional squeezing, “If I Stay” delivers genuine sweetness and affecting tenderness, making it likely to resonate with young audiences seeking catharsis. The film’s central question—whether Mia will choose life or let go—culminates in an empowering, if predictable, declaration of agency: a teen “running the show” amid near-death choices. Rated PG-13; 106 minutes.

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un announced in his New Year’s address that Pyongyang is in the “final stages” of preparing to test-launch an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), framing it as part of ongoing efforts to develop long-range nuclear strike capabilities. Broadcast on state media, the speech asserted that research and development of “cutting-edge arms” is progressing and emphasized strengthening pre-emptive strike and self-defense capacities, with nuclear weapons described as a cornerstone policy as long as the United States and South Korea continue joint military exercises. Kim’s remarks followed a year of intense weapons activity in 2016—two nuclear tests, a satellite launch viewed as a long-range missile technology trial, and frequent ballistic missile launches—and come amid international sanctions that were tightened after Pyongyang’s fifth and largest nuclear test. Analysts have cautioned that, despite the rhetoric and rapid testing pace, North Korea may still be years from a deployable ICBM with a nuclear warhead capable of striking the U.S. The speech was notable for a partly contrite tone: Kim apologized to citizens for unmet goals in 2016 and pledged renewed efforts on their behalf, while also criticizing South Korea’s political turmoil and naming the impeached President Park Geun-hye in denunciation of anti-unification activities. Domestically, he highlighted economic campaigns (the 70- and 200-day battles), flood recovery, and plans to continue a five-year economic strategy with emphasis on science, power generation, heavy industry, and especially light industry and consumer goods. In Seoul, Acting President Hwang Kyo-ahn vowed to bolster military readiness and upheld plans to deploy the U.S. THAAD missile-defense system despite opposition from China and domestic critics, reflecting heightened regional tensions in response to Pyongyang’s advances.

Black Friday turns post-Thanksgiving bargain hunting into a competitive, high-adrenaline endeavor that many local shoppers treat like a sport. Seasoned shoppers like Rosemary Rizzo, who leaves home late on Thanksgiving to queue for midnight openings at outlets, emphasize traveling light, going solo, and meticulous preplanning—subscribing to deal sites, studying circulars while finishing turkey, and mapping an efficient route. Organization at checkout—having flyers, lists, and payment ready—is crucial. Rizzo’s successes include rare finds and steep markdowns; she calls Black Friday her holiday and even considers offering personal-shopping services. For others, like Matt Kane, Black Friday is a contest of strategy: days of research, store reconnaissance, and product placement scouting. Veteran shoppers share practical tips: do your homework by poring over ads and prioritizing must-have items; scout stores beforehand; pay attention to sale windows; and decide what purchases matter most. Bring backup to hold places in line and to split up inside stores to grab multiple items. Prepare physically by sleeping strategically, packing snacks, and fueling with coffee, since many sales start at midnight. Finally, manage expectations and attitude—treat it as intense but fun, and weigh ethical choices about aggressive behavior. For many, the rush of finding deals and completing holiday shopping in hours makes the chaos worth it.

U.S. Army Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl, who was freed from Taliban captivity on May 31 after nearly five years, is en route to the United States and scheduled to arrive at Brooke Army Medical Center in San Antonio, Texas, for continued rehabilitation. Pentagon officials confirm he departed Ramstein Air Base and will arrive early Friday; he has been recuperating at Landstuhl Regional Medical Center in Germany since June 1. Bergdahl, who went missing from his post in Paktika province in June 2009 while serving with the 1st Battalion, 501st Infantry, has not yet spoken with his family as medical staff determine when he is emotionally ready. An Army fact-finding inquiry previously concluded he left his outpost deliberately, but no formal desertion finding exists because intent remains unknown without interviewing him. Reports indicate harsh captivity conditions, including confinement in a dark box and psychological trauma from physical abuse. The swap that secured his release—five Taliban detainees freed from Guantanamo Bay—prompted political controversy over detainee releases, presidential authority and notification of Congress. Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel defended the decision as Bergdahl’s best chance for freedom while facing pointed questioning from lawmakers about the timing and handling of his return and medical assessment.

On a pivotal primary night, Hillary Clinton consolidated her status as the likely Democratic nominee with major victories in Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Illinois, significantly widening her delegate lead over Bernie Sanders. Clinton’s wins—especially in Florida and Ohio—dented Sanders’s momentum after his upset in Michigan and made a November matchup with Republican frontrunner Donald Trump increasingly likely.

Ohio was the most closely watched contest: a Midwestern bellwether where the economy and trade were top voter concerns. Exit polls showed many Ohio voters blamed global trade for job losses; while Sanders had exploited that sentiment in Michigan, Clinton prevailed in Ohio by winning strong support from black voters, older voters, Democrats, and those prioritizing experience and electability. Her campaign emphasized a revamped economic message focused on bringing manufacturing jobs back to the Midwest, deploying heavy organizing and appearances by Bill Clinton and herself in working-class cities. Sanders continued to press economic critique—attacking trade deals, corporate behavior, and Clinton’s Wall Street ties—and drew large crowds, especially among independents and voters under 30, but his gains were not enough to shift the delegate math.

Clinton dominated Florida, capturing large majorities among Hispanics, blacks and female voters, and adding a substantial haul of pledged delegates. Those victories pushed her delegate margin to roughly 300 pledged delegates and a far larger advantage when superdelegates are included—an edge bigger than the one Barack Obama held over her in 2008. Clinton framed her wins as momentum toward the general election, pivoting sharply against Trump in remarks that criticized his rhetoric on immigrants, Muslims and use of torture.

On the Republican side, Donald Trump reinforced his frontrunner status with wins in Florida, North Carolina and Illinois, while Ohio delivered John Kasich his first victory—an important rebuke to Trump in his home region and a boost to anti-Trump conservatives hoping to prevent a straightforward Trump coronation. Marco Rubio’s crushing loss in Florida ended his campaign and underscored the GOP’s ongoing fragmentation, leaving open scenarios that could lead to a contested convention in Cleveland.

Both parties left the night with different dynamics: Democrats appeared to be coalescing around Clinton as the pragmatic choice to take on Trump, while Republicans remained divided among Trump, Cruz and Kasich, producing continued uncertainty in that primary race. For Sanders, the path forward grew much more difficult: he remained competitive in many states and energized many voters, but institutional realities of proportional delegate allocation meant he now needed a string of large-margin victories in big states to have a viable chance.

After a deadly attack on a Tennessee military facility, armed civilians began volunteering to guard recruiting centers nationwide, prompting mixed reactions and official warnings. In Lancaster, Ohio, volunteers stationed at a recruiting office were ordered off property after one guard, Christopher Reed, accidentally discharged his AR-15 while attempting to clear it; no one was injured, and the pavement was damaged. Reed was cited on a misdemeanor charge; he previously had a similar conviction. The shopping center owner cited tenant and public safety and insurance concerns for asking the volunteers to leave. Similar scenes unfolded in Spanaway, Washington, and elsewhere, where landlords and local authorities urged armed volunteers to disperse over liability worries.

Military leadership has cautioned against civilian vigilantes. The Army and Marine Corps issued directives telling recruiters not to interact with armed citizens, to treat them as potential security threats, and to notify law enforcement and property lessors. A Marine Corps memo stressed that well-intentioned volunteers could be counterproductive, risk negligent discharges, deter recruits, and disrupt operations. Groups like Oath Keepers and the “3 Percenters” have organized or encouraged watches, and some volunteers—often veterans—say they act to protect unarmed recruiters. Authorities urge community support through reporting suspicious activity rather than by armed civilian patrols.

BP has filed a federal civil-fraud suit in New Orleans accusing Texas lawyer Mikal C. Watts of inflating its 2010 Gulf oil-spill settlement costs by claiming to represent tens of thousands of “phantom” seafood-industry claimants. BP says it relied on Watts’s representations in agreeing to a $2.3 billion seafood compensation fund and now seeks to halt payments and recover unspent money it labels the product of “brazen fraud.” The company contends Watts claimed more than 40,000 deckhands—about 76–80 percent of projected potential claimants—yet ultimately filed only 648 individual crew claims through the seafood program; of those, BP says only eight were found eligible and 17 remain pending. In related filings under a separate compensation program Watts submitted 43,976 claims; BP’s review found 40 percent used Social Security numbers belonging to someone else, 13 percent used incomplete or dummy numbers, and 5 percent used numbers of deceased people. BP argues the evidence gives an “overwhelming” inference of fraud and that the inflated claimant count produced an undeserved windfall for the class if left unaddressed. Watts’s lawyer insists he acted in good faith, forwarding documentation to the independent special master and denying identity theft or fraud. The controversy has prompted judicial scrutiny—Judge Carl Barbier paused payments while appointing Louis Freeh to investigate—and appellate review; prosecutors executed search warrants at Watts’s office earlier this year and he has resigned from the plaintiffs’ steering committee. Plaintiffs’ lawyers counter that BP is using the Watts allegations to undermine payments to legitimate claimants.

Searchers intensified efforts for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 after authorities shifted the search nearly 700 miles northeast to a new zone in the southern Indian Ocean about 1,100 miles west of Perth. Aircraft from China and Australia reported floating objects on consecutive days; ships recovered several items but investigators concluded none have been confirmed as wreckage from the Boeing 777. The revised area, about 123,000 square miles—roughly the size of New Mexico or Poland—is smaller and closer to Perth, offering better weather and longer on-station time for planes, but remains vast and challenging. Analysis of March 8 radar data, aided by Boeing analysts, indicated the plane likely flew faster and burned fuel sooner than first thought, prompting the redeployment. A multinational flotilla, naval vessels and an Australian ship equipped to detect black box pings are converging on the zone; pingers are detectable for about 30 days. Families, many from China, pressed Malaysian officials for answers as hopes for debris recovery persist and the difficult task of locating wreckage and recorders continues.

Tabloid reports claim Al Gore’s split from wife Tipper after 40 years stems from a two‑year affair with environmentalist Laurie David, who co‑produced his documentary An Inconvenient Truth and divorced Larry David in 2007. Star magazine quotes an unnamed insider saying “Al and Laurie went from friends to lovers,” but Gore friends and a spokeswoman dismissed the story as “complete crap,” and Gore declined comment. Other gossip outlets have floated varying, unproven explanations for the shock separation, from Tipper’s jealousy to rumors about Gore’s sexuality.

The NFL-appointed independent investigation led by attorney Ted Wells concluded that Miami Dolphins guard Richie Incognito, guard John Jerry and center Mike Pouncey engaged in a pattern of harassment against teammate Jonathan Martin, another unnamed young offensive lineman, and an assistant trainer. Wells’ 144-page report, based on more than 100 interviews and thousands of documents and messages, found that the assistant trainer was repeatedly targeted with racial slurs, the other lineman endured homophobic name-calling and inappropriate touching, and Martin was persistently taunted with sexually explicit, racial and other offensive remarks—including graphic references to his sister and later his mother. Investigators determined Incognito was the primary instigator, with Jerry and Pouncey following his lead. Although the report concluded Martin’s teammates did not intend to drive him from the team or inflict lasting emotional injury, it found their conduct amounted to bullying and harassment that contributed to Martin’s departure in October and to his documented emotional distress, including two instances of contemplating suicide in 2013 and a hospitalization after a cafeteria incident.

Wells grappled with complicating factors: Martin’s prior history of bullying, possible depression and an “odd but seemingly close” friendship with Incognito, who often texted and joked with Martin. A consulting psychologist advised Martin’s behavior was consistent with a victim trying to fit in with an abuser. Wells also cited evidence like entries in a fines “kangaroo court” notebook—notes about “breaking Jmart” and efforts to destroy the book—as proof Incognito knew his conduct was improper.

The report criticized certain team culture and oversight, noting Dolphins workplace rules were not fully appreciated and that coach Joe Philbin and front office personnel were unaware of the harassment; investigators said they believed Philbin would have acted had he known. The report discredited some denials from implicated players and staff and found some claims (like a purported physical attack at a 2012 party) exaggerated but still humiliating to Martin.

Incognito’s lawyer blasted the report as erroneous and promised a counter-analysis. The Dolphins, NFL and NFLPA said they would review the findings. Team owner Stephen Ross called the language and behavior “deeply disturbing” and pledged initiatives and new policies to prevent recurrence. Wells and his firm offered no further comment.

Mary Kay Letourneau and Vili Fualaau have maintained an unusually controversial marriage that recently marked its 10th anniversary. Their relationship began when Letourneau, then a 34-year-old sixth-grade teacher, had a sexual relationship with 13-year-old student Vili Fualaau, resulting in two daughters, Audrey and Georgia, and a highly publicized criminal case. Letourneau served about seven and a half years in prison; the couple married in 2005, a year after her release. In an exclusive Barbara Walters interview airing on ABC’s 20/20, the pair reflect candidly on their decade together, acknowledging both the ups and downs of marriage and the extraordinary challenges they've faced. Vili, now 31, says no marriage is without hard times and emphasizes the importance of getting through them together. He also opens up about struggling with alcoholism and depression and feeling unsupported during his teen years, saying the system failed him as a minor. Letourneau, now 53, discusses what has kept their marriage intact despite the vast age difference and public scrutiny, and reveals plans to return to teaching and attempt to have her registered sex offender status lifted. The interview will also introduce their daughters, who are older than Vili was when they were conceived. Both say they expect renewed media intrusion around their anniversary and are focused on protecting their family amid continuing public interest.

The Mississippi special Senate runoff on Nov. 27 decided the last seat of the 116th Congress, determining whether Republicans would hold 52 or 53 seats. The nonpartisan special election pitted incumbent appointee Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, a former state agriculture and commerce commissioner, against Democrat Mike Espy, a former agriculture secretary under Bill Clinton and ex-Congressman. Hyde-Smith led the Nov. 6 jungle primary by a razor-thin margin (41.3% to Espy’s 40.9%), forcing the runoff since no candidate topped 50%.

The race drew heavy national involvement: President Trump held two rallies for Hyde-Smith, the NRSC and Senate Leadership Fund spent heavily, and Democrats countered with surrogates and the Senate Majority PAC. Hyde-Smith’s campaign was marred by controversy after she joked she’d be “on the front row” for a “public hanging,” prompting corporate donors to rescind contributions and intensifying scrutiny of her ties to Confederate-symbol history. Republicans emphasized Espy’s past indictment (he was acquitted) and lobbying work for an Ivory Coast dictator. 

Mississippi’s deep racial polarization makes Democratic victory difficult: black voters (nearly 36–38% of the electorate) vote heavily Democratic, but white voters are strongly Republican, making statewide swings rare. Polling showed Hyde-Smith with a consistent lead; analysts warned that only an unusual turnout surge among black voters or depressed GOP turnout—similar to the Alabama upset in 2017—could hand Espy a narrow win. In the end, Hyde-Smith prevailed, preserving a Republican 53-47 Senate majority.

The day before the 2016 election, Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton published dueling op-eds in USA Today to make final appeals to the national electorate. Each piece largely echoed their campaign themes: Trump reiterated his promise to “drain the swamp” and fix what he called a “rigged system” favoring political insiders, and he referenced Clinton as having “been the subject of an FBI criminal investigation,” omitting Director James Comey’s same-day announcement that she had been cleared again. The Trump campaign did not respond about updating the op-ed after Comey’s statement.

Clinton’s op-ed outlined a vision for a presidency focused on unity and pragmatic problem-solving. She framed the choice as one between inclusive, constructive change and divisiveness, warning that her opponent’s campaign had relied on fear, insults and pitting Americans against each other. Drawing on her experience as first lady, senator and secretary of state, she presented four priorities for her first 100 days: a major investment in job-creating infrastructure and manufacturing, aiming for renewable energy to power every U.S. home within a decade and asking the wealthy and big corporations to pay their fair share; comprehensive immigration reform establishing a path to citizenship while securing borders and targeting violent criminals; a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United to reduce unaccountable money in politics and protect voters’ voices; and end-to-end criminal justice reform to address excessive incarceration for nonviolent offenses. Clinton emphasized she would be a president for all Americans and pledged to work across the aisle. She closed by urging voters to choose change that brings the country together, expressing confidence in America’s potential if citizens invest in one another.

Eight-year-old Chloe-May Kabealo, the sole survivor of a drowning crash in northern New South Wales, has attended the funeral for her mother Stephanie King, 43, and siblings Ella Jane, 11, and Jacob, 7. Hundreds gathered at Tweed Heads Elevation Church to farewell the family after the van slid off a muddy Tumbulgum road into the swollen Tweed River during heavy rains from Cyclone Debbie. Police described Stephanie King as heroic, saying she was trying to free and hold one child when she lost consciousness and drowned; officers believe her efforts helped Chloe escape. Chloe unbuckled her seatbelt, surfaced, climbed the riverbank and ran to a nearby farmhouse to raise the alarm. She was treated for cuts, abrasions and neck pain at Tweed Heads District Hospital. Locals, including former officer Matt Grinham who searched the site, assisted after the crash. Chloe and her father Matt Kabealo have received wide community support; a police-coordinated fundraiser raised over $10,000 and broader donations have gathered tens of thousands to help them. Chloe said her family “were all loved and they’ll never be forgotten,” while her father said he is “shattered” but trying to stay strong for her.

On September 6 in Wasilla, Alaska, a large, alcohol-fueled brawl erupted at a birthday party at Korey Klingenmeyer’s home that involved members of the Palin family. Police audio obtained by media outlets captures chaotic, profane exchanges between Bristol, Willow and Sarah Palin and partygoers in the immediate aftermath. Bristol, distraught and visibly upset, told officers she was shoved to the ground, dragged by her feet, called obscene names and had her shoes and sunglasses taken. She repeatedly said she was defending her younger sister Willow after an older woman allegedly shoved and punched her. Willow alternately accused a 30-year-old man—identified on the tape as Korey in a red shirt—of pushing Bristol down and calling her a “slut,” while Sarah angrily demanded police hold “the bad guys” accountable.

Other witnesses gave conflicting accounts. Some partygoers and a Palin family friend, Matthew McKenna, said Bristol had been aggressive and punched Klingenmeyer multiple times, prompting others to restrain and throw her to the ground. One onlooker noted video of parts of the incident existed. The official police reporting describes Klingenmeyer saying he told Bristol to leave, that she then repeatedly struck him, and that he grabbed and held her arm while pushing her down to stop her.

No charges were filed after the melee. Media recordings show profanity-laced statements, family members pressed and emotional, and Sarah Palin complaining about perceived preferential treatment of others at the scene. The episode has drawn intense public attention and remains a developing story.

A Mississippi teenager launched Change.org petitions after discovering brominated vegetable oil (BVO) — a flame-retardant–linked chemical banned in Europe and Japan — listed in some sports drinks. Her Gatorade petition gained over 200,000 signatures and led PepsiCo to remove BVO from its beverages. She then turned attention to Powerade, noting that fruit punch and strawberry lemonade flavors sold at her school still contained BVO and worried athletes and children were being exposed. Scientific reports cited by the petitioner link BVO and bromine to accumulation in the body and possible effects on hormones, fertility, development and thyroid function. Public pressure and similar ingredient concerns across the food industry have prompted reformulations elsewhere, and Coca-Cola has now confirmed Powerade is “BVO-free,” with some bottles already omitting the ingredient while others still list it, indicating a phased change. The move reflects growing consumer scrutiny of additives and companies’ responsiveness to health-minded customers, especially for products marketed to athletes and youth. The petitioner urged continued awareness and support to ensure safer ingredient choices.

A widely known Kenyan lion named Mohawk was shot dead by Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) rangers on March 30 after escaping Nairobi National Park and injuring a man in Kajiado/Isinya. Mohawk, a 13-year-old black-maned male famed among tourists and often seen with lionesses, had slipped out of the park’s southern, unfenced migration area amid territorial disputes. Hundreds of locals gathered around him, reportedly taunting, throwing stones and taking photos for hours; that crowd’s noise and provocation agitated the animal. When the lion lunged at a boda boda (motorcycle) rider and inflicted deep lacerations, rangers said they had no choice but to shoot because tranquilizer darts would take minutes to immobilize him and could risk more human injuries. Videos and eyewitness accounts showed Mohawk being struck multiple times; critics and many Kenyans expressed outrage online, using #JusticeforMohawk, arguing that rangers lacked proper tranquilizing equipment and that alternative responses should have been attempted. Local officials and conservationists blamed habitat loss, infrastructure projects, and damaged electric fencing around Nairobi National Park for rising escapes. Nairobi National Park, a 117 sq km reserve bordering the city, has seen several recent lion breakouts as urban expansion and construction disturb traditional ranges. Separately, in South Africa, a lion dubbed Sylvester escaped Karoo National Park for the second time; having previously killed livestock, officials initially planned to euthanize him but faced public backlash and are now considering capture, relocation, improved fencing, or transfer to a conservation group—reserving killing only if he poses a major human threat. Both incidents highlight the fraught balance between public safety and conserving lions, whose populations have plunged over decades due to habitat loss, hunting and human-wildlife conflict, and whose vulnerability was spotlighted recently by high-profile killings like Cecil the lion. Wildlife agencies cite limited resources, risky terrain and immediate threats to people as drivers behind lethal responses, while activists press for better preventive measures and nonlethal capture capabilities.

Pro‑Russian demonstrators in eastern Ukraine seized government buildings in Donetsk, Luhansk and Kharkiv in early April, waving Russian flags and demanding Crimea‑style referendums on joining Russia. In Donetsk protesters broke into the regional administration and security service offices, hung a Russian flag, proclaimed a Donetsk People’s Republic and set a referendum date no later than May 11. Activists in Luhansk reportedly seized a weapons cache in a security service building; authorities said several people were injured and arrests had been made. Kharkiv’s main administration was briefly occupied but later cleared, according to Interior Minister Arsen Avakov. Protesters chanted for Russia, called for peacekeeping troops, and urged Putin’s support, while some cited fears of EU and NATO alignment and claimed protection for Russian speakers.

Kiev’s interim leadership accused Moscow and ousted President Viktor Yanukovich of orchestrating the unrest as part of a broader plan to destabilize Ukraine and provide a pretext for Russian forces to cross the border. Prime Minister Arseniy Yatseniuk warned that Russian troops were massed near the frontier and said militants with Russian accents were coordinating actions. Officials in Kiev insisted they would restore order without bloodshed and enacted security meetings and response plans.

Russia has annexed Crimea after a disputed referendum and proposed federalizing Ukraine; Moscow denies direct orchestration but has positioned forces and publicized the eastern demonstrations. Analysts view the eastern seizures as at least partly staged to undermine Kiev, complicate Western support and influence Ukraine’s political future while the interim government struggles with economic reforms and an urgent IMF aid package.

Researchers have identified a new blood-transmissible virus, human hepegivirus-1 (HHpgV-1), that is genetically related to both hepatitis C (a liver-damaging virus) and human pegivirus (generally considered harmless). The discovery, reported in mBio by a Columbia University–led team, came from deep sequencing of archived blood samples from people who had received transfusions or plasma products in the 1970s–1980s. HHpgV-1 sequences were found in two of 46 donors after transfusion and in two of 106 heavily transfused hemophilia patients; in some cases infections persisted for years, but all identified individuals ultimately cleared the virus and none showed evidence of resulting disease. Investigators have not yet isolated live virus or cultivated it in cell culture, but multiple experts judge the genomic findings credible rather than contamination. At present there is no indication HHpgV-1 causes illness, and specialists caution against alarm: current blood screening and modern plasma treatments already reduce transmission risk, and many newly discovered human viruses appear benign or common without clear pathogenicity. The immediate priority is developing antibody tests to assess how widespread HHpgV-1 is, determine prior exposure in larger populations, and evaluate any links to disease through controlled comparisons. The work highlights both the power of deep sequencing to reveal previously unrecognized viral diversity and the ongoing need for surveillance of the blood supply—more than 30 million blood components are transfused annually in the U.S. alone. In the same mBio issue, the team also reported a related novel virus in seals (phopivirus), suggesting a broader and older evolutionary diversity among these viruses and offering potential clues about origins and pathogenic potential of human hepatitis viruses.

Yahoo’s newly appointed CEO Marissa Mayer will receive a substantial compensation package designed to lure her from Google and incentivize a turnaround. Regulatory filings show Mayer could receive close to $60 million in immediate and near-term pay—comprising a $1 million base salary, a performance bonus up to $4 million, a $12 million 2012 equity award (half stock, half options vesting over three years), a $30 million one-time retention award vesting over five years ($15M stock, $15M options), and a $14 million make-whole payment for Google equity she forfeited. Overall, Yahoo expects to pay about $5.4 million this year and roughly $20 million annually thereafter, with total five-year payouts reported up to $100 million. The package was contentious among directors but championed by activist investor Dan Loeb, who helped engineer the hiring. Mayer’s appointment draws attention for her product expertise and potential to revitalize Yahoo amid longstanding struggles.

In 2009, FBI agent James Craig made a breakthrough in the long-running investigation of the Zeus banking malware when a seized New York–based server yielded tens of thousands of Russian- and Ukrainian-language instant-message logs tied to the gang’s Jabber communications. The logs offered a detailed road map of the operation: stolen credentials, lists of victims, operational chatter, and personnel roles. Mandiant and FBI specialists spent months untangling the code and translating slang-heavy chats. The files revealed how the group recruited and managed “money mules” — often students or recent immigrants — who opened accounts, received stolen funds, and withdrew cash just under reporting thresholds. Mules typically kept 5–10 percent, with the rest forwarded overseas. Investigators traced similar mule networks across Europe and estimated attributable thefts of $70–80 million, likely an undercount.

By summer 2010, New York agents alerted banks to suspicious cash-outs and arrested recruiters and other operatives in multiple U.S. cities. Parallel work in Omaha identified key Jabber Zeus figures in eastern Ukraine near Donetsk: Alexey Bron (“thehead”), money-movement specialist; Ivan Klepikov (“petr0vich”), IT and hosting manager; and Vyacheslav Penchukov (“tank”), who ran operations under mastermind Slavik. The gang flaunted profits on cars and vacations. In fall 2010, international raids in Donetsk seized massive amounts of data—nearly 20 terabytes—and led to 39 arrests across four countries, disrupting the network though several leaders escaped.

The suspected creator and ringleader, Evgeniy Mikhailovich Bogachev (aka “lucky12345” and “slavik”), remained elusive. Bogachev, last known to reside in Anapa, Russia, allegedly administered Zeus and later the GameOver Zeus variant, linked to over a million infections and more than $100 million in losses. He was indicted in U.S. federal courts in 2012 and 2014 on racketeering, fraud, computer-crime, identity-theft, and money-laundering charges, but evaded capture as investigators lost his online trace. After seven years on the case, Craig moved on while the hunt for Bogachev continued.

At Rosa Khutor, the men’s Olympic halfpipe became the site of a passing of the torch and sharp criticism of the course. Shaun White, bidding for a third straight gold, delivered an imperfect solo final and finished fourth as Switzerland’s Iouri Podladtchikov stunned with a flawless run anchored by a perfectly landed Yolo flip (1,440 degrees), earning 94.75 points. Japan’s 15-year-old Ayumu Hirano took silver and countryman Taku Hiraoka bronze, marking the first Olympic halfpipe podium without an American since the event’s 1998 debut. Several top riders, including Americans Danny Davis and Greg Bretz, struggled with the pipe’s uneven, choppy conditions; Davis called White’s placement “a gift” and credited the result with showcasing broader talent in the sport. Complaints about the halfpipe’s construction and maintenance surfaced during practice, with athletes urging postponement after bumpy transitions and a deteriorating flat bottom; crews worked overnight to improve it. White withdrew earlier from slopestyle over course concerns and said he’d chosen riskier tricks in the halfpipe to try to win, lamenting, “It just wasn’t my night.” Riders nonetheless acknowledged that the strongest competitors would rise despite imperfect conditions.

Searchers hunting Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 shifted to an underwater phase as a towed pinger locator was deployed to find the aircraft’s black box before its battery expires. Two ships—HMAS Ocean Shield towing a U.S. Navy locator and Britain’s HMS Echo—are sweeping a converging 240 km track in a 217,000–223,000 sq km area about 1,700 km northwest of Perth chosen from satellite data analysis indicating the highest probability of where the plane entered the ocean. The locator must be towed slowly and has a limited detection range, and officials warned the beacon’s battery life is about 30 days, making the effort a race against time. Surface searches continued with up to 14 aircraft and multiple ships, and crews reported several objects sighted but none linked to MH370. Coordinators stressed the importance of finding surface debris to narrow the subsea hunt; drift modelling and physical evidence remain preferred methods when available. The Boeing 777 vanished on 8 March en route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing with 239 people aboard and is believed to have crashed in the southern Indian Ocean after satellite “handshakes” suggested continued flight hours after radar contact ended. Investigators have not ruled out mechanical failure but say evidence points to deliberate diversion; international teams continue intensive search operations.

A Consumer Reports study found store-brand groceries average 30% cheaper than name brands, sometimes saving shoppers up to 52% on items. In 21 taste tests, national brands won seven times, store brands won three, and the rest tied; overall store or tie outcomes were common. Nutrition was similar for most products. Despite stigma—especially among 18–39-year-olds—84% bought store brands last year, which made up nearly a quarter of supermarket sales and $55.5 billion nationally.

Six-year-old Alessandra Perez told a therapist she had seen two adoptive children at her grandparents’ house repeatedly abused — locked in a bathroom with a taped shower curtain, forced to stand in garbage bins, and told to keep silent. That disclosure prompted a brief child-welfare inquiry days before a shocking discovery: Jorge Barahona, 53, a pest exterminator, was found beside his red pickup on I-95 near West Palm Beach with one adopted 10-year-old twin, Nubia, dead in the truck’s bed, doused with acid and wrapped in plastic, and the other twin, Victor, critically injured and soaked in an unknown corrosive. Victor suffered severe chemical burns to his abdomen, thighs and buttocks, exhibited prior fractures, scarring and ligature marks, and is receiving intensive burn-unit care as doctors struggle to identify the agent and treat failing kidneys. Barahona told police he intended to commit suicide after placing Nubia’s body in the truck and gave Victor sleeping pills; he is charged with aggravated child abuse and remains hospitalized. Authorities have removed two other adopted children from the Barahona home to therapeutic foster care while investigations and potential further charges continue.

A large-scale vandalism at Mount Carmel Cemetery in Northeast Philadelphia left roughly 300 gravestones toppled and damaged, authorities said after the destruction was discovered late Saturday and reported Sunday morning. Volunteers are working to upright stones while a GoFundMe has been launched to cover repairs. The incident revived painful memories for the Jewish community; Naomi Adler of the Jewish Federation of Greater Philadelphia called the act “incredibly disgust[ing],” noting it evokes Holocaust-era fears whether or not it was motivated by anti‑Semitism. Mayor Jim Kenney pledged full prosecution of those responsible and urged city residents to stand with Jewish neighbors, and Gov. Tom Wolf called the attack “truly reprehensible,” ordering state resources to assist the investigation. The vandalism follows a recent similar incident in St. Louis and, less than two weeks earlier, damage at Holy Redeemer Cemetery in Philadelphia, though links between cases remain unclear. Multiple rewards totaling $69,000 have been offered for information leading to arrests and convictions, including contributions from the Mizel Family Foundation/Anti‑Defamation League, an anonymous donor, Councilman Allan Domb, Mayor Kenney’s office, and a Fraternal Order of Police lodge. Police continue investigating.

At a town hall in Decorah, Iowa, President Obama clashed with Tea Party activist Ryan Rhodes, who demanded to know whether Vice President Biden had called Tea Party members “terrorists” during the debt ceiling debate. Obama declined to directly confirm Biden said the word, instead pushing back that he, too, has been smeared—called a socialist, accused of being foreign-born, and blamed for taking away freedoms—and urged lowering the rhetoric. He told Rhodes he would discuss it further after the event, and they were later seen in an animated private conversation partially captured on camera, though audio was unclear. Rhodes told Fox News Obama denied Biden made the remark and accused the president of refusing to acknowledge widely broadcast reports, arguing this showed an unwillingness to engage without attacking Republicans. The dispute traces to a closed-door meeting where Rep. Mike Doyle called Tea Party-aligned Republicans “terrorists”; some Democrats said Biden appeared to agree to rally support, but Biden denied using that term. Members of the crowd criticized Rhodes’ confrontational approach, though he insisted he’d “said [his] piece.”

Michelle Hurst, who portrays Miss Claudette on Netflix’s Orange Is the New Black, has awakened after spending 16 days in a medically induced coma following a serious car accident just before the holidays. She remains in the ICU at UNC Chapel Hill Hospital, has opened her eyes and is responsive; doctors had used the coma to prevent movement during multiple surgeries near her spine. Castmates Natasha Lyonne and Matt McGorry shared a fundraising page to help cover medical bills and lost income, and the campaign surpassed its $5,000 goal—raising over $12,000 from more than 200 donors. Updates say she is “progressing slowly, but progressing.”

James Howells, an IT worker in Newport, South Wales, knows the precise location of a hard drive that contains 7,500 bitcoins he mined beginning in 2009, but local authorities refuse to allow him to retrieve it. Howells mined bitcoin on an old Dell M1710 and kept the drive after selling other parts. In 2013, during a home cleanout, he accidentally tossed the drive into a landfill. Since then the site has accumulated hundreds of thousands of tonnes of waste, making recovery complex and hazardous. With bitcoin’s price having climbed dramatically, those 7,500 coins are now worth well into the tens or hundreds of millions of dollars depending on valuation — a sum that has repeatedly renewed public interest in retrieving the drive.

Newport City Council has been approached several times but declines to permit an excavation. Officials cite the huge cost of digging, handling and treating waste, serious environmental risks such as dangerous gases and potential fires, and no guarantee the drive would be found or remain functional after exposure to landfill leachates and corrosion. The landfill holds roughly 350,000 tonnes of waste with about 50,000 tonnes added annually; any independent attempt would be illegal and likely to draw notice. Howells says he has financial backing and has discussed plans with the council, but insists digging a landfill isn’t simple and would require specialist equipment and expertise. He can still monitor the bitcoin address to confirm the coins haven’t moved, and stresses that even if found the data are encrypted and would require his cooperation to access. Howells remains active in cryptocurrency circles and believes the council might change its stance if bitcoin’s value rises high enough to justify the expense.

Crawls of the Obama White House website and subdomains were performed in the months before the administration ended (November 2016–January 2017). The content includes the launch of the @POTUS Twitter account by President Barack Obama from the Oval Office on May 18, 2015, where he announced the account would let him engage directly with the American people and support the administration’s transparency goals. The site lists related official accounts—@WhiteHouse, @VP, @FLOTUS, @DrBiden, @WHLive, @PressSec, @VJ44, @Psaki44, @LaCasaBlanca, and @PeteSouza—and links to a full directory. It also notes features like adding location to tweets, the First Lady’s account management and tweet signature convention (–mo), and archiving/privacy information at wh.gov/privacy.

Michael Clarke Duncan, a towering yet warm presence on screen, died at 54 after suffering a heart attack. The former bodyguard-turned-actor, whose gravelly baritone and gentle-giant persona endeared him to colleagues and audiences, rose to fame with his Oscar-nominated portrayal of death-row inmate John Coffey in 1999’s The Green Mile. That breakthrough role, opposite Tom Hanks, showcased his rare blend of intimidating physicality and underlying sweetness and led to steady work in films such as Armageddon, Planet of the Apes, Daredevil, Talladega Nights, The Whole Nine Yards, Sin City and voice roles in family hits like Kung Fu Panda and Brother Bear. Duncan began acting in his 30s after working as a bodyguard for stars including Will Smith and Jamie Foxx; the murder of Notorious B.I.G., once under his protection, helped push him into acting full time. Born in Chicago in 1957 and raised by a single mother, he supported her through physical labor and security jobs before moving to Los Angeles. Colleagues from Tom Hanks to Steve Harvey expressed shock and sorrow at his passing; his fiancée Omarosa Manigault asked for privacy while plans for memorials are arranged.

On Nov. 9, 1861, seven months into the Civil War, the luxurious 288-foot sidewheel steamer Keystone State vanished in Lake Huron with 33 crew lost; the vessel’s disappearance remained a Great Lakes maritime mystery for 152 years. Launched in 1849 as one of the largest ships on the lakes, the Keystone State left Detroit on Nov. 8, 1861, bound for Milwaukee carrying cargo listed as “iron implements” (farm machinery). Because the ship was on an unusual winter run and farm implements have limited seasonal use, longstanding rumors suggested the manifest masked military supplies or gold bound for the battlefield. No one even knew the ship had sunk until wreckage and the wheelhouse washed ashore more than a week later near Port Austin.

This December, shipwreck hunter David Trotter announced his Undersea Research Associates team discovered the wreck in July about 50 miles north of Michigan’s thumb in under 200 feet of water. Trotter, a retired Ford executive with over 35 years and 100-plus finds, and his team have made dozens of dives to document the site. They located an empty cargo hold, which may reflect crews jettisoning cargo to save the vessel during the storm, but the full reason for the missing manifest items likely won’t be known. The wreck lies further north than historical reports suggested, indicating the ship fought heavy seas before foundering; sidewheel design would have made maneuvering in troughs hazardous, possibly influencing Captain Wilkes Travers’ decisions.

Divers face tight bottom times—15 to 20 minutes—due to depth and long decompression, and a sizable debris field around the wreck remains largely unexplored. No gold has been found so far. Trotter continues to investigate how storm damage, impact with the lakebed, and 152 years of deterioration shaped the site, acknowledging some questions about the Keystone State’s final voyage may never be fully answered.

Two 14-year-olds, Austin Stephanos and Perry Cohen, went missing after taking a 19-foot white single-engine boat out off the Florida coast late last week. The empty boat was discovered Sunday about 67 miles off Daytona Beach; there was no sign of the boys. Families have pleaded with the public to search beaches from Palm Beach to Georgia for debris or clues, suggesting the teens might have fashioned makeshift flotation devices from a white engine cover, life jackets and a cooler.

Oceanographer Mitch Roffer of Roffer’s Ocean Fishing Forecasting Service in West Melbourne is assisting volunteer searchers by analyzing satellite imagery and ocean-current data. Roffer stressed how small variations in current speed and position relative to the Gulf Stream can dramatically change drift trajectories: a quarter-mile-per-hour difference can expand search areas from a few miles to dozens over time. If the boys entered the western edge of the Gulf Stream, Roffer estimated they could now be anywhere from 60 to 180 miles from their starting point, with trajectories extending northward from Cape Canaveral and roughly 30 miles seaward. He posted color-coded maps on social media for volunteer pilots and search teams.

Ted Lund, an outdoors writer and licensed boat captain, emphasized the ocean’s indifference and unforgiving nature, noting how quickly people can find themselves in peril. The Coast Guard continues search efforts as families and communities rally for any information.

The document collects varied 2010 tech and political forecasts and reflections. Analysts predicted growth for Google, Apple (notably a transformative, affordable tablet), YouTube profitability, Android momentum, and 3D TV’s rise. Views differed on netbooks, mobile phones, and companies: optimism for Microsoft’s Zune redesign but skepticism about it entering smartphones immediately; doubts about Palm’s survival; AMD’s prospects tied to Intel settlement funds; HP, Cisco, IBM and Oracle seen as oversold investment opportunities. Trends highlighted include SaaS, cloud services, mobile money, free software models, social-graph analytics, video proliferation, green IT, location-based services and augmented reality, and integration of social features into enterprise apps. Other pieces note social media’s growing influence, the explosion of content, and caution that many high-profile 2010 predictions ultimately proved wrong.

The document compiles multiple reactions to President Donald Trump’s public attacks on NFL players who kneel during the national anthem to protest racial injustice and police brutality. It traces the controversy’s origins to Colin Kaepernick’s protest last season and outlines how Trump’s rhetoric—calling protesting players “sons of b-----s” and urging owners to “get that son of a bitch off the field”—transformed a simmering debate into a full-blown culture war confrontation between the president and professional athletes.

One strand of the commentary situates the kneeling protest within broader democratic values, invoking the 1943 Supreme Court decision West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette. That ruling, written by Justice Robert Jackson, held that the state cannot compel patriotic rituals, affirming that patriotism must be voluntary and that government cannot prescribe orthodoxies of politics, religion, or nationalism. Writers draw on that precedent to argue that true respect for the flag means protecting free expression and diversity of opinion; Trump’s insistence on conformity, they contend, actually disrespects the Constitution and the flag’s meaning.

Another viewpoint treats Trump’s intervention as a calculated cultural strategy. Commentators argue he has repeatedly used cultural flashpoints—immigration, Confederate monuments, and now anthem protests—to energize his base when legislative achievements are stalling. By framing kneeling as anti-patriotic, Trump sought to rally middle-American sentiment against perceived elite athletes and media. Some say that even if pundits overestimate Trump, his stance pressures NFL viewership and could deepen fan alienation; polls and ratings declines have shown many Americans preferred politics kept off the field.

Reactions from the NFL were widespread and largely critical of the president’s bullying tone. Players, coaches, and many owners responded by kneeling, linking arms, or otherwise exercising their rights; owners including Jed York and Shahid Khan publicly supported players’ peaceful protests. Editorial voices compared Trump’s behavior to McCarthy-era persecution, accusing him of stoking division and using the presidency to delegitimize dissent rather than engage on issues of unequal policing.

Conservative commentary counters that kneeling alienates fans and undermines patriotism, suggesting Trump tapped into genuine public sentiment that politics should not dominate sports. Still, across much of the document the dominant defense of the protests is rooted in constitutional values: voluntary patriotism, protection of free speech, and the idea that criticizing the flag in pursuit of social justice can itself be an act of love for country.

A 23-year-old man was hospitalized after deliberately stepping into traffic in Clemson, South Carolina, while imitating the arcade game Frogger. Police say he and two friends were discussing the early-1980s game when he yelled "go" and darted onto U.S. 76 at College Avenue around 9 p.m. Monday, where a white 2010 Lexus SUV struck him. He was taken to AnMed Health Medical Center in Anderson in stable condition and is expected to be released. Clemson Police Chief Jimmy Dixon withheld the man’s name to avoid further discord and said the driver likely won’t be charged. Alcohol is suspected but not yet confirmed pending tests.

Director David Ayer gave fans the first full glimpse of Jared Leto as the Joker by posting an image on Twitter to mark the character’s 75th anniversary. The reveal shows Leto in an extreme, unsettling new interpretation of the Clown Prince of Crime: neon green hair, chalky pale skin, bright red lipstick, silver teeth, and a single purple glove. He also sports numerous tattoos—a repeated “Ha” pattern along his left side, playing cards, a large toothy grin on one arm, a harlequin skull on his chest and the word “Damaged” on his forehead—details that visually tie him to other iconography of the Joker and likely nod to Harley Quinn, played by Margot Robbie in Suicide Squad. Ayer’s caption—“The Suicide Squad wishes you a Happy Anniversary Mr. J!”—celebrated Batman No. 1’s April 1940 debut. The image positions Leto’s take as a bold, menacing shift and the first major Joker portrayal in live-action since Heath Ledger’s acclaimed 2008 performance in The Dark Knight. Suicide Squad, which began filming earlier in the summer, is scheduled for release on August 5, 2016, and features an ensemble cast including Will Smith as Deadshot, Viola Davis as Amanda Waller, Cara Delevingne as Enchantress, Jai Courtney as Captain Boomerang and Joel Kinnaman as Rick Flag. The reveal sparked fan discussion about the character’s look and Leto’s dramatic approach.

Ian David Long, a 28-year-old former Marine, carried out the mass shooting at the Borderline Bar & Grill in Thousand Oaks, California, killing 12 people and a Ventura County sheriff’s sergeant before apparently fatally shooting himself. Law enforcement officials said Long posted messages on social media during the attack asserting he was “bored but sane” and predicting debates over his mental state. Investigators have not confirmed a motive but noted possible personal grievances; some sources and acquaintances told media he had been bullied in school, may have been seeking revenge, and knew patrons at the bar. Long served a tour in Afghanistan and had documented emotional and mental-health struggles, including concerns about PTSD; he had been seen by a mental health specialist earlier in the year. Authorities found signs of recent agitation at his Newbury Park home and had responded previously to a domestic disturbance there. During the rampage, Long—dressed in black and armed with a Glock with an extended magazine—entered the bar around 11:15 p.m., fired inside, fatally shot Sgt. Ron Helus after taking cover, and shot victims in restrooms and escape points. Social platforms removed his accounts; investigations continue into timeline, motive and how social posts were made or posted.

When President Obama hosts British Prime Minister David Cameron this week, the White House may withhold a detail it previously disclosed at state dinners: the specific wines served. During Obama’s first three state dinners — for leaders of India, Mexico and China — menus listed name, vintage and appellation of all-American wines paired with each course, a tradition continued by prior administrations. That practice ceased after the January 2011 dinner for Chinese President Hu Jintao, when one featured wine, a highly rated 2005 Quilceda Creek Cabernet Sauvignon from Washington state, had climbed far above its $115 release price on the secondary market. Subsequent state dinner menus for Germany and South Korea in 2011 named only that “an American wine will be paired with each course.” Wine blogger and NYU instructor Tyler Colman suggested the change may reflect political sensitivity amid a sluggish economy, avoiding perceptions of extravagance. Critics and vintners, however, argue naming wines promotes U.S. winemakers and boosts sales overseas; vintners whose bottles have appeared at the White House reported substantial publicity and export gains — one said China sales quadrupled. Some wines at non-state events have still been disclosed, like Napa selections at a Biden dinner. The White House declined to explain the shift or to disclose recent state-dinner wine selections. The policy change coincided with staff turnover in the social secretary post and an overall cautious approach to highlighting presidential consumer preferences. Vintners view White House selection as both an honor and a valuable business opportunity.

The 2012 presidential campaign saw frequent clashes over factual claims, with debates highlighting where rhetoric outpaced reality. One repeated assertion — that President Obama “doubled the deficit” — is inaccurate. When Obama took office in January 2009, the CBO had already projected a FY2009 deficit of about $1.2 trillion (it ultimately reached $1.4 trillion). The FY2012 deficit was about $1.1 trillion, roughly the same level as when he was inaugurated. Measured as a share of GDP, the deficit fell from about 10.1 percent in 2009 to 7.3 percent in 2012.

Taxes were a major point of contention. Mitt Romney’s campaign was accused of proposing a $5 trillion tax cut over ten years. Romney described his plan as “revenue neutral,” pledging not to add to the deficit, but his proposal to reduce all marginal tax rates by 20 percent would alone reduce revenue by roughly $5 trillion. To offset that, he promised to eliminate or cap deductions and loopholes, but offered few specifics. He floated a cap on itemized deductions at $17,000 per household (with lower caps for high earners) or suggested $25,000–$50,000 thresholds in interviews. Independent analyses, including the Tax Policy Center, found it mathematically unlikely that capping or eliminating deductions just for higher-income taxpayers could fully offset the proposed rate cuts without increasing taxes on many households earning under $200,000 — a group Romney vowed not to raise taxes on.

Health care also sparked competing narratives. Romney warned of a federal “takeover” under the Affordable Care Act; critics noted the law primarily expands private insurance through subsidies and extends Medicaid to millions. The federal government’s role in health spending is projected to grow, with government health spending approaching half of national health expenditures by 2021. Another disputed claim concerned $716 billion in Medicare cuts attributed to Obama’s law. Those savings largely come from reduced payments to providers and insurers, not cuts to beneficiaries’ benefits; indeed, some preventive and drug benefits were enhanced. The reductions extended the solvency of Medicare’s trust fund by several years.

Other campaign claims included overstated failings of green-energy loan recipients — Romney said half had gone bust, when only a few of roughly three dozen DOE loan guarantee recipients were bankrupt — and debates over whether Romney’s tax plan would favor “small businesses.” The federal small-business definition (firms with fewer than 500 employees) means some Trump Organization entities could qualify, but Romney’s plan aimed broadly to lower business taxes for firms big and small, and analyses warned that extending tax cuts for high earners would overwhelmingly benefit the wealthiest taxpayers. Overall, many high-profile assertions from both campaigns required nuanced correction when checked against data and independent analyses.

Denise Simien, 55, of Verona, N.J., was arrested after Port Authority Police alleged she failed to pay more than $16,000 in EZ Pass tolls. Officers began pursuing Simien when they discovered her EZ Pass account had an outstanding balance of $16,633 from over 250 unpaid crossings at Port Authority facilities. While driving a 2007 Toyota SUV on Wednesday, she reportedly ignored police instructions to stop and was later pulled over near the Holland Tunnel entrance by another Port Authority officer. Simien faces charges of theft of services and obstruction of justice and is scheduled to appear in Jersey City Court on July 19. The incident highlights enforcement efforts at major crossings to recover significant unpaid tolls and addresses repeated toll evasion rather than a single missed payment. Also noted in the report is the Internet Archive’s crawl program aimed at preserving web pages and their references to prevent broken links: the archive captures pages as created and their linked content, so future readers can access the original material even if the live pages change or are removed.

Ohio authorities announced arrests in the 2016 massacre that killed eight members of the Rhoden family, saying the killings were meticulously planned and linked to an “obsession with control of the children.” A grand jury indicted four members of the Wagner family—Angela Wagner, 48; her husband George “Billy” Wagner, 47; and their sons George Wagner IV, 27, and Edward “Jake” Wagner, 26—on aggravated murder and numerous other charges, including conspiracy, tampering with evidence, forgery, unlawful possession of a dangerous ordinance, and aggravated burglary. Two additional women—Rita Newcomb and Fredericka Wagner, mothers of Angela and Billy—were arrested on allegations of forging custody documents to keep Sophia Wagner, the 4-year-old daughter of Jake Wagner and victim Hanna Rhoden.

Prosecutors say the Wagners spent months studying victims’ routines and homes, purchasing items allegedly to aid the attacks—brass catchers, ammunition, magazine clips, bug detectors and materials to build silencers—and that most victims were shot as they slept. Authorities emphasized the scale and difficulty of the investigation, noting tens of thousands of hours of work, more than 550 tips and over 550 interviews. Officials dismissed theories tying the crimes to a marijuana business dispute and said they do not believe others were involved.

The Wagners had moved to Alaska in 2017 amid public suspicion but returned to Ohio in 2018; arrests occurred across Ohio and in Kentucky. Their attorney maintains their innocence and looks forward to a full vetting of facts.

Separately, the surviving child’s father, Jake Wagner, won custody of his daughter Sophia and has been raising her while grappling with grief, legal battles and financial strain; he launched a GoFundMe to cover unexpected legal costs. The case remains one of Ohio’s largest homicide investigations, with authorities still urging anyone with information to come forward. Trial logistics may be complicated by publicity and capital charges, and arraignments were pending.

Researchers in Brazil have reported preliminary evidence that ayahuasca, a traditional Amazonian psychedelic brew, may reduce symptoms of treatment-resistant depression quickly and for weeks afterward. In the first clinical test, neuroscientists at the University of São Paulo administered a single mild dose to six volunteers whose depression had not responded to at least one antidepressant. Clinical questionnaires indicated symptom improvement within two to three hours—much faster than standard antidepressants—and statistically significant benefits persisted through a three-week follow-up. Three participants experienced vomiting, a common ayahuasca side effect, but no serious adverse events were reported.

Although promising, the study’s design limits firm conclusions: it involved only six people and lacked a placebo control, so placebo effects cannot be excluded. Experts emphasize that the trial primarily shows tolerability in depressed patients rather than definitive efficacy. Biochemically, ayahuasca plausibly affects mood: it contains DMT, which binds serotonin receptors, and harmine-type alkaloids that inhibit monoamine oxidase A, potentially increasing serotonin and other neurotransmitters—mechanisms shared with conventional antidepressants and other psychedelics under study.

The report fits a broader resurgence in clinical research into psychedelics—ketamine, psilocybin, MDMA and LSD have shown therapeutic potential for depression, anxiety, PTSD and cluster headaches. Larger, randomized, placebo-controlled trials are already underway in Brazil to validate these initial findings and determine safety, efficacy and which patient groups might benefit most.

A large prospective study within the Netherlands Cohort Study (120,852 participants aged 55–69 at baseline in 1986) found that modest daily intake of nuts and peanuts was associated with lower overall and cause-specific mortality over a 10-year follow-up. Multivariable analyses of 8,823 deaths and 3,202 subcohort members showed that compared with non-consumers, those eating 0.1–<5 g/day, 5–<10 g/day, and ≥10 g/day had progressively lower hazards for total mortality (HRs 0.88, 0.74, and 0.77, respectively; trend p = 0.003). Nut consumption was linked to reduced deaths from cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular, respiratory, neurodegenerative, and other causes; cause-specific HRs for ≥10 g/day versus none ranged from 0.56 (neurodegenerative) to 0.83 (cardiovascular). Dose-response relationships were nonlinear, with benefits evident at relatively low intakes (around 10–15 g/day) and little additional gain at higher intakes. Both tree nuts and peanuts showed inverse associations with mortality, while peanut butter showed no relationship. Meta-analyses combining these results with prior cohorts produced summary HRs for highest versus lowest nut consumption of 0.85 for cancer mortality and 0.71 for respiratory mortality. Authors suggest beneficial components in nuts—monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, fiber, vitamins, antioxidants and other bioactives—may underlie the associations, whereas added salt, oils, and trans fats in some peanut butters could negate peanut benefits. Overall, low daily nut intake appears linked to lower risk of death from multiple major causes.

Cocoa police announced misdemeanor charges will be pursued against five teenagers who filmed and mocked 31-year-old Jamel Dunn as he drowned in a pond in July. After initially concluding no crime applied, investigators and the State Attorney’s Office revisited statutes and decided to file charges under Florida Statute 406.12, which requires a person aware of a death to report it to the district medical examiner. Chief Michael Cantaloupe said the statute is usually for medical examiners and may be a novel application in this context; charging documents and evidence have been sent for review. Police declined to name the teens, who are ages 14–16, citing an ongoing investigation. Video shows Dunn struggling while the youths laughed and refused to help; authorities believe Dunn entered the water voluntarily after fence footage. Officials and Dunn’s family hope the case prompts legislation to require reporting or aid and to prevent similar tragedies, while critics note many states do not mandate rendering aid.

Hundreds of University of Iowa students gathered at a candlelight vigil in Hubbard Park to honor Mollie Tibbetts, a 20-year-old psychology student whose body was found after she disappeared while jogging. Her brother Jake urged attendees to meet someone new and make a friend in Mollie’s name, saying she would have done the same. The student-organized event, assembled within a day of the discovery and murder charge, emphasized Tibbetts’ warmth, smile, advocacy for mental health and the positive influence she had on classmates. Speakers including friend Breck Goodman, Dance Marathon leader Charlie Ellis and Student Government president Hira Mustafa asked the community to remember how Mollie lived, to practice kindness, seek campus support if struggling, and to honor other Hawkeye community members who have passed. Jake Tibbetts highlighted the community’s rescue efforts and nationwide support as a better legacy than the crime itself. Meanwhile, attention turned to Cristhian Bahena Rivera, a 24-year-old accused of abducting and killing Tibbetts. Rivera was arrested and charged with first-degree murder; authorities say he led them to the body in a cornfield and allegedly confessed to following her and panicking after she threatened to call police. Rivera appeared in court, faces life without parole if convicted, and an immigration detainer was lodged. Rivera had worked for four years at Yarrabee Farms near Brooklyn, Iowa, under a different name and with documentation his employers believed valid. The Lang family, which owns the farm, has cooperated with investigators but said they were shocked to learn his true identity. They and staff have since received threatening messages from the public, a development they called frightening amid ongoing grief for Mollie and her family.

A violent escape attempt at the Moscow Regional Court left three defendants dead and several people wounded. Authorities say five handcuffed defendants being escorted to a hearing for a gang accused of terrorizing Moscow roads seized sidearms from two guards while in an elevator. When the doors opened on the third floor, three defendants tried to flee and were shot dead by National Guard officers; the other two suspects were seriously wounded. Three law-enforcement personnel were injured, one by gunfire, and two were hospitalized. The defendants were on trial as part of a nine-person group Russian media dubbed the “Grand Theft Auto gang.” Prosecutors allege the group, whose members are originally from ex‑Soviet Central Asia, placed spikes on roads to stop motorists, forced drivers from their vehicles and in many cases shot them dead; they face charges including 17 murders, attempted murders, banditry and related crimes. State outlets also reported that one member had previously fought for Islamic State in Syria, according to a law-enforcement source. Investigations into the shootout are ongoing.

A strong earthquake struck near Okinawa early Saturday, centered about 10 km deep and roughly 52–85 km from Naha. Japan’s Meteorological Agency measured it near magnitude 6.9–7.0 (USGS 7.3) and briefly issued a tsunami advisory/warning for coastal areas, later canceled with no reported tsunami damage. Shaking lasted around 10–15 seconds; local officials, residents and U.S. military bases reported no major injuries or structural damage. Normal operations continued at major facilities.

Out Military, a niche social network for gay and lesbian U.S. service members and supporters, launched recently at outmilitary.com just after President Obama signed the law repealing "don't ask, don't tell." The site—described as a Facebook-like platform—had 53 members in its first week, but its creator, web designer John McKinnon of Bangor, Maine, expects growth as repeal implementation proceeds. Members like Kristin Orta, a Florida National Guard private first-class, say the site provides a social platform to communicate and support openness in service; Vietnam veteran Bill Royal joined hoping to help others who suffered abuse. McKinnon advises caution about posting sensitive details until official policy changes take effect. The WARC files for the crawl are not public.

Emanuel A. Lopes, 20, faces charges in the fatal shootings of Weymouth Police Officer Michael Chesna and 77-year-old Vera Adams. Lopes, who remains hospitalized with a leg wound, is expected to be arraigned either in his hospital bed or in court on murder counts. Authorities say officers initially responded to a report of an erratically driven vehicle and found a crashed BMW. Officer Chesna, a six-year veteran and 42-year-old Iraq and Afghanistan veteran with a wife and two young children, encountered Lopes allegedly vandalizing a home. Morrissey said Lopes struck Chesna in the head with a rock, seized Chesna’s service weapon, then shot him repeatedly in the head and chest. Another officer shot Lopes in the leg; Lopes fled and then reportedly spotted and intentionally shot Adams through her sliding glass door. Chesna was posthumously promoted to sergeant; hundreds attended a vigil and his family received community support as his body was transported to a funeral home.

Court records show Lopes had an extensive prior run-in with police and the justice system: he was arrested in October on charges of dealing cocaine to minors and resisting arrest, was listed as homeless, and released on conditions including random drug testing. He entered an addiction treatment center in November but missed drug screens and faced a probation hearing in April after a violation. He had prior arrests for property damage, including throwing a rock through a bedroom window, and remained free on pretrial probation. Last year Lopes’ mother sought a restraining order citing severe mental health issues and fear of his behavior. Lopes is charged with two counts of first-degree murder, weapons and other offenses; investigations into the crash, motive and his background are ongoing.

Several recent news stories claimed some beards “contain more poo than a toilet,” but these headlines overstate and distort what actually happened. The sensational story began with a local TV segment in New Mexico where a reporter swabbed a small number of men’s beards and sent the swabs to a microbiologist, John Golobic, who cultured bacteria and identified some “enteric” species—types of bacteria normally found in the gut. Reporters and tabloids then leaped from finding gut-associated bacteria to asserting that beards contain feces, which is misleading: gut bacteria on their own are not fecal matter.

There has been no large, peer-reviewed study showing beards are comparable to toilets, only a few small investigations.
