One Anaesthesia paper with small groups found bearded men shed more bacteria than clean-shaven men, and a Journal of Hospital Infection study reported beards were associated with lower prevalence of some pathogens (like S. aureus) on skin, though bearded hospital workers shed more bacteria overall. Both studies were limited in scope and size, and they emphasize that everyone—bearded or not—should follow hygiene practices (hand-washing, face coverings in sterile settings).

In short, the viral claims exaggerate the evidence. Beards can harbor microbes, including some gut-associated bacteria, but there’s no proof they are full of feces or uniquely dangerous; sensible hygiene is the practical takeaway.

The Tennessee Secondary School Athletic Association removed Riverdale and Smyrna girls basketball teams from the postseason and placed both schools on restrictive probation for the rest of the year and through 2015–16 after a referee’s report that players from both teams intentionally tried to lose their District 7-AAA consolation game. Each program was fined $1,500. The referee reported intentional missed free throws, purposeful violations—such as failing to advance the ball over midcourt to force 10-second counts or over-and-back calls—and players standing in the lane to draw three-second violations. He stopped play and admonished the coaches after a Smyrna player nearly shot at the wrong basket. Smyrna won the game 55–29. TSSAA executive director Bernard Childress said the student-athletes “bought into it” and emphasized that educational athletics should teach integrity and sportsmanship. Administrators from both schools met with TSSAA; principals sought permission to continue postseason play if coaches Shawn Middleton (Smyrna) and Cory Barrett (Riverdale) were removed. Riverdale suspended Barrett for the first two games of 2015–16; Smyrna’s Middleton expects further discipline. Riverdale administration contended Barrett discussed bracket possibilities but did not instruct players to lose; Childress countered that Barrett substituted starters out and appeared disengaged. The incident altered regional matchups, advancing Tullahoma and Lawrence County without playing those teams, and sparked local school follow-ups.

Sen. Lindsey Graham faced fierce criticism from conservatives after proposing a compromise to resolve the Guantanamo controversy: urge Republicans to back closing the prison if President Obama sends Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and four co-defendants to military tribunals, and work with Congress to establish a new national-security detention court. Critics from across the right—Sen. James Inhofe, RedState, Glenn Beck, Rep. Pete Hoekstra and others—accused him of betraying conservatives. Graham defended compromise as principled, noting his conservative record and arguing purity politics prevent pragmatic solutions. The White House was reviewing Attorney General Holder’s plan to try KSM in civilian court; Graham urged a framework balancing due process with national security to end the stalemate.

Sigmund Freud long argued that many adult dreams are sexual, and contemporary research supports a strong link between sleep and erotic content. Data from the Kinsey Institute indicate sexual dreams and responses are common: 37% of women at age 45 have experienced orgasm from a sex dream (5% had their first orgasm this way), and 83% of men report nocturnal emissions. Studies find overtly sexual dreams in roughly 70% of women and virtually all men.

While there’s no guaranteed method to force an explicit dream, a 2019 study in Sleep and Hypnosis reported that sleep position appears to influence dream content. Researchers surveyed 670 students about their habitual sleeping posture and dream reports. Those who regularly slept prone (on their stomachs) with arms raised above the head were more likely to report erotic or sexual dreams and specific themes such as being tied up, immobility, or confinement. The single most frequent theme noted was erotomania (De Clérambault’s Syndrome) — the persistent belief of having a secret, often famous, admirer. Investigators hypothesize that pressure on the genitals from the prone position provides mild external sensory stimulation that is incorporated by the sleeping brain into dream narratives. Lead researcher Kai-Ching Yu suggested that the sleeping brain integrates external stimuli into dream content as it attempts to make sense of sensations.

Prone sleeping may increase the odds of sexual dream content, but it has drawbacks: it can compress the spine and contribute to lower back pain. Whether the potential for more vivid erotic dreams outweighs the physical discomfort is a personal choice.

Global markets opened 2016 weak after a disappointing Chinese manufacturing report and a sharp overnight selloff in Chinese stocks triggered a new circuit‑breaker, rekindling growth worries. U.S. indexes fell broadly: the S&P 500 plunged about 1.5% in its worst New Year start in over a decade, the Dow lost roughly 1.6% and the Nasdaq dropped over 2%. Investors sought havens, lifting gold and Treasurys. Tensions between Saudi Arabia and Iran and weak U.S. data added pressure; many sectors and European markets also tumbled. Notable movers included Tesla, Netflix, Amazon and Baxalta; DOJ sued Volkswagen over emissions.

CNN host Piers Morgan described his heated interview with conservative radio host Alex Jones as a vivid demonstration of why stricter gun control deserves attention. Morgan told POLITICO that Jones’s “vitriol, hatred, and zealotry” made him an unwitting “best advertisement for gun control,” and said Jones’s ranting—about guns, a 1776-style rebellion, and conspiracies including 9/11 being an inside job—was frightening given Jones’s influence. Morgan noted Jones’s vast reach—syndication on many networks and large online followings—and warned that Jones’s rhetoric drives fear, gun and ammunition sales, and persuades less discerning followers. Though Morgan anticipated Jones’s shock-jock style and tried to keep the exchange civil, Jones continued through a commercial break and prompted CNN to cancel a planned third segment. Jones, who launched a petition to deport Morgan that gained over 100,000 signatures, later posted a YouTube video alleging threats from the NYPD and Mayor Bloomberg’s “mafia,” claiming he feared for his life after the taping. Morgan vowed to keep pressing for action on gun control until politicians respond, arguing America has become too desensitized to mass shootings.

Pippa Middleton has secured a reported £400,000 book deal with Michael Joseph, an imprint of Penguin, after a bidding contest involving major publishers including HarperCollins and Random House’s Cornerstone. Industry sources say timing was carefully negotiated: Middleton will delay release until after the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee to avoid appearing to profit from royal connections, aiming for a late-autumn launch in time for the Christmas market. The book will be a party-hosting guide with recipes, anecdotes and event-planning advice, drawing on her professional experience at Table Talk and contributions to her family’s Party Pieces newsletter. Her agent David Godwin negotiated the substantial advance, reflecting publishers’ confidence in strong sales. Michael Joseph, known for commercial bestsellers, did not comment. Middleton reportedly impressed executives during her publisher visits. The piece also notes some public skepticism about the deal given her fame linked to royal family ties.

A woman photographing a returning Union Pacific steam locomotive was struck and killed after approaching too close to the tracks at a Henderson crossing near north suburban Denver. The incident occurred about 7:45 p.m. Saturday as the Denver Post Special — Locomotive No. 844 pulling a long consist that had made a daylong trip to Cheyenne Frontier Days — was southbound and had just arrived at the 124th Avenue crossing. The victim, whose name has not been released, was among several people taking pictures; no other injuries were reported. Some reports describe the train as 15 cars, others 21, carrying roughly 700 passengers who were bused back to Denver. Union Pacific acknowledged the fatality via its UP Steam account and said police would assist local authorities; a company spokeswoman said UP is cooperating with the investigation. Locomotive 844 is a well-known, preserved steam engine used by Union Pacific as an ambassador on excursion trips, attracting many railfans who photograph its movements.

Investigators are re-examining 2015 U.S. intelligence intercepts that captured Russian officials discussing associates of Donald Trump, prompted by revelations that Donald Trump Jr. met in June 2016 with Russian lawyer Natalia Veselnitskaya. Some intercepted conversations referenced meetings outside the U.S. involving Russian officials and Trump business associates or advisers. Trump Jr. released emails showing he accepted the meeting after being told the lawyer might have damaging information on Hillary Clinton; he later said the meeting yielded nothing useful and instead touched on a Russian-American diplomatic dispute. Shortly afterward, hacked Democratic emails were made public, which investigators linked to Russian hacking.

As a candidate, Trump expressed admiration for Vladimir Putin and took positions—such as openness to lifting Crimea-era sanctions and questioning NATO commitments—that aligned with Russian interests; the GOP platform at the 2016 convention excluded a plank to arm Ukraine. The president’s legal team declined to comment on the timing; the White House called concerns over the emails and meeting “much ado about nothing.” Trump said he only recently learned of his son’s meeting and did not fault him, calling it a reasonable decision during a nontraditional campaign. He also described asking Putin directly about election meddling, noting Putin’s denial but saying investigators must determine what happened, while insisting there was no collusion.

Chris Brown, 25, was jailed after a Friday arrest for an alleged probation violation and will remain locked up until April 23 after a judge cited his "inability to stay out of trouble." Authorities haven’t officially detailed the violation, but reports say he was expelled from a Malibu rehab for breaking three internal rules: touching a woman despite a unique “two-foot” restriction imposed for his safety, leaving on an unauthorized outing and initially refusing a random drug test (later negative), and disrupting a group session with harsh comments. Brown faces a separate D.C. assault case and was ordered to 90 days’ residential anger-management rehab in November; his probation, due to end in August, may be extended.

The Internet Archive and Wisconsin Historical Society are archiving web pages as they’re created to preserve referenced versions when originals change or disappear, aiming to reduce broken links by providing archived alternatives. Wisconsin’s collection focuses on state agencies, interstate bodies and key social media of top officials, with archived dates and content coverage noted; internal links are usually saved, external links generally aren’t. Separately, children’s horror author R.L. Stine announced he’ll write a live scary story on Twitter for Halloween, continuing his history of short Twitter tales and social-media engagement ahead of a new Goosebumps book and a Scholastic Q&A takeover.

A Wichita 2-year-old is recovering after a small octopus was found lodged in his throat. The child was brought to a hospital Tuesday night not breathing; EMS had transferred him in critical condition. Hospital staff removed a dead octopus with a roughly 2-inch-diameter head, which police say appeared intended for sushi and was not a pet. The boy also had minor facial injuries. His condition has since improved to “good,” and doctors report no current signs of long-term brain injury from oxygen deprivation, though more tests and a child-sensitive interview are planned. Police grew suspicious when the 36-year-old boyfriend’s accounts of how the injuries occurred conflicted with evidence. The boyfriend, identified in arrest records as Matthew Gallagher, was arrested early Wednesday on suspicion of child abuse, questioned by the Exploited and Missing Child Unit, and later bonded out of Sedgwick County Jail. The investigation remains open as authorities continue to assess the cause and circumstances.

Data breaches have compromised over 1.1 billion records since 2005, with major 2018 breaches at companies like Adidas and Macy’s. WalletHub ranked states by identity-theft risk using metrics on complaints, losses, arrests, e-commerce attacks and policy; Nevada, Florida and New Jersey ranked most vulnerable. Experts recommend strong email security, two-step verification, credit monitoring, account alerts and cautious online behavior. The ITRC tracks breaches, methods, affected data types and reporting criteria.

A Chilean mother, Sindy Melany Ortiz, says hospital staff in Talcahuano are restricting her access to her newborn after she admitted smoking marijuana days before giving birth. Ortiz, who says she used cannabis on medical recommendation to relieve arm pain and is not a habitual user, reports she is limited to two hours of daily visitation and is prohibited from breastfeeding her baby. Hospital officials say they followed protocol after tests detected substances they believed could endanger the infant and notified a local court. The court ordered the newborn to remain at Las Higueras hospital pending a hearing. Ortiz says her maternal rights have been violated; hospital representatives maintain the actions were taken to protect the child. The case comes amid ongoing legal change in Chile: in July, Congress approved a bill to decriminalize personal cannabis use and home cultivation (possession up to 10 g and up to six plants), a move intended to ease access for medicinal users and reduce criminalization. The bill still must pass the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, a process that could take years.

New research presented at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2016 suggests that repeated cycles of losing and regaining weight—commonly called weight cycling or yo-yo dieting—may raise the risk of fatal heart disease among postmenopausal women who were normal weight at study start. Investigators led by Dr. Somwail Rasla analyzed self-reported weight histories for 158,063 postmenopausal women, grouping them as stable weight, steady gain, maintained weight loss, or weight cyclers, and followed them for an average of 11.4 years. Normal-weight women who lost and regained weight faced about a 3.5-fold higher risk of sudden cardiac death and a 66% higher risk of coronary heart disease death compared with women whose weight remained stable. In contrast, overweight or obese women who experienced weight cycling did not show increased heart-disease mortality, nor did women who only gained weight or only lost weight without regaining it. The study underscores obesity’s broader role in heart disease risk—alongside high blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, inactivity, poor diet, and smoking—and echoes public-health advice to manage these factors. However, authors caution that the research is observational and cannot prove causation, relies on self-reported weight histories, included relatively few sudden cardiac death cases, and focused only on older women. Further research across broader populations is needed before changing clinical recommendations. Meanwhile, the American Heart Association’s Life’s Simple 7—manage blood pressure and cholesterol, reduce blood sugar, get active, eat better, maintain healthy weight, stop smoking—remains advised.

Former Massachusetts governor Mitt Romney announced he will not take part in the December 27 debate reportedly to be moderated by Donald Trump. Speaking with Fox News’ Neil Cavuto, Romney said unequivocally he would skip that debate, explaining his December schedule is already committed to two debates he has agreed to and to campaigning in early primary states like Iowa, New Hampshire, South Carolina and Florida. Romney said he spoke with Trump about his decision, who “understood my perspective and wished me well.” Cavuto pressed for more detail, but Romney offered no additional color. Romney joins Ron Paul and Jon Huntsman in declining the Trump-moderated event, while Newt Gingrich and Rick Santorum have confirmed they will attend.

Following the Paris attacks, the hacktivist collective Anonymous escalated a long-running campaign against ISIS, posting alleged personal details of suspected supporters and compiling lists of pro-ISIS Twitter accounts and websites for takedown. Anonymous declared “war” and promised its “biggest ever” operation, releasing videos and publishing thousands of account names; at various points it claimed to have flagged or assisted in removing thousands of accounts and taken down dozens of sites. The group uses hacking techniques including distributed denial-of-service attacks, doxxing, and mass reporting to pressure platforms into suspending accounts.

While some affiliated groups (like Ghost Security Group) have coordinated intelligence sharing with authorities, Anonymous’s vigilante style and public exposure of names raise concerns: activists have misidentified people before, and unilateral disruption can hamper official investigations. Analysts warn that removed accounts are easily reestablished, that extremists employ encryption and other countermeasures, and that uncoordinated actions may be more harassment than strategic counterterrorism.

ISIS responded derisively via its “Islamic Cyber Army,” calling Anonymous “idiots” and advising supporters on basic operational security—avoiding suspicious links, altering identifiers, and limiting contacts on platforms like Telegram and Twitter. The episode highlights tensions between grassroots cyber vigilantism and formal law enforcement efforts: outside groups can supply valuable leads, but without coordination their interventions risk being counterproductive or simply temporary.

Over the decade since leaving the White House, former President Bill Clinton has earned $75.6 million from paid speaking engagements, including a record $10.7 million for 52 speeches in 2010, CNN and disclosure filings show. Nearly half of his 2010 income—$4.8 million—came from 18 speeches in 13 countries; the rest were delivered across eight U.S. states and Washington, D.C. Since 2001 he has done 417 paid speeches, averaging $181,000 each, with $44.9 million coming from 215 overseas events. Canada has been his top foreign market ($9.1 million for 54 events), followed by the U.K., Australia and Mexico. Two 2010 events each paid $500,000. Clinton’s speaking earnings have varied with his schedule—2004 was down amid memoir writing and surgery—while his post-presidential book advance and sales added substantially to his income. Disclosure requirements stem from Hillary Clinton’s federal roles.

A simple, longstanding habit produced an unexpectedly warm royal response. Andrew Simes recounts how his grandfather sent a Christmas card to Queen Elizabeth II every year from 1952 until the grandfather’s death in 2011. Their correspondence and a chance meeting created a memorable personal connection: when the grandfather was introduced to the Queen at a reception in Izmir, Turkey, in 1972, she smiled and said, “so it’s you who keeps sending me those lovely Christmas cards.” The Queen later wrote to congratulate him on his 100th birthday. After his grandfather passed at 102, Simes continued the tradition, sending a card the first Christmas after the funeral. In January 2012, he received a reply from Buckingham Palace: the Queen had asked her office to trace the sender and, upon learning of the grandfather’s death, sent condolences to the family. Simes describes being moved to tears by the personal attention and kindness the Queen showed his grandfather and family, and he keeps sending a card every year with the Queen at the top of the list. The story is offered as a reminder that small acts—like mailing a holiday card—can create lasting impressions and occasionally lead to unexpected, heartfelt responses, encouraging others to reach out and brighten someone’s day.

A 10-year-old visiting boy was bitten on the calf while wading in chest-deep water at Daytona Beach Shores, Florida, sustaining minor lacerations treated on scene. He is the second 10-year-old attacked in Florida in a week and marks the fourth reported shark bite this year in Volusia County, an area recently labeled the “shark bite capital” by the International Shark Attack File. Beaches remained open after the incident. Earlier in the week, another 10-year-old off Cocoa Beach suffered more serious injuries. In nearby regions, North Carolina saw two severe attacks within 90 minutes on the same day: a 12-year-old girl lost part of her arm and a 16-year-old boy lost an arm; both were swimming in waist- to chest-deep water near piers. Those incidents prompted Oak Island officials to consider a temporary ban on shark fishing from piers, citing concerns that fishing activity, chumming, and fish cleaning near structures attract sharks into nearshore surf. Some East Coast towns, including Virginia Beach and Myrtle Beach, already restrict shark fishing from piers; enforcement and scientific evidence of effectiveness remain limited. Experts emphasize that increased reported attacks largely reflect more people in the water and improved reporting, not more aggressive sharks. Florida led the U.S. with 28 attacks in 2014, and global attacks slightly declined from 2013 to 2014. Preventive advice includes swimming in groups and avoiding inlets and areas where fishing and chumming occur.

Derek Jeter and actress Minka Kelly have amicably split after three-plus years together, sources and reps confirmed. They remain friends and still care for each other. The breakup comes as Jeter reached the 3,000-hit milestone and Kelly is filming the ABC Charlie’s Angels reboot in Miami; both continue with their careers and personal lives.

Genevieve Kelley, 50, who vanished in late 2004 with her then-8-year-old daughter Mary Nunes during a bitter custody dispute, surrendered to authorities Monday in Lancaster, New Hampshire, ending more than a decade on the run. Kelley and her husband Scott fled New Hampshire after a judge ordered Mary to be produced for evaluation amid accusations that Mark Nunes, Mary’s father and Mark’s ex-husband, had abused the child. Authorities, child welfare investigators and a court-appointed guardian found no evidence supporting the abuse allegations; instead they documented what they described as strong parental alienation by Genevieve. After the couple disappeared in November 2004 and failed to show Mary for school in Colorado, Mark was granted full custody in December 2004 and the Kelleys were later indicted for interference with custody. U.S. Marshals pursued tips across the U.S., Canada and Central and South America, aided by the State Department and Interpol; they noted Genevieve’s fluency in Spanish and past travel to the region. Featured on CNN’s The Hunt, Genevieve was added to the Marshals’ Fugitive of the Week list; Scott Kelley remains a fugitive. Genevieve’s surrender followed outreach from her attorney and months of negotiation; she has said she wants a trial to be vindicated and claims her daughter is safe. She is in Coos County custody and has made an initial court appearance. Mary, now 18, has not been publicly located and her whereabouts remain unknown; authorities and Mary’s father continue to seek confirmation of her wellbeing. U.S. Marshal David Cargill Jr. emphasized that while Kelley’s custody ends a chapter, the priority is learning Mary’s status and ensuring her safety.

Seventeen-year-old Jacqueline “Jackie” Gomez, a MacArthur High School senior, was found dead Saturday morning in a north Houston Hyatt hotel room after attending her school’s prom the night before. Her boyfriend, who spent the night with her in the room on the eighth floor, woke up and discovered she was not breathing and called 911. Police say there were no obvious signs of trauma; investigators are awaiting autopsy results while probing possible contributing factors, including alcohol and prescription painkillers reportedly found in the room. Homicide detectives described the boyfriend as cooperative and said they currently have no reason to believe he contributed to her death, but emphasized they must be thorough.

Friends and classmates described Gomez as outgoing, hard‑working and planning to attend Lone Star College to train as a pharmacy technician; she worked in the pharmacy at a local Kroger and was two weeks away from graduation. Peers recalled her excitement about prom—dressing up, doing nails and sharing details with friends—and some had urged her not to leave with her date. The prom and an after‑party drew other hotel guests’ attention for loud festivities; some who stayed nearby were shocked to learn of the tragedy the next morning. Aldine ISD officials had not commented publicly. Family, friends and the community are grieving and seeking answers about what happened.

An envelope addressed to Sen. Roger Wicker’s Washington office was intercepted at the U.S. Senate’s off-site mail facility after screening revealed a white granular substance that preliminary tests indicated was ricin. Capitol Police hazardous-material teams quarantined the envelope and sent samples to accredited laboratories, including Fort Detrick, for confirmatory analysis; the FBI cautioned that full lab results, which can take 24–48 hours, were needed due to possible inconsistencies in field testing. The letter, postmarked Memphis, Tenn., had no return address; officials said a suspect who frequently writes to lawmakers has been identified, though no arrest was reported immediately. The Senate mail facility was closed for further testing and mail rerouted through the House, and Wicker has been assigned protective detail. Senators were briefed by Homeland Security and FBI officials. Authorities noted that current screening procedures—instituted after the 2001 anthrax attacks—worked as intended; past Senate ricin scares occurred in 2004. Ricin, derived from castor beans, is highly toxic with no antidote.

Norwegian Prime Minister Erna Solberg formally apologized for the post-World War II mistreatment of women who had intimate relationships with German soldiers during the Nazi occupation. Neutral Norway was invaded in April 1940, and some 300,000 German troops were stationed there. SS leader Heinrich Himmler promoted liaisons and encouraged German men to father children with local women as part of Nazi racial policy; Lebensborn maternity homes were established in Norway from 1941. Up to an estimated 50,000 Norwegian women—derisively called "German girls"—had such relationships, and some 10,000–12,000 children were born as a result.

After liberation in 1945, many of these women and their children faced severe reprisals: job dismissals, detention, deprivation of civil rights, expulsion to Germany, and loss of nationality. Children were placed in foster homes or institutions; some later sought compensation. A report by Norway’s Centre for Holocaust and Minorities Studies concluded authorities had violated fundamental legal principles by punishing citizens without trial. Historian Guri Hjeltnes emphasized that women’s relations did not equate to aiding the German war effort and that their “crime” was breaking social taboos.

Solberg delivered the apology during a ceremony marking the 70th anniversary of the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, acknowledging the undignified treatment and the lifelong stigma imposed on many who experienced “teenage love” or lasting relationships with occupying soldiers. Survivors are mostly deceased, but relatives and children of those affected attended; some described the apology as late but historically important. Previous redress efforts included a 2000 apology for the children and legal attempts that faltered due to the passage of time.

A 6.0-magnitude earthquake struck Napa Valley in the pre-dawn hours, the strongest Bay Area temblor in decades, and left a patchwork of destruction — and remarkable community response. The quake, centered near the Napa Airport and ultimately attributed to the West Napa Fault (likely its Browns Valley strand), shook soft valley soils and caused intense local shaking even though only a portion of the fault ruptured. Damage included buckled streets, broken water mains, toppled chimneys and collapsed walls; inspectors red-tagged dozens of buildings as unsafe and hundreds of people were treated for injuries, some serious. Authorities declared a state of emergency for Napa, Solano and Sonoma counties and warned that repairs and recovery would be a long, costly process, with initial damage estimates potentially exceeding $1 billion.

Despite the shock, neighbors, volunteers and local businesses mobilized quickly. Home Depot teams, church groups, contractors and dozens of individual volunteers formed human chains, hauled debris, cleared chimneys, stacked firewood, and helped pack and salvage belongings. Strangers converged to sweep storefronts, transport rubble to dumps, and compile databases of red-tagged homes. Stories of aid ranged from a contractor hauling broken pottery to a volunteer typing addresses for police, to a store manager ferrying supplies and plywood. Volunteer efforts extended to vineyards and wineries, where spilled wine and toppled barrels created dramatic scenes; yet many producers discovered damage was patchy and in some cases less severe than it looked.

The quake activated early-warning systems that provided seconds of advance notice, and scientists are using GPS, aftershocks and field mapping to pinpoint which fault strands ruptured and measure ground shifts. Recovery will take months, officials said, but residents expressed gratitude that the human response — neighbors helping neighbors — matched the scale of the disaster.

U.S. employers added 215,000 jobs in March, a solid gain that reflects ongoing labor-market strength even as overall economic growth has softened. The headline unemployment rate rose slightly to 5.0% from 4.9%, but that partly reflects more Americans re-entering the labor force to look for work, not a widespread pullback in hiring. Job creation was broad-based: construction led with a gain of 37,000 positions—likely helped by warmer weather—while retail and health care also contributed. These additions helped offset continued losses in mining and persistent weakness in manufacturing tied to slow global demand and a strong dollar; low oil prices have cut about 185,000 jobs in mining and related sectors since September 2014.

Wage growth remains modest. Average hourly pay was $25.43, up 2.3% year over year—better than the early recovery years but below the 2.6% peak in December and well under the roughly 3.5% pace typical of a stronger labor market. Sluggish wage gains continue to be a concern for many workers.

Broader economic signals are mixed. Many analysts estimate first-quarter GDP growth around 1% or lower, yet steady hiring suggests employers may view the slowdown as temporary. Consumer spending, a key growth driver, has cooled—rising just 0.1% in February for the third straight month—and households are saving more of their windfall from lower gasoline prices, with the personal savings rate at 5.4% in February. Housing activity softened as existing-home sales plunged 7.1% in February amid limited inventory and rising prices. Overall, jobs remain a bright spot amid uneven growth.

Pepsi pulled a new commercial featuring model Kendall Jenner after a swift and intense backlash for appearing to trivialize recent social justice protests. The ad, created by Pepsi’s in-house team and intended for global TV and digital distribution, shows Jenner leave a fashion shoot to join a cheery, diverse crowd of young protesters. The moment of supposed unity arrives when Jenner hands a can of Pepsi to a police officer, who drinks it; the crowd cheers. Critics argued the vignette co-opted and sanitized real protest imagery, notably evoking a photo of Black Lives Matter protester Ieshia Evans approaching police in Baton Rouge, and reduced meaningful demands to innocuous signs reading things like “Join the Conversation” and heart-and-peace symbols. The spot was widely mocked on social media and in the press for being tone-deaf and exploiting activism for marketing. Pepsi apologized, saying it “missed the mark,” removed the content, halted further rollout and apologized to Jenner for placing her “in this position.” Commentators including late-night hosts lampooned the commercial’s bland corporate messaging and casting choices. Observers noted Pepsi’s timing made the message feel opportunistic; though backlash was fierce online, some marketing experts suggested the hit to Pepsi’s reputation might be short-lived. The incident follows past PepsiCo ad controversies and withdrawals.

21st Century Fox announced it has settled Gretchen Carlson’s lawsuit, issuing a public apology that Carlson “was not treated with the respect and dignity” she and colleagues deserve. Vanity Fair and other outlets reported the settlement is about $20 million and includes a public apology; Fox is also reportedly negotiating settlements with at least two other women. Carlson, who sued former Fox News chairman Roger Ailes in July alleging sexual harassment and retaliation after her on-air demotion and contract nonrenewal, said she is “gratified” Fox took decisive action and will focus on empowering women in the workplace. Ailes has denied the allegations; he resigned after 21st Century Fox launched an internal investigation following Carlson’s complaint and corroborating accounts from more than two dozen women. Reports suggest Fox is settling the suit on Ailes’s behalf though Ailes’s personal financial responsibility is unclear. Carlson’s legal team recorded conversations with Ailes to support her claims and deliberately sued Ailes personally to avoid arbitration clauses in her Fox contract. The scandal exposed long-standing allegations of a misogynistic culture at Fox News — surveillance, intimidation, nondisclosure settlements, and alleged cover-ups involving senior executives. The internal Paul Weiss investigation interviewed many women but, sources say, did not comprehensively probe company hard drives or the broader culture. Roger Ailes’s abrupt ouster left a leadership void and triggered debate among Murdoch family members about Fox’s future leadership; executives were reshuffled and some low- and midlevel figures were ousted. Meanwhile, Ailes’s lawyer has urged New York magazine preserve materials related to its investigative cover story, signaling potential legal pushback to reporting that chronicled the 15-day fall of Ailes and the wider allegations.

At the Conservative Political Action Conference a week after the Parkland, Florida, school massacre, NRA CEO Wayne LaPierre delivered a combative defense of gun rights, blaming gun-control advocates, the media and what he called “socialists” for exploiting the tragedy for political gain. LaPierre condemned Democrats, named high-profile potential 2020 candidates, and accused lawmakers and the press of aiming to erode the Second Amendment rather than protect children. He reiterated long-standing NRA prescriptions: harden schools, increase armed security, and embrace the slogan “to stop a bad guy with a gun, it takes a good guy with a gun.” LaPierre also attacked the FBI for failing to act on warnings about the Parkland shooter and broadened his critique to immigration, opioids and alleged corruption.

NRA spokeswoman Dana Loesch echoed these themes, alleging the mainstream media sensationalize mass shootings and making provocatively racialized comments about coverage. The NRA released a video claiming news outlets profit from such tragedies. Their stance provoked swift criticism from Democrats—Sen. Chuck Schumer called the remarks “out of touch”—and gun-control advocates like Moms Demand Action, who objected to the NRA’s prominent role in post-shooting discussions.

Meanwhile, President Trump and some Republicans signaled willingness to consider modest reforms—tightening background checks, raising the purchase age for semi-automatic rifles to 21 and limiting bump stocks—though those positions conflict with traditional NRA policy. Florida lawmakers prepared legislation to raise the purchasing age. The debate intensified as Parkland survivors pressed for change, creating a sharp national clash over gun policy, school safety and political responsibility.

Spanish police have arrested several suspects after what are believed to be the bodies of missing Dutch volleyball star Ingrid Visser, 35, and her partner Lodewijk Severein, 57, were found buried in a shallow grave in a lemon grove near Alquerías, about 12 km from Murcia. DNA confirmation is pending, but police noted the remains were “extremely tall,” matching the couple’s descriptions. Visser and Severein vanished after checking into a Murcia hotel on 13 May and failing to attend appointments in Spain and the Netherlands; their hired car was later recovered in Murcia. Authorities raided an apartment in Molina de Segura and uncovered evidence of violent crime. Three people have been detained, including Juan Cuenca Lorente, a 36-year-old former director of Murcia’s volleyball club, and two Romanian nationals. Murcia’s police chief indicated the killings may have stemmed from business disagreements between the couple and the suspects; investigators are keeping details confidential as inquiries continue.

Rupert Murdoch flew to London and met privately with the family of murdered schoolgirl Milly Dowler, whose voicemails were allegedly accessed by reporters at the now-closed News of the World. The Dowler family’s lawyer said Murdoch appeared humbled and offered a “full and sincere apology,” acknowledging the wrongdoing fell short of the standards set by his father. The revelations—that messages were deleted, possibly giving the family false hope during the 2002 search—ignited public outrage and intensified a widening phone-hacking scandal. In the wake of the fallout, News International chief executive Rebekah Brooks resigned, becoming the highest-profile casualty; she denies knowledge of illicit activity. Tom Mockridge was appointed her successor, and Les Hinton stepped down as Dow Jones CEO. News Corp. published a written apology and faces multiple investigations in the U.K. and the U.S., including possible hacking of 9/11 victims’ phones. Police have arrested several suspects and recovered a list of some 3,700 potential victims. The scandal has cost News Corp. billions, scuttled its BSkyB bid, and prompted public and parliamentary inquiries.

At Inc.’s GrowCo conference, Dallas Mavericks owner and entrepreneur Mark Cuban sparked debate by candidly acknowledging his own prejudices while addressing the NBA’s recent Donald Sterling controversy. Cuban condemned Sterling’s racist remarks as “abhorrent” but cautioned that forcing an owner to sell a team creates a “slippery slope.” More strikingly, he described everyday impulses—“If I see a black kid in a hoodie and it’s late at night, I’m walking to the other side of the street,” and then switching sides when confronted by a heavily tattooed white man—as examples of biases he recognizes and tries to control. He framed confronting personal bigotry as an entrepreneurial responsibility: rather than ostracize people for prejudiced views, he prefers to engage, educate, and seek solutions within organizations.

Reactions were intense and varied across the media. Some commentators praised Cuban’s honesty and argued that acknowledging bias is necessary for progress; others warned his analogy minimized historical context and likened his remarks to Sterling’s failings. CNN’s LZ Granderson criticized equating hoodie stereotyping with fearing tattooed white men, while NBC and ESPN voices defended Cuban’s intent. Social media and columnists ranged from calling him sincere and constructive to accusing him of poor judgment or political posturing. Cuban later apologized to Trayvon Martin’s family for invoking the hoodie example but reiterated his belief that everyone harbors prejudices and must actively work on them.

The interview also covered Cuban’s business life—his early ventures, the sale of AudioNet to Yahoo, reasons for buying the Mavericks, and leadership style—illustrating a blunt, self-reflective persona who seeks to change culture through engagement rather than simple condemnation. His remarks underscored the complexity of addressing racism publicly: honest admission can prompt necessary conversation but also provoke sharp backlash when context and historical weight are perceived as dismissed.

Seminal new wave band Devo, preparing to tour New Zealand and Australia for A Day on the Green, discussed their return with founding member Bob Casale. Fresh from a U.S. tour with Blondie, Casale described the band’s recent album as a deliberate effort to “be Devo again,” maintaining their signature attention to lyrics and song structure while embracing modern production methods. For the first time they collaborated with outside producers, used focus groups, social networking and file-sharing to write and exchange parts—contrast to their old method of isolating together in a studio. Casale reflected on how the internet and modern distribution have inverted the music industry and cultural role of artists. He lamented contemporary mainstream music’s narcissism and materialism, arguing it reflects a creatively bankrupt, consumer-driven society—unlike Devo’s socially and politically aware origins, rooted in the cultural turmoil around Kent State and the Vietnam era. Visuals and multimedia have always been central to Devo’s expression, and they continue to engage new tech—Casale cited a recent politically themed game critiquing Mitt Romney’s character. The piece also notes Bob Casale’s death at 61; remembered as “Bob 2,” he was praised for engineering, soundtrack work at Mutato and long collaboration with bandmates, leaving a lasting impact on Devo’s sound and multimedia legacy.

On July 21 in Walnut Creek, 21-year-old Scott Bertics fatally shot 19-year-old Clare Orton at her family’s Holton Court home before turning a homemade firearm on himself. Police confirmed Bertics had assembled two unregistered, serial-number-free “ghost guns” from components he ordered online. Investigators found no evidence anyone sold parts illegally or knew of Bertics’ plans, and said the steps he took to assemble the weapons were lawful. Lt. Lanny Edwards noted such kits typically include unfinished lower receivers—the critical firing mechanism that normally bears a serial number—which can be bought as simple pieces of metal alongside triggers, handles and stocks. Websites and police estimates put the cost of parts at roughly $400 to $1,200. Bertics and Orton both had engineering backgrounds: Bertics studied electrical engineering and computer sciences at Stanford, contributed to research on controlling robots with spiking neurons, and took a leave after fall 2014; Orton was an honors environmental engineering student at San Diego State, a dean’s list academic and former high-school athlete. Police said Bertics and Orton had dated previously but were not together since 2013, and they have not disclosed a motive for his visit. Authorities emphasized that while assembling such guns is possible, it requires knowledge and intent. The case highlighted ongoing concerns about untraceable firearms and follows earlier unsuccessful attempts in California to require serial numbers and background checks for gun parts.

The Vancouver Maritime Museum, located in Vanier Park, showcases British Columbia and Canadian seafaring history with the St. Roch—a preserved RCMP schooner famed for circumnavigating North America via the Northwest Passage and Panama Canal—as its centerpiece. Exhibits include model ships, maritime art, the Beaver’s boiler, a fo’c’sle recreation, and interactive family areas like Pirates Cove and the Children’s Maritime Discovery Centre. Visitors praise the hands-on St. Roch tours, kid-friendly activities, knowledgeable staff, and affordable admission (donation evenings on Thursdays). The museum’s dated, modest ambience adds character for many, though some find displays repetitive or in need of refresh. A recent exhibition pairing scrimshaw with sailor tattoo art provoked controversy after a parent complained about explicit 19th-century etchings on whale bone labeled “Hide Your Eyes!” Museum staff say the erotic pieces are displayed high and warned, with more graphic items kept in storage; the dispute has nonetheless increased public interest. Practical notes: limited paid parking nearby and recommended 1–2 hour visits.

A 14-month-old Bronx girl, Xania Samuels, fell from a fifth-floor apartment window and is in critical but stable condition after suffering head trauma. The fall occurred at 11:29 a.m.; emergency responders arrived within minutes after an EMT happened upon the child on the pavement and called 911. Neighbors described her as lying limp with head wounds; she was taken to Jacobi Hospital. Her father said the toddler insisted on wearing a heavily cushioned pink winter coat on an unusually hot day, and the family believes the coat may have softened the impact. At the time of the incident the father was bathing the infant’s twin brother and the mother was at a laundromat. No criminal charges were filed. Residents and the mother told the New York Post there were no window guards in the building; sources indicated none of the upper floors’ windows had legally required guards despite the presence of young children. Neighbors and first responders recounted the father’s shock and the traumatic scene; doctors are hopeful Xania will survive. Additional reporting noted community concern and prior complaints to the landlord were reportedly ignored.

Pittsburgh International Airport will become the first U.S. airport since 9/11 to allow non-ticketed visitors past security checkpoints year‑round, starting Sept. 5, with TSA approval. The change restores pre‑9/11 access so friends and family can enter airside gates, shops, restaurants and view airport artwork. Non‑flyers must register at a special desk, present valid photo ID, and be screened against the no‑fly list before undergoing the same security screening as ticketed passengers. The TSA said it supports the policy but noted no additional staff have been added and there are currently no plans to expand the program to other airports. The move has sparked criticism from airline workers’ unions: Bob Ross, national president of the Association of Professional Flight Attendants, warned the policy could reduce airport safety, lengthen security lines and cause travelers to miss flights. He called the decision “a terrible precedent” and questioned its timing near the anniversary of 9/11, arguing it undermines vigilance. The story was reported by NBC News and covered in the Tribune‑Review; it was written by Theresa Clift. The notice about archived web crawls and the Internet Archive’s "No More 404" effort was included as background on preserving web references.

Newark Mayor Cory Booker won the Democratic U.S. Senate primary decisively, beating U.S. Reps. Rush Holt and Frank Pallone and state Assembly Speaker Sheila Oliver, and will face Republican Steve Lonegan in the Oct. 16 special election to fill the late Sen. Frank Lautenberg’s seat. Booker led with about 59 percent of the vote to Pallone’s 20, Holt’s 17 and Oliver’s 4. He ran as a pragmatic, results-focused centrist who emphasized his accomplishments revitalizing Newark, fundraising advantages, celebrity backing, and ability to work across the aisle, notably with Governor Chris Christie. Opponents attacked his record and business ties—most prominently his stake in tech startup Waywire—but those critiques failed to dent his lead. Booker, a Yale Law and Rhodes scholar who moved to Newark as a young activist and served as mayor, leveraged national visibility and large fundraising to dominate. Lonegan, a conservative former Bogota mayor, prevailed in the GOP primary, setting up a campaign of sharp contrasts ahead.

Billionaire fashion designer Peter Nygård says he’s receiving stem-cell treatments and claims the therapy is reversing his ageing. Living in the Bahamas, the 70-year-old told the Bahamas Tribune that a University of Miami study is monitoring him and that his biomarkers indicate he is “getting younger.” Nygård says he has been undergoing stem-cell therapy for four years and believes he may be taking more treatment than anyone else in the world. He has promoted stem-cell research in the Bahamas and featured in a self-produced video touting the potential of stem cells to cure disease and extend life, even likening himself to a modern-day seeker of the fountain of youth.

Locally, Nygård has explored establishing a stem-cell clinic and has been reported to consider sites in Freeport, including the closed Port Lucaya Resort and nearby marina. These plans follow earlier controversy over a proposed $50 million facility at his Lyford Cay estate, which drew resistance from residents and legal challenges. Fred Smith QC, who led opposition to Nygård’s Lyford Cay development, publicly encouraged Nygård to move any medical tourism investment to Freeport, where authorities and local business leaders would welcome large-scale investment and “roll out the red carpet.” Observers note logistical hurdles and that no formal commitments have been made. Critics and ethicists caution that while stem-cell research holds promise for treating serious illnesses, enthusiasm from wealthy advocates should be viewed skeptically and weighed against ethical, regulatory and community concerns.

During Louisville’s Elite Eight win over Duke, guard Kevin Ware suffered one of the most horrific injuries seen on live sports: an open compound fracture of his right tibia that punctured through the skin and appeared to be snapped in two places. Teammates wept and CBS halted replays; Ware reportedly shouted “Win the game” as trainers stabilized him and he was stretchered out. Surgeons reset the bone, inserted a rod, and closed the wound in a two-hour operation; doctors said infection risk and blood-flow issues make recovery lengthy but not necessarily career-ending. Louisville regrouped to win 85-63 and advanced to the Final Four; teammates honored Ware on court and he hoped to join them in Atlanta. The incident renewed debate over NCAA athlete protections and compensation: Ware faces expensive, prolonged rehab while remaining categorized as a “student-athlete” without workers’ compensation, highlighting broader concerns about medical safety nets for unpaid college players despite massive tournament revenues.

Boulder police and the Boulder County district attorney plan new DNA testing on key evidence in the unsolved 1996 murder of 6-year-old JonBenét Ramsey after a joint 9NEWS/Daily Camera investigation revealed significant problems with earlier DNA interpretations. The inquiry focused on DNA recovered from JonBenét’s panties and long johns and challenged former DA Mary Lacy’s 2008 decision to publicly clear the Ramsey family. Documents from Bode Technology’s 2008 testing showed mixtures on the long johns that likely included genetic material from more than two contributors; independent experts retained by the news organizations concluded the “Unknown Male 1” profile entered into CODIS in 2003 may be a composite rather than an individual’s profile. Those experts also disagreed that the long johns’ DNA definitively “matched” the underwear sample or that its presence on the clothing had no innocent explanation. Emails show Lacy’s office was informed of such ambiguities before issuing the exoneration letter, raising concerns about confirmation bias and the failure to follow double-blind standards. Current DA Stan Garnett and Boulder Police Chief Greg Testa met with Colorado Bureau of Investigation officials about using more sensitive, FBI-required kits (including upcoming Yfiler Plus/Y-STR testing) that examine additional loci and isolate male DNA, which experts say could clarify whether one or multiple male contributors exist. No new testing has been done since 2008, but authorities say they will perform “all reasonable testing” using updated methods. The revelations complicate reliance on the disputed DNA profile, undermine claims that the case is solely a “DNA case,” and could reopen investigative directions previously narrowed by interpretations of the older results. Separately, Dr. Werner Spitz has asked a court to dismiss Burke Ramsey’s $150 million defamation suit over TV accusations, arguing his statements were opinion protected by the First Amendment; the suit disputes that defense.

Diplomatic leaders convened the Quartet’s first top-level meeting in six months at UN headquarters, attended by US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov and UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, with EU representative Baroness Ashton joining by video. They subsequently took part in a UN Security Council debate on the Arab Spring as violence between Israel and Gaza intensified. Israeli airstrikes and rocket fire from Gaza escalated into days of tit‑for‑tat attacks: Israel reported some 180–200 rockets launched from Gaza, wounding Israelis and damaging homes as far north as Gedera and Ashdod, while Gaza medics reported more than 20–25 Palestinians killed and dozens injured. Israel struck militant sites and said it would use all necessary measures to protect civilians; Palestinian officials accused Israel of deadly escalation and urged urgent Security Council action. International reactions included China and UN Secretary‑General Ban Ki‑moon calling for restraint. Egyptian mediators reportedly brokered a ceasefire agreement, though Israeli officials gave no immediate confirmation. Talks between Israel and the Palestinians remain frozen.

A permitted demolition in downtown Philadelphia on Wednesday caused a four-story building to collapse onto the adjacent Salvation Army thrift store at 22nd and Market, killing six people and injuring 13 others. The dead were identified as Kimberly Finnegan, Borbor Davis, Juanita Harmin, Mary Simpson, Anne Bryan and Roseline Conteh; all were found inside the store. Thirteen survivors were pulled from the rubble and taken to hospitals, and a 61-year-old woman, Myra Plekan, was rescued more than 13 hours after the collapse. Witnesses described a sudden, thunderous rumble as walls and framing toppled when heavy equipment allegedly yanked a beam during demolition. Bystanders and citizen rescuers rushed in to help before emergency crews arrived. The city began a wide-ranging investigation amid questions about inspection and permitting: Licenses and Inspections officials said inspections aren’t required during mid-demolition, and the demolition contractor had valid permits. OSHA has been notified. Mayor Michael Nutter praised rescuers and promised scrutiny of oversight practices as cleanup and examination of the site continued and nearby roads remained closed.

When reclusive copper heiress Huguette Clark died at 104, her 2005 wills set off a bitter legal struggle over her $400 million estate. A will drawn six weeks after another largely disinherited distant relatives and directed Clark’s bluff-top Santa Barbara home, Bellosguardo, be turned into a museum holding her art; it named longtime attorney Wallace Bock and accountant Irving Kamsler as executors and gave substantial gifts — including more than $30 million to Clark’s nurse, Hadassah Peri, and bequests to the advisers. Relatives challenged the second will, contending Bock and Kamsler engineered it to gain access and profit: executors normally earn about 2 percent of such estates, roughly $8 million each, and both were named as trustees and beneficiaries of foundation plans tied to the museum.

In December filings, New York’s public administrator accused Bock and Kamsler of massive tax fraud and mismanagement, alleging failure to file federal gift tax returns for roughly $56 million in gifts (1997–2003), understating liabilities, filing false returns, charging for unperformed work, and hiding liabilities that by 2011 allegedly exceeded $82 million with penalties and interest. The public administrator sought their removal; a judge suspended them pending hearings. Kamsler resigned as executor; both men deny wrongdoing. Manhattan prosecutors and the public administrator continue investigations, and relatives seek to intervene and potentially claw back improper gifts, while local leaders hope the estate’s resolution will honor Clark’s legacy.

After nearly three weeks away following the Dec. 14 massacre, Sandy Hook Elementary students returned to classes Thursday at a refurbished middle school in neighboring Monroe, Conn., because their original Newtown building remains a crime scene. More than 400 students, many arriving by bus to streets lined with balloons and welcome signs, reunited with friends and teachers, and parents were allowed to stay in the building for the day. Officials and teachers worked to recreate familiar surroundings: students’ desks, backpacks, coats and lunch boxes left behind on the day of the shooting were transferred to the new site, and the former Chalk Hill Middle School was renamed Sandy Hook Elementary. Donna Page, a former Sandy Hook principal who retired in 2010, returned to lead the school after her successor, Dawn Hochsprung, was killed in the attack.

Counselors, police officers and therapy dogs were present to support students; attendance was robust and Monroe police described the location as “the safest school in America,” while noting security would be gradually scaled back to help restore normalcy. The community response included volunteers who repainted and refitted facilities for younger children, adjusting bathroom fixtures and supplying new furniture and gift boxes for students.

Connecticut Governor Dannel Malloy praised the “Herculean effort” to prepare the Monroe site and announced a 15-member commission to recommend policy reforms by March, focusing on school security, mental health services and gun laws — including scrutiny of high-capacity magazines. The commission will be chaired by Hamden Mayor Scott Jackson. Officials stressed the aim of returning students to learning and healing while addressing broader questions raised by the tragedy for future prevention.

Bodybuilding star Rich Piana collapsed at his Florida home during a haircut and was found with evidence suggesting drug use and long-term steroid use, according to a police report obtained by TMZ Sports. Emergency responders arrived after Piana, 46, suddenly fell in his bathroom; his girlfriend, Chanel, said she could not catch him due to his large size and that he hit his head. A 911 operator instructed Chanel to perform CPR, but she was unable to revive him. Paramedics discovered crushed white powder, a credit card and a straw on a table and administered two doses of Narcan while attempting resuscitation. Chanel told responders Piana had a past opiate addiction but believed he was clean. He was transported to a hospital in a medically induced coma and had not regained consciousness. Officers reportedly found 20 bottles of testosterone in the home; Chanel confirmed Piana had been using steroids for more than 20 years. She also said he had previously experienced a mildly enlarged heart but did not know whether that played a role. Chanel said Piana was still alive, fighting, and asked for prayers.

Half marathons surged in popularity in 2013, becoming the fastest-growing standard U.S. road-race distance. Running USA estimated a record 1.96 million U.S. finishers, a 6% increase from 2012 and more than six times the 1990 total of 303,000. Growth has been driven largely by women, who made up a record 61% of finishers in 2013 (up from 53% in 2006), although male finishers also rose in absolute numbers to over 760,000. Globally, 14 of the 20 largest half marathons were in the U.S., but the three biggest events were overseas: Goteborg (45,126), Great North Run (40,763) and Paris (30,371). Since 2000 U.S. half-marathon finishers quadrupled, and October hosted the most events in 2013.

Portland police announced they have reopened their probe into sexual-assault allegations against former Vice President Al Gore after identifying procedural errors in how the bureau handled the matter in 2009. Chief Michael Reese said command-level supervisors should have reviewed the case and decided whether to pursue it when the complainant, massage therapist Molly Hagerty, went to police last year — her second contact with authorities. Hagerty had told detectives she was groped and kissed during a late-night 2006 massage at the Hotel Lucia, yet police never contacted Gore and did not consult the Multnomah County district attorney’s office. Reese said reopening was the bureau’s decision and pledged a thorough, fair, and expedited investigation while declining further comment during the inquiry.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, a fail-safe facility built into a Norwegian mountain to preserve crop diversity, experienced water intrusion last fall but the seeds were never at risk. In October 2016, unusually high temperatures and heavy rain in Svalbard caused meltwater to enter the tunnel leading to the vault, advancing roughly 15 meters into the 100-meter tunnel before freezing. Statsbygg, the Norwegian government agency overseeing the site’s infrastructure, confirmed the event and said no seeds or the vault itself were endangered; this year no further leaks have occurred. The tunnel was always expected to experience some water intrusion during seasonal thaws—the vault’s inner chambers sit about 110 meters into the mountain and are built into solid rock, with seeds stored at about -18°C. Designers installed pumping stations near the tunnel base because the tunnel was not originally intended to be fully watertight; construction disturbed local permafrost and prevented it from fully re-forming, making the entrance area more vulnerable to meltwater, especially during record heatwaves. Cary Fowler, an architect of the project, noted that some water at the tunnel mouth has occurred annually and typically freezes without reaching the vault. Separately, the facility has been used as intended: for the first time since opening in 2008, seeds were approved for withdrawal to replace material from a gene bank damaged by Syria’s civil war. ICARDA has requested nearly 130 of its deposited boxes—about 116,000 samples including drought-resistant wheat, barley and grasses—to restore collections and support breeding for dry regions. The vault holds over 860,000 samples from nearly all nations and is designed to remain sealed and frozen for centuries even if external systems fail.

A 30-year-old Ugandan hospital technician died of Marburg virus disease in late September, prompting intensive contact tracing and quarantines but no large-scale outbreak. Marburg, a filovirus closely related to Ebola, causes sudden fever, chills, headache and muscle pain after a 5–10 day incubation. By about day five patients often develop a maculopapular rash and then gastrointestinal symptoms; severe cases can progress to jaundice, pancreatitis, multi-organ failure, massive hemorrhage and shock. Transmission requires direct contact with blood, tissues or bodily fluids of infected humans or animals (not airborne). Fruit bats and infected primates have been implicated as sources; notable exposures include visits to caves such as Kitum Cave in Kenya. After the Ugandan death, authorities quarantined roughly 99 contacts—more than 60 were health workers—and tested symptomatic suspects; 11 tested negative and others will be retested if symptoms persist. Uganda’s Ministry of Health and international partners emphasized rapid laboratory capacity, disease detectives and an emergency operations center as key to containment. Historical outbreaks include the first identified in 1967 (31 cases linked to imported African green monkeys), a major 1998–2000 outbreak in DRC (154 cases, 83% fatality), Angola in 2004–05 (252 cases, 90% fatality), and a 2012 Uganda cluster (15 cases, four deaths). Case-fatality rates have ranged roughly 23–90% depending on outbreak and care. There is no specific proven treatment or licensed vaccine; care is supportive, though experimental antivirals have shown promise in animal studies. Early detection, isolation and contact tracing make large uncontrolled spread unlikely.

In Amritsar, a 42-year-old police head constable was found to have swallowed 40 knives over roughly two months, telling doctors he simply “felt like eating them.” He sought medical help for low appetite, weight loss, stomach pain and weakness. Initial ultrasound suggested a solid mass; endoscopy and CT scans revealed multiple metallic knives in his stomach. A five-member team of surgeons, physicians and critical-care specialists performed a five-hour operation to remove the instruments. Some blades were open, some closed, and others were corroded or broken. Dr. Jatinder (Jitendra) Malhotra, who led the team, described the case as the most unsettling surgery in his 20-year career and said the patient appeared to have a psychological disorder driving the behavior. After the procedure the man was reported to be stable and out of danger. The case drew widespread media attention and astonishment.

French prosecutors have filed preliminary charges of complicity in murder, theft and involvement in terrorism against Abdelkader Merah, 29, the brother of Mohamed Merah, who killed seven people before being shot dead by police after a 30–32 hour siege in Toulouse. Abdelkader denies helping commit the attacks, though authorities say inquiries show plausible links; traces of possible explosives were found in his car and he was previously linked to smuggling jihadists. He remains in custody while investigators probe whether Mohamed acted alone. Their mother was released without charge.

On Aug. 15, 2012, the United States men’s national team ended a 75-year drought by beating Mexico 1-0 at Mexico City’s Estadio Azteca, a venue where the U.S. had gone 0-23-1 since 1937. The lone goal came in the 80th minute from defender Michael Orozco Fiscal, who finished a move started by substitutes Brek Shea and Terrence Boyd: Shea cut inside and crossed, Boyd back-heeled to Orozco Fiscal, who poked the ball past goalkeeper Guillermo Ochoa. Tim Howard preserved the victory with key late saves, including denying Javier “Chicharito” Hernández on a deflected shot and a point-blank header. Despite Mexico dominating possession (outshooting the U.S. 15-6 and holding a 10-0 corner advantage) and fielding many regulars returning from the Olympics, the Americans absorbed pressure with a makeshift central defense of Maurice Edu and Geoff Cameron and relied on Howard’s heroics. Coach Jurgen Klinsmann hailed the result as historic and confidence-boosting for his second year in charge as he builds toward World Cup 2014. The match used a half-strength U.S. roster because European club seasons had begun; several usual starters were absent. The win followed a previous historic friendly victory over Italy in Genoa and, beyond the scoreline, symbolically altered the narrative at the Azteca — so much so that Howard joked it was “time to change the sign” in the stadium tunnel listing past U.S. results.

California will stop automatically barring all registered sex offenders from living within 2,000 feet of schools or parks and will instead apply residency restrictions case by case, the state corrections department announced. The shift follows a California Supreme Court ruling this month that found the blanket “Jessica’s Law” restriction unconstitutional in San Diego County and ineffective at protecting the public. Voters approved Jessica’s Law in 2006; critics have long argued such sweeping buffers force many offenders into homelessness or transient living because urban areas rarely offer housing beyond the exclusion zone, making access to jobs and treatment difficult. Under the new policy, high-risk offenders—those with current or prior convictions for lewd acts on a child under 14—will still be barred from living within a half-mile of K–12 schools. For other parolees, residency rules will depend on individual conviction histories and assessed propensity to abuse children. The corrections department will review thousands of parolee cases over about two months; existing restrictions remain during the review. The change drew criticism from Jessica’s Law author and former state senator George Runner, who said it exceeds the Supreme Court’s decision and disregards voter intent. California maintains about 6,000 registered sex-offender parolees and a public Megan’s Law database.

China has been strengthening defenses and repositioning forces along its roughly 880-mile border with North Korea amid rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula and concerns about possible U.S. military action against Pyongyang. Reviews of Chinese military and government reporting, plus expert commentary, indicate Beijing began implementing many measures last year and accelerated them recently. Steps include forming a new border-defense brigade conducting patrols, intelligence gathering and more detailed mapping of the tri-border area with North Korea, Russia and Mongolia, and placing the entire border zone under round‑the‑clock video surveillance using drones, patrol vehicles and advanced cameras.

Chinese officials and analysts emphasize that Beijing’s primary worry is not an invasion but a mass influx of North Korean refugees should conflict erupt. Large refugee flows into densely populated, economically vital northeastern China would pose significant humanitarian, economic and security strains—analogous to regional stresses seen in other refugee crises. Chinese commentators, retired PLA officers and foreign policy analysts have publicly urged contingency planning, including proposals for refugee management and potential military preparations to respond rapidly to instability across the border.

Tensions have heightened as North Korea asserts advances, including claims of ICBM testing, and U.S. officials signal increased pressure on Pyongyang, with some U.S. leaders at times hinting at regime-change options. Beijing has condemned North Korean weapons tests but also criticized U.S. and South Korean rhetoric, calling for negotiations and saying military force should not be the solution. Chinese spokesmen assert the People’s Liberation Army maintains normal combat readiness and training along the border while official outlets warn that if the nuclear issue escalates, war on the peninsula could become unavoidable.

Vote With Your Purse, a study by She Should Run (SSR) and the Center for Responsive Politics, documents a persistent gender gap in U.S. political giving and links declines in women’s donations to reduced female representation in Congress. In 2010 women provided just 26% of recorded federal contributions to candidates, PACs, and parties—down from 31% in 2008—while women make up over 50% of the population but only about 17% of Congress. Key findings show women gave 27% of individual candidate contributions, 21% to PACs, and disproportionately favored Democrats. Yet female candidates outperformed men in fundraising, with incumbent and challenger women raising substantially more than male counterparts. SSR attributes low giving to beliefs that donations don’t matter and a weak link between politics and social change, and recommends framing giving as civic responsibility, clarifying impact, increasing transparency, and creating engagement opportunities to boost women’s political donations.

Trouble at the Top examines how Everest’s growing commercialization, overcrowding, and environmental instability have converged to create a deadly and volatile climbing season. Startling recent images of packed lines of climbers moving between camps underscore the congestion: up to 300 mountaineers were observed between Camps 3 and 4, and many more were crowding summit routes during brief weather windows. While many reached the top, at least four climbers died during that period. Operator Himalayan Experience (Himex) abruptly evacuated its more than 60 clients and staff on May 7, citing unusually warm temperatures, warnings from experienced Sherpas about the Khumbu Icefall’s instability, a giant hanging serac, abundant rockfalls on the Lhotse Face, and recent near-avalanches. Himex’s decision—rare among commercial teams—highlighted how difficult it is for climbers and operators to turn back once invested in a summit bid.

The piece stresses two interacting problems: sheer numbers of largely amateur climbers and deteriorating high-altitude conditions, potentially driven by climate change. Himalayan glaciers have shrunk over 20 percent in 30 years, and warming has made seracs and icefalls more unstable. That instability exacts a disproportionate toll on Nepali high-altitude workers. Historical and recent fatality data show Sherpas face far higher death rates than Western climbers and many other hazardous professions. Sherpas undertake repeated trips through the most dangerous zones—especially the Khumbu Icefall—often while carrying heavy loads and with less oxygen or medical prophylaxis than Western clients. The April avalanche that killed sixteen Nepali high-altitude workers was the deadliest disaster in Everest history and provoked unprecedented Sherpa anger and strikes demanding better compensation, insurance, and government support.

Even as Western climbers benefit from better forecasting, oxygen use, and medical strategies—making ascents statistically safer for them—the commercial model shifts risk onto Sherpas. Meanwhile, media saturation and live dispatches from the mountain glamorize attempts and sustain demand. The result is a spectacle that draws more participants into an increasingly hazardous environment, posing deep ethical, regulatory, and safety challenges for the future of Everest.

Newt Gingrich has long used the slogan “Winning the Future” — indeed, he registered a political group called American Solutions for Winning the Future with the IRS under section 527 on October 6, 2006, and it has been his campaign vehicle since. When President Obama unveiled “Winning the Future” in his 2011 State of the Union, commentators and comedians quickly noted the overlap; Jon Stewart and Stephen Colbert mocked the phrase, and White House adviser Austan Goolsbee laughed during a Stewart segment. Despite Obama’s prominent use, Gingrich continues to use the slogan on his campaign materials and has not objected publicly to the similarity. Gingrich’s spokesman Rick Tyler said the campaign welcomes the overlap and plans to debate directly whose policies will actually “win the future,” framing the shared phrase as fodder for a policy showdown rather than a dispute over ownership.

Bill Cosby’s 2017 criminal trial centers on a single 2004 allegation by Andrea Constand, even though more than 50 women have publicly accused him of sexual assault. Cosby, 79, faces three counts of aggravated indecent assault for allegedly drugging and molesting Constand at his Pennsylvania home. He has denied wrongdoing since Constand first reported the incident to police in 2005. That year’s district attorney declined charges; Constand sued and settled a 2006 civil case. A viral 2014 Hannibal Buress routine renewed scrutiny, prompting dozens of other women to come forward and the unsealing of Cosby’s 2005 deposition, in which he discussed obtaining Quaaludes to give to women — a statement that helped lead to his 2015 arrest.

Legally, the trial will rely primarily on Constand’s testimony and one other accuser the judge allowed to testify to show a pattern of conduct; prosecutors had sought to include many more accounts but were limited to avoid prejudicing the jury. With little forensic evidence and Cosby choosing not to testify, the case is expected to be a classic he-said-she-said contest hinging on witness credibility, timing of reporting, and interpretations of past conduct. Defense strategy is likely to emphasize inconsistencies, the long passage of time, portray Constand’s post-incident behavior as not indicatory of trauma, and depict media and political pressure around reopening the case. Prosecutors plan to use expert testimony on victim behavior and pharmaceutical effects.

Beyond the legal outcome, the trial carries wider cultural significance: it may influence public perceptions of high-profile sexual-assault accusations, affect other survivors’ willingness to come forward, and contribute to national conversations about statutes of limitations, celebrity, race, and accountability. Constand — a former Temple employee and athlete who says she was rendered incapacitated after taking pills and wine — will testify and faces intense cross-examination; many accusers view the prosecution itself as a form of vindication regardless of the verdict.

A rare Northern Song dynasty Ding bowl bought at a 2007 garage sale in New York for $3 sold at Sotheby’s for $2.2 million. The small, thin-walled, ivory‑glazed bowl—about 5.5 inches across—exemplifies top-quality Ding ware: featherlight potting, near-white body that needed no slip, and a glaze that pools in darker “tears.” Its incised lotus spray interior and overlapping leaf exterior show spontaneous, fluid carving; the shape is unusual for Ding but known from contemporary silver examples. Kilns at Quyang, Ding county, Hebei produced such wares, often mimicking precious metal forms for palace use. Only one near-identical bowl exists, in the British Museum. London dealer Giuseppe Eskenazi won the piece; Sotheby’s had estimated $200–300k.

Japanese police have arrested 67-year-old Masaaki Osaka, a fugitive wanted for more than 45 years in connection with the 1971 killing of a police officer during left-wing street protests in Tokyo. Tokyo police confirmed Wednesday that Osaka faces five charges including murder. Public broadcaster NHK and other outlets report he allegedly assaulted a 21-year-old officer with a steel pipe, doused him with petrol and set him on fire during a riot in Shibuya Ward tied to protests against Japan’s recognition of the US military presence. Osaka’s face has been on wanted posters in Tokyo for decades.

Police captured Osaka last month in an apartment in Hiroshima linked to the Chukaku-ha (Japan Revolutionary Communist League, JRCL), a radical left-wing group active in the 1960s–70s. He was initially arrested on a minor unrelated charge—obstructing a police officer—and was identified after DNA testing; fingerprints from the original crime were unavailable. Authorities say he evaded capture for decades by using networks of sympathizers within the JRCL. The JRCL historically organized violent demonstrations, and one alleged accomplice was charged in 1972 but had proceedings suspended for mental illness. Japan abolished the statute of limitations for murder in 2010, allowing prosecution despite the passage of time. Osaka has been transported to Tokyo for further questioning.
