A California woman, Michelle Hadley, was exonerated after spending nearly four months jailed for crimes she did not commit. Orange County prosecutors say 31-year-old Angela Maria Diaz of Phoenix orchestrated an elaborate frame-up, impersonating Hadley in Craigslist “rape-fantasy” ads and fabricating threatening emails to portray Hadley as a violent stalker. Diaz, who married the man both women had been involved with—identified only as “John Doe,” a deputy U.S. Marshal—was arrested in Phoenix and faces numerous felony and misdemeanor charges, including kidnapping, false imprisonment, forgery, grand theft, perjury, and multiple counts of falsely reporting crimes. If convicted she faces up to 12 years and eight months in state prison plus additional county jail time.

Hadley, 30, an MBA student, was arrested twice in mid-2016—first in June and again in July—held on bonds up to $1 million and at one point faced life-threatening charges including attempted forcible rape. The case attracted national attention; Hadley’s mugshot circulated widely. Prosecutors now say Diaz sent the threatening emails to herself—using VPNs and proxies—and posted the Craigslist ads while impersonating Hadley, supplying her own photos and details and luring at least two men to her home before calling police. Diaz also allegedly faked a pregnancy and a cervical-cancer diagnosis, forged doctor’s notes and paychecks, and posed as an attorney; she is accused of altering paychecks and attempting to cash forged checks.

District Attorney Tony Rackauckas called Hadley “an innocent victim of a diabolical scheme” and emphasized clearing her name in court and public opinion. Hadley was released in October after reinvestigation, and her defense attorney worked with prosecutors to trace the emails and other false reports back to Diaz. Diaz awaits extradition and a court date.

Reports suggest Jodie Foster is taking her relationship with photographer Alexandra Hedison very seriously, making significant lifestyle changes to support their future together. According to tabloid accounts, Foster has joined Alcoholics Anonymous and embraced a 12-step program to stop drinking, a move reportedly encouraged by Hedison, a recovering alcoholic with over a decade of sobriety. Friends claim Hedison pushed Foster to address what had become a real issue between them, and Foster’s sobriety has reassured Hedison about their long-term prospects. Insiders say Hedison wants Foster to remain sober for at least a year before they marry, and that the couple—described as "crazy in love"—may already have had a commitment ceremony, sometimes leading to speculation when they were seen wearing matching gold bands. Separately, gossip columns allege Ellen DeGeneres warned Foster against marrying Hedison, citing Ellen’s own marital doubts and past relationship with Hedison, and expressing concern about potential emotional and financial consequences for Foster. These claims come from celebrity tabloids and include speculation about Ellen and Portia de Rossi’s marriage; they should be viewed as unverified celebrity gossip rather than confirmed fact.

California Assembly Majority Leader Ian Calderon (D-Whittier) introduced Assembly Bill 1884, which would require sit-down restaurants to provide plastic straws only upon customer request. The proposal is narrowly targeted—applying to dine-in establishments and excluding bars and fast-food outlets—and Calderon stressed it is not a ban on straws. Under the current California Retail Food Code, violations are misdemeanors punishable by up to six months in jail and/or fines up to $1,000; Calderon clarified that those penalties appear only because the bill is placed within that existing code section and said amendments will remove the severe sanctions as the legislative process proceeds.

Calderon frames AB 1884 as an awareness and behavior-change measure aimed at reducing one-time-use plastic waste that accumulates in landfills, waterways and oceans. His office cited troubling statistics: roughly 500 million plastic straws are used daily in the U.S. (about 1.6 per person), straws and stirrers ranked sixth among items collected on California’s Coastal Cleanup Day (1989–2014), only about 9% of plastics are recycled, and straws are essentially never recycled due to their size and material coding. The bill is presented as a modest step to curb reliance on convenience plastics, reduce environmental harm and encourage consumers to rethink disposable straw usage.

A Dutch father, Hans de Borst, publicly blamed Russian president Vladimir Putin and Russian-backed separatists for the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 in an emotional open letter published on Facebook and in Dutch media. De Borst lost his only child, 17-year-old Elsemiek de Borst, who was traveling from Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur with family when the Boeing 777 was struck on July 17. He described her promising future—strong school performance and plans to study engineering at Delft—and angrily addressed those he holds responsible, saying they have "shot her young life upside down" and signing the letter as "Elsemiek's father… whose life is ruined." The message, translated from Dutch, expresses grief, accusation, and despair toward leaders and separatists implicated by investigators. The report also notes the broader context of archiving online pages to preserve sources as web content changes, mentioning efforts by the Internet Archive to prevent broken links and retain original references.

A community town hall is being held in Dearborn, Michigan, on April 29 at 1 PM to rally against rising anti-Arab and anti-Muslim bias and to counter an Islamophobic conference taking place the same day. Organizers stress that prejudice toward Arabs and Muslims persists nationwide—in bad policy, media spectacles such as the Park 51 controversy, threats like Quran burnings, mosque protests, and anti-Sharia legislation—and that Michigan’s Arab American community has long borne and resisted these attacks. Dearborn residents previously confronted provocateurs such as Terry Jones by marginalizing him and mounting an interfaith response; organizers point to that model of dignified, collective action. The town hall responds specifically to Pamela Geller and Robert Spencer’s “Jessica Mokdad Human Rights Conference,” which appropriates the name of a murdered young Arab American woman to promote a bigoted agenda. Organizers call the exploitation shameful and emphasize that, unlike earlier fringe figures, Geller and Spencer have large followings and frequent mainstream media exposure, making their influence harder to ignore. The Arab American Institute (AAI), together with local groups, will host the event at the Doubletree Hotel (5801 Southfield Road) featuring AAI President Jim Zogby, Executive Director Maya Berry, Eli Clifton (co-author of the investigative report Fear, Inc.), journalist/blogger Sarah Posner, community and interfaith leaders, and Michigan public officials. The town hall aims both to directly challenge the conference’s narrative and to create a community conversation on practical responses to ongoing Islamophobia, affirming commitment to diversity and religious freedom. The piece notes that the Mokdad family and many Muslim women in metro Detroit reject the conference’s use of her name and its message.

Former President George W. Bush canceled a planned Feb. 12 keynote appearance at a Keren Hayesod charity gala in Geneva after growing pressure and legal threats in Switzerland over allegations he authorized torture. Human rights groups said they intended to file a 2,500-page criminal complaint accusing Bush of mistreatment of detainees at Guantanamo Bay, including waterboarding, which Bush has acknowledged in memoirs and interviews. Activists and some politicians urged Swiss authorities to arrest and investigate him under the UN Convention Against Torture, which Switzerland has ratified; rights lawyers argued authorities would be obliged to prosecute or extradite. Organizers cited security concerns and planned protests by leftist groups as the reason for cancelling Bush’s participation, while Swiss officials noted former heads of state enjoy some diplomatic immunity. Rights groups portrayed the cancellation as evidence that accountability efforts can constrain travel for leaders accused of torture and vowed to continue pursuing the case.

Near the Turkish border town of Kilis, Zakaria Deeb and his family — like hundreds of other Syrians — found themselves stranded in a gravel field under plastic sheeting after traveling 100 miles on a false rumor that they would be admitted to a Turkish-run camp. They fled Syria a year earlier because of fighting among rebels, government forces, Kurdish fighters and ISIS; near Kilis, ISIS was clashing with another rebel faction while shells and stray bullets reached across the border, wounding a child in a camp. Their plight reflects a rapidly worsening refugee crisis spawned by nearly three years of civil war in Syria: what U.N. and humanitarian officials call the most challenging displacement emergency in a generation. Refugee numbers jumped from 300,000 a year earlier to 2.1 million, with U.N. forecasts of as many as 3.5 million by year’s end. Host countries — Lebanon, Jordan, Iraq and especially Turkey — are straining under the influx. Camps are full and urban areas bear rising rents, lower wages and social tensions; Lebanon may soon host refugees comprising a quarter of its population. The porous, often lawless border has enabled mass crossings and smuggling networks; Turkish soldiers intermittently chase groups trying to slip in, sometimes returning them. U.N. officials stress the need for sustained humanitarian operations and support for host communities, acknowledging the crisis is likely to persist as fighting continues and large parts of Syria lie devastated.

Former Louisiana governor Edwin Edwards, 86, announced a bid for the U.S. House seat in Louisiana’s 6th District, declaring he can run and is confident he can win despite his past conviction and more than eight years in federal prison for fraud, racketeering and extortion related to riverboat casino licensing. Flanked by his wife Trina and their young son Eli, Edwards framed the campaign as a chance to address local needs, saying he wants to focus on healthcare access—criticizing Gov. Bobby Jindal’s refusal to expand Medicaid—public works, agriculture, oil-and-gas issues, and infrastructure projects like high-speed rail between Baton Rouge and New Orleans. He said he would seek committee assignments to influence those areas, supports the Keystone XL pipeline, and has engaged environmental leader Lt. Gen. Russel Honoré about aquifer concerns. Edwards has a long, colorful political history: four terms as governor, earlier congressional service, a high-profile corruption trial, and a comeback victory over David Duke in 1991. The district leans Republican after redistricting, and analysts view his run as unlikely to flip the seat, though his name recognition could carry him into a runoff. Edwards stresses forgiveness and second chances while maintaining his innocence.

Republican state Sen. Frank Lasee, a candidate for the GOP nomination for Wisconsin’s open 8th Congressional District, is facing scrutiny over where he actually lives after an apartment he says is his primary residence was listed on Airbnb. Lasee lists a De Pere condo as his home address and has claimed he lives there most of the time, but his wife owns a nicer house in Racine—inside Speaker Paul Ryan’s district—raising questions because if Lasee declared Racine as his residence he’d have to run against Ryan. The condo was advertised as a “luxury apartment” for $210 a night and described as close to Lambeau Field; reporters successfully attempted to book it. After inquiries, Lasee’s wife, the Airbnb host, denied a requested stay and the listing was soon removed, though cached copies remain. Lasee acknowledged a “crazy living arrangement,” saying he primarily lives in De Pere and occasionally stays at the Racine house. A prior 2014 complaint over his residency was dismissed by the Government Accountability Board after Lasee produced a 2011 lease that barred subleasing and listed only him and his wife as occupants. Records show Lasee claimed the De Pere address for mileage reimbursements. Critics, including local conservative host Jerry Bader and liberal activist Scot Ross, have questioned his explanations and motives; Lasee says opponents are using the issue as a campaign tactic and declined further comment.

Sant Gopaldas, 36, an activist fasting to protest mining in the Ganga riverbed, was rushed to AIIMS Rishikesh early Saturday after days of fasting at Triveni and Bag ghats since June 24. Admitted to the emergency ward and now in endocrinology, doctors say he was dehydrated with blood sugar at 65, refusing food and treatment; he is receiving IV fluids. Hospital authorities have permission to take measures, including force-feeding, to save his life. His hospitalization comes two days after the death of prominent Ganga activist G.D. Agarwal (Swami Gyan Swaroop Sanand), who died at age 86 after more than 15 weeks on a hunger strike demanding stronger protections and a law to clean the Ganges and halt hydroelectric projects that disrupt its flow. Agarwal’s death—following forced hospitalization when he stopped drinking—prompted national grief, political tributes and calls for an independent probe. Critics say government efforts, including a flagship cleanup launched in 2015, have fallen short, with audits pointing to planning and spending lapses.

Federal and state officials are investigating the suspected shootings of four male California (southern) sea otters after their carcasses washed up on beaches near Santa Cruz over an eight-day period in August. The US Fish and Wildlife Service announced a $10,000 reward for information leading to arrest and conviction in the deaths of three otters found between August 12 and 19; a fourth carcass found August 20 showed a suspected gunshot wound but was too deteriorated for immediate determination. Federal veterinarians determined the animals had been shot days to weeks before being discovered. All four were males. Officials called the cluster of gunshot victims in a small area over a short time “very unusual,” and stressed that killing or harassing federally protected wildlife is a crime. Southern sea otters are protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, California law and the Endangered Species Act; penalties can include fines up to $100,000 and jail time. Once widespread along the Pacific coast, heavy 18th–19th century hunting reduced them to a remnant population; they were listed as threatened in 1977 and today number roughly 3,000, confined between San Mateo and Santa Barbara counties. While oil spills and coastal traffic are primary threats, human killings have occurred before, including an unsolved 2013 case. The carcasses have been sent to the USFWS forensic lab in Oregon for necropsies; anyone with information is urged to contact authorities.

Authorities in Spartanburg County, South Carolina, say Todd Christopher Kohlhepp, 45, has implicated himself in a long-unsolved killing spree after a woman was rescued chained inside a metal storage container on his 95-acre Woodruff property. Sheriff Chuck Wright announced murder warrants charging Kohlhepp in a 2003 quadruple slaying at Superbike Motorsports in Chesnee; Kohlhepp “told us some stuff that nobody else ought to know.” Investigators also say Kohlhepp led them to locations on his land where he claims two other victims are buried, and a third body found in a shallow grave was identified as 32-year-old Charles David Carver, the boyfriend of the woman held captive. Carver died of multiple gunshot wounds. Kohlhepp, a convicted sex offender who had lived a seemingly normal life as a South Carolina real estate licensee and property owner, is jailed without bond on kidnapping charges and faces likely murder charges. Search teams continue to comb the property, where weapons, ammunition, chains and shallow excavations were found. Families of the Chesnee victims and of Carver were informed; loved ones say Kohlhepp’s confession brings answers though not full closure. Investigators warn more remains may be uncovered as the investigation continues.

University Hospital Zurich disclosed that Sergio Marchionne, the longtime chief executive who transformed Fiat and Chrysler, had been receiving recurring treatment for a “serious illness” for more than a year before his death at 66. The hospital said it issued the statement to counter speculation about his care, noting that despite employing “cutting-edge medicine,” Marchionne succumbed to the illness. It declined to provide further details, citing patient confidentiality, and expressed condolences to his family.

Fiat Chrysler Automobiles (FCA) responded that, because of medical privacy, it had no knowledge of the facts of Marchionne’s condition beyond being told he had undergone shoulder surgery. FCA said it was informed by Marchionne’s family on July 20 of a serious deterioration that would prevent his return to work; the company acted and announced leadership changes the following day. FCA declined to say whether the board or chairman had been fully informed earlier.

The revelations prompted questions in the press about how long Marchionne had been ill and what senior executives knew. FCA had warned in its annual report that Marchionne’s role was critical to executing its strategy and acknowledged succession planning challenges. Observers noted that while some firms require top executives to undergo regular health checks, it is uncommon to mandate disclosure of medical conditions. Tributes poured in following his death; Marchionne was widely credited with rescuing Fiat and Chrysler from bankruptcy and multiplying Fiat’s value through decisive dealmaking.

Workers at Goodyear’s loss-making Amiens tyre factory in northern France held the plant’s production director, Michel Dheilly, and human resources chief, Bernard Glesser, captive as part of a long-running dispute over proposed closure. The factory, which Goodyear has tried to sell or shut for five years, has seen violent protests and prolonged negotiations; unions demand a more generous redundancy plan or a buyer. The two managers were guarded but reportedly given water and allowed mobile phones; they spent the night inside the plant and declined some comfort offers. Union leaders described the action as a “reaction of despair,” calling for voluntary redundancies with substantial payouts if no buyer emerges. French “bossnappings” peaked during the financial crisis; while punishable by law, prosecutions are rare and police often avoid intervention to prevent escalation. Goodyear condemned the tactic as counterproductive.

Jodie Foster and photographer Alexandra Hedison secretly married this past weekend, PEOPLE and a rep for Foster confirmed. The Oscar-winning actress and Hedison had been dating since last summer after being spotted together at events and a Fox Studios seminar; sources said their relationship was serious and loving. E! Online first reported the nuptials. Foster, 51, drew attention in 2013 for a Golden Globes speech many saw as her coming-out moment, where she acknowledged past openness with family and thanked her ex-partner, Cydney Bernard.

YouTube stars Liza Koshy and David Dobrik, who together amassed over 20 million subscribers, publicly announced their breakup in an emotional video revealing they split six months earlier. Despite continuing to appear together in recent uploads — including gift surprises like a puppy and a monkey — they decided to end their romantic relationship because they were growing apart and living “separate lives.” In the candid clip they alternate between joking, praising each other and crying, emphasizing that the split was amicable and rooted in personal growth rather than wrongdoing. Both acknowledged the pressures of busy YouTube careers and the unique challenges influencers face when their personal relationships double as public brands. They waited to tell fans because they were initially angry about drifting apart, and they wanted to be honest to prevent fan harassment or speculation. Branding experts say the breakup is unlikely to harm either creator’s career; the pair remain close friends and left open the possibility of reconciling in the future, while many viewers praised the maturity of their separation.

An Australian-led study reported in Archives of Sexual Behavior found men with facial hair are more likely to hold hostile sexist attitudes than clean-shaven men. Over 500 men aged 18–72 from the US and India completed surveys measuring ambivalent sexism and reported their facial-hair status. About seven in ten participants had some beard or stubble. After controlling for age, nationality, education, and relationship status, men with any facial hair scored significantly higher on measures of hostile sexism—beliefs that women are inferior, manipulative, or deserve derogatory treatment—while facial hair did not predict benevolent sexism (protective or chivalrous views). Hostile sexism and nationality were the strongest predictors of whether men had facial hair; Indian participants reported higher facial-hair prevalence and higher sexism scores than American participants. Researchers propose two nonexclusive explanations: men who already hold hostile, patriarchal views may grow facial hair to signal masculinity and dominance, or having facial hair may shape social perceptions that encourage men to adopt more traditionally masculine and hostile attitudes. Prior work showing beards increase perceived dominance and aggression supports these interpretations.

Several residents of Bennington reported a gray squirrel repeatedly attacking people in mid-March. Kevin McDonald said a squirrel jumped onto him while he shoveled snow, scratched him, and leapt back twice after he threw it off. Neighbors on East Street also battled similar squirrel encounters; one woman was bitten on the neck and is receiving rabies post-exposure vaccination on her doctor’s advice. Game Warden Travis Buttle has spoken to two residents and noted the animal vanished quickly, preventing capture and testing for rabies. Vermont Public Health Veterinarian Robert Johnson said squirrels have never been documented to transmit rabies to humans and suggested a formerly tame pet squirrel might lose fear and behave aggressively when encountering strangers. Authorities advise anyone attacked to seek medical advice.

India’s Ayush ministry has distributed a booklet, "Mother and Child Care," compiled by the government-funded Central Council for Research in Yoga and Naturopathy, that gives prescriptive lifestyle guidance for pregnant women: avoid meat and eggs, shun “desire, anger, attachment, hatred and lust,” refrain from sexual thoughts (and purportedly sex after conception), keep calm, avoid “bad company,” have spiritual thoughts, read lives of great personalities, and hang “good and beautiful” pictures in the bedroom to influence the child. The booklet was released by Minister Shripad Naik and defended as a compilation of long-standing yoga and naturopathy practices; Naik and the CCRYN director deny it explicitly advises abstinence from sex. 

Medical professionals and rationalists sharply criticized the guidance as unscientific and potentially harmful in a country with high maternal malnutrition and anemia. Obstetricians note that protein and iron from animal sources are important for pregnant women, and unnecessary dietary restrictions could worsen maternal and fetal outcomes. Clinicians say normal pregnancies do not require abstinence and caution only applies in specific complications. Experts also warn that prescriptive emotional rules are misplaced: while maternal stress can affect fetal development, promoting supportive environments and activities women enjoy is preferable to moral dictates. Critics link the booklet to broader trends promoting traditional or religiously inflected health advice from some right-wing groups, and argue public policy should prioritize evidence-based maternal nutrition and care to reduce India’s high maternal mortality and childhood stunting.

Recent analyses highlight pervasive contamination of homes and the environment by consumer-product chemicals—especially highly fluorinated compounds (HFCs), phthalates, flame retardants, phenols and fragrances—many of which resist breakdown and accumulate in people and wildlife. HFCs (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) form strong carbon–fluorine bonds that provide nonstick, stain- and water-repellent properties but persist for years in bodies and millennia in the environment. Well-studied HFCs have been linked to testicular and kidney cancer, liver malfunction, hormonal and thyroid disruption, high cholesterol, obesity, ulcerative colitis, and reduced birth weight; other fluorinated chemicals raise similar concerns. Scientists worldwide signed the Madrid Statement calling to limit production and use of these chemicals.

A meta-analysis of more than two dozen U.S. studies found 45 chemicals in household dust and showed ten chemicals present in over 90% of samples. Phthalates—used as plasticizers in vinyl, toys, cosmetics and packaging—were the most abundant and are associated in animal and some human studies with endocrine disruption, developmental, respiratory and neurobehavioral harms. Flame retardants and perfluoroalkyl substances also featured prominently; flame retardants ranked highest for likely ingestion by young children. Dust serves as a reservoir: chemicals off-gas or flake from furnishings, textiles, cookware, personal care products and packaging into settled dust that is inhaled, ingested, or absorbed—especially by crawling or hand-to-mouth young children.

Studies also raise concerns about airborne nanoparticles (e.g., magnetite from vehicle exhaust) reaching brain tissue. While causation for diseases like Alzheimer’s is unproven, the potential for harm is being reassessed.

Practical steps include avoiding stain- and oil-repellent products, replacing Teflon with cast iron or ceramic, avoiding certain cosmetics, reducing microwave popcorn/greasy wrapped foods, handwashing, HEPA vacuuming, wet dusting, and staying farther from busy roads. Advocates urge manufacturers to adopt safer alternatives and call for stronger regulatory action—such as reforms to chemical safety laws—to better evaluate and phase out hazardous chemicals.

A former CIA operative, Donald C. Rickard, has admitted that he played a role in tipping off South African apartheid authorities to Nelson Mandela’s whereabouts in 1962, leading to Mandela’s arrest and subsequent imprisonment for nearly 28 years. Rickard’s recorded confession, made to director John Irvin, prompted renewed calls for the CIA and the US government to disclose their involvement and to apologise. Rickard, who later worked as a U.S. diplomat and consular officer in several countries and died aged 88, defended his action by describing Mandela at the time as “the world’s most dangerous communist outside of the Soviet Union.” The revelation triggered strong condemnation from Mandela’s family and political allies. Mandla Mandela, the former president’s grandson, called the tip-off a “betrayal of our nation,” urged President Barack Obama to apologise, and urged the UN to censure the United States. Mandla said the disclosure ended decades of denial about Western complicity in supporting the apartheid regime and stressed that US imperial interests were placed above the liberation struggle of millions in Southern Africa. A veteran political associate of Mandela called the incident “a shameful act of betrayal” that hindered the anti-apartheid struggle. The article also includes Rickard’s obituary details: born in Rangoon in 1928, he and his family fled Burma in 1942, he studied in the US, served in the State Department in posts including Durban and Seoul, married Elaine Grove in 1952, retired to Pagosa Springs, and is survived by six children and a brother. An open memorial service was scheduled at St. Patrick’s Episcopal Church in Pagosa Springs.

Nokia said it will cut up to 10,000 additional jobs, close production and R&D sites in Finland, Germany and Canada, and reduced its earnings forecast — the second profit warning this year — as CEO Stephen Elop presses the biggest overhaul in the company’s history. The measures follow heavy market-share losses to Apple and Samsung and slow Lumia sales on Microsoft’s Windows Phone. Shares plunged about 16–18%, to levels not seen since 1996, cutting market value to well under €10 billion and deepening concern about Nokia’s cash runway; net cash was €4.9 billion at March 31 but analysts warn current burn rates could exhaust reserves within a few years. Nokia expects a worse-than-expected second-quarter loss in its devices unit, with margins below the prior quarter’s negative 3%. The restructuring — which includes closing the Salo plant and facilities in Ulm and Burnaby, selling luxury unit Vertu, and senior executive departures — will cost about €1 billion and aims to reduce devices-unit annual costs roughly to €3 billion by end-2013. Credit-default swap spreads and ratings downgrades underscore investor fears that Nokia could become a takeover target if it cannot stabilize performance.

Four years after entering a Chinese modeling contest simply to win a computer for school, Liu Wen rose from a small town in Hunan to become the first model of Asian descent to walk the Victoria’s Secret runway. At 21 and 5-foot-10, Wen was plucked from a routine casting call and quickly built an international portfolio—covers of Chinese FHM, Marie Claire and Elle, editorials for Vogue, and runway debuts in Milan, Paris and New York for designers including Dolce & Gabbana and Alexander McQueen. Surprised by the casting, Wen described meeting icons like Heidi Klum and balancing ambitions: she once studied to be a teacher and may return to acting or education later. The Victoria’s Secret show itself is an elaborate production: models undergo three to five hours of hair and makeup, multiple artists per model, and extensive body makeup and glitter. Angels don massive, intricate pieces—Marisa Miller’s $3 million bra and heavy, themed wings—making runway performance physically demanding. Participants and producers highlight the spectacle, the grueling prep, and the New York crowd’s enthusiastic reception.

Gallup’s rolling seven-day tracking poll through Oct. 24 shows Mitt Romney leading President Obama 50% to 47% among likely voters, unchanged from the prior day; among registered voters Obama leads 48-47. The Gallup lead has been larger earlier in the week but now aligns more closely with other measures: RealClearPolitics averages Romney up less than one point, and an AP-GfK poll has Romney 47-45. Battleground state polls remain tight — Ohio polls vary from a five-point Obama lead to a tie — and overall state surveys show many toss-ups. Analysis notes Romney’s post-Denver debate bounce appears to have stalled: several recent tracking polls shifted slightly toward Obama, and FiveThirtyEight’s now-cast moved in Obama’s favor by about a point, raising his Electoral College chances. Observers caution that short-term poll swings may reflect noise or delayed reaction to the Florida debate, so momentum claims remain uncertain.

The author, amused by a fondness for fortune cookies, bought 1,050 Panda-brand cookies to study their messages, lucky numbers, and Mandarin phrases. After opening 1,035 (the seller shorted the order), they catalogued 676 unique fortunes, 556 unique lucky-number combinations, and 173 distinct Mandarin vocabulary items. Because the purchase represented contiguous slices of production runs, the sample covered fortunes beginning with letters A–I and W–Y; extrapolating from letter distributions suggests the full fortune corpus might contain roughly 1,200–1,600 unique fortunes.

The lucky numbers were tested against Powerball results from Nov. 1, 1997, to May 27, 2017. Buying a ticket for every fortune-derived six-number combination across 2,043 drawings would have returned $4.4 million on $4.2 million spent, edging out randomized digits’ expected $1.7 million in winnings. This surprising edge is largely attributable to several $1 million-winning drawings that matched frequently occurring fortune combinations. The author cautions this is likely coincidence, cherry-picking, or post hoc alignment rather than proof of genuine luck.

The Mandarin vocabulary on the slips provides about 173 words—roughly the lexicon of a precocious two-year-old—dominated by food terms (74 words), plus 21 verbs and 21 adjectives. It’s useful for ordering and basic needs but not conversation.

Topical coding of fortunes showed only about 22% are predictive; the majority (53%) address “you,” focusing on character and advice rather than prophecy. Common language skews positive and action-oriented: words like “good,” “life,” “never,” and “make” are overrepresented. The author also experimented with a Markov-chain bot to generate new fortunes; results vary from trite to surprisingly apt, exemplified by a memorable original fortune: “You may be disappointed if you fail. But you are doomed if you don’t try.” Overall, fortune cookies are less about predicting the future and more about delivering persona-focused, optimistic prompts and snack-sized Mandarin morsels.

A British judge has granted a death certificate for Richard John “Lord Lucan,” more than 40 years after he vanished following the savage bludgeoning of his children’s nanny, Sandra Rivett, on Nov. 7, 1974. The ruling at London’s High Court allows his son, George Bingham, to become the Eighth Earl of Lucan and formally use the family name. Lucan was accused at a 1975 inquest of murdering Rivett and seriously assaulting his estranged wife, Veronica, who survived and identified him as the attacker. After the murder, Lucan’s blood-stained car was found abandoned in Newhaven; he disappeared and dozens of unverified sightings worldwide followed. Lucan had been treated as dead for probate in 1999, but only the 2014 Presumption of Death Act enabled his son’s recent application for a death certificate. Rivett’s son, Neil Berriman, who opposed the application, said he believes Lucan is dead but stressed that his mother remains the “forgotten victim” awaiting justice. Over the decades theories about Lucan’s fate proliferated: suicide by drowning, escape to foreign countries, or more lurid accounts. One former gambling-set associate recently alleged Lucan shot himself at a private zoo and that his body was fed to a tiger—an unverified anecdote echoing earlier rumors investigators once probed. George Bingham said the ruling brings long-awaited closure, acknowledging the title’s tainted associations but asserting his right to the family name. The mystery remains unresolved in fact, but legally Lucan is now presumed dead and his son may inherit the title.

Celebrity family news: Michael Jordan and wife Yvette Prieto are expecting identical twin girls in April, their first child together and Jordan’s fourth. The couple married April 27 in a lavish Palm Beach ceremony with hundreds of guests. Separately, Bruce Willis and wife Emma Heming-Willis are expecting their second child together; they already share 20-month-old daughter Mabel, and Willis has three older daughters from his prior marriage.

Gustavo “Taby” Falcon, the last of Miami’s notorious “Cocaine Cowboys,” was arrested April 12, 2017, more than 26 years after an arrest warrant was issued on April 10, 1991. Falcon, 55, had disappeared on the eve of a major federal drug indictment that targeted him along with his older brother Augusto “Willie” Falcon and Salvador “Sal” Magluta, who together had smuggled massive quantities of cocaine into South Florida in the 1980s. U.S. Marshals from the Southern District of Florida tracked Falcon to a rented home in a quiet Kissimmee suburb after an exhaustive records search turned up a Florida driver’s license in an alias and a 2013 car-accident report linking that identity to the house shared by Falcon and his wife, Amelia. On the day of the arrest marshals surveilled the property and followed the couple as they rode bicycles; because both wore helmets and sunglasses it took time to positively identify him, but officers eventually stopped him at an intersection, found fraudulent driver’s licenses dating back to 1997, and took him into custody without resistance. Falcon confirmed his identity and was ordered held without bond to be sent to South Florida to face charges of conspiracy to import cocaine. Authorities say he has lived in the Orlando area since 2009 and in the rental since 2012; it’s believed he spent earlier years overseas. His brother and Magluta, once flamboyant traffickers who amassed vast wealth, later faced trials, convictions, and seized assets.

International outrage surged after the Houla massacre in Syria, where more than 100 civilians, including many women and children, were killed. Western states led coordinated expulsions of Syrian diplomats: the United States, Britain, Canada, Australia, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Bulgaria and others ordered top Syrian envoys to leave, and Turkey followed by expelling all Syrian diplomatic staff from Ankara. Japan also expelled Syria’s ambassador while stopping short of severing ties. Damascus denounced the moves as hysteria and retaliated by ordering the Dutch charge d’affaires to leave. The U.N. human rights office reported most victims were shot execution-style, and U.N. observers verified additional killings elsewhere, including 13 bodies in Deir el-Zour bound and shot at close range. Kofi Annan met President Bashar al-Assad but secured no meaningful steps to implement his six-point peace plan; U.N. deputy Jean-Marie Guéhenno warned the mission’s efforts have largely failed. At the U.N. Security Council, members debated responses: Western envoys urged stronger pressure and possible sanctions, while Russia and China opposed outside intervention and new sanctions, calling expulsions counterproductive. U.S. Ambassador Susan Rice warned that if the council cannot act, the conflict could escalate regionally or prompt actions outside the U.N. framework. The U.N. Human Rights Council planned a special session, while violence and shelling continued across Syria.

Renegade Pictures released a trailer for Brittany Murphy’s final film, Abandoned, in which she plays a woman under psychiatric evaluation after her husband disappears; her intense performance drew attention as the actress’s own untimely death unfolded. The article notes a haunting pattern: many stars’ final projects bore dark, ironic parallels to their real-life fates—Heath Ledger’s Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus and The Dark Knight, Aaliyah’s Queen of the Damned, Bruce Lee’s Game of Death, Brandon Lee’s The Crow, Brad Renfro’s The Informers, River Phoenix’s incomplete Dark Blood, and Judy Garland’s I Could Go On Singing. In a separate incident tied to Murphy’s passing, DVD-rental company Redbox removed box-art images for her straight-to-DVD thriller Deadline—whose cover showed her lifeless in a bathtub—and pulled the art from kiosks and its website out of sensitivity while continuing to carry the film.

A federal judge in St. Louis has ruled that Carl and Janice Duffner can be compelled to plant turf grass on their St. Peters property despite Janice’s severe grass allergies. The couple, who have lived in the suburb since 2002, replaced turf with a lush flower garden and other ground cover. St. Peters enacted an ordinance in the past decade requiring homeowners to cover at least 50 percent of their yards with turf grass. After receiving a 2014 notice of noncompliance, the Duffners applied for a variance and were granted one that nonetheless mandated at least 5 percent turf grass. The city warned that failure to comply could result in daily fines—described by the Duffners’ attorney as potentially growing well beyond $200,000—and, in extreme reading, even lengthy prison terms. The Duffners refused to add turf and sued. Their litigation has traversed state and appeals courts, producing mixed results and remands; in 2016 they filed in federal court. On summary judgment, U.S. District Judge John A. Ross largely sided with St. Peters, finding the Duffners’ presented facts insufficient to prevail and granting the city summary judgment. David Roland of the Freedom Center of Missouri, representing the Duffners, called the ordinance “absurd” and the penalties “over-the-top,” announcing an appeal and predicting the case could reach the U.S. Supreme Court. Roland argues the ordinance is dangerous because it forces affirmative use of private property rather than merely restricting harmful uses—he warns it could set a precedent allowing municipalities to require homeowners to install and maintain things like swimming pools. He frames the dispute as a major property-rights case and expects broader advocacy support as the Duffners continue their fight.

An attorney for a teenager identified as Victim 1 said he and other alleged victims plan to testify publicly at Jerry Sandusky’s Dec. 13 preliminary hearing in Centre County, though Sandusky could waive the open session. The teen first reported abuse in 2008; Sandusky faces 40 counts alleging abuse of eight boys over 15 years tied to his charity, The Second Mile. Victim 1 transferred schools after bullying. Attorneys Michael Boni and Slade McLaughlin plan civil suits after the criminal case, naming Sandusky, The Second Mile, Penn State and others. The charity is urging donations to the Pennsylvania Coalition Against Rape while considering its future and seeking to dismiss an injunction request over asset transfers. Sandusky denies the charges; his lawyer says some accusers may recant.

On January 25, 2015, 13-year-old Suhayb Jamal Hassan died after being accidentally shot in his Eagan home. Authorities responded after a 15-year-old brother called reporting his sibling was unresponsive and bleeding, initially claiming the boy had fallen while running with a knife. Emergency crews pronounced Suhayb dead at the scene. Under questioning, the older brother admitted he had accidentally shot Suhayb while the children were playing "cops and robbers." Investigators learned the boys had recently discovered their father's hidden 9 mm handgun, which was initially unloaded but had a loaded magazine nearby. At some point the firearm was loaded—then mistakenly thought to be unloaded—and during play the 15-year-old pulled the trigger, firing one round that struck Suhayb in the chest. An 11-year-old sister was present in the home but did not witness the shooting and was unharmed. Police described the incident as a horrible accident, and no one was in custody or expected to be arrested; the investigation continues and will be forwarded to the Dakota County Attorney’s Office and the Hennepin County Medical Examiner’s Office for review. The victim was an eighth-grader at Blackhawk Middle School; counselors were provided to students. No further information has been released.

Trent Arsenault, a San Francisco-area tech worker who ran an unregulated, one-man sperm donation operation, has drawn federal scrutiny and widespread media attention after the FDA ordered him to cease “manufacturing” semen. Arsenault says he’s helped dozens of couples conceive—claims ranging from 14 to more than 50 pregnancies in various reports—and frames his work as accessible, affordable sperm donation for couples shut out by expensive clinics. His lawyers argue government regulation of his private sexual practices is improper, and his cause picked up support across ideological lines.

But multiple reports and a tipped acquaintance reveal a provocative side omitted from many profiles: Arsenault produces and posts explicit videos and photos of his donations online. He maintains Xtube accounts with hundreds of masturbation videos—viewed millions of times—and hosted explicit galleries on personal sites. He calls himself “donorsexual,” saying the erotic content fuels his sperm production, and admits he does not proactively inform all recipient couples of his pornographic output, though his adult pages link to his donor profile and some recipients discovered him via that work.

Additional background includes Arsenault’s brief stint at the U.S. Naval Academy and a disputed account of leaving amid controversy. Critics argue prospective parents deserve full disclosure that a donor’s activities and history may be publicly accessible and permanently associated with their child’s conception. The FDA’s cease-and-desist and related documents are publicly available for those seeking more detail.

San Diego has launched intensified efforts to curb a hepatitis A outbreak that has killed 15 homeless people and hospitalized nearly 300 over ten months. City crews from Clean Harbors began power-washing sidewalks and streets in downtown areas with a bleach-and-chlorine solution, focusing on zones where large homeless encampments concentrate; cleanings will recur every other week at three designated areas. The city also extended hours for 14 Balboa Park restrooms to 24/7 and the county has installed hand-washing stations and provided 19,000 hepatitis A vaccinations, including 7,300 to at-risk individuals. County health officials had demanded sanitation actions after deeming parts of downtown “fecally contaminated,” and are still evaluating the city’s response. Mayor Kevin Faulconer announced plans to open three large temporary tent shelters—each with 100+ beds, restrooms, showers and on-site services—to immediately house hundreds of homeless people; private donors have pledged funding and at least one shelter could open by December while the city finalizes costs and council approval.

Alan Miller McCarty, 36, disrupted his Daytona Beach trial with repeated outbursts, obscenities and threats, spending much of the proceedings behind one-way glass in a small room after yelling at the presiding judge. Jurors—three women and three men—found him guilty on all charges after about 30 minutes: two counts of threats or extortion and two counts of corruption by threat against a public official. The charges stemmed from phone calls in which McCarty threatened Circuit Judge Stasia Warren, who had ruled against him in an earlier custody dispute, and threatened dispatchers and behavioral health staffers. Judge Matt Foxman, who oversaw the trial, had McCarty removed to the adjacent room when the defendant continued to scream expletives, accuse the court of stealing his papers, and crudely insult the judge; McCarty remained handcuffed and in an orange jail jumpsuit, wearing an electric stun belt beneath his clothing. Prosecutors emphasized that Warren felt frightened and that McCarty’s words were serious, while his attorney argued McCarty was a desperate “squeaky wheel” lashing out after losing access to his children. McCarty claimed his threats were mere words and compared them to the judge’s earlier admonition to quiet him. Following the conviction, McCarty received a 20-year prison sentence, which prosecutors said would allow him ample time to reflect on the gravity of threatening the judiciary. His sentencing hearing is scheduled for Oct. 12.

A federal judge rejected a $125 million settlement between Google and groups representing authors and publishers that would have allowed Google to expand its ambitious book-digitization project. Judge Denny Chin found the deal “not fair, adequate and reasonable,” saying it risked granting Google de facto monopoly power to profit from books without copyright owners’ permission, especially orphan works. The settlement had shifted authors and publishers from opponents to allies of Google, promising wider access to out-of-print titles and new revenue streams, but drew criticism from the Justice Department, competitors like Amazon and Microsoft, academics, and copyright experts over antitrust, privacy and copyright concerns. Chin suggested an opt-in model for rights holders might address problems. Parties now must decide whether to renegotiate, resume litigation, or abandon the settlement.

Years from now—perhaps within a decade—the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) is planned to be switched on in a South of France Alpine forest. When complete it will be among the largest, most complex machines ever built: roughly 100 feet tall, weighing 23,000 tons, and centered on a cavernous vacuum chamber in which a superheated cloud of heavy hydrogen will rotate and twist while being driven by enormous electric currents, particle beams, and concentrated radiation. The hydrogen will be ionized and heated above 200 million °C—far hotter than the sun’s core—so that atomic nuclei fuse, producing helium and releasing intense heat, gamma rays, X-rays, and torrents of high-energy neutrons. No material can contain such plasma, so ITER will confine it in a “magnetic bottle” created by the world’s largest system of superconducting magnets, cooled to near–deep-space temperatures. Achieving controlled fusion would mark decades of preparation and vast investment: ITER’s international organization brings together 35 countries, operates with its own accounting unit, and has seen costs rise steadily; conservative estimates put construction at about $20 billion, making it the most expensive scientific instrument on Earth. If economical fusion is realized, reactors modeled on ITER could supply terawatts of low-carbon power for millions of years using seawater and lithium, with minimal waste and no meltdown risk. The project’s site near Aix-en-Provence will grow into a small scientific city of nearly 40 buildings, including cryogenics and cooling plants. However, ITER recently faced a stinging management assessment: a damning report on leadership and governance prompted the ITER Council to limit the report’s circulation amid fears that its conclusions and anticipated delays could jeopardize funding.

On October 6, 1966, Roger Watson and Dave Brown were drafted together from northwest Detroit, trained at Fort Hood, Texas, and served in the 9th Infantry—both as combat engineer demolition specialists. They became fast friends, spent a month back home before shipping to Vietnam, then lost touch. In Vietnam, Dave heard Roger had been wounded; Roger was shot on March 8, 1968, losing a kidney, portions of his small intestine, and suffering liver damage. Dave never learned whether Roger survived, and later searched the Vietnam Veterans Memorial hoping to find his friend’s name.

Decades later, in Berkley, Michigan, the two men had been living only about 150 feet apart for 18 years without realizing it. Roger befriended his neighbor Peggy Brown while birdwatching; they exchanged pictures and emails. Peggy noticed Roger’s Purple Heart license plate and a “9th Infantry” cap in his car, and during an October email exchange about a hawk asked whether her husband had served in the same unit. That single detail triggered a rapid series of emails and photo comparisons that revealed Roger and Dave were the long-lost Army buddies.

They arranged a meeting at the chain-link fence that separates their yards and instantly recognized one another—shaking hands, embracing, and sharing an emotional reunion after nearly half a century. Now retired—Roger from the Michigan Department of Corrections and Dave a surveyor—both men, in their late 60s, spend time together sharing war stories, coffee, and plans to “share a beer” and watch their grandchildren grow up. Their neighbors and families remain astonished by the improbable reconnection, a reminder of how one small piece of information can reunite lives separated by decades.

Angela Lansbury has issued a clarification after drawing criticism for comments suggesting women must “sometimes take blame” for sexual harassment. In a statement, the 92-year-old actress said she is “devastated” by the backlash and insisted there is “no excuse whatsoever for men to harass women in an abusive sexual manner.” She emphasized her long record of supporting women’s rights and expressed frustration that her remarks were taken out of context, blaming her generation or age without reading her full comments. The controversy began after a Radio Times interview in which Lansbury observed that women “have gone out of their way to make themselves attractive” and said, controversially, that women must sometimes accept blame—though she also called it “awful” that dressing attractively could lead to being assaulted. Critics, including Rape Crisis England & Wales and actress Patricia Arquette, denounced the comments as victim-blaming and harmful. Lansbury’s statement reiterated opposition to harassment and lamented the swift, brutal online reaction, framing her words as misunderstood amid broader debates about sexual violence and accountability.

Rosemont police released surveillance video showing 19-year-old Kenneka Jenkins stumbling alone through the Crowne Plaza Hotel in the early hours of Sept. 9 and disappearing around a corner in a kitchen — the last time she’s seen alive on tape. The clips, drawn from apparently motion-activated cameras, show Jenkins arriving with three people shortly after midnight, later leaving an elevator unsteady and wandering down hallways before moving through an empty kitchen and out of frame. The footage does not show her entering the walk‑in freezer where her body was later found, but the same camera shows no one else entering that area between her disappearance and the discovery; activity is next recorded when a man investigates the corner hours later and returns with police. Jenkins was pronounced dead shortly after midnight on Sept. 10; a body bag is visible in video taken at 4:53 a.m. The Cook County medical examiner has not yet determined cause or manner of death pending further tests.

The family, represented by attorneys Larry Rogers Jr. and Sam Adam Jr., criticized hotel staff and investigators for failing to find Jenkins sooner and said they will pursue their own inquiry and possibly a second autopsy. The case has fueled intense social media speculation and conflicting public statements: the hotel offered to show the family full footage and cover funeral expenses, while activists said they had shown the family snippets; police insist the investigation remains noncriminal so far and have interviewed dozens of people. Jenkins’ mother continues to demand clear answers about how and why her daughter ended up in the freezer.

The United States has deployed 80 military personnel to Chad to bolster intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance efforts in the search for more than 200 Nigerian schoolgirls abducted by Boko Haram from Chibok in mid-April. Largely Air Force members, the unit will operate and support drones and surveillance flights—extending flight time by staging from Chad—while not engaging in ground searches or combat. Half will handle drone launch and recovery and half provide security in Chad. U.S. officials stress the difficulty of locating the girls across dense terrain roughly the size of West Virginia; they may have been split into smaller groups or moved across borders. The U.S. previously sent experts and law enforcement advisers to Abuja. Restrictions limit sharing of some raw intelligence with Nigerian forces amid concerns about their conduct. Nigeria has sought U.N. designation of Boko Haram as a terrorist group to enable sanctions. The kidnappings and escalating attacks, including recent deadly bombings and village raids, have intensified domestic protests and international cooperation to counter the insurgency.

Rebekah (Bekah) Martinez, 22, of Fresno, was reported missing by her mother to the Humboldt County Sheriff’s Office on Nov. 18, 2017, after telling her she was traveling to Humboldt to work on a marijuana farm and would be out of contact for about a week. Her listing later appeared among “The Humboldt 35,” a North Coast Journal package highlighting that county’s unusually high per-capita missing-persons reports. A Trinidad resident, Amy Bonner O’Brien, recognized Martinez from the current season of The Bachelor after seeing the Journal’s slideshow and alerted authorities. The sheriff’s office contacted Martinez by phone and removed her from the missing-persons list. Martinez has been active on Instagram and Twitter throughout, frequently posting about the show; she drew attention on television for her 14-year age gap with the bachelor, Arie Luyendyk Jr., and quipped about the driver’s-license photo used in the missing-persons posting. The broader Journal report examined why Humboldt files so many missing-persons reports—averaging far above the state rate—pointing to California’s permissive reporting rules, chronic runaway youth (especially from foster care), transient cannabis-industry workers who go off-grid, and reporting redundancies. Most reports are resolved quickly; in 2016 the vast majority of adult reports were closed, many juveniles are runaways, and only a handful represent truly unexplained disappearances. Local law enforcement and national databases like NamUs sometimes show inconsistent listings. The piece also profiles long-unsolved cases and families frustrated by slow or stalled investigations, noting that some reported “missing” people are found to be safe or intentionally unreachable, complicating public perception of Humboldt as uniquely dangerous.

The U.S. credit union regulator, the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), sued JPMorgan Securities and Bear Stearns for $3.6 billion, alleging Bear Stearns misled federal credit unions in underwriting and selling mortgage-backed securities that helped sink several wholesale credit unions. This is the NCUA’s second suit against JPMorgan; a prior $1.4 billion claim from June 2011 remains pending. The action joins numerous cases tied to Bear Stearns conduct after JPMorgan’s 2008 acquisition. Separately, Massachusetts fined Morgan Stanley $5 million for ethics and supervision breaches in Facebook’s IPO process, finding a banker scripted the company treasurer’s analyst calls that provided analysts with more detailed revenue numbers than public investors received.

Barrett Township, Pennsylvania, canceled its Halloween parade, 5K Scarecrow Race and trick-or-treating amid a weekslong manhunt for accused cop-killer Eric Frein, believed to be hiding in nearby woods. The usually busy Pocono community has seen dozens of police vehicles and helicopters, roadblocks, hunting restrictions and school closures since the Sept. 12 ambush that killed State Police Corporal Bryon Dickson II and injured Trooper Alex Douglass. Officials worry Frein could exploit Halloween disguises, so a safer “Trunk-or-Treat” will be held at Monsignor McHugh School in neighboring Paradise Township. The state reopened some game lands but kept key search areas closed; hunting remains restricted in several townships. Barrett Township estimates manhunt costs near $40,000, not including lost business revenue.

MIT hosted a “Make the Breast Pump Not Suck” hackathon to tackle long-standing problems with breast pumps and catalyze innovation in maternal and neonatal health. Motivated by parents’ frustrating experiences and a viral New York Times piece on stagnant pump design, organizers—MIT Media Lab researchers and parents—brought 150 engineers, designers, lactation consultants, public-health researchers and users together for a weekend of rapid prototyping, idea-sharing and pitching. The event targeted practical complaints: noisy motors, many hard-to-clean parts, bulky, non-wearable designs, lack of privacy or workplace accommodations, poor data tracking, stigma around pumping and milk, and the inability to lie down while pumping.

Teams prototyped a range of concepts: Compress Express and Second Nature sought quieter, wearable, hands-free systems using gentle compression and massage to mimic baby suckling; PumpIO proposed an open hardware/software platform to collect anonymized milk data and connect pumping moms with lactation support; Helping Hands and Mighty Mom developed hands-free, discreet bras and wearable pumps with integrated logging and analytics. Participants also explored policy solutions for workplace pumping spaces and global affordability to help low-income and working women continue breastfeeding.

The hackathon aimed to seed ideas, collaborations and projects, offering prizes and support from sponsors including Vecna Technologies, Pejman Mar Ventures, Medela, Naia Health and others. Organizers emphasized maternal health’s innovation gap and breastmilk’s documented long-term health benefits for mother and child—arguing better pumps could improve breastfeeding rates, reduce health burdens, and support working parents. The event solicited further ideas, donations, data-visualization help, and outreach to keep momentum toward more dignified, effective, and user-centered breast-pumping solutions.

Anna Fermanova, 24, a U.S. citizen who splits time between Dallas and Moscow, is under house arrest at her parents’ Plano home after federal agents say she attempted to export three advanced night-vision scopes to Russia without the required U.S. State Department license. Acting on a tip, officers searched her luggage at JFK on March 1 and found a Raptor night-vision weapons sight and two other advanced rifle optics hidden in UGG boots; agents seized the devices but allowed her to continue to Moscow. She was arrested when she returned to the U.S. to visit family and has had her passport confiscated while awaiting a New York court appearance. The optics are on the U.S. Munitions List and cannot be exported without approval; one item’s identification numbers reportedly had been obscured. Her attorney, Scott Palmer, says she purchased the scopes legally online for her husband, who intended them for a friend who hunts, and denies she is a spy. Media comparisons to recent Russian espionage arrests have drawn attention, though no link to those cases has been shown.

Geraldine “Gerry” Largay, a 66-year-old Appalachian Trail through-hiker from Tennessee, survived nearly a month after becoming lost in western Maine in July 2013 and documented her final days in a journal recovered with her cellphone. The Maine Warden Service released a 1,579-page case file detailing the disappearance, search efforts and the personal effects found when her remains were located more than two years later. Largay went off-trail July 22 to use the bathroom and could not find her way back. She attempted to text her husband multiple times—first at 11:01 a.m. July 22 (“In somm trouble. Got off trail to go to br. Now lost…”) and again July 23 (“Lost since yesterday. Off trail 3 or 4 miles. Call police for what to do pls.”)—but messages failed to send because there was no cell coverage. After walking to higher ground seeking signal, she decided to remain in place, set up a tent on a pine-needle bed, kept a daily journal and rationed food such as Clif bars and tuna. Her last phone activity was Aug. 6, the date of a torn journal page pleading, “When you find my body, please call my husband George and my daughter Kerry…” The final journal entry is dated Aug. 18, indicating she survived at least 26 days after becoming lost. Wardens found her tent and skeletal remains on Oct. 11, 2015, after a Navy-contracted forester discovered the site on land used for military survival training. The chief medical examiner ruled she died from lack of food, water and environmental exposure; she was about two miles from the trail and roughly a 10-minute walk from a dirt trail. The lengthy, costly 26-month search—one of Maine’s largest—followed many leads, some false, and at times came within 100 yards of her location without finding her. Friends and investigators described Largay as an experienced hiker who nonetheless had a poor sense of direction and avoided carrying heavier packs due to an old back injury. The family has asked for privacy while reviewing the file.

Greek parliament approved a contested austerity package after violent protests and a 48-hour general strike, but observers called the move more symbolic than decisive. The measures, required for continued EU/IMF bailout support, include €50 billion in privatizations, cuts in defense and health spending, tax hikes, and reductions in public-sector employment, though constitutional protections for permanent public workers remain. International leaders welcomed the vote as averting imminent default and enabling further aid, but economists warned it merely buys time without sustained growth or broader European coordination; debt restructuring may still be necessary. Political divisions persist: Prime Minister Papandreou’s Socialist government eked a narrow majority amid party rebellion, and public anger, strikes and street clashes underscored deep skepticism about austerity’s social impact.

Republicans enter the 115th Congress with unified control of the White House and both chambers and an ambitious, long-held conservative agenda focused on dismantling major elements of the Obama era. Their priorities include repealing and ultimately replacing the Affordable Care Act, overhauling the tax code (with big corporate rate cuts), rolling back environmental protections and energy regulations, deregulating financial markets (weakening parts of Dodd-Frank and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau), shrinking the size of government through entitlement changes, and confirming a conservative Supreme Court justice and Trump’s Cabinet picks.

The House has for years signaled this policy vision through bills that repeatedly passed but stalled in the Senate or were vetoed; with Republican control in both chambers and a Republican president, leaders see a rare opportunity to convert those measures into law. Still, there are constraints and divisions. The Senate majority is narrow (52-48), and Democrats retain procedural tools and political leverage. Senate Democrats, led by Chuck Schumer, plan to use Senate processes and public messaging to slow or block elements of the agenda, and they may resist many Cabinet nominees and controversial rollbacks. Nineteen-plus Democrats up for reelection in Trump-won states could be persuadable on some issues, complicating the dynamics.

Immediate early actions are expected on regulation: Republicans will push bills like the REINS Act and the Midnight Rules Act to restrict agencies’ rulemaking power and may use the Congressional Review Act to disapprove many late-term Obama regulations (methane limits, mining rules, payment-disclosure requirements, pesticide restrictions, and more). Leaders emphasize rapid regulatory relief as an economic boon. Repeal of the ACA is slated as a top priority—likely pursued through a quick “repeal and delay” using budget reconciliation to avoid a 60-vote threshold, with replacement deferred for two to four years—an approach criticized as politically risky because it could leave tens of millions without coverage.

Cabinet and judicial confirmations will occupy significant Senate time. Rule changes enacted in 2013 mean most nominations can be confirmed by simple majority, limiting Democrats’ procedural power to block nominees; however, Democrats will use delays, demands for disclosures, and rigorous hearings to contest picks. A high-profile Supreme Court nomination will cap the session’s drama, as Republicans aim for a justice who may overturn landmark precedents.

Tensions exist within the GOP and between Trump and congressional Republicans on trade, Russia-related investigations, and budget/entitlement specifics. Leaders such as Mitch McConnell and Paul Ryan caution against overreach and emphasize performance—aware that midterm elections historically punish perceived failures. Democrats, while weakened, vow active resistance through messaging, floor tactics, and leverage where available, setting up a combative, consequential Congress where enactment will depend on managing intra-party differences, Senate arithmetic, and public reaction.

A large long-term study synthesized data from the Nurses’ Health Study and the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study to quantify how five modifiable lifestyle factors relate to premature mortality and life expectancy in U.S. adults. The five “low-risk” behaviors were: never smoking, body mass index (BMI) 18.5–24.9 kg/m2, at least 30 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous physical activity, moderate alcohol intake, and a high-quality diet (top 40%). Researchers calculated hazard ratios for mortality across a 0–5 lifestyle score, used NHANES to estimate how common these behaviors are in the U.S., and applied CDC death rates to model life expectancy by lifestyle patterns.

Over as much as 34 years of follow-up (122,000+ participants), there were 42,167 deaths. Compared with people with none of the healthy behaviors, those with all five had substantially lower mortality: adjusted hazard ratios were 0.26 for all-cause death, 0.35 for cancer death, and 0.18 for cardiovascular death. The proportion of deaths attributable to not following all five behaviors was large—about 61% for all-cause mortality, 52% for cancer, and 72% for cardiovascular disease. Modeled life expectancy at age 50 differed markedly: women with zero low-risk factors were projected to live 29.0 more years versus 43.1 years with all five (a 14.0-year gain); men showed a 12.2-year gain (25.5 vs. 37.6 years). Much of the benefit was linked to reductions in cardiovascular and cancer deaths, but a substantial share came from other causes.

Limitations include reliance on self-reported behaviors and absence of some clinical risk factors in the models. Nonetheless, investigators and outside experts emphasize the pronounced impact of simple behavior changes—especially smoking cessation, healthy weight, and regular activity—on prolonging life and reducing premature deaths, even when adopted by midlife.

San Francisco Supervisor Scott Wiener publicly disclosed that he takes Truvada daily as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to greatly reduce his risk of contracting HIV. He said he went on PrEP after consulting his physician and wants to remain HIV-negative while helping normalize and destigmatize the prevention tool. Approved by the FDA in 2012, Truvada can reduce HIV risk by up to 99 percent when taken daily and has been endorsed by the WHO, CDC, and local health departments. Wiener represents a district including the Castro, long central to the city’s HIV epidemic, and framed his disclosure as a public-health act intended to encourage people at risk to discuss prevention options with their providers and to reduce shame around sexuality and HIV.

Wiener recounted coming of age during the height of the epidemic and the lingering fear and stigma that followed. He stressed that PrEP complements, not replaces, condoms—both are important—because condom use is inconsistent and not fully protective. He addressed common criticisms: concerns about adherence are real but manageable through education, and evidence does not show that PrEP use increases risky sexual behavior; routine screening of PrEP users may improve STI detection and treatment. Wiener also emphasized PrEP’s relevance beyond gay men—women and others at risk, including those in abusive relationships or trying to conceive with an HIV-positive partner, can benefit.

Barriers remain: cost (Truvada can cost thousands annually), limited access for uninsured people, and some clinicians’ reluctance to prescribe it. Wiener urged expanding access through public programs and insurance coverage and praised organizations and UCSF for advancing research and access. He hopes his disclosure will elevate awareness, reduce stigma, and spur political will to make PrEP widely available so new HIV infections can be dramatically reduced.

A nondescript parking lot at 53 New York Avenue NE in Washington has become the first tangible sign of Elon Musk’s ambitious East Coast Hyperloop vision: a permit was issued allowing The Boring Company to carry out preparatory and excavation work there. The lot, next to a McDonald’s and near the ATF, could become a station in a proposed network that Musk has described as linking New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington with travel times of roughly 29 minutes between New York and D.C. The permit, issued Nov. 29, is preliminary and vague; further approvals would be required to tunnel under city streets and public spaces. D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser visited The Boring Company to learn about its tunneling methods, and the District’s transportation officials are assessing additional permitting needs. Maryland has shown support as well, granting a utility permit for an initial Baltimore–Washington leg that would run under Route 295, though no tunneling has begun.

Musk’s Hyperloop concept envisions pods carrying people—or even cars—on electric sleds through low-pressure tubes or on near-surface tunnels in a Loop system. Stations would be small and widely distributed rather than major grand terminals. The technology leans on magnetic-levitation ideas and low air pressure to minimize drag; variants include passive maglev systems like Inductrack licensed to Hyperloop Transportation Technologies and used by rival Hyperloop One. Engineers say tunneling is technically feasible but costly and complex; safety, integration with existing transit, and practicality remain major challenges. Supporters tout transformative regional mobility; critics point to Musk’s history of overpromising, high infrastructure costs, and concerns that moving cars underground could undercut traditional mass transit. For now, the New York Avenue permit is an early, symbolic step — a stretch before any true race begins.

A mechanical failure on a rotating swing ride called the Zumur at Norwalk’s Oyster Festival caused the attraction to abruptly stop Sunday, sending riders into one another and injuring 18 people, mostly children. Twelve children and one adult were transported to hospitals; an 8-year-old boy remained hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries, while others were treated and released; five refused on-scene care. Witnesses described screams and children lying hurt after the jerking halt. Festival organizers shut down the ride area pending inspection; other rides later reopened. Stewart Amusement, the operator, said the ride had been inspected two days earlier and will be dismantled for further examination as state investigators probe the incident. The crash renewed concerns about inconsistent ride oversight and inspection frequency nationwide.

Before Crystal Palace’s 1-0 Premier League victory over Middlesbrough, the club discovered that one of its team coaches had been heavily vandalised, in what the club believes was an act by opposition fans who mistakenly targeted Palace’s bus. The damage, estimated at around £40,000, involved large red, white and blue graffiti sprayed along one side of the coach, including the words “Crystal Palace.” The incident occurred overnight Friday while the vehicle was parked at a hotel close to Selhurst Park. Palace had loaned the coach to Middlesbrough after Aitor Karanka’s squad flew down to London on Friday, but the vandalised vehicle was not in use by either side for the match; Palace travelled to the game on a different bus. The club confirmed the attack to media, saying police had been informed, and stressed the graffiti was discovered before Saturday’s fixture. Despite the incident and the damage to club property, Crystal Palace secured three valuable points and moved out of the Premier League relegation zone thanks to a single goal from January signing Patrick van Aanholt. The episode drew attention in reports and social media, with outlets noting the apparent confusion by those responsible and reiterating that the defaced coach had not been the transport provided for Middlesbrough on match day. The club is addressing the vandalism through official channels.

Major League Baseball approved a change to intentional walks that lets teams grant one without the pitcher throwing four loopy pitches, using a dugout signal instead. The move aims to speed up games, but it has provoked nostalgia, humor and skepticism. Fans and players noted the small but entertaining drama the traditional four-pitch IBB sometimes produced—errant throws that led to runs, batters swinging at close lobs, and memorable moments now lost. Social media highlighted clips of mistakes and big plays, and joked about replacing the signal with dances or outrageous alternatives. Critics point out the rule’s impact on pace will be negligible: 932 intentional walks across a full season amounted to only a few minutes total, roughly 35 seconds per game saved on average. Still, opponents lamented the loss of quirky, low-stakes rituals that add color to baseball, while supporters argued the minimalist change modernizes play with little practical consequence.

Federal authorities arrested 56-year-old Cesar Altieri Sayoc of Florida in connection with a nationwide mail-bomb campaign that targeted prominent Democrats, major donors, critics of President Trump and media outlets. Investigators traced a fingerprint and DNA from multiple packages to Sayoc and found his white van plastered with pro-Trump imagery, attacks on liberal figures and a “CNN Sucks” sticker. Sayoc was taken into custody near an AutoZone in Plantation, Fla.; FBI agents used flash bangs and later towed the van to an FBI facility.

Sayoc was charged with multiple federal crimes including illegal mailing of explosives, threats against former presidents and assaulting federal officers, carrying a potential sentence up to 48 years. Authorities recovered at least 13-14 packages containing real, crude pipe-bomb devices—packed with powder and broken glass and described as live devices—and intercepted additional suspicious mailings addressed to figures such as Sen. Cory Booker, James Clapper, Sen. Kamala Harris and donor Tom Steyer. No one was injured. Sayoc’s social media showed fervent support for Trump and hostile posts toward targets; he has a prior criminal history including a 2002 bomb-threat arrest. The arrest prompted nationwide law-enforcement and political reactions as officials continued forensic analysis and warned more packages might exist.

Hollywood’s T. rex roar is largely invention: sound designers layered baby elephant cries, tiger chuffs, alligator gurgles and slowed-down small-animal noises to create the cinematic blast. New research, however, argues many dinosaurs likely didn’t roar like mammals at all but produced low, closed‑mouth vocalizations more like pigeons, doves, ostriches or cassowaries. Closed‑mouth sounds are made by directing air into an inflated esophageal pouch or neck cavity while the beak (or mouth) remains closed, producing low-frequency, throaty whooshes or coos used mainly in mating and territorial displays. Scientists analyzed vocal behavior across archosaurs—birds and crocodilians—and found closed‑mouth vocalization in about 52 of 208 bird species studied, concentrated in larger-bodied lineages. Statistical reconstructions indicate this trait evolved independently at least 16 times among birds and appeared in crocodiles too, suggesting the behavior can emerge readily under selective pressures and might have been present in some nonavian dinosaurs, especially the larger species.
