Because vocal organs are soft tissues that rarely fossilize, direct evidence is lacking, but comparative anatomy and bird physiology imply dinosaurs lacked mammal-like vocal cords and may have used air sacs or a syrinx-like organ. Thus, instead of thunderous roars, many dinosaurs might have sounded like booming coos, low hoots or muffled whooshes—intimidating in their own way but very different from Hollywood’s screeches. Further work will combine fossils, physiology and modeling to refine these reconstructions.

At the Super Bowl halftime show, the Red Hot Chili Peppers appeared to mime their instruments while Bruno Mars — who sang live — headlined. Observers noticed Flea’s bass had no cable or wireless pack, and photos plus guitarist Josh Klinghoffer’s histrionics fueled claims the band wasn’t actually amplified. Vernon Reid tweeted about the unplugged bass, and critics compared the scrutiny to past lip-synch controversies involving pop stars. The Peppers’ perceived fakery prompted Flea to post a detailed statement explaining the decision: the band recorded a performance track for the unique, logistics-heavy event and played along with it while Anthony Kiedis sang live. Flea emphasized the group’s long history of genuine live shows, their discomfort with miming in the past, and their belief that in this surreal, one-chance spectacle they should “bring the spirit” rather than pretend instruments were plugged in. He said they could have plugged in to avoid disappointment but chose transparency, likening the set to shooting a music video before millions. Flea expressed gratitude to the NFL and Bruno Mars and said he’d make the same choice again, reaffirming the band’s commitment to authentic live performances on tour.

The Republican 2016 presidential field has swelled to unprecedented size, complicating Gov. Chris Christie’s expected entry and raising the stakes for early exposure and debate inclusion. With a dozen formally declared GOP contenders—including governors and senators—and Jeb Bush’s recent entry, party politics resemble the largest field since 1860. Networks like Fox News and CNN are limiting debate slots to the top 10 in polls, making early polling performance crucial; a Washington Post/ABC poll showed Christie narrowly inside that cutoff, with only five percentage points separating him in eighth place from the leaders and just four points above last place.

Political strategists warn the crowded contest will intensify attacks and demand sharper, earlier positioning. Thomas Schaller observes that big stories and gaffes break through media noise, incentivizing aggressive earned-media strategies. Christie has already engaged in that dynamic, criticizing Rand Paul’s move to let portions of the Patriot Act lapse and mocking Jeb Bush for being “late to the party” on a 4 percent growth plan—while asserting he had previously outlined a similar proposal.

Campaign veterans stress that in such a packed field candidates must stake clear policy territory rather than hedge. Steve Schmidt notes Christie’s advantage in offering detailed plans on entitlements, immigration, taxes and education, which helps define why he’s running and demonstrates leadership style. Yet summertime lower TV audiences and intense competition for limited media space could hinder candidates’ visibility. Historians like Julian Zelizer caution that more candidates mean more debates but less media time per contender.

The crowded field, combined with post-Citizens United outside funding, could prolong the nomination fight into late spring or summer 2016 and even risk a brokered convention, as distributed outside money reduces incentives to drop out. Strategists predict the contest could stretch into June or July, potentially elevating later nominating states such as New Jersey.

Christie’s launch plans emphasize retail campaigning and blunt, unscripted appeals: a no-teleprompter kickoff at his high school, a five-day New Hampshire blitz with town halls, diner stops and family-focused storytelling. His team seeks to project a pragmatic, results-oriented conservative willing to tackle tough issues and govern across partisan lines, while moving past controversies from his governorship.

Researchers described Kulindadromeus zabaikalicus, a 150-million-year-old, 1 m long plant-eating ornithischian from Siberia exhibiting both scales and diverse featherlike integuments. Fossils show small distal hindlimb scales, larger overlapping tail scales, simple monofilaments on the head and thorax, and more complex branched filaments on limbs—features previously known largely from theropod dinosaurs. The finding, published in Science, suggests featherlike structures were not restricted to theropods (the lineage that led to birds) but occurred across major dinosaur groups, implying feathers—or their developmental potential—may have been present in the earliest dinosaurs around 220 million years ago. Authors argue feathers initially served insulation and signaling before being co‑opted for flight; some species may have retained or lost feathers through growth or ecological shifts. The discovery challenges traditional scaly dinosaur reconstructions and expands our view of integumentary evolution, though some paleontologists caution that the filament morphology differs from modern feather branching and that developmental pathways remain debated.

A 12-year-old Arkansas girl, Kali Hardig, who contracted a rare, often-fatal brain infection caused by the amoeba Naegleria fowleri, is showing encouraging recovery signs after experimental treatment and early diagnosis. Kali likely contracted the amoeba during a visit to a now-closed Arkansas water park with a sandy-bottomed lake. Naegleria fowleri enters through the nose in warm freshwater and causes primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), a rapidly progressing illness that destroys brain tissue and typically leads to death. Kali was brought to Arkansas Children’s Hospital on July 19 with a high fever; doctors cooled her body to reduce brain swelling and treated her with an experimental regimen that included a breast-cancer drug. Tests now show no sign of the parasite. She can say a few words—“yes,” “no,” “Hi mama,” “daddy,” and “nanny”—is participating in therapy, and can take a few assisted steps. Physicians caution she may have long-term deficits and will need weeks in hospital care and months of therapy, but she is expected to make significant progress with family and medical support. The CDC notes only 128 U.S. PAM cases from 1962–2012 and recommends precautions to reduce nose exposure to warm freshwater.

The piece argues that the mainstream media and many political analysts have badly misjudged President Trump and Republicans, setting the stage for a large GOP victory in 2018. The author cites columns by Barry Casselman and Scott Adams to show that media narratives have been self-reinforcing and often incorrect. Adams’ list of 20 predictions about Trump — from inability to win the nomination or presidency to economic and foreign-policy failures — is used to illustrate how frequently pundits were wrong. The author singles out coverage of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act as a prominent example of media error: outlets reportedly told Americans the law would raise their taxes, shaped polls around that falsehood, and then continued to portray the legislation as unpopular. A CBS segment is highlighted where three families, expecting tax increases, learned instead they would keep more money—ranging from about $650 to nearly $13,000—undermining media claims. The author contends that as Americans personally experience benefits from the tax cuts, three effects will boost Republicans: voters will be pleasantly surprised and credit GOP effectiveness; media credibility will erode as people compare reality to reporting; and Democrats who opposed the bill will be punished in swing states. The piece concludes that if Republicans communicate truthfully and contrast their record with Democratic alternatives, they can achieve an “astonishing” 2018 victory.

New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman has subpoenaed PepsiCo (maker of AMP), Monster Beverage, and Living Essentials (maker of 5-Hour Energy) seeking documents on marketing and advertising practices for energy drinks. The early-stage probe is investigating whether companies overstate benefits of additives like B-vitamins, taurine, ginseng or guarana while downplaying caffeine’s primary stimulant role, and whether labels omit total caffeine amounts or combine multiple caffeine sources without disclosure. Energy drinks, a fast-growing $8.9 billion U.S. category, are less tightly regulated than sodas; the FDA calls “energy drink” an ill-defined marketing term and raised safety questions about added botanical extracts. If violations of New York food and drug laws are found, firms could face fines and changes to labeling and marketing. Companies declined detailed comment.

English-language online media are rapidly reshaping how news is produced and consumed, and that model is expanding beyond the U.S. Outlets like Business Insider and Quartz are forging international ties—Business Insider with Tencent and Quartz opening an India office—while BuzzFeed, a widely-cited leader, is pushing into new markets including the U.K., India and, after a $50 million funding round, plans for Japan and other non-English-speaking countries by late 2014.

One notable local competitor in Japan is Curazy, a humor and viral-content site launched in January 2014 that already draws about five million unique monthly users and recently closed a JPY 100 million (roughly $964,000) funding round. Run by Laugh Tech with just five full-time staff—CEO Shinnosuke Ito, head of marketing Masahiro Kawasaki and head of business Taisuke Takemoto—Curazy’s founders lack formal media backgrounds but have entrepreneurial experience in tutoring, web sales and design. Laugh Tech began with manga-related projects and a site called Cosmo, winning a “Google Award” at a pitch contest, but user traction led the team to pivot toward viral comedy. They also launched Curazy Pix, a 9gag-like image collection, and expanded to Taiwan with localized translations and content.

Ambitiously, Laugh Tech targets 300 million monthly pageviews and an exit via IPO or acquisition within four years—a steep climb compared with established players like BuzzFeed, which reportedly had 179 million U.S. visits in a single month and 150 million unique users accumulated over years. Still, Curazy’s growth and regional expansion are promising. Ito publicly joked that BuzzFeed should acquire them, but also stressed cultural differences in humor that could make the Japanese market hard for outsiders to dominate. Overall, the piece highlights how nimble local startups can challenge global digital-media entrants by leveraging cultural fit and fast pivots.

Almost a year after proposing Twitter double its 140-character limit, Farhad Manjoo finds the company moving incrementally toward longer, richer posts with its new “expanded tweets.” Rather than removing the 140-character cap, Twitter now lets select publishers append interactive summaries to tweets linking to their content. Expanded tweets reveal headlines (up to 70 chars), snippets (up to 200 chars), bylines, publisher and author handles, images, and playable media—bringing the potential total to about 410 characters of visible information without breaking the core tweet. Manjoo argues this is a sensible evolution: as fewer users rely on SMS, the old limit has become arbitrary, and richer in-tweet previews make links less mysterious, improve news discovery, and can keep users on Twitter instead of constantly sending them elsewhere. Critics worry the feature privileges large outlets and could dilute Twitter’s brevity-driven creativity; Twitter says partners can apply to participate and that rollout is gradual. While expanded tweets edge the service toward a more feature-rich destination—and could enable in-tweet commercial content—Manjoo views them as a practical compromise that deepens conversation while preserving Twitter’s concise roots.

Megyn Kelly’s position at NBC appears increasingly untenable following a week of fierce backlash over comments about blackface on Megyn Kelly Today. After asserting on-air that blackface and “whiteface” could both be problematic but noting that dressing as a character “back when I was a kid” seemed acceptable, Kelly faced swift social-media outrage and internal condemnation. She issued an on-air and written apology, saying she’s rethinking her views and acknowledging the “abhorrent” history of blackface. NBC News chair Andy Lack publicly condemned the remarks at a staff town hall, calling them unacceptable and stressing respect in the workplace.

The controversy accelerated existing turmoil: Kelly had already been the subject of internal criticism since her 2017 hire from Fox, where many colleagues questioned her fit, salary, ratings struggles, and past on-air stumbles. Conversations about winding down or reassigning her 9 a.m. role reportedly pre-dated this week’s episode. Sources tell multiple outlets that Kelly has left CAA, was expected to sign with UTA but will not be represented by them now, and has retained attorney Bryan Freedman as she heads into likely settlement talks with NBC. She is not expected to host for the rest of the week and may be off the program permanently; negotiations about timing and other details continue.

The incident prompted booking fallout—Netflix’s House of Cards talent withdrew guest appearances—and intensified scrutiny inside NBC, where staffers and hosts like Al Roker and Craig Melvin openly criticized her comments. The episode has underscored long-running doubts about her transition from cable opinion journalism to a mainstream morning show.

San Diego’s popular “Floatopia” parties emerged after a 2007 city ban on drinking on beaches inadvertently excluded the water, since the law defined “beach” as sand or land. Partygoers began convening in calm bays and Mission Bay on rafts, inner tubes and inflatable platforms to drink legally a few feet from shore. Events grew large—up to thousands—bringing trash, noise, heavy policing and lifeguard costs, broken bottles and safety concerns about intoxicated people slipping under water. Organizers used social media to spread the idea after a tech worker publicized the loophole. In response, the city council expanded the ban to prohibit alcohol consumption by bathers in the water (effective immediately), aiming to prevent drownings and restore beach safety, while opponents warned of tourism impacts.

Sir Roger Bannister, the first person to run a mile in under four minutes, has died aged 88. His historic 3:59.4 run at Iffley Road, Oxford, on 6 May 1954 held symbolic weight even though it lasted as the official record for only 46 days; it secured his place in athletics history. Bannister also won the mile at the 1954 Commonwealth Games and later built a distinguished medical career as a consultant neurologist. He had been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease in 2011 and revealed the condition publicly in 2014.

Bannister balanced elite running with medical studies at Oxford, having taken up the sport at 17 and narrowly missing selection for the 1948 Olympics before competing in Helsinki in 1952 and finishing fourth in the 1500m. He applied his medical knowledge to devise training and mechanical approaches that helped him target and achieve the four‑minute barrier, aided in the record run by pacesetters Chris Chataway and Chris Brasher. Chataway and Brasher have since died, and John Landy bettered Bannister’s mark a month later. Bannister retired from competitive athletics at the end of 1954 to focus on medicine, was knighted in 1975, and continued running until a 1975 car accident broke his ankle. His passing prompted tributes from across the sporting world, including IAAF president Lord Coe.

A newly installed 950-ton pedestrian bridge at Florida International University collapsed on March 15, crushing eight vehicles on busy Tamiami Trail and killing multiple people. The 174–175-foot span had been swung into place days earlier as an “accelerated” construction effort; it was not yet open to pedestrians. First responders searched the rubble through the night with cranes, dogs and listening devices; at least four to six deaths were reported and multiple people were hospitalized with injuries ranging from bruises to critical trauma. Agencies including the NTSB launched investigations. FIU, contractors FIGG and MCM, and state officials pledged cooperation as authorities work to determine why the newly installed bridge catastrophically failed.

Virginia's peaceful handoff of power included a classic outgoing-governor prank. Newly inaugurated Gov. Ralph Northam and his wife, Pam, discovered pillowcases in the Governor’s Mansion printed with the smiling face of his predecessor, Democrat Terry McAuliffe, along with McAuliffe’s favorite motto: “Sleep when you’re dead.” Northam spent his first night in the mansion with his head on a pillow bearing the 72nd governor’s grinning mug; his wife used a plain pillowcase. Northam also found photos of McAuliffe scattered around the residence and was roused in the early morning by an alarm clock that went off at 3 a.m., which he has not yet located. He texted McAuliffe, who hinted there was more to come. Such practical jokes are a tradition in Virginia, the only state whose governor changes every four years. The article recounts prior stunts: four years earlier, Republican Bob McDonnell left a taxidermied bear in the private bathroom for McAuliffe; McDonnell was once startled by hidden cellphones planted by Tim Kaine that rang; and Mark Warner previously left a life-size cutout of himself in a shower for Kaine. Northam, a Democrat, veteran and pediatrician who beat Republican Ed Gillespie in November, was sworn in as Virginia’s 73rd governor at a chilly Richmond ceremony.

The Vineyard Gazette was sold to Jerome and Nancy Kohlberg for $3.5 million, with $2 million for the newspaper and $1.5 million for real estate; longtime publisher Richard Reston is retiring. Washington Post hired Peter Wallsten for his skill finding overlooked stories. California Supreme Court let stand a $21 million verdict against SF Weekly for predatory ad pricing. Andrea Mitchell received the Sol Taishoff Award honorarium. The 2010 Lowell Thomas Travel Journalism Competition honored Afar, Washington Post, San Francisco Chronicle and Travel Journalist of the Year Andrew McCarthy, among many winners. An essay described Ireland’s recession-hit Doolin sustaining community spirit through traditional music.

Forbes analyzed 2008 IRS county-to-county move data (donated by Alexa to the Internet Archive) to identify U.S. counties attracting — or losing — wealthy households. Leading inbound destination was Collier County, Fla. (Naples), where 15,150 movers averaged $76,161 per person; Florida and Texas dominate the top 20, likely reflecting their lack of state income tax and relatively low personal tax burdens. Greene County, Ga., Nassau County, Fla., Llano County, Texas, and Walton County, Fla. also ranked high. Conversely, wealthy outflows occurred from high-tax states (e.g., New York, California, New Jersey), with Pitkin County, Colo. (Aspen) seeing many affluent residents leave for cheaper nearby areas or big cities. Forbes’ method compared incoming and nonmoving household incomes, limited samples to sizable moves and per-capita incomes ≥$35,000, and noted IRS data limitations and possible undercounts.

During a CNN segment about the controversy over ESPN commentator Jemele Hill, Fox Sports radio host Clay Travis stunned anchor Brooke Baldwin by declaring, “I believe in the First Amendment and boobs.” The remark, delivered while discussing White House pressure on ESPN, left Baldwin incredulous; she asked Travis to clarify whether he meant “boobs” or “booze,” then terminated the interview, cutting his microphone and ending the segment. Baldwin later tweeted that such comments are never acceptable and criticized Travis’s sexism. Video clips and social media reacted swiftly, largely condemning Travis and praising Baldwin’s handling of the incident; colleagues and commentators lauded her quick decision to stop the interview and her visible disgust. Keith Reed, another guest, called Travis’s remark emblematic of the sexism Jemele Hill and other women in sports journalism routinely face. CNN confirmed that Travis would not be booked again and that a planned HLN appearance was canceled. In a longer first-person account Baldwin described her shock, the newsroom’s stunned silence, and the support she received from colleagues and viewers after she cut him off. She framed the episode as part of a broader effort to amplify women’s voices—citing her “American Woman” project—and said she would not host Travis again, urging accountability for demeaning behavior. The incident reignited conversations about sexism on live television and consequences for on-air conduct.

An internal affairs review found that two Salt Lake City police officers who forcefully arrested nurse Alex Wubbels violated department policies and codes of conduct. The July body‑camera footage shows Detective Jeff Payne dragging and handcuffing Wubbels after she refused to allow a blood draw from an unconscious patient without consent, a refusal consistent with University of Utah Hospital policy. The hospital requires either an arrest or a warrant before releasing blood without patient consent; neither condition applied. In the footage Wubbels yells, “I’ve done nothing wrong!” while Payne is heard threatening to retaliate against the hospital’s patient population. Mayor Jackie Biskupski called the footage “unacceptable,” saying it did not reflect the city or its police department. The investigative findings cite possible violations including “conduct unbecoming by a police employee” and breaches of arrest policy. Detective Payne and his watch commander, Lieutenant James Tracy, have been placed on administrative leave and have up to 20 days to respond to the allegations. Biskupski emphasized this is not the final step; the report will go to Police Chief Mike Brown, who will decide on further action. The police department has since amended its blood‑draw request policy to align with the hospital’s rules. Wubbels said she received apologies from the mayor and police chief and accepted them.

At a CNN debate, Rep. Ron Paul responded to a hypothetical about denying care to an uninsured man in a coma by arguing voluntary community and private charity, noting from his medical and church volunteer experience that hospitals hadn’t turned people away. Some audience members shouted agreement. Afterwards, Gov. Rick Perry said he was “taken aback” by cheers for letting someone die, calling Republicans “the party of life” and urging life-protecting policies. Perry defended his support for in-state tuition for children brought illegally to the U.S., framing it as an education, not immigration, issue and saying Texas made the right choice. He also rebutted critiques of his Gardasil vaccine mandate, likening anti-vaccine claims to the debunked autism link and stressing the vaccine’s life-saving intent.

Attorneys for Nanette Kinkade — trustee and executor of the Kinkade Family Trust and estate — have filed for a temporary restraining order against Amy Pinto-Walsh, the late painter Thomas Kinkade’s live-in girlfriend. Filed in Santa Clara County Superior Court by Zuber & Taillieu LLP, the petition alleges Pinto-Walsh breached a confidentiality agreement she signed on Feb. 25, 2011, by speaking publicly about Kinkade’s death and his non-public health condition in an April 7 interview. The proposed injunction would bar Pinto-Walsh from making disparaging statements about Thomas or Nanette Kinkade, publishing or assisting publication of any materials about the family or its companies (Windermere Holdings LLC, Pacific Metro LLC/The Thomas Kinkade Company), and from disclosing proprietary information or trade secrets she learned as a personal assistant and companion. Declarations from family friends and counsel claim Pinto-Walsh had access to business plans, financials, and proprietary painting techniques and has threatened to release confidential materials, including private photos. A hearing is scheduled before Judge Patricia M. Lucas on April 24; opposition deadlines and document submission timelines were set in the court papers.

Rex Tillerson, U.S. secretary of state and former ExxonMobil CEO, is reportedly increasingly frustrated with the Trump administration and may consider leaving his post sooner than previously expected. Multiple CNN and Reuters sources who’ve spoken with Tillerson’s friends and officials say his mood has darkened amid White House turmoil—public rebukes of Attorney General Jeff Sessions, the ouster and replacement of communications staff, the Scaramucci hire, and Sean Spicer’s resignation. Tillerson has chafed at what he sees as White House interference in State Department staffing and policy, including rejected nominees and personnel moves by Johnny DeStefano, and has publicly clashed over coordination failures on issues from the Muslim travel ban to Syria and the Qatar dispute. He’s angered by partisan internal criticism over the administration’s Iran nuclear deal recertification and has lamented his lack of autonomy to run the department in the traditional way. Friends had expected him to stay through the year to complete a State Department reorganization, but two sources now predict a possible near-term “Rexit,” while acknowledging his recent outbursts might be temporary venting. Tillerson’s spokesman disputes claims he plans to depart, emphasizing the need for U.S. global leadership. The reports reflect broader discontent among foreign-policy officials, including national security adviser H.R. McMaster, who are frustrated by disorganization and disputes over U.S. strategy and independence within the administration.

Snoop Dogg was honored with his star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on November 19 outside the El Capitan Theatre, becoming the 2,651st celebrity to receive the accolade. The ceremony, attended by family, friends and industry figures including Dr. Dre, Warren G, Quincy Jones and Jimmy Kimmel, saw Snoop deliver a heartfelt speech thanking many people — and emphatically thanking himself for perseverance, hard work and staying true to who he is. His wife Shante Broadus, children Cori and Julian, and other supporters joined the crowd; longtime friend Martha Stewart was absent but posted supportive comments online. After the unveiling Snoop posed beside his star and posted gratitude to social media, captioning images “Blessed #HollywoodWalkOfFame” and “Thank. U I am humbled.” The honor arrives shortly before the 25th anniversary of his debut album Doggystyle and caps a prolific career: Snoop has sold tens of millions of albums worldwide, earned numerous Grammy nominations, and produced major hits like “Gin & Juice,” “Nuthin’ But a ‘G’ Thang,” and “Drop It Like It’s Hot.” Beyond music, he has expanded into television, film, publishing and entrepreneurship — from VH1’s Martha & Snoop’s Potluck Dinner Party and hosting game and news-format shows to launching a cookbook, From Crook to Cook, and co-founding cannabis media company Merry Jane. He also runs the Snoop Youth Football League and has engaged in varied philanthropic and creative ventures. The star recognizes Snoop’s cross-genre influence, longevity and cultural impact across entertainment, business and community work.

Researchers report a dramatic rise in earthquakes in Oklahoma linked to large-volume wastewater disposal from oil and gas operations. A study published in Science found a roughly forty-fold increase in quake rates between 2008 and 2013, with more than 2,500 earthquakes over magnitude 3 occurring around Jones since 2008. The team modelled how pressurized wastewater injected into deep disposal wells spreads underground and concluded that four high-volume wells in central Oklahoma—pumping about 4 million barrels a month to ~3.5 km depth—are likely responsible for a swarm of tremors occurring as far as 20–35 km from the wells. Wastewater arises both from hydraulic fracturing and from dewatering conventional wells; volumes can be enormous, with water-to-oil ratios sometimes in the hundreds. Increased subsurface fluid pressure reduces friction on faults and can trigger slip if they are close to failure. The researchers note permitted disposal rates in the region nearly doubled between 2004 and 2008 and likely rose further, potentially explaining the geographic breadth and persistence of the seismicity. Company owners of the implicated wells dispute the study’s assumptions and say operations comply with permits. Scientists caution uncertainty remains about the likelihood of even larger induced quakes—small events can precede bigger ruptures—and call for more study and guidance so authorities can limit problematic injection practices while weighing the costs of continued oil and gas production.

On a low hill about 20 miles south of Tbilisi, Georgia, archaeologists have found compelling evidence that people at the Neolithic villages of Gadachrili Gora and nearby Shulaveri Gora were producing true grape wine as early as 6,000–5,800 B.C. Excavations recovered large, rounded pottery jars—similar in form to the qvevri still used by Georgian winemakers—whose fabric contained absorbed organic residues. Chemical analyses detected tartaric acid and other wine-related compounds in eight jars, a molecular “fingerprint” consistent with grape wine. Radiocarbon dates, abundant grape pollen in site soils, and grape-cluster decorations on pottery strengthen the interpretation that these communities cultivated Eurasian grapevine (Vitis vinifera) and made wine on a substantial scale.

The evidence suggests grapes were pressed and fermented in the nearby hills where vines grew; finished wine was then poured into smaller vessels and transported to villages. Unlike many later ancient wines, the residues show no tree resins or other preservatives, implying these were early, relatively pure wines consumed seasonally before spoiling. The jars’ large capacities indicate storage and communal processing—one comparable vessel could have held the equivalent of hundreds of modern bottles.

This discovery pushes back the earliest known example of dedicated grape winemaking by up to a millennium compared with previous finds in Iran and Armenia, and distinguishes pure grape wine from older mixed fermented beverages (such as Jiahu’s rice-honey-fruit brew in China). It illuminates how rapidly Neolithic communities not only adopted agriculture but developed sophisticated horticulture, domestication, and fermentation techniques. Scholars say the results reveal cultural complexity—wine production served social, medicinal, and ritual roles—and tie Georgia’s deep contemporary wine culture to roots stretching back some 8,000 years.

Facebook, with 1.39 billion active users, updated and clarified its Community Standards to give users and its content reviewers clearer guidance on what is and isn’t allowed. The company faces a difficult balancing act: restricting violent, offensive, or illegal material while preserving open expression across a diverse, global audience with varying laws and cultural norms. Past decisions—such as vacillating on beheading videos, inconsistently handling protest pages, and selectively exempting San Francisco drag queens from its real-name policy—have highlighted opacity and inconsistency in enforcement. The clarified rules reiterate longstanding bans (terrorist organizations, pornography, most nudity) while defining nuances: removal of images exposing genitals or fully exposed buttocks, restrictions on some female breast images while allowing breastfeeding and post-mastectomy photos, and explicit prohibition of content promoting sexual violence and revenge porn. Praise or support for violent, criminal, or hateful groups, threats, bullying, and encouragement of suicide or eating disorders are forbidden. Facebook won’t automatically scan for offensive content; it continues to rely on user reports and globally distributed review teams, typically taking up to 48 hours for safety matters, and allows appeals reviewed by humans. Facebook also published its Global Government Requests Report for the latter half of 2014: 9,707 pieces of content were restricted for violating local laws (an 11% increase), led by requests from India and Turkey; government data requests rose slightly to 35,051, with the U.S. making the most. Mark Zuckerberg framed the approach as incremental progress toward giving many people a voice while complying with lawful local orders when necessary.

Orlando International Airport will soon require facial scans of all arriving and departing international passengers, including U.S. citizens, becoming the first U.S. airport to apply biometric checks to every international traveler rather than limited flights or gates. The scans capture a passenger’s image and compare it within seconds to passport photos held in a Department of Homeland Security biometric database to verify identity. While U.S. citizens will technically be able to opt out as at other airports using the technology, privacy advocates say the agency has not adequately publicized that option and a notice about a potential rule change even suggests citizens “may be required to provide photographs upon entering or departing the United States.” Critics worry the expansion at Orlando — which handled about six million international passengers in the past year — massively increases the number of people scanned, raising the likelihood of errors and misidentifications. Research indicates many facial-recognition systems perform worse for racial minorities, women and children because training datasets underrepresent those groups, fueling concerns about unfair outcomes if people are wrongly prevented from boarding. Two U.S. senators, Ed Markey and Mike Lee, have asked the Department of Homeland Security to establish formal rules and vet the program before widening its scope. The move reflects a broader push to integrate biometrics into travel: airports in several cities already use face scans for some departures, airlines like Delta are deploying facial-recognition bag drops, and private services such as Clear store traveler biometrics to speed security. Proponents say the technologies can streamline travel from curb to plane, while opponents caution about privacy, accuracy, and governance gaps.

Investigators probing the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 are increasingly focused on the possibility that someone in the cockpit deliberately diverted and downed the Boeing 777. Within days of the March 8 disappearance en route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing, authorities noted the aircraft’s transponder and ACARS communications were turned off and the jet made a sharp, preprogrammed left turn shortly after last contact—actions consistent with someone trained and familiar with the plane. Military radar later tracked the jet flying west over the Malaysian peninsula and possibly toward either a northern corridor across Central and South Asia or a southern route into the Indian Ocean. Malaysian officials and international partners treat both arcs as possibilities while expanding search efforts across many countries. U.S. and other intelligence officials said cockpit involvement is a working theory but emphasized no final conclusions.

Past crashes—such as EgyptAir 990 and SilkAir 185—have shown how contentious pilot-suicide conclusions can be; investigations often stop short of labeling events suicide even when deliberate action seems likely. An FAA study found pilot-assisted suicides are rare but under-recognized. Malaysian police searched the homes of captain Zaharie Ahmad Shah and co-pilot Fariq Ab Hamid and seized a flight simulator from Zaharie’s house for examination. Investigators are also checking ground staff, engineers, and passenger backgrounds for possible motives or capabilities. Meanwhile search operations have shifted repeatedly; India temporarily suspended its extensive Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal searches pending revised coordinates. Families of the 239 people aboard have grown increasingly frustrated with slow, uncertain public information. Officials continue to analyze satellite pings suggesting the aircraft may have continued transmitting hours after loss of radar contact, but precise location remains unresolved and the international search and investigation continue.

An Austrian climber on his second day ascending El Capitan’s Nose route in Yosemite severed his right thumb when a secondary rope wrapped around it during a fall roughly 1,000 feet below the summit. The thumb fell about 80 feet and landed on a narrow two-by-one-foot ledge, where the climber’s partner retrieved it. The pair summoned Yosemite’s Emergency Communication Center. With daylight limited, park officials opted for a high-angle short-haul helicopter extraction. Rangers were lowered to the wall, hoisted the injured climber to El Capitan Meadow, and he was transferred to an air medical helicopter. He underwent successful thumb reattachment surgery that evening at California Pacific Medical Center in San Francisco. Yosemite officials praised the technical rescue and the Search and Rescue team’s skill and dedication.

Diners at The Good Life Eatery in St John’s Wood, London, watched Ewan McGregor, 46, and Mary Elizabeth Winstead, 32, sit for more than an hour in deep conversation, share a passionate kiss, and then leave together on McGregor’s motorbike. The pair, who co-star as lovers in Fargo’s third series—McGregor as probation officer Ray Stussy (and his twin Emmit) and Winstead as Nikki Swango—were described as relaxed and comfortable by onlookers. Winstead split from husband Riley Stearns in May; McGregor has been married to Eve Mavrakis since 1995, though recent photos showed both without wedding rings and reports say the couple separated in May after 22 years and four children. The Fargo series, filmed in Calgary and aired earlier this year, included intimate scenes between their characters, and Winstead has discussed her character’s genuine feelings for Ray. The episode details and cast interactions, including a Fargo cast dinner in March, have drawn attention amid the sighting and the actors’ personal developments.

Following controversial remarks on his radio show about a recent JetBlue incident, Carson Daly apologized after suggesting gay passengers wouldn’t have been brave enough to restrain a disruptive pilot. On the show he described most passengers as “well-trained dudes” headed to a security conference and quipped that, with his luck, the flight would instead be full of people traveling to a gay pride parade or a “floral convention,” adopting a stereotyped voice. Bloggers and commentators quickly noted the comment ignored real examples of gay bravery, notably Mark Bingham, an openly gay passenger who helped storm United Flight 93 on 9/11. Daly tweeted a brief apology saying he attempted to make fun of himself and “offended others by mistake,” and later issued a fuller statement to GLAAD expressing sincere sadness that his words suggested LGBT individuals don’t confront adversity. He affirmed his long-standing support for gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender rights, called the harm he caused “devastating,” and said he is “proud to be an ally” who will “continue to fight with them.” GLAAD has been in dialogue with Daly and said it looks forward to working with him, while leaving it to the public to judge the sincerity of his remarks.

North Korea presented an American, Arturo Pierre Martinez, 29, to the media Dec. 14 in Pyongyang, saying he illegally entered the country and is seeking asylum in Venezuela. Martinez, from El Paso, Texas, told reporters he crossed into North Korea via a river from China; North Korean statements placed his entry in November. He delivered a lengthy, critical statement denouncing the U.S. political, economic and justice systems, calling U.S. actions abroad akin to criminal plunder and describing American democracy as an illusion favoring the wealthy. He also raised assorted conspiratorial claims, including CIA involvement in drug trafficking, “ultrasonic” devices that induce voices and physical discomfort, and criticism of Western media coverage of North Korea.

Martinez’s mother, Patricia Eugenia Martinez, told CNN her son is bipolar, had earlier attempted to cross into North Korea by swimming a river and was subsequently returned to the U.S. and held in a California psychiatric hospital before being released. She said he later bought a ticket to China after taking out a payday loan, and that the U.S. Embassy in Beijing was searching for him. She expressed relief at seeing him safe after North Korea’s press presentation and said she anticipated his release, though his legal status in North Korea remained unclear.

The press event took place at the People’s Palace of Culture, a venue North Korean authorities have used to display defectors or detained foreigners and for diplomatic signings. Observers noted the timing amid North Korea’s objections to a U.N. human-rights resolution, suggesting Martinez’s appearance could serve propaganda purposes. North Korea recently released other Americans, including Kenneth Bae.

A Southwest Airlines flight from San Francisco to Phoenix was diverted to Los Angeles after a pregnant passenger went into labor and gave birth shortly after takeoff. Flight 623 turned to Los Angeles International Airport where paramedics met the aircraft; the mother and newborn were taken to a hospital in good condition, Los Angeles Fire Department spokesman Erik Scott said. Airline spokeswoman Emily Samuels said a doctor and nurse aboard the plane assisted the woman with help from the flight crew. Passengers described a calm but urgent scene: some heard a call for a doctor, others noticed the woman pacing in the terminal before boarding, and several recalled the distinctive sound of an infant’s cry once the baby arrived. The captain announced the news mid-flight, prompting applause and relief among travelers who initially feared a more serious emergency. Passenger accounts varied: one said it felt “amazing” and praised how calmly fellow passengers and crew responded, while another recalled confusion before the announcement. The aircraft was taken out of service for cleaning; the remaining 111 passengers continued to Phoenix on a different plane, arriving more than two hours late. Southwest did not release the names of the mother or child, and initially withheld the baby’s gender. The airline noted hopefully gaining a “customer for life.” This event echoes a previous Southwest in-flight birth in 2009, when a woman delivered a son on a flight from Chicago to Salt Lake City. Typically, babies born aboard U.S. flights receive a birth certificate from the state where the plane lands. Further personal details about the mother and newborn have not been disclosed.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said her views on same-sex marriage are “evolving” as she reconsiders the issue amid shifting public attitudes. Speaking to the Chugiak-Eagle River Star after addressing a local chamber of commerce, Murkowski acknowledged “a change afoot” in how marriage is viewed nationwide and said she is “reviewing that very closely.” Though she previously supported constitutional amendments defining marriage as between one man and one woman and has tied her positions to Alaskans—who approved a state ban in 1998—she noted influences on her thinking, including conversations with her two young sons and their peers. Murkowski emphasized broader national priorities, questioning the focus on who can marry when issues like sequestration demand attention. She said her future actions will reflect constituent views and that Alaska may eventually revisit its stance, even as other state and federal lawmakers have taken differing positions.

An incident at Rikers Island and broader policy decisions by the city’s jail leadership have raised serious concerns about the treatment of mentally ill inmates and use of force by correction officers. Officer Lameen Barnes’s official report of an encounter with inmate Mr. Dixon described a minimal use of force: Dixon allegedly tried to throw an “unknown liquid substance” at officers, was searched for contraband, refused orders, was restrained and handcuffed to a gurney, and then “escorted to the main clinic for medical examination without any further incident of force used.” That account conflicts sharply with contemporaneous accounts from three people present during the event. Two witnesses, who asked to remain anonymous citing fear of retaliation and their employer Corizon (which contracts with the city to provide jail health care), and a clinician who emailed superiors about the event, say the reality was far more violent. They report Dixon being wheeled into an unmonitored examination area, pleading with medics and social workers—“Don’t leave me… They’re going to kill me”—while about six guards crowded the gurney and one repeatedly punched him in the head.

A similar episode involved another inmate, Mr. Lane, who also had splashed guards with a liquid and who has a lengthy history of severe mental illness and institutionalization. Lane later recounted being punched repeatedly in the face by officers during the confrontation. These accounts suggest a pattern of forceful responses to incidents involving mentally ill inmates.

Separately, city oversight revealed that newly appointed Department of Correction Commissioner Joseph Ponte violated city rules by moving as many as 47 mentally ill inmates into 23-hour confinement without required clinician approvals. Ponte defended the June 13 action as an emergency measure to curb surging violence at Rikers, citing rising slashings and an alleged backlog of inmates who owe time in solitary but remain in the general population. Board members rejected his justification, warning the move endangered inmates—especially those on psychotropic medication or otherwise heat-sensitive—by placing them into uncooled cells contrary to a federal judge’s order. The episode highlights tensions between efforts to control violence on Rikers and obligations to safeguard mentally ill detainees’ health and rights, with critics urging adherence to board standards designed to protect vulnerable prisoners.

Two Marion County, Oregon, commissioners reacted with outrage after a Vancouver Catholic newspaper reported that biomedical waste from British Columbia — possibly including fetal tissue from abortions and miscarriages — has been shipped to and incinerated at the Covanta Marion waste-to-energy plant near Salem to produce electricity. The report, which cited a B.C. Health Ministry confirmation that regional authorities contract with a waste-hauler that ships biomedical waste out of province, sparked local media attention and prompted emergency county action. Commissioners Janet Carlson and Sam Brentano, both publicly pro-life, held an emergency meeting and voted to halt biomedical waste deliveries to the plant until safeguards are in place to ensure fetal tissue is not burned. They also moved to amend county ordinances to explicitly bar fetal tissue from the facility. Covanta Marion, which operates the 28-year-old plant under a county partnership and converts hundreds of tons of waste daily into power sold to Portland General Electric, said it is suspending receipt of the waste stream pending county assurances and stressed it does not solicit such material. Stericycle, the company reportedly transporting B.C. biomedical waste, did not respond. Officials emphasized most medical waste is sealed and includes diverse materials; county leaders said they want to retain other medical disposals while drawing a line against fetal remains.

Multiple reports indicate Yahoo will soon confirm a massive data breach that exposed hundreds of millions of user accounts. Sources describe the incident as widespread and serious; early accounts pointed to roughly 200 million affected records, but some reporting and later company disclosures suggest the figure may be much larger—potentially in the hundreds of millions. The leaked data allegedly includes usernames, hashed or poorly encrypted passwords, birthdates, backup email addresses and other personal details, and some samples date to 2012 or 2014. A known cybercriminal using the handle “Peace” advertised 200 million Yahoo credentials for sale on darknet marketplaces for a small sum in bitcoin, and security reporters verified that some sample addresses matched real accounts.

The timing is especially consequential because Yahoo is completing a $4.8 billion sale of its core business to Verizon; the breach could trigger regulatory scrutiny, legal action, and renegotiation or liability concerns that complicate the transaction. Yahoo initially acknowledged awareness of the claims and said it was investigating, later advising users to change passwords if they hadn’t since 2014. Verizon has said it is monitoring the investigation to assess impacts. The breach underscores risks from reused passwords and inadequate hashing practices and represents a significant reputational and financial blow to Yahoo.

Shortly after the government shutdown ended, President Obama urged Congress to resume comprehensive immigration reform and pass a bill by year’s end, calling it beneficial for the economy, national security and families. But momentum stalled amid partisan mistrust and competing political calculations. Some Democrats worry a quick compromise would blunt an issue that energizes Hispanic voters—who backed Obama overwhelmingly in 2012—and prefer to keep immigration prominent through next year’s campaigns. Republicans remain divided: a Senate bipartisan bill that includes a path to citizenship won approval in June, yet many House Republicans oppose such a pathway and favor piecemeal measures. House leaders, including Speaker John Boehner, say the House won’t back the Senate bill and plan smaller bills; the Senate has resisted scaled-down approaches. Relations poisoned by the shutdown and debt fight complicate talks, with Republicans like Marco Rubio and others saying the president’s tactics have undermined trust. Advocacy coalitions of business, religious, agricultural and tech groups are lobbying hard, but limited House floor days, looming budget and debt deadlines, and internal GOP skepticism make passage before year-end unlikely. Supporters warn the window for major reform may close, especially with 2014’s election-year dynamics ahead.

Motorcycle lane splitting—riding between lanes of moving or stopped traffic—provokes strong reactions from drivers and riders alike. In New Jersey the practice occupies a legal gray area: there is no explicit ban, but state guidance discourages it. The New Jersey driver’s manual warns bikers against “lane sharing” and riding between stopped vehicles. Police can cite riders for failing to “keep right,” and traffic officials caution that lane splitting on highways is risky because drivers changing lanes may not see motorcycles. Riders and advocacy groups, however, argue lane splitting improves safety in stop-and-go traffic by reducing rear-end crash risk, easing overheating, saving time and improving fuel efficiency. Research and agencies offer mixed conclusions: a UC Berkeley 2015 study found lane-splitting motorcyclists in heavy traffic were less likely to be struck from behind or suffer severe injuries, while the NHTSA calls for more study though acknowledges potential escape-route benefits. California alone has formally addressed the practice: AB 51 passed the Assembly unanimously to let the California Highway Patrol set guidelines for safe lane splitting, making California the first state to legalize and regulate it once the governor signs the bill. Debates continue over how specific rules should be, balancing rider safety, driver awareness and enforceability. Meanwhile, efforts to change laws in other states, including petitions in New Jersey, reflect ongoing public interest.

Veterinarian John Robb’s story illustrates a larger upheaval in American pet care as corporate consolidation transforms veterinary medicine. A born-again Christian who believes in protecting animals, Robb sold his first practice to VCA, later bought and ran a Banfield franchise, and ultimately lost it after disputes over vaccine practices. He began giving smaller dogs reduced doses after adverse reactions; Banfield cited vaccine-protocol violations and Connecticut law to seize his charter in 2012. Robb sued and countersued, has picketed, been arrested, and built a “Boycott Banfield” following that channels angry pet owners and former staff. Banfield contends its care is compassionate and aligned with guidelines.

The piece situates Robb’s conflict within the rapid corporatization of veterinary care. Chains like VCA and Banfield—Banfield owned by Mars since 2007—apply retail-style efficiencies: software-guided protocols (PetWare), wellness-plan packages that bundle exams, diagnostics, and vaccines, and centralized targets for revenues and average patient charges. Critics say this encourages one-size-fits-all medicine, overtesting, overvaccination, and a profit-first mentality; defenders argue consolidation enables advanced diagnostics, specialty services, and consistent quality. Veterinary medicine remains lightly regulated compared with human health care; owners pay cash, courts treat pets as property, and malpractice consequences are limited, creating an environment where financial incentives can strongly influence care.

Vaccination practices are central to the debate. Longstanding AAHA guidance favors longer intervals for core vaccines, but many clinics continued yearly boosters—partly because vaccine dosing protocols historically used a uniform volume regardless of animal size. Studies and experts dispute the rate of adverse reactions; some manufacturers have since developed smaller-dose vaccines. Meanwhile, Mars’s pending moves to further consolidate major chains raise alarms that wellness-plan-driven, standardized care will extend to many more clinics, reshaping how Americans obtain medical care for animals and fueling tensions between independent veterinarians and corporate owners.

IntercontinentalExchange (ICE) is set to acquire NYSE Euronext in an about $8–8.2 billion deal, offering roughly $33 a share—two-thirds in stock—representing a roughly 37% premium. Talks could be announced imminently, though they might still falter. The strategic appeal is NYSE Euronext’s derivatives business (including Liffe), underscoring how derivatives and commodities trading have outpaced traditional equities. ICE, founded in 2000 and a fast-growing commodities and derivatives venue, would combine its high-margin operations with NYSE’s scale, creating a group controlling numerous stock and futures exchanges and clearing houses. The deal follows failed prior merger attempts (NYSE with Deutsche Börse and a joint ICE–Nasdaq bid) that faced antitrust obstacles. The merger reflects consolidation trends, electronic trading’s dominance over floor trading, potential cost synergies, and possible regulatory or competitor pushback.

The shooting death of Walter Scott by a North Charleston police officer renewed scrutiny not only of police use of force but also of how the child support enforcement system treats poor noncustodial parents. Scott’s long struggle with child support began years before his death: he was jailed multiple times for unpaid support, lost a $35,000-a-year film job after an early incarceration, cycled through odd jobs and drinking, and repeatedly fell behind again. Court records showed he owed nearly $18,104 at one point and had been jailed three previous times. State law in South Carolina allows county court clerks to issue bench warrants once support is just five days late, and other harsh sanctions—license revocations, wage garnishment, seizure of refunds—can follow. Advocates say these practices trap men in a cycle of debt, unemployment and incarceration because debts keep accruing while men are jailed, undermining their ability to get work and pay support.

Critics, including the S.C. Center for Fathers and Families and the S.C. Appleseed Legal Justice Center, call the state’s “Rule 24” among the strictest in the country and argue that turning family-support issues into policing treats debtors like criminals. A U.S. Supreme Court decision several years ago prompted agencies and courts to reconsider routine incarceration for nonpayment, concluding jail is seldom appropriate for parents who cannot pay. Still, enforcement varies widely by county; Berkeley County alone reported more than 1,100 active bench warrants for nonpayment. South Carolina received an $8 million federal grant to launch “Operation Work,” a program in three counties that helps fathers find employment, attend technical school and suspend child support payments while participants build skills—an alternative to jail that aims to stabilize families and incomes.

Nationally, enforcement practices differ and there is no comprehensive count of parents jailed for nonpayment. Surveys and local reports show thousands are affected: e.g., one in eight South Carolina inmates in a 2009 survey had been jailed for child support, Georgia jailed 3,500 parents in 2010, and New Jersey counties used jail or ankle monitors for many parents. Legal advocates argue that punitive enforcement without addressing poverty perpetuates injustice and that supportive programs are more effective at helping parents meet obligations and prevent cycles like Walter Scott’s.

MTV’s hidden-camera series Punk’d returned to production, filming a new episode in Los Angeles with Taylor Swift as the unsuspecting target. Instead of Ashton Kutcher appearing on camera, Swift was pranked by friend Justin Bieber, a source told Access Hollywood; Kutcher remains an executive producer for the rebooted show he originally launched in 2003. Bieber had recently surprised Swift onstage during her Speak Now tour to perform his hit “Baby.” Separately, Bieber was involved in a minor noon collision in the San Fernando Valley when a Honda Civic reportedly hit his Ferrari; police said there were no injuries and no significant damage. Copyright 2012 NBC Universal.

Ahmed Wali Karzai, the powerful and controversial half-brother of Afghan President Hamid Karzai, was assassinated in Kandahar by a trusted longtime security aide on July 12, removing a divisive but pivotal power broker from southern Afghanistan. Karzai, who chaired the Kandahar Provincial Council and effectively controlled much of the region through tribal, militia, and business networks, was long accused of corruption and ties to the opium trade—charges he denied. His death immediately raised concerns about a dangerous power vacuum in Kandahar, the Taliban’s birthplace, and whether fragile security gains established by a U.S. troop surge could hold. The Taliban claimed responsibility, though motives and any insurgent ties of the shooter remain unclear.

U.S. officials were split about Karzai’s role: military commanders viewed his corruption as undermining counterinsurgency efforts and Afghan legitimacy, while CIA officers and some diplomats relied on him as an indispensable local broker who supplied intelligence, recruited fighters for pro-government forces, and helped keep influential Pashtun tribes aligned against the Taliban. His network controlled logistics routes, security contractors, and patronage that both aided U.S. operations and perpetuated the very patronage system feeding instability. Analysts warn his removal could either allow a cleaner leader to emerge or precipitate violent competition that benefits insurgents. The assassination underscores the deeper contradiction of U.S. policy—relying on “big men” for short-term security while those same alliances impede long-term governance and stability—reinforcing Washington’s impetus to withdraw.

A provocative ad campaign in Colorado promoting enrollment in the state health insurance exchange has drawn heated criticism for its sexualized portrayal of young women. Created by ProgressNow Colorado and the Colorado Consumer Health Initiative, the “Got Insurance?” and “Thanks Obamacare!” ads depict young adults doing keg stands, shotskis, and a woman clutching birth-control pills alongside a man while implying casual sex is now easier because insurance covers contraception. Supporters say the edgy ads target young adults—whose participation is vital to stabilizing premiums—and are intended to raise awareness on social media. Critics, including conservatives and some academics, call the spots demeaning, stereotyping millennials, and trivializing serious healthcare issues amid Obamacare’s troubled rollout and widespread plan cancellations. Organizers defended the campaign’s provocative tone and noted ads aren’t on public transit or billboards; traffic to the campaign site surged. The debate has amplified partisan backlash over the Affordable Care Act and raised questions about whether shock value helps or harms enrollment efforts.

The fleece or down vest has become Silicon Valley’s unofficial uniform, especially among venture capitalists. Often black and commonly Patagonia-branded, the vest is ubiquitous at coffee shops, conferences, and VC offices; HBO’s Silicon Valley even costumed characters in Patagonia vests after the show’s designers observed the trend. VCs and firms like Andreessen Horowitz also hand out embroidered Patagonia vests as high-quality event swag. Practical reasons help explain the craze: Bay Area weather stays cool year-round, making layering sensible, and Patagonia’s reputation for quality and casual authenticity appeals to wealthy tech figures who want to appear grounded. The trend extended to San Francisco International Airport, where a Uniqlo vending machine selling lightweight down vests — priced around $50 and reportedly popular — went viral on Twitter as a punchline about visiting VCs. Uniqlo has been deploying clothing vending machines nationwide; SFO says the vending concept is unique and doing well. Overall, the vest blends practicality, branding, and cultural signaling across Silicon Valley and beyond.

A trove of direct Twitter messages leaked to The Daily Caller revealed Sarah Palin aide Rebecca Mansour mocking conservative figures and even Palin’s daughter, creating a headache for Palin’s operation. Mansour, Palin’s domestic policy adviser, speechwriter and online gatekeeper, sent the messages last year to an online acquaintance who later forwarded them. They include crude descriptions of RedState founder Erick Erickson as “a total douchebag” and a “greasy dumb ass,” dismissive characterizations of Mitt Romney supporters as “wacky” or an “AstroTurf brigade,” and derisive comments about California Senate candidate Chuck DeVore and others. Most explosively, Mansour speculated that Palin might hold daughter Bristol “at arm’s length,” invoked comparisons to other political families, and suggested replacing Bristol’s reported suitor—remarks Mansour later called private and attributed to calming a supporter.

The messages also show Mansour coaching activists to flatter Palin online and reveal internal campaign calculations, such as viewing Nikki Haley’s endorsement as a risky but important move for a possible Palin presidential bid. Mansour even circulated a purported “scoop” about liberal Alaska radio host Shannyn Moore’s finances and sponsorships, name-checking Moore’s partner and invoking a herpes drug in a crude jibe.

When confronted, Mansour initially denied authorship, then said a correspondent fabricated messages; after TheDC authenticated Twitter emails and obtained forensic verification, she shifted to expressions of regret and concern that the revelations would harm her reputation. She declined further context, framing the messages as private conversations with someone she believed to be a friend. Mansour’s current status with SarahPAC was unclear.

Rudy Kurniawan, once celebrated as one of the world’s top wine collectors, was convicted in Manhattan federal court for creating and selling counterfeit wines. Prosecutors detailed how the Indonesian-born collector used his acclaimed palate to blend ordinary and younger wines, re-bottle them with forged labels and pass them off as rare vintage Burgundies and Bordeaux at high-end auctions. French vignerons including Laurent Ponsot, Laurent Roumier and Aubert de Villaine testified that bottles Kurniawan offered bore impossible dates or labels inconsistent with their estates—e.g., vintages predating when a domaine bottled wine or labels from merchants those domaines never used. Ponsot described withdrawing 97 purported Domaine Ponsot bottles from a 2008 New York auction after being alerted, and later confronting Kurniawan, who gave evasive sourcing details. FBI agents arrested Kurniawan in March 2012 after finding hundreds of bottles, labels, corks, stamps and materials in his home consistent with forgery. Evidence included invoices for large purchases of ordinary old bottles and expert testimony linking many counterfeit bottles to him. The defense argued he merely reconditioned bottles or was being scapegoated in a market rife with fakes, but the jury convicted him on fraud counts; he faces sentencing and up to 40 years in prison. The case exposed vulnerabilities in the rare-wine market and underscored how collectors treat bottles as investments rather than beverages.

Hurricane Irma barreled toward Florida early Sunday, its powerful eyewall striking the lower Keys as residents huddled in shelters and hundreds of thousands lost power. The Category 4 storm, with sustained winds around 130 mph and dangerous gusts reported near Key West, was centered just offshore and moving north-northwest toward the Keys and up the Gulf Coast. Tornado warnings were issued for parts of South Florida, and authorities urged people sheltering in the Keys to remain indoors even during the eye’s temporary calm. Utilities reported widespread outages—Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach among the hardest hit—and crews were mobilized for restoration. Officials also warned against dangerous stunts, after a viral Facebook event urged people to “shoot” at the storm; the Pasco County sheriff’s office firmly discouraged firing weapons. Elsewhere, Caribbean islands battered by Irma began recovery efforts, with the Dutch and French reporting less damage than feared from Hurricane Jose.

At the Hayward Russell City Blues Festival, 73-year-old soul singer Lester Chambers was assaulted on stage after dedicating Curtis Mayfield’s "People Get Ready" to Trayvon Martin, moments after George Zimmerman was acquitted. According to police and eyewitnesses, a 43-year-old woman, identified as Dinalynn Andrews Potter of Barstow, leaped onto the stage shouting “it's all your fault” and shoved Chambers, who fell hard. Friends and audience members subdued the attacker; Hayward police arrested her on suspicion of battery, cited and released her pending possible further charges. Chambers, formerly of The Chambers Brothers, was taken to a hospital, treated and released; his family reports bruised ribs, nerve damage, a large welt on his back and he now uses a cane. The family believes the assault was racially motivated and is urging police to pursue hate crime charges; Chambers is Black and the alleged assailant is White. Chambers has a long history in music and advocacy over unpaid royalties and recently raised funds for a new album. The incident occurred amid heightened tensions following the Zimmerman verdict.

Colin Kaepernick, the former San Francisco 49ers quarterback who sparked nationwide debate by kneeling during the national anthem to protest racial injustice, filed a collusion grievance against the NFL. Filed under the league’s collective bargaining agreement (CBA) and handled through arbitration, the grievance alleges team owners conspired to keep him unsigned because of his political protests. Kaepernick opted out of his 49ers contract in March and remained a free agent through the 2017 season despite general league quarterback needs and his solid 2016 statistical finish (16 TDs, 4 INTs in 12 games). Attorney Mark Geragos, who represents Kaepernick, said the grievance followed exhaustive outreach to teams and executives and framed the filing as defending meritocracy and the right to peaceful political protest. The NFL Players Association affirmed it will support and assist Kaepernick in the arbitration process. Media reports note Kaepernick seeks not only redress but could trigger premature termination of the CBA if “clear and convincing evidence” of collusion is found under specific CBA articles; even a single-player collusion finding could have wide consequences. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has denied any blackballing, while some executives express concern teams may avoid the media attention surrounding Kaepernick. Kaepernick maintains he wants to return to playing and is prepared to prove his football value.

Saudi Arabia has launched an ambitious economic overhaul, driven largely by a dramatic fall in oil prices since 2014. Deputy Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) unveiled Vision 2030 and related measures to reduce the kingdom’s dependence on oil, diversify revenue, create jobs, and transform state institutions. Officials say low oil prices—down from above $110 a barrel in 2014 to under $45—have forced urgency on reforms that were already considered necessary for long-term sustainability.

Central to the plan is partial privatization of state oil giant Saudi Aramco, with under 5 percent of shares to be floated. MBS values Aramco at $2–2.5 trillion and expects proceeds and transfers of assets to swell the Public Investment Fund (PIF) from about 600 billion riyals ($160 billion) to as much as 7 trillion riyals ($2 trillion), potentially growing into a $2–3 trillion global investment vehicle. The move is intended to boost transparency, attract investment, and create a large sovereign wealth fund.

Vision 2030 sets ambitious targets: raising non-oil revenue from roughly 163 billion riyals to 600 billion by 2020 and 1 trillion by 2030, increasing private-sector share of the economy to 60 percent, reducing unemployment, and raising women’s workforce participation to 30 percent. Other reforms include encouraging tourism, expanding domestic defense production, reforming education to better prepare youth for a modern economy, easing foreign investment and residency with a proposed “green card,” and introducing new taxes and privatizations.

Analysts applaud diversification but warn implementation challenges and uncertain timelines. The IMF called the plan ambitious but difficult to execute, and skeptics note past reform efforts lacked detail. With a recent budget deficit of about 15 percent of GDP and reserves drawn down, Riyadh faces fiscal pressure. Leaders insist the vision is independent of oil-price recovery, insisting Saudi Arabia must be able to “live without oil” by 2020 and beyond, signaling a major strategic shift for the kingdom.

Authorities in Somerset County, New Jersey, say a Bridgewater woman used children’s drawings to smuggle the prescription opioid Suboxone to her boyfriend in the county jail. Sheriff Frank J. Provenzano announced that staff first spotted “oddities” in mail addressed to inmate Michael Gill on June 15; the corrections K-9 unit alerted to the drawings and Suboxone was found concealed within. Additional letters with children’s drawings arriving June 20 and June 28 also tested positive for suspected Suboxone after inspections and K-9 alerts. Prosecutors allege 37-year-old Casey Giles of Bridgewater attempted to send the narcotic to her 38-year-old boyfriend, Gill of Oxford. Giles was charged with third-degree possession with intent to distribute a controlled dangerous substance and was remanded to jail on $20,000 bail, cash or bond. Gill faces a third-degree charge of attempting to possess a controlled dangerous substance and was held on $10,000 bail. Provenzano declined to disclose the exact concealment method to avoid providing a blueprint for copycats, and praised jail staff for routine mail inspections aimed at keeping the facility, inmates and personnel safe. He noted state rules restrict strip searches in county jails because many detainees are pretrial.

Hillary Clinton announced her 2016 presidential campaign on April 12, 2015, framing her run as a bid to be a champion for everyday Americans. The announcement launched a YouTube channel and campaign hub detailing her platform on issues including climate change, immigration, healthcare, inequality, education and the economy, and encouraging supporters to volunteer and donate. Clinton’s public life spans roles as First Lady of Arkansas and the United States, U.S. Senator from New York, Secretary of State, lawyer, law professor, activist and volunteer. Raised in a Methodist household in suburban Illinois, she attended Wellesley College and Yale Law School, worked for the Children’s Defense Fund, served on the congressional panel probing Nixon, and co-founded Arkansas Advocates for Children and Families. As First Lady she led health care reform efforts and gave a defining speech at the 1995 UN Fourth World Conference on Women declaring “human rights are women’s rights,” sparking global attention to women’s equality. In the Senate she partnered across the aisle on post‑9/11 work and backed initiatives for rural communities, tech partnerships, and local colleges and businesses. As Secretary of State she championed human rights, internet freedom, and opportunities for women, girls, LGBT people and youth worldwide. The campaign launch marked the start of what appeared to be a relatively uncontested Democratic primary, and potentially the first successful major‑party female presidential nomination, adding a new chapter to Clinton’s long, polarizing public career.

Sen. Orrin Hatch, R‑Utah, told reporters during a lunch break in the Senate Judiciary Committee’s hearing for Christine Blasey Ford that Ford was “an attractive, good witness” and “pleasing,” while saying it was “too early to say” definitively whether he found her credible. Hatch added, “I don’t think she’s uncredible.” His choice of the word “attractive” drew attention because all Republican committee members are men and the panel has a female outside counsel questioning Ford. Hatch’s spokesman, Matt Whitlock, later tweeted that Hatch uses “attractive” to describe personalities rather than physical appearance and has used the term for both men and women in the past to mean compelling personalities. Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a pivotal swing vote on Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation, said she found Ford credible “thus far.” The committee is set to hear Kavanaugh later and vote on his nomination the following day.

Scientists probing the smallest scales of existence confront a realm where intuition and established laws break down. Historically, notions of fundamental building blocks have shrunk from grains of sand to atoms, to protons/neutrons and then quarks; today quarks and electrons behave experimentally as point-like, raising problematic infinities in physics. Superstring theory offers one solution by replacing points with tiny loops of string, removing true singular positions, while another proposal treats space-time itself as discrete “grains,” preventing arbitrarily close approaches. Black hole singularities are another candidate for the tiniest entities: classical general relativity predicts infinite density at a singularity, but most physicists expect this infinity signals the clash of general relativity with quantum mechanics and anticipate quantum gravity will reveal finite, ultra-small cores—perhaps far smaller than quarks and comparable to superstrings. Many such proposals converge on the Planck length (about 1.6 x 10^-35 meters) as the scale where quantum-gravitational effects dominate and conventional measurement and determinism fail. At that scale, the universe may reveal extra dimensions, microscopic black holes, or other exotic phenomena, forcing a revision of our deepest notions of space and time.

Fairfax County and Loudoun County authorities investigated the death of a 17-year-old girl found dead in Sterling, Virginia, after she and friends left midnight Ramadan prayers at the All Dulles Area Muslim Society (ADAMS) mosque. Officials identified the victim as Nabra Hassanen of Reston and charged 22-year-old Darwin Martinez Torres of Sterling with murder. Law enforcement has repeatedly stated the case is not being investigated as a hate crime at this time, describing it instead as appearing to be a road‑rage or assault incident, though authorities said they would pursue any bias motivation if evidence emerges.

According to police accounts and mosque officials, Hassanen and a group of four or five teenagers walked from the ADAMS Center toward a nearby IHOP in the early hours of Sunday. A motorist in a red car confronted the group; the driver allegedly got out and assaulted one of the teens. Most of the group ran back to the mosque, reporting that one girl had been left behind. ADAMS personnel immediately alerted both Loudoun and Fairfax law enforcement, who launched an extensive search. Later that afternoon, remains believed to be Hassanen’s were recovered from a pond in the 21500 block of Ridgetop Circle. During the search, officers noticed a car driving suspiciously and arrested Torres; police said they collected several pieces of evidence, including a metal bat reportedly found nearby, and the chief medical examiner would confirm identification and cause of death.

The killing rattled the local Muslim community, particularly because it occurred during Ramadan’s final nights when congregants often attend late prayers and then eat pre-dawn meals together. ADAMS, Northern Virginia’s largest mosque with multiple chapters, said it was “devastated and heartbroken” and provided on-site counselors. Community leaders and public officials voiced condolences: Rep. Barbara Comstock, Virginia’s lieutenant governor Ralph Northam, and Attorney General Mark Herring all condemned the violence and urged support for Hassanen’s family and the ADAMS community. A GoFundMe campaign for the family quickly exceeded its initial goal, reflecting wide support.

The possibility of a bias motive drew national attention because of recent anti-Muslim incidents and an increase in anti-Muslim hate groups reported by the Southern Poverty Law Center. The SPLC’s 2016 census documented a sharp rise in anti-Muslim groups, and Pew analysis of FBI statistics found anti-Muslim violence remains at post‑9/11 levels. Some family members and neighbors expressed concern that Hassanen’s clothing and Muslim identity may have played a role; her mother said investigators told her Nabra had been struck with a metal bat after tripping over an abaya. Police, however, emphasized their current assessment does not indicate she was targeted because of race or religion, while promising to follow all investigative leads as the case develops. A vigil was planned in the Reston area, and the community continues to grieve and seek answers.
