President-elect Donald Trump tapped former Texas governor Rick Perry to lead the Department of Energy (DOE), a choice that surprised many given Perry’s 2011 debate gaffe in which he famously forgot the department’s name and his earlier pledge to eliminate it. Conservatives favored Perry for his managerial record and willingness to challenge DOE’s existing programs; the Heritage Foundation had urged dramatic cuts to DOE’s research, loan, efficiency and renewable programs. Perry’s selection follows tensions during the transition, including a Trump team questionnaire asking DOE to identify employees who worked on Obama-era climate initiatives—a request critics called a “witch hunt.”

Perry, Texas’s longest-serving governor, presided over an oil-friendly, pro-business environment and has long criticized climate science and federal environmental regulations. He served on the board of Energy Transfer Partners, developer of the Dakota Access Pipeline, and received compensation from the company, raising potential conflict-of-interest concerns that would likely require divestment or resignation upon confirmation. Environmental groups decried the pick as an affront to climate policy; Democrats and some critics labeled him unqualified for a science-focused agency that oversees the nation’s nuclear arsenal and national laboratories.

DOE’s budget and portfolio span nuclear weapons maintenance and cleanup (about two-thirds of its spending), basic science, energy research, appliance efficiency standards and loan guarantees for renewable projects. Perry’s track record is mixed: under his governorship Texas saw a dramatic expansion of wind power, yet he opposed federal renewable tax credits and called climate science unsettled. Observers expect Perry to shift DOE emphasis toward fossil fuels and energy independence, potentially slowing appliance efficiency rules and de-emphasizing renewable research. His management skills and deal-making were praised by some former energy officials, but many warned his climate skepticism and industry ties could reshape DOE away from Obama-era priorities if he is confirmed.

An honest act by a teenager turned into a memorable reward. Seventeen-year-old Tristin Budzyn-Baker found actor Chris Hemsworth’s wallet after the star accidentally left it on a restaurant table while dining with his family in a rough area of Los Angeles. Initially unsure whose it was, Budzyn-Baker realized it belonged to the actor who plays Thor and contacted Hemsworth’s management to return it. He even slipped in a request for tickets to The Ellen DeGeneres Show, where Hemsworth was scheduled to appear. The honesty paid off: Tristin and his mother attended the show, and Hemsworth recounted the story onstage. To the teen’s surprise, the wallet still contained cash. Hemsworth handed the money back and added a little extra. He also wrote a special letter of recommendation to support Budzyn-Baker’s bid for the Eagle Scout rank. Host Ellen DeGeneres further rewarded the boy scout by giving him an additional US$10,000, courtesy of Shutterfly. The incident was highlighted as proof that honesty is rewarding, and Tristin’s good deed earned him public recognition, financial gifts, and valuable support for his scouting ambitions. The story was shared widely as an uplifting example of integrity being noticed and appreciated.

A Baton Rouge man, 25-year-old Adonis Forbes, was arrested after a handgun he was handling accidentally discharged Saturday night, killing a 13-year-old boy who was babysitting his children. Forbes and his wife had briefly returned home around 9 p.m. to check on the kids; while Forbes inspected and attempted to fix a malfunctioning handgun at their Tennessee Street residence, the weapon fired and struck Murrain Hawkins in the abdomen. Police found Hawkins down and Forbes administering aid; the teen was rushed to a hospital and pronounced dead. Forbes was questioned, booked on a negligent homicide charge, and released after posting $10,000 bond. It was unclear whether Forbes and Hawkins were related.

Fourteen-year-old Caitlin Sanchez, who became the voice of Dora the Explorer in 2007, sued Nickelodeon, MTV Networks and Viacom claiming a confusing contract left her underpaid despite helping build the show's lucrative brand. Her 41-page Manhattan complaint alleges she was promised $5,115 per episode plus residuals and merchandising cuts but received only minimal merchandising payouts, no residuals, and was made to do more than 100 promotional appearances for little or no pay. Sanchez and her parents say they were rushed into signing the contract and often lost money on travel despite a reported $40 per diem. Nickelodeon responded that Sanchez was properly compensated, that travel and lodging were covered, and that the $40 was only for incidentals. The network also said Sanchez was replaced because her voice changed with puberty, as had occurred with Dora’s original actress. Lawyers for Sanchez maintain the suit seeks unpaid earnings, not to force her continued role.

Steven Beare, a Littleton Police Department officer and Colorado National Guardsman, is missing after attempting a solo climb of Mount Elbrus in Russia. His wife, Olivia, says he arrived in country mid-June and last spoke to her on June 12; he was due back to a checkpoint on June 16 but never reported in. Beare, an experienced alpinist who has summited Mount Kilimanjaro and many Colorado 14ers, was pursuing the Seven Summits. He is also an Army veteran, has been deployed multiple times, and is father to a 20-month-old son while Olivia is pregnant.

A severe, fast-moving storm and subsequent blizzard are believed to have contributed to his disappearance; witnesses reportedly saw him ascend but lost sight in whiteout conditions. Russian high-mountain search-and-rescue teams initially began retracing his route but suspended operations because of the weather. Olivia has been coordinating search efforts from Colorado, hiring private search crews and arranging helicopter searches that have been limited by visibility and visa approvals. The family and colleagues are raising funds through the Colorado Police Officers Foundation to cover private rescue costs, including expensive helicopter time. Colorado Rep. Mike Coffman has contacted the Russian ambassador seeking assistance. The family remains hopeful but fears Beare may be injured or succumb to exposure as rescuers race against time and worsening conditions.

Gilbert P. Hyatt, a Las Vegas inventor now in his mid-70s, has spent decades fighting the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office for decisions on his long-pending applications. Hyatt filed a lawsuit in January seeking court-ordered action on what may be the oldest pending U.S. patent applications—one concerning electronic signals to control machinery that he says has been waiting 43 years, and another on liquid-crystal displays pending for 35 years. The average patent process is about 28 months. Hyatt believes some delays stem from the PTO’s reluctance to risk embarrassment after prior disputes in which his filings drew scrutiny; he has taken the agency to court more than ten times and even prevailed at the Supreme Court in 2012 on evidentiary issues.

Hyatt is no marginal inventor: his 1990 patent on a single-chip integrated circuit architecture provoked industry controversy, generated licensing deals—most notably with Philips that likely earned him over $150 million—and exposed clashes with firms like Texas Instruments. He has also fought California successfully over tax claims, winning a large award now under appeal. The PTO won’t disclose details of his old filings due to confidentiality rules for pre-1995 applications.

Commentators note Hyatt’s technical contributions but argue broader innovation often depends on commercial development, not just ideas. The article connects Hyatt’s plight to wider concerns about patent system reforms that may favor large tech firms over small inventors, urging protections—such as expanded accelerated examination or fee waivers—for independent creators to preserve American innovation.

Neil Edwin Prescott, 28, of Crofton was taken into custody after allegedly threatening to "blow everybody up" at his former workplace and calling himself a "joker," a possible reference to the Aurora, Colo., movie theater massacre. Police recovered about two dozen firearms, accessories and thousands of rounds at his apartment. Prescott was hospitalized for an emergency psychiatric evaluation; no charges are expected while he is treated. Authorities say cooperation among agencies likely prevented a violent episode. Investigations continue.

A devastating fire on the 2500 block of Lexington Street in Harrisburg left a 3- or 4-year-old girl dead and two other children in critical condition at the Lehigh Valley Burn Center, and gutted a row home. Neighbors recalled harrowing scenes of children on the roof, one jumping, another trapped until rescued by firefighters, while smoke and charred debris filled the block. The community and fire crews remained deeply shaken days later: a black curtain draped over Mt. Pleasant Station 8 signaled mourning, and firefighters sat quietly, exhausted from a traumatic shift. As crews rushed to the blaze, Harrisburg Fire Lt. Dennis “Denny” DeVoe was killed when his vehicle was struck at 14th and Walnut streets by a stolen car driven by 19-year-old Khanyae Kendall. Kendall faces multiple charges, including aggravated assault by vehicle while DUI, receiving stolen property, and traffic violations; she is jailed on $200,000 bail and due for a preliminary hearing. Chief Brian Enterline expressed the department’s grief and resolve, praising DeVoe’s leadership and dedication; DeVoe leaves a wife and four children. The city had limited immediate comment on the children’s conditions or identities. GoFundMe campaigns have been created to support both the victims’ family and DeVoe’s family. The article also included general CPSC information urging reports of dangerous consumer products and offering resources for recalls and safety concerns.

An internal News of the World dossier from 2007, based on about 300 emails, reportedly contained “smoking gun” evidence that phone hacking extended beyond a single rogue reporter and indicated four-figure payments to police totaling roughly £120,000. Those emails, held by law firm Harbottle & Lewis, were not passed to the Metropolitan Police until June 2011, prompting accusations of a cover-up by News International executives. The revelations have widened investigations: at least nine journalists and three police officers face potential charges, and senior figures including former editor Andy Coulson and News International chief Rebekah Brooks may be questioned. Scotland Yard assistant commissioner John Yates apologized for earlier handling of the scandal and defended his actions amid calls to resign. The affair threatens Murdoch family executives, may trigger U.S. legal exposure under anti-bribery laws, and has jeopardized News Corp’s BSkyB takeover bid.

The News of the World phone-hacking scandal has provoked intense public outrage and raised questions about criminal liability reaching senior figures at News International. The Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000—used to convict reporter Clive Goodman and investigator Glenn Mulcaire—contains Section 79, which can attach corporate offences to directors or officers if crimes were committed with their consent, connivance, or “attributable to any neglect.” Commentators argue this provision could ensnare executives such as former editor and current News International CEO Rebekah Brooks, who hired a private investigator implicated in hacking the voicemail of murdered teenager Milly Dowler and presided over stories based on illegally obtained messages. Legal counsel caution, however, that applying the “neglect” clause to senior proprietors like Rupert or James Murdoch would be difficult without direct evidence; U.K. prosecutors typically pursue cases they believe can meet the jury’s standard of proof. The scandal has tarnished Murdoch’s influence, prompted calls for inquiries and resignations, jeopardized News Corp.’s bid for full control of BSkyB, and highlighted broader concerns about media ethics, police corruption, and political ties that may have enabled systemic wrongdoing.

Jennifer “Jen” Houle, a 22-year-old Carlson School of Management senior and Pi Beta Phi sorority member at the University of Minnesota, has been missing since the early hours of Friday, March 27. Houle was last seen between 1 and 2 a.m. at Blarney Pub & Grill in the Dinkytown neighborhood of Minneapolis after a night of bar hopping with a friend. The two became separated at the bar; they had earlier encountered Houle’s ex-boyfriend, an interaction friends say stirred emotions. Houle’s purse was found at about 3 a.m. on the 1100 block of 4th Street SE, roughly three blocks from the bar. She is described as 5'5", about 140 pounds, with long blonde hair and blue eyes; she was last seen wearing a green blouse, black leather jacket, black leggings and black boots.

Minneapolis police are investigating and have interviewed the ex-boyfriend and other patrons. The university is cooperating with law enforcement and has offered counseling and support to students. Houle’s sorority sisters have distributed missing-person posters and posted appeals online. More than 200 friends, family and community members held a prayer vigil at her former high school in Stillwater. Authorities urge anyone with information to call 911 or the Minneapolis tipline. The community remains hopeful she will be found safe.

The CNN-sponsored GOP national-security debate highlighted strengths and weaknesses across the Republican field while underscoring divisions on immigration, civil liberties, and America’s role abroad. Newt Gingrich emerged as the night’s standout: his command of debate and greater airtime helped him reinforce front-runner momentum. He also broke with hardline GOP orthodoxy by opposing mass deportation and urging humane legalization measures for some long-resident undocumented immigrants — a stance framed around family values that could help general-election appeal but risks alienating the conservative primary base and inviting attacks as “amnesty.”

Jon Huntsman also fared well, leveraging his foreign-affairs résumé to present measured, expertise-driven positions on Afghanistan, Pakistan and China. His poise and the boost from supportive super PAC spending make New Hampshire a pivotal moment; if his numbers don’t improve soon he may fade. Mitt Romney had a steady, if unspectacular, night: avoiding ganging-up attacks and making competent points on Iran and China, but failing to produce a breakout moment that would distinguish him.

Losers included Herman Cain, who struggled on national-security specifics and seemed increasingly adrift from the debate’s substantive demands. Ron Paul’s anti-interventionist, civil-liberties positions energized his base but underscored his distance from mainstream GOP foreign-policy consensus, limiting broader appeal. Rick Perry, Michele Bachmann and Rick Santorum had flashes—Bachmann’s intelligence-committee credentials helped—but none produced the decisive moment needed to climb the standings.

The debate showcased substantive clashes — notably Gingrich’s immigration gambit, Romney’s steady center-right posture, and competing visions on troop levels and civil liberties — leaving voters clearer on who can credibly handle foreign policy and who may not be viable as the campaign progresses.

The Alabama special Senate primary crystallized a central question: do Donald Trump’s endorsement and Mitch McConnell’s money still carry weight in deeply Republican Alabama? Tuesday’s vote was broadly expected to head to a Sept. 26 runoff because no candidate was likely to clear the 50 percent threshold. Polls and early returns showed former Alabama Chief Justice Roy Moore leading comfortably in the GOP field (about 43.8% with most counties reported), while appointed Sen. Luther Strange—backed by Trump and a McConnell-aligned super PAC—was projected to finish second (around 31.7%) and advance to the runoff. Rep. Mo Brooks trailed and was eliminated.

Strange entered the contest with substantial establishment advantages: the president’s surprise endorsement, a Trump robocall urging support, millions in outside spending pledged by a McConnell-blessed PAC, NRA backing and the trappings of incumbency. Yet his path has been hampered by persistent questions over how he was appointed by disgraced former Gov. Robert Bentley and by grassroots anti-establishment sentiment aimed at figures like McConnell. That baggage kept Strange from being a runaway favorite and made his expected second-place finish a test of whether Trump and the GOP establishment can still shape outcomes in Alabama. If Strange had failed to reach the runoff, it would have been a notable rebuke to both.

Moore, despite prior removals from the state bench for defying federal rulings, sustained a fervent base and led multiple polls in the low- to mid-30s. His campaign expected low turnout to favor him and suggested he could top 35 percent, though still short of an outright win. Moore’s team downplayed the impact of Trump’s endorsement on voter choices.

On the Democratic side, Doug Jones—endorsed by Joe Biden and known for prosecuting civil-rights-era crimes—was competing with a leading but enigmatic candidate named Robert Kennedy Jr. Early polling showed Kennedy with a strong lead in the crowded Democratic primary, but Jones was viewed as the establishment favorite who might capitalize on a fractured GOP to mount a long-shot general election bid in a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in decades.

“Snow White and the Huntsman” reimagines the classic tale as a dark, violent epic rather than a sanitized Disney fable. Director Rupert Sanders and writers Evan Daugherty, John Lee Hancock and Hossein Amini lean into the Grimm roots: bleak medieval landscapes, real menace, and magic born of rage. Charlize Theron’s Ravenna dominates the film—glamorous, cruel, and haunted by a grudging response to a patriarchal world—stealing youth to preserve her beauty. Her complexity invites a degree of sympathy even as she remains terrifying. Kristen Stewart’s Snow White is recast as a fledgling warrior-princess, a modest, earnest heroine caught between two protectors: Sam Claflin’s tidy, noble William and Chris Hemsworth’s rough, magnetic Huntsman, who brings grounded humanity when the film’s operatic opening ebbs. The movie’s dwarfs—played by Ian McShane, Bob Hoskins, Ray Winstone and others, digitally shrunken—are gritty, somber laborers rather than comic relief. Striking production design, Greig Fraser’s earth-toned cinematography and moments of fresh enchantment—a dark-forest slog, a fairy garden—sustain the film’s mythic feel. Though sometimes overwrought musically and melodramatic, the picture succeeds in restoring fairy-tale dread while presenting a modern, battle-ready Snow White.

About 350 U.S. newspapers coordinated on Thursday, Aug. 16, to publish editorials defending press freedom and denouncing President Donald Trump’s repeated attacks labeling the media “the enemy of the people.” The campaign, organized by Boston Globe deputy editorial page editor Marjorie Pritchard, aimed to create a unified response to rhetoric many fear could incite threats or violence against journalists. Major participants included the Boston Globe, The New York Times, Houston Chronicle, Minneapolis Star Tribune, Miami Herald and Denver Post, while some outlets like NOLA.com | The Times-Picayune declined, citing independence.

The Globe’s editorial, headlined “Journalists are NOT the enemy,” emphasized that lies undermine self-government and warned that calling the press an enemy is “as un-American as it is dangerous.” The New York Times’ piece, “A Free Press Needs You,” traced the history of a free press, argued that labeling inconvenient truths as “fake news” is perilous to democracy, and urged readers to subscribe to local papers and engage critically.

Responses to the coordinated action were mixed. Supporters argued a broad, synchronized stand highlighted the stakes for democracy. Critics, including Politico’s Jack Shafer and commentators at outlets like Investor’s Business Daily, warned the effort would reinforce perceptions of a monolithic, partisan press. Shafer predicted the move would feed Trump’s narrative of a national media “cabal” aligned against him, providing fresh fodder for his attacks. Critics also noted many participating papers had opposed Trump in 2016, suggesting the initiative might preach to the choir and fail to persuade skeptics. Some highlighted ironic moments—such as a Globe online ad asking readers to subscribe embedded within its editorial—and questioned whether coordinated editorials would shift public opinion among Trump supporters who are less likely to read newspapers.

The Senate passed a resolution affirming that the press is not the enemy of the people. Trump, meanwhile, continued to taunt participating papers on Twitter and pointed to past sales of the Globe to criticize its motives. The debate underscored tensions over media credibility, partisanship, and the role of coordinated advocacy in defending press freedom.

A newborn baby was found abandoned in Marlborough House Community Park, Stechford, Birmingham, after a German Shepherd named Jade led her owner, 68-year-old Roger Wilday, to bushes where the infant lay wrapped in a towel inside a plastic carrier bag. Roger, out walking his dog on Thursday afternoon, heard a cry, discovered the baby and called 999. He briefly picked the child up at police instruction before emergency services arrived; the baby was taken to Heartlands Hospital. Staff have nicknamed her “Baby Jade” in honour of the rescue dog. Medics say the six-pound infant is “alert, happy and contented” and is being monitored around the clock by paediatricians. West Midlands Police and hospital staff are focusing on finding the mother and reuniting her with the child, urging anyone with information—especially anyone who saw someone carrying a bag from The Entertainer toy shop—to contact them on 101. Forensics are processing the towel and bag, and DNA samples have been taken to help identify the parents. Chief Inspector Ian Green warned the baby could have suffered fatal exposure if not found when she was, and praised the prompt discovery.

The NRA announced that firearms and other weapons would be banned from the arena while Vice President Mike Pence speaks at its annual meeting in Dallas, citing Secret Service security rules that bar weapons where protectees visit. The prohibition — which covers firearms, accessories, knives, ammunition, drones, gun parts, magazines and more — applies before and during Pence’s appearance; elsewhere in the convention center and host hotel lawfully carried weapons are generally permitted in accordance with law. The restriction echoes similar measures used when President Trump spoke to the NRA last year.

Survivors and family members from the Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School shooting quickly condemned the move as hypocritical. Parkland activists including Matt Deitsch, Cameron Kasky and David Hogg questioned why a “gun-free” perimeter is required to keep VIPs safe but not routinely provided to protect schoolchildren. Fred Guttenberg, whose daughter Jaime was killed in the attack, called the situation “enlightening,” arguing the exception exposes a priority to protect those who support the gun industry rather than children.

The policy also drew criticism from some NRA supporters who said disarming attendees for a leadership speech undermines the “good guy with a gun” argument. Others defended the restriction as necessary given Secret Service responsibilities. The NRA did not respond to requests for comment. Pence’s appearance and President Trump’s planned participation at the convention come amid ongoing national debate over gun-policy proposals following the Parkland shooting.

A large retrospective analysis of 2.7 million adverse-event reports found a striking association between dopamine receptor agonist drugs—commonly used for Parkinson’s disease, restless leg syndrome and other conditions—and severe impulse-control disorders such as pathological gambling, hypersexuality and compulsive shopping. Researchers identified 1,580 reports of such behaviors from the U.S. and 21 other countries between 2003 and 2012; 710 of those involved dopamine agonists, producing a disproportionality signal (PRR = 277.6, P < .001) far above that for other drugs. The link was strongest for pramipexole (410 cases; PRR = 455.9) and ropinirole (188 cases; PRR = 152.5), agents with high affinity for the dopamine D3 receptor; a smaller signal was seen for aripiprazole, a D3 partial agonist. Authors urge clinicians to use these medications with caution, monitor patients and caregivers for emerging impulse-control problems, and call for stronger warnings—potentially boxed labels—on prescribing information. Commentators note such behaviors can be subtle or unreported during routine visits yet have devastating financial and social consequences; symptoms often remit after stopping the drug. The findings reinforce earlier reports and suggest D3 receptor activity may underlie these behavior changes, guiding both clinical vigilance and future research.

The North Carolina State Archives and the State Library of North Carolina, Archive-It partners since September 2005, operate under the state Office of Archives and History. Their core mission is to collect, preserve, and make accessible North Carolina’s documentary and material heritage so current and future residents can better understand the state’s past. By safeguarding records and artifacts, the office supports public education and helps protect citizens’ democratic rights through maintaining evidence of previous generations. The organization’s archived web presence is hosted at http://webarchives.ncdcr.gov, reflecting efforts to preserve digital as well as physical resources. In related services, the office highlights features such as optional tweet location information for social media, noting users can add, control, or delete location data associated with tweets when using web or third-party applications, with guidance available for managing tweet location history.

Photographer and biologist Paul Nicklen and members of Sea Legacy filmed an emaciated polar bear on Somerset Island in the Canadian Arctic in late summer, releasing footage in December that quickly went viral. The bear appeared near death: its coat patchy, muscles wasted, one hind leg dragging, scavenging a seasonal Inuit trash bin and chewing remnants like an old snowmobile seat. Nicklen, who has decades of experience with Arctic bears, said the scene “haunts” him; he and his team filmed from roughly 400 feet away and were moved to tears. He has said he did not intervene—feeding wild polar bears is illegal in Canada, he was not equipped to help, and any intervention could have prolonged suffering.

Nicklen shared the footage to show what starvation looks like and to highlight broader concerns about climate change’s impacts on polar bears. Scientists warn that diminishing summer sea ice reduces access to seals, the bears’ primary prey, lengthening fasting periods and increasing starvation risk. Reports from organizations like the World Wildlife Fund and the National Snow and Ice Data Center document declining sea ice and related polar bear stress; some population forecasts predict substantial declines in coming decades. Critics and some viewers cautioned against drawing definitive conclusions from a single animal’s condition, noting uncertainties about age, disease, or injury. Experts, however, say increasing numbers of thin bears have been observed as Arctic ice diminishes. The footage reignited debate over polar bears as emblematic victims of warming Arctic ecosystems and the challenges of translating heartbreaking images into policy action.

Hilary Duff and Canadian hockey player Mike Comrie have married in an intimate Santa Barbara ceremony. The 22-year-old actress and 29-year-old NHL player said their vows Saturday, after Comrie proposed in Hawaii in February. Duff kept the wedding small and personal; her sister Haylie served as maid of honor and their mother escorted her down the aisle. The couple celebrated with close family and friends and thanked supporters for warm wishes.

Rap Genius co-founder Mahbod Moghadam was forced out of the company and resigned from its board after posting insensitive annotations on Elliot Rodger’s 141-page manifesto following the Santa Barbara killings. Moghadam praised the writing and made a misogynistic remark about Rodger’s sister; screenshots published by Valleywag prompted swift backlash. CEO Tom Lehman said Moghadam’s comments “went beyond” attempts to explain the text into “gleeful insensitivity and misogyny,” and that such behavior contradicted Rap Genius’s mission. Sources and investor Ben Horowitz indicated the departure was pressured by company leadership and backers, with Horowitz later clarifying the decision was made by Lehman and co-founder Ilan Zechory. Moghadam apologized on Twitter, calling for reflection and promising to become a better person. The incident added to a pattern of controversial conduct by Moghadam—including prior abusive tweets and a role in a Google SEO controversy—that investors and Rap Genius appear intent to distance themselves from as they try to protect the company’s reputation.

The federal government closed Washington, D.C., area offices Wednesday as a major winter storm threatened the region; non-emergency employees were excused. Forecasts predicted up to 10 inches in the city and more in northern and western suburbs, prompting massive flight cancellations—especially at Dulles and Reagan—and Amtrak reductions. Virginia saw heavier impacts: Gov. Bob McDonnell declared a state of emergency, shelters opened for about 215,000 without power, the National Guard and utility crews were mobilized, and hazardous roads led to early office closures. Coastal states faced flooding and high winds, with coastal flood warnings from Massachusetts to Virginia, evacuations urged, and National Guard deployments. Meanwhile, Washington received less snow than expected, some federal events and hearings were canceled, schools closed across several states, and the storm also earlier battered the Midwest.

A previously unknown early fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen has been discovered in a filing box at the National Archives of Funen in Odense. Retired historian Esben Brage found a six-page handwritten manuscript titled "The Tallow Candle," dedicated "To Mme Bunkeflod, from her devoted HC Andersen." Experts date the work to the mid-1820s, when Andersen was a grammar school student of about 18, meaning it predates his 1830 debut. The short, roughly 700-word story describes a neglected tallow candle that seeks the tinder box’s help to ignite, touching on themes of beauty and worth found in Andersen’s later classics. Curators and Andersen scholars, including Ejnar Stig Askgaard, regard the stylistic simplicity as consistent with an early piece and accept its authenticity, calling the find "sensational." Mme Bunkeflod is believed to have been a vicar’s widow who hosted Andersen, who read to her and borrowed books. The manuscript appears to be a copy of an original now lost; Politiken published an English translation after experts scrutinized the text.

Senate Republicans publicly released a draft of the Better Care Reconciliation Act—a long-sought plan to repeal and replace key parts of the Affordable Care Act—on June 22, 2017. The bill, written largely behind closed doors by a small group of Senate leaders, immediately drew intense criticism and opposition from Democrats, health organizations, protesters and a number of Senate Republicans. Five GOP senators (Ted Cruz, Ron Johnson, Mike Lee, Rand Paul and later Dean Heller) announced they were not ready to vote for the measure, saying it retained too much of Obamacare or failed to protect patients and lower costs. Several other Republicans, including Susan Collins, withheld endorsement pending detailed review; McConnell aimed for a vote before the July 4 recess but acknowledged he faced a narrow path to 50 votes.

Key provisions in the draft include phasing down and eventually ending the ACA’s Medicaid expansion beginning in 2021 and converting broader Medicaid funding into per‑capita allotments or giving states a block-grant option—changes that would limit federal Medicaid growth and, according to analysts, likely reduce coverage and pressure states to cut benefits or eligibility. The bill would also reshape individual market subsidies: it reduces eligibility (capping aid at 350% of poverty rather than 400%), ties credits to less-generous benchmark plans (58% actuarial value vs. the ACA’s 70%), and increases cost sharing expectations, leaving lower-income and sicker consumers with higher out-of-pocket burdens. It repeals the individual and employer mandates for coverage (setting penalties to $0) and imposes a six-month waiting period for people with coverage gaps. The draft eliminates numerous ACA-related taxes, repeals several fees and rescinds certain consumer protections, and for at least one year would bar federal Medicaid funding to certain Planned Parenthood providers.

Release of the draft prompted large protests outside McConnell’s office—ADAPT activists, including wheelchair users, were forcibly removed—and widespread condemnation from Democratic leaders (Chuck Schumer called it “heartless”), medical groups (American Public Health Association, American Psychiatric Association, ACOG) and advocacy organizations urging rejection. The Congressional Budget Office score was expected the following week and its findings were widely anticipated to influence wavering senators. With Democrats united in opposition and Republicans able to lose only two votes, Senate GOP leaders faced urgent negotiations to win enough support while navigating public backlash over secrecy and potential coverage losses.

Håvard Melvaer, a 40-year-old captain of the Norwegian multipurpose supply ship Edda Fjord, described finding the tiny 19-foot SeaCraft linked to missing Florida teens Austin Stephanos and Perry Cohen as an extraordinary stroke of luck. Melvaer was on a voyage from Port Fourchon, Louisiana, to Haugesund, Norway, when, a week into the trip on March 18, his wife urged him outside for fresh air. Stepping out, he immediately saw the small boat bobbing 30 to 40 feet off the ship’s port side; none of the 16-person crew had noticed it, and the bridge lookout was scanning the starboard side at the time. Melvaer emphasized that the sighting involved no special skill, just being in the right place at the right moment, and expressed amazement at how unlikely the chance was, saying the vessel almost seemed to want to be found.

The SeaCraft matches the boat that carried 14-year-olds Austin and Perry from Jupiter Inlet last July and was initially spotted by U.S. Coast Guard teams two days after their disappearance near Daytona Beach; a data marker buoy had been attached but later failed and the boat went missing again. After recovering the craft to remove it from the shipping lane, Melvaer noted the boat was intact with a serial number on its engine and promptly alerted the Coast Guard. The vessel is now packed in a shipping container and expected to arrive at Port Everglades in mid-May; some contents already returned to the families include Austin’s iPhone, two fishing rods and two small tackle boxes. Melvaer, a longtime boater and parent, said he and his crew carefully protected the boat and its contents while aboard and hope the discovery may bring clues or some peace to the grieving families, though he declined to discuss investigative details out of respect for ongoing inquiries.

Former Florida Republican Party chairman Jim Greer, in a 630-page deposition released this week, accused party leaders of internal scheming, financial wrongdoing and discussions about suppressing black votes. Testifying in a lawsuit seeking $130,000 promised in a severance agreement, Greer said legislative leaders and other officials orchestrated a Florida Department of Law Enforcement and grand jury probe to avoid paying him. He described a party in turmoil after disagreements with Gov. Charlie Crist and the rise of the Tea Party, calling some colleagues “whack-a-do, right-wing crazies.” Greer said he wanted fiscal transparency after questions about legislators’ use of party credit cards but was blocked by leaders who warned him not to interfere. Much of the deposition focuses on Greer’s secret business, Victory Strategies LLC, which received nearly $200,000 from the party and prompted criminal charges. Successor John Thrasher called Greer’s allegations absurd and said Greer had to go after secretly forming the company. Greer says the charges and unpaid severance ruined his life, leaving his family destitute and seeking an apology.

President Donald Trump said the intense public scrutiny around sexual misconduct allegations has created “a very scary time for young men in America,” arguing that men can now be treated as “guilty until proven innocent.” Speaking to reporters on the South Lawn before a flight, Trump framed the controversy enveloping Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh as emblematic of a broader political climate that makes it difficult to rebut accusations. He said someone “perfect” their entire life can be accused of wrongdoing and face severe consequences regardless of guilt, and contrasted that by calling it “a great time for women” when asked if he had a message for young women.

Trump’s remarks came amid highly publicized allegations against Kavanaugh: Christine Blasey Ford testified that Kavanaugh assaulted her as a teenager; Deborah Ramirez alleged Kavanaugh exposed himself to her in college; and Julie Swetnick accused she was gang-raped at a party Kavanaugh attended. Kavanaugh vehemently denies all allegations. The White House and Senate Republicans pressed for a swift confirmation, while several GOP senators withheld support pending an FBI inquiry; the White House agreed to expand that probe after criticism it had been too narrow.

The president invoked his own history with accusations, noting that during the 2016 campaign 18 women made allegations against him—claims he denies and has characterized accusers as liars; he also faces a defamation suit from one accuser. Trump warned Democrats that blocking Kavanaugh could energize conservatives and turn the nominee into a martyr ahead of midterms. His comments and stance have intensified debate over the #MeToo movement, due process, and how allegations should be investigated and adjudicated in the political arena.

In La Porte County, Indiana, former postal carrier Kristopher Block is facing criminal charges after investigators say he failed to deliver roughly 17,000 pieces of mail over several months and arranged for much of it to be destroyed. Court records and reporting show that between mid-2016 and early 2017 large quantities of undelivered mail tied to Block’s assigned routes went missing. In February 2017, a deputy in Berrien County, Michigan, discovered about 11,000 pieces of frozen mail in tubs dumped in a ravine; another roughly 6,000 pieces were later recovered from Block’s home after postal investigators visited. Block allegedly admitted to paying a friend $50 per bundle to burn mail he could not finish delivering and said he sometimes handed bundles to his roommate to destroy during his lunch break. He resigned from the Postal Service on Feb. 7, 2017.

La Porte residents reported frequent missed deliveries, missed bills and even missing workers’ compensation checks, prompting some to obtain P.O. boxes. Officials from the U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General stressed that the vast majority of postal employees are honest and that alleged criminal behavior is not tolerated; they urged anyone with information about postal crimes to contact the OIG hotline. Block, 39–40, has been charged in LaPorte Circuit Court with felony official misconduct and misdemeanor theft, and an arrest warrant has been issued though records indicate he had not yet been taken into custody. Authorities have not publicly located or charged the alleged accomplice. Postal and local officials continue to review route impacts and encourage reports of mail theft or fraud.

A German passenger who waited four years for compensation after a Thomas Cook Airlines flight from Vienna to the Caribbean departed 22 hours late has secured a dramatic legal victory that nearly led to an aircraft being impounded. Under EU rules, travelers delayed, denied boarding, or on canceled flights are entitled to fixed compensation based on distance and delay length; this passenger was owed about $680. After the airline failed to deliver the payout, she hired claims firm FlightRight, which took the case to an Austrian court. The court issued a payment order and an official notified Salzburg Airport that he had authority to ground a Thomas Cook jet—an asset worth tens of millions—until the sum was paid. To avoid enforcement, Condor, Thomas Cook’s sister airline, promptly paid the owed amount once notified. Condor spokesman Johannes Winter said the carrier first learned of the claim from the airport and regretted the delay. FlightRight’s legal chief, Jonas Swarzenski, suggested the omission may have been an administrative error but noted airlines sometimes stall to discourage claims; only about 15 percent of EU-entitled travelers actually pursue compensation. The EU regulations apply to flights within the bloc and to certain transatlantic services involving EU carriers, creating stronger passenger protections than in places like the U.S. The case highlights both the potency of legal remedies available under EU law and the practical hurdles many travelers face in claiming what they are owed, underscoring how persistence—or third-party claim services—can force airlines to honor compensation rules.

Glassdoor’s 2017 Employees’ Choice Awards recognize the highest-rated CEOs across six categories in the U.S., Canada, UK, France and Germany, using a proprietary algorithm based on employee reviews from May 2, 2016 to May 1, 2017. The U.S. lists include 100 Highest Rated CEOs (large employers) and 25 Highest Rated CEOs at Small & Medium Companies. Top U.S. CEOs include Benno Dorer (Clorox) at No.1 and leaders such as Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg and Jen-Hsun Huang among the top ten; the small/medium list is led by Justyn Howard of Sprout Social. Seventeen CEOs are recognized in multiple countries. Glassdoor notes CEO approval correlates with strong company culture, senior leadership satisfaction and financial performance. Winners, interviews and methodology are available on Glassdoor.

Researchers reported in Psychological Science that power alters vocal acoustics in measurable ways and listeners use those cues to identify who’s in charge. In studies led by Sei Jin Ko, Melody Sadler and Adam Galinsky, 161 college students read a passage for a baseline recording, were randomly assigned high- or low-power roles for a subsequent negotiation task, then read the same passage again. Compared with low-power participants, high-power participants’ voices rose in pitch, became more monotone (less pitch variability), and showed greater variability in loudness—changes similar to those observed after voice coaching, as with Margaret Thatcher. A second study showed independent listeners could reliably judge which speakers had been assigned high versus low power: they associated higher pitch, louder voices, and louder variability with high-power behaviors and categorized speakers with considerable accuracy. The findings imply that beyond word choice, basic acoustic cues shape perceptions and outcomes in authority contexts. The authors have shared data and materials openly via the Open Science Framework.

Interpol has elected South Korean Kim Jong-yang as its president, defeating Russian candidate Alexander Prokopchuk at the police agency’s General Assembly in Dubai. Kim, 57, a former South Korean police chief and Interpol senior vice-president who had been acting president since Meng Hongwei’s disappearance in China, won by a reported 101 votes to 61. He will serve the remaining two years of Meng’s four-year term. The presidential role is largely ceremonial, with day-to-day operations run by Secretary-General Jürgen Stock, but it carries influence and symbolic importance.

Prokopchuk, also 57 and a Russian interior ministry veteran, was widely seen as the Kremlin’s frontrunner. Human rights groups, Western officials and prominent critics of the Kremlin warned his election risked politicizing Interpol by enabling further abuse of its Red Notice and diffusion systems to pursue dissidents and critics. A bipartisan group of US senators, the UK Foreign Office, and Secretary of State Mike Pompeo publicly opposed Prokopchuk. Lithuania and Ukraine threatened to quit Interpol if he had been elected. Russia called the opposition interference and insisted Prokopchuk would remain a vice-president and continue to strengthen Interpol’s role.

Campaigners and critics, including Bill Browder and Mikhail Khodorkovsky, welcomed Kim’s victory and urged further reforms, especially to the diffusion system. Interpol has tightened Red Notice vetting since 2016, but watchdogs note diffusions can still bypass centralized checks. The vote came amid broader tensions over Interpol’s neutrality following Meng’s detention in China and ongoing concern about member states misusing Interpol tools for political ends.

Georgia’s state senate overwhelmingly passed a resolution urging correction of a long-disputed northern boundary so the state can claim part of the Tennessee River at Nickajack—not for territory’s sake, but for water. The claim rests on an 1818 survey Georgia says misplaced the 35° north parallel about a mile south, robbing Georgia of river access established when it ceded Mississippi territory. Lawmakers, citing severe drought—up to 99 percent of the state affected last December and 80 percent still under drought recently—argue the Tennessee River could supply much-needed freshwater as climate change makes severe droughts more frequent. A similar attempt in 2008 was rebuffed by Tennessee. Georgia’s House Resolution 4 directs the attorney general to seek control of land south of the 35th parallel if no agreement is reached; if Tennessee contests any settlement, Congress would decide. The Tennessee Valley Authority has not recommended the river as a primary water source for North Georgia and says it is not currently involved. Nearby Alabama, also drought-stricken, would likely resist losing water access as well.

An AirAsia jet carrying 162 people disappeared on Sunday while en route from Surabaya, Indonesia’s second-largest city, to Singapore on a scheduled two-hour flight, prompting a multinational search and rescue response and widespread concern among relatives and officials. Flight QZ8501 departed Surabaya at 5:31 a.m. local time (2231 GMT Saturday). The last recorded communication with air traffic control came at 6:13 a.m. (2313 GMT), when the pilot requested a left turn and permission to climb to 34,000 feet (10,360 meters) to “avoid clouds.” Indonesian authorities reported there was no distress signal from the cockpit. AirAsia confirmed the Airbus A320-200 was flying its planned route; Indonesian officials said the aircraft is believed to have gone missing over the Java Sea between Tanjung Pandan on Belitung island and Pontianak on Borneo. In response, a coordinated search operation was launched involving Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia. Indonesia dispatched three aircraft to the area, while Singapore’s air force and navy joined the search using two C-130 transport planes. As the operation got underway, dozens of relatives of passengers gathered at Surabaya’s airport awaiting information. AirAsia’s CEO, Malaysian businessman Tony Fernandes, expressed gratitude for public support on Twitter and said he was traveling to Surabaya to assist and stay with affected families. The incident marked another high-profile air safety event in the region, drawing attention to the ongoing investigation into what caused the disappearance. Authorities continued efforts to locate the aircraft and determine the circumstances, while the public and families awaited news about the fate of those on board. Coverage of the story remained active as search teams worked in challenging conditions.

Doctors have warned about the risks of radical “New Year” detoxes after treating a 47-year-old woman who became critically ill from a mixture of herbal remedies and excessive fluid intake. The patient required intensive care at Milton Keynes hospital after collapsing and having a seizure; tests showed she had dangerously low blood sodium (hyponatraemia). Her regimen included multiple supplements and herbs—milk thistle, molkosan, L-theanine, glutamine, a vitamin B compound, vervain, and valerian root—and she had been drinking large amounts of water, green tea, and sage tea in the days before falling ill.

In investigating the case, clinicians found a similar report of a man with anxiety who developed seizures from hyponatraemia after consuming a herbal preparation containing valerian root, lemon balm, passionflower, hops, and chamomile. The medics, writing in the British Medical Journal Case Reports, emphasize that complementary and “all-natural” products are not harmless and can have side effects, interactions, or contribute to dangerous imbalances when combined or overused. They also note that excessive water intake—often promoted as a way to “purify” the body—can itself be harmful.

The British Dietetic Association echoed these concerns, calling detox marketing nonsense and reminding the public that the body’s organs (skin, gut, liver, kidneys) continually eliminate waste. While staying well hydrated is sensible, overconsumption of fluids can be as dangerous as dehydration. For most people, the BDA advises, maintaining health is best achieved through a balanced diet and regular physical activity rather than pills, special drinks, or extreme cleansing regimens.

Pennsylvania’s highest court has declined to hear actress Sherri Shepherd’s appeal of a lower-court ruling that found her legally responsible for a child born via surrogate before her divorce, leaving intact a decision that surrogacy contracts are binding in the state. Shepherd, the former View co-host, faces a monthly child-support obligation of $4,100 to ex-husband Lamar Sally and has not seen the child, now about one year old. Shepherd spent more than $100,000 on the surrogacy arrangement and sought to void the contract amid divorce proceedings in New Jersey; her attorney expressed surprise that the state Supreme Court declined review. The case is being hailed by surrogacy advocates as Pennsylvania’s first court ruling enforcing a surrogacy contract. Media coverage has followed the couple’s lengthy and public legal fight, with Shepherd describing to Entertainment Tonight that she is coping by staying positive despite emotional strain, and expressing hope that things will work out. Meanwhile, Sally has said he is filming a reality show about his life as a single father and has publicly defended his motives and parenting, saying he wants to shine light on the struggles of single dads. Reports also note Shepherd’s attempts to have her name removed from the child’s birth certificate and claims she has not met or exchanged gifts with the child.

Nearly 100 House Republicans have formally opposed the possible nomination of U.N. Ambassador Susan Rice to be secretary of state. Led by Rep. Jeff Duncan of South Carolina, 97 GOP members sent a letter to President Obama asserting that Rice’s public statements following the Benghazi attack, which killed Ambassador Christopher Stevens and three other Americans, “misleading[ly]” described events and thus “caused irreparable damage to her credibility both at home and around the world.” The letter alleges she is “widely viewed as having either willfully or incompetently misled the American public in the Benghazi affair.” Senators John McCain and Lindsey Graham have indicated they will try to block any Rice nomination, though other Senate Republicans have not pledged a filibuster. President Obama and Senate Intelligence Committee Chairwoman Dianne Feinstein have defended Rice, saying she relied on the best intelligence available at the time; constitutionally, the Senate must give advice and consent on such nominees. Obama is also reportedly considering Sen. John Kerry for secretary of state. Rep. Jim Clyburn has criticized attacks labeling Rice “incompetent,” calling such language coded and inappropriate given her credentials and record.

A Papillon Grand Canyon tour helicopter crashed Saturday evening near Quartermaster Canyon on the Hualapai Nation, killing three passengers and injuring four others. The Eurocopter EC130, carrying six passengers—visitors from the United Kingdom—and a pilot, went down about 5:20 p.m. local time. Hualapai Nation Police Chief Francis Bradley said first responders reached the scene within 30 minutes despite windy, dark and rugged conditions and a 20-minute hike to the wreckage. Rescuers, aided by Nellis Air Force Base aircraft, recovered the three deceased—identified as Becky Dobson, 27; Jason Hill, 32; and Stuart Hill, 30—and evacuated the four survivors to hospitals, including the University Medical Center in Las Vegas. The injured included pilot Scott Booth, 42, who suffered severe limb trauma, and passengers Ellie Milward, 29; Jonathan Udall, 32; and Jennifer Barham, 39. Witnesses reported flames and dark smoke at the site and described survivors running from the burning helicopter. The aircraft sustained heavy damage; authorities said the circumstances of the crash were unknown. The Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board will investigate. Papillon Group CEO Brenda Halvorson expressed condolences and said the company’s priority was passenger and staff care. Papillon, which advertises itself as the world’s largest aerial sightseeing company and flies roughly 600,000 passengers annually, states it follows safety rules exceeding FAA requirements. The company had a previous deadly crash in 2001 near Meadview, Arizona; NTSB investigators attributed that accident to pilot error. Helicopter-crash attorney Gary C. Robb noted Papillon has improved pilot qualifications and maintenance since 2001 but called the latest event a profound human tragedy.

Political coverage emphasizes Florida’s outsized role in the 2016 presidential contest: FiveThirtyEight’s polls-only model puts Florida as the most likely “tipping-point” state with a 19% chance of casting the decisive Electoral College vote, up from 16% two weeks earlier. Pennsylvania is the only other state above 10% (12%). Hillary Clinton’s modest national lead (about 3 points) and narrower lead in Florida (about 1 point) mean she could conceivably lose several Midwestern and light-blue states yet still win by holding Florida, thanks to its racial and ethnic diversity and large Latino and African-American electorates. Florida’s closeness to the national popular margin and its 29 electoral votes—far larger than other near-national-margin states—make it particularly pivotal; losing Florida would sharply reduce Donald Trump’s paths to victory. Separately, an AP-NORC poll finds widespread doubts about Election Day integrity, largely driven by Trump’s unfounded claims the contest could be “rigged.” Only about one-third of Republicans express strong confidence votes will be counted fairly; half of Trump supporters report little or no confidence. Concerns include voter fraud perceptions, support for voter-ID laws, and fears about hacking after reports of probes into state voter registration systems.

The first 2012 presidential debate in Denver delivered a clear short-term victory to Mitt Romney and jolted President Barack Obama’s campaign. Romney, trailing in polls, needed to appear presidential and equal to Obama—and he largely succeeded in the debate’s opening segment by projecting confidence, civility, and command. He distanced himself from the hard-line conservatism of the primaries, promised no tax cuts that add to the deficit without fully detailing how, embraced parts of Simpson-Bowles, and used memorable lines (e.g., proposing to end the PBS subsidy). Commentators said Romney’s tone—measured, informed, and centrist—made him appear a plausible alternative, rehabilitating doubts about his electability. 

Obama, by contrast, seemed subdued, academic, and occasionally tired; pundits and instant-reaction polls described him as defensive and long-winded, unable to land effective zingers or dramatize contrasts on taxes, health care, and congressional obstruction. Analysts argued he missed chances to highlight Romney’s inconsistencies and to indict Republicans for blocking bipartisan health reform. Instant polls from CNN and CBS showed large majorities favoring Romney among debate-watchers and undecided voters; other surveys echoed a post-debate swing toward Romney. 

Forecasts suggested Romney’s victory was more like a field goal than a touchdown—likely to tighten the race modestly but not erase his deficit. With key events ahead (a jobs report, vice-presidential debate, two more presidential debates), the debate altered dynamics and improved Romney’s comeback prospects, while forcing the Obama campaign to recalibrate.

A catastrophic coal-mine fire in Soma, western Turkey, killed hundreds and unleashed national outrage over mining safety and the government’s response. Rescue teams recovered bodies amid smoldering debris; authorities reported at least 283 confirmed dead as recovery continued. Survivors and rescuers described grim conditions—toxic fumes, unstable fires and delays that turned a rescue into a lengthy recovery—while autopsies indicated many victims died of carbon monoxide poisoning. Funerals and mass graves underscored communal grief: women wailed and sang laments as rows of coffins were lowered and relatives pinned pictures of the dead to their clothes.

The disaster sparked widespread protests and strikes. Unions called a nationwide walkout and thousands demonstrated in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir and other cities, confronting police who used water cannons and tear gas. Protesters placed symbolic black coffins at government buildings and chanted “It’s not an accident, it’s murder,” reflecting accusations of negligence. A local Chamber of Electrical Engineers blasted official claims, alleging inadequate gas detection and ventilation systems and asserting the blaze was not simply electrical in origin.

Political fallout intensified after images circulated showing a senior aide to Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan, identified as Yusuf Yerkel, kicking a detained protester during Erdogan’s visit to Soma—an episode that inflamed public anger at what many saw as tone-deaf leadership. Erdogan’s remarks at the site, in which he described mining accidents as common and cited historical examples, were widely criticized as insensitive. President Abdullah Gul and officials promised investigations; prosecutors opened inquiries while political opponents renewed calls for accountability and mine-safety reforms.

A U.S. Transportation Department Office of Inspector General report finds the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is not adequately ensuring airline pilots maintain manual flying skills or are fully trained to monitor complex automated cockpit systems. Investigators concluded the FAA cannot determine how often pilots manually fly and has not made airline training programs sufficiently emphasize manual control and active monitoring. Modern airliners are flown by automation about 90 percent of the time, with pilots typically flying manually only on takeoffs and landings; this increased reliance, plus automation complexity, raises concerns that manual skills are deteriorating.

The report noted deficiencies in oversight: only five of 19 reviewed airline simulator training plans explicitly mentioned pilot monitoring, the FAA issued a 2013 safety alert encouraging more manual practice but did not follow up, and new 2013 training rules lack detailed guidance and do not require compliance until 2019. The watchdog said the FAA lacks the ability to verify whether carriers are implementing the new requirements or whether pilots get more manual flying time.

The findings cite past accidents linked to automation and monitoring failures, including the 2013 Asiana Boeing 777 crash in San Francisco—attributed by the NTSB to weak pilot skills and overreliance on automation—and the 2009 Colgan Air crash near Buffalo, where crews failed to monitor airspeed and misreacted to stall warnings, killing 50. Investigators warned that increasing satellite-based navigation and tighter traffic spacing will further reduce manual flying opportunities. The FAA acknowledged concerns and said it is developing guidance and agreed to work on standards to measure pilots’ manual-flight opportunities, with monitoring guidance hoped for by January 2017.

Sunday talk shows were dominated by discussion of reported Russian interference in the 2016 election, with calls for a special congressional probe and pointed accusations from Democratic operatives. Incoming Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Republican Sen. John McCain and a bipartisan group urged Majority Leader Mitch McConnell to form a select committee on cyber to investigate Russia’s actions, recommend reforms, and propose legislation to modernize U.S. defenses. Rep. Peter King called for an inquiry into whether CIA Director John Brennan leaked information about the hacks to the media.

Former Clinton campaign chairman John Podesta told NBC’s Meet the Press he believes Russians “clearly intervened” to help elect Donald Trump and suggested some Trump associates might have colluded with Russian hackers, though he stopped short of accusing Trump personally. Podesta said Russian diplomats communicated with the Trump campaign and surrogates had contact with WikiLeaks’ Julian Assange. He also revealed the FBI first contacted him about his hacked email account on Oct. 9—two days after WikiLeaks began publishing his emails—and he has had no further contact.

Podesta criticized inconsistent responses from intelligence and law enforcement, contrasting public warnings about Russian interference with FBI Director James Comey’s handling of Clinton-related announcements. He urged a thorough postmortem for Democrats on campaign failures in the Midwest and said electors deserve answers about what Trump’s team knew before casting Electoral College votes. Incoming White House Chief of Staff Reince Priebus said Trump awaits a unified intelligence assessment but asserted the hacks did not change the election outcome.

Vistara, a New Delhi–based domestic airline, has launched "Woman Flyer," a complimentary service aimed at improving solo female travellers’ safety and comfort by guaranteeing non-middle seats and providing ground assistance. Launched in March, the program ensures women who register at least 72 hours before travel receive a window or aisle seat if they haven’t pre-selected one, and offers staff support with luggage, booking airport-authorized taxis, and escorting passengers to pickup points. Vistara says 75–100 women use the service daily and plans to extend it to international routes as the carrier grows beyond its current all-Airbus A320 domestic fleet.

The initiative arrives amid broader concerns about women’s safety in India. High-profile crimes, notably the 2012 gang rape and murder in New Delhi, and frequent reports of street harassment have prompted blunt travel warnings from countries including the United States, the UK, and Australia, which advise women to avoid travelling alone on public transit. International observers and activists link risks to deeper gender-inequality issues; India ranks fifth on a list of countries deemed most dangerous for female travellers by the International Women’s Travel Center.

Globally, cities and transit systems have experimented with women-only transport options—separate train cars and buses—with mixed results: while sometimes effective and popular, critics argue such segregation reinforces the notion that women must be contained for safety and constitutes only a short-term fix. Vistara’s offering is positioned as a customer-service measure to provide peace of mind rather than a structural solution to broader societal problems.

A CNN/ORC national poll conducted July 22–25 finds Donald Trump leading the 2016 Republican field with 18% support among Republicans and Republican-leaning independents, up six points since late June despite aftershock criticism over his remarks about Sen. John McCain. Former Florida governor Jeb Bush follows closely at 15%, within the poll’s margin of error, and Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker holds 10%. No other GOP candidate reached double digits. Fifty-two percent of Republican respondents want Trump to remain in the race; 33% say he should drop out and 15% want him to run as an independent. Among Republicans who have narrowed their choice to one or two candidates, Trump performs stronger (24%) compared with Bush (16%) and Walker (12%). However, many GOP voters (51%) view the contest as wide open. Trump’s broader prospects are weaker: hypothetical general-election matchups show him trailing Democrats Hillary Clinton and Bernie Sanders, and his national unfavorability is high—59% of all registered voters view him unfavorably (42% among GOP voters). Clinton remains the Democratic frontrunner at 56%, with Sanders rising to 19%. Additional polls showed Trump leading in New Hampshire and close in Iowa. The survey sampled 1,017 adults (898 registered voters) and has a ±3.5 percentage-point margin of error.

The Georgia Dome’s planned implosion took a comic turn when a MARTA bus obstructed The Weather Channel’s live feed at the exact moment the 71,250-seat stadium collapsed. Editor Jason Rudge had filmed the crowd and streamed the demolition for 40 minutes from across the street as explosives were set to bring down the 25-year-old former home of the Atlanta Falcons. After a public countdown, a series of blasts initiated the 12-second collapse, producing smoke and rubble — but at the critical moment a bus glided into view and stopped directly in front of Rudge’s camera, obscuring the entire spectacle. Rudge’s frustrated, profanity-laced shouts were captured live; the bus only moved after the dome had crumbled to a pile. The Weather Channel posted a bleeped version to YouTube titled “Bus Photobombs The Weather Channel’s Stream of Georgia Dome Implosion,” and staffers joked about it on Twitter. The clip quickly became a meme, spliced into other sports bloopers by outlets like Sports Illustrated and joked about by the Atlanta Hawks. Slate even produced a playful six-stanza poem commemorating the mistimed obstruction. Though the network missed the implosion visually, the bus’s perfect bad timing became the day’s memorable image.

German police ended a nearly two-day nationwide manhunt by arresting 22-year-old Syrian Jaber Albakr in Leipzig after fellow Syrians detained him in their apartment. Albakr, who arrived in Germany as an asylum seeker in February 2015 and was granted asylum that June, had narrowly evaded a raid on a Chemnitz flat where investigators, acting on domestic intelligence, found about 1.5 kilograms of TATP, the highly unstable homemade explosive used in recent jihadist attacks. Authorities said the explosives were “almost ready, or even ready for usage,” and investigators believe Albakr was preparing a bomb, possibly a suicide vest. Chief Saxony investigator Jörg Michaelis indicated Albakr appears to have had contact with ISIS.

The arrest followed a tip: a man at Leipzig train station hosted Albakr overnight, later recognized him from police appeals broadcast in Arabic, and informed officers; his flatmates restrained and tied Albakr until police arrived. Chancellor Angela Merkel publicly thanked the informant and the police. One Syrian from the Chemnitz flat, identified as Khalil A., was taken into custody as a suspected co-conspirator accused of enabling Albakr’s use of his apartment and assisting online procurement of materials. Authorities also raided another contact’s home.

The case heightened national anxieties after recent ISIS-linked attacks and foiled plots in Germany. Political debate resumed over security and intelligence access to asylum applicants’ files, with Chancellor Merkel’s CDU calling for broader powers for services to vet newcomers.

Maddy Wilford, a 17-year-old junior at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, tearfully thanked first responders and medical staff Monday at Broward Health North after surviving multiple gunshot wounds sustained in the February 14 shooting that killed 14 students and three adults. Wilford, who underwent several surgeries and was released from the hospital within a week, expressed gratitude for the outpouring of support and said she is making a full recovery, though her right arm will need weeks of healing and occupational therapy for tendon damage.

Lt. Laz Ojeda of the Coral Springs Fire Department described the chaotic response at the school and how, upon finding Wilford pale and initially unresponsive, he ultimately elicited a whisper that she was 17. That revelation led him to divert from instructions to transport pediatric patients to a hospital 30 miles away; instead he brought her to Broward Health North, about 10 minutes from the scene. Ojeda and the family credit that decision with helping save her life.

At Broward Health North, Dr. Evan Boyar, medical director of emergency services, said the hospital’s recent active-shooter drill and rapid activation of a “code green” mass-casualty response enabled a seamless and equal treatment of multiple victims. Trauma director Dr. Igor Nichiporenko described Wilford’s injuries—large-caliber gunshot wounds to chest, abdomen and upper arm producing massive bleeding and tissue damage from blast effect—and said she was taken to surgery within 10 minutes for damage-control procedures. Although fragments remain, her chest and abdomen have healed; her youth and resilience contributed to a short hospital stay and prospects for full recovery.

Wilford’s parents voiced deep gratitude to first responders, medical teams and the community. While the family acknowledged broader political debates and scrutiny of law enforcement after the massacre, they focused publicly on healing and the support they have felt, emphasizing the need for communal unity and prayer in the aftermath.

After a wave of rape and bomb threats against women in the U.K., including feminist campaigner Caroline Criado-Perez, MP Stella Creasy and several journalists, Twitter announced policy and staffing changes to better police abusive content. The company updated its rules to define targeted abuse—covering repeated messages from multiple accounts, accounts created solely to harass, one-sided attacks and threats—and said it will add more trust-and-safety staff. Twitter confirmed a wider rollout of an in-tweet “report abuse” button across web and mobile platforms and pledged to simplify reporting. Twitter U.K. will work with the UK Safer Internet Centre to expand user resources and publicize safety guidance. The moves followed public outcry, petitions with over 120,000 signatures, media criticism and police investigations by Scotland Yard’s e-crime unit into multiple malicious communications; two arrests have already been linked to some threats. Twitter’s UK GM apologized and committed to stronger measures to protect users and deter harassment.

US Airways and federal officials are investigating a serious midair near-miss at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport after The Washington Post reported that three US Airways commuter jets carrying 192 people came within seconds of colliding. Controllers reversed the airport traffic flow because of a wind-driven storm, but the change wasn’t fully communicated within the tower. Two outbound flights were cleared as an inbound aircraft continued its approach; one outbound and the inbound closed at a combined 436 mph and were about 12 seconds from impact before the tower controller recognized the error and instructed the inbound to turn. All flights landed safely. The FAA confirmed an investigation and said it will address the communication lapse. The incident adds to a record of operational errors nationwide and past safety controversies at National Airport.

Jonas Bevacqua, 34, co-founder and creative director of Irvine-based streetwear brand LRG (Lifted Research Group), was found dead in his Laguna Beach home; the cause of death remains undetermined and authorities say it does not appear suspicious pending autopsy. Raised in Long Beach and later Laguna Beach, Bevacqua—an adopted U.S.-born Vietnamese—drew on a multicultural upbringing, skate, surf and hip‑hop cultures to create clothing that bridged those influences. He met partner Robert Wright while DJing, launched LRG from his parents’ home in 1999 with early investor help, and grew it into a lifestyle company with music, electronics and skate sponsorships. By 2006 LRG reported $150 million in sales and ranked among Entrepreneur’s fastest-growing companies. Colleagues described him as a visionary, mentor and friend; fans praised him online as a fashion pioneer. Bevacqua is survived by his fiancée, young son, parents and seven siblings. LRG asked for privacy as family mourns.

A libertarian Reason reporter confronted actor Matt Damon at the Save Our Schools March with questions about teacher tenure and incentive-based reforms, aiming to challenge his views. Damon, a multi‑millionaire, appeared dismissive of the reporter’s framing and defended working teachers, turning the encounter awkward for both interviewer and cameraman. Elsewhere, while promoting Friends With Benefits in Moscow, Mila Kunis spoke some answers in her native Ukrainian/Russian, leaving co-star Justin Timberlake without a timely translation feed and creating a few uncomfortable moments during the press junket. The pair later attended the film’s Russian premiere and continued promotion in London.

Two nights after a bruising debate, President Barack Obama and Republican nominee Mitt Romney set aside campaign rancor for the 67th Alfred E. Smith Memorial Foundation dinner at the Waldorf-Astoria, a white-tie charity event traditionally featuring lighthearted roasts by both major-party candidates. Both men skewered themselves, each other, their running mates, and the press while delivering practiced one-liners that landed with the wealthy, mostly Catholic audience.

Romney opened by self-deprecating about his formality and wardrobe, joking it was relaxing to “wear what Ann and I wear around the house.” He ribbed Obama on redistribution, quipped about debate prep—“refrain from alcohol for 65 years” and attack a “straw man”—and mocked coverage that would cast him as dining with rich people while Obama was embraced by Catholics. He also aimed barbs at Bill Clinton’s role supporting Obama and mocked the media’s tendency to bury his positive message.

Obama returned with playful jabs about his debated debate performances—quipping about a “nice long nap” during the first debate—and ribbed Romney for shopping for stores in Midtown and for his awkward foreign trip. He referenced winning a foreign-policy success with Bin Laden and joked about names, wishing he could use his middle name, “Hussein,” as Romney uses “Mitt.” Both men used Vice President Joe Biden as an easy target, trading lines that drew big laughs. Introducing them, Al Smith IV and others added barbs about binders, charity, and the contest’s oddities, making the night a traditional, civil respite amid an increasingly nasty campaign.

American actor Randy Quaid and his wife, Evi Quaid, were arrested Friday night at the U.S. border crossing between Philipsburg, Quebec, and Highgate Springs, Vermont, after U.S. authorities determined they were fugitives subject to extradition on California charges. The couple was detained around 8 p.m.; a Vermont judge set bail at $50,000 each. They face outstanding felony vandalism and related charges from 2010 in Santa Barbara County, where prosecutors allege the pair squatted in a guesthouse of a property they once owned, causing more than $5,000 in damage, and later failed to appear at a court hearing while out on bail.

The arrest followed a string of Canadian immigration encounters. The Quaids had been living in Montreal since February 2013 after fleeing the U.S. in 2010, claiming persecution and alleging threats from so-called “Hollywood star‑whackers.” Evi Quaid, whose father was born in Canada, obtained Canadian citizenship in 2012. Randy Quaid applied for refugee status in 2010, later withdrew that claim, and sought permanent residency; his application was denied in 2012–2013, partly because of alleged fraud accusations in California. He was ordered to leave Canada by Oct. 14 after Immigration and Refugee Board proceedings. Canadian authorities had previously detained him as a potential flight risk during routine check‑ins. The Santa Barbara district attorney indicated prosecutors will seek extradition if the Quaids are returned to the U.S.

Hurricane Michael slammed into the Florida Panhandle as a Category 4 storm, then raced north through Georgia, the Carolinas and Virginia, leaving widespread destruction, flooding and at least 17 confirmed deaths with officials warning the toll will likely rise. Entire coastal towns such as Mexico Beach were devastated—many structures leveled or swept away—and aerial footage showed massive damage. More than one million customers across multiple states lost power; Virginia, North Carolina and Florida reported the largest outage numbers. Search-and-rescue teams, often hindered by blocked roads and downed trees, combed neighborhoods and used dogs and helicopters to reach isolated areas including a psychiatric hospital reliant on generators. Michael caused deadly inland flash flooding, sweeping people from vehicles and inundating rivers in Virginia and the Carolinas; dozens were rescued. Agriculture and industry suffered heavy losses: Georgia reported severe damage to cotton, pecan, peanut and vegetable crops and destruction of dozens of chicken houses, killing millions of birds. Officials set up distribution centers and shelters, while FEMA expanded individual assistance to more Florida counties. Leaders urged patience and warned recovery will be long; experts noted that warming oceans and higher sea levels make storms stronger and surges worse, meaning future hurricanes could intensify more rapidly.

This document reports on a March 2016 crawl of outlinks from Wikipedia and then provides extensive material from Mayors Against Illegal Guns (MAIG), a bipartisan coalition co-founded by New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg and Boston Mayor Thomas Menino.
