MAIG grew to hundreds of mayors and over a million supporters and has repeatedly pushed for stronger gun background checks, limits on military-style weapons and high-capacity magazines, and federal action on gun trafficking. The coalition released investigations showing online sales circumvent background checks, published polls showing strong public and NRA-member support for universal checks, launched ad campaigns and PSAs, organized national rallies and bus tours, and urged Congress and the President to act after mass shootings (Newtown, Tucson, Aurora). MAIG also criticized the NRA, promoted legislation like the Fix Gun Checks Act, tracked state reporting to NICS, and urged websites to curb illegal online gun sales.

Subscribers to streaming services have sued Chicago, challenging the city’s June decision to extend its 9% “Amusement” tax to digital streaming—targeting services such as Netflix, Spotify, Amazon Prime, Hulu and Xbox Live. Filed in Cook County Circuit Court, the suit argues the comptroller illegally imposed what amounts to a new tax without a city council vote, exceeding the authority granted by the municipal code. Plaintiffs say the change injures them by increasing subscription costs and, in Amazon Prime’s case, could make the entire bundled fee taxable if the company does not separately price streaming versus non-streaming perks.

The complaint also contends the tax violates the federal Internet Tax Freedom Act (ITFA), which bars discriminatory internet-only taxes. Plaintiffs allege Chicago treats streamed versions of content differently from physical or mail-delivered formats and applies a higher rate to online performances than to similar in-person events. Xbox Live was singled out as providing services—gaming, communication, cloud storage and broadcasting—that don’t fit the amusement tax’s language.

Chicago officials expect the “Netflix tax” to raise about $12 million annually and say they will defend the ruling vigorously. The dispute highlights growing tensions as local governments seek revenue from cloud and digital services amid declining retail sales tax, while businesses and consumers face legal and compliance uncertainty over how far municipal taxing authority—and the definition of physical nexus—extends.

Senior law enforcement officials have identified the man shot dead outside Endeavour Hills Police Station in Melbourne as 18-year-old Abdul Numan Haider. Haider, whose family is of Afghan origin, had been monitored for about three months and had his passport canceled on national security grounds. Authorities said he had been seen recently displaying what appeared to be an Islamic State flag and had been associated with the radical group Al-Furqan, though he had reportedly distanced himself from the group. Members of a Joint Counter Terrorism team had asked Haider to attend the station to discuss concerns; when officers met him outside, one extended a hand and was stabbed in the arm, and a second officer was stabbed multiple times in the head and body. One officer then shot Haider dead. Both injured officers—one from the AFP and one from Victoria Police—required surgery and were in stable condition. Officials said there were no specific threats identified against the prime minister. The incident prompted community appeals for unity, criticism from Islamic leaders urging caution before conclusions, and broader concern about lone-wolf attacks inspired by IS calls for violence.

Drake L. Kramer, a 21-year-old from San Antonio, remained missing after six days of searches at Grand Canyon National Park. He was last seen Feb. 1 near the Bright Angel Lodge on the South Rim after spending the previous night there and checking out the next morning. Family members reported him missing on Feb. 2; despite extensive search efforts by National Park Service (NPS) Search and Rescue teams, no new clues have emerged. Rangers have combed the South Rim developed area from Hermit’s Rest to Grandview, walking miles along the canyon rim, searching heavily forested areas, deploying dog teams, conducting several over-the-rim technical searches and multiple aerial reconnaissance missions. Posters with Kramer’s photo and description remain posted at South Rim locations.

Because of the lack of leads, the search is being scaled back to a continuous but limited mode, with rangers and pilots searching for clues when in the area. Kramer is described as 5 feet 7 inches tall, 140 pounds, with brown hair and blue eyes, last seen wearing blue jeans and an olive-green sweatshirt. His father, Robbin Kramer, said Drake texted him saying he “needed to be back with Mother Earth” and “set his soul free,” remarks that heightened family concern. Robbin noted Drake’s love of the outdoors and interest in geology but was unsure whether his son had appropriate hiking gear. Authorities ask anyone with information to call the NPS Silent Witness Line at 928-638-7840.

Gordon Gray, a Hollywood producer famed for inspirational, fact-based sports films, and his wife Kristen were devastated in March when their daughters Charlotte, 4, and Gwenyth, 20 months, were diagnosed with an exceptionally rare, fatal neurodegenerative disorder: Late Infantile NCL (a form of Batten disease, CLN6). Told there are perhaps only about 10 sufferers worldwide at any time and no established cure despite the disease being known since 1903, the Grays learned that affected children progressively lose sight, motor skills and independence, typically dying between ages 6 and 12. Refusing to accept the prognosis, they formed The Charlotte and Gwenyth Gray Foundation to fund urgent research. They aim to raise $10–12 million, with an initial $2 million needed to launch trials testing three promising approaches: a gene therapy/vector-virus treatment shown effective in an animal model, stem cell therapy, and small-molecule therapy.

Leveraging Hollywood connections and a steering committee of producers and executives, the Grays secured help from celebrities and social-media platforms. High-profile supporters—including Rihanna, Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson, Megan Fox, Mark Wahlberg and many others—are pledging outreach on Facebook, Twitter and Instagram asking followers to donate $1 each to quickly aggregate funds. The campaign’s math posits that even a small fraction of huge followings could yield millions.

The story of the Bowmans, another American family featured alongside the Grays, underscores the devastation of Batten disease. Bekah and Danny Bowman of Orange County learned this spring that both sons, Titus (5) and Ely (2), have Late Infantile NCL (CLN2). Titus’s decline has been rapid: blindness, loss of speech, mobility and feeding ability, seizures and dependence on a feeding tube; Ely’s positive test confirmed a 25% hereditary risk realized. The Bowmans now focus on cherishing daily moments and raising awareness and funds while managing mounting care needs. The Grays’ highly publicized, celebrity-amplified fundraising has offered the Bowmans hope and greater visibility for a disease that has historically attracted little research funding. The families’ intertwined accounts highlight both heartbreak and determined efforts to accelerate treatments that, if successful, could change outcomes for all children with Batten disease.

James Rynerson, a 38-year-old inmate at the Mesa County Jail in Grand Junction, Colorado, was mistakenly released from custody late last month and enjoyed under two hours of freedom before the error was corrected. Rynerson had been held on a $2,000 cash bond while awaiting prosecution on charges including menacing, disorderly conduct and trespass. According to court records and reporting by the Grand Junction Daily Sentinel, deputies at the jail confused Rynerson with another inmate, Marvin March, and released him in error. Mesa County Sheriff’s Sgt. Henry Stoffel acknowledged that jail employees violated procedure by failing to verify Rynerson’s wristband and photo before processing his release, and said an internal investigation is underway to determine whether policies regarding the housing list and release checks need revision. Sgt. Stoffel credited Rynerson’s wife for discovering the mistake and promptly causing him to return to custody, preventing any extended period of freedom. The incident has prompted scrutiny of booking and release protocols at the Mesa County Jail as officials assess whether additional safeguards or updated procedures are needed to prevent similar mistakes in the future. The reporting source was the Grand Junction Daily Sentinel.

Local police say a man and his 3-year-old son died and a 7-year-old girl is in critical condition after carbon monoxide poisoning in Valley Station. Metro police responded Wednesday morning to the 9900 block of Plaudit Way after a family member found three people unresponsive in the family’s closed garage. Investigators believe the father turned on the car to warm it up while it was inside the garage, allowing carbon monoxide to build up quickly. Juvenal Garcia Mora, 39, and his son Cruz Isaac Garcia, 3, were pronounced dead at the Medical Center Jewish Southwest; their causes and manners of death remain pending as the investigation continues. The 7-year-old was transported under police escort to Norton Children’s Hospital and was last reported in critical condition. Police said the children’s mother was not home when the incident occurred and has been notified. LMPD Lt. Emily McKinley emphasized that such tragedies can happen very rapidly and urged caution during winter: warm vehicles only in well-ventilated areas to avoid deadly buildup of the colorless, odorless gas. Officers said there is no evidence of foul play and that the deaths appear to be a tragic accident. The report noted that carbon monoxide symptoms resemble the flu and that high concentrations can be fatal in minutes.

Three tickets split the record $640 million Mega Millions jackpot, Illinois, Kansas and Maryland each sold a grand-prize ticket, lottery spokesmen confirmed. Each ticket’s pre-tax share was estimated at about $213 million. Maryland’s winning ticket was sold at a 7-Eleven in Baltimore County; Illinois’ at a Red Bud store near St. Louis; details on the Kansas ticket were limited. Winning numbers were 02-04-23-38-46 and Mega Ball 23. The jackpot drew massive ticket sales nationwide, with Americans spending nearly $1.5 billion for this drawing. Maryland also had four $250,000 winners; the retailer there will receive $100,000.

Nearly two months after Anthony Bourdain’s death, CNN will air the final season of Parts Unknown, using footage he filmed in Kenya, Texas (Big Bend), Spain (Asturias), Indonesia and Manhattan’s Lower East Side. Only the Kenya episode — featuring W. Kamau Bell — was complete with Bourdain’s original narration; other episodes will rely on location audio he recorded plus stitched-together pre-recorded interviews and new follow-up interviews with participants to fill gaps. CNN says each episode will feel different but retain Bourdain’s presence through images and voices of those who appeared with him. A special reflection episode and a series finale honoring his impact will also air. CNN will not replace him as host but is developing new unscripted programming inspired by his influence; a premiere date has not been announced.

Ian “Lemmy” Kilmister, the gravel-voiced frontman and founding force behind Motörhead, has died at 70 after a brief battle with cancer diagnosed on December 26. The band announced he passed away at home, surrounded by family and sitting before his favorite video game. Tributes poured in from peers and fans, and Motörhead urged listeners to play his music loud in the days ahead.

Lemmy’s career spanned decades: early stints in 1960s beat groups, work as a roadie for Jimi Hendrix, and prominence with space-rockers Hawkwind—singing their 1972 hit “Silver Machine”—before forming Motörhead in 1975 after being dismissed from Hawkwind following a drug-related arrest. Motörhead’s raw, high-volume sound, which drew on 1950s rock’n’roll roots as much as punk energy, helped inspire thrash metal. With key members “Fast” Eddie Clarke and Phil “Philthy Animal” Taylor, the band released a string of influential records—Overkill, Bomber, Ace of Spades—and reached No. 1 with the live album No Sleep ’til Hammersmith. Motörhead recorded 22 studio albums, including their final release, Bad Magic.

Lemmy cultivated an iconic image—mutton chops, cowboy hat, whiskey and amphetamines, a penchant for Nazi memorabilia that fueled controversy—and lived a hard-living rock lifestyle, later moderating some habits for health reasons. In recent years he faced cardiac and other health issues, used a walking stick, and swapped whiskey for vodka while remaining fiercely dedicated to performing. He never married, embraced the excesses and freedoms of rock’n’roll, and insisted Motörhead were fundamentally a rock’n’roll band. His death marks the end of a singular career and a defining voice of loud, uncompromising rock.

Ryan Seacrest anchored E!’s Oscars red carpet amid renewed sexual misconduct allegations from former stylist Suzie Hardy, which he denies and which E! said lacked sufficient evidence. Observers expected possible snubs; several high-profile actresses, including all five Best Actress nominees, skipped Seacrest’s interviews. Still, he conducted conversations with nominees Allison Janney, Mary J. Blige and Christopher Plummer, plus presenters and stars like Taraji P. Henson—who pointedly told him “the universe has a way of taking care of the good people”—Tiffany Haddish, Kelly Ripa, Diane Warren, Common and others. E! leaned on Giuliana Rancic and offsite coverage from the nearby Roosevelt Hotel, and reportedly considered a brief broadcast delay to avoid confrontations, which the network downplayed as standard practice. The evening mixed polite project-focused chats with moments reflecting broader #MeToo tensions that shadowed the event and shaped guest choices.

Sen. Lindsey Graham will headline a fundraiser Monday for Sen. Ted Cruz’s presidential campaign, illustrating how fractured and fluid the Republican primary has become. Graham, who ended his own presidential bid last December and had campaigned for Jeb Bush, told CNN Cruz isn’t his first choice but is “the best alternative to Donald Trump” and that he will “help Ted in every way I can.” A draft invitation obtained by CNN says the AIPAC meet-and-greet will “honor and support a great friend of Israel and the Jewish people,” and will occur during the AIPAC policy conference in Washington. Graham’s backing marks a notable reversal from earlier in the race when he compared nominating Trump or Cruz to being “shot or poisoned.” Meanwhile, former candidate Marco Rubio, who suspended his campaign after losing Florida’s 99 winner-take-all delegates, told Minnesota supporters he hopes another contender can stop Trump from clinching the nomination and suggested Cruz could be the best conservative alternative. Rubio did not officially endorse Cruz or Ohio Gov. John Kasich. Reflecting on his campaign, Rubio said he saw no viable path forward after the Florida defeat, criticized negative media narratives and Super PAC attack ads for undermining his momentum, and acknowledged how coverage can both help and hurt a campaign. He said he’s “at peace” with leaving the race, remains open to future public service, and emphasized that a nominee perceived by many as having “stolen” the nomination could badly damage the party’s general election prospects.

Last week Rush Limbaugh spent three days attacking Sandra Fluke, a Georgetown law student who argued insurers should cover contraception. After advertisers pressured him, Limbaugh apologized for personal insults—he’d called Fluke a “slut” and made lewd jokes—but he did not retract the arguments behind his rants. Slate columnist William Saletan examines those arguments as representative of many conservative views and frames six key questions raised by Limbaugh’s comments: Is opposition to contraceptive coverage about socialism or disapproval of premarital sex? How much sexual activity is “too much,” given Limbaugh’s repeated insistence that Fluke advocated “so much sex”? Is contraception merely an enabler of sex and therefore undeserving of public support? What consequences should follow from sex—does preventing pregnancy wrongly evade consequences? Is pregnancy prevention a legitimate medical need or an elective luxury comparable to Botox? And what responsibility should men bear in contraception and parenthood enforcement? Saletan urges Limbaugh to clarify policy proposals, for example how he would enforce male responsibility. The piece also notes parallel attacks by actress Patricia Heaton, whose inflammatory tweets about Fluke sparked backlash and were later deleted, underscoring a broader conservative outrage against Fluke.

Christian author and blogger Glennon Doyle Melton publicly announced she is dating retired soccer star Abby Wambach, three months after divorcing her husband Craig. In a heartfelt Facebook post, Melton—known for candid memoirs like Love Warrior—praised Wambach as “deeply sensitive” and “unwaveringly good,” saying her children warmly accept Abby, nicknaming her an “M&M.” Melton said Craig supports their new relationships and emphasized they co-parent and form a “modern, beautiful family.” Both women have navigated recent divorces and personal transformations; Wambach has confronted addiction and revisited faith. Melton, who speaks at Christian venues and affirms same-sex marriage, closed with an all-caps declaration: “I LOVE ABBY.”

Kenny G recently told Bloomberg that he played a small but notable role in Starbucks’ evolution beyond hot coffee, claiming credit for nudging the company toward the Frappuccino. The saxophonist said his uncle was among Starbucks’ earliest investors and introduced him to CEO Howard Schultz; Kenny G became an early investor too. He recalled calling Schultz about a popular blended, milkshake-like drink he’d seen at Coffee Bean and urging Starbucks to offer something similar. “I think that part of the reason that they did Frappuccinos was people like me giving them that kind of feedback,” he said, adding that Frappuccino is his Starbucks drink of choice. Starbucks acknowledged Kenny G as an early friend of the company and thanked “everyone, including Kenny,” who contributed to the Frappuccino’s success.

Starbucks, however, traces the Frappuccino’s in-store origins to two partners who began developing an iced blended beverage in Southern California in 1993. After Starbucks acquired The Coffee Connection in 1994—whose founder and employee had developed and trademarked the original Frappuccino—the drink was introduced nationally under the Starbucks name in 1995, with Coffee and Mocha Frappuccinos. The bottled Frappuccino also launched via a joint venture with PepsiCo and became a major ready-to-drink product. Starbucks says Kenny G also helped the company enter music retail: his Christmas album Miracles was the first record Starbucks sold at the counter in 1994, a successful experiment that led to broader music sales. Background context notes the Frappuccino name derives from “frappe” (a New England milkshake) and “cappuccino,” and that the beverage family has expanded into crème bases, non-dairy options, juice blends, and bottled products—though it has faced criticism over high sugar content. Whether Kenny G “invented” the Frappuccino is debatable, but he undoubtedly influenced Starbucks early on and counts among its formative supporters.

A training accident at Fort Bragg involving an M777 light towed howitzer killed one paratrooper and injured seven others Friday morning, officials reported. The 18th Fires Brigade was conducting artillery live-fire training when the incident occurred; location details weren’t released. Two soldiers were seriously injured—one moved to Duke University Medical Center, the other treated at Womack Army Medical Center—while five were treated and released. The 82nd Airborne Division, Army Criminal Investigative Division and Army Combat Readiness/Safety Center are investigating. Families have been notified and names will be released Saturday; brigade commander Col. Stephen Smith offered condolences and said support is being provided.

JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon survived a shareholder effort to remove his title as board chairman at the bank’s annual meeting in Tampa, held five days after his disclosure of a $2 billion trading loss. Most ballots had been cast before the loss became public; the motion to strip him received 40% support, while his $23 million 2011 pay package was approved with 91% backing. Dimon acknowledged the mistakes as “self-inflicted” and accepted responsibility. The episode battered JPMorgan’s stock, erasing nearly $20 billion in market value before a modest rebound. The loss intensified calls for tougher regulation: President Obama and Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner both cited it as reinforcing the need for stricter rules, and JPMorgan’s chief investment officer Ina Drew resigned over the fallout. Protests and heavy security marked the meeting.

Nearly 30 U.S. Air Force Academy cadets needed medical attention after an unauthorized annual ritual called "First Shirt/First Snow" escalated into a violent melee, officials said. The tradition—where freshmen attempt to throw their cadet sergeant into a snowbank—turned dangerous last Thursday, leaving six cadets hospitalized (since released) and 21 others treated for bruises and lacerations at the academy clinic. Brig. Gen. Gregory Lengyel, commandant of cadets, called the incident unacceptable and said an investigation is underway. An internal email obtained by the Air Force Times, reportedly from Brig. Gen. Dana Born, described the event as devolving into a brawl between freshmen and upperclassmen and noted the ritual has grown more violent over the past two years, producing concussions, a bitten arm and cuts requiring stitches. Born wrote the practice “has gotten out of hand and cannot be repeated,” though Lengyel may permit it to continue if cadets can demonstrate proper order, discipline and risk management. The episode is another reputational setback for the academy, which has faced past scandals including sexual assault investigations, religious favoritism findings, cheating and drug-use incidents.

EU leaders met in Brussels as the Ukraine crisis deepened, warning that the apparent incursion of Russian troops on Ukrainian soil risked pushing the conflict “to the point of no return” and prompting tougher sanctions. Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko told the summit that thousands of foreign troops and hundreds of tanks were operating in eastern Ukraine and warned of the danger of full-scale war. He said he hopes a trilateral meeting with Russia and the EU could produce a ceasefire and that a draft peace plan would be published soon. EU foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton and several leaders, including Lithuania’s Dalia Grybauskaite and Britain’s David Cameron, accused Russia of direct aggression, urged an end to the flow of arms and personnel, and called for support to help Ukraine defend itself. France’s François Hollande and European Commission President José Manuel Barroso backed preparing new economic measures, while some EU members hesitated because of potential economic fallout and the unanimity required for sanctions. NATO estimated at least 1,000 Russian soldiers were in Ukraine; the UN put conflict deaths in the Donetsk and Luhansk regions at roughly 2,600. On the ground, Ukrainian forces reported retreats from towns such as Novosvitlivka and Ilovaisk after rebel advances and alleged Russian armored support; rebels opened a new front toward Mariupol after taking Novoazovsk. The EU signaled it would ask its institutions to prepare further sanctions if Moscow did not reverse course, while also keeping diplomatic channels open and offering financial and reconstruction assistance to Ukraine.

A celebratory night turned catastrophic on the San Mateo-Hayward Bridge when a 1999 Lincoln Town Car stretch limousine burst into flames, killing five women and leaving four survivors among a group of nine friends traveling to celebrate a recent wedding. The women, mostly Filipina nurses in their 30s and 40s who worked across the Bay Area and Fresno, were riding in the rear of the limo when a passenger first tapped the partition and warned of smoke. Driver Orville “Ricky” Brown initially misunderstood, then pulled the vehicle to the bridge shoulder as flames rapidly engulfed the passenger compartment. In under three minutes the back third of the limousine was an inferno. Four women escaped through the small partition opening into the front; several others were pulled by the driver and Good Samaritans but five victims were found huddled near the partition, apparently unable to reach rear exits. Survivors were hospitalized; two victims were later identified as Fresno nurses Neriza Fojas, the bride, and Michelle Estrera. Authorities noted the limo carried nine people despite a limit of eight, but investigators had yet to determine the fire’s cause. The driver speculated an electrical fault; experts pointed to flammable interior materials and the challenges of regulating modified stretch limousines. State regulators said limos aren’t required to have fire extinguishers and modifications often escape stringent oversight. The incident prompted scrutiny of limo safety standards, maintenance practices, and enforcement of seating capacity and certification rules as officials continued their investigation.

Ezra Klein called John Boehner’s Speaker-inaugural speech unusually smart because it emphasized restraint and institutional repair rather than sweeping promises. Instead of positioning himself as a partisan foil to President Obama or launching an ambitious ideological agenda, Boehner stressed humility—calling the House “the people’s House”—and comity, urging openness, respect for minorities, and a reduction of the “scar tissue” between parties. He outlined procedural reforms: three days for members to read bills, smaller committees, more open rules, and efforts to cut spending (starting with Congress’s own budget). Klein praised the speech’s savvy omissions but warned that rhetoric may clash with reality: House rules pushed by Republicans could make deficit-increasing tax cuts easier, and Republicans were already bending rules to vote symbolically on health-care repeal without offsets. Boehner’s instincts impressed Klein, but he cautioned that promises of cooperation often fray under political pressure.

Ben Affleck, 46, has entered a live-in rehabilitation facility to address alcohol addiction, multiple outlets report. People confirms Affleck “is seeking treatment” and that he recognized the need for help. The decision followed a visit from his estranged wife and co-parent Jennifer Garner, who was photographed arriving at his Pacific Palisades home, visibly upset. Garner, Affleck and an unidentified woman later left together and were photographed in a car driven by Garner; they reportedly stopped at a Jack in the Box before heading to a treatment center in Malibu. TMZ first reported that Garner staged an intervention and that Affleck agreed to go into rehab for an extended stay at a facility in Los Angeles County.

Earlier in the week Affleck was photographed accepting an alcohol delivery at his Brentwood home—a box containing Pacifico beer-branded packaging and a blue-cased bottle resembling Johnnie Walker Blue Label—raising concerns, particularly given his new public association with 22-year-old Playboy Playmate Shauna Sexton, who has publicly said she favors whiskey. Sources tell People Garner’s primary concern is Affleck’s sobriety and their ability to co-parent effectively; she is reportedly not pleased about him socializing with a much younger model but is focused on their children’s well-being.

Affleck has a long history of treating alcohol dependence, first entering rehab in 2001 and completing treatment in March 2017, when he publicly acknowledged ongoing work in recovery. Friends have said he attends many meetings and practices meditation and yoga, though he still faces setbacks. Garner filed for divorce in April 2017 after announcing a separation in 2015; the couple remain legally separated but not divorced and continue to co-parent their three children. Sources indicate Garner has delayed finalizing the divorce partly out of concern over Affleck’s sobriety. If you or someone you know needs help, contact the SAMHSA helpline at 1-800-662-HELP.

A 51-year-old Toronto mother gave her 23-year-old son a memorable wake-up call after a domestic argument by sending him a mock invoice for the cost of living under her roof. Posted to Reddit by the son, who uses the handle “Chalipo,” the itemized bill totaled $39,254.17 and included typical household expenses—Internet, cable, gas, his portion of electricity ($1,037), prescriptions, cleaning services and health insurance premiums ($5,726)—alongside larger entries such as $23,550 listed as five years of tuition. The mother also included charges for “specialty meals,” a $600 line for contributions toward gifts (wedding, Christmas, Valentine’s) she helped fund, and a $1,000 fee labeled “being an a**hole and not appreciative of your mother’s support,” a pointed jab at his attitude during their dispute.

The argument began when Chalipo refused to provide information over the phone while his mother was completing an application to enroll his brother in a medication-cost assistance program that required household details. Both later acknowledged the misunderstanding and agreed the son’s reaction was ungracious. The stunt was intended as tongue-in-cheek: the mother told TODAY she did not expect payment, but wanted to make a point and motivate her son to be more appreciative. The tactic worked; Chalipo apologized, reflected on his behavior, and said the invoice helped him grasp how much his mother does for the family. He reposted the note online expecting a laugh, not national attention, and the viral response largely sympathized with the mother—though some criticized her approach. Both mother and son asked to keep their real names private. Chalipo, a part-time worker and full-time radio-broadcast student planning to move out and support his family in the future, says he plans to repay his mother in time.

South Korea’s MERS outbreak, traced to a single traveler who returned from the Middle East in May, has infected at least 95 people and killed seven, with nearly 2,900 people under quarantine at one point. The index patient sought care at multiple facilities after falling ill, visiting clinics in Asan, then St. Mary’s Hospital in Pyeongtaek, and later Seoul’s Samsung Medical Center, where MERS was finally suspected and confirmed on May 20. Crowded wards and emergency rooms allowed extensive hospital-to-hospital transmission: St. Mary’s accounts for about 37 cases (roughly 40 percent of the total), and a patient infected there later sparked at least 35 cases at Samsung by staying in its busy ER. Most infections have occurred in hospitals where infected patients had visited, leading authorities to focus containment on medical facilities.

The pattern—super-spreading events in crowded hospitals combined with frequent family visitation—has been blamed for accelerating spread. Cultural practices of caring for sick relatives in hospitals, and patients’ preference for large, prestigious hospitals, created bottlenecks that exacerbated transmission. South Korea’s government initially withheld the names of affected hospitals, drawing criticism for delayed disclosure and poor early coordination; it later released a list of 29 institutions implicated. That information release, however, caused outpatient numbers to plunge at some facilities.

Public reaction has been significant but not panicked: almost 2,200 schools and kindergartens closed, public events were canceled, mask and sanitizer sales surged, and tourism and attendance at entertainment venues fell. The WHO, while not recommending travel restrictions, sent experts and urged scrutiny of hospital visitation practices; its testing found no alarming viral mutations. South Korean officials declared an “all-out national response,” stepped up tracing (including using cellphone data), fully covered treatment costs, and hoped the outbreak would peak and subside as incubation periods for key cases ended. Critics say the episode highlights systemic information and response failures that must be addressed to prevent similar outbreaks.

Agnes Nixon, a pioneering force in daytime television who created All My Children and One Life to Live, died at 93 in Haverford, Pennsylvania. Celebrated by colleagues including Susan Lucci and Melissa Claire Egan, Nixon transformed soap operas by weaving socially relevant, often taboo issues into mainstream daytime storylines. Early in her career she broke new ground at Guiding Light with a storyline about a woman who discovered cervical cancer after a Pap smear—without using forbidden words—which prompted thousands of viewers to seek tests and later earned Nixon a Pioneer for Health Award. 

Over decades Nixon tackled topics previously absent from soaps: racial integration, interracial relationships, the Vietnam War’s effects, abortion, child abuse, addiction, AIDS, homosexuality and transgender identity. One Life to Live, launched in 1968, featured diverse ethnic characters and plots that forced audiences to confront prejudice; All My Children, which premiered in 1970 and ran 41 years, included the first televised legal abortion storyline and later introduced lesbian and transgender characters. Nixon’s approach avoided didacticism, letting complex plots and characters explore multiple perspectives. 

Despite criticism that soaps were trivial, Nixon insisted they could perform a public service and hold a mirror to social injustices. Her shows influenced other programs, attracted broader audiences, and kept topical daytime drama alive for decades. Called the “queen of modern daytime drama,” Nixon earned many honors including a 2010 Lifetime Achievement Daytime Emmy. She is survived by four children, ten grandchildren and three great-grandchildren. Her legacy endures in the socially conscious storytelling she brought to television.

Operation Blue Roof, run by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers after Hurricane Irma, sends licensed contractors to cover damaged roofs with fiber-reinforced plastic sheeting so homeowners can remain in their primary or permanently occupied rental residences while arranging repairs. The free service excludes vacation rentals and homes with over 50% structural damage; not all roof types qualify. FEMA Region 4 mistakenly tweeted the wrong phone number — 1-800-ROOF-BLU — which connected callers to an adult chat line. After the error was spotted and agencies were contacted, FEMA removed the tweet and reposted the correct contact: 1-888-ROOF-BLU and the program website.

Nearly six months after Robin Williams’s death, a bitter legal fight has erupted between his widow, Susan Schneider Williams, and his three children, Zak, Zelda and Cody, over property and personal items from the actor’s estate. Court filings reveal competing claims: Susan alleges someone entered the family home soon after Robin’s death and removed belongings, while the children contend Susan is trying to reinterpret the clear terms of Robin’s will and trust to keep items that were expressly left to them.

The dispute centers on a mix of financial and deeply sentimental objects accumulated over Williams’s four-decade career: memorabilia, costumes, collectibles, action figures, graphic novels, theater masks, photographs, fossils, bicycles and a watch collection. According to sources tied to the children, the trust specified that personal effects related to his career—such as his Oscar, suspenders from films, and other acting-related items—were destined for the children. The children say Susan can retain items she and Robin acquired during their marriage but accuse her of overreaching by redefining terms like “jewelry” to exclude key pieces the trust intended for them, and by initially refusing them access to the house after his death.

Friends and those close to Williams express sadness that the family has taken the matter to court rather than resolving it privately, saying Robin would be heartbroken to see the posthumous conflict over objects that reflect his life and work. The case underscores how estate language, sentimental value, and family dynamics can collide after a beloved public figure’s passing.

France will introduce a “right to disconnect” on 1 January, requiring companies with more than 50 employees to negotiate rules or produce a charter defining when staff are not expected to send or respond to work emails or smartphone messages outside contracted hours. The law aims to push back against an “always-on” culture that hides unpaid overtime, intrudes on private life and contributes to stress, burnout, sleeplessness and other health problems linked to excessive information flow. The initiative traces back to a 2015 report by labour minister Myriam El Khomri warning about workplace “info‑obesity,” and is part of a broader package of labour reforms introduced in May.

Supporters, including powerful trade unions, say the measure protects the sanctity of private time in a country already notable for a 35‑hour workweek in place since 2000. If employers and staff cannot agree, firms must set a formal charter of good conduct specifying off‑hours. Some companies have experimented with similar practices—Daimler once offered to delete incoming emails during employees’ holidays.

Experts note tensions: workplace researcher Xavier Zunigo says employees value the autonomy and flexibility that digital devices provide and may resist rigid limits. Academic studies, such as “Exhausted But Unable to Disconnect,” find that the obligation or anticipation to answer messages during off hours produces emotional exhaustion and impedes recovery. Surveys suggest many UK workers continue to check email during breaks, highlighting the wider challenge of changing norms beyond France.

A U.S. appeals court has revived a $10 million lawsuit accusing Justin Bieber and Usher of copying parts of a 2008 song called "Somebody to Love" written by Devin Copeland (stage name De Rico) and Mareio Overton. By a 3-0 decision, the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Richmond overturned a 2014 dismissal by a federal judge and said a reasonable jury could find the songs "intrinsically similar." Circuit Judge Pamela Harris wrote that the choruses are similar and significant, noting the phrase "somebody to love" appears in an "almost identical rhythm and a strikingly similar melody." The appeals court rejected the argument that genre differences (Bieber/Usher's dance-pop vs. Copeland's R&B) preclude infringement. The ruling sends the case back to the lower court for trial; publishers including Universal Music Publishing and Sony/ATV are also defendants. Defense lawyers had no immediate comment.

German officials have confirmed that Gudrun Burwitz, the daughter of Heinrich Himmler, worked for West Germany’s foreign intelligence agency (BND) in the early 1960s. Burwitz, who died in May aged 88, was employed as a secretary at the BND’s Pullach headquarters from 1961 until 1963 under an assumed name, BND historian Bodo Hechelhammer told media after the revelation by Bild. Her dismissal coincided with a shift in West German policy toward staff with Nazi-era ties. At the time the agency was led by Reinhard Gehlen, a former Nazi military intelligence officer.

Burwitz never renounced Nazism and spent much of her life defending her father, who as head of the SS was a central architect of the Holocaust. Captured in 1945 as the Third Reich collapsed, Himmler killed himself while in British custody, avoiding trial. Gudrun, born in 1929, was a teenager when the war ended; she and her mother were detained until 1946 and she testified at some postwar trials. She remained a prominent figure among far-right circles, active in Stille Hilfe (Silent Help), an organization that supported former SS men legally and financially and has been linked to neo-Nazi networks and Holocaust revisionism.

Throughout her life Burwitz attended neo-Nazi gatherings and clandestine reunions of former SS officers, maintained personal mementos of her father, and aided individuals convicted of wartime atrocities. Her association with the BND highlights the broader challenges West German institutions faced in addressing personnel with Nazi pasts during the postwar reconstruction era. Authorities said they were making an exception to their usual policy of not commenting on current or former employees because she had died.

Documents leaked by Edward Snowden and reporting by major outlets reveal that the NSA has been systematically copying and searching vast amounts of cross-border email and text communications, including many Americans’ messages, under authority of the 2008 FISA Amendments Act. Though officials have insisted the agency targets only non‑U.S. persons abroad, the leaked “targeting” and “minimization” procedures—endorsed by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court—allow far broader collection. The NSA not only intercepts communications to or from foreign targets but also searches for messages “about” those targets, such as mentions of an email address or phone number, sweeping up “one‑end‑domestic” exchanges. The agency creates temporary clones of selected communication links, runs automated keyword or selector searches, retains matches for human review, and deletes the rest; officials say the process is quick and not bulk storage. But computer scientists note reconstructing routed internet traffic requires capturing nearly all cross‑border packets, effectively amounting to mass collection. The Procedures permit presuming targets are foreigners absent contrary evidence, broaden “foreign intelligence” to include diplomatic and foreign‑affairs content, and allow long retention—sometimes indefinite—of communications that are encrypted, contain foreign intelligence, or show criminality. They also permit retention and sharing of purely domestic and even privileged attorney–client communications. Critics warn these rules erode privacy safeguards, enable dragnet surveillance without individualized suspicion, and build extensive databases of Americans’ communications.

Researchers have measured the mass and density of Kepler-78b, an Earth-sized exoplanet that orbits a Sun-like star every 8.5 hours. Using Doppler radial-velocity observations from two teams—one with HARPS-N and another with Keck/HIRES—scientists independently found a radius of about 1.20 Earth radii and masses of roughly 1.69–1.86 Earth masses. These values yield a mean density near 5.3–5.6 g cm−3, essentially matching Earth’s density and implying a rocky composition with an iron core. Kepler-78b lies extremely close to its star—about 1% of the Earth–Sun distance—giving surface temperatures near 2,000 °C, making it uninhabitable. Its existence is puzzling: standard formation models argue it could not have formed in place inside the star, nor plausibly migrated inward without falling into the star, so its origin remains enigmatic. The planet’s orbit is decaying, and it will likely be destroyed by stellar tides within a few billion years. Although too hot for life, Kepler-78b is important because it demonstrates that Earth-sized, Earth-composition planets exist beyond the Solar System. The result marks a milestone toward identifying true Earth analogs, and upcoming missions like TESS aim to find small transiting planets around nearby, lower-mass stars where masses and potentially habitable conditions will be easier to assess.

Researchers argue that the 3,700-year-old Babylonian clay tablet Plimpton 322 (P322) contains the earliest and a distinct form of trigonometry, predating Greek contributions by over a millennium. Found in southern Iraq and now at Columbia University, the tablet’s four columns and 15 rows of cuneiform numerals were long known to display Pythagorean triples—integer sets satisfying a^2 + b^2 = c^2—but its purpose remained debated. Daniel Mansfield and Norman Wildberger of UNSW reexamined P322, reconstructing damaged entries and interpreting the tablet through an Old Babylonian mindset that prioritized exact numerical ratios. They propose P322 is a ratio-based trigonometric table: instead of angles and approximated sines and cosines, it lists exact ratios of the short side to the long side and to the hypotenuse for right triangles, using Babylonian base-60 arithmetic that yields many exact fractions. This makes the table, they claim, not only the oldest but also completely accurate for the integer-sided triangles it records and potentially useful for surveying and construction. The hypothesis is mathematically plausible and pedagogically attractive, suggesting an alternative, simpler way to teach triangles. However, several historians and specialists call the interpretation speculative; no contemporaneous texts confirm such practical use, and critics argue the tablet may instead be a parameters list for scribal schools. Further study of other Babylonian tablets is needed to confirm the new reading.

Investigators examining the crash of Germanwings Flight 9525 say audio from the cockpit voice recorder supports the theory that co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately locked Captain Patrick Sondenheimer out of the cockpit and initiated a fatal descent into the French Alps, killing all 150 aboard. German tabloid Bild published a purported summary of the recorder’s transcript, though French investigators and the BEA accident agency condemned the leak as a breach of protocol and “voyeurism.” The full audio has not been officially released.

According to the published summary, the flight departed Barcelona 20 minutes late and reached cruising altitude before the captain asked Lubitz to prepare for landing. Lubitz reportedly told him he “can go anytime,” then the captain left the cockpit. Sounds indicate the captain’s seat moving back and the cockpit door clicking shut. Shortly thereafter the aircraft entered a steady descent. Air traffic controllers lost contact and automated alarms—“sink rate” and later “terrain—pull up!”—sounded. The transcript describes the captain banging and pleading: “For God’s sake, open the door!” and “Open the damn door!” Passengers’ screams and the sounds of attempts to breach the door are reported, followed by a wing scraping a mountainside and a final burst of screaming. Investigators recovered the cockpit voice recorder, but the flight data recorder remains missing, leaving unanswered technical questions.

Authorities have focused on Lubitz’s state of mind. Prosecutors say they found torn sick notes in his Düsseldorf apartment, including one for the day of the crash, and media reports—citing unnamed sources—allege prior treatment for depression, anxiety, and possible vision issues that could have threatened his career. Germanwings and medical officials note routine certification tests emphasize physical, not psychological, screening; the airline said it had not been informed of any incapacity.

The leak and rapid media speculation prompted calls for restraint. Airbus chairman Tom Enders criticized sensational TV commentary; European pilot associations and investigators warned against drawing firm conclusions until the flight recorder is recovered and formal inquiries conclude. In Lubitz’s hometown, clergy and residents expressed shock and sympathy for his family even as memorials and grieving continue for the victims.

Al-Qaida leader Ayman al-Zawahri announced the creation of "Al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent" in a 55-minute video released online, declaring the group’s aim to spread Islamic rule and wage jihad across the subcontinent, including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Myanmar. Zawahri presented the new franchise as the result of a two-year effort to unify regional fighters, named Pakistani commander Asim Umar as its field leader, and reaffirmed loyalty to Afghan Taliban leader Mullah Omar. The announcement, packaged by al-Qaida’s As-Sahab media arm and flagged by monitoring group SITE, included incendiary rhetoric from the new group’s spokesman calling Jews and Hindus “apostates” and threatening violence.

Indian states with significant Muslim populations were put on alert and New Delhi’s security apparatus and Home Minister convened to assess the threat, though there were no immediate reports of increased deployments. Analysts say the move is partly propagandistic: al-Qaida is struggling for recruits and relevance against the Islamic State, which has drawn global attention through territorial gains and brutality. India’s under-resourced security services and ongoing conflicts—most notably in Kashmir—create vulnerabilities, but experts note al-Qaida lacks the local depth of longstanding regional militant groups. The Pakistan Taliban distanced itself from rival splinter groups and reiterated allegiance to the Afghan Taliban amid the unfolding announcements.

Clint Bench, born without fully formed arms, has long led an active life—attending college, raising a family, mountain biking, firing a gun and riding roller coasters at Six Flags Over Texas. In May 2012 he says an employee barred him from the Aquaman Splashdown ride, telling him he could not ride because he “does not have hands.” Management cited a policy that riders “must have at least one fully formed arm all the way down to the fingers,” though Bench notes the park’s prior rule required only the ability to grasp—a capability he has. Four months after the incident Six Flags updated its riders’ guide to state riders “must have one full arm.” Bench has sued under the Americans with Disabilities Act, saying the refusal caused embarrassment for him and his children and amounted to discrimination. He seeks damages for suffering and mental anguish and wants assurances the exclusion won’t recur; Six Flags declined to comment while the lawsuit proceeds.

Ko Young-tae, a former national saber fencer and Asian Games gold medalist, has emerged as a central figure in the scandal that led to the impeachment of South Korea’s president, Park Geun-hye. Ko voluntarily went to prosecutors after returning to Korea and underwent about 40 hours of questioning about how confidential materials, including presidential speeches, reached Choi Soon-sil, Park’s longtime confidante. Prosecutors suspect Ko managed companies—The Blue K and Widec Sports—set up by Choi in Korea and Germany, allegedly used to divert funds from the Mir and K-Sports foundations. Details of the interrogation were not released.

Ko’s background is unusual: after retiring from sports he worked at high-end Gangnam host bars, where male hosts serve female patrons. Reports and a former coworker say Ko brought wealthy middle-aged female clients to the bars under the alias Min-woo, and that he and Choi met at one such venue around 2006. With Choi’s help, he launched the fashion brand Villomillo in 2008; the brand gained fame when President Park was seen carrying one of his bags in 2013. Ko supplied Choi—and indirectly Park—with numerous luxury items and bespoke clothing, and cultivated celebrity contacts.

Ko testified publicly and to media that Choi edited presidential speeches, a claim that prompted JTBC to search for and find speech files on a discarded tablet; that discovery was pivotal in escalating the crisis. Ko also revealed CCTV footage showing Choi behaving as if she had authority over presidential aides. In dramatic testimony he recounted how a 2014 quarrel with Choi over her daughter’s puppy—after he left the dog alone while golfing—spurred him to turn evidence over to the press, including videos and documents, which ultimately exposed Choi’s influence and helped trigger mass outrage, investigations, and Park’s impeachment. Ko denies being romantically involved with Choi, calling her a friend, and says he has no regrets for whistleblowing.

At the Cannes Lions festival, author Michael Wolff predicted President Trump’s removal and warned that if Vice President Mike Pence ascended to the presidency, “the media business goes into a deep depression,” calling Pence “literally the most boring person on Earth.” Wolff’s comments amplified attention on Pence’s public persona and private habits—most notably reports that he calls his wife Karen “Mother.” Rolling Stone and several attendees of a 2013 dinner at the Indiana governor’s mansion recounted Pence repeatedly addressing Karen as “Mother,” an oddity that drew surprise and skepticism; Pence’s office denied the claim. The broader portrait of Pence detailed here is unflattering: a deeply conservative politician whose governorship featured controversial stances—opposition to needle exchanges during an HIV outbreak, support for stringent anti-abortion measures, backing a divisive Religious Freedom Restoration Act that provoked economic backlash, and questionable handling of an East Chicago lead crisis. Critics describe Pence as ideologically driven, tone-deaf to marginalized communities, prone to rigid talking points, and politically calculating, yet effective at appealing to social conservatives—qualities that made him an attractive vice-presidential pick for Trump. The piece warns that Pence’s steady conservative agenda, combined with greater power, could have sweeping consequences for women, LGBTQ people, the poor, and public-health policy if he were to assume the presidency.

Former President George H.W. Bush, 92, and his wife Barbara, 91, were hospitalized at Houston Methodist Hospital. George H.W. Bush was placed in the intensive care unit for an acute respiratory issue related to pneumonia; doctors performed an unspecified airway-clearing procedure requiring sedation. Hospital officials said he was stable and resting but would remain in ICU for observation. Barbara Bush was admitted as a precaution after fatigue and coughing. Bush’s chief of staff, Jean Becker, earlier confirmed he was “fine” and expected to be discharged in a few days. President Obama offered prayers and support, calling the couple “as fine a couple as we know.” The report noted Bush’s recent health history, including falls and prior respiratory hospitalizations.

A Quinnipiac University national poll from June 24–30, 2014, of 1,446 registered voters finds troubling ratings for President Barack Obama. Thirty-three percent call him the worst president since WWII, narrowly ahead of George W. Bush at 28 percent; Ronald Reagan is named the best (35 percent). Voters are divided on whether Obama has been better than Bush (39 percent better, 40 percent worse). By party, Democrats overwhelmingly rate Obama positively while Republicans overwhelmingly disapprove. Fifty-four percent say the Obama administration is not competent running government; 48 percent believe he does not pay enough attention to his administration. Job approval stands at 40 percent approve / 53 percent disapprove, largely unchanged from earlier in 2014. Obama receives negative ratings on the economy, foreign policy, health care and terrorism, but positive marks on the environment. Notably, 45 percent of voters say the nation would be better off if Mitt Romney had won in 2012, while 38 percent disagree — a view concentrated among Republicans and some independents. Overall, the poll highlights eroding support across age groups and issues.

E! News and other outlets reported that 18-year-old singer Demi Lovato and 36-year-old actor Ryan Phillippe were secretly involved for a few months in mid-2011. Sources described their liaison as initially “hot and heavy” but casual, and said things cooled after Phillippe’s ex, Alexis Knapp, gave birth to a daughter in early July — news Lovato reportedly didn’t learn until it happened. Lovato’s promotion of her single “Skyscraper” also consumed her attention. Representatives hadn’t commented; one source close to Phillippe denied a relationship.

The Book of Eli is a grim, stylized post-apocalyptic action-drama directed by the Hughes brothers and led by Denzel Washington as the enigmatic, battle-hardened Eli. Wandering a desolate, gray wasteland decades after civilization collapsed, Eli protects a leather-bound King James Bible he regards as divinely important. His quiet, monosyllabic demeanor conceals formidable fighting skills and a ruthless streak: he defends the book and himself with a lethal machete, indifferent at times to innocent suffering. Gary Oldman plays Carnegie, an over-the-top, power-hungry tyrant who rules a re-populated ghost town and obsessively seeks the book to bolster his control; Mila Kunis is Solara, Carnegie’s adopted daughter who flees with Eli, though critics find her miscast and too glamorous for the world. The film’s strengths are its moody visual design, occasional kinetic combat, and Washington’s imposing presence. Yet many reviewers judge it ponderous, heavy-handed in its religious message, and uneven in tone—too brutal to inspire and too slow to satisfy as pure action. Some praise a noteworthy twist near the end, but overall the movie is likened to a handsome, overextended music video or an unwritten graphic novel realized on screen.

A Fort Worth man, identified as 35-year-old Cary Joseph Heath, was arrested on a capital murder charge after two neighbors were found fatally shot early Sunday morning in a south Fort Worth neighborhood. Officers responding to a 4 a.m. robbery report on the 800–900 block of Buffalo Springs Drive discovered two bodies outside the home. Witnesses described hearing multiple gunshots and said the shooter used an assault-style rifle and emptied a magazine, killing two longtime residents. Heath, who lived nearby, was detained the next day at Permenter Middle School in Cedar Hill — where he was employed as a first-year eighth-grade science teacher and a 13-year Air Force veteran — and booked on $1 million bond. The school district placed him on administrative leave and notified parents, though some reported not receiving the alert and expressed alarm that an alleged murderer had been around students. Police have not released a motive or the victims’ identities and initially detained another man for questioning who was not arrested. The investigation was ongoing at the time of reporting.

Sen. Scott Brown, speaking on Boston radio WZLX, joked he was “thank God” Elizabeth Warren didn’t “take her clothes off” to pay for college after Warren, in a Democratic primary debate, contrasted her path—borrowing and working through public school—with Brown’s disclosure that he posed nude for Cosmopolitan in the 1980s to earn money. Brown laughed with the host and defended his own choices and upbringing, saying he went to the “school of hard knocks” and did what he had to do to pay for school. The exchange touched off criticism from Massachusetts Democrats, who called Brown’s remarks gutter politics and demeaning to accomplished women. Warren, a Harvard Law professor who attended University of Houston and Rutgers Law after two years at George Washington University, declined to comment; Brown noted both have been targeted by jabs in the campaign. The incident could hurt Brown’s standing with female voters as he seeks reelection in a heavily Democratic state.

Six-year-old Jacob Hall, who died after being shot Sept. 28 at Townville Elementary School, was honored with superhero-themed memorials that reflected his personality and faith. Jacob remained on life support for three days after the shooting before passing away; the accused 14-year-old gunman has had charges upgraded to murder and faces multiple other counts. Jacob’s mother, Renae Hall, told reporters that her son “wanted to save everybody,” loved the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles and God, and taught her about faith. She planned a nontraditional funeral: Jacob would be dressed in a superhero costume, pallbearers including his uncles and brothers would also wear superhero attire, and attendees were invited to come in costumes or superhero shirts so the service wouldn’t frighten the many children expected to attend.

Visitation was held at Oakdale Baptist Church, followed by a public funeral service where the small casket rested before the altar amid photos and toys. Community members, children and adults alike came dressed as Batman, Superman, Ninja Turtles and other heroes; a Batmobile even traveled from West Virginia for the service. Teachers wore handmade blue capes bearing a Ninja Turtle face and Jacob’s name; his casket featured Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle stickers and figurines. Clergy and family celebrated Jacob’s life, noting his desire to preach and help others, and emphasized forgiveness — Renae Hall said she forgives the accused shooter, believing Jacob would have wanted that.

The Townville community held a balloon release and observed a district-wide moment of silence. Schools planned a Superhero Day in his honor, and officials postponed return to Townville Elementary briefly after the shooting. Jacob’s family and community framed the memorials as a joyful celebration of a boy remembered for kindness, faith and a desire to help others.

Burger King is replacing its 40-year-old slogan “Have It Your Way” with a new tagline, “Be Your Way,” rolling it out across U.S. marketing, including a TV ad. The chain says the new line emphasizes personal expression and lifestyle — encouraging people to live how they want and embrace imperfection — rather than focusing solely on purchase customization. Fernando Machado, senior VP of global brand management, explained the shift aims to move the brand from a functional promise about ordering toward a stronger emotional connection with consumers. The tagline, developed with agency DAVID (WPP), will replace the more recent “Taste Is King” and eventually be used globally; Burger King had already not actively used “Have It Your Way” in the U.S. for some time. Observers note the move follows a trend among fast-food chains to appear hip and culturally relevant, like Taco Bell’s “Live Mas.” But critics warn brands can seem inauthentic trying to be cool, and it’s unclear whether the change will improve Burger King’s long-term image or sales as it competes with rivals and changing consumer preferences favor perceived fresher, higher-quality food. The company’s U.S. same-store sales barely rose 0.1% in the latest quarter.

Marine experts off Sydney carried out a daring, first-of-its-kind rescue to save a critically endangered grey nurse shark that was being choked by an elastic cord wrapped around its gills like a noose. Spotted off Magic Point, a known critical shark habitat, the animal’s labored breathing signaled it was slowly dying. A team from SeaLife sanctuary and aquarium, including divers and a veterinarian, used a clear-plastic “shark sock” to coax and contain the shark. The see-through sock even attracted other sharks, complicating the operation, and rescuers had to wrestle the injured animal into a specialized stretcher. Bringing the shark to the surface, veterinarian Rob Jones cut away the elastic and administered antibiotics to prevent infection. SeaLife’s Rob Townsend cautioned about the dangers of handling wild sharks, noting their constantly visible, sharp teeth. Jones said intervention was essential—without it the cord would have cut deeper into the neck and almost certainly caused death. After treatment the shark swam away; officials expect the serious-looking wound to heal within about a month. With only roughly 1,500 grey nurse sharks left off Australia’s coast, saving even a single individual is significant. The rescue was captured on video by 7News Sydney and highlighted by outlets covering rare and dramatic marine wildlife stories.

President Obama signed a law awarding the Congressional Gold Medal to over 6,000 Nisei veterans — members of the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, the 100th Battalion, and the Military Intelligence Service — who fought for the U.S. in World War II while many of their families were interned. The 442nd became the most decorated unit of its size, famed for rescues like the “Lost Battalion,” despite suffering heavy losses.

The University of Mississippi Medical Center (UMMC) has uncovered extensive unmarked graves on its 164‑acre campus, revealing a tragic legacy tied to the Mississippi State Lunatic Asylum (opened 1855). Radar and excavations discovered dozens of coffins in 2012 and 2013, then roughly 1,000 graves when planning a parking garage east of the dental school; further surveys suggest at least 2,000 coffins and estimates as high as 7,000 burials across about 20 acres. The graves likely include asylum patients, paupers, members of a nearby Black church, tuberculosis victims, and possibly Civil War dead. The finds complicate UMMC expansion: projects such as a proposed parking garage, an American Cancer Society Hope Lodge, and a Children’s Justice Center may need relocation. Exhumation and reburial would cost about $3,000 per body—potentially $21 million—so UMMC is considering an in‑house program costing roughly $400,000 annually over years, plus creation of a memorial, visitors’ center and research lab. The Asylum Hill Research Consortium—anthropologists, archaeologists, historians and other experts—proposes respectful study, DNA registry efforts, and public records. Past research on 66 exhumed coffins has yielded insights into nutrition, disease and oral microbiomes. Descendants and advocates seek identification and dignified treatment of the remains; scholars hope the site becomes a national resource for historical health research and remembrance.

Arron Hughes, a 28-year-old forklift driver from Ruthin, North Wales, stunned friends and authorities by swimming across the Colorado River at the base of the Hoover Dam while on a stag do in Las Vegas. On a 37-hour drinking binge in temperatures around 45–50°C, Hughes impulsively jumped from the 725–726ft-high structure and swam from Arizona to Nevada and back. He estimated the crossing took about 30 minutes and described the view from underneath the dam as “a hell of a sight.” He wore trainers during the swim and said he was driven partly by adrenaline and the encouragement of his companions.

Hughes survived a perilous feat that has claimed many lives at the site; police later noted 275 deaths at the dam in the last decade and that no one had previously survived swimming across its breadth. He escaped being pulled under only because nine of the ten hydroelectric turbines were not operating at the time — one working turbine nearly dragged him in. Police awaited him as he climbed the steep rocky bank; he was handcuffed, taken to the dam office and fined $330 (£250) for “Jumping, diving, swimming from dam’s spillways or other structures.”

Hughes said he hadn’t seen prohibition signs and didn’t realize the danger; his tattoo, “no regrets,” and his penchant for stunts reflect his thrill-seeking nature. The Guinness World Records contacted him but require an adjudicator to validate such a claim, and Hughes refused to attempt the swim again. Reactions have been mixed: friends call him a legend, his mother calls him an idiot, and his father laughed and congratulated him.

New England Patriots receiver Julian Edelman reported a school-shooting threat he spotted in his Instagram comments, leading to the arrest of a 14-year-old in Port Huron, Michigan. While visiting former teammate Danny Amendola in Texas late last month, Edelman received a direct message alerting him to a comment under one of his posts that said a kid planned to "shoot up a school." With the recent memory of the Parkland, Florida, massacre fresh and having become a parent himself, Edelman said he felt compelled to act immediately. He contacted authorities to report the threat.

Port Huron police investigated and located the teen, who admitted to posting the threat aimed at Central Middle School. Officers also recovered two rifles at the boy’s home; police said the weapons belonged to the boy’s grandfather. The 14-year-old has been charged with making a false report of a terrorist threat, a felony punishable by up to four years, and is being held at the Macomb County Juvenile Justice Center. The case underscores how social-media posts can prompt rapid law-enforcement responses, particularly in the wake of high-profile school shootings, and highlights concerns about juvenile access to firearms kept in family homes. The incident began with a concerned tip to a public figure and concluded with intervention by police that prevented a potential violent threat from progressing.

Starbucks announced it will move production of its Ethos bottled water out of California to Pennsylvania over the next six months, citing California’s historic drought and a desire to help conserve local water resources. The company said it is looking for a new West Coast water source and will cut store water use in California by more than 25 percent. The move responds to scrutiny after reports that Ethos water for the Western U.S. was sourced from private springs in Baxter and bottled at a Merced plant—areas classified as facing “exceptional drought.” Starbucks defended its practices by noting the springs are not used for municipal supply, while critics and local officials warn spring extraction can affect downstream users and that groundwater regulation and transparency in California are limited. Starbucks donates 5 cents per Ethos bottle to its Ethos Water Fund and says it has distributed more than $12 million for water and sanitation projects since acquiring Ethos in 2005. The decision comes as California imposes mandatory urban water reductions amid a fourth year of drought and as local tensions rise over bottlers extracting scarce groundwater for profit.

Skin cancer is the most common cancer, and although melanoma makes up less than 2% of skin cancers, it causes the majority of skin cancer deaths. U.S. estimates for 2015 put new melanoma cases at roughly 73,000–74,000 and deaths near 10,000. Lifetime melanoma risk varies by race (about 1 in 40 for whites, 1 in 1,000 for blacks, 1 in 200 for Hispanics) and rises with age, though melanoma can occur in younger people as well. Major risk factors include ultraviolet (UV) exposure, pale skin, a family history of skin cancer, many or unusual moles, previous severe sunburns, and a weakened immune system. Early detection dramatically improves outcomes, and clinicians advise monitoring for changes in moles and other suspicious skin findings.

Because total body mole (naevus) count is an important marker of melanoma risk—each additional mole may raise risk by about 2–4%—researchers from King’s College London assessed whether mole counts on a small, accessible body area could predict total-body counts, simplifying risk assessment in primary care. Using data from 3,594 female Caucasian twins in the TwinsUK study (1995–2003) and replicating findings in a broader case-control dataset, trained nurses recorded moles across 17 body sites. The right arm emerged as the single most predictive proxy for total-body mole burden: women with more than seven moles on the right arm were about nine times more likely to have over 50 moles on the whole body, and those with more than 11 on the arm were more likely to exceed 100 total moles—levels associated with substantially higher melanoma risk. The area above the right elbow and the legs were also strongly predictive; in men, back counts were informative.

Authors suggest that counting moles on an easily reachable site like the arm could help GPs quickly flag patients at highest risk for closer monitoring. Experts caution, however, that mole number is one of several important risk elements—genetic factors and mole appearance (e.g., dysplastic nevi) remain crucial in comprehensive risk evaluation. Overall, the study offers a practical tool to streamline melanoma risk screening in primary care.

Nelson Mandela’s daughters, Makaziwe and Zenani, supported by several grandchildren, have filed a Johannesburg High Court application to remove George Bizos, Tokyo Sexwale and Bally Chuene as directors of two companies, Harmonieux and Magnifique. The firms were reportedly set up by Mandela’s former lawyer Ismail Ayob to channel proceeds from sales of Mandela’s handprints—estimated at over R15 million (about $1.7 million)—for the benefit of Mandela’s family. The applicants allege Bizos, Sexwale and Chuene were never properly appointed by the shareholder via resolution, refused requests to resign, and failed to act with due care, skill and diligence. Makaziwe accuses Chuene of unlawfully registering himself and others as directors. Bizos and Sexwale deny wrongdoing, insisting their appointments reflected Mandela’s wishes; they plan to challenge the application. The Mandela Foundation said it was unaware of the filing.

Since September, allegations that longtime team physician Larry Nassar sexually abused athletes during medical treatments have exploded into a major legal and institutional crisis. At least 140 women and girls have filed lawsuits and about 120 have reported Nassar to police; many suits name Michigan State University (MSU), USA Gymnastics and former employees. Eight suits entered a 90-day court-ordered mediation in September; plaintiffs and nearly all defendants (except USA Gymnastics) have jointly asked to extend mediation 30 days to Dec. 6 while negotiators continue “significant work” and report “substantial progress.” The mediator, Jon Muth, told the judge more remains to be done.

Nassar, who worked with USA Gymnastics from the mid-1990s and at MSU for decades, was fired by MSU after investigative reporting by the Indianapolis Star prompted dozens to come forward. He has pleaded guilty to federal child pornography charges and faces a Dec. 7 sentencing; he also faces 22 state sexual-assault charges that could carry life sentences. Prominent gymnasts including Aly Raisman, McKayla Maroney and Jamie Dantzscher have publicly accused Nassar. Raisman detailed abuse beginning at age 15 in a 60 Minutes interview and in her upcoming memoir, and has criticized USA Gymnastics’ culture and handling of complaints.

MSU’s legal costs have surged: as of Oct. 3, five outside firms billed $4.17 million for 6,812 hours, with top firms charging high hourly rates and single invoices in the hundreds of thousands. USA Gymnastics has itself undergone leadership change and reform: CEO Steve Penny resigned; Kerry Perry will begin Dec. 1; the federation adopted all 70 recommendations from a Deborah Daniels review and has supported creation of the U.S. Center for SafeSport. The litigation and institutional reforms continue as more victims are expected to join suits and accountability efforts proceed.

Newly released court documents from Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou’s bail hearing paint a detailed picture of her ties to Vancouver and outline elements of the defence she and Huawei plan to use if she is extradited to the U.S. Meng was arrested in Vancouver on Dec. 1 at U.S. request on charges accusing her of misleading banks about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom, a company alleged to have facilitated transactions with Iran in violation of U.S. sanctions. She remains in custody as bail proceedings continue.

Affidavits by Meng and her husband disclose two Vancouver properties—one on West 28th Ave. and another on Matthews St.—and describe a 15-year family connection to the city: children who attended school there, summers spent by family members, and plans to reside at the 28th Ave. home if released. The couple offered home equity as bail collateral. Meng cited health concerns, including treatment for hypertension, and argued she is not a flight risk, stressing her reputational stake in Huawei and intent to contest U.S. charges at trial.

Defense filings challenge the U.S. narrative that Huawei controlled Skycom and that Meng knowingly misled banks, noting the prosecution’s reliance on a September 3, 2013 PowerPoint prepared by others. Huawei’s submissions cite compliance reviews, interactions with U.S. regulators, KPMG statements in its annual report, and lack of civil suits or indictments against Huawei by U.S. banks. Crown prosecutors counter that Meng has vast resources, limited meaningful ties to Canada, and citizenship in a country without U.S./Canada extradition, arguing flight risk. Bail hearings are ongoing in B.C. Supreme Court amid diplomatic tensions between China, Canada and the U.S.

On May 4 in Rogersville, Tennessee, 9-year-old Carlie Marie Trent was taken from her elementary school by her 57-year-old uncle by marriage, Gary Simpson, who signed her out under false pretenses. Authorities say Simpson falsely told school staff that Carlie’s father had been in an accident. After removing her, Simpson was captured on security video shopping at a Rogersville Walmart and a Save-A-Lot, buying items investigators say indicate premeditation and intent to hide: a pink and purple plush throw, a green men’s shirt, black men’s pants, girls’ khaki pants, two shades of lipstick and nail polish, a pink folding camp chair, a purple child-sized nightgown, a bikini, girls’ underwear multipack, and nonperishables. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI) says the purchases point to an isolated campsite or rural hideout and warns that Carlie is in imminent danger.

An Amber Alert remains active in East and Middle Tennessee; a Missouri Amber Alert issued after an unconfirmed sighting was later canceled. The pair were last seen in a white 2002 Dodge conversion van, Tennessee tag 173GPS. TBI spokesman Josh DeVine emphasized the seriousness of the case, rejecting social-media theories that Simpson was protecting Carlie and urging the public to trust investigators. More than 1,200 leads across 19 states have been received but no credible sightings confirmed. Rewards totaling at least $25,000 have been offered—$10,000 from two Knoxville banking executives, $10,000 from Carlie’s pediatrician, and $5,000 from the U.S. Marshals.

Carlie is described as 4'8", 75 lbs., blond hair and blue eyes. Simpson is about 5'10", 157 lbs., balding with brown hair. Anyone with information is urged to call 1-800-TBI-FIND, the Rogersville Police Department at (423) 272-7555, or 911 if the vehicle is spotted. Authorities and the family continue an urgent search.

The Supreme Court, in a 5-4 decision, granted Texas’s request to pause a lower court’s ruling that had invalidated two congressional districts and several state House districts across four counties for allegedly diluting minority voters’ influence. By freezing the lower court’s judgment, the Court allowed Texas to keep its current electoral maps in place while the case proceeds on appeal, making it likely the disputed districts will be used in the 2018 midterm elections. The one-paragraph order offered no reasoning; the Court’s four liberal justices—Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Breyer, Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan—said they would have denied the stay. The outcome was hailed as a temporary victory by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who argued redrawing lines so close to election deadlines would “throw the electoral process in disarray.” Voting-rights attorneys and civil-rights groups criticized the move as unjust, saying the legislature’s maps failed to reflect the state’s growing Hispanic population and likely reduced minority electoral power.
