Experts note the narrow 5-4 split suggests challengers face a difficult path before the full Court, and observers pointed to the influence of Justice Neil Gorsuch’s recent addition, which likely prevented a 4-4 split that would have left the stay denied. The decision continues a broader series of federal rulings this year finding Texas policies discriminatory in redistricting and voting regulations.

A Boston-area man, 27-year-old Daniel Morley of Topsfield, Massachusetts, was arrested after police discovered a cache of weapons and suspected bomb-making materials in his home on June 9. A recently unsealed 25-page affidavit says Morley possessed a large stainless-steel pressure cooker, black powder, igniters, metal fragments including ball bearings, hundreds of rounds of ammunition, an assault rifle, a handgun, and other disturbing items such as dismantled cell phones, flex-cuff restraints, a shoebox containing a decapitated bird’s head, and a stabbed, burned stuffed animal. Morley allegedly threatened to hijack an airplane or ship and to burn down his mother’s house; he also is accused of assaulting his mother and her boyfriend. His mother told police he had these materials before the April Boston Marathon bombing, and she said Morley once claimed his best friend bragged about knowing Tamerlan Tsarnaev, one of the Marathon bombing suspects. The FBI Joint Terrorism Task Force is investigating possible influences on Morley and whether any links exist to the Marathon attack, though no connection has been established. A stylized drawing found in his room resembled part of the Boston skyline with an airplane and a figure. Morley was taken into custody after a standoff, is undergoing psychiatric evaluation at Bridgewater State Hospital, and faces multiple charges; additional charges may follow.

The Nunes memo, produced by House Intelligence Committee staff under Chairman Devin Nunes, alleges significant abuses by the Department of Justice and FBI in their use of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) during the 2016 campaign, particularly in obtaining surveillance on former Trump campaign adviser Carter Page. The White House, after review and consultation with intelligence and Justice Department officials, declassified and released the memo, despite FBI warnings that key facts were omitted. The memo asserts the FBI relied heavily on the Steele dossier—compiled by former British agent Christopher Steele and funded by the Democratic National Committee and the Clinton campaign via Fusion GPS and Perkins Coie—while failing to disclose the dossier’s political origins and Steele’s payments to the FISC. It accuses the FBI of omitting information that could be favorable to Page, including Steele’s media contacts, unauthorized disclosures, and bias against Trump documented by Bruce Ohr and others. The memo notes Steele’s source reliability was minimally corroborated, yet his material was crucial to FISA applications and renewals signed by senior officials. It also highlights concerns about agents’ bias, citing texts between FBI officials Peter Strzok and Lisa Page and alleged discussions of “insurance” against a Trump presidency, arguing these issues undermined the integrity of the FISA process.

Comedian Arsenio Hall has filed a defamation lawsuit against singer Sinead O’Connor, seeking at least $5 million in damages after she posted a Facebook rant accusing him of supplying Prince with illegal drugs for decades and of spiking O’Connor herself years ago. The suit, filed in Los Angeles by attorneys Marty Singer and Lynda Goldman, calls O’Connor a “desperate attention-seeker” and says her assertions are “outlandish defamatory lies.” Hall flatly denies ever providing drugs to Prince or having supplied or spiked O’Connor, and notes he has not had contact with O’Connor in 25 years. The complaint frames O’Connor’s post as part of a pattern of media antics and inflammatory social-media behavior intended to attract attention. The filing emphasizes that Hall was falsely characterized in the Facebook post, which labeled him as Prince’s and Eddie Murphy’s “bitch” and alleged long-term involvement in hard drug use by Prince. Hall is pursuing special damages of no less than $5 million, asserting that the false accusations harmed his reputation. The suit seeks to hold O’Connor legally accountable for what Hall’s lawyers describe as malicious and defamatory statements.

Martin Tripp, a former Tesla process technician at the Gigafactory in Nevada, has filed a federal counterclaim accusing Tesla and CEO Elon Musk of defamation and retaliation after the company sued him for alleged hacking, theft, and leaking internal information. Tripp, who says he earned $28 an hour, maintains he was a whistleblower concerned about safety, environmental waste, and quality control—not a “saboteur.” His filing reiterates earlier claims that Tesla generated excessive scrap and reused discarded battery parts, including punctured cells allegedly reworked with glue and returned to production without proper inspections. Tripp alleges the factory’s Manufacturing Operating System (MOS) logged $150–200 million in scrap from January to mid-May 2018 and that tracking systems were disabled, undermining part traceability.

Tesla responded publicly in June by accusing him of running programs that exfiltrated data and by asserting a tip from an anonymous “friend” warned Tripp might threaten violence; law enforcement found no credible threat. Tripp denies hacking (says he can’t code), denies violent intent, and contends Tesla never reasonably verified the alleged tipster. He also challenges Musk’s tweets implying bribery between Tripp and a reporter. Tripp claims the company’s actions and public statements led to threats against him and damaged his reputation; he seeks at least $1 million plus punitive damages for defamation, invasion of privacy, and emotional distress.

The dispute unfolds while Tesla faces intense production and financial pressures amid the Model 3 ramp-up. Tesla has disputed Tripp’s technical assertions and has not publicly responded to the new counterclaim.

Augustus “Gus” Lee, a 20-year-old redshirt freshman defensive back for the University of Richmond and a 2017 Paul VI Catholic High School graduate, was found dead in his snow-covered car near campus on Dec. 11. The Virginia Office of the Chief Medical Examiner ruled the death a suicide by asphyxiation. Lee’s family will donate his brain to the VA–Boston University–Concussion Legacy Foundation Brain Bank, which holds more than 650 specimens for research into traumatic brain injury and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). His mother, Phyllis Lee, said she wondered whether brain injury from contact sports could explain his uncharacteristic actions, noting he had sustained concussions as a youth, including one in middle school that left him unconscious and sidelined for months.

Lee, a multi-sport athlete at Paul VI who played football, lacrosse and track, walked on at Richmond after considering Cornell and Delaware. He transitioned from wide receiver to defensive back, earned special teams playing time, was named MVP of the spring intrasquad scrimmage, and appeared in all 11 games that season. Coaches and teammates remembered him as driven, team-oriented and athletic; Richmond coach Russ Huesman called his loss a tragedy. Friends, including NFL quarterback and former Richmond teammate Kyle Lauletta, paid tribute.

During the season Lee struggled with homesickness and fatigue; midway through he returned home with bronchitis and later reported loneliness and appetite loss to his mother. After a late-night call expressing distress, Lee saw a mental health professional who recommended a neurological screening over winter break. He returned to campus to finish finals; when he missed exams and was unreachable, his roommate alerted his parents and police, who located him early the next morning. Lee is survived by his parents, Phyllis and Chris, and siblings Gillian and Jackson; a funeral is planned in Vienna. Researchers and the Concussion Legacy Foundation said the family’s donation will aid athlete and veteran brain-injury research.

Police in Philadelphia and Los Angeles carried out major overnight operations to clear long-running Occupy encampments after city-imposed deadlines passed. In Philadelphia, authorities moved on Dilworth Plaza around 1 a.m.; crews used heavy equipment to clear debris and hoses to wash the site. Protesters marched through Center City in a four-hour, cat-and-mouse trek—crashing through barricades, confronting lines of bike and mounted officers, and documenting clashes on video—before police made about 52 arrests for failure to disperse and obstruction. Officials reported minor injuries to three officers and one protester whose foot was stepped on by a police horse. Mayor Nutter defended the timing, citing minimized disruption and a pending $50 million plaza renovation; outreach workers helped dozens of homeless encampment residents find placements. In Los Angeles, a force of over 1,000 officers raided the two-month camp near City Hall, using helicopters, barricades and legal observers; more than 200 arrests were reported. Authorities said operations were largely peaceful, aimed at public-safety and sanitation concerns, though protesters vowed to continue activism and some risked arrest to resist removal.

Singer Robin Thicke made a very public, emotional push to salvage his marriage to actress Paula Patton in the days after they announced their separation. Performing in Fairfax, Virginia, Thicke opened up to the crowd, revealing that he and Patton had recently separated and saying, “I’m just trying to get her back.” He dedicated the ballad “Lost Without U,” which he noted is Patton’s favorite, to her and visibly struggled through parts of the performance, at times turning away to hide his emotions and even flubbing lyrics while crying. Throughout the show he wore his wedding ring, signaling his desire to reconcile.

Outside the stage moments and media encounters reinforced the same theme. As he arrived in Washington, D.C., Thicke told a TMZ photog he was “just trying to get her back” and insisted he wasn’t giving up on the marriage. Reports indicate he flew to Canada to persuade Patton—who was filming there—to reconsider, but that attempt failed. Sources told outlets that while Thicke was not blindsided by the split and wanted to save the relationship, Patton chose to end it. The couple, high school sweethearts and parents to 3-year-old son Julian, released a joint statement saying they would “always love each other and be best friends,” but had “mutually decided to separate at this time.”

Media coverage has highlighted tensions that emerged after Thicke’s controversial VMAs performance with Miley Cyrus; insiders said Patton felt “utterly disrespected” by his antics, though Thicke denied the incident caused the marital breakdown. Meanwhile, dramatic gestures continued: large floral deliveries appeared at Patton’s Hollywood Hills home the same day Thicke publicly pleaded for reconciliation—actions widely interpreted as his attempts to woo her back. Additionally, a minor car accident involving Patton, her mother, assistant and the couple’s son on Sunset Boulevard was reported; no injuries were reported. Overall, Thicke’s recent public appearances have combined performance, vulnerability and a clear, ongoing effort to reconcile with Patton.

This collection of pieces examines the growing interest in psychedelic drugs—especially practices like microdosing—and the barriers to rigorous research created by drug prohibition. Microdosing, popularized by figures like James Fadiman and practiced by enthusiasts such as Martijn Schirp, involves taking tiny, sub-hallucinogenic amounts of LSD or psilocybin to boost mood, creativity, focus and mindfulness without full psychedelic effects. Proponents describe subtle benefits—improved productivity, kinder behavior, easier entry into flow states, and reduced symptoms of depression or anxiety—but these reports are anecdotal. Scientists emphasize that plausible biological mechanisms exist: classic psychedelics activate the serotonin 5HT-2A receptor, producing broad brain changes at higher doses and potentially therapeutic effects at low, repeated doses. However, no robust clinical trials have yet validated microdosing’s efficacy; subtle effects are particularly vulnerable to placebo influences. Practical challenges and risks persist: illegal sourcing makes doses unreliable, measurement of tiny LSD quantities is difficult, and frequent use every few days could carry unknown long-term consequences. Broader research into cannabis, MDMA and psychedelics has been stifled by 20th-century legal restrictions, argue researchers like David Nutt, who say those laws impede study of therapeutic potentials and of consciousness itself. The result is scarce funding, costly synthesis, and regulatory hurdles, despite historical and emerging evidence of medical benefits. Advocates call for reform to enable controlled, double-blind studies to determine safety and real clinical value.

John Heath, 68, of Bridgewater pleaded not guilty to the 1984 murder of his wife, Elizabeth Gough Heath, after her remains were discovered in 2010 beneath the floor of a barn in Newtown. Heath was arraigned in Danbury Superior Court wearing oxygen tubes and is held on $1 million bond; he was ordered to surrender his passport. Elizabeth, 30, was reported missing April 6, 1984; John initially told police she had left with $600, though friends said she would not have abandoned their 4-year-old daughter. Her body was found wrapped in bedding and placed head-first into a covered well/cistern during barn renovations; the medical examiner ruled homicide from multiple blows to the head, noting a broken forearm consistent with defensive wounds. Investigators secured an arrest warrant after a tip about a moving truck at Heath’s home. Much of the evidence is circumstantial, and forensic options were limited by time and environmental degradation. The case was continued for appointment of a special public defender and further proceedings.

Hope Hicks, who served as White House communications director during President Trump’s first year, has been named executive vice president and chief communications officer for the new, slimmer Fox that will remain after 21st Century Fox completes its $71.3 billion asset sale to Disney. Reporting to Viet Dinh, Fox’s chief legal and policy officer, Hicks will be based in Los Angeles and assumes the role when the Disney deal closes and the company formally becomes “Fox.” Julie Henderson and other senior communications executives opted not to join the spin-off. Also named Monday was Danny O’Brien as executive vice president and head of government relations; O’Brien brings deep Capitol Hill experience, having served as chief of staff to Senators Joe Biden, Robert Menendez and Robert Torricelli and as staff director for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and most recently led government relations for GE Transportation.

Hicks’s hire reinforces longstanding ties between Fox and the Trump orbit: she joined Trump’s campaign in 2015, served as a senior aide in the White House, and testified in House Russia probes before resigning in February. The appointment drew praise from White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders and criticism from watchdogs who say it further aligns Fox with the Trump communications apparatus. Fox’s New Fox will center on broadcast, Fox News and Fox Sports after selling studio and entertainment assets to Disney.

Canadian Francesca Matus, 52, and her American boyfriend, Drew DeVoursney, 36, were found dead in Belize’s Corozal District after disappearing late April. The couple was last seen leaving a bar in Corozal on April 25. They failed to catch planned flights home; Matus was to fly to Toronto and DeVoursney back to Atlanta. A friend, Joseph Milholen, who was to drive Matus to the airport, found both people missing and their white Isuzu Rodeo absent from her home. The vehicle was discovered abandoned in a sugarcane field near Paraiso on Sunday, prompting extended police and volunteer searches. On Monday evening a search party located the bodies in Chan Chen Village at about 5 p.m. Local authorities initially did not release full details; later reports indicated Belize police were investigating the deaths as homicides and that duct tape had been found around the victims’ wrists. Consular officials from Canada and the U.S. have been notified and are assisting families. Friends and relatives expressed shock and grief; Matus, originally from Sault Ste. Marie and wintering in Belize, leaves two adult children. DeVoursney was a retired Marine and veteran reportedly who had served overseas.

JPMorgan Chase disclosed over $2 billion in trading losses from a hedging strategy tied to obscure credit-derivative indexes, with CEO Jamie Dimon warning losses could rise by at least another $1 billion. The positions centered on the Markit CDX NA IG Series 9 (2017) and related indexes; JPMorgan had sold protection (betting on improving credit) and held complex offsets that became costly as markets moved. The illiquid, widely noticed trades—linked to a trader nicknamed the “London whale”—attracted hedge funds betting against JPMorgan, which pushed index levels higher and amplified losses. Estimates of potential further losses vary widely; some models suggested multi-billion-dollar additional losses, though analysts cautioned such projections ignore hedges and market dynamics. The Federal Reserve is reviewing the scope and appropriateness of the chief investment office’s risks. JPMorgan remains profitable with strong capital, and a dividend cut is deemed unlikely, but the episode has raised regulatory and governance concerns. Chief investment officer Ina Drew resigned; more departures are expected as the bank unwinds the complex, large, and poorly timed positions.

The document mixes several unrelated items. First, it describes an Internet Archive initiative to crawl and archive newly created pages and the pages they reference, preserving versions so broken links can be replaced by archived copies and aiming to eliminate 404s for supported “No More 404” sites. Next, it gives a brief Wikipedia-style bio of Aaron Hillel Swartz (1986–2013): a programmer, writer, political organizer and Internet activist who helped develop RSS, co-founded Creative Commons and worked on web.py and Reddit, became a Harvard research fellow on institutional corruption, and founded Demand Progress, known for opposing SOPA. Finally, a media item reports an online appearance of a 13-track gospel album, Sunday Morning, attributed to former Godfather’s Pizza CEO and 2012 candidate Herman Cain; its authenticity was not fully confirmed, though the album reportedly dates from 15 years earlier and was found via the Daily Caller.

Senate leaders signaled optimism Thursday that bipartisan talks could soon resolve two urgent year-end fights: a $1 trillion omnibus spending bill to fund much of the government through next September and a one-year extension of a payroll tax cut affecting 160 million workers. Harry Reid and Mitch McConnell said negotiations were progressing and could conclude “in the next few days,” as Congress raced to avert a partial shutdown at midnight Friday. The White House pressed for action on the payroll tax and unemployment benefits; Democrats dropped a proposed millionaire surtax but still sought offsets and protections for long-term jobless aid. House Republicans advanced an omnibus negotiated in committee and threatened to move without Democratic support, while disputes remained over GOP policy riders—cuts to unemployment benefits, Keystone XL pipeline language, federal pay freezes, Medicare premium increases for higher-income seniors, and Cuba travel rules. Leaders mulled a short-term two-month extension of tax and benefits as a fallback, with many lawmakers predicting a last-minute compromise despite frustration over the process.

Paul Manafort, President Trump’s former campaign chairman, sued the Justice Department Wednesday seeking to void Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein’s May order appointing Robert Mueller as special counsel and challenging charges Mueller’s team brought against him. Manafort’s 17-page complaint, filed in federal court in Washington, argues Rosenstein exceeded his legal authority by authorizing Mueller to investigate “links and/or coordination” between Russia and the Trump campaign and “any matters that arose or may arise directly from” that probe. Manafort’s attorneys say that wording effectively gives Mueller “carte blanche” to pursue unrelated crimes discovered during the investigation.

The suit contends the indictment against Manafort—alleging fraud, conspiracy and money laundering tied to his lobbying and business work for a Russia-friendly Ukrainian party that ended in 2014—has nothing to do with Trump’s 2016 campaign and reaches beyond the special counsel’s original remit. Manafort and deputy Rick Gates have pleaded not guilty and remain under home confinement awaiting trial. The special counsel’s office declined comment; DOJ called the lawsuit “frivolous.” Legal observers noted defendants commonly try to limit special-counsel reach, but such challenges rarely succeed. The filing intensifies efforts by Trump allies to delegitimize the Russia probe, a tactic criticized by some Democrats and Republicans for politicizing law enforcement.

Former SS guard Oskar Gröning, 93, testified during his trial in Lüneburg as an accessory to the murder of at least 300,000 Jews at Auschwitz-Birkenau, describing the camp’s arrival and selection routines while insisting he had no direct role in killings. The charges focus on May–July 1944, when about 137 trains carrying roughly 425,000 Hungarian Jews reached the complex and, prosecutors say, at least 300,000 were sent straight to gas chambers. Gröning, who worked mainly at Auschwitz I but also performed guard duties at Birkenau, told the court the intake process was “orderly” and that the limited capacity of gas chambers and crematoria sometimes required trains to wait “for the sake of order” until the first was fully processed. He acknowledged moral guilt and asked for forgiveness but left criminal guilt to the court; if convicted he could face three to 15 years in prison.

Survivor testimony, notably from Eva Kor, 81, provided a starkly different account. Kor, torn from her family at age 10 and assigned prisoner A-7063, described chaos on arrival—yelling, dogs, families separated—and horrific medical experiments by Josef Mengele, who experimented on twins. Kor recounted the starvation, abuse, blood draws, injections and the loss of many relatives; she emphasized that her forgiveness was a personal act of healing that did not absolve perpetrators of responsibility. Gröning claimed he rarely stood on platforms and did not take part in selections, saying doctors decided who lived or died. The trial examines both his testimony and the broader machinery of extermination that saw about one million Jews killed at Auschwitz during the Holocaust.

Hawaii state Sen. Clayton Hee, chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, says he and Honolulu police have agreed to remove a longstanding exemption in state anti-prostitution law that appeared to allow officers sexual contact with prostitutes. The department told lawmakers it supports explicitly banning sexual penetration by officers while preserving the ability of undercover officers to make verbal offers to solicit sex during investigations. Honolulu Police spokeswoman Teresa Bell emphasized departmental rules already prohibit officers from engaging in sexual activity with prostitutes and that formalizing the ban would not change investigative practice; undercover work typically uses verbal offers rather than actual sexual contact. 

The change follows public outrage after reporting revealed police lobbying to retain language in the bill that would have carved out law enforcement from prostitution prohibitions; police had earlier persuaded the House to remove a clause that would have explicitly outlawed sexual penetration by officers, arguing such language could hamper undercover operations by signaling limits to suspects. At a recent Senate hearing, Hee pledged to close the loophole; the committee version set to advance removes sexual penetration from the exemption while leaving solicitation by officers permitted for investigative purposes. 

Bell said officers who have sexual contact with prostitutes face internal review and possible discipline, though she could not point to recent disciplinary cases. Anti-trafficking advocate Kathryn Xian, who drafted language to change the exemption, said she was surprised by the police agreement but noted the revisions always preserved the ability to solicit verbally. The move aims to align the statute with public expectations and departmental practice.

Rachel Dolezal, the former president of the Spokane NAACP chapter, defended her identification as black in televised interviews amid intense controversy after her white parents publicly contradicted her claims. On NBC’s Today and in an interview with Savannah Guthrie, Dolezal insisted she identifies as black or “transracial,” rejected the label “white,” and questioned whether birth records prove her biological parentage, acknowledging she has never taken a DNA test. She said she has “experimented” with hair and sometimes uses bronzer but denied altering her skin. Family members and others dispute many of her assertions about her upbringing: her parents, Ruthanne and Lawrence Dolezal, say she is of Czech, Swedish and German descent and deny claims that she was born in a tepee or physically abused as a child. Relatives describe a conventional upbringing in rural Montana; her uncle confirmed a tepee existed years before her birth. Dolezal’s past includes attendance at Belhaven College and a master’s from Howard University, where she focused on the black experience in her art and later sued the school for alleged discrimination. She became active in civil-rights work in Idaho and Washington, taught Africana studies, and advised black student groups. Critics, including transracial adoptees and scholars, argue her self-identification misappropriates blackness and trivializes adoption-related “transracial” experiences, while supporters praise some of her advocacy. Questions also surround credibility beyond race: relatives dispute other personal claims, and several police complaints she filed were not substantiated. Dolezal resigned as NAACP chapter president amid the fallout but continued to assert that racial heritage does not solely determine identity.

Summer 2015 will be remembered as a season of high-profile celebrity breakups, and just before Labor Day another pair joined the list: Avril Lavigne and Chad Kroeger have decided to end their marriage after two years together. The announcement came from Lavigne herself via Instagram, where she shared the news with fans. The couple, whose relationship drew substantial media interest partly because Kroeger is widely recognized as the frontman of Nickelback and Lavigne is a longstanding pop-punk star, married in 2013 after a brief courtship. Their union produced extensive coverage, collaborations, and public appearances, and their separation marks another notable split in a summer crowded with celebrity relationship endings. While fans and tabloids have speculated about reasons, the initial news focused simply on the confirmation of the divorce rather than detailed explanations. The timing—right before the Labor Day weekend—meant the announcement was quickly absorbed into a larger narrative about the season’s breakups. As with many celebrity splits, reactions are mixed: some followers expressed surprise and sadness, others referenced the couple’s relatively short marriage, and commentators weighed in on the pressures that fame can place on personal relationships. For now, the main takeaway is that Avril Lavigne and Chad Kroeger have parted ways after two years of marriage, adding another headline to a summer marked by the end of multiple high-profile relationships.

The 2016 ISU World Figure Skating Championships were held March 28–April 3, 2016, in Boston, Massachusetts—the first time the city hosted Worlds. Skaters competed for world titles in men’s singles, ladies’ singles, pairs and ice dance, and the results determined entry quotas for the 2017 World Championships. Organized by U.S. Figure Skating with the Skating Club of Boston as the local committee, the event used TD Garden (competition and many practices) and DCR Steriti Rink (official practice site for credentialed participants). ISU season-best scores were set, and Argentina made history by fielding its first-ever World Championships representative. Eligibility required skaters be at least 15 by July 1, 2015, and achieve minimum technical element scores at international events; nations could enter one to three skaters per discipline based on 2015 Worlds results.

Key outcomes included Evgenia Medvedeva winning the ladies’ title with a record free skate (150.10), Ashley Wagner earning silver—the United States’ first World ladies medal since 2006—and Anna Pogorilaya taking bronze. In ice dance, Gabriella Papadakis and Guillaume Cizeron won their second consecutive world title, setting a free-dance world record (118.17); U.S. teams Maia and Alex Shibutani (silver) and Madison Chock/Evan Bates (bronze) completed the podium, marking a strong U.S. showing. The championships produced a balanced medal distribution across several countries, with Russia, Canada, France, Spain and the United States among the top finishers.

On March 13 in Landover, Md., an apparent unprovoked attack outside the Prince George’s County District III police station left Officer Jacai Colson dead and a suspect wounded. Chief Henry P. Stawinski III said a man approached the station about 4:30 p.m. and opened fire at the first officer he saw; officers returned fire and engaged the shooter. Colson, a 28-year-old undercover narcotics officer and four-year department veteran who would have turned 29 days later, was mortally wounded and pronounced dead at the hospital. The suspected shooter was also wounded and hospitalized in stable condition. Two men, identified by relatives and officials as brothers Malik and Michael Ford of Temple Hills, were taken into custody; police said one fled after the initial shots and both were questioned, though family members disputed their involvement. Authorities called the incident senseless and vowed an aggressive investigation; the FBI and ATF offered assistance. The shooting prompted a temporary shelter-in-place advisory for nearby residents and left the community shaken. Colson was remembered by coaches and colleagues as a high-character leader and “cop’s cop.” Maryland Gov. Larry Hogan ordered flags at half-staff and expressed condolences as investigators continued to probe motive and circumstances.

George A. Romero, the influential writer-director credited as the father of modern horror and the architect of the contemporary zombie genre, died at 77 after a brief, aggressive battle with lung cancer. Romero passed away peacefully in his sleep while listening to the score of his favorite film, The Quiet Man, surrounded by his wife Suzanne Desrocher Romero and daughter Tina, his longtime producing partner Peter Grunwald and manager Chris Roe confirmed. Born in the Bronx in 1940 and raised in Pittsburgh, Romero studied art and design at Carnegie Mellon before launching a low-budget filmmaking career.

His breakthrough came with 1968’s Night of the Living Dead, made for roughly $114,000. The stark, black-and-white picture—initially ignored by mainstream press—became a midnight-screening sensation and established Romero’s signature blend of visceral horror and social commentary. A copyright error cost him profits from that first film, but he continued shaping the genre with Dawn of the Dead (1978), Day of the Dead (1985), Land of the Dead (2005), Diary of the Dead (2007) and Survival of the Dead (2009). Romero also rewrote Night of the Living Dead for a 1990 remake, collaborated with effects artist Tom Savini, and worked with Stephen King on Creepshow and other projects. His recent work included the Marvel graphic novel Empire of the Dead. Tributes noted his reinvention of zombies, influence on geek culture, and enduring filmmaking legacy rooted in Pittsburgh, now often called the “Zombie Capital of the World.”

On Jan. 18 NASA announced that astronaut Jeanette Epps would not fly to the International Space Station in June as previously planned. The reassignment—Epps was to serve as a flight engineer for Expedition 56/57—means she will remain at the Johnson Space Center awaiting future flight opportunities. NASA declined to explain the decision, saying it is a personnel matter and offering no public rationale. Serena Auñón-Chancellor, previously assigned to other expeditions, was named to take the seat.

Epps’s removal drew particular attention because her flight would have marked the first time an African-American served as a long‑duration crewmember aboard the ISS. The abrupt change provoked criticism from Epps’s family, notably her brother Henry, who posted on Facebook accusing NASA of “oppressive racism and misogyny” and promoted a MoveOn.org petition calling for her reinstatement. The petition and family posts sought transparency from NASA; online signers echoed calls for a credible explanation.

Historically, NASA has reassigned astronauts for various reasons—including medical issues, family illnesses, or undisclosed personnel choices. Examples cited include Ken Mattingly’s last‑minute removal from Apollo 13 after rubella exposure and other reassignments like Don Thomas (medical) and Mark Lee (undisclosed). Agency and space‑flight historians note such changes are not unusual and are typically handled quietly.

Epps, a Syracuse native and member of NASA’s 2009 astronaut class, has not yet flown in space. Her background includes physics and aerospace engineering degrees, time as a NASA fellow, work at Ford, and seven years at the CIA.

A 10-year-old Ventura County girl, identified by the coroner as Jasmine Martinez, died Saturday after collapsing at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California. Jasmine had just exited the Revolution roller coaster and returned to the ride station on Friday when she collapsed. Park staff found her breathing but unconscious; she was airlifted to a hospital and later died. Details about why she collapsed were not immediately available, and the coroner said an autopsy will determine the cause of death. It was not immediately known whether she had any pre-existing medical condition.

Magic Mountain initially temporarily closed the Revolution for review after the incident but soon cleared the ride to reopen that same day after state officials determined there was no evidence to suggest the incident was related to ride operation. Later, following Jasmine’s death, the park again closed the attraction while reviewing the incident. Revolution is a high-intensity roller coaster featuring a 90-foot vertical loop and speeds up to 55 mph; park officials noted more than 45 million visitors have safely ridden it since its 1976 opening. A Magic Mountain spokeswoman expressed sadness, offering thoughts and prayers to Jasmine’s family and friends during their difficult time. An autopsy will provide further answers.

Pop star Lady Gaga made several headline-grabbing appearances and newsworthy moves covered in this mixed report. In Silicon Valley she attended an intimate, high-dollar fundraiser for President Barack Obama at Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg’s home, paying to be a guest among tech elites. The event, held under a tent, reportedly charged up to $35,800 per couple; Gaga arrived in a floor-length sleeveless black lace gown with a dramatic bouffant and veil, which added height. A White House pool report noted she sat at a middle table, stood when the President entered, and that Obama spoke for eight minutes without acknowledging her, though they likely crossed paths during earlier greetings. Gaga had previously expressed a wish to discuss bullying with Obama, but it was unclear whether that conversation took place.

Separately, gossip-focused details circulated about Gaga’s flamboyant aesthetic plans: she’s said to have ordered marquise-style diamond tooth implants—continuing a long tradition of flashy musicians adorning their teeth—with a designer noting the forthcoming fittings ahead of a Thierry Mugler Paris show. The piece riffs on celebrity dental fashion, comparing her to others with jeweled teeth and joking about practical downsides.

On a legal and fan-culture front, Gaga pursued a domain dispute over LadyGaga.org, accusing the site’s owner of bad-faith registration. The site’s operator defended it as a noncommercial fan shrine providing free publicity. A National Arbitration Forum panel ruled the owner had a legitimate interest, allowing the fan site to remain.

Finally, the report covers a brief Las Vegas lodging scramble during the iHeartRadio festival: Gaga checked out of the Cosmopolitan seeking a room with a private pool, relocated to The Palms—where she had a prior stay and access to a private recording studio—and continued preparations for festival performances amid reports of organizational confusion around set times and artist arrangements.

A man driving a suspected stolen car led Los Angeles police on a dangerous, live-televised high-speed chase during Monday evening rush hour, striking multiple vehicles, carjacking a woman at gunpoint and crashing repeatedly before officers shot and arrested him in Montebello. The pursuit began shortly after 5 p.m. when officers attempted to stop a vehicle reported stolen. The driver fled, traveling through downtown and southeast L.A. County on freeways and city streets, sometimes driving the wrong way and reaching speeds around 60 mph. Helicopter footage broadcast live showed the car crashing at least six times, skidding into traffic and onto sidewalks, then coming to rest multiple times only for the suspect to exit and attempt further carjackings.

At one point he approached and forced 22-year-old Elizabeth Yarahuan out of her car at gunpoint; she was shaken but uninjured. The suspect stole her vehicle and continued on I-710 and state Route 60 with at least eight LAPD patrol cars and helicopters tracking him. Heavy traffic in Montebello eventually trapped the stolen vehicle. The man jumped out, attempted to seize another SUV and appeared to brandish a gun while fleeing on foot. Officers pursued; as he tried to carjack yet another vehicle, police fired, wounding him. He was handcuffed at the scene and taken to hospital with multiple gunshot wounds; he was alive hours later. Police recovered a semiautomatic firearm. No officers were injured, and officials said the suspect’s reckless actions endangered numerous motorists and bystanders during the chaotic chase.

PEDAL (Play in Education, Development and Learning) is a research centre in the University of Cambridge’s Faculty of Education, launched in October 2015 with funding from the LEGO Foundation. Its mission is to conduct rigorous academic research into the role of play in young children’s education, development and learning, and to translate findings into evidence-based policy and practice. Play—physical, object-based, symbolic, pretend, and rule-governed—is widely enjoyed and believed to support motivation, well-being, creativity and social competence, but PEDAL was created because the empirical evidence for those claims remains limited and under-researched.

The LEGO Foundation endowed the LEGO® Professorship of Play in Education, Development and Learning to lead PEDAL and fund its work in perpetuity. The university sought an outstanding scholar—preferably from educational or developmental psychology with expertise in play—capable of building an internationally leading research programme, directing the new centre, and fulfilling standard professorial duties (teaching, supervision, examination and administration). The professor will shape PEDAL’s agenda, attract a research team, and advance studies that could inform teachers and policymakers about how playful learning may foster 21st-century skills like problem-solving, teamwork and self-control.

The appointment process was supported by Perrett Laver; applicants needed to submit materials and referee details by 20 January 2017. PEDAL emphasizes interdisciplinary, innovative research methods (for example, GPS studies of outdoor play) and aims to fill gaps in the evidence base so play’s educational impacts can be better understood and applied.

State Representative Daniel B. Winslow, a former district court judge and one-time chief legal counsel to Gov. Mitt Romney, officially entered the special U.S. Senate race, becoming the first Republican to declare. The second-term Norfolk lawmaker said he has committed fully to the campaign, contributing $100,000 of his own money toward an estimated $4–6 million fundraising target. Winslow plans to resign next month from his position as senior counsel at Proskauer to focus on the race, and will travel to Washington to meet with Capitol Hill Republicans and the National Republican Senatorial Committee. He emphasized his fiscal conservatism, problem-solving record and support for Second Amendment rights in announcing his candidacy. Several higher-profile Republicans, including Scott Brown, William Weld and Kerry Healey, have ruled out runs; others still considering bids include state Senate Minority Leader Bruce Tarr, Gabriel E. Gomez, Sean Bielat and Jon Fetherston. Democrats Stephen Lynch and Edward Markey are running. Candidates must gather 10,000 certified signatures by Feb. 27 to appear on the April 30 ballot; Winslow intends to use both volunteers and paid staff to meet that requirement.

On Jan. 24, 1961, a B-52 bomber broke apart over Goldsboro, N.C., dropping two MK39 hydrogen bombs with roughly 3.8–4 megaton yields each — weapons hundreds of times more powerful than those used at Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Newly released and declassified documents, detailed in Eric Schlosser’s reporting and the National Security Archive summary, reveal how narrowly a catastrophic detonation was averted. As the bomber disintegrated, one bomb deployed its parachute (Weapon 1) and completed five of six arming steps; a single low-voltage dynamo switch prevented the final firing signal. The other bomb (Weapon 2) fell free‑fall and struck the ground at about 700 mph, burrowing roughly 12 feet. Impact shock rotated its arm/safe indicator to “armed,” but the crash also damaged critical switch contacts so detonation could not occur. Air Force ordnance personnel later discovered Weapon 2’s arm/safe switch in the “arm” position during excavation, prompting immediate changes to switch design. Analysts from Sandia and the National Security Archive emphasize that the sequence of failures and damage left only narrow margins between safety and catastrophe — Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara later noted that “by the slightest margin of chance… a nuclear explosion was averted.” No one on the ground was killed, and most crew survived, but the declassified accounts underscore how U.S. nuclear weapons policy and device designs of the era allowed multiple near‑disasters. The Goldsboro case is one of dozens of Cold War incidents — 32 pre‑1980 accidents involving nuclear arms disclosed by the Defense Department — and prompted scrutiny of safety mechanisms that, in this incident, all but failed to prevent a domestic nuclear blast.

Charles “Charlie” Hall, inventor of the waterbed, is reintroducing a redesigned waterbed about 50 years after debuting his original concept at a San Francisco art show. Now living on Bainbridge Island with a view of Puget Sound and Seattle, Hall plans to test-market “Waterbed 2018” this spring in a Florida furniture chain, with hopes of broader rollout and an online bed-in-a-box option. The new design keeps the original benefits—body-conforming support and adjustable warmth—while solving past complaints: foam collars replace rigid wooden frames, spandex top covers enhance the floating feel, fiber inserts suppress waves, dual bladders allow independent temperature control, and modern heating systems maintain comfort. Queen and king sizes will be offered; full systems around $2,000.

Hall’s waterbed first gained traction in the 1970s, becoming a counterculture and sexual-revolution icon as well as a practical sleep product. He notes the sensual image helped sales, but people also discovered genuine comfort. After waterbeds peaked in the 1980s and largely vanished due to poor mass-market products and marketing, Hall pursued other inventions (including the Sun Shower) and later won a 1991 patent-infringement suit. He believes millennials may rediscover waterbeds—some nostalgic, others intrigued by novelty—and that modern materials and design can overcome old myths about leaks or structural damage. Hall says the waterbed influenced the mattress industry toward alternatives like memory foam and pillowtops, and he hopes his updated version revives interest.

Olga Goodwin has spent decades pleading to bring home the body of her husband, William Alexander Morgan, the “Yankee Comandante” — an American who became a celebrated guerrilla leader in Cuba’s revolution but was later executed and buried in an unmarked Havana grave. Morgan, a charismatic, mercurial ex-paratrooper and erstwhile petty criminal from Toledo, Ohio, joined anti‑Batista fighters in the Escambray in 1957 and rose to comandante despite early suspicion. He married Olga Rodríguez (later Goodwin), fathered children, and ran development projects like frog farms to aid peasants. At first he trusted Fidel Castro and helped repel plots against the revolution; he even acted as a double agent in an August 1959 sting that exposed a counterrevolutionary strike backed by Dominican dictator Trujillo and others. But as Castro’s government shifted left and consolidated power—sidelining democratic-minded insurgents like Morgan and his Second National Front—the comandante grew disillusioned. Morgan increasingly opposed Communist influence, allegedly began funneling arms to anti‑Castro fighters, and was ensnared in intrigue involving U.S., Dominican and exile plots. Arrested in October 1960, tried for treason in March 1961, he was executed by firing squad at La Cabaña; accounts describe his refusal to kneel and being shot in the knees before death. Olga endured years of imprisonment, beatings, and deprivation before escaping Cuba during the 1980 Mariel exodus and settling in Toledo, where she vowed to recover Morgan’s remains. Renewed attention from books, magazine pieces and television — and thawing U.S.-Cuba relations after prisoner exchanges — have raised hopes his body might be repatriated. Support from Ohio politicians and reporters who have chronicled Morgan’s life has kept his story alive: a complex tale of idealism, betrayal, espionage, love, and the brutal calculus of revolution.

Simone Biles, the 2016 Olympic all-around champion, publicly joined the growing list of gymnasts who say they were sexually abused by former USA Gymnastics and Michigan State University doctor Larry Nassar. In a social media statement ahead of Nassar’s weeklong sentencing hearing, Biles invoked #MeToo, called the abuse “disgusting and abusive,” rejected self-blame, and criticized USA Gymnastics and others for enabling his misconduct. Her disclosure follows earlier statements from teammates and elite gymnasts including McKayla Maroney, Aly Raisman and Gabby Douglas.

Nassar, who worked with Olympic teams across four Games and at MSU from 1997 to 2016, pleaded guilty in Ingham County to seven counts of criminal sexual conduct and faces additional state and federal sentences, including 60 years for child-pornography charges. More than 140 women and girls have accused him of abusing patients under the guise of medical treatment; many victims were children. The sentencing hearing will feature nearly 100 victim impact statements from survivors recounting betrayal, invasive “treatments,” and institutional failures.

Accusers have targeted not only Nassar but USA Gymnastics and MSU for allegedly ignoring complaints, protecting him, and silencing victims. USA Gymnastics expressed sorrow and pledged support, while critics demand deeper leadership changes and accountability. Advocates, led by survivors like Rachael Denhollander, urge systemic reform to prevent future abuse and to hold enabling institutions responsible.

Denver Broncos wide receiver Kenny McKinley, 23, was found dead in his Centennial, Colorado, home in an apparent suicide, authorities said. Arapahoe County deputies discovered his body in a second-floor bedroom with an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. McKinley, a second-year pro who spent 2005–08 at the University of South Carolina, remains the school’s career leader in receptions (207) and receiving yards (2,781). Drafted by Denver in the fifth round of 2009, he played eight games as a rookie—mainly on special teams—and had been on injured reserve this season after knee surgery. Coaches, teammates and Broncos officials expressed shock and sorrow; grief counseling was made available to the team. McKinley is survived by a young son.

Carrie Fisher’s death at 60 after suffering a heart attack aboard a flight from London to Los Angeles stunned fans, colleagues and the entertainment world. Best known as Princess Leia in the original Star Wars films, Fisher was far more than a beloved sci‑fi icon: she was an incisive writer, a sought‑after Hollywood script doctor, a candid mental‑health advocate, and a singular personality who refused to conform to red‑carpet norms.

Fisher came from show‑business lineage as the daughter of actress Debbie Reynolds and singer Eddie Fisher, but she made her own mark through acting, books, and candid public commentary. Her semi‑autobiographical novel Postcards From the Edge and memoirs including Wishful Drinking and The Princess Diarist showcased her razor wit and frankness about addiction, bipolar disorder and recovery. Memorable lines collected from her books and interviews reflect a blend of self‑deprecating humor, blunt honesty about mental illness, and a literary sensibility that turned personal pain into sharp comedy. Many credited her openness about bipolar disorder and depression with helping to reduce stigma and encouraging others to seek help.

Beyond writing and acting, Fisher was a highly regarded script doctor in the 1990s, uncreditedly polishing films such as Hook, Sister Act, Lethal Weapon 3 and The Wedding Singer. Her influence on mainstream Hollywood storytelling was significant even where her name didn’t appear in credits.

Fisher’s personal life and public persona were distinctive and warmly human. She traveled with and adored her French bulldog Gary, who became a familiar presence at interviews, events and on social media. Fisher often described Gary as a therapy dog and companion; their dynamic underlined her mix of vulnerability and comic defiance. She cultivated an idiosyncratic fashion sense—comfortable, witty, and unapologetically herself—which only reinforced her reputation as someone who bucked Hollywood conventions.

Colleagues and fans remember Fisher as fearless, funny and fiercely honest. Her work spanned comedy and drama—films such as The Blues Brothers, When Harry Met Sally and Hannah and Her Sisters, plus many TV guest appearances—while her Star Wars legacy inspired a generation of female fans and helped pave the way for more complex women in genre films. Tributes underscored that while Fisher’s physical presence is gone, her voice—sharp, irreverent and compassionate—will endure.

A Morning Consult poll of 2,200 people gauged favorability for Star Wars characters and found Princess Leia leading with 73 percent, closely followed by Luke Skywalker, Chewbacca, Yoda and R2-D2. Anakin Skywalker scored 55 percent while Darth Vader registered 49 percent, a surprisingly small drop despite Vader’s atrocities. None of the original-trilogy characters landed on the “most hated” list; Jar Jar Binks had a 37 percent approval rating, just below Rey, and even attracted unexpected support from Republican men. The least liked character was Supreme Leader Snoke at 26 percent, below Count Dooku and even Donald Trump’s 32 percent favorability in the poll. The survey also asked whether Star Wars is political: 53 percent said it isn’t, while 17 percent consider it political and 41 percent of that group are bothered by its political tone. Separately, the piece profiles Ahmed Best—Jar Jar’s performer—tracing his Bronx-to-Stomp-to-Skywalker Ranch journey, his early tech and music interests, and how a standout live performance led Lucasfilm casting to hire him for the motion-capture role.

A computer model trained on human ratings of more than 1,000 internet face photos reveals which facial features drive rapid first impressions—typically formed within 100 milliseconds—and shows they cluster into three main dimensions: approachability, dominance and youthful-attractiveness. Researchers at the University of York had volunteers rate photos on social traits like trustworthiness and dominance, then measured 65 facial features (jaw, mouth, eyes, cheekbones, eyebrows, etc.) and used an artificial neural network to link features to impressions. Mouth shape and area—essentially smiling—strongly predict approachability; larger eye shape and area signal youthfulness and attractiveness; and features associated with masculine face shape (eyebrow height, cheekbones, color and texture) relate to perceived dominance. The model could also generate cartoon faces along the three axes; when humans rated these synthetic faces, their impressions matched the intended traits. The team notes many cues are image-specific—expression, lighting, pose and camera angle can alter impressions—so the findings have practical uses for photographers, animators and people choosing profile pictures. The study focused on Caucasian faces to control for cultural factors; cross-cultural work and brain-imaging follow-ups are planned to explore how universal these cues are and whether such impressions can be deliberately shaped.

Groupon’s IPO priced at $20 and opened near $30, briefly valuing the company around $20 billion. Early institutional buyers are flipping shares for quick gains, a common but cautionary sign given Groupon’s small float (<6%). The author argues the stock is overvalued at current levels because Groupon is undergoing a difficult transition: growth is decelerating as the company cuts marketing to reach profitability, its U.S. core is shrinking, and international operations lag. Short-term momentum investors dislike deceleration, which could drive the stock sharply lower—potentially to ~$12 a share or lower—before stabilizing. Long-term the author is bullish: Groupon tapped a huge market and has scale advantages, but predicts mid-single-digit sequential growth settling to 20–30% y/y, with 2013 earnings suggesting a $6–9 billion valuation ($9–13/share). He wouldn’t buy above ~$7/share.

Dallas Cowboys coach Jason Garrett’s brief news conference was consumed by questions about the team’s recent decision to cut wide receiver Lucky Whitehead. Garrett repeatedly stuck to a single line: the team acted in what it believed was “the best interest of the Dallas Cowboys” and would stand by that decision while moving forward. He declined to expand on specifics despite repeated questioning about fairness, rushed judgment, internal knowledge, and why other players with off-field issues remain on the roster.

The firing came after a bizarre mistaken-identity criminal matter in Virginia. Prince William County police confirmed Whitehead — whose given name is Rodney — was wrongly implicated in a Wawa convenience-store shoplifting incident on June 22. Investigators say a suspect without ID verbally gave a name, birth date and Social Security number that matched Whitehead. Officers checked DMV records, compared a photo, and arrested the man, later issuing a July 6 summons for a misdemeanor petty larceny charge. Police now say the identity was falsely provided, they acted in “good faith,” and they will work with prosecutors to officially clear Whitehead while seeking the actual suspect. The department expressed regret for the impact of the error.

Whitehead has consistently denied involvement, noting he was in Dallas until late morning on the day of the incident. His agent, David Rich, criticized the police investigation and blamed it for costing Whitehead his job. Cowboys executive VP Stephen Jones said the team had given Whitehead multiple chances dating to the prior year and chose to go in a different direction. Whitehead said he felt hurt that the team did not let him clear his name and that he was “pretty much being called a liar.” His agent declined to comment on whether Whitehead would seek reinstatement or on comparisons with other players who faced controversy.

Google's 2015 Security Rewards Year in Review shows the company paid over $2 million to more than 300 security researchers for discovering vulnerabilities and participating in its reward programs. A standout case involved Sanmay Ved, who briefly purchased Google.com for $12 on September 29 after Google’s domain briefly became available. Google offered Ved $6,006.13—which the company cheekily said "spells" GOOGLE if you squint—and doubled the payout when Ved pledged to donate it; the funds went to the Art of Living India foundation. Tomasz Bojarski was the most prolific researcher, reporting 70 bugs during the year, including an issue in Google’s vulnerability submission form. 

2015 marked a major expansion: Android joined Google’s Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) in June. By year’s end, Android-related bounties exceeded $200,000, including a single payment of $37,500 to an Android researcher. Google also launched Vulnerability Research Grants—upfront lump sums to support researchers even if they don’t find issues. One grant recipient, Kamil Histamullin from Kazan, used funding to locate a YouTube Creator Studio flaw that could have allowed deletion of any video by altering a URL parameter; Google fixed the issue and awarded him an additional $5,000. 

Established programs continued to produce valuable findings, and Google committed $1 million specifically for Google Drive security research. The report emphasizes continued growth and program evolution in 2016, encouraging researchers to participate and highlighting the tangible benefits of proactive vulnerability discovery.

A Lonsdale, Minnesota restaurant owner drew controversy by posting a sign reading “Muslims Get Out” outside Treats Family Restaurant, with a second line saying “In Support Of St. Cloud.” The message follows a stabbing at a St. Cloud mall in which the suspect allegedly asked victims whether they were Muslim before attacking them. Owner Dan Ruedinger defended the sign, saying he wants people to “stand up” against extremism and asserting it targets extremists, not Muslims generally. He reported increased business after putting up the sign and said he will not remove or change it despite backlash.

Locals reacted with concern: protestors gathered, and residents worried the sign paints the whole Lonsdale community negatively. Payten Estepp, part of a protest group, acknowledged free speech but said the sign gives the town a bad reputation for those passing by. The piece also includes unrelated local details — weather and a personal review of the restaurant’s food and service — noting decent soft-serve ice cream but poor cooked food quality, slow service, and politicized ownership that some feel harms business judgment. The sign remains in place amid community debate over free speech, safety, and town image.

Former Chief U.S. District Judge Vaughn Walker, who retired in February after 21 years on the San Francisco bench, publicly reflected on his landmark ruling striking down California’s Proposition 8, which banned same-sex marriage. Walker said he never considered recusal because he is gay, arguing that a judge’s sexuality is irrelevant and that disqualification on that basis would be a “slippery slope.” He maintains his decision was correct and prefers appellate courts decide the merits rather than dismissing the case on standing grounds after state officials declined to appeal. Walker lamented that the trial wasn’t televised, saying high-profile public trials should be visible. A libertarian-leaning jurist, he now returns to private practice focusing on mediation and arbitration.

New data from the CDC suggest a hopeful shift: after decades of rising numbers, the incidence of new diabetes cases in the United States has declined. In 2014 there were 1.4 million new cases of diabetes, down from 1.7 million in 2008 — the first significant decrease in roughly 25 years after a long period in which annual new diagnoses more than tripled. About 21.9 million Americans now live with diabetes, nearly 10 percent of adults have type 2 diabetes, and over a third have prediabetes, so the burden remains large.

Experts caution that it’s hard to pinpoint a single cause for the reversal. Edward Gregg of the CDC credits the gradual spread of scientific knowledge, education and prevention efforts — programs promoting exercise, healthier diets and lifestyle changes — that can prevent diabetes when sustained. Yet Gregg notes the incidence rate remains roughly 60 percent higher than in the early 1990s, indicating substantial work remains.

Local stories illustrate both the problem and the promise. In Alabama, which has the nation’s highest diabetes prevalence (12.7 percent in 2013), individuals in hard-hit areas like the Black Belt are taking steps to avoid the disease: Lynette Carpenter lost 42 pounds and avoided developing full diabetes after changing her diet and exercising; music teacher Robin Williams lost 33 pounds through diet changes and tracking calories. These personal successes reflect prevention’s potential even amid long-standing poverty and structural inequities that have exacerbated the disease in some communities.

Bolivia publicly rejected a donation of 100,000 chickens from Bill Gates, calling the gift offensive and patronizing. César Cocaric, Bolivia’s minister of development, said Gates should apologize for assuming Bolivians lack the capacity to produce poultry, asserting that the country does not need “gifted chicks” and emphasizing national dignity. Gates had promoted chickens as a simple, cost-effective way to help people living in extreme poverty—easy to care for, nutritious, and a way for women to earn income—announcing an initiative to donate birds to high-poverty countries. His foundation and allies argue that small-scale poultry can improve child nutrition, provide immediate cash for household needs, and empower women because poultry income is often controlled by women and spent on health, education, and nutrition.

Bolivian officials countered with data showing a robust and growing domestic poultry sector. The Bolivian Institute of Foreign Trade (IBCE) reported significant increases in egg and broiler production between 2008 and 2014: per capita egg consumption rose from 130 to 143 eggs annually, and chicken meat consumption grew from 35 to 38 kilos per person. In 2013 egg production exceeded 1.5 billion units, an 11% increase over 2012, with the department of Santa Cruz supplying 59% of eggs. Broiler production reached over 939 million birds between 2008–2013, peaking at 180 million in 2013, and broiler meat production rose from 294,000 to 396,000 tons—a 35% increase. Cooperatives and producers import genetic stock to maintain quality, and major producing regions include Santa Cruz and Cochabamba.

While Gates’ advocacy highlights chickens’ potential to improve livelihoods—especially for women in developing contexts—Bolivian officials view the unsolicited donation as unnecessary and disrespectful given their established, expanding poultry industry.

Rescue teams in Genoa recovered the last three missing victims from the collapsed Morandi motorway bridge, bringing the confirmed death toll to 43. The bodies of three members of one family were found in a car crushed beneath concrete slabs five days after a roughly 200-metre section of the viaduct fell about 45–50 metres during heavy rain, plunging vehicles and debris onto the ground below. Nine survivors remain hospitalized, four critically. Although all reported missing have been accounted for, emergency crews continue searching and stabilizing the site to ensure no one remains under the rubble and to assist investigations.

The tragedy has intensified scrutiny of Italy’s infrastructure and the bridge’s management. Autostrade per l’Italia, the operator and unit of Atlantia, pledged funds for victims’ families, half a billion euros for rebuilding, and support to relocate hundreds displaced by the collapse; its parent company’s shares plunged. The government launched proceedings to revoke Autostrade’s concessions and has set up a commission to probe causes. Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte and other officials promised stricter requirements that concession-holders reinvest profits into maintenance and pledged emergency housing: regional authorities expect about 300 temporary homes within two months and the government allocated €32m. A nationwide infrastructure maintenance plan is due next month.

Historic concerns about the bridge’s design and corrosion emerged: Riccardo Morandi, the bridge’s designer, warned in 1979 about concrete degradation and recommended ongoing rust removal and protective treatment of reinforcements. Engineers have long flagged the bridge’s unusual concrete-encased stay cables and signs of advanced corrosion; repair contracts had been bid in recent months. Public anger and grief remain high: some families rejected a state funeral, criticizing politicians, while residents gathered in Genoa to mourn and voice outrage. Investigations continue to determine the precise causes of the collapse.

Lindsay Lohan’s brief stay at Century Regional Detention Facility in Lynwood, Calif., drew complaints from other inmates who say she’s receiving special treatment and disrupting routine. Maria Medina, a relative of an inmate, told PEOPLE staff sometimes lock down the unit when Lohan receives clothing or other items or needs medical attention; inmates resent the perceived preferential treatment. Los Angeles County sheriff’s spokesman Steve Whitmore denied lockdowns or special treatment, saying it’s “business as usual,” and Lohan’s lawyer Shawn Chapman Holley said Lohan is following rules and in better spirits. Separately, reports say Lohan was taunted by fellow inmates—allegedly yelled at with nicknames like “fire crotch”—and became upset, briefly isolated after shouting at guards. Lohan, 24, is serving a 90-day term but may be released early due to jail overcrowding.

When MongoDB CEO Max Schireson announced in a personal blog post that he was stepping down to spend more time with his family, his decision reignited debates about work-life balance and who gets asked to account for parenting responsibilities. Schireson—who led MongoDB through rapid growth, fundraising and product momentum—said relentless travel between his Palo Alto home and the company’s New York hub (on pace for roughly 300,000 miles this year) forced him to miss important family moments. He noted the asymmetry in public scrutiny: friends and journalists routinely ask his wife how she balances a demanding medical and academic career, but rarely ask him how he balances fatherhood with being a CEO. Citing missed events like his son’s emergency surgery and the family puppy’s accident, he concluded he could not be the “all-in” CEO MongoDB deserved while also being present at home. Schireson will remain as vice chairman and transition the CEO role to Dev Ittycheria, an operations-focused executive with prior CEO experience, who will lead the company’s next growth phase.

The episode is framed in a broader argument: the “having it all” conversation has long focused on women, with public pressure, profiles, and advice aimed disproportionately at female leaders. Schireson’s move and similar signals from men in elite roles suggest the debate must become gender-neutral. The longer essay excerpts underscore research showing family-friendly policies often correlate with better firm performance, retention, and employee engagement, and argue that flexible cultures can foster creativity and innovation by allowing diverse life experiences to inform work. Examples from law and tech show slow but real shifts—alternative fee structures, remote work adoption, and men increasingly asking about work-life balance. The author urges reframing work-family balance as a societal issue affecting both sexes: enabling flexible careers will retain talent, improve firms’ returns on training, and enrich innovation. Schireson’s choice is presented not as retreat but as a candid recalibration that may help normalize parenting priorities for leaders of any gender.

Fox Business Network cut New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie and former Arkansas Gov. Mike Huckabee from next week’s main GOP presidential debate, landing them in the undercard after failing to meet a 2.5% threshold across four major polls (Fox News, NBC/WSJ, Quinnipiac, Investor’s Business Daily). Both finished at 2.25%; Rand Paul just made the 2.5% cutoff. Christie had shown weak, stagnant polling despite praised recent debate performances; Huckabee polled slightly higher in some surveys but still missed. They’ll join Bobby Jindal and Rick Santorum in the earlier debate, while Lindsey Graham and George Pataki failed to qualify for either stage. The primetime debate lineup includes Donald Trump, Ben Carson, Marco Rubio, Ted Cruz, Carly Fiorina, Jeb Bush, John Kasich and Rand Paul.

On Tuesday, NBA Commissioner Adam Silver announced a lifetime ban and a $2.5 million fine for Los Angeles Clippers owner Donald Sterling after audio recordings surfaced in which Sterling made racist remarks about his girlfriend’s association with African Americans. Silver also urged the NBA Board of Governors to force a sale of the Clippers, saying he expected the necessary owner votes; Sterling can fight any sale in court but faces overwhelming public and institutional condemnation. The punishment forbids Sterling from attending games, entering team facilities, participating in personnel decisions, or taking part in league activities.

Silver’s decisive action came hours before Game 5 of the Clippers–Warriors playoff series in Los Angeles. Players, staff and fans turned the game into a public repudiation of Sterling: Clippers personnel wore black, advertisements were covered, cheerleaders dressed in black, and arena LED boards displayed “We are one.” Some players had considered boycotting earlier games, and the team staged a silent protest in a prior contest by hiding logos on warmups. Doc Rivers said the morning’s news brought emotional relief and a sense of justice to the locker room. DeAndre Jordan led the team with a playoff-career-high 25 points in a 113–103 victory that gave the Clippers a 3–2 series lead.

The scandal has also centered on V. Stiviano, the woman on the recording; her lawyer said she did not release the tape and denied a romantic relationship. Sterling’s wife has sued Stiviano seeking to reclaim gifts. Corporate sponsors reacted swiftly: many paused partnerships, increasing pressure on the league. Public figures including Magic Johnson and former players praised Silver’s leadership. Some sponsors later resumed ties after the commissioner’s action.

The episode highlighted tensions between private conduct and public accountability, and set in motion efforts to remove an owner whose remarks many deemed incompatible with the league’s values. The Clippers and their fans, momentarily united by the crisis, see Silver’s move as the start of a healing process.

A Playmobil pirate ship toy sparked outrage after a Sacramento mother, Ida Lockett, discovered its instruction booklet directed her young son to place a metal neck piece around a dark-skinned figurine that appeared to be a shackled captive. Lockett, assembling the set with her five-year-old, said the doll wore no shoes, torn pants and a filthy yellow shirt, and the manual showed the silver accessory snapped around its neck. The set also appeared to include a dungeon-like area, prompting Lockett to call the piece a “slave collar” and describe the inclusion as racist and inappropriate for children’s play.

The toy had been purchased from Toys R Us as a birthday gift from the child’s aunt, Aimee Norman, who posted on Playmobil USA’s Facebook page that she was “MORTIFIED.” Norman urged Playmobil to simply make a regular black pirate and criticized the company’s lack of diversity and sensitivity, adding the hashtag “#Slavery.is.not.a.game.” Sacramento NAACP President Stephen Webb demanded the set be pulled from shelves, calling it “deplorable.”

Playmobil responded to The Washington Post saying the figure was intended to represent life on a 17th-century pirate ship and described the character as a crew member who was a former slave in historical context, not a captive meant to offend. The retailer did not immediately comment. The incident drew mixed reactions online, with some defending historical accuracy and others condemning the inclusion of slavery-themed play accessories in a modern toy line. The story drew local media coverage and prompted calls for action.

Security experts described a massive, sustained cyber-attack that slowed internet traffic worldwide, calling it the largest of its kind. The dispute began after Spamhaus, a nonprofit that maintains blocklists to help providers filter spam, blacklisted Dutch host Cyberbunker, which advertises almost anything except child abuse or terrorism material. Cyberbunker, via a spokesman claiming affiliation, framed the blacklist as an abuse of power and retaliated; Spamhaus alleges Cyberbunker worked with criminal gangs in Eastern Europe and Russia. The attackers used distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) tactics focused on Spamhaus’s Domain Name System (DNS) servers—the internet’s “phone book” that maps domain names to IP addresses. DNS floods are particularly disruptive because DNS servers must be public and cannot be simply shut down without harming the internet. Spamhaus’s chief executive Steve Linford said the group endured more than a week of attacks peaking around 300 Gbps, far above typical major-bank attacks of about 50 Gbps, and that five national cyber-police forces were investigating. Experts warned such power could knock out government or financial systems; collateral damage has already affected global internet services, likened to a motorway clogged not just at the ramps but across the whole carriageway. Arbor Networks and other specialists confirmed the unprecedented scale. Spamhaus remained operational thanks to highly distributed infrastructure—over 80 servers worldwide—and assistance from major companies including Google and CloudFlare, whose involvement drew attackers’ focus to their upstream providers. Analysts pointed to longstanding network configuration flaws—many ISPs do not validate that outgoing traffic really originates from their users—enabling reflection and amplification attacks that are hard to stop without finding and arresting those responsible.

Archaeologists have finally located the long-sought 16th-century Spanish fort San Marcos on Parris Island, South Carolina, part of the former Spanish settlement of Santa Elena. The search, led by University of South Carolina archaeologist Chester DePratter and University of Georgia’s Victor Thompson, used ground-penetrating radar, magnetometers and resistivity meters to image the subsurface across a grid of mapped blocks. Improved computer programs for interpreting remote-sensing data were critical to the breakthrough after more than two decades of intermittent searching and unsuccessful test digs. Historical documents and a drawing established a general area, but no map pinpointed the fort’s position, and organic wooden structures had long decayed. Instead, the team detected post holes, compacted floors and other soil changes left by human occupation—signatures that remote sensing can reveal. San Marcos, built in 1577 by Pedro Menendez Marquez in six days with prefabricated timbers to defend against Native attack, was one of several forts at Santa Elena, a once-thriving Spanish capital founded in 1566. The researchers have now mapped numerous features across roughly 15 acres—wells, houses, posts, ditches, and the footprints of shops, taverns, a church and administrative buildings—and believe they’re close to identifying Menendez de Aviles’ residence by its high-end Chinese ceramics. The findings, to be detailed in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports, will inform further excavation and exhibits at the Santa Elena History Center.

Florida Republican Rep. Brad Drake has proposed legislation to end lethal injection in Florida, replacing it with a choice between electrocution or execution by firing squad. Drake says his idea sprang from a conversation with a constituent at a Waffle House following legal fights over the Sept. 28 execution of Manuel Valle, in which defense lawyers argued a new lethal drug cocktail could cause pain. Drake told supporters lethal injection lets convicted killers “get off that easy” and that harsher, more visceral methods would make inmates “contemplate their fates” daily. He framed the change as common-sense, saying most people would prefer to be “put to sleep,” and called for “put[ting] our pants back on the right way.” Florida used the electric chair starting in 1924 but switched to lethal injection in 2000 after several botched electrocutions and a pending U.S. Supreme Court review; since the switch, 26 people have been executed by lethal injection, including Valle and killers Danny Rolling and Aileen Wuornos.

The proposal drew sharp criticism. Howard Simon of the ACLU of Florida called the bill embarrassing and mocked its Waffle House origins, noting Florida’s troubled death-penalty record and high number of exonerations. The measure will be considered during the 2012 legislative session. The debate intensified after commentator Keith Olbermann publicly attacked Drake on Current TV’s Countdown, using uncensored profanity and labeling Drake a “sociopath,” prompting concerns about civility and media standards.

Chinese media reported that two Guangdong officials were arrested for buying corpses from grave robbers to meet mandatory cremation targets tied to local funeral reform. The case came to light after a resident in Beiliu, Guangxi, discovered his grandfather’s grave had been robbed. Police later arrested a grave robber, who confessed to stealing over 20 bodies from rural cemeteries, bagging them and transporting them by motorcycle into neighboring Guangdong. He said he sold the bodies to two officials from Gaozhou and Huazhou who oversaw local funeral management reforms. The officials, surnamed He and Dong, admitted purchasing corpses to satisfy monthly cremation quotas imposed by local governments based on prior-year populations.
