Dong reportedly bought ten bodies at 3,000 yuan each; He paid 1,500 yuan per body, though the number he bought is unclear. Authorities claimed the purchases were government-approved, and investigations continue. The scandal highlights deep tensions between state-led efforts to encourage cremation to conserve land and entrenched Chinese traditions of ancestor worship that favor intact burials for a peaceful afterlife. In rural areas, strict cremation targets have prompted families to secretly rebury loved ones, while some regions have seen suicides and extreme resistance as people try to secure traditional burials. Grave thefts have been repeatedly reported in Guangxi and elsewhere, provoking outrage because disturbing ancestral tombs is culturally taboo and believed to bring misfortune. The incident underscores the social costs and backlash of top-down burial reforms in communities with long-standing funerary customs.

The Obama administration announced a one-year delay of the Affordable Care Act’s employer mandate, postponing until 2015 the requirement that firms with 50+ full-time-equivalent workers offer health insurance or face penalties. Treasury and White House officials framed the move as necessary to give employers more time to adapt to complex reporting systems and to simplify rules, saying it would allow testing and adjustment of processes without altering other ACA elements like the individual mandate or the planned October 1 exchanges opening. The change was widely welcomed by business groups, including the Chamber of Commerce and retail associations, which had warned that the mandate’s timing and reporting demands could force firms to cut hours or shift employees to part time.

Republicans seized the delay as proof the law was flawed and politically motivated, noting its timing pushes implementation past the 2014 midterm elections and calling for full repeal. Some Democrats defended the flexibility, arguing it was better to implement correctly than quickly. Supporters warned the postponement could reduce employer-based coverage in 2014, potentially pushing more workers to the insurance exchanges and increasing federal subsidy costs; critics feared repeated delays. Administration aides said exchanges and individual penalties remain on schedule, but observers noted the employer reporting pause could complicate verifying subsidy eligibility and affect enrollment dynamics as marketplaces open.

Online dating, which began with sites like Match.com in 1995 and accelerated with apps such as Tinder after 2012, has not only changed how people meet but is reshaping social networks and may be driving greater racial integration and stronger marriages. Social networks typically combine tight-knit clusters of close ties and looser “weak ties” that bridge different groups. Historically, romantic partners were usually embedded within these networks—friends, colleagues, classmates, or community contacts—so cross-group linking was limited.

Researchers Josue Ortega and Philipp Hergovich modelled societies as networks of men and women from different races where marriage requires an existing link. Adding even a few random cross-group links—analogous to online encounters with strangers—dramatically increased predicted interracial marriages and, surprisingly, predicted stronger marriages by measuring average pre-relationship social distance. Empirical U.S. data show a marked rise in interracial unions beginning after the mid-1990s and steepening in the 2000s and again around 2014, coinciding with the growth of dating websites and swipe apps. While population composition shifts and other factors play some role, Ortega and Hergovich argue these cannot fully explain the magnitude of the change, making online dating a plausible primary driver.

Additional studies suggest couples who met online have lower divorce rates, aligning with the model’s prediction of stronger unions. Though the model and correlations do not prove causation, they indicate online dating is creating new social bridges that reduce social distance, increase integration, and may yield societal benefits.

Syrian President Bashar al-Assad said he plans to visit North Korea to meet leader Kim Jong Un, North Korea’s KCNA reported, potentially marking the first time Kim has publicly hosted another head of state in Pyongyang since taking power in 2011. Assad made the remark on May 30 while receiving credentials from North Korea’s ambassador, though Syria’s office gave no immediate confirmation that a trip is planned. The announcement underscores longstanding ties: Pyongyang and Damascus established diplomatic relations in the 1960s and cooperated militarily historically, including North Korean personnel sent to Syria during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war. UN monitors have accused North Korea of assisting Syria on chemical weapons—an allegation both countries deny—while both face international isolation for their respective policies. Assad praised Kim’s leadership and expressed confidence in Korean reunification. The report arrived as Kim has stepped up diplomacy this year with meetings in China and South Korea and ahead of his June 12 summit with U.S. President Donald Trump in Singapore.

Sen. Ted Cruz apologized Wednesday after repeating an old joke about Vice President Joe Biden at a Republican event in Howell, Michigan, shortly after Biden’s son Beau died of brain cancer. Speaking to roughly 650 attendees at a Livingston County Lincoln Day Dinner, Cruz invoked the familiar line — “Vice President Joe Biden… you don’t even need a punch line” — prompting only “faint laughter,” according to Detroit News reporter Chad Livengood. The timing of the joke, which Cruz has used previously in stump speeches, drew swift criticism on social media because the vice president was publicly mourning his 46‑year‑old son, a former Delaware attorney general who died the previous Saturday and was to lie in state and be buried that week.

Within an hour of the speech, Cruz posted an apology on Facebook (and linked it on Twitter), saying it “was a mistake to use an old joke about Joe Biden during his time of grief,” offering sincere regret and prayers for the Biden family. When Livengood asked Cruz about the remark after the speech, the senator walked away without answering; campaign chair in Michigan Saul Anuzis later defended Cruz’s intent, saying he meant no disrespect though “timing could have been better.” Michigan Democrats criticized Cruz’s comments as lacking compassion. Cruz’s Michigan appearance was his first campaign event in the state since launching his presidential bid; his speech also covered policy themes such as a flat tax, repealing Obamacare and appealing to Reagan Democrats.

The Leonid meteor shower peaks overnight Tuesday, November 17 into Wednesday, November 18, producing shooting stars as bits of cometary ice and rock burn in Earth’s atmosphere. Meteors will appear to radiate from the constellation Leo, which rises in the eastern sky around midnight local time across the U.S., though meteors can be seen any time after sunset. This year’s display is mid-cycle—far from the dramatic storms that occur about every 33 years—so expect a moderate rate, roughly one meteor every four minutes, aided by a crescent moon but hampered in many regions by cloudy skies. The shower occurs when Earth crosses debris left by comet Tempel-Tuttle; the comet itself remains far away.

Dominion Diamond Mines and Rio Tinto have recovered a 552.74-carat gem-quality yellow diamond—the largest ever found in North America—at the Diavik mine in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The rough stone, unearthed in October during initial screening at the Diavik recovery plant, is nearly three times larger than Diavik’s previous record find, the 187.7-carat “Foxfire” recovered in 2015. Measuring roughly 33.7mm by 54.6mm, the diamond shows abrasion marks from the recovery process; Dominion describes its survival as remarkable given the fragility of very large stones during mining.

Dominion, which owns 40% of Diavik while Rio operates and holds 60%, purchased the rough through an internal auction and will soon select a specialist cutter to polish the gem. Because of abrasions and its rough condition, the company so far classifies it as “fancy yellow” but cannot provide a value estimate until cutting and evaluation are complete. High-quality fancy vivid or intense yellow stones can command premiums, though yellow diamonds often trade below top white Type IIa stones. The find ranks among the seventh-largest diamonds discovered this century and within the world’s 30 largest finds; historically, the largest remains the 3,106-carat Cullinan from 1905.

The discovery arrives as Dominion adjusts to new ownership under billionaire Dennis Washington and recent executive turnover, and while the global market faces oversupply and pressure on smaller, lower-quality stones—compounded by a weaker Indian rupee and squeezed cutting centers. Dominion plans to choose one of a few master cutters worldwide to maximize the polished stone’s size and value and intends to Canadamark-certify the finished main stone.

Long-time Hubbard, Ohio, residents Rick (Garrick) and Cindy Krlich say they have been subjected to years of sustained horn-honking harassment after a 2007 real estate dispute with the family of former fire chief John Clemente Jr. The conflict began when Krlich bid on a neighboring house in probate; Clemente allegedly demanded he rescind the winning bid, saying the house had been in his family for generations. Krlich contends title nevertheless did not pass to him, and that members of the Clemente family, their friends, and coworkers—including local firefighters and some municipal employees—then launched a campaign of intimidation by repeatedly honking their vehicle horns while passing the Krlich home. The couple say the honking totaled some 5,000 blows over seven years, at one point reaching about 100 times a day and later easing to one or two times daily. The Krlichs installed video and audio surveillance that captured numerous incidents, allegedly involving a wide range of people: a fire truck, police officers from neighboring towns, the Hubbard police chief’s relatives, city council members, and other local officials and employees. Rick Krlich has sued at least 40 alleged honkers, including the Clementes, and filed a federal civil-rights complaint claiming local police and the 9-1-1 center ignored or mishandled his reports and require him alone to follow special “protocols” before accepting complaints. He seeks over $75,000 in damages for violations of the Equal Protection Clause, equipment costs and legal fees. The Clementes deny organizing the harassment; John Clemente says some acquaintances “just” beeped as a goodbye, and both he and Marlene Clemente say Rick’s litigious behavior prompted the town’s opposition. ABC News’ 20/20 invited both families and Hubbard to a peace-and-reconciliation barbecue to confront the dispute.

North Korean leader Kim Jong-il has elevated his youngest son, Kim Jong-un, to four-star general amid a major Workers' Party meeting—the first state media mention of the elusive, Switzerland-educated man believed to be in his late 20s. The promotion, along with Kim’s re-election as party general secretary and the elevation of sister Kim Kyong-hui and other close aides, is widely seen as laying groundwork for dynastic succession despite Jong-un’s lack of experience. Analysts note parallels with Kim Jong-il’s own rise in the 1970s and say the appointments aim to secure continuity of the military-first regime. Kim Jong-il’s reported frailty and past stroke have intensified speculation about succession plans. Pyongyang’s ceremonies and propaganda affirm the leadership cult, while external observers, including the US, watch developments closely given the regime’s nuclear capabilities.

German and French prosecutors say evidence from co-pilot Andreas Lubitz’s tablet and recovered flight recorders indicate he researched suicide methods and cockpit door security in the days before Germanwings Flight 9525 crashed into the French Alps on March 24, killing all 150 aboard. Police reconstructed searches from March 16–23, including queries about medical treatment; prosecutors declined to publish exact search terms. Investigators recovered both cockpit voice and flight data recorders; the flight data recorder was found buried and, despite fire damage to its casing, is expected to yield speed, altitude and control inputs that will clarify Lubitz’s actions. French prosecutors say Lubitz locked the captain out of the cockpit and deliberately put the aircraft into a fatal descent, and a European official described the act as premeditated murder. At the crash site authorities found 470 personal effects and 150 distinct DNA sets matching the passenger count, though identification will take weeks. Reports show Lubitz had a history of depression, saw multiple doctors and obtained sick notes he did not submit to his employer. German officials plan a task force to reassess cockpit door procedures and pilots’ medical oversight while balancing doctor-patient confidentiality.

About 80 percent of the roughly 1,200 participants in the caravan are Hondurans fleeing poverty, political unrest and post-election violence after President Juan Orlando Hernández’s contested swearing-in. For days the group—women, men and children—has marched through southern Mexico, chanting slogans like “out with JOH,” “we aren't immigrants, we're international workers,” and “the people united will never be defeated.” Organized by volunteers with Pueblos Sin Fronteras (People Without Borders), the caravan surprised its organizers with its size and has strained resources in towns where it camps overnight. Organizers and migrants formed self-governing structures—groups of 10–15 with designated leaders, assembled into sectors, plus committees for security, food and logistics—to increase safety and solidarity and to reduce reliance on smugglers and exposure to gangs and cartels. Many hope to claim asylum in the United States; others plan to cross undetected or settle in Mexico. Organizers stress they do not provide legal papers or food, only assistance and coordination; migrants must cover their own costs. The caravan travels by foot, trucks, vans or even the freight train “the Beast,” despite its dangers. Local communities and churches sometimes provide food and shelter. The mass movement poses an enforcement and political challenge for Mexican and U.S. authorities and tests immigration policy amid heated domestic debates over borders and migration.

Mel B has filed for divorce from Stephen Belafonte and obtained a restraining order accusing him of nearly a decade of physical, emotional and sexual abuse. She alleges repeated beatings, choking, threats and humiliation, claiming his violence escalated whenever she succeeded professionally. Specific incidents include alleged assaults in 2007, 2012 and after the 2012 Olympics, injuries that production crews tried to conceal, and a suicide attempt in December 2014 after swallowing a bottle of aspirin. She says Belafonte controlled and degraded her—calling her worthless, threatening to release sex tapes he recorded, and coercing her into sexual encounters with other women; he allegedly recorded some encounters. Mel B also alleges Belafonte impregnated their nanny, pressured her about the pregnancy, and paid the nanny large sums from Mel B’s money. She claims he threatened to use recordings to ruin her career and to involve Child Services to take her children, and that he kept a firearm despite a prior prohibition; ATF later served a search warrant but reportedly did not find the gun. After her father’s recent death and further abusive comments from Belafonte, she sought the restraining order forcing him to leave their home. Belafonte denies the allegations and questions her motives. Despite filing for separation in December, Mel B was recently photographed still wearing a large wedding ring Belafonte bought her.

Lawyers for Krishna “Kris” Maharaj, a 75-year-old British-born former millionaire who has spent 27 years in a Florida prison for the 1986 double murder of business partner Derrick Moo Young and his son Duane, have disclosed 53 witnesses and 498 documents they plan to present to push for a retrial. Miami’s 11th Judicial Circuit will set a date next Wednesday for a full evidentiary hearing — Maharaj’s best chance in decades to prove his innocence. Sentenced to death in 1987 and later resentenced to life, Maharaj’s team says new evidence points to his framing to conceal the involvement of Medellín cartel operatives; defense filings claim the Moo Youngs were laundering cartel money and that cartel members carried out the killings on Pablo Escobar’s orders. Among the proposed witnesses are six who place Maharaj 30 miles away at the time, others who identify an alternate perpetrator and witnesses alleging perjury by key trial witnesses. Documents include hotel records and materials purportedly showing the Youngs’ illicit dealings. Prosecutors argue much of the material is hearsay and inadmissible. Judge William Thomas said a retrial would be granted only if the new evidence would probably produce an acquittal; he will rule on admissibility at the hearing. Maharaj’s attorneys, including Clive Stafford Smith, insist the case for exoneration is overwhelming.

Anonymous street artists plastered Los Angeles with posters depicting Meryl Streep alongside Harvey Weinstein and a red banner reading "She knew," implying Streep enabled or ignored Weinstein’s alleged decades-long sexual misconduct. The posters — echoing artist Barbara Kruger’s style — appeared near Streep’s Pasadena home, by the SAG‑AFTRA building, Hollywood and Highland, and across from 20th Century Fox, which releases Streep’s film The Post. The campaign followed Rose McGowan’s public attacks accusing Streep and other actresses of hypocrisy for planning to wear black at the Golden Globes in solidarity with victims; McGowan has accused Weinstein of rape. Streep responded that she did not know of Weinstein’s crimes and was not deliberately silent, saying his power insulated his behavior. The controversy has sparked wider conversations about complicity, non‑disclosure agreements, and support for survivors, with figures like Amber Tamblyn urging unity rather than public shaming among women seeking change.

Burberry has announced it will immediately stop destroying unsaleable products and phase out real fur, banning rabbit, fox, mink, Asiatic raccoon and angora. The move expands existing reuse, repair, donation and recycling efforts and aligns with its five-year Responsibility agenda to 2022, which aims for product-driven positive change, carbon neutrality and impacting one million people. Burberry highlighted partnerships—Elvis & Kresse to convert 120 tonnes of leather offcuts into goods, and the Burberry Material Futures Research Group with the Royal College of Art—plus work with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation and community programmes in London, Yorkshire and Afghanistan. CEO Marco Gobbetti framed the changes as modern, responsible luxury.

Benny Anders—6'6" showman of the University of Houston’s Phi Slama Jama in the early 1980s—was famous for flamboyant dunks, quotable one-liners and a combustible personality, yet vanished from public view for decades. The defining image: a midair, near-beheading dunk on Louisville in the 1983 Final Four, followed seconds later by a reverse dunk with his team up late, exemplifying Anders’s defiant, take-it-to-the-rack ethos. He was an unmistakable counterpoint to polished stars Clyde Drexler and Akeem Olajuwon—part wild card, part cult figure—who became as much a part of the Cougars’ identity as their big names. After helping drive Houston to consecutive finals, Anders’s college career unraveled: benchings, clashes with coach Guy Lewis, a walkout, reinstatement, and ultimately a gun-possession incident that led to probation and his dismissal. He briefly played overseas, then disappeared.

For years teammates, journalists and fans tried to find him. Reports and tips produced a tangle of dead ends—mistaken identities, conflicting sightings, even paid intermediaries promising contact. The author recounts his own hunt: trips to Bernice, La., and Flint, Mich., inquiries with family and old teammates, and hiring a private investigator, all yielding tantalizing but inconclusive clues. Anders remained elusive, inspiring tall tales and jokes about witness protection.

The mystery was finally broken when filmmaker Chip Rives, making ESPN’s Phi Slama Jama documentary, tracked Anders to the Detroit area with help from former UH player Eric Davis. Anders was located working at a restaurant, appears in the film, and reportedly received an appearance fee. He closes the documentary with, “A brotherly love is a very powerful thing.” Though questions linger about why he withdrew and what he’s done in the intervening years, Anders’s living presence restores the end of a remarkable, enigmatic arc: a brief, audacious athletic flame that left an outsized, unresolved legacy—and, at last, a human face behind the legend.

President Trump signaled a potential breakthrough in stalled immigration talks by saying he is open to a path to citizenship for roughly 690,000 young undocumented immigrants protected under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program. Speaking impromptu to reporters, Trump said DACA recipients could receive provisional legal status that “morphs into” citizenship over a 10- to 12-year period, contingent on Congress approving $25 billion for a U.S.-Mexico border wall plus $5 billion for additional security upgrades. The administration also plans to press for limits on family-based immigration and an end or overhaul of the diversity visa lottery.

White House aides said a fuller “framework” would be released Monday; it likely would grant immediate provisional status to current DACA participants, with eligibility for full citizenship after meeting specified conditions over the ensuing decade. The offer, officials emphasized, would apply only to the roughly 690,000 people enrolled in DACA when Trump ended the program, not the larger pool of up to 1.7 million potential DREAMers some lawmakers and advocates seek to protect. Expanding protections beyond DACA recipients would be left to Congress.

The announcement came amid urgency to resolve immigration before a Feb. 8 funding deadline that could trigger another government shutdown. Reactions were mixed: Sen. Lindsey Graham welcomed Trump’s statement as presidential leadership that could salvage bipartisan negotiations, while other lawmakers and immigrant advocates noted Trump’s past reversals and the lack of Democratic consultation on the plan. Senators have begun coordinating debate parameters; lawmakers warn many contentious details remain—how much wall funding suffices, family immigration limits, and who qualifies—any of which could determine whether a compromise is achievable.

The Hope Diamond, a 45.52-carat, sky‑blue gem now on display at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, has inspired legends of a deadly curse but also serious scientific and historical study. The curse narrative traces loosely to 17th‑century French merchant Jean‑Baptiste Tavernier, who brought a large blue diamond from India to Europe; popular lore says he stole it from a Hindu idol and later died violently, but historians show Tavernier lived and died peacefully and never documented stealing such a stone. The gem became part of King Louis XIV’s collection as the “French Blue,” passed through the French crown, and was stolen during the Revolution. A recut, smaller version surfaced decades later and entered the possession of Henry Philip Hope in 1839, giving the stone its modern name.

Many tragic episodes in owners’ lives—Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette’s execution, Lord Francis Hope’s bankruptcy and marital collapse, Evalyn Walsh McLean’s family tragedies—fed the curse myth, sometimes amplified by owners or jewelers like Pierre Cartier to boost the gem’s mystique and value. Others, like jeweler Henry Winston and the Smithsonian, escaped ill fate; the latter has seen increased museum attendance since acquiring the stone in 1958. A postal worker who delivered the diamond did suffer a streak of misfortune, which further fueled stories.

Beyond legend, recent scientific work by François Farges and Smithsonian curator Jeffrey Post used a rediscovered 17th‑century lead replica and computer modeling to show the French Blue was cut and mounted to produce a sunlike golden effect at its center when set against gold—a symbolic reference to Louis XIV, the “Sun King.” The replica’s dimensions also proved the French Blue and today’s Hope are the same stone, recut after the 1792 theft. Researchers plan a demonstration replica to illustrate the original appearance and continue archival work to confirm the jeweler’s intent. The diamond’s unique boron-induced blue color and red fluorescence under ultraviolet light remain real, measurable attributes that, paired with its storied past, keep public fascination alive—now extended into a Smithsonian‑endorsed adventure video game that educates players about the gem’s history and science.

A recently circulated clip of off-air CBS footage from August 2008 shows anchor Katie Couric preparing promotional pieces on the day John McCain announced Sarah Palin as his running mate. Right-leaning sites claim the leaked raw tape “proves” Couric was mocking Palin; the clearest example cited is Couric’s audible, off-mic reaction upon seeing the Palins’ children’s names—“where the hell do they get these (names)?”—and other brief, dismissive remarks about mooseburgers, Palin’s hometown and female basketball players. Conservatives4Palin and bloggers present this as evidence of contempt and an anti-Palin framing by CBS News. Critics argue the clip reveals early bias that shaped mainstream coverage. Defenders note important context: the footage appears to be unrehearsed, internal moments captured while Couric was preparing copy, likely hearing names for the first time; such an exclamation is unsurprising and doesn’t necessarily indicate sustained prejudice. The broadcast copy itself probably reflected information supplied by the McCain campaign, and Palin later sat for a widely criticized CBS interview, undermining claims of an orchestrated hit. The tape is edited and incomplete, so it lacks full context; CBS’s terse response called the attention to the clip evidence of a slow news day and has not disputed its authenticity. Overall, the material offers a glimpse of informal workplace reactions rather than definitive proof of agenda-driven mockery, and the clip’s selective presentation fuels partisan interpretations more than it settles questions about journalistic bias.

A large, classified unmanned aircraft developed by Northrop Grumman, known as the RQ-180, is reportedly flying and represents a significant advance in combining stealth with aerodynamic efficiency for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR). Funded through the Air Force’s classified budget and awarded to Northrop after competition, the program aims to field a penetrating ISR capability for contested or denied airspace—missions left unmet since the SR-71’s retirement. Officials indicate the RQ-180 carries radio-frequency sensors such as AESA radar and passive electronic surveillance, and may perform electronic attack. Its stealth and long-range efficiency contrast with non-stealthy platforms like the Global Hawk and Predator/Reaper that operate in permissive environments, and it eclipses the smaller RQ-170 Sentinel. Public clues include Northrop financial disclosures showing a large secret contract and entry into low-rate initial production, plus satellite imagery of new hangars at Palmdale and Area 51 sized for a wingspan over 130 feet. The program is expected to be managed by the Air Force’s Rapid Capabilities Office, possibly operated jointly with the CIA as prior secret ISR programs were, and could be operational by 2015. Northrop’s other UAS work, like the carrier-capable X-47B, continues in parallel.

Scientists have reexamined a massive solar storm that narrowly missed Earth on July 23, 2012, concluding it was one of the most powerful in at least 150 years. Daniel Baker (University of Colorado) and colleagues, publishing in Space Weather, report the event was effectively a “superstorm” formed when two coronal mass ejections (CMEs) erupted within minutes of each other and sped through space already cleared by an earlier CME. That combination allowed the cloud to remain unusually fast and energetic; researchers estimate it would have produced a disturbance (Dst) around −1,200 nT had it hit Earth—comparable to the 1859 Carrington Event and far stronger than the −600 nT storm that caused the 1989 Quebec blackout.

Earth was fortunate: the CME tore through Earth’s orbital path about a week after our planet had passed that location. Had it arrived earlier, NASA and study authors say, it could have inflicted catastrophic damage—widespread electrical blackouts, destroyed transformers, disrupted satellites, GPS, radio and communications—potentially costing over $2 trillion and requiring years to repair critical infrastructure. STEREO-A, a sun-orbiting observatory, was struck instead and returned a rich dataset that revealed the storm’s magnetic structure, particle fluxes, and the role of multiple eruptions in preconditioning interplanetary space.

Researchers warn the risk remains tangible: a 2014 analysis by Pete Riley estimated a roughly 12% chance of a Carrington-scale storm hitting Earth within the next decade. Preparations since 2008—better monitoring, operational mitigations like rerouting polar flights and adjusting grid operations—help, but vulnerabilities persist, especially for aging transformers and satellites. Scientists emphasize continued space-weather monitoring and preparedness to reduce societal and economic impacts if such an extreme event occurs.

A Florida couple, Chris and Dana White of Pensacola, say they discovered a hidden recording device pointed at their bed while aboard the Carnival Fantasy on a three-day Caribbean cruise last October. The device was found tucked among TV wires in their stateroom; Chris filmed the discovery and an employee dismantling the unit after ship security was called. The Whites say the device was plugged in, warm, and capable of recording. They felt their privacy had been violated and announced they will never cruise with Carnival again.

Carnival Cruise Line says its shipboard team conducted a full investigation and located a “video transmitter,” but the company maintains it was not connected to an electrical source and therefore “not capable of recording.” Carnival says the safety and security of guests and crew is paramount, that it has taken measures to prevent similar incidents, and that the device was turned over to the FBI for further examination; U.S. Customs and Border Protection was also notified. The couple disputes the company’s description, insisting the device was active when found.

The story was featured on Inside Edition, which plans to air the Whites’ interview and has sought analysis from a surveillance expert using the footage the couple shot. The report also places the incident alongside other recent cruise controversies, such as an episode on Royal Caribbean’s Voyager of the Seas where some 1,300 conference attendees allegedly disrupted passenger experiences with raucous parties and scantily clad performers, prompting refunds and an investigation. The Whites’ case raises concerns about onboard privacy and how cruise lines handle and communicate about security incidents.

Thomas Keith Henderson, 56, a West Virginia Department of Transportation snow plow operator from Elkhorn, was arrested late Wednesday on Burke Mountain near Keystone after a deputy stopped his plow for a defective headlight. The deputy reported smelling alcohol and observing bloodshot, glassy eyes; Henderson failed field sobriety tests. A breath test at the Welch Police Department registered a 0.09% blood alcohol content, above the 0.04% legal limit for commercial drivers. He was charged with DUI (CDL) and defective equipment, arraigned Jan. 30, and released on $500 bond. The DOT confirmed his employment but declined further comment because the matter is ongoing.

The New Museum in New York hosted a program featuring artist Nari Ward in conversation with curator Massimiliano Gioni, coinciding with Ward’s exhibition "We the People." Ward, a prominent sculptor, uses found materials to explore memory and social and political themes. Around the same time, controversy focused on the screening of David Wojnarowicz’s video "A Fire in My Belly, A Work in Progress" at the New Museum after it had been removed from a Smithsonian exhibit. The more-than-30-minute work includes graphic sexual imagery and a scene of ants on a crucifix that offended religious groups, prompting Catholic League president Bill Donohue to protest and lobby Congress to defund the Smithsonian. The Smithsonian removed the piece, spurring debate about artistic freedom and censorship; many galleries sought screening rights after the controversy. New Museum director Lisa Phillips defended free expression, arguing institutions must protect civil liberties. The video is now shown in the New Museum lobby and is available for free viewing.

Vladimir Katriuk, a 93-year-old longtime Canadian resident and beekeeper in Quebec, has died after a prolonged illness, his lawyer Orest Rudzik said. Katriuk had long faced accusations of participating in wartime atrocities as a member of a Ukrainian battalion that collaborated with Nazi forces during World War II. Scholarly research and released KGB interrogations have implicated a man with his name in the March 1943 Khatyn massacre in what is now Belarus, alleging he manned a machine gun outside a burning barn and shot civilians attempting to flee. A 1999 Federal Court ruling found Katriuk lied about voluntary service for German authorities to obtain Canadian citizenship, concluding he belonged to a unit implicated in mass killings, but the court said it could not find direct evidence he committed specific atrocities. In 2007 the Canadian government declined to revoke his citizenship, citing lack of evidence.

Recently, Russia’s Investigative Committee charged Katriuk with genocide and asked Canada to extradite him for trial, a demand Ottawa ignored amid deteriorating Canada–Russia relations over the Ukraine crisis. Canadian Jewish groups had urged action to ensure accountability, while the Ukrainian Canadian Congress and others cautioned against acquiescing to Moscow, calling the request politically motivated. Federal Justice officials reiterated Canada’s stance that war criminals are unwelcome and will be pursued, though Katriuk’s death makes prosecution impossible. Throughout, Katriuk denied wrongdoing and largely refused to discuss his past, focusing publicly on beekeeping; his lawyer characterized him as long-harassed and ailing in his final years.

Twenty-two states and the District of Columbia, led by New York, asked the U.S. Supreme Court to preserve Montana’s century-old ban on corporate campaign spending and to prevent the 2010 Citizens United decision from being used to invalidate state-level restrictions. The brief argues Montana’s Corrupt Practices Act—which requires corporations to use political action committees rather than spend directly from treasuries—differs from the federal rules at issue in Citizens United and is tailored to prevent corruption in state and local races, including judicial and law-enforcement contests. Montana AG Steve Bullock cites historical corruption tied to the Copper Kings as justification; conservative group American Tradition Partnership contends the state law conflicts with Citizens United and has asked the Court to reverse the Montana high court without a hearing. The Supreme Court has temporarily blocked Montana’s law while it considers the case. Supporters, including Sens. John McCain and Sheldon Whitehouse, and groups seeking broader reconsideration of Citizens United argue evidence from recent election cycles shows independent expenditures can foster corruption or its appearance. Legal analysts view a full reversal of Citizens United as unlikely, though a clarification allowing state restrictions remains a possibility.

Minnesota Rep. Michele Bachmann moved to renounce Swiss citizenship after reports that she and some of her children had sought Swiss paperwork. Bachmann said the citizenship was “conferred upon me by operation of Swiss law” when she married Marcus Bachmann, a dual U.S.-Swiss citizen, in 1978, and that she sent a letter to the Swiss Consulate requesting withdrawal to make clear her sole allegiance to the United States. In a statement she emphasized her American birth, pride in U.S. citizenship, commitment to the Constitution, and family military ties. Earlier accounts and a spokeswoman had said the family had sought Swiss citizenship recently because some children wanted to claim eligibility; Bachmann initially called the matter a “non-story” and said the family had only updated documents. The revelation prompted criticism and questions about hypocrisy, given Bachmann’s past attacks on opponents’ patriotism and her role in debates over national loyalty. Opponents and commentators also raised concerns about optics for a member of the House Intelligence Committee, while others defended dual citizenship as common and benign. The episode sparked public commentary about patriotism, hypocrisy and political consequences.

The NYPD arrested 22-year-old Isaiah Thompson after video surfaced of him subway surfing—riding on the outside of a northbound C train in Brooklyn—around 8:30 a.m. between Clinton-Washington and Lafayette Avenue. Captured by commuter Matthew Beary, the clip shows Thompson calmly hanging onto the car and jumping off at Lafayette; it has been widely shared online. Thompson faces reckless endangerment and disorderly conduct charges for this latest incident. Police and multiple outlets say this was at least his third arrest for similar stunts in 2017 (March and November), and some reports claim a fourth September arrest, though authorities couldn’t confirm that. Transit chief Andy Byford condemned the behavior as “incredibly dangerous, disruptive, and foolish,” noting it can cause major delays and death; several fatal and serious subway-surfing incidents in recent years underscore the risk. Thompson could not be reached for comment. Authorities say they will pursue a strong conviction; public reaction mixes shock, fascination, and warnings to simply wait for the next train.

A March 2016 crawl of outlinks from wikipedia.org produced a comprehensive collection that differs from earlier runs in several key ways. Unlike past crawls that targeted only the English Wikipedia, this iteration seeded from all 865 Wikimedia collections, enabling coverage across the many language-specific and thematic wikis for the first time. Duplicate detection was deliberately turned off so the collection would be complete; the team anticipated possible future data sharing and sought to avoid the complexities of referencing duplicates across disparate collections. At the time of reporting, the resulting files were not publicly accessible, though there was an expectation that they might be shared later, with the caveat that sharing linked pointers into other collections presents logistical challenges.

In a separate public-health finding summarized alongside the crawl description, a new annual survey reported a concerning rise in physical inactivity among Americans. The number of people described as “totally sedentary” reached its highest level since 2007. Approximately 83 million Americans aged six and older—about 28% of that population—said they did not once engage in any of 104 specific physical activities during the previous calendar year. This statistic indicates a substantial portion of the population is not participating in even occasional recreational or routine movement captured by the survey’s activity list. The juxtaposition of the technical note about the Wikimedia crawl and the survey’s health data underscores different dimensions of data collection and dissemination: one involving large-scale web-archival practices and the challenges of sharing and de-duplicating link-rich datasets, and the other highlighting the societal implications revealed through population-level survey measurement of behavior and health risk.

A deadly stampede during the Hajj in Mina, near Mecca, killed at least 717 pilgrims and injured 863 as two million worshippers performed the “stoning the devil” ritual, Saudi authorities reported. The crush occurred around 09:00 local time when large groups converged on the Jamarat Bridge; witnesses described chaotic scenes of people climbing over one another, bodies piled on the ground, and frantic attempts to help amid overwhelming crowds. Nationalities among the victims included Iranians—Tehran reported at least 95 dead and 150 injured—Nigeriens, Nigerians, Indonesians and others. Saudi officials, including Crown Prince Mohammed bin Nayef, ordered an inquiry and King Salman demanded an urgent review of Hajj arrangements; some officials blamed pilgrims for disregarding timetables while others, including Iran’s supreme leader, faulted Saudi mismanagement. The disaster follows a crane collapse at the Grand Mosque days earlier that killed over 100. The incident is the deadliest Hajj-related tragedy in decades, reviving memories of past fatal crushes at Mina and highlighting persistent logistical and safety challenges during the pilgrimage.

This document compiles reports and commentary on recurring measles outbreaks in the United States, highlighting causes, impacts, and prevention imperatives. It begins with a historical California epidemic (1988–1990) that produced 16,400 reported cases, 3,390 hospitalizations, and 75 deaths, concentrated among children under five—especially infants under 12 months—and centered in low-income Hispanic communities. Low immunization rates among preschoolers and young adults, limited early funding, and limited public uptake of community immunization campaigns fueled the crisis; direct costs were estimated at $30.9 million. 

More recent outbreaks, including a 2015 cluster traced to Disneyland, again show measles’ capacity to spread rapidly where pockets of undervaccination exist. In that episode about 70 infections spanned five U.S. states and Mexico, most patients were unvaccinated, a quarter were hospitalized, and cases ranged from infants to elderly adults. Officials warned unvaccinated people, pregnant women, infants, and immunocompromised individuals to avoid high-risk settings such as theme parks and airports until containment. Anti-vaccine advocacy groups and a few sympathetic physicians questioned causation and cautioned against alarm, but public-health experts note robust evidence of vaccine safety and emphasize community protection.

A CDC 2011 national summary recorded 222 measles cases across 31 states and 17 outbreaks, a marked rise from prior years; 90% of cases were linked to importations and most patients were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status. Genotyping confirmed multiple imported strains. The report stresses that measles elimination in the U.S. depends on maintaining high MMR coverage (≥95% community immunity), rapid case recognition, laboratory confirmation, timely reporting, outbreak response, and vaccination of all eligible persons, including travelers and healthcare workers. The recurring pattern underscores that importations plus localized undervaccination can rapidly produce outbreaks and that sustained vaccination and vigilance are essential to prevent resurgence.

Republican leaders and pundits are again speculating that House Speaker Paul Ryan could be a fallback presidential nominee if the 2016 GOP convention deadlocks, despite Ryan’s repeated denials. RNC Chair Reince Priebus called the notion “highly unlikely” but conceded it’s possible; Politico reported that some top Republicans privately put heavy odds on a brokered convention and an eventual turn to Ryan. Supporters argue Ryan’s prudence—publicly declining the job—could create leverage similar to his path to the speakership. Ryan, traveling in Israel, firmly rejected overtures on Hugh Hewitt’s show and to The Times of Israel, saying “I’m not running for president” and that one must run to be president. He cited family considerations, the deep bench of GOP candidates, and his belief in campaigning from Iowa onward as reasons for staying out. Critics note practical and political obstacles: nominating someone who didn’t campaign could provoke party chaos; Ryan’s past performance on the 2012 ticket and current polls don’t guarantee national appeal; and a late-emerging nominee would lack campaign infrastructure, messaging, staff, and financing. Despite denials, comparisons to his earlier reluctance over the speakership suggest the speculation will persist through the convention.

A Ride the Ducks sightseeing boat capsized and sank on Table Rock Lake near Branson, Missouri, during a severe thunderstorm on the evening of July 19, 2018, killing many passengers and prompting a major search and investigation. The amphibious vessel was carrying 31 people when heavy winds—reported over 60 mph—and violent waves overwhelmed the flat‑bottomed craft as it tried to head for shore. Initial reports listed at least 11 dead and several missing; later updates raised the toll to 17 fatalities, ranging in age from 1 to 76, including nine members of one Indiana family. Fourteen people survived and seven were injured; several were treated at Cox Medical Center Branson, with two adults critically ill. Authorities and dive teams worked through the night; the National Transportation Safety Board dispatched investigators and the sunken boat was expected to be recovered from about 80 feet of water.

Ride the Ducks Branson, owned by Ripley Entertainment, said it was assisting authorities and that this was its first accident in more than 40 years of operation. The National Weather Service had issued a severe thunderstorm watch and later a warning hours before the storm struck, raising questions about weather warnings, operator decisions, and boat safety. Duck boats have a history of deadly incidents, and past NTSB recommendations have highlighted design and flotation concerns, canopy entrapment risks, and regulatory inconsistencies governing these amphibious tour vehicles. Local officials provided support for victims’ families as the investigation continued.

Two men from the Jersey Shore were arrested after allegedly using a taxi to burglarize a Deal Township home and then refusing to pay the driver, police said. Kenneth Burke, 46, and Timothy Foote, 38, called a cab to a Norwood Avenue residence Friday night and told the driver to wait. They returned with a television and several bottles of liquor, then rode to an Asbury Park apartment and exited without paying. The taxi driver notified Asbury Park police, who alerted Deal officers; investigators found the home had just been burglarized. Burke and Foote face charges including burglary, conspiracy, criminal trespass and theft, are held in Monmouth County jail on $20,000 bail each, and the stolen items were returned to the homeowner.

A tractor-trailer driver who fell from the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel (CBBT) Thursday afternoon died after being rescued, authorities confirmed. The driver, identified as 47-year-old Joseph Chen of Greenville, North Carolina, was hauling seafood for Evans Transports. Chen was pulled from the water by a U.S. Navy MH-60 Sierra crew from HSC-2 that happened to be training nearby; officials said he had been standing on top of the vehicle before being hoisted into the helicopter. He died en route to the hospital. The Medical Examiner ruled the death accidental, citing drowning and hypothermia.

The crash occurred around 12:30 p.m. at mile marker 15 on the southbound side of the CBBT. Video showed a large section of guardrail damaged. Both directions of the bridge were temporarily closed and reopened before 2 p.m. Wind conditions were notable: the CBBT had escalated to Level 2 wind restrictions (winds exceeding 47 mph) later in the day; at the time of the accident there was a Level 1 restriction. Under Level 2 rules, certain tractor-trailers must meet minimum gross payload thresholds to cross. Drivers on the Eastern Shore described feeling trailers pushed by strong gusts and expressed concern about being too light to cross safely.

Meteorologists reported a water temperature of 45 degrees and wave heights of five to seven feet at the time. The Virginia Trucking Association extended condolences to Chen’s family, friends, and coworkers. Chen’s relatives said he was a husband and father and the founder and president of the Turn-N-Burn Motorcycle Club. WAVY noted prior CBBT tractor-trailer incidents, including a 2016 overboard rescue and a fatal 2014 crash. Authorities continue to investigate.

Taxi drivers across Europe staged large protests June 11-12, blocking city centers and airports from London and Paris to Madrid, Berlin, Milan and Barcelona, to denounce Uber and similar mobile car-hailing services for undercutting regulated taxis and threatening livelihoods. More than 30,000 drivers participated, snarling traffic and demanding regulators enforce licensing, insurance and fare rules they say Uber bypasses. London’s black cabs and trainees rallied around Trafalgar and Parliament Squares while Paris drivers slowed major arteries and targeted airports; Madrid and Berlin saw mass marches and coordinated blockades. Protesters argue apps act as illegal taximeters and that private drivers operate without costly taxi licenses; regulators and courts in several countries are weighing restrictions or bans. Uber, backed by substantial new funding and valued in the multibillion-dollar range, pushed back—promoting services, offering discounts, and opening its platform to black cabs in London—arguing it brings consumer choice and jobs. The clashes reflect broader tensions across Europe between entrenched, highly regulated industries and disruptive tech platforms, prompting calls for dialogue and regulatory updates rather than strikes or bans.

During his Galápagos voyage, Charles Darwin noted distinctive finches that later became emblematic of speciation. New research warns that one of those species, the medium ground finch (Geospiza fortis), faces possible extinction within decades due to an introduced parasitic nest fly, Philornis downsi. Although adult flies don’t feed on birds, they deposit eggs in nests; the hatching larvae feed on nestlings and brooding adults, causing severe lesions and mortality among the tiny hatchlings. P. downsi is present across the Galápagos and was first documented in nests in the 1990s after arriving via human activity in the 1960s.

University of Utah scientists collected five years of field data on Santa Cruz Island and experimentally manipulated nest parasite loads using permethrin-treated nests versus water-sprayed controls to quantify direct effects. They incorporated these results into population models under “good,” “neutral,” and “bad” reproductive-year scenarios. In two of three scenarios (neutral and bad), the models forecast extinction: roughly 43–57 years under bad conditions and 65–95 years under neutral conditions; only sustained good reproductive years extended survival to about a century. The researchers stress that similar risks likely apply to other Darwin’s finches, including already critically rare species like the mangrove finch.

The team highlights that reducing infestations by about 40 percent could prevent extinction. Potential interventions include insecticide-treated nests, sterile-male release, parasitoid wasps, or hand-rearing chicks. There remains a slim possibility of rapid evolutionary resistance by the finches, but scientists emphasize urgent human action because the fly’s introduction is anthropogenic. Saving these iconic birds is crucial for biodiversity and for preserving a living laboratory of evolution.

A New Hampshire farm’s wholesome video of a newborn Scottish Highland calf named Diego has sparked a global controversy, drawing both heartfelt support and sharp criticism. Yankee Farmer’s Market in Warner posted a short clip showing the fluffy calf being warmed after a snowstorm, which went viral with roughly 12–13 million views and over 138,000 shares. The post also spurred offers from strangers wanting to adopt the calf and prompted a wave of animal-rights backlash from people who assumed Diego would be separated from his mother or slaughtered.

Owner Brian Farmer says those assumptions are incorrect. Diego was returned to his mother after being dried off; the farm does not produce veal nor slaughter animals on-site, which would require USDA licensing. Farmer emphasizes that his Scottish Highland cattle and American buffalo are raised humanely—roaming pastures, free to graze, and raised without antibiotics or hormones. Diego is intended for registered breeding to help restore a long-established herd tied to Farmer’s Pitcher Mountain Farm in Stoddard, which revived its Highland herd from a low of 12 to about 30 animals since 2013.

Protesters have also used Facebook’s review system to flood the farm with one-star ratings, prompting frustration for Farmer, who feels the attacks conflate ethical concerns about meat consumption with his farm’s practices. The incident has rallied local customers and community members to defend the farm’s open-pasture methods. Farmer says he will keep sharing animal stories to educate the public about humane, small-scale agriculture and the ecological balance between animals, plants, and insects.

This summary covers an FDA safety alert from Sept. 22, 2009, and a 2016 fatality involving a medical alert pendant. The FDA warned that Philips Lifeline pendant personal help buttons—worn on cords around the neck—pose a potential choking and strangulation hazard because their cords are intentionally non–breakaway to prevent the button from falling off. Between 1998 and 2009, the agency was aware of at least six reports of serious injury or death tied to entanglement of these cords with other objects worn around the neck, including three U.S. deaths and one in Canada. Philips Lifeline reported more than 750,000 users in the U.S. and Canada and began notifying customers by letter and updating product labeling to include a choking-warning. The FDA emphasized that risks are higher for people with mobility limitations or who use wheelchairs, walkers, or beds with guard rails, and recommended users consult health care providers to choose the most suitable style of emergency button—such as wrist-worn models or devices with breakaway cords. The notice reminded clinicians and consumers to report adverse events to FDA MedWatch.

The archive also recounts the Feb. 15, 2016 accidental death of 86-year-old Roseann J. DiFrancesco of New Cumberland, Pa. She apparently tripped while using a walker and was found suspended by her medical alert lanyard, which had become caught on the walker handle; the coroner said the lanyard lacked a breakaway feature. Her death was ruled accidental. The reports note debate among manufacturers: breakaway lanyards reduce strangulation risk but can leave the device out of reach, so selection should be individualized with medical advice.

Kuşköy, a remote village on Turkey’s rainy Black Sea coast, looks ordinary—houses on steep hillsides, tea fields, hazelnut orchards—but is notable for its unique whistled language, kuş dili or “bird language.” For generations villagers adapted Turkish syllables into piercing whistles audible over long distances, a practical solution in rugged, noisy terrain. Whistled languages are uncommon but widespread historically—in the Canary Islands, parts of Africa, Southeast Asia, and South America—where they evolved from spoken languages to carry meaning across valleys and forests. A single Turkish phrase like “Taze ekmek var mı?” can become six distinct whistles produced with tongue, teeth, and fingers.

Biopsychologist Onur Güntürkün studied whistled Turkish as a natural experiment in brain organization. The left hemisphere typically dominates language processing while the right handles pitch and melody. Using dichotic listening tests with 31 bilingual speakers of spoken and whistled Turkish, he played different syllables to each ear. With spoken Turkish, participants tended to report the right-ear (left-hemisphere) input; with whistled Turkish, they reported both ears equally, suggesting bilateral early processing. Although dichotic listening is less precise than imaging, the findings imply that brain lateralization for language is more flexible than assumed. Güntürkün speculates whistled language training might help stroke patients with left-hemisphere language damage, much as singing can aid some aphasics.

Despite its scientific and cultural interest, Kuşköy’s whistled language is fading. Once learned in early childhood and used broadly, it survives unevenly: fewer young women know it, and many young men learn it mainly for pride or tourism-driven contests. Modern privacy afforded by texting and changing social needs have reduced everyday use. Still, the language endures in small practical ways—villagers sometimes whistle to communicate when a German-speaking secretary answers Güntürkün’s office phone.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn, the 62-year-old head of the IMF arrested on charges including attempted rape and sexual assault of a Manhattan hotel maid, is being held at Rikers Island under heightened precautions. Following his arraignment, he was placed alone in a wing typically reserved for inmates with contagious illnesses, occupying one cell in a 14-cell unit. He undergoes standard mental-health screening and, after concerns during intake, was put on suicide watch with checks every 15–30 minutes. Authorities say he has not attempted self-harm and appears in good condition. Because he has sleep apnea, he was issued a CPAP machine. As a pre-trial detainee he may wear his own clothes in his cell and leave for limited supervised recreation, but must wear slip-on shoes and a special pocketless gray jumpsuit for visits. He is held without bail pending further court proceedings. The alleged victim remains in hiding, and Strauss-Kahn’s lawyer denies evidence of a forced encounter.

A large, coordinated effort to test reproducibility in psychology attempted to replicate 100 studies from major journals and found that only 39 produced results the replication teams judged to have reproduced the original findings. The replicated effects were generally much smaller: the average effect size in replications was about half that of the originals. Using multiple indicators—statistical significance, effect-size comparisons, subjective team assessments, and meta-analyses—the project reported that 97% of the original studies had significant results versus 36% of the replications; 47% of original effect sizes fell within the replication 95% confidence intervals; and 68% remained significant if original and replication results were combined under a no-bias assumption. Correlational analyses suggested that the strength of the original evidence (for example, original p-values) predicted replication success better than characteristics of research teams. 
 
 The authors and participants emphasize that these outcomes do not mean science has failed; rather, they highlight how difficult reproducible experimentation can be and how essential replication is to self-correction. Replication failures can result from false original findings, replication errors failing to detect real effects, or meaningful methodological differences between contexts (illustrated by a replicated study that differed in participant decision difficulty across universities). The project argues that current incentives favor novel results over replications, which can leave the literature “more beautiful than reality.” To improve trustworthiness, the field should value and standardize high-quality replications alongside new discoveries so science can better identify which results are robust and which require further scrutiny.

University of Cincinnati President Santa Ono publicly revealed that he attempted suicide twice in his youth, a disclosure he made at a mental-health fundraiser and amplified to his more than 70,000 Twitter followers. Ono said he first tried to overdose on cold medicine and beer at 14 and made a second attempt in his late 20s. Now 53, Ono described recovering from depression through medication and professional counseling, and he emphasized that recovery is possible and that stigma should be erased.

Ono shared his story at an Indian Hill event for 1N5, a teen-focused mental health group, which raised more than $115,000. He later posted about his experiences on social media to reach a broader audience and to “break the silence.” Colleagues and campus mental-health professionals praised his candor as courageous and influential. Dr. Phil Diller, who leads University Health Service, said Ono’s openness sends a strong message that highly successful people also face mental-health struggles. Dr. Charles W. Collins of UC’s psychiatry department noted that Ono’s position and recovery can counter the misconception that depression is a weakness and may prompt people to seek help earlier.

Ono’s disclosure is tied to ongoing campus efforts to improve student mental-health resources, efforts he helped accelerate after the 2014 suicide of UC student Brogan Dulle. In the immediate aftermath of Dulle’s death, Ono helped secure five free counseling sessions for any UC student; further care and insurance-covered referrals are available for those needing more help. Dulle’s mother praised Ono’s willingness to share and said his involvement after her son’s death has been supportive.

Ono, son of a Japanese émigré mathematician and an accomplished cellist, said he has been symptom-free for about 25 years and credits family support and treatment for maintaining balance. He urged leaders and legislators to support more suicide-prevention programs and highlighted that many millennials are more empathetic and motivated to address mental-health issues. The article concludes by listing local and national mental-health resources, including UC Counseling & Psychological Services, the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, Crisis Text Line, and others.

A contested Virginia House race between Republican David Yancey and Democrat Shelly Simonds swung dramatically after a recount and a court ruling left the seat tied and control of the House uncertain. On Election Day Yancey led by 10 votes; a recount initially gave Simonds a one-vote victory, prompting Democratic celebrations and Republican concessions anticipating a 50-50 split in the chamber. However, a three-judge panel declined to certify the recount after examining a single disputed ballot that showed marks for both candidates and an additional mark striking out Simonds’s name. The judges—elected by a Republican-controlled legislature—ruled the ballot should be counted for Yancey, producing an exact tie at 11,608 votes each and returning a 50-49 Republican edge in the House until the tie is resolved.

Virginia law requires tied legislative races be decided by lot; the State Board of Elections scheduled a drawing for Dec. 27 using slips in film canisters. The decision followed challenges from Yancey’s team after a recount official expressed regret over how the ballot was handled. Democrats, including caucus lawyer Marc Elias, called the court’s move erroneous and said they were exploring legal options, noting Republicans had initially affirmed the recount outcome. The episode highlighted the power of single ballots and the fragility of election outcomes. Additional recounts in other close House races could further affect control, and House Democrats delayed selecting a speaker while the Simonds-Yancey outcome remains unresolved.

Dozens of concertgoers required medical attention during Avicii’s June show at Boston’s TD Garden, with local reports varying from about 30 to over 80 people affected. Boston EMS and hospital officials said most patients—many aged 16 to 25—suffered from dehydration, alcohol intoxication and possible drug use; Massachusetts General Hospital received 13 patients aged 16–19. Boston EMS described symptoms as largely heat- and alcohol-related and said no patients were in serious condition. About 50 were treated on-site and roughly 36 transported to hospitals, while dozens of ambulances lined Causeway Street as the concert ended. Authorities issued citations for intoxication and drug consumption; three men were arrested on drug charges though not linked to hospitalizations. Attendees and staff described the venue as hot and crowded; TD Garden said it had increased precautions that night, including restricted alcohol sales, extra security and cooling areas. Promoter Live Nation said many taken to hospitals had been stopped before entry. City officials planned meetings with TD Garden leadership; Mayor Walsh emphasized that underage intoxication should not be allowed. Avicii (Tim Bergling) tweeted his concern and well-wishes for those affected. The incident follows other recent festival medical emergencies nationwide.

Burger King is testing a new menu mash-up called the Whopperito, a burrito-style version of its flagship Whopper. First spotted by Grub Grade on signage at several Pennsylvania locations, the Whopperito replaces the burger bun with a flour tortilla while keeping the Whopper’s standard components: flame-grilled beef, American cheese, tomatoes, lettuce, mayonnaise, ketchup, pickles, and white onions. The item follows other recent experiments such as the Whopper Dog, signaling Burger King’s willingness to repackage its signature sandwich in unconventional formats.

It’s not yet known whether the Whopperito is a corporate-sanctioned trial or the work of individual franchisees; Burger King has been contacted for clarification. Availability appears limited to test markets for now, and the company has not announced a wider rollout. Social media reaction has been mixed and often colorful: some Twitter users express disgust or dismay at wrapping a Whopper in a tortilla, while others say they’d try it or appreciate the perceived effort to make the sandwich “a tad more healthy” by removing the bun. The Whopperito concept isn’t entirely new as a DIY pairing—customers have reportedly combined Burger King and Taco Bell items in the past to achieve similar results—but it marks the first time Burger King may be offering such a hybrid directly. Observers and food fans are watching to see whether the Whopperito will expand beyond test locations or remain a limited, experimental offering.

China urged the United States on Wednesday to bar a Taiwanese delegation from attending Donald Trump’s inauguration, warning that such a visit could undermine China-U.S. ties amid concerns Washington might alter the “one China” policy. The delegation, led by former premier Yu Shyi-kun and including security advisers and lawmakers, planned to attend Friday’s inauguration and meet politicians, academics and overseas Chinese. Beijing, which regards Taiwan as a breakaway province with no right to separate diplomatic relations, conveyed its objections to both Trump’s transition team and the Obama administration. Chinese spokeswoman Hua Chunying urged no official contact between U.S. authorities and Taiwan, saying China would send Ambassador Cui Tiankai to the inauguration. Tensions have risen since Trump’s phone call with Taiwanese President Tsai Ing-wen and his remarks that the one-China policy could be renegotiated.

Palau’s president, Tommy Remengesau, is pushing to shift the country’s tourism model from mass to high-end visitors by proposing a law permitting only five-star hotel developments going forward. The aim is “quality rather than quantity”: to attract wealthier tourists who spend more and impose fewer pressures on fragile ecosystems. Investors who build luxury resorts would be expected to provide their own infrastructure—roads, water-treatment systems, power backups—and in return would receive tax breaks and exemptions. Palau depends on tourism for about 85% of GDP, but rising visitor numbers have led to overcrowding, coral reef damage and wildlife disturbance. Chinese package tours, which increased arrivals in recent years while spending little, prompted the government to halve charter flights from China in 2015; Remengesau says that move reduced visitor numbers but increased overall tourist spending. Currently only a few five-star resorts exist around Koror, but with some 500 islands available, the potential is extensive. The proposal emphasizes environmentally sensitive development, though whether future hotels will truly harmonize with Palau’s natural assets remains uncertain.

The Supreme Court refused to narrow a federal law that bars people convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence from possessing firearms, issuing a 6-2 decision that upheld the law’s broad application. Two Maine men had argued their guilty pleas for striking their partners should not trigger the federal ban because their conduct was not intentional or did not fit the statute’s intended scope. Gun-rights advocates supported the men, saying misdemeanor convictions shouldn’t cost individuals their Second Amendment rights, while domestic-violence advocates argued the ban was properly applied to both reckless and intentional misconduct to protect victims. A federal appeals court had already rejected the men’s challenge. By declining to limit the statute, the Supreme Court maintained congressional authority to prohibit firearm possession by those convicted of domestic-violence misdemeanors, preserving the existing legal barrier aimed at reducing the risk of further harm to intimate partners and public safety.

Nigeria’s military says it has arrested the leader of a Boko Haram intelligence cell believed linked to the April abduction of more than 200 schoolgirls from Chibok, along with several women members of the cell. The suspect, named as businessman Babuji Ya'ari, is accused of spying for the militants while posing as a member of a civilian vigilante group and of coordinating deadly attacks in Maiduguri since 2011, and involvement in the killing of the emir of Gwoza in May. The military’s claims could not be independently verified, and Ya'ari has not commented. Boko Haram has demanded the release of imprisoned fighters in return for the girls; the government says it knows the captives’ location but fears a rescue could endanger them. The militant campaign has intensified this year, killing over 2,000 people and expanding attacks—recently including assaults on villages near Chibok that left dozens dead, an attack on a military camp that killed scores of soldiers, and bombings in Abuja. Critics fault the government for slow response; international partners, including the US, have deployed assets to help locate the abducted girls.

The International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) unanimously voted to bar Russia’s track and field team from competing under its flag at the Rio Olympics after concluding Moscow had not done enough to restore confidence following a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) report alleging a state-sponsored doping program. The sanction, unprecedented in Olympic history, extends a suspension that had already kept Russian athletes out of international competition. While Russia won 18 athletics medals, including eight golds, at the last Olympics, none will compete for Russia in Rio; a narrow pathway was created for a few individuals to apply to compete as neutral athletes if they can “clearly and convincingly” show they were subject to credible anti-doping systems and untainted by national manipulation. Whistleblower Yuliya Stepanova’s case was singled out as likely to be viewed favorably.

The IAAF task force, chaired by Rune Andersen, reported that cultural tolerance for doping persists, testing efforts in Russia faced serious obstacles, the Russian Anti-Doping Agency remains noncompliant with WADA codes, and RusAF cannot enforce bans effectively. Interviews revealed denial or dismissal of the independent commission’s findings by key Russian figures; retesting of Beijing and London samples found multiple positives, and evidence suggests laboratory manipulation in Moscow from 2011 onward. The task force noted numerous declined or canceled tests and whereabouts failures.

The decision drew praise from athletes and anti-doping officials as a strong stand for clean sport, while Russian authorities promised challenges and appealed to the IOC. The IAAF emphasized the exception route would be narrowly applied to limit legal challenges, underscoring the priority of protecting clean athletes and the integrity of competition.

The documents debate whether President Obama should seek outside authorization before ordering strikes on Syria, weighing legal, moral, strategic, and practical consequences. One argument insists he should consult Congress rather than act on conscience and military advice alone. Calling Parliament back, as Britain has done, is portrayed as necessary ritual and a source of deliberation: it forces clarity about objectives, constraints, and alternatives. Critics note prior precedent—Libya—where bypassing the War Powers Resolution invited later political theatre and eroded institutional norms; informing and getting Congress’s approval would be neither onerous nor irrelevant given the limited military stakes and the long-term consequences.

Proponents of limited strikes argue U.S. policy toward Syria has failed and that targeted military action, paired with diplomacy, could restore deterrence against chemical-weapons use and reinforce international norms. They point to escalating atrocities, growing death tolls, regional destabilization, and opportunities to pressure Assad’s calculations. Even if strikes are symbolic, they might discourage future chemical attacks and bolster moderate opposition if combined with other support. The red line on chemical weapons, the argument goes, demands some response to preserve credibility and deter mass atrocity.

Opponents counter that a missile strike is a dangerous, hypocritical, and legally dubious gambit that will deepen chaos without a credible follow-on plan. They criticize premature judgments about responsibility for the Ghouta attacks, the sidelining of UN inspectors, and the media’s uncritical role. Skeptics note plausible rebel culpability and cite calls from Russia and other skeptics for full investigations. They warn that even limited Western strikes risk escalation—Assad or allies might retaliate, Hezbollah could strike Western targets, and the intervention may regionalize the war or strengthen jihadist elements. The record of faulty WMD intelligence (Iraq, Sudan) and the West’s selective humanitarian concern fuel distrust. Critics argue the better course is empowering inspectors, securing chemical stockpiles through the UN, pursuing ceasefire and negotiated settlement, and using leverage over rebel backers—rather than symbolic bombing that could worsen the war and civilian suffering.

Across perspectives, common themes emerge: uncertainty about evidence and attribution, ambiguity of military effect, the moral burden of inaction versus the peril of escalation, and the institutional question of whether and how democratic deliberation—Congress, Parliament, or the UN—should constrain executive military action. The texts overall urge careful deliberation, clearer aims, and accountability before any use of force.

A Christmas carol service in Colombo, Sri Lanka, accidentally printed the profanity-laced lyrics of Tupac Shakur’s rap song “Hail Mary” in its programme instead of the traditional Catholic Hail Mary prayer, surprising many attendees. The error occurred at Joy to the World 2016, one of the country’s largest carol services, and photos of the booklet were widely shared on social media over the holiday weekend. The booklet’s opening line—“Makaveli in this … Killuminati, all through your body. The blows like a twelve-gauge shotty”—is from Tupac’s 1997 track, not the thousand-year-old prayer based on passages from the Gospel of Luke. Both the prayer and Tupac’s song call on Mary to intercede for sinners, but the rapper’s lyrics graphically recount sins such as murder and drug dealing, making their appearance in a church programme striking and, to many, inappropriate.

Attendee Andrew Choksy, who photographed the programme, said people around him were initially shocked and unsure whether it was a joke or whether the song would actually be performed. Some older congregants stared at the booklet; others took the mistake with good humour. Organisers at the service made no public explanation at the time, and Choksy’s images circulated online, prompting discussion and surprise. The incident drew attention because of the stark contrast between the sacred text expected at a carol service and the violent, explicit content of Tupac’s song.

On Dec. 22, 2017, at about 2:16 p.m., Madison police arrested 46-year-old barber Khaled A. Shabani at Ruby’s Salon, 627 State St., following an incident in which a 22-year-old male customer said he was injured during a haircut. According to the Madison Police Department and news reports, the customer requested a No. 2 on the sides and about an inch off the top. The situation escalated when the barber allegedly complained the patron was moving and fidgeting, then twisted the customer’s ear. Authorities say Shabani subsequently used scissors to “snip” the customer’s ear, drawing blood, and then used a “zero” clipper to shave a close line down the middle of the man’s head, leaving a visible shave line. Police spokesman Joel Despain described the result as making the victim look “a bit like Larry from the Three Stooges.” After the customer left the shop and returned home, he contacted police. Shabani was taken into custody on suspicion of mayhem and disorderly conduct while armed; the incident report notes mayhem and that disorderly conduct in this context is a county ordinance violation rather than a criminal charge. When reached later, the Madison Police Department said it had no additional information. Shabani pleaded not guilty to the disorderly conduct charge, as reported by the Wisconsin State Journal. The departmental release emphasized that while poor haircuts alone are not criminal, intentionally injuring a patron with scissors—such as by cutting his ear—can result in arrest. For records inquiries, the MPD Records Unit phone number and a Community Crime Map site are referenced in the incident report.

Rockies rookie Trevor Story turned heads in Colorado’s home opener by hitting two homers, becoming the first player in a century to homeroom in each of his first four major-league games and the first rookie ever to do so. Story’s fourth straight game with a long ball extended a torrid start: six homers and 11 RBIs in his first 19 MLB at-bats, with a .368 average and three hits plus four RBIs in Friday’s 13-6 loss to San Diego.
