Elias Sports Bureau notes he’s only the fifth player since 1900 to homer in his team’s first four games of a season, joining Willie Mays (1971), Mark McGwire (1998), Nelson Cruz (2011) and Chris Davis (2013). He also is the only player to record two multi-homer games within his first four big-league games. Story’s early power isn’t solely a Coors Field effect: his first four homers came during the Rockies’ season-opening series in Arizona. Teammates and opponents were stunned—Carlos Gonzalez lauded his fearlessness and Hall of Fame-caliber play, and Padres’ Matt Kemp called the feat impressive. Story, 23, had won the starting job while Jose Reyes was suspended under MLB’s domestic-abuse policy; Story has already donated his helmet and gloves to the Hall of Fame. The Associated Press contributed to reports.

After Donald Trump’s decisive Republican primary victory in South Carolina, observers who once dismissed him as a fringe candidate are now treating his White House bid as a genuine threat. As anxiety grows about the prospect of a reality TV star becoming president, a sharp parody titled "Winter is Trumping" has surfaced, blending Trump footage and audio with iconic Game of Thrones scenes. Created by Huw Parkinson, the video splices Trump into plot moments alongside characters like Littlefinger, Daenerys Targaryen, and Tyrion Lannister, even placing him atop The Wall defending against invaders. The mash-up is nearly seamless, using real Trump lines to make him appear to negotiate, confront dragons and prepare for battle in the brutal, scheming world of Westeros. Though equating a modern politician with a realm where heroes are decapitated and innocence is fleeting may seem extreme, the parody underscores how fitting Trump’s combative, theatrical persona appears within a setting defined by ruthless power plays. David Mack, deputy breaking news director at BuzzFeed News, reported the piece from New York.

A large Libyan military convoy crossed into northern Niger, reaching the Saharan city of Agadez and heading toward Niamey, observers told AFP and AP. Witnesses described several dozen armed pickup trucks; reports suggested Tuareg leader Rissa ag Boula, long linked to Gadhafi, was among those seen. Rumors circulated that members of Muammar Gadhafi’s inner circle—or even one of his sons—might be in the convoy, though this remained unconfirmed. The movement follows accounts that other regime officials fled across the border, and comes as Gadhafi loyalists remained holed up in towns like Bani Walid and Sirte. Gadhafi’s spokesman insisted the leader remained in Libya and was organizing resistance. Rebel negotiators sought peaceful surrenders in loyalist towns to avoid bloodshed while NATO continued strikes near remaining strongholds.

Balloonist Jonathan Trappe, who attempted a transatlantic crossing suspended beneath more than 300 helium-filled balloons, was rescued Friday afternoon after an unplanned landing on Newfoundland’s remote west coast. Trappe had launched from Caribou, Maine, near the New Brunswick border, but said he was burning through ballast too quickly to reach Europe. Facing the choice of landing in isolated woods Thursday night or ditching over the ocean Friday, he chose the former and touched down south of Lark Harbour in the Bay of Islands area. The site was inaccessible by road and largely impassable; local residents’ ATV efforts failed to reach him. Trappe contacted his crew via satellite to confirm he was safe and set up an exposure canopy to wait out the night, posting on Facebook with wry commentary—“Hmm, this doesn’t look like France.” He was ultimately picked up by a helicopter chartered by CBC during an aerial survey; upon meeting a CBC videojournalist he exclaimed, “I’ve never been so glad to see the media.” Trappe, known for cluster-balloon stunts including flying a house inspired by the film Up, framed the outcome as an adventurous success despite missing his original destination.

Jason Van Dyke, the Chicago police officer charged with first-degree murder in the 2014 shooting of 17-year-old Laquan McDonald, has been hired by the Fraternal Order of Police (FOP) lodge in the city’s West Loop, sparking immediate outrage and planned protests. FOP President Dean Angelo confirmed Van Dyke began working for the union about three weeks earlier, earning $12 an hour in a general “jack-of-all-trades” role—duties ranging from office work to rooftop tasks—while he remains suspended from the Chicago Police Department without pay and stripped of police powers. Angelo said the union acted after media inquiries and partly to help Van Dyke’s family, noting threats shut down his wife’s business and he had been unable to find other employment. The FOP framed the hire as consistent with past practice, saying it has provided work for many officers placed in no-pay status and that assistance was based on “sustenance needs of a police officer and his family.”

The move provoked swift condemnation from clergy, activists and community members. Rev. Michael Pfleger called the decision a “disgrace” and urged fellow union members to demand Van Dyke’s firing; his post was widely shared. Protesters organized demonstrations at noon and evening outside the FOP hall, and attempts to enter the building were blocked by police. Activists argued the union was protecting a member accused of shooting a teenager 16 times and compared special treatment to civilian consequences for similar actions. Van Dyke has pleaded not guilty and posted $1.5 million bond after a judge denied a prosecutor’s request to keep him detained. The shooting, captured on video, prompted federal civil-rights scrutiny of the Chicago Police Department and contributed to leadership changes within the force.

Oliver Stone’s four-part Showtime series The Putin Interviews—drawn from more than 30 hours of conversations with Vladimir Putin between 2015 and 2017—offers unusually intimate access to a guarded leader but delivers a documentary that reviewers call both revealing and deeply flawed. Stone’s episodic approach uses dozens of camera angles and extensive B-roll—scenic Kremlin halls, Putin playing hockey, feeding horses, lifting weights, and driving through Moscow—to humanize the ex-KGB president and let him narrate Russia’s grievances against the United States. Putin expounds on NATO expansion, U.S. foreign interventions, Edward Snowden’s asylum, and threats posed by U.S. missile-defense programs, often framing America as the perennial aggressor. His charm, discipline and composure come through, yet so do blunt misogyny, homophobic remarks, selective truths and unproven accusations—moments that make his denials and fabrications more disquieting because they are delivered calmly.

Critics argue Stone’s interviewing style is at times credulous, even solicitous: he often accepts Putin’s assertions without demanding evidence, omits countervailing facts (such as the influence of oligarchs, human-rights abuses, and contested episodes like the Chechen wars), and fails to include meaningful voices from Russian opposition or independent experts. The film’s tone can verge on flattery, allowing Putin to reframe history and U.S.-Russia dynamics while Stone reciprocates with sympathy for anti-interventionist critiques. Ultimately, the series is compelling for its access and intimacy but destabilizing for presenting a powerful, persuasive portrait of Putin that invites unease: it reveals how effectively he controls his image and how little the viewer learns about Russia beyond his carefully curated perspective.

Researchers have rediscovered the Clarion nightsnake, a species not seen in nearly 80 years, on Clarion Island, part of Mexico’s remote Revillagigedo Islands more than 400 miles off the Pacific coast. First recorded by American naturalist William Beebe during a 1936 visit—when he collected a single specimen preserved in a jar—the snake eluded subsequent expeditions and was eventually removed from taxonomic registries amid suspicions the original locality label was mistaken. Smithsonian researcher Daniel Mulcahy, together with Juan Martínez Gómez of Mexico’s Ecology Institute, reopened the case using Beebe’s original field notes and carefully timed fieldwork to match seasonal conditions and nocturnal habits that make the snake cryptic against the island’s rocks. Graduate student Juan Alberto Cervantes was the first of the team to spot a living specimen. The team located 11 snakes matching Beebe’s description and performed DNA analyses showing the Clarion nightsnake is a genetically distinct species most closely related to snakes from the Sonora–Sinaloa mainland coast roughly 500–800 miles away. Scientists speculate the species’ ancestors likely colonized the island via rafting on storm-felled vegetation. The National Museum of Natural History noted this may be the only species ever removed from records due to a presumed locality error and later reinstated. Experts highlight the find’s conservation importance given island ecosystems’ fragility—previously, the Socorro dove vanished in the wild on the Revillagigedo Islands before captive-bred birds were reintroduced. Ongoing monitoring and study are planned to better understand and protect the Clarion nightsnake.

Parsippany police say a hit-and-run early Tuesday left a broken yellow fire hydrant stuck to a car after the vehicle struck the hydrant and a mailbox on Edwards Road. Officer John Garza responded, discovered the scene and followed a trail of water to a Norman Avenue home where he found the 1999 Nissan Quest and the hydrant among garbage cans. The driver, 27-year-old Parsippany resident Domingo Moreno, was located at a nearby diner and arrested. He faces multiple charges including criminal mischief, tampering with evidence, hindering apprehension, failure to report an accident, unlicensed driving, careless and reckless driving, and failure to maintain lane. Moreno was remanded to Morris County jail and turned over to federal immigration officials; police continue investigating.

Gene and Pat Warrington of Ohio, married 69 years, died eight hours apart on Dec. 27 in hospice care in Findlay. Their son Phil said the couple had been inseparable throughout life; they met in junior high and secretly wed as teenagers while Gene was home from boot camp before World War II. A few days before their deaths they spent about 45 minutes together and Gene held Pat’s hand. Recognizing her condition, Phil said his father “decided to die” after returning to his room; Gene died first and Pat passed eight hours later. They raised three children and left seven grandchildren and 12 great-grandchildren.

Sen. Saxby Chambliss (R-Ga.) announced he will retire in 2014 instead of seeking a third term, saying his decision stems from frustration with Washington’s leadership and legislative gridlock rather than fear of a conservative primary challenge. Chambliss cited failures like the 2011 debt-ceiling standoff and the fiscal-cliff vote as reasons he won’t run again. His retirement opens a crowded GOP primary: potential challengers included Reps. Paul Broun and Tom Price and former Georgia Secretary of State Karen Handel, while Herman Cain—though denying plans to run—polls as the strongest hypothetical threat. Chambliss has faced conservative criticism for bipartisan compromise and is unpopular among very conservative Republicans. Democrats view the open seat as a top pickup opportunity, with Atlanta Mayor Kasim Reed and Rep. John Barrow mentioned as possible contenders. The race could shift from safe Republican to competitive depending on the nominee.

Mitchell Guist, a beloved cast member of The History Channel’s reality series Swamp People, died May 14 after falling in a boat on the Belle River in St. Martin Parish. Deputies and witnesses reported Guist appeared to have seizures after the launch; bystander CPR and emergency response were unsuccessful. The cause of death is unknown. Guist and his brother Glenn, both featured as Cajun alligator hunters who live “entirely off the land,” were fan favorites; the show, now in its third season, has been a ratings success, drawing millions and praise for its authentic, unvarnished portrayal of swamp life. The History Channel expressed sorrow, said episodes will air as scheduled, and noted plans to honor Mitchell’s memory while requesting privacy for the family.

Tunisian Prime Minister Mohammed Ghannouchi resigned after weeks of protests demanding removal of figures linked to ousted president Zine al‑Abidine Ben Ali. Ghannouchi, who served under Ben Ali since 1989, said his resignation would protect Tunisians and the revolution; he denied fleeing responsibility. Beji Caid‑Essebsi, a veteran politician, was named his replacement. The move followed violent demonstrations that left several dead, with police using tear gas and arrests, while protesters pressed for a new government and constitution.

In the aftermath of the Boston Marathon bombings and subsequent shootings that left four dead and hundreds injured, Boston’s Muslim community has forcefully condemned the violence and distanced itself from suspects Dzhokhar and Tamerlan Tsarnaev. Investigations continue into whether the brothers acted alone, were linked to militant groups, or were motivated by politics, religion, or assimilation struggles. Authorities say Dzhokhar has claimed they learned bomb-making from an al Qaeda online magazine; Tamerlan reportedly traveled to Chechnya and Dagestan in 2012 and may have become more radicalized. Community leaders wrestle with whether to recognize the suspects as Muslims and whether to permit Islamic burial rites. Many imams and mosques have declined to lead funeral prayers or have not been approached; some say perpetrators of such atrocities have effectively left Islam, while others leave judgment to God and allow family-led rites. Tamerlan’s body remains with authorities for forensic examination; his wife and family have been contacted, and law enforcement continues its probe into the brothers’ motives and connections.

Authorities investigated threats posted on Twitter by a 23-year-old man, identified as Jesus Henry Kong (also known as Jessie Eloah Calix and Jesus Matute), who allegedly wrote messages encouraging shootings and claiming plans to place pipe bombs at several Orange County, Florida, schools. The FBI, Orlando Police and Orange County Sheriff’s Office pursued leads and said they did not believe the threats were credible, noting the suspect does not reside in Florida, but they continued efforts to locate him. The posts targeted William R. Boone High School, Edgewater High School, Colonial High School, Colonial Ninth Grade Center and Liberty Middle School and included explicitly violent and anti‑gay language. Orange County Public Schools informed parents and principals coordinated with law enforcement; classes were not disrupted. Despite authorities’ assessment, attendance dropped sharply: more than 900 students were absent across three named schools, including nearly a third of Liberty Middle School’s enrollment.

New research using more than 1.4 billion deidentified tax records and Social Security death records finds that higher income is strongly associated with longer life expectancy in the United States, and that the gap between rich and poor has widened. Nationwide, men in the top 1% of the income distribution live about 14.6 years longer than men in the bottom 1%; for women the gap is about 10.1 years. Between 2001 and 2014 the top 5% gained roughly 2.3 years (men) and 2.9 years (women) in life expectancy, while gains for the bottom 5% were near zero, increasing inequality over time.

The study also reveals large geographic variation, especially among low-income people. Poor residents of prosperous, dense, highly educated metropolitan areas such as San Francisco, New York and Los Angeles have much higher life expectancies than equally poor people in many rural and industrial Midwest areas (e.g., parts of Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Kansas). For example, a poor person in San Francisco can expect to live about three years longer than a poor person in Detroit. These local differences for low-income groups correlate strongly with health behaviors — smoking, exercise, and obesity — and with local characteristics such as immigrant share, college-education rates, and government expenditures per capita. By contrast, access to medical care, environmental factors, income inequality, and labor market measures were not significant correlates.

Authors and commentators suggest local policies and community culture matter: smoking bans, trans-fat restrictions, walkable environments, social services, paid leave, universal preschool, and public-health initiatives likely contribute to better outcomes. The findings imply that addressing life-expectancy disparities will require targeted local policies and possibly revisions to Social Security and Medicare policy, since wealthier Americans are projected to claim benefits for many more years than the poorest. The study underscores that geography and community-level factors can blunt or amplify the health consequences of poverty.

Britain’s unexpected election outcome delivered continuity at the top and wide ripple effects at home and abroad. Prime Minister David Cameron’s Conservatives secured a slim majority, defying polls that had predicted a hung parliament or gains for Labour. Markets responded positively to the prospect of political stability: the pound strengthened and the FTSE rose as investors cheered continuity after Britain’s economic recovery under the Conservatives, though economists warned a looming EU referendum would keep uncertainty alive.

Cameron has pledged a 2017 referendum on EU membership, raising the specter of “Brexit.” Analysts warn that even the prospect of an exit vote is risky for European and global markets and could reshape Britain’s international role. Cameron faces pressure from euroskeptic rebels within his party and from UKIP’s anti-EU, anti-immigration rhetoric, which has pushed parts of the Conservative base rightward.

The election also exposed deep domestic fractures. The Scottish National Party (SNP) surged, capturing almost all Scottish seats and decimating Labour’s longstanding Scottish base. That outcome revived fears of another Scottish independence referendum and the possibility of Scotland seeking to remain in the EU if Britain votes to leave, complicating the Union and European politics. Labour suffered heavy losses; leader Ed Miliband announced his resignation. The Liberal Democrats were nearly wiped out, prompting Nick Clegg’s resignation, and UKIP’s Nigel Farage resigned after failing to win a seat despite large national vote share.

Immigration and welfare control were central Conservative themes, and the party’s right flank now wields more influence, potentially constraining Cameron despite his majority. Internationally, Britain’s global influence appears diminished relative to Germany’s leadership in EU crises, and foreign policy played only a marginal role in the campaign. With a renewed Conservative mandate but a fractured United Kingdom and an EU referendum on the horizon, the election leaves Britain politically stable in the short term yet facing significant, unresolved tensions.

Australian radio presenters Mel Greig and Michael Christian have publicly apologized and expressed deep distress after nurse Jacintha Saldanha was found dead following a prank call they made to King Edward VII Hospital. The DJs, from Sydney’s 2Day FM, had impersonated Queen Elizabeth and Prince Charles and, after being put through by Saldanha, obtained and later broadcast information about the Duchess of Cambridge’s treatment for acute morning sickness. Saldanha, 46, was later discovered dead; British police are treating the death as unexplained pending a postmortem and possible inquest.

Greig and Christian, who had gone into hiding and undergone counseling, described the outcome as devastating and insisted the segment was intended as a harmless joke. They said the recorded item was normally vetted by others and lawyers before being aired. Southern Cross Austereo, the station’s owner, suspended the DJs’ Hot 30 show, halted all prank calls across its network, suspended 2Day FM advertising, and announced a review of policies and procedures. The company maintains it did not breach laws or codes and attempted to contact the hospital several times before broadcasting.

The incident provoked global outrage, calls for tougher media regulation, and financial fallout for the broadcaster. The hospital criticized the stunt as “appalling,” and Saldanha’s family has requested privacy while authorities in both the UK and Australia cooperate on inquiries.

Jon Favreau warns that House Republicans’ brinkmanship over the debt ceiling and government funding risks an “economic shutdown” far worse than a temporary government closure. Drawing on his unpublished 2011 speech draft about the consequences of default, Favreau describes how failing to raise the debt limit would force delayed Social Security and veterans’ payments, suspend pay for service members, interrupt contractor payments, and undermine global confidence in U.S. debt—raising borrowing costs for every American and potentially triggering a recession deeper than 2009’s. He stresses that raising the debt ceiling does not authorize new spending or increase the deficit; it merely permits the government to pay obligations already incurred. Favreau criticizes Republicans who treat debt-limit votes as leverage to extract policy wins, calling their stance ideological, delusional, and akin to negotiating with a bomb. He contrasts public understanding of a “shutdown” with confusion about “default,” urging repeated use of “economic shutdown” to convey the stakes. Economically, he notes that modern Treasury securities underpin global finance; if U.S. bonds lost their safe-haven status, the consequences could exceed the 2008 crisis. Politically, he argues GOP leaders fear their radical wing and refuse to allow clean votes, leaving only hope that Wall Street pressures or decisive executive action will avert catastrophe. Ultimately he frames default as a self-inflicted disaster driven by political extremism.

Royal Marine David Hart, killed by a Taliban bomb in Helmand province a day before his 24th birthday, arranged for much of his life insurance payout to celebrate his friendships and support fellow servicemen. Hart had taken out a £250,000 policy before deployment and stipulated £100,000 (reported as about $150,000) be used to send 32 friends and their partners on a Las Vegas holiday—his idea of a fitting “lad’s holiday” tribute. He also left around £50,000 for a charity supporting injured Marines and a sum to his family, who have welcomed the friends’ support since his death. Described by comrades and commanders as courageous, selfless and “the perfect commando,” Hart joined the Royal Marines in 2009 and had recently qualified as a combat medic. In his letter he urged mates to “go and have a good time.” Family and friends plan a 170-mile charity bike ride this autumn to raise funds in his memory.

Thailand's Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva declared a state of emergency in Bangkok and nearby provinces after thousands of "Red Shirt" anti-government protesters stormed parliament, demanding dissolution of parliament and new elections. The decree, administered by Deputy PM Suthep Thaugsuban, restricts gatherings of more than five people deemed to instigate unrest, bans spreading information judged a security threat, permits searches, arrests, detention without court orders, surveillance of communications and travel restrictions. Protesters, supporters of ousted PM Thaksin Shinawatra, say Abhisit took office illegitimately; Abhisit offered elections by year’s end. The unrest disrupted the ASEAN summit—Abhisit skipped it—and raised regional concerns about potential violence. The confrontation reflects long-standing divisions between Thaksin’s populist base and opponents since his 2006 ouster.

Nearly seven years after the December 26, 2004 tsunami struck Aceh, Indonesia, a girl long believed dead has reportedly returned to her family. State news agency Antara says 15-year-old Wati, who was eight when she was swept from her mother’s arms, showed up in Banda Aceh seeking to find her home. Found sitting silently in a coffee shop and previously mistaken for a beggar, she reportedly could not recall relatives’ names except for her grandfather, Ibrahim. He and her parents later identified her by a distinctive mole and a scar above her eyebrow. Reporters were not told what happened to her during the intervening years. The 2004 tsunami followed a massive earthquake and killed nearly 170,000 people, with almost 130,000 missing.

Oklahoma’s Department of Corrections and the city of McAlester are disputing ownership of the state’s old electric chair, nicknamed Old Sparky, which is currently unwired and in storage but could be used again if lethal injection is ruled unconstitutional. Corrections spokesman Jerry Massie said the department hasn’t seriously discussed rehiring the chair and thinks its use is unlikely unless lethal injection is invalidated. State law permits use of the electric chair or firing squad only if lethal injection is found unconstitutional. The dispute predates the state’s current scrutiny of execution procedures following the botched April 29 lethal injection of Clayton Lockett, who writhed and appeared to suffer a massive heart attack before dying 43 minutes into the execution. That incident halted executions and led to a stay for Charles Warner, originally slated to die the same night; Warner is now scheduled for execution on November 13. McAlester mayor Steve Harrison told the Guardian he wants the chair displayed publicly as a historical artifact; the chair had been in a McAlester museum until the corrections department reclaimed it. Harrison doubts the old chair, last used in 1966, would be reused if electrocution were reinstated, expecting authorities would acquire a new device. The chair, first used in 1915, was used in 82 executions; the last person executed in it was James French in 1966. City attorney Bill Ervin called it “an antique” and questioned its suitability for modern use. Amid a European-led boycott of execution drugs, some U.S. states have revisited old methods—Tennessee recently approved electrocution when drugs are unavailable, and states like Florida, Alabama, and Virginia retain electrocution as an option; the last U.S. electrocution was in 2013.

Jason Behrens, 44, was arrested in Kearney, Nebraska after his two children texted 911 to report him for drunk driving. The 14-year-old daughter, Mackenzie, and 12-year-old son, Ethan, were traveling with their father toward a Colorado vacation in a rented car when they say he began swerving and nearly caused a head-on collision. Fearful for their lives and reporting that this was not the first time their father drove while intoxicated with them in the vehicle, they repeatedly asked him to stop. After another close call, the children used Buffalo County’s Text-to-911 service to alert dispatch. Police traced and intercepted the family at a Burger King, where officers arrested Behrens; a breath test later showed he was nearly three times Nebraska’s legal limit. He faces DUI and two counts of driving drunk with minors in the car. The children credit the officers with saving them, expressing gratitude and relief; Mackenzie said she had lost trust in their father, and Ethan called the episode the scariest moment of his life. Their mother, Amy Brooks, who has custody for now, said she was angry but relieved her children are safe and hopes the arrest will make others listen. A friend has set up a GoFundMe for the family. Authorities contacted Behrens but had not reached him for comment. Buffalo County is one of two Nebraska counties offering Text 911, launched there a little over a year ago.

Between October 7 and December 4, 2018, a multistate outbreak of Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli O157:H7 sickened 62 people in 16 states and the District of Columbia; illnesses were identified through PulseNet using PFGE and whole genome sequencing (WGS). Patients’ ages ranged from 1 to 84 (median 25); 66% were female. Of 54 with available information, 46% were hospitalized and two developed hemolytic uremic syndrome; no deaths were reported. WGS showed the outbreak isolates were closely related and similar to a 2017 leafy-greens–linked strain but distinct from the spring 2018 romaine outbreak. Epidemiologic interviews found 83% (30 of 36) of interviewed patients ate romaine lettuce, significantly higher than background surveys. Two restaurant-linked illness clusters supported a common food source. FDA traceback pointed to romaine harvested in the Central Coastal growing regions of northern and central California. Environmental sampling at an Adam Bros. Farming, Inc. site in Santa Barbara County found the outbreak strain in sediment from an agricultural water reservoir; WGS linked that isolate to patient strains. Adam Bros. Farming had not shipped romaine since November 20, 2018, and implicated product is no longer for sale. As of January 9, 2019, the outbreak appears to be over; FDA continues investigations into contamination pathways.

EXCLUSIVE: Marvel Studios and director Joe Johnston are widening their search for the lead in The First Avenger: Captain America to ensure they cast the right actor. New reports indicate Marvel has added Chris Evans — known for playing Johnny Storm/Human Torch in two Fantastic Four films — to the candidate pool. Two original frontrunners remain: Mike Vogel (Cloverfield) and Garrett Hedlund (Tron: Legacy). Hedlund was initially wanted but didn’t test due to scheduling and reportedly because his representatives balked at Marvel’s terms, which included options for nine future films and a proposed salary near $300,000. Other testers now out of contention include Chace Crawford, John Krasinski, Scott Porter, Michael Cassidy, and Patrick Flueger. Paramount will release the film on July 22, 2011.

A new study in JAMA finds that although China’s smoking prevalence fell from 30.4% in 1980 to 24.2% in 2012, it has plateaued since 2006 and population growth has produced a record number of smokers. In 2012 China had about 281 million daily smokers—roughly one-third of the world’s smokers—and some estimates reach 350 million. Average daily cigarette consumption per smoker rose from about 15 in 1980 to 22 in 2012, even as global per-smoker consumption edged down slightly. Researchers attribute the global slowdown in declines to stagnant prevalence in populous lower-income countries and the addictive difficulty of quitting. China has enacted partial measures—public-place smoking bans and directives for officials to quit—but weak enforcement and lack of penalties have limited impact. The male-dominated pattern intensified: female smoking fell from 8% to 4% of smokers. Experts warn of rising premature deaths, health-care, economic and social costs unless stronger tobacco-control laws and enforcement are implemented.

A recent body of research led by W. Bradford Wilcox and colleagues, reported and critiqued in multiple outlets, finds that Republicans report somewhat happier and more stable family lives than Democrats. Using individual-level data from the 2010–2014 General Social Survey (GSS), Wilcox and Nicholas Wolfinger show that among married Americans aged 20–60, 67 percent of Republicans say they are “very happy” in their marriages, compared with 60 percent of Democrats and independents. Republicans are also more likely to be married (57% vs. 40% of Democrats) and less likely to be divorced (41% vs. 47% of ever-married Democrats). When researchers control for demographic differences—race, religion, education, and related factors—the raw seven-point partisan gap in marital happiness shrinks to about three percentage points, with compositional differences (especially race and religiosity) explaining over half the advantage. Religious attendance and couple churchgoing are notably associated with higher reported marital satisfaction. The authors acknowledge limitations: the data are cross-sectional and cannot establish causality, and partisan differences in reporting style—Republicans’ greater optimism or tendency to view marriages “through rose-colored glasses”—could influence results. Wilcox also advances a broader claim that at the county and state levels, red areas often have higher marriage rates, lower nonmarital childbearing, and greater likelihood that teens live with both biological parents, challenging earlier views that “blue” areas necessarily produce stronger families. Critics urge caution, noting regional variations (e.g., higher divorce in the South), socioeconomic and racial confounds, and the modest size of the effects. Overall, the research finds a modest Republican advantage in marriage prevalence and self-reported marital happiness, much of which is tied to demographic and religious differences; remaining gaps may reflect attitudes, selection effects, or unmeasured cultural influences, and the causal direction between partisanship and family structure remains unresolved.

A real-world study by Kaiser Permanente in San Francisco found that daily Truvada (emtricitabine/tenofovir) effectively prevented HIV infection: among 657 patients followed for a median of about 32 months after FDA approval in 2012, none acquired HIV. The cohort—largely men who have sex with men, average age 37—remained sexually active, with many reporting decreased condom use and high rates of other STIs (about 30% diagnosed within six months, 50% within a year), yet no new HIV cases were detected. Participants were routinely tested every three months and monitored for side effects; adherence was highlighted as crucial to effectiveness. These outcomes echo prior clinical trials that showed up to 92% risk reduction when PrEP is taken consistently, but the Kaiser study is notable for demonstrating efficacy outside tightly controlled trial settings.

The drug, produced by Gilead Sciences and costing Kaiser patients roughly $50 a month, has drawn controversy: critics feared PrEP might encourage unsafe sex and some community advocates—most prominently Michael Weinstein of the AIDS Healthcare Foundation—label it a “party drug” and caution against broad community-level rollout. The Kaiser study did observe decreased condom use among many participants, reinforcing concerns about risk compensation. Public health authorities, including the CDC, nonetheless recommend PrEP for people at highest risk (e.g., those with HIV-positive partners, sex workers, IV drug users) under clinical supervision. San Francisco health initiatives incorporate PrEP into their Getting to Zero campaign aiming to eliminate new infections, deaths, and stigma.

Kaiser lead author Jonathan Volk describes PrEP as an important new prevention tool that can make HIV management resemble other chronic diseases when used appropriately. Study participants like Paul Marcelin view PrEP as a phase-based option—valuable during periods of heightened risk but not necessarily lifelong. The findings support PrEP’s role in comprehensive HIV prevention while underscoring the need for ongoing monitoring and behavioral counseling.

UN monitors’ commander Maj. Gen. Robert Mood warned in Damascus that violence in Syria had risen to “an unprecedented level,” making observation and mediation impossible and saying his mission cannot be revived without a cease-fire. Turkish and Syrian accounts conflict over the downing of a Turkish F-4 on June 22; Turkey recovered the pilots’ bodies and wreckage with help from undersea explorer Robert Ballard and plans a memorial. In a wide-ranging interview published by Turkey’s Cumhuriyet, President Bashar al-Assad rejected calls for a cease-fire or Kofi Annan’s transitional plan, insisting he retains popular support, blaming Islamist militants and foreign adversaries for seeking to break up Syria, and defending his survival after 16 months of uprising. Assad expressed regret about the plane incident but was sharply critical of Turkish Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan and said bridges with him are “almost” burned. Claims by the Al Nusra Front to recent attacks lent some support to Assad’s terrorist narrative. Iraq’s foreign minister, Hoshyar Zebari, said Baghdad has “solid information” that al-Qaeda operatives are crossing from Iraq into Syria via smuggling routes, prompting Iraq to reinforce its 680 km border to prevent spillover of extremist violence.

Nine-year-old Elina Childs capitalized on the first day of legal cannabis sales in Edmonton by selling Girl Guide cookies outside a pot shop. Accompanied by her father, Seann, Elina brought a wagon with about 30 boxes and walked the line, selling out in roughly 45 minutes at $5 a box. The idea arose when neighborhood door-to-door sales proved slow; customers, some even stopping their cars, responded enthusiastically. Girl Guides officials praised the creative approach, and the viral social media attention prompted questions about appropriateness — organizers said it was acceptable since she wasn’t inside the store. Her father used the event as a teaching moment about legalization and demystifying cannabis; Elina, who has cystic fibrosis, enjoyed the experience and joked about cookies feeling “crummy.”

A 19-year-old man was arrested by the Metropolitan Police Central e-Crime Unit after an investigation into network intrusions and distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks targeting international businesses and intelligence agencies. Searches were carried out at a Wickford, Essex residence; the suspect was detained Monday night on suspicion of offences under the Computer Misuse Act and Fraud Act and is being questioned at a central London police station. The probe involved the FBI and may be linked to attacks attributed to activist hacker groups LulzSec and Anonymous, which recently collaborated on an AntiSec campaign. The UK’s Serious Organised Crime Agency confirmed it suffered a DDoS attack that aligns with the timing. Online reaction was rapid and contradictory: some Anonymous accounts suggested the arrested individual—named by sources as “Ryan,” likely Ryan Cleary—had limited involvement, chiefly running an IRC server used by LulzSec, while LulzSec insisted Cleary is not a member and that their core team remains intact. Internal confusion and mutual distrust among these groups complicate attribution.

Iraq’s security collapse this week exposed deep failures despite years of U.S. training and equipment. Islamist militants led by ISIS rapidly seized Mosul and Tikrit as many Iraqi soldiers surrendered or fled, raising questions about morale, leadership, sectarian divisions and the effectiveness of U.S.-supplied forces. A limited U.S. surveillance program using unmanned aircraft had provided little timely intelligence on the assault. The fall of major cities has triggered mass displacement—up to half a million from Mosul—and raised fears ISIS aims to establish an emirate spanning Iraq and Syria. Reports suggest former Baathists have allied with the jihadis, complicating the threat. Baghdad’s political dysfunction was exposed when parliament failed to secure a quorum to grant emergency powers to Prime Minister Nouri Maliki. Regional actors like Iran, with ties to Shia militias and Maliki, may intervene, potentially deepening sectarian tensions. The U.S. has signaled it will consider “all options,” including air strikes, but rules out sending ground troops; meanwhile it is relocating U.S. defense contractors and personnel amid security concerns. The crisis risks fracturing Iraq along sectarian lines and further destabilizing the region.

Researchers at NIST have demonstrated what they call the world’s most stable clock: an ytterbium optical lattice atomic clock whose ticking rate varies by no more than about one part in 10^18. Reported in Science, the table-sized device traps roughly 10,000 ytterbium atoms cooled to 10 microkelvin in an optical lattice and probes them with a laser oscillating at about 518 trillion cycles per second. Using many atoms and improvements like an ultra-low-noise laser and methods to cancel collision effects, the team built two independent clocks to verify agreement and achieved stability roughly ten times better than previous best results. High stability means precise measurements can be obtained far more rapidly—the new clocks reach levels that a cesium fountain clock needs about five days to achieve in roughly one second—enabling near–real-time sensing. Potential applications include more accurate tests of general relativity, improved GPS and navigation, and sensitive measurements of gravity, magnetic fields, and temperature. The devices remain large and costly, and while stability is established, their absolute accuracy relative to the official second still needs measurement; further work will assess whether they can become new primary time standards.

Odessa police are investigating a brazen theft at Sunset Memorial Gardens & Funeral Home after a woman allegedly removed a wedding ring from an 88-year-old deceased woman, Lois Hicks, while she lay in her casket. The incident occurred April 8 at about 5:27 p.m.; surveillance video later released by police shows a heavy-set white female in a brown long-sleeve sweater, black sweatpants and black sandals entering the funeral home, asking for a restroom, then going into the visitation room and yanking the ring from the victim’s left hand—tearing skin in the process—before fleeing in a red or maroon four-door Saturn. Family members, including daughter Vel McKee, who had been preparing Hicks’s appearance shortly before the theft, described being devastated and said the video and enhanced license-plate images may help identify the suspect. The case is being treated as a state jail felony; no arrests have been made. Anyone with information is urged to contact the Odessa Police Department or Odessa Crime Stoppers at 432-333-TIPS.

House Republicans on the Intelligence Committee voted along party lines to release a classified, GOP-authored memo alleging FBI and Justice Department misuse of surveillance during the Russia probe, setting off a partisan clash with Democrats and career law enforcement officials. Ranking Democrat Adam Schiff said Democrats opposed the release and accused Republicans of politicizing intelligence and selectively publicizing a “distorted” account. The memo reportedly centers on the use of material from the Christopher Steele dossier in FISA applications targeting former Trump campaign adviser Carter Page and alleges senior officials abused the FISA process; it also reportedly notes Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein approved a surveillance extension. Chairman Devin Nunes showed the memo to FBI Director Christopher Wray after Rep. Trey Gowdy urged him to do so; Wray expressed continuing concerns. The panel rejected delaying release to allow broader DOJ and FBI review, though Republicans agreed to share a Democratic rebuttal memo with the full House for members to review. The White House said President Trump had not yet decided whether to clear public release but favors “full transparency,” and has five days to act.

President Trump repeatedly blamed Democrats for the recent surge in family separations at the U.S.-Mexico border, saying “the Democrats have to change their law,” and claiming he “hates” seeing children taken away. Multiple fact checks and reporting show that no law requires separating children from parents who cross the border. The separations increased after the Trump administration, under Attorney General Jeff Sessions, adopted a “zero-tolerance” policy directing prosecutors to criminally charge everyone who crosses the border illegally. Because children cannot be placed in criminal custody, parents prosecuted are often detained separately while their children enter HHS custody. Trump and aides have pointed to prior statutes and court agreements—the Flores settlement, the TVPRA, and past rulings—to argue Democrats bear responsibility, but those measures do not compel separation; Flores limits child detention, and TVPRA protects unaccompanied minors. Congressional proposals offered by House Republicans claim to address separations but mainly would allow indefinite family detention, not prohibit prosecutions that cause separation. Democrats favor reversing the administration policy rather than legislative fixes negotiated without them. The bottom line: the administration’s policy, not a Democratic law, is driving the separations.

A small rural chapel in Champion, Wis., called Our Lady of Good Help, has been officially recognized by the Roman Catholic Church as the site of authentic Marian apparitions — the first in the United States and among only about a dozen worldwide. In 1859 Belgian immigrant Adele Brise reported three visions of the Virgin Mary, who instructed her to teach children the Catholic faith. After a formal two-year diocesan investigation that followed Vatican guidelines, Bishop David L. Ricken of Green Bay declared Dec. 8 that, with “moral certainty,” Brise’s encounters were “of a supernatural character” and “worthy of belief.” Investigators found no evidence of fraud or heresy and noted a history of conversions, reported cures, and other signs associated with the shrine; lore holds that the site and its visitors were spared by the destructive Peshtigo Fire of 1871. The decree has drawn more visitors to the modest chapel and prompted interest from church groups, though it has not produced Lourdes-scale crowds. Local worshipers described a palpable sense of Mary’s presence and comfort, especially in troubled times for the church amid sex-abuse scandals. Church leaders called the recognition a source of hope and spiritual renewal; Bishop Ricken said the decision was based on long-standing devotion and reported answered prayers rather than current controversies. The Vatican typically delegates such determinations to local bishops and investigates apparitions cautiously, often using modern psychiatric tools — not applicable in Brise’s 19th-century case — before granting approval.

D.C. police are investigating the deaths of four people found in a burning Woodley Park home and have released surveillance images of a person of interest. The victims have been identified as Savvas Savopoulos, 46, his wife Amy, 47, and are believed to include their 10-year-old son Philip and 57-year-old housekeeper Veralicia Figueroa. Authorities are treating the blaze as suspicious and the deaths as homicide arson; evidence indicates at least three victims had wounds and one was bleeding from the head and smelled of gasoline. Investigators recovered a 2008 blue Porsche 911 linked to the household — seen near the home around 10:30 a.m. Thursday and later found torched and abandoned in a church parking lot in Maryland — and are seeking information about the car and the person captured on video wearing a dark hoodie. Police are examining neighborhood surveillance footage, interviewing witnesses, and working with ATF agents and evidence teams to establish a timeline and motive. Records and interviews reveal unusual activity before the deaths: tense messages from Savvas, his instruction to a longtime assistant not to come that morning, reports of prowlers and unusual visitors, and a package left at the house as staff traveled to a Chantilly business project Savvas was preparing. The high-profile family were active community donors; two daughters survive. Police ask anyone with information to call 202-727-9099.

Former White House chief strategist Stephen K. Bannon has been effectively shut out of major cable networks and satellite radio following his departure from Breitbart News. Fox News and CNN both confirmed they will not be hiring Bannon after he left Breitbart amid fallout from comments he gave to Michael Wolff for the bestseller Fire and Fury. SiriusXM also announced Bannon will no longer host a Breitbart radio show because Breitbart ended its relationship with him.

Bannon, 64, rejoined Breitbart’s SiriusXM program in December after leaving the White House in August 2017 — a departure President Trump has characterized as a firing. His position at Breitbart became untenable after Wolff’s book quoted Bannon calling Donald Trump Jr.’s 2016 meeting with a Russian-linked lawyer “treasonous” and predicting special counsel scrutiny would “crack Don Junior like an egg on national TV.” Those remarks enraged the president and led Trump to publicly denounce Bannon as having “lost his mind.” Bannon apologized, but the White House rebuffed him. Major backers also withdrew support: Rebekah Mercer publicly cut ties, and Breitbart’s board moved to distance the organization.

Bannon’s influence had waned amid tensions with the president and controversial associations. Networks have signaled they may book him as a guest, but as of the latest reports Fox, CNN and SiriusXM are declining to hire him in any ongoing role, marking a significant professional setback.

Researchers propose that the most devastating mass extinction in Earth’s history, the end-Permian “Great Dying” about 252 million years ago, was driven not solely by volcanism but by a bloom of methane-producing microbes. The archaeon Methanosarcina, which can convert organic carbon into methane, may have rapidly proliferated after acquiring new genes via horizontal gene transfer. Massive Siberian eruptions likely released large amounts of nickel into the oceans, a key nutrient that would have fueled Methanosarcina’s growth. This microbial expansion could have emitted vast quantities of methane (and later CO2), triggering intense greenhouse warming, ocean acidification, and deoxygenation over tens of thousands of years. These changes match geological carbon records showing a sustained rise in carbon gases that volcanic emissions alone cannot explain. The resulting environmental stresses wiped out an estimated 90+ percent of marine species and about 70 percent of land vertebrates, ended the long run of trilobites, and reshaped post-extinction ecosystems; recovery of land vertebrate diversity took tens of millions of years and set the stage for later groups like dinosaurs. The hypothesis underscores microbes’ capacity to radically alter the global carbon cycle, though uncertainties remain about nickel sources, timing of Methanosarcina’s evolution, and whether multiple kill mechanisms contributed.

U.S. federal judges in at least five states issued orders blocking enforcement of President Donald Trump’s executive ban on travel and refugee resettlement from seven Muslim-majority countries, sowing confusion at airports and spurring widespread protests and legal challenges. Rulings from judges in New York (Brooklyn), California, Massachusetts, Virginia and Washington prevented deportations or detentions of affected travelers, including legal permanent residents and approved visa or refugee holders. Some local court orders went further than others—Boston’s judge barred detention and removal of approved refugees, visa holders and green-card holders entering from the listed countries—while New York’s order focused on stopping removals. Lawyers and activists reported uneven compliance by federal officials: some Border Patrol agents refused lawyer access to detainees despite court orders, and authorities said they would “comply with judicial orders” while still enforcing vetting measures. The order, which halts travel from Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen for 90 days and suspends refugee resettlement for 120 days (indefinitely blocking Syrians), ignited global criticism, protests at major airports and condemnations from state attorneys general, lawmakers, civil society and foreign leaders. Dozens of lawsuits were filed nationwide by firms and NGOs arguing constitutional and statutory violations. The administration defended the measure as necessary for security, while opponents warned it discriminates on religious grounds and breaches U.S. and international legal protections.

A British Airways Airbus A320 approaching Heathrow from Geneva was struck by an object believed to be a drone on Sunday afternoon while descending over Richmond Park at about 1,700 ft. The jet was carrying 132 passengers and five crew; it landed safely, was inspected by engineers and cleared for its next flight. No injuries or visible damage were reported, and British Airways said it would fully assist the Metropolitan Police, whose aviation security unit at Heathrow is leading the investigation. No arrests have been made. Police asked the public to report any drone debris found in the Richmond area.

Officials and industry groups stressed the seriousness of the incident. The Met’s aviation policing commander warned the event illustrates the “very real dangers” of reckless or malicious drone use. The Civil Aviation Authority called flying drones near airports “totally unacceptable.” The British Airline Pilots Association said it was “only a matter of time” before a strike occurred and urged stricter enforcement, registration, tracking and electronic safeguards such as geo-fencing to prevent drones entering restricted zones.

Analysis from technology and aviation experts highlights gaps in knowledge and regulation: existing UK law already bans flying drones above 400 ft or beyond unaided line of sight and allows penalties up to five years’ imprisonment, but enforcement is difficult. There have been rising numbers of near-misses at UK airports; the UK Air Proximity Board and other bodies have recorded numerous incidents in recent years. Unlike the US, the UK did not then require drone registration, though the government planned consultations on unmanned aircraft strategy. Researchers and pilots also note there is little experimental data on the effects of drones impacting jet engines or windscreens; some modeling suggests such strikes could cause significant engine damage, reinforcing calls for testing, better technology for detection and avoidance, and stronger regulation and enforcement.

Former CIA Director David Petraeus resigned after admitting an extramarital affair with his biographer, Paula Broadwell. Retired Col. Peter Mansoor said Petraeus is keeping a low profile to focus on his family, calling the affair morally wrong but not illegal. Broadwell and Petraeus ended their relationship months ago but stayed in contact professionally. The affair was uncovered during an FBI probe into anonymous, harassing emails sent to Tampa socialite Jill Kelley; that probe expanded to examine Gen. John Allen’s communications with Kelley. Broadwell’s security clearance has been suspended and investigators searched her home and materials; officials say prosecution over classified leaks appears unlikely. Petraeus will testify privately before the House Intelligence Committee on the Benghazi attack.

Tampa police are investigating a third slaying in Seminole Heights in 11 days, heightening fear in the neighborhood and prompting a heavy law-enforcement response. Interim Chief Brian Dugan announced the death of 20-year-old Anthony Naiboa, who was found shot near North 15th Street and East Conover Street around 8 p.m. after accidentally taking the wrong bus. Naiboa’s killing follows the Oct. 9 slaying of 22-year-old Benjamin Edward Mitchell and the Oct. 11 death of 32-year-old Monica Caridad Hoffa, all victims found near bus stops and all apparently unconnected to one another by prior relationship or obvious motive. Dugan said the proximity and timing strongly suggest the incidents are linked and described the situation as terrorizing the neighborhood, though he stopped short of formally labeling the suspect a serial killer. The FBI is assisting the Tampa Police Department alongside support from the Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office, St. Petersburg Police, ATF and Crime Stoppers, which together are offering a $25,000 reward for information leading to an arrest. Police have saturated the area with officers, collected surveillance footage, canvassed residents and released video of a person seen near the first murder, urging the public to review footage and report tips without making assumptions about the individual’s appearance. Families of victims are grieving together; community members report fear about patronizing local businesses. Dugan encouraged residents to remain vigilant—keep porch lights on, stay in groups, avoid walking alone—but not to be confined to their homes. Authorities asked anyone with information to contact police or Crime Stoppers.

Seventy-five-year-old Sandra Layne was convicted of second-degree murder and a weapons charge for fatally shooting her 17-year-old grandson, Jonathan Hoffman, last May. Layne fired ten shots, striking him six times; prosecutors say she left him wounded and returned to shoot him again. The jury rejected her claim of self-defense after a five-hour testimony in which she said she feared Jonathan—who had tested positive for synthetic marijuana—and alleged he demanded money and struck her. Crucial evidence was Jonathan’s dying 911 call—“My grandma shot me. I’m going to die. Help. I got shot again”—which jurors replayed repeatedly and said influenced their verdict. Jonathan’s parents, Jennifer and Michael Hoffman, called the verdict vindication that restored their son’s reputation after Layne portrayed him negatively at trial. Layne, who wept as the verdict was read, faces at least 14 years in prison; her defense says she is devastated.

A major genomic study led by Adam Boyko at Cornell analyzed 185,805 genetic markers from 5,392 dogs—including 549 free‑breeding “village dogs” from 38 countries and 4,676 modern purebreds across 161 breeds—to trace the origins and spread of domesticated dogs. The team reports that genetic diversity is highest in Central Asia around modern‑day Nepal and Mongolia, and that diversity radiates outward to neighboring regions (Afghanistan, India, Egypt, Vietnam), consistent with a single origin there. Village dogs, which are genetically more diverse and represent longstanding local populations, proved crucial to the analysis because modern pure breeds are genetically narrow, largely European, and mostly created in the last ~200 years. The study thus offers strong evidence that dogs were domesticated from Eurasian gray wolves at least 15,000 years ago in Central Asia, after which village dog populations rapidly fanned out across Asia.

The researchers improved on past work by sampling many village dog populations and by analyzing autosomal markers inherited from both parents rather than relying mainly on mitochondrial or sex‑chromosome DNA. Their results argue against multiple independent domestication events and suggest later European influence explains the predominance of European lineages in the Americas and South Pacific. The team speculates hunter‑gatherers in Central Asia may have driven wolves toward scavenging and tameness under changing ecological and demographic conditions, initiating domestication.

Some experts welcome the scale and clarity of the result but caution it is not definitive: sampling gaps (notably southern China) and reliance on present‑day genomes mean ancient DNA from archaeological remains will be needed to corroborate or refine the origin location. A consortium led by Greger Larson is pursuing ancient-genome analyses to test these conclusions further.

Two weeks after Haiti’s earthquake, many survivors around Port-au-Prince still face desperate shortages of food and fuel despite international aid. In response, local initiative Muncheez, a corner pizza restaurant that had been unaffordable to most, transformed itself into a free community kitchen. Co-owner Gilbert Bailly began by cooking perishable ingredients rather than letting them spoil, then accepted donations from nearby businesses and neighbors. When local contributions dwindled, Bailly’s nephew raised money and brought a truckload of food from the Dominican Republic. Muncheez now serves about 1,000 people daily—lines wrap around the building and some wait hours. Recipients include Leonce Bell, who lost his home and job and lives in a public park; he spares his plate for his child. The grassroots effort has drawn attention from aid groups such as World Vision, which now delivers sacks of dry food so families also leave with staples like bulgur and lentils. Bailly says running the kitchen keeps him busy and hopeful.

Silicon Valley’s signature perk of free, high-end campus meals is drawing municipal pushback as cities try to protect local businesses and street life. Mountain View has barred Facebook from fully subsidizing meals for roughly 2,000 employees at its new Village at San Antonio Center offices: under a 2014 agreement, on-site meal subsidies cannot exceed 50%, although Facebook may pay in full if employees dine at public restaurants. The measure grew out of complaints that Google’s extensive workplace cafeterias harmed nearby restaurants by diverting lunch crowds and potential workers. City officials and business owners argue that when employees remain inside campuses, local shops and eateries lose vital foot traffic and vitality, especially as mixed-use developments aim to link housing, transit and retail.

Supporters, including the Golden Gate Restaurant Association, favor broader San Francisco proposals to ban workplace cafeterias in new developments (not retroactive), suggesting alternatives like vouchers to buy from local vendors. Opponents, including labor unions, warn that banning cafeterias may eliminate good jobs that offer decent pay, benefits and pensions—café workers at Facebook recently unionized for raises and healthcare. There are also concerns about fairness and unintended effects on employment.

Mountain View hopes similar conditions might apply to future tech expansions; other Bay Area cities vary—Cupertino and San Jose currently have no such prohibitions. Local food-business owners and food-hall operators say limiting subsidized in-house meals would help independent restaurants survive and encourage tech workers to engage with the broader community. Tech firms and some developers are exploring compromises such as public food halls and partnerships with neighborhood vendors.

In August 2015, 17-year-old Vera Mol from the Netherlands died during a bungee jump organized by Aqua21 Aventura on a highway viaduct in Cantabria, northern Spain. Standing on a 130-foot-high bridge at about 8:30 p.m., she was the last of 13 teenagers in the group when the instructor issued an instruction that has become central to later proceedings. He intended to tell her “don’t jump” or “no jump” to prevent her from leaping before safety checks were complete, but the court concluded that his pronunciation of “no jump” could plausibly have been heard as “now jump.” Ms. Mol then jumped while her harness was not yet secured to the bridge, fell, and died. 

An appeals court in Cantabria has upheld a ruling that the instructor and the director of the organizing company face potential criminal charges, including negligent homicide, if prosecutors pursue the case. Judges highlighted the instructor’s “poor English” as a contributory factor, noting that correct phrasing such as “don’t jump” should have been used and that he should have verified the participant’s age—Vera was under 18. The court also referenced allegations that bungee jumping from that road bridge may be banned by Spanish regulation. The ruling centers on communication failings and procedural lapses that, the court found, could have prevented the tragedy.

Authorities in Santa Barbara are investigating the “horrific” slayings of three people — identified as Dr. Weidong “Henry” Han, his wife Huijie “Jennie” Yu, and their 5-year-old daughter Emily — after a welfare check Wednesday evening at their gated seven-acre Greenhill Way property between Goleta and Santa Barbara. Deputies discovered evidence prompting a suspicious-death investigation; detectives executed a search warrant and coroner investigators collected the remains early Thursday. County and state forensics teams and the Sheriff’s Coroner processed the scene; autopsies were planned to determine cause and manner of death. Sheriff’s spokespeople said early indications suggest the attack was not random, and detectives are working around the clock to identify who is responsible. Han, 57, founded the Santa Barbara Herb Clinic and was a practitioner and author in Chinese herbal and Western medicine; the home was purchased in 2012. The family’s deaths shocked the local community — Emily attended Foothill Elementary — and prompted school counselors to advise families. Investigators briefly entered Han’s clinic as part of inquiries, and authorities requested anyone with information call the sheriff’s tip line. Further updates were expected from law enforcement.

A Dallas pet-sitting company’s bid to extract up to $1 million from a Plano couple over a one-star Yelp review has been dismissed. Prestigious Pets and owner Kalle McWhorter sued Michelle and Robert Duchouquette for defamation, business disparagement and breach of a nondisparagement clause after the couple posted a negative October 2015 review saying the betta fish’s tank looked murky, billing was incorrect and the company tried to charge to return keys; the couple said dog care was fine. The suit began as a roughly $6,700 small-claims filing, was refiled in state district court with expanded claims and a damages increase to $200,000–$1 million after the dispute drew national attention. The Duchouquettes moved to dismiss under the Texas anti‑SLAPP law (Texas Citizens Participation Act), which protects speech about matters of public concern. On Friday a Dallas County district judge granted the motion and dismissed the case; the court also ordered recovery of fees and sanctions under the statute. Prestigious Pets’ attorney said the company is reviewing options and may appeal, defended enforcing its contract and alleged harassment of the owners, while noting the sitter had not agreed to clean the fish bowl. The Yelp review remains up and the company’s Yelp page carries a consumer alert warning that the business may be trying to silence reviewers. Advocates framed the dismissal as a win for free expression and a rebuke of attempts to use litigation to chill criticism.

Seattle police responded Sunday afternoon to a disturbance in a University District apartment where officers, after hearing arguing and threats, forced entry and found a man strangling a woman. They pulled the man off, performed CPR until medics arrived, and the victim was rushed to Harborview Medical Center with life-threatening injuries. The suspect, identified in police documents as 21-year-old Casey Henderson, also a University of Washington student, was arrested and booked into King County Jail on investigation of domestic violence assault; bail was set at $1 million. Initial reports said both the suspect and the victim had taken LSD and the suspect told detectives he became paranoid, believed the woman was plotting against him, and admitted to punching and strangling her. A neighbor who called 911 reported hearing violent pounding, threats and shouting. The 22-year-old female victim, also a UW student, later died at the hospital; police upgraded the investigation to a homicide and prosecutors expected to file formal charges. The victim’s name has not been released. A judge found probable cause to hold the suspect pending charges. The case underscores a deadly campus domestic attack involving alleged drug use and extreme violence.

Target CEO Gregg Steinhafel defended the retailer’s four-day delay in publicly disclosing a major data breach, saying the pause after confirming the intrusion on December 15 was necessary to secure systems, begin forensic work, prepare stores and call centers, and ready customer notifications. Steinhafel told CNBC that by 6 p.m. on December 15 Target had removed malware from the point-of-sale access point and was confident guests could shop without added risk. The breach, which ran from November 27 to December 15, initially was disclosed as affecting up to 40 million payment cards but later was found to have exposed personal information — names, addresses, phone numbers and emails — of as many as 110 million customers. Target launched a public apology campaign and pledged to investigate fully. The incident came amid similar holiday-season intrusions at other U.S. retailers: Neiman Marcus confirmed a December hack, and Reuters reported at least three other unnamed retailers suffered smaller breaches. The attacks underscore growing concerns about magnetic-stripe card vulnerabilities and have renewed calls for wider adoption of more secure “chip-and-PIN” cards, though costs and implementation timing remain contentious.

Forbes’s Celebrity 100 ranks entertainers by pretax earnings (May 1, 2011–May 1, 2012) and media visibility across print, TV, radio, online and social media. Earnings estimates come from industry insiders; management and agent fees aren’t deducted. Media exposure is quantified via Google blogs, Factiva, LexisNexis, magazine cover counts, and social metrics from Twitter and Facebook. Data are combined by an algorithm and celebrities are categorized by profession. Jennifer Lopez tops the list with $52 million and huge fame after reinvigorating her career via American Idol, endorsements, a Kohl’s clothing line and fragrances, plus strong social media followings. Oprah is second, earning $165 million from her media empire despite her syndicated show ending, while Justin Bieber is third with $55 million and growing tech investments. Lady Gaga falls to fifth with $52 million. New entrants include Kim and Khloe Kardashian and Ashton Kutcher—who leveraged TV and tech investments to debut at No. 51 with $24 million. The feature team is led by editor Dorothy Pomerantz.

Workers clearing debris after the deadly Camp Fire sparked outrage after posting insensitive photos from destroyed properties, prompting firings and possible criminal charges. The Town of Paradise used advanced laser-based road surveys by ARRB Group, funded in part by a North Valley Community Foundation donation, to document roadway conditions before and after heavy equipment moved through town; council action on the ARRB contract was noted. Separately, cleanup contractor Rob Freestone — employed as a third-party worker on the PG&E response and also linked to Bigge Crane and Rigging — posted inflammatory images on Facebook from the Camp Fire zone. Screenshots shared on the Town of Paradise page showed workers posing in a burned RV, a man jumping on a scorched trampoline with an insulting caption, and a photograph of a dead cat staged with a beer bottle. Paradise police said they learned of the posts via social media and will pursue applicable criminal charges; investigators are considering whether Freestone violated rules about entering evacuated zones, since he appears to have been acting outside his cleanup responsibilities when he took and shared the photos. PG&E and Bigge took immediate steps: PG&E removed the worker from the response effort, and Bigge terminated three employees identified in the incident, condemning their conduct as inconsistent with company values. The actions came amid broader scrutiny of PG&E’s role in the fire, including lawsuits alleging equipment failures that sparked the blaze.

Stephanie Clifford, known as Stormy Daniels, has publicly sought to tell the truth about an alleged past relationship with Donald Trump and the efforts by Trump and his then-attorney Michael Cohen to silence her, including an unsigned nondisclosure agreement and threats of large damages if she speaks. She filed a lawsuit in Los Angeles to void the NDA and has offered to return the $130,000 payment she received in exchange for being allowed to speak; Trump and Cohen did not respond. Daniels says she needs funds for legal fees, costs tied to litigation and arbitration, security, and potential damages.

Separately, Daniels publicly distanced herself from attorney Michael Avenatti, accusing him of filing a defamation suit against Trump without her consent, launching a new crowdfunding campaign using her name without permission, and refusing repeated requests for accounting of a legal defense and safety fund. While she praised Avenatti’s advocacy, she criticized his lack of client deference and unclear handling of donated funds and is uncertain whether she will retain him. Avenatti defended his actions, saying a retention agreement allowed funds for his fees and that most donations covered security and other expenses; he also denied taking legal fees from the crowdfunding. Legal experts warned Avenatti could face malpractice exposure if he sued over Daniels’ objections. Daniels’ disputes with Trump, Cohen, and now tensions with Avenatti come amid broader legal fallout involving Cohen’s guilty plea for campaign-related payments and Avenatti’s own controversies.

SpaceX announced Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa as its first private passenger for a planned lunar flyby aboard the company’s yet-to-fly Big Falcon Rocket (BFR). Maezawa, 42, founder and CEO of online fashion retailer Zozo and noted art collector, revealed he plans to make the trip in 2023 and will invite six to eight artists to join him, asking them to create works after their return. SpaceX founder Elon Musk said Maezawa’s deposit is substantial and will materially offset BFR development costs, which Musk estimates around $5 billion, though he cautioned the mission is not guaranteed and depends on many test flights and the unproven rocket. If realized, the mission would be the first human travel beyond low Earth orbit since Apollo missions ended in 1972; the flight will be a “free return” loop around the Moon rather than a landing. Maezawa has amassed fame for his Basquiat purchase and flamboyant lifestyle; he sees the trip as preferable to short suborbital hops offered by rivals such as Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic. SpaceX has dramatically changed the industry with reusable Falcon rockets and is pursuing ambitious timelines for BFR orbital tests and eventual Mars missions, though Musk’s targets have historically slipped. The announcement also comes amid unrelated controversies surrounding Musk and market reactions that briefly pressured Zozo shares.

A new Colorado Tourism Office (CTO) study indicates legal recreational marijuana is becoming a notable factor in travel decisions to Colorado. Surveys conducted by Strategic Marketing and Research Insights (SMARI) in October and November of potential summer visitors exposed to the state’s “Come to Life” ads found marijuana laws influenced nearly 49 percent of respondents to some degree—22 percent saying it was “extremely influential,” 20 percent “very much,” and 7 percent “somewhat.” Yet only 8 percent of actual Colorado tourists reported visiting a dispensary, the same share as the previous year; among those who did, 85 percent said marijuana was a primary motivator, up sharply from 29 percent in 2014. SMARI cautioned the questions may not capture people deterred by legalization, and its survey director urged better follow-up questions.

The CTO’s ad campaign, which does not mention marijuana and cost over $5.3 million, was credited with generating an estimated 2.1 million leisure trips and $2.6 billion in economic impact, a strong return on investment. Tourism leaders are divided on how openly to address cannabis: some, like former CTO chief Al White, now acknowledge its growing influence, while new CTO head Cathy Ritter calls for more research. Localities such as Telluride cautiously include pot in messaging.

Separate research from Fort Lewis College suggests dispensary customers mainly seek other Colorado attractions and view legal marijuana as “icing on the cake”; many value tested, legal product. Researchers expect marijuana’s tourism pull to lessen as other states legalize, and industry advocates urge better visitor education and promotion within legal constraints.

Tension erupted at Jerusalem’s Western Wall after a court ruling allowed the Women of the Wall, a feminist and pluralist prayer group, to conduct non‑Orthodox customs there without being arrested. About 100 women and male supporters gathered for a monthly service in which some wore prayer shawls (tallit) and tefillin; thousands of ultra‑Orthodox protesters—many yeshiva students and schoolgirls called by rabbinic leaders—converged to oppose them. Clashes broke out: protesters hurled chairs, water, coffee, garbage and stones, spat at participants, and stoned the bus that later transported the women; three men were detained and two police officers sustained light injuries. Police formed cordons to protect the women, restrained attackers and made a few arrests, marking a shift from prior practice when Women of the Wall members themselves were often detained. The confrontations highlighted a wider struggle in Israel between secular and ultra‑Orthodox authorities over religious life and control of holy‑site customs. Political figures, including Natan Sharansky, have been pressed to broker a compromise—one proposal would create an expanded mixed‑gender prayer zone—while U.S. Jewish support for the group adds international pressure to resolve the dispute.

A European collaboration (OPERA) reports neutrinos traveling from CERN to Italy arriving about 60 nanoseconds earlier than light would, implying a velocity exceeding light by ~20 parts per million. The result, based on ~16,000 time-of-flight measurements over 730 km with a quoted 10-ns uncertainty, challenges Einstein’s special relativity and would be revolutionary if confirmed. OPERA’s spokesperson Antonio Ereditato stresses caution: the team could not find instrumental effects but invites scrutiny and independent replication. Many physicists are skeptical, pointing to possible systematic errors—particularly in GPS-based timing—and urge confirmation from other experiments (Fermilab, T2K). While statistically significant, the claim awaits reproduction; extraordinary implications demand extraordinary evidence, so the community is examining methods and seeking independent tests before accepting any revision of fundamental physics.

A New Jersey mother, 32-year-old Tova Gerson of Bergenfield, has filed a federal class-action lawsuit claiming Century 21 shorted her 80 cents after applying a $5-off-$50 coupon pro rata when she returned one item from a Jan. 10 purchase. Gerson bought about $106–$108 of goods, returned a $17.97 child’s outfit on Jan. 19, and received $17.17 after the store reduced her refund to account for the coupon’s share. She alleges the practice “unjustly enriched” the retailer and deprived customers of the coupon’s full benefit, arguing she would have purchased items separately if she’d known. The suit, seeking at least $5 million and alleging hundreds or thousands affected, was filed by her lawyer father, Harry Katz, who has sued other retailers over similar coupon disputes. Century 21 did not comment.

Four Paws International rescued the only surviving animals from the Montazah al-Morour Zoo in war-ravaged Mosul and relocated them to Jordan for veterinary care and a fresh start.
