In February vets found Simba the lion and Lula the bear abandoned in cages, filthy and suffering from severe neglect after months of fighting in the city left the zoo nearly destroyed and most animals dead from starvation or violence. Dr. Amir Khalil, an Egyptian-Austrian vet who led the mission, reported both animals had multiple health issues: Lula had pneumonia and very poor teeth, and Simba suffered from bad teeth and joint problems and later developed a respiratory issue. Obtaining export permits from Iraqi authorities took weeks, and an initial evacuation attempt was delayed when the transport lorry was held at a checkpoint for nine days. After securing the necessary paperwork, Four Paws flew Simba and Lula to Jordan, where they will receive proper medical care and rehabilitation. The relocation marks a hopeful new chapter, freeing the animals from the dangers of war.

Prime Minister David Cameron, with just 18 weeks until the General Election, is intensifying a campaign that frames the vote as a stark choice between “competence or chaos.” In an exclusive Mail on Sunday interview he pledges to “hit the ground running” with education and welfare reforms within the first 50 days of a second term and repeatedly stresses economic stewardship as the Tories’ central message, accusing Labour of risking an extra £13.5 billion in interest through reckless spending. Cameron underscores his willingness to press EU leaders, notably Angela Merkel, for reforms ahead of a promised 2017 referendum, saying he will “rule nothing out” if Britain’s “red lines” are ignored. Personal touches—family Christmas anecdotes, his bond with Samantha, and musical tastes—soften the political edge. He praises his close rapport with Barack Obama, who reportedly calls him “bro,” and courts party unity while delicately addressing potential post-election leadership tensions involving Boris Johnson and Theresa May. Overall, Cameron projects confidence while campaigning across marginal seats to defend his economic record.

Bill Hudson recounts a deeply painful Father’s Day incident that he says laid bare a long-simmering family rupture with ex-wife Goldie Hawn and their two eldest children, actors Oliver and Kate Hudson. After a beach day with his youngest daughter, Bill discovered an old family photograph Oliver posted on Instagram labeled “Happy Abandonment Day,” tagging Kate. Both Oliver and Kate also publicly thanked Goldie’s long-term partner Kurt Russell as “Pa” in Father’s Day posts. Bill says the posts were a calculated, malicious provocation that reopened decades of hurt over custody, alienation, and public narratives that have painted him as an absentee father.

In a raw interview, Bill declared he no longer recognizes Oliver and Kate as his children, asking them to stop using the Hudson name and vowing to “break all ties.” He accuses Goldie of “wilfully alienating” the kids after their 1981 split, alleging she rewrote the family story to favor a myth of a perfect family with Kurt Russell. Bill describes early devotion to Oliver and Kate, recounting Oliver’s near-fatal newborn illness and many years of active parenting, but says Goldie’s increasing fame, alleged infidelity, and control over custody access eroded their relationship. He says he tried mediation, weekend visits, letters and gestures to reconnect, but believes a “drip, drip” of negative messaging poisoned the children’s perceptions. Deeply wounded by Oliver’s timing and intent, Bill says their relationship is over and that he is mourning the loss of the bond despite their being alive. The piece situates this family conflict in a broader, decades-long Hollywood saga of love, fame, and fractured parenthood.

A new UCLA study challenges the idea that “sex addiction” or hypersexuality is a true addiction. Researchers measured brain responses (P300 event-related potentials via EEG) to sexual and neutral images in 52 people who reported difficulty controlling their viewing of sexual images. Although participants’ questionnaire scores matched those seeking help for hypersexual problems, the study found that brain responses to sexual stimuli were not linked to measures of hypersexuality or compulsivity. Instead, P300 amplitudes correlated only with levels of sexual desire: people with higher libido showed stronger neural responses to sexual images. The findings contrast with addiction research showing heightened cue-reactivity in substance addicts and cast doubt on applying traditional addiction models to compulsive sexual behavior. Authors note earlier DSM-5 debates and mixed research: hypersexual disorder was considered but not included, and previous studies relied on questionnaires or resting measures. Critics argue compulsive sexual behavior may reflect impulse control, mood regulation, or attention differences rather than neural dependence—there are no “sex receptors” producing withdrawal like substances. Researchers call for more experimental work to clarify mechanisms and caution against prematurely medicalizing diverse sexual behaviors simply because they cause personal or social problems. Replication is needed to confirm these implications.

In 1864 the Confederate submarine H.L. Hunley became the first sub to sink an enemy ship, destroying the USS Housatonic with a spar-mounted copper torpedo filled with about 135 pounds (61 kg) of black powder. The Hunley then sank, and when it was raised in 2000 researchers found eight crewmen seated at their stations with no obvious injuries, escape attempts, or decisive hull damage—leaving their sudden deaths a long-standing mystery. New research led by biomechanist Rachel Lance, published in PLOS ONE, used scaled experiments and historical analysis to test whether the Hunley’s own blast could have killed its crew via transmitted shock waves rather than by drowning, suffocation, or hull breach.

Lance built a one-sixth scale model of the Hunley (the “CSS Tiny”), instrumented it with internal and external pressure gauges, and ran both shock-tube and live black-powder tests in a pond. Her experiments showed that an underwater explosion near the thin iron hull would flex the hull rapidly, producing a secondary “backface” pressure wave that traveled into the interior airspace. That transmitted wave, though it left little or no external structural damage, would impart a sharp-rising pressure to the bodies inside—especially impacting lungs and other gas-filled tissues—causing pulmonary hemorrhage and traumatic brain injury consistent with instantaneous incapacitation and death. Scaling and archival data suggest each crewman had less than a 16% chance of survival from the blast exposure.

The findings reconcile why the men remained at their stations with closed hatches and pumps: a lethal blast would have killed or disabled them instantly without leaving skeletal traces. While some Hunley investigators remain cautious and other naval studies have differed, Lance’s hands-on blast measurements provide a plausible and testable explanation for the Hunley’s fate and illustrate how underwater blast transmission through thin structures can be fatal even when visible damage is minimal.

After more than five decades in broadcast journalism and nearly 40 years at ABC News, Barbara Walters announced she will retire from appearing on television in summer 2014. Walters, who co-created and has hosted ABC’s daytime program The View since 1997, confirmed on the show that she plans to remain on The View through next season, then step down, though she will continue as a co-executive producer and will help select new co-hosts. ABC said she will still anchor and report occasional specials for the network and participate in retrospectives marking her career.

Walters, who will turn 84 in September, has repeatedly deflected retirement rumors following a recent health scare, but announced her decision on-air, saying she is “perfectly healthy” and choosing to slow down to “sit in a sunny field” and admire the talent who will follow her. The announcement aired with notable guests in the studio, including New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg and Disney/ABC CEO Bob Iger, who praised her influence on television journalism.

Her career began in 1961 at NBC’s Today, where she advanced from researcher to reporter, and later joined ABC in 1976 as the first woman to co-anchor an evening newscast. Walters went on to host 20/20, conduct landmark interviews with global leaders and celebrities, and create signature specials. ABC will mark her retirement year with retrospectives of her specials and a multi-part career tribute, while praising her path-breaking contributions to TV news.

On Jan. 12, 2015, a Yellow Line Metro train heading toward Virginia stopped in the tunnel south of L’Enfant Plaza in Washington, D.C., and thick smoke quickly filled the cars and tunnel. Passengers described chaotic, frightening conditions: lights went out, visibility fell to near zero, and many struggled to breathe. Riders tried to stay low, shared inhalers, performed CPR on those who collapsed, and some self-evacuated by walking through the tunnel back toward the station or climbing a vent shaft after the third rail power was shut down. Firefighters reached the train and escorted passengers out; one firefighter was also injured. D.C. Fire and EMS said 84 people were hospitalized and more than 200 evaluated; three remained in critical but stable condition. Metro General Manager Richard Sarles announced one female passenger died; her identity and cause of death were not immediately released. The incident prompted large-scale emergency response, closure and evacuation of L’Enfant Plaza—an important transfer hub serving five lines—temporary suspension of portions of the Green and Yellow lines, and shuttle and reroute arrangements (Blue Line service used as an alternate for Yellow Line riders). NTSB investigators reported electrical arcing involving the third rail and its power supply prior to the smoke; water on the tracks may have helped propagate smoke. The FBI assisted Metro Transit Police as part of standard protocol. Riders recounted long waits—some said firefighters took up to 40 minutes to arrive—and confusion over communication and shuttle logistics even after evacuation. Metro turned on tunnel fans and cut third-rail power to clear smoke; L’Enfant later reopened for certain lines while Green/Yellow restrictions remained. Metro pledged investigation; officials warned a final NTSB report could take months. The episode drew widespread public and social-media attention and scrutiny of Metro safety and emergency response.

Crystal Matrau-Belt, 24, delivered her son Jeremiah James Matrau-Skokan at Bronson Methodist Hospital in Kalamazoo, Michigan, last Saturday. Hours later she learned that her fiancé, Emil Skokan III, 34, and her mother, Peggy Nichols, 53, were killed in a car crash while driving to the hospital to be there for the birth. Emil lost control of the car on South 26th Street near Cork Street in Comstock Township and the vehicle struck a tree; authorities said speed was a factor.

Crystal had been induced because she was 39 weeks along and had high blood pressure. During labor she experienced a drop in blood pressure and opted for an emergency C-section; she spoke with Emil shortly before the operation—the last time she heard from him. Her stepmother stayed with her through delivery. After the birth, family members eventually told Crystal that Emil and her mother had died; she described the moment as devastating and struggled to reconcile the joy of welcoming Jeremiah with the loss of two central people in her life.

Crystal and Emil had only just agreed on the baby’s name—Jeremiah—and chose James as his middle name after her stepfather. She sees Emil’s expressions and features already in the infant and finds some comfort in that resemblance. Emil, who would have turned 35 the following day, is survived by Jeremiah and two older sons, Emil IV and Kayden. He had been preparing for the baby—cleaning the house and setting up a bassinet—and was described by Crystal as caring, hardworking and devoted to family. Nichols had been especially excited to meet her first biological grandchild and had bought much of his wardrobe and gear.

Funeral arrangements were set for both Emil and Nichols later in the week. Crystal is expected to be discharged to attend the services. She urged others to cherish every moment, reminding people that life can change suddenly and unexpectedly. Fundraising efforts for the family are underway.

Late Saturday’s police shooting of 23-year-old Sylville K. Smith in Milwaukee’s Sherman Park neighborhood set off two nights of unrest, with fires, looting and clashes between residents and police. Officers say Smith, an African‑American man with a lengthy record, was armed and turned toward a pursuing officer during a brief foot chase; body‑camera footage reportedly shows the gun in his hand. Police Chief Edward Flynn described the entire encounter as lasting 20–25 seconds and said the officer, also African‑American, faced a credible threat. The decision to release video lies with the state Department of Justice.

Saturday night’s violence left businesses burned, cars overturned, windows smashed and multiple officers injured; 17 people were arrested. An 18‑year‑old man was reported shot Sunday night amid continued unrest, and officers rescued a shooting victim and took him to hospital in an armored vehicle. Police moved through the area in riot gear, declared unlawful assemblies, made arrests and later pulled back after tensions eased. The National Guard was put on alert but not deployed.

Community leaders, clergy and elected officials held meetings, urged calm and began cleanup efforts. Residents expressed mixed reactions: sorrow, anger over persistent poverty and segregation, and calls for dialogue and political engagement. Some defended the police; others emphasized longstanding economic and social grievances. Vigils and peaceful marches were held for Smith, while local leaders and the police union debated accountability, transparency and public safety as the city sought a path forward.

Simone Battle, a 25-year-old singer who rose to fame on the U.S. X Factor and later joined girl group G.R.L., was found dead in her Los Angeles home on September 5. Law enforcement and media reports say her father discovered her hanging in a bedroom closet; authorities described the death as an apparent suicide, though the coroner’s autopsy was pending. Battle had competed on X Factor in 2011, acted on shows like Everybody Hates Chris and Zoey 101, and joined G.R.L. in 2013; the group had recently released an EP and the single “Ugly Heart.” RCA, Kemosabe, Reign Deer Entertainment and G.R.L. founder Robin Antin released statements expressing devastation and condolences. Friends, bandmates and fellow artists mourned her loss.

The Boston Globe published a satirical front page envisioning an America under Donald J. Trump to dramatize what its editorial board called a deeply disturbing and un‑American vision. Framed as an exercise in “taking a man at his word,” the parody imagines headlines about mass deportations, a stalled border wall, and even a pet named after China’s first lady, illustrating the paper’s alarm at Trump’s rhetoric and promises. The Globe argues that Trump’s campaign combines appeals to political violence, hostility toward the press, and explicit scapegoating of minorities—traits more typical of demagogues abroad—and warns his rise could embolden dangerous followers. With Trump unlikely to clinch the 1,237 delegates outright, the paper urges Republicans to prepare for a contested convention and to consider blocking his nomination. It calls for an honorable alternative, naming figures like Paul Ryan or Mitt Romney as potential convention choices, and stresses the need for principled resistance rather than political expediency or selecting another extreme nominee. Ultimately, the Globe asserts the GOP must prioritize democratic norms and reject a demagogue even at electoral cost.

The Washington Post announced several style changes reflecting evolving language use: email (no hyphen), website, Walmart, mic (short for microphone), and conditional acceptance of the singular they. Bill Walsh, the paper’s style steward, explains that these updates were resisted until usage forced them to reconsider. Some changes—like mike versus mic—grew from confusion between abbreviations and short forms; MIC on devices is an abbreviation not meant to be pronounced, yet mic overtook mike in common usage by 2005. Walmart became acceptable because the company’s branding shifted even though its legal name remained Wal-Mart Stores Inc., and the Post stopped routinely using corporate suffixes, allowing the more familiar form in most references.

Walsh frames the Post’s conservative approach as preserving the paper’s voice and credibility, especially in hard news, but acknowledges that language shifts coalesce into broader norms: phrases like mic drop make the older spelling anomalous. He admits personal purism about some forms but accepts pragmatic adaptation.

The most debated change is permitting singular they in instances when recasting a sentence as plural is impossible or awkward, and to respect people who identify outside the gender binary. Walsh had long hesitated but was persuaded by increased visibility of gender-neutral individuals and practical newsroom needs. Coverage from other outlets and copy-editing conferences shows growing acceptance: singular they has deep historical roots (Chaucer, Shakespeare, Austen), and resistance largely arose from 18th-century Latin-influenced prescriptivism. Modern usage has accelerated amid transgender and non-binary visibility, institutional endorsements (e.g., some newsrooms, Facebook’s interface, Canadian government), and style shifts at major outlets like the New York Times experimenting with honorifics such as Mx.

Commentators and language historians argue singular they is a practical, historically attested, and inclusive solution to English’s lack of a gender-neutral singular pronoun. The Post’s cautious policy—prefer rewriting, allow they when needed—mirrors broader, gradual acceptance, driven by both real-world usage and respect for individuals’ identities. The changes reflect the interplay of linguistic evolution, editorial judgment, and cultural shifts toward inclusivity.

A Southwest Airlines flight from Chicago to New Jersey made an unscheduled landing in Cleveland when an outer layer of a window cracked; the pilots did not declare an emergency and cabin pressure was never lost, the airline said. Flight 957 landed safely Wednesday morning with no injuries and the aircraft has been taken out of service for maintenance review. The incident follows a recent deadly accident two weeks earlier in which an engine failure led to a window blowout and one passenger’s death.

Aviation experts explained that modern airliner windows consist of multiple acrylic plies—typically an outer and an inner pane—designed so the inner layer can sustain pressure if the outer layer fails. Jim Lee of Lee Aerospace noted each pane is built to withstand two to four times normal flight pressure, and said an outer-ply crack, while alarming to passengers, is not usually dangerous. Airline consultant Robert Mann said windows are periodically polished to remove tiny cracks from sun and chemical exposure, and he supported the crew’s decision to land promptly. Flight instructor Anthony Roman added that such problems should be caught during regular inspections. Investigators expect to analyze the damaged window microscopically to determine whether fatigue or another cause led to the failure.

Neighbors say Randy and Amy Loughner, parents of accused Tucson shooter Jared Lee Loughner, are devastated and considering a public statement — their first since the massacre that left six dead and wounded many, including Rep. Gabrielle Giffords. The couple, long-time residents of a modest ranch house north of Tucson, largely avoided neighbors and valued privacy; few saw them after the shootings and deputies cordoned off their property. Neighbor Wayne Smith, who brought in their mail, reported Randy had written a statement but was unsure when to release it and wanted to coordinate with the sheriff’s office. Residents recalled the Loughners as reclusive and sometimes hostile; Randy reportedly didn’t work after Jared’s birth while Amy held a steady job. Authorities say Jared had psychological problems and planned the attack; the parents told investigators they hadn’t realized the severity of his issues. The family has otherwise been unreachable amid the community’s shock.

Bruno, a seven-year-old chocolate Labrador, has been discharged to return home after nearly a month of intensive veterinary care following his rescue from an abandoned three-metre well near the Billesbergers’ farm in the Estevan area. Missing since Sept. 17, he was found Oct. 14 by the family when their other dogs led them to the well. Severely emaciated—having lost about half his body weight—and suffering wounds and sores from prolonged time in water and attempts to escape, Bruno initially received emergency care at Prairie Animal Health Centre in Estevan. After several days he developed refeeding syndrome, a dangerous metabolic complication that can follow prolonged starvation, prompting referral to the Western College of Veterinary Medicine in Saskatoon.

At the college Bruno spent nearly 22 days in the Veterinary Medical Centre and ICU, monitored around the clock. Treatment included careful, gradually increased feeding with electrolyte and mineral supplementation (phosphorus, magnesium, potassium), IV support, cold laser therapy for paw and hindquarter injuries, and physiotherapy. Clinicians praised his progress: once barely ambulatory and food-driven, he regained energy, wagged his tail, and began showing his old personality. Veterinarians plan to document the case so others can learn from the multidisciplinary approach involving nutritionists, internists, rehab specialists and surgeons. Owners John and Cindy Billesberger, grateful to local and Saskatoon veterinary teams, said Bruno will continue a special diet and rehab at home and is expected to thrive back on the farm with his canine companions.

During the early days of the 2017 San Fermin festival in Pamplona, Spain, the famed daily running of the bulls produced multiple injuries but no life-threatening outcomes. Over the first two days five people were gored; several more suffered knocks and falls. On Sunday the third run, featuring bulls from the Puerto de San Lorenzo ranch making their debut, was unusually fast—completing the 930-yard cobbled course in 2 minutes, 22 seconds—and relatively calm, with four men (three Spaniards and one Frenchman) treated for minor injuries. A brown bull named Huracan broke away and charged through the crowds, briefly catching a runner by a pant leg and dragging him a short distance, though he escaped without serious harm. 

American runner Bill Hillmann, a 35-year-old author and 12-year veteran of the event, was gored again during the festival—his second major goring since 2014. A 1,200-lb bull, Sentido, jabbed a horn into Hillmann’s buttocks and flipped him; initial shock masked the pain and he walked to medics. Doctors later found a deep wound requiring stitches and a drainage tube; he spent 36 hours in hospital and was released walking but sore. Hillmann, who has been gored multiple times and previously required extensive recovery, says he remains devoted to the bulls and Pamplona’s culture and intends to run again before the festival ends. His experiences are being filmed for an interactive documentary exploring the role of foreign runners. The nine-day fiesta, attracting tens of thousands worldwide and popularized by Ernest Hemingway’s The Sun Also Rises, continues amid its dangerous traditions and devoted participants.

Residents of Hawaii’s Big Island faced escalating danger as Kilauea’s eruption spread lava, toxic gas and seismic unrest across the lower East Rift Zone. Authorities warned a wind shift could carry rising sulfur dioxide levels into southeast communities; SO2 and fine particulates in vog can cause acute respiratory distress, especially in children, the elderly and those with lung disease. About 2,000 people were evacuated from Leilani Estates and nearby subdivisions after roughly 15 fissures opened, destroying some 36 structures. Geologists reported continuing ground cracking and earthquakes as magma drains and migrates through deep conduits, keeping the chance of new surface eruptions “decent.” Scientists caution Kilauea may enter a rare explosive phase, potentially hurling multi-ton “ballistic blocks” up to 800 meters and showering pea-sized ejecta and ash a mile or two downwind; the summit area inside Hawaii Volcanoes National Park was closed indefinitely. Authorities removed 50,000 gallons of flammable pentane from the nearby Puna Geothermal Venture to avert catastrophe if lava reached the plant. Air-quality teams detected no immediately dangerous SO2 near fissures, but hospitals reported more respiratory visits in some areas; monitoring equipment is being installed. Governor David Ige requested a federal disaster declaration, saying mass evacuation might exceed state and county capacity. Officials warned of possible acid rain, ecological impacts, and that other lower East Rift Zone neighborhoods could become threatened as activity evolves.

Gloria Hiroko Chapman says her husband, Mark David Chapman, told her two months before John Lennon’s murder that he had planned to kill the Beatle, but claimed he didn’t because his love for her stopped him and he’d thrown the gun away. When news of Lennon’s death reached her in Hawaii on December 8, 1980, she realized Mark had lied. Now 67, Gloria has waited nearly four decades as Mark, 63, serves 20 years to life for the killing and faces a parole hearing for the tenth time in August. Despite past abuse, long separations and pressure to divorce, Gloria—guided by her faith—remained loyal, making annual conjugal visits and praying for his release. She hopes recent parole board shifts toward assessing in-prison behavior will favor his freedom, despite opposition from Yoko Ono.

During the early-morning massacre at Pulse nightclub in Orlando, News 13 producer Matthew Gentili was staffing phones at the downtown newsroom less than two miles away when he received a call he later described as “the most serious call I’ll ever get in my life.” Around 2:45 a.m., amid frantic viewer inquiries about the shooting, Gentili answered in his usual way: “News 13, this is Matt.” The caller asked if he knew about the shooting, then interrupted to declare, “I’m the shooter. It’s me. I am the shooter.” According to Gentili, the man said he carried out the attack for the Islamic State and began speaking rapidly in Arabic; Gentili asked him to speak English. The caller repeated, “I did it for ISIS. I did it for the Islamic State,” and, when asked his location, replied with an expletive before hanging up after declining to add anything more. Gentili heard no background noise during the brief exchange. After his 12-hour shift he was interviewed by the FBI; while federal agents would not confirm the identity of the caller, News 13’s managing editor matched the incoming number to Omar Mateen. The call followed Mateen’s earlier brief 911 conversations in which he pledged allegiance to IS. Gentili says the experience has profoundly affected him and altered how he will answer calls in the future.

Bill Watterson, the famously reclusive creator of Calvin and Hobbes, has produced new public artwork for the first time in nearly two decades. He contributed the cover illustration for Stripped, a documentary by cartoonist Dave Kellett and filmmaker Frederick Schroeder that celebrates comic strips and examines the newspaper industry; Watterson also provided a brief voice-over interview. Watterson said he wasn’t otherwise involved but enjoyed creating a playful, somewhat bawdier poster image inspired by the film’s title and themes. Stripped, funded via Kickstarter, will be released on iTunes April 1 and on DVD April 2. Separately, Watterson donated a 6" x 8" oil painting of Petey Otterloop from Richard Thompson’s Cul de Sac to Team Cul de Sac, a fundraising project benefiting Parkinson’s research and the Michael J. Fox Foundation. That piece—Watterson’s first art seen by his syndicate in 16 years—supports a book and other efforts to raise funds for the cause.

Rob Porter, White House staff secretary and a close aide to Chief of Staff John Kelly, resigned after two ex-wives publicly accused him of physical and emotional abuse. Colbie Holderness produced photos of a blackened eye and recounted being punched and choked during their marriage; Jennifer Willoughby described being dragged from a shower and cited a 2010 protective order. Both women said they spoke to the FBI during Porter's security-clearance review in 2017. Porter denied the allegations but stepped down amid mounting pressure. The White House initially defended him—Kelly and others praised his professionalism—but reversed course after the photos surfaced. Porter had been influential in vetting material for President Trump and shaping policy, making his departure a significant blow to West Wing operations and raising questions about the handling of background-check information.

Swaddling—wrapping a baby snugly in a blanket to calm them and reduce startling—has seen a resurgence as parents use it to soothe crying and promote sleep. While long used in many cultures, several UK experts warn tightly swaddling infants can harm hip development by forcing legs straight and restricting the natural “frog” or flexed-abducted position needed for healthy hip joints. Professors and orthopaedic consultants, writing in Archives of Disease in Childhood, link restrictive swaddling with developmental dysplasia of the hip and note other risks such as overheating, increased cot-death risk if placed prone, and possible effects on breastfeeding or respiratory infections. Organisations including the Royal College of Midwives, Great Ormond Street clinicians, the Lullaby Trust and NCT advise caution: avoid heavy wraps, never cover the head, never place swaddled babies on their stomach, and allow leg movement. Safe alternatives and instructional videos show hip-healthy swaddling techniques and stress tailoring advice to cultural practices.

Ramineh Behbehanian, 50, was arrested April 29, 2013, on suspicion of attempted murder after police say she placed two bottles of orange juice tainted with isopropyl rubbing alcohol into a Starbucks open-air refrigerated display in South San Jose. A customer watching the line saw her place the bottles and alerted staff; an employee noted Behbehanian’s license plate as she fled. Employees smelled something toxic, called 911, and hazardous-materials technicians confirmed the presence of a potentially lethal concentration of isopropyl alcohol. No one drank the juice. Behbehanian, who holds a master’s in physical chemistry and chemical engineering and worked for Janssen/Johnson & Johnson, was arrested at her home about five miles away and jailed without bail. Authorities have not disclosed a motive and said they do not know if she targeted anyone or had planned similar acts elsewhere. Starbucks removed and destroyed remaining juices and notified nearby stores.

Researchers have documented a bizarre, long-lived wood ant aggregation living inside an abandoned Soviet nuclear weapons bunker near Templewo, Poland. The bunker, built in the Cold War and buried with trees planted above, ended up beneath a large Formica polyctena colony. A rusted ventilation pipe in the nest roof now funnels hundreds of thousands of worker ants each year into the subterranean storage chamber, where they cannot escape. Discovered when scientists investigating bats entered the site, the underground population has been monitored since 2013 and described in the Journal of Hymenoptera Research.

Conditions inside the bunker are harsh: constant darkness, very low temperatures (rarely above about 50°F/10°C), and a paucity of obvious nutritious food. Despite this, workers continue to build and maintain a mound and perform normal worker tasks. However, extensive searches found no evidence of reproduction—no queens, no larvae, pupae, or empty cocoons—so the underground group appears to be a non-reproductive aggregation of sterile workers sustained only by the yearly inflow of fallers from the surface colony. Mortality is high; researchers recorded vast “ant cemeteries” around the mound, with densities suggesting millions of dead bodies accumulated over time. A small detrital ecosystem—mites and other invertebrates—feeds on those remains, and bat guano or scavenged invertebrates may supply some nutrients, though the ants’ exact food sources remain uncertain.

The team notes that, in principle, a queen could enter and found a reproductive population or the colony could adopt an alien queen, but without reliable nutrition and warmth raising brood seems unlikely. Thus the bunker population persists as a grim, dystopian workforce: a large, aging mass of non-reproductive workers maintained only by continual accidental reinforcement from the surface nest. The study highlights an unexpected and haunting ecological legacy of Cold War infrastructure on insect societies.

A widely shared video captured a man being forcibly removed from United Airlines Flight 3411 at Chicago O’Hare on April 9, 2017, triggering public outrage. The flight, bound for Louisville, had been overbooked and United needed seats for crew members who had to reach Louisville for subsequent flights. United initially sought volunteers at the gate, offering $400, a hotel night and a Monday flight; when no one accepted, the offer rose to $800. Passengers were already allowed to board, and the carrier later said a computer would randomly select four people to give up their seats. Two people complied, but one passenger, identified as Dr. David Dao of Elizabethtown, refused, saying he needed to see patients Monday morning.

Video posted by passenger Audra D. Bridges shows officers speaking with Dao, then grabbing and dragging him down the aisle as he screams; his face was later seen bloodied. Bridges and other passengers reported that multiple aviation security officers boarded, the man was thrown against an armrest, removed from the plane, then later allowed to reboard before the flight departed about two hours late. Passengers, including children, were visibly upset. United initially stated the customer refused to leave voluntarily and law enforcement was called, apologizing for the overbooking. CEO Oscar Munoz later called the incident “upsetting,” said the airline was conducting a review, reaching out to the passenger, and working with authorities.

Chicago’s Department of Aviation placed the officer who pulled the man from his seat on leave and said the actions did not conform to standard operating procedures; all three individuals seen speaking with the passenger were confirmed as aviation security officers. The episode spawned widespread criticism, multiple headlines, and follow-up coverage about airline bumping practices and United’s handling of the situation.

Apple announced its new touchscreen device would be called the iPad, sparking a wave of mockery and gendered critique online. Critics and bloggers derided the name—Business Insider called it "terrible"—and social media quickly turned the discussion toward menstruation jokes, with "iTampon" trending on Twitter. Commenters lamented the absence of women on Apple’s announcement stage and questioned whether marketing had considered female perspectives. Some writers compared the backlash to early jibes about Nintendo’s Wii, which still sold strongly despite ridicule. Apple promoted the iPad as "a magical and revolutionary device" but offered no comment to critics. A recurring joke highlighted a practical limitation: you can’t use an iPad while swimming.

Researchers analyzed data from 1,656 married U.S. adults aged 57–85 drawn from the 2005–2006 National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project to examine how marital characteristics relate to sexual outcomes. Key findings show that people in their first marriage report more frequent sex than those who have remarried, though marriage order did not relate to reported physical pleasure or emotional satisfaction. Frequency of sex follows a curvilinear pattern across marital duration: it is higher in the early years, declines over time, but shows a modest rebound among couples who have been married longer than about 50 years—a small subgroup given the age cohort. Gender differences emerged in the timing of sexual frequency: men in younger marriages reported more frequent sex than women in younger marriages, suggesting gendered dynamics early in marriage. Authors propose explanations but caution about causal interpretation because the study is cross-sectional. They speculate that perceived relationship permanency and increased investment in long-term partners may help sustain or revive sexual activity in very long marriages, while those who remarry might feel less permanence and thus engage less frequently. The research contributes to a limited but growing literature on older adults’ sexual behavior, challenging ageist assumptions by showing that regular sexual activity remains common into later life despite health declines and bereavement. The study’s authors call for future research to explore mechanisms behind these patterns.

The article explores the curious phenomenon of spite houses—small, odd-shaped homes built deliberately to annoy neighbors—and centers on Seattle’s famous Montlake Spite House while reviewing an art show themed around spite. Spite, distinct from ordinary anger, is portrayed as a hardened, cherished grievance that drives people to monumentally irrational acts: building a structure solely to spite someone. The Montlake Spite House, at 2022 24th Avenue East, is a wedge-shaped bungalow built in 1925, narrow to just 4.5 feet at one end and roughly 830–860 square feet overall. Popular origin stories include a jilted wife building on a tiny awarded parcel after a divorce or a landowner responding to a lowball offer by erecting a pie-slice house that forced his neighbor to move; other accounts suggest pragmatic design choices to fit a lot. Its quirky layout—requiring cooks to stand to the side to open the oven—has become local lore, and the house has sold multiple times at rising prices. The piece notes that many states, including Washington, have “malicious erection” statutes to enjoin or remove spite structures, reflecting how common and disruptive such acts have been historically.

The essay then ties spite houses to an art exhibition, Spite House, at Lawrimore Project. Curators Yoko Ott and Jessica Powers assembled works that attempt to channel spite’s formal planning and moral absurdity; some pieces succeed more than others. A gallery installation by SuttonBeresCuller, ironically, burned just before opening—likely from an accidental fire—which lent a visceral intensity to the show. Works by Aaron Young, Andrew Dadson, Bert Rodriguez, and others engage boundary-stomping, obstruction, and aesthetic rebuke, though the critic finds many pieces less personally vehement than true spite houses. Overall, spite houses and the exhibition reveal long-running neighborhood conflicts, performative ownership, and the peculiar beauty of obstinate, self-defeating acts.

On the second anniversary of Egypt’s uprising against Hosni Mubarak, massive anti-President Mohamed Mursi protests erupted across Cairo, Suez, Alexandria, Port Said and other cities, leaving five people dead in Suez, including one security officer, and hundreds wounded. Thousands gathered in Tahrir Square, accusing Mursi and the Muslim Brotherhood of hijacking the revolution, pushing an Islamist-tinged constitution, and failing to fix a plunging economy. Street battles, arson at state and Brotherhood offices, and clashes with riot police—who used tear gas and barriers—marked the day. The Brotherhood largely stayed off the streets, staging charity drives instead. Opponents demand constitutional overhaul, protection of rights, judicial independence and an end to perceived Brotherhood domination.

Lt. Col. Eric E. Schultz, 44, a veteran Air Force test pilot, died after an aircraft crash during a training mission Tuesday evening at the Nevada Test and Training Range, about 100 miles northwest of Nellis Air Force Base. The crash occurred around 6 p.m.; Schultz was assigned to an Air Force Materiel Command aircraft. Base officials confirmed the fatality Friday and said the type of aircraft involved is classified and not releasable. Investigators are probing the incident. After the crash, Nellis officials concentrated on search, recovery and next-of-kin notification, which contributed to the delayed public release of details. It’s unclear whether Schultz died at the crash site or whether anyone else was aboard. The accident came one day before a separate training mishap at the same range, when two A-10C Thunderbolt II jets from Nellis’ 57th Wing crashed around 8 p.m.; both A-10 pilots ejected safely and were treated and released. Both the fatal crash and the A-10 incident are under investigation; the service has not said if the two events are related. Schultz, an Annapolis High School graduate, joined the Air Force in 2001 after a career that included civilian test piloting and significant technical roles. He logged more than 2,000 flight hours across multiple aircraft, including the F-35 and F-15E, flew combat close air support missions in Afghanistan, and held advanced degrees including a Ph.D. in aerospace engineering. He is survived by his wife Julie, five children, and extended family.

Swiss researchers have revived clinical LSD research after a roughly 40-year pause, reporting results from a small trial testing lysergic acid diethylamide combined with psychotherapy to reduce death-related anxiety in cancer patients. Published in the Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, the study administered supervised 10-hour LSD sessions—so-called "trips"—to mostly terminal patients to help them confront painful memories and feelings. Participants underwent about 30 sessions across two months. One patient described a session as a mystical but distressing revisiting of long-suppressed memories; clinicians consider such distress potentially therapeutic because it enables emotional processing.

The protocol compared a full LSD dose (200 micrograms) with a lower dose. One year after treatment ended, patients who had received the full dose showed a roughly 20 percent decrease in anxiety, while those on the lower dose experienced increased anxiety; the low-dose group was later offered the full dose after the trial. No serious adverse effects were reported. Because the trial enrolled only a small number of participants, the investigators caution against drawing firm conclusions—the results did not reach statistical significance—but they view the study as a positive sign for renewed clinical investigation into psychedelics.

Advocates and researchers hope to reframe LSD research beyond its countercultural associations and reintroduce rigorous laboratory study. Rick Doblin, director of the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies, called for bringing these substances "back to the lab" as part of a broader psychedelic renaissance, noting the potential clinical value and acceptable safety profile observed in this trial.

After recent police killings in Ferguson, New York and nearby Cleveland, Akron’s youth-led Akron PeaceMakers created and began distributing a glossy two-sided “You and the Law” palm card to every middle and high school student in the city. The card, funded by the group’s $1,500 fundraising to print 50,000 copies, lists 15 practical points advising how to behave during police encounters—things like staying calm, answering identity questions, keeping hands visible on the steering wheel and avoiding insults toward officers. It also urges broader common-sense avoidance of trouble and, importantly, gives instructions and phone numbers for documenting and reporting alleged police misconduct on the card’s reverse.

The project sprang from outrage after the November shooting of 12-year-old Tamir Rice in Cleveland and other national incidents. PeaceMakers President Myia Culbreath and peers said they wanted a constructive response beyond protests: to educate peers so encounters don’t escalate. Mayor Don Plusquellic and city officials, including Assistant Police Chief Charles Brown and retired Sgt. Willa Keith, advised the youths during development. The cards carry personal resonance: Billy Soule, the mayor’s community relations liaison and PeaceMakers director, recounted his son’s experience being pursued by officers while carrying a toy gun and credited compliance with saving his life.

Students’ reactions at local schools have ranged from interest to debate. Some praise the preventive, de-escalation focus; others emphasize that the cards must also hold police accountable. The PeaceMakers intentionally included reporting steps to balance guidance on compliance with empowerment to seek redress later. Organizers plan broader community distribution—to churches, block watches and board meetings—and hope to extend the program to adults and possibly abroad. Observers, including Mayor Karen Freeman-Wilson of Gary, Ind., see the initiative as a potential model for mayors nationwide seeking ways to bridge police-citizen divides.

Law enforcement sources confirmed that James T. Hodgkinson, the 66-year-old gunman who opened fire at a congressional Republican baseball practice in Alexandria, Virginia, carried a handwritten list that included the names of at least three GOP members of Congress. The names identified by officials were Representatives Mo Brooks (Alabama), Jeff Duncan (South Carolina) and Trent Franks (Arizona). Brooks and Duncan had been at the practice; Duncan left before the shooting began. Authorities stress the list did not include explicit threats and at least one source said it should not necessarily be characterized as an “assassination list,” though it indicates Hodgkinson had recently focused on a small group of people. Law enforcement also found multiple writings among Hodgkinson’s possessions and photos of the ballfield on his cellphone.

The attack occurred around 7 a.m. Wednesday; Hodgkinson was fatally shot by police. Five people were struck, including House Majority Whip Rep. Steve Scalise, who as of Thursday remained in critical condition with some improvement but facing further surgeries and rehabilitation. None of the other injured individuals were reported to be on the list.

Federal investigators are probing Hodgkinson’s motives, reviewing social media posts that displayed anti-Republican and pro-Bernie Sanders sentiments, and believe he had recently moved from Illinois to Alexandria and was living in his vehicle. The ATF traced the recovered weapons—a 9 mm handgun and a 7.62 caliber rifle—and so far has found no evidence they were obtained illegally. The investigation into his intentions and connections continues.

Scientists have found initial evidence that inhaled air-pollution particles can pass through pregnant women’s lungs and lodge in their placentas, potentially explaining how pollution harms fetal development. In a small London study presented at the European Respiratory Society congress, researchers examined placentas from five non-smoking women who delivered healthy babies. They isolated about 3,500 placental macrophage cells—immune cells that engulf harmful particles—and identified 72 dark particles in 60 cells. Electron microscopy showed these particles resembled sooty carbon particles seen in lung macrophages. While further analysis is required for definitive identification, investigators say the most plausible explanation is that these are combustion-derived particles that traveled from the mother’s lungs to the placenta. Researchers caution they cannot yet prove the particles cross into the fetus, but note placental impairment alone can directly affect fetal health. The findings build on extensive epidemiological evidence linking maternal air pollution exposure to premature birth, low birth weight and long-term health and cognitive impacts; larger studies in London and elsewhere have described substantial population-level risks. Experts at the congress emphasized the public-health implications, noting damage can occur even below current regulatory limits and urging stricter air-quality policies. Separate research presented at the same meeting found children with early, persistent asthma—often associated with pollution—have worse educational outcomes. Investigators and public-health leaders called for increased awareness among clinicians and the public, and for urgent policy action to reduce exposure to toxic air, especially for pregnant women and young children.

When the government announced it would declassify a copy of the Pentagon Papers 40 years after The New York Times first published them, it initially said 11 words would remain secret — then reversed course and released the full 7,000-page report. That brief censorship sparked widespread curiosity and a guessing game among historians, security analysts and even the report’s authors, who could not identify which words might still be sensitive decades later. Daniel Ellsberg, who leaked the Papers to oppose the Vietnam War, said he was “stumped.” Leslie H. Gelb, who directed the task force that produced the study, likewise could not imagine where the words came from, though he suggested they might relate to peace-negotiation material omitted from early leaks. The New York Times invited readers to propose candidates via Twitter using the hashtag #pentagon11, turning the mystery into a public, participatory puzzle.

A small Adelaide café, Viscous Coffee, has created an extreme caffeinated drink called the Asskicker (or Ass Kicker) that has drawn attention for its potency and health implications. Invented by owner Steve Benington for an emergency nurse who needed to stay awake on night shifts, the beverage blends four espresso shots with two strengths of cold drip and milk; the cafe claims it contains roughly the caffeine equivalent of 80 standard cups or about five grams of caffeine per large serving. Benington says the recipe has been moderated from its original form—an earlier version reportedly kept the nurse awake across three days—and the drink is intended to be sipped slowly over three to four hours to provide sustained alertness rather than a brief, intense spike. Viscous warns customers—especially those with high blood pressure or heart conditions—and Benington personally discusses the drink with patrons to dissuade those unprepared for its effects. Reported overdose signs include shakes, sweating, dilated pupils, vertigo and nausea; experts note that individual sensitivity varies widely and that serious effects have occurred with far lower doses in susceptible people. While a fatal dose is often cited near 18 grams consumed rapidly, some researchers estimate about 10 grams could be lethal for some; the Asskicker’s five grams is substantial but below those extreme levels. Broader context notes caffeine is the world’s most-used psychoactive drug, with average adult intake around 300 mg/day and both potential benefits (reduced risks of some diseases) and harms (hypertension, gastrointestinal issues, withdrawal). Medical and public-health voices urge caution and moderation; many recommend two to four cups of coffee daily rather than such concentrated brews.

A YouTube clip of a behind-the-scenes moment from Charlie Chaplin’s 1928 film The Circus sparked renewed online debate when Belfast fan George Clarke posted footage showing a woman who appears to be holding a small dark object to her ear and speaking while walking. Clarke, who describes himself as a devoted Chaplin follower and says he studied the clip for over a year, says he repeatedly rewound and zoomed the segment and cannot explain her gestures; he floated the idea she might be a time traveler using a mobile phone. The video, posted in October 2010, attracted over 1.3 million views and a wide range of viewer theories—from hearing aid or obscure period device to joking suggestions—while Clarke says screenings and festival viewings produced no conclusive explanation, leaving the short clip an enduring internet mystery.

Former President George W. Bush’s official portrait was unveiled at the White House, showing him in the Oval Office with hands on a chair—a conventional political pose that looks toward an undefined future. One notable detail: the portrait includes Bush’s favored painting, the work he placed by his desk and named his 1999 memoir A Charge to Keep after. Bush long described the image as depicting 19th-century Methodist circuit riders, aligning with his faith and self-image, but critics have challenged that interpretation. Jacob Weisberg argued the painting’s title and meaning differ, linking it instead to a 1918 Country Gentleman story about a son defending inherited land—an ironic contrast to Bush’s account. Some aspects of the dispute remain debated, including possible confusion between similar Kommer illustrations, but the connection to Methodist missionaries appears unlikely. The event also highlighted how presidential portrait artists are chosen—presidents select their painters from many submissions, often with first-lady or curator input—and that official portraits are privately funded through the White House Historical Association rather than by taxpayers. Portraits form part of the White House’s historical record.

Authorities have upgraded charges against Jesse L. Matthew Jr., the man accused in the disappearance and death of University of Virginia sophomore Hannah Graham, to capital murder, exposing him to possible death penalty if convicted. Matthew, 33, was previously charged with first-degree murder after Graham, 18, vanished from a Charlottesville outdoor mall on Sept. 12 and her body was found weeks later in a wooded area about 10 miles from campus. Prosecutors allege Matthew abducted Graham “with intent to defile,” indicating an intended sexual assault; such aggravating factors allow a capital charge in Virginia. Albemarle County’s commonwealth’s attorney initially declined to seek capital murder after consulting Graham’s family but later upgraded the charge at a court hearing. Matthew also faces separate charges from a 2005 attack in Fairfax City, where authorities say his DNA was found under the victim’s fingernails. Surveillance and witness accounts place Matthew and Graham together the night she disappeared.

Vice President Joe Biden chose Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor to administer his oath of office, making her the fourth woman and first Hispanic to swear in a president or vice president. President Barack Obama will be sworn in by Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., who will preside at both the private, constitutionally required ceremony on Sunday, Jan. 20, and the public inauguration on Monday, Jan. 21. The private swearing-in will be small and family-centered at the White House Blue Room, with a larger public ceremony on the Capitol’s west front expected to draw up to 800,000 people. Biden praised Sotomayor as a friend and a justice committed to justice and opportunity.

Obama’s subdued Sunday ceremony reflects tradition when Jan. 20 falls on a Sunday; he will deliver his formal second inaugural address Monday, setting the stage for his second-term priorities—economic recovery, immigration reform, tighter gun laws and winding down the war in Afghanistan—with detailed policy plans to follow in the State of the Union. The weekend included civic events such as a National Day of Service. Roberts and Obama’s relationship, testy since a 2009 oath flub and strained over decisions like Citizens United, remains consequential as the Court may continue to shape major policy disputes during Obama’s second term.

A Winton Hills woman treated for an STD at University of Cincinnati Medical Center has filed a lawsuit after an employee allegedly posted her medical record, including her diagnosis of syphilis, to a Facebook group called "Team No Hoes" in September 2013. The suit, filed in Hamilton County Common Pleas Court, names UC Medical Center, employee Ryan Rawls, an unnamed nurse, and the woman’s ex-boyfriend, Raphael Bradley. Attorney Mike Allen says Bradley persuaded the employees to release and share a screenshot of the patient’s record, which was also emailed to the closed group; commenters called the plaintiff derogatory names. The lawsuit alleges negligent supervision, invasion of privacy, emotional distress, malice and ongoing harassment, including phone calls to the plaintiff and her child, and seeks over $25,000 in damages and a jury trial. UC Health declined detailed comment on pending litigation; CEO Lee Ann Liska reminded staff that unauthorized access or sharing of protected health information is a serious violation and can result in termination. The plaintiff seeks procedural changes to prevent future breaches.

A US special forces detachment ambushed near Tongo Tongo, Niger, in early October fought alone for hours after most accompanying Nigerien troops reportedly fled within minutes, according to serving and retired officers. Twelve US soldiers from the 3rd Special Forces Group and about 30 Nigeriens had been on a “train and equip” mission when roughly 50 militants attacked with small arms, RPGs and mortars. The rear half of the patrol was trapped in an ambush kill zone; roughly half the Nigerien force was killed or fled, leaving small American groups—about six men each—to fight multiple attackers. An unarmed US drone arrived quickly but provided no strike capability. French Mirage fighters from Mali responded to airstrike requests but allegedly refused to engage, citing poor weather, terrain and inability to distinguish friend from foe; ground reinforcements, including French special forces, reached the site by helicopter after about two hours and evacuated survivors. Four US soldiers and five Nigerien troops died; one US soldier, Sgt La David Johnson, was found two days later, possibly after an attempted kidnapping. The incident has prompted a US Africa Command investigation, ignited debate in Washington over oversight of overseas missions, and raised questions about mission risk, intelligence failures and interpartner coordination.

Tiger Woods began the PGA Championship strong—three early birdies had him tied for the lead—then imploded, carding three double bogeys and multiple other bogeys for a 77 in the opening round at Atlanta Athletic Club. The 7-over total left him tied for 129th, far behind leader Steve Stricker’s 63. It was Woods’ highest opening-round score in a major and among his worst major rounds overall. Woods blamed trying to play by feel instead of trusting his swing, saying he’s “not at that point yet.” He struck trouble with errant irons and frequent sand shots, including a ball that found a pond and another buried in a bunker, and finished having been in sand a dozen times. At 35, Woods faces the risk of missing the cut—something he’s rarely done—and jeopardizing his FedEx Cup standing and remaining PGA season.

In 1890 Thomas Edison attempted to bring recorded sound into homes with some of the earliest talking dolls. About 500 two-foot-tall dolls were produced, each with wooden limbs, a metal body and a tiny spring-wound phonograph inside activated by a crank at the back. Edison loaded short, familiar verses—nursery rhymes and prayers—onto fragile wax cylinders so listeners would recognize the content despite very poor sound quality. Recordings recently scanned by a government lab and made public reveal those voices for the first time in decades, and listeners describe them as unnerving. Jerry Fabris, curator of sound recordings at the Thomas Edison National Historical Park, notes that the unsettling effect likely comes in part from a female factory worker who read in a high, childlike voice to simulate a little girl. Even Edison found the dolls’ sound unpleasant, and they were commercially unsuccessful for practical reasons: they were expensive (roughly $200 in today’s money), didn’t have moving mouths and the audio was not clear enough to seem lifelike. Edison discontinued production after about a month and reportedly called them “little monsters.” The dolls also tap into a long cultural discomfort: talking toys occupy an established horror subgenre because they sit in an uncanny middle ground—familiar and human-like, yet clearly not alive. Georgetown scholar Caetlin Benson-Allott links that reaction to Freud’s concept of the uncanny and to lingering childhood associations when dolls were imagined as living. The dolls’ combination of primitive technology and simulated life highlights how giving objects power or agency can provoke a deep, persistent apprehension that the power might somehow come back at us.

Hamilton County Coroner Dr. Lakshmi Sammarco said she could not determine what caused the severe, fatal brain damage sustained by 22-year-old University of Virginia student Otto Warmbier, who was detained in North Korea for 17 months and died June 19, 2017, shortly after his return to the U.S. Her Sept. 11 report cites complications from chronic anoxic/ischemic encephalopathy—lack of oxygen and blood to the brain—from an “unknown insult” more than a year before his death. The manner of death was listed as undetermined. Warmbier’s family declined a full autopsy; Sammarco performed an external exam and CT “virtual autopsy,” and said further autopsy would not add useful information after such prolonged injury. UC Health doctors found no evidence of botulism, fractures or healing fractures; a forensic dentist likewise found no trauma to teeth, contradicting the parents’ TV description that Otto’s teeth looked “rearranged.” Warmbier’s body appeared well-nourished with skin in good condition and no bedsores, suggesting he received regular care, though it bore multiple scars consistent with medical procedures. North Korea denied torture, attributing his coma to botulism and a sleeping pill. Sammarco emphasized that without testimony from those present during the initial injury, the cause may never be known. President Trump and Warmbier’s parents have publicly accused North Korea of torture.

A stovepipe hat long presented as Abraham Lincoln’s prized beaver-fur chapeau — the centerpiece of a $25 million acquisition by the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library Foundation in 2007 and appraised at $6.5 million — lacks firm evidence tying it to the 16th president, according to previously undisclosed reports obtained by WBEZ. The foundation quietly commissioned a 2013 review by senior curators from the Smithsonian and the Chicago History Museum and later sought DNA testing from the FBI; neither produced confirmation of Lincoln provenance. The curators’ report concluded documentation was insufficient to assert Lincoln ever owned the hat and urged the museum to “soften its claim,” avoid using the hat in exhibitions until further research, and even consider asking seller Louise Taper to take it back if better evidence could not be found.

FBI analyses in 2015 compared DNA recovered from the hat with samples from Lincoln-related items tied to his assassination night and hair samples. Results showed contemporary handling DNA on the hat and no conclusive match to Lincoln; the lab described remaining DNA as limited and inconclusive. The testing was carried out under secrecy—agents reportedly disguised as a news crew at the museum—prompting concern from current museum director Alan Lowe, who says he only recently received the full reports and has paused display of the hat pending internal investigation.

Foundation vice chairman Nick Kalm maintains the foundation still believes the hat could be Lincoln’s, noting gaps in provenance research and calling the investigations responsible though disappointing. The episode has fueled criticism from lawmakers over transparency as the financially strained foundation seeks state aid and private donations to repay loans tied to the Taper collection. Museum leaders say they will not exhibit the hat again until rigorous authentication and internal review are completed.

Richard Grenell, an openly gay longtime Republican communications operative, resigned less than two weeks after joining Mitt Romney’s presidential campaign as Foreign Policy and National Security Spokesman. Grenell said he left because the “hyper-partisan discussion of personal issues” had diminished his ability to speak clearly and forcefully about foreign policy, and he thanked Romney for treating his sexual orientation as a “non-issue.” His departure followed intense criticism from social conservatives and anti-gay groups who objected to his appointment, notably pieces in the National Review and Daily Caller and attacks from the American Family Association. Conservative commentators questioned whether Grenell’s loyalty to the GOP would hold if Democrats changed positions on same-sex marriage. The campaign largely kept Grenell out of public foreign policy roles during the controversy, did not publicly defend him to conservative critics, and sources say senior Republicans unsuccessfully urged him not to resign. Separately, scrutiny intensified over Grenell’s past Twitter activity: he deleted hundreds of tweets that mocked public figures, including Hillary Clinton, Rachel Maddow and Callista Gingrich, which drew criticism from both liberals and conservatives. Campaign manager Matt Rhoades said the campaign was disappointed but respected his decision, noting Grenell’s strong qualifications.

Less than a week before they were found dead, Honey Sherman was cheerfully planning a Florida visit with her husband, billionaire Apotex founder Barry Sherman. The couple, prominent philanthropists in Toronto’s Jewish community, were discovered Friday in their North York mansion hanging from a railing by their basement lap pool. Police later reported the cause of death for both as “ligature neck compression.” Homicide detectives have taken over the investigation, though officials initially described the deaths as “suspicious” and said they could not yet say if foul play was involved. Media reports and unnamed police sources briefly floated a murder-suicide theory; the Shermans’ grown children and many friends strongly rejected that possibility, calling such suggestions irresponsible and inconsistent with their parents’ character. There were no signs of forced entry and no note was found. A real estate agent assisting with the sale of their recently listed $6.9–7 million home reportedly discovered the bodies. The loss shocked colleagues, neighbours and public figures, including Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Toronto Mayor John Tory, who noted Barry Sherman’s business contributions and job creation. Barry, 75, built Apotex into a global generics company and was estimated to be worth about $4.77 billion; Honey, 70, was an active philanthropist and board member of several institutions. Friends described Barry as a devoted workaholic and Honey as warm, social and relentlessly charitable. The investigation continues as the community seeks answers.

On his first trip to Europe since taking office, US Vice-President Mike Pence delivered a firm message to NATO allies at the Munich Security Conference: Europe must increase defence spending. Speaking after German Chancellor Angela Merkel, Pence said several major allies “do not have a credible path” to meeting NATO’s target of 2% of GDP on defence and urged them to “do more.” He noted only five NATO members — the US, UK, Estonia, Greece and Poland — met the 2014 commitment. Pence reiterated that the US remains “unwavering” in its support for the transatlantic alliance but reminded listeners of Article 3’s burden-sharing expectation alongside Article 5’s mutual defence pledge, echoing President Trump’s prior warnings about financial contributions. He framed his remarks as carrying the president’s message while also seeking to reassure partners of continued US commitment. On Russia, Pence said the US seeks new common ground but will hold Moscow accountable and insisted Russia must honor the 2015 Minsk agreement on Ukraine. Merkel countered the pressure on defence budgets by arguing Germany will meet pledged increases over a decade but resisted faster rises, saying military capacity, not just spending, matters and highlighting development aid as a security component. She called for multilateral cooperation against a shifting world order and defended press freedom amid broader tensions with the new US administration.

The IUCN’s latest Red List update reveals a sharp, largely unnoticed decline in giraffe numbers: from roughly 151,000–163,000 in 1985 to about 97,500 in 2015, a drop of roughly 36–40% over three decades. As a result, the giraffe (Giraffa camelopardalis) has been uplisted from Least Concern to Vulnerable. The assessment treats giraffes as one species with nine subspecies; of these, five are declining, one stable and three increasing. Declines are worst in central and eastern Africa — some subspecies, like the Nubian giraffe, have fallen by as much as 95% locally — while populations in southern Africa have grown due to effective park management and translocations for tourism-driven conservation.

Primary drivers are habitat loss and fragmentation from expanding human populations, agriculture, mining and infrastructure; illegal hunting and poaching; human–wildlife conflict; and civil unrest, which makes giraffes easy targets in war-torn areas where communities may rely on bushmeat. Conservationists describe the trend as a "silent extinction" because giraffes’ iconic status masks their precarious situation. Experts stress that solutions exist: targeted management of protected areas, national conservation strategies, monitoring (e.g., SMART patrols), and greater funding and attention following the IUCN listing could reverse declines.

The Red List update also highlights broader biodiversity concerns: over 85,600 species have been assessed, with more than 24,000 threatened. New assessments include 742 newly recognized bird species (11% threatened), first evaluations of crop wild relatives critical for food security, and comprehensive freshwater species reviews. IUCN urges urgent action to safeguard species and genetic resources vital for ecosystems and human well-being.

After the FBI search of his properties, President Trump shifted from a cooperative legal posture to a far more confrontational strategy, hiring Rudy Giuliani and Emmet Flood to replace John Dowd. Giuliani immediately launched a public-relations offensive against Special Counsel Robert Mueller, promoting dubious and unfounded theories—such as claims the FBI “planted a spy” in Trump’s campaign—and accusing Mueller’s team of misconduct without evidence. The legal team has also tried to undermine key witnesses like former FBI Director James Comey, arguing Comey’s own actions and an inspector general report weaken his credibility.

Giuliani has repeatedly changed the terms and deadlines for whether Trump will submit to an interview with Mueller, now demanding that Mueller first present evidence that Trump committed a crime and show that an interview is necessary because all other avenues were exhausted. The strategy appears aimed at delaying resolution until after the midterm elections and eroding public confidence in the investigation, forcing Mueller into a subpoena-and-court battle or producing a written report to Congress. Polling suggests these efforts have had some effect: Mueller’s favorability has declined, especially among Republicans. Team Trump and congressional allies have continued to press and discredit Mueller and Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein, framing the inquiry as a “witch hunt” to influence public opinion and potential impeachment prospects.

Filmmaker Michael Bay was involved in an altercation on Oct. 17, 2013, while beginning location shooting for Transformers: Age of Extinction in Hong Kong, but his representatives stressed he was not seriously hurt. Reports said two men approached Bay on set demanding roughly $13,000 and attacked him; Reuters added one assailant allegedly injured Bay’s right cheek, though damage was reported as minor and filming resumed. BBC and local accounts suggested the men might have been seeking “disturbance fees” from businesses disrupted by the production.

Bay’s press representative, Gabriela Gutentag, offered a more detailed version saying a drug‑impaired man wielded an air‑conditioning unit and swung it at Bay, who ducked, wrestled the unit away and avoided injury. Security and police subdued and arrested multiple suspects; police scuffled with assailants and arrested three men, while later accounts mentioned four arrests tied to assaults on officers. Bay described the attacker on his website as “like a Zombie” from World War Z, recounting that the man lifted several guards and even bit a guard’s Nike shoe. Bay and the crew reported no serious injuries and resumed filming the same day. He noted that being recognizable abroad can attract attention, but emphasized the production continued without further incident.

Researchers led by Rachel Winograd at the University of Missouri studied whether alcohol truly changes personality or merely amplifies certain traits. Prior surveys found drinkers consistently report marked shifts across the Five Factor Model when intoxicated, but experimental evidence was limited. To test this in the lab, the team recruited 156 participants who first reported their typical sober and “drunk” personalities. Groups of friends returned to the lab, had baseline breath tests, and then consumed either Sprite or vodka-and-Sprite drinks calibrated to reach about .09% blood alcohol concentration. After a 15-minute absorption period, friends completed group tasks designed to elicit a range of behaviors while both participants and outside observers rated personalities from video.

Participants’ self-reports indicated changes across all five major factors: they felt more extraverted and emotionally stable (less neurotic) and less conscientious, open, and agreeable after drinking. Observers, however, saw far fewer shifts: only extraversion reliably increased in intoxicated participants, specifically in gregariousness, assertiveness, and activity level. The authors suggest this discrepancy stems from perspective differences—drinkers experience internal changes that may be genuine yet subtle or invisible to observers, while raters accurately report externally visible behavior. The team acknowledges demand characteristics or expectancies could influence self-reports and calls for replications in natural drinking settings. They emphasize exploring clinical implications, such as integrating findings into interventions to mitigate alcohol’s harms. Co-authors include Douglas Steinley, Sean P. Lane, and Kenneth J. Sher.

Chaos erupted on a JetBlue red-eye from Portland to JFK when an intoxicated 18-year-old, Robert “Sandy” Vietze of Warren, Vt., allegedly urinated on a sleeping 11-year-old girl during the flight. The girl had been briefly unattended while her father and sister used the lavatory when Vietze, seated five rows behind, stumbled up and emptied his bladder onto her, witnesses said. Vietze later told police he had consumed eight alcoholic drinks and “did not realize” he was urinating on the child. The girl’s father—reported to be a Stage 4 cancer patient—confronted Vietze midstream, creating a loud scene; flight attendants intervened, separated the men, and attempted to clean and comfort the traumatized girl. Roughly an hour before landing, another passenger suffered chest pains and vomited, prompting a medical call from the cockpit. On arrival at JFK, Port Authority officers met the aircraft: two escorted the ill passenger off and four took Vietze into custody. He received a federal summons for indecent exposure and was released; prosecutors later declined to pursue charges. Vietze, who had been on a U.S. Ski Team developmental roster, was reportedly removed from the team amid the fallout. JetBlue confirmed an incident aboard but declined further comment.

Ridley Scott’s Prometheus is an ambitious, visually striking sci‑fi thriller that mixes pulp horror, philosophical musing and blockbuster spectacle — and often betrays an uneasy balance among them. The film nods openly to Scott’s own Alien and Blade Runner: it shares DNA with Alien in its body‑horror beats and claustrophobic exploration, while offering the world‑building grandeur and moral questioning audiences expect from Scott. It opens with a baffling, memorable prologue suggesting life’s seeding by an alien “engineer,” then follows archaeologists Elizabeth Shaw (Noomi Rapace) and Charlie Holloway (Logan Marshall‑Green), who interpret prehistoric pictograms as pointing to extraterrestrial creators. Backed by billionaire Peter Weyland (Guy Pearce), a multinational crew aboard the starship Prometheus seeks answers about humanity’s origins.

Technically the film dazzles — Arthur Max’s Giger‑tinged production design, Dariusz Wolski’s cinematography and effective 3‑D heighten atmosphere — and Michael Fassbender’s android David is a standout, giving sly, unnervingly human performance. Charlize Theron and Idris Elba add strong support. But critics note Prometheus pushes too hard for grand answers while leaving many questions unresolved; its thematic ambition sometimes outstrips narrative clarity, and some plotting choices feel conventional or implausible. The film’s horror is more creepy than truly terrifying, and its final act turns chaotic. Still, Prometheus remains engrossing: a thought‑provoking, visually sumptuous entry that tantalizes with big ideas even as it frustrates those wanting tidy explanations or the focused suspense of Scott’s best work.

The Department of Defense’s 1033 program has funneled military surplus to campus police nationwide, with at least 117 colleges receiving items ranging from clothing to grenade launchers and MRAP armored vehicles. Universities such as the University of Central Florida and Hinds Community College obtained grenade launchers repurposed for tear gas or flares; Central Florida also received 23 M-16 rifles. Supporters say the program offers scarce-budgeted campus forces critical gear at minimal cost, enabling preparedness for rare but catastrophic scenarios like active-shooter incidents, and can include mundane supplies as well as tactical equipment. Critics counter that militarized gear is poorly matched to the common problems on campuses—alcohol incidents and sexual assault—and risks chilling free expression and reshaping police culture toward viewing communities as threats. Ferguson protests intensified scrutiny, prompting calls from lawmakers and President Obama for reviews and possible limits or training requirements. Advocates emphasize transparency, administrative oversight, and accredited training to govern use; opponents warn that even with safeguards, the presence of military-grade weaponry on campuses has potential cultural and civil-liberty consequences that merit rethinking the program’s scope.
