One year ago the entertainment world looked very different: Harvey Weinstein was an acclaimed film producer, Kevin Spacey a Broadway favorite, and figures like Morgan Freeman and Mario Testino enjoyed near-unassailable reputations. Rose McGowan was better known for her role on the TV show Charmed than as a high-profile accuser. Everything shifted when news broke that McGowan was among eight women who had been paid by Weinstein to keep quiet about alleged sexual assaults. That revelation ignited a sweeping reckoning across Hollywood and beyond: stories about powerful men’s abusive behavior proliferated, and hundreds of prominent men were accused, exposed, and in many cases fired or otherwise held to account.

The piece reflects on the upheaval of the past year, noting how quickly reputations crumbled as survivors came forward. It highlights that the movement extended past individual scandals to a broader cultural moment that empowered victims and spurred institutions to respond. The anniversary is framed as both a milestone and a reminder of the emotional toll: survivors have endured a year of triggers and difficult reckonings, even as the movement has brought progress.

Included in the text are excerpts from McGowan’s social media commentary, clarifying that she did not call the #MeToo movement a lie and emphasizing her distinction between criticizing Hollywood systems like Time’s Up and supporting survivors’ experiences. She expresses exhaustion with mischaracterizations of her statements and reaffirms solidarity with fellow survivors, calling the anniversary one of the hardest years of her life but also expressing pride and resolve—“Onwards. #RoseArmy.”

Overall, the summary underlines how the Weinstein revelations catalyzed a transformative, painful, and still-unfolding confrontation with sexual misconduct in entertainment and other arenas, centering survivors’ voices amid ongoing debates about accountability and change.

Researchers at the University of Siena report that bright light exposure may boost sexual satisfaction in men with low libido by raising testosterone. In a small trial of 38 men diagnosed with disorders causing diminished sexual interest, half received 30 minutes of morning light-box therapy each day for two weeks; the control group used an adapted box emitting much less light. After treatment the active group’s self‑reported sexual satisfaction scores rose from about 2/10 to roughly 6.3/10 — roughly a threefold increase — while the control group’s scores remained near baseline (about 2.7). Measured testosterone in the treated men increased from approximately 2.1 ng/ml to 3.6 ng/ml; levels did not change in controls. Lead researcher Prof. Andrea Fagiolini suggested the testosterone rise likely explains the improved sexual satisfaction and proposed that light therapy may act by inhibiting the pineal gland or producing other hormonal effects. The team situates the findings in a seasonal context, noting that testosterone naturally declines in northern latitudes from November to April and rises thereafter, and that light-box treatment may mimic increased natural daylight. Light boxes — bright fluorescent lamps used to simulate sunlight and commonly to treat seasonal affective disorder — send signals via the retina to brain centers regulating sleep, appetite, mood and reproductive functions. The authors caution the study is small and preliminary, so light therapy cannot yet be recommended clinically; larger trials are needed to confirm efficacy and safety and to compare light therapy with existing treatments such as testosterone replacement or medications. The work will be presented at the ECNP Congress in Vienna.

A Virgin Mary statue stolen from a Lyndonville, Vermont, nativity scene in January 2016 has been found unharmed and returned to the Lyndon Ecumenical Council. Lyndonville Police Chief Jack Harris recovered the statue from a storage area in an apartment building after receiving a tip. Municipal Administrator Justin Smith had earlier identified the missing figure in photos of the building’s interior taken by the town health officer during an inspection. Police say the building houses mostly college students, and investigators do not expect to determine how the statue ended up there. A smaller statue of the baby Jesus that was stolen at the same time remains missing. The Caledonian-Record first reported the recovery.

Lauren Bacall, who died at 89, left an estate of about $26–26.6 million and specified a $10,000 bequest to care for her papillon, Sophie. Court papers filed in Manhattan Surrogate’s Court show Bacall named her son, actor Sam Robards, to look after Sophie and provided the five-figure sum for the dog’s upkeep. The bulk of her estate—including her famed Dakota apartment, royalties, and remaining trust funds from her late husband Humphrey Bogart—was divided among her three children: Leslie Bogart, Stephen Humphrey Bogart, and Sam Robards. She also left $250,000 to each grandchild, with those funds intended for college and the remainder accessible at age 30. Two long-time employees received modest bequests ($20,000 to Maria Santos and $15,000 to Ilsa/Isla Hernandez). Bacall’s will, signed in 2013, named her children executors and asked they respect her wish to keep certain personal letters, diaries and memorabilia private. A lifelong dog lover, Bacall often appeared in public with Sophie; her decision to provide for the pet follows a broader celebrity pattern of leaving funds for animals, from modest amounts to high-profile cases like Leona Helmsley’s bequest.

A recent neighborhood clash in Washington, D.C., highlights a broader urban debate about limiting new liquor licenses. In Shaw/Dupont, local activists proposed a moratorium on new bars and restaurants along nightlife corridors like 14th and U Streets; a pro-growth countergroup, In My Backyard—D.C., mobilized and outnumbered opponents at a public session, so the ban appears unlikely to pass. The writer argues these local “NIMBY” impulses are common—from New York’s Lower East Side to parts of Chicago and many California counties—but are often given undue weight by city regulators. Such deference to immediate neighbors, the piece contends, imposes costs on cities because bars and restaurants are vital engines of small-business growth, job creation, tax revenue, and vibrant street life.

The clustering of nightlife venues mirrors other industry agglomerations—auto firms in Detroit or tech in Silicon Valley—and generates complementarities: late-night food sellers, music venues, and bars mutually boost one another’s value. Moratoria that keep clusters intact but block new entrants foster higher prices and stagnation, as underperformers can free-ride. Urban neighborhoods, with small, idiosyncratic spaces ill-suited to big-box retail, are particularly appropriate for dining and drinking establishments; e-commerce pressures on retail make restaurants an especially durable urban economic sector.

Rather than blanket license bans, the author recommends city-level decisions that weigh citywide benefits and that address nuisance concerns proactively—more policing, street cleaning, and targeted services—so nightlife can expand without imperiling quality of life. The piece notes public-health and social costs from excessive drinking—tens of thousands of deaths annually and large economic burdens—and acknowledges critiques linking more bars to violence and hospitalizations. Alternatives like cannabis substitution are discussed in other debates, but the primary policy thrust here is promoting nightlife as legitimate economic development: supporting small, locally owned food and drink businesses and treating liquor licensing as a matter of citywide planning, not purely local sentiment.

Heavy rains from the remnants of Subtropical Storm Alberto caused severe flooding, landslides and a dam scare in western North Carolina, prompting mass evacuations before officials later allowed residents to return. Overnight rainfall totals of roughly 4 to 6 inches swelled creeks and rivers across McDowell County, forcing mandatory evacuations below Lake Tahoma after a landslide near the dam raised concerns about its integrity. The National Weather Service issued urgent warnings—“ACT NOW TO PRESERVE YOUR LIFE”—and a flash flood emergency for the area; engineers later inspected the dam and deemed it safe, and evacuations were lifted by midmorning Wednesday. County officials said several thousand people had been affected, with around 2,000 evacuated from campgrounds and communities and roughly 200 in shelters. Flooding reached levels not seen since 2004, damaging roads, closing sections of I-40 after a mudslide, and producing multiple water rescues that caused five minor injuries. Gov. Roy Cooper declared a state of emergency for western North Carolina. The storm’s heavy rains also caused deadly incidents elsewhere: a television anchor and photojournalist were killed when a tree crushed their vehicle. Flash flood watches persisted across many states from Alabama to Illinois as Alberto’s remnants moved inland. No fatalities were reported from the McDowell County flooding.

House Speaker John Boehner asked President Obama to move a requested Sept. 7 joint session jobs address to Thursday, Sept. 8, citing logistical and security needs and noting the House doesn’t reconvene until 6:30 p.m. Boehner’s letter did not directly cite that Obama’s preferred Sept. 7 date conflicted with a Republican presidential debate that night, but the clash set up an early political showdown as Congress returned from recess. The White House initially said Sept. 7 and an 8 p.m. time had been cleared with House Republicans; Boehner’s office denied signoff and accused the White House of bypassing long-standing protocol. Press secretary Jay Carney called the overlap with the GOP debate a coincidence and defended Obama’s choice, saying the president wanted to speak directly to Congress about jobs after hearing voters’ concerns over the summer. Republicans, including RNC Chair Reince Priebus and conservative commentators like Rush Limbaugh, called the timing political and accused Obama of trying to undercut GOP events. The revised Thursday date also promises competition with the NFL season opener, a major television draw. The White House confirmed Obama agreed to move the speech to Sept. 8.

Staten Island police have detained a 54-year-old man as a person of interest in a series of three fake bomb incidents this month believed to be motivated by jealousy, sources said. Investigators say the inert devices—found Sept. 2, Sept. 12 and most recently Saturday—were left in residential areas (Port Richmond, Randall Manor and Grymes Hill) inside laptop bags, a backpack and a suitcase. They included propane containers, liquids, wires, nails and screws; one had a nine-volt battery and another a clock not wired to the device. Each carried a threatening note in Spanish naming a 35-year-old target who lives on the same block and recently married a 32-year-old woman the suspect liked. No explosives were present, but the NYPD formed a task force and evacuated homes while the bomb squad examined the items. The suspect was taken for questioning at the 121st Precinct; charges are pending. Police say terrorism is not suspected and ask anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers.

Nearly two years after 15-year-old Bartlomeij “Bart” Palosz died by suicide on the first day of his sophomore year at Greenwich High School, his parents have sued the town and school district, alleging longstanding, unaddressed bullying contributed to his death. Court filings portray years of name-calling, teasing, theft, physical assaults—including being hit with a locker requiring stitches, kicked, and having his shoelaces tied together—and property damage like a smashed smartphone. School records disclosed in the suit include a middle-school “sharings” form describing Bart as “very socially awkward,” regularly bullied, needing social work, and unlikely to report incidents. Teachers and administrators documented concerns but, the suit contends, failed to follow the district’s anti-bullying policies: they did not properly investigate, report, notify parents, discipline perpetrators, or create safety and support plans. Bart’s grades and behavior deteriorated; he posted suicidal messages online in June 2013 and survived an earlier attempt. On Aug. 27, 2013, after his sister—his protector—had graduated, he returned home and used a family firearm to end his life. The family seeks damages and hopes the lawsuit will spur policy and response changes to prevent future tragedies. The town must respond by Sept. 8.

Thomas Piketty, the influential French economist and author of the best‑selling Capital in the Twenty‑First Century, has publicly declined nomination to France’s highest decoration, the Legion d’honneur. Piketty told AFP he refused because “I do not think it is the government’s role to decide who is honourable,” adding that the government would be better occupied with reviving economic growth in France and Europe. Once close to the Socialist Party, Piketty has grown critical of President François Hollande’s policies, making the refusal a pointed rebuke of the administration. Capital, a nearly 600‑page study of income inequality that became an international sensation and sold hundreds of thousands of English‑language copies, drew high praise—including from Nobel laureate Paul Krugman—and vigorous debate, particularly in the United States. Refusals of the Legion are rare but not unprecedented: past decliners include Jean‑Paul Sartre, cartoonist Jacques Tardi and the Curies. Piketty’s decision underscores his insistence that honors should not be bestowed by political authorities and highlights ongoing tensions between public intellectuals and the government over economic priorities.

Glen James, a homeless man in Boston, found a backpack at South Bay Mall containing a passport, $2,400 in cash and nearly $40,000 in traveler's checks. He flagged down police and turned the bag in; officers and store staff helped locate the owner and return the property. City police honored James with a special citation for his honesty. News of his action prompted Ethan Whittington, a 27-year-old accounts manager from Midlothian, Virginia, to create a GoFundMe campaign to reward and help James. The fundraiser quickly went viral, surpassing initial goals and drawing donations from across the US. Reports of the drive show contributions growing well past $88,000 and approaching or exceeding $110,000 in some accounts; Whittington later raised the target to $250,000 so James might afford a home. Whittington said the outpouring restored his faith in people and was “a statement to everyone in America.” He has spoken with James by phone and plans to meet him in Boston to arrange how the money will be used. James said he would not have kept any of the found money.

Google revealed new details and visuals for Project Glass, showing how the wearable will function and inviting broader public testing. The glasses use a small display above and to the right of the right eye (viewed via a mirrored block), so on-screen elements won’t dominate the wearer’s field of view as some point-of-view images suggest. Voice activates the device with the wake phrase “OK, Glass,” enabling hands-free photo and video capture, web search, directions, translations, reminders (like flight alerts), messaging, and sharing via messaging or Google+ Hangouts. An automatic photo mode can snap images at preset intervals. To expand testing beyond developers, Google launched a contest (#ifihadglass) asking people to submit 50-word pitches on Google+ or Twitter by Feb. 27; winners can purchase Glass for $1,500 and must attend a pick-up event in New York, San Francisco, or Los Angeles. Google showcased use cases—performers streaming backstage, tourists translating on the spot, and families video-chatting—to illustrate real-world applications.

Ross Cassidy, who became close friends with former Russian spy Sergei Skripal after he moved to Salisbury in 2010, says he believes Sergei and daughter Yulia—both critically ill after the novichok nerve-agent attack—are so severely damaged they should be allowed to die. Cassidy described warm neighborly ties, driving Sergei to Heathrow to collect Yulia days before they were found collapsed. He has assisted police but was barred from visiting them in hospital and is haunted by guilt for not considering their fate sooner. Viktoria Skripal, Sergei’s niece, says their chances of recovery are slim and, if they survive, will likely be lifelong invalids. The attack has provoked broad international backlash: more than 23 countries expelled over 115 Russian diplomats, NATO reduced Russia’s mission, and global pressure on Moscow continues amid denied responsibility.

Community members in Richmond, Indiana, gathered for a candlelight vigil to support the family of a 14-year-old, identified as Brandon Clegg, who died by a self-inflicted gunshot after exchanging fire with police at Dennis Intermediate School. The teen was not a student at the school but lived nearby. Authorities say Clegg had taken another family member hostage and was driven to the school; his mother, Mary York, called 911 around 8:11 a.m. to warn that he was headed there armed. That tip prompted a rapid police response and allowed the school to go into lockdown, a step officials say likely prevented further casualties. Officers confronted the teen outside; he shot out glass in a locked entry door and ran into the building, where he was contained on a second-floor stairwell and then killed himself. No students or staff were hurt. Dozens attended the vigil to pray with and support Clegg’s mother; organizer Shawn Wright emphasized she “saved a lot of lives.” Family members described Clegg as having been bullied, expressing shock and sorrow. The Indiana State Police said the investigation remains ongoing and the middle school stayed closed following the incident.

At the 2011 Values Voter Summit straw poll, Ron Paul won decisively with 36.9% (732) of 1,983 ballots, a return to his organized convention-strength showing, aided by Campaign for Liberty supporters who bought many passes. Herman Cain placed second with 22.5% (447), followed by Rick Santorum at 16.3% (323). Rick Perry, despite heavy campaign effort, finished fourth with 8.4% (167), hindered by perceptions of being "heartless" and Cain’s likability. Michele Bachmann drew 7.9% (157), Mitt Romney just 4.4% (88), Newt Gingrich 2.7% (54), and Jon Huntsman 0.1% (2). Organizers noted Paul’s supporters were highly mobilized. The results underscored this audience’s skepticism of Romney and highlighted Santorum’s modest rise, while Perry and Bachmann struggled to energize the crowd.

Oliver Stone will write and direct a feature film adaptation of Luke Harding’s The Snowden Files, dramatizing the disclosures by former NSA contractor Edward Snowden and the Guardian’s reporting. Stone, who has publicly defended Snowden as a hero for revealing alleged Fourth Amendment violations, announced he’s begun scripting and will produce the movie with longtime partner Moritz Borman as a European co-production, aiming to start filming before year’s end. The Guardian is collaborating on the project; editor-in-chief Alan Rusbridger praised the story’s impact on public understanding of government surveillance. Stone called the subject “one of the greatest stories of our time” and acknowledged the cinematic challenge it presents. His film joins another high-profile adaptation: Sony Pictures acquired rights to Glenn Greenwald’s No Place to Hide, to be produced by James Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. The competing projects reflect continuing global interest in Snowden’s revelations and their implications for privacy, government power and journalism.

A faction of 9/11 conspiracy theorists is threatening to protest Charlie Sheen’s live appearances, claiming the actor has betrayed their movement. Sheen previously voiced belief that the World Trade Center collapses resembled a “controlled demolition,” aligning him publicly with 9/11 skepticism. Mark Dice, a visible member of the 9/11 Truth Movement, says fellow theorists are upset that Sheen has shifted focus to sensational personal behavior—“bragging about smoking crack and sleeping with hookers”—rather than continuing to “ask hard questions” about 9/11 and the wars that followed. Dice says he has tried to contact Sheen without success and warns that if Sheen does not address the issue, he and several others will stage protests outside Sheen’s upcoming shows. The report also notes a broken link to the original Yahoo! page.

Researchers and health officials report compelling evidence linking Zika virus outbreaks to sharp increases in cases of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), a rare neurological disorder in which the immune system attacks peripheral nerves, causing muscle weakness and sometimes life-threatening paralysis. A multi-country analysis led by Dr. Marcos A. Espinal at the Pan American Health Organization examined confirmed and suspected Zika infections and GBS incidence across Bahia (Brazil), Colombia, the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Honduras, Suriname, and Venezuela. During Zika transmission periods, GBS rose two- to nearly ten-fold above baseline in these sites—for example, Venezuela saw an 877 percent increase (expected ~70 cases but 684 recorded), Colombia reported 320 cases versus an expected ~100, and El Salvador’s cases doubled from 92 to 184. Altogether roughly 1,474 GBS cases accompanied some 164,237 Zika reports in the studied period. Men had a 28 percent higher reported incidence than women, and incidence rose with age. Clinicians warn this spike places substantial strain on health systems because about one-third of GBS patients require ventilatory support and intensive care. Puerto Rico documented its first Zika-linked death from GBS and reported thousands of Zika infections—including many in pregnant women—raising concerns about both GBS and Zika-related congenital defects such as microcephaly. While other infections can trigger GBS, investigators found no similar association with dengue in their analysis. Public health authorities recommend enhanced surveillance for GBS as a potential indicator of Zika activity and emphasize prevention of mosquito exposure, especially for pregnant women.

On New Year’s Day, 10 states raised their minimum wages—mostly via automatic cost-of-living adjustments—by amounts from a dime to 35 cents. Rhode Island enacted its first raise in five years through legislation. Nearly a million workers benefit, with Washington reaching $9.19 while nearby Idaho remains about $2 lower. Supporters say steady, small annual increases reduce turnover and provide predictability; opponents warn higher wages may cost jobs or deter hiring for entry-level positions. Businesses report tighter margins and modest price or staffing adjustments to cope.

In 1996 Alexa Internet began donating crawl data to the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine—background to the following piece by J.K. Rowling about founding Lumos after seeing a distressing newspaper photo of a caged child in an institution. Shocked into action while pregnant, she campaigned and helped establish Lumos to expose and end the institutionalisation of children. Rowling emphasizes that most of the roughly eight million institutionalised children worldwide are not orphans but separated from families due to poverty, disability, lack of services, or discrimination. Institutions inflict measurable, often irreversible harm: malnutrition, developmental delays, psychological trauma, higher risk of abuse and trafficking, and lifelong exclusion and poverty. Harm occurs even in well-resourced institutions; cosmetic improvements don’t solve the problem. Lumos argues the solution is family- and community-based care—investing in inclusive education, health services, poverty support, foster care and adoption alternatives. Donor priorities shape outcomes. Lumos cites successes: Moldova saw a 70% reduction in institutionalised children since 2007; Bulgaria cut numbers by 54% and increased foster carers by 440%; demonstration projects in the Czech Republic sharply reduced admissions. Rowling calls elimination of institutionalisation by 2050 achievable, a moral and economic imperative, and urges public engagement via #Letstalklumos.

Online dating’s rapid growth has spawned a market for quick background checks and prompted state regulation as users worry about scammers, married people posing as singles, sexual predators, and felons. Companies founded by former law-enforcement officers and mobile apps now offer inexpensive criminal searches—often requiring only a name and birthdate—to help daters vet matches. New York and New Jersey have enacted laws requiring dating sites to post safety tips and disclose whether they perform criminal checks; some firms like True.com screen applicants and reject a small percentage. But dating sites and experts warn checks are imperfect: public databases are incomplete, county records vary, and screenings can create a false sense of security. Privacy and misuse risks also exist, especially with mobile apps sharing personal information. Legal protections under the Communications Decency Act limit sites’ liability, though critics expect challenges when sites accept fees or know of criminal behavior. Safety advocates urge caution: meet in public, verify identities, and don’t rush trust despite available screening tools.

Nancy Reed, 77, of Kingwood, died Sept. 15 from flood-related necrotizing fasciitis after falling in her flooded home and sustaining blunt trauma to her arm, the Harris County Institute of Forensic Sciences reported. Her death, linked to complications from a wound that became infected, is the county’s 36th officially tied to Hurricane Harvey. Reed, a former teacher, community volunteer, and operator of LivingTributes.com, was treated at Memorial Hermann hospitals before she died; a memorial service was held at First Presbyterian Church of Kingwood. Reed was the second known Harvey-related case of flesh-eating bacteria in the area; rescuer J.R. Atkins contracted a severe infection from an insect bite while aiding neighbors in Missouri City but survived after intensive treatment and multiple surgeries. Health officials warned that necrotizing fasciitis—a rapid, potentially fatal soft-tissue infection often caused by group A strep or other organisms—can arise after flood exposure and stressed prompt medical care, proper disposal or disinfection of items touched by floodwater, and ongoing research into treatments and vaccines.

Russian forces moved into Ukraine's Crimean peninsula in early March 2014, prompting a sharp international crisis. Unidentified, Russian-speaking armed men in military-style uniforms—often without insignia—seized airports, government buildings and key infrastructure in Crimea, while its newly installed pro‑Russian leader, Sergey Aksyonov, asked Moscow for help and moved a referendum forward. Russian President Vladimir Putin secured parliamentary authorization to deploy troops “to protect Russian citizens and the Black Sea Fleet,” framing the action as a response to threats to compatriots; Ukraine denied those claims.

Ukraine’s interim government declared mobilization, put forces on high alert, and warned that military intervention would mean war. The situation triggered urgent diplomacy: President Obama warned of consequences for violating Ukrainian sovereignty, Secretary of State John Kerry condemned what he called Russian “invasion and occupation,” and other Western leaders urged de‑escalation. The UN and NATO called for calm. Russia defended its actions as protecting interests and blamed the EU for unrest. Tension spread to eastern Ukrainian cities, where pro‑Russian demonstrations and clashes heightened fears the crisis could widen beyond Crimea and further damage Russia‑West relations.

A middle school student in Menifee, California, who dressed as Elsa from Disney’s Frozen for a school “Disney” spirit day was ordered by school officials to remove his gown and wig because administrators judged it was creating a disruption. The incident happened before classes on a Thursday in a quad area at Ethan A. Chase Middle School, where many students were gathered and taking photos. The student, identified in local reports as 13-year-old Austin Lacey, told KTLA he wore the costume “for fun” and that he likes to “go all out.” He said classmates asked to take selfies with him and reacted positively.

Romoland School District Superintendent Dr. Julie Vitale issued a statement explaining the principal’s action: there was no indication the student was conveying any particular message, and the removal was done to stop a general disruption to the school environment, in accordance with district policies. Vitale also confirmed the student faced no discipline and completed the school day.

Several students interviewed after school described the episode as not problematic. Eighth-grader Kassandra Melara said it “wasn’t a disruption” and noted that many students were taking pictures with Austin. Another peer, Natalia Alvarez, who said she knew Austin and supported his ASB president campaign, described him as a helpful, high-achieving student who gets along well with others.

The account highlights tensions schools can face balancing student expression and maintaining orderly environments during spirited events. Officials framed the intervention as a policy-based response to crowds and potential disorder; some students and the student’s family viewed the moment as lighthearted and well-received by peers.

Security footage captured a dramatic sinkhole that opened beneath the National Corvette Museum in Bowling Green, Ky., swallowing eight iconic Corvettes into a roughly 40-foot-deep cavity. The museum posted multiple videos showing the collapse, the cars disappearing and interior views of the pit. Engineers must inspect the site before any recovery or repairs can begin, and no timetable has been set for removing the vehicles or restoring the affected wing.

When Paris began removing and selling thousands of tons of its historic cobblestones as part of a circular-economy effort, entrepreneur Margaux Sainte-Lagüe saw an unusual souvenir business opportunity. Riding her Vespa past jackhammers on the Champs-Élysées, she bought five tons of chiseled granite that had been unearthed during public works, cleaned them in a central workshop, and launched Mon Pavé Parisien. Each roughly five-pound stone is real Paris street material sourced from city stockpiles and is hand-painted or customized — offerings include a tricolor French-flag design, a gilded version with 22.5-carat gold leaf, and a May 1968–inspired piece inscribed “sous les pavés.” Sainte-Lagüe has personalized stones for clients ranging from Paris’s mayor to foreign newlyweds and sells them online for roughly $63–$157, with plans to place pieces in concept and souvenir shops.

The municipal program, started in 2016 and expanded in 2018–19, salvages granite blocks first laid centuries ago and resells them to reduce waste and recoup funds; the city may extract millions of tons over time. Most reclaimed stones go to builders and landscapers, but demand from tourists, collectors and designers has grown. Though key sites like the Arc de Triomphe remain intact, many other streets are being resurfaced, creating a steady supply. For buyers, Sainte-Lagüe pitches a tactile fragment of Parisian history — a literal piece of the city once walked by generations of Parisians and famous artists.

Adacia Chambers, 25, is jailed without bail on four counts of second-degree murder after allegedly driving her 2014 Hyundai Elantra into a crowd at the Oklahoma State University homecoming parade, killing four people and injuring dozens. The crash occurred at 10:31 a.m. near the parade’s end, after the car reportedly struck an unmanned police motorcycle and then plowed into spectators just blocks from Boone Pickens Stadium. Victims include retired OSU professor Marvin Lyle Stone, his wife Bonnie Lynn Stone, 23-year-old University of Central Oklahoma student Nikita Nakal (also reported as Nikita Prabhakar), and 2-year-old Nash Lucas. About 47 were treated; 17 remained hospitalized with four in critical condition, and 11 victims were under 13.

Chambers’s attorney, Tony Coleman, says she was arrested on suspicion of DUI but displayed none of the typical signs of intoxication; toxicology results are pending. Coleman expressed concern about Chambers’s competency, citing mental illness, possible untreated diabetes, insomnia, and a blackout period she cannot recall. He plans to request a psychiatric evaluation and competency hearing. Friends and family said she had not been drinking; she had been participating in the prior night’s homecoming “Walk Around” and left for a 9 a.m. shift at a nearby restaurant but left soon after arriving.

Witnesses described chaotic scenes of people thrown into the air, smoke, and widespread panic. Families of the injured kept vigil as surgeries and treatments continued. OSU held a somber remembrance before its game, even as the university and local community began coping with the tragedy. Investigations continue.

This piece debates the culture of instant outrage and forced apologies after offensive remarks, sparked by Robert De Niro’s joke at a Michelle Obama fundraiser about “a white first lady” and Newt Gingrich’s demand for an apology. The author criticizes performative indignation — from reactions to De Niro to outrage over David Axelrod’s “Mittzkrieg” pun — arguing apologies often become meaningless theater. Bill Maher’s New York Times plea, “Please Stop Apologizing,” is highlighted for calling for amnesty on insincere public apologies and urging people to simply tune out offensive speech. Yet the column notes Maher’s own abusive commentary on Sarah Palin undermines his stance and points out a distinction between edgy satire and dehumanizing rhetoric that corrodes civil discourse. While recognizing free speech protections, the article endorses a higher standard of civility and unity, invoking Barack Obama’s 2004 appeal that Americans resist division and treat one another as fellow citizens rather than enemies.

A federal appeals court has affirmed a $25 million settlement with students who sued over Trump University, ending a challenge that sought a public trial. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco finalized the settlement after it had been approved by a lower court last March. The challenge was brought by Florida bankruptcy lawyer Sherri Simpson, who paid roughly $19,000 for Trump University workshops and mentorships and wanted to opt out of the class action to pursue her own trial. The three-judge panel rejected her interpretation of earlier notice language that she said guaranteed an additional opportunity to opt out, concluding that a reasonable class member would not have read the notice that way. Judges Jacqueline Nguyen, Andrew Hurwitz and Steven Logan also found the settlement fair and reasonable given the legal and practical complexities of trying fraud claims against a president-elect or sitting president on the eve of an inauguration.

Trump University operated from 2005 to 2010 and was accused of using deceptive marketing and high-pressure sales tactics at free workshops to sell costly programs and mentorships, with prices ranging from about $1,495 for a one-year apprenticeship to $35,000 for “Gold Elite” classes. The consolidated cases included lawsuits from California and a New York suit led by Attorney General Eric Schneiderman. Trump paid the settlement in January 2017; funds were held in escrow pending appellate approval. The court said plaintiffs are expected to recover about 80–90 percent of amounts paid. Simpson declined to pursue further appeals so payments to roughly 4,000 class members could proceed. Schneiderman and plaintiffs’ attorneys welcomed the ruling as delivering restitution to victims of what they called a “sham university.”

U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and many others demanded accountability as Flint, Michigan’s long-developing water crisis erupted into a national scandal. Flint switched in April 2014 from Detroit’s Lake Huron-supplied system to the Flint River to save money while awaiting a new pipeline. That river water proved highly corrosive; state officials failed to require corrosion-control treatment, allowing lead to leach from aging pipes into the drinking supply. Residents complained immediately about taste, smell and appearance and reported health problems, but state regulators repeatedly reassured the public the water was safe. It took until fall 2015 for state leaders, including Gov. Rick Snyder, to publicly acknowledge elevated lead levels after Dr. Mona Hanna-Attisha and others publicized findings that children’s blood-lead levels had risen. Sanders said Snyder “knew long ago” and should resign for the administration’s inaction that poisoned hundreds of children and exposed thousands more.

Independent researchers, notably from Virginia Tech, found dangerously high lead in many homes—median 90th-percentile readings far above EPA action levels, with some samples reaching thousands of parts per billion. City tests sometimes undercounted lead by sampling after flushing. The crisis has prompted widespread testing, distribution of bottled water and filters, nutritional interventions to mitigate lead uptake, and mobilization of resources—Snyder declared a state of emergency, activated the National Guard, and requested federal aid. President Obama issued a federal emergency declaration, enabling FEMA support and initial funding for water, filters and other supplies; larger disaster aid was denied because statutes typically cover natural disasters.

Public-health experts now advise treating all Flint children under six as exposed; testing can miss past exposure because blood-lead declines over weeks while lead accumulates in bone and tissue. Concerns remain about long-term effects, the need to replace service lines (potentially costing up to $1.5 billion), and whether Legionnaires’ disease spikes are linked to the water. Critics argue state response was slow and insufficient, and calls for accountability and sustained federal and state resources continue.

This project harvested Wikidata and DBpedia records for military conflicts and imported cleaned sets into nodegoat to create interactive geotemporal visualizations. From Wikidata, optional SPARQL queries yielded 2,657 battles with dates and locations; DBpedia provided 4,022 (or 10,116 with deeper queries). The combined dataset reached 12,703 records. The visualization supports timelines, color-coded periods, provenance highlighting, links to source items, and person-event connections (e.g., movements between battles and birth/death data). Data cleaning was required, especially for DBpedia dates and sparse Wikidata references; CSVs were produced for use.

On the night of May 8–9, 2018, Earth passes between the sun and Jupiter, placing Jupiter at opposition — rising at sunset, highest at midnight, and setting at sunrise — and marking the best time all year to observe the planet. Jupiter is near its closest approach (May 10) and shines brighter than any star in the night sky, second only to Venus among planets and surpassed only by the sun and moon in overall brightness. In 2018 it appears in front of the constellation Libra, outshining nearby 2nd-magnitude Zubenelgenubi by over a hundredfold. Oppositions occur roughly every 13 months, shifting by about a month each year (2017’s was April 7; 2019’s will be June 10). The Juno spacecraft is orbiting Jupiter, sending back unique polar views and infrared videos of massive cyclones. Jupiter is a gas giant — more than 11 times Earth’s diameter and about 2.5 times the combined mass of all other planets — with a mostly hydrogen-helium composition, a likely solid core, metallic hydrogen deep inside, rapid rotation, banded cloud structure and long-lived storms like the Great Red Spot. Binoculars or small telescopes reveal the four Galilean moons and cloud-top detail, making opposition an excellent opportunity for stargazers.

An online campaign led by Aberdeen activist Suzanne Kelly has successfully pressured Robert Gordon University to revoke the honorary doctorate it awarded Donald Trump in 2010 and has also generated a high-profile petition calling for the US presidential candidate to be banned from entering the United Kingdom. The university announced it was rescinding the honorary DBA after concluding that “statements” Trump made during his campaign were “wholly incompatible with the ethos and values of the university.” Supporters of the campaign were urged to thank the university and to back further actions via online petitions.

Separately, Kelly launched a petition on the UK government petitions site arguing that Trump’s remarks about Muslims and other groups constitute hate speech and therefore make him unfit to be allowed entry under existing “unacceptable behaviour” exclusion criteria. The petition rapidly accumulated signatures—initial reports cited tens of thousands, later accounts recorded more than 300,000—surpassing the 100,000 threshold that triggers consideration by Parliament’s Petitions Committee and opens the possibility of a Commons debate. The committee planned to review the petition in early January. The Home Office noted the home secretary has powers to exclude individuals but had not indicated action against Trump.

The push to ban Trump followed widely reported comments in which he proposed barring Muslims from entering the United States and made disparaging remarks about parts of London, prompting criticism from UK political figures including David Cameron, Jeremy Corbyn, Nicola Sturgeon and Boris Johnson. Kelly, who has campaigned against Trump’s local projects in Aberdeen and previously sought the university revocation via a separate petition and 38 Degrees campaign, framed the ban petition as a stand against hate speech and a call for consistent application of exclusion rules regardless of wealth or influence.

Texas will end the practice of allowing condemned inmates to choose last meals after Lawrence Russell Brewer’s execution Wednesday. Brewer, put to death for the 1998 hate-crime killing of James Byrd Jr., requested an extravagant final meal — two chicken-fried steaks, a triple-meat bacon cheeseburger, fried okra, a pound of barbecue, three fajitas, a meat-lover’s pizza, a pint of ice cream and a slab of peanut-butter fudge with crushed peanuts — though officials said he did not eat it. The large, costly request prompted criticism that granting such choices is inappropriate for someone sentenced to death. Sen. John Whitmire, chair of the Senate Criminal Justice Committee, formally urged Brad Livingston, executive director of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, to stop the practice. The decision marks an immediate policy change affecting the handling of final requests for inmates scheduled for execution in Texas.

The Missionary Church of Kopimism, founded in 2010 to treat copying and sharing information as sacred, has been officially recognized as a religion in Sweden. The movement, whose symbol is “Kopimi” (pronounced “copy me”) and whose rituals include acts of copying and connecting, grew from about 1,000 to 3,000 members before recognition. After earlier rejections, authorities required the group to formalize a prayer or meditation practice; once that was done the National Judicial Board granted religious status. Founder and philosophy student Isak Gerson says state recognition will strengthen members’ identity and may encourage more people to admit their beliefs privately. While the status does not legalize file sharing or copyright infringement, Kopimists hope their beliefs might be considered in future legislation. The church remains open to new members and urges continued sharing online.

Eric Swenson, 64, co‑founder of Thrasher magazine and key figure behind Independent Trucks, died by suicide June 20, 2011, outside the Mission Police Station in San Francisco. A private man and longtime Potrero Hill resident, Swenson reportedly walked to the station’s front doors and shot himself; friends believe chronic pain from a severe motorcycle leg injury decades earlier contributed. He co‑founded High Speed Productions (Thrasher, Juxtapoz, Slap), Ermico Enterprises, Independent Trucks and Deluxe Distributions, helping transform skateboarding from a passing fad into a distinct subculture with new equipment that enabled vertical skating and aerial tricks. Colleagues remember him as a humble, hardworking “doer” who preferred building and fixing over the spotlight. He is survived by his wife Linda McKay and sisters Rebekah Engle and Sonja Taylor; services were private.

China and the United States entered talks after Chinese naval forces seized a U.S. Navy unmanned underwater glider in the South China Sea, an episode Washington called one of the most serious military incidents between the two countries in years. Beijing said military channels were working to “appropriately handle” the matter but gave few details. The Pentagon described the glider as a roughly 3-meter, $150,000 commercial off-the-shelf vehicle operated by civilian contractors from the USNS Bowditch while collecting unclassified scientific data about 57 miles northwest of Subic Bay in international waters; the U.S. lodged a diplomatic protest and demanded its return. The Bowditch and a Chinese ship were within about 450 meters during the encounter; no shots were fired. Chinese state media quoted officials suggesting the device was initially found as an “unidentified” object and that a smooth resolution was expected, while some retired Chinese navy figures defended the seizure. The incident exacerbated already strained ties after President-elect Donald Trump’s call with Taiwan’s president and his rhetoric on trade and Taiwan; Trump tweeted condemnation and then suggested the U.S. might tell China to keep the drone. Analysts say the seizure risks further inflaming tensions amid China’s South China Sea militarization and questions about future U.S.-China relations under Trump.

Global reactions poured in after Donald Trump’s surprise victory in the 2016 U.S. presidential election, sparking a mix of congratulations, concern and anxiety across regions, markets and political leaders. Many governments and leaders signaled readiness to work with the incoming administration while expressing varied expectations about future policies. China’s Xi Jinping congratulated Trump and emphasized constructive management of differences; Beijing’s state media, however, depicted the vote as evidence of American political crisis. Russia’s Vladimir Putin and Russia’s parliament welcomed the result and expressed willingness to restore better ties. European leaders, including Germany’s Angela Merkel and EU officials, underlined shared values and urged continued trans-Atlantic cooperation despite differences. NATO’s Jens Stoltenberg affirmed the importance of U.S. leadership for the alliance even as Trump’s criticisms of allies’ defense spending raised concerns.

In Latin America, reactions were sharply focused on Mexico, where Trump’s campaign rhetoric—threats to renegotiate or rip up trade deals, large-scale deportations, and a U.S.-Mexico border wall—generated alarm. The peso plunged sharply, hitting record lows as investors feared economic fallout. Mexicans following results expressed shock and dread about personal and economic consequences. Cuba feared a reversal of the recent U.S. opening, worrying that a Trump administration might undo tourism and business gains. Across the region, leaders were cautious but many offered congratulations.

In Asia and the Middle East, leaders and officials sent congratulatory messages while signaling priorities. Japan’s Shinzo Abe and Australia’s Julie Bishop stressed the importance of the U.S. alliance in the Asia-Pacific. India’s Narendra Modi, the Philippines’ Rodrigo Duterte and Turkey’s leadership congratulated Trump and sought continuity or cooperation on respective concerns. Iran’s foreign minister stressed the importance of U.S. adherence to the nuclear deal, while the Taliban called for U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan.

Markets reacted turbulently. Initial panic gave way to a rebound in U.S. equities as investors anticipated pro-business policies—lower taxes and deregulation—especially given Republican control of government. Bond yields rose on inflation expectations, the dollar strengthened, and commodities and emerging markets experienced volatility. The Mexican peso and some global markets bore the brunt of uncertainty, reflecting widespread apprehension about how Trump’s policies might reshape trade, security and international relations. Overall, the world’s response combined pragmatic outreach with apprehension about the implications of a Trump presidency.

Chicago Officer Jason Van Dyke, charged with first-degree murder in the October 2014 killing of 17-year-old Laquan McDonald, had bond set at $1.5 million after a Cook County judge viewed dashcam footage showing Van Dyke firing 16 shots, many after McDonald fell. Van Dyke, who turned himself in Nov. 24, posted the required $150,000 and was released. The grainy, silent dashcam video—made public when charges were filed—sparked citywide demonstrations and calls for Police Supt. Garry McCarthy’s resignation. The mayor announced a Task Force on Police Accountability to review oversight and training, with recommendations due by March 31, 2016. Van Dyke’s attorney disputes that the full incident is captured on video; the next court date is Dec. 18.

An off-duty California Highway Patrol sergeant is being lauded for honesty after finding more than $120,000 in cash in two bank deposit bags on a Concord roadway in September. While driving in a personal car, she swerved to avoid the bags, made a U-turn, inspected them and discovered stacks of $100 bills. Despite friends urging otherwise, she immediately alerted authorities and turned the money over to Concord police. Officers tracked down the rightful owner and returned the life savings. The 20-year CHP veteran, who asked to remain anonymous, said she acted to set an example for her children and because integrity matters when no one is watching. CHP Golden Gate Division Chief Avery Browne praised her conduct.

Hurricane Harvey struck the Texas Gulf Coast late Friday as a powerful Category 4 storm with 130 mph winds, then slowed and weakened as it moved inland, becoming a Category 1 hurricane and later a tropical storm. The slow-moving system dumped torrential rain—some locations reported more than 16–20 inches already, with forecasts of up to 40 inches in places—and threatened “catastrophic” inland flooding across a wide area from Corpus Christi to Houston. Harvey caused extensive wind and structural damage in coastal communities such as Rockport and Corpus Christi, where roofs, schools and businesses were damaged, senior housing roofs collapsed and communications and emergency response were hampered. Nearly 300,000 customers lost power, cell service outages were reported, and authorities issued boil-water advisories. Search-and-rescue operations mobilized hundreds of personnel, Coast Guard crews rescued dozens, and the governor activated service members and shelters; evacuees were transported and hotel taxes waived. Federal disaster aid was authorized, and President Trump and FEMA officials coordinated response efforts. The storm also disrupted oil and gas production and halted many flights and port operations, leaving recovery and flooding threats to dominate the days ahead.

Archaeologists and a geophysics team will this week scan the grounds of Waltham Abbey Church in Essex to test a long-debated alternative to the traditional account of King Harold II’s death at the Battle of Hastings in 1066. The Stratascan team that helped locate Richard III will use ground-penetrating radar on October 14—the battle’s anniversary—at a site near the east wall about 15 yards from Harold’s reputed tomb. The work, commissioned and funded (£2,000) by amateur historian and stonemason Peter Burke, may be filmed for a documentary exploring whether Harold survived the battle and died decades later as a hermit. 

Conventional histories—reinforced by the Bayeux Tapestry and contemporary Norman accounts—hold that Harold was struck in the eye by an arrow and hacked to death by Norman knights; some medieval sources report his body was dismembered. Burke has spent five years investigating an alternative narrative found in a 12th-century manuscript, Vita Haroldi, housed in the British Library, and argues the English tradition suggests Harold may have been gravely wounded, treated (possibly in Winchester), escaped to Germany, and lived until about 1090. He posits scenarios including a concealed burial, a headless knight placed to hide Harold’s fate, or the remains of an elderly, scarred man consistent with his theory.

English Heritage granted non-invasive scanning permission, noting the survey will not disturb important remains; any excavation would require further consent because the site is consecrated and archaeologically sensitive. Local historians caution the site has been heavily disturbed by later building works, making a find unlikely. Burke remains hopeful that if the scan uncovers human remains fitting his description, DNA tests and further study could prompt major revisions to the accepted history of England’s last Saxon king.

Reality star Kim Kardashian West was robbed at gunpoint in a private Paris residence early Monday, held briefly by five armed men disguised as police who escaped with millions in jewellery. Masked and wearing fake police armbands, the assailants arrived around 3 a.m., threatened and handcuffed the building concierge on rue Tronchet in the chic 8th arrondissement, forced him to show them Kardashian West’s apartment, then tied her up and locked her in a bathroom before fleeing on bicycles. Police say a jewellery box worth about €6m and a ring worth €4m were taken, along with phones; investigators believe only two of the five entered the flat. Kardashian West, attending Paris Fashion Week, was “badly shaken but physically unharmed” and flew back to New York after giving a statement. Her husband Kanye West abruptly ended a U.S. festival performance citing a “family emergency.” The incident revived debate over Paris security: opposition politicians criticized the city administration, while the mayor called the attack rare and urged political restraint ahead of national elections. The robbers remain at large as the investigation continues.

Extremist and fringe publications found in Tamerlan Tsarnaev’s apartment and connections the Tsarnaev brothers had with a conspiracy-minded neighbor suggest their influences extended beyond Islamist radicalism to a wider exposure to anti-government and conspiratorial beliefs. Tamerlan, who died after a confrontation with police following the April 15 Boston Marathon bombing, encountered many of these materials through Donald Larking, a West Newton man whose family had a long relationship with the Tsarnaevs after their mother worked as a personal care aide. Attorney Jason Rosenberg says Larking, who sustained brain damage from a 1974 shooting, shared fringe literature and espoused views that included 9/11 and the Newtown shootings as government plots; he also kept publications that question the Holocaust. Neighbors and a former landlady confirmed salvage of extremist print items from Tamerlan’s Cambridge apartment, including publications tied to Confederate imagery and groups labeled anti-Semitic by watchdogs. Larking befriended the brothers while they assisted with his quadriplegic wife; he later converted to Islam at the mosque they attended and remained close to Tamerlan. Prosecutors additionally allege Dzhokhar downloaded jihadist writings and instructions for making pressure-cooker bombs, linking the brothers’ attack to violent Islamist materials as well as broader conspiratorial influences.

Cleanup and technical teams are working inside the FAA Air Route Traffic Control Center in Aurora after a deliberate fire, smoke and water damage disrupted operations. Brian Howard, 36, a Naperville resident and eight-year contract employee who handled telecommunications at the facility, has been charged with one felony count of destruction of aircraft or aircraft facilities. Authorities allege he entered the basement early Friday with a hard-sided suitcase, cut radar feeds, damaged communications and set gas-soaked rags on fire near sensitive equipment, forcing a ground stop at Chicago O’Hare and Midway. The attack severed radar links and damaged the host computer; adjacent FAA centers are handling the affected airspace at a greatly reduced capacity, managing roughly 25 percent of normal operations and routing aircraft through only three corridors. The disruption caused massive cancellations—1,550 at O’Hare and 470 at Midway—and delays nationwide, with ripple effects at major hubs. Howard is hospitalized with self-inflicted stab wounds after paramedics found him wounded in the basement; a private Facebook message he sent beforehand reportedly declared his intent. Officials stress the act appears isolated and not terror-related. Investigations continue, with evidence collection and searches of Howard’s home underway. The FAA is bolstering staffing at nearby centers; repair timelines and center reopening remain uncertain, and airlines urge travelers to check flight status.

United Airlines has rolled out a redesigned boarding process intended to reduce gate congestion and speed boarding. After months of testing in Chicago and Houston and earlier trials at LAX, the carrier moved from five boarding lanes to a simpler two-lane system while retaining five numbered boarding groups. Lane 1 (blue) will serve pre-boarding elites—Premier 1K, Global Services, active military, customers with disabilities, and families with young children—plus Groups 1 and priority Group 2 passengers (including some Chase cardholders and those who purchased priority access). Lane 2 (green) handles Groups 3–5, with Groups 3–5 asked to remain seated until called. United will also send push notifications through its mobile app when boarding begins, triggered when the first boarding pass is scanned, helping travelers avoid lingering at the gate if flights are delayed or loaded early.

The change responds to frequent complaints about gate crowding as passenger numbers grow—United carried about 155 million passengers in a recent 12-month period—and to observations that five separate lanes created idle standing passengers and jams, especially during delays. The new approach aims to segment boarding while preventing the "magnet" effect of early line-ups. United’s system aligns with peers: American uses two lanes; Delta uses four. A notable distinction is United’s expanded pre-boarding access for top-tier elites to board before the official sequence. United frames the rollout as customer-driven, having tested variants across thousands of flights, and expects gateside notifications and the two-lane structure to reduce waiting and improve recognition of elite customers. The update is being implemented across airports this week.

Ireland voted decisively to legalize same‑sex marriage in a landmark referendum, with 62% supporting the change and a 60.5% turnout — about 1.2 million Yes votes to 734,300 No. Every constituency but Roscommon‑South Leitrim approved the amendment; many Dublin districts recorded over 70% Yes. Jubilation erupted at Dublin Castle as results arrived, with politicians, campaigners and celebrities celebrating. Prime Minister Enda Kenny called it pioneering leadership; Minister Leo Varadkar described Ireland as a “beacon of light.” Youth turnout and social media were credited with driving the result. The Catholic Church, long influential but weakened by past scandals, acknowledged the social shift; Archbishop Diarmuid Martin urged the Church to reassess. No campaigners congratulated the winners while voicing ongoing concerns about religious freedom and constitutional change. The referendum made Ireland the first country to approve marriage equality by popular vote.

Giovanni DeGarimore, owner of Giovanni’s Fish Market in Morro Bay, made headlines after buying a 70-pound octopus—later named Fred—from a crab fisherman in San Luis Obispo County solely to release it back into the ocean. DeGarimore paid “a couple hundred dollars” for the animal and returned it to the water the next day. A spokesperson said the decision reflected Gio’s personal connection to the ocean: he’s an avid diver who once had a close encounter with an octopus in Fiji and has since felt conflicted about selling them, despite his livelihood depending on seafood sales. The market’s Facebook post about Fred has been widely shared, and DeGarimore said freeing the octopus “might not change the world, but I’m going to do one thing and if it only makes me and Fred happy, that’s okay too.” The article also highlights octopus intelligence and behavior, noting incidents like a two-spotted octopus dismantling a valve at the Santa Monica Pier Aquarium and historical aquarium mischief. Comparative psychologist Jennifer Mather, who has studied octopuses for decades, explains their problem-solving, tool-like use of suckers, play behaviors, distinct personalities, and unusually centralized nervous systems—features that help explain why these solitary cephalopods evolved notable intelligence.

House Republicans, led by Oversight Committee Chairman Rep. Jason Chaffetz (R‑Utah), introduced an impeachment resolution against IRS Commissioner John Koskinen, asserting he violated the public trust during the probe into the IRS’s targeting of conservative groups. The move came days after the Justice Department closed its investigation without charges. Chaffetz accuses Koskinen of failing to preserve 422 backup tapes that might have contained Lois Lerner’s missing emails, misleading Congress by saying relevant documents were turned over and not notifying lawmakers when evidence was irretrievably lost. Eighteen committee Republicans sponsored the measure, which now moves to the House Judiciary Committee. The IRS strongly disputes the allegations, saying it fully cooperated with investigations. Democrats, led by ranking member Rep. Elijah Cummings (D‑Md.), denounced the effort as partisan grandstanding that wastes taxpayer money and resembles prior politically charged probes like Benghazi and Planned Parenthood. They note substantial IRS cooperation—alleged costs of $20 million and 160,000 employee hours—and say there is no evidence supporting the impeachment charges. Pursuing impeachment of an agency head is rare and a significant escalation beyond contempt proceedings.

Florida authorities captured a 12-foot, 120-pound Burmese python in Port St. Lucie after neighbors reported a very large snake in a residential block. Officers responded Friday when signs pointed to a predator preying on neighborhood pets; police found a dead cat and suspect the python killed it and may be responsible for several recent disappearances of other cats. Sgt. John Holman located the snake concealed in waist-high brush and, with other officers, removed and secured the animal. Although Florida banned Burmese pythons in 2012, police said this particular python belonged to an owner who held a license to keep it.

A former Bronx-Lebanon Hospital physician, Dr. Henry Bello, entered the hospital on June 30, 2017, concealed an assault rifle under his lab coat and began shooting after seeking out a doctor he blamed for his 2015 forced resignation. Bello had been dismissed amid complaints, including a sexual harassment scandal, and former colleagues describe him as aggressive, loud and threatening; he allegedly warned co-workers after his ouster that he would return to kill them. Dr. Kamran Ahmed, whom Bello reportedly had named as a target, told the New York Post he was surprised and baffled to be singled out because Bello “never argued” with him and had been relatively cordial. Ahmed, a family medicine physician who specializes in early detection and treatment of dementia, was not working that day and thus escaped the attack. Bello first encountered Dr. Roger Green on the 16th floor, demanded to know why Green hadn’t helped him when he was in trouble, then produced an AM-15 rifle; Green fled and raised the alarm. Bello proceeded to the 17th floor, where he fatally shot Dr. Tracy Sin-Yee Tam, a 32-year-old family medicine doctor covering a shift, and wounded six others. He briefly set fire to a nurses’ station before dying of a self-inflicted gunshot. Six victims were hospitalized, one critically. Investigators later searched Bello’s recent Bronx residence and recovered the rifle’s box; the weapon had been purchased at a Schenectady gun shop on June 20. Bello had earlier sent an email to the Daily News blaming colleagues for ending his medical career. Hospital staff held a grief-stricken meeting to support one another in the aftermath.

Al-Qaeda announced it is holding 70-year-old American development expert Warren Weinstein, who was abducted from his Lahore home on Aug. 13. In a recording, leader Ayman al-Zawahri said Weinstein, who led J.E. Austin Associates’ Pakistan office and worked on USAID-funded projects, would be freed only if the U.S. halted airstrikes in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Somalia and Yemen and released all al-Qaeda and Taliban detainees. Pakistani colleagues and beneficiaries described Weinstein as a helpful, long-time development practitioner who boosted Pakistan’s dairy and gem sectors—facilitating $63 million in investment, creating jobs, arranging scholarships for tribal-area students, and aiding university dairy facilities. U.S. and Pakistani authorities have not identified his captors; militants are suspected. His employer says he is in poor health and has provided kidnappers a list of needed medications.

The Boy Scouts of America revoked the charter for Troop 98 and its affiliated Cub Scout pack at Rainier Beach United Methodist Church in Seattle after the church refused to remove openly gay Scoutmaster Geoffrey (Geoff) McGrath. The BSA informed parents and leaders that because the church would not follow BSA policy barring gay adults from leadership, it was no longer an authorized charter partner; a local community center has been offered as a new sponsor. Troop 98, formed after last year’s contentious BSA vote allowing gay youth but not gay adults, has about 15 boys and includes children from immigrant families and two boys with gay fathers. Rev. Monica Corsaro said the church expected the move, called it unilateral, and insisted it would continue supporting McGrath and the youth program even if it could no longer use Boy Scout logos, uniforms, or the Scout name. McGrath, a married Eagle Scout and software engineer, said he was shocked and criticized the BSA for dissolving the units without proper dialogue. The gay fathers of one scout said they were offended and had no plans to transfer to the offered troop. The dispute highlights ongoing tensions within the Boy Scouts over its exclusion of openly gay adult leaders despite permitting gay youths.

Just days into his tenure as President Trump’s national security adviser, Michael T. Flynn was questioned by the FBI about late-December phone calls with Russia’s ambassador, Sergey Kislyak. Investigators concluded Flynn had not been fully forthcoming about whether he discussed U.S. sanctions imposed by the Obama administration after alleged Russian interference in the 2016 election. Acting Attorney General Sally Yates and a senior Justice Department official alerted White House counsel Don McGahn on Jan. 26, and the president was briefed that same day. Despite this, Vice President Mike Pence was not told that Flynn had misled him until Feb. 9, after media reports prompted an inquiry. Flynn resigned on Feb. 13, just 24 days after taking his West Wing office, amid conflicting accounts about whether he left voluntarily or at the president’s request.

Flynn acknowledged giving “incomplete information” to Pence and others, attributing it to the “fast pace” of the transition, but insisted in interviews that he “crossed no lines” and that discussions focused on the expulsion of 35 Russian diplomats rather than sanctions. White House counsel reviewed the matter and concluded there was no legal violation, but officials said the erosion of trust — especially after Flynn misled the vice president — made his position untenable. The FBI had interviewed Flynn in the early days of the administration, and reports indicate agents likely had access to call records or transcripts during questioning.

Flynn’s departure intensified scrutiny of Trump-Russia ties and prompted bipartisan calls for investigations. Some Republicans, including Sen. Lindsey Graham and Sen. John McCain, urged congressional inquiries; Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell said the intelligence committee was already examining related allegations. House Intelligence Committee Chairman Devin Nunes emphasized probing the source of leaks, while Democrats demanded briefings and broader probes into contacts between Trump associates and Russian officials. The White House reacted by accusing leaking intelligence sources of politicizing classified information; President Trump and allies framed the story as driven by “illegal leaks,” with conservative commentators asserting the media sought to undermine the administration.

Legal analysts said prosecution under the Logan Act was unlikely, but Flynn could face charges if he knowingly lied to the FBI, a felony under 18 U.S.C. § 1001. Some former prosecutors noted a genuine faulty memory can be a defense, but questioned how Flynn could forget such recent, consequential conversations. Flynn’s rapid rise and fall raised wider concerns among U.S. allies about the administration’s Russia policy and deepened perceptions of chaos in the White House’s early days.

On June 27, 2017, a blue police helicopter attacked Caracas government sites, firing shots at the Interior Ministry and dropping grenades on the Supreme Court. President Nicolás Maduro called it a "terrorist attack," saying 15 shots were fired and four grenades were dropped, one failing to detonate; no injuries were reported. Authorities identified the pilot as police officer Oscar Pérez, who posted a video declaring a coalition of soldiers, policemen and civilians rising against "tyranny" and demanding Maduro’s resignation and immediate elections. Pérez—who has film-actor credits—appeared in fatigues flanked by armed, masked men, urging Venezuelans and military bases to join the uprising under constitutional articles he cited. The helicopter was later found on the northern Caribbean coast; Pérez remained at large. The incident intensified an already volatile crisis marked by months of anti-government protests, looting and clashes that left dozens dead. Opposition figures suggested the raid might be staged by the government to justify repression; Maduro accused foreign interference and links to former officials. The attack coincided with judicial moves weakening dissident prosecutor Luisa Ortega Díaz and preceded a contested July 30 vote to form a Constituent Assembly—an action opponents say would cement Maduro’s power.

Domnica Cemortan, a Moldovan dancer who was on the bridge of the Costa Concordia when it struck rocks off Giglio in January 2012, testified at Captain Francesco Schettino’s trial that they had been romantically involved. Under threat of criminal penalty she admitted the relationship and said she boarded as a non-paying passenger after working briefly for the cruise operator in December 2011. She recounted dining at the captain’s table the night of the disaster, being invited onto the bridge as Schettino performed a close sail-past, and helping other passengers into lifeboats before boarding one herself. Cemortan said Schettino urged her to “save herself,” that she retrieved his laptop from his cabin, and later handed it back on Giglio. Her courtroom appearance and remarks—“When you are someone’s lover no one asks you for any explanations”—drew gasps and intense media attention. Schettino faces charges including manslaughter, causing a shipwreck and abandoning ship; 32 people died and he could face up to 20 years in prison. Witnesses testified the captain had ordered a very close approach to Giglio; his defense cites faulty watertight doors and blames the helmsman. The ship was righted after a major salvage effort and is slated for removal.

Nick Stoeberl, a 24-year-old artist and comedian from California, has been verified by Guinness World Records as having the longest tongue, measuring 10.1 cm (3.97 in) from tip to the middle of his closed top lip. His record appears in the Guinness World Records 2015 book, the 60th-anniversary edition, which showcases many feats and includes augmented reality features. Stoeberl discovered his unusually long tongue as a child imitating Gene Simmons of KISS; his father’s fandom inspired the pose that revealed his unusually long lingua. He enjoys the attention his unique trait brings, boasting he can lick his nose and even his elbow, though he jokes that tongue hygiene takes longer each morning. His measurement surpassed the previous record held by Brit Stephen Taylor (9.8 cm) since 2002.

The story also highlights another contender: 18-year-old Adrianne (Adrienne) Lewis from Michigan, who claims a 4-inch tongue and has been promoting her ability online—demonstrating she can touch her elbow, nose, chin and even her eye with assistance. Lewis has drawn viral attention on Facebook and YouTube and is reportedly in talks with Guinness World Records to have her tongue officially measured and possibly replace Stoeberl as the record holder. The piece connects readers to Guinness World Records’ social channels and the 2015 book for further record-breaking stories and videos.

ABC is reviving Roseanne with an eight-episode, straight-to-series order slated for midseason, nearly 20 years after the original sitcom ended. Network president Channing Dungey announced the multicamera revival, which will follow the working-class Connor family confronting "the economic challenges of living paycheck to paycheck in 2018." Returning cast members include Roseanne Barr, John Goodman, Sara Gilbert, Laurie Metcalf, Michael Fishman and Lecy Goranson; Sarah Chalke will also return in a new role. The revival was championed by Gilbert and reunites original executive producers Barr, Tom Werner and Bruce Helford, with Whitney Cummings and Tony Hernandez also onboard; Carsey-Werner produces. The pickup reflects a broader trend of revivals—Will & Grace, The X-Files, Twin Peaks and others—and networks’ efforts to engage working-class viewers in the post-2016 media landscape. Roseanne will be ABC’s only multicamera comedy in 2017–18 after the network canceled other multicam shows, and its return underscores both nostalgia and continued interest in established franchises to attract audiences.

John Oliver devoted a Last Week Tonight segment to seriously dissecting Donald Trump’s proposal to build a Mexico–U.S. border wall. He highlighted major problems: wildly inconsistent cost estimates from Trump ($4–$12 billion) versus expert estimates of at least $25–$26 billion, and no credible evidence Mexico would pay. Practical and legal geography complicates construction—much of the border follows the Rio Grande and treaties prevent obstructing the river, so past fencing sometimes ended up inland, even cutting off U.S. land. Effectiveness is questionable: many unauthorized immigrants initially enter legally and overstay, and physical barriers can be bypassed by ladders, ropes, or tunnels. Oliver also addressed the racialized rhetoric framing immigrants as criminals, noting research shows immigrants commit crime at lower rates than native-born citizens. Satirically, he suggested a cheaper, less harmful alternative—buying every American an electric waffle iron—arguing it would cost less, avoid diplomatic fallout, and at least make waffles.

A Cobb County, Georgia police lieutenant has been fired after dashcam video from a July 2016 traffic stop showed him making a racially charged remark. The clip captures Lt. Greg Abbott, who is white, interrupting a woman who said she was afraid to move her hands to retrieve her cellphone and saying, "But you're not black. Remember, we only shoot black people. Yeah. We only shoot black people, right?" The video was obtained by WSB-TV through an open-records request and brought to the department's attention, prompting an internal investigation and Abbott’s placement on administrative leave before his termination.

Police Chief Mike Register announced the firing, saying such comments are inexcusable and have no place in law enforcement. Register stressed that, regardless of context or intent, the remarks were inappropriate and inconsistent with the values he has sought to instill since becoming chief in June. He noted that the internal review found Abbott claimed to have been sarcastic and attempting to de-escalate what he saw as an uncooperative passenger, but Register emphasized that the words spoken were the decisive factor. Although Register said he has known Abbott for years and viewed him as honorable, he concluded the comment warranted dismissal.

Local Black community leaders welcomed the swift action but warned the incident may reflect broader issues in the department. Deane Bonner of the Cobb County NAACP called the racial interjection particularly troubling and potentially systematic. Ben Williams of the Cobb County Southern Christian Leadership Conference praised the chief’s transparency, suggesting the disclosure itself was significant in addressing police conduct in the county. Abbott’s attorney had previously said Abbott cooperated with the probe; he did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the firing.

Cyprus authorities investigated reports that a bright object streaked over the Troodos mountains shortly before midnight, producing a blue glow, a loud explosion and ground shaking. Police and the Geological Department said there’s no sign the object struck the ground and it likely exploded in the sky; searches are underway for any remaining debris. Hundreds of calls came in from across the south of the island, especially Nicosia and Limassol, but there were no casualties or damage reported. The civil aviation authority logged no unusual pilot reports and flights operated normally. Officials said the phenomenon was most likely a meteor; meteorites that reach the surface can provide scientists with information about the early solar system. Investigations continue.

Four Japanese students say they were handed a €1,100 bill after dining near St Mark’s Square in Venice, prompting outrage from locals and an official probe. The students reported paying for four large Fiorentina steaks, a fried fish platter, water and service; other reports suggest costly wine and aperitifs may have been included. Three women who dined with them at a different venue reportedly paid €350 for three plates of seafood pasta.
