The students filed a complaint with police in Bologna, where they study, and Venice authorities have opened an investigation after the citizens’ group Gruppo 25 Aprile publicized the case.

Venice Mayor Luigi Brugnaro vowed to seek justice if the episode is confirmed, saying officials will check the complaint. Media reports did not name the restaurant but described it as owned by a Chinese woman and run by an Egyptian. Gruppo 25 Aprile criticized widespread overcharging in tourist-heavy areas, noting that just 1.1% of restaurants in that part of Venice are locally owned, compared with 50% across the historic centre. The group plans to post tourist advisories to help visitors avoid being overcharged and warned that harming Venice’s reputation hurts residents.

The incident follows other high-profile billing disputes: a British family said they paid over €500 at a trattoria and a Japanese couple complained of being charged €120 for lobster pasta priced by weight. Mayor Brugnaro has defended some merchants, arguing visitors should expect to pay more and even chided tourists for not speaking Italian. His stance drew criticism from residents’ groups who accuse city leadership of tolerating practices that damage Venice’s image even as the mayor pursues measures to limit overtourism, including restrictions on accommodation and cruise ship access.

UNESCO experts who examined a wreck off Haiti have concluded it is not Christopher Columbus’s 1492 flagship, the Santa Maria, but a later vessel from the late 17th or 18th century. The team, led by former Spanish underwater museum head Xavier Nieto Prieto, based this on artefacts at the site—especially copper-alloy fasteners—arguing that such construction techniques postdate Columbus’s era. The site lies in the general area contemporary accounts place the wreck, but farther offshore than expected. A metal tube once photographed there, believed by US investigator Barry Clifford to be a 15th-century lombard cannon, has since been removed. Clifford had earlier claimed his find “strongly suggested” it was the Santa Maria and urged full excavation; Professor Charles Beeker of Indiana University also considers the site a strong candidate and criticizes UNESCO’s refusal to allow further US-led work.

UNESCO noted the Santa Maria’s remains might instead lie buried under coastal sediments or marshland and plans searches in both seabed and land locations, a proposal some scholars dispute given reef barriers and ambiguous diary editions. Critics say UNESCO’s report overlooked photographic evidence of possible early cannon, neglected prior expedition records, and did not conduct tests (e.g., ballast provenance or bronze dating) that could clarify the artefacts’ ages. Clifford insists the lombards are “smoking-gun” evidence and welcomes further investigation, while UNESCO urges more comprehensive, standards-compliant research to settle the question.

Tiffany & Co. reported a modest rebound in sales for the third quarter ended Oct. 31, marking its first increase in two years as net sales rose about 1–1.2% to roughly $949m and net income increased to $95.1m. The company cited stronger traffic in Japan and China—China sales grew in double digits—and said U.S., Canada and Latin America declines slowed to their smallest pace in five quarters. Fashion jewelry, especially gold bracelets from the “Tiffany T” line, and renewed focus on diamond engagement rings and lower-priced silver pieces under $500 helped performance. Comparable-store sales fell about 2%, better than some analyst expectations, and the results lifted Tiffany’s shares to their biggest gain in 15 months.

However, Tiffany warned that election-related protests and heightened security around Trump Tower—next to its iconic Fifth Avenue flagship—have depressed foot traffic and could continue to weigh on sales at that store, which accounts for less than 10% of worldwide net sales. CEO Frederic Cumenal expressed cautious optimism about early improvements but said more sustained positive data is needed before declaring a turnaround. The company reaffirmed its full-year forecast of declining sales and adjusted EPS and remains watchful of near-term risks to holiday-period demand.

A new 200-page report by Conflict Armament Research (CAR), based on three years of fieldwork in Iraq and Syria, documents how weapons from diverse global sources—including U.S. supply chains and European factories—ended up in Islamic State (ISIS/IS) hands. CAR traced more than 40,000 recovered items using serial numbers and markings, revealing that many arms were looted from Iraqi and Syrian stockpiles but that new transfers into the Syrian conflict also boosted ISIS’ arsenal. In one striking case, an anti-tank missile sold to the U.S. Army by a Bulgarian manufacturer appeared in ISIS possession just 59 days after export, suggesting minimal intermediaries and possible diversion via Syrian rebel groups. CAR tied weapons supplied by or via the U.S. and Gulf states to Syrian opposition factions that later had items diverted to ISIS. Chinese and Russian-made weapons account for over half of the documented small arms, while more than 30 percent originated in EU states like Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary and Germany. CAR also found older and unusual items—such as a 1941 Mauser rifle—and stockpiles indicating internal ISIS logistics, including Chinese light machine guns issued with amphetamines. The report warns that international arms transfers into complex conflicts risk rapid diversion, enabling ISIS not only to wage local insurgency but to retain an exportable capacity for violence beyond the region.

John McCone, an industrialist-turned-CIA outsider, replaced Allen Dulles as director of central intelligence in November 1961 after the Bay of Pigs fiasco. Tasked by John F. Kennedy with restoring order and oversight, McCone remained director under Lyndon Johnson and testified to the Warren Commission after Kennedy’s assassination, asserting the CIA had no evidence linking Lee Harvey Oswald to any conspiracy. For decades critics alleged the agency hid information. A once-secret 2013 report by CIA historian David Robarge, quietly declassified in 2025, largely confirms those suspicions: McCone and other senior officials were “complicit” in withholding “incendiary” material from the Warren Commission in what the report calls a “benign cover-up.” Most consequentially, the agency suppressed knowledge of long-running CIA plots to assassinate Fidel Castro—some involving the Mafia—thereby preventing the commission from investigating whether Cuba-related retaliation motivated Kennedy’s murder.

Robarge’s article portrays McCone as hands-on in restricting the CIA’s cooperation, favoring “passive, reactive and selective” assistance and even directing staff to keep the commission focused on the conclusion that Oswald acted alone. The report raises additional withheld items: possible CIA contacts with Oswald and post-defection surveillance under the mail-opening program HTLINGUAL. McCone later claimed ignorance of the Castro plots, but Robarge concludes that he had been informed earlier and misled investigators. The piece implicates other figures—including Allen Dulles, a Warren commissioner, and Robert Kennedy, who had overseen anti-Castro covert action—in a tangled post-assassination response. While reaffirming that Oswald was the gunman, the report concedes that the agency’s nondisclosures likely undermined the commission’s credibility and left unresolved questions, and 15 redactions in the public release indicate remaining classified secrets.

Rosie O'Donnell revealed on her blog that she suffered a nearly fatal "widow maker" heart attack last week but initially kept it private. In a poetic post, she recounts helping a woman in a parking lot, then later developing chest pain, arm soreness, nausea, clammy skin and vomiting. She Googled symptoms, took an aspirin, but didn’t call 911. The next day a cardiologist’s EKG led to hospitalization, where doctors placed a stent for a 99% blockage in her LAD. O'Donnell warns women to recognize heart attack signs, heed inner warning signs, and call 911—stressing many women don’t seek emergency help.

Actor Neal McDonough quit ABC’s Scoundrels three days into filming because he won’t perform sex scenes; the married Catholic father-of-three has long refused such roles and reportedly risked losing up to $1 million. ABC called it a “casting change,” while insiders say McDonough sticks to his principles despite career cost. Separately, Christopher Ryan and Cacilda Jethá’s book Sex at Dawn argues modern American marriage struggles stem from a mismatch between evolved human sexuality and the recent institution of lifelong monogamy that arose with agriculture. Drawing on anthropology, primatology and anatomy, they suggest pre-agricultural humans practiced more communal, less sexually possessive arrangements, and cite evidence like testicle and penis morphology and bonobo behavior to support historical non-monogamy and sperm competition. The authors advocate tolerance, open discussion, and realistic expectations about love, sex and marriage rather than prescribing a single alternative arrangement.

U.S. District Judge Denise Cote ruled that Nomura Holdings and Royal Bank of Scotland misled Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac by selling defective mortgage-backed securities before the 2008 crash, calling the deception “enormous.” In a 361-page opinion after a three-week bench trial, Cote found offering documents did not accurately describe underlying loans and concluded 45–59% of loans in sampled securities had material underwriting defects; in many appraisals home values were inflated. The decision entitles the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), as conservator for Fannie and Freddie, to seek damages—Cote indicated FHFA could recover about $624.4 million less payments already received, leaving roughly $450 million potentially due. The ruling follows large settlements FHFA secured earlier—about $17.9 billion from other banks—and may prompt more settlements to avoid adverse judgments and publicity. Nomura said it will appeal and maintains it was candid; RBS declined comment. Cote rejected defenses blaming the housing crash alone and found bank misconduct exacerbated losses. She barred certain defense evidence at trial, a factor that may complicate appeals. FHFA was ordered to propose final damages based on the ruling.

A judge in Phoenix ordered the release of Leslie Merritt Jr., a man charged in a series of freeway shootings that unnerved the city the previous year, after his bond was reduced to zero and he was allowed to return home under electronic monitoring. Merritt, who had faced a $1 million bond and had been jailed in solitary for seven months, celebrated and embraced family and lawyers as he walked from the courtroom. He has pleaded not guilty to counts including drive-by shooting and aggravated assault. Defense attorneys argued ballistic testing and phone records cast doubt on the case against him and provided an alibi; they also noted that similar freeway shootings continued after his arrest, suggesting the real shooter remained at large. Judge Warren Granville imposed a gag order preventing lawyers and officials from publicly discussing the evidence that prompted the bond change. Arizona Department of Public Safety and the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office declined comment under the gag order. Detectives arrested Merritt on Sept. 18 after a series of incidents in August and September that struck 11 vehicles and triggered heightened patrols; authorities had labeled the attacks the work of a “domestic terrorist,” and Governor Doug Ducey tweeted “We got him!” five minutes after the arrest. Granville set a May 18 court date and cautioned Merritt to appear; Merritt assured the court he would. Separately, in Alabama, state troopers reported a fatal shooting in Blount County after a driver suspected of shooting at motorists earlier that morning fled, crashed and exchanged gunfire with officers; the suspect was later pronounced dead and identities have not been released.

During Libya’s uprising against Moammar Gaddafi, thousands of people disappeared, adding to decades-long detentions and unresolved cases. Rebel leaders estimate nearly 60,000 went missing during the six-month conflict; only about 10,000 freed prisoners have been accounted for after rebels opened Gaddafi’s jails in Tripoli. Families fear many remain in secret detention centers or mass graves. The notorious Abu Salim prison—site of a 1996 massacre of roughly 1,200 inmates—held Abdul Rauf for 48 days. He described brutal daily beatings, electric shocks, severe overcrowding—sharing a cell with 70 men—and dire sanitation and food shortages, yet brought hope to long-imprisoned inmates when he told them of the uprising. His release, amid rebel advances and inside help from guards, reunited him with tearful family celebrations. Elsewhere, survivor Muneer Masoud Own recounted being detained in a warehouse near the 32nd Brigade with roughly 175 others; after days of abuse and deprivation, guards allegedly tossed a grenade into the packed building and opened fire. Residents later recovered about 150 charred bodies and other graves, many victims unidentifiable, leaving families with haunting uncertainty.

Libyan leader Colonel Muammar Gaddafi gave an interview in Tripoli asserting he remained loved and supported by his people, denying widespread protests and rejecting calls to quit. Speaking calmly at a beachfront restaurant to BBC, ABC and the Sunday Times, he insisted he held no formal office to resign from and claimed power rested with the people. He dismissed reports of demonstrations, blaming unrest on al-Qaeda, “terrorists” and drugged youths who seized weapons, and denied using force against civilians—saying any strikes targeted military or ammunition depots. Gaddafi angrily accused Western leaders of betrayal and alleged they sought to recolonize Libya; he challenged accusations of foreign bank accounts and laughed at suggestions he would go into exile. He invited UN fact-finding missions and criticized sanctions, an arms embargo, asset freezes and travel bans imposed by the EU and others.

International leaders reacted strongly. US UN Ambassador Susan Rice called him “delusional” and unfit to lead; Secretary of State Hillary Clinton condemned the use of “mercenaries and thugs” and said Gaddafi should go if it would stop violence, while the US froze $30bn in Libyan assets. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon said Gaddafi lost legitimacy by declaring war on his people. Despite Gaddafi’s defiance, protesters have seized eastern towns, clashes continued in Misrata and Zawiya, and about 100,000 people fled unrest, with mass crossings into Tunisia reported. Government efforts to quell dissent included cash handouts to families and threats of force if dialogue failed.

U.S. officials say the Pentagon has contingency plans to send small special-operations teams into Syria to secure or destroy chemical weapons if the White House decides intervention is necessary, following President Obama’s warning that use or threatening movement of Assad’s chemical arsenal would cross a “red line.” Planners emphasize protecting stockpiles from falling into rebel, Al Qaeda–linked, Hezbollah or other militant hands, possibly using stealth raids and precision strikes to neutralize agents without dispersal. U.S. intelligence estimates Syria holds hundreds of tons of sarin, mustard gas and sought VX, though age and degradation make lethality uncertain. Sites and production facilities are near Aleppo, Hama, Homs and Latakia; surveillance by satellites and drones is ongoing but Athens-level detailed operational orders await White House direction. Meanwhile, fierce fighting continues: government forces have shelled Damascus, bombarded suburbs and battled in Aleppo, with high civilian casualties and reports of executions. The conflict, now a civil war with tens of thousands killed, risks regional destabilization. Russia doubts Syria would use chemical weapons; diplomats urge international, not unilateral, responses.

New details have emerged about Demi Moore’s hospitalization after she was rushed to the hospital Monday night following an apparent seizure at a small birthday dinner at her Beverly Hills home. Guests — described as a small group of girlfriends including Jennifer Meyer — said the 49-year-old actress had been “pretty hyper” and “acting crazy” during the evening, intermittently leaving and returning to the gathering. After dessert she reportedly began convulsing, prompting a friend to call 911. Paramedics transported her to a nearby hospital; her publicist described the care as treatment for exhaustion and to improve her overall health.

Reports and anonymous sources have tied Moore’s condition to longer-term struggles: claims surfaced that she has been battling anorexia and substance issues, including alleged Adderall use, energy drink consumption, starvation, and experimentation with inhalants. Friends noted emotional turmoil following her recent divorce from Ashton Kutcher and the death of her longtime AA sponsor, which may have worsened relapse risks. Kutcher, who was in Brazil, was said to be “deeply concerned” and returning to Los Angeles. Moore was later reported released and potentially seeking treatment.

Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway and JPMorgan Chase announced a joint effort to curb health-care costs and improve services for their U.S. employees by creating an independent, non–profit-incentivized company. The three employers, together covering more than 1.1 million workers, said the initial emphasis will be technology solutions to simplify health care, improve transparency and boost patient satisfaction and outcomes. Leaders—Todd Combs (Berkshire), Marvelle Sullivan Berchtold (J.P. Morgan) and Beth Galetti (Amazon)—will spearhead planning, but many operational details, headquarters and long-term plans remain undecided.

Executives framed the move as a long-term experiment rather than a finished plan. Warren Buffett called rising health costs a “hungry tapeworm” on the economy and urged unknown talent to find better approaches; Jeff Bezos and Jamie Dimon emphasized the complexity of health care and the potential to benefit employees and possibly all Americans. Observers said employer-driven disruption is overdue given misaligned incentives across innovation, delivery and insurance. Analysts and consultants noted technology—especially information sharing and AI—could reduce spending if initiatives extend beyond these companies’ employees, but warned meaningful change will take time and faces skepticism.

The announcement rattled markets: shares of several health-care firms plunged—Express Scripts, Aetna, CVS, UnitedHealth and others fell sharply—while Amazon edged up and Berkshire and J.P. Morgan dipped slightly. Insurers and benefit managers signaled interest in learning more, even as questions linger about scope, scalability and whether the venture can become a true industry challenger.

Frank Taaffe, once one of George Zimmerman’s most vocal defenders during the Trayvon Martin case, has publicly reversed course and testified to a federal grand jury that Zimmerman may have racially targeted Martin. Taaffe, a fellow neighborhood-watch volunteer who repeatedly appeared on national TV to defend Zimmerman—portraying Martin as suspicious and Zimmerman as a community protector—now says a mysterious phone call he received two years ago, featuring racist remarks about Martin, might have come from Zimmerman. Initially believing it a prank, Taaffe told the FBI this year he now suspects the caller was Zimmerman and that Zimmerman racially profiled the teen. He said personal losses—the deaths of two sons and damage to family relationships over his earlier support for Zimmerman—helped shift his perspective and motivated him to “clear his conscience” and try to make amends with Martin’s family.

Taaffe’s media role was controversial long before his recantation. Investigations revealed a lengthy criminal history, convictions and arrests including DUI and trespassing, domestic-violence complaints, and a past burglary charge. His public commentary repeatedly aired virulent, racially charged views on podcasts and social media; he defended racial profiling on grounds of alleged neighborhood crime and attacked black communities and public figures. Despite lacking legal or forensic expertise, networks repeatedly used him to discuss technical trial issues, where his claims—about drugs, injuries, and forensic evidence—often drew pushback.

Taaffe maintains he acted from conscience and First Amendment rights when initially defending Zimmerman, but now says Zimmerman should not have followed Martin and that he believes race played a role. He has no clear evidence the caller was Zimmerman and admits others could have placed the call, but he volunteered his grand jury testimony in hopes of atonement as DOJ continues its civil-rights inquiry.

Yulia Skripal, 33, who was poisoned along with her father Sergei Skripal in Salisbury by a nerve agent, is reported to be improving rapidly and is no longer in a critical condition. Salisbury District Hospital described her state as stable; she has responded well to treatment and remains under 24-hour specialist care. Doctors and hospital leadership praised staff for their work. Sergei Skripal, 66, a former Russian double agent believed to have been the primary target, remains in critical but stable condition. Detectives believe both were exposed to the nerve agent novichok, with the highest concentration found smeared on Sergei Skripal’s front door; lower concentrations were detected at other town locations. Police have placed precautionary cordons, including around a children’s play area at Montgomery Gardens near the Skripals’ home, and are searching those areas. About 250 counter-terrorism detectives are working on the investigation, examining over 5,000 hours of CCTV, 1,350 seized exhibits and identifying 500 witnesses. At least 130 people may have been exposed; Wiltshire officer Detective Sergeant Nick Bailey, who was also exposed, has been discharged. The UK government attributes responsibility to the Russian state, an accusation Moscow denies. The incident prompted a major international response: at least 26 countries expelled Russian diplomats, and Russia has announced reciprocal measures, including expulsions and closures. The long-term health consequences for the Skripals remain uncertain.

San Juan County, Utah, declared a state of emergency and threatened to take control of several federal park areas after National Park closures left local businesses and tourism-dependent communities at risk. The county commission, led by commissioner Phil Lyman, planned to remove barricades at Natural Bridges National Monument and reopen sites including Hovenweep, Rainbow Bridge, parts of Canyonlands, and the Hite Marina in Glen Canyon National Recreation Area. Officials described the move as civil disobedience and mobilized at least 60 personnel—sheriff’s deputies, search-and-rescue volunteers, firefighters, EMTs—plus portable toilets, garbage trucks and mobile command centers, arguing the action was needed to protect the local economy, which they say is 70 percent reliant on park visitors. Commissioners sought state financial aid and notified the National Park Service; park officials warned the plan is illegal and could prompt citations, fines and jail time. County leaders said they would provide sanitation, trash removal, search-and-rescue and law enforcement at reopened sites while avoiding intimidation of federal employees and maximizing media attention. Governor Gary Herbert offered to deploy state resources and asked the president to authorize funding or staffing to keep parks open.

William McCormack, a 43-year-old Bronxville investment banker, has sued Lawrence Hospital Center and surgeon Dr. Michael Kerin after he required a second appendectomy in the Adirondacks about a year after an operation at the Bronxville facility that was supposed to remove his appendix. McCormack alleges that on Jan. 27, 2013, Kerin performed an appendectomy at Lawrence Hospital and provided an operative report, electronically signed, stating the appendix had been removed. McCormack was told the procedure was successful. In early March of the following year, while in Lake Placid, he suffered severe stomach pain and underwent emergency surgery at Adirondack Medical Center, where surgeons found his appendix still intact. Court papers say Lawrence Hospital’s pathology department received a specimen labeled “appendix” from the 2013 surgery but issued a final diagnosis noting “no evidence of appendix.” The lawsuit contends the hospital failed to notify McCormack of the discrepancy and ignored the mistake. McCormack seeks unspecified damages for pain, suffering and undergoing surgery twice. Lawrence Hospital said it is investigating and does not comment on pending litigation; Kerin did not respond to requests for comment.

Actor George Takei posted on Facebook defending his characterization of Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas as a “clown in blackface,” calling “blackface” a theatrical term for a white actor darkening his face to play a black buffoon and insisting his use of the phrase was “theater lingo” and “not racist.” Takei argued that Thomas has “abdicated and abandoned his African American heritage” by suggesting slavery did not strip human dignity and by commenting on Japanese American internment—an event Takei, a survivor, pointed to when criticizing Thomas. 

A critic responding to Takei’s defense rejected his explanations point by point. They argued the problem was not Takei’s intent but that he uttered a racist remark and appeared unaware that such language is unacceptable. The critic rejected Takei’s framing of blackface as a quaint theatrical term, stressing its well-known, ugly racist history and calling Takei’s minimization condescending and ignorant. They also challenged Takei’s assertion that Thomas “abandoned” his race, questioning who has the right to label someone a traitor to their race based on politics and warning against political litmus tests that effectively erase identity. 

On Takei’s claim that he accurately represented Thomas’s views on slavery and internment, the critic said Takei had mischaracterized Thomas’s dissent, taken it out of context, and displayed willful blindness. The piece notes that many in Hollywood remained silent, with a few, like Marc Lamont Hill, publicly condemning Takei.

A class-action lawsuit and multiple criminal and civil actions have thrust Jacksonville pediatric dentist Dr. Howard Schneider, 78, into intense scrutiny. Plaintiffs in a suit filed in Duval County allege decades of physical and psychological abuse of mostly low-income, non-English-speaking children treated at his practice, calling it a “house of horrors.” Claims include assault, battery, false imprisonment and intentional infliction of severe emotional distress; lawyers say they have identified at least 60 victims and estimate there could be hundreds more. Allegations range from unnecessary extractions (parents say healthy baby teeth were removed) and performance of procedures without adequate anesthesia, to children being restrained, choked until unconscious, left with visible injuries, and threatened into silence.

The wave of complaints prompted protests outside his clinic, viral videos from parents, and an Attorney General Medicaid fraud probe. Schneider was charged with 11 counts of Medicaid provider fraud for allegedly billing for unnecessary procedures and collecting nearly $4 million over five years; he has pleaded not guilty. He surrendered his license and closed his practice, and has settled over 100 related civil suits without admitting wrongdoing.

In criminal proceedings, defense and prosecution medical experts disagreed on Schneider’s competency to stand trial. A judge appointed a third psychologist to evaluate him; a November hearing was set to address competency, and no trial date is established. Investigations and evidence include parental testimony, former-employee accounts, and expert observations that his consent forms and records were inadequate, sedation was minimal, and dental work quality was poor. Schneider denies mistreating children and maintains he used anesthesia and practiced competently.

DJ Samantha Ronson, 33, was arrested Monday morning near Baker, California, on suspicion of DUI after being pulled over for speeding at about 10:30 a.m. Authorities say she initially refused a roadside breathalyzer and performed poorly on field sobriety tests, leading to her arrest and transport to the Barstow jail (Baker substation). Once at the station she agreed to take an evidentiary breathalyzer and reportedly blew over the legal limit. Ronson, who DJ’d at Lavo in Las Vegas the previous night, was released several hours later while the District Attorney decides whether to file charges.

John Tice, president of the Brevard Hall of Fame in Melbourne, Florida, is leading an initiative to repatriate Jim Morrison’s remains from Paris to Morrison’s birthplace in Melbourne. Morrison, the iconic and controversial Doors frontman, was born Dec. 8, 1943, at the former Brevard Hospital and later died in Paris in July 1971, where he was buried at Père Lachaise Cemetery. Tice, who founded the nonprofit Hall of Fame in 2012 and also serves on the West Melbourne city council, says Melbourne has scant visible ties to Morrison despite his local origins and prominent status in rock history. The Hall of Fame currently features a modest Morrison display—posters, two Doors records, a framed will, donated books and a replica street sign—positioned among displays honoring other local celebrities like Kate Upton, Doug Flutie and Kelly Slater.

Tice reports hearing that Paris cemetery officials have indicated Morrison’s grave lease is nearing expiration and that vandalism concerns might prompt relocation. He claims the cemetery once offered to move the remains to Morrison’s Vernon Place birth home but that the homeowner declined; Tice plans to contact Père Lachaise directly and would pursue fundraising and legal steps if officials agree. He acknowledges the idea will prompt mixed reactions locally—some supportive, others critical given Morrison’s controversial past, including legal troubles that led him to leave the U.S. Tice also notes common local misconceptions, such as the false rumor that Morrison graduated from Melbourne High; his family moved away when he was an infant. He is awaiting a response from Paris authorities before taking further action.

Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and senior adviser, denied any collusion with Russia after a closed-door interview Monday with Senate Intelligence Committee staff and in an 11-page statement released beforehand. He said he had “no improper contacts,” did not rely on Russian funds for his businesses, and sought to be fully transparent about his security-clearance SF-86, which he blamed on an assistant prematurely submitting a draft. Kushner acknowledged four contacts with Russian-linked individuals during the campaign and transition: a brief April 2016 exchange with then-Ambassador Sergey Kislyak at a foreign-policy event, attendance at a June 2016 Trump Tower meeting with a Russian lawyer that he described as a “waste of time,” a Dec. 1 transition meeting with Kislyak where he discussed receiving a Syria briefing and suggested (and was rebuffed on) using an embassy channel, and a Dec. 13 meeting with Sergey Gorkov of state-connected VEB bank, which Kushner said concerned Russia’s economy and goodwill rather than business deals. His account disputes reporting that he sought a secret backchannel or had multiple calls with Kislyak. Critics note that Kushner’s detailed assertions create many factual claims investigators can verify, and some discrepancies with other accounts have prompted calls for further scrutiny and likely additional congressional or FBI follow-up.

The document is a round-up of film reviews centered on the new romantic comedy Did You Hear About the Morgans? and several other recent releases. Did You Hear About the Morgans? stars Hugh Grant and Sarah Jessica Parker as a quarrelsome Manhattan couple who witness a murder and are placed in federal witness protection in rural Wyoming. Critics find the film lifeless and padded with awkward pauses; its premise—city sophisticates humbled by red-state life—never yields much humor. Sam Elliott and Mary Steenburgen play dignified hosts; the screenplay and direction by Marc Lawrence are seen as formulaic, with some amusement derived from Grant’s reliable deadpan. Another perspective in the piece calls the movie a lightweight, enjoyable throwaway that demonstrates Grant’s comic steadiness and Lawrence’s knack for snappy tunes, though it remains conventional rom-com fare.

Also reviewed is Crazy Heart, starring Jeff Bridges as worn country singer Bad Blake. Adapted by Scott Cooper from Thomas Cobb’s novel, Crazy Heart is praised as a rare, adult American film about rehabilitation and emotional reckoning; Maggie Gyllenhaal co-stars and the movie is lauded for restraint and tenderness. Shorter notes cover Fall Down Dead, a pulpy exploitation thriller with gory set pieces and an unsatisfying sequel setup, and Home, Ursula Meier’s unsettling debut about an insular family pushed toward paranoia when a nearby highway reopens.

Nearly a year before Attorney General Jeff Sessions fired FBI deputy director Andrew McCabe for “lack of candor,” McCabe had authorized a federal criminal inquiry into whether Sessions lied to Congress about contacts with Russians, multiple news outlets reported. The probe began after Sens. Patrick Leahy and Al Franken urged the FBI in March 2017 to investigate “all contacts” Sessions may have had with Russian officials and whether any laws were broken. Sessions had testified during his January 2017 confirmation that he had no contacts with Russians; later reporting and his own acknowledgments revealed he met Russia’s ambassador, Sergey Kislyak, during the campaign and had been aware of adviser George Papadopoulos’s Russian contacts. Sessions recused himself from the Russia investigation, placing oversight with Deputy AG Rod Rosenstein; the matter was later transferred to Special Counsel Robert Mueller. Sessions’s lawyer said Mueller’s team interviewed the attorney general and informed them the matter was closed without charges for false statements or perjury. It is unclear how actively the FBI pursued the inquiry before Mueller’s interview or whether other Sessions-related lines remain open. McCabe, who denies misleading investigators, was dismissed after an inspector general concluded he lacked candor in a separate matter involving media contacts about the Clinton Foundation; his firing occurred less than 48 hours before his planned retirement.

A series of short items note a few unrelated updates and observations. First, a reader can subscribe to email notifications for Bo Petersen’s posts; the site confirms when a notification is saved and warns if saving fails. Notifications are delivered once daily, only when new matching items exist, and include a link to the new content. Next, social media-style lines highlight a great white shark, “Mary Lee,” tagged and cruising the U.S. East Coast, with a tracking link to OCEARCH for live location details. Another brief line reiterates the general region—East Coast of the U.S.—as the shark’s current area. Finally, a historical note explains that since 1996 Alexa Internet has been donating its web crawl data to the Internet Archive. Those daily crawl datasets are incorporated into the Wayback Machine after an embargo period, helping preserve web history. Altogether, the items mix content subscription instructions, wildlife tracking, and web-archiving background: a notification service mechanic, a tagged shark’s tracked presence along the U.S. East Coast, and the archival practice by which Alexa’s crawls have been flowing into the Internet Archive for decades to populate the Wayback Machine once any embargoes expire.

At the Democratic Platform Committee meeting in Orlando, Bernie Sanders’ push for explicit opposition to the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) failed to win a direct prohibition; instead the committee adopted broader language opposing “trade agreements that do not support good American jobs.” Sanders’ team expressed disappointment, though many speakers reportedly voiced anti-TPP views. Despite that setback, Sanders secured notable platform victories — most prominently the inclusion of a $15 federal minimum wage — and remains influential as he considers endorsing Hillary Clinton.

On the same day, Clinton moved to narrow policy gaps with Sanders by announcing substantive health proposals shaped in part by discussions with his campaign. She pledged to increase mandatory funding for Federally Qualified Health Centers by $40 billion over the next decade, effectively doubling primary-care investments for low-income and underserved populations that serve roughly 25 million Americans. Clinton also reaffirmed support for a “public option” within the Affordable Care Act exchanges and proposed allowing people aged 55 and older to buy into Medicare. Her plan, she said, would be paid for through savings, innovations, and tax reforms targeting loopholes and the wealthy.

Sanders praised Clinton’s health plan as an important step toward universal, affordable care, calling it likely to save lives and cut costs. The convergence on health and education proposals signaled growing compromise between Clinton and Sanders camps and set the stage for his expected endorsement, which could help bring progressive supporters into Clinton’s fold ahead of the general election.

Tropical Storm Isaac forced the Republican National Convention to postpone its opening day, shortening the event and canceling several Monday appearances, including Donald Trump’s much-hyped slot. Trump, in Florida to receive a Sarasota GOP award, said he had been given a “big role” and might return but likely would head back to New York; his spokesman insisted the planned spectacle would have been memorable. At the reception Trump reiterated his long-running birther claims about President Obama and urged Republicans to abandon political correctness and “fight fire with fire.” 

Despite the shortened schedule, GOP leaders opened the convention briefly and vowed to press criticism of Obama throughout the week, framing the event to contrast Obama’s record with Mitt Romney’s purported managerial strengths. Organizers monitored the storm while planning major speeches and the formal nomination of Romney and Paul Ryan. The convention also grappled with fallout from Rep. Todd Akin’s controversial remarks and outside attacks like MoveOn.org’s ad targeting Romney and Ryan, as polling showed a close race with voters seeing Obama as more in touch on many issues.

Archaeologists have exposed a remarkably well-preserved Neolithic rectangular house on the edge of Marden Henge in Wiltshire, revealing flint tools dropped on its floor more than 4,300 years ago. The structure, made smart with tonnes of white chalk stamped into a plaster-like surface, is unusually regular and level for its age and is described by Dr Jim Leary of the University of Reading as among the best-preserved houses of the period found in Britain. Excavations have recovered finely worked flint arrowheads and blades, decorated pottery with residue of last meals, shale and copper bracelets, a small Roman brooch and even a vole jawbone. Charred grain and seed assemblages recovered will help reconstruct diet and agriculture.

Evidence including pig bones from at least 13 animals and scorch marks around a charcoal pit indicate the house was likely used for large communal feasting rather than permanent residence; after abandonment the site was deliberately cleaned and neatly covered so it would not be reused. The building sat within a small earth-banked circle on a terrace overlooking a mound, part of the enormous Marden Henge complex whose ramparts once rose about three metres and enclosed some 15 hectares — larger than Avebury and far surpassing Stonehenge in scale. Leary suggests sites like Marden showcased status and power by mobilising huge labor forces.

The landscape, long obscured by fertile farmland, modern roads and buildings, is being reexamined through a multi-year Vale of Pewsey project involving Reading University, Historic England, AHRC and Wiltshire Museum. Recent work at nearby Wilsford henge also uncovered a 4,000-year-old burial of a child in fetal position wearing an amber necklace. The excavations will continue, with public open days planned to display finds and tours as part of a nationwide archaeology festival.

A small Piper PA‑31 twin‑engine aircraft crashed off the coast of Long Island Saturday afternoon amid severe thunderstorms, killing at least two people and leaving two missing. East Hampton Town Police identified those on board as 70‑year‑old builder Bernard (Ben) Krupinski, his 70‑year‑old wife Bonnie Krupinski, 22‑year‑old grandson William Maerov and 47‑year‑old pilot Jon Dollard. The plane went down about 1.5–2 miles south of Indian Wells Beach/Amagansett shortly before 3 p.m.; controllers lost radar contact during a storm that likely included strong downdrafts. Two male bodies were recovered amid floating wreckage—one by an East Hampton lifeguard on a Jet Ski and another by the U.S. Coast Guard—while a search for the remaining two was briefly resumed and later suspended. Authorities have not publicly confirmed which victims were recovered. The National Transportation Safety Board and the FAA will investigate the cause of the crash. Ben Krupinski, an East Hampton native and prominent builder to celebrities such as Martha Stewart, Billy Joel and Roger Waters, was well known locally for massive luxury projects and philanthropic acts; his businesses and family ties are central to the East Hampton community. The crash follows another fatal small‑plane accident on Long Island earlier that week.

Orofino police investigated the disappearance of 17-year-old Kristian Perez after he left the Orofino High School prom on April 15. Perez signed out of the event at 9:32 p.m. and did not return home; his mother reported him missing. Investigators recovered his tuxedo jacket, one shoe and his broken cellphone near a relative’s vehicle he had used to get to the prom. A canine tracking team followed a path suggesting Perez walked west from the National Guard Armory (the prom venue) to a nearby parking area along U.S. Highway 12, where officers believe he may have entered a vehicle. The department obtained a search warrant for Perez’s cell phone records and is reviewing calls and texts for leads. Agencies in surrounding areas were notified after a possible sighting in Lewiston; surveillance footage later showed the person was not Perez. Orofino officials asked the public for any information and provided a tip line, 208-476-5551. School officials activated crisis protocols and made counselors available to students and staff. On April 18 the department located Perez at a residence on Indio Avenue in Orofino after a tip; he was found in good health and taken into custody on a runaway charge. The homeowner, 26-year-old Tyson Imel, may face charges for assisting Perez; the investigation remains ongoing.

Ben Affleck’s The Accountant opened at No. 1 with an estimated $24.7 million, demonstrating Affleck’s continued box-office draw. The Gavin O’Connor-directed film, made for about $44 million, blended action with a cerebral premise and benefited from marketing that emphasized Affleck’s star power; critics were lukewarm (51% on RottenTomatoes) but audiences rewarded it with an A CinemaScore. Kevin Hart: What Now? finished second with $11.98 million, outperforming Hart’s 2013 concert film debut and already recouping its $10 million budget; it earned 78% on Rotten Tomatoes and an A-minus CinemaScore. The Girl on the Train held third with $11.97 million in its second weekend; Miss Peregrine’s Home for Peculiar Children and Deepwater Horizon followed in fourth and fifth. Toy-based Max Steel flopped, grossing just $2.2 million and receiving no early critic screenings. Nate Parker’s The Birth of a Nation suffered a steep 61% second-weekend drop to $2.7 million, jeopardizing its awards prospects. Final box-office numbers were pending.

Accessory Outlet, an online retailer, has drawn legal scrutiny for hiding extreme consumer penalties in its Terms of Sale and then enforcing them against at least one customer. The buried clause prohibits buyers from filing complaints, chargebacks, disputes, public reviews, Better Business Bureau complaints, social media posts, or even threatening to do any of those things within 90 days of purchase — or face a $250 “damages” penalty plus continuing fees. The terms also require all disputes to be resolved by binding arbitration in New York City, at the parties’ expense.

A Wisconsin woman, represented by Public Citizen, sued after ordering a $39.94 iPhone case on July 6, 2014. When the item didn’t appear to have been processed by USPS, she asked to cancel the order. Accessory Outlet claimed it had shipped, provided a tracking number that didn’t check out, and then threatened to impose the $250 penalty when she warned she would request a chargeback. The company told her it would send the debt to collections, damaging her credit, and warned it would bill hourly fees for any correspondence and impose a $50 flat fee for disputes. When she said she would get a lawyer, the retailer replied with aggressive messages including “You are playing games with the wrong people.”

The customer later received the case nine days after the alleged shipment, but it was warped and unusable. Her complaint argues she never agreed to the hard-to-find Terms, which were not acknowledged during checkout, and that the clauses are unconscionable and unenforceable. Public Citizen’s attorney calls the hidden, gag-like terms and bullying emails unlawful attempts to silence customers. Investigations also found Accessory Outlet falsely displayed endorsement badges (BBB, Angie’s List, buySAFE, Trusted Shops) and the BBB noted the company was not accredited and was asked to remove its badge.

The Internet Archive is crawling and saving web pages as they’re created and as they reference other pages, aiming to preserve the exact versions cited so links won’t break when originals change or disappear. The goal is to replace dead links with archived versions to keep context intact. In Alabama’s special U.S. Senate race, Democrat Doug Jones defeated Republican Roy Moore, narrowing the Senate Republican majority to 51–49. Jones, a former prosecutor, capitalized on Moore’s sexual-misconduct allegations and national Democratic support; his win energized Democrats ahead of 2018. Election day saw heightened security, DHS monitoring for threats, and unusual turnout patterns—more young and Black voters in some Republican areas. Moore campaigned amid controversy, briefly appearing at his watch party and voting on horseback; his campaign barred The Washington Post from its event. The race drew intense national attention and scrutiny.

Singer-songwriter Ryan Adams and actress-singer Mandy Moore have mutually decided to end their nearly six-year marriage, the couple said in a joint statement asking for privacy. Married in March 2009, they kept their relationship largely private despite occasional collaborations: Moore worked with Adams on her music and contributed background vocals to his projects, and Adams appeared on her recordings. Adams has faced health struggles, including Ménière's disease, which influenced his melancholic 2014 self-titled album. Separately, actor Patrick Dempsey and wife Jillian Fink, married since 1999, are also splitting; Fink reportedly filed for divorce citing irreconcilable differences and seeks joint custody and support.

Pete Davidson stirred fresh reaction from ex-fiancée Ariana Grande after a promo for Saturday Night Live showed him jokingly proposing to musical guest Maggie Rogers. In the clip, Davidson asks Rogers, “Hey Maggie, I’m Pete. You wanna get married?” When she declines, he quips he’s “0 for 3,” referencing his string of failed relationships. The skit prompted Grande to respond on Twitter — in a now-deleted post she wrote, “for somebody who claims to hate relevancy u sure love clinging to it huh,” and later tweeted “thank u, next,” a pointed nod to moving on. Grande also quote-tweeted a fan who said SNL would “milk their breakup,” adding only an ellipsis. The exchange follows the swift, highly publicized breakup between Grande and Davidson, who became engaged after dating only weeks this summer and split in October. Both have covered matching tattoos from their brief engagement. Reports described the split as mutual and attributed the breakup in part to timing and Grande’s need to grieve and heal following other personal losses. Davidson has frequently referenced his romantic life in comedy, and this SNL gag continued that pattern, drawing sharp public attention from his famous former partner.

New research published in The Lancet reveals that in 2013 complications from preterm birth became the leading global cause of death for children under five, surpassing infectious diseases. Of an estimated 6.3 million under-five deaths that year, nearly 1.1 million were due to prematurity—965,000 in the first 28 days and 125,000 between one month and five years. Pneumonia and childbirth complications remain major causes (935,000 and 720,000 deaths respectively). The shift toward neonatal causes reflects successful reductions in infectious disease mortality from investments in vaccines, bed nets, antibiotics and treatments, while preterm mortality has declined more slowly and the global prematurity rate has risen to 15.1 million births annually.

The highest absolute burdens of preterm deaths are in India, Nigeria, Pakistan, DR Congo and China, while some West African countries facing Ebola have among the highest rates. High-income countries can also show large shares of under-five deaths due to prematurity because infectious deaths are rarer; Macedonia, Slovenia and Denmark top the percentage list. In the U.S. 28.1 percent of under-five deaths stem from prematurity, equating to about 8,100 deaths and reflecting persistent disparities by race.

Global responses include intensified advocacy, the Every Woman Every Child movement, WHO-led Every Newborn Action Plan (ENAP), and four major research initiatives totalling roughly $250 million. Key programs include the Global Coalition to Advance Preterm Birth Research, March of Dimes’ $75 million campaign, UCSF’s $100 million Preterm Birth Initiative, and GAPPS-funded projects. Research spans 20 disciplines, investigating triggers of labor, uterine signaling, biomarkers, genetics, microbiome and social determinants, with hopes for breakthroughs in three to five years.

Proven interventions—family planning, infection prevention, reduced elective early C-sections, Kangaroo Mother Care—could prevent many deaths; KMC alone might save up to 450,000 newborns yearly. New implementation programs (e.g., USAID’s Every Preemie–SCALE) and global collaborative networks aim to scale evidence-based care, especially in high-burden countries like Ethiopia, India and Nigeria. World Prematurity Day mobilizes partners worldwide to raise awareness and spur commitments to reduce preterm birth and newborn mortality.

Ikea and the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission announced a nationwide repair program covering about 27–29 million chests and dressers after reports that unsecured units can tip over and fatally crush children. The action follows at least three confirmed child deaths tied to Ikea Malm and other dressers, including a Minnesota toddler, Theodore “Ted” McGee, who died in February when a bureau toppled onto him. Two earlier Malm incidents in 2014 and 2015 also resulted in child fatalities. Though labeled a recall, Ikea’s remedy is not to take back furniture but to provide free wall-anchoring kits and publicize anchoring instructions; consumers can get kits at stores, online, or by phone. Ikea has sent hundreds of thousands of kits and says it will expand outreach; the company expressed sorrow and pledged to work with regulators on safer designs. CPSC Chair Elliot Kaye praised the step but urged Ikea and the industry to produce inherently more stable furniture, noting European standards are stricter and that expecting all consumers—especially renters—or all parents to anchor furniture is unrealistic. Safety advocates argue calling the action a “repair program” weakens urgency versus a recall and stress many consumers remain unaware or do not install restraints. Industry groups say they’re exploring design and technology solutions. Attorneys representing affected families are pursuing lawsuits and pressing for buybacks or replacements with safer units. CPSC data show furniture and TV tip-overs cause numerous deaths and tens of thousands of injuries annually, underscoring the broader safety concern.

When George Talley’s 1979 Corvette vanished from Jefferson Avenue in Detroit in July 1981, he assumed it was gone forever. Last week the silver Corvette resurfaced in Columbia, Mississippi, after Michigan’s Southwest Commercial Auto Recovery unit was alerted when someone tried to register two 1979 Corvettes under the same VIN. Working with Mississippi authorities and the National Insurance Crime Bureau, investigators traced the car back to Talley; his insurance claim had never been paid, so he remains the owner. The car reportedly runs, has about 47,000 miles, and is being held at the Hattiesburg police station. Talley, now 71, was stunned and worried about retrieving it until General Motors Executive Vice President Mark Reuss, having heard Talley’s story on WJR radio, offered to have GM pick up and deliver the Corvette to him at the company’s expense. Talley awaits scheduling details.

CBS News veteran Bob Schieffer, 78, announced he will retire this summer after a 46-year career with the network and 24 years as host of Face the Nation. Speaking at Texas Christian University, his alma mater, Schieffer reflected on his start in Fort Worth radio, reporting in Vietnam, and a long rise through newspapers, local TV and CBS. He praised colleagues and credited mentors and his wife for support. Schieffer highlighted CBS’s current strength—especially Face the Nation and CBS This Morning—and said that timing his retirement ahead of the 2016 presidential campaign made sense. CBS is considering internal candidates Major Garrett, Norah O’Donnell and John Dickerson, and outside options like Jake Tapper and Jonathan Karl, with no final decision announced.

In Haverfordwest, Pembrokeshire, a dramatic and unusual insect episode unfolded when a queen bee became trapped in the boot of a silver Mitsubishi Outlander and roughly 20,000 bees followed her, covering the car and causing alarm in the town. The swarm was first noticed as a large “brown splodge” on the car’s rear after the owner parked to shop. Tom Moses, a Pembrokeshire Coast National Park ranger, called the local beekeepers and helped for about three hours, eventually coaxing many of the bees into a cardboard box. Moses and other helpers were stung several times during the rescue; he reported stings to his head, neck and ears and took antihistamines. Roger Burns of Pembrokeshire Beekeepers, a retired doctor with 30 years’ experience, explained the queen likely found something sweet and entered a gap in the boot mechanism. Burns and colleagues used a box to collect the swarm but a gust of wind blew the box off the car roof and the queen slipped back into the boot. Later, unintentionally, the car owner drove off with the queen still hidden, and the swarm continued to trail the vehicle—witnesses reported bees on the boot the next day. Beekeepers eventually recovered many of the insects, but the episode left a queen-less box of bees behind. Observers described the sight as spectacular and worrying, given the busy high-street location outside a pub and the potential danger to passersby and the insects. Beekeepers stressed the value of bees and urged people not to harm swarms. Participants called the two-day pursuit by thousands of bees both surprising and amusing, yet unprecedented in Burns’ experience.

Tom Hanks quietly continued a years-long tradition of supplying coffee to the White House press corps by gifting a new espresso machine to the press break room. Reporters found the upgraded “super deluxe” machine and a note from the Oscar-winning actor urging them to “Keep up the good fight for Truth, Justice, and the American Way. Especially for the Truth Part.” Hanks first noticed the press area relied on vending-machine coffee during a Bush-era visit and bought an espresso maker then, later replacing it in 2010 after finding it dirty and worn during a screening visit. The recent delivery, spotted during the early days of the Trump administration, included a card illustrated with American troops and continues Hanks’s tongue-in-cheek support for journalists covering the White House.

JPMorgan Chase disclosed that losses in its Chief Investment Office (CIO) have swollen to $5.8 billion and that internal reviews of about 1 million emails and tens of thousands of voice tapes indicate traders may have concealed the full extent of the damage by misstating position prices. The bank reported a $4.4 billion trading loss tied to a wrong-way bet on credit derivatives in its London unit, driven by trader Bruno Iksil’s oversized positions, pushing second-quarter net income down 9% to $4.96 billion. First-quarter results were restated, reducing prior net income by $459 million. CEO Jamie Dimon, who initially minimized the issue, is meeting analysts to address the fallout; CIO Ina Drew retired shortly after the disclosure. JPMorgan has overhauled CIO management, said all synthetic-credit-derivatives staff have left, and may claw back compensation from responsible individuals. The bank offset some losses with securities sales, warned losses could rise by up to $1.6 billion in an extreme scenario, and faces broader pressures from low interest rates, weaker markets and regulatory probes.

The document compiles media coverage and commentary about celebrities’ reactions to controversial political figures and events, centering on threats by public figures to leave the United States if disliked candidates win, and a lengthy feud between Donald Trump and Rosie O'Donnell. Many entertainers—Whoopi Goldberg, Rev. Al Sharpton, Raven-Symoné, Jon Stewart, Cher, Rosie O’Donnell, Samuel L. Jackson, Sienna Miller, Bryan Cranston and others—publicly joked or vowed they would emigrate if Donald Trump or another objectionable candidate were elected. These declarations are framed as both genuine expressions of distress and as attention-grabbing media moments; past examples include Eddie Vedder and Stephen Baldwin, who threatened to move after prior elections but remained. The text notes grassroots responses like the tongue-in-cheek “Cape Breton If Donald Trump Wins” campaign offering refuge to detractors, and reports reactions from Trump’s sons who offered to pay airfare for departing celebrities, framing such threats as political endorsements.

A substantial portion recounts the decade-long, highly publicized Trump–Rosie O’Donnell feud: its origins in 2006 over Miss USA controversies, repeated barbs on Twitter and television, exchanges during O’Donnell’s stints on The View, and mutual insults over the years. The timeline covers key moments—public insults, health-related tweets, debate references, and social-media back-and-forths—through Trump’s 2016 campaign and presidency. O’Donnell’s evolving responses, from calling Trump names to active protest after his 2016 victory, are highlighted. Overall, the piece illustrates how celebrity reactions, social media disputes, and personal feuds intersect with modern political discourse, often amplifying controversy and public attention.

RadarOnline reports that Ben Affleck visited Lindsay Lohan during her stay at Cliffside Malibu, sparking renewed rumors she might appear in his film Live by Night. A former patient at the treatment center said Affleck arrived late one night with an assistant a few days before Lohan’s July 2 birthday and stayed about an hour. According to the source, he discussed the possibility of a role; Lohan allegedly told fellow patients she would have dark hair and an Irish accent for the part. The insider framed Affleck as checking on Lohan, noting his own past struggles with substance abuse, while also relaying Lohan’s claim that he was being flirty—something the source dismissed as typical embellishment. A person close to the movie denied Lohan is being considered for the project, but did not deny Affleck’s visit. Separately, preview promos for Lohan’s upcoming Oprah Winfrey interview on OWN show probing questions about addiction, accountability, and whether she can “turn it around.” Winfrey has described Lohan as “honest,” “authentic,” and looking “strong” and “healthy.” The full interview airs Sunday, Aug. 18 at 9 p.m.

Administration lawyers have presented President Barack Obama with four options for restructuring the National Security Agency’s bulk phone‑metadata surveillance program, according to officials. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the Justice Department completed the review ahead of the president’s March 28 deadline and delivered options ranging from retaining the program with changes to ending it. The proposals are: (1) leave the metadata with phone companies and have the NSA access specific records on request, maintaining carrier control of stored data; (2) transfer custody of the metadata to another government entity (for example the FBI or potentially overseen by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court) to separate the investigators from the database itself; (3) place the data with a private, non‑telecommunications, non‑government third party—a less favored approach that Obama criticized as effectively outsourcing a government function while adding expense, legal uncertainty and little public confidence; and (4) terminate the program entirely, a politically bold option considered unlikely. Public statements from Obama have recently favored one of the first two options, emphasizing reduced concentration of authority and improved oversight, but administration officials have not announced a final decision or timeline for implementing changes.

Congress raced over the weekend to avert a potential government shutdown as a midnight Monday deadline loomed for passing funding for federal agencies. The House approved a continuing resolution early Sunday to fund government operations through Dec. 15, but it attached contentious provisions aimed at the Affordable Care Act: a one-year delay in major provisions and repeal of the 2.3 percent medical-device tax. Those additions set up an immediate clash with Senate Democrats and the White House, which have vowed to reject any changes to the health law and which President Obama would veto.

House Speaker John Boehner’s move to push delay and repeal measures stems largely from pressure from conservatives within his Republican conference, who demanded a robust confrontation over the health law and have the votes to complicate Boehner’s leadership on fiscal matters. Republicans also hope the Senate might accept repeal of the medical-device tax — an idea that has previously drawn bipartisan support in test votes — giving the House a political win. But key Senate Democrats, including Sen. Amy Klobuchar, have cautioned against attaching such measures to a short-term funding bill, and Senate leadership is confident it can defeat the amendments.

The Senate, scheduled to reconvene Monday afternoon, could simply table the Republican amendments under rules allowing a simple majority to remove them. Senate Democratic leaders, led by Majority Leader Harry Reid, have counseled a hardline approach: resist concessions and force Republicans to pass a clean funding bill or bear the responsibility for a shutdown. Reid urged President Obama not to participate in a largely symbolic White House meeting with congressional leaders, arguing it would create the false impression of serious negotiation. Democrats argue that any small concession would invite even larger GOP demands later, including on the debt ceiling, and that political fallout from a shutdown would damage Republicans.

If neither side yields by the deadline, options include a very short-term continuing resolution to buy negotiating time, or a partial government shutdown that would immediately ratchet up pressure on both parties. Local leaders are warning of severe economic and service impacts if shutdown occurs. The Washington region, heavily dependent on federal employment and contracting, could lose roughly $200 million per day and see hundreds of thousands of jobs affected. Federal services would be curtailed: new Social Security and Medicare applications paused, no new NIH clinical trials enrollments, halted housing and small-business loans, and closures of national museums, parks and the National Zoo — a serious tourism blow. Local jurisdictions have set aside reserve funds in anticipation, and officials warn of cascading effects on state and local programs that rely on federal activity.

As the standoff continued, the responsibility for avoiding a shutdown largely rested with House Republicans: either pass the Senate’s clean short-term funding or return to the House with another plan that Democrats would likely defeat, risking a shutdown for the first time in nearly two decades.

Chinese leaders signaled renewed engagement with North Korea as Premier Wen Jiabao and President Hu Jintao met visiting senior North Korean official Jang Song-thaek in Beijing. The meetings, following Jang’s six-day visit to China, sought to rebuild ties after tensions prompted by a recent North Korean rocket launch. Wen urged Pyongyang to allow market mechanisms greater scope to revive its economy, improve laws and regulations, attract business investment, and reform customs—steps aimed at reducing North Korea’s dependence on Chinese aid. Hu and Wen expressed support for stronger bilateral relations; Hu praised Jang’s contributions to friendship between the neighbors. China and North Korea also agreed to deepen economic cooperation through developing special economic zones at Rason and Hwanggumphyong, with Chinese investment and plans for manufacturing, logistics, tourism, IT, agriculture and garment industries. Despite supporting some sanctions over Pyongyang’s nuclear tests, Beijing is cautious about measures that could destabilize the regime and trigger refugee flows. Trade and investment flows remain limited compared with South Korea, though Chinese exports to the North increased recently and about 100 Chinese firms have invested non-financially in North Korea.

Dove, long known as a pioneer of “femvertising” through its Real Beauty campaign, aimed to extend its message of body positivity with a limited-edition set of six body-wash bottles shaped to mimic different female body types. Marketed in the U.K. and described by Dove and its agency Ogilvy as a celebration of diversity—“from curvaceous to slender, tall to petite”—the stunt sought to translate decades of brand messaging into product design and to thank women who have promoted the Real Beauty conversation on social media.

The intent echoes Dove’s focus on issues such as ageism, stereotypes that erode girls’ confidence, and the disconnect between women’s self-perceptions and how others see them. Executives framed the bottles as a simple, tangible reminder that beauty comes in “a million different shapes and sizes,” supported by research the brand cites about social-media pressures on women. Ogilvy described the idea as a compact expression of Dove’s legacy intended to marry message and product.

But the move quickly provoked criticism and mockery online. Twitter users turned the bottles into memes, comparing them to everyday containers (wine jugs, drink bottles, cleaning-product jugs) and lampooning the notion that toiletry packaging stands as a meaningful representation of women’s bodies. Critics called the campaign silly at best and patronizing at worst, arguing that few women feel oppressed by the shapes of their soap bottles and that the stunt trivialized deeper structural issues around body acceptance and discrimination.

Commentary went further to accuse Dove of exploiting the insecurities it claims to address: selling empowerment while ultimately selling product. Observers noted the irony that Dove’s parent company Unilever also owns brands like Axe, which markets male-targeted products using traditional sexist tropes—highlighting corporate hypocrisy beneath the body-positive rhetoric. Practical critiques also emerged: differing bottle shapes could awkwardly emphasize bodies at the point of purchase, require shoppers to choose a proxy for their own figure, and even create functional disparities (some shapes being easier to grip or less prone to tipping), which would inadvertently suggest a “better” body shape.

Some commentators argued the campaign missed the real work of making beauty less central to self-worth—saying cosmetic packaging cannot substitute for structural changes that reduce the importance of appearance. Others questioned whether the limited run and gifting-only distribution reflected uncertainty about commercial viability.

In sum, while the Real Beauty Bottles were conceived as a playful, tangible extension of Dove’s long-running message about diversity and self-acceptance, the execution exposed tensions inherent in corporate-led feminism. The stunt illuminated how brand-driven empowerment can be perceived as superficial, commodified, and sometimes counterproductive—especially when the symbolic gesture overshadows the substantive changes critics say are needed.

Talcum powder, made from the mineral talc, is used widely in cosmetics because it absorbs moisture and reduces friction. Natural talc can contain asbestos, a known cause of lung-related cancers when inhaled; consumer talc in the U.S. has been asbestos-free since the 1970s. Scientific inquiry has focused on occupational inhalation of talc (miners, millers) and whether genital use of talc-based powders raises ovarian cancer risk. Laboratory studies of asbestos-free talc have been inconsistent, with some animal experiments showing tumors and others not. Human studies have likewise produced mixed results. Many case-control studies report a small increase in ovarian cancer risk associated with perineal talc use, but these can suffer recall bias. Prospective cohort studies, less subject to that bias, have not found an increased risk. If any increased individual risk exists, it appears small, though widespread use makes the question important. Occupational studies of miners and millers are complicated by variable asbestos contamination and other workplace exposures; no increased lung cancer risk has been linked to cosmetic talcum powder use. Limited and inconsistent evidence exists for links to endometrial or other cancers. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies talc with asbestos as carcinogenic, inhaled asbestos-free talc as “not classifiable” for human carcinogenicity, and perineal use of talc-based powders as “possibly carcinogenic.” The U.S. National Toxicology Program has not completed a full review. Given uncertainty, people concerned about talc may choose to avoid or limit use of talcum products. Concurrently, a series of high-profile U.S. lawsuits has produced multi-million-dollar verdicts against Johnson & Johnson alleging failure to warn consumers that baby powder caused ovarian cancer; the company contests the science and is appealing. Research continues.

Malaria, a mosquito-borne parasitic disease, causes fever, chills and flu-like illness and can be fatal if untreated. Globally, hundreds of millions of cases and hundreds of thousands of deaths occur annually, mostly among African children. Control efforts—especially insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs), indoor residual spraying, rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs)—have substantially reduced malaria incidence and mortality since 2000, but funding and rising resistance remain serious challenges.

Recent research from Mali reveals a worrying mechanism undermining ITN effectiveness. Two closely related African malaria vectors, Anopheles gambiae and Anopheles coluzzii, experienced brief breakdowns in reproductive isolation that allowed hybridization. In 2006, A. coluzzii acquired an entire "island of divergence" on chromosome 2L from A. gambiae, carrying multiple insecticide-resistance alleles. This introgression occurred as large-scale bed net distributions began, suggesting that increased insecticide exposure acted as a selective pressure favoring hybrids and sweeping the resistance-linked genomic region through A. coluzzii populations. The work, led by Gregory Lanzaro and colleagues and published in PNAS, provides a clear example of adaptive introgression driving rapid evolution of insecticide resistance in an animal species.

The findings underscore an urgent need to diversify vector-control strategies and develop new tools—novel insecticides, biological agents like bacteria or fungi, and genetic approaches—to counter rising mosquito resistance. Continued surveillance of resistance, sustained funding, and accelerated deployment of alternative interventions are critical to maintain malaria control gains.

Steven Spielberg’s long-anticipated adaptation of Roald Dahl’s The BFG underperformed badly at the U.S. box office over the Independence Day weekend, raising questions about timing, marketing and audience appeal rather than the talents of Spielberg or Dahl. The $140 million Disney-backed fantasy opened to roughly $18.6–$22.3 million across the three- and four-day frames and placed fourth that holiday weekend; early international returns were also weak. Those figures leave the film reliant on overseas markets to recoup costs and mark one of Spielberg’s most conspicuous commercial disappointments in decades if the trend continues.

Critically, The BFG did respectably: it held around a 71 percent critics’ score on Rotten Tomatoes, an A- CinemaScore from opening audiences and commendations for Mark Rylance’s motion-capture performance as the gentle giant and for the film’s lavish special effects and dreamlike visuals. Still, reviewers and audiences often found the movie “unremarkable” — beautiful to look at but lacking the darker edges and emotional depth of Dahl’s book. The film’s tonal middle ground, neither fully a children’s blockbuster nor a richly layered family drama, may have left both demographics under-served.

Several practical causes contributed to the weak launch. The title’s acronym (BFG) and relative unfamiliarity of the source material in the U.S. hindered instant recognition; the cast lacked major box-office draws; and visual advertising struggled to convey the film’s tender relationship-driven core. Timing was also poor: it opened against established family fare, particularly Disney/Pixar’s Finding Dory, and during a holiday weekend when many potential viewers were traveling. Industry analysts noted Dahl lacks the franchise pull of contemporary properties like Harry Potter, and that Spielberg’s recent work has skewed toward prestige dramas rather than event family blockbusters.

In sum, The BFG’s failure appears driven by positioning, marketing and generational awareness more than a collapse of Spielberg’s craftsmanship or Dahl’s storytelling. If it stays modest domestically, the film may still be rescued by overseas grosses, but for now it stands as a high-profile example of how even acclaimed filmmakers can struggle when a project misreads the market and moment.

A lighthearted encounter in Washington, D.C., has drawn wide attention after a female Metropolitan Police Department officer broke up a park fight and ended up in a spontaneous dance-off with a 17-year-old girl. The incident occurred Monday afternoon on K Street SW when officer intervention dispersed the disturbance. As 17-year-old Aaliya Taylor — a Ballou High School senior — began dancing to Silentó’s hit "Watch Me (Whip/Nae Nae)," the officer challenged her, saying she could do better. Surprised but amused, Aaliya accepted the challenge. Onlookers laughed and cheered as the officer matched Aaliya step for step performing the “Nae Nae.” The two declared the contest a tie and exchanged a friendly hug; the officer asked for Aaliya’s name and smiled, an interaction Aaliya said changed her perception of police. She commented, “Oh yeah, we need more cops like you,” highlighting the positive community impact of the brief, humanizing moment. Aaliya posted video of the dance-off to Facebook, where it rapidly went viral—garnering over 279,000 views in less than 24 hours. The Metropolitan Police Department confirmed the officer in the clip is with their department, and Mayor Muriel Bowser referenced the episode on Twitter, praising D.C.’s innovative community-safety approaches and noting that a D.C. police officer even performed the “Nae Nae.” The playful exchange between officer and teen has been embraced online and locally as an example of friendly, rapport-building policing that resonated with residents, especially youth, by turning a tense situation into a positive community moment.

The Toronto Zoo is investigating after a video posted online appears to show a woman climbing over a protective boardwalk barrier to retrieve a hat from a Sumatran tiger enclosure while the tiger lunges from behind a second fence. The woman grabs the hat and returns to onlookers amid shouts condemning her actions; another visitor intervenes. Zoo communications director Jennifer Tracey said staff learned of the incident from the video and are seeking witnesses. No zoo staff were at the tiger pen at the time; the attendant assigned to that area also cares for other animals and may have been elsewhere. Multiple signs warned visitors not to cross barriers. City bylaws bar entering enclosures and could lead to fines up to $2,000, bans, or other penalties once the person is identified.

Florida Memorial University has become the headquarters for the Trayvon Martin Foundation, established by Trayvon’s parents after the 17-year-old’s 2012 death and George Zimmerman’s subsequent acquittal. The foundation’s offices, located on a second-floor library space at the historically black university, are filled with artwork—mostly images of a hooded young man—and serve as a reflective, spiritual meeting place. A ceremony inaugurating the space drew about 100 people, including local officials, foundation members and Miami residents, and featured prayers, remarks from the university president Roslyn Artis, and speeches by Trayvon’s parents, Sybrina and Tracy Fulton. The university offered financial support and hopes the site will be a “learning laboratory” inspiring students to address violence and civic issues.
