The foundation focuses on assisting families affected by violent crime and promoting nonviolence; it distributes wristbands and hosts memorial displays and programs like the Black Male College Explorers, a college-prep and leadership initiative highlighted by the Fultons. Sybrina Fulton emphasized the universal nature of the work and her connections with other parents who lost children to gun violence. Separately, George Zimmerman—acquitted in Trayvon’s death—filed divorce paperwork claiming no job or steady home, significant legal debts and modest assets.

A member of the family that founded Purdue Pharma, a company sued by more than 1,000 jurisdictions over its role in the U.S. opioid crisis, has been listed as an inventor on a newly issued patent for an opioid-use-disorder treatment. Dr. Richard Sackler, a former Purdue president and son of one of the company’s founders, is named among six inventors on a patent issued in January for a new formulation of buprenorphine. The drug, already FDA-approved in tablet and film forms to treat opioid addiction, is described in the patent as a rapidly dissolving sublingual wafer intended to reduce diversion and potentially treat pain in humans and animals. Critics told the Financial Times they were disturbed the patent might allow a Sackler family member to profit from treatments addressing a crisis their company is accused of contributing to; Purdue denies liability in the lawsuits. The family’s philanthropic donations have come under increasing scrutiny amid legal disputes, including consolidated cases in Ohio and a Massachusetts suit naming the family. Congress has requested a deposition of Sackler from a settled 2015 Kentucky case — reportedly the only instance a family member was questioned under oath about OxyContin marketing and addiction risks. Purdue did not comment on the patent and has publicized efforts to combat addiction, including support for safer prescribing, naloxone donations, and a recent $3.4 million contribution toward a low-cost naloxone nasal spray.

Manufacturers have quietly slimmed down paper products while touting improvements, leaving shoppers to decide whether changes are acceptable. Kimberly-Clark, for example, introduced a “15% bulkier” Kleenex tissue but reduced sheet count by 13%, a practice the industry calls “desheeting.” Toilet paper has undergone similar shrinkage: narrower rolls, larger cardboard cores, fewer sheets per roll and smaller sheets. With Americans reportedly using about 46 sheets per day on average, these shifts matter for value and performance.

Consumer Reports evaluates toilet paper on strength, softness, disintegration and ease of tearing, and recent tests identified two top performers. White Cloud 3-Ply Ultra sold at Walmart earned a Best Buy designation at roughly 25 cents per 100 sheets thanks to excellent strength and softness along with very good disintegration and tearing performance. Charmin Ultra Strong also ranked among top picks; it achieved excellent tearing ease but scored lower on other attributes and costs about 41 cents per 100 sheets.

Several brands fared worse: Scott 1000 (about 8 cents per 100 sheets) was neither soft nor strong. Marcal Small Steps (about 25 cents) was nearly as harsh as Scott 1000 and did not tear easily. Cottonelle CleanCare with Touch of Soft Cotton proved less soft than its name implies and, at roughly 44 cents per 100 sheets, was pricier than nearly all other tested tissues. The tests also show that brand name alone isn’t a reliable guide—different products from the same brands (Scott, Cottonelle, Charmin) varied significantly in performance. In short, consumers should scrutinize sheet counts and test results rather than rely on packaging claims or brand reputation.

An iguana that crawled onto a power line caused a blaze on a pole and cut electricity to The Palms Care Center in Lauderdale Lakes, Fla., forcing the temporary relocation of 20 residents to hospitals. Broward Sheriff Fire Rescue said the reptile was electrocuted, igniting the pole fire and knocking out power Friday afternoon. The nursing home was running on a generator but only half the building’s air conditioning worked, so staff and firefighters moved residents into cooled areas when possible. Due to overcrowding and as a precaution, 20 patients without reliable A/C were transported to nearby hospitals; none were in distress. Power was restored shortly before 11 p.m., and patients were to return after evaluation. The facility is licensed for 120 beds.

Hillary Clinton has quietly begun positioning herself for a possible 2016 presidential run by re-engaging on high-profile issues, taking organizational refuge in the Clinton Foundation, and signaling a schedule of public policy speeches. In a forceful address to the American Bar Association in San Francisco, Clinton criticized the Supreme Court’s decision weakening the Voting Rights Act and condemned a wave of state-level voting restrictions—particularly photo ID laws and cuts to early voting—as efforts that disproportionately burden minorities and undermine democratic access. She urged Congress to repair the Voting Rights Act, called for stronger Justice Department enforcement, and asked lawyers to help protect ballot access. The speech reinforced her alignment with Democratic base priorities—voting rights, gay marriage, and civil-rights protections—and served as an early, deliberate policy statement reminiscent of a candidate’s platform.

Concurrently, Clinton is taking a leading role at the rebranded Clinton Foundation alongside Bill and Chelsea Clinton. Her move provides an institutional platform to pursue her preferred issues—women and girls, early childhood development, and global economic and health initiatives—while maintaining distance from day-to-day Washington battles. Foundation stewardship offers Clinton both a public-facing vehicle to shape messaging and an organizational base for future political activity, though it invites fresh scrutiny and management tests following internal reviews and Chelsea’s expanded role.

Taken together, Clinton’s ABA speech, announced upcoming addresses on national security and global leadership, and formal integration into the foundation signal a deliberate, measured re-entry into national debate. While she has not declared a candidacy, these steps build issue credibility, keep her prominent with core constituencies, and lay groundwork for a potential 2016 campaign.

Jamaica’s Parliament has passed landmark legislation decriminalizing small amounts of marijuana and creating a framework for a regulated medical cannabis industry. Under the new law, possession of up to 2 ounces (56.6g) is treated as a petty, non-arrestable offence punishable by a ticket rather than a criminal record, and individuals may cultivate up to five plants on any premises. The act also formally permits Rastafarians to use ganja sacramentally and allows tourists with foreign medical prescriptions to apply for permits to buy limited amounts legally.

The legislation establishes a cannabis licensing authority to regulate cultivation and distribution for medical, scientific and therapeutic purposes, opening the door to health tourism, product development and commercial cultivation of medical ganja and industrial hemp. Jamaican officials point to local scientific advances—such as Canasol for glaucoma—as an example of the island’s potential in cannabis-derived products. Commerce Minister Anthony Hylton described the sector as holding “great potential” amid Jamaica’s ongoing IMF loan programme.

Government leaders emphasized the reforms do not amount to laxity on drug trafficking; National Security Minister Peter Bunting stressed continued enforcement against illegal plots and transnational trafficking, noting Jamaica’s international treaty obligations. U.S. counter-narcotics officials reiterated that trafficking into the United States remains illegal and urged compliance with UN drug conventions.

The move follows a regional and international trend of easing cannabis restrictions—several U.S. states and Uruguay have adopted liberal policies—and marks a significant shift in Jamaica’s decades-long debate over ganja, aiming to correct historic criminalization disproportionately affecting poor, predominantly black Jamaicans and to integrate traditional cultural practice with a regulated industry.

The Houston Rockets have been sold by Leslie Alexander to local billionaire Tilman Fertitta, who called acquiring his hometown team “a dream come true.” League sources told ESPN Fertitta agreed to pay $2.2 billion—a record price for an NBA franchise—pending NBA Board of Governors approval. Fertitta, owner of Landry’s, Inc. and Golden Nugget Casinos, will also operate the Toyota Center and reportedly has no partners in the deal. Alexander praised Fertitta as a capable successor. The sale drew attention amid Hurricane Harvey recovery, and celebrity interest — including rumored bids involving Beyoncé — ultimately did not prevail.

Pennsylvania State Police say 47-year-old Michele Leonard of Somerset was arrested twice for suspected drunk driving after crashing her car on the same day. Troopers responded to an initial crash around 5 p.m. Saturday; Leonard was taken into custody, tested for blood alcohol, and then released from the state police barracks. Details about to whom she was released were not provided. According to police, after her release Leonard paid a stranger $3 for a ride back to her disabled vehicle, got back into it, and began driving. About an hour after the first crash, she again lost control near Waterlevel and Lowry Roads, sideswiping a parked car and plowing into a shed owned by Stanley Fisher. Fisher said he saw the car speed down his driveway and hit the shed, destroying costly tools and the structure; crews were salvaging what remained and moving items into paid storage until a new shed is built. Fisher removed Leonard’s keys and quoted her saying, “I can’t get another DUI. I already have one today.” Charges are pending receipt of blood-alcohol test results. Leonard declined to comment when reached at her home.

Democrats faced an awkward reality as their candidates prepared to debate: median household income fell during President Obama’s term and only barely recovered, leaving incomes stagnant—a glaring vulnerability for a party defending the administration’s economic record. Census data show 2014 median household income was $1,656 below January 2009; private Sentier Research indicates incomes only recently nudged above mid-2009 levels by 1.3 percent. Republicans have highlighted this problem but struggle to offer convincing solutions that reconcile their principles with voters’ wage anxieties.

GOP contenders criticize Obama—saying inequality rose and the middle class “hollowed out”—but many oppose popular remedies like raising the federal minimum wage. Only Rick Santorum endorsed a specific modest increase; others, including Jeb Bush and Carly Fiorina, prefer state-level decisions. Some Republicans have flirted with indexing the minimum wage to inflation in past cycles, but several present candidates oppose hikes or favor tiered/entry-level exceptions. Marco Rubio’s comments that $10–$11 an hour is insufficient yet opposing a rise exemplify the tension.

Republicans generally favor tax cuts and deregulation to spur growth—approaches with mixed historical results on median incomes. Meanwhile, a significant Obama initiative—the Labor Department’s proposed overtime rule expanding salaried workers’ overtime eligibility—has received little attention from GOP hopefuls but could become a debate topic once finalized. Overall, wage stagnation poses political and policy challenges that neither party has fully resolved.

The author, a long-time watcher of Apple events since 1998, condemns Phil Schiller’s justification for removing the iPhone 7’s 3.5mm headphone jack—calling Schiller’s invocation of “courage” absurd and offensive by equating a product decision with historical acts of bravery. The piece argues Apple replaced a universal, high-quality wired audio standard with proprietary Lightning and wireless solutions for dubious reasons: greed, arrogance, and poor judgment rather than technical necessity. The author insists wired audio generally sounds better than wireless and shares a personal conversion back to wired headphones after experiencing superior sound from Bose QuietComfort in-ear cans, undermining Apple’s push to wireless. Concerns include loss of simultaneous charging and headphone use without clumsy dongles, the fragility and easy loss of AirPods, and the need to buy expensive adapters—issues presented as user-hostile rather than innovative. The author also rejects Apple’s “space is at a premium” rationale and mocks the emphasis on features like stereo speakers and the Taptic Engine, suggesting most users wouldn’t trade universal headphone compatibility for such internal components. Removing the jack also breaks compatibility with many third-party accessories that used the port, from card readers to sensors. The verdict: Apple’s move deepens its walled garden, undermines the old “it just works” simplicity, forces customers to pay for convenience, and provokes justified anger rather than praise.

A San Francisco federal judge ordered Wells Fargo to return about $203 million to California customers after finding the bank used a “high-to-low” transaction posting scheme to maximize overdraft fees. U.S. District Judge William Alsup’s 90-page ruling called the practice profiteering, saying it drained accounts faster by clearing larger items first and generated more $25–$35 overdraft charges. Alsup also faulted Wells Fargo for burying disclosures about the policy and allowing a “shadow line of credit” that let transactions post when customers lacked funds. The decision directs Wells Fargo to stop resequencing transactions and to reverse fees from Nov. 15, 2004, through June 30, 2008; the bank says it will appeal and has modified some policies. The ruling applies only to California plaintiffs but could influence a consolidated federal class action in Miami involving dozens of banks accused of similar practices; nationwide, overdraft fees totaled billions. New federal rules requiring opt-in for overdraft protection are also taking effect, limiting automatic overdraft coverage unless customers consent.

President Trump criticized the FBI minutes before speaking at the agency’s National Academy in Quantico, calling recent documents “really, really disgraceful” and saying “it’s a shame what’s happened with the FBI.” He was referring to Justice Department disclosures including politically charged text messages from an agent who had disparaged Trump during the 2016 campaign. Trump said “we’re going to rebuild the FBI” and suggested there are “a lot of very angry people” over the revelations. He again dismissed Robert Mueller’s Russia probe as “a Democrat hoax” and asserted “there is absolutely no collusion.” Asked about pardoning Michael Flynn, who has pleaded guilty and appears to be cooperating with Mueller, Trump said, “I don’t want to talk about pardons with Michael Flynn — yet,” while White House lawyer Ty Cobb later denied pardon consideration. At Quantico, however, Trump tempered his attack, largely refraining from criticizing the bureau in his speech and instead championing a pro–law enforcement, “law and order” agenda. He promised loyalty to police, vowed to crack down on gangs such as MS-13, and defended policies easing local access to surplus military equipment. The president’s earlier criticisms, along with disclosures about edits to the Comey draft and anti‑Trump texts by an FBI agent, have intensified scrutiny and prompted defenses of the bureau by FBI leaders and associations.

Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed a recently publicized dossier alleging ties between Russia and President-elect Donald Trump as "fake" and part of an effort to undermine Trump's legitimacy. Speaking in Moscow, Putin said the unverified memos — compiled by former British spy Christopher Steele and circulated among U.S. intelligence and political leaders — were being used in an "ongoing acute political struggle" in the United States. He called those behind the dossier "worse than prostitutes," mocked its salacious claims about Trump's behavior in a Moscow hotel, and questioned the notion that Russian intelligence would pursue an American billionaire. Putin suggested opponents might even try to provoke Maidan-style unrest in Washington to block Trump from taking office, and he criticized late-December U.S. sanctions as attempts to tie the president-elect’s "hands and feet." The dossier alleges, among other things, that Russians funneled hacked Democratic documents to WikiLeaks in exchange for Trump sidelining Ukraine, and that kompromat could be used to blackmail Trump. Trump has labeled the dossier "fake news" and shrugged off low approval polls as rigged; Martin Luther King III said Trump spoke of representing all Americans in a private meeting. Russian spokesmen said there are no planned additional Putin-Obama contacts beyond their November Peru meeting.

On June 5, a woman identified only as Avital says a Southwest agent in Las Vegas told her her cleavage was “inappropriate” and she could not board a 6 a.m. flight to New York unless she buttoned her flannel. Wearing a loose cotton sundress, flannel and scarf, Avital refused to conceal herself and boarded. She later called the interaction “slut shaming,” noting a man nearby wore a T‑shirt with a condom display and was not confronted. Southwest apologized and offered her a refund, citing Contract of Carriage language that lets staff refuse transport for lewd or patently offensive clothing and asking customers to use “good judgment” for a family‑focused onboard atmosphere. The incident highlights a pattern of complaints against Southwest: prior passengers were removed or shamed for perceived immodesty, size, or other subjective reasons, and some received apologies only after publicizing their stories. Critics urge clearer, published dress‑code rules to prevent individual employees from exercising vague discretion that can humiliate travelers.

Scientists have discovered that Saturn’s outermost ring, the Phoebe ring, is far larger and composed of much finer material than previously thought. Originally detected in 2009 by the Spitzer Space Telescope, the faint ring was known to extend between about 128 and 207 Saturn radii (RS). New infrared observations from NASA’s Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) show the ring actually stretches from roughly 100 RS to about 270 RS—more than 270 times Saturn’s radius—making it the largest ring in the system by a wide margin. If Saturn were the size of a basketball, the ring would extend nearly two-thirds the length of a football field outward.

The Phoebe ring is invisible to the naked eye and seen only in infrared because its particles absorb sunlight and glow thermally. Analysis indicates the dusty component is dominated by very small grains: roughly 90% of the cross-sectional area comes from particles smaller than a soccer ball, and many grains are microns in size. Larger bodies (radii >10 cm) contribute at most about 10% of the ring’s visible area. This skew toward tiny particles may reflect the ring’s radiative and collisional physics and could offer insight into the Saturn system’s history.

The ring likely originates from the dark, distant moon Phoebe; impact ejecta from Phoebe appear to have produced a vast, long-lived debris cloud. Because orbital decay times at such distances are enormous—possibly longer than the age of the solar system—material persists rather than coalescing into another moon. The Phoebe ring’s unexpected scale and composition challenge simple textbook ideas about ring evolution and suggest similarly extended, faint rings or clouds might exist around other giant planets.

In a turbulent election year the tea party has loomed large rhetorically, reshaping debate, toppling incumbents and elevating new conservative figures. But a Washington Post canvass of hundreds of local tea party groups finds a looser, less organized reality: many groups are small, diffuse, and only loosely connected to national organizations. Of more than 1,400 possible groups identified, The Post verified and reached 647; 70 percent reported no political campaigning this year. Most lack formal candidate slates, national leaders, significant funds, or clear, unified goals. Local chapters often describe themselves as forums for like-minded discussion rather than electoral machines, emphasizing limits on spending and government size while generally downplaying social issues. National outfits such as FreedomWorks and Tea Party Express, run by experienced operatives, contrast sharply with the sporadic grassroots chapters. The Post found uncertainty about the true scope of the movement—some listed “groups” are tiny or transient—and noted anger and distrust of government as key motivators. That diffuse, internet-enabled structure makes the tea party both omnipresent and hard to pin down politically, posing a vexing asymmetrical challenge to establishment figures, including President Obama.

McDonald's operated in Bolivia for 14 years with eight locations but consistently lost money and shut down in 2002, leaving Bolivia the only country in the Americas without the chain. A documentary, Why did McDonald’s Bolivia go Bankrupt?, explores why Bolivians largely rejected the fast-food model. Interviewees — including cooks, sociologists, nutritionists and educators — say Bolivians distinguish between hamburgers and “fast food,” viewing a proper meal as one prepared with care, time, hygiene and dedication. That cultural standard made McDonald’s quick, processed offerings unattractive. The case is often cited as a rare example of popular resistance to a global corporate food model.

Since its 1955 discovery by amateur fossil hunter Francis Tully in Illinois’ Mazon Creek deposits, the oddball Tully monster (Tullimonstrum gregarium) has confounded paleontologists. Its strange mix of features—eyestalks, a long toothed proboscis, a torpedo-shaped body and triangular tail—led to wildly differing interpretations over decades: worm, mollusk, arthropod, conodont, or an entirely unique phylum. The fossil’s fame grew—Illinois even named it the state fossil—because Mazon Creek’s exceptional preservation yields many detailed impressions of this soft-bodied animal, typically 12 inches long (up to about 18 inches).

A multidisciplinary team from the Field Museum, Argonne National Laboratory, Yale University and the American Museum of Natural History used advanced imaging at Argonne’s Advanced Photon Source plus study of roughly 2,000 Field Museum specimens to resolve the long-running mystery. Published in Nature, their work presents strong evidence that the Tully monster is a vertebrate on the stem lineage leading to lampreys. Key findings included chemical signatures—zinc in the eye stalks—similar to vertebrate fossil eyes, identification of structures interpreted as gill openings like those of primitive fishes, and crucially a reinterpretation of a previously identified “gut trace.” That light, two-dimensional structure is better explained as a notochord, a primitive backbone, whose curvature through the tail region matches lamprey-like anatomy rather than shark or other fish patterns.

Researchers emphasize there was no single dramatic revelation but a convergence of morphological, chemical and imaging evidence that increasingly pointed toward a lamprey-related chordate. The result moves Tullimonstrum out of “problematica” and onto the vertebrate tree, resolving a paleontological puzzle that intrigued scientists for more than half a century.

At a tense UCLA meeting, the University of California Board of Regents approved a 32% undergraduate fee increase to be phased in by next fall, raising basic fees to about $10,300 plus roughly $1,000 in campus charges and significant additional room, board and book costs. Hundreds of students from multiple campuses protested outside, chanting, beating drums, linking arms and staging sit-ins and tent encampments; some barricaded themselves in Campbell Hall and a group occupied a classroom building. Fourteen demonstrators were arrested earlier. Students warned the hike would especially hurt undocumented and minority students and those from low-income families, forcing some to work more, take leaves or abandon college. Only the student regent opposed the increase; UC President Mark Yudof cited state budget cuts and urged exploring financial-aid options.

A major Australian Crime Commission report has concluded that doping is widespread across Australian professional sport, with peptides and hormones being used by athletes and facilitated by sports scientists, high-performance coaches and other sports staff. The investigation found multiple players across different codes using banned substances and identified the involvement of organized-crime syndicates in supplying drugs, noting a growing criminal footprint in the market. Although no individuals were named, the commission warned the problem crosses sporting codes and is evolving, drawing parallels with the U.S. investigation into Lance Armstrong while stressing the Australian threat is current. The Australian Football League and National Rugby League are under particular scrutiny. Former ASADA head Richard Ings described the findings as the “blackest day in Australian sport,” underscoring the severity of the systemic issue.

Reports claim Jersey Shore star Nicole “Snooki” Polizzi is about three months pregnant by boyfriend Jionni LaValle, despite her recent denials on Good Morning America. The news, breaking amid filming of her spinoff with Jenni “JWoww” Farley in Jersey City, has tabloid and production implications: sources say she may sell the announcement to US Weekly and producers might be hiding a growing bump during delays. The piece situates Snooki’s situation within a broader social trend—rising births to single young women—and argues her challenges mirror those faced by many expectant single mothers, only magnified by celebrity. Concerns are raised about how pregnancy will affect Snooki’s career built on party-centric antics, her endorsement deals, and public image, and whether she can parlay the pregnancy into televised content. The article also notes Snooki’s history of heavy drinking, prompting sensational questions about fetal alcohol risks, while leaving open whether producers view the news as a liability or opportunity.

The document reports that the U.S. Intelligence Community inspector general informed Congress that a limited review of Hillary Clinton’s private-server emails found classified intelligence in some messages that lacked classification markings. IG Charles McCullough sampled 40 emails and identified four that “contained classified [intelligence community] information” and said none bore classification or dissemination markings; State FOIA officials warned there could be hundreds of classified messages among the roughly 30,000 emails Clinton provided. The four remain classified, a spokeswoman said. The development prompted conflicting media and Justice Department statements about whether a criminal probe was requested; inspectors general reportedly asked DOJ to examine potential mishandling, but no decision to open a criminal investigation had been made. Clinton responded by calling reports inaccurate, noting previous denials that she sent classified information, and saying she’s released pages and will answer congressional questions while focusing on campaign issues. Republicans, including House Speaker John Boehner and Rep. Trey Gowdy, urged Clinton to surrender her server for forensic review, criticizing her judgment and alleging national-security risks. Democrats including Rep. Elijah Cummings contested some assertions about who sought criminal inquiry. The piece recounts State Department IG memos finding “hundreds” of potentially classified emails and concerns about future public releases. Separately, Clinton told the AP she accepts responsibility for using a private account, has been transparent, and called the controversy a distraction that hasn’t harmed her campaign efforts. The document also includes lengthy portions of Executive Order 13526 detailing classification, declassification, safeguarding, oversight, and penalties for handling national-security information.

Pete Kostelnick, 29, completed a coast-to-coast run from San Francisco to New York City in 42 days, 6 hours and about 30 minutes, smashing the 36-year-old transcontinental record held by Frank Giannino Jr. (46 days, 8 hours, 36 minutes). Kostelnick averaged just over 72 miles per day and covered roughly 3,067 miles, finishing on the steps of New York City Hall on Oct. 24 after an 87-mile final leg that began at midnight. Giannino greeted him at the finish, helped hold the banner, and presented a gold baton in a symbolic passing of the record. Kostelnick, accompanied by a small escort and greeted by crowds chanting and running with him, described the effort as more mentally and emotionally taxing than physical, crediting support from fans and strangers across the country. He began the run on Sept. 12, and despite ankle and shin trouble that forced a rest day early on and a couple of falls, he steadily grew stronger. Kostelnick’s interest in the record was sparked five years earlier after meeting ultra-runner Marshall Ulrich; after winning the Badwater Ultramarathon twice, he felt ready. Ulrich and other endurance veterans praised the achievement as possibly the most significant running feat in decades, noting Kostelnick’s choice of the longer, more challenging northern route through the Sierra and Rockies. Supported by a dedicated crew, rigorous calorie intake, multiple GPS trackers, and witness logs, Kostelnick’s performance awaits Guinness verification. He plans rest time with his wife and, for now, no more running.

Researchers have restored meaningful bladder control in rats with severe spinal cord injuries by coaxing damaged nerves to regenerate across a surgically created gap. The team, led by Jerry Silver at Case Western Reserve, removed a segment of spinal cord, grafted a peripheral nerve taken from the rib into the gap, applied an enzyme (chondroitinase) to digest scar tissue, and added a growth factor to stimulate axon growth. Over months, axons extended through the graft and beyond—about 2 cm—reconnecting with neural circuits that control urination. After six months the rats could largely decide when to urinate and even showed slight leg movement, though they did not regain walking. This is the first demonstration that nerve regeneration can restore bladder function after a devastating cord injury in animals. Experts call the advance important because loss of bladder control causes serious medical complications in people with spinal injuries. Researchers caution that further studies in larger animals are needed to assess safety and efficacy before human trials, and several technical challenges remain. If translatable to humans, the approach could improve quality of life and reduce kidney damage from catheter dependence.

Robert D. Monroe, 50, of Shorewood has been criminally charged with 13 felony counts alleging he cast multiple ballots in several 2011–2012 elections. A Milwaukee County complaint says Monroe used addresses in Shorewood, Milwaukee and Lebanon, Indiana, and in some instances voted in the names of his son and his girlfriend’s son. The complaint alleges two ballots in the April 2011 Wisconsin Supreme Court race, two in the August 2011 Alberta Darling recall, five in the 2012 Walker-Barrett gubernatorial recall, one illegal ballot in an August 2012 primary, and two ballots in the November 2012 presidential election. Prosecutors say Monroe cast an in-person absentee ballot in Shorewood on Nov. 1, 2012, then drove to Indiana and voted there on Nov. 6 using an Indiana driver’s license; he owns a house in Indiana. The investigation began in Waukesha County after questions about an absentee ballot linked to his son, then shifted to Milwaukee and tied into records from another John Doe inquiry. Investigators say DNA testing on absentee ballot envelopes found only Monroe’s DNA and that text messages show he urged family members to register and vote. The complaint describes Monroe as a health-care executive with an MBA and notes he has discussed attending law school. He faces up to 18 months in prison, two years’ extended supervision and $10,000 fines per count. Monroe is not in custody; his initial appearance is July 17. He is represented by attorneys Franklyn Gimbel and Steven McGaver.

The Transportation Security Administration announced that, beginning April 25, passengers may carry small pocketknives and certain sporting equipment onto U.S. flights for the first time since 9/11. Allowed items include knives with retractable blades under 2.36 inches (6 cm) and narrower than 1/2 inch, up to two golf clubs, hockey and lacrosse sticks, billiard cues, ski poles and some novelty or lightweight bats. TSA Administrator John Pistole said the change aligns U.S. rules with international standards, speeds checkpoints by reducing time spent confiscating non-threatening items and lets screeners focus on threats that could cause catastrophic damage, such as non-metallic explosives. Some knives—those with locking blades or molded handles—and box cutters and razor blades remain banned. The decision drew strong criticism from flight attendant unions, who argue these items increase risks to cabin crew and passengers and will crowd overhead bins. TSA defended the move by citing hardened cockpit doors, armed marshals and trained crew as existing protections.

Florence’s mayor, Dario Nardella, has begun an experiment to discourage tourists from eating and loitering on the steps of historic churches by hosing those areas and nearby pavements at lunchtime. The initiative started with the steps of the Basilica of Santa Croce and Santo Spirito; workers pour water over steps so anyone who sits there will get wet. Nardella framed the measure as a gentler alternative to fines, aimed at restoring “decorum” and protecting cultural sites rather than targeting tourists broadly. He blamed day-trippers who spend only hours in the city and leave litter on UNESCO-listed streets, while stressing that visitors remain welcome and that eating while walking is not banned. The move drew mixed reactions online: some locals called it elitist or feared it would deter visitors, while others joked that picnickers would not mind being sprinkled in hot weather. Nardella clarified the city will not use “water cannons” but simply clean steps and evaluate whether to extend the practice to pavements. The step-hosing is part of wider efforts to manage mass tourism in Italy’s heritage cities: Florence has tightened rules on restaurant sourcing and rejected a McDonald’s piazza application, and Venice has introduced capacity controls and bans on new takeaway outlets in its centre. Nardella argues such measures protect historic sites from the pressures of millions of visitors each year.

Syrian President Bashar al-Assad’s rare public speech at the Damascus Opera House dashed hopes for negotiation and risked prolonging the country’s 21-month civil war. Analysts said Assad barely acknowledged international mediator Lakhdar Brahimi’s proposals and instead framed the uprising as driven by “murderous criminals” and foreign-backed terrorists, refusing to accept a transitional government or meaningful concessions. His stance complicates Russia’s diplomatic sheltering of Damascus and could prompt Brahimi to abandon his mission, forcing the “Friends of Syria” to choose between more aggressive intervention or a protracted conflict. The United Nations estimates over 60,000 dead; neither government nor rebels appear close to decisive victory. Fighting continued near Damascus, Idlib, Aleppo and Hama, with reports of bombardment, sieges, and civilian flight. Western governments condemned Assad’s remarks—U.S. officials called them evidence of regime brutality and irrationality—while Iran praised the plan. Domestically, supporters celebrated; critics said the speech entrenched divisions and offered no accountability for arrests or airstrikes. Assad thanked military personnel, vowed to stay, and appealed to Syrians who hadn’t “sold” the country to foreigners. Observers warned his defiance signals a long, bleak struggle with few good outcomes and reinforced fears the conflict will drag on.

Kansas House Bill 2453, passed 72-49, would let businesses and state employees refuse service to same-sex couples on religious grounds, broadly covering “public accommodations.” Critics warn it enables widespread discrimination—grocers, hotels, hospitals, ambulances and public agencies could deny service or eject patrons, with those defendants immune from civil suits and entitled to recover attorneys’ fees. The bill’s vague language, especially clauses covering transactions “related to” marriages or civil unions, could permit denial of service based on perceived sexual orientation or suspected wedding planning. Supporters frame the measure as protecting religious liberty amid court challenges to bans on gay marriage and cite cases where vendors were penalized for refusing wedding-related services. The measure sparked national backlash, business opposition and mobilization on social media. Senate President Susan Wagle and other Republican leaders signaled most Senate Republicans oppose the bill as written, prompting plans for substantial revisions—likely removing public employees and narrowing scope—after employers and chambers warned it would harm hiring, tourism, and be unworkable.

In September 2017, 68-year-old grandfather William Hannah, hospitalized at Salford Royal after being hit by a car, died the day after a routine lung washout was mistakenly performed with cleaning detergent instead of saline. Hannah had suffered a traumatic brain injury and multiple fractures and was on a ventilator in critical care when he developed a lung infection. According to the family’s lawyers and the hospital’s internal serious-incident report, a doctor asked a healthcare assistant for saline; the assistant instead handed an unlabelled bottle containing a detergent solution prepared for cleaning equipment. The doctor, unaware of the mix-up, used the solution to wash out Hannah’s lungs. The error was discovered only when the doctor later sought the cleaning fluid to sterilize instruments. Staff attempted to remove the detergent by performing an additional washout, but Hannah’s condition worsened and he died the following day. The hospital’s review cited multiple contributing factors: an unstocked trolley, distractions from other life-critical tasks, poor two-way communication, lack of bottle labeling, inadequate staff training, and insufficient risk assessment. Salford Royal NHS Foundation Trust apologized, acknowledging that Hannah did not receive the standard of care it expects, and said it has introduced measures to prevent recurrence. The family criticized the trust’s handling of the investigation as lacking compassion and are pursuing legal action to hold the hospital accountable and ensure lessons are learned. An inquest at Bolton Coroner’s Court and hearings beginning February 2019 will further examine the circumstances and the extent to which the error contributed to his death.

Reports reveal that Iranian-linked hackers penetrated U.S. industrial-control systems multiple times, including a previously undisclosed 2013 breach of a small New York dam and a major intrusion into Calpine Corp.’s networks that exposed detailed engineering diagrams and credentials for dozens of power plants. Investigators say intruders in the dam case probed defenses but did not take control; the breach briefly raised alarms at the White House after it was initially misidentified as an attack on a larger Oregon facility. Security researcher Brian Wallace uncovered the Calpine intrusion while tracing unrelated malware; attackers had stored more than 19,000 stolen files on unsecured FTP servers, including 71 plant schematics, usernames and passwords, and configuration maps enabling remote access and masking of malicious activity. Cylance’s analysis linked activity to Iran-based IP addresses and Persian-language snippets, though definitive government attribution remains uncertain. Experts warn such incursions fit a broader pattern of nation-state teams—from Iran, Russia and China—mapping U.S. grid and industrial networks to leave stealthy footholds that could be exploited if geopolitical conditions change. DHS statistics show industrial-control incidents rising (295 in fiscal 2015), and agencies caution aging, Internet-connected systems, insecure contractor relationships, and proliferation of smart meters create many vulnerabilities. Analysts say an orchestrated attack on a handful of critical stations could trigger prolonged, costly blackouts, while defenders note that causing a nationwide outage would be difficult though not impossible. The episodes have prompted calls from lawmakers for clearer cyberwarfare thresholds and response standards, and led DHS and industry to expand briefings and assistance—but officials acknowledge defenses lag, especially among smaller utilities outside federal regulation. Overall, the disclosures underscore the stealthy accumulation of operational knowledge by foreign hackers and persistent concerns about the U.S. energy sector’s readiness to prevent or respond to a damaging cyberattack.

War for the Planet of the Apes concludes Matt Reeves’s contemporary trilogy with a stirring, soulful, and morally resonant war drama that often eclipses its genre trappings. Reeves and co-writer Mark Bomback craft a film that synthesizes homage to the original 1960s “Apes” kitsch with a rich, new mythology centered on Caesar (Andy Serkis), the motion-capture-created chimp leader whose emotional depth and moral complexity anchor the story. After an attack on the apes’ forest home by a fanatic military commander known as the Colonel (Woody Harrelson), Caesar sets out on a revenge mission that threatens his role as a diplomatic leader and tests his nobler instincts. Joined by loyal Maurice (Karin Konoval), a mute orphaned girl the apes adopt (Amiah Miller), and an anxious former zoo ape called Bad Ape (Steve Zahn), Caesar’s small band moves from guerilla conflict to an epic, heartbreaking rescue and escape narrative that evokes The Great Escape as well as darker historical parallels.

The film leans into weighty themes—internment camps, refugees, the Holocaust, biblical imagery, and modern topicality like walls and purity rhetoric—sometimes with blunt symbolism, especially in the Colonel’s fanaticism and his project to build a barrier. Yet the movie keeps its dramatic focus: violence has consequences, leadership is costly, and dehumanization can blind people to sentience beyond their species. Technical accomplishments stand out; motion-capture performances render the apes’ emotions convincing, and steady editing keeps action clear. Small humanizing moments—a gorilla adorning a girl with blossoms, Bad Ape’s childlike trauma—add poignancy amid the brutality.

Though occasionally heavy-handed politically and featuring a few caricatured humans, the film remains a thoughtful, adult blockbuster that prioritizes character, moral weight, and cinematic experience over franchise product. Its emotional sweep and disciplined storytelling make it a fitting and powerful conclusion to this era of Planet of the Apes.

Apple’s iOS 7 introduced a clean, minimal visual design but added extensive motion: zooming folders and apps, sliding app switcher, full-screen transitions and a parallax home screen. While many users find this dynamic, people with vestibular disorders or motion sensitivity report dizziness, nausea and vertigo triggered by the new animations. Reports from developers and users describe feeling ill during app transitions and needing to close their eyes or avoid using upgraded devices; some have reverted to iOS 6 phones. Experts explain the issue as visual-vestibular conflict—when perceived self-motion from screen effects contradicts inner-ear signals of being stationary—affecting a minority of people but far more severely among those with vestibular dysfunction. Apple’s “Reduce Motion” setting only disables parallax and does not stop zooming or sliding, leaving few effective remedies. Advocates urge Apple to acknowledge the problem, offer comprehensive system-level controls to disable motion, and engage with accessibility communities. Developers are encouraged to provide in-app options to limit animations and ensure effects serve functional purposes. Until broader fixes arrive, affected users are left with limited coping strategies like resting, avoiding triggers, or not using their devices.

Former tennis star Jennifer Capriati was rushed to a Riviera Beach, Florida, hospital after a reported possible drug overdose, TMZ says. Paramedics responded to a hotel call early today and transported her; her father told TMZ she is recovering well. Capriati, who turned pro at 13, won 14 career titles including three Grand Slams and Olympic gold in 1992. After early success and massive earnings as a teenager, she struggled in the mid-1990s with injuries, legal troubles, stays in rehab and loss of endorsements. She resurged to win the 2001 Australian and French Opens and the 2002 Australian title, but later faced further injuries and depression and has not returned to competitive tennis.

U.S. officials say at least 16 Americans — possibly including government employees and family members — have been affected by mysterious "incidents" in Cuba that began in late December 2016. State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert called the situation unprecedented and said symptoms have varied widely, including headaches, vision problems, balance and walking issues, memory loss, nausea and hearing loss. Medical evaluations reviewed by CBS News diagnosed some diplomats with conditions as serious as mild traumatic brain injury and probable central nervous system damage. Some affected personnel were medically evacuated to Miami; others remained in Cuba. Authorities report the harmful episodes appear to have ceased since spring, no device has been found, and investigations are ongoing. U.S. agencies on the ground in Havana include the FBI and the State Department’s Bureau of Diplomatic Security; the Cuban government denies involvement but has been contacted and is said to be cooperating, though not jointly investigating. U.S. actions have included asking two Cuban diplomats in Washington to leave, framed as holding Cuba responsible under the Vienna Convention for protecting diplomats. Separately, Treasury removed numerous Cuba-related domain names from a sanctions list, a move officials say reflects delisting of a single company with many sites rather than broad policy change.

When sixth-grader Cruz Riojas arrived in Linda Hooper’s Brown Elementary classroom in the early 1980s, he was a feared, violent student — a “holy terror” who threw chairs, attacked classmates and used humor to mask deeper pain. He was two years behind in reading, classified as special education, and carried the scars of a chaotic home: a one-room lean-to shared with his mother, five half-siblings and an abusive stepfather known as “No. 5.” Cruz wore the same clothes daily, came to school with lice multiple times, and had learned to fight for attention and survival.

Hooper, a veteran teacher, initially vowed she’d quit rather than have him in her class, but found herself responsible for him when fellow teachers repeatedly sent Cruz to her room. Over that difficult sixth-grade year she began engaging him in small classroom tasks and later hired him for odd jobs with her husband, Gale. Those gestures — steady attention, pay he could keep, a clean wardrobe, and a safe home — slowly transformed Cruz. He ran 7.5 miles to the Hoopers’ house after fights at home and increasingly sought refuge there. When his stepfather kicked him out at age 12, Cruz’s mother brought him to hide behind an 18-wheeler and asked Linda to keep him “for the weekend.” He never left.

With continued support, including special-education teacher James Harris who helped him academically, Cruz tested out of special education by high school graduation, attended Texas Tech, and later worked in payroll in San Antonio. Though the Hoopers feared social stigma — acknowledging that in the early 1980s white families seldom adopted Mexican children — their bond deepened. Cruz longed to honor them: shortly before his 30th birthday he asked to be legally adopted. In January 1998 he became Cruz Hooper in a formal ceremony with his wife, Anel. The family now includes two children; the Hoopers have four daughters and cherish Cruz as the son who carried their name forward.

Hooper reflects that welcoming Cruz changed her life and teaching: she began seeing every student as a potential “Cruz.” Cruz credits perseverance and the Hoopers’ unwavering care for his turnaround. For both, the relationship that began in a turbulent classroom grew into enduring family, proof, they say, that patience and love can rewrite a child’s future.

Actress Melissa Gilbert, known for Little House on the Prairie, is facing significant tax troubles after the IRS filed a $360,551 federal tax lien covering 2011–2013. Gilbert says the recession, a divorce and fewer acting opportunities led to the liability; she has negotiated an installment plan to pay it off. California previously filed $112,527 in tax liens against her since 2013. The IRS breaks the debt into $219,989 for 2011, $99,405 for 2012 and $41,157 for 2013. Gilbert and husband Timothy Busfield moved to Howell, Michigan, in 2013, renting a Victorian home and becoming active locally—she’s written a cookbook, My Prairie Cookbook, signed books in the area and joined charity events. Landlord Brenda Korth says rent was paid on time and the couple were welcome in town. The couple are relocating within the county; Busfield says the move is unrelated to the tax debt.

A woman in Kings Mountain, North Carolina, ended a nationwide manhunt for Dylann Storm Roof after recognizing him from police surveillance images and a distinctive license tag. Debbie Dills saw a man with a bowl haircut in a car she’d seen described in news reports, called her husband and 911, and alerted authorities. Roof was arrested in Shelby, N.C., at a traffic stop shortly afterward; he cooperated and waived extradition to South Carolina. Roof, 21, is accused of killing nine people during a prayer meeting at Emanuel AME Church in Charleston, an attack widely denounced as a hate crime. In the days following the shooting, a clearer portrait emerged: friends said Roof recently reconnected with a childhood friend and began voicing racist views, referencing the Trayvon Martin case and incidents in Baltimore, and advocating segregation and violent action on behalf of the “white race.” His social media displayed symbols associated with former white-ruled regimes in Africa, and court records show recent adult charges including a pending felony drug case and a misdemeanor trespassing charge. The Southern Poverty Law Center said Roof was not previously on its radar but, judging from his online presence, appeared to be a “disaffected white supremacist,” highlighting concerns about domestic extremist violence.

On October 22, 2016 (New Zealand time), Dr. Gordon Hamilton, a University of Maine climate scientist working with the U.S. Antarctic Program (USAP) managed by the National Science Foundation (NSF), was fatally injured when the snowmobile he was operating fell into a crevasse in a heavily crevassed area known as the McMurdo Shear Zone (SZ), about 25 miles south of McMurdo Station. The SZ is a perilous, roughly three-mile-wide, 125+-mile-long region where the Ross and McMurdo ice shelves meet; ice there can be up to 650 feet thick. Dr. Hamilton’s body was recovered and will be returned to his family in Maine. An accident investigation has been opened by USAP.

Hamilton, an accomplished glaciologist, had been leading research using robotic platforms equipped with ground-penetrating radar to map and study ice-shelf stability and identify buried crevasses. At the time of the accident his science team was camped about 200 yards from a USAP South Pole Operations Traverse crevasse remediation team; both teams included experienced personnel and mountaineers and had received crevasse and glacial safety training. They had been identifying and filling crevasses earlier in the week and were beginning work on a newly identified crevasse when the incident occurred. NSF and polar program leaders expressed sorrow and emphasized the inherent risks of Antarctic fieldwork. Hamilton is survived by his wife, Fiona, and their two children.

A Pembroke Pines Arby’s sparked controversy after Sgt. Jennifer Martin says she was effectively denied service at the drive-through because she is a police officer. According to Martin’s report, clerk Kenny Davenport took her card but then manager Angel Mirabal approached the window and told her “he doesn’t want to serve you because you are a police officer.” Martin said she felt uncomfortable, was handed her food amid laughter, and later received a refund and the manager’s contact information; Davenport did not give his contact. The incident prompted protests by officers’ wives and calls from local police unions for a national Arby’s boycott and for the employees involved to be fired. Broward and Dade County police unions condemned the episode as part of a troubling trend of disrespect toward law enforcement. Pembroke Pines Police Chief Dan Giustino called Arby’s corporate office; CEO Paul Brown and SVP Scott Boatwright apologized, saying the behavior was unacceptable and not representative of the company, and Giustino accepted the apology and considers the matter closed. Arby’s issued a statement calling it an isolated matter and promising follow-up training. Davenport and his grandfather, however, say the remark was a poorly judged joke made during a busy shift and have asked that it not be blown out of proportion. The dispute has drawn strong local reaction and heightened scrutiny of how Arby’s will handle corrective action.

Jeffrey Zaslow, a 53-year-old Wall Street Journal reporter and bestselling author based in West Bloomfield, died in a car accident in northern Michigan. According to the Antrim County Sheriff’s Office and reports from Fox 2 Detroit, Zaslow lost control on a snow-covered stretch of M-32 near Elmira and collided with a semi-truck; the crash occurred after a book-signing in Petoskey. A Philadelphia native, he was married to Fox 2 anchor Sherry Margolis and was father to three daughters: Jordan, Alex and Eden.

Known for empathetic, emotionally resonant nonfiction, Zaslow coauthored The Last Lecture with Randy Pausch, which grew from a Journal column and a viral online video into a global bestseller. Other notable works include The Girls from Ames, Highest Duty about Captain Chesley Sullenberger, Gabby: A Story of Courage and Hope with Rep. Gabrielle Giffords and Mark Kelly, and his most recent book, The Magic Room, set in a Michigan bridal shop. He had earlier succeeded Ann Landers in a Chicago Sun-Times advice-column contest and wrote a popular WSJ relationships column. Colleagues remembered him as outgoing, meticulous and deeply moved by family moments; arrangements are pending.

A Long Island mother, Kathi Fedden, has filed a federal wrongful-death lawsuit after her 29-year-old son, Peter Fedden, was killed in a high-speed, alcohol-related crash in July 2013. The suit alleges that earlier that night Peter was involved in a separate crash while “severely intoxicated” and visibly injured, but Suffolk County police officers — who the complaint says were friendly with him because he owned a deli that provided steep discounts to officers — drove him home instead of arresting him or otherwise preventing him from continuing to drive. According to the complaint, officers towed Peter’s car to a nearby schoolyard, told other parties at the scene to leave without taking witness statements or photographs, placed Peter in the back of a squad car, and then dropped him at his Commack residence where multiple vehicles were parked. Moments later he took his mother’s car, drove at speeds over 90–100 mph and fatally crashed into a marketing firm in Hauppauge, causing substantial property damage and four months of repairs.

The lawsuit names Suffolk County and specific officers, as well as the Ruby Tuesday restaurant where Peter allegedly drank earlier that evening. It contends a bartender there served him excessive alcohol and lacked training to recognize intoxication. Peter’s attorney produced what he said were numerous police organization cards found on Peter the night he was killed to suggest familiarity with officers. Suffolk County declined comment due to pending litigation. The marketing firm owner called the suit frivolous, arguing Peter endangered the community by getting into a second car. The complaint seeks significant damages — reports cite amounts of $30 million and $130 million — alleging police actions “created the events leading to Peter’s wrongful death.”

Ken Mehlman’s public revelation that he is gay, confirmed in an Atlantic interview, is a significant moment in American politics. As President Bush’s 2004 campaign manager and RNC chairman from 2005–2007, Mehlman is the most prominent Republican to come out, and his disclosure forces colleagues and the party to reckon with gay identity beyond caricature. Friends and former associates have reacted with support; GOP figures like Michael Steele and Ed Gillespie framed Mehlman’s announcement as personal and consequential, noting generational shifts in attitudes toward same-sex marriage within the party. Mehlman has begun advocating for gay marriage from inside the GOP, advising the American Foundation for Equal Rights and arguing that marriage equality fits conservative principles—individual freedom, limited government, and the social virtues of marriage. His stance reframes support for same-sex marriage as compatible with socially conservative values, not merely liberal or libertarian ideology. Reactions range from respectful encouragement to sharp criticism and calls for apology over past Republican anti-gay strategies during his tenure. Regardless, Mehlman’s openness may further normalize homosexuality among conservatives and could help provide Republican-friendly arguments for marriage equality, potentially influencing party debate and public opinion.

A week of Quran burnings by U.S. military personnel in Afghanistan set off deadly violence that has exposed a major vulnerability in the U.S. exit strategy: reliance on small advisory teams living and working alongside Afghan security forces. After the burnings, an Afghan security official killed two senior NATO officers and an Afghan in uniform shot two American troops, highlighting repeated "insider" attacks that have rattled confidence in Afghan partners. NATO’s top commander pulled foreign advisers from key Afghan ministries, and several countries temporarily withdrew hundreds of military and civilian advisers. President Hamid Karzai urged calm and endorsed the withdrawals, but protests continued, including attacks that wounded American soldiers and left dozens of Afghans dead. U.S. officials pledged continued partnership, yet much cooperation is suspended and rebuilding trust is uncertain. Advisers—small teams far more exposed than large combat units—may have to limit time spent with Afghan counterparts, undermining effectiveness. Experts warn that the advisory model requires deep, constant engagement to work and will always carry fratricide risk rooted in cultural tensions. Plans call for U.S. troop reductions from 100,000 to 68,000 by summer and full NATO combat withdrawal by 2014; some analysts estimate 25,000 advisers could sustain Afghan forces, but only if advisers accept heightened personal risk.

A major draft federal report—the Third National Climate Assessment—concludes that human-driven climate change is already altering U.S. weather, ecosystems and infrastructure, and warns of substantially higher temperatures this century if emissions remain unchecked. Compiled by more than 240 scientists and experts, the 1,193-page assessment finds “unambiguous evidence” of warming: heat waves, longer hotter summers, heavier downpours, regional floods and droughts, melting glaciers and Arctic sea ice, rising seas, and increasing ocean acidity. Average U.S. temperatures have risen roughly 1.5°F since 1895, with most of that increase occurring since 1980. The report projects another 2°F to 4°F rise in most regions in the coming decades. By 2100, temperatures could increase 3°F–5°F if global emissions are sharply reduced after 2050, or as much as 5°F–10°F under continued high-emissions pathways. The assessment details regional impacts—stressed water supplies and threatened specialty crops in the Southwest, coastal flooding and erosion in California and the Southeast, more extreme precipitation in the Northeast and Midwest, and heightened heat- and drought-related risks across the West—and warns U.S. infrastructure and public health are already being affected. Environmental groups and former officials called for tougher actions, including stricter power plant carbon standards and expanded investment in community resilience. Some lawmakers, chiefly Republicans including Rep. Lamar Smith, challenged aspects of the science and plan to scrutinize the findings. The draft, produced under the Global Change Research Act, is open for public and scientific review through April; a National Research Council review will follow and a final assessment is expected in early 2014. The report stops short of prescribing policy but underscores the scale of risks tied to future emissions choices.

Cuba has developed a promising therapeutic lung cancer vaccine, Cimavax, but U.S. trade restrictions long prevented its wider use. During New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo’s recent visit to Havana, Roswell Park Cancer Institute finalized an agreement with Cuba’s Center for Molecular Immunology to bring Cimavax to the United States and pursue FDA approval and clinical trials. Roswell Park CEO Candace Johnson said the Cuban center will provide manufacturing documentation, toxicity data, and prior trial results; she hopes to file for testing within six to eight months and start trials within a year. Cimavax, produced after 25 years of research and offered free in Cuba since 2011 at about $1 per dose, does not directly attack tumors but induces antibodies against epidermal growth factor (EGF), slowing tumor growth and metastasis. A 2008 Phase II trial found recipients lived on average four to six months longer. While not a definitive cure, researchers see potential for preventive use and applications against other EGF-related cancers. Cuban biotech has a strong track record—developing interferon, vaccines for meningitis B and hepatitis B, and monoclonal antibodies—despite limited resources and decades of sanctions. Other Cuban candidates, like Racotumomab, are also under collaboration. Though Obama eased some restrictions on medical equipment, full research partnerships depend on Congress lifting the embargo. Cuomo’s delegation also facilitated tech and business deals, signaling that engagement may expand U.S.–Cuban scientific collaboration.

Russian president Vladimir Putin donned a number 11 jersey to play in an exhibition game at the All-Russia Festival of the Night Hockey League in Sochi, joining retired Soviet stars like Vyacheslav Fetisov and Pavel Bure. Footage showed him missing several close-range attempts—sometimes needing gentle taps from teammates to convert—but he eventually scored amid cheering fans. State media credited him with multiple goals and assists, claims not fully verified. The festival, begun in 2011 for over-40 amateurs, attracted 108 teams this year and political figures including Defense Minister Sergey Shoigu. The event came as another example of Putin’s staged macho publicity: past stunts include riding a horse bare-chested, posing with a tranquilized polar bear and snow leopard, scuba “discoveries” of ancient vases, and shooting darts at a whale for research.

Snap has begun selling its video-recording Spectacles directly online in the U.S. at Spectacles.com for $129.99, ending the limited vending-machine and pop-up-only distribution that produced long lines and high resale prices. Previously available through roving Snapbot vending machines and a now-closed NYC pop-up, the sunglasses record circular 10–30 second videos viewable in any phone orientation and come in three colors. Shipping is estimated at two to four weeks, purchases are limited to six pairs per household, and Snap now offers a $49.99 charging case and $9.99 cord (no longer sold on Amazon). Snap says the slow rollout helped test fit and demand; despite positive user response, the company acknowledged in its IPO filing that Spectacles have not yet generated significant revenue and near-term production costs may exceed related income. The move to online sales aims to broaden availability, boost user content creation, and demonstrate potential hardware revenue ahead of Snap’s public offering — even as questions remain about future camera products and profitability.

Facebook plans to unveil a long-rumored music platform at its f8 developer conference on Sept. 22 that will let users listen to music from within Facebook and see what friends are playing. Rather than hosting or streaming content itself, Facebook will integrate third-party services as content providers; reported launch partners include Spotify, Rdio and MOG, with others such as Rhapsody and Slacker also mentioned. The move aims to increase time spent on Facebook by making music a social, discoverable experience—sharing songs, playlists and listening activity among friends—and could extend to other media like movies if expanded. The deeper integrations could boost smaller streaming services by driving subscriptions through social exposure, although Facebook says there’s nothing new to announce. Observers note the strategy contrasts with vendors that host music on their own servers and that past social-network music attempts (e.g., MySpace) didn’t guarantee long-term success.

U.S. officials say Russian-linked hackers breached the White House’s unclassified computer network last year and gained access to sensitive, non-public details of President Obama’s schedule. Although the White House described the intrusion as affecting only an unclassified system, investigators told CNN and other outlets that the hackers could view intimate, real-time information—such as meetings and calls—that is tightly controlled and highly valuable to foreign intelligence services. The intrusion appears to have been routed through the State Department, where attackers had already established a foothold. Investigators believe the compromise began with a phishing email sent from a hijacked State Department account that delivered malware to a White House machine. The FBI, Secret Service and U.S. intelligence agencies treated the incident as among the most sophisticated attacks on government networks, tracing code and markers to actors they assess are linked to Russia, though official spokespeople declined public attribution.

Officials emphasized that classified networks were not believed to be compromised and stressed protocols that require classified work to occur on separate, more secure systems. Still, the breaches prompted shutdowns and security upgrades of the unclassified White House network and contributed to broader concern inside government about persistent Russian cyber operations. The revelations spurred calls from some lawmakers for stronger cybersecurity measures and legislation. The intrusions also intensified scrutiny of federal cyber defenses, coming amid heightened U.S.-Russia tensions over Ukraine and other geopolitical disputes.

In spring 2004 Swiss electrical engineer Raphaël Domjan imagined a daring test: circumnavigate the globe in a vessel powered entirely by solar energy. With financial backing from German entrepreneur Immo Stroeher and a design by New Zealander Craig Loomes, the 115-foot catamaran MS Turanor PlanetSolar was built from lightweight carbon material and outfitted with 38,000 photovoltaic cells charging six banks of lithium-ion batteries. Launched from Monaco in September 2010, the world’s largest solar boat completed a 37,294-mile voyage in about 584 days, finishing in Hercule Harbor after crossings of the Atlantic and Pacific, passage through the Panama and Suez canals, and stops from Miami and Cancún to Brisbane, Singapore and Abu Dhabi. The slow, deliberate trip included promotional stops, an encounter with pirates and occasional waits for sunlight, but demonstrated solar technology’s potential for marine use and sustainability. With the mission accomplished, Domjan and his team plan a book and documentary, and are weighing options for the vessel’s future—from scientific platform to green luxury yacht or mobile solar battery.

President Donald Trump’s first foreign trip as president — a nine-day, five-country swing across Saudi Arabia, Israel/Palestine, the Vatican, Belgium and Italy — was built around heavy religious symbolism and high-stakes diplomacy. Framed by the White House as a pilgrimage to the birthplaces of the three Abrahamic faiths and a bid to project American strength and unity, the itinerary was also intended to rebuild ties with allies, press regional partners on security issues and broadcast a message of cooperation among Jews, Christians and Muslims. But the trip came as Trump’s administration was beset by controversy at home and abroad, complicating the mission.

Administration officials, including National Security Adviser Gen. H.R. McMaster, cast the tour as unprecedented in combining visits to sites central to Judaism, Christianity and Islam. The White House listed three principal goals: project U.S. power, strengthen relationships with world leaders, and promote a message of religious unity. A stated focus was countering extremist ideology and rallying Muslim leaders to oppose radicalism, beginning with a high-profile speech in Riyadh to leaders from more than 50 Muslim-majority countries.

Yet many observers questioned whether Trump, whose campaign and early months in office included divisive rhetoric about Muslims, controversial comments about Jews and a public spat with Pope Francis, was the right messenger for a tour so explicitly couched in religious themes. Critics stressed his sparse history of personal religious observance, past statements like “Islam hates us,” and administration policies such as travel restrictions targeting several Muslim-majority countries. The involvement of aides like Stephen Miller — associated with hardline immigration views — in drafting the Riyadh speech raised further concern that the address might alienate Muslim audiences or conflate Islam with terrorism. Experts warned against implicitly endorsing Saudi religious models or failing to address Saudi human-rights issues while celebrating its custodianship of Islam’s holiest sites.

In Israel and the West Bank, Trump aimed to reaffirm U.S. support for Israel while encouraging a resumption of Israeli-Palestinian talks. Stops included Yad Vashem, the Israel Museum, the Western Wall, and Bethlehem, where he would meet Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas. The White House emphasized Trump had not come with a formal peace plan and would not serve as an arbiter of details, but would reiterate concerns about Israeli settlement expansion outside major blocs and say he had not abandoned a two-state solution. Diplomatic friction emerged over whether the Western Wall is in Israeli sovereign territory; U.S. officials’ ambiguous comments provoked Israeli unease and prompted the administration to emphasize the visit’s religious rather than political intent. Logistical issues also forced the cancellation of a planned helicopter landing at Masada, shifting that part of the program to the Israel Museum.

In Rome, Trump met Pope Francis, who signaled he would listen and seek common ground rather than preach. The Vatican encounter was carefully choreographed and brief — an opportunity to open channels despite earlier mutual criticism over immigration and borders. Brussels and Sicily would test Trump’s relations with NATO and other Western leaders as he sought reassurances from allies on burden-sharing and conveyed his “America First” economic and security priorities at the G7.

The trip’s promise — to reassert U.S. global leadership, present unity across faiths, and stabilize frayed relationships — was tempered by risks: domestic scandals that shadowed the president, prior inflammatory rhetoric that complicated outreach, and the diplomatic minefields of contested holy sites and regional politics. Advisers hoped the religious framing might capture public attention and provide a platform for bridging divides, but analysts cautioned that missteps or a lack of nuance could amplify tensions instead of healing them.

Many close to Jeb Bush say his presidential bid began to stumble in Dallas, where early senior staff meetings were held in a Hyatt at Dallas/Fort Worth airport — a pragmatic but awkward choice that signaled disorganization to donors and GOP insiders. What began as a centralized, inexpensive way to gather a geographically scattered team soon highlighted deeper problems: tensions between longtime Bush loyalists and new advisers, rapid hiring, and disputes over how to allocate resources between his official campaign and the allied Right to Rise super PAC. Those frictions intensified as Bush underperformed on the trail and in polls, culminating in a team shake-up that replaced the expected campaign manager role and elevated Danny Diaz while moving David Kochel to a strategist position focused on early states.

Bush’s exploratory effort projected confidence bolstered by fundraising prowess, but that strength created inflated expectations. Promises that the super PAC would raise massive sums fell short of early projections, and the campaign’s strategy — assuming a dominant financial advantage would deter rivals and that voters wouldn’t focus on him until later — proved flawed. On policy and delivery, Bush’s moderate stances on immigration and education alienated parts of the conservative base, while his wonky, lecture-like interactions failed to connect emotionally. A series of missteps culminated in a damaging mid-May interview sequence about the Iraq war, where inconsistent answers crystallized worries about his judgment and reluctance to distance himself from his brother’s legacy.

As rivals like Marco Rubio, Scott Walker and Rand Paul surged, and John Kasich prepared to compete for donors, Bush’s standing shifted from presumed front-runner to one of several top-tier candidates. Bush, traveling and speaking overseas, urged patience and framed the reorganization as corrective rather than catastrophic. Allies hope his financial resources and new management will steady the campaign as it pivots to more aggressive tactics against GOP rivals while he emphasizes retail campaigning and sustained competition in every state.

European counterterrorism forces disrupted an imminent Islamist plot against police in Belgium and France after coordinated raids led to 17–27 detentions across several countries and a shootout in Verviers that left two suspected attackers dead and a third wounded. Belgian authorities said 13 suspects were arrested in Belgium—most in Molenbeek, Brussels, Berchem and Verviers—and two in France; other media and intelligence reports described additional arrests across France, Germany and the Netherlands as part of a wider sweep. Investigators believe the Verviers gunmen were Belgian nationals who had returned from fighting in Syria and that the cell had planned to kill police officers on the street and attack police stations. Police recovered weapons, ammunition, explosives, police uniforms, radios, false documents and significant cash at the Verviers address; further material was seized in Molenbeek.

Belgian prosecutors emphasized the operation dismantled an active logistic network and averted a major attack, with officials likening the prevention to stopping “a second potential Paris.” Western intelligence sources told CNN they are monitoring as many as 20 sleeper cells—120–180 people—across France, Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands, raising fears of copycat or coordinated strikes. France deployed large security forces and put 122,000 officers, gendarmes and troops on patrol; Belgium kept heightened alert and placed troops on standby.

Separately, arrests in Paris targeted people linked to the recent Charlie Hebdo and kosher supermarket attacks; German raids detained suspected ISIS recruiters. Europol warned that decentralized, semi-independent extremists returning from Syria complicate detection, requiring closer international cooperation. Governments across Europe tightened security at synagogues, Jewish schools and transportation hubs amid continuing investigations and concerns about further attacks.

A hydroelectric project in southeastern Laos collapsed Monday, unleashing massive flooding, killing at least 19 people and leaving dozens missing as rescue teams search devastated communities. Officials said a saddle dam at the Xepian-Xe Nam Noy (Xe-Pian Xe-Namnoy) complex in Attapeu province failed, releasing an estimated five billion cubic meters of water that swept away homes and rendered more than 6,000–6,600 people homeless across multiple villages. Boats and emergency teams, including company, government and Red Cross responders, have been mobilized amid appeals for clothing, food, clean water, medicine and cash. Prime Minister Thongloun Sisoulith halted government business to oversee relief efforts.

The $1.02–$1.2 billion project, still under construction and slated to begin operations in 2019, is a joint venture led by South Korean firms SK Engineering & Construction and Korea Western Power, with Thailand’s Ratchaburi Electricity Generating Holding and the Lao Holding State Enterprise among partners; Thai lenders provided most financing. The 410 MW development was designed to export about 90% of its power to Thailand. Company sources cited unusually heavy rains and possible overflow of an auxiliary dam; investigators are determining whether overflow or structural collapse occurred. The disaster highlights long-standing environmental and social concerns about Laos’ aggressive hydropower expansion, which affects Mekong flows and ethnic-minority communities in resettlement zones. Information flow is constrained by Laos’ tight media environment.

The 2019 Golden Globe nominations produced many surprises and notable snubs across TV and film. TV surprises included The Good Place, Bodyguard and Who Is America?; big omissions were The Handmaid’s Tale, Westworld, Atlanta, GLOW, Maniac and Patrick Melrose. Several expected acting nominees—Sterling K.
