Brown, John Krasinski, Liev Schreiber, Bob Odenkirk, Jodie Comer, Ted Danson and Sam Elliott—were left out, replaced by newcomers like Stephan James and Billy Porter. In film, Cold War, Ethan Hawke (First Reformed), Nicholas Britell’s score (If Beale Street Could Talk) and Mary Poppins’ original songs were snubbed, while Vice and Mary Poppins Returns earned multiple nods. Overall the HFPA favored fresh choices and network comedies, confounding many predictions.

A Baltimore County police officer, identified as 29-year-old Amy Caprio, was killed Monday afternoon in Perry Hall while responding to a report about a suspicious vehicle. Caprio, a nearly four-year veteran honored previously for solving package-theft cases, confronted occupants of a black Jeep Wrangler on Linwen Way; witnesses said they heard a pop and saw the Jeep strike her. She was rushed to MedStar Franklin Square Medical Center and pronounced dead at 2:50 p.m. Authorities recovered the Jeep and found damage to a nearby patio door, leading investigators to believe a burglary may have been in progress. Body-camera footage and an autopsy were to be reviewed to determine whether she was shot, struck by the vehicle, or both.

A massive, hours-long manhunt ensued in the suburban neighborhood, with residents ordered to shelter in place, roads closed, and nearly 2,000 students held in schools until parents were allowed to pick them up. Initially police sought multiple suspects described as potentially armed and dangerous; by Tuesday a 16-year-old, Dawnta Anthony Harris, was charged as an adult in Caprio’s slaying and three other teenage males were reported in custody. Investigators employed aviation, K-9 units, and heat-sensing technology during the search.

Caprio was remembered as dedicated and effective—praised by colleagues for solving widespread thefts, named Parkville Precinct officer of the month, and described as athletic and community-minded. Governor Larry Hogan ordered flags at half-staff through her funeral week. Funeral services were scheduled later in the week; the department and community mourned the first female officer in county history to die on duty and the loss of a promising, highly regarded officer.

Minutes after President Donald Trump’s lengthy Thursday press conference, critics called it “unhinged” and “wild.” Over roughly 77–80 minutes in the East Room, Trump oscillated between combative, jocular and defensive, using the forum to assault the media, defend his administration after a chaotic first month, and revisit campaign-era themes. The event was ostensibly to announce Alexander Acosta as labor secretary, but it quickly turned into an unscripted, wide-ranging confrontation with reporters about Russia, leaks, policy plans and personal grievances.

A central thread was Trump’s attack on the news media. He repeatedly labeled coverage he dislikes “fake news,” arguing that leaks about his associates’ alleged contacts with Russia were real but the coverage of them was false or slanted. He told reporters the public no longer trusts them and blamed biased reporting for making his job harder. At times he singled out outlets — most notably CNN — deriding its ratings, accusing it of “anger and hatred,” and upgrading his usual “fake news” label to “very fake news.” He also suggested he would make a good reporter himself, claiming he knows when a story is good or bad and accusing journalists of turning positive items negative.

Russia and the fallout around former National Security Adviser Michael Flynn dominated many exchanges. Trump insisted he had no ties to Russia and called the whole “Russia” narrative a ruse, saying leaks were likely coming from the Obama administration. He defended firing Flynn, saying Flynn was dismissed for misleading Vice President Pence rather than for conversations with the Russian ambassador. Pressed on whether his campaign had contact with Russian officials, he repeatedly refused to provide specifics, offering only “not that I know of” at one point, and refused to telegraph military responses to provocations such as a Russian spy ship or North Korea’s missile tests.

On foreign policy Trump mixed tough rhetoric and outreach. He mused that better relations with Russia would be “a good thing,” but also warned grimly about the consequences of nuclear war, saying “nuclear holocaust would be like no other.” He mocked Hillary Clinton’s 2009 “reset” with Russia — notably the “stupid plastic button” incident — and repeated unproven claims that she allowed Russia to acquire a large share of U.S. uranium.

Domestically, Trump touched on a range of priorities and personnel issues. He pledged an Obamacare replacement plan by mid-March and said the administration had ordered a Pentagon plan to defeat ISIS, who he described as a “small group” that “spread like cancer,” though he overstated how much territory the group had recently lost. On immigration, he defended the troubled rollout of his travel ban, blamed Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly for advising against a longer lead time, and promised a revised executive order. He offered a sympathetic tone toward DACA recipients, saying he would “deal with DACA with heart,” while still stressing immigration enforcement.

The press conference also featured awkward personal moments: Trump asked black reporter April Ryan to set up a meeting with the Congressional Black Caucus, chided a Jewish reporter about anti-Semitic incidents, and made exaggerated or incorrect factual claims — including overstating his Electoral College margin and other statistics. He dismissed corrections from reporters and touted a Rasmussen poll showing favorable approval numbers.

Responses to the performance were polarized. Supporters and some conservative commentators praised his candor and combative stance toward the media, saying he answered questions and reclaimed the narrative. Critics and several journalists called the event chaotic, misleading on facts, and disrespectful to the press. Observers noted the president’s reliance on grievances and media attacks as a familiar communication strategy that may please his base but risks alienating skeptics and undermining trust in institutions. Overall, the press conference underscored the turbulent, confrontational tone that has marked Trump’s early presidency.

Researchers at the Universities of Nottingham and Bristol have uncovered how animals link changing day length to seasonal fertility. Published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study identifies vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) as the missing messenger between melatonin-producing brain regions and hormone-producing cells in the pituitary gland. Melatonin, secreted by the pineal gland during night, encodes day length and has long been known to influence seasonal traits such as reproduction, coat growth and antler development. Until now, how melatonin signalled to the distinct pituitary region that controls sex hormones remained unclear after nearly 30 years of inquiry.

Using sheep as a model, the team—led by Dr. Domingo Tortonese, Professor David Bates and Dr. Jennifer Castle-Miller—found that melatonin duration determines which VEGF isoform is produced in a specific pituitary area. Long winter nights drive production of VEGF forms that inhibit blood-vessel growth, limiting vascular connections between pituitary regions and stimulating sex-hormone production associated with winter breeding. Shorter summer melatonin exposure favors VEGF variants that promote angiogenesis, increasing connectivity and acting as an anaphrodisiac. Thus, seasonal VEGF-driven vascular remodelling conveys melatonin’s timing signal to hormone-producing cells.

The discovery explains seasonal reproductive timing in sheep and suggests ways farmers might adjust lambing times to improve survival amid climate change. It also raises broader questions about seasonal regulation in other species, including possible implications for human seasonal biology and pituitary-related endocrine disorders. The full paper, “Mechanisms Regulating Angiogenesis Underlie Seasonal Control of Pituitary Function,” is published in PNAS.

JC Penney drew ridicule on social media after a baffling tweet that looked like it was typed by someone drunk or otherwise incoherent. The retailer’s Sunday evening post—“Who kkmew theis was ghiong tob e a baweball ghamle. #lowsscorinh 5_0”—appeared tied to the Super Bowl but made little sense. Follow-up tweets continued the odd tone, including a garbled shout at the Seahawks, and the account briefly offered no explanation. Users mocked the brand, suggesting an intern was intoxicated, the account was hacked, or it was an ill-conceived marketing stunt; jokes and retweets piled up across Twitter. The episode came amid scrutiny of J.C. Penney’s pricing strategies after TIME reported the company was raising prices to mark them down again for Valentine’s Day, a tactic critics call price anchoring. The retailer later apologized, attributing the messages to tweeting with mittens.

The Bank of England announced Jane Austen will replace Charles Darwin on the £10 note, likely entering circulation around 2017, after public outcry over an earlier decision that would have left no women (other than the monarch) represented on British banknotes. New governor Mark Carney said the bank had listened and would celebrate a broader diversity of historical figures; he also pledged a review to make the selection process more transparent. Campaigner Caroline Criado-Perez, whose petition and protests drew tens of thousands of supporters, welcomed the decision and the promised review. Austen’s portrait on the note is adapted from her sister’s sketch and the design includes her writing table, Godmersham Park, an illustration of Elizabeth Bennet, and the Pride and Prejudice quote “I declare after all there is no enjoyment like reading!” The change restores female representation alongside Elizabeth Fry and Florence Nightingale and comes amid concern that future monarchs will be male, making non-royal women on currency increasingly important.

A March Washington Post-ABC News poll finds President Obama’s approval slipping to 50 percent as public confidence in his economic stewardship weakens since his January inauguration. In December he led congressional Republicans by 18 points on who could better handle the economy; by March that advantage narrowed to 44–40, with “neither” rising. Independents and some core supporters moved toward disapproval. The survey shows frustration with Washington amid the sequester: a slim majority disapproves of automatic cuts, yet most report no personal effect; nonetheless large majorities expect harm to the economy, military, and services and favor bipartisan talks to end cuts. On issues, Obama and Republicans are roughly even on gun control and close on immigration and spending priorities. Most reject cuts to Medicaid and raising Medicare’s eligibility age, while 56 percent back limits on high-income tax deductions. Congress’s approval remains abysmal at 16 percent. The poll sampled 1,001 adults March 7–10 (±3.5 points).

Josh Browder, a 19-year-old Stanford student and self-taught coder, created DoNotPay, an AI “robot lawyer” that has helped contest 160,000 of 250,000 parking tickets across London and New York, winning about 64% and overturning over $4 million in fines. Browder began the project after receiving roughly 30 parking tickets at 18 and built a chat-like interface that asks simple questions (e.g., visibility of parking signs) to determine if an appeal is viable, then guides users through the appeals process for free. He argues that many ticketed drivers are vulnerable and exploited as revenue sources, and that the formulaic nature of appeals makes them well suited to automation, saving people costly lawyer fees.

Beyond parking disputes, Browder has applied blockchain technology to socially sensitive legal problems: he built a tool enabling HIV-positive people to create a permanent, anonymous blockchain record proving they disclosed their status to partners, addressing cases that surface decades later when companies and records vanish. He believes blockchain’s permanence can reshape law and financial technology.

In interviews, Browder expresses skepticism about government involvement in innovation, favoring minimal regulation and suggesting politics often distract from problem-solving. He’s expanding DoNotPay to new areas—flight-delay claims, refugee legal guidance, and rights information for HIV-positive individuals—and exploring a developer platform enabling legal experts (not just coders) to build helpful legal bots. DoNotPay is available at DoNotPay.co.uk.

President Barack Obama will not attend Justice Antonin Scalia’s funeral Saturday, the White House confirmed, choosing instead to pay respects on Friday while Scalia’s body lies in repose in the Supreme Court’s Great Hall. Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama will visit the Court Friday; Vice President Joe Biden and his wife Jill Biden, who share Scalia’s Catholic faith, will attend the funeral Mass at the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception. Press Secretary Josh Earnest emphasized the president’s intent to honor Scalia’s life and service and declined to specify Obama’s Saturday plans, rejecting suggestions that the president was shirking respect or prioritizing recreation. The decision generated criticism from conservative media and some commentators who viewed it as a partisan snub, while others close to the Scalia family and former clerks defended the choice as appropriate and practical. Historically, presidents do not consistently attend justices’ funerals; President George W. Bush attended Chief Justice William Rehnquist’s funeral in 2005, but precedents are sparse. Scalia’s death at 79 has intensified a looming political battle over his replacement: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell urged waiting until after the 2016 election, while Obama insisted the Constitution empowers him to nominate a qualified successor. Some Republicans signaled openness to hearings; others remained committed to blocking a confirmation. Obama praised Scalia as a “brilliant legal mind” and, despite political tensions, reiterated respect for his service while preparing to nominate a replacement though no nomination is expected while Congress is in recess.

LOOK magazine's latest issue, out now, teases celebrity scoops, fashion trends and lifestyle features, and urges readers to grab a copy from newsagents or download the digital edition. A key story claims Tom Cruise has written an emotional letter to ex-wife Katie Holmes a year after their high-profile split. Insiders say Cruise, now 51, penned the note as July—anniversary time—approached, hoping to rekindle friendship if not more. Sources suggest he chose a letter because phone contact would be unwelcome, kept the tone measured rather than over the top, and expressed lingering care and understanding about why Holmes left. The piece reports Holmes, who has been building a new life in New York with their daughter Suri, was touched and found the letter cathartic, though she likely isn’t interested in resuming the relationship. Other LOOK highlights mentioned include warnings about royal baby safety, new-season fashion picks, stories on cyber “ratters,” Kristen Wiig’s reflections, and makeup artists’ celebrity tips. The issue also promotes accessible high-street finds and invites iTunes ratings. The note about Alexa Internet adds that since 1996 its crawl data have been donated to the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine.

Since the 2010 discovery that non-African humans carry 1–4% Neanderthal DNA, researchers have speculated about its effects on modern traits. A new study published in Science by John Capra, Corinne Simonti and colleagues directly links Neanderthal genetic variants to numerous clinical traits by comparing genomes and electronic health records from 28,000 individuals of European ancestry in the eMERGE network. The analysis found that surviving Neanderthal DNA has subtle but significant influences across immunological, dermatological, neurological, psychiatric and reproductive traits. Some findings reinforce prior hypotheses: Neanderthal-derived variants affect keratinocyte biology and increase risk of sun-induced keratoses. Other results were unexpected—one Neanderthal locus elevates risk of nicotine addiction, and many archaic snippets are associated with psychiatric and neurological outcomes, with some variants increasing and others decreasing depression risk. The authors suggest many retained Neanderthal alleles were once adaptive during early non-African migrations (e.g., a variant promoting faster blood coagulation might have helped fend off infections) but can be maladaptive today by raising stroke, embolism or pregnancy complication risks. The team identified associations by mapping individual Neanderthal-derived segments in each genome to billing-code phenotypes in medical records. The work demonstrates a new approach to study recent human evolution’s phenotypic legacy and paves the way for deeper analyses using richer clinical data such as lab tests and physician notes.

The Philae lander, carried by ESA’s Rosetta spacecraft, successfully touched down on Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko and returned historic images and science data—but has since run low on power and entered a hibernation-like state. After an unexpectedly bumpy touchdown that left Philae lodged on its side in the shadow of a cliff or boulder, its harpoons failed to anchor it and one leg was left pointing upward. Limited sunlight reached its panels—about 1.5 hours rather than the expected 6–7—so its primary battery, designed to last roughly 60–64 hours, could not be replenished. Engineers deployed the drill and a 1.2 m sampling arm and reported the drill extended about 25 cm and that the SD2 instrument completed a down-and-up cycle; COSAC was chosen to analyse samples because it uses less power. In a last effort to improve solar charging, controllers commanded Philae to lift and rotate about 35 degrees, nudging it into a slightly sunnier orientation, then used remaining battery power to transmit final data. Contact was later re-established but power remains marginal; if solar charging remains insufficient Philae will sleep until the comet nears the Sun in 2015, when increased illumination might reboot the lander and allow further science. Despite the setbacks, mission leaders call the operation a historic and largely successful achievement.

Matthew McConaughey is returning to the University of Texas at Austin this fall to teach an upper-level filmmaking course at his alma mater. The Oscar-winning actor will co-teach the class alongside director Gary Ross (The Hunger Games) and university lecturer Scott Rice, admitting 30 students to the once-a-week course offered through the Moody College of Communications. The class will take students behind the scenes of Free State of Jones by showing film clips and recorded video lessons in which McConaughey, Ross and Rice explain creative and technical choices; the course will include at least one on-campus visit by McConaughey. Open to juniors and seniors with no prerequisites or extra fees, the course marks McConaughey’s second time coteaching this material — a similar offering ran in spring 2016 when students signed nondisclosure agreements and restrictions on photos and video were enforced because the film had not yet been released. McConaughey, a 1993 UT graduate in radio, television and film, is a frequent campus visitor known for attending football games and giving motivational talks.

Mary H. Musselman, an 81-year-old Sebring resident, was arrested after repeatedly feeding black bears despite warnings and court orders. Musselman initially received diversion after authorities learned she had been putting out food for bears; after violating that agreement she was placed on probation Jan. 24 with an explicit one-year ban on leaving food for wildlife. Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) officers found clear evidence she continued to feed animals—numerous bowls and trays of birdseed and corn, hanging feeders, and food on the ground—and filed a probation violation. During the arrest, Musselman allegedly resisted officers, kicked them, and threatened to kill an FWC officer once released; she faces charges including violation of probation, resisting an officer with violence, and battery on a law enforcement officer. The matter began in November 2012 after reports that she had been feeding bears for months; one bear that had been regularly fed was euthanized because it became a public-safety risk. FWC spokesman Gary Morse emphasized that feeding bears causes them to lose fear of humans, creating dangerous, habituated animals that usually cannot be relocated and often must be euthanized. FWC has actively educated local residents—canvassing homes and using media—to reduce human-bear conflicts. Musselman’s supporters say she is a longtime, gentle animal lover and possibly unable to grasp the court orders; she remained jailed without bond pending a March court appearance.

Scarlett Johansson tops this year’s list of highest-paid actresses with $40.5 million in pretax earnings from June 1, 2017 to June 1, 2018, largely thanks to her role as Black Widow in Marvel’s Avengers films. Johansson quadrupled her 2017 earnings, unseating Emma Stone. Angelina Jolie is No. 2 with $28 million, boosted by upfront pay for Maleficent 2, while Jennifer Aniston ranks third with $19.5 million, driven mainly by lucrative endorsements; her pay is expected to rise with an Apple series with Reese Witherspoon (No. 5; $16.5 million). Jennifer Lawrence remains on the list despite recent box-office misses, supported by franchise roles and a Dior contract. The top 10 collectively earned $186 million pre-tax, up 16% from 2017. Newcomer Gal Gadot (No. 10; $10 million) benefited from Wonder Woman’s success and endorsements. The report highlights persistent gender disparities—female speaking roles remain limited, only two women exceeded $20 million this year—and notes many top earners are over 40 and pursue producing or endorsements to create opportunities.

RadarOnline reports the California Attorney General is conducting a preliminary inquiry into allegations that former Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger used state-funded security — California Highway Patrol officers and vehicles — to escort women into his suite at the Sacramento Hyatt Regency, allegedly to conceal sexual liaisons. Veteran hotel security officer William Taylor claims he witnessed CHP dignitary protection ferries of scantily clad women to the governor’s private wing; he reportedly passed a polygraph and is likely to be interviewed. The Attorney General’s office declined comment. Calls for investigation into possible misuse of state or campaign funds have come from lawmakers and Democratic Party officials after Schwarzenegger admitted fathering a child with a former housekeeper. Schwarzenegger’s PR team and attorney deny Taylor’s claims; multiple CHP retirees and the Hyatt manager also dispute the allegations, calling them untrue.

Dawn Wells, best known as Mary Ann from Gilligan’s Island, is the subject of an urgent fundraising effort launched by friend Dugg Kirkpatrick. The GoFundMe campaign seeks nearly $200,000 to cover mounting medical bills, IRS penalties, and related costs. Organizers say Wells suffered severe financial losses after the 2008 banking crash and later endured a life-threatening surgery and complications from an accident that required two months of hospitalization and long recovery. Kirkpatrick reports Wells broke her knee this year while still recuperating from prior surgery problems; she has since lost her home and faces difficulty securing an assisted-living placement geared to entertainment-industry residents because of outstanding debt. The fundraiser’s goal was increased to offset platform fees, and funds are intended to be withdrawn by a designated person on Wells’s behalf. In its first 10 days the campaign raised nearly $120,000. Kirkpatrick, who appears from his social posts to have worked as a hairstylist for Wells, says she has no family support and is trying to be moved into a Glendale, California facility that serves film and TV professionals. Media outlets have reached out to Wells, her agent and Kirkpatrick for comment. Supporters and fans are being asked to donate and share the campaign to help the long-time actress facing medical, financial, and housing crises.

Ukrainian forces withdrew from the strategic rail hub Debaltseve after intense fighting in what Kiev and Western officials called a breach of a recent Minsk ceasefire. Dozens of tanks and troop columns retreated toward Artemivsk amid footage showing separatists raising their flag and claims they now control the town. President Poroshenko described the pullout as “planned and organised,” while NATO warned the offensive jeopardised the wider agreement and accused Russia of supporting separatists. Reports said heavy shortages, civilian suffering and casualties occurred; around 7,000 civilians remained trapped. Observers could not access Debaltseve to verify claims.

Harper Lee’s enduring classic To Kill a Mockingbird owes a crucial debt to a New York couple, Joy and Michael (Marion Martin) Brown, who gave Lee the financial freedom to finish her novel. After moving from Monroeville, Ala., to New York, Lee struggled to write while working as an airline reservations clerk. In Mary McDonagh Murphy’s documentary Hey Boo: Harper Lee & To Kill a Mockingbird, the Browns recount how, on Christmas Eve 1956, they slipped an envelope into Lee’s tree offering “one year off” to write whatever she pleased. Lee later described the gift as a “sure thing.” The Browns’ loan—kept secret for decades and later revealed in Charles J. Shields’s biography—allowed Lee to complete the manuscript that would be published in 1960 and win the Pulitzer Prize in 1961. Michael Brown, a Broadway lyricist and creator of shows such as the massively performed “Wonderful World of Chemistry” at the 1964 World’s Fair, and Joy, a former ballerina, provided the means from modest windfalls; Lee repaid the loan, the Browns say. Lee’s Manhattan years were difficult but socially rich—she followed Truman Capote’s literary circle, often noting only that she was from Alabama and working on a book. After Mockingbird’s success—an initial print run of 5,000 copies that vastly underestimated demand—the novel sold some 30 million copies worldwide, translated into over 40 languages. Lee later retreated from public life, and questions about a contested biography remain unresolved, but the Browns’ pivotal, generous role in bringing Mockingbird into being is now widely acknowledged.

Dick Clark returns to co-host Dick Clark's New Year's Rockin' Eve for its 40th anniversary on Dec. 31, appearing alongside Ryan Seacrest on ABC. Seacrest has shared duties since 2005 after Clark’s 2004 stroke left him with impaired speech; Regis Philbin substituted that year. Despite health challenges, the 82-year-old remains actively involved in production, calling the show “one of his children.” The nearly six-hour broadcast features retrospectives of four decades of performances and 29 live acts, headlined by Lady Gaga in Times Square, with Justin Bieber, Pitbull, Florence + the Machine, Nicki Minaj, Beyonce (from London) and others joining from New York and Los Angeles. The program leads ABC’s prime-time coverage and historically draws larger audiences than competing networks. Producers emphasize Clark’s continued presence as meaningful to viewers and insist on live broadcasts with no taped backups.

Jahmel Binion, a Warren man with hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia—a rare genetic condition causing reduced sweating, sparse hair, missing teeth and distinctive facial features—filed a lawsuit in Macomb County Circuit Court against Shaquille O’Neal, Trey Burke and rapper Waka Flocka Flame. Binion alleges the celebrities mocked a selfie he posted, reposting or parodying it to a national audience of about 8.4 million, and claims invasion of privacy, defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence. Though O’Neal and Burke later apologized and contacted Binion, the suit says the apologies were belated and that the ridicule publicly disclosed embarrassing private facts, placed him in a false light and caused severe emotional harm. Binion, who has struggled with employment and health risks from overheating, founded the antibullying campaign Hug Don’t Judge and seeks more than $25,000 in damages.

Nearly 50 years after the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Olympics, the International Olympic Committee has clarified its records to list Vivian and Ronald Joseph as the official bronze medalists in pairs figure skating. The long, convoluted dispute began when West Germans Marika Kilius and Hans-Jürgen Bäumler—heavy favorites who finished second behind Soviets Ludmila Belousova and Oleg Protopopov—were found to have signed a contract to perform professionally during the Games, violating amateurism rules. After an IOC probe, the Germans returned their silver medals in January 1966; Canada’s Debbi Wilkes and Guy Revell were elevated to silver and the Josephs, originally fourth, received bronze. The Josephs recalled a subdued medal presentation in Chicago and assumed the matter settled. In 1987, however, the IOC executive board quietly reinstated the Germans’ medals following lobbying that many skaters held similar contracts and others had not been sanctioned; the West Germans were deemed “rehabilitated.” The IOC did not inform U.S. Figure Skating or Canadian officials, nor request the return of redistributed medals, leaving record books and media guides inconsistent for decades. The uncertainty left the Josephs and Wilkes unsure how to represent their Olympic status in life. A 2013 New York Times inquiry prompted action; this year the IOC confirmed that the Soviets remain gold, Canada and West Germany are co-silver medalists, and the Josephs retain bronze. The siblings expressed relief and vindication, though Vivian said the medal itself was not their proudest achievement.

Iraq’s president nominated veteran Shiite politician Haider al-Abadi to form a new government, deepening a political crisis as the country battles an Islamic State insurgency. Incumbent Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki rejected the move as illegal, vowed to fight it, and filed a challenge with the Supreme Court, while remaining caretaker premier during Abadi’s 30-day window to build a cabinet. Maliki stressed his control over security forces, prompting deployment of armored vehicles and a tank around Baghdad’s Green Zone and mobilization of loyal militia elements, heightening fears of a potential clash. Yet many in Maliki’s State of Law coalition have defected, with 38 of 96 lawmakers publicly backing Abadi; analysts say Abadi can likely form a majority including Kurdish and Sunni support. The U.S. government and President Obama voiced support for Abadi and conditioned expanded aid on Iraq forming an inclusive government that bridges sectarian divides. Washington has intensified military support against IS, conducting airstrikes and supplying weapons to Kurdish peshmerga. Abadi, a British-educated former communications minister, vowed to curb IS influence but faces the dual challenge of unifying fractured politics and restoring effective, cohesive security forces.

Yad Vashem recently received a remarkable artifact: a yellowed 1930s Nazi family magazine whose cover featured the image of the ideal “Aryan” baby—who turned out to be Jewish. The infant was Hessy Levinsons (later Hessy Taft), born in Berlin in 1934 to Jacob and Pauline Levinsons, Latvian-born singers who had moved to Berlin for musical careers. In 1935 Hessy’s mother took her six-month-old to a prominent photographer, Hans Ballin, for a portrait. Months later the photograph appeared on the cover of Sonne ins Haus and on widely distributed postcards; Joseph Goebbels is said to have selected the image. Terrified that publication would expose them, Hessy’s mother confronted Ballin, who revealed he had known the family were Jewish and deliberately submitted the photo to mock Nazi racial ideology. He later told Hessy he wanted “to make the Nazis ridiculous.” Recognized by a distant aunt but never identified by Nazi authorities, Hessy was kept at home for safety. The family endured increasing persecution—Jacob lost jobs and was once arrested on a trumped-up charge—and fled Germany, moving between Latvia, Paris, and, aided by the French resistance, to Bordeaux and Nice. Denied U.S. visa extensions, they obtained Cuban visas and lived in Havana until 1949, when they emigrated to the United States. Hessy became a chemistry professor in New York. Donating her magazine to Yad Vashem, she said she felt “a little revenge” and “something like satisfaction” at having been the unwitting foil to Nazi propaganda.

An Algerian court sentenced a man to two years in prison after he posted a shocking image on Facebook appearing to show him dangling his baby cousin out of a 15th‑floor window in Algiers with the caption, “1000 likes or I will drop him.” The child in the photo looked terrified and bewildered, and the post sparked widespread outrage online. Users who saw the image called for the man to be prosecuted for child abuse, and authorities pursued the case amid intense public pressure. The defendant claimed the photo had been doctored—telling Ennahar news that protective balcony bars visible at the scene had been removed by others editing the viral image—but the court found this explanation unpersuasive. Prosecutors argued the act was carried out to attract views and likes on social media. After reviewing the evidence, the court convicted him and imposed the two‑year prison term. The incident and its legal outcome underscored concerns about social media stunts that endanger children, the speed at which disturbing content can spread online, and the role of courts in responding to viral abuses. (Last update: 21 June 2017)

Fourteen-year-old Valentina Maureira, a Chilean girl with cystic fibrosis, made a public plea for assisted death in a video posted to social media that went viral and drew national attention. Speaking from a hospital bed, Valentina asked to speak urgently with President Michelle Bachelet and requested authorization for “the injection to put me to sleep forever,” saying she was tired of living with the illness. Cystic fibrosis, a hereditary disease that progressively damages the lungs and other organs, has already claimed the life of Valentina’s older brother; her father, Freddy Maureira, described her long history of suffering, including five operations and persistent symptoms such as vomiting and headaches. A spokeswoman for Santiago’s Universidad Católica clinic confirmed Valentina is a patient there and described her condition as stable, without an immediately life-threatening situation. The public plea prompted a response from the government and from Bachelet herself, who visited Valentina after the video circulated. Government spokesman Álvaro Elizalde said the health ministry is in contact with the family to ensure Valentina receives medical and psychological support but made clear that euthanasia cannot be authorized: current Chilean law bars assisted dying. The episode reignited debate in Chile about end‑of‑life choices and palliative care. Euthanasia remains illegal in Chile, where the Catholic Church remains influential and abortion is heavily restricted; Bachelet’s government has pursued some social reforms, including a bill to relax abortion rules, but has not proposed changes to euthanasia policy. The case highlighted tensions between personal suffering, legal limits, and broader ethical and political questions about assisted dying in Chile.

Pete and Alisha Arnold, a 30-year-old married couple from Apple Valley, Minnesota, launched BirthOrNot.com to let the public vote on whether they should keep or abort Alisha’s third pregnancy. Since September they’ve posted pregnancy updates and ultrasounds; a PollDaddy poll asks, “Should We Give Birth or Have an Abortion?” with the abortion option leading narrowly as the poll closes December 7. The couple say they’re undecided about parenting after two recent miscarriages and will weigh the poll heavily—though not bindingly—before the 20-week cutoff for abortion. Pete frames the experiment as a civic lesson about voting’s consequences; critics note major flaws: most pro-choice people aren’t actively pro-abortion, online trolls can skew results, and the forum trivializes a deeply personal, emotional decision. Commentators have called the stunt misleading, offensive, or a pro-life publicity ploy; others argue it undermines the principle that reproductive choices should remain private. The episode prompted condemnation, debate about ethics and parenting fitness, and calls for alternatives like adoption if the couple won’t responsibly decide for themselves.

The page begins with a Yahoo! “not found” notice advising users to check the URL, try Yahoo! home or services, use the site search or Help Central. Beneath that, a blog post excerpt recounts Bill Ayers’ recurring sarcastic claim that he wrote Barack Obama’s Dreams from My Father. Posted March 28, 2011 by Allahpundit and sourced via American Thinker, the item relays John Hawkins’ reading of Ayers’ remark as mockery. It describes a 2009 encounter in Reagan Airport where a conservative blogger confronted Ayers; upon learning she was conservative, Ayers reportedly boasted he authored the book at Michelle Obama’s behest and offered to split royalties if she could prove it. When challenged that he might have merely edited it, he supposedly doubled down, claiming full authorship. The author suggests Ayers delights in baiting people who believe conspiracy theories, using the outlandish claim to expose gullibility, though acknowledging readers may interpret his intent differently. Related posts are listed afterward.

Multiple sources tell The Federalist that the New York Times is preparing another piece critical of Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh, this time focusing on a 1983 letter he wrote organizing a high‑school “Beach Week.” After failing to corroborate sexual‑assault allegations, the Times has reportedly queried classmates about the tongue‑in‑cheek note that lists logistics, costs, sleeping arrangements, inside jokes and warnings to neighbors about “loud, obnoxious drunks.” Classmates confirm Kavanaugh organized the trip and describe the letter as innocuous evidence of his organizational skills and youthful camaraderie. They recall frequent large backyard parties and heavy drinking among peers but emphasize longtime friendships and many alumni endorsements supporting Kavanaugh. The Federalist criticizes the Times’ earlier reporting on yearbook jokes and a story about a possible ice‑throwing incident, calling those efforts smears. Kavanaugh’s lawyers say the note was simply to organize Beach Week; the Senate awaits an FBI supplemental background check before voting on his confirmation.

President Obama’s $3.8 trillion 2013 budget blueprint emphasizes higher taxes on the wealthy, new investments in infrastructure and education, and selective spending cuts, while largely avoiding major entitlement reform. Framed around fairness—“everyone gets a fair shot”—the plan would raise about $1.5 trillion by letting Bush-era tax cuts expire for high earners, taxing carried interest as ordinary income, enacting a “Buffett Rule” preventing millionaires from paying under 30% tax, and imposing new levies on big banks and energy tax breaks. It funds priorities like $30 billion to modernize schools, $30 billion to retain teachers and first responders, $476 billion over six years for surface transportation, and an $8 billion, three-year Community College to Career Fund to train two million workers and expand technical and internship programs.

To meet Budget Control Act caps, discretionary spending is constrained—projected to fall from 8.7% of GDP in 2011 to 5.0% by 2022—with $24 billion in cuts in 2013 and $520 billion over a decade, plus $217 billion in selected mandatory-savings proposals. Defense spending would decline modestly; Medicare and Medicaid cuts total about $360 billion over ten years. Despite these measures, deficits remain large—$1.33 trillion in 2012 and $901 billion in 2013—and the budget adds roughly $7 trillion to public debt from 2013–2022. Critics say the omission of deep entitlement reforms leaves long-term fiscal risks unresolved, and Congress—divided politically—must accept, amend, or reject the proposal.

The Texas Rangers are investigating an incident in Venezuela in which catcher Yorvit Torrealba struck an umpire during a winter-league game. Video that circulated online shows Torrealba, playing for Leones del Caracas, striking out swinging, arguing with home-plate umpire Dario Rivero Jr., and then using an open hand to push the umpire’s facemask after a brief face-to-face confrontation. Rangers GM Jon Daniels acknowledged the club is aware and will look into the episode but said details are limited and possible disciplinary action “depends on circumstances.” Torrealba is entering the second year of a two-year, $6.25 million contract with Texas; he hit .273 with seven homers and 37 RBIs in 113 regular-season games last year but saw reduced postseason time after Mike Napoli became the club’s primary catcher. Commentators called the act inexcusable and disappointing given Torrealba’s reputation for passion and leadership.

The document combines a brief note about web archiving efforts with a report on actress Allison Williams’s public comments about her father, journalist Brian Williams. The archiving passage explains that crawls are being conducted to capture web pages as they are created and the pages they reference, preserving the versions that existed when the citing pages were written. The Internet Archive’s aim is to replace or supplement broken links with links to those preserved snapshots so visitors can see the original sources and avoid lost context; the broader stated objective is to fix broken links across the web through “No More 404” crawls.

The larger portion of the text covers Allison Williams’s appearance at 92Y on February 18 in conversation with Seth Meyers. Known for her role as Marnie on HBO’s Girls and her title turn in NBC’s Peter Pan Live!, Williams spoke about her career and training—her theater background, improv work with Yale’s Just Add Water, and a BA in English—before addressing her father’s controversy. This marked her first public statement about Brian Williams’s six-month suspension from NBC for fabricating aspects of a 2003 Iraq report. She defended him personally, calling him honest, caring, and committed to journalism, and said the episode had been very hard but that the family felt supported by outreach from strangers as well as loved ones. She emphasized her belief in his integrity and eagerness for his return to television, sharing a personal anecdote about him calling from Iraq to keep a promise to attend her ninth-grade father-daughter dance as an example of his character.

An Aeroméxico Embraer 190 carrying 103 people — 99 passengers (including two infants) and four crew — crashed just after takeoff from Guadalupe Victoria International Airport in Durango, Mexico, on Tuesday afternoon. The mid-sized jet went down around 16:00 local time amid heavy rain and stormy conditions. Eyewitnesses and officials said a sudden strong gust or turbulent air current rocked the aircraft shortly after liftoff; the plane’s left wing struck the ground, ripping off two engines, and it skidded into scrubland about 300 meters from the runway before coming to rest and catching fire.

Passengers and crew escaped using evacuation slides and by exiting through breaks in the fuselage; many walked away on their own. Video and images showed heavy damage and a column of smoke rising from the scene. Dozens were treated for injuries; state civil protection reported around 85 people with mostly light injuries and 37 hospitalized, while the state health department said two passengers were in critical condition. The pilot was among the most seriously hurt but was reported in stable condition after surgery. Reports described at least one child with burns and passengers who lost passports and documents in the fire.

Aeroméxico expressed deep regret and said families of those affected are in their thoughts. Preliminary statements from airport operators and the governor attributed the accident to bad weather; investigators will recover the flight recorders and probe the cause, a process expected to take months. Embraer dispatched technicians to support the investigation. The aircraft, serial number 190-173, was built in 2008 and leased to Aeroméxico in 2014. U.S. officials offered investigative assistance. No fatalities were reported.

The CIA drew widespread criticism for live-tweeting the raid that killed Osama bin Laden, posting an hour-by-hour, real-time style account five years after the 2011 operation. Using the hashtag #UBLRaid, the agency’s social media account narrated mission milestones with exact timestamps—helicopters departing from Afghanistan, two helicopters descending on the Abbottabad compound with one crashing, the assault continuing, Bin Laden being found on the third floor and killed at 3:39pm, and President Obama receiving confirmation of probable identification several hours later. The decision to present the events “as if it were happening today” was intended to mark a defining moment of President Obama’s legacy and to spotlight the CIA’s role in the top-secret operation. Reaction on Twitter skewed negative, with users calling the move “grotesque and embarrassing” and sharing memes and GIFs expressing dismay; other users defended the posts. The tweets followed the CIA’s typical historical and artifact-focused content but stood out for their dramatized timeline. On the anniversary, CIA Director John Brennan reflected on the broader fight against Islamist extremist groups, saying Bin Laden’s death dealt a symbolic and strategic blow to al-Qaeda but warning the threat was not eliminated. He urged continued focus on dismantling related extremist networks, citing the global reach of IS and the necessity of targeting its leadership.

20th Century Fox has fired Bryan Singer as director of the Queen biopic Bohemian Rhapsody after a series of on-set absences, clashes with lead actor Rami Malek, and escalating tensions that forced production to halt on Dec. 1. The studio said Singer was “no longer the director,” citing his “unexpected unavailability” and a pattern of unreliable behavior that required cinematographer Newton Thomas Sigel to step in on multiple shooting days. Sources say the situation included a confrontation between Singer and Malek—nonphysical but involving Singer throwing an object—and that actor Tom Hollander briefly quit over Singer’s conduct before returning. Malek reportedly complained to studio executives about Singer’s unreliability and unprofessionalism; Fox executives had warned Singer before production began that such behavior would not be tolerated, and a Directors Guild representative monitored the set. Singer denies the misconduct narrative, saying he asked Fox for time off to tend to a gravely ill parent and to address his own health, and claims the studio refused to accommodate him. He says he and Malek had resolved earlier creative differences and continued working together until just prior to Thanksgiving. Another insider says Singer has claimed post-traumatic stress from on-set tensions. With roughly two weeks of principal photography remaining, Fox, New Regency and producer Graham King plan to name a replacement director within days. Despite the turmoil, the film—with Rami Malek as Freddie Mercury and supporting cast including Ben Hardy, Joe Mazzello and Gwilym Lee—remains expected for its planned December 2018 release.

Michael Cohen, a lawyer and senior advisor to Donald Trump, sparked outrage when he told the Daily Beast that “by the very definition, you can’t rape your spouse,” while defending Trump against a decades-old allegation from ex-wife Ivana Trump. The claim relates to a 1993 book by Harry Hurt III, which cites a divorce deposition in which Ivana said she felt “raped” after a violent 1989 encounter with Trump. The book describes Trump tearing out clumps of Ivana’s hair, ripping off her clothes and forcing himself on her; Trump has long denied the incident and the scalp surgery referenced. Ivana’s statement, provided to the author by Trump’s team and included in the book, acknowledged she had said her husband “had raped me” in a deposition but sought to clarify she did not intend the term in a “literal or criminal sense,” instead describing emotional violation. Cohen insisted Ivana meant emotionally violated and also threatened legal action against reporters and the Daily Beast for using the word “rape” with Trump’s name, issuing aggressive warnings about lawsuits and personal ruin. Media outlets corrected Cohen: New York abolished the marital rape exemption in 1984, making his legal claim inaccurate. The episode renewed scrutiny of Trump’s past remarks and handling of sexual-assault issues, prompted back-and-forth between the campaign and reporters, and left open questions about whether the allegations or Cohen’s conduct would affect Trump’s political standing.

Polish historians have published what they describe as the most comprehensive online list to date of SS commanders and guards who served at the Auschwitz-Birkenau complex, aiming both to document perpetrators and assist in bringing surviving suspects to justice. Compiled by historian Aleksander Lasik over more than 30 years and released by the state-run Institute of National Remembrance together with the Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial, the SS KL Auschwitz Garrison list draws on archives in Poland, Germany, Austria, the United States and limited Russian sources. It contains more than 8,500 Auschwitz-specific entries and Lasik’s broader research database includes over 25,000 names from various German-run camps; his work continues as the list remains incomplete. Entries—available in Polish, English and German—typically include birth date and place, nationality, education, military service, party affiliation and, where available, photographs. Judicial documents are attached for those who were tried; for example, Rudolf Höss’s entry includes a photocopy of his 1947 Krakow death sentence. The project’s organizers hope the searchable archive will preserve historical links and provide investigators with leads, particularly since archives in some countries remain less accessible. Lasik suggested up to 200 former Auschwitz guards could still be alive; historians estimate only about 12% of Auschwitz guards were ever tried. Nazi hunter Efraim Zuroff praised the publication as important and potentially practically useful if it reveals names unknown to prosecutors. Auschwitz operated 1940–45, where roughly 1.1 million people—about 1 million Jews, up to 75,000 Poles, some 21,000 Roma and about 15,000 Soviet POWs—were murdered.

A Navy MH-53 Sea Dragon from Helicopter Mine Countermeasures Squadron 14 crashed into the Atlantic about 20 miles east of Cape Henry during a training mission, killing two sailors and leaving a third missing. Lt. Wesley Van Dorn, 29, and PO3 Brian Collins, 25, died at Sentara Norfolk General Hospital; Lt. Sean Christopher Snyder, 39, remained missing after exhaustive search efforts over more than 600 square miles were suspended that afternoon. Five crew were aboard; four were pulled from the water, two later died, one remained serious and one fair. Rescue teams from the Navy, Coast Guard, Virginia Beach fire and police, and several ships recovered wreckage scattered across a half-mile debris field. Investigators opened a probe into the cause; officials noted the aging MH-53 fleet’s troubled safety record but said there were no plans to ground Sea Dragons. Separately, a U.S. HH-60 Pave Hawk crashed in eastern England, killing four airmen.

Lena Dunham’s reported $3.5–3.7 million book deal has reignited debate about corporate publishing’s priorities. Critics argue the large advance exemplifies a risk-averse, profit-driven industry that chases perceived instant hits—“the next Bossypants”—rather than investing broadly in diverse literary talent. The author, a former Random House employee, contrasts the current model with Barney Rosset’s Grove Press ethos: small advances, loyalty to writers, and patience that builds a lasting backlist and cultural legacy. The critique suggests that that same multi-million-dollar sum could fund hundreds of modest advances or dozens of substantial ones, potentially nurturing future literary heavyweights whose works would endure and, cumulatively, outsell a single celebrity-driven book. Corporate houses, accountable to shareholders and quarterly results, lack the long time horizon needed for that approach, which helps explain why nimble indie presses—Graywolf, McSweeney’s, Soho, Bellevue Literary and others—are winning awards and cultural relevance. Defenders of the Dunham deal note her cultural reach and the demand for candid, relatable essays about work, gender, fashion, and everyday life; her proposal promises fresh, practical stories that may resonate beyond celebrity gloss. The broader tension remains: short-term commercial bets versus patient cultivation of literature with lasting impact.

Pope Francis used his Wednesday audience in St. Peter’s Square, timed with World Environment Day, to condemn a growing “culture of waste,” especially the daily disposal of good food. He recalled grandparents’ habits of saving leftovers and said consumerism has made people insensitive to food’s value; “throwing away food is like stealing from the table of the poor and the hungry.” Citing UN figures, about 1.3 billion tonnes of food—one third of production—is lost or wasted annually, with consumer behavior and oversized portions a major cause in industrialized countries. The pope linked materialism to indifference toward human suffering, noting market dips provoke outrage while homelessness and hunger are treated as normal. He urged Catholics to defend the poor, practice austerity, care for creation, and cultivate responsibility toward the environment. Italian farmers’ group Coldiretti welcomed his recognition of agriculture’s role.

In February, Amanda Carpenter, formerly Sen. Ted Cruz’s communications director, was briefly trapped in an Amtrak elevator at Baltimore–Washington International Airport and tweeted to her more than 90,000 followers asking for help. She also posted a photo showing the elevator’s inspection certificate had expired. Amtrak initially responded within 16 minutes on the day, saying BWI agents were aware and working to get her out. Months later, on Sept. 7, Amtrak’s official Twitter account replied to her original plea asking if she was “still in the elevator,” a response prompted not by a new incident but by a recent retweet of her February post. Amtrak quickly explained the mix-up, noting that someone had retweeted Carpenter’s old tweet and the message had resurfaced. The exchange, a lighthearted social media mistake rather than a serious brand blunder, drew attention and amusement online. Amtrak followed up by offering Carpenter a free ride on its Acela service as an olive branch. While brands frequently make missteps on Twitter, this incident stood out for being an honest, relatable error—an old plea brought back into view by the mechanics of social sharing—and for Amtrak’s candid, conciliatory responses that acknowledged the confusion and tried to make amends.

Dr. David Newman, a prominent emergency physician at Mount Sinai Hospital and author, surrendered to police after being accused of sexually abusing two female patients while they were under his care. Arrested by the NYPD’s Manhattan Special Victims Division, Newman was arraigned on charges including sexual abuse and forcible touching and held on $150,000 bond ($50,000 cash). He has been suspended from Mount Sinai pending the criminal and internal investigations.

The most serious allegation, arising from an incident on Jan. 11, involves a 22-year-old patient who said she was being treated for a shoulder injury when Newman allegedly administered an extra shot of morphine, rendering her incapacitated. She contends Newman then fondled her breasts, masturbated, and ejaculated on her face; she preserved the semen-stained hospital gown and bedding as evidence and turned them over to police. Authorities are awaiting DNA lab results; prosecutors sought a court order to obtain Newman’s DNA for comparison. Police sources and reports say nurses typically administer morphine at the hospital, leading prosecutors to suggest Newman may have had access to additional medication.

A separate woman, also 22, came forward claiming that in September she sought treatment for a severe head cold and was groped by Newman during a chest exam. Accounts vary on Newman’s age in reports (40 or 45), but widely note his prior standing as an Iraq War veteran, educator, and author of a book critiquing modern medicine. Colleagues and some supporters have defended him or urged caution, while Mount Sinai and other observers expressed shock and concern about abuse of medical power.

Newman’s lawyer said he has no criminal record and at one point said Newman volunteered a DNA sample; the defense called him a good doctor with a family. Investigators believe there may be additional victims and encouraged anyone with relevant experiences to come forward. Newman is due back in court on Feb. 23.

A Missouri appeals court judge has been appointed to take over Ferguson’s municipal court and implement reforms after a scathing U.S. Justice Department report prompted by the fatal police shooting of Michael Brown. The Missouri Supreme Court named Judge Roy L. Richter to hear all pending and future municipal cases and to overhaul court policies to protect defendants’ rights and restore integrity. Richter will assume control on March 16 and will be aided by staff from the state court administrator’s office.

Ferguson Municipal Judge Ronald J. Brockmeyer resigned, saying his departure would help restore public confidence and aid the city’s “healing process.” The city began seeking his permanent successor, while reactions from city officials were limited. Gov. Jay Nixon praised the Supreme Court’s actions.

The DOJ report found instances of racial profiling and bigotry by police and criticized a profit-driven municipal court system in the predominantly black suburb. It said Ferguson relied on fines and fees for roughly $3.1 million—about a quarter of its 2015 budget—and routinely imposed monetary penalties that led to arrest warrants and jail for missed payments or court dates. The report also documented forgiven tickets for officials, suggesting a racial double standard. The city recently fired court clerk Mary Ann Twitty. Public reaction to Richter’s appointment was mixed, with some seeing it as a needed step and others calling for more sweeping change.

In Emeryville, startup Ripple Foods is preparing to enter the national alternative-dairy market after raising $15 million in 2015. Founded by Adam Lowry and Neil Renninger—veterans of climate science and sustainable-product companies—Ripple makes a pea-based milk using a method that isolates protein from split yellow peas to produce a neutral-tasting, smooth white protein base. Blended with water, sunflower oil, stabilizers and flavoring, the resulting vegan beverages come in plain, sweetened, vanilla and chocolate varieties and deliver 8 grams of protein per serving—matching cow’s milk and standing out in a non-dairy category where many options are low in protein.

Ripple’s product avoids common allergens (soy, nuts), is gluten- and GMO-free, and supplies about 45% of daily calcium per serving; the company says that calcium is highly bioavailable because it’s associated with the protein. The sweetened version contains roughly half the sugar of cow’s milk, though the company uses cane sugar rather than the naturally occurring lactose found in dairy; founders argue the high protein content keeps the drinks low glycemic.

Lowry emphasizes Ripple’s environmental benefits: the company claims its milk uses roughly 96% less water than almond milk and 98.5% less than cow’s milk, and a 93% smaller carbon footprint versus traditional dairy. Current reliance on French-grown peas raises emissions, but Ripple plans to source all ingredients from U.S. suppliers by the end of 2016 and pursue an organic label. The founders are also seeking patents on their flavor- and color-removal technology, which could enable broader use of diverse plants in dairy alternatives and new pea-based products like yogurt. Bay Area stores will begin carrying Ripple products imminently, with national rollouts to follow.

Thomas S. Monson, the 16th president of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, died at age 90 in his Salt Lake City home after nearly a decade leading the faith and more than five decades in senior church leadership. Known for his warmth, storytelling and relentless personal ministry, Monson rose from bishop at 22 to become the youngest modern apostle in 1963 and was sustained as church president in February 2008. He cultivated a pastoral, hands-on style—visiting the sick, comforting the bereaved and responding to spiritual promptings—which defined his public image and endeared him to multiple generations of Mormons.

Monson’s presidency emphasized humanitarian outreach, temple building, expansion of missionary work, and institutional adjustments to respond to a globalizing church. His most consequential policy moves included lowering missionary minimum ages in 2012—triggering a surge in missionaries—and championing disaster relief and welfare programs. His tenure also grappled with contentious social issues: the church’s prominent support for California’s Proposition 8 in 2008, a 2015 policy concerning same-sex couples that provoked intense criticism, and ongoing debates about gender roles and immigration. Under Monson the church sought greater historical transparency through published essays addressing difficult aspects of Mormon history.

A World War II Navy veteran with degrees from the University of Utah and BYU, Monson balanced institutional leadership with personal interests—fishing, pigeons, Boy Scouts and the Utah Jazz—and was widely regarded as a compassionate, approachable prophet. Russell M. Nelson, the senior apostle, is expected to succeed him under church protocol. Monson’s legacy is a blend of pastoral care, humanitarian expansion and stewardship through a turbulent era for both the church and American society.

The number 13 and Friday the 13th carry a strong cultural stigma as unlucky, influencing behavior from skipping the 13th floor to avoiding weddings or driving that day. Scientific evidence, however, does not support an inherent unluckiness. Researchers like Igor Radun argue no number is intrinsically lucky or unlucky; perceptions arise from belief and selective memory. A frequently cited 1993 BMJ paper suggested a 52% higher hospital admission risk from transport accidents on Friday the 13th, but its authors later said it was a tongue-in-cheek Christmas edition piece. Subsequent studies produced mixed results: some reported gender differences in accidents, others refuted them. Analyses of lottery draws (UK Telegraph) found 13 drawn less often than some numbers since 1994, but such patterns are not predictive. Superstition clearly affects behavior—wedding vendors report fewer bookings or offer discounts on Friday the 13th, while some couples embrace it or ignore the taboo. Historical anecdotes and psychology explain the fear: cultural lore, religious associations, confirmation bias, and notable figures avoiding 13 reinforce the myth, though empirical support remains weak.

Two sisters, Nazila, 35, and Lida Sharaf, 33, have pleaded not guilty to multiple child-abuse charges after being accused of tightly swaddling seven infants at Universal Preschool in Livermore so severely the babies couldn’t move or breathe easily. Arrested last week, the sisters were arraigned on three felony counts and four misdemeanors each and released on reduced $340,000 bail. Court and jail attendees noted both are pregnant; Lida is due in July and Nazila is about 4½ months along. Investigators say staff used heavy-duty knots, sometimes covered infants’ faces, and raised room temperatures to induce sleep; three of the affected infants reportedly had upper respiratory conditions. No children showed medical injuries in exams. State officials closed the facility, seek license revocation and banned the women from licensed child-care work; Lida had faced a prior swaddling-related shutdown in 2010. Their attorney insists there was no intent to harm.

Assailants attacked Microsoft’s Athens offices pre-dawn, ramming a van through the front entrance and detonating an incendiary device that burned the building’s ground floor; there were no injuries. Police said three people were initially in the van, two masked gunmen armed with pistols and a machine gun forced security guards out, then reversed the vehicle into the doors and ignited camping gas canisters and gasoline containers. Forensic teams examined the burned-out van and charred entrance; damage was estimated around €60,000. No group immediately claimed responsibility. Authorities linked the tactic to past anarchist or left-wing extremist attacks amid Greece’s austerity-driven unrest. Microsoft closed the office while assessing damage.

A series of court rulings has put major talc-related verdicts against Johnson & Johnson (J&J) into question as plaintiffs who say the company’s talc-based baby powder caused ovarian cancer face legal setbacks. In Los Angeles, a judge threw out a $417 million jury award to Eva Echeverria, who alleged daily use of J&J baby powder from the 1950s until 2016 caused her ovarian cancer. Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Maren Nelson cited jury misconduct, trial errors, lack of convincing evidence of malice by J&J and an excessive damages award, and granted the company a new trial. Echeverria’s attorneys said they will appeal despite her death; they contend J&J knew of talc risks for decades. J&J maintains cosmetic-grade talc does not cause ovarian cancer and said it will continue to defend the product’s safety.

Separately, a Missouri appeals court vacated a $72 million award to the family of Jacqueline Fox, an Alabama woman who had been awarded $10 million in actual damages and $62 million punitive in an earlier St. Louis trial. The appeals court ruled Missouri lacked proper jurisdiction, citing a recent U.S. Supreme Court decision limiting where plaintiffs can sue corporations not based in the state where injuries occurred (the Bristol-Myers Squibb/Plavix precedent). That ruling threatens many St. Louis lawsuits—over 1,000 filed—because most plaintiffs are nonresidents. J&J has appealed multiple verdicts, arguing lack of jurisdiction in nonresident cases, while plaintiffs’ lawyers counter that the company’s Missouri packaging and labeling establish ties. Scientific evidence on talc is mixed: most large studies find no or weak links between genital talc use and ovarian cancer, though some smaller studies and the International Agency for Research on Cancer classify genital talc use as “possibly carcinogenic.”

Protesters in Durham, N.C., toppled a nearly century-old Confederate soldier statue outside the old county courthouse on Aug. 14, 2017, during a rally against racism sparked by the deadly white nationalist violence in Charlottesville. Dozens initially gathered, then more than 100, representing groups including the Triangle People’s Assembly, Workers World Party, Industrial Workers of the World, Democratic Socialists of America and antifa, chanted and circled the 15-foot bronze soldier. A protester climbed a ladder, looped a cord around the statue and, as it somersaulted from its pedestal, the crowd cheered and some kicked the fallen monument. Sheriff’s deputies and police recorded the action but did not intervene; no arrests were reported. Demonstrators briefly blocked intersections, marched past the new police headquarters construction site, and later dispersed peacefully. The action drew criticism from Gov. Roy Cooper, who urged lawful removal of such monuments. Durham officials said they would research the statue’s history and the state law—enacted in 2015—that generally prevents removal of “objects of remembrance” on public property without state approval. The monument’s base is inscribed “In memory of ‘the boys who wore the gray,’” and North Carolina hosts about 100 clearly Confederate-related memorials.

By midday Friday protesters had gathered outside Tunisia’s Interior Ministry, celebrating and debating the likely fall of President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali. Many credited Al Jazeera and social media, especially the #sidibouzid feed, with creating nationwide solidarity. The crowds—largely middle-class professionals, including many young women without veils—said Tunisia’s distinctive Bourguiba-era education and social policies produced a broad, empowered middle class. Anger focused on the Trabelsi family, accused of monopolizing key sectors and looting wealth. Ben Ali tried appeasements—firing ministers, pledging investigations, promising reforms and early elections—but promises, tear gas and bullets failed; police at times stood idle. Thousands rallied on Avenue Bourguiba, chanting “Ben Ali, out!” and accusing the regime of killings. The unrest, triggered by economic despair and a self-immolation, drove tourist evacuations, diplomatic fallout, resignations and mounting death toll disputes as Tunisia confronted a potential political rupture.

Athens stocks fell sharply after reopening following a five-week shutdown, with banks plunging for a second day and dragging the main index down 1.2% on Tuesday after a 16.2% collapse Monday. The banking index hit its 30% daily loss limit amid fears lenders need €10–25 billion in recapitalization after large deposit outflows. Non-financials largely recovered—19 of 25 blue chips rose; retail, airlines and gaming shares gained—suggesting bargain hunters bet on low valuations. Greece is negotiating a bailout with creditors and aims to finish a deal soon, while the economy slips back into recession; the Commission forecasts a 2–4% contraction and manufacturing and sentiment have deteriorated. U.S. mutual funds typically hold only tiny Greek exposures.

A participatory artwork at the Folkestone Triennial has launched an impromptu gold rush: German artist Michael Sailstorfer buried 30 bars of 24-carat gold, worth about £10,000 in total, in the sand of the Outer Harbour beach. Organisers revealed the project, Folkestone Digs, shortly before low tide opened access and encouraged the public to dig for the bullion — finders keepers. The bars vary in size and are marked “Made in London,” though metal washers were also buried to confound detector users. Curator Lewis Biggs and Situations director Claire Doherty framed the scheme as both playful and thought-provoking: the mass digging will produce ephemeral land art as sandcastles and trenches form and are subsequently reclaimed by the tide, and the uncertainty over whether all bars are recovered means the work “lasts forever.” Biggs highlighted questions the project raises about value—whether recovered bars are best sold as gold, treated as artworks, or kept as souvenirs—and predicted a mix of visitors and locals turning up to dig. Sailstorfer stayed away to let the piece “unfold”; his past work alters perceptions of place through simple interventions. The event forms part of the third Folkestone Triennial (30 Aug–2 Nov), which features over 20 commissions including works by Yoko Ono, Andy Goldsworthy and others, and aims to reframe the town’s cultural future.

Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, sharply criticized President Donald Trump’s decision to decertify Iran’s compliance with the 2015 nuclear deal and warned that Tehran would “shred” the pact if the United States formally abandons it. Speaking to students and in comments carried by Iranian state media, Khamenei dismissed Trump’s remarks as “rants and whoppers” and called him “foul‑mouthed” and “mentally retarded,” while accusing the U.S. of deceit and of backing extremist groups. He said Iran would not be the first to violate the accord but vowed to rip it “into pieces” if Washington tore it up. 

Khamenei pressed European governments to move beyond verbal support for the agreement and take concrete steps to resist U.S. pressure, arguing that European companies and governments benefit from the deal through trade and energy projects and therefore should protect it. He cited post‑deal business deals—aircraft sales by Airbus, Total’s gas agreements and Renault’s car contracts—to underline Europe’s stake in preserving Iran’s access to international markets and crude oil revenues needed for Iran’s economy. 

While Trump’s decertification sends the issue to Congress, which has 60 days to consider restoring sanctions, European leaders and the EU have urged the U.S. to remain in the multilateral deal. Khamenei framed the U.S. move as retaliation for Iran’s regional influence and role fighting ISIS, promising that Iran and its people would resist and that America would be defeated if it attempted to scuttle the agreement.

AirlineRatings.com’s 2017 Airline Excellence Awards recognized top carriers across categories. Air New Zealand claimed Airline of the Year for a fourth consecutive year, excelling across audit criteria. Virgin Australia and Virgin Atlantic retained Best Cabin Crew, with Virgin Australia also taking Best Business Class. Etihad won Best First Class and Best Long Haul (Middle East/Africa). Emirates earned Best In-Flight Entertainment. Qantas secured three wins: Best Domestic Airline Service, Best Lounges, and Best Catering. Delta remained Best Long-Haul (Americas); Singapore Airlines was Best Long-Haul (Asia). Low-cost honors included Scoot, Norwegian, and Kulula.com, while EVA Air, All Nippon, Cathay Pacific, and Lufthansa made the top 10.

A 51-year-old German tourist, identified as Oliver Park, died after falling from a ledge at Machu Picchu while attempting a mid-leap photo. Officials and witnesses say Park bypassed a security cordon and entered an off-limits area near a cliff edge overlooking the Inca citadel. He asked another visitor to photograph him as he posed with his back to the abyss; as the stranger took the camera, Park lost his balance, slipped about 10 feet onto a narrow ledge, then plunged approximately 130 feet (about 100 meters) into a ravine. Rescuers reached the site around an hour and a half later and recovered his body; it was transported by train to a morgue in Cusco. Park’s death is the latest in a series of accidents tied to tourists posing for photos in hazardous locations — including recent falls at other Peruvian sites and worldwide incidents involving selfies near cliffs, wildlife, trains, and waterways. Machu Picchu, a UNESCO World Heritage site perched roughly 8,000 feet above sea level, has long posed risks; Peru limits daily visitors to 2,500 to protect the ruins and improve safety, but some tourists still ignore warnings and venture into dangerous zones to capture dramatic images.

The document collects strong criticism of Washington Post columnist Richard Cohen for a passage in which he characterizes “people with conventional views” as needing to “repress a gag reflex” at the sight of New York mayor Bill de Blasio’s biracial family and mentions his wife’s past same-sex relationship. Critics argue that Cohen’s phrasing normalizes and excuses visceral disgust at interracial marriage, effectively portraying such reactions as merely “conventional” rather than racist, and reveal a deeper discomfort with modern, diverse America. Multiple excerpts and commentaries point out the historical and social ignorance implied by Cohen’s tone—mocking his surprise at depictions of slavery’s brutality and accusing him of repeatedly producing racially insensitive columns. Commentators note the disconnect between Cohen’s background as a liberal New Yorker and his apparent regression to reactionary language, suggesting his writing habitually projects archaic or prejudiced views onto “others” while denying personal culpability when called out. Critics also fault the Post’s editing, implying his prose goes unvetted, and urge owner Jeff Bezos to consider the paper’s business interests by reevaluating the publication of such columns in a majority-black city. The collection frames Cohen as a recurring figure who alternates bland political pieces, bad jokes, and racially charged commentary, followed by self-defensive responses when controversy erupts. Defenders’ claims that he was merely describing others’ views are seen as implausible given his framing—prefacing the description with “today’s GOP is not racist.” Overall, the assembled pieces call for accountability: they demand better editorial oversight, rejection of language that normalizes racial disgust, and—some say—Cohen’s removal from the paper.

Arkansas presents a paradox for anti-Obamacare politics: its shift from conservative Democrats to Republicans makes Democratic targets like Sen. Mark Pryor vulnerable, yet the state’s Republican legislature adopted a Medicaid “private option” that splits the GOP coalition and stops Arkansas from joining broader resistance to the Affordable Care Act. That political complexity allowed groups like Americans for Prosperity to run aggressive ads—sometimes misleadingly—about canceled plans, even after the state had extended such plans through 2017. Nationally, on April 1, 2014, President Obama announced roughly 7.1 million people had chosen plans through ACA marketplaces, a milestone that exceeded revised administration goals despite earlier website troubles. The number’s significance is political and symbolic, though it leaves key implementation questions unanswered: how many were previously uninsured, the age and health mix of enrollees, and how many paid premiums. The administration hailed grassroots outreach, celebrity endorsements, and last-minute enrollment pushes for the surge, while Republicans continued to criticize the law’s rollout and effects, vowing repeal. Polling showed public opinion creeping slightly more favorable: a narrow plurality supported the ACA. Administration officials argued the debate should shift from repeal to defending implementation, even as Republicans prepared to make Obamacare a central midterm issue.

Washington voters narrowly approved Referendum 74, legalizing same-sex marriage and making Washington the third state (with Maryland and Maine) to adopt marriage equality by popular vote. With about three-quarters of ballots counted, R-74 led roughly 52–48 percent; opponents conceded as the margin held. Supporters celebrated across Seattle’s Capitol Hill and at news events, calling the outcome historic and a step toward equality. Gov. Chris Gregoire and bill sponsor Sen.
