Ed Murray praised the result as correcting past injustices; Murray predicted marriages beginning in December would be a healing moment. Preserve Marriage Washington and other opponents expressed disappointment, blaming political and funding disadvantages; the anti-R-74 campaign raised about $2.7 million versus roughly $12 million from pro-equality donors, including Bezos and Gates. Though the measure lost in most counties, it won overwhelmingly in populous King County, securing its statewide lead. The law allows civil marriages while protecting religious organizations from being compelled to perform them. The vote continues a recent trend toward marriage equality via legislation, courts and now direct voter approval.

This morning in New York City some polling places opened late after ballots and poll books were misdelivered. Voters waited while officials retrieved correct materials, others used affidavit ballots, and some left. NYC requires poll workers to arrive at 5 a.m., giving just one hour to set up; by contrast, many jurisdictions routinely set up polling sites before Election Day, sometimes the night before or over the weekend, allowing time to detect misdeliveries, sign shortages, absent workers, or other problems. City officials cite security concerns for keeping voting materials locked until Election Day to prevent theft, while election experts note tamper-evident seals and logs can secure at least some equipment and supplies ahead of time. Meanwhile, news organizations have mobilized collaborative projects to monitor and report voting problems and debunk hoaxes. ProPublica’s Electionland links more than 400 newsrooms, sharing tips from social media, a national hotline, and local reporting to surface issues like long lines, voter intimidation, and misinformation. Regional teams and journalism students will mine trends and verify leads; partners include The New York Times and USA Today, though some outlets declined. Other efforts include Votecastr, publishing real-time turnout-based projections from key precincts. Organizers say collaboration helps catch and correct problems in a high-stakes, polarized environment rife with hacking fears and false tampering claims, though critics may portray coordinated coverage as biased.

Researchers at the University of Waterloo led by PhD candidate Gordon Pennycook examined why some people find grand-sounding but meaningless statements—termed “pseudo-profound bulls***” by the authors—impressive or insightful. The study defines such statements as syntactically coherent collections of buzzwords that imply depth without conveying actual meaning or truth. To operationalize the concept, the team used an online generator that produces aphoristic, wise-sounding sentences (e.g., “This life is nothing short of an unveiling quantum leap of mythic rejuvenation”) and presented these alongside genuine philosophical quotes and mundane sentences to almost 300 participants. Subjects rated each sentence’s profundity on a one-to-five scale and completed other measures assessing cognitive ability, reflective thinking, and belief tendencies.

Findings show a clear pattern: individuals who rate pseudo-profound statements as meaningful tend to score lower on measures of cognitive ability (including verbal, fluid intelligence and numeracy) and are less reflective. They are also more prone to ontological confusions—mistaking vague language for substantive claims—and more inclined toward conspiratorial ideation. Additionally, receptivity to such statements correlates with higher endorsement of religious and paranormal beliefs and greater acceptance of complementary and alternative medicine. While most participants correctly identified mundane sentences as unremarkable, many rated the generated pseudo-profound sentences similarly to actual mystical or spiritual tweets by public figures, demonstrating the persuasive veneer of such language.

The researchers conclude that the tendency to perceive vague, meaningless statements as profound is a legitimate psychological phenomenon, systematically related to cognitive and personality variables of theoretical interest, and reflective of broader patterns in how people evaluate and are influenced by superficially impressive language.

Doctors Without Borders (MSF) is demanding an independent international probe after a U.S. airstrike hit its Kunduz trauma hospital in Afghanistan, killing dozens including 12 MSF staff. President Obama phoned MSF president Dr. Joanne Liu to apologize and express condolences, and the White House pledged support for U.S., NATO and Afghan investigations, but MSF says those internal probes are insufficient. The charity called for activation of the International Humanitarian Fact‑Finding Commission (IHFFC), a Geneva Conventions body created in 1991 that has never been used; it requires consent from a state party to begin work, and neither the U.S. nor Afghanistan are signatories. MSF argues the IHFFC could independently establish what happened, why, and who is responsible, warning that letting the incident go unchecked would erode protections for medical facilities in war. U.S. commanders say the hospital was struck accidentally while providing close air support to Afghan forces; accounts of who requested the strike and why have shifted. MSF describes scenes of patients burning in beds and staff operating on colleagues; it says GPS coordinates had been shared with all authorities and stresses that hospitals enjoy special protected status under international humanitarian law.

On Dec. 12, 2016, Bakersfield police shot and killed 73-year-old Francisco Serna early Monday morning after responding to a call about a man allegedly brandishing a handgun in the 7900 block of Silver Birch Avenue. Officers arrived about 12:30 a.m.; when a witness pointed to Serna standing in a neighbor’s driveway, an officer fired multiple rounds. Serna was declared dead at the scene about 1:15 a.m. The Bakersfield Police Department initially reported the man had been carrying a gun and was not complying with commands, but no weapon was found at the scene. Family members say Serna — who lived with his wife and daughter and had moved to Bakersfield years earlier to be near family — suffered early-stage dementia, often took late-night walks, did not own a gun, and had previously prompted nonviolent police visits after triggering a medical alarm. Officers involved were placed on administrative leave while the shooting was investigated. The Kern County coroner listed cause of death as multiple gunshot wounds and manner of death as homicide. An autopsy showed five of seven bullets fired by the officer struck Serna; at least one passed through him and three rounds hit a nearby home.

Washington state Republicans Matt Shea, David Taylor and Bob McCaslin introduced House Bill 1015 to bar public stadium authorities, local governments and private operators leasing public venues from forbidding licensed concealed carry holders from bringing pistols into stadiums and similar facilities. Affected venues would include CenturyLink Field and Safeco Field. Currently stadiums can prohibit certain items, including firearms, even though carrying a firearm to games isn’t broadly illegal under state law. The NFL said it opposes the proposal, noting it forbids weapons in its stadiums, and the league’s policies and game-day logistics (bag rules, security) make permitting guns complicated. Critics warn of increased danger where alcohol, heated rivalries and crowd altercations occur. The bill faces likely opposition in Democratic-leaning Washington.

Former Florida governor Jeb Bush published a massive archive of emails from his eight-year governorship online in the name of “transparency,” but the release exposed a large amount of private constituent data and prompted criticism for its careless handling of sensitive information. Bush’s site hosted hundreds of thousands of messages—sources put the total between roughly 275,000 and 333,000—and initially made raw Outlook (.pst) files and searchable calendars available. Many emails included full names, email addresses and other personal details; some even contained home addresses, phone numbers, medical information and Social Security numbers. Observers and security researchers quickly flagged the risk: Identity Finder reported more than 12,000 people had their name, birthdate and SSN exposed in the archive, while journalists and researchers found medical and personnel records and emotionally personal appeals that were never intended for broad public dissemination.

Bush’s team said the files replicated public records held by the Florida Department of State under Florida’s broad Sunshine Law, and his spokesperson asserted redaction efforts had been made. Florida law, however, treats Social Security numbers as confidential and exempt from public disclosure; legal experts noted the state’s custodian of records bears responsibility for preventing release of exempt data. Critics argued that even if the records were legally obtainable, publishing them without redaction was tone-deaf and breached reasonable expectations of privacy. Some correspondents expressed embarrassment and dismay that private messages—some explicitly pleading they not be published—were now public.

After media scrutiny, Bush’s site removed the raw PST downloads and later removed or redacted personal data from many entries; his campaign said it would take down personal information it found. Nonetheless, copies had already proliferated online and been archived elsewhere, underscoring how once released, sensitive data can be difficult or impossible to fully retract. The episode highlighted both the hazards of indiscriminate public-data dumps and the limits of “transparency” when it exposes vulnerable individuals to privacy and identity-theft risks.

Edgar Wright’s Baby Driver is a turbocharged, music-fueled summer thriller that blends precise choreography, dark humor and high-octane car chases into an exuberant, often dazzling whole. Ansel Elgort stars as Baby, a soft-spoken young Atlanta getaway driver with chronic tinnitus who drowns the constant ringing in his ears behind an ever-present personal soundtrack. That music becomes the film’s organizing force: Wright times stunts, editing and even gunfire to songs ranging from the Jon Spencer Blues Explosion to Simon & Garfunkel, making each set piece feel like a needle-drop dance number and giving the action a visceral, you-are-there urgency bolstered by in-camera stunts and Bill Pope’s cinematography.

Baby works for Doc (Kevin Spacey), a calculating crime boss who relies on Baby’s near-supernatural steering to pull off robberies. Doc assembles a volatile crew — the unhinged Bats (Jamie Foxx), the menacing Griff (Jon Bernthal), the oddly affable Buddy (Jon Hamm) and his tough partner Darling (Eiza González) — and when one job goes wrong Baby’s desire to escape the life spikes the stakes. The film slows only briefly for Baby’s romance with diner waitress Debora (Lily James), whose sweetness and dream-of-the-West optimism create a pleasing counterpoint to the escalating violence. Elgort’s largely silent performance relies on expressive eyes and physicality; he makes Baby sympathetic and compelling in a demanding role.

Wright’s direction is the movie’s dominant pleasure: building on a concept he’d tinkered with since a 2003 music video, he executes meticulously timed sequences and cleareyed homages to genre touchstones — Walter Hill’s The Driver, Point Break, Reservoir Dogs and Heat — without feeling derivative. Supporting performances go big; Jon Hamm and Jamie Foxx, in particular, deliver show-stopping turns. Rated R, 113 minutes, Baby Driver is pure pop cinema — a bold, kinetic, joyfully crafted film that feels custom-made for the summer.

Conal O’Rourke, a Northern California resident with 20 years’ experience in corporate controllership, says a year-long billing nightmare with Comcast led to his firing from PricewaterhouseCoopers and has prompted him to threaten legal action. After moving to San Jose in early 2013 and signing up for Comcast TV and Internet because no rival service was available, O’Rourke encountered repeated billing and service errors. His first bill arrived late and misspelled his name; it also included charges for three “additional HD outlets” at $26.25 per month, fees for cable boxes he says he never activated, and a promotional HBO package that disappeared after three months instead of the promised nine. Multiple calls and store visits failed to fix the issues.

Problems escalated in late 2013 when his Internet service became unreliable and, while traveling overseas, he returned to find 12 pieces of Comcast equipment on his doorstep and a December bill topping $2,000 that included $1,820 for devices he insists he never ordered—items such as an “AnyRoom Hub” and a “Pace Host.” O’Rourke returned the equipment to a San Jose Comcast store and handed a detailed spreadsheet documenting the errors to employee Matt Doblias, who said he’d review it but later claimed not to have received the file.

Frustrated, O’Rourke sent a sarcastic, unsent “nomination” letter criticizing the store’s customer service. Billing errors persisted and Comcast allegedly referred his account to collections. After an agitated call with an assistant in the controller’s office—during which O’Rourke pressed about accounting accuracy and regulatory oversight—Comcast internal alarms were reportedly triggered. O’Rourke has compiled voluminous documentation (invoices, spreadsheets, photos, notes, correspondence) and, represented by attorney Maureen Pettibone Ryan, is demanding a full retraction and apology, reinstatement at PWC, and $100,312.50 by October 14 or he will file suit. The case raises questions about billing practices, customer service failures, and how disputes can escalate when corporate accounting and consumer complaints collide.

A study published in the Journal of Medical Toxicology analyzing National Poison Data System calls from 2000–2012 finds a large and growing burden of poisonings from dietary supplements, with children disproportionately affected. Researchers at Nationwide Children’s Hospital reported 274,998 supplement exposures—about one call every 24 minutes—with the rate of supplement-related calls rising nearly 50% from 2005 to 2012. Seventy percent of exposures occurred in children under six (99% unintentional), and overall 82.9% of calls were unintentional. Symptoms commonly included rapid heart rate, vomiting, nausea, irritability, drowsiness and dizziness. Although only 4.5% of exposures produced serious medical outcomes, children bore most of the harm: 1,818 yohimbe exposures were reported over ten years, 512 classified as serious, with one death linked to yohimbe. Across the study period, 34 deaths were associated with supplement exposures, including six tied to ma huang (ephedra) and three to homeopathic agents.

Certain products accounted for the largest shares of calls and the worst outcomes. Homeopathic agents were the single largest category (36% of calls), followed by botanicals (31.9%) and hormonal products (15.1%). The most dangerous groups—energy products, botanicals, and cultural medicines—had the highest proportions of serious outcomes. Notable hazardous botanicals included yohimbe (linked to arrhythmias, seizures, kidney failure) and ma huang (linked to strokes and heart attacks), the latter banned by the FDA in 2004; that ban coincided with a temporary drop in poison calls.

Authors and poison-center directors urge stronger protections: child-resistant packaging, caregiver education, and tighter FDA oversight. Because dietary supplements are not reviewed or approved as drugs, product quality, labeling, and contamination vary widely. They recommend treating supplements as medicines—storing them out of children’s reach—and call for regulatory steps, particularly for risky products like yohimbe and stimulant-containing energy supplements.

Footage and reports from the devastating Oso, Washington, mudslide in late March 2014 documented both dramatic rescues and grim discoveries as search-and-recovery operations continued. Helicopter video captured a young boy, 4-year-old Jacob Spillers, being plucked from the mud after the hillside above the North Fork Stillaguamish River collapsed on Saturday, sending a milewide torrent of debris across Highway 530 and through the Steelhead Haven neighborhood. Jacob was one of the few immediate survivors from his household; his mother, who was elsewhere, survived, while his stepfather Billy Spillers and three siblings remained missing. 

By Tuesday, officials had recovered additional bodies, raising the confirmed death toll to 16, and said they believed they had located eight more bodies under packed mud that has in places reached 20 feet deep and become as hard as concrete. The number of people reported missing swelled to 176 as families scrambled to account for loved ones; authorities cautioned that the list included duplicates and hoped the tally would shrink after verification, but they also shifted toward a recovery posture and called in mortuary assistance. 

Rescue and recovery efforts were hampered by hazardous terrain, worsening weather and the risk of further slope movement. Dozens of responders—including the National Guard, FEMA teams, trained dogs and sonar and thermal equipment—worked alongside local volunteers through wreckage of twisted vehicles, shattered homes and contaminated water. Officials noted the slide’s enormous scale—estimated at roughly 175 million cubic feet—and said monitoring and stabilization would be needed as engineers assessed ongoing risks. The disaster prompted a federal emergency declaration and left the close-knit community reeling as hopes for additional survivors faded.

PolitiFact named "death panels" its inaugural Lie of the Year after Sarah Palin’s August Facebook post claimed Democratic health-care proposals would create government boards to decide whether seniors and the disabled deserved care. Palin’s phrase — apparently original — rapidly spread through broadcasts, talk shows and town halls, driving intense public debate and drawing comparisons to Nazi-era euthanasia. The charge grew from earlier, false claims by conservatives that Medicare would mandate counseling to encourage euthanasia; in fact the provision merely allowed optional Medicare-paid physician consultations about advance directives. PolitiFact and health policy experts debunked the allegation, rating related claims Pants on Fire, but Republicans amplified the fear, energizing opposition and resonating with voters worried about rationing and end-of-life costs. Polls found roughly 30 percent believed death panels were part of reform, with belief split largely by party. Democrats argued the claim illustrated unreasonable Republican obstruction; President Obama called it a deliberate lie. Palin has refused to retract the phrase, saying it effectively warned people about potential rationing and comparing her rhetoric to Reagan’s provocative language. The episode highlighted the potency of political misinformation and its chilling effect on civil discourse.

An Army dress rehearsal ahead of Donald Trump’s 2017 inauguration used military stand-ins to ensure the real event would run smoothly. At Fort McNair on Jan. 15, members of the U.S. Army Band “Pershing’s Own” portrayed President-elect Trump, Melania Trump, Vice President-elect Mike Pence and Karen Pence while rehearsing the parade route, swearing-in movements, security escorts and media arrangements. Band vocalist Sgt. Maj. Greg Lowery, 53, played the part of Trump and even bought a red tie to “look the part,” while Spc. Sara Corry, from Capistrano Beach, California, stood in for Melania. MSG Neil Ewachiw acted as Mike Pence and M Sgt. Leigh Ann Hinton as Karen Pence. The four were chosen by command and auditioned primarily for height and movement compatibility rather than facial resemblance, though some people noted likenesses. Rehearsals aimed to set microphone heights, lighting and camera angles and to rehearse escort procedures—details critical to both safety and how the ceremony would appear to the world. Participants described the experience as thrilling and meaningful, emphasizing the peaceful transfer of power as a cornerstone of democracy. The Joint Task Force National Capital Region directed the single dress rehearsal, giving the stand-ins one opportunity to work out any kinks before the inauguration.

Boston police arrested 34-year-old homeless man Bodio Hutchinson after he allegedly lunged at and stabbed two unarmed park rangers on Boston Common in an unprovoked attack. A 46-year-old sergeant was critically wounded in the abdomen and underwent surgery at Massachusetts General Hospital; a 23-year-old rookie ranger sustained less serious wounds and was treated at Tufts Medical Center. Witnesses followed Hutchinson, provided cellphone video, and helped police capture him in the Public Garden; officers recovered a knife from Frog Pond. Commissioner William Evans said Hutchinson has a violent criminal history and faces attempted murder counts plus outstanding assault and drug charges. Officials are reviewing park safety and resources.

The western Indian state of Gujarat has enacted an amendment to its Animal Preservation Act that imposes the country's harshest penalties for cow slaughter and related activities. Under the change, killing cows can now carry a life sentence, while transporting beef is punishable by up to 10 years in prison. Monetary fines have also been doubled from 50,000 to 100,000 rupees. State officials framed the move as reflecting cultural values: Minister of State Pradipsinh Jadeja said the cow is a symbol of Indian culture and the amendments were made “in consultation with the people,” while Chief Minister Vijay Rupani has repeatedly advocated “harsh” punishments for cow killing. The law will take effect after the state governor’s approval.

The amendment comes against a backdrop of rising vigilante violence linked to cow protection. The article recounts a recent deadly attack in neighboring Rajasthan in which a Muslim man, Pehlu Khan, died after being beaten by a mob that accused him and others of transporting cows for slaughter. Video showed victims beaten with sticks and iron rods; the attackers released a Hindu truck driver after warning him not to carry cattle. No arrests had been reported in that case. Such incidents are part of a broader pattern since Prime Minister Narendra Modi took office in 2014: hard-line Hindu activists and self-styled cow-protection groups have increased efforts to stop cattle transport and press for beef bans, actions that have disproportionately affected poor and minority Muslim communities for whom the beef trade is an important livelihood. Rumors about beef consumption have sparked other fatal vigilante attacks in northern India in recent years.

Facebook, Inc. builds products for users, developers and advertisers, enabling people to connect, discover and share with friends and family, and allowing developers to integrate apps and sites via the Facebook Platform. Advertisers can target more than 900 million monthly active users using demographic and interest data. In late 2013 Facebook made some corporate moves: Mail.Ru Group sold its remaining Facebook shares in September, Facebook acquired Mobile Technologies on September 25, and in October it bought Onavo Inc.

At a Menlo Park event, Facebook unveiled Graph Search, its major push into helping users find content from within the social network. With over a billion users, hundreds of billions of photos and trillions of social connections, Facebook faces a huge indexing challenge. CEO Mark Zuckerberg described Graph Search as designed to take precise queries and return precise answers drawn from the user’s social graph. Rather than returning web links like traditional search engines, Graph Search surfaces content—people, photos, videos, games—shared within a user’s network. Queries such as “games my friends play” return results based on one’s connections, keeping relevance grounded in social relationships.

Graph Search directly competes with initiatives like Google’s Search Plus Your World, but Facebook’s advantage is a much larger, more active social graph. The feature also threatens third-party recommendation services such as Yelp, Foursquare and Path, which operate on far smaller datasets. For web content not present on Facebook, the company has partnered with Microsoft’s Bing to deliver external results. The broader strategic aim is clear: encourage users to find what they need inside Facebook and reduce the frequency of leaving the network. Bloomberg noted Facebook held a press event to reveal this new capability, with live reporting on the announcement.

Derrick Deanda, a Good Samaritan who rescued a father and three children from a rollover crash in Elk Grove, California, was later mailed a $143 first-responder fee by the Cosumnes Community Services District. Deanda stopped at the scene in September 2015, broke a van window to free the occupants and suffered a small cut. When emergency crews arrived, paramedics checked him, gave him a bottle of water and recorded his information. Months later he received a bill for the “first-responder” assessment. Deanda posted the bill and photos of the crash on Facebook, saying he asked for water to clean his wound and was surprised to be charged for what he considered a minimal check. He questioned whether charging Good Samaritans discourages people from helping at accidents.

Deputy Chief Mike McLaughlin confirmed the district billed Deanda because he was technically a patient after the cut and emphasized the department applies the same billing standards for every patient. The district instituted the fee two years earlier to help avoid fire station brownouts. McLaughlin called the situation unique in his 28-year career and said there is an appeals mechanism; he expressed a desire to have the fee waived in this case and make things right. Deanda plans to appeal and hopes the charge is resolved before it goes to collections.

A comprehensive international assessment published in Nature shows Antarctica’s ice loss has accelerated sharply since the 1990s, with roughly 2.7–3 trillion tonnes of ice shed since 1992. Satellite and airborne observations—synthesized by the Ice sheet Mass Balance Inter-comparison Exercise (IMBIE), combining 24 independent methods and data from some 10–15 satellites plus ground and air measurements—reveal average annual losses rising from about 84 billion tonnes per year (1992–2011) to roughly 200–241 billion tonnes per year (2012–2017). That increase has tripled Antarctica’s contribution to global sea-level rise since the previous multi-method assessment: Antarctica now adds about 0.6 mm per year to sea level, and overall global sea-level rise runs near 3 mm per year from multiple sources. Most losses are concentrated in West Antarctica and the Antarctic Peninsula, where warm ocean waters are undermining marine-terminating glaciers and the collapse of ice shelves has allowed upstream ice to accelerate. West Antarctica’s loss rose from ~53 to 159 billion tonnes per year across the record; the Peninsula increased from ~7 to 33 billion tonnes annually. East Antarctica shows modest gains—on the order of a few billion tonnes per year—that do not offset losses elsewhere and may reflect short-term snowfall variability. Researchers caution ocean warming and changing winds are driving the melt by thinning glacier fronts from below; bedrock uplift (isostatic rebound) may locally slow retreat but is unlikely to halt the ongoing dynamic losses. Projections suggest Antarctica could contribute significantly to century-scale sea-level rise—possibly adding on the order of 16 cm by 2100 in many scenarios—heightening the need for governments to plan coastal defences and for continued, robust observations to refine forecasts.

Arlington police are appealing for public help after a deadly road-rage shooting on Interstate 30 late Wednesday afternoon claimed the life of 26-year-old Fort Worth woman Brittany Daniel. According to investigators, the incident occurred between 6:45 and 7:00 p.m. near the Cooper Street exit as Daniel was driving east with a co-worker, Jasmine Thomas, who was riding in the front seat. Thomas said an erratic, dark-colored small four-door sedan repeatedly swerved alongside them; after a brief verbal exchange, a light-skinned black or Hispanic man in his mid-20s reportedly rolled down a backseat window and fired at least two shots. Daniel was struck, managed to pull over and asked Thomas to call 911, but she was pronounced dead about 7:30 p.m. at Texas Health Arlington Memorial Hospital. With no surveillance footage, police seek anyone who was driving on I-30 between Cooper and Center streets during that time and might have information. Tips can be given to Detective Steve Griesbach at 817-459-5325 or anonymously to Tarrant County Crime Stoppers at 817-469-TIPS. Daniel’s family is pleading for justice.

A France Telecom worker in his late 50s, employed for more than 30 years and father of four, died by suicide after setting himself on fire on company premises in Mérignac near Bordeaux shortly after arriving at work. Colleagues and union representatives said staff were “overwhelmed” and deeply affected. The incident revived scrutiny of a wider crisis at the company that began in 2008: dozens of employees took their own lives amid major restructuring as the former government agency transformed into the private firm now known as Orange. Unions have blamed restructuring measures, repeated internal transfers, heightened work pressure and allegedly unattainable performance targets for creating unbearable conditions for some staff. A 2010 labour inspection reported 19 suicides, 12 attempts and multiple cases of severe depression or forced work stoppages tied to the company’s policies; union counts have been higher. Legal action has followed: former France Telecom CEO Didier Lombard, six other executives and Orange itself face trial on charges of engaging in or assisting psychological harassment (“moral harassment”), a crime punishable by up to two years’ imprisonment and fines. Lombard and others deny wrongdoing. The controversy previously forced senior resignations and remains a focal example of the human cost of aggressive corporate restructuring.

People have long wondered how astronauts relieve themselves in space; the answer evolved pragmatically from simple, necessity-driven solutions into more engineered systems as missions grew longer. Early Mercury flights originally omitted any bathroom provision because missions were planned to be very short. In practice, however, astronauts endured long waits on the launchpad and flights that could extend beyond initial plans. Alan Shepard famously wet his suit before his suborbital Freedom 7 flight after being denied a chance to exit the capsule; mission control later allowed him to disable biomedical sensors and urinate into his suit, the oxygen flow soon drying him. Gus Grissom used a makeshift garter-and-condom setup attached to a collection bag, an ad-hoc fix that was soon replaced by a dedicated external urine-collection tube and bag with one-way valve. Gordon Cooper’s Faith 7 added multiple bags and the ability to pump urine overboard or return samples for study.

As missions lengthened with Gemini, fecal containment became necessary. Crews were given low‑residue diets and provided adhesive-lined tube bags containing moisture-absorbing crystals; using them was awkward and missions like Gemini 7 produced unpleasant smells noted by recovery crews. Apollo offered slightly more space but still minimal privacy: astronauts sometimes stripped down to simplify cleanup, and moonwalkers wore collection bags plus diapers (maximum one-sixth gravity helped contain waste). Diapers were seldom used deliberately, but accidental leaks occurred—Charlie Duke found a wet boot after ascent from the Moon. Over months-long ISS missions, toilet technology improved and crew privacy became important for mixed-gender teams. Throughout, solutions were driven by pragmatism: human biology met engineering constraints, producing humble but essential systems that kept spaceflight possible.

Pope Francis arrived in South Korea for a five-day visit, his first trip to Asia as pontiff and the first papal visit to the country in 25 years. He opened the trip by urging renewed efforts for peace and reconciliation on the divided Korean Peninsula, calling for diplomacy, listening and dialogue instead of "mutual recriminations, fruitless criticisms and displays of force." His arrival coincided with North Korea firing several short-range projectiles into the sea, underscoring regional tensions. Francis met President Park Geun-hye, exchanged condolences with relatives of Sewol ferry victims, and will beatify 124 Korean martyrs to inspire evangelization in a country whose Catholic Church has grown significantly. He also plans to attend Asian Youth Day and hold a reconciliation Mass at Myeong-dong Cathedral. Organizers had invited North Korean Catholics to the Mass, but Pyongyang declined. While South Korea’s church is seen as a model for growth and outreach, North Korea permits virtually no independent religious practice. En route, Francis sent greetings to China’s leader, a rare exchange given the lack of Vatican-Beijing diplomatic ties; his plane was allowed to use Chinese airspace, which Vatican spokesmen called a sign of détente.

General Mills has voluntarily recalled about 10 million pounds of flour — including select Gold Medal, Wondra and Signature Kitchens SKUs — after a multistate outbreak of E. coli O121 sickened 38 people across 20 states between Dec. 21, 2015, and May 3, 2016. The CDC found roughly half of those ill reported making homemade items with flour before falling sick, and some reported using General Mills brands; about 10 people were hospitalized and no deaths were reported. The company said E. coli O121 has not been detected in any of its flour products or its manufacturing facility, and it has not received direct consumer reports of confirmed illnesses. Most of the recalled flour was produced at General Mills’ Kansas City plant and was distributed to many major grocery chains. General Mills called the recall “out of an abundance of caution,” offering replacement and reminding consumers that raw dough or batter should never be eaten because flour is a raw agricultural product that can carry pathogens; cooking or baking kills such bacteria. The company provided UPCs and “better if used by” dates to identify recalled packages and set up an informational web page and hotline (1-800-230-8103). Health officials advise anyone ill to see a physician and report confirmed E. coli O121 infections to local health authorities.

A class-action suit claimed Taco Bell’s beef is only 36% meat, prompting CEO Greg Creed to rebut the allegation. Taco Bell says its seasoned beef is 88% USDA-inspected beef and 12% seasonings, water and other ingredients — including 3–5% water, 3–5% spices (salt, chili, onion and tomato powders, garlic, cocoa, sugar and proprietary Mexican spices/natural flavors) and 3–5% oats, starch, yeast, citric acid and similar components. Creed called the lawsuit’s facts wrong, promised legal action, and emphasized ingredient transparency on Taco Bell’s website. The broader commentary notes recurring “fake food” controversies—from blueberry substitutes and non-maple syrup in McDonald’s oatmeal to processed chicken nuggets and low chocolate content in candy—urging consumers to research ingredients and decide what they’ll eat.

The Tamiment Library Economic and Social Justice Web Collection, begun in 2010, archives webpages of left- and progressive-oriented organizations addressing economic and social justice topics such as corporate accountability, immigrant rights, unemployment, homelessness, urban justice, healthcare reform, and wealth redistribution. The collection places heavy emphasis on the Occupy Wall Street movement (established September 2011), documenting diverse Occupy-related sites and working groups under a distinct series and tag. Materials preserved include YouTube videos, PDFs, blog posts (Tumblr, WordPress), petitions, news feeds, audio, and other media used to document activities, publicize events, and build awareness. Most sites are crawled quarterly, with weekly or monthly captures during intense activity; the archive preserves only publicly available content and cannot capture password-protected or robot-excluded pages, and linked or deeper pages are sometimes missed.

Also featured is Micah White’s The End of Protest, in which the Occupy co-creator contends that traditional protest no longer effects lasting change despite massive recent mobilizations. White diagnoses activism at a crossroads—innovation or irrelevance—and proposes a unified theory of revolution plus eight tactical principles for future movements. He frames Occupy as a “constructive failure” that revealed both limits and pathways forward, urging multi-century timescales, broader political engagement (dominating elections, governing cities), and a spiritual and social revolution. White’s activist background and writings lend authority to his provocative, forward-looking playbook for reinventing protest.

“The Road” is a faithful but emotionally incomplete film adaptation of Cormac McCarthy’s bleak Pulitzer-winning novel. Directed by John Hillcoat and scripted by Joe Penhall, it follows a nameless man (Viggo Mortensen) and his son (Kodi Smit‑McPhee) as they trudge across an ash‑strewn, post‑apocalyptic America toward the coast, hauling their few belongings in a shopping cart and avoiding marauding survivors who may resort to cannibalism. The production design, costumes and performances—especially Mortensen’s guarded intensity and Smit‑McPhee’s unshowy vulnerability—evoke the book’s stark world and haunting relationship between parent and child. Flashbacks with Charlize Theron and a fragile Robert Duvall add texture, yet critics argue the film lacks McCarthy’s transformative prose and the novel’s transcendent emotional heft. Hillcoat’s restrained, realistic approach produces disturbing, powerful images but stops short of the deeper, poetic resonance that made the book more than an endurance test. Ultimately, “The Road” is a strong, somber film that honors its source yet falls short of fully capturing its moral and literary force.

The Senate Judiciary Committee proceeded with a scheduled Friday vote on Brett Kavanaugh’s Supreme Court nomination after a contentious, day-long hearing featuring Kavanaugh and accuser Christine Blasey Ford. Key Republican senators—particularly Jeff Flake, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski—were being watched closely as they weighed whether to advance the nomination; Flake voiced uncertainty late Thursday. GOP leaders aimed for a full Senate vote the following week while acknowledging they could only afford one defections in their 51-49 majority. The White House praised Kavanaugh’s forceful defense as decisive and aligned with President Trump’s combative style, despite some aides’ concerns that Ford’s testimony was credible and that GOP questioning, led by prosecutor Rachel Mitchell, was uneven. Tennessee Sen. Bob Corker announced support, while others continued private deliberations. The outcome remained uncertain as senators weighed testimony, credibility and political consequences.

Last week’s flurry of reporting revived the long-standing hunt for Bitcoin’s creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, by pointing to Australian entrepreneur Craig Steven Wright as the likeliest candidate — or, alternately, as the architect of an elaborate hoax. Wired and other outlets compiled a cache of leaked emails, archived blog posts, company records and a purported trust document that together draw a detailed line between Wright and early Bitcoin activity. Key items include pre-launch blog posts from 2008–2009 referring to a forthcoming “cryptocurrency paper,” a PGP key linked to an address similar to Nakamoto’s, and a now‑deleted January 2009 post about Bitcoin’s beta. Leaked messages imply Wright discussed a P2P distributed ledger as early as mid‑2008 and planned to invest heavily in hardware to “get [his] idea going.” A PDF signed by the late computer forensics expert David Kleiman references a “Tulip Trust” holding 1.1 million bitcoins — the same massive, unmoved cache widely attributed to Nakamoto — and Wright’s firms’ audited records show multi‑million‑dollar bitcoin holdings consistent with unusually large early accumulation.

Wired confronted Wright; encrypted replies came from an account routed through the Panama-based Vistomail service Nakamoto used. Wright’s responses were evasive, alternating between denial, claims of privacy and hints that “too many already know secrets.” Much of the evidence is circumstantial: Wright’s technological background, cypherpunk mailing-list involvement, libertarian bent, academic claims and supercomputing projects fit the Satoshi profile. Yet investigators found that some blog posts were edited or restored years later, raising the possibility they were retroactively altered to create incriminating breadcrumbs.

If Wright truly is Nakamoto, consequences would be profound: control over a vast coin reserve, influence on community debates, and legal and market ramifications if those coins became movable. Authorities also raided Wright’s home in Australia in a tax-related probe following the reports. Conversely, inconsistencies in Wright’s academic and technical claims keep open the alternative: a patient, sophisticated hoax. The mystery remains unresolved, but the Wired dossier places Wright as the most compelling—and most controversial—candidate to date.

U.S. District Judge Bernard Friedman struck down Michigan’s ban on same-sex marriage and same-sex adoption, ruling the 2004 Marriage Protection Amendment unconstitutional for denying equal protection. He issued a 31-page opinion after a nine-day trial, finding the state’s expert testimony not credible and siding with plaintiffs April DeBoer and Jayne Rowse, Hazel Park nurses who sued to marry and adopt each other’s special-needs children. Friedman did not issue an immediate stay, prompting Attorney General Bill Schuette to seek an emergency stay from the 6th U.S. Circuit Court; Schuette vowed to continue defending the amendment. Washtenaw, Oakland and Muskegon counties opened clerks’ offices briefly to issue licenses; other counties planned to wait pending appeals. The ruling reflects shifting public attitudes and adds Michigan to states recognizing same-sex marriage, while lawyers predict the issue may ultimately be resolved by the U.S. Supreme Court.

Heavy fighting erupted at Tripoli’s international airport as rival militias battled for control, killing at least six to seven people and wounding dozens. Clashes pitted forces from Zintan, which had guarded the airport since Gadhafi’s fall in 2011, against rival militias reported to include fighters from Misrata. Explosions, rockets and anti-aircraft fire sent thick black smoke over the capital, trapped families inside the terminal and prompted civil aviation authorities to close the airport for at least three days; many international carriers canceled flights. Casualty figures varied by report, with one account citing 25 wounded and another 36. The United Nations temporarily relocated some international staff and warned of deteriorating security. The government condemned the assault as unauthorized, while pro-Misrata supporters said the operation aimed to remove Zintan control and hand the site to authorities. The violence highlights persistent militia rivalries in post‑Gadhafi Libya, where armed groups fill security vacuums, undermining state authority, disrupting oil production and deepening a political crisis that followed contested parliamentary elections.

The document criticizes LeBron James and the media circus around his televised free-agent announcement, "The Decision." The first voice lashes out, calling James vain and manipulative for staging an hour-long ESPN special and accusing ESPN of pandering. The author dismisses James’s charity pledge as performative, compares the spectacle unfavorably to Kevin Durant’s low-key contract move, and blames James for stringing along fans and seeking adulation over basketball. The piece labels the stunt a selfish, overblown marketing con. A second, more measured voice argues the broadcast reflects public interest and media logic, noting ESPN framed the event as news with analysis and additional interviews. That column suggests James and his team bungled promotional opportunities—poor use of his website and social media—and missed building engagement and a marketing database. Both views agree the episode is outsized, reflecting modern sports-media spectacle and James’s evolving public image.

Oprah Winfrey expressed regret that a brief incident during a trip to Zurich became a media storm after she said a sales assistant at a high-end boutique refused to show her a 35,000 Swiss franc (about $38,000) crocodile handbag because the clerk assumed, based on her appearance as a Black woman, that she couldn’t afford it. Speaking at the Los Angeles premiere of Lee Daniels’ The Butler, Winfrey said she was sorry the episode “got blown up,” and clarified she had not named the store and saw the episode as an isolated incident, not an indictment of Switzerland. She described being judged despite carrying a “black card” and earning substantial income, and said customers should be able to request items without being sized up. The boutique’s owner and Swiss tourism officials apologized, but the sales assistant, speaking anonymously to a Swiss paper, denied the accusations, calling Winfrey’s account absurd. The clerk said she offered other bags, noted the expensive item was displayed high on a frame, and said she would never refuse a customer or act on racist grounds. The staffer said she feels powerless amid the fallout and hopes the misunderstanding ends.

This document presents two complementary innovations in pelvic-floor fitness: kGoal, a smart Kegel trainer for women from Minna Life, and Private Gym, an FDA-registered pelvic muscle training program for men from The Private Gym, LLC. Both address the long-neglected pelvic floor muscles, which support bladder control, pelvic stability, recovery after childbirth, sexual function, and overall comfort; weakness can lead to incontinence, pain, and diminished sexual performance.

kGoal is a connected device-and-app system: a squishable, vented vaginal “pillow” with an external arm houses pressure sensors and vibrational motors to deliver real-time tactile, visual, and auditory biofeedback. The app stores exercise history, suggests tailored workouts developed with pelvic-floor physical therapists and doctors, and aims to make training engaging through gamified interactions. kGoal emphasizes comfort (medical-grade silicone, splash resistance, USB charging), adaptability to anatomy, and Bluetooth Low Energy compatibility (iOS initially, Android planned). The team cites user testimonials and expert endorsement from a UCSF pelvic-floor therapist, and sought Kickstarter funding both for manufacturing capital and user-driven design input. Production ramp-up was slated post-campaign with shipping expected by December.

Private Gym targets men with an eight-week program combining instructional DVD training with patented resistance equipment that fits around the erect penis, using magnetic weights to provide measurable resistance. Developed with urologists and pelvic physiotherapy experts (including research-backed methods), Private Gym promotes benefits such as stronger erections, reduced premature ejaculation, improved urinary control and prostate support. The release highlights clinical evidence that pelvic-floor exercises can improve male erectile function and urges men to incorporate pelvic training as part of preventive and restorative sexual health care.

Together these products reflect a growing trend to quantify and modernize pelvic-floor training with biofeedback, personalized programs, and home-use devices.

Search teams hunting wreckage of AirAsia Flight QZ8501, which crashed into the Java Sea with 162 people aboard, reported finding multiple large parts of the Airbus A320 on the seabed. Indonesia’s search-and-rescue chief said sonar detected four major objects, the largest about 18 metres long, while another account cited two big fuselage pieces and an oil slick. Poor underwater visibility, strong currents and rough seas have hindered ROV and diver inspections, though Russian and other international teams stood ready to investigate when weather permitted. About 30 bodies have been recovered so far; officials warned many victims may have sunk after several days. The black boxes remain unfound. Weather is a leading theory: Indonesia’s meteorological agency released an analysis suggesting the aircraft likely encountered severe conditions and possible icing that damaged engines; radar traces reportedly showed an unusually steep climb before the crash. Authorities also suspended AirAsia’s Surabaya–Singapore service after saying the carrier lacked permission to operate the route on the Sunday of the accident and launched a review of its schedules and permits. AirAsia’s Indonesian unit pledged full cooperation with investigations as families awaited further recovery and identification efforts.

The Coast Guard has ordered Taylor Energy to develop a new containment plan and hire a contractor after federal estimates dramatically raised the daily leak rate from the company’s wrecked offshore platform off southeast Louisiana. New government figures put the Taylor Energy well leak between 10,500 and 29,000 gallons per day—five to 13 times higher than last year’s estimates—potentially making it one of North America’s largest, longest-running spills. The Coast Guard demanded that any new containment eliminate surface sheens and avoid prior system failures, threatening fines up to $40,000 per day for noncompliance.

Taylor Energy, which says full containment could cost more than $1 billion, disputes the new estimates and blames chronic sheens on oil and gas seeping from oil-saturated seafloor sediments rather than from leaking wells. The company points to sediment and sheen samples containing drilling fluid—likely from post-Hurricane Ivan well-plugging work in 2004—to argue the visible surface films originate from disturbed seabed contamination, not pressurized well flows. Taylor’s scientists note the site’s wells were low-pressure and that prior production required pressurized gas injection, making sustained high-rate leaks improbable.

Environmental groups and earlier remote-sensing analyses have long challenged Taylor’s contention that pollution was minimal; Skytruth and partners previously documented sheens more than 20 miles long and estimated smaller but significant daily releases. Federal scrutiny mounted beginning in 2016, and the Coast Guard’s recent pronouncement cites a “worst-case” release in the hundreds of barrels per day. Taylor contests the validity and transparency of the new government calculations, suggesting they may support federal retention of remaining trust funds set aside for response work.

If the high-end estimate is accurate, the site could have discharged roughly 150 million gallons over 14 years—comparable in total volume to the BP Deepwater Horizon release—though the sheen has not been documented reaching shore or causing large-scale fisheries or wildlife die-offs. Advocates stress that even sustained smaller discharges can harm Gulf ecosystems and call for immediate, thorough remediation and study of environmental impacts.

Kathleen Dawn “Kat” West, a 42-year-old wife and mother from Calera, Alabama, was found partially nude and dead outside her home on Jan. 13. Police have classified her death as a homicide but have released no details about the cause of death, and no arrests have been made. The discovery—made early Saturday morning by a neighbor’s daughter—left West face down near the street, bleeding from the head, with a cell phone and a green liquor bottle reportedly nearby; police have not confirmed that account. West lived in a house she and her husband built in 2015 with their 12-year-old daughter; neighbors described the family as private and the neighborhood as typically tranquil. West’s mother, Nancy Martin, has launched an online fundraiser to help cover funeral costs and issued the family’s only public statement, asking for prayers and support while defending her daughter’s character and faith. West presented herself publicly as a stay-at-home mom but also maintained subscription-only online accounts under the name Kitty Kat West, posting revealing photos and operating a paid adult site. That online presence has drawn intense attention: private Facebook groups with thousands of members have formed to speculate about her death, circulating theories—ranging from a deranged subscriber to involvement by family members—despite no public evidence linking her internet activities to the homicide. Local police have warned that widespread speculation and media repetition of unverified details have hindered the investigation. Media coverage, including syndicated reports, highlighted West’s online work and asked whether it played a role in her killing, though authorities have provided no confirmation. Friends and family have largely remained silent, and the community continues to grapple with the shock and unanswered questions surrounding her death.

The U.S. handed over Ali Mussa Daqduq, a suspected Hezbollah operative accused of organizing a 2007 Karbala raid that killed five U.S. soldiers, to Iraqi custody as American forces complete their withdrawal. The Obama administration had sought to keep Daqduq in U.S. custody—discussing options with Iraqi leaders and considering transfer to a U.S. military commission or Guantánamo—but Baghdad refused to allow him to leave Iraq and the 2008 U.S.-Iraq security agreement required detainees be returned. National Security Council spokesman Tommy Vietor said the administration obtained Iraqi assurances that Daqduq will be tried. Republicans, including Sens. John McCain, Lindsey Graham, Joe Lieberman and Mitch McConnell, sharply criticized the decision, calling it “disgraceful” and warning Iraq’s history of releasing detainees raises the risk Daqduq could be freed and return to violence. The transfer marks the last detainee handover as U.S. troops complete their exit by month’s end.

Police in parts of Britain are warning the public after a recent craze of people dressing as clowns and deliberately frightening others. Greater Manchester Police received a call at about 8:35pm reporting that people wearing clown masks had driven up to and scared children on Park Road in Stretford. Social media users described a white car with clown-costumed occupants who chased and left children “petrified.” Earlier reports included sightings of a “scary clown” in Ashton-under-Lyne and incidents in Leigh. Cheshire police said they have had a small number of reports and denounced the behaviour as unacceptable, noting that while Halloween is near, deliberately terrifying children and vulnerable people could amount to an offence; anyone witnessing such activity or intimidated by it should call 101.

Parents expressed alarm on social media, recounting children left tearful, unable to sleep, or afraid to walk to school alone, and urged those involved to stop. In other regions, national reports said some people in clown outfits have acted suspiciously and even wielded knives while following or threatening people. Gloucestershire police logged six such reports, and incidents were also noted in Durham and Suffolk; suspects often fled before officers arrived, and no arrests were immediately reported.

Chelsea Handler signed off Chelsea Lately after seven years with a star-studded, irreverent finale that captured the show’s blend of self-mockery, celebrity banter, and loose chaos. Calling her run “seven years of ridiculous stupidity,” Handler acknowledged how the show traded earnestness for gossip-fueled, late-night release—embracing tabloid fodder and mocking both herself and the culture that sustained her. That tone made her uniquely appealing: candid, off-script quips often outshone scripted panel segments, and celebrities welcomed the relaxed, unpredictable environment where they could seem more real. The finale featured fake interventions from Jennifer Aniston, Sandra Bullock and Mary McCormack, a flustered exchange with ex-boyfriend 50 Cent, Miley Cyrus and a massive curtain-call musical number with Gwen Stefani, Melissa McCarthy, Gerard Butler and many more. Handler’s departure was less somber than defiant—she plugged her Netflix move on-air—underscoring a career built on audacity, polarizing humor, and an unapologetic middle finger to convention.

Seven advertisers had suspended advertising on Rush Limbaugh’s radio program after his remarks about Georgetown law student Sandra Fluke, bringing renewed pressure on sponsors and the host. ProFlowers announced on Facebook it would halt ads, saying Limbaugh’s comments were a personal attack that did not reflect company values. The move followed campaigning by women’s groups, including UltraViolet, which said 91,000 people had signed a petition urging ProFlowers to pull its ads and urged a permanent cut-off. Other companies that suspended advertising included Quicken Loans, Sleep Train, Sleep Number, Citrix, Carbonite and LegalZoom, according to the Associated Press.

Limbaugh had called Fluke a “slut” and “prostitute” after she advocated for expanded contraceptive coverage under an Obama administration rule; he equated her position with wanting to be “paid to have sex.” The remarks drew criticism across the political spectrum: Republicans Newt Gingrich, Rick Santorum and Ron Paul criticized Limbaugh, and a Mitt Romney adviser said Limbaugh’s apology was “appropriate,” adding that extreme rhetoric should be toned down on all sides.

Carbonite CEO David Friend said the comments were offensive, especially to parents of daughters, and announced withdrawal of advertising despite having planned a meeting with Limbaugh to express concerns. The controversy highlighted advertiser sensitivity to hosts’ editorial content and public backlash.

The NTSB apologized after a summer intern mistakenly confirmed offensive, fake pilot names to KTVU regarding Asiana Flight 214, which crashed at San Francisco International Airport on July 6. The intern acted beyond his authority; the NTSB clarified it does not release or confirm crewmember names to media and vowed corrective action. KTVU aired the fraudulent names live, later retracting them and apologizing, saying it had relied on an NTSB confirmation and failed to verify the source’s role. The station’s mistake spread online, drawing criticism from the Asian American Journalists Association and prompting Asiana to consider legal action for reputational harm to the pilots. The NTSB emphasized its commitment to releasing only appropriate factual investigation details and expressed deep regret over the incident.

Laura Cunliffe, 23, of Hoyland near Barnsley, has been jailed for 14 weeks after admitting causing unnecessary suffering to her four-month-old kitten, Mowgli, whom she put into a microwave and switched on. Cunliffe placed the black-and-white cat in the appliance and ran it; she removed the animal after about a minute but it initially survived despite catastrophic internal injuries and died about 90 minutes later. At Barnsley Magistrates’ Court, District Judge John Foster described the act as “utterly horrendous cruelty” to a pet that had trusted and relied on her. Cunliffe’s solicitor stated she suffers from long‑standing psychotic depression and has been sectioned under the Mental Health Act around 20 times. As she was sentenced, relatives in the public gallery protested that she did not understand what was happening and blamed failures in medical services. The court imposed a lifetime ban on Cunliffe keeping animals, with no application to lift the ban allowed for five years. The RSPCA commented on the case’s sadness and the prolonged suffering the kitten endured, noting sentencing is a matter for the courts.

Google offered free Wi‑Fi at 47 U.S. airports through January 15, 2010, and extended the offer to Virgin America flights within the continental U.S., aiming to help holiday travelers during delays. The initiative, backed by partners like Time Warner Cable, Boingo Wireless and Advanced Wireless Group, covers many airports (e.g., Boston Logan, Houston IAH, Las Vegas McCarran, Seattle SeaTac) but omits major hubs such as Chicago O’Hare, LAX, Minneapolis–St. Paul, Dallas–Fort Worth and New York area airports. Microsoft’s Bing partnered with JiWire to provide alternate free access at hotels and some airports in exchange for a Bing search, covering locations like JFK, Midway, O’Hare and Dulles. Google also launched a holiday photo contest via Picasa and encouraged donations to three charities through Google Checkout, matching donations up to $250,000; the airport with the most donations by January 1, 2010, would receive $15,000 to donate. Google notes no payment info is required but may collect aggregate non‑personal data.

Stephen Lancaster Dennis, 49, of Harpersville, Alabama, has been charged with one count of bank theft for stealing $196,000 in quarters from the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta while working as a money processing manager at Brink’s Birmingham facility in early 2014. Federal authorities say Dennis swapped coin-filled ballistic bags with bags packed with beads, leaving only about $1,000 in quarters visible through each bag’s plastic neck window. In total investigators concluded he removed 784,000 quarters — roughly $196,000 — over a period from Jan. 1, 2014, through his last day of employment on Feb. 20, 2014.

An April 2014 audit of the Federal Reserve Coin Inventory discovered four ballistic bags that contained beads and minimal coins. The FBI’s investigation determined Dennis had accessed the coin room on Feb. 16, 2014 — a Sunday when he was not scheduled to work — collected four empty skids and ballistic bags, filled the bags with beads, and placed the substituted skids and bags back into Brink’s coin storage. Brink’s stored U.S. currency and coin for customers, including the Atlanta Fed, and each ballistic bag in that inventory held up to $50,000 in quarters.

Dennis has agreed to plead guilty under a plea agreement and to repay the $196,000 to Brink’s; the company already reimbursed the Federal Reserve for the loss. U.S. Attorney Joyce White Vance and FBI Special Agent in Charge Roger C. Stanton emphasized that what may have seemed like a “nickel and dime” theft amounted to a major bank heist, and that Dennis now faces federal sentencing. The maximum penalty for bank theft carries up to 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The case was investigated by the FBI and is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Henry Cornelius.

At the AARP Life@50+ event, President Barack Obama and GOP vice-presidential nominee Paul Ryan traded sharp attacks over Medicare and the 2010 Affordable Care Act. Obama, appearing by satellite, argued the law strengthened Medicare by cutting waste and fraud, expanding preventive care and lowering prescription costs, calling Republican claims that $716 billion was taken from Medicare “simply not true.” Ryan, speaking in person, insisted Obamacare weakened Medicare and called for repeal, repeating the $716 billion figure and saying the law turned Medicare into a “piggy bank,” which drew loud booing from AARP members. The disagreement highlights Medicare as a key battleground issue, especially in swing states like Florida. Romney released his 2011 tax return showing $13.7 million in income and a 14.1% effective federal tax rate; Democrats, including Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, called the disclosure insufficient and pressed for earlier returns. Campaign tensions continued nationwide as candidates crisscrossed battleground states, with both sides accusing the other of dishonesty and debating leadership and policy direction ahead of November.

A Toyota Corolla driven by Nabila Altahan ended up suspended from a telephone pole guy wire in Mendon Wednesday evening after the driver reacted too quickly to sudden directions from a GPS to turn around. The incident occurred around 8 p.m. on westbound Route 4 across from Sugar & Spice Restaurant; police say the GPS alerted that the car had passed its destination, prompting Altahan to leave the lane and veer off the road onto the pole’s wire. A witness at a nearby miniature golf course reported seeing Altahan jump from the suspended vehicle. State Police and Rutland City Fire Department responded; both occupants were uninjured, authorities said.

Solar Impulse 2 resumed its round-the-world, fuel-free attempt with a takeoff from Nagoya after a frustrating four-week grounding. Flight engineers seized a clear-weather window over the Pacific and in a pre-dawn scramble launched the solar-powered aircraft from Nagoya Airport, where it had sheltered since an unscheduled diversion from Nanjing, China. Project spokeswoman Elke Neumann said the team was relieved and quickly packing the hangar; a cargo plane will transport the inflatable hangar and support crew to Kalaeloa Airport near Honolulu, where the plane is expected to land after an estimated nonstop flight of about five days and nights. The team had postponed an earlier restart at the last minute to ensure safety, drawing disappointment from supporters and journalists. The project thanked Japanese hosts, including Aichi Governor Hideaki Omura, the Swiss Embassy and sponsors Schindler and ABB, for assistance during the extended stay. Swiss pilot and co‑founder André Borschberg entered a “point of no return” after takeoff and must now complete the roughly 120-hour Pacific crossing; turning back to Japan is no longer an option. Success would set records for longest solo flight duration and greatest distance by a solar-only craft. Delays have reduced the schedule margin and could force pauses into next year; the plan is for Solar Impulse to continue on to the U.S. mainland, cross the Atlantic, and finish the circumnavigation in Abu Dhabi.

Senate Republican leaders Mitch McConnell and John Cornyn sent June 27 letters warning six major sports leagues—the NFL, MLB, NBA, NHL, PGA and NASCAR—against assisting the Obama administration in promoting the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare). The senators argued that because the law is divisive and unpopular, leagues risk damaging their apolitical brands by partnering to publicize its benefits. The letters follow Health and Human Services Secretary Kathleen Sebelius’ admission she spoke with the NFL about possible outreach, though she said no agreement existed. McConnell and Cornyn recited conservative critiques of the law, suggested the administration might use policy retaliation to extract support, and urged leagues to alert them if pressured so Congress could investigate. Republicans have been working to impede ACA implementation and have probed HHS for seeking industry help. Democrats countered that public-private partnerships are not unprecedented, citing a 2007 Red Sox–Massachusetts effort to promote Romneycare. House Republican Steve Scalise also sent inquiries to NFL and NBA commissioners about HHS requests. The NFL later said it had no plans to engage on Obamacare and denied being pressured, noting only that it had been contacted. HHS and the White House did not comment.

Federal health officials and politicians debated mandatory 21-day quarantines for U.S. health workers returning from Ebola-affected West Africa after states including New York, New Jersey and Illinois required them following a case in New York. Dr. Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, warned that such quarantines—imposed after Dr. Craig Spencer, a Doctors Without Borders physician, tested positive for Ebola—could unintentionally deter clinicians from volunteering where they are most needed. Fauci argued the science shows Ebola is not contagious until symptoms appear and that active, direct monitoring of asymptomatic returnees can protect the public without broadly restricting volunteers. He called mandatory quarantines “draconian,” urged that returning health workers be treated respectfully as heroes, and stressed that stopping the epidemic in Africa is the best domestic protection. New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie defended his state’s quarantine policy as necessary to protect residents of his densely populated state and the New York metro area. He rejected Fauci’s voluntary-monitoring approach, citing concerns about compliance and public examples of rule-breaking, and predicted broader adoption of quarantines. Rep. Darrell Issa criticized the Obama administration’s handling of the crisis and questioned leadership choices, arguing that lack of trust has driven state-level action; he also suggested a military or experienced crisis manager would be preferable to the appointed Ebola coordinator. The debate highlights tensions between public health science, risk perception, political pressure, and the practical need to sustain volunteer medical staffing to curb the epidemic at its source.

Commissioner Rob Manfred denied Pete Rose’s 2015 application for reinstatement, upholding Rose’s placement on Major League Baseball’s permanently ineligible list for betting on baseball since Aug. 23, 1989. Manfred’s three-page written decision emphasized the inviolability of Rule 21, which bars any participant with a duty to perform in a game from wagering on baseball, and explained that reinstatement requires objective evidence that an applicant has fundamentally changed and no longer poses a risk of future violations. Manfred found Rose’s submission “well short” of that standard, expressing doubt Rose fully understands or accepts the scope and harm of his misconduct. He pointed to inconsistencies between Rose’s claims—most notably his long insistence he never bet as a player—and documentary evidence, including a betting notebook linked to Rose associate Michael Bertolini and corroborating elements of the 1989 Dowd Report. Manfred also criticized Rose for admitting to recreational legal betting on horses and sports, including baseball, during their interview, and noted Rose initially denied current betting before later conceding it. The decision declined to resolve Rose’s separate Hall of Fame eligibility—Manfred said that determination is for the Hall of Fame, whose bylaws already bar individuals on baseball’s ineligible list. Manfred acknowledged Rose’s exceptional on-field accomplishments and said Rose may participate in approved ceremonial activities that pose no integrity risk. Reds CEO Bob Castellini said the club respects the ruling and appreciates the commissioner’s clarity that Hall consideration is a separate matter. The report references newly public documents—pages from Bertolini’s seized betting notebook—that indicate Rose bet extensively on baseball, including on the Cincinnati Reds while a player-manager in 1986. Investigators, including John Dowd and former postal inspectors, say the notebook furnishes written proof tying Rose’s wagering to organized crime-linked bookmakers, undermining Rose’s long denials and reinforcing MLB’s position that reinstatement is inappropriate.

When Silk Road was shut down and charges announced in October 2013, authorities called it “the most sophisticated and extensive criminal marketplace on the Internet.” From January 2011 until closure, several thousand vendors sold hundreds of kilograms of illegal drugs and illicit goods to more than 100,000 buyers, generating over $213 million in revenue, prosecutors said. Ross Ulbricht, accused operator under the alias Dread Pirate Roberts, allegedly took millions in commissions. The site’s appeal lay in anonymity: it ran on the dark web and used bitcoin, a hard-to-trace digital currency. Ulbricht was convicted in February after a 13-day trial on multiple counts, including distributing narcotics via the Internet and running a continuing criminal enterprise—charges that could carry life sentences. Prosecutors also alleged he commissioned five murders, though no killings were proven; they used the allegations to argue he would use violence to protect his operation. Two other high-profile, bitcoin-related prosecutions followed: Charlie Shrem, a visible bitcoin entrepreneur and founder of BitInstant, pleaded guilty to aiding an unlicensed money transmitting service and was sentenced to two years in prison; his case signaled regulatory scrutiny of bitcoin businesses, including New York’s proposed BitLicense. Meanwhile, investigations into Silk Road unraveled corruption among law enforcement: former DEA agent Carl Force and ex–Secret Service agent Shaun Bridges were charged with stealing bitcoins and laundering funds seized during the probe. Prosecutors allege Force extorted Ulbricht and diverted bitcoins to personal accounts and offshore holdings; Bridges is accused of siphoning over $800,000 in bitcoin through Mt. Gox and wiring proceeds to personal accounts. These cases underscored both crime facilitated by bitcoin and law enforcement vulnerabilities during the Silk Road takedown.

Syrian government forces massed around Aleppo as heavy shelling and helicopter strikes battered rebel-held neighborhoods, raising fears of a major, possibly devastating assault on the country’s commercial capital. Activists and residents reported checkpoints, sniper positions, street clashes, random shelling, power shortages and thousands fleeing; dozens were reported killed in and around Aleppo amid mounting civilian displacement. Rebels — including foreign fighters — claimed control of parts of the city and said they had seized some police stations, while the army reinforced outskirts with troops, tanks and armored columns but appeared to await further orders. International alarm grew: the U.S. warned of a potential massacre yet resisted calls for military intervention, and Russia, Iran and Turkey signaled competing geopolitical interests, with Turkey threatening action against Kurdish militants near its border and closing border crossings to commercial traffic. Fighting also intensified in Damascus and southern suburbs, Yarmouk camp saw deadly strikes, and diplomatic defections and debates about opposition unity underscored Syria’s deepening fragmentation as the conflict escalated.

Ava DuVernay’s Selma marks the first major feature focused squarely on Martin Luther King Jr.’s pivotal role in the 1965 Selma-to-Montgomery campaign, presenting a sweep of political drama and an intimate portrait of King as a strategic, conflicted leader rather than a flawless icon. David Oyelowo portrays King with nuance—flawed, brilliant, insecure—and DuVernay deliberately avoided direct use of King’s famous speeches because the MLK estate had already licensed those rights to DreamWorks and Steven Spielberg. By paraphrasing King’s rhetoric in Paul Webb’s script, the film captures King’s cadence and meaning without literal quotations, sidestepping legal entanglements and collaborative strings attached to licensed material. That choice also frees the movie from mere impersonation or hagiography and allows inclusion of lesser-seen activists like Diane Nash and James Bevel, even if some historical compressions and contested portrayals—especially of President Lyndon Johnson—have sparked debate. Beyond Selma’s creative decisions lies a broader controversy: the MLK estate’s aggressive copyright enforcement, which has long restricted use of King’s speeches in books, films, documentaries and commemoration, sometimes extracting large fees or settlements. Copyright’s extended terms mean King’s speeches remain under estate control until at least 2039, limiting public access to words central to American history. Critics argue the estate’s monetization and tight control conflict with King’s mission of free public discourse; supporters counter that protecting his image prevents misuse. Selma’s achievement is thus twofold: a powerful filmic vindication of King’s leadership and a reminder of how copyright and family stewardship shape which historical voices reach the public.

Bernardo Bertolucci, now confined to a wheelchair after a disastrous series of back surgeries, has found renewed purpose directing Me and You, a film adapted from Niccolò Ammaniti’s novel that suited his limited mobility because it is largely set in a basement with few characters. Once an imposing figure in cinema, Bertolucci speaks candidly about using filmmaking as therapy after depression and describes directing with improvisation, a method learned from Jean Renoir. His career, from early work with Pasolini to triumphs like The Conformist and The Last Emperor, has been marked by ambition and controversy. The most enduring scandal remains Last Tango in Paris (1972), notably the notorious “butter” scene in which Marlon Brando performs a simulated anal sex act on 19-year-old Maria Schneider. Bertolucci has admitted that he and Brando devised the detail on the day and did not inform Schneider, wanting her “reaction as a girl, not as an actress.” Schneider said the moment wasn’t scripted, left her humiliated, and contributed to long-term personal struggles; she called the experience akin to feeling “a little raped.” Bertolucci has alternately expressed regret at not being able to apologize after her death but defended his artistic choices, comparing directorial decisions to controversial artworks. The resurfacing of a 2013 interview in which he reiterates those admissions provoked widespread outrage on social media, with actors and filmmakers condemning the lack of consent and calling the maneuver abusive. Bertolucci acknowledges ruthlessness in pursuit of results and recounts past incidents where he pushed actors to extreme ends. Now older and less mobile, he watches television and reflects on psychotherapy’s impact on his work, while the Last Tango debate continues to shadow his legacy.

The Florida U.S. Senate race between Democratic incumbent Bill Nelson and Republican Gov. Rick Scott is headed to an automatic recount after Scott took a razor-thin lead of under 0.5 percent out of more than 8 million votes. Nelson’s campaign announced the recount early Wednesday and said the late result was disappointing but not a concession. As of an updated statement the margin was within the half-percent threshold that triggers a statewide review under Florida law. County supervisors in all 67 counties must recheck tallies, initially with a noon deadline (Nov. 10) to complete the first round, and Nelson’s team is sending monitors statewide and working with Democratic attorney Marc Elias of Perkins Coie. Elias signaled scrutiny of certain supervisors, citing a report about Madison County’s GOP supervisor, appointed by Scott, who made pointed remarks about Nelson. Scott’s campaign criticized Nelson for pursuing the recount, calling it a desperate and embarrassing tactic and asserting the race is over.
