Scott has already declared victory and delivered remarks emphasizing unity and his businesslike approach to Washington if elected to the Senate.

A Chicago TV station apologized after a staff member mistakenly used a Nazi-era symbol while airing a Yom Kippur segment. WGN-TV anchor Tom Negovan described the Jewish Day of Atonement as a graphic behind him showed a yellow Star of David patch with the German word “Jude” on striped material resembling concentration camp uniforms. Viewers noticed the offensive image, and Marc Karlinsky posted a photo to Twitter, sparking widespread criticism. News Director Jennifer Lyons issued an apology, calling the use of the artwork an “unfortunate mistake” and saying “ignorance is not an excuse.” General Manager Greg Easterly and station officials said the image came from their image bank and they failed to recognize it was an offensive Nazi symbol. The station apologized on-air and on Twitter, pledged to review in-house policies, and said changes had been made to prevent similar oversights. Officials expressed embarrassment, regret, and promised to do better and to guard against repeating the error.

Two commuter trains collided head-on Monday evening in Granges-près-Marnand in western Switzerland, injuring dozens and leaving one locomotive driver missing, officials said. The crash around 6:45 p.m. on the Payerne–Lausanne regional line injured at least 40 people, five seriously, though Swiss TV put the toll at 44 with four seriously hurt. Rescue teams including paramedics, firefighters, police and an air rescue helicopter worked at the scene. Crews sought to pry open a crushed cab to recover the missing driver. Authorities have launched an investigation; service between Payerne and Moudon was suspended until at least midnight.

Commercial satellite images released Nov. 28 by the Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS) show far more extensive damage from the Nov. 12 explosion at an Iranian military base near Bidganeh than Iran’s description implied. A DigitalGlobe image from Nov. 22 reveals most buildings on the sprawling, secured compound were destroyed or heavily damaged, with debris still present and little heavy equipment visible, suggesting the blast itself caused most of the wreckage. The explosion killed 17 military personnel, including missile program founder Gen. Hassan Tehrani Moghaddam; Iran called the incident an accident and said setbacks would be brief. ISIS reports the blast likely occurred during a volatile missile-engine procedure tied to a major missile development milestone, though imagery cannot distinguish accident from sabotage.

Tonight Show host Jay Leno agreed to a substantial pay cut and roughly 20–25 staffers were laid off as NBC restructured the late-night program’s budget. Though still the top-rated late-night show, The Tonight Show reportedly only breaks even financially, in part because production costs did not fall when Leno returned to late night after his brief 2009–10 prime-time experiment. Leno, whose prior salary was reported between $25–30 million, volunteered to reduce his pay—estimates of his new salary vary around $20–30 million—to help preserve jobs; his spokesman later said Leno’s foremost concern was his staff’s well-being. Many senior staffers also accepted pay cuts. The weekly production budget, once about $2.3 million (the same as Leno’s prime-time budget), will be trimmed to roughly $1.7 million, closer to its level during Leno’s earlier tenure. The cuts follow broader NBC cost trimming under new ownership and come amid prior network staff reductions; NBC declined to comment, and the initial report came from Deadline Hollywood.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg will officiate a same-sex wedding at the Kennedy Center this weekend, likely the first time a sitting Supreme Court justice has done so. The bride and groom are Kennedy Center president Michael Kaiser and government economist John Roberts. Ginsburg, an opera enthusiast and longtime friend of Kaiser, called the role an honor and a statement in favor of equal treatment for marriages. The ceremony of about 220 guests features prominent arts and civic figures. The event follows the Court’s landmark June rulings expanding federal recognition of same-sex marriages and striking down part of an anti-gay marriage law; Ginsburg was in the majority. She said justices had avoided officiating such ceremonies before decisions were reached but expects others will follow; she also has another same-sex wedding scheduled for September.

Kuwaiti telecom Zain released a three-minute Ramadan TV advertisement confronting extremism that quickly went viral across the Middle East and provoked intense debate. Launched at the start of Ramadan, a high-TV-viewing season, the music-driven spot intercuts a man assembling a suicide belt with everyday family scenes and the aftermath of a bus bombing. A child’s voice accuses the bomber: “You’ve filled the cemeteries with our children and emptied our school desks,” while survivors of past attacks confront him and rebut his religious phrases — for example, when he intones “there is no god but Allah,” a man counters, “You who comes in the name of death, he is the creator of life.” The ad culminates with Emirati singer Hussein al-Jassmi joining survivors to urge mercy over violence and to “bomb extremism with mercy,” a refrain meant to replace hatred with love.

The production features real survivors and re-enactments of notorious incidents: a bride from a 2005 Amman wedding bombing, victims of the 2015 Kuwait mosque attack, and others. It also includes an actor portraying Omran Daqneesh, the Aleppo boy whose bloodied image after an airstrike went global. Zain, which has run widely viewed peace-themed adverts in previous years, did not comment on the campaign.

Public reaction split. Many praised the ad’s emotional power and its message against violence; the spot garnered millions of online views and supportive social-media responses. Critics argued the ad oversimplifies extremism, exploits victims in a corporate commercial, and misrepresents realities in places like Syria where many victims were harmed by regime actions rather than jihadi groups. Commentators noted that tackling extremism requires deeper political, social, and economic engagement beyond a slogan-led media push. The campaign has thus reopened conversation about the ethics and effectiveness of persuasive corporate messaging on sensitive political and humanitarian issues.

Across the U.S., communities from Florida to Iowa, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Ohio are confronting a resurgent, deadlier heroin epidemic that is reshaping arrests, emergency responses, prosecutions and lives. In Orange County, Florida, deputies reported at least 11 heroin overdoses within 24 hours in the Blossom Park area, prompting stepped-up patrols; some victims were hospitalized and at least one died. Similar clusters and surges are evident elsewhere: Cedar Rapids saw heroin account for 85% of overdose calls in a recent year, and Eastern Iowa counties are submitting rising numbers of suspected heroin exhibits to state labs. Iowa authorities warn heroin is spreading via metropolitan distribution hubs and becoming more lethal because dealers are increasingly cutting heroin with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid up to 80 times more potent, turning each use into “spinning the chamber” of a loaded gun.

Regions such as New Jersey report dramatic rises: 781 heroin-related deaths in 2014 and tens of thousands entering treatment for opiates. Small towns and Rust Belt counties like Washington, Pennsylvania, and Marion, Ohio, describe days with double-digit overdoses, often involving fentanyl-laced batches, and fatalities that devastate families. First responders increasingly carry naloxone (Narcan), which can temporarily reverse overdoses, but officials stress it’s a short-term rescue—addiction treatment and long-term recovery resources remain scarce. Programs like Vivitrol (an extended-release opioid blocker) help some stay sober but have limits, and some users switch to other drugs.

Law enforcement is pursuing suppliers and prosecuting dealers, but legal and evidentiary challenges have complicated convictions in fatal-overdose cases. The epidemic’s demographics have shifted: young adults, women and suburban or middle-class users are prominent, often transitioning from prescription opioids to cheaper, more dangerous heroin. Community responses combine harm reduction, expanded treatment access, prevention efforts and tougher prosecution of high-level traffickers, but officials warn the crisis will worsen without substantial increases in treatment capacity, interdiction and public-health strategies. Families across affected towns continue to grieve, push for solutions and support those seeking recovery.

Danish toy maker Lego Group has become the world’s largest toymaker by revenue and profit, driven largely by the success of The Lego Movie and related products. In the first half of 2014, Lego’s revenue rose about 11% and net profit increased roughly 14% to 2.7 billion kroner ($480 million) on sales of 11.5 billion kroner. CFO John Goodwin credited Lego Movie merchandise for a significant boost across Europe, the Americas and Asia, and said the company hopes that momentum will continue with the movie’s DVD release later in the year. The film itself opened strongly—making $69 million in its debut weekend and grossing nearly $260 million to date—which helped fuel demand for sets, including popular new releases like a celebrated female scientists set that sold out on Lego’s website over a weekend. Lego’s performance outpaced rivals: it surpassed Mattel, which has faced slumping global sales and weaker demand for Barbie and Fisher-Price lines, and posted revenue more than 30% higher than board-game giant Hasbro. The privately held, family-owned company—founded by the Kirk Kristiansen family in 1932 and employing about 12,000 people—reported only half-year figures publicly. Rising popularity has even attracted crime: U.S. police this summer uncovered theft schemes involving more than $300,000 worth of Lego products. Executives are focused on sustaining strong sales into the holiday season.

A University of North Carolina study published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition finds that fast food itself is not the primary cause of childhood obesity; rather, eating at fast-food restaurants is one behavior within a broader unhealthy dietary pattern established at home. Examining NHANES data from 2007–2010 on 4,466 children aged 2–18, researchers classified kids by what they ate when not eating fast food (a “Western” pattern high in saturated fat and added sugars versus a “prudent” pattern rich in fruits, vegetables and lean proteins) and by the proportion of calories coming from fast food (nonconsumers, low consumers ≤30%, high consumers >30%). Results showed children following a Western pattern had the highest overweight/obesity rates even if they rarely ate fast food; conversely, children with a prudent diet were less likely to be overweight even when they frequently consumed fast food. Low and high fast-food consumers were 1.5 and 2.2 times more likely, respectively, to follow a Western pattern. Authors argue location of food purchase matters less than overall dietary quality and caution that targeting fast-food outlets alone is insufficient to curb child obesity. The study, funded by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, urges addressing home food environments and broader behaviors such as sugary drink consumption and limited fruits and vegetables.

New research explains how Southeast Asian “flying” snakes glide: by flattening and shaping their bodies into a saucer-like cross section that gives favorable aerodynamics. Published Jan. 29 in The Journal of Experimental Biology, the study led by biomechanist Jake Socha shows that when a paradise tree snake (Chrysopelea paradisi) launches from a high branch it splays its ribs, flattens its body, curls into an S-shape, and undulates while airborne. Those movements transform the snake’s cylindrical form into an unusual, UFO-like airfoil that produces lift comparable to many other gliding animals and, at small scale, to a scaled-down airplane wing. Researchers 3-D printed the snake’s cross-section and tested models in a water tunnel to mimic airflow; measurements showed the saucer shape generated sufficient lift across most angles to explain observed glides. The real snakes may perform even better, and investigators are now probing why they undulate once or twice per second while gliding. Though ingeniously solving an engineering problem, the shape would not scale to large, fast aircraft — so don’t expect snake-shaped airliners.

The House GOP tax overhaul unveiled in November proposes eliminating the federal adoption tax credit, drawing sharp criticism from adoption advocates, conservatives who view it as a pro-family policy, and some Republicans. The credit, created in 1996 and expanded over time, helps families offset adoption costs—often tens of thousands of dollars for private or international adoptions—and provides higher amounts for special-needs adoptions. In 2017 the maximum credit was about $13,570 and it phases out for higher-income households. Crucially, the credit is nonrefundable: families who owe little or no federal income tax cannot claim its full benefit, which limits its reach among lower-income adoptive parents.

Advocates had feared the credit’s removal after House Ways and Means Chair Kevin Brady earlier signaled that certain once-in-a-lifetime provisions might be cut in favor of broader permanent tax changes. They argue the credit is a modest expense to the federal government—costing a few hundred million dollars annually—but yields larger social and fiscal returns by encouraging foster-care adoptions and reducing long-term costs associated with children remaining in foster care (less criminal-justice involvement, special education, and other public spending). Researchers estimate each dollar spent supporting foster-care adoptions returns several dollars in benefits.

Critics also say making the credit refundable would better support lower-income families and sibling-adoptions, yet efforts this year to make it refundable have been undercut by the proposed repeal. Supporters of repeal, including Brady, counter that broader tax cuts and an increased child tax credit will help families more consistently, though opponents say those changes don’t address the concentrated, upfront costs of adoption. The proposal has provoked bipartisan concern and could complicate passage as the tax bill proceeds. The final legislation’s details remain uncertain, but advocates warn that removing the credit could make adoption—especially private and international placements—harder for many families and might reduce the number of children who find permanent homes.

On May 11 at 8:26 a.m., a 40-person team at VCU Medical Center in Richmond, Va., delivered sextuplets—three boys and three girls—by cesarean section to Ajibola Taiwo, a native of western Nigeria who was 30 weeks and two days pregnant. The infants weighed between 1 pound, 10 ounces and 2 pounds, 15 ounces and are doing well in the Children’s Hospital of Richmond at VCU neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). The delivery was the hospital’s first set of sextuplets and followed months of intensive prenatal management, including pre-delivery drills and resuscitation exercises coordinated among maternal-fetal medicine, labor and delivery, nursing, anesthesia, respiratory, neonatal medicine, social work, nutrition, cardiology and chaplain services. The Taiwos, who had tried to conceive for 17 years, initially saw four heartbeats at their first ultrasound and learned in January at VCU that they were expecting six. Parents and staff have practiced kangaroo care—skin-to-skin contact—to support bonding, temperature regulation and breastfeeding. Hospital leaders praised the teamwork required for simultaneous premature deliveries; the NICU is level 4 and can provide any needed subspecialty care. Ajibola was discharged May 18, and the couple remain actively involved in their babies’ care. The hospital and family are not currently facilitating media requests.

Hillary Clinton made a rare post-election public appearance at UNICEF’s annual Snowflake Ball to surprise and honor pop star Katy Perry with the Audrey Hepburn Humanitarian Award. Clinton’s unexpected arrival prompted a sustained standing ovation as she praised Perry’s humanitarian work, energy and compassion, saying Perry brings the same spirit Audrey Hepburn brought to UNICEF. She noted Perry’s enormous social reach and quipped that Perry “might have some competition,” a jab at the president-elect’s Twitter presence. Clinton highlighted Perry’s lyrics about resilience and called her a necessary champion “now more than ever.”

Perry, an ambassador for UNICEF since 2013, was visibly moved to tears. Clinton cited Perry’s field visits to Madagascar and Vietnam and credited her with raising more than $1 million for UNICEF on tour. In her acceptance remarks, Perry thanked Clinton for helping her use her platform beyond music: “Hillary has lit that voice inside of me, and that light will never go out,” she said, pledging that her humanitarian work is only beginning. Perry also made a pointed reference to climate change, saying she’d helped highlight its effects and calling for unity, empathy and ongoing commitment to children’s welfare globally.

The gala at Cipriani Wall Street, hosted by Octavia Spencer, celebrated UNICEF’s work and has raised $27 million over 11 years. The evening included performances by Sara Bareilles and the cast of The Color Purple and honored others such as Moll Anderson. Clinton’s appearance was one of her first public events since conceding the presidential race, and the exchange underscored the close ties between Perry and Clinton during the campaign, while keeping the focus on humanitarian advocacy and continued activism.

A federal advisory panel recommended that women in their 40s need not have routine mammograms, sparking controversy. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force cited low cancer prevalence in that age group and high false-positive rates—costly follow-ups and anxiety—as reasons to change screening guidance, recommending biennial screening for ages 50–74 instead. Critics say the rationale feels like a cost-benefit decision favoring system efficiency over individual women; some see it as patronizing and politically timed amid health care reform debates about cutting "unnecessary" tests to expand coverage. The American Cancer Society and several lawmakers, including Rep. Debbie Wasserman-Schultz, oppose the change and call for hearings. HHS Secretary Kathleen Sebelius clarified the task force’s recommendations are not government policy, urged women to consult doctors, and noted Medicaid and other plans will continue covering mammograms.

NBC News chairman Andrew Lack has reached a tentative deal to keep Brian Williams at the network after his six‑month suspension ends in August, though Williams will not return to anchor NBC Nightly News. Lester Holt, who filled in for Williams, will become the permanent Nightly News anchor — the first African‑American solo weekday network nightly news anchor — and receive a significant pay increase. Williams, who was suspended after admitting he “misremembered” and exaggerated several accounts of his reporting — including a 2003 Iraq helicopter incident and other on‑the‑record anecdotes — will take a reduced role: serving as an MSNBC breaking‑news and special‑reports anchor and as NBC’s breaking‑news fill‑in when Holt is unavailable. The network said its internal review found Williams made numerous inaccurate statements about his field experiences, mostly on late‑night programs and public appearances years after events, but concluded the errors did not generally occur on NBC news platforms. Williams issued public apologies and began meetings with staff; NBC says he will take a substantial pay cut from his prior contract. The network will not publish the full investigation. Executives hope the compromise prevents further embarrassment and leverages Williams’s strengths on breaking stories while preserving Nightly News’s credibility under Holt.

At a tech conference in Rancho Palos Verdes, California, Hillary Clinton blamed a wide range of factors for her loss in the 2016 presidential election while reiterating that she accepts responsibility for “every choice” her campaign made. Speaking at Recode’s Code Conference with Kara Swisher and Walt Mossberg, Clinton argued that the decisive late shift against her stemmed not from campaign mistakes alone but from external forces and structural weaknesses: a late FBI letter about her private email server from James Comey; Russian cyberattacks and a coordinated misinformation effort; an underresourced Democratic National Committee data operation; media coverage that she said treated the email story like “Pearl Harbor”; and a pervasive assumption that she would win.

Clinton singled out Comey’s public letter to Congress just over a week before Election Day as a pivotal moment that cost her critical ground. She criticized the news media for sensationalizing the email controversy and for failing to focus on substantive policy reporting on television, suggesting that coverage helped define the campaign on the wrong terms.

The former secretary of state placed major emphasis on alleged Russian interference, describing hacks of the DNC and her campaign chairman’s emails, the rapid release of material via WikiLeaks, and the proliferation of fake-news websites as a novel form of “weaponized” information technology. Clinton expressed the belief that Russians could not so effectively tailor and time the dissemination of stolen documents without guidance from Americans, posing direct questions about whether they were “coordinating with, and colluding with” U.S. operatives—an issue she framed as fair to investigate, though she did not outright accuse the Trump campaign of collusion during this session.

Clinton also criticized the DNC’s data capabilities, saying the organization provided her a weaker infrastructure after she secured the nomination while Republicans had heavily invested in data between 2012 and 2016. She lamented broader institutional weaknesses in the Democratic Party, calling it “bankrupt” and poor at building necessary operational capacity and content to support campaigns.

Addressing other factors, Clinton rejected claims that her paid speeches hurt her more than comparable payments to male politicians, framing such attacks as tinged by sexism. She described Trump as an impulsive leader and called his reported plans to pull out of the Paris climate agreement “totally incomprehensible.” Clinton declined to run for office again but vowed to remain politically active, saying she is “not going anywhere” and remains “unbowed and unbroken.” She urged Democrats to focus on upcoming gubernatorial races and the 2018 midterms, arguing that flipping the House is realistic if the party organizes effectively.

At a TED Talk with Gayle King in Vancouver, Serena Williams revealed that her pregnancy photo was shared on social media by accident. The 35-year-old, who’s engaged to Reddit co‑founder Alexis Ohanian, said she’d been photographing her growing bump weekly while on vacation and had planned to wait several more days before posting. Instead, she accidentally pressed the wrong button and the image went public; she only realized after missed calls. Williams noted she’s usually careful about saving weekly photos, and the slip-up didn’t worry her. A week earlier she’d posted a mirror selfie showing her 20‑week bump in a custom yellow suit, and her representative later confirmed she and Ohanian are expecting their first child this fall. At the TED event she also discussed returning to tennis after the baby, referencing Roger Federer’s longevity and expressing hope her child will be in the stands cheering her on as she works to regain championship form.

Tom Cruise and Katie Holmes’ divorce was finalized quickly and quietly. Holmes filed for divorce on June 28, seeking sole custody of their six-year-old daughter Suri, and the couple reached a settlement within days. Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Matthew Cooper signed the judgment and the court papers were sealed. Reports say Holmes was awarded primary physical custody and the agreement imposed limits on Suri’s exposure to the Church of Scientology. A source close to Cruise told E! News he is “very happy and relieved” to be moving forward, prioritizing being a good father under the terms of the confidential deal.

Scientists in South America have discovered that larvae of the Argentine horned frog (Ceratophrys ornata) emit brief, clear, metallic-like distress calls when threatened. Dr. Guillermo Natale and colleagues heard the sound while netting tadpoles and later reared wild adults to study the behavior. The tadpoles, naturally aggressive and carnivorous toward other species’ larvae, produce 0.05-second pulses by forcing air from early-developing lungs; even three-day-old larvae can call. Sounds occur when prodded or contacted, underwater and more often when removed from water, and may deter cannibalism among conspecifics. This is the first reported case of underwater sound production by vertebrate larvae, suggesting many aquatic larvae might also communicate acoustically and prompting further study of its development and social function.

The document is a long, mixed-response appraisal of Red Nose Day Actually, a 10–12 minute Comic Relief reunion of Richard Curtis’s 2003 ensemble rom‑com Love Actually. It compiles critiques, recaps, fan reactions and column snippets that oscillate between fondness, exasperation and outright dismissal.

The piece summarizes what the short revisits: familiar characters (Prime Minister David, Natalie, Billy Mack, Jamie and Aurelia, Mark, Juliet and Peter, Rufus, Daniel and Sam) reappear with tidy updates—Grant’s PM is re‑elected and still dancing (this time to Drake), Martine McCutcheon remains unchanged, Bill Nighy’s Billy Mack is still plugging charity singles, Rowan Atkinson’s Rufus now sells red noses at Sainsbury’s, Colin Firth and his Portuguese wife have three children, and Sam and Joanna are reunited and apparently engaged. Kate Moss turns up as Mark’s model wife; Emma Thompson and Martin Freeman are absent (Thompson declined out of respect for the late Alan Rickman; Freeman was busy). Gregor Fisher’s character Joe is written as deceased in the short, which some find needlessly morbid.

Reaction is divided. Some viewers delighted in nostalgia, clever callbacks, and the sight of the cast together; social media celebrated Grant’s dance and cameo surprises. Fans praised Curtis’s intent to draw attention and donations for Comic Relief. Others criticized the sketch as thin, joke‑light and clumsily assembled—texted‑in performances, contrived poignancy, and recycled gags that felt weak rather than warm. Specific complaints include Andrew Lincoln’s “creepy” cue‑card return, Jamie’s persistent Portuguese incompetence (a potentially deeper, passive‑aggressive marital signpost), and a missed opportunity for sharper commentary (e.g., avoiding political satire despite a chance to reference contemporary leaders).

Several columnists defend the reunion’s purpose: it was fund‑raising, not a full cinematic sequel, so charitable outcomes trumped comedic perfection. Yet many lament that the short didn’t consistently earn laughs and occasionally relied on sentimentality or strained gags. Overall, Red Nose Day Actually offers a bittersweet, uneven nostalgia trip—delightful for devoted fans and useful for charity, but flawed as comedy or as a substantive sequel.

At the 90th Academy Awards, three of Harvey Weinstein’s most prominent accusers—Ashley Judd, Salma Hayek and Annabella Sciorra—joined to present a video montage focused on equality and representation, and to publicly reflect on the momentum of the #MeToo and Time’s Up movements. Sciorra opened by acknowledging the progress made since many survivors began speaking out, noting that “the journey ahead is long, but slowly a new path has emerged.” Judd emphasized that change is being driven by “the powerful sound of new voices” uniting in a chorus that declares “time’s up.” Hayek saluted those who broke through biased perceptions based on gender, race and ethnicity to tell their stories, and the trio spoke about ensuring that the next decades empower equality, diversity, inclusion and intersectionality.

The montage featured other industry figures—Mira Sorvino, Kumail Nanjiani and Greta Gerwig among them—underscoring the importance of representation in Hollywood. Sorvino highlighted that Time’s Up has amplified voices across all walks of life. Each presenter has publicly recounted allegations against Weinstein: Judd told The New York Times about inappropriate behavior and coercive bargaining during a business meeting; Hayek wrote in an op-ed about threats and intimidation during the making of Frida; and Sciorra detailed a violent encounter in her New Yorker account. Weinstein has denied non-consensual sex allegations and disputed specific claims while admitting to some “boorish behavior” in a spokesperson’s statement. The piece also directs readers to support the Time’s Up Legal Defense Fund, which provides legal aid to survivors of workplace sexual harassment and assault. The 2018 Oscars took place March 4 at the Dolby Theatre and were broadcast live on ABC.

Wolfram Alpha’s new ImageIdentify tool offers quick, automated guesses about what appears in uploaded photos, demonstrating both impressive successes and amusing failures. After a few seconds, the site returns a computer-generated identification—sometimes accurately naming breeds of dogs, specific flowers, or simple objects like pizza, and other times giving vague, incorrect, or humorous results (e.g., calling Yosemite’s Half Dome “elevation,” a gecko a “night lizard,” or mistaking an Apple TV remote for an alligator clip). Stephen Wolfram acknowledges the system “won’t always get it right,” but notes the mistakes often resemble human errors. Trained on “a few tens of millions” of images—including challenging examples like cats in spacesuits, sloths in party hats, and even Chewbacca—the system can recognize about 10,000 common everyday objects. It still struggles with specific people, art, and nonstandard items, and can be unreliable under heavy demand, sometimes returning “please try again” errors. ImageIdentify keeps a thumbnail of uploaded images and collects them to continue training the model, so users should consider privacy before submitting photos. Beyond casual use, Wolfram envisions the technology applied to large photo collections to identify, categorize, and generate statistics about visual content—useful for travel logs, dietary analysis from food photos, or integration into other apps. Developers can incorporate the recognition capabilities through Wolfram’s programming and cloud tools, positioning ImageIdentify not just as a novelty but as a foundation for broader image-recognition features in various services.

Omran Daqneesh, the young Syrian boy whose dust- and blood-covered image in an ambulance became an international emblem of Aleppo’s civilian suffering, has reappeared in photos and a short video posted by a pro-government TV presenter. The footage, shared by Kinana Allouche and other pro-regime outlets, shows Omran and his father in government-controlled west Aleppo; the boy appears in good health for the first time since the August airstrike that wounded him and later killed his older brother, Ali. In the clip Omran’s father, Mohammed Daqneesh, accuses opposition groups and international media of exploiting his son’s image “to trade in his blood,” says he refused offers to leave Syria for propaganda purposes, and claims he changed Omran’s name and cut his hair to protect him from alleged threats. The family’s move into regime-held territory followed the rebels’ withdrawal and government forces’ recapture of eastern Aleppo last December. Observers caution that the interview may not reflect the family’s free will: independent analysts note that civilians now living under government control face pressure, and Syria’s government has previously used media appearances to promote its narrative. The resurfacing of Omran has reignited debate over the wartime use of children’s images by all sides for propaganda—mirroring past cases like Bana Alabed—and underscores continuing concerns about coercion, disinformation, and the humanitarian cost of Syria’s conflict, which has killed an estimated 465,000 people since 2011.

Ron Paul’s “We are all Austrians now” praised “Austrian economics,” but the label is ambiguous. Classical figures like Hayek influenced mainstream policy, yet Paul’s reference aligns with Ludwig von Mises and Murray Rothbard’s stricter strand, which rejects almost all government stabilization, monetary stimulus, and regulation. Austrians argue low interest rates cause “malinvestment” and inevitable busts, a view critics say ignores expectations and fails to explain why investors wouldn’t avoid doomed projects. The essay contrasts this with mainstream and Wicksellian ideas: recessions stem from a gap between the natural rate of interest and actual rates, which central banks can normally close by cutting rates. After the financial crisis the natural rate fell below zero, limiting policy tools, but gradual recovery narrows the gap. Renewed credit, rising durable-goods demand, and housing starts—especially multifamily—should drive employment and spending, aiding state revenues and reversing public-sector cuts. The result: a meaningful recovery from a low base, not a late-1990s-style boom.

The U.S. Department of Labor has filed multiple federal lawsuits and an administrative action against the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS), several church leaders, and associated businesses following a multi-year probe into alleged child labor and wage violations tied to the 2012–2013 pecan harvest. The complaints accuse FLDS leadership, including Bishop Lyle Jeffs and ranch supervisor Dale Barlow, of pulling students in Hildale, Utah, and Colorado City, Arizona, out of school for weeks to work unpaid at the Southern Utah Pecan Ranch. Investigators identified about 1,400 workers who harvested pecans without pay, including as many as 175 children under 13, performing tasks from tree pruning and equipment operation to picking, bagging and shelling pecans. The DOL seeks back wages for workers and is pursuing $1.9 million in penalties for child labor violations. Separate filings target Paragon Contractors Corp. and owner Dan Jessop for allegedly violating a 2007 injunction addressing prior child labor issues; a former young worker testified she worked long hours and helped manage sign-in sheets. Wage and Hour Division chief David Weil emphasized the agency’s commitment to protecting vulnerable workers and enforcing child labor laws.

In March 2014, Russia’s annexation of Crimea sparked international condemnation, targeted sanctions and significant economic fallout. Western powers imposed travel bans, asset freezes and restrictions on Russian individuals, banks and businessmen close to President Vladimir Putin—measures that have driven capital flight, stock-market losses and ruble weakness. Russia’s Micex index plunged double digits, investors withdrew billions, and ratings agencies shifted Russia’s outlook to negative amid fears of broader industry sanctions affecting finance, energy and defense. Visa and MasterCard briefly halted services for sanctioned banks, prompting public anxiety and proposals in the Duma for a national payment system that could isolate Russia further. Kremlin allies dismissed the penalties as limited or politically useful, while Putin’s popularity rose domestically after annexation. U.S. lawmakers pursued tougher measures linked to corruption, with the arrest of Ukrainian billionaire Dmitry Firtash in Vienna raising the prospect of disclosures about Gazprom dealings that could broaden sanctions. Western leaders canceled the planned G8 summit in Russia and warned of escalating sectoral sanctions if Moscow did not de-escalate. Analysts warned that prolonged restrictions could tip Russia into recession, fracture its elite’s ties to the West and deepen geopolitical confrontation.

A first-year University of Calgary student’s earnest attempt to find a missed connection sparked an unexpected social phenomenon and a new friendship circle. After meeting a Dutch exchange student named Nicole at a campus bar, Carlos Zetina said she gave him a phone number that turned out to be wrong. To avoid appearing disrespectful for not following up, he used the university email directory to message 246 people with “Nicole” or variations in their names, pleading that if any Nicole was from Holland and thought Nietzsche was depressing, she should text him.

Rather than irritation, the mass email produced amusement and camaraderie. Recipients began exchanging messages, many teasingly impersonating the supposed Nicole before the group coalesced. PhD candidate Nicolette Little and student Nicole DuGraye helped organize the responders into a Facebook group called “Nicole From Last Night.” About 20 of the women met at a pub for a meetup they dubbed the “Congress of Nicoles,” greeting one another by name and enjoying the novelty. The story went viral on Twitter under #nicolefromlastnight, drawing widespread attention and supportive reactions.

The real Nicole, who had no university email address, learned of the stunt through social media and later posted in the group, explaining she’d recently acquired a Canadian number and had likely given Zetina a wrong digit by accident. She reached out to him, and they planned to meet again. Members of the newly formed Nicole group said they intend to continue meeting monthly and welcomed the serendipitous “girl gang” and its role in reconnecting the pair. What began as a quirky search for a missed connection ended with laughter, new friendships and a likely date.

A quick-thinking boater without a fire extinguisher managed to extinguish a blaze using whatever was at hand, impressing onlookers despite doubts and commentary in the background. The scene shows a speedy good Samaritan deftly handling the situation, putting out the fire effectively while looking confident and capable. Observers praised the daring intervention and the dramatic moment captured, noting that the quick action turned a potentially dangerous situation into a successful rescue and left viewers admiring the person’s composure and skill.

Police in Ludhiana, Punjab, arrested multiple suspects after a newborn was reportedly sold through a Facebook-arranged deal. The baby’s grandfather allegedly kidnapped the infant from his daughter soon after birth, falsely telling her the child was stillborn, then sold him to hospital staff for 45,000 rupees. The infant changed hands again and was posted for sale on Facebook; a businessman allegedly offered 800,000 rupees. Authorities rescued the baby and returned him to his mother; suspects face kidnapping charges carrying up to seven years’ imprisonment. Officials warned the case may reveal wider child‑trafficking networks in India.

Fueled, a New York City mobile app firm led by Ryan Matzner, says they don’t build every pitch they get. They hand-pick ideas and subject them to a rigorous vetting process to polish concepts before design and development. The company observes the app market is saturated—there really is “an app for that”—which makes truly new, viable ideas rare. Fueled compiled a list of repeatedly pitched but ill-advised concepts. Examples deemed generally terrible include “Airbnb for public parking” (too much hassle for too little reward), Tinder-style apps for dogs, GPS-based local chat networks (geo-networking repeatedly failed to gain traction), “pee break” alerts, and shock-therapy wearables that zap sedentary users. Some ideas are simply unrealistic given technical or market constraints: apps promising to find bars with happy-hour deals, custom emoji packs (iOS won’t let you add system emojis), building a full point-of-sale system (huge effort and sales force required), or services that need large user networks before proving value. Fueled also fields common entrepreneur missteps: people trying to sell ideas without execution capability, wildly mismatched budgets versus scope, and underestimating development complexity. The firm emphasizes focusing on feasible, well-polished concepts rather than novelty alone.

President Obama, speaking from Martha’s Vineyard on Aug. 14, 2014, appealed for calm after the fatal shooting of 18-year-old Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri, calling the death “heartbreaking and tragic” and urging healing, peaceful protest and transparency in the investigation. He condemned looting and violence while also denouncing excessive police force and the detention of journalists. The Department of Justice and federal investigators are involved; Obama said he directed Attorney General Eric Holder to ensure a thorough review.

In Ferguson, Gov. Jay Nixon shifted operational control to Capt. Ronald S. Johnson of the Missouri State Highway Patrol to soften the police response after nights of clashes, tear gas, armored vehicles and arrests. Johnson, a Ferguson native, pledged to protect protesters’ rights and rebuild trust. Local leaders, including Sen. Claire McCaskill and clergy, urged demilitarization of the response and organized peaceful marches. Community scenes varied from calm, clergy-led processions and cleanup efforts to looting, fires at a QuikTrip and confrontations that injured civilians and officers. Journalists were arrested, prompting national press organizations to demand protection of First Amendment rights; the ACLU sued St. Louis County for police records.

The unrest exposed racial tensions in a predominantly black town policed largely by white officers, raising wider debate about policing practices. Anonymous hackers claimed to target county websites and released an unverified officer name, intensifying concerns. Local businesses suffered revenue losses; schools delayed reopening. Civil-rights groups called for federal action and accountability. Federal, state and local authorities continue investigations amid calls for transparency and community reconciliation.

A surprising media-foreign policy exchange emerged after Russian President Vladimir Putin published a New York Times op-ed: the English edition of the Russian news site Pravda.ru tentatively agreed to publish a column by U.S. Senator John McCain criticizing Putin’s leadership. Dmitry Sudakov, Pravda’s English editor, welcomed a submission despite expecting strong disagreement with McCain’s views; he said the piece would be published in English and translated into Russian so local readers could see McCain’s arguments. The exchange began when McCain, joking on CNN about wanting to write for Pravda given Russia’s limited press freedoms, prompted The Cable to contact Pravda. McCain’s communications director, Brian Rogers, promptly confirmed the senator would be glad to submit a piece and suggested topics including Russian democracy and human rights and Putin’s alleged support for Syria’s regime. The story notes Pravda.ru is distinct from the Soviet-era official organ—post-Soviet, it is an anti-Western independent site—and mentions Paul Craig Roberts as a U.S. contributor (a point Rogers corrected as Roberts was not a senator). McCain’s camp later emailed Pravda promising a submission by Wednesday; the article was updated to note Pravda.ru lacks a print edition.

Twenty-five years after the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum heist, authorities released previously unseen surveillance footage showing an unidentified man being admitted through the same rear entrance used by the thieves about 24 hours before the March 18, 1990 robbery. The low-resolution tape, captured at about 12:49 a.m. on March 17, shows a car pulling up, a man exiting and being buzzed in by a guard, spending roughly three minutes in the reception area, then leaving. The vehicle matches the general description of a car reported near the museum shortly before the theft. Investigators reopened and re-examined original evidence and hope public identification of the man or vehicle will yield new leads toward recovering the 13 stolen works, including Vermeer’s The Concert, three Rembrandts (including The Storm on the Sea of Galilee), and a Manet, valued at least $500 million. The FBI and U.S. Attorney’s Office urged anyone with information to contact them; the museum offers a $5 million reward for recovery of all works in good condition. The footage refocuses attention on former guard Richard Abath, who admitted protocol violations on the night of the robbery but has denied involvement; officials did not confirm he is the guard shown. The robbers, posing as Boston police, entered through the same door, subdued and bound the guards, and escaped with the works. No one has been charged; the statute of limitations for theft has expired, though possession-related charges remain possible and authorities have considered offering immunity for return of the pieces. The release aims to generate fresh tips in the largest unsolved art theft in the world.

The document reports two major, unrelated items. First, the U.S. and China jointly introduced new U.N. sanctions targeting North Korea to hinder Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programs after its recent atomic bomb test. The sanctions were presented as a significant step to impede North Korea’s weapons development.

Second, IBM’s Sequoia supercomputer at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory was ranked the world’s fastest system, achieving 16.32 sustained petaflops on the Top500 list and reclaiming the top spot for the U.S. Sequoia, a 96-rack IBM Blue Gene/Q system with about 1.6 million cores and 1.6 PB of memory, surpasses Japan’s Fujitsu K Computer (10.51 petaflops). It is more energy efficient—consuming 7.9 MW versus K’s 12.6 MW—and is intended to run high-resolution simulations for the U.S. nuclear stockpile stewardship program, supporting life-extension programs and reducing the need for underground testing. IBM claims Sequoia can perform in an hour what would take billions of people years by hand, and NNSA officials emphasize its role in ensuring weapon safety, informing policy, and advancing U.S. leadership in high-performance computing.

Habeas corpus—the Great Writ—protects individuals from indefinite government detention without cause by requiring the executive to justify custody before a neutral judge. Enshrined in Magna Carta and the U.S. Constitution’s first article, it is a fundamental safeguard against arbitrary executive power. The 2006 Military Commissions Act (MCA) undermined this protection by stripping habeas rights from Guantánamo detainees and from any non-citizen, including lawful U.S. permanent residents, whom the executive labels “enemy combatants.” Many held at Guantánamo lack substantive evidence against them: most were sold to U.S. forces for bounties by regional warlords rather than captured on a battlefield, and of roughly 800 detainees only ten have been criminally charged. Civil rights groups like the Center for Constitutional Rights (CCR) have persistently filed habeas petitions to force judicial review, and the Supreme Court has repeatedly had to address detainees’ rights, with a June 2007 term set to reconsider multiple cases. Critics argue the MCA creates a second-class justice system that erodes the constitutional balance by permitting executive detention without meaningful judicial oversight—contrary to historical practice, as suspensions of the writ have been rare, brief, and limited to active combat zones. Separately, a novel New York case broadened habeas discourse by seeking the writ on behalf of two Stony Brook research chimpanzees, Hercules and Leo. The court initially issued an order to show cause—an unprecedented step toward recognizing legal personhood for cognitively complex animals—though subsequent amendments struck “writ of habeas corpus” language. The Nonhuman Rights Project continues to press such cases, arguing that habeas principles can aid efforts to secure bodily liberty for nonhuman beings. Overall, the text warns that weakening habeas corpus imperils liberty for all.

The UK government has approved a controversial plan to build a 1.8-mile (2.9 km) dual-carriageway tunnel beneath the A303 near Stonehenge to remove traffic noise and visual intrusion from the World Heritage Site. The scheme, part of a wider £2bn (about $2.45bn) regional road upgrade between the M3 and M5, aims to ease chronic congestion on the busy trunk road that runs yards from the monument and attracts over 1.3 million visitors a year. Supporters, including the National Trust and Transport Secretary Chris Grayling, say the tunnel will restore tranquillity—letting visitors hear skylarks instead of constant traffic—and improve journey times and local communities’ connectivity. A public consultation runs until March 5.

Opponents, led by the Stonehenge Alliance and many archaeologists, warn the dual two-lane tunnel could cause “irreparable damage” to the richly layered Stonehenge landscape and its complex archaeology, arguing any tunnel should be significantly longer (they propose at least 2.7 miles) or forego new road building at the site. Critics highlight the site’s broader prehistoric context—buried henges, barrows and acoustic landscapes—arguing research and preservation risk being sidelined. The project revives long-running debates: balancing better public access and aesthetic restoration against protecting and fully understanding the monument’s extended archaeological setting.

YouTube invested about $100 million to fund roughly 160 original channels over the past year as part of a push to make the site more TV-like and attract advertisers. Now it’s reviewing those deals and plans to renew financing for only about 30–40 percent of partners, meaning it will not reinvest in up to 60 percent of channels. Renewals, starting with the January cohort, will mirror prior contracts—advances of roughly $1–$5 million for a year of exclusive content—and YouTube will notify winners soon. Channels not renewed can remain on the site, but YouTube will keep all ad revenue until its initial investment is recouped. Renewal decisions hinge mainly on engagement (especially watch time) and cost-efficiency rather than immediate ad revenue performance. Early lessons: celebrity attachment alone didn’t guarantee success; channels that prioritized audience-building did best. The top new channels now average more than a million views weekly, and YouTube’s overall viewing time has grown substantially, helping attract upfront advertisers like Geico and others. Despite progress, YouTube still trails TV in total viewing time and many producers struggle to recoup investments, but the initiative has shifted industry perceptions of YouTube as a serious programming funder.

House Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi on Thursday rejected linking funding for President Donald Trump’s proposed U.S.-Mexico border wall to legal protections for young immigrants (so-called Dreamers). Speaking as she campaigns to be House speaker in January, Pelosi said the two issues are separate and that Democrats will not trade Dreamer safeguards for money for the wall. Her remarks came as the House and Senate approved a brief stopgap funding extension through Dec. 21 to keep the government open; Trump has said he will sign that extension to allow time for ceremonies honoring the late President George H.W. Bush. White House pressure continues: Trump warned by tweet of potential “Big danger” at the border and urged Pelosi and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer to approve wall funding. Pelosi urged the lame-duck Congress to pass six appropriations bills already agreed upon and to move a separate Homeland Security funding measure that would address border security without necessarily including a physical wall. Most Democrats view the wall as “immoral, ineffective and expensive,” she said, noting Trump’s broken promise that Mexico would pay for it. Schumer backed a bipartisan Senate plan that would provide $1.6 billion for fencing and technology, not for the 30-foot concrete wall Trump envisions, and urged passage of appropriations to avoid a shutdown. Republicans are divided: Appropriations Chair Richard Shelby prefers bundling Homeland Security with other unresolved bills, while Sen. Roy Blunt warned the pivotal question is whether Trump will accept a package without wall funding or trigger a shutdown.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell emerged as the decisive Republican who helped end a 16-day government shutdown and avert a potentially catastrophic U.S. debt default, but his bipartisan maneuvering deepens political risks as he runs for reelection in Kentucky. Facing a fractured GOP and a House that repeatedly failed to produce a viable resolution, McConnell found himself, by his account, “caught in a cul‑de‑sac” with the “worst hand” he’d ever been dealt. With House Speaker John Boehner effectively overrun by hard‑right members who pushed a shutdown strategy to try to defund or delay the Affordable Care Act, Senate Democrats seized leverage. McConnell, long regarded as a consummate dealmaker, scrambled in the final 24 hours to broker a solution that would reopen the government and raise the debt ceiling temporarily.

This was the fourth time in under three years McConnell has played a central role forging bipartisan fiscal deals—two tax agreements and two debt‑limit measures—each aimed at averting financial crises. That record underpins McConnell’s defense of his recent actions: he argues that stepping into bipartisan negotiations during national crises is precisely the leadership qualification he will run on in both his upcoming Republican primary against Matt Bevin and the general election against a Democratic challenger. Still, walking that line is politically treacherous. Conservative activists and Bevin accuse McConnell of betraying GOP principles by cutting deals with Democrats, while opponents on the left cast him as part of Washington dysfunction.

The immediate shutdown drama began with a hardline House strategy to use funding and the debt ceiling to extract concessions on Obamacare. Boehner, who pledged to avoid a shutdown, was overtaken by his conference as roughly 80 House Republicans backed a shutdown tactic that leadership could not control. Democrats—united behind President Obama and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid—refused to concede. Reid, relishing the leverage, engineered talks that ultimately left McConnell with limited options and forced bi‑partisan negotiations under Democratic terms. McConnell sought conservative concessions where possible, such as repeal of the medical device tax that helps fund the health law, but the final agreement largely gave Democrats what they wanted while postponing future fights over spending and the next debt ceiling.

The settlement extended government funding to Jan. 15 and raised the debt ceiling until Feb. 7 with no binding strings—essentially returning to a version of what Republicans had rejected weeks earlier. The outcome underscored how the tea‑party driven strategy backfired: it united Democrats, weakened Boehner’s authority, damaged GOP poll standing, and left Senate Republicans scrambling to limit political fallout. McConnell’s defenders emphasize his ability to secure stability and protect prior concessions—like the 2011 Budget Control Act’s spending caps and the permanent extension of most Bush‑era tax cuts—but critics say repeated bipartisan bailouts erode conservative credibility and could complicate his reelection messaging. As McConnell himself put it, he was on the “two‑yard line” with a shaky offensive line, trying mainly to punt to better field position—an apt metaphor for a leader balancing crisis management with fraught political calculations at home.

International efforts have completed the destruction of Libya’s chemical weapons, a difficult but important milestone that also informed the larger Syrian disarmament program. Libya’s final two tons were small compared with Syria’s 1,300 tons, but their elimination posed acute challenges: remote desert geography, harsh weather, local tribal conflict, and the risk of theft by militants. The stockpile dated to Muammar Gaddafi’s 2004 decision to hand over nuclear know-how and chemical agents; Libya originally declared 24.7 metric tons of sulfur mustard and later revealed nearly two additional tons hidden in munitions, raising the total to 26.3 tons. After the 2011 civil war left the disposal site ransacked, the fragile transitional government signaled it would finish destruction, seeking Western assistance despite sovereignty sensitivities. The U.S. Nunn-Lugar program provided $45 million, and contractors rebuilt and secured the site; Canada and Germany contributed infrastructure and logistics. Inspectors found bulk containers largely intact; both bulk agents and the newly found combat-ready munitions—artillery shells, rockets and bombs—were destroyed using a Dynasafe static-detonation chamber that thermally neutralized agents and scrubbed the gases. The Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons supervised the technically demanding operation. U.S. officials expressed confidence no other unconventional caches remain, calling the operation the culmination of an international effort to prevent weapons of mass destruction from falling into terrorist hands. The report also included wider post-Gaddafi revelations about his regime’s abuses and clandestine activities from former insiders.

Katie Couric is close to signing with ABC for a syndicated daytime talk show and contributions to ABC News, with an announcement possible as soon as Monday. Her five-year CBS contract ends this weekend, and Scott Pelley will replace her on CBS Evening News, a debut her announcement could overshadow. Couric had considered staying at CBS or moving to ABC after talks with several networks; she previously co-hosted Today. ABC aims to fill the daytime void left by Oprah, amid broader schedule changes including cancellations of two soaps.

Megyn Kelly debuted Megyn Kelly TODAY on NBC’s 9 a.m. hour on September 25, 2017, marking a deliberate shift away from the hard-edged political journalism that made her a star at Fox News. Speaking to a live studio audience that included her mother and husband, Kelly opened by saying she was “kind of done with politics for now,” explaining she wanted the program to offer laughter, inspiration, occasional tears and “a little hope” to start viewers’ days. The premiere was positioned as a reintroduction: she shared personal background, including the death of her father when she was 15, and invited audience participation, saying each morning would begin with dialogue between host and crowd.

The hour combined celebrity interviews, lighter segments and an uplifting field piece. Kelly hosted the cast and creator of the Will & Grace reboot, spotlighting the show’s cultural impact, and engaged in playful taped bits with Today colleagues—biking with Al Roker and cooking with Matt Lauer—while receiving a welcoming toast from the Today family. The program closed with a “Settle For More” segment inspired by Kelly’s memoir, highlighting a 77-year-old Chicago nun’s efforts to improve a troubled neighborhood; sponsors contributed donations on air.

NBC packaged Kelly as part of the broader Today franchise and leaned on advertiser support, weaving branded promotions into the debut. Critics noted the show’s effort to soften Kelly’s image and emulate daytime icons like Oprah, while questioning whether the lighter, inspirational tone can be sustained amid a news cycle saturated with politicized stories. Reviewers pointed out awkward moments—missed cues, an uneven cadence, and an ill-timed joke—and observed that many topics, even uplifting ones like neighborhood revitalization or gun violence prevention, are inherently political. The central challenge identified is striking a credible balance: Kelly aims to avoid constant political coverage, but politics permeate many everyday issues, and viewers will watch to see whether she can authentically inhabit a warmer morning show persona and maintain relevance without reverting to her combative, hard-news instincts.

Reese Witherspoon and husband Jim Toth, newly married on March 26 at her Ojai estate, were spotted vacationing in Belize with her two children from her previous marriage, Ava (11) and Deacon (8). Observers described them as a relaxed, happy family who didn’t seek VIP treatment on arrival and blended in as ordinary tourists. Their wedding at Libby Ranch was intimate and joyful, attended by friends and family; Witherspoon wore a rose-hued Monique Lhuillier gown with tulle, Chantilly lace, and floral details, later switching to a white silk Lhuillier minidress. Ava served as maid of honor in a matching custom Lhuillier dress. 

In interviews around the time of her wedding, Witherspoon reflected on balancing fame, family and career. She acknowledged the costs of celebrity—lost privacy and the constant public scrutiny—but said she feels fortunate and supported by close friends and family. Turning 35 prompted introspection about aging, motherhood and identity; she described parenting as humbling and surprising, noting her daughter’s growing independence. Witherspoon emphasized that family and creating a stable home guide her choices more than career ambition.

Professionally, she remains adventurous: preparing physically for varied roles, from circus training and working with an elephant for Water for Elephants to action-comedy This Means War. Directors and co-stars praised her professionalism, bravery and comedic timing, while critics have sometimes found her miscast. She’s developing a Peggy Lee biopic with Nora Ephron and values character work that transforms her. Throughout, Witherspoon presents as warm, private, resilient and focused on cultivating a balanced life amid Hollywood pressures.

President-elect Donald Trump in December publicly pressured defense contractors over the soaring costs of major Pentagon programs, most notably demanding that Boeing price a comparable alternative to Lockheed Martin’s F-35 stealth fighter. Trump’s tweet asking Boeing to “price-out a comparable F-18 Super Hornet” came after meetings at Mar-a-Lago with Pentagon officials and the CEOs of Lockheed and Boeing, and immediately moved markets: Lockheed shares fell roughly 2% in after-hours trading while Boeing ticked up.

Trump’s involvement illustrates a departure from presidential norms: federal procurement is a highly technical, rule-bound process overseen by career contracting officers guided by the Federal Acquisition Regulation. Historically, presidents have shaped procurement through broad executive orders (for example, Obama’s contractor labor and nondiscrimination policies), but targeting specific companies or contracts is unprecedented. Experts warn Trump’s willingness to publicly threaten and intervene in individual contracts could be used as leverage to reward allies, punish perceived offenders, or score political points.

Federal contracts include termination clauses that give the government flexibility: termination for default (rare and punitive) and termination for convenience (common, permitting contractors to recover costs and sometimes profit). Legal precedent makes proving bad faith by the government extremely difficult; courts require a high threshold of proof. Contract law scholars say it’s theoretically possible for the administration to use convenience terminations against specific companies, and while contracting officers are supposed to act independently, political pressures and appointee loyalty make acquiescence likely in practice.

Experts cautioned that even the threat of executive intervention can have broad consequences. Companies facing tweet-driven public pressure or risk of termination may raise prices to hedge uncertainty, slowing down acquisition timelines and increasing overall program costs. Contracting officers, fearful of presidential criticism, may proceed more cautiously, further delaying acquisitions. Some firms may avoid suing the government over alleged bad-faith actions because litigation risks jeopardizing other contracts.

The F-35 program itself has long faced technical setbacks and cost growth—its lifetime acquisition cost is estimated at roughly $379 billion—while the Super Hornet lacks the F-35’s stealth and advanced sensor fusion. Analysts note the two aircraft are from different generations; to make the Super Hornet comparable would require significant redesign, testing and expense. Trump has also discussed modernizing and expanding the U.S. nuclear deterrent, a potential policy shift that would intersect with defense procurement priorities.

Overall, Trump’s direct, public intervention in procurement signals a new dynamic: his “bully pulpit” approach can immediately affect company fortunes and inject instability into long-term defense programs, risking higher costs, slower procurement, and strained industry-government relations even if formal legal authority to compel specific contract actions remains constrained.

Charlie Rangel, once a consummate political operator who helped free Hillary Clinton from the East Wing and turn her into a successful New York Senate candidate, was publicly censured by the House after a two-year ethics battle. The 80-year-old Harlem Democrat stood stone-faced as Speaker Nancy Pelosi read House Resolution 1737, rebuking him for failing to pay taxes on a Dominican beach home and improperly using his office for charitable fundraising. Rangel angrily protested the censure on the House floor and at a news conference, calling the vote “very, very, very political” and insisting on his honesty. Friends and some colleagues defended him, arguing his behavior mirrored routine practices in Congress and that far worse transgressions have gone unpunished. Critics countered that Rangel deserved punishment. The episode exposed Congress’s weak self-policing: rules governing members’ behavior proved lax and inconsistently enforced, with most transgressors escaping sanction. Rangel’s fall was thus both a personal tragedy and a broader indictment of an institution unable to apply consistent ethical standards.

A 6-year-old Quincy, Massachusetts boy named Robbie dialed 911 during Memorial Day weekend to report that his father, Michael Richardson, drove through a red light while they were out running errands. The Quincy Police Department shared the recorded call on Facebook, where Robbie calmly told the dispatcher, “My daddy went past a red light,” and explained they were on their way to a car wash. The dispatcher asked to speak with Robbie’s father, who realized what had happened, apologized and laughed it off, and no ticket was issued. Robbie, who aspires to be a police officer and enjoys playing in a toy cruiser, said his mother taught him how to call 911 and that a red light means stop. Parents Michael and Joleen used the incident as a teaching moment, explaining 911 is for emergencies; Joleen said she hadn’t expected him to actually call. Michael praised Robbie’s resolve—“when he says he’s going to do something, he does it”—and the family joked about future consequences, with Robbie saying he’d call an eye doctor if his dad ran another red light. Detective Karen Barkas called the call “pretty unique.”

Sen. Mark Udall, a strong advocate for government transparency and a member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, urged President Obama to support maximal declassification of the committee’s 6,300‑page study of the CIA’s detention and interrogation program, warning he might oppose a key CIA nomination unless oversight obstacles are removed. McClatchy reports the CIA’s Inspector General has referred possible malfeasance to the Justice Department tied to the still‑unreleased report, amid allegations the CIA monitored computers used by Senate aides reviewing agency documents—potentially breaching an agreement and raising legal questions under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. The dispute marks a rare and severe breakdown between the CIA and its congressional overseers over findings that the CIA misled the Bush administration and Congress about harsh interrogation techniques, including waterboarding, and that those techniques did not yield intelligence leading to the bin Laden raid. The White House has tracked the clash but has not intervened directly, while asserting a summary of findings should be declassified with necessary redactions. The committee discovered the CIA withheld an internal review that corroborates some committee findings, intensifying demands for transparency and White House control over declassification decisions.

Rodney Todd, a 36-year-old father who worked in dining services at the University of Maryland Eastern Shore and cared for his seven children, and all seven children — ages 6 to 15 — were found dead of carbon monoxide poisoning in their modest Princess Anne, Md., rental home. Authorities discovered the bodies Monday after coworkers and school staff became concerned when Todd failed to show up for work; his supervisor last saw him March 28. Police said the family appeared to have been sleeping and that a gasoline-powered generator with an empty tank was found inside the house. Investigators believe the generator was running to provide light and heat after electricity to the home had been cut off.

Delmarva Power said it had disconnected a stolen electric meter at the address on March 25 for safety reasons and had not cut service for nonpayment since there was no record of a request to reconnect after the Todds moved in. The utility and Maryland’s Public Service Commission are being investigated and the utility subpoenaed for records. State rules prohibit routine winter shutoffs for nonpayment without special filings, though utilities may disconnect service without notice if they find hazardous conditions or tampering.

Friends and relatives remembered Todd as a devoted, private father who took care of his children’s daily needs; his stepfather and mother described the children as lively and close-knit. The children’s mother, Tyisha Chambers, expressed shock and regret, saying she would have helped had she known. Officials used the tragedy to warn about the dangers of indoor generator use and carbon monoxide’s odorless, colorless threat, urging installation of detectors and proper generator placement outdoors and away from buildings. The case underscores risks for vulnerable families dealing with power loss and limited resources.

Former tennis champion Boris Becker has sparked controversy by claiming diplomatic status with the Central African Republic (CAR) to seek immunity from UK bankruptcy proceedings. Becker’s legal team told the High Court in London that he was appointed in April as an attaché for sport, culture and humanitarian affairs to the EU by the CAR, arguing that under the 1961 Vienna Convention his diplomatic role protected him from legal process unless the CAR president and foreign minister lift his immunity. A photograph of Becker with CAR President Faustin-Archange Touadera and a passport image circulated as supporting evidence.

However, CAR officials have strongly disputed his claim. Cherubin Moroubama, chief of staff at the foreign ministry, told AFP the passport’s serial number matches a batch stolen in 2014, lacked the foreign minister’s signature and stamp, and described Becker’s purported job title as nonexistent or inconsistent with sporting duties. Foreign Minister Charles Armel Doubane called the passport a “clumsy fake” and said an inquiry would be launched into who issued it; he also said nomination alone is insufficient without his signature to recognize a diplomat. The CAR embassy in Belgium earlier confirmed issuing a diplomatic passport, but CAR authorities later denied Becker is an official diplomat.

Becker, a three-time Wimbledon champion declared bankrupt in 2017 over debts to private bank Arbuthnot Latham, said the bank’s action was “unjustified and unjust” and framed his attaché role as a way to contribute to sport in one of the world’s poorest nations. His lawyers have not yet responded to CAR officials’ accusations that the passport and appointment are invalid.

The document mixes two topics: the Internet Archive’s effort to crawl and preserve webpages to prevent link rot, and a critical review of Justin Timberlake’s Super Bowl halftime performance, especially in relation to Prince.

The Internet Archive crawls new pages and the pages they reference to capture versions as they existed when written. The aim is to replace broken links or supplement them with archived versions so readers can see the original intent of authors. This “No More 404” campaign seeks to fix broken links across the web by preserving referred content at the time of creation.

The larger portion critiques Timberlake’s halftime show in Minneapolis. Reviewers judged it a serviceable, athletic, and largely fumble-free 12-minute set that revived his earlier pop choreography and closed with the crowd-pleasing “Can’t Stop the Feeling.” He began in a staged nightclub bit and moved across platforms with many dancers; he revived “Rock Your Body” and introduced a band called the Tennessee Kids. The set included a projected video tribute to Prince rather than a controversial hologram, which some saw as an acceptable homage while others considered it inadequate. Critics argued the performance lacked the depth, musical risk and emotional resonance of Prince’s legendary 2007 halftime show; Prince fans were especially uneasy given Prince’s complex history with Timberlake. Sound issues and reliance on backing tracks were noted, as were awkward moments—most memorably Timberlake taking a selfie with a teenager mid-song. Overall, the show was more athletic than artistically memorable and did little to dispel controversy around Timberlake’s recent PR challenges.

In 1999 Bain Capital and Madison Dearborn bought $75 million in Stericycle, a fast-growing medical-waste disposal firm that later became a target of anti-abortion activists for handling waste from abortion clinics. SEC filings obtained by Mother Jones list Mitt Romney — then founder and chief executive of Bain — as having voting and dispositive power over more than two million Stericycle shares and identify him as sole shareholder or officer of several Bain entities involved in the purchase; one filing bears Romney’s signature. Bain and Romney have said he left Bain in February 1999 to run the Salt Lake City Olympics and had no role in later investments, describing his status as retired or on a part-time leave. But other contemporaneous filings and press notices describe him as retaining ownership, occasional management input, and committee membership; Romney also kept ownership of Bain-related entities incorporated after his supposed departure. Stericycle’s growth after the buyout was rapid and profitable for Bain: by 2001 Bain sold part of its stake for about $88 million and realized roughly $49.5 million total by 2004. The company had a troubled safety and regulatory history in the 1990s, with OSHA citations and state fines, and later antitrust settlements. The documents raise questions about the timing and nature of Romney’s exit from Bain and whether he truly had no involvement in Bain’s investments after February 1999.

The Rio Olympics produced a mixture of historic triumphs, stirring human moments and embarrassing missteps, leaving a legacy both brilliant and flawed. Michael Phelps again topped the medal chart, adding six medals — five gold — to extend his career total to 23 Olympic golds and 28 medals overall. The United States dominated the podium, driven by multi-medal performances from stars such as Simone Biles and Katie Ledecky (each with five medals) and Kim Rhode, who earned a medal in her sixth consecutive Games. Biles, in particular, emerged as a defining figure in Rio; her power, precision and charisma made her an almost household name and a likely future record-breaker in gymnastics.

Usain Bolt sealed a perfect Olympic farewell by anchoring Jamaica’s 4x100 relay to gold, finishing his Olympic career with an emphatic kiss of the finish line and nine golds in nine finals. Other standout moments included a pure act of sportsmanship when Abbey D’Agostino helped rival Nikki Hamblin finish a 5,000-meter race despite tearing a knee ligament — an episode that captured the Olympic spirit. Monica Puig became a breakout star by securing Puerto Rico’s first Olympic gold in tennis, inspiring widespread emotion back home.

There were also poignant personal and national stories: Rafaela Silva, raised in Rio’s City of God favela, won judo gold, a near-movie script of local triumph. Brazil achieved a storybook ending when Neymar converted the decisive penalty to give the host nation men’s soccer gold in shootout drama against Germany, producing one of the most celebrated moments of the Games.

Not all moments were noble. Ryan Lochte’s fabricated robbery tale became one of Rio’s biggest embarrassments, drawing legal and reputational fallout. Organizational spins and odd press lines from Rio organizers — encapsulated by spokesman Mario Andrada’s memorable quips about chemistry and numbers — highlighted the Games’ chaotic side. Still, amid infrastructure issues and controversy, Rio delivered unforgettable performances, emotional breakthroughs and moments that embodied both the best and most human sides of the Olympic ideal.

Finally, commentary from Australia reflected on gymnastics’ profile gap: while the U.S. benefits from broad media exposure and widespread youth participation fueling elite success, Australia’s limited coverage and participation are cited as reasons for weaker results, implying that broader media focus and investment could elevate the sport nationally.

Lincoln University has instituted a controversial policy requiring undergraduates with a body mass index (BMI) over 30 to either lower their BMI or take a one‑semester “Fitness for Life” course combining exercise, nutrition education and discussion of obesity risks before they can graduate. The rule affects dozens: 92 freshmen (19% of the incoming class) initially had BMIs above 30, and about 25 seniors who never lost weight or completed the class now risk delayed graduation. Supporters, including James DeBoy, chair of the health, physical education and recreation department, frame the requirement as a public‑health responsibility amid high obesity and diabetes rates, especially in African‑American communities, and cite improvements seen in class participants. Critics—students and outside experts—call it discriminatory, question its effectiveness for long‑term weight loss, and raise concerns about personal rights and the university’s role in policing students’ bodies.

Saturday Night Live’s Melissa McCarthy portrayal of Sean Spicer provoked more White House discomfort than sketches lampooning Donald Trump directly.
