Though Trump did not tweet about the sketch, sources told Politico the administration was especially upset that Spicer was impersonated by a woman—an element they found emasculating and damaging to his authority. Spicer himself has tried to downplay the skit, joking about McCarthy’s gum-chewing and suggesting he’d rather focus on the president’s agenda, but allies worry the viral send-up deepens his credibility problems after earlier missteps. The episode tapped into broader patterns: Trump’s history of gendered responses to media figures, feuds with women such as Megyn Kelly and Rosie O’Donnell, and an obsession with image and perceived strength. That context helped fuel a Twitter campaign urging SNL to cast O’Donnell—Trump’s decade-long public antagonist—in a prominent role, with many suggesting she play Steve Bannon or even Trump when Alec Baldwin is unavailable. O’Donnell replied she’d be willing to “serve” if asked. Commentators noted SNL rarely casts by social media consensus, but the idea resonated because mocking Spicer with a woman seemed to strike a particularly sensitive nerve in Trump world. Some observers argued portraying Bannon as a sinister power broker is already embarrassing for the administration; casting O’Donnell could be an especially pointed provocation, likely to infuriate the president.

A 13-year-old boy, Gregory Jean Jr., was rescued from a concealed compartment in a Jonesboro, Georgia home after his biological mother alerted police that he was being held and abused. Officers discovered the boy after he used a phone app to text and send a photo of the garage to his mother, who relayed the information to the 911 center. Initial police searches of the house turned up nothing; the family denied knowledge of the child and gave conflicting statements. Sgt. Joanne Southerland insisted officers return and, shortly after midnight, found a hidden space behind a linen closet leading into the area between the garage and attic. The compartment contained only wooden beams and insulation; Southerland said it was a place where no person should be living. The boy appeared frightened but calmed down after officers reassured him and later thanked them. Police say he had been physically assaulted that night—thrown down stairs and punched—and earlier punished for trying to leave. Gregory’s father, 37-year-old Gregory Jean Sr., and stepmother, 42-year-old Samantha Joy Davis, were arrested on charges including false imprisonment, cruelty to children and obstruction; Davis is on probation for a 2004 child cruelty case involving another child. Three teenage children of Davis were also arrested on similar charges. Authorities have not detailed how long the boy had been hidden or whether he had been reported missing to registries, saying the investigation is ongoing. Neighbors described the household as outwardly normal. Officials emphasized they would take such calls seriously and pursue all leads to ensure a child’s safety.

The Associated Press removed a two-week-old tweet that summarized its August review of Hillary Clinton’s meetings as secretary of state, saying the message “fell short of AP standards by omitting essential context.” The original Aug. 23 tweet read, “More than half those who met Clinton as Cabinet secretary gave money to Clinton Foundation.” AP leader for standards John Daniszewski explained the analysis actually focused on 154 discretionary in-person or phone meetings with non-government individuals, 85 of whom were foundation donors. That subset excluded the many government and foreign-official meetings that comprised much of Clinton’s schedule, a distinction the tweet failed to convey. AP replaced the message with a more precise line: “Many of the discretionary meetings Clinton had at State were with people who gave to Clinton Foundation,” and announced a new policy subjecting tweets to the same internal review and correction process as other AP content. Clinton and her campaign criticized the original report as misleading and defensive, saying meetings with global figures were based on their stature, not foundation ties. The story also intersected with broader debates over Clinton’s emails and foundation practices during the 2016 campaign.

Amedeo Modigliani’s 1917 reclining nude Nu couché (sur le côté gauche) sold at Sotheby’s New York for about $157.2 million during the May 14, 2018 Impressionist & Modern evening sale, the highest price in Sotheby’s history though below a prior $170 million record for the artist. One of only five Modigliani nudes ever auctioned, the large work—infamous when first shown in Paris for provoking a police shutdown—had a $150 million pre-sale estimate and was consigned reportedly by Irish owner John Magnier, who bought it in 2003 for $26.9 million. The sale underscored renewed strong demand for early 20th-century masterpieces amid a competitive spring season featuring Picasso, Monet, Munch and O’Keeffe.

Researchers at Johns Hopkins and the NIH report that a single neonatal dose of a sonic hedgehog (SHH) pathway agonist restored cerebellar growth and improved learning in mice engineered to model Down syndrome. Published in Science Translational Medicine, the study used mice bearing extra copies of roughly half the genes on human chromosome 21; these mice normally have smaller cerebella and impaired spatial learning. A one-time injection on the day of birth normalized cerebellar size into adulthood and unexpectedly rescued performance on a water-maze test, matching untreated normal mice. Although learning and memory are typically associated with the hippocampus, the treatment produced cognitive benefits without obvious hippocampal cell changes, suggesting improved cerebellum–hippocampus communication may underlie the effect. Investigators caution the SHH agonist’s systemic activation of growth pathways could produce harmful side effects—such as increased cancer risk—so the compound is not ready for human use. The team plans to seek more targeted strategies to harness SHH signaling safely; they stress any future therapy would be one of multiple approaches rather than a cure for Down syndrome’s complex cognitive features.

Rodney King was reportedly upbeat and excited about returning to celebrity boxing shortly before his death. Damon Feldman, a longtime acquaintance who worked with King on the boxing circuit, told TMZ he spoke with King at 4:00 PM the day before and that King was looking forward to an August match with Jose Canseco; a June 29 press conference was scheduled to announce the fight. Feldman said King was thrilled to be working again and getting back in the ring. King, 47, was found dead early that morning at his Rialto, California home. According to sources cited by TMZ, King’s fiancée told friends he had been drinking all day Saturday and had smoked marijuana in the hours before he died. She reportedly went to bed around 2:00 AM and later awoke to King screaming in the backyard; she found him naked and then heard a splash, discovering him at the bottom of the pool. Paramedics were unable to revive him.

This document reviews research showing that mustached bats (Pteronotus parnellii) display hemispheric asymmetry in auditory processing analogous to humans: the left auditory cortex favors fine temporal resolution while the right favors finer spectral resolution. The bat species, found from southern Sonora to Brazil, roosts in caves and prefers moist habitats; it has a wingspan up to 1.9 feet and is IUCN “Least Concern.” Framed by the Heisenberg-Gabor Limit (the acoustic uncertainty principle that constrains simultaneous time and frequency precision), the authors contrast “closed-system” views that human speech mechanisms are unique with “domain-general” models (ASTIR: Asymmetry for Spectral versus Temporal Integration and Resolution) predicting similar asymmetries across species that rely on refined spectrotemporal hearing. Mustached bats rely on CF-FM echolocation and rich social calls; their auditory cortex contains specialized subregions (DSCF for Doppler-shifted CF processing and FM-FM for delay/range) that process spectral and temporal features respectively. Electrophysiological studies found left-right differences in DSCF neurons: left-side neurons in males show faster latencies, greater responsiveness to rapid FM rates and shorter integration windows (temporal specialization), whereas right-side neurons prefer longer, narrower-band stimuli (spectral specialization). Females show weaker asymmetry. These findings argue against human-only closed-system accounts and against brain-size or handedness explanations, suggesting sex-dependent ASTIR is evolutionarily conserved and may inform studies of human language disorders and speech recognition. The authors call for more behavioral, pharmacological, and imaging work to probe mechanisms and the functional significance of sex differences.

An Omaha man traveling with his toddler was left distraught at an airport check-in when an agent told him his daughter, who had just turned two, was over the free-infant age limit by two months and would require a paid ticket. The father, unable to afford the unexpected cost or rebooking on short notice, stepped aside to make calls, visibly upset as he hugged his daughter. A fellow passenger, Kevin Leslie, witnessed the scene and later shared it on Facebook. A woman nearby overheard the exchange and intervened, telling the agent she wanted to buy the little girl’s ticket. When told the fare was $749, she calmly paid with her credit card. The relieved father repeatedly thanked her and asked for her name so he could repay her, but she refused and walked away, saying, “Don’t worry about it.” Leslie’s post went viral after he recounted the moment on the Love What Matters Facebook page. Within hours, people identified the Good Samaritan as Debbie Bolton, co-founder and global chief sales officer of Norwex. Norwex confirmed Bolton’s identity and praised her generosity. Company colleagues and independent consultants described Bolton as humble, caring and consistently giving, citing personal encounters that reflected her compassion, including working with Mother Teresa when she was 19. Norwex leaders and employees said the act was in line with her character and expressed pride in her deed. Leslie said he shared the story to highlight people who do kind things without seeking recognition; Bolton, who called her gesture something anyone might do, expressed surprise at the attention and said she hopes the story inspires others to make positive impacts in people’s lives.

Popstar: Never Stop Never Stopping is a sharp, affectionate mockumentary from the Lonely Island trio—Andy Samberg, Akiva Schaffer and Jorma Taccone—who wrote and star in the film, with Schaffer and Taccone directing. Clocking in at about 86 minutes and rooted in the same satirical mock-doc tradition as This Is Spinal Tap and A Mighty Wind, the movie lampoons modern pop stardom while also demonstrating genuine affection and understanding for the culture it skewers.

Samberg plays Conner4Real, a Bieber- and boy-band-like superstar who rose to fame with his group, the Style Boyz, and then splintered off into an inflated solo career. The plot follows the release of Conner’s latest flop album, his public meltdown and the ensuing push—by industry forces and nostalgia—to reunite with his former bandmates (played by Taccone and Schaffer). The film mines contemporary pop phenomena: manufactured celebrity, stunt PR, DJs-as-deities, social-media martyrdom, talentless entourages, desperate cultural appropriation, and the cycle of youth-vs.-nostalgia that shapes today’s charts.

Rather than merely piling on one-liners, Popstar blends broad, obscene humor (there are many memorable dick jokes) with pointed industry satire and surprising heart. It mirrors the format of music documentaries—archival footage, talking-head cameos and celebrity interviews—featuring real stars like Mariah Carey, Usher, Questlove and others who play themselves offering faux-critical takes on Conner. Supporting comic talent including Bill Hader, Sarah Silverman, Tim Meadows, Joan Cusack and Imogen Poots add texture and laughs, while Chris Redd shines as a rising rapper whose presence highlights Conner’s fall.

Popstar succeeds because it both understands and admires pop music’s absurdities. It skewers fame without cruelty, offers smart commentary on celebrity culture, and still delivers infectious, deliberately dumb songs and visual gags. The result is consistently funny, surprisingly empathetic and a fitting cinematic extension of the Lonely Island’s best work.

A new Public Policy Polling survey found only 24% of voters support the Senate GOP’s Graham-Cassidy bill to repeal and replace Obamacare, while 50% oppose it. The measure, sponsored by Sens. Lindsey Graham and Bill Cassidy, would convert ACA insurance subsidies and Medicaid expansion funds into state block grants, letting states design their own programs. The poll — cited by Democratic groups defending the ACA — also found 46% of voters would be less likely to back a member of Congress who voted for Graham-Cassidy, while 23% would be more likely. Seventy-seven percent agreed with Jimmy Kimmel that no one should be denied coverage due to cost, and 68% said senators should wait for a Congressional Budget Office score before voting; only 21% disagreed. The Brookings Institution estimated the bill could leave at least 21 million people uninsured by 2026. Senator John McCain announced he could not “in good conscience” support the bill without a CBO analysis, dealing a major blow to the GOP effort; Sens. Rand Paul and Susan Collins have also signaled opposition or reluctance, making passage unlikely.

The 51st Country Music Association Awards opened with a somber tribute and a sharp dose of satire. Darius Rucker led an all-star country ensemble—Keith Urban, Lady Antebellum, Tim McGraw & Faith Hill, Garth Brooks, Reba McEntire and others—in a moving rendition of Hootie and the Blowfish’s “Hold My Hand,” honoring victims of the recent Route 91 Harvest Festival shooting in Las Vegas. Hosts Carrie Underwood and Brad Paisley broadened the tribute to include victims of other recent mass shootings and the hurricanes that struck Texas, Florida, the Caribbean and Puerto Rico. The salute followed controversy earlier in the week after the CMA initially issued guidelines asking journalists not to question artists about the Las Vegas attack; the association later rescinded and apologized for the restrictions amid backlash. While emphasizing the show’s role in lifting spirits, Paisley and Underwood did not avoid politics. The pair mocked the withdrawn “politics-free” ban in their opening monologue and performed a pointed parody—“Before He Tweets,” set to Underwood’s “Before He Cheats”—lampooning President Donald Trump’s frequent, late-night tweeting and referencing White House excess and nuclear tensions with North Korea. The gag balanced humor with a cautionary line about the stakes of impulsive presidential tweets. Their performance marked the tenth consecutive year the duo hosted the CMA Awards, blending tribute, comedy and cultural commentary.

Recent reports and industry moves show shifting patterns in both homebuying and TV advertising. Zillow’s September analysis found millennials (ages 18–34) are now the largest group of U.S. homebuyers, though they tend to buy later than previous generations. Spencer Rascoff, Zillow’s CEO, explained that limited starter-home inventory is pushing millennials to rent longer and skip traditional starter homes. When they do buy, many opt for larger, more expensive first houses—sometimes reaching million-dollar price points—reflecting a major generational shift in timing and expectations.

Separately, Fox is experimenting with six-second TV ads, debuting them in high-profile sports broadcasts such as the Dallas Cowboys–Denver Broncos game and expanding across NFL, MLB, college football and other properties. T-Mobile and Visa are among the early adopters; T-Mobile pairs six-second spots with its 30-second ads to mimic short-form digital content, while Visa will use brief spots to promote Hurricane Harvey relief and has committed $1 million to the effort. Fox executive Bruce Lefkowitz and advertisers say shorter ads better capture attention—especially among younger viewers—and reflect digital viewing habits. Fox charges rates similar to 15-second units and limits the number of six-second spots to preserve value. The move addresses competition from ad-light digital platforms and attempts to improve the TV experience, though advertisers remain cautious about economics and whether paying premium rates for reduced clutter is justified.

U.S. home values are falling faster across many major metros, with the Wall Street Journal reporting year-over-year declines in all 28 tracked areas in Q4. Price drops intensified in hard-hit cities like Miami, Orlando, Atlanta and Chicago, and spread to previously resilient markets such as Seattle and Portland. Weak buyer demand and tight credit, plus rising inventories, are driving declines; many markets now have unsold supplies well above the six-month balance point. Foreclosures, underwater mortgages and potential bank-led distressed sales could worsen conditions. Homeownership rates fell and vacancies remain high, while renting has increased. Some pockets (e.g., Sacramento, San Diego, core urban centers) show healthier activity, but overall recovery may take years without stronger job growth.

The New York Times told HarperCollins it will not include Sen. Ted Cruz’s new book, A Time for Truth, on its upcoming bestseller list despite strong first-week sales. According to Nielsen BookScan, the hardcover sold 11,854 copies in its debut week—more than 18 of the 20 titles that will appear on the Times list for the week ending July 4, and more than several recent conservative releases. The book ranks highly on other charts (No. 4 on the Wall Street Journal, Publishers Weekly, and BookScan hardcover lists, and No. 1 at the Conservative Book Club). When HarperCollins asked for an explanation, the Times said the title did not meet its inclusion criteria, noting that the paper applies uniform standards and analyzes sales patterns beyond raw numbers to ensure the list reflects “authentic best sellers.” The Times later said evidence suggested sales were largely due to strategic bulk purchases; HarperCollins and the Cruz campaign declined to comment.

NATO leaders met in Wales to reorient the alliance toward defending Europe amid Russia’s destabilizing actions in Ukraine. They approved a rapid-reaction “spearhead” force drawn from member states—several thousand troops, with air, sea and special-forces support—able to deploy to an Eastern European crisis within 48 hours. The unit will have a permanent command staffed on rotation and pre-positioned supply depots to avoid flying in all equipment. The measure is a compromise after members balked at permanently stationing troops on the eastern flank; NATO insists this won’t violate the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act. Canada was asked to contribute but offered only cautious consideration, reflecting domestic budget cuts and reluctance to meet the UK’s call for NATO allies to boost defence spending to 2% of GDP. 

Meanwhile, Ukraine reported heavy setbacks: forces withdrew from Luhansk airport after clashes with what Kiev says are Russian tanks and battalion-sized formations. President Petro Poroshenko accused Russia of “direct and undisguised aggression,” while Moscow denied direct intervention and pressed for talks on regional “statehood.” EU leaders prepared tougher sanctions targeting finance and energy if Moscow did not pull back; some members wary due to energy dependence. Russian officials signaled they will revise military strategy in response to NATO moves, warning of further deterioration in relations. Analysts called the summit a watershed—NATO must demonstrate resolve or risk losing credibility.

Multiple news reports and court filings revealed that Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential campaign and the Democratic National Committee helped fund research that produced the now-notorious dossier alleging links between Donald J. Trump, his associates and Russia. The arrangement was brokered through Perkins Coie attorney Marc E. Elias, who retained Washington research firm Fusion GPS in April 2016. Fusion GPS, which had previously researched Trump for an unnamed Republican client during the GOP primary, subcontracted former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele to compile a series of reports alleging Russian efforts to aid Trump and that Moscow had compromising material on him.

Perkins Coie’s letter, unsealed amid a subpoena fight over Fusion GPS’s bank records, released the research firm from client-confidentiality obligations and confirmed that the Clinton campaign and the DNC shared the cost of the work through late October 2016. The exact sums paid were not disclosed. Campaign officials and some DNC leaders said they were not aware of the specifics or Fusion GPS’s role; former Clinton spokesman Brian Fallon said he first learned of the dossier after the election but would have tried to verify and publicize its claims pre-election.

The dossier was later given to the FBI, which used parts of Steele’s reporting in its counterintelligence probe; the special counsel’s team also interviewed Steele. Intelligence agencies assessed with high confidence that Russia intervened to help Trump. Trump has dismissed the dossier as false and politically motivated, while congressional Republicans have sought to discredit Fusion GPS and identify its clients. Fusion GPS has resisted disclosure, citing confidentiality and constitutional protections, and has fought subpoenas challenging the release of its financial records.

JPMorgan Chase will commit $100 million over five years to help Detroit recover from its record municipal bankruptcy, providing a mix of loans and grants for housing repairs, blight removal, job training and economic development. The investment arrives as Detroit negotiates a bankruptcy exit plan amid roughly $18 billion in long-term debt and a federal judge’s upcoming decision. State lawmakers are considering nearly $200 million in public funds as part of a “grand bargain” with philanthropic contributions to protect pensions and the city’s art collection, a proposal that faces political caution about using taxpayer money. JPMorgan’s package—announced publicly by CEO Jamie Dimon with local officials—aims to bolster revitalization and reduce the risk of future fiscal distress. Half the funds will reach community projects lacking capital; $25 million will assist demolition and blight efforts via groups like the Detroit Land Bank Authority and the Blight Removal Task Force. The remainder includes $12.5 million for workforce training, $7 million for small-business support and $5.5 million for economic-growth initiatives such as a streetcar project. The move follows JPMorgan’s broader urban investments and comes after the bank’s recent high-profile legal settlement.

Researchers sequenced the coelacanth genome to illuminate genetic changes tied to vertebrates’ move from water to land. As a lobe-finned fish closely related to the tetrapod ancestor, Latimeria allowed distinction between genes lost in tetrapods and those absent in ray-finned fishes. Over 50 genes present in the bony-fish ancestor but missing in tetrapods were identified, including components of FGF, TGF-β/BMP and WNT pathways and many developmental transcription factors. Functional data from zebrafish link many lost genes to fin, ear, kidney, tail, eye and brain development, suggesting targeted gene loss accompanied morphological shifts like fin-to-limb and ear remodeling. In contrast, homeobox gene coding sequences remained largely conserved. The team also mapped 44,200 conserved non-coding elements (CNEs) that arose in ancestral tetrapods; these are enriched for regulatory activity (p300 binding) and associate with genes for olfaction, morphogenesis, cell differentiation and immune functions, reflecting terrestrial adaptations. Comparative analysis of HOX-D regulatory deserts found a coelacanth–tetrapod shared enhancer (island 1) that drives limb expression in transgenic mice, supporting co-option of an ancestral lobe-fin regulator in autopod evolution. Adaptive changes were detected in the hepatic urea-cycle enzyme CPS1 during the tetrapod transition. Finally, a conserved HOX-A CNE near Hoxa14 shows activity in extra-embryonic blood-island tissues, suggesting possible roles in the evolution of extra-embryonic structures such as the placenta. The coelacanth genome thus reveals both gene loss and regulatory innovation underlying the water-to-land transition.

On Christmas Eve, actor Ben Affleck announced via Facebook that he will not run for the soon-to-be-vacant Massachusetts Senate seat expected after John Kerry’s confirmation as secretary of State. Affleck said he loves Massachusetts and politics but prefers to focus on work with the Eastern Congo Initiative, veterans’ causes, hunger awareness, and filmmaking. His post noted he expects “some phenomenal” candidates to emerge. Earlier the same day, Ted Kennedy Jr. also ruled out a bid. Kennedy, son of the late Sen. Edward Kennedy, said he is grateful for support but considers Connecticut his home; he did not close the door on future public service. Their decisions leave a familiar Democratic field intact, with Massachusetts Reps. Michael Capuano, Stephen Lynch and Ed Markey frequently mentioned as potential contenders. On the Republican side, former Sen. Scott Brown—defeated by Elizabeth Warren in November—remains a strong likely candidate with statewide name recognition. President Obama has pledged to help raise money and campaign for the eventual Democratic nominee. Observers say a Kennedy entry would have reshaped the race, but his absence maintains a broad Democratic contest.

Economists call “efficiency wages” the practice of paying workers above the market rate to gain loyalty, effort and lower turnover. Walmart’s recent experiment with higher pay, better scheduling and extensive training—called “the investments”—tests that theory at massive scale. Beginning in early 2015, new executives reversed years of aggressive labor-cost cutting after customer surveys and sales showed decline. Walmart committed $2.7 billion to raise average pay, introduce training academies, and offer clearer career paths and more predictable schedules. Early results show improved customer-service ratings, rising sales at established stores and 90 consecutive weeks of better “clean, fast, friendly” scores. Store managers report attracting applicants seeking careers rather than stopgap jobs. Yet U.S. operating income is down as labor costs rise, and Walmart’s stock has underperformed, leaving investors skeptical about near-term profitability. Critics say the measures are partial—some raises depend on completing long training, and scheduling changes are limited in scope. The experiment matters beyond Walmart: if large employers embraced efficiency wages, it could boost productivity and consumer demand economy-wide. For now, Walmart’s changes show promise for workforce and customer experience but remain an uncertain long-term business bet.

At the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), Mitt Romney narrowly beat Rick Santorum 38% to 31% in the straw poll, a result Santorum downplayed on CNN’s State of the Union. Santorum suggested some campaigns have boosted results by buying tickets and bussing supporters—an accusation he framed generally and tied to long-standing questions about Ron Paul’s past successes at CPAC—while insisting his own campaign did not “rig” turnout. He said he wouldn’t engage in that kind of politics. Romney’s campaign promptly rejected Santorum’s implication. Spokeswoman Andrea Saul countered that Romney legitimately won both the CPAC straw poll and a separate nationwide CPAC survey of conservatives, and pointed to Romney’s victory in the Maine caucuses as proof conservatives are coalescing around someone they see as capable of changing Washington and not as a “creature of Washington.” Meanwhile, Ron Paul expressed bemusement at Romney’s self-description as a “severe” or “serious” conservative on CBS’s Face the Nation, saying he was unsure what Romney meant and inviting Romney to clarify his claim. In separate coverage, new White House Chief of Staff Jack Lew defended President Obama’s handling of contraception policy affecting Catholic institutions. Lew told Candy Crowley the administration’s Friday “accommodation” represents the president’s consistent position and is the furthest step he will take to persuade Catholic bishops. When asked whether health insurers would cover contraception costs for church-run hospitals and schools, Lew said insurers would indeed bear those costs and might even pay less overall because contraception can reduce pregnancy-related expenses. The pieces highlight intra-party disputes on the right and ongoing tension between the Obama administration and faith leaders over reproductive coverage.

Irish lawmakers passed the Protection of Life During Pregnancy Bill after a marathon two-day debate, legalizing abortion only when a woman’s life is at risk—either because continuing the pregnancy would be fatal or because she is suicidal. The Dáil approved the measure by 127 to 31, forcing Prime Minister Enda Kenny to push the bill through despite strong opposition from Catholic clergy and conservative members of his party; five Fine Gael deputies were expelled for voting against it and one minister, Lucinda Creighton, was ousted after dissenting. The law responds to a 2012 case in which a woman died after being denied a termination but does not extend to pregnancies resulting from rape or to fatal fetal anomalies, nor does it end the thousands of Irish women who travel to Britain annually—about 4,000 last year—for abortions. Rights groups and anti-abortion activists have already threatened legal challenges; critics argue criminal penalties of up to 14 years and exclusions for many cases will leave many women with no choice but to travel, seek clandestine pills, or take legal action. Public protests and tense scenes both inside and outside parliament underscored deep national divisions.

The Muslim Brotherhood, Egypt’s long-banned Islamist opposition, is sharply divided between younger, pragmatic activists and an older, conservative leadership, raising uncertainty about its post-Mubarak role. Youth leaders like 29-year-old Moaz Abdel Karim embraced democratic pluralism, women's rights, and alliances with secular groups, helping organize the January protests that toppled Hosni Mubarak and calling for a unity government and free elections. In contrast, Supreme Guide Mohamed Badi and other hard-liners have voiced anti-Western and anti-Israel rhetoric, supported jihadist causes, and favor an Islamic state. The movement’s internal tug-of-war was deepened when state crackdowns in the 2000s targeted moderates, empowering conservatives who pushed a 2007 platform limiting women’s and Christian political roles and proposing clerical oversight of laws. Moderates insist such positions were misrepresented. As the Brotherhood seeks legal party status and pledges not to field a presidential candidate, observers—domestically and abroad, including Israel and U.S. officials—are wary about which faction will prevail and how genuinely democratic the group’s future agenda will be.

Legal documents obtained by TMZ allege that radio legend Casey Kasem is in severely diminished mental and physical condition. Filed by his daughter Julie, the papers state an examining physician found major impairments in Casey’s short-, long- and immediate-term memory, severe disorganized thinking, significant difficulty communicating verbally, problems with simple calculations, planning and reasoning, and moderate hallucinations. The filings say he has advanced Parkinson’s disease, is mostly bedridden and may have early-onset dementia after declining over three to four years. Julie is seeking a conservatorship to control Casey’s health care and alleges his wife of 33 years, Jean, has isolated him from his children, preventing phone contact for months. Jean is reportedly contesting the move to transfer control away from her.

Scientists have analyzed DNA from a jawbone (Oase 1) found in Peștera cu Oase, Romania, and discovered it carries the highest proportion of Neanderthal ancestry identified in any modern human to date. Oase 1 lived roughly 42,000–37,000 years ago, among the earliest anatomically modern humans in Europe. Genetic sequencing shows that 6–9.4% of this individual’s nuclear genome came from Neanderthals—about 2.3–3.6 times more Neanderthal DNA than seen in present-day non-Africans or in several other ancient modern humans previously sequenced. The Neanderthal-derived segments in Oase 1’s genome are unusually large, indicating a very recent Neanderthal ancestor: likely within four to six generations (the equivalent of a great-great-grandparent) and possibly as recent as 100–150 years before the individual lived. This provides direct evidence that interbreeding between Homo sapiens and Neanderthals occurred not only in the Near East but also later in Europe. Despite living in Europe, Oase 1 appears to have contributed little genetically to later Europeans; his genome shares more variants with present-day East Asians and Native Americans than with modern Europeans, suggesting he belonged to an early “pioneer” population that did not persist in Europe’s ancestral lineages. The findings refine timelines of human–Neanderthal interactions and reinforce that Neanderthals were not distant, primitive cousins but contemporaries who interbred with incoming modern humans. The jawbone was excavated in 2002; improvements in DNA techniques enabled successful sequencing and these new insights into early human population dynamics in Europe.

On the 33rd anniversary of eight-year-old Christy “Luna” Luna’s 1984 disappearance from Greenacres, Fla., the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office launched an unusual social media campaign: for three days they let an imagined, first-person Christy “take over” their Facebook and Twitter accounts, narrating what she might have experienced during and after her abduction. Christy, who vanished after walking 500 feet to Belk’s General Store to buy cat food on Memorial Day weekend, became a familiar missing-child face decades ago—appearing on billboards, milk cartons and television—yet no arrest or recovery followed. The department’s posts recreated the day’s timeline: a family trip that turned out not to be Disney, an afternoon nap by Christy’s mother Jennie Johnson, the girl’s solo errand and the discovery she was gone. Tweets ranged from tender pleas aimed at Christy’s mother to chilling imagined moments of fear and struggle. Reactions were mixed—many thanked the office and expressed emotion, while others called the approach creepy or inappropriate. The campaign aimed to generate fresh tips; it was inspired by a similar Royal Canadian Mounted Police effort that produced leads without arrests. Investigators over the years probed several suspects, including Victor Wonyetye—linked by rumor to other missing girls but never charged—and neighborhood residents Willis and Chuck Rambo; none were conclusively tied to Christy. Her mother has vowed never to stop seeking answers. The sheriff’s final post asked the public to share Christy’s story and help bring her family closure.

A Memphis woman, Faith Pugh, says she feels betrayed after a date allegedly stole her car and used it to take another woman on a date the same night. Pugh had agreed to go out with Kelton Griffin, a former high school acquaintance who contacted her out of the blue. When he arrived, he had been dropped off by someone else and didn’t bring a vehicle. They took Pugh’s black Volvo but stalled when Griffin couldn’t decide where to go, eventually stopping at an Airport Area Marathon gas station. Griffin asked Pugh to buy cigars and, while she was inside, drove off in her car. Pugh’s mother picked her up, and later she received a text from her god sister saying Griffin had asked her out. Pugh asked for the location and, with help from her god sister’s GPS, the women tailed Griffin until losing and then re-locating him at the Summer Drive-In on Summer Avenue. There they found Griffin in Pugh’s Volvo; her god sister had driven him and even paid their admissions. Police arrested Griffin that night and charged him with theft of property. WMC’s report notes he had prior arrests, including a 2016 incident involving an alleged robbery after dining out. Pugh said she never wants to see him again and hopes he remains jailed for a long time.

Samsung’s updated SmartTV privacy policy and related industry moves have sparked major privacy concerns by revealing how voice, camera and usage data may be captured, transmitted and shared. The policy explicitly warns that spoken words containing personal or sensitive information may be captured and transmitted to third parties for voice-recognition processing, and that disabling voice recognition stops the feature but not other Samsung data collection about TV usage. Samsung also notes data encryption, on‑screen microphone indicators, and that owners can disconnect Wi‑Fi to limit data flow. The SmartTV supplement details broad telemetry collection used to build personalised recommendations—watch and search histories, clicks, device identifiers, IP address and cookie data—and explains that third‑party apps may independently collect data. Camera features (gesture control, facial recognition) can be disabled or covered, though disabling them removes those services; facial images are stored locally but usage metadata may still be collected. The policy’s capacious language led critics to compare SmartTVs to Orwellian “telescreens,” a parallel amplified on social media and by privacy advocates. Similar industry choices, such as Microsoft’s always‑listening Kinect for Xbox One, which accepts voice wake words even when the console is off, have intensified the debate about the “internet of things.” Companies stress technical safeguards and user controls, but critics warn that pervasive microphones and cameras in homes could allow unprecedented data collection and raise risks if devices or services are compromised.

After the Senate’s failed attempt to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act, President Donald Trump urged changing Senate rules to eliminate the 60-vote threshold for most legislation and require only a simple 51-vote majority. Trump tweeted that Republicans must “immediately go to a 51-vote majority, not senseless 60,” despite the “skinny” repeal bill actually being pursued through budget reconciliation — a process that already required only 51 votes. The measure fell 49-51 after Sens. John McCain, Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins joined Democrats and independents to oppose it. Trump later acknowledged parts of health-care changes could pass with 51 votes but argued many important bills still need 60. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has repeatedly opposed abolishing the legislative filibuster, and Republicans have struggled to advance their agenda without bipartisan support; other major measures such as spending bills would still require 60 votes to overcome filibusters. Trump also chastised defecting senators for letting “the American people down” and suggested letting Obamacare “implode,” a position Democrats criticized as harmful.

Defense Secretary James Mattis delivered a spirited pep talk to U.S. service members during a recent overseas trip to Jordan, Turkey and Ukraine; a video of the remarks circulated on social media. Speaking to troops in an informal setting, Mattis acknowledged the deep partisan tensions at home and urged personnel to “hold the line” until the nation recovers mutual respect and cohesion. He contrasted two American strengths—“the power of inspiration” and “the power of intimidation”—saying the military embodies the latter, ready to protect families, country and allies, while expressing confidence the nation will regain its inspirational power.

Mattis thanked troops for their service, said he had “flunked” retirement and praised young service members as selfless and energetic. The remarks echoed themes he used previously at West Point and were widely interpreted as a subtle rebuke of domestic turmoil following the violent white-supremacist rally in Charlottesville and debate over the administration’s handling of such events. The remarks preceded President Trump’s presidential memo directing the Defense Department to halt new enlistments by transgender individuals and to end Pentagon-funded gender reassignment surgery except for ongoing cases. That directive—announced after Trump’s earlier tweet—had reportedly surprised military leaders and drawn criticism from service members, veterans, civil-rights groups and lawmakers like Sen. John McCain, who warned against removing currently serving transgender troops solely on the basis of gender identity rather than medical and readiness standards.

Detroit’s aggressive campaign to shut off water for tens of thousands of overdue accounts has provoked sustained protest and accusations of human-rights violations. Activists staged demonstrations at Homrich, a contractor hired by the Detroit Water and Sewerage Department (DWSD) to disconnect service, temporarily blocking trucks and prompting multiple arrests for disorderly conduct. Protesters — including religious leaders and local officials — say shutoffs disproportionately harm the poor, elderly and families with children in a city with a 44% poverty rate and rising average bills now near $75 monthly, well above the national average. They point to alleged inconsistencies in enforcement, noting large commercial and state debts (a golf course owes $437,000; the state owes about $70,000) while households owing small amounts are cut off. DWSD defends the campaign as necessary to recoup roughly $175 million in unpaid bills and to limit rate increases for paying customers; it reports nearly half its accounts are delinquent and has executed thousands of residential shutoffs since April. The department announced a $1 million assistance fund and says payment plans exist, while also preparing to target delinquent commercial accounts. Activists, backed by a U.N. panel urging reconnections, vow escalating civil disobedience if shutoffs continue, and local leaders have urged federal intervention to address the crisis.

A 27-year-old French-Canadian university student, Alexandre Bissonnette, was charged with six counts of first-degree murder and five counts of attempted murder after a deadly shooting at the Centre Culturel Islamique de Québec during evening prayers that left six men dead and at least 19 wounded. Bissonnette, who made a brief, silent court appearance in restraints and did not enter a plea, was arrested after calling 911 and surrendering to police near Île d’Orléans. Authorities treated him as the lone suspect; another man initially detained was later identified as a witness and released. Investigators have not publicly stated a motive, but friends, activists and social media evidence linked Bissonnette to far-right, nationalist views, including support for France’s Marine Le Pen and anti-multicultural positions, prompting concerns the attack was driven by anti-Muslim hatred. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Quebec Premier Philippe Couillard called the assault a terrorist act; Trudeau spoke at a vigil and reassured Canada’s Muslim community of solidarity. The victims included a butcher, a university professor and other community members; families and officials expressed grief. The shooting prompted increased security around mosques and solidarity vigils across Canada. Canadian authorities said terrorism charges could follow depending on the investigation.

The FDA approved AquAdvantage, the first genetically engineered animal cleared for human consumption, concluding after extensive scientific review that it is as safe and nutritious as conventional Atlantic salmon. Developed by AquaBounty, the salmon carries a Chinook growth-hormone gene and an ocean pout gene that together speed growth so market size is reached in about 18 months instead of three years. FDA scientists examined the company’s data and peer-reviewed studies, finding the genetic changes stable over generations, food from the fish safe for humans and animals, no undue harm to the engineered fish, and confirmation of the faster-growth claim. The agency also completed environmental assessments and determined approval would not significantly impact U.S. ecosystems, citing strict containment measures at land-based facilities in Panama and Canada and requiring production only at specified, inspected sites; initial approval does not permit U.S. breeding or rearing. The decision drew sharp criticism from food-safety activists, environmental groups, and Alaska lawmakers, who fear escapes could harm wild stocks and warn the approval may set a precedent for more GE animals. AquaBounty says its fish are sterile females and argues their product could ease pressure on wild fisheries. Retailers including Whole Foods and Trader Joe’s have pledged not to sell the fish, and critics plan to continue efforts to limit market adoption. FDA chose not to require special labeling because it found no material nutritional differences; it released guidance on voluntary GE labeling and invited public comment. Observers note initial U.S. market impact will likely be small, making the fish uncommon in stores for now.

During a March 21 speech to university students in Jerusalem, President Barack Obama was briefly interrupted by a heckler who reportedly shouted demands for the release of Jonathan Pollard, a former U.S. Navy intelligence analyst imprisoned for sharing secrets with Israel. Obama dismissed the interruption with humor, telling the audience his team had “arranged for that” because it made him “feel at home,” and quipping he wouldn’t be comfortable without “at least one heckler.” The episode drew applause and was framed as part of lively debate. Obama has previously been heckled in high-profile U.S. speeches; he has said Pollard committed “a serious crime” and there were no plans to release him.

Oscar-winning actor Sean Penn faces misdemeanor battery and vandalism charges after an October confrontation with a photographer outside a Brentwood store. Los Angeles prosecutors allege Penn kicked the photographer and broke his camera; TMZ footage shows Penn charging, striking and shouting “get out!” though the camera remains in the photographer’s hands. Penn, who lives in San Francisco, is due in Los Angeles Superior Court on March 22 and could face up to 18 months in jail if convicted. The arrest recalls past incidents: a suspended sentence 25 years ago for attacking British journalists when his then-wife Madonna was photographed, and a 1987 altercation on a film set.

Separately, the piece chronicles Penn’s intensive humanitarian work in Haiti since the 2010 earthquake. He founded J/P Haitian Relief Organization and manages a sprawling camp hosting tens of thousands, overseeing medical care, sanitation and security. The article profiles other celebrity aid efforts, local activists and the harsh realities of cholera, gangs and political instability. Penn discusses personal strains—including a costly divorce from Robin Wright and custody impacts—that partly freed him to spend extended time in Haiti, where he now says he intends to remain involved long-term.

Oklahoma Gov. Mary Fallin signed Senate Bill 1023, preventing cities and counties from setting local minimum wages, sick-day rules or vacation requirements. Supporters say the ban protects the state’s economy and small businesses from increased labor costs that could drive jobs away, citing concerns that mandated local raises would raise consumer prices and harm employment. Fallin and proponents pointed to analyses suggesting higher minimum wages could cost jobs and argued many minimum-wage workers are part-time students. 

Critics contend the law targets an Oklahoma City grassroots effort to put a $10.10 minimum-wage question to voters; organizers had been gathering signatures for a local initiative to raise the city’s wage above the federal $7.25 level. Attorney David Slane, the petition author and spokesman, called the law an affront to voters’ rights and said the group will pursue alternative options, including a statewide petition or legal challenge. Opponents, including some lawmakers, called the measure morally wrong given that many low-wage workers are adults supporting families. Economic research cited by opponents disputes the student-worker stereotype, noting most affected workers are over 20, many full-time and with children.

Former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani removed himself from consideration for a role in President-elect Donald Trump’s incoming administration, most notably the secretary of state post, the transition team announced. Trump praised Giuliani as “extraordinarily talented and patriotic” and a close friend whose campaign dedication and counsel he values, saying he could be called on for advice or a future role. The team said Giuliani withdrew on Nov. 29, though he remained discussed internally for weeks afterward.

Giuliani publicly campaigned for secretary of state, but told Fox News he stepped aside because the process had become “confusing” and burdensome for Trump; he judged he could be more effective as an outside adviser and wanted to return to his private legal and consulting work. He emphasized he had pursued only the secretary of state role and was not interested in other cabinet posts. Allies framed the withdrawal as a gracious choice by a loyal supporter to avoid distracting the transition.

Rex Tillerson, ExxonMobil’s CEO, emerged as the leading contender for secretary of state, with Mitt Romney, Sen. Bob Corker, retired Adm. James Stavridis, John Bolton and former Ford CEO Alan Mulally also under consideration. Transition aides said Giuliani’s self-promotion and controversial media appearances harmed his prospects; some aides also worried he lacked the stamina for the job’s demands. Questions about his paid work for foreign governments and potential conflicts were reportedly under legal review, complicating his candidacy despite assertions from Trump’s team that he had been vetted.

Giuliani’s withdrawal leaves him returning to private-sector work while remaining a supporter and informal adviser to Trump; transition officials indicated they respected his decision. Some allies expressed disappointment at his not being chosen but expect he will continue to counsel the president-elect in various capacities.

A World Health Organization and U.S. National Cancer Institute study warns smoking imposes massive health and economic burdens worldwide, costing over $1 trillion annually while causing about 6 million deaths a year now and projecting roughly 8 million by 2030 — a one-third increase. More than 80% of those deaths will occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where about 80% of smokers live. Although global smoking prevalence is falling, the absolute number of smokers is rising. The peer-reviewed, 688-page report emphasizes tobacco use as the leading preventable cause of death and finds the economic losses from health care and lost productivity far exceed global tobacco tax revenues (about $269 billion in 2013–2014). Governments currently spend under $1 billion on tobacco control and have largely underused effective, low-cost measures: higher tobacco taxes and prices, comprehensive smoke-free laws, bans on tobacco marketing, and prominent pictorial health warnings. Taxes could also fund mass media campaigns and cessation services. Tobacco regulation faces legal and trade tensions as countries consider plain packaging, which standardizes cigarette packs and removes branding. Australia’s pioneering plain-pack law, introduced in 2011, faced multiple international challenges. Philip Morris Asia’s investor-state arbitration against Australia was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, a decision welcomed by public health advocates as protecting a proven policy that has contributed to falling smoking rates in Australia and may encourage other nations. Australia still faces a separate World Trade Organization complaint, but its government remains committed to defending plain packaging as a legitimate public-health measure.

This document contains two distinct pieces: a brief note about web archiving efforts by the Internet Archive and a longer report on feline behavior based on the work of British biologist John Bradshaw.

The Internet Archive segment explains that targeted crawls capture webpages as they are created and also archive the pages those new pages reference. The aim is to preserve the exact versions that existed when an author linked to them, so that when referenced pages change or disappear, people can still access the original context. The Archive hopes archived links will be used in place of broken links or as companion links so readers can see what the page’s author intended. The ultimate goal stated is to eliminate broken links across the web by crawling supported “No More 404” sites.

The larger portion summarizes Bradshaw’s insights into why domestic cats greet humans with tail-up postures and rubbing behavior. Bradshaw, director of the Anthrozoology Institute at the University of Bristol and author of Cat Sense, explains that cats use the tail-up/rub sequence as a friendly greeting among themselves—typically a smaller cat signaling deference and friendship to a larger one, such as a kitten to its mother. When cats became domesticated 5,000–10,000 years ago, they adapted this ritual to communicate affection to people. Bradshaw emphasizes that owners should let cats initiate interactions; cats often need to perform the tail-up/rub ritual before feeling comfortable, and approaches initiated by people can shorten interactions. He also notes that purring does more than express contentment: it can be an attention-seeking or reassurance signal rooted in kitten behavior to keep a mother still while nursing. Finally, Bradshaw lists three feline signs of affection—tail-up/rubbing, resting in contact, and mutual grooming—and notes a cat need only show one to indicate fondness. The summary points readers to Bradshaw’s book and its website for more.

Researchers isolated 3,900 Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeasts from Sauvignon Blanc grapes, forests, and spontaneous ferments across six New Zealand wine regions. Microsatellite genotyping identified 295 distinct genotypes and region-specific sub-populations. The study selected representative genotypes from each region—prioritizing common alleles so that on average at least 60% of each regional population’s common alleles were represented—to test whether genetic differences in native yeasts influence wine chemistry.

Using sterilized, homogenized Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc juice, the team fermented single genotypes (six per region) and regional co-inoculations (all six genotypes together), in triplicate across three batches, yielding 112 successful single-genotype ferments after excluding anomalous fermentations. They quantified 39 volatile compounds and standard wine parameters by GC-MS and FTIR. Multivariate analyses (PERMANOVA and constrained correspondence analysis) showed that the region of yeast origin significantly affected volatile profiles: geographic origin explained roughly 10–13% of variation, rising to nearly 20% when only genotypes with clear regional ancestry were considered. Pairwise comparisons highlighted Nelson yeasts as most chemically distinct, while Awatere and Wairau were least distinct. Individual ANOVAs indicated 29 of 39 compounds varied by region; key drivers included esters like ethyl isobutyrate, ethyl-2-methyl butanoate, ethyl butanoate, and β-damascenone, contributing fruity and floral notes.

Genetic distance based on microsatellites correlated significantly with chemical profile distance, supporting a genetic basis for the observed phenotypic differences. Co-fermentation of regional genotypes produced profiles distinct from simple blends of single-genotype wines, but co-ferments tended to weaken regional signals, and blending more strongly eroded regional signatures. Overall, the study provides experimental evidence that regional yeast populations contribute a measurable, though modest, component to wine “terroir” by shaping volatile chemistry during fermentation.

Steve Jobs’ resignation as Apple’s CEO marks a formal end to his daily leadership but may not radically alter Apple’s immediate direction. Jobs will remain chairman of the board, and Tim Cook—who had been running day-to-day operations since January during Jobs’ medical leave—has been promoted to CEO and added to the board. The board expanded from seven to eight members; other directors include Andrea Jung, Arthur Levinson, William Campbell, Millard Drexler, Al Gore and Ronald Sugar.

Apple’s operational transition had been gradual: Jobs continued to influence major decisions and public appearances this year (he unveiled the iPad 2), and many upcoming products—iPhone 5, iPad 3 and future devices—were already in development under Jobs’ influence. Observers argue the timing of his resignation was strategic: Apple was at a commercial high with record earnings and poised to ship the next iPhone, giving Cook space to lead without being overshadowed by Jobs’ immediate presence.

Analysts see competing internal tendencies shaping Apple’s future. Tim Cook’s strengths lie in supply-chain mastery and operational control, turning Apple into a highly efficient, cash-rich enterprise. Another strand emphasizes Apple’s marketing prowess and product cadence; a third, quieter strand comprises deeper innovation and design leadership. Concerns remain about whether Apple will continue to produce breakthrough “next” products without Jobs’ visionary role, or lean more heavily on control, litigation and incremental product evolution. The company’s path forward will depend on which faction—operations, marketing, or innovation—asserts dominance.

After Twitter announced plans to overhaul its verification system, it removed the blue check marks from several prominent far‑right figures, triggering dramatic reactions. Some users, such as Tim “Baked Alaska” Gionet, were permanently banned; Gionet responded by livestreaming a public meltdown. Laura Loomer, a controversial right‑wing activist and former Project Veritas employee known for provocative stunts, reacted particularly angrily to losing verification, comparing her treatment to the beginnings of the Holocaust — a claim made even after a verified user pointed out the ludicrousness of equating social‑media policy with genocide. Although Twitter stripped verification from white‑supremacist figures like Richard Spencer and Jason Kessler, they remain active on the platform, underscoring a broader criticism: Twitter’s moves often aim to avoid appearing to endorse extremists without actually barring them, a half‑measure that does not fully address harassment and radicalization enabled by the service.

Separately, Loomer was banned from ride‑sharing services Uber and Lyft after a daylong anti‑Muslim tweetstorm blaming all Muslims for a New York terror attack carried out by a former Uber driver. She urged creation of a non‑Muslim ride service and posted inflammatory photos, prompting swift backlash, celebrity criticism, and the companies’ deactivation of her accounts; Loomer said she would pursue legal action. Critics label her an alt‑right provocateur rather than a legitimate journalist.

McDonald’s has withdrawn and apologized for a U.K. television advertisement that many viewers said exploited childhood bereavement. The 90-second spot produced by Leo Burnett followed a young boy asking his mother about his late father and wondering what they had in common; at the end they discover a shared favorite McDonald’s menu item, the Filet-o-Fish. After the ad began airing on May 12, it prompted widespread criticism on social media and nearly 100 complaints to the Advertising Standards Authority. Viewers described the commercial as “shameful,” “cynical,” and “vulgar,” arguing it trivialized grief by suggesting a fast-food meal could soothe profound loss.

Bereavement charity Grief Encounter said it received “countless calls” from parents whose bereaved children were distressed by the advert. Its founder, Dr. Shelley Gilbert, called the spot insensitive and inappropriate, arguing that a brand should not imply a meal can cure emotional pain or substitute for meaningful remembrance practices. Several bereaved parents reported their children were upset or confused, and critics noted the ad’s timing—close to Father’s Day—made it especially ill-judged. McDonald’s issued a public apology, saying causing upset was never the intention and that the campaign aimed to reflect the brand’s role in everyday life “in good and difficult times.” The company announced it would remove the advert from all media within the week, review its creative process, and is reviewing customer feedback to prevent similar missteps. The ASA said it would assess complaints to determine whether an investigation was warranted.

Joseph P. Kennedy III’s announcement that he will leave his Middlesex County district attorney’s office to run for Barney Frank’s congressional seat has reignited hopes of a Kennedy return to national politics and bolstering Massachusetts Democrats. The move ends a period in which no Kennedys have held elected federal office for the first time since 1947, following a string of family setbacks and retirements. Supporters praise Kennedy’s pedigree—Stanford, Harvard Law, Peace Corps service—and his prosecutorial experience, including a recent shift from Cape Cod to Middlesex County to build a stronger political base. Some family loyalists, however, preferred he gain a longer record in the courts, perhaps as a district attorney, before seeking Congress. The campaign is framed not just as a dynastic comeback but as a strategic chance for Democrats to reclaim Massachusetts’ deep-blue identity after the shock of Scott Brown’s 2010 Senate victory. A youthful, telegenic Kennedy could help energize Democratic voters and complement other rising liberals like Elizabeth Warren, offering the party a potential route to redemption in the Bay State.

This satirical roundup lists recent “losers” — individuals, products, and institutions that have fallen from influence or relevance. Highlights include Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid al-Maktoum mocked for seeking funds from Abu Dhabi; Google Buzz, an unwanted social add-on; and Leonid Tyagachev, whose Russian Olympic results disappointed. Obsolete tech like standalone TomTom GPS units and Palm’s Pre phone are sidelined by smartphones. The Space Shuttle is dismissed as passé compared with rockets. Deposed leaders Kurmanbek Bakiyev, Mamadou Tandja, and Manuel Zelaya are noted for losing power and exile or arrest. Cultural touchstones dim: Rue McClanahan is eclipsed by Betty White, Gourmet magazine folded after 68 years, and the U.S. Metric Association’s president is joked about as irrelevant. The tone is mocking and humorous.

Acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) is a rare but severe, polio-like neurological condition that has re-emerged in the United States, primarily affecting children. Between January and August 2016, the CDC confirmed 50 cases across 24 states—more than double the total for all of 2015—and signals have mirrored the 2014 spike when 120 cases clustered in many states. AFM produces sudden limb weakness, facial droop, difficulty swallowing or breathing, urinary retention and spinal gray-matter lesions visible on MRI; many patients report a preceding febrile or respiratory illness. Severe cases can require ventilator support and long, often incomplete recoveries: in 2014 most children improved partially but only a few fully recovered.

The underlying cause remains unproven. AFM has been temporally associated with enteroviruses—particularly enterovirus D68 (EV‑D68)—and other viruses such as adenoviruses and West Nile virus, but direct causation has not been established. Respiratory samples from some AFM patients have tested positive for EV‑D68 and other enteroviruses, and animal models infecting mice with EV‑D68 have produced similar paralysis and suggest IVIG may offer protection; however, CDC testing of spinal fluid in many cases has not consistently identified a pathogen.

No specific, proven therapy exists beyond supportive care and intensive rehabilitation (physical, occupational and speech therapy); occasional experimental use of IVIG or other agents has been reported. Public-health officials urge vigilance, timely reporting of cases, specimen submission for testing, and preventive measures—hand washing, avoiding sick contacts, disinfecting surfaces and staying current on vaccinations—to reduce viral spread while investigations continue. Families affected emphasize frustration at the unknowns and the devastating, long-term impact on children’s lives.

Researchers and startups pursuing diagnostics from a single drop of blood face significant biological and practical challenges, despite intense interest in less invasive "lab on a chip" technologies. Many patients dislike conventional venous draws, and clinics in low-resource settings need simple, noninvasive testing options, which has driven investment and innovation. However, an experiment at Rice 360° Institute for Global Health measured basic parameters—hemoglobin and platelet counts—in seven fingerprick drops taken from each of 10 people and found substantial variability among drops from the same individual. Authors Meaghan M. Bond and Rebecca R. Richards-Kortum warned in The American Journal of Clinical Pathology that relying on a single fingerprick sample can be misleading; in their work they found averaging six to nine drops was required to approach the accuracy of standard venous draws. The findings underscore why high-stakes claims about single-drop diagnostics attract scrutiny: Theranos, which promised many tests from just a few drops, has recently faced regulatory action and public controversy. Other companies, such as Genalyte, are pursuing single-drop approaches more cautiously, backing work with peer-reviewed studies and initially targeting specific areas like autoimmune diseases (lupus and rheumatoid arthritis) rather than broad-spectrum screening. Overall, the science suggests that variability in capillary samples must be addressed if single-drop diagnostics are to match conventional lab accuracy.

A man identified as Gul Ahmed (about 25) went on a deadly rampage in Charsadda district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, killing 10 members of his extended family in a pre-dawn attack after a long-running dispute over a rejected marriage proposal to his cousin. Police say Gul and accomplices burst into the home of his uncle, Hazrat Jamal, around 3:00 a.m., firing an AK-47 and killing Jamal, his wife, four sons (ages include 28, 25, 15, 10) and four daughters — among them Naveeda (26), the woman Gul had sought to marry. Two children and four women were among the dead. Villagers took the bodies to the local hospital for autopsy, prompting protests when male doctors performed examinations of female victims due to lack of female staff. Authorities say Gul had earlier, in November 2014, murdered his own parents and two brothers — reportedly over the same marriage dispute or a dowry disagreement — and was a proclaimed offender who was never arrested. Police have launched raids and tightened security at nearby entry points as Gul remains at large. The killings spotlight violent responses to arranged-marriage and dowry conflicts in the region.

A rare but serious bacterial infection linked to dogs and cats left Wisconsin man Greg Manteufel with life-altering injuries after what doctors believe began as a routine interaction with a dog. In late June 2018 Greg became suddenly ill, developing symptoms that progressed rapidly to septic shock. Blood tests identified the cause as Capnocytophaga canimorsus, a bacterium commonly found in the mouths of healthy dogs (up to about 60–74%) and cats (roughly 17–57%). While the bacteria are normal in animals and rarely cause human disease, in uncommon cases they can invade people through bites, scratches, or even close contact such as a lick, and cause severe infections.

Capnocytophaga infections most often affect tissues connected to the mouth and throat—periodontal disease, respiratory tract and eye infections—but can also enter the bloodstream. When bacteremia occurs it can lead to septicemia, endocarditis, abscesses, and inflammation of eyes, face, lymph nodes or the brain’s membranes. Sepsis can trigger widespread inflammation, dangerously low blood pressure, and reduced blood flow to extremities; in Greg’s case this led to tissue death in his limbs. Within days doctors amputated both feet and, after further damage, performed amputations through both knees. Parts of his hands were also removed and reconstructive surgery is planned for extensive facial and nasal damage. His wife and family report Greg remains mentally strong and grateful to be alive, taking recovery one day at a time.

Clinicians stress such outcomes are extremely rare—infectious disease specialists note that more than 99% of people with dogs will never experience this—but people with weakened immune systems or other risk factors should consult their doctors about safe pet interactions. Preventive guidance emphasizes avoiding bites and prompt wound care; most contact with pets does not lead to infection. The family has launched a GoFundMe to help cover prolonged medical care, surgeries, prosthetics and support during Greg’s long recovery.

Kevin Curran, a veteran television comedy writer and producer, died at his Los Angeles home after a long illness. He was 59. A Harvard College graduate and former Harvard Lampoon editor, Curran met future Simpsons showrunner Al Jean at school. He joined The Simpsons staff in 2001 and served most recently as co-executive producer, writing notable episodes including “I’m Spelling as Fast as I Can,” “Don’t Fear the Roofer,” and co-conceiving and co-writing the 2002 “Treehouse of Horror” segment “The Island of Dr. Hibbert.” During his Simpsons tenure he shared three Emmy Awards and earned numerous nominations. Earlier in his career Curran won three consecutive Emmys (1985–87) as part of the writing team on Late Night With David Letterman. In the 1990s he worked on Married...With Children, voiced the family dog Buck on that show in many episodes, and was executive producer of the WB’s Unhappily Ever After alongside creator Ron Leavitt. His other credits include the short-lived ABC comedy The Good Life. Curran is survived by a son and daughter with his former partner, author Helen Fielding. Colleagues and friends posted tributes on social media, with Al Jean remembering him as brilliant, hilarious and big-hearted. Cynthia Littleton contributed to reports on his passing.

The White House’s reluctance to address the status of National Security Adviser Michael T. Flynn deepened after senior policy aide Stephen Miller, who was sent to speak for the administration on several Sunday shows, declined to say whether President Trump still has confidence in Flynn. When NBC’s Chuck Todd asked Miller directly, Miller said that was a question for the president, Vice President Mike Pence or Chief of Staff Reince Priebus and repeatedly noted the White House had not given him anything specific to say. The choice to deploy Miller — whose portfolio does not include foreign policy — appeared deliberate, allowing the administration to avoid a substantive public defense or explanation of Flynn’s actions.

Flynn’s position is imperiled by reports that he may have misled colleagues, including Pence, about his communications with Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak in the weeks before Trump’s inauguration. The FBI has been reported to be investigating those contacts, examining whether Flynn discussed U.S. sanctions and whether any actions crossed legal lines aimed at preventing private citizens from conducting foreign policy. Flynn initially denied discussing sanctions; a Washington Post report citing multiple current and former officials contradicted that, and his representative later softened Flynn’s denials, saying Flynn could not be certain the topic never came up. Since the report, the White House has largely avoided publicly backing Flynn; Trump said he was unaware of the Post story and later tweeted approval of Miller’s comments without addressing Flynn directly.

Separately, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer urged Trump to abandon his travel-ban executive order entirely, calling it ineffective for security, unconstitutional as a religious test, and harmful economically. Schumer argued that real vulnerabilities lie in visa-waiver countries where extremists could enter more easily than refugees from the seven targeted nations, and warned the policy could deter skilled immigrants and harm U.S. job growth. Meanwhile, the White House signaled it may pursue additional executive actions or appeals after a federal appeals court blocked the travel ban, with Miller vowing to explore “every single possible action” to keep the country safe.

Miami Gardens Police Chief Stephen Johnson was arrested in a Broward County undercover sting for soliciting a prostitute at a Dania Beach hotel and was immediately fired. Deputies say an escort ad on Backpage led Johnson to call and negotiate $100 for a “two-girl” encounter; when he arrived at the room he handed over cash and was arrested. Video and audio of the transaction were recorded; officers found two condoms in his pocket. Johnson, 53, bonded out on a $300 bond and apologized, attributing his poor judgment to on-the-job stress. His dismissal came amid recent controversies in Miami Gardens, including protests after a fatal officer-involved shooting and prior allegations of department misconduct. Assistant Chief Antonio Brooklen was named interim chief while city leaders stressed commitment to integrity and repairing community trust.

Roger Ebert’s review of Catherine Hardwicke’s 2011 Red Riding Hood finds the film a visually capable but thematically timid teen melodrama. Amanda Seyfried’s presence anchors the movie; her beauty and on-screen magnetism are frequently exploited, but the director’s attempts to deepen the fairy tale’s adult themes of sex and death come off weak and cautious. Hardwicke updates the story with modern touches—electronic music, contemporary styling, a dreadlocked grandmother and a proto-hippie witch—but these choices sometimes feel like pandering or sloppy design. Gary Oldman chews scenery as Father Solomon, while the computer-generated wolf lacks menace. The narrative flirts with the idea of Red as predator as well as prey and borrows from feminist retellings without fully committing, leaving girl-power imagery largely superficial. Ebert criticizes the film’s earnest tonal confusion—crossing Twilight-style teen romance with werewolf hokum—and highlights striking aerial shots even as he finds the overall execution preposterous and unconvincing.

Pope Francis capped a packed day in New York by celebrating Mass for 24,000 people at Madison Square Garden, transforming the arena into a spirited religious gathering where congregants applauded and cheered. He urged New Yorkers to care for the marginalized—immigrants, the homeless, the uninsured and forgotten elderly—and insisted God lives in cities, freeing people from anonymity and selfishness. Earlier he addressed the UN on climate change and inequality, visited the National September 11 Memorial & Museum where he laid a white rose and prayed with victims’ families, and rode through Central Park greeting tens of thousands. Events included interfaith services, meetings with workers and schoolchildren, musical performances, and warm exchanges with Cardinal Dolan and civic leaders. He left asking attendees to pray for him.

At a major evangelical conference in Nashville, Jeb Bush reignited controversy by saying, “I’m not sure we need half a billion dollars in funding for women’s health programs” while criticizing Planned Parenthood and asserting abortion should never be government-funded. The remark, intended to appeal to religious conservatives, prompted immediate Democratic backlash — including direct tweets and speeches from Hillary Clinton — and forced Bush to say he “misspoke” and to clarify his comments. His campaign then issued a corrected statement stressing the need to fully fund community health centers and rural clinics while singling out the roughly $500 million in federal funding for Planned Parenthood, which he and others argued should be redirected in light of allegations about fetal tissue sales. 

The episode follows a string of recent Bush gaffes on issues such as worker hours and Medicare, raising concerns about his unscripted style ahead of the GOP debate. Reporters also revisited his Florida gubernatorial record: Medicaid enrollment and costs rose during his tenure even as some women’s programs he championed—like the Mary Brogan Breast and Cervical Cancer Early Detection Program and related funding initiatives—drew bipartisan attention. Democrats suggested the comments could be damaging in future campaign ads.

A deadly fire swept through a state police station detention center in Valencia, Venezuela, killing 68 people, the country’s attorney general, Tarek William Saab, said. Saab said 66 of the dead were men and two were women; four prosecutors were assigned to investigate. Relatives who had gathered outside the facility seeking information clashed with police and were driven back with tear gas and riot squads, leaving many distraught and frantic to learn whether loved ones had survived. Local accounts and a nonprofit monitor, A Window to Freedom, said violence began with a disturbance—possibly an armed detainee shooting an officer—and that inmates set mattresses alight as flames spread through overcrowded cells. Rescuers reportedly had to breach a wall to free some prisoners; photos showed badly burned victims removed on stretchers. Activists and relatives criticized chronic overcrowding and poor conditions in Venezuelan jails, where detainees often remain long-term in temporary holding cells and where corrupt guards and armed groups enable weapons and drugs. Officials vowed a thorough probe, while opposition lawmakers demanded transparent information for grieving families amid wider concerns about long-running lawlessness and deadly clashes in the country’s detention facilities.

President Barack Obama honored veterans at Arlington National Cemetery on Veterans Day, laying a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknowns and speaking at the Memorial Amphitheater about the nation’s obligation to those who served. He paid tribute to generations of service members and focused on the post-9/11 generation that fought in Iraq and Afghanistan, noting this was the first Veterans Day in a decade without U.S. troops fighting in Iraq and that a decade-long Afghanistan war is winding down.
