Obama stressed that ceremonies cannot fully repay veterans’ sacrifices and urged Americans to support the more than one million service members transitioning to civilian life in coming years. He called for faster, more responsive care and benefits, specifically pushing to reduce the veterans’ claims backlog and improve treatment for those with PTSD. Later he and First Lady Michelle Obama, plus Vice President Joe Biden and his wife Jill, greeted families in Section 60, where recent war dead are buried.

A 20-month-old boy, Zymeir Perry of Allentown, died Saturday at Lehigh Valley Hospital-Cedar Crest, six days after his 19-year-old mother, Johnesha Perry, allegedly pushed him from the 52-foot-high Hamilton Street Bridge into the Lehigh River. Witnesses say she kissed him, shoved him over the railing, then jumped in herself, telling onlookers “it was her time.” Officer Joseph Ianetta and another officer pulled the child from the river about 700 yards downstream and performed CPR; Zymeir was later declared medically brain dead and life support was withdrawn. An autopsy found blunt force trauma and drowning. Johnesha Perry, initially charged with attempted homicide and other counts, was later charged with criminal homicide and remains jailed; prosecutors will provide further details Monday.

At the White House’s annual “Made in America Product Showcase,” Rep. Claudia Tenney discovered that the spoons used to serve refreshments—bearing the Oneida Ltd. brand—were made in China, highlighting a gap between the administration’s patriotic event and actual procurement. Tenney and others have long lobbied the White House to buy flatware from Sherrill Manufacturing, the Upstate New York company that remains the last American flatware maker after former Oneida Ltd. shifted production overseas. Sherrill’s president, Matt Roberts, and co-founder/CEO Greg Owens, both former Oneida executives who reopened the Sherrill plant in 2005, displayed their Liberty Tabletop stainless-steel line and Betsy Ross designs at the event. They met mixed responses: a White House hospitality staffer expressed interest and Owens said Trump privately promised in November to buy their products, but follow-up had been slow. Owens reported some progress—production up 33 percent, workforce rising from 42 to 54, expected net income over $5 million, and sizable federal orders from the Navy and State Department. Despite visits from top advisers like Wilbur Ross and Peter Navarro, Sherrill’s presence underscored tension between Made-in-America rhetoric and actual purchasing choices.

A group of nine prisoners convicted of drug offences in Indonesia faced imminent execution after receiving 72-hour notices and spending apparent final hours with relatives on Nusakambangan prison island. The group includes Australians Myuran Sukumaran and Andrew Chan, Filipina Mary Jane Veloso, four Nigerians, a Brazilian, and an Indonesian; a tenth, Frenchman Serge Atlaoui, had his execution delayed amid ongoing legal challenges. Relatives of Chan and Sukumaran were visibly distraught: Sukumaran’s sister collapsed and had to be carried, and family members described the final visit—reported to last about five hours—as “torture.” Media reported the Australians were denied their chosen spiritual advisers and were limited to Christian guides appointed by authorities, a decision condemned by families as a final indignity.

Indonesia’s government defended the executions as necessary to combat a severe domestic drugs problem, with the attorney-general stressing that judicial reviews could not overturn prior rulings and that foreigners lack standing before the Constitutional Court. Jakarta ended a moratorium on executions in 2013 and maintains some of the world’s toughest drug penalties. International appeals for clemency—from Australia, the Philippines, the United Nations, and the Council of Europe—failed to sway President Joko Widodo, and high-profile pleas, including from actors and Filipino boxer Manny Pacquiao on behalf of Veloso, were unsuccessful.

Authorities followed customary execution preparations: ambulances carrying coffins arrived at the port, heavy security cleared media, and families made last visits. Chan and Sukumaran, arrested with others in 2005 for attempting to smuggle heroin to Australia, were deemed ringleaders and sentenced to death in 2006; remaining Bali Nine members serve long prison terms. Reports indicated all nine would be executed together by firing squad, with only three of 12 shooters carrying live rounds.

New analyses of data from NASA’s Cassini spacecraft strengthen the case that Saturn’s icy moon Enceladus hosts a warm, chemically active ocean beneath its south-polar ice shell. Cassini detected tiny silica-rich particles in Saturn’s E-ring and magnetosphere that researchers trace back to plume material ejected from Enceladus. Laboratory experiments and modeling indicate those particles form only under hydrothermal conditions: hot (at least about 190–200°F) water interacting with rock on the ocean floor, dissolving silica and later precipitating uniformly small particles as hydrothermal fluids cool. The particle sizes and chemistry also imply an ocean with modest salinity (below ~4%) and alkaline pH (roughly 8.5–10.5), broadly Earth-like in key respects. Tidal heating from Saturn and other moons is likely a major heat source, but some scientists argue tidal friction alone may not suffice; ongoing water–rock chemical reactions could supply additional heat. That combination—liquid water, heat, and organic and inorganic chemicals such as methane, carbon dioxide and nitrogen—makes Enceladus one of the most promising places in the solar system to search for life, analogous to Earth’s hydrothermal-vent ecosystems. The evidence is indirect: Cassini sampled the ring and magnetospheric dust rather than directly sampling plume vents, but independent researchers find the hydrothermal interpretation plausible. Upcoming targeted Cassini flybys, including a low pass near Enceladus’ surface, should collect higher-fidelity plume data. Future missions with modern instruments or landers would be required to directly search for biosignatures and fully characterize Enceladus’s subsurface environment.

Meet the Press, long the flagship of Sunday political talk shows, is in decline under moderator David Gregory, provoking internal concern and program changes. Once dominant under Tim Russert, NBC’s program has fallen to third place behind CBS’s Face the Nation and ABC’s This Week, enduring a three-year ratings slide and record lows among the key 25–54 advertiser demographic. Gregory acknowledges the challenge and says he and new executive producer Rob Yarin are retooling the show—speeding pacing, shortening interview segments, broadening topics and adding features like “Meeting America”—to modernize the format and attract a wider audience. Competitors are also evolving: ABC’s This Week has become more magazine-like under young EP Jonathan Greenberger, while Face the Nation’s Bob Schieffer prefers continuity and minimal change. NBC reportedly commissioned outside consulting last year to assess how Gregory connects with viewers; the network later described the work as brand, not psychological, consulting. Gregory faces the lingering comparison to Russert’s legacy and controversy over past on-air incidents, but supporters argue time could favor him as veteran rivals age. Network bosses appear committed to fixing Meet the Press rather than immediately replacing its host.

Mahin Khan, an 18-year-old Arizona man indicted on terrorism and conspiracy charges, was assaulted by other inmates while jailed after his arrest, according to court records and multiple news outlets. The attack occurred on July 2 at Maricopa County’s Towers Jail, where Khan had been placed in medium-security general population after declining an offer of voluntary segregation. He sustained minor, non-life-threatening injuries, was evaluated at a hospital, and has since been moved to segregated housing at Lower Buckeye Jail. Sheriff Joe Arpaio has ordered that Khan and any future inmates charged with similar offenses be automatically placed in segregation. Khan is accused of plotting attacks on Motor Vehicle Division and other government offices in Maricopa and Pima counties between April 2015 and July 1, 2016, and the FBI alleges he sought contact with the Pakistani Taliban and individuals to obtain firearms. He pleaded not guilty on July 12 and remains held without bond; a bond hearing and further court dates are pending, with public defenders seeking to seal future proceedings to protect his right to a fair trial and his family’s safety.

Lady Gaga, born Stefani Germanotta in 1986, rose from theatrical training and early New York gigs to global superstardom by reinventing pop for the Internet age. After failed Def Jam beginnings she signed with Interscope, teamed with RedOne, and delivered breakout hits like "Just Dance," "Poker Face," and The Fame (2008). She followed with The Fame Monster, Born This Way, Artpop, Joanne, collaborations with Tony Bennett, film and TV roles, awards, and major tours. Known for provocative performance art, she debuted a drone-powered flying dress, Volantis, at her ArtRave launch for ARTPOP, blending fashion, tech, and spectacle.

Since late February, following Russian forces’ seizure of Crimea, abductions, beatings and intimidation of Ukrainian activists, journalists and minority groups have become widespread across the peninsula. Incidents include the apparent disappearance of two men seized at Simferopol station after handling a pro-Ukrainian parcel; threats that forced activist Igor Kiriushchenko to flee Sevastopol after armed militiamen raided his apartment; and the severe beating of ATR journalist Ibraim Umerov while attempting to film a seizure. Investigative journalist Sergiy Mokrushin estimates up to ten activists missing. Many perpetrators are linked to pro-Kremlin self-defense groups that incorporate former Berkut riot police and “titushkas,” reportedly adopting the same tactics used during Kyiv’s EuroMaidan. These forces now patrol streets and guard Berkut barracks, backed by Russian military presence after a March 16 referendum that led to Crimea’s transfer to Russia. The takeover has driven over 500 people, including activists and Crimean Tatars, to seek refuge elsewhere, and Ukrainian border guards report harassment. Psychologist Iryna Brunova-Kalisetska notes pro-Russian euphoria and mimicry of Maidan-style organization, but warns fear keeps many from protesting. Firsthand accounts from detained female AutoMaidan activists describe humiliations, mock executions and detention by mixed forces; they were eventually released after interrogation by Russian military, who treated them comparatively respectfully and allowed them to leave, underscoring chaos and danger for dissenters in Crimea.

Danielle Fishel, best known as Topanga from Boy Meets World, married longtime boyfriend Tim Belusko on Oct. 19 in a candlelit ceremony at Vibiana in downtown Los Angeles. The 32-year-old bride wore a strapless white-lace gown, carried a bouquet of dark purple flowers, and featured bridesmaids in midnight-blue dresses to match the autumnal color scheme. Around 200 guests attended, including Fishel’s on-screen husband Ben Savage, who she jokingly calls her “first husband.” After the ceremony, guests moved to a courtyard for cocktails. Fishel celebrated the day on Twitter, calling it “one of the most amazing days” and saying the love in the room was “palpable and overwhelming.” Shortly after photos ran in Us Weekly, Fishel faced cruel online comments about her weight. While on her honeymoon she responded strongly on Twitter, defending her 5’1″, 107-pound frame, condemning the trolls’ cruelty, and urging people to stop judging others’ appearances, ending on a defiant, humorous note about gaining weight on the trip.

To mark Princess Charlotte’s second birthday on May 2, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge released a new photo taken by Kate at Anmer Hall in April. In the image Charlotte wears a navy bow and a yellow cardigan; her parents thanked well-wishers and said they were “delighted to share” the portrait. The family will celebrate privately at home; the date follows the May Day holiday, making it easy for friends and relatives to attend. Charlotte has had a busy year: she made her first royal tour to Canada, showed off her personality at public events, joined Christmas services, and will be a bridesmaid at aunt Pippa Middleton’s wedding on May 20, with brother Prince George as page boy. Previous candid portraits by Kate have sparked strong public interest.

A class-action lawsuit filed in federal court accuses CNN, Turner Broadcasting and parent company Time Warner of systemic racial discrimination, alleging long-standing practices that limit Black employees’ pay, evaluations, promotions and job security. Brought by Celeslie Henley, a former CNN executive administrative assistant, and Ernest Colbert Jr., a long-time TBS manager, the 40-page complaint relies in part on Turner-provided data and statements from roughly 20–30 other current and former employees. It contends Black staff—especially men—receive disproportionately lower performance scores, are promoted far less often, and are terminated at higher rates than white colleagues. The suit charges written and unwritten promotion practices allow supervisors to handpick candidates subjectively, effectively excluding qualified African-Americans and keeping them out of senior, high-pay divisions such as Media Group, Legal and Strategy. Henley says she faced race-, sex- and pregnancy-based mistreatment and was fired in retaliation after complaining to HR; Colbert claims years of underpayment, missed job descriptions, denied promotions and lost performance records. The filing frames these issues as company-wide, spanning back to at least 1997, and seeks class status for Black salaried and mid-level managers nationwide. Attorney Daniel Meachum, who also represents DeWayne Walker in a separate $50 million suit, says he has compiled complaints for three years; CNN and Turner have declined comment on pending litigation.

An Australian vessel searching for Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 detected two more acoustic signals consistent with aircraft black-box pingers, offering a “great lead” in the month-long hunt. The Defence Vessel Ocean Shield, towing a U.S. pinger locator, recorded pings Tuesday at about 4:27 p.m. and 10:17 p.m. Perth time lasting roughly five-and-a-half and seven minutes; these followed two earlier acoustic events detected Saturday. Analysis by the Australasian Joint Acoustic Analysis Centre found a stable 33.331 kHz signal pulsing at 1.106-second intervals, judged unlikely to be natural and consistent with a flight data recorder. Retired Air Chief Marshal Angus Houston said the detections narrowed the search to a single 75,423 sq km zone about 2,261 km northwest of Perth, enabling tighter visual search patterns and coordinated aerial and naval assets. Teams prepared sonar buoys and are poised to deploy an autonomous underwater vehicle once location certainty improves, mindful that pinger batteries are rated for 30 days and signals appear weakening. Despite intensified efforts—dozens of aircraft and ships scouring the area—no wreckage has yet been found, leaving families desperate for definitive evidence of the aircraft’s fate.

John Wayne, the enduring Hollywood icon known as "The Duke," has survived serious health battles and remains resolutely active at 71. After losing a lung to cancer in 1964—the result of heavy smoking—and undergoing open-heart surgery this spring to replace a defective valve, Wayne has repeatedly defied expectations about his toughness and recovery. His latest surgery, performed in Boston, astonished surgeons with his resilience; the valve replacement even used a pig valve, and his voice, once threatened by arterial complications, has returned. Despite doctors’ orders to take it easy, Wayne is walking daily around his Newport Beach neighborhood, spending weekends captaining his yacht The Wild Goose, and fishing—once catching an enormous Mahi-Mahi with his son. He candidly criticizes earlier studio press releases that concealed his cancer treatment and says the truth inspired thousands of letters from fans and patients who found hope in his survival. Wayne plans to work on a new film, Beau John, a contemporary-family story that could win him another Oscar. Ever sentimental but unbowed, he admits the public’s goodwill moved him to tears and insists he’s still hungry for more life and work.

Love bombing is a grooming and control tactic in which someone overwhelms a target with excessive flattery, attention, promises of deep connection, gifts, and constant contact to gain power and compliance. Used by abusers, cult leaders, and other manipulators, it exploits victims’ need for belonging and approval. Children of narcissistic parents are especially vulnerable because they were conditioned to seek external validation, people-please, and survive emotional neglect; when they encounter emotional predators in adulthood, they can more easily be ensnared.

Love bombing is often paired with intermittent reinforcement—sporadic rewards of affection or praise amid periods of coldness, criticism, or abuse. That unpredictable pattern creates longing, instability, and a trauma bond: victims cling to rare positive moments, interpreting small kindnesses as evidence the abuser “isn’t all bad.” This dynamic amplifies attachment much like gambling fuels addictive behavior.

Three vulnerabilities common to survivors of narcissistic parenting increase susceptibility to love bombing: 1) After chronic hypercriticism, over-the-top praise disarms and mirrors longed-for acceptance, making targets reliant on external validation; immunity strategy—cultivate internal validation and surround yourself with genuinely supportive people. 2) Having been triangulated or pitted against siblings, survivors crave special attention and may tolerate later triangulation by new partners; immunity strategy—identify what makes you irreplaceable and avoid negative self-comparison. 3) Growing up emotionally alone, survivors mistake intense early flattery for deep connection; immunity strategy—distinguish between quick flattery and slowly built, reciprocal trust and consistency.

Recognizing love bombing involves noticing accelerated closeness, excessive compliments tied to requests, and contact that later flips to control. True connection develops over time through consistent, respectful behavior—not sudden performance-level devotion.

A graduation ceremony at Madison Square Garden for 884 new NYPD officers turned ugly when Mayor Bill de Blasio was met with boos, jeers and turned backs as he urged recruits to confront problems they “didn’t create.” The hostile response echoed prior incidents: officers turning their backs during the mayor’s eulogy at Detective Rafael Ramos’s funeral and other symbolic displays after the December murders of Detectives Wenjian Liu and Ramos. Those gestures, organized or encouraged by union leadership, were meant to signal distrust of the mayor but instead portrayed the department as juvenile, entitled, and unworthy of its “New York’s Finest” reputation.

The tensions followed the non-indictment of Officer Daniel Pantaleo in Eric Garner’s death and de Blasio’s public acknowledgment that his Black son is at greater risk during police encounters. After Liu and Ramos were murdered by an assailant who explicitly cited anger over police killings, the city briefly had an opportunity for unity and reflection. Instead, union president Patrick Lynch accused the mayor and protesters of having “blood on their hands,” a claim widely seen as ignorant given the shooter’s own violent history and mental state. Lynch also advocated a deliberate slowdown in enforcement; tabloid reports confirm sharp drops in summonses and arrests since the killings, reflecting both fear and possible retaliatory disengagement.

Critics argue police are a privileged, protected class who chose this dangerous work and can quit if pressures mount, whereas victims like Eric Garner had no such escape. The piece catalogs long-standing examples of police violence against marginalized New Yorkers but notes progress: stop-and-frisk has diminished and public protest has pushed the city toward accountability. Still, the NYPD’s recent public displays of contempt and self-pity risk squandering any credibility and further alienating the communities it serves.

Detroit police found 12-year-old Charlie Bothuell V alive in a basement tunnel system of his family’s Nicolet Place townhouse after a nearly two-week disappearance. Officers discovered a makeshift hiding spot—behind a barricade and a 55-gallon drum—during the fourth search warrant at the home. Charlie, who had been homeschooled and put through a strict daily exercise routine, told investigators his stepmother, Monique Dillard‑Bothuell, helped conceal him and supplied food. A PVC pipe with blood on it was seized as evidence; blood was also reportedly found in the boy’s room and on clothing, prompting investigators to initially consider homicide. Charlie was treated at Children’s Hospital and released to his biological mother after interviews with the FBI and other agencies. Police took Monique Dillard‑Bothuell into custody on an outstanding bench warrant for violating probation related to a prior guilty plea for purchasing a pistol without a permit. Child Protective Services removed two younger children, ages 4 and 10 months, from the home. The father, Charlie Bothuell IV, admits to disciplining his son but denies abuse; prosecutors are expected to seek child-abuse charges against him and possibly charges against the stepmother. Investigators noted an underground tunnel connecting units; the stepmother’s uncle, attorney Godfrey Dillard, lives nearby, but any connection remains unclear. The case remains under active investigation.

After a June 26 arrest in New York City following a string of public drunken episodes, Shia LaBeouf was spotted back in Los Angeles clutching Alcoholics Anonymous literature and soon checked into rehab, RadarOnline reports. Observers said he appeared nervous and reluctant but aware he needed help. The appearance of the AA “Big Book” highlighted a long, troubled history with alcohol: LaBeouf attended AA meetings as a child with his father, showed early promise in his career, but by 2007 and 2008 had multiple alcohol-related arrests, including for intoxicated behavior and DUI. He once celebrated 60 days sober at an AA meeting and publicly admitted to being an alcoholic in 2011 after a bar brawl, attending meetings in New York and L.A. Nonetheless, by 2012 he publicly boasted of drinking moonshine and experimenting with LSD for roles, signaling relapse. The most recent incidents included a Times Square chase of a homeless man, being arrested at a Broadway performance, and charges in NYC for harassment, disorderly conduct, and trespass after heavy margarita consumption. Separate reports recount additional disruptive behavior, such as being banned from a Los Angeles restaurant after urinating outside.

North Korean Foreign Minister Ri Yong Ho told Russia’s TASS that President Donald Trump’s UN remarks have “lit the wick of war,” warning the United States it will be made to pay “with a hail of fire.” Ri framed Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programs as a guaranteed regional deterrent—the “sword of justice”—and said North Korea will not negotiate away its weapons. His comments follow months of escalatory actions: North Korea’s multiple missile tests and a sixth nuclear test, and the U.S. response including a high-profile UN speech in which Trump threatened to “totally destroy” North Korea and dubbed Kim Jong Un “Rocket Man.” The exchange of insults has intensified with allied shows of force such as U.S. B-1B bomber flights with Japan and South Korea near the peninsula. Ri said North Korea is near its goal of achieving a balance of power with the U.S. and insisted final scores be settled by force, not words. While some U.S. officials, including Secretary of Defense Jim Mattis, still emphasize seeking a peaceful resolution, critics in Congress warn that bellicose rhetoric risks escalating toward broader conflict.

Less than three months before the Boston Marathon bombings, Tamerlan Tsarnaev filed a federal petition to change his first name to “Muaz,” honoring Emir Muaz, a slain Dagestani rebel, and reflecting a nickname reportedly given to him during a 2012 visit to the Caucasus. On the Jan. 23, 2013 form he framed the change in political terms, saying Russians had terrorized his home country and he needed to “help.” Authorities believe Tamerlan became deeply radicalized during that 2012 trip, attempting unsuccessfully to join insurgents in Dagestan and returning with a strong desire to attack the U.S. The name-change filing, YouTube activity with militant material, mosque tirades and other evidence have strengthened the view that Tamerlan was the principal radicalizing force behind the April 2013 attacks that killed three and injured more than 260. Defense lawyers for his younger brother, Dzhokhar, seek evidence that multiple FBI contacts—allegedly including requests to act as an informant—heightened Tamerlan’s paranoia and contributed to his actions. Prosecutors counter that they have no evidence the FBI solicited him as an informant. Dzhokhar, now facing capital charges, has pleaded not guilty; his lawyers argue he acted under Tamerlan’s domination and seek records on the brothers’ radicalization, surveillance, immigration files and other materials to mitigate culpability and oppose the death penalty.

Researchers at Melbourne’s Murdoch Children’s Research Institute have developed an experimental peanut-probiotic therapy that appears to provide long-term tolerance to peanut allergy in children. The treatment, called PPOIT, combines gradually increasing amounts of peanut flour with high doses of the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus taken daily for about 18 months. The probiotic is thought to modulate immune responses and create conditions that allow the immune system to become tolerant of peanut protein.

In the original clinical trial begun in 2013, 28–48 allergic children received either the probiotic-plus-peanut regimen or placebo; by the end of treatment 82 percent of those given PPOIT could eat peanuts without allergic reactions, compared with a small fraction of the placebo group. A follow-up assessment up to four years after treatment found that approximately 80 percent of children who had achieved initial tolerance were still eating peanuts freely and showed no signs of allergic reaction; many passed formal challenge tests confirming sustained tolerance. Lead researcher Professor Mimi Tang reported that participating children have been able to resume normal diets and social activities with markedly reduced anxiety.

Peanut allergy affects around 3 percent of infants and is a leading cause of anaphylaxis in young children. The team views these results as evidence that long-term tolerance, not just temporary desensitisation, is an attainable treatment goal for food allergies. The institute plans to pursue commercialisation with venture capital partners, hoping a shelf product could be available within about five years pending larger trials and regulatory steps.

Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel failed to secure an outright second term, falling short of the required 50% and forcing a runoff against Cook County Commissioner Jesus “Chuy” Garcia on April 7. With roughly 98–99% of precincts reported, Emanuel received about 45% while Garcia garnered roughly 34%; businessman Willie Wilson and Ald. Bob Fioretti trailed with single-digit shares. Emanuel vastly outraised opponents—raising more than $13–16 million and deploying thousands of TV ads and a high-profile endorsement and visit from President Barack Obama—yet could not overcome voter discontent over school closings, teacher conflicts, and crime. Garcia, a progressive who entered the race late and had far fewer funds, capitalized on grassroots support, endorsements from the Chicago Teachers Union, and appeals to neighborhoods he argued Emanuel had neglected, casting the mayor as aligned with wealthy interests. Low turnout and pockets of strong Hispanic and progressive support propelled Garcia to win multiple wards. The runoff narrows the choice to Emanuel versus Garcia and shifts campaign dynamics: Emanuel retains a fundraising edge but now must confront Garcia one-on-one while Garcia seeks to unite anti-Emanuel voters and expand his coalition.

Nancy Gordeuk, founder and principal of TNT Academy in Stone Mountain, Georgia, was fired by the school’s board after a racially charged remark at a recent graduation went viral. During the ceremony she mistakenly dismissed attendees before the valedictorian spoke and, amid commotion, said, “Look who’s leaving, all the black people.” Video circulated widely and prompted outrage. In an email apology she called the remark “racist,” said her emotions got the best of her, and asked for forgiveness. The board’s dismissal letter cited “recent events” and pledged continued support for graduates and commitment to the school’s educational services. Her son faced separate social media controversy amid the fallout.

For over three years, Lauriann Bartell has been in a coma after losing oxygen to her brain during emergency surgery for a bleeding ulcer. Her husband Mike has been her full-time caregiver while also caring for their six children; older children help when possible, but the family faces mounting medical bills and risk losing their home. A GoFundMe was created to ease financial strain and share their story. On October 20, Taylor Swift donated $15,500—signed “Love, Taylor, Meredith and Olivia Swift”—to the campaign, which boosted visibility and inspired further donations. By that report the fund had raised about $26,000 of a $40,000 goal. The family and organizers appreciate prayers, shares, and support.

A New York woman is asking a Connecticut jury to hold her then-8-year-old nephew legally responsible for injuries she says he caused by leaping into her arms at his birthday party four years ago. Jennifer Connell, a 54-year-old Manhattan human-resources manager who has no children, sued Sean Tarala of Westport after the March 18, 2011 incident at the Tarala family home. Connell testified that Sean, who had just received his first two-wheeler and was riding it excitedly, saw her and shouted “Auntie Jen, Auntie Jen,” dropped the bike, ran at her and “flew” into her arms. The impact, she says, made them tumble to the ground and left her with a broken wrist and ongoing difficulties. Although she did not complain at the time because it was his birthday, Connell describes subsequent life disruption: living in a Manhattan third-floor walk-up has been harder, everyday tasks and social activities such as holding a hors d’oeuvre plate at a party are more difficult, and her quality of life has been affected. She is seeking $127,000 in damages and asks a six-member Superior Court jury in Bridgeport to find the boy liable; the lawsuit argues that “a reasonable eight years old under those circumstances would know or should have known” that a forceful greeting could cause such harm. The boy, now 12, appeared in court with his father; his mother died last year. Connell emphasized she loves Sean but believes he should be accountable for what she calls negligence and carelessness that resulted in her injuries, losses and harms.

At Mexico City’s televised presidential debate, a brief visual moment overshadowed policy discussion: model and former Playboy playmate Julia Orayen, serving as an edecan (a traditional event hostess), walked onstage in a tight white dress with a plunging neckline to present cards assigning speaking order. Her 24-second appearance provoked gasps, whistles and widespread Twitter attention; journalists and viewers debated whether she had “stolen the show.” The Federal Electoral Institute (IFE) said an independent production company hired Orayen and apologized for the “production error” and distracting attire. IFE councilors said they had requested sober dress but did not identify the producer; the hired TV producer defended the choice, saying Orayen was chosen for her height relative to other applicants and that the dress was her selection. Some candidates and commentators criticized the moment as inappropriate for a serious debate and as reflecting a macho stereotype in Mexican public life. The incident sparked morning-show discussions and prompted vows to avoid similar distractions at the second debate scheduled for June 10.

Widespread Arab protests sparked forceful crackdowns across the region as governments sought to prevent uprisings like those in Tunisia and Egypt from spreading. Libya faced the bloodiest repression: security forces, including snipers and alleged foreign mercenaries, fired on funeral marches in Benghazi, killing many and prompting international condemnation and an Internet blackout. Yemen saw violent clashes in Sanaa between protesters and government supporters, leaving several wounded and at least one dead. Algeria’s police used clubs to disperse demonstrators, while Bahrain briefly withdrew troops from Pearl Square after a deadly assault, though distrust remained. Egypt and Tunisia took tentative reform steps. Protests reflected anger over repression, corruption, unemployment and long-ruling authorities, with governments increasingly resorting to violence to retain control.

Ursula K. Le Guin, a towering figure in speculative fiction, died at 88, prompting a wide outpouring of tributes from fellow writers, public figures, publishers and readers. Over her prolific career she produced more than 20 novels, dozens of poems and essays, over 100 short stories, numerous children’s books and translations. Her work, translated into over 40 languages and selling millions of copies worldwide, blended fantasy and science fiction with literary ambition and pronounced feminist and humanistic concerns. Le Guin won multiple Hugo and Nebula Awards as well as the National Book Awards’ Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters.

Colleagues and admirers emphasized how deeply she influenced contemporary writers and the genre itself. Stephen King called her “a literary icon,” while N. K. Jemisin credited Le Guin as “one of the reasons” she became a writer, noting how Le Guin’s short story “The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas” echoed through Jemisin’s own Broken Earth trilogy. Neil Gaiman, who once presented her with a lifetime achievement award, described her work as “written on my soul” and mourned her as a “deepest and smartest” writer and a “glorious funny prickly person.” Other voices—from politicians like Sen. Ron Wyden to science communicators such as Hank Green—expressed grief and admiration, urging people to read her books and listen to her recent recordings.

Tributes highlighted Le Guin’s role in expanding what fantasy and science fiction could achieve: serious social thought rendered through myth and metaphor, and inclusive worlds populated by diverse characters. Many noted her insistence on literature’s humanizing potential, recalling her explanation that speculative fiction could make the future more livable and humane. Her death leaves a significant void in imaginative literature, but her influence endures through the countless writers and readers shaped by her work.

Egypt held the final phase of its first parliamentary elections since Hosni Mubarak’s ouster as prosecutors resumed their high-profile trial of the former president. Voting in nine governorates — including Sinai and Brotherhood strongholds in the Delta — could cement gains by Islamist parties, especially the Muslim Brotherhood’s Freedom and Justice Party, which had captured a large share of seats in earlier rounds. Analysts said the third phase was likely to underline Islamist control but might not dramatically alter Parliament’s overall character; estimates varied on whether the Brotherhood could secure an outright majority. The vote intensifies an emerging power struggle between the elected assembly and the ruling military council, which insists it will retain key executive powers until presidential elections are held. Economic fallout from the unrest has hit tourism, foreign reserves and the stock market. In Cairo, prosecutors portrayed Mubarak as a “tyrant” who engineered a plan to install his son Gamal, accusing him of enabling Interior Ministry violence that led to hundreds of deaths during the 18-day uprising. Mubarak, who has pleaded not guilty, and his sons face corruption and complicity-in-killing charges; the prosecution urged the court to impose the harshest penalties as testimony continued. Demonstrators plan renewed protests on the revolution’s anniversary.

A 51-year-old Orange County woman was rescued by helicopter after slipping and becoming stranded on a 50-foot steep slope behind her Silverado Canyon home while trying to retrieve her adopted kitten. Around 8 a.m., she climbed the hill off Kitterman Drive; while descending she slid, injured her ankle and suffered scrapes, unable to climb up or down. Neighbors called 911 after hearing her calls for help. An urban search-and-rescue firefighter rigged a harness and a firefighter rappelled from an Orange County Fire Authority helicopter to hoist both the rescuer and the woman to safety. Paramedics evaluated her; she declined hospitalization and was driven home. The kitten descended safely on its own. Authorities advised leaving food and waiting, as cats typically come down by themselves.

The New York Federal Reserve may have known as early as August 2007 that London Interbank Offered Rate (Libor) submissions were flawed. Barclays told the Fed it had raised concerns then and engaged U.S. officials repeatedly through October 2008. The Fed says market monitoring after the crisis produced anecdotal reports and that in spring 2008, following Bear Stearns’ failure, it queried Barclays and later shared reform suggestions with British authorities. Congressional leaders have sought transcripts and briefings to determine what U.S. regulators knew and whether they acted sufficiently amid crisis firefighting. Barclays paid $453 million to U.K. and U.S. authorities after admitting manipulation; its top executives resigned. Investigations have widened to more than a dozen global banks. Critics say regulators, including the New York Fed, could have pushed harder or embedded staff in the Libor process to verify submissions. The episode exposed unclear regulatory responsibility over benchmark-rate integrity and prompted calls for systemic reform.

For six years Turkish police searched for Kenan Oner’s missing parents before unearthing their dismembered remains this April in a garden behind the family home in Iznik, Bursa province. Oner, 56, a former bank manager, was arrested at his apartment after officers executed a warrant tied to a separate forgery conviction. Found calmly sitting in the dark, he asked the officers, “Did you dig the garden?” and was handcuffed. Investigators now also suspect Oner of killing his wife, who vanished in 2005; police believe her remains may have been concealed within the apartment’s walls. Oner has declined to comment on the murder allegations.

The case has riveted Turkish media and the public, eliciting comparisons to the film Seven for its grisly details. Authorities describe Oner as meticulous, organized and educated, noting he kept extensive records—thousands of documents and hourly movement notes—including a hand-drawn map marking an “X” in his parents’ garden and entries such as “I dug my dad’s garden, I am very tired.” Police say his primary motive appears financial: a bitter inheritance dispute with his parents and siblings. The couple reportedly held over $2 million in assets and had refused to give Oner his share.

Oner’s criminal history is complex. In the 1980s he fled to France amid political turmoil and was later convicted there for killing a Turkish acquaintance for money, stealing identity documents and returning to Turkey. He received a life sentence in 1998 but was paroled about seven years later. Suspicion after his parents’ disappearance lingered but lacked bodies until investigators discovered forensic evidence linking the remains to them. A forgery conviction—Oner allegedly withdrew $150,000 using his mother’s forged signature—triggered renewed searches that ultimately produced the bodies. Facing potential life imprisonment in a country without capital punishment, Oner now awaits trial amid intensive, sensational media coverage.

Manti Te’o’s widely told story of playing through the grief of losing a girlfriend to leukemia unraveled when investigators revealed the girlfriend, “Lennay Kekua,” never existed. Notre Dame and Te’o say he was the victim of an elaborate online hoax, having developed an emotional relationship by phone and internet and believing she died in September—the same day his grandmother actually passed. The tale had propelled Te’o into national sympathy and helped fuel his Heisman Trophy runner-up finish. Deadspin’s reporting found no records of Kekua at Stanford, no death certificate, and traced the woman whose photo was used; she had never met Te’o. Questions persist: why Te’o sometimes described in-person meetings with Kekua, why he referenced losing a girlfriend after reportedly receiving calls that she was alive, and whether he or others embellished the story. Notre Dame said Te’o learned the truth Dec. 6 and informed coaches Dec. 26; he has largely declined public questioning. Media critics faulted journalists for failing to verify the narrative, while the NCAA said it was monitoring developments as doubts and scrutiny continued.

An EgyptAir domestic flight, MS181 from Alexandria to Cairo, was hijacked on 29 March after takeoff and forced to divert to Larnaca, Cyprus. The lone hijacker claimed to be wearing a suicide explosive belt; Cypriot authorities later told airline officials the device was fake. After a tense morning of negotiations, most passengers were released and the hijacker surrendered; no one was injured. Video showed a man identified by Cypriot officials as Seif Eldin Mustafa leaving the plane with hands raised, and other passengers and at least one crew member escaping, including a crewman who exited via a cockpit window.

Reports about the hijacker’s motives conflicted: some accounts said he wanted to contact an estranged Cypriot wife and hand her an envelope, while others said he demanded the release of female prisoners in Egypt. Cypriot President Nicos Anastasiades suggested the incident was not terrorism-related, quipping that “always there is a woman involved.” A four‑page Arabic letter was reportedly handed over on landing; a woman thought to be his wife later arrived at the airport. Official statements varied on the hijacker’s identity, and confusion persisted during early reporting.

The flight carried about 56 passengers and six crew (initial counts varied); among passengers were 26 foreigners from several countries including the US, UK, Netherlands, Belgium, France, Italy, Greece and Syria. Larnaca airport was closed temporarily and flights were diverted.

The incident renewed concerns about Egyptian airport security—already under scrutiny since the October suicide bombing of Metrojet Flight 9268—highlighting how a passenger described as “mentally unstable” could pass through screening with a convincing fake device and how easily bluff threats can disrupt aviation and further damage Egypt’s fragile tourism industry.

Ari Mahler, a Jewish registered nurse at Allegheny General Hospital, publicly recounted treating Robert Bowers after the Oct. 27 Tree of Life synagogue massacre, where 11 worshippers were killed. Mahler, whose father is Rabbi Mark Joel Mahler, wrote on Facebook that Bowers, who yelled “kill all the Jews” as he was brought in, thanked him for saving his life and for showing kindness. Mahler did not disclose his Jewish identity to Bowers and said he treated the suspect the same as any patient, guided by compassion and professional duty.

Mahler described looking into Bowers’ eyes and seeing confusion rather than “evil,” characterizing him as lonely, easily influenced by propaganda, and craving attention. He suggested Bowers was manipulable by those with platforms who exploit fear. After the encounter, Mahler broke down and later met with Allegheny General Hospital president Dr. Jeff Cohen—also Jewish and a Tree of Life congregant—who praised Mahler and other staff who set aside personal feelings to care for the suspect. Cohen described Bowers as “lost,” not the “face of the devil,” and said the immediate caregivers honored their professional mission despite the emotional strain.

In his post, Mahler recounted lifelong experiences with anti-Semitism—swastikas, hateful notes, and bullying—and said the shooting did not surprise him given current climate. He explained he often downplayed his Jewishness to ease social friction. Mahler framed his decision to show empathy as a way to honor the victims and counter hatred, ending with an appeal to love as the meaningful response to evil. His account underscores the tensions between personal trauma, professional ethics, and the enduring need for compassion after targeted violence.

This collection of articles and reader responses explores why some people — including Czech supermodel Karolina Kurkova — appear to have no visible belly button. Kurkova’s smooth navel drew attention after a Victoria’s Secret runway appearance, prompting speculation about whether it’s a natural anomaly, the result of infancy surgery, or cosmetic alteration. Her representative later confirmed she had an operation as an infant; surgeons and commentators suggest an umbilical hernia or other congenital abdominal condition (such as gastroschisis) is the likely cause. Such conditions often require early surgery that can change the navel’s appearance, sometimes leaving a scar or smooth indentation instead of a typical “innie” or “outie.” Alternative explanations include rare birthing practices (lotus births where the cord is left to drop off), premature birth, or routine newborn cord-clamping variations that influence final appearance.

Adults can also lose or have their belly button reconstructed after abdominal operations, skin grafts, or tummy tucks; cosmetic umbilicoplasty is performed to reshape navels for aesthetics, or to reattach a repositioned navel during a tummy tuck. The pieces include many reader anecdotes describing umbilical hernia repairs, childhood surgeries, surgical removal by older practitioners, and photo retouching of models’ navels for magazine spreads. One later story recounts a Houston woman who lost her belly button following a tummy tuck and hernia repair and is pursuing legal action after claiming inadequate counseling about the risk; her surgeon says reconstruction is possible once healed. Overall, the coverage emphasizes that absent or altered navels are usually medical or surgical outcomes rather than mysterious or cosmetic-only choices, and that photo editing can also hide real anatomy.

Israel beefed up security around the funeral of former Prime Minister Ariel Sharon after two rockets were reported fired from the Gaza Strip hours before the burial, though they appeared not to have landed in Israel and caused no injuries or damage. Media said the rockets likely fell into the sea; a Reuters reporter heard explosions in northern Gaza that sounded like impacts, and Israeli outlets suggested militants may have been testing weapons. The government deployed increased police forces and, reportedly, an Iron Dome interceptor near Sharon’s family ranch at Sycamore Farm—about 10 km (6 miles) from Gaza and within range of Palestinian rockets that have struck the area before. The military declined to comment on some details.

Sharon, who died at 85 after eight years in a coma, received state honors: a memorial in parliament in Jerusalem and an afternoon burial near his ranch, attended by U.S. Vice President Joe Biden and delegations from 18 countries. Israeli officials said they warned Gaza’s Hamas rulers not to permit rocket fire during the funeral, with one security source warning of severe consequences for provocations; Hamas and other factions issued no immediate response. Israel increased aerial patrols and kept forces on alert to spot and pre-empt launches. Tensions with Gaza and broader regional issues, including Iran’s interim nuclear deal and stalled peace talks with the Palestinian Authority, framed Biden’s brief visit and meetings with Israeli leaders.

An East Liverpool police officer, Patrolman Chris Green, accidentally overdosed after coming into contact with what officers believe was fentanyl during a traffic stop Friday night. Around 8:50 p.m., officers stopped a blue Monte Carlo on Lisbon Street after observing what they suspected was a drug transaction. The driver, 25-year-old Justin Buckle, and passenger, 24-year-old Cortez Collins, were seen trying to dispose of white powder inside the car; officers found powder on the seat, floor, shoes, and even on an open soda can. After arresting both suspects, Green followed protocol by donning gloves and a mask to search the vehicle, but some powder remained on his shirt. Back at the station he instinctively brushed it off, later passing out from an overdose. He received one dose of Narcan at the station and three additional doses at East Liverpool City Hospital and is reported to be fine. Buckle and Collins have been charged with tampering with evidence; both waived preliminary hearing rights and were held on $100,000 bond. The incident underscores growing dangers fentanyl poses to officers and has led to changes in police procedures, including ceasing field testing of suspected drugs.

A Swedish team led by Dr. Mats Brännström at the University of Gothenburg has begun transferring embryos into four of nine women who received uterine transplants in an experimental effort to enable them to carry their own biological children. The recipients, born without a uterus or who lost one to cancer, had produced eggs via IVF before receiving wombs donated by mothers or close relatives. Brännström said he expects three or four of the seven remaining recipients might ultimately give birth, while one or two could miscarry and one or two may not become pregnant; he would not confirm any current pregnancies. Two of the nine transplants were later removed due to complications, and four patients experienced mild rejection episodes. Recipients will take low-dose immunosuppressants during pregnancy and be monitored as high-risk; Brännström plans to remove transplanted wombs after a maximum of two pregnancies. The work follows failed prior attempts in Turkey and Saudi Arabia and parallels planned programs elsewhere using deceased donors. Experts praise the step but caution about donor risks, ethical issues of living donors, and uncertainties about whether transplanted uteri will adapt blood flow and physiology adequately to support fetal growth; a live birth would validate the approach.

St. Joseph Abbey, a Benedictine monastery near New Orleans, began selling handcrafted caskets to help recover income lost when Hurricane Katrina damaged its timberlands. The monks invested in a woodshop and built simple, blessed caskets priced far below typical funeral-home offerings. Soon after they publicized the venture, Louisiana regulators sent a cease‑and‑desist order, citing a law that only licensed funeral directors may sell “funeral merchandise.” Complying would force the abbey to become a full funeral establishment or stop sales. After failed legislative attempts to change the law, the abbey sued with help from the libertarian Institute for Justice, arguing the ban is protectionist and violates due process and equal protection. U.S. District Judge Stanwood Duval Jr. struck down the restriction as economically protectionist; the state board has appealed. The case highlights broader legal tensions: courts generally defer to economic regulations if a “rational basis” exists, but federal appeals courts are split on whether protectionism violates constitutional limits. The Institute for Justice hopes an appeals decision will attract Supreme Court review. Abbot Justin Brown says the suit hasn’t disturbed monastery life and that, historically, monks have often clashed with civil authorities.

Jason Alexander apologized after recounting on The Howard Stern Show why Seinfeld’s showrunners killed off his character George Costanza’s fiancée, Susan Ross (played by Heidi Swedberg). Alexander had explained that he struggled to find comedic chemistry with Swedberg — their instincts and timing often “misfired” — and that tension among the cast contributed to the decision to end the engagement arc in Season 7 with Susan’s death by licking poisonous envelope glue. He said fellow cast members, including Julia Louis-Dreyfus, began to echo his concerns after working more with Swedberg, and that Larry David ultimately conceived the inventive finale. After the Stern appearance drew criticism and suggestions he’d disparaged Swedberg personally, Alexander took to Twitter to apologize and clarify. He emphasized he and the cast liked Swedberg, called her “a kind, lovely person,” and insisted comments about “killing” referred to the character, not the actress. He regretted his retelling might diminish her, said he’d meant to defend her, and apologized directly to Swedberg. The piece notes Swedberg continued acting afterward and now plays and teaches ukulele while leading the Sukey Jump Band. Alexander’s apology urged fans to enjoy reruns and to understand the creative, not personal, reasons behind Susan’s exit.

Heirs of prominent German-Jewish art dealer Alfred Flechtheim have sued the State of Bavaria and the Bayerische Staatsgemaldesammlungen in U.S. federal court, seeking return of eight paintings they say were lost to Nazi-era seizure and trafficking. Plaintiffs Dr. Michael Hulton, Flechtheim’s grand‑nephew, and Penny Hulton, widow of Flechtheim’s heir, contend Flechtheim fled Berlin for Paris in May 1933 under Nazi persecution and was forced to leave behind works that later entered Bavarian collections. The lawsuit alleges Bavaria refused requests to restitute the works despite public commitments to “fair and just” handling of Nazi‑looted art; several of the disputed pieces are reportedly displayed at Munich’s Pinakothek der Moderne.

The eight paintings include six by Max Beckmann—Duchess of Malvedi; Still Life with Cigar Box; Quappi in Blue; Dream—Chinese Fireworks; Champagne Still Life; Still Life with Studio Window—plus Juan Gris’s Cruche et Verre sur un Table and Paul Klee’s Grenzen des Verstandes. The complaint argues any Bavarian title is defective because ownership traces to seizures enabled by state-sponsored Aryanization and persecution, and challenges Bavarian assertions that Flechtheim sold the works pre-1933.

Plaintiffs point to the Gurlitt affair—Hil­debrand Gurlitt’s role selling “degenerate” art and the 2012 discovery of Cornelius Gurlitt’s cache—as evidence of Nazi-era art trafficking linked to Bavarian institutions. Flechtheim, a key promoter of the avant-garde, died impoverished in London in 1937; his widow later died amid deportation threats. Bavaria has indicated the claims lack merit and disputes jurisdiction; its lawyers have not further commented. The case is Hulton et al. v. Bayerische Staatsgemaldesammlungen et al., SDNY.

The Supreme Court upheld the EPA’s “good neighbor” rule in a 6–2 decision, a major win for public health and downwind states. The rule, issued in 2011, requires roughly 28 eastern states and about 1,000 power plants to limit emissions of nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide that travel across state lines and form smog and soot linked to asthma, lung disease and premature deaths. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, writing for the majority, described the challenge regulators face accounting for the “vagaries of the wind” and endorsed the EPA’s cost‑based, pragmatic approach to allocating emissions reductions as “permissible, workable and equitable.” The Court also rejected the D.C. Circuit’s view that the EPA must apportion blame precisely state by state or first give upwind states another chance to craft their own plans; instead it deferred to the agency’s technical expertise in fashioning the remedy.

Justice Antonin Scalia, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, dissented, warning that the EPA’s method represented unchecked bureaucratic power and criticized the cost‑focused allocation as effectively redistributing burdens based on ability to pay. The ruling drew praise from the EPA and health groups as life‑saving regulation and warnings from industry and some scholars that it sidelines state primacy and expands administrative authority. Chief Justice Roberts and four other justices joined Ginsburg; Justice Alito recused himself.

The Officer Down Memorial Page has launched ODMP K9 to honor police canines killed in the line of duty. The piece chronicles numerous preventable deaths of K-9s left in vehicles that became deadly heat traps, focusing on specific cases and broader patterns. Primo, a six-year-old Belgian Malinois with the New Orleans Police Department, died of heat shock in May 2009 after being left in a squad SUV; his body temperature approached 110°F. Investigations produced mixed outcomes: his handler, Officer Jason Lewis, initially faced felony charges, later pleaded to a misdemeanor, was reinstated, but no longer works with K‑9s. The article notes at least 29 confirmed K‑9 deaths in hot cars between April and September across 14 states, citing BuzzFeed and PETA findings, while acknowledging the true number is unknown because no federal agency tracks such deaths. Other tragic cases include Ike (Arizona corrections), Hades and Vegas (Bexar County, Texas), Sasha (Warwick, Georgia), and Beny (Montville, Ohio). Causes range from forgetfulness to misplaced trust in vehicle air conditioning; many dogs chewed to escape and suffered seizures or organ failure. Experts explain dogs’ limited cooling ability—primarily panting—and susceptibility of thick-coated breeds like German shepherds and Belgian Malinois to heat stroke. The article highlights preventive technology—heat-alert systems (Hot Dog/Hot‑N‑Pop)—which can roll down windows, activate fans, or sound alarms, costing roughly $500–$1,000 per vehicle. Some agencies have installed them; others have not, even after grant-funded purchases remained unused. K‑9s are expensive investments (often exceeding $50,000 over time) and vital partners in tracking, detection, and public safety. Advocacy groups urge mandatory installation of heat-alert systems and stronger departmental policies, training, and accountability to prevent needless deaths.

CVS Caremark announced it will stop selling cigarettes and other tobacco products in all CVS/pharmacy stores by October 1, saying tobacco sales conflict with its evolving role as a health-care company. CEO Larry Merlo framed the move as aligning retail practice with the company’s mission to improve health outcomes; CVS employs 26,000 pharmacists and nurse practitioners and operates over 800 MinuteClinic locations. Chief Medical Officer Troyen Brennan and public-health groups praised the decision as consistent with efforts to reduce smoking-related chronic disease and premature death (about 480,000 U.S. deaths annually). CVS plans a national smoking-cessation program this spring offering counseling, treatments, and online resources across stores and clinics, and expanded support for pharmacy benefit management members. The change follows growing expectations that pharmacies act as health-care providers rather than tobacco retailers and brings CVS into closer alignment with medical organizations that oppose tobacco sales in pharmacies. Financially, CVS expects to lose roughly $2 billion in annual tobacco-related revenue—about 1.6% of sales—reducing annual EPS by an estimated 17 cents (6–9 cents impact in 2014), but management expects to offset the profit effect through other opportunities while strengthening long-term growth prospects.

Yo is a minimalist mobile app that lets users send a single notification — the word “Yo” — to contacts. Conceived when Mobli CEO Moshe Hogeg asked Or Arbel to build a one-button alert for his assistant, Arbel developed the app in eight hours and launched it in April. Despite—or because of—its simplicity, Yo attracted wide attention after raising $1 million from angel investors led by Hogeg. That funding and rapid virality provoked both amusement and scepticism across social media and tech circles.

Arbel calls Yo “context-based messaging”: the meaning of a Yo depends on who sends it and when. Use cases range from lightweight personal signals (a quick “thinking of you” to a partner) to notifications about events—Yo’s team even manually delivers goals during the World Cup—and potential integrations with publishers and brands to alert subscribers when content or services update. The founders emphasize efficiency: sending a Yo takes fewer taps than composing a message in other apps.

Yo’s supporters see it as a new notification channel and a frictionless communication layer; critics view investor enthusiasm as symptomatic of a frothy tech market eager to fund viral simplicity. Arbel plans to expand via an API for partners while resisting feature bloat to preserve simplicity and privacy. Whether Yo represents a durable innovation in lightweight messaging or a momentary curiosity in a speculative funding environment remains to be seen.

In a rare posthumous twist in Washington’s 30th legislative district, Democratic incumbent Rep. Roger Freeman—one of the state’s two black legislators—died of colon cancer in late October, days after ballots were mailed. Despite his death, early returns showed Freeman leading Republican challenger Jack Dovey by about six percentage points, roughly 53–47 percent. Many voters remained unaware of Freeman’s passing and continued to vote for him; local reporting captured residents who had cast ballots for the deceased incumbent only to learn of his death afterward. Because Washington conducts elections by mail and accepts ballots postmarked by Election Day, votes already cast remained valid.

State law provides a clear but uncommon remedy: if Freeman wins, Democratic precinct leaders in the district will nominate three candidates, from which the King and Pierce County councils will jointly appoint an interim Democrat to serve until a special election next year fills the remaining year of the two-year term. If the Republican had won, he would assume the seat at the next session. The episode reflects other U.S. instances where deceased candidates have won or advanced in elections, prompting appointments or special elections. Officials noted the rarity of the situation but confirmed existing protocols to preserve party representation and allow voters the final say in the subsequent special election.

The Olsen twins’ luxury label The Row is seeing brisk demand for a $39,000 crocodile-skin backpack at Barneys New York. Ashley Olsen told Women’s Wear Daily it “was the first thing that sold off the shelf,” and Barneys introduced the pricey bags in July to compete with ultra-expensive handbags and attract younger high-spending customers. Amanda Brooks, Barneys’ fashion director, said the pieces aim to appeal to shoppers who value classic, long-lasting designs and exclusivity — “you also might be the only one who has it.” The bag’s rapid sell-through suggests the strategy succeeded.

Freestyle Releasing is positioning Old Fashioned, a faith-based romantic drama, as a direct counterprogramming alternative to Fifty Shades of Grey by opening both films on Valentine’s Day 2015. Written, directed by and starring Rik Swartzwelder, Old Fashioned tells the story of a former frat boy who pursues an “old-fashioned” courtship with a free-spirited woman played by Elizabeth Ann Roberts. Its tagline, “Chivalry makes a comeback,” signals an intentional embrace of conservative, God-centered romance and an explicit avoidance of sexual content; the filmmakers describe the movie as exploring “Godly romance” and a “higher standard in relationships” without shaming those who have made mistakes. Freestyle, fresh off the surprising commercial success of God’s Not Dead (which grossed over $60 million), is marketing Old Fashioned as a David-vs.-Goliath challenge to the heavily hyped, big-budget Fifty Shades adaptation, acknowledging the disparity in screens, marketing muscle and buzz but betting there is a sizable audience seeking a wholesome alternative to objectification and domination on screen. Co-president Mark Borde called Old Fashioned the first faith-based theatrical release aimed specifically at the underserved Christian singles market. Producers include Swartzwelder’s Skoche Films, Nathan Nazario, Dave DeBorde and Nini Hadjis; the cast also features Dorothy Silver, Tyler Hollinger, Lejon Woods, Maryann Nagel and Joseph Bonamico. The announcement followed closely after Universal released the first trailer for Fifty Shades and amid other Valentine’s weekend studio releases.

A Kentucky discussion group formed to promote restoration of the Constitution, liberty, and Second Amendment rights advertises itself as a forum for peaceful debate and information about open carry and related events. The group emphasizes moderation by members’ common sense, includes links to open-carry resources, and displays a Second Amendment dollar image; it disclaims any encouragement of violence and aligns topically with other liberty-focused Meetups. Amid this organizing effort, a violent incident in Lexington highlighted the heated tone of 2010 races: video showed Lauren Valle of MoveOn.org shoved to the ground and then stomped by two men after she approached Republican Senate nominee Rand Paul with a mock award. One assailant, Tim Profitt — identified as a Bourbon County coordinator for Paul — admitted stepping on Valle’s head and was identified by police and served with a criminal summons to appear before a Fayette County judge. The Paul campaign publicly disavowed the volunteer and condemned violence, calling any aggression deplorable and unacceptable.

Damien Hirst’s major retrospective at Tate Modern ends with a luxury gift shop selling high-priced branded souvenirs echoing his famous works. Chief among them is Hallucinatory Head, a limited run of 50 plastic skulls painted like his spin pieces, priced at £36,800. Other items include a £10,500 set of china plates, £700 a roll of butterfly wallpaper, a £480 skateboard, a £310 deckchair and a £195 umbrella. The show displays Hirst’s signature pieces — the formaldehyde shark, bisected animals, spin paintings, the maggot-feeding A Thousand Years, live butterflies in And Out Of Love, and the diamond-encrusted skull For The Love Of God, valued at about £50 million. The exhibition opened amid criticism from Julian Spalding, who called Hirst a “con artist” and urged collectors to sell before values drop. Hirst defends market-driven prices, likening art’s value to demand for Rembrandts or designer jeans. The exhibition runs from April 4 to September 9.

After Ferguson unrest drew attention to police tactics, the Pentagon quietly released detailed spreadsheets of its 1033 Excess Property Program, which has transferred over $4.3 billion in surplus military gear to local, state and federal law enforcement since 1997 (including $449 million in 2013). The itemized list ranges from mundane chargers and televisions to rifles, armored mine-resistant vehicles, helicopters, bomb‑squad robots and even trumpets and snowshoes. Many small departments — town police, college forces and rural sheriffs — received heavy equipment, including grenade launchers and MRAPs. California agencies received over $160 million worth. The disclosure marks a policy shift after years of FOIA denials.

Investigators intensified their search Thursday night for convicted killers Richard Matt, 48, and David Sweat, 34, after their weekend escape from Clinton Correctional Facility in Dannemora, New York. Clinton County District Attorney Andrew Wylie said K-9 units tracked scents from the prison to a nearby gas station that houses a Subway, and followed a trail east toward Cadyville. Authorities reviewed surveillance video from the station and found a shoe- or boot-print and a food wrapper; they believe the pair may have rummaged for food in a trash bin and possibly bedded down in the area. Roads including Cringle Road were closed as searches continued, and officials used infrared technology to aid nighttime searches. Residents in Cadyville and nearby communities were advised to stay indoors and lock doors; Saranac Central School closed for the day.

State police closed State Route 374 east of Dannemora to West Plattsburgh after what they called a promising lead. Hundreds of officers have combed woods, farms and structures in the region “behind every tree, under every rock,” New York State Police Superintendent Joseph D’Amico said. Searches extended beyond the immediate area after reports of two suspicious men spotted in Willsboro during a late-night storm and intelligence suggesting Vermont was discussed as a possible destination; Vermont troopers and vessels scanned Lake Champlain and nearby campsites. Officials have not ruled out travel to Canada — only about 20 miles north — or elsewhere in the U.S. Digital billboards displaying the fugitives’ photos were posted across multiple states. Law enforcement cautioned the public to remain vigilant, noting fugitives might not stay local.

The escape reopened historical context: Clinton Correctional Facility, opened in 1845, has a long record of escapes by digging, disguise or scaling walls. Accounts from the early 20th century describe elaborate tunneling escapes into sewer systems, including a meticulous 1903 breakout by Peter James after years of secret tunneling. Historians note escapes are uncommon but recurring, often thwarted when the public spots someone unfamiliar. Former escapee Timothy Vail, who fled Elmira Correctional Facility in 2003 and was recaptured two days later, expressed sympathy and tactical admiration for Matt and Sweat, advising patience and silence while warning that the fugitives’ biggest danger is their own behavior and impulse to act rashly.

The document contains three compact film reviews with a sardonic tone. Bitch Slap is described as a low-budget, green-screen homage to exploitative, hot-women-in-peril movies: flashy costumes, gratuitous close-ups of the actresses, interminable fistfights, scant humor, and a muddled, Memento-inspired treasure-CIA plot. It offers a few fun moments—a water fight, an unhinged villain, abrupt make-outs—but underuses stunt coordinator Zoë Bell and ends predictably without delivering promised payoffs. Daybreakers is a vampire thriller set when humans are livestock for the undead; Ethan Hawke’s hematologist seeks a blood substitute while Willem Dafoe’s re-humanizing vampire hints at a cure. The film gestures at social critique—resource exhaustion and elite selfishness—but is undone by wooden characters, predictable scares, and gloomy cinematography, with conspicuous Chrysler placements. Wonderful World stars Matthew Broderick as Ben Singer, a burned-out former children’s performer turned misanthropic proofreader whose life is nudged back toward warmth by his Senegalese roommate’s sister (Sanaa Lathan). The debut writer-director Joshua Goldin delivers promising but uneven work: character moments reveal potential, yet the script is thin, predictable, and fails to fully explore motives, leaving strong actors in improbable situations.

The Khizanat al-Qarawiyyin library in Fez, founded in 859 and widely regarded as the world’s oldest, has undergone a multimillion-pound restoration and is due to reopen to the public. Architect Aziza Chaouni, a Fez native appointed in 2012, led the sensitive project aimed at preserving the library’s fabric while making it a living resource for locals, students and researchers rather than a tourist relic. Structural repairs addressed long-standing problems—blocked drainage, moisture, cracked beams and broken tiles—and revealed surprises such as an ancient sewage system. To protect fragile manuscripts, teams installed a new underground canal and sewerage system to control humidity, created a secure, climate-controlled room for the most precious works (including a ninth-century Kufic Qur’an on camel skin and an original of Ibn Khaldun’s Muqaddimah), and equipped a conservation lab with digital scanners and machines to treat and digitize texts. Restoration also included refurbished woodwork, courtyard fountains, a new chandelier and sustainable features like solar panels and water collection. The project dovetails with wider efforts to revive Fez’s medina as a cultural and spiritual capital—cleaning the river, renovating quarters, and hosting festivals—while guarding heritage amid regional threats. King Mohammed VI inspected the works and is expected to inaugurate the library before the end of 2016.

Transparency International’s 2013 Global Corruption Barometer, based on responses from over 114,000 people in 107 countries, found that 27% of respondents paid a bribe in the past year. Bribe-paying was especially acute in Liberia and Sierra Leone, where more than 75% reported paying bribes, while two-thirds overall said they refused when asked. Police and the judiciary were most associated with bribery: nearly one-third of citizen contacts with police involved a bribe, and 24% involved the judicial system. In countries that view police as most corrupt, an average 53% were asked for bribes by police; in those viewing the judiciary as most corrupt, 30% faced judicial bribe demands. Over half believe corruption has increased in two years; the average seriousness rating was 4.1/5, worst in Liberia and Mongolia (4.8). More than 50 countries named political parties the most corrupt institutions, and public confidence in governments’ anti-corruption efforts fell from 31% in 2008 to 22% in 2013.

Toronto Mayor Rob Ford, speaking in a hoarse, quiet voice at City Hall, revealed he has been given a “50-50” chance of surviving liposarcoma, a rare cancer, and described the diagnosis as the worst thing he’s endured. He said chemotherapy has left him exhausted and emotional — “some nights, I just cry myself to sleep” — and acknowledged the strain on his young children as he copes with treatment and its toll. Ford apologized for occasional pauses and hoarseness during his remarks, attributing them to chemo, and described returning briefly to his office to handle paperwork and read get-well cards.

After being hospitalized in mid-September, Ford withdrew from the mayoral race and instead registered to run for his former Ward 2 (Etobicoke North) city council seat, a ward he represented from 2000 to 2010. He has 13 opponents; polls still show him with a substantial lead. Ford said he might not be well enough to attend all-candidates debates and shrugged off criticism about running while undergoing treatment: supporters want his name on the ballot, and if voters feel he cannot serve they can choose another candidate.

Reactions among opponents were mixed. Businessman Andray Domise called Ford’s candidacy “highly irresponsible” unless Ford actively campaigns, debates, releases a platform, and canvasses. Community developer Luke LaRocque said it’s a personal decision and difficult to argue Ford shouldn’t run. Ford missed a Ward 2 debate but briefly attended a mayoral debate where his brother Doug was participating, leaving early due to illness; he has been seen canvassing at least once since discharge.

Meanwhile Doug Ford continued campaigning for mayor, unveiling a $9-billion, 32-kilometre subway plan similar to Rob’s earlier proposals but prioritizing a downtown/Yonge relief line alongside other subway extensions, promising funding from other government levels, public-private partnerships, asset sales and air-rights rather than new costs to residents.

NOAA Fisheries has declared an "unusual mortality event" after 30 large whales were found dead in the western Gulf of Alaska since May, about three times the historical average for the region. The strandings include 11 fin whales, 14 humpback whales, one gray whale and four unidentified cetaceans. The declaration mobilizes additional federal, state and tribal resources and launches a rigorous, collaborative investigation through NOAA’s Marine Mammal Health and Stranding Response Program and the Working Group on Marine Mammal Unusual Mortality Events.

A leading hypothesis is toxins from a harmful algal bloom, but officials emphasize there is no conclusive evidence linking algal toxins to the deaths. Investigators have been able to collect useful samples from only one of the 30 Alaska carcasses; two necropsies were performed recently on whales found off British Columbia, where six large whale deaths have also been reported since May. Sample collection is hampered by logistical challenges across vast, remote coastline, safety issues such as large bears scavenging carcasses, and many whales remaining afloat or inaccessible for full necropsies. These factors limit the immediate ability to identify causes, forcing reliance on environmental data, historical records and mortality patterns in other marine life.

NOAA urges the public to report sightings of dead or distressed whales to local hotlines (Alaska: 877-925-7773; B.C.: 1-800-465-4336) but to avoid touching or approaching animals. Investigations may take months or years, and updates will be posted on NOAA’s unusual mortality event website as findings emerge.

Fraternity brothers from Pi Kappa Alpha at California State University, Chico, are facing federal criminal charges after an alleged initiation binge in Lassen National Forest in April that left a campsite heavily damaged. According to a federal complaint, camper Jon Elam told authorities he visited the camp the weekend of April 21 and encountered about 80 people. He was met by Evan Jossey—the fraternity president from Pleasant Hill—and three other men who identified themselves as Chico State fraternity members and said they planned an initiation ceremony that night. The U.S. Forest Service alleges the group illegally cut down more than 32 trees, fired firearms, and left the campground in disarray; a visitor later photographed the wreckage. Surveillance images released by officials reportedly show young men purchasing tools believed to have been used in the vandalism. Each implicated member faces charges including vandalism, illegal firearms violations, and damaging federal land. The chapter has no house; its Facebook page denies at least some allegations and reports that members have received threats from the community. Fellow students and other fraternities have expressed disapproval—Chico State student Mark Anderson described the conduct as “poor judgment and planning”—and a Forest Service representative voiced disbelief at the apparent disrespect for public lands. The fraternity and Jossey are scheduled to appear in court on June 26, 2017, and authorities indicate additional charges may follow.
