Separately, an archival note explains that web crawls aim to preserve pages and their references so links remain accessible even if original pages change or disappear—part of an effort to reduce broken links by storing contemporaneous versions for future reference.

A 14-year-old Clayton County girl, Ayvani Perez, returned to her Ellenwood home Wednesday night nearly 48 hours after being abducted. Neighbors saw her arrive, and authorities said she was found in "seemingly good health" at a Conyers residence and evaluated by police. Investigators arrested Wildrego Jackson, 29, and Juan Alberto Rodriguez, 40, in connection with the case; Jackson faces conspiracy to commit kidnapping charges and has a long criminal history including assault, drug and weapons offenses, while Rodriguez is being held on immigration-related charges. Police say two armed men forced entry early Tuesday, demanded money and jewelry, and kidnapped Ayvani; those two men match sketches released previously and remain at large. Authorities would not disclose how federal agents located Ayvani. Reporting revealed a past link between Rodriguez and Ayvani’s mother, Maria Corral: both were arrested in a 2012 Henry County drug probe that found 500 pounds of marijuana, though charges were later dropped. Neighbors expressed relief and gratitude that Ayvani is home safe, while questions remain about the circumstances of the abduction.

Sienna Miller is set to join legal action against the News of the World and Scotland Yard over alleged phone hacking after discovering private investigator Glenn Mulcaire had her mobile numbers, account details and voicemail PIN. Her lawyers said she will seek a judicial review of the Metropolitan Police’s handling of the case, joining others including John Prescott, Brian Paddick, Chris Bryant and journalist Brendan Montague in action led by Bindmans. Miller learned only in October 2009 that police held evidence from Mulcaire’s 2006 arrest and complained police delayed informing her despite signs her voicemail had been interfered with. Former News of the World reporters Sean Hoare and Paul McMullan have been interviewed by police under caution after alleging widespread hacking; Hoare claimed editor Andy Coulson asked him to hack, a claim Coulson denies. Parliament’s standards committee will consider whether phone hacking breaches parliamentary privilege. Other public figures, including Steve Coogan and Chris Tarrant, are also pursuing legal action.

California Gov. Jerry Brown declared a statewide drought emergency after a fourth year of severe dry conditions and the Sierra Nevada’s April 1 snowpack measured at just 5% of average—the lowest since records began in 1950. Announcing the order in a snowless Sierra meadow, Brown urged Californians to change water habits and warned the drought could persist. The executive order targets urban water use with measures including banning median strip watering, removing 50 million square feet of turf for drought-tolerant landscaping, rebate programs for high-efficiency appliances, and requiring drip or microspray irrigation for new developments using drinking water. Golf courses, campuses, and cemeteries must reduce water use, and agencies will use tiered rates to discourage waste. The order seeks a 25% statewide urban reduction in 2013 and directs the State Water Resources Control Board to issue regulations, assign local targets, and enforce compliance—fines up to $10,000 per day. Critics said the order doesn’t sufficiently address agricultural consumption; the order does require groundwater data sharing from agricultural districts in depleted basins. Officials noted many Southern California agencies already pursue rebates and tiered pricing. With reservoir replenishment limited by minimal snowmelt and Central Valley growers facing severe cuts, officials warned further restrictions, including wider outdoor watering bans, may be necessary.

A rare "Blue Moon"—celebrated as a second full moon in a calendar month by popular usage—brightened clear skies, inspiring photographers and social media buzz. Historically, however, the traditional definition is the third of four full moons in an astronomical season; that interpretation dates back farther and remains valid among astronomers. The modern, simpler definition arose from a mistaken 1943–1946 Sky & Telescope article and stuck in public imagination. Although most Blue Moons aren't actually blue, volcanic ash or other atmospheric particles have painted moons blue in history (notably after Krakatoa in 1883, El Chichon in 1983, and Pinatubo in 1991). The next calendar-month Blue Moon arrives July 31, 2015; the next seasonal-type falls May 21, 2016.

In Cleveland, the shocking discovery that three women had been found alive after years missing prompted fresh scrutiny of past investigations and the people involved. Fernando Colon, 49, who had been questioned by the FBI in 2004 about the disappearances of Gina DeJesus and Amanda Berry, said he followed the recent revelations closely. At the time Colon worked as a neighborhood security guard and, with his step-daughter, was reportedly the last person to see DeJesus before she vanished. The 2004 probe and its fallout left him stigmatized; he said community suspicion that he was involved “was just devastating.” Colon is also personally connected to the case’s prime suspect, 52-year-old Ariel Castro: Colon was married to Castro’s ex-wife and was stepfather to Castro’s four children. In 2004 Colon was convicted of two counts of gross sexual imposition for molesting two of Castro’s daughters and remains registered as a sex offender. He alleges Castro manipulated the situation—he claims Castro orchestrated accusations and even testified at Colon’s trial—to deflect attention from Castro’s own crimes. Colon says that when he spoke to the FBI in 2004 he pointed them toward Castro as a suspect in the girls’ disappearances, and he now plans to seek an appeal of his molestation conviction in light of evidence emerging against Castro. Veteran Cleveland private investigator Chris Giannini, who worked on Colon’s defense, supports the view that Castro warranted greater scrutiny years ago. Giannini noted Castro’s routine presence around his daughters and their friends, his reluctance to allow visitors to his home, and his job as a school bus driver on the route where the girls were last seen; he believes police should have checked Castro’s house and questioned him more thoroughly. Separately, archival coverage from 2004—an “America’s Most Wanted” segment—features an interview with Arlene Castro, Ariel Castro’s daughter, who said she was the last person to see Gina DeJesus and described giving her 50 cents for a pay phone call before parting ways. At the time, police dog tracking followed DeJesus’ scent from that pay phone down the block until the trail went cold. The FBI had not responded to queries about Colon’s current allegations.

Maria Rose Belding, a 20-year-old American University sophomore, co-founded MEANS Database (Matching Excess And Need for Stability) to bridge the gap between massive food waste and widespread hunger in the U.S. Sparked by witnessing a pantry discard thousands of boxes of expired macaroni while people waited for food, Belding built MEANS to let donors, food banks, and pantries post surplus food online or via app; nearby recipients receive notifications, claim items, and arrange pickup. In its first year MEANS rescued roughly 4,000 pounds (about two tons), grew to more than 200 donor and recipient accounts representing over 2,000 partner agencies across 24–27 states, and won several awards including GW’s New Venture Competition and a L’Oréal Paris Women of Worth prize.

MEANS differentiates itself from larger food-rescue organizations by enabling participation by small organizations and individuals who operate at scales too small for big players. The platform emphasizes data-driven efficiencies: it uses data science to predict which pantries will need resources, to manage logistics, and to compile a public directory—an effort driven by the discovery that roughly half of online listings for emergency food providers have incorrect contact information. Belding’s co-founder, Grant Nelson, developed MEANS’ technology; together they’ve grown the team to a staff of about 11 plus interns and volunteers.

To achieve sustainability beyond grants, MEANS plans a model allowing retailers to claim tax benefits for donations; MEANS would track required documentation and take a small fee while the service remains free to users. Future goals include launching that revenue program, expanding coverage to untapped states, and improving the nationwide directory of pantries. Balancing school and leadership, Belding credits math and data science for turning a simple idea into a scalable solution that pairs empathy with entrepreneurial rigor to reduce food waste and alleviate hunger.

Nicky Hilton Rothschild and husband James Rothschild are expecting their first child this summer, confirmed by multiple outlets. The newlyweds, who married at Kensington Palace in July after an August 2014 Lake Como engagement, have been sharing the news with close friends and family and are reportedly “over the moon.” The 32-year-old heiress has spoken fondly about marriage and her wedding dress, and sister Paris Hilton has expressed enthusiasm about becoming an aunt. Insiders say Nicky is excited and feeling great as she prepares for motherhood.

On Oct. 22, 2013, 13-year-old Andy Lopez was shot and killed by Sonoma County Deputy Erick Gelhaus after deputies saw him walking with an airsoft BB gun resembling an AK-47. Gelhaus fired eight rounds, striking Lopez seven times. The shooting sparked immediate local, state and national protests, with activists decrying it as an example of police brutality and the militarization of law enforcement. Hundreds participated in coordinated demonstrations — a “National Day of Action for Andy Lopez” — in Santa Rosa, Oakland, San Francisco and other cities to demand accountability and justice.

After an exhaustive investigation, Sonoma County District Attorney Jill Ravitch announced on July 7, 2014, that no criminal charges would be filed against Gelhaus. Ravitch released a 52-page summary concluding Gelhaus reasonably believed he faced a deadly threat; prosecutors found his use of lethal force was lawful. The report introduced new details, including toxicology showing significant THC in Lopez’s system, which experts said could have impaired his judgment and reaction time. Investigators re-interviewed witnesses, consulted outside experts, conducted ballistic and 3D trajectory analyses, and reviewed hundreds of interviews and evidence items.

The decision provoked outrage from Lopez’s family, attorneys and activists, who called it unjust and pledged to continue protesting and pursue a federal civil rights lawsuit. Sheriff Steve Freitas and others urged reforms such as clearer markings for imitation guns and pledged reviews of deputy-involved shootings, while local leaders asked demonstrators to remain peaceful. The case left the community deeply divided and grieving, with calls to rebuild trust between residents and law enforcement.

Violence in the U.S. has declined since 1995 but remains uneven across states. 24/7 Wall St.’s peacefulness index ranks Maine most peaceful and Louisiana least, using crime, homicide, gun ownership, and incarceration data. Wealth, employment, and local conditions like vacant housing influence violence. The summary spotlights the 10 least peaceful states—Arizona, South Carolina, Florida, Missouri, and Arkansas among them—each with high violent crime and related social challenges.

The document chronicles the U.S. federal government’s partial shutdown and the concurrent debt-ceiling showdown in mid-October 2013, highlighting intense Senate negotiations, partisan maneuvering, economic alarm and international concern. As the shutdown entered its third week and the Treasury warned it would exhaust extraordinary borrowing authority by about Oct. 17, Senate leaders raced to craft a short-term deal to reopen the government and avert a default. Democrats, sensing political leverage as public opinion penalized Republicans, resisted any agreement that would lock in extended sequester cuts for 2014. They pushed instead for reopening the government immediately with a shorter spending deadline and a later deadline to raise the debt limit, seeking new budget talks to address sequestration and long-term fiscal issues.

Republicans, notably Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, backed a bipartisan proposal spearheaded by Sen. Susan Collins that would reopen the government and prevent default while keeping sequestration-level spending through mid-January or longer. GOP senators warned against undoing the Budget Control Act’s spending caps, arguing the party could not retreat. Some centrist and conservative Democrats engaged in negotiations with Collins but publicly declined to endorse the plan in its then-current form. House conservatives, meanwhile, insisted on concessions targeting the Affordable Care Act as a condition for funding — a nonstarter for Democrats and the White House, which said it would not pay a ransom to reopen government.

Markets and global leaders voiced alarm: IMF chief Christine Lagarde warned of worldwide disruption from a U.S. default, foreign holders of U.S. debt fretted, and U.S. economic indicators and consumer confidence were already showing strain. Polls showed broad public disapproval of congressional Republicans’ handling of the crisis. Lawmakers publicly expressed optimism about an imminent bipartisan compromise that would fund operations into January and extend borrowing authority into early 2014, but procedural hurdles, House factionalism and unresolved policy disputes left the outcome uncertain even as analysts warned key payments could be missed by early November. International commentary urged reforms to reduce global dependence on U.S. political stability, underscoring the diplomatic and economic fallout of the impasse.

President Obama is convening a meeting with House and Senate Democrats on Capitol Hill to map out strategies for protecting the Affordable Care Act (ACA) from Republican repeal efforts expected when the 115th Congress and President-elect Donald Trump take office. The session, confirmed by Democrats and first reported by Politico, will be held at 9 a.m. in the Congressional Visitors Center auditorium and will include top Democratic leaders. Republicans plan an early move to repeal the ACA, possibly using reconciliation to bypass the 60-vote Senate threshold; GOP leaders have floated delaying the repeal’s effective date by up to three years to allow time for a replacement. That prospect has put Democrats into rapid strategy mode: some are open to negotiating a replacement, but most oppose repeal. Incoming Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has vowed to block both repeal and a conservative replacement, challenging Republicans to produce an alternative. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi and others are emphasizing the law’s achievements—extending coverage to more than 20 million people, allowing young adults to remain on parents’ plans, protecting those with preexisting conditions, and slowing health-care cost growth—while acknowledging problems like premium increases in certain states. Democrats are also planning broader resistance to GOP plans to alter Medicare and Medicaid, organizing a “day of action” on Jan. 15 led by Schumer, Pelosi and Bernie Sanders to rally grassroots support. The meeting may also touch on other issues Obama has championed, including Dodd-Frank and environmental protections, as Democrats prepare to defend these policy gains.

On Sept. 18, Breckenridge resident Jack McAtee, 27, crashed his black sedan off the road into Dillon Reservoir after veering onto a paved bike path, rolling across gravel and going airborne before plunging into the water. Miraculously, he swam to the surface with only a cut above his left eye. McAtee told a trooper he had fallen asleep at the wheel; the trooper judged him not under the influence but noted erratic mood swings. Family members later said McAtee had recently stopped taking medication for bipolar disorder. Authorities took him to the hospital, then to the Summit County jail for evaluation, and a psychologist before releasing him around 11 a.m. on Sept. 19 with $67, a red hoodie and a tan hat. He was never seen again.

McAtee had a history of disappearing briefly when off medication, but this time he did not reappear. The family mobilized widespread searches, posting missing-person flyers from Summit County to truck stops along I-70 and beyond, following one trooper’s offhand suggestion that Moab would be a destination to hitchhike west. They pursued leads across the West — Moab, Alaska, northern California, Slab City, Burning Man — and canvassed homeless shelters, truck stops and small towns where people live off the grid. They emphasized the missing blue TREK mountain bike as key evidence and urged hunters, shelter workers and “travelers” communities to watch for him. Search teams, the Summit County Sheriff’s Office and Breckenridge rescue groups conducted extensive ground, canine and aerial searches; the family enlisted social media and offered a reward.

After nearly a year of searching, in August hikers found a skull on Peak 1 in the Tenmile Range near Frisco. DNA testing identified it as Jack’s. The family announced that they now have closure that their son is gone, while law enforcement continues to investigate manner and cause of death. Throughout the ordeal, the McAtee family maintained public appeals, updates and charitable efforts in Jack’s memory and expressed gratitude for widespread community support.

In July 2012, 26-year-old Caitlan Coleman of Stewartstown, Pennsylvania, and her husband Joshua Boyle set off on an adventurous backpacking trip through Central Asia that ultimately led them into Afghanistan. Initially in “safe” Central Asian republics, the couple ceased regular contact by late September; family received a final message on Oct. 8, 2012, from an internet cafe in an “unsafe” part of Afghanistan. In 2013 the Taliban’s Haqqani network claimed they had kidnapped Caitlan and Joshua; officials believe they have been held in Pakistan. Over the following years the family learned harrowing details: Caitlan gave birth to two sons while in captivity, and videos released by the captors show the couple pleading for their lives and warning that their children will be killed unless Afghan authorities change policies on executing Taliban prisoners. The authenticity and date of the latest video remain under review by U.S. and Canadian authorities; the Taliban said it was recorded in 2015.

Friends and family recall Caitlan as generous, devout, optimistic and naively trusting—a small-town woman with a wanderlust that, combined with Joshua’s intense interest in Afghanistan and Islam, helped propel the couple into danger. The tale’s shocking domestic normalcy—“the girl next door” becoming a hostage and mother in captivity—has made it hard for her community and the wider public to process. Media coverage has been sporadic, and the family has largely stayed private, hampering broader awareness.

Critics argue U.S. hostage recovery efforts were disjointed for years; retired Green Beret Jason Amerine testified that no coordinated push had initially occurred to free the civilian hostages. Reforms led to creation of the Hostage Recovery Fusion Cell in 2015, credited with releasing dozens of hostages, but political constraints, the risk of operations in Pakistan, and official reluctance to negotiate with terrorists complicate prospects. Meanwhile Caitlan’s loved ones live in prolonged grief and uncertainty—unable to grieve fully, fearing for her health and the children’s welfare, and frustrated that public attention has waned despite the continuing moral urgency of securing their release.

Johann Breyer, an 89-year-old former SS guard accused of involvement in mass killings at Auschwitz, died Tuesday night in a Philadelphia hospital the day before a U.S. magistrate approved his extradition to Germany, his lawyer said. Magistrate Timothy Rice found probable cause that Breyer was the person sought for aiding and abetting murder and wrote that no statute of limitations protects murder suspects. German authorities had issued a 2013 warrant charging Breyer with 158 counts of accessory to murder, tied to trainloads of victims brought to Auschwitz from May to October 1944—alleging complicity in killings of roughly 216,000 Jews. Breyer, who immigrated to the U.S. in 1952 and became a citizen, acknowledged serving as an SS guard but maintained he was stationed away from the camp’s killing operations and did not participate in atrocities. His attorneys cited frail health, dementia and heart problems; he had been held without bail pending extradition and a final U.S. government review.

European regulators are probing reports that some televisions may be programmed to reduce power use during official energy-efficiency tests, producing more favorable lab results than they deliver in real-world viewing. Independent investigations, including work by an EU-funded consortium ComplianTV and national agencies such as Sweden’s Energy Agency, found that certain TVs sharply lower brightness and power when a standard 10-minute IEC test film is played. ComplianTV observed one Samsung LCD model’s power drop from about 70W to 39W within a minute. Samsung denies deliberate cheating, saying the change is caused by an out-of-the-box “motion lighting” feature that reduces backlight in response to on-screen motion and operates both in homes and labs. Campaigners warn the practice resembles the Volkswagen emissions “defeat device” scandal and call for tougher oversight. The European Commission says it will follow up, verify the findings, assess the scale and whether devices render products non-compliant, and plans to clarify ecodesign rules to outlaw defeat devices. Regulators note manufacturers self-test and file results, with only some independent checks, and stress more testing is underway to determine whether any firms are intentionally detecting test patterns and switching to lower-energy modes, potentially misleading consumers and understating real-world energy use and emissions.

Perez Hilton (Mario Lavandeira Jr.) announced on his blog that earlier this month he became a father to a healthy baby boy. In a post titled "A Very Important Message from Perez," the 34-year-old expressed joy and gratitude, noting the infant has "lots of hair" and calling the child a cherished addition to his family. Hilton shared a photo cradling the newborn but did not disclose the baby’s name, the birth mother, or whether surrogacy or adoption was involved. He thanked fans for their support and said he’s humbled and ready for fatherhood.

President Trump’s pardon of former Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio capped a long political friendship and provoked widespread controversy. Trump, who and Arpaio had bonded over the “birther” movement and immigration enforcement, privately pressed Attorney General Jeff Sessions in the spring to drop Arpaio’s criminal case; Sessions advised against it. Trump then decided to allow the case to proceed, reserving the option of clemency if Arpaio were convicted. After Arpaio was found guilty of contempt for defying a federal order barring racial profiling and detention of suspected undocumented immigrants, Trump issued a pardon Aug. 25 without consulting the Justice Department and bypassing the customary review process. The move was prepared inside the West Wing with advocacy from advisers including Stephen Miller and Steve Bannon and with White House Counsel’s Office staff readying paperwork and talking points; Arpaio’s lawyers were asked whether he would accept a pardon. Trump’s action, timed amid other contentious Friday-night announcements and a looming hurricane, drew immediate criticism from Democrats and some Republicans, including Sens. John McCain and Jeff Flake and Speaker Paul Ryan, who said the pardon undermined respect for the rule of law and rewarded misconduct. Critics noted Arpaio’s history of accusations—racial profiling, mistreatment of inmates, and civil-rights violations—and argued presidents should avoid intervening in specific cases. Supporters framed the pardon as correcting a politicized prosecution and hailed Arpaio as a law-and-order ally. The episode heightened concerns about White House interference with Justice Department independence and intensified debates over presidential use of clemency, politicized justice, and the administration’s direction on immigration and civil-rights enforcement.

Astronomers have captured the first direct image of a large strand of the long-predicted cosmic web by using a distant quasar as a “cosmic flashlight.” Observations with the 10-metre Keck I Telescope revealed a glowing hydrogen nebula about two million light-years across around quasar UM287, roughly 10 billion light-years away. The quasar’s intense radiation fluoresces the cold gas, making visible a filament that appears to trace underlying dark matter structures predicted by cosmological simulations. The result supports the standard model in which dark matter forms a filamentary scaffold that ordinary matter follows, producing gas filaments, galaxies, and clusters at nodes. Unlike previous indirect detections via gravitational lensing or absorption studies, this is a direct image of diffuse intergalactic gas lighting up the filament. The team also found “dark galaxies” — denser clumps within the nebula — and report about ten times more gas than typical simulations predict, suggesting either resolution limits in models or missing physics in galaxy formation. Published in Nature, the discovery offers new ways to map missing ordinary matter and study how galaxies grow within the cosmic web.

Archaeologists in northern Greece have uncovered a large, well-preserved Hellenistic tomb near Amphipolis, dated to about 300–325 B.C., and described by officials as one of the largest ancient graves found in Greece. Excavations that began in 2012 have revealed an elaborate burial complex featuring a 4.5‑metre‑wide approach road, frescoed walls, a 497‑metre marble outer wall and an entrance flanked by two headless, wingless sphinxes. A five‑metre lion sculpture discovered nearby a century ago is believed to have once crowned the mound. The site appears unlooted and archaeologists expect to enter the tomb soon to determine who is buried there; they suspect it belonged to a prominent Macedonian of the era. Although the tomb dates to the end of Alexander the Great’s lifetime and has prompted speculation, Culture Ministry officials say there is currently no evidence linking the burial to Alexander or his family. The find has drawn national attention—Prime Minister Antonis Samaras called it “especially significant”—and the area remains tightly guarded as researchers prepare to open the burial chamber and learn more about its occupant and historical context.

Heavy fighting continued in Gaza despite international calls for a cease-fire, with Israeli airstrikes and ground operations targeting Hamas infrastructure, including tunnels and alleged militant sites. Palestinian health officials reported over 1,100 dead and more than 6,500 wounded, many civilians and children; at least eight children died when shells struck a beach-area refugee camp during Eid al-Fitr celebrations. The IDF said 53 Israeli soldiers and several civilians have been killed; ten soldiers died in recent ground clashes and tunnel attacks. Israel stressed its campaign aims to destroy Hamas tunnels and said it would press operations as long as attacks continue. World leaders, the UN and regional mediators urged a durable truce and humanitarian relief; UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon called for an immediate halt to the violence.

Researchers report that whale sharks, the largest living fish, are increasingly frequenting the Azores, a volcanic archipelago in the central North Atlantic, likely driven by rising sea surface temperatures and associated ecological changes. Analyzing 16 years (1998–2013) of tuna-boat observer sightings, scientists found a marked increase beginning in the exceptionally warm year of 2008, after which whale sharks became regular visitors. The animals, which prefer 26.5–30 °C waters, are now drawn to the Azores’ warmer patches at the northern edge of their historical range. Sightings were more common near seafloor features such as seamounts and slopes that boost productivity (chlorophyll-a) and thus prey availability. Fishermen have long used whale sharks—locally called “pintados”—to locate tuna, since tuna often school beneath the sharks. The study suggests large marine species can shift distributions regionally with climate change, potentially reshaping ocean ecosystems and tourism (e.g., whale-shark watching). Authors call for further research into reasons whales remain in summer—food, mating, or other factors—and urge placing these shifts in the context of longer-term oceanic change. Findings published in PLOS ONE.

President Donald Trump spent Thanksgiving week at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach and returned to his West Palm Beach golf course on a sunny Friday, using Twitter to press urgent legislative priorities. In an early-morning post the day after Thanksgiving he urged both parties to unite on a "major Border Security package, which will include funding for the Wall," calling it "time for action" after decades of debate. That stance comes as Congress faces a Dec. 7 deadline to fund parts of the government and amid Trump's willingness to allow a shutdown if wall funding is not included. His push conflicts with newly empowered House Democrats, who oppose wall funding, and follows a summer in which he discouraged bipartisan immigration efforts until Republicans regained seats—a strategy that failed in the midterms. Trump also urged passage of criminal justice reform, saying Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and Democratic leader Chuck Schumer "have a real chance" to act, though McConnell has warned there may not be enough lame-duck floor time. Separately, Trump accidentally tagged a Schumer fan account instead of the senator in a tweet. Over Thanksgiving he called troops, answered reporters, visited a Coast Guard station and dined at Mar-a-Lago.

The piece traces the recent surge of hybrid pastries—croissant-doughnut mashups like Dominique Ansel’s Cronut and Maury Rubin’s pretzel croissant—placing them in a broader history of pastry innovation and commerce. Pastry, the author argues, often leads culinary innovation because confectioners are alchemists who transform basic ingredients into entirely new textures and flavors. This creative tension is intensified by internal rivalries among bakers, pâtissiers, and restaurant pastry chefs, which fuels experimentation. Rubin, a former TV producer trained in Paris, pioneered New York’s pretzel croissant at City Bakery after a chance kitchen pairing produced a salty-sweet hybrid that bridged savory and sweet breakfast preferences; its profitability also reflects rising ingredient costs that squeeze traditional bakers. Rubin admires innovation but criticizes the blog-driven hype around fads like the Cronut, seeing them as “hula-hoop” phenomena that owe much to social media. Dominique Ansel’s Cronut emerged from classical French training applied in a small SoHo bakery focused on creativity and freshness; its viral launch created long lines, trademark protection, and strict production limits. The Cronut’s success—and corporate responses like Dunkin’ Donuts’ mass-market “Croissant Donut”—raises questions about commercialization, authenticity, and whether such hybrids will become enduring staples or short-lived crazes.

Syrian Deputy Foreign Minister Faisal Mekdad signaled a modest shift in the government’s stance by inviting talks with Syrian religious and community leaders who influence fighters, acknowledging links between armed opposition elements and parts of Syrian society. That concession contrasted with Damascus’s long-held portrayal of the rebellion as a foreign-led conspiracy, but practical negotiations remain stalled because the opposition is fragmented and it is unclear who can both deliver fighters and be acceptable to the regime. Mekdad expressed confidence that President Bashar al-Assad’s government had gained the upper hand militarily and diplomatically, citing the decision to surrender chemical weapons—to avoid U.S. strikes—as consistent with those gains. He also asserted, controversially, that rebels, not government forces, had fired the chemical munitions that killed hundreds in Damascus suburbs in August, a claim disputed by U.S. officials and some U.N. inspectors’ findings. Mekdad even urged an international push for Israel to relinquish its unacknowledged nuclear arsenal, framing it as a next diplomatic step. Meanwhile, the war has killed over 100,000 and displaced millions.

Jessica Raubenolt, 24, and her 21-month-old daughter Lillia, visiting from Ohio, were killed while crossing Bayshore Boulevard in Tampa after being struck by a Ford Mustang driven by 18-year-old Cameron Herrin. The mother and child were legally crossing at an intersection when witnesses said the Mustang and a gold Nissan, driven by 17-year-old John Alexander Barrineau, were racing northbound, changing lanes and revving engines shortly before the crash. Raubenolt was pronounced dead at Tampa General Hospital; Lillia died the following day after being on life support.

Cameron Herrin and Barrineau were arrested at the scene and charged with two counts each of vehicular homicide and street racing; both posted $10,000 bail and were released. Tristan Herrin, 20, a passenger in the Mustang and Cameron’s brother, faces a misdemeanor racing charge and was released on $500 bail. All three are recent graduates of Tampa Catholic High School and had no prior Florida criminal records. Family members described Jessica as a devoted mother, health and fitness advocate, and community-minded gardener who had met her husband at Kent State; they were in Florida while her husband trained for a pilot certification. Her uncle publicly forgave the young men, praying for their families and hoping something positive would result from the tragedy. The diocese and community have expressed condolences as the investigation continues.

Argentine agriculture’s rapid shift to biotech soy and associated chemical-intensive practices has produced a public-health crisis in rural provinces, an Associated Press investigation found. Since the mid-1990s adoption of genetically modified seeds and “no‑till” planting, farmers initially reduced some spraying but then increased agrochemical use as weeds became resistant and multiple annual harvests proliferated. Nationwide application rose roughly ninefold since 1990; an AP analysis shows Argentine farmers now apply about twice the pesticide concentrate per acre as U.S. farmers. In practice, chemicals are often handled and applied recklessly: crop-dusters spray near homes and schools, workers mix and load poisons without protective gear, banned buffer zones are ignored, runoff and drift contaminate wells and rivers, and discarded containers are reused for household water. Provincial rules vary widely and enforcement is weak; a federal environmental statute designed to halt harmful activities has never been used against agricultural spraying. Doctors and epidemiologists report alarming trends in farming regions: cancer rates two to four times the national average in Santa Fe, a quadrupling of congenital defects in Chaco after biotech expansion, and studies finding pesticides in 80 percent of children tested in one contaminated neighborhood. Individual tragedies — such as former worker Fabián Tomasi, now severely neurologically impaired after years of unprotected exposure — underscore the human cost. Scientists call for systematic, long-term epidemiological and toxicological studies of real-world chemical mixtures, while activists press for enforcement of existing limits and stronger protections for communities.

A new Action on Sugar analysis of 131 hot flavoured drinks sold by major UK coffee chains found alarmingly high sugar levels: 98% would receive a “red” (high) label per serving, and 35% contain as much or more sugar than a can of Coca‑Cola (about 9 tsp). The worst single product was Starbucks’ Venti Hot Mulled Fruit (Grape with Chai, Orange and Cinnamon) at 99 g of sugar — roughly 25 teaspoons, more than three times the recommended adult daily free sugar limit (7 tsp). Other extreme examples include Costa’s large Chai Latte (≈80 g, 20 tsp), Starbucks White Chocolate Mocha Venti (≈74 g, 18 tsp), and KFC’s Mocha (≈59 g, 15 tsp). Overall, 55% of drinks surveyed contain the equivalent of, or more than, the maximum recommended adult/teen daily sugar intake (30 g / 7 tsp). Even items marketed as “healthy,” such as large chai and matcha lattes, contained 11–13 teaspoons per serving. Action on Sugar highlights that oversized servings contribute to excess intake — Starbucks’ larger 454 ml and 568 ml sizes are notably bigger than competitors’ typical 340 ml medium. The campaign calls for mandatory reformulation targets, stricter labelling, bans on unhealthy product marketing and promotions, and a 20% tax on sugar‑sweetened drinks. Experts urge chains to cut added sugar, improve transparency, stop selling extra‑large sugary drinks and promote smaller or sugar‑free alternatives. Starbucks has pledged a 25% reduction in added sugar in “indulgent” drinks by 2020 and points to lighter options and in‑store nutrition information.

Journalists watching the second day of Supreme Court arguments over the constitutionality of the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate widely reported a bleak outlook for the Obama administration. Observers said Solicitor General Donald Verrilli appeared unprepared as justices, especially swing-voter Anthony Kennedy, pressed skeptical questions. Media commentators framed the session as a disaster for the administration: CNN’s Jeffrey Toobin called it “a train wreck” and predicted the law would likely be struck down; others used similarly dire metaphors. Reports noted aggressive skepticism from conservative justices Antonin Scalia, Samuel Alito, Chief Justice John Roberts and Clarence Thomas, who together constitute a conservative bloc that Kennedy could potentially join or break from. Because the mandate’s survival depends on at least one conservative justice siding with the government, Kennedy’s pointed questioning and apparent hostility were seen as particularly ominous. However, the piece cautions against overreaction: the Supreme Court’s deliberations are opaque, and media “tea leaf-reading” can exaggerate outcomes. While courtroom reports signaled trouble for the mandate, the final decision remains uncertain until the justices officially rule.

A violent shootout at a wedding in northern Afghanistan’s Baghlan province left around 20–21 people dead and multiple others wounded, underscoring the country’s fragile security. The clash erupted late Sunday in Deh Salah (Dih Salah) district during a celebration attended by roughly 400 people. Officials’ accounts vary slightly: provincial police spokesman Jawed Basharat reported 20 killed and 10 wounded; district police chief Gulistan Qusani put the toll at 21 dead and said victims were all male guests aged 14–60; other officials cited eight wounded and noted two teenage victims among the dead. Authorities say the fighting began after a verbal altercation between two armed groups at the wedding, escalating when a local security official fired warning shots and both sides then traded gunfire. Some officials suggested simmering local rivalries and a recent assassination of a relative of a provincial police official at the event may have triggered the violence. Investigators have been dispatched to the scene. The incident echoes other deadly wedding-related shootings and attacks across Afghanistan—ranging from celebratory gunfire misfire incidents to insurgent bombings and raids—highlighting how both militant attacks and local feuds claim civilian lives. The violence comes even as Afghan officials have begun talks with the Taliban and planned follow-up negotiations aimed at securing a ceasefire; militant offensives and attacks on civilians, however, have continued, including recent bombings and insurgent activity in northern provinces.

The Backstreet Boys announced 21 new dates for their Larger Than Life Las Vegas residency, running July 25 to Nov. 17, with presale for fan-club members already open and general tickets on sale Friday. During a live Twitter Q&A at the platform’s Los Angeles office, the group revealed they’ve chosen a new single and teased it will arrive “real soon.” A brief upbeat clip with the lyric “baby don’t go breaking my heart” was played; Howie Dorough called it mid-tempo and Kevin Richardson praised its piano, synths and hook. The band is working on their 10th studio album to coincide with their 25th anniversary, likely due in 2018, and may add the new song to their Vegas set.

A Baton Rouge mother, 30-year-old Schaquana Evita Spears, was arrested after admitting she struck three of her sons—ages 10, 12 and 13—after finding them burglarizing a neighbor’s home. Deputies say the boys stole electronics, a hoverboard and other items from a nearby residence; Spears ordered them to return the property and then disciplined them by whipping them with an RCA cord. The 13-year-old told child services he was struck multiple times and had lacerations and bleeding on his arms, leg, shoulder, back and stomach. The 12-year-old had cuts on his arm and the youngest a small scratch. Spears was booked on two counts of cruelty to juveniles; bail was initially $2,500 and she was released after a judge reduced it. Her attorney insists her actions did not constitute abuse and argues the arresting agency acted hastily.

The arrest sparked a heated public debate over where to draw the line between permissible parental discipline and criminal child abuse. Some neighbors and strangers defended Spears—her neighbor, whose house was burglarized, said Spears should be commended for protecting her children from criminal behavior; others across the country offered financial support for her bail and welfare. East Baton Rouge District Attorney Hillar C. Moore III said parental discipline is allowed but will review the case, noting the presence of marks and possible open wounds. Louisiana’s child welfare head, Marketa Garner Walters, stated that discipline becomes abuse when it leaves cuts, burns, blood or bruises, urging people to consult child development resources. Spears, a single mother of six and small-business caterer with no prior convictions, said she thought she was doing the right thing; her children are temporarily with their grandmother while officials review the situation.

Eight-year-old Safyre Terry, who survived a 2013 arson that killed her father and three younger siblings and left her with severe burns and the loss of a hand and foot, received an outpouring of global support after she told family she only wanted Christmas cards. Her aunt and guardian, Liz Dolder, expected only a few, but Safyre’s wish went viral. To date she has received more than 300,000 letters and cards and thousands of packages from around the world; one delivery included 195,000 items in a single day that required multiple mail trucks and a rented cargo vehicle. Schenectady Postmaster John Reilly and volunteers have been helping the family sort and open the mail, and the community plans to photograph the sprawling collection with a drone as a thank-you.

In addition to the mail, Safyre and her family have benefited from extensive charitable support. Baking Memories 4 Kids, a nonprofit that funds vacations for children with life-threatening illnesses, surprised Safyre and her extended family with a fully funded weeklong trip to Walt Disney World in February, including accommodations arranged with Give Kids the World. The surprise came during a difficult hospital stay in which Safyre had undergone more than 50 surgeries, including a recent amputation; the nomination was made by a classmate who had been helped by the same charity. A YouCaring fundraiser for Safyre has raised over $300,000, far exceeding its original $15,000 goal. Cards and gifts can still be sent to Safyre at P.O. Box 6126, Schenectady, NY 12306.

At the National Cancer Moonshot Summit, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) and IBM Watson Health announced a two-year public-private partnership to bring IBM’s Watson for Genomics into VA care with the goal of providing precision oncology for 10,000 veterans. Watson for Genomics will process de-identified genetic alteration files from tumor DNA sequencing, rapidly identify likely cancer-driving mutations, and generate evidence-ranked treatment options and links to supporting research and clinical trials. This automation aims to scale precision medicine across the VA—America’s largest integrated health system, which treats roughly 3.5% of the nation’s cancer patients—and to increase the number of veterans who can access targeted therapies by nearly 30-fold compared with current capacity.

The collaboration addresses a major bottleneck in precision oncology: the time- and labor-intensive process in which molecular tumor boards of specialists review sequencing results and literature to recommend therapies. IBM says Watson can sift vast, disparate data and surface clinically relevant insights within minutes, triaging straightforward cases to treating oncologists while flagging complex cases for expert review. Early validations with more than 20 cancer centers indicate Watson’s recommendations align closely with what multidisciplinary teams would recommend.

VA leaders highlighted veterans’ disproportionately high cancer burden and framed the program as a way to democratize access to advanced treatments regardless of geography. IBM emphasized that data and insights from Watson will be shared with the research community to advance genomic research and broader clinical benefit. The VA’s prior investments in cancer research and IBM’s development of cognitive computing and the Watson Health Cloud form the foundation for the initiative. If successful, the partnership could markedly expand precision oncology delivery across the VA, accelerate individualized treatment decisions, and contribute research findings back to the academic community.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, 85, was hospitalized after a fall in her office Wednesday evening that resulted in three fractured ribs on her left side. She initially went home but sought care at George Washington University Hospital the next morning due to discomfort; tests confirmed the fractures and she was admitted for observation and treatment. The fall forced her to miss the formal investiture of new Justice Brett Kavanaugh. Ginsburg, the court’s oldest member and leader of its liberal wing, has a long history of serious health challenges—surviving colon and pancreatic cancers and receiving a coronary stent in 2014—and previously fractured ribs in 2012. Appointed by President Bill Clinton in 1993, she has been influential on gender-discrimination and reproductive-rights jurisprudence and said in 2018 she planned to serve at least five more years. The court pledged to provide updates as they become available.

The Senate Standing Committee of Correspondents has tabled Breitbart News’ application for permanent Senate Press Gallery credentials and will not renew the outlet’s temporary Capitol access when it expires at the end of May. Committee members cited unresolved questions about Breitbart’s editorial independence, ties to former chairman Steve Bannon and to the Mercer-funded Government Accountability Institute, inconsistent information about its masthead and lack of a proper Washington office. CEO Larry Solov said Breitbart is independent, that a listed managing editor had resigned, and that office searches are ongoing. The committee said Breitbart may reapply if it resolves concerns; meanwhile temporary credentials for three staffers will lapse.

A Manhattan criminal judge has ordered Twitter to turn over a Brooklyn writer’s tweets to prosecutors investigating his role in the Occupy Wall Street Brooklyn Bridge arrests, highlighting how public social media posts can be used as evidence. Judge Matthew Sciarrino Jr. rejected arguments that Twitter’s users retain exclusive control over their content once posted publicly, writing that “what you give to the public belongs to the public.” The subpoena sought all of Malcolm Harris’s tweets from shortly before the Occupy protests began in 2011 through year-end; prosecutors say the messages might contradict Harris’s expected defense that police had escorted protesters into the roadway. Harris’s lawyer moved to quash the subpoena as overly broad and improperly served; the judge dismissed the motion partly because Twitter’s terms grant it broad distribution rights and the tweets had been public. Twitter itself contested the subpoena but was ordered to comply. The ACLU filed a friend-of-the-court brief urging that courts require warrants for such requests and allow users an opportunity to oppose them.

The ruling occurs amid broader disclosure from Twitter about law enforcement demands: from January through June the company received 849 government requests for user data, granting 63% overall and 75% of U.S. requests (679). Twitter says U.S. agencies made 80% of requests and that government demands have risen sharply in 2012. The company notifies users of requests unless legally barred and preserves requested data when asked; it complied with none of six foreign government requests cited and removed 5,275 tweets after complying with 38% of 3,378 copyright takedown requests. The developments underscore growing tensions between public social-media expression, user privacy, and law enforcement’s use of pervasive digital records.

Reports say Mike Huckabee will launch the Huckabee Post, an online news site seeking reporters via a Craigslist ad and listing offices in New York and Washington, D.C. The ad describes the venture as covering politics, U.S. and international news, media, sports and general news. Representatives had not responded to inquiries. The move follows a trend of conservative personalities turning personal brands into media outlets, like Glenn Beck’s TheBlaze and Andrew Sullivan’s The Dish. Huckabee, former Arkansas governor (1996–2007) and 2008 Republican presidential contender who briefly led that race, has kept the door open to another presidential bid in 2016. He’s been conducting interviews and meeting potential donors while weighing the financial and professional costs of campaigning, including giving up Fox pay if he mounts a serious run. Huckabee’s appeal combines social conservatism, evangelical ties and blue-collar resonance; polling shows strength in early states, but fundraising concerns and the challenge of translating media visibility into votes remain central obstacles.

An advanced tsunami early-warning system that could have reduced fatalities in the recent Sulawesi disaster remains stalled in testing after years of delays, inter-agency disputes and lack of modest funding. The high-tech network of seafloor sensors, acoustic signaling and fiber-optic links was developed as a successor to post-2004-basin efforts and built to prototype with $3 million from the U.S. National Science Foundation and partners including Woods Hole and Indonesian scientists. But the project never moved past the prototype because agencies could not agree on responsibilities and a final 1 billion rupiah (~$69,000) to complete cabling was not delivered. That gap left Indonesia reliant on a weaker system of 134 tidal gauges, land seismographs, some sirens and text alerts; none of 22 buoys set up earlier are functioning due to vandalism, theft or lack of maintenance. When a magnitude-7.5 quake struck near Palu and Donggala, waves up to 6 meters killed at least 832 people, exposing limitations in detection, model assumptions (which often ignore submarine landslides and complex multi-event sequences) and public preparedness. Power outages disabled sirens and many residents did not evacuate. Experts stress that the prototype could provide authoritative detection in 1–3 minutes versus far longer from current gauges, and that seafloor surveys will be needed to determine whether the tsunami arose from vertical motion on a mostly strike-slip fault, submarine landslides, or a combination. Failure to finish the network and improve public training contributed to the tragedy.

Merriam-Webster released the sixth edition of The Official Scrabble Players Dictionary, adding more than 300 entries and expanding the official lexicon players may use. Notable inclusions are the short, game-changing two-letter word OK, interjections like ew and yowza, and zen, all useful for the strategy of fitting and scoring on tight boards. The update also adds qapik — one of roughly 20 new playable q-words that do not require a following u — which players prize for opening flexibility. High-scoring playable terms include bizjet (especially as a plural for a bingo play), and several vowel-rich words such as arancini. Merriam-Webster consulted the North American Scrabble Players Association during the revision and omitted a contested candidate, RBI, after competitive players raised concerns despite some recognition of rib-ee in usage.

The new edition reflects changing language patterns tied to texting and social media: transcribed speech (ew, mm-hmm), slang and tech terms now seen often in writing (emoji, facepalm, botnet, bokeh), and culturally borrowed words that have become mainstream (bibimbap, cotija, sriracha, schneid). Editor Peter Sokolowski singled out macaron as a favorite on meaning rather than score. The official Scrabble dictionary, first issued by Merriam-Webster in 1976, now contains over 100,000 words and is periodically refreshed to mirror evolving English usage and Scrabble play.

An elderly Bedford, Pennsylvania, homeowner and her daughter were shocked to find an unknown man living in an upstairs closet of the woman’s two-story house after hearing noises. The woman, in her 80s and largely confined to the first floor because of mobility issues, had a caretaker who had introduced them to her boyfriend, later identified as Mark Potts. Police say Potts had moved several suitcases, a duffel bag and other personal items into the upstairs room and had been secretly residing there for several weeks without bringing new furniture. When officers located him, Potts was carrying a small handgun. Bedford County District Attorney Bill Higgins said the intruder’s presence likely destroyed the homeowner’s sense of security; Potts faces criminal trespassing charges. Authorities are also investigating the caretaker’s role, and Higgins expects charges against her for allegedly assisting Potts. The incident highlights vulnerabilities faced by immobile seniors and raises concerns about oversight of caretakers and home security.

A hydrogen or steam-related explosion tore off the outer wall and roof of Fukushima Daiichi’s No. 1 reactor building after the March quake and tsunami disabled power and crippled cooling systems. Authorities vented pressure to protect containment, and Japanese officials said the reactor’s inner steel containment remained intact even though the turbine/concrete structure was heavily damaged. Traces of radioactive materials, including cesium, were detected outside the plant, indicating fuel damage, and some workers suffered radiation sickness; up to 160 people may have been exposed. Officials distributed guidance to nearby residents—stay indoors, seal openings, use wet towels and iodine—and urged calm while assessing core conditions. Experts warned a meltdown risk if core cooling failed; the presence of spent fuel in a nearby pool added concern. Analysts and agencies differed on severity: many stressed design differences from Chernobyl that would limit releases even if core damage occurred, while others cautioned the situation remained very serious and uncertain until workers can inspect fuel—possibly months. Tepco’s decision to flood the core with seawater suggested the plant might be abandoned, and every hour of restored cooling was deemed crucial.

Researchers at Georgia Tech used ThermoChemical NanoLithography (TCNL) with an atomic force microscope to create "Mini Lisa," a grayscale Mona Lisa replica just one-third the width of a human hair (~30 microns wide). The team heated the AFM cantilever tip and lowered it pixel-by-pixel onto a polymer "molecular canvas" whose surface sites were protected by capping groups. Local heating triggered confined nanoscale chemistry: more heat produced a higher concentration of new surface molecules and therefore lighter tones when stained with fluorescent dye; less heat produced darker tones. Pixels measured 125 nm and the image was 240 × 320 pixels. Currently TCNL can pattern amine and carboxyl group gradients, but researchers expect compatibility with other chemistries and properties (e.g., graphene conductivity). TCNL offers high spatial resolution, relatively fast processing, and potential applications in nanoelectronics, optoelectronics, bioengineering, lab-on-a-chip devices, and scalable smart-material surface patterning.

After spending nearly a year aboard the International Space Station, astronaut Scott Kelly arrived in Houston about two inches taller than his identical twin, Mark — a temporary effect caused by spinal elongation in microgravity. Kelly and Russian cosmonaut Mikhail Kornienko spent 342 days on the ISS to help scientists study long-term spaceflight impacts ahead of future missions to Mars. NASA used Mark as an Earthbound control in a unique twin study examining genetic expression, aging, immune function, arterial plaque, vision changes, cognition, and gut microbiome shifts. Fresh blood samples and parallel psychological tests improve data quality. Kelly was welcomed home by family, Gabrielle Giffords, and dignitaries; he emphasized the mission as NASA’s achievement and looks forward to public briefings and reuniting with loved ones.

Joan Fontaine, the Oscar-winning actress celebrated for her delicate beauty and portrayals of vulnerable romantic heroines, died Dec. 15 at her home in Carmel, Calif. She was 96. Fontaine rose to stardom in the late 1930s and early 1940s, becoming best known for her work with Alfred Hitchcock: she earned an Academy Award nomination for Rebecca (1940) opposite Laurence Olivier and won the 1942 best actress Oscar for Suspicion (1941) opposite Cary Grant—making her the only actor to win an Oscar for a Hitchcock film. She also received a nomination for The Constant Nymph (1943) and gave notable performances in Jane Eyre (1943), September Affair (1950), Ivanhoe (1952) and the racially charged Island in the Sun (1957).

Born Joan de Beauvoir de Havilland on Oct. 22, 1917, in Tokyo to British parents, Fontaine moved to the U.S. as a child when her mother pushed her and sister Olivia into acting. Her early career included bit parts and a breakthrough in The Women (1939), which led to a contract with producer David O. Selznick. Fontaine adopted her stepfather’s surname as a stage name. She battled studio demands and at times was dropped by RKO, later fighting for stronger roles and alternating high and low points in her filmography.

Fontaine’s life was marked by one of Hollywood’s most enduring sibling feuds with her older sister, Olivia de Havilland; tensions that began in childhood continued through awards ceremonies and family disputes and ultimately led to a permanent rift after their mother’s death in 1975. Fontaine wrote about this rivalry in her 1978 memoir No Bed of Roses.

Beyond acting she was an accomplished pilot, prize-winning balloonist, Cordon Bleu-level cook and interior decorator. Married four times, she had two daughters. Fontaine continued to work on stage and television into later decades and remained a notable figure in film history for her sensitive performances and classic Hollywood presence.

A new NBC News/Wall Street Journal poll finds Americans increasingly anxious about security following Islamic State’s beheadings of U.S. journalists and its rapid gains in Iraq and Syria. Forty-seven percent now say the United States is less safe than before 9/11—up sharply from 20 percent in 2002 and 28 percent last year—while only 26 percent believe the country is safer. Awareness of the beheadings is near-universal at 94 percent, higher than recent major news events the poll has tracked. More than six in ten respondents favor military action against ISIS. President Obama planned a primetime address outlining an expanded campaign relying on intensified airstrikes, allied support, and no large-scale ground deployments; officials warn the effort could take years. Pollsters and commentators say the public, though war-weary, has “woken up” to the threat. Analysts trace the broader struggle against Islamist militancy from the 1979 Iranian revolution through 9/11, Afghanistan and the 2003 Iraq invasion, arguing the current conflict is long-term and complex. Views differ on causes and remedies: some blame U.S. policy failures and regional politics for creating a vacuum that helped ISIS, while others fault recent troop withdrawals. Experts caution there may be no quick victory—terms like “manageable” goals replace “winnable”—and some liken the likely duration to a prolonged Cold War–style contest with high human cost.

The writer wakes with a hangover after several drinks and reflects on Kristi Coulter’s essay arguing that many modern women drink to cope with living in a sexist world. That piece resonated widely and sparked debate: some critics say men drink for similar reasons and that capitalism, not patriarchy, is to blame. The author acknowledges patriarchy shapes many choices but finds it hard to prove it drives particular behaviors like drinking. Cultural models—Olivia Pope, Sex and the City—also normalize booze as coping and bonding, blurring cause and effect.

Now newly sober, the author notices ubiquitous alcohol cues: rosé displays, workplace bottles, drink-centric events, and classes combining wine with yoga or cooking. Social rituals often presume drinking—farmer’s-market sympathy recommends “wine immediately,” company events pressure you to sip, and baby showers or movie nights center alcohol. Women frequently toast hardships with drinks: after sexist workplace panels the author and friends celebrate with pricey cocktails, laughing and numbing rather than demanding change. That behavior can comfort and bond, and the author admits wine sometimes catalyzed decisive actions—ending relationships or career shifts—but worries it can also mollify and perpetuate inaction.

Sober, the author grows angrier at the relentless expectations placed on women: performative empowerment, unpaid labor, harassment, and shrinking rights. She rejects the “24-hour woman” ideal and the cultural myth that women must do everything. Recovery brings clarity and solidarity: quieter, deliberate pleasures, mutual recognition among women, and plotting tangible change. The conclusion: whether booze is a symptom of patriarchy or broader exhaustion, the important question is what women do when they gather—let’s strategize together, with or without wine.

The Trump administration announced it will terminate Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for about 200,000 Salvadoran immigrants on Sept. 9, 2019, giving them 18 months to leave, seek lawful residency, or prepare for return to El Salvador. TPS had been granted after devastating 2001 earthquakes. Officials said the decision reflects El Salvador’s recovery — rebuilt schools, homes and hospitals and millions in aid — and argued TPS was always meant to be temporary. The move is part of a broader push to tighten immigration enforcement; in recent months the administration also ended TPS for Haiti and Nicaragua and may end Honduras’ status later this year. In all, changes to TPS could expose roughly 250,000 people to deportation over two years.

Advocates and immigrant groups condemned the decision, warning it ignores ongoing violence, political instability and a weak economy in El Salvador, and will break up families: about 275,000 U.S.-born children have a parent who is a TPS holder. Individual stories underscore the stakes: Salvadorans who have lived and worked in the U.S. for decades, pay taxes and raise U.S.-born children face uprooting. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce urged extensions, citing labor impacts in construction, food processing, hospitality and healthcare. Congressional Democrats called for permanent solutions but face political hurdles, as talks over protections for Dreamers and tougher immigration measures complicate negotiations. Supporters of restriction argue long extensions have undermined TPS’s temporary intent. El Salvador’s government welcomed the delayed termination and said it will seek alternatives and press the U.S. Congress for protections for its citizens.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet donated crawl data to the Internet Archive; these daily inflows are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo. Separately, a group led by Russian scientist Dr. Igor Ashurbeyli has proposed creating Asgardia—a self-styled “nation in space” intended to be independent of Earthbound states. Announced in Paris and promoted online, Asgardia borrows its name from Norse myth and aims to foster peace, broaden access to space technology, and protect Earth from cosmic and man-made threats like space debris and asteroids. The project envisions a legal, scientific and technological platform rather than an immediate orbital settlement: its initial territory would be a single satellite planned for launch, while citizens would remain physically on Earth but also claim Asgardian citizenship. Ashurbeyli says once registrations exceed 100,000, Asgardia could apply to the UN for state status. The initiative plans public competitions to design a flag and anthem and emphasizes inclusivity—“any human living on Earth can become a citizen.” Proponents argue Asgardia could create an independent regulatory framework, shifting responsibility for space activities from nation-states to the new entity and opening access for countries lacking space agencies. Critics and space-law experts caution that Asgardia faces major legal obstacles: the Outer Space Treaty ties liability to launching states, and international recognition requires territory, population, and acceptance by other nations. Historical precedents, like the unrecognized “Nation of Celestial Space,” suggest skepticism, though thousands registered interest rapidly after the launch announcement.

A $6.3 million grant from The Leona M. and Harry B. Helmsley Charitable Trust will fund efforts to improve survival after cardiac arrest across Iowa. The Iowa Department of Health will use the money to buy LUCAS 2 Chest Compression System devices for ambulances and hospitals and to provide training for their use. The LUCAS 2 automates chest compressions, enabling longer, more consistent CPR delivery than manual compressions. Each device costs about $10,000, and studies suggest LUCAS-style devices can improve CPR outcomes by roughly 5 to 50 percent. The grant leverages the Helmsley trust’s philanthropy; Leona Helmsley, historically known as the “Queen of Mean,” left a large estate that has been the subject of legal scrutiny. Separately, in New York, nine years after her death, a court dispute over her estate resumed: the state attorney general challenged a requested $100 million executor fee sought by executors of Helmsley’s roughly $4.78 billion estate. The attorney general called the fee “astronomical” and sought a substantial reduction, potentially cutting it by about 90 percent. Together, the items underline continuing public and legal impacts from Helmsley’s fortune—funding life-saving health equipment in Iowa while prompting high-profile legal contestation over executor compensation in New York.

The 111th Congress adjourned after a tumultuous two years that balanced sweeping legislative achievements with deep public frustration. Dominated by Democrats, it enacted the largest package of laws since the 1960s: an $814 billion stimulus that created or saved about 3.3 million jobs, comprehensive financial reform, major health-care overhaul extending coverage to millions, pay-equity measures, expanded children’s health programs, FDA tobacco and food-safety powers, confirmation of two Supreme Court justices, and ratification of the New START arms treaty. In a lame-duck session it extended tax cuts, repealed “don’t ask, don’t tell,” and aided 9/11 responders. Yet intense polarization, town-hall unrest and the rise of the Tea Party produced a voter backlash that cost Democrats the House and trimmed their Senate edge. Economically, markets rebounded and some firms recovered, but high unemployment and partisan gridlock leave future legislative progress uncertain.

XPRIZE has launched a three-year global competition to spur rapid advances in ocean mapping technology, offering a $7 million purse and the prestige of being an “XPRIZE Winner.” Despite covering about 70 percent of Earth, only roughly 5–7 percent of the ocean floor has been meaningfully mapped—more of the moon and Mars are charted than our own seafloor. The Shell Ocean Discovery XPRIZE, announced at the AGU Fall Meeting in San Francisco and run in partnership with NOAA and Shell, aims to change that by encouraging teams worldwide to develop robotic platforms capable of operating to depths up to 4,000 meters.

Competing systems must be launched from shore or air and complete tasks including producing high-resolution seafloor maps, capturing high-definition images of specified objects, and identifying notable features in a “treasure hunt” assessment. Testing will proceed in stages at 2,000 m and then 4,000 m. The top prize distribution includes $4 million for first place, $1 million for second, $1 million split among other top teams, and an extra $1 million “bonus” funded by NOAA for systems that can detect and follow chemical or biological signals in the water column—useful for locating hydrothermal vents or deep-sea life.

XPRIZE frames the challenge as highly interdisciplinary, requiring underwater robotics, computer vision, digital imagery, and more. It’s the third in a five-prize Ocean Initiative series aimed at addressing critical ocean challenges by 2020; previous prizes focused on oil spill cleanup and ocean pH sensors. Registration is open to anyone worldwide for nine months, with tests scheduled after registration closes. XPRIZE and partners emphasize openness and broad participation to accelerate innovation and uncover the deep ocean’s unknowns. For details and registration, teams are directed to the XPRIZE ocean discovery website.

NORAD’s long-running Santa-tracking tradition has shifted mapping partners: after five years with Google, NORAD teamed with Microsoft Bing and will run its Santa Tracker on Microsoft’s Windows Azure and Bing Maps this Christmas Eve, also offering Windows 8, Windows Phone 8, and Android apps. NORAD says the split was mutual and not due to any problems; Google will continue its own Santa-tracking efforts with a new route algorithm, a Santa Tracker website, a Chrome extension, Android app, and social updates. Both services begin tracking on Dec. 24 (NORAD at 2 a.m. ET, Google at 2 a.m. PT). NORAD’s decades-old effort—dating to 1955—uses radar, satellites, “Santa Cams,” and fighter jets to mock-authoritatively follow Santa, and draws millions of users annually; NORAD expects roughly 25 million visitors this year. NORAD updates will also be available via Twitter, Facebook, a dedicated phone line (1-877-HI-NORAD), and email, while Google will keep hosting related videos on YouTube and offer interactive Santa-themed features and games.

Liana Barrientos, a 39-year-old Bronx woman, was arrested and faces multiple charges after authorities say she married 10 men between 1999 and 2010 in what prosecutors allege was a marriage-for-immigration scheme. She was arrested after failing to pay a subway fare with her niece and is charged with theft of service and criminal trespass; she had earlier been arraigned on two felony counts of filing a false instrument, pleading not guilty. The indictment centers on a 2010 marriage to Salle Keita, where Barrientos allegedly filed a marriage license asserting it was her first and only marriage. Investigators from ICE and Homeland Security brought the case to the Bronx DA after discovering multiple prior nuptials—nine between 1999 and 2002—many overlapping, with Barrientos at one point married to as many as eight men simultaneously and currently believed to be married to four. Seven of the grooms came from countries flagged by authorities (Egypt, Turkey, Georgia, Pakistan, Mali). One spouse, Rashid Rajput of Pakistan, was deported in 2006 after a Joint Terrorism Task Force probe. Prosecutors say several of the men later sought permanent status based on marriage to Barrientos; when denied, some filed for divorce and attempted to refile using other marriages. Records show she used her real Social Security number on marriage documents but varied the spelling or form of her name. In one instance she admitted receiving money for her actions, yet told Homeland Security she hadn’t met nine of the men. National security experts warned the pattern reveals weaknesses in oversight. If convicted on the false-instrument charges, Barrientos faces up to four years in prison.

Peggy Sue Gerron Rackham, the Texas woman who inspired Buddy Holly’s 1958 hit “Peggy Sue,” died Monday at University Medical Center in Lubbock at age 78, hospital officials confirmed. Her family authorized confirmation of the death but asked that further details not be released. Gerron, born in Olton, Texas, later moved to Lubbock, where she attended high school and became part of the social circle that included Holly and his friends. She remained closely associated with the singer’s legacy and in 2008 published a memoir, Whatever Happened to Peggy Sue?: A Memoir by Buddy Holly’s Peggy Sue, timed to mark the 50th anniversary of the song. The book drew on roughly 150 diary entries Gerron kept during the years she knew Holly; she said the memoir was intended to “give him his voice” and recalled Holly as “probably one of the best friends I ever had.” Gerron married Jerry Allison, the drummer for Holly’s band The Crickets; the couple later divorced. Family members noted that the song’s naming had an informal origin: her son-in-law, Tom Stathos, said the tune initially had a different working name—reportedly “Cindy Lou,” the name of Holly’s niece—before Allison persuaded Holly to change it to “Peggy Sue” to impress her. Buddy Holly, who also wrote hits like “That’ll Be the Day” and “Maybe Baby,” later wrote a sequel-style song titled “Peggy Sue Got Married.” Holly’s life was cut short in the Feb. 3, 1959 plane crash in Iowa that killed Ritchie Valens and J.P. “The Big Bopper” Richardson. Lubbock honors Holly’s memory at the Buddy Holly Center, celebrating him as the city’s most famous native son. The report concludes with unrelated notes about web archiving efforts to preserve pages and fix broken links.

Cerro Gordo, a 19th-century mining ghost town in the Inyo Mountains near Death Valley, has been sold to a group led by Brent Underwood and Jon Bier for $1.4 million, after being listed at $925,000. The closing took place on Friday the 13th, a fitting date for a town famed for its Wild West history — at its height it produced large quantities of silver and lead, swelled to around 5,000 people, and was notorious enough that a listing joked it “averaged a murder a week.” The property comprises more than 300 acres, 22 remaining structures — including a saloon with two out-of-tune pianos, an abandoned hotel (Belshaw Bunkhouse), church, bunkhouse, superintendent’s house and hoist house — and patented mining claims. Many artifacts are preserved in an onsite museum, and the town was protected from looters while in family hands for decades.

The buyers assembled a Los Angeles–based investor group that includes entrepreneurs and hospitality figures; their offer was chosen over higher bids because the sellers favored their preservation-minded plan and commitment to public access. Underwood, who runs a backpacker hostel in Austin, says the goal is to maintain the town’s historical integrity while making selective renovations to host visitors. Initial work — estimated at about $1 million — will focus on structural stabilization, securing water (there’s no running water currently), and enabling extended stays. Plans include adding Wi-Fi, refurbishing select buildings for lodging, and eventually hosting events such as writing retreats, music and theater performances, dining experiences, photo shoots, stargazing, and guided hikes.

Longtime caretaker Robert Desmarais, who has lived in Cerro Gordo for over two decades, will remain. Both buyers and the seller’s family emphasize stewardship of the site’s cultural significance: the new owners want to tell its story, preserve artifacts and architecture, and open the unique historical destination to a wider public while protecting its Wild West character.

Jordan Peele’s Get Out is a debut feature that fuses genre craft with a pointed racial critique, delivering both genuine terror and incisive satire. Drawing on influences from Guess Who’s Coming to Dinner, Rosemary’s Baby and Invasion of the Body Snatchers, the film uses familiar horror conventions not to lampoon but to intensify its social message: racism operates not only through overt hostility but through liberal complacency, fetishization and microaggressions. Peele—already renowned for his documentary-quality parody work on Key & Peele—proves himself a confident filmmaker who controls tone, pace and suspense with unusual maturity for a first feature.

The story follows Chris (Daniel Kaluuya), a 26-year-old photographer who visits the estate of his white girlfriend Rose’s (Allison Williams) affluent parents. Rose assures him of their liberal bona fides, yet subtle and then increasingly menacing incidents — from a suspiciously slow police interaction to backhanded comments about Chris’s “genetic makeup” — escalate into a nightmare. The Armitage family, led by Catherine Keener and Bradley Whitford as a psychiatrist and neurosurgeon, are disturbingly polite, and their black housekeeper and groundskeeper display hypnotic servility that hints at something far more sinister. LilRel Howery’s Rod offers comic relief and a wary counterpoint as Chris’s skeptical best friend.

Peele’s strengths lie in casting, atmosphere and a handheld-camera anxiety that keeps the viewer aligned with Chris’s growing paranoia. Kaluuya’s expressive, watchful performance anchors the film; supporting actors are uniformly strong. The film opens with a prologue that plays on contemporary fears about black vulnerability in white suburbs, setting expectations the movie then subverts in several “rug-pull” moments.
