Peele borrows nods to Kubrick in his surreal hypnosis sequences, marrying visual rigor to the film’s thematic core.

Ultimately, Get Out is a memorable, righteous horror film: frightening, funny and deeply relevant. It refuses to separate entertainment from social commentary, transforming everyday racial anxieties into visceral cinematic terror while demonstrating Jordan Peele’s emergence as a major new voice in genre filmmaking.

The It Gets Better initiative seeks support to help LGBT youth through donations, participation, and spreading hope. Contributions fund resources, awareness, suicide prevention, and anti-bullying programs. Supporters can record and submit It Gets Better videos or share written stories if they don’t have video equipment. People are encouraged to take the pledge to actively promote the project’s message of hope. Financial support is also welcomed by purchasing items from the project’s store, buying the It Gets Better book, or donating $25 to send a book to a local library or school to further community impact.

Airbus’s A350 XWB aims to make long-haul flying less grueling for passengers, airlines, and crews by combining advanced materials, aerodynamic design, and cabins tuned to human biology. More than half the aircraft’s structure uses carbon fiber–reinforced plastic, reducing weight, corrosion risk, and fuel needs. Larger, bird-inspired wings (about 20% bigger and 10% wider than prior generations) and a redesigned flap system that follows the flight path instead of the wind cut drag, noise, and improve low-speed performance. Paired with ultra-efficient Rolls‑Royce engines, Airbus claims roughly 25% better fuel economy versus similar competitor models. To combat jet lag, the cabin features LED lighting that shifts color temperature to mimic natural daylight and align with circadian rhythms; air is refreshed every two to three minutes and cabin pressure is maintained at a 6,000-foot equivalent for greater comfort. The slightly wider fuselage yields marginally roomier economy seats and easier aisle movement, while interiors and avionics follow an open, adaptable architecture so airlines can reconfigure cabins and update systems more easily over the jet’s projected 30-year life. Backed by $15 billion in R&D and 2,600 flight-test hours, the A350—already in service with carriers like Qatar Airways—aims to outcompete Boeing’s long-range models, though operational teething issues remain a watchpoint.

Britain announced a plan to ban sales of new petrol and diesel cars and vans from 2040 as a central measure in a wider clean-air strategy intended to protect public health and meet pollution limits. Environment Secretary Michael Gove framed the phase-out as essential to curb health harms and climate damage from internal combustion engines. The government pledged roughly £1.4–£3 billion in measures covering investments in ultra-low emission vehicles, charging infrastructure, retrofitting public transport, targeted scrappage schemes, local air-quality grants, and support for cycling and walking. Local authorities will receive funding and must produce plans to tackle pollution hotspots, with measures including retrofitting buses, reprogramming traffic lights, changing road layouts and, as a last resort, introducing “clean air zones” that could levy charges on the most polluting vehicles.

The announcement follows legal pressure after a judge found the prior plan unlawful and echoes France’s similar 2040 deadline. Proponents and experts see the signal as accelerating the inevitable shift to electric, plug-in hybrid and hydrogen vehicles, though current uptake is small and barriers remain: cost, range anxiety and charging availability. Industry leaders warn that achieving the transition will demand major investment, planning and industrial capability to avoid job losses. Campaigners and city leaders welcomed the long-term commitment but urged immediate, concrete actions and funding—especially scrappage support and stronger local measures—arguing the government must rapidly reduce illegal pollution that is linked to thousands of premature deaths annually.

On Wednesday, Elizabeth Midlarsky, a Jewish professor at Columbia University’s Teachers College who researches and teaches about the Holocaust, discovered two red spray-painted swastikas and the anti‑Semitic slur “Yid” in the entryway to her private office. Shocked and shaken, she reported the vandalism to campus security; a different staff member had entered the office earlier that morning and noticed nothing unusual. The NYPD Hate Crimes Task Force is investigating the incident as aggravated harassment. Midlarsky, 77, a longtime faculty member whose work on Holocaust-related topics and public visibility previously made her a target, noted the act in the context of a broader national rise in anti‑Semitic crimes and changing cultural climate. Her office had been vandalized before in 2007, when a swastika was spray‑painted on her door and anti‑Semitic flyers were left in her mailbox; no arrests were made in that case. The current episode is part of a wider pattern of threats at Teachers College this week: three professors received manila envelopes bearing swastika images, and a former African‑American professor received a noose image, according to the NYPD. Columbia and Teachers College leaders condemned the attacks. Thomas Bailey, president of Teachers College, called the graffiti an expression of hatred with no place in society and pledged cooperation with police to find the perpetrator, reaffirming the college’s commitment to a respectful, safe environment. Both the Office of University Life and Barnard College issued statements denouncing the act and expressing support for Jewish students and faculty. No arrests have been made.

President-elect Donald Trump tweeted that burning the American flag should be a crime, suggesting penalties including loss of citizenship or up to a year in jail. His proposal clashes with longstanding Supreme Court precedent: in Texas v. Johnson (1989) and United States v. Eichman (1990), the Court ruled flag burning is protected symbolic speech under the First Amendment and struck down laws banning desecration. Stripping citizenship as punishment would also run afoul of earlier rulings and constitutional protections; a 1958 decision rejected expatriation as criminal punishment and legal analysts called Trump’s suggestion unconstitutional. Trump’s tweet prompted mixed reactions from fellow Republicans: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell publicly defended the Court’s decisions and the First Amendment, as did House leaders like Kevin McCarthy and Rep. Justin Amash, who warned against abridging free speech. Some lawmakers, including John McCain, said they disapproved of flag burning but acknowledged the legal protection. The debate was reignited amid post-election protests where flags were burned and campus controversies, such as Hampshire College removing its flag. Historically, Congress has twice tried to ban flag desecration and a constitutional amendment has been proposed repeatedly but never passed.

The document is a sprawling compilation of celebrity business ventures, cultural influence, and media tidbits, stitched from many sources. It opens noting that since 1996 Alexa Internet has donated daily web crawl data to the Internet Archive, which feeds the Wayback Machine after embargoes. Much of the rest catalogs high-profile celebrity successes and spectacular failures in business and branding. A listpiece highlights 15 failed celebrity ventures—examples include Hulk Hogan’s short-lived Pastamania restaurant and Vince McMahon’s XFL, a one-season football league undermined by poor talent and wrestling-style storylines. The article underscores how fame does not guarantee business acumen, though large personal fortunes can soften fallout. Interspersed are profiles of major celebrity entrepreneurs: Gene Simmons of Kiss emphasizes relentless monetization and massive merchandising—over 5,000 licensed items—while maintaining a teetotal, work-focused persona. Jay-Z receives an extended profile tracing his rise from Brooklyn’s Marcy Projects to a diversified brand empire: Roc-A-Fella Records, Rocawear (sold for $204 million), sports and hospitality ventures, a $150 million Live Nation deal, and cultural clout that reaches politics. The piece emphasizes his philosophy—“you are the product”—and his ability to translate artistic credibility into business legitimacy while arguing hip-hop’s broad social influence. Lighter entertainment fragments cover Jessica Simpson’s on-camera gaffes and celebrity alcohol and beverage ventures: Justin Timberlake’s 901 tequila, Clooney’s Casamigos, Fergie’s Voli vodka, Diddy’s stake in Cîroc, Brangelina’s Miraval rosé, Bethenny Frankel’s Skinnygirl line, Kenny Chesney’s rum, Hanson’s “Mmmhops” beer, and others—demonstrating how stars leverage fame into lifestyle brands with mixed results.

President Donald Trump visited Cedar Rapids, Iowa, for his first trip to the state since taking office, delivering a familiar, campaign-style rally as he sought to shore up support amid growing troubles in Washington. Speaking for over an hour to an enthusiastic crowd at a community college and later a downtown arena, Trump attacked the media, derided the Russia probe as a “witch hunt,” and framed his tenure as a streak of victories despite limited legislative progress and sub-40 percent approval ratings in many polls.

Trump repeatedly touted economic indicators—job gains and a rising stock market—as proof that his policies are working. He praised wealthy members of his team, such as top economic adviser Gary Cohn and Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross, arguing he preferred affluent appointees for certain posts (“I just don’t want a poor person — does that make sense?”). He also previewed continued efforts to secure funding for a border wall with Mexico, floating the idea of building a “solar wall” and noting that solar proposals had been submitted to the Department of Homeland Security.

The president reveled in recent Republican special election successes in Georgia and South Carolina, celebrating a string of GOP wins and mocking Democratic efforts, including criticism of the large sums spent in the Georgia race for Jon Ossoff. He cast those outcomes as validation of his base’s strength and sent tweets and a post-rally text boasting that the “MAGA Mandate is stronger than ever.”

Despite embracing the campaign atmosphere, Trump acknowledged political headwinds: his legislative agenda was stalled, Democrats were unlikely to cooperate on major initiatives such as health care overhaul, and he faced an ongoing federal probe into possible Russian interference and links to his campaign. He invoked the near-fatal shooting of Rep. Steve Scalise as a unifying moment but remained pessimistic about short-term bipartisan breakthroughs.

On foreign policy, Trump spoke about the “bad hand” of challenges like North Korea’s nuclear program and expressed frustration with perceived limited help from China despite his working relationship with President Xi Jinping. The rally also featured typical elements of his political events—hecklers removed by police, “Drain the Swamp” signage, and frequent jabs at opponents—underscoring Trump’s comfort and apparent preference for energizing rallies over governing from the White House.

Clint Eastwood’s American Sniper dominated Super Bowl weekend box office, earning $30.7 million in its third weekend—just shy of the $31.1 million record set by 2008’s Hannah Montana concert but surpassing Dear John’s $30.5 million for the second-highest Super Bowl weekend ever. The film also became the highest-grossing war movie domestically ($247.98 million), overtaking Saving Private Ryan. New releases fared modestly against the NFL-focused weekend: Project Almanac and The Loft opened after delays and drew weak interest, while family favorite Paddington held strong with about $8.5 million. Project Almanac (B CinemaScore) and Black or White ($6.5M, A- CinemaScore) aimed at younger and adult audiences respectively; Black or White featured Kevin Costner and Octavia Spencer and saw mostly viewers over 25. The Loft underperformed with $2.9 million. Overall theater attendance dipped for the game day.

Federal prosecutors have recommended felony charges against retired Gen. David Petraeus for allegedly mishandling classified information, though no charges have been filed and Attorney General Eric Holder must decide whether to prosecute. The recommendation follows an FBI cyberstalking probe that began when Jill Kelley, a friend of Petraeus, reported anonymous threatening emails about her relationship with him. Agents traced the messages to Paula Broadwell, who had been researching Petraeus for a biography, and while examining her emails uncovered evidence of an extramarital affair between Broadwell and Petraeus that reportedly began in 2011 after he became CIA director. Petraeus resigned from the CIA three days after President Obama’s re-election and publicly admitted the affair, calling his conduct “extremely poor judgment” after 37 years of marriage. President Obama, shortly after the resignation, said he had no evidence Petraeus disclosed classified information in a way that harmed national security and lauded Petraeus’s career, expressing hope the matter would remain a “single side note.” Investigators, however, concluded the disclosures—regardless of demonstrable harm—constituted a significant security breach for a highly trusted intelligence official and urged charges, noting that lower-ranking officials have been prosecuted for lesser leaks. The FBI director, James Comey, declined to explain delays in the probe when asked, and Justice Department spokesman Marc Raimondi and Petraeus’s lawyer provided no substantive comment. Some officials view media leaks about the recommendation as pressure on Holder to act.

Ford has unveiled the F-Series Super Duty Limited, a top-tier heavy-duty pickup that blends near-luxury appointments with extreme towing capability. The Limited range includes F-250, F-350 and F-450 4x4 crew-cab models; the F-250 starts at $80,835, the F-350 at $82,010 and the F-450 at $87,100 (destination included). With every option checked the F-450 can reach about $94,455—prices comparable to flagship luxury sedans. Ford promotes the Limited as a truck for “successful ranchers to contractors to RV owners,” noting Lariat, King Ranch and Platinum trims already make up over half of Super Duty sales.

Under the hood, all Limited models use Ford’s 6.7-liter Power Stroke V8 diesel, rated at 440 hp and 925 lb-ft of torque, enabling towing capacities up to roughly 30,000 pounds—Ford likens this to the weight of an F-35 fighter. Interiors emphasize handcrafted luxury: two-tone Camelback leather, heated and ventilated front seats, heated rear seats, Miko suede headliner, dark ash wood trim and a laser-etched serial number on the center console. Exterior cues include a satin-finish twin-bar grille, chrome accents and quad-beam LED headlamps.

Technology and safety features are extensive and largely class-exclusive: SYNC 3, a high-definition 360-degree camera with Trailer Reverse Guidance, trailer-aware BLIS, adaptive steering and cruise control, lane-keeping alerts and forward collision warning with brake support. The Super Duty Limited will arrive at dealerships in single- and dual-rear-wheel configurations this winter, offering buyers heavy-duty capability wrapped in premium touches.

A Hungarian arrest warrant shows that Sebastian Gorka, a former Trump deputy assistant, was wanted on a weapons-related charge during his seven months at the White House. Hungarian outlet 444 and BuzzFeed News reported the warrant, which lists the offense as “firearm or ammunition abuse” and was issued on Sept. 17, 2016. The warrant was filed with the Budaörs police station in Budapest; little additional detail is provided and Hungarian authorities did not respond to requests for comment. 444 suggested the alleged incident might date back to as early as 2009. Gorka, who moved to the U.S. in 2008, denied the report on social media and declined to say whether any incident could have occurred during a visit to Hungary. During his White House tenure—where his exact duties as a deputy assistant were often described as vague—Gorka met with Hungarian officials, including Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó. He left the White House in August 2017 after reportedly being pushed out by Chief of Staff John Kelly. Gorka has a well-documented interest in firearms: he once had a pistol confiscated at Reagan National Airport in 2016 and has described carrying two pistols, a knife, a tourniquet and a copy of the U.S. Constitution as his “everyday carry.” Critics have questioned his counterterrorism credentials and ties to fringe right-wing groups.

A Bloomberg Businessweek investigation alleges that Target was warned about a malware breach nearly two weeks before acting, but failed to respond. Target had contracted FireEye and installed its $1.6 million detection system, including honeypot servers and a Bangalore-based monitoring team. According to the report, FireEye’s response center alerted Target HQ on November 30 and again on December 2, but Minneapolis did not act. Computer logs cited by Businessweek contradict Target’s earlier public statements and congressional testimony that the company only learned of the intrusion in mid-December after contact from the Department of Justice. FireEye’s system can automatically remove detected malware, but auditors say Target’s security team disabled that function, leaving rapid human intervention as the only line of defense — which apparently failed. The article paints this as a series of security “blunders,” suggesting inaction by Target rather than failure by FireEye. Target’s CIO at the time, Beth Jacob, resigned; CEO Gregg Steinhafel said the company is conducting a full probe. The report also points to a possible perpetrator, a Ukrainian carder known as “Rescator,” but cautions there is no definitive proof linking him to the alias Andrey Khodyrevskiy.

Bread is a particular menace for people with dysphagia—chewing it soaks up saliva and forms sticky balls that resist swallowing—so researchers and companies are developing alternatives and treatments to restore safe, appealing eating. Japan’s EN Otsuka launched iEat Bread in 2015: enzyme-treated bread that looks, tastes and feels like the real thing but absorbs almost no saliva, is easily mashed by the tongue, and is far less sticky. Elsewhere, teams use molds and 3D printing to reshape puréed foods into familiar-looking dishes; the EU-funded PERFORMANCE consortium and German firm Biozoon produced 3D-printed peas, pasta and a full meal (roast pork with gnocchi), with commercial availability possible within a few years. Making modified diets more palatable may have clinical importance: a study found stroke patients put on thickened liquids or purées were likelier to become dehydrated than those on regular diets, possibly because unappealing textures reduce intake. For those who cannot swallow at all, mechanical and biological interventions are advancing. Peter Belafsky’s Swallow Expansion Device—a small implant that mechanically opens the upper oesophageal sphincter when pulled—entered a phase I trial; trials are also testing drugs like donepezil, muscle stem-cell therapies, and methods to reduce radiation damage or physically dilate constricted oesophagi. The article follows Samantha (Sam) Anderson’s harrowing experience: after sudden dysphagia linked to shingles-damaged cranial nerves, she suffered weight loss, malnutrition, choking and social isolation, required an 18-month feeding tube, and learned complex swallowing techniques and restrictive diets. Under specialist care, medication and therapy she slowly regained function, now eating with caution and hope, joining trials for further improvement. Her story highlights the physical, emotional and social toll of swallowing disorders and the need for greater awareness and tailored treatments.

The Pentagon announced late Friday that Defense Secretary Jim Mattis will delay implementation of the policy allowing openly transgender people to enlist or be commissioned until at least Jan. 1, 2018. Mattis approved the services’ recommendation to defer accessions so they can review how accepting transgender applicants might affect “readiness and lethality.” The six-month postponement applies only to new recruits and officers; an estimated 15,500 transgender service members already serving may remain. The delay came shortly before a July 1 deadline set under former Secretary Ash Carter. Service leaders including the Army and Marine Corps had sought more time, and the lack of a final accession policy already prevented commissioning some transgender academy graduates. Advocates and researchers criticized the move: the Palm Center warned it forces prospective troops to conceal their identity, and a RAND study found negligible readiness impact. LGBT military groups called the decision disappointing and urged lifting the restriction after the delay.

New scientific analyses reported in the Harvard Theological Review bolster Harvard professor Karen L. King’s claim that a small Coptic papyrus fragment—the so-called “Gospel of Jesus’s Wife,” which includes the line “And Jesus said to them, ‘My wife,’” and “She will be able to be my disciple”—shows no clear signs of modern forgery. Carbon dating and ink analysis indicate the papyrus and ink are consistent with ancient materials: a second radiocarbon test returned a mean date around 741 A.D., and micro-Raman spectroscopy found the ink qualitatively similar to carbon-based inks used on other ancient Egyptian papyri. Microscopic imaging also failed to confirm alleged suspicious ink pooling visible in low-resolution photos. King, who stresses the fragment is not evidence that the historical Jesus was married, argues it likely reflects early Christian debates about women, family, and celibacy and may have been copied from an earlier Greek text. Her article addresses criticisms—including claims the fragment is a modern pastiche of the Gospel of Thomas or contains a typo lifted from an online edition—arguing parallels with Thomas are not decisive and that some supposed grammatical errors appear in authentic Coptic texts. Skeptics remain unconvinced: Egyptologist Leo Depuydt labels the piece a modern forgery with amateurish Coptic and grammatical blunders, arguing similarities to Gospel of Thomas and errors point to a cut-and-paste fake. Absolute proof remains elusive because destructive ink-dating would harm the tiny fragment; promising nondestructive methods are in development. The fragment’s provenance is murky, and debate continues among specialists about authenticity and significance, even as King hopes attention can shift from questions of forgery to the fragment’s implications for understanding early Christian views on gender and celibacy.

Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg donated about $1 billion in Facebook stock to the Silicon Valley Community Foundation, marking the largest gift in the foundation’s history. The contribution is part of Zuckerberg’s broader pledge to give away more than half his wealth and follows a similar donation last year that has since appreciated substantially as Facebook’s shares surged. The foundation will help allocate the donated assets over time; it previously managed Zuckerberg’s $100 million pledge to Newark schools and channeled his contributions to the Breakthrough Prize. Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan focus on education and health causes but have kept many specifics private.

Simultaneously, Facebook announced a new stock offering to raise nearly $1.5 billion by selling 27 million shares, while Zuckerberg will sell roughly $2.3 billion of his own shares—mostly to cover taxes tied to exercising an option to buy 60 million additional shares. After these moves Zuckerberg’s voting control will slip only modestly, from 65.2% to about 62.8%, and he will still hold roughly 444.2 million shares. The company has not designated uses for the offering proceeds; speculation about acquisitions resurfaced after reports of a rejected $3 billion Snapchat bid. Facebook’s strong mobile ad growth has driven its stock recovery since the troubled 2012 IPO, making it a dominant online ad seller behind Google.

A new Emerson College poll released Monday shows Sen. Ted Cruz (R) leading Rep. Beto O’Rourke (D) by a single point in the competitive Texas Senate race, with Cruz at 38% and O’Rourke at 37%. Four percent of respondents prefer another candidate and 21% are undecided. The survey of 550 likely voters was conducted Aug. 22–25 and carries a 4.4-point margin of error, meaning the race is statistically tied. The finding comes amid growing momentum for O’Rourke, who is polling strongly among younger voters: he leads Cruz in the 18–34 and 35–54 age brackets. Cruz maintains advantages with voters aged 55–74 and those 75 and older. Emerson notes O’Rourke’s favorable ratings—37% of registered voters view him positively—which could challenge Cruz in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in three decades. Other recent data and ratings shifts reflect the tightening contest: an NBC News–Marist poll last week showed Cruz up by four points, and the Cook Political Report moved the race from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican.”

Candy Spelling’s 57,000-square-foot Holmby Hills mansion, long touted as the most expensive U.S. home with a $150 million asking price, is reportedly in contract to be sold to 22-year-old heiress Petra Ecclestone, daughter of Formula One boss Bernie Ecclestone. Known as “The Manor,” the five-acre French chateau-style estate built by Aaron Spelling in 1991 features extravagant amenities—bowling alley, beauty salon, flower-cutting and china rooms, multiple gift-wrapping rooms, a library, a “Prince Charles suite,” a double staircase inspired by Gone With the Wind, and parking for 100 cars. The sales price was not disclosed. Ecclestone, who owns a large Chelsea townhouse in London, plans to split time between Los Angeles and London after an upcoming wedding. Candy Spelling, who has downsized to a Century City condominium, declined comment. The transaction, if completed, would highlight continued influence of wealthy foreign buyers even as U.S. real-estate prices struggle amid a prolonged downturn.

At Howard University’s commencement, President Barack Obama delivered an explicitly racialized yet broadly framed address urging graduates and activists to pair passion with political engagement. He praised a new generation of black activists — including Black Lives Matter organizers, “black Twitter” voices and named individuals like Brittany Packnett — for raising awareness about systemic inequality, especially in policing and mass incarceration. But he insisted awareness alone is insufficient: structural change requires lawmaking, cultural shifts and sustained participation in electoral politics.

Obama commended activists who sat at negotiating tables and helped shape policy, highlighting Packnett’s role on his 21st-century policing task force. He urged willingness to compromise and accept imperfect victories as part of long-term progress: “You consolidate your gains and then you move on to the next fight from a stronger position.” He also warned students against silencing opponents, recommending rebuttal and persuasion “on the battlefield of ideas.”

Responses from movement leaders reflected a pragmatic consensus: disruption and protest create political pressure, but must be coupled with engagement. DeRay Mckesson argued that street pressure produced forums such as the policing task force, while cautioning that failing to participate in policy processes can yield unsatisfying reforms — for example, a step like body cameras that many activists view as inadequate. Samuel Sinyangwe acknowledged Obama’s point that awareness matters but emphasized its role alongside policy and culture change, including confronting bias that contributes to police killings.

Prominent online activist April Reign noted that disruptive tactics have forced politicians to address issues they might otherwise ignore, citing interruptions of Sanders and Clinton as catalysts for conversation about race and accountability. Still, many applauded Obama’s unapologetically black tone: he encouraged graduates to “be confident in your blackness,” celebrated cultural figures like Prince and Ta-Nehisi Coates, and highlighted gains in education and representation while warning of a persistent “justice gap” linking underfunded schools to incarceration.

Obama broadened the moral imperative, urging graduates to expand their empathy beyond black communities to refugees, immigrants, the rural poor, transgender people — and even middle-aged white men affected by economic dislocation — proposing a coalition-minded politics. His message: combine moral imagination, grassroots pressure and electoral strategy — not just hashtags, but votes — to secure lasting change.

New Jersey faced a critical shortage of road salt amid repeated winter storms, but a 1920 federal law known as the Jones Act prevented rapid transport of a 40,000-ton shipment waiting in Searsport, Maine. The state requested an emergency waiver from the Department of Homeland Security to allow a foreign‑flagged ship—the bulk carrier Anastasia S—to move the salt directly to Port Newark in about a day and a half, but DHS denied the request or indicated a waiver was unlikely. Without the waiver, New Jersey must rely on slower, American‑flagged barge options that would take weeks and require multiple trips, carrying only portions of the shipment at a time. State officials warned supplies would last only through one or two more storms; several municipalities had already curtailed salting, left roads untreated, or resorted to blending salt with brine and using sand to stretch reserves. The decision recalled past controversy over Jones Act waivers—DHS granted one after Hurricane Sandy in 2012 but refused waivers in other crises, including the Gulf oil spill. New Jersey leaders, including DOT officials and Governor Chris Christie, urged relief, while shipping industry groups stated domestic carriers were responding and that any waiver request would be reviewed under federal law. Senators from New Jersey did not comment.

Investigators reported that residue from Tannerite, a commercially sold binary explosive used as an exploding rifle target, was found on at least one of the devices in the Chelsea, Manhattan bombing that injured 29 people. Tannerite is marketed as two inert components—commonly an oxidizer such as ammonium nitrate and a metal fuel like powdered aluminum—that are safe separately but form an explosive mixture when combined. The ATF classifies such products as binary explosives but does not regulate sales because the parts are not explosive until mixed. The manufacturer and its investigator have questioned whether their product was actually used, noting company testing indicates Tannerite detonates only from the impact of a high‑velocity rifle round, not by fuses, flames, low‑velocity impacts, or electrical triggers; law enforcement has not publicly confirmed the ignition method. Experts caution binary mixtures can be dangerous when misused—especially if enclosed in containers which generate shrapnel—and note ammonium nitrate has been involved in major past blasts. The ATF has warned the public about binary explosives and urges reporting of suspicious purchases or large orders by uninformed buyers. States such as Indiana have pursued tighter retail controls. Ahmad Khan Rahami faces charges including five counts of attempted murder in connection with the linked bombings.

TMZ Sports reports PGA legend John Daly praising President Barack Obama’s golf game as “pretty good,” but saying he doesn’t compare to the all-time presidential golf GOAT, George H.W. Bush. The piece mixes a social admonition—urging people not to judge, bully, or publicly shame others, and to live in gratitude and happiness—with Daly’s lighthearted ranking of presidential golfers. The short item combines celebrity sports commentary with a broader reminder to treat people kindly rather than “making an example” of them, while celebrating Bush’s reputed golfing prowess over Obama’s solid play.

On Jan. 2, 1988, a newborn boy was found dead and frozen in a Meriden parking lot, wrapped in a blanket near a tree. Local clergy named him David Paul, meaning “God’s beloved little man.” The Meriden Police Department unofficially adopted the child, funded his burial at Walnut Grove Cemetery and has held annual memorials ever since to honor him and all abused, neglected or abandoned children. The baby, full-term with blond hair and blue eyes, was never identified and no one was charged; investigators sought the mother believing trauma led to the abandonment rather than to punish her. At a recent memorial, about 20 officers, retired Chief Robert Kosienski and the Rev. Alden Barnes attended, with Barnes praying for children and noting the memorial’s added resonance after the Sandy Hook tragedy a year earlier. The gathering also highlighted Connecticut’s 2000 Safe Haven law allowing parents to leave infants under 30 days at hospitals anonymously so they enter state custody.

BMX legend Dave Mirra, who died by a self-inflicted gunshot in February at age 41, was posthumously diagnosed with chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), marking the first confirmed case in an action sports athlete. University of Toronto neuropathologist Dr. Lili‑Naz Hazrati identified trademark tau protein deposits in Mirra’s frontal and temporal lobes that were indistinguishable from those seen in former football and hockey players with CTE. At the Mirra family’s request, Hazrati sent anonymized slides to multiple U.S. and Canadian neuropathologists; all independently confirmed the diagnosis. CTE is a progressive neurodegenerative disease linked to repeated head trauma that can cause memory loss, dementia, depression and impulse-control problems; it can currently be diagnosed only after death. Mirra’s brain injuries included a fractured skull and blood clot after being struck by a car at 19, numerous concussions sustained over a long BMX career, and later involvement in other high-risk sports. His widow, Lauren Mirra, reported personality and mood changes in his final year and has called for greater awareness and research to enable earlier detection and prevention. Mirra, a dominant figure in freestyle BMX with a then-record 24 X Games medals, a video game franchise and MTV exposure, will be honored posthumously at the National BMX Hall of Fame and with a Dave Mirra event at the X Games. Researchers continue to study CTE staging in his brain. The family plans to create a platform for CTE awareness and research as his legacy prompts discussion about brain injuries across sports.

Marcia Clark, the former Los Angeles County prosecutor who led the O.J. Simpson murder prosecution, says she blames herself for the controversial not-guilty verdict in the double-homicide trial. In a Dateline NBC interview with Josh Mankiewicz airing Sunday, Clark reflected on the trial’s inner workings and the emotional impact of the jury’s decision. She described hearing the foreman read “Not guilty” as “physically painful,” and said she immediately thought of Ron Goldman and Nicole Brown, believing the verdict was wrong. Clark reiterated that, despite her self-blame, the prosecution faced barriers in convincing the jury: “There was no way to reach that jury. There was no way to make them believe. There really wasn’t.” 

The preview also revisits the infamous moment when Simpson tried on the gloves the prosecution said were worn by the killer—a scene Clark says she opposed. She told Mankiewicz the decision to have Simpson try on the gloves “was not my call,” attributing it to co-counsel Christopher Darden, who later apologized. Clark responded that it was okay and suggested that even without that misstep, the case was unlikely to be won. 

The Dateline special, timed amid renewed interest following FX’s The People v. O.J. Simpson: American Crime Story, includes interviews with numerous figures connected to the case, including Kris Jenner, Denise Brown, Fred Goldman, Alan Dershowitz and Kato Kaelin. The two-hour episode aims to provide deeper context and personal perspectives on one of the most scrutinized trials in modern American history. Dateline, on air since 1992, continues its investigative storytelling under anchors like Lester Holt and correspondents including Mankiewicz.

A viral video shot near Pripyat in the Chernobyl exclusion zone shows a fox calmly assembling and carrying away an enormous sandwich, carefully stacking slices of bread and cold cuts before holding the multi‑layered meal in its mouth. Journalists from RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service reportedly gave the bread and meat to the animal; the clip has drawn more than a million views and highlights the animals’ lack of fear around humans. Since the 1986 nuclear disaster and subsequent evacuation, wildlife—particularly foxes, wolves and bears—has grown in the largely human‑free area. The report also notes a major 2015 forest fire in northern Ukraine that threatened to spread toward the abandoned Chernobyl plant. More than 300 firefighters, three planes and a helicopter were deployed; Prime Minister Arseny Yatseniuk said the blaze was contained and radiation levels remained normal. The stricken Reactor 4, the site of the 1986 explosion and fire, is covered by a concrete casement that Ukrainian authorities planned to reinforce. The footage underscores both the changing wildlife dynamics and ongoing safety concerns in the exclusion zone.

The Library of Virginia, a long-standing Archive-It partner since September 2005, functions as the Commonwealth’s official archival agency and reference library at Virginia’s seat of government. As one of the nation’s leading research institutions focused on Virginia’s history, politics, and culture, it maintains extensive holdings that draw researchers from across the United States and around the world to its Richmond facilities as well as to the library’s growing array of online digital resources. The institution’s dual role—preserving state records and supporting historical research—positions it as a central repository for primary materials about Virginia and a public-facing library that supports scholarship, education, and civic life. In parallel to institutional developments, the document touches on broader contemporary communication and marketing trends. Significant sums are being invested in SMS messaging campaigns as mobile marketing becomes an increasingly integral advertising tool. Small businesses, in particular, are adopting mobile strategies to discover new and engaging ways to reach existing and prospective customers, signaling the growing importance of mobile channels in outreach and commerce. Additionally, social media platforms provide location-based features: users can add city or precise location information to posts made via the web or third-party applications, and retain control over privacy through options to delete location histories. Together, these themes highlight evolving practices in information access, preservation, and modern digital communication.

The document describes two distinct topics: an archiving initiative by the Internet Archive and a fatal shooting of a Modoc County deputy. The Archive’s crawls aim to capture webpages as they are created and the pages they reference, preserving versions that existed when an author wrote a page. By saving both primary pages and their linked content, the Archive seeks to prevent link rot—pages becoming changed or removed—and to provide preserved versions that can replace broken links or serve as companion links so readers can see what an author originally intended. The broader goal described is ambitious: to fix broken links on the web by systematically archiving supported “No More 404” sites and their references. Separately, the document reports a deadly incident on Oct. 19 in Modoc County. Deputy Jack Hopkins was killed while responding to a disturbance about eight miles south of Alturas; he was shot as he entered a property and died instantly. Authorities say suspect Jack Lee Breiner, 47, fled and later exchanged gunfire with another deputy, sustaining wounds. Breiner has been charged with murder and additional offenses related to the killing. The piece juxtaposes efforts to preserve digital records with a local law-enforcement tragedy.

The Alaska Senate race underscored Sarah Palin’s mixed political influence: Lisa Murkowski, having lost the Republican primary to Palin-backed Joe Miller, appears to have prevailed as a write-in—an outcome that weakens Palin’s standing in her home state. Nationwide, Palin endorsed about 60 candidates; with several races unresolved she’s near a split between winners and losers. Of 34 House endorsements, only 15 won; in the Senate she had about five victories among 12 efforts. High-profile successes—Vicky Hartzler defeating Ike Skelton and Michael Grimm beating Michael McMahon—were offset by notable losses like Joe Miller’s likely defeat and Sean Bielat’s failure in Massachusetts. GOP strategists say Palin picked ideological allies over electability, boosting her brand and grassroots name recognition even as many endorsements flopped. Critics argue her focus on political spectacle, limited staffing and identity-based “mama grizzlies” messaging curtailed broader effectiveness. Emerging Republican figures such as Rand Paul and Marco Rubio now command more substantive influence; Palin’s national standing is diminished until she decides on a 2012 run.

A study investigating how people engage with online privacy policies and terms of service (TOS) found overwhelming evidence that users rarely read the fine print, even when it contains extreme “gotcha” clauses. Researchers created a fictitious social network, NameDrop, with privacy and TOS documents modeled on real examples (about 8,000 and 4,000 words). Hidden in those documents were startling provisions: one permitting broad data sharing (including with the NSA and other agencies) and another absurdly requiring users to assign their firstborn child to the site until 2050. Of 543 undergraduate participants, 399 skipped the policies entirely via a “quick join” clickwrap; among the rest average reading times were 73 seconds for the privacy policy and 51 seconds for the TOS—far too short to meaningfully process thousands of words of legalese. Overall, 98% of participants missed the inserted “gotcha” clauses; only about 10–11 noticed. The paper echoes prior work showing low policy readership across demographics and finds information overload predicts ignoring TOS and policy changes. Qualitative responses describe policies as nuisances to be bypassed to achieve digital goals. The authors conclude that current lengthy, dense policies fail at comprehension, allowing companies wide latitude so long as clauses are disclosed, and call for improved accessibility and tools.

The Economist Intelligence Unit’s Worldwide Cost of Living Index 2014, a twice-yearly survey that has run for over 30 years, compares more than 400 individual prices across 160 products and services in cities worldwide. It covers food, drink, clothing, household supplies, personal care, rents, transport, utilities, schools, domestic help and recreation, producing comparative indices for use by HR and finance managers to set expatriate allowances and compensation. For the report all cities are benchmarked against New York (index = 100). The 2014 results name Singapore as the most expensive city, driven primarily by a strong Singapore dollar and high costs for cars, utilities and clothing. Although Singapore’s cost-of-living relative to New York fell over the past 12 months, a roughly 40% currency appreciation and steady inflation over the past decade have moved it up the rankings. The EIU positions itself as a trusted source of rigorous global business intelligence.

Mitt Romney secured the Republican presidential nomination at a hurricane-delayed convention in Tampa, where New Jersey’s roll call formally clinched his victory. The GOP quickly ratified a conservative platform favoring immediate tax cuts, a 20% income tax bracket reduction, repeal of Obama’s health care and Wall Street reforms, and strict anti-abortion language. Ann Romney was slated for a prime-time speech to humanize her multimillionaire-turned-politician husband. The convention, compressed by Hurricane Isaac fears, featured tense moments with Ron Paul supporters and highlighted the economy—Romney’s perceived strength—amid 8.3% unemployment. Democrats countered on immigration, Hispanics, women, and likability as campaign season intensified.

The Internet Archive is crawling and archiving newly created pages and the pages they reference so that when referenced pages change or disappear, links can point to the version that existed when a page was written. The aim is to reduce broken links across the web by replacing or supplementing dead links with archived versions, part of supported "No More 404" site crawls. Separately, a Morro Bay Burger King suffered about $35,000 in damage after employees, tricked by a prank caller claiming to be from the fire department, smashed windows and a manager used a car to ram the building. The restaurant closed Sunday for repairs and is expected to reopen Tuesday at 6:30. The suspended manager and others involved are under investigation; anyone with information, photos, or video is asked to contact Morro Bay Police or Det. Mark Martin.

Former President Bill Clinton’s lengthy, impassioned speech at the Democratic National Convention sought to cast President Barack Obama as a pragmatic problem-solver thwarted by Republican intransigence, while offering a broad case for Obama’s re-election. Clinton praised Obama’s stimulus, college-aid expansion, renewable energy efforts and the Affordable Care Act, arguing those policies benefit the middle class and that Americans are “better off” than four years earlier. Pundits across outlets lauded Clinton’s performance as a powerful, clarifying message that could energize swing voters and improve Democrats’ standing. Commentators called it substantive, charismatic and potentially decisive for the campaign.

But fact-checkers and critics noted omissions and half-truths. The coverage points out that gridlock is not solely the GOP’s fault: Democrats and Obama sometimes resisted compromise (e.g., Rahm Emanuel’s combative approach, Obama’s limited follow-through on Simpson-Bowles recommendations, and the failed 2011 “grand bargain” that collapsed amid dissent on both sides). Claims that Obamacare tamed health-cost growth were contested: low spending growth largely reflected weak economic demand, not demonstrable effects of still-unimplemented law provisions; employer premiums continued rising. Clinton’s evocation of his 1990s economic success also omitted the late-term downturn and his support for the Glass-Steagall repeal, a move critics link to later financial instability. And his jab about ignoring fact-checkers drew attention to Clinton’s own history of misleading statements during the Lewinsky scandal. Overall, Clinton’s speech was praised for style and persuasion, but analysts urged scrutiny of selective framing and important context the speech left out.

Martin Gill and his partner have fostered two brothers in North Miami for four years; the children, now four and nine, have flourished under their care. After the boys’ biological parents’ rights were terminated in 2006, Gill and his partner sought to adopt them. Florida law, however, automatically bars adoption by gay people despite permitting gay and lesbian individuals and couples to serve as foster parents since 1977. With ACLU assistance, Gill challenged the adoption ban; a juvenile court judge granted the adoption last November. Florida’s attorney general immediately appealed, so the legal outcome remains unresolved, but the boys continue to live with Gill and his partner for now. Separately, an extensive web crawl dataset from March–December 2011 is described. Conducted with Heritrix and a new distributed HQ crawler, the crawl began from an Alexa top-1-million seed list and amassed 2.7 billion captures across roughly 2.27 billion unique URLs and 29 million hosts. The team notes operational issues—missed embedded resources and repeated crawls of some sites—that skew country-level results. The dataset is available for research requests via archive.org, though access may be limited.

President Barack Obama said the United States will not send ground troops to Yemen or Somalia despite growing al Qaeda activity there, telling People magazine he plans to work with international partners to keep Americans safe. Obama noted al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), based in Yemen, appears linked to the attempted Christmas Day airline bombing, and that al Shabaab controls large areas of Somalia. Gen. David Petraeus, head of U.S. Central Command, echoed that U.S. forces will not be deployed on the ground in Yemen, saying Yemen’s government does not want them and Washington will instead provide assistance. The U.S. plans to more than double security aid to Yemen from $70 million to at least $150 million and increase economic support, alongside contributions from regional partners. Officials emphasize intelligence and partner cooperation to target terrorist camps, while Petraeus cautioned that al Qaeda remains capable of periodic attacks despite overall degraded capability.

Mitch Carter, a former Bakersfield High School student, sued the Kern High School District after suffering severe injuries, including a traumatic brain injury, during a 2010 pep rally dog pile. Carter had been dressed in a chicken costume for a skit mocking an opposing school’s mascot when members of the football team attacked him, punching, kicking and piling on. Jurors found the district negligent. During the civil trial, attorneys exposed lapses in school safety, conflicting accounts among administrators and the district police, and disputed testimony about who witnessed the incident. Defense counsel called the attack “embarrassing and inexcusable” but said it was sudden and unknown to staff; plaintiffs’ attorneys accused the district of a conspiracy and cover-up. Coach Paul Golla’s testimony—he said he was not in the gym—was contradicted by a USC scout who said he sat next to Golla as the pile formed, fueling calls from plaintiffs for administrative accountability and firings of those who lied. The trial featured dramatic moments, including plaintiff attorney Nicholas Rowley donning a chicken suit during closing arguments. Facing a potential award reportedly exceeding $45 million, the district and its insurers chose to settle. The Kern High School District agreed to pay $10.5 million—largely covered by Everest National Insurance—to cover Carter’s healthcare costs. District officials said they will reevaluate safety policies; Carter expressed hope the settlement will prevent future harm and said he aspires to attend law school to help others.

Texas finalized rules requiring hospitals, clinics and other health facilities to cremate or bury fetal remains instead of disposing of them in sanitary landfills, a move set to take effect Dec. 19. The Department of State Health Services advanced the measure after months of public comment and hearings that generated more than 35,000 submissions. Supporters, including Gov. Greg Abbott, argued fetal remains should not be treated as medical waste and said the rules protect public health and safety. The Health and Human Services Commission later clarified the rules do not apply to miscarriages or abortions occurring at home and do not require filing birth or death certificates, preserving confidentiality.

Reproductive-rights groups, providers and some medical and funeral-industry representatives sharply opposed the regulation, saying it creates logistical, financial and ethical burdens that will impede access to abortion and traumatize patients. NARAL Pro-Choice Texas and allies rallied outside the state health department, delivering over 5,500 petition signatures opposing the rule; advocacy groups pledged possible legal challenges, calling the policy an intrusion on women’s beliefs and an attempt to restrict abortion access. Critics also noted the potential for high costs in cremation or burial per case, though the department contends new methods won’t increase total facility costs because they would offset current disposal expenses.

The rule change bans previously permitted disposal methods for fetal tissue—such as incineration, grinding and landfill disposal after treatment—while retaining standard procedures for other human tissue. Some Republican lawmakers have signaled support and may codify the requirements legislatively; opponents say the issue raises complex legal and philosophical questions about ownership and status of biological material removed from patients.

Monday Properties plans to demolish two aging Rosslyn office buildings at 1401 Wilson Blvd and 1400 Key Blvd, including the underground parking garage where Bob Woodward met “Deep Throat” (FBI official Mark Felt) during the Watergate investigation. The garage, built in the early 1960s and marked by an Arlington County historical plaque installed in 2011, will be removed as part of a proposed redevelopment that must pass Arlington’s 1–4 year site plan process. Monday envisions a mixed-use project with a 32-story residential tower, a 29-story office tower, roughly 500,000 sq ft office, 385,000 sq ft residential, 60,000 sq ft retail and public open space. The plaque will likely be removed for construction and reinstalled or otherwise commemorated; Monday says it will explore ways to honor the site’s history. Timing depends on approvals; work likely won’t start before 2016–2017.

Rep. Louie Gohmert said Wednesday there is no personal animosity between him and Attorney General Eric Holder, despite a heated confrontation between the two during a House Judiciary Committee hearing the previous day. Speaking on Fox & Friends, the Texas Republican described Holder as “a likable guy” but asserted that the attorney general is failing to fulfill his duties. Gohmert criticized Holder for allegedly making subjective, “personal choices” about whom to prosecute, accusing him of selective enforcement and saying that, if Holder were doing his job, he would provide requested Justice Department documents related to an Islamic charity based in Texas.

The verbal clash at Tuesday’s hearing involved Gohmert pressing Holder for those documents and also touched on the Fast and Furious gun-tracking controversy. At one point Holder, visibly agitated, pointed his finger at Gohmert and warned him, “You don’t want to go there.” Both men exchanged barbs about not needing lectures from the other, and the back-and-forth drew attention across political media. Gohmert reiterated that his concerns were about oversight and the Justice Department’s transparency, not personal hostility toward Holder.

Holder, for his part, referenced the episode during a speech Wednesday to Al Sharpton’s National Action Network, partially departing from his prepared remarks to address how he had been treated by the House committee. He framed the treatment as part of a broader pattern of “unprecedented, unwarranted, ugly, and divisive adversity” faced by the Justice Department and the Obama administration’s justice initiatives. Without naming Gohmert, Holder implied that no prior attorney general or president had to endure such treatment from Congress.

Other Republicans were also confrontational: Rep. Blake Farenthold publicly stated he would not question Holder because, in his view, Holder should “be in jail.” The exchange generated video and social media coverage, with outlets posting footage and commentary. The dispute underscores ongoing partisan tensions over DOJ document requests, investigations like Fast and Furious, and broader complaints from some Republicans about selective law enforcement under the Obama administration.

Indian police and medical staff are trying to identify a girl, aged roughly 8–12, who was found living among monkeys in the Katarniaghat forest in Uttar Pradesh. Villagers first spotted her naked, emaciated and roaming with a group of monkeys; attempts to approach were repelled by the animals. In January a police officer managed to rescue her after monkeys attacked him, and she was taken to a primary health center and then to the government hospital in Bahraich.

On arrival she was malnourished, had long tangled hair and nails, wounds on her body, and displayed behavior described as "monkey-like": walking on all fours, screeching, growling, clawing, refusing to eat from plates and taking food from the floor. She could not speak but reportedly understood commands and smiled. After treatment her condition improved—she began walking upright, eating with her hands, and reacting less violently, though she remains nonverbal. Medical staff have cleaned and trimmed her hair and nails and are treating her wounds; officials say psychological and specialized medical care will be needed to reintegrate her slowly.

Police are reviewing missing-children reports to identify her and determine how long she lived in the forest and whether she was abandoned. Authorities plan to move her to a juvenile home or specialized facility once stable; Lucknow medical college may offer further care. Local officials have dubbed her "Forest Durga" and media comparisons to Kipling’s Mowgli have spread, though the girl’s past and the duration of her forest life remain unclear.

Sen. Orrin Hatch easily won the Utah GOP primary, defeating tea party-backed challenger Dan Liljenquist and securing a path to a likely seventh Senate term. Hatch, a six-term incumbent, overcame vulnerability earlier this year—when conservative activists and convention delegates seemed to favor change—by building an unprecedented campaign operation, spending about $10 million on ads and organizing new delegates. He also won key endorsements, including from Mitt Romney, and shifted rightward on some issues, earning recent high scores from the American Conservative Union while pledging this would be his final term and emphasizing a potential role as Senate Finance Committee chairman if Republicans regain the majority. Liljenquist criticized Hatch for contributing to the national debt but suffered from weaker resources. Hatch’s victory made him the favorite against Democrat Scott Howell in November. Across the country on primary night, Rep. Charles Rangel narrowly prevailed in New York despite past ethics and health troubles, while other notable contests included an upset in Oklahoma and primary wins for Hakeem Jeffries and Mitt Romney in his home state.

Bob Dylan’s long Q&A with Bill Flanagan, posted exclusively on bobdylan.com, explores his three-disc standards project Triplicate, his approach to singing classic popular songs, and memories of fellow legends. Dylan explains why he issued three interconnected 32-minute discs, preferring live horn sections and tight arrangements, and describes how age and life experience let him inhabit these songs more fully. He rejects the label “nostalgic,” calling the standards truthful and present, and credits arrangers like James Harper while embracing imperfections from live takes. Dylan recalls encounters with Frank Sinatra, Elvis Presley, John Wayne and jazz figures like Ornette Coleman and John Coltrane, and mourns recent losses—Muhammad Ali, Merle Haggard, Leonard Cohen—saying their deaths left “empty spaces.” He also discusses influences, recording practices, and why certain songs resonate for him now.

The Justice Department found a pattern of “unreasonable and in some cases unnecessary force” by the Cleveland Division of Police after reviewing nearly 600 use-of-force cases from 2010–2013. Attorney General Eric Holder announced that Cleveland and the DOJ have agreed on principles leading to a consent decree that will require an independent monitor to oversee reforms. Investigators documented excessive deadly force (including shootings and head strikes), unnecessary less-lethal force (Tasers, chemical spray, fists), and disproportionate force against the mentally ill and those in crisis. They found poor tactics that put officers in situations where avoidable force becomes likely, inadequate training and supervision, and failures to properly investigate or discipline misconduct and report use-of-force incidents. The probe cited high-profile incidents, including a 2012 chase where officers fired 137 shots, killing two unarmed occupants, and episodes of prisoners being kicked, stunned while restrained, pepper-sprayed through spit hoods, and a driver shot inside his car. Holder framed the Cleveland findings amid a national conversation about police-community trust, referencing other investigations like those into Michael Brown, Eric Garner, and Tamir Rice.

Chicago police say two juveniles are in custody and could soon face charges in the fatal shooting of 15-year-old Javon (Jovan) Wilson, the grandson of U.S. Rep. Danny Davis. Authorities described the Nov. 18 slaying in the Englewood neighborhood not as a random home invasion but as a targeted dispute that began over a pair of basketball shoes. Officer Michelle Tannehill and department spokesman Anthony Guglielmi said detectives are interrogating the suspects and expect to file first-degree murder charges; the juveniles’ identities and exact ages have not been released.

Police say the assailants were known to the victim and had a prior history or relationship with him. According to Davis and investigators, Wilson was at home with family—an uncle, a 16-year-old sister, a 14-year-old brother and an 8-year-old brother—when two teens entered and argued with him. During the confrontation, a 15-year-old boy allegedly produced a gun and shot Wilson in the head while his mother was out picking up dinner. A 17-year-old girl is reported to have accompanied the shooter. Officers characterized the killing as senseless—an escalation of a dispute over clothing into deadly gun violence.

Rep. Davis, newly re-elected to his 11th term, mourned his grandson as a typical, improving 15-year-old who loved basketball and music and whose grades were getting better. He used the tragedy to lament the pervasive availability of guns and the normalization of youth violence, asking where a 15-year-old could have obtained a firearm. Family members and friends expressed grief and called for greater community involvement, prayer and improved relations with police to help stem such killings.

Chicago has experienced a sharp rise in shootings and homicides this year, with hundreds of killings and several high-profile victims, underscoring the city’s struggle with gun violence as investigators move toward charging suspects in this case.

Bill de Blasio emerged as the surprising front-runner in the Democratic mayoral primary, narrowly exceeding the 40 percent threshold that would avoid a runoff. With about 40.2 percent of the vote and 97 percent of precincts reporting, he led former city comptroller Bill Thompson, who had roughly 26 percent. If de Blasio falls below 40 percent when absentee and provisional ballots are counted, he would face Thompson in an October runoff. De Blasio’s campaign, built on a critique of widening economic inequality and policing practices, struck a broad chord: he performed strongly across boroughs, with women, and among black voters. He pledged to end racial profiling, overhaul stop-and-frisk, replace Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly, and tax the wealthy to fund universal prekindergarten—ideas that resonated with voters eager to move beyond Michael Bloomberg’s 12-year tenure.

Christine Quinn, once the early front-runner and Bloomberg ally, finished third with about 16 percent, hampered by backlash over her role in extending Bloomberg’s term. Anthony Weiner’s campaign collapsed after new sexting revelations, leaving him with about 5 percent. Bill Thompson, backed by unions and establishment figures, framed himself as a fiscally responsible, experienced alternative but failed to consolidate enough nonwhite support.

On the Republican side, Joseph Lhota, former MTA chairman and Giuliani deputy mayor, won the nomination over billionaire John Catsimatidis, positioning a tough-on-crime, pro-Bloomberg continuity platform for the November general election. Scott Stringer defeated Eliot Spitzer in the comptroller’s race, and Letitia James and Daniel Squadron headed to a Democratic runoff for public advocate. The city’s electorate signaled a strong desire for change after Bloomberg’s era, making the fall campaign pivotal.

Since the late 1970s, China has transitioned from a closed, centrally planned economy to a more market-oriented one, achieving over a tenfold GDP increase since 1978 through gradual reforms—agricultural decollectivization, price liberalization, fiscal decentralization, state-enterprise autonomy, private sector growth, capital markets, and trade opening—while retaining industrial policy, state support for key sectors, and restrictive investment controls. By 2017 China was the world’s largest economy by PPP, largest exporter, and biggest trading nation, though per-capita income remained below the global average. Currency policy evolved from a dollar peg toward a basket reference, with episodes of appreciation and depreciation and tighter capital controls since 2015. Major economic challenges include high savings and corporate debt, local government off-balance liabilities, real estate speculation, overcapacity, uneven regional development, rapid population aging, environmental degradation, and the need to boost consumption and innovation. The 13th Five-Year Plan stresses innovation and rebalancing, but state dominance and renewed support for SOEs persist. Rising global interests and regional disputes have driven a significant military buildup and increased defense spending, prompting concern among neighbors and the U.S. while Beijing stresses a defensive posture.

Halle Berry and ex Gabriel Aubry clashed in court over their 6-year-old daughter Nahla’s hair after Berry accused Aubry of having the child’s naturally curly hair straightened and highlighted while in his care. Berry’s lawyer argued Aubry, who is white, was trying to make Nahla appear less African American; Berry, who is biracial, has previously said she identifies as black and wants Nahla to embrace her heritage. Neither Berry nor Aubry attended the hearing in person, but a judge ruled that neither parent may alter Nahla’s natural hair color or texture and ordered her hair be allowed to grow back naturally. The dispute is one of several in the couple’s bitter custody battle since their 2010 split; they share joint custody. Separately, Berry has reportedly sought to reduce child support from about $16,000 a month to roughly $3,000, alleging Aubry is unemployed and relying on payments despite being capable of working. The fight reflects deeper tensions over race, parenting and control in their co-parenting relationship.

President Barack Obama began a three-day trip to Jamaica and Panama aimed at strengthening ties with Caribbean and Central American nations amid shifting regional dynamics. Arriving in Kingston—the first sitting U.S. president to visit Jamaica since 1982—Obama’s low-key welcome included brief meetings with Prime Minister Portia Simpson Miller and an unscheduled 20-minute visit to the Bob Marley Museum, where he said he remained a fan. The trip, which precedes the Summit of the Americas in Panama, follows increased U.S. focus on the region through immigration measures, outreach to Cuba and efforts to address migration from Central America. Energy security is central to Obama’s agenda as Washington seeks to fill gaps from Venezuela’s retreat as a regional energy patron; the U.S. has promoted cooperative energy solutions and hosted a Caribbean Energy Security Summit. The tour also responds to China’s growing economic footprint in the Caribbean through infrastructure financing. Obama will meet Caribbean Community leaders and hold a town-hall with young regional leaders to engage the next generation.

This collection of reports centers on three related episodes involving media, politics and public reactions: an Oval Office encounter between President Donald Trump and RTÉ reporter Caitríona Perry; CNN’s retraction and ensuing resignations over a story about a Trump aide and Russia; and the White House’s use of a conservative undercover video to attack the network.

Caitríona Perry, RTÉ’s Washington correspondent, was inside the Oval Office to cover President Trump’s congratulatory phone call to new Irish Taoiseach Leo Varadkar. While the call was in progress, Trump remarked broadly about the “beautiful Irish press,” beckoned Perry over and asked her to identify herself. He then told Varadkar on the line that Perry “has a nice smile on her face so I bet she treats you well,” before she laughed and returned to her seat. Perry posted a short clip to Twitter and later described the incident as “bizarre,” saying she had been expecting to film from outside a White House window but was invited inside and “caught his eye.” The exchange provoked a polarized reaction online: many criticized the president’s behavior as demeaning and symptomatic of workplace sexism, arguing a journalist should be treated professionally rather than commented on for her looks. Others defended Trump’s remark as a harmless compliment and questioned whether women can no longer accept compliments.

Separately, CNN quietly accepted the resignations of three journalists — Thomas Frank, Eric Lichtblau and Lex Haris — after retracting an online story about an alleged pre-inaugural meeting between Trump aide Anthony Scaramucci and the head of a Russian investment fund. The retraction and resignations furnished the White House with fresh ammunition in its prolonged campaign against what it labels “fake news.” White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders highlighted a video released by conservative activist James O’Keefe’s Project Veritas showing a CNN producer, John Bonifield, criticizing the network’s Russia coverage as ratings-driven. Sanders called the footage “a disgrace to all of media,” urging Americans to watch it and implying systemic problems at CNN reaching “directly from the top.”

CNN defended diversity of opinion among employees and stood by Bonifield, while critics on the right demanded broader accountability, including calls for CNN president Jeff Zucker’s removal. Trump tweeted that CNN had been “caught cold,” lumping several mainstream outlets into a “fake news” category. The controversy emerged at a politically awkward moment for the administration amid intense scrutiny over the Russia probe and stalled legislative priorities, and it reinforced the broader, adversarial dynamic between the White House and major news outlets.

Swiss authorities arrested two Syrian men in Geneva after traces of explosives were found in their car, prosecutor Olivier Jornot said. The men, who spoke Arabic, had Syrian passports and had "recently arrived" in Switzerland; they were stopped because their behavior attracted police attention amid heightened vigilance following the November 13 Paris attacks. Jornot clarified the vehicle bore traces of explosives and had at one point been used to transport explosives, but there was no sign the men had toxic gas or were necessarily the ones who transported them. They are suspected under Swiss law of manufacturing, concealing and transporting explosives and of breaching prohibitions on groups like al-Qaeda and Islamic State. Authorities stressed the two were not among four other men whose photographs were released in connection with searches for suspected jihadists. The arrests came as Geneva raised its threat level to three, deploying armed police to sensitive locations after Swiss officials said a foreign authority—reported by media to be US intelligence—had warned of a possible IS cell in the area. Officials said there was no indication of a concrete planned attack.

A Philadelphia Common Pleas jury awarded $2.5 million to Austin Pledger, now 20, after finding Janssen Pharmaceuticals (a Johnson & Johnson subsidiary) failed to adequately warn that its antipsychotic Risperdal could cause gynecomastia—abnormal breast development in males. Pledger, diagnosed with autism, began taking Risperdal in 2002 at age 8 for irritability. At that time the drug was not FDA-approved for children; its label then indicated a low risk of gynecomastia. By 2006, when the FDA approved Risperdal for use in children and updated labeling to note high prolactin levels (a hormone linked to breast growth), Pledger had already begun developing size 46DD breasts. His mother testified about the profound emotional impact; Austin was ruled incapacitated, so she described behaviors such as covering himself after showers and distress over his appearance. His breasts can only be removed surgically via mastectomy, a decision complicated by his condition and adolescence.

The case is significant as the first Risperdal gynecomastia lawsuit to go to trial in Philadelphia after many settlements and is one of more than 1,200 Risperdal suits filed there. It also recalls J&J’s $2.2 billion settlement two years earlier resolving criminal and civil claims of illegally marketing Risperdal to children and the elderly. Former FDA commissioner David Kessler testified for the plaintiffs that Janssen knew of the risks. Janssen disputes the verdict, saying the FDA-approved label properly warned patients and doctors, that Risperdal benefits many, and that it will seek to overturn the decision. The jury’s finding highlighted competing accounts over whether Pledger’s family and physician were adequately informed before treatment began.

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a rapidly developing, potentially fatal complication of diabetes that can appear within 24 hours and may be the first sign someone has diabetes. Common early symptoms include excessive thirst, frequent urination, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, weakness, shortness of breath, fruity-scented breath and confusion. Home testing can reveal high blood glucose and elevated urine ketones. People who are ill, stressed, or recovering from injury should monitor blood sugar frequently and may use over-the-counter urine ketone tests. Immediate medical contact is advised if vomiting prevents keeping down food or liquids, blood sugar remains above target despite home treatment, or urine ketones are moderate to high. Emergency care is necessary when blood glucose is consistently over 300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L), ketones are present and a doctor cannot be reached, or multiple DKA symptoms occur. Untreated DKA can be fatal.

A separate case in Sydney underlines that danger: two parents were charged with manslaughter after their six-year-old diabetic son died following attendance at a week-long “self-healing” course in April 2015. Emergency services found the child unconscious at a nearby hotel; he died at the scene. Police allege gross negligence and deliberate denial of insulin and food. The course, run by Hongchi Xiao—who promotes a harsh therapy called paidalajin combining fasting, stretching and skin-slapping—has been linked to another death in England and Xiao remains sought by authorities. The clinic that rented space for the seminars said the boy was not its patient. The parents were granted conditional bail and face up to 25 years in prison if convicted.

Coffee culture’s evolution has brought more nuanced flavors to the fore, but for many consumers caffeine potency still rules. A recent entrant to the “world’s strongest coffee” race is Black Insomnia, a South African brand launched in 2016 that now claims to be the most highly caffeinated coffee available and has begun selling in the U.S. via Amazon (16-ounce bags for $19.99). After independent testing in Switzerland, Black Insomnia says its blend beats longtime rival Death Wish Coffee: Caffeine Informer lists Black Insomnia at about 702 mg of caffeine per 12-ounce cup versus Death Wish’s 660 mg—both well above the 400 mg daily limit health experts recommend for most adults. For perspective, a typical 12-ounce cup of coffee contains roughly 150 mg of caffeine and a can of cola only about 34 mg. Black Insomnia attributes its high caffeine to using robusta beans, which carry more caffeine than arabica, and claims to retain a pleasant flavor profile—“walnut and almost sweet”—without extreme bitterness or acidity. However, the staggering caffeine content raises safety concerns: Mayo Clinic guidance cited alongside the product’s arrival notes that up to 400 mg daily is generally safe for most healthy adults, while higher or sensitive individuals may experience side effects such as insomnia, nervousness, rapid heartbeat, tremors, or gastrointestinal upset. Caffeine can interact with medications and some supplements, and pregnant or breastfeeding people should consult doctors about limits. For those wanting to cut back, experts recommend tracking intake, reducing consumption gradually, choosing decaf or herbal options, and heeding product labels to avoid unwanted interactions or withdrawal effects.

President Obama faces historically poor midterm results: his party lost 63 House seats in 2010 and was expected to lose another 5–12 (or more) in the subsequent midterm, putting his two-midterm House losses at roughly 68–75 seats—potentially the worst since Harry Truman, whose two midterms cost Democrats 83 House seats. Comparisons note Reagan, Clinton and George W. Bush each had one bad midterm paired with a milder one, and Senate trends vary by president. Democrats lost six Senate seats in 2010 and were projected to lose 5–10 more, giving Obama a possible Senate midterm loss total of 11–16—short of Truman’s party loss of 17 but comparable to Eisenhower-era GOP losses. Analysts attribute the defeats to partisan polarization and the president’s leadership and centrism missteps. Looking ahead to 2016, six vulnerable GOP senators elected in Obama-won states (Kirk, Toomey, Johnson, Portman, Ayotte, Rubio) could make the map favorable to Democrats, potentially limiting any Republican Senate majority’s longevity. Both parties are eyeing pick-ups and defensive races, with Democrats optimistic about a short-lived GOP Senate majority if achieved.

Two 17-year-old students and acquaintances at Plano East Senior High School, Ritu Sachdeva and Hillary Kate Kuizon, were found dead within hours of each other over a weekend in Murphy, Texas. Relatives discovered Sachdeva at her home shortly after midnight Sunday; Kuizon’s body was located hours later in a wooded area near Kimbrough Stadium. Murphy police say both deaths are being investigated as likely suicides, with no evidence of foul play so far. Investigators are interviewing family members to determine whether the deaths are connected and to explore rumors of a possible suicide pact. The medical examiner will determine official causes of death.
