Distinctive morphology, including large raptorial claws and an oblique membranous division on the basal segment of the anterior lateral spinnerets, marks it as a very unusual, ancient haplogyne lineage and suggests Trogloraptoridae may be sister to other Dysderoidea families. Many aspects of its biology remain unknown—diet and mating behaviors have not been observed, and captive individuals refused offered prey. The discovery highlights the Klamath-Siskiyou region’s role as a refugium for ancient taxa and suggests more cryptic species may await discovery in its inaccessible habitats.

A London School of Economics analysis of the Millennium Cohort Study — which follows about 18,000 British children — reports that children born to mothers in their thirties tend to perform best on early cognitive tests and show advantages in health and development compared with children of mothers in their twenties or forties. Published in Biodemography and Social Biology and led by researcher Alice Goisis, the study highlights several likely explanations: first-time mothers in their thirties are more often better educated, have higher incomes, are more likely to be in stable relationships, adopt healthier lifestyles, seek earlier prenatal care and plan pregnancies. Those socioeconomic and behavioral factors likely contribute to improved outcomes for children at age five. The analysis also found that mothers in their forties are more likely to breastfeed, read to their children and smoke less, but their children showed higher rates of obesity and their mothers reportedly played with their children less than younger mothers — though the sample of mothers in their forties was small (only 53), prompting the authors to call for more research. Critics note limits of the study: cognitive test scores at age five are a narrow measure of “intelligence,” and early-life advantages tied to parental resources (better schools, nutrition, and enrichment) do not necessarily predict all future accomplishments or different forms of intelligence. The report arrives against a backdrop of rising maternal age in the UK (average maternal age rose from 24.5 in 1980 to 28.1 today) and contributes to ongoing debates about the best timing for parenthood, while underscoring socioeconomic factors that shape child development.

Michael (Mike) Oreskes, NPR’s senior vice president for news and editorial director, resigned after multiple accusations of sexual harassment spanning decades surfaced. He acknowledged wrongdoing in a statement, apologized to those he hurt, accepted full responsibility, and informed NPR CEO Jarl Mohn of his decision to step down. Oreskes had been placed on leave shortly before resigning; Mohn named Chris Turpin interim news chief.

The allegations emerged publicly after The Washington Post reported that two women said Oreskes, while Washington bureau chief at The New York Times in the 1990s, abruptly kissed them during meetings about job prospects — in both accounts the women said he unexpectedly kissed them and used his tongue. Those women filed formal complaints with NPR in mid-October and spoke to the Post on condition of anonymity. NPR had earlier received a separate complaint from an employee, Rebecca Hersher, who went public with her account of a 2015 encounter when Oreskes visited NPR. Hersher, then a 26-year-old assistant producer, said a career counseling meeting turned into a three-hour dinner that veered into personal and sexual topics, left her uncomfortable, and undermined her confidence; she reported it to NPR’s human resources, which formally rebuked Oreskes and notified senior executives. Hersher said she felt the network’s response at the time was appropriate and she suffered no retaliation.

NPR emphasized it takes harassment concerns seriously; CEO Mohn urged staff to come forward with any issues and said the organization reviews such matters promptly to ensure a safe, productive workplace. Oreskes had previously served as a vice president and senior managing editor at The Associated Press before joining NPR in 2015.

Elisabeth Hasselbeck sparked criticism on The View for suggesting some older women become lesbians because men their age pursue younger partners, leaving them without male companions. She argued late-in-life same-sex relationships may arise from a search for companionship rather than sexual preference. Co-host Joy Behar rebuked the notion as “ridiculous,” insisting sexual orientation isn’t a choice people suddenly make and noting many were constrained by societal expectations to marry. Hasselbeck, a conservative known for contentious remarks — including past comments about the morning-after pill and victim-blaming Erin Andrews — drew ire from viewers and colleagues for oversimplifying and stereotyping lesbian identity.

Myanmar has begun releasing another group of political prisoners as part of reforms promised by President Thein Sein during a recent European visit. Officials said 69–73 detainees were freed from various prisons on Tuesday, bringing the number of political prisoners below 100 for the first time in years. The releases follow Thein Sein’s pledge in Britain to free all remaining political prisoners by year-end. A 19-member Committee to Scrutinise Remaining Political Prisoners—composed of former detainees, government appointees and mediators—reviews cases to distinguish criminal offenders from those jailed for political reasons and meets monthly to oversee the process. Activists and advocacy groups welcomed the releases but cautioned they often occur in small batches and noted that repressive laws remain in force; new arrests and trials of peaceful protesters continue. Before this round, roughly 200 political detainees were believed imprisoned. Authorities, embassies and NGOs sometimes report differing counts, and rights groups are still compiling names of those released.

In northern Italy, two white Chow Chow dogs painted to resemble giant pandas were seized from a travelling circus near Brescia after visitors—especially children—paid to pose with them. The animals, originally imported from Hungary, had been dyed and displayed as rare Chinese bears; the ruse reportedly attracted paying families until a tip-off prompted intervention by Italy’s environmental police. Officials said the dogs were generally healthy but had watery eyes, likely worsened by repeated camera flashes. Authorities removed the animals on animal-cruelty grounds and cited problems with their paperwork: the dogs were six months younger than stated, raising charges related to false passports and potentially defrauding customers. The circus denied mistreatment, with its secretary insisting the animals are obviously dogs and were well cared for, and the animals have since been returned although they may no longer be used in shows. The episode echoes a trend in China where dyed Chow Chows, marketed as panda-like companions and commanding higher prices, have gained popularity. Italian authorities are pursuing legal action against the circus owner for animal cruelty, falsified documents, and cheating customers.

A man calling himself Nolan Daniels posted a Facebook photo claiming to hold one of the two winning tickets in Wednesday’s roughly $588 million Powerball jackpot and pledged to give $1 million to a random person who shared his image. His account—active since 2008—showed a smiling Daniels with a ticket listing the winning numbers 5-23-16-22-29 and Powerball 6. The post went viral, being shared tens to hundreds of thousands of times and prompting frantic online participation. Daniels warned skeptics they would be excluded from the promised drawing. But lottery officials have only confirmed one winning ticket, held by Cindy and Mark Hill of Dearborn, Missouri, who took a lump sum; the Arizona purchaser has not publicly claimed the prize. Multiple red flags suggest Daniels’s claim is fraudulent: the ticket in his photo displays the white-ball numbers out of numerical order, which real Powerball tickets do not do, and surveillance footage of the Arizona winner does not match Daniels. Authorities and observers consider the Facebook giveaway a hoax.

Construction workers in Gdansk, Poland, unearthed a marble bust of Adolf Hitler during work in the inner garden of the National Museum. The 50 cm (20 in) high head, weighing about 60 kg, bears the inscription "Thorak 1942," identifying it as a work by Josef Thorak, a favored sculptor of the Third Reich known for monumental pieces commissioned for official buildings and public spaces. Museum officials say the bust was deliberately buried some 60 cm underground, likely in 1945 as the Soviet army approached; had it been found immediately after the war, it likely would have been destroyed. The sculpture was struck by a shovel during digging but appears to be in good condition after decades underground. Lech Lopuski, a curator in the museum’s sculpture department, suggested it may originally have been part of the municipal museum’s director’s office when Gdansk (then Danzig) had a predominantly German population and the building served as the municipal museum. Despite repeated gardening and fountain installations over the years, the bust remained concealed. The National Museum has no immediate plans to exhibit the piece; director Wojciech Bonislawski said it will be placed in storage for scientific study to determine who ordered it, where it stood, and how it came to be in the museum grounds. The find highlights Thorak’s prominence: his works ranged from heroic figures to monumental horses, two of which—10 m bronze horses that once stood outside Hitler’s chancellery—were recovered by German police after being missing since 1989. The discovery raises sensitive questions about provenance, historical context, and how to handle artworks associated with the Nazi regime.

NPR fired longtime news analyst Juan Williams after he told Bill O’Reilly on Fox News that he becomes nervous on airplanes when he sees people in Muslim dress. The network said his comments on The O’Reilly Factor were inconsistent with NPR’s editorial standards and undermined his credibility as a news analyst. NPR executives had previously warned Williams about using the NPR name on Fox and about public remarks that veered from journalistic ethics. CEO Vivian Schiller defended the termination, saying analysts shouldn’t offer controversial personal opinions in a way that reflects on NPR; she later apologized for a hasty remark comparing Williams’ feelings to matters for “his psychiatrist or his publicist.” Williams maintained he was not bigoted and said his reaction stems from 9/11-related anxiety; he said he had also urged protecting constitutional rights and avoiding blanket stereotyping. The Council on American-Islamic Relations criticized his remarks, while some media figures, including Whoopi Goldberg, defended him. Fox News quickly signed Williams to a multi-year contract; he wrote columns for FoxNews.com and vowed to defend his view as honest discourse.

Katherine Heigl has returned to Hollywood after stepping back in 2009 to focus on family and reassess her career. Once a rom‑com mainstay, she says she overdid romantic comedies, felt creatively unchallenged and grew disillusioned with the industry that “suddenly turned on” her. The break gave her space to rethink goals and silence the noise; now she’s back with a US TV series, State of Affairs, and the animated film The Nut Job. Heigl insists she still loves rom‑coms but wishes she'd diversified into different genres earlier — perhaps a superhero or psychological thriller — and has negotiated a 15‑episode season limit on State of Affairs so she can return to Utah and maintain a healthier life‑work balance. She describes this phase as the next stage of adulthood while acknowledging she remains partly “a Hollywood animal.” The piece also notes Marie Claire’s August 2014 issue includes trend reports and interviews with Miranda Kerr, Taylor Schilling and Kate Upton, and promotes its digital availability. Separately, the article recounts on‑set tension between Ryan Gosling and Rachel McAdams during The Notebook, with director Nick Cassavetes revealing Gosling once asked to replace McAdams mid‑scene. After a heated confrontation and a cooling‑off moment, their working relationship improved, though the pair later had a tumultuous off‑screen romance that lasted intermittently until 2007.

A powerful storm system soaked much of Texas over several days, producing flash floods, rescues and a freight train derailment as the remnants of Hurricane Patricia moved north. Patricia, downgraded to a tropical depression after making Category 5 landfall in southwestern Mexico, threatened to add heavy rain across South and East Texas. Some areas saw up to 20–21 inches of rain in 24 hours, prompting widespread flash flood watches and warnings through the weekend and into Monday for Houston, Galveston, Corpus Christi, San Antonio, Austin, Waco and other regions.

In Navarro County near Corsicana a 64-car Union Pacific freight train derailed after floodwaters washed out tracks; one locomotive and several cars were partially submerged. Two crew members swam to high ground and were rescued; no injuries were reported. Authorities carried out dozens of swift-water rescues and closed major highways including Interstate 45, causing long traffic backups. In San Antonio, a man walking his dog was swept into a drainage ditch and remained missing; the dog survived. Other incidents included a motorist in Temple rescued after his car floated away and numerous flight cancellations and power outages—about 100 flights canceled at Dallas-Fort Worth. Local officials issued voluntary evacuations for vulnerable coastal areas like Bolivar Peninsula amid concerns about heavy rain, high tides and possible isolation from emergency services.

Bernie Sanders has again thrust single-payer health care into the center of Democratic politics by unveiling a “Medicare for All” bill in the Senate. The proposal seeks to replace the United States’ patchwork system—largely organized around employer-sponsored private insurance and the Affordable Care Act—with a universal, government-run insurance program modeled broadly on single-payer systems in other developed countries. Sanders frames health care as a right and argues that the only sustainable solution to the country’s health-care crisis is a single national program covering every man, woman and child.

The bill would expand Medicare from its current senior-focused role to cover all Americans. It promises comprehensive benefits—hospital and doctor visits, prescription drugs, mental health and substance-abuse treatment, maternity care, vision, dental and more—largely eliminating premiums, deductibles and co-payments for covered services. Sanders and supporters say the plan would be largely financed through progressive tax changes (higher taxes on top earners, capital gains, estates and employers) while existing health-care spending would be folded into the new system. Sanders’ campaign claims the plan would save families and businesses trillions over a decade, though independent evaluations and experts note substantial debate over the net savings and the plan’s true fiscal impact.

The rollout is more political than legislative: Sanders concedes the measure has virtually no chance of passing a Republican-controlled Congress, yet its real purpose is to shift the Democratic debate and set a long-term policy goal. Indeed, the bill has attracted a notable number of Democratic co-sponsors—progressive senators and several potential 2020 presidential contenders, including Elizabeth Warren, Kamala Harris, Cory Booker and Kirsten Gillibrand—transforming support into a practical litmus test for the party’s leftward flank. Polling indicates growing public openness to federal responsibility for universal coverage, and many Democrats believe embracing ambitious options helps define party identity and pressure moderates.

Still, the proposal exposes deep divisions within the Democratic caucus and raises strategic concerns. Senate leaders and many vulnerable Democrats—especially those in Republican-leaning states—have resisted endorsing full single-payer. Figures like Chuck Schumer and Nancy Pelosi emphasize shoring up and defending the Affordable Care Act as the immediate priority. Centrist and some pragmatic liberals argue Medicare for All could be politically toxic in a general election, risk alienating voters satisfied with employer coverage, and impose large tax increases that require clear, credible financing details; some cite Vermont’s failed state-level single-payer attempt as cautionary. Several Democrats, including Chris Murphy and Brian Schatz, have proposed compromise paths—a Medicare or Medicaid “buy-in” or public-option approaches—that would expand government coverage without fully displacing private plans.

Policy experts underscore additional trade-offs. Single-payer could reduce administrative waste and standardize payments—lowering prices by adopting Medicare-like fee schedules—yet Sanders’ version is more generous than most international single-payer systems and removes nearly all cost-sharing, which could spur greater utilization and raise costs. It would also increase payments to providers now reimbursed at Medicaid rates. Crucially, Sanders’ bill initially provided limited financing detail, promising later revenue proposals; critics say concrete, transparent funding plans are essential to judge feasibility.

In short, Sanders’ Medicare for All has succeeded in moving the health-care debate left and rallying progressives, while provoking resistance among centrists and politically vulnerable Democrats. Whether it will become the Democratic Party’s standard-bearer—or remain an aspirational benchmark that shapes future policy choices—remains uncertain. The bill is likely to stay symbolic in the near term, but its emergence signals Sanders’ growing influence on the party’s agenda and a sustained push to expand government-provided health coverage.

David Oliver Relin, a journalist and adventurer best known as co-author of the 2006 best seller Three Cups of Tea, died Nov. 15 in Multnomah County, Ore., at 49. His family said he suffered from depression and took his own life. Relin built a reputation in the 1990s reporting humanitarian stories—child soldiers, travels in Vietnam—and was drawn to Greg Mortenson’s narrative about building schools in Pakistan and Afghanistan. Relin and Mortenson’s relationship was fraught from the start; Relin publicly said Mortenson should not have been a listed co-author. The book sold more than four million copies but came under scrutiny after CBS’s 60 Minutes and Jon Krakauer’s Three Cups of Deceit questioned key episodes and alleged some Central Asia Institute schools did not exist and funds were mismanaged. Mortenson admitted some inaccuracies; Relin faced legal and financial strain, hiring counsel as a federal suit was later dismissed. Relin finished a new book on doctors curing cataract blindness due spring 2013. He is survived by his wife, Dawn; his mother; stepfather Cary Ratcliff; and sisters Rachel Relin and Jennifer Cherelin.

Austin voters rejected a company-backed measure and upheld a City Council ordinance requiring fingerprint-based criminal background checks for ride-hailing drivers, handing Uber and Lyft a high-profile defeat. In a costly, closely watched showdown, the two firms spent more than $8 million—the most expensive municipal campaign in Austin history—to try to repeal the rule, outspending opponents roughly 80-to-1. Voters sided with the fingerprint requirement by 56 to 44 percent. Both companies said their existing screening was sufficient; Lyft called the council rules incompatible with “true ridesharing” and announced it would suspend Austin operations, while Uber expressed “disappointment” at having to halt service. Mayor Steve Adler said the companies are “welcome to stay” and offered to continue negotiations, but analysts and the firms’ hardball past suggest they may not quickly resume service. The outcome produces mixed results: proponents of Proposition 1 and public-safety advocates welcome stricter vetting and reduced risky mid-street pickups, while customers and drivers face disruption. Austin is heavily car-dependent; without Uber and Lyft, riders may pay more for taxis or rely on a less-than-ideal transit system, and drivers who depended on significant earnings from app-based work must scramble for alternatives. The Austin vote could embolden other cities considering fingerprint checks, showing that regulators and campaigns can survive intense industry spending. The situation remains fluid since the rule originated in City Council action and legal and political maneuvering may continue.

Researchers at ETH Zurich have engineered an anti-theft surface for ATMs inspired by the bombardier beetle’s chemical defense. The beetle stores hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinone separately and mixes them to expel near-boiling caustic spray; ETH researchers mimicked this by packing honeycomb-patterned plastic films with hydrogen peroxide in one layer and manganese dioxide in another, separated by a thin lacquer. Impact ruptures the lacquer, the chemicals mix, and a violent catalytic reaction produces hot foam, steam, oxygen and heat (infrared shows foam temperatures reaching about 80°C). The ejected foam is dyed to mark stolen banknotes and thieves; researchers also propose embedding DNA nanoparticles to trace cash back to its source. Unlike the beetle’s enzymatic catalyst, manganese dioxide offers a cheaper lab alternative. The foam is less a spray than an oozing, heat-bearing foam, and the design is likened to a fuse—small mechanical input releasing larger chemical energy. Still experimental with no immediate rollout, proponents suggest broader applications for deterring vandalism or protecting goods and even preventing animal damage in forestry and agriculture.

Briggs Fussy and Brittney Husbyn’s romance reads like a storybook full circle. The couple first crossed paths as children: in 1995, a 3-year-old Briggs served as ring bearer and Brittney as flower girl at Briggs’s godmother’s wedding in Minnesota. Neither recognized the other beyond that single childhood moment—Briggs admits he “didn’t really remember the wedding part at all,” and Brittney says her main recollection was his distinctive name. Years later, they unexpectedly reunited in high school when Brittney sat in front of Briggs in government class. Brittney’s curiosity led her to check with her mother, and the unique name tipped her off. A photo she had from the childhood wedding matched one Briggs’s family had hung in their hallway, revealing their shared past. Though they were both seeing other people at the time, the pair began dating two years after the reconnection and eventually enrolled together at Mankato State University. On Jan. 10, surrounded by 310 family and friends, Briggs and Brittney married—recreating the walk down the aisle they had once shared as toddlers. Friends and relatives, especially Briggs’s godmother who originally brought them together, delight in the serendipity of their story. The newlyweds have embraced the attention their reunion has attracted and plan to preserve the articles and memories to someday show their children. Their journey—from childhood roles at a wedding to becoming bride and groom themselves—continues to captivate those who hear it.

Mira Sorvino has issued a public apology to Dylan Farrow and renounced working with Woody Allen after re-examining Farrow’s longstanding sexual-abuse allegations against the director. Sorvino, who won an Oscar for Allen’s 1995 film Mighty Aphrodite, wrote an open letter in HuffPost acknowledging she was a “naïve young actress” who accepted the media’s framing of Farrow’s claims as part of a custody dispute and failed to look deeper. She emphasized that Allen never behaved inappropriately toward her, but said that personal experience does not excuse having “turned a blind eye” to Dylan’s story because she did not want it to be true.

Sorvino explained that her decision to revisit Farrow’s allegations followed conversations with Ronan Farrow and her own experience going public about being sexually harassed by Harvey Weinstein. After sharing her Weinstein story with Ronan and learning more about the public record around Dylan’s accusations, Sorvino said she found the evidence compelling and concluded Dylan had been telling the truth. She expressed sorrow for having admired and benefited from Allen’s work while failing to support Dylan for years, and vowed never to work with Allen again. Sorvino framed the moment as part of a broader reappraisal of powerful figures and the need to expose abuse even when it involves beloved artists.

Her statement follows similar public regrets from actresses Ellen Page and Greta Gerwig, who have also distanced themselves from Allen. Sorvino closed her letter with praise for Dylan’s courage, an explicit belief in her account, and solidarity with victims of abuse.

A New England Journal of Medicine analysis found that firearm injuries and deaths dip sharply during National Rifle Association (NRA) annual conventions. Researchers Anupam Jena (Harvard) and Andrew Olenski (Columbia) examined nearly 76 million private insurance claims from 2007–2015, comparing injury rates during convention dates with the three weeks before and after. Nationally, firearm injury rates fell about 20% during conventions (from 1.5 to 1.2 per 100,000), while in states hosting conventions the decline was larger—around 50–63% (from 1.9 to 0.7 per 100,000). The reductions were concentrated among men and were most pronounced in the South and West and in states with higher gun ownership. The study found no corresponding drop in gun-related crime, suggesting the decline stems from reduced firearm use rather than reduced criminal activity. Authors propose several explanations: many gun owners and staff of shooting venues attend conventions (sometimes thousands traveling hundreds of miles), ranges or hunting grounds may close, and convention-goers may be the more frequent firearm users whose absence lowers exposure and accidental injuries. The findings, the authors argue, indicate guns pose risks even for experienced users and that decreased exposure leads to fewer injuries—analogized to driving, an inherently riskier activity than walking. External experts endorsed the plausibility, noting unreported unintended discharges are not captured. The NRA criticized the study as illogical, arguing conventions draw only a small fraction of gun owners. Separately, following recent mass shootings, membership and activity in the NRA and other gun-rights groups reportedly surged, reflecting mobilization when supporters feel threatened; whether such growth will affect policy remains uncertain amid rising public support for stronger gun laws.

A man identified as 29-year-old Carnell Marcus Moore opened fire inside the ticketing area of Terminal B at Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental Airport on May 2, 2013, wounding no one but causing panic as passengers scrambled. Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) special agent heard the shots from an office about 150 feet away, confronted Moore and ordered him to drop the gun. The agent fired one shot as Moore turned toward him; Moore simultaneously shot himself and was pronounced dead at the scene. Authorities recovered a Smith & Wesson AR-15 with a fully loaded magazine in a black suitcase nearby and additional .223 ammunition in Moore’s car. Earlier that day Moore had posted ominous messages on Facebook indicating an intent to commit violence; a handwritten note found on his body said he had decided instead to "kill myself" and mentioned struggling with a "monster inside." Parts of Terminal B were closed and later partially reopened; the rest of the airport remained operational. No other injuries were reported. An autopsy was scheduled, and investigators executed searches at Moore’s Beaumont residence.

Starbucks has updated its North American dress code to allow greater personal expression while maintaining a neat, professional appearance. Effective immediately, employees (partners) may wear a broader palette beyond solid black and white—permitted tones now include gray, navy, dark denim, brown and some patterns—along with dark-wash jeans, shorts, skirts, dresses and other standard work pants. The policy also softens headwear restrictions to allow beanies, fedoras and “other suitable hats” (still banning bucket hats, sports caps, berets and cowboy hats). Most notably, partners may now dye their hair any color, so long as the coloring is permanent or semi-permanent to meet food-safety standards; temporary dyes, hair chalk or glitter that could pose safety issues remain restricted.

The change responds to long-running partner feedback and a petition on Coworker.org that drew nearly 15,000 signatures demanding freedom to use unconventional hair colors as self-expression. Starbucks frames the update as aligning workplace attire with what partners already wear in their daily lives, improving comfort and morale while preserving the chain’s recognizable look anchored by the green apron. Select locations, including the 47th & Broadway store, Reserve stores and the Seattle Roastery, piloted the relaxed standards and reported positive customer reaction.

Despite the loosening, the policy still excludes brightly colored shirts, certain prints, hoodies, distracting socks and UGG boots, and retains food-safety-driven limits like restrictions around nail polish and excessive jewelry. Executives say the move complements broader employee-focused initiatives and modernizes the brand’s in-store image by balancing individuality with professionalism.

Two men from Douglas, Georgia, Michael Mancil, 30, and James Dryden Jr., 22, were arrested by Coffee County sheriff’s investigators after allegedly plotting to attack the High Frequency Active Auroral Research Program (HAARP) facility in Alaska, a scientific ionospheric research installation now owned by the University of Alaska Fairbanks. Authorities say the pair were motivated by long-standing conspiracy theories that falsely claim HAARP manipulates weather, controls minds, or traps souls. Investigators described the arms cache they seized as “like something out of a movie,” finding nine firearms including four AR-15s, four Glock handguns and a Remington rifle, plus two to three thousand rounds of ammunition, radios, two flak jackets, $5,500, and a small amount of marijuana. The plot came to light during a drug-sale probe into Mancil and after a local gun shop reported attempts to buy large quantities of weapons. Coffee County Sheriff Doyle Wooten noted concern about a recent, drastic change in Mancil’s behavior. Detective Michael Vickers said the suspects allegedly confessed to believing God told them to destroy HAARP and discussed seeking access to the facility by targeting scientists. UAF officials emphasized that HAARP conducts legitimate atmospheric research and has faced threats before but nothing on this scale; they thanked Georgia investigators for the arrests. Mancil and Dryden face charges including methamphetamine sales, marijuana possession, and possession of a weapon during a crime; additional charges are pending.

Steve Aisthorpe, now 55, has expressed relief and a measure of closure after the remains of his two friends, Icelandic climbers Kristinn Rúnarsson and Þorsteinn Guðjónsson, who vanished on Pumori more than 30 years ago, were recently recovered. The three-man expedition had been attempting Pumori, a nearly 23,500 ft peak on the Nepal–Tibet border, in October 1988. Aisthorpe fell ill mid-expedition and descended to the village of Pheriche; he encouraged Kristinn and Þorsteinn to attempt the summit without him. They were last seen alive at about 21,650 ft on 18 October 1988. After they did not return, Aisthorpe led searches, summoned help, and took part in a helicopter search five days later, but found no trace; he left the area convinced the pair had fallen from the face into a deep crevasse. Decades later an American mountaineer discovered remains at the snout of the glacier below the route, consistent with the glacier having slowly carried the bodies down over the years. Local climbers returned the remains to Kathmandu and relatives attended a cremation; ashes were taken back to Iceland. Aisthorpe recalled the raw loneliness of finding the empty tent in 1988 and the long period of uncertainty that followed. He described how faith and prayer sustained him then, and said the recent discoveries have stirred many emotions but also brought people together and should help families find peace. Two rolls of camera film recovered in a jacket pocket have been sent to Australia for development and could offer further clues. Aisthorpe plans to travel to Reykjavík to meet the families and pay his respects.

Alec Baldwin was honored at Spike TV’s One Night Only: Alec Baldwin tribute at Harlem’s Apollo Theater, where a string of friends, family and co-stars celebrated his three-decade career — and offered plenty of ribbing. The evening featured a surprise appearance by former president Bill Clinton, who opened with a jibe at Donald Trump before praising Baldwin’s long-standing interest in politics, his early backyard filmmaking and his commitment to helping others. Clinton joked that Baldwin should consider running for office again. Robert De Niro joined in mocking Trump and lauded Baldwin’s SNL impersonation, urging him to keep satirizing the president. Throughout the night colleagues including Julianne Moore, Tracy Morgan, Jane Krakowski and Jack McBrayer paid tribute, while Baldwin’s brothers shared childhood memories and his daughter Ireland delivered a self-deprecating roast, referencing her notorious 2007 voicemail from her father and noting their restored relationship. Baldwin closed the show with barbed thank-yous, skewering friends and family — including De Niro, Moore and producer Lorne Michaels — with comic insults rather than heartfelt remarks. The special is scheduled to air July 9 on Spike TV. Separately, Baldwin confirmed to CNN he will reprise his notable Donald Trump impression on Saturday Night Live this fall, though his busy schedule means appearances will be limited.

The family of Walter L. Scott reached a $6.5 million settlement with the city of North Charleston that bars further civil claims over his death. The City Council unanimously approved the agreement, which city attorneys called the largest of its kind in South Carolina and comparable to settlements in other high-profile police killings nationwide. Scott, a 50-year-old black man, was fatally shot on April 4 by white officer Michael T. Slager; bystander cellphone video showed Slager firing at Scott’s back as he ran away. Slager was fired, jailed April 7, and indicted on murder charges in June; he has denied culpability. 

City officials and Scott family lawyers said they negotiated the settlement over months to avoid a civil lawsuit, depositions and prolonged publicity, and to allow both the family and the city to move forward. About $1 million is expected from the state Insurance Reserve Fund and the remainder from the city’s fund balance; officials said it will not affect the city’s bond rating. The settlement also protects current and former city employees from suit. Family representatives described the payout as bittersweet but historic and hoped it sends a message that excessive force will not be tolerated. A portion of the funds will be donated to flood relief. 

The case follows other major settlements—such as Eric Garner in New York ($5.9 million) and Freddie Gray in Baltimore ($6.4 million)—and has intensified national debate about policing, use of force, and the role of video evidence, which has played a key role in recent prosecutions and public scrutiny. The criminal case against Slager will continue.

A Pittsburgh man is suing Kennywood Entertainment, alleging he contracted a damaging eye parasite after being splashed on the Raging Rapids ride on July 2. Robert Trostle and his wife, Krystsina, say they observed the ride’s water was “dirty, stagnant and sludge-like” and noted a nonworking waterfall while waiting in line. Near the ride’s end Trostle was splashed in his left eye; the lawsuit contends that microsporidia, a parasite that can erode the cornea, was present in the ride water and entered his eye then.

Trostle experienced immediate discomfort that progressed over days to severe pain, itching, redness, sensitivity to light and inflammation. Initially treated for acute conjunctivitis on July 5 with antibiotics, his condition worsened and he was diagnosed with microsporidia keratitis on July 14. He underwent a painful surgical scraping to remove the parasite, was kept in a dark room for two days, and surgeons were unable to eliminate the organism entirely because it had penetrated deeper eye layers. The suit alleges ongoing issues—blurry and impaired night vision, persistent redness, itchiness, dryness, inflammation, pain—and that microsporidia remain present.

Filed in Allegheny County Common Pleas Court, the negligence claim seeks damages exceeding $35,000 and accuses Kennywood of failing to maintain adequate water-inspection policies for the ride. Attorney Alan Perer said health department water samples were taken but results have not been released despite Right-to-Know requests. The Allegheny County Health Department confirmed an ongoing investigation and coordination with state and federal agencies. Kennywood declined detailed comment, calling the parasite allegation unproven and noting safety is a top priority. The complaint cites a broader context of rare but serious infections linked to contaminated recreational waters.

Wind shear—the change in wind speed or direction with height—is a primary control on hurricane formation and decay. In the tropics, shear is usually considered vertically between roughly 850 mb (~5,000 ft) and 200 mb (~40,000 ft). Analysts often compute shear averaged over a large radius (e.g., 700 miles) around a storm; that 200–850 mb measure is useful but crude because it may miss smaller-scale or mid-level jets (for example along the Saharan Air Layer) that can impose damaging shear unseen in broad-layer charts. Sparse upper-air observations over the ocean further limit detection of damaging shear, which can unexpectedly weaken developing cyclones.

Tropical cyclones are heat engines powered by latent heat release during condensation. Vertical shear disrupts the storm’s vertical alignment and the balance between low-level inflow and upper-level outflow, removing heat and moisture from the core and reducing efficiency. Classic research by Bill Gray showed large zonal (east–west) shear strongly inhibits development; meridional shear matters less. As a rule of thumb, shear ≤20 kt favors intensification, and rapid intensification is common when shear is ≤10 kt. However, very large storms can sometimes withstand much larger shear (e.g., Hurricane Wilma).

Operational shear diagnosis uses satellite-derived wind fields (e.g., CIMSS), subtracting low-level from upper-level winds while removing the cyclone’s own circulation to show the environmental shear and direction overlaid on moisture imagery. Real cases, such as Tropical Storm Gabrielle (2007), illustrate how differential wind directions with height produced local shear variations that inhibited convection near the center.

Cape Verde hurricanes originate near the Cabo Verde Islands and often become large, intense storms as they cross the Atlantic; Irma (2017) is an example. Forecast uncertainty over longer ranges reflects competing model solutions and evolving steering patterns: a strong ridge can force a westward track into the Caribbean and potentially toward the U.S., while weaker ridging can allow recurvature away from land. Seasonal factors—neutral ENSO, warm Atlantic sea-surface temperatures, and active African waves—have contributed to an above-normal 2017 season.

WWF charged a Brandenburg public order chief after he authorised local hunters to shoot a European bison found near Lebus on the Oder, saying “giving permission to shoot a strongly protected animal without a clear potential threat is a criminal offence.” The bison — Europe’s largest land mammal and listed as “strongly protected” and “vulnerable” — had likely wandered from Ujście Warty National Park on the German-Polish border. Brandenburg officials defended the decision as protection of the public; critics, including the Environment Minister, argued bison are not generally dangerous and could have been tranquillised. WWF blamed a lack of trained staff and pointed to past poor handling of wolves and elk.

The piece then turns to Poland’s Białowieża Forest, a storied refuge for bison, wolves, lynx and bears. Once hunted to near extinction—only about 50 remained in the early 20th century—intensive conservation and reintroductions have grown global numbers to over 4,600, with Poland hosting significant free-ranging populations. Night footage from Białowieża shows bison fending off wolves, illustrating their resilience; adults, weighing up to 2,200 lb, lack natural predators except when wolves target calves.

Despite recovery successes, challenges persist: low genetic diversity (descended from seven ancestors), disease risks, human-wildlife conflict, and controversial management practices such as winter feeding and annual culls (up to 50 animals). Rewilding advocates urge less intervention and larger, varied habitats; critics of strict forestry management argue parks are often run to protect trees rather than whole ecosystems. Cross-border issues—including a frontier fence splitting bison populations and differing hunting laws—complicate conservation. Białowieża remains a mix of ancient, untouched fragments and managed forest, emblematic of Europe’s struggle to reconcile wildlife recovery with human land use.

Facebook and Microsoft struck a patent deal that goes beyond routine IP trading and signals a broader strategic alignment against Google. Microsoft bought 925 patents and applications from AOL for about $1.056 billion, then agreed to sell roughly 70 percent (about 650 patents) to Facebook for $550 million while keeping roughly 275 patents for itself. Microsoft will license the patents Facebook acquires and grant Facebook a license to the 275 patents it retains. The split likely leaves Facebook with patents tied to mobile, web and instant messaging technologies, and Microsoft with search-related patents.

The transaction bolsters Facebook’s intellectual property holdings ahead of its expected IPO and arms it in ongoing litigation, notably its patent clash with Yahoo, which has sued Facebook over advertising patents; Facebook has countered. Observers frame the move as largely defensive and politically strategic: assembling a patent portfolio provides leverage in disputes and deterrence against suits and “patent trolls.” Analysts and commentators see the partnership as part of a tightening Microsoft–Facebook relationship driven by a common rival, Google. Google dominates search and has pursued social features (Google+) and mobile (Android), matters that threaten both firms in different ways. Microsoft’s previous collaborations with Facebook include sharing social data for Bing search; Redmond also owns a small Facebook stake.

The deal leaves some open questions—how patents will be divided in detail, whether Facebook will seek more patents directly from AOL, and how it will use the acquisitions in litigation or competitive strategy. Yahoo said the deal won’t affect its lawsuit; Microsoft emphasized it values relationships with both Facebook and Yahoo. Overall, the agreement underscores how major tech firms are using patent portfolios as strategic tools in a landscape heavily shaped by Google’s dominance.

Last week’s big IP dust-up hit the brony community when Hasbro issued takedown notices to PonyArchive.org, a major fan site that hosted high-quality episodes of My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic. PonyArchive—popular with international fans and about 30,000 weekly visitors—initially refused, claiming protection by fictional Princess Celestia and asserting distance from U.S. law. After a second notice it removed episodes and posted a profanity-laced farewell, provoking heated debate among bronies. Many fans criticized PonyArchive’s immature response; others lamented losing access and turned to torrents. The episode underscores tensions between intellectual property enforcement and devoted online fandom. Bronies—adult fans, often male, who embraced the 2010 reboot for its strong writing and heart—originated partly on 4chan and grew into a lively subculture with blogs, art, meetups and conventions. Despite site shutdowns, the community persists, showing how high-quality children’s programming can attract unexpected adult audiences while clashing with corporate rights enforcement.

A former Royal Canadian Mint employee, 35-year-old Leston Lawrence, has been sentenced to 30 months in jail and ordered to pay a $190,000 fine after being found guilty of stealing 22 solid gold “pucks” from the mint’s Ottawa facility. Lawrence was convicted in November of stealing the pucks, laundering 17 of them through Ottawa Gold Buyers and related offences including possession of property obtained by crime, conveying gold out of the mint and breach of trust. He sold the 17 pucks for about $130,000 between 2014 and 2015; their estimated market value is roughly $190,000. The crown had sought a three-year sentence while the defence argued for 18 months and contended lax mint security facilitated the thefts.

The evidence was largely circumstantial: no one was seen taking the pucks and there was no video of the thefts, though the pucks matched the mint’s unique ladle and Vaseline and latex gloves were found in Lawrence’s locker. He also set off a metal detector more often than co-workers, but secondary wand checks failed to detect metal. Four unsold pucks were recovered from a safety deposit box. Lawrence reportedly used proceeds to buy a house in Jamaica and a boat in Florida.

Ontario Court Justice Peter Doody ordered repayment of the fine within three years of release or an additional 30 months’ imprisonment. The mint said it has since strengthened security—upgrading screening, cameras to HD real-time monitoring, and staff scanning training—to prevent similar incidents.

A group of Spokane, Washington, men in their 20s placed a Craigslist ad seeking a “generic dad” to man the grill for a Father’s Day weekend barbecue in mid‑June. Applicants must have at least 18 years of experience being a dad and 10 years’ grilling experience, and must bring their own grill; burgers and hotdogs will be supplied. The ad's creators, who don’t live with their fathers and say none of them can fill the “barbecue dad” role, want someone who can talk about stereotypical dad topics—lawnmowers, building decks and Jimmy Buffett—and will be paid in food and beer. Dane Anderson told KHQ‑TV that several people have responded to the posting. The report cites KHQ‑TV and archived online references.

Ford said it will largely abandon traditional passenger cars in North America and concentrate on trucks, SUVs and commercial vehicles, leaving only the Mustang and a new Focus Active crossover in its car lineup. The move reflects shifting consumer demand and follows broader industry trends favoring higher-riding, more versatile vehicles. By 2020 Ford expects nearly 90% of its North American offerings to be trucks, SUVs or commercial models.

The announcement accompanied first-quarter results: $1.7 billion in profit, 43 cents per share (beating estimates by 2 cents), and $42 billion in revenue—up 7% year-over-year. Pretax profit fell 14% to $2.2 billion, with the company attributing much of the reported quarterly profit increase to a lower effective tax rate. Higher commodity costs—aluminum, steel and copper—were a significant drag, costing roughly $500 million this quarter and an expected $1.5 billion for the year. Regionally, North America and Europe were profitable while South America, Asia/Pacific and Middle East/Africa posted losses.

Ford plans additional cost reductions of $11.5 billion through 2022 on top of prior cuts, and will reduce capital expenditure plans by $5 billion over 2019–2022. Executives did not rule out further staffing changes. The strategy includes expanding hybrid and electric options across key SUVs and trucks to capture growing market share in electrified vehicles.

Armed civilian groups and self-styled militias have mobilized in response to President Trump’s warnings about migrant caravans moving through Mexico, vowing to travel to the U.S.-Mexico border to "observe and report" or to assist law enforcement. Groups such as the Texas Minutemen and the Minuteman Project say volunteers — some armed, some equipped with drones and night-vision gear — are converging on border areas from Texas to New Mexico. Their leaders claim they will support Border Patrol and the military, though how many will actually show up remains uncertain. Military planning documents obtained by Newsweek warn commanders that roughly 200 unregulated militia members could deploy, sometimes operating as "citizen patrols" and, in isolated past incidents, allegedly seizing National Guard equipment. Border officials have not issued specific orders about militias but plan community outreach; they caution that volunteers should not interfere with official operations.

Local reaction is mixed. Some ranchers and organized local volunteer groups reject outside militias, refusing entry to strangers and stressing that property owners prefer vetted, local responders. Residents worry militias could be "trigger-happy," damage property, or complicate law enforcement. Small border towns like Columbus, N.M., report a handful of self-described militiamen arriving; local leaders urge calm, emphasize good cross-border relations, and warn that federal authorities should handle border security. The situation highlights tension between grassroots armed activism and official control as troops prepare to support border operations.

Manuel “Meme” Uribe, once recognized by Guinness World Records as the world’s heaviest man, died at 48 in Monterrey, Nuevo Leon. Uribe had reached a peak certified weight of about 1,230 pounds (560 kg) in 2006 but later reduced to roughly 867 pounds (394 kg). Confined to his bed since about 2002 and unable to walk, he relied on his mother and friends for feeding and care and left home only rarely. He was taken to a hospital on May 2 after experiencing an abnormal heartbeat; emergency workers had to use a crane to move him. Doctors have not yet certified the official cause of death, though he suffered cardiac arrhythmia and was believed to have liver problems. Uribe’s weight struggles dated back to adolescence, when he already weighed over 250 pounds, and ballooned further after 1992. He had a history that included living briefly in the United States and selling tacos in Dallas. In 2008 he married Claudia Solis, a wedding notable as one of the few times he left home in recent years.

House Speaker Paul Ryan released a slick, 45-second video titled “Politics These Days” promoting a unity message for House Republicans under his “#ConfidentAmerica” agenda. In the clip, Ryan condemns identity politics and urges Republicans to inspire voters around shared values and common humanity rather than divide them. The production, which resembles a campaign ad and reprises remarks he made to Capitol Hill interns, has reignited speculation that the Wisconsin Republican could become a compromise presidential nominee if the GOP faces a contested convention this summer.

Ryan has repeatedly and publicly denied any interest in running for president, saying bluntly that he is not a candidate and will not accept a nomination. His office and spokeswoman AshLee Strong have firmly disavowed “Draft Ryan” efforts and threatened legal action against organizers. Still, observers point to past behavior—most notably his initial reluctance to accept the House speakership last year before ultimately taking the job—as reason to doubt his categorical denials. Prominent Republicans, including former Speaker John Boehner and Rep. Tom Cole, have at times praised Ryan as a possible unifying alternative. As the convention approaches and divisions deepen within the party, the video ensures Ryan will remain central to debate about the GOP’s direction and potential contingency plans.

The Humane Society of Missouri’s Disaster Response Team rescued a small white dog named Soshe from a Pender County home submerged by Hurricane Florence and reunited her with her owner. The owner had evacuated and was stranded in Wilmington, unable to return to her flooded house; she contacted rescuers when she learned Soshe was trapped inside. The nine-member HSMO team made three boat attempts to reach the area, facing roof-high floodwaters that made houses hard to identify and suffering a boat breakdown on their third try. They paddled half a mile after the breakdown and, as water receded enough to spot the right house, heard Soshe barking. Two rescuers forced the front door and found the dog perched on a floating living-room couch, where she had likely spent almost a week. Soshe was dried, cared for, and delivered to a friend before being reunited with her tearful owner. The team spent 10 days assisting in North Carolina alongside partners, saving multiple animals, transporting others to shelters, and aiding Coast Guard animal unloading. Donations were solicited to support ongoing efforts.

Army Staff Sgt. Robert Bales intends to plead guilty to the 2012 massacre of 16 Afghan villagers to avoid the death penalty, his attorney John Henry Browne told the AP. The plea deal—pending approval by a judge and his commanding general—requires Bales to recount the killings in court; a June 5 hearing is set, with sentencing-phase proceedings in September to determine life imprisonment with or without parole. Browne described Bales as “crazed” and “broken,” citing PTSD, a traumatic brain injury, alcohol and drug use, and multiple deployments, but said his mental state did not meet the legal standard for insanity. The attack, in Kandahar province, also wounded six and provoked Afghan outrage and strained U.S.-Afghan relations. Afghan families demanded execution; some threatened revenge if Bales is not hanged. Browne warned the plea could inflame tensions but said his priority is saving Bales from execution.

A striking new pedestrian attraction in Vietnam’s Bà Nà Hills has drawn international attention for its dramatic, theatrical design. Known as Cau Vang or the Golden Bridge, the roughly 150-meter (nearly 500-foot) walkway opened in June as part of the Thien Thai Garden development at the mountain resort outside Da Nang. Perched around 1,000–1,400 meters (3,280–4,600 feet) above sea level, the bridge appears to be lifted into the sky by two enormous stone-colored hands that emerge from the hillside, an image intended to evoke “giant hands of gods pulling a strip of gold out of the land.” TA Landscape Architecture (Ho Chi Minh City) led the design, and TA Corporation contributed to the landscape concept; the project was built in under a year and forms part of a reported $2 billion investment to boost tourism in the area.

The bridge’s path is edged with purple lobelia chrysanthemums and offers sweeping views of the verdant mountainscape and the resort’s attractions. It complements existing draws at Bà Nà Hills—such as a replica French village, formal gardens, a cable car system once ranked among the world’s longest and highest, and Fantasy Park—and has already hosted events including a bridal fashion show. Visitors’ reactions emphasize the surreal, cloudlike sensation of walking the elevated span and the lifelike quality of the sculpted hands.

Cau Vang joins a global family of iconic, statement footbridges—ranging from mechanically unfolding and DNA-inspired structures to living root bridges and sunken pathways—that function as sculptural landmarks as much as practical crossings, drawing tourists, photographers, and selfie-seekers worldwide.

Researchers Christopher A. Thorstenson, A. D. Pazda, and A. J. Elliot designed and ran two experiments testing whether induced emotion alters basic color perception. Participants were randomly assigned to watch brief film clips that induced sadness (a two-minute grayscale clip of Mufasa’s death from The Lion King), amusement (a stand-up comedy clip), or a neutral screensaver; the clips in the second experiment were converted to grayscale to control for color exposure. After viewing, participants identified highly desaturated color patches (red, yellow, green, blue) presented twice in randomized order, and reported their emotional state. Across both experiments, sadness reliably impaired accuracy in discriminating colors along the blue–yellow axis but did not affect discrimination along the red–green axis. Amusement and neutral conditions did not show this impairment. The authors note the effect is axis-specific, arguing that a general drop in arousal or engagement would have produced broader deficits across color axes. They speculate that dopamine—a neurotransmitter implicated in mood disorders and in retinal processing—might mediate the blue–yellow sensitivity change, citing parallels with clinical conditions (e.g., ADHD, depression) that show blue perception deficits and altered dopamine function; however, dopamine was not measured in these studies. The findings support the idea that emotion can influence low-level visual processes and suggest that common metaphors linking mood and color (e.g., “feeling blue”) may reflect perceptual as well as linguistic associations. All authors contributed to design, data collection, analysis, and manuscript preparation.

A massive magnitude-8.9 (later revised to 9.0) earthquake and tsunami struck northeastern Japan on March 11, 2011, crippling infrastructure and triggering a multi-facility nuclear crisis at Fukushima. The quake and flooding severed power to the Fukushima Dai-ichi complex, disabling cooling systems. With backup power failing at one unit, operators faced rapidly worsening temperatures in reactor vessels. To relieve pressure and avoid catastrophic core damage, officials vented radioactive steam that contained hydrogen produced when overheated zirconium cladding reacted with water. They knew venting risked a hydrogen explosion but judged it preferable to a total meltdown. The containment building at Unit 1 later exploded; seawater and boron were then used in desperate, nonstop cooling efforts until electrical power and normal systems could be restored. Experts warned that continued temperature rises could melt uranium fuel, breach the stainless-steel reactor vessel and containment floors, and release deadly radioactive material—potentially requiring measures akin to Chernobyl’s entombment and rendering surrounding land uninhabitable for long periods.

Beyond the nuclear emergency, the quake-tsunami disaster produced immense human and material devastation: official estimates put the death toll above 10,000 in some hard-hit prefectures, with thousands confirmed dead, many more missing, and widespread injuries. Hundreds of thousands were displaced, often without power, water or food; rolling blackouts were imposed nationally. Rescue and relief operations expanded, including military deployments and international aid, but access remained limited in many inundated areas. Cities and towns—Sendai, Rikuzentakata, Minamisanrikucho and others—suffered catastrophic damage, scenes of rubble, fires and desperate survivors underscored the scale of Japan’s worst crisis since World War II.

Fitch Ratings placed the United States' long- and short-term sovereign ratings on Rating Watch Negative on October 15, 2013, keeping the 'AAA' IDRs but signaling elevated downgrade risk. The move reflects high-weight concerns about Congress failing to raise the federal debt ceiling before Treasury's extraordinary measures run out, exposing the Treasury to volatile cash flows and possible payment delays. Fitch warned prolonged brinkmanship could undermine confidence in the U.S. dollar’s reserve status and weaken perceptions of government effectiveness, harming growth and funding costs. Despite this, Fitch cited strong fundamentals—large, diversified economy, reserve-currency benefits, improved deficit reduction since 2010, and stabilizing debt ratios—as reasons the U.S. retains 'AAA'. Resolution of the watch depends on the debt-ceiling outcome and longer-term fiscal prospects.

Chelsea Handler has relocated her late-night show, Chelsea Lately, from a cramped Santa Monica studio to the much larger Stage 1 at Universal Studios, a space with history as the former home of The Jack Benny Show and Conan O’Brien’s short-lived Tonight Show. The move, debuting Monday at 11 p.m. on E!, brings several practical and creative upgrades Handler relishes — including a private shower in her office so she no longer has to walk past lined-up audience members in a robe after using an industrial shower downstairs. The new set expands audience capacity from 75 to about 200 while aiming to preserve the show’s intimate, participatory feel; Handler stresses her comedy depends on strong audience involvement and plans interactive bits like picking crowd members for onstage games. Improved sound and lighting systems and more space open possibilities for bigger staging and gags involving sidekick Chuy Bravo. For the studio christening, close friend Jennifer Aniston will be the first guest, followed by Fergie, Miley Cyrus and Christina Aguilera later in the week — a string of female guests Handler hopes will “give the stage their blessing.” Handler, who has hosted since 2007 and draws strong female 18–34 viewership, says she’s committed to the show and ready to go “full throttle.” A playful shower sketch with Sandra Bullock also marked the move.

British investigators have contacted Australian authorities after skeletal remains of a fair-haired young child were found in a suitcase beside a highway near Wynarka, South Australia. The remains, discovered in mid-July by a passing motorist, are believed to be of a girl aged roughly between 2½ and 4 (police later widened the estimated range to two to seven). South Australia Police say the child was likely killed elsewhere at some point after 2007 and the suitcase was left beside the Karoonda Highway between four weeks and four months before discovery. Clothing items and a distinctive handmade quilt with 25 octagonal patches—seven of which have been digitally released to the public—were found with the remains. One fabric piece featuring musical notes was traced to manufacture in New York around 2008. Forensic testing is under way in Adelaide, and investigators believe the girl met a violent death; foul play is certain but cause and circumstances remain unclear.

The high-profile disappearance of British toddler Madeleine McCann in 2007 prompted media and public speculation about a link because Madeleine was a blond three-year-old when she vanished in Portugal. Scotland Yard confirmed it had made inquiries with Australian counterparts. South Australian officials, including Detective Superintendent Des Bray and Police Commissioner Grant Stevens, have repeatedly stated there is currently no evidence connecting the Wynarka remains to McCann and warned against speculation. Investigators hope public recognition of the quilt, clothing or suitcase will yield leads; hundreds of calls to Crime Stoppers have already been received. Authorities urge anyone with information to come forward.

An 86-year-old Port St. Lucie man, William J. Hager, has been arrested and charged with first-degree premeditated murder after telling deputies he shot his 78-year-old wife, Carolyn Hager, because she was ill and he could no longer afford her medications. Deputies responded to a verbal disturbance May 16 at the Hagers’ Meadowlark Lane home. Upon entering, Hager reportedly told officers, “I have bad news. I shot my wife at 7:30 this morning,” and later apologized that he hadn’t called earlier because he wanted to tell his children first. Investigators found Carolyn dead from a gunshot wound to the head in a bedroom. According to the arrest affidavit, William Hager said he had been contemplating killing his wife for several days because she was suffering; she had previously expressed a desire to die but never explicitly asked him to kill her. Neighbors described the couple as sweet and were shocked; one neighbor noted Carolyn appeared to be in “excruciating” back pain despite her otherwise warm demeanor. Authorities and community clinic staff confirmed Carolyn had long-term health problems, including severe arthritis, and the couple had financial struggles—records show a 2011 bankruptcy and William once took a job at Sears to help pay for medications. Officials would not disclose specific prescriptions due to HIPAA. The sheriff’s office emphasized that community resources exist for those facing medical and financial crises, and urged using helplines like 2-1-1. Hager was booked without bond and remains in the St. Lucie County Jail.

Researchers have discovered a vast, year‑round liquid water reservoir buried within Greenland’s firn — the partially compacted snow layer — overturning assumptions about where surface melt goes. Found in southeast Greenland in 2011 when drillers struck slushy, water‑soaked firn at depths of 5–50 meters despite air temperatures around −15°C, the aquifer spans roughly 70,000 km² (about the size of Ireland or West Virginia) and holds an estimated 140 billion tonnes of water. That volume is equivalent to about 0.4 mm of global sea level rise — roughly half of Greenland’s annual contribution — and represents a previously unrecognized storage pool for meltwater. 

The water remains liquid because heavy late‑summer snowfall in these high‑accumulation regions insulates the buried firn, preventing freezing during winter. Radar surveys and additional drilling confirmed widespread pockets of liquid in areas of high snowfall. Scientists do not yet know the water’s age or ultimate fate: it may be draining to the ocean slowly, feed sudden drainage events, lubricate the ice sheet base and accelerate glacier flow, or act largely as temporary storage. The aquifer also functions as a heat sink that could affect how the ice sheet responds to warming, especially as surface melting intensifies and extends to higher elevations. 

Researchers plan further fieldwork to determine connectivity to ocean drainage and the implications for ice dynamics and sea level projections. The discovery adds complexity to models and observations of Greenland mass loss and is important for improving predictions of future sea level rise.

Democratic strategist Hilary Rosen sparked widespread backlash after telling CNN that Ann Romney has "never worked a day in her life." Rosen argued that Ann Romney hasn’t faced the dual pressures of earning a paycheck while raising children like many American women, and questioned Mitt Romney’s use of his wife as an authority on women's economic concerns. The remark drew swift bipartisan condemnation—Ann Romney posted her first tweet defending stay-at-home parenting as hard work, and Obama aides including Jim Messina and David Axelrod called Rosen’s comments inappropriate and urged family remain off-limits. Rosen defended and clarified her point on Twitter and in a Huffington Post column, stressing she admires homemakers but was critiquing whether Ann Romney represents most women’s economic struggles. The controversy prolonged media attention and risked political fallout on gender issues for both campaigns.

Fourteen-year-old Emanuel Zayas, who had traveled from Cuba with his family to Miami for treatment, died after surgery to remove a massive facial tumor. The growth, which initially seemed like a pimple when it first appeared, eventually ballooned to a size larger than a basketball and weighed about 10 pounds. Although surgeons determined the tumor was benign, they worried its size posed life-threatening risks, including suffocation or catastrophic neck injury. Emanuel’s condition was identified as polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, a disorder in which bone is replaced by scar-like fibrous tissue, leading to deformities and weakened structures. Dr. Robert Marx, chief of oral and maxillofacial surgery at the University of Miami Health System, had learned of Emanuel’s case after seeing photos and X-rays shown by missionaries at a medical conference and arranged for surgery at Holtz Children’s Hospital at Jackson Memorial. Following the operation, Emanuel died; Dr. Marx expressed sadness that the physiological stress of surgery overwhelmed the boy’s compromised anatomy and said their hopes of both saving his life and improving his quality of life were not realized. He offered condolences and called Emanuel “a very brave young man.” Emanuel’s family plans to donate his body to science to help researchers better understand polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. The case drew coverage from the Miami Herald and NBC 6, and the story was reported by Brett Molina.

A Minnesota couple anonymously dropped a $500,000 check into a Salvation Army red kettle at Cub Foods in Rosemount over the weekend, the largest single kettle donation ever recorded in the Twin Cities and, confirmed by national headquarters, the largest in the country. The previous Twin Cities record was $25,000; the charity says a typical kettle collects about $30 an hour. The check cleared Monday; the couple asked to remain anonymous and have given substantial kettle gifts before, though not at this level. Salvation Army staff learned a day or two beforehand and retrieved the kettle. The donors said they gave to encourage others to be generous, to honor one donor’s father who served in World War I and appreciated Salvation Army “doughnut lassies,” and because they once relied on discarded grocery food themselves. Maj. Jeff Strickler called the gift “a true blessing” as the Twin Cities campaign pursues an $11.6 million goal, having raised roughly $2.2 million so far. Separately, an anonymous benefactor known as “St. Grand” recently left $1,100 in several kettles. The Salvation Army continues to seek volunteers to staff 575 kettle locations and supports thousands with meals, shelter and toys.

A weeklong manhunt is underway for suspected killer William (Billy) Boyette Jr., 44, and alleged accomplice Mary (Mary Craig) Rice, 38, after a multi-state crime spree across the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama that left three women dead and a fourth shot. Authorities say the pair have been hiding in woods in northwest Florida, prompting doubled patrols and a public warning: surrender or be killed. Santa Rosa County Sheriff Bob Johnson and Escambia County officials updated the public, releasing surveillance images and a new photo of Rice taken at a Walmart days after two of the murders. Investigators now consider Rice a suspect with a capital murder warrant rather than a hostage, saying evidence indicates she had opportunities to flee or seek help.

Timeline: Jan. 31 — Boyette allegedly killed Alicia Greer, 30 (his girlfriend), and Jacqueline Moore at the Emerald Sands Inn in Milton, Fla.; Feb. 3 — Peggy Broz, 52, was allegedly killed in Lillian, Ala.; Feb. 6 — Boyette is accused of shooting Kayla Crocker, 28, during a Beulah, Fla., home invasion, stealing her white 2006 Chevy Cobalt, and fleeing with Rice. Crocker is expected to survive; her 2-year-old was unharmed. Surveillance showed the suspects later at a Shell and Hardee’s. Authorities believe Boyette altered his appearance by shaving his head and goatee and that Rice dyed her hair orange. Boyette is described as armed, dangerous, with a lengthy violent-crime history and substance abuse issues. Deputies are searching wooded areas, using dogs and investigating possible camps; a $10,000 reward was paid for a tip leading authorities to the suspects’ whereabouts. Officials urge anyone with information not to approach the suspects and to call police immediately.

Indiewire published its annual predictions charts for the 86th Academy Awards, covering all major categories ahead of the March 2, 2014 broadcast and encouraging readers to subscribe to their awards newsletter. Ellen DeGeneres was announced as the Oscars host, tweeting the news and recalling her prior 2007 turn; producers Craig Zadan and Neil Meron praised her warmth and humor. The producers were rehired earlier, and Cheryl Boone Isaacs’ recent election as Academy president set the stage for planning. DeGeneres’ selection signals a shift to a gentler tone after criticism of Seth MacFarlane’s prior hosting.

On the morning of December 16, gunmen from Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) stormed the Army Public School and Degree College in Peshawar, scaling an undefended back wall and igniting the deadliest terrorist attack in Pakistan’s recent history. Seven attackers wearing suicide vests entered the male-only section where students aged roughly five to 18 — many the children of army personnel — were taking exams. They moved classroom to classroom, firing indiscriminately and executing pupils and staff; some victims were also burned. By evening, authorities reported at least 145 dead, including roughly 132 children and numerous teachers and soldiers, and more than 100 wounded. The school’s principal, Tahira Qazi, and several teachers were among the victims.

Survivors described scenes of horror: students hiding under benches, being shot at point-blank range, and playing dead amid bloodied corridors. Rescue efforts involved elite commandos who fought through the complex for hours; all attackers were eventually killed. Witnesses said the attackers used diversionary explosions and came prepared with ammunition and supplies, indicating they did not expect to survive. The TTP later claimed the assault was revenge for army operations in tribal areas and said older male students were targeted, a claim widely condemned as implausible and damaging.

The massacre provoked national and international outrage. Pakistan declared three days of mourning; Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif vowed to intensify the fight against militancy and lifted a moratorium on the death penalty for terrorism cases. Pakistan’s military reported air strikes against militant positions in Khyber and North Waziristan in the aftermath. Global leaders, including President Obama and Nobel laureate Malala Yousafzai, condemned the atrocity. Mass funerals, vigils and frantic blood drives followed as Peshawar and the nation grappled with profound grief and renewed determination to combat the insurgency.

President Obama’s medical reports and public appearances have made his nicotine habit highly visible. Doctors have described him as in “excellent” health overall but noted occasional smoking and recommended continued smoking-cessation efforts, specifically nicotine gum. Obama has long struggled to quit cigarettes, admitting relapses and using Nicorette gum regularly — on Air Force One, during ceremonies, and on foreign trips — prompting criticism from some observers who deemed chewing gum disrespectful at diplomatic events. Critics, including commentators and foreign bloggers, framed the behavior as undignified, while others pointed out chewing gum’s broad popularity in countries like China, where Wrigley dominates the market and the average person buys multiple sticks yearly. Beyond tobacco, Obama’s exam flagged borderline-high cholesterol and chronic tendinitis in his left knee linked to basketball; physicians advised dietary changes, leg-strengthening exercises, routine immunizations, dental care, and follow-up cancer screening in five years. Overall, he remains fit for duty with targeted health recommendations.

Hackers identifying with Anonymous in Mexico disrupted at least two websites tied to Pope Benedict XVI’s upcoming visit, claiming the trip is a political maneuver to boost the conservative National Action Party (PAN) ahead of July elections. The Mexican Episcopal Conference said its papal-visit page was blocked by a “cyber attack,” hampering logistics and visitor information for events beginning in Guanajuato, a PAN-governed, heavily Catholic state. Anonymous IberoAmerica credited operations named “Pharisee” and “freeloader,” and Anonymous Mexico posted a video arguing the visit wastes funds that could aid the poor and will be used to sway Catholic voters for PAN candidate Josefina Vázquez Mota. The timing drew scrutiny despite the government saying President Calderón invited the pope in 2007; critics also questioned why Mexico City was excluded, with the Vatican citing high altitude concerns. Security is a major focus: the pope is expected to address rampant drug violence that has claimed tens of thousands of lives, and local authorities, church leaders and even cartels have signaled restraint during the visit. Major events include a meeting with Calderón and a large open-air mass.

Chicago authorities have shut a Lawndale corner store after investigators found clerks selling synthetic cannabinoids suspected in a cluster of severe bleeding cases. Illinois health officials have issued repeated warnings: since early March, dozens of people who reported using synthetic pot—often called K2, spice, or labeled as herbal or liquid incense—have sought emergency care with alarming hemorrhagic symptoms. Initially 17 cases were reported; state tallies rose to 32 people treated for significant bleeding after using these products, with no deaths reported so far.

Symptoms have included nosebleeds, bleeding gums, blood in urine, coughing up blood, bleeding from eyes and ears in some reports, and unusually heavy menstrual bleeding. Most cases were reported in the Chicago area (including Cook, Will, DuPage, Kane and McLean counties), but a concentration emerged in central Illinois—Tazewell and Peoria counties reported a combined 16 cases. Patients said they acquired products from convenience stores, dealers, or friends.

Health officials stress that synthetic cannabinoids are a changing mix of hundreds of chemicals that can cause hallucinations, psychosis, violent behavior, kidney injury, and now unexplained bleeding—an unexpected and severe development. Regulators suspect manufacturers tweak chemical formulas to evade bans, complicating detection and linking products to illnesses. Investigations continue to identify a common contaminated product or ingredient. The Illinois Department of Public Health and clinicians advise anyone experiencing unexplained bleeding or bruising after using synthetic cannabinoids to seek immediate emergency care.

A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to immediately restore CNN chief White House correspondent Jim Acosta’s press credentials after they were revoked following a heated exchange with President Trump at a press conference. U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee, granted a temporary restraining order after finding that the White House’s process for the suspension violated due process under the Fifth Amendment. Kelly concluded that the government could not specify who initially ordered the revocation and that the post-hoc explanations offered by the White House were insufficient.
