He also found Acosta suffered irreparable harm, rejecting the government’s argument that CNN could simply send other reporters to cover the president. The larger lawsuit CNN filed, alleging viewpoint discrimination under the First Amendment and procedural violations, continues; the ruling returns Acosta to the White House while litigation proceeds. The dispute began after an on-camera confrontation in which Trump called on another reporter and Acosta clashed with a White House intern over a microphone; the White House initially accused Acosta of improper physical contact, circulated a doctored video, then shifted to accusing him of unprofessional behavior. Media organizations widely criticized the ban as unprecedented and threatening to press freedom; several filed amici briefs supporting CNN. The White House signaled it would draft rules to address the court’s due-process concerns and said it would continue to contest the matter.

This document surveys several archaeological discoveries and the complex history of the swastika as a symbol. It opens with a 1939 Nazi May Day parade image in Berlin and explains that the hooked cross—called swastika from Sanskrit svastika, meaning “good fortune”—is an ancient motif found across Neolithic Eurasia, India, Indonesia and pre‑Christian Europe and remains sacred in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism. Late 19th‑century archaeology, notably Heinrich Schliemann’s finds at Troy, revived interest in the motif; nationalist and racialist movements then appropriated it to promote Aryan identity. The Nazi Party formally adopted the Hakenkreuz in 1920 and made it central to propaganda, transforming its connotations into an emblem of racist ideology and genocide, as described by Hitler in Mein Kampf. The piece then shifts to modern geoglyph discoveries enabled by satellite imagery: a huge elk‑shaped stone geoglyph in the Ural Mountains, Russia, possibly dating to the Eneolithic (4th–3rd millennia BCE) based on lithic artifacts and partial excavation, which—if confirmed—would predate Peru’s Nazca Lines. It reports over 50 earthen geoglyphs in northern Kazakhstan—squares, rings, a swastika and huge mounds up to 1,312 ft—where excavations uncovered hearths and structures suggesting ritual use. Finally, it describes thousands of stone “wheels” across the Middle East (Syria, Jordan, Saudi Arabia): circular stone structures with spokes, often on lava fields, visible from the air, poorly dated but possibly up to 2,000 years old, whose function—ritual, funerary, territorial marking—remains unresolved. The account emphasizes how satellite mapping is revealing widespread, ancient landscape art worldwide and how meanings of symbols can be radically transformed over time.

NASA researchers using a new satellite method have revealed that slow, low flames burning beneath the Amazon canopy—so-called understory fires—have destroyed far more forest than recent deforestation. Between 1999 and 2010 these hidden fires burned over 33,000 square miles (85,500 km²), killing 10–50% of trees in affected patches and leaving long recovery times. Understory fires spread slowly and modestly visible at the surface, so they were previously underestimated; the study in Philosophical Transactions B gives the first regional estimate for the southern Amazon. Fire risk at regional scale is driven chiefly by climate—low nighttime humidity and reduced soil moisture—rather than by adjacent clearing, although human ignitions (campfires, cigarettes, land management) provide sources. Scientists warn these widespread burns likely add significant, undercounted carbon emissions and are investigating soil moisture and other climate precursors to improve prediction and accounting.

On 3 June the Guardian published an interview in which actor Michael Douglas said the throat cancer he discussed was “caused by something called HPV, which actually comes about from cunnilingus.” Douglas’s spokesman, Allen Burry, quickly disputed media portrayals that the actor had claimed oral sex caused his own cancer, saying Douglas only discussed causes of oral cancer generally and intended to note HPV as one known risk. The Guardian denied misrepresenting Douglas: only the actor and reporter Xan Brooks were present, and the paper posted an audio clip and verbatim transcript of the exchange. Press coverage and public statements escalated: some outlets reported Douglas blamed his cancer on a sexually transmitted virus contracted via oral sex, while Burry insisted Douglas never stated that was the specific cause in his case and declined to confirm whether Douglas tested positive for HPV. At an American Cancer Society event Douglas framed his remarks as a public-service announcement about HPV — a virus that can cause oral cancer and for which vaccines exist — saying he hoped to raise awareness. His ex-wife and current wife made no further public health revelations; the controversy centered on how Douglas’s comments were reported and interpreted.

This large UK survey of 3,432 higher-education staff and students aged 18–40 examined whether bereavement by suicide carries a specific risk for later suicidal behaviour compared with other sudden deaths. Participants who, since age 10, had experienced sudden bereavement of a close contact were classified by the respondent’s perception of cause (sudden natural, sudden unnatural, or suicide). The study used validated self-report measures to distinguish suicidal ideation and suicide attempts that occurred after the bereavement, adjusting for nine prespecified confounders including prebereavement psychopathology and prior suicidality. Researchers compared suicide-bereaved people to those bereaved by sudden natural causes, and separately to those bereaved by sudden unnatural causes, tested whether relatedness to the deceased modified risk, and examined perceived stigma as a potential mediator.

Key findings: compared with sudden natural deaths, bereavement by suicide was associated with a higher probability of postbereavement suicide attempt (adjusted OR ≈1.65) and with increased odds of occupational drop-out (adjusted OR ≈1.80). When compared with sudden unnatural deaths, suicide bereavement showed similar odds of suicidal ideation and attempt but greater odds of poor social functioning. Relatedness to the deceased (blood relative vs non-blood contact) did not modify associations, indicating risk extends to peers and friends. Adding perceived stigma to models attenuated associations to nonsignificance, suggesting stigma and reduced help-seeking may partly explain elevated risks. Sensitivity analyses largely supported robustness of findings, though repeated exposure to multiple sudden losses attenuated associations.

Strengths include a large population-based sample, baseline adjustment for prebereavement vulnerabilities, and standardized measures. Limitations include sampling from higher-education institutions with female and higher-education overrepresentation, possible selection and recall biases, reliance on self-reported exposure classification, and residual confounding. The authors recommend clinicians assess suicide history among friends as well as relatives, employers consider workplace support, and further research and trials to reduce stigma and identify interventions for people bereaved by suicide.

When Jane Austen died in 1817 at 41, her writing desk passed down through family and was entrusted to the British Library in 1999. In a drawer were three pairs of spectacles long believed by family tradition to have belonged to Austen. The British Library’s Conservation team and Birmingham Optical recently examined the lenses with a lensmeter. All three were convex (“plus”) lenses for longsightedness — consistent with needing help for close work — but their strengths differ markedly: a wire-framed pair at +1.75 DS in both eyes, a tortoiseshell pair A at +3.25 DS, and a much stronger tortoiseshell pair B around +4.75–+5.00 with slight astigmatic correction. London optometrist Professor Simon Barnard suggested possible explanations: Austen may have been naturally longsighted and progressively required stronger reading lenses as her vision worsened, using the strongest pair for very close tasks like fine embroidery. Barnard also noted that some systemic illnesses can change refractive needs; diabetes can induce cataracts but would likely have been fatal then, making sequential prescriptions less likely. He pointed to arsenic exposure as a plausible cause of progressing cataracts, since arsenic — common in 19th-century medicines and environments — is known to cause cataracts. Earlier theories for Austen’s death include Addison’s disease, cancer, and Hodgkin’s lymphoma; an arsenic hypothesis was previously advanced by writer Lindsay Ashford. The Library cautions limitations: the glasses may have been bought off-the-shelf, might not have been prescribed or even worn by Austen, and provenance cannot be proven beyond family tradition. The Library published the results to invite further specialist input; the spectacles are now on public display and scholars are already engaging with the findings.

Forty coffins from Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 were flown from Kharkiv to Eindhoven on Dutch and Australian military aircraft, arriving amid national mourning in the Netherlands. Relatives, Prime Minister Mark Rutte and members of the royal family awaited the arrivals; churches tolled bells, a minute’s silence was held and 40 hearses transported the remains to military barracks in Hilversum for identification by DNA, dental records and fingerprints. Dutch officials warned identification could take weeks or months; more corpses are expected to be flown out. International teams, including British DVI experts, will assist. Accusations swirl that pro‑Russian separatists tampered with evidence and delayed recovery. US intelligence points to an SA‑11 missile fired from eastern Ukraine. Fighting in the region continues.

The Met Gala drew its usual mix of daring fashion, celebrity drama and viral moments this year, with standout looks and missteps sparking conversation online. Solange Knowles made a memorable entrance in a printed Giles mini-dress with pronounced pleating that created a layered, fan-like 3-D effect—an eccentric, statement-making choice in line with her style. Her Instagram quip, “When @cartier is your date, and Giles is your dress,” highlighted the evening’s blend of high fashion and personal flair. Observers wondered whether she might upstage sister Beyoncé, who has a history of dramatic arrivals.

Beyoncé herself faced criticism: she arrived two hours late and wore a revealing dress that some compared unfavorably to previous Met Gala controversies. The timing and outfit drew a strong reaction from fans and commentators alike. Meanwhile, Sarah Jessica Parker commanded attention with a towering Philip Treacy headpiece—an audacious, flaming headdress that quickly became meme fodder. Twitter users likened it to everything from the fire emoji and the villain Aku from Samurai Jack to Jafar, Darth Maul, Kirby, and the Human Torch; but SJP’s fearlessness and theatricality were undeniable.

Not every celebrity scored a win. Jennifer Connelly’s Louis Vuitton lace sheath with oversized sleeves overwhelmed her frame, and Maggie Gyllenhaal’s Roland Mouret gown featured awkward strap and waist details that critics called a “hot mess,” reinforcing old fashion taboos like mixing black and brown.

Context for the evening: the Met Gala, formally the Costume Institute Gala, is an elite fundraiser and kickoff for the annual exhibit—this year focused on “China: Through the Looking Glass”—and is overseen by Anna Wintour. The event continues to blend couture, celebrity culture and occasional controversy, from last year’s infamous Solange-Jay Z elevator incident to spontaneous, now-deleted backstage moments captured on social media. With filmmakers and heavy security present, stars alternated between spectacular and polarizing looks, ensuring the gala remains both a fashion showcase and a pop-culture highlight.

Home Secretary Alan Johnson has refused to block the extradition of Gary McKinnon to the US despite new medical evidence showing he has Asperger’s syndrome, severe major depression, panic attacks and a “fixed-psychological conviction he will kill himself” rather than be extradited. Consultant psychiatrist Prof Jeremy Turk warned suicide was an “almost certain inevitability.” Johnson said the material was not materially different from evidence before the High Court and that assurances from US authorities address McKinnon’s needs; he noted McKinnon would not serve time in a supermax if convicted and repatriation would be pursued. McKinnon’s family and campaigners condemned the decision, plan urgent judicial review, and warn he could be extradited by Christmas. Critics say the Extradition Act is unfair to UK citizens.

The TF-2 (Transition) is a roadable aircraft designed to integrate air and ground travel in a single passenger cabin so travelers need not change vehicles. It takes off like a helicopter, flies like an airplane and drives on roads using electric propulsion, modern materials and manufacturing. Classified as a light-sport aircraft despite exceeding the 1,320 lb limit by 120 lb via an FAA exemption, the two-seat Transition folds its electrically powered wings, drives on highways at about 30 mpg, and cruises at 115 mph with a 460-mile range and 450 lb payload. It needs a 1,700-foot runway, fits in a standard garage, costs about $194,000, and has 70 preorders with $10,000 escrowed deposits; proponents cite increased flexibility and safety since it can drive home in bad weather.

Iran announced it will bolster its naval presence in the Gulf to assert control over three disputed islands — Greater and Lesser Tunb and Abu Musa — claimed by the United Arab Emirates. IRGC Commander Mohammad Ali Jafari said the Guards are expanding naval defense capabilities and inaugurated a fifth naval defense zone at Bandar Lengeh specifically tasked with protecting the islands near the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil route. The 41-year dispute has strained ties, with past diplomatic threats and visits inflaming tensions. Separately, Iranian media reported a domestically made VTOL drone able to hover and fly silently will be unveiled, claims that are difficult to independently verify.

Portland officials decided to drain 38 million gallons from Mt. Tabor’s Reservoir 5 after surveillance footage appeared to show an 18-year-old, identified as Dallas Swonger (also reported as Dallas Delynn), urinating near the open-air storage pool early Wednesday. Though Water Bureau tests the next day found no urine-related toxins, bureau leaders and city Commissioner Nick Fish said they would proceed with emptying and cleaning the reservoir to eliminate even a remote public-health risk. The move drew widespread ridicule and second-guessing nationally and internationally because Reservoir 5 holds up to 50 million gallons while a typical adult bladder contains only a couple of cups—making the risk of contamination extremely small. Public-health experts echoed that view: Anna Harding of Oregon State University said urine would be “very, very, very, very diluted” and not a significant microbial threat. Still, city officials emphasized a precautionary stance and followed professional advice.

The decision also reignited political debate about Portland’s water governance. Kent Craford, a leading proponent of a ballot measure to transfer water control to an independently elected district board, called the flush a poor use of water and money and framed it as evidence that a different governing body might make better decisions.

Swonger granted an explicit, profanity-laced interview denying he urinated in the water, saying he relieved himself on a reservoir wall. He and two friends received trespass citations; Swonger was additionally cited for public urination and faces potential further charges. He lamented becoming a national spectacle and criticized the city for wasting water, noting he’d seen dead animals in the reservoirs. City officials noted a history of similar incidents and past flushes; Mt. Tabor’s open reservoirs must be disconnected from the water system under federal mandates by 2015, which adds context to the controversy.

British police investigating the Manchester Arena suicide bombing halted sharing information specifically about the probe with US counterparts after a series of leaks to American media, actions that sparked anger across UK government and security circles. The suspension followed initial disclosures in US outlets identifying the bomber as Salman Abedi and, later, publication by the New York Times of forensic photographs showing bloodstained fragments, a destroyed backpack and bomb components. UK officials described the unauthorised disclosures as a grievous breach of trust that risked undermining a major counter-terrorism investigation and causing fresh distress to victims’ families.

The pause in information-sharing was limited to the Manchester inquiry; other UK-US intelligence exchanges continued. After diplomatic interventions at the NATO summit in Brussels — where Prime Minister Theresa May told President Trump shared intelligence must remain secure — British police resumed the specific Manchester information flow following “fresh assurances.” The US stated it would investigate the leaks and take steps to prevent recurrence. US and UK leaders and ministers publicly condemned the announcements, and the US acting ambassador to the UK called the leaks “reprehensible.”

Investigators say the bomber, 22-year-old Manchester-born Salman Abedi of Libyan descent, likely did not act alone and that the attack reflected a network rather than a lone-wolf incident. Eight men were in custody in the UK, including Abedi’s older brother, and Libyan authorities detained Abedi’s father and younger brother; Libyan officials reported the younger brother had confessed to knowing “all the details” of the plot. Police described arrests and searches as “significant,” recovering items deemed important to the inquiry, and carried out raids with controlled explosions. Authorities stressed the probe is ongoing and called for public vigilance.

Forensic analysis of crime-scene material — some of which had been circulated before publication — suggested a carefully prepared improvised explosive device packed with nuts and screws as shrapnel, powered by a substantial 12-volt lead-acid battery, and possibly initiated by a handheld switch. Images implied a powerful, high-velocity charge; this complexity raised concerns that an experienced bomb-maker or assistance may have been involved, although some sources have said Abedi could have constructed the device himself.

The attack killed 22 people and injured over 100; victims named include children and young concertgoers, with the youngest confirmed death an eight-year-old girl. The bombing prompted Britain to raise its terror threat level to “critical,” deploy troops to high-profile sites, and prompt national mourning and solidarity actions in Manchester. The affair has spurred renewed debate about limits of intelligence sharing, the pressures on MI5 and police resources in monitoring suspects, and calls for those responsible for the leaks to be held accountable.

White House officials and some attendees of a contentious immigration meeting are disputing reports that President Donald Trump used the word “shithole” to describe Haiti and certain African nations. Early accounts said Trump referred to those countries as “shithole countries,” prompting widespread condemnation. But on Sunday morning shows and in subsequent commentary, several Republicans who were at the meeting either defended the president, said the phrase was misreported, or said they could not recall the exact words he used.

National Review’s Rich Lowry offered a possible explanation for the conflicting accounts: his sources say the president may have used a closely related vulgarity—“shithouse countries”—rather than “shithole.” On ABC’s This Week, Lowry said his understanding is that Trump said “S-house” rather than “S-hole,” though he stressed that Trump did make the broader disparaging remarks and that the general tenor of the discussion has been reported accurately. Lowry’s suggestion has been picked up as a potential reason why figures like Senators David Perdue and Tom Cotton appear to be denying the more widely circulated quotation, claiming instead a different word or expressing uncertainty.

The debate highlights how small differences in heard or reported profanity can become focal points in political defense and media discussion, even as multiple sources agree that the meeting included offensive remarks about immigrants from Haiti and African nations. Mediaite first reported these differing accounts, and the clip of Lowry’s remarks aired on ABC News.

A Los Angeles photographer, identified as a supposed third mistress of motorcycle builder Jesse James, says he hired her for styling in 2008 and then exchanged emails and texts with her for about a year. She claims their physical relationship was brief—only four sexual encounters—yet she has preserved 195 text messages, some explicit, in which James repeatedly pressed for photos and meetings and wrote lines like, "I'll be your monkey." Representatives for James were not reached for comment. Separately, stripper Melissa Smith publicly detailed a two‑year affair with James that began in 2006 after he contacted her via MySpace. Smith says they met about every two months, once had sex on his couch without a condom, and that he showed enthusiasm for her breast augmentation. Star magazine published photos, including a jean jacket reading "Jesse's Girl" she says he gave her. Smith, who has had recent legal troubles including a 20‑day jail stint for assaulting an officer and a DUI, called Bullock to consider divorce, calling James "a serial cheater."

Chelsea Manning, the former Army intelligence analyst who leaked more than 700,000 military and State Department documents to WikiLeaks, said she felt a duty to the public and did not believe her disclosures endangered national security. In her first televised interviews since her May release from the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth—after seven years of a 35-year sentence commuted by President Barack Obama—Manning reiterated she acted alone and accepted responsibility for her choices. She described being driven by the human consequences she witnessed in Iraq: what began as filtered statistics and reports became, to her, “people” suffering death and destruction. Manning explained she sought to provoke public debate and did not think the leaks would harm national security, arguing that as a subject-matter expert she knew the material intimately. She said formal channels for raising concerns “don’t work.” Convicted by court-martial under the Espionage and Computer Fraud and Abuse Acts, Manning pleaded guilty to some charges and was acquitted of aiding the enemy; her was the longest imprisonment of any U.S. leaker. Manning also discussed her gender transition and the severe struggles she faced in prison, including two suicide attempts and a fight for hormone treatments she says are lifesaving. Her legal team’s advocacy led to her becoming the first military prisoner to receive transition-related health care and influenced broader policy changes on transgender service. Now off duty while appealing her conviction, Manning has been publicly documenting post-prison life on social media and expressed gratitude to Obama for the second chance he afforded her. She said she retains respect for the military and identifies simply as herself.

Swiss voters will decide June 5 whether to adopt a landmark guaranteed income proposal that would grant every adult citizen and legal resident $2,600 a month tax-free and $650 per child. Brought to the ballot by artists, writers and intellectuals using Switzerland’s direct-democracy system, the plan would provide the stipend regardless of employment, income or wealth. Supporters argue the payment would allow people to reduce hours without losing a decent standard of living, increase workforce motivation, and humanize the economy. For example, a family of two non-working adults and two children could receive about $6,500 monthly tax-free.

The proposal is unprecedented at a national level and comes as debates about universal basic income gain traction in parts of Europe and beyond. Switzerland’s high per-capita wealth—around $85,000—makes such a generous plan more conceivable there than in many countries. Still, polls suggest the measure is likely to be defeated.

Critics warn it would undermine work incentives and strain public finances; estimated annual costs are about $200 billion. Backers suggest funding through measures such as raising the 8% value-added tax, but the government warns that significant tax increases or spending cuts would be necessary and that the scheme could not fully replace existing social security. Prominent observers elsewhere, like Robert Reich in the U.S., say broad acceptance of such ideas may only come after greater job and wage disruption. Whether the Swiss vote succeeds or fails, the national referendum marks a major step in bringing basic-income discussions into mainstream policy debate.

Top military leaders and Army commanders warn that suicides and family crises among service members are likely to rise as thousands of troops return from repeated deployments and resume longer home-station tours. Admiral Mike Mullen said he expects growing challenges for families as bases such as Joint Base Lewis-McChord and Fort Hood swell with returning soldiers. The Army has seen record suicide rates, and Fort Hood reported a surge this year—14 confirmed and six suspected suicides so far—prompting exhaustive reviews, off-post visits, and scrutiny of privately owned weapons. Commanders cite multiple stressors—repeated deployments, PTSD, family and financial problems, and substance abuse—and emphasize leadership, prevention programs, reducing stigma about mental-health care, and buddy-awareness training to identify at-risk soldiers and curb the trend.

In a wide-ranging “60 Minutes” interview aired October 14, 2018, President Donald Trump offered forceful, often combative views on climate change, foreign policy, domestic politics and his own administration, reiterating themes that have defined his presidency while resisting scientific consensus and deflecting criticism.

On climate change, Trump backed away from his long-standing claim that global warming is a “hoax” but remained skeptical about human influence. He told Lesley Stahl, “I think something’s happening. Something’s changing and it’ll change back again,” and said he’s uncertain that warming is manmade. He emphasized economic concerns—saying he did not want to “give trillions and trillions of dollars” or lose “millions and millions of jobs”—and challenged scientists’ motives, asserting they have political agendas. His remarks came days after a major Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change report warned of mounting climate risks and contrasted with long-term temperature records showing steady warming.

On the disappearance and presumed murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, Trump promised “severe punishment” if Saudi culpability is established but stopped short of explicitly endorsing cutting arms sales to Riyadh. He cited potential job losses at U.S. defense firms and suggested there are alternate ways to punish Saudi Arabia while insisting an investigation is underway.

Trump described his personal diplomacy with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un positively, saying he trusts Kim and emphasizing the lack of recent missile or nuclear tests. He framed their rapport—at times using hyperbolic language—as a pragmatic tool to reduce threats, even while acknowledging Kim’s brutal human-rights record.

On trade and China, Trump defended his tariff strategy as leverage to secure fairer access to Chinese markets, insisting he’s not trying to crush China’s economy but to force negotiations. He repeatedly cast the European Union as having taken advantage of the U.S. on trade and challenged the conventional praise of NATO, insisting allies must pay their fair share and even suggesting he knows more about alliance fairness than Defense Secretary Jim Mattis.

Regarding Russia, Trump maintained he has been tough with Vladimir Putin despite public perceptions to the contrary; he conceded Putin is “probably” involved in assassinations and acknowledged Russian meddling in the 2016 U.S. election but also alleged, without presenting evidence, that China and other countries meddled as well.

Trump defended his handling of domestic controversies: he took credit for helping secure Brett Kavanaugh’s Supreme Court confirmation—saying his provocative Mississippi speech was decisive—and dismissed ongoing reports of White House “chaos” as fake news while admitting he doesn’t trust everyone in the West Wing. On special counsel Robert Mueller’s Russia probe, he refused to pledge not to shut it down but said he had no intention of doing so and reiterated his denial of any collusion.

Throughout the interview, Trump alternated between boasting about his administration’s accomplishments—tax and regulatory cuts, a strong economy—and expressing frustration at the media and political adversaries, calling Washington a “vicious” and deceptive place. The tone ranged from defiant to defensive as he sought to justify policy choices and frame his approach to leadership.

Kanye West was voluntarily hospitalized for exhaustion and sleep deprivation after canceling the remaining dates of his Saint Pablo tour, sources tell PEOPLE and E! News. Contrary to some reports, he was not placed on a 51-50 psychiatric hold or restrained; friends say a minor gym altercation occurred, he was deemed medically stable, and he sought help at his physician’s recommendation. Family and friends, including wife Kim Kardashian West, are supporting his recovery—Kim canceled a planned Angel Ball appearance and flew back to Los Angeles to be with him. Representatives and sources emphasize confidence that he will recover.

The tour cancellation—21 dates—raises major financial questions: Billboard estimated refunds for over 300,000 tickets amounting to roughly $27.3 million. Industry-standard tour insurance typically covers cancellations for illness or injury if an independent medical practitioner confirms the performer cannot continue, but policies often exclude claims tied to drug use, unreasonable or capricious behavior, or pre-existing conditions. Live Nation, the promoter, likely carries its own policy that may cover different liabilities, leaving a complex picture about who bears costs. Insurance professionals note exhaustion is harder to prove than a clear physical injury, so coverage is uncertain until further medical details and policy specifics emerge. Meanwhile, media reports claiming he was handcuffed and taken for psychiatric evaluation conflict with sources insisting he sought treatment voluntarily.

New research led by San Diego State University seismologist Tom Rockwell indicates the San Jacinto fault — a 130-mile strike-slip system running from Imperial County through Anza, Ocotillo Wells and Borrego Springs into Riverside County and the San Bernardino Valley — may be capable of larger earthquakes than previously thought and could at times rival the San Andreas in strength. Historically, the largest credible quake on the San Jacinto was estimated at magnitude 7.5. Rockwell’s field studies, centered near Hog Lake by Anza and published in Pure and Applied Geophysics, examined evidence for 21 seismic events on the fault over the past 4,000 years. The results suggest the central and northern sections of the San Jacinto can fail together, producing events in the magnitude 7.6–7.7 range. If a rupture were to propagate onto the San Andreas, an event approaching magnitude 8.0 could be possible, although the researchers found no clear evidence that such a crossover rupture has occurred within the last couple of millennia. The San Jacinto is part of the broader plate-boundary system between the Pacific and North American plates; together with the San Andreas it accounts for roughly 80 percent of the plate slippage in the region. Rockwell, a leading authority on the San Jacinto, has been central to mapping the fault’s trace and reconstructing its seismic history. Instrumental history includes a magnitude 6.5 quake on the San Jacinto in April 1968 and a 6.7 event on the Superstition Hills strand in November 1987, both of which were strongly felt in San Diego. The study underscores a reassessment of seismic hazard in Southern California, highlighting potential for larger, multi-segment ruptures on faults previously considered less catastrophic than the San Andreas.

Michel Fourniret, the French serial killer nicknamed the “Ogre of the Ardennes,” has admitted to the 1990 murder of British language student Joanna Parrish, her family lawyer said. Fourniret, already serving life imprisonment since 2008 for the rape and murder of seven girls and young women, was interviewed last week by two instructing magistrates in Paris and, according to lawyer Didier Seban, made detailed, repeated confessions acknowledging he killed Parrish and another teenager, Marie-Angele Domece. Seban described the development as a remarkable resolution to a long legal battle and said he hoped a trial would soon follow. Parrish, 20, a Leeds University student working as a language assistant in Auxerre, Burgundy, disappeared in 1990; her body was found on May 17, 1990 and autopsy results showed she had been raped and beaten. Domece, who had learning disabilities, went missing in July 1988 and her body has never been recovered. Fourniret had been charged in 2008 with the kidnapping and murders of both girls, but an appellate court dismissed the case in September 2011; in June 2012 that dismissal was annulled and investigations resumed on new leads. Fourniret’s wife, Monique Olivier, who was convicted in 2008 of complicity in five murders and sentenced to life with a long minimum term, had twice accused and later retracted accusations against him regarding these two cases; she will likely be questioned again, Seban said. Paris prosecutors declined to comment while investigations continue, and Fourniret’s lawyer also made no comment. Parrish’s family, who have long suspected Fourniret, expressed shock but hope for closure.

On May 22, 2017, a suicide bombing at the Manchester Arena devastated concertgoers leaving an Ariana Grande performance. The attack, which detonated in the foyer near an exit at about 10:33–10:35 p.m., killed 22 people including children and injured roughly 50–59 others, some critically. Witnesses described a massive explosion, smoke, blood and debris, and scenes of chaos as thousands fled a packed 21,000-capacity venue. Social media and videos captured panicked crowds, while parents frantically sought missing children. Greater Manchester Police’s counterterrorism unit treated the blast as a likely terrorist incident. Authorities later identified the bomber as 22-year-old Salman Abedi, who was killed in the explosion; police investigated whether he acted alone and arrested at least one other person in connection with the attack. Islamic State claimed responsibility on messaging channels, though its account contained contradictions and lacked independent confirmation from U.K. or U.S. officials. The attack prompted Britain to raise its terrorism threat level to “critical,” deploy additional armed officers and consider military support at public events. National leaders condemned the “cowardly” assault; Prime Minister Theresa May and other world leaders expressed solidarity. Local communities mobilized to help—offering shelter, free rides and medical assistance—and thousands attended a vigil for the victims. Ariana Grande and many artists expressed sorrow and support; her team and opening acts confirmed they were safe. The bombing, Britain’s deadliest since 2005, prompted heightened security and widespread grief across the U.K. and beyond.

Rick Calamaro, a 46-year-old club promoter and longtime personal assistant and close friend of actor Charlie Sheen, was found dead in his Los Angeles apartment on Sunday. Authorities believe he had been deceased for several days before discovery. Reports say the apartment contained numerous prescription pain medications and an open bottle of alcohol. Calamaro was known to be present during Sheen’s widely publicized 36-hour drug binge in October 2010, and since then some have speculated he may have influenced Sheen’s substance problems or even supplied drugs. The cause of Calamaro’s death has not yet been determined, and at the time of the report Charlie Sheen had not issued a public statement about his former assistant’s death. The case remains under investigation.

Hard-line Iranian students stormed two British diplomatic compounds in Tehran, overrunning gates, smashing windows, burning the Union Jack and hauling down pictures of the queen in protests tied to new Western sanctions over Iran’s nuclear program. The assaults followed parliament’s move to downgrade ties with Britain. Protesters hurled petrol bombs and stones, set a car ablaze, and briefly occupied the ambassador’s residence and a separate Qolhak compound; Iranian news agencies reported six staff were briefly held but later freed. Police clashed with demonstrators, fired tear gas, and arrested some intruders; Iranian officials said the actions were not government-planned and expressed regret, while Britain condemned the failure to protect its staff and warned of “serious consequences.” The U.N., U.S. and EU also strongly condemned the attacks. The incidents amplified long-standing Anglo-Iranian tensions and internal political struggles between hardliners and the government over how to respond to sanctions.

Heather Locklear posted a heartfelt Instagram video celebrating daughter Ava Sambora’s 21st birthday, captioned “Happy Birthday Sweet Child of Mine.” The 57‑year‑old showed framed photos and praised Ava as “the kindest, funniest, smartest, most beautiful child,” joking about “spanking you 21 times” and flipping an ace and queen to mark 21. Locklear is in long‑term rehab for substance abuse and mental health treatment after a June incident that led to arrest and a possible overdose. She celebrated her own recent birthday at the facility. An EMT plans to sue Locklear over alleged injuries from that episode; criminal charges are pending.

Peter Ascoli’s biography and Aviva Kempner’s documentary revive the story of Julius Rosenwald, the German-Jewish son of immigrants who transformed Sears, Roebuck into America’s largest retailer and became a major, if underappreciated, philanthropist. Rosenwald rose from a clothing apprenticeship to lead Sears from 1908, building a business empire and later founding Chicago’s Museum of Science and Industry. More enduring, however, was his commitment to social improvement—especially for African Americans in the segregated early 20th-century United States.

Influenced by Rabbi Emil Hirsch, the race riots in Springfield in 1908, and the ideas of Booker T. Washington, Rosenwald directed substantial resources to Black education and community development. Rather than simply donating funds outright, he pioneered a matching model: when he contributed to Tuskegee, Washington urged him to allocate a portion to build six rural schools. Rosenwald’s approach required one-third from his Fund, one-third from local Black communities, and one-third from local White sources. That template helped finance more than 5,300 “Rosenwald schools,” dramatically increasing access to basic education across the Jim Crow South. The Rosenwald Fund later shifted to support promising Black artists and cultural figures, becoming, as poet Rita Dove calls it, “the single-most important funding agency for African-American culture in the 20th century.”

Kempner’s film, screening at the NAACP convention, stitches archival footage with interviews from figures like Maya Angelou, John Lewis, Julian Bond and others who attended Rosenwald schools or benefited from his patronage. Viewers and attendees—some who only discovered the source of their school’s name decades later—testify to the fund’s deep, often personal legacy. Rosenwald gave away roughly $62 million in his lifetime and intentionally dissolved his fund in 1948, believing his mission should not become perpetual. His efforts exemplify an American Jewish tradition of tikkun olam and a hands-on philanthropic model that paired wealth with community partnership to expand education and culture for African Americans.

Astronomers have discovered that comet 103P/Hartley 2 contains water with a deuterium-to-hydrogen (D/H) ratio nearly identical to Earth’s oceans, challenging previous conclusions that comets could supply at most about 10% of terrestrial water. Using infrared observations from the Herschel Space Observatory, Paul Hartogh and colleagues measured Hartley 2’s D/H and found it roughly half the deuterium fraction seen in several earlier-studied comets, all from the distant Oort Cloud. Hartley 2 likely originated in the Kuiper Belt, much closer to the Sun than Oort Cloud objects, suggesting compositional diversity among comets. The finding expands the possible sources of Earth’s water—where earlier meteorite and asteroid analyses matched ocean D/H and thus were favored—and implies cometary contributions might be far greater than thought, perhaps even supplying most of Earth’s water in principle. Researchers caution the result is not definitive: more measurements of Kuiper Belt comets are needed, and dynamical models of early Solar System delivery mechanisms may require revision. Upcoming facilities like ALMA should help resolve how much cometary material contributed to Earth’s oceans.

Storm Barney swept across the UK and Ireland, prompting warnings against taking “storm selfies” as powerful winds, fallen trees, power cuts and disrupted flights were reported. Gusts reached 78mph in County Carlow, Ireland, and forecasters warned southern Britain—especially Wales and central England—could see inland gusts up to 70mph and higher coastal gusts later on. Natural Resources Wales warned of strong onshore winds and large waves along the west coast; modest flood impacts were expected due to low tides, but alerts could be issued if needed. The Environment Agency and RoSPA cautioned that people risking dramatic weather selfies endanger themselves and rescuers. RoSPA stressed that getting swept out to sea can be rapidly fatal. Barney followed Storm Abigail and was driven by successive Atlantic low-pressure systems; a separate warning covered heavy rain for north-west England and Wales in coming days.

The piece places these warnings in the broader context of a global spike in dangerous “selfie” incidents. It recounts numerous recent tragedies—people killed falling from cliffs or buildings, struck by trains, gored by bulls, drowned, electrocuted, injured by animals or guns—prompting authorities from Russia to Mumbai to designate “no-selfie zones,” run safety campaigns, and post warnings at tourist sites to curb risky behavior.

Court records unsealed in the Griswold triple-slaying reveal a premeditated plot in which suspects conspired with the victims’ son to trade drugs for guns kept in a safe at his parents’ home. Text messages show 21-year-old Matthew Lindquist arranging to show the safe’s location in exchange for cash and drugs hours before his parents’ burned home was discovered on Dec. 20. Investigators say Lindquist told an associate when his father usually slept and suggested the basement door was unlocked so the plan could look like a robbery.

Ruth Correa, 23, of Hartford, who has been charged with multiple counts including murder, robbery, arson and home invasion, told police she and her brother, Sergio Correa, went to the Lindquist home that night. According to her detailed statements in a 17-page arrest affidavit, the scheme unraveled when Matthew panicked, fled and was chased into nearby woods. Ruth Correa said Sergio hit him with a machete, then both siblings stabbed him — she admitted stabbing him about 10 times — and left his body in the woods; his remains were later found in May.

Ruth Correa described entering the house through the unlocked basement, confronting Kenneth and Janet Lindquist, and a violent struggle over safe keys. She recounted Sergio striking Kenneth with a bat, restraining and assaulting Janet, and forcing Ruth to assist in stealing items. She said they doused areas with a flammable liquid and set the home alight. The parents’ bodies were found inside the burned residence; autopsy reports ruled both deaths homicides involving blunt-force injuries and, for Janet, smoke inhalation and thermal injury.

Sergio Correa, incarcerated on unrelated charges, has not been formally charged in this case; his lawyer says he denies involvement. The affidavit provides gruesome, corroborated details of the robbery-turned-murder and the role of texts and drug debt in prompting the fatal events.

Jeffrey, 56, and Jeanette Navin, 55, an affluent Connecticut couple, vanished after being last seen Aug. 4 near their home in Easton. Relatives reported them missing Aug. 7; their pickup was found Aug. 9 in a Merritt Parkway commuter lot. Easton police initially treated the disappearance as a likely spur-of-the-moment trip—because the Navins often traveled—but relatives said they normally notify family and described bank accounts as untouched, denying that reported financial troubles motivated any departure.

Investigators have escalated the inquiry: the State Police Western District Major Crime Squad has taken over, detectives searched a Bridgeport house owned by the couple’s son, and evidence from the abandoned truck was sent to a state forensic lab. Authorities are reviewing phone, bank and credit-card records, interviewing friends and colleagues, and searching the couple’s rental home in Easton. As of reporting, no foul play has been confirmed, but police say they are keeping all possibilities open.

Public records show the Navins had long-running financial and legal troubles. HSBC filed foreclosure papers in 2007 over a Guilford retreat purchased with a $1.3 million mortgage; after missed payments the debt swelled to about $2.2 million by 2014 and a recent appeal was denied. Connecticut Light & Power (now Eversource) pursued about $130,000 in unpaid electric bills; other foreclosures and mortgage releases appear in records. Jeffrey runs J&J Refuse; their son is listed as its operations manager. Jeanette is a 18-year paraprofessional at Weston Intermediate School and is described as beloved by the district. Family, attorney and officials express shock and hope for their safe return while the probe continues.

Two FBI employees who previously worked for Special Counsel Robert Mueller—agent Peter Strzok and FBI lawyer Lisa Page—exchanged roughly 375 text messages during the 2016 campaign that criticize Donald Trump and other political figures. The Justice Department turned the messages over to Congress and released them to the media before the inspector general’s final report, prompting controversy and partisan backlash. Mueller removed Strzok from the Russia probe immediately after the department learned of the texts in late July; Page had already left the special counsel’s team.

The texts, revealed in excerpts, include repeated disparaging references to Trump—calling him an “idiot” and “a loathsome human”—as well as expressions of support for Hillary Clinton and derisive remarks about other political figures including Bernie Sanders, Martin O’Malley, John Kasich, Attorney General Eric Holder and prospective AG Jeff Sessions. Some exchanges suggest worry about Russian interference and WikiLeaks activity; others convey personal reactions to campaign events and anxiety about Trump’s electoral prospects. Several messages hint the correspondents discussed work matters and internal assessments—one refers to “Andy’s office,” possibly Deputy Director Andrew McCabe, and another frames a contingency as an “insurance policy” against an unlikely Trump victory.

Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee criticized the DOJ’s pre-IG-release sharing of the texts and sought a review of the decision, demanding details on who authorized distribution and which reporters saw the materials. Deputy AG Rod Rosenstein defended the decision, saying DOJ consulted the inspector general and career ethics advisers and found no legal barrier to release. Critics argued the disclosures transformed an internal investigation into a partisan spectacle and risked unfairly damaging career employees before any formal finding of wrongdoing. Supporters of GOP probes point to the messages as evidence of potential bias affecting both the Russia investigation and the Clinton email inquiry; Democrats counter that private political views are protected speech and reflect sentiments many held at the time.

Susan Olsen, best known for playing Cindy Brady on The Brady Bunch, was dismissed from her Los Angeles radio co-hosting role after a string of homophobic and abusive Facebook messages directed at an openly gay actor. Olsen, 55, co-hosted LA Talk Radio’s “Two Chicks Talkin’ Politics” on December 7, during which guest Leon Acord-Whiting — an openly gay actor — criticized her on Facebook for spreading what he called “outrageous misinformation” and for advancing inflammatory, partisan claims during the broadcast. Acord-Whiting urged the station to remove Olsen, saying he would not appear on or listen to shows that continued to employ her and calling her behavior “dangerous and unprofessional.” Olsen responded publicly on Facebook the next day, calling Acord-Whiting “this little piece of human waste” and noting he had blocked her before she could reply. The confrontation escalated when Acord-Whiting posted a screenshot of a private Facebook message that Olsen allegedly sent him, which contained multiple slurs, sexual taunts and threats, and explicit, homophobic language. In the wake of the messages, LA Talk Radio announced on December 9 that it had severed ties with Olsen. The station emphasized its ongoing collaboration with the LGBT community and stated it would not tolerate hateful speech from anyone associated with its programming, saying Olsen had “veered off the direction in which we are going.” The firing follows public backlash over her conduct and reflects the station’s stated commitment to inclusivity and respectful discourse.

Following a deadly shooting at Canada’s Parliament and rising calls by terrorist groups to target officials, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security announced heightened security at federal buildings in Washington, D.C., and other major cities. Secretary Jeh Johnson framed the measures as precautionary—not prompted by specific, credible intelligence of an active plot—but justified by recent attacks on government personnel and ongoing global threats. The Federal Protective Service, responsible for more than 9,500 federal facilities and 1.4 million daily visitors or occupants, will implement sensitive, varying security enhancements that will be continually re-evaluated. Officials declined to disclose exact locations or tactics because of law-enforcement sensitivity. DHS said the changes began over the weekend and were only publicly disclosed later. President Obama condemned the Ottawa violence; DHS emphasized vigilance, intensified law enforcement, border protection, and intelligence sharing to better protect U.S. government installations and personnel.

As U.S. combat troops prepare to leave Iraq by the end of 2011, the Obama administration plans a large civilian-led effort backed by contractors to fill the security and training roles. The State Department will assume police training—primarily via contractors—and run two new $100 million diplomatic outposts to defuse tensions between Iraqi forces and Kurdish pesh merga. To protect diplomats and civilians in a still-dangerous environment, private security guards would more than double to as many as 7,000, defending five fortified compounds, operating surveillance radars and drones, searching for roadside bombs, and staffing quick-reaction forces. Some experts warn that a tiny residual military presence may be insufficient for tasks like training on new heavy equipment, airspace protection, and counterterrorism, and suggest thousands of troops might be needed post-2011—though political sensitivities and the Iraqi agreement limit public discussion. The transition, renamed Operation New Dawn, reflects a shift from combat to civilian-led support and diplomacy.

In the wake of the Newtown school shooting, Hollywood rapidly altered publicity and premiere plans for multiple holiday releases out of respect and sensitivity. Paramount revised marketing for Tom Cruise’s Jack Reacher, reportedly removing a clip of Cruise firing a semi-automatic from promotional spots, and postponed a Pittsburgh premiere and a Lincoln Center screening featuring a discussion with Cruise and director Christopher McQuarrie. The Weinstein Company canceled the Los Angeles premiere of Quentin Tarantino’s violent Django Unchained while still holding a private cast-and-crew screening; the company cited national mourning. Tarantino defended film violence as part of storytelling, while co-star Jamie Foxx acknowledged that movies’ violent content can have an impact. Studios have revisited other promotions too: Warner Bros. had previously delayed Gangster Squad after the Colorado shootings to remove a theater gunfight scene, and Fox pulled red-carpet events and broadcasts to avoid insensitivities. Across the entertainment world, events were postponed or modified, NFL games observed moments of silence, and artists and celebrities publicly offered condolences, reflecting a broad industry response to the tragedy.

On October 24, The Crimson revealed a “scouting report” produced by members of Harvard’s 2012 men’s soccer team that evaluated incoming women’s soccer recruits on their physical appearance and sexual appeal. Six members of the women’s 2012 recruiting class—Brooke Dickens, Kelsey Clayman, Alika Keene, Emily Mosbacher, Lauren Varela, and Haley Washburn—publicly responded, rejecting anonymity and describing the report as painful evidence of a widespread culture that objectifies women. They explained that while initially they dismissed such behavior as “normal,” the disclosure and ensuing media attention forced them to confront the emotional impact, the betrayal by friends, and the broader implications for women’s safety and dignity. They called for men to help end this behavior, urged unity among women, and urged campus-wide cultural change.

Subsequent reporting showed similar practices were not isolated: the men’s cross country team maintained annual spreadsheets ahead of a joint dance that sometimes included sexually explicit comments about female athletes. Team messages indicate such documents dated back to at least 2012, and contributors discussed removing access as concerns mounted. Cross country captain Brandon Price acknowledged past harm, said team culture has shifted, and asked teammates to disclose problematic content before the university discovered it.

Harvard canceled the remainder of the men’s soccer season after the Office of the General Counsel found the practice continued beyond 2012 and found the soccer team initially untruthful. University leaders and athletics officials emphasized intolerance for demeaning behavior. The men’s soccer team later issued a collective apology, accepted responsibility, described internal culture changes since 2013, and pledged education, accountability, and collaboration to combat sexism across athletics and campus.

New filings in a long-running civil case tied to the Caylee Anthony tragedy have renewed controversy. Dominic Casey, a private investigator who worked on the Anthony matter, filed a 15-page affidavit in Casey Anthony’s bankruptcy proceedings alleging that Anthony had a sexual relationship with her former defense attorney, Jose Baez, and that Baez once told him Anthony had killed her daughter and hidden the body. Casey also claims he unexpectedly saw Anthony naked at Baez’s office. Baez vehemently denies the allegations, calling them “unequivocally and categorically” false and asserting he always met Florida Bar ethical standards; he says legal action is forthcoming. Dominic Casey has a history of sensational, unproven statements about the case, including past suggestions he wasn’t sure that remains found near Anthony’s home were Caylee’s. His deposition has been filed in Roy Kronk’s civil suit against Anthony—Kronk, who found remains in 2008, sued in 2011 alleging Anthony and her lawyers falsely accused him of the child’s death. Anthony’s bankruptcy delayed Kronk’s suit; it now proceeds in bankruptcy court as Kronk seeks to overcome bankruptcy protections to recover defamation damages. Anthony’s lawyers have moved to strike Casey’s testimony and demanded records he claims to possess. Casey did not respond to requests for comment.

Kisspeptin is a peptide family, encoded by the KiSS-1 gene, that plays a central role in activating and maintaining human reproductive function. Discovered while searching for metastasis suppressors, KiSS-1 produces a 145–amino-acid precursor cleaved into shorter kisspeptins (e.g., 54-, 14-, 13-, 10–amino-acid forms) that bind the GPR54 receptor. Kisspeptin triggers gonadotropin release by activating GnRH neurons and thereby initiates puberty; individuals lacking functional kisspeptin signaling fail to undergo puberty. Animal studies show single or repeated kisspeptin injections stimulate gonadotropins and can advance pubertal timing or override energy-deficit–induced reproductive suppression. In seasonal breeders, kisspeptin levels track day length and control fertility, with potential agricultural applications. Clinically, manipulating kisspeptin signaling offers therapeutic promise: receptor antagonists might suppress sex-hormone-driven cancers, while kisspeptin agonists could treat delayed puberty, some infertility forms, hypothalamic amenorrhea, or trigger ovulation in IVF.

Recent human imaging research demonstrates kisspeptin enhances limbic and paralimbic activity in response to sexual and romantic stimuli, correlating with reduced sexual aversion, increased reward-related responses, improved positive mood, and attenuated negative mood. Effects were specific to sexual and bonding cues and occurred without altering testosterone, oxytocin, or cortisol acutely. These findings position kisspeptin as a neuroendocrine modulator linking hormonal and emotional components of reproduction and suggest potential treatments for psychosexual disorders and mood disturbances associated with reproductive dysfunction. Further studies are needed to map neuronal pathways, assess safety, and explore therapeutic applications.

Juneau Mayor Greg Fisk was found dead Monday in his home on Kennedy Street after his adult son discovered the body and called 911. Police and Capital City Fire/Rescue responded to a call received about 3:30 p.m.; Fisk was pronounced dead at the scene. The cause of death is pending an autopsy by the State Medical Examiner, with results expected within several days. Juneau Police emphasized the investigation remains in its early stages and called rumors of an assault speculative; detectives are preserving and documenting all evidence as they investigate. The City and Borough of Juneau canceled evening Assembly meetings in response to the death. Deputy Mayor Mary Becker, a longtime friend of Fisk, described the news as devastating and said she will assume acting mayor responsibilities per state law while the city’s attorney outlines necessary legal steps. Fisk had been elected mayor in October, defeating incumbent Merrill Sanford by a wide margin. Officials characterize the case as an unattended death; authorities continue to investigate and will release updates as more information becomes available. This is a developing story.

Lady Gaga will begin a Las Vegas residency at the Park Theater (Monte Carlo/MGM) starting in late 2018, running through 2019 with possible extensions into 2020. Reports vary on length and pay: one account cites 36 shows at about $400,000 per performance; another claims up to 74 dates and a near-$100 million valuation. Insiders say the widely circulated $100 million for 60 shows figure is inaccurate. The schedule was adjusted to accommodate Gaga’s film work on A Star Is Born and to allow rehearsal time. The Park Theater, seating about 5,200–6,300, hosts major headliners; Gaga has previously teased and performed in Las Vegas.

The National Archives released a final, large batch of JFK assassination records Thursday, comprising 19,045 documents — the largest single release under the JFK Assassination Records Collection Act of 1992. The release fulfills much of a congressional mandate that originally set a 25-year deadline for disclosure, but President Trump earlier granted agencies a six-month extension to re-review sensitive files. At the request of the FBI and CIA, Trump kept some material sealed, concluding in a memo that certain documents are “of such gravity” that immediate disclosure could jeopardize national security. He ordered a further agency review over the next three and a half years to decide which of the remaining files can be released. About 15,884 records have now been partially released, many with redactions, and will undergo additional review during that period. The Archives published searchable indexes and download links, including previously secret items such as 1978 House testimony from CIA Mexico City station chief David Atlee Phillips, who called Lee Harvey Oswald a lone, unstable actor. Historians, researchers and enthusiasts continue to comb the newly available material for insights into the assassination and related Cold War operations, while some names and addresses of living people remain redacted.

Germany's largest rock festival, Rock am Ring at the Nürburgring near Koblenz, was halted and evacuated on Friday amid “concrete indications” of a possible terrorist threat, with organisers and police ordering the site cleared for safety. About 90,000 people were expected over the three-day event. Authorities detained three men, hired to install security barriers and suspected of Salafist links, but they were released after searches found no imminent danger. Security had already been bolstered to 1,200 officers following the Manchester concert bombing. Organisers and the region’s interior minister defended the precautionary shutdown; after intensive searches, police cleared the site and allowed live music to resume the next day.

Cesar Millan, star of Dog Whisperer and current Nat Geo WILD host of Cesar 911, is under investigation by Los Angeles County Animal Control after a citizen complaint about alleged animal cruelty at his Santa Clarita Dog Psychology Center. Authorities confirmed an officer visited the center and the case is active; details are limited. TMZ reported the complaint involves a dog injuring a potbellied pig during a training session. Nat Geo WILD responded, saying a clip from a recent Cesar 911 episode showing a French bulldog/terrier mix named Simon chasing and nipping a pig lacked full context. The network provided an additional clip and said Millan used precautions—initially a long lead—and tended the pig’s wound promptly; the pig recovered with no lasting harm and the dog’s aggression was successfully rehabilitated, avoiding separation or euthanasia. Critics and petitioners contend Millan’s methods are inhumane, allege he uses animals as bait, and call for his shows to be removed from the air. The American Humane Association said it received complaints, noted the segment appeared to violate its Guidelines for the Safe Use of Animals in Filmed Media, and urged the industry to include their oversight on reality productions; they are not usually invited to monitor reality TV. Petitioners cite California cruelty statutes and encourage witnesses to contact animal control with concrete evidence; investigators indicated the case will remain open for a year to allow more testimony.

President Donald Trump criticized NFL players who protested during the national anthem at preseason games, tweeting that they were “taking a knee when they should be standing proudly” and accusing many of being “unable to define” their cause. He urged players to “be happy, be cool,” called games an inappropriate place for protest, suggested they find other avenues, and warned that those who don’t stand should be “Suspended Without Pay.” His comments followed several demonstrations Thursday night: Philadelphia Eagles players Malcolm Jenkins and De’Vante Bausby raised their fists, while Miami Dolphins receivers Kenny Stills and Albert Wilson kneeled. Jenkins and teammates wore shirts highlighting racial disparities in incarceration. Contrary to the president’s claim, kneeling players have repeatedly stated their protest is against racial injustice and police brutality, a movement sparked by Colin Kaepernick in 2016. The protests have expanded over two seasons, prompting NFL owners in May to approve a policy allowing fines for failing to stand, though enforcement is paused as the league negotiates with players. Critics view anthem protests as disrespectful to the flag and anthem, while supporters argue athletes are using their platform to spotlight systemic injustice and exercise free speech. Trump previously denounced kneeling players at a rally, and his remarks helped broaden the controversy. Colin Kaepernick and others publicly supported recent protesters; the NFL Players Association had not immediately commented on the newest wave of demonstrations.

North Korean state media say leader Kim Jong-un climbed Mount Paektu, the country’s highest peak, with photos showing him on the snowy 2,750-metre summit alongside hundreds of fighter pilots, top army and party officials. Rodong quoted Kim saying the climb “provides precious mental pabulum more powerful than any kind of nuclear weapon.” Mount Paektu, a volcanic peak on the China border, is sacred in Korean folklore and central to propaganda that glorifies the Kim dynasty and its claimed “Mount Paektu bloodline.” The regime has long claimed Kim Jong-il was born there, though many historians say he was born in Russia. The visit follows a pattern of staged “field guidance trips” by Kim to factories, bases and symbolic sites to project energy and connect with the people. State media’s recent biographical claims — such as Kim allegedly driving at age three — echo earlier mythical stories about Kim family feats. Meanwhile, the country faces severe economic hardship and food insecurity while prioritizing military and nuclear development, according to UN reports.

Josh Greenberg, co‑founder and former CTO of music‑streaming startup Grooveshark, was found dead at age 28 in his Gainesville home Sunday evening by his girlfriend. Police told his mother, Lori Greenberg, there was no evidence of injury, drugs, foul play, or suicide; the medical examiner’s autopsy disclosed no cause of death and toxicology results are expected in two to three months. Friends and family say Greenberg had been healthy and not on medication. His girlfriend, Abby Mayer, last spoke with him early Sunday morning and discovered him after returning later that day.

Greenberg and Sam Tarantino launched Grooveshark as University of Florida freshmen in 2006. The service peaked with tens of millions of users and roughly 145 employees, but faced major lawsuits from record labels alleging widespread copyright infringement. Grooveshark shut down in April after settling with major labels; Greenberg reportedly felt relieved by the settlement and was looking forward to new projects. He had been working on other music‑related mobile applications and community training initiatives, including Grooveshark University, the Summer with the Sharks internship program, and the Gainesville Dev Academy.

Widely regarded as a mentor and technology pioneer in Gainesville, Greenberg helped found the Founders Pad incubator and the Gainesville Technology Council and co‑created MaidSuite. Colleagues praised his mentorship, vision, and local impact. He is survived by his mother Lori, brother Jacob, and grandparents. Friends plan a memorial in Gainesville and say they intend to continue his legacy of mentoring and community contribution.

A disturbing incident in Phuket, Thailand, saw 20-year-old Wuttisan Wongtalay livestream himself hanging his 11-month-old daughter and then taking his own life, police said. Relatives who viewed the Facebook Live alerted authorities; police later discovered both bodies in an abandoned hotel. Officials said the killing followed a dispute in which Wuttisan accused his wife of neglect and suspected her of having another relationship. The broadcast was removed by Facebook about a day later; copies briefly appeared on YouTube and were taken down after media notification. Thai officials have given the grieving mother time before questioning. The case adds to mounting criticism of social platforms’ handling of violent live content, coming shortly after a U.S. murder was streamed on Facebook Live and after other global incidents—standoffs, suicides, sexual assaults and killings—were shown online. Facebook acknowledged it must improve controls and is exploring faster review processes, resharing prevention, and AI flagging, while rejecting calls to end live streaming. The tragedy prompted anger and sorrow in Thailand and renewed debate over the responsibilities of tech companies policing real-time user broadcasts.

Researchers have advanced a potential stem cell therapy that partially repairs heart damage after heart attacks, though significant challenges remain before human trials. In experiments with macaque monkeys, scientists at Shinshu University generated heart muscle cells in the lab from donor skin cells chosen for close genetic matching. After inducing heart attacks in five animals, they injected 400 million lab-made cardiomyocytes into the damaged areas. Over 12 weeks the transplanted cells replaced roughly 16% of scarred tissue, electrically integrated with host myocardium, and improved cardiac pumping function. Results were published in Nature.

However, all treated monkeys developed abnormal heart rhythms (arrhythmias) after transplantation. While these arrhythmias were not fatal in this and earlier similar studies, they present a serious safety concern that must be explained and resolved before human use. Lead researcher Yuji Shiba expressed confidence the post-transplant arrhythmia can be managed, and other experts noted potential interim measures such as implantable defibrillators to prevent sudden cardiac death while arrhythmias subside.

Experts welcomed the work as an important step toward regenerating damaged hearts and highlighted the appeal of having banks of pre-prepared, HLA-matched cell lines to avoid the lengthy, costly process of making patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)–derived cardiomyocytes. Still, immune suppression was required even with close matching, and incomplete or imperfect integration of transplanted cells could underlie arrhythmic risk. Given the prevalence and mortality of heart disease—hundreds of thousands of heart attacks annually in countries like the UK and US—novel therapies are urgently needed, but further research is needed to improve safety, understand mechanisms of arrhythmia, and determine clinical strategies before trials in people can proceed.

The White House quietly corrected its official transcript of President Donald Trump’s Rose Garden press conference after an exchange in which he insulted ABC News reporter Cecilia Vega went viral. The press event, marking the US-Canada-Mexico trade agreement, included a moment where Vega was waiting for a microphone and Trump said she was “shocked that I picked her. Like in a state of shock.” When Vega replied, “I’m not, thank you, Mr. President,” Trump retorted, “That’s okay. I know you’re not thinking, you never do.” The initial transcript released hours after the event misquoted Trump as saying, “I know you're not thanking. You never do,” prompting the White House to correct the wording to reflect the insulting remark. Vega asked a question about Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh, which Trump initially refused to answer, saying he would only take trade-related questions, though he later returned to allow her to ask the Kavanaugh question. The interaction drew online attention and criticism; Vega tweeted that a news conference allows any question and invoked the First Amendment. The correction highlights scrutiny over official records of presidential remarks.

A widespread Facebook bug briefly labeled many living users as deceased by displaying the site’s memorial banner on their profiles. The error, which affected a large number of accounts including that of CEO Mark Zuckerberg, caused a banner reading “We hope people who love [user] will find comfort in the things others share to remember and celebrate [his or her] life” to appear atop profiles not meant to be memorialized. Users posted reassurances—some humorous—clarifying they were alive, while journalists and observers reacted with bemusement and satire. Facebook said the message was intended only for “memorialized profiles” and that the bug mistakenly posted it to other accounts; the company called the incident “a terrible error” that was fixed quickly and apologized. The social network introduced the memorial feature in 2015 to give families a place to share memories if a person dies; accounts can be memorialized when Facebook is notified of a death, or users can choose to have their account deleted after death. The brief glitch reignited discussion about social media grief practices and prompted lighthearted coverage as well as concern from users surprised to find themselves unexpectedly declared dead online.

North Korea has upped its rhetoric, warning it may carry out “a new form of nuclear test” after the U.N. Security Council condemned Pyongyang’s recent medium-range missile launches. The Korean Central News Agency quoted the foreign ministry saying future Korean People’s Army drills will include “more diversified nuclear deterrence” and did not rule out novel nuclear testing methods. The launches—two Rodong missiles capable of reaching Japan—follow months of shorter-range tests and a 2013 nuclear detonation that North Korea says advanced its arsenal, though it likely lacks intercontinental delivery capability to strike the U.S. mainland.

Analysts and satellite imagery suggest North Korea has been excavating Punggye-ri’s West and South Portals in ways that could create multi-detonation tunnel complexes rather than single-use shafts. If tunnels branch from main drifts, Pyongyang could conduct multiple tests from the same site, enabling a higher testing cadence—especially if its fissile material output from Yongbyon increases. While Punggye-ri likely cannot host very large thermonuclear blasts safely, an uptick to annual or more frequent tests would change the strategic landscape and challenge current policies of strategic patience.

Following the Aurora movie-theater massacre, Republican presidential hopeful Mitt Romney said Monday it was “not a time to be talking about the politics associated with what happened,” while noting his Massachusetts record on gun restrictions. Romney reminded viewers that as governor he signed the first state assault-weapons ban, outlawing AR-15–style rifles like one used in the attack, and described that law as a bipartisan compromise that both sides celebrated. Speaking to CNBC’s Larry Kudlow, Romney argued that where “people of reasonable minds” can find common ground, he favors such legislation rather than one party forcing measures through. Still, he asserted additional laws would not have prevented the Colorado shooting, saying Colorado already had “very stringent laws” and that the core problem is individuals who commit “unthinkable, unimaginable, inexplicable” acts. Romney urged communities to focus first on reaching out to one another and later on policy. Both campaigns paused aggressive campaigning and ads immediately after the shooting and offered subdued remarks, but Romney indicated the brief pause was ending as campaigning resumed. He also criticized President Obama’s campaign for running predominantly negative ads, though trackers find both campaigns’ advertising overwhelmingly negative.

A chartered British Aerospace 146 carrying the Brazilian soccer team Chapecoense, club officials, journalists and crew crashed into a mountainous area near Medellin, Colombia, late Monday, killing most aboard and ending the small club’s breakthrough season in devastating fashion. Authorities reported six survivors among 77 people; the death toll was revised to 71. The team had been flying from Santa Cruz, Bolivia, to the first leg of the Copa Sudamericana final against Atletico Nacional. Chapecoense’s improbable rise—from Brazil’s lower divisions to continental finals—made the loss resonate across Brazil and international football, prompting days of mourning, canceled matches and offers of support from major clubs and confederations. Atletico Nacional asked that the title be awarded to Chapecoense as a tribute.

Rescue teams recovered the plane’s cockpit voice and flight data recorders from wreckage scattered on a mountainside; investigators were analyzing them. Colombian authorities initially said the jet experienced an electrical failure as heavy rain and thunderstorms developed during approach. Flight-tracking data show the aircraft entered a holding pattern south of Medellin, circling several times and descending from about 21,000 to 15,550 feet before radar contact was lost. Officials have not ruled out fuel exhaustion; a surviving flight attendant reportedly told rescuers the plane ran out of fuel minutes before impact.

The aircraft was operated by LaMia, a Bolivian-registered charter airline that had flown prominent teams and national squads in recent months. Experts noted the BAe 146’s limited range and the high-altitude, terrain-challenging approach into Jose Maria Cordova airport, combined with bad weather and any electrical outage, could create catastrophic conditions, particularly late in flight if fuel was low.

Three players survived — Alan Ruschel, Helio Zampier (Neto) and Jakson Follmann — though all were seriously injured, with one undergoing amputation. Among the deceased were coach Caio Junior, players, club staff and 20 journalists. Chapeco, a city of about 200,000, was left in shock as funerals and tributes unfolded. Investigators warned it may take months to determine the definitive causes of the crash.

Sudbury Police posted a holiday reminder after stopping a small blue sedan on Route 20 that was largely obscured by a very large Christmas tree. The department shared the photo on Facebook to urge motorists to transport trees and other items safely.
