Police Chief Scott Nix later told Boston.com there had been a single tree on the car; the family received a warning “in the spirit of the holidays.” An officer helped secure the tree more safely and marked it with caution tape. The department said the image was intended as a public safety reminder to move items responsibly on vehicles.

ONE® Condoms has launched myONE® Perfect Fit, a U.S. condom line offering an unprecedented 60 sizes (10 lengths × 9 circumferences) to address longstanding fit complaints. Released after seven years of research and regulatory work—including updating testing standards and securing FDA clearance—myONE aims to solve common problems: condoms that are too long or short, too loose or too tight. Historically, standard U.S. condoms were required to be at least 6.7 inches long with nominal widths of 1.9–2.2 inches, fitting properly only about 12 percent of men. myONE’s lengths span 4.9 to 9.4 inches and circumferences from 3.5 to 5.0 inches, adding 28 sizes larger than the leading XL and 27 sizes smaller than average condoms. ONE says this range should fit nine out of ten men, reducing issues such as slipping, discomfort, lost sensation, loss of erection, and increased STI and unintended pregnancy risk associated with poor fit.

Manufacturing 60 sizes posed major technical and financial challenges: creating many different cylindrical glass molds and modifying production lines. Despite this, ONE invested in specialized manufacturing and partnered with long-time manufacturer Karex Berhad. To help users find the right size, myONE offers a printable FitKit, online measurement tools, and sample kits (one size plus adjacent sizes) for a $2 shipping fee refunded on a next purchase; discreet shipping is available. ONE also pledged one million free condoms to promote proper fit and increase usage.

The launch builds on public health goals to normalize condom use and reduce STI/HIV transmission. Independent research cited shows mean erect penile length about 14.15 cm and circumference 12.23 cm—data that informed size offerings. While experts remain cautious about the public-health impact, ONE positions myONE as a smart, comfortable, affordable solution that could change perceptions and boost condom use. For more information or press materials, visit myonecondoms.com.

David Neevel, a Portland physicist, artist and inventor, built a quirky machine to remove the creme from Oreos because he prefers the cookies. Commissioned by Oreo for its "Cookies vs. Creme" campaign, Neevel’s contraption—the Oreo Separating Machine (OSM)—was assembled from scrap aluminum, wood, a hatchet and dental floss in his garage. It halves cookies with a lowered hatchet blade, uses mechanical arms to lift and transfer the halves to a router table, and strips away the creme. Neevel says the electric-powered device took about two weeks and many long hours to complete, during which he sacrificed time with friends, family and his dog. The video of him describing the build, his disdain for creme and his folksy catchphrase is entertaining and reminiscent of Portlandia-style humor; viewers praised his ingenuity and personality. Oreo plans a series of similar separator videos featuring other inventors, with additional designs to be revealed. While Neevel’s machine is more novelty than necessity, it’s an enjoyable example of creative problem-solving and hands-on engineering driven by personal preference.

A 15-year-old girl from Mississauga was cautioned by Ontario Provincial Police after she dialed 911 last Tuesday from a rental cottage in Trent Hills to report that her parents had “forced her” to go on vacation. Officers from Northumberland OPP attended the cottage on the Trent River, about 180 kilometres northeast of Toronto, to ensure everyone’s safety and to determine whether the situation involved coercion or an abduction. After interviewing all occupants and confirming the teen was safe, police concluded there was no real emergency and characterized the call as “a case of a teenager being a teenager.” Const. Stephen Bates noted the call was not an appropriate use of the emergency number and warned that such calls tie up resources that could be needed by others in genuine crisis. The teen was formally cautioned for misuse of 911. The incident drew light-hearted commentary, with reports noting a collective eye-roll from teens across Canada, while authorities reiterated the importance of reserving emergency lines for real threats to safety.

A woman’s engagement announcement on Facebook accidentally revealed another life update: she was pregnant. Miranda Levy posted a joyful photo of herself and her fiancé showing off an engagement ring, but friends quickly noticed a pregnancy test visible in the lower-left corner of the image. Initially unaware of the extra detail, Miranda wondered why so many people were asking if she was expecting; once she saw the test box in the photo, she confirmed the news with a follow-up post: "Hey we're having a baby, too." Miranda said she was delighted to be marrying “the love of my life” and described herself as “truly blessed,” noting the ring wasn’t a real jewel but that material things didn’t matter. The slip-up prompted reminders to double-check and crop photos before posting to social media to avoid unintentional reveals. Despite the faux pas, friends and onlookers offered congratulations on both the engagement and the pregnancy. The story circulated with the lesson: always inspect images carefully before sharing them online.

Late Friday night at Ripley’s Aquarium of Canada in downtown Toronto, a naked man climbed over a barrier, stripped, and jumped into the Dangerous Lagoon — a 2.9-million-litre exhibit housing sand tiger sharks, green sawfish, sea turtles and other species. Visitor video shows him calmly breaststroking among sharks and doing a backward flip off the rocks before emerging. On-site security asked him to leave shortly before 10:30 p.m.; he got out, slipped past staff into a crowd where a woman appears to hand him clothing, dressed, and left the aquarium despite requests to remain for police.

No animals, patrons or staff were injured, but officials described the stunt as “extremely dangerous,” endangering the man, marine life and staff who attempted to remove him. Aquarium management said it is cooperating with authorities and will press appropriate charges.

Investigators later linked the swimmer to an unrelated earlier attack that night: around 8 p.m. a 34-year-old man was randomly assaulted outside Medieval Times after the suspect had been ejected for disruptive behaviour; the victim suffered serious facial injuries and a broken tooth. Toronto police identified the suspect with public help as David Weaver, about 35–40 years old, of Nelson, B.C., wanted for assault causing bodily harm, mischief, trespassing and indecent exposure. He remains at large. Police ask anyone with information to contact them or Crime Stoppers. Authorities have launched an investigation; the aquarium did not immediately comment further to media.

A second inquest has reaffirmed that singer Amy Winehouse, 27, died in 2011 from alcohol toxicity after accidentally consuming a lethal amount of alcohol. Dr Shirley Radcliffe at St Pancras Coroner’s Court recorded a verdict of death by misadventure, matching the original October 2011 finding. Winehouse’s blood alcohol was 416mg per 100ml—more than five times the UK drink‑drive limit—and two empty vodka bottles were found beside her bed. The post‑mortem suggested respiratory arrest; no illicit drugs were detected and police found no suspicious circumstances. Winehouse’s GP, Dr Christina Romete, testified she had seen Amy the night before and that Amy “specifically said she did not want to die,” also noting a history of an eating disorder. The rehearing followed revelations that the deputy coroner who oversaw the first inquest, Suzanne Greenaway, lacked required qualifications; her appointment by senior coroner Dr Andrew Reid led to his resignation and disciplinary action.

An apparent suicide at the historic Berkeley City Club on Durant Avenue prompted a large emergency response and evacuation Tuesday afternoon after a woman in her 80s reportedly used a toxic chemical in her third-floor room. Police, fire and UC officers, along with hazardous-materials crews and bomb technicians, responded around 2 p.m.; the victim left a note warning first responders about the dangerous substance. Authorities later said the chemical was sodium azide, a gas‑forming salt used in airbags that is highly toxic when mixed with water. Durant Avenue was closed for hours, buses diverted, and the club evacuated; no injuries were reported. Investigators worked to remove the material and make the building safe while the death remained under investigation.

Hayden Kennedy was a prodigious and unconventional climber whose life mixed bold achievement with controversy and tragedy. From his teenage years he impressed peers—on his first El Capitan route he displayed the skill and calm of a future elite climber—and he grew up steeped in mountaineering through his father Michael Kennedy, a noted alpinist and longtime Climbing magazine editor. Forgoing college to pursue climbing, Hayden supported himself with sponsorships and odd jobs and earned grants to fund expeditions. His résumé spans hard sport and bold alpine lines: first ascents like Carbondale Short Bus (5.14-) and new routes on K7 and the Ogre (Baintha Brakk), a 10-hour all-free ascent of Hallucinogen Wall, and audacious alpinism in Patagonia including a near bolt-free first ascent of Cerro Torre’s southeast face with Jason Kruk. That Patagonia climb sparked intense debate after they removed more than 100 bolts from the historic Compressor Route, leading to threats, arrest, and jail time; supporters and detractors argued over ethics and respect for mountaineering history.

Hayden embraced a lighthearted, unstressed approach—“trying to have fun and not take it too seriously”—even after close calls, like a harrowing North Twin attempt. In October 2017, while skiing near Bozeman with girlfriend Inge Perkins, an avalanche buried and killed her; Perkins’ beacon was turned off. Kennedy survived but later returned home and died by suicide. His family honored his openness. Hayden had long avoided media attention, preferring climbing as a personal pursuit. In his later writings he reflected on loss, mortality, and the fleeting nature of partners and summits—insights that now resonate amid the shock of his and Perkins’ deaths.

A frightening carjacking in Atlanta ended without physical harm to two infants but left a father shaken. On a Saturday night at a Texaco station on Martin Luther King Jr. Drive, Lester Chaney stopped to pay after his pump card failed and admits he left his Toyota Camry running while he went inside. Surveillance footage captured a man sprinting to the unattended vehicle, jumping in and driving off with Chaney’s one-year-old twin daughters, Nadia and McKenzie, asleep in the back seat. Chaney said he ran to the car and tried to unlock the door as the suspect fled, but the thief drove away before he could reach them.

Police located the vehicle a short time later—about a quarter of a mile from the station—in the parking lot of an apartment complex. According to authorities, McKenzie remained buckled in her car seat inside the abandoned car, while Nadia had been taken out of the vehicle and left in a nearby wooded area. Remarkably, both girls had been sleeping through the ordeal and were found unharmed. The report does not make clear whether the suspect was aware there were infants in the car when he stole it, nor does it provide details about a suspect description or arrests. The incident highlights the serious risks of leaving a vehicle running and unattended, and it drew intense concern from the father and the community before the safe recovery of the twins. The story was reported by local station WSB-TV and originally covered by Cox Media Group.

At a Buffalo rally before New York’s April 2016 primary, Republican front-runner Donald Trump energized a large crowd with familiar themes—promising to revoke trade deals, repeal Obamacare, rebuild manufacturing jobs, and “build that wall.” He repeatedly attacked rivals (“Lyin’ Ted Cruz,” “Crooked Hillary”) and blamed NAFTA and other agreements for job losses in Buffalo and across New York. Trump praised local first responders and invoked 9/11, though he mistakenly referred to the attacks as “7-11.” He vowed to remain combative rather than adopt a more “presidential” tone until he secures victory, urging supporters to vote and deliver him New York’s delegates. The event, introduced by Rex Ryan and featuring local backers like Carl Paladino and Rep. Chris Collins, drew roughly 11,000–12,000 attendees; police ejected about 20 protesters and arrested six. The rally coincided with internal campaign changes—Trump moved new hires Paul Manafort and Rick Wiley into greater roles and allotted $20 million for upcoming primaries—while polls showed him leading New York Republicans by a wide margin (54% to Kasich’s 25% and Cruz’s 16%).

In Indianapolis, a homeowner believes her pet pig, Dumplin, may have scared off burglars who smashed in through her back door but left without taking anything. The single mother of four discovered extensive damage—the door was ruined and boarded up—after the break-in while her family was away. Police suggested the intruders likely encountered Dumplin and decided not to continue, though it’s unclear if that’s definitive. The owner rescued the full-grown pig earlier this year and praised him as a loving companion, urging others to consider adopting pigs from shelters. The neighborhood has seen a string of recent burglaries; police have not yet identified suspects and are seeking tips from the public.

The Miami Dolphins have dismissed offensive line coach Jim Turner and head trainer Kevin O’Neill following release of Ted Wells’ independent investigation into locker room misconduct. Owner Stephen Ross said the language and behavior documented in the report violated the organization’s core values; after an internal review he concluded both staffers, while dedicated, had shown poor judgment. Ross called the situation a teaching moment for the team and for sports in general. Head coach Joe Philbin acknowledged responsibility for creating a respectful team culture, calling the behaviors “disappointing and unacceptable” and pledging accountability going forward. According to the Wells report, Turner tolerated and participated in harassment of players, lied to investigators, and pressured Jonathan Martin to defend teammate Richie Incognito publicly. NFL Media indicated Turner was not expected to attend the NFL Scouting Combine. The Dolphins recently hired former Texans line coach John Benton as an assistant and he could be tapped to help replace Turner; Philbin and GM Dennis Hickey will address the media at the combine. The story was also discussed on the “Around The League” podcast.

A new study from Austin’s Pecan Street Research Institute challenges the long-standing rule that rooftop solar in the Northern Hemisphere must face south to be optimal. Testing 50 Austin homes during summer, researchers compared south- and west-facing fixed solar arrays. Contrary to installer models predicting up to 30% losses for west orientations, the study found west-facing systems produced about 2% more energy over a normal day and far outperformed south-facing panels during late-afternoon peak hours. From 3–7 p.m., west-facing arrays generated 49% more electricity, helping homeowners cut their peak grid draw by 65% versus 54% for south-facing systems. Pecan Street CEO Brewster McCracken noted these reductions are comparable to powerful residential demand-response tools and could ease grid stress by aligning generation with evening household demand and reducing surplus exports utilities struggle to absorb. The findings could broaden the viable market for residential solar—making east-west roofs attractive—especially where utilities price peak versus off-peak hours. Researchers and industry observers caution results may vary by region and season (the study covered summer only) and that incentives and local weather patterns will affect optimal orientation decisions.

One year after Robert Mueller was appointed special counsel to probe links between Russia and President Trump’s 2016 campaign, the investigation has quietly secured multiple indictments and five guilty pleas while revealing little else. Mueller, a former FBI director and Vietnam veteran with bipartisan appointments, assembled a team largely screened from partisan hiring and bound by professional ethics; many staffers are registered Democrats, though Mueller himself is a Republican. Major developments include charges against Paul Manafort, Rick Gates, George Papadopoulos, Michael Flynn, Alex van der Zwaan, and a February 2018 indictment of 13 Russian nationals and three entities. Key unresolved legal questions loom: whether Mueller can subpoena or indict a sitting president, whether Trump can fire Mueller (only the acting attorney general can under DOJ rules, though political routes exist), and whether pardons could blunt the probe (a self-pardon is legally unclear and pardons wouldn’t necessarily halt investigative leads). The inquiry’s future may hinge on novel constitutional and statutory court rulings.

A 6-year-old autistic boy who slipped away from family at a Mount Vernon park was found driving a small battery-powered ATV onto the Bronx River Parkway late Sunday, then safely recovered by Good Samaritans. Around 7 p.m. the child left a park near South Seventh Avenue and rode the blue miniature vehicle about a mile to Oak Street, where he took the ramp onto the northbound parkway. Drivers reported seeing the little boy in the far right lane, with cars passing at highway speeds. Multiple motorists slowed and boxed him in to protect him from traffic; witnesses describe one rescuer grabbing and holding the frightened child who repeatedly called for his mother. Three motorists are credited with surrounding the ATV, allowing someone to exit a vehicle, remove the boy and his toy from the roadway, and bring him to the shoulder. Police arrived shortly afterward, took the child to Montefiore Mount Vernon Hospital for observation, and confirmed he was unharmed before reuniting him with his family in Westchester County. The incident, which began when relatives lost sight of him at the park and led to many 911 calls, is under investigation. Good Samaritans involved have been praised for preventing a potentially tragic outcome.

Ford has added a new, Ford-licensed 1967 Mustang convertible body shell to its restoration parts lineup, joining reproduction ’65 and ’67 and ’69 fastback shells. Made by Dynacorn, the shell is stamped from modern automotive-grade “virgin” steel slightly thicker than the original and uses updated welding and reinforcements in known stress areas for improved strength and fit. It ships rustproofed and primed, ready for painting and assembly, and accepts original-era big-block engines (390, 427, 428) or modern powertrains without modification. More than 90% of required components are available as Ford-licensed reproduction parts. The shell is listed at $15,995.

A jaguar escape at New Orleans’ Audubon Zoo left eight animals dead and the park grappling with shock and questions. The male jaguar, Valerio, slipped from his enclosure Saturday and mauled nine animals; six were initially reported dead, and two more—a fox and an alpaca—died later, leaving one injured fox alive. Staff sedated and returned Valerio to his night house; no people were hurt. Inspections found the exhibit roof was compromised, and officials said keeper error was not initially suspected. The zoo reopened Sunday but many exhibits remained empty, grief counselors were offered to staff, and visitors and members debated the ethics and safety of zoos. Visitors left notes and tributes for the killed animals, underscoring the episode’s emotional impact.

China announced it will suspend all coal imports from North Korea for the remainder of the year, a move Beijing said complies with the U.N. Security Council’s tougher sanctions imposed in November 2016 after Pyongyang’s fifth nuclear test. The Commerce Ministry and customs agency published a joint notice saying the ban covers coal produced in North Korea, including shipments already declared to customs but not yet released. The restriction revokes an earlier, narrower ban China enacted in April 2016 that had allowed some coal flows for civilian use. Coal is North Korea’s principal export and a critical source of foreign currency; most of that coal has historically gone to China, Pyongyang’s largest trade partner and main provider of aid. By cutting off coal imports, Beijing increases economic pressure on North Korea to abandon its nuclear and ballistic missile programs. The decision comes amid rising tensions after North Korea’s recent ballistic missile test and growing international calls—highlighted by pressure from the U.S. administration—to take a firmer stance on Pyongyang. China has long maintained it has limited leverage over North Korea, but the new import suspension signals Beijing’s frustration with North Korea’s continued defiance of U.N. resolutions.

Over the July holiday weekend, Walmart, Sears and Amazon removed a poster from their marketplaces showing the main gate of the Dachau concentration camp bearing the Nazi slogan “Arbeit macht frei” (“work makes you free”), after shoppers and Holocaust-related groups expressed outrage. The image had been listed and promoted as home décor, prompting accusations of tastelessness and insensitivity. Walmart apologized, saying the item was sold by a third-party marketplace seller, that it was “horrified,” and that it had the seller remove the publisher from inventory. Sears likewise said the listing violated its guidelines and was removed; a screengrab shared online highlighted an especially jarring page where “similar items” included ovens, prompting further condemnation due to ovens’ association with crematoria. Amazon also pulled the item; it did not immediately comment to ABC News. The incident revived concerns about online retailers’ handling of Nazi and Holocaust-related material. Retail platforms face criticism for allowing offensive memorabilia and denial literature to be sold—eBay previously changed policies after outrage over Holocaust items, and Amazon has faced scrutiny for hosting works like Mein Kampf and Holocaust denial publications. The episode underscores challenges in policing third-party listings and content sensitivity.

Sentiment entering 2017 was split: supporters expected strong growth from tax reform and deregulation, while skeptics like Paul Krugman warned against 3%+ GDP forecasts. Stocks rose over 20% in 2017, making Wall Street broadly bullish for 2018, with some firms forecasting higher S&P targets. The author cautions against extrapolating recent trends and long-range crystal-ball predictions, though he leans toward modest optimism: global PMI strength and repatriated offshore cash could lift U.S. multinational earnings, especially if the corporate tax rate falls near 20%, potentially enabling 15% earnings growth and $150 S&P earnings. Buybacks have peaked and may give way to a capex cycle. Fortune’s 2018 outlook predicts tax reform without 3% GDP (around 2.5%), higher Fed rates (about 2.25% by year-end), oil near $55/barrel, home-price growth slowing to ~4.1%, and a revived IPO market.

Washington led U.S. English-language TV ratings during the World Cup, continuing a trend with ESPN’s Monday Ghana–USA broadcast earning an 11.8 overnight rating in the Washington market — the highest in the country and notably above New York (10.2), Hartford/New Haven (10.1) and Boston (10.0). In Washington and Baltimore it was the highest overnight rating ever for a World Cup group-round match on any network. Through 14 matches, D.C. tops ESPN networks’ local averages (5.0), followed by San Francisco (4.4) and New York (4.1). D.C. repeatedly led local ratings for other matches this week and outpaced typical local sports telecasts; the Ghana–USA telecast averaged a 7.0 overnight on ESPN and drew about 15.9 million viewers across ESPN and Univision, setting network records.

Billboard named Lady Gaga its 2010 Artist of the Year, after she jumped from last year’s Top New Artist to the summit thanks to strong chart showings from The Fame and The Fame Monster and singles like “Bad Romance.” Taylor Swift was No. 2, marking back-to-back top-two finishes. Eminem was No. 3 and Lady Antebellum the top group at No. 4, aided by “Need You Now.” Ke$ha won Top New Artist with “TiK ToK” reigning nine weeks at No. 1.

Sean “Diddy” Combs publicly mourned his ex-partner Kim Porter three days after her sudden death, posting a heartfelt social media tribute describing his struggle to accept the loss. Porter, 47 (reported at 46 in some outlets), was found dead Thursday at her Toluca Lake, California home; authorities responded to a 911 call reporting a patient in cardiac arrest, and reports say she had experienced flu-like symptoms for weeks, but no official cause of death has been released. Diddy, 49, wrote that he has been “trying to wake up out of this nightmare” and expressed profound grief and disbelief, calling their bond “unexplainable,” saying they were “more than best friends” and “more than soulmates.” He signed the message “Super Black Love.” A representative confirmed Porter’s passing to media outlets. Porter and Combs had an on-again, off-again relationship lasting about 13 years; they remained close after separating in 2007. Together they share three children: son Christian (20) and 11-year-old twin daughters Jessie James and D’Lila. Porter also had an older son, Quincy, whom Diddy adopted; Quincy is Porter's child from a previous relationship with producer Al B. Sure!. The family and fans have been left mourning amid limited official details about the circumstances of her death.

Nicholas D. Kristof recounts a 1,700-mile road trip across Iran from Mashhad to Tabriz and Tehran after receiving a rare journalist visa and permission to travel unescorted. He found striking warmth toward Americans—often effusive—despite occasional state slogans like “Death to America.” Many Iranians blamed their own leaders more than the U.S. for economic suffering tied in part to Western sanctions. Compared with his 2004 visit, Kristof found greater discontent and fear: after the 2009 crackdown, public criticism stops short of activism, and people worry about being recorded or quoted—some begged that video not be used. Views varied widely by education and media access: farmers and less-educated citizens who rely on state television often supported the regime, while others—shopkeepers, businessmen, separatists, and disillusioned religious practitioners—were sharply critical. Kristof sees Iran as an authoritarian state under strain and suggests its system may eventually collapse unless war triggers a nationalist rally that would strengthen the ayatollahs. He plans more reporting to follow.

The FAA ordered emergency inspections of about 175 older Boeing 737s worldwide—80 in the U.S., mostly Southwest’s 737-300/400/500 fleet—after a Southwest 737-300 suffered a five-foot fuselage tear and rapid decompression en route from Phoenix to Sacramento. The order targets aircraft with a specific manufacturing process and over 30,000 flight cycles, using eddy-current scans to detect hidden fatigue cracks; ultrasound and X-ray follow-ups are used if needed. NTSB investigators and Southwest found additional cracks at the riveted seam where two skin panels join; corrosion and enlarged rivet holes likely contributed. Southwest grounded many 737-300s, found cracks in several planes, and canceled flights. Officials said the incident could prompt broader, costlier inspection requirements for aging airframes and has renewed scrutiny of aging-aircraft safety and inspection programs.

The Justice Department filed suit against North Carolina, charging that the state’s recently enacted voter-ID law and related voting changes violate the Voting Rights Act by discriminating against African-Americans. Attorney General Eric Holder announced the complaint in Greensboro, asserting the law was intentionally designed to reduce minority participation and that its “purpose, intent and effect” discriminate on the basis of race. The DOJ asks a court to bar enforcement of the photo-ID requirement and to place North Carolina back under a preclearance regime—requiring federal approval of future voting-rule changes—by invoking a rarely used “bail in” provision of the Voting Rights Act. Until the Supreme Court’s June Shelby County v. Holder decision struck down the statute’s formula for who must preclear, 40 North Carolina counties were subject to preclearance; DOJ and civil-rights groups have since sought to recreate that oversight through litigation.

North Carolina’s law, signed by Republican Gov. Pat McCrory, mandates government-issued photo ID to vote (student IDs excluded) and curtails other practices: it eliminates the first seven days of early voting, ends same-day registration during early voting, and bars counting provisional ballots cast at the wrong precinct. DOJ officials cited a state elections study finding more than 300,000 registered voters lacked DMV-issued ID; African-Americans are disproportionately represented among those without IDs and among users of early and same-day registration. Holder and civil-rights advocates said there is little evidence of widespread voter fraud—the principal rationale cited by supporters of voter-ID laws—and argued that reductions in early voting bear no logical tie to preventing fraud.

The federal suit follows an August DOJ challenge to Texas’s voter-ID and redistricting actions and comes amid heated debate: proponents say photo ID safeguards election integrity, while opponents and the NAACP call the North Carolina law a concerted attack on voting rights that will disenfranchise minority and vulnerable voters. DOJ did not specify a requested duration for any preclearance order for North Carolina; similar requests in Texas seek a ten-year oversight period.

A viral video of Bloodhound Gang bassist Jared Hasselhoff stuffing a Russian flag down his pants and whipping it between his legs during a July 31 concert in Odessa provoked a major diplomatic and legal uproar. The stunt, filmed and widely circulated online, led to the band being barred from performing at the Kubana festival in Russia and reportedly assaulted by nationalist demonstrators and self-described Cossacks at an airport in Anapa. Russian authorities launched a criminal investigation and the Interior Ministry said a specialized unit opened a case for desecration of the national flag, an offense punishable by up to a year in prison; prosecutors also began reviewing regional music festivals. Some lawmakers suggested the incident was a deliberate provocation, while cultural critics warned that authorities’ heavy-handed reaction could fuel a new cultural "iron curtain" that isolates Russia from Western influences. The U.S. ambassador called the stunt “disgusting” but condemned the violence against the band, noting U.S. free speech protections for flag desecration. Ukraine also opened investigations into alleged desecrations there, and calls arose to ban the musicians from Russia and Ukraine. The episode underscored how unscripted acts can inflame tensions amid worsening U.S.–Russia relations.

The Supreme Court on November 2 declined the Trump administration’s emergency request to halt a landmark climate lawsuit brought in 2015 by 21 young plaintiffs who argue the federal government has violated their constitutional rights by allowing dangerous climate change to proceed. In an unsigned order, the justices said the government had not met the extraordinary standard required to stop the case before trial, though Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch would have granted the stay. The Court suggested the administration could seek relief from the Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals and possibly return to the Supreme Court later. 

Known as Juliana v. United States, the suit seeks a court-ordered national remedial plan to reduce greenhouse gases and phase out fossil fuel reliance, aiming to lower atmospheric CO2 to 350 ppm by 2100. The government contends the claims rest on unprecedented legal theories—like a substantive due process right to particular climate conditions—and that courts lack authority to order such sweeping policy changes. Both the Obama and Trump administrations have tried to dismiss the case, arguing separation-of-powers and burdens of discovery, but lower courts repeatedly allowed it to proceed. 

Plaintiffs’ counsel say they will push the Oregon district court to reschedule the long-awaited trial; they maintain the youth already suffer irreparable harm from climate impacts and emphasize the strength of their evidence. The case has inspired similar global litigation; proponents point to successes like the Dutch Urgenda and Colombian rulings as models for using courts to compel stronger climate action. The path ahead remains uncertain, hinging on appellate review and trial-stage developments.

A recent viral craze over a discontinued McDonald’s “Szechuan” McNugget dipping sauce — originally a 1998 Mulan promo — has highlighted a thriving market for nostalgic, rare, and regional packaged foods. The frenzy began after an episode of Rick and Morty referenced the sauce, sparking online campaigns and fan demand. One buyer paid an astonishing $14,700 on eBay for a 20-year-old packet found in an old car, topping 186 bids; other listings asking far less also appeared. The episode and ensuing social-media push even prompted a Change.org petition and some tentative comments from McDonald’s that they “never say never” about a return. 

This episode is part of a broader niche economy where collectors, sellers, and nostalgic consumers trade in discontinued sodas, snacks, and candy. Sodafinder.com curator Brian Florence stores around 400–600 12-packs at a time and drives long routes to source regional and discontinued soft drinks, selling many for $15–$25 per case and sometimes much higher for rare items. Vendors like Patrick Meynders sell Canadian Dunkaroos to U.S. buyers; others hawk discontinued regional sodas such as Dublin Dr. Pepper or rare flavors like Nehi Grape and Buffalo Rock Ginger Ale. Many sellers warn that discontinued items are out of date, sold “drink at your own risk,” but buyers often seek taste-linked memories rather than culinary fidelity. 

Marketing researchers note nostalgia’s power: the flavor ties to memory and feelings of simpler times, though expectations can lead to disappointment when products don’t match childhood recollections. Sellers balance sourcing, pricing, and logistics—Florence times road trips, rents vans, and adjusts prices by demand—while some customers buy to consume, others as collectors. The Szechuan-sauce bidding spectacle underscores how pop culture can suddenly turn an obscure food relic into a high-value collectible.

Dozens of African-American pastors met privately with Donald Trump at Trump Tower on Nov. 30, 2015, in a contentious session that left no clear endorsement and highlighted deep divisions over his rhetoric. The meeting, originally billed by the campaign as an endorsement event with 100 black clergy and a press conference, was scaled back after backlash from other black faith leaders and an open letter in Ebony criticizing Trump’s “racially inaccurate, insensitive and incendiary rhetoric.” Many invited pastors said they accepted the invitation to challenge Trump rather than to endorse him.

During roughly two-and-a-half hours of discussion, several pastors demanded that Trump apologize to the black community—and to Mexicans—for inflammatory comments and for condoning rough treatment of a Black Lives Matter protester at a rally. Others counseled him not to apologize, arguing his outspoken style had propelled him to the top of polls. Trump portrayed the meeting as full of “love” and said attendees did not ask him to change his tone, asserting that his blunt approach has won him strong support. Some pastors, however, said he gave noncommittal responses about softening his rhetoric.

Attendees criticized Trump’s mocking of a New York Times reporter’s disability and his earlier tweet with misleading crime statistics. Some emerging from the session voiced hope that Trump’s “heart” had been seen; others remained uneasy about his comments about minorities, women and Muslims. The episode underscored the Republican front-runner’s fraught relationship with minority communities and the challenge of courting African-American support amid controversy over his style and statements.

An online video showing American hunter Josh Bowmar spearing a black bear in Alberta has prompted public outrage and a government response. The footage, posted in June and filmed in May near Swan Hills northeast of Edmonton, shows Bowmar throwing a roughly two-metre spear with a 40-centimetre blade into a baited bear, a strike later captured via a GoPro mounted on the spear. Bowmar celebrates on camera, returns the next day with outfitters John and Jenn Rivet, and finds the bear dead about 50–70 metres from the hit site. He insists the animal “died immediately” and defends the act as humane and ethical; critics dispute that account and warn of the risk an injured animal might flee and suffer.

Alberta’s Ministry of Environment and Parks condemned the act as “archaic” and “unacceptable,” ordered fish and wildlife officers to investigate potential charges under existing laws, and said it will introduce a ban on spear hunting this fall as hunting regulations are updated. The Alberta Fish and Game Association, which consults with government, had already seen spear hunting as a legal grey area under 2016 weapon definitions and supports clearer prohibitions to ensure ethical, quick kills using firearms or bows. Bear baiting, the method used to attract the animal, is legal in restricted areas.

The video drew intense online criticism, tabloid headlines in the U.K., threats against Bowmar, and condemnation from animal welfare groups including the Humane Society, comparing the backlash to previous high-profile trophy hunting controversies. Bowmar, a former collegiate javelin thrower and fitness personality, has defended his actions and his hunting record.

The Samsung Galaxy Note 7 launched in 2016 as a remarkably refined, feature-packed flagship: a 5.7-inch Quad HD Super AMOLED HDR-capable display widely praised as the best smartphone panel at the time; a refined, compact glass-and-metal design with dual subtle curved edges; 4GB RAM, Snapdragon 820/Exynos 8890 options, 64GB storage plus microSD, IP68 water resistance, USB-C, and a 3,500 mAh battery with fast wired and wireless charging. Its signature S Pen was improved (0.7 mm tip, 4,096 pressure levels, new software like GIF capture, Translate and Glance), and it introduced an iris scanner and Secure Folder for extra security. Reviewers lauded camera quality, battery life, productivity features and polished TouchWiz, calling it arguably the best big phone ever.

However, the Note 7 campaign ended in disaster. Multiple devices from the initial production run—and later replacement units—experienced battery overheating and fires. Samsung recalled about 2.5 million phones, halted production, and eventually discontinued the model. U.S. carriers and regulators urged users to power down and return devices; airlines banned the device. Replacement units initially cleared by Samsung and the U.S. CPSC later showed similar failures, prompting a full pullback. Review scores were revoked and editorial guidance strongly advised against buying or using Note 7 units. The reviews remain as an archive of a phone that combined technical brilliance with a catastrophic safety failure.

Tracy Fain, a mother of two, suffered a catastrophic brain aneurysm and stroke on August 7 while accompanying her 7-year-old son Ethan to a post-operative appointment at Egleston Hospital to remove stitches from injuries sustained in a December dog attack. She lost consciousness in the hospital lobby, was rushed to Emory for emergency surgery to relieve brain pressure and stop bleeding, and was placed in a medically induced coma. Although initial treatment stabilized her and showed some brain activity, her condition deteriorated and doctors later declared her brain dead. The family, who had hoped for a recovery after the emergency surgery, experienced compounded grief: Ethan had been severely mauled months earlier—losing an ear and undergoing reconstructive surgery—and the family had already faced the recent sudden death of Tracy’s nephew. Tracy’s mother, Sandra Moore, has expressed profound heartbreak and struggled with why these tragedies have struck her family, pleading for Tracy to fight and praying for a miracle. The family asks for prayers and support during this devastating time, and those wishing to help financially can donate via the family’s GoFundMe at https://www.gofundme.com/496vn2w.

Last summer Democrats said the tea party movement was an AstroTurf creation of corporate interests. With the grassroots conservative resurgence now a clear force, some on the left have shifted to treating tea partiers as the adversary. The Agenda Project, a new progressive group founded by Erica Payne, has launched the "F*ck Tea" project to "dismiss the tea party and promote the progressive cause." The effort, rooted in New York fundraising circles and linked to Payne’s work with liberal donor networks like the Democracy Alliance, sells merchandise and distributes mocking content and polling meant to portray tea party supporters as misinformed. Its materials highlight survey claims: many activists distrust climate science, favor stricter abortion rules, back figures like Glenn Beck, and express anti-immigration and anti-gay-recognition views.

Emerson College will launch a Bachelor of Fine Arts in Comedic Arts beginning fall 2016, turning an already strong comedy program into a full major. The hands-on curriculum, developed by Martie Cook and offered across Emerson’s Boston and Los Angeles campuses, blends theory and practice: students will study comedy history and the art and theory of laughter while producing sketch and sitcom performances, writing jokes for stage and screen, learning comedy editing and production, and building portfolios of scripts to show agents and producers. The program grows out of a popular minor, “Comedy: Writing and Performance,” and includes partnerships with industry groups such as the Upright Citizens Brigade; faculty include working professionals and the college expects guest master classes from prominent comedians. Emerson touts a long list of successful alumni—including Jay Leno, Denis Leary, Bill Burr, Iliza Shlesinger and others—as evidence of its comedic pedigree. Supporters say the major meets cultural demand, since millennials increasingly consume news and culture through comedy. Alumni and comedians note the value of formal training for developing craft and market-ready work, though some emphasize that practical stage experience, like frequent open mics, remains essential for aspiring stand-ups. More details will be posted on Emerson’s website.

Latter-day Saints teach that monogamy—one man and one woman—is God’s enduring law of marriage, but that on certain occasions in biblical and early Latter-day Saint history the Lord commanded plural marriage (one man with more than one woman). Joseph Smith received a revelation on plural and eternal marriage (Doctrine and Covenants 132) emerging from his Old Testament study; under that revelation he introduced plural marriage incrementally in the 1840s, sealing some women to himself and authorizing others to enter plural unions. Early practice was kept confidential, producing a sparse and sometimes ambiguous historical record.

Plural marriage was understood by participants as a commandment meant in part to “raise up seed” and to bind families eternally through priesthood sealings—an extension of restored temple keys and ordinances. In Nauvoo and later Utah, plural families reported both hardships and blessings. The practice altered social patterns: it increased marriage opportunities, reduced per-capita wealth inequality for some women, encouraged ethnic intermarriage among immigrants, and promoted strong group cohesion. Most polygamous men had only two wives; women could choose to divorce or remarry, and some unions involved very young brides by the standards of the time.

Federal anti-polygamy laws beginning in 1862, Supreme Court affirmation in 1879, and prosecutions in the 1880s pressured the Church. In 1890 President Wilford Woodruff issued the Manifesto declaring submission to U.S. law, largely ending new plural marriages in the United States, though some occurred later in Mexico and Canada. A 1904 Second Manifesto made new plural marriages grounds for excommunication. Since then, Church leaders have repeatedly taught that the Church does not authorize plural marriage.

Plural marriage remains one of the most challenging aspects of the Restoration. While it provoked persecution and personal sacrifice, descendants of those who entered plural unions include many faithful Church members. Today the Church honors those pioneers while teaching that plural marriage is no longer practiced.

Miss America 2015 Kira Kazantsev, a trilingual Hofstra honors student and advocate for women’s health, faced controversy after reports emerged that she was expelled from the Alpha Phi sorority in late April 2013 for hazing pledges while serving as recruitment committee president. Jezebel cited an anonymous source alleging Kazantsev and a friend subjected new members to verbal abuse, degrading tasks, and physically taxing activities—accusations said to be retaliation for how Kazantsev herself had been hazed. Hofstra’s code strictly prohibits hazing and threatens campus removal for offenders; the university investigated and, according to sources, expelled Kazantsev from the chapter, barring her from sorority events. Alpha Phi’s national and Hofstra chapters did not publicly celebrate her Miss America win, and public records and photos show her active participation in chapter events. The Miss America Organization said Kazantsev had been “fully transparent” with them about the termination and praised her academics and service. Kazantsev denied the hazing allegations in a statement and on Good Morning America, explaining her termination stemmed from a joking email taken out of context and asserting she never engaged in name-calling, physical hazing, or degradation. The episode sparked debate over accountability, campus hazing culture, and how past student conduct should factor into public roles.

PETA slammed Kim Kardashian after she posted video of herself riding captive dolphins in Mexico, calling her actions “intrusive,” “dangerous,” and harmful to the animals. Kardashian’s Instagram noted a “double dolphin ride” and plans to show her daughter photos of swimming with dolphins and kissing a sea lion. PETA Senior VP Lisa Lange responded that while Kardashian can leave the pool, the dolphins cannot, describing “swim-with” programs and touch tanks as invasive, stressful, and risky for both animals and humans. The organization says such interactions lead to injury, illness from foreign bacteria, anxiety, aggression, and shortened lives. The piece broadens the critique to aquariums and marine theme parks, arguing these facilities confine highly social, wide-ranging cetaceans to tiny tanks, force them to perform, separate families, and cause physical and psychological harm—collapsed dorsal fins, damaged teeth, chronic injuries, and premature deaths are cited. Notable examples include Tilikum and Lolita; statistics show many orcas and dolphins die young in captivity. The article notes international moves to ban or restrict captivity (Chile, Costa Rica, India, etc.) and urges readers to avoid visiting marine parks that keep cetaceans, pressure institutions to rehabilitate rather than breed, leaflet, contact officials, and support legislation to protect marine mammals.

Nike has announced the HyperAdapt 1.0, its first broadly offered self-lacing shoe that realizes the long-standing sci-fi promise popularized by Back to the Future II. The shoe uses pressure sensors in the sole to detect when a wearer steps in; that triggers a battery-powered system of tiny pulleys and spools that cinch the shoe’s throat, tightening the fit automatically. Manual adjustment remains possible via plus and minus buttons on the sides, and holding a button for two seconds fully loosens the shoe for removal. Nike describes the design as a consumer-ready evolution of the company’s commemorative Air Mags, which were never intended for mass release though a few were made and gifted to figures like Michael J. Fox. The HyperAdapt 1.0 will be sold this holiday season in three colors, but initially only to Nike+ members; pricing is TBD. Nike says the battery lasts about two weeks per charge. Designers John Hoke and Tinker Hatfield emphasize that HyperAdapt is a platform: after a few wears the shoe learns preferred settings, and future versions could make automatic, biometric-driven micro-adjustments—integrating into a broader ecosystem of adaptive wearables. The trade-offs include potential malfunctions and the need to recharge—new conveniences with new dependencies.

David Steele, 42, a veteran sprint car racer and multiple United States Auto Club national champion, was killed Saturday night in a crash during the Southern Sprint Car Shootout at Desoto Speedway in Bradenton, Fla. Steele — a two-time Little 500 winner, 2004 USAC Silver Crown champion and the defending Southern Sprint Car Series champion — was pursuing his 100th Florida sprint car victory. Early in the 35-lap main, his car made contact while passing, hooked wheels, flipped airborne, struck the outside retaining wall and spun before coming to rest. Track medics responded immediately but Steele was pronounced dead at the scene. The track paused activities and released condolences to his family; colleagues and drivers expressed shock and grief on social media. He is survived by his wife, Lynn Bunn Steele, and three young children.

The New York Times revealed that the NSA collects millions of images daily from electronic communications and analyzes them with facial-recognition tools. From that volume, roughly 55,000 images each day are deemed “facial-recognition quality.” Leaked 2011 documents (from Edward Snowden) show the agency has expanded reliance on both in-house and commercial software—such as Google-owned PittPatt—to process photos from social media, email, messaging, videoconferencing and other channels. Officials touted facial recognition as offering “tremendous untapped potential” for tracking targets and treating biometric data alongside written and oral communications. The NSA says it cannot access U.S. driver’s-license or passport databases and would need court approval to collect Americans’ imagery as content, yet it declined to confirm whether it gathers social-media photos by means other than communications intercepts. Experts have long warned about privacy risks: Facebook’s automatic tagging and high-accuracy DeepFace work have increased the volume of tagged images that could feed surveillance. U.S. privacy laws do not expressly protect facial-recognition use, and cross-border communications may allow the agency to obtain Americans’ images indirectly. The disclosures amplify concerns about scope and oversight of biometric surveillance.

The Queen has become Britain’s longest-reigning monarch, surpassing Queen Victoria after 23,226 days, 16 hours and around 30 minutes on 6 February 2015. Speaking in the Scottish Borders at age 89, she thanked well-wishers for their “touching messages of great kindness,” adding she had never aspired to the title. Her brief public engagement included opening the new Scottish Borders Railway with Prince Philip; a Thames flotilla and gun salute marked the day in London. Politicians and Commonwealth leaders paid tribute, calling her a steady, selfless symbol of service across generations. Business in Parliament was briefly suspended for tributes, and ministers will present bound cabinet papers from 1952. Buckingham Palace released official photos from her private audience room; the Queen is spending her usual summer break at Balmoral and is expected to mark the milestone privately, with no large public celebrations planned.

Patton Oswalt and Meredith Salenger were married on November 4, 2017, at the Jim Henson Company lot in Los Angeles, announcing the union with shared photos showing Salenger walking down the aisle with Oswalt and his daughter Alice. The couple went public in June at the Baby Driver premiere and announced their engagement in July; Oswalt proposed playfully, hiding the ring in a marzipan Star Wars Slave I and joking about being maced before she said yes. Their relationship began early in 2017 via messages and quickly deepened over months of nightly conversations, and they moved toward marriage after a period of intense grieving and therapy for Oswalt. 

Oswalt, 48, had been widowed when his first wife, Michelle McNamara, died unexpectedly in April 2016 from a mix of prescription drugs and an undiagnosed heart condition. Her death left Oswalt a single parent to their daughter Alice, and he has been open about the profound grief and the slow process of healing—including removing his wedding ring about a year after her death. He and Salenger faced some online criticism for the timing of their engagement; both defended their relationship publicly, noting the support of Michelle’s family and emphasizing their intention to honor Michelle’s memory while creating a loving family life for Alice. Oswalt has described his renewed happiness with Salenger as a hard-won new beginning and said he continues to prioritize being a present father for Alice.

John W. Caltabiano Jr., a 49-year-old man from Catskill, New York, was sentenced to 57 months in federal prison after a jury found him guilty of conspiring to fraudulently obtain Social Security Disability and state workers’ compensation benefits by pretending to be nearly blind. Beginning with a 2006 workplace incident in which he lost sight in one eye, Caltabiano falsely represented that his other eye was impaired and collected disability payments from 2008 to 2010. Investigators later obtained videos and photos showing him performing activities inconsistent with blindness: driving a pickup truck, walking unassisted into stores, exercising at a gym, holding doors open and apparently reading. These images undermined his claims and demonstrated continued independence, despite public appearances in which his girlfriend, Colleen McCarten, led him into hearings to bolster the ruse.

Federal authorities say Caltabiano’s scheme could have netted more than half a million to over a million dollars had it continued; he was ordered to pay $27,784 in restitution and will serve three years of supervised release after imprisonment. McCarten received probation after being convicted alongside him. Officials emphasized that disability fraud burdens taxpayers and depletes funds intended for genuinely disabled people. The Social Security Administration’s Office of the Inspector General and the U.S. Attorney’s Office prosecuted the case, stressing ongoing efforts to detect and prosecute benefit fraud and protect public trust. Judge Mae A. D’Agostino and prosecutors also noted Caltabiano’s extensive and disturbing criminal history during sentencing.

Underwater pumping to remove about 500,000 gallons (more than 2,300 tonnes) of fuel from the Costa Concordia began Sunday, nearly a month after the ship struck a reef and capsized off Giglio. After weather and rescue delays, Dutch salvage firm Smit and an Italian partner started on the first of 15 tanks holding roughly 84% of the fuel; operations should run 24/7 and last about 28 days. Valves will be fitted and oil warmed and pumped out while seawater is forced in to replace it. The grounding killed 17; 15 remain missing. Captain Francesco Schettino faces charges including manslaughter and abandoning ship; investigators continue and memorials have been held.

In May 2015, Russia’s RATAN-600 radio telescope recorded a brief, strong radio spike at 2.7 cm (≈11 GHz) from a patch of sky that aligns in right ascension with the Sun-like star HD 164595, about 94–95 light-years away in Hercules. The reported amplitude was ~750 mJy. The detection was circulated among SETI researchers by Alexander Panov and presented by a team led by N.N. Bursov with collaborators including Claudio Maccone. The signal was seen only once in 39 observations and has not been published in a peer-reviewed paper; the team urged permanent monitoring and planned to discuss the finding at the IAC SETI committee meeting in September 2016.

If the emission were an isotropic beacon from HD 164595, the inferred transmitter power would be enormous—about 10^20 W—comparable to a Kardashev Type II civilization. If beamed toward Earth, the required power drops to roughly 10^13 W, near total current human power usage and consistent with a Kardashev Type I capability. However, experts stress these are speculative back-of-envelope estimates and that terrestrial interference, military satellite transmissions, receiver bandwidth effects, or microlensing of a background source are plausible. The Russian receiver’s wide 1 GHz bandwidth could dilute narrow-band signals, complicating interpretation.

Follow-up observations by the Allen Telescope Array and other facilities initially found no repeat signal across targeted bands, and Russian statements later suggested no confirmed extraterrestrial emission. The candidate remains intriguing but unconfirmed; without repeat detections or independent confirmation, it must be treated as an interesting anomaly warranting continued, careful monitoring rather than evidence of alien intelligence.

Actress Amy Adams gave up her first-class seat on a Delta flight from Detroit to Los Angeles to an American serviceman, choosing to sit in coach instead. Jemele Hill of ESPN recounted spotting Adams glance at the soldier, speak with her companion and then leave her first-class seat so the serviceman could be moved up. A fellow passenger, Ernest Owens, took a selfie with Adams and said she told him she’d long wanted to do something like that. Adams told Inside Edition she did it “for the troops,” not for attention. Fans praised her gesture on Twitter; observers noted Adams was born on a U.S. military base and spent part of her childhood in a military family.

A U.S.- and Russia-brokered cease-fire in Syria took effect at sundown, aiming to halt fighting between the U.S.-backed opposition and the Russian- and Iranian-backed Syrian government. The weeklong truce permits continued government and Russian strikes on ISIS and al-Qaida-linked militants; if the lull holds for seven days, Washington and Moscow will begin intelligence sharing and coordinated targeting of extremist groups. Syrian President Bashar Assad publicly supported the deal and made a rare appearance in Daraya for Eid al-Adha prayers, stressing a drive to “reclaim every area from the terrorists.” Russia said it will keep striking jihadist targets and set up a joint U.S.-Russian center to coordinate operations and use drones to monitor compliance.

Mixed reactions came from rebel factions, some cautious or skeptical, with concerns the pause might favor the regime. Activists reported government bombardments in several opposition areas hours before the truce, and jihadists continued offensive operations in parts of Quneitra and Aleppo. Humanitarian groups hope the cease-fire will allow aid into besieged cities like Aleppo; Turkey pledged to send relief to northern towns. The U.N. and international officials urged careful monitoring; Staffan de Mistura said his office would assess the start of the truce before commenting. Observers cautioned previous agreements have failed, leaving the cease-fire’s durability—and the fate of millions of displaced Syrians—uncertain.

Over the weekend Adele addressed rumors she’d be the 2017 Super Bowl Halftime performer, saying she declined because “that show is not about music” and she “can’t dance.” Speaking at a Los Angeles concert, she said organizers had been “very kind” but she’d turned the idea down. The NFL and sponsor Pepsi issued a joint statement saying they’d spoken with several artists but had not extended a formal offer to Adele or anyone else, and they’re focused on assembling a great show for Houston on February 5. Tabloid reports had suggested the league pursued her; she’s currently on a sold-out world tour behind the album 25.

Former US President Barack Obama, in his first interview since leaving office, warned about the dangers of irresponsible social media use and the resulting distortion of public understanding. Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, guest-edited by Prince Harry, Obama cautioned that online platforms can create “entirely different realities” where people become cocooned in information that reinforces their biases, contributing to social Balkanisation and the spread of misinformation. He urged leaders to help recreate a common online space that supports diverse voices without fragmenting society.

Obama suggested that face-to-face interaction remains essential to counteract extreme online views: while social media allows people with shared interests to convene, meeting offline—at pubs, places of worship or in neighbourhoods—reveals the complexity of individuals and builds common ground. Although he did not name his successor, Donald Trump—known for prolific Twitter use—Obama’s remarks implied concern about leaders and citizens alike relying on narrow information sources.

Reflecting on life after the presidency, Obama described mixed feelings upon leaving office: serenity at having completed a term and relief at personal freedoms, coupled with concern about unfinished work. He praised his wife Michelle for her partnership and cited Obamacare as a major achievement, noting that about 20 million previously uninsured Americans gained coverage. Optimistic about the future, he argued that problems are solvable if people engage, volunteer and participate in their communities, and he asserted that today’s world is healthier, wealthier, better educated and more tolerant than in the past.

Prince Harry, who also interviewed Obama in a light-hearted “lightning round,” focused his guest-editing on issues including the armed forces, mental health, youth crime and climate change. When asked about inviting Obama to his wedding to Meghan Markle, Harry kept the guest list a secret.

A U.S. Navy guided-missile destroyer, USS John S. McCain, collided with a commercial oil tanker near Singapore on August 21, sustaining a large gash to its port side that flooded berthing, machinery and communications compartments. Ten sailors remain missing and several were medevaced to Singapore; multinational search-and-rescue efforts by Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and the U.S. are ongoing. The incident prompted Adm. John Richardson, Chief of Naval Operations, to order an operational pause across fleets and a rapid, wide-ranging review of the 7th Fleet’s personnel, maintenance, equipment, operational tempo and surface warfare training. Adm. Phil Davidson, head of U.S. Fleet Forces, was named to lead the inquiry.

The McCain collision is the second major mishap involving U.S. 7th Fleet ships in two months: on June 17 the USS Fitzgerald struck a container ship off Japan, killing seven sailors and resulting in the removal of top Fitzgerald officers after investigations pointed to poor seamanship and watchstanding failures. Other recent incidents include the cruiser USS Antietam running aground in Tokyo Bay in February, causing an oil spill, and USS Lake Champlain colliding with a South Korean fishing vessel in May. These events have intensified internal scrutiny of training, certifications, maintenance, and career management within the fleet.

Adm. Richardson said investigators will consider all possibilities, including cyber intrusion or sabotage, though he stressed there is currently no evidence of hacking. The possibility has drawn attention from cyber experts and former military information-warfare personnel who note the regional operational environment—high traffic chokepoints like the Strait of Malacca and Singapore Strait—could complicate navigation and make ships vulnerable to interference. Some cybersecurity professionals suggested scenarios such as GPS spoofing or malware affecting navigation systems, citing previous spoofing incidents reported in other regions. Others, however, argue such attacks would likely affect many vessels in the area and that standard naval navigation procedures and lookouts should mitigate reliance on a single system.

The Navy’s expedited review aims to identify root causes and corrective actions quickly, with leaders seeking frequent updates as investigations continue into whether systemic problems, human error, technical failures, or other factors contributed to the McCain collision. The Associated Press contributed reporting.

A militant raid on the In Amenas gas plant in Algeria left at least 37 foreign hostages dead, including three Americans whose bodies were recovered by the FBI, and many others injured or missing. Algerian forces stormed the complex after militants—claimed by Mokhtar Belmokhtar and said to include fighters from several African countries and at least one Canadian—seized workers intending to move hostages to Mali. Prime Minister Abdelmalek Sellal defended the rapid, forceful military response as necessary to prevent a larger catastrophe and vowed to resist Islamist enclaves in the Sahara. Western governments expressed mixed reactions: Britain and France backed Algeria, while some criticized its harsh tactics and called for addressing underlying grievances fueling militancy.

Congress in 2011–2012 is on track to be the least productive post–World War II, enacting just 61 laws in 2012 and 90 in 2011 out of 3,914 introduced—under 2% became law—according to U.S. House Clerk records. The 112th Congress’s two-year total is the lowest in 65 years, even worse than President Truman’s so-called “do-nothing Congress.” By comparison, other low-output years, like 1995 (88 laws), were followed by rebounds; the 104th Congress produced 245 laws in 1996. Critics note many House-passed economic measures stalled in the Democratic-controlled Senate. When Democrats controlled Congress in the 111th, 258 laws passed in 2010 and 125 in 2009, including the health care law. The 112th’s stalemate included failure of the bipartisan “Super Committee” to agree on $1.2 trillion in deficit reduction and unresolved items: Bush tax cuts, a replacement for $109 billion in automatic cuts, drought relief, the farm bill, and postal reform. The legislative inertia correlates with record-low public approval: Gallup found just 10% of Americans approved of Congress, mirroring other polls showing approval as low as 9%.

President Trump told reporters he would beat Oprah Winfrey in a hypothetical 2020 matchup but doubted she would run. Speaking during an immigration meeting, he called Oprah “a lot of fun,” said he knows her well, and recalled appearing with his family on one of her final talk-show episodes. The exchange followed widespread discussion about Winfrey’s Golden Globes speech and reports that she is “intrigued by the idea” of a presidential bid, according to friend Gayle King and other associates. Media attention suggested Winfrey could disrupt the Democratic primary and present a strong challenge to Trump. Trump has praised Oprah previously on Twitter and once considered her an ideal running mate when he briefly contemplated a presidential run in 2000.

United Nations human rights experts have ruled that Ireland’s restrictive abortion laws violated the rights of Amanda Mellet, a Dublin woman who in 2011 was denied an abortion after doctors told her the fetus had a fatal congenital heart defect. The 29-page decision by the UN Human Rights Committee concluded that forcing Mellet to choose between carrying a non-viable pregnancy to term or travelling abroad for a termination amounted to discrimination and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. The panel said Ireland’s legal framework places the rights of an inviable fetus above those of the pregnant woman, an arbitrary imbalance that cannot be justified, and found the underlying criminal law discriminatory because it primarily burdens pregnant women with criminal liability.

The committee ordered Ireland to provide Mellet with an effective remedy, including financial compensation and access to psychological and state-supported bereavement services, and to prevent similar violations by amending domestic law — including, if necessary, the constitutional protection that equates the unborn child’s right to life with the mother’s. The ruling criticized barriers to clear medical information and the chilling effect on healthcare providers who fear criminal sanctions for discussing or facilitating abortion options. Ireland, which allows abortion only when a woman’s life is at risk, is not compelled to comply but faces mounting domestic and international pressure. Rights groups welcomed the decision; anti-abortion groups and church leaders condemned it. The government has indicated the matter will be considered by a citizens’ assembly and said changes would require constitutional amendment.

The Rich Earth Institute in Brattleboro, Vermont, is testing human urine as an alternative to chemical fertilizers. Since 2012 volunteers have donated hundreds to thousands of gallons of urine—about 3,000 gallons from 170 people last year—and the group hopes to collect 6,000 gallons this season. Urine is rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, nutrients plants need that are otherwise mined or synthesized. Field trials beginning in 2012 showed promising results: urine-treated hay fields yielded roughly double the production of unfertilized controls, prompting a USDA SARE grant and expansion to additional farms. International research, notably Swedish and Nepalese studies, supports urine’s fertilizer potential when combined with compost, sometimes matching or replacing mineral fertilizers. Rich Earth addresses safety concerns by sanitizing stored urine via solar pasteurization or warm greenhouse storage and is studying pharmaceutical residues in donated urine with university partners. Practical barriers include public “ick” factors and logistics of collection; urine-diverting toilets are touted as a scalable solution. Despite regulatory scrutiny and cultural resistance, proponents argue urine recycling can close nutrient loops and reduce environmental harm from conventional fertilizers.

In October Sen. Al Franken secured a strong amendment to the FY2010 Defense appropriations bill barring the government from contracting with companies that force employees to forgo court access for workplace sexual assault and related claims. The Senate approved it 68–30, and despite reconciliation rumors the provision survived largely unchanged. It bars contractors from restricting suits over assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, or negligent hiring practices, and preserves a Title VII provision allowing suits against both perpetrators and employers for contracts of $1 million or more. A narrow national-security waiver lets the Defense Secretary block a case that imperils safety—but only with a personal, public explanation to Congress. Separately, a Dallas woman, Lynda Darden, sued Halliburton alleging pregnancy discrimination after being fired in June 2009 following a transfer; her attorney Todd Kelly, known for representing sexual-assault plaintiffs against Halliburton/KBR, says the company poorly treats women. Darden seeks back and front pay, claiming her termination was a pretext for discrimination.

A gray two-piece dress worn by Vivien Leigh as Scarlett O’Hara in the 1939 classic Gone With the Wind sold for $137,000 at a Heritage Auctions sale in Beverly Hills, topping more than 150 items from the private collection of Jim (James) Tumblin. Tumblin, who worked for decades in Universal Studios’ hair and makeup department, first acquired the outfit in the early 1960s after spotting it on the floor at Western Costume Company where it was about to be discarded. He negotiated a $20 purchase after seeing a Selznick International Pictures label and “Scarlett production dress” written in ink. That modest buy helped seed a massive archive of Hollywood memorabilia—Tumblin amassed more than 300,000 artifacts over the years and toured the collection nationwide.

The auction featured a wide array of evocative film pieces. Other notable sales included a straw hat worn by Leigh for $52,500; Clark Gable’s gray wool trousers and jacket, worn as Rhett Butler during the door-kicking scene, for $55,000; and a black bonnet worn by both Leigh and Olivia de Havilland for $30,000. Additional lots highlighted the film’s cultural footprint: Leslie Howard’s tattered Confederate uniform, a presentation script signed by producer David O. Selznick that once belonged to Hattie McDaniel, and Sidney Howard’s typewriter. Some costumes have faded or required restoration—Tumblin noted the Scarlett dress’s original slate blue-gray has mellowed to light gray—but provenance and screen use kept bidders engaged.

Tumblin, who has long promoted Hollywood history through exhibitions and loans to institutions, said selling the collection will allow others to see the pieces in museums; he retains Vivien Leigh’s Oscar. The sale underscores enduring public interest in one of cinema’s most iconic films.

On the eve of George Washington’s birthday, AP writer Jesse Washington explores why the surname Washington is disproportionately African-American. The 2000 U.S. Census counted 163,036 people with that name; about 90 percent were black, far higher than any other common surname. The pattern traces to slavery and Reconstruction, when newly freed blacks adopted surnames. Some historians suggest freed people chose Washington out of pride in the nation and its first president, whose fame and published will—freeing his enslaved people after his wife’s death—were widely known. Others argue the name could preserve ties to powerful plantation families or reflect naming after an ancestor’s owner or plantation. Yet scholars caution that most enslaved people did not necessarily carry their owners’ surnames; George Washington’s own records often listed slaves by first name only, and only a handful bore his last name.

The article recounts Washington’s complex relationship with slavery: he inherited and acquired many slaves, treated them relatively better by contemporary standards, grew opposed to slavery late in life, and freed those he enslaved in his will. Historians note that naming choices were varied—some freed people picked names out of admiration, for pragmatic ties, or simply at random (as Booker T. Washington later recounted). The surname’s racial perception affects lives today: many black Washingtons assume the name is exclusively African-American; white Washingtons sometimes face misidentification or subtle bias. Studies show “black-sounding” names can reduce job callbacks. Whether coincidence, strategy, or homage, the prevalence of Washington among African-Americans encapsulates the contradictions of American history and identity.

Facebook has effectively blocked all mention of the rival social network Tsu.co across its platforms, including Facebook itself, Facebook Messenger and Instagram, removing millions of posts and warning users that links to Tsu are “unsafe.” Beginning Sept. 25, Facebook began rejecting posts or messages that contained “tsu.co” and retroactively deleted or disabled access to many existing posts that referenced the site—Tsu says the total removed exceeded 9–10 million posts. Users who simply type “Tsu” without the “.co” can sometimes get through, but any direct link is blocked.

Tsu is a small, invite-driven social network that shares most advertising revenue with its users: the company keeps about 10%, the creator gets 45%, and the rest is distributed among the chain of inviters. That revenue-sharing model incentivizes users to post, recruit and drive traffic to Tsu pages—behavior Facebook characterizes as spammy. Facebook’s official stance is that developers and outside services may not financially incentivize sharing on Facebook because it encourages mass, low-quality posting and harms user experience. Facebook says it would lift the block if Tsu prevented users from simultaneously posting to both platforms.

Tsu’s founder Sebastian Sobczak and many users call Facebook’s move anti-competitive, arguing the ban targets a business model that could threaten Facebook’s ad-dominated revenue. Affected creators—from photographers and models to hobbyists—report lost content and reach; one user said some 7,500 posts mentioning Tsu were deleted. Tsu counters it operates similarly to services like YouTube, paying creators based on ad revenue generated by their content rather than paying for direct posting to Facebook. The dispute highlights the power major platforms wield over what users can share and how smaller rivals’ growth can be stifled when platform policies and enforcement collide with emergent business models.

Former professional wrestler Bret “The Hitman” Hart announced on Instagram that he is battling prostate cancer. The 58-year-old WWE Hall of Famer, who survived a 2002 stroke and has endured other health challenges, said he will undergo surgery in the coming days. In his message Hart acknowledged fear and hesitation but vowed to fight “with one shield and one sword,” driven by determination, fury for life, and the love that has sustained him. Hart’s long and decorated wrestling career includes five world heavyweight championships in the WWF/WWE and two in WCW, plus five WWE U.S. heavyweight title reigns. He retired after a concussion in 1999 and is a prominent member of Canada’s Hart wrestling family: his father, Stu Hart, was a noted wrestler and trainer, and his brother Owen Hart died in a 1999 accident when he fell while being lowered into the ring at Kemper Arena. The announcement drew attention to Hart’s resilience and legacy in professional wrestling as he prepares for his next confrontation—this time with cancer.

Brandon McGraw, a 33-year-old Marine based at Camp Lejeune, died while skydiving in Euroa, Victoria, Australia, during a trip his wife won on The Ellen DeGeneres Show. Cherilyn McGraw, a special education teacher, had earned the pair a trip to Australia by winning a contest in January; they finally traveled in mid-November. Cherilyn completed a tandem skydive safely, then Brandon — an experienced jumper and veteran of Afghanistan and Iraq who enjoyed extreme sports — performed a solo jump with Euroa Skydive.
