Witnesses described his descent as initially flawless: he floated under a good canopy for three to four minutes. As he came in to land, however, his parachute suddenly exhibited unexplained complications, veering left and right before he slammed into the ground. He went into cardiac arrest and was pronounced dead at the scene around 12:30 p.m. The Euroa Skydive school, which had operated for 30 years without a fatality, is investigating the incident. Friends and family mourned publicly: Cherilyn posted a final photo of Brandon smiling on the plane and paid tribute to him as her “hero” and “angel,” noting he was happy doing what he loved. Military officials and colleagues described him as an extreme-sports enthusiast with many jumps to his credit. Authorities continue to probe the cause of the parachute failure and the sudden complications that ended his descent.

The document is a concentrated, multi-voice critique of Newt Gingrich’s 2012 presidential bid, arguing he is ill-suited to represent conservative principles or win a general election. Former Reagan administration officials and conservative commentators charge Gingrich with repeatedly attacking Ronald Reagan and undermining Reagan-era policies—especially on confronting Soviet expansion in the Third World—despite later claiming Reagan’s mantle. A March 21, 1986 floor statement is cited in which Gingrich called Reagan’s efforts “failing” and labeled administration strategies “pathetically incompetent,” a record critics say exposes Gingrich as anti-Reagan. 

Prominent conservatives—including Tom DeLay, Bob Dole, National Review editors, Ann Coulter, and others—warn that Gingrich’s temperament, erratic leadership as Speaker, personal scandals, and transactional ties to Washington (notably payments from Freddie Mac) make him a risky nominee. They portray him as a political huckster, likening him to Bill Clinton in charmlessness and moral opportunism: skillful at rhetorical attacks and media performance but lacking steady executive experience, broad electability, and consistent small-government credentials. Critics contrast Gingrich with Mitt Romney and Rick Santorum, arguing Romney’s executive record and Santorum’s statewide appeal better position them to govern and win. 

Gingrich’s debate strengths—attacking the media and rallying conservative anger—are viewed as insufficient for a general election, where he would need to persuade independents and withstand counterattacks. Conservatives also highlight policy inconsistencies: Gingrich’s past positions on health-care mandates, immigration, and entitlements have shifted, undermining claims of ideological purity. The overall conclusion from these conservative framings is that nominating Gingrich would be a high-stakes gamble, risking not only electoral defeat but broader conservative policy goals.

Jennifer Aniston introduced new boyfriend Justin Theroux to close friends, including Courteney Cox and Chelsea Handler, at a small party last Friday, a source told PEOPLE. The couple, who met last fall while filming Wanderlust, are "doing great"; Theroux is described as edgier than Aniston’s usual partners. Separately, reports of tension between Aniston and longtime friend Courteney Cox surfaced in Us Weekly, alleging Aniston disapproves of Cox’s behavior following her trial separation from David Arquette—specifically Cox socializing with Cougar Town co-stars and delaying divorce paperwork, which reminds Aniston of her own ex, Brad Pitt. Meanwhile, Brad Pitt and Cox were seen together at a birthday dinner for manager Cynthia Pett-Dante at Beso, where they hugged, chatted and appeared relaxed and happy, according to an onlooker. The gathering included other celebrities and seemed cordial, with no reported awkwardness.

U.S. leaders and policy experts warned that avoiding the “fiscal cliff” at year’s end will require political compromise, balanced measures and urgent action to prevent damaging economic fallout. IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde urged a “balanced solution” combining revenue increases and spending cuts, warning that failing to reach a deal would erode confidence and prompt rapid market declines. She favored a comprehensive fix over a short-term patch.

Former Sen. Alan Simpson and Erskine Bowles, co-chairs of the Simpson-Bowles commission, similarly stressed that higher taxes on the wealthy alone won’t solve the deficit. Simpson predicted top rates will likely rise; Bowles noted restoring Clinton-era rates would raise roughly $400 billion over ten years — small relative to the annual trillion-dollar deficit — and emphasized the need for spending restraint, particularly slowing healthcare cost growth to match economic growth. Bowles warned that going over the cliff could cost about 2 million jobs and push unemployment toward 9 percent, calling such an outcome a disaster.

Sen. Bob Corker suggested Republicans may need to concede the tax fight to President Obama—preserving current rates for about 98 percent of Americans while letting rates rise for the top 2 percent—to focus GOP leverage on spending and entitlement reform next year, including using the debt ceiling debate to press for concessions.

Meanwhile, political maneuvering and potential candidacies surfaced: Newt Gingrich and others predicted Hillary Clinton would be virtually unbeatable for the 2016 Democratic nomination if she runs. Newark Mayor Cory Booker said he’s weighing a 2013 gubernatorial bid against Gov. Chris Christie and a possible Senate run. Overall, commentators signaled cautious optimism that negotiations—led by Obama and House Speaker John Boehner—have begun to “tango,” giving some hope a deal can be reached.

A CDC review of 1,075 contact lens–related infections reported to the FDA from 2005–2015 found that unsafe lens use and poor hygiene are causing serious, sometimes long-term eye injuries. Nearly one in five reported infections resulted in eye damage — including corneal scarring, reduced vision or the need for corneal transplant — and over 10% required emergency or urgent care. Even “minor” infections can be painful and highly disruptive, with some patients needing daily doctor visits or hourly eye-drop treatments.

Researchers and eye-care experts emphasize that contact lenses are medical devices that require proper fitting and care. Common, easily avoidable risky behaviors cited in more than a quarter of reports include sleeping in lenses, wearing lenses longer than recommended, “topping off” solutions (adding new solution to old), using tap water to clean or store lenses, sharing contacts, and failing to replace lens cases regularly. Sleeping in lenses raises infection risk six- to eightfold. The CDC and professional groups urge wearers to follow simple precautions: have annual eye exams, buy lenses from reputable sources with a prescription, never share lenses, use only appropriate disinfecting solution, toss and replace lens cases every three months, and replace lenses on the schedule prescribed.

The report was released ahead of Contact Lens Health Week to promote safe practices. While serious infections are relatively uncommon among the roughly 41 million U.S. contact lens users, the findings underscore the preventable nature of most problems and the importance of vigilance to protect vision.

In Chillicothe, Ohio—a small Rust Belt town of about 21,000—at least six women have vanished in just over a year, and four bodies have been recovered, many dumped in waterways outside town. The victims share troubling commonalities: most struggled with drug addiction, often turned to prostitution to support their habits, and some knew one another, fueling fears that a serial killer or human traffickers may be targeting vulnerable women. Local law enforcement, county sheriffs, state investigators and FBI analysts have formed a task force to investigate, compiling profiles and scouring patterns such as the consistent disposal of bodies along creeks and rivers. Families and friends, frustrated and grieving, criticize police responses as slow or dismissive, saying earlier missing-person reports were not taken seriously. Several women’s disappearances began in May 2014 with Charlotte Trego and Tameka Lynch; Lynch’s body was later found in Paint Creek and ruled likely due to multiple drug overdoses, though her family suspects foul play. Subsequent disappearances and deaths include Wanda Lemons, still missing; Shasta Himelrick, whose death was ruled a suicide though friends doubt it; Timberly Clayton, found shot and for which a convicted sex offender is a named suspect; and Tiffany Sayre, discovered wrapped in a sheet in a drainage pipe and ruled a homicide. The task force has received more than 100 tips and is reexamining earlier cases previously labeled suicides or overdoses. Residents report rising fear, accuse authorities of neglecting low-income, addicted women, and worry the pattern may extend to nearby cities. Families continue vigils and demand answers and justice as investigations proceed.

Public Health England (PHE) is investigating a UK case of multidrug-resistant gonorrhea in a man who acquired the infection during sex in Southeast Asia. This strain showed high-level resistance to the standard first-line dual therapy—azithromycin and ceftriaxone—marking the first global report of gonorrhea resistant to both drugs. The patient, who later sought care in the UK, reportedly had a regular partner at home who has tested negative so far; PHE is tracing other sexual contacts to limit onward transmission.

Gonorrhea, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and transmitted through unprotected vaginal, oral, or anal sex, can be asymptomatic, especially in women and some men, or cause discharge, painful urination and bleeding. If untreated it may lead to pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, and can be passed to infants during childbirth. Health officials say the infection exhibited resistance to most commonly used antibiotics, though analysis suggests one remaining antibiotic might still be effective; the patient is being treated and follow-up testing is planned.

Experts have long warned of rising antimicrobial resistance in gonorrhea, including a 2015 azithromycin-resistant outbreak in the UK. Officials including PHE’s Dr. Gwenda Hughes emphasize enhanced surveillance and partner tracing to contain resistant strains. Sexual health leaders warned that cuts to public health funding and sexual health service reductions risk worsening the situation by weakening prevention, testing, and treatment capacity just as more resistant gonorrhea strains emerge.

Sandra Bullock was not blindsided by Jesse James’s quick engagement to tattoo artist Kat Von D. Sources say Jesse gave Sandra a heads-up before the news broke; she isn’t thrilled but has accepted that he’s moving on. Sandra’s main focus remains caring for her adopted son Louis and maintaining stability for him. Though she and Jesse aren’t close, they keep lines of communication open, and Sandra was prepared for the announcement. Jesse praised Kat as his best friend and love, calling 2010 the best year of his life. Kat and Jesse, who began dating after his split from Bullock, plan to balance homes between Los Angeles and Austin.

Cheryl Strayed’s memoir and film Wild—subtitled “From Lost to Found on the Pacific Crest Trail”—have inspired many to see long-distance hiking as a route to personal healing. Strayed’s candid account of hiking roughly 1,100 miles while recovering from addiction, divorce, and grief resonated widely, boosting book sales, earning Hollywood attention, and drawing large numbers to the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT). The Pacific Crest Trail Association (PCTA) reports sharp increases in interest since the movie’s release—web traffic jumped dramatically and permit requests rose—contributing to a multi-year surge in long-distance hikers. Historically rare, thru-hikes have climbed from hundreds to thousands annually; in recent seasons more than 1,000 attempted the full route, and in peak years permit systems fill rapidly, yielding roughly 3,000 northbound starts within a narrow season window.

This surge raises concerns about preparedness, environmental impact, and community strain. Strayed’s success can inadvertently encourage “deliberate ineptitude”—people setting out unprepared, hoping the trail will fix life problems. Inexperienced hikers may endanger themselves, degrade fragile desert ecosystems, create new campsites, leave human waste, and impose costs through rescues and logistics. Even experienced folks can act poorly, harming the trail’s reputation. In response, the PCTA instituted a daily permit quota in 2015 to disperse starts and limit damage; volunteers and managers monitor impacts and warn of potential interventions like shelters if degradation worsens.

The PCTA and Strayed promote responsible hiking via campaigns like #responsiblywild, emphasizing Leave No Trace, water protection, waste management, and safe campfires. Practical advice remains crucial: good timing to avoid dangerous snow or floods, adequate budgeting (a thru-hike can cost around $6,000), proper gear choices, and building competence before attempting the PCT. While the trail continues to offer transformative experiences to many, advocates urge prospective hikers to prepare, respect communities and ecosystems, and act as ambassadors of the trail.

United States Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, 79, was found dead in his room at Cibolo Creek Ranch near Marfa, Texas, on February 13, 2016. Presidio County Judge Cinderela Guevara, who was notified by the sheriff and remotely pronounced him deceased at 1:52 p.m., said his heart had stopped during sleep and that the death certificate would list a natural cause—likely myocardial infarction (heart attack). Guevara consulted with Scalia’s personal physician, who reported seeing the Justice earlier in the week for a shoulder injury and other chronic ailments; after that conversation she determined an autopsy was unnecessary. Scalia had told companions on Friday evening he felt unwell and retired early; he missed breakfast and lunch and was later discovered unresponsive. His remains were discreetly transported overnight under escort by Texas Department of Public Safety troopers and U.S. Marshals to Sunset Funeral Home in El Paso, arriving around 3:30 a.m. Sunday. The funeral home embalmed the body as required by Texas law before interstate transport and is collecting information for the official death certificate; Guevara will sign the document once details are complete. Scalia, appointed by President Ronald Reagan and the court’s longest-serving justice since 1986, had been on a hunting and relaxation trip with a friend from Washington. His death prompted immediate national attention and statements about the vacancy on the Supreme Court; President Obama said he intended to nominate a successor before his term ended.

In June 2009 a mother of a fourth-grader at Miramonte Elementary discovered disturbing letters allegedly written by teacher’s aide Areceli Luisjuan to her 11‑year‑old son. One note expressed romantic feelings — “When I was writing this letter, I was crying… I like when you put your arm around my shoulder… Don’t tell nobody about this!” — and was signed “Sad Girl.” The mother found a crying drawing and a cell number in her son’s room, confronted school staff and later met with the aide, the teacher and an assistant principal; she says Luisjuan admitted writing the letters and likened her affection to a grandmother’s. The mother alleges initial complaints to the school and sheriff’s deputies were not taken seriously. L.A. Unified says Luisjuan no longer works for the district, though officials have struggled to locate records of the incident. The revelation came amid a broader criminal probe at Miramonte after veteran teacher Mark Berndt was arrested on multiple lewd conduct counts, accused of binding, blindfolding and sexually abusing students and photographing them, and of feeding students semen as part of a “tasting game.” A second teacher, Martin Springer, was charged with fondling a seven‑year‑old. Attorneys for victims allege additional staff may have been complicit. The district temporarily reassigned the entire Miramonte staff while investigators continue their review.

The document examines Donald Trump’s atypical candidacy and the question of his motive, arguing that unlike past major-party nominees who clearly sought the presidency, Trump’s behavior often clashes with any rational path to winning. He is historically unpopular outside a core base, has become more divisive rather than pivoting to the center, and sometimes fails to perform routine nominee tasks — such as contacting major donors. Two possible explanations are offered: incompetence or an alternative, shrewd plan to profit from his political persona. The campaign has already damaged aspects of his branding business as clients distance themselves, undermining the traditional revenue Trump once gained from licensing his name. Reporters suggest he may be exploring a different avenue: launching a media venture built around his devoted audience. Sources say he’s discussed creating a “mini-media conglomerate” beyond Trump Productions LLC, possibly with input from Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, who see a monetizable loyalist base underserved by existing conservative outlets. While spokespeople deny any active plans, Trump’s mastery of the attention economy — dominating coverage, leveraging social media, and often sidestepping or punishing traditional outlets — makes such a project plausible. The document also includes an Associated Press-style account of President Trump’s Syria troop-withdrawal decision, portraying it as a hasty choice influenced by a phone call with Turkish President Erdoğan that surprised and alarmed U.S. advisers. Finally, the piece draws a cultural parallel to the 1992 mockumentary Bob Roberts, portraying its titular media-savvy, populist candidate as a prescient template for Trump: a charismatic, wealthy celebrity who manipulates media and rallies populist resentment, illustrating how entertainment, outrage, and political ambition can blend into a lucrative, demagogic brand.

In November 2011 a head-on crash on Flat Shoals Road in south Fulton County killed 35-year-old Glen Walker and 16-year-old Joshua Jenkins and left Sandra Walker with a traumatic brain injury; two Walker children were not seriously hurt. Authorities say Tamara Matthews’ minivan veered into oncoming traffic, causing the collision that also killed her own teenage son. Nearly two and a half years later Matthews pled guilty to misdemeanor homicide by vehicle and failure to maintain lane. A judge sentenced her to 36 months of probation and 500 hours of community service, directing that some service honor the lives of her son and Glen Walker. In court Matthews apologized; during a tearful victim-impact statement Sandra Walker forgave her and embraced Matthews afterward, saying she wanted her to know she understood Matthews was suffering too. Separate brief local coverage noted an unrelated Surfside Beach motorcycle crash that injured two people.

Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor issued an emergency order late Tuesday temporarily exempting a small group of Catholic nuns, the Little Sisters of the Poor, from part of the Affordable Care Act that requires employer health plans to cover contraceptives. Acting on the nuns’ appeal hours before the mandate’s New Year’s Day effective date, Sotomayor gave the government until Friday to respond; her stay applies only to these nuns and other nonprofits on the same Christian Brothers Employee Benefit Trust, not to the law itself. The Little Sisters and their lawyers argued they would face severe fines if forced to comply and contended the administration’s “accommodation” — a self-certification allowing insurers to provide contraceptive coverage without direct employer payment — still violates their religious beliefs. The order comes amid multiple legal challenges by religious organizations and closely held corporations, including Hobby Lobby and Conestoga Wood, over whether employers with religious objections must facilitate contraception coverage. The Supreme Court will hear related corporate cases in March, and the administration has defended the mandate as protecting women’s access to contraception.

New research shows a powerful new driver of Arctic sea-ice loss: warm Atlantic waters intruding and mixing upward beneath the ice, a process researchers call “Atlantification.” Long-term mooring arrays, drifting sensors and satellites reveal that warm Atlantic currents, delivered via a Gulf Stream offshoot, have increasingly risen and mixed into surface layers across the Eurasian basin. Historically, a cold halocline layer (CHL)—a fresher, colder surface cap—kept Atlantic warmth trapped below and preserved multi-year summer ice, especially north of Siberia. Over roughly the last decade this barrier has weakened or vanished in winter in many places; one mooring recorded the Atlantic layer’s top rising from 140 m to 85 m in a decade. The result is more vertical mixing, warmer winter surface waters, and much-reduced summer ice persistence: regions that formerly lost less than a month of ice annually now remain ice-free more than three months. Across the Arctic Ocean, sea ice extent has fallen about 13% per decade since satellite records began, and thickness has declined by roughly 1.7 m since the 1970s. The study finds that whereas 2000s melt was mainly air-driven, ocean heat now contributes about equally, creating a positive feedback loop of less summer ice → weaker stratification → more ocean heat at the surface → further ice loss. Freshwater inputs from rivers and permafrost thaw could modulate this trend, but winds might disperse that freshwater. Atlantification also has ecological and climatic implications—altering nutrient mixing, primary productivity, ocean chemistry and potentially regional weather and geopolitics as the Arctic shifts toward a more Atlantic-like state.

Terry Wayne Ward’s funeral in Crown Point was a lively, fitting farewell that matched the humor and character captured in the viral obituary his daughter Jean Lahm wrote. Ward, 71, who died Jan. 23 after a stroke, was remembered not with a somber, formulaic notice but with a warm, witty portrait that reflected the man himself: a onetime AT&T worker who amassed “roughly 3,000 rolls of black electrical tape” and joked about being colorblind while faced with a tangle of wires. Lahm, who works at Geisen Funeral Home and surprised family by writing the humorous obituary, used anecdotes and laughter to celebrate a father who “couldn't give a damn about most material things” and who lived to make others laugh. 

At the service, Lahm shared stories—like spotting her dad working roadside at a substation—and encouraged attendees to remember his lighthearted spirit. Mourners laughed, toasted with Heinekens, and gathered afterward in the reception center to reminisce. The obituary struck a chord far beyond the funeral: strangers sent condolences and flowers, an online guestbook amassed more than 700 signatures, and people who’d never met Ward expressed that they wished they had. Lahm noted how humor helped the family heal and how the obituary shifted readers’ focus from how he died to how he lived. 

The piece argues that obituaries should define lives rather than merely list facts. Ward’s sendoff—both the obituary and the celebratory funeral—served as a reminder that honoring personality and shared laughter can be a powerful, restorative way to grieve and remember.

Julian Assange, founder of WikiLeaks, told RT in an extensive interview that the material his site has published is only a fraction of what exists and that far more damaging secrets remain hidden. He argued many revelations in 2010 exposed real events people did not know about and urged skepticism toward mainstream media, which he says often collaborates with state and corporate interests to censor or sanitize information. Assange said WikiLeaks released secret and confidential documents but not the most sensitive “top secret” material, which he believes still exists. On the Middle East uprisings he saw genuine change in places like Egypt but labeled Libya’s unrest as driven by distant state actors. He condemned social networks, especially Facebook, as massive surveillance tools that aggregate personal data accessible to U.S. intelligence via built-in interfaces, criticizing Google and Yahoo similarly. Discussing Guantanamo cables, he defended the timing of releases amid operational constraints and accused the U.S. of “people laundering” detainees to avoid legal protections. He criticized media partners—particularly The Guardian and The New York Times—for over-redaction and protecting commercial interests over public right to know. Facing extradition pressures from Sweden and a U.S. grand jury, Assange called ignorance the “number one enemy” and blamed poor media for enabling wars through misinformation.

What began as a routine family boating trip off Noank, Connecticut, on June 26 turned into a nightmare for Clare Shaw and her family when their 8-month-old Shiba Inu puppy, Ryder, slipped out of his harness and fell into the ocean. The family and local responders searched extensively—backtracking along the shoreline for hours, coordinating with the Coast Guard, and enlisting people on shore—but they could not find the little dog. Convinced he couldn’t swim and likely lost, the Shaw family returned home distraught, packed Ryder’s things and lit a candle in his empty crate while coping with the possible loss.

Refusing to give up hope, Shaw posted to Facebook asking if anyone had seen Ryder. That post was shared nearly 100 times on community lost-and-found pages. Meanwhile, three friends—Phil Q. Bigelow, Patrick Jullarine and Tommy Nahornick—were out fishing when they spotted a small, frightened dog in the water about a half-mile out. They maneuvered their boat to the pup, and Tommy scooped him aboard with a single reach. They dried and rehydrated him, nicknamed him “Nemo” for being lost and found, and made him comfortable with food, a collar and toys while they tried to locate his owners.

Bigelow emphasized they were simply in the right place at the right time and didn’t consider themselves heroes. An equine veterinarian later connected the dots between the rescue and Shaw’s Facebook plea by linking two community posts, allowing the reunited owners and puppy to be brought back together. Shaw expressed immense gratitude for the community, social media’s reach, and everyone who shared, prayed and helped bring Ryder home—calling his safe return “a true miracle.”

Italy's highest court was set to decide the fate of Amanda Knox and her former Italian boyfriend Raffaele Sollecito in the long-running, high-profile murder case of British student Meredith Kercher, found dead in the Perugia apartment she shared with Knox on Nov. 2, 2007. Kercher had been sexually assaulted and her throat slashed. Knox and Sollecito were convicted in 2009, freed by an appellate court in 2011, had those acquittals voided by the Court of Cassation in 2013, and were reconvicted in Florence in 2014—Knox to 28 ½ years and Sollecito to 25—together with finding they acted in concert with Rudy Guede, who is serving 16 years.

Several outcomes were possible from the highest court’s review. If the Florence convictions were upheld, Florence prosecutors would issue orders to execute the sentences. Sollecito, who remained in Italy, would likely be taken into custody promptly. Knox, a U.S. citizen living freely in the United States who has said she will never return willingly to Italy, would prompt a more complex process: prosecutors would request extradition through the Justice Ministry, which would decide whether to seek her return. Although Italy and the U.S. have an extradition treaty and no formal legal bar to a request, extradition decisions can involve political discretion. Italy might alternatively propose Knox serve any sentence in the United States. The timing of any extradition request could take months.

Alternatively, the court could order a new appeals trial, sending the case back to reconsider specific aspects; Italy’s system has seen repeated appellate rounds before. The Court of Cassation must issue written reasoning for such a decision within 90 days, and no new trial date can be set until that reasoning is released. Less likely but possible is an outright acquittal by the high court—effectively closing criminal proceedings against Knox and Sollecito, restoring travel freedoms (including Knox’s ability to return to Italy without arrest and Sollecito’s passport), and ending the case.

A recent magazine interview with a Florence appellate juror claiming insufficient evidence and suggesting the verdict was not unanimous drew attention, but such internal deliberations are sealed, unanimity is not required, and the interview would likely have little legal impact on the Court of Cassation’s deliberations.

Everybody’s Fine is a sentimental, Americanized remake of Giuseppe Tornatore’s Stanno Tutti Bene that flounders under artificial emotion and clumsy characterization. Robert De Niro plays Frank, a widowed, working-class retiree who, despite a lung condition and being counseled to rest, takes a cross‑country trip by bus and train to surprise his four grown children—without calling ahead. Each child, played by Kate Beckinsale, Sam Rockwell, Drew Barrymore and an absent New York artist, maintains a happy facade that collapses under scrutiny: they’re secretly unhappy and deceptive, hiding lives that disappoint their demanding father. Director–writer Kirk Jones strips subtlety from the original and replaces it with syrupy scoring and broad sentiment; the film’s portrayal of American life feels inauthentic, and Jones’s outsider treatment of U.S. culture is often awkward. De Niro’s earnestness can’t fully rescue a script that traffics in predictable revelations and thinly sketched family dynamics. Visually polished but emotionally hollow, the movie ultimately delivers a banal moral—truth matters—after a long, unconvincing buildup.

Twitter has sued the U.S. government to block a demand that it reveal the identity of the operator of @ALT_uscis, a prominent “alt” account that emerged after President Trump’s inauguration to criticize immigration policy and other administration actions. The company filed the suit in federal court in San Francisco after U.S. Customs and Border Protection served an administrative summons seeking the account’s login records, IP addresses, phone number and mailing address. Twitter says the summons—issued under a statute tied to import duties—lacks proper legal authority and that forcing disclosure would chill anonymous, pseudonymous political speech protected by the First Amendment.

The lawsuit names DHS Secretary John Kelly, acting CBP Commissioner Kevin McAleenan and two CBP agents as defendants. Twitter informed the account holder of the summons and plans to contest the order; the ACLU has pledged to join the defense, calling anonymous political dissent a “bedrock American value.” Twitter and DHS declined further comment; CBP did not discuss pending litigation. The alt-government accounts, including @ALT_uscis, have claimed insider perspectives and alleged misconduct by immigration agencies. Observers note the government’s request is unusual in non-criminal, non-national-security cases, and experts say the summons may be an improper use of customs law to unmask a critic.

The High Court has blocked the extradition of Lauri Love, a British-Finnish student accused of hacking into multiple US government and intelligence agency systems between 2012 and 2013. Lord Chief Justice Ian Burnett and Mr Justice Ouseley ruled extradition would be "oppressive" given Love’s medical vulnerabilities—Asperger syndrome and severe depression—and the substantial risk he would attempt suicide if sent to US custody, where he might face solitary confinement and inadequate mental-health safeguards. The judges noted that prosecuting Love in the UK would not be oppressive and urged the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) to pursue domestic prosecution with assistance from US authorities, stressing the gravity of the alleged offences and harm to victims.

The decision, greeted with cheers in court, overturns an earlier magistrates’ ruling and a 2016 home secretary extradition order. Love and his supporters argued repeatedly that extradition would be life-threatening; psychiatrists and evidence about US prison procedures informed the court’s concern. Love said the ruling could set an important precedent for how neurodiverse and mentally ill defendants are treated, and that he hoped others in similar positions would be tried at home. Liberty and other human-rights advocates welcomed the judgment as recognition of vulnerability and family ties, calling it shameful that Love and his family endured the ordeal.

The CPS has 14 days to decide whether to seek leave to appeal to the UK Supreme Court. Legal commentators say the ruling will force UK and US prosecutors to more carefully weigh where to try cases of concurrent jurisdiction, paying greater attention to defendants’ connections to the UK.

Texas’s new “campus carry” law (SB 11), signed by Gov. Greg Abbott, allows licensed individuals to carry concealed handguns into university buildings, dorms, classrooms and other spaces at public colleges and universities beginning August 1, 2016 (community colleges in 2017). The law makes Texas the eighth state with such a mandate and limits institutions’ ability to enact blanket bans; schools may only designate certain locations gun-free. The measure sparked immediate resistance at the University of Texas (UT), where faculty, students, staff, parents and alumni formed Gun Free UT and gathered petitions and social-media support opposing campus carry. Nearly 200 UT faculty pledged to refuse guns in their classrooms; petitions gathered thousands of signatures.

Critics — including UT faculty such as English professor Lisa Moore and economist Daniel S. Hamermesh — argue the law threatens campus safety, academic freedom and classroom dynamics. Moore, who teaches gay and lesbian studies, recounts past incidents of intimidation and a semester when a disruptive student required an armed guard; she worries that the presence of concealed weapons will chill discussion of controversial topics (religion, sexuality, feminism, abortion, transgender issues), push professors to avoid debate or ban student interaction, and make vulnerable students feel unsafe. Some instructors say they may restrict class formats, hand out grades to avoid confrontation, or dismiss class rather than risk confronting an armed student. Hamermesh, a retired professor contracted to teach large classes, resigned from teaching to avoid the increased perceived risk and said campus carry could harm faculty recruitment and the university’s reputation.

Others, like UT spokesman Gary Susswein, note the university is consulting stakeholders to craft implementation policies. Opponents emphasize that increased firearms do not necessarily reduce violence and that responsibility for response should remain with law enforcement. The debate has intensified following recent campus shootings elsewhere and has prompted some faculty to consider relocation or civil disobedience (e.g., posting “no guns” signs), raising questions about how higher education will balance legal mandates, safety, free speech and pedagogy.

A wave of Middle East and international developments centers on regional unrest, Israel’s security concerns, and global reactions to Syria and Iran. Turkish Prime Minister accused Syrian President Assad of “state terrorism” as rebels claimed to have downed a Syrian fighter jet and hackers allied with Damascus struck Al-Jazeera. Egypt’s President Morsi urged Assad to go and criticized Israel’s commitment to Palestinian peace, while China signaled support for a “political transition” in Syria. Jordan’s Muslim Brotherhood vowed mass protests for reforms. In Gaza-related news, an Islamist extremist group said Hamas arrested 20 members amid rocket-fire crackdowns. In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Iran’s possible nuclear capability dwarfs other threats, citing media reports of accelerated Iranian nuclear work and intensifying domestic debate over potential military action despite U.S. calls for diplomacy. The Israeli cabinet moved to streamline decisions; security drills and home-front preparedness increased. Other Israeli items: Netanyahu cut short a security meeting over a leak, the IDF began evacuating Migron caravans, and a Home Front Command drill was planned at Hadassah Hospital. U.S. Democrats removed wording naming Jerusalem as Israel’s capital from their platform.

Media Rights Capital (MRC) and Netflix have responded to new sexual misconduct allegations against Kevin Spacey stemming from his time on House of Cards. A CNN report published multiple accounts from current and former crew members who described a pattern of inappropriate behavior by Spacey toward predominantly young, male staff. Among those who spoke anonymously, a former production assistant accused Spacey of putting his hands down the assistant’s pants while driving him to set and later cornering and touching him in the actor’s trailer. Other crewers described repeated nonconsensual touching—shoulder massages from behind, stomach touches, pulling hands toward Spacey’s crotch—and crude sexual comments on set. Some witnesses said the conduct was widely observed but rarely reported because employees feared retaliation or losing jobs.

MRC acknowledged a prior 2012 complaint about Spacey and said immediate action was taken then, including Spacey participating in training; the company said no further complaints had been made to them until now. In response to the recent disclosures, MRC established an anonymous complaint hotline, provided crisis counselors and sexual-harassment legal advisors, suspended production and said it will continue to investigate any formal claims. Netflix said it sent a representative to set, is collaborating with MRC, suspended production during a review, and reported being aware of one five-year-old incident that had been resolved.

The CNN revelations follow Anthony Rapp’s BuzzFeed allegation that Spacey made a sexual advance toward him when Rapp was 14. Spacey apologized to Rapp while denying memory of the encounter and publicly announced he is gay—a move that drew criticism. Spacey’s representatives later said he is seeking evaluation and treatment; his publicist and talent agency have since severed ties. Production on House of Cards was suspended and its sixth season designated the show’s last as the industry confronts broader sexual-misconduct reckonings.

TransCanada Corp. responded to President Barack Obama’s November denial of the Keystone XL pipeline permit by launching two legal actions: a NAFTA Chapter 11 arbitration claim seeking more than US$15 billion in damages and a federal suit in Houston arguing the permit denial exceeded presidential constitutional powers. The company said it will also record a C$2.5–2.9 billion after-tax writedown in the fourth quarter tied to the decision. TransCanada contends the U.S. rejection was arbitrary, politically motivated and unprecedented for a cross-border Canadian pipeline, arguing its application met the same criteria used to approve similar projects and that activists politicized the issue to influence politicians’ environmental credentials. Lawyers for TransCanada characterize the US$15 billion as an initial estimate of lost asset value after billions invested in infrastructure intended to transport Canadian oil sands and Bakken crude to Gulf Coast refineries. Critics and environmentalists maintain the rejection was a legitimate policy choice to curb greenhouse gas emissions and protect land and water from spills; groups like Bold Nebraska and 350.org denounced the suit as a shareholder-appeasing move or an attempt to force harmful fossil-fuel expansion. The Canadian government declined detailed comment, noting TransCanada’s legal right to sue while emphasizing broader North American energy discussions with the U.S. remain ongoing.

Legislators in several U.S. states are reconsidering alternative execution methods as lethal-injection drugs grow scarce. In Wyoming, a committee is drafting a bill to permit firing-squad executions after the state’s corrections director said it lacks execution drugs; Wyoming has one death-row inmate, Dale Wayne Eaton. Utah Rep. Paul Ray plans to revive a firing-squad option, arguing it causes instantaneous death; Utah already allows firing squads for those sentenced before a 2004 ban. The push follows high-profile botched lethal injections elsewhere.

Separately, Tennessee’s Republican governor signed a law allowing electrocution if lethal-injection drugs cannot be obtained. The measure, passed overwhelmingly by the legislature, uniquely permits the state to impose electrocution without offering inmates a choice; experts expect legal challenges on unavailability proofs and Eighth Amendment cruelty claims. Supporters cite European drug export restrictions that have left many states unable to procure execution drugs. Thirty-two states retain capital punishment, almost all relying on lethal injection; the Supreme Court has historically upheld various methods but bars gratuitous pain under the Eighth Amendment.

In Lausanne, negotiators struck a tentative framework late Wednesday into Thursday for limiting Iran’s nuclear program, but key details remain unclear and provoked immediate criticism. Energy Secretary Ernest Moniz and Iran’s delegation haggled through the night over whether Iran may pursue research on advanced centrifuges—more efficient machines that would shorten a pathway to a bomb. The administration’s fact sheet allows “limited research and development” on next-generation centrifuges according to an agreed schedule and parameters, and bars enrichment with those machines for ten years, but it does not disclose the schedule or parameters. Critics, notably Israeli sources and several U.S. senators, called that vagueness dangerous.

Other unresolved or fuzzily described issues include the disposition of Iran’s large stockpile of low-enriched uranium. The framework requires Iran to “reduce” it from over 10 tons to a few hundred pounds, but does not specify whether Iran must export most of the material or may dilute it domestically—a point Tehran insisted upon late in talks. Dilution can still be reconverted, though some experts argue reconversion would be laborious and the choice partly reflects Iranian domestic politics.

Perhaps most problematic is Tehran’s past weapons-related work. The International Atomic Energy Agency reports Iran has not answered most questions about alleged bomb design work and has denied access to the Parchin military site. The framework pledges “an agreed set of measures” to address IAEA concerns but gives no specifics.

Congressional reaction was cautious and bipartisan: lawmakers demanded full details and reserved the right to act, with Senate Foreign Relations Chairman Bob Corker pursuing a bill for congressional review. Republican leaders signaled tough scrutiny and potential pushes for new sanctions, while the White House warned it would veto measures that undercut diplomacy. The administration urged patience, stressing the framework must be turned into a detailed deal by June 30 and warning that premature congressional interference could imperil international unity and the chance for a diplomatic resolution.

USDA projects U.S. 2014/15 total rice supplies at 282.6 million cwt, up 2.8 million from last month due to a higher production forecast. The first survey-based U.S. crop estimate for 2014/15 is 228.8 million cwt, a near 21 percent increase year-to-year. Yield is forecast at 7,560 pounds per acre (up 91 pounds from last month but slightly below last year’s record); harvested area is unchanged at 3.03 million acres. Long-grain production is forecast at 169.3 million cwt; medium- and short-grain combined at 59.5 million cwt. Imports are projected at 21.0 million cwt, down 9 percent. Total use is forecast at 243.0 million cwt, up 3.0 million from last month and 12 percent above the prior year, with domestic/residual use at 134.0 million and exports at 109.0 million cwt. Ending stocks are projected at 39.6 million cwt, slightly below last month but 21 percent higher than the previous year. Prices: long-grain $12.00–13.00/cwt; medium/short $17.50–18.50 (up $0.50); all-rice $13.80–14.80 (up $0.30).

Globally, 2014/15 production is trimmed 2.1 million tons to 477.3 million (still a record), with lower crops in Bangladesh, Brazil, Indonesia, and India. World ending stocks fall 3.2 million tons to 105.4 million, down 4.7 million from last year.

Separately, California’s historic drought has cut state sushi-grade short- and medium-grain plantings by about 25 percent, threatening supply for premium Japonica rice used in sushi. While overall U.S. rice production is up, California is the primary producer of the preferred sushi varieties; reduced acreage and water allocations mean higher prices are likely for sushi restaurants and exporters, though impacts nationwide and on menus remain uncertain.

On New Year’s Eve, Mariah Carey’s headlining set on Dick Clark’s New Year’s Rockin’ Eve suffered visible technical problems that sparked widespread attention, criticism and conflicting accounts over blame. Carey began with “Auld Lang Syne” but struggled on “Emotions” and “We Belong Together,” telling the crowd she couldn’t hear through her in-ear monitors. Her manager, Stella Bulochnikov, and publicist Nicole Perna accused production of failing to fix in-ear issues despite multiple warnings before the live broadcast, saying the team changed battery packs but the monitors never worked and that producers proceeded to air the performance regardless. They portrayed Carey as having rehearsed and taken the gig seriously, only to be “set up to fail.” Dick Clark Productions (DCP) denied responsibility, calling any suggestion they intentionally compromised an artist defamatory and noting that initial investigation found no production involvement in the difficulties. Multiple industry sources and Billboard reporting indicate the in-ear feed was on the wrong frequency, with two insiders blaming Carey’s tech team—supporting DCP’s position that production systems were functioning. A production source also accused Carey of inadequate rehearsal, even claiming she used a body double earlier. Amid the dispute, audio producer Robert Goldstein said monitors worked perfectly on his end. The incident drew public reactions: Josh Groban briefly joked about lip-syncing in a deleted tweet and later apologized for any offense, while Carey responded to the controversy on Twitter with “Shit happens,” wishing fans a happy new year. The episode highlights the complexities of live TV production and competing narratives when failures occur.

A leaked draft of a United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) report warns that global efforts to curb climate change are dangerously behind schedule, raising the risk of severe economic disruption. If emissions are not sharply reduced within about 15 years, current technologies may be unable to avoid catastrophic warming, forcing future generations to rely on unproven, costly methods to remove greenhouse gases from the atmosphere and store them underground. The draft highlights that governments still subsidize fossil fuels far more than clean energy, encouraging new coal and other high-emission projects even as renewable deployment grows too slowly to offset rising fossil-fuel emissions—especially in fast-developing economies. Nuclear’s share of low-carbon energy is declining, and rich countries’ apparent emission reductions partly reflect outsourcing production to nations like China. The Kyoto Protocol has been ineffective partly because major emitters did not participate fully, and the successor treaty isn’t due to take effect until 2020 with uncertain ambition. The report stresses the hard choice: accept some near-term economic costs to avoid far larger future damages, or risk overshooting targets that would likely require expensive carbon removal strategies that could compete with food production.

Domestically, U.S. environmental groups pressed President Obama to apply a strict “climate-impact” test to energy decisions—including the Keystone XL pipeline, fracking, Arctic drilling, and coal leases—criticizing the administration’s “all of the above” policy as incompatible with deep emissions cuts. The push creates a rift with the White House, which argues it is reducing emissions through regulatory steps while still supporting domestic fossil-fuel production. With political and industry opposition mounting on both sides, critical permitting and regulatory choices this year could shape whether policy aligns with the urgent scientific warnings in the IPCC draft.

Thor: The Dark World held No. 1 for a second weekend with a studio estimate of $38.5 million, a 55% drop that brings its domestic total to $147 million against a $170 million budget and positions it to surpass the original Thor’s $181 million. The big surprise was The Best Man Holiday, which opened far above expectations with $30.6 million from 2,024 theaters, an A+ CinemaScore and strong word-of-mouth; the low-budget sequel (about $17 million) should be highly profitable. Limited releases Nebraska and Dallas Buyers Club posted strong per-theater averages. Next weekend’s big shake-up: The Hunger Games: Catching Fire.

Multiple reports detail the escalating 2014 Ebola crisis and responses at home and abroad. Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan pledged $25 million to the CDC Foundation to support U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Ebola response work in Guinea, Liberia, Sierra Leone and other at-risk areas; the grant came from their fund at the Silicon Valley Community Foundation and follows other major donations such as Paul Allen’s $9 million gift. CDC Director Tom Frieden urged rapid international action to stop Ebola at its source.

The World Health Organization warned the epidemic was intensifying: WHO officials reported the outbreak’s death rate had risen to about 70 percent and cautioned there could be as many as 10,000 new cases per week within two months if the global response did not scale up. WHO noted 4,447 deaths and roughly 8,914 probable or suspected cases, with urban centers—Freetown, Conakry and Monrovia—of particular concern. WHO and aid groups emphasized isolation and care but recognized overwhelmed health systems and the need for practical measures like protective kits for families and basic community clinics.

In the United States, attention turned to Texas Health Presbyterian Hospital after the death of Thomas Eric Duncan, a Liberian visitor who died of Ebola, and the subsequent infection of nurse Nina Pham. Medical records show about 70 staff participated in his care, raising concerns about potential exposures. The CDC broadened contact monitoring while investigating possible breaches in protective protocols; experts stressed strict donning and doffing procedures are vital to prevent transmission.

Doctors Without Borders reported 16 staff infected and nine deaths among its workers and criticized insufficient international aid on the ground. Meanwhile, individuals affected included freelance cameraman Ashoka Mukpo, evacuated from Liberia to Nebraska; initial fundraising highlighted high evacuation and treatment costs, although NBC later agreed to cover his medical bills. Overall, the reports depict a rapidly worsening epidemic demanding urgent global coordination, resources, and rigorous infection-control practices.

A video circulating online shows hooded figures performing what appears to be a ritual and culminating in a woman being stabbed on the grounds of CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research. The footage, shot beneath the large illuminated statue of the Hindu deity Shiva that stands on the campus as “a gift from India,” depicts robed people moving around the statue while one woman collapses and is apparently stabbed; the cameraman reacts with expletives and flees before the clip ends. CERN confirmed the video was filmed on site but said it was made without permission, calling it a spoof and warning it could cause misunderstanding about the laboratory’s scientific work. The statue’s presence at CERN is tied to a metaphor linking Shiva’s cosmic dance to the “cosmic dance” of subatomic particles; India is an observer state at CERN. The organisation emphasized its multicultural, collaborative mission to study fundamental particles and denied any occult intent. CERN indicated the participants — many temporary visitors and scientists from around the world use the site, especially in summer — likely let “their sense of humour go too far,” and noted that the campus has security measures and ID checks; the woman in the video appears identifiable. The incident has revived long-standing public anxieties and conspiracy theories about CERN’s work, including fears about creating black holes, opening portals to other dimensions, or disproving God, claims that CERN has repeatedly rebutted. The lab added a clarification to its FAQ and social media, stating the ritual video is fictional and that it does not condone such spoofs, which can misrepresent and alarm the public about its scientific activities.

An informal American Farm Bureau Federation survey finds the classic Thanksgiving Day dinner for a family of 10 cost $49.04 this year, down slightly from $49.48 in 2012 and below the 2011 cost of $49.20. The AFBF shopping list for the meal includes a 16-pound turkey, bread stuffing, sweet potatoes, rolls with butter, peas, cranberries, a carrot-and-celery relish tray, pumpkin pie with whipped cream, and beverages (coffee and milk), with quantities sufficient for 10 people and plenty of leftovers. The turkey remained the most expensive single item at $21.76—about $1.36 per pound—representing a roughly 3-cent-per-pound decrease and a 47-cent drop for the whole bird versus 2012, making it the largest contributor to the overall price decline. LPL Financial’s Jeffrey Kleintop highlighted the AFBF release and quipped, “There’s no inflation on the table.” The item also notes web-archiving efforts to preserve pages and prevent broken links over time.

Twin sisters Kristin and Candace Hermeler, 29-year-old Australians, carried out a planned suicide pact at an Arapahoe County gun range in Colorado. Kristin died from a self-inflicted gunshot; Candace shot herself simultaneously and survived in serious condition. Investigators found a 1999 Time magazine cover depicting Columbine shooters among their belongings and discovered that Kristin had written sympathetic letters in 1999 to Columbine survivor Brooks Brown, describing herself as “rejected, victimized and ostracized.” The sisters had communicated with the Browns by phone and letters when they were 18, saying they had been bullied. During their Colorado visit, they did not contact the Browns. Authorities say the twins rented two pistols at the Family Shooting Center, fired at targets for about 90 minutes, then turned the guns on themselves; surveillance, physical evidence, and Candace’s statements led law enforcement to conclude it was suicide and attempted suicide, not foul play. Candace initially was defensive and later refused to discuss motives. The case has drawn international attention and raised questions about bullying, twin psychological bonds, and suicide pacts. Family asked for privacy and thanked responders; investigators have not released range surveillance footage.

The document chronicles the controversy surrounding an unverified dossier alleging ties between Donald Trump and Russian operatives, its origins in opposition research, the role of intelligence and media, and the political fallout. The dossier, compiled by former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele of Orbis Business Intelligence, began as paid opposition research during the Republican primary and later was funded by a Democratic client or an independent donor. Fusion GPS commissioned Steele, who leveraged Russian contacts and native speakers to collect reports alleging long-term Russian efforts to cultivate Trump—through kompromat, business inducements, and other covert tactics—and specific allegations, including a purported Prague meeting involving Trump lawyer Michael Cohen. Steele delivered memos beginning in June and continued through December; concerned about their gravity, he passed material to the FBI and reportedly to his country’s intelligence service.

Senator John McCain learned of the dossier at the Halifax security forum, met an emissary who vetted the source, and eventually handed the documents to FBI Director James Comey on December 9. The FBI included a summary of the reports in a classified briefing for President Obama and President-elect Trump in mid-January; the briefing was leaked to CNN. BuzzFeed then controversially published the unredacted dossier, drawing heavy criticism for airing anonymous, unvetted allegations that its own editor said had “serious reason to doubt.” Questions arose about the source of the unredacted copy and whether intermediaries or the original client leaked it.

Reactions were polarized. Civil-rights groups such as the Anti-Defamation League and the Anne Frank Center condemned Trump for comparing the dossier controversy to the Holocaust, calling his remarks insensitive and demanding explanation or apology. Within media and political circles, voices split between those insisting the dossier merited investigation—some Democrats called for sanctions on Russia and independent probes—and skeptics warning against treating anonymous claims as truth. Journalists including Dean Baquet of the New York Times declined to publish the dossier earlier, citing lack of corroboration.

A longer critique in the text frames the episode as symptomatic of a “Deep State” clash, arguing intelligence agencies and sympathetic media amplified unverified allegations to sabotage Trump, and warning that this undermines journalism and democratic legitimacy. The critique cites prior public interventions by former intelligence officials backing Hillary Clinton and suggests motives rooted in preserving the postwar security order. Conversely, many lawmakers and commentators stressed the need for fact-finding: some Democrats avoided directly questioning Trump’s legitimacy pending evidence, while others urged transparency, further investigation into alleged links between Trump aides and Russia, and safeguarding electoral systems.

Overall, the document traces a complex chain—from private opposition research to international intelligence channels, from classified briefings to public leaks—that produced a highly charged, divisive public debate about credibility, media ethics, national security, and how democracies should handle unverified but potentially consequential intelligence.

Comedian and talk‑show host Bill Maher used a Wednesday night appearance on Jimmy Kimmel Live to sharply criticize mainstream Muslim attitudes and to urge U.S. liberals to more forcefully defend free speech after the Charlie Hebdo massacre in Paris. Maher, a longtime critic of Islam, argued that while most individual Muslims would not carry out such attacks, “hundreds of millions” worldwide support them or excuse violence when the Prophet Muhammad is mocked. He accused many American liberals of turning a blind eye to extremism out of political correctness and called for unequivocal condemnation of both the killings and the purported motivations behind them. Maher said religions are “stupid and dangerous” and defended the right to insult religious beliefs as core to free speech. He cited an unnamed study to argue that many majority‑Muslim countries score poorly on women’s rights and noted harsh penalties for homosexuality in some states. Maher’s remarks, which included scathing commentary about cultural sensitivity and later about Bill Cosby, drew a mixed reaction: some praised his defense of free expression while others—moderate Muslims and fellow liberals—have criticized him for intolerance and broad generalizations. The segment rekindled debate over how to confront extremism without alienating Muslim communities.

An Aeroflot Boeing 777 en route from Moscow to Bangkok hit a sudden patch of clear-air turbulence about 40 minutes before landing, injuring 27 people. The turbulence occurred in clear skies with no visual warning, so crew could not give advance notice to fasten seatbelts; Aeroflot and the Russian embassy in Thailand said many of the injuries resulted from passengers not wearing seatbelts. Of the 313 people on board, 24 injured were Russian and three Thai. Fifteen people, including a child, were admitted to Bangkok hospitals; three required surgery—two for multiple leg fractures and one for broken ribs—and by evening 14 remained hospitalized. Russian officials said none of the injuries were life-threatening and there were no spinal compression fractures, contrary to earlier reports. Footage shared by passengers showed people lying in aisles and cabin items scattered. Passengers described being hurled into the ceiling and fearing a crash as the shaking persisted. Aeroflot noted the pilot had over 23,000 flight hours and pointed out that clear-air turbulence—caused by differing air masses and invisible to radar—is difficult to predict; roughly 750 such incidents are recorded annually in civil aviation. Aeroflot will cover medical costs.

The twelve jurors who acquitted Casey Anthony of first-degree murder were publicly identified after a three-month court-ordered delay intended to protect their safety. Jurors ranged in age and background—retirees, parents, service workers, teachers, and students—from Pinellas County. They declined media interviews and had already refused collective comment. The panel convicted Anthony only on lying to law enforcement, sparking significant public anger and threats that motivated the delayed release.

Police in the Bronx are investigating after the body of a newborn girl — her umbilical cord still attached — was found dead outside a seven-story apartment building on West 183rd Street in Morris Heights. The infant was discovered in a courtyard alley after reportedly falling several stories shortly after 2:40 p.m.; surveillance footage captured at least part of the fall. The New York Fire Department said the baby was found unresponsive and declared dead at the scene. Authorities say criminality is suspected but no arrests have been made. The baby’s mother was located, taken to a hospital and was being questioned at the 52nd Precinct; the father was questioned and released after saying he was unaware of the pregnancy. The Administration for Children’s Services confirmed an investigation but could not disclose whether it had prior involvement with the family. Neighbors described shock and disbelief, with many gathering outside as detectives and crime-scene teams worked. Residents expressed heartbreak and confusion, some defending neighbors and wondering how such a tragedy could occur. Building management declined comment while police continue to piece together how the infant came to fall and whether she was alive when she fell.

Two months after United Airlines launched what it billed as the airline industry's first bug-bounty program, Florida security researcher Jordan Wiens received the program’s first major reward: one million MileagePlus miles. Wiens, owner of Vector 35, submitted reports of two vulnerabilities he believed were remote code execution (RCE) flaws in United’s customer-facing web properties after about six hours of targeted, careful testing. United verified his U.S. citizenship and that the research was performed on U.S. soil before crediting his account with two deposits that together totaled 1,000,000 miles.

United’s program, announced in May amid controversy over a high-profile researcher being barred from a flight, rewards eligible security reports with miles rather than cash. The payout scale ties severity to miles: 50,000 miles for lower-severity issues such as cross-site scripting (XSS) or CSRF, 250,000 miles for medium-severity issues like authentication bypass, brute-force or PII disclosure risks, and the top award of 1,000,000 miles for RCE vulnerabilities. The approximate cash value of the million miles is roughly $25,000, making it competitive with many commercial cash bounties.

United’s rules restrict scope to United-operated, customer-facing websites and apps and explicitly exclude internal systems, partner sites, onboard Wi‑Fi/entertainment/avionics, and aggressive testing methods such as brute-force or automated scans. Submissions must include detailed reproduction steps and the researcher’s legal information; successful reports are paid once vulnerabilities are remediated. The program also imposes eligibility limits (e.g., no current or former United employees or residents of sanctioned countries) and confidentiality and indemnity obligations.

Wiens, who had never participated in a commercial bounty program before, praised United for running the program and said he plans to use the miles for family travel. He declined to disclose technical details of the vulnerability to avoid jeopardizing the award or remediation.

Brandon Jenkins, a prospective student, has sued the Community College of Baltimore County (CCBC), alleging he was denied admission to its radiation therapy program because he expressed his religious belief. Jenkins applied for the Fall 2013 cohort, completed the exam and a five-person interview panel. When asked what was most important to him, he replied, "My God." The American Center for Law and Justice (ACLJ), representing Jenkins, says this was the only time he mentioned his faith. After rejection, program director Adrienne Dougherty told Jenkins in email that “religion is a major part of your life” and that “this field is not the place for religion,” advising him to omit such beliefs in future interviews. The ACLJ contends that singling out religion as a basis for denial is unlawful and a First Amendment violation; it seeks an injunction to admit Jenkins and unspecified damages. CCBC declined to comment on litigation, noting a commitment to diversity; its lawyer cited other factors, including higher GPAs among applicants, Jenkins’s 3.2 GPA relative to others, a decade-old criminal charge, and his desire to remain in Maryland. The suit argues those cited reasons were pretextual and that faith was improperly used to disqualify him.

Republican insiders in Iowa, New Hampshire, South Carolina and Nevada increasingly accept that Donald Trump is a durable contender: POLITICO’s weekly Caucus survey finds he could win two of the first four contests, though his grip on Iowa is fragile. After seven months of weekly polling of top state strategists, operatives and activists, roughly three-quarters of GOP insiders in New Hampshire and South Carolina now say Trump would prevail if voting were today. South Carolina respondents cited voter anger over immigration and security as boosting Trump. Insiders view Iowa and Nevada as more organizationally demanding; many now favor Ted Cruz in Iowa, marking the first time Cruz leads insiders there, while Nevada insiders split between Trump and Marco Rubio, whose Mormon outreach and ground game are credited. Ben Carson has faded from earlier prominence.

On the Democratic side, insiders overwhelmingly say Hillary Clinton would win in all four early states, reporting that she has blunted Bernie Sanders’ summer surge. Nevada Democrats praise Clinton’s superior organization; New Hampshire insiders say Sanders has lost momentum and electability concerns favor Clinton.

Separately, a Reuters/Ipsos rolling poll showed Trump’s national Republican support dipping from 43% to 31% in five days after controversial post‑Paris remarks and other gaffes, though he remains the front-runner.

Severe hail, wet weather and fungus cut France’s champagne grape yields by about 40% this year—the worst in at least 40 years—contributing to a 20% fall in total French grape output and poor harvests across Europe. However, immediate shortages are unlikely: champagne ages at least 15 months, producers blend multiple vintages, and reserves exceed three years. Exports and prior surpluses cushion large houses, though smaller growers and domestic sales face pressure amid economic weakness.

A Department of Homeland Security inspector general report found that the Secret Service improperly accessed and widely disseminated sensitive personnel records about Rep. Jason Chaffetz while he was investigating the agency’s repeated security lapses. Between March 24 and April 2, 2015, about 45 employees queried Chaffetz’s 2003 Secret Service job application nearly 60 times; the IG concluded only four accesses were arguably legitimate. Assistant Director Edward Lowery emailed colleagues urging that “some information that he might find embarrassing needs to get out,” and at least one employee admitted telling a reporter. The information subsequently appeared in news outlets. The report criticized the agency for violating the Privacy Act and for poor stewardship of protected data, noting the spread reached many headquarters offices, field offices and supervisory levels; dozens of staff members acknowledged sharing the material internally. Secret Service Director Joseph Clancy and DHS Secretary Jeh Johnson apologized to Chaffetz and pledged accountability. Chaffetz called the conduct intimidating and vowed to continue oversight. Ranking panel Democrat Elijah Cummings and others said those who fail ethical standards should not remain in the Service. The IG investigation faced criticism for allowing Secret Service internal affairs inspectors to participate in interviews, raising concerns about conflicts of interest and potential chilling effects on whistleblowers.

A multinational team led by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) is racing to study a marine ecosystem exposed for the first time in about 120,000 years after a colossal iceberg, A-68, calved from the Larsen C ice shelf in July. A-68, an estimated trillion tons and roughly twice the volume of Lake Erie, reduced Larsen C’s area by about 12% and uncovered roughly 3,600 square miles of ocean now open to sunlight. The researchers will spend about three weeks aboard the RRS James Clark Ross to sample a 2,200-square-mile section of the newly revealed seabed, collecting seafloor animals, microbes, plankton, sediments and water and recording surface mammals and birds. Expedition leader Katrin Linse emphasizes urgency: scientists must document conditions before sunlight-driven colonization and ecological change transform the under-ice community. BAS science director David Vaughan frames the mission as an unprecedented opportunity to probe how polar continental shelves respond to climate-sensitive change, noting logistical challenges including sea ice, low temperatures and hazardous ice-filled waters. Recent Greenpeace submarine dives have already revealed the Antarctic seafloor “carpeted with life,” showing rare squids, starfish and diverse organisms that may be vulnerable when the environment shifts. While the Larsen C calving cannot be directly linked to anthropogenic warming, longer-term trends show regional ice-shelf retreat, glacier acceleration and contributions to sea-level rise. The expedition, operating under CCAMLR permissions, aims to deliver a baseline snapshot of a hidden ecosystem, improving understanding of resilience and vulnerability in Antarctic marine habitats and informing conservation efforts, including proposals for a large Antarctic ocean sanctuary.

A Central California woman, Myrna Arias, has sued Intermex Wire Transfer LLC in Kern County Superior Court, alleging she was fired after uninstalling a company-required Xora (now ClickSoftware) app that tracked employees’ locations continuously. Arias, who worked as a sales executive and account manager from February to May 2014, says Intermex’s regional vice president John Stubits instructed her and other staff to install the StreetSmart/Xora app on their company-issued iPhones. The app’s GPS function recorded employees’ exact locations and purportedly could not be disabled outside work hours. After researching the software and asking a trainer whether off-duty monitoring would occur, Arias says Stubits admitted employees would be monitored 24/7 and bragged he could see her driving speed and routes. Arias accepted GPS tracking during work hours but objected to constant monitoring during personal time, likening the app to an ankle bracelet and warning it was illegal. She uninstalled the app; shortly thereafter Stubits reprimanded her, and she was fired a few weeks later.

Her complaint accuses Intermex of invasion of privacy, retaliation, unfair business practices, wrongful termination, labor code violations and intentional interference with contract, and seeks an injunction plus general, special and punitive damages exceeding $500,000. Arias’ attorney Gail Glick says the app’s clock-in/out feature did not stop background GPS tracking and that management used the data to report employees’ speeds, routes and time at customer locations. The suit also alleges Intermex’s president phoned Arias’ prior employer, NetSpend, leading to her termination there and making it harder for her to find new work. Intermex had not commented by press time. Arias’ attorneys say they will pursue the case aggressively to obtain justice and damages for the alleged illegal and intrusive monitoring.

Senators Heidi Heitkamp (D-N.D.) and Joe Donnelly (D-Ind.) announced support for same-sex marriage, notable because they represent reliably Republican states. Their statements framed marriage equality as an extension of non-discrimination and inclusion, and they join a growing group of Democratic senators backing the issue. The article examines why Senate endorsements have surged—from 8 in 2008 to 50 recently—far faster than the steady, linear rise in public opinion. Using a dataset of every senator-year since 1997 and variables including party, DW-Nominate ideology scores, birth year, and modeled state and national public support, a logistic regression finds ideology and state-level support as the strongest predictors of endorsement. Party loses predictive power once ideology is accounted for. A simple linear model underestimates the recent spike in endorsements, so the author tests a “majority model” that gauges the probability same-sex marriage has reached majority support nationally and in each state; this better reproduces the rapid uptick in endorsements. The conclusion: senators appear to time endorsements around perceived majority thresholds. As same-sex marriage becomes unambiguously majority-supported, endorsements will likely decelerate—remaining opponents will be driven by state-level politics, principle, or primary concerns.

Wesley Snipes began serving a three-year federal sentence at the minimum-security Federal Correctional Institution McKean in Lewis Run, Pennsylvania, after being ordered to surrender. The 48-year-old actor was convicted in 2008 on three misdemeanor counts of willful failure to file income tax returns; prosecutors say he failed to file for at least a decade and owed $2.7 million on $13.8 million of income from 1999–2001, while alleging he hadn’t paid taxes on roughly $38 million earned since 1999. Snipes, acquitted of more serious felony charges, maintained he relied on tax advisers and described himself at sentencing as an “idealistic, naive, passionate, truth-seeking, spiritually motivated artist.” He sought last-minute relief, filing appeals including an emergency motion for a new trial and expressing plans to seek Supreme Court review; he also told Larry King he believed there were irregularities in his case and asked not to be “sent up the river yet.” McKean’s minimum-security camp—no perimeter fences, about 300 nonviolent inmates living in two-man barracks—offers daily routines, chores that pay pennies an hour, limited commissary spending, recreational and religious activities, and strict rules like five daily head counts. Officials stress all inmates are treated equally despite Snipes’s fame.

Robin Roberts made a highly publicized return to Good Morning America after a 173–174 day medical leave following a bone marrow transplant to treat myelodysplastic syndrome (M.D.S.), a rare blood disorder likely tied to earlier breast cancer treatment. Celebrated on-air and online, her comeback was framed as a victory over daunting odds: doctors had warned she might not survive, and she described agonizing pain and a near-coma before rallying. ABC integrated her into the show’s coverage while she recuperated, and co-anchors frequently referenced her recovery during her absence. Executives say her return bolsters the show’s hopes of extending its lead over NBC’s Today, particularly among key demographics. Roberts will resume gradually—initially a few days a week—while her doctors monitor her stamina and vision under studio lights; she’ll appear at the Oscars and on a forthcoming 20/20 special. ABC plans to continue featuring regulars Elizabeth Vargas and Amy Robach. The broadcast drew widespread viewer support, brief conciliatory gestures from Today, and emotional relief among colleagues who emphasized that, beyond ratings, the primary celebration was that Roberts survived and returned.

A Sinking Spring, Pa., neighborhood was shaken after the deaths of Megan and Mark Short and their three children—Liana, 8; Mark Jr., 5; and Willow, 2—found Saturday in an apparent murder‑suicide. Police discovered gunshot victims and a handwritten note after a relative reported Megan missed a lunch date; a handgun was located near one adult. Investigators said the couple had “domestic issues,” but did not disclose who fired the shots. The family dog was also shot. Counseling was offered at the Wilson School District for students and parents.

Neighbors described Megan as planning to leave the marriage; she had posted on Facebook that she was moving Aug. 6 and commented that she was leaving a 16‑year marriage after engaging with an article about emotional abuse. A neighbor, Angie Burke, shared messages showing Megan had found a potential rental and hoped to relocate. Other neighbors recalled Megan’s advocacy for organ donation and her public recounting of the trauma surrounding daughter Willow’s severe congenital heart defect and transplant.

Willow’s medical saga drew local and national attention: born with a complex heart defect, she received a transplant as an infant and faced ongoing challenges, including struggles to obtain life‑sustaining immunosuppressant drugs. Megan wrote about PTSD stemming from those experiences. The family was involved in organ‑donor advocacy and parish life. Authorities and community leaders asked for prayers and provided support resources as the investigation continues.

Ken Bone, the undecided voter who sat in a red sweater at Sunday night’s presidential debate, became an instant internet sensation after asking a question about energy policy.
