From his close vantage point, Bone told CNN the debate “almost felt like watching mom and dad fight,” criticizing the “bickering and name calling” that filled much of the 90-minute event. He praised moderators Martha Raddatz and Anderson Cooper for doing a “great job” under difficult circumstances and said that amid the rhetoric there were still substantive answers if viewers could “dig through” the noise.

Bone’s moustache, sweater and the sight of him photographing the emptying debate hall with what looked like a disposable camera fueled social media affection. He gained thousands of followers and joked he had to wear the sweater again because “it's more famous than me.” He explained the sweater was a backup after he ripped his trouser seat that morning, scrapping a favored suit.

Bone said he hadn’t known during the debate that Donald Trump had invited several women who accused Bill Clinton of sexual misconduct to sit in the audience. He called that move “uncalled for,” saying it had little to do with Hillary Clinton’s fitness for office and accusing Trump of dredging up opponents’ pasts while asking to forget his own. The debate left him less certain: previously leaning toward Trump, Bone said Clinton’s composure and answers had impressed him and muddied his choice further. Media outlets quickly capitalized on the moment, even suggesting where to buy “Ken Bone” sweaters.

A major analysis published in Science Advances concludes that Earth is undergoing a sixth mass extinction driven by human activities, even under the most conservative assumptions. The study’s authors used a recently revised, higher “background” extinction rate (2 extinctions per 10,000 species per 100 years) and conservative modern counts from the IUCN (only species confirmed extinct, and a second estimate including “extinct in the wild” and “possibly extinct”). Despite these cautious choices, 20th‑ and 21st‑century vertebrate extinction rates are eight to 100 times greater than the background rate. For example, 477 vertebrates have gone extinct since 1900 versus nine expected under the background rate; overall documented extinctions since 1500 number in the hundreds, and many more species are functionally extinct or declining. Amphibians show particularly sharp, accelerating losses; many extinctions reflect habitat destruction, overexploitation, invasive species and emerging diseases, and climate change—pressures amplified by human population growth and consumption patterns. The authors emphasize that their approach likely underestimates true losses because IUCN listings are conservative and population extirpations (which degrade ecosystem services) are not fully represented. They estimate that the vertebrate species lost in the last century would have required 800 to 10,000 years to disappear under natural rates, indicating unprecedented rapid biodiversity decline. While some experts urge caution about declaring a full mass extinction yet, the paper argues avoiding one will demand rapid, greatly intensified conservation to protect habitats, curb overexploitation, and address climate change; otherwise recovery would take many millennia and human well‑being would be severely affected.

Two nearly simultaneous explosions rattled churches in Las Cruces, New Mexico, on Sunday morning, injuring no one but leaving worshippers shaken and property damaged. The first blast occurred around 8:20 a.m. at Calvary Baptist Church when a device placed in a mailbox outside an administrative entrance detonated as people were gathering for services. About 30 congregants were inside; witnesses described seeing bomb parts and an Eveready battery among debris. Roughly 20–30 minutes later, a second explosive detonated in a trash can just outside the front entrance of Holy Cross Catholic Church during the 8 a.m. Mass, shattering the building’s glass and prompting an orderly evacuation. Monsignor John Anderson recounted being in the middle of communion when the noise occurred; he said the timing likely prevented injuries because many were kneeling and away from the doors. Damage at both sites was described as relatively minor.

Local, state and federal agencies — including Las Cruces Police, New Mexico State Police, the ATF, FBI and Department of Homeland Security — responded, assisted by bomb squads and canine units. Officials have not confirmed motives or suspects and are investigating whether the incidents are connected, though police say the proximity in time and targets makes a link likely. Authorities cautioned other churches to be vigilant and avoid investigating suspicious items themselves. New Mexico Gov. Susana Martinez condemned the attacks, calling them cowardly and pledging law enforcement will pursue those responsible. Community leaders urged continued worship with increased prudence and security measures, and a rally called for forgiveness and unity in the wake of the events.

Researchers from Harvard (Andrew Reece) and the University of Vermont (Christopher Danforth) report that Instagram photos can reveal markers associated with depression. Analyzing roughly 44,000 images from 166 users, the team trained algorithms on objective image features—hue, brightness, saturation, face detection, vividness, and filter choice—and compared algorithmic assessments with human ratings of happiness, sadness, likability, and interestingness. The computer model outperformed average human raters and showed higher predictive success for depression than general practitioners in their testing context, even identifying signs prior to formal diagnosis. Depressed users tended to post darker, bluer, and more faded images, were more likely to use the black-and-white “Inkwell” filter (while non-depressed users favored warmer “Valencia”), posted slightly more photos with faces but with fewer people per image, and received more comments but fewer likes. Human judgments correlated poorly with the computational signals, indicating machines detect patterns people don’t consciously use to label photos as “sad.” Authors stress that such tools would be for screening and early detection—augmenting, not replacing, clinicians—and caution against overinterpretation; the preprint has not yet been peer-reviewed. They envision opt-in, privacy-conscious applications that prompt users to seek care when algorithmic markers suggest elevated risk.

Dominique Venner, a 78-year-old far-right writer and activist, shot himself at the altar of Paris’s Notre Dame Cathedral in the afternoon, in front of about 1,500 visitors who were evacuated without incident. Venner, known for nationalist essays denouncing immigration and the “decline” of European civilization, left a final essay on his website and a recorded message read on Radio Courtoisie in which he framed his suicide as a deliberate political protest. He criticized France’s recent law legalizing gay marriage and adoption and condemned immigration from North Africa, declaring that “words must be backed up with acts” and that spectacular symbolic gestures were needed to “re-awaken” national memory. National Front leader Marine Le Pen called his death an “eminently political act” intended to wake the French, while other party figures praised him as an intellectual protesting societal decadence. Venner, a former soldier in the Algerian War who once belonged to the OAS, had a long career publishing right-wing history and military works; his publisher noted his next book’s title, "A Western Samurai," and observers compared his act to Yukio Mishima’s ritual suicide. Cathedral officials expressed shock, cancelled masses, and planned a vigil; authorities and the interior minister noted the emotional impact of the incident.

James Wesley Howell, 20, of Jeffersonville, Indiana, faces criminal charges in both California and Indiana after authorities discovered weapons and alleged child sexual abuse tied to his movements. In California, Howell was arrested in Santa Monica on June 12 after police found a loaded assault rifle with magazines altered to allow about 60 rounds to be fired rapidly and roughly 15 pounds of explosive-ready chemicals in his car. He was charged in Los Angeles with three felony weapons and ammunition counts, pleaded not guilty, and had bail set at $2 million. Howell told officers he was driving to a large gay pride event in West Hollywood; his arrest came hours after the mass shooting at an Orlando gay nightclub, prompting heightened alert among law enforcement and event organizers, though investigators have not determined whether he planned violence at the parade.

Separately, prosecutors in Clark County, Indiana, charged Howell with one count of child molestation for an incident on May 31. County Prosecutor Jeremy Mull said Howell took a 12-year-old girl to a state forestry property and had sex with her; the girl had met Howell through an adult friend connected to a local car club. The girl’s mother reported the allegations on June 2. Howell was interviewed by detectives on June 7 and left Indiana afterward; Mull indicated it’s logical Howell fled to California after learning of the investigation and plans to seek his extradition. Records show Howell had prior incidents involving threats with a gun and was on probation forbidding weapons possession and leaving Indiana. Federal agents searched his home in Jeffersonville but gave no details. Defense and family lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

After Bill Cosby was sentenced Tuesday to three to ten years in prison for drugging and sexually assaulting Andrea Constand in 2004, his defense team mounted a forceful public response, accusing the justice system of racism and sexism and framing the conviction as part of a broader “sex war.” Speaking in the rain, Cosby’s publicist Andrew Wyatt characterized the trial as “the most racist and sexist trial” in U.S. history, likened it to a “public lynching,” and compared Cosby’s fate to the contemporary accusations against Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh. Wyatt also criticized expert witnesses, alleged audio evidence was falsified, and invoked historical persecution of Black men — even referencing Jesus — to argue Cosby was unfairly targeted. Members of Cosby’s team previously invoked Emmett Till in their rhetoric. The judge, Steven T. O’Neill, also designated Cosby a “sexually violent predator,” which mandates lifelong monthly counseling. Following sentencing, Cosby, 81, briefly remained in county custody before being transferred to SCI Phoenix, a recently opened state prison near Philadelphia, where officials said he would be processed, housed initially in a single cell near the infirmary, and assessed for safety and long-term placement. Prison officials noted provisions for his medical and psychological needs and said the goal is eventual placement in general population and access to required programming during incarceration.

Rotisserie chickens are often cheaper than roasting your own because supermarkets use soon-to-expire raw chickens and other perishables to make prepared foods rather than throwing them out. Reporter Cat Vasko discovered that grocers transform unsold produce and meat into hot-bar items, deli salads and rotisserie chickens to recoup value and reduce spoilage. This practice allows stores to offer lower prices on both cooked and raw items and mitigates waste that would otherwise be a net loss. Sell-by and best-by labels are about quality, not safety, and are often conservative; experts and resources note many foods remain good past their labeled dates. Retailers still discard significant inventory but also deliberately repurpose near-expiration goods; industry sources and former executives acknowledge this strategy and vendors of rotisserie equipment market waste-reduction programs. Buying prepared items can therefore be safe, economical, and environmentally beneficial: it saves consumers time and money, helps stores lower costs, and reduces wasted food and the resources used to produce it.

A U.S. government intelligence report, shared with law enforcement in recent weeks, warns that Islamic State (ISIS) may be manufacturing legitimate-looking Syrian passports using seized government assets, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and news outlets reported. The Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) intelligence briefing says ISIS likely accessed passport-printing machines, blank passport booklets and Syrian government biographical and fingerprint records after seizing offices in Raqqa and Deir ez-Zour. That access raises concerns about counterfeit documents and identity theft, and the report notes individuals holding passports “issued” in ISIS-controlled cities might already have traveled to the United States. The primary source for the assessment was rated at moderate confidence. FBI Director James Comey and State Department officials have publicly acknowledged concern over ISIS’s apparent capability to produce fraudulent passports. The report highlights that fake Syrian passports are widespread inside Syria and can be bought for a few hundred dollars, with backdated stamps also available. It also documents at least one passport found in Turkey bearing a designator tied to an ISIS-controlled printing location. HSI warns that if ISIS’s passport production is not curtailed, the group’s ability to operate beyond its territories will grow, posing heightened international security risks.

On Christmas Day thieves broke into The French Laundry in Yountville and stole 76 highly collectible bottles from the restaurant’s wine cellar, with an estimated value of at least $300,000. The haul was targeted: most bottles were from Burgundy legend Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (including multiple Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, Richebourg, Grands Échezeaux and Romanée St. Vivant vintages) and several cult Napa Cabernets from Screaming Eagle, plus other rare labels and Dom Pérignon. Chef-owner Thomas Keller publicly appealed to the wine community for tips and said the restaurant is cooperating with law enforcement as it rebuilds its cellar during a planned kitchen remodel. Keller warned stolen bottles will likely raise red flags if offered publicly, and asked anyone with information to contact authorities.

Sinn Féin leader Gerry Adams was arrested and questioned at Antrim police station over the 1972 IRA abduction and murder of Jean McConville, a widowed mother of ten and one of Northern Ireland’s “Disappeared.” After four days he was released pending a file being sent to the Public Prosecution Service. Adams denied involvement, criticized the timing during an election, and said he had voluntarily contacted police months earlier. The case draws on Boston College interviews and has renewed calls for justice from McConville’s family.

The fourth GOP debate in Milwaukee was a steadier, more policy-focused affair than prior clashes, yielding few game-changing moments but clarifying the field’s pecking order: Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz continued to outshine rivals, Jeb Bush delivered his best debate showing yet, Donald Trump was oddly muted, and Ben Carson struggled on substance.

Rubio and Cruz again emerged as the most polished performers. Rubio blended ease and command across topics — from immigration to military spending — and produced memorable lines (including a quip about welders vs. philosophy majors) while deftly confronting Rand Paul on defense spending. Cruz reinforced his appeal to conservative grassroots voters, delivering crisp, populist-ready attacks on Washington and memorable sound bites about the tax code and national defense. Both men appear to have solidified their status as the strongest contenders.

Jeb Bush, who entered the night under intense pressure after prior weak showings, steadied himself. He demanded more speaking time, avoided another disastrous confrontation with Rubio, and landed sharper, more concrete lines — notably criticizing Donald Trump’s mass-deportation plan as impractical and warning that such rhetoric helps Hillary Clinton. Bush’s performance reassured donors and supporters that he can at least “stop the bleeding,” though analysts caution that modest improvement won’t transform his standing: better debate form improves optics but may not revive his struggling candidacy.

Donald Trump returned to his combative style in spots but largely felt ancillary. His answers recycled familiar themes without substantive depth, and a few remarks earned boos. Despite a relatively weak night, his polling remained largely unaffected in observers’ eyes. Ben Carson, by contrast, had one of his shakier nights: he struggled on foreign policy questions about defeating ISIS, offered vague prescriptions, and took minimal speaking time.

Immigration dominated early exchanges, exposing deep GOP divisions. Trump defended building a southern wall and mass deportation; Kasich and Bush criticized that approach for being unrealistic and politically harmful. Cruz defended Trump and framed immigration as an economic issue for many voters. Defense spending and America’s global role produced another major clash, pitting Rubio and Cruz’s muscular foreign-policy views against Rand Paul’s restraint and fiscal objections.

Moderators kept the debate comparatively substantive and restrained, which some viewed as welcome, though critics said the format’s limits reduced candidate-to-candidate combat and produced many rehearsed talking points and clichéd personal anecdotes. Overall, Milwaukee clarified strengths and weaknesses without altering the race’s trajectories: Rubio and Cruz consolidated momentum, Bush regained footing but not dominance, and the contest looked set to slog on into the nominating season.

Shia LaBeouf has withdrawn from the upcoming Broadway revival of Lyle Kessler’s Orphans, citing “creative differences,” a month before previews begin. The 26-year-old, who had little theater experience, was set to appear alongside Alec Baldwin and under director Daniel Sullivan; the production still plans to open April 7 with previews from March 19. No details were given about the disputes or a replacement. Orphans, first staged in 1983 and adapted to film in 1987, is frequently revived regionally. LaBeouf, known for Transformers and the latest Indiana Jones, recently said he’s moving away from blockbusters toward riskier indie projects. He has upcoming roles in Robert Redford’s The Company You Keep and Lars von Trier’s Nymphomaniac. The release about LaBeouf’s exit was published alongside unrelated theater coverage about Tom Hanks’ Broadway debut in Nora Ephron’s Lucky Guy, reflecting Broadway’s continuing draw for film stars.

Afghanistan’s High Peace Council said it will allow a Taliban liaison office in Qatar to begin peace talks but insisted no foreign power may intervene without Kabul’s consent. The council, responding to reports that the U.S., Qatar and Germany had secretly arranged an office in Doha, set 11 conditions for engagement: the Taliban must halt violence against civilians, cut ties with al Qaeda and other terrorist groups, accept the Afghan constitution and preserve gains made since their ouster, and include recognized representatives from both sides. Kabul prefers any office be in Saudi Arabia or Turkey but will tolerate Doha if Afghan sovereignty is respected. The council also said Pakistan’s support is necessary because many insurgents are based there. Tensions with the U.S. rose over prisoner transfers from Guantanamo to Doha; Kabul demands custody of Afghan detainees. The document notes setbacks to reconciliation, including the assassination of peace council head Burhanuddin Rabbani and persistent Taliban rejection of talks while foreign troops remain.

The Supreme Court unanimously ruled that an Indiana farmer, Vernon Hugh Bowman, infringed Monsanto’s patent by planting and replanting soybeans containing Monsanto’s Roundup Ready gene without paying the company. Farmers who buy Monsanto’s patented seeds typically agree not to save seeds for replanting and must repurchase them annually. Bowman avoided those contracts for a later-season crop by buying mixed seeds from a grain elevator, planting them, applying Roundup, and saving seeds from survivors to sow future crops. Lower courts had found this constituted infringement, and Justice Elena Kagan, writing for the Court, affirmed that decision while stressing its narrow scope. Kagan held that the patent exhaustion doctrine allows a buyer to resell or consume a purchased patented item but does not permit creating new copies of the patented product without permission. Rejecting Bowman’s “blame-the-bean” claim that seeds self-replicated independently, she emphasized Bowman actively controlled reproduction across generations. The ruling protects inventors of self-replicating technologies—such as biotech, vaccines, cell lines, and software—by preserving patent value, though it does not settle all future cases involving self-replicating products. The decision drew praise from biotech industry leaders and criticism from farm and food-safety advocates who say it favors corporations over farmers.

Facebook analyzed about one million US English status updates using the LIWC word categories to identify linguistic and psychological patterns. Key findings: older users write longer updates, use more prepositions, articles, religious and family terms; younger users use fewer articles, more profanity, anger words, and self-references (“I”), and discuss school more. People with many friends use “you” and talk more about music and sports, are less emotional, and mention family less. Time of day matters: positive emotion words peak in the morning while negative emotions rise after 10 p.m.; references to sleep, work, and leisure follow daily routines. Posts with positive words get more likes but fewer comments; negative posts get more comments. Finally, friends show linguistic homophily, using similar word categories to one another.

One day before the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics opening, Google unveiled a pro-LGBT homepage Doodle: Olympic-themed silhouettes colored like the rainbow pride flag, appearing on all national Google sites including Russia’s. Clicking it links to the Olympic Charter text declaring sport a human right and condemning discrimination. The move highlighted global concern over Russia’s anti-"homosexual propaganda" law and President Putin’s statements. Some brands like AT&T and American Apparel voiced opposition; major Olympic sponsors had not. The Doodle was widely seen as a pointed, silent rebuke of Russia’s policies.

In mid-July in Forsyth County, Georgia, Nicole Bahret discovered her 18-year-old son, Mackean Robertson, had been killed in a three-car crash when she drove up to the wreck and recognized his vehicle. Bahret said she had seen and spoken with Mackean about an hour before the collision; he had asked to hang out with friends and she approved. Deputies reported that a white 2010 Mercedes SUV driven by 17-year-old Natalie D’Allen collided with Mackean’s white 2005 Honda Accord, causing the Honda to slide into the path of a westbound green Nissan Pathfinder. Mackean was pronounced dead at the scene; occupants of the other vehicles were hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries. Investigators said a teen driver’s failure to yield caused the crash; charges were pending while the probe continued. D’Allen later turned herself in and posted bond. Mackean, a recent Georgia Cyber Academy graduate who previously attended Forsyth Central High School, had started a job and enjoyed music, travel, and time with family and friends. He had attended local schools and was described by relatives and friends as joyful, always smiling, and well liked. Hundreds attended his funeral, with Forsyth Central’s marching band escorting his body from the church; the school planned a memorial on August 12. Bahret, a former special education teacher at Forsyth Central, expressed deep grief and said friends and family have been helping her cope. A fundraising page set up to assist with funeral costs raised more than $15,000. Authorities issued a correction clarifying that D’Allen caused the crash, not Robertson.

A forthcoming study in the European Journal of Personality suggests people can glean aspects of personality from body odor alone. Researchers in Poland had 30 men and 30 women wear cotton T‑shirts for three nights without fragrances or odorous foods; each donor completed a personality questionnaire. One hundred men and 100 women then rated shirts’ scents for five traits. Raters’ judgments reliably matched donors’ self‑reports for extraversion, neuroticism and dominance, though not perfectly. Accuracy for extraversion and neuroticism was comparable to judgments from short videos. Dominance was detected best across sexes, hinting at a mate‑choice role. Authors suggest physiological or hormonal differences (sweat, bacteria, testosterone) may drive scent cues; results are preliminary and require cross‑cultural replication.

Taylor Swift sparked intense speculation about new music after she wiped her social media clean and then returned August 21, 2017 with a short, cryptic video of what appears to be a snake’s tail. The blackout—deleting Instagram, Tumblr, post-2011 Tweets and replacing her website with a black screen—happened three days earlier and fell on the three-year anniversary of the 1989 era, fueling fan theories that a new album (commonly dubbed TS6) was imminent. Director Joseph Kahn, who worked with Swift on 1989 videos like “Bad Blood” and “Wildest Dreams,” reacted publicly: he quoted her tweet with a smiley face and joked that “In 30 minutes, as a show of power, @taylorswift13 will blot out the sun,” a tongue-in-cheek nod to both her celebrity and the 2017 solar eclipse happening then.

The snake imagery resonated because of Swift’s highly publicized 2016 feud with Kanye West and Kim Kardashian, when she was flooded with snake emojis and branded “a snake.” Many commentators and fans read the new posts as Swift leaning into that label—reclaiming and repurposing the symbol as part of a reinvention. Media outlets and social users compared the teaser to dragons and Game of Thrones, joked about eclipsing the solar event, and pointed to industry clues: sources told Us Weekly Swift had quietly been recording a new pop album aimed for a fall release to follow 1989’s massive success. The rollout—social purge, coded website changes, and enigmatic clips—set off a flurry of reactions, memes, and predictions that Swift’s next era, possibly tied to the snake motif, was about to begin.

Los Angeles prepared for a highly publicized 53-hour closure of a 10-mile stretch of Interstate 405 through the Sepulveda Pass to allow Caltrans to partially demolish a bridge and add a high-occupancy vehicle lane as part of a $1 billion widening project. Officials warned the shutdown would snarl the region—250,000 vehicles normally use that segment daily—potentially severing the San Fernando Valley from coastal communities and prompting comparisons to an apocalypse of traffic dubbed “Carmageddon.” City leaders urged people to avoid travel; Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa advised staying home or vacationing, and celebrities and social-media stars were recruited to spread the message. Anticipating massive congestion, many local merchants rolled out promotionary tactics and discounts to lure or serve stranded customers. Offers ranged from pet portrait discounts (“4-0-fido”) to tattoo and jewelry markdowns, restaurant prix-fixe dinners and bar specials, theme-park promotions for local zip codes, and novelty “Caltrans Orange” cotton candy. Aviation firms marketed aerial alternatives: JetBlue announced $4 shuttle flights between Burbank and Long Beach, while Briles Wing & Helicopter sold 15-minute luxury helicopter rides over the jam for a premium. Some businesses worried discounts wouldn’t overcome the disruption; Pacific Park on the Santa Monica Pier feared loss of typical summer visitors. The closure also evoked the 405 corridor’s long history of transformation: from Native trails and a 1930s Sepulveda Boulevard celebrated then quickly overburdened, to the 1960s engineering feat that carved the Big Cut and opened the modern eight-lane freeway amid huge earthmoving and concrete pours. The project’s scale and cultural imprint underscore Los Angeles’s deep dependence on freeways—and the persistent social and economic ripples when they are taken offline.

Occupy Wall Street marked its two-month anniversary with a citywide Day of Action that tested the movement after authorities cleared Zuccotti Park earlier in the week. Protesters planned morning attempts to disrupt Wall Street, midday gatherings at transit hubs across the five boroughs, student walkouts, a mass rally at Foley Square backed by unions, and a march across the Brooklyn Bridge. A heavy police presence, barricades and permits constrained access to key sites, but thousands nonetheless rallied and marched, with many actions centered on Lower Manhattan.

Clashes between protesters and police erupted repeatedly. Early confrontations near the New York Stock Exchange produced arrests as demonstrators tried to block workers, and police raids on and around Zuccotti Park led to scuffles, baton strikes and mass detentions. By midafternoon reports cited hundreds arrested—official totals reached into the low hundreds—with dozens injured among protesters and officers; several cops suffered injuries from thrown objects and liquids. Authorities confiscated devices that could be used to lock protesters to structures. High-profile arrests included City Councilman Jumaane Williams.

While many actions were peaceful—subway protests, union-backed rallies, creative projections on buildings—tensions were high as the city balanced accommodating First Amendment rights with restoring order. Organizers and volunteers worked to regroup the movement after the park sweep, arguing the eviction may have strengthened resolve by filtering out casual participants.

A man camping at Little Harbor Campground on Catalina Island was gored by a bison the afternoon of Saturday, Feb. 17, authorities said. The incident occurred around 5:15 p.m. while the camper was sitting on a log and a bison grazed nearby. When the animal moved closer, the man stood to move away and the bison charged, goring him in the left arm, Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Sgt. Ray Ward said. Los Angeles Fire Department personnel treated the man on scene and he was airlifted to Harbor-UCLA Medical Center. Bison roam freely on the island’s back side near the campground and are common there, though Ward stressed attacks are rare; visitors sometimes forget they are wild animals because they can appear domesticated. The man’s injury severity was not immediately released.

A North Carolina judge is considering whether to grant a new trial in the 1996 murder conviction of Daniel Green in the killing of James Jordan, father of basketball star Michael Jordan, according to reporting by the Charlotte Observer. Green was convicted in March 1996 after testimony from his alleged accomplice, Larry Martin Demery, who told jurors that he and Green approached James Jordan’s car intending to rob him and that Green shot Jordan after he awoke from a nap and saw them. 

Green’s attorneys, Scott Holmes and Ian Mance, have filed for a new trial, presenting new evidence they say undermines the conviction. Their key claims include a sworn statement from the jury forewoman alleging she conducted her own investigation into the murder during the trial in violation of the judge’s instructions, and an affidavit from a former Robeson County newspaper editor who says Demery admitted to committing the murder himself. Defense lawyers also challenge forensic evidence that reportedly linked Jordan’s blood to Green’s car, raising doubts about the reliability or interpretation of that state forensic expert’s findings.

The state has until the end of April to respond to the defense filing. After the state’s response, Robeson County Superior Court Judge Robert Floyd will decide whether to grant Green a new trial based on the newly presented materials and procedural concerns. The filings and the judge’s impending decision bring renewed attention to a high-profile case that has persisted for three decades. (This report also notes, separately, that starting in 1996 Alexa Internet has donated crawl data to the Internet Archive, contributing to the Wayback Machine.)

Former Rhode Island governor and senator Lincoln Chafee, whose Democratic presidential bid struggled with near-zero poll numbers and only about $30,000 raised, announced he was ending his long-shot 2016 campaign at the DNC Women’s Leadership Forum. Chafee, an anti-war candidate known for his focus on foreign policy and opposition to the Iraq War, had stumbled during a recent Democratic debate and faced public questioning about his viability. He declared his campaign in June on a platform he called “Prosperity Through Peace,” and used his farewell remarks to reiterate his plea for giving peace a chance. Chafee cited the recent consolidation of the Democratic field—Hillary Clinton’s strong week, Jim Webb’s withdrawal, and Joe Biden’s decision not to run—as factors influencing his choice to exit. A spokeswoman had not immediately commented on his plans following the announcement.

The single vice-presidential debate between Vice President Joe Biden and Rep. Paul Ryan became a high-stakes, must-win moment for both tickets after the first presidential debate shifted momentum toward Mitt Romney. Biden, meeting with advisers in Delaware, prepared an aggressive approach intended to spotlight Romney’s “47%” remarks and to draw sharp contrasts between the Obama administration’s policies and the Romney-Ryan agenda. Democrats hoped Biden could recapture initiative for the ticket by attacking Ryan’s fiscal proposals—particularly Medicare cuts in the House GOP budget—and by underscoring Romney’s inconsistent positions on Ryan’s plan.

Ryan, preparing in Florida, aimed to present himself as a credible, policy-savvy alternative and to shore up doubts about whether the GOP ticket deserves four more years. Known as a “numbers guy,” Ryan’s wonky budget mastery is both his strength and risk: it can help defend Romney-Ryan plans in detail, but deep policy talk had previously undermined President Obama in the presidential debate by bogging him down. Ryan needed to translate technical competence into accessible arguments that reassure voters he could serve as commander-in-chief if needed.

Key themes media and campaigns flagged included whether Biden would attack Romney directly rather than only Ryan, whether he could forcefully link Romney to Ryan’s proposals, and whether Biden would put Social Security back into play by highlighting Ryan’s past support for partial privatization. Biden’s style—combative, quick with jabs—made him suited to highlight risks older voters fear from proposed Medicare cuts, while the age gap between Biden (69) and Ryan (42) underscored a broader choice between experience and fresh direction.

The debate also drew controversy about moderator impartiality after conservative outlets questioned Martha Raddatz’s past social ties to Barack Obama—an angle widely lampooned in the press. Broadcast outlets like CNN emphasized broad access to coverage and interactive features. Both campaigns viewed a clear win as transformative and a clear loss as damaging; a draw would likely be spun variably but might preserve GOP momentum. Overall, the matchup tested Biden’s ability to score political blows and Ryan’s capacity to humanize wonkish policy for a national audience.

On a bleak February day in 1944 in the eastern French village of Gemeaux, two young Jewish sisters, Denise and Micheline Lévy, were arrested at school and forced outside into the snow with their parents, grandparents, an aunt and uncle, a cousin and other Jewish families. A gendarme snatched their dolls — one pink, one blue — from the girls as they were bundled toward deportation to Auschwitz, flinging the toys to the ground. The sisters never returned. A village shopkeeper picked up the abandoned dolls and gave them to the grandmother of Frédérique Gilles, a local teacher. For three generations the family kept the dolls and the memory of the girls and that day alive, preserving a small but poignant physical remnant of the community’s loss and the human face of deportation. On a recent Sunday, Gilles presented the dolls to the Shoah Memorial, the Holocaust museum in Paris, transferring custody of these objects and the story they embody to an institution dedicated to remembrance and education.

The account of the dolls’ preservation highlights both the intimacy of personal memory and the role of families and communities in safeguarding fragments of history that might otherwise be lost. It also underscores how ordinary objects can become powerful witnesses: toys abandoned in the snow came to symbolize the severed childhoods and erased lives of Holocaust victims. The donation to the museum ensures the dolls will be conserved, contextualized, and shown to broader audiences as part of efforts to remember and teach about the Holocaust. Preserving such artifacts and their stories contributes to collective memory and helps future generations grasp the human consequences of persecution and state-sponsored violence.

Nebraska honored late punter Sam Foltz during its season opener against Fresno State by sending out a ten-man punt formation with no punter on a 4th-and-4, prompting players, opponents and fans to clap and cheer in remembrance of Foltz and Michigan State’s Mike Sadler, who died in a car crash in July. After roughly a minute and a delay of game penalty, the team punted. Foltz had been Big Ten Punter of the Year, led the conference with a 44.2-yard average, and was on the Ray Guy watch list.

Clint Eastwood’s American Sniper, a commercial and awards-season success, has sparked debate in Hollywood over its portrayal of warfare and snipers. The biographical drama about Navy SEAL Chris Kyle—America’s most lethal sniper—earned a record January box-office opening, $105.2 million over four days, and six Oscar nominations including Best Picture and Best Actor for Bradley Cooper. While many praised the film’s craft and Cooper’s performance, several prominent figures criticized its perceived pro-war or glorifying elements.

Seth Rogen tweeted that the movie “kind of reminds me” of the fictional propagandistic film shown in the third act of Quentin Tarantino’s Inglourious Basterds, implying a troubling similarity; he later softened his comment, saying he “liked American Sniper” but that it reminded him of the Tarantino scene. Documentary filmmaker Michael Moore sparked even sharper discussion when he tweeted that snipers are “cowards,” noting his uncle was killed by a sniper in World War II. Moore later clarified that his initial tweets were not directly about Chris Kyle or the film, posting a longer Facebook note that both praised Bradley Cooper’s work and criticized aspects of Eastwood’s storytelling—accusing the film of conflating Vietnam and Iraq and featuring characters who call Iraqis “savages.” Moore also acknowledged anti-war elements and the tragic ending involving Kyle’s death at the hands of a fellow veteran.

The backlash drew responses from other public figures and ignited broader conversation about how wartime violence and veterans are depicted. Supporters included Jane Fonda, who tweeted her admiration for the film. Warner Bros. declined to comment. The debate highlights tensions between honoring military service, examining the psychological toll of combat, and the cultural implications of cinematic portrayals of war.

Russell Armstrong, 47, was found dead in Los Angeles in an apparent suicide weeks after his estranged wife Taylor Armstrong filed for divorce and after their marital conflicts were aired on Bravo’s The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills. Authorities reported he was found hanged at a friend’s home; the coroner’s office awaited autopsy and toxicology results. Coverage and friends’ accounts highlighted mounting pressures: public allegations of abuse by Taylor, looming divorce and litigation, past financial troubles including earlier bankruptcy and reports of renewed money problems, and a recent $1.5 million lawsuit. Russell and his attorney said the show amplified their personal and financial stress—Russell told reporters the program “pushed us to the limit,” and friends said he blamed reality TV for “ruining” his life. Media observers and scholars have criticized reality formats for manufacturing drama, exhausting participants, and intensifying vulnerability; producers and networks face questions about whether to air or reedit season-two episodes scheduled shortly after his death. Russell is survived by his daughter with Taylor and two sons from previous relationships. Family and Bravo have requested privacy; officials and his lawyer described his recent mood as depressed but not obviously suicidal.

A new study published in Occupational & Environmental Medicine found an association between higher levels of pyrethroid metabolites in children and their mothers and increased behavioral difficulties at age six. Pyrethroids are synthetic insecticides widely used in head-lice treatments (permethrin is a common example) and some mosquito repellents. Researchers measured five pyrethroid metabolites in urine samples collected from nearly 300 women during early pregnancy and later from their 6-year-old children. Home visits included behavioral assessments by psychologists, dust sampling, and questionnaires covering socioeconomic and lifestyle factors. Child behavior was evaluated using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, focusing on altruism, internalizing behaviors (e.g., withdrawal, inability to seek help), and externalizing behaviors (e.g., defiance, disruption). Three metabolites—trans-DCCA, cis-DBCA, and cis-DCCA—were most frequently detected. Key findings: higher maternal cis-DCCA during pregnancy linked to greater risk of internalizing behaviors in children; higher 3-PBA in children’s urine associated with higher risk of externalizing behaviors; and overall, children with the highest pyrethroid metabolite levels were about three times likelier to show abnormal behaviors. Researchers suggest pyrethroids might alter neurochemical signaling, but emphasize these are correlational results, not proof of causation. Experts cited call for more rigorous studies. Given widespread use—CDC estimates up to 12 million U.S. head-lice infestations yearly—parents may be concerned; alternatives include alcohol-based treatments, ivermectin, and non-pyrethroid products such as Sklice or more natural options like Licefreee.

A UC San Diego study published in Infection and Immunity finds that cigarette smoke makes MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) markedly harder to kill and more virulent. Researchers exposed MRSA to cigarette smoke extract and compared it with unexposed bacteria in lab cell cultures and mouse models. Macrophages—the immune cells that engulf pathogens—were less able to kill smoke-exposed MRSA: these bacteria were about four times more resistant to macrophage killing. Smoke-exposed MRSA showed increased resistance to reactive oxygen species and to antimicrobial peptides, both key innate immune defenses, and adhered better to human cells, enhancing invasion. Changes to the bacterial cell wall appear to underlie this heightened resistance; effects were dose-dependent and persisted for at least 24 hours, suggesting potential transmission to progeny. In mice, smoke-exposed MRSA caused higher mortality. Related earlier work indicated e-cigarette vapor can produce similar but weaker effects—cigarette smoke induced roughly tenfold greater surface changes than e-cigarette vapor. The authors conclude cigarette smoke not only harms host immunity but directly stresses pathogens, prompting adaptive changes that increase severity of infection, offering another public-health reason to avoid smoking.

Sen. David Perdue sparked controversy after citing Psalm 109:8 during remarks at the Faith and Freedom Coalition’s “Road to Majority” conference, saying, “We should pray like Psalms 109:8 says. It says, ‘Let his days be few, let another have his office,’” referring to President Barack Obama. Perdue’s office and spokeswoman Megan Whittemore (and Caroline Vanvick in other accounts) insisted he did not wish harm on Obama, arguing he was urging prayer for leaders and criticizing media for “pushing a narrative to create controversy.” The line prompted laughter in the audience but drew sharp criticism from Democrats, who accused Perdue of effectively praying for the president’s death; Kristen Orthman, a spokeswoman for Senate Minority Leader Harry Reid, cited the remark as evidence of extreme rhetoric at the conference.

Observers noted the broader context: Psalm 109 is an imprecatory psalm that curses enemies, and the verse Perdue quoted is followed by harsher lines calling for bereavement and ruin. Scholars weighed in: Harvard’s Michael Coogan called such psalms examples of calling on God to punish enemies and suggested Perdue likely spoke tongue-in-cheek, while Graham Cole of Trinity Evangelical found the usage puzzling but not necessarily a literal wish for death. The passage has a history in conservative circles—dubbed the “Obama Prayer”—and has previously provoked controversies when public officials referenced it.

New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie is expected to decide within days whether to enter the presidential race, weighing the practical difficulties of a late campaign against political opportunity. Christie spent much of the weekend consulting with aides, family and his wife about the logistics and viability of an 11th-hour bid, reflecting concerns in his inner circle about the increasingly compressed calendar and the heavy demands of launching a national campaign on short notice. He attended a New Jersey National Guard event Sunday but declined to answer reporters’ shouted questions about his intentions. The situation underscores the challenge for any prospective late entrant: organizing staff, fundraising, message development and ballot access quickly enough to compete effectively. Operatives familiar with the matter have been discussing strategy and feasibility, probing whether Christie can marshal the resources and momentum needed to make a meaningful impact. The broader context includes archived news sites and other media sources that track political developments and commentary. Those archives—covering a range of formats and viewpoints, often progressive—note that archived copies may differ from original web content for technical, privacy or other reasons. Christie’s imminent announcement could reshape the field, but substantial hurdles remain for a successful late start.

Two weeks before the Paris attacks, Brussels police shut a Molenbeek café, Les Beguines, after finding customers with drugs and ashtrays with partially smoked joints. The bar had been run by brothers Brahim and Salah Abdeslam until they sold it about six weeks ago; Brahim retained majority ownership on company papers while Salah served as manager. Neighbors and friends describe the brothers as ordinary, sociable men who drank, smoked and played cards at the cafe — behavior at odds with the Islamist motives now linked to the attacks. Brahim, 31, detonated a suicide vest at the Comptoir Voltaire in Paris, wounding bystanders, while Salah is now Europe’s most wanted man and the subject of an intense manhunt. Family members and acquaintances say they saw no signs of radicalization; a brother held briefly by police was released with an alibi. Belgian media and court documents show Les Beguines was ordered closed for five months after an August raid which found a “strong smell of drugs” and customers carrying illegal substances. Reports link Salah’s past to petty crime and to acquaintances like Abdelhamid Abaaoud, believed by French investigators to have coordinated the attacks from Syria. The arrests and siege in Molenbeek spotlight the district’s social problems—youth unemployment, overcrowding, and alleged jihadist networks—and have prompted Belgian officials to vow a crackdown. The community remains stunned that men who led commonplace, secular lives could be tied to such deadly violence.

The House on Friday passed the "Keep Your Health Plan Act" 261-157, allowing insurers to renew or sell individual policies canceled under the Affordable Care Act that don’t meet its new standards. Thirty-nine Democrats broke with party leadership to support the bill despite a White House veto threat; only four Republicans opposed it. The vote highlighted political pain for vulnerable Democrats facing tough 2014 reelection races and intensified pressure on Senate leaders to act. President Obama had announced an administrative fix Thursday to let insurers renew existing plans for most of 2014, which blunted but did not eliminate defections. Republicans argued the House bill restores a broken presidential promise—“if you like your plan, you can keep it”—and accused the administration of relying on administrative maneuvers instead of Congress. Democrats warned Upton’s measure would undermine the ACA by creating a “shadow market” of substandard plans that could destabilize insurance exchanges and raise rates; they argued the president’s limited, time-bound fix was preferable. Procedural moves blocked Democratic alternatives that would have extended canceled policies only temporarily. The bill’s prospects in the Democratic-led Senate are uncertain and Obama has vowed to veto it. Both sides framed the fight as political and policy clashes over implementation missteps and protecting consumers versus preserving ACA reforms.

Facebook has launched its App Center, a centralized discovery hub for web and mobile apps that personalizes recommendations using user ratings and friends’ activity. Rolling out first in the U.S. and then to its 901 million users, the store opens with over 600 apps including Draw Something, Pinterest, Nike+, Stitcher Radio, Ghost Recon Commander, Jetpack Joyride and others. The App Center isn’t a replacement for Apple’s App Store or Google Play; rather it links out to those stores for downloads while serving as a curated directory that highlights “high-quality” apps based on engagement and feedback.

Accessible via Facebook’s iOS and Android apps and at Facebook.com (desktop and mobile), the App Center tailors suggestions by the apps you and your friends use, and organizes offerings into categories like Games, Entertainment, Music and News. On desktop it shows recommended and friends’ apps, detailed app pages, and web-playable apps or links to platform stores. The mobile version is more streamlined—opening to “Social Picks” and Top Apps—but offers fewer browsing categories and occasionally obscures platform compatibility, which can cause download errors if a link points to an unavailable platform.

Designed to keep users engaged on Facebook and drive app discovery, the App Center arrives amid debates about platform control and the broader economic growth in mobile apps, a market projected to generate substantial revenue in coming years.

The Jets defeated the Bengals 24-14 in an emotional AFC wild-card win in Cincinnati, advancing to the divisional round. Rookie quarterback Mark Sanchez played superbly, completing 12 of 15 passes for 182 yards and a touchdown and becoming the fourth rookie QB to win a playoff game. The team played turnover-free football, overcame an early deficit, and sealed the game with two late sacks. Coach Rex Ryan, visibly moved, dedicated the lone game ball to grieving owner Woody Johnson. The victory, the second over Cincinnati in six days, bolstered the Jets’ belief they’re serious postseason contenders.

Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder publicly apologized for the Flint water crisis and pledged full responsibility for fixing what he called a “catastrophe.” In his State of the State address he acknowledged residents “face a crisis you did not create,” apologized—“I’m sorry I let you down”—and promised transparency by releasing his 2014–2015 emails about Flint. Snyder outlined immediate actions: door-to-door distribution of bottled water, filters, replacements and testing kits (over 21,000 homes visited), and proposed budget measures to keep Flint on Detroit’s water through 2016, replace pipes and school fixtures, and fund local health follow-up staff. He requested $28 million from legislators for short-term needs including bottled water and filters, fixture replacement in schools and hospitals, treatment and testing for children with high lead levels, behavioral-health services, support for youth health centers, an infrastructure integrity study using outside experts, and utility aid for the city. Snyder vowed accountability for those responsible.

The crisis began in April 2014 when Flint switched from Detroit’s Lake Huron supply to the Flint River to save money; corrosive river water, untreated for corrosion control, leached lead from aging service lines. Virginia Tech researchers later found dangerously high lead levels in some homes. Flint reverted to Lake Huron water in October 2015, but pipe damage remained. Residents, local leaders and lawmakers criticized the state response as slow and inadequate; protests demanded Snyder’s resignation and legal teams filed multiple lawsuits alleging constitutional and negligent misconduct. Snyder defended his actions in interviews, saying state officials acted when they knew elevated blood lead levels, but conceded failures by the Department of Environmental Quality and vowed to rebuild trust while providing ongoing aid and remediation.

Two young Indonesian friends who had studied together in Australia are at the center of a high-profile murder investigation after newlywed Wayan Mirna Salihin, 27, died following a sip of Vietnamese iced coffee in Jakarta. Mirna collapsed after complaining the drink tasted bad at the Olivier cafe in Grand Indonesia Mall and later died in hospital; police say cyanide was found in her stomach and in the coffee. Jessica Kumala Wongso, who ordered Mirna’s drink and had studied with Mirna and another friend, Hani, in Australia, has been arrested and named a suspect. Authorities say Jessica’s statements were inconsistent with other evidence, and investigators have collected around 20 witness statements, carried out a reenactment, and assembled multiple expert inputs — forensic, forensic psychiatry and criminal experts — to build the case. Police say they have four of five evidentiary items required under the Criminal Code to name a suspect and will present the dossier to prosecutors; they also sought assistance from the Australian Federal Police to clarify the friends’ relationships from their time studying abroad. Jessica denies involvement; her uncle and lawyer, Yudi Wibowo, insists she is innocent and has requested a second autopsy, questioning the initial procedures. Investigators have questioned Hani repeatedly, placed a household staff member in protection as a key witness, and synchronized witness testimony, lab results, CCTV and reenactment findings as they prepare to proceed to trial.

Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio emerged quickly as the leading candidate during the conclave that elected him Pope Francis, winning on the fifth ballot with at least the required two-thirds majority. Observers say early ballots included “courtesy” votes for many names, but votes consolidated around Bergoglio after private discussions and congregations where cardinals debated the need to reform and streamline the Vatican bureaucracy. Journalists reported that Bergoglio, Cardinal Angelo Scola and Cardinal Marc Ouellet initially led; Scola had a solid European and American base but was weakened by opposition tied to Curia controversies and the Vatileaks scandal. Bergoglio’s candidacy benefited from broad support, including strong backing from Latin American electors, and from his reputation as a persuasive, reform-minded pastor who had urged purification of church structures.

Despite being 76—older than some cardinals preferred given concerns about papal longevity—Bergoglio’s age was seen as both a spur to action and less threatening to conservatives. He was viewed as theologically sound yet pastoral and down-to-earth, able to connect with the developing world where Catholicism grows. His election marked the first non-European pope in more than a millennium and the first from the Americas. Publicly, Francis impressed with humility: he asked the crowd for their blessing, chose the name Francis, refused an elevated throne, rode the bus with fellow cardinals, and even returned to his hotel to collect luggage and pay the bill. Vatican insiders and observers described his selection as driven by personality, pastoral credibility, and a desire for renewal in church governance.

Conservative activist Andrew Breitbart, who exposed a photo sent from Rep. Anthony Weiner’s Twitter account to a woman, says he holds an explicit, uncensored image he’ll publicize if Weiner retaliates. Weiner has admitted the crotch photo was his and acknowledged inappropriate contact with six women over three years via social media and phone. Breitbart described the explicit image as an “insurance policy” against reprisals and suggested more women could come forward if Weiner invites further scrutiny. Breitbart later showed the uncensored photo on Sirius radio, where hosts photographed and circulated it online, making the image widely available despite its unsuitability for television. Observers note the explicit photo may deepen public reaction and further damage Weiner politically.

Nashua authorities said they believe a body recovered Sunday from the Merrimack River is that of 16-year-old Jacob Goulet, a Nashua High School North student who disappeared during an intense rainstorm Friday night. A Massachusetts State Police helicopter spotted a body near Parlee Farms in Tyngsborough around 11:38 a.m.; Tyngsborough crews and Nashua divers recovered the body by about 12:20 p.m. Police are awaiting positive identification by the Massachusetts chief medical examiner, but said the clothing and description match Goulet.

Goulet’s parents filed a missing-person report Saturday after he did not return home from a friend’s house. Surveillance video showed him near an open sewer behind 75 Main St. Friday night, and a caller later reported personal items — a baseball cap and an umbrella — near the uncovered drain. City officials and family members believe Goulet may have fallen at least 20 feet into an interceptor sewer that connects to the wastewater treatment system and can overflow into the Merrimack during heavy storms. The cover, about 4 by 4 feet, should not have been open; officials said they are investigating how it came off. The city resecured the cover Sunday and has inspected roughly 1,000 feet of the sewer system so far.

A massive multi-agency search over the weekend included Nashua police and fire dive teams, public works crews, state police, Fish and Game, and private contractors using sewer cameras. The community has been rocked by the likely loss: classmates, neighbors and strangers left flowers and tributes at a memorial, the school prepared grief counseling for students, and a GoFundMe was launched to help with funeral expenses. Nashua leaders expressed condolences and vowed to investigate the sewer safety issue.

Secretary of State John Kerry’s offhand proposal that Syria avert U.S. military strikes by surrendering its chemical weapons unexpectedly opened a diplomatic avenue that could spare military action. Russia, Syria’s main backer and arms supplier, immediately endorsed the idea: Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov urged Damascus to place chemical stockpiles under international control and destroy them, and Syria’s foreign minister welcomed the proposal. The United Nations secretary-general and Britain’s prime minister quickly supported the concept, and President Obama called it “a potentially positive development,” saying it deserved a hard look.

The article argues the Obama administration should pursue this route despite well-founded skepticism about Assad’s reliability and Russia’s motives. Removing and destroying Syrian chemical weapons under international supervision would reduce civilian risk and create longer-lasting deterrence without immediate U.S. strikes. For credibility, Assad must allow immediate access to monitors; Russia must cooperate with the U.S. and U.N. to catalog, verify, and timetable the removal and destruction, backed by a U.N. Security Council resolution that condemns chemical weapon use, authorizes the operation, and sets consequences for noncompliance.

Prominent critic Michael Doran warns the plan may be a sham that lets Assad and Putin avoid consequences and boxes in the U.S. He tweeted eight “truths” arguing Assad will not truly relinquish his weapons, Russia will exploit negotiations, and the U.S. has lost coercive leverage after congressional resistance to strikes. In an interview he urged demanding immediate, verifiable steps—rapid accession to the chemical weapons convention, site listings, and immediate monitoring—while acknowledging such measures require credible follow-up U.S. policy, potentially including stronger support for opposition forces. Doran also cautions that lengthy inspections and negotiation could be gamed, echoing the U.N. Iraq WMD experience, and that embracing Russia and Assad risks signaling U.S. weakness to allies. The diplomatic proposal provides a pause and potential political opening, but success hinges on rapid, enforceable verification and sustained international resolve.

Middlesex County authorities are investigating the suspicious disappearance of 23-year-old mother TerriLynn St. John after she was last seen early Tuesday morning at her Mill Wharf Road home. Family members say St. John went to her car around 7:30 a.m. to prepare to take her two young children to daycare and that a struggle was evident near the vehicle. Her father reported jewelry scattered nearby and her cell phone found in the bushes. The children, ages three and one, were discovered at home alone but unharmed by relatives who had gone to check when she did not show up for work.

Major Michael Sampson of the Middlesex Sheriff’s Office characterized the case as a missing person under suspicious circumstances and said it was too soon to determine whether she was abducted. Investigators have identified and interviewed four persons of interest, including St. John’s boyfriend; those questioned have cooperated and provided DNA samples now being tested at the Richmond crime lab. A K9 unit, air surveillance, and searches on foot have been used, and neighboring jurisdictions and Virginia State Police are on standby to assist if needed.

Officials urged anyone who saw anything unusual in the area early Tuesday to come forward and called on the tight-knit community to share tips directly with law enforcement rather than relying solely on social media. Sampson noted that unverified online posts create extra work by forcing investigators to chase leads that could distract from primary investigative efforts. TerriLynn is described as a white female, 5'6", 130 pounds, with blonde hair and blue eyes, last seen wearing a blue Outer Banks hoodie and bearing several tattoos. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Middlesex Sheriff’s Office.

On July 4, 2016, multiple suicide bombings struck Saudi Arabia, including an explosion near the Prophet Muhammad’s Mosque in Medina, a blast near the U.S. Consulate in Jeddah, and attacks in the Shiite-majority area of Qatif in the Eastern Province. State-linked media reported a suicide bomber detonated near a security building outside the Prophet’s Mosque, igniting car fires; initial reports on casualties were unclear. Witnesses said the blast shook the area during Ramadan’s final days when many pilgrims were present. In Jeddah a man detonated explosives when guards approached near the heavily fortified consulate; he died and two security officers were lightly wounded, with no consular staff harmed. In Qatif a suicide vest and a car bomb exploded near a Shiite mosque as residents were breaking the fast; no immediate fatalities were reported but the region has been targeted previously by IS-affiliated attackers. Saudi authorities said the Jeddah attacker was a non-Saudi resident; investigations continued and no group immediately claimed responsibility.

The coordinated strikes highlighted the extremist threat facing the kingdom, which backs U.S.-led efforts against the Islamic State. King Salman vowed to crack down “with an iron hand” on those radicalizing youth, while the U.N. human rights chief called the Medina attack “an attack on Islam itself.” Saudi leaders, including Crown Prince Mohammed bin Nayef, reassured the public about security efforts. The U.S. Embassy warned Americans to be cautious, and regional arrests in Kuwait suggested broader concern about IS-linked plots targeting Shiite worshippers during Ramadan.

Philadelphia’s civic malaise has prompted an unusual get-out-the-vote effort: The Philadelphia Citizen, co-founded by Larry Platt and Ajay Raju, announced a lottery that will award $10,000 to one person who votes in the Nov. 3 municipal election. The promotion—publicly launched by Platt alongside former mayors John F. Street and ex-GOP candidate Sam Katz—aims to spark conversation and boost turnout after chronically low participation (only 27% in the May 2015 primary). The prize money comes from the Pamela and Ajay Raju Foundation. Organizers plan to randomize among all 1,686 voting divisions, visit the chosen polling place on Election Day, and give the first voter leaving that site the $10,000 check, subject to eligibility checks; if ineligible, a random voter from the division’s turnout list will be selected. Supporters point to a similar Los Angeles experiment where a $25,000 prize coincided with higher turnout among informed residents, though its overall impact was debated. Local election-law attorneys at the announcement said the nonpartisan incentive is legal so long as voters aren’t instructed to support a specific candidate. Reactions were mixed: some civic leaders called the effort a pragmatic experiment to revive participation, while critics argued it demeans voting and confuses incentives. Organizers emphasize the prize is not an endorsement and hope the contest prompts broader engagement and discussion about reforms—like automatic registration and same-day registration—to address long-term turnout decline.

Peggy Frank, a 63-year-old U.S. Postal Service carrier of roughly 28–30 years, was found unresponsive in her mail truck in Woodland Hills on a day when temperatures soared into the upper 110s. Paramedics attempted resuscitation but she was pronounced dead at the scene. The Los Angeles County coroner completed an autopsy but deferred the official cause of death pending additional tests; officials noted she had some unspecified medical history. Frank had recently returned to work after months off with a broken ankle and was months away from retirement. Family members and coworkers described her as upbeat and hardworking; relatives say she had suffered heat stroke the previous summer.

The death reignited concerns about postal workers’ safety in extreme heat because USPS delivery vehicles lack air conditioning. Coworkers reported cabin temperatures can run 10–15 degrees hotter than outside, and relatives blamed the Postal Service for not doing enough to protect employees. USPS issued a statement expressing condolences and noting a national Heat Illness Prevention Program that mandates training and advises hydration, shade, proper clothing, and carrying water and ice. Federal OSHA has previously cited the Postal Service after heat-related incidents, including a willful violation tied to a carrier’s death in 2012. Investigations into Frank’s death are ongoing, and family members urge procedural changes to prevent similar tragedies as heat waves intensify.

Usaamah Rahim, a 26-year-old security guard whom authorities say was radicalized online, was fatally shot by FBI-led counterterrorism agents in Boston after allegedly waving a large military knife and refusing to drop it. Investigators say Rahim initially plotted to behead activist Pamela Geller but then decided to attack police officers—calling them "the easiest target"—and bought three fighting knives. He had been under 24-hour surveillance as part of a probe into Islamist extremist activity and had discussed violent plans with associates, including David Wright, who was charged with obstructing the investigation for allegedly destroying Rahim’s phone and faces detention. Police showed video to community leaders to address disputed accounts that Rahim was shot in the back while on a cellphone; leaders said the footage contradicted that claim but remained inconclusive on some details. Local and federal authorities continue investigating potential wider connections.

General Motors is recalling about 1.205 million late-model pickup trucks and large SUVs worldwide, including roughly 1.02 million vehicles in the United States, because of a steering defect tied to electronically controlled power steering. The recall affects certain 2015 Chevrolet, GMC and Cadillac pickup trucks and sport-utility vehicles. According to a filing with federal safety regulators and a company statement, the problem can cause a temporary loss of power steering that may return suddenly, leaving drivers with unexpected steering resistance or a brief loss of steering assist. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration warned this condition can make steering difficult, particularly at low speeds, and increase crash risk. GM has received reports of 30 crashes and two injuries potentially linked to the issue, but no deaths. Dealers will remedy the defect by updating the power steering module software at no cost to vehicle owners. This action follows a similar GM recall in 2017 that affected nearly 800,000 pickup trucks worldwide for the same problem, highlighting ongoing challenges as automakers increasingly rely on software to manage mechanical vehicle functions.

A massive leak of more than 250,000 U.S. diplomatic cables, first obtained by WikiLeaks and shared with major newspapers, exposed candid assessments, covert efforts and awkward diplomacy spanning decades. Early publication began after German magazine Der Spiegel’s pages were sold prematurely. The documents include blunt personal descriptions of world leaders—Kim Jong-il’s alleged epilepsy, Muammar Gaddafi’s “voluptuous blonde” nurse, Angela Merkel dubbed “Teflon,” Hamid Karzai “driven by paranoia,” Putin an “Alpha Male” and Medvedev “afraid, hesitant”—and claim U.S. officials thought President Obama “prefers to look East” and “has no feelings for Europe.” Governments warned the release could endanger lives; WikiLeaks said critics feared accountability. Newspapers including The New York Times, The Guardian, Le Monde, El País and Der Spiegel published material selectively, redacting names of vulnerable sources.

The cables reveal secretive U.S. efforts and diplomatic bargaining: attempts to remove Pakistani highly enriched uranium, contingency planning for a collapsing North Korea and energetic negotiations to relocate Guantánamo detainees. They document corruption allegations—Afghan officials carrying large cash sums—global hacking campaigns tied to China, arms flows from Syria to Hezbollah, and friction with European governments over legal probes into CIA activities. The trove spans 1966–2010 but is concentrated post-2007, offering a raw chronicle of U.S. foreign relations in the post-9/11 era: managing terrorism, balancing rising China and resurgent Russia, countering Iran’s nuclear program, and navigating the messy, human realities of statecraft.

Satellite data show Greenland’s ice sheet experienced an unprecedented, rapid melt in July: between July 8 and July 12 melting expanded from about 40% to roughly 97% of the surface, a record in over 30 years of observations. Three independent satellites (ISRO’s Oceansat‑2, and NASA’s Terra/Aqua MODIS, plus a U.S. Air Force sensor) confirmed the event, which stunned researchers who initially suspected a data error. Scientists attribute the widespread thaw to a persistent “heat dome” — a strong ridge of warm air lingering over Greenland from roughly July 8–16. The melt reached unusually high elevations, with signs even near Summit Station (~3.2 km altitude). Researchers noted this episode sits alongside multi‑decadal trends of earlier, longer, and more frequent summer melting across the ice sheet. Consequences include added contribution to sea‑level rise (Greenland currently accounts for about one‑fifth of annual rise) and Arctic warming feedbacks. While similar events may occur infrequently in natural cycles, repeated occurrences would be worrisome and are consistent with expectations from human‑driven climate warming.

Researchers are finding that awe—a feeling of encountering something vast that transcends understanding—may have unique, measurable benefits for health, decision-making, social behavior, and well-being. Multiple studies summarized here link awe to reduced inflammation markers (lower interleukin-6) in college students, suggesting possible physical-health advantages distinct from other positive emotions. Laboratory experiments from Stanford and Minnesota show awe expands people’s subjective sense of time, increasing patience, reducing materialism, and boosting willingness to volunteer. Berkeley researchers propose two complementary explanations for why awe matters. Distally, awe may have evolved to bind individuals into cooperative social groups: experiencing awe reduces self-focus, embeds people in larger collectives, and promotes generosity and resource-sharing—behaviors demonstrated in experiments where awe increased helping and cooperation. Proximally, awe stimulates curiosity, wonder, and creative thinking, encouraging people to persist on difficult tasks and to generate more novel ideas. Everyday experiences—sunrises, music, nature, acts of kindness, even a perfect burrito—can elicit awe; it’s not as rare as assumed, occurring roughly every few days for many people. Preliminary evidence links routine awe to longer-term increases in well-being and curiosity, and researchers speculate that lack of awe might contribute to stress-related health burdens in disadvantaged populations. Scholars recommend seeking more daily awe—pausing to notice what overwhelms comprehension—as a simple, accessible practice with potentially broad psychological, social, and physical benefits.

A UPS Airbus A300-600F cargo plane crashed on approach to Birmingham-Shuttlesworth International Airport before dawn, coming down about a half-mile north of the runway and breaking apart across roughly 300 yards. The pilot and co-pilot were killed; no ground injuries were reported. There was no distress call before impact. Wreckage smoldered, delaying recovery of the flight recorders, and investigators from the NTSB and FAA are probing the cause. Weather was calm with light showers; debris and damaged power lines affected nearby buildings.

Bobby Fuller’s death on July 18, 1966, remains a haunting mystery for friends and family. Found slumped in his car outside his Hollywood apartment with a can of gasoline nearby, police ruled the cause of death inhalation of gasoline and labeled it either a suicide or an accident. That conclusion has been vehemently rejected by those who knew him. Family and friends cite blood and abrasions on Fuller’s body and his temperament as reasons to doubt a self-inflicted or accidental explanation. Younger brother Randy Fuller insists Bobby would never have taken his own life, especially given their elderly mother’s presence in town at the time, and believes Bobby “got in a bad situation” with the wrong person. Musician Rod Crosby and longtime acquaintance Boyd Elder describe Fuller as polite, not self-destructive, and unlikely to intentionally harm himself. A persistent rumor suggests Fuller became entangled with a low-level mobster jealous over a woman Fuller was seeing, leading to a violent confrontation that spiraled out of control—“disorganized crime” rather than a planned hit. With more than three decades passed, those close to Fuller say the truth may never be known. Interest endures, however: the Entertainment Channel planned a program on Fuller, and a biography and related events continue to revisit his life and enigmatic death.

Tony Trapani, 81, of Grand Rapids, Mich., discovered a letter last year that revealed he had a son he never knew about. While cleaning out his late wife’s filing cabinet, Trapani found a 1959 letter from a woman who wrote that her five-year-old son, born November 13, 1953, was his child. The boy, Samuel Childress, is now 61. Childress said his mother had told him she mailed the note but assumed Trapani ignored it; he grew up in Pennsylvania believing his father didn’t want to meet him. Trapani and his late wife had been unable to have children, and he now believes his wife intercepted and hid the letter for decades. Tearful and stunned, Trapani described Childress as “my full son that I’ve had my whole life,” while also expressing bewilderment that his wife concealed the message. The two men met for the first time recently and are spending time catching up and building the relationship they missed over six decades. They plan to take a paternity test to confirm the biological link. Both are trying to focus on making the most of their newfound connection rather than dwelling on the past secrecy that kept them apart.

The government launched a “Tech Surge” to fix Healthcare.gov, bringing in dozens of engineers, developers, designers and analysts from the public and private sectors, including Red Hat, Oracle, Google, and others. Two highlighted contributors are Michael Dickerson, a site reliability engineer on leave from Google working with general contractor QSSI to stabilize high-throughput components and improve reliability and performance, and Greg Gershman, a developer/entrepreneur and former Presidential Innovation Fellow working with CGI to optimize performance and make development more agile for faster improvements. QSSI coordinates the effort to ensure experts are used efficiently against a prioritized punch list. The surge supplements ongoing 24/7 work to resolve bugs that have hampered enrollments; officials expect continued fixes through the planned target dates. For more info, visit hhs.gov/healthcare or healthcare.gov/contact-us.

After months of leaks and anticipation, Lady Gaga’s nine-minute "Telephone" video, featuring Beyoncé, premiered March 11 on E! News. Part short film, part dance spectacle, it mixes pop-culture references—from Caged Heat and Kill Bill to David LaChapelle-style color—with over-the-top costumes, celebrity cameos and heavy product placement. Written by Gaga and director Jonas Åkerlund, the clip opens in a women’s prison where Gaga endures a lurid, stylized confinement before answering a phone and launching into the song. After a provocative yard dance sequence she’s bailed out by Beyoncé, who arrives in the “P—y Wagon.” The pair race into the desert, stop at a diner where Beyoncé poisons a rude Tyrese Gibson and other patrons, and perform campy choreography amid the bodies.
