Interludes include a bizarre “Let’s Make a Sandwich” skit with blatant Wonder Bread and Miracle Whip logos and surreal visual gags. The video closes with Gaga and Beyoncé driving into the sunset as “To Be Continued...” appears. Bold, ambitious and cinematic, "Telephone" is hailed as a major pop-media event—packing humor, shock and spectacle—and cements Gaga’s reputation for theatrical blockbuster videos.

A court hearing in the sexual-assault case against former IMF chief Dominique Strauss-Kahn was postponed two weeks to Aug. 1 so both sides can continue investigating, prosecutors and his lawyers said. Strauss-Kahn has pleaded not guilty to charges that he assaulted a Sofitel maid in Manhattan; prosecutors have questioned the maid’s credibility after she admitted lying about various matters. His lawyer urged dismissal, while the district attorney said the probe is ongoing and the victim’s attorney said the case should go to trial. Separately in France, novelist Tristane Banon—who accused Strauss-Kahn of a 2003 attempted rape—was interviewed by police in a preliminary inquiry, and Strauss-Kahn’s team filed a slander complaint against her.

Doug “Deo” Odolecki stood on a Parma, Ohio, sidewalk holding a white poster board reading “Check point ahead! Turn now!” to warn drivers about a nearby DUI checkpoint. Parma Police Lt. Brian McCann asked him to remove the instruction to “turn now,” saying it obstructed police business; Odolecki refused and was cited by Officer James Manzo. Odolecki, who has used the same sign for two years without issue, said officers “tried to be as civil as they could knowing they were violating someone’s rights.” His attorney, John Gold, is representing him pro bono, arguing the instruction to turn is protected First Amendment speech and that Odolecki posed no safety hazard while standing on the sidewalk. Ohio law requires police to notify the public about checkpoints in advance, and a pending bill would let drivers warn others by flashing headlights.

Deputy Sheriff Patrick Rohrer was fatally shot and his partner seriously wounded while transporting a prisoner to the Wyandotte County Correction and Court Services Building around 11:15 a.m. In a separate story, Oconee County, Georgia Sheriff Scott Berry used Facebook to announce a tongue-in-cheek cancellation of Valentine’s Day for men across a large swath of the state after an ice storm closed many stores. Berry declared a “NO VALENTINES DAY ZONE” from north of I-16 to the Georgia–Tennessee border, excusing men from buying typical Valentine’s items until February 18 so they could recover from the weather. He told Fox News the proclamation came after seeing numerous store closures; his chief deputy called it typical “hijinks.” Berry clarified the order won’t be enforced and admitted he won’t follow it at home. The post was widely shared—over 1,500 times—and drew some criticism, including a protest call from a Michigan area code. The Associated Press contributed to the report.

Flappy Bird, the unexpectedly viral mobile game created by Hanoi developer Dong Nguyen, was removed from both Apple’s App Store and Google Play after Nguyen announced he would pull it down, saying he “could not take this anymore.” The simple yet infuriating game—tapping a bird through gaps between green pipes—launched in May 2013 but shot to the top of download charts in early February 2014, reportedly earning roughly $50–55,000 a day from ads and achieving up to 50 million Android downloads. Nguyen tweeted the 22-hour warning before disabling downloads; users who already had the app could continue to play. His decision sparked intense backlash, with some fans issuing extreme threats and widespread media attention, generating hundreds of thousands of retweets. Nguyen, who developed Flappy Bird alone over a few nights and said he did not want investors or to sell the game, cited stress and unwanted publicity rather than legal reasons for the removal. Rumors that Nintendo had sent a warning were denied by Nintendo. Industry observers suggested Nguyen’s choice might avoid potential legal risks and noted the game’s hit-driven, uncertain long-term investment appeal.

Former President George W. Bush took part in the viral Ice Bucket Challenge to raise awareness and funds for ALS, accepting nominations from several people including his daughter Jenna Bush Hager. In a video posted to his Facebook page, Bush initially joked that being splashed was “not presidential” and said he would write a check instead—only to have former First Lady Laura Bush pour a bucket of ice water over him, quipping that the check was hers to avoid ruining her hair. After the soak, Bush nominated his predecessor, Bill Clinton, to take the challenge, noting it was a belated birthday gift. The Ice Bucket Challenge has been a widespread social-media phenomenon, generating millions for ALS research—nearly $22.9 million in three weeks and at one point $15 million reported—while celebrities and public figures joined in. President Barack Obama declined to be doused but donated to an ALS charity. Jenna Bush Hager helped arrange her father’s participation; the stunt highlighted both the campaign’s fundraising success and its appeal across political and celebrity circles.

A chartered LaMia British Aerospace 146 carrying Brazil’s Chapecoense soccer team crashed near Medellin, Colombia, on its way to the Copa Sudamericana final, killing most aboard and leaving only a handful of survivors. The flight, departing from Santa Cruz, Bolivia after originating in Sao Paulo, declared an emergency late Monday night with reports of electrical failure and, according to other pilots in the area, radio messages saying the plane was running out of fuel and requesting an emergency landing. The aircraft struck a mountainside in poor visibility and heavy rain; rescuers recovered the wreckage and eventually all bodies, with Colombian officials confirming dozens of identifications. Initial counts of fatalities varied in reports but the tragedy devastated the small southern Brazilian club, which had risen rapidly through the divisions and reached its first major international final this season.

Among the few survivors were three Chapecoense players, a journalist and two crew; some required major surgery, including one player who underwent an amputation and others treated for severe trauma. Survivors described darkness and panic before impact and credited following safety procedures for staying alive. Investigations began with black boxes recovered and international aviation experts assisting. The loss prompted national mourning in Brazil, an outpouring of global condolences from the soccer community, tributes and planned wakes in Medellin and Chapecó, and Atletico Nacional’s public wish that Chapecoense be awarded the Copa Sudamericana title in their honor.

Passengers on United Express Flight 5449 from San Francisco to Boise were forced to restrain a woman who began screaming “I am God” and attempted to open an aircraft cabin door mid-flight. Video released online shows fellow travelers tying the woman’s feet and holding her down in the aisle until the Embraer 175, operated by SkyWest Airlines with 73 people aboard, landed safely in Boise. Authorities met the plane at the gate and took the woman for medical evaluation. Experts noted that opening a pressurized cabin door in flight is impossible, though the attempt still alarmed passengers. Boise police said they will forward a report to the prosecutor for charging consideration, and the FBI may also review the incident.

Oxford-based Oxitec has engineered insects designed to collapse pest populations by passing on lethal genes. For olive growers, Oxitec created male olive fruit flies carrying a gene that kills female offspring in the larval stage; males survive but cannot sustain the population once females vanish. In lab trials the engineered males outcompeted wild males and caused population crashes within about ten weeks. Oxitec has applied to Spain’s National Biosafety Commission for a small, contained field trial under mesh over six trees in Tarragona. Meanwhile, a larger release in Brazil aims to suppress Aedes mosquitoes that spread dengue by releasing males whose offspring die before breeding; prior trials reduced local mosquito numbers by 80–96 percent. Proponents argue the approach is species-specific and preferable to broad-spectrum insecticides, requiring less household access and minimizing collateral environmental harm. Critics, including GeneWatch UK, warn of insufficient oversight, unpredictable spread, ecological interactions, and reinvasion risk, urging more study before wider deployment.

The long-running legal tussle over whether Nestlé can trademark the distinctive four-finger Kit Kat shape has been sent back to the EU Intellectual Property Office after the European Court of Justice dismissed appeals from both Nestlé and Mondelez. Nestlé had sought EU-wide protection for the “four trapezoidal bars on a rectangular base,” first granted in 2012, but Mondelez challenged it, pointing to competing four-finger bars such as Norway’s Kvikk Lunsj (made since 1937) and its own Leo bar. A 2016 lower EU court ruled Nestlé had not proven the shape was recognised as distinctive across every EU member state—missing evidence for countries including Belgium, Ireland, Greece and Portugal. The ECJ upheld that standard: distinctiveness must be shown across the entire EU, not merely in a significant part. The decision means EUIPO must reconsider its earlier registration; it could remove the mark unless Nestlé supplies stronger, pan‑EU evidence, though national trademarks for the shape remain in some countries (France, Germany, Spain, Italy). Nestlé says the fight isn’t over and may reapply with additional proof. The case underscores broader issues for brand protection across diverse national markets in the EU and echoes other high-profile confectionery disputes, such as Toblerone’s shape and Cadbury’s purple.

Geraldine “Jerri” Kramer, now 72 and living in Fortville, Indiana, is urgently trying to find the son she was forced to give up for adoption in 1963. At 19, unmarried and pressured by her parents and a priest, Kramer stayed at St. Elizabeth Girls Home in Indianapolis and gave birth on June 10, 1963. She named the healthy, curly-haired infant “Jack” after her father and briefly held him before nurses took him away; Catholic Social Services never told her where he went. The secret of the pregnancy was known only to her younger sister and remained hidden from her future husband, Joseph, whom she married in 1966. The loss left Kramer with a lifelong ache — she has prayed for him nightly and marked his age through the years.

With declining health from diabetes and heart disease, Kramer asked her five children to help search for the son she last saw more than five decades ago. In late November, her family posted a plea and photo on Facebook saying, “If you were born 6-10-63 you’re our older brother; we’re looking for you.” The post has been widely shared—over 40,000 times—reflecting how social media is increasingly used to locate separated relatives when legal records are sealed. Kramer’s eldest daughter, Marie Henson, revealed the secret to the family in 1988 to dissuade her own child from being adopted; she and Kramer’s other children are determined to find their eldest sibling.

Indiana is a mutual-consent state: adoption records remain sealed unless both parties register to unseal them. Adoption agencies can perform searches for a fee, but matches only occur if both sides have registered. The Kramers hope their brother, now about 52, has had a good life and might welcome contact. They continue filing searches, sharing the plea online, and praying for a “Christmas miracle” so Kramer can tell him she has loved him for years and finally reunite with the son she’s longed to know.

A Northern California couple has secured a $2.5 million settlement from the city of Vallejo and its police department after investigators initially dismissed the woman’s elaborate 2015 abduction as a hoax. Denise Huskins and her then-boyfriend Aaron Quinn reported that a masked intruder had drugged them in their Mare Island home, bound them, and kidnapped Huskins, who was held two days and sexually assaulted before being released outside her family’s home in Southern California. Vallejo police publicly suggested the episode resembled the fictional plot of Gone Girl and called it fabricated, but later apologized after evidence tied disbarred, Harvard‑trained attorney Matthew Muller to the crime. Muller had spied on the couple with a drone, broke into their home with a fake gun, forced them to drink a sedative, and recorded himself sexually assaulting Huskins. He also sent anonymous emails to a reporter claiming an elite criminal team was responsible. Muller pleaded guilty and is serving a 40-year federal sentence; prosecutors found items linking him to the abduction, including a stolen computer. Huskins sued the city and officers for defamation and emotional distress, and a federal judge allowed the case to proceed, saying alleged conduct could be deemed “extreme and outrageous.” The city admits no wrongdoing in settling. The couple’s attorney called the settlement a message that victims should be believed and praised the couple for enduring the ordeal.

Muhammad Ali, one of the most celebrated athletes and cultural figures of the 20th century, died at 74 in a Phoenix hospital after being admitted with a respiratory illness complicated by Parkinson’s disease. His spokesman said he died of septic shock from unspecified natural causes. Ali, a three-time world heavyweight champion who first won the title at 22 by beating Sonny Liston, had been living with Parkinson’s for more than three decades; his struggle with the disease was a poignant part of his later public life.

News of his death prompted an outpouring of tributes from around the world. US President Barack Obama praised Ali as “the greatest” whose fight outside the ring helped shape modern America, noting his courage in standing up for civil rights and refusing the Vietnam draft — a stance that cost him his title and nearly his freedom but ultimately elevated his moral stature. Former president Bill Clinton, British Prime Minister David Cameron, Sir Paul McCartney, Ringo Starr, Tiger Woods and many leading boxers and sports figures, including George Foreman, Mike Tyson, Floyd Mayweather, Manny Pacquiao and Oscar De La Hoya, paid homage. Promoter Don King and longtime friend Bob Arum recalled Ali as a transformative global figure whose personality and activism transcended sport.

Colleagues and opponents remembered Ali’s charisma, wit and principle as much as his skills: his “rope-a-dope” win over Foreman in the 1974 Rumble in the Jungle in Kinshasa and epic bouts with Joe Frazier are enduring sporting milestones. Foreman described Ali as “beautiful” and “something greater than a boxer.” Promoters and reporters highlighted his genius for publicity and irrepressible confidence, while friends stressed the sacrifices he made for his beliefs, including giving up large purses to defy the draft.

Public memorial plans included a funeral in Louisville, Kentucky, with eulogies from Bill Clinton and Billy Crystal and a public procession. Fans and fellow athletes around the globe paid tribute, reflecting on Ali’s athletic brilliance, moral courage and the compassion that, many said, made the world better for his having lived.

A shooting in Strasbourg on the evening of Dec. 11, 2018, near the city’s famed Christmas market left four people dead and 11 wounded, prompting a massive security response, a city-wide lockdown and an anti-terror investigation. Authorities identified and sought a suspect with a criminal record who had previously been flagged as a possible extremist; prosecutors opened a probe on suspicion of murder and attempted murder linked to a terrorist enterprise. Gendarmes had earlier visited the suspect’s home to arrest him but found him absent and reportedly discovered explosive materials. Soldiers and police swarmed the market and surrounding neighborhoods; witnesses recounted hearing multiple gunshots, screams and orders from security forces to stay inside. Several wounded were in critical condition. One of the dead was reported by a witness to be a Thai tourist who succumbed despite CPR attempts; an ambulance reportedly took more than 45 minutes to arrive. The gunman appeared to target civilians, not soldiers patrolling the market, and was wounded by soldiers during the response, according to a police union official. The attack triggered the lockdown of the nearby European Parliament and mobilized national leadership—Interior Minister Christophe Castaner and the Paris anti-terror prosecutor traveled to Strasbourg, and President Emmanuel Macron paused a meeting to monitor the situation. The incident rekindled memories of a thwarted al-Qaida-linked plot aimed at the Strasbourg market around the turn of the millennium; that earlier conspiracy had led to convictions in 2004. Authorities urged residents to avoid the area and remain indoors as the hunt for the shooter continued and emergency services managed the aftermath. Contributors to reporting included John Leicester and Angela Charlton.

From 1659 to 1681, Puritan authorities in Massachusetts legally banned Christmas, fining anyone who "observed" the day — by avoiding work, feasting, or other celebrations — five shillings. The ban reflected Puritan leaders’ view that December 25 held no biblical sanction and had become a rowdy, indulgent custom; Increase Mather condemned its "compotations," revelry, and excesses. Earlier customs like wassailing—where poorer colonists demanded food and drink from wealthier households, sometimes violently—underscored the holiday’s unruly reputation. Though the ban was regional (Jamestown settlers celebrated without incident), Puritan prohibitions shaped New England for centuries: town criers proclaimed "No Christmas" while mince pies and puddings were forbidden and work was once mandatory on the day. After royal control was restored in the 1680s, Governor Sir Edmund Andros sponsored Christmas services, even guarded by redcoats, and observance slowly returned, yet Boston remained reticent into the 19th century—schoolchildren risked expulsion for skipping class on Christmas in 1869. Other sects, like Quakers and some Baptists and Presbyterians, also eschewed the holiday, making Christmas observance a marker of denominational differences in early America.

Old City Cemetery in Lynchburg, Virginia, is a 27-acre “history park,” public garden, and active burial ground that draws over 33,000 visitors annually, making it the city’s most visited historic site. Established in 1806, it is the oldest municipal cemetery in Virginia still in use. The site includes five small museums that interpret the lives of nearly 20,000 people interred there and features extensive plantings, including Virginia’s largest public collection of antique roses. The gates are open daily from dawn to dusk.

Recently, cemetery staff and archaeologists have uncovered the remains of dozens of Civil War soldiers in a section known as “Yankee Square.” Beginning in April, a 45-by-10-foot trench revealed red and orange markers indicating Confederate burials; the team located 35 to 40 graves in this latest excavation, adding to 50 found the previous year. Assistant director Ted Delaney said the project aims to identify each soldier, place individual markers noting names, units, and dates of death, and provide closure to descendants. Cemetery records and detailed undertaker’s notes are aiding identification; when finished, about 80 Confederate soldiers are expected to be properly identified. Delaney noted that Union soldiers once buried in the same plot were exhumed and removed in 1866.

The work is part of an effort that began in April 2013 and is supported by an annual $2,500 grant from the Virginia Department of Historic Records Work. The cemetery’s discoveries echo efforts elsewhere to locate and restore unmarked military graves. One example is Sam Ricks of the Sons of Confederate Veterans in Pennsylvania, who located the unmarked grave of Nathan Tiernon Walton— a Virginia Military Institute cadet and New Market veteran—at Philadelphia Memorial Park in 2008, enabling Walton’s descendants to finally place a long-held Southern Cross of Honor marker. Such projects combine archaeology, archival research, and family involvement to restore recognition to forgotten soldiers.

This morning’s early NFL game in London set the tone for the league’s response to President Donald Trump’s recent attacks on players who kneel during the national anthem to protest racial injustice. Many players on both teams knelt while others and Jacksonville Jaguars owner Shad Khan linked arms — a visible demonstration of solidarity that comes after two days of Trump’s public condemnations. More protests were expected later in the day across the league.

The controversy generated a stream of reactions on television and social media. Former White House adviser and Fox News contributor Karl Rove argued Trump had mishandled the moment and was losing politically. Rove suggested the president could have encouraged respect for the flag by emphasizing the sacrifices that built the country and appealing aspirationally to why citizens should stand, despite America’s imperfections. Instead, Rove said, Trump’s call for punitive measures — telling owners to fire players who do not stand — contradicted his prior stance opposing federal interference in team matters and cast him unfavorably in the public eye.

Conservative voices also weighed in. Mike Huckabee criticized kneeling players on Fox News, saying he wished protesting athletes would instead express gratitude for opportunities they enjoy playing in the United States, and admonished media perceived as defending protesters over those praying on the field.

Former Bills coach Rex Ryan, who once supported Trump by introducing him at a rally, publicly regretted that association after the president’s incendiary comments. Speaking on ESPN, Ryan called Trump’s language — including labeling players “son of a bitch” and urging their firing — appalling, and defended players he knows from locker rooms as decent men undeserving of such attacks. In the wake of Trump’s remarks, players, teams, owners, the NFLPA, league officials, and former players and coaches have broadly criticized the president’s divisive rhetoric, amplifying the national debate over protest, patriotism, and racial justice.

Scott Strzelczyk, a Carroll County resident, legal activist and radio host, launched a July 2013 campaign to separate Maryland’s five western counties—Frederick, Carroll, Garrett, Allegany and Washington—into a new state dubbed Western Maryland (or West Maryland). Frustrated by what he and supporters describe as domination by Montgomery County, Prince George’s County and Baltimore City, Strzelczyk argues western residents lack representation in Annapolis and face oppressive laws and taxes. He cites Maryland’s Declaration of Rights to justify reforming government. The movement’s Facebook page has drawn modest attention—about 2,200 likes—and organizers plan public outreach and meetings to engage county officials and residents. Critics and officials, including Rep. John Delaney’s office, dismiss the idea as impractical; Delaney’s communications director called it “utterly ridiculous,” noting constituents haven’t raised this issue in local offices. Historically, the only successful U.S. intra-state secession created West Virginia in 1863; modern attempts nationwide (e.g., Baja Arizona, North Colorado, Jefferson) have largely failed. Experts say constitutional hurdles are high—state legislature and Congressional approval are required—making success unlikely, though efforts reflect a growing rural-urban political divide over issues like gun rights, taxes, marriage and regulation. Western Maryland counties contain 11% of the state population with mixed wealth and poverty; supporters say a new state would better reflect local values and governance. Organizers acknowledge logistical and legal challenges—funding, infrastructure, debt allocation and governance—but hope the threat of secession will force negotiations and give western residents a stronger voice.

A tightly controlled NIH study led by Kevin Hall offers some of the clearest human data yet on whether cutting carbohydrates or fat is better for reducing body fat. Published in Cell Metabolism, the research confined 19 adults with obesity to a metabolic ward for two separate two-week stays in which all food and activity were controlled. Each stay began with five days on a baseline diet, then six days with a 30% calorie reduction achieved either by removing only carbohydrates (keeping fat constant) or by removing only fat (keeping carbs constant); protein was unchanged. Participants switched conditions between visits, and researchers measured calories consumed, fat intake, fat oxidation, insulin secretion, and calculated body fat loss rates.

Contrary to claims that carb restriction is uniquely effective for shedding body fat, the study found that calorie-for-calorie, restricting dietary fat produced greater net body fat loss than restricting carbohydrates. As predicted by Hall’s prior mathematical simulations, the low-carb intervention did lower insulin secretion and increase fat burning, but the reduced-fat intervention produced a larger imbalance between fat eaten and fat burned, yielding more body fat loss over the short test periods—about a 68% higher rate in one report. The model and observed data agreed, and extended-model projections suggest that over longer times the body tends to minimize fat-loss differences between diets that supply equal calories but different carb-to-fat ratios.

Hall cautions against broad diet prescriptions from this single, small study: the sample was limited (19 people), the menus and confinement don’t mirror real-world dieting or long-term adherence, and ease of sticking to a diet remains crucial. His team will next study how low-carb and low-fat diets affect brain reward circuits to understand why individuals respond differently to diets. For now Hall recommends choosing the diet one can maintain, while recognizing that not all calories are exactly equal in how they influence short-term body fat change.

A cluster of pediatric cases of a rare, paralysis-causing illness has re-emerged in the Pacific Northwest, and one child has died. Six-year-old Daniel Ramirez of Bellingham, who had been treated at Seattle Children’s Hospital for more than two weeks after developing cold-like symptoms and rapid paralysis, was taken off life support and died. Daniel was one of eight children hospitalized there with polio-like signs that include sudden weakness or paralysis of one or more limbs, loss of muscle tone and reduced reflexes. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) in eight of nine children admitted with these symptoms at Seattle Children’s. The patients range from 3 to 14 years old and come from several counties in Washington; the cases occurred over about six weeks.

AFM is a rare condition affecting the spinal cord; its exact cause remains unclear though it has been linked to enteroviruses, West Nile and other infectious agents. There is no specific treatment, and care is largely supportive. Nationwide this year, the CDC has investigated a substantial rise in AFM, with dozens of cases across many states; the Washington child is the only known fatality reported. Oregon has also seen a resurgence: three cases since August, including two children and an adult, with one adult linked to West Nile virus. Families of prior AFM patients describe long, uncertain recoveries and urge more research. Public health officials recommend hygiene measures—handwashing and covering coughs—and prompt medical evaluation for any sudden limb weakness. Hospitals await further CDC investigation into the recent regional cluster.

The trial opened in L’Aquila of six prominent Italian scientists and a former civil protection official accused of manslaughter over the 6.3 magnitude earthquake of 6 April 2009 that killed 309 people and destroyed much of the city and surrounding villages. Prosecutors say the seven, who sat on the government Serious Risks Commission, gave a reassuring public statement a week before the quake after reviewing hundreds of low-magnitude tremors, providing what the indictment calls an “approximate, generic and ineffective assessment” and “incomplete, imprecise and contradictory information.” Defendants face up to 15 years in jail and civil claimants, including the local council, seek €50m in damages; the civil case will run alongside the criminal trial. The experts argued they had warned that precise earthquake prediction is impossible and urged stricter enforcement of anti-seismic building measures; defenders and thousands of scientists contend the prosecution effectively puts science on trial. Only one defendant, former deputy Civil Protection technical head Bernardo De Bernardinis, attended the opening. Survivors and relatives counter that the reassurances led many to stay indoors and die; victims’ groups seek accountability and improved risk communication. The trial was adjourned until 1 October.

A Pennsylvania woman, Michele G.M. Kalina, was charged with criminal homicide and five counts of abuse of a corpse after forensic testing linked her to the remains of five infants found between late July and early August in her Reading home and a nearby landfill, prosecutors said. Kalina, 44, had been jailed since an August 9 arrest following her teenage daughter’s discovery of remains in a living-room closet. Investigators recovered four sets of infant remains from the apartment—each stored in individual plastic containers, one encased in cured cement—and a bone and cooler were later found at the Conestoga Landfill. DNA testing identified Kalina as the mother of four infants and tentatively linked a man described as her long-term boyfriend to three as the father; the fifth infant’s parentage was inconclusive. A forensic pathologist found four deaths consistent with asphyxia, poisoning, or neglect. Kalina, a nurse’s aide who reportedly hid multiple pregnancies from family, is held without bail; prosecutors will decide specific homicide counts before trial. Her public defender declined to comment.

Tyler County emergency managers issued a stark, life-or-death evacuation order as flooding from Tropical Storm Harvey intensified: officials announced the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers had opened flood gates to 100 feet, predicting river rises to about 79–82 feet, and warned residents “GET OUT OR DIE!” Those refusing evacuation were told they shouldn’t expect rescue and were urged to mark their Social Security numbers for identification. Harvey, having made a second landfall in Louisiana, dropped prodigious rains across Southeast Texas—8–15 inches in many communities and averages up to 27 inches in parts of Harris County, with localized totals near 50 inches—causing catastrophic urban and rural flooding.

Across the region, emergency responses included block-by-block searches in Houston, mass sheltering, National Guard deployments, and rescues of stranded nursing-home residents. The storm and its aftermath caused widespread infrastructure impacts—an Arkema chemical plant explosion after power and refrigeration failures, toppled oil storage tanks spilling crude, overwhelmed 911 centers and massive property damage. The confirmed death toll rose above 30 and was expected to climb as waters receded and searches continued; many fatalities involved people swept away in vehicles or trapped in homes, and some deaths occurred during rescue or recovery efforts. Officials cautioned that additional deaths could occur in the recovery phase from accidents or carbon monoxide exposure. While forecasters downgraded Harvey to a tropical depression, heavy rain and flooding threats lingered farther inland, and authorities urged residents to heed evacuations and safety warnings to reduce further loss of life.

Lee Daniels’ The Butler topped the box office again with $17 million in its second weekend, pushing its total to $52.3 million and surpassing Daniels’ previous North American best, Precious. The Weinstein Co. saw strong holdover performance as The Butler’s audience broadened racially and skewed younger. New Line’s R-rated sleeper hit We’re the Millers dipped just 25%, earning $13.5 million this weekend and reaching $91.7 million domestically. Three new releases underperformed: Mortal Instruments: City of Bones opened weakly with $9.3 million (five-day $14 million) and struggled despite a built-in YA audience; Edgar Wright’s The World’s End debuted well for its size with $8.9 million and the top per-theater average; horror You’re Next opened modestly at $7.1 million. Woody Allen’s Blue Jasmine expanded to 1,200 theaters, while Jobs tumbled nearly 60% to $3 million.

House Republican leaders face growing pressure to bring a bipartisan China currency bill to the floor as the Senate moves toward passage. Democrats, led by Rep. Mark Critz, are pushing a discharge petition (177 signatures so far) to force a vote, arguing the measure addresses alleged Chinese undervaluation of the renminbi and protects American jobs. Many House Republicans support action but worry about Speaker John Boehner’s opposition—he called the bill “dangerous” and warned it could trigger a trade war. GOP leaders urge caution; some members say they’ll sign the petition only if President Obama vows to sign the bill. The White House has expressed concern about WTO legality and effectiveness. China warned the U.S. that such legislation could harm bilateral ties, stall global recovery and risk retaliation, while also linking tensions to U.S. arms sales to Taiwan. Political stakes are high ahead of 2012 elections.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz responded to a New York Times report that he failed to disclose personal loans from Goldman Sachs and Citigroup on his Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings during his 2012 Senate campaign, calling the omission an “inadvertent filing question” and a “filing error.” Cruz said the underlying facts have long been disclosed on other filings and promised to amend any FEC reports if needed. The Times reported that Cruz and his wife, Heidi—who worked at Goldman Sachs at the time—took out low-interest personal loans that helped finance his campaign; those loans appeared on his congressional financial-disclosure forms but not on his FEC campaign reports. Campaign aides framed the issue as semantic and said the campaign would consult the FEC. The loans totaled between $500,001 and $1 million across both banks according to Senate disclosure ranges: a margin loan from Goldman initially listed at $100,001–$250,000 and later increased to $250,001–$500,000, plus a Citigroup line of credit of $250,001–$500,000. Cruz’s campaign has long emphasized that he personally fronted roughly $1.43 million for the race by selling stock and using personal savings and loans; it said the particular loan in question was repaid in full but did not specify how. Legal experts noted that campaign rules require disclosure of the original source of funds used to finance campaigns, so failing to report bank loans to the FEC could violate rules. Goldman and Citigroup declined to comment.

In early July 2016, 41-year-old artist Betsy Davis, who had spent three years losing control of her body to ALS, invited more than 30 friends and family to a two-day farewell she called a “rebirth.” Under California’s newly enacted End-of-Life Option Act, Davis planned to end her life with prescribed medications and organized a detailed weekend in Ojai that would culminate in that choice. Her invitation warned attendees: “These circumstances are unlike any party you have attended before, requiring emotional stamina, centeredness and openness,” and set one rule: don’t cry in front of her.

Guests flew in from across the country and filled a home with a wraparound porch for cocktails, pizza, music, a cello and harmonica, screenings of a favorite film, and a playful fashion show where friends modeled outfits Davis had chosen. She rolled among rooms in her electric wheelchair, chatted, distributed “Betsy souvenirs,” and encouraged laughter and celebration even as everyone knew what was coming. Her sister Kelly wrote about the experience for Voice of San Diego, describing the tension between grief and respect for Davis’s decision.

On the evening of July 24, wearing a kimono bought during a post-diagnosis trip, Davis took a combination of morphine, pentobarbital and chloral hydrate at 6:45 p.m. with her sister, caretaker, doctor and massage therapist present. She died about four hours later. Friends described the gathering as a final performance and a dignified, self-directed end; some opponents of assisted suicide warned of risks to vulnerable people. Those who attended plan to reconvene next June to scatter her ashes.

Tom Hardy’s career and persona are a study in controlled chaos: handsome and Hollywood-famous, yet fiercely drawn to dark, difficult roles. He lost a bet with Leonardo DiCaprio over an Oscar nod for The Revenant and honored it with a tattoo reading a DiCaprio-chosen phrase — reluctantly, and only after DiCaprio rewrote it legibly. Hardy’s extensive ink collection signals loyalty to lovers, family and his agent Lindy King, who he credits for his Hollywood break. Raised in West London, he battled substance addiction and brushes with the law before training at the Drama Centre and landing early roles in Band of Brothers and Black Hawk Down. Sober since 2003, his raw experiences fuel transformative performances in Bronson, Stuart: A Life Backwards, Legend and The Revenant. He resists prettified leads, preferring villains and complex antiheroes, and co-created the gritty period drama Taboo, which he’s producing and starring in. A devoted but sleep-deprived new father, Hardy oscillates between indie experiments and blockbuster work (Mad Max, Dunkirk), remaining mercurial, magnetic and unapologetically himself.

Researchers at NYU Langone Medical Center investigated why long-term Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) members often report little or no craving for alcohol, examining brain responses when members confronted drinking-related cues. In what is believed to be the first study of AA members’ brain physiology, 20 long-term AA participants who reported no cravings in the prior week were scanned while viewing images of alcoholic drinks and people drinking. Images were shown twice: once after the participant read neutral newspaper material and again after reciting an AA abstinence-promoting prayer. All subjects reported some craving after viewing the images, but cravings were significantly reduced following the prayer. Functional MRI revealed increased activity in prefrontal cortex regions involved in attention, as well as areas implicated in emotional control and semantic reappraisal—the cognitive reframing of emotional situations—when participants prayed. Senior author Marc Galanter, MD, suggests the findings indicate that long-term AA involvement equips members with an ability to use AA experiences, like prayer, to blunt alcohol-triggered cravings, possibly reflecting physiologic brain changes accompanying a “spiritual awakening” and a shift in perspective toward drinking. Earlier studies linking spirituality and reduced drinking after treatment are consistent with these results. The study, supported by the John Templeton Foundation and published in the American Journal of Drug and Alcohol Abuse, adds evidence that prolonged AA participation may produce measurable neural changes that help diminish craving and support abstinence.

Jan Chamberlin, a five-year member of the Mormon Tabernacle Choir, resigned after deciding she could not in good conscience sing at President-elect Donald Trump’s inauguration. In a letter later posted to Facebook she said repeated sleepless nights, prayer and soul-searching led her to conclude participation would betray her values and damage her self-respect: “I could never ‘throw roses to Hitler.’ And I certainly could never sing for him.” Chamberlin warned the choir’s appearance would harm its image and networking and alienate many who already feel betrayed.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints emphasized that choir participation is voluntary, that roughly 215 of the choir’s 360 members have volunteered for the trip, and that selection is limited by the inaugural committee and by a lottery system. Church spokesman Eric Hawkins stressed the choir’s historical role in presidential events—performances at past inaugurations and parades—and framed the invitation as a nonpartisan demonstration of support for freedom, civility and a peaceful transition of power.

The choir’s decision provoked strong internal reaction: an online petition authored by Affirmation past-president Randall Thacker gained nearly 19,000 signatures from Mormons worldwide arguing the choir’s participation misrepresents the church’s 15+ million members and endorses values they view as sexist, racist, misogynistic and xenophobic. Responses have been mixed, and Chamberlin reported receiving hate messages after publicizing her resignation. LDS leaders have not commented on whether other members have resigned.

A small archive of six typewritten letters from Harper Lee to her close friend, New York architect Harold Caufield, failed to meet its reserve at Christie’s New York and did not sell. The lot, estimated up to $250,000, included correspondence written between about 1956 and 1961—a crucial period during which Lee wrote Go Set a Watchman and recast it into To Kill a Mockingbird. Four letters predate the 1960 publication of Mockingbird; together the eight pages offer an unusually intimate window into Lee’s creative struggles, loyalties, private humor and conflicted feelings about her Southern hometown, religion and public visibility.

Christie’s described the collection as “poignant and especially rare.” Some letters are signed with playful pseudonyms—“The Prisoner of Zenda,” Francesca da Rimini—or initials like “Nelle.” Contents range from reflections on her ailing father Amasa Coleman Lee, the model for Atticus Finch, to an exuberant December 12, 1960 note reacting to glowing reviews: “We were surprised, stunned & dazed by the Princeton review… all that lovely, lovely money is going straight to the Bureau of Internal Revenue tomorrow.” Other passages reveal homesickness for her Manhattan apartment, frustration with creative blocks in small-town Monroeville, skepticism about Presbyterian theology, and worries that her civil-rights views were being gossiped about locally.

The letters resurfaced after Caufield’s death; they passed through a rare-books dealer to a private collector who consigned them to Christie’s. Few of Lee’s personal letters have appeared publicly—correspondence is rare because friends have tended to protect her privacy—so the cache drew attention as an unusually candid record of the years surrounding her sudden literary breakthrough. Critics and Lee’s publisher noted she was a deeply private figure and might be disappointed at the sale of personal letters. The auction unfolded shortly before the July release of Go Set a Watchman, which renewed public focus on Lee’s life and limited published output.

A wave of violent and often chaotic protests swept much of the Muslim world after the release of a 14-minute anti-Islam video denigrating the Prophet Muhammad. Demonstrations erupted from North Africa to South Asia, with thousands gathering outside U.S. embassies and consulates. In Tunis, protesters scaled the embassy wall, planted a black Islamist banner and clashed with police who fired tear gas and shots; thick black smoke rose as police battled stone-throwing crowds. In Khartoum, hundreds stormed the German Embassy, setting fires and burning vehicles; part of the building was aflame. Violence and arson also struck Tripoli, Lebanon, where protesters burned fast-food restaurants, leaving one dead and dozens wounded. Security forces in Yemen, Egypt and elsewhere used tear gas and live rounds to repel crowds from diplomatic missions. Egypt’s President Morsi urged protection of foreign missions and condemned the Libya attacks that killed the U.S. ambassador, while Secretary of State Clinton denounced the film as reprehensible and unrelated to the U.S. government. Protests ranged from peaceful rallies in Malaysia and parts of Pakistan to large, often ultraconservative-driven, confrontations in Baghdad, Jerusalem, Sanaa and Jalalabad.

Rep. Michele Bachmann, a leading conservative and 2012 presidential candidate, has vocally campaigned against big government spending and federal programs, yet records show her family and interests have benefited from government funds. Marcus Bachmann’s counseling clinic, Bachmann & Associates, received nearly $30,000 in state grants since 2006—largely for staff training financed in part by federal funds—and more than $137,000 in Medicaid reimbursements for treating low-income mentally ill patients since 2005, according to state records obtained by reporters. Bachmann lists the clinic among her assets and has minimized the payments publicly, calling them one-time training funds that did not benefit the clinic directly. Separately, a family farm in Wisconsin in which she remains a partner received nearly $260,000 in federal farm subsidies between 1995 and 2008; Bachmann has said she personally didn’t get subsidy payments, though her disclosures show farm income between about $32,500 and $105,000 in some years. While she has denounced the 2008 farm bill as laden with “pork,” she later urged USDA commodity purchases to support local dairy and pork producers. Critics say these ties undercut her anti-spending rhetoric; Republican strategists advise she address the discrepancies. Bachmann’s office did not fully respond to requests for comment.

Producer Adi Shankar launched a crowdsourced spec-script contest earlier this year to address the controversy around The Simpsons’ long-running character Apu Nahasapeemapetilon, criticized after Hari Kondabolu’s documentary for perpetuating a racist stereotype. Shankar sought a script that would subvert, evolve or write Apu into a more nuanced, realistic portrayal of Indian-Americans — ideally produced by Fox as an episode — but after selecting a winner he says he’s heard from multiple sources that The Simpsons plans to quietly drop the character instead. Shankar calls that move “cowardice,” arguing a satire known for cultural commentary should confront, not avoid, the issue. He worries sidelining Apu misses an opportunity to broaden representation and heal cultural tensions through storytelling.

The Grand Prize winner is Vishaal Buch, an Indian-American family doctor and former Air Force pilot from Bethesda, Maryland. Buch’s spec envisions Apu transitioning from Kwik-E-Mart owner to thriving businessman and expands the story to include other prominent Indian-Americans, using humor to underscore diversity and individuality. Shankar praises the script as clever, authentic and non-preachy, and says Coverfly is helping Buch translate it into proper screenplay format. He also named Tasha Dhanraj second place.

Believing Fox will not produce the episode, Shankar plans to realize Buch’s script via his Bootleg Universe channel, where he’s previously produced viral fan-driven shorts and where he serves as co-showrunner on Netflix’s Castlevania. He’s open to involving Simpsons voice actors, even Hank Azaria. Fox and The Simpsons offered limited responses; executive producer Al Jean later disputed Shankar’s claim that the show would write Apu out, and Fox noted Apu’s recent brief appearance. Shankar, undeterred, intends to produce the episode himself if necessary.

As dusk falls at some Cuban sinkhole caves, Jamaican fruit bats erupt in clouds, and Cuban boas lie in wait—sometimes in numbers—draped from cave ceilings to snatch bats midflight. Vladimir Dinets, a research assistant professor at the University of Tennessee, documented this behavior during field observations in Desembarco del Granma National Park. Over eight nights he recorded snake positions and hunting outcomes and concluded that the boas were not simply coincidentally occupying the same spots but actively positioning relative to one another, producing a deadly curtain across the passage that greatly improved capture success.

Dinets observed that individual boas routinely chose different segments across nights, undermining the idea that all snakes were selecting the same microhabitat by preference. Instead, the first boa would pick a spot and arriving snakes would place themselves nearby; when three or more boas hung together bats had far fewer safe paths through the entrance and often collided with or came within striking range of a snake. Statistical records showed group hunters captured prey more reliably and faster than solitary individuals. Dinets emphasizes this challenges the old view of reptiles as mainly solitary and cognitively limited; coordinated hunting in reptiles is rarely documented, with crocodilians and monitor lizards being notable exceptions.

Similar mass-roost predation has been observed in Puerto Rico and Mexico’s “Cavern of Serpents,” though those accounts lacked quantitative analysis. Dinets cautions that proving true social cooperation would require controlled experiments; some herpetologists have criticized the strength of the coordination claim. He also warns that boas face threats from hunting and the pet trade, and dwindling numbers could disrupt group hunting dynamics. The study, published in Animal Behavior and Cognition, highlights both a striking natural spectacle and gaps in understanding of snake social and hunting behavior.

Comedian and actress Amy Schumer has combined personal news with political activism, declining to appear in Super Bowl LIII commercials to stand with Colin Kaepernick’s protest against racism and police brutality. On Instagram she urged white NFL players to kneel as well, warning that failure to do so makes them complicit, and announced she told her representatives she would refuse Super Bowl ad offers this year. Schumer framed the boycott as a way to hit the NFL through its advertisers, acknowledging the limited nature of her sacrifice. Her post drew supportive comments from figures like Diddy, Jessica Seinfeld and Christie Brinkley; it was unclear if she had been courted for a Super Bowl spot. Separately, Schumer used an Instagram collaboration with journalist Jessica Yellin to reveal she is expecting her first child with husband Chris Fischer. The pregnancy announcement was posted alongside political messaging: Yellin’s #NewsNotNoise campaign, which aims to demystify political jargon ahead of the midterm elections, posted Schumer’s candidate recommendations and appended “I’m pregnant—Amy Schumer” at the end. Schumer has a recent track record of high-profile activism — she was reportedly detained protesting Brett Kavanaugh’s Supreme Court nomination, has advocated for gun control, supported transgender rights, and urged artists to pull out of NFL halftime events in solidarity with Kaepernick. Tying her baby news to a voting reminder reflects her long-standing commitment to political causes and voter engagement.

ABC's Tom Llamas accompanied First Lady Melania Trump on her first solo Africa tour—visiting Ghana, Malawi, Kenya and Egypt—to promote her "Be Best" children's initiative and to sit for an extended interview airing in "Being Melania." The trip featured high security, visits to orphanages, conservation sites and cultural landmarks, and drew intense attention to her wardrobe choices, including an "I really don't care. Do U?" parka worn during a Texas border visit and a pith hat in Egypt. In the exclusive interview she addresses sensitive subjects often avoided by the White House: she says organizations have declined to partner with her because of politics, expresses empathy for women in the #MeToo movement while also insisting that allegations require evidence, and defends her husband amid past accusations. On the Brett Kavanaugh controversy she called him "highly qualified," noted Dr. Ford was heard and the FBI probe completed, and said she would "move on." She also described offering candid advice to the president but acknowledged he doesn't always follow it. The sit-down promises more revelations, including why she launched an anti-cyberbullying focus and her reflections on public perceptions.

Today Alaska will release 24,199 pages of emails sent and received by Sarah Palin during her early years as governor, responding to requests first made in 2008 amid her vice-presidential nomination. The long, costly review was complicated by Palin’s use of private Yahoo accounts, necessitating retrieval from multiple officials and repeated deadline extensions; lawyers reviewed documents and will withhold about 2,353 pages for privilege and redactions. Media organizations will pick up paper boxes in Juneau and create searchable archives. While the archive may yield noteworthy insights into Palin’s office and political dealings, withheld material and missing private-to-private messages mean the record won’t be fully comprehensive.

President Trump prepared to announce his Supreme Court nominee to replace Justice Anthony Kennedy, narrowing a longer list to three likely federal appeals judges: Brett Kavanaugh, Raymond Kethledge and Amy Coney Barrett. The choice, coming less than four months before the midterms, has energized conservative activists who want a reliably originalist justice to shift the court for decades. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell privately urged Trump toward Kethledge or Thomas Hardiman, arguing they would face fewer confirmation hurdles than Kavanaugh, whose extensive paper trail from 12 years on the D.C. Circuit and prior White House and Starr investigation roles could complicate Senate approval. Prominent conservative voices lined up behind different candidates: radio host Hugh Hewitt promoted Kethledge as “Gorsuch 2.0” and highlighted political upside in swing-state Michigan; ACU chairman Matt Schlapp and Fox host Laura Ingraham backed Kavanaugh for his conservative rulings and jurisprudential influence; Ben Shapiro favored Barrett as the most reliable originalist; Mark Levin and figures like Jim DeMint, Adam Brandon of FreedomWorks, and Erick Erickson pushed for Sen. Mike Lee, while others accepted alternatives such as William Pryor. Democrats and some Republicans urged a nominee not intent on overturning Roe v. Wade; Trump said he would not question candidates about the case. The debate combined strategic confirmation calculus with ideological priorities as the president readied a prime-time announcement.

In January at Stony Brook University Hospital, surgeons performed a rare corrective operation on the Howard triplets—Hunter, Jackson and Kaden—who were born with craniosynostosis, a condition in which skull plates fuse too early and can restrict brain growth. The three boys, born Oct. 22, 2016, underwent separate endoscopic surgeries over two days when they were about 11 weeks old. Surgeons used small incisions and instruments including a harmonic scalpel to remove a strip of bone and reopen fused seams; all three recovered quickly and went home two days later.

Craniosynostosis affects roughly one in 2,000–2,500 births, but having it in a set of triplets—especially non-identical triplets (two identical, one fraternal)—is extraordinarily rare. Stony Brook pediatric neurosurgeon Dr. David Chesler estimated the probability of this specific presentation at about one in 500 trillion and said the team could not find reports of other triplets with the condition. Beyond cosmetic concerns, untreated craniosynostosis can put pressure on the brain and jeopardize vision and development, so timely surgery was important.

Postoperative care includes wearing custom orthotic helmets 23 hours a day for six to nine months to help reshape the skulls; the boys’ head shapes already look rounder and normal three months after surgery. Parents Amy and Mike Howard—who conceived the triplets without fertility treatments—expressed relief that the procedures went well and said the boys are thriving: Kaden is easygoing, Hunter is talkative and Jackson is the “tough one.” The family is adjusting to life with three infants and three cats, grateful that the surgery gave their sons a healthier start.

Detective Eric Smith, 40, a veteran of the Jackson Police Department’s Robbery-Homicide Division, and murder suspect Jeremy Powell, 23, were both found dead after gunfire erupted during an interview at Jackson police headquarters Thursday evening. Powell was being questioned in connection with the April killing of 20-year-old Christopher Alexander, whose body was found stabbed. Officers elsewhere in the building heard shots, entered the third-floor interview room and discovered both men had been shot multiple times. Authorities did not release a detailed sequence of events; councilman Chokwe Lumumba said he was told Smith was shot by the suspect but did not know how Powell died. The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation has taken over the probe. The department, city officials and community leaders mourned Smith, described as a decorated, well-respected detective and family man, while police headquarters remained locked down as investigators worked.

Actor Jon Bernthal has said he observed troubling behavior from Kevin Spacey while working with him on the 2017 film Baby Driver, and that those impressions preceded the wave of sexual misconduct allegations that surfaced in late October and November 2017. Bernthal told SiriusXM he “lost a ton of respect” for Spacey after meeting him on set, describing the actor as having rubbed him “the wrong way,” behaving like “a bit of a bully” and treating other people on set in ways Bernthal found inappropriate. He emphasized he never witnessed the specific sexual misconduct now alleged, but said he was glad to leave the production and recalled others later reached out to him about their own reactions.

Those remarks came amid a growing list of accusations against Spacey dating back decades. The initial, high-profile allegation came from Anthony Rapp, who said Spacey made sexual advances toward him when Rapp was 14; Spacey apologized and publicly came out as gay. Numerous other men—some named, some anonymous—then accused Spacey of groping, attempted rape, or other unwanted sexual advances occurring at locations including the Old Vic theater in London, sets and private parties. Allegations range from teen victims to men in their 20s and older and include claims from former colleagues and production staff that Spacey created a toxic work environment on House of Cards. In response, Netflix cut ties with Spacey and the actor was removed from the upcoming All the Money in the World, with Christopher Plummer recast to replace him; legal and police inquiries were reported in several instances. Spacey’s representatives said he is seeking evaluation and treatment.

When Diana Carrillo and three companions went to the Saint Marc Pub-Cafe in Pacific City, Huntington Beach, they expected a casual outing but instead experienced what they viewed as discriminatory treatment. Carrillo, 24 and from Irvine, says that when they were seated a waiter asked her, “Can I see your proof of residency?” She had her ID out and was stunned; the waiter then asked the same question of the other three women, saying he needed to confirm they were residents before serving them. After speaking with a manager—who apologized—the group left. Carrillo posted the incident on social media on March 11, where it drew attention. The restaurant issued a public apology three days later stating the behavior does not represent the St. Marc brand. Kent Berden, senior director of operations, said the waiter was fired for violating corporate policy; he reported the waiter claimed the question had been asked “in a joking fashion.” Carrillo rejected that explanation, saying the exchange felt hostile and reflected broader fears tied to national political climate, noting her parents are immigrants and expressing concern about rising hostility. The restaurant contacted Carrillo afterward, offering VIP treatment and pledging to donate 10 percent of that weekend’s sales to a charity of her choice; Carrillo declined the VIP offer but accepted the donation and asked it be given to Orange County Immigrant Youth United, which the restaurant agreed to do. The piece notes this was the restaurant’s first complaint since opening in 2015. Contact details for the writer and an archival note about web crawls were included.

Mariano Barbosa Jr., a Manhattan hotel security director, was arrested and charged with setting eight fires at two hotels over four years, fire officials said. Barbosa, 30, of West New York, N.J., worked as director of security at Yotel on 10th Avenue and 42nd Street and had previously been a security officer at the SoHo Grand. Fire marshals say he started fires from 2009 through this month in hallways, stairwells and in front of exit doors — locations chosen to maximize danger — and was on duty when they occurred. The blazes, set between about 10:11 p.m. and 5:09 a.m., were quickly extinguished; two firefighters suffered minor injuries in a February incident. Officials allege Barbosa’s motive was to make the hotels less popular and thereby reduce rowdy clientele and parties, making his job easier; investigators say he hoped incidents would be blamed on patrons, curbing events. Authorities say he admitted to voluntary questioning, which led to his arrest on charges including arson, reckless endangerment and criminal mischief. Yotel is cooperating with investigators; the SoHo Grand declined comment. Barbosa’s wife protested his arrest, calling him hardworking and devoted to their three young sons; a co-worker described him as a “normal person,” expressing surprise at the allegations. Fire Commissioner Salvatore Cassano condemned the alleged conduct as endangering lives for personal gain.

Amur, an Amur tiger, and Timur, a goat kept in the same enclosure at a Russian safari park near Vladivostok, have had a falling-out after months of attracting public fascination as an unlikely pair. The friendship began in November when keepers placed Timur with Amur expecting the tiger to kill him; instead the two bonded and resisted separation, with Amur roaring when separated. A park-released 30-minute video captures the relationship’s unraveling: Timur repeatedly provoked Amur, even rubbing his horns through the tiger’s fur for hours. Eventually the tiger snapped, leapt on the goat, mauling and tossing him to the snow. Staff distracted Amur with a live rabbit so keepers could rescue Timur, who lay stunned before being taken for veterinary examination. Vets found him in good health though shaken and needing rest. Park director Dmitriy Mezentsev said Timur sends greetings and vows to be less cocky; the pair have been separated for now while veterinary staff monitor recovery and managers consider whether reunification is appropriate. The episode reinforced speculation about why Amur has not eaten Timur—choosing to discipline rather than kill.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s newly arrived ambassador to Germany, Richard Grenell, immediately warned German companies to halt business in Iran after Trump announced the U.S. withdrawal from the 2015 Iran nuclear deal and plans to reimpose sanctions. Posting on Twitter hours after presenting his credentials in Berlin, Grenell said U.S. sanctions “will target critical sectors of Iran’s economy” and urged German firms to “wind down operations immediately.” The move, delivered by Trump in a televised White House address, risks increasing tensions in the Middle East, straining relations with Germany and other European allies, and disrupting global oil markets. German industry reacted nervously, noting that European companies could face U.S. fines if Iranian partners land on U.S. sanctions lists. Grenell takes the Berlin post nearly 16 months after his predecessor left. A Republican foreign policy writer and long-time Twitter user, Grenell served as a U.S. spokesman at the United Nations from 2001–2008 and later contributed to Fox News; he worked with John Bolton when Bolton was U.S. UN ambassador. Senate confirmation on April 26 made Grenell the highest‑ranking openly gay official in the Trump administration, after a delayed confirmation amid Democratic objections over past online and televised remarks Grenell characterized as attempted humor rather than insults. His arrival was celebrated at a high-profile New York party featuring Trump family allies, Fox personalities and other conservative figures.

Angelyne long stood as one of Los Angeles’s most persistent enigmas: a self-fashioned blonde bombshell whose ubiquitous pink billboards and pink Corvette made her a local cultural icon from the early 1980s onward. Her persona—glamorous, coy, emblematically “famous for being famous”—preceded any clear biographical facts. She marketed herself relentlessly: hundreds of billboards, bus-shelter ads, merchandise sold from her trunk, paid appearances, tiny film roles and occasional records. She charged steep licensing and appearance fees, cultivated a rigid control over her image, and insisted on preserving mystery as part of her brand, refusing offers for reality TV and saying she’d save personal revelations for memoirs.

Recent reporting by Gary Baum and research by a genealogist claim to have unmasked Angelyne as Renee Tami (born Ronia Tamar) Goldberg, born in Poland in 1950 to Holocaust-survivor parents who endured ghettos and camps before emigrating via Israel to Los Angeles. Records, yearbook photos and family testimony—such as that from a former husband and a stepsister—support the claim that the billboard diva grew up in L.A.’s Jewish community, later remade herself into the quintessential Hollywood fantasy: bleached hair, dramatic cosmetic surgery, and a persona that reads as deliberately non-Jewish. Angelyne’s longtime spokesman Scott Hennig denies the identification, calling such attempts “ridiculous,” while Angelyne herself declines to discuss her origins and has sometimes implied the past is hers to monetize.

The revelation reframes Angelyne as both an entrepreneurial performance artist and a person shaped by trauma and reinvention: a woman who escaped a painful family history by meticulously inventing a public identity. Whether the newly surfaced documents and testimony fully settle her origins or simply add another layer to her myth, they underscore the complicated interplay between image, commerce, secrecy and survival in Angelyne’s uniquely Los Angeles life.

In 2009 Richard Walker, head of a South African surgical-supply firm, discovered counterfeit spinal screws among returns from U.S. distributor Spinal Solutions LLC. Tests showed some screws were not medical-grade titanium, had uneven threads and potentially toxic markings—signs they were knockoffs. Despite an employee alerting the FDA in 2011 and an on-site inspection, Spinal Solutions continued selling implants until it collapsed under debt in 2013. Investigations and lawsuits now allege the company sold counterfeit hardware nationwide, mixing fake and genuine screws in surgical kits sent to hospitals in California, Nevada, Texas, Wisconsin and Maryland.

Spinal Solutions’ founder Roger Williams lived lavishly—private jets, courtside NBA seats, luxury cars—while the company accrued massive debts and allegedly enticed surgeons with plane rides, consulting contracts and cash. Former employees and pilots describe envelopes of cash and other perks used to secure business. Plaintiffs’ lawyers say some surgeons received kickbacks; doctors deny knowingly using substandard parts. One machinist, 85-year-old William Crowder, admitted making copies of screws after being asked by an operations manager; he later stopped when payment fell. Another contractor performed laser etching that could mimic authentic logos.

Patients like Derika Moses, who endured chronic pain, infections and multiple surgeries, now fear metal left in their spines might be counterfeit and dangerous. U&I Corp., a South Korean manufacturer whose logo appeared on some hardware, identified several pieces as fake. More than 30 lawsuits have been filed alleging counterfeiting and fraudulent billing—charging insurers and workers’ compensation inflated prices for substandard devices. The FDA issued warning letters and inspected the company but allowed it to operate while it attempted fixes; the full scope of harm and number of affected patients remain uncertain. Attorneys warn thousands could be impacted and seek accountability.

Cleveland officer Timothy Loehmann has given his first public account of the fatal shooting of 12-year-old Tamir Rice, telling investigators he believed he faced an “active shooter situation” and thought Tamir was an adult. Loehmann’s written statement, released by Cuyahoga County prosecutors as evidence read to a grand jury, says he and partner Frank Garmback repeatedly yelled “show me your hands” as Tamir reached toward his waistband and then saw a weapon. Loehmann said he exited the patrol car—explaining he was trained that “the cruiser is a coffin”—and fired two shots, believing the object was a handgun; it later proved to be a nonlethal airsoft pellet gun. Garmback’s statement describes driving over a curb and skidding across grass to approach the reported suspect, noting the car “did not stop where and when I intended,” and that he believed the object in Tamir’s hand was real. Surveillance footage shows the encounter was extremely brief, with critics saying the officers had only seconds to act.

Tamir’s family attorneys denounced the release and the officers’ unsworn written statements, calling their accounts “preposterous” and arguing the timeline was too short for the officers’ claimed observations and commands. They also criticized Prosecutor Timothy McGinty for making selective evidence public—expert reports released by his office concluded the shooting was justified, while the family’s experts disagreed—and asked for a special prosecutor. McGinty defended the transparency of the grand jury process. The grand jury is considering whether to indict Loehmann and Garmback; public debate continues over officer tactics, the handling of the investigation, and whether the officers’ versions of events would withstand cross-examination. Tamir’s mother testified to the grand jury, urging jurors to find probable cause to indict.

Indonesian search teams continued battling severe weather to recover remains and wreckage from AirAsia Flight QZ8501 after debris and bodies were first spotted Tuesday. Conflicting reports emerged about underwater detections: one local search official said sonar may have found wreckage on the seabed, but the national search chief said the main aircraft has not yet been located. Search-and-rescue authorities have recovered seven bodies—four men and three women, including a cabin crew member—and found floating debris, including an emergency exit, life jacket, children’s shoes and luggage, roughly 60–120 miles from the jet’s last known position over the Java Sea. Heavy rain, strong winds, high seas and shifting currents hampered diving and helicopter operations; sonar searches and dozens of ships continued in a concentrated zone near the Karimata Strait while international assets, including U.S. Navy vessels and patrol aircraft, joined the effort. Families gathered at crisis centers in Surabaya and Pangkalan Bun endured anguished waits, fainting and anger over media coverage; many provided DNA and photos to aid identification. The Airbus A320 lost contact after pilots requested to climb to avoid bad weather, then disappeared without a distress call. Investigators stress that recovery of the flight data and cockpit voice recorders is crucial to determine cause; experts have suggested possibilities from aerodynamic stall to weather-induced engine damage, but no conclusions can be drawn until the black boxes are recovered.

Walt Disney Co. sparked outrage after filing 10 U.S. trademark applications on May 1 for “Día de los Muertos” across products including toys, cereals and jewelry, anticipating an untitled Pixar feature inspired by the Mexican Day of the Dead. The studio said the filings were meant to protect a potential film title and related activities, but announced it would withdraw the trademarks after backlash and a decision to change the film’s title. Critics and community leaders called the move offensive and inappropriate, arguing the centuries-old, indigenous-rooted holiday—a sacred cultural tradition observed across Mexico, Latin America, Europe and the U.S.—should not be owned or commercialized by a corporation. A Change.org petition opposing the trademark quickly gathered thousands of signatures; commentators compared the stunt to Disney’s 2011 bid to trademark “Seal Team 6,” which the company also abandoned after criticism. Community organizers urged respect for cultural heritage over corporate branding.

Reuters and commentary pieces report Facebook’s IPO roadshow was set to begin May 7, with shares expected to start trading May 18. Founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg, who had largely stayed offstage during earlier IPO preparations, was reported to be participating in the roadshow. Regulatory review related to Facebook’s recent acquisition activity was said to be near completion, removing a timing hurdle. The offering was expected to raise at least $5 billion, likely making it the largest Silicon Valley IPO, amid strong investor interest reminiscent of Google’s debut.

Separately, analysts warned investors to temper enthusiasm. Facebook’s updated S-1 showed decelerating revenue and user-growth trends and notable margin compression: operating margin fell year-over-year and quarterly EPS pressure increased. Mobile usage—now a large and growing share of activity—poses a monetization challenge, and Facebook’s acquisition of Instagram raised governance and valuation concerns given Zuckerberg’s decisive role and the premium paid. Some argued Facebook should delay IPO until it demonstrates improved margins and a clearer mobile monetization path rather than rushing to market.

Pop star Justin Timberlake made headlines for returning to his Tennessee roots to participate in early voting in Memphis. Though he primarily lives in California and also owns property in Nashville, Timberlake flew back home to cast his ballot, promoting civic participation with an Instagram selfie taken just before he voted. In the post, he urged followers to take advantage of early voting where available or to vote on Election Day, writing, "Hey! You! Yeah, YOU! I just flew from LA to Memphis to #rockthevote !!! No excuses, my good people! There could be early voting in your town too. If not, November 8th! Choose to have a voice!" His appearance drew excitement from local voters and fans, who shared reactions online when they spotted the star at polling locations. One Twitter user joked about her mother “freaking out” seeing Timberlake in line to vote. The coverage also noted a legal detail: Tennessee prohibits ballot selfies, meaning voters should be cautious about photographing their marked ballots even if taking a pre- or post-vote selfie is common. The article highlighted that users can add location information to tweets and have the option to delete their Tweet location history, a reminder about digital privacy when sharing voting activity. Overall, Timberlake’s visit and social-media post combined celebrity influence, a get-out-the-vote message, local enthusiasm, and a brief nod to voting privacy rules, illustrating how public figures can draw attention to civic engagement while prompting reminders about legal and privacy considerations around sharing voting moments online.

The writer bought 50 Cent’s The 50th Law expecting hustler wisdom and found entertaining revisionist anecdotes but little about his music craft. Recent albums felt disconnected from fearlessness and street immediacy; Before I Self Destruct instead aims to court listeners who prefer his harder, earlier tracks. The album has strong, menacing moments—“The Invitation,” “Death to My Enemies,” and especially “So Disrespectful”—and potent production from Dr. Dre and others that underscores transactional, amoral themes tied to money, betrayal and hurt. Yet the record drags in the middle, sometimes reverting to post-2001 muddiness and failed hit attempts. Despite flashes of ferocity and skill (notably on “Psycho” with Eminem), the album ultimately fails to fully restore 50’s former dominance.

Rupert Murdoch and former supermodel Jerry Hall have announced their engagement in the births, marriages and deaths column of the Times of London. The 84-year-old media mogul and 59-year-old Hall, who were introduced in Australia by Murdoch’s sister and niece, have been dating for about four months and surfaced publicly at last October’s rugby World Cup final. They became engaged over the weekend in Los Angeles while attending Golden Globes events. The Times notice, published 12 January and bordered in black, named their children and said the couple are “delighted to announce their engagement.” Guardian Australia estimated a classified ad could cost close to £300, though Murdoch likely did not pay full price; extra was reportedly spent for the black border. The pair’s relationship has prompted mixed reactions in media and social circles, with friends and spokespeople calling Murdoch “very happy” and crediting Hall with bringing him renewed vigor, while some insiders mocked the pairing. The engagement would be Murdoch’s fourth marriage and Hall’s second, depending on the legal status of her 1990 Bali ceremony with Mick Jagger.

Since 2009 the beef industry has run the Masters of Beef Advocacy (MBA), a checkoff-funded PR and training program that has taught nearly 3,000 students and producers how to defend beef production. Supported with at least $240,000 by the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association, the MBA offers online modules—now updated as MBA 2.0—covering sustainability, nutrition, animal welfare, beef safety and the industry’s history. It recruits young land-grant students and aspiring farmers, encouraging public outreach through presentations, social media, media interviews and an alumni Facebook group. Trainees like Carrin Flores and others see the program as a way to protect their agricultural futures against critics such as Michael Pollan, whose books and speeches have energized campus debates about industrial farming. MBA participants say they’re not “Astroturf” but express genuine concern about balancing environmental critiques with the need to feed a population and preserve farm livelihoods as beef consumption and young-farmer numbers decline.

Hurricane Isaac battered the northern Gulf Coast as it crawled inland over Louisiana, producing prolonged heavy rain, storm surge and damaging winds that left hundreds of thousands without power and prompted widespread rescues and emergency operations.
