New Orleans Mayor Mitch Landrieu imposed a dusk-to-dawn curfew and warned of strict anti-looting enforcement as the city weathered sustained tropical-storm-force gusts and flooding; he said drinking water remained safe and urged caution during cleanup. Isaac’s slow movement intensified impacts: levees and rural protections in Plaquemines Parish were overtopped, inundating homes, stranding residents in attics and on roofs, and prompting consideration of an intentional levee breach to allow floodwater to drain. Dozens were rescued by boats, and the National Guard, FEMA and military helicopters were deployed for search-and-rescue. At peak tallies more than 817,000 customers across several Gulf states lost power; utilities warned outages could last days. Storm surge reports included an 11-foot reading at Shell Beach and localized flooding up to a foot or more over levees; as many as 800 homes in Plaquemines may have significant water damage. Tornado warnings and flash-flood watches accompanied Isaac’s slow march, and officials cautioned that inland flooding—the leading cause of hurricane deaths—remained a major danger even as winds began to ease.

Public Health England (PHE) has confirmed two children from the same family in the Charnwood area of Leicestershire have died after contracting E. coli and developing haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS), a serious complication that affects the kidneys. The siblings were treated in the past two weeks; their ages and identities have not been released. PHE said the cases are not currently being treated as an outbreak, but investigators are working with environmental health officers and local partners to determine how the children became infected, reviewing the family’s recent movements and collecting environmental samples from the home. Tests are being run on the bacterial isolates to identify the exact E. coli strain, a process expected to take at least a week. PHE consultant Dr Lauren Ahyow noted that E. coli infections vary from mild illness to severe bloody diarrhoea, often without fever, and that HUS, while relatively rare, can be very serious—particularly in young children and elderly people. Potential exposure routes include contaminated food, contact with farm animals, and infected water; authorities continue to investigate these possibilities. PHE expressed condolences to the family and urged vigilance while inquiries proceed.

Michael Julian, the NYPD’s newly appointed deputy commissioner in charge of training, announced a campaign to curb officers’ profanity and reduce unnecessary force, saying both behaviors drive civilian complaints. Julian argued many officers curse “for effect” and can be taught to control their language, noting his claim that 30% of Civilian Complaint Review Board (CCRB) complaints involve a curse word. He said commanders have already succeeded at precinct level and new training begins next week. On use of force, Julian stressed that NYPD officers are not routinely brutal in the Rodney King sense but sometimes deliver an “extra kick” or punch fueled by adrenaline after chases; he promised techniques to help officers manage emotions and avoid excess force. The retraining follows the July order after Eric Garner’s death in a chokehold. CCRB data show complaints about discourteousness have fallen slightly year-over-year, and the CCRB chairman has likewise condemned officers’ foul language. Julian said officers will welcome instruction on self-control as well as legal rules.

Los Angeles police arrested San Francisco 49ers linebacker-defensive end Aldon Smith at Los Angeles International Airport after he indicated he had a bomb while being screened in Terminal 1. According to airport and LAPD officials, Smith was randomly selected for secondary screening, became belligerent and made a comment suggesting he possessed a bomb before proceeding toward the gate. Los Angeles Airport Police detained him at the gate after he continued to be uncooperative; he was booked on a false bomb report charge, which carries up to a year in jail, and posted about $20,000 bail that night. The 49ers’ general manager expressed disappointment and declined further comment pending facts. Bystanders, including a former Marine, recorded the encounter. This episode is Smith’s latest legal trouble: in November he pleaded not guilty to three felony counts for illegal possession of an assault weapon stemming from a 2012 party, and earlier this year he spent time in an alcohol treatment center after a second DUI arrest, missing five games. Separately, a Chicago-to-Sacramento Southwest flight was diverted to Omaha after a passenger allegedly tried to open a rear door midflight; fellow passengers and air marshals restrained him and he was removed, and the flight arrived about two hours late.

A new study led by Columbia University’s Earth Institute and published in The Cryosphere finds Greenland’s surface reflectivity (albedo) has been declining since the mid-1990s and could be up to about 8–10% darker by 2100. Using three decades of space-borne multispectral data (1981–2012) and regional model simulations, the team documents a statistically significant summertime albedo decrease beginning around 1996—about 0.02 per decade in observations—confined to regions that melt in summer, while the high dry-snow zone shows no trend. Two self-reinforcing processes drive the darkening. First, as snow melts, older, dirtier layers loaded with light-absorbing impurities (dust, soot) are exposed and concentrated at the surface, increasing absorption. Second, melt–refreeze cycles enlarge snow grain size; larger grains scatter less sunlight (especially in the infrared) and absorb more energy. These feedbacks make the surface increasingly sensitive to solar input: warming promotes melt, melt reduces albedo, and reduced albedo accelerates further melting. The study investigated external soot sources (wildfire and aerosol trends) and found no consistent increase to explain the darkening, suggesting the effect arises mainly from exposure and concentration of existing impurities plus grain-growth processes rather than increased atmospheric deposition. Model projections under warming scenarios indicate continued darkening through the century; results may be conservative because current models underpredict melting and often omit impurity effects. The darkening increases meltwater runoff and sea-level implications, highlighting a dangerous feedback loop tied to human-driven warming.

George Zimmerman, acquitted last year in the 2012 shooting death of 17-year-old Trayvon Martin, is living a very different life now: on the move, financially strained and frequently targeted with death threats. In his first interview with the Orlando Sentinel, Zimmerman described attending a firearms expo in Lake Mary — where he posed for photos, shook hands and greeted gun enthusiasts — as a relatively low-key, “friendly” appearance that didn’t require special protection. He carries a semi-automatic handgun for personal safety and says his Twitter feed is flooded with threats. Public reactions vary: some people express support and surprise that he seems soft-spoken and kind, while others react with fear or hostility. Zimmerman said he receives invitations from strangers and tries to lead a normal life despite celebrity status and constant scrutiny. He also travels frequently for speaking engagements and legal meetings, rarely staying in one state more than a month. Recently he launched a website to communicate directly, posting, among other things, portraits he painted of the four Americans killed in Benghazi; he plans to give originals to the families and sell replicas to raise money for veterans’ charities.

A large Danish study reported in JAMA Pediatrics finds that prenatal use of acetaminophen (paracetamol/Tylenol) is associated with a higher likelihood that children will later be diagnosed with ADHD or related hyperactivity disorders. Researchers analyzed data from more than 64,000 mother–child pairs from the Danish National Birth Cohort. About half of the mothers reported using acetaminophen during pregnancy. Those who ever used it had a 29% higher risk of an ADHD diagnosis and a 37% higher risk of hyperkinetic syndrome; longer use (20+ weeks) and later-pregnancy exposure were linked to greater risks, including a reported 50% increase in likelihood of ADHD medication use. The authors caution the findings show association, not causation, and could reflect confounding factors such as maternal infection, undetected viral illness, genetic predisposition, or postnatal acetaminophen use. Laboratory studies suggesting hormone-like effects of acetaminophen on fetal development motivated the research. Experts urge pregnant women to weigh risks and benefits: avoid chronic or long-term use when possible, use minimal effective dose for brief periods, and consider nonpharmacological pain relief when appropriate. Drug makers and some clinicians note no randomized trials prove causality and advise consulting physicians before use.

A systematic individual-level meta-analysis examined whether swaddling—wrapping an infant tightly with head exposed—affects sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) risk. From a comprehensive search to December 2014, four case–control studies (760 SIDS cases, 1,759 controls) from England, Tasmania and Chicago met inclusion criteria. Study methods and swaddling definitions varied, and prevalence of swaddling ranged widely (5.7%–35.7% among control groups). Across studies, 17.5% of SIDS infants had been swaddled for their last sleep versus 10.8% of controls.

Pooled results showed heterogeneity (I2 = 65.5%), so a random-effects model gave an age-adjusted odds ratio (OR) of 1.58 (95% CI, 0.97–2.58), borderline significant. Excluding the most recent UK study reduced heterogeneity (I2 = 28.2%) and produced a significant pooled OR of 1.38 (95% CI, 1.05–1.80). Risk varied markedly by sleep position: swaddled infants placed prone had the highest SIDS risk (OR ~13.0), followed by side (OR ~3.16) and supine (OR ~1.93). Data suggested increased swaddling-associated risk with age, with infants ≥6 months showing higher odds (OR ~2.53). Many swaddled infants who died were found prone after being placed supine or on their side, implying rolling while swaddled is hazardous.

Limitations include small number of heterogeneous studies, inconsistent swaddling definitions, and incomplete adjustment for confounders (e.g., bed-sharing). Despite uncertainty, findings reinforce current guidance to avoid placing infants prone or on their side—especially if swaddled—and suggest clinicians and guidelines consider advising cessation of swaddling by the age infants begin rolling (around 4–6 months). Further, better-standardized, contemporary research on swaddling technique, age limits, and interactions with sleep environment is needed.

A legal battle has erupted between Harper Lee, the reclusive author of To Kill a Mockingbird, and the Monroe County Heritage Museum in Monroeville, Alabama, the town that inspired her novel. Lee, now in poor health, filed a federal trademark infringement suit seeking to bar the museum from using the book’s title, characters, and related imagery to promote activities or sell merchandise. Her lawyers allege the museum has increasingly exploited her fame—particularly after her 2007 stroke—and even opposed her trademark application while demanding a royalty-free license. The complaint points to the museum’s website, gift shop goods, local logos, and long-running theatrical productions as evidence that the institution trades on Lee’s work rather than merely preserving local history.

Museum attorneys deny the claims, calling the lawsuit “false” and “meritless,” and warn that a successful suit could destroy the nonprofit, which they say brings tourists and modest revenue to the town and has honored Lee’s legacy for decades. The dispute has deepened community divisions in Monroeville, where the museum stages annual performances in the restored county courthouse that inspired the novel’s trial scenes and attracts about 30,000 visitors yearly. Complicating matters are questions about who is acting for Lee: associates, family members, and a local attorney thought to hold power of attorney may be driving the litigation. Earlier lawsuits this year—over Lee’s copyright and trademark filings—reflect broader concerns about protecting her estate amid declining health. The conflict has intensified local debate over preserving cultural heritage versus commercial use of a singular American literary legacy.

Researchers at MIT, the University of Sheffield, and Tokyo Institute of Technology have developed an ingestible origami robot that unfolds from a swallowed capsule, is steered by external magnetic fields, crawls across the stomach lining, and can remove swallowed button batteries or patch wounds. Presented at the International Conference on Robotics and Automation, the device continues Daniela Rus’s lab work on origami robots and targets a clear clinical problem: each year about 3,500 button-battery ingestions are reported in the U.S., and prolonged contact with tissue can cause severe burns.

The robot is built from two outer structural layers with a middle layer that shrinks when heated; slits in the outer layers determine folding. For biocompatibility the team chose a malleable structural material (dried pig intestine, like sausage casing) and a biodegradable shrinking layer called Biolefin. To recover stiffness lost with the softer material, the design uses fewer slits and folds that increase stiffness along specific axes. The rectangular robot features accordion folds, pinched corners that act as traction points, and a permanent magnet embedded in a forward fold. External rotating magnetic fields produce principally rotational forces: quick rotations spin the device, slower ones make it pivot around a foot; the same magnet can pick up a button battery.

Propulsion combines stick-slip locomotion with fluid thrust—about 80% friction-based motion and 20% water propulsion—making it effective in the stomach’s acidic, fluid environment. The team tested performance in a silicone model tuned to pig-stomach mechanics, filled with water and lemon juice. Results show reliable unfolding from a dissolvable capsule, locomotion, and battery retrieval, though work remains on sensors, autonomous control, and alternative materials for broader clinical use. Colleagues praise the concept as a creative, practical response to a pressing health need.

Ford Motor Co. announced it will end more than 90 years of vehicle production in Australia, closing its Geelong engine plant and Broadmeadows assembly plant in Victoria and ceasing local manufacturing in October 2016. The shutdown, expected to cause about 1,200 job losses, was blamed on sliding sales, high operating costs and a strong Australian dollar. Ford Australia chief executive Bob Graziano said the business case was unsustainable, with Australian costs much higher than in other regions—particularly wages—despite government efforts to support the auto industry.

Recent discussion traces a rising informal usage of because that drops clauses and "of" to take a bare noun or other short element—e.g., "No work tomorrow because holidays" or "Because science." Linguists call it "because+noun" or "because NOUN." It functions like a terse, jocular prepositional-like device that signals an obvious, weakly argued, or playful cause and suits online brevity. Variants accept nouns, verbs, adjectives, interjections, and occasional adverbs ("Because yay," "because tired," "because cooking"). Analyses note constraints—bare nouns are common and emphatic—yet the slot can host longer phrases. Historical and corpus searches reveal precedents in speech and media going back decades, though edited writing rarely uses it outside quotes. Proposed origins include elliptical "because, hey" constructions, child–parent exchanges, and meme spread. The form appeals because of its economy and humorous grammatical violation; it proliferates online and may influence analogous compressions with words like but, so, and thus, though formal acceptance remains uncertain.

Lindsay Lohan scrambled to shore up her court record ahead of a Los Angeles hearing as prosecutors prepared to seek jail time for alleged probation violations tied to a past DUI and a misdemeanor necklace theft. A probation report set for Judge Stephanie Sautner’s review described Lohan as in “substantial compliance” with her sentence, but Los Angeles City Attorney spokesman Frank Mateljan said the office still planned to ask the court to incarcerate her because she failed to follow a key term: performing community service at the Downtown Women’s Center. Authorities say Lohan was terminated from that program for repeatedly missing appointments; she had been ordered to complete 480 hours of community service by April 2012, including 350 hours at the shelter and 120 hours at the coroner’s office. Lohan’s camp says she completed a shoplifting course, has been seeing a psychologist, and shifted her shelter hours to the American Red Cross, where her spokesman said she worked nearly every day the prior week. Observers note the judge could impose a stern warning or jail, since the original order required full compliance. Lohan previously spent two weeks in jail for probation violations in 2010 and a month under house arrest earlier this year; even if jailed at the hearing, she could likely post bail pending a violation hearing.

The document compiles several news items surrounding Donald Trump’s presidential transition and early presidency: his inauguration schedule, a freeze on U.S. funding for Palestinian refugees, potential areas of bipartisan cooperation with Democrats, market reactions to Trump’s comments on the dollar, public opinion polling on Trump’s favorability and policy expectations, and the slow pace of his Cabinet confirmations.

The inauguration timeline details events from Jan. 19–21, including a Lincoln Memorial concert, a wreath-laying at Arlington, church services and tea at the White House, the Jan. 20 Capitol ceremony where Trump uses Lincoln’s Bible and is sworn in by Chief Justice John Roberts, a parade down Pennsylvania Avenue, evening inaugural balls, and a Jan. 21 interfaith National Prayer Service at the Washington National Cathedral.

Separately, the Trump administration reportedly froze $125 million intended for the UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) pending a review of U.S. aid to the Palestinians after they suspended contacts following U.S. recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital. Diplomats warned that cutting or withholding significant U.S. support could be catastrophic for UNRWA and worsen humanitarian conditions in Gaza and refugee camps; Israeli officials expressed concerns and urged gradual disengagement rather than abrupt cuts.

Analysis of potential cooperation suggests Democrats could work with Trump on select issues—trade renegotiation (including NAFTA), raising the minimum wage, infrastructure spending, allowing Medicare to negotiate drug prices, and protecting Social Security—though such alignments risk alienating party bases.

Markets reacted when Trump told The Wall Street Journal he favored a “weaker” dollar, heightening investor concerns. Polling from ABC/Washington Post found Trump entered office with unusually low transition approval and favorability compared with recent presidents, though many expect him to do well on the economy and jobs; large partisan and demographic divides shape views on his agenda.

Finally, Trump faced an unusually slow Cabinet confirmation process hampered by ethics issues, Democratic tactics, complex financial disclosures for nominees, and scheduling constraints—raising the likelihood that many posts would remain unfilled well after Inauguration Day.

Recent disclosures suggest the NSA can collect vast amounts of Americans’ communications and metadata, including call logs, emails, chats and location data. While some mainstream technologies are vulnerable, practical steps can reduce exposure. Use Tor Browser to hide your IP and browse anonymously by routing traffic through multiple relays (but still use HTTPS or end-to-end encryption for sensitive data). For instant messaging, use OTR (Off-the-Record) enabled clients like Adium or Pidgin to get end-to-end encrypted chats so servers only see ciphertext. For secure voice, choose audited, open-source apps such as Silent Circle or Redphone, which provide end-to-end encryption and claim no backdoors. However, metadata — who you call, when and where — is hard to hide; turning a phone off or removing its battery is the only reliable way to prevent location tracking. Encryption protects content, but preventing linkage and pattern analysis remains difficult.

Joe Miller formally conceded the Alaska Senate contest to Sen. Lisa Murkowski, ending his post-election legal challenges to her historic write-in victory. At an Anchorage news conference, Miller said he would abide by the courts’ rulings despite disagreeing with them and would not pursue further appeals, including to the U.S. Supreme Court. He maintained a defiant tone about policy differences and pledged to keep “sounding the alarm” on state and national issues, while denying ill will toward Murkowski. Miller repeatedly said he had not personally contacted Murkowski to concede, joking he didn’t have her phone number. The dispute centered on how voter intent should be interpreted when write-in names were misspelled; a federal judge rejected Miller’s narrower reading, finding it would undermine election integrity. Murkowski’s campaign welcomed the end of the contest and noted she’ll continue serving Alaska for six years. Miller left future political plans, including a possible 2012 House run, undecided.

Conservationists are using selective “back-breeding” to recreate an auroch-like bovine — the Tauros — to restore lost grazing dynamics across Europe. The auroch, a large wild cattle species that roamed Europe for 250,000 years until its extinction in Poland in 1627, is seen as a keystone herbivore whose intensive grazing historically shaped mosaic habitats and supported biodiversity. Ronald Goderie, founder of the Tauros Project, began breeding cattle from modern breeds retaining auroch ancestry (from Spain, Portugal, Italy and the Balkans) in 2008. By crossing these breeds and testing offspring DNA against the sequenced auroch genome, the program aims to produce animals that resemble the original in form, behavior and self-sufficiency — the fourth generation is now released into the wild in Spain, Portugal, Croatia, the Czech Republic and Romania; Goderie hopes to reach a close approximation by the seventh generation around 2025.

Working with Rewilding Europe, the Tauros have been exposed to natural pressures including wolves and show signs of “de-domestication,” defending themselves and functioning as landscape engineers. Supporters argue that reintroducing large bovines can recreate grazing regimes necessary for diverse habitats. Critics and the IUCN warn of ecological and social risks, stressing careful risk assessment, habitat suitability and potential impacts on people, flora and fauna. Some conservationists note that restoring herbivores may also require restoring predators to re-establish balanced ecosystems.

Hurricane Sandy, though not yet made landfall, is already reshaping the final week of the U.S. presidential campaign by forcing President Obama and Mitt Romney to alter schedules and prompting temporary suspension of early voting in places like Maryland and D.C. The storm could significantly affect early voting and turnout across the East Coast and Great Lakes, potentially altering poll results and the election’s dynamics. Research by Reeves and Gasper suggests voters punish incumbents for severe storm damage but reward officials who visibly respond well; presidents may gain modestly from disaster declarations, while governors often gain more. Polling may be skewed if millions are unreachable—Voorhees models a hypothetical loss of 15 million respondents leaning Democratic, which could depress Obama’s national poll standing by about one percentage point, though pollster weighting can mitigate this. Turnout effects are uncertain: Northeast resilience and recovery could lessen disruption by Election Day, but inland areas—sometimes conservative—could also be hit. The storm’s vast and unpredictable footprint makes state-level impacts hard to forecast. Campaign plans and media focus will change, but public safety should be the priority for those in harm’s way.

A report commissioned by Nestlé and produced by U.S. fair-labor group Verité found widespread abusive labor practices in Thailand’s seafood sector that supply global companies, including Nestlé. Migrant workers—mainly from Cambodia and Myanmar—are frequently lured with false promises, charged excessive recruitment fees, trapped in debt, had pay withheld, had identity documents confiscated, and in some cases were verbally or physically abused or sold to boat captains. Verité identified indicators of forced labor, trafficking and child labor among sea- and land-based workers, echoing prior investigations by media and NGOs and prompting lawsuits in the U.S. alleging slavery-linked seafood in products sold by retailers and food companies. The Thai industry’s problems have led to international pressure, including U.S. trafficking reports and EU warnings about import restrictions; Thailand’s government says it is taking enforcement steps.

Nestlé acknowledged the systemic nature of the risks—“virtually all companies sourcing seafood in the Thai seafood sector are exposed to the same risks”—and published an action plan and commitments to eliminate forced labor from its Thai seafood supply chain. Measures include improving traceability of raw materials, audits, grievance channels for workers, training for captains and owners, banning IUU fishing and trans-shipments at sea, and working with NGOs, suppliers, the Thai government and multi-stakeholder groups such as the ILO. Nestlé aims to report progress publicly and said it will apply sustained, collaborative efforts to address this complex issue across its seafood sourcing.

A June Gallup poll finds 29% of Americans favor closing the Guantanamo Bay detention facility and moving detainees to U.S. prisons, while 66% oppose it — a view little changed since 2009 and across multiple Gallup surveys. The poll was conducted days after the exchange that freed Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl in return for five Taliban detainees. Public opinion remains divided over negotiating with terrorist groups to secure Americans’ release. President Obama has long pledged to shutter Guantanamo, most recently reiterating that goal at a West Point commencement, but he still lacks broad public backing, including among many Democrats: 41% of Democrats now support closure versus 54% opposed. Republican support for closure has been consistently low, dipping to 8% in 2009; independent support has fallen from 37% in 2007 to 28% in 2009. Over the past 13 months, 17 inmates have been transferred out, including the five exchanged for Bergdahl, leaving 149 detainees. The White House is considering case-by-case transfers and reportedly drafting options to override a congressional ban on bringing detainees to the U.S., a move that would mark a significant use of executive power and likely draw strong congressional pushback. Observers note that shrinking detainee numbers or developments in the Bergdahl case could shift public sentiment.

Every June, nearly 10 million Chinese high school seniors sit the gaokao, the high-stakes national college entrance exam that often determines access to top universities and long-term career prospects. The exam is taken over multiple days, lasts many hours, and is widely viewed in China as a life-defining test; roughly one in four test-takers will not secure a university place. The intense national focus around gaokao season includes symbolic clothing choices, public displays of support, and commercial responses—companies like Nike selling gaokao-themed shirts—reflecting the exam’s cultural prominence.

Foreign universities are increasingly responding to gaokao’s timing and importance by adapting admissions practices to recruit strong Chinese applicants. The University of New Hampshire (UNH) announced it will accept gaokao scores, becoming the first U.S. flagship state school to formally evaluate Chinese applicants using those results. UNH’s initiative aims to admit outstanding Chinese students after gaokao results are released in late June, enabling some accepted students to begin studies as early as the January term or potentially the following semester, rather than waiting a year. Applicants must also submit English test results, participate in a video interview, and provide transcripts; UNH is still finalizing whether SAT/ACT requirements will be waived.

The University of San Francisco and many institutions in Europe, Australia, and Canada already accept gaokao scores, with USF running an admissions-by-gaokao program that emphasizes gaokao’s criterion-referenced strengths and expedites visas and enrollment. International students—particularly Chinese students who often pay full tuition—are an important revenue source for U.S. universities. These recruitment efforts come amid U.S. government scrutiny and tightened visa policies for some Chinese students, which could affect future enrollment patterns.

Variants of the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene—commonly called e2, e3, and e4—affect risk for multiple diseases by altering lipid handling and other processes. Each person inherits two copies, producing six possible genotypes, and different alleles are associated with distinct health outcomes. APOE e4 is a well-established risk factor for cardiovascular disease and neurodegeneration. Carriers of one or especially two e4 alleles have an increased tendency to develop atherosclerosis, the progressive buildup of fatty deposits and fibrous tissue in arterial linings that narrows vessels and raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. e4 is also strongly linked to higher likelihood of developing Alzheimer’s disease. In contrast, the e2 allele is connected to different risks and paradoxes: homozygosity for e2 (two e2 copies) greatly raises the risk of the rare disorder hyperlipoproteinemia type III. That condition produces elevated blood cholesterol, triglycerides, and beta–very low–density lipoproteins (beta-VLDLs), which can cause xanthomas (small yellow skin growths) and accelerate atherosclerosis. Intriguingly, adults with e2 variants may accumulate more brain amyloid plaques yet show fewer clinical dementia symptoms in some studies, suggesting complex effects on pathology versus clinical presentation. APOE variants have also been investigated in age-related macular degeneration (AMD); some studies suggest e4 might be protective or delay onset while e2 could increase risk or precipitate earlier symptoms, but findings are inconsistent. Overall, APOE alleles clearly influence lipid-related diseases and Alzheimer’s risk, while their roles in conditions like AMD remain uncertain and warrant further research.

Scout LaRue Willis staged a public protest against Instagram’s anti-nudity policy by walking topless through Manhattan’s Lower East Side and posting photos to Twitter with the hashtag #FreeTheNipple. Willis—daughter of Bruce Willis and Demi Moore—captioned one image “What @instagram won’t let you see #FreeTheNipple” and another “Legal in NYC but not on @instagram,” highlighting the inconsistency between New York City law, which has allowed female toplessness since 1992, and social media censorship. Willis’s avatar referenced a topless magazine cover that led to Rihanna’s Instagram suspension in April. Her photos, taken by Mario Sorrenti, and her vocal tweets followed Instagram’s removal of earlier content, including a sweatshirt she designed that featured topless models; Willis’s Instagram account was eventually disabled. She criticized Instagram for flagging images of breasts, even those of breast cancer survivors, and changed her Instagram middle name to “Areola” in defiance. The #FreeTheNipple movement, supported previously by figures like Miley Cyrus and Cara Delevingne and explored in a documentary of the same name, frames the issue as a fight against prudish or inconsistent censorship of female bodies online. Willis continued to press Instagram publicly but reported no response.

A Houston couple discovered a stranger had taken control of their internet-connected baby monitor and camera, using its speaker to hurl obscene insults at their sleeping 2-year-old daughter and then at the parents. Marc Gilbert heard the voice while doing dishes after his birthday; as he and his wife approached, the intruder called their daughter profane names and berated the parents before Gilbert unplugged the device. Fortunately the toddler is deaf and her cochlear implants were off, so she slept through the incident. The family believes the attacker exploited a known vulnerability in Foscam wireless IP cameras that security researchers disclosed earlier in the year, a flaw that could allow remote control of many devices. Researchers warned most Foscam units were still running old firmware; a June Foscam update later added prompts to change default admin credentials and allowed renaming the default admin user. Security experts advise changing default usernames and passwords, using strong, non-dictionary passwords, enabling strong wireless encryption, and keeping device firmware current. The Gilberts have unplugged their camera permanently and urged other parents to secure routers, cameras, and any associated web accounts to prevent similar intrusions.

Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and senior adviser, has had his White House security clearance restored after months of uncertainty tied in part to Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation. Kushner has cooperated extensively, providing documents and participating in multiple lengthy interviews—including two sessions with Mueller’s team and testimony before congressional committees. His attorney, Abbe Lowell, said Kushner answered all questions and helped expedite conclusions of the probes. Kushner’s interim clearance was stripped in February amid a broader overhaul of access procedures following staff controversies; his application was also complicated by initially omitted foreign contacts that were later added. White House officials attribute delays to administrative backlog and the complexity of his background, while some feared legal trouble tied to his contacts with Russians and his transition-era role. With permanent clearance restored, Kushner can access highly classified briefings and sensitive foreign intelligence relevant to his diplomatic portfolio.

During a National Assembly session in Paris, Green MP Véronique Massonneau was forced to interrupt her speech on pension reform after UMP conservative Philippe Le Ray began making chicken-like noises. Massonneau snapped at Le Ray, “That’s enough. Stop that, I’m not a hen!” but the heckling continued until Assembly President Claude Bartolone intervened, condemning the behavior and calling it unacceptable and childish. The episode provoked national outrage and accusations of sexism, with calls for Le Ray to be officially reprimanded; Deputy Minister Pascal Canfin described the conduct as degrading and deserving punishment. A video of the incident circulated online, though the noises are not clearly audible. Bartolone has summoned party whips for an extraordinary meeting to address the matter.

Scientists are alarmed by widespread intersex conditions in male bass across the northeastern United States and beyond. A USGS and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service reconnaissance of 19 national wildlife refuges found 85 percent of male smallmouth bass and 27 percent of male largemouth bass showed "characteristics of the opposite sex," typically immature eggs within testes. Similar high rates have been reported in parts of the Potomac and Susquehanna rivers and in other studies across U.S. river basins, and intersex traits have been documented in about 37 fish species worldwide.

Researchers suspect estrogenic endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) as the principal culprits. These include natural and synthetic hormones from human pharmaceuticals (notably birth control), hormones in livestock manure, herbicides such as atrazine, pesticides, and plastic-associated chemicals like BPA. Such compounds can disrupt hormone signaling at very low concentrations, altering gene expression (epigenetic effects), reproduction, immune function and potentially reducing fertility across generations. Lab work with synthetic estrogen EE2 showed lowered fertilization success in offspring and a 30 percent drop in fertilization in grandchildren.

Although the reconnaissance identified contaminated refuges, it did not analyze water or fish tissues for specific chemicals, so direct attribution remains uncertain. Scientists warn that even protected, ostensibly pristine refuges are affected, meaning contamination is pervasive. Addressing the problem will be difficult and costly—upgrading wastewater treatment, limiting runoff and reducing pesticide use face logistical and political challenges—but experts urge targeted actions to trace sources and reduce known estrogenic inputs to protect aquatic ecosystems and wildlife health.

A deadly fire in Colts Neck, N.J., on Tuesday left two adults and two children dead and is being investigated as a possible arson, Monmouth County Prosecutor Christopher J. Gramiccioni said. The blaze began around lunchtime at a large home on Willow Brook Road and burned into the evening. Three bodies were found inside the house; a fourth — identified by sources as 50-year-old homeowner Keith Caneiro — was found dead on the lawn with an apparent gunshot wound that did not seem self-inflicted. Officials have not officially released victims’ names. The Caneiro family members reported killed include Keith’s wife, Jennifer, 45, and two of their children, according to law enforcement sources and NJ Advance Media reporting.

Earlier on Tuesday, a separate fire occurred at the Ocean Township home of Keith’s brother, Paul Caneiro, where officials are also probing possible links between the two blazes. Prosecutors said they are investigating whether the incidents are connected but have not reached any conclusions. Neighbors described Paul as visibly distressed after his home caught fire before dawn; he remained at the scene through midday. Paul and Keith grew up in Brooklyn, later moved to New Jersey, and worked together in business ventures: public records and social media show Keith co-owned a technology firm, Square One, and EcoStar Pest Management in Asbury Park, where Paul was also involved.

Public profiles show Keith held a Columbia bachelor’s degree and had taken courses at Harvard Business School; he also held an active real estate license and had owned the Colts Neck property since 1999. The prosecutor’s office expects to release more information. Authorities continue to investigate both fires and possible criminal causes.

A newborn boy was found barely breathing in a dumpster at a Houston apartment complex early Tuesday morning, rescued with his umbilical cord still attached. Maintenance worker Carlos Michel discovered the infant upside down inside a white plastic trash bag after hearing crying while handling refuse at the Reserve at Windmill Lakes on Almeda Genoa Road around 8 a.m. He described the baby as cold and possibly only hours old. Paramedics transported the child to Hermann Hospital, where he is reported to be doing fine. Police and Child Protective Services are investigating and searching for the parents; officers suspect the mother may be a teenage resident of the property. The trash bag contained food leftovers and papers resembling homework with a student’s name, which investigators are examining for leads. Authorities noted Texas’s “Baby Moses” law—allowing a parent to leave an infant at any facility offering 24-hour medical care—aims to prevent such dangerous abandonments and encourage safer alternatives for parents in crisis.

Taylor Swift likens fame to “walking around with a cat on your head”: attention can be flattering but also invasive. On set for the “Shake It Off” video—an operation codenamed Project Sparrow with intense security—she’s candid about paranoia over privacy, fearing hidden cameras, wiretaps and leaks. Despite that, she feels freer than ever: excited about her new pop-focused album 1989, a move to New York, and a contented single life. Swift bought a Tribeca penthouse (and the unit across the hall for her security) and a Rhode Island summer home; she describes domestic pleasures—pets (kittens Meredith and Olivia), friends, cooking, and a garden—and brushes off criticism around renovations to her Rhode Island seawall.

1989 marks a deliberate shift from country-pop crossover to “blatant pop,” co-produced with Max Martin and influenced by Eighties pop. Unlike previous records, it contains fewer vindictive “diss” tracks; her songwriting is more reflective than scorched-earth, though one aggressive track, “Bad Blood,” targets another woman who Swift says tried to sabotage her arena tour by poaching staff. Swift declines to name the target publicly, preserving her usual mix of coyness and control; the ensuing media speculation connected the song to Katy Perry, who later tweeted a Mean Girls reference suggesting she’d been suggested as the subject.

Swift says she’s chosen friendship over dating, having not dated since her split with Harry Styles; instead she’s cultivated close female friendships (Karlie Kloss, Lena Dunham, Lorde) and embraced feminism. She remains fiercely protective of her image and work, refusing to let tabloid narratives trivialize her songs. Still, she engages warmly with fans—often under tight guard—and balances her tremendous public visibility with private routines, creative discipline, and a clear artistic reinvention.

The 2017 Baywatch film, directed by Seth Gordon and starring Dwayne Johnson, Zac Efron, Alexandra Daddario, Priyanka Chopra and Ilfenesh Hadera, aims to translate the campy appeal of the long-running TV series into an R-rated big‑screen comedy but largely fails. Built around the familiar beach spectacle of slow‑motion runs and attractive lifeguards, the movie initially leans into self-parody and playful chemistry—especially between Johnson’s stoic head lifeguard Mitch Buchannon and Efron’s washed-up Olympian Matt Brody—delivering a few laughs and a confident first half. The ensemble includes token recruits like Kelly Rohrbach’s C.J., Hadera’s Stephanie, and comic‑relief Ronnie Greenbaum (Jon Bass), whose awkwardness is meant to be endearing but often reads as grating.

Problems mount when the flimsy premise tries to expand into an actual crime plot: Brody and the Baywatch team uncover a drug‑smuggling operation run by resort owner Victoria Leeds (Chopra), exposing corruption among local officials. The screenplay, credited to multiple writers, stumbles in trying to make Baywatch about something more than its gimmicks; the tone slips into tasteless, male‑oriented humor—frequent profanity, crude sexual jokes, and extended gags about male anatomy—that veers toward juvenile rather than clever. Cameos from original TV cast members are undercut by having their names revealed early, spoiling what might have been fun surprises.

Overall, Baywatch offers some visual gags, a few amusing set pieces, and the star appeal of Johnson and Efron, but its larger ambitions drown in an overlong, half‑baked plot and broad, lowbrow humor. It’s essentially a well‑bodied but brainless beach movie: temporarily diverting but ultimately forgettable, delivering what many expect from the brand—red swimsuits and slo‑mo runs—without the wit or heart to elevate it.

A 43-year-old Italian man who had been in a minimally conscious state for nearly two years after a car accident experienced a transient but striking recovery of speech and interaction after receiving the sedative midazolam, according to a published case report. The patient had been comatose for 40 days post-accident, then emerged into a minimally conscious state: he showed sleep–wake cycles and limited voluntary behaviors (eye opening, reaching) but could not communicate or follow simple commands. Over the following year his cognition and movement worsened, with slowed motions and repetitive actions resembling catatonia.

Two years after the injury, clinicians preparing him for a CT scan administered midazolam, a benzodiazepine typically used for preoperative sedation and ICU unconsciousness. Minutes after injection he became alert, spoke by phone, recognized familiar routes, congratulated family, and interacted appropriately, though he had no memory of the accident or its consequences. The effect lasted about two hours and then dissipated. To test causality, physicians repeated midazolam and again observed rapid improvement: the patient conversed, solved simple arithmetic, and followed written commands. Brain scans taken before, during and after administration localized drug-affected regions previously associated with catatonia, a syndrome of profound unresponsiveness that can respond to benzodiazepines.

Authors note this is the first report of midazolam producing such an “awakening” in a minimally conscious patient. While midazolam’s short-term efficacy was clear, its continuous use is impractical outside ICUs. Trials with lorazepam produced agitation, so clinicians switched to carbamazepine, which helped sustain improved interaction. The report suggests some prolonged minimally conscious patients may harbor reversible, catatonia-like components responsive to GABAergic drugs, but broader study is needed. The case appeared in Restorative Neurology and Neuroscience.

At the Republican National Convention in Cleveland, Donald J. Trump’s nomination was made official amid the collapse of a last-ditch conservative revolt and a tightly managed push to present party unity. After weeks of plotting by anti-Trump conservatives—many energized by Ted Cruz supporters—efforts to use party rules or delegate maneuvers to block Trump ultimately failed. The roll call formally put Trump over the top, and attempts to cast dissenting votes or force a rules change were repeatedly rebuffed by party leaders and convention officials.

Conservatives’ plans were hampered by several factors: they lacked a viable alternative nominee, they were outnumbered by Trump loyalists and party regulars who accepted the primary results, and they faced vigorous coordination between the Trump campaign and the Republican National Committee. Delegations that tried to register dissent encountered procedural obstacles. Utah’s delegation announced votes for Cruz but state GOP rules permitted votes only for active candidates at the convention, so the presiding officer awarded Utah’s votes to Trump. In Alaska and other places, delegate splits were overruled by convention officials citing rule discrepancies, underscoring how party control of the gavel and rulings made a revolt impractical. Colorado’s dissident delegation, among others, ultimately stood down amid a sense that unity against Hillary Clinton trumped intra-party conflict.

With the nomination secured, the convention’s programming shifted to selling Trump’s message on jobs and family under the theme "Make America Work Again." High-profile speakers, including former rivals-turned-supporters Chris Christie and Ben Carson, tried to emphasize economic arguments and Trump’s business experience. Christie delivered an aggressively accusatory address aimed at Hillary Clinton that fused hyperbolic charges with theater: he led the crowd in mock verdicts and chants of “Lock her up!” Critics characterized the speech as an alarming example of political rhetoric that verged on criminalizing policy disagreements, likening it to a prosecutor’s performance that invited a mob-style condemnation rather than sober debate.

The evening also showcased members of the Trump family as political assets. Tiffany Trump and Donald Trump Jr. delivered polished, effective speeches designed to humanize their father and present him as both caring and results-driven. Tiffany offered a personal portrait that softened Trump’s image, while Donald Jr. tied family privilege to policy proposals like school choice and portrayed his father’s persistence as an asset. Their performances were widely viewed as among the night’s strongest moments.

Several figures came away damaged. House Speaker Paul Ryan, who had publicly expressed misgivings about Trump, presided over the roll call and formally declared Trump the nominee; his visible role made his earlier reservations appear hollow. State delegates and announcers who enthusiastically endorsed Trump on camera risked future political attacks in swing states. And former Attorney General Michael Mukasey was criticized for attacking Clinton’s handling of emails after previously defending controversial counterterrorism measures, creating a perception of hypocrisy.

Overall, the RNC’s second night solidified Donald Trump’s official nomination, displayed a party willing to suppress dissent in favor of unity, and relied heavily on emotional attacks against Clinton and family-centered messaging to rally the base ahead of the general election.

John Sidney McCain Sr. (August 9, 1884 – September 6, 1945) was a distinguished U.S. Navy admiral who commanded the Fast Carrier Task Force in World War II. Born in Teoc, Mississippi, he attended the University of Mississippi before graduating from the U.S. Naval Academy in 1906. Early in his career he served with the Asiatic Squadron and took part in the American occupation of Veracruz. Between the world wars he served aboard several battleships and auxiliaries; his first command was the cargo ship Sirius. In 1936, at age 51, McCain became a Naval Aviator and commanded the aircraft carrier Ranger from 1937 to 1939, helping develop carrier tactics. During World War II he led air forces in the Western Sea Frontier and the South Pacific Force, though a failure to order requested reconnaissance contributed to the Allied defeat at the Battle of Savo Island during the Guadalcanal campaign. He later served as Chief of the Bureau of Aeronautics and Deputy Chief of Naval Operations (Air). In 1944 he succeeded Marc Mitscher as commander of the Fast Carrier Task Force, conducting sustained carrier operations that supported major amphibious campaigns; his tactics in protecting cruisers Canberra and Houston earned him the Navy Cross. McCain’s forces struck widely across the Pacific, sinking many ships and destroying thousands of enemy aircraft. He witnessed Japan’s surrender on September 2, 1945, and died four days later; he was posthumously advanced to admiral and buried at Arlington National Cemetery. He was the patriarch of a naval family: his son John S. McCain Jr. became an admiral, and his grandson, John McCain III, served as a Navy captain and U.S. senator. USS John S. McCain (DDG-56) commemorates him and his son.

Zimbabwe’s first lady, Grace Mugabe, was involved in two separate incidents this week that drew significant media attention. In Harare, local state media reported she injured her ankle when the presidential limousine moved as she was getting in after returning from a medical trip to Singapore; her shoe was run over and she was treated at a clinic and discharged. A police motorcyclist escorting the motorcade also reportedly fractured his arm in a separate crash on the airport road. Presidential spokesman George Charamba characterized the vehicle episode as a “freak car incident.”

Separately, in Johannesburg, 20-year-old model Gabriella Engels accused Grace Mugabe of violently assaulting her with an extension cord at the Capital 20 West Hotel in Sandton after Engels visited Mugabe’s sons. Engels described being beaten repeatedly, sustaining a deep gash to her forehead and blood over her arms and hair, while bodyguards allegedly watched without intervening. She posted photos of her injuries and filed a police complaint in South Africa alleging assault with intent to do grievous bodily harm. South African police and officials issued mixed statements about whether Mugabe had handed herself over; Police Minister Fikile Mbalula later said she cooperated and handed herself in and would appear in court, while police noted negotiations were ongoing and the investigation was advanced. Diplomatic immunity was discussed as dependent on whether Mugabe was in the country on official business. Zimbabwean officials have not offered substantive comment on the assault allegations.

The young woman known worldwide as the "Delhi gang-rape victim" is remembered by her family as a brave, affectionate, hardworking 23-year-old who dreamed of becoming a doctor and building a hospital in her ancestral Uttar Pradesh village. Raised in a lower-middle-class family that moved to Delhi in 1983, she insisted on education despite financial strain; the family sold land to fund her studies. Her brother last spoke to her the evening she went missing after a bus journey; hours later police called saying she had been taken to hospital. She suffered horrific injuries after being attacked by six men on a private bus, and later died in a Singapore hospital. Five men have been charged with murder, gang rape and criminal conspiracy; a sixth, a juvenile, will be tried separately. The case has ignited nationwide anger, mass protests and calls for swift, severe punishment including the death penalty. Authorities have set up fast-track courts and review panels to reform laws and improve women’s safety, while legal experts warn against hasty legislation that could compromise fair trials. The family mourns and urges the brothers to focus on their exams despite overwhelming grief.

A new body of research helps explain why women outlive men almost everywhere: a surge in excess male mortality began around the late 19th and early 20th centuries as infectious disease control, better nutrition and healthier behaviors sharply cut death rates, but men did not benefit as much as women. A USC-led study of cohorts born 1800–1935 in 13 developed countries found that for people born after about 1880, female mortality fell roughly 70% faster than male mortality for ages over 40. The divergence began as early as 1870, concentrated between ages 50–70, and largely diminished after age 80. Much of the excess male mortality was attributable to cardiovascular disease rather than infectious causes; smoking explained only about 30% of the post-1890 sex gap. Researchers suggest this pattern implies sex-specific biological vulnerabilities or protective factors for heart disease in midlife, and call for further study of diet, exercise, genetics, cellular biology and links to later brain health. Complementary commentary highlights sex differences in stem cell regulation and hormonal effects—estrogen appears to boost certain regenerative capacities in females and may extend lifespan in experimental settings—underscoring that sex profoundly influences aging, lifespan and healthspan and should be a controlled variable in aging research. The USC study appears in PNAS.

Wine bottles have changed little since the 1800s, and one persistent nuisance — wine dripping down the bottle's neck after pouring — has long been treated as inevitable. Daniel Perlman, a biophysicist at Brandeis University and prolific inventor, studied the problem with slow‑motion footage and found the culprit partly lies in the hydrophilic nature of glass, which encourages liquid to cling to the bottle lip and run back along the neck. His simple but effective solution is a tiny circular groove cut around the bottle opening: roughly 2 millimeters wide and 1 millimeter deep. That miniature moat interrupts the wine stream so a drop cannot bridge the gap without climbing against gravity or having enough momentum to jump the groove. In demonstrations, the grooved bottle pours cleanly with no dripping, outperforming the traditional design and eliminating the need for napkin “bandanas” or aftermarket pourers. Perlman hopes manufacturers will adopt the modification, but widespread uptake would require the groove to be incorporated during production rather than added later as an accessory, which raises questions about manufacturing changes and licensing. Perlman is currently discussing the idea with bottle makers. If producers embrace the tweak, a simple, low‑profile redesign could finally end two centuries of drips and spare wine lovers the familiar annoyance.

The rollout of the Affordable Care Act has been a public-relations and policy debacle, undermining confidence in the government’s ability to expand health coverage. Widespread coverage has focused on two problems: a dysfunctional federal exchanges website and the revelation that many people cannot keep their existing plans despite President Obama’s repeated assurances. While some canceled plans were substandard and replacement plans often offer better coverage or subsidies, most Americans have heard only the negative headlines: canceled policies, sticker shock, and a broken site. Local news will magnify individual stories of rate increases and angry consumers, keeping the controversy in the public eye for months even if technical glitches are soon resolved.

Critics argue that the ACA’s design—built as a market-based, technocratic compromise to win moderate support—inevitably produces coercive outcomes that irritate millions, unlike straightforward government programs such as Medicare or Medicaid. Democrats, including moderates who weakened the bill to secure passage, own the law and its consequences. Appeals for bipartisan fixes now ring hollow because the crucial compromises were made when Democrats had greater leverage. The administration’s insistence that nobody is forced out of their plans contradicts the law’s architecture and political reality. Ultimately, the rollout’s failures may leave the uninsured worse off politically and could strengthen opposition rather than foster cooperation.

Selena Gomez revealed she underwent a kidney transplant over the summer because of complications from lupus, and the donor was her longtime friend and actress Francia Raisa. Gomez shared photos from the hospital — including the two friends holding hands in their beds and images of her post-surgery incision — and explained she had been laying low and not promoting her new music because she was recovering. She thanked her medical team, family and friends, and expressed deep gratitude to Raisa, calling the donation “the ultimate gift and sacrifice.” 

Gomez has publicly managed lupus for years: she disclosed receiving chemotherapy for the autoimmune disease in 2015 and has spoken about its mental-health impacts, including anxiety, panic attacks and depression. In 2016 she took a career break to focus on her health, describing the need to be proactive and encouraging others to address their own issues. In later interviews she said she hoped using her platform would raise awareness and help others. 

Lupus is a chronic inflammatory disease in which the immune system attacks the body’s tissues and organs, potentially affecting the skin, joints, kidneys, blood, brain, heart and lungs. It can be triggered by genetic tendencies, infections, certain drugs or sunlight, is often challenging to diagnose, and currently has no cure — though treatments can manage symptoms. Gomez’s transplant underscores both the serious kidney risks lupus can pose and the life-changing impact of living organ donation.

Google announced it is exploring expansion of its Google Fiber gigabit internet and TV service, asking 34 cities across nine metropolitan areas to complete a checklist to assess what it would take to build fiber networks there. The metros include Phoenix, Atlanta, San Jose, Salt Lake City, Nashville, San Antonio, Portland (Ore.), Charlotte and Raleigh-Durham. Google emphasized it will work with city leaders to map networks, evaluate local construction challenges, and use existing infrastructure such as utility poles and conduit to reduce disruption. Local factors—topography, housing density and existing utilities—will influence final decisions. The company said it aims to announce which cities will get Fiber by the end of the year, but cautioned that no commitments are guaranteed.

Google Fiber, which runs fiber directly to homes offering symmetric 1 Gbps service, currently serves parts of Kansas City and Provo and has agreements for Austin and some Kansas City suburbs. Expansion could significantly grow its customer base, strengthen its negotiating leverage for TV content, and pressure incumbent cable and phone providers to increase speeds. Observers expect Google may not expand to all nine regions but that the move signals broader national ambitions. The company declined to disclose customer totals or profit timetables; the rollout strategy favors neighborhoods showing concentrated demand to avoid costly piecemeal builds.

Former President George H.W. Bush was released from Maine Medical Center after four days of treatment for a fractured vertebra sustained in a fall at his Kennebunkport summer home. Spokesman Jim McGrath said Bush, 91, was "very grateful" and in good spirits; doctors reported no nerve damage or neurological deficits and do not expect surgery. Attending physician Dr. William D’Angelo said the fracture should heal in three to four months. Bush, who has a form of Parkinson’s and uses mobility aids, is the oldest living former president.

North Korea announced it had successfully tested a hydrogen bomb on Wednesday, saying the device was miniaturized and part of its effort to deter the United States. The underground explosion produced a seismic event (USGS magnitude 5.1) near the Punggye-ri test site—the same location used in 2006, 2009 and 2013—prompting regional alarm, evacuations near the Chinese border, and immediate international condemnation. Pyongyang’s state media hailed the test as a “perfect success” and a demonstration of national strength, timed two days before leader Kim Jong Un’s birthday.

The U.S., South Korea, and outside nuclear experts expressed deep skepticism that the detonation was a full thermonuclear (H‑bomb) device. Initial U.S. analyses and seismic yield estimates suggested the blast was similar in size to previous fission tests; experts proposed it could have been an A‑bomb, a “boosted” fission device with some fusion fuel, or a failed two‑stage thermonuclear attempt. No radiation was detected by South Korean agencies immediately after the event.

The U.N. Security Council called an emergency session and said it would work on significant new measures, likely tougher sanctions. In Washington, Republicans criticized the Obama administration and sought broader penalties on foreign firms dealing with Pyongyang; presidential candidates urged stronger action while Hillary Clinton called for more sanctions and enhanced missile defenses. China and Russia condemned the test, with Beijing lodging a protest. The episode intensified regional tensions, underscored North Korea’s persistent push to advance its nuclear capabilities, and renewed debate over how the international community should impose real costs to halt Pyongyang’s program.

The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (MFA) exhibited material from Tomb 10A at Deir el-Bersha—an important Middle Kingdom (MK) necropolis about 250 km south of Cairo—highlighting a mutilated, bandage-wrapped mummified head discovered when George A. Reisner’s MFA–Harvard team excavated the tomb in 1915. Tomb 10A belonged to a powerful MK nomarch named Djehutynakht (either IV or V) and his wife, who also bore the name Djehutynakht. Although tomb robbers had looted valuables and damaged the burials, excavators recovered one of the largest MK funerary assemblages known: decorated cedar coffins, canopic jars, pottery, nearly 60 model boats, and the famed “Bersha procession” relief group. The governor’s outer coffin remained largely intact except at the head end; in the disturbed burial chamber archaeologists found a decapitated torso and a mummified head placed atop the governor’s coffin. CT scans in 2005 showed extensive post-mortem facial bone loss, preventing confident morphological sexing despite male-leaning cranial features (robust mastoids, occipital/temporal regions, and gonial flaring). Because prior ancient DNA work on Egyptian remains often failed or produced contamination, the MFA collaborated with the FBI Laboratory to attempt genetic sex determination. Traditional forensic PCR-based methods typically require relatively long DNA fragments and have limited utility for highly degraded samples. The team therefore used high-throughput shotgun sequencing, which can recover very short ancient fragments without targeted PCR. By drilling a pristine molar and extracting tooth powder, investigators obtained damaged but authentic ancient DNA and, through sequencing, determined the individual was biologically male—strongly indicating the head belonged to the governor Djehutynakht rather than his wife. This study demonstrates that modern sequencing methods can overcome longstanding barriers to analyzing severely degraded Egyptian remains and resolve century-old archaeological questions.

The Paterno family argued removing Joe Paterno’s statue doesn’t aid Jerry Sandusky’s victims or heal Penn State; they urged uncovering the full truth and criticized the Freeh report as an incomplete, prosecutorial document that denied Paterno due process. They noted Paterno lacked a hearing, counsel couldn’t interview key witnesses, and critical evidence remains undisclosed. Separately, the NCAA announced pending “corrective and punitive measures” after the Sandusky scandal and Freeh’s finding that top leaders repeatedly concealed abuse. NCAA leaders—including President Mark Emmert—called the case unprecedented and signaled willingness to use severe penalties beyond past precedent. The Freeh report highlighted decentralized compliance failures and urged an honest review of institutional culture; Penn State said it was ready to respond.

Sergey Kislyak, Russia’s long-serving ambassador to the United States, has suddenly become the central figure in a growing Washington controversy over the Trump administration’s ties to Moscow. Normally low-profile and a fixture on the diplomatic circuit—hosting cultural events, dinners and “jazz diplomacy” nights—Kislyak’s routine engagement with U.S. officials has drawn intense scrutiny after contacts with him implicated two senior Trump aides. Michael Flynn resigned as national security adviser after misleading the White House and the FBI about his December calls with Kislyak, and Attorney General Jeff Sessions recused himself from Justice Department investigations after acknowledging two 2016 meetings with the ambassador that he had not disclosed during his confirmation hearing. Sessions’ omission and subsequent recusal have fueled calls for his resignation and intensified probes into whether Russia sought to influence the 2016 election.

Kislyak, 66, is a career diplomat fluent in English who has represented Moscow in Washington since 2008, after earlier postings including NATO and Belgium and service in the Foreign Ministry on arms control. Colleagues describe him as intelligent, charming, firm and fiercely loyal to Kremlin positions—willing to press Moscow’s line on Ukraine and sanctions in sometimes testy exchanges. Observers note his extensive network in Washington and his deliberate outreach to officials, which Moscow likely views as strategic engagement with potential U.S. allies. That networking is standard ambassadorial practice, but in the fraught post-election context it has become politically explosive.

U.S. intelligence reports and some media have suggested Kislyak may have ties to Russian intelligence or act as a recruiter, claims Moscow angrily rejects as “fake news” and “total disinformation.” Experts contacted by reporters expressed skepticism about labeling him a spy, noting instead that he is a trusted emissary who is often recalled to Moscow. Kislyak himself has publicly lamented the nadir in U.S.-Russia relations while insisting that better ties are possible; he has promoted cultural exchange and argued against caricatured depictions of Russia.

Now at the center of inquiries into possible Russian interference and contacts with the Trump team, Kislyak’s routine diplomatic interactions are being reevaluated amid allegations that Moscow ordered hacks of Democratic targets during the 2016 campaign. Whether his role is simply that of a persistent envoy or something more covert remains disputed, but his contacts have already reshaped the early months of the Trump administration and propelled Kislyak from diplomatic society into the heart of a major U.S. political storm.

JetBlue is giving away a surprise volunteer getaway as part of its For Good Month. On Nov. 27 the airline will charter a flight from JFK carrying 50 winners and their companions to an undisclosed “Destination Good” city it already serves. Winners will learn the location only the morning they depart and will spend three immersive days doing volunteer work tied to JetBlue For Good’s priorities: youth and education, community, and the environment. U.S. residents 18+ can enter at jetbluecheckinforgood.com by Oct. 26, answering philanthropic questions and submitting a 150-word statement; winners are notified by Nov. 20.

A genetic survey of 400 pythons captured in South Florida over a decade has revealed that at least 13 individuals carry mitochondrial DNA from the Indian rock python, indicating past hybridization with the invasive Burmese python population that has overrun the Everglades. USGS researchers had expected a mostly homogenous Burmese lineage from snakes descended from released or escaped pets in the 1980s, but the unexpected “tangled family tree” suggests maternal Indian python ancestry in a small subset. Indian rock pythons differ from Burmese pythons in being smaller, faster, more terrestrial, and perhaps more aggressive—traits that, if combined through hybrid vigor, could enable some Everglades snakes to exploit drier habitats and expand their range more quickly. However, the mitochondrial-only finding means the signature is inherited maternally and does not by itself prove broad genomic mixing or a new species. Scientists caution that behavioral consequences are uncertain and that hybridization could also produce outbreeding depression. The discovery complicates already faltering control efforts against an estimated many-thousand-strong python population that has devastated small mammal communities. Researchers plan further genomic and ecological studies to clarify how hybrid ancestry, climate change, and adaptation may influence the invasion’s future.

Prince Andrew became the first senior royal to join Twitter, launching an account under the handle @TheDukeOfYork with an inaugural tweet reading "Welcome to my Twitter account - AY," the initials indicating posts personally written by him. The move, framed by his office as a natural extension of his long-standing interest in new technology, coincided with his visit to open the Duke of York Award for Technical Education at a University Technical College. Responses were mixed: supportive messages and advice about adding a personal touch appeared alongside mocking and critical reactions referencing his association with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and jokes confusing him with other figures. A palace spokesman emphasized the duke’s commitment to free speech and to using Twitter to tell people what he is doing; the account followed two golf clubs and two official royal accounts (@BritishMonarchy and @ClarenceHouse). BBC coverage noted that when the royals engage on social media extra security measures are sometimes needed to block abusive posts. Within two hours the account had gained over 3,000 followers.

Star Wars momentum from The Force Awakens is set to continue with a steady release schedule of new films over the next several years. First up is Rogue One: A Star Wars Story, directed by Gareth Edwards and written by Gary Whitta and Chris Weitz, arriving December 16, 2016. Set after the Empire’s rise, it follows a rogue band of Rebels on a desperate mission to steal Death Star plans; the cast includes Felicity Jones, Diego Luna, Riz Ahmed, Ben Mendelsohn, Mads Mikkelsen, Donnie Yen, Forest Whitaker and others. Episode VIII, written and directed by Rian Johnson and featuring many Force Awakens alumni (including Daisy Ridley and Mark Hamill), is scheduled for December 15, 2017, though plot details remain scarce. A Han Solo anthology film, directed by Phil Lord and Christopher Miller with a script by Lawrence and Jon Kasdan, aims to explore young Han’s origins and is due May 25, 2018. Colin Trevorrow will direct Episode IX (2019) with Rian Johnson credited as writer. A Boba Fett anthology is tentatively planned for 2020. Dates and personnel may change, but Disney’s plan promises frequent Star Wars installments.

Rachel Barton Pine, once a rising violin prodigy from Chicago, rebuilt a public music career while coping with life-changing injuries from a 1995 Metra train accident that cost her left leg above the knee and severely damaged her right leg. At 20 she had already won major international competitions and earned acclaim, but the accident interrupted a trajectory toward the world’s top orchestras. Thrown from a train while trying to retrieve a valuable 1617 Amati violin that had trapped her, she was dragged more than 300 feet, lost much of the skin and bone in her legs, developed osteomyelitis, and survived dozens of surgeries, prolonged hospital stays and addiction withdrawal. She later endured post-traumatic stress and long, fraught legal battles that culminated in a multimillion-dollar settlement, which she uses to pay ongoing medical expenses.

The story charts Barton’s extraordinary early talent—rigorous practice from toddlerhood, early orchestral debuts, prize wins in Leipzig, Budapest, Vienna, Genoa and Brussels, and praise from leading figures such as Daniel Barenboim—and then the abrupt derailing of that promise. Recovery included painstaking reconstructive surgery, years of rehabilitation, and painful adjustments in personal relationships: a long estrangement from her mother and siblings, followed by gradual reconciliation. She met Greg Pine during recovery; he became her partner, caregiver and later husband, accompanying her on tours and helping her manage inaccessible backstage terrain and onerous medical regimens.

Despite recurring infections, dozens of operations and relentless medical appointments, Barton continues to perform superbly—touring with solid regional orchestras, teaching, founding a charity to help musicians in need, and advocating for music outreach—though she longs for the elite orchestral stages she believes she might have reached. She balances pride in artistic resilience with frustration over compromised mobility, ongoing health risks, and sacrifices such as postponing family plans until her medical situation stabilizes. Her performances still earn standing ovations, testimony to enduring talent even as she remains a work in progress physically and professionally.

Controversial rapper Azealia Banks unexpectedly announced on Twitter that she planned to vote for Donald Trump in the 2016 presidential race, arguing—using blunt, provocative language—that Trump alone had the courage to "bust up big business" and criticizing Hillary Clinton and Bernie Sanders as ineffective or insincere on issues affecting minorities. Banks framed politicians generally as dishonest and suggested putting “a piece of shit in the White House” might be as honest as the country gets.

Separately, the Associated Press compiled major campaign developments with the Iowa caucuses imminent. Ted Cruz and allied super PACs challenged Donald Trump to a one-on-one debate in Iowa, offering $1.5 million to veterans’ charities if he agreed; Trump dismissed the proposal and refused to attend a Fox News debate amid a feud with the network, opting instead to host a veterans’ fundraiser in Des Moines. Cruz and other Republicans mocked or criticized Trump’s boycott; Marco Rubio called it a sideshow as he prepared for debate prep. Trump’s team announced endorsements and local allies in South Carolina.

On the Democratic side, Bernie Sanders met President Obama and—while open to an additional New Hampshire debate—requested three more debates overall, with conditions. Sanders pledged to remain positive and resist negative campaigning against Hillary Clinton, who also supported holding more debates. Other items: campaign theatrics, a tomato-throwing arrest at a Trump event, weather concerns for caucus-goers, and parody and ad activity from other campaigns.

China plans to attempt the first-ever landing on the moon’s far side before 2020, a senior engineer involved in the country’s lunar program announced on state television. The Chang’e 4 mission, described by Zou Yongliao of the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ moon exploration department, aims to investigate geological conditions on the moon’s far side — the hemisphere permanently turned away from Earth — with the longer-term objective of installing a radio telescope there. Because radio transmissions from Earth cannot directly reach the far side, China would deploy additional satellite capability to relay communications: an orbiting spacecraft would receive signals from the landed probe and forward them to Earth, a commonplace solution analogous to orbiters relaying signals from Mars rovers. Placing sensitive radio astronomy instruments on the shielded far side could fill an observational gap and enable low-noise exploration of the universe. Chang’e 4 would follow earlier steps in China’s methodical lunar program, which has launched orbital probes, landed a rover in 2013, and planned a 2017 mission to return lunar samples to Earth — a success that would make China the third country after the U.S. and the Soviet Union to do so. Beijing has also hinted at eventual crewed lunar ambitions as part of its broader, steadily advancing space program.

Thirty-five years after William and Michelle Becker were found drowned near a Mattituck marina, New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) officers are renewing efforts to get answers, offering a $15,000 reward for information. The couple left a dinner party shortly before midnight on March 10, 1981. William, a 43-year-old DEC police officer and 15-year agency veteran, was discovered about 12 hours later in the Matt-A-Mar marina, his foot caught on a swim platform and his arm tangled in electrical cable; he was still in his dark green uniform and had a lump on his head. Michelle, 36, who ran a local beauty salon and was mother to three children, was found about 20 hours after the couple left the party, roughly 40 feet from her husband; her slippers were on the dock near the host’s boat. Suffolk County police ruled the deaths accidental and closed the case in 1983, with authorities initially concluding William may have drowned trying to save Michelle, who could not swim.

Relatives and some colleagues have long doubted that explanation.
