Family members note it was cold and dark, the couple’s home was only half a mile away, William reportedly feared water, and the host’s boat was under repair — circumstances that made a spontaneous trip to the dock unlikely. DEC Police Maj. Scott Florence, who re-examined the case in the 1990s, pointed to scene details that raised questions: a kitchen table on the boat had come apart and William’s clip-on uniform tie was found on the floor, suggesting a possible struggle. The DEC officers’ union and fraternal organizations funded the reward, the largest in the department’s history, hoping the 35th anniversary will prompt new witnesses to come forward. Suffolk County Homicide detectives say they welcome any new information. Family members, frustrated by what they view as a rushed initial investigation, continue to seek closure and urge anyone with knowledge to speak up before memories fade.

From January 17 to February 24, 2018, researchers led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health conducted a randomized household survey across Puerto Rico to estimate excess deaths related to Hurricane Maria. They sampled 3,299 households using a geographically stratified design: 900 administrative units (barrios) were ranked by remoteness (travel time to cities ≥50,000), grouped into eight percentile categories, and 13 barrios were randomly selected per category, plus one each from the two inhabited offshore islands. In each sampled barrio, 35 household locations were chosen from OpenStreetMap building layers; when a sampled point was nonresidential, empty, or refused, interviewers substituted a nearby visible household randomly. Data collectors interviewed one adult per household with a brief questionnaire capturing household composition during 2017, births, moves, and deaths, plus monthly access to electricity, water, and cell service. No personal identifiers were recorded; GPS data were aggregated, consent was obtained, and the study received IRB exemption.

Using a hybrid census approach, the team treated missing-but-not-known-dead individuals as alive, constructed survey weights from inverse selection probabilities, and used official 2016 population and mortality data for comparisons. They estimated the crude post-hurricane mortality rate for Sept 20–Dec 31, 2017 without weighting (finding no remoteness-specific clustering), assumed Poisson-distributed deaths to derive standard errors and confidence intervals, and compared the post-hurricane rate to the same period in 2016.

From their survey extrapolated to Puerto Rico’s population, researchers estimated approximately 4,645 excess deaths between Sept 20 and Dec 31, 2017 (a 62% rise in mortality), which they rounded above 5,000 to reflect assumptions; the 95% confidence interval ranged widely (about 800 to 8,500). The study attributes much of the sustained elevated mortality to interrupted or delayed medical care—about one-third of post-storm deaths—and documents prolonged infrastructure failures (e.g., electricity outages exceeding 100 days for many households). The authors note household surveys can undercount deaths if households were destroyed and missing from sampling, suggesting their estimate may be conservative, and recommend larger surveys to narrow uncertainty. The findings highlight implications for aid, preparedness, and family closure, and complement other analyses that also found higher-than-official death tolls.

A row of new luxury homes in Chesterton, Cambridge, was graffitied overnight with large Latin lettering reading “Locus in domos Loci Populum,” a phrase that turned out to be nonsensical Latin—likely the result of someone using an online translator to render “local homes for local people.” The stunt, painted across four riverside houses marketed at around £1.25m each, drew national attention more for its choice of language than for clarity: classicists noted every word misfires, and commentators linked the error to Google Translate’s limitations. The graffiti also included anti-currency signs—Dollar, Euro and Yen—with “go away,” and phrases like “local lives,” signalling opposition to foreign investment and the sale of community assets; the houses occupy the former Penny Ferry pub site. Observers speculated about the graffitist’s motives: an attack on elitist Establishment symbols associated with the University, a protest against developers pricing out locals, or a deliberately debased Latin jab at corporate-speak. The piece’s author, a Cambridge classicist, read further cultural hints—regendered pedestrian iconography and mixed political signals—and found the protest both revealing and muddled. Locally, the incident highlights broader housing tensions: Cambridge average house prices are among the highest in Britain (roughly £475–500k), many homes are bought by outsiders, and wages lag far behind. Police are investigating the criminal damage; the developer is removing the graffiti and reviewing security. The protest’s aim is clear but its execution left the message blunted.

A gunman identified as 28-year-old Gene Evin Atkins was arrested and held on $2 million bail after a midday shooting, police chase and a nearly three-hour hostage standoff at a Trader Joe’s in Los Angeles’ Silver Lake neighborhood. Authorities say Atkins shot his grandmother seven times and wounded another woman at a South L.A. home before driving away with the injured woman. Officers tracked the car, exchanged gunfire during a pursuit, and the vehicle crashed into a pole outside the supermarket. The man then ran into the store, firing at police as he entered; bullets shattered the store’s glass doors and frightened customers and employees dove for cover. A 27-year-old Trader Joe’s employee, Melyda Corado, was later identified by coroner’s officials as the woman who was shot and killed; it was unclear whether she was struck by police or the gunman’s fire. Atkins took an estimated 40 to 50 people hostage inside the store. He made a series of demands, and crisis negotiators engaged him throughout the standoff. Around 6:30 p.m., Atkins handcuffed himself and surrendered, exiting the store surrounded by several hostages. His grandmother remained hospitalized in critical condition. Six other people, ages 12 to 81, were transported to hospitals in fair condition; none had been shot. Officials praised law enforcement and emergency personnel for their response, which Mayor Eric Garcetti said likely saved lives. Witnesses described chaotic scenes of employees and customers escaping through windows and being rescued by police.

Sen. Bernie Sanders used a major Georgetown University address to cast his “democratic socialism” as part of a long American tradition, aligning it with the economic-rights emphasis of Franklin D. Roosevelt and Martin Luther King Jr. Seeking to demystify the label “socialist,” Sanders insisted he does not advocate government ownership of small businesses or the means of production; instead he emphasized economic security as a core element of freedom. He urged policies such as health care as a right, free college tuition, investment in jobs, a living wage, paid family leave, and public funding of elections, arguing these reforms combat a corrupt political system and an overly powerful billionaire class. Sanders invoked Roosevelt’s 1944 “second Bill of Rights,” proposing a modern revival of economic rights that he says America has yet to realize.

Speaking days after the Paris attacks, he also called for a new international security organization—like NATO but broader—to include current NATO members, Russia, and Arab League states to address contemporary threats. The speech drew a large, enthusiastic student audience, though some, like Georgetown senior Livia Matteucci, expressed skepticism about achieving such goals in a gridlocked Congress.

Commentators noted Sanders’s attempt to bridge socialism and liberalism, reviving a New Deal-era rhetoric that once united diverse left factions but fractured during the Cold War. His appeal is strongest with younger voters for whom Cold War-era divisions are less salient, opening space for renewed debate about social democracy in the U.S.

The Metropolitan Opera’s 2014 staging of John Adams and Alice Goodman’s controversial 1991 opera The Death of Klinghoffer provoked intense public debate, protests and heightened security at Lincoln Center. Police presence was heavy; bags were checked and Met general manager Peter Gelb briefed performers about enhanced measures. The production drew protesters—including former Mayor Rudy Giuliani, ex-Gov. David Paterson, Representatives Carolyn Maloney and Peter King, and groups led by Jewish and conservative religious organizations—who accused the work of romanticizing or excusing terrorism for portraying the 1985 Achille Lauro hijacking and the murder of Leon Klinghoffer. Demonstrators included some in wheelchairs and a vocal rally across from the opera house; counterprotesters and supporters of artistic freedom also gathered. The Anti-Defamation League mediated a compromise: the Met canceled international theater and radio broadcasts but proceeded with live New York performances, a move that pleased few.

Supporters argued the opera grapples with complexity rather than endorsing violence. Artistic figures like Oskar Eustis and critics noted that Klinghoffer and his family are among the most sympathetic characters and that dramatizing the hijackers’ humanity does not equal glorification. Critics such as Rabbi Avi Weiss and members of the Klinghoffer family said the work creates false moral equivalencies and can inspire violence; the daughters declined the opera’s framing in the program. The opera’s history has been contentious since its Brussels premiere and U.S. debut, spawning cancellations, debates and mixed receptions over decades. Defenders emphasize the opera’s powerful music and the emotional weight of Marilyn Klinghoffer’s closing aria, arguing that the piece ultimately centers personal loss and forces audiences to confront painful realities rather than celebrate terrorism. The Met maintained that the work is neither anti-Semitic nor celebratory of terror, and performances ran through Nov. 15, 2014, amid continued controversy.

After 53 days and an immense multinational effort, the search for Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 is entering a more costly, technologically intensive phase. The jet vanished March 8 with 239 people aboard; despite more than 300 flights, 3,000+ flight hours, and searches covering roughly 4.6 million square kilometers, no wreckage was found in the primary search zone in the southern Indian Ocean. Australian, Malaysian and Chinese officials will meet in Canberra to audit all collected data—especially the satellite “pings” that guided the current search—to confirm interpretations and assumptions.

Authorities plan to expand the search into deeper, previously unmapped waters and intensify seabed mapping and underwater searches. The next phase will rely on specialized private-sector equipment: deep-diving autonomous underwater vehicles, tendable towed side-scan sonar and other rare devices (only a handful globally). The U.S. Navy’s Bluefin-21 will continue missions but is depth-limited and costly (about $40,000/day); tenders will be issued for deeper-capable systems expected in the water within one to two months. Australia estimates the new phase will cost about $60 million and discussions will cover cost-sharing. Officials emphasize avoiding long gaps in operations, learning from prior searches like Air France 447, while acknowledging the search’s increasing difficulty and uncertain prospects.

Philippine officials angrily condemned Dan Brown’s depiction of Manila as “the gates of hell” in his novel Inferno. Brown’s book includes a character who, after visiting, describes Manila as plagued by six-hour traffic jams, choking pollution, massive poverty and a thriving child sex trade. Metropolitan Manila Development Authority chairman Francis Tolentino, who said Brown has never visited the country, sent a public letter to the author and publishers demanding correction and insisting Manila is instead “an entry to heaven,” emphasizing residents’ Catholic faith, compassion and good character. Tolentino also disputed the severity of traffic and denounced what he called religious insinuations. Some Filipinos agreed with Brown online, and commentators noted persistent poverty despite economic growth — recent government figures put poverty at 27.9 percent. Former disputes over The Da Vinci Code were also recalled, and calls for Manila’s rehabilitation were voiced by local politicians.

Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is the most common form of cardiomyopathy, typically affecting adults aged 20–60. It usually begins in the left ventricle, where heart muscle stretches, thins, and the chamber enlarges; the condition can progress to the right ventricle and atria. As the heart dilates, contraction weakens and pumping ability declines, potentially causing heart failure with symptoms such as breathlessness, fatigue, and swelling in the ankles, legs, abdomen, and neck veins. DCM can also cause valve problems, arrhythmias, and intracardiac blood clots. It goes by multiple names depending on cause or context — alcoholic, congestive, diabetic, familial, idiopathic, ischemic, peripartum, and primary cardiomyopathy. Causes include coronary heart disease, heart attack, high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid disease, viral infections (myocarditis), HIV, toxins (e.g., cobalt), certain recreational drugs, and some chemotherapy agents; up to one-third of cases are inherited, and many remain idiopathic. Separately, fatty liver disease — accumulation of fat in liver cells — can occur even inlight drinkers but heavy alcohol use increases risk. Alcohol-related fatty liver (ALD) may be asymptomatic or cause right-upper-abdominal discomfort; it is reversible with abstinence but can progress to alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis, liver failure, and life-threatening complications if drinking continues. British singer George Michael, who died at 53, was found by a coroner to have died of dilated cardiomyopathy with myocarditis and fatty liver; his partner Kenny Goss and family have been mourning while awaiting final toxicology and funeral arrangements.

Mantecore, the white tiger long associated with Siegfried & Roy, died March 19 at age 17 after a short illness, the entertainers announced. Zoologists note 17 is near the lower end of a typical tiger lifespan. Mantecore—often spelled “Montecore” in reports—was the animal involved in the October 3, 2003 onstage incident at The Mirage in which Roy Horn sustained a severe neck bite. Horn lost significant blood that night, but he and his partners have consistently argued that a stroke and subsequent brain swelling, not a predatory attack, were the underlying causes of his partial paralysis and the end of his stage career. Siegfried & Roy maintain Mantecore acted protectively, dragging Horn backstage after Horn suffered the stroke; Horn has repeatedly corrected media language calling the event an “attack.” After the incident, the tiger was quarantined for 10 days, cleared of disease or abnormal behavior, and returned to exhibit at The Mirage’s Secret Garden of Siegfried & Roy and later alternated time between the attraction and Horn’s estate. Horn called Mantecore a brother and credited the tiger with raising awareness for conservation and preservation. He said it was his honor to be beside the animal at the end and expressed that Mantecore’s spirit will live on with Siegfried & Roy and their fans.

Christopher Kennedy Lawford, an actor, author and member of the Kennedy political dynasty, died at 63 after suffering a medical emergency in Vancouver, his cousin Patrick J. Kennedy told the Associated Press. Lawford was living with his girlfriend and working to open a recovery center; he had been doing hot yoga shortly before the incident. A coroner’s autopsy was expected to determine the exact cause of death.

The only son of Patricia Kennedy and actor Peter Lawford, Christopher grew up between Hollywood and the Kennedy circle, later recounting celebrity moments and family pressures in his 2005 memoir Symptoms of Withdrawal. He began using drugs as a teenager, spiraled into heroin and opioid addiction in the 1970s, and experienced homelessness and arrests before achieving sobriety at 30. He became a prominent advocate for recovery, writing several books including 2015’s What Addicts Know, and helped others—including cousin Patrick—through their own recovery journeys.

Lawford maintained a steady acting career with roles on General Hospital, All My Children, appearances on Frasier and The O.C., and a small part in Terminator 3. He is survived by his sisters Sydney, Victoria and Robin, and his children David, Savannah and Matt.

Police in Cleveland have arraigned 52-year-old Ariel Castro on multiple counts after three women — Amanda Berry, Georgina “Gina” DeJesus and Michelle Knight — and Berry’s young daughter were found alive after nearly a decade of captivity in his home. Castro appeared silent at his arraignment, held on $8 million bond, and faces charges including kidnapping and rape. Cuyahoga County Prosecutor Timothy McGinty said prosecutors will seek additional counts for each act of sexual violence, every day of kidnapping and all felonious assaults; he also plans to ask a grand jury to consider “aggravated murder” charges tied to the termination of pregnancies, a charge that can carry the death penalty in Ohio. Investigators allege horrific abuse: Michelle Knight reported being forced to miscarry multiple times after being starved and beaten; Berry gave birth in captivity, delivering in a tub, and the newborn briefly stopped breathing before surviving. Authorities are reviewing more than 200 seized items and suspect writings that may explain motives, while state crime-lab DNA testing was expedited. Two of Castro’s brothers were arrested then released with no charges. Family members and neighbors expressed shock and devastation; Castro’s daughter said she is disgusted and devastated. Officials say the rescued women need time, space and careful debriefing as they recover from prolonged trauma.

The not-guilty verdict for Casey Anthony in the death of her two-year-old daughter Caylee provoked widespread public outrage and sparked a grassroots push for new law. A central issue in the trial was that Anthony did not alert authorities after Caylee’s disappearance; the child was last seen June 16, 2008, but Caylee’s grandmother waited until July 15 to notify police. Anthony was convicted only on four misdemeanor counts of lying to investigators. In response, Oklahoma mother Michelle Crowder launched a Change.org petition and Facebook page urging Congress to pass “Caylee’s Law,” which would make it a federal felony for a parent or guardian to fail to report a missing child. The petition quickly gained thousands of signatures per hour and became one of Change.org’s fastest-growing campaigns; a related Facebook campaign has nearly two million people pledging to leave porch lights on for Caylee.

A comprehensive review of 67 studies concludes that serious vaccine complications are very rare and that immunization benefits far outweigh risks. Commissioned by federal health officials and led by RAND researchers, the analysis—published in Pediatrics—reassures parents that there is no credible evidence linking vaccines to autism or leukemia. The report updates and echoes a 2011 Institute of Medicine review, finding that while some vaccines are associated with adverse events, these are uncommon and typically mild or transient.

Noted risks include a small increase in fever-related seizures after MMR and some influenza vaccinations; these seizures are usually benign and leave no long-term harm. Rotavirus vaccines (RotaTeq, Rotarix) are tied to a rare intestinal blockage, intussusception, at an estimated one to five additional cases per 100,000 doses; experts point out rotavirus infection itself can also cause this problem. Other rare associations, such as thrombocytopenic purpura with varicella and MMR, were acknowledged.

Researchers emphasize balancing these minimal risks against vaccines’ massive public-health benefits: preventing hundreds of millions of illnesses, millions of hospitalizations, and hundreds of thousands of deaths over children’s lifetimes. The authors hope the findings will support clinicians in counseling families, though they recognize entrenched vaccine hesitancy may persist.

The U.S. Geological Survey has raised its estimate for the chance of a magnitude 8.0-or-greater earthquake striking California within the next 30 years to about 7%, up from roughly 4.7%. The revision reflects an improved understanding that faults across California form an interconnected system and that ruptures can jump from one fault to another, enabling multi-fault, mega-quakes. Historically rare, an M8+ event would release vastly more energy than the 1994 Northridge (M6.7) quake; the last Southern California mega-quake is thought to have been about M7.9 in 1857. Recent large California quakes—including the 1992 Landers (M7.3), 1999 Hector Mine (M7.2) and a 2010 Baja event—have demonstrated fault-jumping behavior, and even the 2011 Tohoku (M9.0) quake in Japan involved multi-fault rupture with catastrophic consequences. The updated forecast examined more than 250,000 fault-based earthquake scenarios across roughly 300 faults (versus far fewer in earlier models), producing a revised recurrence expectation of about one M8+ event every 500 years (previously one every ~600 years). The southern San Andreas is highlighted as the most likely site for a large quake; that segment has a 19% chance of producing M6.7+ shaking in 30 years. Overall, there is a >99% chance of at least an M6.7 event statewide within 30 years, a 93% chance of M7+, and a 48% chance of M7.5+. The forecast refines risk estimates for planning critical facilities but does not enable precise timing of earthquakes.

U.S. Navy leaders have launched an intensive probe into whether compromised computer systems played any role in the August 21 collision of the guided-missile destroyer USS John S. McCain with a merchant tanker, and they are making cyber forensic work a standard part of future accident investigations. Vice Adm. Jan Tighe and Vice Chief Adm. Bill Moran said teams from U.S. 10th Fleet, the Navy’s cyber command, were sent to Singapore to capture shipboard computer and network data and to assess whether the reported aft-steering failure was caused by cyber tampering. Although investigators so far have no indication that a cyberattack caused either the McCain crash or the June 17 USS Fitzgerald collision, the simultaneity of both incidents prompted commanders to look closely at digital intrusion as a potential factor. The two collisions together killed 17 sailors, triggered leadership removals and a temporary operational pause ordered by Chief of Naval Operations John Richardson, and raised questions about readiness in the Pacific amid growing regional threats. Early assessments have focused on crew training, situational awareness breakdowns and operational strain across the fleet, but intelligence officials have long warned that adversaries could potentially spoof ship systems—displaying false positions or sensor data—to blind commanders and create hazardous situations. The Navy has set aside about $1.5 billion for cyber defenses through 2023 and intends to institutionalize cyber forensics in all mishap investigations so authorities and trained personnel are routinely available to determine whether digital interference occurred. Commanders stress ships must be able to “fight through” cyberattacks and maintain redundant communications and monitoring to preserve safety and command continuity.

A 10-year-old Houston girl, Britton Joniec, underwent emergency endoscopic surgery after swallowing a metal bushing from a fidget spinner. Her mother, Kelly Rose Joniec, recounted that on the drive home from a swim meet she heard Britton retch, then saw her turning red and drooling; Britton indicated she had swallowed something after putting a spinner bushing in her mouth to clean it. Urgent care staff could not determine whether the object was in the airway or esophagus, so Britton was rushed to Texas Children’s Hospital in The Woodlands. X-rays showed the nickel-sized bushing lodged in her esophagus; a gastroenterologist removed it using an endoscope. Joniec described the ordeal as terrifying but ultimately resulting in a positive outcome and urged parents to be cautious. She warned that bushings can pop out easily and represent a choking hazard, especially for younger children (she highlighted children under 8). The incident has drawn wide attention on social media and sparked renewed discussion about fidget spinner safety. Originally designed as a therapeutic aid for children with ADHD or autism, the spinning toys have become a widespread craze—so much so that some schools have banned them because they distract students. Joniec’s experience serves as a reminder that popular toys can have unforeseen risks and that caregivers should supervise use and heed age-appropriate warnings.

At the Nathan’s Famous July Fourth hot dog eating contest on Coney Island, Joey “Jaws” Chestnut captured his 10th title by consuming a record 72 hot dogs and buns in 10 minutes, topping his 70-dog mark from 2016. Carmen Cincotti placed second with 62; Matt “The Megatoad” Stonie finished third with 48. Chestnut said he trains like a marathoner, gradually increasing intake before the contest. In the women’s division, Miki Sudo won her fourth straight crown with 41 hot dogs; Michelle Lesco was second with 32 and record-holder Sonya Thomas third with 30. Thousands watched the televised event. Outside, PETA handed out vegan hot dogs, and five demonstrators trying to unfurl a banner in the crowd were arrested, though they were not affiliated with PETA.

A new global study warns rising temperatures and more frequent heat waves will make it harder for many commercial aircraft to take off, forcing weight reductions, delays or cancellations. As air warms and becomes less dense, wings produce less lift, so fully loaded planes at some airports may not be able to achieve safe takeoff performance during the hottest hours. The Columbia University-led analysis projects that on the hottest part of the day between 10 and 30 percent of fully loaded flights could need to offload fuel, cargo or passengers—or wait for cooler conditions—by mid- to late-century. Global average temperatures have risen about 1°C since 1980 and could climb a further ~1–3°C this century, while annual maximum daily temperatures at airports are projected to rise 4–8°C by 2080, amplifying heat-wave impacts.

Using 27 climate model projections and performance data for common jets at 19 busy airports, the authors estimate that, under unchecked emissions, payload or fuel capacity cuts might reach about 4 percent on the hottest days (roughly 12–13 seats on a 160-seat plane); with strong mitigation this could fall to ~0.5 percent. Airports with short runways, high elevation or very hot climates—such as New York’s LaGuardia and Dubai—face the greatest risk; some aircraft at these sites could be weight-restricted much of the time during extreme heat. Temperate airports with long runways like JFK, Heathrow and Charles de Gaulle are less vulnerable.

The study highlights broader cascading economic effects for an industry with thin margins. Possible adaptations include revised scheduling to cooler hours, airframe or engine redesigns, or runway expansions where feasible; researchers urge incorporating climate risks into aviation planning.

Sophia Chua-Rubenfeld, eldest daughter of Amy Chua—the author of Battle Hymn of the Tiger Mother—served as valedictorian and delivered her high school commencement speech, jokingly teasing her mother’s controversial parenting memoir. An audience member confirmed she opened by quipping that instead of writing an original speech she would read from her mom’s book. Her school named a single valedictorian for the class of 2010–2011, with the class president serving as salutatorian. Sophia, who has blogged to address family rumors, applied to Harvard, Yale and UVA and hinted she chose Harvard. Amy Chua, a Yale law professor, faced intense criticism after excerpts of her memoir—meant as satirical—were widely interpreted as endorsing strict child-rearing.

Jack McCullough, 76, was ordered released and granted a new trial after DeKalb County Judge William Brady threw out his 2012 conviction for the 1957 abduction and murder of 7-year-old Maria Ridulph. McCullough had been serving a life sentence in what was one of the oldest cold cases ever prosecuted. DeKalb County State’s Attorney Richard Schmack, who reviewed the case after inheriting it, concluded in a six-month probe that there was “clear and convincing evidence” McCullough was wrongly convicted and asked the court to free him.

Schmack’s review examined some 4,500 pages of records—FBI and police reports, grand jury and trial transcripts, affidavits and other documents—and found new evidence supporting McCullough’s long-held alibi that he was about 40 miles away in Rockford trying to enlist in the Air Force when Maria vanished. Crucial to the finding were newly obtained AT&T phone records showing a collect call placed at 6:57 p.m. from a Rockford pay phone to McCullough’s home, consistent with his account. Schmack also faulted trial rulings that excluded certain evidence and highlighted false or problematic testimony used to convict McCullough, including an identification by Maria’s playmate made decades later from a photo array.

Maria disappeared Dec. 3, 1957 while playing in the snow; her body was found 144 days later near the Iowa border. McCullough maintained his innocence throughout. Family members of the victim remain unconvinced and have sought a special prosecutor to try to keep him behind bars. The judge’s ruling focused on procedural and evidentiary failings rather than pronouncing guilt or innocence.

Multiple media reports claimed a major explosion at Iran’s underground Fordow uranium-enrichment site last week, alleging a blast on Monday at 11:30 a.m. that badly damaged the facility and trapped about 240 people. The story, originating on WND and attributed to a defected Iranian intelligence officer, said Fordow—buried roughly 300 feet under a mountain and housing some 2,700 centrifuges enriching to 20%—was partially destroyed. The report blamed Israel, suggesting sabotage timed ahead of Israeli elections, and warned of possible retaliation. Israeli officials gave mixed reactions: one minister welcomed damage to Iranian assets, while foreign ministry sources and intelligence contacts said they had no reliable confirmation. Iranian authorities, including the deputy head of the Atomic Energy Organization and military commanders, denied any explosion, calling the reports Western propaganda aimed at influencing nuclear talks. The IAEA and diplomats said they had no evidence of an incident. Analysts noted Fordow’s strategic importance and the plausibility of covert sabotage but emphasized the claims remain unverified and contentious.

South Korean intelligence briefed lawmakers that North Korea appears to be moving an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), though details on timing, direction and transport remain unclear. The briefing followed Pyongyang’s sixth nuclear test, which seismological data and state media suggest was its most powerful yet and which North Korea claimed was a hydrogen (thermonuclear) bomb potentially mountable on a long-range missile. Weapons experts caution that pairing a warhead and missile can’t be confirmed without an actual nuclear-tipped ICBM launch.

The test came after a summer of missile activity, including two lofted long-range launches in July and an intermediate-range missile in August that overflew Japan. South Korea’s National Intelligence Service warned lawmakers that North Korea might conduct a lower-angle ICBM launch into the North Pacific, and had reportedly dug additional tunnels at its test site, allowing for more detonations “anytime.”

Seoul responded militarily and diplomatically: South Korea’s Navy, Air Force and Army held live-fire exercises off the east coast to demonstrate readiness, with the Navy warning it would “immediately destroy” provocations. Diplomats at the UN condemned the test; U.S. Ambassador Nikki Haley said the United States would circulate a resolution seeking the strongest sanctions. South Korea and the U.S. agreed to lift restrictions on the payload weight of South Korean ballistic missiles, but tensions surfaced between President Moon Jae-in’s engagement-oriented approach and President Trump’s harder-line rhetoric, prompting concerns that visible cracks could be exploited by Pyongyang. Analysts warn North Korea may time another provocative launch around its Sept. 9 national holiday to maximize attention.

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un delivered a televised New Year’s address—the first such broadcast since 1994—calling 2013 a year for “creations and changes” and urging a “radical turnabout” to transform the impoverished state into an “economic giant.” He emphasized improving the economy and raising living standards while reiterating that military strength remains essential to national power. Kim also called for removing confrontation with South Korea and urged both sides to honor past inter-Korean agreements, a conciliatory tone coming after conservative Park Geun-hye’s election in Seoul. However, he set prerequisites South Korea may resist, and offered no concessions on Pyongyang’s nuclear program. The speech followed two long-range rocket launches under Kim’s rule—one failed in April and a December launch Pyongyang said succeeded—prompting UN Security Council deliberations. Kim watched the new year in with a musical performance; his remarks blended familiar propaganda themes without mentioning the United States or explicitly addressing nuclear disarmament.

Gasoline prices have finally begun their seasonal decline after a delayed and volatile summer marked by refinery and pipeline problems. The national average fell to about $3.72–$3.67 after peaking near $3.86–$3.87, but remains historically high for this time of year and about $0.27 above last year. Analysts expect continued drops as inventories rise and demand falls, possibly shaving up to $0.50 by late November to roughly $3.30–$3.35 nationally. California remains far costlier, averaging about $4.51.

On June 10 The New York Times briefly posted then pulled a Michael Barbaro article profiling the women entangled in Anthony Weiner’s sexting scandal; a production note said the piece went up “before it was ready.” Though removed, much of the 1,342-word story was reconstructable from Google cache results. The article sympathetically portrayed several women—some who sought publicity, some who were exposed unwillingly—arguing the scandal has continued to upend their lives even as Weiner re-emerged running for New York mayor. Lisa Weiss, a Nevada blackjack dealer who leaked messages to RadarOnline and later appeared on Inside Edition, described severe fallout: taunting customers, ostracizing coworkers, press camps outside her home and ongoing emotional harm. Traci Nobles, a Georgia fitness instructor forced to quit her job at a Young Women’s Christian Organization after messages surfaced, is working on a book. Gennette Cordova, a college student when she received an image from Weiner, withdrew from classes and moved to escape scrutiny. Some women formed online support among themselves; reactions to Weiner vary—Weiss and Nobles at times express support for his comeback. Porn actress Ginger Lee urged him not to run, saying renewed headlines retraumatize them. Weiner issued apologies saying he was “deeply sorry” for upheaval and vowed not to discuss private exchanges as the mayoral campaign keeps the episode alive.

North Korea issued an air-raid warning early Thursday, likely part of a defense drill, Seoul’s Unification Ministry said after monitoring a Pyongyang radio broadcast. The alert told military units to stand ready amid heightened tensions as North Korea conducts large-scale drills concurrent with annual South Korea–U.S. exercises. Pyongyang angrily denounced U.S. B-52 flights over the peninsula and warned that U.S. bases in Guam and Japan are within its “striking range,” promising corresponding military actions. The rhetoric follows North Korea’s recent nuclear test and rocket launches, and new U.N. sanctions that have provoked further threats, including talk of pre-emptive strikes. Analysts say Kim Jong Un’s regime seeks to bolster its military deterrent and domestic standing, forcing the U.S. and allies to reassess strategy and boost defenses.

Following the U.S. commando raid that killed Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad, Pakistan’s army ordered a reduction of U.S. military personnel in the country to “minimum essential” levels and warned it would review military and intelligence cooperation if similar unilateral strikes recur. The statement, issued by Army Chief Gen. Ashfaq Kayani, sought to counter domestic criticism accusing Pakistan’s security services of failing to protect sovereignty or of harboring bin Laden. It acknowledged “shortcomings” in Pakistani intelligence while alleging the CIA withheld later intelligence developments after initial ISI cooperation. Washington expressed confusion and restraint, balancing congressional pressure over continued aid with the need to protect a vital counterterrorism partnership. U.S. officials voiced doubts that bin Laden could have lived in a garrison town without some local assistance; Pakistani leaders emphasized sovereignty violations and called for investigations, even as past probes have produced limited revelations. The episode deepened mistrust and risked straining U.S.-Pakistan ties.

An English historian has identified what may be the earliest clear instance of the word “fuck” in a legal record dated 1310–1311. Dr Paul Booth of Keele University found the name “Roger Fuckebythenavele” recorded three times in the Chester county court plea rolls (first on 8 December 1310, again 25 May 1311, and finally as outlawed on 28 September 1311). Booth suggests the entry is likely a nickname rather than a clerk’s joke and proposes two interpretations: either it records an actual awkward sexual attempt by an inexperienced youth, later publicized—perhaps by a spurned lover—or it was used metaphorically to mean a dimwit who would attempt sex in such a way. Before this discovery, the earliest widely cited use with clear sexual meaning was in the ca. 1475 poem Flen flyys (“fvccant vvivys of heli”), while a 1278 name, John le Fucker, has been argued to reflect a different word (fulcher, “soldier”) and thus not necessarily the modern expletive. Linguist Jesse Sheidlower notes the word’s Germanic roots and cognates in Dutch, German, and Swedish with sexual and motion-related senses. Booth, an honorary senior research fellow and co-director of the Gascon Rolls project, plans to publish his findings in Notes and Queries and has informed the Oxford English Dictionary. The entry illuminates medieval naming practices and coarse nicknames—other curious examples include medieval epithets referencing testicles and crude language—underscoring how archival work can revise the known history of everyday language.

A North Carolina judge ruled that Marcus Robinson’s death sentence must be reduced to life without parole because prosecutors’ racially influenced jury selection tainted his trial, marking the first use of the state’s 2009 Racial Justice Act. Superior Court Judge Greg Weeks found that race played a “persistent, pervasive and distorting” role: prosecutors struck black jurors more than twice as often as whites statewide and 2.6 times as often in Cumberland County, based on a Michigan State University study. Weeks concluded the statistics supported an inference of intentional discrimination, undermining the jury’s neutrality and court integrity. Robinson, convicted in the 1991 killing of a white teenager, will be moved off death row; prosecutors plan to appeal. The decision could affect more than 150 pending Racial Justice Act claims. The ruling has sparked debate—supporters hail it as a landmark reform addressing racial bias in capital cases, while prosecutors and some lawmakers dispute the study’s scope and seek to repeal the law.

Police removed eight human remains from Johnson Family Mortuary in east Fort Worth after the building’s landlord, who had asked the mortuary to vacate about two weeks earlier, found unattended bodies and called authorities. Fort Worth police said the remains ranged from infant to adult and were in varying stages of decomposition. Homicide investigators executed a search warrant on suspicion of abuse of a corpse; the Tarrant County medical examiner is now identifying the bodies and notifying next of kin. No arrests have been made and the investigation is ongoing.

Co-owner Dondre Johnson called the discovery a misunderstanding, saying some remains were embalmed and in caskets, including one slated for shipment to Nairobi, and that refrigeration is not legally required. He and his twin brother Derrick—who says he is a part-owner but had not been present for weeks—insist the business has been operating legally and plan to continue serving families. The mortuary’s state license expires this month and the Texas Funeral Service Commission is investigating the business in five open complaints. Authorities urge anyone who thinks a relative may be among the deceased to contact the medical examiner.

A fast-moving winter storm that began in the Midwest continued Friday across the Northeast, dumping snow, freezing rain and ice that created widespread travel chaos, large power outages and at least eight deaths across the eastern U.S. The mix brought up to a foot of snow in places, heavy freezing-rain accumulations elsewhere, and prompted school closures, long commuter delays and hundreds of flight cancellations. About 200,000 customers across four states were without power Friday evening; Pennsylvania alone reported roughly 105,000 outages, mostly in the west. The National Weather Service said snow in the Northeast should end Saturday morning, but warned of continued gusty winds, coastal flooding and additional snow from a cold front moving in through the weekend.

The hazardous conditions contributed to multiple deadly crashes: victims included a 60-year-old woman in Indiana, fatalities in Ohio and Maryland, two dead in a Mississippi tour-bus crash, and three killed in separate Arkansas incidents. Transportation systems were severely impacted in the New York metropolitan region: hundreds of vehicle crashes stalled traffic on the George Washington Bridge and other arterials, Port Authority Bus Terminal and Newark airport were overwhelmed with stranded travelers, and NJ Transit warned of continued bus delays and cancellations because drivers reached federally mandated rest limits. FlightAware reported thousands of delays and nearly 2,000 cancellations at the storm’s peak; Newark Liberty was among the hardest hit airports.

Officials faced criticism for preparedness. New York Mayor Bill de Blasio and New Jersey leaders pledged reviews after many commuters were stranded for hours, students sheltered overnight at schools, and highways such as a 30-mile stretch of I-78 saw vehicles stuck. Some Massachusetts towns received more than nine inches of snow, northern New England reported four to eight inches, and parts of the region reduced interstate speeds. Emergency crews continued clearing roads and restoring services as travel disruptions and hazardous conditions persisted.

UPS has taken its drone experiments from remote test sites into residential settings by trialing an octocopter launched and recovered from a moving delivery truck. In a test in Lithia, Florida, UPS and supplier Workhorse Group demonstrated the HorseFly UAV system: an octocopter that docks on a rooftop mount on a delivery van, lowers a caged payload into a hatch where a driver loads it, then flies autonomously to a nearby destination and returns to a truck that has moved on. The drone recharges through a physical connection while docked and is claimed to have a roughly 30-minute flight time, top speeds near 45 mph, weighs about 9.5 pounds, and can carry up to 10 pounds—sufficient for many residential parcels.

UPS says the truck-launched-drone approach differs from prior tests and could improve network efficiency and reduce emissions by avoiding long road miles for single rural stops—for example, dispatching a drone from a route to serve one distant address and letting the vehicle continue. Workhorse built the drone and the custom electric vehicle used in the trial; UPS has already purchased a fleet of Workhorse electric trucks and aims for a system that can be adapted to many vehicle types.

Regulatory and operational hurdles remain: FAA rules currently restrict commercial drones from flying over uninvolved people and require line-of-sight operation, limits that could constrain practical distances and routes even if drivers could maintain visual contact. The test reflects growing industry momentum—Amazon and others are also active in residential drone delivery research and pilots, each pursuing different technical approaches to last-mile automation.

The Hollywood Reporter published a detailed investigation alleging that the American Humane Association (AHA), the nonprofit charged with monitoring animal welfare on film and TV sets, has repeatedly concealed animal deaths and downplayed abuses to maintain good relations with Hollywood producers. Reporter Gary Baum documents numerous troubling incidents beyond the well-known deaths of three horses on HBO’s Luck, including a dog punched by its trainer on Eight Below, a chipmunk dropped and stepped on during Failure to Launch, and scores of sheep and goats dying during a production hiatus on The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey. Sources—many anonymous—say AHA often excuses such events as unintentional or irrelevant because they occurred off-camera. The investigation quotes AHA board member Candy Spelling appearing to defend the organization’s “No Animals Were Harmed” end-credit wording by implying monitoring applies only while cameras roll, a stance that drew sharp criticism and calls for government oversight.

AHA responded with a public rebuttal defending its seven-decade record and insisting the THR piece misrepresents its work. The organization cites a 99.98 percent on-set safety rate and stresses that most reported incidents were accidental, unrelated to production activities, or occurred outside its jurisdiction. AHA provided specific rebuttals—saying a sick dog in Our Idiot Brother died of cancer unrelated to filming, a horse linked to War Horse died in transit after being checked out of production, and the Hobbit deaths occurred when animals were not under AHA supervision. AHA notes it voluntarily inspected the Hobbit farm afterward and recommended safety changes that production implemented.

The statement outlines reforms the group says it has already enacted: creating a Scientific Advisory Committee to review its guidelines, appointing Dr. Kwane Stewart to head the program, recruiting licensed veterinarians as Certified Safety Representatives in major filming regions, and instituting a policy to commission independent investigations whenever an animal is seriously injured or dies on set. AHA emphasizes its mission-driven history, claiming to protect roughly 100,000 animal performers annually across 2,000 sets and insisting it continually improves oversight to prevent abuse. The dispute highlights tensions over accountability, transparency, and the adequacy of existing protections for animals in entertainment.

Buckingham Palace announced that Prince Philip, 95, the Duke of Edinburgh and husband of Queen Elizabeth II, will stop carrying out public engagements this autumn. The palace said the queen fully supports his decision; he will continue to lead many charities but will no longer attend events actively. No new health details were provided, though Philip has experienced heart problems in the past while maintaining a busy public schedule. Earlier reports of an unusual royal household meeting had provoked speculation and false reports about the couple’s health, including that Buckingham Palace’s flag had been lowered. Philip and the queen appeared well at recent engagements—he opened the Warner Stand at Lord’s cricket ground, joking and inspecting the new facility.

A March 2016 crawl collected outlinks from wikipedia.org across all 865 wiki collections, with duplicate detection disabled to preserve completeness for potential sharing; the files are not publicly accessible. Separately, a CNN report notes Jerome Corsi’s book Where’s the Birth Certificate? reached No. 6 on the New York Times Best Sellers list, reviving the “birther” claim that President Obama is not a natural-born U.S. citizen. Despite Obama releasing his long-form Hawaiian birth certificate, polls showed 17% still doubted his birthplace, down from 25% earlier.

The piece centers on Eddie Murphy’s brief, controversial return to Saturday Night Live for its 40th anniversary and a backstage anecdote from Norm Macdonald about why Murphy declined to perform a Bill Cosby impersonation. The article opens with a sarcastic lampooning of Cosby’s current stature—still a draw, wealthy, recently honored in museums—contrasting that with the multiple sexual-assault accusations against him, setting an ironic tone about public sympathy. Norm Macdonald recounted on Twitter a planned Celebrity Jeopardy! bit in which Eddie Murphy would enter in a multicolored Cosby-style sweater, silently play the Cosby role for comic effect, then speak as Cosby to huge laughter. Macdonald says he spent an hour convincing Murphy to do it; Murphy ultimately refused, deciding the laughs weren’t worth “kicking a man when he’s down.” That decision was praised publicly, with Cosby himself expressing appreciation and commentator Piers Morgan endorsing Murphy’s restraint. The article then shifts to audience reaction to Murphy’s actual SNL appearance: after an introductory bit by Chris Rock, Murphy spoke briefly—less than a minute—without performing a classic character. Viewers and critics reacted with disappointment and ridicule, calling the cameo needy, unfunny, and awkward. A moment of on-air confusion, where Murphy appeared to check with producers and suggested doing the bit again before the broadcast cut to commercial, amplified the awkwardness. NBC later edited the online version to remove the fumbling. Media reaction and tweets are quoted, lampooning Murphy’s cameo and defending his indifference to critics by reminding them of his box-office misfires. The article reiterates Macdonald’s account that Murphy consciously refused to parody Cosby out of principle, choosing not to add to the public pile-on. It closes by noting that Cosby publicly thanked Murphy and references a 1987 Raw appearance as context for what audiences “missed.”

The killing of 25-year-old Drummer Lee Rigby in Woolwich has prompted intense scrutiny of Britain’s security services after it emerged the two men shot and arrested at the scene, identified as Michael Adebolajo, 28, and Michael Adebowale, 22, had previously been known to MI5. Rigby, a father and soldier who had served in Afghanistan, was attacked in broad daylight on a south-east London street; footage and witness accounts show the assailants used large knives and a cleaver and later confronted armed police. Passers-by filmed one suspect, bloodied, proclaiming he had killed the soldier because British forces “kill Muslims every day.” Armed officers arrived about 13 minutes after the first emergency call; police fired eight shots, wounding both suspects, who remain under armed guard in hospital in stable, non-life-threatening condition.

Government and security figures defended intelligence agencies, noting the difficulty of monitoring everyone in a free society. Communities Secretary Eric Pickles stressed parliamentary inquiry but warned against expecting omnipresent surveillance. Former MI6 counterterrorism head Richard Barrett and other experts highlighted the challenge of distinguishing radical views from a turn to violent extremism, especially when suspects may operate in small, locally focused groups. Former Met commissioner Lord Blair called for a prompt review to ensure the security services acted properly.

Video obtained by media outlets shows the attackers apparently luring police by dragging the victim into the road and then attempting to ambush officers; one suspect charged at a patrol vehicle while the other aimed a handgun. Two further arrests—of a man and a woman—were made on suspicion of conspiracy to murder, and searches continued at multiple addresses. Community and Muslim leaders condemned the attack, while thousands are expected to gather in solidarity against extremism and to mourn Rigby, remembered by family as a loving son, husband, father and protector.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Turkey has shared audio recordings related to the Oct. 2 killing of journalist Jamal Khashoggi with Saudi Arabia, the United States, Germany, France and Britain, asserting that those countries have listened to the conversations and “know.” Turkish authorities have previously said they possess a recording purportedly documenting the murder inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul, though its existence had not been officially confirmed until Erdogan’s remarks. Turkey maintains a 15-member Saudi team flew to Istanbul and that the killers and the location of Khashoggi’s remains are known; Ankara seeks extradition of suspects. Turkish sources told Al Jazeera traces of acid were found at the Saudi consul-general’s residence, near the consulate, where Turkish investigators believe Khashoggi’s body was chemically disposed of. Istanbul prosecutors said he was strangled on entry and his body dismembered. Saudi Arabia initially denied involvement, then offered shifting explanations—first that Khashoggi left the consulate, then that he died in a fight, later calling it a rogue, premeditated murder—while Riyadh has arrested 18 people and dismissed five officials. Erdogan suggested some Saudi officials tried to hamper the probe and said he might press the issue in a possible meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump in Paris.

Correction: An earlier claim that this winter solstice would be the longest night ever was incorrect. While Earth's rotation is gradually slowing over geologic time because of tidal interactions with the Moon, year-to-year variations from geologic and climatic processes can speed or slow rotation. Over the past ~40 years, data show a slight net speed-up (partly from polar ice melt and mass redistribution), and 20th-century trends were variable; the longest night in recorded history likely occurred in 1912. The author apologizes for the error.

Separately, the winter solstice—occurring on December 21 or 22 in the Northern Hemisphere—does mark the shortest day and longest night of the year at any given location in that hemisphere. This happens because Earth’s axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees; during the December solstice the Northern Hemisphere is tilted farthest from the Sun, making the Sun follow its lowest arc across the southern sky. Conversely, the Southern Hemisphere enjoys its longest day on this date. At local solar noon on the solstice, shadows are longest; the effect grows with latitude, so high-latitude places like Fairbanks see only a few hours of daylight.

Practical details: sunrise and sunset shift to the southernmost points on the horizon on the solstice. However, the earliest sunset and latest sunrise in many mid-latitude locations do not fall on the solstice—earliest sunsets often occur in early December and latest sunrises in early January—because of the interplay between Earth's axial tilt and its elliptical orbit, which alters "solar time" relative to clock time. Finally, the coldest days typically lag the solstice by weeks; despite increasing daylight after the solstice, the Northern Hemisphere continues to lose heat for a while, so average coldest periods often arrive in January depending on region, ocean influence, and snow cover.

Bourbon’s soaring popularity has created what many fear is a temporary shortage rooted not in missing ingredients but in past production choices: distillers in the 1990s simply underestimated today’s demand. Bourbon must age in oak barrels to develop its characteristic flavors, a process that takes years and cannot be sped up by simply distilling more. That time dependency, combined with a shortage of new American oak barrels and hoarding of limited releases by collectors and deep-pocketed buyers, has made sought-after long-aged bottlings scarce. Evidence is mostly anecdotal—many enthusiasts report trouble finding previously available bottles—but sales have jumped sharply over the past decade, intensifying pressure on supply.

Entrepreneurs and some distillers are experimenting with ways to compress aging from decades to months or even days. Techniques include using much smaller barrels to increase wood-to-spirit contact, adding toasted oak chips and agitation, applying ultrasonic energy, increasing oxidation in tanks, and pressurizing stainless steel vessels with wood segments. Firms like Tuthilltown, Copper Fox, Terressentia, Cleveland Whiskey and others have developed various rapid-aging methods and blends to approximate traditional profiles and to bring products to market sooner. Some companies even blend tiny fast-aged reserves with older stocks to achieve desired character.

While these methods can produce drinkable whiskey and help fill market gaps, many experts remain skeptical. Chemically, aging involves complex transformations—aldehydes turning into acids and then esters—that unfold over time; speeding up extraction of wood compounds doesn’t always accelerate those reactions. Accelerated spirits are often described as “hot,” “raw,” or thin, lacking the rounded complexity of long-aged bourbon. Large legacy distillers generally dismiss quick-aging as inferior and continue to invest in traditional methods. The shortage, therefore, is likely temporary as more barrels mature, but conventional solutions will take years; rapid-aging innovations may ease shortages but so far haven’t universally matched the quality of time-aged bourbon.

Researchers at the March of Dimes Prematurity Research Center Ohio Collaborative studied 3,485 Nordic mother–baby pairs and found maternal height influences pregnancy duration and preterm birth risk. Using genetic analyses (Mendelian randomization, maternal and fetal genetic scores, and haplotype transmission), they showed birth length and birth weight are mainly driven by fetal genetics: transmitted height-associated alleles from parents had strong effects on newborn size, while nontransmitted maternal alleles did not. In contrast, gestational age appears to be causally affected by maternal height independent of fetal genotype. Maternal nontransmitted height alleles were associated with longer gestation, and each 1 cm increase in maternal height corresponded to about 0.3–0.4 additional days of pregnancy and roughly a 3% lower preterm risk. Authors note the mechanism may involve maternal lifetime nutrition or environment and emphasize findings derive from well-nourished northern European cohorts, so results may differ where malnutrition is common. The study highlights distinct maternal versus fetal genetic contributions to fetal growth versus pregnancy length and underscores the importance of understanding causes of preterm birth.

Sonya Thomas narrowly defended her women’s title at Nathan’s Famous Fourth of July Hot Dog Eating Contest in Coney Island, consuming 36.75 hot dogs and buns in 10 minutes to edge Juliet Lee’s 36. That was a sharp decline from Thomas’s 45-dog record last year. In the men’s event, Joey Chestnut extended his dominance, winning a seventh straight crown and breaking his own mark by eating 69 hot dogs and buns in 10 minutes, topping his prior record of 68. Matt Stonie finished second with 51 and Tim Janus third with 50. The century-old contest drew thousands despite nearby park closures; ceremonial weigh-ins featured Mayor Michael Bloomberg and plenty of hot-dog puns. Competitive-eating veterans remain far ahead of the chasing pack.

Hurricane Sandy struck the East Coast days before Halloween, disrupting celebrations, commerce and safety routines across many communities. Retailers had counted on a roughly $8 billion holiday haul, but while most consumers had already bought costumes and supplies, small businesses that depend on last-minute shoppers faced heavy losses—one Virginia costume shop feared up to $50,000 in lost profit. Major events were curtailed: New York’s Greenwich Village parade went ahead but expected far fewer participants and about a 50% revenue drop. Pumpkin patches, fundraisers and restaurants also closed or postponed, harming seasonal revenues and charitable programs.

Power outages, flooding, downed trees and dangerous debris made trick-or-treating unsafe in many areas. Officials and parents wrestled with whether to cancel or postpone celebrations; New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie initially tweeted plans to reschedule and later signed an executive order moving Halloween in New Jersey to Nov. 5, citing ongoing hazards and recovery needs. Numerous municipalities shifted trick-or-treating to the weekend or later; some kept curfew times. Safety guidance urged avoiding dark neighborhoods, downed lines, debris and flooded streets and emphasized short, visible costumes and staying away from hazards.

For families unable to go out, alternatives included indoor candy hunts, “trunk-or-treat” gatherings, or small community events once areas are safe. Child mental health experts recommended parents model calm, reassure children that the storm is over, and restore routines to ease anxiety. Across the region, the immediate focus remained on rescue, cleanup and assessing widespread damage even as communities tried to preserve some Halloween normalcy.

A 20-year-old Burbank man, identified as Richard Pananian, died in a high-speed rollover crash on the southbound 5 Freeway near the 134 overpass around 7 a.m. CHP investigators say Pananian was driving a 2004 Ford Fiesta at a high rate of speed and passing vehicles on the right shoulder when he suddenly veered left and struck the rear of a 2004 Ford F-150 traveling in the No. 4 lane. The Fiesta then rolled multiple times; Pananian, apparently not wearing a seat belt, was ejected about 20–30 feet and landed on the walkway ledge of an overhead Colorado Street exit sign. His badly damaged car rolled back onto the roadway. Paramedics pronounced him dead at the scene; CHP noted it was unclear whether the fatal injuries resulted from the initial impact or the subsequent ejection and strike with the sign. The F-150 driver and two passengers were uninjured. Authorities did not immediately know if drugs or alcohol played a role. Firefighters used ladders to recover the body, which remained on the sign for several hours while lanes were temporarily closed. Pananian reportedly worked for an auto sales company in Van Nuys.

Sotheby’s will auction the original 1926 ink map of the Hundred Acre Wood by E.H. Shepard—the iconic illustration that opens A.A. Milne’s Winnie-the-Pooh—on 10 July, estimated at £100,000–£150,000 ($133,000–$200,000). Described by Sotheby’s specialist Philip Errington as “probably the most famous map in English literature,” the sketch appears in the first edition and in Disney’s adaptations. Four additional Shepard drawings, unseen publicly for nearly 50 years and depicting scenes such as Christopher Robin saying goodbye to Pooh, Eeyore, Rabbit, and a game of Pooh-sticks, will also be offered; the group is valued at £310,000–£440,000. Shepard collaborated with Milne on four books in the 1920s, and renewed collector interest fuels the sale.

Vancouver police Const. Peter Colenutt was praised after jumping into icy Lost Lagoon in Stanley Park to rescue a large dog that had broken through thin ice while chasing a ball. Officers were alerted around 4:30 p.m. by a resident; upon arrival they found the exhausted dog struggling to stay above water. Colenutt removed parts of his uniform, took one end of a rescue rope while colleagues held the other, and waded out to reach the animal. He returned to shore with the dog; both were cold but uninjured. The rescue was documented in photos and shared on social media, drawing widespread appreciation and gratitude for the officer’s quick action and care. The incident drew attention because Colenutt had recently received the Vancouver Police Board’s Chief Constable’s Commendation for a June 2016 water rescue, when he and another officer swam roughly 100 metres to assist a panicked swimmer and kept the person afloat until a police boat arrived. Tweets and comments applauded the officer’s “act of kindness” and noted the dangers of icy water. Police and witnesses clarified the dog had chased a ball, correcting an initial tweet that said a bird was involved. Vancouver Police shared the images and confirmed both dog and officer were okay after the rescue.

Cardinal Donald Wuerl, the archbishop of Washington, D.C., announced he will travel to Rome to discuss asking Pope Francis to accept his resignation, a step that could mark the departure of one of the highest-ranking U.S. Catholic prelates amid a widening sexual-abuse crisis. Wuerl, who previously served as bishop of Pittsburgh from 1988 to 2006, has been criticized after a Pennsylvania grand jury report found that, during his Pittsburgh tenure, he reassigned or allowed the retirement of priests accused of abusing children rather than taking stronger disciplinary action. The report — the most extensive U.S. inquiry since the Boston scandal of 2002 — documented evidence that at least 1,000 people were sexually abused by some 300 clergy over 70 years, and suggested the true numbers may be higher. Although the grand jury did not accuse Wuerl of personally abusing anyone, it said he informed the Vatican in 1989 about accused priests yet later approved reassignments and even financial assistance for one accused priest. In response to the fallout, Wuerl requested that his name be removed from Cardinal Wuerl North Catholic High School; the Pittsburgh diocese confirmed the school is now North Catholic High School. Wuerl has cancelled a planned speech at the World Meeting of Families in Dublin and said he first submitted his resignation at age 75, as required, and will seek a resolution with Pope Francis so the archdiocese can “move forward” toward healing and renewed oversight.

President Barack Obama’s announcement that he would use executive authority to shield millions of undocumented immigrants from deportation drew swift praise from Democrats and fierce backlash from Republicans, illustrating the deep partisan divide over immigration and setting the stage for a contentious political battle.

Democrats celebrated the move as necessary relief for families and a morally right step in the face of congressional inaction. Leaders such as House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi and members of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus called the action “bold” and “courageous,” while emphasizing it is a temporary measure that cannot substitute for comprehensive legislation. Prominent immigration advocates on Capitol Hill, including Reps. Luis Gutiérrez, Linda Sánchez and Raúl Grijalva, lauded the relief but urged lawmakers to pursue permanent reform through Congress, noting the Senate had passed a bipartisan overhaul in June 2013 that the Republican-led House refused to consider.

Republicans reacted with outrage, framing Obama’s unilateral action as an unconstitutional power grab that undermines the rule of law. Speaker John Boehner accused the president of ignoring the public will and diminishing trust needed to govern; other GOP figures, including Rep. Trey Gowdy, warned against executive “fiat.” Incoming Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and House leaders said Congress would respond forcefully in 2015, floating options such as litigation, rescinding funding for immigration agencies, pursuing stand-alone immigration bills, or targeting White House nominees. Yet leadership also sought to temper calls for extreme measures—impeachment talk and a government shutdown—urging a measured response to avoid repeating past political damage.

The announcement intensified intraparty tensions within the GOP. Tea party and conservative hardliners vowed aggressive pushes—Sen. Ted Cruz suggested refusing confirmation votes for Obama’s nominees, and Rep. Steve King even raised impeachment as a remote possibility—while more moderate Republicans urged restraint to avoid alienating Latino voters and the broader electorate. Party elders such as Sen. John McCain and Sen. Lindsey Graham counseled against inflammatory rhetoric and overreaction.

Public reaction was equally mixed. Immigrant-rights activists, families, and supporters celebrated at watch parties nationwide, viewing the policy as life-changing for many who would no longer live in fear of abrupt family separations. Yet critics—from sheriffs to vocal conservative activists—said the move was inappropriate, incomplete, or politically reckless. Many immigrants and advocates noted the policy still left millions without status and urged Congress to craft a permanent, comprehensive solution.

Overall, Obama’s executive actions provided immediate but limited relief and crystallized the political battle lines: Democrats framing the move as a necessary but interim step toward legislation, and Republicans vowing retaliation and legal challenges while wrestling internally over how confrontational that response should be.

The piece revisits The Simpsons’ 1995 episode “Lisa’s Wedding,” which imagined life in 2010, and evaluates which predictions came true. Many comedic forecasts landed: soy snacks and widespread celebrity arrests are everyday realities; satellite dishes and thousands of cable channels became common eyesores; credit cards at vending machines are routine; Prius-like car designs appear; and motion-controlled gaming, Kindle-like readers, and networked classrooms exist in some form. The Rolling Stones surviving into old age and overcrowded classrooms also rang true. Other predictions missed the mark: cryogenic resurrection remains fantasy, robot butlers and British servants didn’t materialize, and redesigned airplanes mostly reflect cost-cutting rather than innovation. Video phones flopped despite available tech—people increasingly avoid face-to-face interaction. Fox didn’t morph into a hardcore sex channel but spawned Fox News, and news consolidation didn’t create a single mega-network; instead, 24-hour news expanded hours of yelling with little more real news. Wristwatch communicators are niche or toy-like, and while some devices echo early PDAs, they failed to revolutionize life the way imagined. The piece frames these findings as one side of a two-part look, promising a follow-up about the episode’s worst predictions.

House Speaker John Boehner sharply criticized President Obama’s renewed focus on the economy, calling the planned speeches a “big set-up” aimed at justifying higher taxes and more stimulus spending. Boehner and other House Republicans urged Obama to work with Congress instead of giving speeches, and touted GOP bills—like approving the Keystone pipeline, cutting regulations, and delaying parts of the 2010 healthcare law—as real job-growth measures. Boehner insisted Republicans will not lift the debt ceiling without substantial spending cuts and entitlement changes, signaling a likely fall showdown that could risk a shutdown or default. Democrats, including the White House and Senate leaders, rejected negotiations tied to the debt limit, calling for a “clean” increase to avoid repeating the 2011 fiscal crisis.

Pentagon investigators concluded that Undersecretary of Defense for Intelligence Michael Vickers provided restricted information to filmmakers of Zero Dark Thirty and referred the matter to the Justice Department, multiple U.S. officials said. The referral, sent in September, centers on a finding that Vickers disclosed the name of a U.S. Special Operations Command planner who helped design the May 2, 2011 raid that killed Osama bin Laden. Identifying certain special-operations personnel can be classified or sensitive for personal-security reasons, and unauthorized disclosure can violate the law. The Justice Department has so far declined to bring criminal charges.

Vickers, a former Army Special Forces and CIA paramilitary officer who advises Defense Secretary Leon Panetta and has been discussed as a possible CIA director nominee, denied wrongdoing. Pentagon spokesmen and a senior defense official described him as an outstanding intelligence professional and framed the referral as routine when unauthorized disclosures are suspected. The inspector general’s report remains open; officials said investigators found no evidence the White House leaked classified material, though they did not interview key White House figures. The IG is still probing other potential disclosures to the filmmakers.

The inquiry was prompted by Rep. Peter King’s request and by Judicial Watch-released documents showing a July 2011 meeting in which Vickers discussed making a SEAL planner available to the filmmakers. Filmmakers Kathryn Bigelow and Mark Boal say they received no classified information. The episode spotlights broader disputes over classification boundaries, leak prosecutions under the Obama Justice Department, and debates about how much information the government should share with the entertainment industry.

Johnny “Thumper” Duckworth, a longtime busboy at Randy’s Southside Diner on Orchard Mesa, Colorado, became the focus of local admiration after he found $3,000 in cash on the diner floor on December 15, 2015 — and turned it in without hesitation. Duckworth, who has worked at Randy’s for nine years and averages about 25 hours a week, discovered an envelope behind booth number 10 while doing routine cleaning. Inside were thirty $100 bills and an ATM deposit slip. He handed the envelope to his employer, owner Randy Emmons, who took it to the bank. Bank staff used the deposit slip to identify the owner, regular customer Darrell Cox, and contacted him. Cox, surprised to learn the bank had his lost money, returned to the diner and publicly thanked Duckworth, later giving him $300 from the recovered funds as a personal tip and writing a heartfelt note calling him a “super honest guy.” Emmons and coworkers described Duckworth as hardworking, uncomplaining, and generous despite his own struggles: he rides a bike to work in winter, his car has broken down, and medical bills garnish his paycheck, leaving him staying intermittently with friends and family. The community’s response extended beyond Cox’s tip. A GoFundMe campaign titled “Tip Thumper” was launched to raise money to help Duckworth with immediate needs — car repairs, housing, and outstanding medical debts — and quickly surpassed its initial $3,000 goal, reaching more than $3,800. Local media coverage highlighted Duckworth’s integrity and the employer’s praise, with Emmons calling him one of the hardest-working people he’s ever met and noting he would happily employ more people like him. The story resonated as a small-town reminder of honesty and community support: a modest, dependable employee returned a large sum he clearly needed, and his act of integrity was rewarded by both the original owner and a broader wave of donations and public goodwill.

A massive manhunt in northern New York ended with the capture of escaped convict David P. Sweat after a 22- to 24-day search that also saw fellow escapee Richard W. Matt killed. Authorities pieced together Matt’s final days after discovering multiple burglarized hunting camps near Malone and Owls Head. One camp yielded soiled underwear later matched to Matt by DNA and suggesting he was sick from spoiled food or contaminated water; another camp showed evidence of alcohol consumption. Matt, 49, appeared unkempt and ill when a tactical team found him with a 20-gauge shotgun; he did not fire but was shot and killed. Investigators believe Matt had been outdoors for an extended period and possibly intoxicated when killed. Sweat remained at large until a New York State Police sergeant spotted him near the Canada border in Constable; after a brief chase the sergeant fired two shots, wounding the unarmed Sweat, who was taken to medical centers and listed in critical condition. Throughout the search, roughly 1,200–1,300 federal, state and local officers scoured rugged terrain, using roadblocks, ATVs, helicopters and infrared; they sought DNA links from camps and suspected tactics by the fugitives to foil tracking dogs. Officials stressed the importance of interviewing Sweat to uncover how the pair escaped Clinton Correctional Facility and who aided them.

On Sept. 19, 2018, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) announced that Cargill Meat Solutions of Fort Morgan, Colo., was recalling about 132,606 pounds of ground beef made from the chuck portion of carcasses because it may be contaminated with Escherichia coli O26. The products were produced and packaged June 21, 2018, bore establishment number “EST. 86R” inside the USDA mark of inspection, and were shipped to retail locations nationwide under brands including Our Certified, Excel, Sterling Silver, Certified and Fire River Farms, in various package sizes with July 11 use-or-freeze dates. FSIS and CDC investigations linked raw ground beef to an E. coli O26 outbreak identified on Aug. 16; traceback tied case-patients to ground beef supplied by the Cargill plant. The epidemiological inquiry found 17 illnesses and one death, with onset dates from July 5–25, 2018. E. coli O26 is a shiga-toxin producing E. coli (STEC) that typically causes diarrhea (often bloody) and vomiting 2–8 days after exposure; severe cases can progress to hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), especially in young children, older adults and immunocompromised people. FSIS urged consumers to discard or return recalled products, check freezers, and cook ground beef to 160°F using a thermometer. Cargill said affected products have been removed from stores and that it is reviewing facilities. FSIS posted distribution lists and provides hotlines and online resources for consumers.

In late October at Yale, an email from Erika Christakis, an associate master of Silliman College and lecturer in child development, ignited a campuswide debate over racial sensitivity and free speech. Christakis challenged a college advisory urging students to avoid racially insensitive Halloween costumes, arguing universities should allow provocative or offensive expression as part of maturation and inquiry. The message surfaced amid other racially charged incidents, including allegations a fraternity barred black women and longstanding concerns about a residential hall named for slaveholder John C.
