Calhoun. Outrage among many students of color led to large protests in November demanding action from administrators and an improved racial climate. Administrators, including President Peter Salovey, responded with initiatives to expand faculty in race- and ethnicity-related fields and other measures intended to quell tensions. Faculty reactions split: nearly 70 signed a letter defending the Christakises’ free-speech rights, while many more signed a separate letter siding with students’ claims of racism and marginalization. Under intense scrutiny, Erika Christakis announced she would step down from teaching, citing concern that the campus climate no longer supported the civil dialogue and open inquiry needed to address pressing societal problems. Her husband, Nicholas Christakis, said he will take a spring 2016 sabbatical and not teach to focus on research and Silliman students. Students and colleagues expressed mixed responses, noting both the value of her courses and disappointment over her departure.

Elizabeth Rathburn, 56, of Grosse Pointe Park, Michigan, pleaded guilty to wire fraud for her role in a scheme in which she and her husband, Arthur Rathburn, sold and rented human remains through their company, International Biological, Inc., while concealing that some specimens were infected with HIV and hepatitis B. Prosecutors say the couple bought diseased cadaver parts at a discount, misrepresented them as disease-free to medical and dental schools and professional groups, and profited by charging substantial fees for body parts used in training and research. In one notable incident, Elizabeth admitted bringing infected remains to an anesthesiology conference in Washington, D.C., in 2012 after falsely representing them as safe. As part of her plea agreement she faces four to ten months in prison, must pay $55,225 restitution to the American Anesthesiology Association, and has agreed to testify against Arthur Rathburn at his upcoming trial. Arthur, who has pleaded not guilty to charges including transporting hazardous materials and making false statements, is accused of gruesome and unsafe handling practices: dismembering cadavers with chainsaws and other nonstandard tools, stacking heads atop one another, and shipping severed heads in blood-filled coolers—one shipment allegedly labeled deceitfully as containing Listerine. Federal agents raided a Detroit warehouse in 2013 and seized more than 1,000 body parts, which were stored at the Wayne County Morgue. Arthur faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted; his trial is scheduled to begin April 5. Elizabeth has cooperated with authorities and notified them of prohibited contact from Arthur, underscoring her role as a witness against him. Attorneys for both declined immediate comment.

With under eight weeks to go and the first debate imminent, the presidential contest is unusually close. National polls show Hillary Clinton holding a slim lead over Donald Trump: about 46–48 percent to Trump’s 41–44 percent in head-to-head tests, depending on the survey and whether likely or registered voters are counted. When third-party options are offered, the two major candidates’ margins tighten or tie—Gary Johnson and Jill Stein draw enough support in some polls to erase Clinton’s edge among likely voters. Quinnipiac, CBS/New York Times, and other polls conducted in early to mid-September consistently show narrowing gaps amid momentum favoring Trump compared with earlier months, prompting heightened concern among Democrats and some GOP unease.

Voter enthusiasm and the strength of support are notable factors: fewer Democrats report high enthusiasm now than in August, while Republican enthusiasm remains steady; Trump backers report higher “very enthusiastic” levels than Clinton supporters. Most supporters say their choice is set, though many cite opposition to the other candidate rather than strong positive reasons. Demographic patterns persist—Trump leads among men, whites (especially without college degrees), and older voters; Clinton leads among women, non-whites, college-educated whites, and younger voters, though her youth margins lag Obama 2012 levels. The campaign has also been marked by concerns about candidate health and transparency: over 40 percent of voters wanted more medical records from each candidate (polling largely conducted before recent releases). Polling samples and margins of error vary; forecasts still generally favor Clinton but with reduced probabilities.

The document debates whether the Obama administration was right to withhold gruesome post-mortem images of Osama bin Laden. Supporters of suppression, including President Obama, White House press secretary Jay Carney, and Republican Rep. Mike Rogers, argue that releasing graphic photos would inflame anti‑American sentiment, create propaganda for extremists, and risk U.S. troops overseas. Obama framed the decision as avoiding images that could become icons to rally support for al-Qaida; Carney emphasized sensitivities and potential harm to U.S. interests. Rogers warned that such images could complicate troops’ missions, likening the potential effect to how insurgents might react if images of American victims were circulated.

Opponents counter with several arguments. One line of critique holds that photos wouldn’t decisively convince conspiracy-minded skeptics—digital-era deniers would claim doctored images—so the evidentiary value is limited. Another view rejects the notion that withholding images protects national security or dignity; some argue that transparency is essential, and that hiding the photos fosters conspiracy, infantilizes the public, and sets a dangerous precedent for censoring “news that’s too gruesome to reveal.” Some commentators insist the images are part of the historical record and that the public can be trusted to view them, given prior exposure to violent imagery from events like 9/11, Abu Ghraib, and other wartime footage. There’s also discussion of releasing helmet-cam video, possibly edited to remove operational details.

A stronger critique focuses not just on photos but on handling the body: calls for full forensic procedures—autopsy, forensic testing, detailed photography—argue that burying bin Laden at sea and suppressing evidence undermines transparency. Critics worry the rapid burial and limits on evidence fuel suspicion about how he died and whether procedures were properly followed. Legal voices contend that in a democracy doubts should be resolved toward disclosure, that Congress and the press might rightfully demand access, and that sunlight is the best disinfectant for public trust. The document captures competing priorities: operational security and preventing propaganda versus openness, accountability, and the public’s right to verify the facts.

Martin Shkreli, the controversial “pharma bro” convicted on three counts of securities fraud, is again drawing legal trouble after provocative social media behavior while free on $5 million bail. Prosecutors asked a federal judge to revoke his bail, calling him a danger to the community after a now-deleted Facebook post offering $5,000 to anyone who would “grab a hair” from Hillary Clinton during her book tour. The Justice Department said the post forced a substantial Secret Service response and that Shkreli’s large online following raises the risk someone might take his offer seriously. The motion also cites other instances of harassment, including prior posts targeting writer Lauren Duca, and notes that Shkreli declined to meet with Secret Service agents seeking to question him. His attorneys must respond by Tuesday, with a hearing set for Sept. 14. Unrepentant on social media, Shkreli later called the hair-post “just a prank” while urging authorities to investigate Clinton instead. He faces up to 20 years in prison for his convictions but is expected to receive a lesser sentence given no prior record; his defense plans to appeal and has sought to overturn one conspiracy-related verdict as legally insufficient. Shkreli is also widely known for raising the price of the drug Daraprim from $13.50 to $750 per dose.

Records obtained by the Associated Press show Louisiana has spent more than $1,067,000 fighting a three-year lawsuit over extreme heat on death row at Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola — a sum that could buy an air-conditioning system the state refuses to install. U.S. District Judge Brian Jackson has expressed amazement at the legal costs, noting lawmakers are making painful budget cuts while the corrections department and attorney general’s office continue the litigation. Jackson has said the expense is “stunning” and questioned whether the state’s position is driven by management concerns, politics or ideology.

The suit was filed by three inmates with medical vulnerabilities after Jackson ruled more than two years ago that Louisiana subjects prisoners to cruel and unusual punishment when the heat index on death row exceeds 88 degrees. Temperatures there routinely pass that threshold and have reached heat-index levels above 100. Plaintiffs describe cells as like “a sauna” or “an oven.” The state maintains its current remedies — one cold shower a day, ice chests in cells and fans — are sufficient, and argues that ordering air conditioning could prompt costly nationwide litigation and burdens on prison systems.

Cost estimates differ: a plaintiffs’ expert said cooling death row’s six tiers would cost about $225,000 excluding engineering and operating costs; a state engineer in 2014 proposed nine units to cool all eight tiers. Jackson cited a state remediation plan suggesting a roughly $1 million mechanical fix could resolve the issue and end the case. So far, most legal bills have gone to private attorneys; the state also paid monitoring contractors and expert witnesses, and settled fee awards to the inmates’ lawyers for about $490,000. Last year the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals limited remedies to the three plaintiffs and invited the state to provide relief without installing air conditioning. Jackson is set to hear testimony on whether the current measures adequately protect the plaintiffs as summer approaches.

Footage and photos from Guangzhou’s Grandview Aquarium, located inside a busy shopping mall, have sparked international outrage by exposing severely inadequate conditions for dozens of captive animals. Images and videos released by Animals Asia and circulated widely show two polar–brown bear hybrids, six young beluga whales, five walrus calves, Arctic wolves and other species confined to small, dimly lit, barren enclosures where animals display signs of severe stress and abnormal behavior. Bears pace repeatedly, wolves lie listlessly, and marine mammals swim in tight circles; visitors bang on glass and shout to elicit reactions and selfies. Critics and welfare experts describe the facility as a “prison” or the “saddest zoo in the world,” arguing that the enclosures deny animals the space, environmental complexity and social conditions they need for physical and mental health.

Animals Asia launched a petition urging the aquarium’s closure that has attracted hundreds of thousands of signatures and prompted viral discussion on Chinese social media. The charity says public pressure has prompted the aquarium’s management to engage with them; Animals Asia’s director reports site visits, openness to advice, and some immediate changes such as providing snow and beginning enrichment programs for the bears. Nevertheless, the facility remains open and commercially unaffected, and activists caution that incremental improvements fall short of solving the fundamental issue of keeping wide-ranging, social and marine species in a mall for entertainment and profit.

Animals Asia and allied groups continue to press Haichang Holdings, the operator, for deeper reforms or closure, arguing that only sustained public objection, boycotts and regulation will protect the animals’ welfare and end such exploitative attractions.

The Justice Department told a federal court it no longer needs Apple’s help to unlock the iPhone 5C seized from San Bernardino shooter Syed Farook because investigators, with help from an unnamed third party, successfully accessed the device’s data. DOJ prosecutors asked the magistrate to vacate a February order that had compelled Apple to build software disabling the phone’s security features so agents could brute-force the passcode. The development ends this specific legal fight but not the broader national debate over encryption, privacy and law enforcement access to digital evidence.

Apple reiterated its stance that forcing a backdoor would set a dangerous precedent and weaken security for millions of users worldwide. The company said the case should never have been brought and stressed its commitment to privacy and security. DOJ spokespeople framed the outcome as a continuation of efforts to obtain crucial digital information—whether through manufacturer cooperation, court orders, or external technical means—and said they will pursue all available options to aid investigations.

Key details remain undisclosed: neither the FBI nor the government named the third party or described the technique used, and officials would not say whether the exploit works on other iPhones or whether they will share the method with Apple. Reports have speculated about forensic firms such as Cellebrite, but no confirmation has been offered. Security experts noted that the method’s existence implies a vulnerability in that iOS generation, meaning Apple will likely need to identify and patch the flaw without government assistance. The resolution avoids an immediate legal precedent but raises fresh questions about device security, disclosure practices, and the balance between privacy and public safety.

The 2010 remake of Clash of the Titans retools the 1981 mythic adventure into a loud, hollow blockbuster that prioritizes spectacle over story. Producers and writers graft modern macho tropes, recycled epic visuals and added romantic interest onto the Perseus myth, yielding a thin script full of exposition, plot holes and underwritten characters. Sam Worthington’s inert Perseus spends much of the film sidelined while beefy supporting warriors do the heavy lifting; Mads Mikkelsen and Ralph Fiennes provide the few vivid moments. Director Louis Leterrier stages frenetic, often incoherent action, and the retrofit 3-D adds little immersive value. Set pieces and monsters are occasionally effective, but the narrative lacks rhythm, internal logic or emotional stakes, turning the quest into a checklist of CGI encounters culminating in a perfunctory kraken climax. Critics call it a market-driven, soulless, forgettable spectacle—big, noisy and not worth the premium ticket.

Stiles Zuschlag, a senior from Lebanon, Maine, says Tri-City Christian Academy (TCCA) in Somersworth, N.H., told him he was no longer welcome after he revealed he is transgender. Zuschlag, who had attended the private Christian school since kindergarten and was on track to be valedictorian with a 3.89 GPA, told Seacoast Media Group that during an August meeting with administrator Paul Edgar he was told he was “going down the wrong path,” urged to confess his sins, stop testosterone treatments, and seek Christian counseling. He was reportedly barred from returning to the school campus and offered alternatives such as homeschooling. Edgar declined to comment, citing family privacy and TCCA admissions confidentiality.

Unable to continue at TCCA, Zuschlag transferred to Noble High School in North Berwick, Maine, where staff immediately accommodated his pronoun, bathroom and locker-room preferences and where he says he now feels accepted; he was even nominated “Prince of Homecoming.” Zuschlag began transitioning in 2015, changed his name to Stiles Maverick Zuschlag, and started testosterone in 2016 with medical supervision. His mother and younger sister have supported him, though he experienced bullying at TCCA from some classmates citing religious texts.

New Hampshire education officials noted TCCA does not receive federal funds through the state office; legal experts quoted say religious schools can legally ask students to leave regardless of federal funding. Local public schools like Noble and some communities have adopted transgender-inclusive policies to protect students, while private religious schools vary in approach. Zuschlag says he feels stung by TCCA’s decision but remains determined to excel academically and live openly at his new school.

Mariner Energy has a recorded history of offshore accidents and safety lapses in the Gulf of Mexico, including at least a dozen incidents investigated by federal regulators, six with possible violations and three fines. Incidents from 2006–2009 include a corroded storage tank leak after Hurricane Katrina; worker falls without proper fall protection (resulting in a $30,000 penalty); welding-related fires; a flash fire and explosion during decommissioning that violated the company’s safety procedures; a minor tow strike on a well; a blowout when a rig hit shallow gas; a drilling accident causing an eye injury; a cleaning-operation fire that caused ~$40,000 damage; a leaking valve pollution event; falls while repairing Hurricane Ike damage; a methanol-tank explosion burning a worker; and unsafe crane decommissioning. A separate 2010 Vermilion 380-A platform fire sent 13 workers into the Gulf but caused no fatalities and little oil spill; it renewed scrutiny of offshore safety amid the Deepwater Horizon crisis and debates over drilling moratoria and regulation.

Jon Gosselin, the former Jon & Kate Plus 8 star and father of eight, will perform an adult dance routine at Dusk Nightclub’s Untamed Male Revue in Caesars Atlantic City on April 1, his 40th birthday. Gosselin, 39, confirmed to outlets he’s part of the Senate DJ group at Dusk, helps with promotion and occasionally DJs; he says promotion has been more rewarding financially and emotionally. Club owner Eric Millstein told PEOPLE the performance is “R-rated, not X-rated,” choreographed by an ex-Vegas showgirl with costumes, and likened the revue to Magic Mike and Thunder from Down Under. Millstein said Gosselin has rehearsed weekly and the club plans future celebrity appearances; the show aims to be polished rather than sleazy, with female emcees. Gosselin called the gig “integral” and said joining the group made him feel part of a brotherhood. He’s undertaken various jobs since leaving reality TV, including past stints as a cook and DJ.

Hannah Pewee, a college student in Grand Rapids, Michigan, was asked to leave Woodland Mall on a 90-degree day after an anonymous shopper reported her “inappropriate” dress. Pewee posted a photo of her outfit — denim cutoff shorts and a tank top — on Facebook, saying she was surrounded by other women dressed similarly and that being singled out left her embarrassed and shaken. Her post criticized what she called slut-shaming and stressed that people dress for the heat; it quickly went viral, drawing hundreds of supportive comments and thousands of shares.

Woodland Mall’s publicly posted code of conduct requires “appropriate attire, including shirts and shoes” and bans clothing with inappropriate words or graphics, but it contains no stated rules on short length. Pewee noted that if stricter standards exist, they should be made public so shoppers can make informed choices. After the post gained attention, mall management contacted Pewee, apologized for how security handled the incident, and told media they are “working to make things right.” The mall said it will revise its website clothing policy for clarity and instruct security on better handling such situations.

Pewee told Mashable that retailers must recognize changing styles and be transparent if they enforce dress codes, so consumers can decide whether to patronize those venues. The episode joined a broader pattern of dress-code policing that disproportionately affects women, especially during warm weather, and sparked debate about public standards, enforcement, and respect for personal autonomy.

Aubri Degeffered, a three-year-old who had celebrated her birthday two weeks earlier, was abducted during a carjacking Sunday evening in Milwaukee and found safe later that night. Around 6:50 p.m. a suspect forced the driver out of a red four-door 2013/2014 Volvo XC60 in the 4900 block of W. Chambers St. and fled with Aubri inside. The same red Volvo, bearing Wisconsin plates 409-XBP, was later linked to an attempted strong-arm robbery at a Brookfield gas station on W. Bluemound Road about 7:30–7:35 p.m. Milwaukee and Brookfield police released photos of the vehicle and suspect. Acting on citizen tips, Jefferson County deputies located Aubri and recovered the SUV in Lake Mills shortly before 11 p.m.; a 32-year-old suspect was taken into custody. Authorities canceled the Amber Alert; charges are expected to be presented to the Milwaukee County DA as the investigation continues.

Gavin Paul Zimmerman, a 19-year-old Mormon missionary from West Haven, Utah, has died after falling from a cliff at Cape Solander in Kurnell, a popular whale-watching site in southern Sydney. Zimmerman, who had been serving in the Sydney Mission since August, slipped while taking photographs with other missionaries and friends. Authorities recovered his mobile phone containing images taken moments before the fall that show him close to the cliff edge. Lifeguards, alerted to the incident, reached the scene by jetski; one lifeguard dived about eight metres to retrieve the unconscious young man, performed CPR on the jetski and onshore, and emergency services continued resuscitation efforts, but Zimmerman could not be revived. Police and local officials stressed the dangers of venturing onto rocks below the lookout and urged visitors to remain on the designated whale-watching platform and obey signage. Sutherland Mayor Carmelo Pesce noted this was the second fatality at Cape Solander in six weeks and said council and National Parks and Wildlife would consider additional safety measures and public education. Zimmerman's parents, Raymond and Jeanette, and Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints leaders described him as a bright, devoted young man who loved his mission, enjoyed sharing his faith, and had been active in high school sports and church leadership. Friends remembered his enthusiasm for Australia and plans to complete his mission next year. Authorities continue to warn visitors about slippery rocks and cliff hazards.

Lacey Spears, 26, was arraigned in Westchester County after being indicted on second-degree depraved murder and first-degree manslaughter charges in the January death of her 5-year-old son, Garnett. Garnett, who had a feeding tube and a documented history of medical problems on social media, died at Maria Fareri Children’s Hospital after toxic levels of sodium were found in his system. Authorities allege Spears systematically poisoned him by administering salt through his feeding tube and researched the effects online. The medical examiner ruled the death a homicide in April.

Prosecutors say investigators compiled evidence from hospital records, surveillance, computer and phone data, witness interviews and testimony from neighbors who observed Spears feed Garnett. Doctors had previously told Spears that Garnett’s sodium spikes were “metabolically impossible,” prompting a state child-abuse investigation before his death. Neighbors reported Spears asked one to dispose of a feeding bag shortly before Garnett died; that bag later tested high for sodium. Detectives probed Spears’ movements across Alabama, Florida, Tennessee and New York and drew links to possible Munchausen syndrome by proxy, a disorder in which a caregiver fabricates or induces illness in a child for attention.

Spears pleaded not guilty and was held without bail; she faces up to 25 years to life on the murder charge plus additional manslaughter exposure. The case, described as among the first Munchausen-by-proxy inquiries in the social-media era, has prompted scrutiny of past reports to child-welfare agencies and raised questions about why warning signs were not acted upon sooner. The next court date is July 2.

New York Times reporter James Risen defended his Page One story revealing Pentagon research that estimates Afghanistan may hold nearly $1 trillion in untapped mineral wealth—lithium, copper, iron, rare earths and more—after facing sharp online criticism. Critics argued the revelations weren’t new, questioned the timing amid worrying reports on the Karzai government and Petraeus’s testimony, and suggested the piece could be a Pentagon information operation. Risen rejected those charges, saying he relied on new fieldwork by a Pentagon team led by Paul Brinkley that connected Soviet-era maps, USGS aerial surveys and recent ground studies to produce fresh assessments. He lashed out at bloggers who challenged the reporting, later apologizing for his heated remarks. The reporting traces how decades-old Soviet data and sophisticated US surveys coalesced into a comprehensive valuation only recently assembled by the Pentagon task force, which is helping Afghanistan prepare for international bids. Officials warn development could take decades and carry risks: corruption, intensified conflict over resources, environmental harm, and geopolitical competition, notably from China.

President Trump spent the weekend at his Bedminster golf club reviewing judicial records, philosophies and temperaments of about five finalists to replace retiring Justice Anthony Kennedy, though he had not interviewed them as of Saturday. He spoke extensively with White House Counsel Don McGahn and plans to announce a nomination on July 9. The short list reportedly centers on five federal appeals judges: Brett Kavanaugh, Amy Coney Barrett, Thomas Hardiman, Raymond Kethledge and Amul Thapar, including two women. Trump said he will not ask candidates about Roe v. Wade. Senate confirmation is expected to be contentious; Republicans hold a 51-49 majority, making swing votes from Senators Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski especially pivotal. The FBI background checks continue.

When Zoe Averianov (formerly Zoe Lemon) was 10 years old she tossed a small plastic bottle containing a handwritten note into the sea as she left Hull on a ferry bound for Belgium on 12 September 1990. In that childhood message she introduced herself — saying she was 10, liked ballet, played the flute and piano, and had a hamster called Sparkle and fish called Speckle — and asked the finder to write to her. She had long since forgotten the bottle. 

More than two decades later, just before Christmas, Zoe was surprised when her parents arrived with a piece of post from Europe addressed to her maiden name. Inside was her original letter and a reply from a Dutch couple, Piet and Jacqueline Lateur, who live near Rotterdam. Piet discovered the bottle while walking his dog among debris on the dikes of the Oosterschelde near Serooskerke. He kept Zoe’s note and wrote back, saying he had found the message during one of his many walks and that he was keeping her little letter on his piano.

Now 33 and living in Salford (working in a jewellery shop), Zoe has been moved by seeing her childhood handwriting and has been exchanging emails with Piet, who has sent photos of the find site. The story highlights the unexpected journeys messages in bottles can take and the small, enduring human connections they can create across time and distance.

Former Florida Governor Jeb Bush told WHAS11 News he is "not running for President," dismissing recent speculation that he might enter the 2012 Republican field and extend the Bush family’s political legacy. In Louisville to speak at the National Conference of State Legislatures about education reform, Bush spotlighted Florida’s gains in student performance, especially among Latino students, and emphasized state-led initiatives as the source of that success. He also held a fundraiser for Senate candidate Rand Paul, noting Paul’s stance that education policy should be driven locally rather than federally. While praising Florida’s reforms, Bush acknowledged President Obama’s contributions to education policy. Introduced by NCSL President Don Balfour as a reformer who “did not abandon reforms in tough times,” Bush argued that adults—not students—bear responsibility when kids aren’t learning and called education the key to solving social problems. The piece also briefly references efforts by the Internet Archive to preserve web pages and fix broken links.

Three French construction workers who discovered a hidden hoard of gold while working on a house in Normandy have been charged with theft after attempting to keep and sell the loot. The treasure, found in glass jars on the property and believed possibly buried during World War II, included 16 gold bars (each weighing about one kilogram) and roughly 600 US $20 gold coins dating from the mid-1920s. Valued at about €900,000 ($1.2 million), the stash was not reported to the homeowners; instead the men, aged 20, 33 and 40, sold items to a local coin collector. Their scheme unraveled when one worker deposited unusually large cheques, alerting tax authorities. Investigators later arrested the men; they confessed and authorities seized vehicles, motorcycles and hundreds of thousands of euros. The three are due to appear in court in Evreux, northwest of Paris, and the coin collector faces charges of handling stolen goods, which he denies. The anonymous homeowners said they had joked with the workers before the discovery—“If you find any treasure, be sure to tell me!”—and later learned of the theft only when police contacted them, leaving them shaken.

A new study in Science finds that up to half of Earth’s water predates the Sun, implying much of our water formed in the cold interstellar cloud that birthed the solar system rather than being produced during planetary formation. Researchers probed the origin of water by measuring the ratio of deuterium (heavy hydrogen) to ordinary hydrogen. Earth’s elevated deuterium levels are inconsistent with formation solely in the relatively warmer protoplanetary disk around the young Sun and instead point to an older reservoir of water that survived the star-formation process. That heavy-water signature requires very cold conditions and enough energy to drive reactions that bind hydrogen, deuterium and oxygen—conditions found in dense, cold interstellar clouds. Two competing explanations have long existed: water formed in the pre-solar molecular cloud versus water synthesized later in the protoplanetary disk. The new measurements support the pre-solar-cloud origin for a substantial fraction of terrestrial water. If water routinely survives stellar birth and if other planetary systems form similarly, then wet environments may be common across the galaxy. That raises the prospects that many exoplanets could acquire abundant water and potentially develop conditions suitable for life. Tim Harries of the University of Exeter, a co-author, noted that this ancient water heritage suggests our Solar System’s formation is not unique, boosting the likelihood that exoplanets form with water resources necessary for life. This dovetails with estimates that billions of exoplanets reside in habitable zones where liquid water could persist.

Jack Yufe, who died Monday at 82 in a San Diego hospital, lived a life that read like a cinematic paradox: separated from his identical twin brother Oskar Stohr six months after their 1933 birth in Port of Spain, Trinidad, the pair were raised in radically different cultures—Jack as a Jew in Trinidad (later serving in the Israeli navy and settling in San Diego as a retail proprietor) and Oskar as a Catholic in Nazi Germany (joining the Hitler Youth and working later as a miner and welder). Their reunion at age 21 was awkward and bristly; across decades they oscillated between rivalry and deep fascination. Their story drew international attention and made them central figures in the landmark Minnesota Twin Study, which probed nature versus nurture by examining twins raised apart. Psychologist Nancy L. Segal, who studied the brothers for years and wrote about them in books including Indivisible by Two, recounted how despite divergent upbringings the twins shared striking, specific similarities—same dress and glasses at one meeting, identical gait and nervous tics, matching quirks (such as flushing toilets before and after use, loud sneezes in elevators, and disliking a flower on a table). Those parallels challenged researchers’ assumptions about the sources of behavior. Yet profound differences remained: conflicting views about politics, religion and history—Oskar’s identification with German soldiers angered Jack—and an enduring competitive, hot-tempered dynamic described as love-hate. Jack’s son and wife remembered him as old-school, generous but firm in business, and devoted to family. Oskar died of cancer in 1997; Jack is survived by his wife Ruth, children Anita, Hovi, Debvra and son Kenneth, and stepsons Renee and Enrique Vega. Their lives remain a compelling testament to the complex interplay of genetics and environment.

Bobbi Kristina Brown, the 22-year-old daughter of Whitney Houston and Bobby Brown, died on July 26 after nearly six months in a coma. She was found unresponsive in a bathtub at her Roswell, Georgia, home on Jan. 31 by boyfriend Nick Gordon and was initially placed in a medically induced coma for brain swelling. After months on life support and a move in March to a long-term care facility near Atlanta, her condition worsened in June and her family transferred her to Peachtree Christian Hospice so she could spend her final days peacefully. The Houston family confirmed her death in a statement saying she passed surrounded by family and was “finally at peace in the arms of God,” and they thanked supporters for their love over recent months. News of her passing prompted numerous condolences from celebrities and friends on social media. Bobby Brown, who had returned to Atlanta after the birth of his daughter Bodhi Jameson Rein, spent time with family and reportedly took comfort in believing his daughter was reunited with her mother. Fulton County medical examiners said an autopsy will be needed to evaluate what led to her death, but noted the long interval between the Jan. 31 incident and her death will complicate interpretation of findings and reconstruction of events. A police report had described the initial incident as a drowning.

Wesley Morris’s critique argues that biopics turn icons into untouchable saints, and that when filmmakers revere subjects too much they lose the messy humanity that makes for compelling cinema. That problem, he contends, afflicts 42, Brian Helgeland’s restrained Jackie Robinson film. Concentrating on Robinson’s 1947 rookie season with the Brooklyn Dodgers, the movie frames him largely as a moral exemplar whose restraint is instrumentalized by Branch Rickey (Harrison Ford) and used to teach white America to change. Morris praises certain scenes—most notably an extended sequence of Philadelphia manager Ben Chapman’s racial abuse and Robinson’s private explosion of rage—but faults the movie’s lack of psychological depth. Chadwick Boseman shows athletic joy and restrained fury on the field, yet Helgeland’s script reduces Robinson to a symbol, “medicine” for the nation, rather than a fully developed character. Nicole Beharie is praised but underwritten; many black characters are flattened into models of virtue or support roles, and some comic or sentimental touches—like a precocious child destined to be Ed Charles—feel cloying. By centering white converts and elevating Rickey, the film shifts focus from Robinson himself and reads more like an allegory about integration—or even a parable about a hypothetical openly gay player—than a rich sports drama.

In contrast, Morris admires Danny Boyle’s Trance for its audacity: a sleek, sensorial noir about an art heist, amnesia, and hypnosis that dances between reality and manipulation. With kinetic camerawork and a disorienting style, Boyle, writer John Hodge, and actors James McAvoy, Rosario Dawson, and Vincent Cassel deliver a dizzying thriller whose moral confusion and technical bravura make its narrative oddities forgivable.

An appended personal column recalls meeting Robinson as a boy and defends 42’s importance despite its flaws: it reminds viewers why Robinson’s courage and dignity mattered, though some critics find the filmmaking conventional and sentimental.

HMD Global has unveiled the Nokia 8, its first true Android flagship under the revived Nokia brand, aiming to re-establish the name against Apple and Samsung. Priced at €599 and due in early September in Europe, the 5.3-inch, 7.9 mm aluminium phone pairs a high-resolution display with a Snapdragon 835, 4 GB RAM and 64 GB storage. Design-wise it favors a clean, classic aluminium finish and larger bezels rather than the near‑bezelless trend. Its standout features focus on camera and audio: dual 13-megapixel rear cameras developed with Carl Zeiss (one color, one monochrome), a 13 MP front camera, and a “Dual Sight” mode—marketed as the “bothie”—which records or photographs simultaneously from front and rear lenses and can livestream split‑screen feeds directly to Facebook or YouTube. Nokia’s OZO-derived spatial audio captures 360-degree sound for richer playback, especially in live streams. Reviewers call the bothie and 360° audio interesting but not obviously game-changing versus rivals. The Nokia 8 lacks some premium touches like waterproofing, wireless charging and ultra-thin bezels, leaving it competitive but not class-leading on design. HMD must rely on strong pricing, marketing and the nostalgic Nokia name to carve out market share in a crowded high-end segment dominated by Apple and Samsung.

Weight Watchers International is struggling as consumers shift to digital calorie- and activity-tracking tools, reporting a holiday-quarter loss and continued member defections. CEO Jim Chambers said the company’s turnaround, begun last year, is taking longer than expected after a weak start to 2015. In response, Weight Watchers will cut an additional $100 million in costs and forecast lower profit—its full-year earnings guidance of $0.40 to $0.70 per share falls well below analyst expectations. The stock plunged 35%, its biggest decline since the 2001 IPO, after revenue fell for an eighth consecutive quarter and active subscribers declined 15% to 2.51 million. Revenue dropped 10% to $327.8 million, missing estimates.

Industry trends are eroding Weight Watchers’ traditional subscription model. Fitness trackers and mobile apps are proliferating: Juniper Research projects fitness trackers in use globally will triple to about 57 million by 2018, and smartwatches—spurred by Apple Watch—are expected to become dominant. Nielsen data show over 51 million U.S. adults use health-tracking apps. Analysts say lower-cost trackers and free apps make it harder to justify Weight Watchers’ fees unless the brand modernizes. The company has integrated some devices (Fitbit, Jawbone, its ActiveLink) and launched a new ad campaign and magazine redesign, but executives admit more change is needed.

Observers suggest Weight Watchers’ best growth path lies in corporate and health-plan partnerships, where structured programs can offer value that standalone apps may not. The company recently partnered with Humana to provide discounted programs through certain insurance plans, reflecting a strategic shift toward institutional clients.

Mexico announced a major security escalation in its northeastern states of Tamaulipas and Nuevo León, deploying more troops and federal police in a new "Coordinated Operation Northeast" to reclaim territory contested by rival cartels. The move targets violence following the split of the Gulf cartel and its former enforcers, the Zetas, which has sparked assassinations, grenade attacks, roadblocks, school closures, refugee flows and the discovery of 72 murdered migrants. Officials cited geographic factors that make the border region a prized trafficking route and said reinforcements aim to prevent cartel regrouping after recent captures and killings of leaders. Authorities gave few operational details. Separately, federal police arrested Carlos Montemayor, the alleged new leader of a Beltrán Leyva faction linked to kidnappings and killings near Acapulco, signaling continued pressure on organized crime amid public doubts about the drug war’s success.

The 74th Golden Globe Awards delivered a night of laughs, emotion and clear winners, blending comedic bits, political barbs and heartfelt tributes. Host Jimmy Fallon opened with a star-studded, prerecorded musical number spoofing La La Land that included Tina Fey, Justin Timberlake and various nominees, but his live monologue ran into trouble when the teleprompter malfunctioned. Fallon rolled with it, riffing on the 2016 election, comparing President-elect Donald Trump to Game of Thrones’ King Joffrey, joking about Russian involvement in the vote tally, and even quipping about Mariah Carey’s New Year’s Eve mishap. His attempts at broader humor met with mixed results, though he landed several memorable lines and staged genuinely moving tributes to Carrie Fisher and Debbie Reynolds.

La La Land dominated the evening, sweeping its seven nominations and breaking Golden Globe records by taking home the most awards for a single film. Ryan Gosling and Emma Stone won Best Actor and Best Actress in a Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy, respectively, while Damien Chazelle earned Best Director and Best Screenplay. Gosling dedicated his award to Eva Mendes and her family; Stone celebrated dreamers and credited the film’s spirit. Casey Affleck won Best Actor in a Motion Picture – Drama for Manchester by the Sea, and Isabelle Huppert’s upset victory over Natalie Portman for Best Actress in a Drama surprised many observers.

Television honors highlighted fresh voices and breakout successes. The People v. O.J. American Crime Story continued its awards momentum, with Sarah Paulson winning Best Actress in a Limited Series and the show securing Best Television Limited Series. The Crown took Best TV Drama, unseating heavy contenders including Westworld, Stranger Things, This Is Us and Game of Thrones. Tracee Ellis Ross earned a milestone win for Best Actress in a TV Comedy for Black-ish, becoming the first Black actress to win that category since 1983. Donald Glover’s Atlanta and its cast enjoyed emotional recognition, and several first-time nominees made notable impressions.

Comedy moments peppered the ceremony. Amy Schumer and Goldie Hawn, promoting their upcoming film Snatched, presented Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy with a mother-daughter routine that leaned into Hawn’s trademark giggle and jokey teleprompter flubs. Kristen Wiig and Steve Carell mined darkly funny territory while presenting the animated film category, ultimately seeing Zootopia win. Billy Bob Thornton’s bemused acceptance speech included a surreal feud joke with Bob Odenkirk, and John Oliver–style quips appeared throughout.

The evening’s most powerful moments were emotional and political. Viola Davis delivered an affecting introduction for Meryl Streep’s Cecil B. DeMille Award, praising Streep’s artistry and humanity; Streep’s own acceptance speech addressed the presidential election and urged a vigilant press, concluding with a ringing call to make art from heartbreak. The ceremony also paused for an In Memoriam highlight honoring Carrie Fisher and Debbie Reynolds. Overall, the Globes mixed glamor, satire and activism, crowning La La Land’s big night while giving space to both comedic frivolity and serious reflection.

Last night a close friend called to say Dr. Prabhjot Singh, a young Sikh American professor at Columbia and a physician at Mt. Sinai, had been brutally attacked on a public street and was en route to the hospital. When family arrived they found him bloody, bruised and with a fractured jaw; many teeth were displaced and he was unable to speak. NYPD officers, including the Hate Crime Task Force, were already at his bedside. Singh said his assailants taunted him as they beat him, shouting “Osama,” “terrorist,” and other anti-Muslim remarks. He recalled being punched repeatedly until he fell, then receiving further blows as he lay on the sidewalk; at one point someone reached inside a coat as if for a gun, and others pulled at his beard. He could not or would not describe his attackers in detail. Singh had been on an evening walk after dropping his wife and one-year-old son at home. A respected public-health leader, Singh directs Systems Management at Columbia’s Earth Institute, serves on faculty at the School of International and Public Affairs, and works to expand affordable care in underserved communities like Harlem. The attack fits a disturbing pattern: recent assaults on Sikh Americans, including a Fresno beating, an Orlando-area shooting, and the 2012 Oak Creek gurdwara massacre. Researchers note widespread association of turbans with terrorism, reflecting ignorance that fuels violence. The authors call for solidarity among marginalized groups and broader community bridges to stop hate and prevent further attacks. Kiran Kaur and Justin Collins contributed.

The two pieces critique current airport security as invasive, inefficient, and theatrical. One writer lampoons the culture of resistance sparked by incidents like a flight attendant’s dramatic escape and John Tyner’s viral refusal of a TSA pat-down, framing “Don’t touch my junk” as the rallying cry against intrusive checks. He argues that much airport screening is pointless, humiliating, and fails to address real threats—pointing out pilots with intent could crash planes without weapons—and calls out the taboo against profiling that prevents focused enforcement. The second piece traces the TSA’s post-9/11 expansion into a 67,000-employee bureaucracy whose searches, scanners, and liquid bans haven’t clearly improved security; GAO and internal tests show screeners miss threats. It proposes replacing blanket measures with risk-based screening: low-risk travelers (crews, vetted frequent flyers) get expedited biometric passes; high-risk individuals are screened based on intelligence-driven watchlists; everyone else undergoes standard metal-detector and carry-on X-ray checks with limited random secondary screening. Together the pieces urge reform toward smarter, less humiliating, evidence-based airport security.

Court documents in a Riverside County civil case reveal 72-year-old singer Etta James is gravely ill, diagnosed with dementia, an organic brain syndrome and currently undergoing treatment for leukemia. Dr. Elaine James said Etta requires round-the-clock in‑home care, cannot sign her name, and needs help feeding, dressing and toileting, though she recognizes family. The dispute concerns control of just over $1 million held for her care: husband Artis Mills seeks authority to manage or move the funds, while son Donto James asks a neutral third party oversee disbursements to avoid family conflict. A hearing is scheduled.

The Sky 1 airing of The Simpsons episode “Fraudcast News” sparked a social media storm as viewers noted its uncanny timeliness amid the Murdoch phone-hacking saga. The episode centers on Lisa Simpson creating a paper that denounces tycoon Montgomery Burns; Burns retaliates by buying up Springfield’s media, prompting residents to start their own newspaper. The show includes the line, “it’s impossible to control all the media, well unless of course you’re Rupert Murdoch,” which viewers seized on. Tweets called the screening “brilliant” and “hilarious,” with many joking that Sky’s broadcast was more than coincidence given Rupert Murdoch’s unfolding bid for BSkyB and his company’s central role in the scandal. Sky insisted the timing was coincidental and unrelated to Murdoch’s affairs.

Meanwhile, real-world fallout continued: Rupert and James Murdoch were summoned to appear before the UK Parliament’s Culture, Media and Sport Committee to face questions about phone-hacking by News of the World; the committee also invited Rebekah Brooks. News International said it would cooperate with requests. The Murdochs’ appearance is not legally binding because they are not British citizens, but public pressure mounted. The company awaited formal requests; the hearing was set for July 19.

Separately, revelations emerged that during the initial 2006 Scotland Yard inquiry into phone hacking, five senior police investigators discovered their own mobile messages had likely been intercepted by the tabloid. That raised concerns the police may have curtailed their probe from fear of being exposed in the press. Allegations about some officers’ private conduct later surfaced in other outlets, and senior figures like Andy Hayman and John Yates faced scrutiny. Parliament planned further hearings with Hayman, Yates and others to probe why the original investigation was limited and whether victims’ status affected its scope. Calls for accountability and resignations intensified as the scandal widened.

Fiat Chrysler Automobiles is recalling 1.4 million vehicles after security researchers demonstrated a remote hack of a Jeep at highway speeds. The vulnerability affects models with 8.4-inch touchscreens across 2013–2015 Dodge, Chrysler, Ram and Jeep lineups, including Viper, Ram pickups and chassis cabs, Grand Cherokee, Cherokee, Durango, Chrysler 200/300, Dodge Charger and Challenger. Researchers Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek showed code that could commandeer entertainment systems to access dashboard functions, transmission, brakes and potentially steering from a distant laptop; they intend to publish part of the exploit around the Black Hat conference. FCA says it has applied network-level protections, pushed over-the-air patches and will provide USB devices for further security updates. The company reports no known injuries, complaints or accidents and is acting “out of an abundance of caution.”

Apparel retailer Gap Inc. said it will raise U.S. hourly wages to $9 in June 2014 and $10 in June 2015, a move affecting about 65,000 store employees and following the White House announcement raising the minimum wage for federal contract workers to $10.10 an hour in 2015. Gap, which owns Old Navy, Banana Republic, Athleta and other chains, noted most of its store, call center and distribution employees already earn above the $7.25 federal minimum. CEO Glenn Murphy framed the increases as a business investment rather than a political statement, saying higher pay for frontline workers should produce strong returns for the company. President Barack Obama praised Gap’s decision after signing an executive order to raise wages for new and replacement federal contracts beginning Jan. 1, 2015, and called on other employers to follow suit. Separately, Wal‑Mart — the nation’s largest private employer — said it remains neutral on the federal minimum-wage order and is evaluating the proposal’s impact; a Wal‑Mart spokeswoman emphasized most of its full-time store associates already earn above state and federal minimums and denied reports it had committed to supporting the increase.

On July 26, 2017, University Hospital nurse Alex Wubbels was handcuffed and briefly arrested by Salt Lake City Detective Jeff Payne after she refused to allow a blood draw from an unconscious, burn-injured patient, William Gray. Payne had come seeking Gray’s blood after a serious crash in which another driver died; Logan investigators requested a draw, which is routine in severe collisions. Wubbels explained, citing hospital policy and the law, that blood could not be drawn from an unconscious patient without the patient’s consent, a warrant, or the patient being under arrest. Body-camera footage released publicly showed Payne acknowledging that none of those conditions applied yet insisting he had authority. After consulting hospital officials, Wubbels continued to refuse; Payne then grabbed and handcuffed her and put her in a patrol car as she protested.

The incident sparked widespread outrage after Wubbels’ attorney released the video. Salt Lake City Mayor Jackie Biskupski and Police Chief Mike Brown personally apologized to Wubbels, calling the footage unacceptable and announcing changes to blood-draw policies and officer training. Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill asked for a criminal investigation for transparency and accountability; the Unified Police Department agreed to conduct the probe. An internal affairs investigation was already underway, and Payne was placed on administrative leave, along with a second unnamed officer connected to the confrontation.

Police reports indicated confusion: Payne claimed a lieutenant had ordered the arrest; the lieutenant later learned the hospital routinely draws blood and investigators often obtain warrants to access those results. Another officer noted Logan authorities said they lacked probable cause for a warrant. The department subsequently revised its policy to require subject consent or a search warrant for blood draws and to remove “implied consent,” emphasizing adherence to search-and-seizure law. Hospital leaders and nursing organizations defended Wubbels, praising her for following law and protocol and warning the arrest sent chilling signals about patient and nurse safety. Public reaction included protests, petitions, and national attention. Wubbels accepted the mayor and chief’s apologies and expressed hope that the episode would prompt positive change.

People reports that Jennifer Aniston and her boyfriend Justin Theroux have moved in together. According to an unnamed source cited by People.com, the couple chose to rent a house jointly while they continue searching for an ideal home to purchase. The move represents a step forward in their relationship as they combine households on a temporary basis during the house-hunting process. The source emphasized that renting is an interim solution as they look for a permanent property. No additional details about the rental, the location, or their future plans were provided in the brief People item, which directs readers to the full story on People.com for more information.

Firefighter Michael R. Davidson, 37, a 15‑year veteran of the FDNY assigned to Engine Company 69, died after being critically injured battling a five‑alarm fire at a Harlem building where the film Motherless Brooklyn was shooting. The blaze began around 11 p.m. in the basement of the five‑story former St. Nick’s Pub on St. Nicholas Avenue. Davidson, serving as the nozzleman on the first‑arriving crew, descended with colleagues into the basement; conditions rapidly deteriorated, and he became separated from his group. Firefighters later found him unconscious; he was taken to Harlem Hospital and succumbed to his injuries. Two other firefighters suffered serious burns and were hospitalized; three civilians had minor injuries. Davidson, cited four times for bravery during his career, leaves his wife Eileen and four young children (daughters 7, 3, 1 and a 6‑year‑old son). He came from a family of firefighters—his retired father served in the same house and his brother is an 11‑year veteran. The FDNY and city officials including Commissioner Daniel Nigro and Mayor Bill de Blasio expressed profound grief; a procession escorted his body to a Long Island funeral home and mourners gathered at his firehouse. Producers of the film expressed sorrow and said they alerted authorities as soon as smoke was noticed. Investigators have not yet determined the fire’s cause.

During Game 3 of the World Series in Houston, Astros first baseman Yuli Gurriel provoked controversy after hitting a second-inning home run off Dodgers pitcher Yu Darvish. Television replays showed Gurriel making a slant‑eyed gesture toward his own face and appearing to mouth a derogatory Spanish term. Gurriel, a 33‑year‑old Cuban who played in Japan in 2014, apologized through an interpreter, saying he did not intend to offend and explaining he’d been joking about his lack of success against Darvish—he was 1-for-7 versus the pitcher before the homer. He acknowledged using the word “chinito,” a term he said is commonly used in Cuba to refer to Asians but admitted is offensive in Japan. MLB said it was aware of the incident and that Commissioner Rob Manfred intended to speak with Gurriel; discipline was possible. Darvish, who is of Japanese and Iranian descent and pitched professionally in Japan before joining MLB, called the gesture “disrespectful,” noting it offended Asian fans and the organization but urged learning and moving forward rather than escalating anger. Dodgers teammates expressed disappointment; outfielder Enrique (Kike) Hernandez called the act unfortunate and said he’d leave any punishment to the league. An MLB source indicated the Dodgers were “very upset,” especially given the current social climate. Astros manager A.J. Hinch described Gurriel as remorseful. The incident attracted wide attention amid MLB’s increasing intolerance for hateful speech; Manfred was expected to meet with Gurriel before Game 4 at Minute Maid Park.

Former Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney faced a combative question-and-answer session while stumping at the Iowa State Fair’s Des Moines Register soapbox, where a few hecklers challenged him on Social Security, Medicare and tax policy. Pressed on why he wouldn’t raise the Social Security payroll tax cap or protect Medicare benefits, Romney raised his voice, told the crowd “If you want to speak, you can speak. But right now, it’s my turn,” and later admonished dissenters that they could vote for someone else if they disagreed. Most notable was his defense of corporate tax policy with the remark, “Corporations are people, my friend,” arguing that corporate earnings ultimately go to individuals who create jobs. Democrats quickly seized on the line as evidence Romney is out of touch, and the DNC circulated coverage calling it “BRUTAL.” Romney spokesman Eric Fehrnstrom defended the comment, saying corporations are run by people who hire workers. The incident came two days before the Ames Straw Poll and a GOP debate in Iowa.

President Trump attacked Sen. Dianne Feinstein after she released the transcript of a Senate Judiciary Committee interview with Glenn Simpson, co-founder of opposition research firm Fusion GPS, which commissioned the dossier alleging ties between Trump's 2016 campaign and Russia. Feinstein, as the committee’s top Democrat, had authority to publish the August transcript and her staff assisted in the interview. On Twitter, Trump labeled her “Sneaky Dianne Feinstein,” accused her of releasing the testimony “totally without authorization,” and urged a tough primary challenge. He reiterated his long-standing claim that the Russia investigation is a “Witch Hunt,” insisted there was no collusion and said Democrats know it, and urged Republicans to take control. Trump also complained that Russia and the world are mocking the U.S. over the probe. The clash highlights continuing partisan tensions over the probe’s release and oversight.

Retiring Tennessee Senator Bob Corker, chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has publicly broken with President Donald Trump in a way that has energized media attention, intra-party debate, and a Twitter feud. Corker, who once courted roles in the Trump administration and praised Trump during the campaign, recently warned in interviews that the president’s temperament and behavior risk putting the country “on the path to World War III.” He has said that senior officials such as Rex Tillerson, Jim Mattis, and John Kelly “help separate our country from chaos,” and described daily efforts inside the White House to contain the president’s worst instincts. Corker, who decided not to seek reelection, argues that stepping out of electoral politics has freed him to speak more candidly and to focus on his last 15 months in office.

Trump responded angrily on Twitter, calling Corker “liddle” and accusing him of lacking the “guts” to run for reelection while also reminding readers of Corker’s past role in the Iran nuclear deal. The president and his allies portrayed Corker’s remarks as politically timed and hypocritical. White House press secretary Sarah Sanders dismissed Corker’s claims and defended Trump’s successes. The back-and-forth intensified preexisting Republican fractures and raised broader questions about GOP strategy going into the 2018 midterms, where the party’s narrow Senate majority and vulnerable House majority are at stake.

Commentators and critics seized on Corker’s volte-face as emblematic of establishment hypocrisy. Many noted Corker’s earlier support and accommodation of Trump and argued that his recent denunciations are politically convenient because he is retiring and potentially positioning himself as a more acceptable anti-Trump figure in the Republican mainstream. Critics contend that Corker and other establishment Republicans share responsibility for Trump’s rise by failing to mount or sustain credible resistance during the campaign and by prioritizing short-term partisan control. They argue that understanding and remedying that failure is essential to preventing future populist insurgencies.

The episode also intersected with Steve Bannon’s plans to support insurgent, anti-establishment challengers to incumbent Republican senators, raising the prospect of primaries that could further fracture the party. Bannon-backed efforts have already had an impact, notably in Alabama, and Bloomberg reported Bannon targeting several incumbent senators. With tax reform expected to be the GOP’s main achievable legislative aim, party leaders are under pressure to produce a visible victory to assuage voters and shore up incumbents.

Beyond policy stakes, many observers urged fellow Republicans to publicly address Corker’s claims: whether they agree that the president’s behavior poses a national risk and whether congressional leaders are sufficiently checking the White House. The debate underscores a deeper question about whether the Republican establishment will acknowledge and correct the political and moral failures that critics say enabled Trump’s ascendancy—or continue the same patterns that produced him.

Researchers from the Universities of Exeter and Zurich have found that chestnut-crowned babblers, social birds from the Australian Outback, use combinations of simple vocal elements to create distinct meanings—a basic form of compositional signalling previously thought unique to humans. Unlike most songbirds, these babblers do not sing long, continuous songs; their vocal repertoire consists of discrete calls built from smaller acoustically distinct sounds. The team identified two elements, labeled A and B, that are reused in different orders to signal different behaviours. In flight the birds emit an A-B sequence; when prompting chicks to feed they use B-A-B. Playback experiments showed listening birds reliably interpreted the sequences: they looked to the sky when hearing the flight call and toward nests when hearing the feeding call. Crucially, when researchers recombined elements—constructing flight calls from feeding elements and vice versa—birds still distinguished the meanings, demonstrating that the different signals arise from rearrangements of the same meaningless sound units rather than wholly different calls. The authors liken this to a rudimentary form of phoneme structuring, where the arrangement of meaningless sound elements changes meaning, analogous to how humans form words from phonemes. Co-author Andy Russell suggests combining existing sounds to create new meanings is faster evolutionarily than inventing entirely new calls. The study, published in PLOS Biology, offers the first demonstration outside humans that rearranging meaningless elements can generate new meaning, and the researchers propose it represents a potential early step toward the elaborate language systems humans use. They note the simplicity of the structure but argue it could mirror an initial stage in the evolution of combinatorial signalling in hominid ancestors, and they anticipate similar capacities may exist in other species.

GQ’s weekly Washington power roundup crowns Hillary Clinton the most powerful person in D.C. this week, driven less by formal authority than by a newly energized public image. A viral Tumblr called “Texts From Hillary,” created by two young D.C. communications professionals, transformed a candid photo of Clinton texting on a military plane into a meme casting her as calm, in-charge, and even glamorous. Rather than lampooning her, the meme expresses admiration: the image reframes Clinton from the embattled, abrasive candidate of 2008 into a composed, effective Secretary of State whose competence has bolstered her appeal.

The meme exploded rapidly—tens of thousands of shares, large followings on Tumblr and Twitter, and mainstream coverage—prompting its creators to retire the project at peak popularity. Commentators argue the phenomenon reflects a broader rehabilitation of Clinton’s standing. Unlike other Obama administration figures whose reputations suffered in office, Clinton’s has improved; her low-profile, policy-focused role as Secretary of State fits a traditional, apolitical mold that has won broad approval. Gallup showed her favorability near 66 percent, including unusually strong numbers among Republicans, reinforcing the sense of resurgence.

Analysts note that Clinton’s competence is most admired when she’s seen working rather than campaigning, and that her restrained role during contentious partisan battles has preserved her cross-partisan appeal. That popularity has reignited 2016 speculation, with some Democrats urging another presidential bid even as Clinton downplays a return to electoral politics. Observers caution that a renewed campaign would likely erode some bipartisan goodwill, but her tenure as a respected, battle-tested public servant makes her a dominant political figure and a focal point of ongoing debate about future presidential contenders.

At the 60th Grammy Awards in New York, Bruno Mars dominated, winning all six awards for which he was nominated, including album of the year for 24K Magic, record of the year for its title track, and song of the year (shared with seven co-writers) for "That's What I Like." Mars dedicated his wins to R&B songwriters who shaped the genre. Despite high expectations for hip-hop, Jay-Z—who led nominations with eight—left empty-handed, and Kendrick Lamar, while winning five Grammys (best rap album, best rap song, best rap performance, best rap/sung performance, and best music video), did not capture the top general-field categories. Lamar opened the show with a powerful, politically charged performance featuring striking visuals and choreography.

The ceremony included emotional and politically resonant moments: Kesha delivered a stirring performance of "Praying" supported by the Resistance Revival Chorus and several artists amid her legal struggle with Dr. Luke, introduced by Janelle Monáe invoking Time’s Up. A tribute to the Las Vegas shooting victims featured Maren Morris, Eric Church and Brothers Osborne performing "Tears in Heaven." Many attendees wore white roses in solidarity with Time’s Up and #MeToo.

Other notable winners and performances: Chris Stapleton won three country awards and paid tribute to Tom Petty; Little Big Town won for "Better Man"; Lady Gaga, Sam Smith, Pink and Childish Gambino all delivered standout performances. The Rolling Stones won a Grammy for best traditional blues album; Ed Sheeran won best pop vocal album. The show, hosted by James Corden, mixed music with comedy skits and honored posthumous winners including Carrie Fisher and Leonard Cohen.

Officials have reopened the 1981 drowning death of actress Natalie Wood as a homicide investigation after new information and publicity prompted detectives to take another look. Wood disappeared from the yacht Splendour off Santa Catalina Island on Thanksgiving weekend 1981 while aboard with her husband Robert Wagner and actor Christopher Walken. At the time her death was ruled an accidental drowning. The L.A. County Sheriff’s Department says recent contacts from people claiming additional information — including a letter from an unidentified third party — led homicide detectives to revisit the case. Sheriff Lee Baca indicated detectives want to speak with the boat’s captain after comments he made recounting the night on the 30th anniversary of Wood’s death. 

Renewed attention stems largely from a 2008 book co-authored by Marti Rulli and Splendour captain Dennis Davern, which depicts drinking, Quaaludes, a heated argument between Wagner and Walken, a subsequent loud altercation between Wagner and Wood, and the captain hearing thumping sounds before Wood vanished. The book alleges Wagner resisted allowing the captain to call the Coast Guard and that witness accounts later conflicted with initial statements. Investigators have interviewed Rulli and Davern and traveled to locations connected to the case; no one has been officially named a suspect. The Wagner family says it supports the department’s review and wants new information vetted for credibility.

A Laysan albatross known as Wisdom—first banded in 1956 and now at least 63 years old—is again a mother on Midway Atoll after surviving the tsunami triggered by Japan’s 9.0 quake. Both Wisdom and her newly hatched chick were seen alive about a week after 5-foot waves struck Sand Island in the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, which hosts roughly 71% of the world’s Laysan albatross population. The tsunami killed an estimated 2,000 adult albatrosses and about 110,000 chicks at the refuge, but Wisdom’s survival and successful chick-rearing exemplify remarkable longevity and resilience: officials estimate she has raised at least 30–35 chicks over her long breeding life and has likely flown millions of miles. Laysan albatrosses spend much of the year at sea, returning to nest and raise a single chick per year; incubation and rearing require many months and both parents alternately brood and feed the chick with nutrient-rich stomach oil. Conservationists highlight ongoing threats to albatrosses, including marine debris—an estimated five tons of plastic are fed to Midway chicks annually—longline fishing bycatch, contaminants, invasive predators, and sea-level rise that reduces nesting habitat. Midway staff and volunteers monitor the colony’s health; Wisdom’s continued success underscores the value of protecting seabirds and their ocean ecosystems.

A Minnesota woman, 19-year-old Monalisa Perez of Halstad, was charged with second-degree manslaughter after fatally shooting her boyfriend, Pedro Ruiz III, during an attempted YouTube stunt. Perez, who is pregnant, was released on $7,000 bail; the charge carries up to 10 years in prison. According to the Norman County sheriff’s criminal complaint, Ruiz proposed making a video in which Perez would fire a bullet into a book he held against his chest. Perez told investigators she fired from about a foot away, using a .50-caliber Desert Eagle pistol—an exceptionally powerful handgun—after Ruiz had set up cameras to record the stunt. Earlier the same day, Perez tweeted that they were “probably going to shoot one of the most dangerous videos ever. HIS idea not MINE.” Ruiz had previously shot a book without it penetrating fully and had been encouraging Perez to try the stunt. Family members described Ruiz as a thrill-seeker who often added dangerous twists to his activities; an aunt called him “our little daredevil.” The couple posted numerous prank and stunt videos on YouTube, with Perez expressing aspirations for larger subscriber counts. Ruiz’s aunt said he rationalized risky stunts as ways to gain fame and viewers. Authorities located the Desert Eagle at the scene and confirmed Perez’s account of the weapon used. Perez has posted about 18 videos on her channel since May, including a recent fair visit, and the fatal shot killed Ruiz instantly. The case has drawn attention to the perils of online stunt culture and legal consequences when such acts go tragically wrong.

Twelve hours after House Majority Leader Eric Cantor’s upset primary loss, a rapid leadership scramble is underway. Pete Sessions, chair of the House Rules Committee, is aggressively courting support to replace Cantor, using calls, emails and mass texts. Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy has also been in frequent contact with members but is holding off a formal campaign until Cantor decides whether he will remain in leadership through the term. Potential contenders for majority leader include Reps. Jim Jordan, Cathy McMorris Rodgers, Jeb Hensarling and GOP Vice Chair Lynn Jenkins; several have begun outreach and are weighing bids. For the whip slot, Steve Scalise and Peter Roskam have effectively declared interest and are building support, while Sessions and Tom Price are other possibilities. Conservative members are reportedly pressing for Cantor to step down immediately, though there is no effort to challenge Speaker John Boehner. Cantor has met privately with allies and GOP leaders and has not announced his plans; his decision will shape floor operations and conference dynamics in the coming days. House Republicans scheduled a caucus meeting to address the fallout and next steps.

The piece is a magazine-profile centered on Scarlett Johansson during a late-afternoon encounter in a dim hotel bar. Playful and candid, Johansson engages in a lighthearted handwriting exercise—writing and comparing cursive and print versions of an old proverb—revealing a willingness to be spontaneous and amused by small, unserious experiments. The scene balances intimate observational detail (her sandy, resonant voice, casual tracksuit, sunglasses) with notes on her temperament: outwardly aloof in photos but, in person, witty, generous, and down-to-earth. At 28 she is intensely busy—film releases, stage work, and high-profile franchises—yet already thoughtful about career strategy, theater and producing as hedges against aging out of leading roles. She describes exhaustion from long shoots and strange glamour (standing in bogs with expensive jewelry) and expresses a craving for simple pleasures: long sleep, reading the paper, and a low-key “staycation.” The profile frames Johansson as savvy about celebrity’s demands, unromantic about fame’s trappings, and pragmatic about future choices. The document also contains appended celebrity news blurbs—short items about Johansson’s later becoming a mother and separate brief pieces on Alyssa Milano’s newborn—tacked on as additional entertainment-industry updates.

The document contains two linked accounts of tensions between big beer conglomerates and the craft beer community, and an Internet Archive effort to preserve web references. First, it explains that the Internet Archive is crawling and archiving pages and their referenced links so that when referenced pages change or disappear, a preserved version can be linked instead—an effort aimed at fixing broken links across the web, including supported “No More 404” sites.

The rest focuses on craft-beer backlash against Anheuser-Busch InBev (AB InBev) and allied brands. Black Project Spontaneous & Wild Ales disclose deep ethical objections to AB InBev’s strategies, accusing the company of aggressive, predatory actions that threaten American craft beer. As a result, Black Project won’t continue business ties with Wicked Weed following its sale to AB InBev: they’re refusing to associate with the collaboration beer aging in Asheville, will repurpose the beer brewed with Wicked Weed into a non-collaboration blend, and will skip the Wicked Weed Funkatorium Invitational. They express personal goodwill toward Wicked Weed’s people despite the business split.

The document also critiques Budweiser’s Super Bowl advertising, which mocks craft-beer culture while AB InBev continues acquiring craft labels and marketing faux-indie products like Shock Top. The ads emphasize Budweiser’s oppositions—“Not Small,” “Not Sipped,” “Not Soft,” “Not a Fruit Cup,” “Not Imported,” “Not for Everyone”—positioning Bud drinkers as proud, untrendy, and masculine. Observers view the ads as deliberately provocative: not to win over craft fans, but to reassure and rally Bud’s existing customer base amid perceived insecurity about craft-beer trends.

In closing arguments at Oscar Pistorius’ murder trial in Pretoria, chief prosecutor Gerrie Nel accused the defense of advancing contradictory and dishonest theories to avoid a murder conviction for the fatal shooting of Reeva Steenkamp on Feb. 14, 2013. Nel criticized Pistorius’ lawyers for alternately arguing that he acted in self-defense—mistakenly believing an intruder was in the house—and suggesting he lacked criminal responsibility because he was “startled” and accidentally shot through a closed toilet door. Nel said those two defenses could not be reconciled. The prosecution maintains Pistorius intentionally shot Steenkamp after an argument; the defense has maintained he fired by mistake, thinking an assailant was in the toilet and that she was in the bedroom. Pistorius faces a murder charge plus three separate firearms-related charges, including an alleged earlier accidental discharge at a Johannesburg restaurant, Tashas. He has pleaded not guilty to all counts. With no jury in South Africa, Judge Thokozile Masipa, assisted by two legal clerks, will determine whether Pistorius is guilty of murder, guilty of negligent killing or culpable homicide, or not guilty. Conviction for premeditated murder carries 25 years to life. Masipa reminded both sides they had until the end of Friday to finish final arguments, quipping about working over the weekend. The courtroom showed written arguments and testimony transcripts as proceedings continued.

A Pompano Beach man, Scott Simon, 24, was arrested on a first-degree murder charge after allegedly pocket-dialing 911 while plotting a killing, law enforcement said. On May 5, a recorded 911 call captured Simon telling someone he would follow and kill 33-year-old Nicholas Romondo Walker of Lauderhill. Minutes later Walker was shot multiple times as he entered I-95 south at Commercial Boulevard; his car crashed into a guardrail and caught fire. Fire rescue extinguished the blaze, but Walker died at the scene. Broward Sheriff’s Office detectives say Simon likely orchestrated the attack but was not the triggerman; they are seeking two other suspects, including the shooter and a second man seen in a black 2012 Buick GS. Investigators believe an earlier argument at a Waffle House may have sparked the violence; surveillance footage shows a confrontation and the vehicles leaving the restaurant. Simon remains jailed without bond. Authorities are asking the public for tips and offering up to $1,000 through Crime Stoppers. The recorded 911 call will not be released.

Scotland Yard has contacted Australian police after the apparent suicide of Jacintha Saldanha, a 46-year-old nurse at King Edward VII’s Hospital, days after she answered a prank call from 2Day FM presenters Mel Greig and Michael Christian, who posed as the Queen and Prince Charles.
