The DJs, taken off air and on indefinite leave, are receiving intense counselling and have expressed a desire to speak to the media. Southern Cross Austereo, 2Day FM’s owner, held emergency board meetings, suspended advertising, and is reviewing broadcast processes after strong criticism from the hospital’s chairman and advertisers pulling support. The station says the pre-recorded spoof was legally cleared, but legal experts note possible breaches of New South Wales’ Surveillance Devices Act and a potential ACMA inquiry into licence or industry rule breaches. New South Wales Deputy Commissioner Nick Kaldas confirmed lines of communication are open with the Met but said no requests to interview staff had been made; he emphasised there is no suggestion a crime has been committed. The Duchess of Cambridge is recuperating from severe morning sickness; the Duke cancelled an appearance to spend time with her. The tragedy has prompted public mourning and calls for accountability.

With just days left in the Obama White House, Michelle Obama made a warm, upbeat farewell appearance on The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon, who devoted the entire episode to the first lady. Fallon, who began hosting as the Obamas entered the White House, said he and his daughters were moved by President Obama’s recent farewell address. Michelle laughed about her own daughters’ reactions—Malia cried while Sasha stayed home studying—and described the end of the administration as “surprisingly emotional.” She said children are her deepest concern, expressing a desire for them to face the future without fear and to move forward “with strength and with hope,” regardless of background.

The first lady pledged to remain active on causes she championed, especially promoting higher education and healthier school lunches, saying, “I’m not done. I’m too young.” She urged that progress made on school meals be preserved. Fallon kept politics light, asking about her meeting with incoming First Lady Melania Trump; Michelle said she offered advice on creating a safe White House space for family and would help Melania or Ivanka if they wanted her assistance.

Segments mixed humor and heartfelt moments: Fallon surprised fans who recorded thank-you messages by having Michelle emerge from behind a curtain to hug them; she played a competitive round of Catchphrase with Fallon, Dave Chappelle and Jerry Seinfeld; and the show closed with Stevie Wonder performing a medley dedicated to her. Fallon and Obama exchanged playful thank-you notes—he praised her as a style icon and activist; she thanked Barack for being her “silver fox.” The evening let Michelle Obama say goodbye on her terms—celebratory, personable, and focused on continuing public service.

The United States announced a range of measures in response to Uganda’s 2014 anti-homosexuality law, which President Yoweri Museveni signed in February, strengthening penalties for same-sex activity and introducing life sentences for "aggravated homosexuality" (including sex with minors or when one partner is HIV-positive). The law also criminalizes lesbianism and penalizes those who assist or counsel LGBT people, prompting reports of increased abuses and detentions. In retaliation, Washington cut or redirected tens of millions in aid, imposed visa restrictions on Ugandans believed to be involved in human rights violations or corruption, and canceled a planned U.S.-sponsored regional military exercise. Specific funding changes included halting $2.4 million for a community policing program after a police raid on a U.S.-funded health project, shifting some health ministry salary and travel support to NGOs, and reallocating $3 million earmarked for a national public health institute to another African country; a National Institutes of Health meeting was moved to South Africa. The U.S. emphasized it would continue humanitarian assistance and counter-insurgency cooperation—Ugandan troops remain central to African Union efforts against al Shabaab and the search for Joseph Kony—but said it would defend LGBT rights globally. Kampala rejected pressure to repeal the law, framing it as a sovereign decision not subject to foreign blackmail.

Former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates and former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper testified before a Senate Judiciary subcommittee on May 8, producing a high-profile hearing that added fresh scrutiny to the Trump administration’s handling of Michael Flynn and broader Russia-related inquiries. Yates’ testimony focused on her January warnings to White House Counsel Don McGahn that then–National Security Adviser Flynn had misled senior officials about communications with Russia’s ambassador, Sergey Kislyak, and was therefore susceptible to Russian blackmail. She said she met McGahn on Jan. 26 and again on Jan. 27 to convey the urgency of the matter; Flynn was not dismissed until Feb. 13, 18 days later, after reporting revealed he had lied to Vice President Mike Pence. That delay raised immediate questions about the White House’s response and judgment in retaining Flynn in a position with access to sensitive intelligence while he might be compromised.

Yates also recounted how she learned of Trump’s travel ban executive order from the media on Jan. 30, the same day she was fired after refusing to defend the order in court. She defended her decision, arguing the order raised legal and constitutional concerns and that she acted on legal judgment rather than policy preference. Throughout the hearing she denied leaking classified information despite President Trump’s tweets implying otherwise; Clapper likewise denied being an anonymous source in media reports related to Trump and Russia.

Clapper confirmed that U.S. intelligence received sensitive information from U.K. and other European allies during 2016 about contacts between Trump associates and Russian officials. He also testified he was unaware of the FBI’s counterintelligence investigation into possible Trump–Russia ties until FBI Director James Comey disclosed it publicly in March, suggesting the probe had been tightly held within law enforcement channels.

Republican senators pressed Yates on her refusal to defend the travel ban and probed Clapper about leaks and prior investigations, while Democrats used the hearing to underscore concerns about Flynn’s conduct and Russia’s meddling. Although the testimony produced no smoking-gun evidence of collusion, it intensified scrutiny of administration decision-making, highlighted unanswered questions about why Flynn remained in his post after being warned, and contributed to the incremental accumulation of facts across multiple investigations that could bear on broader inquiries into election meddling and contacts between Trump associates and Russia. Social media and the White House reacted sharply, including ridicule over Trump briefly changing his Twitter banner to feature one of his own tweets denying collusion.

A 12-year-old boy was stopped by police in Broken Hill, far-west New South Wales, after attempting to drive alone across much of Australia. Officers from the Broken Hill Highway Patrol pulled the vehicle over on the Barrier Highway Saturday morning when they noticed a hazardous defect—its bumper dragging on the ground—and discovered the driver was a child. Police said the boy had already driven roughly 1,300 kilometres across New South Wales from Kendall on the east coast and said he intended to continue to Perth, a journey of about 4,000–4,300 kilometres that would cross the long, harsh Nullarbor Plain. That crossing alone typically takes visitors several days and requires carrying extra fuel, water, food and spare parts because services are sparse; wildlife such as emus, kangaroos, wombats and even feral camels pose night-time hazards. Authorities arrested the boy, took him to the Broken Hill police station, and later released him into his parents’ care; inquiries were ongoing and police said they hoped to speak with the family. The case prompted public astonishment and questions about how he paid for fuel, who taught him to drive, whether his parents had reported him missing, and what motivated the attempt. Commentators noted he spent at least one night alone on the road and praised that he was unharmed, while authorities and the public remained concerned and curious as the investigation continued.

A 2-year-old girl, Leasia Carter, died after being left unattended in a locked car for about 16 hours in Baltimore’s Belair-Edison neighborhood, authorities said. Police were called around 5:15–5:30 p.m. Monday to the 3400 block of Juneway/Brendan Avenue after a man discovered the unresponsive child buckled in a car seat. Paramedics transported her to Johns Hopkins Children’s Center in critical condition; she later died. Investigators determined the vehicle had been closed for roughly 16 hours, with much of that time during daytime heat when outside temperatures neared 89°F. By the time she was removed, Leasia had suffered second-degree burns consistent with prolonged exposure to extreme heat inside a closed vehicle.

Her father, 31-year-old Wilbert Carter, who had sole legal custody, was arrested and charged with second-degree murder and child abuse. Police obtained a warrant and took him into custody Monday; he is being held at Central Booking. In interviews and charging documents, Carter said he had consumed about five alcoholic drinks Sunday and had limited memory of events. He reported that a friend drove his car to Brendan Avenue around midnight; family members said they saw him return home around 7 a.m. and he later woke about 4 p.m. and began searching for his daughter when he could not find her. A cousin told him his car was still parked on Brendan Avenue, where he then found Leasia.

Neighbors said Carter had another child with him when he initially searched. Authorities noted Carter has a prior history of heavy drinking. Officials and safety experts reiterated that temperatures inside parked cars can reach lethal levels within ten minutes, and issued reminders never to leave children, pets, or the elderly unattended in vehicles. Research shows heatstroke is a leading non-crash vehicle-related killer of children, with many cases involving caregivers who inadvertently forget children in the back seat.

Archaeologists excavating the ancient and medieval fortress and port of Burgos (Poros) on Cape Foros near Burgas, Bulgaria, uncovered a tiny sixth‑century lead tube reliquary containing ashes said to be from the grave of John the Apostle (St. John the Theologian) in Ephesus. Discovered in a 6th‑century Early Christian basilica during 2014 digs and announced in 2015 by Milen Nikolov of the Burgas Regional Museum of History, the 2.2 cm by 1.7 cm tube is decorated with cross motifs and likely arrived with a pilgrim who visited Ephesus, a major healing pilgrimage center where “manna” was believed to appear annually at John’s tomb. Bulgarian archaeologists note only 43 such lead tube reliquaries are known worldwide; the Burgas example resembles clay tubes produced in Ephesus, supporting its origin. The site has also yielded other finds—a Late Antiquity latrine, Roman inscriptions, multiple building phases from the 3rd–6th centuries, and a 10th‑century Bulgarian royal seal—highlighting the long, multi‑period occupation and the fortress’s regional significance.

Rescue excavations in 2006–2007 beneath a future shopping center in Tulln, Lower Austria, uncovered a unique, nearly complete camel skeleton in a backfilled cellar associated with a late 17th‑century urban deposit. Initial misidentification as a horse or cattle was overturned by distinctive cervical vertebrae, mandible and metapodials. Coins and a medicinal bottle recovered in the same fill date the context to the late 1600s, a period when Ottoman troops operated in the region during the 1683 campaign toward Vienna. While camel remains are known sporadically across Europe from Roman to early modern times, this is the first fully preserved camel skeleton documented in Central Europe, enabling a rare integrative study combining archaeology, osteology and ancient DNA.

Morphological and metric analyses produced mixed features: some long bones were slender like dromedaries, others robust like Bactrian camels, and metacarpals resembled Bactrian form. Ancient DNA results clarified this ambiguity, identifying the animal as an F1 hybrid (Tulu) with a dromedary mother (maternal mitochondrial haplotype common in modern dromedaries) and Bactrian paternal contribution. Osteopathologies—symmetrical lesions on scapulae and humeri and periostitis of the mandible—suggest repeated mounting activity consistent with a riding animal rather than a heavy beast of burden. The specimen was a male, roughly seven years old and possibly castrated.

The authors interpret the camel as an “exotic” animal kept by townspeople—perhaps left by Ottoman forces, presented, and then neglected or died naturally—rather than butchered. Its preservation offers direct archaeozoological and genetic evidence for hybrid camels used historically in Anatolia and by Ottoman military or associated networks, illustrating past animal exchange and husbandry practices in Central Europe.

Gabino Zavala, a Mexico-born auxiliary bishop of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles who rose from humble beginnings to oversee the influential San Gabriel pastoral region, resigned after revealing he is the father of two teenage children. Long known as a popular, approachable leader and a vigorous advocate for social and economic justice—campaigning against the death penalty, supporting immigrant rights, promoting labor protections, and leading Pax Christi USA—Zavala stopped public ministry after informing Archbishop José Gomez in December. The Vatican accepted his resignation, with Gomez telling parishioners the news was “sad and difficult” and noting the children live with their mother in another state; the archdiocese has offered spiritual care and financial help for college costs. Church officials investigated and found no misuse of church funds. The case, disclosed during Gomez’s early tenure, has prompted shock and renewed debate over priestly celibacy. While some theologians call the rule outdated, Pope Benedict and Vatican policy remain committed to celibacy, though married Anglican converts are occasionally exempted.

A grassroots effort to create a 51st state, often called North Colorado, largely fizzled Nov. 5 as voters in several key counties rejected advisory measures asking county commissioners to pursue secession. Weld County, the movement’s most populous backer, overwhelmingly voted no (about 58% to 42%), a sharp rebuke of commissioners who had led the push citing perceived neglect of rural priorities like agriculture, oil and gas. Overall, five of 11 counties—Kit Carson, Washington, Phillips, Cheyenne and Yuma—approved asking commissioners to explore secession, while Elbert, Lincoln, Logan, Moffat, Sedgwick and Weld voted against. The ballot was a symbolic straw poll asking whether commissioners should pursue statehood; actual secession would require state and congressional approval, a rare and difficult process last seen in 1820 with Maine. Proponents argued the vote highlighted rural frustration with Front Range-driven legislation such as stricter gun laws and renewable-energy mandates and said the campaign succeeded in raising rural issues. Organizers plan continued activism, including a proposal to give counties equal representation in a reformed state senate and backing statewide candidates sympathetic to rural concerns. Local leaders defended the exercise as listening to citizens, not a publicity stunt.

Tracy Rosner, a third-grade teacher at Coral Reef Elementary in Miami-Dade County, has filed a federal lawsuit alleging employment discrimination after being denied reassignment to an Extended Foreign Language (EFL) track that requires one hour per day of foreign language instruction. Rosner, who does not speak Spanish, says she requested the reassignment in May 2015 and was rejected because the school’s principal required foreign language teachers to actually speak the language they teach. Her complaint argues she was otherwise fully qualified and that the school could have assigned someone else to deliver the one-hour Spanish component while she handled other responsibilities. 

Rosner’s attorneys contend the policy of hiring only Spanish-speaking teachers disproportionately disadvantages non-Spanish speakers in Miami-Dade County, where Spanish speakers form a majority, and thus discriminates on the basis of race—Rosner is white. After being denied the reassignment, Rosner alleges the principal retaliated by doubling her workload and making her teach all subjects rather than only reading and language arts. She filed complaints with the superintendent and the district’s civil rights office; administrators found no probable cause and closed the case. 

The lawsuit claims Rosner suffered harm including a less desirable position, emotional pain, suffering, mental anguish, inconvenience, and loss of enjoyment of life as a direct result of the alleged retaliation and rights violations. Miami-Dade School Board attorneys have not yet filed a court response and did not comment. Rosner did not respond to requests for comment.

The 40-piece Chicken McNugget is McDonald’s most calorie-dense menu item, at 1,880 calories—nearly a full day’s recommended intake and enough to feed several people. 24/7 Wall St. reviewed about 500 McDonald’s items and found that large sandwiches and big-portion items dominate the highest-calorie list; the Big Breakfast with Hotcakes and a large biscuit ranks second at 1,310 calories. Some beverages are also calorie-heavy—a 16-ounce M&M’s McFlurry has 930 calories and a Large Oreo Frappe 810—so a plausible single lunch (sandwich, medium fries, McFlurry) can exceed 2,000 calories. Calories don’t capture full nutritional risk; for example, the 630-calorie Premium Grilled Chicken Bacon Clubhouse contains 1,740 mg of sodium. The analysis used McDonald’s nutritional data to compile the 50 highest-calorie items.

A Florida woman was arrested after allegedly shooting at houseguests she said were too loud. According to Bay County Sheriff’s Office officials, 32-year-old Alana Annette Savell told investigators guests came over, began drinking and became noisy. Savell and her boyfriend reportedly followed a violent “rule”: after asking someone to leave three times, she should retrieve a handgun and shoot at the ground; if that failed, she was to shoot the person in the leg. Acting on that plan, Savell armed herself with a .22-caliber pistol and fired from the doorway toward the guests’ feet. One woman was struck in the leg and taken to a hospital; Savell’s boyfriend was also hit in the leg by a bullet. Savell was booked on a charge of aggravated battery with a firearm and jailed; it is unknown whether she has obtained an attorney. Separate unrelated reporting noted that e-cigarettes and other battery-powered devices occasionally catch fire, citing an earlier New York incident.

Salman, a 12-year-old jaguar on a one-year breeding loan to Delhi’s National Zoological Park from Thiruvananthapuram Zoo, is being returned after staff concluded he is “too fat to breed.” Brought to Delhi in October 2014 to mate with a female named Kalpana, Salman reportedly showed no interest in mating during the year and instead prioritized food, often finishing meals other jaguars left behind. Keepers described him as lazy and gluttonous; despite efforts to slim him with a strict diet and more time in a larger enclosure to encourage exercise, he remained lethargic and unresponsive to Kalpana’s advances. Zoo curator Riaz Khan said officials lost hope of breeding and decided to send him back, arguing the jaguar was not fulfilling the purpose of the loan. Some staff noted relocation stress can curb breeding in previously proven sires, and pointed out other male jaguars in the park have also failed to sire cubs with Kalpana. Salman’s exact weight has not been officially measured at Delhi, though keepers estimate it exceeds 100 kg—above the typical jaguar range—and maintain this contributed to his mating disinterest.

Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) warned that Donald Trump is “a wrecking ball” threatening to dismantle the Republican Party, criticizing Trump’s recent rhetoric that broadly labels many immigrants as criminals. On CNN’s State of the Union, Graham said Trump’s comments and their adoption by some conservatives mark a “defining moment” the GOP must reject to retain moral authority and win national elections. He argued such language alienates Hispanic voters — “friends, neighbors and relatives” of immigrants — and damages the party’s capacity to govern. While acknowledging border problems, Graham advocated practical measures: doubling border patrol agents, tripling drones and addressing visa overstays. He contrasted policy solutions with what he called “demagoguery,” warning Republicans who embrace Trump’s tone are “digging their own political graves.”

Former Sen. Jim Webb (D-Va.), also running for president, criticized Trump’s abrasive immigration remarks as cheapening the 2016 campaign and contributing divisive rhetoric unfit for a commander in chief. Webb, positioning himself as an alternative Democrat, argued the party has moved left and pledged to champion working-class voters who feel neglected by both parties, suggesting his campaign can bring a different tone and focus to national politics.

Mathew Carpenter, a 22-year-old Australian, launched ShipYourEnemiesGlitter.com as a joke—offering to anonymously mail glitter-filled letters to “enemies” for $9.99. The site’s snarky copy (“we fucking hate glitter” and “the herpes of the craft world”) went viral, drawing millions of visitors, thousands of orders, and over $20,000 in sales within days. Overwhelmed by demand, Carpenter paused orders and begged people to stop buying the “horrible” product, then listed the business on Flippa. After bidding surged, an anonymous buyer purchased the site for about $85,000. Carpenter included the site, domain, and press leads in the sale, offering transition support and a non-compete. He noted simple margins ($5.99–$7.99 per order) and potential to scale via outsourcing, product extensions, and branding on the letter included with each mailing. Several copycats have already emerged to fill continued interest.

On Oct. 3, 1995, O.J. Simpson was acquitted of the murders of his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman in a trial that captivated the nation. The case transformed Simpson—from Heisman Trophy winner, Hall of Fame running back and popular actor and spokesman—into a polarizing figure whose notoriety endures. Although found not guilty criminally, Simpson was held liable in a 1997 civil suit and ordered to pay $33.5 million to the Brown and Goldman families, of which they have collected less than 1 percent.

Simpson’s fortunes declined after the trial. Once earning substantial income from endorsements (he reportedly made $550,000 a year from Hertz in 1992) and possessing multimillion-dollar assets, he defaulted on his Brentwood mansion mortgage in 1997 and now has a much reduced estimated net worth of about $250,000. His NFL pension, roughly $25,000 per month, is legally protected from civil judgments.

In 2007 Simpson led a group that entered Las Vegas hotel rooms to recover sports memorabilia he asserted belonged to him. That incident resulted in a 2008 conviction on 12 counts—including armed robbery, kidnapping and assault with a deadly weapon—and a nine-to-33-year sentence. He has served nearly nine years at Nevada’s Lovelock Correctional Center and was paroled on lesser counts in 2013. As of a recent Nevada parole hearing, Simpson appeared virtually before the board seeking release; if granted, he could be freed as soon as Oct. 1. Media interest in the decision is intense, and public opinion remains sharply divided. Supporters point to Simpson’s model prison behavior and age in parole considerations, while critics warn against any return to the spotlight given his fraught history and unresolved civil judgment.

The aftermath of Hurricane Harvey revealed both the strengths and strains of American civic response: immediate, grassroots rescue efforts contrasted with deep political polarization that threatens coordinated national recovery and longer-term planning. Harvey’s catastrophic flooding and loss of life rekindled debates over two major fault lines: how Congress funds disaster recovery, and how climate change is altering storm risks.

Funding fights have become increasingly partisan. Historical precedents—post-Katrina aid in 2005 and Hurricane Sandy relief in 2012—show congressional battles over whether disaster assistance should be offset by cuts elsewhere. Prominent conservatives have pushed for offsets to prevent expanding federal debt, turning emergency aid into zero-sum fights between regions. Those debates delay aid and frame help for one community as harm to others, undermining the principle of government sharing risks beyond the capacity of individuals or localities. Observers warn that if Texas aid is again tied to cuts in other programs, partisan rancor will outpace public compassion and slow recovery.

The second, more profound debate concerns climate change. Scientists caution that individual storms can rarely be attributed solely to climate change, but the consensus is that warming amplifies several risk factors: higher sea levels raise storm surge; warmer air holds more moisture, increasing potential rainfall; and warmer ocean surface temperatures fuel stronger storms. For Harvey specifically, Gulf sea surface temperatures were unusually warm and a deep warm layer likely helped rapid intensification. Thermodynamics implies roughly a 3–7 percent increase in atmospheric moisture per degree Celsius, translating into heavier precipitation and flooding risk. Some researchers suggest climate-driven changes in atmospheric circulation—like weakening or shifting jets and expanded subtropical highs—may increase the persistence of storms, causing events to stall and dump extraordinary rain over single regions, as Harvey did.

Recent scientific work goes further, linking anthropogenic warming to alterations in large-scale temperature gradients, jet stream structure, and resonant planetary wave patterns that favor long-duration extreme weather in summer. Analyses of climate models (CMIP5) and observational temperature datasets find trends consistent with a “fingerprint” of conditions favoring quasi-resonant amplification of planetary waves—conditions that have become more likely with Arctic amplification and greenhouse forcing. While internal variability complicates detection, anthropogenic-only model runs show a stronger, more robust trend toward these QRA-favorable temperature patterns.

Politics complicate responses to these scientific realities. The Trump administration’s skepticism—withdrawal from the Paris Accord and rollback of emissions regulations—reflects regional economic priorities tied to fossil fuels, even though some high-risk coastal states depend economically on those industries. Media and partisan actors have also politicized coverage: cable pundits criticized questions about climate links as opportunistic, while commentators and scientists argued that ignoring climate context during disaster coverage abdicates journalistic responsibility and squanders a brief window when public attention could support systemic change.

Experts stress that mitigation and adaptation are not interchangeable. Adaptation—better infrastructure, land-use planning, and social safety nets—is essential but costly and uneven; without mitigation, adaptation becomes increasingly futile and inequitable. Harvey therefore surfaces a broader moral and policy choice: whether to recognize and address climate-driven risk multipliers now through emissions reductions and equitable adaptation, or to continue reactive, partisan approaches that leave vulnerable communities repeatedly exposed.

Researchers analyzing sediment from the bottom of the 1993 GISP2 ice core have identified a 2.7‑million‑year‑old silt layer beneath Greenland’s Summit, revealing a pre‑glacial tundra landscape preserved under the ice. Using beryllium‑10 isotopic dating—which accumulates in surface soils exposed to cosmic rays—the team found levels comparable to long‑lived Arctic tundra and consistent with a stable surface that existed for roughly 200,000 to 1 million years before being buried. The findings, published in Science, imply that at least at this Summit “pinprick,” the Greenland Ice Sheet has persisted through major natural warm periods of the Pleistocene without fully melting, including interglacials as warm as those expected in coming decades. The preservation is explained by cold‑based ice at the core base that is frozen to bedrock and thus protects rather than erodes underlying soils; the lowest 10–15 meters of the core are frozen and the ice above is deformed but not basal‑erosive. Earlier work found similarly ancient preserved landscapes elsewhere in Greenland, and researchers are now seeking comparable records in Antarctica. The study underscores both the ice sheet’s past endurance and the uncertainty posed by rapid human‑driven warming today.

A Pennsylvania couple married a week earlier was arrested after allegedly attempting to shoplift $1,049.26 worth of groceries and party supplies from a Wegmans the afternoon of their planned wedding reception. Brittany M. Lurch, 22, and Arthur Phillips III, 32, both of Centre Hall, were observed on surveillance loading numerous items into two shopping carts and leaving the store without paying, then pushing the carts to a waiting Hyundai. Police say the pair told officers the merchandise was intended for their 5:30 p.m. reception. Reported stolen goods included seafood orders such as a shrimp platter, two spiral hams, vegetable and appetizer trays, eggs, a punch bowl, utensils and dinnerware for eight, soda, turkey, and various personal items like toothbrushes, a polo shirt and razor blades. The couple were arrested and booked on misdemeanor retail theft and receiving stolen property charges and remained in the Centre County jail on $2,500 bail. Officers also found a glass pipe with marijuana residue in the car; Phillips faced an additional paraphernalia charge. Both waived their right to a preliminary hearing.

Hollywood’s sexual-harassment revelations continued with multiple developments: Nickelodeon producer Chris Savino, creator of The Loud House, apologized on Facebook after up to a dozen women accused him of sexual harassment. Reports detailed offers of work for sexual favors, explicit messages, and long-standing rumors; Nickelodeon confirmed Savino was fired and no longer involved with the series, which will continue production. Separately, New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman opened a civil rights investigation into The Weinstein Co., subpoenaing company records to probe pervasive harassment or discrimination after dozens accused co-founder Harvey Weinstein of assault. Actress Ashley Judd will give a televised interview about her earlier allegations against Weinstein.

President Donald Trump announced that the United States, Britain and France had launched precision strikes in Syria in retaliation for an alleged chemical attack by President Bashar al-Assad’s government. Speaking from the White House, Trump said the strikes were intended to punish Assad for using internationally banned chemical weapons and to create a strong deterrent to prevent future attacks. Explosions and heavy smoke were reported over Damascus as the operation began; Syrian state media said air defenses had responded.

Trump framed the operation as limited to degrading Syria’s chemical weapons capabilities — including strikes against aircraft, military depots and chemical facilities — and said the U.S. was prepared to “sustain” pressure until chemical attacks stop, though he also reiterated that America does not seek an indefinite presence in Syria. He criticized Russia and Iran for supporting the Assad regime, saying their associations with “murderous dictators” are damning and urging them to change course; he reminded that Russia had guaranteed a 2013 deal for Syria to dismantle its chemical arsenal.

French President Emmanuel Macron affirmed France’s participation, calling Syria’s alleged use of chemical arms a crossed “red line” and saying the operation targeted the regime’s clandestine chemical capabilities. The strikes follow a year after a U.S. Tomahawk missile attack on a Syrian airfield, which had limited long-term effect. Questions remain whether the allied action signals a broader political strategy to end the war without leaving Assad in power, and U.S. officials considered risks including Russian forces and the safety of roughly 2,000 American troops in-country.

A UNICEF report released ahead of International Day of the Girl (11 October) finds that girls aged 5–14 worldwide shoulder a disproportionate share of unpaid household work, spending 40% more time on chores than boys — the equivalent of 160 million extra hours per day. The study, Harnessing the Power of Data for Girls: Taking stock and looking ahead to 2030, provides the first global estimates of children’s time spent on tasks such as cooking, cleaning, caring for family members and collecting water and firewood. Disparities begin early: girls aged 5–9 spend 30% more time on household duties (about 40 million extra hours daily), and the gap widens in adolescence, with 10–14 year-olds spending 50% more time (about 120 million extra hours daily). The report highlights that much of girls’ work is invisible and undervalued, often involving adult responsibilities like childcare and elder care, which reduces time for play, study and socializing. In some contexts, chores such as fetching water or firewood also expose girls to risks like sexual violence. Regional and country-level findings show particularly large gender gaps in South Asia and the Middle East and North Africa, while Burkina Faso, Yemen and Somalia have the largest disparities; 10–14 year-old girls in Somalia spend the most time on chores — about 26 hours weekly. UNICEF officials emphasize that quantifying these burdens is a vital step toward achieving gender equality under the Sustainable Development Goals and unlocking benefits for girls and societies, including improved education, economic growth and reduced poverty.

Researchers have reconstructed a detailed portrait of LUCA—the Last Universal Common Ancestor—by mining nearly 2,000 modern microbial genomes. Facing the complication that microbes frequently exchange genes horizontally, William Martin and colleagues used stringent criteria: they sought gene families present in at least two bacterial and two archaeal species. From some 6.1 million protein-coding genes grouped into ≈286,514 clusters, they identified 355 protein families traceable by phylogeny to LUCA. Because these genes are not universally distributed, their functions illuminate LUCA’s physiology and environment.

The inferred traits portray LUCA as an anaerobic, thermophilic, single-celled organism that fixed carbon via the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway and depended on hydrogen (H2) and carbon dioxide as primary substrates. Its biochemistry was rich in iron–sulfur (FeS) clusters and radical reaction mechanisms and required cofactors and metals such as flavins, S-adenosyl methionine, coenzyme A, ferredoxin, molybdopterin, corrins, and selenium. Evidence also points to nitrogen fixation and specialized nucleoside modifications in its genetic code. Phylogenies place modern clostridia and methanogens—organisms with similar metabolisms—as basal within their domains, supporting continuity from LUCA-like metabolisms.

These results bolster hypotheses that life began in geochemically active, oxygen-poor settings—most plausibly hydrothermal vents or similar environments where geological processes supply H2, CO2, and iron. The findings strengthen the idea of an autotrophic origin of life driven by ancient, metal-dependent biochemistry rather than a later oxygenated, pond-like scenario.

A U.S. cyber intelligence firm, iSight Partners, uncovered a long-running espionage campaign—dubbed "Sandworm Team"—that for about five years targeted NATO, the European Union, Ukrainian entities, and companies in the energy and telecommunications sectors. Researchers say the attackers recently began exploiting a previously unknown vulnerability present in most versions of Microsoft Windows, using sophisticated, novel malware and social-engineered phishing documents to infect systems. iSight found clues in code and choice of targets pointing to Russian origins and believes the operation is likely supported by a nation-state because its objectives appear espionage-focused rather than criminal. While iSight could not confirm what specific data was stolen, the content of phishing lures and target profiles suggests interest in the Ukraine crisis, diplomatic matters, energy and telecom topics.

The firm notified Microsoft of the vulnerability and delayed public disclosure to allow a fix; Microsoft planned an automatic update rollout. iSight said it alerted some victims but would not provide details; it also reported evidence of infections in several Ukrainian government systems though could not remotely confirm particular compromised machines. The malware used an attack method that bypassed most known defenses, leading researchers to conclude a large share of targeted systems were likely infected. iSight intended to release a detailed 16-page report to clients. The investigation adds to a string of private-sector findings linking highly capable cyber campaigns to actors tied to Russia, including previous research by Kaspersky Lab into broad attacks on government and military targets. No comment was immediately available from Russia, NATO, the EU or Ukraine.

Fox News host Laura Ingraham mocked Taylor Swift on Twitter after Swift’s endorsed candidate lost the Tennessee Senate race. Ingraham tweeted, “Hey @taylorswift13, haters gonna hate. #shakeitoff,” referencing Swift’s hit song, following Republican Marsha Blackburn’s victory over Democrat Phil Bredesen for the Senate seat previously held by Bob Corker. Swift had publicly revealed she voted for Bredesen and had earlier endorsed him and Jim Cooper for the House, explaining she could not support Blackburn despite generally wanting to vote for women in office. Blackburn’s win likely dimmed Democratic hopes of flipping control of the Senate. Swift’s foray into politics was notable because it was a rare, explicit endorsement from the singer.

A Massachusetts court approved release of 192 pages of Mitt Romney’s 1991 testimony in the divorce-related litigation of Staples founder Tom Stemberg, but kept a gag order preventing Stemberg and his ex-wife Maureen Sullivan Stemberg from publicly discussing the case. The transcripts show Romney testified that Staples issued a new “D” class of shares before its IPO, convertible into common stock, to help finance Stemberg’s divorce settlement—an action Romney described as a favor to facilitate a settlement. Romney portrayed Stemberg as an optimistic entrepreneur who downplayed risks when raising funds. Lawyers for Romney, Stemberg and Staples did not oppose release; Romney’s lawyer dismissed accusations as politically motivated and false. Gloria Allred, representing Sullivan Stemberg, sought both transcript release and removal of the gag order, warning the testimony is incomplete without her client’s statements. Staples’ market values cited in the filings rose substantially in the years following Romney’s testimony.

This sprawling compilation centers on Bob Dylan’s disputed but ultimately lauded place in literature and popular culture, weaving critical praise, fan obsession, biographical detail, and reflections on his career and persona. The Nobel Prize in Literature awarded to Dylan ignited debate: some balk at calling pop lyrics “literature,” others celebrate the recognition of new poetic forms within the American song tradition. Supporters argue that Dylan’s words are inseparable from his music—lines from songs like “It’s Alright, Ma,” “Visions of Johanna,” and “Brownsville Girl” are cited as examples of language that resonates deeply precisely because of their vocal and musical delivery. The Nobel citation—“for having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition”—both honored and provoked analysis of Dylan’s evolution, including his late-career recordings of Great American Songbook standards and his long habit of upending classifications placed on him by critics.

The text traces Dylan’s creative arcs: the early protest-folk phase, the electric breakthroughs of the mid-60s, the Blood on the Tracks introspection of the 1970s, and later reinventions that kept expanding the possibilities of song. It addresses the perennial controversy over whether his non-musical writings (e.g., the prose Tarantula) qualify him as a traditional literary figure. Commentators emphasize that Dylan’s potency lies in phrasing and performance, the way a simple line can encapsulate complex truth.

A large portion of the material explores Dylan’s personal mystique and fraught relationship with fame: his secrecy, his “Never Ending Tour,” and an almost religious fan culture that can veer into obsession (collectors seeking relics, extreme archivists). Anecdotes from collaborators and admirers—Bruce Langhorne, Joan Baez, Allen Ginsberg, and others—illustrate both his genius and unapproachable tendencies. Episodes like the “Judas!” concert reaction, his 1966 motorcycle accident, and stories of difficult interviews underscore Dylan’s evasive public stance.

The piece also situates Dylan among peers and contenders for literary honors, contrasting him with novelists, poets, and the wider Nobel conversation, while asserting his enduring influence on singers and writers. Ultimately, it argues that Dylan’s significance—ambiguous, provocative, and singular—transcends neat categorization: he remains a vital, if enigmatic, force whose work continues to be reassessed and celebrated.

Ana-Alecia Ayala, 32, who won widespread attention for dancing through chemotherapy, has died after a year-long battle with uterine sarcoma. Diagnosed in December 2015, the rare tumor originated in her uterus and spread to her ovaries and the lining of her stomach; a later recurrence appeared on her spleen. Ayala underwent surgery that removed most of the tumor, then more aggressive inpatient chemotherapy when the new tumor was discovered. She spent difficult stretches separated from her 3-year-old daughter — at one point holding the child’s birthday party in her hospital room with nurses joining in song.

Known for an upbeat video she and her “chemo buddy,” Danielle Andrus, posted from the hospital — dancing to viral tracks like “Juju On That Beat” — Ayala hoped to change perceptions of cancer. The clip quickly drew tens of thousands of views and led to appearances and widespread support. She credited Danielle, whom she met in a 2015 fitness group, for sitting through chemo sessions with magazines, crafts and encouragement, and for pushing her to share the video. Ayala urged fellow patients and loved ones to “not look at cancer as a death sentence” and to embrace joy, silliness and presence amid hardship, calling laughter the best medicine. Surrounded by family, loved ones and a family priest, she passed away in the hospital; a GoFundMe remained for those wishing to contribute.

U.S. Rep. Elizabeth Esty, a Connecticut Democrat and vocal #MeToo proponent, has apologized after reports that she failed to promptly protect and discipline staffers who say they experienced threats, violence and sexual harassment by her former chief of staff, Tony Baker. Esty acknowledged learning in 2016 via a third party about allegations that a former employee had been harassed and physically harmed. She said she demanded Baker receive counseling, ordered an internal review, and fired him three months later after that review indicated the harassment and threats were part of a broader pattern. Esty has expressed remorse for delaying action, for not advancing the investigation faster, and for having “even the slightest assistance” in his pursuit of subsequent employment; Baker later worked briefly as Ohio state director for Sandy Hook Promise, though he no longer works there and has denied some allegations. Ahead of media reports, Esty met with leaders of Connecticut women’s groups and domestic violence advocates, who described her as remorseful and intent on making improvements, while also urging more information be disclosed. Critics, including the Hartford Courant editorial board and the state GOP, called for her resignation; some Connecticut Democrats voiced disappointment but noted her acknowledgment of mistakes. Esty requested a House Ethics Committee review of her conduct and later announced she will not seek reelection, saying stepping down at year’s end is in the best interest of constituents and family and pledging to work to strengthen workplace protections in her remaining months.

A new study challenges the long-held belief that black rats drove repeated European plague epidemics after the Black Death. Researchers led by Prof. Nils Christian Stenseth (University of Oslo) analyzed 7,711 historical plague outbreaks alongside European tree-ring climate records to test whether climatic conditions favored a rat-flea-human transmission cycle. They found no correlation between European weather and plague recurrence, undermining the theory that rat reservoirs and local climate fluctuations repeatedly ignited epidemics. Instead, the team identifies Central Asian giant gerbils as a likely source: years with wet springs followed by warm summers boost gerbil and flea populations across large areas of Central Asia, increasing Yersinia pestis circulation in wild rodent-flea systems. Those conditions, combined with intense medieval east–west trade (e.g., the Silk Road), could have enabled repeated introductions of plague into European port cities and subsequent continent-wide spread. The researchers plan to sequence ancient Y. pestis DNA from European skeletons; high genetic diversity between waves would support multiple Asian-origin introductions, whereas low diversity would be expected from a persistent European rat reservoir. The article notes plague persists worldwide in enzootic foci; from 2010–2015 there were 3,248 reported cases (584 deaths), and WHO lists the Democratic Republic of Congo, Madagascar, and Peru as most endemic. It also highlights general plague biology, clinical forms (bubonic and pneumonic), transmission routes, treatment with antibiotics, prevention measures, outbreak control strategies (vector/rodent control, isolation, chemoprophylaxis), and WHO surveillance and response guidance.

A Purdue University–led analysis of data from the Within-Family Differences Study finds that being a mother’s apparent favorite in adulthood is not necessarily protective and may even be linked to greater depressive symptoms. The longitudinal project followed 725 adult children from 309 families, with mothers aged 65–75 when the study began in 2001, and collected data in two waves seven years apart. Researchers measured four dimensions of perceived maternal favoritism/disfavoritism — emotional closeness, conflict, pride, and disappointment — and assessed depressive symptoms among the adult children.

Contrary to expectations that closeness would uniformly benefit well-being, adult children who thought they were emotionally closer to their mother than their siblings reported the highest levels of depressive symptoms. Elevated depressive symptoms were also observed among those who perceived themselves as the child their mother was most disappointed in or with whom she had the greatest conflict. The investigators interpret these findings as reflecting ongoing social comparison among siblings: both positive and negative differential treatment can generate distress through comparisons and altered family dynamics, such as increased sibling tension and caregiving expectations for the favored child.

Analyses by race revealed one notable difference: black adult children appeared particularly distressed when they perceived themselves as the child in whom their mother was most disappointed. No gender differences were found; sons and daughters were similarly affected. The authors plan to examine paternal favoritism next and to explore predictors of maternal favoritism. The study highlights that perceived parental preferences continue to matter in midlife and can influence psychological well-being through comparison-based processes.

Google UK marketing director Dan Cobley told Bloomberg TV that iOS 6 users could still “use Google Maps by downloading them or going to the Google Maps website” after Apple replaced Google Maps in the new OS. That comment was puzzling because Google has not released a dedicated Google Maps app in the App Store for iOS 6 (only Google Earth is available), and mobile Safari lacks a way to download offline Google Maps. SearchEngineLand contacted Google about when a native Maps app — possibly with turn-by-turn navigation — might arrive; Google reiterated its goal to make Google Maps available to everyone regardless of device, browser, or OS, but gave no timeline. In the meantime, users missing Google Maps are advised to consider third-party mapping apps; 9to5Mac compiled a list of comparable alternatives. The article also links to related items mocking iOS 6 Maps failures, and other tech and gadget roundups and promotions.

Inmates in Florida’s prisons plan a statewide, month-long strike beginning on Martin Luther King Day to protest unpaid labor, harsh conditions and commissary price gouging. Dubbed Operation Push, the coordinated action will include refusing work assignments and avoiding purchases to pressure the Department of Corrections financially and demand reforms. Organizers, who remain anonymous to avoid retaliation, cite recent use of prisoners as unpaid cleanup crews after Hurricane Irma and longstanding grievances: no wages for prison labor, lack of parole, exorbitant commissary prices, brutal conditions, overcrowding, mistreatment of mentally ill inmates, unexplained deaths in custody and suppression of inmates’ rights. Advocacy groups support the strike with solidarity rallies outside prisons. Critics and rights groups call Florida’s practices “slave labor,” noting Florida is one of few states that pay inmates nothing and still lacks parole for many offenses. The state’s corrections department has said it will ensure safe operation but has not detailed its response. Activists argue the demands are reasonable and necessary for rehabilitation and public safety; tensions remain high after past lockdowns, alleged abuses, and lawsuits over treatment of prisoners.

These articles compile the final days, circumstances, and aftermath of Robin Williams’ August suicide, blending eyewitness accounts, family statements, and reporting on his health, finances and career. Photos surfaced showing a gaunt, subdued Williams at a Bay Area art-gallery reception about a day before his death; attendees recalled him laughing and engaged, not drinking, and talking about projects such as a homeless-superhero script. He was later found dead in his Marin County home on Monday, seated in his bedroom with a belt secured around his neck; there was no suicide note. A longtime assistant and friend, Rebecca Erwin Spencer, discovered his body and called 911. The coroner cited asphyxia by hanging and noted superficial cuts on his wrist; toxicology results were expected weeks later.

Multiple sources describe Williams’ deepening depression in the weeks before he died. Reports say he was sleeping excessively—up to 18–20 hours a day—had little appetite, and was struggling to get out of bed. Friends and insiders stressed that depression had shadowed much of his adult life and that humor often served as his coping mechanism. He had recently completed voice work for the indie film Absolutely Anything and had entered rehab for “deep depression” earlier in the summer.

Speculation about financial troubles circulated online after his death, but his longtime publicist, Mara Buxbaum, denied financial strain as a cause. She pointed to his estimated $50 million net worth, valuable Napa and Tiburon properties, and likely estate planning via living trust, arguing the family was provided for. Williams himself had sometimes joked about downsizing and the appeal of steady TV work; he had taken the CBS series The Crazy Ones partly for creative reasons. Colleagues and fans responded with grief and tributes, and authorities and mental-health voices urged anyone struggling with suicidal thoughts to seek help.

Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine and Pike County Sheriff Charles Reader confirmed investigators are examining a Facebook threat that named one victim as they probe the execution-style killings of eight Rhoden family members at four rural Pike County properties. All autopsies are complete, crime scenes remain closed with roadblocks in place, and search warrants have not yet been filed. More than 100 personnel are assisting the lengthy investigation; authorities have interviewed 30+ people and urged anyone with tips to call provided hotlines. DeWine said marijuana grow operations were discovered at three of the four locations—about 200 indoor plants in one site—suggesting commercial production; investigators are considering whether the grows, a drug-turf dispute, cartel ties or a family feud could be motives, but no direct link has been established. Reader said the killings were planned and targeted, advising surviving family members to be armed and warning the community. The victims—seven adults and a 16-year-old—appear to have been shot while sleeping in some cases; infants and small children found unharmed. The killings have left the close-knit town shaken, with fewer attendees at local events and a $25,000 reward offered for information. Authorities continue to withhold many investigative details while pursuing leads. A memorial fund for the family has been set up at Fifth Third Bank.

Actor Ron Livingston publicly defended his sister, Jennifer Livingston, after the La Crosse, Wisconsin news anchor’s emotional on-air rebuttal to a viewer’s cruel email went viral. Livingston praised Jennifer’s dedication to her job, family, and community and called her a longtime role model. The controversy began when viewer Kenneth Krause emailed the WKBT-TV anchor, telling her her “physical condition hasn’t improved for many years” and that she shouldn’t be a role model for young people, especially girls. Jennifer, a 37-year-old mother of three, said the message made her feel bullied and responded on air, prompting widespread support. Krause later issued a statement that reiterated his position without much contrition, framing his remarks as concern amid an “epidemic of obesity” and suggesting Jennifer should “transform herself” on camera over the next year; he even offered to give advice or support. The exchange drew national attention: Soledad O’Brien discussed the story on CNN’s Starting Point and pressed Jennifer about whether she’d consulted station management before responding—Jennifer said her news director backed her, especially after her husband posted the email on Facebook and public support surged. O’Brien also named Krause on air and read his statement, noting the strong backing Jennifer received from viewers and public figures, including her actor brother Ron Livingston.

A 10-year-old Guatemalan girl with cerebral palsy, Rosa Maria Hernandez, was detained by U.S. federal immigration officers after passing a Border Patrol checkpoint while being taken for emergency gallbladder surgery in Corpus Christi, Texas. Brought to the United States as an infant by her undocumented mother, Rosa Maria had initially been treated at a specialty center in Laredo; local doctors said Driscoll Children’s Hospital in Corpus Christi was the nearest facility able to perform the operation. Because the transport route required driving through a checkpoint, Rosa Maria’s U.S. citizen cousin, Aurora Cantu, who carried a notarized letter from doctors explaining the emergency medical transport, drove her to Corpus Christi. Border Patrol permitted the trip but dispatched agents to follow them, and those agents remained at the hospital while Rosa Maria recovered.

Hospital officials would not confirm whether immigration agents were present, citing patient privacy. Immigration policy generally advises avoiding enforcement at “sensitive locations” such as hospitals, absent supervisory approval or exigent circumstances, but Customs and Border Protection (CBP) said it enforces immigration laws and escorted the child for medical care then would process her once medically cleared. After discharge, CBP agents escorted Rosa Maria by ambulance to the Bexar County Juvenile Detention Center in San Antonio rather than releasing her to family, despite her mother and grandfather being in the U.S. (the mother is undocumented; the grandfather is a permanent resident). Her lawyers contested the detention, noting Rosa Maria’s significant medical and developmental needs (attorneys say her mental capacity is closer to a 5- or 6-year-old). Authorities initially discussed moving her to a Houston detention center but ultimately routed her to San Antonio; Homeland Security officials said they would expedite a review to determine whether she can return to her mother, a process that typically takes months. Advocates and attorneys criticized the action as part of a broader shift toward more aggressive enforcement, noting that hospitals, schools, and places of worship previously regarded as de facto safe zones are increasingly subject to immigration actions. The case underscores tensions between emergency medical care access for undocumented patients and current immigration enforcement practices; it is developing and has drawn legal and public scrutiny.

On Christmas Eve 2017 the author unexpectedly encountered Ken Starr—the independent prosecutor whose 1998 investigation into President Clinton dragged her, then a 24-year-old White House intern, into a public scandal. She describes the surreal meeting: his warm, intrusive demeanor, his polite inquiry about her wellbeing, and her urge to remind him that his pursuit had terrorized not only her but her family, by threatening to prosecute her mother and probing relatives. That moment precipitates a reflection on the long shadow of 1998—both personally and nationally. Diagnosed with PTSD from being publicly outed and vilified, she recounts years of therapy and the struggle to reclaim her narrative after being gaslighted and labeled. The piece situates her trauma within a broader cultural wound: the Clinton–Starr saga unfolded amid an evolving media landscape—early web publishing, cable news, and tabloidization—that blurred private and public boundaries and amplified gossip into national spectacle. The author invokes George Lakoff’s family metaphors to argue the scandal ruptured national trust, turning a “family matter” into state crisis and leaving the country without a consoling voice. Psychologist Jack Saul observes elements resembling collective trauma—social rupture, scapegoating, and a constricted public narrative—though 1998 wasn’t a traditional “Big T” catastrophe. The author sees signs of progress in the #MeToo era: survivors now find solidarity and platforms that were absent two decades ago. Still, she remains in the process of integrating her past—grappling with agency versus victimhood, re-evaluating long-held internal scripts, and seeking the power to retell and reshape the story that has dominated her life. Her hope is that cultural reckoning will finally allow personal and collective healing.

Rep. Robert E. Andrews (D-N.J.) announced his resignation after 23 years in Congress, leaving a legislative record notable more for quantity than enacted laws. He introduced 646 bills—the most of any representative since he arrived—but only four passed the House and none became law. While that might suggest an unusually poor success rate, Andrews and observers say this metric misreads modern lawmaking. Contemporary Congress often advances policy through massive “moving vehicle” bills stuffed with provisions from many members; freestanding bills rarely pass. Andrews argues his strategy was to craft and stockpile legislative language so his ideas could be inserted into larger, must-pass legislation. He estimates about 110 of his ideas ultimately became law after being incorporated into others’ bills or companion measures. Examples include changes to Tricare and orthotic-device insurance rules; in some cases private-sector or agency actions mirrored his proposals despite his bills failing. Andrews’s influence peaked despite a backbench role and setbacks after Republicans took the House in 2011 and questions about campaign spending. His career highlights how congressional impact often occurs off the public roll call through legislative collaboration and insertion.

Archaeologists have confirmed that Jamestown colonists resorted to cannibalism during the "starving time" winter of 1609–1610. Forensic analysis of remains uncovered in 2012 revealed a 14-year-old English girl, dubbed "Jane," whose skull and tibia bear butchery marks consistent with axes, cleavers and knives used to remove flesh, tongue and brain—techniques similar to contemporary animal butchery. The girl’s bones were found in a fort cellar amid animal remains and debris from a fortwide cleanup. Historical accounts long hinted at cannibalism; records report corpses exhumed and eaten and at least one execution for murder and consumption. Researchers say the pattern of cuts, their sequence, and microscopic analysis rule out animal damage, indicating human action during extreme famine when only 60 of about 300 colonists survived. A facial reconstruction and the remains will be displayed at Jamestown’s museum.

Marin County ruled Robin Williams’ August 11 death a suicide by asphyxia from hanging. The 63-year-old was found in a Tiburon home closet wearing black clothes, with a belt around his neck and cuts on his wrist; a pocketknife with his blood and prescription medications were nearby. Toxicology showed antidepressants, caffeine and levodopa for Parkinson’s; no alcohol or illegal drugs were detected. Widow Susan Schneider said Williams had severe depression, anxiety, early Parkinson’s and a recent increase in paranoia; he’d been sleeping separately due to restless movement and insomnia. Investigators found no explicit suicide notes or searches, though items and behaviors—like giving away watches and researching medications—were noted. His death prompted widespread mourning and reflections on his career and struggles.

During World War II, the German battleship Tirpitz—dubbed "the beast" by Winston Churchill—was sheltered in northern Norway’s fjords and shielded with artificial smoke to evade Allied reconnaissance. In 2016, dendrochronologists led by Claudia Hartl from Johannes Gutenberg University discovered that this wartime camouflage left a long-lasting ecological fingerprint in the surrounding forests. While surveying trees near Kåfjord, Hartl and colleagues found extremely narrow or nearly absent growth rings in many pines and birches dated to 1945, signaling a sudden, severe environmental shock. Initial hypotheses such as insect outbreak or extreme cold proved unlikely. A local Norwegian researcher suggested a link to the Tirpitz, which had been producing chemical smoke—likely chlorosulphuric acid mixed with water—to create dense fog around the anchorage. That smoke drifted into adjacent forests, stripping needles from evergreen pines and impairing photosynthesis. Hartl returned to establish five test sites from a few hundred meters up to about ten kilometers from the former berth. Close to the fjord, over 60 percent of trees showed virtually no growth in 1945; effects persisted up to four kilometers away, where more than half the trees were severely affected and took on average eight years to recover. Some trees exhibited growth gaps lasting nine years, and young stands that appeared in the 1950s indicate tree mortality from the chemical exposure. The research, presented at the European Geosciences Union meeting, illustrates how wartime activities can leave durable environmental signatures and suggests similar “warfare dendrochronology” effects might be found elsewhere where artificial smoke or chemicals were used during WWII.

French authorities said early signals from the automatic detection system aboard EgyptAir Flight 804 indicated smoke in multiple locations moments before the Airbus A320 vanished from radar over the eastern Mediterranean, though the cause of the crash that killed all 66 aboard remains undetermined. The French air accident agency cautioned that smoke-warning messages “generally mean the start of a fire” but stressed no conclusions should be drawn yet. Investigators are examining all possibilities, including terrorism, and have reviewed passenger lists and begun questioning ground staff at Paris’ Charles de Gaulle Airport. The jet had reportedly been cruising normally when it suddenly lurched, rolled and plunged about 38,000 feet into the sea without issuing a distress call. Search teams from Egypt, Greece, Britain, France, the U.S. and Cyprus scoured a wide area after Egyptian forces located debris around 180 miles north of Alexandria; the deep waters complicate recovery, though black box pings can be detected to far greater depths. Photos and video released by the Egyptian military showed scattered wreckage—seats, life jackets, clothing and personal items. Egyptian authorities lean toward a terrorism explanation, and experts note the erratic flight could suggest an onboard blast or cockpit struggle, but no group has claimed responsibility and no firm evidence has emerged. The crash risks further harming Egypt’s fragile economy and tourism industry. French officials met bereaved families in Paris, pledging solidarity and a full investigation.

The piece criticizes Emma Watson for starring as Belle in Disney’s live-action Beauty and the Beast, arguing that her participation undermines her feminist credentials. While acknowledging Watson’s activism—her HeForShe work, speeches, and book initiatives—the writer contends she should have avoided affiliating with Disney, a company rooted in conservative, stereotypical portrayals of women. The core complaint is that Disney’s “princess” narratives consistently center romance, passive femininity, and male rescue, merely repackaged as empowerment through superficial updates (Belle “inventing” a washing machine, corset removed). Statistical examples are cited to show that female characters in Disney films often have less dialogue than males—even decreasing over time—and that modern heroines remain unrealistically thin and secondary to active male counterparts. The author dismisses claims that Disney has become progressive, calling rebrands like Tangled, Brave, and Frozen cosmetic rather than structural change. Public reactions to Watson’s Vanity Fair shoot—some accusing hypocrisy for her revealing photo, others defending choice and agency—are noted, alongside criticism of media figures who weaponized the image to question her feminism. The essay concludes that while Watson is a natural fit for a princess role, if she genuinely sought to empower girls away from passive tropes, she should use her influence to make original, feminist-led films that actively challenge patriarchal narratives rather than reinforce Disney’s entrenched brand.

Two months before a rare fatal alligator attack at Walt Disney World, Reedy Creek firefighters were warned to stop feeding two alligators that had been frequenting a pond behind Fire Station 3, emails obtained after the June incident show. Reedy Creek is the special taxing district that governs the Disney resort. The reptiles—a juvenile and a smaller adult estimated at about 4–5 feet—were reported near the station’s dumpster and parking lot, making communicators uneasy about walking to their cars. Communications captain Claude Rogers emailed fire command on April 20 saying the feedings were illegal, had attracted the animals into the lot, and that Animal Control had been notified; he asked crews to stop. Dispatcher Dan Lewis had earlier complained the gators were “not docile” and were coming out more often because people were feeding them.

Two months later, an alligator believed to be 4–7 feet ambushed 2-year-old Lane Graves while he waded at Seven Seas Lagoon by the Grand Floridian Resort, killing him; his father was injured by a second alligator during the rescue. Disney posted warning signs, removed crocodilian characters, and reiterated its policy to relocate small gators and call licensed trappers for larger ones. It is unclear whether the fire-station pond gators were removed or connected to the lagoon attack; Reedy Creek administrator John Classe said relocation seemed unlikely because an alligator would have to travel across roadways to reach the lagoon. Wildlife experts note feeding wild alligators is illegal in Florida because it conditions them to lose fear of people and can create dangerous “nuisance” animals.

Two websites offering “Dinner with Donald Trump” looked almost identical — one official Trump campaign site, the other a separate operation run by 25-year-old Maryland resident Ian Hawes. Hawes’s PAC, American Horizons, used a look-alike site (dinnerwithtrump.org), aggressive Facebook advertising and email solicitations to gather donations from more than 21,000 people, raising roughly $1.1 million and amassing an email list of over 410,000 entrants. In its first three weeks the PAC spent over $108,000 on Facebook ads and raised about $350,000, with the single largest payment — $133,000 — going to CartSoft LLC, a payment-processing company Hawes founded and owns. Federal filings describe that spending as “media” or “media purchasing.” Hawes maintains the PAC has no ties to Trump and denies operating a scam, saying contributors can request refunds (he reported processing about 110). But many donors POLITICO contacted — including people who gave $265, $1,015 and more — said they believed they were contributing to Trump’s campaign and only discovered via fine print that the PAC was unrelated. The PAC’s contest did not promise an intimate dinner; small type disclosed winners would receive two tickets to a sponsor-selected fundraising event with Trump and other attendees. After POLITICO’s reporting, the Trump campaign sent Hawes a cease-and-desist accusing him of defrauding donors. Hawes has since registered other politically themed domains copying Trump branding, including crookedhillary2016.org and imwithtrump.org, and his operation appears designed to monetize supporters and build lists for future solicitations. Observers, including an FEC commissioner, warned that current enforcement offers limited consumer protection against deceptive internet-era political fundraising. Hawes declined to specify his personal take from the operation; his PAC ended June with about $88,197 on hand.

Allen Christopher Ivanov, 19, has been charged in a Mukilteo, Washington mass shooting that killed three 19-year-olds and injured a fourth after investigators say he brought a recently purchased AR-15 to a house party where his ex-girlfriend was present. Court documents and an affidavit of probable cause released by Mukilteo police describe Ivanov’s actions and statements during and after the Aug. 1 attack. He told detectives he bought the rifle about a week earlier for target practice, planned to take safety classes, and viewed the weapon “as a symbol of power.” After spotting his ex, Anna Bui, at the party with another man, Ivanov returned to his car, read the rifle’s owner manual, loaded a magazine he had bought earlier that day, and then approached the home around midnight.

According to the affidavit, a male partygoer discovered Ivanov hiding near a living-room window and said, “No, no, no.” Ivanov said he was scared, flipped the rifle’s selector, and opened fire; he later told police that once he pulled the trigger it was too late to stop and his adrenaline took over. He entered the house, fatally shot Bui, and killed Jake Long and Jordan Ebner. He also shot an 18-year-old, Will Kramer, who was hospitalized in serious condition. Ivanov fired from a balcony and the roof until his magazine was empty, then returned to his car and drove off; he was arrested about 90 minutes later on Interstate 5.

Detectives report prior text messages Ivanov sent to a Kentucky contact about committing a mass shooting and social-media posts suggesting he had contemplated violence. At a brief video court appearance he was ordered held without bail and barred from contacting victims’ families. Prosecutors plan to file formal charges, which may include aggravated first-degree murder and could allow capital penalties. Friends and classmates described shock and grief; some recalled Ivanov’s temper and desire for control, while his parents’ attorneys say the family is devastated.

On Feb. 4, 2004, Mark Zuckerberg launched thefacebook.com from his Harvard dorm, offering a clean, college-only social network that quickly stood out among contemporaries like Friendster, MySpace and Orkut. Its focus on student profiles, searchable class and house directories, and a spam-free layout helped it spread rapidly; within a year it hit a million users even before photos were added. Zuckerberg promised eventual monetization; Facebook turned a profit in 2009 and by its tenth year reported roughly $1.5 billion in profit on nearly $8 billion revenue. Over time the site layered transformative features—News Feed, Like buttons—and less memorable experiments that Facebook’s own anniversary timeline omits. To mark its tenth birthday, Facebook launched several features including “A Look Back,” a personalized video of a user’s top posts and photos, and debuted a new iPhone app, Paper. The Look Back project required large-scale engineering work—media storage and the Moonshot team optimized servers so video rendering fell from 17 minutes to one—producing retrospective montages for hundreds of millions of users. Zuckerberg framed the milestone as a chance to reflect and reiterated Facebook’s mission to connect people while serving its global community.

Kathryn Bigelow’s Detroit dramatizes the July 1967 Algiers Motel siege—an episode of white police brutality during the larger Detroit riots that left the city under martial law. The film centers on the night when three Black youths were killed and several motel guests tortured as Detroit police and National Guard troops, responding to reports of a sniper, descended on the seedy motor hotel. Bigelow and screenwriter Mark Boal reconstruct the escalating violence as a chain of bad decisions, racist intent and chaotic fury, staging much of the movie as cinéma vérité: handheld camerawork, documentary footage, sparse scoring and a relentlessly harrowing centerpiece that spares little relief.

Characters include rising singer Larry Reed (Algee Smith), his friend Fred (Jacob Latimore), security guard Melvin Dismukes (John Boyega), Vietnam vet Greene (Anthony Mackie), and two white visitors who by chance are at the motel. The main antagonist is the trigger-happy patrolman Philip Krauss, embodied by Will Poulter, whose casual cruelty and the command structure that tolerates it drive the night’s atrocities. Bigelow portrays some officers and guards as appalled witnesses, but the system’s failure is emphasized when reprimands don’t amount to accountability and suspected perpetrators return to duty. The film concludes by noting that the Algiers events were never fully explained and that the subsequent prosecutions faltered when key confessions were ruled inadmissible.

Critics praise Detroit’s visceral power and moral urgency: it’s an unflinching indictment of systemic racism and police violence that resonates half a century later. But reviewers also fault Boal’s script for spreading itself over many characters without deepening individual backstories, making the film more situational than personal. Bigelow’s immersion-first approach delivers a maddeningly imperfect yet honorable work—brutal, sobering, and designed to leave audiences unsettled rather than comforted.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman’s 2013 visit to Pyongyang — where he famously sang “Happy Birthday” to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and played in a friendly basketball game — highlighted the opacity surrounding the young ruler. Kim’s birthday is observed on January 8, but the exact year of his birth remains unclear; South Korean and other analysts list 1982, 1983 or 1984 as possibilities. North Korean state media do not officially confirm his age, and personal details such as the birth of his daughter were only publicly revealed by outsiders like Rodman and former associates. Unlike the grand, state-orchestrated commemorations for his grandfather Kim Il Sung (Day of the Sun) and his father Kim Jong Il (Day of the Shining Star), Kim Jong Un’s birthday has been comparatively low-key during his first years in power, with modest distributions of sweets and basic items rather than major public spectacles. Analysts suggest this may be deliberate — to cultivate humility or avoid drawing scrutiny to his youth and relative inexperience. Since assuming power in 2011, Kim has consolidated authority, overseen nuclear and military developments, and carried out political purges, most notably the 2013 execution of his uncle Jang Song Thaek. Despite limited travel and few foreign meetings, Kim’s profile grew internationally amid incidents like the Sony cyberattack tied to the film The Interview. China publicly sent birthday congratulations in 2015, wishing Kim success in advancing socialism.

A large randomized trial (ACOSOG Z0011) assessed whether complete axillary lymph node dissection (ALND) benefits women with clinical T1–T2 invasive breast cancer who had 1–2 sentinel lymph node (SLN) metastases. Among 891 patients treated with lumpectomy, whole-breast irradiation, and adjuvant systemic therapy, participants were randomized to ALND (median 17 nodes removed) or SLN dissection (median 2 nodes). After median 6.3 years, 5-year overall survival was 91.8% with ALND and 92.5% with SLND alone; disease-free survival was similar. ALND caused substantially more morbidity (infections, seromas, paresthesias, lymphedema). The trial found no survival or recurrence benefit from ALND for this patient group, supporting omission of ALND to avoid harm when contemporary multimodality therapy is used.

Concern is growing for nine-year-old Maëlys De Araujo, who disappeared in the early hours of Sunday while attending a family wedding in Pont-de-Beauvoisin, Isère, southeastern France. She was last seen in a children's room at about 03:00 local time. Guests initially searched the hall and grounds for about an hour after the DJ announced she was missing, then notified police. Maëlys attended the event with her parents, older sister and other relatives from nearby Jura.
