A large-scale search involving around 100 personnel — police, firefighters, volunteer rescuers, divers, cavers, dog handlers and a helicopter — has combed dense vegetation, sewers, the wedding hall, the river Guiers (dived twice) and the surrounding area but has so far found no trace. Sniffer dogs reportedly lost the child’s scent at the venue car park, and three dogs failed to pick up the trail beyond that point, prompting investigators to consider that she may have left the site in a vehicle. Investigators have opened a kidnapping inquiry while cautioning against premature conclusions; prosecutors say both accidental and criminal scenarios remain under review.

Authorities have interviewed roughly 140–180 wedding guests and are also questioning about 70 people who attended two nearby social events that night. They are checking criminal records of attendees, reviewing photos and videos from the party, and have searched the wedding hall’s caretaker’s house and car. Maëlys is described as 130 cm tall, weighing 28 kg, with tanned skin, brown eyes and chestnut hair, last seen in a white sleeveless dress. Police have appealed for witnesses and any information to help locate her.

Alyssa Milano and Minnie Driver publicly rebuked Matt Damon after his ABC News interview asserting that sexual misconduct exists on a “spectrum” and cautioning against a “culture of outrage.” Damon acknowledged the #MeToo moment as necessary and empowering but argued distinctions matter — placing rape and child molestation at the criminal end requiring prison, while calling other misconduct “shameful and gross” and suggesting some cases might be better addressed through investigation, rehabilitation or dialogue. He praised Louis C.K.’s statement acknowledging wrongdoing as a sign “we can work with that,” and speculated that social-media-driven consequences might incentivize denial rather than accountability. Damon also discussed Harvey Weinstein, saying he knew Weinstein’s womanizing reputation but hadn’t seen criminal acts, and predicted confidentiality-driven settlements would decline as public scrutiny rises.

Milano responded on Twitter, condemning Damon’s framing that segregates behaviors and stressing that “the micro makes the macro”: chronic, normalized harassment creates the system that enables the worst abuses. She called the outrage righteous and labeled sexual misconduct and violence a “systemic disease,” using #MeToo. Driver called Damon “tone deaf” and “part of the problem,” arguing men cannot be the arbiters of what abuse feels like and warning against creating hierarchies of suffering. She rejected attempts to minimize or compartmentalize abuses such as exposure or harassment versus assault, insisting “it’s all fucking wrong” and urging men to listen and support rather than judge. Both women framed the debate as about systemic misogyny and the need to center survivors’ experiences rather than let powerful men define or soften culpability.

Lemhi County authorities have named DeOrr Kunz Jr.’s parents, Jessica Mitchell and DeOrr Kunz Sr., as suspects in the toddler’s disappearance after determining the couple have been inconsistent and “less than truthful” during the investigation. DeOrr, who turned three on Dec. 30, went missing from a family camping trip near Leadore on July 10, 2015. Despite extensive searches, no trace of the boy has been found.

Sheriff Lynn Bowerman said investigators grew increasingly concerned after multiple interviews and follow-ups with the FBI and behavior analysts in January revealed changing and conflicting accounts. When confronted, the parents reportedly declined to provide clarifying information. Bowerman said he believes the parents “know where he is” and whether he is alive, and called them the top persons of interest, though neither has been arrested and no warrants have been issued. He emphasized caution: prosecutors and federal partners are involved and he will not charge the couple prematurely for fear of jeopardizing the possibility of finding DeOrr.

Private investigators hired by the family earlier said abduction or an animal attack seemed unlikely. The sheriff asked the public to share any observations about interactions between the parents and DeOrr. Bowerman also addressed fundraising concerns after the family raised about $15,000 for private investigators; he cautioned donors given the parents’ suspect status. Family members, including DeOrr’s aunt, maintain the parents’ innocence and urge the public not to judge until facts are known. The investigation remains active and officials continue to seek information to locate DeOrr and resolve the case.

Randall Margraves, father of three daughters who testified that Larry Nassar sexually assaulted them, lunged at the disgraced former team doctor during an Eaton County, Mich., sentencing hearing after two daughters delivered victim impact statements. Margraves asked Judge Janice Cunningham for a short private meeting with Nassar — first five minutes, then one minute — which she refused. Visibly enraged after hearing details he said he had not known and seeing Nassar’s reactions in court, Margraves charged toward Nassar shortly before 10 a.m. He was stopped by Nassar’s attorney and restrained by multiple deputies, handcuffed by MSU Detective Andrea Munford, and led from the courtroom. Margraves shouted he wanted “one minute” with the doctor and later apologized, saying he lost control but regained it in a holding cell. Judge Cunningham found him in direct contempt but declined to impose jail time or a fine, explaining she could not punish him given the extraordinary emotional circumstances and acknowledging a parent’s understandable rage while warning against vigilantism. Assistant Attorney General Angela Povilaitis urged others not to copy Margraves’ behavior, saying violence would only empower Nassar. Margraves held a news conference expressing remorse, describing his daughters’ pain, lamenting his trust in institutions that enabled Nassar, and hoping Nassar faces divine punishment. The attempted attack drew notable courtroom security response and renewed focus on the wide scope of Nassar’s abuse; more than 250 victims have come forward, and Nassar already faces lengthy prison terms from prior state and federal sentences.

Serena Williams returned to training in Palm Beach Gardens after months off for injury and a pulmonary embolism, sharing a photo of herself serving in a hot-pink bodysuit on Twitter. Still on blood thinners and avoiding long flights, she’s been cleared for light cardio but has no set timetable; Wimbledon or the U.S. Open are likeliest comeback targets. Kim Clijsters suffered severe ankle ligament damage at a wedding and faces four to six weeks out. Meanwhile, Ryan Sweeting won his first ATP title in Houston, and teens Christina McHale and Melanie Oudin will represent the U.S. in Fed Cup play.

A massive Mega Millions jackpot—estimated at $636 million—drew fevered ticket buying ahead of Tuesday night’s drawing, producing at least two confirmed winning tickets matching numbers 8, 20, 14, 17, 39 and Megaball 7. The headline prize was updated from $586 million the prior day; if a single winner opts for the lump-sum cash option, that payout would be roughly $341.2 million. If no one wins, the pot could climb toward $950 million for Friday’s drawing. Strong last-minute sales historically drive big jackpots: game officials said as much as 70% of tickets are bought on drawing day, and recent demand covered an estimated 65–75% of the 259 million possible number combinations. The frenzy pushed the jackpot close to the U.S. record $656 million Mega Millions prize from March 2012.

Winners face important practical and legal choices. First, sign and photograph the ticket, then store it securely—safe deposit boxes or a home safe are recommended. Consult a trusted attorney and an experienced certified financial planner (and limit who you tell) to decide between the lump-sum or annuity and to arrange tax, estate and trust planning. Check whether your state allows anonymity; only a few do. Consider hiring PR help and security, take time off or travel to avoid immediate publicity, and know claim deadlines. Finally, check lesser-prize tickets too—large amounts often go unclaimed each year.

The Internet Archive is running crawls to preserve web pages as they are created and the pages they reference, aiming to save the versions that existed when an article was written so broken links can be replaced with archived copies. This effort, part of a “No More 404” initiative, seeks to reduce link rot by keeping contemporaneous snapshots accessible.

Separately, pop star Kesha, 28, has publicly described a personal transformation away from her earlier glitter-drenched party-girl image. In a candid Vogue interview she revealed she entered rehab in January for an eating disorder after spiraling under public scrutiny and praise for extreme thinness. Kesha said she associated nearly fainting from hunger with positive feedback, though internally she was unhappy. Since treatment she’s focused on health and self-acceptance, making a daily effort to be kind to herself and embrace her body. She doesn’t regret her past flamboyant stage persona—recalling odd rituals like using beer as adhesive before rolling in glitter—but says she no longer does practices that harmed her skin. Glitter isn’t gone entirely from her aesthetic.

Kesha is also involved in a high-profile legal battle with producer Dr. Luke, whom she accuses of sexual, physical, verbal and emotional abuse; he denies the allegations and has countersued for defamation. A New York judge recently denied her request to record outside their contract, prompting public outcry and support from many celebrities. Artists including Jack Antonoff and Zedd offered to produce music for her, and Taylor Swift donated $250,000 to assist Kesha during the dispute.

As the special election for Anthony Weiner’s former House seat nears, POLITICO obtained a sealed 1986 interim child-custody ruling that portrays Democratic candidate David Weprin negatively. Justice Bruce Wright described Weprin as “heedless” of his young son’s welfare, “extremely temperamental,” and acting in ways that “shock the conscience,” citing incidents such as leaving the child with a doorman and allegedly locking himself and the toddler in a cold bathroom. The contentious divorce was labeled “warlike,” and Wright denied Weprin expanded custody. A later 1989 ruling by Judge Burton Sherman, however, found Weprin’s ex-wife prone to “feign and exaggerate” and ultimately granted Weprin full custody; the parents later shared custody. The release of the old file—possibly obtained at the courthouse—became campaign fodder. Weprin’s campaign blasted the disclosure as dirty politics by Republican Bob Turner allies. The race itself is unexpectedly close in Democratic-leaning New York’s 9th District, influenced by local demographics, Weprin’s campaign missteps, and President Obama’s weak approval. Turner has run aggressive ads, including a controversial mailer about the Ground Zero mosque, and national Democrats have poured nearly $500,000 into TV ads to try to hold the seat.

Texting while driving is widely illegal and dangerous, but recent court decisions have begun probing whether people who send texts to drivers can be held liable when those drivers crash. A Pennsylvania wrongful-death suit arising from a fatal collision alleges the driver was distracted reading and replying to texts; the judge allowed the estate to include two remote texters as defendants, rejecting the notion that only drivers can bear responsibility simply because statutes target drivers. The ruling follows a 2013 New Jersey appellate decision that likewise recognized third-party texting liability in principle but affirmed dismissal in that case because the remote sender lacked evidence she knew the recipient was driving or would read the message while driving.

Both courts set a demanding standard for liability: a sender may be civilly liable only if they knew—or had “special reason to know” from their relationship or prior experience—that the recipient was driving and was likely to view the message immediately, creating a foreseeable risk of harm. Liability theories discussed include aiding-and-abetting under Restatement § 876 and direct negligence for actively distracting a driver. Courts stress that mere sending of a message, without knowledge the recipient will read it while operating a vehicle, is insufficient to impose duty, because overly broad liability would be unfair and impractical.

These rulings are part of broader legal attention to distracted driving—parallel developments include lawsuits against apps (e.g., Snapchat over a speed-measuring feature) and proposed “textalyzer” legislation to let police check phones after crashes. Scholars say these decisions could mark a cultural and legal shift toward treating distracted driving more like other stigmatized, harmful behaviors (such as drunk driving), potentially deterring risky texting. Still, plaintiffs face high evidentiary burdens to show a sender knew the recipient would read a message while driving; many cases thus will fail unless specific facts demonstrate the sender’s knowledge or active encouragement.

West Africa is facing the deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, with more than 650–670 deaths reported and infections continuing to rise across Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea. Governments have stepped up emergency measures: Liberia closed schools, ordered markets near borders shut, sent most civil servants home for 30 days, declared quarantines in some areas and deployed security forces to enforce restrictions and accompany aid workers. Fear, denial and mistrust in affected communities have hampered response efforts—residents have barricaded towns, hidden sick relatives, and in one case set fire to part of the health ministry—while some aid groups have withdrawn nonessential staff. International organizations including the Peace Corps, Samaritan’s Purse and Serving in Mission evacuated volunteers after staff infections; two American aid workers infected in Liberia were in serious condition. The virus, which spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids and has an incubation of 2–21 days, poses particular risk to healthcare workers and family caregivers. Authorities warn the outbreak could worsen and potentially reach new countries without rapid improvement; there is no vaccine or specific cure, only supportive care.

Johnson County authorities arrested Marvin E. “Buddy” Potter Jr., 60, and Jamie Lynn Curd, 38, on first-degree murder charges in the Jan. 31 slayings of 36-year-old Billy Clay Payne Jr. and 23-year-old Billie Jean Hayworth in Mountain City. The couple’s infant was found unharmed in the mother’s arms and is now with family. Sheriff Mike Reece called the motive “senseless and stupid,” saying Potter was angry about internet and phone communications between the victims and his daughter, who had complained harassment after being deleted as a Facebook friend. Investigators from the sheriff’s office and the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation interviewed 150–170 people; Potter and Curd remained prime suspects and were questioned and polygraphed, after which Curd cooperated. The victims, who lived with Payne’s father who last saw them before leaving for work, were found with gunshot wounds; Payne also had his throat cut. Potter and Curd were arraigned; bond matters are pending.

Arizona’s Republican-controlled Legislature passed SB 1062, a contentious measure permitting businesses, churches or individuals to use asserted religious beliefs as a defense against discrimination claims, sending it to Governor Jan Brewer. The House approved the bill 33-27 after the Senate’s party-line 17-13 vote. Supporters, including the Center for Arizona Policy and bill sponsor Sen. Steve Yarbrough, framed it as a First Amendment protection against “activist” courts and an effort to let people live and work according to their faith. They cited cases where vendors refused services for same-sex ceremonies and were sued, arguing the law simply clarifies existing protections.

Opponents — Democrats, civil liberties groups, the ACLU of Arizona, business organizations and LGBT advocates — warned the bill legalizes discrimination against gay and lesbian people and could be invoked broadly to deny goods or services to many protected classes. They said it risks economic fallout and boycotts similar to reactions after SB1070, with the Greater Phoenix Economic Council urging Governor Brewer to veto. Critics argued the measure would send an exclusionary message nationwide and could undermine local non-discrimination ordinances. Brewer, who vetoed a similar bill last year, has been noncommittal; supporters hope a revised version will earn her signature, while detractors continue to lobby against it, warning of legal and reputational consequences for Arizona.

Camp Cloverleaf is a year‑round traditional 4-H camp on Lake Francis in Lake Placid, Highlands County, Florida, offering a relaxed atmosphere with modern conveniences. Its private grounds and waterfront permit fishing, canoeing, kayaking and swimming; facilities include climate‑controlled cabins for up to 150 overnight guests, conference rooms for 15–125, a dining hall, an air‑conditioned auditorium and a campfire circle seating 150. Additional amenities include an outdoor pavilion with a large barbecue grill, a lighted recreational field, audiovisual equipment, wireless internet and recreational gear by request. The camp hosts school field trips, church retreats, family reunions, business meetings, teacher in‑service training, civic and athletic groups, weddings and more, and runs environmental education programs using 4‑H curriculum or custom activities. Resident Director Steve Cooper and Assistant Director Bill Tillett manage reservations; contact info and the camp address are provided online, and summer Gator Adventures sessions serve youth ages 8–13.

On June 22, 2018, more than two dozen attendees at the Cloverleaf 4‑H camp fell ill: Highlands County officials reported 33 children and three adults experienced nausea, vomiting and headaches; some were transported to two local hospitals. The Health Department is investigating; no cause was immediately determined.

Greece confirmed it would not make a €1.6 billion loan repayment to the International Monetary Fund due June 30, underscoring the severity of its financial crisis. Government ministers said they lacked the funds unless a deal with creditors unlocked €7.2 billion in frozen bailout aid; talks collapsed over the weekend and capital controls and a six-day bank shutdown followed when the European Central Bank halted expansion of emergency funding. IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde warned Greece would be in default from July 1 if the payment was missed; the IMF characterized a missed payment as being “in arrears.” A default could push Greece closer to leaving the euro if the ECB cut off emergency liquidity for Greek banks, though analysts think a default need not immediately force an exit and the ECB was expected to keep providing lifelines at least through the week. The crisis set the stage for a July 5 referendum on creditor-imposed bailout terms, with eurozone leaders urging a “yes” vote and warning that a “no” could be interpreted as rejecting engagement and pointing toward an exit from the euro. Reporting by Lefteris Papadimas; writing by Deepa Babington.

ISIS released a new propaganda video threatening attacks in France, Italy, the United States and elsewhere, naming landmarks and hinting at plots against major Western cities. The footage features suspected ISIS fighters threatening to blow up the White House, strike Paris again, and even speak of a “conquest of Rome.” The Vatican’s St. Peter’s Square was recently showcased on the cover of the group’s online magazine. In response, Italy deployed roughly 1,000 army personnel to bolster security around Rome and the Vatican; the U.S. Embassy in Rome warned Americans to remain vigilant, highlighting St. Peter’s Basilica, Milan’s Duomo and La Scala, as well as houses of worship, restaurants, theaters and hotels, as potential targets. A related ISIS video circulated Wednesday appeared to threaten New York City, showing Times Square, Herald Square and other Manhattan sites intercut with shots of homemade explosive devices and a bomber donning a suicide belt. New York and federal authorities said there is no specific or credible threat at this time but increased precautions: the NYPD deployed additional members of its anti-terrorism squad and maintained heightened vigilance in coordination with the FBI and Joint Terrorism Task Force. Mayor Bill de Blasio, Police Commissioner Bill Bratton and other officials urged New Yorkers to carry on with daily life, stressing resilience and caution. Analysts note that even if parts of the video recycle earlier footage, ISIS remains a potent, well-funded extremist group with continuing ambitions to strike Western targets.

Brett Morgen’s Kurt Cobain: Montage of Heck is a deeply intimate, family-approved documentary that peels back the myth to reveal the man behind Nirvana’s anguished songs. Premiering in theaters and on HBO, the 132-minute film draws from an unprecedented trove of Cobain’s personal archives—Super-8 home movies, journals, drawings, audio montages and unreleased music—made available by his family, widow Courtney Love and daughter Frances Bean Cobain. Morgen uses this material to construct a layered, often devastating portrait that begins at the beginning: a bright, blue-eyed toddler proud to announce “I’m Kurt Cobain,” whose early sweetness gradually yields to adolescent restlessness and depression.

Montage of Heck unfolds as a series of visual and aural montages—an editing tour de force—where home movies, animated sequences that bring Cobain’s scribbled journals to life, concert footage, and intimate domestic recordings collide with a dense soundtrack of Nirvana tracks, demos and taped narration. The film traces Cobain’s uneasy childhood amid his parents’ divorce, his search for belonging that led to forming a surrogate family in Nirvana, underground success with Bleach, and the explosion of global fame with Nevermind. Interviews are sparse but pointed—Courtney Love, Krist Novoselic, and early girlfriends provide context—while Frances Bean, who was too young to remember her father, says the documentary allowed her to “know” him in an unfiltered way and confirmed his love for her.

Morgen resists hagiography, showing Cobain’s contradictions and private failures alongside moments of tenderness. Some scenes are painfully intimate—most notably a home video suggesting intoxication while Love trims their toddler’s hair—that may unsettle fans used to idealized narratives. The film stops short of dramatizing Cobain’s 1994 suicide, noting it tersely, instead assembling evidence of insecurity, shame, and addiction that contributed to his decline. While it doesn’t fully answer ultimate questions about his death or fully chart his musical evolution, Montage of Heck succeeds as a revelatory, artful mosaic: it gives us Kurt Cobain, warts and all, through the artifacts he left behind. Critics hail it as both a virtuoso editing achievement and an emotionally wrenching, necessary reexamination of an icon. Grade: A.

A recent cross-sectional study in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics examined whether daily apple consumption is linked to better sexual function in women. Researchers surveyed 731 sexually active Italian women aged 18–43 with no history of sexual dysfunction, excluding those on certain medications or with depression. Participants reported apple intake and completed the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI), which assesses desire, arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction and pain. Women were split into Group A (one to two apples daily; n=343) and Group B (less than one apple per day; n=388). Group A scored significantly higher on total FSFI and specifically on the lubrication domain (p = 0.001 for both; Cohen’s d reported), and multivariate analysis identified daily apple intake as an independent predictor of better FSFI scores (p = 0.002). Authors propose mechanisms including antioxidants, polyphenols and phytoestrogens (e.g., phloridzin) in apples—particularly concentrated in peels—that might enhance genital blood flow and lubrication, similar to effects attributed to red wine and chocolate. The researchers caution that the study’s cross-sectional design and sample size limit causal conclusions and call for further research, including investigation of the role of apple peels.

Natasha Exelby, a casual ABC contributor and former Wake Up! co-host, was the focus of national attention after a viral weekend blooper in which she appeared startled on live TV when cameras returned to her unexpectedly. The clip, showing her playing with a pen and then gasping when she realised she was back on air, drew widespread public sympathy and support rather than condemnation. Colleagues and public figures — including journalists, Bill Shorten, Russell Crowe and Kevin Rudd — rallied for her, sharing their own on-air mishaps and calling for her reinstatement. A petition for her return gathered thousands of signatures.

Initial reports said Exelby had been removed from on-air duties; the Daily Telegraph claimed she’d been “banned.” ABC management was criticised in the wider debate because the broadcaster had previously faced scrutiny over more serious vetting failures, most notably allowing a controversial figure on a live panel without repercussions for staff. The ABC denied Exelby was sacked. Director of News Gaven Morris said no one would be punished for a blooper, stressed that live TV errors are human and that Exelby remains a casual contributor. He acknowledged she is not currently doing on-air shifts and that performance management processes are being followed. Sources told Guardian Australia she had been “read the riot act,” offered further training, and might return to on-air roles later. Exelby declined to comment beyond thanking supporters. The ABC reiterated that contributors’ shift details are confidential and that she has been booked on an as-needed basis.

Former New York Governor George Pataki suspended his Republican presidential campaign, acknowledging his bid never gained traction in a GOP moving sharply rightward. Pataki, 70, announced the decision in a two-minute televised message in early primary states obtained via equal-time rules after Donald Trump’s SNL appearance. He framed his goals as defeating radical Islam, shrinking Washington’s power, and uniting the country, but his moderate positions—support for abortion rights, past gun-control measures and a willingness to compromise with Democrats—clashed with primary voters’ appetite for insurgent outsiders. Out of office since 2006, Pataki struggled with low name recognition and minimal polling (around 0–1 percent), raised little money, and failed to reach main debate stages. His criticism of Trump drew harsh rebukes and did not improve his standing. With this exit, 12 Republican candidates remain.

The Senate Intelligence Committee voted 10-5 to advance Gina Haspel’s nomination as CIA director, effectively clearing the way for near-certain Senate confirmation and making her the first woman to lead the agency. Haspel, currently deputy director with a 30-year CIA career, won most Republican support and endorsements from several Democrats. She acknowledged in a letter that the CIA’s enhanced interrogation program—whose abuses included waterboarding at a Thai “black site”—was a mistake and said she would not restart such methods. Her record drew strong criticism from some Democrats and two Republicans, Senators Ron Wyden and Rand Paul, and Senator John McCain voiced concerns about her role in the interrogation program.

In June 2018, Seattle’s City Council voted 7-2 to repeal a recently passed “head tax” on large employers that was designed to raise about $47–48 million a year for affordable housing and homeless services. The tax would have charged roughly $275 per full-time employee at firms with at least $20 million in annual revenue, affecting about 585 employers; Amazon alone would have paid an estimated $12 million annually. The repeal followed an intense, noisy council meeting in which supporters and opponents clashed, with protesters chanting and displaying opposing banners.

The reversal came after major local employers—including Amazon, Starbucks and others—backed a “No Tax on Jobs” campaign and quickly raised substantial funds to qualify a referendum for the November ballot. Business opposition, combined with worries that the city lacked the resources to win a costly campaign, led several council members who had sponsored the law to change course. Proponents called the repeal a betrayal, arguing the levy was a necessary progressive revenue source to address a persistent homelessness crisis: local counts showed about 12,000 people experiencing homelessness in the region and hundreds of related deaths, despite the city already spending tens of millions annually.

City leaders and Mayor Jenny Durkan framed the decision as pragmatic, citing the political and financial realities and promising continued efforts, increased accountability, and alternative partnerships to address homelessness. The episode highlighted tensions over corporate influence, the responsibilities of booming employers in high-growth cities, and the challenges of funding social services amid rapid economic change. Mountain View, Calif., meanwhile, continued moving ahead with a similar proposal targeting Google, underscoring divergent local dynamics.

David Knowles, a 77-year-old retired nurse and long-time St John Ambulance volunteer, survived a sudden cardiac arrest while delivering a CPR lecture to his church first-aid group in Exeter. Shortly after beginning the session, he felt dizzy and weak, lay down, and realized his condition was serious. Although some trainees initially thought he was role-playing a demonstration, Knowles calmly instructed them that his symptoms were real and told them exactly what to do before he lost consciousness. One trainee, Karol Chew, a fellow parishioner and former nurse, called emergency services and began CPR when he stopped breathing. Paramedics arrived and transported him to the Royal Devon and Exeter Hospital, where he suffered a further cardiac arrest and a pulmonary embolism and was placed in a medically induced coma. Knowles later woke from the coma about two and a half weeks after the incident and spent a total of five weeks in hospital. Doctors feared potential brain damage and damage to his internal organs, and predicted a lengthy rehabilitation, but he has since made what clinicians describe as excellent progress. He is mentally alert, walking unaided, exercising, and recuperating at home in Newtown, Exeter. St John Ambulance noted that had Knowles collapsed while preparing the class alone, with no one present to begin resuscitation, his outcome would likely have been fatal. Knowles credits his trainees’ quick response and CPR for saving his life and continues to remain active with St John Ambulance as it marks its 140th anniversary.

Antony Britton, a West Yorkshire escapologist, narrowly survived a “Buried Alive” stunt when he lost consciousness while attempting to free himself from handcuffs beneath six feet of soil. The Linthwaite performer aimed to emulate—and surpass—Harry Houdini by escaping unaided from a standard grave at the Escape for Life festival in Slaithwaite Spa, a charity event raising funds for Leukaemia & Lymphoma Research (soon to be rebranded Bloodwise). About nine minutes into the attempt, soil compacted around him, collapsing an air pocket and crushing his chest; he became unable to inhale and passed out. Crew members, having monitored his likely position, used a mechanical digger and then hand-balled soil to retrieve him. He was pulled out unconscious, had his mouth and throat cleared, given oxygen in a waiting ambulance, and later regained consciousness. Britton sustained a cracked rib, scratches and bruises but described the rescue as well-executed and credited his team and digger operator for preventing a fatal outcome. He revealed he was only about two feet from the surface when rescued and said the experience felt like “seconds away from death.” Britton, who runs the not-for-profit and has performed other dangerous stunts, said he will recuperate for a few weeks and is unlikely to attempt the Buried Alive escape again. He noted the stunt’s risky history, referencing failed attempts by Houdini and Alan Alan and a fatality in 1992.

A 31-year-old Chinese tourist identified as Mr L. became inadvertently entangled in Germany’s asylum system for 12 days after seeking help for a theft while touring the country. Speaking only Mandarin, he first went to local authorities to report a stolen wallet but somehow signed what was interpreted as an asylum application. He was fingerprinted, medically examined and transferred about 220 miles to a refugee shelter in Dülmen, where staff provided food and pocket money like other asylum seekers. Staff noticed he behaved differently from typical refugees: he was well dressed, repeatedly asked for his passport and tried to explain his situation, but language barriers prevented understanding. Initial efforts using translation apps failed. Only after Red Cross workers turned to a nearby Chinese restaurant for help did they learn he was a tourist who wanted to continue to France and Italy, not seek refugee status. Christoph Schlütermann of the German Red Cross described the episode as the man having “set machinery in motion that he couldn’t get out of,” and lamented the complexity of Germany’s bureaucratic asylum procedures—especially amid a large recent influx of more than a million refugees from countries such as Syria, Iraq and Afghanistan. Authorities say only a small number of Chinese seek asylum in Germany. A regional official noted the man had signed papers at a processing camp with a Mandarin interpreter present, suggesting some awareness of the steps taken; however an amended report clarifies there is no police record of a robbery in Heidelberg and asylum cannot be applied for at Heidelberg town hall. The tourist was eventually released and resumed his European trip, reportedly amused rather than upset.

Eli Rosenbaum has spent his career as the Justice Department’s most prominent Nazi hunter, dedicating decades to tracking down and removing from the United States former Nazi perpetrators who quietly settled here after World War II. Hired as an intern in 1979 soon after the Office of Special Investigations was created, Rosenbaum rose to direct Human Rights Enforcement Strategy and Policy and has helped pursue 137 cases, winning 107 denaturalizations or deportations. His work spans famed prosecutions tied to Sobibor and other camps and the less-known, painstaking investigations of auxiliaries and guards whose roles supported mass murder.

Rosenbaum describes the work as a race against time: suspects are elderly, documentation is scarce, witnesses are dwindling, and relevant records were often behind Cold War barriers. Investigators sift through tens of thousands of names, fragmentary archival traces, and sometimes Soviet-era files that U.S. courts and agencies initially distrusted. The cases are “ultimate cold cases,” requiring historians, lawyers and researchers to stitch together evidence—like a report of a rifle butt break mentioning an operation that killed 4,000 at Trawniki—to link individuals to specific atrocities. The U.S. legal remedy, however, is limited: denaturalization and deportation rather than criminal trials for the original wartime crimes, which are left to other countries.

Rosenbaum’s motivation is personal and moral. Raised in a Jewish home where the Holocaust was seldom discussed, a television reenactment of the Auschwitz trial shocked him as a child. He finds interviews with survivors both heartbreaking and compelling, and interrogations of accused perpetrators “surreal.” Though the work has exacted personal tolls—long hours and emotional strain—he returns again and again, convinced pursuing every living perpetrator is the least owed to victims.

The article profiles Jakiw Palij, a frail nonagenarian living in Queens, identified as a Trawniki guard and stripped of U.S. citizenship yet effectively un-deported because no country will accept him. His case illustrates both the moral urgency and the practical limits of Rosenbaum’s mission: a complex, imperfect pursuit of justice across decades and borders.

David Welch, 54, left his Manhattan, Kansas home on Sept. 2 without telling anyone and drove away in his maroon Pontiac Montana. His family reported him missing within days, and law enforcement was notified, but no leads surfaced for weeks. Nearly seven weeks later, on Oct. 18, a passerby on a desolate stretch of Interstate 70 in Utah—about 850–900 miles from his home—discovered Welch’s overturned van in a deep ravine. Tire tracks showed the vehicle went straight off the road; investigators suspect he may have fallen asleep at the wheel and rolled down the embankment. Welch was found dead inside the mangled vehicle; authorities believe he survived in the ravine for an unknown number of days or weeks and used that time to write private love notes to his wife of 32 years and their four sons. The contents of the notes were given to the family. His death leaves unanswered questions about why he had driven so far from home and how long he endured before dying.

A hijacked beer delivery truck ploughed down Drottninggatan, Stockholm’s busy pedestrian street, and crashed into the Åhléns department store on Friday, killing four people and wounding about 15. Police detained a 39-year-old man from Uzbekistan, previously flagged in intelligence as a marginal figure, on suspicion of terrorism; investigators said they were confident they had the right person but have not ruled out other accomplices. Authorities discovered a suspicious “technical device” in the truck’s cab that could be a bomb or incendiary item; forensic and bomb-disposal teams were examining it. Ten victims remained hospitalized, including a child and two in intensive care. The attack echoed recent vehicle-ramming assaults in Europe, and Sweden tightened border controls and increased police presence amid fears of copycat acts. National leaders showed defiance and unity: Prime Minister Stefan Löfven declared a national day of mourning and vowed to preserve Sweden’s open, democratic society, urging citizens to carry on; the king and Crown Princess also paid respects. Public reaction mixed shock and resolve, with memorial flowers near the damaged storefront. Police said the suspect had appeared in past intelligence but was not recently under active investigation; international security services are cooperating. An official minute’s silence was planned Monday to honor the dead as Sweden grappled with the rare, deadly attack.

Former Massachusetts Republican Scott Brown, who lost his Senate seat in 2012 and a 2014 comeback bid in New Hampshire, has spent recent months working as a volunteer bike mechanic at Gus’ Bike Shop in North Hampton, N.H., while continuing an active triathlon and cycling lifestyle. Brown described how he shifted from basketball to duathlons after a serious eye injury, winning his age group in his first race and developing a passion for cycling. He recounted racing in the Spanish Pyrenees, touring local culture after events, thrilling descents, heat-exhaustion races requiring IV fluids, and a severe crash that damaged his knee but didn’t end his athleticism. Brown trains around two to two-and-a-half hours daily, often splitting triathlon disciplines, and enjoys tandem rides with his wife—including a rainy 111-mile Pan-Mass Challenge. He owns four bikes, including two tandems, and has learned full bike assembly while helping younger mechanics. Politically, President Trump nominated Brown as U.S. ambassador to New Zealand in April 2017; Brown previously backed Trump and was a Fox News contributor. Separately, Fox host Andrea Tantaros filed a lawsuit alleging Brown made sexually inappropriate comments and touched her in 2015; Brown denies the claims. Brown remains a visible regional fixture who emphasizes camaraderie in the triathlon community and encourages newcomers to just start riding.

Jennifer Love Hewitt and actor Brian Hallisay secretly married and welcomed their first child, a daughter named Autumn James Hallisay, on November 26. The couple, who met on Lifetime’s The Client List and announced Hewitt’s pregnancy in June, kept the baby’s sex a surprise and held a gender-neutral shower. Hewitt has spoken about embracing motherhood after her mother’s recent passing.

The document outlines India's severe child protection crisis, highlighting widespread deprivation and endemic child sexual abuse. India has 430 million children facing malnutrition, high under-five mortality, low birth registration, and millions out of school. Surveys and studies reveal alarming abuse rates: a 2007 government study (12,500 children) found 53% had experienced sexual abuse and over 20% severe abuse, though methodology targeted vulnerable groups so figures aren’t nationally representative. Other studies (RAHI, Save the Children/Tulir) report high prevalence, often perpetrated by known individuals (uncles, neighbors), with boys frequently affected and many victims never reporting incidents. Official statistics and UN/UNICEF warnings underscore the scale—one in three rape victims is a child, and thousands of children are raped annually. Media exposure and public outrage have pressured legal reforms, including India’s 2012 law criminalizing child sexual abuse, and institutions like the NCPCR (established 2007) now monitor child-rights laws and investigations. Nevertheless, systemic failures persist: weak social services, inadequate policing, and horrific cases (Nithari murders, Falak’s death) demonstrate ongoing gaps in prevention, protection, and support for vulnerable children.

In April 2008 Congressman Dennis Kucinich bought a sandwich wrap at the Longworth House Office Building cafeteria and bit down on an unpitted olive that allegedly cracked a tooth. This month he sued Restaurant Associates and three other companies, seeking $150,000 for negligence and breach of implied warranty, claiming “serious and permanent dental and oral injuries” requiring multiple surgeries. The complaint offers few details about costs or delayed timing. A spokesman called it a private legal matter.

A centuries-old embalmed head found in 1919 at the Royal Basilica of St. Denis—long rumored to be King Henry IV’s—has become the focus of a contentious forensic dispute. In 2010, Philippe Charlier and colleagues used CT imaging and digital facial reconstruction to identify the mummified head, with soft tissues intact, as that of Henry IV, citing facial features and injuries consistent with historical accounts. However, a new genetic study by researchers at the University of Leuven compared Y‑chromosome markers from the head with samples from three living Bourbon male-line descendants and found no match. The Belgian team also tested a blood-soaked handkerchief said to bear Louis XVI’s blood; that sample likewise failed to match Bourbon DNA. Critics argue the Y‑chromosome test is limited, contamination or degraded ancient DNA could skew results, and disputed paternity in royal lines might explain mismatches. Two coauthors of the original 2010 paper have asked for its retraction, saying the identification lacked sufficient rigor. Experts note facial reconstruction is better at exclusion than definitive ID, and multiple tissues or further genetic work would be needed to resolve whether the head truly belonged to Henry IV.

Will and Jaden Smith sat for a New York magazine Q&A to promote After Earth, a postapocalyptic sci-fi film Will conceived watching his son on The Karate Kid set. The movie’s father-son premise—an elite soldier forced to watch his injured son survive alone on a hostile, future Earth—mirrors Will’s anxiety about parenting amid fame: the pain of letting children make dangerous mistakes and hoping lessons stick. Throughout the interview Will frames life as pattern-seeking—“a student of patterns,” even “at heart…a physicist”—offering examples ranging from the sun’s reliability to Oscar trends. Jaden echoes a belief in an ultimate “theory of everything,” suggesting human mathematics haven’t yet evolved to grasp it, calling it “multidimensional mathematical.” Both reject simple religious labels, preferring to study world religions, and insist family creativity—not fame—is their priority.

They discuss family dynamics on set: Jaden views their film work as a collaboration, Willow (12) commands attention and chose to step back from stardom at school’s expense, and Jada Pinkett Smith is the vigilant, corrective presence. Will defends letting his children choose careers, recounts structuring their home as an “artist’s haven” with systems to capture ideas, and stresses teaching financial literacy after his own tax troubles. The interview also drew skeptical commentary: a critic lampoons Will and Jaden’s grandiose, sometimes vague pronouncements about patterns and theory, suggesting their fame insulates them from reality checks. The piece mixes earnest parental philosophy, family anecdotes, and moments that critics found perplexing or self-important.

On April 19, 2013, after a chaotic night in the Boston suburbs, authorities captured Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev, the surviving suspect in the Boston Marathon bombings, following a massive daylong manhunt that had shut down large parts of greater Boston. Earlier that day, a citywide “shelter in place” order had been issued as law enforcement searched for the fugitive, who had escaped a shootout in Watertown that left his older brother, Tamerlan Tsarnaev, dead. The two brothers—ethnically Chechen immigrants who had lived in the Boston area—are accused of planting low-tech bombs at the marathon finish line that killed four people and injured more than 170.

The standoff ended late Friday when police surrounded a boat behind a home in East Watertown, where Dzhokhar, believed wounded, was found hiding under a tarp. The arrest came after an intense, hours-long search that involved swat teams and federal investigators, house-to-house searches, and a temporary lockdown of Boston and nearby suburbs. Earlier, the brothers allegedly shot and killed MIT Police Officer Sean Collier as he sat in his cruiser, carjacked an SUV, forced the driver to withdraw cash, and went on a rampage that included throwing explosives at pursuing officers. In Watertown they engaged in a fierce gunbattle, during which Tamerlan was wounded—apparently by an explosive that detonated in his hand—and then dragged under a car and later died at a hospital. A transit police officer was also shot and subsequently treated and released.

Investigators in Washington and Boston began probing the brothers’ backgrounds, motives, and any potential outside assistance. The FBI confirmed it had interviewed Tamerlan in 2011 at the request of a foreign government but found nothing warranting further action. Both brothers had shown some interest in radical Islamic ideologies, according to social media and family reports, but officials said there was no evidence of additional conspirators. The investigation continued, and the city grappled with the immediate aftermath: the Boylston Street memorial was moved, the crime scene remained closed, and communities sought answers as authorities pursued any remaining leads.

North Korea regularly stages elections that mimic democratic processes but serve authoritarian ends. Voting is compulsory for citizens over 17, and turnout is reported as near-universal (commonly 99.7–99.98%), with state media attributing nonparticipation to being abroad or at sea. Ballots present a single, regime-approved candidate per district, chosen by the Democratic Front for the Reunification of the Fatherland under the Workers’ Party. To “vote yes” citizens deposit an unmarked ballot; to register dissent they must cross out the sole candidate’s name in a special booth—an act made perilous by lack of secrecy and surveillance. As a result, abstention or a “no” vote is widely viewed as treasonous and can bring severe punishment, including political criticism, restrictions or worse.

Beyond validating predetermined outcomes—local assemblies and the Supreme People’s Assembly function largely as rubber stamps—elections operate as an administrative and security tool. They act as an unofficial census, organized by neighborhood units (inminban) and electoral registers, letting authorities detect absences, locate defectors, and enforce population control. Defectors report returning from China to avoid repercussions for missing election day. The process also provides opportunities for regime reshuffles; past votes have coincided with constitutional or personnel changes, purges and consolidations of power. Rituals on election day emphasize loyalty: public displays, rallies, portraits of Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il, and obligatory bows. While the DPRK maintains additional nominal parties within the Front, real authority rests with Kim Jong Un and the Presidium. Observers see these staged elections as a Soviet-style legacy that the regime maintains to project legitimacy, mobilize the populace, monitor dissent, and reinforce the cult of the Kim family rather than to permit genuine political choice.

Police in Bentonville, Arkansas, arrested 31-year-old James Andrew Bates on suspicion of first-degree murder in the November 22, 2015 death of 47-year-old Victor Parris Collins, according to a probable cause affidavit and local reporting. The Arkansas State Crime Lab ruled Collins’ death a homicide by strangulation with drowning as a contributing cause. Bates called 911 that morning saying he found Collins dead in the hot tub on his back patio. He had hosted Collins and two others the previous evening to watch a football game; one guest left before midnight and another returned home near 12:30 a.m., leaving Collins and Bates in the hot tub. Bates later told police he slept and claimed to have found Collins floating hours later.

When officers searched the property they found Collins floating face up in a hot tub with water tinted red and containing bodily fluids and blood. Injuries observed on Collins included a black eye, a cut eyelid, swollen and bruised lips, and bleeding from his mouth and nose. Blood spatter and diluted blood spots were found on hot tub cushions, the cover, and sides; investigators later determined the blood belonged to Collins. The patio and hot tub rim had been hosed down and a hose had been used despite freezing temperatures—evidence detectives deemed consistent with a struggle and an effort to wash away traces of the incident. Broken eyeglasses, Collins’ wedding ring, and a broken shot glass were recovered from the bottom of the spa.

Investigators documented injuries on Bates consistent with a physical altercation and noted phone records showing multiple cancelled calls overnight that Bates later claimed were accidental butt-dials—an explanation detectives disputed given the phone’s security and timing. Witness interviews indicated Collins was alive when one guest left, and that guest showed no signs of a struggle.

Importantly, investigators also obtained smart-home data. Utilities records showed unusually high water usage—about 140 gallons—between 1 and 3 a.m., far above typical usage and consistent with hosing down the patio. Detectives say they were able to pull data off an Amazon Echo speaker found in the home; Amazon declined to provide Echo-stored audio without a valid legal demand but did supply Bates’ account details and purchase records. The use of Echo data and IoT device logs in criminal probes raises privacy and reliability questions. Bates’ attorney argues home technology should not be used against clients, while others note such audio and device records could be strong evidence if accurate. Bates remains jailed without bond. Collins, a former Georgia law enforcement officer, is survived by his wife and five children; memorial services were held in Arkansas and Georgia.

A 64-year-old former airman, Jeffrey Michels, has been arrested and charged with desertion after vanishing from Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota 40 years ago. Michels failed to report for duty on July 6, 1977, and was located on October 12 living in Sanford, Florida, under the alias Jeffrey Lantz. Records indicate he used that name to obtain a Florida construction business license in 1998 for Atlantic Development Corporation. He lived there with a wife and children while maintaining the false identity. The Air Force Office of Special Investigations took him into custody; because there is no statute of limitations for military desertion, Michels will face a court-martial. Desertion carries severe theoretical penalties, from dishonorable discharge and multi-year imprisonment to death in wartime under extreme circumstances, though the military rarely imposes the harshest sentences—fewer than one percent of deserters received prison time during the Iraq War, per New York magazine. The case drew public attention after a July Facebook post to the “Veteran Doe” group identified a possible match; that post was later removed. Michels’s arrest coincides with heightened visibility of desertion cases: Army Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl recently pleaded guilty to desertion and misbehavior before the enemy for leaving his Afghanistan post in 2009 and subsequently being held captive by the Taliban until 2014. Military records on deserters are incomplete, but internal estimates place outstanding cases around 50,000.

Bald eagles are increasingly visible across eastern Massachusetts, delighting residents and signaling recovery of the species and regional waterways. Recent local sightings included two eagles along the Neponset River in Milton, one photographed by Tom Palmer of the Neponset River Watershed Association — his first-ever eagle sighting — and earlier reports of two eagles on the frozen Charles River near the Longfellow Bridge. Other observations have come from Spy Pond in Arlington, Jamaica Pond, Chestnut Hill Reservoir and areas near Milton, Waltham, Lynnfield and Framingham. Social media and community message boards have been buzzing with photos and reports.

State and conservation experts say the rise in sightings reflects a larger comeback that began after the species’ reintroduction at Quabbin Reservoir in 1982. By 2014 there were about 46 known eagle territories in Massachusetts; last year that number rose to 51 confirmed breeding pairs — the most since reintroduction — and officials expect more undocumented pairs. Winter counts are bolstered by birds migrating south from northern New England and Canada to find open water and food, concentrating eagles along shorelines and rivers.

The return of eagles illustrates improving water quality and habitat availability, plus reduced shooting and greater tolerance of human presence. At the same time, growing eagle numbers bring new threats: collisions with vehicles when eagles scavenge roadkill and lead poisoning from fragments in hunter-removed gut piles. Rehabilitation centers report more eagles admitted now than a decade ago, reflecting both population recovery and continuing conservation challenges. Observers and stewards express excitement at seeing the national symbol thriving in urban and suburban landscapes.

A decade-old women’s clinic in north Metro Atlanta is being forced to retire its name, Isis Women’s Health Care, after receiving dozens of death threats and hostile calls from people confusing the practice with the terrorist organization commonly called ISIS. Founded by Dr. Hughan Frederick ten years ago and named for the Egyptian goddess of motherhood, the clinic grew from a single employee in a small subleased space near North Fulton Hospital into a three-office practice employing nearly 30 people and affiliated with North Fulton Hospital and Emory Johns Creek Hospital. Over the years the Isis name became associated locally with “a better birth experience,” but recent international news coverage of the violent extremist group — labeled ISIS, ISIL, or the Islamic State by different outlets — triggered public misunderstanding and anger that made staff and patient safety a concern. Frederick describes the decision to change the name as painful: the clinic has invested a decade and thousands of dollars building its brand, and now must replace signage, pamphlets, websites and business cards. Rather than simply lament the loss, the practice plans to treat the rebranding as a positive opportunity and is inviting the community to help choose a new name. The new company name will be unveiled March 31 at the clinic’s Mansell Road office, marking a new chapter while the clinic remains open.

New research and reviews highlight two distinct alcohol-related health concerns: a heightened cancer risk when drinking and smoking, and myths about mixing alcoholic drinks and hangovers.

A meta-analysis published in The American Journal of Gastroenterology found that people who both smoke and drink face nearly double the risk of developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) compared with those who only smoke or only drink. This study is the first to quantitatively assess interaction between alcohol and tobacco for ESCC risk. Researchers conducted a systematic search of population-based case-control and cohort studies and calculated synergy factors to estimate multiplicative interactions. They confirmed that alcohol and tobacco are independent, exposure-dependent risk factors for ESCC, but their combined use markedly amplifies carcinogenic potency. Lead author Anoop Prabhu emphasized the need for physicians to target prevention efforts at individuals who use both substances. The National Cancer Institute estimated over 18,000 new U.S. esophageal cancer cases and more than 15,000 deaths in 2014.

Separately, longstanding folk wisdom about “never mix” (wine and beer) has little scientific support. Hangover severity is driven mainly by total alcohol consumed, drinking speed, dehydration, hormone changes, immune disruption, and toxic metabolites. Congeners—non-ethanol byproducts (e.g., acetaldehyde, fusel oils, tannins)—also worsen hangovers; darker spirits like bourbon have far higher congener levels than clear spirits such as vodka, and studies show higher hangover ratings after bourbon versus vodka at matched intoxication. No rigorous trials show that mixing different drinks per se increases hangovers; apparent effects likely stem from higher alcohol intake, choice of high-congener beverages, or impaired judgment while drinking. Tried hangover remedies lack solid evidence of efficacy.

Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, the Army psychiatrist accused of the 2009 Fort Hood shootings that killed 13 and wounded over 30, rested his case without calling witnesses and declined to make a closing statement as prosecutors urged the military jury to convict on premeditated murder charges that would permit seeking the death penalty. Prosecutors, led by Col. Steve Henricks, laid out detailed evidence they said showed Hasan planned the attack—buying a high-tech weapon, practicing, using laser sights, choosing Nov. 5 because his unit was processing for deployment, and targeting soldiers while leaving many civilians unhurt. Hasan has acted as his own lawyer but largely remained silent at trial, offering little courtroom defense beyond an early admission he was the shooter and media leaks asserting his jihadist motives. The judge barred certain motive-related evidence and defenses; the jury paused deliberations overnight after requesting testimony readbacks and a base map, to resume consideration of guilt and possible capital punishment.

Robert Farmer, 26, was sentenced to a maximum of 16 years after pleading guilty to 21 felony counts of animal cruelty for torturing and killing neighborhood cats in San Jose’s Cambrian Park. Arrested in October 2015, police found a dead, bloody cat in his car along with fur-covered gloves, a hunting knife and other evidence; DNA tests linked him to multiple victims. Authorities say he killed up to 16 cats though only a few bodies were recovered. Victims’ owners and dozens of activists packed the courtroom, grieving pets lost over months when outdoor cats vanished and owners kept animals indoors. While prosecutors sought to require Farmer to register as a sex offender—citing veterinary findings suggesting possible sexual abuse of one cat—the judge declined, saying the evidence and expert consensus did not meet the burden for that order. Farmer received credit for about 646 days already served; with credits and county confinement he could be released much sooner, possibly in roughly 4½ years, according to his attorney. Conditions of his sentence include probation, mandatory counseling, a 10-year ban on owning or caring for animals, and staying away from Cambrian Park.

Steven Aftergood of the Federation of American Scientists suggested that had Clinton’s emails been requested quietly under the Freedom of Information Act rather than becoming a public controversy, more of the correspondence might have been withheld as classified. He noted that State Department practice treats much of a secretary of state’s records as potentially containing “foreign government information,” and that as the department’s top classification authority Clinton had broad discretion over what was designated classified. Aftergood argued this makes it unlikely she would face charges for unauthorized retention, since she could determine classification status. Clinton aides countered that the secretary rarely needed to send classified material from a personal account: she was typically accompanied by aides with secure BlackBerrys and laptops and received classified material in hard copy or through secured channels while traveling. Her office said she communicated with foreign officials mainly in person, by correspondence and by phone, and their review found only one email with a foreign official (from the U.K.). The piece noted that while officials have been punished for storing classified information on personal devices, such cases are uncommon; for example, former CIA director John Deutch was pardoned after pleading to a misdemeanor for keeping classified material on personal computers. Meanwhile, the State Department intends to expedite release of roughly 900 pages of Benghazi-related emails from Clinton’s private account and will review the broader set of about 55,000 pages over several months. Spokeswoman Jen Psaki said the department will check for FOIA-exempt national security material and apply consistent redaction standards; Clinton insists she did not send classified material via her private email.

Charles Krauthammer argues that Americans prefer pragmatic philosophy over rigid ideology, citing Edmund Burke’s respect for tradition and context. He assesses Paul Ryan’s vice-presidential pick as potentially consequential for 2012, unlike most Veep choices since Lyndon Johnson’s boost to JFK. Democrats’ “Mediscare” attacks portray Ryan as threatening elderly benefits; Republicans should counter by clarifying Ryan’s plan spares those over 55 and by attacking Obama for cutting Medicare to fund Obamacare. If Republicans shift the debate to Obamacare, they force Democrats to defend policy weaknesses and expose Obama’s limited economic agenda—Krauthammer calls Obama’s proposals trivial amid stagnant growth and rising debt. Ryan’s selection also nationalizes the election, making it ideological and reviving the 2010 dynamic that favored conservatives. Beyond 2012, Ryan could become the defining Republican figure for a generation, much as Nixon, Bush and others rose from vice-presidential or running-mate prominence. As a movement conservative, Ryan embodies a disciplined, limited-government conservatism contrasting with “compassionate conservatism” and Obama’s liberalism. Whether Romney wins, Ryan’s campaign performance could secure him long-term leadership of the party.

Most Holy Redeemer, a Roman Catholic parish in San Francisco’s Castro district, finds itself at a tense crossroads after archdiocesan intervention halted drag-queen emcees from two charity events at the church’s Ellard Hall. The parish, with a congregation of about 450–550 — roughly 80 percent gay or lesbian — has long been a celebrated, welcoming spiritual home in a neighborhood where gay culture is everyday life. The archdiocese’s refusal, initially blamed on incoming Archbishop Salvatore Cordileone, stirred deep anxiety about anti-gay sentiment and raised fears that the parish could face more severe restrictions or even closure under new leadership. Church leaders and parishioners reacted with a mix of frustration and caution: business manager Mike Poma urged patience with the newly arrived pastor, Rev. Brian Costello, noting Costello’s inclusive public message and his unfamiliarity with Castro culture; Costello, however, sought guidance from the archdiocese and was rebuffed. The controversy intensified long-standing sensitivities after past events pushed boundaries — notably a performance involving a crucifix-shaped dildo — which even some gay parishioners found offensive. Despite the dispute, Most Holy Redeemer remains spiritually vibrant, known for powerful music and meaningful services that have drawn visitors and renewed faith for many. The larger context is the arrival of Cordileone, a figure prominent in the Proposition 8 fight and vocal about limiting Communion for those in sexual relationships he deems contrary to church teaching. His appointment signals Vatican and U.S. bishops’ renewed emphasis on traditional doctrine, prompting anxiety among gay Catholics who worry about being marginalized even as church officials insist on outreach and pastoral care. The parish and its supporters now await how the new archbishop’s leadership will shape the church’s role in a community where faith and gay identity are deeply intertwined.

Donald J. Trump used Twitter to weigh in on the killing of Nykea Aldridge, a cousin of N.B.A. star Dwyane Wade, who was shot and killed while walking with her baby in Chicago. In a morning tweet — in which he initially misspelled Wade’s name — Mr. Trump linked the tragic death to his broader campaign message, asserting that incidents like this validate his warnings about violence in minority communities and predicting that “African-Americans will VOTE TRUMP!” The first tweet offered no immediate condolences to the victim’s family; only later in the day did Mr. Trump post a separate message expressing sympathy for the family of the slain woman. The episode illustrates Mr. Trump’s ongoing strategy of courting African-American voters by highlighting poverty, violence and dysfunction in “inner cities,” portraying such conditions as proof that his candidacy addresses community safety and broader social breakdown. The tweets drew attention partly because of the personal tragedy involved and partly because of the political framing of the incident. The initial misspelling of Wade’s name and the delayed expression of condolence also drew notice. The exchange underscores how political figures increasingly use breaking personal tragedies on social media to reinforce policy narratives and electoral appeals, while prompting debate over tone, timing and the appropriateness of leveraging victims’ stories for political gain.

MSNBC’s Lawrence O’Donnell and guest Goldie Taylor suggested Mitt Romney’s appearance at the NAACP convention was strategic — possibly intended to provoke boos from African-American attendees to appeal to racist GOP voters. Taylor argued Romney wasn’t there to engage the black community substantively, noting he didn’t repudiate voter ID laws and that mere rhetoric won’t win black votes without policy commitments. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi echoed that the boos may have been calculated. Congressional Black Caucus chair Rep. Emanuel Cleaver criticized Romney’s opposition to Obamacare at the NAACP but praised him for showing up. Conservative commentator Rush Limbaugh reacted angrily, defending Romney’s business record and asserting Romney used the forum to broadcast his economic message to a wider audience, not to win the convention crowd. Limbaugh dismissed the booing as predictable, accused the left of mischaracterizing repeal of Obamacare, and argued Obama avoided the NAACP because of unmet expectations on black employment. Observers disagreed on whether Romney sought confrontation or genuine outreach, with debate focused on intent, policy substance, and political optics.

The film Blind, starring Alec Baldwin as a novelist who becomes blind after a car crash, has provoked criticism for casting an able-bodied actor in a high-profile disabled role. Disability advocates, led publicly by the Ruderman Family Foundation, condemned the choice as “crip-face,” likening it to the offensiveness once associated with white actors portraying Black characters. Jay Ruderman, the foundation’s president, argued that portraying disability as a costume should become universally unacceptable, just as the industry moved away from racially insensitive casting practices.

The Ruderman Family Foundation, which campaigns for greater representation of disabled people in media, pointed to data it released last year showing a stark disparity: people with disabilities make up nearly 20% of the U.S. population, yet about 95% of disabled characters on television are played by able-bodied actors. The group previously criticized casting decisions in films such as the 2016 drama Me Before You, where Sam Claflin played a banker left paralyzed after an accident. That film, and now Blind, are cited as examples of missed opportunities to hire disabled performers and to present more authentic portrayals.

Blind’s trailer debuted Wednesday. Demi Moore co-stars as a married socialite who, under a plea bargain, becomes caregiver to Baldwin’s character; the two begin an affair and Moore’s character must choose between her husband and the novelist. Directed by Michael Mailer, the film premiered at the Woodstock Film Festival on Oct. 13 and is slated for worldwide release on July 14 by Vertical Entertainment.

Mitch Daniels, Indiana’s Republican governor and a rumored presidential contender, challenged expectations at a conservative American Enterprise Institute speech by praising parts of the Obama administration’s education agenda, endorsing a federal role and national standards, and commending the administration’s handling of Osama bin Laden. Daniels presented himself as a pragmatic, wonkish alternative to the GOP’s more combative figures, emphasizing teacher accountability focused on student growth, support for vulnerable children, and expanded full-day kindergarten funded by increased state education spending. He softened typical conservative positions—acknowledging a place for collective bargaining, invoking “social justice,” and limiting private-school voucher eligibility to students with two semesters in public school—while deploying self-deprecating humor and folksy anecdotes to appeal to moderates. Yet his record reveals contradictions: after urging Republicans to de-emphasize social issues, he moved to sign a stringent anti-abortion bill cutting Medicaid funding to Planned Parenthood clinics, banning abortions after 20 weeks, and mandating potentially misleading counseling about fetal pain and risks. Critics argue Daniels’s mix of fiscal hawkishness, technocratic language, and selective social conservatism exposes him as a tactician who can charm elites while pursuing hardline policies that undermine the moderation he publicly touts.

Sacha Baron Cohen’s Showtime series Who Is America? continued its shock-satire run by ambushing former Alabama Chief Justice and Senate candidate Roy Moore. In a segment airing July 2018, Cohen, in character as Israeli anti-terrorism expert Col. Erran Morad, presented Moore with a fake “pedophile detector” wand that supposedly senses a hormone linked to pedophilia. The device repeatedly beeped when waved in front of Moore but not when waved in front of others. Moore, who faced multiple sexual-misconduct allegations during his 2017 Senate campaign, protested his innocence on camera, saying he’d been married 33 years and had never faced such accusations; he walked off the set, calling the exchange cutting the conversation and denouncing the stunt as disrespectful to Israel and religious conservatives.

Moore issued a longer statement after learning he’d been duped, saying he was invited to Washington to receive an award for supporting Israel, that expenses were paid and he received no personal remuneration, and that he had been misled. He characterized Cohen’s tactics as trickery and deception and warned Showtime that airing the segment could prompt legal action to defend his honor and character. Moore framed the ambush as an attack on religious conservatives and America’s values, invoking his past military service and readiness to “defend her again.”

The episode fits Who Is America?’s pattern: guests are lured into absurd scenarios where their reactions can reveal prejudices, gullibility, or indignation. Other figures targeted on the show include Sarah Palin, Dick Cheney, Bernie Sanders and several controversial individuals whose willingness to play along produced revealing — and sometimes alarming — moments that critics say expose moral blind spots and gullibility across the political spectrum.

The document lampoons the trend of taking and sharing funeral selfies on social media, highlighting the shock and discomfort many feel when people post photos from funerals with flippant captions and hashtags like “#funeral” or “#sadday.” It frames the behavior as part of a self-centered “circle of YOLO,” imagining even relatives snapping selfies at someone’s funeral. The piece references a Tumblr page collecting such images that has drawn media attention—including a light, scripted segment on Good Morning America—and mocks both the sensational coverage and the creator’s flippant responses. The author notes the Tumblr’s blue-template quirks and expresses mild annoyance at formatting, then points readers to the site’s press page and interviews for context. The creator says they probably won’t keep updating the Tumblr, treating it as a static statement unless paid to continue, and signs off with a sardonic choice: follow them on Twitter or take a funeral selfie and risk global ridicule. The tone is satirical and critical of social-media insensitivity.

Alexander “Sasha” Shulgin, who died at 88, was a pioneering chemist, psychonaut, and advocate for cognitive liberty. Celebrated for rescuing and popularizing MDMA (Ecstasy) in the 1970s, he synthesized and cataloged more than a hundred novel psychoactive compounds over decades working from a backyard laboratory in California. Shulgin meticulously tested many compounds on himself, his wife Ann, and trusted collaborators, producing influential books PIHKAL and TIHKAL that document syntheses, dosages, and subjective effects. Licensed by the DEA for a time to analyze controlled substances, he later lost that privilege after public exposure of his work; nevertheless his publications ensured many molecules persisted in circulation. He believed in legalizing drugs with sensible safeguards and promoted therapeutic research into psychedelics. Admired and controversial, Shulgin’s legacy includes vast chemical archives, enduring influence on psychotherapy, rave culture, and ongoing scientific inquiry into the chemistry of consciousness.

Iran has executed Vahid Mazloumin, nicknamed the "Sultan of Coins," and another man after convicting them of "spreading corruption on earth" for allegedly hoarding about two tonnes of gold coins to manipulate local prices. Arrested in July, Mazloumin was accused of operating a speculative network that stockpiled coins; the other executed man was said to be linked to the network and involved in coin sales. Both were hanged following quick trials handled by special courts established after Iran’s Supreme Leader approved expedited judicial measures in August to punish suspected financial crimes; some trials have been broadcast on state television. Amnesty International condemned the executions as "horrific," arguing that the death penalty is prohibited under international law for non-lethal offenses such as financial corruption and criticizing the fast-tracked proceedings as showing a disregard for due process. The cases come amid sharp economic distress: the rial has plunged roughly 70% against the US dollar since renewed US sanctions targeting Iran’s oil and finance sectors, driving demand for hard assets like gold coins and dollars. Authorities have arrested many small currency and gold dealers recently as Tehran struggles to stabilise markets and cope with a cost-of-living crisis that has fuelled public protests.

House and Senate negotiators unveiled a $1.1 trillion, 1,582‑page omnibus spending bill to fund federal discretionary programs for fiscal 2014, implementing the December bipartisan budget agreement and aiming to avert another shutdown. The package largely eases sequester cuts without restoring agency budgets to pre‑sequester levels, reflecting compromise between GOP spending restraint and Democratic priorities.

Key funding moves include $1.012 trillion for regular discretionary spending, $92 billion for overseas operations (including Afghanistan and Syrian refugee assistance), and $6.55 billion for domestic disaster relief. The bill fully restores Head Start to $8.6 billion — a roughly $1 billion increase over current funding — and raises National Institutes of Health funding to $29.9 billion (an increase over sequester levels but below last year’s pre‑sequester request). It also partially restores funds for medical research, job training, and creates new programs addressing sexual assault in the military. Federal civilian employees and military personnel would receive a 1 percent pay raise.

Republicans secured tighter funding for financial regulators (modest increases for the CFTC and SEC) and policy riders on issues from coal financing to TSA staffing: TSA screening staff capped at 46,000 with more support for private screeners; Homeland Security construction funding trimmed; restrictions on conferences, travel and awards were added. The omnibus contains dozens of controversial policy riders: bans on enforcing new incandescent bulb efficiency rules, continued prohibition on transferring Guantanamo detainees to the U.S., conditions on aid to Libya and Afghanistan, limits tied to Egypt, and continued bans on federal funding for most abortions. It also blocks implementation of certain Justice Department gun‑tracking programs and seeks detailed DHS ammunition reporting.

Leaders framed the bill as necessary compromise to keep the government open through Oct. 1 and restore budget stability. Chairmen Hal Rogers and Barbara Mikulski touted bipartisan achievement; the White House urged swift passage.
