Short‑term continuing resolution votes were planned to buy time for floor action this week, but conservative opposition and outside groups warned some Republicans might defect. Overall, the omnibus reduces spending relative to recent years while resolving many discrete policy and funding conflicts.

Japanese authorities upgraded the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear crisis from Level 5 to Level 7 on the International Nuclear and Radiological Event Scale, placing it alongside Chernobyl as a “major accident.” The decision followed re-evaluation of cumulative releases—principally iodine-131 and cesium-137—after the March 11 quake and tsunami disabled cooling systems and triggered explosions and fires. Regulators estimated total iodine-131 emissions at roughly 370,000–630,000 terabecquerels by averaging different measurements, and converted those figures to an equivalent of about 500,000 TBq—above the Level 7 threshold described as “several tens of thousands” of TBq. Officials emphasized Fukushima’s releases so far amount to about one-tenth of Chernobyl’s estimated 5.2 million TBq, noting critical differences: Chernobyl experienced an open graphite fire and an exploded reactor core, while Fukushima’s reactor pressure and containment vessels remained largely intact. Japanese authorities said current on-site releases are much smaller and that there have been no confirmed acute radiation deaths like those in Chernobyl’s immediate aftermath.

Nevertheless, the upgrade prompted expanded evacuations, adding several towns and hot spots with elevated soil and produce contamination to the exclusion zone. Greenpeace reported vegetables and a playground with radiation above government guidelines, urging school delays. Ongoing aftershocks and a recent battery fire have hampered stabilizing work; repeated quakes have forced temporary worker withdrawals and risk disrupting makeshift cooling systems. Officials stressed the rating reflects cumulative past releases, not a sudden current escalation, and urged calm while acknowledging the crisis could persist for months and cleanup take years. Public unease grew, fueling large anti-nuclear demonstrations and deepening concern about risks posed by Japan’s many reactors.

Keith Olbermann’s abrupt departure from MSNBC, announced suddenly on Friday night, appears to have been the end result of weeks of negotiations rather than an immediate firing. Multiple outlets report long-standing clashes between Olbermann and network management, predating Comcast’s takeover, and say both sides had been maneuvering toward an exit. TMZ and others claim money and control were key factors: Olbermann’s agent pushed for higher pay, NBC refused, and Comcast viewed him as a “loose cannon.” Reports say Olbermann negotiated an exit package worth well over $7 million that curtailed his television appearances for a short, defined period but allowed future online activity; negotiations reportedly lasted about seven weeks with Patty Glaser among the negotiators. Deadline and the New York Times emphasize Olbermann had expressed a desire to leave previously and even staff learned of his decision when he announced it on air; one exec worried Comcast would be blamed if he left immediately after the takeover. Amid the media coverage, speculation about Olbermann’s next moves surfaced: possibilities include contributing to Aaron Sorkin’s behind-the-scenes cable-news script, returning to sports writing (an MLB.com blog reference appeared briefly on his Twitter), or other online projects. Observers note he’s likely under a gag or noncompete clause limiting public commentary for a time; meanwhile his Twitter silence has only amplified interest in his future plans.

The document collects profiles and dispatches from TIME’s 2014 Person of the Year package, portraying a world shaken by epidemics, uprisings and geopolitical shifts through human stories and leadership portraits.

Central is the Ebola crisis: reporters and first-person accounts describe how the outbreak exploded in West Africa and tested global public-health systems. Nurses, doctors and local responders—MSF teams, Samaritan’s Purse, Liberian clinicians and contact tracers—risked their lives to staff improvised treatment centers, trace contacts and perform burials amid denial and scarce resources. Personal narratives (Kaci Hickox, Iris Martor, Dr. Kent Brantly, Nina Pham, Drs. Jerry Brown, Mosoka Fallah, Philip Ireland and others) convey fear, sacrifice, faith and the emotional toll of caregiving: long shifts in stifling PPE, patients dying alone, the stigma faced by survivors and volunteers, and chaotic quarantine policies that sometimes deterred helpers. TIME crowns these “Ebola fighters” as Person of the Year for buying the world time and exposing systemic weaknesses in outbreak response.

Interwoven are profiles of other consequential figures and movements of 2014. Jack Ma’s Alibaba story illustrates explosive Chinese entrepreneurial scale and the blend of diplomacy, strategy and culture behind its global expansion. Massoud Barzani’s leadership of Iraqi Kurdistan is examined amid the rise of ISIS, Kurds’ de facto autonomy, and the regional complexities of potential statehood. The U.S. Ferguson protests and the broader Black Lives Matter outcry are traced from local tragedy to national mobilization, showing how grassroots activists rewired public conversation about race and policing. Finally, Vladimir Putin’s annexation of Crimea and posture toward the West are contextualized as an imperial revival with heavy economic and diplomatic costs.

Taken together, the pieces portray 2014 as a year of frontline courage, societal awakenings and geopolitical realignments—moments when individuals and communities confronted failure, risk and possibility.

At a recent Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation staff meeting, Bill Gates recounted two encounters with Donald Trump in which the former president displayed an unusual focus on Gates’s daughter and raised basic questions about vaccines and infectious diseases. Gates said Trump first met his daughter Jennifer, now 22, at a Florida horse show and then returned minutes later by helicopter, an ostentatious move that underscored Trump’s attention. When Gates first spoke with Trump in New York in December 2016, he recalled being unsettled by how much Trump seemed to know about his daughter’s appearance, a detail that made Melinda Gates uncomfortable. The pair met again at the White House in March of the following year. In both meetings, Gates said, Trump asked whether vaccines were “a bad thing” — reflecting Trump’s consideration of a commission to investigate alleged vaccine harms after reportedly receiving advice from vaccine-skeptic voices such as Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Gates advised against such an inquiry, calling it “a dead end.” He also described Trump asking twice whether HIV and HPV were different, prompting Gates to explain the clear distinctions. MSNBC’s All In with Chris Hayes aired the footage and noted the Gates Foundation had not yet commented. Commentators seized on the exchange to criticize Trump’s priorities, suggesting he devoted more energy to commenting on women’s appearances than to learning policy. The item also noted NHS guidance summarizing the medical differences between HPV and HIV.

Australian TV presenter Karl Stefanovic conducted a year-long on-air experiment to highlight the gendered double standard in how celebrities’ clothing is judged. Frustrated by the constant scrutiny his female co-hosts, notably Lisa Wilkinson and Samantha Armytage, faced over their appearance, Stefanovic wore the same inexpensive navy suit virtually every day for a year—altering only shirts and ties—to see whether viewers would notice or comment. He reported that no one did, and used the lack of reaction as evidence that men’s wardrobes escape the intense public critique women endure. The stunt, kept secret from everyone on the Today show except Wilkinson and one colleague, was framed as a protest-prank and a demonstration of empathy for women who are routinely judged more harshly for what they wear, how they look, and even how they speak. 

The story generated substantial social media attention and international coverage from outlets including the BBC, the Irish Independent, the New York Daily News and Jezebel. Many praised Stefanovic for using a simple, visible act to translate an everyday injustice into a conversation about sexism; Australian feminist commentators and online communities like Destroy the Joint lauded the stunt as meaningful allyship. Some voices, however, cautioned that the stunt risked reducing feminism to a superficial media moment and pointed out that broader policy issues affecting women—such as economic and social reforms—remain urgent and under-discussed. The piece prompted broader reflection on how public attention is disproportionately focused on women’s appearances and how symbolic acts can spark debate about entrenched gender biases.

Sen. Cory Booker delivered an unprecedented, emotional denunciation of fellow Sen. Jeff Sessions during Sessions’ confirmation hearing for attorney general, arguing his conscience compelled him to speak despite Senate norms. Booker, flanked by civil rights leader Rep. John Lewis and Congressional Black Caucus Chair Rep. Cedric Richmond, said Sessions’ record shows hostility to civil-rights protections and would not advance justice for marginalized communities. Booker warned Sessions would not be a leader on racial bias in policing, voting rights, immigrant rights, LGBTQ protections or efforts to reduce mass incarceration, urging the Senate to consider those stakes for the Justice Department’s leadership.

Booker acknowledged past collegial work with Sessions—citing their joint effort to honor Selma marchers—but said personal rapport cannot excuse policy consequences. Lewis and Richmond echoed concerns, with Lewis stressing that an attorney general must “stand up, speak up and speak out” for those discriminated against. Sessions’ defenders, including former staffer William Smith and Republican senators, countered that accusations mischaracterize Sessions’ record and praised his integrity and law-and-order credentials. Committee Republicans largely defended Sessions, and observers expected his confirmation to succeed with the GOP Senate majority.

Booker’s vocal opposition drew wide media attention and partisan commentary, with critics suggesting the speech also raised his national profile as a potential 2020 presidential contender.

VICE confirmed reporter Simon Ostrovsky has been safely released after being held by militia in eastern Ukraine. Vice thanked supporters and said he is in good health but offered no further details to respect his family’s privacy. BBC’s acting Moscow bureau chief tweeted that Ostrovsky was free and heading to Donetsk.

Scientists have discovered an extensive hydrological system beneath the Antarctic ice sheets, where geothermal heat, pressure, ice movement, and the insulating ice allow liquid water to persist at the bed. In depressions these waters form hundreds of subglacial lakes, some isolated and others linked by channels and saturated sediments that ultimately drain into the Southern Ocean as ice becomes floating shelves. The interdisciplinary WISSARD (Whillans Ice Stream Subglacial Access Research Drilling) project is accessing Subglacial Lake Whillans and the nearby grounding zone at the Ross Sea margin to study ice dynamics, microbiology, biogeochemistry, and geophysics. Using radar, seismic surveys, GPS, and sterile drilling, the team plans to sample a water cavity about 750 meters below the ice and recover basal ice cores during a focused campaign. A Nature paper reports unequivocal evidence of active microbial life far beneath the West Antarctic Ice Sheet: single-celled Archaea that metabolize ammonium and methane were retrieved from a lake untouched by sunlight for millions of years. This confirms long-speculated sub-ice ecosystems and highlights contamination-safe techniques. Discovering life in such extreme, dark, isolated environments broadens the search for life elsewhere—inviting comparisons to methane lakes on Titan and subsurface oceans on Europa—and reinforces interest in missions to icy worlds in the coming decades.

An international research team, led by the University of Aberdeen as part of the EU-funded RuminOmics project, has found promising early evidence that selective breeding can substantially reduce methane emissions from ruminant livestock—cows, sheep, goats and deer. Methane, produced mainly by belching during digestion, wastes 2–10% of animals’ feed energy and is a potent greenhouse gas. In a preliminary study of 25 dairy cows, individual methane output proved consistent across different diets: low emitters remained low and high emitters remained high. That consistency suggests genetic factors influence emissions, enabling breeding for lower methane production while improving feed efficiency and profitability. The project will expand to about 1,400 animals to quantify genetic effects and develop breeding tools. Researchers caution dietary changes can trade off other environmental harms—like increased nitrogen losses—so their goal is to reduce both methane and nitrogen impacts while enhancing production efficiency, providing an integrated approach to shrink livestock’s climate footprint.

Janet Killough Barreto, wanted in Mississippi on charges including manslaughter of a child, multiple counts of child abuse and neglect, and witness tampering, was arrested in Portland after five years on the run. Authorities say she and her husband, Ramon Barreto, allegedly traveled to Guatemala in 2005–2006 to obtain children through a local adoption agency and then brought them to the U.S., where the children were reportedly malnourished, physically abused, forced to sleep on plywood-bottomed beds, and subjected to brutal punishments such as being duct-taped to beds, punched in the stomach, and having their heads submerged in water. In 2008, one adopted 2-year-old girl died as a result of the abuse. Janet Barreto was arrested in 2008, released on bond, later arrested in 2009 for witness tampering, released again, and then failed to appear for trial two months later. Added to the U.S. Marshals Service “15 Most Wanted” list in June 2013 with a reward up to $25,000, she reportedly used aliases and altered her appearance to evade capture. The couple, using the names Emily and Juan Chavez, were detained at Jantzen Beach Center after a tip placed them in Oregon; an 11-month-old boy found with them was taken by Child Protective Services. Both were booked in Multnomah County jail and face extradition to Mississippi.

Republican Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker was asked Sunday whether he is considering a 2016 presidential run and argued that governors make stronger presidents than members of Congress. Walker said governors bring a fresh, bottom-up approach and executive experience “from outside of Washington” that contrasts with what he described as an “old, tired, top-down approach” coming from D.C. When questioned about fellow Wisconsin Republican Rep. Paul Ryan—often mentioned as a potential candidate after his 2012 vice-presidential run—Walker praised Ryan, calling himself “the president of the Paul Ryan fan club,” but emphasized that beating Hillary Clinton would require a message framing her as emblematic of Washington establishment politics and promoting state-level, grassroots alternatives. Democrats quickly pushed back: Democratic National Committee spokesman Michael Czin welcomed Walker’s preference for governors as nominees but argued that the GOP’s gubernatorial wing is “every bit as broken and dysfunctional” as its congressional wing. Czin criticized Walker’s record, asserting Wisconsin lags the nation in job growth, and cited other GOP governors—Chris Christie’s tenure coinciding with credit downgrades and Rick Perry’s Texas having high poverty—as evidence against the party running on gubernatorial records. Separately, House Oversight Chairman Darrell Issa, fresh from a trip to Iraq, told ABC’s This Week that the Baghdad government remains “quite delusional” about the urgency of the fight with ISIL and appears focused on long-term training rather than immediate combat readiness. Issa said he would support authorization of the U.S. campaign against ISIL, argued that Iraqis—not Americans—should handle ground combat, and expressed confidence that Kurdish forces, supported by U.S. airpower and technical assistance, will fight effectively.

Floodwaters that inundated much of Queensland left Brisbane and numerous upstream towns reeling as residents waited for waters to recede and for the full scale of the destruction to emerge. The slow-motion inundation of Australia’s third-largest city crested just shy of 1974 record levels, sparing a worse catastrophe but still swamping about 30,000 homes and businesses, emptying the CBD and forcing thousands into evacuation centers. At least 25 people were confirmed dead, with 61 missing—most from flash-flooded Toowoomba and the Lockyer Valley—and officials warned more bodies were likely as search teams reached remote hamlets. Soldiers and police scoured debris-strewn floodplains where tractor-trailers were snapped, cars dangled from trees, and whole houses were reduced to slabs. Premier Anna Bligh called it possibly the nation’s worst natural disaster; early damage estimates and lost economic output, including impacts on coal exports and crops, pointed toward multi‑billion-dollar losses. Stories of rescue and sacrifice emerged: a mining magnate’s helicopter saved dozens stranded on roofs, while a boy who died helping family members was hailed a hero. Authorities cautioned it could be days before residents could safely return, and many homes may never be habitable again.

Taylor Swift addressed recent accusations that she’s “terribly calculated and mean,” comments initially tweeted and later deleted by Grizzly Bear’s Edward Droste. In a lengthy GQ cover interview by Chuck Klosterman, Swift — though the article does not name Droste — called such insinuations “highly offensive,” arguing that thoughtful planning and professional care for her work have been twisted into a critique of her personal life. She stressed that careers require hard work, not mere luck, and that being deliberate about choices shouldn’t be viewed as manipulative.

The interview covers Swift’s creative process, public image, friendships and fame. She explains that her confessional songwriting naturally intertwines art and life, which invites tabloid speculation; she accepts some of that trade-off, noting she never names subjects of her songs and sometimes guides interpretations to deflect unwanted assumptions. For example, she insists “Bad Blood” was about losing a friend rather than a romantic breakup, a response she acknowledges was strategic.

Swift also discusses her media habits: after a period in 2013 when she avoided the internet because coverage centered on her dating life, she now monitors public narrative to detect recurring themes that might shape perception. She defends her selective pop shift on 1989 against label pressure, emphasizing artistic autonomy and self-awareness as safeguards against the pitfalls she observed in other artists’ careers.

Personal anecdotes punctuate the piece — from the infamous 2009 Kanye West VMA incident (which she calls a pivotal, accidental moment) to her nightly meet-and-greets and how she avoids loneliness by connecting with fans and rewatching Friends. Throughout, Swift rejects the pejorative “calculating” label while acknowledging she plans carefully: to her, self-awareness and intentionality are protective and creative tools, not signs of malice.

Tronc Inc. has cut roughly half of the New York Daily News’s editorial staff as part of a push to make the century-old tabloid more digitally focused and to concentrate reporting on breaking news—especially crime, civil justice and public responsibility. The reductions follow Tronc’s purchase of the paper last fall for a reported $1, after years of declining print circulation and revenue. An internal memo told staff the company had restructured and redefined operations but “has not gone far enough,” prompting the steep layoffs and a reallocation of resources toward faster-turn coverage aimed at digital audiences.

Editor-in-chief Jim Rich and managing editor Kristen Lee were among those dismissed; Tronc named Robert York, editor of the Morning Call in Allentown, Pennsylvania (another Tronc property), to lead the paper. The move drew criticism and worry about the future of local watchdog journalism in the nation’s largest city: the Daily News had recently shared a Pulitzer with ProPublica for exposing misuse of eviction rules by the NYPD and has a history of investigative work on housing, first responders and municipal accountability. Reporters and veterans expressed concern that ambitious, time-intensive projects would be difficult to sustain with a much smaller staff and that newsroom morale had already been eroded by prior cuts and remote work trends.

Tronc—owner of titles including the Chicago Tribune and The Baltimore Sun—has faced controversy for its digital-first strategy and prior newsroom upheavals, which have spurred unionization drives and prompted observers to question whether the scaled-back Daily News can continue robust metro reporting.

U.N. humanitarian coordinator for Iraq Lise Grande warned that the offensive to retake Mosul from the Islamic State could become the largest, most complex humanitarian crisis of 2016. In a worst-case estimate, up to 1 million civilians could flee, with 700,000 needing shelter—far exceeding existing capacity. Current emergency sites hold about 60,000 people; plans to expand to 22 sites would raise capacity to roughly 400,000, still well short of needs. Grande highlighted the estimated 1.2–1.5 million civilians remaining in Mosul who could be trapped in fighting, noting IS has booby-trapped areas, placed snipers, and may use chemical weapons or human shields, or forcibly expel civilians. Reports surfaced of smugglers demanding exorbitant fees—up to $10,000—to extract people. Residents inside Mosul described living in fear: airstrikes, bombardment, and IS tactics such as hiding among civilians, IEDs, and executions of attempted escapees. Many stay home as fleeing is dangerous or impossible; leaflets urging civilians to remain sheltered were dropped by coalition aircraft. Locals expressed desire for IS’s removal but fear sectarian reprisals, particularly from Shia militias, and prefer Kurdish peshmerga over sectarian forces. Preparations continue, but humanitarian capacity and security concerns leave the population extremely vulnerable.

San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick sat during the national anthem for each of the team’s three preseason games to protest racial oppression and police brutality, and he plans to continue until he sees meaningful change. His action prompted a players-only meeting where Kaepernick and teammates discussed his motives. Kaepernick emphasized the protest is not an attack on the military; rather, it’s aimed at systemic injustices he has witnessed and experienced, citing police killings of black men and personal incidents of racial profiling. He said the decision was deliberate, informed by conversations with peers and mentors like Dr. Harry Edwards, and that he won’t recruit teammates to join him—each must choose individually given potential consequences.

Responses from players were mixed but largely respectful: many said they wouldn’t have protested that way because the anthem evokes sacrifice and soldiers, yet they acknowledged the importance of the issues Kaepernick raised and respected his right to act. Leaders including NaVorro Bowman, Torrey Smith, Daniel Kilgore, Bruce Miller and others stressed team unity, saying the squad will support Kaepernick as a teammate while keeping focus on winning. Kaepernick also criticized political figures and noted plans for future, concrete initiatives beyond symbolic protest, asserting he could accept being cut if necessary because he believes he is doing the right thing.

Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell publicly condemned white supremacist violence and rhetoric following the deadly Charlottesville rally, saying “there are no good neo-Nazis” and asserting that the nation must have “no tolerance for an ideology of racial hatred.” McConnell declared that those who espouse such views do not represent American ideals or freedoms and urged everyone to “stand against hate and violence, wherever it raises its evil head.” His remarks came after President Donald Trump drew widespread criticism for saying there were “very fine people on both sides” of the Charlottesville clashes and for faulting the “alt-left” along with white supremacists. Trump later explicitly condemned neo-Nazis and the KKK, but many Republican lawmakers criticized his initial response. The violence in Charlottesville culminated in the death of Heather Heyer, who was killed when a man allegedly aligned with far‑right views drove into a crowd of counterprotesters during a “Unite the Right” rally. McConnell, who has a record on civil rights issues and was privately troubled by the president’s handling of the episode, warned that white nationalist groups are planning a rally in Lexington, Kentucky over Confederate statue removals and said those groups’ messages “are not welcome in Kentucky” or anywhere in America.

West Africa is facing the deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, with the World Health Organization reporting about 1,201 confirmed, suspected and probable cases and UN figures showing 672 deaths across Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia. The epidemic began in Guinea in February and has since spread to Liberia and Sierra Leone; Nigeria reported its first imported case when a Liberian official, Patrick Sawyer, flew to Lagos and later died. High-profile medical casualties include Sierra Leone’s lead Ebola doctor Sheik Umar Khan and Liberian physician Samuel Brisbane; two American health workers in Liberia have also been infected.

Ebola transmits through direct contact with an infected person’s bodily fluids and has an incubation period up to 21 days. The current outbreak’s fatality rate is around 60 percent, though Ebola strains can kill between 50 and 90 percent of those infected. Symptoms often begin like flu—fever, muscle pain, vomiting and diarrhea—and can progress to internal and external bleeding in a portion of patients. There is no specific cure or licensed vaccine; treatment is supportive (fluids, fever control) while experimental therapies are under development.

Responses have escalated: airlines such as Asky and Arik Air have suspended flights to Liberia and Sierra Leone and screen passengers from Guinea; Liberia has closed most border crossings, deployed police at airports to enforce screening, quarantined affected communities, and suspended football and other large gatherings. In Nigeria, Lagos quarantined and closed a hospital after Sawyer’s death and is tracing dozens of contacts; WHO teams are assisting contact tracing in Nigeria and Togo. International agencies, including U.S. officials and WHO, warn the outbreak exceeds single-country capacities and urge coordinated, multisectoral responses and intensified public-awareness and hygiene measures to contain further spread.

Alan Dershowitz has joined Harvey Weinstein’s legal battle over access to The Weinstein Company’s emails, filing a declaration in Delaware Bankruptcy Court as a consultant to Weinstein’s attorney Benjamin Brafman. Weinstein seeks personal and business records held by the company, arguing the materials could exonerate him amid numerous sexual misconduct allegations and ongoing criminal investigations by authorities in New York, the UK and Los Angeles. Weinstein’s lawyers contend due process is at stake and that discovery could reveal whether any company property for sale belongs to Weinstein. Dershowitz, the former Harvard Law professor and high‑profile commentator and defense lawyer, asserts Brafman has a constitutional right to review potentially exculpatory emails under Brady and related jurisprudence. He argues the emails have no legitimate commercial value to the bankrupt company and their only noncommercial value is to Weinstein’s defense and negotiations with prosecutors and civil claimants. Dershowitz says he may prepare a supporting memorandum, signaling a willingness to play a larger role in the effort to obtain the disputed records as the company unravels amid scandal.

Mayim Bialik, known for her role on Blossom, wrote about sex and fertility on Kveller, a Jewish parenting site, blending modern fertility knowledge with traditional Jewish practice. Referencing the Torah’s instruction to count “seven days” and the later-added five, Bialik and the article’s author link this timing to ovulation around day 12 of the menstrual cycle—matching contemporary guidance in books like Taking Charge of Your Fertility (TCOYF). The piece argues that Jewish tradition long recognized natural fertility patterns and that mikveh immersion on the night of ovulation historically marked readiness to resume sexual relations. The mikveh is portrayed as a meditative, sanitary ritual that heightens anticipation after a period of sexual separation, which some say revitalizes marriages. The article counters the critique that Judaism reduces women to baby-makers by noting that Orthodox practice allows birth control when appropriate and that sexual satisfaction is explicitly protected in a woman’s ketubah (marriage contract). Bialik emphasizes that Judaism celebrates sex—encouraging intimacy especially on Shabbat—and that sexual relations are not solely for procreation; when not fertile (pregnancy, menopause), sex is freely encouraged. The overall message celebrates Jewish tradition’s practical focus on living well: loving, reproducing when ready, honoring rituals, and enjoying sex within marriage.

In a contentious Orlando debate, Republican presidential hopefuls Mitt Romney and Rick Perry dominated the stage, trading barbs over immigration, health care and Social Security while seven other candidates struggled for attention. The Fox News– and Google-sponsored event focused less on jobs and more on explosive cultural issues, with audience participation and YouTube-submitted questions shaping the discussion. Romney and Perry arrived intent on undermining the other’s conservative credibility. Romney assailed Perry’s Texas policy that grants in-state tuition to children of undocumented immigrants, calling it a “magnet” and arguing illegal entrants receive benefits unfairly; Perry defended the policy passionately, saying denying education to children brought here through no fault of their own showed a lack of heart and drawing boos and counterattacks from rivals. 

The two also clashed over past writings and positions: Romney accused Perry of previously endorsing letting states run their own Social Security-style pensions, while Perry accused Romney of editing his book to remove praise for Massachusetts’ health plan—labelled “Romneycare.” Both accused the other of flip-flopping on issues like gun rights and abortion. Perry, despite polling strength, gave several meandering answers—particularly on foreign policy—and struggled to land a decisive blow against Romney; Romney remained relatively unscathed, insisting he knows where he stands. 

Other candidates—Herman Cain, Ron Paul, Jon Huntsman, Newt Gingrich, Rick Santorum, Michele Bachmann and Gary Johnson—had limited impact, though Santorum and Bachmann also attacked Perry on immigration. Broad consensus targeted President Obama’s economic record, with calls to cut taxes and regulations. The debate underscored a battle over character and consistency as Romney and Perry jockeyed for front-runner status ahead of the primaries.

WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange, facing Swedish rape allegations and growing calls for prosecution or worse from international figures, warned he has distributed a 1.3-gigabyte encrypted “insurance” file that would be unlocked if he is arrested, tried, harmed or forced to surrender. The file reportedly contains unredacted US diplomatic and military documents—material withheld from prior publications to protect sources—and is protected by a strong 256-bit key. Assange denies the sexual-assault claims, calling them a smear possibly linked to political pressure; Swedish prosecutors say the investigation is independent. Bradley Manning, a jailed US Army analyst, is believed to have leaked the documents. US officials have considered Espionage Act options, while supporters and lawyers say WikiLeaks has faced cyberattacks, surveillance and efforts to criminalize journalistic activity.

At CPAC, the NRA hosted a session billed as "NRA university," aimed at equipping attendees with talking points to defend gun rights and counter what it called "gun control myths." Presenters argued that registering all guns and ammunition would not reduce gun violence but merely restrict law-abiding citizens’ Second Amendment rights. An NRA speaker minimized accidental gun deaths — claiming firearms account for only 0.5% of such fatalities — and quipped that people are more likely to be hurt by a hammer than an assault weapon. To lampoon mainstream notions of “assault weapons,” one male presenter juxtaposed a 20-second Arnold Schwarzenegger machine-gun clip from Predator with footage of several shooters firing single-round AR-15-style semi-automatics, prompting laughter. A female NRA speaker declared a high-stakes fight for Second Amendment rights and credited NRA success to the passion of roughly four million gun owners amid a U.S. population of about 313 million. She acknowledged the NRA’s vigorous efforts to oppose Obama but conceded difficulty winning young voters, urging NRA university graduates to change that trend. Separately at CPAC, Sarah Palin delivered an energetic speech packed with barbs at Obama, critiques of political consultants, calls for grassroots authenticity, and a litany of memorable one-liners aimed at energizing conservative activists for the next election.

The California State Auditor’s annual investigations report found multiple instances of improper governmental activities across state agencies from July 2017 to June 2018. Investigations substantiated misuse of state time, inaccurate attendance, wasteful spending, and misuse of property. Notable cases: two Fresno State facilities workers failed to account for over 5,100 hours, costing ~$111,000; a Kern Valley employee left early, costing ~$9,000; a DMV data operator slept on the job over ~2,200 hours (2014–2017), costing >$40,000 while supervisors failed to properly discipline her; a nursing director reassigned a friend LVN, wasting nearly $30,000; CDCR overpaid an analyst (~$3,000); CSU Dominguez Hills bought an unused $7,000 charger; a Cal Fire assistant chief built an unauthorized structure using on-duty staff. The auditor handled 1,481 cases and issued nonpublic reports addressing nepotism and other management misconduct.

Following a bruising week for his campaign, Donald Trump spent Saturday defending controversial remarks as he began a three-day push toward Wisconsin’s primary. Speaking at rallies in Racine and later in Eau Claire, Trump sought to blunt criticism over comments on NATO, nuclear weapons and particularly abortion, while also expressing regret for retweeting an unflattering photo juxtaposing rival Ted Cruz’s wife with his own wife, Melania. He called the retweet “a mistake” and said he would not do it again.

Trump framed the backlash as unfair media treatment, saying he was being held to a different standard than other candidates and insisting his words were taken out of context. He defended his “Face the Nation” comment — “The laws are set. And I think we have to leave it that way” — calling the exchange “perfect” and arguing the network edited his remarks, despite the full video showing otherwise. The abortion controversy was broader and deeper: earlier in the week he had suggested women should be punished for obtaining abortions if the procedure were ever banned, a position his campaign quickly reversed, and his subsequent statements have alarmed conservatives and opponents alike.

The flap has intensified worries within the Republican Party about Trump’s weak standing with women voters and whether that would make him unelectable against Democratic front-runner Hillary Clinton. Trump’s response has been to emphasize free media coverage and to highlight family surrogates: he said Melania will campaign with him Monday and Ivanka will return in a week or so to help burnish his appeal to women.

Despite tense moments between supporters and protesters outside, Trump’s three events were otherwise peaceful. In interviews he reiterated he would “be myself” and suggested he plans no specific strategy to win over women beyond using Ivanka and arguing he respects women, while deflecting questions about past behavior and the broader political fallout.

At a January town hall in Council Bluffs, Iowa, New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie told an Omaha fifth-grader, Jacob Royal, that if elected president he would roll back the Obama-era school lunch rules and let parents decide what children eat. Royal, wearing a suit and GOP pin, complained that lunches have worsened since Michelle Obama promoted healthier meals, saying he misses square pizza and “crispitos” and dislikes “gluten-free stuff.” Christie responded that the first lady “has no business” dictating school menus and that using government to mandate her preferences is inappropriate. He emphasized that parents, not the federal government or the first lady, should make those choices and said he “doesn’t care” what students eat at school, even while acknowledging he supports healthier eating in general. The exchange came against the backdrop of the Healthy, Hunger-Free Kids Act and 2012 nutrition standards that increased fruits and vegetables and limited sugar, salt and fat; reviews of those policies have been mixed, with some improved nutrition data and other studies showing students discard produce. Christie noted past support for the first lady’s goals but framed the initiative as overreach. Royal said he was satisfied and hopeful his favorite lunches might return under Christie. Some attendees agreed that government should not mandate school nutrition.

Federal agencies are reexamining marijuana as scientific evidence accumulates, and new research highlights significant mental health risks from potent cannabis varieties. The FDA is conducting an eight-factor scientific and medical analysis—at the DEA’s request—to reassess marijuana’s Schedule I classification (highest abuse potential, no accepted medical use). The review, which informs HHS recommendations and DEA scheduling proposals, may take unspecified time. Rescheduling would not legalize marijuana federally but could ease research barriers, banking reluctance, and tax restrictions for state-legal businesses. Historically, limited U.S. research has hampered reassessment: only one federally authorized cultivation site (University of Mississippi, overseen by NIDA) supplies studies. NIDA has funded roughly 30 marijuana benefit studies and approved over 500 related research grants, with funding rising from $6 million (2003) to over $30 million (2012). Critics argue federal agencies have focused on harms and slowed rescheduling.

Separately, a major six-year study from King’s College London, to be published in Lancet Psychiatry, links high-potency “skunk-like” cannabis to a threefold increased risk of psychosis compared with non-users and associates potent-cannabis use with 24% of new psychosis cases examined. Daily users faced up to a fivefold risk. The study of about 780 adults found milder forms like hash—richer in CBD, which may counteract THC’s psychosis effects—were not linked to increased risk. Researchers call for clear public messaging, clinician screening about cannabis type and frequency, and prevention efforts, arguing eliminating high-potency use could prevent many psychosis cases. Public Health England and the Home Office echoed concerns; advocates note regulation could permit safer product choices. Meanwhile, the FDA maintains it has not approved marijuana for any medical indication despite interest in conditions ranging from neuropathic pain to seizure disorders.

Sales of Geiger counters and potassium iodide (KI) supplements jumped across the U.S. after Japan’s quake-and-tsunami–damaged reactors raised public fears of radiation reaching North America. Retailers quickly sold out as consumers placed mass orders; suppliers and pharmacies reported back-orders and overwhelmed hotlines. Experts and government agencies, including the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, said the risk to the United States is negligible and any radiation arriving would be undetectable and pose no health threat. KI protects only the thyroid from radioactive iodine and must be taken shortly before or after exposure; it does not shield other organs or types of radiation. Officials urged restraint, though some public demand persists and renewed debate over household KI stockpiles near U.S. plants has resurfaced.

Roger Stone, a longtime friend and former adviser to President Donald Trump, warned in a TMZ interview that if Congress moves to impeach Trump, the country could descend into a violent, even civil war–level conflict. Speaking at an airport baggage claim, Stone argued impeachment proponents are mostly people who didn’t vote for Trump and should “get over it,” boasting that Trump’s campaign spent far less than the opposition yet prevailed. He issued a stark warning: “Try to impeach him. Just try it. You will have a spasm of violence — an insurrection — in this country like you have never seen before… Both sides are heavily armed.” Stone, who served in the Nixon White House, said this is not 1974 and predicted that any politician voting for impeachment would be “endangering their own life.” He framed his comments as a prediction, not advocacy of violence. The remarks come as a small group of House Democrats has introduced impeachment articles over issues including Trump’s firing of FBI Director James Comey and his response to violence at a white supremacist rally. Democratic leadership, including Nancy Pelosi, favors an independent commission to investigate Russia’s election interference and Trump’s connections instead of immediate impeachment.

The Miami Caliente’s inaugural Lingerie Football League season mixed high-level athleticism with harsh physical cost and promotional controversy. Quarterback Anonka Dixon, a gifted 33-year-old with exceptional arm strength and mobility, epitomized the league’s competitiveness — slipping tackles, evading sacks, and powering Miami into playoff contention despite playing in satin and lace uniforms. The games were brutal: collisions, concussions, torn ACLs and other injuries were common, and Miami lost multiple players to season-ending knee injuries. The league markets itself as male-targeted entertainment — “beautiful women and football” — prompting debate about exploitation versus empowerment; players call it both demeaning and liberating, likening it to burlesque or early roller derby. Off the field, management clashed with media and players: two top Miami stars were placed on probation for posing in shoulder pads during a photo shoot, and a reporter was banned from coverage after critical reporting. The season highlighted the tension between serious athleticism, sensational marketing, and strict, image-focused league control.

Netflix’s board adopted a shareholder rights plan—a “poison pill”—after activist investor Carl Icahn disclosed a 9.98% stake, aiming to block hostile attempts to gain control the board deems not in shareholders’ interest. The plan issues one right per common share, letting holders buy one one-thousandth of a preferred share at $350, exercisable if an investor acquires 10% (20% for certain institutional 13G holders) without board approval; it dilutes a hostile acquirer and includes provisions to double value if a triggering investor pursues a merger or asset sale. Icahn criticized the move as poor governance and discriminatory for its low 10% threshold and objected to lack of shareholder vote, while Netflix defended the action as reasonable to protect long-term shareholder value. The rights plan expires Nov. 2, 2015.

After years of requests and repeated refusals, Facebook is finally preparing to test a Dislike-style feature, CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced during a town-hall Q&A. But the company’s version won’t be a simple downvote or a tool for public judgment. Zuckerberg emphasized that Facebook has avoided a traditional Dislike button because it doesn’t want the platform to become a place where people upvote or downvote others’ posts — a dynamic that can encourage harassment and turn personal sharing into a popularity contest. Instead, the new feature is intended to let people express emotions beyond the default positivity of the Like button, particularly empathy in response to sad or difficult moments. 

Details are sparse, and Facebook suggests the functionality may not look like a literal “Dislike” button; it could be one of several alternative reactions users choose from, and users might have input on which reactions are available. The company is trying to design the feature so it becomes “a force for good” rather than a tool for negativity or targeted dislike, and Zuckerberg repeatedly framed the goal as enabling simple, one-click expressions that fit situations where a Like feels inappropriate. 

The change represents a notable shift from Facebook’s historically positive-facing features such as Moments and comes amid wider debate over how social platforms surface and quantify sentiment. A broadly implemented Dislike-like option could affect how individuals and brands post and how news spreads, since Facebook is a major traffic source for publishers. Facebook’s careful language and staged testing reflect sensitivity to these potential consequences and recent controversies on other platforms that have struggled with upvoting/downvoting dynamics. The company says testing is imminent, but specifics and rollout plans remain unclear.

For the first time in over a decade, the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) and Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) have opened a lottery for thousands of part-time “casual” longshore jobs at the Los Angeles–Long Beach ports, triggering a surge of applicants. Local postal shops sold out of the 4x6 postcards required to enter the raffle as hundreds of thousands — perhaps up to a million according to PMA estimates — rushed to apply. InterOptimis, the firm handling the drawing, will alternately pick from public-submitted cards and union-issued cards until they reach the target number; the union says 2,400 names will be drawn, though timelines mention 3,400. Winners become casuals, paid about $25 an hour initially with no benefits; over years of accumulated hours some may earn full-time union positions that include generous pay (full-time averages cited between $123,000 and $161,000) and lifelong benefits. The lottery renews intense hopes: applicants describe it as a rare pathway to stable, well-paid blue-collar work in an era of shrinking unionized opportunities. Longtime casuals worry the influx will reduce their chances of elevation and that employers favor part-timers; many casuals have endured years or even decades of intermittent work, commuting to the dispatch hall daily and cobbling together other jobs. Advocates note the ports’ automation and slow post-recession demand have limited hires, making these slots especially coveted amid a weak labor market for non-college workers.

Around 500 years after it vanished en route to India, a richly laden Portuguese vessel believed to be the Bom Jesus has been unearthed in Namibia’s Sperrgebiet, the restricted diamond zone along the Atlantic coast. The site was discovered accidentally in April 2008 when De Beers–operated Namdeb miners bulldozing sand struck a mass of metal, wood and pipes. Archaeologist Dieter Noli identified the find as a shipwreck; marine archaeologist Bruno Werz and others subsequently led excavations. The cargo and artifacts align closely with 16th-century records—most notably the Memorias das Armadas—and date the wreck to the 1525–1538 period, consistent with the Bom Jesus’s loss in 1533. 

The preservation is unusually good: large quantities of copper ingots aboard likely acted as a preservative, their toxic properties inhibiting organisms that normally consume buried wood and organic material. Strong storms and treacherous seas along the Namibian coast account for many shipwrecks there, but the Sperrgebiet’s century-long restricted status limited human disturbance and aided preservation. 

Excavators recovered some 5,438 artifacts including roughly 2,000 gold coins in mint condition, Portuguese silver coins, bronze cannons, muskets, navigational instruments, pewter and copper tableware, more than 50 elephant tusks, five anchors and tonnes of copper ingots. A coin-stuffed chest apparently remained intact under collapsed superstructure, explaining the exceptional state of the currency. Namdeb now guards the site and stores sensitive organic finds in damp conditions per 16th-century conservation practice. Talks have been held about exhibiting the wreck in a museum, but no formal plans have been confirmed. The discovery is hailed as a major maritime-archaeological find and may solve one of the Age of Exploration’s enduring mysteries.

Canada’s national police force, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP), has approved a policy allowing Muslim women officers to wear the hijab while on duty. Announced formally this week after being adopted in January, the change aims to reflect Canada’s diversity and encourage more Muslim women to consider careers with the Mounties. The RCMP developed and tested three hijab designs, choosing one that won’t interfere with duties; no officer has yet requested to wear it. The move follows earlier accommodation of religious dress — notably the 1990 decision allowing Sikh officers to wear turbans — and aligns the RCMP with other services in Toronto, Edmonton, parts of the U.S., the U.K., Sweden, Norway and Police Scotland, which have integrated headscarves into uniform policy. Ottawa framed the decision as a stand against islamophobia, contrasting it with recent French bans on garments like burkinis. Public Safety Minister Ralph Goodale’s office and the RCMP commissioner endorsed the policy as a step to boost representation in the force.

A new large-scale study led by UC Davis researcher Cuihua “Cindy” Shen directly challenges the stereotype that men are inherently better video game players than women. Using anonymous server records and account-registered gender from over 11,000 players across two massively multiplayer online role-playing games—more than 9,000 EverQuest II players in the U.S. and about 2,000 Chevaliers’ Romance III players in China—researchers measured how quickly men and women advanced levels, controlling for key confounds. Because raw levels reflect time invested, the team compared leveling speed rather than absolute level and excluded top-level characters who could not progress further. They also statistically accounted for playing time, character class choice (e.g., healers vs. damage dealers), and guild membership. Initial raw data showed women at lower levels, but that difference vanished when these factors were controlled: women advanced at least as fast as men, and in some models surpassed them. The study is notable for using real-world game logs across two games and cultures, unlike prior lab studies with brief tasks. Authors link findings to broader issues: persistent online harassment (e.g., Gamergate) and cultural stereotypes may discourage women from gaming and from pursuing STEM pathways where gaming experience can serve as an entrée. The research suggests perceived female inferiority in gaming stems from confounding behaviors—less overall playtime and different game roles—not innate skill. Shen and colleagues argue that debunking this myth, promoting female-supportive communities, and designing less hostile game environments could reduce the stereotype’s self-fulfilling effects and help broaden participation in gaming and related tech fields.

Kanye West and Kim Kardashian West attended opening night of The Cher Show on Broadway, where Jarrod Spector stars as Sonny Bono. Spector publicly called out Kanye after noticing him looking at his cellphone during the performance, tweeting, “Hey @kanyewest so cool that you’re here at @TheCherShow! If you look up from your cell phone you’ll see we’re doing a show up here. It’s opening night. Kind of a big deal for us. Thanks so much.” Kanye quickly apologized on Twitter, explaining that the dynamics of Cher and Sonny’s relationship moved him and Kim to hold hands and sing “I Got You Babe,” and asking pardon for his “lack of etiquette,” while praising the cast’s energy and the production as a “master piece.” Kim gushed about Cher as “seriously the most amazing beautiful person ever.” Reviews of the musical are mixed: critics note its affectionate recreation of Cher’s TV-era glitz and lifetime of hits, but say the script is clichéd and emotionally distant. Standout elements include Bob Mackie’s extravagant costumes, strong performances—especially Spector as Bono—and the three actresses who portray Cher at different stages, whose combined strengths help lift the uneven show.

Diane and Larry Moyer of a 70-acre farm near Columbus own multiple exotic animals, including five kangaroos, and recently drew attention when Diane brought an eight-month-old joey named Jimmy into a McDonald’s in Beaver Dam. A customer complained, prompting a Dodge County sheriff’s deputy to ask the Moyers to leave; they complied and were not ticketed. Diane, who says she is disabled and uses Jimmy as a support/therapy animal with a doctor’s approval, has routinely taken him to public places—restaurants, church, even a movie theater—and says patrons often ask to pet him. Local authorities say the couple is well known and have dealt with them before. The Moyers have kept kangaroos for years—Diane has owned seven over eight years and currently cares for Perry, Anna, Ruby, Charles and Jimmy—and also maintain sheep, goats, emu, deer, horses, poultry and more. Diane bought the kangaroos from a Missouri livestock market; females cost about $1,000 and males $2,000. Her farm is USDA-licensed and inspected for animal health; she also coordinates with the state DNR for deer. Kangaroo care is expensive—imported milk and special feed cost hundreds monthly—and the animals require secure enclosures. Diane says she rarely faces negative reactions and plans to continue caring for and possibly expanding her exotic animal collection.

Florence Henderson, best known as Carol Brady on the 1969 sitcom The Brady Bunch, has died at 82. She passed away at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles after suffering heart failure, surrounded by family and friends; she had been hospitalized only a day earlier, her manager Kayla Pressman said. Born Florence Agnes Henderson on Feb. 14, 1934, in Dale, Indiana, she was the youngest of ten children. After high school she studied at the American Academy of Dramatic Arts in New York and launched a career on Broadway in shows such as Wish You Were Here, Fanny, The Girl Who Came to Supper and South Pacific. She transitioned to television, guest-hosted The Tonight Show in 1962, and was a Today Girl on NBC’s Today in 1959–60. Henderson achieved international fame starring in every episode of all five seasons of The Brady Bunch and later reprised Carol Brady in numerous spin-offs, reunion projects and The Brady Bunch Movie. Her post‑Brady career included guest roles on series like The Love Boat, Murder, She Wrote, Ally McBeal and 30 Rock, reality TV appearances including Dancing with the Stars and The Surreal Life, and hosting duties on Retirement Living TV’s The Florence Henderson Show and TNN’s Country Kitchen. She married Ira Bernstein in 1956, with whom she had four children; they divorced in 1985. In 1987 she married Dr. John Kappas, who died in 2002. Henderson earned a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1996 and is survived by her four children and five grandchildren.

An Internet Archive initiative crawls and preserves web pages as they are created and the pages they reference, aiming to maintain access to the versions that existed when a page was written. By storing these contemporaneous copies, the Archive hopes sites will replace or supplement broken links with links to the archived versions so readers can see what the original authors intended. The broader goal is to eliminate broken links across the web by archiving supported "No More 404" sites.

Separately, police in Norwalk, Ohio, arrested 18-year-old Anthony Damante of Milan on drug trafficking charges after a marijuana delivery gone wrong. A woman who left a store to buy lottery tickets returned to find a sandwich bag labeled "Sour Kush" and smelling of marijuana on her front seat. Surveillance footage showed another woman exchanged money with Damante and went into the store while he left about 40 grams of marijuana in the wrong unlocked car. Court records did not indicate whether Damante has an attorney. Information came from the Sandusky Register.

Brazil’s lower house of Congress opened a heated, three-day debate over whether to impeach President Dilma Rousseff on charges of breaking budget laws by manipulating 2014 accounts to boost her re-election. The session was raucous: pro-impeachment lawmakers chanted “Dilma Out,” while pro-government supporters rallied nationwide amid fears of violent clashes. Police erected metal fences and planned cordons in Brasilia and Rio to separate opposing crowds expected in the tens of thousands. Rousseff denies wrongdoing, her allies argue prior presidents used similar accounting, and she is not directly implicated in the Petrobras kickback scandal, though opponents link the corruption probe to her party. The attorney general called the impeachment a “violent act,” and Rousseff sought a last-minute injunction from the Supreme Court to halt proceedings; a majority denied the request, leaving Sunday’s crucial vote intact. If 342 of 513 deputies approve, the case goes to the Senate; polls and recent party defections indicate two-thirds support impeachment, with analysts forecasting at least 350 votes in favor. If the Senate approves a trial, Rousseff would be suspended and Vice President Michel Temer would assume the presidency, facing the task of stabilizing an economy mired in recession and widespread political scandal. Public TV planned live coverage of the decisive roll call.

Retail site Yandy.com removed a “Brave Red Maiden” Halloween costume after widespread backlash over its sexualized take on The Handmaid’s Tale imagery. The outfit, inspired by Margaret Atwood’s dystopian novel and the Hulu series, was marketed as a bright red mini dress with a cape and high heels, a provocative departure from the story’s white bonnets and full red cloaks that symbolize the handmaids’ enforced fertility and oppression. BuzzFeed News highlighted the costume and the wave of critical responses on Twitter, where reactions ranged from bewilderment and disgust to dark humor and occasional praise for possible subversion.

Yandy issued a statement saying the costume had been intended to reference recent uses of the handmaid costume as a protest symbol and to celebrate women’s empowerment, but acknowledged that many people saw it as a symbol of women’s oppression. Citing the “sincere, heartfelt response” and numerous personal stories it received, the company decided to remove the item from its site. Critics on social media called the product tone-deaf and an example of commodifying suffering; some joked about the impracticality of mixing protest attire with nightlife, while a few argued the sexy reinterpretation might unintentionally subvert the original symbolism. The outlet ultimately pulled the costume, and shoppers still have access to other “sexy” costume options elsewhere. The incident underscores tensions around commercialization of political protest imagery.

NASA has renamed its ambitious Sun mission the Parker Solar Probe to honor Eugene Parker, the University of Chicago astrophysicist who predicted the solar wind in 1958. Parker, who turned 90 in June, was long doubted but later vindicated by observations; NASA’s decision marks the first time the agency has named a spacecraft after a living researcher. At the renaming event Parker received a model of the probe, a chip carrying his photographs and seminal paper, a plate bearing an inscription of his choosing, and NASA’s Distinguished Public Service Medal.

The Parker Solar Probe (formerly Solar Probe Plus) is a roughly car-sized spacecraft built by Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory. Scheduled for launch in summer 2018 on a Delta IV Heavy, the probe will spend about seven years making repeated close passes of the Sun, using seven Venus gravity assists to shrink its orbit. Ultimately it will come within about 3.7–4 million miles (under 10 solar radii) of the solar surface—seven times closer than any previous spacecraft—where it will encounter extreme heat and radiation. Designed to survive temperatures up to roughly 1,370°C (about 2,500°F), the probe uses a 4.5-inch-thick carbon-composite heat shield and retractable solar arrays with active cooling so the instruments inside can remain near room temperature.

The mission’s chief scientific goals are to trace the flow of energy that heats the corona and accelerates the solar wind, determine the structure and dynamics of plasma and magnetic fields at the wind’s sources, and investigate mechanisms that accelerate and transport energetic particles. Instruments aboard will measure electric and magnetic fields, capture particles (electrons, protons, alpha particles), study turbulence, and image solar structures. Scientists expect the probe to observe where the solar wind transitions from subsonic to supersonic and to probe particle acceleration processes that produce dangerous high-energy events.

Beyond fundamental stellar physics, the mission aims to improve understanding and forecasting of space weather—coronal mass ejections and energetic particle events that can damage satellites, threaten astronauts, disrupt HF communications and GPS, and induce geomagnetically induced currents that can damage power grids. Costing roughly $1.5 billion and described by researchers as risky but essential, the Parker Solar Probe pushes engineering limits to achieve observations that could transform knowledge of our star and help protect technology and infrastructure on Earth.

The 1993 Jack in the Box E. coli outbreak, which sickened over 600 people and killed four children, prompted a nationwide shift in burger-cooking practices after it showed that cooking patties to the then-standard 140°F did not reliably kill E. coli O157:H7. Washington state had already raised its recommended minimum internal temperature to 155°F, but many restaurants hadn’t adopted the change. In the aftermath, chains revised protocols to prevent similar tragedies. Despite that, a resurgence of gourmet burger restaurants and gastropubs serving medium-rare, pink-centered burgers has revived concerns. Outbreaks continue: in 2014 Wolverine Packing Co. recalled 1.8 million pounds of ground beef tied to 12 E. coli illnesses; undercooked preparation at restaurants was suspected. The federal food code permits serving undercooked burgers if restaurants provide written menu warnings and servers verbally inform customers of risks, and some establishments go further by sourcing suppliers that test for E. coli. Food safety experts note, however, that testing is not foolproof and other pathogens like Salmonella and Campylobacter remain risks. The code specifies 155°F for 15 seconds (or 158°F instant) to kill pathogens; lower temperatures require longer hold times, which preclude a pink center. Experts caution that terms like “medium-rare” are imprecise and that true informed consumer choice depends on clear communication—something studies suggest is often lacking. Overall, raw or undercooked meat and raw milk remain hazardous despite culinary trends.

A planned Oxygen special, All My Babies’ Mamas, featuring Atlanta rapper Shawty Lo and the 11 children he fathered with ten women, has ignited national controversy. Critics — led by Sabrina Lamb, a children’s nonprofit CEO who launched a Change.org petition that garnered nearly 28,000 signatures — argue the show exploits children, normalizes unprotected sex and harmful stereotypes, and treats the mothers and offspring as spectacle. Lamb calls the term “babies’ mama” a slur, says the mothers “need therapy and condoms,” and warns the program would be akin to a “modern-day minstrel” or auctioning children for entertainment. The Parents Television Council echoed concerns, labeling the premise “crass, irresponsible and exploitative,” and pledging to pressure advertisers. Oxygen responded that the special aims to portray one unique, complicated family rather than stereotype any demographic, and plans to continue development. Shawty Lo defended himself in interviews, saying he provides for and cares for all his children and urging fathers to be present in their kids’ lives; he acknowledged past hardships and said many women came when he gained wealth. Some PR and media voices defended airing such reality content as a depiction of reality that parents should contextualize. The dispute spotlights tensions over reality TV ethics, child exploitation, responsibility of networks, and cultural representation.

At the 63rd Cannes Film Festival, Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives won the Palme d’Or. Xavier Beauvois’s Of Gods and Men took the Grand Prix, Mahamat‑Saleh Haroun’s A Screaming Man won the Jury Prize, and Mathieu Amalric earned Best Director for On Tour. Lee Chang‑dong won Best Screenplay for Poetry. Juliette Binoche was Best Actress; Javier Bardem and Elio Germano shared Best Actor. Camera d’Or went to Leap Year.

A major Lancet modeling study by teams from Imperial College London, WHO and others predicts substantial gains in life expectancy across 35 high‑income and emerging economies by 2030, with South Korea projected to lead. Korean women’s average life expectancy could climb from about 84 in 2010 to roughly 91 by 2030, while Korean, Australian and Swiss men may reach about 84 years. Several other countries — France, Japan, Spain, Canada, New Zealand and the Netherlands among them — are also expected to see notable increases, narrowing the historical female–male gap as male lifestyles converge with women’s.

The study combined 21 forecasting models and found gains driven mainly by reductions in infant mortality and cardiovascular diseases, better childhood nutrition, education and broad access to medical care. South Korea’s rapid economic development and relatively equitable distribution of health benefits are highlighted as key reasons for its dramatic improvement.

By contrast, the United States is predicted to lag: modest increases would leave U.S. life expectancy in 2030 near 79.5 for men and 83.3 for women — comparable to Croatia and Mexico and the lowest among the nations studied. The authors attribute the U.S. underperformance to high inequality, lack of universal healthcare, rising deaths from drugs, alcohol and mental‑health causes, obesity, and persistently high infant and maternal mortality. The study notes its projections use data through 2013 and do not reflect the U.S. downturn in life expectancy after 2015, which could mean even worse outcomes. The authors stress that unexpected events and policy changes (for example, health‑insurance reforms) could materially alter forecasts and urge planning for aging populations and more equitable health systems.

Ford Motor Co. moved quickly to block use of its trademark by supporters of Toronto Mayor Rob Ford after the mayor signed shirts reading “Ford Nation” that incorporated the automaker’s blue oval at a United Way event. A Ford spokesman said the company did not grant permission and has asked that the use stop. The corporate action comes as Rob Ford — who last week admitted to using crack cocaine and being intoxicated in public — said he purchased illegal drugs while in office during a heated city hall session in which many councillors urged him to take a leave to confront his problems.

Newly released court documents and a police search-warrant application in the case against Alexander “Sandro” Lisi, a friend and occasional driver for the mayor, provide a detailed and damaging portrait of Ford’s conduct and of dysfunction inside his office. The documents compile allegations from staffers who say they bought alcohol for Ford, observed his substance abuse, and covered for or tolerated his lies denying a crack-video’s existence. Many allegations remain unproven and Ford has not been charged, but the material paints a picture of frequent impairment, erratic behaviour and abusive conduct.

Former staffers reported that Ford often kept light hours, frequently disappeared during the workday, and repeatedly drank heavily in public and private settings. One account says staff bought Iceberg vodka for him and that, on at least one occasion, Ford drank while driving — allegedly becoming “rambling and incoherent.” Staffers described episodes of alleged physical and verbal abuse: pushing employees into walls, slurs aimed at staff, threats, and alleged assaults at venues including strip clubs. Some staff told police they had grave concerns about his fitness to drive while impaired; others failed to corroborate certain incidents when questioned, complicating the investigation.

The documents also reveal tension between Rob Ford and his brother Doug, and the influence of associates such as Lisi. Lisi, previously convicted of threatening to kill a woman, is charged with drug trafficking and extortion in relation to efforts to retrieve the crack video; police filings do not specify who directed him. The papers recount the notorious 2013 Garrison Ball appearance, where staffers say Ford was intoxicated, nearly incoherent, and later asked to leave, and the rowdy Bier Markt St. Patrick’s Day episode when Ford allegedly hurled racial insults at a taxi driver and behaved lewdly.

Former chief of staff Mark Towhey advised Ford to choose among fighting the scandal, resigning, or taking a leave; Ford subsequently fired him. Amid the revelations, Ford’s market namesake, Ford Motor Co., defended its trademark, while investors in the automaker continued to push the stock higher. The mayor has repeatedly denied some allegations and defended himself in public, even as pressure mounted from councillors and continued media scrutiny.

On Feb. 13, 2013, more than 40 environmental activists—including Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Julian Bond, actress Daryl Hannah, Bill McKibben, NASA scientist James Hansen and Sierra Club director Michael Brune—tied themselves to the White House gate protesting the proposed Keystone XL tar sands pipeline. They were arrested for failing to disperse and released on $100 bond. Protesters warned the pipeline would increase greenhouse gases and spill risks; supporters, including labor and the oil industry, touted jobs and energy security. The action marked the Sierra Club’s first leadership arrest and preceded a planned large Mall rally.

Kensington Palace has confirmed that Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will marry on Saturday 19 May 2018 at St George’s Chapel, Windsor Castle. The engagement, announced in November, will be followed by Markle’s baptism and confirmation into the Church of England before the service. Choosing a Saturday departs from recent royal practice—previous royal weddings more often fell on weekdays—and was described as “unusual, but not unprecedented,” with the BBC’s royal correspondent noting it gives more people the chance to attend but did not prompt a government Bank Holiday. The date creates a notable clash: the FA Cup Final traditionally takes place that same day, an event Prince William normally attends as FA president and where he presents the trophy. An FA spokesman congratulated the couple and framed the coincidence positively, saying both occasions would bring millions together. The palace said the Royal Family will cover costs for the ceremony, music, flowers and reception. The wedding comes about a month after the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge are expected to welcome their third child. The couple spent Christmas at Sandringham with the Queen and made their first official engagement together in Nottingham.

Vallejo authorities have launched a major search after 29-year-old Denise Huskins, a physical therapist at Kaiser Permanente in Vallejo, was reportedly abducted from a Mare Island home early Monday and a ransom demand was communicated during the incident. Huskins’ boyfriend, identified in public reports as 30-year-old Aaron Quinn, told police he saw her forcibly taken from his residence in the 500 block of Kirkland Avenue and reported her missing to authorities around 1:55 p.m., many hours after the alleged abduction occurred. Police have not explained the delay in reporting. Investigators are interviewing Quinn but say he is not being treated as a suspect or person of interest at this time; public records list him as the homeowner and the registered owner of a 2000 white Toyota Camry that was taken from the home and later recovered at an undisclosed Vallejo location.

Local, county and federal resources — including the FBI, dive teams, sonar equipment, search-and-rescue crews and cadaver dogs — have been deployed. More than 100 personnel and up to 75 dedicated investigators have been combing Mare Island’s waterfront, marshland and surrounding streets; search teams focused on a stretch of shoreline after searchers and sonar detected a possible object in the water during low tide. Detectives also examined and dusted the residence for fingerprints and limited details publicly, citing investigative concerns.

Huskins, originally from Southern California and formerly associated with Southern California Orthopedic Institute, moved to Vallejo in 2014. Her family, including her father who traveled from Huntington Beach, is cooperating with police and pleading for her safe return. Authorities ask anyone with information to contact the Vallejo Police Department at 707-648-4524.

In a wide-ranging TIME interview, President Obama defended his foreign-policy record and domestic priorities after three years in office. He argued his administration ended the Iraq War, weakened al-Qaeda—most notably killing bin Laden—and reinforced alliances with NATO, Japan, South Korea and Israel while engaging multilateral institutions. Obama described a recalibrated U.S. leadership that accepts rising powers like China and India, insists on shared international rules, and pursues engagement rather than containment in Asia. On Iran, he emphasized unified international pressure and diplomacy to prevent a nuclear weapon while keeping military options available. He acknowledged mixed results in Afghanistan: counterterrorism successes but difficult, long-term stabilization and governance challenges that will take decades and Afghan ownership. Domestically, Obama said foreign policy depends on economic strength at home and defended his approach to deficit reduction, noting he created the Simpson-Bowles commission and has sought balanced cuts and revenues despite Republican resistance to new revenue. Responding to critiques of being aloof, he said family priorities and a focus on mission—not Washington socializing—explain his style, and he blamed congressional partisanship, not personal relationships, for legislative gridlock.

Jean S. Harris, the former headmistress of an elite girls’ school whose 1981 trial for the shooting death of Dr. Herman Tarnower drew national attention, died at 89. Arrested March 10, 1980, Harris’ case—depicting a love triangle among the cultured, 56-year-old Harris; Tarnower, the wealthy cardiologist and author of The Complete Scarsdale Medical Diet; and his younger office assistant, Lynne Tryforos—dominated headlines for more than a year. Harris said she drove to Tarnower’s Purchase, N.Y., home intending to kill herself after learning of his affairs; during a struggle she claimed the .32-caliber gun discharged and Tarnower was shot four times. Officers found her leaving the scene and a gun in her glove compartment; she reportedly told a detective, “I did it.” Convicted of second-degree murder in 1981 and sentenced to 15 years to life, Harris spent 12 years at Bedford Hills, where she counseled inmates, created a center for infants of prisoners and later founded Children of Bedford to support their children. Her trial sparked debates about gender, aging and power; supporters framed her as a vulnerable, dependent woman, while critics said her testimony and jealous correspondence made jurors find her story not credible. Granted clemency in 1993 after health issues, she remained an advocate for prison reform.

At a Wisconsin Right to Life fundraiser, Sarah Palin warned that acceptance of abortion rights could lead to rationed care or devaluation of the elderly and disabled, suggesting liberal policies risked de facto euthanasia. She energized about 5,000 supporters with personal stories, anti-abortion appeals, and critiques of Democrats and Nancy Pelosi, while hinting at possible 2012 ambitions. Fox News fact-checked her inaccurate claim that the Obama administration moved “In God We Trust” to the coin’s rim; the coins were authorized by Republican Congress and President Bush.

In Bruce v. Boardwine, the Court of Appeals of Virginia resolved a dispute over parental rights that arose after Joyce Bruce became pregnant using sperm provided by longtime friend Robert Boardwine through nonmedical, at-home insemination (repeated attempts with a turkey baster). Bruce had sought a child she could raise alone, believing that a pregnancy achieved without sexual intercourse would prevent any claim by the biological father. Although the two discussed a written agreement, none was signed. Boardwine testified he intended to be involved in the child’s life—expecting to attend events and participate in educational and health decisions—while Bruce maintained she would be the sole parent and later limited his contact after a falling out. Bruce did not list Boardwine on the birth certificate or notify him immediately of the birth; after several strained visits, she told him to stop coming.

Virginia’s statute on assisted conception relieves a “donor” of parental status only when conception results from “intervening medical technology,” listing examples such as artificial insemination by donor and in vitro fertilization. The appeals court interpreted “medical technology” narrowly, concluding that the statute applies only to procedures involving medical professionals or conventional medical or surgical treatment. A kitchen implement used at home—a turkey baster—does not qualify.
