Because Bruce’s conception method fell outside the statute’s protections, Boardwine’s paternity, established by DNA testing, carried legal consequences. The court affirmed that Boardwine is J.E.’s father and is entitled to pursue and receive visitation (and joint custody considerations), rejecting Bruce’s appeal and leaving in place parental rights for the biological father despite the unconventional conception method.

The text is a long, heated discussion of the decades-old accusations that filmmaker Woody Allen molested his then–seven-year-old adopted daughter Dylan Farrow during his relationship with Mia Farrow, and the ways public opinion, media coverage, family divisions, and the criminal and custody investigations shaped the narrative. The author begins by arguing that presuming Dylan a liar by default—treating Woody’s reputation as more deserving of protection than her credibility—is emblematic of “rape culture.” He insists the presumption of innocence in legal contexts does not require ordinary people to ignore the broader probabilities: while courts must demand proof beyond a reasonable doubt, individuals may reasonably believe Allen likely abused Dylan given patterns of sexual violence and the unlikelihood of coordinated false accusations. He acknowledges he might be wrong but sees the balance of probabilities favoring Dylan.

Interwoven is Robert Weide’s lengthy Daily Beast piece recounting his involvement with a Woody Allen documentary and his reaction to renewed online uproar after Dylan’s Vanity Fair interview and Mia and Ronan Farrow’s tweets. Weide separates two distinct controversies: Allen’s later relationship with Mia’s adopted daughter Soon-Yi (which he disputes many common misconceptions about) and the molestation allegation from 1992. He details the Connecticut investigation, the Yale-New Haven team’s inconclusive report leaning toward coaching or a troubled child, the videotape of Dylan with on/off recording, nanny depositions alleging pressure from Mia, and Judge Elliot Wilk’s custody decisions. Criminal investigators ultimately declined to file charges; a prosecutor’s “probable cause” comment later drew disciplinary scrutiny. Weide stresses ambiguities: inconsistent statements, destroyed investigator notes, contested motives, and the different incentives for a famous man versus an accuser in the court of public opinion.

The narrative also covers family splits: Moses Farrow publicly defending Allen and accusing Mia of poisoning the children, Dylan’s firm insistence that her memories are truthful, and Ronan’s social-media condemnations. The account closes noting Woody’s continued career and family life with Soon-Yi, Mia Farrow’s humanitarian work, the ongoing pain and moral complexity, and the author’s stated sympathy for Dylan alongside skepticism about certain evidentiary claims. The piece underscores how celebrity, media, and family dynamics complicate seeking truth and justice in high-profile abuse allegations.

Daily Duo profiles introduce Misty and Lukas: Misty is a musician whose bold image and style draw comparisons to Grace Jones, while Lukas is devoted to neonatal care, focusing on supporting premature infants. Both were recently chosen as promising new talents for the Daily Duo feature.

The rest of the document shifts to a lengthy look at Kate Upton’s rapid ascent in modeling, sparked by the power of social media. At 19, Upton transformed from relative obscurity into a cultural phenomenon after a viral YouTube clip of her doing the Dougie at an NBA game helped propel her visibility. That exposure led to representation by IMG’s Ivan Bart and high-profile editorial work, and ultimately to being named the Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue cover model — a role that has traditionally launched major careers. The text emphasizes how social platforms have altered traditional pathways to fame across entertainment industries, with industry figures noting that online followings can eclipse conventional TV or runway credentials.

Upton’s wholesome, curvaceous 5'11" figure and mainstream appeal mark her as “bigger than fashion” to some, though fashion insiders remain divided; critics argue her look is too commercial or obvious for certain high-fashion or Victoria’s Secret runways. The piece frames her success as emblematic of shifting industry dynamics where marketability and pre-existing platforms increasingly matter.

David Bowie’s comeback album, The Next Day, is a striking, mature return that both echoes his past and addresses the present. Produced with longtime collaborator Tony Visconti and recorded with familiar players, it channels elements of Bowie’s Berlin, Ziggy, Tin Machine and Eighties eras while remaining immediate and muscular: concise rock arrangements of drums, bass and jagged guitars are shaded by keyboards, sax and ambient guitar. The cover’s redacted Heroes image signals the album’s palimpsest of memory and reinvention.

Lyrically, the record often focuses outward—celebrity, conflict, greed, moral decay—though moments like “Where Are We Now?” are nostalgic and melancholic. Songs range from the stalking funk-rock title track’s indictment of fame and betrayal to the brittle social observations of “The Stars (Are Out Tonight),” the bitter lament “Love Is Lost,” the surreal “How Does the Grass Grow?,” and the epic, vitriolic “You Feel So Lonely You Could Die.” Musical references and quirks—recurring motifs, vocal effects, and lifted hooks—reward close listening without making the album a museum piece. The Next Day is urgent, perplexing and rewarding: a compelling, thoughtful comeback that revisits Bowie’s mythos while confronting contemporary anxieties.

Campus Pride says Chick-fil-A’s WinShape Foundation stopped funding the most controversial anti–same-sex-marriage groups after 2011, citing access to the foundation’s 2011 IRS Form 990. Executive director Shane Windmeyer said the nearly $6 million in outside grants now focus on youth, education, marriage enrichment and local communities; previously funded groups like the Family Research Council, Eagle Forum and Exodus International no longer appear. Windmeyer acknowledged WinShape still supports groups that oppose same-sex marriage on biblical grounds, such as the Fellowship of Christian Athletes, but said they lack hard-edged political agendas. The dispute followed Chick-fil-A President Dan Cathy’s 2012 comments supporting a “biblical” family, prompting boycotts and counter-support events. After dialogue between Windmeyer and Cathy, Campus Pride suspended a national college campaign to seek common ground and urged campuses to protect LGBT students amid ongoing controversy.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers at the Pharr-Reynosa International Bridge in Texas intercepted a tractor-trailer on Jan. 10 that appeared to be carrying fresh carrots from Mexico. An imaging scan and a canine inspection revealed 2,817 carrot-shaped packages containing a total of 2,493 pounds of suspected marijuana, with an estimated street value of about $499,000. Port Director Efrain Solis Jr. noted the creativity of drug smuggling organizations and praised officers’ vigilance. Homeland Security is assisting the investigation. Authorities previously seized over $1 million in drugs disguised as carrots and cucumbers at the same bridge on Dec. 2, underscoring recurring concealment tactics.

Capt. Bruce Kevin Clark, a 43-year-old Army nurse deployed to Tarin Kowt, Afghanistan, died April 30 during a Skype call with his wife, Susan, who watched him suddenly pitch forward unresponsive. From their El Paso home more than 7,000 miles away, Susan says she saw a bullet hole in a closet behind him and immediately contacted base emergency services; after two hours and numerous calls, two military personnel arrived, checked his pulse, and Clark was pronounced dead. The family released a statement describing what Susan witnessed to counter speculation and honor Clark. The Army initially ruled the death non-suicide and non-combat related but said official cause will await autopsy and toxicology results; later announcements indicated no bullet wound was found on Clark’s body. Military officials explained the delayed response by saying Susan’s calls were routed through multiple stateside commands before reaching Afghanistan. Clark, who joined the Army in 2006 after earning a nursing degree from SUNY Brockport, was assigned to William Beaumont Army Medical Center in El Paso and had deployed in March. He is survived by his wife and two daughters, ages 3 and 9. The circumstances prompted public speculation, and the investigation and rumors are likely to continue.

LaVar Ball minimized reports of a feud with President Donald Trump in a CNN interview, while refusing to publicly thank Trump for his role in securing the release of LaVar’s son, LiAngelo Ball, from Chinese detention. LiAngelo and two other UCLA freshmen, Jalen Hill and Cody Riley, were detained in Hangzhou after admitting to shoplifting from multiple stores, including Louis Vuitton. Their detention occurred during Trump’s 12-day Asia trip, and the president later tweeted that he had helped save the players from potential prison terms of up to 10 years. The players and UCLA later acknowledged the president’s assistance, but LaVar repeatedly insisted his own efforts — and work by unnamed “boots on the ground” — were primarily responsible for getting his son home. He said he didn’t need to thank everyone who helped and suggested other parties, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, might deserve acknowledgment if thanks were due. LaVar also questioned accounts that Trump intervened to stop a long prison sentence, noting that negotiations may have been underway before the president’s involvement. He dismissed the idea of being at war with “the most powerful man in the world,” asking rhetorically why he would take Trump on. The exchange escalated after Trump posted sharp tweets calling LaVar “very ungrateful” and suggesting he should have left the players in jail.

Samantha Bee plans to host a gala in Washington, D.C., on April 29 called “Not the White House Correspondents’ Dinner,” positioned as an alternative to the traditional White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) dinner amid strained relations between the Trump administration and the press. Bee and Full Frontal producers will stage the event at the Willard Hotel simultaneous with the WHCA dinner and expect TBS to broadcast it, though details remain tentative. Originating after the election, the idea aims to create a joyful, media-focused evening without supplanting the WHCA event; proceeds will benefit the Committee to Protect Journalists. Bee said the gala may spotlight “unsung journalists” and include “super fans,” and insisted the move is motivated by concern for press freedom under the Trump presidency rather than commercial promotion. The effort fits a broader trend of late-night hosts expanding beyond traditional broadcasts—Stephen Colbert, Seth Meyers and others have created events and social strategies to retain fragmented audiences. Bee’s Full Frontal, renewed through 2017, has already experimented with social-media extras and satirical content; she says this gala is serious and intended to ensure journalists and comedians have a forum to roast the president if the WHCA dinner’s future is uncertain.

Researchers at the University of Washington discovered that fruit flies (Drosophila hydei) perform ultra-fast, plane-like evasive maneuvers when threatened, rolling and pitching their bodies to execute banked turns instead of simple yaw turns. Captured at 7,500 frames per second across 92 escapes and 3,566 wing beats, flies were seen reorienting in less than one-hundredth of a second—about two wing beats—enabled by wing flapping around 200 Hz. Using expanding-shadow stimuli and infrared illumination to avoid disturbing the insects, the team quantified subtle wing adjustments that generate rapid forces, then reproduced the motions on a robotic fly in viscous fluid to measure forces. Despite tiny brains denser than humans’, flies perform remarkably complex, precise sensorimotor computations. Researchers aim next to map the neural circuitry translating visual input into these explosive motor outputs, insights that could inform engineering and neuroscience.

James D. Watson, co-discoverer of DNA’s double helix, has been at the center of a recent controversy after making remarks to Britain’s Sunday Times Magazine suggesting that black people are less intelligent than whites. The comments, reported by Charlotte Hunt-Grubbe, touched off swift condemnation in the U.K.: planned appearances promoting his new book Avoid Boring People were canceled by the Science Museum, the University of Edinburgh, and other hosts. Watson, 79, apologized, calling himself “mortified” and insisting he did not mean to imply genetic inferiority and that “there is no scientific basis for such a belief.” Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory suspended his administrative responsibilities amid the uproar and he canceled the remainder of his U.K. engagements and returned to the U.S.

The episode rekindles debate over Watson’s pattern of provocative remarks over the decades — earlier comments included controversial views about sexuality, eugenics-like hypotheticals, and derogatory observations about colleagues — and highlights persistent tensions between a scientist’s stature and public accountability. The piece notes that contemporary science offers no agreed definitions of “race” or “intelligence,” and IQ testing is known to contain cultural biases; biological explanations for group differences remain unproven.

Separately, Christie’s New York announced the December 4 auction of Watson’s 1962 Nobel Prize medal, estimated at $2.5–3.5 million, the first time a living recipient’s medal will be offered. The sale includes his Nobel speech notes and lecture drafts. A portion of proceeds will support scientific and charitable causes. The release recounts Watson’s formative biography: precocious education, collaboration with Francis Crick leading to the 1953 Nature paper, academic leadership at Harvard and Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, authorship of influential books (The Double Helix), and role in the early Human Genome Project. While his scientific legacy is monumental, the recent controversy underscores how Watson’s public statements complicate his standing today.

After Whitney Houston was found dead at 48, sales and downloads of her music surged dramatically. Seven of her records hit Amazon’s top 10 best-sellers and multiple songs and albums reappeared in iTunes’ charts; her Greatest Hits compilation reached number two on Amazon and her cover of “I Will Always Love You” topped iTunes. Observers expected sustained demand to keep her catalogue high on charts for weeks as tributes poured in.

Controversy arose when Sony Music reportedly raised the wholesale price of Houston’s 1997 album The Ultimate Collection early Sunday, which automatically pushed the iTunes retail price from £4.99 to £7.99. Apple later restored the original price. Fans criticized the timing as an attempt to capitalize on the tragedy, though an industry insider said the wholesale change was a pricing error discovered when Sony reviewed Houston’s catalogue after her death. The Ultimate Collection and Whitney – The Greatest Hits were both among iTunes’ top three albums at midday Monday. Apple and Sony declined to comment.

Marvin Gaye’s family has taken legal steps to block further use of “Blurred Lines” after a jury found Pharrell Williams and Robin Thicke had copied elements of Gaye’s 1977 hit “Got to Give It Up.” The jury ordered Williams and Thicke to pay about $7.4 million to three of Gaye’s children. The family filed an injunction to prevent copying, distributing and performing the song and asked the court to amend the verdict to include rapper T.I. (Clifford Joseph Harris Jr.) and labels Universal Music, Interscope Records and Star Trak Entertainment. Seeking to protect Gaye’s musical legacy, the family said in a statement that the digital age increases risks of infringement and that preserving copyright standards ensures music remains valued. The injunction could strengthen the family’s leverage to secure royalties, songwriting credits or other concessions. “Blurred Lines,” a major 2013 hit, sold over 7 million U.S. tracks, dominated pop charts for months and received two Grammy nominations.

Former skating champion Tonya Harding expressed sympathy for Nancy Kerrigan and her family after the death of Kerrigan’s father, Daniel Kerrigan. Harding’s representative noted Tonya’s own recent loss — her father Al Harding died in April — and said she understands the family’s grief. Daniel Kerrigan, 70, died following an altercation at the family’s Massachusetts home on Jan. 24; his son Mark was charged with assault in connection with the incident, pleaded not guilty at arraignment, and was held on $10,000 bail. A cause of death had not been determined, though Daniel’s wife Brenda said he may have suffered a heart attack. The tragedy has resonated through the skating community: Olympic silver medalist Paul Wylie described Nancy as “really struggling” but gracious in responding to well-wishers, and Olympic champion Kristi Yamaguchi offered condolences, praising Daniel and Brenda for their support of skaters. Separately, Nancy’s parents sued her older brother in 2008, alleging he failed to repay $105,000 they had provided for his mortgage, bills and other expenses while he served time for assault, drug and property charges.

Steven Avery’s 2003 release from a wrongful 1985 sexual assault conviction made him a local symbol of miscarriage of justice in Manitowoc County and a national figure in the innocence movement. His exoneration prompted apologies, local welcome, and spurred law enforcement reforms—the “Avery task force” produced what became the Avery Bill, recently enacted to improve eyewitness identification, interrogation practices and evidence handling. Avery toured the Capitol, testified before lawmakers, and was hailed by some as a hero of reform.

Weeks after reclaiming his life and amid a pending $36 million civil suit for his wrongful conviction, Avery, 43, was arrested and charged with the October 31 killing and mutilation of photographer Teresa Halbach. Authorities reported finding Halbach’s car and remains at Avery’s salvage yard, blood from both in the vehicle, her car key in his trailer, and Avery’s DNA on the key using the same technology that had freed him. The new case stunned his attorney, Stephen Glynn, who warned of the damage to the cause of criminal justice reform, and dismayed innocence advocates who fear public backlash despite statistics showing reoffense among exonerees is rare.

Reactions are sharply divided. Avery’s family insists he is innocent and that evidence was planted; they and some county residents say the community is reliving an injustice. Critics on talk radio and blogs argue the Innocence Project’s work might indirectly have enabled a dangerous man’s release, citing Avery’s prior record. The Wisconsin Innocence Project and national advocates urge separating the new allegations from the proven wrongful conviction, emphasizing their mission to both exonerate the innocent and see the guilty held accountable. Politically and legally, the arrest has complicated Avery’s civil suit, muted legislative attention to compensating him, and cast a shadow over the reforms and public perceptions that grew from his earlier case. The questions raised by his prosecution—about evidence handling, potential motive for framing, and interrogation of co-defendants—remain hotly contested.

The West African Ebola outbreak beginning in late 2013 is the largest and most geographically widespread in history, centered in Guinea and spreading into Sierra Leone and Liberia. By late June the World Health Organization reported roughly 600 cases and about 367 deaths (updates later cited ~390+ deaths and 567 cases in some reports). The responsible agent is Zaire ebolavirus, the deadliest of known Ebola species, historically killing as many as 79–90% of infected people in some outbreaks. Ebola typically spills over from animal reservoirs—likely bats—when people handle or eat infected wildlife; it then spreads between humans through direct contact with blood or other bodily fluids or contaminated materials. Symptoms begin like flu and can progress to vomiting, diarrhea and in many cases hemorrhage from orifices; death usually follows from multi-organ failure within 6–16 days.

This outbreak has been amplified by social, political and health-system factors: health workers in West Africa often lacked Ebola training, travel patterns helped geographic spread, unsafe burial rites and denial or mistrust of health efforts have hampered containment, and communities sometimes hide sick relatives or destroy supplies. Médecins Sans Frontières called the situation “out of control,” reporting overwhelmed teams and urging urgent resource mobilization. WHO plans regional coordination meetings to improve surveillance, contact-tracing, communication and cross-border cooperation. Transmission requires close contact with infectious fluids, so risk of global spread is low but not zero; public education, isolation, protective procedures and strengthened healthcare response are critical to control the epidemic while treatment remains largely supportive and vaccines/drugs are under development.

Canadian authorities concluded that 31-year-old Glee actor Cory Monteith died from a lethal combination of heroin and alcohol. The British Columbia Coroners Service reported that autopsy and toxicology results indicated "mixed drug toxicity, involving heroin and alcohol." Monteith’s body was found July 13 in a Vancouver hotel room, where officials noted evidence consistent with a drug overdose. The actor had a long history of substance abuse and had attended rehab earlier that year.

Larimer County is confronting a surge in suicides this year, with 77 confirmed deaths to date, including three involving children under 18. Two of those juvenile fatalities occurred in Fort Collins within days of each other: an 11-year-old girl who died Nov. 16 and an 11-year-old boy who died Saturday. The coroner’s office has not released their names; local reporting and an obituary identify the girl as a sixth-grader at Lincoln Middle School and the boy as a student at Blevins Middle School. Last year the county recorded 83 suicides, the highest in at least a decade, and two youth suicides; December 2014 was particularly deadly with 11 deaths. The Poudre School District has increased counseling services at the affected schools and says it has expanded student mental-health supports and suicide-prevention training over the past five years. The girl’s family and community members have linked her death to ongoing bullying that began in elementary school; they describe prior signs of depression and episodes serious enough to require counseling and alternative coursework, though authorities have not publicly confirmed bullying as a factor in either death. Neighbors and classmates held a candlelight vigil and balloon launch for the girl, and both families are raising funds to cover medical and funeral expenses. Survivors and relatives are calling for deeper, more effective anti-bullying responses in schools and urging students to seek help, hoping the tragedies prompt meaningful change and greater validation of young people’s feelings. A combined vigil was planned outside Colorado State University to honor both children.

General Mills’ non-GMO Original Cheerios and Post Foods’ non-GMO Grape Nuts have been reformulated to remove ingredients from genetically engineered crops, but the new versions contain substantially fewer vitamins. New Original Cheerios now list only 2% of the daily value for riboflavin (vitamin B2) per serving, down from 25%, while Post’s Grape Nuts no longer include vitamins A, D, B12 or B2. Neither company has explained the reductions. Experts and industry sources say the change likely reflects the difficulty of sourcing vitamins and nutrient additives that can be verified as non-GMO: many vitamins are produced by fermentation using microbes or feedstocks (corn, sugar beet) that may be genetically modified, and microencapsulation often uses corn- or soy-based ingredients. Obtaining the documentation required for Non-GMO Project verification is complex because manufacturers guard proprietary formulas. Market research shows many consumers express GMO concerns, but most won’t pay more; nonetheless, a vocal subset and retail trends have driven rapid growth in non-GMO labeling despite supply-chain challenges.

Michael Wolff’s profile and excerpts capture Donald Trump as a media-savvy performer whose campaign and presidency are driven less by coherent policy than by spectacle and personal magnetism. In a relaxed June 2016 interview at his Beverly Hills home, Trump repeatedly celebrates the “phenomenon” of his candidacy—its fame, crowds and media domination—arguing that success itself trumps substantive critique. He delights in mutual flirtation with hosts like Jimmy Kimmel, relishes relationships with media moguls (Rupert Murdoch, Sumner Redstone, Leslie Moonves) and entertains entertainment-industry allies such as agent Ari Emanuel, who offered to craft convention film coverage. Trump claims he need not pivot to win women, Hispanics or blacks because he will “remake the electoral math” through sheer bigness and charisma; he eschews policy nuance and displays ignorance on issues like Brexit while insisting his spontaneity—speaking without teleprompters—connects him to voters.

Wolff’s White House account, drawn from extensive access for Fire and Fury, depicts chaotic governance: inexperienced, often infighting senior staff; a revolving door of officials (Flynn, Priebus, Spicer, Bannon among others); and the unusual centrality of family (Ivanka, Jared) and young aides (Hope Hicks). Staff oscillate between defending Trump and despairing at his impulsiveness, repetition and craving for “wins.” Factional battles—Jared and Ivanka versus Bannon and others—produce leaks, screaming matches and resignations. Despite achieving the tax bill, the administration is portrayed as unmoored, sustained partly by media acolytes and Trump’s billionaire confidants. Wolff leaves a stark impression: a presidency run more as a show business enterprise centered on a charismatic, mercurial figure than a conventional, steady exercise of governance.

Last year’s high-profile claim that DNA from hairs attributed to the Himalayan “yeti” matched an ancient polar bear has been re-evaluated and challenged. Bryan Sykes and colleagues reported in 2014 that two hair samples—one from a creature shot decades ago in Ladakh and another found in Bhutan—matched mitochondrial DNA from a 40,000–120,000-year-old polar bear jawbone, suggesting an unrecognized polar bear–brown bear hybrid might live in the Himalayas. That idea attracted widespread attention and speculation that such a bear could underlie yeti lore.

Subsequent re-analyses have undermined that conclusion. Eliécer Gutiérrez of the Smithsonian and a colleague re-examined the same sequence fragments and found the DNA segment Sykes’s team used is insufficiently informative to distinguish between brown bears and certain polar bears. By consulting publicly available sequences in GenBank, they concluded the hair samples most plausibly come from the Himalayan brown bear (a high-altitude subspecies of Ursus arctos), not a distinct or hybrid species. Earlier critiques published in the same journal also argued Sykes’s group relied on a limited mitochondrial fragment and should have sequenced additional regions to confirm the surprising polar-bear link.

Sykes has acknowledged database-search limitations but maintains the samples are not from unknown primates and says fresh tissue would be needed for definitive answers. Other experts note bears—especially Himalayan brown bears that sometimes stand bipedally—can account for many yeti sightings. Historical analyses of other purported yeti hairs have similarly identified known species (e.g., Himalayan goral). Overall, current evidence does not support a taxonomically unrecognized bear in the Himalayas; the simpler explanation is that the samples derive from the Himalayan brown bear.

Two separate tragic drownings of young children were reported in the Northeast. In Londonderry, Vermont, 5-year-old Jaxon Lawrence died at Dartmouth-Hitchcock Medical Center two days after falling off a toy flotation device in Lowell Lake. His 55-year-old grandmother, Julie Lawrence, attempted to rescue him but began struggling; rescuers found both unresponsive and pronounced the grandmother dead at the scene. Jaxon’s 9-year-old brother attempted a rescue and swam for help; he is in good health. Meanwhile in Milford, New York, 3-year-old Andrew Durkin went missing from a seasonal home and was found about 17 feet from a dock in the Susquehanna River by an underwater recovery team. Resuscitation was attempted, but he later died at a hospital; authorities ruled his death an accidental drowning. Corrections clarified spellings and locations.

A large study of 8,207 sleep-related infant deaths from 24 states (2004–2012) found distinct risk patterns for younger (0–3 months) versus older (4–12 months) infants. Overall, 69% of infants were bed-sharing at death; 58% were male and most were non-Hispanic white. Younger infants were much more likely to be bed-sharing at the time of death (about 74% of deaths in that group) and to be found sleeping on an adult bed or on/near a person. Older infants were more likely to be found prone and in sleep areas containing objects such as blankets, pillows, or stuffed animals (about 39% of older-infant deaths involved objects); 18% of older infants had changed from back or side to prone. The study examined associations rather than proving causation, but authors conclude that risk factors vary by developmental stage and that prevention should reflect these differences.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) reiterates evidence-based safe-sleep recommendations for infants up to 1 year: always place babies on their backs for sleep on a firm, flat surface that meets Consumer Product Safety Commission standards; room-share (keep baby’s sleep area in parents’ room) for at least six months; avoid bed-sharing and never let infants sleep on couches or armchairs. Keep soft objects, loose bedding, bumper pads, and toys out of the sleep area. Newborn skin-to-skin contact is encouraged shortly after birth, but infants should be placed on their backs in a bassinet when the mother must sleep. Swaddling is acceptable if done safely and stopped once the baby attempts to roll. Parents should follow AAP guidance and consult pediatricians with questions.

Dartmouth College charged 64 students with honor-code violations after uncovering widespread cheating in the “Sports, Ethics and Religion” course, part of a broader pattern of academic dishonesty at elite U.S. schools. Professor Randall Balmer discovered students used handheld “clicker” devices to answer questions for absent classmates, enabling false attendance and participation. He reported 43 students to the college judicial board; another 21 later confessed. Balmer, who designed the class partly to help student-athletes, said the incident left him “burned” and eroded trust between faculty and students. An appeals process is underway to determine suspensions; Dartmouth policy warns cheating can lead to suspension or separation. Balmer ultimately reduced the accused students’ marks by a letter grade rather than fail them, after “many sleepless nights.” The case echoes prior scandals—Harvard’s 2012 exam probe and UNC’s long-running “paper classes” scheme—prompting debate about whether a culture prioritizing success over integrity contributes to rising cheating. Dartmouth officials declined detailed comment until the disciplinary appeals conclude.

When President Trump added chief strategist Steve Bannon to regular meetings of the National Security Council, the move set off an immediate online backlash and intensified debate about who shapes U.S. policy. The hashtag #StopPresidentBannon trended nationally as thousands criticized Bannon’s new role, pointing to his tenure as head of Breitbart News and alleging the outlet promoted racist, sexist and anti‑Semitic views. Twitter users questioned why a former media executive would be elevated above seasoned national security professionals, with many calling his influence a threat to democracy and national safety. White House spokespeople defended the decision, noting Bannon’s prior Navy service, business background, and perceived geopolitical insight, and saying his presence helps inform the president’s final judgments. Trump also adjusted the NSC structure to make Bannon a regular attendee of the principals committee while limiting the director of national intelligence and the chairman of the Joint Chiefs to discussions relevant to their expertise. Critics, including Sen. Tim Kaine, denounced the changes as placing “questionable people” on the NSC. The episode highlighted deep partisan fears about the administration’s decision‑making and the role of ideological advisers in shaping security policy.

Researchers identified a novel Thogotovirus, named Bourbon virus, after isolating it from the blood of a previously healthy man from Bourbon County, Kansas, who died in 2014 following acute febrile illness. The patient had a recent tick bite and developed fever, nausea, diarrhea, myalgia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes. He received doxycycline empirically for presumed tickborne disease but deteriorated over 11 days with multiorgan failure, respiratory distress, shock, and fatal cardiac arrest. Extensive testing for known bacterial, viral, fungal, and parasitic causes, including common tickborne pathogens and Heartland virus, was negative. Viral culture revealed cytopathic effect; plaque assays and next-generation sequencing showed an orthomyxovirus closely related to Dhori and Batken viruses. Phylogenetic analyses placed the novel agent within the Thogotovirus genus. Transmission is suspected to be tickborne given exposure and season, but vectors and reservoirs remain unknown. Public health actions underway include searching for additional human cases, vector and reservoir studies, and development of diagnostic assays; prevention focuses on avoiding tick bites.

Meryl Streep responded publicly after Rose McGowan criticized several actresses, including Streep, for planning to wear black at award shows to protest sexual harassment. McGowan accused them of silence and hypocrisy, saying accepting awards without effecting change was problematic; she specifically called out Streep for “happily working with the pig monster,” referring to producer Harvey Weinstein, whom McGowan alleges raped her. Streep said she was hurt by the attack and insisted she had not known about Weinstein’s crimes “in the 90s” or later. She denied being deliberately silent, saying she neither tacitly approved of rape nor knew such abuse was occurring. Streep described minimal contact with Weinstein—only once visiting his office in 1998 for a meeting—and said she was never invited to his hotel room. She emphasized that Weinstein functioned more as a marketer and producer, distributing films by many filmmakers, and that not everyone associated with his films knew about his misconduct. Streep expressed support for a legal defense fund for victims and conveyed sympathy for McGowan’s pain. She said she had tried to reach McGowan through mutual contacts and left her phone available, hoping for a conversation that never happened. McGowan later deleted the tweet attacking Streep and apologized for an unrelated insult about Weinstein’s estranged wife’s fashion line, but has not directly reconciled with Streep. Over fifty women have accused Weinstein of sexual misconduct; he denies non-consensual allegations.

With North Korea deciding just a month before the Winter Games to send a delegation, organizers had little time to alter the opening ceremony. Director Song Seung-whan said he only modified one segment to acknowledge the North’s presence and focused mostly on contingency plans for extreme cold. Rehearsal tweaks included shoe spikes for dancers and testing electronics for freezing temperatures; fortunately the actual night was milder, near 28°F. Song also struggled to stage a large production—1,300 performers plus 700 volunteers—on a “very limited” budget, joking it was far less than Beijing’s. IOC president and 1976 fencing gold medalist Thomas Bach appeared; North Korean dignitaries Kim Yo-jong and Kim Yong-nam attended, briefly greeted by South Korea’s President Moon Jae-in. The Parade of Nations emphasized warmth and practical style—Team USA wore Ralph Lauren heated jackets—while several countries stood out for distinctive flagbearer outfits (Sweden, Mexico, Tonga) and appealing apparel (Belarus, Iran), and tropical teams like Jamaica and Bermuda managed to look good despite the cold.

Windi C. Thomas, 44, pleaded guilty Monday to third-degree murder in the March death of her boyfriend, 44-year-old Keeno Butler, at their east Erie apartment. Under a plea agreement with prosecutors, Thomas accepted a recommended state prison sentence of 18 to 36 years; sentencing is set for Dec. 21. Judge William R. Cunningham accepted the plea, and Assistant Erie County District Attorney Jeremy Lightner dropped related charges including aggravated assault, reckless endangerment and possession of an instrument of a crime. The agreed range reduces the statutory maximum for third-degree murder (20 to 40 years) by two to four years. Court-appointed attorney Mark Del Duca characterized the outcome as fair for both sides. Family members disagreed: Butler’s sister, Sandra, said Thomas deserved a longer term, even life. According to police affidavits, Thomas admitted to cutting Butler’s hand with a folding knife, striking him with a table leg and positioning part of her body on his head; investigators noted Thomas weighs about 300 pounds while Butler weighed about 120. The medical examiner ruled the homicide caused by respiratory insufficiency from neck and chest compression, worsened by blunt head trauma. Thomas remains jailed without bond pending sentencing, and Butler’s family continues to grieve.

Pope Francis used a wide-ranging interview with Italy’s Corriere della Sera to reiterate core Catholic teachings while signaling a more pastoral, pragmatic tone on several contentious issues. Reaffirming that marriage is “between a man and a woman,” he nonetheless acknowledged that states may legitimately create civil unions to ensure legal and economic protections—comments that Vatican officials later urged not be over-interpreted. The remark was notable as the first time a pope has even tentatively accepted civil unions, reflecting earlier instances when some bishops, and Francis as Archbishop of Buenos Aires, showed openness to alternatives to marriage for same-sex couples.

On contraception, Francis praised Pope Paul VI’s courage in maintaining the ban but emphasized the need for mercy and attention to concrete situations, suggesting ongoing, in-depth reflection ahead of bishops’ meetings in 2014 and 2015 on issues like contraception and divorced Catholics receiving communion. He urged greater inclusion of women in decision-making roles beyond purely functional tasks, noting church leaders are engaged in “deep reflection” about their role.

Addressing the clergy sexual abuse crisis, Francis acknowledged the deep wounds inflicted on victims and argued the church has shown openness and transparency, while lamenting that the institution has been singled out for attack. The Vatican said it would study a recent critical U.N. report charging inadequate acknowledgement and response.

Francis also rejected the “mythology” of a celebrity pope, calling portrayals of him as a “Superpope” offensive and stressing his normalcy—he laughs, cries, sleeps and has friends like anyone else. He described Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI as a “wise grandfather,” saying they agreed Benedict should remain visible and participate in church life rather than be hidden away.

Separately, the Vatican opened the papal gardens at Castel Gandolfo to the public, offering guided tours of historic Barberini gardens and papal villas—part of Francis’s broader openness in tone and access during his first anniversary as pope.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet donated crawl data to the Internet Archive; those daily captures are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo. Separately, a Game of Thrones Season 6 spoiler: actor Dean-Charles Chapman, known since 2014 as King Tommen Baratheon, previously appeared in Season 3 as Martyn Lannister. Martyn and his brother Willem were taken hostage by Robb Stark’s forces and later killed by Lord Rickard Karstark, prompting Robb to execute Karstark. Fans noticed the resemblance (and IMDb lists Chapman in both roles), meaning Chapman played two related Lannisters. While this doesn’t impact the main plot, it fuels playful theories—like the “Tommen is a faceless man” idea—and highlights how casting reuse and Lannister incest in-universe can explain identical appearances.

While jogging on a familiar wooded trail near her Hope, Maine, home on June 3, 21-year-old Rachel Borch was attacked by a raccoon that she immediately suspected was rabid. The animal blocked the narrow path, charged at her with its teeth bared and latched onto her thumb. With no object to defend herself and the trail too tight to pass, Borch wrestled with the raccoon, which clawed her arms and legs. After dropping her phone into a puddle, she dragged the animal into the muddy water and, fearing it would continue to bite, held its head under until it stopped struggling. Bleeding and hysterical, she ran home, and her family retrieved the carcass and turned it over to the Maine Warden Service; the Maine CDC later confirmed the raccoon tested positive for rabies.

Borch was treated at Pen Bay Medical Center and has begun post-exposure prophylaxis: rabies vaccine doses, immunoglobulin, tetanus and antibiotics for puncture wounds, with her final shot scheduled soon. Hope Animal Control Officer Heidi Blood warned that one infected animal usually signals others nearby and reminded residents that infected wildlife often show unusual daytime activity or erratic behavior. The Maine CDC reports wildlife rabies is common; as of June 7 there had been 20 positive animals in 2017, compared with 64 in 2016. Blood emphasized rabies is nearly always fatal if untreated and urged people to avoid wild animals and keep pets vaccinated. Borch, a vegetarian, called the encounter surreal and said she will never view raccoons the same way.

Ben Affleck has publicly confirmed via Facebook that he recently completed treatment for alcohol addiction, calling it “the first of many steps being taken towards a positive recovery.” The 44-year-old noted this isn’t his first encounter with addiction—he previously entered rehab in 2001—and said he will continue to confront the issue. Affleck emphasized family and parenting throughout the statement, thanking his friends and family and specifically praising his estranged wife and co-parent Jennifer Garner for supporting him and caring for their three children while he “did the work.” Reports indicate he entered treatment soon after the Oscars; sources suggest his alcohol struggles had been recurring. Despite past professional setbacks—such as his directoral film Live by Night underperforming and his exit as director of The Batman—Affleck will still star in and produce the upcoming Batman film and appears in Justice League. He framed his recovery as both personal responsibility and an example for his kids about seeking help without shame.

This HRC study examines why people adopt or abandon vegetarian and vegan diets, focusing on contrasts between current vegetarians/vegans (about 2% of U.S. adults) and former ones (about 10%). Using a representative sample of over 11,000 adults, the report finds that a majority who try vegetarianism/veganism eventually revert: only about one in five who adopt the diet maintain it long-term, while 84% return to eating animal products. Many lapses occur quickly—one-third abandon within three months and over half within a year—and most who switch do so rapidly: 65% of former vegans/vegetarians transitioned in days or weeks, compared with 53% of current vegans/vegetarians. Common factors linked to lapsing include social pressures (feeling different, living with non-vegetarian partners), rapid transitions, weak social ties to other veg people, persistent cravings, and viewing the diet as primarily a health choice rather than an identity. Current vegetarians/vegans more often cite multiple motivations (animal welfare, environment, health), suggesting diverse messaging helps retention. The study recommends reframing advocacy toward reduction rather than strict elimination, promoting gradual transitions, stronger community support, and messaging that acknowledges challenges. These insights aim to move animal-free diets from the margins toward broader, more sustainable adoption.

The Daily Show began in 1996 as a loose satire of television news under Craig Kilborn, blending pop culture bits and field pieces. In 1999 Jon Stewart took over amid skepticism from staff and industry observers. Stewart, coming off failed TV ventures but seasoned by writing and acting work, aimed to reshape the program from broad spoofing into pointed satire with a clear point of view. Early months were turbulent: Kilborn-era writers resisted changes, producing an acrimonious “fuck-you meeting,” and Stewart had to assert control, firing or sidelining resistors while recruiting allies who shared his sensibility.

Ben Karlin joined as head writer in 1999 and quickly forged a productive partnership with Stewart, emphasizing righteous anger and targeting powerful institutions rather than eccentric individuals. Karlin brought writers from The Onion aesthetic; David Javerbaum, a fast, multi-talented writer, soon followed. On-camera talent shifted too: Stephen Colbert, Steve Carell, Mo Rocca and others became regular correspondents, bringing character-driven reporting that parodied the authoritative styles of network news and newsmagazines. Colbert’s insurance-salesman persona and Carell’s bumbling local-anchor act proved especially potent.

A turning point came during the 1999–2000 campaign coverage. The correspondents’ field work at New Hampshire and on John McCain’s Straight Talk Express signaled the show’s new direction: instead of ridiculing fringe eccentrics, they began to deconstruct political theater and media processes. A famous moment—Carell’s awkward, revealing exchange with McCain—demonstrated that the show could expose political absurdities while remaining funny and relevant. Stewart and his team realized their niche: bridging the gap between staged public appearances and the backstage meetings that actually shape events.

By refocusing targets on politicians and the media, tightening editorial control, and cultivating smart writers and fearless correspondents, Stewart transformed The Daily Show into a sharper, politically engaged satire that anticipated the coming fragmentation of cable news and the internet’s rise, positioning the program to become a defining voice for younger, media-savvy viewers.

In 2009 a small landscape, “On the Shore of the Seine,” surfaced in the headlines as the so-called “flea‑market Renoir” after Martha Fuqua (who earlier used the name Marcia Fuqua) tried to sell it at auction. Fuqua told Potomack Company auctioneers she had bought the painting in a $7 box of trinkets at a West Virginia flea market. Days before that sale the Baltimore Museum of Art (BMA) discovered internal records showing the same Renoir had been stolen from its collection in 1951; the FBI seized the work and opened an investigation. A federal judge in Alexandria must now decide whether Fuqua or the museum keeps the painting.

Because Fuqua’s account conflicted with other evidence, reporters and investigators dug into the work’s recent history. Multiple former acquaintances of Fuqua recall the small, ornately framed painting hanging in the studio of her mother, Marcia Fouquet — a Goucher College and Maryland Institute College of Art–trained artist who reproduced masterworks, including Renoir. Robert Musser, who lived with and dated Fouquet in the late 1970s and early 1980s, and two others who visited her studio in the 1990s all remember the tiny framed piece with a plaque reading “Renoir.” That memory complicates Fuqua’s flea‑market origin story.

Months before the Potomack notice, Fuqua had offered the painting to Quinn’s Auction Galleries, claiming an estate provenance and envisioning a $1 million price; she refused to leave the work for further study. Quinn’s alerted the FBI after learning of the Potomack sale and the BMA’s theft records. Potomack had sought authentication from Bernheim‑Jeune and the Art Loss Register; the Paris gallery confirmed the painting as a Renoir, and the register listed no match.

Fuqua claims to be an “innocent owner” under federal law; the statute of limitations for the 1951 theft has expired, but possession or transportation charges could still be possible. The FBI has shown particular interest in who accompanied Fuqua to Quinn’s and in the painting’s unclear chain of custody, while Fouquet and Fuqua have largely declined public comment as litigation proceeds.

French authorities have charged a 23-year-old man with preliminary terrorism offenses after he allegedly plotted attacks targeting President Emmanuel Macron and minority groups during the Bastille Day events. Police arrested the suspect in the Argenteuil suburb following tips from users of a videogame chat room, where he reportedly said he wanted to buy a gun. Investigators say his plans were vague and seemingly not finalized; they found three kitchen knives in his vehicle and internet searches on possible targets. After his arrest he reportedly admitted wanting to attack “Muslims, Jews, blacks, homosexuals.” The suspect had previously been convicted last year for condoning terrorism after praising Anders Breivik and received a three-year sentence with half suspended. Macron will preside over the July 14 military parade on the Champs-Élysées — which he will attend alongside U.S. President Donald Trump — then travel to Nice to mark the anniversary of the 2016 truck attack that killed 86 people. Security concerns are heightened after recent incidents on the avenue, including two attacks on police earlier this year.

Early Thursday morning near Edna, Texas, a traffic stop escalated into a fatal crash after a 2003 Ford Explorer fled from officers. Police attempted to stop the SUV for a violation on U.S. 59; the driver refused, leading to a roughly ten-minute pursuit. Around 1:30 a.m., the vehicle lost control, ran off the road, and rolled multiple times, ejecting several occupants. Six people died—four at the scene and two later at hospitals—and about ten others were injured; most survivors are in stable condition. Authorities estimate 14–15 people were inside; the Explorer’s rear seat was folded and the middle seat removed to create space. Two people who fled the scene were later arrested. Investigators suspect human smuggling: some victims have been identified as nationals of Honduras, Guatemala and Mexico, and many survivors were turned over to U.S. Border Patrol. Texas authorities note U.S. 59 is a frequent corridor for human- and drug-trafficking.

As Congress negotiates the federal budget during the lame-duck session, two senators from opposite parties are quietly collaborating on online-gambling legislation. Nevada’s influential Democratic Sen. Harry Reid, backed by casino interests, and Arizona Republican Sen. Jon Kyl, who has historically opposed betting, are pushing to include language in a package that would both expand and restrict various forms of internet wagering. Central to the proposal is creating an Office of Online Poker Oversight within the Department of Commerce to regulate online poker activity. The initiative, long discussed behind closed doors, has not been publicly introduced but could be tucked into budget negotiations. The bill’s mixed approach—permitting some online betting while curbing other types—reflects competing interests and a desire to bring federal structure to internet gambling, especially poker. By coupling expansion with limits and placing oversight in a federal agency, the measure aims to balance industry growth, consumer protections and legal clarity. Its discreet development underscores political sensitivities and the potential for significant regulatory change if lawmakers move to incorporate it into end-of-session budget legislation.

A mass methanol poisoning in Irkutsk, Siberia, after people drank a hawthorn-scented bath lotion sold as alcohol has become one of the worst such incidents in modern Russian history. Initial reports gave death tolls around 49–55; later local media raised the number to at least 58, with dozens more hospitalized and many in critical condition. Irkutsk regional health minister Oleg Yaroshenko warned that nearly half of those still alive have little chance of survival because they arrived at hospitals too late after ingesting large doses. Victims ranged from 25 to 62 years old and included a doctor and a kindergarten teacher; many bodies were found at home, indicating victims had no time to seek help. Survivor accounts describe drinking what seemed like vodka but later waking blind and paralyzed. Labels on the confiscated product falsely claimed it contained ethyl alcohol; tests showed it contained toxic methanol, which the body metabolizes into formaldehyde and formic acid, causing blindness, organ failure, and death. Police discovered an illicit workshop producing the contaminated lotion and various bootleg vodkas and have detained several suspects and seized hundreds of liters of product. Analysts note surrogate alcohol consumption is common in Russia amid poverty and sanctions, worsening risks from illicitly produced drinks.

Rush Limbaugh on his radio show mocked the Republican establishment for being “shocked” by Rick Santorum’s three-state wins, calling them insulated from grassroots sentiment. Limbaugh rejected media claims that conservative voters were simply following his lead, insisting Santorum’s success reflected genuine dissatisfaction with Mitt Romney and Santorum’s appeal as an uncorrupted conservative. He defended his audience as thoughtful, warned the GOP not to dismiss voters’ choices as his influence, and said he wasn’t surprised by Santorum’s victories. Limbaugh has avoided endorsing to preserve credibility but had earlier remarked that “everybody is guilty” of some transgression except Santorum. 

After wins in Missouri, Minnesota and Colorado, Santorum spoke to pastors in McKinney, Texas, clarifying he is not running to be “pastor in chief” while urging clergy to be more active. He emphasized defending the nation’s moral foundations, criticized the Obama administration over religious-freedom and contraception policy, and lamented political costs of speaking on moral issues. Santorum shared personal stories—his late son and daughter Bella’s struggle with Trisomy 18—drew strong emotional support, and raised funds in Texas while condemning intolerance toward those opposing same-sex marriage.

Marianne and Erin Krupa of Montclair, N.J., along with two other women, have sued Richard J. Badolato, commissioner of the New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance, arguing that the state’s infertility insurance mandate discriminates against lesbian couples. New Jersey law requires most major insurers to cover medically necessary infertility treatments, defining infertility in terms that presume heterosexual intercourse — the inability to impregnate another person, the inability to carry a pregnancy to live birth, or failure to conceive after one or two years of unprotected sex depending on age. Plaintiffs and their lawyer, Grace Cretcher of Beranbaum Menken, contend that this wording excludes nonheterosexual women and forces them to pay out of pocket for costly procedures like artificial insemination and in vitro fertilization (IVF), treating them as second-class citizens. 

The Krupas say they have spent roughly $50,000 on treatments, endured multiple miscarriages and painful medical complications, and still face reduced or denied coverage. After initial denials from Horizon, Erin appealed and later received some coverage only after severe complications and a doctor’s intervention; the couple exhausted allotted cycles and continued treatment at their own expense. Another plaintiff, Sarah Mills, reports using credit cards and anticipating loans to continue treatment after denial of coverage, describing emotional strain and fear of accumulating debt. 

Medical experts quoted say the mandate’s language creates a discriminatory double standard that limits access to optimal care when insurance would determine what treatments patients can afford. Fifteen states require fertility coverage; California and Maryland have updated mandates to be sexual-orientation neutral. New Jersey legislators have proposed bills to redefine infertility to include a physician’s determination, but those measures have not advanced from committee. The Department of Banking and Insurance declined to comment on the pending litigation. The plaintiffs seek damages for treatment costs and systemic change so same-sex couples receive equal insurance coverage for fertility care.

The Justice Department and FBI have launched the largest post-conviction forensic review in U.S. history to determine whether flawed microscopic hair and fiber analysis by the FBI Laboratory led to wrongful convictions or deserves new trials. The review covers all FBI hair and fiber examiners’ work since at least 1985 and may reach earlier cases if records exist. It was prompted by a Washington Post investigation that reported department officials had long known forensic problems existed but had not comprehensively reviewed or notified affected defendants. The review will be assisted by the Innocence Project and the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers.

Early findings reveal systemic failures: of 28 examiners in the hair-comparison unit, 26 overstated matches in ways favoring prosecutors in more than 95 percent of reviewed trials, according to the Innocence Project and NACDL. The probe has identified roughly 2,500 cases with declared hair matches, including about 32 death-row defendants; many defendants were never informed. Where possible, federal authorities are offering new DNA testing and will drop certain procedural objections to appeals. But biological evidence is often lost, and only some states explicitly allow appeals based on recanted expert testimony or new science.

The review has exposed longstanding gaps in forensic standards and oversight: the FBI lacked written standards for hair testimony until 2012, and many examiners trained hundreds of state and local analysts to testify similarly. Lawmakers and forensic experts have urged root-cause analysis and structural reforms, including stronger scientific standards and removing crime labs from prosecutorial control. Critics say the scandal underscores how courts admitted scientifically unsupported testimony for decades, producing a “mass disaster” of potentially wrongful convictions that will be difficult to remediate.

The Congressional Budget Office released a report offering over 100 deficit-reduction options, several of which would reduce or restructure military and veterans’ pay and benefits. These options, intended to inform lawmakers negotiating a new debt-cutting deal, include capping military pay raises, increasing TRICARE fees, restoring limits on concurrent receipt, narrowing VA compensation eligibility, and tightening Individual Unemployability (IU) benefits.

CBO suggests capping annual basic pay raises at 0.5 percentage points below civilian wage growth could save about $25 billion from 2015–2023; critics warn it could harm recruitment, retention, and future retirement payouts. Raising TRICARE costs for retirees—by adding initial out-of-pocket costs and higher cost-sharing for TRICARE-for-Life users or increasing fees for working-age retirees—could save billions but might discourage preventive care. Restoring the ban on concurrent receipt of retired pay and VA disability pay could save $108 billion but would reduce income for many disabled retirees and ignores distinctions between longevity pay and compensation for service-connected injury. Narrowing the VA’s broad “service-connected” standard or eliminating compensation for certain conditions could save about $20 billion, while restricting IU benefits for older veterans could save $15 billion. CBO frames these as options, not recommendations, acknowledging trade-offs between fiscal savings and veterans’ welfare.

Joy Milne, a 65-year-old woman from Perth, Scotland, has prompted new Parkinson’s research after she realized she could detect a distinctive odor associated with the disease. Milne first noticed a subtle musky smell from her husband Les years before he developed visible symptoms; he was diagnosed with Parkinson’s at 45 and died at 65. She later encountered the same scent on other people with Parkinson’s after joining Parkinson’s UK, and mentioned it to researchers, who took her observation seriously.

Researchers at Edinburgh University tested Milne using t-shirts worn by six people with Parkinson’s and six without. She correctly identified all six Parkinson’s samples and initially marked one control as positive; that man was diagnosed with Parkinson’s eight months later, meaning Milne had effectively been 12/12 correct. Scientists hypothesize that biochemical changes in skin secretions such as sebum produce a disease-specific odor early in Parkinson’s. Identifying the molecular signature of that odor could lead to a simple diagnostic test—potentially a forehead swab—that would transform diagnosis and enable timely treatment and clinical trial recruitment.

Parkinson’s UK is now funding collaborative research in Manchester, Edinburgh, and London to study roughly 200 people with and without Parkinson’s. Swabs will be analyzed molecularly and smelled by Milne together with olfactory experts from the food and drink industry. Charity leaders stress that an objective, early diagnostic test would be life-changing: it would replace largely observational diagnosis methods used since the disease was first described in 1817, allow earlier intervention, better monitoring, and improve opportunities for affected people to access research and treatments. Milne hopes her accidental discovery will help others beginning their Parkinson’s journey.

California secessionists, organized under the Yes California or “Calexit” banner, can now begin collecting the roughly 585,407 signatures needed to place a nationhood proposal on the November 2018 ballot after the state attorney general approved the measure’s language. The movement surged on social media after Donald Trump’s 2016 victory and taps into long-standing separatist sentiments—similar to past southern secession talk after Barack Obama’s election—amplified by a contentious national outcome. Supporters argue California’s distinct cultural attitudes and progressive policies on immigration and the environment, combined with its enormous economy (comparable to France’s GDP) and status as a “donor state” to the federal government, make independence conceivable. They contend Trump-era national policies and threats—such as withholding funds from sanctuary jurisdictions—have intensified desire for autonomy. California already has strong protections limiting cooperation with federal immigration enforcement and legislators are considering further restrictions, strengthening perceptions of a de facto sanctuary state.

Despite publicity and an estimated 7,000 volunteers mobilizing for signatures, the path to secession is nearly impossible. If the initiative makes the ballot, a simple majority would amend the state constitution to authorize a 2019 independence referendum—but that referendum’s ground rules demand 55 percent approval and at least 50 percent turnout among registered voters, a hard threshold given past midterm turnout. Even a successful California vote could not lawfully effect secession without a U.S. constitutional amendment requiring two-thirds congressional approval and ratification by three-fourths of states; unilateral secession has been tried only once, with catastrophic results. Ultimately, Calexit functions more as a symbolic protest against Trump-era policies and a lightning rod for political fury than a viable prospect for statehood.

Newly released, heavily redacted documents have intensified scrutiny of New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie after they linked senior aides and Port Authority appointees to the September closures of lanes leading to the George Washington Bridge. The shutdowns caused days of severe traffic congestion in Fort Lee, delayed emergency responders, and sparked accusations that the lane closures were politically motivated retaliation against the town’s Democratic mayor, Mark Sokolich, who did not endorse Christie’s reelection. Christie, a likely 2016 presidential contender, denied prior knowledge of any plan to close lanes and expressed outrage at being misled by a staff member, saying the behavior was “unacceptable” and promising accountability, though his office would not confirm whether anyone had been or would be fired.

The documents, turned over by Port Authority official David Wildstein under subpoena and obtained by The New York Times and other outlets, show intimate discussions among Christie’s staff, Port Authority appointees, and his campaign about how to react as the scandal unfolded. An August 13 email from deputy chief of staff Bridget Kelly — “Time for some traffic problems in Fort Lee” — and Wildstein’s “Got it” reply have become central. When New York appointees reopened the lanes after four days, Wildstein and Kelly expressed panic; Wildstein allegedly assured her that David Samson, Christie’s chosen Port Authority chairman, was “helping us to retaliate.” The pair worked with gubernatorial spokesman Michael Drewniak to craft public statements blaming a traffic safety review and asserting contact with Fort Lee police.

Two Port Authority officials, Wildstein and Bill Baroni, resigned in December after testifying they had violated protocols and concealed plans. Other aides, including former campaign manager Bill Stepien, appear in emails but are not directly linked to ordering the closures. The controversy threatens to damage Christie’s reputation as a straight-talking leader and complicates his national ambitions.

Less than 200 km from New Delhi, Indian authorities ended a week-long standoff by arresting Sant Rampal, a 63-year-old self-styled guru, at his fortified Hisar ashram in Haryana. Rampal faced contempt charges and a 2006 murder case; he repeatedly ignored court summonses and was accused of using followers to resist arrest. The attempt to detain him sparked violent clashes between police and devotees, with images of petrol bombs, gunfire, stones, tear gas, water cannons and bulldozers dominating Indian television. At least six people—including four women and an 18-month-old child—died; authorities said the bodies showed no visible injuries and suspected deaths from illness due to lack of timely medical care. More than 200 people were injured and about 270 arrested on charges including rioting, illegal detention, attempt to murder and waging war against the state. Police evacuated over 16,000 followers by bus and train before the arrest, though thousands reportedly remained on site during the operation. Rampal denied charges and rejected allegations that he used followers as human shields, saying they acted on their own and that he regretted the deaths. The episode revived difficult questions about handling religiously motivated camps: law enforcement must balance force with restraint, using police and paramilitary units rather than the army, to minimize bloodshed while enforcing the law. Comparisons to past sieges such as Waco and Operation Blue Star highlighted how faith-driven loyalty can complicate state intervention. The Punjab and Haryana High Court had criticised authorities’ earlier reluctance to arrest Rampal, setting a final deadline that precipitated the operation.

The Tarrant County Medical Examiner ruled that a 52-year-old Dallas woman, identified as Rosa Ayala-Goana (family has also used Rosy Esparza), died of “multiple traumatic injuries due to [a] fall from roller coaster” after being ejected from the Texas Giant at Six Flags Over Texas. Her time of death is listed as 7 p.m., and the manner is “accident.” Witnesses said she expressed concern that the safety bar had not fully engaged before the 14-story ride began. Six Flags closed the Texas Giant and said it will remain closed until internal and external investigations, including assistance from Gerstlauer Amusement Rides (manufacturer of the coaster’s cars), are complete; Arlington police will defer to those inquiries. Company officials offered condolences but no further details. State records show the Texas Giant had 14 reported injuries from 2008–2013, mostly minor; experts note such self-reported figures may understate problems and don’t capture near-misses. The ride, originally wooden and renovated in 2010 into a steel-hybrid coaster, had its most recent safety permit in February after an annual engineering inspection. As a precaution, Six Flags also temporarily closed a similarly constructed coaster, Iron Rattler, pending the outcome of the investigation.

A Nebraska faith ministry has launched a fundraising campaign to buy out four beer stores in Whiteclay, a tiny village bordering the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, where alcoholism and related problems are rampant. The Lakota Hope street ministry, led by founder Bruce BonFleur and his wife, aims to raise at least $6.3 million to close the shops that sold 3.5 million cans of beer in 2015 despite Whiteclay having only about a dozen residents. The reservation is officially dry and struggles with high rates of fetal alcohol syndrome and extreme poverty. BonFleur says he has spoken with the store owners and believes they are willing to sell; the stores are already under growing legal and political pressure as state liquor regulators plan to review their licenses soon. The ministry’s campaign, called “B.O.B.S. Whiteclay P.L.A.N.” (Buy out the beer stores; Promote the Lakotas as a nation), envisions replacing the outlets with constructive community spaces—ideas range from a roller skating rink or movie theater to parks and a Makerspace that would offer art supplies, equipment, mentoring, and an online storefront to help local artists earn income. Reaction in the community is mixed: longtime activists like Frank LaMere oppose paying owners off and want licenses revoked, while protest leader Olowan Martinez cautiously supports redevelopment if the buyout succeeds. Some locals fear bootleg sales or displaced drinking and question whether closing the shops would reduce harm or merely shift it elsewhere. The Nebraska Liquor Control Commission is scheduled to discuss the licenses amid concerns about inadequate local law enforcement; some county officials have even recommended license renewal to avoid potential increases in intoxicated driving.

While jogging in Chicago, actress-comedian Amy Schumer stopped into a Six Corners Mattress Firm seeking to use the restroom. Store employee Sagine Lazarre let her, then later was surprised when the jogger asked which mattress was her favorite and said she wanted to buy it for her as thanks. Schumer purchased the roughly $2,000 mattress on the spot; Lazarre only realized afterward that her benefactor was the Snatched star after seeing the name on the credit card and Googling her. Lazarre, who had recently moved into a new apartment in Woodridge with her daughter, called the gift “amazing” and “mind blowing.” She recognized Schumer’s comedy but was stunned during the interaction and even suspected a prank at first. Schumer mentioned she lives in New York and visits Chicago often. WGN News reported the story after speaking with Lazarre; requests for comment to Schumer and her representatives were not returned.

An anonymous hacker calling themselves “thedarkoverlord” has followed through on a threat to leak episodes of Orange Is the New Black season five after allegedly failing to extort Netflix. The hacker posted the season premiere and, shortly before 6 a.m. ET Saturday, uploaded the first 10 episodes to the Pirate Bay in ten files totaling about 11.46 GB. Variety and the Associated Press could not independently verify the authenticity of the files. Netflix’s official release date for season five is June 9; the streamer may consider moving that date now that much of the season has surfaced online. Netflix said a production vendor used by several major studios had its security compromised and that authorities including the FBI are involved. Thedarkoverlord claims to have also obtained unreleased content from ABC, Fox, National Geographic and IFC, apparently stolen in a late-2016 attack on post-production firm Larson Studios; the hacker said only the first 10 of 13 OITNB episodes were taken because the heist occurred before the final three existed. The hacker demanded an unspecified ransom and taunted Netflix publicly, warning other networks they can still pay to avoid leaks. Netflix did not immediately comment on the ransom specifics. Industry observers note that leaks of a flagship title like OITNB could hurt Netflix’s subscriber growth and stock, especially as the company expected strong additions in the April–June quarter. The series had been renewed through season seven and remains one of Netflix’s most-watched originals.

Global stocks rose as U.S. benchmarks hit record highs following President-elect Donald Trump’s surprise victory, which has boosted expectations of deregulation and fiscal stimulus, including infrastructure spending. The Dow traded above 19,000 for the first time, with the S&P 500, Nasdaq and Russell 2000 also at historic levels. Gains were broad-based across Europe and Asia—France, Germany and Britain climbed, while Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong, Australia and China all rose. Oil prices were firmer on growing expectations OPEC will agree production cuts. The Chinese yuan weakened, and the dollar strengthened versus the yen as markets weighed stimulus optimism against policy uncertainty.

Sinéad O’Connor’s recent appearance at Ireland’s Bray Music Festival reignited debate about fame, aging and public scrutiny. Once instantly recognizable for her shaved head and haunting voice after her 1990 breakout with “Nothing Compares 2U,” the 44-year-old drew shock online for a changed look—short dark hair, glasses, a mesh top and a fuller figure. Media outlets and commenters ridiculed and speculated, with many snide remarks about weight gain. Critics framed the reaction as schadenfreude: O’Connor’s outspoken past and refusal to conform to pop-star aesthetics have long made her a target, and seeing her depart from the gamine image unsettles observers who equate worth with youthful looks. The coverage overlooked context: O’Connor is a mother of four, has struggled publicly with bipolar disorder, has spoken about medication-related weight changes, and emphasizes that she’s no longer the same young pop star. Despite periods out of the limelight, she’s continued recording and touring, and her voice remains powerful and emotionally resonant. The episode underscores a broader cultural problem—celebrity bodies are unfairly policed—and serves as a reminder that aging, health and self-acceptance deserve respect rather than ridicule.

Autumn Veatch, 16, survived for two days in rugged North Cascades terrain after a small Beech A-35 plane she was in with her step-grandparents, Leland and Sharon Bowman, crashed. Found Monday after hiking out, she reached Highway 20 via the Easy Pass trail, caught a ride with hikers to Mazama, and was driven by a motorist to the Mazama Store, where employees called 911. She was taken to Three Rivers Hospital in Brewster with minor burns, dehydration, exhaustion and treatable rhabdomyolysis; officials said her injuries were non-life-threatening. In a brief phone call from the hospital to her father and friends, Autumn said the plane crashed after flying into clouds, that she tried to pull the Bowmans from the wreckage, and that they seemed to have died on impact or shortly after. Authorities had not confirmed the condition of the Bowmans as of Monday night, and the downed plane had not yet been located. Searchers used Autumn’s account and cellphone data to narrow the search area; difficult terrain of rocks, trees and steep ridges complicates recovery efforts. Rescuers celebrated Autumn’s survival but continued searching for the aircraft and the other occupants, while family and friends expressed relief and sorrow.

Republican leaders abruptly withdrew from White House debt-ceiling negotiations Thursday, centering their protest on the inclusion of tax increases. House Majority Leader Eric Cantor first announced he would not attend a scheduled meeting, saying Democrats’ insistence on revenue measures made talks untenable until President Obama “resolve the tax issue” personally. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell and Sen. Jon Kyl amplified the message, questioning Obama’s engagement and portraying him as favoring higher taxes over a bipartisan deficit plan. Cantor’s exit, arranged conspicuously via The Wall Street Journal, surprised some GOP colleagues and came after a Boehner-Obama meeting. Democrats accused Cantor and Kyl of abandoning GOP negotiators to avoid owning potential revenue deals; several Democrats suggested the departures signaled an expectation that revenue would be necessary. With Kyl’s subsequent withdrawal, no Republican remained at the negotiating table, leaving four Democrats and Vice President Biden’s team to continue talks amid rising pressure as the debt deadline looms.

The American Customer Satisfaction Index (ACSI) finds U.S. car owners are growing less satisfied, with average satisfaction falling to 79/100 — a 3–3.7% drop and the lowest level since 2004. The decline follows a record number of safety recalls (nearly 64 million vehicles last year), which, along with rising new-car prices (average about $33,453), have heightened owners’ expectations and frustrations. ACSI director David VanAmburg and others note that stronger post-recession pricing and fewer incentives make buyers feel sticker shock, while increased defects and lengthy recall repairs dent perceived quality.

Luxury brands fared best: Lexus leads at 84, followed by Acura, Lincoln and Mercedes-Benz (83). BMW, Subaru and Toyota scored 82; Hyundai, Buick, Cadillac, Honda, Mazda and Volkswagen also scored at or above 80. Import brands dominate higher ratings, with 77% of above-average scores going to Japanese, Korean and European makes.
