Domestic performance slipped, largely driven by Fiat Chrysler (FCA) nameplates. Fiat ranks lowest at 73, with Chrysler (74) and Jeep (75) also anchoring the bottom. ACSI’s survey covered owners of vehicles 6 months to 3 years old, capturing recent ownership experiences; analysts advise buyers to consider long-term trends when choosing brands. Fiat Chrysler disputes the findings, citing other studies that praise certain Fiat models.

President Trump warned he would be “very angry” if Republicans fail to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act, saying he’s waiting for the bill to reach his desk and reiterating GOP promises to undo what he called a “failed” experiment. His comments, excerpts from an interview with Pat Robertson airing on the 700 Club, followed earlier, more sanguine remarks in June that a failure would be “okay.” Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell is scrambling to corral moderates and conservatives before a planned push, extending the Senate’s session into August and urging colleagues to drop procedural objections so debate can proceed. McConnell and allies argue that blocking a motion to proceed would deny the public a chance to see and vet Republican ideas.

Key conservative holdouts include Sens. Ted Cruz and Mike Lee, who insist on an amendment allowing insurers to sell any plans so long as at least one complies with federal rules. Critics—including insurers’ trade group—warn that such a change could siphon healthy people into bare-bones plans, driving up premiums for older and sicker enrollees and harming those with pre-existing conditions. McConnell can afford only two defections; several senators (Rand Paul, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski among them) are seen as possible no votes or remain undecided. Leadership has limited disclosure of bill details to minimize opposition, but GOP senators are negotiating tweaks—led by Sens. Mike Rounds and Bill Cassidy—to make the Cruz-Lee idea more palatable and secure enough votes to advance the measure.

Country music legend Merle Haggard, a Bakersfield native and pioneer of the Bakersfield sound and Outlaw Country movement, died at 79 on his birthday, surrounded by family at his home near Redding, California. His manager Frank Mull and son Ben Haggard confirmed he succumbed to pneumonia after repeated hospitalizations for double pneumonia that forced recent tour cancellations with Willie Nelson. Haggard had 40 No. 1 hits, numerous awards, and was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1994; his song "Mama Tried" was recently added to the National Recording Registry. Friends and peers, including Willie Nelson, expressed deep sorrow at his passing.

San Francisco’s experiment with dockless electric scooters unraveled as City Attorney Dennis Herrera on Monday sent cease-and-desist letters to Bird, Lime and Spin, citing numerous complaints that riders were operating on sidewalks, without helmets, and leaving scooters obstructing pedestrian right-of-way. The devices had proliferated rapidly since March, backed by venture capital and echoing the dockless bike boom; Bird in particular became ubiquitous. Herrera provided photos showing scooters strewn on sidewalks and people riding without helmets, calling them a “public safety hazard.” California law requires helmets, prohibits sidewalk riding and carrying passengers; companies ask users to agree to those rules via app tutorials, but enforcement proved weak. Supervisor Aaron Peskin worked on a municipal permitting scheme mirroring stationless bike rules to give SFMTA and Public Works authority to permit operators and remove unpermitted devices; fines would begin at $125 per scooter. The Board of Supervisors unanimously approved legislation requiring permits, user education, and removal powers; SFMTA hopes to open permitting by May 1. Companies responded with mitigation steps: Bird piloted a requirement that riders photograph parked scooters, and Lime pledged to distribute helmets, enhance outreach, require end-of-ride parking photos, and emphasize that sidewalk riding is illegal. Critics note scooters are often less dangerous than private cars, while some residents and disabled users complain about impediments and safety risks. The city seeks regulation rather than an outright ban.

Democratic strategist James Carville dismissed several GOP presidential contenders during an appearance on Good Morning America, delivering blunt assessments of Rick Perry, Mitt Romney and Herman Cain. Carville argued Romney’s main liability is perceived inconsistency—calling him a “serial wind sock”—but suggested little else stands between Romney and the nomination. He declared Herman Cain a “national distraction” who will not be the Republican nominee. Carville was most scathing about Rick Perry, saying Perry should “get out of the race and go back to Texas,” arguing Perry is “in over his head”: unable to debate, give speeches, hold positions, or handle television, despite campaign cash. Carville also mocked a Cain adviser seen smoking in a campaign video, saying the aide appeared “drunk or stoned.” The segment, with minimal pushback from host George Stephanopoulos, reinforced Carville’s partisan critique that Cain’s appeal is fleeting and Perry’s campaign is effectively finished, leaving Romney as the likely frontrunner.

The document covers three loosely connected topics: the Internet Archive’s “No More 404” crawls, Heinz’s new Super Bowl ad and campaign, and the rising popularity—and controversy—of mayonnaise.

The Internet Archive is conducting crawls to capture pages as they are created and the pages they reference, preserving the versions live when content was written. The aim is to replace or accompany broken links with archived snapshots so references remain meaningful even if original pages change or disappear.

Heinz released its first Super Bowl commercial in 16 years: a feel-good, lightly comic spot from Cramer-Krasselt that riffs on “If You’re Happy and You Know It,” using bottle-bottom slaps instead of claps. The :30 TV ad (with a :50 online cut) mixes Americana visuals and comic beats, ending with a grandmother squeezing the last of her ketchup. Tagged #ifyourehappy and headlined “Where there’s happy, it has to be Heinz,” the spot is part of a “Show Us Your Heinz” campaign. Special bottles with QR codes link to the campaign through Feb. 23, offering more than $400,000 in prizes including five grand-prize trips to major sporting events.

Separately, mayonnaise recently surpassed ketchup in U.S. sales—about $2 billion versus $725 million—sparking debate. Chefs praise mayo’s versatility and flavor base, while detractors deride its texture and composition, often substituting aiolis, Greek yogurt, or other spreads. The divide shows mayo’s role as both a beloved staple and a polarizing ingredient in modern kitchens.

San Francisco’s defense dominated New Orleans in a 36-32 playoff thriller, setting the tone early with hard hits and opportunistic play. Donte Whitner’s crushing hit on Pierre Thomas knocked the running back out and signaled the 49ers’ physical approach; Whitner also drew a pass-interference penalty earlier. San Francisco forced five Saints turnovers, including Dashon Goldson’s first-quarter interception that ended Drew Brees’ NFL-record streak of 226 postseason passes without an INT. Tarell Brown added another interception, while special teams’ Blake Costanzo and Madieu Williams each forced fumbles. Justin and Aldon Smith pressured Brees all day—Justin recording a sack in the third quarter—while Patrick Willis and NaVorro Bowman stifled the run. Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio’s “old-fashioned” scheme and Jim Harbaugh’s first-year leadership propelled the Niners (14-3) back to the NFC championship at Candlestick against the Giants. Alex Smith’s late touchdown to Vernon Davis sealed the comeback.

In the AFC, the Baltimore Ravens advanced with a 20-13 win over the Houston Texans by protecting the ball and creating turnovers. Baltimore intercepted rookie T.J. Yates three times, including an Ed Reed clincher near the goal line, and benefited from a physical defense led by Reed and Ray Lewis. Arian Foster rushed for 132 yards—the first 100-yard postseason rusher vs. Baltimore—but Houston’s turnovers and missed opportunities cost them. The Ravens, 9-0 at home, will face New England next Sunday.

Vanilla Ice (Robert Van Winkle) revealed he dated Madonna in 1991 when he was 24 and she was 33, calling the relationship "exciting" and saying she was a "great lover." He said he ended the relationship after Madonna published her 1992 coffee-table book Sex, which included intimate photos of them and images suggesting she was with other men. Feeling betrayed and humiliated, Vanilla Ice described the book as "disgusting and cheap," saying it made him look like a product and appeared pornographic; he broke up with her despite her claim she hadn’t slept with those men. He currently appears on the U.K. show Dancing on Ice.

A U.S. federal judge has ruled that the company long collecting royalties on "Happy Birthday To You" does not hold a valid copyright in the song’s lyrics, finding that the original 1893 transfer of rights covered only the melody and specific piano arrangements. The tune originated as "Good Morning to All," written by Kentucky sisters Mildred and Patty Hill; the familiar birthday lyrics surfaced later in the early 20th century. Judge George H. King concluded that Clayton F. Summy Co., which acquired rights from the Hills and whose successor Warner/Chappell later bought those assets, never acquired copyright to the words. Warner/Chappell had enforced licensing fees—reportedly about $2 million a year—charging filmmakers, advertisers and others for commercial uses since buying the catalog in 1988.

The lawsuit was brought by filmmakers and musicians who had been charged licensing fees while making a documentary and other projects. Plaintiffs seek restitution of licensing fees paid over decades; the court will address damages later. King’s 43-page opinion explored historic publications and contracts, finding the 1935 copyright registration ambiguous and focused on arrangements rather than lyrics, and observed conflicting evidence about authorship of the birthday words. Warner/Chappell said it is reviewing the opinion and considering options, likely appeal. Legal experts caution that the ruling applies in the U.S. and that elements of the song could remain protected elsewhere, so commercial users should still seek counsel before using it internationally.

Researchers in the UK report that “temperature contagion” is real: merely observing someone else experiencing cold can produce small, measurable drops in an observer’s peripheral skin temperature. In a PLoS ONE study, 36 healthy volunteers sat in a 21°C room while watching short videos of actors placing one hand into steaming (warm), iced (cold), or neutral water. Participants’ left and right fingertip temperatures and heart rates were recorded continuously. Viewing cold-hand videos produced a modest but reliable reduction in observers’ hand temperatures (mean right hand ≈ −0.1°F, left hand ≈ −0.4°F), while warm and neutral videos produced no change; heart rate remained unchanged. The effect was stronger for cold stimuli and more pronounced in observers’ left hands. Researchers suggest the asymmetry may reflect greater perceptual salience of ice versus fleeting steam and note prior work showing decreases in skin temperature are easier to elicit than increases.

The authors link this peripheral physiological mirroring to emotional contagion and perception–action mechanisms (e.g., mirror neuron systems), proposing that top-down processes can recruit thermoregulatory pathways to simulate another’s state and support empathy and social understanding. Individual differences in empathy predicted sensitivity to temperature contagion in a complex way: empathic concern correlated positively, while a broader emotional-empathy score correlated negatively. The study extends evidence for autonomic contagion, relates to historical and clinical data on volitional temperature changes, and suggests potential relevance for social-cognitive disorders.

Reactions, a short video series from the American Chemical Society, explores the chemistry behind the perfect grilled cheese. Cheese melting behavior depends largely on its protein structure: casein proteins form spherical micelles held together by calcium and containing fat. These micelles normally repel one another due to negative surface charge, but lactic acid produced during aging reduces pH and weakens those repulsive forces. As acidity increases, micelles clump into chains that trap water and fat, producing a gooey mass when heated. Aging and acidity therefore determine whether a cheese melts smoothly or breaks into oily, curdled clumps. The video highlights an ideal pH window—about 5.3 to 5.5—for grilling cheeses; above that range cheeses may not melt fully, and below it they can release oil and collapse. Practical takeaways: choose cheeses with the right acidity and moisture—Gouda, Gruyère, and Manchego are recommended, and mild cheddar is preferable to sharp cheddar because it has a higher pH and more forgiving texture when heated. The segment also points viewers to The Kitchen as Laboratory and other sources on milk proteins and cheese texture, and offers cooking tips in a related “We Tried It” investigation to help you turn ingredient knowledge into a reliably gooey grilled cheese.

A full translated letter from British diplomats in Quito warns Ecuador that granting Julian Assange asylum would not change Britain's legal duty to extradite him to Sweden under the European Arrest Warrant and the Extradition Act 2003. London urged Quito to continue diplomatic talks to agree a joint text allowing Assange to leave the Ecuadorian Embassy voluntarily; it said safe passage requests after asylum would be refused and suggested revoking the embassy’s diplomatic status under the Diplomatic and Consular Premises Act as a last resort. Ecuador announced it would grant Assange asylum, citing violated rights and fear of possible U.S. persecution, turning the case into a diplomatic standoff. Britain insists police will arrest Assange if he steps outside the embassy for breaching bail. Protests and arrests occurred outside the embassy. Legal and practical options for smuggling him out are viewed as unworkable, and critics warn that breaching diplomatic protections would set a dangerous precedent.

Retired South Korean Lieutenant General I.-B. Chun warned at a London forum that a U.S. or allied military strike on North Korea would face an extraordinarily entrenched, ideologically driven defense that differs sharply from recent wars in Iraq or Afghanistan. Drawing on nearly four decades in the South Korean military and his experience living close to the Demilitarized Zone, Chun described North Korea as “one huge barracks” where the Kim cult and juche ideology produce deep indoctrination. He cited defectors’ retained loyalty, neighborhood surveillance groups that punish entire families for dissent, and pervasive military training from adolescence as evidence that North Koreans would resist fiercely. Chun outlined concrete military challenges: extensive underground infrastructure, a massive standing army of 1.3 million with 7.7 million reserves, 200,000 special forces, large conventional artillery aimed at Seoul, chemical and biological stockpiles he estimated at 2,500–5,000 tons, and a thousand aging jets possibly used in suicide-style strikes. He assessed recent ICBM tests as close but not yet reliable for a heavy nuclear warhead to reach Washington, suggesting a diplomatic window remains if Pyongyang acts now. Chun nevertheless insisted that peace requires preparation for war and that military action must be a last resort—“like having a toothache and having to pull out all of your teeth.” Other speakers noted North Korea’s cyber capabilities and Beijing’s strategic tolerance of a nuclear North as preferable to greater U.S. presence in Asia. While Chun expressed confidence in U.S.-ROK alliance airpower prevailing in a conflict, he warned the human, political, and humanitarian costs of any invasion would be immense and unpredictable.

Former South African President Nelson Mandela, 94, was hospitalized late Wednesday for a recurring lung infection and is "responding positively" to treatment, the presidency said. President Jacob Zuma asked South Africans and the world to pray for "Madiba" and respect the family’s privacy while doctors continue observation and care. Mandela, who was conscious when admitted, has a long history of respiratory illness dating to tuberculosis contracted during 27 years in prison on Robben Island; he spent nearly three weeks in hospital in December for a lung infection and gallstone surgery. World leaders, including President Obama, sent well wishes. Mandela, South Africa’s first post-apartheid president and Nobel laureate, remains a revered global statesman.

NOAA has released the first high-resolution images from its newly launched GOES-16 (formerly GOES-R) satellite, marking a leap forward in weather observation and forecasting. Launched from Cape Canaveral on Nov. 19, GOES-16 carries the Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI), which delivers imagery with four times the spatial resolution, five times greater coverage, and three times the spectral channels of its predecessors. The ABI can produce a full-disk Earth image every 15 minutes, a continental U.S. image every five minutes, and can target regional areas as often as every 30 seconds, enabling rapid, detailed monitoring of severe weather, hurricanes, wildfires, volcanic eruptions, and other high-impact events.

The initial images, taken Jan. 15 and publicly released later that month, showcase clear views of the Western Hemisphere, including dust plumes off Africa, storms over Argentina, cloud movement on the U.S. West Coast, a Northeast storm system, Mexico and Central America with pinpointed fires and smoke, and a Feb. 7 tornado outbreak over Louisiana. NOAA emphasizes these richer images will improve the timeliness and accuracy of watches, warnings, and forecasts, potentially saving lives. GOES-16, positioned about 22,300–23,000 miles above Earth in geostationary orbit, will be operational by November 2017 as either GOES-East or GOES-West. Its successor, GOES-S (GOES-17), is undergoing testing and will follow after launch to expand the enhanced GOES constellation.

Legendary singer Pat Boone, 79, faces an arrest warrant after failing to appear in court in a lawsuit tied to condos sold aboard an unlaunched luxury cruise liner. The builder of the ship lost a suit brought by some investors and was ordered to pay over $800,000 in attorneys’ fees. Lawyers, still unpaid, have attempted to recoup fees from buyers of the ship’s condos, and Boone was subpoenaed to testify. He did not attend the hearing, prompting the judge to issue the warrant; Boone was reportedly vacationing in Hawaii with his wife. Boone tells TMZ the warrant is a misunderstanding: his only involvement was agreeing to be a spokesperson for the project once it launched, which hasn’t happened, and he knows little about the development. He says he plans to appear in court but doubts his testimony will assist the litigant. He also joked about the publicity surrounding the incident.

This ProPublica–Houston Chronicle investigation chronicles a steep decline in outcomes at Baylor St. Luke’s Medical Center’s once-celebrated heart transplant program, revealing avoidable complications, leadership turnover, and institutional failures that harmed patients and families. Between mid‑2014 and 2016 the program’s one‑year survival rate lagged well behind national averages — about 85% versus 91.4% — meaning roughly twice as many patients died within a year than expected. Federal regulators cited the program for significantly worse‑than‑anticipated outcomes and threatened to cut Medicare funding; the hospital later submitted a corrective plan.

The report documents multiple catastrophic cases: patients whose donor hearts failed, surgeons who inadvertently stitched through major veins, prolonged recoveries lasting months, device malfunctions in operating rooms, and emergency measures that nonetheless resulted in strokes, organ failure, or death. Several experienced clinicians left amid the turmoil; new leadership choices, including hiring Dr. Jeffrey Morgan as surgical director in 2016, proved controversial. Colleagues reported surgical errors early in his tenure, and two malpractice suits from his previous institution surfaced. Hospital leaders defended hiring decisions and said patient mix and sicker, older referrals partly explain outcomes; they also assert survival rates improved after program changes. Critics counter that peer centers have achieved better results with comparable or sicker patients.

Staff cuts and ownership transitions after the hospital’s 2013 sale to a national chain are portrayed as contributing factors, as are failures in transparency and communication: families recount being uninformed or receiving conflicting explanations, and some received massive bills. The piece balances patient and family narratives with medical records, staff interviews, regulatory data and hospital responses, portraying a historic program struggling to reconcile its storied legacy with current performance and patient safety failures.

"Zebra" is American medical slang for leaping to an exotic diagnosis when a common explanation is likelier, based on Dr. Theodore Woodward’s aphorism: "When you hear hoofbeats, think of horses not zebras." It cautions trainees against availability bias and attraction to novel, striking cases, though clinicians remind that rare diagnoses must be considered and definitively ruled out when criteria permit. The obscure-diagnosis term fascinoma exists. Misdiagnosis examples include attributing necrotic skin lesions to recluse spider bites where such spiders are absent. Some conditions labeled zebras, like Ehlers–Danlos and hypermobility syndromes, are underdiagnosed and have adopted the zebra as a symbol. The concept appears in pop culture (Scrubs, House, SVU, a Harvard parody video). Related aphorisms: Sutton’s law, Occam’s razor, Leonard’s law, and Hickam’s dictum. A separate news item: two Universoul Circus zebras briefly escaped in West Philadelphia in 2015 but were safely recaptured with no injuries.

Marc Anthony and model Shannon de Lima announced they are divorcing after two years of marriage, issuing a joint statement Dec. 18 saying they "mutually and amicably decided to end our two-year marriage" and asking for privacy. Reports said the split was decided earlier this year because they "didn’t have enough in common." Anthony filed for divorce in Florida Dec. 16. Rumors swirled after Anthony kissed ex‑wife Jennifer Lopez at the Latin Grammys; sources suggest Anthony may still have feelings for Lopez, though no reconciliation is confirmed.

The document contains two distinct pieces: a positive reaction to a Budweiser Super Bowl commercial and a discussion about the NFL’s awkward use of Roman numerals for future Super Bowls. The Budweiser ad, called "Flash Fans," surprised two Port Credit, Ontario beer-league hockey teams by staging a faux documentary and then filling an empty arena with passionate, body‑painted fans. Players’ delighted reactions captured the joy of amateur sport, reminding viewers that many professionals began as everyday players who love the game. The writer praises the ad as inspirational marketing that honors grassroots passion.

The second piece examines a marketing dilemma: Roman numerals, long used to stylize Super Bowls, will make Super Bowl L (2016) look like an oversized "L"—a pop-culture sign for "loser." The NFL values the mystique Roman numerals add, but brand experts and advertisers suggest creative fixes—emphasizing Arabic numbers for the 50th, redefining L as "learning," "love," or "largest," or designing city-specific logos. The article traces the "L" gesture’s rise in pop culture and notes the league is already planning for the anniversary while weighing numeral aesthetics, merchandising concerns, and possible host-city tie-ins.

California Gov. Jerry Brown signed AB 60, allowing immigrants in the U.S. illegally to obtain state driver’s licenses, making California the latest of at least 11 states to adopt such measures. The licenses, expected by late 2014 or early 2015, will carry a special designation and a notice that they are not federal ID and cannot prove work or benefits eligibility. Supporters — including police chiefs, insurance authorities and immigrant advocates — say the law will improve road safety by ensuring drivers are tested and insured, reduce fear of driving and prevent car impoundments that led to immigration screenings. Critics warn of identity fraud, possible conflict with federal law, and disputed safety outcomes seen in other states. State officials estimate 1.4 million applicants in three years and $140–$220 million in initial processing costs, partly offset by fees. The law includes anti-discrimination protections and bans using the license as evidence of immigration status; implementation details and acceptance by other entities remain uncertain.

A reported ownership group led by former Florida Governor Jeb Bush and ex-New York Yankees captain Derek Jeter has the winning $1.3 billion bid to buy the Miami Marlins from longtime owner Jeffrey Loria, according to people familiar with the deal. The sale remains unofficial until a contract is signed and approved by Major League Baseball; MLB vetting is required for all investors and for Bush as the intended “control person.” The buyer group reportedly includes at least five investors whose identities and South Florida ties haven’t been disclosed. Competing bids came from Wayne Rothbaum and a group led by Tagg Romney. Loria, who bought the team in 2002 for about $158 million, is expected to leave with more than $1.2 billion. The Marlins, who play in Marlins Park (opened 2012), have struggled with attendance—averaging roughly 24,313 this season, 24th of 30 clubs—and with low regional TV revenue; their Fox deal pays about $20 million annually, the lowest in MLB and expires after 2020. The new ownership could seek stadium naming rights and a reworked TV contract to boost revenues. Reports say Bush intends to retain manager Don Mattingly and president of baseball operations Mike Hill, while Jeter plans an active role. MLB commissioner Rob Manfred has expressed support for a former player like Jeter joining ownership. The transaction could take months to finalize amid MLB approval and other details.

Wild birds feeding on winter berries are sometimes getting intoxicated after early frosts and thaws promote fermentation in fruit. When starches in berries convert to sugars and thawed fruit is invaded by yeast, alcohol forms. Species that gorge on such berries—Bohemian waxwings, robins, thrushes and others—can become uncoordinated, fly into buildings and cars, stumble on roads, or suffer fatal collisions. Wildlife and law-enforcement officers have received multiple reports of disoriented birds; some communities even temporarily house stunned waxwings in animal units until they sober. Experts note that most affected birds are only mildly tipsy and recover within hours, though young or inexperienced birds are more vulnerable. Documented fatalities and postmortems have sometimes revealed alcohol in liver samples, but routine testing is rare because alcohol dissipates quickly and leaves no distinctive lesions. Birds adapted to berry diets often have relatively large livers that help detoxify alcohol, but urban settings with hard surfaces and glass increase the risk of lethal impacts. Advisers recommend placing an intoxicated but uninjured bird in a ventilated box to sober up and using window decals to reduce strikes. Researchers suggest that changing weather patterns—more frequent freeze-thaw cycles tied to warming—may increase occurrences, though longer-term data are needed.

This collection assembles news and social media material produced in the run-up to the September 25, 2017 Kurdish independence referendum in Iraqi Kurdistan. It gathers reporting from regional news outlets aligned with different Kurdish political parties as well as posts by influential individuals, capturing competing narratives, party positions, official statements, campaign messaging, and public reaction. Materials document the Kurdistan Regional Government’s push for a vote on statehood, messaging emphasizing historical grievances, self-determination, and security concerns; political rivals’ calculations and critiques; and responses from local communities and minority groups. The archive reflects regional media practices, partisan framing, and efforts to shape domestic and international opinion, including appeals to the U.S., EU, and neighboring states. It also records social media dynamics: mobilization, debate, patriotic appeals, and alarm at potential economic and military repercussions. Together the sources illuminate the political context, strategic aims of Kurdish parties, fears of escalation with Baghdad and neighboring countries, and the information environment that shaped voter perceptions and the referendum’s domestic and international fallout.

Nancy Kotowski, Monterey County superintendent of schools, acknowledged this week that she had a long-term intimate relationship with the Rev. Mike Manning, a prominent Southern California priest now on leave after the liaison was reported by the San Bernardino Sun and published in The Herald. Kotowski said the physical aspect of their relationship ended about three years ago, though she described their bond as a committed, 30-year partnership and objected to media labeling it an “affair.” Manning, 70, and Kotowski, 59, are second cousins who did not grow up together; he entered the seminary at 14 and the pair reconnected when she was in her late 20s. Family members have known of and accepted their closeness, Kotowski said, and have welcomed them at gatherings. The couple discussed whether Manning should leave the priesthood to marry, communications the Sun reported. Kotowski said she supports Manning’s vocation and that they are now embracing celibacy, acknowledging the struggle but saying they honor God’s calling. She hopes the revelation will prompt dialogue within the Catholic Church about obligatory clerical celibacy and whether it is right for all people. Kotowski said she has done nothing illegal and declined to detail the duration of the relationship’s physical phase or past relationships.

In his state-of-the-nation address ahead of a March presidential election, Vladimir Putin showcased a suite of new Russian strategic weapons and framed them as a decisive response to Western policies and alleged attempts to contain Russia. Speaking to lawmakers and elites, he presented video and animations of intercontinental ballistic missiles, hypersonic systems, a nuclear-powered cruise missile, and autonomous underwater drones, claiming these weapons render existing missile defenses “useless.” Putin highlighted the RS-28 Sarmat ICBM, the Avangard hypersonic glide vehicle, the Kinzhal air-launched hypersonic missile, and a purported “doomsday” submarine-launched torpedo/cruise system; he asserted some systems are already tested or deployed. He warned that any attack on Russia or its allies would be treated as a nuclear attack and met with instantaneous response.

The militarized portion of the two-hour speech followed domestic policy pledges — to halve poverty, raise life expectancy, boost pensions, expand daycare, and double urban infrastructure spending — though funding details were scarce. Putin portrayed Russia as possessing “huge potential” but needing to improve living standards, noting about 20 million Russians remain below the poverty line. The address doubled as campaign messaging: with opposition leader Alexei Navalny barred and polls indicating broad support, Putin signaled strength to both domestic audiences and the West. Western officials downplayed surprises, saying Moscow’s capabilities are factored into assessments, while criticizing animations depicting attacks on U.S. soil as irresponsible. The presentation underscored renewed great-power competition in advanced weaponry and technology.

On November 23, 2015, Los Angeles Superior Court Judge William C. Ryan exonerated Luis Vargas, who had spent 16 years in prison after being convicted in 1999 for three sexual assaults. Vargas was sentenced to 55 years to life based largely on eyewitness identifications; he consistently maintained his innocence. While incarcerated, Vargas learned about a string of similar attacks by an unidentified serial offender dubbed the “teardrop rapist” — named for a teardrop tattoo under the eye — and contacted the California Innocence Project (CIP), which took his case in 2012.

CIP pushed for modern DNA testing of evidence from one victim’s rape kit and clothing. In 2013 the tests detected genetic material from at least two contributors: the victim and a profile matching the teardrop rapist, not Vargas. Prosecutors later acknowledged that the advanced technology used to exclude Vargas’ DNA was not available in the late 1990s. They also noted inconsistencies in eyewitness accounts: some victims earlier were less certain in lineups and described two teardrop tattoos, while Vargas had only one faded mark. The district attorney’s office conducted an extensive review and ultimately approved Vargas’ release.

At the exoneration hearing Judge Ryan ordered Vargas released, though he was briefly transferred to federal custody because his green card had been revoked after his conviction; his attorneys expected his return home soon. Family members expressed relief and long-awaited hope — Vargas’ daughter described the emotional toll his incarceration took on her life and her wish for him to be present for future milestones. The court’s action acknowledges a wrongful conviction tied to eyewitness error and evolving DNA science and highlights the ongoing search for the still-unidentified teardrop rapist, suspected in dozens of Los Angeles-area assaults.

NBC's rebooted Celebrity Apprentice, now hosted by Arnold Schwarzenegger, premiered Monday but failed to win its 8 p.m. timeslot, drawing about 4.9 million viewers across the two-hour telecast, according to Nielsen. That was behind ABC’s The Bachelor (nearly 6.6 million) and CBS’s four-sitcom block (over 6 million). Schwarzenegger’s debut represented a steep drop from Donald Trump’s last season hosting in 2014–15, when the show averaged 7.6 million viewers and a substantially higher 18–49 demo rating—roughly 46% higher than Monday’s numbers. NBC heavily promoted the post‑Trump relaunch and weathered controversy over Trump retaining an executive producer credit and stake in the franchise, though he will reportedly be compensated by MGM. The premiere also faced tough competition from The Bachelor and the Penn State–USC Rose Bowl on ESPN, factors NBC acknowledged when comparing this launch to last year’s premiere, which lacked major sports competition. Early critical reviews of Schwarzenegger’s turn were mixed, but NBC noted the episode delivered a strong lead-in for the new game show The Wall, which retained most Apprentice viewers and performed well in the 10 p.m. slot among younger audiences.

A dam at the Germano iron-ore mine in Minas Gerais, southeastern Brazil, burst Thursday, sending clay-red mud and floodwaters down valleys and devastating nearby villages. Samarco, a joint venture of BHP Billiton and Vale, said the cause was not yet known and pledged to prioritise care and environmental mitigation. At least 15 people are believed dead and 45 missing, according to local reports, though official counts remained uncertain; other sources reported one confirmed death and dozens missing. Bento Rodrigues, about 7 km below the dam, and Paracatu de Baixo were heavily affected and about 600 residents were evacuated to higher ground. Rescue crews, police, firefighters and army units searched for survivors amid concerns about toxic tailings contaminating rivers. Authorities and company executives warned that fuller assessments would follow at daylight.

Jessica Simpson is engaged to former NFL player Eric Johnson, UsMagazine.com and her rep confirmed. The couple began dating in May; Johnson’s divorce from stylist Keri Johnson was finalized five months later. Simpson, 30, and Johnson’s relationship progressed quickly—he joined her for her 30th birthday in Italy—and she has publicly praised him as her best friend. She was spotted wearing a sizable ruby-and-diamond ring at a Kansas City mall and plans to spend Thanksgiving in New York while performing in the Macy’s Parade. The engagement news comes days after Simpson’s ex-husband Nick Lachey announced his engagement to Vanessa Minnillo. Family and friends expressed happiness for the pair; Simpson has said she’s longed for marriage and children and suggested she’s hopeful about planning a future with Johnson.

The author announces the end of a beloved project as they complete a master’s thesis and prepare to relocate for Ph.D. studies. They express deep gratitude to readers for shaping their life and work, noting the project’s unexpected, delightful impact. The Feminist Ryan Gosling book remains available and the site will stay online; the author invites anyone curious about future personal projects to follow them via their website. They close with a warm farewell: “Goodbye, girl, and thank you.”

The piece then shifts to Ryan Gosling’s heartfelt Golden Globes acceptance speech for Best Actor in a Motion Picture — Musical or Comedy for La La Land. Gosling combined signature wit with sincere thanks, joking about being mistaken for Ryan Reynolds before turning to acknowledge his partner Eva Mendes. He praised her for holding the family together while he filmed: raising their daughter, being pregnant with their second child, and supporting her brother during his battle with cancer. Gosling credited her sacrifices for enabling his achievement, dedicated the award to his daughters Amada and Esmeralda, and wished to honor the memory of Mendes’s brother, Juan Carlos Mendez, who died the previous April. The speech sparked widespread online affection, with many fans reacting emotionally and praising Gosling’s warmth, generosity, and romantic sincerity.

A federal judge in Virginia ruled Tuesday that federal law protects a transgender student who sought to use the boys’ bathroom at his school, denying the Gloucester County School Board’s request to dismiss the student’s lawsuit. The decision is a significant win for Gavin Grimm, a transgender male who began challenging his high school’s bathroom policy in 2015 after being barred from using the boys’ restrooms; he has since graduated. Grimm’s case contends that the school board’s policy violated his constitutional rights and federal protections against sex discrimination. Represented by the ACLU, Grimm argued that Title IX — the federal law prohibiting sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programs — covers discrimination based on gender identity. U.S. District Judge Arenda L. Wright Allen concluded that Grimm has sufficiently pled a Title IX claim, specifically under a gender-stereotyping theory, after reviewing the facts and relevant legal analyses. The judge also ordered the parties to schedule a settlement conference. The case has moved through the courts for several years: Grimm took the matter to an appeals court, and a federal appeals court in Chicago issued a similar ruling in a different but related challenge in May 2017. The most recent decision sends the dispute back to the lower court level for further proceedings rather than dismissing Grimm’s claims.

An experienced walker, 53-year-old Jane Wilson of Stockport, died after falling from Snowdonia’s Tryfan while she and her husband tried to find a safe route down using a smartphone app, an inquest heard. The couple, who had been scrambling and walking together for six years, decided against continuing to the summit at dusk on 25 March and instead traversed the mountain’s west face—known for loose rock and steep sections—relying on Mr Wilson’s Ordnance Survey app. Mr Wilson said his wife went a short distance ahead to check the route; after asking if it was safe and agreeing they would proceed only together, he heard exclamations and a rockfall. Realising she had fallen, he moved to a safer ledge, raised the alarm, and was later guided to safety by Ogwen Valley Mountain Rescue Team members. Rescuers found Mrs Wilson’s body about 150 metres below, having tumbled 20–30 feet down a vertical cliff into an area called Notch arrete; she had a fractured skull and multiple severe injuries. The coroner returned a verdict of accidental death. Rescue team leaders and mountain safety spokespeople stressed the limitations of smartphone maps—smaller, less detailed displays and battery risk—and advised carrying paper maps and using compass navigation. Teams noted Tryfan often generates incidents, warning that although the North Ridge is a superb scramble, it can be hazardous to the unwary and that lighter footwear may be unsuitable for such rough terrain.

Rocker Ted Nugent visited President Donald Trump at the White House Wednesday night with former Alaska governor Sarah Palin and musician Kid Rock. Palin posted photos of the Oval Office meeting showing her speaking with Trump and Jared Kushner, and the group posing near a portrait of Hillary Clinton. Nugent celebrated the visit on Facebook with boastful, inflammatory language; he has a history of vitriolic remarks about Hillary Clinton, Barack Obama and others, including past calls for violence. The meeting underscores the Trump White House’s decision not to release visitor logs and prompted widespread online reaction.

Vice Admiral Scott A. Stearney, a 36-year Navy veteran and native of Chicago, was found dead at his residence in Bahrain on December 1, 2018, while serving as commander of U.S. Naval Forces Central Command, U.S. Fifth Fleet and Combined Maritime Forces. The Navy said there was no evidence of foul play; the Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the Bahraini Ministry of Interior are cooperating in the investigation. Chief of Naval Operations Admiral John Richardson called the news devastating, describing Stearney as a decorated professional, devoted husband and father, and a good friend. Rear Admiral Paul Schlise, deputy commander of Fifth Fleet, assumed command immediately, with Vice Admiral Jim Malloy en route to Bahrain to take interim command. 

Stearney graduated from the University of Notre Dame with a B.A. in Economics, was designated a Naval Aviator in 1984, and graduated from the Navy Fighter Weapons School. He held an M.S. in National Resource Strategy from the National Defense University. Operationally, he flew the F/A-18 Hornet in multiple strike fighter squadrons, commanded VFA-131 and Carrier Air Wing Seven aboard USS Dwight D. Eisenhower, and served in Kabul as chief of staff for Joint Task Force 435 and Combined Joint Interagency Task Force 435. Ashore, he was an instructor at the Navy Fighter Weapons School and held senior staff roles including aide to the chief of naval operations and director of operations at U.S. Central Command. His flag commands included Joint Enabling Capabilities Command, Strike Force Training Atlantic, Carrier Strike Group 4, Navy Warfare Development Command and director of operations, CENTCOM. He earned the Defense Superior Service Medal, Legion of Merit and Air Medal, logging over 4,500 mishap-free flight hours and more than 1,000 carrier arrested landings.

Ninety-three-year-old American World War II veteran Norwood Thomas flew from Virginia to Adelaide after reconnecting online with his wartime sweetheart, 88-year-old Joyce Morris, and the pair reunited for the first time since 1945. They first met in London in 1944 before Thomas left for Normandy; letters and a misunderstanding ended their contact and both later married others. Widowed and divorced respectively, they were reunited last year when Morris’s son found Thomas’s name and relatives arranged Skype calls that revived long-dormant feelings. Their reunion, featured on Australian television, was funded by hundreds of donations and supported by Air New Zealand. They embraced warmly and plan to spend Valentine’s Day together, reflecting on what might have been.

A review of student responses to the National Assessment of Educational Progress (the Nation’s Report Card) finds many U.S. students feel insufficiently challenged and not well engaged in rigorous learning. Analysis of the student questionnaire shows substantial shares reporting schoolwork is “too easy”: 37% of fourth-graders for math, 29% of eighth-grade math students, and large proportions saying civics and history are often or always too easy (51% and 57% in eighth grade; roughly mid-50s for twelfth-grade civics and history). Many students report low engagement in reading and writing: about a third of eighth-graders read fewer than five pages daily and rarely write long answers; 39% of twelfth-graders hardly ever write about class readings. Science and technology access is limited—72% of eighth-grade science students say they are not taught engineering and technology. Large fractions of middle- and high-school math students do not feel they are “always or almost always” learning, and many students report difficulty understanding teachers’ questions. Disadvantaged and minority students are less likely to have access to rigorous opportunities and to understand instruction compared with higher-income and white or Asian peers. The authors urge stronger, more challenging standards (e.g., Common Core), expanded use and study of student surveys to inform teacher evaluation and policy, and sustained reforms to ensure equitable, high-quality learning for all students.

An eight-year-old Canadian boy developed temporary allergies to fish and nuts after receiving a blood transfusion while being treated for medulloblastoma, a new case report in the Canadian Medical Association Journal describes. The child, who had no prior food allergies, experienced anaphylaxis within 10 minutes of eating salmon a few weeks after transfusion, and four days later had another reaction after eating a chocolate peanut butter cup. Skin-prick testing and blood work suggested the boy had acquired immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies to salmon and peanuts—antibodies that mediate allergic reactions. Investigation traced the plasma-containing blood product to a donor who reported allergies to nuts, fish and shellfish; the donor’s remaining donations were removed and the person was barred from future donations. Physicians treated the boy with antihistamines and advised avoidance plus carrying an epinephrine injector. Importantly, because the boy’s own immune system had not produced the IgE, clinicians expected the allergy to be temporary; indeed, by about five months IgE levels to salmon and peanut were undetectable and his parents successfully reintroduced those foods under medical guidance by six months. Transfusion-acquired allergies are rare but previously reported: other cases have documented temporary allergy transfers via plasma. Blood services in the U.S. and Canada do not screen donors for allergy history beyond excluding those with active symptoms on the donation day, since IgE testing of donors would not reliably predict clinical allergies and could unnecessarily reduce the donor pool. Researchers urge clinicians to be aware of this phenomenon and call for more study to assess frequency and potential prevention strategies without compromising blood availability.

This piece stitches together two small but notable inauguration-era moments involving President Obama and others. First, it recalls a 2010 Wall Street Journal Magazine interview in which fashion designer Thom Browne criticized Obama’s wardrobe, saying the president “could be dressed so much better” and suggesting politicians avoid dressing above constituents’ expectations. Browne contrasted this with the Queen Mother, who maintained sartorial standards during wartime because the public wanted to see a figure who looked like a monarch. Second, the article recounts a 2013 inauguration flub: during the oath, Obama stumbled on the word “States,” starting “The office of the president of the United Sta—” and briefly hesitated. The piece links that moment to the 2009 incident when Chief Justice John Roberts misstated key oath wording, noting that despite rehearsal the tradition remained imperfect. The correct oath wording is provided for clarity. The article closes by inviting readers to contribute reactions or story ideas to the author, Alexander Abad-Santos.

The American Cancer Society (ACS) recommends cervical cancer screening begin at age 21 to detect cancers and, importantly, precancerous changes that can be treated. Women 21–29 should have a Pap test every three years; HPV testing is not recommended for primary screening in this group except as follow-up to abnormal Pap results. From age 30 to 65 the preferred approach is co-testing (Pap plus HPV) every five years; an acceptable alternative is Pap testing alone every three years. Women with compromised immune systems or in utero DES exposure may need more frequent screening per their health care teams. Screening can generally stop at age 65 for women with adequate prior screening and no history of serious precancers (CIN2/3), though those with such histories should continue for at least 20 years after the abnormality. Women who have had a total hysterectomy for benign reasons can stop screening; those with the cervix retained must continue. Annual screening is discouraged. HPV vaccination does not eliminate the need for screening. The ACS guidelines do not apply to women already diagnosed with cervical cancer, precancer, or HIV.

A new study published in Cancer finds U.S. cervical cancer mortality has been substantially underestimated because prior rates didn’t adjust for women no longer at risk after hysterectomy. After adjustment, death rates rose markedly—particularly widening racial disparities: the adjusted mortality is 10.1 per 100,000 for Black women versus 4.7 per 100,000 for White women. Researchers caution the data covered 12 states but likely represent national trends. Experts say the larger-than-recognized disparity likely reflects unequal access to screening, HPV vaccination, and care. Cervical cancer is largely preventable through screening and HPV vaccination, yet vaccination coverage remains low and many women lack access to recommended services, underscoring a need to improve prevention, screening access, and adherence to guideline-based care.

Qantas’ new in-flight safety video, introduced by Hollywood actor and airline ambassador John Travolta, has drawn criticism from some airline staff who describe it as “cringeworthy,” “corny” and “tacky.” The three-minute clip, shown before every domestic and long-haul flight, opens with Travolta in a pilot’s uniform saying, “This is your captain speaking — well, maybe not today,” and praising “the guys on the flight deck and the greater team” for safety. Several anonymous cabin crew and pilots have objected to Travolta fronting the message instead of a “real pilot,” suggesting that Captain Richard de Crespigny—who handled the QF32 emergency and saved 466 lives—would be a more appropriate choice. Crew members also resent being referred to as “the team,” calling the term demeaning and likening it to fast-food terminology, and worry the celebrity-led presentation trivializes the safety briefing, especially after recent aviation incidents. Qantas, however, says feedback has been positive from both staff and customers and describes the video as engaging. The debate underscores tensions between marketing choices that use celebrity appeal and operational staff preferences for professional representation in safety communications.

A late amendment to the House health care bill banning use of federal subsidies for insurance that covers elective abortions has energized antiabortion advocates and set up a major Senate fight. The provision, pushed by conservative Democrats and strongly lobbied for by Roman Catholic bishops, would bar abortion coverage in plans bought with newly created federal subsidies and in a government-run plan. Supporters call it a necessary safeguard against public funding of abortions; opponents warn it could reduce access by prompting insurers to drop abortion coverage from plans sold in the subsidized marketplace. Women could still pay out of pocket or buy separate riders, though analysts note few do and many avoid billing insurers for abortions. The amendment passed amid a fractious House debate, with 64 Democrats supporting it and many liberals promising to fight its inclusion in final legislation. Senate Democrats are now divided, and leaders anticipate a contentious debate as they reconcile House and Senate bills, which also differ on funding, a public-plan option, employer mandates and other key provisions.

A record $550 million Powerball jackpot is up for grabs, the largest in Powerball history and second-largest U.S. lottery prize ever, prompting huge public interest even though the odds of winning remain astronomically low. The chance of a single ticket matching the Powerball jackpot is about 1 in 175,223,510—marginally better than Mega Millions—making a win far less likely than many other rare events. For perspective, dying from a bee sting is roughly 1 in 6.1 million, dying from lightning about 1 in 3 million, drowning or other beach fatalities about 1 in 2 million, and a shark attack about 1 in 11.5 million. An amateur golfer making a hole-in-one is about 1 in 12,500, while consecutive holes-in-one sit at roughly 1 in 156 million—still slightly less likely than the Powerball jackpot.

Ticket sales have surged as the jackpot climbed; officials estimate Americans will have purchased more than $1 billion in Powerball tickets by drawing time, with some 105,000 tickets sold per minute and a roughly 60 percent chance that the winning combination will have been sold. Despite that, lottery officials caution there’s no guarantee of a winner in this drawing.

Winners’ real-life experiences underscore both the shock and challenges of sudden wealth. Mary and Brian Lohse, recent $202 million Powerball winners, went from financial strain and foreclosure threats to hiring lawyers and financial advisers, fielding unsolicited requests from strangers, and deciding to give back to their community (including helping fund a new high school football stadium). Advisors urge anyone who does win to immediately sign and secure the ticket, assemble a trusted team of lawyers and financial professionals, and delay public announcements to manage finances and privacy responsibly. The odds are long, but if luck strikes, careful planning is essential.

Actor Shia LaBeouf was caught on video headbutting a man during a heated altercation at the Hobgoblin pub in South London. The clash reportedly stemmed from insults about his girlfriend's mother; LaBeouf can be heard shouting, "What are you saying about my girl's mom? Are you f**king kidding me bro?" A woman—likely his companion—pleads for him to stop as the confrontation escalates. This incident adds to LaBeouf’s history of bar fights: he was involved in another brawl at the same pub in November 2012 and was beaten outside a Vancouver bar in 2011. Afterwards, an apparently intoxicated LaBeouf apologized, calling himself “super normal,” expressing remorse and insisting he reacts when people disparage his girlfriend’s mother.

John Mackey, Whole Foods’ CEO, argued against expanding government-run health care, warning of unsustainable deficits and likening Obama’s reforms to control akin to fascism (later calling that term a poor choice). He advocates market-based reforms: expanding high-deductible plans with Health Savings Accounts, equalizing tax treatment for individual policies, allowing interstate insurance competition, repealing coverage mandates, tort reform, price transparency, Medicare restructuring, and voluntary tax-deductible donations to help the uninsured. Mackey emphasizes individual responsibility for health, blaming obesity and lifestyle-related diseases for most healthcare costs and promoting plant-based, low-fat diets to prevent degenerative illness. He frames health care as a service best delivered through voluntary market exchanges, opposes government-imposed entitlement expansion, and champions consumer choice and employer/employee-directed benefit decisions.

A Wirecutter investigation and tests of children’s headphones found many models can reach unsafe volumes under certain conditions and that only a few reliably limit sound to safe levels. Audiologist Brian Fligor (WHO working group) advised comparing results to the widely used 85 dBA safety benchmark. The Wirecutter team used objective lab measurements (pink noise, pop tracks, LEQ) with an ear/cheek simulator and chose an iPod touch as a realistic loud source. They discovered most “volume-limited” kid’s headphones are passive: resistors in the cord reduce output but can be defeated by louder source devices or headphone amplifiers, so many sets can exceed safe limits. Active, digitally limited models are far safer in this regard.

The overall Wirecutter children’s pick was the Puro BT2200 ($99.99): Bluetooth, strong digital limiting when wireless, good sound, noise reduction features, and 18–22 hour battery life. Its wired cable must be plugged in correctly—reversed connectors can bypass limits and produce very loud output. Runners-up that stayed under 85 dBA despite cords included lower-cost models: Onanoff Buddyphones Explore ($29.99) favored by toddlers though outgrowable, and the JLab JBuddies Studio ($29.99) for ages 4–11.

Tests of ambient-noise isolation showed only four models provided meaningful blocking of backseat/airplane frequencies; in-ear models (Etymotic ETY-Kids3, Puro IEM200) performed best. The report emphasizes adults must monitor total noise exposure and that combining effective isolation with true electronic limiting is the safest approach.

Karl Smith, a 38-year-old inmate serving a 99-year sentence for a 2008 armed robbery and attempted murder, stunned a Chicago courtroom by confessing that he committed a 2003 murder for which his identical twin, Kevin Dugar, has been imprisoned since 2003. On the witness stand Smith told the judge, “I’m here to confess to a crime I committed that he was wrongly accused of.” The shooting killed Antwan Carter and wounded Ronnie Bolden after a gunman fired into a small crowd; Bolden later identified “Twin” — the street name used by the brothers — as the shooter. At trial in 2005 Dugar was convicted largely on eyewitness testimony and given a 54-year sentence despite no confession or physical evidence; one eyewitness had recanted at trial and another identified Dugar in a photo lineup that did not include Karl. The twins, who were extremely close growing up, frequently impersonated each other and remain almost indistinguishable today. Smith says he first admitted the killing to Kevin in a 2013 letter, repeated the confession in a signed sworn statement in 2014, and only recently revealed it in court. Prosecutors are skeptical, arguing Smith “has nothing to lose” by taking the blame after his own conviction was upheld and that his account doesn’t match independent eyewitness statements. If the judge finds Smith’s confession credible, Kevin Dugar could be granted a new trial; Judge Vincent Gaughan has not yet ruled. Their mother insists Karl is telling the truth.

Former first lady Michelle Obama, speaking Thursday at the American Institute of Architects’ annual conference in Orlando, used her first major post–White House appearance to describe adjusting to private life, rule out a future run for office, and emphasize ongoing public-service commitments. She said the harsh realities of politics — “the knives” and the toll on family — make her unwilling to ask her children to endure another campaign. She added that working outside elected office frees her from “political baggage” while still allowing substantial impact.

Obama spent 45 minutes in a Q&A discussing priorities she intends to pursue, especially girls’ education worldwide, citing her Let Girls Learn initiative, and pressing to combat violence against women and expand women’s access to healthcare. She and Barack Obama are also focused on plans for the Barack Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, considering building design and programming to benefit the city and beyond.

She avoided mentioning President Donald Trump directly, although she quipped about media coverage of his first 100 days and described restraining tears when saying goodbye to White House staffers on Inauguration Day. The Obamas have largely stayed out of the spotlight since January but promise continued public-service engagement.

Researchers have reported compelling new evidence linking Zika virus infection during pregnancy to severe fetal brain damage, strengthening concerns that the virus causes microcephaly. A case detailed in the New England Journal of Medicine involved a European woman who developed Zika-like symptoms at 13 weeks while living in Brazil. Early ultrasounds at 14 and 20 weeks were normal, but after she returned to Europe an ultrasound at 29 weeks revealed severe fetal abnormalities. An abortion was performed at 32 weeks and autopsy of the fetus showed striking neuropathology: microcephaly, a smooth brain surface lacking normal folds, calcifications indicative of inflammation, and fluid accumulation. High loads of Zika virus RNA and evidence of viral replication were found exclusively in brain tissue; the complete viral genome sequenced from the fetal brain matched strains circulating in French Polynesia (2013) and Brazil (2015). Extensive testing excluded other common infectious causes of congenital brain damage (dengue, yellow fever, West Nile, rubella, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis) and no genetic causes were identified, suggesting the virus preferentially targets neural tissue.

An accompanying editorial and other reports, including CDC findings of Zika in brain tissue from miscarriages and newborn deaths, consider this among the strongest biological links yet between Zika and congenital central nervous system injury. Separate research from Brazil found alarming ocular abnormalities in about one-third of 29 infants with microcephaly, further indicating combined brain and eye damage. Public health agencies have warned pregnant women to avoid Zika-affected areas; no vaccine or specific treatment exists. While this evidence greatly increases the plausibility that Zika causes fetal brain malformations, definitive proof of causality, the role of asymptomatic maternal infections, trimester-specific risks, and precise mechanisms require larger, long-term studies and animal models.

Michael Brown’s funeral in St. Louis on Aug. 25 drew thousands who mourned the 18-year-old and pressed for change in policing, voting and community accountability. Held at Friendly Temple Missionary Baptist Church, the service filled a 2,500-seat sanctuary and overflow rooms, with roughly 2,000 more on church grounds. Brown’s closed casket, topped with a St. Louis Cardinals cap, stood beside large photos of him in cap and gown; he had been due to start vocational training to become an HVAC technician days after his death.

Family members and clergy remembered Brown as a “kind, gentle soul” with growing Christian faith and ambitions—he once told relatives “one day, the world will know my name.” His mother and father wrote moving letters read at the service. Relatives urged mourners to channel grief into civic action: Eric Davis called for voting to effect change, and speakers repeatedly urged peaceful protest and restraint so Brown’s name would not be associated with violence.

Civil rights leaders, celebrities and officials attended, including the Rev. Al Sharpton, the Rev. Jesse Jackson, Spike Lee, Sean Combs, Martin Luther King III, and White House representatives. Sharpton emphasized the need to address policing nationally and warned against actions that would tarnish Brown’s memory. Brown’s great-uncle, Rev. Charles Ewing, framed his death as part of a larger cry for justice alongside other national tragedies.

The funeral came amid ongoing legal and federal probes into Officer Darren Wilson’s shooting of the unarmed teen on Aug. 9—a case marked by conflicting witness accounts and controversy over a police-released convenience-store video. Outside, the town showed signs of calm: protesters honored a “day of silence,” schools reopened with staff trained to support stressed students, and a solemn procession accompanied Brown’s burial at St. Peter’s Cemetery. The service blended intimate remembrance with a clarion call for reform, healing and civic engagement.

A new study links a pineapple pesticide that contaminated Hawaii’s milk supply in the 1980s to brain changes associated with Parkinson’s disease. Researchers led by Dr. Robert Abbott examined 449 Japanese-American men from a long-term aging study in Hawaii who reported their midlife milk intake and later donated their brains for autopsy. Men who drank more than 16 ounces of milk daily at baseline had roughly 40 percent fewer neurons in the substantia nigra—a brain region whose cell loss characterizes Parkinson’s—compared with men who drank less than two cups per day. The investigators detected residues of heptachlor epoxide, a breakdown product of the organochlorine insecticide heptachlor, in a higher proportion of brains from heavy milk drinkers (90 percent) than from non-milk drinkers (63 percent). Heptachlor had been used in Hawaiian pineapple farming and likely entered the cows’ feed; most agricultural uses were banned in the U.S. by 1988, though related compounds persist in the environment. The cell loss appeared decades after exposure, consistent with Parkinson’s long prodromal phase. Intriguingly, the association between milk consumption and neuron loss was not present among men who had ever smoked, echoing prior observations that smoking is linked to lower Parkinson’s risk by an unclear mechanism. Authors caution that the study shows association, not definitive causation: milk intake was measured only once, milk samples were unavailable, and alternative explanations exist. Experts and the Parkinson’s Disease Foundation emphasize the need for further research into environmental exposures, diet, and Parkinson’s risk. The findings underscore concerns about persistent pesticides entering the food chain and suggest diet and contamination merit deeper study as contributors to neurodegenerative disease.

Two sets of human remains were found this week in a rural area south of Kansas City, Missouri. One set has been positively identified as 21-year-old Jessica Runions, who disappeared Sept. 8, 2016 after leaving a party. Her burned 2012 Chevy Equinox was found Sept. 10, 2016; a man arrested shortly afterward, 28-year-old Kylr Yust, has been charged with knowingly burning the vehicle and pleaded not guilty. With Runions’ remains recovered, the Kansas City police are treating her death as a homicide and working with medical examiners to determine cause of death. A second set of remains was found nearby; authorities say identification could take weeks or months and have not confirmed whether they belong to 17-year-old Kara Kopetsky, who vanished in May 2007 and has been a long-standing person of interest in relation to Yust. Kopetsky’s family reported she had filed a protective order against Yust days before her disappearance. No charges connect Yust to Kopetsky’s case at this time. The families of Runions and Kopetsky have joined forces—searching, raising awareness with “Justice for Jessica and Kara” signs, and supporting one another—vowing to pursue answers and justice. Yust is in custody; his attorney says he faces only the vehicle-burning charge for now and is preparing for trial. Law enforcement continues searching the scene for additional evidence.

John Sandoval, 52, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and was sentenced to 25 years in prison, with five years of parole, for the 1995 killing of his estranged wife, Kristina “Tina” Tournai Sandoval. His sentence was backdated to August 2010, when he was first convicted of first-degree murder; that conviction had been overturned on appeal in 2016 and a new trial was imminent. As part of a plea deal reached three weeks before the retrial, Sandoval led investigators to Tina’s remains, which were exhumed from beneath the grave of World War II veteran Arthur Hert at Sunset Memorial Garden cemetery in Greeley. Her body was tightly wrapped and found about 21 inches below the bottom of the grave. Cemetery workers had unknowingly buried the veteran over her remains in 1995.

Tina disappeared after a planned meeting with Sandoval on Oct. 19, 1995. Despite circumstantial evidence—Sandoval was the last person seen with her, had fresh scratch marks, and had acted as a convicted peeping Tom and stalker—the case went cold because authorities could not locate a body. Sandoval initially remained silent for 22 years; prosecutors say he only disclosed the burial location to avoid life imprisonment. The district attorney and family wrestled with accepting a plea that reduced Sandoval’s sentence but allowed recovery of Tina’s remains. The family ultimately agreed, citing the emotional toll and their desire to reclaim and bury Tina properly. Authorities exhumed Hert’s casket temporarily with the veteran’s family’s consent and later reinterred him with full honors.

Prosecutors continue to investigate specifics of Tina’s death; the coroner’s forensic autopsy had not yet determined cause of death at the time of the plea. Family members described Tina as brilliant and loving, and expressed relief that her remains were found so they can finally lay her to rest, while condemning Sandoval as her murderer.

A large Chinese study suggests drinking very hot tea greatly raises esophageal cancer risk—but primarily in people who also smoke or drink alcohol. Researchers followed about 456,000 adults aged 30–79 who were cancer-free at baseline for roughly nine years. Participants reported their tea-drinking frequency and perceived temperature as “warm,” “hot,” or “burning hot,” along with tobacco and alcohol use. Overall, hot or burning-hot tea alone was not linked to higher cancer risk. However, among daily alcohol drinkers and regular smokers, consuming burning-hot tea daily was associated with up to a fivefold increase in esophageal cancer compared with people who drank tea less than weekly. For smokers, daily boiling-hot tea doubled risk versus infrequent tea drinkers. The investigators and outside experts propose that repeated thermal injury from very hot liquids may damage the esophageal lining, increasing inflammation and cell turnover or impairing barrier function, thereby making tissue more susceptible to carcinogens in smoke and alcohol. The study is observational and relied on self-reported tea temperature, a key limitation. Prior research and a 2016 review have linked beverages hotter than about 65°C (149°F) to esophageal cancer. Authors emphasize that avoiding tobacco and excessive alcohol remains the most important prevention strategy, and that people who do not smoke or drink heavily likely do not need to stop drinking tea.

The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear challenges from Kansas and Louisiana seeking to bar Planned Parenthood and similar providers from state Medicaid programs, leaving in place several federal appeals court rulings that protect those providers. The petitions did not concern federal funding for abortions—which is already prohibited—but state attempts to exclude clinics that provide abortions (with privately funded abortion services) from receiving Medicaid reimbursements for other care, such as cancer screenings, prenatal services, contraception and ultrasounds. Three conservative justices—Clarence Thomas, Neil Gorsuch and Samuel Alito—dissented, saying the Court should resolve conflicting lower-court rulings and that patients in different circuits now face unequal rights. Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh joined the four liberal justices in declining review, signaling an institutional desire to avoid high-profile, politically charged disputes this term and preserve the Court’s nonpartisan reputation after contentious confirmation fights. The cases stem from 2015 undercover videos that claimed Planned Parenthood profited from fetal tissue sales; investigations later found no wrongdoing, but several states nonetheless moved to defund affiliates. Planned Parenthood, which says abortions are a small share of its services, argued the exclusions were unlawful discrimination tied to politics. Anti-abortion groups criticized the Court’s inaction and urged administrative or legislative routes to cut funding. The decision leaves a split among appellate courts intact: most circuits protect providers, while at least one has allowed states greater discretion.

Seattle’s 2018 sweetened-beverage tax—1.75 cents per ounce—was sold by then-mayor Ed Murray as a public-health and revenue measure to curb sugar consumption, fund programs like a year of free community college for public high-school graduates, and subsidize healthy food for low-income families. The tax covers sodas, sports drinks, kombucha and other sugary beverages that don’t list milk as the primary ingredient, and it has produced stark price increases for bulk buyers: a Costco case of Gatorade rose from $15.99 to $26.33. Retailers have reacted visibly—Costco has posted signs directing shoppers to stores outside Seattle that avoid the levy—and early evidence suggests cross-border shopping is already draining city sales and tax revenue, echoing outcomes seen in Philadelphia and Cook County, Illinois.

Critics argue the tax is regressive, hitting low-income families hardest, and that it fails to target all high-sugar drinks—Starbucks beverages, many milk-based drinks, and food-stamp purchases are exempt—creating perceptions of inconsistency and unfairness. Opponents range widely, from libertarians to labor unions and retailers, and in Cook County the backlash, litigation, operational confusion, and heavy industry spending led to repeal within months. Supporters, including public-health groups, maintain sugary-drink taxes are defensible tools to reduce obesity- and diabetes-related costs and improve public health.

The policy’s practical effects remain contested: proponents stress behavior change and long-term health gains, while critics point to immediate price shocks, lost local sales, legal fights, and potential harm to businesses and low-income consumers. Debate continues regionally—Washington lawmakers have reintroduced a statewide soda-tax bill—reflecting polarized views on whether such measures improve health or simply redistribute spending and economic activity.

Salt Lake City police shot a male who officers say was wielding a broomstick late Saturday evening, critically wounding him and triggering several hours of unrest downtown. The incident occurred around 8 p.m. near a homeless shelter adjacent to a shopping center and movie theater. Authorities say officers were called to break up a fight; when they arrived they found a man striking another person with a broomstick and tried to intervene. According to Detective Ken Hansen of the Unified Police Department, the man attempted to attack an officer, and one or both responding officers fired, striking the man twice in the torso. He was hospitalized in critical condition Sunday morning. Investigators have not released the victim’s identity or confirmed his age; accounts conflict, with bystanders and some news reports identifying him as a teenager while Hansen said he was older than 16. Details such as the number of shots fired, distance between officers and the victim, whether the broomstick was modified, and whether the victim had any other weapon remain unclear. After the shooting, bystanders became hostile, shouting obscenities and throwing rocks and bottles at police. Salt Lake City called for aid from neighboring departments—Unified, West Valley City, Sandy and University of Utah police—bringing nearly 100 officers, some equipped with riot shields, to the scene. Officers barricaded four blocks, detained multiple people, and closed a TRAX light rail stop, briefly disrupting transit for nearby Utah Jazz game attendees; trains resumed service around 11 p.m. Police have not released the officers’ identities and said the investigation is ongoing, with more details to be released later.

Emojipedia acknowledged criticism of several 2018 sample emoji designs and issued updates. After release of 157 new emojis, feedback prompted revisions to the skateboard, DNA, and lobster images. Skateboard legend Tony Hawk advised redesigning a dated board; the updated emoji is modeled on his board and simplified for clarity at emoji size. The DNA double helix was corrected from left‑handed to the scientifically standard right‑handed twist. Outcry from Maine residents and others over the lobster’s missing pair of legs led Emojipedia to add two legs and tweak the tail. Emojipedia kept a four‑heart smiling face despite its three‑heart name; final vendor designs may vary.

The United States and China — the world’s two largest economies, energy consumers and greenhouse-gas emitters — jointly announced ambitious post‑2020 climate targets, recognizing that neither can solve global warming alone. Together they produce about 40 percent of global emissions, so coordinated action is essential to building momentum toward a strong international agreement in Paris in 2015. The pledge follows a year of bilateral cooperation through the U.S.–China Climate Change Working Group and is intended to encourage other nations to submit ambitious contributions at upcoming U.N. negotiations, beginning in Lima.

The U.S. commitment: reduce net greenhouse‑gas emissions 26–28 percent below 2005 levels by 2025, roughly doubling the pace of reductions compared with 2005–2020 and putting the country on a long‑term trajectory toward roughly 80 percent cuts by 2050. The target is presented as ambitious but feasible, grounded in sectoral analysis and expected to deliver public‑health, air‑quality and energy‑security benefits. It builds on President Obama’s earlier 2009 goal of a 17 percent cut by 2020; the U.S. is on track to meet that target, aided by rapid expansion of renewables (wind tripled, solar increased tenfold) and EPA proposals to limit carbon from existing power plants.

China’s commitments: to peak CO2 emissions around 2030 — sooner if possible — and to raise the share of zero‑emission energy (renewables and nuclear) to about 20 percent of total consumption by 2030. Achieving that share would require deploying roughly 800–1,000 gigawatts of additional low‑carbon generation, an amount comparable to China’s existing coal capacity and nearly equal to current U.S. generation capacity.
