The joint announcement signals a breakthrough in climate diplomacy, with former adversaries aligning to lead the global transition toward a low‑carbon economy and to spur a durable international climate agreement.

An Australian prospector has uncovered a remarkable 145-ounce (4.1-kilo) gold nugget worth more than $250,000 in Victoria’s famed Golden Triangle. The find, informally named “Friday’s Joy,” was detected only about 30 cm below ground in an area already believed to be worked over, underscoring that significant deposits can still be found in long-prospected regions. The finder, who wishes to remain anonymous, first mistook the object for rubbish or an old horseshoe and was astonished to realize its true nature. An experienced prospector of more than ten years, he was part of an agreement with friends to split proceeds from any large finds; he plans not to retire but to buy a van for travel and continued prospecting. After discovery he washed the nugget, wrapped it in foil and kept it overnight in his oven; it is now secured in a bank vault and a replica is being made ahead of a planned auction.

The nugget’s discovery was made with a Minelab metal detector, likely the GPZ 7000, which the company markets as a major advance in gold-detection technology using its Zero Voltage Transmission (ZVT) system. Minelab celebrated the user’s success, noting that the find highlights how much gold remains in Victoria. Friday’s Joy is comparable in value to notable Australian nuggets such as Cindy’s Pride and surpasses last year’s 87-ounce “Fair Dinkum,” found by Mick Brown and auctioned for $175,000. The story illustrates the passionate, technology-driven hobby of modern prospecting, where advanced detectors can still turn up life-changing discoveries.

Florida authorities ordered an emergency shutdown Wednesday of the Rehabilitation Center at Hollywood Hills after a power failure that disabled the facility’s air conditioning preceded the deaths of eight residents and the evacuation of 115 patients. Gov. Rick Scott directed the Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA) to issue a moratorium preventing the center from admitting new patients and demanded answers; AHCA and the Department of Children and Families were already investigating. Hollywood police opened a criminal probe.

The outage was linked to damage from Hurricane Irma. Nursing home administrator Jorge Carballo said a transformer-related power failure left the air system inoperable. An HVAC technician reported that a fuse controlling the unit popped during the storm and had not been replaced despite repeated calls to Florida Power & Light (FPL); he said restoring the fuse would take about 30 minutes once FPL acted. FPL noted the facility had not been identified as “top-tier” critical infrastructure in county planning, though portions of the building had power restored. The company said the event highlights gaps in emergency preparedness.

Three residents died at the facility and five others died after being transported to nearby hospitals. The deceased were identified by the Broward Medical Examiner as Carolyn Eatherly, Miguel Antonio Franco, Estella Hendricks, Betty Hibbard, Manuel Mario Medieta, Gail Nova, Bobby Owens and Albertina Vega. Causes of death are pending. Hospital officials reported many evacuees suffered respiratory distress, dehydration and heat-related problems; at least a dozen were in emergency care and officials warned the death toll could rise.

Larkin Community Hospital, adjacent to the nursing home and owned by the same interests, also evacuated 18 behavioral health patients. The Rehabilitation Center and its owners have a history of citations and at least one pending negligence lawsuit. Local authorities conducted welfare checks at dozens of other eldercare facilities; Memorial Healthcare set up a hotline for worried family members. Officials emphasized accountability if investigations show neglect.

Homeland Security Adviser Tom Bossert defended President Donald Trump’s controversial tweet that circulated a GIF of Trump body-slamming and punching a figure with the CNN logo superimposed, telling ABC’s This Week that “no one would perceive that as a threat.” Bossert, appearing with co-anchor Martha Raddatz, said he had seen the tweet for the first time on the show and argued that cable news often treats the president unfairly; he praised Trump’s use of Twitter and other social media as a way to speak directly to the public. Raddatz questioned whether the GIF was the kind of communication a president should use and suggested it could be seen as threatening. Bossert pushed back, asserting the president has a right to respond to what he characterized as biased coverage. The adviser’s comments drew sharp criticism on the program’s roundtable, notably from CNN contributor Ana Navarro, who accused Bossert of ceding moral ground and called the tweet “an incitement to violence,” warning it could put media members at risk. The episode is the latest in a pattern of incendiary Trump tweets that have generated controversy since his campaign and into his presidency. Trump has defended his social media habits as “modern day presidential,” arguing they were instrumental to his 2016 victory and rejecting calls from some Republicans and commentators to restrain his direct, combative communications with the public.

Sixteen-year-old Mackenzie Wethington is recovering in an ICU after surviving a near-impossible skydiving accident in which she fell about 3,500 feet. The first-time jumper was airlifted to the University of Oklahoma Medical Center after the crash and is awake, breathing on her own and listed in fair condition. Doctors describe her survival as miraculous given the severity of her injuries, which include a lacerated liver and kidney, multiple fractures throughout her body, and broken teeth. Trauma surgeons said her injuries are comparable to those sustained in a car collision at 40–50 mph, yet they expect her to recover fully within roughly six to eight weeks.

Accounts differ about what happened during the jump. Mackenzie’s father, Joe Wethington, said only half of her parachute deployed and that she went into an uncontrollable spiral, with ground crew urging her to cut away and deploy the reserve. Bob Swainson, owner of the Pegasus Air Sports Center where the jump took place, maintained the parachute opened completely and suggested technical factors or the jumper’s body position may have induced a dangerous rotation.

Medical experts and physicists explain that a rare combination of factors likely contributed to her survival. Pediatric and trauma specialists called her recovery extraordinary, noting young, healthy bodies tolerate trauma better. Physicist James Kakalios emphasized the role of air resistance, turbulence, and how the body’s orientation during a fall can dissipate energy and reduce impact force. Survival from great heights is uncommon, but not unheard of, when circumstances and luck align. Mackenzie’s family calls her a “miracle,” grateful that she is expected to get better despite the horrific accident and initially grim expectations from emergency responders.

Scientists are investigating evidence that a distant, massive ninth planet may exist in our solar system — but it’s not the doomsday “Nibiru” of internet rumors. The real Planet Nine hypothesis, advanced by Caltech astronomers Konstantin Batygin and Mike Brown, rests on multiple indirect clues from objects in the outer solar system rather than any threat to Earth. Based on gravitational effects on distant Kuiper Belt objects, Batygin says there are now five observational lines pointing to a hidden planet; removing this single explanation would force astronomers to invent five different theories to account for the anomalies.

The initial 2016 study noted that six distant Kuiper Belt objects share unusually aligned, elongated orbits and are tilted about 30 degrees relative to the solar system’s main plane. Simulations including a Planet Nine also predict a population of bodies with extreme 90-degree tilts; five such high-inclination objects are already known. Subsequent work suggests Planet Nine could slowly tilt or make the entire planetary plane precess over billions of years, helping explain why the planetary orbital plane is inclined roughly 6 degrees to the Sun’s equator. The planet’s influence may also account for some Kuiper Belt objects orbiting opposite to the usual direction.

If Planet Nine exists, Batygin and Brown estimate it would be roughly ten times Earth’s mass and located about 20 times farther from the Sun than Neptune — extremely distant and dim. They are now searching with the Subaru Telescope on Mauna Kea to detect it directly. Alternative analyses of new trans-Neptunian surveys suggest the patterns might also arise from observational bias, so Planet Nine remains unconfirmed. Finding it would also align our system with the common “super-Earth” class seen around other stars and shed light on its origin, whether formed here or captured.

A bitter power struggle in Iran pits President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad and his ally Esfandiar Rahim-Mashaei against Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and the clerical establishment. Mashaei, Ahmadinejad’s chief of staff and rumored successor, has reportedly sought secret outreach to the United States and promoted a reduced role for clerics—moves that alarm Khamenei’s camp. Tensions flared when Ahmadinejad tried to assert control over the intelligence ministry, prompting the resignation and then the reinstatement of its minister by Khamenei, an unusual public rebuke of the president. Conservative clerics have launched harsh public attacks, labeling Ahmadinejad’s circle “the perverted team” and warning of impeachment or worse; some accused the president’s associates of supernatural practices and arrested dozens of Mashaei allies. A controversial documentary about the imminent return of the Hidden Imam further fueled clerical outrage. The dispute reflects broader regional upheaval from the Arab Spring and underlines divisions in Tehran over openness to the West versus clerical retrenchment.

Less than a week after Brad Pitt proposed, Angelina Jolie received a new U.N. title: special envoy for the High Commissioner for Refugees, a step up from her longtime role as goodwill ambassador. The appointment, focused on crises that displace people—such as Afghanistan and Somalia—will have Jolie continue traveling to refugee camps and representing the U.N. on occasion, relaying messages to governments and partners. Tabloid coverage has predictably mixed serious reporting with lighter concerns, most notably whether Jolie’s new status might imperil the large engagement ring Pitt reportedly spent a year designing. Estimates of the ring’s value vary widely—Us Weekly suggested around $250,000; other reports cite figures up to $500,000—and tabloids offered tongue-in-cheek security advice: avoid damaging substances, consider leaving the ring in a safe or wearing a duplicate when traveling, and dress inconspicuously or turn the stone inward. 

Meanwhile, media chatter has also turned to the financial value of potential Jolie-Pitt wedding photos. Market insiders say celebrity magazine economics have cooled since 2008; whereas their twins’ images once fetched $14 million and earlier couple photos brought in about $1 million, wedding images today might command significantly less—estimates range from around $2 million to $5 million for worldwide rights, depending on access and content. Other coverage touched on the likelihood of a prenuptial agreement given the couple’s combined wealth, speculation about Jennifer Aniston’s reaction, and the family-centered proposal moment when Pitt presented the ring to Jolie in front of their six children.

Scientists have uncovered a 99-million-year-old partial dinosaur tail preserved in Myanmar amber, offering an unprecedented three-dimensional glimpse into dinosaur feather structure and arrangement. Described in Current Biology, the specimen was purchased at an amber market by Lida Xing after a seller mistook the bushy inclusion for plant material. CT scans and microscopic study revealed eight articulated vertebrae and dense feathering around a 1.4-inch appendage likely from a juvenile coelurosaur roughly sparrow-sized. Because modern birds and close Cretaceous avialans have fused tail vertebrae (a pygostyle), the flexible unfused tail indicates a non-avialan dinosaur. The feathers show a poorly developed rachis and an open, flexible vane more like modern ornamental feathers than stiff flight feathers; dorsal feathers were darker while ventral feathers were pale, suggesting roles in camouflage, signaling, or thermoregulation rather than flight. Chemical analysis of a cross-section, produced when the amber had been shaped for jewelry, detected ferrous iron—decomposition product of hemoglobin—raising hope for future pigment and molecular studies. The find resolves limitations of flattened fossil impressions by preserving spatial feather arrangement in three dimensions and underscores that more such specimens may exist, sometimes mistaken for plant debris. Researchers continue to search amber markets and mines, anticipating further discoveries as access to Myanmar deposits improves.

At the U.S. Professional Wing Eating Championship in Buffalo, three lightweight women dominated, consuming nearly 500 chicken wings in 12 minutes to outpace seven men. Miki Sudo, 28, of Las Vegas, won with 178 wings; Michelle Lesco of Tucson took second; five-time champion Sonya “The Black Widow” Thomas placed third with 141. Sudo, who weighs 115 pounds and turned pro in April after competing as an amateur, also won Saturday’s Buffet Bowl contest. Notably absent was last year’s winner Joey Chestnut. The trio’s combined weight was 345 pounds—less than one male contestant’s 407 pounds—prompting astonished and joking reactions from spectators. Fourth-place finisher Yasir Salem, 19, had recently completed an ironman. Festival founder Drew Cerza reported higher Sunday attendance and an overall crowd of 72,000, down from 80,000 the previous year. Attendees sampled wings from 32 vendors, including Dinosaur Bar-B-Que and Anchor Bar, alongside new items like spicy Buffalo rolls and vegetarian “wings,” while emcee George Shea kept the crowd energized with rapid-fire banter.

Audrey Parker, a 57-year-old Halifax woman with Stage 4 breast cancer, died by medically assisted death on Nov. 1 after publicly urging changes to Canada’s assisted-dying law. Parker had been planning what she called a “beautiful death” and wanted to live longer — ideally to Christmas — but the federal law’s requirement that patients be mentally competent to confirm consent at the moment of death forced her to schedule earlier than she wished. She feared cancer spreading to her brain would rob her of that capacity. In her final Facebook post she called the law “poorly thought out” and asked Canadians to pressure MPs to remove the late-stage consent requirement for people already assessed and approved for medical assistance in dying (MAID). Her post drew thousands of shares, reactions and supportive comments.

Responses from politicians and officials have varied. Federal Justice Minister Jody Wilson‑Raybould said the government was not considering legislative changes, though Liberal MP Darren Fisher and others signaled openness to listening to constituents’ views. Halifax-area MPs offered mixed or limited responses; some expressed respect and interest in ongoing conversation. Nova Scotia Premier Stephen McNeil and Halifax Mayor Mike Savage paid tribute but deferred to federal jurisdiction.

The current MAID law, enacted in 2016 after the Supreme Court decision, permits adults with grievous, irremediable conditions to seek assisted death but bars advance requests — a provision intended to protect vulnerable people. Critics argue it forces some to die earlier or endure pain by reducing medications to stay lucid. Expert panels originally recommended limited advance requests for certain cases, but the enacted law excluded them while commissioning a Council of Canadian Academies review on advance requests and other exclusions; that evidence summary is due in December but will not include recommendations. Parker’s death has intensified public debate and advocacy, including calls to amend the law (proposed as “Audrey’s Law”) so approved patients need not give consent at the final moment.

The Parkland, Florida, shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School on February 14 left the nation reeling and prompted immediate local, state and national responses to aid victims and honor those who acted bravely. The U.S. Army awarded the Medal of Heroism posthumously to three JROTC cadets—Alaina Petty, Peter Wang and Martin Duque—recognizing their acceptance of danger and extraordinary responsibility. Wang, 15, reportedly held a door open so classmates could escape; Petty and Duque, both 14, were remembered by family and friends for their warmth, talents and community involvement.

The massacre, blamed on former student Nikolas Cruz, killed 17 and wounded many more; Cruz allegedly triggered fire alarms and used an AR-15. Authorities arrested him about an hour later. Broward County has since received broad support and organized relief efforts: Lutheran Church Charities sent at least 18 trained Golden Retriever “comfort” dogs and handlers to console students, staff, families and first responders. Blood donation centers called for replenishing O-negative supplies after treating victims.

Financial and logistical assistance has been mobilized. The Broward Education Foundation’s official Stoneman Douglas Victims’ Fund on GoFundMe quickly raised millions to support victims, survivors and counseling; a volunteer steering committee led by community leaders and the National Center for Victims of Crime was formed to ensure transparent distribution. Florida’s attorney general pledged to cover funeral expenses for the victims. JetBlue and Lyft offered free travel and ground transport for families, and JetBlue partnered with local groups for a blood drive. Individual memorial and scholarship funds, including one in memory of 14-year-old Alex Schachter to promote school safety and music education, were also created to honor the victims and support prevention and healing.

U.S. federal health officials released draft CDC guidelines saying the medical evidence shows the benefits of male circumcision outweigh the risks and urging insurers to cover it. The guidance stops short of directing parents to circumcise newborn sons, acknowledging personal, cultural and religious choices, but recommends clinicians counsel parents and sexually active uncircumcised men—especially those at higher HIV risk—about benefits and harms. The CDC’s review cites strong evidence that circumcision reduces a man’s risk of acquiring HIV from a female partner by 50–60%, lowers risk of genital herpes and certain HPV strains by about 30% or more, decreases infant urinary tract infections, and reduces penile cancer risk. It notes benefits are modest and partial: circumcision hasn’t been shown to lower HIV transmission from infected men to women, nor to reduce risk during male-to-male anal sex. Complication rates are low—about 0.5% in newborns, rising to 9% in ages 1–9—mostly minor bleeding and pain. The draft, published in the Federal Register, opens a 45-day public comment period and will undergo peer review before finalization. The recommendations echo the American Academy of Pediatrics’ stance and are expected to draw opposition from anti-circumcision activists who decry elective infant genital surgery.

Police were called to Oakdale Elementary in Rock Hill after a nine-year-old student became disruptive when a teacher confiscated iPads from noisy pupils. According to a police report, the boy crawled under a desk, flipped multiple chairs, and, after being taken into a hallway, repeatedly stomped on the 26-year-old teacher’s foot. Two other teachers and an assistant principal restrained him; the teacher sustained a bruised, swollen left foot. Officers arrived after the student had calmed and released him to his mother. Two other students were also disorderly during the September 26 incident but were separated and calmed by staff.

A recent Lancet Psychology study and related research challenge traditional assumptions about inner experiences like hearing voices and dreaming. An online survey and detailed analysis of 153 voice-hearers led by Angela Woods (Durham University) found vast diversity in how people experience voices. Contrary to the stereotype tied to schizophrenia—angry, commanding hallucinations—many report voices as internal characters with distinct personalities that converse or reflect exaggerated versions of everyday inner dialogues. Up to 15% of people who hear voices lack any psychiatric diagnosis. Some experiences include physical sensations (e.g., tingling), and voices can range from distressing to comforting. Woods and colleagues argue the auditory label is inadequate and urge broader research perspectives and more nuanced clinical approaches: therapy can help people reinterpret voices as parts of themselves and address underlying subconscious concerns. The full study appears in The Lancet Psychology.

Separately, Patrick McNamara and Kelly Bulkeley argue in Frontiers in Psychology that dreams historically fueled religious beliefs by presenting vivid, involuntary encounters with other beings. REM sleep produces immersive experiences that ancient people plausibly interpreted as communications from gods or ancestors. Evolutionary tendencies to attribute agency—favoring false positives to avoid danger—heighten readiness to see significance in dream figures. Dreams also foster theory-of-mind attributions and engage brain systems that ascribe value, making them fertile ground for creating supernatural-agent concepts. McNamara and Bulkeley conclude that human brains are naturally primed to generate god concepts through dreaming, helping explain religion’s deep psychological roots.

A rare protest disrupted oral arguments at the U.S. Supreme Court when Noah Newkirk of Los Angeles rose from the public gallery and shouted slogans opposing the 2010 Citizens United ruling, including “Money is not speech,” “Corporations are not people,” and “Overturn Citizens United.” The interruption occurred during a patent-fees case and came near the end of arguments. Court police quickly removed Newkirk after a brief scuffle; he was charged under a federal statute that forbids “haranguing” or uttering “loud threatening or abusive language” inside the Supreme Court building. Chief Justice John Roberts, without commenting on the disturbance, told counsel they had three minutes remaining. The justices made no public remarks about the incident and the official transcript did not record the outburst. Such courtroom protests are uncommon; officials cited past disturbances years earlier. The interruption underscored ongoing public tensions over campaign finance rules and highlighted the court’s strict courtroom decorum and security procedures.

Ivanka Trump attended the Broadway debut of Come From Away with Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, sitting between Trudeau and U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley. The high-profile audience included cabinet members, former Canadian prime minister Jean Chrétien and around 150 UN ambassadors, part of a wider diplomatic presence as Canada campaigns for a temporary UN Security Council seat. Trudeau introduced the show, opening with light jokes about New York’s wintry weather before praising the Canada–U.S. relationship and the story’s message of neighbourliness and mutual support. 

Come From Away, written by Canadian duo Irene Sankoff and David Hein and directed by Christopher Ashley, dramatizes the real events in Gander, Newfoundland, after Sept. 11, 2001, when 6,579 passengers on 38 diverted planes were sheltered by local residents. The musical, which had successful regional runs prior to its March Broadway opening, balances tearful and comic moments and explores themes including prejudice against Muslims—highlighted in a subplot about an Egyptian man rebuffed from helping despite being a skilled chef. 

The evening, arriving amid news about a U.S. court pausing a controversial refugee and travel ban, underscored the play’s timely themes of welcome and solidarity. Trudeau and Ivanka had previously met at a White House roundtable on women in the workforce; their shared appearance at the show drew attention to diplomatic and political ties between Canada and the United States.

Nearly four years after her death, the U.S. Army has released the final photograph taken by Spc. Hilda I. Clayton, a 22-year-old visual information specialist with the 55th Signal Company (Combat Camera), moments before a mortar tube accidentally exploded during an Afghan National Army (ANA) mortar validation exercise in Laghman Province on July 2, 2013. Clayton, of Augusta, Ga., was killed along with an Afghan photographer she was training and several ANA soldiers. The image, published in Military Review alongside the Afghan photographer’s picture, underscores the partnership between U.S. and Afghan forces as ANA units assumed greater responsibility and highlights that Clayton shared the risk while documenting those efforts.

Military Review framed her death as symbolic of female soldiers increasingly facing hazards on par with men. Clayton’s service was honored in memorials at Forward Operating Base Gamberi and at Defense Information School, where her name was added to the DINFOS Hall of Heroes. Combat Camera named its annual best combat camera competition after her—the Spc. Hilda I. Clayton Best COMCAM Competition—to celebrate her dedication and sacrifice. The widely shared photograph has renewed public interest in her story and brought tributes from colleagues and civilians alike, reflecting both the hazards of wartime documentation and the enduring impact of her work.

Country star Jason Aldean visited University Medical Center on Sunday, one week after the Oct. 1 massacre at the Route 91 Harvest festival that left 58 dead and hundreds injured. The hospital thanked Aldean on Facebook, saying he spent time with critically injured patients and helped lift spirits. Aldean’s pregnant wife, Brittany, posted an Instagram photo of the couple looking toward Mandalay Bay and called the visit “surreal,” praising the strength of those fighting for their lives and saying the meeting helped begin the healing process. Aldean had been performing at the festival when the shooting began and had appeared on Saturday Night Live the day before.

Effigies of Black lynching victims were found hanging in prominent locations on the University of California, Berkeley campus the morning of a scheduled Black Lives Matter protest, provoking controversy over whether they were provocative protest art or racist intimidation. Three cardboard cutouts—two male and one female—displayed names and dates of historical lynching victims; one reportedly bore the hashtag “#ICantBreathe” and identified a 1911 victim, Laura Nelson. Two effigies hung from Sather Gate arches and a third was found in a tree near Bancroft Lane. Campus officials and police launched an investigation but had not identified who placed the effigies or their intent, and university spokespeople described the motive as unclear. Social media and campus reaction split: some saw the images as misguided, inflammatory and racially terrorizing, while others argued they might be guerrilla public art intended to force historical connections between lynching, state violence, and contemporary police brutality. UC Berkeley faculty weighed in—one social psychology professor called the display without redeeming qualities given protest volatility, while an African American studies professor suggested it might aim to provoke thoughtful discussion about historical repression and modern policing. Campus clergy and student leaders condemned the terrorizing effect, though a black student union representative said the group did not know who was responsible and hoped the images were meant to draw attention to the issues. About 300 people attended a largely peaceful Berkeley protest that afternoon; many later joined a larger Oakland demonstration, where 45 arrests were made. Authorities retained two effigies as evidence and students took down the third.

NASA-supported observatories report the sun is weeks to months away from reversing its magnetic polarity — a routine event that occurs about every 11 years at the peak of the solar cycle. Stanford researchers say the north pole has already flipped and the south pole is close behind, signaling the midpoint of solar maximum. As the field reverses, the heliospheric current sheet — a vast, wavy surface extending billions of kilometers from the sun’s equator — becomes more rippled, causing stormier space weather when Earth crosses its waves. That increased turbulence can affect satellites, astronauts and cosmic-ray exposure, though the wrinkled current sheet also improves shielding from high-energy cosmic rays. This solar maximum is unusually weak compared with past cycles, with fewer sunspots and lower overall activity, but the polarity flip remains a significant, regular milestone for solar and space-weather science.

A Quinnipiac poll released Sept. 10 found Bernie Sanders leading Hillary Clinton 41% to 40% among likely Iowa Democratic caucus-goers, with 12% for Joe Biden and 3% for Martin O’Malley. The shift is notable: in July Quinnipiac showed Clinton up 52–33. The survey, conducted Aug. 27–Sept. 8 with 832 likely caucus participants (±3.4%), coincides with other polls showing Sanders gaining in New Hampshire and reflects fallout from Clinton’s email controversy and questions about her connection with voters. Gender splits are stark: Clinton leads women 49–35, while Sanders leads men 49–28. Favorability measures show Sanders (+72 net) and Biden (+70) outpacing Clinton (+56); Sanders scores higher on honesty and empathy, though Clinton retains strong marks for leadership and crisis temperament. Voters prefer experienced Washington candidates (54% want in‑Washington experience; 69% say Washington experience better prepares a president). Separately, Clinton endorsed small-dollar public matching of donations to curb big-money influence—an idea that would advantage Sanders’ grassroots fundraising, given his high share of small contributions. While pollsters caution against overreading one survey and Clinton remains the overall front‑runner, the results signal growing momentum for Sanders and send concern through Democratic establishment circles.

British Airways suffered a major IT outage that disrupted thousands of passengers over a long weekend, prompting CEO Alex Cruz to apologise “profusely” while rejecting claims the failure stemmed from outsourcing or cyberattack. Cruz told Sky News the blackout began about 09:30 on Saturday when a power surge caused catastrophic damage to communications hardware and messaging across BA’s systems; he said local data-centre issues were handled by local staff and that there’s no evidence of a cyberattack or data breach. The backup systems failed to restore normal operations promptly.

The outage led to mass cancellations and delays at Heathrow and Gatwick, with around 75,000 customers affected, hundreds of flights delayed or cancelled across BA and sister carriers (including Iberia and Air Nostrum), and many passengers sleeping overnight in terminals. By Monday BA had restored most services, operating over 95% of flights and all long-haul departures from Heathrow, though short-haul disruption and a backlog of passengers and luggage continued. Cruz promised an exhaustive investigation and committed to follow compensation rules; experts estimate costs could exceed £100m depending on claims and whether BA can classify the incident as “extraordinary circumstances.”

Critics—including the GMB union and IT commentators—argue the problem exposed risks from recent restructuring and outsourcing of IT, saying loss of in-house expertise may have hampered disaster recovery. BA denied outsourcing caused the outage and said stranded passengers could rebook within six months; couriers will deliver remaining baggage and customers were advised to check flight status before travelling to airports.

This document describes two main things: a web-archiving project and a tragic accidental shooting at a Punta Gorda, Florida, citizens police academy.

The web-archiving component explains that these records are pre-inauguration web crawls for the End of Term Web Archive, a collaborative effort to preserve the U.S. federal government’s web presence at each change of administration. Carried out in fall and winter 2016 to capture content before the January 20, 2017 inauguration, the crawls include publicly accessible government sites on .gov and .mil domains, relevant non-.gov domains, and government social media. The goal is to archive pages and their referenced links so that when original pages change or disappear, preserved versions remain accessible—helping prevent broken links and support historical research. The project’s portal is noted at eotarchive.cdlib.org and mentions a “No More 404” effort.

The news narrative centers on 73-year-old Mary Knowlton, a retired librarian and Punta Gorda resident, who was killed during a citizens police academy simulation when a police officer’s firearm discharged a live round. The academy—meant to educate residents about police work and strengthen community relations—had 35 participants that night. Knowlton volunteered to play a victim in a lethal-force role-play; the shot proved fatal. Chief Tom Lewis called it a “horrible accident” and said the department was unaware live ammunition was available. The Florida Department of Law Enforcement was asked to investigate how live rounds entered the scenario. The officer involved has been placed on administrative leave. The community and city officials offered condolences and counseling; Knowlton’s family asked for compassion over vengeance. The piece notes the broader role of citizens police academies in improving police-community relations and situates this tragedy amid national conversations about policing.

Three college friends faced a moral test when a shabby couch they bought at a Salvation Army thrift store yielded an astonishing $40,800 in cash. In March 2014, SUNY New Paltz student Reese Werkhoven, Mount Holyoke graduate Cally Guasti, and graduate Lara Russo discovered pockets and envelopes full of twenties while unpacking the couch. Initially stunned and briefly tempted by the windfall—dreams of paying loans, travel, or buying a car flickered—they debated whether to keep any of it. Parental advice urged discretion and a search for the owner. Finding a deposit slip with a woman’s name, they called and learned she’d indeed stored money in the couch for decades: her husband had saved cash for her before he died, and she continued tucking funds into the couch until health issues led family to replace it and donate it while she was in rehab. The students drove to return the money, met the grateful 91-year-old widow, and handed over the cash. The woman rewarded them with $1,000 for their honesty. The trio later reflected that keeping the money would have felt profoundly wrong.

Sony unveiled the PlayStation 4, a next-generation console focused on the gamer rather than the living room. Led by system architect Mark Cerny, Sony prioritized developer-friendly design—choosing a familiar x86 CPU and unified GDDR5 memory to simplify development compared with the PS3’s complex architecture. The console includes an HDD, an advanced GPU, and features like quick suspend/resume save states, background downloads, and a secondary processor to enable playing while games download. The DualShock 4 adds a Vita-style touchpad, light bar for motion tracking, a share button, and a headphone jack; a 3D stereo camera accessory can track controller movement. Social integration is central: easy gameplay video sharing, spectator modes, real-name profiles, mobile app tie-ins, and Ustream integration for streaming. Demos showcased impressive graphics, facial detail, and lighting, though not a revolutionary leap. No native PS3 backward compatibility was announced; cloud streaming promises access to older titles. PS4 targets Holiday 2013 with pricing and final design still unannounced.

Hours before the mass shooting that left Latina Verneta Herring and her 8-year-old son dead, Sanford police twice responded to disputes between Herring, 35, and her boyfriend, Allen Dion Cashe, 31. Body-camera footage released by Sanford police shows an early-morning confrontation at a Wawa gas station around 3:20 a.m., in which the couple argued over house and car keys and traded accusations. About 20 minutes later officers were called to Herring’s home on Hays Drive. In that encounter, officers characterized the incident as a “civil matter,” said Herring was “making false accusations,” and at one point told a third party on the phone to “stop calling 911,” adding “we’re going to handle it.” Cashe was briefly handcuffed and placed in a patrol car but was released after officers determined there was no reason to arrest anyone. Officers on scene speculated Cashe might be afraid he would hurt Herring, and Herring reportedly expressed frustration that she should have lied and claimed Cashe had struck her. Friends and community members have criticized Sanford police for not doing more.

Around 6:30 a.m., roughly three hours after the initial calls, investigators say Cashe used an AK-47–style rifle to fire an entire magazine, killing Herring—shot seven times—and later her 8-year-old son, Branden, who died days after the attack. Herring’s 7-year-old son, her father, and two bystanders were also shot; four survivors remain hospitalized, three stable and one critical. Cashe reportedly told investigators he was upset about Herring calling police and taking his keys. He remains jailed without bond, facing charges including premeditated murder, multiple attempted homicide counts, possession of a weapon by a convicted felon, and a parole violation. City leaders expressed sorrow and noted the broader problem of domestic violence.

President Trump’s lawyers are advising him against submitting to a broad, face-to-face interview with special counsel Robert Mueller, primarily because they fear he could incriminate himself by making false statements and potentially be charged with lying to investigators, according to multiple news reports. The legal team believes Mueller has not satisfied the “high threshold” necessary to compel a presidential interview and is urging Trump to refuse an extensive in-person session. They hope that by declining voluntarily, Mueller may be unwilling to escalate to a subpoena seeking to force the president to testify.

This counsel clashes with Trump’s public and private eagerness to speak with Mueller; the president has said he looks forward to answering questions under oath and maintains there was no collusion and no obstruction. The decision over whether to cooperate with prosecutors is looming and consequential. If Trump declines, Mueller could subpoena him to appear before a grand jury, prompting a potentially months-long courtroom confrontation over whether a sitting president must answer questions under oath—an issue that could reach the Supreme Court.

Refusal also carries political risks: it would likely fuel accusations that the president is concealing wrongdoing and could extend the special counsel inquiry well into the midterm elections or beyond, prolonging legal and political uncertainty for Republicans and the administration.

The University of Canterbury (UC) is preparing to bring a unique 15th-century English illuminated genealogical scroll—the Canterbury Roll—into the digital age and open it to global study. Dating from the Wars of the Roses and stretching about five metres, the Roll traces English lineage from mythical origins through the late Middle Ages. Acquired by UC in 1918 and once owned by Sybilla “Nurse” Maude, it remains the only genealogical roll of its kind in the southern hemisphere and is described by UC medieval historian Dr Chris Jones as New Zealand’s most significant medieval artefact.

To mark the centenary of its acquisition, UC is producing a new, sophisticated digital edition and English translation to be released publicly in 2018. Unlike typical static photographic reproductions, UC’s version will be fully scrollable, zoomable and interactive. The Canterbury Roll Project is student-driven: Latin transcriptions and the translation have been completed by current and former UC students through internships in the Arts Digital Lab, giving participants practical skills in transcription, coding and teamwork.

In January, a British scientific research team led by Professor Haida Liang from Nottingham Trent University will visit Christchurch to apply advanced imaging and sensing techniques to the Roll. Their groundbreaking tests aim to reveal hidden writing and other features never before explored on this type of manuscript. The project situates the Roll both as a vital piece of European history and as part of New Zealand’s evolving cultural story, now recontextualised for teaching and wider public access.

Gravy, an event-finding app, ranked the greenest U.S. cities not by building efficiency or per-capita carbon footprints but by counting the number of environmentally themed events held annually. While a glut of awareness-focused festivals doesn’t guarantee substantive environmental progress, the volume of public, eco-oriented events signals a city’s visible commitment to environmentalism and often correlates with other green rankings. Gravy’s list of the five “Most Earth-Friendly Cities” highlights this measure and pairs each city with a unique Earth Day activity. Separately, Alexa Internet has been donating web crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996, which is added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo.

Families of Sandy Hook victims are pressing their case against Remington Outdoor Co. before the Connecticut Supreme Court, seeking to revive a lawsuit dismissed under federal law that shields gunmakers from liability. The plaintiffs — nine victims’ families and a surviving teacher represented by attorney Josh Koskoff — argue Remington’s military-style marketing of its AR-15 Bushmaster intentionally targeted a “younger demographic” of men prone to violence, including shooter Adam Lanza, and thus amounted to negligent entrustment or a violation of Connecticut consumer-protection law. Koskoff told justices Remington “courted” people like Lanza by linking the rifle to macho vigilantism and military identity in ads using phrases such as “perform under pressure” and “consider your man card reissued,” increasing the risk the weapon would be used for mass harm.

Remington’s counsel, James Vogts, maintained the 2005 Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act (PLCAA) bars such claims and that manufacturers are not legally responsible for criminals’ actions, urging application of established law. Justices queried both sides at length about negligent entrustment — a doctrine traditionally applied where a seller knows a specific buyer poses a risk — and whether advertising can ground liability. The lower court dismissed the suit in 2016; the high court’s decision could send the case back for discovery, allowing scrutiny of Remington’s marketing and potentially setting new legal ground. Observers note the novel use of negligent entrustment against a manufacturer could prompt further appeals, possibly to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Archaeologists working on a roadway near Gliwice, Poland, uncovered a group of unusual burials that appear to be ritualized "anti-vampire" interments rather than wartime graves. The skeletons were found with heads severed and placed on their legs, a treatment interpreted as a deliberate attempt to prevent the dead from rising. Such measures—decapitation, suspension by the neck until the head separated, or placing the head away from the body—reflect medieval and early-Christian-era practices in Slavic regions aimed at neutralizing suspected revenants. Other documented anti-vampire methods include driving stakes through chests, as seen in Bulgarian finds, and wedging bricks into mouths, evidenced by a 16th-century Venetian plague burial researched by forensic anthropologist Matteo Borrini. These customs grew from a mix of superstition and ignorance about decomposition: delayed putrefaction, bloating, and blood seeping into the mouth could be misread as postmortem feeding. Accusations of vampirism often followed calamities such as plagues or crop failures, serving as a scapegoating mechanism. The Gliwice graves lacked personal artifacts—no jewelry, buckles, or buttons—so their precise dating remains uncertain, but they provide compelling evidence of historical responses to feared revenants.

President Obama announced that he has authorized two limited but consequential U.S. actions in Iraq: targeted airstrikes against Islamic State (ISIL/ISIS) forces if they threaten U.S. personnel or facilities, and a humanitarian operation to rescue and sustain thousands of civilians trapped on Mount Sinjar. The moves respond to a rapid ISIL advance across northern Iraq that has threatened Irbil (Erbil)—home to a U.S. consulate, diplomats, and military advisers—and created a humanitarian emergency among Yazidi and other minority populations.

The humanitarian mission began with U.S. military airdrops over Mount Sinjar, delivering 8,000 prepackaged meals and 5,300 gallons of water via one C-17 and two C-130s escorted by F/A-18 fighters. Officials reported 72 bundles dropped in a brief mission and left open the possibility of additional airdrops. The displaced include perhaps 10,000 to 40,000 Yazidis—estimates vary up to tens of thousands—who fled ISIL’s campaign of killings, forced conversions, enslavement of women, and explicit threats of systematic destruction that U.S. officials called potentially genocidal. Trapped high on a barren mountain with little food or water, many face death by dehydration or slaughter if they descend.

To protect U.S. personnel and key locations such as the consulate in Irbil and the embassy in Baghdad, Obama authorized targeted strikes against ISIL convoys advancing toward Irbil. U.S. surveillance—manned aircraft and drones—has been intensified over the area, and U.S. aircraft reportedly struck ISIL artillery positions threatening Kurdish defenses near Erbil after militants fired on Kurdish troops. The U.S. force presence in Iraq remains limited: several hundred advisers, mainly Special Forces, continue to assess and support Iraqi and Kurdish forces, while Pentagon officials emphasize that American combat troops will not return to large-scale ground combat. The administration frames its actions as necessary, focused, and contingent on Iraqi requests and coordination with Kurdish peshmerga.

Obama stressed that military force is neither a cure-all nor the preferred primary instrument, reiterating that the durable solution is political reconciliation among Iraq’s communities and a more inclusive Iraqi government. Washington conditioned broader support on Iraq forming a responsive government; Iraqi leaders have been moving toward naming a new prime minister and building consensus. The U.S. intends to work with regional partners and the U.N. to expand humanitarian relief, strengthen Iraqi forces, and prevent further atrocities, while consulting Congress on ongoing decisions. The administration seeks to limit intervention to protecting Americans and averting mass civilian slaughter, even as it weighs risks of mission creep.

Iceland has seen a tourism boom: visitors have grown from under 500,000 in 2010 to an expected 2.4 million this year, despite a population of about 350,000. The surge followed global attention on the 2010 Eyjafjallajökull eruption, increased exposure in TV and film (including Game of Thrones and The Secret Life of Walter Mitty), and creative promotion by Iceland’s tourism bodies. After the 2008 recession and the disruptive 2010 eruption, government and industry cooperated on crisis communications and then shifted to marketing Iceland as a year-round destination while encouraging visitors to explore beyond Reykjavik.

Promote Iceland has run quirky campaigns — from local-hosted stays predating Airbnb to the Iceland Academy video series offering playful cultural primers like “How to Eat Like an Icelander” and “How to Avoid Hot Tub Awkwardness.” Cultural tourism also draws music fans eager to see the origins of artists such as Björk and Sigur Rós, and many travelers seek the Northern Lights and the island’s dramatic natural features: glaciers, waterfalls, volcanoes, lava fields, geothermal pools and geysers.

Air connectivity from North America has expanded, notably through Wow Air and Icelandair, which offer cheap transfer routes and free stopovers that let passengers see Iceland on the way to Europe. Icelandair emphasizes its longstanding stopover option and recently promoted Iceland’s imagery via themed planes (Northern Lights and a glacier-themed aircraft with interior and exterior glacier motifs). HomeAway listings in Iceland rose 68% in a year while demand grew 81%, reflecting expanded lodging and tour offerings.

The influx has led to more tour itineraries and growing accommodation inventories, but also raises issues such as access to attractions on private land, changing glacier conditions that can alter visitor expectations, and the need for local stewardship as popular sites—from the Blue Lagoon to glacial lagoons and coastal wreck sites—continue to draw crowds.

The Senate released final details of a broad tax package totaling about $858 billion over 10 years and began debate to prevent income-tax increases for nearly all Americans on Jan. 1. The agreement, brokered by President Obama and Republican leaders, would extend current tax rates for two years for all brackets, renew long-term unemployment benefits for 13 months, cut Social Security payroll taxes for one year, and extend many energy-related tax incentives including ethanol subsidies and credits for wind, solar, efficiency and transit. It lowers the estate-tax top rate to 35% with a $5 million inflation-indexed exemption, drawing sharp Democratic criticism. House Democrats openly rebelled, chanting “Just Say No” and passing a nonbinding resolution demanding changes, arguing the deal favors the wealthy and excluded rank-and-file Democrats from talks. Senate leaders expected passage with bipartisan support despite concerns that the package would substantially increase the federal deficit and deepen intra-party tensions for Democrats heading into divided government.

Chechen insurgent leader Doku Umarov has claimed responsibility for the 24 January suicide bombing at Moscow’s Domodedovo Airport, which killed 36 and injured about 180. In a video posted on the Kavkaz Tsentr site, Umarov, leader of the self-styled “Caucasus Emirate,” said the attack was ordered by him as retaliation for “Russian crimes in the Caucasus” and warned of further “regular, deeper and more aggressive operations,” claiming hundreds of recruits ready to carry out suicide attacks. Authorities identified the bomber as a 20-year-old from the North Caucasus and said several foreigners were among the dead. The bombing prompted President Dmitry Medvedev to sack transport and security officials, tighten airport and transport security, and vow the country would not be cowed, though public concern about future attacks remains high.

House Republicans nominated 45-year-old Rep. Paul Ryan as House Speaker, succeeding John Boehner after a 200-43 secret-ballot vote. Ryan, who initially resisted, agreed to run to unify a fractured GOP and pledged procedural reforms and broader rank-and-file input. He faces conservative challengers, must secure 218 floor votes, and will be formally elected by the full House Thursday.

Melania Trump gave her first extended public defense of Donald Trump after a 2005 “Access Hollywood” tape surfaced showing him making lewd comments about women, calling the remarks offensive and inappropriate but saying she accepted his apology and they were “moving on.” In interviews with Fox & Friends and CNN’s Anderson Cooper, she described the tape as “boy talk,” saying it didn’t reflect the man she knows and suggesting Trump was “egged on” by the host. She repeatedly defended her husband’s character, insisting “I believe my husband,” and arguing that many allegations are politically motivated and lack factual support. Melania challenged specific accusations — notably a People magazine account by journalist Natasha Stoynoff — saying details were untrue and that her lawyers have threatened to sue. She urged that any claims of sexual misconduct be resolved in court and emphasized that accusations without evidence are “damaging and unfair.” 

Melania acknowledged the language was unacceptable and said Trump apologized; she asked the public to accept that apology, noting the tape was many years old and portraying her husband as “real” and “raw” because of his entertainer past. She defended his record of employing and supporting women and recounted seeing other women make advances toward him. While she agreed with Michelle Obama that non-consensual kissing or groping is sexual assault, she would not label what was said on the tape as assault, saying “he didn’t say he did it.” 

She also criticized the mainstream media as dishonest and biased, blaming coverage for undermining Trump and saying outlets sensationalize small excerpts instead of his policy messages. Separately, reports indicate that Billy Bush and NBC have reached a confidential financial settlement ending his employment after the tape’s fallout; Bush reportedly felt scapegoated and was reportedly satisfied with the settlement amount.

President Trump escalated a public feud with his former aide Omarosa Manigault Newman, calling her a “dog” and a “crazed, crying lowlife” on Twitter after she accused him of racism and cognitive decline. Omarosa, promoting her memoir Unhinged, has claimed she heard a recording of Mr. Trump using the N-word during his time on The Apprentice and has released several secret recordings tied to her firing and those allegations. The White House, pressed on whether any tapes might surface, would not guarantee none exist; Press Secretary Sarah Sanders said she had never heard Trump use that epithet and framed the president’s insults as attacks on integrity rather than race.

Omarosa said Trump disrespects women and African-Americans and confirmed she has been interviewed by Special Counsel Robert Mueller, though she declined to discuss details. The Trump campaign filed arbitration against her for allegedly breaching a 2016 nondisclosure agreement. Controversy centers on a newly reported CBS recording of a 2016 conference call in which aides, including Katrina Pierson and Lynne Patton, discuss how to handle a purported tape of Trump using the slur; Pierson’s earlier denials were contradicted by the audio, but she later said she had been placating Omarosa. The dispute has produced conflicting statements and intensified scrutiny over recordings, the campaign’s handling of the allegations, and Omarosa’s practice of secretly recording conversations.

A viral video showing 11-year-old Keaton Jones of Knoxville, Tennessee, tearfully describing daily bullying at Gibbs Middle School sparked a nationwide outpouring of support from celebrities, athletes and the public. Posted by his mother, Kimberly Jones, the clip captures Keaton saying classmates call him “ugly,” mock his nose, tell him he has no friends, pour milk on him, shove ham into his clothes and throw bread at him. Keaton explains he sometimes asks his mother to pick him up because he’s too afraid to go to lunch and pleads that people “different” shouldn’t be criticized for what they can’t control. His mother urged parents to talk with their children and offered words of resilience to victims.

Within days the video drew tens of millions of views across platforms and trended under #StandWithKeaton. High-profile figures weighed in: Snoop Dogg reposted the video and offered friendship; actors Chris Evans and Mark Ruffalo invited Keaton to the Avengers: Infinity War premiere and praised his courage; NASCAR’s Dale Earnhardt Jr. and country star Kelsea Ballerini sent messages of support. Local and college athletes also mobilized—University of Tennessee players, including wide receiver Tyler Byrd, pledged to visit Keaton’s school and show support, while Tennessee Titans tight end Delanie Walker invited the family to a game.

The response highlighted broad condemnation of bullying, community solidarity with victims, and calls for parents and schools to address harassment and create safer environments for children.

Ten years ago on Aug. 28, 2005, National Weather Service meteorologist Robert Ricks faced a grave responsibility as forecast coordinator at the Slidell office serving New Orleans. With Hurricane Katrina imminent, Ricks chose to issue an unusually stark bulletin — now preserved in the Smithsonian alongside his grandmother’s rosary — to convey the imminent danger. Labeled "URGENT... SPECIAL MESSAGE," the warning described unprecedented destruction: most of the area uninhabitable for weeks or longer; half of well-built homes suffering roof and wall failure; all gabled roofs failing; vast numbers of trees snapped or defoliated; and water shortages making human suffering "incredible by modern standards." Ricks later said he agonized over each line, drawing on local history and his own experience surviving Betsy and Camille in the Lower Ninth Ward. He felt compelled to leave every validated phrase in the message rather than dilute its urgency. The bulletin and Ricks’s emotional, direct language—echoed in other high-impact forecasts like Gary Szatkowski’s personal plea during Superstorm Sandy—reflect a shift at the National Weather Service toward more candid, forceful communications in true emergencies. Although Ricks wished he had been wrong about the storm’s scale, the forecast proved accurate; the devastation confirmed his warnings. Returning to work after the storm, he and colleagues—some who had lost homes and were still wearing the clothes from that day—continued to carry the burden of telling their community the terrible truth they could not afford to soften.

Water for Elephants, adapted from Sara Gruen’s Depression-era novel, is a polished but muted cinematic take on a traveling circus love triangle. Directed by Francis Lawrence with a screenplay by Richard LaGravenese, the film follows Jacob Jankowski (Robert Pattinson), a former veterinary student who joins the Benzini Brothers circus after his parents’ deaths, and becomes entangled with star performer Marlena (Reese Witherspoon) and her cruel husband, ringmaster August (Christoph Waltz). The movie captures the story’s broad strokes—the circus’s itinerant life, Rosie the elephant’s emotional presence, and the simmering jealousy that fuels conflict—but many critics found it too cautious. Pattinson’s narration and underplayed chemistry with Witherspoon blunt the romance; James Newton Howard’s ubiquitous score smooths rather than sharpens mood; and the film often shies away from the harsher grit of circus life that made the book memorable. Waltz’s menacing August is the film’s strongest element, providing the only real edge. Visually sumptuous and faithful to the source, Water for Elephants ultimately lacks the raw spark and cathartic payoff critics felt it needed.

Stranded overnight at Las Vegas’ McCarran Airport, Richard Dunn turned boredom into a playful guerrilla music video, lip-syncing Celine Dion’s 1996 cover of “All By Myself.” With the terminal nearly empty, he improvised camera rigs from everyday items: luggage tape supplied by a departing ticket agent, a wheelchair with a tall pole to mount his iPhone, the extended handle of his computer bag, and strategic padding to get the right angles. He used moving walkways for dolly shots and sprinted up an escalator after recording to prevent his makeshift rig from toppling. Midway through the four-and-a-half-minute clip he cheekily recreates the famous Flashdance waterfall silhouette using a water bottle, a gag that helps push the video’s delightfully cheesy tone over the top. Dunn edited and uploaded the solo production to Vimeo, and it quickly resonated online, racking up nearly half a million views soon after release. The stunt even drew playful attention from Celine Dion herself, who reportedly wanted to meet him.

A white nationalist “Unite the Right” rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, devolved into violence Saturday, leaving three people dead and dozens injured. Hundreds of white nationalists and counter-protesters clashed in multiple violent encounters throughout the day, prompting local and state authorities to declare a state of emergency and order people to disperse. Tensions had begun Friday with torchlit marches and continued into Saturday with fights, chemical sprays and physical confrontations downtown.

The worst incident occurred around 1:30 p.m. on the Downtown Mall when a silver Dodge Charger accelerated into a crowd of counter-protesters on Water Street, then reversed and fled. Thirty-two-year-old Heather Heyer was killed; at least 19 others were injured and treated at local hospitals (other reports put injuries higher). Witnesses described bodies thrown into the street and severe trauma at the scene. After a brief pursuit, police arrested 20-year-old James Alex Fields Jr. of Maumee, Ohio. Fields was charged with second-degree murder, three counts of malicious wounding and leaving the scene; he was being held without bond awaiting a bond hearing and first court appearance.

Later Saturday, a Virginia State Police helicopter assisting law enforcement monitoring the unrest crashed outside Charlottesville, killing two troopers: Lt. H. Jay Cullen and Trooper-Pilot Berke M.M. Bates. Authorities linked the crash to the day’s law-enforcement activity, though exact circumstances remained under investigation.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Virginia, the Richmond FBI field office and the Justice Department announced a civil rights investigation into the vehicular attack. State police also announced additional arrests for disorderly conduct, assault and unlawfully carrying a concealed weapon related to the day’s clashes. Rally organizer Jason Kessler and prominent alt-right figures like Richard Spencer disavowed the violence and urged dispersal; public officials and the First Lady called for peace as vigils were held that night. The events prompted national outrage and intensified scrutiny of extremist demonstrations and law-enforcement responses.

This morning’s Senate Intelligence Committee hearing with Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey and Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg on misinformation, content moderation and foreign interference was disrupted by Infowars host Alex Jones, who attended the open, public proceeding. Jones, recently banned or suspended from platforms including Twitter, YouTube and Facebook for violating terms of service, has claimed bans boosted his profile even as audience data show Infowars’ reach is shrinking. Seeking attention, Jones confronted Senator Marco Rubio in a hallway during a hearing recess, interrupting Rubio’s interview and accusing U.S. platforms of engaging in censorship comparable to China’s. Rubio attempted to answer, then tried to ignore him; Jones persisted, taunted Rubio as a “snake,” “little gangster thug” and “frat boy,” and laughed obnoxiously. When Jones reached to touch Rubio’s shoulder, Rubio recoiled and warned him, “Don’t touch me again, man,” later saying he would “take care of” Jones after Jones accused the senator of trying to have him arrested. Jones livestreamed his entrance and sat in the first row of the hearing, mere feet from the tech executives during testimony. The confrontation underscored tensions around content moderation, platform bans, and conservative complaints of Silicon Valley bias amid the broader hearing on social media’s role in foreign influence and misinformation.

In the closing weeks before the 2018 midterms, President Donald Trump publicly cast the elections as a personal referendum—urging supporters at rallies to “vote for me”—while privately preparing to distance himself if Republicans suffer big losses. According to people familiar with his private remarks, Trump tells confidants the real contest is 2020, not 2018, and plans to blame congressional leaders, particularly House Speaker Paul Ryan and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, for any failure to hold GOP majorities. He reportedly tells associates that “these are their elections” and says if they “screw it up, it’s not my fault.” The president is also expected to attack the media as part of any post-election response, and aides anticipate early-morning, unfiltered tweets assigning blame elsewhere.

Trump does express confidence in Republican prospects, crediting McConnell’s handling of the Brett Kavanaugh confirmation and continuing an intense campaign schedule. But the White House appears to lack a formal post-election messaging plan; aides expect Trump to lead the narrative and resist taking responsibility if results go poorly. This would break with recent presidential precedent—George W. Bush accepted blame after the 2006 losses and Barack Obama acknowledged responsibility after the 2010 midterms—leaving Republicans to brace for finger-pointing even as some allies defend Trump’s efforts on the campaign trail.

Democrats, meanwhile, have been dampening expectations for a sweeping “blue wave,” arguing that talk of inevitable victory can suppress turnout. DNC chair Tom Perez and Sen. Bernie Sanders warned publicly against assuming an easy win, casting the races as close and emphasizing turnout. Democrats still hope to reclaim the House—pointing to consistent leads on the generic ballot and polls showing advantages in congressional control—but see the Senate map as more difficult: many Democratic incumbents are defending seats in states Trump carried in 2016.

Both parties see risks and opportunities. Republicans have been energized by Trump’s rallies and immigration rhetoric, including claims—without evidence—linking Democrats to a migrant caravan, and by appeals to nationalist themes. That strategy aims to boost GOP turnout, especially in rural and red-state Senate contests, but could alienate suburban and moderate voters crucial to House control. Early voting data showed Republican-affiliated turnout outpacing Democratic-affiliated turnout in several key states (Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Montana, Tennessee and Texas), while Democrats led only in Nevada, raising concerns that enthusiasm gaps favoring Democrats earlier in the season may be closing.

High-profile races reflect these tensions. In Texas, Trump campaigned for Sen. Ted Cruz against Democrat Beto O’Rourke, with both sides drawing large crowds; in Georgia, voter-roll purges and election administration by GOP Secretary of State Brian Kemp sparked litigation and concern among Democrats. Early voting patterns also varied by gender and geography, and as of Oct. 22 more than 5 million votes had been cast early or absentee nationwide. With both parties mobilizing messaging and turnout strategies, the outcome remained uncertain and potentially consequential for control of Congress and the political narratives that would follow.

A mass shooting at Santa Fe High School, southeast of Houston, left 10 people dead and 10 wounded on a Friday morning, authorities said. Seventeen-year-old student Dimitrios Pagourtzis was arrested and charged with capital murder; a judge denied him bond. Officials found explosive devices at the school and nearby, and federal prosecutors were considering additional weapons-related charges. Authorities say Pagourtzis used a sawed-off shotgun and a .38 revolver taken from his father; investigators recovered homemade bombs including pipe-style and pressure-cooker-like devices. Texas Governor Greg Abbott said the suspect had journal entries and material on his devices indicating intent to kill and to commit suicide afterward, though Pagourtzis told authorities he lacked the courage to take his own life.

The attack began in an art classroom, where students described the gunman wearing a trench coat and a “Born to Kill” T-shirt. Survivors recounted chaos, sheltering, and narrow escapes; a school resource officer engaged the shooter and was hospitalized after arm surgery. Two substitute teachers and several students were among the victims. Families and community leaders publicly mourned, and the Pakistani Embassy confirmed exchange student Sabika Sheikh was killed. Public figures responded: President Trump ordered flags at half-staff and reactivated his school safety commission; NFL player J.J. Watt offered to pay funeral expenses.

The shooting reignited national outrage over school gun violence and debate over prevention measures, as students and officials recalled prior activism and blasted the recurring pattern of such attacks. Schools in the district closed through Tuesday as the community grappled with grief and investigations continued.

Cynk Technology Corp., a purported social-network operator with no revenue, assets and only one reported employee, saw its stock surge astonishingly in mid-2014 and was suspended from trading by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The SEC cited concerns about the accuracy and adequacy of market information and potentially manipulative transactions. Before the SEC suspension, the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority and OTC Markets had already flagged the stock as suspicious; OTC Markets marks such issues with a skull-and-crossbones “buyer beware” warning that prompts brokerages to lock trading. Cynk’s stock jumped from 6 cents on May 15 to an intraday high of $21.95 on one day—an increase of as much as 36,000 percent—before closing lower; the extreme run attracted intense coverage and commentary across business blogs and mainstream outlets. Observers say the spike may have been enabled by difficulty shorting the thinly traded penny stock and by brokerage compliance systems preventing selling after dramatic moves. Regulators and market participants criticized such episodes as damaging to investor confidence and small-company capital formation. Cynk’s filings show a $1.5 million net loss and no revenue for nine months in 2013; filings list Marlon Sanchez as the company’s lone officer at that time and later filings name a Javier Romero as CEO, but Cynk’s claimed Belize headquarters and other details proved dubious. Cynk operates the Introbiz.com site, which sells contact information for public figures and accepts payments online. The SEC and other authorities were investigating the surge and the company’s opaque structure and disclosures.

Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner on Sunday sharply criticized Mitt Romney’s campaign assertion that most jobs lost under President Barack Obama have been among women, calling the claim a “ridiculous way” to frame the nation’s economic problems. Speaking on ABC’s This Week, Geithner argued the jobs crisis began in early 2008 and initially hit men harder because it was concentrated in construction and manufacturing. Pressed on Romney’s specific figure—92.3 percent of jobs lost being among females—Geithner said the argument had been “largely debunked” and characterized such attacks as political fiction rather than fact-driven debate.

Also on Sunday, Republican National Committee Chairman Reince Priebus dismissed President Obama’s proposed “Buffett Rule,” a minimum tax rate on millionaires, as largely symbolic and insufficient to address the federal deficit. Speaking on CNN’s State of the Union ahead of a Senate vote, Priebus called the measure a “shiny little object” and estimated that the revenue it would raise would pay for only about 11 hours of government operations, suggesting it would fail to meaningfully impact the budget shortfall.

In Washington oversight news, Rep. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.), chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, predicted that the Secret Service scandal tied to Obama’s recent trip to Colombia likely wasn’t an isolated incident. On CBS’s Face the Nation, Issa warned that investigations should explore how often misconduct like this has occurred, not just the current episode involving 11 to 20 agents. He questioned whether the agency needs broader reforms to protect principals from potential blackmail or compromised personnel, noting that five military members were later reported to be connected to the scandal involving local prostitutes.

On the political and cultural front, Rep. Michele Bachmann (R-Minn.) attacked Democratic strategist Hilary Rosen for saying Ann Romney “has never worked a day in her life,” calling the remark “shocking and insulting” and predicting women would be upset. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) acknowledged Rosen’s apology but called the comment “wrong and inappropriate.” Bachmann and Gillibrand sparred sharply on issues affecting women, including contraception; Bachmann said she was “very seriously looking” at endorsing Romney to help unite the Republican Party.

Marco Lavoie, a 44-year-old experienced outdoorsman from Quebec, was rescued after surviving roughly three months alone in the remote northwestern Quebec wilderness near the Nottaway River and Lake Matagami. He began a planned two-month canoe and hiking trip on July 16, but did not return. His family reported him missing on October 21, prompting searches that were repeatedly constrained by early snow, high winds and rugged terrain. After about eight days of ground searches and weather delays, a helicopter crew spotted Lavoie on October 30/31; they could not land, so officers hiked in and carried him more than a mile—one officer reportedly shouldering him for nearly two hours—to the chopper.

Police say Lavoie was hypothermic, severely dehydrated and near starvation when found. He was initially too weak to speak, drink or even swallow, and had lost a very large portion of his body weight—reports say about 90 pounds or roughly half his body mass. Medical staff placed him on IV fluids; authorities warned he likely would have died within 24–48 hours had he not been rescued.

Investigators believe a bear attacked Lavoie’s campsite mid-trip, eating his food and destroying his boat and survival gear. The bear did not injure him, allegedly because his German shepherd intervened; accounts conflict about the dog’s fate, with some sources reporting the dog was killed and later eaten by Lavoie to survive—a claim police declined to confirm. Survival experts told journalists that, given the sparse plant life in the Canadian Shield and prolonged food deprivation, desperate measures sometimes preserve life and that Lavoie’s endurance and decisions likely kept him alive. Locals cautioned the Nottaway River is particularly hazardous and not advisable to traverse alone. Lavoie remains hospitalized in very serious condition as authorities await his recovery to obtain more details.

Susan Schneider Williams recounts the painful decline and death of her husband, actor Robin Williams, from diffuse Lewy body disease (LBD), aiming to deepen clinicians’ understanding of patients and caregivers and to humanize the research they do. Over 2013–2014, Robin developed a constellation of puzzling symptoms—constipation, insomnia, loss of smell, anxiety, panic, delusions, memory loss, paranoia, tremor, visual-spatial problems, motor slowing, and severe fluctuations in cognition and alertness. Many signs were subtle at first and misattributed to isolated conditions; psychiatric medications sometimes worsened his state because people with LBD commonly have extreme medication sensitivity. Despite therapy, exercise, medication adjustments, and specialist consultations, his decline was swift and devastating. He was diagnosed with Parkinson disease in late May 2014, but the postmortem autopsy three months after his suicide revealed widespread Lewy body pathology throughout his brain and brainstem—one of the worst cases the reviewing physicians had seen—with massive loss of dopamine neurons and Lewy bodies present in nearly every brain region, including the amygdala, explaining acute anxiety and paranoia. Schneider Williams describes the intimacy of their seven-year partnership and the heartbreak of watching a brilliant, beloved partner “drown” as his mind disintegrated. She reflects on whether an earlier diagnosis would have helped, concluding that without a cure it might only have prolonged suffering; nonetheless she immersed herself in LBD research and advocacy, joining the American Brain Foundation board. She urges clinicians and researchers to persist—transforming Robin’s suffering into meaning by pursuing advances that may spare other families similar torment.

The “digital native” — people born around 1980 or later who supposedly innately understand and learn differently with technology — is a widely cited but increasingly challenged concept. Originating in Marc Prensky’s 2001 essay, the term contrasted “digital natives” with “digital immigrants” and has influenced education, marketing and workplace practices. Businesses target millennials as tech-first consumers, and many schools have retooled curricula and learning environments on the assumption younger students demand multimedia, collaborative, tech-driven teaching.

However, recent analyses question whether a distinct, tech-savvy generation actually exists. A review by the Higher Education Academy and a June paper in Teaching and Teacher Education (Kirschner and Bruyckere) find no convincing evidence that younger people learn differently, possess superior digital skills, or are better at multitasking than older cohorts. Empirical work shows many millennials use technology passively to consume information, much like older generations, and that multitasking during lectures or meetings reduces cognitive performance for anyone. Critics argue that treating students as a special cognitive group risks adopting faddish policies that don’t improve learning and may harm it.

Marc Prensky has said his metaphor was meant to describe cultural attitudes, not innate ability; he now emphasizes “digital wisdom” and mutual learning across generations. Still, scholars like Jean Twenge note that generations can differ in habits, values and preferences even if fundamental cognitive processes remain stable. The sensible takeaway is to avoid blanket assumptions about abilities based on birth year: redesign teaching and workplace practices on evidence of what actually improves learning and performance, not on the myth of inherently tech-native minds.

The Tomah VA Medical Center is notifying 592 patients that they may have been exposed to Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C or HIV after a yearlong violation of infection-control rules in its dental clinic. From October 2015 through October 2016 a dentist used his own instruments, cleaned and reused them rather than following VA policy requiring sterile or disposable equipment.
