The practice was discovered when a temporary assistant noticed the improper procedures and reported them. Acting Medical Center Director Victoria Brahm said the dentist knowingly violated protocols — he had used VA equipment appropriately during orientation but chose to use his own tools against procedure. The provider has been removed from patient care and reassigned to an administrative role while the VA referred the matter to the Office of Inspector General to assess possible criminal charges.

The VA describes the risk as limited to patients of that single provider and says there is no evidence yet that anyone contracted an infection, but it is offering precautionary, no-cost screening and will provide free treatment to anyone who tests positive. Testing is available through Dec. 22 at Building 400, Room 1054 on the Tomah campus (weekdays 8 a.m.–5:30 p.m.; Saturdays 8:30 a.m.–noon). A 24-hour hotline, 888-598-7793, handles questions and appointments. The incident has renewed veteran concern in the region about care quality; Tomah has faced prior scrutiny over prescribing practices and staffing challenges. The VA reports an internal investigation was completed Oct. 31 and staff are reviewing records to verify patient safety and implement improvements.

Prosecutors at London’s Old Bailey told the phone-hacking trial that the now-defunct News of the World intercepted voicemails belonging to Kate Middleton and Prince Harry while Kate was dating Prince William. Evidence included transcripts of intimate messages — one in which William calls Kate “babykins” and recounts nearly being shot during a military exercise — which police say were recorded by private investigator Glenn Mulcaire. The revelation is the first allegation that the Murdoch tabloid accessed a royal’s personal phone, though earlier cases involved royal aides. Prosecutors displayed a 2006 “target evaluation” list seized from Mulcaire naming royal staff and showed police-found royal phone directories taken from former royal correspondent Clive Goodman’s home. The trial accuses former editors Rebekah Brooks, Andy Coulson and others of conspiring to intercept communications from 2000–2006; some defendants deny charges. The scandal prompted the Leveson inquiry into press ethics and media–state relationships.

A small preliminary study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that inhaled oxytocin improved social behavior in 13 adults with high‑functioning autism or Asperger’s. After receiving nasal oxytocin, participants made more eye contact when viewing faces and engaged more responsively in a ball‑tossing game. The hormone, linked to bonding, trust and maternal behavior, has been shown in other studies to reduce repetitive behaviors and improve emotion recognition. Researchers and outside experts called the results promising but preliminary, noting oxytocin’s short duration and the need for larger, controlled trials—especially in children—to assess safety, long‑term effects and therapeutic potential for core autism symptoms.

Target is launching a new budget wine line called California Roots: five $5 bottles made from California grapes—chardonnay, pinot grigio, moscato, cabernet sauvignon and a red blend—rolling out to about 1,100 Target stores that sell alcohol beginning Sept. 3. The retailer positions the collection as “carefully crafted with premium, California-grown grapes,” offering tasting notes and suggested pairings for each varietal. The move follows Target’s broader strategy to expand its alcohol selection—boosting craft beer and wine assortments and adding liquor in roughly 300 stores through remodels, larger footprints and new licenses. Target has seen mid-single-digit sales gains in adult beverages and is also opening several small-format stores and renovating locations as part of its turnaround, aiming to attract urban, college and value-minded shoppers.

A Secret Service prostitution scandal in Cartagena led to several dismissals and resignations and raised questions about agency culture and leadership. Among those ousted was supervisor David Chaney, who drew attention when old Facebook photos showed him standing near Sarah Palin during the 2008 campaign and joking, “I was really checking her out, if you know what i (sic) mean?” Palin called the posts embarrassing and quipped, “You’re fired!” The incident involved 11 Secret Service members and about 10 military personnel allegedly bringing prostitutes to hotel rooms the night before President Obama’s Summit of the Americas arrival; a dispute over payment made the matter public. The agency recalled, replaced and suspended implicated staff, revoked clearances, and fired three so far. Lawmakers and officials warned more dismissals could follow as formal investigations proceed in Colombia and the U.S. Counsel for Chaney and another supervisor, Greg Stokes, says the probe is incomplete and defenses are premature.

NBC10 Investigators exposed a man, calling himself Eric, who openly used a handheld cell‑phone jammer on SEPTA buses to silence people talking on their phones. Caught on undercover video after a rider reported repeated lost calls, Eric admitted buying the device online and “taking the law into my own hands,” saying phone conversations in public are rude. He initially believed jamming cell service was a gray area but, after being told it’s illegal, said he would dispose of the jammer. Federal law prohibits use, possession, sale or manufacture of jammers; penalties include fines and jail. Experts warn such devices pose serious public‑safety risks by potentially blocking GPS, two‑way radios and emergency calls, disrupting communication between crews, dispatch and 911. SEPTA says its systems are resilient and buses have panic buttons and other ways to summon help, but riders remain unnerved. Reporters noted the practice is more widespread on some commuter lines, where others admit using jammers to mute loud callers without guilt.

A Yale Law student preparing to interview for federal clerkships says professors Jed Rubenfeld and Amy Chua warned her about Judge Brett Kavanaugh’s apparent preference for female clerks with a “certain look.” The student, who asked to remain anonymous, recalls Rubenfeld pairing that remark with a warning about Alex Kozinski, then under suspicion for sexually harassing clerks. Though Rubenfeld did not describe the “look,” the student inferred it concerned physical appearance. Chua reportedly told a group of students last year that it was “not an accident” Kavanaugh’s female clerks “look like models” and offered to coach students on how to dress, even inviting photos to advise on outfits for interviews. The student found the counsel off-putting but ultimately interviewed with Kavanaugh and experienced nothing unusual; she later clerked elsewhere.

Chua, known for helping students secure prestigious clerkships and author of Battle Hymn of the Tiger Mother, defended Kavanaugh as an “exceptional mentor to his female clerks” and stressed his selection was based on excellence and produced diverse clerks. Travis Lenkner, a former Kavanaugh clerk, called the “certain look” notion absurd and emphasized formal dress standards. Observers note that advising students on interview attire is normal, but singling out a judge in this way raises troubling implications and can sound sexist. Yale has been alerted to concerns about Rubenfeld’s conduct, and an internal review reportedly exists; Chua is hospitalized and unreachable for detailed comment. The revelations add to the contentious public scrutiny surrounding Kavanaugh’s Supreme Court nomination amid separate assault allegations.

A growing trend in expensive cities: mobile IV therapy to treat hangovers and acute dehydration. The I.V. Doctor, founded by New York urologist Dr. Elliot Nadelson and his son Adam in December, brings intravenous hydration plus anti-nausea, anti-heartburn and anti-inflammatory medications to clients in homes, offices and hotels across New York and the Hamptons. For about $249 the most popular “full cocktail” is administered by one of roughly 60 nurses in the city (12 more in the Hamptons), who typically deliver around 200 ml of fluid over 35–40 minutes. Clients range from celebrities and athletes to a large contingent of finance professionals who value rapid recovery after late nights of client entertainment and long work hours. Users say the treatment isn’t a miracle but can lift them from feeling like a “2” to a “7,” enabling them to return to work the same day. The service markets convenience and discretion—nurses hook clients up in conference rooms, hotel suites or beach houses—and encourages pre-booking, especially on busy weekends.

Similar businesses have already thrived elsewhere: Las Vegas’s Hangover Heaven runs 24/7 clinics and offers at-room service for additional fees, illustrating high demand among tourists. The Nadelsons plan expansion to Chicago and are targeting Hamptons clientele via social media. They and other physicians view such offerings as supplemental income amid financial pressures in medicine; some doctors now supplement practice work with elective procedures or side services. Proponents argue the treatments help with hangovers, food poisoning, flu and post-event recovery, while critics question necessity. Early customers, like a Hamptons rental party and a Wall Street sales trader, report real, practical benefits and repeated use.

A team of cave divers and scientists working with the Gran Acuífero Maya (GAM) project has confirmed that two major flooded cave systems off Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula are connected, creating the world’s longest known underwater cave. After roughly ten months of targeted exploration near Tulum, explorers found a previously unmapped channel linking the 263-kilometer Sac Actun system with the 84-kilometer Dos Ojos system. The unified network measures about 347 kilometers (216 miles), surpassing other regional systems such as Ox Bel Ha and becoming the planet’s longest submerged cave system. By speleological convention the combined system retains the larger name, Sac Actun (“White Cave”).

Leaders of the effort—GAM director and underwater archaeologist Guillermo de Anda and lead diver Robert Schmittner—describe the achievement as the culmination of years of painstaking mapping and diving. The cave averages roughly 20 meters deep, with sections ranging from around 2 to 100 meters. It contains numerous dry or partially dry chambers where researchers have documented more than 100 archaeological contexts: remains of extinct fauna, evidence of some of America’s earliest human inhabitants, Mayan artifacts, ceramics, graves, cave paintings and ancient structural modifications such as walls and stairways. These finds link the aquifer’s history from the Pleistocene through pre-Hispanic Maya occupation to the colonial era and highlight the cenotes’ cultural and religious importance to the Maya.

Beyond archaeology, the system represents a vital fresh-water reservoir and supports notable subterranean biodiversity. GAM’s next priorities include further mapping, water-quality and biodiversity studies, conservation planning, and searching for additional interconnections among nearby systems — including a neighboring 11-mile system dubbed “the mother of all cenotes.” The discovery strengthens understanding of the region’s hydrogeology, heritage and the need to protect these fragile underground resources.

Saudi Arabia will move its official weekend from Thursday-Friday to Friday-Saturday starting June 29, a royal decree said, aligning the kingdom with other Gulf Cooperation Council states and aiming to reduce friction with global markets. Ministries and monetary bodies will adopt the change; schools will switch in the next academic year. Officials and market participants framed the shift as an economic modernization step that could help prepare the kingdom’s $400 billion stock market for broader foreign access. Currently non-resident investors participate only through share swaps and ETFs. Global banks including Deutsche Bank, HSBC, Morgan Stanley and Credit Suisse have been positioning in Riyadh amid expectations Saudi markets may open to direct foreign investment as soon as next year, potentially attracting large inflows. Index provider MSCI has upgraded neighboring UAE and Qatar, increasing pressure on Saudi Arabia to accelerate reforms to qualify for emerging-market status. The change is expected to ease cross-border trading hours, reduce lost opportunities from mismatched workweeks, and complement recent regulatory moves by the Capital Market Authority to modernize market rules.

An 11-year-old girl, Evha Jannath, died after falling from the Splash Canyon water ride at Drayton Manor theme park in Staffordshire during a school trip. Park staff rescued her and an air ambulance took her to Birmingham Children’s Hospital, where she was later pronounced dead. Evha, a Year 6 pupil from Jameah Girls Academy in Leicester, had borrowed suitable trip clothing from school so she could attend. Her family and school described her as loving and always smiling; the school and park closed for the day as a mark of respect. Staffordshire Police and the Health and Safety Executive have opened investigations. The incident prompted other parks to close similar rapids rides temporarily and renewed scrutiny of ride safety after past tragedies.

Barnes & Noble is rethinking its Nook strategy after e-reader and tablet sales plunged 34% in the fiscal fourth quarter ending April, prompting a broader shift. The company will continue selling Nook products and keep designing its black-and-white e-readers, but will pursue a partnership to outsource production of Nook HD tablets and may co-brand future devices with a third-party manufacturer. CEO William Lynch emphasized the company is not exiting the device business and said more details will follow. The move follows industry talk that Microsoft, which owns a 17.6% stake, might buy the Nook brand; Microsoft declined to comment. Barnes & Noble reported a $118.6 million fourth-quarter net loss, revenue down 7.4% to $1.3 billion, and digital sales fell nearly 9%. The company will still open about five new stores while closing 15–20.

Twitvid is rebranding as Telly and offers an early preview at telly.com; existing Twitvid users can log in with their accounts and find their videos already migrated. Separately, Stefanie Gordon, an event planner flying to Palm Beach, unexpectedly documented the space shuttle Endeavour’s final launch from her plane. She photographed and filmed the launch on her iPhone and posted an image to her roughly 1,800 Twitter followers. Her post quickly went viral, attracting calls from major outlets like ABC, the BBC and CNBC and about 1,000 new followers, forcing her to disable @mention alerts to save battery. Gordon says the view was awe-inspiring, she didn’t expect the attention, and she’s even shared her LinkedIn resume on Twitter as she looks for a job.

Alex Van Der Zwaan pleaded guilty to making false statements to FBI agents and the special counsel's office in Robert Mueller’s probe of Russian election interference. Prosecutors allege Van Der Zwaan lied about his final communications with former Trump campaign aide Rick Gates and another individual, then deleted requested emails. The lies concerned work he did for a firm hired by Ukraine’s Justice Ministry preparing a 2012 report on Yulia Tymoshenko’s trial; that report, produced by Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, was reportedly arranged by Paul Manafort for pro‑Yanukovych interests. Van Der Zwaan, a former Skadden London associate, was fired in 2017; the firm says it has cooperated with authorities. Gates is reportedly nearing a plea deal that could involve testimony against Manafort.

When White House counsel Kathryn Ruemmler received notice on April 24 about an upcoming inspector general report indicating the IRS had improperly targeted Tea Party and other conservative groups, she and senior aides, including Chief of Staff Denis McDonough, decided not to brief President Obama until the audit was complete and public. They believed that shielding him from premature information would protect him from any appearance of interfering. The White House’s cautious, lawyer-led approach aimed to preserve executive-branch prerogatives and avoid jeopardizing the presidency during a fraught second term beset by the IRS controversy, the Benghazi fallout, and Justice Department leak investigations.

Their plan unraveled when IRS official Lois Lerner disclosed the agency’s extra scrutiny of conservative groups on May 10, creating a communications crisis that made the administration look out of touch with its agencies. Ruemmler, described by colleagues as a “lawyer’s lawyer” who prioritizes legal process and protecting the president, argued against intervening before facts were clear; critics countered she should have at least briefed Obama for crisis planning. The White House’s inconsistent public explanations, chiefly by press secretary Jay Carney and adviser Dan Pfeiffer, damaged credibility and prompted PR strategy sessions with former campaign and Clinton aides to refocus messaging and the president’s agenda.

Commentary also criticized media coverage that trivialized Ruemmler with a separate profile on her shoes, highlighting gendered double standards: appearance-focused reporting on powerful women can undermine perceptions of competence. Supporters praise Ruemmler’s restraint and legal focus, while detractors call for more political and media savvy; the episode underscores tensions between legal caution and political management in the West Wing.

Danish police say inventor Peter Madsen told investigators and the Copenhagen court that Swedish freelance journalist Kim Wall died in an accident aboard his homemade UC3 Nautilus submarine on the night of 10 August, and that he subsequently "buried her at sea" in an unspecified part of Køge Bay. The court case is held behind closed doors; the substance of Madsen’s account was released after requests by defence and prosecution. Madsen, 46, who designed and owned the 18‑metre vessel, is charged with negligent manslaughter and remains suspected of deliberately sinking the submarine; police say they will not release further investigative details. Authorities from Denmark and Sweden have now mapped the Nautilus’s route through the Øresund and Køge Bay between its departure on 10 August and when it was relocated the following morning. Intensive searches—using divers, sonar, helicopters and ships—are under way along that track as teams try to recover Wall’s body; she was not found when the raised submarine was examined. Wall, 30, had boarded the submarine to research a feature about Madsen and was reported missing by her partner when she did not return. Madsen initially claimed he had dropped her ashore that night and later said he was alone when technical problems caused the vessel to sink; his lawyer stresses he pleads not guilty and has not admitted wrongdoing. The investigation continues.

Raymond Reinke, 55, of Pendleton, Oregon, pleaded guilty August 23, 2018, to four misdemeanor charges arising from multiple incidents in Yellowstone and Grand Teton National Parks, including a high-profile episode in which he aggressively provoked a bison. U.S. Magistrate Judge Mark Carman accepted a plea agreement that reduced five original misdemeanors to four and imposed a combined jail term of 130 days (with credit for 21 days served). Sentencing also included $70 in fees, five years of unsupervised probation, a ban on alcohol and bars while on probation, required substance abuse evaluation and treatment if needed, alcohol testing and searches upon reasonable suspicion, and a five-year ban from Yellowstone, Grand Teton, and Glacier National Parks. Some charges—being under the influence in Grand Teton and a disorderly conduct count in Yellowstone—were dismissed. Reinke, who has a long prior criminal history without felonies and has publicly identified as an alcoholic, apologized in court to the bison. Authorities described his harassment as among the most egregious animal disturbances they’d seen; the judge noted Reinke was fortunate the bison did not retaliate. Park officials reaffirmed their commitment to protecting wildlife and visitors, reminding the public to respect park rules and stewardship of public lands. Court records are available via PACER.

Police in El Cerrito are asking for the public’s help after a violent robbery may have been solved by a suspect’s own selfies. According to authorities, a teenage El Cerrito High School student was walking to class while talking on her iPhone when a car pulled up and a woman jumped out, demanded the girl’s phone and backpack, and began punching her when she refused. The victim was struck in the head several times, lost consciousness, suffered facial injuries, and later required recovery time. Several days afterward, while recuperating, the teen discovered new photos had appeared in her iCloud account and recognized the smiling woman in the selfies as her attacker. Police believe the suspect unintentionally uploaded the images from the stolen phone to iCloud, likely unaware of automatic cloud syncing. The department has released the photos and received many tips. Students reacted by warning peers to avoid flaunting valuables; one advised not showing off phones to reduce theft risk, while another called the suspect’s actions “kinda dumb” for taking incriminating pictures. Authorities continue to investigate and seek assistance identifying and apprehending the woman.

In Sedro-Woolley, Washington, the owner of Lucky Teriyaki asked local law enforcement not to dine at the restaurant after four Skagit County deputies finished lunch there, drawing swift attention and conflicting accounts. Sheriff Will Reichardt posted on the Skagit County Sheriff’s Office Facebook page that two deputies who went to pay were told by the owner that other customers didn’t like law enforcement and that deputies were no longer welcome. Reichardt said his chief deputy later called the owner, who reiterated the request and asked that the message be spread to other law enforcement agencies.

The sheriff’s post quickly went viral, provoking thousands of shares and a flood of comments. Some social media users condemned the owner’s action as wrong and insulting to officers, while others defended the right of businesses to refuse service if customers felt uncomfortable. The Sedro-Woolley Police Department said it was disappointed but would keep responding to businesses as needed. Nearby business owner Mike Bennett said the community generally shows strong support for deputies and was surprised by the incident.

Through an interpreter, Lucky Teriyaki’s owners explained the episode as a major misunderstanding driven by language barriers and fear after receiving online and phone death threats. They said the situation began when an employee noticed other customers had spilled soup and water and, not understanding why the customers were upset, wondered aloud whether the deputies’ presence had caused it. The employee asked the deputies if they were about to leave; later, attempts by law enforcement to clarify the matter were hampered by miscommunication. The owners expressed remorse, invited police to eat for free at Lucky Teriyaki on July 18, and said they welcome officers. Separately, Dave North, owner of The Bullpen Sports Bar & Grill, plans a police appreciation fundraiser in early August for the Behind the Badge Foundation, with participating restaurants and details to be announced.

Twin explosions rocked Damascus near 7 a.m., striking the heavily guarded Syrian army command headquarters by Omayyad Square, shattering nearby windows and sending thick black smoke over the capital. State media and witnesses reported a car bomb and an explosive device detonated near the compound, followed by hours of heavy gunfire and fierce clashes around and inside the military complex. Witnesses described panicked soldiers and sounds of shooting from within the building, and the British-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported casualties on both sides. The army said no senior commanders were harmed but acknowledged several guards were wounded and blamed “terrorists” for the attack. Ambulances rushed in as police sealed off the area, set up checkpoints, and snarled traffic into and out of Damascus.

The violence underscored rebels’ increasing reach in targeting regime power centers during the civil war that began in March 2011 and has killed tens of thousands. The strikes came amid other recent bombings in Damascus, including a July attack that killed top officials. Internationally, the conflict dominated U.N. discussions, with Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon calling for action while the Security Council remained paralyzed by Russian and Chinese vetoes. Separately, Iranian Press TV reported its correspondent Maya Nasser was killed in the area during the fighting, and its bureau chief was injured; the network blamed states it accused of arming militants.

Investigators released a suspect description for an attempted abduction near Ketner Lake on May 28 as they seek any leads that might connect that incident to the Oct. 5 abduction and murder of 10-year-old Jessica Ridgeway. Police say a 22-year-old woman jogging near Ketner Lake — about a half-mile from Jessica’s home and just south of Witt Elementary School — was grabbed from behind by a man who tried to put a chemical‑soaked rag over her mouth. She escaped and called 911. The assailant was described as white or light‑skinned, 18–30 years old, about 5'8", with brown hair and a medium build. No vehicle description is available. Westminster police are reviewing other attempted abductions in the Denver metro area and seeking tips about unusual behavior or people who changed habits around Memorial Day or Oct. 5. Authorities also ask the public to watch for someone owning or wearing a distinctive cross linked to the suspect. Call Westminster police at 303‑658‑4336 or email PDamberalert@cityofwestminster.us with information.

Artist Ryan Mendoza, who salvaged the dilapidated Detroit home where civil-rights icon Rosa Parks once lived, wants to return the reconstructed house from Germany to the United States. Mendoza removed the home's facade about a year ago to prevent demolition, shipped it to Berlin, and refashioned it as an artwork to give international audiences a closer connection to Parks’ life and legacy. He says the timing is urgent as America confronts debates over Confederate monuments and the resurgence of white nationalism; he believes Parks’ home would serve as a corrective symbol and reminder of the struggle for justice and equality.

Mendoza, a 45-year-old painter who lives in Germany, has invested more than $130,000—much from selling his own work—to disassemble, move and rebuild the roughly 21-by-21-foot house and is now finishing the interior. The project has drawn thousands of visitors in Berlin and attention from public figures; Germany’s vice chancellor Sigmar Gabriel has championed returning the house and even wrote to Michelle Obama on the matter. In the U.S., Mendoza says Detroit cultural institutions have shown limited interest, but several museums and one foundation—the Nash Family Foundation—has pledged up to $40,000 to help ship it back. Mendoza hopes the house will be displayed in a prominent U.S. venue, perhaps in Washington, D.C., or New York, so Parks’ legacy can be more visible amid ongoing national conversations about memory and monuments.

Researchers in Japan have successfully grown an adult-size human ear from induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells, marking a notable advance in regenerative medicine. Teams at the University of Tokyo and Kyoto University cultured human iPS cells into cartilage cells, formed them into numerous microscopic cell "balls," and loaded these into three slender biodegradable tubes molded in the shape of a human ear. The ear-shaped construct was implanted under the skin of a rat; over about two months the tubes dissolved and left a roughly 5-centimeter, living ear-like cartilage structure. Photographs show the ear on the rat’s back. The researchers say the reconstructed ear could be used to treat people born with missing or malformed ears, and because it is a living graft it could grow as a child grows; they hope to begin human clinical trials in about five years.

The ear growth builds on broader worldwide bioengineering progress: teams are developing artificial kidneys using human cells and nanofilters, lab-grown intestines and “gut-on-a-chip” models for diagnostics, bioengineered intervertebral disc therapies, windpipes and bladders from patient cells, early-stage liver “buds,” and hybrid or biologically enhanced artificial hearts. Advances in making blood vessels from patient cells and scalable artificial skin production also promise improved treatments. While risks remain—illustrated by complications in high-profile cases—scientists continue pursuing tissue engineering to address organ shortages and repair traumatic or congenital defects.

Florida Gov. Rick Scott and state lawmakers unveiled what they described as the most significant Florida gun-control proposal in decades in response to the Parkland school massacre. The plan, announced amid massive student protests, would raise the minimum age to purchase any firearm, including semiautomatic rifles, from 18 to 21 (with exceptions for active-duty military, National Guard, law enforcement and spouses), ban bump stocks, strengthen background checks and waiting periods, and require those involuntarily committed under the Baker Act to temporarily surrender guns until a court hearing. It would also bar people subject to injunctions for stalking, domestic violence or similar protections from purchasing or possessing firearms, create a new “Violent Threat Restraining Order,” and enhance penalties for threats to schools and for possessing guns when legally prohibited.

Scott proposed a $450 million school safety initiative to place a resource officer in every public school (one per 1,000 students), fund metal detectors and hardened infrastructure, mandate active-shooter training and drills, create anonymous “See Something, Say Something” reporting tools, and establish threat-assessment teams. A separate $50 million mental-health package would expand counseling, embed Department of Children and Families case managers in sheriff’s offices, and fund special law enforcement-mental health teams.

The proposals split opinion. Survivors and many Democrats criticized Scott for not banning AR-15–style assault rifles, a key student demand, and for stopping short of broader measures. Some students welcomed elements like the 21-year age floor, increased officers, and mental-health funding but opposed arming teachers. Scott explicitly rejected arming teachers, countering President Trump’s proposal. Experts and education leaders argued arming teachers is dangerous and unrealistic, noting training limits, risks in chaotic shootings, and harms of increased policing in schools—especially to marginalized students. The plan marks a significant political break with the NRA in Florida, drawing both praise from local law enforcement and criticism from gun-rights advocates.

Seven men have been charged in the 2014 hazing death of University at Albany student Trevor Duffy; authorities allege the group forced Duffy to drink a 60-ounce bottle of vodka, causing his death. The men were reported to have identified themselves as members of Zeta Beta Tau (ZBT), specifically claiming affiliation with the Epsilon Gamma chapter, but the national fraternity and the university say the group was never recognized and had no official ties to ZBT. In response, Zeta Beta Tau released a formal statement distancing itself from the men and denouncing their actions. The Indianapolis-based national organization emphasized that the individuals involved were not, and have never been, members of ZBT, and characterized them as a “rogue group” illegally using the fraternity’s name and materials.

ZBT announced it has retained legal counsel and plans to sue the individuals for falsely representing themselves, deceiving the public, and damaging the fraternity’s reputation. The statement noted that ZBT’s name, symbols, slogans, and materials are protected by U.S. copyright and trademark law, and warned that unauthorized use—such as representing oneself as a chapter member or wearing ZBT letters—could prompt legal action. Founded in 1898 as the world’s first Jewish fraternity, ZBT has chapters on more than 90 campuses and over 130,000 undergraduate and alumni members.

Attorney Paul DerOhannesian, who represents accused student Joseph Angilletta, said the fraternity’s move appears aimed at distancing itself from the tragic event. He acknowledged being informed of the lawsuit but was not prepared to comment further on his client’s defense.

The Bramble Cay melomys (Melomys rubicola), a small mosaic‑tailed rodent found only on Bramble Cay at the northern tip of Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, has been confirmed extinct on its sole known island population following comprehensive surveys. Intensive searches in 2014—using cameras, traps and systematic searches led by Queensland authorities and University of Queensland researchers—produced no records, confirming local extirpation. Historic data show a steady decline: estimates fell from at most several hundred animals in 1978 to 93 in 1998, then to just 10–12 detections in the early 2000s, with the last confirmed sighting in 2009. The island’s area above high tide decreased markedly (from about 4 ha in 1998 to 2.5 ha in 2014), and researchers attribute the primary cause of the melomys’ disappearance to repeated seawater inundation that dramatically reduced herbaceous vegetation the species depended on—especially the succulent Portulaca oleracea—and eliminated daytime refuges. With Bramble Cay only about 3 m above high tide and subject to seasonal erosion, storm surges and extreme high water events over the previous decade, the study concludes that anthropogenic climate change—sea‑level rise and increased intensity/frequency of bad weather—was almost certainly the root cause. While the report notes a remote possibility that an undiscovered population exists in nearby Papua New Guinea’s Fly River delta, searches of other Torres Strait islands have found none. The loss is significant because it likely represents the first documented mammalian extinction attributed primarily to human‑driven climate change. Conservation groups warn this case underscores Australia’s mammal extinction crisis and call for substantial funding to protect other vulnerable native species.

Sebastian Gorka, a deputy assistant to President Trump and ally of Steve Bannon, has left the White House amid internal disputes over the administration’s direction. Gorka’s exit came one week after Bannon’s ouster; Gorka published a resignation letter, saying “forces that do not support the MAGA promise” had become ascendant and that the most effective way to support the president was from outside the White House. He criticized the administration’s recent Afghanistan policy speech for omitting references to “Radical Islam” and for listing operational objectives without defined strategic victory conditions, arguing the omissions signaled a loss of campaign principles and a continuation of flawed policy.

A White House official disputed that Gorka resigned, stating only that he no longer works at the White House, and another aide suggested his removal reflected Chief of Staff John Kelly’s reshaping of staff. Questions were raised about whether his wife, Katie Gorka, a Department of Homeland Security official, would remain.

Gorka, formerly a national security editor at Breitbart and a Marine Corps University fellow, focused in the West Wing on counterterrorism, the Muslim Brotherhood, the Qatar crisis, and China. He was more prominent as a media surrogate than as an internal policymaker and was frequently defended by Bannon. His tenure was controversial: critics accused him of extremist ties, citing past Breitbart work and a Hungarian medal he wore; defenders said such charges were unfair and personal attacks extended to his family.

Following his departure, House Democrats proposed amendments to bar federal funds for Gorka and Stephen Miller’s salaries, accusing them of fostering white supremacist-friendly policies—amendments unlikely to reach the floor. Gorka’s future role, including a possible return to Breitbart, remained unclear.

An Amtrak Cascades passenger train derailed early Monday morning on its inaugural run along the new Point Defiance Bypass near DuPont, Wash., sending 13 cars off an overpass onto Interstate 5, killing three people and injuring more than 70. The train, carrying 80 passengers, five crew and a technician, was traveling about 80 mph when it entered a curve where the posted speed limit drops to 30 mph. NTSB data from the rear locomotive’s event recorder confirmed the excessive speed. Witnesses and investigators described mangled cars, some dangling over the highway, and chaotic rescue work that included cutting victims from crushed cars and using ladders to reach trapped passengers. Good Samaritans and medical professionals on the scene aided first responders.

The derailment occurred on a newly upgraded 14.5-mile corridor that had undergone a roughly $181 million retrofit to shorten travel time between Seattle and Portland. Although the line is equipped for positive train control (PTC) — a system designed to prevent overspeed incidents — Amtrak officials said PTC was not yet operational on this segment; testing was still underway. Federal regulators had mandated PTC nationwide after earlier deadly crashes, but full implementation has been repeatedly delayed.

Investigators have not determined why the train was traveling so fast. The Washington State Patrol, NTSB and other agencies are continuing the probe. The wreck closed southbound I-5 and disrupted regional rail service; Governor Jay Inslee declared a state of emergency. The crash revived debates over infrastructure investment and speed-control technology on U.S. rail lines.

A 5-year-old Texas girl, Allison Anderwald, is being hailed as a hero after home surveillance caught her saving her mother, Tracy Anderwald, when Tracy suffered a seizure and sank to the bottom of a backyard pool in Portland, Texas. Tracy, 34, had been enjoying a mother-daughter swim with Allison when she suddenly blacked out, sank four feet to the pool floor and did not surface for more than five minutes. Realizing her mother hadn’t come up, Allison dove down, pulled Tracy to the shallow end and flipped her so Tracy’s head was out of the water. Tracy’s sister, Tedra Hunt, was walking toward the house when Allison ran to her; Hunt called 911 and emergency responders transported Tracy to CHRISTUS Spohn Hospital Corpus Christi-Memorial. Doctors later told the family that had Tracy remained underwater any longer she likely would not have survived. Initially doctors had low expectations for Tracy’s recovery and feared possible neurological damage, but she awoke the next morning, underwent tests, and was released from the hospital a few days later. Tracy, who has never had a seizure before, will follow up with a neurologist to determine the cause. Family members described Allison as calm and instinctive during the crisis; she had been swimming since about two-and-a-half and was taught water safety. Hunt, emotional about nearly losing her sister after their father’s death two years earlier, called Allison’s action a miracle and credited their late father as a “guardian angel.” The family hopes the incident highlights the importance of early swim lessons and teaching children how to respond in water emergencies. Tracy affectionately calls Allison “our little mermaid and my little hero.”

US ambassador to New Zealand Scott Brown has acknowledged being the subject of an official US State Department inquiry after allegations that he made inappropriate remarks during a July trip to Samoa, where he also serves as the US representative. Brown spoke publicly about the complaints in an interview alongside his wife, Gail Huff, saying he wanted to address “innuendo and rumour” about his conduct at an event in Apia held to celebrate 50 years of the Peace Corps in Samoa.

Brown confirmed that State Department investigators visited Wellington to examine what occurred. He described the complaints as stemming from comments he made at a party, where he told attendees they looked “beautiful” and suggested they could earn hundreds of dollars working in the US hospitality industry. Brown and Huff said they were unaware those remarks would be taken as offensive. Brown added that, as an ambassador, he had been reminded to be “culturally aware of different cultures and sensitivities,” noting that common language does not prevent different meanings across cultures.

Huff said the incident’s lesson was that they would “be very, very careful about what we say and how it’s perceived.” The Guardian reports that the complaints originated from two serving female Peace Corps members. The newspaper sought comment from the US State Department, the US Embassy in Wellington and the US High Commission in Samoa in August but had not received responses by the time of reporting. A spokesperson for the US embassy in Wellington later said only that “Ambassador Brown has nothing to add to the comments he made in this afternoon’s interview.”

Brown was President Donald Trump’s first ambassadorial appointment after Trump took office. The matter has drawn attention amid heightened scrutiny of diplomatic conduct and cultural sensitivity during overseas postings. The article also references archival efforts by web crawlers to preserve pages and combat broken links, though that detail is ancillary to the primary report on the ambassadorial complaint.

A Baltimore judge ruled that the prosecutions of six police officers charged in Freddie Gray’s death will proceed in separate trials and refused to remove State’s Attorney Marilyn Mosby or dismiss the charges. At a packed pretrial hearing, Judge Barry Williams denied defense motions alleging prosecutorial misconduct by Mosby, saying her May comments, while troubling, did not deprive the officers of a fair trial and that marriage to a city councilman was not grounds for recusal. Williams also concluded that trying all six together would be “not in the interest of justice” because key evidence admissible against some defendants would be inadmissible against others, so the officers will face six separate trials. The officers—Caesar Goodson Jr., Sgt. Alicia White, Lt. Brian Rice, Officer William Porter, Edward Nero and Garrett Miller—face charges ranging from second-degree assault and misconduct in office to manslaughter and, for Goodson, second-degree “depraved-heart” murder. Outside the courthouse, dozens of largely peaceful protesters rallied and marched, briefly blocking roads and resulting in one arrest; tensions flared near the Inner Harbor. Williams admonished attorneys for overheated rhetoric and sought orderly proceedings as the high-profile case, which has prompted national debate about policing and race, moves forward.

A recent Facebook report highlighted how quickly online language shifts, showing that “LOL” has declined into one of the least-used ways to show laughter on the social network. The drop in LOL’s popularity appears tied to demographics: older users are disproportionately the ones still using it, while younger people favor emoji and other text-based laughter like “haha” or “hehe.” The piece suggests the decline is partly cultural—what was once trendy in the early internet era is now seen as outdated—and partly generational, with older adults maintaining earlier habits. The report doesn’t fully account for ironic or playful uses of LOL (or similar expressions), but the usage data is clear: fewer people employ LOL, and those who do skew older. Explanations floated include older users not adopting emoji keyboards, misunderstanding LOL’s meaning, or simply sticking with a familiar habit. Regardless of cause, the takeaway is that LOL’s cultural prominence is fading as emoji—especially the 😂 face—becomes the dominant way younger users convey laughter online. The trend illustrates broader, rapid evolution in online language and expression.

Nearly half of the edible seafood supply in the United States is lost each year due to inefficiencies across the supply chain and consumer behavior, according to a study in Global Environmental Change by researchers at Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future. The authors estimate the U.S. edible seafood supply at about 4.7 billion pounds annually and calculate total losses of roughly 2.3 billion pounds. Losses break down to about 1.3 billion pounds discarded by consumers, 573 million pounds lost as bycatch when fishers unintentionally catch non-target species, and 330 million pounds lost during distribution and retail.

The study finds that consumers account for the largest share of waste (51–63 percent), followed by bycatch (16–32 percent) and distribution/retail losses (13–16 percent). The wasted seafood contains enough protein to meet the annual needs of more than 10 million people and could close about 36 percent of the gap between current U.S. seafood consumption and the 2010 Dietary Guidelines recommendation of eight ounces per person per week. Achieving that guideline would otherwise require roughly doubling the current seafood supply.

Authors caution that not all lost seafood can or should be recovered for human consumption—bycatch is often better avoided than eaten, and seafood’s short shelf life complicates redistribution. They recommend prevention-focused strategies across government, industry, and consumers: reducing allowable bycatch, offering smaller portion packaging, promoting frozen options, and other measures to minimize loss and make the seafood system more efficient and sustainable. The findings arrive amid broader U.S. efforts to halve food waste by 2030.

At the 18th Critics' Choice Movie Awards in Santa Monica, Ben Affleck’s Iran-hostage drama Argo won best picture and Affleck took best director, a strong precursor for the Oscars. Jennifer Lawrence had a standout night, winning both best actress in an action movie for The Hunger Games and best comedic actress for Silver Linings Playbook; Silver Linings Playbook also won best comedy. Daniel Day-Lewis won best actor for Lincoln, and Jessica Chastain won best actress for Zero Dark Thirty. Anne Hathaway received best supporting actress for Les Misérables, while Judd Apatow earned the Louis XIII Genius Award. The ceremony, hosted at Barker Hangar and broadcast on The CW, highlighted how critics’ choices often forecast Academy Award trends.

A violent storm swept across northern Europe and much of the United States, leaving coastal flooding, travel chaos and several deaths in its wake. In Britain, hurricane-force winds produced the largest tidal surge in 60 years along parts of the eastern coast, flooding about 1,400 homes, prompting evacuations and forcing the Thames Barrier in London to close twice. In eastern England cliffs were eroded and houses at Hemsby fell into the sea. Britain recorded two storm-related fatalities; overall at least eight people died across northern Europe (Britain, Sweden, Denmark and Poland). Flood warnings and stronger coastal defenses limited casualties compared with historic events such as the 1953 and 1962 surges, though further tidal surges were forecast for some areas including Hamburg and parts of the Danish Roskilde fjord where towns were evacuated and the Viking Ship Museum boarded up windows. Airports and rail links across northern Europe saw widespread cancellations and thousands stranded; in Copenhagen over 1,000 spent the night at the airport. The storm boosted German wind-power generation dramatically, briefly supplying roughly 35% of the country’s output. Separately, a severe winter storm gripped much of the U.S., bringing record cold in Dallas/Fort Worth, heavy snow and ice across the mid-Atlantic and Plains, hundreds of crashes, hundreds of flight cancellations, multiple fatalities and state emergencies in Tennessee and Arkansas.

Beyoncé and Jay-Z’s daughter Blue Ivy may invite a few teasing remarks about color-learning in kindergarten, but her name isn’t the most outlandish among celebrity children. Though distinctive, Blue Ivy stands relatively tame compared with some Hollywood monikers like Audio Science, Pilot Inspektor, Moon Unit and Apple. The music power couple’s choice still avoids the most extreme eccentricities, and their daughter won’t exactly blend into a classroom of ordinary Catherines. Celebrity baby names range from quirky to bizarre, and outlets such as HuffPost Parents have highlighted and even invited readers to pick future top baby names.

Ben Bernanke will hold the Fed’s first-ever scheduled news conference Wednesday at 2:15 p.m., prompting calls for tougher media scrutiny about why the Fed is tolerating prolonged high unemployment despite claiming tools to reduce it. The article argues Bernanke could commit to keeping rates at zero longer, tolerate temporarily higher inflation, or explicitly reject extended joblessness, but has been cautious, citing inflation risks. Critics who always fear inflation have limited power, so responsibility rests with Bernanke. Core inflation remains low, making runaway inflation unlikely, while the costs of sustained unemployment—lost savings, worse health, permanent scarring, and political dysfunction—are severe. The FOMC kept rates at 0–0.25%, ends its $600 billion bond-buying on June 30, noted a moderate recovery, and reiterated rates will stay low for an extended period. Updated forecasts will be released before the news conference.

China’s official economic data face serious credibility questions even as the economy slows to its weakest growth in years. A 2007 remark by Li Keqiang — later revealed by WikiLeaks — that GDP statistics are “man‑made” and “for reference only” underscores lasting doubts. Official second‑quarter growth was 7.6%, down from 8.1%, marking the sixth consecutive quarterly slowdown and the slowest pace in three years. Analysts note internal inconsistencies: provincial GDP totals exceed the national figure by about 10% due partly to double counting, registered urban unemployment has barely budged near 4%, while electricity consumption and rail cargo have weakened faster than GDP, suggesting numbers may be smoothed upward. China measures industrial output and corporate profits relatively well thanks to legacy reporting systems, but tracking services and household consumption is weaker; retail figures can be inflated by government and state enterprise purchases. Market watchers use alternatives — bank loans, electricity use, rail freight, earth‑moving equipment sales, and surveys like the China Beige Book — as better economic gauges. Beijing has reformed data collection, centralizing reporting and working with international agencies, but opacity remains, and some see withholding methodological details as preserving flexibility to adjust figures. Policymakers have cut rates and reserve requirements to cushion the slowdown while seeking a gradual rebalancing from investment toward consumption.

Most modern Thanksgiving foods—turkey, cranberry sauce, stuffing, pumpkin pie—aren’t strictly what the 1621 Plymouth feast featured. Contemporary accounts like Edward Winslow’s describe “wild fowl” and five deer gifted by the Wampanoag leader Massasoit, plus abundant fish and shellfish—no explicit turkey mention. Turkey became central later: Bradford’s journals (reprinted in 1856) and its status as an American bird helped popularize it, and Lincoln’s 1863 national Thanksgiving cemented traditions. Practical reasons favored turkey: large size to feed families, limited utility compared with chickens or cows, and rarity compared with pork. Cranberry sauce likely wasn’t at the first meal either—sugar was scarce and the sweetened sauce appears in records only by 1663—though native peoples used cranberries extensively (fresh, dried, in pemmican, dyes, and medicines). Native pemmican—dried meat, tallow, and cranberries—was a long-lasting energy food crucial to trade. Colonists adapted cranberries to European recipes once sweeteners like honey and later cane sugar were available, helping cranberry dishes and pies rise in popularity. Pumpkins were eaten but not as baked pies—pilgrims lacked flour, butter, and ovens—but pumpkin preparations evolved into pies by the 17th century. As for drinks, hard apple cider was likely common: apples grew locally, cider was England’s popular beverage, and colonists brewed cider and distilled applejack. Today cider is resurging alongside revived interest in heirloom apples and regional craft producers.

Luke Irwin, a rug designer in Wiltshire, accidentally uncovered one of Britain’s most significant recent archaeological finds while having electricians lay an underground power cable to light a converted barn. Drilling revealed a hard layer 18 inches down that proved to be Roman mosaic—prompting Historic England to intervene. Subsequent excavation showed the mosaic formed part of a vast, high-status Roman villa dating from about AD 175–220, remodelled several times before the fifth century and left largely undisturbed for more than 1,400–1,500 years.

Archaeologists say the three-storey villa would have dominated the valley and rivals other major sites like Chedworth. Finds so far include an exceptionally fine mosaic, Purbeck marble slab beneath the Irwins’ house (likely Roman), a perfectly preserved well, high-status pottery, brooches, coins, animal bones, a suckling pig, and hundreds of discarded oyster and whelk shells that indicate live shellfish were transported from the coast in barrels of saltwater—evidence of great wealth. A stone coffin of a Roman child had been repurposed as a flowerbed until its significance was realised. Wall remnants appear to survive more than a metre high beneath alluvial sediment.

Historic England’s Dr David Roberts describes the untouched site as “unparalleled in recent years,” offering a rare chance to study Roman elite life and the poorly understood transition between Roman Britain and the early post-Roman (fifth-century) period; timber structures from that era suggest continuity of occupation after imperial collapse. The site has been protected for preservation, with further research planned pending funding. Irwin said uncovering artifacts untouched for over a millennium around his home was a powerful, mind‑blowing experience.

British Prime Minister Theresa May announced the expulsion of 23 Russian diplomats after concluding it was "highly likely" the Russian state ordered the March 4 nerve-agent attack on former Russian double agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia in Salisbury. Both remain critically ill after exposure to Novichok, a Soviet-era nerve agent; May said the expulsions— the largest from the UK in three decades—plus asset freezes and a boycott of the 2018 World Cup by senior royals and ministers, would degrade Russian intelligence capabilities in the UK for years. London set a midnight deadline for Moscow to explain how the nerve agent was used; when it failed to provide a credible response, Britain acted and invited the OPCW to investigate. Russia dismissed the accusations as a "circus show" and a "hostile action," with its UN envoy accusing Britain of rushed conclusions and even suggesting other countries could be responsible. 

U.S. responses were mixed. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson had called Russia "clearly" responsible, and U.N. Ambassador Nikki Haley delivered a strong statement at the Security Council declaring the United States "stands in absolute solidarity" with Britain and urging the Council to hold Russia accountable, warning that failure to act would endanger other cities. The White House later echoed solidarity, but President Donald Trump’s public comments were measured and delayed—he said he would wait for facts before condemning Russia—drawing criticism from former diplomats who expected immediate, unequivocal support for the UK and worry that ambiguity might embolden Moscow. The episode recalls the Litvinenko poisoning and has intensified calls for coordinated international action.

This report, using National Hospital Discharge Survey (NHDS) data from 1979–2010, presents national and regional estimates of male newborn circumcisions performed during the birth hospitalization. It emphasizes that these estimates exclude circumcisions done outside hospitals (e.g., ritual procedures) or after discharge, so they should not be interpreted as overall prevalence of male circumcision in the United States. Nationally, the in-hospital newborn circumcision rate fell about 10% over the 32-year period, from 64.5% in 1979 to 58.3% in 2010, with a high of 64.9% in 1981 and a low of 55.4% in 2007. Trends were not linear: rates declined in the 1980s, rose through the 1990s, then declined again in the early 2000s—changes that coincided with shifting American Academy of Pediatrics guidance on routine newborn circumcision. Regionally, patterns diverged. The Northeast showed no steady trend, fluctuating between roughly 61% and 70%. The Midwest mirrored national patterns, ranging from about 69% to 83%. The South increased until the late 1990s then declined, with rates between about 54% and 66%. The West saw the most pronounced decline: a 37% drop from 63.9% in 1979 to 40.2% in 2010, with steep decreases in the 1980s and continued decline through the 2000s (low of 31.4% in 2003). NHDS, the only reliable national historical source for in-hospital newborn circumcision, identified procedures via ICD-9-CM code 64.0. Trends were analyzed with JoinPoint software to detect statistically significant changes. The report notes comparisons with other data sources showed modest differences (under 6% for any year) and points readers to NCHS resources for further data access.

As Hurricane Sandy’s immediate destructiveness eased, the brief interruption it caused in the presidential campaign was ending and both campaigns began returning to politics while continuing disaster response. President Obama delayed campaign stops to oversee federal relief, visiting the Red Cross, coordinating with officials and touring damage in New Jersey with GOP Gov. Chris Christie, who praised his response. That visibility offered political benefits but also kept Obama off the trail during the campaign’s final days, risking lost momentum tied to high-profile travel and early-vote mobilization.

Mitt Romney paused a planned Dayton rally and turned it into a storm-relief event, helping load supplies and urging donations, then resumed campaigning in Florida with events Wednesday. Both campaigns sought to balance sensitivity to victims with the urgency of closing a tight race. The Republican operation also launched aggressive ad buys aiming to expand the battleground map into states like Pennsylvania, Michigan and Minnesota; allies were spending millions while Obama’s team countered with its own airtime and dismissed Republican moves as signs of weakness.

A heated exchange intensified over a Romney ad suggesting Obama’s auto bailout benefited China, specifically alleging Jeep production would move there. Chrysler and Fiat executives refuted that claim, and Obama’s campaign countered with its own spot. With Election Day days away, both sides scrambled to manage optics: Obama leveraging incumbency and disaster leadership, Romney emphasizing compassion and continued retail campaigning. Campaign strategists agreed both must re-engage quickly while avoiding appearing overly political amid ongoing recovery.

President Trump used Twitter to accuse the media of treating his son unfairly after reports that Donald Trump Jr. met a Russian lawyer during the 2016 campaign, arguing that “fake news” and “phony unnamed sources” are “DISTORTING DEMOCRACY.” He contrasted scrutiny of his son with Hillary Clinton’s controversies and thanked Michael Caputo for defending the administration, as well as attendees of the U.S. Women’s Open where he recently appeared. The New York Times report about the June 9, 2016 meeting — which included Paul Manafort and Jared Kushner and described the attendee as a “Russian government lawyer” offering damaging Clinton information — intensified questions about possible campaign links to Russia.  

Michael Caputo, a former Trump campaign communications adviser with unusually deep Russia ties, told CNN he never heard anyone in the campaign discuss Russian involvement. Caputo, who lived and worked in Russia in the 1990s and later ran a PR firm with Moscow ties, denied wrongdoing in a pre-testimony interview and said the campaign was too frenetic for any organized collusion. He resigned from the campaign in June 2016 after tweeting about Corey Lewandowski’s dismissal. Caputo has been characterized by critics as part of a “tarantula web” of Russian links and labeled “Putin’s image consultant” by Rep. Jackie Speier, a charge he denied, saying his work for Gazprom Media was mischaracterized.  

Caputo testified for three and a half hours behind closed doors to the House intelligence committee, reiterating he had no knowledge of contacts between the campaign and Russia and describing the hearings as a debunking of what he calls the “Russia collusion delusion.” Lawmakers including Tom Rooney, Adam Schiff, Eric Swalwell and Denny Heck attended his session.

Howard Stern sat for a more-than-three-hour interview with Rolling Stone writer Neil Strauss at SiriusXM, forming the basis of a new cover story that probes his personal life, career and future. Stern opens up about the trauma of his divorce from ex-wife Alison and the chaotic period that followed before he met his current wife, Beth. He discusses longtime therapy, his role as an interviewer—defending his habit of cutting guests off as a way to keep shows fresh—and his evolving work schedule. Although Stern recently renewed his contract, he says he once believed he might leave radio; now he plans to reduce workload over time, moving from four taped days a week toward perhaps three shows weekly so he can pursue other interests.

The interview touches on the painful situation of former sidekick Artie Lange, who attempted suicide early last year and has been off the air since. Lange has spoken with Stern about possibly returning, but Stern says he is cautious: he does not feel strong enough to handle the situation on air and prioritizes Lange’s staying alive over sensationalizing his struggles. A lighter moment came when Stern coaxed Strauss into revealing a private detail about Strauss’s girlfriend during an on-air exchange that delighted Stern’s audience.

The feature is supplemented with archival links and past Rolling Stone profiles of Stern, including pieces from 1990, 1994 and 1997, and earlier coverage of Artie Lange, placing the new interview in the context of Stern’s long public career and personal trials.

Eighteen House Republicans have formally nominated President Donald Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize, submitting a letter to the Norwegian Nobel Committee that credits him with pressing for denuclearization on the Korean Peninsula and helping to end the 68-year wartime stalemate between North and South Korea. Led by Rep. Luke Messer (R-Ind.), the lawmakers argue Trump “worked tirelessly to apply maximum pressure on North Korea” and united the international community — notably engaging China — to implement a stringent sanctions regime they call among the most successful in history. Messer announced his intent to nominate Trump after a landmark inter-Korean summit in which North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korean President Moon Jae-in pledged to pursue the elimination of nuclear weapons on the peninsula and to enter talks with the U.S. aimed at formally ending the Korean War, which has technically continued since the 1953 armistice.

Trump is slated to meet Kim in late May or June, marking the first meeting between a sitting U.S. president and a North Korean leader. Ahead of that summit, North Korea has agreed to suspend nuclear and long-range missile tests and announced the planned shutdown of a northern nuclear site as a goodwill gesture. Voices across the political spectrum have reacted cautiously optimistic: Senate Foreign Relations Chairman Bob Corker praised the administration’s role in rallying pressure on Pyongyang and said Trump would deserve a Nobel if the diplomacy succeeds, while urging skepticism given North Korea’s history of broken commitments. Retired Gen. Michael Hayden also credited the combination of sanctions, diplomatic isolation, and military signaling for bringing Kim to the table, though he criticized Trump’s earlier bellicose tweets toward the North Korean leader as unwise. Overall, supporters hail diplomatic momentum; critics and analysts warn that verification and follow-through remain critical.

Eat Pray Love, adapted from Elizabeth Gilbert’s bestselling memoir, follows Julia Roberts as Liz Gilbert, a well-off New York writer who abandons a failing marriage and an unsatisfying affair to spend a year seeking herself across Italy, India, and Bali. The film leans heavily on romanticized visuals — sumptuous food, sunlit landscapes, colorful locals, and handsome men — while treating Eastern spirituality superficially. Director Ryan Murphy retains the book’s itinerary-driven structure (Eat, Pray, Love) and its touristic pleasures, but struggles to translate Gilbert’s intimate, confessional voice to the screen. Roberts brings warmth and magnetic charm, making even mundane pleasures feel sensuous, and Javier Bardem provides appealing romantic chemistry. Richard Jenkins stands out with a grounded, emotionally rich performance in the Indian ashram sequences, elevating scenes that otherwise feature archetypal, often one-dimensional characters. Though visually alluring and easy to enjoy as an armchair travelogue or late-night watch, the movie’s polish and pleasantness mask a thinness: its spiritual lessons feel clichéd and its self-discovery arc remains comfortably familiar rather than challenging, leaving viewers with an attractive but shallow portrait of personal transformation. C+

On Tuesday, President Donald Trump abruptly fired FBI Director James Comey, who had led the bureau’s investigation into possible coordination between Trump campaign associates and Russia during the 2016 election. The administration cited Comey’s handling of the Hillary Clinton email probe—particularly his public rebuke of Clinton last July and his announcement reopening the investigation shortly before the election—as grounds for dismissal, relying publicly on a memo from Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein criticizing Comey for breaching DOJ norms. Trump’s letter to Comey said new leadership was needed to restore public trust.

The sudden ouster provoked immediate bipartisan concern and demands for an independent or special prosecutor to oversee the Russia probe. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the timing and rationale suspect, warned the move could be a cover-up if the Justice Department does not appoint a special prosecutor, and said the decision could chill future FBI directors. Schumer and others noted troubling parallels to Watergate-era firings and pointed to recent dismissals of other officials investigating the administration. Republican Chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee Richard Burr and several other senators expressed unease about the timing and potential impact on ongoing investigations, while some Republicans defended Rosenstein’s role.

Comey learned of his termination while speaking to FBI staff in Los Angeles; Deputy Director Andrew McCabe became acting director. The firing intensified calls for independent oversight of the Russia investigation, as even some Republicans joined those urging extra scrutiny. The episode also drew attention to internal White House discussions—reports tied advisers including Roger Stone to support for dismissal, though Trump denied recent contact—and raised questions about why the administration waited until now to remove Comey. Meanwhile, subpoenas and grand jury activity related to associates such as Michael Flynn continued, underscoring the broader investigative context.

Researchers from MIT, the U.S. Army Research, Development and Engineering Command (RDECOM), U.S. Special Operations Command and industry partners are developing the Tactical Assault Light Operator Suit (TALOS), an ambitious effort to give soldiers enhanced protection, strength and situational awareness reminiscent of science- fiction “Iron Man” suits. TALOS prototypes aim to integrate advanced armor, sensors, communications and power systems. Key concepts include “liquid” or magnetorheological armor that hardens on impact, wound- detection sensors with foam sealants, 360-degree/night-vision camera systems, wearable heads-up displays like Google Glass, and external exoskeleton frames to amplify strength and speed. Developers stress the focus is practical protection—survivability during door-entry assaults—rather than flight. Technical hurdles remain: power sources (heavy batteries or pumps) and weight pose significant limits, and many components are still experimental. Timelines are cautious: some components are underway, a basic prototype was targeted within roughly a year, with more complete working prototypes expected in two to three years. Critics warn of overreliance on tech or false security, but proponents argue TALOS could markedly improve individual soldier survivability if engineering challenges are solved.

Nearly four centuries after the Dutch East India Company ship Batavia was wrecked on Morning Reef in the Houtman Abrolhos in 1629, archaeologists have uncovered a new grave on tiny Beacon Island that sheds fresh light on one of Australia’s most horrific maritime massacres. The Batavia went aground on its maiden voyage with some 340 people aboard; many reached nearby islands but, in July 1629, a calculated and brutal mutiny led by undermerchant Jeronimus Cornelisz produced a wave of killings. More than 120 survivors — including women and children — were murdered by musket fire, stabbing, strangulation, poisoning, drowning and throat-cutting; some women were kept and repeatedly raped. When the captain returned from seeking help, mutineers were punished: several had their right hands cut off and were hanged; some lesser offenders were repatriated to Holland and two men left ashore as punishment.

The new discovery is the 11th skeleton found on Beacon Island since the 1960s and the first located through systematic archaeological excavation. Found about 1.5 metres down, the largely intact skeleton—thought to be an adolescent—lay with arms crossed and the skull oddly positioned; two musket balls were recovered nearby. A human tooth found in 2013 guided excavators back to the area, and mutton-bird activity helped reveal likely sites. Forensic experts are examining the remains to learn more about identity, diet, origins and cause of death; initial signs point to violent death though no obvious trauma on the skull was noted.

Led by the University of Western Australia and funded through an Australian Research Council project, the international team regards the find as vital for understanding early European habitation in Australia and the Batavia tragedy’s global historical significance. Plans under the Roaring Forties project include a virtual-reality presentation to interpret Beacon Island over time and broaden recognition of Dutch-era sites in Western Australia.

An anonymous donor has given $34 million to benefit underserved residents of Oakland, distributed through the San Francisco Foundation. The gift, arranged in February and required to be “on the streets” by summer, will fund initiatives across jobs, housing, education, health care and technology. The foundation — which has a $1.3 billion endowment — will disburse funds to nonprofits, with about $6 million dedicated to Oakland public schools for early-childhood education, African-American student achievement and community coordinators. Citywide, the investment is expected to create roughly 2,500 jobs and build 731 affordable housing units; about one-third of the funds target East Oakland specifically, where estimates include 813 jobs and 136 affordable units. Grants include $4 million for Oakland Codes and awards to re-entry and workforce programs such as a $1 million restaurant worker training program from the Ella Baker Center for Human Rights. Local leaders, including Mayor Libby Schaaf and Councilman Larry Reid, praised the donation as transformative and timely amid rising rents and displacement from the Bay Area tech boom. Officials did not reveal the donor’s identity but emphasized the importance of philanthropy partnering with government to ensure equitable prosperity.

An emergency response unfolded after an estimated 1 million gallons of acidic, metal-laden wastewater was accidentally released Wednesday from the abandoned Gold King Mine near Silverton, Colo. A U.S. EPA-led crew working to secure the mine and reduce long-term metal pollution reportedly triggered the discharge, sending an orange-brown plume down Cement Creek into the Animas River. The sludge, containing heavy metals and sediment, traveled through San Juan and La Plata counties and reached Durango by Thursday evening, then continued downstream toward New Mexico. 

Local authorities closed the Animas River to all recreational use—tubing, rafting and kayaking—indefinitely until test results clarify contaminant types and concentrations. Durango halted pumping raw water from the Animas to protect its reservoir, suspended transfers of untreated water to a college and a golf course, and asked residents to conserve water; stores near the city saw heavy bottled-water purchases. Farmington, N.M., and other downstream communities shut off intake pumps and warned residents and agricultural users to avoid the river. Officials advised keeping pets and livestock out of the water.

Preliminary concerns focused on iron, aluminum, cadmium, zinc and copper; pH at one monitoring site dropped from 7.8 to 5.8, indicating increased acidity. Agencies noted Cement Creek and upper Animas already suffer longstanding metal contamination and limited fish populations. Colorado Parks and Wildlife placed fish cages at several river sites to monitor acute impacts. EPA teams, state and local health and environmental agencies are sampling and investigating downstream locations to determine the plume’s composition, persistence and ecological effects. The release has raised local unease—especially since an EPA action caused it—and officials say test results are expected within 24–48 hours to guide further public-health and environmental decisions.

Ryan Lock, a 20-year-old chef from Chichester, died on 21 December near Raqqa while fighting with the Kurdish People’s Defence Units (YPG) against Islamic State (IS/ISIS). Having told his family he was going on holiday to Turkey in August, Lock—who had no prior military experience—joined the YPG as a volunteer. Kurdish sources and forensic examination indicate he sustained a gunshot wound under the chin, consistent with suicide, and likely shot himself rather than be captured after he and four comrades were surrounded during a fierce firefight in the village of Ja'bar. The YPG reported the five fighters showed “considerable resistance” before being killed; Lock’s body was later recovered from IS-held territory and transported into Iraq for repatriation. Rights activist Mark Campbell praised Lock’s action as an act of bravery that denied IS a propaganda victory. Lock, who attended school in Havant, Hampshire, is the third British national reported killed fighting with Kurdish forces against IS. His father, Jon Plater, expressed gratitude to the YPG for returning his son; the Foreign Office continues to advise against travel to Syria.

Authorities intensified the search for 22-year-old Sahray Astina Barber after she was reported missing early Monday from her apartment complex on Northpark Boulevard, directly across from California State University, San Bernardino (CSUSB). Barber, a graphic design student at the Art Institute of California–Inland Empire who does not attend CSUSB, was last seen around 6 a.m. as she might have been heading to a nearby bus stop. Her roommates discovered several of her belongings strewn on the lawn and personal items including a laptop and cellphone were later found in vegetation about 30 yards from the bus stop. Police dispatched multiple teams — including mounted and motorcycle units — to search chaparral and sage hills north of the campus but had found no sign of her by Wednesday afternoon.

The disappearance comes amid a string of violent incidents near campus, including two separate attacks at the university and an attempted kidnapping, prompting heightened campus security and student concern. CSUSB released a composite sketch of a suspect in the campus attacks; investigators are exploring whether those incidents and Barber’s disappearance are connected but have not confirmed links. San Bernardino police have assigned a large detective contingent, questioned Barber’s ex-boyfriend and roommates, and sent her laptop to a high‑tech crime unit for analysis. Barber is described as about 5'8", 125 pounds, with long red-brown hair and green eyes. Police asked anyone with information to contact Detective Dan Han or the San Bernardino Police Investigations Bureau, referencing case number 2015-26028. Her parents pleaded publicly for her safe return.

NBC’s three-hour live staging of The Sound of Music, starring Carrie Underwood as Maria and Stephen Moyer as Captain von Trapp, was an ambitious, costly effort that showcased memorable songs but ultimately failed to fully capture the emotional heart of the classic. The production spent reportedly $9 million on a cavernous set that accommodated Alpine landscapes, the Nonnberg Abbey, the Von Trapp household and a final concert space, and it assembled strong supporting talent—Audra McDonald as Mother Abbess, Laura Benanti as Elsa, and Christian Borle as Max—alongside experienced producers Craig Zadan and Neil Meron and directors Rob Ashford and Beth McCarthy-Miller.

Critics agreed the musical numbers remained the show’s saving grace: Rodgers and Hammerstein’s timeless score—from “My Favorite Things” to “Climb Ev’ry Mountain” and “Do-Re-Mi”—was delivered well, particularly by MacDonald, whose “Climb Ev’ry Mountain” was a standout, emotionally resonant moment that even moved Underwood to tears. The supporting cast generally received praise for bringing energy and craft to their roles, and the telecast avoided major technical flubs despite the complexity of a live broadcast.

The principal criticism centered on the leads. Underwood proved vocally capable—she belted the big moments convincingly—but critics found her acting shallow, lacking the guileless, nuanced warmth Julie Andrews brought to the iconic film role. Her Maria was often described as visually correct but emotionally flat, taking most of the broadcast to build enough confidence to be affecting.
