Moyer, while a stronger singer than some predecessors, was judged unable to convincingly convey the Captain’s inner transformation; his steely stoicism came off as clenched rather than deeply felt.

The hybrid presentation—shot like a film on a massive soundstage with no visible audience—left the broadcast feeling stagebound yet deprived of theatrical immediacy, muting laughter and applause and diluting energy. Some noted the stage script’s differences from the famous film adaptation made certain moments feel oddly staged or truncated. In sum, NBC’s live Sound of Music was impressive in scale and intermittently moving thanks to standout supporting performances and the enduring score, but it played, in one critic’s words, like “very expensive karaoke” when its leads failed to fully sell the story’s emotional core.

The piece frames a public clash between Paul Krugman and Ben Bernanke over Federal Reserve policy amid a slow recovery and high unemployment. Krugman argues the Fed should tolerate higher inflation—raising its target to about 3–4 percent for several years—to lower real interest rates, encourage spending, ease debt burdens, and stimulate growth. Bernanke calls that approach reckless, warning it could un-anchor inflation expectations, reduce the Fed’s flexibility, and spark unpredictable harms. The Fed has already cut short-term rates to near zero, provided emergency lending in 2008–09, and purchased over $2.5 trillion in long-term securities, yet recovery remains weak. Samuelson notes risks of Krugman’s plan: wages might lag prices, eroding purchasing power; consumers could save more out of fear; investors might demand higher yields, undermining stimulus. He sides with Bernanke, cautioning that flirting with inflation is dangerous given historical lessons from the 1970s and limits to monetary policy. The broader lesson: economists and the Fed cannot control every outcome, and overambitious fixes risk harmful side effects.

Ken Stern, drawing on a decade at National Public Radio, argues in With Charity for All that much of the American nonprofit sector is failing its stated missions. He contends that while some charities are clearly and intentionally fraudulent—paying outsized CEO salaries, diverting funds to phone banks, and sending little to beneficiaries—many other problems are structural and systemic. The ease of obtaining tax-exempt status from the IRS, weak or absent state oversight, and donors’ susceptibility to emotionally charged words like “veteran,” “children,” “hope,” and “cancer” create an environment in which questionable organizations can flourish. Stern emphasizes how time-consuming and difficult it can be for ordinary donors to investigate charity finances, which compounds the potential for misuse.

Beyond outright scams, Stern focuses on organizations that arguably should not receive charitable classification or the tax advantages that come with it. He critiques nonprofit hospitals for frequently delivering no more charity care than for-profit counterparts while enjoying tax benefits and competitive advantages. Similarly, he scrutinizes college football bowl games and cultural institutions such as opera companies, suggesting some principally exist to serve donors or to underwrite lavish expenses—golf outings, high salaries, travel, and entertainment—rather than to advance a clear public good. Stern’s broader point is that the sector’s incentives and lack of accountability create perverse outcomes: entities can be legally charitable without operating in ways that meaningfully serve the needy. A separate note indicates a cautious approach to endorsing charities: rather than broadly labeling organizations good or bad, the referenced evaluators focus narrowly on identifying and thoroughly vetting the very best giving opportunities for donors.

Two former bodyguards of Brazilian model Gisele Bündchen and her husband, US football star Tom Brady, were sentenced to five years in prison for shooting at photographers during the couple’s April 2009 wedding celebrations at a seaside home in Costa Rica. A court in Puntarenas convicted Costa Rican Miguel Solís and Colombian Alexander Rivas of attempted murder; a third defendant, Manuel Valverde, was acquitted. The photographers had been confronted and ordered to surrender camera memory cards; as they drove away a guard fired, but no one was injured. Each convicted man was also ordered to pay five million colónes (about $10,000) in damages to each photographer. Neither defendant testified at trial. The incident was documented as part of web archiving efforts to preserve original page versions.

A false tweet posted from the Associated Press’ Twitter account claiming “Two Explosions in the White House and Barack Obama is injured” briefly wiped out a 125–145 point Dow Jones gain after it spread widely. The AP quickly said its account had been hacked, suspended the feed, and staff reported deceptive phishing emails preceded the breach. White House spokesman Jay Carney and other officials confirmed the president was unharmed. The Syrian Electronic Army claimed responsibility; it had previously targeted multiple news outlets’ Twitter accounts. The market rebound was rapid once the falsehood was exposed, underscoring how fast social-media misinformation can move financial markets.

The document is a forceful critique of President Obama’s energy policies and of the “drill, baby, drill” response from Republicans, arguing that both political narratives oversimplify complex realities. One strand, advanced by Charles Krauthammer, accuses Obama of ideological hostility to oil — labeling it the “fuel of the past” — and of actively restricting drilling in strategic domestic areas (Mid-Atlantic, Florida Gulf, broader Gulf of Mexico, ANWR, and federal lands in the Rockies). Krauthammer singles out the veto of the Keystone pipeline as proof of anti–domestic-oil bias, claiming the veto sacrifices jobs, strategic resources, relations with allies, and U.S. economic security while enriching unfriendly producers. He dismisses Obama’s energy optimism (electric cars, algae fuels) as techno-idealism that has already produced failures (Solyndra, Ener1, weak Chevy Volt demand) and lampoons Energy Secretary Steven Chu’s past comments favoring higher gas prices. Krauthammer insists increased domestic production would keep dollars and jobs at home and reduce dependence on hostile powers, so restricting drilling is irresponsible amid rising pump prices.

A second strand, more skeptical of simplistic drilling prescriptions, points out that U.S. oil and gas production has surged thanks to fracking and horizontal drilling—largely independent of Obama-era policy—and that this “hydrocarbon boom” has not produced sharply lower gasoline prices or a big employment payoff. It argues that environmental costs of fracking have been underplayed and that energy policy has had limited influence on global oil prices. The piece concludes that while high gasoline prices are politically damaging and painful, neither unfettered drilling nor wishful investment in futuristic alternatives alone offers a clear or immediate solution.

Statistical methods, especially Bayesian inference, have long helped search teams locate lost vessels and aircraft and could refine the hunt for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370. Bayes’ approach begins with prior probabilities—educated guesses about where an object might be—and updates them as new data arrive (radar, satellite pings, ocean currents, search coverage, and evidence about how communications were cut). This yields a probability distribution over locations that can be revised when hypotheses change, for example when deliberate diversion becomes more plausible than accident, shifting likely locations farther from Kuala Lumpur. Metron Scientific Solutions used such methods successfully in the Air France 447 search: analysts combined crash theories, historical crash data, sensor performance and prior search effectiveness to produce grids of probabilities; after re-evaluating an assumption about beacon signals they identified a new area that led to the wreck and black boxes. Bayesian approaches force explicit accounting for uncertainty and conflicting evidence, but require subjective judgments—estimating beacon survival rates or sensor detection probabilities—that can influence outcomes. Critics warn that quantifying uncertain priors can be misleading if treated as definitive, and some question Bayes’ fit when evidence dramatically changes scenarios. Yet proponents argue Bayesian methods bring disciplined, updateable reasoning that outperforms instinctive decision-making. For MH370, the complexity of sparse data, damaged or absent signals, and vast ocean means Bayesian tools can guide searches but cannot guarantee discovery; without new breakthroughs the plane may remain lost on the ocean floor.

A small, rusty-brown pebble found in 2004 near Bexhill, Sussex, has been identified as the first likely example of fossilized dinosaur brain tissue. Discovered by amateur fossil hunter Jamie Hiscocks and studied by a team coordinated originally by the late Professor Martin Brasier, the specimen probably came from an iguanodontian dinosaur of the Early Cretaceous (~133 million years ago). Using scanning electron microscopy, researchers report mineralized remains interpreted as meninges (the protective membranes around the brain), collagen strands, tiny capillaries, and possible fragments of cortical tissue preserved as mineral “casts.” The team suggests the head settled in acidic, low-oxygen water—similar to a bog—where soft tissues mineralized before total decay, enabling exceptional preservation.

The preserved structures show similarities to the brain coverings of modern birds and crocodiles, dinosaur descendants. Unusually, the fossilized tissue appears pressed against the skull’s roof, raising speculation that some dinosaurs might have had brains filling more of the cranial cavity than in many modern reptiles; however, researchers caution that taphonomic processes (collapse during decay and burial) could explain this arrangement, and no firm conclusions about intelligence can be drawn. The find is reported in a Geological Society of London special publication honoring Brasier and has drawn both interest and skepticism from paleontologists, who note the extraordinary nature of the claim and call for high evidentiary standards and access to the specimen for broader study.

Ignite Restaurant Group, the parent company of Joe’s Crab Shack, is piloting a no-tipping policy at 18 of its 131 locations as part of a wider response to rising federal and local minimum-wage debates. Under the trial, restaurants eliminate tips and instead pay workers higher fixed hourly wages determined by factors such as employees’ historical compensation and their role importance. Ignite CEO Ray Blanchette framed tipping as “an antiquated model” and said the no-tipping approach moves the company “above the fray” of minimum-wage conversations nationwide. The pilot sites—located across Utah, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Illinois, Michigan, Nebraska and Kansas—are not adding service charges to checks; the company acknowledged small menu price increases in some cases. Blanchette said the company expects lower employee turnover because staff will shift from variable tip-based earnings to stable pay—citing an example contrast of roughly $14 an hour under the fixed model versus $2.25 an hour base pay for tipped workers in some states where tips are expected to make up the difference to meet minimum wage standards. Joe’s Crab Shack operates two Orange County locations (Newport Beach and Garden Grove near Disneyland) that are not part of the pilot, and the company declined to disclose specific salary figures. The move follows a similar high-profile change by New York restaurateur Danny Meyer, who announced a phased elimination of tipping across his Union Square Hospitality Group restaurants, starting with The Modern; Meyer plans menu price increases to fund higher employee wages. The article also briefly notes broader efforts—such as web archiving “No More 404” crawls—to preserve online references so links remain accessible even as pages change or disappear.

Susan Carland, a Muslim sociologist and lecturer at Monash University and wife of TV host Waleed Aly, has turned sustained online abuse into a force for good. Targeted daily by Twitter trolls with racial slurs and vitriol aimed at her hijab and faith—ranging from calls for her to leave Australia to accusations that she supports oppression and violence—Carland initially tried engaging, blocking, muting and ignoring. None felt satisfactory. Instead, she chose to "repel evil with what is better," inspired by a Koranic injunction, and pledged to donate $1 to UNICEF for every hateful tweet she receives. 

Although she began the practice months earlier, media attention noted that within just a few weeks her tally exceeded $1,000. Carland explains that donating to UNICEF felt especially appropriate because children often suffer directly from hatred expressed as war, poverty and injustice; turning each ugly message into tangible aid transforms virtual hostility into real-world help. The pledge is both a personal coping strategy and a public affirmation of her beliefs: rather than allowing anonymous hostility to define her, she embraces a response rooted in the ethical teachings of her faith. 

Carland—who converted to Islam at 19 after a Christian upbringing—says the campaign has brought unexpected benefits. It has made her more secure and relaxed in her identity and recommitted her to the "beauty" of her tradition. What once provoked anger now becomes “a chalk-mark” toward the next donation installment. Her approach reframes abuse as an opportunity to generate goodness, making each act of hate an impetus for charity and resilience.

A student opened fire at Berrendo Middle School in Roswell, N.M., on the morning of Jan. 14, 2014, injuring two classmates before being taken into custody. The suspect, identified as 12-year-old seventh-grader Mason Campbell, brought a 20-gauge shotgun—allegedly concealed in a bag or instrument case—and fired in the school gym. An 11- or 14-year-old boy was shot in the face and remained in critical condition after surgery; a 13-year-old girl, later identified as Kendal Sanders, was shot in the arm and was reported in satisfactory condition after treatment. A social studies teacher, John Masterson, and State Police Lt. Gary Smith intervened; Masterson persuaded the shooter to drop the gun and Smith detained him. Campbell was later transferred to a psychiatric hospital as authorities executed search warrants at his locker, home and the bag and worked with prosecutors on potential charges. The school had practiced active-shooter training and was locked down; students were reunited with parents at a mall. The community held prayer vigils as officials and families grappled with the trauma, and state and federal authorities monitored the situation.

UPMC Presbyterian is investigating whether fungal infections found in three transplant patients are linked to mold recently discovered in its cardiothoracic intensive care unit (CTICU). Hospital officials disclosed that two heart-transplant patients who died last year had invasive fungal infections—one with rhizomucor (died June) and another with rhizopus (died October)—and both had stayed in a CTICU room where mold was later found. A more recent lung-transplant patient tested positive for lichtheimia and remains hospitalized; that detection on Sept. 3 prompted immediate testing and the temporary closure and cleanup of the 20‑bed CTICU. UPMC says the role of mold in the earlier deaths cannot be definitively determined, and families were notified; the hospital emphasized clinical complexity and the staggered timing of cases as reasons the cluster was not publicly disclosed earlier.

Preliminary testing indicates the three patients harbored different but related fungi from the zygomycetes group. The specific mold identified in the ICU walls and toilets has not been publicly named and reportedly differs from the patient isolates. UPMC has engaged infection prevention experts and a private remediation firm; the state health department is overseeing review. Hospital officials and outside specialists note that such fungi are uncommon in hospitals and typically require water or construction-related disturbances to proliferate. UPMC had recent deconstruction work on adjacent facilities, a potential contributing factor under review, though outside consultants called UPMC’s response—including ICU closure—proactive.

Public reaction includes alarm from patients’ families. Local experts stress that mold rarely causes severe illness in healthy people but can threaten immunocompromised patients—such as transplant recipients on immunosuppressive drugs. UPMC has launched a public blog to post investigation updates and says it will continue reviewing cases from the past year to determine any link and prevent future occurrences.

Scientists have described two remarkable fossil discoveries that illuminate ancient life and arthropod evolution. In Myanmar amber, researchers identified a tiny, unusual predatory cockroach, Manipulator modificaputis, dating to about 100 million years ago. Barely 1 cm long, it combines features reminiscent of crane flies, praying mantises and modern cockroaches: a triangular, highly mobile head on a long neck, large lateral eyes plus a second pair on the crown, elongated mouthparts and legs, narrow body and wings. Found by Ziggi Ellenberger and analyzed by Peter Vršanský and Günter Bechly, the specimen belongs to the Manipulatoridae and is interpreted as a solitary, nocturnal hunter that pounced or seized prey with spined legs and frequently took flight. Some experts, however, dispute aspects of this lifestyle, arguing its long, gracile legs indicate ambush or gap-traversing behavior rather than fast pursuit. The find joins other fierce Cretaceous cockroaches from Myanmar, many predatory lineages of which went extinct, leaving only mantises among that superorder’s top predators today.

Separately, Moroccan paleontologists have uncovered dozens of spectacular soft-bodied fossils of Aegirocassis benmoulae, a giant anomalocaridid up to seven feet long that filtered plankton about 480 million years ago. Exceptionally preserved specimens reveal netlike frontal appendages adapted for suspension feeding during the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event. These fossils also preserve previously hidden dorsal swimming flaps, clarifying how two-branched arthropod limbs evolved: the flaps are precursors of the upper branch. With thousands of additional unstudied specimens from the site, researchers expect more insights into early arthropod diversity and the evolution of major body plans.

Auto makers are racing to make 2014 the year cars truly go online, partnering with Silicon Valley to build modern, connected infotainment systems that match consumers’ smartphones and tablets. At CES, Google unveiled the Open Automotive Alliance with automakers including GM, Honda, Audi, Hyundai and chipmaker Nvidia to adapt Android for vehicles. The move aims to give car companies a common, rapidly evolving platform that benefits from Android’s dominant developer ecosystem, extensive hardware testing, and existing Google services like Maps and search.

Traditionally, automakers favored stable, proprietary software for safety and reliability, creating varied in-car systems (Ford’s MyFord Touch with Microsoft, QNX from BlackBerry, Linux variants or in-house solutions). Those fragmented approaches force app developers to write multiple versions and slow feature rollout. Past collaboration efforts such as the Genivi Alliance produced limited results. Android’s scale and third-party familiarity promise lower costs, faster innovation and easier app availability.

Tesla exemplifies the “computer on wheels” trend with its large touchscreen and integrated apps. Startups such as CloudCar propose aftermarket computing modules to modernize older cars, while Ford’s Palo Alto lab and open-sourcing of some vehicle software show automakers experimenting with new development models. Overall, the industry is shifting toward standardized, upgradable, internet-connected vehicle platforms to meet consumer expectations and compete in a mobile-first world.

A white Balch Springs, Texas, police officer, Roy Oliver, surrendered and was booked on a murder warrant in the April 29 shooting death of 15-year-old Jordan Edwards. Oliver posted a $300,000 bond and was released after turning himself in following the Dallas County Sheriff’s Office’s issuance of the warrant, which says evidence indicates Oliver “intended to cause serious bodily injury and commit an act clearly dangerous to human life that caused the death.” Edwards was a passenger in a car of teens leaving an unruly house party when officers responded to reports of intoxicated teens. Initial police statements claimed the vehicle backed toward officers “in an aggressive manner,” but body-camera footage later showed the car was driving away when Oliver fired into it with a rifle, shattering the passenger-side window and fatally wounding Edwards. Another officer reportedly used his weapon to break the car’s rear window before Oliver fired multiple rounds as the car passed. Oliver was fired by the department for policy violations; his personnel records show a 2013 suspension tied to courtroom conduct and required anger-management training and at least one prior reprimand for disrespect on a call. The case reignited national attention on police shootings of unarmed black civilians, coming the same week as other high-profile federal and local decisions in similar cases. Edwards’ family filed a wrongful-death lawsuit; their attorneys and supporters said the murder charge is a necessary step though a conviction is not assured. Investigations and reviews are ongoing.

An imaginative, cavern-style one-bedroom, two-bath house in Malibu resembling "The Flintstones" is listed at $3.5 million. Set on nearly 23 mountaintop acres, the free-form home features cave-like interiors, vaulted living and dining ceilings, expansive glass with ocean views, a fireplace and a wine cellar. Public records show long-running TV personality Dick Clark and his wife as owners. Diane Carter of Coldwell Banker’s Malibu Colony office is the listing agent.

A rumored new poem by Jay-Z, published by Britain’s NME if authentic, reportedly signals he’s retiring the word “bitch” from his vocabulary now that daughter Blue Ivy Carter has arrived. Quoted lines suggest a shift in perspective—recognizing past use of the word in his music and business but rejecting it now that he’s a father. The piece contrasts with Jay’s recent collaborative track “Watch the Throne,” which includes the line “That’s My Bitch,” highlighting how parenthood may be altering his artistic choices. Beyonce, in her first interview since giving birth, emphasized that she and Jay-Z intend to raise Blue in a “normal loving family,” with Jay described as an “inspirational” and hands-on dad who will change diapers. Beyonce also mentioned celebrity friends lined up to babysit—specifically Destiny’s Child alum Kelly Rowland, who kept in touch throughout the pregnancy and is eager to help. She pushed back on exaggerated reports about their hospital stay, saying security at Lenox Hill was tight for their daughter’s safety but many stories were overblown. The full interview appears in Star magazine.

The document criticizes both President Obama’s tone and House Speaker John Boehner’s tactics during the 2011 debt-ceiling standoff, arguing both misrepresented the facts and misread ordinary citizens. It objects to Obama’s condescending line that many Americans “have probably never heard” of the debt ceiling, noting citizens do hold views and understand its basic purpose: allowing the nation to pay obligations already incurred. The piece contends Obama misstated the effect of his requested $2.4 trillion increase, which would permit additional spending beyond already appropriated funds. Boehner, meanwhile, is depicted as disingenuous—insisting the president sought a “blank check,” shifting positions, and escalating demands to satisfy the Tea Party base by tying a balanced-budget amendment to any hike, a move portrayed as politically risky and likely unserious. The author recounts failed negotiation dynamics: initial talks with about $400 billion in difference, Republicans rejecting revenue increases, and Republicans later walking away from a possible “grand bargain.” The essay critiques Obama’s rhetorical choices—overusing household-budget analogies and claiming Americans most want compromise—while praising parts of his speech advocating balanced cuts, revenue from the wealthy, and protecting entitlements. It warns Republicans are willing to risk economic harm for political advantage and expresses skepticism about reaching a clean, responsible resolution.

On January 31, 2018, a rare and striking lunar event will occur: a total lunar eclipse coinciding with a Supermoon and a Blue Moon. The Virtual Telescope Project is coordinating a free livestream of the eclipse beginning at 11:30 UTC, partnering with several astrophotographers across Australia and the U.S. and using the “Pearl” telescope at Tenagra Observatories; later that day they will also broadcast the Supermoon rising over Rome’s monuments starting at 16:00 UTC. The eclipse itself will be widely visible across the Pacific: best views will be in central and eastern Asia, Indonesia, New Zealand and most of Australia in the evening, while Alaska, Hawaii and northwestern Canada can watch the whole event. For much of North and Central America, moonset will cut observations short, and in places farther west in Asia, India, the Middle East and Eastern Europe the eclipse will be underway as the moon rises. The total phase lasts about 77 minutes, during which Earth’s atmosphere bends sunlight into the shadowed Moon, producing the characteristic reddish “blood moon” appearance and causing the Moon’s lower limb to look brighter than its upper limb. Historically this alignment is uncommon: the last total eclipse of a Blue Moon occurred on March 31, 1866, making the 2018 event the first of its kind in nearly 152 years. The Jan. 31 Supermoon is the third in a sequence that began in early December 2017 and continued on Jan. 1, 2018; supermoons appear about 14% larger and 30% brighter than full moons near apogee. Observers are encouraged to watch near moonrise for the “moon illusion” that accentuates size, to photograph the Moon with landmarks for scale, and to use fast shutter speeds for sharp images. Unlike solar eclipses, lunar eclipses and supermoons are safe to view with the naked eye.

A Visalia high school science teacher, 52-year-old Margaret Gieszinger, was arrested after videos circulated showing her cutting a student’s hair in class and loudly singing the "Star Spangled Banner" as students fled. The incident occurred during first-period chemistry at University Preparatory High School, located on the College of the Sequoias campus. In footage reviewed by police and media, Gieszinger approaches a student seated in a chair, announces “free haircuts,” cuts portions of his hair despite his objections and attempts to leave, then follows him out of the classroom with scissors. She is also seen grabbing at another girl’s hair before other students ran from the room. Students said she had shown earlier troubling behavior that week, including a Monday outburst over a missing test that left a student in tears and prompted complaints that were not apparently acted on. College of the Sequoias police arrested Gieszinger at her home on suspicion of felony child endangerment (corporal injury to a child) and booked her into the Tulare County jail with bail set at $100,000. The Tulare County Office of Education and school officials said all students are safe; the district has placed Gieszinger away from the classroom and assigned a qualified substitute for the rest of the semester. The superintendent sent mental-health counselors to support students, and the incident will be submitted to the Tulare County District Attorney’s Office. Records show Gieszinger had previous credential suspensions in 2007 and 2016; details were not provided. The case has prompted criticism about prior student complaints and administrative response.

Florida’s coral reefs have been suffering an ongoing, multi-year disease outbreak since 2014 that is unprecedented in geographic reach, species affected and mortality. First noted near Key Biscayne, the outbreak spread rapidly: by 2015 it covered roughly 55 linear miles from Pompano Beach to Biscayne National Park, continued through the Florida Keys in 2016–2017, reached St. Lucie Inlet in the north and Looe Key in the lower Keys by 2018. The event has killed millions of corals and hit foundational species—especially brain and star corals—so hard that in some areas their loss constitutes a local ecological extirpation. The disease often causes tissue to slough off the skeleton, leading to whole-colony death within weeks and leaving skeletons vulnerable to algal overgrowth and further decline.

State and partner response since 2015 has involved documenting distribution, prevalence and impacts; searching for likely pathogens (current evidence points toward bacterial agents for at least some cases); investigating environmental contributors such as elevated sea temperatures, pollution, turbidity and sedimentation; experimenting with interventions (from antiseptic epoxies to targeted antibiotic treatments); and expanding monitoring through citizen science programs like SEAFAN and Reef Ambassador initiatives. DEP convened regional coordination calls and several workshops in 2017 to develop sampling, intervention planning and laboratory analysis frameworks.

Scientists emphasize that causes are likely multifactorial—warming seas and degraded water quality probably exacerbate disease—and that restoration via lab-reared, disease-resistant corals (e.g., Mote Marine Lab’s propagation and outplanting efforts) will be critical while researchers continue to identify pathogens and effective treatments. Public reporting of observations and reducing local stressors are encouraged to aid recovery.

Verizon agreed to buy Yahoo’s core internet businesses for about $4.8–4.83 billion in cash, ending Yahoo’s run as an independent pioneer of the early web. The sale covers Yahoo’s web services—email, news, finance, sports, Tumblr, Flickr, Yahoo Answers, fantasy sports and ad technology—and some real estate, but excludes stakes in Alibaba and Yahoo Japan (combined market value around $40 billion) and certain intellectual property, which will remain with the independent company that plans to rename itself and stay publicly traded. The transaction is expected to close early next year.

Verizon, which paid $4.4 billion for AOL in 2015, will combine Yahoo with AOL to build a larger mobile-media and advertising business it hopes can better compete with Google and Facebook. Yahoo’s properties still draw about 1 billion monthly users, offering Verizon content, audience and ad inventory to monetize across its more than 140 million wireless subscribers. Executives such as AOL’s Tim Armstrong and Verizon’s Marni Walden (who leads new business and media strategy) are central to integrating Yahoo into Verizon’s push beyond connectivity into video, content and advertising technology. Verizon CEO Lowell McAdam framed the purchase as accelerating Verizon’s move into cross-screen mobile media.

The deal highlights Yahoo’s decline from a dot‑com-era heavyweight to a company whose core business became worth far less than its valuable Asian equity holdings. Yahoo’s stock rose modestly on the news; Verizon’s market cap is substantially larger. Analysts note regulatory and privacy risks: proposed FCC rules requiring explicit opt‑in for ISPs to use customer browsing and location data could hamper Verizon’s ability to enhance ad targeting using network-derived data. Critics warn the combination of an ISP’s data and large content properties raises privacy concerns.

Verizon sees acquisitions like AOL and Yahoo as essential to scale its media ambitions, even while questions remain about whether the combined properties can meaningfully dent the dominance of incumbent digital ad leaders.

Lady Gaga delivered a powerful, widely praised Oscars performance of "Til It Happens to You," the song she co-wrote with Diane Warren for the documentary about campus sexual assault, The Hunting Ground. Seated at a white piano and surrounded by survivors who wrote messages on their arms, Gaga’s stirring rendition became one of the ceremony’s most emotional moments. The singer revealed afterward that many close to her — including her grandmother and aunt — learned she was a survivor only by seeing the performance. In an Instagram post, Gaga (Stefani Germanotta) explained she had kept her assault secret for years out of shame and religious guilt, believing for a decade that it was her fault. She first publicly discussed the rape in a 2014 Howard Stern interview, describing the song “Swine” as stemming from that trauma and the healing work that followed. Though she did not win the Oscar (the award went to Sam Smith’s Bond theme), Gaga said performing lifted a weight and made her feel she no longer had to hide. She thanked the 50 survivors who joined her onstage for their bravery and credited her fiancé, Taylor Kinney, for supporting and loving the “survivor” in her. The performance was widely noted as a milestone for sexual assault survivors.

The start of 2013 brought not only New Year celebrations and federal “fiscal cliff” drama but also thousands of new state laws that quietly took effect, ranging from consequential reforms to quirky restrictions. Overall state legislative activity has declined since 2009, but many states enacted measures responding to public concerns and high-profile cases. Examples include California’s expanded mandatory reporting rules for K–12 and higher education staff after the Sandusky scandal, and “Caylee’s Laws” in California and Illinois that penalize caregivers who fail to report a child’s disappearance or death within 24 hours. Maryland and Maine legalized same-sex marriage, while New Hampshire and Montana enacted new abortion-related restrictions. Consumer protections also rose: California strengthened tools against mortgage fraud and barred large lenders from foreclosing while reviewing loan-modification requests. Employment and immigration saw changes—Pennsylvania and several other states required E-Verify for public-works contractors, and Montana moved to withhold some state services from undocumented immigrants. Other laws reflected local priorities and oddities: Illinois banned motorcycle wheelies and the sale of shark fins, Concord, Massachusetts outlawed plastic bottles, Wellington, Kansas limited households to four cats, North Carolina made stealing large amounts of unused cooking oil a felony, and Kentucky prohibited releasing feral hogs. Advocates say these laws show lawmakers responding to voters’ concerns, though experts question whether legislation is always the best solution.

Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservatives won a majority in Ontario’s 2018 provincial election, toppling the Liberals after 15 years and making Ford the new premier. The result followed a tumultuous campaign: Ford, a populist and brother of the late embattled Toronto mayor Rob Ford, emerged as an outsider who appealed to frustrated voters seeking change. Kathleen Wynne’s Liberals were reduced to a rump and she resigned as leader; the NDP became official opposition under Andrea Horwath, and the Greens won their first seat with Mike Schreiner in Guelph.

Ford ran a tightly controlled, media-limited campaign that emphasized simple, tangible promises — large tax cuts, lower gas and hydro rates, cheaper beer, more infrastructure spending — while pledging to eliminate the deficit by finding government “efficiencies.” His platform was criticized as imprecise and largely uncosted until late in the campaign, with few details on funding. Despite controversies (associations with his brother’s scandals, party nomination disputes, a lawsuit by Rob Ford’s widow, and campaign-finance questions), Ford’s message resonated across rural conservatives and “Ford Nation” supporters in Toronto. Analysts say his clear, repeatable pitch and team strategy unified varied voter blocs, translating anger with the Liberals into a decisive electoral victory — though a majority of voters overall did not necessarily back him.

Rachel Uchitel quietly married boyfriend Matt Hahn in Nevada after several months living together in San Francisco; records show they obtained a marriage license and filed it. Uchitel, 36, and Hahn, 26 and a former Penn State football player turned San Francisco businessman, are expecting a child—she tweeted she’s five months pregnant. Uchitel rose to fame after a 2009 affair with Tiger Woods and subsequent publicity.

JBS Tolleson, Inc. is recalling about 6.9 million pounds of raw, non-intact beef products, including ground beef, packaged July 26–Sept. 7, 2018, because they may be contaminated with Salmonella Newport. Products bear “EST. 267” inside the USDA mark and were distributed nationwide. Epidemiologic and traceback investigations linked raw ground beef from JBS to 57 illnesses in 16 states (illness onset Aug. 5–Sept. 6); 14 hospitalizations reported. Consumers should not eat recalled products, should throw them away or return them, and cook ground beef to 160°F. Contact JBS or USDA hotlines with questions.

Edvard Munch’s 1895 pastel-on-board version of The Scream sold at Sotheby’s in New York for $119,922,500, a record price for an artwork at auction. The only version remaining in private hands, it drew five bidders and sold to a telephone buyer. Owner Petter Olsen will use proceeds to fund a museum and cultural complex in Hvitsten, Norway; three other versions reside in Norwegian museums.

"O: A Presidential Novel," published anonymously, is a 368-page speculative political novel set during the 2012 presidential election that blends fact and fiction about Barack Obama's presidency. Simon & Schuster says the author "has been in the room with Barack Obama" and "spent years observing politics," sparking widespread Washington guessing. Leading suspects include Joe Klein (who anonymously wrote Primary Colors), former White House press secretary Robert Gibbs, ex-chief of staff Rahm Emanuel, Politico reporter Ben Smith, and even Obama himself — with joking suggestions like the presidential teleprompter. The novel reads like brisk campaign fiction, paced more like Game Change than What It Takes, and emphasizes campaigns’ relationships with the press, suggesting the author is a political reporter or press staffer. It sketches Obamaland figures such as a thinly veiled David Axelrod and a spurned Chicago protege, portrays an unflattering Arianna Huffington stand-in named Bianca Stefani, and includes the specific detail of a character with myelodysplastic syndrome. The author’s anonymity remains the book’s main allure.

US lawmakers sharply criticized Pakistan after a tribal court sentenced surgeon Shakeel Afridi to 33 years for allegedly helping U.S. intelligence verify Osama bin Laden’s presence, warning the conviction could jeopardize U.S. aid. Senators Carl Levin and John McCain called the sentence “shocking and outrageous,” praised Afridi’s role in locating bin Laden and urged his immediate pardon, saying his imprisonment harms U.S.-Pakistan ties and congressional willingness to fund Pakistan. The dispute compounds tensions over Pakistan’s alleged ties to extremists, U.S. concerns about drone strikes, and stalled cooperation after bin Laden’s killing near a Pakistani military academy. Separately, a U.S. drone strike in volatile North Waziristan killed ten suspected militants, following another strike a day earlier. Such strikes, viewed by many Pakistanis as sovereignty violations causing civilian casualties, fuel anti-American sentiment and prompted Pakistan’s parliament to demand an end to them. Pakistan also closed NATO supply routes after a border air raid killed Pakistani troops, straining talks on Afghanistan logistics.

Rising violence in eastern Ukraine prompted President Petro Poroshenko to cancel a scheduled working visit to Turkey and remain in Kyiv to manage the crisis. Poroshenko cited a sharp escalation in the Donetsk region, especially around Amvrosiivka and Starobeshevo, accusing Russian troops of being brought into Ukraine. He said the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) would meet to plan next steps, Ukraine would urgently seek a UN Security Council meeting for international assessment, and would ask European partners to convene an emergency EU Council meeting. The cancelled trip had included seven bilateral meetings tied to the Turkish president’s inauguration.

On the ground, the southeastern port town of Novoazovsk appears to be under control of Russia-backed separatists after days of shelling; Associated Press reporters encountered rebel checkpoints and were barred entry. Rebels say they entered Wednesday, and local officials reported shelling overnight in Donetsk city that killed at least 11 people. A pro-Russian rebel leader claimed 3,000–4,000 Russian citizens are fighting with separatists, many described as former or on-leave military personnel; Russia denies covert military involvement. Ukraine’s security council described the forces in Novoazovsk as Russian troops and said Ukrainian units withdrew to save lives and reinforce Mariupol’s defenses.

International reactions included U.S. and European leaders demanding explanations from Moscow and calls for Russia to stop supporting rebels. The OSCE held a special meeting in Vienna. Analysts warn the separatists may be seeking a land link between Russia and annexed Crimea and control over the Sea of Azov. The conflict’s human toll remains high, with thousands killed, many wounded, and large displacement within Ukraine and into Russia.

During a Salvation Army fundraiser at the Tega Cay Wal-Mart, an anonymous donor dropped a single coin into a red kettle that was later appraised at roughly $1,200 by Brownlee Jewelers. The coin’s value was confirmed locally, and Salvation Army organizers expect to sell it and use the proceeds to support their programs. Details about the specific type of coin or the donor’s identity were not disclosed. The gesture highlights a generous, unexpected contribution that significantly boosted the local collection effort. Organizers expressed appreciation for the donation, noting that such surprises can make a meaningful difference in fundraising outcomes and directly benefit community services provided by the Salvation Army.

“Loose Tweets Destroy Fleets” is the Air Force’s modern reminder to guard social media posts because casual sharing can reveal critical operational or personal information to adversaries. U.S. Air Forces Central’s message from Al Udeid Air Base included an image of F-16s and warned that ISIS sympathizers and “lone wolves” have used online avenues to locate and threaten service members. Capt. Jonathan McDonald stressed avoiding mission details and detailed personal data, and urged checking privacy settings. OPSEC (Operations Security) aims to keep sensitive information from enemies; Master Sgt. Aaron Miller noted failures could endanger missions and national policy. Practical OPSEC tips include following the Critical Information List, using secure phones, encrypting emails, shredding notes, and routing media queries to public affairs. Units have OPSEC managers to report incidents; Air Force Instruction 10-701 provides guidance. The “loose tweets” slogan, previously used by the Navy and Army, has drawn media attention and mixed public reactions while reinforcing that seemingly harmless posts can have serious consequences for service members’ safety.

German and Norwegian police report that an iron gate bearing the infamous Nazi slogan "Arbeit macht frei" ("Work sets you free") believed stolen from the Dachau concentration camp in 2014 has been recovered in western Norway. Norwegian authorities in Bergen located the gate after receiving an anonymous tip and shared photos showing the ironwork propped in a storeroom; Bavarian police said the images make it "highly likely" the gate is the original. The gate, about 1.87 meters high and weighing roughly 100–108 kg, was taken on 2 November 2014, an act that provoked public outrage and drew condemnation from leaders including then-Chancellor Angela Merkel. No arrests were reported immediately, and police did not disclose the precise find location or the identity of the tipster. Officers said the gate is in acceptable condition, with paint flaking, and will be returned to German authorities as soon as practical.

Dachau, near Munich, was established in 1933 shortly after Hitler’s rise to power and became a model for the Nazi concentration camp system. Initially used for political prisoners, it later held Jews, foreigners and other persecuted groups; more than 41,000 people died there before U.S. forces liberated the camp on 29 April 1945. The original gate had been replaced with a replica installed in 2015 to mark the 70th anniversary of liberation. The theft echoes a 2009 incident in which an "Arbeit macht frei" sign was stolen from Auschwitz; that sign was later recovered in pieces and the perpetrators prosecuted.

A 45-year-old man was arrested after attempting to smash the protective case of Salisbury Cathedral’s Magna Carta with a hammer on Thursday afternoon. Alarms and a silent alert were triggered; staff, volunteers and members of the public restrained the suspect until police arrived. The outer glass was breached in three places but the inner glass and the charter itself were undamaged, and no injuries were reported. The cathedral evacuated briefly; the document has been removed for safekeeping while the case is repaired and a facsimile will be displayed. The arresting suspect faces suspicion of attempted theft, criminal damage and possession of an offensive weapon and is being questioned at Melksham police station.

Minnie Driver, now 42, reflects on a career that promised stardom but never quite reached it. Still working steadily, she praises her new indie Hunky Dory—a raw, live-sung British musical she’s proud of despite budget limits and a cut singing scene—and jokes about wanting roles like Glee. Her public image suffered after the 1998 film Hard Rain, on-set conflicts, and a misquoted remark about Judi Dench, prompting a media retreat. She reveals her son Henry’s father was a writer on her show The Riches; though once distant, he’s now more involved. Driver describes motherhood as life-changing, making her less self-centred and more selective about work. She hopes for another US TV series, aims for big directors and an Oscar, and values balance between career and parenting.

The piece centers on a fierce media and political fight after Ted Cruz swept Colorado’s Republican delegates at the state convention. The Drudge Report led an aggressive narrative framing Cruz’s wins as illegitimate, running numerous accusatory headlines—“rigged,” “cheating,” “1 MILLION REPUBLICANS SIDELINED”—and shaping social-media discourse, according to Zignal Labs. Cruz fired back on radio, accusing Drudge of serving as an attack organ for Donald Trump’s campaign and claiming Drudge now pushes Trump talking points rather than news. Drudge countered by highlighting an older interview in which Cruz praised the site.

The article frames the dispute as more than routine campaign sour grapes: right-wing outlets allied with Trump, including Drudge and Breitbart, risk alienating grassroots activists whose support Cruz would need at a contested convention in Cleveland. Ironically, the Democratic National Committee began attacking Cruz too, echoing Drudge’s theme that his candidacy is divisive.

Much of the analysis disputes Drudge’s portrayal of Colorado as a disenfranchising sham. The state’s delegate-selection rules—changed months earlier to elect unbound delegates at assemblies rather than a binding presidential straw poll—were public and known. Critics argue the system benefits highly organized activists; however, the account stresses Trump’s campaign failed to organize, send Trump himself, or match Cruz’s ground game. Several media responses called Drudge’s headlines misleading or sensationalized, noting isolated incidents were exaggerated into mass disenfranchisement claims.

The broader roundup includes related campaign developments: Trump invoking Ayn Rand’s Howard Roark, delegate skirmishes hurting Trump in other states, and polling showing Trump and Clinton strong in New York. Other news briefs cover NFL brain-injury research, Zika developments, corporate and legal stories, and various political and cultural items. Overall, the Colorado clash illustrates how delegate rules, grassroots organization, and media amplification are reshaping perceptions and tensions within the GOP primary.

An 8-year-old girl testified at the murder trial of her mother, 25-year-old Jessica Dutro, recounting a pattern of severe abuse that prosecutors say led to the 2012 death of Dutro’s 4-year-old son, Zachary Dutro-Boggess. The girl, who was seven when Zachary died, told jurors that Dutro and her then-boyfriend, 24-year-old Brian Canady, frequently punished the children with “lickins” that left marks, forced long timeouts facing the wall with hands raised, and hit them if their arms dropped. She testified that both adults beat Zachary until he was sick and that her mother told her not to talk about being hit. Zachary was taken to a Portland hospital on Aug. 14, 2012, with trauma to his abdomen and torn bowels; he was removed from life support two days later. Canady has pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter and second-degree assault. Prosecutors allege Dutro abused three children and neglected to seek timely medical care for Zachary; the surviving children now live with relatives. At trial, prosecutors introduced a Facebook message in which Dutro used a slur and wrote that Zachary “walks and talks like” he would be gay and that Canady would have to “work on” him—evidence the judge allowed as showing motive and a pattern of torture. Searches Dutro reportedly made the day Zachary died—on anger management, parenting classes, free items, and sex with strangers—were also ruled admissible.

The document mixes technical seed-description data for a web crawl with a film review and movie-theater listing, plus notes about Alexa’s data donations. The seed for “Wide00014” specifies crawling rules: include slash pages from every web domain, rank all URLs with more than one incoming inter-domain link (using Wide00012 inter-domain links), limit to the top 100 ranked URLs per domain, and include top-ranked pages (up to 100) from every linked-to domain using the Wide00012 navigational link graph. Interspersed is a New York Times–style review of the 2010 comedy The Other Guys, directed by Adam McKay and starring Will Ferrell and Mark Wahlberg. The reviewer describes a bait-and-switch tone: a closing-credit sequence of charts about financial scandals suggests a sharper satire than the film actually is. Instead, McKay plays to wide-ranging silliness and verbal riffing, showcasing Ferrell as mild-mannered, explosively passive detective Allen Gamble and Wahlberg as his volatile partner Terry Hoitz. Comic highlights include a whispered funeral brawl and a spoof of action-hero personas by Dwayne Johnson and Samuel L. Jackson, with support from Michael Keaton, Rob Riggle and Damon Wayans Jr. The document also contains a long theater/movie listing and a note that since 1996 Alexa has donated crawl data to the Internet Archive, which feeds the Wayback Machine after embargo periods.

An Egyptian court has sentenced 25-year-old singer Shaimaa Ahmed, known as Shyma, to two years in prison after finding her guilty of “inciting debauchery” and publishing an indecent film over a provocative music video. The clip for her song “I Have Issues” features scenes of Shyma dancing in underwear, performing suggestive acts such as pouring milk over a banana before eating it, licking an apple, and tasting cake icing. The video drew more than a million views quickly but also provoked conservative outrage. The director of the video was also handed a two-year prison sentence in absentia and fined; Shyma received a fine of 10,000 Egyptian pounds and can appeal the verdict. Arrested on November 18, Shyma told prosecutors she did not intend to offend and later apologized on a now-deleted Facebook post, saying she had not anticipated the intense backlash and that the director had included some controversial scenes without her consent. She appeared in court wearing a niqab and was photographed reading the Quran while awaiting sentencing. The case follows a pattern in Egypt of criminal prosecutions targeting women in entertainment: last year three women were jailed for six months each for dancing in music videos after being convicted of inciting debauchery. Separately, another popular singer, Sherine Abdel Wahab, faced a trial and a two-month performance ban by the Egyptian Musicians Syndicate after joking that drinking from the Nile could cause schistosomiasis, which led to accusations of “spreading provocative publicity.” Human rights and free-expression advocates say such prosecutions reflect growing restrictions on artistic expression and personal freedoms in Egypt’s conservative social and legal environment.

Leslie Kahn, 61, of Epping, New Hampshire, found herself stranded in her backyard pool on Aug. 11 after a ladder step broke while she was exiting. With one foot on the broken rung she cracked her knee and lacked the upper-body strength to pull herself out. Alone at home and without her cellphone, Kahn improvised: she used a pool pole to drag a chair holding her iPad close enough to access the internet and posted a “911” plea for help on a local Facebook group, Epping Squawks. Responses came within minutes. Neighbors, a nearby woman, and police arrived and tried several rescue ideas—repairing the ladder, placing a chair in the water (which proved unstable)—before someone produced a step ladder that allowed Kahn to climb out safely. A breast cancer survivor, Kahn reflected that life alternates between helping others and needing help herself; she expressed gratitude and humor about the episode, thanking the community for its quick response and saying she was laughing through the ordeal. The incident illustrates both personal resourcefulness and the rapid, positive impact of social media and neighborly assistance.

The Federal Reserve’s bank stress tests mostly cleared major U.S. lenders, but it rejected parts of several capital plans, notably Citigroup’s request to raise dividends and repurchase shares. Citigroup passed the test overall but showed a projected Tier 1 common ratio of 4.9% under the Fed’s severe recession scenario—below the 5% minimum if it pursued higher payouts. CEO Vikram Pandit said Citi will work with regulators to return “meaningful” capital while satisfying requirements. SunTrust, Ally and MetLife also fell short on proposed distributions; Ally and SunTrust plan to submit revised plans. The Fed’s scenario assumed 13% unemployment, a 50% stock decline and 21% house-price drop, producing aggregate losses of $534 billion. JPMorgan and Wells Fargo won approval for larger payouts, boosting investor confidence in the banking recovery.

Cory Booker, the 44-year-old mayor of Newark, easily won the New Jersey Democratic primary for the special U.S. Senate election to fill the late Frank Lautenberg’s seat, taking 59% in a four-way race. He will face Republican Steven Lonegan in October in a contest New Jersey is unlikely to lose to a Republican. Booker's victory crystallizes a larger debate on the left: many progressive commentators criticize him as too cozy with Wall Street and Silicon Valley, overly self-promotional, and insufficiently committed to structural reforms. Critics from Salon, Slate, and elsewhere argue he represents a neoliberal, elite strain of Democratic politics, useful to the party mainly as a high-profile nonwhite figure who can boost turnout. Others on the left concede he is pragmatic and effective—capable of delivering results and being a valuable advocate when aligned with liberal priorities. Booker’s biography—Stanford class president, Rhodes Scholar at Oxford, Yale law degree, charitable work, and anti-corruption fights in Newark—supports the image of a highly accomplished, media-savvy politician. He campaigned as a uniter and pragmatist rather than an ideologue, appealing to a broad electorate. Observers note speculation about his national ambitions; supporters see a rising star, detractors fear a centrist, media-focused senator rather than a progressive legislator.

Colin Kaepernick’s anthem protest has spread across sports, and the Seattle Seahawks may join in solidarity. Cornerback Jeremy Lane has been sitting during the anthem and plans to continue; teammates Doug Baldwin and Bobby Wagner have discussed joining him, and Wagner suggested any action would be a team decision rather than individual. Baldwin has exchanged messages with veterans who supported his tweets defending the protest and has been in contact with Kaepernick. Coach Pete Carroll supports Lane’s right to express himself and won’t dictate player actions; the organization won’t punish them. Teammates, including Michael Bennett, voiced support for the right to protest. All eyes will be on the Seahawks at their September 11 opener.

A Brussels appeals court has ordered retired King Albert II of Belgium to undergo a DNA paternity test in a long‑running case brought by 50‑year‑old artist Delphine Boël, potentially resolving whether he is her biological father. The court’s ruling, reported by Boël’s lawyers, overturns an earlier decision and requires the 84‑year‑old former monarch to submit to a saliva test within three months or face a legal presumption that he is her father. Albert, who abdicated in 2013 after 20 years on the throne and thus lost his immunity from such court orders, has denied Boël’s claim for more than a decade. Previous court‑ordered testing excluded Jacques Boël, a scion of one of Belgium’s wealthiest industrial families, as her father. Boël, who has two children, has sought legal confirmation of her identity since a 1999 biography of Queen Paola alleged Albert fathered a daughter from an extramarital relationship in the 1960s. Her lawyers welcomed the ruling as a “strong affirmation of the principle of acting in the interests of the child.” The court’s decision could still be legally challenged by Albert’s representatives. The royal household had no immediate comment; Albert now has no formal public role. The outcome would carry personal and reputational consequences but would not affect the current succession, where Philippe’s family, including heiress Princess Elisabeth, remains in line.

Democratic Sen. Jon Tester claimed victory over Republican Rep. Denny Rehberg in a closely watched Montana Senate race and urged Congress to set aside partisanship to address the nation’s pressing problems: the federal deficit, taxes, the economy and the flood of secret outside political spending. Speaking in Great Falls shortly after being declared the winner, Tester—who led by about 16,000 votes with 48.5% to Rehberg’s nearly 45% and Libertarian Dan Cox at 6.5%—called for transparency from outside groups that spent an estimated $30 million on the contest, much of it by nonprofits that hide donors. Tester praised Rehberg’s public service after the congressman conceded and expressed hope lawmakers will pursue deficit reduction, tax reform, and pass Tester’s long-stalled wilderness/jobs bill to balance conservation and logging. Vote counting continued in several counties due to delays, but the Associated Press called the race early Wednesday. The report also notes other Senate outcomes nationally, including wins by Democrats in North Dakota and elsewhere.

Pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) candidate Tsai Ing-wen won Taiwan’s presidential election decisively, taking roughly 60% of early counted votes while ruling Kuomintang (KMT) candidate Eric Chu trailed at about 30%. Chu conceded and resigned as KMT chair while Premier Mao Chi-kuo also stepped down. Tsai is poised to become Taiwan’s first female president, promising to preserve the status quo of de facto independence while refusing to endorse the idea that Taiwan and China are one nation. Her victory reflects public unease over a sluggish economy, low wages, housing affordability and worries about growing dependence on mainland China. Voters signaled a desire to keep Beijing at arm’s length despite benefiting from cross-strait trade and exchanges. Observers expect Beijing to take a cautious “wait-and-see” approach but warn it could use diplomatic or economic pressure if Tsai appears to move toward formal independence. Tsai urged dignity and reciprocity in cross-strait relations and pledged to avoid provocations, cooperate with other parties, and uphold Taiwan’s democracy. The election also diminished the KMT’s long dominance, and the legislature’s final balance remained uncertain amid gains by independents and smaller parties.

A high-speed passenger train derailed near Santiago de Compostela, northwestern Spain, on the night of July 24, killing around 80 people and injuring many more in one of Europe’s deadliest recent rail disasters. The eight-carriage Madrid–Ferrol service, carrying over 200 passengers, left the tracks on a curve about 2–3 miles from Santiago, slammed into a concrete wall, jack‑knifed and caught fire. Security footage captured the train hurtling into the bend, one carriage flying meters and some cars overturning and tearing apart; survivors described scenes “like hell.” About 94 people were hospitalized, dozens in critical condition; victims included at least one American and other foreign nationals. Emergency crews, hospitals and volunteers responded, hospitals flooded with blood donors, and local festivities for St. James’s feast day were canceled. The veteran driver, Francisco José Garzón Amo, 52, survived with minor injuries and was under police guard in hospital and formally being questioned. Investigators say the train may have been traveling at roughly 190–200 kph (around 120 mph) where the limit was about 80 kph; the driver allegedly admitted excessive speed. Authorities are probing why onboard speed-control systems failed to brake the train and whether technical, human or systemic factors caused the crash; Renfe and Adif launched inquiries. Spain’s prime minister and the king visited the scene, national mourning was declared, and forensic teams and specialists were deployed to aid identification and the ongoing investigation.

Disneyland arrested 22-year-old outdoor vendor Christian Barnes after a small explosion from a dry-ice device in a trash can in Mickey’s Toontown on Tuesday evening. The blast injured no one but prompted a two-hour evacuation of the children’s area. Anaheim police say fragments of a plastic bottle suggested dry ice was used; Barnes was booked on suspicion of possessing a destructive device, held on $1 million bail, and is cooperating with investigators. Disneyland said it is working closely with authorities; police found no significant damage or links to other local incidents.

U.S. forces and allies carried out humanitarian airdrops and airstrikes to relieve the Iraqi town of Amerli, which has been besieged by ISIS fighters since mid-June. Amerli, home to under 20,000 mostly Shiite Turkmen residents, faced severe shortages of food, water, power and medical care, prompting U.N. and human rights warnings of an “imminent massacre.” Rear Adm. John Kirby said the U.S. coordinated drops with Australia, France and the U.K., and U.S. strikes targeted ISIS positions to protect the humanitarian operation. Video from Iraq’s defense ministry showed desperate scenes similar to those of Yazidis trapped on Mount Sinjar earlier in the month. Turkmen, a small Iraqi minority with cultural ties to Turkey, have long been targeted by Sunni extremists; Amerli itself was hit by a deadly 2008 truck-bomb attack.

Separately, the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported that ISIS abducted hundreds of Yazidi women and girls in Iraq and transported many into Syria, where roughly 300 have reportedly been “distributed” among fighters. SOHR confirmed at least 27 cases of women sold or married to ISIS militants for about $1,000 each in areas around Aleppo, Raqqa and Al-Hasakah. The group described ISIS attitudes toward captives as “spoils of war,” and U.N. agencies and human-rights bodies have warned of forced conversions, trafficking and broad displacement: since early August about 122,600 people from Sinjar have fled to Kurdistan.

Violence across Iraq continued, with suicide bombings and roadside attacks killing and wounding soldiers near Baghdad. U.S. Central Command reported expanded strikes near Mosul to support Iraqi and Kurdish defenses and critical infrastructure, bringing its Iraq tally to over 115 strikes. Regional leaders, including Saudi King Abdullah, urged a strong international response to the expanding ISIS threat, warning it could reach Europe and the U.S. if unchecked. In Lebanon, ISIS released videos showing the beheading of a captured soldier and threatening others after clashes and temporary militant seizures near the Syrian border.

Mobile phones in Broadway theaters have become a flashpoint, highlighted by two recent, widely shared incidents that underscore growing tensions between performers and audiences. In early July, 19-year-old Nick Silvestri leapt onto the set of Hand to God and attempted to plug his iPhone into a realistic-looking prop outlet. The stunt — filmed and posted online — provoked immediate security intervention and online ridicule. Silvestri later held a press conference, apologized, blamed alcohol and ignorance of theater norms, and denied the episode was a publicity stunt, though journalists questioned the timing given Hand to God’s box-office struggles. He acknowledged learning about theater etiquette and said he wouldn’t repeat the act. Coverage revealed how viral attention can both shame and reward such misbehavior, with Silvestri enjoying newfound followers even as producers used the moment for publicity.

A few days earlier, Patti LuPone made headlines by snatching a texting audience member’s phone mid-performance in Shows for Days without breaking character. LuPone, long outspoken about audience rudeness, lamented that phones and LEDs “destroy” the theatrical world and said she sometimes considers whether she wants to keep working on stage. Her intervention — and past incidents, including stopping shows for ringing phones or photos — illustrate performers’ growing impatience.

These episodes reflect a cultural clash: traditional theater etiquette values a dark, silent auditorium, but younger, tourist and mobile-native audiences often treat constant connectivity as normal. The theater community appears determined to resist that erosion of the live experience, using direct performer intervention, public rebukes, and social pressure to preserve the shared, immersive nature of theatrical performance.

In Texas City, a neighborhood tragedy unfolded when four dogs — three pit bulls and a mixed breed — escaped through a hole in a shared fence and attacked a family’s 10-year-old beagle, Bailey, killing her. Thirteen-year-old Brittany Baker returned from school to hear yelping and screams and witnessed the attack, describing the dogs chasing and pouncing on Bailey. Her father, Steve Baker, said the dogs “shook her like a rag doll” until she bled out. Police and animal control arrived quickly and eventually secured the dogs; the owners repaired the fence hole afterward. Texas City police declared all four animals “dangerous” under city ordinance, which requires owners who keep declared dogs to confine them in a secure, at least six-foot-high enclosure with mechanical locks, microchip/tagging, warning signs, annual registration, and $100,000 liability insurance. The owner has 15 days to appeal the designation.

The incident prompted community concern and comparisons to tougher ordinances elsewhere, such as recent League City rules requiring microchips, fluorescent collars, and holding dangerous dogs at the shelter pending hearings. Initially the Bakers sought awareness rather than punishment, but the case escalated when the neighbor, Emerald White, sued the Bakers for up to $1 million, alleging she was seriously injured retrieving her dogs from the Baker yard and claiming the Bakers failed to confine Bailey. Steve Baker said he was shocked to be sued after his family’s loss. City officials and both families have been involved with animal control and legal processes as the situation proceeds.

A detective testified at a preliminary hearing for 18 Penn State fraternity members accused in the fatal hazing of 19-year-old pledge Timothy Piazza, saying surveillance video from the Beta Theta Pi house showed Piazza “looked dead, he looked like a corpse.” Detective David Scicchitano described footage from the night of Feb. 2 that captured Piazza after he was ordered to drink during a pledge event involving heavy alcohol consumption. Prosecutors say he consumed a life-threatening amount and suffered multiple falls that left him seriously injured.

Scicchitano said the video shows Piazza’s first serious fall at 11:22 p.m., after which he was unconscious, limp, eyes closed and bearing a bruise on his abdomen. Through the night and into the early morning, surveillance shows him falling repeatedly, hitting his head and stomach, rolling on the floor and staggering toward the lobby and basement stairs. By about 3 a.m. he was left alone on a couch, and he isn’t seen again on tape until brothers later find him in the basement. When carried upstairs, Piazza had labored breathing and had “lost all color,” prompting some fraternity members to fear he had died. The defendants delayed calling 911 until nearly 12 hours after his first fall.

Piazza, a sophomore from Lebanon, New Jersey, died at a hospital on Feb. 4 from a traumatic brain injury and severe abdominal bleeding; toxicology showed a dangerously high blood-alcohol level. The charges against various members include involuntary manslaughter and felony aggravated assault, and the Beta Theta Pi chapter itself is a defendant. Penn State has permanently banned the fraternity, citing a persistent pattern of excessive drinking, drug use and hazing. Piazza’s parents attended the hearing; his father notably left the courtroom with his wife as the video was shown.

A sudden eruption of Kilauea on Hawaii’s Big Island forced widespread evacuations, damaged homes and cut power as intense seismic activity and gas emissions continued. Beginning with hundreds of small earthquakes over several days, the crisis escalated when fissures opened in the East Rift Zone and lava emerged in Leilani Estates and nearby Lanipuna Gardens. A magnitude 6.9 quake — the strongest since 1975 — was among more than 110 temblors in 24 hours, and USGS confirmed numerous fissures ejecting lava and steam. At least one home and another structure were destroyed, county officials said, and officials warned that additional vents and lava outbreaks were possible and unpredictable.

Mandatory evacuations affected roughly 1,500–1,700 residents; shelters opened at Pahoa and Keaau community centers. Officials activated the Hawaii National Guard, declared states of emergency, closed much of Hawaii Volcanoes National Park and imposed temporary flight restrictions. Power outages impacted about 14,000 customers; Puna Geothermal Venture suspended operations. Fire and civil defense teams reported extremely high sulfur dioxide levels in evacuation zones, posing acute risks to the elderly, children and those with respiratory conditions; authorities urged immediate removal from affected areas. Social media and drone footage documented lava fountains, burning vegetation and a lava flow snaking through neighborhoods. Officials emphasized safety, restricted access to impacted areas, and set up recovery centers and entry protocols for residents to retrieve belongings when conditions permit.

Reality-TV figure Jon Gosselin is embroiled in a messy publicity storm involving girlfriend Hailey Glassman and Octo-mom Nadya Suleman. Glassman accused Jon of emotional abuse on TV, but a source close to Jon claims the on-air confession was staged for money and exposure: Jon allegedly orchestrated the appearance to attract producers and earn fees. That same insider says Jon was indeed negotiating a quirky reality show with Suleman and hoped to be paid handsomely for staged dates, despite his public denials. The source paints Jon as financially strained, leveraging controversy to revive his career while neglecting responsibilities to his children and estranged wife Kate. Publicly, Jon has apologized, expressed a desire to reform, and said he and Hailey are “slowing things down,” while Hailey describes herself as “semi-single” and taking time for herself.

No jackpot winner was drawn Tuesday for Mega Millions, so the prize swelled to an estimated $502 million for Friday’s drawing (cash option $301 million). The numbers Tuesday were 7, 25, 43, 56, 59 and Mega Ball 13. This marks the fourth time the jackpot has topped $500 million in the game’s 16-year history. The roll began after the last jackpot win Jan. 5 ($451 million). Since then there have been 33 prizes of $1 million or more. Mega Millions is played in 44 states, D.C. and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Republican Senate candidate Pete Hoekstra released a Super Bowl ad featuring a young Asian woman speaking in broken English amid rice paddies, blaming Sen. Debbie Stabenow’s spending for U.S. job losses. The spot and an accompanying site using Chinese imagery drew immediate backlash as racially insensitive from both Democrats and some Republicans. Asian-American groups in Michigan condemned the use of negative stereotypes; GOP consultant Nick De Leeuw called the ad “appalling.” Hoekstra defended the ad as satirical and focused on economic competition, saying it targeted Stabenow’s record, not Asians or China, and asserted it generated positive response. Democrats countered by highlighting Hoekstra’s own spending record and lobbying career, launched rebuttal websites and ads, and used the controversy to raise funds. The ad aired regionally and will run on GOP-targeted cable shows.

Daybreakers reimagines vampire lore as a dark, satirical near-future: by 2019 a plague has turned most people into corporate, suit-clad vampires who commute at night, drink blood-laced coffee and farm humans for hemoglobin. Ethan Hawke plays Edward Dalton, a remorseful vamp-hematologist trying to develop a synthetic blood substitute for his profit-driven employer (Sam Neill) as supplies run dangerously low and “subsiders” — feral, bat-like creatures — begin to emerge. He encounters a human resistance led by Claudia Karvan’s Audrey and Willem Dafoe’s charismatic Elvis, who may hold the key to a cure. Directed and written by Australian brothers Michael and Peter Spierig, the film mixes inventive worldbuilding and grim humor — vamp-mobiles, blood-baristas and corporate vampirism as a metaphor for resource depletion — with pulpy, R-rated gore and retro B-movie thrills. Critics praise the premise, Hawke’s brooding turn and Dafoe’s scene-stealing energy, and admire the visual flair and satirical bite. But many note the script’s holes and a mid-film sag: inventive ideas outpace character and plot development, leaving a less satisfying climax despite striking atmosphere and clever concept.

On August 7, Deborah Skouson of St. George posted a simple, heartfelt plea on Facebook: her 10-year-old daughter Cami, who has autism, insists on wearing one specific pink, flower-and-heart shirt from Target and the original had become too faded to use. After finding a few duplicates on eBay but needing more reliable backups, Skouson asked friends and followers to sell or donate identical shirts, offering to cover shipping. The request quickly exploded across social media, accumulating over 22,000 shares, pickup by local news and the large Love What Really Matters page, and offers from people around the world. Within a week she had received or been promised roughly 135 shirts—far more than the few she had hoped for. Donations came from as far away as Germany, England and the Philippines, and even Target contacted her offering to make larger versions so Cami can wear the same shirt into adulthood; Skouson tearfully accepted. Skouson said the flood of kindness has been deeply moving and changed how she views the internet, making her feel connected to many people. She explained that Cami, who started fifth grade on August 11 and is one of five children, prefers sameness, so keeping that exact shirt is important to her wellbeing. Skouson acknowledged a handful of critics who argue she is feeding an “obsession,” but she defended her decision: as Cami’s mother she knows what helps her daughter, and if the shirt brings comfort, she will keep finding it. The story highlights how social media can mobilize empathy and practical support for families managing autism.

A CTA Route 148 articulated bus crashed at Michigan Avenue and East Lake Street around 5:50 p.m. on June 2, 2015, killing 51-year-old Aimee Coath of Flossmoor and injuring eight others, including the bus driver. The bus reportedly ran a red light, struck two pedestrians and several cars, jumped a curb and came to rest on a sidewalk near 205 N. Michigan Ave. Witnesses described chaotic scenes, screams, people pinned under the bus and bystanders aiding victims until ambulances arrived; at least 10 ambulances responded. Coath was freed from beneath the bus and later pronounced dead at Northwestern Memorial Hospital. The driver, hired less than a year ago, was ticketed for running a red light and failure to exercise care; authorities are investigating and reviewing onboard video and drug test results.

Two recent college graduates have embraced the tiny-house movement by turning trailers into mobile homes and hitting the road with their dogs and much-reduced possessions. Kelly Tousley and Curtiss O’Rorke Stedman left their 1,200-square-foot Juneau rental in June and moved into a handmade tiny house on a utility trailer—98 square feet of living space they outfitted over eight months for about $8,600. The glossy exterior hides a snug interior with vinyl floors, lime-green walls, a bench that folds into a queen bed, a small kitchenette, a curtained bathroom (no running water), and solar panels for electricity. Curtiss, a high-school English teacher and musician, decided to pursue his music career full time and Tousley quit her job working with autistic children so they could travel together for at least a year. They pared down to essentials with playful curbside giveaways and tough goodbyes—Curtiss parting with plants grown from his great-great-grandmother’s clippings and Kelly giving up sentimental clothing.
