Friends and family were surprised but mostly supportive; even Kelly’s builder grandfather was impressed when they successfully installed trailer windows. Their route will span the Alaska road system and the Lower 48, aiming for nomadic adventure rather than conventional homeownership. Meanwhile, another couple, Kristin and Tony Schillaci, recently returned to Santa Fe after spending a year on the road in an 18-foot 1980 Coachman, traveling 25,000 miles to 30 juried art shows across 35 states to sell Kristin’s fine art photography—also accompanied by two large dogs. The stories highlight a growing willingness to downsize materially in favor of mobility, creative careers, and experiential living. Kelly and Curtiss invite followers to track their journey at paygasnotrent.com.

A powerful 7.2 magnitude earthquake struck eastern Turkey near Van, centered north-east of the city, causing widespread destruction across Van province and the town of Ercis. Authorities reported at least 265 dead and 1,140 injured, with the toll expected to rise as rescue teams reach outlying villages. Nearly 970–1,000 buildings were destroyed, including dozens in Ercis and several in Van; up to 80 buildings and a student dormitory collapsed in Ercis alone. Rescue crews, heavy machinery, dogs and medics have been working to pull survivors from rubble amid hundreds of aftershocks; some trapped people were reached after calling on mobile phones. Tens of thousands spent cold nights outdoors; many were treated in hospital gardens due to overwhelmed facilities. Deputy officials coordinated tent and food distribution, while international offers of aid arrived. Officials warned that mud-brick village homes were especially vulnerable and that building regulations had often been ignored. The quake—shallow and followed by significant aftershocks—was the deadliest in Turkey since the 1999 disasters.

Funny or Die launched "Live Funny or Die" on Nov. 8 to cover the 2012 presidential campaign with satire, debuting an introductory video that features comedians impersonating several GOP candidates and President Obama. The sketch includes portrayals of Mitt Romney, Ron Paul, Michele Bachmann, Rick Perry and a heavily lampooned Herman Cain — played by Mike Tyson — who delivers absurd, pizza-themed lines. Darrell Hammond channels a mashup of his Clinton and Trump impressions for Rick Perry, while Reggie Brown appears as Obama to deliver a blunt lesson about online attention: cats and breasts. The parody compresses campaign clichés into internet-era humor: Romney’s awkward self-promotion, Bachmann’s family-centric gaffes, Paul’s framing anxieties, Perry’s folksy crudeness and Cain’s simplistic slogans. The piece mocks how politicians try to court viral audiences, closing with a jokey reminder that online appeal often reduces serious debate to attention-grabbing gimmicks.

In 2014, Lund University chemistry professor Charlotta Turner received a distressing text from her PhD student Firas Jumaah saying he might not finish his thesis because he feared he would not return to Sweden. Jumaah, a Yazidi from Iraq, had gone back to visit family as violence escalated: ISIS launched a brutal offensive in northern Iraq, massacring and enslaving thousands of Yazidis. When ISIS reached the area near his family’s village, Jumaah found them hiding in a disused bleach factory amid gunfire. He contacted Turner in desperation, telling her his situation was hopeless.

Refusing to abandon her student, Turner contacted Lund’s then security chief, Per Gustafson. Gustafson arranged rapid assistance through a security company with global transport and protection capabilities. Over several intense days a rescue operation was organized: two Land Cruisers carrying four heavily armed contractors reached Jumaah’s hiding place, evacuated him, his wife and two young children, and drove them to Erbil Airport. Jumaah later described the rescue as feeling both privileged and guilt-laden because he had to leave other relatives behind. Fortunately, his remaining family survived the ISIS occupation.

Back in Sweden, Jumaah completed his PhD and now works for a pharmaceutical company in Malmö. The family has almost repaid the university for the cost of the rescue. Gustafson described the episode as unprecedented for a university. Turner said she was driven by outrage that ISIS had penetrated their academic community and by a sense of obligation to help a student in mortal danger. The episode highlights the extraordinary lengths a university and an individual professor went to save a student from violent persecution.

The piece argues that the early 2000s will be remembered as the Superhero Era and warns that the genre is approaching oversaturation. Studios, especially Warner Bros., are rushing to match Marvel’s output—Warner announced plans for 10 DC-based films from 2016–2020, including Batman v Superman, Suicide Squad, solo Wonder Woman, two Justice League films, The Flash, Aquaman, Shazam, Cyborg, and a rebooted Green Lantern. The author calls this strategy short-sighted: mass-producing superhero pictures risks accelerating audience fatigue just as past trends (film noir, westerns, spy films) eventually waned.

Warner’s track record with DC adaptations is mixed: while Batman and Superman reliably draw crowds, other attempts (Catwoman, Jonah Hex, Green Lantern) flopped. The studio’s tonal approach—darker, more somber fare compared with Marvel’s humor-driven hits like Guardians of the Galaxy—could limit broader appeal. Warner is also betting on less-established actors for key roles (Gal Gadot, Ezra Miller, Jason Momoa, Ray Fisher), which may or may not resonate commercially despite some welcome diversity and the long-overdue female-led Wonder Woman movie.

The broader landscape shows signs of cooling: overall box office is down versus previous years, and even big hits like Guardians have lower tallies than earlier blockbusters. The article suggests that rather than racing to outproduce Marvel, Warner might be better served by picking quality and originality over sheer quantity to avoid hastening the genre’s decline.

The piece concludes with a roundup of related superhero industry chatter—potential Civil War plotlines, Michael Keaton’s openness to reprise Batman with Tim Burton, Hawkeye solo speculation, and a Lego Batman spin-off—illustrating how expansive and crowded the field has become.

Netflix will release the documentary Virunga, executive produced by Leonardo DiCaprio and directed by Orlando von Einsiedel, on November 7 both on Netflix and in New York and Los Angeles theaters. The film follows park rangers in Virunga National Park, Democratic Republic of Congo, who protect endangered mountain gorillas from poachers, armed militias and resource-extracting industries. Virunga spotlights an embattled team including an ex-child soldier turned ranger, an orphan-gorilla carer and a Belgian conservationist. The documentary has won awards at festivals such as Tribeca, DOXA and AFI. DiCaprio described the partnership as an opportunity to inform and inspire action on biodiversity and conservation, while Netflix touted the film’s emotional impact.

Leaked emails from former Secretary of State Colin Powell portray him sharply criticizing Donald Trump, dismissing investigations into the 2012 Benghazi attack as a “witch hunt,” and expressing frustration over being tied to Hillary Clinton’s email controversy. Powell confirmed the authenticity of the emails, which were first reported by BuzzFeed and published by DCLeaks—sites U.S. officials and reporters have linked to actors with possible ties to Russian intelligence. In messages to a former aide, Powell called Trump a “national disgrace” and an “international pariah,” said Trump was “in the process of destroying himself,” and condemned the “birther” movement as racist. He also wrote that any outreach to black voters by Trump would be ineffective, saying “he takes us for idiots,” and criticized Trump’s past demands for President Obama’s birth certificate and school records. In correspondence with former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, Powell characterized the long-running Benghazi congressional probes as “stupid” and noted blame across multiple parties, including intelligence agencies and, to some extent, Hillary Clinton. Other leaked notes show Powell frustrated at being dragged into Clinton’s email controversy, complaining that publicity cost him business and expressing ambivalence about voting for Clinton despite respecting her. The cache—allegedly spanning June 2014 to August 2016 and reportedly numbering thousands of messages—includes exchanges suggesting friends expected an eventual endorsement of Clinton; Powell has publicly described himself as a lifelong Republican who twice endorsed Barack Obama. The releases have raised concerns among Democrats and cybersecurity experts about foreign-linked interference in U.S. politics.

Michael Lohan, 49, announced his engagement to Kate Major, 27, with whom he’s been close for five years. Lohan told UsMagazine.com he values their strong friendship and waited to announce the engagement until his family situation with daughter Lindsay was addressed; he has been urging her to enter rehab. He proposed after discussing plans with Major and getting approval from her father during a recent Florida visit. Major and Lohan plan to have children in the future and are already making wedding plans for later this year at Oheka Castle in New York; Major says she’s “really happy” and called the ring “gorgeous.” Major noted she and Jon Gosselin do not speak, but she wished him and Kate Gosselin the best. Earlier text describes Internet Archive crawls aimed at preserving web pages to prevent broken links by archiving referenced content.

House of Cards will end with its forthcoming sixth season, TVLine reports. The decision, Netflix confirms, was made months earlier and isn’t a reaction to actor Anthony Rapp’s allegation that Kevin Spacey made a sexual advance toward him when Rapp was 14. Production on Season 6 began this month, and the final season will premiere in 2018. Season 5 shifted power to Robin Wright’s Claire Underwood, and showrunners said there was more to explore beyond the presidency. Spacey issued a statement apologizing if the encounter occurred, acknowledged past same-sex relationships, and was criticized by advocacy groups.

Secretary of State John Kerry made a series of forceful public remarks about two major international crises: the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine and the violence between Israel and Hamas in Gaza.

On MH17, Kerry said it is "pretty clear" that separatists shot down the airliner and likely received significant Russian support. Citing U.S. intelligence and other evidence, he asserted that a sophisticated missile system had been transferred from Russia into separatist hands and that Ukrainian forces did not possess such a system in that area at the time. Kerry described confirmation that, within the previous month, convoys carrying armored personnel carriers, rocket launchers, tanks and artillery crossed from Russia into eastern Ukraine and were handed to separatists, and that separatists had received Russian training. He pointed to video evidence reportedly showing a launcher moving back into Russia with at least one missile missing, reports of separatists tampering with the crash site, removing wreckage and taking bodies, and other indicators tying the group to the attack. Kerry warned that the compromised and limited access to the crash site — monitors were initially given just 75 minutes, then three hours — has "seriously compromised" the investigation and called for full access, calling the situation a "moment of truth for Russia."

Separately, Kerry expressed hope for a swift ceasefire in the Israel–Hamas fighting, supporting an Egyptian initiative and saying the U.S. was working intensively to secure a halt to hostilities. He defended Israel’s right to defend itself against rocket attacks while warning that terrorism cannot be rewarded and preconditions cannot dictate negotiations. Kerry also drew scrutiny for an open-mic remark critical of aspects of Israel’s operations; he stood by his candid reaction while reiterating support for Israel’s security and acknowledging the difficulty of protecting civilians in wartime.

The World Food Programme (WFP) produced a July assessment warning severe hunger among Rohingya in northern Rakhine State, finding more than 80,000 children under five were “wasting” and calling for aid for over 225,000 people. After the Myanmar government requested its removal, the six-page report was pulled from public view and replaced with a statement that WFP and Myanmar were “collaborating on a revised version” and that the original should not be cited. WFP leadership later said the assessment should be republished and stood by its findings, while acknowledging conditions likely deteriorated after an August 25 insurgent attack prompted a harsh military crackdown and mass displacement. Humanitarian agencies, including WFP, have been denied access to much of the conflict zone and are pressing Myanmar to allow unhindered aid deliveries. Critics say the UN’s handling of the Rohingya crisis—including alleged suppression of reports and prioritizing relations with the government to secure access and funding—has muted warnings about the plight of roughly 1.1 million Rohingya in Myanmar. The crackdown has driven over half a million Rohingya into Bangladesh, where displaced people face overcrowded camps, limited rights, and precarious living conditions. Bangladesh registers arrivals but hesitates to formally recognize them as refugees; officials are consolidating camps for security and management despite concerns from aid workers about health, rights, and long-term prospects.

Orange County authorities released new photos and details as their manhunt continued for three inmates who escaped the Orange County Central Men’s Jail and for several people suspected of aiding them. Sheriff Sandra Hutchens said five people were arrested in connection with the breakout and that more arrests were expected; she identified some arrestees as gang members tied to Vietnamese gangs in Westminster and Garden Grove but gave no names to avoid compromising the investigation. The escapees — Hossein Nayeri, Jonathan Tieu and Bac Duong — remain at large and are considered armed and dangerous. A $200,000 reward is being offered for information leading to their capture, and hotlines have been established for tips.

The inmates escaped sometime after a 5 a.m. head count on Friday and were not discovered missing until an evening count, giving them roughly 16 hours’ lead time. Hutchens called the delay “every sheriff’s nightmare” and said the department is reviewing policies and procedures; officials have already revised head-count practices to require more thorough verification of inmate movements. Investigators believe the escape involved outside help and are also probing possible inside assistance. Deputies say the trio cut through half-inch steel bars and plumbing ducts, accessed an unsecured recreation roof, and used bed sheets to rappel to the ground before fleeing on foot; authorities described the cuts as professionally executed, suggesting tools not made inside the jail.

Nayeri, considered the likely mastermind due to his military background and the severity of charges against him, has been held since 2014 on allegations including kidnapping and torture. Tieu and Duong are documented gang members facing violent-crime charges; new images of Duong’s tattoos were released to aid identification. Since the escape, deputies have served at least 30 warrants as the investigation continues.

Senate Intelligence Committee Chairwoman Dianne Feinstein said there is no evidence linking terrorism to the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, which vanished en route to Beijing more than three weeks earlier. Speaking on CNN’s State of the Union, Feinstein acknowledged speculation but stressed that investigators have not found anything to suggest a terrorist act. She described the multinational search as “a very difficult mission,” noting that the involvement of many countries underscores limitations in current methods and calculations for locating the plane. Feinstein declined to discuss specific U.S. intelligence capabilities or whether more advanced satellites could be used, saying American intelligence is not purpose-built for air-crash investigations and she would not detail what assets exist. Separately, Russian Ambassador to the United States Sergey Kislyak told ABC’s This Week that Russia has no intention of withdrawing from Crimea, insisting the peninsula is now part of the Russian Federation and that Russian forces are conducting exercises on Russian territory. Rejecting characterization of Russia as a weakened regional power, Kislyak argued Russia’s significance spans from Europe to Asia. He suggested a possible diplomatic path involving constitutional revision in Ukraine, framing the main problem as tensions between the interim Ukrainian government and the rest of the country.

Freedom Industries Inc. filed for Chapter 11 protection in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in the Southern District of West Virginia after a Jan. 9 chemical spill that contaminated the Elk River and the state’s largest water system. Company president Gary Southern signed the filing, which lists assets and liabilities each in the $1 million–$10 million range, notes at least 200 creditors, and states the top 20 creditors are owed $3.66 million. The leak came from a storage tank and its containment area at a Freedom-owned facility; the document reports the tank appears to have been pierced through its base by an object. One current theory is that a nearby broken water line caused the ground beneath the tank to freeze during cold weather just before the spill. The contamination forced officials to advise residents in a nine-county area around Charleston to avoid using tap water except for flushing toilets, closing some businesses and schools for days; most restrictions have since been lifted. State records show the leaking terminal hadn’t been inspected since 2001, when a different, more tightly regulated owner operated it; Freedom bought the terminal the month before the spill.

Researchers have detected minute tidal effects in Scotland’s Loch Ness caused not by the moon directly moving the loch’s water but by the land beneath it flexing in response to ocean tides in the nearby North Sea. The phenomenon, called ocean tidal loading, occurs when changing sea levels about 13 km east of the loch increase pressure on the seafloor and deform the solid Earth. This deformation subtly tilts the basin that holds Loch Ness, causing water to slosh so that one end becomes about 1.5 millimeters deeper than the other depending on the North Sea tide phase. The team from the National Oceanography Centre (UK) and the University of Porto used distributed pressure sensors along the loch’s 35 km length to measure depth changes with astounding precision—0.1 mm depth resolution and tilt accuracy better than 10^(-8) over the full distance. The measurements demonstrate Loch Ness functions as one of the world’s longest and most accurate natural tiltmeters and may represent the first documented case in a European lake of tidal land shifts driven by remote ocean tidal loading.

Multiple news outlets reported that former National Security Adviser Susan Rice requested the unmasking of U.S. persons whose identities had been redacted in intelligence reports that incidentally captured communications involving members of the Trump transition and campaign. According to sources cited by Bloomberg, Fox News and other outlets, Rice requested the names in dozens of instances during the months between the November 2016 election and President Trump’s January 2017 inauguration. Those unmasked identities were reportedly distributed widely within the National Security Council, to some Defense Department officials, and to senior intelligence leaders including then-Director of National Intelligence James Clapper and CIA Director John Brennan.

The underlying surveillance cited involved incidental collection: conversations intercepted while monitoring foreign officials, some of whom were discussing the Trump transition or communicating with Trump transition members. Under normal practice, the identities of U.S. persons intercepted incidentally are masked in intelligence summaries—labeled generically as “U.S. Person One,” for example—unless an unmasking is justified by a demonstrable national security, law enforcement or foreign intelligence need. Sources told Fox News and other outlets that the reports relating to the Trump transition included political content—who Trump aides were meeting, their views on foreign policy, and plans for the incoming administration—and that some summaries were written in ways that made the masked individuals’ identities obvious even before any official unmasking.

The pattern of Rice’s requests came to light during a National Security Council review of unmasking policy conducted by NSC senior director for intelligence Ezra Cohen-Watnick. He discovered multiple requests and raised the matter with White House counsel; subsequently, Cohen-Watnick was directed to end his own review. House Intelligence Committee Chairman Devin Nunes, who had previously said he had seen incidental surveillance reports that concerned him, viewed related logs and briefed the White House before publicly describing that names had been unmasked. Nunes has been criticized for viewing documents on White House grounds rather than through the committee’s usual channels; Democrats said it was improper that he alone had access initially. Ranking member Adam Schiff later reviewed the reports but voiced concern that the material had not been shared more broadly with committee members.

Legal and political commentators noted that Rice’s unmasking requests do not substantiate President Trump’s earlier tweet accusing former President Obama of wiretapping Trump Tower—no evidence has emerged to support that allegation. Civil liberties advocates caution that the standard for unmasking is broad and can be stretched to encompass political intelligence. NBC, CBS and other mainstream outlets provided varying degrees of coverage, with some reporters and networks defending the legality of unmasking when done for legitimate intelligence reasons, while others treated Rice’s role as politically troubling.

The revelations prompted calls for congressional inquiries to determine why the unmaskings occurred, what the unmasked reports contained, whether distribution of the names was appropriate, and whether any dissemination led to unauthorized leaks. Rice publicly has been largely silent on the unmasking specifics; she told PBS in March she knew nothing about reports that Trump aides had been monitored and said she was surprised by Chairman Nunes’ disclosures. The episode has intensified scrutiny of both the Obama administration’s handling of intelligence during the transition and of congressional oversight practices.

In his final address to the United Nations General Assembly, President Barack Obama urged nations to defend democratic values, maintain open international engagement and address the dislocations caused by globalization rather than retreat into isolationism or strongman rule. Acknowledging persistent global dangers—ongoing violence in the Middle East, the rise of extremist networks, refugee flows, terrorism, North Korea’s nuclear advances and widening inequality—Obama argued these challenges cannot be solved by force or walls. “A nation ringed by walls would only imprison itself,” he warned, a clear rebuke to isolationist and nativist movements at home and abroad. He emphasized diplomacy over military solutions in conflicts such as Syria, noting that outside powers cannot indefinitely force communities with deep sectarian divides to coexist.

Obama highlighted foreign-policy accomplishments from his administration—normalizing relations with Cuba, the Iran nuclear agreement, cooperation on climate change, reductions in terrorist safe havens and assistance to nations like Myanmar—while conceding that many problems remain unresolved. He criticized Russia’s attempts to reclaim influence by force and cautioned against militarizing disputes such as those in the South China Sea, urging adherence to international law. On the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, he said progress requires mutual recognition: Palestinians rejecting incitement and Israel acknowledging it cannot permanently occupy Palestinian land.

Central to Obama’s message was a call for a “course correction” in global integration: preserve the benefits of open markets, technology and interdependence, but ensure those gains are broadly shared and that economic, political and cultural disruptions are addressed. He warned against authoritarian strongmen who respond to discontent with crackdowns or scapegoating, which risk domestic repression or foreign conflict. Urging democracies to “speak out forcefully” for freedom and dignity, Obama framed his appeal as pragmatic—asserting that accountable governance, human rights and cooperation remain the most durable foundations for global stability and progress.

Twitch streamer AnaPlaying had an unexpected live-stream mishap while playing League of Legends: flicking a lighter near her head, she accidentally set her hair on fire. For several seconds she didn’t realize; when she did notice she quickly patted out the flames. Though visibly shocked, she appeared uninjured and laughed about the incident with her viewers, brushing it off as an embarrassing but harmless moment. The clip highlights how quickly an ordinary moment can turn chaotic during live streams, and how streamers and audiences often treat such fails with humor.

Justice Anthony Kennedy’s retirement exposes how broken Supreme Court selection has become after the partisan chaos following Justice Antonin Scalia’s death. In 2016 Senate Republicans refused to consider Merrick Garland, inventing a rule barring election-year confirmations; Democrats retaliated by filibustering Neil Gorsuch, prompting Republicans to eliminate the Supreme Court filibuster. This tit-for-tat “Senate syndrome” has left nominations highly politicized: the majority can install lifetime justices with little minority input, yet opposite-party control often freezes seats for years. The stakes are enormous—justices serve decades and decide issues from elections funding to abortion and healthcare—so both parties treat nominations as existential fights. That incentivizes justices to time retirements politically and presidents to pick the youngest ideologically aligned nominees. The author proposes deescalation through term limits—suggesting ten-year, nonrenewable terms (or longer bipartisan proposals like 18 years)—to regularize vacancies, reduce stakes, discourage strategic retirements, and restore predictability and moderation. With Kennedy’s July 31 resignation, Senate Republicans vowed a swift confirmation before the midterms, while Democrats urged delay, setting up another intense, high-stakes confirmation battle likely to shape the Court and the 2018 elections.

Pedro Viloria, a McDonald’s drive‑thru attendant in Doral, Fla., leapt into action when a customer—an off‑duty Miami‑Dade police officer—suddenly lost consciousness while ordering breakfast for herself and her two children. After preparing the order, Viloria returned to the window and saw the driver struggling to breathe; she then passed out, her foot slipped off the brake, and the SUV began rolling down the drive‑thru lane. Surveillance footage shows Viloria jumping through the service window and pulling the officer from the vehicle just as it stopped against the curb. He directed the children to call 911 and comforted them while a firefighter, an off‑duty paramedic and other first responders who were already in or near the restaurant rushed to assist. A second McDonald’s employee performed CPR and helped revive the woman on scene before she was transported to the hospital for further treatment. McDonald’s praised Viloria’s “hero” actions in a statement, noting pride in his quick response and acknowledging the role of the unnamed coworker and emergency personnel in ensuring the officer received timely care. As of the latest updates, Miami‑Dade Police Detective Daniel Ferrin had not released information on the woman’s condition. The story was reported by local outlets and the Associated Press.

Central Europe faces severe flooding as the Danube and Elbe surge to record levels after heavy rains and a saturated spring. Hungary warns of its worst floods ever: the Danube is set to crest at unprecedented heights in Nagybajcs and Budapest, prompting evacuations, military reinforcements, sandbagging and concerns about a toxic sludge reservoir near Komarom. Budapest officials expect defenses to hold but thousands may still be affected. In Germany the swollen Elbe threatens Saxony-Anhalt and has already inundated areas downstream, forcing mass evacuations and causing widespread damage; Dresden’s center was spared. The Czech Republic focuses on large-scale pumping and cleanup after affecting hundreds of communities. At least 15 deaths have been reported across the region, with economic losses potentially rivaling the 2002 floods.

Researchers analyzing data from South Korea’s 2007–2009 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (10,711 adults) examined links between instant noodle consumption, overall dietary patterns, and cardiometabolic risk. They identified two main dietary patterns: a traditional pattern (rice, fish, vegetables, fruit) and a “meat and fast-food” pattern (meat, soda, fried and fast foods, including instant noodles). While neither pattern as a whole was directly associated with metabolic syndrome, the meat-and-fast-food pattern was linked to greater abdominal obesity and higher LDL cholesterol, whereas the traditional pattern was associated with lower elevated blood pressure and trends toward less abdominal obesity. Crucially, independent of these patterns, women who ate instant noodles at least twice weekly had a 68% higher prevalence of metabolic syndrome; this association was not seen in men. Authors and outside experts noted limitations: cross-sectional design cannot prove causation, and higher sodium intake or foods consumed with noodles might drive risks. The report sparked strong reactions in Korea, where instant noodles (ramyeon) are an ingrained, inexpensive staple and cultural comfort. Researchers advised occasional consumption (once or twice a month) is unlikely harmful, but frequent intake—several times a week—appears unwise for long-term cardiometabolic health, particularly for women.

As caterer Tyonne Johns cleared plates and packed folding chairs after a wedding reception at Ellanor C. Lawrence Park in Chantilly, Va., a dispute over ownership of the chairs escalated into violence. Park employee Kempton A. Bonds, 19, insisted the chairs were park property; Johns, 35, owner of Chef Tyonne catering, said they were hers. Tensions had been building earlier that night: witnesses say Bonds, a facilities attendant who had worked for the Fairfax County Park Authority since 2015, cut power to the reception’s junction box, abruptly stopping music and leaving about 80 guests without amplification just before the cake cutting. Bonds had called police at 9:24 p.m. to complain about disorderly conduct and noise; officers later logged the incident as resolved. Later, during the chairs dispute, police say Bonds produced a pocketknife and stabbed Johns in the upper body. Officers found her at the park around 10:50 p.m.; she died at a local hospital. Bonds remained at the scene and was arrested, charged with second-degree murder, held without bond, and fired by the park authority. Friends and colleagues remembered Johns as an ambitious, meticulous chef and entrepreneur, mourned by family and coworkers who praised her warmth and professionalism. The park authority expressed shock and condolences as the investigation continues.

Facebook announced it will roll out face-recognition assistance for photo tagging, prompting confirmation from users rather than automatic tagging and preserving existing privacy controls: users receive notifications when tagged, can remove tags, limit who tags them, and opt out of having their name suggested. The system will compare faces against a limited subset of friends—likely the 30 most-communicated-with—to improve accuracy and will leverage prior tags. Experts note face recognition remains difficult, especially at large scale, so Facebook’s “human in the loop” confirmation approach helps. The feature will start in the U.S. with a gradual rollout. Separately, Facebook’s revenue is expected to reach about $2 billion in 2010 as advertising and user growth surge, amid ongoing privacy scrutiny and improvements.

Sausage Party surprised at the box office with a $33.6 million debut, giving struggling Sony a hit and marking the biggest August opening for an animated film. The R-rated, profanity- and sex-joke-heavy comedy, backed by Annapurna and featuring voices like Seth Rogen and Kristen Wiig, was praised as fresh amid sequels and reboots. Suicide Squad stayed No. 1 with $43.8 million but suffered a steep 67% second-week drop. Disney’s Pete’s Dragon opened to $21.5 million—disappointing given strong reviews—while Jason Bourne and Bad Moms continued to perform steadily. Smaller releases like Florence Foster Jenkins and Hell or High Water showed promising niche success.

If all goes well, NASA’s Curiosity rover will touch down on Mars around 1:17 a.m. Eastern, with a confirmation signal reaching Earth about 13 minutes, 48 seconds later. But silence after landing wouldn’t necessarily mean disaster — it could result from communications gaps. Curiosity transmits on X-band directly to Earth until Gale Crater rotates out of view a few minutes before touchdown, and it also sends rich UHF data to the Mars Odyssey orbiter, which relays to Earth. If Odyssey cannot point correctly because of a recent wheel issue, it might miss the signal; the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter will be listening but only recording for later playback. If immediate relay fails, follow-up passes by orbiters and a later direct link could confirm a successful landing hours afterward. The final descent is preprogrammed and unsteerable in real time, using an untested sky-crane maneuver; engineers are “rationally confident, emotionally terrified.” The landing is a global spectacle; Mars missions historically succeed only about a third of the time worldwide, though the U.S. has the best record.

The University of Alberta cancelled a scheduled “Spoon Bending and the Power of the Mind” workshop after the presenters withdrew. The session, listed under Pediatric Integrative Medicine rounds, had been to address reiki and energy therapies, acknowledging their lack of evidence while discussing why patients and therapists use them. The workshop’s presenter, Edmonton energy healer Anastasia Kutt, advertised an “experiential” guided meditation/energy transfer promising most participants could bend cutlery by mind power, and explicitly noted it would not be a scientific evaluation. The event drew public criticism—especially from University of Alberta law professor Timothy Caulfield—and widespread social media mockery, with critics decrying the university’s apparent institutional support for unproven practices. Commentators linked the flyer to classic spoon-bending conman Uri Geller and expressed concern that academic medical centers are increasingly embracing complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) modalities like reiki and acupuncture without sufficient skepticism. Critics argue such acceptance reflects a broader problem in “integrative” or quackademic medicine, where pseudoscientific therapies are combined with evidence-based care. The cancellation and subsequent campus protests highlight tensions between promoting patient choice in care and maintaining rigorous scientific standards in medical institutions.

Law enforcement launched an intense manhunt for Christopher Jordan Dorner, a 33-year-old ex-LAPD officer suspected of killing three people in a revenge campaign after his 2008 dismissal. More than 100 officers scoured snowy, forested terrain around Big Bear Lake after Dorner’s burned pickup was found on a U.S. Forest Service road; footprints led away but yielded no capture. Search teams, including ski-masked SWAT, dogs and investigators, checked cabins, sheds and hundreds of homes across eight square miles while aircraft were grounded by snowfall. Authorities guarded more than 40 people named in Dorner’s manifesto — a conspiracy-laden online screed promising “unconventional” violence — and searched his and his mother’s homes. Officials confronted false sightings statewide, worried Dorner’s military and police training, survival skills and possible premeditation could enable ambushes; residents were warned and schools closed amid frigid, hazardous conditions.

Rebels from the Seleka coalition seized Bangui over a weekend assault, forcing President Francois Bozize to flee and prompting his whereabouts to remain unclear. Rebel leader Michel Djotodia declared himself president and pledged a 2–3 year transition with elections, saying he would respect the January Libreville power-sharing accord and keep Prime Minister Nicolas Tiangaye in place. The African Union suspended the Central African Republic and imposed sanctions, travel bans and asset freezes on Seleka leaders. The UN, US, France and regional states condemned the coup and urged respect for the agreement and restoration of services. Fighting killed scores, including at least 13 South African soldiers and many wounded, and looting in Bangui raised humanitarian alarms. The collapse of the peace deal followed Seleka accusations that Bozize reneged on commitments, notably integrating rebels into the army. The country’s chronic poverty and resource wealth complicate the fragile outlook.

Alexa Internet has been donating its crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996; these daily inflows are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo. One seed set, Wide00014, focused on “slash pages” from every domain — a ranked list of URLs with more than one incoming inter-domain link (ranked by inbound links using the Wide00012 inter-domain graph), capped at the top 100 URLs per domain — plus the top-ranked pages (also up to 100) from every linked-to domain based on the Wide00012 navigational link graph.

Separately, reports describe Natalie Portman’s private wedding to Benjamin Millepied in Big Sur. The ceremony, described variably as hosting 60 to 100 guests, was an intimate, traditional Jewish evening event at a private coastal residence on August 4. Attendees reportedly included Diane Sawyer and Mike Nichols, Ivanka Trump, Macaulay Culkin, Rashida Jones and Rodarte designers Kate and Laura Mulleavy. Portman wore a simple tea-length Rodarte gown with sheer full-length sleeves, reflecting her understated style. The reception featured a vegetarian meal—consistent with Portman’s vegan diet—and hip-hop DJ sets into the early morning. Coverage noted the conspicuous absence of Portman’s Black Swan co-star Mila Kunis, prompting speculation about whether Kunis chose not to attend because of Culkin’s presence or other reasons. Insiders described Portman as happy and glowing as she celebrated with close family and friends.

Oscar Pistorius, the South African Paralympic sprinter known as the “Blade Runner,” is expected to be released from Pretoria prison on parole around August 21 after serving roughly ten months of a five-year sentence for culpable homicide in the February 14, 2013, killing of his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp. Pistorius shot Steenkamp through a locked bathroom door and has long maintained he mistook her for an intruder. After a lengthy trial he was found guilty of culpable homicide rather than murder; prosecutors are appealing that verdict and will seek a murder conviction in a Supreme Court of Appeal hearing set for November. If convicted of murder on appeal, Pistorius could face at least 15 years or life imprisonment.

Under South African rules, Pistorius is eligible for “correctional supervision” after serving a sixth of his sentence and is likely to serve the remainder under house arrest with parole conditions such as no alcohol or drugs and participation in psychological and anger-management programs. He has been held in a single cell for protection at Kgosi Mampuru prison and is allowed limited exercise. His legal team says he is isolated but coping, hopes to work with disadvantaged youth upon release, and has turned down book and film deals despite financial strain. Steenkamp’s family expressed dismay that ten months’ incarceration is insufficient punishment, saying incarceration must serve as a deterrent and hold offenders accountable. Pistorius’s lawyers and supporters argue he must rebuild his life while facing continuing legal uncertainty and public scrutiny.

Pacific Life announced it will stop running ads on Tucker Carlson’s Fox News program “in the coming weeks” after an on-air segment in which host Tucker Carlson called the “immigration crisis” in the United States a force that makes the country “poorer and dirtier and more divided.” The company’s decision followed backlash on social media after a Pacific Life commercial — touting the insurer’s 150 years of protecting families — aired immediately after Carlson’s opening monologue. In a statement posted to Twitter, Pacific Life said it “strongly disagree[s] with Mr. Carlson’s statements” and emphasized that its customer base and workforce reflect national diversity “something we take great pride in.” The insurer said it will reevaluate its relationship with the program and pull all advertising from the show during that review.

Fox News responded through a spokesperson who characterized the criticism as “unfortunate and unnecessary distractions,” accusing left-wing advocacy groups of weaponizing social media to pressure advertisers and asserting the network would continue to support and work with its advertisers. Carlson’s monologue included additional inflammatory remarks about immigrants, calling them “cynical shake-down artists who have been watching too much CNN,” which intensified calls from critics on Twitter urging sponsors to drop his program. The network’s defense and Pacific Life’s withdrawal underscore the broader tension between media outlets, controversial on-air commentary, and advertiser responses in the social media age.

Amazon’s Prime Day, launched as a July experiment and code-named “Piñata,” has evolved into a major retail event designed to boost mid-year sales, enroll Prime members and test systems ahead of the holiday season. First held in 2015 to mark Amazon’s 20th anniversary, Prime Day was inspired in part by Alibaba’s Singles’ Day and aimed to stimulate otherwise slow July retail activity. Early iterations suffered glitches and criticism—sites briefly crashed at launch, and many deals were seen as clearing out low-quality inventory—yet Amazon iterated quickly, expanding inventory, spreading deals throughout the event, and improving pricing guarantees.

Prime Day now runs roughly 30 hours across multiple countries and promotes both Amazon’s hardware (Kindle, Fire tablets, Fire TV, Echo family) and third-party sellers who account for more than half of units sold on the site. Amazon touts Prime Day as a “branding” and data-gathering opportunity: it increases consumer engagement with services like Alexa and Echo, stress-tests logistics and software, and helps level out sales across the year. Prime members—estimated at tens of millions and spending far more annually than non-members—are the core target; Prime trials also qualify for deals, helping drive new sign-ups.

The event’s breadth has prompted many traditional retailers to counter with their own sales, while some major chains skip it. Amazon promises that lightning deals will be the lowest price for each item on its site in the prior 365 days, and frequently offers Alexa-exclusive discounts. Despite early-day site and checkout problems affecting some customers in past years (spawning the hashtag #PrimeDayFail), Amazon reported record-breaking Prime Day sales in later events, with strong device and category sales and improved customer sentiment compared to the inaugural year.

For shoppers, Prime Day offers genuine bargains but requires vigilance: deals are numerous, staggered, and often limited in quantity. Tools like the Amazon app (watch and waitlist features), Alexa voice prompts, browser extensions, price trackers such as CamelCamelCamel, and deal aggregators like SlickDeals help buyers monitor and verify prices to avoid “hype” or recycled discounts. Tax considerations also matter: as of 2017 Amazon collects sales tax in most U.S. states, so Prime Day purchases are typically not tax-free. Prime Day has become an established annual shopping holiday that both reflects and reinforces Amazon’s larger strategy to build a dominant commerce and services ecosystem.

A Laurel County man, Ernest (Chris) Chumbley, is charged with murder after admitting he shot his wife, Virginia Chumbley, early Wednesday morning, saying he did it at her request to end her suffering. Deputies found Virginia with two gunshot wounds at the couple’s Greenlawn Subdivision home around 2:30 a.m. Ernest called 911, telling the dispatcher, “I’ve shot my wife,” and later told reporters from the Laurel County Detention Center that her ongoing battle with breast cancer left her in severe pain and she asked him to “stop the pain.” He described the act as granting her last wish and insisted it was not murder; he pleaded not guilty in Laurel District Court and is held on $200,000 cash bond. Neighbors described a loving, long marriage of more than 20 years and said Virginia had been suffering, sometimes gasping at night. Authorities said the investigation is in its early stages, with additional interviews planned and an autopsy underway in Frankfort. Ernest is scheduled for a preliminary hearing on Sept. 5. Funeral arrangements for Virginia remain pending.

The Brazilian Senate voted on Wednesday to convict and remove President Dilma Rousseff, suspending her for the remainder of her term in a 61–20 decision. She was found guilty of manipulating the federal budget to hide worsening economic conditions, charges she and supporters have called politically motivated. Rousseff, Brazil’s first female president and a leading figure of the leftist Workers’ Party, had been suspended in May pending trial. Her ouster ends 13 years of Workers’ Party rule that saw economic expansion and major social gains but later severe recession and corruption scandals that eroded political support. The impeachment trial featured dramatic, marathon proceedings: Rousseff testified for 14 hours and some 66 senators spoke during the lengthy session, which included emotional moments from both prosecutors and defense counsel. Although her removal was expected to include an eight-year ban from public office, a subsequent Senate vote fell short of the necessary threshold (42–36), so she retains the legal right to run again. Rousseff has signaled she may appeal to Brazil’s Supreme Court, though prior appeals in the process were unsuccessful, and has indicated plans to return to Porto Alegre if she leaves office. Interim President Michel Temer was sworn in immediately following the vote.

UPDATE: The body of 19-year-old TeNiya Elnora Jones has been found. The University of Kentucky student, from Fort Myers, had been reported missing after a swimming accident in the Mediterranean off Tel Aviv. Jones was studying abroad this summer with a program run by the Council on International Educational Exchange (CIEE). On Saturday evening she and several other students entered the sea; a strong current pulled them out. Two students reached shore, but Jones did not. Israeli authorities conducted a primary search and rescue effort, with assistance and coordination from the U.S. Embassy in Israel, the State Department, and officials in Washington. The University of Kentucky, including President Eli Capilouto and the International Center led by Associate Provost Sue Roberts, notified and stayed in close contact with Jones’s family, CIEE, and federal and local officials. UK arranged travel for Jones’s mother and grandfather to Tel Aviv and Roberts planned to travel to meet them and authorities. CIEE and UK confirmed the other students are safe and coordinated their return to Amman, Jordan; the program, which began in June, was scheduled to conclude this week. The Jones family had endured earlier tragedy when TeNiya’s brother Samuel was fatally shot last December. The report also notes web archival crawls intended to preserve referenced pages to prevent broken links.

Three new papers in Science report that dramatic, rapid climate variability in East Africa helped drive important behavioral and technological shifts among hominins by about 320,000 years ago. Excavations in Kenya’s Olorgesailie Basin reveal the oldest securely dated Middle Stone Age (MSA) industry yet—small, standardized, retouched blades and points—displacing earlier, larger Acheulean hand axes that persisted there from about 1.2 million to 499,000 years ago. Age control comes from argon and uranium dating of volcanic ash layers, though a sedimentary gap between 499,000 and 320,000 years leaves some uncertainty about the transition’s tempo.

Microscopic and chemical soil analyses show frequent, rapid swings between wet and dry conditions around 320,000 years ago, when anatomically modern Homo sapiens were emerging. Researchers argue these environmental stresses made food resources unpredictable, favoring greater mobility, innovation, and long-distance social connections. Supporting this, many MSA artifacts at Olorgesailie were made from obsidian sourced 25–50 km (and in some cases farther) away; at one site obsidian comprised a large fraction of artifacts. The presence of large raw obsidian chunks worked at the site suggests transport and exchange, not casual procurement during travel—evidence for burgeoning trade or social networks. Teams also recovered 88 pigment lumps, some ground or cut, indicating early symbolic behavior or social signaling.

Although no hominin fossils were found at Olorgesailie and it remains unclear whether H. sapiens or close relatives made these tools, the finds align with genetic dates for H. sapiens origins (350,000–260,000 years ago) and challenge views of a late “human revolution.” Scholars caution that demographic shifts might also explain innovations, and that the relationship between species and behaviors across Africa remains complex. Nonetheless, Olorgesailie furnishes strong evidence that mobility, exchange, specialized tools, and symbolic materials were established much earlier than once thought.

CareerCast’s 2017 rankings identify the nation’s best and worst jobs by weighing environment, income, outlook, and stress. Among the best jobs highlighted are several high-paying, fast-growing roles driven by healthcare demand, aging populations, and increased data and software use. Ten notable positions:

- Speech pathologist: median pay $73,410, 21% growth; treats communication disorders in schools and hospitals, often requires a master’s degree.
- Occupational therapist: $80,150, 27% growth; helps patients with disabilities perform daily tasks.
- Software engineer: $100,690, 17% growth; strong demand, especially for applications developers.
- Mathematician: $111,100, 21% growth; needed for data modeling, usually requires a graduate degree.
- Tenured university professor: $72,470, 13% projected growth (includes untenured faculty); offers substantial job security but requires a Ph.D. and lengthy tenure review.

Overall BLS projects 7% employment growth across all occupations from 2014–2024. CareerCast’s top jobs tend to combine above-average pay and outlook; math and medical fields are well represented. The full rankings and methodology come from CareerCast and BLS data.

A 20-year analysis of U.S. mortality data (1993–2012) published in JAMA Pediatrics examined suicide in children aged 5 to 11 years to characterize trends by sociodemographic groups and method. Across the period, 657 children in this age range died by suicide (an average of nearly 33 per year); 84% were boys (553) and 16% girls (104). Hanging or suffocation was the leading method (78.2%, 514 of 657), followed by firearms (17.7%, 116) and other methods (4.1%, 27). 

Overall crude suicide rates for 5- to 11-year-olds remained essentially stable between the first (1993–1997) and last (2008–2012) five-year windows (1.18 to 1.09 per million; incidence rate ratio [IRR] = 0.96; 95% CI, 0.90–1.03). However, that apparent stability concealed significant divergent trends by race. Suicide rates increased significantly among black children (from 1.36 to 2.54 per million; IRR = 1.27; 95% CI, 1.11–1.45) and decreased significantly among white children (from 1.14 to 0.77 per million; IRR = 0.86; 95% CI, 0.79–0.94). These racial differences were concentrated among boys: black boys’ suicide rate rose (1.78 to 3.47 per million) while white boys’ rate declined (1.96 to 1.31 per million). Changes among girls were smaller and not statistically significant, though the rate for black girls rose from 0.68 to 1.23 per million while white girls’ rates remained stable.

Method-specific trends showed a significant decline in firearm suicides overall (IRR = 0.69; 95% CI, 0.57–0.85) and among white boys (IRR = 0.72; 95% CI, 0.59–0.88). Suicide by hanging/suffocation increased significantly among black boys (IRR = 1.35; 95% CI, 1.14–1.61), but overall rates by hanging/suffocation or other methods did not change significantly across the study.

The authors emphasize that the overall stable rate masks an important emerging racial disparity—rising suicide incidence among young black children—which merits further surveillance and research to identify risk, protective, and precipitating factors (e.g., exposure to violence, traumatic stress, disciplinary practices, early puberty) and to guide culturally informed prevention strategies.

Antarctic notothenioid fishes produce antifreeze proteins (AFPs) that bind to internal ice crystals and prevent their growth, a key adaptation allowing survival in subzero Southern Ocean waters. However, these same proteins also inhibit melting, producing a paradox: AFPs protect against freezing but stabilize ice once it exists, potentially causing lifelong accumulation of internal ice. Researchers measured melting behavior of AFP-stabilized ice both in vitro and in vivo and analyzed a decadal seawater temperature record from McMurdo Sound. They directly observed superheated ice—ice that persists above the expected equilibrium freezing/melting point—in serum samples and in purified AFP solutions. Live fishes retained internal ice at temperatures more than 1 °C above the normal melting point for at least 24 hours, and at lower temperatures for days; field experiments confirmed superheated ice occurs naturally in wild fishes. While most summers in the 1999–2012 record exceeded the fishes’ equilibrium melting point, temperatures never reached the higher thresholds needed to reliably melt AFP-stabilized ice. Thus, seasonal warming is unlikely to clear internal ice routinely. The findings reveal an antagonistic pleiotropic effect of AFPs: they confer essential freezing avoidance but also cause melting inhibition that may lead to persistent, potentially harmful internal ice accumulation, with unknown long-term physiological consequences.

The U.S. economy posted a distorted but still resilient jobs picture in September as Hurricanes Harvey and Irma temporarily depressed payrolls. The Labor Department reported a loss of 33,000 jobs—the first monthly decline in nearly seven years—largely driven by a 105,000 drop in restaurants and bars in Florida’s tourism sector. About 1.5 million people were unable to work because of the storms, the highest such number in 20 years, and many hourly workers who missed paychecks were counted as not working in the payroll survey. At the same time, the unemployment rate fell to 4.2 percent from 4.4 percent, the lowest since February 2001, because the household survey (used to calculate the rate) counted many temporarily absent workers as employed. Labor force participation rose and the share of adults with jobs climbed to 60.4 percent—the best since January 2009—suggesting underlying labor-market strength outside the hardest-hit areas. Average hourly earnings jumped 0.5 percent month-over-month and 2.9 percent year-over-year, a gain that likely reflects the temporary absence of lower-paid workers in affected regions. Other indicators show momentum: service-sector and manufacturing surveys hit multi-year highs, and auto sales surged as storm victims replaced damaged vehicles. Economic damage estimates are large—Moody’s pegs Harvey losses at $76–$87 billion, Irma $58–$83 billion, and preliminary losses from Maria remain substantial. Overall, a short-term hurricane hit masked continued broader economic resilience.

French Riviera city of Nice reeled after a Bastille Day truck attack that killed 84 people and wounded hundreds. As night fell on the Promenade des Anglais, residents and visitors gathered for vigils—leaving candles, flowers and toys for child victims—while police cordoned off areas to protect mourners. Witnesses described chaos: Swedish couple Christina and Bengt Adlers recalled hiding in a restaurant kitchen for hours after seeing the white truck and hearing gunfire. The attacker, 31-year-old Mohamed Lahouaiej Bouhlel, was killed by police after driving a rented 19-ton refrigerated truck for more than a mile through crowds watching fireworks. Authorities described evidence of premeditation: security footage showed Bouhlel driving the Promenade days earlier, he emptied his bank account, and he reportedly sent a text at 10:27 p.m. saying “Bring more weapons” shortly before the attack. French investigators widened their probe after detaining additional suspects, including an Albanian couple alleged to have supplied weapons and a man believed to have received Bouhlel’s text; seven others had been held earlier, with Bouhlel’s ex-wife later released. The Islamic State claimed Bouhlel as a “soldier,” although officials continued to investigate whether the group directly orchestrated or merely inspired the attack. The toll included many unidentified victims and dozens critically wounded; overall 256 people were reported injured with 85 hospitalized. The assault intensified public anger over apparent security lapses but, within days, life partially resumed as beachgoers returned to the Promenade des Anglais.

U.S. President Donald Trump said he would consider intervening in the Justice Department’s extradition case against Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou if doing so served U.S. national security interests or could help secure a major trade agreement with China. Meng, arrested in Canada on Dec. 1 at U.S. request and accused of misleading banks about Iran-related transactions that risked breaching U.S. sanctions, was granted CAD 10.3 million (USD 7.5 million) bail by a Vancouver court shortly after Trump’s comments. The president told Reuters he would act “whatever’s good for this country,” including intervening if it would facilitate “certainly the largest trade deal ever made.” He said the White House had discussed the matter with the Justice Department and with Chinese officials, though he had not personally been contacted by China’s Xi Jinping. Meng’s detention has intensified diplomatic tensions: Canadian authorities arrested her on the U.S. request, and in apparent retaliation a former Canadian diplomat, Michael Kovrig, has been detained in China. Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said his government is taking the situation of the detained Canadian very seriously, maintaining direct contact with Chinese diplomats and providing consular support to the family. Analysts warned Trump’s remarks risk confirming Chinese suspicions that Meng’s arrest was politically motivated, potentially complicating legal processes and diplomatic efforts amid broader U.S.–China trade negotiations.

This document explains Pennsylvania’s inheritance tax: what it applies to, who pays, rates, exemptions, deadlines, and where to find more information. Inheritance tax is charged as a percentage of the value of a decedent’s estate transferred to beneficiaries, whether by will, intestacy, or operation of law, and the rate depends on the recipient’s relationship to the decedent.

Pennsylvania’s current rates are structured by class of heir:
- 0% on transfers to a surviving spouse, and to a parent from a child age 21 or younger.
- 4.5% on transfers to direct descendants and other lineal heirs.
- 12% on transfers to siblings.
- 15% on transfers to all other heirs, with the exception of charities, exempt institutions, and government entities that are tax-exempt.

Jointly owned property between spouses is exempt from the inheritance tax. Since July 1, 2012, certain farmland and other agricultural property can also be exempt when transferred to eligible recipients; specifics and eligibility requirements are described in Inheritance Tax Informational Notice 2012-01.

Payment timing and discounts: inheritance tax becomes due at the decedent’s death and is considered delinquent if unpaid nine months after death. A 5% discount is available if the tax is paid within three months after death.

For taxpayers and administrators seeking more detail or practical guidance, the document points readers to additional resources: a brochure titled “Pennsylvania Inheritance Tax and Safe Deposit Boxes” for frequently asked questions, and the Tax Compendium for detailed and historical information about Pennsylvania inheritance tax provisions and practices.

The devastation caused by Typhoon Haiyan in the central Philippines triggered an immense international relief effort amid chaotic conditions, severe infrastructure damage and widespread insecurity. The storm, one of the most powerful on record, struck with winds around 195 mph and tidal surges up to 20ft, leaving whole villages flattened across Leyte and Samar. The UN estimates more than 11 million people were affected; official Philippine fatalities exceeded 2,300 and were widely expected to rise, while some early local estimates feared as many as 10,000 dead.

The UK committed substantial support: more than £20m in aid, deployment of the aircraft carrier HMS Illustrious (with 900 crew, seven helicopters and water-purification capability) to relieve destroyer HMS Daring, a Royal Air Force C-17 transport, and a 12-person medical team requested by the Philippines. The Disasters Emergency Committee’s UK appeal raised £23m in 48 hours, with charities and agencies mobilizing planes, ships and personnel. Other nations contributed significantly: the US sent an aircraft carrier USS George Washington, destroyers, aircraft and thousands of military personnel and supplies; Japan pledged funds, troops and medical teams; aid also came from Australia, China, South Korea, the UAE, the European Commission, the Asian Development Bank and others.

On the ground, relief operations faced major logistical bottlenecks: roads, bridges and the damaged Tacloban airport impeded distribution, with much aid initially stuck in Manila or Cebu. Military and humanitarian flights began delivering food, water, medical supplies, heavy machinery and field hospitals, and the US presence boosted helicopter capacity to ferry supplies and move people. NGOs like Save the Children, Oxfam and the Red Cross reported initial deliveries but stressed the urgent need to get more aid into remote islands and worst-hit communities.

Security and public order were serious concerns. Tacloban experienced reports of looting, violence and clashes over supplies; a nighttime curfew and the deployment of troops and police aimed to restore order. Mass burials began as bodies were cleared from streets; authorities attempted identification procedures. Health risks escalated—lack of clean water, sanitation and damaged clinics raised fears of cholera, pneumonia, dengue and other disease outbreaks. Medical teams treated injuries, childbirths and chronic conditions under strained conditions, while evacuations continued for those in critical need.

Despite immense challenges, relief steadily increased, logistics hubs in Cebu and Ormoc were established, and international and local responders worked to provide emergency shelter, water, food and medical care. The scale of destruction, the complexity of distribution, and the urgent public-health threats underscored the need for sustained long-term assistance to help survivors rebuild.

Donald Trump’s presidential campaign is planning a Republican National Convention in Cleveland (July 18–21) that will showcase not only politicians but a heavy roster of sports figures and entertainers. Ivanka Trump said the lineup will include “athletes to coaches” and industry leaders rather than a “ho-hum lineup of the typical politicians.” Campaign aides have reportedly tried to book several retired athletes, coaches and sports executives to appear, including Mike Tyson, Mike Ditka, Bobby Knight and NASCAR CEO Brian France. Attendance confirmations have been rocky: Tyson and France announced they would not attend, Ditka said he was willing but had not been asked, and roles for any sports figures — whether speaking onstage or simply appearing — remain unclear. Trump has touted athlete endorsements throughout his campaign, naming supporters such as Tom Brady and others he hopes to invite. In addition to sports personalities, third-party groups have arranged musical acts around the convention — Journey, Bret Michaels, Rick Springfield, Martina McBride, Rascal Flatts and The Band Perry — funded by private organizations, not the RNC. Organizers unveiled a large LED-stage design at Quicken Loans Arena as planning continues amid mixed confirmations.

After an EF-5 tornado devastated Joplin, Mo., killing at least 126 people, officials and volunteers struggled Thursday to reconcile a list of more than 230 people reported missing. Many listed were actually alive but unreachable because cell service was spotty or phones were lost; the AP found multiple cases of survivors — including 75-year-old Sally Adams, who laughed when told she was on the list while sitting outside her destroyed home — who had been reported by relatives via hotlines or Facebook. Authorities acknowledged some overlap between missing and confirmed dead, including nursing home residents, and the Red Cross said at least nine on the list were deceased. Identification of victims has been slow as forensic teams collect DNA, dental records and other identifiers to prevent misidentification.

NASA's Voyager 1 has entered a newly identified region near the solar system's edge called a "magnetic highway," where the Sun's magnetic field lines connect with interstellar ones, permitting lower-energy heliospheric particles to stream outward and higher-energy cosmic rays to flow inward. Instruments detected a fivefold rise in high-energy particles and a thousandfold drop in low-energy particles, signaling an environment more like interstellar space; yet Voyager's magnetometer still measures an East-West field orientation tied to the Sun, not the expected North-South interstellar field. Voyager first encountered this region July 28, 2012, with repeated crossings before settling there Aug. 25. Scientists view the highway as likely the last layer before the heliopause—the boundary marking the end of the heliosphere—but estimates for true entry into interstellar space range from months to a few years. Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is now the most distant human-made object (~122 AU) and continues sending data while mission teams monitor its final approach beyond the Sun's magnetic influence.

Conservative host Sean Hannity publicly attacked Fox colleague Megyn Kelly on Twitter after she criticized both presidential candidates for avoiding tough interviews. On The Kelly File, Kelly said Hillary Clinton limits her interviews to comfortable settings and that Donald Trump largely confines himself to friendly outlets like Hannity’s show, limiting outreach. Hannity responded by tweeting that Kelly “clearly” supports Clinton and telling her she should be mad at Hillary, noting Trump had talked to her. When urged to stand by colleagues, Hannity replied, “Sure. When they stand by me.” The exchange ignited wide reaction across media and social platforms, with commentators from CNN, MSNBC and other outlets mocking the spat and debating its significance for Fox News amid the post-Roger Ailes era. Some noted the irony of in-house attacks as the network approached its 20th anniversary; others questioned whether Hannity’s behavior could breach employment rules or reflect deeper divisions about Fox’s future and its relationship with Trump. Reports later indicated the two appeared to have reconciled. The incident highlighted tensions among Fox personalities over partisan alliances and interview practices during the 2016 campaign.

A photo of an elderly man dining alone at an In-N-Out Burger with a portrait of his late wife beside him went viral after several people who witnessed the scene shared it online, prompting a flood of reactions praising the couple’s lifelong devotion. Twitter user Madina Bashizadah posted an image of the man sitting in a restaurant booth with a laminated photo propped up next to his meal; she said she immediately began to cry when she noticed the picture and learned from others that the woman had passed away. Other patrons approached the man, and he gladly spoke about his sweetheart, recounting a sweeping love story that captured listeners’ hearts.

Accounts from multiple witnesses, including an imgur user named “soulrose,” describe how the couple first met at 17, were separated when he went to war and her family moved, and then spent a decade searching for one another. The serendipitous reunion reportedly occurred when the man described his search to a barber; the barber called out his daughter, who turned out to be the woman he had been seeking. They married soon after and stayed together for 55 years until her death in 2009. The man keeps a laminated photo of them—one side showing them older together, the other a youthful portrait—whenever he goes out, even to eat.

Witnesses relayed his gentle reflections: he considered himself wealthy in love rather than money, and urged others to tell their spouses “I love you” often. The poignant images and story struck a chord online as an emblem of enduring love and devotion.

A Las Vegas justice of the peace denied Floyd Mayweather Jr.’s emergency request to be released from jail or moved to house arrest, rejecting his claims that poor-quality food and water in custody threatened his health and career. Justice Melissa Saragosa ruled that water is available around the clock and that Mayweather’s alleged malnourishment is self-imposed because he refuses the meals provided. The judge also found his complaints about being unable to train unfounded, noting that the detention center offers adequate space and time for physical activity even if it does not match his prior regimen.

Mayweather, 35, began serving a three-month sentence after pleading guilty last year to reduced domestic battery charges related to an assault witnessed by two of his children. His lawyers argued he was losing muscle tone and consuming far fewer calories than usual; his personal physician claimed Mayweather was eating under 800 calories daily instead of his normal 3,000–4,000 and disliked tap water. Prosecutors and the judge dismissed those concerns, with a prosecutor bluntly noting, “It’s jail,” and Saragosa calling his condition self-induced. The judge ordered him to complete the remainder of his sentence behind bars.

Danish police announced that divers recovered the head and legs of Swedish journalist Kim Wall from Køge Bay; earlier her headless torso had washed ashore in August and was identified by dental records. Wall disappeared after boarding a homemade submarine on August 10 with its inventor, Dane Peter Madsen, who was rescued when the vessel sank. Madsen is charged with her killing; he denies wrongdoing, claiming she died accidentally after being struck by a heavy hatch and that he later panicked and disposed of her body at sea. Police say remains and clothing were found in separate bags weighted with metal, along with a knife. An autopsy on Wall’s head found no skull fractures; investigators are focusing on her neck and throat to determine cause of death. Authorities also reported finding images on a laboratory computer they believe show women being strangled and decapitated; Madsen says the computer was shared and not solely his. Divers continued searching for additional body parts. Investigators matched blood from the submarine to Wall’s torso and allege her body was cut into pieces and weighted to sink. Madsen remains in custody pending further investigation and court hearings; if convicted of murder he faces five years to life. Wall was a freelance journalist with bylines in major international outlets.

Sean Spicer used a surprise Emmys comedy bit on Sunday to lampoon his contentious six-month run as White House press secretary, but he also conveyed a measure of contrition. In a Monday interview he told The New York Times he regretted one of his most notorious moments: charging into the briefing room after President Trump’s inauguration to dispute accurate news reports that President Obama’s inauguration drew a larger crowd. “Of course I do, absolutely,” Spicer said, acknowledging the incident that became emblematic of his combative relationship with the press.

Spicer resigned this summer after repeated clashes with journalists and a public falling-out over Anthony Scaramucci’s brief appointment as communications director. Since leaving the White House he has embraced a celebrity trajectory, seeking to parlay his visibility into paid speaking gigs and television opportunities. His Emmys appearance — mocking his own inaugural briefing line by quipping that this would be “the largest audience to witness the Emmys, period” — was widely interpreted as an attempt to rehabilitate his image with entertainment and media elites.

Reactions were mixed and sometimes mocking; late-night host James Corden joked about kissing Spicer at the after-party and used the moment for comic fodder, denying and then joking about the photo. Spicer’s tenure remains controversial for misleading statements and an adversarial approach to the press, but his recent entertainer-friendly turn signals a bid to reshape his public persona and leverage newfound fame in the private sector.

Arnold Schwarzenegger plans a return to films now that his California governorship ended. He tweeted that his agency, CAA, can again take offers seriously. Best known for the Terminator series, he did occasional cameos during his tenure, like in The Expendables. Schwarzenegger has read several scripts, including one about a compassionate Nazi soldier, and says he’ll adapt roles to his age, seeking more dramatic challenges while acknowledging limits on action.

Senator John Thune announced he will not run for president, saying he and his wife considered the idea after encouragement from many supporters but decided he can better serve the country in the Senate. Thune cited three reasons: his role in the Senate (including a new Finance Committee seat and potential leadership opportunities with Jon Kyl’s retirement), concerns about the strain a campaign would place on his family, and poor timing. He emphasized fighting for America’s future “in the trenches” in Washington.

Pressure is mounting on the Metropolitan Police to widen its phone-hacking probe after MP Tom Watson alleged that private investigator Jonathan Rees targeted politicians, royals and sensitive intelligence figures for Fleet Street clients, notably News International. The Guardian and others report Rees—formerly of Southern Investigations and linked to the Mirror Group and News of the World—may have accessed bank details and other private data belonging to Tony Blair, Jack Straw, Peter Mandelson, Alastair Campbell, members of the royal family (including Kate Middleton in 2005), senior police figures such as Sir John Stevens and John Yates, and Bank of England officials. Rees is also accused of commissioning computer hacking that exposed MI6 informers. Scotland Yard is believed to hold “boxloads” of paperwork from long-running inquiries into Rees’s corrupt police links and alleged illegal news-gathering, but says many allegations fall outside Operation Weeting’s remit and are under consideration. News International denies Watson’s specific claims.

Carlo M. Cerutti, 50, was arrested at his duplex near NorthTown Mall after a neighborhood confrontation escalated into a violent attack involving a sword, according to court documents. The incident began when Cerutti’s wife argued with a neighboring man, accusing him of putting trash in her garbage can. Following the dispute, Cerutti allegedly rushed out of his home wielding “a large sword-type weapon with multiple blades” and attempted to swing it like a hatchet. The victim raised his hands to block the blade and managed to wrest the weapon away from Cerutti. A second neighbor witnessed the altercation and called police, leading to Cerutti’s arrest on Saturday. The account, provided in official documents, frames the episode as an assault prompted by a dispute over garbage cans. No further details about injuries, charges filed, or subsequent legal proceedings were provided in the available summary. The case reflects a dramatic escalation from a routine neighbor disagreement to dangerous, weapon-involved conduct.

An Airbus A320 operated by Germanwings crashed in the French Alps on March 24, 2015, killing all 150 people aboard, including 144 passengers and six crew. The jet, flying from Barcelona to Düsseldorf, plunged in an unexplained eight-minute descent less than an hour before landing. Investigators recovered a black box and pulverized debris scattered across steep, remote slopes; the impact was described as extremely violent with the largest wreckage pieces the size of small cars. Authorities found no distress call or radio contact after the descent began, deepening the mystery about the cause. French, German and Spanish leaders pledged thorough investigations; officials said there was no sign of terrorism at the time. Among the victims were two opera singers, two babies, and 16 German tenth-grade students and two teachers from Josef-Koenig-Gymnasium in Haltern am See, returning from a Spanish exchange program. The small town of Haltern and the Spanish village of Llinars del Vallès were plunged into grief, with candles, memorials and church vigils. Rescue teams faced difficult access, harsh terrain and worsening weather. Germanwings and parent Lufthansa called it an unprecedented tragedy; mourning and inquiries continued as officials awaited detailed analysis from the flight recorders.
