Google’s year-end search recap for 2014 highlights what captured global attention most. Topping the list was the public reaction to Robin Williams’ suicide, which drove spikes in searches for his films, “carpe diem” and depression. Other major trending topics worldwide included the World Cup, the Ebola outbreak, the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, the Ice Bucket Challenge, the mobile game Flappy Bird, bearded drag performer Conchita Wurst, ISIS, Disney’s “Frozen,” and the Sochi Winter Olympics. The US list mirrored the global trends but emphasized Ferguson/Michael Brown and the Ukraine-Russia conflict instead of Wurst and Sochi. Notably, 2014 marked a rare year without an Apple product in Google’s top trending searches, and Flappy Bird became one of the first mobile apps to reach the top 10 for rising interest. Google’s rankings reflect year-over-year increases in search interest rather than raw volume, offering insight into what topics surged in public curiosity over the past year.

PayPal has terminated its payment agreement with Infowars after an internal review found the site “promoted hate and discriminatory intolerance against certain communities and religions,” citing violations of its acceptable use policy. Infowars was given ten days to find alternate payment processors. The decision follows prior deplatforming of Infowars and Alex Jones by Facebook, YouTube, Twitter and app stores amid longstanding controversies including harassment of Sandy Hook victims’ families and conspiracy claims. Infowars and allies portray the PayPal ban as politically motivated election meddling and financial censorship coordinated by rival media, advocacy groups and sympathetic lawmakers, warning it sets a dangerous precedent for conservatives’ access to commerce. PayPal and critics like Right Wing Watch disagree: PayPal framed the move as enforcing its values and policies. Infowars says it is exploring legal options.

A French court fined Air France 10,000 euros and ordered the airline to pay 3,000 euros in damages to Horia Ankour, a 30-year-old nursing student, after she was removed from an April 2012 flight to Tel Aviv because she was not Jewish. Ankour had been traveling to join the “Welcome to Palestine” campaign, during which hundreds of activists tried to enter Israel and authorities pressured airlines to cancel roughly 300 flights. While prosecutors called the removal discriminatory, Air France said Ankour’s name appeared on a list of undesirables provided by Israeli authorities and that she would not have been allowed into Israel. The court ruling sided with Ankour, deeming the action unlawful and discriminatory.

Swiss mountaineer Erhard Loretan, 52, died in a climbing accident on his birthday while leading a client on the Gruenhorn in the Bernese Alps. The pair fell about 200 meters from roughly 3,800 meters; Loretan was killed and his 38-year-old client was seriously injured and hospitalized. Loretan, from Fribourg, was the third person to summit all 14 peaks above 8,000 meters, noted for a 1986 Everest ascent without supplemental oxygen in 40 hours. His career had been marred by a 2001 tragedy when he fatally shook his seven-month-old son; he pleaded guilty to negligent manslaughter and received a four-month suspended sentence.

Web series have long been a haven for creators seeking freedom from traditional media — think Joss Whedon, Felicia Day, Issa Rae — and now major stars are embracing the format too. Jerry Seinfeld’s new Crackle series, Comedians in Cars Getting Coffee, debuted with a casually polished 13–15 minute episode in which Seinfeld picks up Larry David in a 1952 VW Beetle, they drive, eat breakfast, and riff on life and comedy. The premise is simple: vintage cars, coffee stops, and relaxed conversation. The episode revels in small-talk minutiae — cigars versus cigarettes, underwear preferences, dietary fastidiousness — and occasionally touches on deeper notes, like how lifestyle choices affected David’s marriage. David even pronounces Seinfeld has “finally made a show about nothing,” a winking nod to their shared legacy.

Though it’s presented as spontaneous, the production is highly crafted: crisp visuals, rapid editing, varied camera angles, and sumptuous close-ups that give the easy chat a glossy sheen. That tension between intimacy and polish can distance viewers, making the episode feel like a well-produced promotional vignette of two comedy legends enjoying themselves. Yet their rapport — likened to “the Lennon–McCartney of comedy” — remains compelling, and the format showcases the pair’s ability to mine humor from the trivial.

Seinfeld’s move online reflects a broader trend: established stars are using the web to experiment without network constraints, reach fragmented audiences, and exploit new viewing habits on digital devices. Alongside projects like Tom Hanks’s Electric City, Comedians in Cars underscores how the internet is no longer just an incubator for newcomers but a creative playground for veterans who want low-stakes, flexible formats — and a place perfectly suited for wasting time, as the show cheerfully admits.

President Trump reacted to reports that an FBI informant contacted members of his 2016 campaign, calling any such action a “really big deal” and suggesting it could amount to political infiltration. The New York Times reported an unnamed informant—described as an American academic teaching in Britain—had reached out to advisers George Papadopoulos and Carter Page, who had been flagged for suspicious contacts with Russia-linked individuals. Conservative outlets and social media had circulated the informant’s identity. Trump previously tweeted that an FBI representative had been “implanted” in his campaign “for political purposes,” calling it potentially the “all time biggest political scandal,” and later framed the matter as an “infiltration.” He contended the truth would emerge only if Congress obtains documents House Republicans and the Senate Judiciary Committee have sought but that the Justice Department has resisted releasing. The reporting ties back to Papadopoulos’s April 2016 conversation with an Australian diplomat, who relayed that Russians claimed to have dirt on Hillary Clinton—a exchange that reportedly helped trigger the FBI’s investigation and ultimately Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s probe into possible coordination between Trump campaign officials and Russian election interference. Congressional Republicans, including Rep. Jim Jordan, have demanded access to sensitive and classified materials about the investigation and the informant’s identity, arguing that disclosure is necessary to determine whether the FBI’s actions were politically motivated. DOJ refusals have intensified GOP frustration and stoked calls for transparency.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg sparked a major controversy in July 2016 by making unusually candid, politically charged comments criticizing then-presidential candidate Donald Trump. In a set of interviews originally connected to research for a book on Chief Justice John Roberts, Ginsburg reiterated and expanded on remarks she had given to the New York Times, calling Trump “a faker,” accusing him of inconsistency, excess ego and refusing to release his tax returns, and saying she could not imagine what the country would be like with Trump as president. Those comments, delivered from her chambers, were striking because sitting justices traditionally avoid public statements about active political campaigns to preserve the appearance of judicial impartiality.

Ginsburg’s remarks immediately provoked backlash across the political spectrum. Republican nominee Trump demanded her resignation and later tweeted that her mind was “shot.” Prominent conservatives, including House Speaker Paul Ryan, labeled the comments inappropriate and biased, warning they undermined public confidence in the Court’s impartiality given that justices must later adjudicate matters that may hinge on presidential actions or campaigns. Commentators and ethicists widely noted that her statements violated longstanding norms — and, by some readings, aspects of judicial ethics guidance that counsel judges to refrain from political activity or endorsements.

Observers also highlighted the practical ramifications: a publicly stated antipathy toward a candidate creates grounds for recusal requests from that candidate’s side in any litigation touching on campaign or presidential matters, potentially complicating the Court’s composition in politically sensitive cases. Critics warned that Ginsburg’s off-the-bench commentary set a dangerous precedent that could encourage similar behavior from other justices and further politicize the judiciary.

At the same time, defenders and some commentators framed Ginsburg’s actions as a deliberate, conscience-driven departure from customary restraint. They argued she weighed the risks of breaching judicial decorum against what she viewed as an extraordinary threat posed by Trump’s candidacy and felt compelled to warn the public. Given her age and established legacy, some suggested Ginsburg judged she had less to lose by speaking out and hoped to mobilize opposition to a candidate she deemed perilous to democratic norms.

The episode rekindled broader debates about the Code of Conduct for United States Judges — which, while formally applicable to lower federal judges, informs expectations of behavior for all jurists. The Code emphasizes canons requiring judges to uphold the judiciary’s integrity, avoid impropriety or its appearance, refrain from political activity, and disqualify themselves where impartiality might reasonably be questioned. Commentators pointed to these canons in arguing Ginsburg’s comments compromised public confidence in the Court even if they reflected genuine personal views.

Beyond the immediate controversy, the affair underscored perennial tensions: the balance between judicial candor and institutional neutrality, the limits of off-the-bench expression by high-court justices, and how singular moments of frankness can reshape perceptions of judicial legitimacy and fuel partisan battles over the courts.

Ali Elmezayen, 44, an Egyptian national living in Hawthorne, California, has been charged in federal court with fraud and identity theft after prosecutors say he deliberately drove his car off a Port of Los Angeles pier on April 9, 2015, killing his two severely autistic sons and attempting to profit from accidental-death insurance policies. Authorities allege Elmezayen spent roughly a quarter of his modest reported income to buy more than $6 million in coverage for himself, his longtime partner Rabab Diab, and three sons in 2012–2013, and repeatedly called insurers to confirm that claims filed more than two years after policy inception would not automatically trigger investigations. The plunge occurred two years and 12 days after the final policy took effect. Witnesses reported the vehicle accelerating and flying off the wharf; Elmezayen escaped through an open driver’s window and swam to safety, Diab—who cannot swim—was rescued by a fisherman, and the two boys, ages 8 and 13, were found dead in child seats. Federal agents say Elmezayen collected over $260,000 from insurers and wired more than $170,000 to Egypt; prosecutors obtained seizure of about $80,000 from a bank account. He faces charges including mail and wire fraud and aggravated identity theft for allegedly posing as Diab in communications with insurers and making false statements that the deaths were accidental. The Los Angeles County district attorney had earlier declined to file charges, citing insufficient evidence; a police mechanic found brake issues but could not determine whether corrosion after submersion caused them. At a detention hearing judges cited credibility concerns and denied bail, noting the alleged “ghastly scheme” and flight risk. If convicted, Elmezayen faces up to 20 years on fraud counts plus a mandatory consecutive two years for identity theft.

Researchers have described a new genus and species of shrew rat, Hyorhinomys stuempkei (hog-nosed shrew rat), from Mt. Dako on the northern peninsula of Sulawesi, Indonesia at about 1,600 m elevation. Known only from the type locality and five trapped specimens, the species combines a suite of unusual morphological traits not seen together in other Indonesian murines: a large, flat, pink hog-like nose with forward-facing nostrils; very large ears (~21% of head and body length); extremely long procumbent lower incisors; very long urogenital hairs; prominent, medially bowing hamular processes on the pterygoids; and unusually long articular surfaces on the mandibular condyles. It also lacks the coronoid process on the dentary, indicating reduced jaw musculature consistent with a diet that does not require heavy chewing; stomach contents and observations indicate consumption of earthworms and beetle larvae. Morphologically and genetically the new taxon groups with Sulawesi’s endemic “shrew rats” — long-faced, carnivorous murines — and Bayesian and likelihood analyses of five unlinked genetic loci place Hyorhinomys as sister to a clade of Melasmothrix, Paucidentomys, and Echiothrix, with the Sulawesi water rat Waiomys mamasae as the next relative. This discovery raises the known Sulawesi shrew rat diversity to six genera and eight species and highlights remarkable morphological disparity among a small clade. The find, made by international teams from LSU, Museum Victoria, and Indonesian institutions during remote high-elevation surveys, underscores Sulawesi’s complex biogeography and the likelihood of further undiscovered endemic mammals in understudied montane habitats.

A highly publicized custody dispute ended with Los Angeles County social workers removing 6-year-old Lexi from the Santa Clarita home where she had lived with foster parents Rusty and Summer Page for four years. The Pages, who have three biological children and had hoped to adopt Lexi, fought for custody after she was placed with them at 17 months following her birth parents’ struggles with substance abuse and the father’s criminal history. Lexi’s placement became governed by the Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) because court findings determined she is 1/64th Choctaw through her father, even though he had no reservation ties and the family in Utah who were awarded custody are not Native American but related by marriage to Lexi’s father.

A recent court order required Lexi’s transfer to the Utah relatives so she could be kept with siblings who already live there; one sister will live with the Utah couple and another lives nearby. The removal, captured on social media and covered by news outlets, showed a tearful child clutching a teddy bear as she was carried from the Pages’ home amid protests and an online petition that gathered tens of thousands of signatures. The Pages and supporters argued the child would be harmed by being uprooted from the only family she had known; the court found they did not prove likely emotional harm and ordered compliance with ICWA.

LA DCFS and advocates for ICWA emphasized that the law’s intent is to keep American Indian children connected to extended family and tribal communities and that agency staff are bound to follow court orders. National and tribal organizations defended the decision as consistent with ICWA’s goal of prioritizing extended family placement and tribal interests. The Pages have appealed to the California Supreme Court and requested Lexi be returned pending appeal. The case highlights ongoing controversies over ICWA’s application and debates about children’s best interests versus tribal and statutory protections.

A transcript released Friday shows Camille Cosby’s February deposition in a federal defamation suit brought by seven women accusing Bill Cosby of sexual assault was contentious and largely nonresponsive. Over multiple hours, Camille frequently invoked marital privilege, declined to answer questions about conversations with her husband, and at times refused to continue, saying “I’m done.” Attorneys for the plaintiffs read portions of Bill Cosby’s 2005 deposition in which he admitted obtaining Quaaludes to give to women he wanted to have sex with, but Camille said she had no understanding of those statements and denied ever obtaining Quaaludes for herself or others. She also declined to state opinions on whether her husband acted with deceit or lacked integrity, with her counsel instructing her not to answer questions about private communications. The deposition was one of several legal developments around Cosby: his criminal trial in Pennsylvania for an alleged 2004 assault remains pending, and separate civil suits continue. In Los Angeles, Gloria Allred said Hugh Hefner gave sworn testimony in a sexual-battery case brought by Judy Huth alleging an encounter at the Playboy Mansion in the 1970s; the contents remain sealed. Additional accusers have filed suits alleging incidents at the Playboy Mansion, and nearly 50–60 women have publicly accused Cosby of misconduct over decades, allegations he denies.

A Madrid provincial court found 85-year-old gynecologist Eduardo Vela responsible for abducting Inés Madrigal as a newborn in 1969, falsifying her birth records and handing her to an unrelated woman who was certified as her mother. Judges said the trial “indisputably proved” Vela committed unlawful detention, document forgery and certification of a nonexistent birth at the San Ramón clinic, long accused as a hub of Spain’s “stolen babies” network. However, the court acquitted him on criminal punishment because the statute of limitations had expired: Madrigal turned 18 in 1987, and the 10-year limitation for unlawful detention meant her 2012 complaint arrived too late. DNA tests confirmed Madrigal’s account, though her biological parents were never located. Madrigal, now 49 and president of the Murcia branch of SOS Stolen Babies, called the verdict “bittersweet,” saying she would appeal to Spain’s Supreme Court and continue seeking justice and answers. Her lawyer argued the limitation should not apply because she only learned she had been stolen — not merely adopted — in 2010 when her adoptive mother revealed details; many courts, however, have dismissed other cases for similar timing reasons. The trial was the first to reach court over large-scale child trafficking during and after Franco’s regime, a practice that targeted single, poor or politically disfavored mothers and may have affected tens of thousands, with some children allegedly sent abroad.

McDonald’s is giving away 10,000 free bottles of its iconic Big Mac “special sauce” at participating U.S. locations to promote two new Big Mac variations: the smaller Mac Jr. (a Big Mac without the middle bun and second patty) and the larger Grand Mac (with one-third-pound patties). The bottles will be distributed Thursday, with specifics on locations and how to claim them announced shortly before. This U.S. giveaway is a first for the chain and celebrates the Big Mac, introduced in 1968 and famous for its “special sauce” line in the 1975 jingle. The product relaunch aims to boost sales after a recent U.S. dip and to re-engage Millennials, many of whom reportedly haven’t tried a Big Mac.

An eastern South Dakota egg farm, Dakota Layers in Flandreau, confirmed infection with highly pathogenic H5 avian influenza, marking the state’s largest single poultry outbreak to date. The operation, which houses about 1.3 million laying hens and supplies roughly 90,000 dozen eggs daily (about 70% shipped to California), reported unusually high mortality in one barn and alerted state veterinarians. South Dakota State University lab testing confirmed H5; officials were working to determine whether it is the H5N2 strain responsible for massive Midwest losses. If H5N2, the virus would be part of an outbreak that has already killed more than 33 million U.S. poultry, hitting neighboring Minnesota and Iowa particularly hard. State and USDA teams planned to euthanize the flock—likely using carbon dioxide—and were determining carcass disposal methods; prior responses have used burial and composting. Dakota Layers’ CEO said the farm had implemented extensive biosecurity measures that nonetheless failed to prevent infection.

Nationwide, the outbreak has drastically affected egg supplies and prices. Iowa, the top egg-producing state, lost about 23 million hens; overall, over 33.5 million birds have been affected, prompting forecasts of the first annual drop in U.S. egg production since 2008. The loss of liquid “breaker” eggs—used by bakeries, food processors and restaurants—has driven wholesale breaker-egg prices to record highs, disrupting industrial users and prompting businesses to stockpile or switch to shell eggs. The USDA authorized $330 million in assistance; governors in multiple Midwest states declared emergencies and mobilized resources. Industry leaders expect continued biosecurity vigilance, prolonged cleanup timelines, and price pressures that could persist as flocks are repopulated and affected facilities are sanitized.

Following the death of 25-year-old Freddie Gray from a severe spinal injury sustained while in Baltimore police custody, Prince responded with music and activism. Gray’s April 19 death, after being arrested for carrying a knife, sparked protests that turned violent and led to six police officers being charged with crimes ranging from second-degree murder to assault. In the wake of those events, Prince recorded a new, unreleased song titled “Baltimore,” explicitly addressing unrest in Baltimore and broader socio-political issues tied to repeated killings of young Black men. The song, described by his publicist as a tribute to Baltimore residents and a call for peace, includes lyrics mourning Michael Brown and Freddie Gray, urging an end to violence and gun prevalence, and pleading for love and action: “Enough is enough, it’s time for love… It’s time to hear the guitar play.”

Prince previewed the soul-rock track during a private session at Paisley Park with his band 3rdEyeGirl, performing a moving live rendition that featured an extended guitar solo. He plans a “Rally 4 Peace” concert at Royal Farms Arena in Baltimore on Mother’s Day, where he is expected to debut the song; attendees are asked to wear something gray as a symbolic gesture. The event aims to foster healing and reflection amid national concern over police violence. Prince has a history of weaving social commentary into his work and intends to use his platform to confront indifference and advocate for change.

Peter Jackson’s film adaptation of Alice Sebold’s The Lovely Bones is visually ambitious and uneven, marrying sentimental family drama, serial-killer suspense and fantastical afterlife imagery in a way that often unsettles the story’s balance. Saoirse Ronan is unequivocally the film’s heart—her radiant, natural performance as Susie Salmon, a 14-year-old murdered in 1973 who narrates from an “in-between” realm, consistently grounds the movie and delivers its most affecting moments. Jackson and his collaborators recreate a vividly imaginative afterlife—fields turning to oceans, oversized ships-in-bottles and surreal landscapes—powered by Weta Digital effects and Andrew Lesnie’s cinematography. Those sequences frequently work and capture the novel’s comforting meditation on absence.

However, the film leans heavily into the grotesque aspects of the murder and the killer, Stanley Tucci’s George Harvey, whose quietly chilling portrayal and detailed creepy lair receive prominent screen time. That emphasis, along with sometimes cartoonish tonal shifts—from gentle fantasy to grisly detail—undermines the emotional coherence and softening that made the novel widely appealing. Mark Wahlberg and Rachel Weisz give committed turns as Susie’s grieving parents, though the film’s erratic tone constrains their impact; Susan Sarandon’s Grandma veers overly broad. Ultimately, The Lovely Bones contains striking, often moving moments—largely thanks to Ronan and the dreamscape visuals—but never fully reconciles its competing impulses, producing a film that is compelling yet inconsistent.

Poland’s Senate approved a contentious bill criminalizing assertions that the Polish nation or state were responsible for Nazi crimes, punishable by fines or up to three years’ imprisonment; the measure awaits presidential signature. Supporters, including President Andrzej Duda and the ruling Law and Justice (PiS) party, argue it defends “historical truth” and combats misleading phrases like “Polish death camps,” which they say falsely imply state responsibility for Nazi-run extermination sites established after Germany’s 1939 invasion. The law exempts artistic and scientific activity, but critics fear it could muzzle research and discussion about individual Polish complicity in Nazi atrocities—an area where many historians cite clear evidence, including denunciations of Jews and local participation in massacres such as Jedwabne.

The bill provoked strong Israeli condemnation: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called it an attempt to rewrite history and deny the Holocaust, and Israeli MPs from across the political spectrum moved to strengthen Israel’s Holocaust-denial laws to criminalize minimizing collaborators’ roles, and to provide legal aid to survivors prosecuted abroad. Israel postponed a planned visit by a senior Polish official in protest. The U.S. State Department urged Poland to reconsider, warning of damage to free speech, scholarship, and strategic relationships.

Domestic Polish reactions are mixed: government officials defend the law as protecting national dignity, while some media, artists, politicians, and Jewish community members argue it overreaches and risks stifling honest historical inquiry, deepening international tensions rather than resolving them.

Bathrooms.com teamed up with U.K. chocolatiers Choccywoccydoodah to create an extravagant novelty bathroom suite made entirely of Belgian chocolate and promoted on Bathroomsweets.com, a playful site launched after CEO Ian Monk noticed many online searches mistakenly used “bathroom sweets” instead of “bathroom suites.” The Maderno Sweet collection comprises a chocolate bidet and basin (each about 210,000 calories and priced at £7,000 and £9,000 respectively), a colossal chocolate bath (roughly 8 million calories, £50,000), and a dark-chocolate toilet (about 980,000 calories, £14,000). The full set totals roughly 9.4 million calories and is listed for about $133,040, with individual pieces also available. Items are made to order, requiring a two- to three-month wait, and Bathroomsweets.com says the suite has a six-month edible shelf life but can be kept at room temperature for years if not eaten; a varnish layer can be added for longer preservation. The site cautions the chocolate fixtures are decorative only and will melt if exposed to direct sunlight, radiator heat, or hot liquids, so they aren’t functional bathrooms despite their sumptuous appearance.

Katie Couric’s show released three voicemails Manti Te’o says were left by his deceased girlfriend, Lennay Kekua, ahead of his interview. The messages include one before her first chemotherapy session, one accusing Te’o of infidelity, and one dated Sept. 11, 2012—the day she claimed to have been released from hospital before "dying" on Sept. 12. Reports say hoaxer Ronaiah Tuiasosopo later admitted posing as Kekua by disguising his voice. Couric reviewed Te’o’s phone records showing dozens of calls, some lasting hours, to a single number; ESPN noted over 1,000 calls across four months.

Boston’s New England Holocaust Memorial was vandalized again Monday evening when a 17-year-old allegedly threw a rock through one of the memorial’s glass panels etched with concentration camp identification numbers. Witnesses helped police identify and detain the Malden teen, who was tackled by bystanders and charged with willful destruction of property; because he is a juvenile his name was not released. Authorities are investigating whether the act qualifies as a hate crime. The incident occurred shortly before 7 p.m., coming less than two months after a 21-year-old with a history of mental illness shattered another panel and two days after the violent white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Va. Regional ADL director Robert Trestan and Jewish Community Relations Council executive director Jeremy Burton called the vandalism a painful blow to the community and urged caution until motives are known. Boston Mayor Martin J. Walsh and Police Commissioner William Evans condemned the act, and police briefly cordoned off the site while public works crews cleaned shattered glass. The memorial reopened around 9 p.m., with at least one officer posted overnight. Visitors and survivors’ descendants at the site described the attack as shocking and heartbreaking, emphasizing the memorial’s importance in standing against hatred.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has dismissed mutual genocide claims brought by Croatia and Serbia over atrocities during the 1991-1995 Croatian war of independence. Croatia had accused Serbia of committing genocide in places like Vukovar in 1991, where the town was devastated during a three-month occupation, tens of thousands of ethnic Croats were displaced and about 260 Croat men were detained and killed. Serbia counter-sued, alleging Croatia committed genocide by expelling more than 200,000 ethnic Serbs during the 1995 Operation Storm. Judge Peter Tomka ruled that while forces on both sides committed serious violent acts and deliberately forced minority populations from areas they controlled, neither side presented sufficient evidence of the specific intent required to constitute genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention. The court noted that ethnic cleansing, though grave, does not automatically equate to genocide unless there is intent to physically destroy a group. The decision ends a 16-year legal process that had heightened tensions but also offered a chance to reset relations; Serbian officials called for a new chapter with Croatia, while Croatian leaders said they accepted the ruling despite dissatisfaction. The ICJ’s verdict follows prior international tribunals’ findings that, although widespread crimes occurred in the Yugoslav wars, proving genocide remains legally demanding.

Dan Adler, a Democratic candidate in California’s crowded primary to replace Rep. Jane Harman, is attracting attention for a bizarre, potentially offensive ad campaign. Backed by former Disney CEO Michael Eisner, Adler’s spots aim for viral shock value: one shows him with a multi-ethnic crowd touting his appeal to Asian voters by noting he’s married to a Korean and, as a Jew, understands minority status, while an accented Korean immigrant awkwardly asks, “What’s a mensch?” Other ads include former child star Patty Duke saying “Dan Adler: He Gets Shit Done,” and one where Adler’s young son repeats the line before Adler performs a special-effects dunk. The stunts echo deliberate online-driven, weird ad tactics.

A mummified monk discovered in north-central Mongolia has drawn wide attention and mystified scientists, monks and the public. Found on January 27 wrapped in cattle skins and seated in the lotus position, the remains were apparently hidden in a house in Ulaanbaatar after being taken from elsewhere — authorities say a 45-year-old man, named only as Enhtor, stole the relic from a cave in the Kobdsk region and intended to sell it on the black market. Police arrested him and the body is now guarded at the National Centre of Forensic Expertise for forensic examination.

Early visual assessments date the relic to roughly 200 years old, though no peer-reviewed verification has been published. Mongolian Buddhist scholars and some international observers suggest the corpse may be connected to the famed Buryat lama Dashi-Dorzho Itigilov, whose own preserved body, exhumed in 2002, became a miraculous symbol for many followers. The identity of the newly found monk remains unconfirmed.

Religious experts, including Dr. Barry Kerzin — a physician to the Dalai Lama who has cared for meditators — interpret the state of the corpse as tukdam, a rare, advanced meditative state in which a practitioner’s consciousness reportedly remains after clinical death. Kerzin described tukdam as sometimes leading to a “rainbow body” phenomenon, where the body gradually shrinks and only hair, nails and clothes remain; prolonged tukdam is considered a step toward Buddhahood and associated with spiritual benefit for others. Mongolian professor Ganhugiyn Purevbata noted the posture and hand positions as consistent with deep meditative tradition rather than ordinary death.

Scientists are investigating how the remains are so well preserved; Mongolia’s cold conditions can naturally mummify organic material, and there is precedent for “accidental mummies” in frigid regions. For now the case blends religious belief, forensic inquiry and criminal intrigue as authorities seek to determine the monk’s identity, cause of preservation, and legal consequences for trafficking cultural heritage.

President Obama, vacationing on Oʻahu, briefly halted his golf outing after the son of family friend Dr. Eric Whitaker suffered a minor beach injury. White House deputy press secretary Bill Burton confirmed the first family was fine; the boy was examined, released, and returned to play. Obama left Luana Hills Country Club in a rapid motorcade to check on the child, then resumed golfing until sundown. The incident initially prompted concern—an ambulance and heightened Secret Service activity drew media attention—but officials said no stitches were required and the child was treated at the vacation compound rather than transported to The Queen’s Medical Center. Earlier that morning Obama held a short press appearance at Marine Corps Base Hawaiʻi, addressing the attempted Christmas Day airline bombing and condemning Iran’s suppression of protests. Marines on base appreciated their encounters with the president.

A South Florida scuba diver, Christopher Le Cun, is suing Florida Power & Light (FPL) after being sucked into an intake pipe at the St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant on July 12, 2015. Le Cun and a friend had tied their boat to a yellow buoy offshore and dove to investigate submerged structures beneath it. Le Cun says there were no visible warnings on the buoy; FPL counters that the buoy has read “stay back 100 feet” since the plant opened and that a protective cap covers the intake. Le Cun describes being suddenly pulled into a 16-foot-diameter, quarter-mile-long pipe that draws about 500,000 gallons per minute to cool the reactors. He spent roughly four to five terrifying minutes tumbling through darkness, fearing death and imagining turbine blades, while thinking of his family. Eventually he saw a faint light, was expelled into a cooling pond, and encountered an employee who helped him call his wife. FPL told reporters the diver “intentionally swam into one of the intake pipes after bypassing a piece of equipment” and would not comment on pending litigation. Le Cun’s suit alleges inadequate safety precautions and seeks changes to prevent future incidents. The story echoes a near-identical episode in 1989 when diver William Lamm survived being carried through 1,600 feet of pipeline into the plant’s cooling pond; Lamm also reported no effective protection despite a concrete cap and nearby buoy. Le Cun says the experience left him shaken and with nightmares; he’s uncertain whether he will scuba dive again.

A major sewer main break at Valley Forge National Historical Park on Tuesday forced road closures and prompted a multi-agency emergency response after raw sewage gushed into Valley Creek. The failure occurred around 10:30–11:00 a.m. in the Valley Creek Trunk Sewer Force Main near Routes 252 and 23 in Tredyffrin Township; the 30-inch pipe is jointly used by several nearby townships and boroughs. Initial estimates of the spill ranged from thousands of gallons per minute up to several million gallons total—reports cited figures between roughly 5,000 gallons per minute and as much as 3–5 million gallons entering the creek, which flows to the Schuylkill River. Crews worked overnight to remove the broken pipe and planned to install a replacement the following morning; extensive damage assessment, traffic control and resurfacing were expected to keep multiple park roads closed for days. Officials engaged contractors and consultants; authorities said the leak likely poses limited human risk but could threaten local wildlife.

Ricky Gervais and Mel Gibson shared an awkward moment at the Golden Globes when Gervais, hosting, jabbed at Gibson with dark humor. Gervais blamed NBC for the situation, quipped about Gibson’s alcoholism, and said he’d prefer a drink with Gibson over Bill Cosby. When Gibson returned to the stage, he teasingly told Gervais, “I love seeing Ricky every three years because it reminds me to get a colonoscopy,” prompting Gervais to reappear and put an arm around Gibson. Gervais then asked a censored question referencing Gibson’s infamous 2006 DUI arrest—when Gibson insulted a female officer with the phrase “sugar t—s”—eliciting uncomfortable laughter. Throughout the ceremony Gervais targeted other celebrities too, including Sean Penn, Caitlyn Jenner, and a jab at The Martian being considered a comedy. The summary recalls Gervais’s pattern of incendiary Golden Globes monologues: his 2010 debut skewered Hollywood vanity with crude sexual jokes and celebrity barbs; 2011 amplified the insults toward many A-listers; and by 2012 his act, though toned down, still produced controversial lines about Jodie Foster, Madonna, and a bleeped slur about Spanish-speaking actors. The encounter highlighted Hollywood’s uneasy mix of redemption, provocation, and spectacle.

ISIS released a propaganda video featuring two deaf-mute militants who deliver a sign-language message with Arabic and English subtitles. The clip opens with “We, the deaf and mute, direct our message to the Islamic world,” then urges Muslims in Europe to join ISIS and threatens to slaughter its enemies. One fighter identifies himself as a traffic policeman for ISIS in Mosul and says he and his brother alternate duties directing traffic. Titled “From Who Excused To Those Not Excused,” the video implies disability is no excuse to avoid jihad. It concludes with the pair wiring and launching two rockets reportedly aimed at nearby Peshmerga fighters.

This document describes two distinct items. First, an extensive web crawl conducted from 9 March to 23 December 2011 using a new distributed crawling system (HQ software by Kenji Nagahashi) with Heritrix (3.1.1-SNAPSHOT). The crawl began from Alexa’s top 1 million sites and captured 2,713,676,341 items across 2,273,840,159 unique URLs and 29,032,069 hosts. Robots.txt was respected and only a few sites were manually excluded. The crawl was experimental and had operational issues: some embedded or linked resources were not fetched because URL queues grew too large, and repeat crawls of some Argentinian government sites skew country results. The organizers invite requests for access via info@archive.org but may restrict sharing. Second, a separate report summarizes sequencing of the tammar wallaby genome (Macropus eugenii), the third marsupial sequenced after the Tasmanian devil and opossum. Led by Australian researchers and collaborators, the study identified genes linked to hopping and other marsupial traits, examined developmental gene regulation, and highlighted milk-borne antibiotics protecting pouch-young. The team sees the genome as a valuable resource for understanding mammalian evolution and potential human disease insights.

Tim Tebow canceled a scheduled April 28 speaking engagement at First Baptist Dallas, the megachurch led by controversial pastor Robert Jeffress. Tebow, then a New York Jets backup likely facing a trade or release, had been set to give two sermons at the church’s new $130 million facility. In a tweet announcing his withdrawal, Tebow cited “new information” brought to his attention and said he wanted to avoid controversy while continuing to use his platform to share “Faith, Hope and Love.” First Baptist Dallas issued a statement saying Tebow phoned Jeffress to explain he needed to avoid controversy for “personal and professional reasons” but hoped to speak there at a future date. The cancellation followed widespread criticism of Jeffress for inflammatory remarks about Islam, Mormonism and homosexuality — including calling some religions from “the pit of hell,” suggesting Muslims promote pedophilia, and claiming a high AIDS rate among gay people. Commentators said Tebow’s withdrawal was a cautious rebuke of intolerance, though some urged a stronger public denouncement. The church defended Jeffress as preaching “the whole counsel of God.”

Sir Elton John reflected on his 1973 album Goodbye Yellow Brick Road during a TODAY interview, saying listening to it again left him emotional and moved him to tears because it reminded him of a more innocent time. The record, which sold over 30 million copies, marked a creative peak but also preceded a period of drug and alcohol abuse for the then-26-year-old musician. Now sober for more than two decades, John expressed regret but no anger about his past, calling his substance choices curious missteps he wouldn’t repeat. Music remains his enduring passion and refuge through life’s highs and lows; he said he loves songwriting and still thrills at hearing extraordinary young artists like Lorde. The interview’s second part will address his upcoming marriage to long-time partner David Furnish. Furnish told a columnist they plan a quiet registry wedding in England in May with their two sons, Zachary and Elijah, and a few witnesses. The couple entered a civil partnership in 2005, which they say unexpectedly deepened their commitment. Both praised recent legal changes enabling same-sex marriage in England as a joyous step that reflects societal progress and personal fulfillment.

Republican presidential candidate Ben Carson has longstanding business and personal ties with Pittsburgh dentist Alfonso A. Costa, who pleaded guilty in 2007 to health care fraud after an FBI probe found Costa billed insurers for procedures not performed. Despite the potential 10-year federal sentence, Costa avoided prison after Carson—who described Costa as “one of my closest, if not my very closest friend”—testified at the 2008 sentencing hearing and petitioned a judge for leniency. Costa, whose license was revoked, received one year of house arrest, 100 hours of community service, and more than $294,000 in fines and restitution; his probation was later reduced. Carson and his wife invested in commercial real estate through Costa; financial disclosures show those investments have earned them between $200,000 and $2 million annually. Corporations tied to the Carsons purchased a Pittsburgh office building whose mailing address and deed contacts link to Costa’s real estate firm, and Costa continues to feature his association with Carson’s Carson Scholars Fund in promoting his business. Costa’s son has worked for Carson’s campaign and a related political committee.

The relationship contrasts with Carson’s public stance calling for harsh penalties for health care fraud. In his 2013 book America the Beautiful, Carson advocated severe punishments—loss of medical license, forfeiture of possessions, and at least ten years in prison—citing extreme deterrence. The report also includes critiques of Carson’s broader healthcare ideas (like universal Health Savings Accounts, standardized insurer rates, and limiting insurer profits), arguing many are poorly informed or impractical. Observers note the discrepancy between Carson’s punitive public rhetoric and his private efforts to secure leniency for a close associate convicted of fraud.

Las Vegas police arrested 19-year-old Erich Nowsch in connection with a fatal road-rage shooting that left 44-year-old Tammy Meyers dead. Authorities say Nowsch was taken into custody after a brief standoff at his mother’s home a block from the Feb. 12 crime scene. Police believe he was the shooter but are still seeking at least one other suspect involved in the incident. Nowsch faces felony charges including murder, attempted murder and unlawful discharge of a firearm from a vehicle; a court hearing was scheduled for Monday morning.

According to investigators, the episode began earlier that evening after Meyers and her teenage daughter were involved in a road-rage confrontation near a junior high while the daughter was receiving a nighttime driving lesson. After the other vehicle sped by and the daughter honked, the other driver stopped and threatened the family, police said. Meyers drove home and, accompanied by her armed 22-year-old son, went looking for the suspect vehicle because she wanted to keep the situation away from her house. They briefly followed a car they believed was involved, then returned home. A short time later a silver or gray car pulled up and someone inside opened fire. Meyers was hit outside her home and died two days later; her son returned fire with a properly registered firearm.

Meyers’ husband, Robert, said the family knew Nowsch; the couple and Nowsch lived within walking distance and his wife had spent time mentoring and helping the young man at a nearby park. Robert defended his son’s actions and criticized media coverage he felt portrayed his family unfairly. Homicide Capt. Christopher Tomaino confirmed investigators were not aware until the arrest that the families knew each other and declined to specify how many weapons Nowsch had. Nowsch is being held at the Clark County Detention Center as the probe continues.

Outrage erupted after Cecil, a well-known 13-year-old lion from Hwange National Park in Zimbabwe, was killed in early July, prompting criminal charges, international condemnation and a social-media storm. Conservationists say American hunter Walter James Palmer, a dentist from Minnesota, paid about $50,000 for the hunt. Local authorities and the Zimbabwe Conservation Task Force allege that Palmer and professional hunter Theo Bronkhorst lured Cecil out of the park by tying a dead animal to a vehicle, then shot him with a bow and arrow; when that did not immediately kill the lion, they tracked him for roughly 40 hours and finished him with a gun. Cecil was reportedly beheaded and skinned, and attempts were made to remove his GPS tracking collar, which was part of an Oxford University research project. The head was later seized as evidence.

Bronkhorst and landowner Honest Trymore Ndlovu were arrested and appeared in court on poaching-related charges and for lacking the required permit or quota; both were granted bail and face up to 15 years in prison if convicted. Zimbabwean officials said they were seeking Palmer as well and indicated he could face charges. Palmer has left Zimbabwe; in public statements he expressed regret, said he believed his guides had secured proper permits, and claimed he was unaware the lion was a collared local favorite involved in research. He also said he would cooperate with inquiries. U.S. records show Palmer pleaded guilty in 2008 to making a false statement to wildlife authorities over a black bear hunt, receiving probation and a fine.

The killing triggered fierce international backlash. Social media and review sites inundated Palmer’s dental practice with angry messages; protesters left stuffed animals at his clinic, and petitions demanding justice gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures. Zimbabwean hunting and conservation figures criticized the act as reckless and damaging to conservation and tourism—arguing that an iconic lion like Cecil was more valuable alive. The incident intensified debate over trophy hunting practices, quotas and enforcement in Africa, spotlighting tensions between hunting revenues and wildlife protection.

A 37-year-old female caretaker was killed by a Bengal tiger at Terra Natura zoo in Benidorm at about 5pm. The victim, who had worked at the park for eight years, was found inside the tiger’s enclosure; authorities believe she entered the area while performing cleaning tasks and may have left a door open by oversight. Emergency services, including Red Cross medics, arrived to find her already dead. Zoo staff anaesthetised the tiger so the body could be recovered; sources say the tiger did not escape and the enclosure was away from public view, so visitors did not witness the attack. Terra Natura, an “immersion” park housing more than 1,500 animals of about 200 species, has launched an investigation. Staff expressed shock and distress. Police inquiries are ongoing. The incident echoes a previous fatal mauling at a UK zoo in 2013 involving a Sumatran tiger.

A deadly crash on a notorious southbound stretch of the Bronx River Parkway killed seven members of one family, including three children, after their SUV plunged off the road near the Bronx Zoo. Police say driver Maria Gonzalez was traveling about 68 mph in a 50 mph zone when her vehicle clipped the concrete median, damaged a tire, crossed lanes, struck a curb and vaulted over a 4-foot fence, landing six stories below. All seven occupants, three generations returning from a family gathering, died of blunt-force trauma; autopsies ruled the deaths accidental. The tragedy revived criticism of that roadway segment, which has seen similar fatal incidents over the years. Attorney Eric Buckvar, who previously sued over a 2006 crash at the same location, called the area the “Bermuda Triangle” and faulted authorities for not widening the road or improving safety despite past warnings. Bronx officials pledged to examine safety fixes as the community mourned and organized funerals and aid for the grieving relatives.

Around 6,400 tins of Heinz baked beans with sausages were stolen from a parked curtain-sided Scania lorry after thieves cut a large hole in its side. The theft occurred overnight in a lay-by on the A441 at Cookhill, near Redditch, Worcestershire, while the driver slept in the cab. Thieves removed one full pallet and part of another between about 8:45pm Monday and 5:30am Tuesday. West Mercia Police are appealing for information, particularly about anyone trying to sell large quantities of Heinz baked beans in suspicious circumstances.

Nine-year-old Kieran Sorkin, born with bilateral microtia and deafness, has had new ears reconstructed from his own rib cartilage at Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH). Microtia, an underdevelopment of the external ear, affects roughly one in 100,000 babies; about 100 children a year in the UK are born with one or both ears missing. Kieran, who previously received surgery to implant a hearing aid and now hears with assistance, underwent a six-hour bilateral operation led by consultant plastic and reconstructive surgeon Neil Bulstrode. Cartilage from six ribs was harvested, carved into ear frameworks using an outline of his mother’s ear as a “family template,” and grafted beneath the scalp. Suction was applied to shape the skin to the new contours. Performing both reconstructions at once helped ensure balance and the best cosmetic result. The procedure is primarily cosmetic and intended to boost Kieran’s confidence and social integration; he had struggled at his first school because he looked different but has since transferred to a school with a deaf unit. Parents describe the result as transformative for his self-esteem. Kieran will have a follow-up surgery in six months to refine ear projection; the cartilage reconstructions should be long-lasting. GOSH and the UCL Institute of Child Health are researching tissue-engineering alternatives—growing cartilage from a child’s own fat-derived stem cells—to create ears less invasively in future, but such methods remain experimental.

An 85-year-old American-built wooden schooner, the Nina, and her seven-person crew have been missing in the Tasman Sea since early June after sailing from New Zealand toward Australia. The classic 70-foot vessel left the Bay of Islands on May 29 for Newcastle and last communicated with shore on June 3–4 from about 370–400 nautical miles northwest of New Zealand. Meteorologist Bob McDavitt took a satellite-phone call from a crew member, Evi, who asked how to avoid deteriorating weather; he advised heading south and, later, to stay put and ride out a storm. A final text from Evi on June 4 read, “ANY UPDATE 4 NINA? … EVI.” Subsequent radio, satellite and emergency-beacon contacts failed, and friends alerted authorities on June 14.

Maritime New Zealand and its Rescue Coordination Centre have conducted communications checks and two aerial searches extending toward the Australian coast, finding no trace. The Nina carries a tracking device, satellite phone and emergency buoy, yet none have transmitted since early June. The skipper is U.S. national David Dyche; passengers include five other Americans and one 35-year-old Briton, ages 17–73. Rescuers cite severe storm conditions around the outage—winds up to 110 km/h and waves to 8 meters—and consider scenarios from communications loss or drifting to lifeboat abandonment or catastrophic sinking. Searchers say they have “grave concerns” and are evaluating next steps.

In early October, fierce Diablo winds fanned nearly simultaneous wildfires across Northern California’s North Coast, producing an unprecedented and deadly conflagration that devastated communities around Santa Rosa, Napa and Sonoma counties. The Tubbs Fire, named for its origin near Tubbs Lane north of Calistoga, exploded on the night of Oct. 8 and within roughly four hours ran about 12 miles into west Santa Rosa. Fueled by sustained 40–70+ mph gusts and abundant dry fuels, the blaze moved at roughly 3 mph—about an acre a minute—spewing embers far ahead of the flame front, igniting spot fires and overrunning neighborhoods while many residents were asleep. The fire crossed Highway 101, surged into commercial districts and densely packed neighborhoods such as Fountaingrove and Coffey Park, destroying thousands of structures, flipping cars and killing dozens; the regional death toll reached at least 40 across four counties. Firefighters and first responders described scenes of homes and familiar landmarks erased, people fleeing in the dark, and dramatic rescues—one Battalion Chief finding a half-naked couple huddled in a pool and ferrying them out through roaring heat.

Scientists and fire officials documented violent fire whirls or “fire tornados” during the Tubbs and other North Bay blazes: vortices formed when intense heat drew in air that, combined with strong winds and obstructions, spun into tornado-like columns capable of ripping trees out, peeling roofs, lifting vehicles and amplifying damage. Experts compared the event’s ferocity to historic wind-driven fires (e.g., the 2003 Cedar Fire, 1991 Oakland Hills) and noted that such phenomena require extreme winds, steep pressure gradients and dry fuel—conditions that were abundant that night. Similar fire vortices have been filmed worldwide recently, including deadly fires in Portugal; researchers say video of these events may help improve understanding and response but underscore how unpredictable and destructive wind-driven wildfires can be.

North and South Korea’s leaders met in Pyongyang for a three-day summit that produced a broad, largely conditional agreement on reducing military tensions and advancing denuclearization. South Korean President Moon Jae-in announced North Korean leader Kim Jong Un agreed to shut down key missile test facilities at Tongchang-ri — including an engine test site and a launch pad — permanently and in the presence of international experts, and to halt rocket and nuclear testing in the meantime. Kim also expressed willingness to close the Yongbyon nuclear complex if the United States undertakes unspecified reciprocal measures. The two Koreas committed to reconnecting rail lines east and west across the heavily militarized border, resume joint economic projects such as the Kaesong factory park and Mount Kumgang tours, expand family reunions, and bid to co-host the 2032 Olympics. Militarily, they agreed to withdraw guard posts from the demilitarized zone, set up a joint military committee, establish no-fly zones near the border, and suspend test firing there to reduce accidental clashes. Kim invited to visit Seoul “in the near future,” which would be historic if it occurs. Washington welcomed the pledges and invited North Korean officials to talks, but U.S. and outside experts voiced skepticism: commitments are conditional, lack detailed verification, and may not constitute irreversible denuclearization. The summit is seen as confidence-building but leaves major diplomatic and verification challenges ahead.

Bon Jovi’s scheduled debut concerts in mainland China—planned for Beijing, Shanghai and Macau later this month—were abruptly canceled a week before the first shows after promoter AEG Live Asia said permits had been pulled. Chinese authorities reportedly flagged past visuals linked to politically sensitive subjects: a 2009 music video referencing the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and a 2010/2011 performance backdrop that included an image of the Dalai Lama. China’s Ministry of Culture, which controls approvals for foreign performers, is widely believed to have intervened, though official reasons were not published. AEG promised full refunds and apologized for the inconvenience; Bon Jovi’s management did not comment.

The cancellation adds Bon Jovi to a growing list of Western artists whose China plans have been derailed over perceived political issues. Earlier this year Maroon 5 pulled Beijing and Shanghai dates amid speculation that a band member’s attendance at the Dalai Lama’s birthday prompted authorities’ disapproval. Taylor Swift drew scrutiny over merch referencing “1989,” potentially conjuring Tiananmen associations. Historically, acts like Björk, Bob Dylan and Oasis have faced bans or cancellations after gestures or statements seen as sympathetic to Tibet or critical of Chinese policy. Promoters warn that the spate of last-minute cancellations has heightened fear and financial risk among event organizers, while disappointed fans lament lost travel and tickets, with some urging fans to travel abroad for safer concert experiences.

The 2017 Academy Award nominations produced plenty of surprises and notable snubs despite strong showings for films like La La Land, Moonlight and Manchester by the Sea. Martin Scorsese’s religious epic Silence, which underperformed at the box office and was ignored at the Golden Globes, received only a cinematography nod — a surprise given Scorsese’s storied Oscar history. Amy Adams, buoyed by Arrival’s critical acclaim and industry buzz, missed a Best Actress nomination in a crowded category. Finding Dory, despite critical praise and over $1 billion worldwide, failed to land a Best Animated Feature slot. Denzel Washington’s acclaimed turn in Fences earned acting recognition for co-star Viola Davis but left Washington out of Best Director contention. Annette Bening’s restrained lead in 20th Century Women was overlooked amid tough competition from more flamboyant performances by the likes of Meryl Streep and Isabelle Huppert. Deadpool and other genre or crowd-pleasing films such as Sully and The Founder were also shut out of major categories, as were notable individual performances from Hugh Grant, Aaron Taylor-Johnson and Taraji P. Henson, the latter a surprising omission despite Hidden Figures’ Best Picture and supporting recognition. Conversely, some underdog successes included Viggo Mortensen’s Best Actor nod. The nominations also highlighted increased diversity, with seven actors of color recognized, renewing discussions about representation in Hollywood.

After Robin Williams’ death, his daughter Zelda Williams was driven off Twitter and Instagram by trolls who blamed her for his suicide and sent graphic, altered images. Zelda, 25, said she could not bear the messages and asked followers to petition Twitter to block the accounts responsible; Twitter removed several accounts and pledged to update policies. Del Harvey, Twitter’s VP of trust and safety, said the company will expand policies on self-harm and private information and improve support for family members of deceased users.

The incident highlights a broader, ongoing problem of persistent abuse on Twitter. Imani Gandy, senior legal analyst at RH Reality Check, described daily harassment she faces—rooted in race, gender, and even attacks on her medical condition—and chronicled futile attempts to stop one persistent harasser, including blocking thousands of accounts and reporting abuse. She noted troubling cases where Twitter deemed rape threats not in violation of its rules. Twitter offers reporting tools and a “Report Abuse” button introduced after high-profile abuse campaigns, but critics say these tools are inadequate against adversaries who simply create new accounts.

Advocates suggest improvements such as adopting features from third-party tools like Block Together, which automates blocking and shares blocklists. Media critic Soraya Chemaly argued that Twitter’s strong free-expression stance may limit protections for vulnerable users, and warned that when platforms fail to protect victims, the targeted users—like Zelda—are often the ones who leave.

An oil production platform owned by Mariner Energy exploded and caught fire Thursday off the Louisiana coast; all 13 crew members survived after donning insulated “Gumby” survival suits and were rescued from the water. The platform, Vermilion Oil Rig 380, sits in about 340 feet of water roughly 92 miles south of Vermilion Bay and was reportedly undergoing maintenance rather than producing at the time. Initial reports of a one-mile-long, 100-foot-wide oil sheen prompted Coast Guard monitoring, but later aerial and on-scene inspections found no visible spill. Mariner Energy shut down seven active production wells on the platform; the company and regulators are investigating the cause. The fire was extinguished by afternoon. Federal records show Mariner had multiple past incidents and fines in the Gulf. Officials emphasized the difference from April’s Deepwater Horizon disaster—this platform operated in shallow water with redundant shutoff valves, making spill response and containment easier if needed.

Seth Meyers and his wife Alexi Ashe welcomed their second child, son Axel Strahl, in a dramatic delivery on April 8 — born in the lobby of their apartment building before they could reach the hospital. Meyers, 44, recounted the story on Late Night the next day, thanking the NYPD, who arrived shortly after Axel and helped cut the cord, and neighbors who warmed the baby with towels from a dryer until emergency personnel took over. He choked up while praising his wife and revealed Axel’s middle name honors Ashe’s grandparents, who met in an Austrian hospital after liberation from a concentration camp. Meyers shared a photo of Alexi holding newborn Axel as he knelt beside them, and fans flooded social media with congratulations. The couple also have a 2-year-old son, Ashe Olson.

After President Trump’s June 12 summit with Kim Jong Un, he announced the U.S. would halt “very expensive” and “very provocative” annual joint military exercises with South Korea. The Pentagon formally suspended several large drills— including Ulchi Freedom Guardian and others slated for summer—characterizing the move as a good-faith measure tied to negotiations. The next major drills, notably spring’s Foal Eagle and Max Thunder, remain uncertain; planning for them is preliminary and no final decisions have been made. On Tuesday, Defense Secretary Jim Mattis said the U.S. has no plans at this time to suspend any more exercises, stressing the earlier suspensions were not open-ended and were intended to support diplomacy. He declined to say whether resuming exercises would be provocative and deferred denuclearization questions to Secretary of State Mike Pompeo. Washington’s diplomacy with Pyongyang appears stalled: Trump canceled Pompeo’s planned trip, citing insufficient progress, and North Korea has warned talks could falter. U.S. officials remain skeptical about Pyongyang’s willingness to relinquish nuclear arms, and Washington has signaled it may resume military pressure and sanctions if negotiations do not advance.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren fiercely challenged Wells Fargo CEO John Stumpf over the bank’s fake-account scandal, demanding his resignation, the return of his compensation, and criminal investigations by the DOJ and SEC. The case involves Wells Fargo paying $185 million in penalties after roughly 5,300 employees were fired for creating millions of unauthorized accounts to meet aggressive “cross-selling” targets. Warren repeatedly confronted Stumpf with evidence that he praised cross-selling in earnings calls from 2012–2014, arguing those efforts boosted Wells Fargo’s stock and enriched him personally by more than $200 million. She accused him of “gutless leadership” for not holding senior executives accountable and for blaming low-paid employees pressured by quotas. Stumpf defended cross-selling as “deepening relationships” and frequently told senators he lacked specific expertise—saying he wasn’t a lawyer, compensation expert, or credit consultant—while offering limited answers on clawbacks for former executive Carrie Tolstedt or relief for customers whose credit was harmed. Other senators, including Patrick Toomey, expressed skepticism that thousands of employees independently committed similar fraud without systemic pressure. The hearing highlighted public outrage over accountability at big banks and renewed calls for stronger consequences for executives when widespread customer harm occurs.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle disclosed further wedding details for May 19 at Windsor Castle. Both of Meghan’s divorced parents, Doria Ragland and Thomas Markle, will attend and meet senior royals during the week before the ceremony; Ragland will ride with Meghan to the castle and Thomas will walk her down the aisle. Harry will have his brother William as best man; Meghan will have no maid of honor. All bridesmaids and page boys will be children, possibly including Prince George and Princess Charlotte; newborn Prince Louis will not attend. Diana’s family will be represented—one sister, Jane Fellowes, will give a reading—and Harry is keen to involve his late mother’s relatives. The couple will spend the night before apart and will remain in the UK after the wedding, delaying their honeymoon. Photographer Alexi Lubomirski will shoot the official photos.

The Navy’s review of Aaron Alexis’s military record after the Washington Navy Yard killings found several missed warning signs and recommended that future security reviews include any available police reports, even those that didn’t lead to charges or convictions. Alexis, who killed 12 people before being shot dead by police, had an honorable discharge, a Secret-level clearance, and multiple prior incidents involving firearms and disorderly behavior. A 2004 Seattle arrest—known to the Office of Personnel Management via fingerprint checks when Alexis joined the Navy Reserve in 2007—was summarized to investigators as tire deflation during a dispute, but police records show he fired a .45-caliber pistol and was charged with malicious mischief; the charge was dismissed after the victim declined to press charges. That firearm detail was omitted from the personnel report the Navy received, and Alexis did not disclose the incident on his security questionnaire, saying the charge had been dismissed and would be removed. Additional incidents included arrests in Georgia (disorderly conduct, 2008) and Fort Worth (discharging a firearm in 2010), the latter prompting efforts to administratively separate him from the Navy until no charges were filed; he left three months later with an honorable discharge. Alexis had reported hearing voices and microwave attacks. The Navy concluded it could not know how clearance adjudication would have differed with full police documentation and forwarded recommendations to Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel to require inclusion of police documents in personnel investigations.

Over a holiday weekend in January 2016, a predominantly white armed militia occupied the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge in Oregon, demanding that federally managed land be transferred to local ranchers, loggers, and miners. Leaders Ammon and Ryan Bundy insisted they did not want to hurt anyone but refused to rule out violence if authorities attempted to remove them. Despite the group's explicit threat of force and the takeover of a federal building, much of the mainstream media framed the incident as a “peaceful protest,” prompting public outcry and comparisons to how coverage might differ if protesters were black or Muslim. Social media users highlighted perceived double standards, noting harsher language and alarmist narratives directed at Black Lives Matter demonstrations—often labeled violent or criminal—whereas the Oregon occupation initially received muted, descriptive coverage. Commentators traced these disparities to implicit racial bias: decades of research shows subconscious dehumanization and differential threat perception toward black people and Muslims, influencing policing, public reaction, and media framing. Studies cited include work showing officers more likely to dehumanize black individuals and quicker to shoot black suspects in simulations. Critics argue newsrooms must recognize and correct for implicit biases to ensure consistent, accurate coverage of armed protests and public safety risks regardless of protesters’ race or religion.

The Florida chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR-FL) filed a federal lawsuit against Florida Gun Supply in Inverness after owner Andy (Andrew) Hallinan declared the shop a “Muslim-free zone” in a July Facebook video. Hallinan said his action followed the July 16 Chattanooga shootings and expressed a “moral and legal responsibility” to refuse to arm or train anyone he believed might harm others. CAIR-FL argues the policy constitutes unlawful religious discrimination under federal public-accommodations law and asks the U.S. District Court in Fort Lauderdale for an injunction barring the shop from discriminating or segregating customers on the basis of religion. CAIR-FL leaders stressed that American Muslims have the same rights to purchase guns, take safety classes, and use ranges as other citizens and said they tried to resolve the matter amicably before suing.

Hallinan’s attorney, Robert Muise of the American Freedom Law Center, called the lawsuit frivolous and contended any refusals are based on public-safety concerns, not religion; he suggested possible sanctions against CAIR. Muise also pointed to past controversies involving CAIR’s inclusion on an unindicted co-conspirator list in the Holy Land Foundation case. CAIR responded that Hallinan rescinded a planned meeting with its executive after receiving pressure and wrongly lumped the group with terrorists. The dispute has drawn national attention and raised broader questions about religious discrimination, public safety, and constitutional rights.

Multiple recent studies raise concerns that widely used proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)—drugs like omeprazole, lansoprazole, esomeprazole and pantoprazole—may be linked to serious long-term harms, though causality remains unproven. A large JAMA Internal Medicine analysis compared PPI users and nonusers in two U.S. cohorts (the ARIC study and Geisinger health records). After adjustment, PPI use was associated with a modestly higher incidence of chronic kidney disease: 10-year absolute CKD risk estimates rose from 8.5% to 11.8% in one cohort and from 13.9% to 15.6% in the other. Authors emphasized observational design and potential confounding; they urged reducing unnecessary PPI prescriptions because many appear inappropriate and long-term use is common. A related JAMA Neurology study from Germany found that among 73,679 adults 75+ without dementia, regular PPI prescriptions were associated with a 44% higher risk of incident dementia (hazard ratio 1.44). Investigators noted limitations—lack of lifestyle and over‑the‑counter use data—and called for randomized trials to evaluate causality. Mechanistic and laboratory work offers possible biological links: a PLOS ONE study showed lansoprazole and other PPIs increased production of several amyloid-β species in cell models and raised soluble Aβ40 in mouse brains, suggesting PPIs can affect amyloid metabolism; other research ties PPIs to nutrient deficiencies, infections, and cardiovascular or kidney risks. Clinicians stress that PPIs benefit many patients with serious acid-related disease and should not be stopped precipitously, but experts recommend careful assessment of indications, limiting unnecessary long-term use, monitoring for side effects, and discussing risks versus benefits with patients.

Late reports from the Washington Post and New York Times in December 2016 alleged that U.S. intelligence concluded Russia actively intervened in the presidential election to help Donald Trump win. The CIA reportedly assessed that Russian cyber intrusions and information operations were intended not merely to disrupt but to favor Trump, an allegation amplified by claims that Russia hacked the Republican National Committee yet conspicuously did not publish GOP materials—raising concerns that Moscow might be holding leverage. Both Russia and WikiLeaks denied direct government-to-Wikileaks links, and reporting relied on anonymous intelligence sources, prompting calls for the administration to make evidence public.

The revelations ignited intense partisan fallout. President-elect Trump and his transition team dismissed the CIA’s credibility, comparing it to flawed WMD intelligence and calling reports "fake news," while Trump used Twitter to attack unrelated topics—patterned behavior when facing damaging stories. Critics highlighted that Trump had previously praised Vladimir Putin and seemed willing to accept hacked material during the campaign. The stories also implicated Republican Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, who reportedly discouraged a pre-election public warning from officials and threatened to frame such disclosures as partisan, a stance that drew sharp condemnation and questions about prioritizing party over national security. McConnell’s refusal to recuse himself from his wife Elaine Chao’s forthcoming Cabinet confirmation added to the conflict-of-interest concerns.

Responses varied across Washington. President Obama pushed to release a formal intelligence report before leaving office, concerned Trump might ignore the findings. Bipartisan congressional leaders, including Lindsey Graham and Chuck Schumer, called for investigations and potential retaliation; options discussed ranged from hearings and sanctions to broader measures in Syria and Ukraine. Analysts argued Congress could pressure Trump via public hearings, legislation, and a war of words to force tougher stances on Russia—or alternatively hope Russian actions reveal their true adversarial intent. Many commentators demanded transparent, evidence-based inquiries; even then, proving that Russian actions determinatively swung the election could remain elusive unless direct manipulation of vote counts is shown. The episode underscored deep fractures: between intelligence and politics, within the Republican Party, and over how to safeguard American democracy from foreign influence.

President Obama, concluding the Summit of the Americas in Cartagena, called for a thorough, rigorous investigation into a prostitution scandal that led to 11 U.S. Secret Service agents being sent home. He emphasized that agents must act with “dignity and probity” and that all U.S. personnel abroad should meet the highest standards; if allegations are true, he said he would be “angry.” The agents were placed on administrative leave and interviewed by the Secret Service’s Office of Professional Responsibility after being removed and replaced before Obama’s arrival. The Defense Department also opened an inquiry after five servicemen on the advance team were found to have violated curfew at the same hotel. Colombian police alerted the U.S. Embassy after a dispute over payment involving one agent. The scandal shifted media focus from the summit, drawing criticism in Colombia and raising concerns in Washington. House Oversight Chairman Darrell Issa suggested the number involved might be higher and warned such breaches could enable blackmail, urging better preventative systems. The alleged participants include both special agents and uniformed division members.

Donald Trump will receive his first classified intelligence briefing tomorrow at the FBI’s New York Field Office as the Republican presidential nominee. Career staff from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence will lead the session, which will cover major global threats and emerging concerns; the FBI will merely host because the site houses secure SCIF rooms. Trump plans to bring Chris Christie and retired Lt. Gen. Michael Flynn, fueling speculation about possible Cabinet roles. Nominees do not need security clearances to get these briefings, a long-standing practice affirmed by DNI James Clapper despite partisan objections. Briefings provide analysis, not the most sensitive sources or methods, and both nominees are expected to receive multiple sessions before Election Day.

Josephine Crook, 49, was arrested Friday night in Alhambra on suspicion of commercial burglary after allegedly stealing women’s undergarments from a Kohl’s on South Fremont Avenue. Police say she concealed the items in an empty purse and left without paying. Officers also reported she was found in possession of possible burglary tools, including wire cutters and scissors. Crook was taken into custody around 7:15 p.m., booked at the Alhambra Police Department, and held with bail set at $20,000, according to Los Angeles County inmate records. She was scheduled to make her first court appearance Wednesday at Alhambra Municipal Court. No further details were immediately available.

More than 1,000 metres of overhead cabling were stolen overnight on Friday from land off the A1133 at Newton-on-Trent in Lincolnshire, causing a village-wide blackout that lasted several hours. Police say the theft affected power supplies and prompted immediate disruption as local residents and services coped with the outage. This incident follows a similar theft in August at Normanby-Le-Wold, indicating a worrying pattern of cable thefts in the county. Authorities emphasise the extreme dangers posed by stealing live or decommissioned cabling, both to thieves and the public, and note the broader impacts such crimes have on communities, businesses and emergency responses. Investigators are appealing to anyone with information or who witnessed suspicious activity in the area to contact Lincolnshire Police on 0300 111 0300 to assist with enquiries and help prevent further incidents.

Bloomberg reported that a group of Russian hackers infiltrated Dow Jones servers seeking early access to market-moving information to trade on before publication.
