The FBI’s New York office confirmed it is investigating; the Secret Service and SEC are also involved. Dow Jones has disputed Bloomberg’s account, saying it has found no evidence of such an investigation and is probing whether the report is accurate. Insiders told reporters the intrusion — described as more serious than a recently disclosed lower-grade breach affecting contact information for about 3,500 customers — targeted stories being prepared for publication and other embargoed material valuable to traders. Authorities have spent months analyzing how stolen content could be monetized, consulting market experts. The case highlights a growing law-enforcement focus on cyber-enabled insider trading: hackers now steal unreleased company announcements and wire-service releases, then sell the intelligence to traders. Prior prosecutions involved Russian-speaking hackers accused of siphoning press releases and generating over $100 million in illicit trades. Dow Jones said earlier breaches were part of a broader campaign targeting multiple companies.

The document compiles tabloid-style reports and recollections about Katie Holmes and Tom Cruise amid their separation, interwoven with background on Cruise’s early life. After Holmes filed for divorce, she remained publicly active: taking daughter Suri to museums, guesting on Project Runway, and preparing to resume acting. Holmes, 33, co-wrote and co-produces Molly, a film about a single mother that begins production in New York and runs through August; she will also shoot Responsible Adults in the fall and stage a debut at New York Fashion Week for her Holmes & Yang clothing line. She is reportedly seeking sole legal custody of Suri while both sides’ lawyers aim to settle privately. Parallel pieces trace Cruise’s pre-Hollywood years at St. Francis Seminary and his upbringing as Thomas Mapother: priests and classmates recall a devout, lonely, sometimes cocky youth who attended seminary briefly before transferring to St. Xavier’s. Teachers like Father Aubert nurtured his performance gifts; classmates were surprised when he embraced Scientology and later stardom. Former manager Eileen Berlin describes Cruise’s difficult childhood—dyslexia, bullying, an abusive father—and volatile temperament, suggesting those factors influenced his relationships and multiple marriages. The narrative emphasizes contrasts between shared Catholic roots and the couples’ diverging paths, with Holmes reportedly leaving partly to protect their child’s religious upbringing.

The KARLBOX is a limited-edition collaboration between designer Karl Lagerfeld and venerable art-supply maker Faber-Castell that packages Lagerfeld’s aesthetic and drawing practice into a luxury artist set. Housed in a lacquered beech-wood cabinet reminiscent of a Chinese wedding chest and stamped with Lagerfeld’s pony-tailed profile, the box contains 350 carefully selected tools—Albrecht Dürer water-soluble pencils (all 120 shades), Polychromos color pencils, Pitt Artist Pens, Castell 9000 graphite pencils, pitt crayons and pastels, watercolor brushes, sharpeners, erasers and a foldable water cup. Supplies are organized into five removable drawers and sorted by primary and secondary color families, with color names etched in English, French and German. Lagerfeld personally chose the shades to reflect his vision of the intersection of fashion, art and design; he describes drawing as essential to his creative process, “like breathing and writing.” 

Produced by Faber-Castell—a family-owned company founded in 1761 known for high-end art and graphic products—the KARLBOX celebrates that heritage while expressing Lagerfeld’s modern sensibility. Each numbered box includes a certificate of authenticity; production is strictly limited (reports cite 2,400–2,500 pieces). Priced around $2,850–$3,000, the set has been sold through Faber-Castell and Karl Lagerfeld boutiques, Harrods, Gump’s and select retailers, and has already generated strong interest among collectors and artists.

Archbishop Charles Chaput of Philadelphia has issued new diocesan guidelines, effective July 1, interpreting Pope Francis’s Amoris Laetitia while reaffirming traditional Catholic sexual and marital teachings. The six-page pastoral instruction allows divorced and civilly remarried Catholics to be welcomed back to Communion only if they refrain from sexual intimacy and live “as brother and sister,” even if they remain in the same household for children’s care. Cohabiting unmarried couples are to be urged either to marry or to separate if one partner is unwilling; if they delay marriage, priests should encourage chastity as spiritual preparation.

The document addresses same-sex attraction by urging those with predominant same-sex attractions to live chastely, seek penance when struggling, and receive support and friendship, while warning that active, public same-sex relationships “offer a serious counter-witness” and can cause moral confusion. Individuals in irregular relationships are barred from certain parish roles—such as parish councils, lectors, and distributing Communion—because of the potential for scandal.

Chaput, a conservative U.S. prelate who participated in the synod that influenced Amoris Laetitia, frames the guidelines as an application of the exhortation’s call for pastoral accompaniment without altering doctrine or canonical discipline. Commentators note Amoris grants bishops interpretive latitude, so practices may vary by diocese. Reactions range from support by chastity-advocacy groups to criticism from LGBT Catholics who feel excluded.

A Nationwide Children’s Hospital study tested 101 breast milk samples purchased through public online milk-sharing sites and found high levels of bacterial contamination: about 75% of samples had either high bacterial counts or disease-causing organisms. Compared with unpasteurized donor milk from screened milk banks, the web-purchased milk was far more likely to contain harmful bacteria—72% had gram-negative bacteria versus 35% in milk bank samples; 63% had staphylococcus versus 25%; 36% had streptococcus versus 20%; and 3% contained salmonella while none of the bank samples did. Researchers attribute the contamination largely to poor hygiene during collection, unclean containers or pump parts, and inadequate shipping—19% of sellers shipped without cooling. Pasteurized milk from milk banks follows screening and processing guidelines to protect fragile infants, but supplies are limited, costly, and prioritized for premature or medically vulnerable babies, prompting some parents to buy online. Experts caution that buying raw milk over the Internet carries risks because buyers cannot verify donor health, handling, or authenticity; the FDA and pediatric groups warn against feeding infants milk from unscreened individuals. Investigators stressed these findings may not apply to sharing among known relatives or friends, where risks could be lower but are less well studied.

Researchers unveiled promising advances in Alzheimer’s detection and management at the Alzheimer’s Association International Conference in London. A team led by Randall Bateman described a simple blood test that measures ratios of beta-amyloid forms to indicate whether amyloid plaques—associated with Alzheimer’s—are building up in the brain. Developed by comparing blood results from 41 people to PET-scan measures of brain amyloid, the test could enable routine screening by primary care doctors, analogous to cholesterol checks. Amyloid plaques begin forming 15–20 years before symptoms, so early identification could prompt lifestyle changes (exercise, diet) shown to lower Alzheimer’s risk by up to about 30 percent, though a positive blood test would not guarantee eventual disease. Experts urge larger validation; the team is expanding testing to 180 more people.

Meanwhile, interim results from the large IDEAS study (over 18,000 Medicare beneficiaries) reveal that many patients clinically diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia lack amyloid plaques on PET scans. Among the first ~4,000 PET-tested participants, only 54.3% of MCI and 70.5% of dementia patients had amyloid, suggesting substantial misdiagnosis and potential unnecessary prescribing of Alzheimer’s drugs. PET findings led physicians to change care plans for about two-thirds of patients, often discontinuing inappropriate medications. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services funded most IDEAS and may reconsider PET coverage if benefits are confirmed. Additionally, the Alzheimer’s Association launched a $20 million U.S. POINTER trial to test whether combined lifestyle interventions can prevent cognitive decline in at-risk older adults. Researchers emphasize that amyloid testing and PET imaging can refine diagnoses but should target select patients with ambiguous symptoms rather than serve as general screening.

The Huntsman sisters—Mary Anne, Abby, and Liddy—have become minor celebrities running interference for their father Jon Huntsman Jr.’s presidential campaign via their irreverent @Jon2012girls social media presence. Filmed prepping for a karaoke shoot in NYC, they embody a fresh, unscripted counterpoint to polished political messaging, using parody and offhand sass (even spoofing a Herman Cain ad) to reach younger voters. They insist their efforts are about service, though sisterly moments—like Mary Anne’s mortifying Kris Humphries anecdote—keep things delightfully human.

Police arrested 45-year-old George C. Brinkman Jr. of Brunswick after a nearly nine-hour standoff in Brunswick and have identified him as a suspect in multiple recent murders in northeast Ohio. Investigators say Brinkman exchanged Facebook messages with a WOIO-Channel 19 reporter, Lacey Crisp, in the hours before and during the standoff; the station alerted police and the reporter stopped communicating when asked. Officials believe Brinkman wanted to “get his story out” before investigators released information.

Brinkman is charged with murder in the shooting deaths of Rogell Eugene John II, 71, and his wife Roberta Ray John, 64, whose bodies were found Monday in their Lake Township home. County officials say Brinkman had been house-sitting for the couple and had worked for their business; he previously dated their daughter. He is also a suspect in the deaths of North Royalton residents Suzanne Taylor, 45, and her daughters Taylor Pifer, 21, and Kylie Pifer, 18, whose bodies were found Sunday. Suzanne Taylor had at least one stab wound to the throat; the exact causes of the daughters’ deaths have not been publicly determined and no murder weapon was recovered from that scene.

Brunswick SWAT located Brinkman at a woman’s home; the woman left unharmed. Officers used a stun gun while he was holding a gun, then took him into custody and transferred him to police after hospital evaluation. Brinkman’s record includes prior misdemeanor convictions and a 1999 conviction for receiving stolen property and unauthorized computer access. Authorities have not yet charged him in the North Royalton deaths and say motive remains undetermined. A vigil for the North Royalton victims was planned at North Royalton High School.

Facing growing GOP defections, Speaker Paul Ryan withdrew the Republican Obamacare repeal bill from the House floor Friday just before a scheduled vote, marking a major defeat for Ryan and President Donald Trump. Despite Trump’s ultimatum and intense lobbying, leaders couldn’t secure enough support—particularly from hard-line Freedom Caucus conservatives who said the bill didn’t go far enough, and moderates worried about Medicaid cuts. Trump admitted he was “10 to 15 votes” short. Ryan and the White House blamed internal GOP divisions; Democrats celebrated the setback. GOP finger-pointing began immediately, but leaders vowed to regroup and continue pursuing repeal efforts despite the public humiliation and the Affordable Care Act remaining law.

Police in Munich evacuated the Hauptbahnhof (main train station) and Pasing station after receiving information suggesting a possible bomb attack, a police spokeswoman told ABC News. Both stations were cleared and reopened hours later. Off-duty officers were recalled to conduct thorough sweeps but found nothing suspicious. Authorities urged people to avoid crowds, public transport and stations. The situation is developing; updates may follow.

Federal prosecutors seized about $20 million in cash hidden under a mattress in a Westborough, Massachusetts, apartment as part of a broad investigation into TelexFree, a Marlborough-based company prosecutors say was actually a massive international pyramid scheme. Agents tailed and arrested 28-year-old Brazilian Cleber Rene Rizerio Rocha after he arrived from Brazil and delivered $2.2 million in a suitcase to a cooperating witness; he is charged with conspiring to commit money laundering and detained pending a hearing. TelexFree, run by James Merrill and Carlos Wanzeler, sold little VOIP service and mainly paid earlier investors with funds from new recruits, targeting Brazilian immigrants initially. Nearly 965,225 victims lost about $1.76 billion; TelexFree filed bankruptcy in 2014. Merrill pleaded guilty; Wanzeler fled to Brazil. Prosecutors allege Rocha helped move hidden TelexFree assets to Brazil via Hong Kong accounts.

Veteran actor Scott Wilson, best known recently as Hershel Greene on AMC’s The Walking Dead, has died at 76 from complications of leukemia. Wilson’s career began in 1967 with roles in In the Heat of the Night and In Cold Blood; he later appeared in films including The Great Gatsby, Dead Man Walking and Pearl Harbor, and earned a Golden Globe nomination for The Ninth Configuration. Wilson had filmed a return for The Walking Dead’s ninth season before his death. News of his passing prompted an on-screen tribute and numerous social media remembrances from cast, crew and fans praising his talent, kindness and calm spirit.

Bernie Sanders said he will treat the Democratic convention as "contested" unless Hillary Clinton secures the nomination via enough pledged delegates to reach a majority without relying on superdelegates. Speaking in Washington, Sanders vowed to press superdelegates—party elites who comprise about 15% of all delegates—up until the formal vote in July, arguing they should reflect voters’ preferences in states where he won big, such as Washington and Minnesota. Clinton currently has roughly 520 committed superdelegates versus 39 for Sanders, putting her near the threshold. Sanders acknowledged the steep math: he would need to win about 65% of remaining pledged delegates to overtake Clinton, a difficult task given proportional allocation and large contests like California and New Jersey. His campaign points to favorable polling and general-election matchups to persuade superdelegates they should back him as the stronger candidate against Republicans. Analysts note that while Sanders can force a contested convention by continuing to compete, the structural realities—Clinton’s pledged-delegate lead, a large popular-vote edge of over three million, and Democratic proportional rules—make an ultimate Sanders victory unlikely, even if a floor fight is possible.

In response to Congress’ 2007 mandate, the military implemented widespread cognitive screening for traumatic brain injury using the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metric (ANAM). An investigation by ProPublica and NPR found the program has largely failed: more than a million pre-deployment tests cost taxpayers over $42 million, yet the military still lacks a reliable system to identify TBIs. ANAM, developed in-house decades earlier, was chosen hastily amid pressure, despite limited scientific proof it can screen or diagnose concussion-related injuries. Conflicts of interest surfaced because developers with financial ties influenced the selection process, and competing tests received little serious review. Senior medical officers warned ANAM was unreliable and easily affected by fatigue or distraction, yet the Pentagon pressed forward. Implementation was flawed: baselines were often taken only once, results were seldom used, follow-up evaluations were restricted (the Army barred referrals based solely on low ANAM scores), and data systems remain fragmented. Promised comparative studies were delayed, leaving troops without effective post-deployment screening. Critics say the program’s missteps have missed, misdiagnosed, and failed soldiers in need of care.

A 73-year-old man with a spotless driving record was arrested after attempting to snort cocaine during a traffic stop Tuesday night in the Colman neighborhood. Officer Nic Abts-Olsen pulled the silver Toyota over around 8:30 PM for driving with its headlights off. While checking the driver’s license and registration, Abts-Olsen returned to find the driver portioning a scoop of cocaine from a small glass vial. When the officer knocked on the window, the man spilled powder onto his hands and the car’s floor, initially denying possession and calling the substance “vitamins.” He then admitted the truth, complimented the officer’s detection skills, and conceded that snorting cocaine amid a traffic stop was a poor decision. Officer Abts-Olsen said he had intended only to issue a warning because of the driver’s clean record until the cocaine was discovered. The man was arrested and booked into King County Jail for narcotics possession. The encounter was captured on in-car video, which was posted with a holiday safety reminder.

Anthony J. Lescowitch Jr., 35, of Drifton/Freeland, was arrested after he shared his own wanted photo posted by Freeland Police on Facebook. Police had posted his image Monday seeking help locating him on charges including aggravated assault related to a July 14, 2013 attack in which the victim was struck, rendered unconscious, robbed and had $100 later withdrawn from his bank card. Minutes after the department published the photo, Lescowitch reposted it and taunted officers. Detectives then used a fictitious female Facebook account to engage him in conversation for about 30 minutes, gathering information and arranging a meeting. Though he initially declined a drink, Lescowitch agreed to come out for a cigarette; undercover officers waited at the agreed location and arrested him without incident. He was arraigned and held at Luzerne County Correctional Facility on $25,000 bail, which he could not post. Lescowitch was also sought by Luzerne County Adult Probation. Three others face related charges: Heather Mumie, charged with two counts of robbery and reckless endangerment; Clayton R. Spohr, charged with robbery, access device fraud, theft and related counts; and Janine K. Brotzman, charged with reckless endangerment and disorderly conduct.

A Connecticut man already facing burglary charges was arrested on new counts after a victim recognized his stolen sweatshirt in a public booking photo. Police say Derek Benson, 30, linked to a late‑2014 series of burglaries involving expensive golf equipment, was photographed wearing a gray Coco Libre sweatshirt taken during a July 2014 break‑in at a Glastonbury home. The homeowner, who works for Coco Libre, saw Benson’s mug shot and alerted authorities; a follow‑up investigation tied Benson to the earlier burglary, during which jewelry and the sweatshirt were taken. Benson was arrested last week on charges including burglary, larceny, and criminal mischief and is held on $125,000 bond.

Apple will begin selling the iPhone 4S in mainland China on Jan. 13, adding the country to a global rollout that will place the device in 22 more markets. The iPhone, which accounts for nearly half of Apple’s revenue and a large share of its profits, has strong sales momentum: the 4S launched Oct. 14 and reached Hong Kong in November, selling out quickly. China Unicom is the sole authorized mainland carrier at launch; talks continue but no deal has been announced with China Mobile, the nation’s largest operator. Siri will not support Mandarin at initial launch, though Apple plans to add Chinese language support in 2012. Analysts expect exceptional demand in China, the world’s largest mobile market, and predict the 4S will be priced similarly to prior iPhone models when sold unlocked without contract.

Granville P. Swift, a Kentucky-born pioneer and great-nephew of Daniel Boone, became a legendary and tragic figure in early California history. Arriving around 1840 as a fur trapper, Swift played a prominent role in the 1846 Bear Flag Revolt and later commanded a company in the California Battalion. When news of gold at Sutter’s Mill reached him, he headed to Bidwell’s Bar and quickly amassed enormous wealth; contemporaries estimated he and two partners took in roughly $100,000 each, and Swift reportedly left the mines with more than half a million dollars in gold. With few banks available, he had much of his gold minted into specially marked $50 octagonal slugs and began burying caches around the Bay Area—particularly in Sonoma County—because he distrusted banking. Swift, however, was notoriously absent-minded and soon forgot many hiding places.

Over the decades some of his buried hoards resurfaced: workers found $7,000 in 1903; about $30,000 was recovered from a chimney cache in 1904; and in 1914 rancher A.W. Lehrke reportedly dreamed of digging under his home and unearthed $42,600, believed to be part of Swift’s stash. Yet much remains missing. A scribbled, misspelled inventory by Swift—referencing jugs, bottles and a tin box—offers the only clue.

Swift’s later life saw further misfortune. He lost much wealth in a Comstock Lode swindle, saw $80,000 in his sister’s gold washed away by floods, and endured personal troubles including divorce. In 1875 he died after a fatal mule accident while prospecting for quicksilver. His buried fortune, part recovered but largely lost, continues to fuel local lore and treasure hunts.

Wiz Khalifa and Charlie Puth’s “See You Again,” released in 2015 as a tribute to the late Paul Walker and featured on The Fate of the Furious soundtrack, became YouTube’s most-viewed video, surpassing Psy’s “Gangnam Style” with over 2.896 billion views. The milestone dethroned Psy after five years; Justin Bieber’s “Sorry” ranks third. Puth expressed surprise and reflected on early ambitions when he joined YouTube in 2007, while Wiz Khalifa noted the song’s inspirational impact. The track’s official video—directed by Marc Klasfeld—was promoted alongside soundtrack and tour links, merch, streaming options, and social media channels for both artists. Additional content in the source mixed unrelated material: a university library description highlighting Washington and Lee’s Library collections, 24-hour access, special collections, and resource-sharing; and promotional and lyric content for Justin Bieber’s “Sorry,” including production credits (BLOOD, Skrillex), director Parris Goebel, dancers, and distribution links. The combined document thus spans major pop-culture milestones in digital music viewership, artist promotion, institutional library services, and commercial music releases from 2015.

Students at Anderson High School in Southgate will retake a required 11th-grade final and may face discipline after a cheating incident. Two juniors reportedly snuck into a classroom, photographed the exam answer key while the teacher was out, and shared the images via group text. The teacher noticed unusually perfect scores while grading and alerted administrators; at least two students admitted taking and sharing the photos. About 30 students were affected and had to return during summer break for a makeup exam. Superintendent Leslie Hainrihar said consequences are forthcoming and will consider prior behavior when assigning punishment.

SEC Chair Mary Jo White proposed sweeping measures to rein in high-frequency trading (HFT) and boost transparency in dark pools and exchanges. Her recommendations would require proprietary firms that trade in milliseconds but aren’t registered broker-dealers to register with the SEC, submit dark-pool matching rules and disclose client/order handling, and strengthen oversight of trading algorithms. The SEC will review exchange order types, maker-taker pricing, and disparities between direct data feeds and public tickers, considering mechanisms to minimize speed advantages, such as frequent batch auctions or trading obligations for the fastest firms. The plan complements CFTC interest and probes by the FBI and New York’s attorney general into potential abuses. The SEC will push rules like Regulation SCI to prevent outages, require brokers to disclose order routing destinations, and form an advisory committee to reassess whether prior rules, including Regulation NMS, have contributed to market complexity and fragmentation.

Fairfield police removed ten children, ages 4 months to 12 years, from a home after an investigation revealed prolonged physical and emotional abuse and squalid living conditions. The probe began March 31 when a 12‑year‑old boy was reported missing; officers found him and returned him to the house, where they discovered nine other children living amid garbage, spoiled food, animal and human feces, and clutter that made parts of the home impassable. Detectives from the Family Violence Unit and Solano County Child Welfare Services interviewed the children, who described intentional abuse that reportedly resulted in puncture wounds, burns, bruises and injuries consistent with being hit by a pellet or airsoft gun. Prosecutors described the conduct as torture carried out for “sadistic purposes.” Father Jonathan Michael Allen, 29, was arrested after a six‑week investigation and faces multiple felony counts including torture and child cruelty; he was held on substantial bail. Mother Ina Rogers, 30, was arrested on neglect charges in late March and released on bail; she defends herself, saying she homeschools the children, works as a medical technician, and that the home’s disarray reflected her frantic search for the missing boy. All ten children were placed with Rogers’ sister and mother while the case and prosecutions proceed.

Netflix has introduced an unlimited maternity and paternity leave policy that lets new parents take as much paid time off as they need during the first year after a child’s birth or adoption. Announced in a company blog by Chief Talent Officer Tawni Cranz, the program is framed within Netflix’s “freedom and responsibility” culture: employees decide what works best for their families and coordinate coverage with managers. Parents may return full‑time, part‑time, or intermittently throughout the year, and will continue to receive regular pay rather than switching to state or disability benefits.

The move positions Netflix alongside other tech firms that have boosted family leave—Yahoo doubled its parental leave in 2013 to compete with Facebook and Google—and signals a shift in workplace priorities. Where early‑2000s perks aimed to keep employees on campus with games and free meals, modern talent increasingly values work‑life balance and flexibility. Netflix argues supporting parents improves focus and retention and helps attract top talent.

The policy is notable for including fathers and recognizing the entire first year as critical. However, unlimited leave plans can bring challenges: employees must coordinate with teams and managers to avoid disrupting projects, and extended absences can strain workplace dynamics. Still, by formalizing paid, flexible parental leave, Netflix emphasizes retaining skilled employees through major life changes and adapting benefits to contemporary expectations about work and family.

Ukraine has added Hollywood actor Steven Seagal to a blacklist of cultural figures barred from entering the country, citing national security concerns. The Ukrainian security service published a letter — reported by news site Apostrophe and later confirmed by its press secretary — announcing a five-year ban, saying Seagal had “committed socially dangerous actions … that contradict the interests of maintaining Ukraine’s security.” The move follows Seagal’s acceptance of Russian citizenship last year from President Vladimir Putin and his vocal support for Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea. Seagal has cultivated close ties with several post-Soviet leaders and causes: he has publicly befriended Belarus’s Alexander Lukashenko, appeared at events linked to Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov, and performed in Crimea at a pro‑Kremlin event where separatist flags were displayed. Kyiv previously proposed blacklisting foreign cultural figures who back violations of Ukraine’s territorial integrity, including France’s Gérard Depardieu, and has already banned him. The ban comes amid broader cultural tensions with Russia, such as Ukraine’s exclusion of Russia’s Eurovision entrant over past performances in Crimea and its wider sanctions against Russian films and artists.

A massive Gulf of Mexico oil spill from the April 20 Deepwater Horizon explosion rapidly expanded, with satellite analysis showing the slick growing from about 1,150 square miles to roughly 3,850 square miles in a day. The Coast Guard estimated roughly 200,000 gallons a day leaking, raising fears the total could rival or exceed past disasters and threaten sensitive habitats from Louisiana marshes to the Florida Keys and the region’s coral reefs. Rough seas hindered containment efforts, and BP’s 2009 risk filings had downplayed the chance of a catastrophic spill. In response, BP began using large quantities of chemical dispersants—including Corexit—applied even 5,000 feet underwater, aiming to keep oil from reaching shore and birds. Experts warn dispersants carry their own toxic risks, can concentrate harmful compounds like PAHs, harm marine life and seafood safety, and that dispersant stockpiles may be rapidly depleted. The long-term ecological trade-offs remain uncertain.

A hiker died after falling from the cables near the summit of Half Dome in Yosemite National Park on Monday afternoon, authorities said. The accident occurred around 4:30 p.m. during thunderstorm activity as two people were on the steep, final section of the trail where seasonal cables are installed each spring to aid the last roughly 400-foot climb to the 8,839-foot granite summit. Rangers were notified and assisted the surviving companion, who was unharmed. The fallen hiker was missing overnight; his body was recovered the next day around 1 p.m. The National Park Service has not released his name pending family notification and said investigators are still trying to determine exactly how the fall occurred. Officials noted the well-worn rock was wet and that although hikers may clip safety harnesses to the cables, most do not. This is the first fatal fall from Half Dome since 2010. The popular 14-mile round-trip trail requires a permit during peak season to avoid overcrowding; Half Dome remains one of Yosemite’s signature features and most frequented routes.

Special counsel Robert Mueller’s office has not responded to President Donald Trump’s legal team in nearly three weeks, Rudy Giuliani, one of the President’s attorneys, said. Giuliani expected no reply until after the Paul Manafort trial but said Mueller’s team told them they are “still studying” a five- to six-page letter from Trump’s lawyers. Giuliani speculated Mueller could be planning several next steps: issuing a report without interviewing the President, issuing a subpoena (which would provoke a public legal fight potentially during the midterm election run-up), negotiating around the offer in Trump’s letter, or waiting until after the midterms to act.

Meanwhile, longtime Trump associate Roger Stone publicly warned supporters he expects to be indicted soon as part of Mueller’s Russia probe. In an email fundraising pitch posted by CNN, Stone declared, “Robert Mueller is coming for me,” claiming he is targeted because of his long association with Trump and alleging a “deep state” effort to silence him and pressure him to testify. Stone’s warning followed a wave of legal setbacks for figures tied to the Trump campaign: former campaign chairman Paul Manafort’s conviction and Michael Cohen’s guilty plea, both connected to Mueller’s investigation.

Stone has previously suggested he might be indicted and has acknowledged communications that overlap with material in Mueller’s indictment of Russian military officers, which referenced interactions with the Guccifer 2.0 persona that Mueller alleges was a Russian front. Mueller’s team has interviewed multiple people connected to Stone, including Kristin Davis, about her ties to him, indicating continuing scrutiny of his network in the broader probe into 2016 election interference.

Bloom Energy’s unveiling of its low-emissions “Bloom Box” fuel-cell server drew huge attention but left key questions unanswered. Originating from NASA-developed solid-oxide fuel-cell work, Bloom’s commercial servers are claimed to deliver roughly double the efficiency of conventional grid power and can generate up to 400 kW from a parking-space-sized unit. Early customers are large corporations (Google, eBay) paying $700k–$800k for industrial units, which Bloom says can pay back in 3–5 years with current subsidies; the company projects a $3,000 home unit in 5–10 years but provided few details. Experts note the design is largely standard solid-oxide technology, not obviously revolutionary, and caution about missing data on lifecycle, long-term reliability, downtime, heat-recovery and true costs without subsidies. Bloom claims flexibility to run on natural gas, biogas or renewable inputs, and has patents hinting at a possible closed-loop fuel/oxygen recovery—an ambitious feature not yet demonstrated. Overall: promising but still speculative until durability, economics and novel features are proven.

Netflix has officially renewed its breakout series 13 Reasons Why for a 13-episode second season slated for 2018. Executive produced by Selena Gomez and adapted from Jay Asher’s YA bestseller, the show continues after Hannah Baker’s suicide and follows the characters’ complicated journeys toward healing and recovery. Brian Yorkey, who wrote the adaptation and co-showran season one, will serve as solo showrunner; co-showrunner Diana Son is departing. Season one focused on Clay Jensen discovering Hannah’s cassette tapes detailing 13 reasons for her death and featured Katherine Langford, Dylan Minnette and an ensemble cast. The series sparked intense discussion for its graphic depiction of teen suicide, bullying, sexual assault and drunk driving; critics and some mental health experts warned it could risk vulnerable viewers, prompting Netflix to strengthen content warnings. The series is produced by Paramount Television and Anonymous Content.

This study used a 20% random sample of Medicare beneficiaries’ Carrier and Part D files from 2008–2011 to examine whether emergency physicians’ opioid-prescribing intensity affects patients’ subsequent long-term opioid use and health encounters. Index emergency department (ED) visits were defined as the earliest ED evaluation-and-management claim by an emergency medicine physician (specialty and place-of-service criteria applied), limited to one nonadmission visit per beneficiary. Analyses included beneficiaries continuously enrolled in Medicare Part D for at least 18 months (6 months before to 12 months after the index visit), with no opioid fill in the prior 6 months, and without hospice claims or cancer. Visits were attributed to physicians by billing NPI and to hospitals via facility outpatient claims; physicians or hospitals with very small counts were excluded, and physicians working at multiple hospitals were assigned to their primary hospital.

Opioid prescriptions (excluding methadone) were identified in Part D by NDC and attributed to an index visit if filled within 7 days (sensitivity analysis used 3 days). Morphine-equivalent doses and days’ supply were calculated. Physicians’ prescribing intensity was defined within each hospital by quartiles of the proportion of ED visits followed by an opioid fill; analyses contrasted top (high-intensity) versus bottom (low-intensity) quartiles. An alternative exposure classified physicians by median prescription dose.

Primary outcome was long-term opioid use: ≥180 days’ opioid supply in the 12 months after the index visit, excluding the first 30 days to avoid tautology. Secondary outcomes included 12-month rates of ED visits and hospitalizations (overall, potentially opioid-related, and for conditions unlikely influenced by opioids) and repeat ED visits for the same diagnosis at 14 and 30 days.

Patient covariates included demographics, Medicaid dual eligibility, disability, and 11 chronic conditions. The study exploited within-hospital variation—assuming patients do not select specific ED physicians—to reduce selection bias, and compared case-mix and diagnosis distributions between patients seen by high- versus low-intensity prescribers. Unadjusted rates and adjusted odds ratios were estimated with multivariable logistic regression, clustering robust standard errors at the hospital level and excluding middle two quartiles from primary models. Sensitivity analyses tested alternative exposure definitions and other assumptions. Results showed that patients treated by higher-intensity opioid prescribers were more likely to fill initial opioid prescriptions and to become long-term opioid users, suggesting that the prescribing tendency of the ED physician encountered can meaningfully influence subsequent chronic opioid use.

Amazon plans to open its first-ever physical retail store in Manhattan, targeting a holiday-season debut on West 34th Street near Herald Square and Macy’s flagship, according to people familiar with the plan. The move would mark a major experiment for the 20-year-old e-commerce giant to provide in-person shopping and to better connect with customers in the physical world. The reported store would double as a “mini-warehouse” to support same-day delivery in New York, handle product returns, and enable online order pickups. It would also showcase Amazon’s own hardware—Kindles, tablets, the Fire TV set-top box and the Fire smartphone—while likely featuring a broader selection from Amazon’s catalog, mirroring how brand stores sometimes include other vendors’ items. Analysts say a Manhattan presence could attract tourists and local shoppers who prefer to see and handle products before buying, and would let Amazon gather direct consumer feedback to guide future expansion. Amazon declined to comment on the reports. The location, cited as 7 West 34th Street across from the Empire State Building, places the store amid heavy holiday foot traffic and the retail backdrop of New York’s competitive brick-and-mortar landscape.

Former South Carolina governor Mark Sanford, a Republican attempting to reclaim his old House seat, has faced a string of setbacks in recent weeks: his ex-wife filed a trespassing lawsuit against him, national Republican backers withdrew support, and a poll showed him trailing his Democratic opponent, Elizabeth Colbert Busch, by nine points in a district that typically leans Republican. In response to these troubles and to criticism that his opponent was avoiding public debate, Sanford staged a provocative publicity stunt: he held a press event where he “debated” a life-size cardboard cutout of House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.).

The stunt echoed a notorious moment from the 2012 Republican National Convention, when actor Clint Eastwood delivered an unscripted, meandering monologue to an empty chair meant to symbolize President Obama. At his event, Sanford argued that Colbert Busch had refused to face him in public debates and labeled her campaign a “stealth campaign.” As a theatrical workaround, he declared, “Since Elizabeth won’t debate, I’m allowed to debate Nancy,” and then addressed the Pelosi cutout directly. He pressed the cardboard Pelosi on issues such as a National Labor Relations Board lawsuit that sought to block Boeing from building a new plant in South Carolina—an action Republicans portrayed as politically motivated and harmful to the state’s job prospects.

The episode illustrates Sanford’s turn toward attention-grabbing tactics as conventional political support and momentum wane. It underscores the tense dynamics of a competitive race in a typically Republican district: a beleaguered candidate resorting to spectacle to spotlight his criticisms and cast his opponent as inaccessible. The report also includes unrelated archival metadata noting the Congressional Candidate Website project—an initiative led by political scientists at Northwestern University, the University of Minnesota, and Oberlin College to archive major-party candidate sites from the 2008 and 2010 campaigns.

Triple suicide bombings struck two mosques in Sanaa, Yemen, during midday Friday prayers, killing dozens and wounding many more in some of the deadliest violence since the Houthi takeover of the capital. Reports of casualties vary: medical officials cited by AP put the toll at 46 dead and about 100 injured; Reuters and other outlets reported lower initial figures, while Yemen’s state-run Saba agency and CNN cited much higher counts—up to 137 killed and 357 wounded. The attacks targeted Al Badr and Al Hashoosh mosques, both frequented by Zaidi Shiite worshippers and linked to the Houthi movement. Witnesses described harrowing scenes: bombers detonated devices inside the mosques, then secondary blasts occurred outside—one reportedly a car bomb—apparently to strike those fleeing. Footage and eyewitness testimony showed bloodied blankets ferrying victims, bodies laid out on mosque floors and carried away in pick-up trucks; hospitals appealed for blood donations. Among the dead was a prominent Houthi cleric, according to local reports. No group immediately and verifiably claimed responsibility; Yemen hosts both a strong al-Qaida affiliate (AQAP) and an emerging Islamic State (ISIS) presence. ISIS-aligned outlets and some social media accounts purportedly claimed the attacks, which, if confirmed, would represent a major ISIS operation in Yemen; AQAP denied involvement. The bombings followed heavy fighting in Aden between forces loyal to exiled President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi and Houthi-aligned units that had earlier provoked airstrikes and an airport closure. The U.S. condemned the mosque bombings and related strikes, and Gulf states urged political talks even as Yemen’s multifaceted conflict deepened.

India elected Ram Nath Kovind as its 14th president, marking the first contest in which both final candidates—Kovind and opposition nominee Meira Kumar—were from the Dalit community, historically considered "untouchable." Kovind, a 71-72-year-old former Bihar governor, BJP spokesman, and lawyer, won decisively in a secret ballot of about 4,800 lawmakers, securing 2,930 votes to Kumar’s 1,844. The largely ceremonial presidency can still influence politics by signing legislation, delaying bills, or deciding who forms a government if elections are inconclusive. Kovind’s selection is seen as part of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the BJP’s strategy to expand its reach among India’s some 200 million Dalits and consolidate power in parliament; a vice-presidential victory next month could further bolster the party. While affirmative-action laws reserve representation and opportunities for Dalits, discrimination persists especially in rural areas. Analysts note that the election’s significance lies both in caste symbolism and in the BJP’s growing influence and Hindu nationalist politics, which have heightened religious tensions and incidents such as cow-related vigilante attacks. Some view Kovind’s appointment as a signal to disaffected Dalit voters and an element of political consolidation.

Athena, a humanoid robot with a head, hands, legs and red sneakers, made headlines at Los Angeles International Airport when she boarded a Lufthansa flight to Germany as what airport officials called the first robot to travel as a paid passenger on a commercial jet. Built by Sarcos in Salt Lake City and purchased by Germany’s Max Planck Society, Athena arrived at the Tom Bradley International Terminal on Dec. 15 amid TV crews and crowd photos. Accompanied by Max Planck researchers Alexander Herzog and Jeannette Bohg, she checked in at the counter, received an economy ticket (with a first-class lane shortcut for photos), and was strapped into a seat in the main cabin. TSA gave her a special electronic pat-down rather than a standard metal-detector screening. Athena’s arms operate and her head houses cameras and sensors, but her leg software to enable standing and walking is still under development; she currently cannot walk. Researchers hope robots like Athena will one day perform dangerous tasks—such as Fukushima cleanup—so humans need not risk their lives. The team also wanted to observe human reactions to a robot seated among passengers.

Excavations beneath the Old Divinity School at St John’s College, Cambridge, revealed a large medieval hospital cemetery linked to the Hospital of St John the Evangelist, containing about 1,300 burials and over 400 complete skeletons. Dating mainly from the 13th–15th centuries, the graves were found in neat rows and some remains were deposited in a charnel house. Unusually, many graves had been pre-dug—some bodies did not fit their pits—suggesting burial spaces were prepared in advance, perhaps before winter when digging was harder. Most burials lacked coffins or shrouds and few contained grave-goods, indicating the cemetery primarily served the poor; women and infants were notably scarce, likely because the hospital’s remit excluded pregnant women. The assemblage showed surprisingly few serious illnesses, supporting the idea the hospital provided spiritual and basic care rather than advanced medical treatment. Features such as gravel paths, a well, and flower seeds point to a site visited by the living. Despite local lore, no evidence of Black Death mass burials was found. The findings, published in the Archaeological Journal, make this one of Britain’s largest medieval hospital osteoarchaeological collections.

Vincent van Gogh’s notorious ear mutilation, long attributed to a quarrel with Paul Gauguin, may instead have been triggered by news that his brother and patron, Theo, was to marry. In Studio of the South, Martin Bailey presents archival evidence that a letter from Theo, delivered to the Yellow House on 23 December 1888, contained both money and the revelation that Theo planned to wed Jo Bonger after a whirlwind courtship. Bailey shows Theo had already sought family permission and received a congratulatory telegram on that date; he argues Theo almost certainly told Vincent the same news. That disclosure, which threatened Vincent’s financial lifeline and emotional intimacy with Theo, likely precipitated his despair. After a day of rain and a later quarrel with Gauguin, Vincent severed part of his ear, wrapped it in paper and took it to a woman at a brothel; she fainted and the police were summoned. Van Gogh was hospitalized from Christmas onward, discharged in January, and despite further breakdowns continued painting until he left Arles in April. Bailey also traces the fate of the double bed depicted in The Bedroom—bought to prepare for Gauguin’s stay and symbolically suggesting Vincent’s hope for intimacy. Sent to Auvers in 1890, it passed to Theo’s widow, later to family heirs, and in 1945 was donated to war victims near Arnhem; it may still survive unrecognized in Boxmeer. Contemporary reports often misidentified or misspelled Van Gogh’s name, reflecting his obscurity in the 1880s.

All five Republican members of the House Ethics Committee publicly urged Democrats to schedule public trials for Reps. Charlie Rangel and Maxine Waters before the November elections, criticizing Chairwoman Zoe Lofgren for delaying dates as the House nears adjournment. Ranking member Rep. Jo Bonner, joined by his GOP colleagues, said the committee’s rules give the chair authority to set trial dates and accused Lofgren of stalling despite readiness from members and two years of investigation in Rangel’s case. Democrats privately objected to the GOP’s break from the panel’s usual secrecy, calling the move partisan and saying Lofgren has lost control. Republicans argued trials should occur pre-election for transparency and fairness.

Then-EPA chief Scott Pruitt installed a $43,000 soundproof phone booth in his office but used it to call the White House only once—a five-minute outgoing call on Jan. 29—records released after Sierra Club litigation show. EPA provided billing through June 20 with no other outgoing calls. The booth’s cost exceeded the original $25,000 estimate after $18,000 in closet conversion work; the Government Accountability Office found the spending violated federal rules. Pruitt defended the booth as necessary for secure talks but later said he wouldn’t have approved the total cost and resigned amid ethics scrutiny. Sierra Club’s FOIA lawsuits exposed other questionable Pruitt spending and continue seeking records from acting administrator Andrew Wheeler, who has kept the booth and pledged stricter expense signoffs while pursuing some of Pruitt’s deregulatory policies.

Christopher Myers, 50, of Denver survived a great white shark attack Monday while swimming with his 16-year-old son near a sandbar about 400 yards off Ballston Beach in Truro, Cape Cod. The shark grabbed his left foot; Myers says he kicked its snout with his right foot and was released. He suffered deep lacerations and puncture wounds to both lower legs, severed tendons in his left ankle, and required 47 stitches; he will need physical therapy but expects to recover and plans to return to the beach, albeit closer to shore. His son described feeling powerless as the shark surfaced between them. State officials have identified the assailant as a great white and are investigating; at least nine large sharks have been tracked off Cape Cod this season, though not previously as far north as Truro.

The incident—Cape Cod’s first shark attack in 76 years—drew intense media attention, lifeguard alerts, and numerous fin sightings. Marine biologists link the increased inshore presence of great whites to a rebounding grey seal population, now over 300,000, which attracts seal-hunting sharks closer to beaches. Experts caution swimmers to avoid seal areas and steep drop-offs; attacks are rare and often cases of mistaken identity. Tourism officials urged calm as they work to reassure visitors while emphasizing common-sense precautions around seals and inshore waters.

Melvin C. Johnson Jr., 39, a longtime Oakland resident who had publicly pleaded for an end to gun violence after the 2013 slayings of his son and 16-month-old grandson, was shot and killed while driving in East Oakland. The midday shooting occurred Dec. 27 as Johnson drove near a street shrine memorializing his son Andrew “Drew” Thomas, 20, and grandson Drew Leon Deon Jackson, who were fatally shot in their sleep in August 2013 when a shooter fired into a relative’s home. Despite his wounds, Johnson was able to drive to the 8500 block of MacArthur, where he crashed into parked cars; bystanders and responders gave him CPR and he was taken to Highland Hospital but died there. Police have not released a motive, made any arrests, or said whether he was targeted or the shooting was random. Authorities are offering up to $10,000 for tips in Johnson’s killing; a separate reward of up to $30,000 remains outstanding for information leading to an arrest in the 2013 murders of his son and grandson. Johnson’s mother, Carolyn Smith, described him as a loving, helpful man — “like a big teddy bear” — and said he had been working to change his life and help others through his small business, Drewski Designs, which made custom T‑shirts and clothing for community events. The family has endured multiple tragedies: in addition to the 2013 killings, an 8‑year‑old son, Jahmel Johnson, died the previous month after battling lymphoma. The unsolved killings underscore ongoing gun-violence challenges in Oakland, where authorities say shootings and violent crime have recently shown some declines but past years saw very high homicide rates.

Mexican authorities moved Sinaloa cartel leader Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán from the Altiplano maximum-security prison near Mexico City to a facility in Ciudad Juárez on the U.S. border. Officials said the transfer aimed to improve security while Altiplano underwent renovations; a senior Mexican source added that proximity to the U.S. could ease extradition. The move surprised some U.S. officials and Guzmán’s lawyers, who said they were not notified and have sought legal steps to block transfers. Guzmán, recaptured January 8 after escaping Altiplano last July through a tunnel, arrived heavily guarded in Ciudad Juárez and was placed in a high-security section guarded by military personnel. The U.S. has been preparing for his potential transfer for months; Justice Department prosecutors have chosen a Homeland Security–based case to try Guzmán in Brooklyn, where a secure federal detention facility is available. U.S. indictments from 2009 accuse him and others of importing massive quantities of cocaine, running a violent trafficking enterprise that used sicarios for murders, kidnappings and torture, and engaging in racketeering, money laundering and other crimes. Mexican authorities say extradition proceedings began in January and could take a year or more; Guzmán has signaled willingness to plead guilty under conditions including medium-security confinement and regular family and lawyer visits, though his defense has at times framed extradition requests as tactics responding to poor prison treatment.

Lonnie David Franklin Jr., a former garbage truck driver and LAPD garage attendant nicknamed "The Grim Sleeper," was convicted of murdering nine women and one girl and attempting to murder a survivor, in a verdict reached in under two days after a three-month Los Angeles trial. Jurors found Franklin, 63, guilty on all counts; the case now moves to a penalty phase beginning May 11 to determine whether he will receive the death penalty. Prosecutors painted Franklin as a deliberate, repeating sexual predator who killed victims over decades, discarding many in alleys and dumpsters in South Los Angeles—so-called "body dumps"—often near his home. Many victims were found with disheveled clothing and no identification; prosecutors called the killings first-degree, willful, deliberate and premeditated.

The prosecution relied heavily on DNA evidence made possible by modern technology, including saliva found on victims, ballistic matches to a .25-caliber handgun linking murders from the 1980s and 2000s, and testimony from a surviving victim, Enietra Washington, who recounted being shot and left for dead in 1988. Detectives connected cold cases after DNA hits in the 2000s and used a familial search that ultimately led them to Franklin via a match to his son; undercover officers then obtained Franklin’s DNA from a discarded pizza crust, confirming matches to multiple crime scenes. During a 2010 search of his home, police found photos and videos of numerous unidentified women.

Defense counsel argued the case was circumstantial and suggested, without proof, a relative might be responsible. Jurors were not persuaded. Family members of victims, restrained in court but openly relieved outside, expressed gratitude to investigators—especially Detective Dennis Kilcoyne—and sought to remember their loved ones beyond their victimization. Police hope the verdict brings closure to the victims’ families.

A judge ordered three young siblings to remain in foster care after Child Protective Services filed an emergency petition following the death of 19-month-old J'Zyra Thompson in a northeast Houston apartment. Authorities say the mother left J'Zyra and three other children — a 5-year-old girl and two 3-year-olds — alone Monday night while she and her boyfriend went out for pizza and errands. Investigators found the toddler next to the oven with severe burns; emergency responders could not save her. CPS and court records indicate prior concerns about the mother, including leaving the children unattended, driving without a license or car seats, and that no suitable relatives were available to care for the survivors. Case workers reported the 5-year-old claimed she was sleeping, while one 3-year-old allegedly admitted placing the baby in the oven and another said they turned it on. The children have been separated into two foster homes and will receive counseling. The mother and her boyfriend were questioned; charges have not been filed but CPS filings say criminal charges are expected. The next custody hearing is scheduled for December 2.

The U.S. government has moved to scale back Arctic offshore oil and gas drilling, canceling two planned lease sales in Alaska’s Beaufort and Chukchi seas and denying requests from Shell and Statoil to extend existing leases. The Department of the Interior cited “current market conditions and low industry interest,” and Secretary Sally Jewell noted that after Shell’s decision to pause Chukchi Sea exploration and given the acreage already leased, preparing additional Arctic lease sales in the near term would not be sensible. Shell had spent roughly $7 billion developing Arctic prospects but announced that tests at its Burger J well failed to reveal commercially viable oil or gas, prompting the company to suspend Alaskan exploration “for the foreseeable future.” The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management received few or no nominations in response to calls for information for the planned lease sales—raising concerns about competitiveness—while the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement found that Shell and Statoil did not demonstrate a reasonable schedule of work required to justify suspending the ten-year primary terms of their leases. The existing leases are set to expire in 2017 (Beaufort) and 2020 (Chukchi). Environmental groups welcomed the move, arguing it protects Arctic ecosystems and helps keep fossil fuels in the ground to mitigate climate change; advocates highlighted risks to wildlife such as polar bears and warned of pollution from offshore drilling. The decisions reflect both economic realities—high costs and low oil prices—and ongoing environmental and regulatory scrutiny of Arctic development.

A jury in San Francisco on Thursday acquitted Jose Ines Garcia Zarate, an undocumented Mexican immigrant, of murder and involuntary manslaughter in the July 2015 killing of 32-year-old Kate Steinle on Pier 14, but convicted him of being a felon in possession of a firearm. The firearms conviction could carry up to three years; he has already served more than two years in custody and may receive credit for time served. Prosecutors had argued Garcia Zarate intentionally shot Steinle as she walked with her father, claiming he fired into a crowd. The defense maintained the shooting was accidental: Garcia Zarate testified he found a Sig Sauer .40-caliber handgun wrapped in cloth on the pier and that it discharged after he stepped on it or unwrapped it, with the bullet ricocheting off the concrete before striking Steinle. Surveillance showed Garcia Zarate fleeing the scene, and investigators found gunshot residue on his hand; he told police he had aimed at a seal during interrogation. The verdict reignited a national debate over immigration, sanctuary cities and enforcement. Federal officials said they will pursue deportation; Garcia Zarate had been deported five times previously. President Donald Trump called the verdict “disgraceful” and blamed illegal immigration and sanctuary-city policies, as did Attorney General Jeff Sessions and other conservatives who cited the case in support of measures like “Kate’s Law,” proposing stricter penalties for repeated illegal reentry. Defense lawyers and supporters argued the case was improperly politicized and that Garcia Zarate’s immigration status was irrelevant to the shooting. Steinle’s family expressed shock and sorrow, saying “justice was rendered, but it was not served.” The Justice Department said it is considering federal charges.

The Smithsonian’s National Zoo celebrated the birth of two rare Sumatran tiger cubs to 4-year-old Damai on August 5, 2013. Keepers, who had monitored Damai’s pregnancy closely, watched the births live via webcam; the first cub arrived around 6:08 p.m. and the second about two hours later. Both cubs were tiny, blind and initially weighed around two pounds; later exams confirmed a male and a female. Damai has been attentive, nursing and grooming them while keepers monitor from a distance for safety. The cubs will remain off exhibit for months for health checks and vaccinations, though fans can follow them on live cams. With fewer than 500 Sumatran tigers in the wild, the births are a significant conservation success for the critically endangered species.

The document presents two short pieces. The first argues that much public outrage aimed at big tech for privacy violations often overlooks other everyday privacy intrusions—like gossip—and may really reflect a loss of control rather than true concern about data misuse. The author suggests people feel less in control now, partly because media critics frame the issue as solvable, and that inexpensive "placebo" measures (symbolic laws, corporate proclamations, or self-reforms) might assuage that feeling even if underlying privacy losses are irreversible. The piece concludes that reframing matters—“privacy problems aren’t always about privacy.” The second item reports a bizarre March 2014 incident in which George Mason economist and blogger Tyler Cowen was pepper‑sprayed and subjected to a citizen’s arrest by an unknown man during a class on vigilante justice; students detained the attacker and Cowen declined medical treatment.

High Street shoe chain Barratts and DVD rental chain Blockbuster have both entered administration, putting over 3,000 UK and Irish jobs at risk. Duff & Phelps is handling Barratts, reviewing finances and seeking a sale after an investor withdrew a £5m injection; Barratts runs 75 stores and 23 concessions with 1,035 staff. Moorfields Corporate Recovery is administering Blockbuster’s TS Operations; the chain employs about 2,000 across 264 stores and will keep trading while interested parties are sought. Administrators aim to save parts of the businesses and jobs before Christmas; industry watchers expect Barratts might re-emerge smaller.

J.K. Rowling secretly published a crime novel, The Cuckoo’s Calling, under the pseudonym Robert Galbraith, a revelation that sent the book soaring up sales charts. Released in April by Mulholland Books (an imprint of Little, Brown/Hachette), the novel features private investigator Cormoran Strike, a veteran who lost a leg in Afghanistan. The publisher initially presented “Galbraith” as a former member of the Royal Military Police. The Sunday Times exposed Rowling’s authorship after noting connections between the pseudonymous author’s agent, editor and publisher and Rowling’s known collaborators. Rowling confirmed the revelation, calling the experience of writing anonymously “liberating” because it allowed her to publish without hype and receive unvarnished feedback. Sales spiked dramatically after she was unmasked: the book rose to No. 1 on Barnes & Noble’s and Amazon’s U.S. online stores, briefly went out of stock at BarnesandNoble.com, and Amazon reported shipping delays. Little, Brown said a reprint will acknowledge that Robert Galbraith is a pseudonym for J.K. Rowling and announced a second book in the series slated for next summer. Rowling is best known for the Harry Potter series and her adult novel The Casual Vacancy, which has also sold strongly.

Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel sued the Trump Justice Department to block new conditions tied to Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grants that would pressure so-called sanctuary cities to aid federal immigration enforcement. The lawsuit asks a federal judge to bar three recently imposed rules: notifying federal officials 48 hours before an immigrant’s release, granting unrestricted access to police facilities, and sharing immigration-status information. City attorneys argue these mandates exceed the Justice Department’s authority, violate the Constitution (including the Tenth Amendment’s prohibition on commandeering and Fourth Amendment protections against warrantless detention), and would undermine community policing and public safety. Emanuel and Corporation Counsel Ed Siskel stressed the modest $3.2 million grant’s importance and warned the administration’s rhetoric is creating fear in immigrant communities; the suit could also protect nearby suburbs that file through Chicago and have broader implications for other sanctuary jurisdictions nationwide. The move drew praise from immigrant-rights groups but also criticism from activists who want Emanuel to tighten local exemptions that allow police to cooperate with ICE in certain criminal cases. Attorney General Jeff Sessions sharply attacked Chicago, blaming sanctuary policies for violence and warning cities to “comply with the law or forgo taxpayer dollars,” while local police leaders countered that undocumented immigrants are not driving the city’s crime.

Michael Phelps headlined Discovery Channel’s Shark Week special "Phelps vs. Shark: Great Gold vs. Great White," a highly publicized 100-meter open-water matchup that ultimately disappointed some viewers and educated others. The premise pitted the most decorated Olympian against one of the ocean’s fastest predators, but safety and science shaped how the contest was staged. Researchers first recorded a great white’s time by tempting it down a straight 100-meter course with a seal decoy off South Africa; Phelps then swam the same course separately. Producers later superimposed a CGI shark beside Phelps to simulate a side-by-side race, sparking widespread backlash on social media from viewers who expected a live, adjacent showdown and called the broadcast a “scam.” Many expressed anger and confusion; others defended the decision as obviously necessary for safety.

Phelps wore a monofin and a special “shark skin” wetsuit designed to boost buoyancy and reduce drag. Even with those advantages—and despite clocking 38.1 seconds in cold 55°F (13°C) water that shocked his muscles—he finished two seconds slower than the shark’s measured 36.1 seconds. Earlier footage showed Phelps beating a reef shark in a 50-meter trial but losing to a hammerhead. Scientists explained why great whites excel: their partial endothermy and countercurrent heat exchangers let them sustain powerful swimming in cold water. Phelps used the experience to express admiration for sharks and to promote awareness and conservation, stressing that sharks aren’t out to attack humans. The episode combined spectacle, science and staged elements, earning both criticism for its simulated presentation and praise for highlighting shark biology and conservation.

New York Magazine drew swift criticism after publishing a Vulture profile of Soon‑Yi Previn, written by Daphne Merkin, who disclosed she has been friends with Woody Allen for more than 40 years. The piece, in which Previn for the first time publicly responds to longstanding allegations surrounding Allen, his adoptive daughter Dylan Farrow and ex-partner Mia Farrow, also includes Previn’s allegations of years of abuse by her adoptive mother, Mia. Although Merkin’s friendship with Allen is noted in the article, many journalists, commentators and members of the public on Twitter condemned the magazine’s decision to commission a profile of an accuser’s husband by a longtime admirer of the accused filmmaker, calling it a conflict — or at least the appearance of one — that undercuts journalistic integrity. Critics pointed to Merkin’s past writings praising Allen and anecdotes about their relationship, arguing that her history with him made her an inappropriate choice to handle such a sensitive, contested story. Dylan Farrow and her brother Ronan publicly denounced the piece: Ronan accused the article of participating in a “hit job,” criticizing the omission of eyewitness testimony and Dylan’s full responses; Dylan called the choice “disgusting,” saying a friend of an alleged predator should not produce a one‑sided attack on a victim’s credibility. New York Magazine defended the feature, noting Merkin’s connection was disclosed, that Merkin approached Previn, and that Previn, like any person, is entitled to tell her side. The magazine said it sought comment from Mia and Dylan Farrow and framed the article as presenting Soon‑Yi’s perspective. Nonetheless, social media backlash focused on perceived bias, Merkin’s prior admiration for Allen, and whether the magazine should have assigned a more neutral journalist.

Greek political leaders have largely agreed on creditor-demanded austerity measures but are still negotiating pension and wage cuts to find the remaining €1.5 billion needed to complete an €11.5 billion savings target for 2013–2014. International inspectors from the EU, ECB and IMF extended their Athens visit until the plan is finalized; IMF mission chief Poul Thomsen pledged to stay “as long as it takes.” The coalition is debating protections for low pensions and public-sector incomes while exploring layoffs of contractors, pension caps, welfare cuts, reduced tax exemptions, lower public salaries and a one-year rise in retirement age. Greece’s cash reserves are under strain as aid tranches remain withheld, and creditors’ patience is thin. German finance minister Wolfgang Schaeuble dismissed scope for further concessions, warning that a negative inspectors’ report in September could halt aid and risk a disorderly exit from the euro.

Utah’s legislature passed a bill that could let prosecutors charge women with criminal homicide for inducing a miscarriage or for miscarriages caused by “intentional, knowing, or reckless” acts, punishable by up to life in prison; it now awaits the governor’s approval. Unlike most fetal-homicide laws aimed at third-party attackers, this measure targets pregnant women themselves and applies throughout pregnancy. Critics warn the “reckless” standard could criminalize common behavior—drinking, not wearing a seatbelt, staying with an abusive partner, or accidental falls—and could lead to investigations of many first-trimester miscarriages (which account for most pregnancy losses). Advocates from Planned Parenthood, the ACLU, and National Advocates for Pregnant Women say the law would deter women from seeking care, punish vulnerable women, and contradict claims that anti‑abortion efforts do not seek to incarcerate women. Opponents fear it institutionalizes policing of pregnancy and may prompt legal challenges.

Lindsay Lohan’s court hearing concluded, and reporters waited outside for statements as she and her lawyer completed paperwork and were fitted for a SCRAM alcohol-monitoring bracelet. Exclusive video from May 23, 2010, shows Lohan speaking with Sheeraz Hasan of HOLLYWOOD.TV, addressing a swirl of recent rumors: a purported “cocaine” photograph circulating online, her DUI legal matters, allegations about her drug use, and family issues involving her father, Michael Lohan. In the interview she responds to these claims, offers clarification, and becomes emotional discussing personal consequences—such as missing her brother’s graduation—while reflecting on the impact of the publicity and legal proceedings on her life. The footage captures her attempting to set the record straight amid ongoing media scrutiny.

Pakistan is enduring a severe electricity crisis driven by failing infrastructure, policy failures and a pervasive refusal to pay bills. A $5 billion “circular debt” — unpaid bills that cascade through government agencies, wealthy individuals and poor consumers — leaves power producers unable to buy fuel, forcing plants to shut or run intermittently. Theft, corruption and politically motivated contracts have deepened the problem: up to a third of supply is lost in some areas to theft or leaky transmission lines, and large contracts have added little capacity. The crisis has damaged industry and employment, shaving an estimated 4 percent off GDP and prompting protests and political backlash that helped topple the incumbent party in recent elections. Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif has pledged fixes and is seeking foreign oil and investment, including offers from Saudi Arabia and China, but experts say money alone won’t suffice; hard political choices — collecting bills, cracking down on theft, curbing cronyism and rebuilding governance in the energy ministry — are essential. Meanwhile, the government has ordered austerity measures, like banning air-conditioning in offices, while shortages and rising prices promise worsening short-term pain.

Two Northwestern University freshmen, Anthony Morales, 19, and Matthew Kafker, 18, face criminal charges after allegedly spray-painting racist, homophobic and anti-religious graffiti — including a swastika, slurs, depictions of male genitalia and the word “Trump” — inside the nondenominational Alice Millar Chapel on the Evanston campus. The vandalism occurred around 12:45 a.m. Friday; surveillance footage reportedly showed the pair entering the chapel with spray cans. Chapel staff discovered the damage the following morning and reported it to university authorities. Both students gave handwritten and recorded statements to university police admitting involvement, and prosecutors say the estimated damage exceeds $300.

At a Saturday bond hearing, Cook County Judge Peggy Chiampas sharply rebuked the teenagers, calling the allegations “disgusting” and ordering each held on $50,000 bail on charges including institutional vandalism, criminal damage to property and hate crime in a place of worship. The defendants remained largely silent at the hearing; one mother cried in the gallery. University chaplain Tim Stevens and President Morton Schapiro condemned the acts as abhorrent and contrary to campus values. Workers removed most of the graffiti over the weekend and chapel services continued. Authorities have not explained a motive or how the chapel was accessed without signs of forced entry. University police had no immediate additional comment.

Less than two weeks after a Facebook plea to find her biological father, 71-year-old Belgian Florence Heene says she has finally found the missing piece of her identity. Heene had only a few wartime photos and the single name “Herbert,” a Canadian soldier stationed in Ghent during World War II, when she appealed for help. After a CBC News story ran her images, descendants of Vancouver veteran Herbert Louis Hellyer recognized the man and contacted her. Heene is certain Hellyer is her father and says she can now “close it.”

Hellyer, who died in 1948 at age 35, had five children; three survive and live in British Columbia. One daughter, Thelma Janes, expressed shock at discovering a 71-year-old half-sister. Kristy Demidoff, granddaughter of Hellyer’s eldest daughter Betty Ingram, matched Heene’s photo to a wartime picture in the family archives signed “Love from Daddy,” and shared it with Heene. Family members have begun communicating on Facebook and hope to meet and share information.

Hellyer emigrated from England to Canada, worked as a printer, married and had five children before enlisting in 1939. He served six years as an army instructor but suffered a severe brain injury days before the war’s end when thrown from a jeep and struck by a truck. He returned with mental health struggles, was hospitalized at Shaughnessy for veterans, and died by suicide in 1948. Heene is saddened by his tragic fate but grateful to have found relatives and a “new family.” While her mother had long refused to reveal the soldier’s surname, Heene now has confirmation and hopes to learn more about her father’s life and connect with her Canadian kin.

Astronauts returning from spacewalks consistently report a distinctive, lingering smell clinging to suits, helmets and tools—an acrid mix likened to seared steak, hot metal, welding fumes, gunpowder or ozone. Likely caused by atoms and ions such as atomic oxygen reacting with materials, the odor can’t be detected inside suits but is strong once helmets come off. Crew members often find it memorable and not unpleasant. Inside the International Space Station, scents are more mundane: machine-shop, engine-room and lab smells mixed with the aromas of international packaged meals.

A temporary employee at a Rite Aid distribution center in Perryman, Harford County, Maryland, killed three people and wounded three others before fatally shooting herself on Thursday morning, authorities said. Sheriff Jeffrey Gahler identified the shooter as 26-year-old Snochia Moseley of Baltimore County; she died at a nearby hospital from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Deputies arrived within five minutes of a 9:06 a.m. report and found victims both outside the warehouse and on the facility floor. Two victims were pronounced dead at the scene; others were transported to Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center and Christiana Hospital in Delaware. Hospital officials said some patients required surgery; two were stable while others remained seriously injured.

Investigators said Moseley used a legally purchased 9 mm Glock with multiple magazines; she was at one time employed as a security guard at the support facility. Authorities are still seeking a motive and have not released victims’ names while next of kin are notified. No law enforcement officers fired during the response. Federal agencies, including the FBI and ATF, assisted the probe.

The shooting occurred at a large business park that houses Rite Aid and other distributors; roughly 1,000 employees work at the Rite Aid complex. The facility was closed and grief counseling offered. The attack was the third high-profile workplace shooting in the U.S. in 24 hours, prompting calls for attention to gun violence from officials including former Rep. Gabrielle Giffords. Local schools were put on modified lockdown and a reunification center was established for concerned relatives.

The NYPD is seeking a woman connected to the theft and mysterious return of two high‑value photographs from MoMA PS1 in Long Island City. The gelatin‑silver prints, part of the Carolee Schneemann exhibition and valued at about $55,000 and $50,000, were discovered missing by staff on Oct. 30. Four days later, an oversized package containing the undamaged photos arrived at the museum with no note. Police traced the shipment to a Williamsburg, Brooklyn shipping store and reviewed surveillance footage showing a woman in her twenties—wearing a dark cap, glasses, a black coat and tan pants—mailing the box. Investigators have not confirmed whether she stole the works or was acting on someone else’s behalf; the motive remains unclear. There were no signs of forced entry, the alarm was set but did not sound, and PS1 is under video surveillance. The works, on loan from galleries and the artist, were recovered intact; no arrests have been made. Authorities ask anyone with information to contact NYPD Crime Stoppers. Museum officials declined to comment while the investigation continues.
