During a Phoenix speech, Donald Trump invoked “antifa” to suggest the far left is as violent as the far right after the Charlottesville clashes. That framing — echoed by surrogates and folding “antifa” together with terms like “alt-left” — masks a real asymmetry: over the decade ending in 2016, right-wing extremists were responsible for the vast majority of politically motivated killings, while antifa supporters have not been linked to killings. Antifa is not a unified national organization or an ideological movement with a single program; it is a mantle for a loose, local, often male-dominated network concentrated in places like Texas and the Northwest that emphasizes direct confrontation with white supremacists. Members range from anarchists to various Marxists and others uninterested in labels. What binds them is action and style: confronting, exposing, shaming, and sometimes physically opposing racists. Some draw inspiration from militant left groups of the past, prize hypermasculine bravado, and accept force as necessary when legal or political channels seem futile. Few antifa groups routinely carry firearms, though groups like Redneck Revolt have displayed rifles to protect crowds. Many mainstream leftists, including Noam Chomsky, view antifa as a small, counterproductive fringe that hands rhetorical victories to the right. Still, as antifa grows amid a larger anti-Trump wave and in the face of heavily armed right-wing militias and permissive open-carry laws, the risk of further violent clashes — potentially worse than Charlottesville — rises unless police and communities contain escalation.

WEN, the celebrity-stylist Chaz Dean’s sulfate-free “cleansing conditioner” sold by Guthy‑Renker and via infomercials, is the subject of a nationwide class-action lawsuit brought by more than 200 women in 40 states alleging severe hair loss, scalp injury, and related harms. Plaintiffs claim the product can cause hair to fall out in clumps, produce bald spots, clog drains, and provoke scalp irritation and rashes. Court papers assert WEN contains a caustic ingredient that triggers a damaging chemical reaction and that Guthy‑Renker suppressed negative feedback by removing reviews and blocking comments on Facebook. Lead plaintiffs’ counsel say chemists hired for the case found the product “contains virtually no cleanser,” arguing it behaves like lotion that remains in follicles and causes buildup and breakage.

WEN defenders and many fans counter that the products help certain hair types and deny any defect; Guthy‑Renker contends WEN is not responsible for hair loss. Experts warn proving causation will be difficult because female hair loss has many potential causes—genetic, hormonal, styling, or product buildup—and WEN’s worldwide sales involve multiple formulas, complicating ingredient analysis. Notably, some formulations include hydroxycitronellal, banned in the EU for immune-toxicity concerns. Both sides are pursuing mediation and have agreed to limit public statements while seeking a possible settlement. The case highlights tensions between product marketing, consumer reports, and scientific proof of harm.

The Internet Archive has been conducting crawls to preserve webpages as they are created and to capture the pages they reference, with the aim of preserving the version of a referenced page that was live when an author wrote a piece. By archiving both new pages and the pages they link to, the Archive hopes content creators and site maintainers will replace or supplement broken links with links to the archived versions, preserving context and intent even when original pages change or disappear. This initiative, part of a “No More 404” effort, seeks to reduce the prevalence of broken links across the web.

Separately, Los Angeles authorities have identified a long-unidentified victim of the 1992 Los Angeles riots: 18-year-old Armando Ortiz Hernandez. His identity was confirmed recently through a fingerprint taken from his left middle finger, Los Angeles County coroner’s spokesman Ed Winter said. Hernandez’s body was found May 2, 1992, inside an auto parts shop that had been set on fire during the riots; his cause of death was listed as inhalation of smoke, soot, carbon monoxide and thermal burns. Officials did not say whether his prints had been previously checked in databases, and attempts to reach family members were unsuccessful. The 1992 unrest, triggered by the acquittal of four white officers in the beating of Rodney King, resulted in 53 deaths and more than 2,000 injuries over several days.

Nine former NHL players filed a federal lawsuit in Manhattan alleging the league “intentionally created, fostered and promoted a culture of extreme violence” that exposed players to repeated head trauma and long-term health damage. The plaintiffs — including well-known enforcers Dan LaCouture, Jack Carlson and Michael Peluso — accuse the NHL of failing to warn players about concussion risks, hiding information, and profiting from violence. The complaint highlights the enforcer role, historical celebrations of fighting, and cites films and teams that glorified aggression. Some plaintiffs recount severe post-career problems—Peluso reports concussion-related seizures and depression; LaCouture describes concussion symptoms after a 2004 hit. The suit seeks compensatory and punitive damages and demands a jury trial; lawyers say a settlement like the NFL’s $765 million deal is desirable though litigation may proceed. The NHL, which established a concussion study in 1997 and has modified rules more recently, said it is satisfied with its player-safety record and will defend vigorously. This case follows other suits, including Derek Boogaard’s family’s wrongful-death claim and a larger group action from earlier eras.

Elle’s October 25th-anniversary issue, featuring 25 women in their 20s, sparked debate because Gabourey Sidibe appears on one of four separate covers in a close-up portrait while Megan Fox, Lauren Conrad and Amanda Seyfried get full-body shots. Critics argued the Sidibe cover looked different in troubling ways: her skin appears noticeably lighter than usual, the shot is awkwardly cropped—omitting the standard three-quarter, centered composition used for other women—and her hairstyle (a visible weave) was unflattering. Salon and others called the presentation a form of fetishization or patronizing treatment. Observers linked the skin-lightening suspicion to a recurring industry pattern in which retouching makes women of color appear lighter and alters how men of color are depicted. Elle responded that Sidibe’s image was not retouched more or less than the others and that the portfolio featured varied treatments to reflect different stories; they defended the choice, saying Sidibe was selected for “who she is.” Supporters note that landing a cover is a milestone for Sidibe, who has been frequently sidelined by fashion magazines and previously left off high-profile spreads. Critics counter that when magazines misrepresent the bodies or skin of full-figured women of color, the coverage can feel less like a triumph and more like another industry misstep.

The London School of Economics is investigating allegations that a Nazi-themed drinking game at a students’ union skiing trip in Val d'Isère led to a brawl in which a Jewish student’s nose was broken. Around 150 athletics union students attended the trip. The LSE Jewish Society said the assault followed the student objecting to a Ring of Fire variant arranged into a swastika, with participants required to "salute the Führer." The injured student told the Guardian that while the game itself was familiar, the antisemitic taunts and personal insults that followed after he left the game escalated matters and left him deeply upset. Student and university leaders condemned the behavior: LSE and the students’ union said they are investigating and will take disciplinary action if allegations are proven, stressing zero tolerance for antisemitism and racism. Athletics union and SU officials described the actions as those of a small minority at odds with institutional values. The incident echoes wider concerns about antisemitism on campuses after recent reports of similar behavior elsewhere.

The document covers two main stories: a critique of current spectrum allocation and developments in the U.S.-China trade dispute over soybeans. Entrepreneur Declan Ganley argues that the auction-based model for allocating mobile spectrum—used in the U.S. and other countries—favors large incumbents with deep pockets, stifling innovation and recreating a top-down structure he likens to feudalism. He contends that this model disadvantages U.S. and European carriers competing fiercely for customers and profits, while China’s state-backed, concentrated operators can sustain investment and potentially pull ahead in 5G deployment. Ganley and his firm, Rivada Networks, advocate replacing auctions with a wholesale, electricity-style market that would enable dynamic access and pricing and broaden participation. Elements of the Trump administration have signaled openness to spectrum sharing; advisors and commentators have suggested wholesale approaches could aid U.S. competitiveness, though some analysts remain skeptical about whether such a shift would deliver promised benefits.

Separately, the report details immediate effects of retaliatory Chinese tariffs on U.S. agricultural exports after Washington imposed duties on Chinese goods. A U.S. soybean carrier raced to reach Dalian before levies took effect but likely missed the window. U.S. soybean cash prices plunged to near-decade lows, while Brazilian exporters benefited from surging premiums as China pivots to Brazilian supplies, buying significant volumes and widening the price gap—raising prospects of a quarter‑to‑quarter shift in trade patterns.

A surprise birth on the remote Brazilian archipelago of Fernando de Noronha has produced the first baby on the island in 12 years, despite a long-standing policy banning local childbirths. The 22-year-old mother, who did not want to be named, said she and her family were unaware she was pregnant; she went into labor at home late Friday, discovered the newborn in the bathroom, and the baby girl was helped by the child’s father and later taken to the island hospital. Fernando de Noronha, a national maritime park renowned for beaches and wildlife and home to about 3,000 residents, lacks a maternity ward and requires expectant mothers to travel roughly 230–370 km to the mainland for delivery. Local authorities confirmed the incident, and residents have been donating clothes and assistance to the family. Strict population controls remain in place to protect the reserve.

At memorial events and Sunday shows following Sen. John McCain’s death, friends and former colleagues defended his daughter Meghan’s pointed criticism of President Donald Trump, saying it reflected McCain’s character. Sen. Lindsey Graham and ex-Sen. Joe Lieberman praised Meghan’s directness and honored the late senator’s Senate legacy, describing McCain as fearless, devoted to the institution, and irreplaceable. Former Secretary of State John Kerry contrasted today’s leadership unfavorably with McCain’s bipartisan approach, calling current political figures “so-called leaders” operating in a “fact-less world.” Former Defense Secretary Leon Panetta urged Democrats to await Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s report before pursuing impeachment, warning that efforts to undermine Mueller could backfire and that Mueller’s findings will determine next steps, including potential obstruction considerations tied to actions against the investigation.

ESPN commentator Rob Parker sparked widespread outrage after questioning whether Washington Redskins quarterback Robert Griffin III was “really” black because he has a white fiancée. Parker’s on-air remarks on First Take prompted criticism across social media and from figures like NFLPA chief DeMaurice Smith, who said people must be held accountable for offensive comments. Parker initially defended himself on Twitter, calling critics “uneducated” and “silly,” and hinted the discussion would continue on First Take, but he stopped tweeting and ESPN later suspended him indefinitely while conducting a review, calling the remarks inappropriate. The episode is part of recurring racial controversies in the NFL this season, from scrutiny of Colin Kaepernick’s tattoos to debates over Cam Newton’s treatment, and commentary that resurrects dated stereotypes about black quarterbacks. Griffin’s father called Parker’s comments provocative rather than plainly racist, while critics argued such generalizations are unhelpful and echo past racialized questioning of black athletes.

An orca known as J35 or "Tahlequah," a 20-year-old member of the endangered Southern Resident J Pod, carried her dead newborn calf for at least 17 days and roughly 1,000 miles in waters off Washington and British Columbia. The unprecedented, highly publicized episode—during which she pushed and balanced the calf on her rostrum, sometimes with other pod members taking turns—drew global attention and reinforced scientific views that cetaceans have complex emotional lives and can exhibit mourning-like behaviors. Observers recorded mournful calls and close family support; J35’s son J47 stayed nearby and other relatives appeared to feed and assist her, likely sharing the physical burden. Photographs and shore-based telephoto images indicated J35 remained in good physical condition despite concerns that the prolonged effort could harm her.

The calf was first seen alive only briefly after birth on July 24, and researchers await necropsy results to determine whether it was stillborn or died shortly after. The loss compounds a broader population crisis: the three southern resident pods (J, K and L) total just 75 individuals and have had no surviving births since 2015. Scientists attribute declines mainly to dwindling Chinook salmon stocks—the orcas’ preferred, energy-rich prey—plus threats from noise, pollution and disturbance. Some researchers warn the population may have as little as five years of reproductive opportunity left to recover without significant intervention.

Officials from U.S. and Canadian agencies worked with volunteers to keep boats away and monitor the pod, urging the public to respect regulations and report whales in distress. The episode prompted calls for stronger conservation action—especially measures to restore Chinook runs and reduce human impacts—so this culturally and genetically distinct population might survive.

Mike Megna, a 44-year-old former Marine and Pompton Lakes police officer, believes his rare kidney disease stems from three weeks he spent working at Ground Zero after the Sept. 11 attacks. He and his brothers searched for survivors and helped clear debris; Megna returned nearly daily for about three weeks. Years later he began urinating blood and developed chronic anemia. After extensive testing his condition was recently diagnosed at the Mayo Clinic as a newly named, extremely rare form of kidney disease — monotype atypical anti–glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) nephritis — one of only about 20 documented cases worldwide. In this disease, defective antibodies produced by bone marrow attack the kidneys’ filtering membranes; treatment options are limited and doctors advised watchful waiting because chemotherapy risks outweigh benefits. Prognosis is slow progression toward eventual dialysis in several years.

Megna has been unable to work since 2011 and is on disability, his finances strained; his house in West Milford has been foreclosed. He received some compensation earlier for respiratory and digestive conditions from the Victim Compensation Fund, but his kidney disease is not on the official list of 9/11-related illnesses covered under the James Zadroga Health and Compensation Act. That program requires published, peer-reviewed epidemiologic evidence that an illness occurs at higher rates in exposed responders than in the general population before adding a condition. Researchers at Mount Sinai are conducting kidney studies; previous research suggested a link but was not decisive. Officials say they will reconsider adding kidney disease after relevant studies are published, but Megna says he cannot wait years. Frustrated, he bought billboards and launched DoRightByMike.com to press authorities and seek help, urging the head of the World Trade Center Health Program and appealing publicly for action so he can obtain compensation to cover mounting losses. Clinicians acknowledge causation is biologically plausible but say the tiny number of cases makes statistical proof difficult, leaving Megna trapped between clinical reality and bureaucratic requirements.

New U.S. guidelines update the definition of Alzheimer’s for the first time in nearly 30 years, framing it as a continuum that can begin years before dementia is evident. The guidance adds earlier stages, including a pre-symptomatic phase with brain changes and a middle phase of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) where daily function remains largely intact. Biomarkers—amyloid, tau, brain atrophy and spinal fluid or blood measures—are highlighted as crucial for earlier detection and research, but are not yet recommended for routine clinical use because tests lack standardization and clear abnormal cutoffs. Clinical diagnosis will still rely on clinician judgment, and there is no proven disease-modifying therapy yet. The guidelines aim to spur research, enable earlier planning for patients and caregivers, and prepare for future treatments that could be more effective if started earlier.

Paul Ceglia, a 39-year-old New Yorker who sued Facebook and CEO Mark Zuckerberg in 2010 claiming an 84% stake in the company, has been federally indicted on wire and mail fraud charges for allegedly fabricating evidence. Authorities say Ceglia did contract Zuckerberg in 2003 for work, but created a falsified agreement claiming Zuckerberg granted him at least a 50% interest in Facebook. He’s accused of forging emails, destroying evidence and pleaded not guilty; each count carries up to 20 years. Ceglia was arrested last month and faces a November federal court appearance. His Ohio attorney, Dean Boland, has moved to withdraw, joining several prior counsel who left the case. Facebook has sought dismissal, calling the suit a fraud and arguing documents were forged and the claim is time-barred.

Tens to thousands of Afghans staged violent protests in Kabul over reported Quran burnings in the U.S., chanting anti-American and anti-government slogans days before parliamentary elections. Demonstrators burned tires, waved Taliban flags, hurled stones and blocked roads; police say some protesters fired pistols. Security forces fired warning shots and into the air to disperse crowds; witnesses and officials reported at least one killed and five wounded, including two with gunshot wounds. Authorities and observers warned the Taliban may be exploiting the outrage to turn demonstrations into anti-government unrest ahead of the vote.

Amanda Palmer and Jason Webley’s concept album Evelyn Evelyn introduces a fictional pair of conjoined twins, Eva and Lyn Neville, through theatrical, genre-hopping songs and spoken-word interludes that tell their picaresque tale of marginalization, abuse, and oddball adventures. The project mixes cabaret, folk, country, ’80s pop pastiche and ukulele-driven numbers; highlights include the show-tune “Have You Seen My Sister Evelyn,” the folky “You Only Want Me ’Cause You Want My Sister,” the power-ballad “My Space,” and a stripped-down cover of Joy Division’s “Love Will Tear Us Apart.” The album features a cameo-heavy chorus — including Frances Bean Cobain, “Weird Al” Yankovic, Tegan and Sara, Gerard Way and Andrew WK — though guests are blended into the mix rather than spotlighted. Frances Bean Cobain, while praised for her singing, is noted more for her visual art and distinctive personal drive. Evelyn Evelyn is eccentric and divisive but rewarding for listeners willing to engage with its darkly whimsical world.

On Nov. 21, 2012, former Florida Highway Patrol trooper Robert Boody’s retired police dog, Drake, a 5-year-old German shepherd, was shot and later euthanized. The shooting led to the arrest of then-16-year-old Ivins Rosier. During a recorded November 2012 interrogation, Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office Detective Philip DiMola pressed Rosier, telling him, “If you shoot that dog and he dies, that’s murder of a law enforcement officer.” Rosier ultimately confessed, and investigators tied him to the scene with GPS ankle monitor records placing him inside Boody’s home the night of the incident. Rosier was charged as an adult and tried this week on felony counts including cruelty to animals with a firearm, burglary of a dwelling with a firearm, and shooting into a building. The jury convicted him on those felony counts. Circuit Judge Robin Rosenberg ordered the now-17-year-old held without bail at the Palm Beach County Jail; she sentenced him to 23 years in prison. Defense attorneys Jack Fleischman and Rachel Preefer said they will seek a new trial and pursue other legal challenges. They plan to renew a pretrial argument that Rosier’s indictment violates his right to be sentenced as a juvenile, which would carry substantially lighter penalties. Fleischman also maintains there is insufficient evidence to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt despite the confession and GPS data.

House and Senate Democratic leaders said they reached an understanding with President Donald Trump to protect hundreds of thousands of young undocumented immigrants and pursue border security measures that would not include Trump’s proposed contiguous border wall. After a White House dinner, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic Leader Nancy Pelosi said they agreed to move quickly to enshrine Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) protections into law and craft a bipartisan border-security package excluding the wall. A person briefed on the talks said the deal would center on bipartisan DREAM Act-style legislation providing eventual citizenship for DACA beneficiaries. The White House called the meeting “constructive,” while Trump said he favored protections for “dreamers” but insisted on “massive border security” and maintained he would pursue the wall later. The apparent pact marks another instance in which Trump bypassed GOP leaders to negotiate with Democrats, following earlier bipartisan deals on spending and the debt ceiling. Republicans, especially House conservatives, expressed alarm; hard-liners warned a deal could alienate Trump’s base. Leaders acknowledged many details remain to be negotiated and that congressional Republican unity is uncertain. Schumer and Pelosi said they hoped to finalize legislation quickly, but Speaker Paul Ryan and GOP members signaled further deliberation and resistance within their conference.

Leaked emails from hacked AshleyMadison servers reveal that a former Avid Life Media (ALM) CTO, Raja Bhatia, claimed in November 2012 to have exploited a security flaw in competitor Nerve.com, exfiltrating its entire user database and gaining the ability to alter records, convert users between paid and unpaid status, and fabricate messages. Bhatia emailed CEO Noel Biderman and COO Rizwan Jiwan, and allegedly posted a sample to GitHub. Six months later Biderman asked Bhatia whether ALM should disclose the vulnerability to Nerve; the leaks don’t show a reply or confirm any disclosure. Bhatia had been ALM’s founding CTO (2007–2010) and elsewhere acknowledged AshleyMadison’s own poor security practices, admitting passwords were likely stored without proper cryptography. The broader Biderman email cache (January 2012–July 2015) — released by the Impact Team alongside a dumped user database — shows ALM considered buying Nerve and other properties, debated security audits, and later faced the massive breach that exposed millions of users. The dump also included sensitive personal and corporate documents from Biderman’s inbox. If Bhatia did hack Nerve, he could face charges under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. The revelations deepen scrutiny of ALM’s conduct and security failures amid ongoing fallout from the AshleyMadison breach.

An annual Chronicle of Higher Education report on 2011–12 compensation for public university presidents found sharply rising pay at the top and growing use of lucrative deferred and severance arrangements. Pennsylvania State University’s Graham B. Spanier was the highest-paid public university president that year at $2.9 million, a total that included $1.2 million in severance and $1.2 million in deferred compensation; he had been forced out in November 2011 over the Jerry Sandusky child sex abuse scandal. Other presidents with total pay above $1 million were Jay Gogue of Auburn ($2.54 million), E. Gordon Gee of Ohio State ($1.90 million), and Alan G. Merten of George Mason ($1.87 million). The report documents a “sea change” in compensation, with some packages reaching $2 million-plus and many more presidents clustered in the $600,000–$700,000 range (28 executives, up from 13 the prior year). Median total compensation for public research university presidents was $441,392 (up 4.7%), and median base salary was $373,800 (up 2%). Other top earners included leaders at Ball State, Michigan, Virginia Tech, UC, Florida, and Texas.

Archaeologists from the University of Buckingham have declared Amesbury, Wiltshire — the parish that includes Stonehenge — Britain’s oldest continuously occupied settlement, with evidence of habitation dating back to about 8,820 BC. Carbon-dated aurochs bones from the Blick Mead/Vespasian’s Camp site indicate continuous use of the area through each millennium since then, pushing Amesbury’s origins roughly 1,100 years earlier than Thatcham, the previous record-holder. The team, led by David Jacques, argues the finds reshape understanding of the Neolithic transition: rather than Stonehenge being built in an empty landscape by incoming continental farmers, its earliest monuments grew out of a long-established local Mesolithic community that cleared land, built timber monuments, and attracted visitors across wide regions.

Excavations recovered an extraordinary 31,000 worked Mesolithic flints from a 16-square-metre area in just over 40 days, plus large-game remains (aurochs, red deer, wild boar) and evidence of feasting, including frog bones. The site’s warm, constant spring — producing a distinctive pink hue on flints via algae — and proximity to the River Avon likely made it a longstanding focal point and “Mesolithic London,” drawing people from both west and east. Researchers say Blick Mead fills a chronological gap between early timber posts (8,820–6,590 BC) and Stonehenge’s stone phases (~3,000 BC), suggesting indigenous hunters and homemakers were central to the area’s monument-building traditions. The discovery has been recognized by Guinness World Records and filmed for forthcoming documentaries.

Old Rag Mountain is Shenandoah National Park’s most popular — and one of its most hazardous — hikes. The circuit spans about nine miles with significant elevation change and a strenuous rock scramble that requires good upper-body strength; children and shorter adults often need assistance. Hikers are advised to plan carefully: allow seven to eight hours, bring at least two quarts of water per person, wear sturdy ankle-supporting shoes, pack light (many prefer fanny packs to backpacks for the scramble), carry a headlamp, check the forecast and avoid wet or icy conditions, stay with your group and on the trail, and never let children run ahead. Pets are prohibited. Weekday visits reduce crowding; parking fills quickly on weekends and the trail’s narrow passages can create long waits. All hikers must use the large parking area at the Old Rag Fee Station and have a valid Shenandoah entrance permit; parking along road shoulders is prohibited. Patrols have been increased and some spaces are reserved for staff and search-and-rescue. Overnight camping is limited and restricted above 2,800 feet; backcountry permits are required. Numerous resources — including Old Rag Mountain Stewards, hiking websites, guidebooks, and Shenandoah NP pages — offer maps, trip suggestions, and safety information to help visitors prepare.

Separately, in April 2016, 31-year-old Fairfax County firefighter and paramedic Nicole K. Mittendorff was reported missing after failing to show for a shift. Her 2009 Mini Cooper was found near the White Oak Canyon Trail, close to Old Rag. Described as a 5'6" white female, 125 lbs., with blonde hair and green eyes, she had last contacted her family on April 13. State, park, and federal authorities searched by ground and air; family and community organized search efforts, a Facebook page (Find-Nicole), and a prayer vigil while urging anyone with information to contact Virginia State Police.

A scientist has published a practical guide to reduce deaths from radioactive fallout after a small nuclear detonation in a city. Michael Dillon of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory used mathematical modeling to determine the “optimal shelter exit time” — when people should leave an initial, often poor-quality shelter to reach better protection without incurring excessive radiation risk. His analysis, published in Proceedings of the Royal Society A, focuses on low-yield blasts (0.1–10 kilotons). Key findings: if adequate shelter (for example, an underground or thickly built interior space) is reachable within 15 minutes, people in flimsy or basement-less dwellings should remain where they are for up to 30 minutes after the blast before relocating. If a better shelter is within five minutes, however, evacuees should move there immediately and skip closer, inadequate buildings. Rapid access to suitable shelters could save between 10,000 and 100,000 lives in a single low-yield detonation, the study estimates. Dillon stresses simplicity: quickly assess the quality of immediate shelter and the travel time to superior protection. Practical factors such as traffic, mode of travel, and the availability of adequate nearby shelters complicate planning; over 20 percent of U.S. households lack basements. Dillon is mapping shelter distribution across the U.S. to inform emergency planning, emphasizing that these guidelines are one component of a broader nuclear incident response strategy.

The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR) reported that the Islamic State (IS) executed 1,878 people in Syria between June 28, 2014—when IS declared a “caliphate”—and December 27, 2014. The majority were civilians: 1,175 victims, among them four children and eight women, killed by beheading, shooting or stoning across Deir Ezzor, Raqqa, al-Hasakah, Aleppo, Homs and Hama. Of those civilians, 930 belonged to the al-Shaitaat (Shaitat) tribe from eastern Deir Ezzor, which rose up against IS after clashes over control of oilfields; a mass grave of 230 Shaitat was reported discovered on Dec. 17. SOHR also documented 502 regime soldiers and militiamen executed after capture, 81 fighters from Jabhat al-Nusra and other rebel or Islamic battalions executed following arrest or battlefield capture, and roughly 120 IS members—largely foreign fighters attempting to return home—executed for “exceeding the limits in religion” or trying to flee. SOHR cautioned the true death toll is likely higher due to missing persons, detainees in IS prisons, and unresolved disappearances— including dozens of Kurds missing since IS’s September attack on Ayn al-Arab (Kobani). International reporting notes IS has publicized many executions; U.S.-led coalition air strikes continued against IS positions in Syria and Iraq during this period.

George Herbert Walker Bush, who died at 94, served as the 41st U.S. president, leading a swift victory in the 1991 Persian Gulf War and guiding the U.S. through the peaceful end of the Cold War, the dissolution of the Soviet Union and German reunification. A World War II Navy pilot—shot down in the Pacific and awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross—he returned home, married Barbara Pierce, finished at Yale and built a career in Texas oil before entering politics. His résumé included two terms in the House, ambassador to the United Nations, envoy to China, chairman of the Republican National Committee, CIA director and vice president under Ronald Reagan. Elected president in 1988 promising a “kinder and gentler nation,” his pledge “Read my lips: No new taxes” later backfired when he agreed to tax increases amid a recession, eroding support and contributing to his 1992 loss to Bill Clinton. Known for loyalty, steadiness during crises and international statesmanship, he later forged bipartisan friendships—most notably with Clinton—worked on humanitarian causes in retirement, and saw his eldest son, George W. Bush, become president. He was predeceased this year by his wife, Barbara.

The bodies of three Israeli teenagers—Eyal Yifrach (19), Gilad Shaar (16) and Naftali Frenkel (16), a U.S.-Israeli citizen—were found in a shallow grave near Hebron on Monday, after they went missing on 12 June while hitchhiking home from West Bank religious schools. Israeli officials said the youths were likely shot soon after being abducted; investigators reported signs consistent with them being killed inside a stolen car and that their bodies were later buried under stones near Halhul. The discovery followed a massive search that included arrests of more than 400 Palestinians and clashes that left several Palestinians dead; families of Palestinians killed have complained their losses received less attention.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu blamed Hamas, declaring “Hamas is responsible and Hamas will pay,” and vowed retribution. Hamas denies involvement and warned Israel against escalation, while a small group calling itself Ansar as-Dawla al-Islamiya claimed responsibility—an assertion that could not be independently verified. The Israeli military named two alleged suspects, Marwan Kawasme and Omar Abu Aysha, and demolished their West Bank homes; footage showed extensive damage. Israeli forces also carried out raids in Jenin and other West Bank areas, and an 18-year-old Palestinian was killed during an operation there.

In response to rocket fire from Gaza—18 projectiles reported since Sunday—Israel launched dozens of air strikes, targeting sites it said were linked to Hamas and Islamic Jihad; Gaza health officials reported wounded civilians and blackouts after hits on infrastructure. International reactions included condolences and calls for restraint: President Obama urged Israeli-Palestinian cooperation to find perpetrators and warned against steps that could further destabilize the region; the UN urged maximum restraint. While Israeli leaders insist on decisive action, some officials signaled reluctance to become mired in a prolonged conflict, and funeral ceremonies for the teens were marked by national mourning and heightened tensions across Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories.

A large US study published in the BMJ suggests that adherence to a Mediterranean diet—rich in vegetables, fruits, nuts, legumes, whole grains, olive oil and fish, and low in red and processed meat—is associated with longer leukocyte telomeres, a marker of cellular aging. Researchers analyzed data from 4,676 healthy women in the Nurses’ Health Study, comparing dietary patterns from food-frequency questionnaires with telomere length measured in blood. After adjusting for age, BMI, smoking, physical activity, calorie intake and other factors, higher Mediterranean diet scores correlated with longer telomeres; the trend remained significant across multivariable models. The investigators estimated that each one-point increase in the diet adherence score corresponded to roughly 1.5 fewer years of cellular aging, so a three-point improvement equated to about 4.5 years—comparable to differences between smokers and non-smokers. No single food component stood out, highlighting potential synergistic effects of the overall dietary pattern. Authors propose reduced oxidative stress and inflammation as plausible mechanisms. Limitations include the cross-sectional design, single telomere measurement, possible residual confounding and limited ethnic diversity of the cohort. While results are supportive, experts caution they do not prove causation.

Alaska’s GOP Senate primary between incumbent Sen. Lisa Murkowski and Joe Miller remains too close to call as state election officials report more than 20,000 absentee and questioned ballots still to be processed. Miller led by 1,668 votes after Election Day. Of the outstanding ballots, 11,266 absentees have been returned so far (from over 16,000 requested), plus 658 early votes and 8,972 questioned ballots; many are expected to be Republican. Officials plan staged counts through early September, and some questioned ballots may be disqualified. Miller, buoyed by Sarah Palin’s endorsement, said he expects to hold his lead and warned against any legal challenges if he prevails. Murkowski’s camp urged patience and noted she’s considering all options, including a possible Libertarian run if she loses; the Alaska Libertarian Party and its candidate have discussed stepping aside. National attention has escalated amid concerns about legal intervention and party involvement.

New research from the University of Lincoln used a rigorously controlled, counterbalanced adaptation of Ainsworth’s Strange Situation Test (SST) to investigate whether domestic cats form secure attachments to their owners in the same way dogs and human infants do. Twenty owner–cat pairs completed two versions of a nine-episode SST in an unfamiliar room involving the owner, a stranger, separations and reunions. The team focused on three operational features of attachment: proximity/contact seeking, a secure-base effect (more exploration/play in the presence of the caregiver) and distress at separation.

Most putative behavioural measures were unreliable across test repetitions or influenced by episode-order effects, reducing their value for assessing attachment. Cats did vocalise more when the owner rather than the stranger left, but this alone was insufficient to infer secure attachment; vocalisation may reflect frustration or learned reinforcement (e.g., previous attention or feeding), not panic-like separation distress. Measures that would indicate a secure base—greater exploration, reduced vigilance, or increased play when the owner was present—were not consistently observed. Marking (body rubbing) shifted over the test: early episodes showed more marking toward the stranger (possibly to reduce arousal/familiarize), while later episodes showed increased marking of the owner, suggesting familiarity dynamics rather than attachment. Passive behaviours often reflected inhibition or anxiety rather than relaxation.

The authors conclude that adult cats are typically more autonomous than dogs in social contexts: while many cats show social preferences for their owners, these relationships do not usually meet Bowlby’s operational definition of a secure attachment based on safety and security provision. The SST may not be fully appropriate for cats, and alternative methods are needed. Separation-related problems reported in some cats may reflect frustration rather than classical attachment-based distress. Individual variation exists, and a minority of cats might form stronger attachment-like bonds, but this is not the norm.

During the early hours of March 12–13, 2014, a suspected drunken driver, later identified as Rashad Charjuan Owens (also reported as Rashad Owens), drove through temporary police barricades on Red River Street in downtown Austin during the South by Southwest (SXSW) festival. The vehicle plowed into a crowd of concertgoers, killing two people—a Dutch cyclist and an Austin woman on a moped—and injuring 23 others, five critically. Witness photos and captions documented frantic bystanders administering CPR, paramedics transporting victims, and authorities working the scene. The driver reportedly attempted to evade a checkpoint after an incident at a Shell station near I-35 and 9th Street; he was tased and taken into custody and faces capital murder charges. Austin Police Chief Art Acevedo and SXSW Managing Director Roland Swenson addressed the media, describing the crash as intentional and confirming the festival would continue. The community responded with vigils and a candlelight service at St. David’s Episcopal Church, where the mayor and police leaders joined mourners. Photos showed crime scene tape, floral tributes, and crowds near venues such as the Mohawk, underscoring the shock across the festival and city. Emergency units, including University Medical Center staff, briefed media on victims’ conditions as investigations proceeded.

After announcing he would resign on Wednesday following the Brexit vote, British prime minister David Cameron was heard merrily humming to himself as he walked back into Number 10. The short, jaunty snippet—captured on microphone before he removed it—prompted a flurry of speculation and online reaction. Commentators compared the tune to everything from the West Wing theme and Winnie-the-Pooh to the Dam Busters fanfare; ITV political editor Robert Peston likened it to a Pooh-style ditty, while Classic FM called the notes “Beethoven-esque.” Some analysts suggested a Wagnerian fanfare or even the opening of Shostakovich’s Fifth Symphony. A closer musical reading described a brisk 3/4 time with an anacrusis, a confident leap followed by an uneasy descent creating “harmonic doubt,” and the decisive spoken “Right” landing on the next bar—interpreted as a contemporary, almost theatrical flourish. Twitter responses ranged from amused to interpretive, with some viewing Cameron’s relaxed hum as a sign of relief at leaving office. Media and musical commentators treated the brief moment as a light, revealing coda to his resignation, inviting playful reworkings and symbolic readings of his farewell tune.

Leonardo DiCaprio will star as H.H. Holmes in Paramount’s long-gestating adaptation of Erik Larson’s The Devil in the White City, with Martin Scorsese directing. Paramount acquired the rights after a competitive auction; Billy Ray is writing the screenplay. DiCaprio and Jennifer Davisson’s Appian Way, Stacey Sher, Scorsese, Rick Yorn and Emma Koskoff produce, and Paramount executives Marc Evans and Elizabeth Raposo will oversee. DiCaprio first joined the project in 2010; the story interweaves architect Daniel H. Burnham’s 1893 Chicago World’s Fair with Holmes’s “murder castle,” where he lured and killed dozens of young women. The film reunites DiCaprio and Scorsese after The Wolf of Wall Street and marks a major studio commitment to a longtime passion project.

A 36-year-old Colorado woman, Michelle Marie Thompson of Arvada, was arrested Feb. 28 for trespassing at the New York Mets’ First Data Field in Port St. Lucie after repeatedly returning to the complex and refusing to leave, according to a police report. Team staff first confronted Thompson Feb. 26 after she had been loitering around the facility since early morning asking about Tim Tebow, who had arrived for minor league camp. An officer noticed a sticker on her license that read “I (heart) Jesus/Tim Tebow.” When asked why she was there, Thompson claimed she was in a relationship with Tebow and, when pressed about the nature of that relationship, giggled and answered “all of the above.” She also told officers she was living with Tebow in Jacksonville, saying her Colorado address was not current. Mets executive Paul Taglieri asked that she be removed; she was told to return to her vehicle and leave the area and was advised it would be best to leave St. Lucie County. Two days later she returned and was arrested; she remained in the county jail on $750 bail. Tebow said he feels safe at the facility, hopes Thompson gets help, and that players are trained to focus and rely on security when issues arise.

The document surveys shifts in photography, cloud services and operating‑system openness, then reports a tech product launch. The writer argues that long experience—especially with cameras—gives perspective and counsels against endless complaints about digital photography, suggesting that criticism often overlooks progress. A sidebar explains why developers should care about Apple’s CloudKit: iCloud’s many moving parts can be powerful but historically brittle, producing confusing outages and cryptic errors for developers; CloudKit aims to provide a clearer framework for cloud storage and sync. The piece also notes Apple’s growing openness, comparing the company’s 2014 Yosemite public beta approach to the original public previews of OS X in 2000, highlighting a shift toward inviting user feedback before release. Finally, an article excerpt reports that Samsung and Google jointly unveiled the Galaxy Nexus smartphone running a new Android release in Hong Kong, timed just after Apple revealed the iPhone 4S—part of Samsung’s broader push to expand its presence in a fiercely competitive, litigious smartphone market.

Cobalt, a silvery-blue metal essential to lithium-ion batteries, is fueling a new mining rush similar to 19th-century gold booms. Once typically recovered as a by-product of copper and nickel mining, rising demand driven by electronics and electric vehicles has pushed cobalt into primary focus. Global consumption has jumped—from about 75,000 tonnes in 2011 to an expected 122,000 tonnes this year—with prices rising sharply. Around 300 companies worldwide are now exploring cobalt deposits, and major miners are expanding output in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which supplies over 60% of mined cobalt. China dominates refining. In the United States, after decades without significant cobalt extraction, several firms are reviving projects in Idaho, Montana, Missouri, Alaska and elsewhere. Companies such as First Cobalt and eCobalt aim to develop domestic mines within a few years, partly to reduce reliance on imports and to offer ethically sourced, “made in America” cobalt that may command a premium. U.S. policymakers labeled cobalt a critical mineral earlier this year. However, the DRC’s vast reserves and growing production mean the U.S. will likely still import significant volumes. The boom has a dark side: escalating demand has intensified exploitative and dangerous mining practices in the DRC, including child labour and hazardous working conditions documented by Amnesty International and others. Advocacy and proposed laws—such as Australia’s Modern Slavery Bill—seek to force companies to audit supply chains and reduce links to abuses. Meanwhile, researchers pursue cobalt-free battery chemistries, but scalable alternatives remain five to ten years away, suggesting cobalt will remain important in the near term.

A pair of female capybaras escaped from their pen at Toronto’s High Park Zoo on May 24 while staff were moving a third capybara into the enclosure. More than two weeks later, one remained at large and was briefly spotted Marching through headlines and social media after being seen swimming at the south end of High Park near The Queensway. Breakfast Television cameraman Bertram Dandy encountered one of the animals while setting up for a weather shot; he described it as “ninja-still,” like a log, before it clambered up a bank. An earlier sighting on June 5 led city staff to set traps the next morning; traps were visible in the park as officials continued efforts to recapture the duo, nicknamed “Bonnie and Clyde” by the public.

Capybaras are the world’s largest rodents, semi-aquatic grazers native to South America. In the wild they can reach well over four feet in length and weigh up to about 175 pounds (some captive individuals have exceeded 220 pounds). Adaptable and capable swimmers, they often flee into deep water when threatened and can remain mostly submerged, surfacing far away to evade predators. They are generally nonaggressive toward humans and more likely to retreat than bite, though they have been known to bite on rare occasions.

The escape drew widespread public attention—with parody social accounts, an online game, and quips from Mayor John Tory—but also raised concerns from animal-welfare advocates. ZooCheck warned the High Park Zoo could face charges under Ontario’s animal cruelty laws, citing the facility’s history of previous escapes, including a peacock that ran free for days the prior year and a 2009 incident where multiple animals escaped after enclosures were opened. Experts also warned that while capybaras adapt well in summer, Toronto winters are likely too harsh for them to survive if they remain at large.

National Louis University is offering a heavily discounted Groupon for a graduate-level introductory teaching course, marking the first time an academic university has used the site to attract students. The three-credit course, designed for those with no prior teaching experience who hold an undergraduate degree, will be offered only at the Chicago campus and runs Monday evenings from late September to December. Regular tuition is $2,232; the Groupon price is $950, a nearly 60% reduction. The deal goes live Tuesday, will remain available through Wednesday or until it sells out, and is limited to 25 slots with a minimum 15 buyers required for the offer to activate. While the class counts toward a graduate degree, it represents only three of the 36 credits needed to graduate; further enrollment requires the university’s standard admissions process. University officials say the promotion aims to expose prospective teachers to the profession’s realities and encourage committed candidates, while Groupon calls it an experimental, career-starting opportunity for subscribers.

Former President Barack Obama broke with tradition by publicly criticizing President Donald Trump’s Jan. 27 executive order limiting immigration, backing airport protesters and saying, through spokesman Kevin Lewis, that Obama “fundamentally disagrees with the notion of discriminating against individuals because of their faith or religion.” Lewis added that protesters represent the civic engagement expected when American values are at stake. The order indefinitely bars Syrian refugees, suspends all refugee admissions for 120 days, and temporarily bars travelers from seven predominantly Muslim countries. Its implementation caused chaos at airports as some refugees, visa holders and even permanent residents were detained or turned away, prompting legal challenges including a temporary federal stay won by the ACLU. The White House defended the policy as counterterrorism, with Trump likening it to a 2011 Obama-era pause on Iraqi refugee processing. Reporting shows that 2011 actions were a limited, targeted rescreening after two Iraqi refugees in Kentucky were tied to attacks, not a broad visa ban. Experts note the contrast: Obama’s response addressed a specific threat and one country, while Trump’s order was wider and religion-linked in effect.

The FBI’s annual Crime in the United States report showed violent crime in 2015 rose compared with 2014 but stayed well below the high rates seen in the 1990s. The national violent-crime rate reached 372.6 incidents per 100,000 people, up from 361.6 in 2014, though far lower than the 1996 peak of 636.6. The agency estimated 1,197,704 violent crimes in 2015, a 3.9 percent increase from 2014, but still 0.7 percent below 2011 and 16.5 percent below 2006. Property crimes declined an estimated 2.6 percent from the previous year.

Murders rose to an estimated 15,696 in 2015, up from 14,164 in 2014; the increase in violent crime was most pronounced in large cities and concentrated in segregated, impoverished neighborhoods. The South had the highest levels of violence: its murder and manslaughter rate, 45.9 per 100,000, was more than double rates in the West, Midwest and Northeast. Rape, assault and property crime rates were also markedly higher in that region. Chicago saw a notable local increase—54 more murders in 2015, a 13 percent jump, according to the Brennan Center.

The report arrived amid a politically charged atmosphere, with the presidential campaign likely to spotlight public safety. Donald Trump emphasized rising crime to advocate aggressive tactics such as stop-and-frisk; Hillary Clinton favored stricter gun controls and national guidelines on police use of force. Experts and officials cautioned against reverting to overly aggressive policing; FBI Director James Comey had warned that scrutiny of police practices might chill enforcement, while reform advocates urged community policing and alternatives to incarceration for nonviolent offenses. Some law‑enforcement voices noted a shift from a “warrior” to a “guardian” mentality and urged policies that address underlying neighborhood conditions to reduce violent crime sustainably.

Flu season is approaching and vaccination rates remain low — under half of adults get a flu shot despite influenza affecting up to 20% of people yearly. To boost convenience and uptake, Uber is running a one-day on-demand flu prevention drive called UberHEALTH in more than 35 U.S. cities. On Thursday from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., users who open the Uber app can select “UberHEALTH” to request a $10 wellness pack delivered by Uber; recipients can then request up to ten free Fluzone® flu shots administered by a registered nurse from Passport Health at that same visit. Nurses will handle all paperwork and consent; vaccinations are available for ages 4 and up. The wellness pack includes a water bottle, tissues, hand sanitizer, lollipop and tote. Last year’s pilot in four cities delivered over 2,000 vaccinations, and a study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine found nearly 80% of users said they wouldn’t have been vaccinated without the service, suggesting convenience reaches a “hard-to-reach” group. Organizers expect high demand, plan for thousands of doses and say Uber, Passport Health and Epidemico are subsidizing costs. John Brownstein, Ph.D., an epidemiologist at Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, has joined as Uber’s health adviser. A VaccineFinder link is provided for those outside participating cities or unable to access UberHEALTH.

An 18-week-old Irish baby, Megan, survived after being presumed miscarried and after her mother, Michelle Hui, was given abortion medication. Hui, 31, experienced a miscarriage around six weeks’ gestation and, after five scans at Dublin’s Rotunda Hospital that concluded she had lost the pregnancy, was given the standard two-pill medical abortion regimen and sent home. A follow-up pregnancy test—intended to check for retained tissue—was positive, and during preparation for a dilation and curettage to clear clots, doctors detected a fetal heartbeat. They discovered Hui had been carrying twins and one fetus had miraculously survived both the miscarriage and the effects of the abortion medication. Megan was born healthy on February 25, weighing just under six pounds; she joins siblings Mya, 4, and Noah, 2. Medical staff called the case extraordinary—so unusual it’s been written up in journals—and midwifery experts say they’ve never seen survival after mifepristone in such circumstances. Hui described intense emotions: devastation, disbelief, anger at missed scans, and overwhelming gratitude that her daughter is healthy.

President Obama announced U.S. recognition of the National Coalition of Syrian Revolutionary and Opposition Forces as the legitimate representative of the Syrian people, saying the coalition is now sufficiently inclusive and representative. The decision, following moves by Britain and the EU, gives the coalition new diplomatic legitimacy and allows closer U.S. support for political organization and eventual post‑Assad governance, though it falls short of recognizing state authority or granting access to Syrian government assets. Obama emphasized responsibilities for the coalition to be representative and to protect women’s and minority rights. The U.S. stopped short of supplying weapons now, saying arms might be considered only if they clearly promote a political solution; providing arms remains a future possibility. The president warned against supporting extremist factions, specifically singling out Jabhat al‑Nusrah and noting its recent U.S. terrorist designation and sanctions. Critics say recognition may be too late and does little to alter battlefield dynamics, and many armed rebels resent the absence of stronger U.S. assistance.

A video filmed at a Whataburger in San Antonio on July 4 showed a man approach a group of teenagers and take a “Make America Great Again” hat from one teen, then throw a drink at the table while shouting a racial slur. The footage went viral, garnering more than 2 million views and widespread online outrage. The teen whose hat was taken identified himself as 16-year-old Hunter Richard; he told local media he supports the president and would prefer political conversation over aggression. Richard later posted on Instagram a photo of himself wearing a MAGA hat with a caption indicating he was unbothered by the theft; the post was liked by Donald Trump Jr., who now follows the account.

San Antonio police arrested 30-year-old Kino Jimenez at his Universal City home and charged him with theft of a person; officials say the arrest was made without incident. Social media users had circulated Jimenez’s name and photo after the clip spread. Whataburger issued a statement saying the company was shocked by the video, that no employees were involved or witnessed the incident, and that they are supporting the San Antonio Police Department’s investigation.

The clip was removed or set to private by its original poster but remains available elsewhere online. The episode prompted reactions from political figures, including a comment from then–Trump 2020 campaign manager Brad Parscale offering to send a signed hat and expressing support for the teenager. The incident highlighted tensions around political symbols and public confrontations.

James Robert Jones, 59, was arrested by U.S. Marshals in Pompano Beach, Florida, after living under a false identity for decades. Jones, convicted in 1974 of premeditated murder and aggravated assault while serving as an Army private at Fort Dix, was sentenced to 23 years at the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth. He escaped from that maximum-security military prison in 1977 and had been on the run for 37 years. Army investigators, believing Jones to be in Florida, asked Marshals for help in January. Marshals matched his prison photograph to a Florida driver’s license issued in 1981 under the name Bruce Walter Keith, and began surveillance. Jones, who had been living in Deerfield Beach since at least 2005 and working in Pompano Beach, surrendered peacefully when approached. He told authorities he expected capture someday and had been close to retirement in his assumed life, which included “significant others.” Jones will be extradited to Kansas to resume his sentence and likely face additional charges for the escape.

On April 7, 2017, the United States launched a significant military strike against the Syrian government, firing nearly 60 Tomahawk cruise missiles from two destroyers at the Shayrat air base near Homs. The strike, ordered by President Donald Trump in response to a chemical attack days earlier in Khan Sheikhoun that killed scores of civilians — including many children — targeted runways, hangars, a control tower and ammunition areas. U.S. officials said the base was used to launch the chemical attack; Syrian and Russian sources disputed the attribution of responsibility for the gas incident and Syria denied using chemical weapons.

The attack marked the first direct U.S. strike on forces loyal to President Bashar al-Assad in the six-year civil war and represented a sharp policy shift by the Trump administration. Trump framed the action as a necessary response to prevent further use of chemical weapons and urged other nations to join in ending the carnage in Syria. U.S. military spokesmen said effort was made to avoid Russian personnel; Moscow acknowledged being warned in advance but condemned the strike as an act of aggression that violated international law and suspended a key Russia-U.S. memorandum meant to prevent aerial incidents over Syria.

International reactions were sharply divided. Western allies including Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Israel, and NATO officials largely supported or described the strike as proportionate, with some calling it a potential catalyst for renewed political pressure on Assad. Turkey and Saudi Arabia, both opponents of Assad, welcomed the action. Conversely, Russia and Iran — Assad’s main backers — strongly criticized the strike, warned of escalation, and questioned U.S. motives and timing. Critics also suggested the strike risked damaging U.S.-Russia relations and complicating efforts to build a coalition against ISIS.

Within the United States, congressional reaction split across unusual lines. Many senior Republicans and Democrats praised the strike but urged a broader strategy and consultation with Congress for any escalation. Libertarian and liberal lawmakers, including Senators Rand Paul and Tim Kaine and Rep. Barbara Lee, argued the president lacked constitutional authority to strike without congressional authorization and called for debate.

Analysts warned of risks: alienating Russia, undermining efforts against ISIS by destabilizing Syria further, and exposing a lack of a comprehensive U.S. plan to achieve a political solution. Syrian opposition figures and some residents of Khan Sheikhoun hoped the strike might deter further chemical attacks but expressed skepticism that a single strike would halt widespread government air operations, noting many other operational air bases remain. The strike reinvigorated global debate over intervention, the enforcement of norms against chemical weapons, and the legal and strategic limits of unilateral military action.

Rough Night is a raunchy R-rated comedy about five college friends who reunite in Miami for a bachelorette weekend that spirals into a darkly comic catastrophe. Scarlett Johansson plays Jess, a now-conservative state senate candidate engaged to Paul W. Downs’s Peter; Jillian Bell is Alice, the party-obsessed, needy friend who instigates the reunion; Ilana Glazer portrays Frankie, a zealous activist; Zoë Kravitz is Blair, newly divorced and stressed by custody issues; and Kate McKinnon appears as Pippa, an effervescent Australian who complicates group dynamics. After heavy drinking, drug use, and a male stripper mix-up, a man ends up dead in the house in what the women insist is an accident. What follows is a frantic, often farcical cover-up as the friends debate culpability and attempt to dispose of the body while navigating jealousy, rivalry, and surveillance by sleazy neighbors played by Demi Moore and Ty Burrell.

Directed and co-written by Lucia Aniello, with co-writer Paul W. Downs, Rough Night leans into the “women behaving badly” subgenre that’s proliferated in recent years. The film’s novelty isn’t its premise—which echoes the 1998 dark comedy Very Bad Things and borrows from The Hangover, Bridesmaids, and Weekend at Bernie’s—but its female-centric spin, the candid banter among the women, and the “female gaze” Aniello brings. Performances are uneven but often enjoyable: Johansson finds a breezy, no-nonsense rhythm as a conflicted grown-up, Glazer imbues Frankie with lived-in nuance, and Bell is the movie’s comic spark with sharp timing and painfully earnest delivery. McKinnon provides zippy, scene-stealing moments, though her accent-based jokes sometimes feel thin.

Rough Night shines in its first act and in moments of raw, competitive camaraderie; its darker black-comedy turns are less consistent and some gags fall flat. Still, the film offers enough bold, bawdy laughs and vivid character exchanges to be a crowd-pleasing, if derivative, summer comedy that underlines the need for more women filmmakers across both bold and mainstream commercial fare. Critics gave it mixed marks—roughly a C+—noting it’s entertaining but not particularly original or fully satisfying.

Last year Transparent California reported that BART janitor Liang Zhao Zhang earned $271,243 in 2015 — about $57,945 in base pay and roughly $162,050 in overtime — prompting scrutiny about how such pay was possible. KTVU’s investigation reviewed BART timecards, public records, and station surveillance and found patterns that raised more questions than answers. Timecard data show Zhang worked extraordinarily long stretches, including a stint in July 2015 when he logged 17-hour days for 18 consecutive days. Over four years (2012–2015) he earned more than $705,000 in pay and benefits. BART confirmed 49 other janitors earned over $100,000 in 2015 and said no law prevents employees from working excessive voluntary overtime.

KTVU obtained station video that appears to show Zhang repeatedly entering a storage closet at Powell Street station and remaining inside for extended periods — examples include 54- and 90-minute stays on one day and 90- and 78-minute stays on another. Zhang told investigators he used that time for meal breaks, but BART policy designates a separate break room and gives employees 30-minute lunches; the agency said it does not track breaks. Investigators also found timesheet irregularities, including 16 missed clock-ins or outs in one year and three unverified entries over two months.

BART officials defended the overtime, saying Zhang signs up for extra shifts and fills work others won’t because Powell Street requires frequent cleanup of human waste and needles. Management says supervisors approved his timesheets and that no audit is planned. Critics, including Transparent California’s Robert Fellner, call the pay and oversight “obscene” and a sign of management failures, urging audits of overtime practices and timesheet verification. BART acknowledged cleanliness problems at Powell Street but maintains systems exist to ensure work is completed.

On August 3, 2012, LGBT advocacy group Rights Equal Rights launched a global boycott of Amway/Alticor and related family-owned businesses in response to Amway president Doug DeVos’s $500,000 donation to the National Organization for Marriage (NOM), revealed in the Doug and Maria DeVos Foundation’s IRS 990 filing. Rights Equal Rights framed the boycott as a consequence for major financial support of organizations that actively oppose LGBT equality. NOM has been prominent in contesting marriage-equality measures and defending like-minded corporations such as Chick-fil-A; activists said such donors enable campaigns that harm LGBT Americans. The boycott targets Amway affiliates, including businesses connected to the DeVos family, and will monitor donors to anti-gay campaigns in upcoming ballot fights in Minnesota, Maryland, Maine, and Washington. Media coverage cited the donation and subsequent backlash, noting Amway’s response that the gift reflected the DeVos family’s personal political beliefs and that Amway’s business is open to all. The controversy followed a broader national debate where companies and executives—Chick-fil-A, Google, General Mills, Ben & Jerry’s, Kraft—took public stances on same-sex marriage, each drawing support and boycotts depending on their positions.

These articles revisit the long-unsolved death of actress Natalie Wood, who drowned off Catalina Island in late November 1981 after disappearing from the couple’s yacht, Splendour, during a trip with husband Robert Wagner and actor Christopher Walken. Initially ruled an accidental drowning, the case was later reclassified as drowning with “undetermined factors,” and the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department reopened investigations multiple times, naming Wagner a person of interest in 2011. The renewed scrutiny and fresh allegations have kept the story in the media decades later.

Lana Wood, Natalie’s sister and a former actress, gave an exclusive interview to the “Fatal Voyage: The Mysterious Death of Natalie Wood” podcast and has repeatedly accused her former brother-in-law, Robert Wagner, of wrongdoing. In the podcast she recounts being warned—by late talent agent Rowland Perkins—that Wagner had effectively blacklisted her in Hollywood after Natalie’s death, a move that she says ended her acting and production prospects and forced her into various odd jobs. Lana told investigators and media she believes Wagner “has something to hide” and has suggested he may have played a direct role in Natalie’s death.

Dennis Davern, the yacht’s captain who at first described the death as an accident, has since said he now believes Natalie was murdered and alleges he heard a fight between Wagner and Natalie and that Wagner later prevented him from calling for help and coached him on a false story. Wagner, now in his late eighties, has consistently denied any involvement and declines to discuss the case; his representative harshly criticized Davern and Lana for revisiting the tragedy.

podcasts, renewed police inquiries, and TV interviews (including “Dr. Phil”) continue to surface new testimony and controversies, keeping public interest alive and the debate over what really happened on the Splendour unresolved.

South Park’s 21st-season premiere, “White People Renovating Houses,” lampooned white nationalism and featured scenes that unintentionally triggered real smart speakers. Throughout the episode, characters yelled commands at cartoon Alexa and Google Home devices; because the assistants respond to hearing their wake words, many viewers reported their own Amazon Echo and Google Home units repeatedly activating. Tweets and clips showed devices adding vulgar items like “titty chips” and “hairy balls” to shopping lists, setting alarms for 7 a.m., and otherwise acting up until some viewers unplugged them. The stunt was in line with South Park creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone’s irreverent style; they’ve said this season would mostly return to standalone episodes after last season’s serialized arc. The show’s use of wake words rekindled concerns about media inadvertently controlling voice assistants — a problem previously seen when a Burger King ad prompted Google Home responses. The outlet contacted Amazon and Google for comment and potential fixes; no response was reported in the piece.

President-elect Donald J. Trump announced he will nominate David M. Friedman, a bankruptcy lawyer and close adviser aligned with the Israeli far right, to be U.S. ambassador to Israel. Friedman has no diplomatic experience and holds outspoken positions at odds with longstanding U.S. policy: he has questioned the necessity of a two-state solution, likened left-leaning American Jews to Jews who aided Nazis during the Holocaust, endorsed Israeli settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, and said he does not believe annexation of the West Bank would be illegal. In the transition statement announcing his nomination, Friedman said he looked forward to serving “from the U.S. embassy in Israel’s eternal capital, Jerusalem,” signaling a potential break with decades of U.S. practice of keeping its embassy in Tel Aviv until final status negotiations determine Jerusalem’s fate. Moving the embassy to Jerusalem would be politically charged, anger Palestinians who claim east Jerusalem as their capital, and isolate the U.S. diplomatically from many allies. Trump advisers have insisted he intends to follow through on his campaign promise; one discussed option would have Friedman operate out of a U.S. consulate in Jerusalem, effectively rebranding it as the embassy. The nomination drew sharp criticism from liberal Jewish groups and raised questions about how such a policy shift would be implemented and its impact on the Israeli-Palestinian peace process.

Malaysian authorities concluded that VX, a banned and extremely potent nerve agent, was used to kill Kim Jong-nam, the estranged half brother of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, after he was attacked in Kuala Lumpur’s airport on Feb. 13. Swabs from his eyes and face reportedly tested positive for VX, and one of the two women accused of smearing something on his face later vomited, though neither she nor the other suspect showed severe symptoms. VX is an oily, tasteless, persistent V-type agent that can kill from skin exposure in minutes; it is banned under the Chemical Weapons Convention, which North Korea has not signed. Experts note only a tiny amount is lethal, and forensic puzzlement remains over how the alleged attackers apparently avoided fatal exposure — some suggest they may have been given antidotes. Malaysia detained three people and sought several North Korean nationals, including an embassy official, prompting diplomatic confrontation: Pyongyang vehemently denied involvement, accused Malaysia of fabricating evidence, declined to confirm the victim’s identity as Kim Jong-nam, and warned Malaysia it bears responsibility because the death occurred on its soil. Outside assessments long estimate North Korea possesses large chemical stockpiles and production capacity, including VX, raising concerns about its global reach and past sharing of capabilities. The case has severely strained Malaysia–North Korea relations and raised public-safety and international-security alarms.

Multiexport Foods, Inc. of Miami expanded a voluntary recall announced Dec. 22, 2012 for Paramount Reserve cold smoked salmon (12-oz twin pack and 1.25-lb pack) due to possible Listeria monocytogenes contamination. The products, UPCs 688264867050 and 688264866640, were distributed Nov. 12–Dec. 21 to retail outlets including Wal‑Mart’s Sam’s Club across 42 states and Puerto Rico. No illnesses have been reported. Consumers may return affected packages for a full refund. Tampa Bay Fisheries, Multiexport and Walmart are cooperating with the FDA.

The trial of Samsung vice‑chairman Lee Jae‑yong, widely regarded as the de facto head of the Samsung conglomerate, has opened in Seoul on charges including bribery, embezzlement, hiding assets overseas, perjury and concealing criminal profits. Lee, detained since February, was not present at the preliminary hearing; his lawyers denied all charges on his behalf and disputed aspects of the special prosecution’s case. Four other Samsung executives indicted alongside him also deny wrongdoing.

Prosecutors allege Lee conspired to funnel roughly 41–43 billion won (about $36–38 million) to foundations and individuals tied to Choi Soon‑sil, a confidante of President Park Geun‑hye, in return for government support for a 2015 merger that consolidated Lee’s control over Samsung. Samsung has acknowledged donations totalling 20.4 billion won to two foundations but insists these were customary contributions made under government request and not bribes. Lee has admitted providing a horse and funds to support Choi’s daughter’s equestrian career, saying he regrets it.

The case is a central strand of the broader scandal that precipitated President Park’s impeachment after revelations that Choi, who held no official role, influenced state affairs and edited speeches. Park denies criminal wrongdoing but has apologised for her relationship with Choi; Choi faces her own trial on corruption and coercion charges. South Korea’s constitutional court is expected soon to rule on whether Park’s December impeachment will be upheld; if it is, she will lose immunity and face potential prosecution.

The Lee trial, described by prosecutors as the nation’s “trial of the century,” is slated to run for months and has intense domestic and international attention due both to the sums involved and to concerns about chaebol influence on politics. A conviction could lead to years or life in prison, and regardless of outcome the proceedings cloud leadership succession at Samsung and risk reputational damage to the company even as it seeks to recover from recent product setbacks.

President Donald Trump created confusion on Friday about House Republican immigration plans by telling Fox & Friends he would not sign a “more moderate” proposal, then hours later the White House clarified he supported both a conservative Goodlatte bill and a compromise leadership bill and would sign either. The day’s back-and-forth threatened to undercut GOP leaders’ efforts to hold votes next week and exposed divisions between conservative hard-liners and centrists who negotiated the compromise. The leadership package, negotiated with White House input and reflecting elements of Trump’s “four pillars,” would fund the border wall, end the visa lottery, curtail chain migration, expand border and interior enforcement, and create a pathway to citizenship for young undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children (Dreamers). White House spokesman Raj Shah said Trump had misunderstood the morning interview and was referring to a Democratic-backed moderate plan that would codify DACA without enforcement measures. Trump then tweeted that any immigration bill “MUST HAVE” wall funding, end catch-and-release, eliminate the visa lottery and move to merit-based immigration—requirements included in the compromise. Conservatives and some centrists remained uneasy; a president’s rejection would have left GOP leaders asking members to oppose their own president and risked derailing the compromise. Senior White House adviser Stephen Miller had been encouraging support for the leadership bill, but conservative backlash and Trump’s earlier TV comments briefly stalled vote-counting and prompted GOP leaders to seek clarification. Democrats oppose both GOP bills, and passage remains uncertain given intra-party fractures and potential defections.

When Brett Kavanaugh left the Senate hearing room for lunch during his Supreme Court confirmation hearing, Fred Guttenberg — whose 14-year-old daughter Jaime was killed in the Parkland school shooting — said he reached out, introduced himself and offered his hand. Multiple videos and photos show Kavanaugh looking at Guttenberg, then turning and walking away without speaking or shaking his hand. The White House initially said an “unidentified individual” approached Kavanaugh and that security intervened “before the Judge was able to shake his hand,” but Guttenberg and the footage dispute that account. A White House spokesman later said he stood by his statement despite the apparent contradiction.

Guttenberg, now a prominent gun-control advocate, had been invited to the hearing by Senator Dianne Feinstein and said he attended hoping to convey the human consequences of gun policy to Kavanaugh, who has written that assault-weapon bans are unconstitutional and whose confirmation is supported and funded by the NRA. Gun-control activists and some Parkland students criticized Kavanaugh’s refusal to acknowledge Guttenberg as revealing both character flaws and the real-world implications of his pro-gun legal views. After the lunch break, Guttenberg says security removed him from the room for about 15 minutes, took his license and questioned him; he believes Kavanaugh may have pointed him out to security. Not all Parkland parents reacted the same: Andrew Pollack, who also lost a child in the shooting, defended Kavanaugh and urged against “weaponizing Parkland” for political ends.
