The episode added to tensions surrounding Kavanaugh’s confirmation and highlighted the emotional and political stakes tied to his stance on the Second Amendment.

Fidget spinners, a major toy trend, have been found to contain dangerously high levels of lead in tests conducted by the U.S. Public Interest Research Group (U.S. PIRG) and a CPSC-accredited lab. U.S. PIRG tested 12 spinners sold in Target stores and online; two models distributed by Bulls i Toy—Fidget Wild Premium Spinner Brass and Fidget Wild Premium Spinner Metal—showed alarming contamination. The brass spinner’s center circle tested at 33,000 ppm and an arm at 22,000 ppm of lead, vastly exceeding the 100 ppm federal limit for children’s products; the metal model’s center and arm tested at 1,300 ppm and 520 ppm respectively. U.S. PIRG retested to confirm results and urged Target and Bulls i Toy to recall the products and investigate the source of contamination. Target and the manufacturer have resisted recalls, pointing to product labeling that indicates ages 14+ and citing the Consumer Product Safety Commission’s (CPSC) current classification of many spinners as “general use” rather than toys—thus not subject to children’s lead limits. Advocates including Kara Cook-Schultz of U.S. PIRG and parent activist Tamara Rubin argue spinners are marketed and sold alongside children’s toys and pose risks, especially to young children who more easily ingest lead. The CPSC warns there have been other spinner hazards (choking, batteries, fires) and so far has declined to reclassify spinners. U.S. PIRG calls for reclassification of fidget spinners as toys, broader testing, recalls of contaminated models, public notification, and stronger enforcement to prevent lead exposure.

Pedro Aguayo Ramirez, known as Hijo del Perro Aguayo, died early Saturday after sustaining a neck injury during a match in Tijuana, Baja California. Video shows he fell unconscious on the ropes, apparently after a flying kick from Oscar Gutierrez (Rey Mysterio Jr.). The bout continued for nearly two minutes before participants and the referee realized Aguayo was seriously hurt; he was taken to a nearby hospital and pronounced dead about 1:30 a.m. An autopsy found trauma to the neck and a cervical fracture, and authorities opened a possible manslaughter investigation. The event organizer, The Crash, did not comment. Aguayo, 35, a 20-year veteran and son of lucha libre legend Pedro "Perro" Aguayo, led Los Perros de Mal and held several championships. The Tijuana commission called it a tragic accident, and colleagues expressed sorrow.

Retired Gen. Alexander M. Haig Jr., who served as White House chief of staff under Richard Nixon, NATO supreme allied commander, and Ronald Reagan’s secretary of state, died at 85 of complications from a staphylococcal infection. Haig rose rapidly through military and governmental ranks, earning distinction in Korea and Vietnam and later serving as Henry Kissinger’s deputy. As Nixon’s chief of staff during Watergate, he became a central figure—urging Nixon to destroy tapes, confronting the Saturday Night Massacre, arranging congressional and legal meetings, and ultimately smoothing the path to Nixon’s resignation in 1974. Critics labeled him the “37½ president”; Haig denied brokering Nixon’s pardon. Confirmed as NATO commander by Presidents Ford and Carter, he retired from the Army in 1979, briefly led United Technologies, ran unsuccessfully for the 1988 Republican presidential nomination, and served as Reagan’s turbulent secretary of state until 1982. Known for his distinct “Haigspeak,” he remained active in business and commentary, survived by his wife Patricia, three children, and eight grandchildren.

The document compiles several political news threads from late 2016, centering on WikiLeaks revelations about the Clinton Foundation, media and campaign clashes surrounding Megyn Kelly and Newt Gingrich, and Donald Trump’s efforts to bolster his brand and campaign by opening a Washington, D.C., hotel — all against the volatile backdrop of an election season rife with fear and anger among voters.

A hacked November 2011 memo published by WikiLeaks alleged that Douglas Band, a top aide to former President Bill Clinton, and another chief fundraiser for the Clinton Foundation pressured corporate donors to steer business opportunities and lucrative paid speaking engagements to Bill Clinton. The memo reportedly detailed extensive fundraising efforts and how those efforts sometimes translated into large speaking fees and other paid work for the former president. The disclosure added to scrutiny of the Foundation’s fundraising practices and the intersections between philanthropy and paid political or private engagements.

In media and campaign politics, Newt Gingrich’s on-air accusation that Fox News host Megyn Kelly was “fascinated with sex” and uninterested in public policy sparked widespread backlash. Donald Trump applauded Gingrich’s attack, and his campaign’s social-media director publicly criticized Kelly as biased. Karl Rove appeared on Kelly’s show to defend her and chastise Trump for misusing time that should be devoted to campaigning, given the narrow timeline before Election Day. The exchange underscored tensions among conservative media figures and campaign operatives and highlighted disputes over journalistic tone and focus.

Meanwhile, reporting from Trump rallies in several states captured a mix of fervor, denial of polls, and alarm among supporters about the prospect of a Hillary Clinton presidency. Interviews with attendees revealed a belief in a “silent majority” not reflected in polls, mistrust of institutions, and some extreme rhetoric suggesting the possibility of violence if Clinton won. Many supporters expressed fear about their future — economic anxiety, Second Amendment concerns, and apocalyptic visions — while others insisted they would accept election results but worried about division and unrest.

Seeking to repair both his campaign momentum and personal brand, Donald Trump staged a high-profile ribbon-cutting for his refurbished D.C. hotel, framing it as proof of executive competence and a metaphor for what he could do for the country. Critics questioned the timing and optics — with the event listed on his campaign site and attended by campaign aides — and Hillary Clinton seized the chance to contrast her campaign with what she portrayed as Trump’s self-promotion and past business controversies. The hotel opening, amid protests and heavy media attention, illustrated how Trump blended commercial interests with campaign messaging in the final days before the election.

"The Grey" retools Liam Neeson’s recent action-star persona into a lean, somber survival drama that echoes Jack London and Hemingway. Neeson plays John Ottway, an Arctic oil-field sharpshooter who survives a plane crash with a handful of roughneck coworkers and must guide them through a frozen Alaskan wasteland stalked by a merciless pack of wolves. Director Joe Carnahan and co-writer Ian Mackenzie Jeffers strip the story to elemental terms: building fires, improvising weapons, finding food, keeping watch — practical tasks that fuel suspense while supporting deeper meditations on mortality, faith, masculinity and regret. Ottway is taciturn and haunted by memories of a lost wife; his quiet compassion and lethal skills give the film emotional ballast and a moral seriousness rare in action fare. The ensemble cast (including Dermot Mulroney, Frank Grillo, Nonso Anozie and Dallas Roberts) are sketched through behavior rather than backstory, and Carnahan resists caricature while allowing the men to ruminate on fear, courage and God. The wolves — large, relentless antagonists designed with heavy CGI — make nature an implacable adversary, though some critics found their depiction overblown. Overall, "The Grey" is a technically assured, brooding January surprise: a brutal, lyrical survival picture that treats death thoughtfully and keeps viewers invested in each hard-fought moment. Runs 1:57; rated R.

A Sicilian former mobster-turned-informant, Vincenzo Calcara, has offered explosive claims linking the Mafia to two high-profile Vatican-related incidents. Calcara told investigators that Mehmet Ali Agca, the Turkish gunman who shot Pope John Paul II in St. Peter’s Square in 1981, acted as a Mafia-hired hitman. He named jailed boss Salvatore “Toto” Riina and ex-mayor Antonio Vaccarino as the organizers, and alleged a third accomplice, “Antonov,” was subsequently murdered and secretly buried near Milan. Sicilian magistrates have forwarded transcripts of Calcara’s testimony to Rome, but searches for the alleged burial site turned up nothing and prosecutors have expressed skepticism about parts of the story; Antonio Marini, who investigated the assassination attempt, said there is no firm evidence the Mafia ordered the killing. Calcara also accused high-ranking Vatican figures and Sicilian criminals of laundering money, and his allegations coincide with a new arrest warrant for imprisoned Mafia treasurer Pippo Calo. Separately, Calcara wrote a six-page letter to Pope Francis offering to confess three “very important secrets,” claiming he could shed light on the 1983 disappearance of 15-year-old Emanuela Orlandi, daughter of a Vatican employee. He told La Repubblica he believes revealing the truth would expose a system connecting the Vatican to “deviant entities.” The revelations come amid Pope Francis’s stern public condemnations of the Mafia and ongoing public interest in unresolved Vatican-era mysteries.

A major new PayScale study of about 1.4 million full-time employees over two years finds that the gender pay gap persists even after controlling for marital and family status, job, industry, seniority, geography, education, and generation. On average, women with year-round full-time jobs earn roughly 79 percent of what men do, and when PayScale adjusts for common explanatory factors the controlled gap remains: women make about 2.7 percent less than comparable men. That shortfall appears across virtually every industry and occupation tracked. Even in sectors where one might expect parity, women earn less—between about 1.3 percent less in real estate and 5.4 percent less in mining, quarrying, and oil and gas—and women earn less in nearly all of the hundreds of Bureau of Labor Statistics job categories analyzed.

Education does not eliminate the gap. Young women now outpace men in degree attainment, but the wage gap exists at every education level and widens at the top: the adjusted gap is 2.2 percent for associate-degree holders, grows to 4.7 percent for MBA holders and 5.1 percent for PhD holders. Advancement also fails to close the gap; it widens with seniority—entry-level women earn about 2.2 percent less than comparable men, while female executives earn roughly 6.1 percent less.

Family dynamics contribute: the controlled gap is largest between married men with children and married women with children, reflecting both discrimination against mothers and women’s greater likelihood of altering careers for caregiving. Occupational segregation—women concentrated in lower-paid, less-specialized jobs like teaching and nursing—also depresses lifetime earnings, producing an earlier peak for women’s median pay (around $49,000 from age 40 onward) versus men’s continuing growth into their 50s (median about $75,000). Experts cited in the report point to both discrimination and persistent “head-of-household” pay expectations for men as ongoing drivers of the gap, and note that the disparity is substantially larger for women of color.

“The Way, Way Back” is a warm, witty coming-of-age indie set on a Cape Cod beach that balances humor and emotional truth without descending into teen-movie cliché. Written and directed by Nat Faxon and Jim Rash—whose screenplay first appeared on the 2007 Black List—the film feels authentic and conversational, preserving the script’s quirky voice. It centers on 14-year-old Duncan (Liam James), who endures the awkward, sometimes cruel attentions of his soon-to-be stepfather Trent (Steve Carell) during a family vacation at a beachfront house called Riptide. Duncan’s mother Pam (Toni Collette) is tender and conflicted, trying to make a new family work while uncertain and vulnerable.

Duncan finds refuge at Water Wizz, a rundown local water park run by the charismatic, Peter Pan–like Owen (Sam Rockwell). Owen’s easygoing mentorship and the camaraderie of the park’s staff help Duncan regain confidence and perspective. The film thrives on contrasts: Trent’s aggressive, humiliating behavior versus Owen’s flawed but supportive guidance; adult messiness against adolescent isolation. Supporting performances add color—Allison Janney excels as the loud, lonely neighbor Betty, Maya Rudolph provides warmth as Owen’s right-hand, and AnnaSophia Robb plays Duncan’s tentative romantic interest.

Technically accomplished with a sun-drenched score by Rob Simonsen and solid production values, the movie navigates domestic comedy on the edge of tragedy with tenderness and sly humor. It’s an affecting summer escape about connection, growth, and the small moments that reshape a young life.

Matt “Megatoad” Stonie, one of Major League Eating’s top competitors, set a new bacon-eating record in Daytona by consuming 182 slices in five minutes—more than six pounds of cooked bacon and roughly 28,000 mg of sodium, according to sponsor Smithfield. Stonie said the bacon was cooked “a little crispy” so he wouldn’t have to chew much and that he was well prepared from longer contests where he eats 10–15 pounds. He described competitive eating as his job: he focuses on texture and saltiness rather than flavor, though he still loves bacon and is particular about its preparation. MLE hadn’t previously held an official bacon contest; unofficial records were around 54 slices. Stonie, ranked second to Joey “Jaws” Chestnut, has recently set multiple Florida records, including a 14.5-pound cake, and remains a frequent rival of Chestnut.

Following a June 5 demolition accident in Philadelphia that killed six and injured 13, lead inspector Ronald Wagenhoffer recorded a one-minute cellphone message saying, "It was my fault," admitting he never inspected the adjacent demolition site after a citizen complaint. He was found dead of an apparent suicide days later. City officials defended L&I’s actions and said Wagenhoffer had offered to remain working; the mayor urged support for staff. Investigations include criminal charges against excavator operator Kane Robert and scrutiny of contractor Griffin Campbell. Lawsuits allege gross negligence; calls grew for stricter demolition oversight and inspections.

Oscar-winning actress Jennifer Lawrence was aboard a private Beechcraft 400 Beechjet that made an emergency landing Saturday at Buffalo Niagara International Airport after experiencing engine trouble. The aircraft, en route from Louisville, Kentucky, to Teterboro, New Jersey, was diverted after a possible left engine failure at cruising altitude; sources say one engine failed at 31,000 feet and the other failed during the unscheduled descent. Pilots landed safely at 1:15 p.m. with two crew members and two passengers aboard. Lawrence was confirmed as a passenger and uninjured. The plane was moved to Prior Aviation; its departure status is unclear.

A federal judge in Texas ruled the Affordable Care Act (ACA) unconstitutional, declaring the entire 2010 law invalid after Congress removed the tax penalty enforcing the individual mandate. The December ruling by Republican-appointed Judge Reed O’Connor has major political resonance but little immediate effect: the ACA remains in force while appeals proceed, enrollment via HealthCare.gov continues, Medicaid expansion and protections like coverage for young adults and no lifetime limits remain scheduled to take effect Jan. 1. The Justice Department declined to defend the mandate earlier in 2018, prompting Democratic-led states to step in and pledge appeals; California Attorney General Xavier Becerra said the coalition will fight the ruling in court. Legal scholars widely criticize O’Connor’s severability reasoning—most say Congress’s 2017 decision to remove the penalty while leaving the rest of the law intact shows intent to keep the ACA—and expect the 5th Circuit to stay the ruling pending review, with further appeals likely and potential Supreme Court resolution only if lower courts uphold O’Connor. Politically, Republicans face a dilemma: the public increasingly supports core ACA elements like protections for pre-existing conditions, complicating GOP options after failed repeal efforts and Democrats’ midterm gains. Experts warn legal uncertainty could unsettle insurance markets, raise future premiums, and reduce consumer participation. Many lawmakers from both parties urge preserving popular ACA provisions, suggesting legislative fixes would offer the most stability—yet partisan divisions make comprehensive agreement difficult. The legal and political battle is likely to continue for months or years.

BP’s board is weighing three choices for its $10.5 billion annual dividend amid intense pressure from the Obama administration and investors after the Gulf of Mexico oil disaster. Options reportedly include suspending the dividend for two quarters, paying it in bonus shares, or escrowing the cash while continuing cleanup funded from operating revenues unless needed. The debate follows President Obama’s escalating criticism of BP’s response as he makes his fourth Gulf trip and prepares for a nationally televised Oval Office address outlining plans to compel BP to fund an escrow for victims’ claims. The administration demands “substantial” money be placed with an independent mediator to handle economic and cleanup claims; Senate Democrats have proposed a $20 billion fund. BP insists it will pay claims tied directly to the spill but resists open-ended liability, fearing unchecked exposure and shareholder backlash. BP executives, including CEO Tony Hayward and chairman Carl-Henric Svanberg, will meet Obama midweek. The standoff has provoked market and political fallout, complicated by higher government estimates of daily leak rates and intensifying congressional scrutiny.

Hadiya Pendleton, a 15-year-old sophomore and majorette from King College Prep, was fatally shot in a Chicago park after finishing final exams and days after performing in President Obama’s inauguration events. Four years earlier, as a sixth-grader, she had appeared in an anti-gang public service video urging peers to “say no to gangs and yes to a great future.” On the afternoon of the shooting, Hadiya and friends took shelter from rain under a canopy when a gunman jumped a fence and opened fire; Hadiya was hit in the back and later died at Comer Children’s Hospital. Police say she and her friends were not gang-involved and may have been mistaken for rivals; the suspect fled in a white Nissan. The city increased the reward for information to $24,000, and no arrests have been reported. Her father called for justice. Rev. Jesse Jackson and others planned a march at the killing site, emphasizing broader causes of violence beyond gun laws. The White House expressed condolences.

European Council President Herman Van Rompuy convened an emergency coordination meeting of senior EU officials—joined by ECB President Jean-Claude Trichet, Eurogroup chair Jean-Claude Juncker, Commission President José Manuel Barroso and Commissioner Olli Rehn—after a sharp sell-off in Italian assets raised fears the sovereign debt crisis could spread to Italy. Italian 10-year bond spreads hit euro-era highs, pushing yields near levels some bankers say could threaten Italy’s finances; shares in UniCredit plunged and the Italian stock index fell. Market worries reflect Italy’s high debt (about 120% of GDP), sluggish growth and political tensions between Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi and Finance Minister Giulio Tremonti. The session also aimed to prepare a eurogroup meeting on private-sector involvement in a prospective second Greek bailout and the results of bank stress tests. Officials remain deadlocked over how to secure voluntary private contributions without triggering a selective default; Germany and others favor imposing losses or swaps, while the ECB resists. Observers warned more decisive, long-term solutions will be needed to restore investor confidence.

Thieves broke into the Armstrong Air & Space Museum in Wapakoneta, Ohio, late Friday and stole a solid-gold, 5-inch replica of the Apollo 11 lunar module that had been presented to Neil Armstrong. The alarm at the museum prompted police response, and investigators later found the small model missing. The museum stressed on Facebook that artifacts belong to the public and that theft deprives many visitors of shared history.

The 18-karat gold models were commissioned by French newspaper Le Figaro and made by Cartier as gifts to the three Apollo 11 crew members—Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins—after their 1969 return. Each contained a microfilm listing names of readers who contributed to the presentation. Only three such models were made; Cartier reportedly bought Collins’ model back at auction in 2003 for $56,000. The museum and police said the item’s collectible value is difficult to determine.

Retired NASA agent Joseph Gutheinz Jr., who has experience recovering stolen moon rocks, said the burglars likely intend to melt the replica for gold rather than sell it intact, noting a moon rock at the museum was left behind—suggesting the thieves were after quick cash, not collectibles. Melting would make recovery and prosecution far more difficult. Authorities including the Wapakoneta police, the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation and the FBI are investigating. Wapakoneta, Armstrong’s hometown, hosts the museum that opened in 1972 and houses unique artifacts tied to Armstrong and NASA history. No further updates or details about surveillance footage have been released.

A new archaeological investigation suggests William Shakespeare’s skull may have been stolen from his grave at Holy Trinity Church in Stratford-upon-Avon. Led by Staffordshire University archaeologist Kevin Colls, the team used ground-penetrating radar (GPR) to examine the playwright’s burial non-invasively for a Channel 4 documentary marking the 400th anniversary of his death. Their GPR data indicated an unusual disturbance at the head end of the grave—material appears to have been dug out and replaced—providing fresh support for a long-standing, often-dismissed story that trophy hunters stole Shakespeare’s skull in 1794, a claim first printed in 1879. Colls said the disturbance makes it “very, very convincing” that the skull is not in the church. The team also investigated a separate local legend that Shakespeare’s skull was kept in a Worcestershire church crypt; forensic analysis showed the skull there belonged to an elderly woman, not the Bard. Other findings revise aspects of Shakespeare’s burial: he and his wife Anne Hathaway were laid in shallow, roughly one-meter-deep graves beneath the church floor, not in a deeper family vault, and there was no evidence of coffin nails or metal—suggesting he was wrapped in a shroud rather than buried in a coffin. Holy Trinity’s vicar, Patrick Taylor, urged caution, saying the evidence does not definitively prove the skull was taken and that the mystery of what lies under the stone remains. The documentary “Secret History: Shakespeare’s Tomb” presents these results and will air on Channel 4.

Aretha Franklin delivered an unusually long, 4-minute-35-second rendition of the national anthem before the Detroit Lions–Minnesota Vikings Thanksgiving game, stretching the traditional two-minute performance into a slow, churchlike piano-accompanied spiritual. The crowd at Ford Field applauded repeatedly, and responses split between admiration—calling the Queen of Soul untouchable and entitled to take her time—and social-media jokes about delayed kickoffs, time-of-possession, Colin Kaepernick kneeling, Thanksgiving chores, and Johnny Manziel quips. Some compared the halftime gripe over Andy Grammer’s brief set, arguing Franklin’s stature warrants indulgence; others praised her storied six-decade career, 20 Grammys, Kennedy Center Honor and Presidential Medal of Freedom. The performance echoed Franklin’s history of vocal surprises, from stepping in for Pavarotti in 1998 to later performing “Nessun Dorma” for the Pope.

New research from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business finds that a candidate’s voice can matter more than their written résumé in shaping perceptions of competence. In a series of experiments led by Professor Nicholas Epley and Ph.D. candidate Juliana Schroeder, MBA students prepared identical pitches in written and spoken form. Independent evaluators either read transcripts, listened to audio, or watched videotaped pitches. Those who heard the audio rated candidates as more intelligent, thoughtful and competent than those who read the same words; video added no further advantage beyond audio. Listeners also reported greater liking for candidates and higher willingness to hire them. A follow-up experiment had trained actors read candidates’ written pitches aloud; listeners again judged those candidates as more intelligent and more hireable than evaluators who read the original texts. Crucially, the effect held even with professional recruiters who routinely hire from Chicago Booth. The researchers conclude that speech conveys not just content but signals of reasoning capacity and thoughtfulness—qualities employers use to judge intellect. The findings, titled “The Sound of Intellect: Speech Reveals a Thoughtful Mind, Increasing a Job Candidate’s Appeal,” will appear in The Journal of Psychological Science, suggesting that letting your voice be heard can materially boost job prospects.

The Spanish-language version of HealthCare.gov, CuidadoDeSalud.gov, launched more than two months after the English site and mirrored many of its problems, leaving Spanish-speaking Americans underserved during the initial enrollment wave. The site arrived Dec. 6, close to the Jan. 1 coverage deadline, but users and enrollment navigators reported technical glitches, slow navigation, broken links that pointed to English pages, and difficulties uploading required documents. Translations were frequently awkward, grammatical or literal—often described as “Spanglish” or machine-generated—making dense insurance terminology harder to understand. Call centers and in-person navigators were overwhelmed; Spanish-only callers constituted a small share of hotline contacts, and many areas lacked enough bilingual staff. As a result, relatively few Spanish enrollments occurred in states with large Latino populations, including California and New Mexico. Advocates say these failures undermined trust and missed an opportunity to reach a high-uninsured group, though federal officials noted phone and paper options and pledged fixes. Community clinics and navigators stepped in to assist vulnerable Spanish speakers, focusing now on the March 31 enrollment deadline.

Fred Beckey, a legendary and eccentric mountaineer who achieved more first ascents than any other American climber, died in Seattle at 94. Close friend and longtime caretaker Megan Bond said he passed from congestive heart failure at her home after four days in hospice. Born in Germany and raised in Seattle, Beckey developed his love of the mountains with the Boy Scouts and The Mountaineers club and went on a seven-decade climbing career marked by raw tenacity and audacity.

Beckey completed as many as a thousand previously unclimbed routes across Alaska, the Canadian Rockies, the Pacific Northwest and beyond, including notable 1954 new routes on Denali (then Mt. McKinley), Mount Deborah and Mount Hunter. He and his brother Helmut gained early renown with a striking 1942 second ascent of Mount Waddington. Beckey also climbed in the Himalayas and China.

A prolific author, he wrote more than a dozen mountaineering books, most famously the three-volume Cascade Alpine Guide detailing hundreds of North Cascades peaks. Admirers and collaborators praised his humor, scholarship and uncompromising commitment to climbing. Filmmaker Dave O’Leske chronicled him in the documentary "Dirtbag: The Legend of Fred Beckey."

Even into his 90s Beckey was planning expeditions and still climbing with careful partners; Bond said they had been preparing a Himalaya trip and recently climbed in Squamish. He is survived by his brother Helmut. Private burial and a public memorial in November are planned.

A team from UCLA and Stanford reports carbon isotope evidence suggesting life may have existed on Earth by 4.1 billion years ago, roughly 300 million years earlier than previous chemical indicators. The researchers analyzed over 10,000 zircons from Jack Hills, Western Australia—durable, mm-scale minerals that trap and preserve their formation environment. One 4.1-Ga zircon contained two graphite inclusions fully encased in crack-free zircon, ruling out recent contamination. Isotopic analysis showed a high 12C/13C ratio in the graphite, a signature often associated with biological carbon because enzymatic carbon fixation preferentially incorporates 12C. The zircon’s age is determined by uranium–lead ratios; the graphite is at least as old as the host zircon. The authors argue this may push the origin of life into the Hadean, implying life began quickly after Earth formed and perhaps survived or re-emerged following the late heavy bombardment around 3.9 Ga. The finding challenges views of an inhospitable early Earth and supports environments capable of hosting organic material. However, the interpretation is debated: inorganic processes (e.g., Fischer–Tropsch-type reactions) can also produce 12C-rich carbon, and isotope data alone cannot definitively prove biology. While not universally accepted as proof, the study compels reconsideration of how ancient the biosphere might be and motivates further searches for cryptic early-life records.

U.S. hospitals are conserving supplies and in some cases delaying care amid a national shortage of intravenous sodium bicarbonate, a basic but critical drug used from emergency resuscitation to chemotherapy support and open‑heart surgery. The shortage has persisted since about February after production problems at one of the nation’s two suppliers disrupted supply chains; confidentiality agreements have kept the specific issue undisclosed. The second supplier, Amphastar, could not fully absorb the surge in demand, and both companies warned the New York Times that normal supplies might not resume until at least June or August.

Sodium bicarbonate solution must be sterile and precisely formulated, so it cannot be substituted with household baking soda, and only two U.S. manufacturers produce it. Hospitals and pharmacists are therefore rationing vials for essential uses: correcting dangerously acidic blood, treating certain poisonings, easing pain during procedures, and supporting specific chemotherapy and cardiac operations. The scarcity has prompted some facilities nationally to postpone surgeries and cancer treatments and to transfer critically ill patients; one Alabama hospital delayed seven open‑heart surgeries and sent a patient elsewhere. Other systems, like OSF HealthCare and UnityPoint Health‑Peoria, report partial deliveries and tighter stewardship but have avoided drastic service cutbacks so far.

Experts say this episode illustrates a broader trend of shortages of inexpensive generics caused by factors including limited suppliers, aging manufacturing plants, raw material constraints, industry consolidation, and low profit incentives that discourage reinvestment. The Food and Drug Administration is working with manufacturers and is considering measures such as temporary importation to alleviate the scarcity. The FDA notes progress on shortages over recent years but still lists about 50 drugs currently in short supply.

This Economic Policy Institute briefing paper updates earlier work estimating the employment effects of growing U.S. goods trade deficits with China and quantifies Wal‑Mart’s role as a major conduit for Chinese imports. Between China’s 2001 WTO entry and 2013, the U.S. goods trade deficit with China rose sharply and, according to EPI methodology using an input‑output model, eliminated or displaced about 3.2 million U.S. jobs. Wal‑Mart, as the nation’s largest retailer and largest importer of ocean containers, is estimated conservatively to have accounted for 11.2 percent of U.S. goods imports from China in 2013—about $49.1 billion—and for roughly 15.3 percent of the deficit’s growth from 2001–2013. That Wal‑Mart share of trade flows corresponds to at least 415,400 U.S. jobs displaced over 2001–2013, including 314,500 manufacturing jobs (75.7 percent of Wal‑Mart‑related losses). Manufacturing losses are emphasized because these jobs typically pay higher wages and provide better benefits, especially for workers without college degrees. The report critiques Wal‑Mart’s 2013 pledge to buy more U.S. products—finding fewer than 4,100 specific U.S. manufacturing jobs identified to date—and concludes the retailer’s imports have displaced many more jobs than its promises create. The paper also attributes China’s export competitiveness to currency management, large purchases of U.S. assets, and labor repression, arguing U.S. policy should address exchange‑rate and labor‑standards practices. Overall, the brief contends Wal‑Mart’s import practices have been an important factor in an unbalanced U.S.–China trade relationship that has weakened U.S. manufacturing and wages.

Former hacker Adrian Lamo, who informed authorities about Army intelligence analyst Bradley Manning, says Manning likely had help from Boston-area hackers to leak massive classified files to WikiLeaks. Lamo told investigators he knew about five local people—including MIT and Boston University students—interviewed by Army and FBI agents; he alleges some provided encryption software, training, and even physically transferred documents to WikiLeaks. Lamo insists Manning lacked the technical and political expertise to act entirely alone and that associates with information-security backgrounds and antiwar views aided him. Those interviewed deny involvement and are not formally considered accomplices by officials. A recent MIT graduate acknowledged meeting and emailing Manning about security but denied any role in the leaks. Manning was arrested in May and charged with leaking a helicopter attack video, over 150,000 diplomatic cables, and thousands of Afghan war reports. Separately, WikiLeaks volunteer Jacob Appelbaum was detained and had devices seized returning from Europe; he was later questioned by FBI agents at DefCon. Appelbaum, a Tor project researcher and public WikiLeaks spokesman, defends leaks as exposing wrongdoing and rejects claims that volunteers directly endanger lives. Investigations continue into Manning’s ties to the hacker community and possible civilian assistance.

Arizona Republican Senator John McCain said it’s “worth looking into” whether Texas Senator Ted Cruz is eligible to serve as president, acknowledging uncertainty about the issue and suggesting the Supreme Court might need to weigh in. Speaking on KFYI’s Chris Merrill Show, McCain contrasted his own 2008 eligibility questions—he was born on a U.S. military base in the Panama Canal Zone—with Cruz’s situation: Cruz was born in Canada to an American mother and held dual U.S.-Canadian citizenship until he renounced the Canadian status in 2014. McCain said his Canal Zone birth differed from being born on foreign soil and that he isn’t a constitutional scholar, but he doesn’t think it’s illegitimate to examine Cruz’s eligibility. He recommended Cruz get ahead of the controversy, as McCain did in his own campaign.

The exchange follows public comments by GOP frontrunner Donald Trump, who told the Washington Post Cruz’s Canadian birth could be “a big problem” for the party, and uncertainty expressed by Senator Rand Paul. McCain’s remarks revived a wider narrative about establishment resistance to Cruz—who has long been a polarizing figure in Washington and a frequent target of McCain’s criticism. Observers note McCain’s questioning keeps the story alive beyond partisan attacks, potentially influencing media framing and the Republican primary dynamic, though it’s unclear the comments will significantly hurt Cruz’s standing with his anti-establishment supporters.

IndyStar is updating coverage of a shooting at Noblesville West Middle School on May 25, 2018. At about 9:06 a.m. dispatchers received reports of an active shooter; police from multiple agencies responded quickly. Authorities say a male student left class and returned with two handguns, then opened fire; a teacher and a student were wounded. A male student was detained at the scene. The teacher, identified by parents as Jason Seaman, a science teacher and youth football coach, reportedly intervened to stop the shooter and was shot three times; he was undergoing surgery but was awake and talking en route to the hospital, according to family. Victims’ identities and exact conditions have not been released. Students were evacuated, bused to Noblesville High School, and reunited with anxious parents; the middle school remains a crime scene and investigators say there are no additional suspects. Officials noted a separate threat that prompted a high school lockdown was likely unrelated. Local, state and federal officials—including Vice President Pence and Gov. Eric Holcomb—offered support. The incident renewed debate over school safety and gun access: recent Indiana legislation added funding and safety measures but drew criticism for not restricting firearms. The Indiana State Teachers Association urged action beyond prayers to prevent future tragedies. The Red Cross is available to assist, and the story is being updated as new information emerges.

Southwest Flight 812 from Phoenix to Sacramento suffered a sudden fuselage rupture at about 34,400 feet on April 1, forcing an emergency descent and landing in Yuma; oxygen masks deployed and passengers experienced brief loss of consciousness, but no serious injuries among 118 passengers and five crew were reported. Photos showed a several-foot hole in the cabin roof. The NTSB and FAA opened investigations; investigators removed fuselage sections and flight recorders. Southwest grounded about 79 similar Boeing 737-300s for inspections, canceling roughly 300 flights, while Boeing and regulators probed causes including possible metal fatigue and maintenance history.

A third victim of Asiana Airlines Flight 214 died Friday at San Francisco General Hospital: a girl under 18, a Chinese national, who had been critically injured when the Boeing 777 clipped a seawall, spun off the runway and caught fire. Earlier, police confirmed a 16-year-old Chinese passenger, Ye Meng Yuan, had been run over by an airport fire truck as crews sprayed foam, though investigators don’t yet know whether she was already dead. Another teen, Wang Lin Jia, also died. Dozens were treated; six remain hospitalized as NTSB crews began dismantling the wreckage and the runway reopened.

After President Trump announced the U.S. would withdraw from the Paris climate agreement, France mounted an immediate and public rebuttal. The French Ministry of Europe and Foreign Affairs reposted the White House’s promotional video with corrective on-screen captions disputing several Trump administration claims. Where the U.S. warned of millions of lost industrial and manufacturing jobs, France countered that major U.S. companies such as ExxonMobil, Schneider Electric and Microsoft disagree. The French edits also changed “badly negotiated” to “comprehensively negotiated,” corrected assertions about a supposed $3 billion UN “slush fund” by noting U.S. per-capita contributions are lower than some peers, and reframed MIT’s assessment of Paris from “negligible” impact to “a step in the right direction,” citing MIT researchers who said Trump misinterpreted their work.

French President Emmanuel Macron amplified the response, urging U.S. climate scientists and experts to consider France “a second homeland” and urging collective responsibility to “make our planet great again,” a riff on Trump’s slogan. France, along with Germany and Italy, released a joint statement rejecting any renegotiation of the accord. EU, UN and global leaders—including China, Japan and Pacific nations—expressed regret and concern, warning withdrawal risks severe environmental and geopolitical consequences, while some officials predicted the U.S. may eventually rejoin.

Brussels Airport announced a partial reopening for passengers 12 days after suicide bombers destroyed its departure hall, killing 16 at the airport and 19 in a metro attack. Initial operations will be minimal — three Brussels Airlines flights to Faro, Athens and Turin — and capacity limited to about 800 departing passengers per hour (around 20% of normal). Temporary outdoor check-in zones, tents for passenger and baggage screening, random vehicle checks, license-plate cameras, and increased armed police and military patrols will be used; access will initially be by car and taxi only. Authorities hope to restore full capacity by early July, ahead of summer holidays. The closure has cost carriers and the hospitality sector heavily: Brussels Airlines estimates €5 million daily losses, while many airlines have diverted services to regional airports like Charleroi, Liege and Ostend.

Research finds that Facebook use after breakups can prolong distress and impede personal growth. Two related studies (Marshall, 2012) surveyed college-age participants about Facebook interactions with exes and their postbreakup adjustment. One study identified three Facebook harassment behaviors—Covert Provocation, Public Harassment, and Venting—which were each associated with cyber obsessional pursuit (COP) and obsessive relational intrusion (ORI). People who engaged in COP were nearly six times more likely to perpetrate ORI, and stalking behaviors often occurred both online and offline. The larger study (N=464) tested whether remaining Facebook friends with an ex and actively surveilling an ex’s profile predicted worse outcomes beyond offline contact and personality or relationship factors. Facebook surveillance (frequency of checking an ex’s page or friends list) correlated with greater current distress, negative feelings, sexual desire, longing for the ex, and reduced personal growth—even for those not Facebook friends with their ex. Paradoxically, those who remained Facebook friends reported less negative emotion and longing but showed lower personal growth, perhaps because continued weak-tie exposure reduces opportunities for meaning-making and growth. Findings are correlational but suggest avoiding online exposure to an ex may aid emotional recovery and have implications for social media use and stalking laws.

A WWF report released Dec. 12, 2011, highlights 208 species newly described in 2010 across the Greater Mekong region — a biodiversity hotspot spanning Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam and Yunnan province in China. Discoveries included 145 plants, 28 reptiles, 25 fish, seven amphibians, two mammals and one bird, with notable finds such as a monkey with an Elvis‑style crest, a psychedelic gecko, a self‑cloning skink, five carnivorous plants and a distinctive leaf warbler. WWF stressed that these scientific gains contrast sharply with escalating threats: habitat loss, deforestation, overdevelopment and climate change are driving rapid biodiversity decline, exemplified by the recent extinction of Vietnam’s Javan rhino. WWF urged Greater Mekong leaders meeting in Myanmar (Dec. 19–20) to prioritize biodiversity in regional planning, arguing that protecting nature is essential for long‑term sustainability and that failing to do so will cost the region its irreplaceable natural heritage.

Authorities investigating the Turpin household in Perris, California, revealed a disturbing case of prolonged alleged abuse and neglect involving 13 children who appeared severely malnourished and developmentally stunted. Deputies discovered six minors and seven adults in a dark, malodorous home; three individuals were reportedly chained to furniture. A 17-year-old daughter escaped through a window with a cellphone and alerted authorities, leading to the rescue. Medical experts warn recovery will be slow and complex: prolonged malnutrition likely caused growth stunting and nutritional deficiencies, and refeeding must be carefully managed to avoid complications. Long-term psychological damage, including PTSD from deprivation of normal childhood interactions, will require sustained mental-health support. The minors are receiving care at Riverside University Health System Medical Center, while the seven adults—initially mistaken for minors due to their size—are treated at Corona Regional Medical Center; hospital officials described them as stable and hopeful. Parents David Allen Turpin, 56, and Louise Ann Turpin, 49, remain jailed with $9 million bail each; investigators say they are believed to be the biological parents. The family had registered an in-home private school, Sandcastle Day School, with California’s Department of Education; the agency noted it lacks authority to inspect private schools. Child Protective Services had no prior contact with the family. Riverside County plans to seek court authorization to oversee and place the children, possibly with relatives after checks, while a meticulous investigation continues into the duration and motive for the alleged abuse.

In August 2017 the FDA and Abbott (formerly St. Jude Medical) announced a corrective action—a firmware update—for about 465,000 radio-frequency-enabled implantable pacemakers to reduce risks from documented cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Researchers had shown that commercially available equipment and third-party programmers could potentially communicate with and reprogram devices, and that hospital monitoring systems sometimes lacked basic protections (no logins, unencrypted patient data including SSNs and names). Abbott’s firmware update, approved by the FDA and available beginning August 29, 2017, requires in-person installation during a roughly three-minute visit; devices manufactured after August 28, 2017 include the update preloaded. During the update the pacemaker temporarily operates in backup mode but essential functions remain available. The FDA and Abbott do not recommend device replacement and report no known patient harm from these vulnerabilities. The update will require authorization from Merlin Programmer or Merlin@home Transmitter for future communications. Known, low-probability update risks include incomplete reloads, loss of settings, or, very rarely, complete device failure. Providers should discuss risks and benefits with patients, consider each patient’s dependence on pacing, and follow guidance (including printing device settings before update). The FDA will monitor and work with manufacturers, researchers, and health organizations on device cybersecurity and urges reporting of adverse events via MedWatch. Patients with questions should consult their physicians or Abbott’s resources.

President Donald Trump had a previously unreported one-on-one exchange with Russian President Vladimir Putin during a Group of 20 leaders’ dinner in Hamburg, Germany, prompting conflicting accounts and concern. The White House acknowledged Trump “spoke briefly” with Putin at the close of the dinner, saying leaders circulated freely and the encounter was routine social small talk; it denied reports of a separate private meeting and called suggestions the White House tried to hide anything “false, malicious and absurd.” Trump also dismissed press reports as “Fake News” on Twitter.

Multiple news outlets and attendees, however, described a longer, more private conversation lasting up to an hour, during which Trump apparently left his chair to speak directly with Putin, who was seated next to First Lady Melania Trump. Some foreign leaders found the episode “weird” and unsettling, and critics noted there is no U.S. government record or American interpreter present for the exchange, raising national security and transparency concerns. U.S. intelligence agencies have concluded Russia attempted to influence the 2016 election, and several congressional investigations and a special counsel probe are ongoing into Russian interference and possible ties to Trump associates. Separately, the White House announced Trump plans to nominate Gov. John Huntsman as U.S. ambassador to Russia.

Peter Hamby reviews Mark Halperin and John Heilemann’s Double Down, a behind‑the‑scenes chronicle of the 2012 presidential campaign that trades sweeping structural analysis for juicy insider detail. The book spotlights tensions—most explosively between Mitt Romney’s team and New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, after a vetting file from Romney aides revealed damaging allegations about Christie—and relishes campaign theater: tempers, gaffes, vomit backstage, and eyebrow‑raising anecdotes about candidates and surrogates. Halperin and Heilemann spend heavy time on the chaotic Republican primary while portraying Obama’s operation as disciplined and Romney’s as reactive. Critics may fault the pair’s reliance on anonymous sources and anecdote over data, yet their portraiture captures candidates’ temperaments and human flaws that shape voters’ choices. The book also spreads wider implications: readers will debate its ethics and the media’s appetite for scandal. A separate excerpt notes a stark Obama quote about drone warfare, prompting discussion of the administration’s expanded targeted‑strike campaign.

The Wine Institute’s latest figures show Vatican City leads the world in per-capita wine consumption, with residents drinking an average of 74 litres annually — about 105 bottles per person. That level is roughly double the average in France or Italy and about three times higher than in the UK. Observers note the Vatican’s atypical, homogeneous population helps explain the statistic: residents tend to be older, predominantly male, highly educated and often dine in larger groups, all factors linked with higher wine intake. Ceremonial duties — including regular Communion wine — also contribute. Vatican City’s tiny population of roughly 800 makes per-capita measures especially sensitive to outliers, and the presence of a single, nearly tax-free supermarket reportedly supplying most of the city-state’s wine further skews consumption figures. Other microstates also appear high on the Wine Institute’s list, suggesting size and demographic composition, more than sheer volume, drive these rankings. The report’s underlying web crawl details and WARC files are not publicly accessible.

Airbus’s research team in Toulouse has filed a striking patent for an unconventional aircraft architecture that reimagines the passenger cabin as a circular, 360-degree seating space enclosed within a delta-wing, teardrop-shaped fuselage. The top view resembles a doughnut inside a triangular French pastry (a “Jésuite”), a comparison the patent text even playfully acknowledges by noting the removal of almonds to improve aerodynamics. The design’s stated aim is to address shortcomings of conventional cylindrical cabins—specifically heavy, sealed end structures needed to withstand pressurization and limited passenger capacity—by redistributing loads and potentially increasing seating density in an amphitheater-like arrangement. The U.S. filing, naming investors Patrick Lieven, Romain Delahaye and Catalin Perju, describes the concept as a “simple, economic and efficient solution” to pressure-geometry problems. Airbus stresses the idea is only one of hundreds of patent filings intended to protect intellectual property and not a committed development program. Significant technical, regulatory and infrastructure barriers would face any effort to commercialize such a radical shape: emergency exit rules conflict with proposed below-deck boarding hatches, and airports might need major modifications—echoing challenges seen with the A380. For now the concept remains futuristic artwork on paper rather than an imminent aircraft.

A recent paper, "The Physics of Baking Good Pizza," examines why authentic Neapolitan Margherita pizzas baked in brick ovens are hard to replicate at home and offers a physics-based method to approximate them in a conventional electric oven. The authors—two physicists and a food anthropologist who sampled Roman pies—describe how wood-fired brick ovens, heated to roughly 625°F (330°C) or higher, deliver uniformly distributed radiant heat from curved walls and a stone floor. That combination rapidly bakes a thin pizza in about two minutes, producing a soft, elastic interior, charred flecks on the crust, and perfectly melted toppings. In contrast, common home ovens use metal trays or racks with much higher thermal conductivity; metal transfers heat to the dough far faster than brick. If you bake at the same extreme temperatures on metal, the bottom will burn long before toppings are cooked. Using a thermodynamic analysis (their equation #13), the authors calculate that to mimic brick-oven conditions in an electric oven you should lower the temperature to about 450°F (230°C) and bake for roughly 170 seconds, adjusting time upward for wetter toppings because evaporation extracts heat. Their conclusion: while a home oven can’t fully match a stone-fired pie eaten in Rome, understanding heat transfer lets you get closer—otherwise consider other dishes (they’ve also studied steamed dumplings).

CEO fraud, also called “fraude au président” or business email compromise (BEC), is a highly effective social-engineering scam in which attackers impersonate senior executives, lawyers, or trusted vendors to trick employees into wiring money to fraudsters. Targeted, low‑tech attacks use look‑alike domains, hacked inboxes, and publicly available corporate data (LinkedIn, websites) to craft convincing, urgent messages that bypass spam filters and antivirus tools. France has been particularly hard hit: since 2010 an estimated €465m was lost and about 15,000 firms affected, with high-profile victims including Michelin, KPMG and Nestlé. One noted case involved Etna Industrie, whose accountant almost sent €500,000 after receiving emails and phone calls supposedly from the CEO; €100,000 was temporarily lost but later recovered after a court found the bank at fault. French‑Israeli gangs, notably Gilbert Chikli’s network, have been linked to many attacks. Globally the FBI and security firms report dramatic rises: the FBI cites $2.3bn in losses across thousands of victims and a 270% increase in identified incidents since 2015; other estimates top $2bn in two years. Losses per incident average $25,000–$75,000 but can reach millions. Recommended defenses include two‑factor authentication for email, multi‑channel verification (phone calls) for transfers, restricting public disclosure of operational details, employee phishing education, and prompt reporting to banks and authorities when targeted.

The Ediacaran biota, a diverse group of soft-bodied organisms that flourished in warm shallow seas roughly 570–541 million years ago, have long perplexed scientists because their strange shapes leave ambiguous relationships to modern life. Dickinsonia, a flattened, ribbed oval that could exceed a metre in length and bore a central ridge, has been variously assigned to fungi, protists, lichens, or animals. A new study in Science applies molecular biomarker analysis to remarkably preserved Dickinsonia specimens from the White Sea region of northwest Russia and provides strong chemical evidence that Dickinsonia was an animal.

Researchers extracted and analyzed sterol-derived molecular fossils preserved in thin films of organic matter on the fossil surfaces. Sterols are group-specific biomolecules: animals produce cholesterol derivatives, while fungi and many algae produce different sterols. The Dickinsonia samples contained overwhelmingly cholesterol-derived compounds (up to 93% of the sterane signal), whereas surrounding sediments were dominated by ergosteroids indicative of green algae. The team validated their methods on other Ediacaran fossils and interpreted the cholesterol signal as a robust signature that Dickinsonia was an animal, pushing confirmed animal existence back to about 558 million years ago—well before the Cambrian explosion.

The approach helps resolve decades of debate by combining morphological imprint studies with molecular chemistry, offering a new tool to classify other enigmatic Ediacarans. While preservation biases and the antiquity of these molecules leave some uncertainty, experts praise the rigor and see this as a major step toward understanding early multicellular evolution and the transition to the animal-dominated world of the Cambrian.

Flynn McGarry is a precocious 16‑year‑old chef whose culinary ambition and media savvy are shaping an unconventional path toward a high‑end restaurant career. Having graduated high school early and already running popular supper clubs in New York and Los Angeles, McGarry will open a 12‑seat pop‑up called Eureka in the Village, serving a 14‑course tasting menu three nights a week. Priced at $160 per person with an optional $80 wine pairing, the pop‑up is sold out through September. McGarry treats the venture as practical training: a way to learn restaurant operations without committing to a permanent space. His dishes are imaginative and meticulously developed — examples include a three‑week‑aged beet bourguignon with fermented beet butter and a tomato‑lobster dumpling in rose‑hip tea — and he plans to rotate items frequently to keep the menu fresh.

McGarry is also pursuing broader exposure and resources. He hopes to star in a reality travel show that would pay for his global apprenticeships in top kitchens, accelerating his goal to become the youngest Michelin‑starred chef. Though he resists overthinking media attention, he embraces self‑promotion as essential to modern creative work, arguing that publicity enables opportunities he couldn’t otherwise afford, especially at 15 when his mother must accompany him.

His longer‑term plan is methodical: move to New York at 17, stage at elite restaurants such as Eleven Madison Park for about a year, then open his own place by 19—mindful of rising real estate costs. McGarry openly sets lofty benchmarks—Michelin stars and elite rankings—to motivate himself, saying he thrives on pressure and wants to build “one of the best restaurants in the world.”

School bus drivers in New York City, members of Amalgamated Transit Union Local 1181, launched their first strike since the 1970s over city plans to bid out roughly 1,100 private bus contracts without Employee Protection Provisions (EPPs). About 8,800 drivers and matrons walked picket lines at depots across the city, with other unions pledging not to cross them. The strike immediately disrupted service for roughly 152,000 students—about 14% of the public school population—including some 54,000 students with disabilities who face particular hardship; overall attendance dropped 2.5% and special-education attendance fell dramatically in some areas.

City officials scrambled to respond: students received free MetroCards to use subways and buses, and parents were to receive cards after a 72-hour programming delay. Parents driving children are eligible for 55-cent-per-mile reimbursements; cab users must submit weekly receipts. The city and bus companies have hired replacement, nonunion drivers who must complete three days of testing and training before starting, so service restoration is uncertain. The companies asked the NLRB to halt the strike, saying they’ll suffer financially.

Union leaders vowed to continue until job protections return to the bids; city officials say such guarantees may violate competitive-bidding rules. No negotiations were scheduled, leaving the strike’s duration unclear and families bracing for a potentially prolonged disruption.

Mike Brown, a Caltech planetary scientist famed as the self-styled "Pluto killer," has helped discover more than 30 distant dwarf planets and asteroids and played a central role in the 2006 reclassification of Pluto. His detection of Eris — initially thought to be larger than Pluto and about 25 percent more massive — helped prompt the International Astronomical Union to formalize a planet definition that relegated Pluto to dwarf-planet status. Brown says Eris’s greater mass, not Pluto’s volume, exposed the need to rethink what constitutes a planet and led to broader recognition of many Pluto-like bodies in the Kuiper Belt.

Now Brown and his colleague Konstantin Batygin have published new mathematical modeling and computer simulations arguing there is strong indirect evidence for a true ninth planet, dubbed Planet Nine. They infer its existence from the peculiar clustering and orbital behavior of several distant small bodies: their perihelia and orbital orientations appear sculpted by a massive, distant perturber. Their models suggest a planet five to ten times Earth’s mass, roughly two to four times Earth’s diameter, on a highly elongated orbit tens of times farther from the Sun than Neptune — possibly taking 10,000–20,000 years per circuit. Brown estimates the odds of its reality as perhaps 90 percent; others are cautiously optimistic but stress that direct observation is required.

Observers on multiple continents are now searching for it. Brown emphasizes that formal discovery requires direct imaging and orbital confirmation; their paper functions as a treasure map pointing to where telescopes should look. If found, Planet Nine would likely qualify as a planet under IAU criteria because its gravity would clearly sculpt the surrounding population. Brown downplays naming ambitions and acknowledges luck will play a role in who spots it first. Whether Planet Nine exists remains unconfirmed, but the new analysis has reinvigorated searches and revived discussion about our solar system’s architecture.

University of Missouri officials are investigating multiple allegations involving the Delta Upsilon (DU) fraternity, including potential use of date-rape drugs and other misconduct tied to parties this fall. Records obtained by ABC 17 News show at least two open investigations: one by the school’s Title IX office into claims that active DU members allegedly gave new members pills and instructed them to drug women to incapacitate them for sexual activity, and a separate Office of Student Conduct inquiry linked to a racially charged confrontation that culminated on DU’s front lawn Sept. 27 and led the national organization to place the Columbia chapter on emergency suspension. The chapter had been placed on disciplinary probation a day before the lawn incident after problems at parties on Aug. 27 and Sept. 10, which included an alcohol overdose requiring ambulance transport for a 20-year-old woman, an altercation that pushed a man down stairs, and an 18-year-old who hit her head after excessive drinking. DU had previously received two university warnings for underage drinking and noncompliance with police during a theft probe. A police report describes a Sept. 16 medical call for an 18-year-old found disoriented and partially unclothed in a residence hall with fecal smearing on walls; she reported drinking at multiple locations including DU, was taken to hospital where urine was tested for drugs, and could not recall whether she had sex that night. MU spokespersons and DU national communications say investigations remain ongoing; DU says it’s cooperating and previously reduced membership and tightened policies. Possible outcomes range from expulsion of individuals to the university withdrawing recognition of the chapter, barring campus privileges and event participation.

Bill O’Reilly devoted a segment of his Friday show to attacking Sandra Fluke, the Georgetown law student who had urged insurance coverage of contraception and was subsequently insulted by Rush Limbaugh. O’Reilly echoed Limbaugh’s core argument — that Fluke wants taxpayers to pay for her sex life — though he did not use Limbaugh’s extreme epithets. He framed Fluke’s request for birth-control coverage under a university health plan as an improper demand on other people’s money, asking rhetorically if he should bankroll students’ sexual activity. O’Reilly extended the logic with provocative comparisons, suggesting that if society must subsidize Fluke’s “activities,” then taxpayers should also cover his college football uniform if an injury imposes costs, or men’s gym memberships to keep them fit. He cast Fluke’s position as part of a broader progressive agenda and an attack on American freedom, asserting that “the progressive colossus” seeks payment so she can attend Georgetown Law “with an active, healthy social life.” The segment aligned O’Reilly with Limbaugh’s stance even as advertisers and many critics condemned Limbaugh’s harsher language.

Fox News host Sean Hannity promoted a bizarre, unfounded claim that Kehinde Wiley’s official portrait of Barack Obama contains “secret sperm cells,” sparking widespread ridicule. Hannity linked to a now-deleted article on his site and tweeted that the portrait featured “inappropriate sexual innuendo,” citing a close-up detail of Obama’s temple as supposed evidence. The article alleged Wiley had concealed sperm-like motifs in his work and recycled a 2008 New York Times note that Wiley’s patterned backgrounds have sometimes been likened to abstractions of sperm. Parts of the conspiracy traced back to a 4chan post that circulated the same close-up image. The piece also recycled an old quote and controversy about a different Wiley painting—misrepresented as a threat to white people—to sensationalize the story. Both the tweet and the article were removed within hours; Hannity issued a statement blaming his web staff for publishing content “not reviewed by me” and said it did not reflect his voice. The episode followed broader debate over Wiley’s nontraditional, widely praised portrait, which Obama defended at the National Portrait Gallery unveiling, praising Wiley’s attention to dignity, representation, and challenging conventional views of power and privilege.

Astronomers are disputing a reported detection of Gliese 581g, a low-mass planet thought to orbit in the habitable zone of nearby star Gliese 581. Vogt et al. combined historic Keck radial-velocity data and published HARPS measurements through 2008 with new high-cadence Keck observations and reported a ~3σ signal consistent with a ~3+ Earth-mass planet in a temperate, circular orbit. Concerns were raised about false-alarm probability estimates and difficulties disentangling signals in tightly packed systems. At IAU 276 in Torino, the Geneva HARPS team, with ~50% more data than used by Vogt et al., said they cannot confirm the planet; forcing a solution produces a negative signal, suggesting the detection may be spurious. The HARPS group cannot definitively rule out the planet, and additional high-precision, high-cadence observations over the next year or two are expected to resolve the issue.

The Senate control contest on Election Day is extremely close — essentially a coin flip. Polling models give Democrats a slight edge: about a 52–53% chance to win a majority, and a roughly 16% chance of a 50-50 Senate where the vice president breaks ties. Structural factors help both sides: Republicans defend 24 of 34 seats up in 2016, many in states Obama won in 2008 or 2012, giving Democrats pickup opportunities; but incumbency generally helps Republicans, and GOP incumbents often outperform Trump. The Senate map and presidential coattails have produced tight correlations between Clinton’s standing and Democratic chances in Senate races.

Democrats need a net gain of five seats for a majority (four for a tie). FiveThirtyEight highlights 11 key races plus two wild cards. Likely/probable Democratic pickups include Illinois (Mark Kirk vs. Tammy Duckworth) and Wisconsin (Ron Johnson vs. Russ Feingold). Pennsylvania (Pat Toomey vs. Katie McGinty) leans Democratic. Tossups that could decide the chamber include Missouri (Roy Blunt vs. Jason Kander), Nevada (Joe Heck vs. Catherine Cortez Masto), and New Hampshire (Kelly Ayotte vs. Maggie Hassan). Plausible pick-ups: Indiana (Evan Bayh vs. Todd Young) and North Carolina (Richard Burr vs. Deborah Ross). Longshots: Florida (Marco Rubio vs. Patrick Murphy) and very longshots in Arizona and Ohio. Wild cards: Colorado (Michael Bennet) and Louisiana’s jungle primary.

Individual race dynamics vary: recruitment, incumbency, local demographics, turnout, and candidates’ handling of Trump shaped close contests. Some Democrats’ chances depend heavily on Clinton’s performance and turnout in key counties; Republicans bank on incumbents’ advantages and Trump’s strength in certain states. Because polls can be off in the same direction across races, surprises remain possible, but many simulations show a razor-thin outcome — tied or 51-49 scenarios are common — making the Senate outcome as fraught as the presidential contest.

The document contrasts two eras of John McCain’s political character. In 2000, during his insurgent primary bid against George W. Bush, McCain rejected dirty politics—refusing negative ads and delivering a concession speech that praised honor and principle after his loss amid vicious smears. Yet by 2008, McCain’s campaign adopted many of those same tactics against Barack Obama: insinuating ties to radicals, circulating robo-calls and flyers, and pushing personal attacks that even unnerved him at moments. Critics, allies, and admirers saw this as a betrayal of the principled “happy warrior” image that had attracted centrists and independents. The piece also notes lingering animosity between Bush and McCain—Bush once privately admitted he might not even vote for McCain despite endorsing him.

After nearly a year stalled, comprehensive food-safety legislation moved forward in the Senate during the lame-duck session. The bill, S. 510, backed by Sen. Dick Durbin, HELP Chair Tom Harkin and advocates like The Pew Charitable Trusts, cleared a 74-25 cloture vote to limit debate and advance toward final passage. The measure—less contentious than the House version—would boost FDA authority to trace outbreaks, require more frequent and thorough inspections of processing plants (including imports), grant HHS stronger recall powers, and mandate a joint national food-safety plan with USDA. The HELP Committee approved an earlier draft unanimously in November 2009; the House passed its own bill in July 2009. Key sticking points remain: Sen. Jon Tester seeks exemptions for small farms to avoid undue burdens, and Sen. Dianne Feinstein pushes limits on bisphenol-A in containers. Industry groups and farm advocates are lobbying hard on both amendments. Opponents like Sen. Tom Coburn argue the bill adds costly bureaucracy without fixing core problems. With bipartisan co-sponsors but unresolved differences with the House, rapid reconciliation would be required to send a final bill to the president before the session ends.

PepsiCo is launching Gatorade Zero, the brand’s first no-sugar, no-carb sports drink, to recapture consumers moving away from sugary beverages. Debuting in Lemon-Lime, Orange and Glacier Cherry, it arrives as sports-drink volume fell and rivals like coconut water and flavored electrolyte waters gain traction. Gatorade, long dominant in the roughly $8 billion US category, has seen sales and share slip amid health-conscious trends and competition from Powerade Zero and newer brands like BodyArmor. PepsiCo previously added lower-sugar and organic lines; Gatorade Zero aims to offer athletes hydration without sugar and counter emerging competitors.

Tesla’s board confirmed it has repeatedly met to discuss CEO Elon Musk’s surprise proposal to take the company private, following Musk’s tweet that he had “funding secured” to offer $420 per share—implying a roughly $72 billion deal before debt and potentially the largest buyout ever. A terse statement from six independent directors said Musk “opened a discussion” last week about how being private could better serve Tesla’s long-term interests and that funding was addressed; three directors, including Musk and his brother Kimbal and Steve Jurvetson, did not join the statement. The announcement raised multiple questions: whether the board was satisfied that funding really was secured, why the talks weren’t disclosed in Tesla’s recent SEC filing, and whether Musk’s tweet was an appropriate way to notify investors. Regulators have shown interest and experts note legal, financing and structural uncertainties—especially given Tesla’s lack of consistent profits and how many shareholders might choose to stay public—while the stock has seen volatile swings since the revelation.

Police are searching for 21-year-old Oscar Ramiro Ortega after shots were fired near the White House and Washington Monument; no one was injured and no bullets were initially found in surrounding buildings, cars or trees. Authorities located Ortega’s crashed car near the Theodore Roosevelt Bridge containing a semi-automatic rifle and shell casings, and have issued a felony warrant for carrying a dangerous weapon. Ortega, described as a Hispanic male about 5'11", 160 lbs, has a criminal record across Idaho, Texas and Utah and is believed to have been in the Washington area for weeks. The Secret Service later found a bullet stopped by the White House’s inner glass and another on the exterior, raising concern the rounds may be linked to the incident. Officials say Ortega may be mentally ill, had been previously stopped by police the same day, and might have exhibited a fixation on the White House. Investigators urge Ortega to come forward as they assess his motives and potential threat.

President-elect Donald Trump spent Sunday continuing transition activities at his Bedminster, New Jersey golf club while publicly criticizing entertainers on Twitter. He attacked Saturday Night Live after seeing parts of the show, calling it “totally one-sided, biased” and demanding “equal time,” criticizing Alec Baldwin’s portrayal of him as ignorant on foreign policy. Trump also renewed his complaints about the Broadway musical Hamilton, insisting the cast and producers “should immediately apologize to Mike Pence for their terrible behavior” after Vice President-elect Mike Pence attended a performance Friday night where actor Brandon Victor Dixon addressed him from the stage about concerns regarding the incoming administration. Trump called the production “highly overrated” in his tweets, some of which he subsequently deleted. Meanwhile his transition team continued vetting candidates for cabinet and other posts. Trump’s Bedminster schedule for the day included meetings with New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani and Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach; he had met Saturday with Mitt Romney and retired Marine Gen. James Mattis, a possible nominee for Defense. Trump indicated he might announce some appointments imminently and said “Numerous patriots will be coming to Bedminster” as he works to “MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!”

Essex Police dropped drug charges against Lamarr Chambers after he spent 47 days in custody refusing to use the toilet following an arrest on 17 January in Harlow. The 24-year-old, from Brixton, was suspected of having swallowed Class A drugs during a police chase. During detention he remained under constant surveillance, received daily medical visits, and was routinely provided food and water, but repeatedly declined medical treatment and opportunities to go to hospital. Prosecutors discontinued the possession-with-intent-to-supply and driving charges, citing insufficient evidence and public interest considerations, and Chambers was released on 5 March on medical and legal advice. Police had repeatedly sought custody extensions at seven court hearings while waiting for him to pass the suspected evidence; social media tracked the saga under Essex Police’s #PooWatch. Authorities say this may be the longest recorded period anyone has gone without using the toilet while in custody. After his release he was re-arrested on suspicion of being concerned in the supply of a Class A drug, released on bail, and taken to hospital with a medical professional. Deputy Chief Constable BJ Harrington emphasized the need to balance detainee welfare with securing evidence in suspected internal concealment cases. Reporting restrictions were lifted.

Yahoo sued Facebook in U.S. District Court in San Jose, alleging infringement of 10 patents covering messaging, news feed generation, social commenting, ad display, click-fraud prevention and privacy controls. The complaint argues Facebook built much of its social-network model using Yahoo’s earlier patented technologies and quotes Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg acknowledging that “getting there first is not what it’s all about.” Yahoo seeks unspecified damages after failed licensing talks; it had reportedly been demanding fees and said other companies have licensed its patents.

The timing is notable: Facebook is preparing a high-profile IPO that could value it near $100 billion, and experts say companies are vulnerable to patent suits during IPO processes. Yahoo, which has seen declining revenue and recently appointed Scott Thompson as CEO, retained Quinn Emanuel, a firm active in major tech patent cases. Only two patents reportedly directly target social-networking features; most relate to online advertising. Yahoo holds a much larger patent portfolio (over 3,300 patents/applications) than Facebook (about 160), giving it leverage. Facebook said it learned of the suit through media and expressed disappointment that a longtime partner resorted to litigation. The case is Yahoo Inc. v. Facebook Inc., No. 12-cv-1212.

Carla Stefaniak, a 36-year-old Hallandale Beach resident who lived in the Tampa area for 12 years, disappeared while on a birthday trip to Costa Rica with her sister-in-law, April Antonieta (also referred to as April Burton). The two traveled together and had been sharing upbeat moments from their trip; CBS4 received cheerful cell phone clips from their vacation. Antonieta returned to the U.S. a day early on Nov. 27; she said Stefaniak drove her to the airport, returned the rental car, and then took an Uber to the Airbnb where she was staying. According to Antonieta, the Uber driver later offered Stefaniak a one‑hour tour of San José, which Carla accepted. She communicated with Antonieta throughout the evening, reporting heavy rain and power outages after being dropped off at the Airbnb around 8 p.m.—that was the last contact. Stefaniak was scheduled to fly home to Miami at 1 p.m. the next day, Nov. 28, but never boarded. Relatives say Stefaniak’s social media fell silent and her last texts referenced intermittent power. Family members have spoken with the Airbnb owners, an Uber driver and security guards; some report she left early the following morning around 5 a.m. in an unknown car.
