Her brother and other relatives have traveled to Costa Rica to search; Antonieta has contacted the Miami FBI, the U.S. Embassy and Senator Marco Rubio’s office. A #FindingCarla flyer and a GoFundMe have been launched to support the search as family and friends seek any tips or assistance from authorities.

Hurricane Sandy — later classified as a post-tropical “superstorm” — battered the U.S. East Coast as it merged with other weather systems, creating a vast, damaging storm that affected tens of millions. Making landfall near southern New Jersey late Monday, Sandy brought record storm surges, widespread coastal flooding, destructive winds and major disruptions across a huge swath of the Northeast and into inland and Appalachian regions.

The storm’s impacts were state-by-state and varied from coastal inundation to heavy inland snow. New Jersey and New York suffered severe coastal flooding: Atlantic City and neighboring shore towns saw streets and boardwalks submerged, cars underwater and sections of boardwalk ripped away. Lower Manhattan recorded a surge near 14 feet, inundating subway stations and flooding electrical substations, which precipitated massive outages in the city. New York City closed its transit system, evacuated low-lying neighborhoods and shut down its airports; a construction crane collapsed in midtown, prompting evacuations. Con Edison preemptively cut power to protect equipment, but by late Monday hundreds of thousands in the New York area were still without electricity.

Massachusetts and New England endured punishing winds and high seas that toppled trees and power lines, closed roads and shuttered schools and businesses. Coastal towns prepared for storm surges exceeding six feet and some areas opened shelters; Cape Cod and the southern coast reported the highest gusts and significant coastal flooding. Across the Northeast and mid-Atlantic, utilities warned outages could last days because high winds made repairs dangerous.

In the mid-Atlantic, Maryland and Delaware enforced driving bans and positioned National Guard and staging resources; Ocean City experienced extreme surge and erosion. Washington, D.C., halted rail service; taxis were permitted a temporary emergency fare. Pennsylvania faced wind gusts up to 75 mph and heavy rain; speed and vehicle restrictions were imposed on highways. Connecticut, Rhode Island, New Hampshire and Vermont declared emergencies, closed schools and opened shelters; New Hampshire urged drivers off roads and activated Guard troops.

Inland and western areas saw unusual effects: Sandy’s western flank interacted with cold air to produce heavy, even blizzard-level snow in parts of West Virginia, Virginia, Kentucky and the southern Appalachians — with up to several feet possible at high elevations. The storm also disrupted travel nationwide, canceling thousands of flights and leading Amtrak to suspend most Northeast Corridor service. The New York Stock Exchange closed; many colleges, government offices and public services were shuttered.

Tragically, Sandy caused multiple fatalities across states and had already killed dozens in the Caribbean. At sea, the tall ship HMS Bounty sank off North Carolina; most of its crew were rescued but some remained missing. Utilities and emergency crews mobilized large mutual-assistance efforts to restore power and respond to damage. Restoration work began as winds eased, with out-of-state repair crews and National Guard units deployed. Authorities warned that the slow-moving, large storm would continue to produce dangerous conditions — coastal flooding, downed trees and prolonged outages — through the following days and urged residents to heed evacuation and safety orders.

The UN has reported that the number of Syrians who have fled the conflict and sought refuge in neighboring countries has reached one million. UNHCR said more than 400,000 people became refugees since January 1, 2013, and roughly half are children, most under 11 and often traumatized. Major host countries—Lebanon, Jordan, Turkey, Iraq and Egypt—are severely strained: Lebanon’s population rose by about 10%, Jordan’s services are stretched, and Turkey has spent over $600 million establishing camps. The symbolic millionth refugee, 19-year-old mother Bushra, described crowded, precarious living conditions with her two children in Tripoli, Lebanon. UN High Commissioner António Guterres warned Syria is “spiralling towards full-scale disaster” and that humanitarian capacity is dangerously stretched, urging greater international support for host countries. Donor funding lags badly—only about 25% of the regional response plan is funded—leaving agencies struggling to meet urgent needs. Without a political solution, UNHCR insists more funds are urgently required to save lives and ease suffering.

A series of political and election stories unfolded: Senator Rand Paul staged an almost 11-hour Senate floor protest against renewing the Patriot Act as the Justice Department warned the NSA’s bulk phone-records program could end without reauthorization. Hillary Clinton urged childcare be a national priority and pushed Republicans for more federal support while she maintained a low-key Iowa campaign approach. Jeb Bush criticized President Obama’s Iraq withdrawal but stopped short of promising more troops. Internationally, Burundi delayed parliamentary votes amid deadly unrest, and Ireland debated legalizing same-sex marriage. Back home, Florida’s Miami-Dade County struggled to process a massive backlog of absentee and provisional ballots after lengthy lines and operational problems, delaying results and keeping the statewide margin narrow enough to risk a recount. Third-party tallies showed Gary Johnson, Jill Stein, Virgil Goode and others still accumulating votes as final counts continued.

A powerful winter nor’easter struck the Midwest and Northeast around New Year’s, bringing heavy snow, strong winds, coastal flooding risk and dangerously cold temperatures that threatened commutes and travel for the first workday after the holidays. Forecasts called for generally 6–12 inches across interior southern New England and New York, with up to a foot or more in places and localized amounts above that — Boston could receive 10–18 inches, parts of Massachusetts up to 2 feet, and Long Island faced blizzard conditions with 8–10 inches and 35–45 mph gusts. Airlines and airports were heavily impacted: more than 2,200 U.S. flights were canceled Thursday, with O’Hare, Newark and LaGuardia among the worst hit. States declared emergencies and preemptively closed or restricted major roadways; officials warned of whiteout conditions, drifting snow and wind chills plunging well below zero. The storm disrupted daily life—schools closed, shelters prepared for more occupants, and residents stocked shovels and salt or planned to work from home. After the snowfall, an even colder air mass was expected to linger, bringing some of the coldest temperatures in years across the region and prolonging travel and safety concerns.

Twelve-year-old Ananya Vinay, a Fresno sixth-grader who won the 2017 Scripps National Spelling Bee, became the unexpected center of a controversy after a CNN interview in which anchor Alisyn Camerota joked that the now-famous internet typo “covfefe” might have its root in Sanskrit — “which is what you’re probably, uh, used to using,” she said. The remark, made after Camerota and Chris Cuomo quizzed Vinay on the made-up word, drew immediate criticism on social media as presumptive and racially insensitive because Vinay is Indian American. Critics argued the comment reinforced the automatic “othering” of brown Americans by assuming a cultural or linguistic connection based solely on heritage; commentators asked whether similar assumptions would be made about white or Jewish winners. CNN defended Camerota, saying the Sanskrit line was a recycled joke from an earlier segment and not intended to reflect bias, calling accusations of racism “extremely cynical.” Observers and writers noted the broader issue: even casually intended jokes can perpetuate a patronizing mindset that treats children like Vinay as less American regardless of birthplace or upbringing. The episode sparked debate on how seemingly benign remarks reveal deeper assumptions about identity and belonging, and how repeated microaggressions — polite or joking — contribute to a sense of exclusion among successful American-born minorities. Many felt the moment detracted from celebrating Vinay’s achievement and reflected a wider pattern of questioning where people of color truly “belong.”

A viral video showing staff at a Westport, Massachusetts, car dealership berating a pizza delivery driver over roughly $7 in change sparked public outrage, an apology from the dealership’s management, and a grassroots fundraising surge that raised more than $11,000 for the driver. The driver, identified as Palace Pizza employee Jarrid Tansey, had delivered about $42 worth of food and was handed $50. Believing the extra $7 to be a tip, he left and was later called back to return the change; a surveillance-style clip captures the resulting exchange in which Tansey questions why he was handed a bill only to be summoned back, while office workers insist they needed correct change. The interaction escalates: a woman threatens Tansey physically and colleagues laugh; another man demands Tansey’s manager be called so the driver could be fired. The dealership’s sales manager, Gary Batista, issued a statement apologizing “for the actions that led to this situation” and said the owner plans to offer Tansey a cash donation; one implicated female employee was terminated and at least one participant was not an employee. The video, initially posted to YouTube and LiveLeak before being taken down or made private, prompted viewers to act. Amanda Rogers, who saw the clip, set up a GoFundMe titled “Get Jarrid his tip money!” which collected roughly $11,500 by Thursday night, with many donors giving in $7 increments. Palace Pizza reported an outpouring of support and calls; the dealership’s owner and son visited to apologize in person. The incident led to negative online reviews for F&R Auto Sales and disrupted the dealership’s communications.

Governor Rick Scott declared a state of emergency for Martin and St. Lucie counties (later expanded to include Lee and Palm Beach) in response to extensive blue-green algal blooms fouling South Florida waterways and beaches. The executive order lets state and local agencies redirect flows into and out of Lake Okeechobee and accelerate water storage projects intended to reduce harmful discharges to the St. Lucie and Caloosahatchee estuaries. Scott blamed federal inaction—specifically delayed repairs to the Herbert Hoover Dike and insufficient U.S. Army Corps of Engineers measures—for forcing large releases from Lake Okeechobee that carry nutrient-rich water fueling blooms. The Corps began reducing east/west discharges after local pressure.

Scott directed the Florida Department of Environmental Protection to deploy extra staff for faster surveys and sampling, buy on-site microcystin test kits for quicker toxin screening, and launch a public hotline to report blooms. The Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission was asked to continue offshore surveys. The South Florida Water Management District was instructed to store more water north of the lake (Kissimmee Chain of Lakes), increase southward flows where feasible, and pursue dispersed storage projects.

The blooms have created health and economic threats: beaches closed ahead of the Fourth of July weekend, tourism and local businesses suffered, residents reported foul odors and wildlife—manatees—struggling in thick mats. Tests from mid-June showed Lake Okeechobee algae with toxin levels over 20 times WHO hazard thresholds. Scientists warn that thickening and dying blooms release toxins and can trigger fish kills by depleting oxygen. Local leaders and federal senators urged storing and treating more water southward while noting long-term restoration funding gaps and the complexity of balancing flood risk, water supply, and ecosystem health.

The Washington State Health Department and other authorities described the Fukushima crisis as a layered technical failure following a catastrophic earthquake and tsunami. Reactors scrammed correctly and control rods inserted, but loss of power disabled cooling pumps; diesel backups were flooded. Without cooling, decay heat boiled off water, pressure rose, and operators vented and injected seawater and boron—measures that damage reactors but reduce broader risk. Explosions damaged outer buildings though containment largely held; some radioactive isotopes were released but officials called levels minimal for public health. Media, bloggers and opportunistic vendors amplified fear with inaccurate measurements and worst-case plume maps. U.S. officials emphasized monitoring and stockpiles of potassium iodide, but gave limited public detail on plant seismic design limits, fueling concern. Commentators argued against panic and cautioned that while nuclear incidents merit scrutiny and lessons—especially backup power and passive cooling designs—the earthquake and tsunami’s human and economic devastation far outstrips reactor impacts.

The case of 23-month-old Alfie Evans, a British toddler with a degenerative neurological condition, returned to the Court of Appeal as his parents sought permission to take him to Italy for further treatment. High Court Justice Anthony Hayden had rejected the parents’ latest appeal, calling his ruling the “final chapter” in Alfie’s life after concluding further treatment was futile because Alfie had little brain function and would not improve. Despite that, the parents, backed by the Christian Legal Centre and supported internationally—most notably by Pope Francis and Italian authorities—were given a chance to press their case before appeal judges.

Alfie, treated at Alder Hey Children’s Hospital in Liverpool since December 2016, had life support withdrawn on Monday following prior court decisions permitting withdrawal. His parents and lawyers claimed he showed signs of surviving without ventilator support and even “significantly better” health, prompting renewed applications to move him to Vatican-linked Bambino Gesù Hospital in Rome. Italy offered a military plane for transfer and granted Alfie citizenship to facilitate travel. Pope Francis personally met Alfie’s father and appealed for the parents’ wishes to be honored.

Hospital and legal representatives maintained there was no new medical evidence to counter previous findings that Alfie’s brain had been irreversibly damaged and that further treatment would be futile. Appeal judges noted that, while Alfie might not feel pain, the capacity for awareness or appreciation of life had been destroyed. The hospital emphasized it continued to prioritize Alfie’s comfort, dignity and privacy while supporting the family as they spent final time with him. The family has exhausted multiple legal avenues following an earlier High Court decision allowing withdrawal of ventilation.

French authorities mounted a massive pre-dawn raid in Saint-Denis on Nov. 18 linked to the Nov. 13 Paris attacks that killed 129 people and wounded over 350. Police and elite RAID units besieged an apartment building after intelligence — including tapped phones, surveillance and a witness tip — suggested suspects, possibly including alleged ringleader Abdelhamid Abaaoud, were holed up. The seven-hour operation involved more than 100 officers, helicopters, snipers, robots and drones; officers fired nearly 5,000 rounds and used explosives to try to breach a reinforced door. A woman detonated an explosive vest during the assault and at least two people were killed; another body was found riddled with bullets but identities remained unconfirmed pending forensic work. Seven people were arrested at or near the scene and additional nationwide raids since the attacks have produced dozens more arrests, seizures of weapons and hundreds of searches. Investigators also recovered a phone near the Bataclan containing a message and venue map that aided probes. President François Hollande said France was “at war” with terrorism and sought to reassure citizens to resume daily life while extending emergency powers. European nations raised alerts and tightened security as the continent reeled from the coordinated IS-linked attacks.

When Lady Gaga headlined this year’s Super Bowl halftime show, questions swirled about whether she would make a political statement. The NFL’s Mark Quenzel insisted artists avoid election or presidential commentary to preserve the Super Bowl as a unifying communal event. Gaga said she could only promise to convey the themes she’s long championed— inclusion, equality, love and compassion—leaving viewers to judge whether that unified America.

Gaga opened with a brief duet of “God Bless America” and Woody Guthrie’s “This Land Is Your Land.” Though she omitted Guthrie’s angrier verses—those that include “No Trespassing” and scenes of hungry people at relief offices—choosing the song was still a pointed act. Guthrie originally wrote the piece as a critique of Irving Berlin’s “God Bless America,” and his fuller lyrics are associated with protest movements, including recent demonstrations against proposed immigration bans and border walls. Arlo Guthrie and The New Yorker note the song’s roots in Woody’s politicization and labor sympathies.

Gaga’s set balanced overt pop spectacle with inclusive messaging. She performed hits like “Born This Way,” delivering explicit lyrics celebrating LGBTQ identities—arguably the first televised Super Bowl use of the word “transgender”—alongside grand staging, dancers of varied skin tones and genders, and theatrical acrobatics. Critics argue that within the NFL’s commercial, tightly managed context, Gaga managed a subtle act of activism: packaging a progressive, inclusive message inside a universally palatable pop show. Whether intentionally subversive or simply true to her brand, Gaga’s halftime performance threaded celebration and quiet political signaling, inviting audiences to “read between the lines.”

The EPA reached a settlement with Magnolia Waco Properties (Magnolia Homes), alleging violations of the Toxic Substances Control Act’s Renovation, Repair and Painting (RRP) Rule after reviewing Fixer Upper renovation footage. EPA found evidence of noncompliance at 33 properties where required lead-safe work practices—firm certification, assigning certified renovators, pre-renovation lead pamphlets, posting work-area warnings, and containment measures—were not followed. Magnolia cooperated, obtained EPA firm certification, trained staff, and brought active projects into compliance. The settlement includes a $40,000 civil penalty, a $160,000 supplemental environmental project to abate lead hazards in Waco homes and child-occupied facilities, enhanced compliance management and reporting, and public outreach: a lead-safety segment already aired on Fixer Upper and a promised Chip Gaines video on safe renovation practices to be posted within 90 days.

Burning Man organizers and participants are dealing with an unexpected and widespread insect infestation across the Black Rock Desert build site. Photos and eyewitness reports circulating on social media and the Voices of Burning Man blog describe swarms of unidentified, large biting bugs that are everywhere—under wood piles, blown up in inches-deep drifts against tents, embedded in carpets, and clustered around the Man Base, Commissary tent and Depot. The critters reportedly crawl on and into people, have bitten attendees leaving red welts, and even been found inside clothing, visors and mouths. Medical staff treated at least some workers suffering from bites. An amateur entomologist on the blog suggested winged ants and stink bugs; other commenters recalled similar, temporary plagues in past years.

Organizers don’t know the origin: possibilities include mass hatching after an unusually wet spring and summer, hitchhiking in on wood deliveries, or more fanciful theories. The build has enjoyed unusually calm, dry weather so far, which paradoxically may favor this emergence; leaders hope continued heat and dryness will reduce numbers. Some joked about extreme measures if not. Alongside reports of the infestation, the blog also profiles long-time Burner families and second-generation workers, underscoring the community’s resilience and humor even as they cope with a potentially miserable, pervasive pest problem.

Crew member Youngjoo Hwang has sued actor Fred Savage and Fox, alleging harassment, assault, battery and discrimination while working on the Fox series The Grinder in 2015. In the suit and at a press conference, Hwang says Savage created a hostile work environment, repeatedly berated her, gave “dirty looks,” rolled his eyes, hurled profanities and cultivated a reputation for verbally abusing and intimidating female crew. She alleges one incident when she was brushing dandruff from Savage’s suit as part of her costume duties, he told her not to touch him and then “violently struck” her arm three times. Hwang says she was fearful of reporting the behavior because supervisors discouraged complaints; she quotes an executive producer as saying, “I’m not even sure what Fred did constituted harassment and I don’t think you should report it to HR.” Her attorney, Anahita Sedaghatfar, also says other women on set filed complaints, though she would not identify them or give specifics. Hwang seeks unspecified emotional distress damages.

Savage and Fox have both strongly denied the allegations. Savage issued a detailed statement calling the claims “absolutely untrue,” saying he cooperated with what Fox described as an “extensive internal investigation” that found no evidence to substantiate the accusations, and asserting he has always treated colleagues professionally. Fox likewise said it investigated and found no wrongdoing and will “vigorously defend against these unfounded claims.” Sedaghatfar counters that Fox did not conduct an independent investigation and that Savage’s lawyers have refused to communicate with her or Hwang. The Grinder aired from 2015–2016. This suit follows a previously settled 1993 sexual harassment claim against Savage from his Wonder Years era.

On Sunday in Berkeley, a planned right-wing “No to Marxism” rally largely collapsed, but thousands of left-wing demonstrators and about 150 black bloc/antifa participants showed up. While most of the day remained largely peaceful with small, contained skirmishes, a violent incident occurred when a man associated with right-wing organizer Joey Gibson—later identified as 54-year-old Trump supporter and video blogger Keith Campbell—was chased, knocked down and attacked by a group of anti-fascist protesters who kicked and struck him with a flagpole. Al Letson, host of Reveal from the Center for Investigative Reporting, was covering the rally and intervened: seeing a mass of people converging on the fallen man and fearing for his life, Letson dropped his equipment and dove on top of the victim to shield him from further blows. Letson says he acted as a human first, putting journalistic detachment aside to prevent potential fatal harm—citing the recent Charlottesville death as motivation—and invoking a moral impulse to protect another person’s humanity regardless of ideology. The episode, captured on video and shared widely, has been used by critics of antifa; Letson and Reveal’s editor defended the action as a human response rather than taking sides. Campbell later said he has bruised ribs and kidneys and has temporarily relocated for safety; he did not remember Letson’s intervention until he saw the footage. Letson reflects that antifa’s violence risks creating a false equivalency between those fighting fascism and white supremacists, complicating how the media and public perceive and report these confrontations.

After 79 years, 97-year-old Margaret Thome Bekema of Walker, Michigan, received an honorary high school diploma from Catholic Central High School, fulfilling a lifelong wish she had to graduate with the Class of 1936. Bekema left school during her junior year at 17 when her mother was struck with cancer and her father called on her to care for the household and her three younger siblings. The sacrifice, she said, “broke her heart,” but she did the work—cooking, cleaning and making clothes—without complaint. Over the years she worked in clerical roles for the armed forces during World War II and later taught preschool for 17 years at Grace Episcopal Church. At a ceremony held at the Yorkshire and Stonebridge Manor senior community, Bekema donned a mortarboard and honor cords as Principal Greg Deja presented her with an official honorary diploma and alumni certificate. Family, friends and school officials praised her lifetime of service and sacrifice, calling her example inspiring and aligned with the school’s core values. Bekema, a widow, is a mother, grandmother and great-grandmother who treasures faith and community.

A federal judge has awarded Jose R. Martinez $8,000 after he was trapped more than 30 minutes on Disneyland’s “It’s a Small World” ride on Nov. 27, 2009. Martinez, a San Pedro resident paralyzed since age 16 who uses a wheelchair and suffers diabetes, hypertension and anxiety disorder, was stuck in the ride’s “Goodbye Room” when the attraction broke down the day after Thanksgiving. Lawyer David Geffen said employees evacuated others but could not assist Martinez, the music looped loudly, and staff failed to summon firefighters; Martinez experienced panic, high blood pressure and autonomic dysreflexia as his bladder filled. Judge James Selna found Disneyland breached a duty to warn disabled guests they might be trapped during outages and awarded $4,000 for pain and suffering plus $4,000 under the Americans with Disabilities Act. Disneyland said it believes it provided appropriate assistance and is disappointed the court did not fully agree; it has since addressed first-aid station access issues.

Students at Pittsburg High School in Kansas uncovered questionable credentials for their newly hired principal, Amy Robertson, prompting her resignation days after the discovery. The Booster Redux, the school newspaper, spent weeks investigating Robertson’s background after a routine interview raised red flags. Six student journalists, guided by their adviser Emily Smith (who recused herself because she served on the hiring committee), traced Robertson’s graduate degrees to Corllins University, a private institution whose website was nonfunctional and which federal and accreditation databases did not recognize. Students found multiple reports describing Corllins as a diploma mill and noted that accrediting and government sources had no record of the school; the U.S. Department of Education could not verify its existence. They also located Gulf News articles about Robertson’s prior work in Dubai, including a 2012 report that Dubai’s education authority had suspended the license of a school with which Robertson was associated and later closed the institution after repeated “unsatisfactory” inspections.

Robertson, who earned a bachelor’s degree from the University of Tulsa and has lived in Dubai for nearly two decades, told reporters her degrees were “authenticated by the U.S. government” and that Corllins had accreditation when she obtained her MA (1994) and PhD (2010). She declined to answer students’ questions directly. Pittsburg Community Schools Superintendent Destry Brown said the district relies on the Kansas Department of Education to approve credentials and acknowledged that Robertson was not yet licensed in Kansas; she would have had to obtain licensure through coursework and testing. After a closed-board meeting, Robertson resigned and the board reopened the principal search. Students’ reporting drew local, state and national attention and praise from professional journalists; the superintendent said he would meet with the students to thank them, and acknowledged responsibility for the oversight. The episode highlighted the rigor of student journalism, protections for student press under Kansas law, and the importance of vetting qualifications for public school leaders.

Panic! at the Disco frontman Brendon Urie publicly embraced the label of pansexual in a Paper magazine interview, saying he’s “married to a woman” and deeply in love but is also attracted to men and ultimately “likes a person” regardless of gender. Calling his statement “me coming out as pansexual,” Urie explained he values people whose “heart’s in the right place.” He reflected on the band’s queer-supportive anthem “Girls/Girls/Boys” from their 2013 album Too Weird to Live, Too Rare to Die!, noting that although he originally wrote the song about his first threesome, fans reframed it as a message of coming out and self-acceptance—a reinterpretation he praised. Urie also discussed his past “stage gay” antics, such as making out with bandmates or friends while intoxicated, acknowledging it made some uncomfortable. He recently appeared on Broadway in Kinky Boots, a show celebrating drag and LGBT themes, and Panic!’s latest album, Pray for the Wicked, was released on June 22.

Howard G. Buffett, son of investor Warren Buffett, purchased hundreds of belongings of civil rights icon Rosa Parks that had been stored in a New York warehouse for years and frequently fought over in court. Buffett said his foundation plans to donate the items—among them Parks’ Presidential Medal of Freedom, Congressional Gold Medal, photographs with presidents, a pillbox hat she may have worn on the Montgomery bus, a signed postcard from Martin Luther King Jr., documents from civil rights meetings, personal letters and clothing—to a museum or institute to ensure public access and preservation. The artifacts had been removed from Parks’ Detroit home following legal disputes over her will and were kept by Guernsey’s Auctioneers since 2006. Guernsey’s president valued the collection at $10 million; the buyer and overseeing judge reached an agreement this summer and closed the transaction last week. Though Buffett initially declined to disclose the sum, a lawyer for Parks’ heirs said the purchase price was $4.5 million, with commissions and allocations—12.5 percent to the auction house, 20 percent of the remainder to Parks’ relatives, and the balance to the Rosa & Raymond Parks Institute for Self Development. Buffett emphasized his goal was preserving the materials “for the public’s benefit.”

Hospitals say they’re struggling because Medicare and Medicaid don’t pay enough. But an Axios review of 84 of the nation’s largest not-for-profit hospital systems — which together reported $535.5 billion in revenue — shows they offset thin patient-care margins with substantial investment and deal income. Those systems earned $14.4 billion in operating profit from patient care last year, an operating margin of 2.7%. When Wall Street income (stocks, bonds, credit-default swaps), accounting gains from mergers and acquisitions, and other investment returns are included, their combined surplus rose to $35.7 billion, a 6.7% total profit margin — more than double the prior year. While these margins are modest percentage-wise, applied to huge revenue they generate large dollar profits. Financial health varied: integrated insurers like Kaiser Permanente fared extremely well, while others such as Partners HealthCare lost ground. Academic systems including Northwestern Memorial and University of Colorado Health posted some of the highest margins. Critics note consolidation and aggressive investing have turned many systems into Fortune 500–style organizations wielding financial and political power; consolidation often leads to higher prices and premiums rather than cost savings. Experts say dominant market positions and investment luck help explain the profits. The American Hospital Association acknowledged booming markets buoy investment returns and argued positive margins are needed for medical advances, while blaming Medicare and Medicaid for underpayment; it said investment income is reinvested, though funds frequently support revenue-boosting projects. The analysis focuses on the wealthiest systems; many smaller, rural, and public hospitals continue to struggle with low payments, declining patient volumes, and weaker negotiating power.

Republican Sen. Pat Roberts narrowly defeated tea-party-backed challenger Milton Wolf in the Kansas GOP primary, 48% to 41%, with two minor candidates splitting the rest. The result, aided heavily by national Republican resources, thwarted another Tea Party attempt to unseat an incumbent this cycle. The National Republican Senatorial Committee, chaired by Kansas Sen. Jerry Moran, deployed staff to Johnson County—Wolf’s home base—making tens of thousands of calls and knocking on over 10,000 doors; Roberts’ campaign says they reached more than 200,000 GOP households. Roberts tied Wolf in Johnson County by a razor-thin margin and ultimately prevailed statewide. Roberts, 78, emphasized unity in his victory remarks, warning against intraparty infighting, while Wolf criticized Roberts for being too tied to Washington. Wolf, a radiologist and distant relative of President Obama, ran as a hard-line conservative with backing from some tea-party groups but was hurt by controversial social-media posts and Roberts’ attacks. Roberts will face Democrat Chad Taylor in November in solidly Republican Kansas. The race reflects a broader pattern this cycle of establishment Republicans successfully defending incumbents in primaries.

The piece criticizes progressive figures—especially Michael Moore and briefly Keith Olbermann—for supporting Julian Assange after rape allegations surfaced. It opens with stark statistics about low reporting, arrest, prosecution, conviction, and imprisonment rates for rape, arguing that taking accusations seriously is vital for progressives. Moore posted $20,000 bail for Assange and urged distrust of “official” accounts, a stance the author says dismisses and harms alleged victims. The article rebuts misleading claims about the Swedish charges (noting they involve alleged force, non-consensual sex without a condom, and sex with an asleep woman) and condemns victim-blaming, doxxing of complainants, and progressive failure to prioritize sexual-assault survivors. It calls for accountability from progressive leaders: demand they unequivocally oppose rape apologism, support survivors, apologize publicly, and redirect resources to anti-sexual-assault causes.

An unusual Oakland County civil case centers on Lori Cichewicz, who is suing her doctor for “wrongful conception” after he told her in 2008 that her fallopian tubes were blocked and she could not become pregnant. Based on that assurance, Cichewicz did not undergo permanent sterilization or use contraception. Three years later she became pregnant and in April 2011 gave birth to a daughter, Reagan, who has Down syndrome. Cichewicz, now 50, says the unplanned pregnancy and the consequences—raising a special-needs child at her age, financial strain, and the emotional toll of uncertainty about her daughter’s future—caused significant distress. She emphasizes she always intended to give birth and loves her daughter, calling her a joyful and cherished member of the family, but says the pregnancy itself was unwanted and stressful because of the doctor’s alleged misguidance.

Her lawsuit seeks damages for emotional distress tied to the unplanned conception, not for the costs of raising a child with Down syndrome. Legal analysts and her attorney frame the claim as akin to medical malpractice: the doctor’s erroneous statement that she could not conceive allegedly led her to make decisions she otherwise would not have made. A Michigan appeals court ruled unanimously that Cichewicz may pursue compensation for the stress and emotional harm of the unplanned pregnancy but cannot recover damages for the expenses of raising her child. The case has been returned to Oakland County Circuit Court and is expected to go to jury trial in the coming months unless settled. Calls to the doctor and his attorney were not returned. The case highlights the limited but recognized scope for wrongful conception claims—permitting recovery for pregnancy-related distress while barring awards for child-rearing costs.

Uber is moving aggressively into autonomous-vehicle research, announcing a partnership with Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) to open the Uber Advanced Technologies Center in Pittsburgh focused on mapping, vehicle safety and self-driving technology. The collaboration will fund faculty chairs and graduate fellowships, tap CMU’s robotics expertise and National Robotics Engineering Center talent, and create local jobs. TechCrunch and other outlets report Uber has been hiring heavily from CMU’s Robotics Institute and NREC to staff the effort, intending to develop core technology, vehicles and infrastructure away from Silicon Valley. The move appears driven partly by competitive pressure from Google, a major investor in Uber that has been developing its own driverless-car program and reportedly prototyping a ride-hailing app. That dynamic has strained the prior alliance—Google provided Maps integration and venture funding, and its board representative has raised concerns about competing services—prompting Uber to build in-house capabilities. Google’s head start in autonomous miles, mapping data and technical depth poses an existential threat if it fields an on-demand driverless fleet; Uber’s Pittsburgh center is an attempt to close that gap and secure its future in automated urban transport.

Florida researchers have confirmed that three Nile crocodiles were captured in South Florida between 2000 and 2014, raising concern that more of the large, potentially dangerous reptiles could be present. University of Florida scientists used DNA analysis to identify the animals as Crocodylus niloticus and found the three were genetically identical, indicating a common source. Their DNA did not match samples from Nile crocodiles housed at licensed facilities such as Disney’s Animal Kingdom, suggesting the animals were likely introduced through the pet trade or by an unpermitted private collector rather than from legal exhibits. The captured individuals—a hatchling found on a Miami porch, a 4-foot female taken at a park, and another female trapped twice and later euthanized after recapture in Everglades National Park—demonstrate that Nile crocodiles can survive, grow quickly (one juvenile grew 28% faster than comparable wild counterparts), and persist in Florida’s subtropical environment. Scientists warn that if Nile crocodiles became established they could prey on native birds, fish, mammals and even American crocodiles and alligators, threaten livestock, and degrade the genetic integrity of the endangered American crocodile via hybridization. Although there is currently no confirmed breeding population, researchers urge a scientific risk assessment to evaluate establishment and spread, noting Florida’s Atlantic and Gulf coasts offer suitable climate. Officials and scientists stress this episode highlights the wider invasive-species problem in Florida and the risks tied to the unregulated wildlife trade.

Congressional committees expanded investigations this week after allegations that up to 12 U.S. Secret Service employees engaged with prostitutes in Cartagena while on advance detail for President Obama’s Summit of the Americas trip. Senate Homeland Security Chairman Joe Lieberman said the panel will ask whether the incident was an isolated lapse or part of a wider pattern and will hold public hearings; he indicated no evidence so far that classified information was compromised. House Homeland Security Chairman Peter King demanded a minute-by-minute timeline and warned more firings are likely; six Secret Service members have left, one was cleared of serious misconduct but faces administrative action, and five are on leave. Lawmakers and advisers voiced support for Director Mark Sullivan and called for rigorous review. David Axelrod and others stressed the actions of a few should not tarnish the agency’s overall professionalism. Some members, including Sen. Susan Collins and Rep. Carolyn Maloney, suggested increasing the number of female and minority agents as one way to reduce future misconduct. The military is also probing several troops.

A Texas state representative from Cypress has filed a resolution asking Texans to stop using the Chilean flag emoji to represent the Texas flag. House Concurrent Resolution 75, submitted Thursday, urges residents not to substitute the Republic of Chile’s flag emoji for the Lone Star flag in digital communication. The move reflects persistent confusion and mistakes online: because the emoji for Texas does not exist, some Texans have adopted the Chilean flag emoji as a proxy, despite clear differences between the real flags. The resolution does not create penalties; it is an advisory appeal meant to discourage the informal practice.

The document also mentions efforts by web archivists to preserve online content through targeted crawls. Those crawls capture pages as they are created and archive the pages they reference so that if linked pages change or are removed, the archived versions remain accessible. The Internet Archive and similar projects aim to replace broken links with links to archived copies or to include companion links showing the original content as authors intended. This “No More 404” approach is part of a broader goal to fix broken links across the web and maintain a reliable historical record of online material.

Additionally, playful cultural items are referenced: a Houston rapper, Trae Tha Truth, has been turned into an emoji set reflecting his image and local hip-hop culture. Photos of those custom emojis accompany the story, underscoring how emojis are used to represent people, places and identities in modern digital life.

The Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 disaster intensified international tensions and a scramble for answers as remains of the 298 victims were moved through government-controlled Kharkiv en route to the Netherlands. A refrigerated train carrying bodies arrived amid criticism over delays and poor handling of remains at the rebel-held crash site near Hrabove, where wreckage remained unsecured and observers reported possible unrecovered bodies. The catastrophe heightened pressure on EU foreign ministers in Brussels to toughen sanctions on Russia, which Western officials accuse of supplying separatists with the Buk missile system used to down the Boeing 777; 193 victims were Dutch nationals.

Russia mounted an alternative narrative, airing detailed military briefings and satellite and radar claims on state television that suggested a Ukrainian fighter jet or Ukrainian missile batteries might have been involved. Russian generals presented radar and imagery they said showed a second aircraft near MH17 and movements of Ukrainian missile systems into the area. Moscow denied supplying the rebels with Buks and urged investigators to consider multiple possibilities, while U.S. and European officials dismissed Russian assertions as propaganda aimed at muddying responsibility and undermining sanctions. Kiev denied involvement, saying its jets were grounded and that its missile systems were accounted for; it posted intercepted calls allegedly implicating rebels. The U.N. Security Council unanimously called for an independent international investigation as diplomatic blame-trading continued amid calls for stronger action against Russia.

The House Intelligence Committee voted unanimously to release a classified Democratic memo that aims to rebut a Republican memo alleging FBI and Justice Department abuses in surveillance tied to the Russia probe. The Democratic document now goes to President Trump for a five-day review; the White House said it will “consider” the request as it did the GOP memo. Democrats say their memo provides a point-by-point counter to Republican claims that the FBI relied improperly on Christopher Steele’s dossier and concealed its funding by the Clinton campaign and the DNC when seeking a surveillance warrant for former campaign adviser Carter Page. Democrats and some Republicans dispute the GOP memo’s portrayal and worry the effort is meant to discredit the FBI and hinder Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation. Rep. Adam Schiff, who led the Democratic memo effort, criticized the GOP process—saying Democrats shared the memo with the FBI and Justice Department for professional redactions, unlike Republicans—and accused the GOP chairman of refusing to clarify possible White House involvement in drafting the Republican document. President Trump has also attacked Schiff personally on Twitter.

A hate crime investigation is underway after the Chicago Loop Synagogue at 16 S. Clark St. was vandalized early Saturday when a suspect affixed swastika stickers to the front doors and smashed a plate glass window. Chicago police responded at 12:20 a.m. after a “criminal damage in progress” call. Surveillance video shows a white male in dark clothing and a dark face mask exiting a dark-colored SUV—possibly a Toyota Highlander—placing two swastika stickers on the doors, then producing a metal object to break the glass before fleeing. No arrests had been made Saturday night as Area Central detectives continued their investigation. Community activist Raul Montes Jr. announced a reward for information leading to the vandal’s arrest and conviction. The American Jewish Committee’s Chicago office condemned the attack, noting it comes amid rising anti-Semitic incidents across the country; AJC Chicago Director Amy Stoken emphasized that the Jewish community will not be intimidated and urged unity against such hatred. The incident was reported amid a broader weekend pattern of swastika vandalism in multiple U.S. cities, including other episodes of anti-Semitic graffiti on public transit and defacement of a Rice University statue. In New York, separate subway passengers quickly removed Nazi graffiti from a train using hand sanitizer, an act captured in photos and widely shared online, illustrating both the spread of anti-Semitic vandalism and rapid community responses. Authorities in Chicago continue to investigate the synagogue attack as a hate crime while seeking tips from the public.

Facebook distanced itself from and condemned comments its director Marc Andreessen posted on Twitter after India’s telecom regulator blocked Facebook’s Free Basics program. Free Basics offered a limited set of internet services at no charge to people with little or no connectivity. India’s regulator ruled the program violated net neutrality by privileging certain services, saying equal access to all online content must be preserved. Andreessen, a prominent venture capitalist and board member at Facebook, responded angrily, calling the decision “morally wrong” because it denied poor people partial connectivity, and then posted a now-deleted tweet suggesting anti-colonialism had been “economically catastrophic for the Indian people for decades.” Those remarks were widely interpreted as endorsing colonialist sentiments and drew immediate backlash.

Andreessen apologized, withdrawing his comments “in full and without reservation.” Facebook’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg publicly repudiated the tweets, calling them “deeply upsetting” and saying they did not reflect his or Facebook’s views. A company spokesperson echoed the rejection. Andreessen Horowitz offered no further comment.

The episode highlights tensions as Silicon Valley pushes into developing markets with connectivity projects — from Facebook’s Free Basics to Google and SpaceX exploring balloons and satellites — while grappling with differing regulatory frameworks and sensitivities about sovereignty, historical context, and net neutrality. It also occurred amid broader high-level outreach between U.S. tech leaders and Indian officials, signaling the growing geopolitical and commercial stakes of global internet expansion.

The Centre for Economics and Business Research (CEBR) warned that 2012 could mark the start of a breakup of the euro, forecasting a 60% chance that at least one country will leave the eurozone by year’s end and a 99% probability of breakup within a decade. The warning comes amid growing strains: the euro posted its second consecutive annual loss versus the dollar, hit decade lows versus the yen, and banks face writedowns on sovereign debt that could force bailouts or nationalizations across major French and German lenders. European leaders are racing to stabilize Spain and Italy and finalize fiscal rules after a December summit; French and German leaders are due to meet in January with a full accord expected by March. German Chancellor Angela Merkel acknowledged 2012 would bring turbulence but vowed to do everything to save the euro. Greek Prime Minister Lucas Papademos said the coming months are crucial as Greece seeks to secure a €130 billion bailout and negotiate debt relief. Public opinion in Germany is divided on whether the crisis can be resolved.

Forbes’ 2018 list of the world’s 100 highest-paid athletes included no women, the first time in eight years. Boxer Floyd Mayweather topped the list with $275 million; NBA players dominated overall. Serena Williams, the year’s highest-paid female athlete at $18 million, missed the roughly $22.9 million cutoff—partly because she took time off after having a baby. The omission renewed debate over persistent gender pay gaps in sports, highlighted by recent fights for equity by the U.S. Women’s National Soccer and Hockey teams. Former and current athletes, including Abby Wambach, Billie Jean King and Kaillie Humphries, urged broader discussion and male allyship to address entrenched disparities.

La-Sonya Mitchell-Clark, 38, of Youngstown, reunited with her biological mother, Francine Simmons, after nearly 40 years — and discovered they had unknowingly worked at the same company for years. The reunion followed the Ohio Department of Health’s recent decision to open birth records for people adopted in Ohio between Jan. 1, 1964 and Sept. 18, 1996. When Mitchell-Clark received her original birth record, it named Simmons as her mother. A Facebook search revealed a Francine working at InfoCision in Boardman, the same teleservices firm where Mitchell-Clark has been employed for four years; Simmons has worked there about ten years. After reaching out through social media, Mitchell-Clark received a phone call from Simmons. The emotional conversation brought tears of joy as mother and daughter learned they live just six minutes apart in Youngstown and had likely crossed paths at company events and in hallways without knowing their connection.

The discovery also revealed three other biological sisters, including Kamala Cummings, another InfoCision employee, and Maisha Cummings, who reflected on the astonishing coincidence that both sides had been searching for one another. Simmons, who was 14 when she became pregnant and 15 when La-Sonya was born, said she had always wanted to reconnect but didn’t know how. Mitchell-Clark’s adoptive parents have supported her search and will be part of the growing family’s life. The story highlights the broader impact of Ohio’s policy change: more than 400,000 people can now access original birth records to learn family medical history or potentially reconnect — though outcomes vary, and agencies caution that reunions can be emotionally complex.

Raul Ramirez, a 32-year-old Salvadoran immigrant, will be sentenced to three years in state prison after pleading guilty to sexual penetration by force in a case overseen by Santa Clara County Judge Aaron Persky. Ramirez admitted fingering his female roommate for five to ten minutes against her will in November 2014, apologized to police, and had bail set at $200,000. The three-year minimum prison term under his plea deal contrasts sharply with the six-month county jail term and probation given to former Stanford swimmer Brock Turner—also sentenced by Persky after his 2015 conviction for sexually assaulting an unconscious woman. That disparity has fueled criticism that Persky showed favoritism to Turner, a young, white, privileged athlete, while treating Ramirez, a poor Latino immigrant, more harshly. Critics, including Stanford professor Michele Dauber—who is leading a recall campaign against Persky—argue Persky could have pursued a lesser charge or negotiated a deal that avoided prison for Ramirez, as happened for Turner. Defenders and some legal experts counter that statutory differences, charge selection, and the defendants’ responses (Turner contested guilt; Ramirez pleaded guilty) help explain disparate outcomes, and that judges require discretion to temper overly punitive sentencing. A poll of Santa Clara voters showed strong support for recalling Persky, especially among women and younger voters, with many believing race and privilege influenced Turner's lenient sentence. Meanwhile, a contingent of Stanford Law graduates urged caution, warning that recalling a judge over a sentencing decision could undermine judicial independence and chill future discretionary mercy.

Vicki Gardner, executive director of the Smith Mountain Lake Regional Chamber of Commerce, was seriously wounded during the August shooting at Bridgewater Plaza while being interviewed live by WDBJ reporter Alison Parker and photojournalist Adam Ward. Gardner was shot in the chest, rushed to Carilion Roanoke Memorial Hospital, underwent emergency surgery and initially listed in stable condition. By the morning update she had been upgraded to good condition and was recovering. Her husband, Tim Gardner, told reporters the couple has received overwhelming community support and urged people to continue visiting and enjoying Smith Mountain Lake as the best way to help. Gardner, a longtime chamber leader since 2002 and a well-known local tourism advocate, had been speaking about the lake’s 50th anniversary and related events when the attack occurred. A prayer vigil was held for her at Bethlehem United Methodist Church in Moneta. The shooting also killed Alison Parker and Adam Ward. Investigators later searched the gunman Vester Flanagan’s rental car and found items including a wig, multiple magazines of ammunition, letters, and other personal effects; Flanagan died hours later at a hospital.

In Carson City, Nevada, state pension chiefs Steve Edmundson and his predecessor Ken Lambert have quietly transformed the Nevada Public Employees’ Retirement System by moving nearly all stock and bond allocations into passive index-tracking securities. Managing about $35 billion together, the duo shifted 42% of assets to the S&P 500, 18% to international stocks, and 30% to U.S. Treasury bonds, retaining only modest private equity and real estate holdings. Their rationale: most active managers fail to outperform benchmarks over long periods, and persistent fees—small in percentage terms but large in absolute dollars for big funds—erode returns. By eliminating many active managers, Edmundson and Lambert expect to save roughly $4 million annually in fees and reduce long-term costs; one basis point equals $3.5 million for their fund. They argue indexing also reduces temptation to react to short-term market noise, an important discipline for a pension that must serve workers decades from now. Their approach contrasts with traditional views that large institutional investors can consistently hire outperforming managers; Nevada’s returns have ranked ahead of many peers during the decade-long move toward indexing, according to consultants Callan Associates. The piece notes a broader institutional reevaluation—New York City and CalPERS have questioned the value of expensive active managers—though CalPERS’ stance remains ambivalent. Edmundson and Lambert emphasize simplicity, patience, and the discipline to “do nothing” amid market volatility; when tempted to trade, they instead clear their heads by running trails. Their radical adoption of passive investing for a major pension fund marks an uncommon but increasingly influential stance in public fund management.

Claiming new Shakespeare authorship is risky: past computational attributions have been retracted. Still, a growing group of scholars now contend that 325 additional lines appended to Thomas Kyd’s The Spanish Tragedy around 1602 were written by William Shakespeare. Douglas Bruster’s recent paper builds on earlier work by Gary Taylor, Gordon McMullan, and especially MacDonald P. Jackson and Jonathan Bate’s colleague Eric Rasmussen, as well as external advocacy by G. K. Hunter and Duncan Salkeld, and follows J. Charlotte Vickers’s influential 2012 case. Bruster focuses less on stylometric parallels than on orthographic and palaeographic evidence: he identifies 24 characteristic spelling patterns (shortened past tenses, single medial consonants, variable spellings) and nine textual “corruptions” in the printed Additional Passages that match idiosyncrasies in the handful of pages widely attributed to Shakespeare’s handwriting (notably the Sir Thomas More manuscript fragments in the British Library). He argues some awkward lines result from printers’ misreadings of Shakespeare’s script—turning seemingly clumsy passages into elegant verse once corrected. Prominent editors, including Rasmussen and Jonathan Bate, plan to include the material in upcoming scholarly editions, and Bruster will print it in the 2016 Bankside Riverside edition. Critics caution that collaborative Elizabethan theater and commercial pressures complicate attribution, and some remain wary of expanding the canon. Nonetheless, Bruster’s methodical, handwriting-based case has convinced many that these Additional Passages likely bear Shakespeare’s “fingerprints.”

President Donald Trump has confirmed he is “looking at the possibility” of meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in July, prompting concern among U.S. officials and European allies. The White House said national security adviser John Bolton will visit Moscow next week, accompanied by NSC staffers including Fiona Hill, to make preparatory arrangements and discuss possible venues such as Vienna. Sources say a summit could be scheduled just before or after the NATO summit in Brussels (July 11–12), with Trump also planning a state visit to Britain. Critics warn a bilateral meeting would legitimize Putin—who U.S. intelligence blames for 2016 election interference, is accused of ordering a nerve-agent attack in Britain, and backs Syria’s Bashar Assad—and could undercut allied pressure and sanctions imposed over Crimea and other actions. Trump, who has pushed for warmer ties with Russia and suggested readmitting Russia to the G7, argues engagement can yield cooperation on issues like counterterrorism. Allies fear the optics and timing, especially given NATO’s focus on Russian aggression and the Skripal poisoning in the U.K. Administration officials say preparations have been underway for weeks and Trump is unconcerned about optics amid ongoing probes into alleged campaign collusion with Moscow.

This long piece centers on the tragic case of Scott Stevens, a once-respected chief operating officer who became ensnared by slot-machine gambling and ultimately killed himself after embezzling millions to feed his addiction. On August 13, 2012, after losing thousands at the Mountaineer Casino, Stevens mailed a detailed letter to his wife explaining financial instructions, called lawyers, announced his intent to die, and shot himself in the casino parking lot. His wife Stacy later sued the casino and machine manufacturer, alleging the industry’s systems helped destroy him.

The article situates Stevens’ story within the broader rise of modern electronic gaming machines (EGMs) and the gambling industry’s business model. Since the late 20th century casinos expanded nationwide and shifted revenue dependence to electronic slots and video poker. EGMs now account for the majority of casino profits and are engineered—through technologies like virtual reel mapping, multiline play, “near misses,” “losses disguised as wins,” and uneven symbol distributions—to increase play duration and revenues. These features exploit human reward systems and research showing near-misses and frequent small “wins” prolong engagement, especially in vulnerable or addicted players.

Legal efforts to hold casinos or manufacturers accountable have largely failed, but plaintiffs’ attorneys like Terry Noffsinger have pursued novel product-liability strategies akin to early tobacco litigation, arguing machines are deliberately designed to addict. Studies estimate 1.1–1.6 percent of U.S. adults have gambling disorders, with millions more at risk; problem gamblers generate a disproportionately large share of casino income. Casinos use data from loyalty cards, cameras, and ATMs to identify and cultivate high-value “whales,” offering perks that encourage continued losses. Neuroscience explains how addiction undermines control—reward pathways and prefrontal inhibition are altered—making it hard for addicts to stop despite devastating personal consequences. The article frames Stevens’ death as both a personal tragedy and a symptom of an industry whose technology and marketing strategies can prey on human vulnerability.

A gunman identified as former Bronx-Lebanon Hospital doctor Henry Bello opened fire inside the Bronx hospital Friday afternoon, killing at least one woman and wounding six others before apparently killing himself. Officers found Bello, wearing a white lab coat and carrying ID, dead on the 17th floor from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot; a woman’s body was nearby. Five of the six wounded on the 16th floor were in serious condition. The shooter, who had previously worked at the hospital, entered around 2:50 p.m. with a rifle concealed in his coat; motive appears tied to a workplace dispute.

President Barack Obama and first lady Michelle Obama reported combined assets valued between $1.8 million and $7 million for 2013 on financial disclosure forms released by the White House. The forms, which list holdings in broad ranges, show the couple’s largest jointly held assets were Treasury notes worth between $1 million and $5 million. Their portfolio reflects retirement and college savings vehicles typical for a family in their 50s, including Vanguard funds and education plans. Royalties from Obama’s books—Dreams From My Father, The Audacity of Hope and Of Thee I Sing—totaled between $70,000 and $165,000 in 2013, down from a much larger range in 2011. The Obamas carry a 30-year mortgage on their Chicago home valued between $500,000 and $1 million with a 5.625% interest rate. Vice President Joe Biden reported assets of $276,000 to $940,000, including a jointly owned Wilmington rental property; he refinanced last year and holds mortgages at about 3.375%. The Bidens donated $50,000 from an award to Pennsylvania anti-domestic violence groups. The Obamas paid $98,169 in federal taxes on $481,098 adjusted income; the Bidens paid $96,378 on $407,009. The administration continues to post these disclosures online; the Office of Government Ethics certified the reports and the White House said neither official has conflicts of interest.

Actress Marcia Strassman, best known as Julie Kotter on the 1970s sitcom Welcome Back, Kotter and as the mother in Disney’s Honey I Shrunk the Kids and its sequel, died Oct. 25 at her Sherman Oaks home after a seven-year battle with breast cancer. She was 66. Her sister Julie Strassman confirmed the death and praised Marcia as “the funniest, smartest person I ever met,” noting her courage after doctors once gave her 2½ years to live. News of her passing was first shared online by longtime friend and director Bob Weide; fellow performer Cher also posted condolences. Born April 28, 1948, in New York City and raised in New Jersey, Strassman moved to Los Angeles at 18. She began her career as a singer in the late 1960s and had early TV appearances including The Patty Duke Show and a recurring role as nurse Margie Cutler on M*A*S*H before breaking out on Welcome Back, Kotter (1975–79). Over five decades she worked steadily in TV and film—roles on Booker, Tremors, Third Watch, Providence and voice work on Aaahh!!! Real Monsters—and appeared in The Aviator (1985). Active in progressive causes and breast cancer fundraising, she served on the Screen Actors Guild national board beginning in 2010. Strassman is survived by her daughter, costume designer Elizabeth “Lizzie” Collector, her brother Steven, and her sister Julie. Services are pending; donations to cancer charities have been requested in lieu of flowers.

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences faces intense criticism and a daunting task to diversify its overwhelmingly white, male membership after two consecutive years of all-white acting nominees sparked the #OscarsSoWhite controversy. A Los Angeles Times and Washington Post analysis found little progress since 2012: roughly 91% of voters are white and 76% male, with small gains for women and minorities. The academy pledged to double women and diverse members by 2020 and adopted rules to remove inactive voters, but its 6,200 lifetime members and strict branch eligibility make rapid change difficult. Powerful branches—executives and directors—remain especially homogeneous, with executives about 96% white and directors overwhelmingly male and older, shaping which films get made and promoted. Industry structural problems—studio hiring, financing, and gatekeeping—limit the pipeline of qualified diverse candidates. Some members warn reforms risk ageism or tokenism, while supporters say systemic change is overdue and must start with diversified hiring and funding in Hollywood so more varied talent can qualify for academy membership and awards recognition.

Dabbing is a simple dance move in which a person drops their head into the bent crook of a slanted, upward-angled arm while extending the opposite arm straight out. Emerging from the Atlanta hip-hop scene in the mid-2010s, the dab became a youth fad and internet meme by 2015, used as a playful or triumphant gesture. Its precise origin was disputed among artists—names like Skippa Da Flippa, Migos, Peewee Longway and others were mentioned—but Migos later credited Skippa as the originator. The move resembles sneezing into one’s elbow and even appears in earlier media, such as a 2009 Metro Station video.

The dab entered mainstream culture through celebrities and athletes: Jason Derulo taught James Corden to dab, and NFL quarterback Cam Newton popularized it with a widely publicized celebration in November 2015. Politicians and public figures across the globe—from Hillary Clinton and UK deputy leader Tom Watson to Emmanuel Macron and Norway’s Prince Sverre Magnus—have performed it, sometimes provoking amusement or criticism. It spread into sports, K-pop, and memes, often used to punctuate musical drops or celebrate goals. In Saudi Arabia the gesture was controversially banned as allegedly referencing drug culture, leading to arrests and public censure. Overall, dabbing evolved from a regional dance into an international cultural shorthand.

Joy Dianne Covey, a pioneering tech executive and Amazon’s first chief financial officer, died at 50 after a bicycling collision on a rural stretch of Skyline Boulevard in San Mateo County. Authorities reported a southbound minivan turned left in front of her while she was traveling downhill; she was pronounced dead at the scene. The 22-year-old driver remained and cooperated; drugs or alcohol do not appear involved and the investigation continues.

Covey joined Amazon in late 1996 and served as CFO from December 1996 to September 1999, staying with the company until April 2000. She played a central role in Amazon’s early growth, overseeing financial strategy, international expansion, product launches and orchestrating its 1997 initial public offering. Her unconventional, long-term approach to Wall Street—prioritizing sustainable business decisions over short-term appeasement of investors—was instrumental in shaping Amazon’s trajectory. Fortune named her one of the 50 Most Powerful Business Women in America during her tenure.

Her path to prominence was unorthodox: she left high school at 15, worked as a grocery clerk, then completed a bachelor’s at Fresno State in two-and-a-half years before earning both a J.D. and an M.B.A. from Harvard in 1989. In later years she focused on family, travel, environmental causes and philanthropy, founding the Beagle Foundation and serving as treasurer and director for the Natural Resources Defense Council. She also served on boards including JetBlue. Colleagues remembered her intellect, independence and adventurous spirit. She is survived by her young son and a legacy as a decisive, influential figure in the rise of e-commerce.

Facebook’s highly anticipated IPO on Nasdaq disappointed investors Friday, closing at $38.23—just $0.23 above its $38 offering—after an eventful, volatile debut. Shares opened late following a 30-minute Nasdaq delay and traded as high as $45 before falling amid heavy volume, technical glitches, and a broader market selloff that erased early gains. Analysts cited the massive share supply, high pricing, and investor skepticism about Facebook’s advertising and long-term prospects as factors. Underwriters, led by Morgan Stanley, intervened using overallotment shares to stabilize the price. The offering raised over $16 billion and valued Facebook near $104–105 billion despite first-day anticlimax.

Iranian authorities postponed the trial of two American hikers, Shane Bauer and Josh Fattal, arrested near the Iran-Iraq border in July 2009, citing the absence of the third detainee, Sarah Shourd, who was released on $500,000 bail in September and returned to the United States. Judiciary spokesman Qolamhossein Mohseni-Ejei said the delay would allow Shourd to return or for her case to be handled separately. The hikers maintain they were unaware they had crossed into Iran while hiking in Iraqi Kurdistan; Shourd has denied spying charges and described their trip as a benign camping outing. Their lawyer said he had not been notified of the postponement. The case has become entangled in broader U.S.-Iran tensions, with Tehran suggesting the Americans might be part of a prisoner swap for Iranians jailed in the U.S. Iranian officials have publicized allegations of mistreatment of Iranians in American prisons. U.S. officials, including State Department spokesman Philip Crowley, have emphasized uncertainty about exactly where the trio crossed the border but criticized Iran for holding them too long. Bauer and Fattal remain in Evin prison while diplomatic efforts continue.

The Panama Papers leak exposed extensive use of offshore companies by relatives of China’s top leaders, revealing how secrecy jurisdictions like the British Virgin Islands facilitate opaque links between political power and business. Internal files from law firm Mossack Fonseca, shared by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists, name family members of eight senior Communist Party figures as clients or controllers of offshore entities. Notable cases include Jasmine Li, granddaughter of Jia Qinglin, registered as sole shareholder of two BVI firms while a Stanford undergraduate; Xi Jinping’s brother-in-law Deng Jiagui, who appeared on BVI shareholder registers for multiple companies; and Li Xiaolin, daughter of former premier Li Peng, connected to a BVI firm and Swiss accounts. Other named relatives include the brother of former vice-president Zeng Qinghong, Tian Jiyun’s son, Hu Yaobang’s son Hu Dehua, and the son-in-law of senior vice-premier Zhang Gaoli.

The documents do not prove that the politicians themselves benefited, and there are legitimate reasons to use offshore structures—cross-border lifestyles, investment protection, and commercial convenience. Nonetheless, the leaks highlight how secrecy havens can conceal potentially lucrative intersections of big business and political influence in China. Chinese authorities have aggressively censored reporting on the revelations, blocking social media posts and some news websites, reflecting sensitivity about officials’ family wealth amid Xi Jinping’s high-profile anti-corruption campaign that emphasizes both integrity and appearances.

Mossack Fonseca maintained that it applies due diligence and that much offshore work is legal; the firm says it was the victim of a hack. The wider Panama Papers trove—11.5 million documents—exposes how global elites use shell companies, trusts and foundations to obscure ownership, sometimes to evade tax or sanctions but often legally. The disclosures have provoked international investigations and political fallout elsewhere, such as Iceland’s prime minister resigning after his offshore ties were revealed. The revelations intensified debate over tax havens’ role in facilitating secrecy, potential illicit flows from developing countries, and the difficulty of reforming a system that benefits wealthy and politically connected actors worldwide.

Police in Chiapas, Mexico, discovered 513 migrants packed into two trailer trucks bound for the United States after X-ray scanners revealed human shapes inside the cargo. Found at a checkpoint near Tuxtla Gutierrez, many migrants had clung to cargo ropes and suffered dehydration during the journey from the Guatemalan border. The trucks had holes punched in the roofs but lacked sufficient air and water. Those detained—mostly from Guatemala, plus migrants from El Salvador, Ecuador, India, Nepal, China, Japan, the Dominican Republic and Honduras—included 32 women and four children. Authorities arrested four suspected smugglers; migrants said smugglers charged about $7,000 each. The incident, one of Mexico’s largest migrant seizures in recent years, highlights human-smuggling risks and the growing use of X-ray scanners to detect clandestine transport.

John Goodlett, a 25-year-old new employee at Enterprise Rent-A-Car in Tulsa, Oklahoma, has become an internet sensation after a customer posted a photo of him helping her with her twin infants while processing her rental. Coty Vincent had come to the branch after a hit-and-run damaged her car. With 11-month-old twins and only single car seats—no double stroller—she asked Goodlett for assistance. He lifted one of the boys out of his car seat, held him while typing with one hand and continued to serve her, allowing Vincent to hold the other child and complete the transaction. Vincent, herself 25 and a single mom, said she expected he might hand the child back quickly, but instead he calmly juggled work and childcare “like a champ.” She photographed the moment and posted it to Facebook, praising him as “one of the most compassionate and caring people” and urging others to “Be a John.” After sharing with twin parent groups, the post went public and quickly went viral, garnering hundreds of thousands of reactions and tens of thousands of shares across platforms.

Goodlett, surprised by the widespread attention, said the act came naturally to him—he’s a twin and lives with his sister—and hopes the story encourages everyday kindness and mutual help. His branch manager, Marlyn Jones, noted that colleagues had already praised Goodlett’s eagerness and service; Enterprise corporate offered a gift card for his gesture, which Goodlett donated to a local Boys & Girls Club run by the Salvation Army for scholarships and equipment. Enterprise also contacted Vincent and provided a double stroller to ease her outings with both boys. Vincent said she’s heartened that such a small act resonated broadly, reminding people of everyday decency amid broader social stress: little gestures like holding doors, smiling, and helping others can make a real difference. The image of Goodlett holding one of the twins while working became a simple, viral emblem of compassion and community.

A routine traffic stop near Bisbee, Arizona, turned into an unexpected roadside delivery on Nov. 14 when Trooper Miguel Rincon helped a woman who gave birth in her grandmother’s car. Rincon was preparing to cite a speeding driver when another vehicle pulled up and a panicked woman said her granddaughter’s water had broken. Courtney Benavidez, who had been in labor only about an hour and a half and hadn’t expected the baby for another two weeks, went into labor so quickly she delivered before Rincon could reach her. Rincon left his traffic stop, grabbed gloves and blankets, and returned to find Benavidez already holding her newborn son. He wrapped the baby—named Carter Jett, a nod to his rapid arrival—in blankets and cared for mother and infant until emergency medics arrived. Both were taken to Canyon Vista Medical Center in Sierra Vista and released the next day in good health. Rincon, a Department of Public Safety trooper since 2008, called the incident the most surprising moment of his career and credited his experience as a father for helping him stay calm during the unexpected roadside birth.

A start-up called Fantex unveiled a novel exchange allowing investors to buy tracking stocks tied to an individual athlete’s future earnings. Backed by Silicon Valley and Wall Street executives, Fantex plans to issue shares linked to earnings from playing contracts, endorsements and appearances. Its inaugural offering centers on NFL running back Arian Foster: Fantex will pay Foster $10 million up front in return for 20 percent of his future earnings and will offer 1.06 million shares at $10 each, trading only on a Fantex-operated exchange. The company expects to pay dividends and collect commissions on secondary trades, but shareholders gain no governance rights or direct control over Foster’s brand. Regulators’ filings enumerate extensive risks—career-ending injury, performance slumps, illiquidity, insider trading concerns and opaque valuation—making the investment highly speculative. Fantex’s founders include seasoned entrepreneurs and financiers, and the firm hopes to expand to other athletes and celebrities. Commentary in the document situates Fantex amid a broader trend of novel, often risky investment products—like motif funds and bitcoin vehicles—enabled by postcrisis deregulatory changes and eager capital, warning ordinary investors to beware of flashy, illiquid offerings that can funnel wealth to the information-rich.

Viktor and Amalija Knavs, Melania Trump’s parents, were naturalized as U.S. citizens in a private New York ceremony after more than a decade living in the United States as permanent residents, their lawyer Michael Wildes said. Wildes praised family reunification and said their path to citizenship followed the same legal process as others. Sources told CNN Melania sponsored her parents’ green cards, a category of family-based visas President Trump and allies have sought to curb as “chain migration.” The White House and first lady’s office declined to comment, citing privacy. The retired Slovenian couple, in their early 70s, have frequently traveled with the Trumps and moved near Washington after the inauguration. Critics of current policy argue curbing family sponsorship would sharply reduce legal immigration unless replaced by a clear alternative.
