Gwyneth Paltrow’s lifestyle brand Goop has become a lucrative but contentious wellness empire, drawing criticism from medical professionals and watchdog groups for promoting unproven, sometimes potentially dangerous health claims. What began in 2008 as a personal newsletter has expanded into e-commerce, a supplement line, and paid “In Goop Health” summits featuring eccentric therapies—yoni (jade) eggs, earthing, leech facials, crystal healing, oxygen bars and supplements—generating millions in traffic and venture funding. Critics highlight a pattern of marketing products or third-party items with explicit or implicit disease-treatment claims unsupported by reliable scientific evidence. TINA.org documented more than 50 such instances (e.g., claims about infertility, depression, psoriasis, cancer prevention) and, after limited remediation by Goop, filed complaints with California prosecutors urging enforcement. The site’s medical credibility is further disputed by prominent physicians, most notably obstetrician-gynecologist Dr. Jen Gunter, who has publicly and repeatedly debunked Goop’s sexual- and women’s-health advice—calling out jade eggs, vaginal steaming, and misleading breast-cancer assertions—and defended evidence-based practice. Goop responded with a post, “Uncensored: A Word From Our Doctors,” defending alternative approaches and featuring contributions from affiliated clinicians; that post prompted further rebuttals, including criticism that some “Goop doctors” do not fully endorse the brand’s content. Former contributors have urged Goop to audit its health content. Regulators and skeptics warn that marketing unsubstantiated health claims exploits consumers, and call for clearer substantiation or removal of deceptive statements as Goop plans more summits and continues to expand its wellness business.

CIA Director John Brennan held a rare, live televised news conference to address fallout from a Senate Intelligence Committee report that harshly criticized the CIA’s post‑9/11 interrogation program. Brennan struck a defensive but conciliatory tone: he praised the “overwhelming majority” of CIA personnel for faithful service, acknowledged the agency “fell short” in oversight, and said some officers used techniques that “had not been authorized, were abhorrent and rightly should be repudiated by all.” He repeatedly used the agency’s term “enhanced interrogation techniques” rather than “torture,” saying he would “leave to others” how to label the practices. Brennan maintained detainees subjected to EITs supplied “useful and valuable” information that was used in operations, including the hunt for Osama bin Laden, but conceded it is “unknown and unknowable” whether the information resulted from the harsh techniques. He disputed the Senate panel’s implication that the CIA intentionally misled Congress and officials, while accepting that internal reviews had identified program flaws and accountability failures. Brennan criticized aspects of the report’s handling—particularly that the committee did not interview CIA officers—and said he thought recent disclosures were “over the top.” Senate Intelligence Chair Dianne Feinstein’s office countered Brennan in real time via tweets defending the report’s sourcing and conclusions. The exchange underscored continuing contention over the program even as officials express a desire to move past the controversy.

CNN is reformatting its struggling 8 p.m. program. Beginning Monday, Parker Spitzer — co-hosted by Eliot Spitzer and Kathleen Parker for four months — will be renamed In the Arena and converted to an ensemble format centered on Spitzer, with contributors including E. D. Hill and Will Cain plus other guests. Kathleen Parker is stepping down to focus on her syndicated column and other writing, though she will appear occasionally. CNN says the revamp aims to present balanced, multi-perspective discussion and analysis after Parker Spitzer failed to gain ratings traction amid backstage tensions. Executives deny it will simply become “The Eliot Spitzer Show,” but the change elevates Spitzer’s role.

Winter cold snaps across parts of the Northern Hemisphere have prompted predictable public confusion and sceptical commentary questioning global warming. Columnists and politicians seized on local and short-term cold weather in Britain and elsewhere to argue against long-term warming, wrongly conflating weather with climate. Scientists point out that natural variability can produce severe cold spells even as the long-term global temperature trend rises: 2009 ranked among the planet’s warmest years since 1880, and regions such as Alaska, northern Canada, North Africa and the Mediterranean have been warmer than usual. The current pattern reflects a strongly meandering jet stream that lets Arctic air plunge south in some places while allowing warmth elsewhere. Experts stress single events don’t disprove climate change; instead, climate change may increase extreme weather frequency, and forecasts predict the present pattern should moderate in coming weeks.

Chelsea Manning, the former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who leaked hundreds of thousands of classified documents to WikiLeaks in 2010, is the subject of a high-profile Vogue feature that includes photographs by Annie Leibovitz and a beach shot of Manning in a red swimsuit. Manning, who came out as transgender the day after her 2013 sentencing and served seven years before President Obama commuted her remaining sentence in May 2017, has been living in New York since her release. The Vogue profile traces her troubled childhood in Oklahoma, early internet refuge, military service, the Iraq deployment that gave her access to sensitive files, and the moral and personal reasoning behind her disclosures. It recounts her difficult prison experience—solitary confinement, suicide attempts, and the fight to receive hormone therapy—and describes her reentry into public life: social outings in New York, energetic appearances at LGBTQ events, a buoyant social-media presence, and plans to write a memoir while exploring new interests like programming in Rust.

The piece portrays Manning as reflective and determined, accepting responsibility for her actions while arguing that formal channels often fail those who witness government wrongdoing. Reactions to the Vogue profile were polarized: many praised the photoshoot and Manning’s courage, while critics condemned both the commutation and Vogue’s decision to spotlight a controversial figure. Conservative commentary, exemplified by National Review, framed Manning as a traitor whose celebrity status and acclaim reveal troubling politicized double standards. Supporters counter that Manning’s motives and the broader debate about secrecy, accountability, and transgender visibility merit serious discussion. The article leaves Manning at a crossroads—free and publicly visible, yet still deciding how to shape her future.

The intimate, bittersweet musical Once was the big winner at the Tony Awards, taking home eight trophies including Best New Musical and Best Actor for Steve Kazee. Adapted from the 2006 indie film about an unlikely romance between a Czech flower seller and an Irish street musician in Dublin, the stage version features songs by Marketa Irglova and Glen Hansard, notably the Oscar-winning "Falling Slowly." Cristin Milioti starred opposite Kazee and was nominated for Best Actress in a Musical. Once beat out larger-scale contenders such as Newsies, Nice Work If You Can Get It and Leap of Faith, and its creative team earned recognition as well: director John Tiffany and playwright Enda Walsh won Tonys, and Bob Crowley and Natasha Katz won for scenic and lighting design respectively. Hosted by Neil Patrick Harris at the Beacon Theatre, the ceremony also honored Clybourne Park (Best Play) and revivals including Death of a Salesman and The Gershwins’ Porgy and Bess.

A 400-pound Siberian tiger named Bashuta will not be euthanized after mauling a 25-year-old man who leaped from a moving Bronx Zoo monorail into the Wild Asia tiger enclosure. The man apparently vaulted the 16-foot perimeter fence and spent about 10 minutes alone with Bashuta before zoo staff used a fire extinguisher to drive the tiger away and called him into a holding area. The visitor suffered bites and punctures to his arms, legs, shoulders and back and broke an arm and a leg; he was in stable condition and his family requested privacy. Zoo Director Jim Breheny said the tiger “did nothing wrong” and was returned to his night holding area; Bashuta, 11, has been at the zoo three years and will be back on exhibit. Officials noted there are no surveillance cameras in that part of the exhibit, pledged a safety review, and emphasized the incident was an isolated, deliberate act by the visitor.

Nora Ephron, a gifted essayist, journalist, novelist, playwright and Oscar‑nominated screenwriter-director, died at 71 after a prolonged blood disorder. Raised in a show‑business family—her parents were successful Broadway and Hollywood writers—she absorbed the dictum “Everything is copy,” turning personal life and cultural observations into sharp, witty prose. A Wellesley graduate, Ephron began as a reporter at the New York Post, moved into magazine journalism at Esquire and New York, and produced celebrated essay collections like Crazy Salad and I Feel Bad About My Neck. Her candid, mordant voice probed feminism, aging, marriage and media with Dorothy Parker–like dryness.

Ephron parlayed literary renown into a major film career: her screenplays include Silkwood (1983), When Harry Met Sally (1989) and Sleepless in Seattle (1993); she also wrote and directed films such as You’ve Got Mail and Julie & Julia. She received three Academy Award nominations and became one of the rare prominent female writer-directors in Hollywood. Heartburn transformed her painful breakup with Carl Bernstein into bestselling fiction and film. Friends and collaborators ranged from Mike Nichols and Rob Reiner to Meryl Streep and Tom Hanks. Survived by husband Nicholas Pileggi, sons Jacob and Max Bernstein, and sisters who are also writers, Ephron remained a sharp chronicler of modern life until her death.

Comedian Russell Brand continued publicly discussing his recently finalized 14-month marriage to pop star Katy Perry, giving largely sympathetic, measured comments across multiple high-profile interviews. On Piers Morgan’s show he said he still felt “great feelings of compassion and warmth” for Perry. On Howard Stern’s Sirius/XM program Brand expanded on the relationship’s arc: deeply in love when they married in India, later realizing “this isn’t really working out” as practical realities — careers, long distance and differing schedules — took their toll. He described the marriage as “lovely” but said it mostly failed for practical reasons, adding that both he and Perry are happy now.

Brand repeatedly declined to air intimate details that might hurt Perry, saying he didn’t want her to read tabloid twists that would sadden her. He confirmed he and Perry discussed children but refused to elaborate. He denied various lurid tabloid claims — including friction with Perry’s parents, whom he called “lovely” — and rejected the idea of pursuing financial claims on Perry’s earnings, saying he has a good job and isn’t “into taking money from women.”

When Stern probed whether Brand was dating Isabella Brewster, he neither fully confirmed nor denied but joked some reports were true and spoke of enjoying single life. Brand grew uncomfortable when Stern analyzed lyrics from Perry’s song “Wide Awake,” insisting interpretations were arbitrary and reiterating his respect and affection for her and pride in her work.

This website, FramingPaterno.com, argues that mainstream media created a false narrative around the Jerry Sandusky case that wrongly framed longtime Penn State coach Joe Paterno and devastated his legacy, the university, and its football program. The site insists it is not defending child sexual abuse nor promoting a literal conspiracy; rather, it claims an incompetent, ratings-driven press misreported facts and refuses to correct its mistakes. Initially focused on defending Paterno, the project expanded after two years of investigation and two prison interviews with Sandusky, concluding both men suffered injustice and that key allegations are doubtful if examined impartially. The site hosts a documentary, The Framing of Joe Paterno, online books, interviews, polls, events, and extensive commentary challenging the Freeh Report, media coverage, and institutional actions. It promotes alternative analyses, transcripts, and eyewitness material, organizes public events and outreach, and encourages legal challenges and public scrutiny of Penn State’s Board and the NCAA. Separately noted: a mistaken Penn State mailing invited convicted Sandusky to renew season tickets, for which the university apologized, calling it a database error from a mass mailing.

The Food and Drug Administration warned that breast implants—both saline and silicone—may be associated with a very small but measurable increase in risk for anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (ALCL), a rare immune-system cancer distinct from breast cancer. Cases have involved lymphoma developing in the scar tissue capsule around implants, producing late-onset symptoms such as lumps, pain, swelling, asymmetry and fluid buildup. Roughly 60 cases worldwide have been reported vs. millions of implant recipients, suggesting an excess but still extremely low absolute risk. Some patients have been cured by removing the implant and capsule; others require chemotherapy or radiation. The FDA is not yet certain implants cause ALCL or how; it is asking physicians to report cases to MedWatch, working on a registry with plastic surgeons, and will add information to implant labeling. Women with implants and no symptoms need routine care but should report changes to their doctors.

Nevest Coleman, 49, returned to work Monday as a groundskeeper for the Chicago White Sox after spending 23 years wrongfully imprisoned for a 1994 rape and murder. DNA testing ultimately led prosecutors to vacate his conviction last November, and a Cook County judge issued a certificate of innocence this month. Coleman’s reinstatement followed outreach from his childhood priest and supporters who contacted the White Sox; after an interview in February the team welcomed him back to Guaranteed Rate Field, the ballpark he last knew as Comiskey Park.

Coleman described his first day back—power-washing the Gate 4 entrance by the team’s 2005 World Series commemoration plaza—and the emotional reconnection with former colleagues who remained on the grounds crew. Longtime head groundskeeper Roger “The Sodfather” Bossard embraced him and joked he had “saved his spot.” Supervisor Jerry Powe and coworker Harry Smith, who worked alongside him in the 1990s, helped ease his return. Coleman said he felt like family, proud to come to work and eager to regain independence: “I don’t have to worry about everybody giving me things. I can support myself now.”

During incarceration, Coleman kept out of trouble, read extensively, worked in a prison job making socks, and sustained hope through family support. He had not seen his children since they were toddlers; he now calls his children and grandchildren daily and relishes ordinary freedoms—simple acts like showering and sitting on his porch. Coleman hopes to move onto full-time staff and even joked that now that he’s free, he wants the White Sox to win a World Series. The team issued a statement expressing gratitude that “justice has been carried for Nevest” and looks forward to welcoming him at the ballpark.

On Saturday, a gunman in an armored van attacked Dallas police headquarters, leading to a chase that ended on Interstate 45 in Hutchins. Authorities say the shooter identified himself as 35-year-old James Boulware and told officers he intended to blow up police because they “took his child and accused him of being a terrorist.” Police have not yet publicly confirmed his identity pending a medical examination. After a police sniper shot the man through the van’s windshield, concerns about explosive ordnance—pipe bombs found near the headquarters and later inside the van—prevented officers from immediately recovering the body. A robot was used to approach the vehicle; authorities warned the public that detonations might be heard while they worked to secure the scene. Two loud blasts were reported around noon as officials attempted to neutralize explosives believed to be inside. Police spokesman Maj. Max Geron said the van contained at least two pipe bombs and had ports in its walls designed to fire weapons. No one aside from the gunman was injured. Family members described Boulware as having a history of family violence and said he blamed police for losing custody of his middle-school-aged child. His mother declined to speak to media; his father said he had seen no warning signs the night before and had believed his son planned to live in a van and travel.

U.S. and China jointly unveiled new U.N. sanctions aimed at slowing North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs after its recent atomic test. Separately, mounting evidence shows pests overcoming biotech crop protections: western corn rootworms have damaged fields planted with Monsanto’s Bt corn, with confirmed resistance in four Iowa sites and suspected cases in Illinois. Rootworms historically adapted by shifting egg-laying to soybeans, and resistance has already arisen to some pesticides. Contributing factors include consecutive planting of Bt corn and inadequate planting of non‑Bt “refuges” that dilute resistance. Monsanto stresses current products still perform on most acres, offers refuge seed mixes and alternative traits, and is developing new technologies (including RNA interference) to counter resistance. Critics warn reliance on single solutions fosters “superweeds” and “superinsects,” requiring ever‑novel, costly fixes.

At the National Prayer Breakfast, President Donald Trump blended jokes with policy, using the platform to tout his leadership, defend tough diplomatic calls and press a major change to church-state rules. He quipped about Arnold Schwarzenegger’s poor Apprentice ratings and reassured listeners about difficult phone calls with foreign leaders, but his most consequential pledge was to “get rid of and totally destroy the Johnson Amendment,” the 1954 tax-code provision barring tax-exempt organizations—including churches—from endorsing or campaigning for political candidates. Trump framed repeal as expanding religious freedom, saying clergy should speak “freely and without fear of retribution,” and tied his message to defending religious values against terrorism and ideological threats. He also defended his restrictive immigration executive order and promised vetting reforms to ensure newcomers embrace U.S. values of religious and personal liberty.

Critics — civil-liberty advocates, legal scholars and many religious leaders — warn repeal would invite partisan politics and unregulated “dark money” into houses of worship, turning churches into de facto Super PACs able to channel tax-deductible donations into campaigns without disclosure. Polling indicates most Americans and many clergy oppose clergy endorsements from the pulpit. Opponents say Trump’s push reflects pressure from the religious right, notably supporters like Jerry Falwell Jr., who argue enforcement chills conservative speech. Protesters outside the breakfast included evangelical author Ann Voskamp and former Obama faith adviser Michael Wear, who urged compassion for refugees and called for rescinding travel bans. Legal experts note that fully removing the Johnson Amendment requires Congress; the president can, however, influence enforcement. The debate highlights tensions between free-speech claims, tax policy and the separation of church and state, with potential consequences for campaign finance transparency and the political role of religious institutions.

Poland’s deputy defense minister Bartosz Kownacki provoked an international spat by insulting France after Paris revoked an invitation to the Euronaval 2016 defense exhibition. Kownacki told TVN24 that “the French side officially invited us a long time ago and now they are showing us the door,” adding that “these are the people we taught to eat with a fork a couple of centuries ago,” a historical jibe meant to explain their behavior. The invitation cancellation, communicated via the Polish Embassy in Paris and confirmed to AFP, followed a breakdown in talks over Poland’s planned purchase of 50 Airbus Caracal helicopters. Poland halted negotiations and moved to buy US Black Hawks, prompting sharp criticism from Airbus CEO Tom Enders and tension with Paris; President François Hollande postponed a visit to Warsaw. There is disagreement over which side ended the helicopter talks. Kownacki’s fork remark is historically dubious—while some link European fork use to Polish connections with King Henry III, historians suggest he likely encountered forks in Venice—and has been condemned domestically by liberal opposition figures and even by Beata Mazurek, a spokeswoman for the governing Law and Justice party, as “unfortunate” and undiplomatic. Media and commentators mocked the gaffe—Polityka quipped he was committing “diplomatic suicide by fork”—and opposition MPs called for his dismissal. The episode is another diplomatic misstep for Poland’s defense officials amid broader controversies surrounding the ruling Law and Justice party and its recent confrontations with EU partners.

Standard & Poor’s downgraded Italy’s long-term rating to A from A+ and cut its short-term rating, citing a weak economic outlook, political gridlock, and doubts about promised fiscal savings. The move, which caught markets off guard while Moody’s delayed its review, pushed Italy’s 10-year yields higher—peaking up 16 basis points and settling around 5.6%—and widened the spread over German bunds to about 382 basis points. Analysts warned the downgrade could raise borrowing costs as Italy readies nearly €30 billion of bond issuance, testing investor appetite and possibly pressuring the euro. Rome angrily rejected S&P’s assessment, defending its majority, fiscal measures and growth plans. The episode renewed concerns that the sovereign-debt crisis could overwhelm euro-area rescue capacity, stoke bank vulnerabilities (notably in France), and prompt greater ECB bond purchases or other policy steps.

When chess meets livestreaming, the result is a cultural remix that’s reshaping the game’s image and audience. Traditional images of stoic grandmasters give way on Twitch to chaotic, music-driven broadcasts like Eric Hansen’s Chessbrah: long, party-inflected streams featuring trash talk, profanity, and spontaneous antics that deliberately break chess stereotypes. Hansen, a Canadian grandmaster who earned his title at 20, pioneered chess livestreaming by treating fans as part of his daily life and combining the communal European chess scene with North American showmanship. Despite early backlash from chess purists, Chessbrah’s mix of personality and high-level play attracted viewers and other titled players, helping normalize chess as an eSport.

More instructional, low-key figures like IM John Bartholomew built large followings by creating accessible teaching videos that demystify chess fundamentals for beginners. His calm, explanatory style contrasts with Hansen’s brash persona but shares the same platform-driven growth: YouTube and Twitch let players monetize engagement through subscriptions and donations. Chess.com and IM Danny Rensch occupy the center, professionalizing online chess with leagues (PRO Chess League), programming, and partnerships with Twitch that emphasize fast-paced formats, fan interaction, and accessible commentary. This model helped draw massive audiences to events like Carlsen–Nakamura Speed Chess finals.

Streaming’s growth hasn’t solved deeper problems: sexism and harassment persist, making moderation and supportive communities crucial—illustrated by players like Alexandra Botez who returned to streaming only after adding strong moderation. Still, with celebrity players, streamed tournaments, and IRL finals in venues like San Francisco, chess is evolving into a mainstream eSport: faster formats, personality-driven channels, and interactive broadcasts are introducing new fans while changing how the centuries-old game is played, taught, and watched.

Chef Tom Colicchio renamed his Beekman Hotel restaurant from Fowler & Wells to Temple Court after discovering Fowler & Wells’ connection to phrenology, a discredited 19th-century pseudoscience that linked skull shape to mental traits and was used to justify discrimination and slavery. Colicchio said deeper research into Fowler & Wells revealed beliefs antithetical to his values, prompting the change.

Phrenology, though thoroughly debunked, was once internationally popular and was invoked both to defend and to oppose slavery. Quentin Tarantino’s Django Unchained dramatizes phrenology’s use to rationalize racial hierarchy: a plantation owner cites skull features as proof of Black submissiveness. That cinematic image mirrors real figures like Charles Caldwell, a Kentucky doctor and slave owner who embraced phrenology and argued that Africans’ supposed “tameableness” made them apt for enslavement. Caldwell corresponded approvingly that Africans “must have a master,” illustrating how phrenological claims were deployed to legitimize slavery.

Paradoxically, many influential abolitionists also embraced phrenology. Reformers such as Lucretia Mott, George Combe, and Horace Mann endorsed phrenological ideas or engaged with its literature. Some anti-slavery advocates argued that perceived natural timidity or other traits meant emancipated Africans would not seek violent revenge and that society had a duty to assist them—using the same pseudoscientific framework to argue for humane treatment and emancipation. Thus, in the 19th century, scientific racism and abolitionist thought were not mutually exclusive; phrenology served as a malleable tool for conflicting moral and political ends.

Chinese state media announced that Bo Xilai, once a star in the Communist Party, has been expelled and will “face justice.” Xinhua said the decision followed party discipline probes that found decades of misconduct: taking massive bribes, abusing power—notably in the Neil Heywood murder cover-up involving his wife, Gu Kailai—and maintaining improper sexual relationships. The announcement, timed just before the 18th Party Congress set to open on November 8, transfers Bo’s case to judicial authorities and signals leaders’ intent to extinguish the populist momentum he built in Chongqing through Maoist-style campaigning and heavy state spending.

Bo’s downfall began when his police chief, Wang Lijun, fled to a U.S. consulate and exposed Gu’s role in Heywood’s death; Gu received a suspended death sentence and Zhang Xiaojun, a family aide, was convicted. Wang was sentenced to 15 years for his crimes. The public reaction mixed relief and anger, raising broader concerns about systemic corruption and how Bo rose so high. Analysts see the harsh handling as an effort to restore party credibility and ensure an orderly leadership transition amid economic and geopolitical challenges. Bo is believed detained and likely faces a lengthy prison term.

Iran warned it treats U.S. and Israeli interests as one and would retaliate against both if attacked, Navy commander Ali Fadavi said, rejecting any separation between Washington and the "Zionist regime." The remarks followed denials of reports that the U.S. had negotiated staying out of an Israel-Iran conflict and amid U.S. election debate over policy toward Tehran. Iran has showcased missile and military capabilities, insisting its nuclear work is peaceful, while Israel sees a nuclear Iran as existentially threatening. Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu has pressed for a harder line; Israel would expect U.S. backing for any strike, though U.S. military leaders have warned against unilateral Israeli action. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Martin Dempsey said a strike would likely only delay Iran’s program and opposed U.S. complicity, urging sanctions and diplomacy. Dempsey also cautioned on Syrian intervention complexities and noted NATO’s role in Afghanistan transition.

Comedian Kevin Hart launched a Hurricane Harvey Relief Challenge, posting an Instagram video pledging $25,000 to the American Red Cross and urging high-profile peers—Beyoncé, Jay-Z, Dwayne Johnson, Chris Rock, Jerry Seinfeld, Justin Timberlake and others—to match his donation. His call to action helped spur other celebrity contributions and public awareness. Coldplay performed a one-off song called “Houston” in Miami as a tribute, while Kim Kardashian’s family donated $500,000. Sandra Bullock pledged $1 million to relief efforts, saying she’s “grateful I can do it” and stressing the need for people to take care of one another.

Ryan Seacrest has been named Kelly Ripa’s new co-host on Live, marking a major shift in the morning TV landscape. The announcement was confirmed by two sources and revealed on-air, where Ripa thanked the rotating guest hosts who filled in after Michael Strahan’s abrupt departure for Good Morning America. Seacrest, a frequent guest during the yearlong search, embraced Ripa on stage; he will co-host daily and serve as an executive producer, giving him influence similar to Ripa’s. The move brings Seacrest back to network morning television and pits Live directly against NBC’s Today and its forthcoming 9 a.m. show led by Megyn Kelly. Seacrest will move to New York but will maintain other roles, including radio shows and hosting New Year’s Rockin’ Eve; ABC plans a new radio studio for him. The decision caps a wide-ranging search involving many celebrities.

News Corporation raised its bid to take full control of the 61% of BSkyB it does not already own, offering 700p per share in cash—valuing the stake at about £7.8bn—after an initial 675p proposal was rejected as too low. BSkyB’s independent directors again called the offer “significantly undervalued” and said regulatory and pre-financing conditions created uncertainty, though they agreed to talks aimed at reaching an agreed proposal. BSkyB indicated it would accept a bid only if it exceeded 800p per share. News Corp said it would fund a “significant portion” of the deal from cash reserves, reduce reliance on advertising, and boost global reach; it and BSkyB have entered a cooperation agreement to progress regulatory filings. BSkyB appointed an empowered committee; advisers include Morgan Stanley and UBS for BSkyB, and Deutsche Bank and J.P. Morgan Cazenove for News Corp. Shares jumped about 21% in early trading.

Donald Trump, the front-runner for the Republican presidential nomination, faced sharp foreign-policy questioning from conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt in a Thursday interview that produced awkward exchanges and illustrated gaps in Trump’s knowledge of key Middle East figures and groups. When Hewitt asked if Trump knew “General Soleimani” and the “Quds Forces” (referring to Iranian Maj. Gen. Qasem Soleimani and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Quds Force), Trump said yes but appeared to confuse “Quds” with the Kurds. Hewitt corrected him; Trump insisted he thought Hewitt had said “Kurds.” Hewitt pushed on other names — Hassan Nasrallah, Ayman al-Zawahiri, Abu Mohammad al-Julani, and Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi — and Trump admitted he didn’t know all of them “without a scorecard,” saying he expected the landscape to change and promising strong military leadership. Hewitt later put the same questions to Carly Fiorina; she fared better, recognizing Soleimani and the Quds Force and distinguishing Hamas from Hezbollah while admitting occasional name confusion. The interview raised questions about whether such moments could damage Trump’s atypical campaign momentum; Trump dismissed Hewitt’s approach as “gotcha” questioning and maintained he wouldn’t reveal responses to hypothetical military provocations. Hewitt will ask foreign-policy questions at the upcoming second Republican debate. Separately, the NYPD has intensified active-shooter training for the public and media following recent workplace attacks, emphasizing the ABCs — Avoid, Barricade, Confront — and advising people to follow officers’ instructions during incidents.

Little Caesars is rolling out a limited-time Bacon Wrapped Crust DEEP! DEEP! Dish pizza beginning Feb. 23, featuring more than 3½ feet of bacon wrapped around the crust, plus bacon sprinkled on top and pepperoni. The Detroit-style, 8-corner deep-dish pie — priced at about $12 and available at participating locations from 4–8 p.m. and by request through late April — replaces the chain’s Soft Pretzel Crust Pizza. CEO David Scrivano and SVP Edward Gleich framed the launch as part of Little Caesars’ efforts to innovate while delivering value and fun. The idea reportedly sprang from an R&D team member who once ordered a bacon-wrapped filet and inspired the bacon-crust concept. The move taps into America’s continuing bacon craze: domestic bacon sales have risen for five straight years to roughly $4 billion, and bacon has appeared in many novelty items from milkshakes to sundaes. Analysts note bacon’s appeal as an indulgent, emotionally resonant comfort food and a symbolic pushback against wellness trends. However, concerns include operational complexity — wrapping crusts could slow service — and poor portability compared with other menu items. Nutritionally, a single slice is indulgent: about 450 calories, 23 grams of fat, 830 mg sodium and 40 mg cholesterol.

Germanwings co-pilot Andreas Lubitz, 27, who investigators say deliberately crashed an Airbus A320 into the French Alps killing 150, had a documented history of mental-health treatment, German media report. Bild and ARD cite internal records saying Lubitz underwent about 18 months of psychiatric care after a “serious depressive episode” around 2009; notes recommended regular psychological assessments. Lufthansa acknowledged a lengthy interruption in his training six years earlier but said Lubitz was later cleared to resume, passed all subsequent checks and was deemed fit to fly. French prosecutors, having reviewed cockpit voice recordings, offered no definitive motive but say Lubitz locked the captain out of the cockpit and initiated a rapid descent while the captain attempted to re-enter; an emergency axe was reportedly used in an effort to break the door. German police searched Lubitz’s Düsseldorf flat and his parents’ home in Montabaur, seizing items including a computer; authorities said one significant clue was found but it was not a suicide note. In response to the crash, several airlines pledged policy changes to ensure two crew members remain in the cockpit. Investigations continue, including recovery of the flight-data recorder and forensic work at the crash site.

A new study suggests excess vitamin B12 can promote acne by altering the behavior of common skin bacteria, particularly Propionibacterium acnes. Researchers compared bacterial gene expression from people with acne and those with clear skin and found the B12 synthesis pathway differed between the groups. When volunteers received B12 injections, bacterial gene expression shifted: production of bacterial B12 was repressed and, in some cases, the bacteria increased production of porphyrins—compounds that trigger inflammation associated with pimples. In lab cultures, adding B12 caused P. acnes to produce more porphyrins, supporting the proposed mechanism linking high B12 levels to acne in susceptible individuals. The effect appears variable: only a subset of people may develop breakouts after supplementation. Investigators caution the results do not prove causation and call for larger randomized trials; past studies have been mixed, and some suggest anti-inflammatory roles for B12. Clinicians say it’s premature to advise patients to stop supplements, especially since B12 is essential for nerve function and blood formation. The research highlights how diet and supplements can affect skin microbes and may guide future targeted acne therapies.

Airbnb is offering a chilling Halloween prize: an overnight stay for two in Paris’s Catacombs, the vast underground ossuary that holds the remains of about six million people. The contest, announced Oct. 13, invites adventurous entrants to explain on Airbnb’s site why they’re brave enough to sleep in the tunnels, with submissions due by midnight on Oct. 20. Winners will spend the night on Oct. 31 and experience a specially arranged visit that blends history, atmosphere and theatrical frights. The evening includes a guided exploration of the labyrinthine passages and bone-lined galleries, a private concert taking advantage of the unique subterranean acoustics, and a storyteller who will share macabre tales designed to unsettle and entertain. Guests are reminded to treat the site with reverence—“respect the Catacombs as you would your own grave”—and must follow rules such as no pets. The listing playfully warns that “you can be assured there will be a monster under your bed,” and promises that dawn will find winners as the only living people to wake up inside the Catacombs. The contest is limited to pairs—couples or friends, maximum two people.

Less than two weeks before the U.S. presidential election, Donald Trump’s campaign released a targeted TV ad for Indian-American viewers in which he speaks some Hindi and borrows Narendra Modi’s 2014 campaign slogan—“Ab ki baar Modi sarkaar”—replacing Modi’s name with his own. The ad, built from footage of his Oct. 15 speech to Indian Americans in Edison, N.J., emphasizes warm U.S.–India ties and praises Modi as an energetic reformer. It links Trump’s tough rhetoric on “radical Islamic terrorism” with imagery of the 2008 Mumbai hotel attacks, suggesting security credentials that might appeal to some voters.

Campaigning in languages beyond English is common—Hillary Clinton ran Spanish and Haitian Creole ads—but this is likely the first targeted Hindi ad. Its practical impact is uncertain: polls show Trump far behind Hillary Clinton among Indian-American voters (one cited survey had 7% for Trump versus 70% for Clinton), and the group backing the ad, the Republican Hindu Coalition led by donor Shalabh Kumar, represents a narrow constituency; Kumar and his family have given substantial funds to Trump and helped organize the Edison event.

Reactions in India were largely critical or amused. Street interviews in Delhi described the ad as tone-deaf and reductionist—addressing Hindus as if they were all of India—and many respondents called the effort insincere, unconvincing, or reflective of a candidate unfit for office. Critics warned the approach risked endorsing the politics of Hindu majoritarianism and questioned whether Trump’s overtures would translate into trust or votes among Indian Americans or broader international audiences.

A Las Vegas blackjack dealer released Facebook chats to RadarOnline.com that she says were with Rep. Anthony Weiner, adding to his admission of inappropriate online conversations with six women. The messages are sexual; one exchange from Sept. 28 shows flirtatious, explicit language and requests for photos. The dealer, identified online as @liberallisa and said to be from Milwaukee and a UW-Milwaukee alum, reportedly described Weiner as “sooo hot and such a liberal.” Another woman, Meagan Broussard, a 26-year-old single mother from Texas, says she exchanged dozens of sexual photos and messages with Weiner after liking a video of him; shirtless photos of Weiner surfaced Monday. Republicans pushed for Weiner’s resignation, and Democrats largely refrained from defending him. The scandal also drew satirical coverage, including a Daily Show bit in which Jon Stewart mocked the fallout.

Wells Fargo has moved to punish top executives as it confronts a massive scandal in which employees opened roughly two million unauthorized accounts to meet sales targets. CEO John Stumpf agreed to forfeit about $41 million in unvested stock awards, will not receive a 2016 bonus, and will take no salary while an independent board investigation proceeds. Carrie Tolstedt, former head of the community banking unit where the misconduct occurred, will give up about $19 million in unvested awards, receive no severance, and will not get a 2016 bonus; she also agreed not to exercise some stock options. The board said additional clawbacks or employment actions could follow depending on the probe’s findings.

Regulators fined the bank $185 million earlier in September, calling the practice “widespread illegal” behavior; Wells Fargo has fired more than 5,300 employees tied to the scheme. State actions followed: California dropped Wells Fargo as a bond underwriter and broker-dealer for a year. Lawmakers, including Senator Elizabeth Warren, harshly criticized Stumpf, demanding resignations and repayment of compensation, and he faces tough hearings before the Senate and House financial panels. The Labor Department has launched a “top-to-bottom” review, and federal prosecutors may pursue civil or criminal charges. Wells Fargo is contacting customers to confirm account authorizations, will send confirmation emails after new account openings, and insists it is tightening controls, though critics question whether the measures and executive penalties go far enough.

Terry Jones, a marginal Florida pastor who planned to burn Qur'ans on the ninth anniversary of 9/11, drew disproportionate global attention. Jones claimed—probably inaccurately—that he’d secured a concession to move a proposed Manhattan Muslim community center; the claim helps him avoid losing face while stoking controversy. Media organizations largely exercised restraint: Fox and CNN refused to show images, the AP barred distribution of footage or detailed descriptions, and NBC said it would film but not air live. Newsrooms debated the journalistic value of broadcasting such provocations, with editors arguing images of deliberate offense add nothing. Coverage amplified international reactions, including Afghan protests and warnings from military leaders that the stunt could endanger troops. Fringe imitators like Westboro Baptist have tried similar acts but received little attention; the incident prompted media self-critique about fueling extremist publicity and highlighted tensions between free expression and responsible coverage.

Beginning in 1996, Alexa Internet began donating daily web crawl data to the Internet Archive, which the Archive ingests into the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. These continuous crawls aim to capture pages as they are created and the pages they reference so that, as content changes or disappears, archived versions remain available. The Archive’s goal is to reduce broken links online by encouraging references to archived snapshots—either replacing dead links or providing companion links so readers can see what authors originally cited. Supported “No More 404” sites are part of this effort.

Interspersed in the source material are reflections on fascism’s historical and contemporary resonance. Quotations from Anne Applebaum, Al Gore, and John Grisham underscore how the rhetoric of totalitarian struggle framed World War II and how early denial or minimization of threats like Hitler’s regime was common. These excerpts and a brief note about the interwar rise of fascism in Europe remind readers of the persistent relevance of that history.

A different thread recounts a 2016 cultural moment: Merriam-Webster reported “fascism” as its most-looked-up word of the year, making it the leading candidate for Word of the Year. The dictionary’s Twitter account wryly urged followers to look up other words to dethrone “fascism,” promoting whimsical alternatives like “flummadiddle” (“something foolish or worthless”). Social media responses ranged from earnest attempts to game the rankings to playful engagement, illustrating how public anxiety, historical terms, and internet-era behaviors intersect in how language trends emerge and are contested.

In recent weeks violence linked to Mexico’s drug war has surged, claiming multiple public officials and prompting vigilantism. Near Monterrey, suspected drug hitmen gunned down Prisciliano Rodriguez, mayor of Doctor Gonzalez, and another passenger as he drove to his ranch; he is the fourth mayor killed in just over a month. Earlier slayings occurred in Santiago (Nuevo León), Hidalgo (Tamaulipas), and San Luis Potosí. Nuevo León and Tamaulipas have become flashpoints as Gulf cartel and its former enforcers, the Zetas, battle over U.S. smuggling routes, increasingly targeting officials, police and journalists. President Felipe Calderón, who deployed tens of thousands of troops against cartels in 2006, condemned the killings but faces mounting pressure as more than 29,000 people have died in drug violence since his offensive began. Monterrey’s business reputation has suffered—over 450 drug killings in the state this year prompted U.S. consulate advisories. In another sign of eroded trust in security forces, residents of Ascensión, Chihuahua—fed up with rampant kidnappings—pursued and captured suspected abductors, stormed a military base, and in mob actions caused the deaths of two youths accused of kidnapping, then demanded firings of local police, illustrating how communities are resorting to self-help amid failing protection.

Scientists have discovered that the Pacific nudibranch Chromodoris reticulata can detach, regrow and reuse its penis, a previously unreported reproductive strategy. Researchers in Japan observed 31 mating events in specimens collected from shallow coral reefs. These simultaneous hermaphrodites position their right sides together so each can inseminate and be inseminated. After brief copulations lasting seconds to minutes, individuals detached their external, thread-like penis and left it behind. Remarkably, within about 24 hours each slug regenerated a new penis from a large coiled structure stored internally; this internal spiral tissue appears compressed and undifferentiated, unfolding and differentiating into the replacement organ. The slugs could perform this cycle up to three times in succession, each separated by roughly a day, though it remains unclear whether further regeneration occurs after internal reserves are exhausted. Microscopic examination showed the penis bears backward-pointing spines, which likely hinder withdrawal and may function to displace rival sperm from a mate’s storage before the donor’s own sperm are delivered. Researchers propose that shedding a spiny penis is a trade-off: losing immediate mating capacity but gaining paternity advantage through sperm displacement. While other animals sometimes lose sexual organs after mating (some spiders, periwinkles, and land slugs), C. reticulata appears to be the first known species capable of repeatedly regrowing and reusing a “disposable” penis.

Amanda Knox’s account of her four years in an Italian prison has resurfaced ahead of her memoir, Waiting to Be Heard, and a primetime interview, rekindling debate about the conditions she describes versus contemporaneous records. The memoir portrays Capanne prison in Perugia as traumatic, alleging sexualized behavior by at least one male guard, a false HIV scare, invasive medical examinations, and other humiliations. Tabloid and magazine excerpts amplify claims of guards “hitting on” a powerless detainee and a female inmate propositioning her. HarperCollins publishes the memoir April 30.

However, handwritten documents Knox wrote while incarcerated, prison diaries later published in Italy, letters to her lawyers, witness recollections and US consular cables paint a more nuanced — sometimes contradictory — picture. Her prison diary contains passages describing staff as “really nice,” notes a well-stocked library and television, recounts a guard offering comfort when she cried, and records boredom softened by consular-sent books. In letters she said she was given time to write statements for police, contradicting memoir depictions of being rushed into naming Patrick Lumumba. Accounts from a fellow inmate recall Knox as popular, engaged in music and theatre, employed in the dispensary, and visited often by US embassy officials, who reviewed her case repeatedly between 2007 and 2009.

Italian lawyers and diplomats have not publicly corroborated claims of mistreatment. With Italy’s Supreme Court having ordered a retrial in Florence, key memoir passages may be examined anew in court. Meanwhile Knox, now back in Seattle, continues to maintain her innocence as legal battles persist.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev will be formally sentenced to death for the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings, but whether he will speak at the hearing remains uncertain. Defense attorneys have not said if the 21-year-old will accept the court’s invitation to address victims and survivors before the judge imposes the jury-recommended death penalty. During the trial the public heard from Tsarnaev only indirectly: Sister Helen Prejean, a longtime death-penalty opponent who met him several times, told jurors he expressed remorse, saying “No one deserves to suffer like they did.” Prosecutors countered with video footage showing Tsarnaev flipping off a jail camera, suggesting a lack of contrition.

Legal experts largely advise against him speaking. They note the judge must impose the death sentence and that a statement carries little legal upside and risks backfiring—particularly if Tsarnaev offers justification or a political rant. Comparisons were drawn to other convicted terrorists: Timothy McVeigh quoted a Supreme Court dissent at his execution hearing, Zacarias Moussaoui denounced America at his sentencing, and Abu Hamza used his time to protest prison conditions. Some observers suggest a sincere, consistent display of remorse could help in future clemency efforts, but that would require sustained behavior beyond a single courtroom statement.

More than 20 victims and family members are expected to speak at the hearing; many have already said the death sentence is justice. Several survivors, including Celeste Corcoran and her injured daughter, chose not to attend, saying engagement would only add stress and would not affect Tsarnaev. Defense counsel emphasized their primary goal was sparing Tsarnaev’s life, but acknowledged the risks if he personally addresses the court.

Actress who says Harvey Weinstein raped her two decades ago expressed disbelief and relief on Megyn Kelly Today after Weinstein’s early-morning arrest, reflecting widespread Hollywood reaction to the mogul’s fall. Separately, Morgan Freeman issued an apology following a CNN report in which eight women accused the 80-year-old actor of inappropriate behavior across professional settings—on sets, at his production company and in interviews. The allegations include unwanted touching and comments about women’s bodies; several accusers said they did not report incidents for fear of losing work. Freeman’s statement to Entertainment Tonight said he would never intentionally offend or make anyone feel uneasy and apologized to anyone who felt uncomfortable or disrespected, insisting it was never his intent. 

But the CNN story and archival interview footage highlight examples that put his apology in context. In 2015, author and activist Janet Mock recounted an ET junket interview about Freeman’s film Five Flights Up in which he commented on her dress and body as she sat across from him; Mock criticized the encounter as emblematic of men in power treating women’s bodies as theirs to claim. Entertainment reporter Chloe Melas, co-author of the CNN piece, described her own 2017 junket experience while six months pregnant, alleging Freeman inspected her and made repetitive, suggestive remarks on camera; studio HR later said they could not corroborate her account. The report underscores broader concerns about workplace power dynamics and why many women in entertainment have historically felt unable to speak up.

In March 2014 a 19-year-old Colorado resident died after ingesting an entire THC-infused cookie that contained about 65 mg of THC, roughly six times Colorado’s recommended single serving (10 mg). The cookie had been purchased legally by a 23-year-old friend, and a store clerk instructed buyers to cut it into six pieces and eat one serving at a time. Initially the teen ate one piece but, feeling no effect after 30–60 minutes, consumed the remainder. Over the next hours he displayed erratic speech, hostile and incoherent behaviors, and severe agitation. Approximately 2.5 hours after finishing the cookie he jumped from a fourth-floor balcony and died from fall-related trauma. An autopsy and toxicology on chest cavity blood found delta-9 THC at 7.2 ng/mL—above Colorado’s 5.0 ng/mL per se driving threshold—and 49 ng/mL of the inactive metabolite; no other drugs were detected. Investigators noted the decedent had no known history of alcohol abuse, illicit drug use, or mental illness, and was likely marijuana-naïve. The case, documented by Colorado health authorities and the CDC’s MMWR, highlights unique dangers of edible cannabis: oral THC absorption is slower and peak blood levels occur 1–2 hours after ingestion, so users may ingest multiple servings before feeling effects, increasing risk of intense intoxication, anxiety, or psychoticlike symptoms. In response to overconsumption incidents, Colorado instituted packaging and labeling rules in February 2015 limiting single servings to 10 mg THC or requiring clear demarcation and mandating potency testing. The report calls for improved public health messaging and regulatory measures to reduce edible-related harms.

Sally Hootnick lost her iPad after an American Airlines flight into JFK and used MobileMe’s GPS tracking to follow it from her home in Manlius, N.Y. After leaving messages with the airline’s lost-and-found, she discovered the iPad at a Long Island address and alerted American Airlines and Port Authority police, but saw no prompt action. She monitored the device as it moved repeatedly between JFK, Los Angeles, and San Francisco, leading her to suspect an airline employee was using it. Frustrated, she sent messages to the iPad and used an app to make it beep every two minutes to harass whoever had it and encourage its return. Only after she threatened to contact a consumer protection agency did American Airlines corporate security call and a police detective speak with her; the airline declined further comment due to an ongoing investigation. Hootnick later replaced the iPad and deactivated wireless service on the old device, so she can no longer track it; she believes the tablet is likely unusable to the thief and may ultimately be discarded.

Friends and colleagues had repeatedly warned veteran war reporter Kenji Goto and amateur contractor Haruna Yukawa to avoid Syria’s most dangerous areas, but both ignored cautions and traveled into zones controlled by the Islamic State (IS). The two met during an earlier detention in northern Syria in April 2014; Goto helped secure Yukawa’s release then. Goto, 47, a respected Japanese freelance journalist who founded Independent Press in 1996 and campaigned on child-rights issues, returned to Syria in October to report firsthand on civilians and children suffering in conflict. He kept contacts and believed they would protect him, despite colleagues’ pleas. Yukawa, 42, a widower with no military background who set up a private military company in 2014, went to Syria seeking on-field experience and business chances—training briefly with Free Syrian Army fighters and later seeking to supply medical goods and ambulances. He reportedly re-entered Syria in July and was believed captured by IS in August. On Jan. 20 a video showed a masked man threatening to kill both unless Japan paid $200 million within 72 hours. Tokyo has verified their identities and vowed to use all diplomatic channels to secure their release, dispatching a counterterrorism team to Jordan and analyzing the video for manipulation. Families, friends and aid groups have appealed for their safe return as Japan maintains its humanitarian stance in the Middle East.

An 87-year-old Grand Rapids man, Howard Arthur Klein, will not be prosecuted on a solicitation charge stemming from a late‑June prostitution sting, prosecutors announced. Klein was cited June 26 near Broadway Avenue NW and Leonard Street after police said he approached what they believed to be a prostitute; two female detectives were working as decoys during the operation. Klein was one of several people detained in two sting operations in areas between downtown Grand Rapids and Alger Street SE. Other arrests included Tia Booth (32) and Tammy Glautney (45), who faced prostitution-related charges, and two men, Paul Alan Leys (indecent exposure) and Felipe Reuben Manuel (solicitation). Klein was not taken into custody because of his age and was arraigned July 8. He denied attempting to solicit a prostitute, saying he thought the woman was someone he knew from church. After reviewing the matter, Kent County Prosecutor William Forsyth dismissed the charge, noting Klein’s advanced age, lack of any prior criminal record, and reported struggles with dementia. Forsyth said prosecution was unnecessary — Klein faced a maximum of 93 days if convicted — and concluded there was no compelling reason to continue the case against him.

A Trader Joe’s assistant manager, 27-year-old Melyda Corado, was fatally struck by an LAPD officer’s bullet during a chase and shootout with suspect Gene Evin Atkins in Silver Lake on Saturday, LAPD Chief Michel Moore said. Investigators determined an officer’s round hit Corado as she was exiting the store after hearing Atkins’ car crash into a light pole outside the Trader Joe’s on Hyperion Avenue. Corado ran toward the entrance just as Atkins, who had been firing a semiautomatic pistol at pursuing officers, also ran toward the store. Officers returned fire, discharging eight rounds; one round struck Corado’s arm and entered her body. She collapsed behind the manager’s desk and later died. Atkins, 28, had earlier allegedly shot his 76-year-old grandmother multiple times and shot a 17-year-old girlfriend, then forced the girlfriend into the grandmother’s car. Police traced the vehicle and pursued Atkins into Silver Lake, where the crash occurred. Atkins entered the store, fired at officers, and held a standoff while about 40 people inside scrambled for cover; some escaped through a window and others were carried out by police. The girlfriend was hospitalized in fair condition; the grandmother remains in critical condition. Atkins surrendered after several hours and was treated for a gunshot wound to his arm. He faces more than 30 charges, including murder, attempted murder counts, hostage-related charges and felony evading; bail was set at $18.7 million. The incident left the community mourning, with a growing memorial and a GoFundMe raising funds for Corado’s funeral. Reactions were mixed: some criticized police gunfire toward the store, while others defended officers’ split-second decisions under life‑threatening circumstances. Chief Moore expressed sorrow and emphasized the tragedy of the outcome.

The annual Canadian UFO Survey, released by Winnipeg-based Ufology Research, found 1,267 reported UFO sightings in 2015—an increase from 2014 and the second-highest total since the group began compiling reports in the late 1980s (behind 2012’s 1,981). Compiler Chris Rutkowski described sightings from coast to coast, with an unexpected surge from Quebec (35% of reports, up from a typical 5–15%). Reports came from 17 sources, including Transport Canada, National Defence, the National UFO Reporting Center and social media, and included accounts from pilots, police and other credible observers.

Most sightings were explainable—stars, planets, aircraft, fireballs, drones or camera artifacts—but about 12% remained unexplained. When filtered to “high-quality” cases with multiple sources or on-site investigations, unexplained incidents drop to roughly 1–3%. One high-quality unexplained case occurred in Manitoba: a couple reported a silent, dark triangular object with colored lights that did not resemble known aircraft.

The report catalogs hundreds of varied accounts—fireballs, hovering lights, disc- and diamond-shaped craft, and a handful of close encounters describing humanoids or alleged abductions. Researchers stress they report what witnesses say, not proof of extraterrestrials, and explore possible psychological, cultural or physical explanations. Rutkowski suggests increased public interest, more attention to the sky (not just cellphones), and proliferation of devices like drones and smartphones all influence reporting trends, while noting continued curiosity about life beyond Earth.

The 2010 remake of The Wolfman updates Universal’s 1941 classic with a star-studded cast—Benicio Del Toro, Anthony Hopkins, Emily Blunt—and director Joe Johnston aiming to bridge old-school gothic atmosphere and modern gore. Set in 1891 Blackmoor, England, Del Toro’s Lawrence Talbot returns to investigate his brother’s death, is bitten by a werewolf, and undergoes brutal full-moon transformations that lead to bloody rampages. Critics praise the film’s visual beauty, period mood, and some effective scenes (notably a medical amphitheater transformation), and commend Emily Blunt’s subtle presence and Hopkins’s ominous cameo. Yet many reviews fault the production: Del Toro’s subdued Talbot lacks emotional connection; supporting roles are underused; the makeup and creature effects (Rick Baker’s designs mixed with CGI) often read as campy or dated; and the grafting of graphic violence onto a restrained gothic tale feels uneven. Overall, The Wolfman is seen as an accomplished-looking but ultimately unnecessary, uneven remake that fails to recapture the haunting potency of the original despite genuine craft and occasional pleasures.

Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, sharply rebuked U.S. President Donald Trump after the United States withdrew from the 2015 nuclear agreement (JCPOA). Meeting teachers in Tehran, Khamenei called Trump’s remarks “ludicrous and shallow,” asserted “you can’t do a damn thing,” and accused Trump of telling “more than 10 lies.” He warned the president’s threats targeted both Iran’s people and its theocratic system, and declared that Iran would not continue fully implementing the deal unless Britain, France and Germany provided practical guarantees they could withstand U.S. pressure. President Hassan Rouhani and parliamentary speaker Ali Larijani said Iran would watch how European partners respond; Rouhani said the deal could survive if Europe defied Washington.

Hardliners welcomed the U.S. pullout, with Revolutionary Guards commander Mohammad Ali Jafari congratulating Iran and MPs burning a paper U.S. flag and the JCPOA text, chanting “death to America.” Analysts warned the move strengthens conservatives and weakens reformists, raising fears for Iran’s fragile economy and possible domestic strife. Ordinary Iranians reacted with worry: the rial plunged, dollars were hoarded, and many feared war or long-term economic hardship. The IAEA has repeatedly verified Iran’s compliance, but Tehran said it might resume higher-level enrichment if the pact collapses. European powers professed commitment to preserving the deal, while critics like Israel and Saudi Arabia praised the U.S. decision.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) prepared to cast a pivotal vote on net neutrality rules after nearly a year of debate, with Chairman Tom Wheeler’s proposal expected to reclassify broadband as a common-carrier service under Title II of the Communications Act. That shift would give the FCC stronger authority to police Internet service providers (ISPs) and prohibit discriminatory practices like paid “fast lanes,” while extending full net neutrality protections to wireless traffic—a significant move given that a majority of Internet use now occurs on mobile devices.

The debate split industry and political lines. Major web companies and civil-rights groups—alongside musicians and consumer advocates—backed Wheeler’s approach as necessary to preserve an open Internet and protect competition, innovation and free expression. They argued that without Title II powers, the FCC could lack adequate enforcement tools. Millions of public comments poured in, mostly supporting regulation. President Obama had urged the FCC to adopt stronger rules, framing the Internet as essential infrastructure that shouldn’t let providers “pick winners and losers.”

ISPs and many Republicans warned the Title II reclassification was excessive and risked chilling investment, innovation and network management needed to handle wireless congestion. Opponents criticized the potential regulatory uncertainty and signaled likely legal challenges. Some lawmakers, like Rep. Greg Walden, promoted alternative legislation banning blocking and paid prioritization without applying utility-style rules. Former FCC commissioners and analysts predicted court battles and continued political wrangling regardless of the FCC vote, noting the rules would be a benchmark reshaped by courts, Congress and the marketplace.

Wireless carriers raised specific concerns about how rules would treat network management and “zero-rating” plans—where certain apps don’t count against data caps. Some carriers, like Sprint and T-Mobile, expressed openness to regulation, while others warned it would constrain congestion management. The FCC indicated zero-rating would be assessed case-by-case.

Analysts cautioned the order would change legal authority more than immediate consumer experience; broadband prices and daily service might not shift overnight. Still, supporters said the debate had permanently reframed public expectations about the Internet’s future, and opponents prepared for court challenges, making the FCC vote a defining but not final milestone in the net neutrality saga.

President Trump announced his support for the First Step Act, a bipartisan criminal justice reform bill that combines prison-conditions improvements with sentencing changes aimed at reducing recidivism and easing overly harsh punishments for many nonviolent drug offenders. The measure would require the Justice Department to create a risk-and-need assessment system to steer prisoners toward rehabilitation, expand time credits for good behavior and add credits for participation in job training and reentry programs, and ban practices like shackling pregnant women. It also directs the Bureau of Prisons to place inmates, when possible, closer to home. 

The bill would roll back parts of 1990s-era mandatory minimums: it ends most life sentences under the “three strikes” drug provision (except for those with prior serious violent felonies), curbs “stacking” of firearm charges, and would allow judges greater discretion in sentencing nonviolent offenders. It would also retroactively apply the 2010 Fair Sentencing Act, potentially shortening many disproportionately long crack-cocaine sentences. Advocates estimate the reforms could free thousands, provide relief for elderly and terminally ill inmates, and fund reentry programming.

Support is broad but not unanimous. The Fraternal Order of Police and many conservatives have been won over after carve-outs for certain fentanyl offenses; some law enforcement officials and conservative senators, like Tom Cotton, remain opposed citing safety concerns. Jared Kushner has led White House efforts; Trump, wary of appearing soft on crime, framed the bill as tough on hardened criminals while addressing racial disparities. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell must gauge whether 60 votes exist to bring the measure to a floor vote during the lame-duck session. Public figures from across the spectrum, including Van Jones and Kim Kardashian West, urged Congress to act.

Nineteen-year-old Lucas Ransom, a UC Santa Barbara junior described by his mother as a “fearless athlete with the sweetest heart,” was fatally attacked by a large shark while boogie-boarding with a friend at Surf Beach near Lompoc. The pair entered glassy, six-foot surf around 9 a.m.; about 45 minutes later, witnesses and his friend Matthew Garcia said a shark suddenly seized Ransom roughly 100 yards offshore. Garcia recounted Ransom saying “Help me, dude” before being pulled under. Ransom suffered catastrophic injuries—the left leg was reportedly ripped off at the pelvis—and bled to death before rescuers could reach him. Vandenberg Air Force Base personnel pronounced him dead at the scene. Authorities closed Surf Beach and two nearby beaches for at least 72 hours as state and federal officials worked to identify the species. Shark experts told reporters the attack and injuries are consistent with a large great white, likely 14–20 feet long, which often assaults surface prey from below and can mistake surfers for seals. While great whites cause about 75% of fatal shark attacks, experts stress such incidents remain exceedingly rare.

HBO Now, HBO’s standalone streaming service, launched primarily on Apple devices (iPhone, iPad, Apple TV) and via Cablevision’s Optimum Online, letting U.S. customers subscribe directly through iTunes for $14.99/month with a 30-day free trial. The service essentially mirrors HBO Go’s content—about 2,000 titles including HBO’s full slate of originals and a large on-demand movie library—so cable subscribers don’t gain exclusive extras at launch. The app’s interface is familiar: navigation includes Watchlist, Series, Movies, More, Search, and Settings, and users can add shows to Watchlist from anywhere. Playback performs well, streaming HD promptly with minimal buffering so far; backend delivery is handled by MLB Advanced Media, though peak demand (e.g., Game of Thrones premiere) will test reliability. Early registration saw hiccups, and the user agreement reserves HBO’s right to alter simultaneous-stream and registered-device limits or crack down on password sharing; authorized users are intended for household members. The Apple TV app is functional but visually bland compared with iOS layouts, where browsing is smoother. For Apple ecosystem users, signing up is straightforward and low-risk because of the month trial; non-Apple cord-cutters must wait for broader platform support or use Cablevision/website access for now.

Republican nominee Donald Trump escalated intra-party tensions by refusing to endorse House Speaker Paul D. Ryan and Sen. John McCain in their primary contests, marking an unusual public split with top GOP leaders who had backed him but criticized his conduct. In a wide-ranging Washington Post interview, Trump said he was “not quite there yet” on Ryan’s re-election in Wisconsin and reiterated he had “never been there” for McCain, citing disappointment in McCain’s record on veterans. Trump praised Ryan’s primary opponent Paul Nehlen—who defended Trump’s attacks on Khizr Khan—and tweeted thanks to Nehlen, prompting speculation about a possible endorsement. Ryan’s team denied soliciting Trump’s endorsement and predicted a comfortable win. The standoff follows Ryan’s tepid endorsement of Trump earlier and his rebuke after Trump’s remarks about the Khans, which also drew a sharp rebuke from President Obama, who called Trump “unfit to serve” and urged Republicans to withdraw support. The episode highlighted widening GOP fractures: Rep. Richard Hanna announced he would back Hillary Clinton, and other senators who criticized Trump faced public rebuke from the nominee. Trump defended his actions as responses to media bias and pledged to shape debate terms, suggested excluding third-party candidates, and threatened future “anti-certain candidate” super PACs if he lost.

Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh faced intense, wide-ranging questioning during the Senate Judiciary Committee’s confirmation hearings, with Democrats pressing on abortion, presidential power, judicial independence and past associations. Kavanaugh described Roe v. Wade as an “important precedent” repeatedly reaffirmed, citing Planned Parenthood v. Casey as “precedent on precedent,” but did not indicate how he would rule on future challenges. He repeatedly declined to answer hypothetical questions about presidential powers — including self-pardons, subpoenas and pardons tied to testimony — saying such matters could come before the court. Kavanaugh called the sexual misconduct allegations against his former mentor, Judge Alex Kozinski, a “gut punch,” said he was shocked and unaware of them before they became public, and supported efforts to improve harassment reporting in the judiciary. He emphasized judicial independence, citing a ruling favorable to an unpopular defendant as evidence. The hearing was marked by protests and partisan clashes, fact-checking of senators’ claims about illegal abortion deaths, and debate over Kavanaugh’s past testimony and writings as Democrats probe records and positions.

Santa Monica College announced that 26-year-old student Marcela Franco died Sunday from wounds suffered in Friday’s shooting spree, making her the fifth fatality. Marcela, who had registered for summer classes, was with her 68-year-old father, college groundskeeper Carlos Navarro Franco, when gunman John Zawahri opened fire on their SUV as they drove onto campus to buy textbooks; Carlos died at the scene. Zawahri, 23, was later killed by police in a shootout inside the college library. Authorities say the rampage began minutes earlier at a house set ablaze where Zawahri’s father, Samir, 55, and brother, Chris, 25, were found dead. Zawahri, armed with high-powered weapons and large amounts of ammunition, wounded several others and carried out largely random attacks across Santa Monica. The college has started a memorial fund for the Franco family and plans a campus memorial.

Keith Urban and Nicole Kidman maintain a deliberately private, deeply connected marriage despite busy, globe-spanning careers. Urban, 45, revealed on The Ellen DeGeneres Show that while he’s touring and taping American Idol in the U.S. and Kidman, 46, shoots in London, they preserve intimacy through phone calls rather than texts or emails—sometimes sharing sexy selfies privately—and prioritize direct, vocal communication. In a Vanity Fair cover interview with Sam Kashner, Kidman reflects on her past and present: marrying Tom Cruise at 23 left her young and needing time alone to grow; meeting Urban brought her “great love” she hadn’t been sure would return. Recalling her role in The Hours, she describes how portraying Virginia Woolf, including repeatedly filming a suicide scene, led her to choose life and foster a renewed appreciation for living during a low point. Kidman discusses the isolating intensity of fame—how a couple enveloped in a celebrity bubble can find it intoxicating and intimately bonding—and how parenthood reframes public attention when seen through her children’s eyes. Now based in Nashville with Urban and their two daughters, she embraces stepping away from Hollywood’s relentless business side to protect family life and pursue an “idiosyncratic” path. Motherhood, she says, has been healing for their marriage but also creates a persistent tension between nurturing family and fulfilling her artistic passions.

A glitch in American Airlines’ pilot schedule-bidding system inadvertently allowed many pilots to remove themselves from December flights, leaving thousands of holiday-period trips without assigned cockpit crews. The Allied Pilots Association (APA) told members the failure left roughly 15,000 flights — about 19,000 cockpit seats — initially unfilled across major hubs including Miami, Dallas-Fort Worth, Chicago O’Hare, LaGuardia and Philadelphia. Pilots had loaded schedules in early December and then, because the system allowed it, were able to take holiday days off en masse.

American said it has fixed the issue, is using reserve pilots, and is offering pay incentives—up to 150 percent of hourly pay, the contractual maximum—to pilots who pick up open trips. The carrier expects to avoid cancellations and said it is working with the APA to resolve staffing and get customers to their destinations. The union has filed a grievance, asserting management’s unilateral solution and the way overtime pay was restricted violate the pilots’ contract, and urged caution about accepting assignments handled improperly.

The incident recalls prior industry disruption from scheduling problems, and while the financial toll is unclear, stock reaction showed investor sensitivity to higher labor costs. American continues efforts to cover late-December flying and reach a negotiated fix with the union.

Jacob Brundage, a 39-year-old professional poker player from Lakeland, Florida, had a panic-inducing start to a World Series of Poker night when he realized a black tote holding $7,000 in cash and playing chips was missing. He left the bag in the backseat of an Uber minivan after a June 1 ride from The Venetian to the Rio. Attempts to reach the driver through the app failed until Brundage encountered Uber staff promoting the service at the Rio, who helped track down the vehicle. After more than an hour, the driver called—his phone battery had died—and agreed to return. The bag was exactly where Brundage left it; relieved, he rewarded the driver $200 and gave $100 to the Uber team for assisting. Uber spokeswoman Maui Cheska Orozco said people often leave items in rideshares, but this may be the most valuable item reported left in a Las Vegas Uber. Brundage called the driver’s honesty “a miracle.”

Filmmaker Quentin Tarantino joined hundreds of demonstrators in New York City on Saturday to protest police brutality and demand justice for people killed by police. The event, organized by RiseUpOctober and held at Washington Square Park before a roughly two-mile march up Sixth Avenue, featured speakers including Cornel West and activist Carl Dix. Protesters carried photos and signs bearing the names and dates of mostly young Black victims, chanted through megaphones and recounted stories of those killed. Tarantino, who flew in from California to attend, said, “I’m a human being with a conscience… if you believe there’s murder going on then you need to rise up and stand up against it. I’m here to say I’m on the side of the murdered.” The day remained peaceful with officers cordoning a traffic lane for marchers; no arrests were reported.

Several speakers underscored personal loss: Marion Gray-Hopkins recalled her son Gary Hopkins Jr.’s 1999 death, and Temako Williams, walking arm in arm with Cornel West, described the unresolved wound of her son La-Reko Williams’ 2011 death despite a federal jury finding excessive force and awarding $500,000. Organizers emphasized the protest’s focus on those allegedly killed by police, with Dix noting that the march would proceed despite recent events.

Tensions surfaced because the demonstration occurred days after NYPD Officer Randolph Holder was fatally shot while pursuing a suspect.
