The city’s largest police union, the Patrolmen’s Benevolent Association, condemned Tarantino and called for a boycott of his films, with president Patrick Lynch accusing him of “peddling… ‘Cop Fiction.’” Relatives of Officer Holder and some former officers expressed hurt and protest; a retired officer conducted a solo seven-and-a-half-mile march to City Hall in support of the NYPD. City officials have pledged reforms to rebuild trust between police and communities, even as national attention remains fixed on fraught police-community relations.

A West Long Branch, New Jersey homeowner, Joe Hornick, faces municipal charges for flying Donald Trump "Make America Great Again" flags on his property more than 30 days before the state’s June primary. Borough ordinance bars political signs earlier than 30 days before an election and requires removal within five days after. Hornick, who’s displayed two flags day and night since February and reportedly replaces them after they’ve been torn down, was ticketed after a complaint; his municipal hearing is set for April 20 with possible penalties from a $100–$2,000 fine to 90 days in jail. Hornick says he will not remove the flags and is prepared to accept jail time if necessary.

The American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey deems the ordinance likely unconstitutional. Deputy legal director Jeanne LoCicero notes political signs are protected speech and cannot be time-limited; once a community allows flags it cannot favor some messages over others. Legal commentators cite the U.S. Supreme Court’s Reed v. Town of Gilbert (2015), holding that content-based sign restrictions are generally unconstitutional, and City of Ladue v. Gilleo (1994), which limits permissible municipal regulation of residential signs. Borough officials have not provided further comment; the case could prompt a legal challenge over free speech and discriminatory enforcement of flag and sign regulations.

Two men, Dereck James “D.J.” Harrison, 22, and his father Flint Wayne Harrison, 51, were in custody after a day-long manhunt in Wyoming tied to the alleged abduction and assault of a Utah mother and her four daughters, ages 13 to 18. The victims were reportedly lured to a Utah home in Centerville, north of Salt Lake City, on Tuesday for a barbecue, where the men allegedly bound them with wire and duct tape. As some of the girls and their mother tried to escape, they were assaulted with a baseball bat; the girls ultimately broke free, fled the house, and one called 911. By the time police arrived the suspects had fled.

Flint Harrison surrendered to Sublette County authorities early Saturday and cooperated with investigators to find his son. A manhunt focused on the Half Moon Lake area northeast of Pinedale after authorities discovered a makeshift campsite and evacuated a campground; residents of the roughly 2,000-person town were urged to shelter in place. Deputies arrested Dereck without incident Saturday night about a mile from a roadblock. The Sublette County Sheriff noted Dereck was believed to have been armed with multiple weapons and had threatened law enforcement. Centerville police said Dereck had extensively used methamphetamine and appeared to have targeted the mother in retaliation, mistakenly believing she had turned him in. Both men will be extradited to Utah to face charges; Flint is registered in Wyoming as a sex offender for a 2001 attempted forcible sexual abuse conviction, and it is unclear if additional Wyoming charges will follow.

Wheaton College removed former U.S. House Speaker J. Dennis Hastert’s name from its public policy center after he was federally indicted for lying to the FBI about large cash withdrawals tied to $3.5 million in payments to a longtime acquaintance. Hastert, a 1964 Wheaton alumnus who had donated his congressional papers to the school and for whom the college had named the J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy, resigned from the center’s Board of Advisors shortly after the indictment. The college re-designated the program as the Wheaton College Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy, stressing it will continue its mission of teaching about free enterprise, limited government, and the role of Christian worldview in public life while upholding “the highest ethical and academic standards.” Wheaton said it respected Hastert’s public service and noted he is entitled to due process, but also pledged to pray for all involved, including any victims. The indictment renewed scrutiny of other honors and positions Hastert held: he resigned from the CME Group board and from a role at lobbying firm Dickstein Shapiro, and a proposed $500,000 state statue in his honor was shelved earlier at his request. The college said the future of Hastert’s archived papers was under review and reiterated it is not implicated in the allegations.

Nineteen-year-old Jonathan Brussow of Rockford, Michigan, was killed during a family vacation on March 5 in Eleuthera, Bahamas, after a massive rogue wave swept him from a cliff near the Glass Window Bridge into the sea. Brussow, a 2016 Rockford High School graduate described by loved ones as adventurous and full of passion, had quietly asked his girlfriend Athena Williams’ family for permission to marry her the night before the tragedy. The couple had known each other since middle school and had planned a life together; Williams recounts that Brussow already had their wedding envisioned and often spoke of marrying her.

Just before dawn the morning of the incident, Brussow left with Athena’s brother, Eric, for a hike to a high cliff—at least 70 feet—where the two men planned to talk about the proposal. While sitting at the cliff’s highest point, both were struck by a freak surge; Eric managed to cling to a rock and eventually pull himself to shore despite serious injuries (broken ribs and cuts), then ran for help. Jonathan did not return. Friends and family launched immediate searches, contacting the U.S. Embassy, the Coast Guard, and local authorities; local Bahamians also joined extensively in the search effort, providing food, water and assistance without asking for money.

After days of searching in difficult conditions—complicated by a tropical storm—a search party recovered Brussow’s body on March 9, hundreds of yards from the impact site, in a depression that had briefly formed and later dried. His father flew to the island; the family issued a statement likening the storm that both brought him into the world and took him away, calling him “Stormy” for his passionate spirit.

The family initially used a GoFundMe to reward anyone who might have found Jonathan alive; they have repurposed it to cover repatriation costs, reimburse search expenses, and fund safety improvements—led by Eric—near the Glass Window Bridge, including warning signs and rescue equipment. They also hope to help the island hospital acquire needed equipment such as a mammogram machine. Athena remains grateful for the islanders’ support and urges the community to celebrate Jonathan’s life and honor his memory.

Rochester-area Assemblyman Bill Nojay, a 59-year-old Republican known for his outspoken conservative views, died Friday morning after an apparent self-inflicted gunshot at Riverside Cemetery. Police said an officer responding to a welfare check at 9:22 a.m. saw Nojay shoot himself; he was pronounced dead at the scene. Colleagues reacted with shock.

Nojay, first elected in 2012 to represent the 133rd Assembly District, had a history of high-profile, often contrarian activity in Albany and beyond: he vocally opposed the SAFE Act, co-chaired Donald Trump’s New York campaign committee, hosted a conservative radio show, and worked as an election attorney and consultant in international settings. He was admired by some for his fierce advocacy for upstate concerns and unafraid rhetoric, but he frequently split with fellow legislators and ruffled feathers.

At the time of his death, reports linked Nojay to several legal probes. He reportedly failed to appear in court to face embezzlement charges tied to a trust fund he managed and was to surrender that day. Local reporting also said the FBI had investigated his role in a business connected to Rochester’s $1.3 billion school modernization program. Separately, Cambodian prosecutors had pursued fraud allegations related to Akra Group, an agricultural venture Nojay helped form; a Phnom Penh dentist accused the company of taking $1 million. Federal agents had subpoenaed documents tied to that investment. Nojay lived in Pittsford with his wife and three children and faced a primary challenge this week; his challengers suspended campaigns after his death.

A widespread internal practice at Bloomberg allowed reporters to view Bloomberg Terminal subscriber usage data, raising privacy and client-trust concerns after The New York Post first highlighted a Goldman Sachs incident. A Bloomberg preliminary review reportedly found “several hundred” reporters had used the capability; Bloomberg employs over 2,400 journalists. The technique involved the “Z function” to list subscribers at a firm and a UUID function that revealed background details: contact information, last login times, chats with support, and weekly function-usage stats. Bloomberg says traders’ specific securities or trades were never visible and has disabled those newsroom functions, centralized data-security efforts, and appointed a client data compliance officer. Goldman complained after a reporter cited a partner’s lack of terminal activity; Bloomberg executives and Matt Winkler, editor in chief, apologized and reiterated terminal-use policies. Regulators including the Federal Reserve are probing whether their officials’ usage was monitored. Former employees recounted casually viewing officials’ usage patterns, and JPMorgan sources said reporters used login data to infer trader suspensions during high-profile events. Competitors like Thomson Reuters emphasized stricter separation of editorial access. Bloomberg characterizes the practice as a mistake and says reporters now have only the same customer-relationship data clients see.

White House officials gave mixed signals about Veterans Affairs Secretary David Shulkin’s future as reports swirled that President Trump may remove him this week. Deputy press secretary Hogan Gidley said Trump “at this point in time” has confidence in Shulkin, praising some of his accomplishments while reminding that all appointees serve at the president’s pleasure and could be replaced when the president chooses. Gidley and Raj Shah declined to confirm personnel moves, noting the president can act with or without a ready replacement. CNN and the AP reported Trump signaled to associates he’s preparing to oust Shulkin amid internal rebellion and multiple investigations into alleged spending abuses, including acceptance of Wimbledon tickets and contentious travel for Shulkin’s wife. One AP source placed the likelihood of a near-term departure at roughly 50-50. The White House has reportedly been vetting several potential successors—names floated include Pete Hegseth, Jeff Miller, Keith Kellogg, Michael Kussman, Toby Cosgrove and Leo Mackay Jr.—and deputy secretary Tom Bowman would serve as acting head if Shulkin leaves. Shulkin has denied wrongdoing and said internal agency discord has hampered reforms, while the White House presses for personnel who will execute its veterans’ care agenda.

A Southwest Airlines flight bound for Dallas turned back to Seattle after crew discovered a life‑critical cargo—reported as a human heart—had been left on board. The heart had arrived in Seattle from Sacramento and was supposed to be unloaded for processing; after takeoff the pilot announced the plane would return because the shipment needed to reach its Seattle‑area destination within its allotted time. Passengers reacted with shock and concern, researching viability windows for whole‑organ transplants. Southwest said the flight returned to ensure timely delivery; the package was unloaded after the three‑hour diversion and later reached its intended destination. Details remained unclear initially about whether the tissue was a whole heart or parts and whether any patient was endangered. Sierra Donor Services and LifeNet Health later clarified the shipment contained heart tissue—valves—destined for processing rather than an intact organ for immediate transplant; such tissue has a much longer viable transport window and can be stored for years after processing. The courier had boarded the box in error and a representative called the incident highly unusual but said the tissue ultimately arrived safely. The flight departed again after a five‑hour delay.

Sarah Palin, during a visit to Paul Revere’s house in Boston, offered a mistaken and widely noted retelling of Revere’s famous midnight ride. In remarks picked up by ABC News’ Sheila Marikar, Palin said Revere “warned the British” by “ringing those bells” and riding through town to send “warning shots and bells” to show colonists would remain “secure … free … and … armed.” In fact, Revere’s mission was to warn patriot leaders John Hancock and Samuel Adams about the approaching British troops; he traveled covertly and did not rely on bells or alert the British. Media coverage highlighted the error with a mix of correction and satire, underscoring both the public expectation of historical knowledge from political figures and the media’s tendency to amplify gaffes. The episode prompted commentary about public memory of the Revolution and Palin’s grasp of basic historical facts.

A cybersecurity report from Trend Micro links the hackers behind last year’s Democratic National Committee breach—known as Fancy Bear, APT28 or Pawn Storm—to recent phishing campaigns targeting Emmanuel Macron’s French presidential campaign and groups tied to German political parties. Trend Micro says the attackers registered decoy domains mimicking Macron’s party En Marche! (for example onedrive-en-marche.fr and mail-en-marche.fr) to trick campaign staff into surrendering credentials, using tactics similar to those used against the DNC (which employed lookalike domains such as actblues.com). Macron’s digital director confirmed attempted intrusions but said defenses held and no supporter data were compromised.

The report also documents attacks on German-affiliated foundations Konrad Adenauer Stiftung and Friedrich Ebert Stiftung, linked respectively to Angela Merkel’s Christian Democratic Union and the Social Democratic Party; Germany faces federal elections in 2017. Trend Micro notes Fancy Bear’s typical pattern: phishing as an entry point followed by deployment of bespoke malware (X-Agent) and reliance on a global network of reusable command-and-control servers. Unusually long-lived servers and a rising number of second-stage servers—growing from five in 2013 to 26 in October 2016—suggest the group is increasing operations and does not seek to remain covert. U.S. intelligence and many experts consider Fancy Bear to be a Russian espionage operation; Moscow denies interfering in foreign elections.

The Heartland Institute, a Chicago-based conservative think tank known for promoting climate skepticism, launched a highly controversial billboard campaign in early May 2012 that equated belief in man-made global warming with infamous criminals and dictators. The digital and poster series—briefly featuring Ted Kaczynski, Charles Manson, and Fidel Castro and suggesting future inclusion of figures like Osama bin Laden—asked viewers if they still believed in global warming, implying that prominent advocates are murderers, tyrants, and madmen. Heartland defended the campaign as highlighting that these figures publicly called for drastic action on climate change and framed mainstream climate advocates as radical and unethical, citing incidents such as “Climategate” and the leak of Heartland’s own funding documents. The stunt drew immediate ridicule and embarrassment; the Kaczynski billboard was removed within 24 hours and the campaign prompted questions about potential fallout—whether corporate donors and scheduled conference speakers might withdraw support. Critics condemned the strategy as an extreme, guilt-by-association propaganda tactic that illustrates a broader breakdown on the right: refusal to accept scientific consensus and reliance on provocative, alarmist messaging rather than substantive debate.

A massive Gulf of Mexico oil leak off Louisiana—about 50 miles offshore from a rig that exploded and sank—was spilling roughly 42,000 gallons a day, creating a slick up to 42 by 80 miles. With the slick within 20 miles of fragile Mississippi Delta wetlands, Coast Guard officials weighed controlled burns using fireproof booms to protect marshes, though burns produce smoke and leave residue. BP, Transocean and federal teams have yet to seal the well; remote submarines, a dome capture and a relief rig are being tried but won’t stop flow immediately. Investigations with subpoena power were opened into the explosion.

Some musicians complain about low streaming payouts; Vulfpeck turned that complaint into an experiment. The small funk band released Sleepify, a ten-track album of silence intended to be streamed repeatedly by fans so streaming royalties could fund a tour. The stunt plays as both publicity and a business workaround—an ironic commentary on how digital platforms assign value to plays rather than musical content. Sleepify has already become Vulfpeck’s most-played release on Spotify, with roughly 1.1 million streams translating to an estimated $6,700–$9,400 based on reported per-track payouts. That won’t finance a major tour, but it’s meaningful pocket money for a band that rarely performs live.

Band member Jack Stratton praises Spotify for discovery—about 10 percent of new fans come through it—while noting YouTube brings many visitors even if per-play revenue there is lower. The silent-album approach also boosted interest in their real music. Spotify’s response was amused and mildly dismissive, likening Sleepify to John Cage’s 4’33”.

The stunt highlights broader issues: distributed computing and automated traffic can be harnessed for legitimate science or abused for fraud. Bots already plague digital advertising, costing brands millions. While bot-driven streaming could theoretically amplify royalties, it faces technical hurdles (account limits, detection) and ethical problems. Spotify pays out roughly 70 percent of revenue pro rata by overall plays, so gaming plays would divert funds from other artists and undermine the ecosystem. Vulfpeck’s project is therefore a clever, provocative loophole that raises questions about fairness, platform incentives, and how we value recorded music in the streaming era.

Search teams in New Mexico recovered the body late Sunday of Walter Scheib, a 61-year-old former White House executive chef who had been missing since he went hiking alone in the mountains near Taos on June 13. Scheib’s vehicle was found days earlier at the Yerba Canyon trailhead, and his body was located about 1.7 miles from the base of the Yerba Canyon Trail. Authorities have not released a cause of death or additional details about the discovery, and rescue officials were still gathering information. The rugged terrain, high altitudes—some trails exceed 12,000 feet—and dense vegetation hampered search efforts that involved ground teams, aircraft, National Guard units and search dogs. Scheib served as executive chef at the White House from 1994 to 2005, hired by then–First Lady Hillary Clinton and remaining through part of George W. Bush’s administration. He was known for promoting modern American cuisine, co-authored the 2007 memoir White House Chef: Eleven Years, Two Presidents, One Kitchen, and later ran a private chef business. Tributes and reflections on his career noted his role in shaping White House menus and his public profile as a chef who balanced service, culinary innovation and the intense demands of feeding the First Family.

This week’s political landscape has brought the consequences of the 2010 Citizens United ruling into sharp relief, as the rise of super PACs reshapes campaigns, fuels negative advertising, and provokes calls for reform. Bernie Sanders used a national platform to push for a constitutional amendment to overturn the decision, arguing corporations are not people and shouldn’t have broad free-speech rights to buy elections. The Iowa caucuses offered the first extensive presidential test of super PAC influence: Restore Our Future, backing Mitt Romney, spent roughly $2.7–3 million in Iowa and has been credited with damaging Newt Gingrich’s standing through relentless negative ads. Gingrich, who had previously hailed Citizens United as a free-speech victory, complained of being “Romney‑boated,” yet he and other conservatives largely continue to defend the legal framework that enabled outside spending. Campaigns themselves often outspent their allied super PACs, but some candidates benefited from outside groups that could raise and spend unlimited funds—raising new concerns about coordination, disclosure, and the appearance of corruption.

Commentators and legal scholars have highlighted how Citizens United and follow-on rulings opened the door to candidate-specific, well-funded independent groups run by former campaign aides or donors, undermining the idea of true independence and transparency. Critics argue the decision ignored the corrupting potential of unregulated money.

Contrastingly, the Montana Supreme Court recently upheld a century-old state ban on corporate election spending, invoking Montana’s unique history of corporate political domination and corruption to justify stricter limits. That ruling, and strong dissents denouncing corporate personhood, mark a countervailing judicial effort to blunt super PACs’ reach—though the decision may face reversal at the U.S. Supreme Court. Overall, the post‑Citizens United era is exposing tensions between free-speech doctrines, political reality, and growing public unease about money’s role in American elections.

Two-time Oscar winner Tom Hanks unexpectedly became a central figure in the resolution of a Los Angeles domestic assault case after serving as a juror. The trial had been underway since the previous week, and the defendant faced up to a year behind bars for a misdemeanor domestic violence charge. Defense attorney Andrew Flier prepared for closing arguments Wednesday, but proceedings shifted after prosecutors disclosed that another Los Angeles City Attorney’s Office lawyer had spoken with Hanks outside the courtroom to thank him for jury service. Flier moved for a mistrial, alleging prosecutorial misconduct. In a Wednesday hearing, both sides negotiated a resolution: the defendant pleaded to a reduced charge of disturbing the peace and was fined $150. A City Attorney’s Office spokesperson confirmed the interaction with Hanks and said the office would review the matter. CNN sought comment from Hanks’ representatives but received none. The alleged victim’s response was unavailable; prosecutors do not identify domestic violence claimants, and no parties issued public statements. Flier initially worried Hanks’ celebrity might sway the jury but, after voir dire, had found Hanks to appear fair and suitable for the panel. Flier noted Hanks’ amiable demeanor and the post-court attention from photographers and fans; Hanks reportedly told the defense he “was going to vote the way of justice,” without revealing which side that would be.

Jane Fonda’s life and career have been defined by reinvention, activism and controversy, most prominently her 1972 trip to Hanoi during the Vietnam War. The visit, during which she was photographed sitting on a North Vietnamese anti-aircraft gun, earned her the enduring nickname “Hanoi Jane” and decades of denunciation from U.S. veterans and critics. In the HBO documentary Jane Fonda in Five Acts, director Susan Lacy examines her complex public journey—from sex symbol and Hollywood star to outspoken activist and fitness entrepreneur. On The Late Show with Stephen Colbert, Fonda acknowledged the gun photo as a “bad thing” and a “betrayal,” saying she immediately regretted the image and would “go to my grave regretting that.” She insisted she never intended to be against American soldiers, noting prior and subsequent work with veterans, including the film Coming Home. Fonda has defended her trip as personally enlightening, recalling that Vietnamese hosts sang words about equality and rights before she was led to the weapon and photographed—an act she later suggested might have been a setup. Her activism drew ferocious opposition at the time, including efforts by President Nixon to silence her, and the controversy resurfaces periodically, as when Megyn Kelly referenced the photo during a feud this year.

Sacha Maujean and her family have been thrown into crisis after her youngest daughter, two-year-old Rumer Maujean (also called Rumer Rose), was diagnosed with an advanced neuroblastoma in December. A wake-up trip to Cairns Base Hospital revealed an 11 cm cancerous tumor in Rumer’s adrenal gland; further testing at Brisbane’s Lady Cilento Children’s Hospital on Christmas Eve confirmed stage 3 neuroblastoma with an estimated 50% chance of recovery. The family has been relocated to Brisbane for intensive treatment and likely long-term care, with an anticipated disruption of around two years away from home, family and friends. Queensland Health provided flights and temporary hospital accommodation, but the emotional and financial strain remains severe: Rumer’s father, Adam Koessler, left his job to support her through chemotherapy, complementary nutrition and natural therapies, and round-the-clock care.

The story has attracted strong community support in Cairns and beyond. Local fundraising efforts, including GoFundMe pages, have already raised thousands; the family hopes to reach goals such as $20,000 to cover living costs, treatment-related expenses and to make their temporary living situation more comfortable. Updates on Rumer’s treatment schedule, progress and needs have been shared via social media pages.

Also highlighted are broader tensions around access to medicinal cannabis. Adam Koessler faced legal trouble in January 2015 after administering cannabis oil to his daughter; his case spurred debate about parental rights, compassionate use, and the decriminalisation of medicinal cannabis in Australia. Supporters point to other families who faced similar legal battles but saw positive outcomes. For now, the family seeks donations, community support and privacy as Rumer undergoes chemotherapy and recovery efforts. Links to donation pages and social updates have been widely circulated for those who wish to help.

CNN suffered its worst ratings stretch in decades in the second quarter of 2012, registering its lowest primetime quarter since 1991 and steep declines across dayparts and key demographics. Primetime averages fell to 446,000 total viewers and just 129,000 adults 25–54—drops of roughly 35% and 41% from the prior year—while Total Day averaged 319,000 viewers and 95,000 in 25–54, declines of about 35% and 45%. Network executives point out that Q2 2011 benefited from several major breaking-news events (e.g., Osama bin Laden’s death, the Royal Wedding) that buoyed viewership, whereas Q2 2012 was relatively quiet. Still, CNN’s losses were notably deeper than those at rivals: Fox News and MSNBC also retreated in the 25–54 demo (down 14% and 18%, respectively), but CNN’s drop was more than double those rates in the demo and far worse in total viewers.

Individual CNN programs saw sharp audience erosion. Piers Morgan Tonight averaged only 137,000 viewers in 25–54, a 32–33% year-over-year decline—the worst 9 p.m. quarter in network history. Anderson Cooper 360 is down significantly (with the 10 p.m. airing off about 48% in the demo), Erin Burnett OutFront fell roughly 45% in 25–54, and Wolf Blitzer’s Situation Room lost large shares as well. Overall, CNN’s primetime average placed it well behind Fox News (which remained the clear leader with roughly 1.79–2.14 million primetime viewers depending on measures) and behind MSNBC.

Insiders cite fallen morale, stale primetime offerings and an identity crisis: while Fox and MSNBC have embraced opinionated, personality-driven programming that attracts steady audiences, CNN has largely stuck to nonpartisan journalism and has struggled to adapt its strategy. The network noted June month-to-month improvements—Cooper up 5%, Morgan up 9%, Burnett stronger—and emphasized a commitment to nonpartisan, quality journalism over chasing ratings gains.

About 15 heavily armed gunmen ambushed two vans carrying millions in jewels on the A6 motorway near Avallon in Burgundy, forcing out the drivers in the middle of the night and escaping with the haul. The attackers abandoned and burned the vans nearby; forensic teams searched the scene but the jewels remain missing. No injuries were reported. Authorities, treating the case as organized crime, are combing the region for suspects; investigators note similarities to past high-profile thefts, including those linked to the Pink Panther network and several spectacular Paris heists in recent years.

A fatal shooting at Butler High School in Matthews, North Carolina, unfolded Monday morning after an argument between two male students escalated into gunfire in a crowded hallway as students were arriving for the day. The victim was transported to a hospital and later died. A school resource officer quickly arrested the student suspected of firing the shot; investigators recovered the weapon but had not immediately disclosed its type or the students’ names or ages. Matthews Police Capt. Stason Tyrrell said surveillance video shows the incident stemmed from a fight between the two students and described it as an isolated event. The campus was placed on lockdown for about two hours while police secured the scene; counselors and psychologists were made available because many students witnessed the shooting. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools Superintendent Clayton Wilcox expressed sorrow that the fatality involved a student shooter and said the district is reviewing security procedures, noting concern over how a young person obtained a handgun. By late morning the lockdown was lifted, families could pick up students at the main entrance, and classes continued for those remaining. Dozens of anxious parents had gathered outside during the lockdown; footage showed students leaving in tears and reuniting with family.

Andy Roddick announced he will retire from professional tennis after the US Open, revealing the decision on his 30th birthday and calling the tournament his final event. He said recurring injuries and a waning ability to commit fully—physically and emotionally—led him to conclude he didn’t want to “disrespect the game by coasting home.” Roddick, who reached world No. 1 and won the 2003 US Open, continued competing during the tournament, defeating Rhyne Williams in the first round and slated to face Bernard Tomic next. His coach Larry Stefanki confirmed Roddick had been considering retirement for months, noting physical breakdowns and diminished focus. Over a distinguished career Roddick compiled a 610–212 record, 32 singles titles, more than $20 million in prize money, four other major finals, a year-end No. 1 ranking, a 2007 Davis Cup title, and nine straight years in the top 10. Praised for competitiveness and leadership, he plans to focus on his foundation, media work, family and staying connected to the sport even after stepping away from the tour.

A partisan budget standoff over the Affordable Care Act triggered a U.S. government shutdown beginning Oct. 1, 2013, halting many services and jeopardizing pay for more than 800,000 federal employees. The shutdown followed failed negotiations between a Republican House, which pushed short-term funding measures tied to delaying the ACA’s individual mandate and eliminating health subsidies for lawmakers and staff, and a Democratic Senate that rejected those amendments. President Obama and congressional leaders traded accusations as the midnight funding deadline passed; the administration ordered agencies to implement contingency plans.

By law, core functions tied to national security, public safety and mandatory benefits continue. Active-duty military, some national security personnel, Social Security and Medicare payments, and the U.S. Postal Service remained operational, and Congress passed a limited measure to keep military pay flowing. However, many federal workers were furloughed, and employees required to work faced possible pay delays. Agencies provided guidance: supervisors would notify staff whether to report, furloughed employees could spend limited hours securing work before leaving, and voluntary work during furloughs was prohibited.

The shutdown’s impacts were broad and immediate. National parks, museums, and the Smithsonian closed; NASA furloughed almost its entire workforce except for mission-critical operations such as ISS support. The Department of Defense sent about 400,000 civilian employees on unpaid leave, while many FAA safety inspectors, NTSB staff, and other regulatory personnel were stood down. Passport and visa processing slowed, small-business loan processing and many permitting functions halted, and programs like WIC, some veterans’ benefits, and Head Start faced interruptions if the shutdown continued. Agencies funded by mandatory or alternative revenue streams—such as certain health exchanges, the Postal Service, Amtrak, and some transportation programs—remained active.

The political divide within the Republican ranks—between hard-liners insisting on ACA concessions and moderates wary of the fallout—complicated resolution. Democrats warned that a prolonged shutdown could merge into a more perilous fight over raising the federal debt limit, which risked broader economic harm. Public opinion polls suggested voters disapproved of using a shutdown to challenge health-care law, and many worried about effects on services and federal workers reliant on paychecks and benefits. The duration of the shutdown depended on Congress and the White House reaching a funding agreement.

A severe late-December storm system spawned multiple tornadoes across the South and Midwest, killing at least seven people and injuring dozens as it moved through Arkansas, Missouri and nearby states around New Year’s Eve. In northwestern Arkansas, a tornado struck the hamlet of Cincinnati before dawn, killing three residents and flinging homeowner Chris Sisemore across the street; he survived with minor injuries. In Missouri, three people died near Rolla—two at a Lecoma farm where debris from mobile homes was scattered—while another victim later died at a hospital. Fort Leonard Wood suffered heavy damage when a tornado with estimated winds of 136–165 mph destroyed about a dozen homes in an officers’ neighborhood. Additional storms damaged homes, churches and boats around St. Louis County, and a possible touchdown near Petersburg, Ill., damaged about two dozen houses. Unseasonably warm Gulf moisture ahead of a cold front provided the instability for these winter tornadoes. Tornado watches and flash-flooding were reported across parts of Mississippi, Alabama and Louisiana as the system continued east.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid named Sens. Patty Murray, Max Baucus and John Kerry to serve as the Democratic picks on a 12-member “super committee” charged with finding over $1 trillion in deficit reduction by year’s end. Murray will be a co-chair; House Speaker John Boehner will choose the Republican co-chair plus two House members. House and Senate leaders will each appoint additional members. Reid praised the trio for budget expertise and bipartisan experience. Murray’s role drew Republican criticism because she chairs the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, prompting RNC chief Reince Priebus to call for her withdrawal. Democrats aim to defend entitlements and push for revenue options if Republicans reject tax increases. Kerry, Baucus and Murray pledged bipartisan, balanced work; Pelosi urged public deliberations to protect Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security.

A Chronicle of Higher Education analysis of federal data found Harvard led research universities with a 98% six-year graduation rate for students who enrolled in 2002, followed by Yale (97%) and Notre Dame (96%). Among public research universities, Virginia topped the list at 93%, with William & Mary and UC Berkeley close behind. The Chronicle compared six-year completion rates for cohorts entering in 1996 and 2002 and noted that one-third of institutions had lower rates by 2008; some attribute declines to students taking longer than six years. The study covered more than 1,000 four-year colleges and adjusted for year-to-year fluctuations by averaging adjacent years.

Interviews Before Execution was a weekly Henan provincial TV programme in central China that ran for just over five years, attracting nearly 40 million viewers. Hosted by reporter Ding Yu, the show featured face-to-face interviews with convicted murderers shortly before execution. Producers selected cases from court reports with approval from the Henan high court; they avoided political cases and disputed convictions and focused on violent murders intended as public warnings. Ding argued the condemned wanted to be heard and sometimes expressed remorse or final messages; she became a well-known figure, nicknamed “Beauty with the Beasts.” The series’ episodes included harrowing stories—young college graduates who killed for money, and Bao Ronting, an openly gay man whose case drew high ratings—followed until execution. The programme drew international attention after a documentary about its making circulated, prompting foreign media coverage. Authorities abruptly cancelled the show, citing “internal problems,” and replaced it with another legal affairs programme. The series also fed debate about China’s death penalty: judges on the programme noted recent legal shifts—Supreme Court review of death sentences and occasional leniency for mitigating factors—while some voiced that abolition might be a future goal.

Vint Cerf, a pioneer of the Internet and Google vice-president, warned at the American Association for the Advancement of Science meeting that relying solely on digital storage risks creating a “digital Dark Ages” in which future historians cannot reconstruct the early 21st century. Cerf noted that if we think in terms of centuries—1,000 or 3,000 years—preserving the raw bits is not enough: future researchers will also need the context and software environments that make digital objects interpretable. He likened the potential loss of our records to gaps in knowledge from post‑Roman Western Europe, where missing written records leave historians puzzled.

Cerf stressed that digitization is often assumed to prolong the life of photographs, documents and other artifacts, but that assumption may be wrong. Digital files can “evaporate” if not saved or become unreadable when the software or operating systems required to render them become obsolete. He invoked Doris Kearns Goodwin’s use of preserved correspondence to reconstruct historical conversations, suggesting a 22nd‑century historian might be unable to perform similar reconstructions for our era because the necessary digital evidence would be gone or unusable.

The problem is acute for legal and other important records: historians and institutions may lose perspectives that only emerge over long timescales. Cerf proposed institutionalizing preservation thinking and highlighted a technical concept called “digital vellum,” being explored at Carnegie Mellon. Digital vellum involves taking a comprehensive snapshot at storage time that captures the item plus the software, runtime and environment needed to reproduce it later. Such snapshots could allow future machines to faithfully render files, games or spreadsheets even centuries hence, preventing inadvertent loss of cultural and legal memory.

Google’s new social network Google+ appears to be losing early momentum, according to Experian Hitwise data and observer accounts. U.S. visits to Google+ fell about 3% to 1.79 million in the week ended July 23, following a 283% surge the prior week, and average time spent on the site dropped 10% to 5 minutes 15 seconds. Experian’s traffic measurement excludes mobile and third-party app activity, so the figures are partial. Launched in limited invite-only beta on June 28, Google+ reached more than 10 million users within weeks, and Google reported high sharing activity. Still, anecdotal reports and site analytics suggest engagement is cooling: referral traffic from Google+ is declining, users report checking less frequently, and shared content often centers on Google itself rather than diverse user posts. Features like Hangouts retain some appeal, while Sparks and the maintenance burden of Circles may hinder ongoing use. Observers warn that sustaining user retention is the critical next phase for Google+, and that initial signup momentum must be translated into compelling, repeatable reasons for users to return and engage.

Two former servers at the Hard Rock Café in Universal Studios, Orlando, Christopher Grant and Benjamin Aguda, have sued Hard Rock Café International in Orange Circuit Court, alleging wage-and-tip violations under Florida and federal law. The complaint asserts that for nearly three years they were paid less than Florida’s minimum wage while the company improperly used a tip credit by requiring servers and bartenders to share tips with kitchen employees—specifically “expediters” who garnish and prepare plates. Plaintiffs and their attorneys contend that such tip-sharing is unlawful unless all participants customarily and regularly receive tips, and that allowing kitchen staff into the tip pool effectively reduced frontline workers’ pay. Attorneys described the practice as robbing diners’ gratuities from the servers who served them. The suit argues Hard Rock should have known the arrangement violated labor law and deprived servers of legally required wages.

U.S. researchers report that some of the water detected on the Moon originates from the solar wind. Analyzing glassy grains of lunar regolith returned by Apollo missions, the team found water and hydroxyl with low deuterium levels, indicating hydrogen supplied by the Sun rather than from cometary or asteroidal sources. Solar-wind protons implanted in the airless, unprotected lunar surface react with oxygen bound in rocks to form water-bearing molecules. The discovery, published in Nature Geoscience, adds a new mechanism for producing water on the Moon and suggests similar processes could operate on other airless bodies like asteroids and moons such as Deimos. Lead author Yang Liu highlights potential value for future human settlement—water could be consumed or electrolyzed into hydrogen and oxygen for fuel—though some scientists caution that extracting usable amounts from regolith may be difficult and that current conclusions are based on tiny samples. The finding broadens understanding of inner Solar System water sources beyond delivery from icy bodies beyond the snow line.

The White House circulated talking points urging allies to say President Donald Trump was "entirely correct" in his handling of the violent Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, insisting "both sides" bore responsibility. The memo echoed Trump’s contentious remarks at a Trump Tower news conference and reiterated that he condemned hate groups while promoting unity and American founding principles. It cited anecdotal reports and social-media posts suggesting counter-protesters (described as "antifa" or the "alt-left") used clubs, and urged critics and media to focus on violence on all sides and the administration’s steps — including a Justice Department civil-rights probe and prior prosecutions — to hold violent extremists accountable.

The guidance prompted widespread backlash. Republican leaders, including House Speaker Paul Ryan, Sen. Marco Rubio, Sen. Tim Scott and Rep. Charlie Dent, demanded unequivocal condemnation of white supremacists and rejected moral equivalence between racists and those opposing them. Some Republicans and business leaders criticized Trump more sharply than usual; Sen. John McCain explicitly rejected any moral equivalency. Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Brian Schatz, condemned Trump’s equivocation, saying his words signaled sympathy with white nationalists. The controversy deepened after Trump alternated between naming hate groups and reverting to blaming "many sides," fueling bipartisan outrage and departures from the White House’s intended messaging.

Paris Saint-Germain announced it will replace its regular Fly Emirates sponsor on the front of its jerseys with the message “JE SUIS PARIS” for its next two matches — Wednesday’s Champions League game against Malmö and Saturday’s Ligue 1 home match versus Troyes. The move, approved by Emirates, is a larger, more prominent tribute than an earlier gesture when players wore the phrase in small print over their hearts. The change honors victims of the Nov. 13 Paris attacks claimed by ISIS that killed more than 129 people. The Saturday fixture at Parc des Princes will be especially emotional: it is PSG’s first home game since the attacks, and the club has positioned itself as a civic symbol for the city. PSG also observed a minute of silence for the victims. The decision underscores how clubs may forego lucrative front-of-shirt sponsorship space to offer public solidarity after national tragedies.

Rapper Eminem’s headlining set at the Bonnaroo music festival in Tennessee provoked fear and a heated online debate after concertgoers reacted to loud blasts that many said sounded like gunshots. Videos circulating on social media show fans screaming and ducking as the noises rang out during Eminem’s performance of “Kill You,” a track from his 2000 album The Marshall Mathers LP. Attendees and commenters described being traumatized and startled—some leaving the show—and several invoked recent mass-casualty incidents at public events as context for why realistic weapon sounds were especially alarming. Social media personality Andrea Russett, who said she has mild PTSD, called the use of the shot-like blasts “extremely irresponsible and distasteful,” recounting that the effect reduced her to tears and prompted people around her to drop instinctively to the ground.

The incident sparked divided responses online. Critics argued that festival organizers or the artist should have warned the audience about potentially triggering sound effects; others said such effects are an established part of Eminem’s live repertoire and that the song dates to long before recent mass shootings. Supporters pointed out Eminem has used similar sounds at other festivals, including Governor’s Ball the week prior, and that audiences have long encountered dramatic effects in rock and hip-hop performances.

Eminem’s representatives issued statements calling reports of gunshot sound effects inaccurate: they said the noises were produced by a pyrotechnic concussion—a loud booming effect used by many artists—and noted the effect has been part of his live shows for over a decade without prior complaint. The exchange highlighted broader tensions over performance theatrics, audience safety, and sensitivity to trauma in the wake of public mass violence.

The document reports the Islamic State’s (ISIS/ISIL) killing of 26-year-old American aid worker Peter Kassig (also known as Abdul-Rahman), and examines the implications for other Western hostages and ISIS’s propaganda and ransom practices. Kassig, a former U.S. Army Ranger turned emergency medical technician who founded a relief group to aid Syrian refugees, was seized in October 2013 while delivering supplies. A video released by ISIS showed a masked militant standing over a severed head identified as Kassig’s and included graphic mass beheadings of Syrian military personnel; unlike prior execution videos, Kassig was shown already beheaded and not forced to read a statement. His parents and the U.S. government confirmed their anguish; President Obama and Secretary of State John Kerry praised Kassig’s humanitarian work and noted his conversion to Islam, which his family said was sincere.

With Kassig’s death, ISIS has killed five Westerners it was holding. A 26-year-old American woman, captured in August 2013 while doing aid work and the only remaining U.S. hostage known to be held by ISIS, remains in captivity; U.S. officials and her family have withheld her name for safety. ISIS’s intentions for her are unclear; notably she did not appear at the end of the Kassig video, breaking the group’s prior pattern of showing the next intended victim. ISIS has reportedly demanded exorbitant ransoms—over $6 million—for American prisoners, but U.S. policy forbids paying ransoms and warns families they could face prosecution. Analysts and officials argue that the high ransom demands signal ISIS’s primary interest in using Western hostages for propaganda and recruitment rather than for straightforward ransom revenue.

The Kassig video differed from earlier ISIS productions: unusually long and more graphically brutal, with historical narration glorifying ISIS’s rise and calls to join the fight, plus lingering close-ups of militants’ faces and a location identified near Dabiq. The release may reflect desperation amid mounting setbacks: U.S.-led airstrikes have helped retake key sites like the Baiji refinery and intelligence efforts have pressured ISIS leadership. The broader hostage-rescue effort has been hampered by U.S. refusal to negotiate ransoms, interagency friction, and the complex dynamics among militant groups in Syria, leaving the fate of remaining Western captives uncertain.

A fragile ceasefire and evacuation deal for rebel-held eastern Aleppo, brokered by Russia and Turkey, unraveled amid renewed shelling and conflicting demands from pro-Assad allies, notably Iran-backed militias. Buses sat idle as civilians and fighters waited; reports said Iranian militias blocked departures and held nearly 1,000 people at checkpoints. Rebels pledged to honor the agreement, while Iran-linked militias—whose fighters led the assault—insisted on additional conditions, including evacuations from besieged pro-government villages and recovery of fighters’ remains. Russia said shelling resumed in response to rebel attacks; opposition and independent monitors said government and allied forces continued bombardment and summary executions. The UN reported reliable evidence that pro-Assad forces and allied militias executed at least 82 civilians in areas retaken by government troops, prompting calls for UN observers and humanitarian oversight. International actors expressed outrage: US and European officials blamed Syria, Russia and Iran for civilian suffering and potential war crimes; Turkey and Russia agreed to act as guarantors of a revised deal reportedly set to restart evacuations. Tens of thousands of civilians remained trapped in dire conditions—short of food, water and medical care—while the fall of eastern Aleppo would mark a decisive victory for Assad and a dire humanitarian turning point.

Medicinal Genomics, a startup led by Kevin McKernan, released raw sequencing reads for the Cannabis sativa genome via Amazon’s EC2, marking an early public step toward mapping the plant’s DNA. The dataset comprises about 131 billion bases of shotgun reads fragmented into hundreds of thousands of snippets; McKernan estimates the genome is roughly 400 million bases. Sequencing was performed in Amsterdam and cost about $200,000. McKernan, with a background on the Human Genome Project and in sequencing technology firms, intends the data to enable research into cannabinoids beyond THC—such as CBD, which has shown anti-tumor effects—and to support genome-guided breeding, regulation, and potential therapeutic production. The draft has not yet been peer-reviewed or assembled, though Medicinal Genomics plans annotations and tools for researchers and regulators to explore medical applications.

Justin Timberlake tells Vanity Fair he hasn’t spoken to ex Britney Spears in roughly nine or ten years, wishing her well but noting their teen relationship—two “small-town kids” thrust into massive fame—was shaped by circumstance and couldn’t endure into adulthood. Reflecting on life as Mouseketeers turned pop stars, he calls their existence abnormal—“little kids with big toys”—and says growing up changed them. Timberlake praises Jessica Biel as the most significant person in his life and says he wants a family someday, though he worries couples commit to who someone is now rather than who they’ll become; staying together requires changing together. He explains why celebrities often date each other: mutual understanding of fame offers refuge. Professionally, Timberlake isn’t ruling out more music but downplays immediate plans, notes forthcoming film work including Friends with Benefits with Mila Kunis, and recalls the practical awkwardness of filming intimate scenes while joking about showing off on-screen now before “gravity” sets in.

Alaska Governor Bill Walker announced he will use executive authority to expand the state’s Medicaid program under the federal Affordable Care Act, aiming to cover more than 20,000 uninsured Alaskans in the first year. Walker, an independent who has repeatedly faced resistance from the Republican-controlled legislature, said Alaska will accept $146 million in federal funds available for Medicaid expansion. He cited nearly 30 other states that have accepted expansion funds, arguing the move is “commonsense” because it benefits residents, economies and state budgets.

Walker’s administration submitted the request for federal funds while noting expected fiscal and economic gains: an estimated $1 billion in federal healthcare dollars over six years, about $100 million in state savings, and roughly 4,000 new jobs, according to a letter from budget director Pat Pitney. By applying directly to Washington, Walker seeks to bypass the legislative roadblocks that have blocked previous expansion efforts since he took office after the 2014 election.

Under Alaska law, the Legislative Budget and Audit Committee can review requests for federal funds when the legislature is not in session. The committee has until Sept. 1 to either support the request or recommend a special legislative session. Committee chairman Rep. Mike Hawker described the panel’s role as largely procedural, affecting the timing of fund availability.

Opponents, including Republican state Senator John Coghill, warn of future fiscal risks if the federal government retreats from its funding commitments, saying current spending could burden future taxpayers. The move places Alaska among states embracing Medicaid expansion despite partisan divides that have left many southern and central states opting out.

CNN's New York offices and studios were evacuated Thursday night after a phoned-in bomb threat that claimed five devices were inside the building. The New York Police Department investigated and later determined the threat was not substantiated, issuing an all-clear. In an internal memo to staff, CNN Worldwide president Jeff Zucker informed employees that the NYPD had given the all-clear and that the building was secure and safe to return to in the morning. He thanked local authorities for their swift action and commended employees for their patience and professionalism during the evacuation. Law enforcement sources noted the threat originated from a caller who asserted the presence of multiple devices, prompting the precautionary evacuation and response. After searches and safety checks, officials concluded there was no credible threat, allowing staff to resume normal operations. CNN and NYPD communicated the resolution via the memo and a tweet, respectively, reassuring staff and the public that the situation had been resolved without incident. No injuries or damage were reported, and the network’s facilities were declared safe.

A new report from the special inspector general for Afghanistan reconstruction raises serious doubts about the U.S. strategy of funding large infrastructure projects to bolster counterinsurgency efforts. The inspection finds major programs funded through the Afghan Infrastructure Fund are badly delayed, risk outlasting the U.S. combat presence, and may create an “expectations gap” the Afghan government cannot close. One highlighted case, the “Kandahar Bridging Solution,” relied on costly diesel generators to supply roughly 25 megawatts to Kandahar until a hydropower turbine can be installed—yet the turbine will provide less power and won’t arrive for years, and Afghanistan cannot afford diesel once U.S. funding ends. Senior commanders argued more electricity would win popular support, but some officials, including Maj. Gen. Kenneth Dahl, found no evidence of improved employment, stability or government backing. The inspector general also flagged a $23 million Helmand road where landowners weren’t compensated and noted four electricity projects worth over $300 million remain uncontracted despite claims of counterinsurgency benefit. Critics, including Sen. Claire McCaskill, say there’s no data showing these projects improved security and warn against simply “throwing money” at reconstruction. The State Department and U.S. Embassy defend the projects as signaling long-term commitment. New inspector John Sopko plans closer scrutiny of project design, not just implementation.

President Barack Obama warned that Moammar Gadhafi must immediately halt attacks on civilians or face enforcement of a U.N. resolution through international military action. Speaking March 18, 2011, Obama said a cease-fire, withdrawal of Gadhafi’s forces from key cities, and restoration of power, water and humanitarian access were non-negotiable. He emphasized the U.S. would act within an international coalition, would not deploy ground troops to Libya, and has already imposed sanctions, frozen assets, and delivered humanitarian aid to neighboring countries. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton was dispatched to Paris for allied talks as Britain, France, NATO and regional partners planned implementation, including a possible no-fly zone.

In a thrilling World Cup opener in Sochi, Portugal and Spain fought to a 3-3 draw thanks to Cristiano Ronaldo’s sublime hat-trick. Ronaldo opened from the spot after drawing a foul, added a second when David De Gea spilled a shot, and completed the salvo with a sensational late free-kick — his first from a direct free-kick at major tournaments after 44 prior attempts. The performance made Ronaldo the oldest World Cup hat-trick scorer, put him among players to score in four World Cups, and moved him level with Ferenc Puskas on international tallies. Spain’s Diego Costa impressed with two robust, decisive strikes, and Nacho briefly gave Spain the lead with a spectacular effort. The draw was seen as fair: Spain dominated possession but suffered individual lapses, while Portugal’s resilience and Ronaldo’s brilliance earned them a vital point.

A 2-year-old boy, Yoshiki Fujimoto, was found safe on Aug. 15 about 68 hours after going missing on Suo-Oshima (Yashiro Island), Yamaguchi Prefecture. He had disappeared on Aug. 12 after setting off toward a beach with his 66-year-old grandfather and 3-year-old brother; after walking roughly 100 meters toward the beach, Yoshiki said he wanted to go home and began returning on his own, then vanished. A large search involving hundreds of police, firefighters, volunteers, drones, thermal cameras, search dogs and helicopters concentrated on areas around his great‑grandfather’s home but initially did not search the mountain where he was ultimately found. 

A 78-year-old volunteer, Haruo Obata from Oita Prefecture, climbed a mountain trail northeast of the house and, after calling repeatedly, heard Yoshiki reply “I’m here.” Obata found him barefoot and sitting on a moss-covered rock in a mountain stream, feet in the water, and wrapped him in a towel. The boy happily accepted candy and was able to converse with his mother and grandmother when reunited. He was taken to hospital with dehydration, scratches and tick bites but no major injuries and is expected to remain under observation for several days.

Experts described the outcome as a “miracle,” noting favorable conditions likely helped: access to shade and stream water, the toddler’s limited stress and unpredictable two-year-old behavior that may have kept him from wandering further. Some rescuers later expressed regret that the mountain hadn’t been searched earlier. The family expressed relief and gratitude, while the grandfather apologized for momentarily taking his eyes off the child.

Harry Shearer, the veteran voice actor behind key Simpsons characters such as Mr. Burns, Ned Flanders and Principal Skinner, announced he is leaving The Simpsons after 26 seasons. Shearer tweeted that he wanted “the freedom to do other work,” and suggested his exit followed a contract dispute, saying a lawyer for producer James L. Brooks informed him, “‘Harry will not be part of it, wish him the best.’” Executive producers Matt Groening, Al Jean and Brooks confirmed Shearer declined “the same deal the rest of the cast accepted” and said the show will continue, quipping “Maggie took it hard.” They plan to recast Shearer’s characters “with the finest voiceover talent available” rather than retire them. Fox had recently renewed the long-running series for two more seasons through 2017; most of the other voice cast signed two-year extensions for seasons 27 and 28, and production on season 27 has begun without Shearer. Brooks publicly appealed for further talks on Twitter. The Simpsons has faced tense contract negotiations before—most notably in 2011 when the cast accepted pay cuts after difficult bargaining—yet previously retained its core voices. The season 26 finale will air Sunday on Fox.

Severe flooding in southeastern Louisiana has created an urgent need for blood donations, and South Texas Blood and Tissue Center (STBTC) in San Antonio is trying to help fill that gap while already facing its own shortages. STBTC officials say summer months are challenging for blood collection because many donors are students who leave for vacation, and the Zika virus has further reduced donor eligibility: anyone who traveled to Zika-affected areas must wait 28 days after return before giving blood. The center now offers Zika testing for donated blood, requiring only an additional consent form. STBTC emphasized there is no substitute for human blood and all types are needed; donors can find locations at southtexasblood.org.

Experts warn that once floodwaters recede, mosquito-borne disease risks—including Zika and West Nile virus—could rise. Peter Hotez of Baylor’s National School of Tropical Medicine warned that eggs laid in containers like buckets or tires can survive surges and hatch after floods, potentially increasing Aedes aegypti populations in coming weeks. The CDC’s Ben Beard agreed monitoring in the coming weeks is crucial but said he does not expect a significant increase in Zika-carrying mosquitoes, noting that this species may be more easily washed away. No local Zika cases have been confirmed in Louisiana, though unreported cases are possible. Authorities say increased mosquito counts would prompt an intense response to prevent virus spread. Public-health officials continue broader monitoring and preventive actions nationwide as Zika remains a pressing concern, with ongoing discussions around surveillance, funding, mosquito control, and vaccine research.

BuzzFeed’s CEO Jonah Peretti announced the company has terminated a planned advertising agreement with the Republican National Committee that had reserved space for the fall election cycle, saying BuzzFeed will not accept ads for Donald Trump. The buy — reported by Politico to be worth about $1.3 million — was signed in April, but Peretti said the tone and policy proposals of Trump’s campaign, including a proposed ban on Muslim travel and rhetoric targeting immigrants, women and the press, made continuing the arrangement untenable. Peretti framed the decision as a business judgment rooted in protecting employees’ freedoms and ability to work, comparing refusal to run Trump ads to BuzzFeed’s choice not to run cigarette advertising for health reasons. Editor-in-chief Ben Smith emphasized the move was a publisher/business decision, not an editorial one, and said BuzzFeed News’ campaign coverage would remain unchanged. The RNC did not comment to BuzzFeed, while RNC strategist Sean Spicer told CNN the committee never intended to use BuzzFeed’s reserved space and criticized BuzzFeed for rejecting a candidate “under investigation.” BuzzFeed staffers noted the site’s relationship with the Trump campaign has already been strained, with reporters previously denied credentials and targeted by Trump. The action follows prior instances of BuzzFeed taking public policy stances, and echoes moves by other outlets — such as Huffington Post — that have declined Trump campaign ads or marked coverage with editorial labels. BuzzFeed declined to elaborate on the ad-buy’s size or further details.

Since the Harvey Weinstein allegations and the rise of the #MeToo movement, many have framed the moment as a cultural tipping point in confronting sexual harassment and assault. But public accusations against powerful men are not new: in 1991 law professor Anita Hill testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee about alleged sexual harassment by Clarence Thomas as his Supreme Court confirmation loomed. Hill endured intense questioning and attacks on her credibility during a hearing led by then-Senator Joe Biden. Thomas was ultimately confirmed.

Decades later, Biden has expressed regret for how the hearings played out and has apologized to Hill, saying he wished he had done more to protect her from aggressive questioning and to prevent sexist remarks from committee members. In an interview with Teen Vogue’s editor in chief Elaine Welteroth, Biden said he believed Hill, voted against Thomas, and later worked to ensure women would serve on the Judiciary Committee. He acknowledged failing to subpoena three women he had hoped would corroborate Hill’s testimony, explaining he feared they would not support her and that the committee’s narrow margin made the outcome precarious. “I wish I had been able to do more for Anita Hill,” he said.

Hill and others have criticized Biden’s past actions as insufficient, arguing his apologies lack full ownership of the committee’s treatment of her and the broader missed opportunity to model best practices for hearings involving allegations of sexual misconduct. Hill stressed that the harm extended beyond her personal experience: women were watching for leadership that would protect them and promote equality, and the hearings instead signaled unfair treatment.

Both Hill’s experience and the current #MeToo moment highlight the need for cultural change. Biden, through initiatives like the “It’s on Us” campaign and work on campuses, says he aims to help shift norms so abused women no longer question themselves. He sees the present movement as a chance to reshape how sexual harassment and assault are addressed and prevented.

Apple has rejected the first Apple Watch app built solely to play fart noises from the wrist. Fart Watch let users trigger canned flatulence sounds on an iPhone placed under a cushion by tapping a big “Fart” button on the Watch. Apple declined the submission citing App Store rules that bar duplicate, low-value apps—specifically naming fart and burp apps—and trademark guidelines. The rejection notice bluntly stated it noticed the app was “primarily a fart app” and that such apps are not accepted on Apple Watch. Observers note the decision supports the Watch’s upscale image, despite many fart apps existing on the iPhone; the developer now plans a decorative strap accessory called WatchPops.

Prince and Rose Adams, a 45-year-old couple from St. John in the U.S. Virgin Islands, won a “Win an Inn” essay contest to acquire the 210-year-old Center Lovell Inn and Restaurant in Maine. The contest was organized by retiring innkeeper Janice Sage, who said she modeled the giveaway on a contest she had won 22 years earlier. Sage said entrants submitted 200-word essays and paid a $125 entry fee; although she had hoped for 7,500 entries, she received fewer but said the fees provided sufficient retirement funds. The Adamses plan to close their Caribbean-style restaurant and aim to open the Maine inn by July 10. However, dozens of unsuccessful entrants have organized as the Center Lovell Contest Fair Practices Commission and allege deceptive advertising and unfair advantage because Sage’s contest language reportedly said restaurant or inn owners would not receive preferential treatment. Maine State Police said they are investigating whether the contest violated state law on games of skill, which bars operators from partially or fully controlling outcomes; the probe focuses narrowly on potential violations and should conclude within a week. Officials suggested contestants consult private attorneys for other remedies.

Rep. Pete Sessions (R-Texas) announced Thursday night that he was ending his bid to become House majority leader, effectively leaving Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.) as the lone prominent candidate to replace Rep. Eric Cantor (R-Va.), who suffered a shock primary defeat. Sessions, chairman of the House Rules Committee and former head of the House GOP campaign committee, said he withdrew after concluding that the effort required to mount a successful campaign would have caused “unnecessary and painful division” within the Republican conference. His exit came after a brief but intense push for support immediately following Cantor’s loss; Sessions struggled to overcome McCarthy’s institutional advantages as the party’s vote counter and top fundraiser and failed to consolidate the GOP’s right flank, where some conservatives had favored fellow Texan Jeb Hensarling, who also declined to run. Speaker John Boehner’s decision to hold a secret-ballot leadership election on June 19, soon after Cantor’s announcement, further limited challengers’ time to organize. Other high-profile conservatives—Paul Ryan, Tom Price and Jim Jordan—also passed. Rep. Raúl Labrador is considering a challenge, but McCarthy is widely expected to be elected and will leave the whip race open, where contenders include Rep. Peter Roskam, Rep. Steve Scalise and Rep. Marlin Stutzman. Cantor will remain majority leader through July 31 to aid transition.

In Beaumont, shoppers have begun staking out spots for Black Friday bargains weeks in advance, with two longtime participants—Vicky Torres of Cabazon and Juanita Salas of Beaumont—camping outside the Best Buy at 1650 Second St. The pair arrived last Wednesday and say they’ve done this together before. Wrapped in blankets and armed with mittens, snacks and hot coffee, they trade off overnight shifts to hold their place and hope to snag deals like a 50-inch HDTV advertised for about $199. Jacob Alva, Salas’ husband, stands in line periodically to keep her spot and provide practical support—food, charged cell phones and bathroom breaks—though he himself does not camp. He also notes he feels safe because police and store security are present. Store manager Eric Tschudy observes that the number of “campers” increases every year and that regulars like Vicky are welcome. The practice reflects shoppers’ desire to stretch limited budgets: many in line say deep discounts after Thanksgiving are essential for buying Christmas gifts on fixed incomes. While some onlookers praise their dedication, others call them “stupid” or “crazy,” and sometimes ask for favors like saving spots—requests the campers politely decline. As retailers push Black Friday earlier, even opening on Thanksgiving evening, committed bargain hunters are adapting by arriving earlier and staying longer to secure advertised specials.

A Los Angeles jury awarded casino mogul Steve Wynn $20 million after finding that "Girls Gone Wild" founder Joe Francis defamed him by claiming Wynn threatened to have Francis killed and buried in the desert over a gambling debt. The verdict broke down into $5 million for statements Francis made to a TMZ producer and $11 million for remarks on Good Morning America; punitive damages up to $60 million may be considered. Francis contends trial errors and argues some statements were privileged court communications; he also claims the threat was real but has not produced the alleged supporting email.

James Cameron’s long-awaited Avatar, his first film in 12 years, lives up to much of the hype: a visually dazzling, emotionally engaging sci-fi epic that could reshape the cinematic experience. Set in 2154 on the lush moon Pandora, the story follows paraplegic marine Jake Sully (Sam Worthington), who inhabits a genetically engineered Na’vi “avatar” to help humans exploit a precious mineral, unobtanium. The human mission is split between scientists, led by Sigourney Weaver’s Grace, who advocate understanding and relocation, and militaristic forces under Colonel Quaritch (Stephen Lang), who favor annihilation. Predictable echoes of colonialism, Vietnam and contemporary geopolitics underpin the narrative, yet Cameron’s laborious worldbuilding — from Na’vi language and fauna to clan history — and his “emotion capture” performances give the characters authenticity and heart. The 3D presentation is a calculated, mostly restrained triumph: moments of spectacle are thrilling, though the extended 161-minute runtime in stereoscopic format can fatigue viewers. Highlights include the awe-inspiring final battle and intimate scenes like Jake’s awakening in avatar form and his romance with Neytiri (Zoe Saldana). Avatar is entertaining, poignant and likely to be influential — a technical milestone and awards contender.

A London lawyer proposed to his girlfriend by hiding a marriage proposal in The Times cryptic crossword — believed to be the first such proposal in the puzzle’s 85-year history. Matthew Dick arranged with puzzle editor Richard Rogan to insert clues whose answers, when read together, spelled out his intent. Tuesday’s puzzle included a six-letter clue, “Pretty Welsh girl widely thought not to be all there,” yielding “Delyth,” and an eight-letter clue, “‘Will you marry me,’ say, that’s forward also rude!” whose answer was “proposal.” Other themed answers included “birthday,” “wishes” and a clue ending in “Matthew,” tying into the moment when Dick produced the ring. The couple, celebrating Delyth Hughes’s birthday in Cornwall, reacted with emotion and humor: Hughes was “dumbfounded,” paused for about 30 seconds and joked “No” before saying “Yes.” Dick, 38, admitted his hands were shaking; Hughes, 39, called the stunt “typical” of his cheeky, geeky nature. Rogan, contacted via Twitter, confirmed he thought it was a one-off and joked they “won’t be doing it again.” The story drew attention as an inventive, personal public proposal.

Comedian Stephen Colbert’s crude joke about a metaphorical sexual relationship between President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the May 1 episode of The Late Show prompted over 5,700 complaints to the FCC from viewers across the political spectrum. Samples released by the agency show callers objecting on grounds of indecency, hate speech and homophobia. Some parents said they had to answer questions from children; others—both supporters and critics of Trump—called the joke beneath American broadcasting standards and urged fines or sanctions against CBS. Several complaints argued the line demeaned gay people by using homosexuality as an insult, including comments from a trans man who objected despite disliking Trump. Critics also argued media bias, saying similar jokes wouldn’t target Democrats. FCC Chairman Ajit Pai confirmed the agency is reviewing the complaints—a routine process that does not indicate merit—though he offered no update. Media law experts say enforcement is unlikely: Colbert’s expletive was bleeped and The Late Show airs at 11:30 p.m. within the FCC’s “safe harbor,” and obscenity standards are strict. Attorneys noted the segment had political context and lacked the prurient intent required to meet the obscenity test, making regulatory action improbable.

Actor Liam Neeson’s nephew, 31-year-old Ronan Sexton, is critically ill after falling about 20ft from the top of a telephone kiosk on Brighton promenade early last Sunday. He sustained serious head injuries and was first taken to Royal Sussex County Hospital, then transferred to Hurstwood Park Hospital in Haywards Heath, where he remains. The accident occurred around 4am while he was out with friends and is not being treated as suspicious. Ronan’s mother, Bernadette Sexton—Liam Neeson’s sister—has been at his bedside, and Neeson has been informed.

North Korea’s third nuclear test deepened regional tensions and spotlighted China’s fraught role as Pyongyang’s main patron. The test, which North Korea said used a miniaturized device with greater explosive force than prior blasts, drew near-universal condemnation, an emergency U.N. Security Council meeting and a Chinese summons of the North Korean ambassador. Beijing publicly expressed “strong dissatisfaction” and urged restraint and a return to six-party denuclearization talks, but stopped short of committing to punitive measures that might destabilize the regime or trigger refugee flows into China.

Analysts underline Beijing’s dilemma: China likely will back tougher U.N. language and sanctions, yet is unlikely to abandon its long-standing policy of shielding North Korea as a buffer against U.S. influence. China’s military and Communist Party links to Pyongyang, fear of chaos on the border and strategic caution limit Beijing’s leverage. The test embarrasses China and complicates the new leadership transition to Xi Jinping, whose response could signal Beijing’s willingness to cooperate more closely with Washington and Seoul.

Washington vowed to augment sanctions and reassured allies of U.S. defense commitments, while experts warned the test may accelerate regional missile defenses and edge North Korea closer to a credible warhead deliverable by missiles. Pyongyang framed the test as a response to U.S. hostility and prior U.N. sanctions. Observers see a recurring cycle: sanctions provoke further provocations as the impoverished regime pursues nuclear deterrence and international relevance, leaving few attractive policy options for the international community.

China stunned global markets by altering how it sets the yuan’s daily reference rate, triggering a rapid devaluation that sent the currency to multi-year lows and roiled stocks, bonds and commodities worldwide. The People’s Bank of China said it would base the daily midpoint more on market signals—including the prior day’s close—aiming to make the tightly managed renminbi more market-oriented. The move produced a 1.9% drop on Tuesday and another roughly 1.6% fall Wednesday, with offshore rates even weaker.
