Markets feared further declines, since the yuan trades within a 2% band around the reference rate.

Officials framed the step as a reform to liberalize the exchange rate and invited IMF approval; the IMF called it a welcome step if implemented prudently and suggested a path to an effectively floating rate over two to three years. Yet many analysts and politicians viewed the change through a competitive lens: a cheaper yuan would boost struggling exporters, worsen foreign competitors’ positions and risk a “currency war.” U.S. lawmakers, notably Senator Chuck Schumer, criticized the move as manipulative, while the Treasury responded more measuredly. The action complicated Federal Reserve rate deliberations by adding disinflationary pressure globally, weakening prospects for an imminent U.S. hike.

China’s economic slowdown—slower export growth, weaker factory data and sliding commodity demand—underpinned the decision. Authorities say they do not intend an uncontrolled depreciation, and state banks intervened to temper moves, but some policymakers reportedly favor a larger overall devaluation to support domestic growth, leaving significant uncertainty about the yuan’s next path and its global repercussions.

A previously private chapter of pop history resurfaced when a breakup letter Tupac Shakur wrote to Madonna while in jail became public and was announced for auction. Madonna had acknowledged a past romantic involvement with Tupac in 2015; TMZ later published the 1995 letter in which the rapper explains why he ended their relationship. In the note Tupac acknowledges that Madonna being seen with a Black man would not harm her career and might even enhance her image, but he says he feared damaging his own public persona and disappointing “half of the people who made me what I thought I was.” He apologizes for any pain he caused, frames himself as a young man with limited experience handling a relationship with “an extremely famous sex symbol,” and says he has since grown “spiritually and mentally.” The letter quotes Madonna as having said she was “off to rehabilitate all the rappers and basketball players,” and he expresses regret at having hurt her. TMZ reports the letter will be auctioned July 19–28 by Gotta Have Rock and Roll with a $100,000 starting bid; previous Tupac correspondence has fetched well over six figures. Observers noted the poignancy of the text — a reminder that celebrity relationships carry the same insecurities and difficult choices as others — and even commented on Tupac’s striking handwriting.

Italy’s national statistics agency Istat will include prostitution, illegal drug sales and trafficking in contraband cigarettes and alcohol in its 2014 GDP calculations, aligning with new EU/Eurostat national accounts methodology. Announced for implementation starting in September with prior-year figures adjusted, the change updates a system dating to 1995 and also adds research and development and arms expenditures to GDP. Istat acknowledged difficulties in measuring illicit activity, but estimates the inclusion could raise Italian GDP by about 1–2 percent. A larger GDP would lower deficit-to-GDP ratios, potentially easing pressure on Prime Minister Matteo Renzi’s target to narrow the deficit to 2.6 percent. The Finance Ministry declined to comment.

Sen. Rand Paul defended and stood by his aide Jack Hunter amid controversy over Hunter’s past provocative radio persona and writings that praised John Wilkes Booth, mocked Abraham Lincoln, and used a Confederate-themed ski mask. Paul condemned those views as “absolutely stupid,” affirmed he is not a secessionist or enemy of Lincoln, and said Hunter—who co-wrote Paul’s first book and served as his social media adviser—had never acted discriminatorily. Paul argued people can outgrow youthful provocations and maintained a zero-tolerance stance for racism, saying he would fire anyone he believed to be a white supremacist. Under intense scrutiny, Hunter resigned to avoid distracting Paul and to resume work as a pundit, recanting some past remarks and retiring the “Southern Avenger” persona. Supporters and former colleagues described Hunter as talented and professional, while critics said his history revived broader GOP tensions about states’ rights, slavery’s legacy and mainstreaming libertarian-leaning conservatives. Hunter says he’s now more libertarian and tolerant and wants to defend his views independently.

Astronomers have confirmed the most distant galaxy yet detected, z8_GND_5296, whose light began traveling to Earth 13.1 billion years ago, when the universe was roughly 700 million years old. The team identified the faint infrared source in Hubble images, then used spectroscopic observations with Keck Observatory’s MOSFIRE instrument to measure a secure redshift of about 7.5, surpassing the prior record of 7.2. Spectroscopy of the Lyman-alpha emission line provided the definitive distance, avoiding false positives that imaging alone can produce (such as dusty nearby galaxies or cool brown dwarfs). Though only one of 43 Hubble-selected candidates returned a clear spectroscopic detection in two nights at Keck, z8_GND_5296 is notable for an extreme star-formation rate—about 330 solar masses per year—unusual for its small, dwarf-like mass and potentially characteristic of early, gas-rich galaxies. The discovery sheds light on the epoch of reionization, when the first stars and galaxies ionized the primordial hydrogen fog. Researchers say pushing to even higher redshifts (z ~10) is feasible in principle but awaits more powerful facilities like the James Webb Space Telescope and next-generation extremely large telescopes.

President Obama’s likely selection of former Nebraska Sen. Chuck Hagel as secretary of defense has triggered a contentious reaction on Capitol Hill, drawing guarded support from some Democrats and sharp criticism from many Republicans. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell said Hagel should receive a “fair” confirmation hearing and that he will evaluate whether Hagel’s views align with the responsibilities of the job. McConnell, who once praised Hagel’s national security voice when Hagel left the Senate in 2009, declined to reaffirm that praise as Republicans highlight concerns about Hagel’s past remarks on Israel and Iran.

Republican opposition has been vocal and personal. Sen. Lindsey Graham labeled the potential nomination “in-your-face,” calling Hagel “out of the mainstream” and warning he would be “the most antagonistic secretary of defense toward the state of Israel in our nation’s history,” citing Hagel’s past comments on negotiations with Iran and Hamas and opposition to labeling Hezbollah as terrorists. Freshman Rep. Tom Cotton, an Iraq and Afghanistan veteran, said he would vote against confirmation, criticizing Hagel’s past statements on the Iraq surge and his positions on Iran, Hezbollah, Hamas and Israel. Sen. Ted Cruz accused the president of ignoring bipartisan criticisms and suggested the pick reflects political calculation.

Democrats defended Hagel’s credentials. Senate Majority Whip Dick Durbin called him a “serious candidate,” noting his Vietnam service and roles on the Foreign Relations and Intelligence committees. Overall, Hagel’s anticipated nomination promises a hard-fought confirmation battle focused on his foreign policy record, views on Israel and Iran, and qualifications to lead the Pentagon.

After the U.N. authorized a no-fly zone and "all necessary measures" against Libya, Col. Muammar Gadhafi’s government abruptly announced a cease-fire, prompting skepticism from rebels, military experts, and civilians. Rebel commander Khalifa Hifter and residents of Misrata reported continued bombardment, and activists say Gadhafi is concealing heavy weapons among civilian areas to use human shields and complicate Western strikes. Analysts call the cease-fire likely tactical brinksmanship aimed at delaying or undermining Western plans; some suggest internal government divisions or a distancing maneuver by Gadhafi. Britain and other allies moved warplanes and ships into position, and leaders vowed determination to enforce the resolution. Commentators remain conflicted about intervention: it could protect civilians and reinforce a new "Responsibility to Protect" norm and inspire regional uprisings, but failure or prolonged conflict risks civilian casualties, regional backlash, and a quagmire reminiscent of Iraq or Afghanistan. The outcome hinges on whether international action quickly collapses Gadhafi’s regime or spirals into a protracted, costly war.

The Academy Award nominations announced this morning stirred both praise and outrage. Big winners like Boyhood, Birdman and strong acting nods (Laura Dern, Edward Norton, Mark Ruffalo) largely reflected critical favorites, but notable omissions exposed deeper problems. Jennifer Aniston’s widely anticipated Cake nomination didn’t materialize — replaced by Marion Cotillard — illustrating the unpredictability and hype-driven nature of awards season. More troubling were snubs with cultural weight. The acclaimed Swedish film Force Majeure was left out of Best Foreign Language Film, a baffling omission many saw as short-sighted. Most consequentially, Selma received only Best Picture and Best Original Song nominations; Ava DuVernay was denied a Best Director nod, and David Oyelowo missed Best Actor. Given Selma’s critical and audience acclaim, its exclusion from directing, acting, screenplay, editing and cinematography categories feels like more than campaign mishap and has been interpreted as symptomatic of the Academy’s lack of diversity.

The director slate—Inárritu, Linklater, Miller, Anderson and Tyldum—consists solely of men, and the acting nominees skew white. The piece argues this outcome underscores systemic bias: Academy voters are overwhelmingly white and male, and despite efforts by president Cheryl Boone Isaacs to broaden representation, progress remains stalled. DuVernay’s omission is framed not only as an artistic injustice but as potentially harmful to her future opportunities in a Hollywood that still disadvantages women and people of color. The nominations raise urgent questions about whose stories and creators receive recognition and the real costs of institutional exclusion.

The mayor of Kharkiv, Hennadiy (Gennady) Kernes, was critically wounded in an apparent assassination attempt on Monday when an unknown gunman shot him in the back while he was jogging. Kernes underwent a two-hour operation for severe chest and abdominal wounds; hospital officials said organs were damaged, bleeding was stopped, and he remained in intensive care in a life-threatening condition. Kernes, a wealthy former Yanukovych supporter turned pro-unity politician described as a "mini-oligarch," has faced accusations from rivals about criminal origins, which he has denied.

The attack came amid escalating unrest in eastern Ukraine, where pro-Russian separatists continue to seize administrative buildings and detain opponents. On Monday gunmen in unmarked uniforms occupied the local government building and reportedly the police station in Kostyantynivka, raising the flag of the self-proclaimed Donetsk Republic; the town lies near Sloviansk and Donetsk, both under separatist control. Clashes and tensions have persisted in Kharkiv as well, where pro-Ukrainian and pro-Russian demonstrators recently scuffled, leaving several injured.

Separatists are also holding Western observers from the OSCE—initially eight, one released for medical reasons—with captives paraded before media by masked militants claiming they were spies. Kyiv and Western governments accuse Moscow of supporting the insurgency; Russia denies involvement.

In response, the United States expanded sanctions, targeting seven additional Russian officials (including two linked to Putin’s inner circle) and 17 companies with asset freezes and visa bans, and signaled more measures to deter alleged Russian aggression. EU ambassadors met to consider further sanctions; Western leaders framed measures as aimed at altering Kremlin calculations rather than personally targeting President Putin.

Ugandan army officials and U.N. sources say Joseph Kony’s naming of his 22-year-old son, Salim Saleh, as deputy and field commander of the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA) may signal a weakening of the long-running guerrilla group. Uganda’s top general, Sam Kavuma, told reporters that the appointment reflects Kony’s diminished control: many senior commanders have been killed or gone into disarray, fighters are split into autonomous gangs, and defectors identify Salim as the most influential figure after his father. Salim, reportedly raised in the bush with the LRA and named after a relative of President Yoweri Museveni, previously handled Kony’s personal security. Despite setbacks, the LRA continues to evade capture and conduct attacks across remote border regions of the Central African Republic (CAR), South Sudan, Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo, with several hundred fighters estimated to remain. U.N. officials, including Abou Moussa, say African-led military efforts and rebel defections have greatly reduced killings, abductions and displacement, though they warn against complacency until Kony is removed. A recent U.N. report suggests Kony and other leaders may have sought refuge in Sudan’s Kafia Kingi area; Sudan denies harboring them. The Security Council praised progress and urged continued action until the LRA no longer threatens civilians.

The ACLU of Michigan alleges Detroit police have been forcibly removing homeless people from the Greektown entertainment district, stuffing them into vans and abandoning them miles away—sometimes outside city limits—and filed a complaint with the U.S. Justice Department after a yearlong investigation. The ACLU calls the practice “inhumane, callous and illegal,” saying officers harass people for their appearance, confiscate any money, and drop them in unfamiliar, potentially dangerous neighborhoods with no safe way home. Several detailed accounts of victims were included: Andrew Sheehan says he was taken at least four times and once left eight miles away at the Detroit–River Rouge boundary; Dennis B. reports multiple removals and being left on Detroit’s east side; Charles E., who suffers seizures and leg ulcers, was driven to Southwest Detroit and walked two hours back; Elvin D. was told he’d be taken to a warming center but was dropped off in Dearborn; and Marvin S. was allegedly taken 14 miles to Allen Park and told to get out. A warming center alerted the ACLU to the issue, and outreach workers note many victims then walk long distances to shelters or churches for help. Detroit Police Chief Chester Logan said he will review the complaint before commenting. The ACLU demands the city stop the practice and treat homeless people with dignity.

The Supreme Court on Monday declined Virginia Attorney General Ken Cuccinelli’s request to fast-track review of President Obama’s health care law, sending challenges back through the usual federal appeals process. Cuccinelli, a leading opponent, sought immediate Supreme Court review to end what he called “crippling and costly uncertainty,” but the Obama administration opposed the plea. The court’s rare intervention is typically reserved for wartime or constitutional crises; instead hearings are already scheduled in three federal appeals courts in May and June. The matter could still reach the high court in time for a decision by early summer 2012. To date five district judges have ruled: two Republican appointees (Florida and Virginia) struck down the law in whole or part, while three Democratic appointees (Michigan, Virginia, D.C.) upheld it. Major provisions are already being implemented, including Medicare payment changes and allowing children up to 26 on parents’ policies. The one-sentence order showed no indication any justice, including Elena Kagan, recused herself.

Mischa Barton has sued her mother and one-time manager, Nuala Barton, accusing her of long-running financial exploitation, fraud and manipulation. Filed in Los Angeles Superior Court, the complaint brands Nuala a “greedy stage mother posing as a talent manager” who controlled Mischa’s finances, misrepresented earnings, and used her daughter’s name and assets for personal profit. Mischa alleges Nuala lied about the actress’s pay on the film The Hoarder, forged her signature, pocketed the difference and collected a 10% management fee; she also claims Nuala entered her into endorsement deals and launched a Mischa Barton handbag line and a London boutique without giving Mischa any of the proceeds. 

The suit asserts Nuala created business entities that gave her exclusive financial control, doled out allowances sporadically, and induced Mischa to buy a $7.8 million Beverly Hills house in 2006—structuring the purchase so Nuala obtained half-ownership, then borrowing against the property and effectively barring Mischa from the home while Nuala and Mischa’s father live there. Mischa contends neither parent has worked outside her career in over a decade and accuses them of relying on her earnings to support their lifestyle. 

Seeking unspecified actual damages, treble punitive damages and legal fees—documents put the amount in controversy above $25 million—the five-count complaint includes breach of fiduciary duty, breach of oral contract and conversion. Mischa is now represented by APA and LINK for management and by Venable LLP lawyers Alex Weingarten and Leslie Eggers in the lawsuit. Nuala’s attorney has declined to comment, saying they had not yet received the complaint.

A new Global Slavery Index by Walk Free estimates about 29.8 million people are enslaved worldwide, a figure higher than previous estimates and covering 162 countries. Slavery takes many forms—bonded labour in quarries and kilns, debt bondage, forced marriage, sexual exploitation, child abduction for war, unpaid work on fishing boats, and hereditary “chattel” slavery. Nearly half of the victims are in India (about 13.9 million), followed by China (2.9 million), Pakistan (2.1 million), Nigeria, Ethiopia, Russia, Thailand, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Myanmar and Bangladesh. When measured per capita, Mauritania has the highest prevalence—around 4 percent of its population—where chattel slavery persists across generations, followed by Haiti with widespread child domestic exploitation (“restavek”), then Pakistan, India, Nepal and several West African and Eastern European countries. Even wealthy nations show higher-than-expected numbers of slaves, with researchers estimating six to ten times more victims than official case counts suggest. Walk Free says the index provides a crucial baseline to measure progress and guide policy, stressing that better measurement is essential to combat modern slavery effectively.

A historic warmth sweep across Southeast Alaska on Thursday shattered a century-old March temperature record. Klawock, on Prince of Wales Island northwest of Ketchikan, reached 71°F, surpassing the previous statewide March high of 69°F set in Ketchikan in 1915. The National Weather Service noted it as the warmest official March temperature recorded in Alaska. Other Southeast communities also logged new daily March 31 highs: Ketchikan hit 65°F, Sitka, Juneau, Yakutat (57°F) and others recorded unusually high readings for late March. This extreme warmth follows a trend: March 2016 produced the warmest monthly average temperatures on record for multiple Southeast locales, including Juneau, Sitka, Klawock, Haines, Petersburg, Skagway and Ketchikan. The Weather Service tweeted the preliminary Klawock measurement and its significance relative to the 1915 record. The event underscores an ongoing pattern of anomalously warm conditions in the region during that period. (Separately, Alexa Internet has been donating web crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996; those crawls are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo.)

Two days after Bernie Sanders’ decisive New Hampshire victory, he and Hillary Clinton met in the sixth Democratic primary debate in Milwaukee. Overall the evening reinforced Clinton’s steadiness and raised questions about Sanders’ ability to broaden his appeal and manage delicate political terrain.

Hillary Clinton delivered arguably her best debate performance of the campaign. Calm and in control, she spent the first half hour puncturing Sanders’ health-care plan and depicting him as an idealist whose proposals would be difficult to enact. She effectively tied Sanders to a pattern of criticism of President Obama, portraying herself as protective of the administration’s legacy — a move calculated to reassure black voters who remain strongly attached to Obama. Clinton avoided many of the debate’s potentially damaging topics (paid speeches, State Department inquiries), and when pressed about heavy contributions to her super PAC she stumbled briefly but recovered. Her composed responses, especially on why many young New Hampshire women didn’t support her, helped neutralize prior missteps by her surrogates.

Bernie Sanders struggled to expand his appeal beyond his base. Although he showed improved foreign policy knowledge, he faltered on domestic issues — his supposed strength — often defaulting to familiar attacks on millionaires, billionaires, and Wall Street. A notable gaffe occurred when he asserted he’d handle race relations better than President Obama; the comment played poorly and left him vulnerable to Clinton’s attacks framing his critiques of Obama as disloyal. Sanders’ frequent animated reactions and occasional petty one-liners undercut his credibility at moments.

The debate elevated issues championed by Black Lives Matter, with both candidates addressing police violence and systemic racism more directly than in past cycles. Barack Obama emerged politically advantaged as Clinton defended his record and used his achievements as a shield against Sanders’ critiques. Wall Street figures and Democratic-friendly financiers fared poorly politically; both candidates attacked financial-sector excesses, leaving many donors uneasy. In a memorable foreign policy exchange Sanders emphatically repudiated Henry Kissinger, scoring a rhetorical win that resonated with younger voters.

In sum, the debate solidified Clinton’s image as the steady, electable front-runner while underscoring Sanders’ challenges persuading broader Democratic constituencies and navigating politically sensitive comparisons to a popular president.

Rupert Murdoch’s News Corp has agreed to sell a controlling stake in three Chinese TV channels and the Fortune Star film library to China Media Capital (CMC), a state-backed private equity fund, marking a decisive retreat from efforts to build a broadcasting business in China. The assets—Xing Kong, Xing Kong International, Channel [V] Mainland China and 757 Chinese-language films—are jointly valued at about $300m, with the deal estimated near $160m; News Corp will reportedly retain close to 50 percent. The move reflects regulatory and commercial realities in China, where authorities tightly control media while promoting select groups to project Chinese content abroad. CMC gains overseas distribution access; News Corp frames the deal as an opportunity to grow the venture with local partners.

Republican momentum continued in recent elections, with gains in both the House and Senate and the survival of a high-profile Republican governor in Wisconsin. Gov. Scott Walker, a potential 2016 presidential contender who drew intense Democratic opposition after pushing through laws that weakened public-sector unions, remained in office despite being a major target; he had previously survived a recall effort two years earlier. The GOP’s strengthening position was evident in notable House pickups, where Republicans unseated several veteran Democrats. In West Virginia, former Democrat-turned-Republican Evan Jenkins defeated 19-term incumbent Nick Rahall, one of the last white Democrats to retain a seat in the increasingly Republican South. In Georgia, Republican Rick Allen beat five-term Rep. John Barrow, another Southern Democrat who had withstood GOP dominance for years. These results reflect a broader trend of Republican advances that are moving the party closer to a Senate majority while expanding its already substantial House advantage. The shifting political landscape highlights continued partisan realignment in Southern districts and reinforces the GOP’s electoral strength ahead of future contests.

Hillary Clinton was speaking at the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries convention in Las Vegas when a woman with platinum-blond hair rushed past security, threw a sandal and scattered papers toward the stage, then walked briskly to the exit. Clinton dodged a projectile near her head, joked about initially thinking it was a bat and quipped about not having played softball, then smoothly continued her keynote to applause. The protester, who was not credentialed and was escorted out by hotel security and the Secret Service, reportedly also dropped a document. Clinton discussed recycling’s economic and environmental benefits, international trade, Syria and Russia’s actions in Crimea, urged tougher trade enforcement, criticized political polarization, and took audience questions. The rest of the event proceeded without incident.

A 62-year-old Federal Protective Service employee, Eulalio “Leo” Tordil, was arrested Friday in Aspen Hill, Maryland, after a day of shootings that left three people dead and three wounded across Prince George’s and Montgomery counties. Authorities allege Tordil fatally shot his estranged wife, Gladys Tordil, outside High Point High School in Beltsville on Thursday; a man who tried to intervene was also shot. A protective order had been issued against Tordil in March, and his employer had removed his duty weapon and placed him on administrative duties.

On Friday morning, Tordil is accused of shooting a man to death and wounding two others in the Westfield Montgomery Mall parking lot in Bethesda; police believe two victims were shot while coming to the aid of the first. About 11:50 a.m., a woman was found fatally shot in her car outside a Giant grocery store in Aspen Hill. Investigators worked to determine whether the three incidents were connected; by late afternoon officials said Tordil was the alleged gunman in all three.

Plainclothes officers tracked Tordil’s silver 2015 Hyundai Elantra and surveilled him for about an hour as he visited stores and ate at Boston Market. Officers rammed and boxed in his vehicle in a shopping center parking lot; Tordil surrendered without incident and a weapon was recovered. Prince George’s County charged him with first-degree murder and related counts in his wife’s killing; Montgomery County investigations and potential charges were pending. Shelter-in-place orders for schools were lifted after the arrest.

China’s National Space Administration has released hundreds of high-definition photos, videos and data from its 2013 Chang’e‑3 mission, including stunning images of the lunar surface taken by the Yutu (“Jade Rabbit”) rover and lander. Yutu, which landed December 14, 2013, suffered mobility and power problems and stopped moving January 25, yet continued transmitting until October of the following year. The release is a rare display of openness.

A strong solar flare and associated coronal mass ejection (CME) from a sunspot in mid‑July 2017 produced a geomagnetic storm that made the Northern Lights visible across much of Canada and into the northern United States. The flare, an M‑class event, emitted X‑rays that caused a minor radio blackout over parts of Asia and hurled a cloud of charged particles into space. While most of the CME missed Earth, part of the expanding cloud swept past the planet, interacting with Earth’s magnetic field and funneling particles into the upper atmosphere near the poles to create auroras.

NOAA’s Space Weather Prediction Center issued a geomagnetic storm watch and recorded G2 (moderate) storm conditions by mid‑morning; levels were forecast to dip to G1 (minor) early evening then return to G2 between about 8 p.m. and 2 a.m. EDT, with a possibility of brief G3 (strong) spikes. As a result, auroras were expected across most of Canada and as far south as parts of the northern U.S., including Montana, the Dakotas, Minnesota, Wisconsin, northern Illinois, Michigan, northern New York and New England — reaching cities such as Minneapolis, Chicago, Detroit, Buffalo, Syracuse, Albany and Boston. Visibility depends on clear, dark skies away from light pollution; viewers were advised to let their eyes adjust for 30–40 minutes and avoid bright lights for best viewing.

During a GOP debate, Brian Williams asked Governor Rick Perry—without naming Cameron Todd Willingham or citing the scientific evidence that undermined the arson case—whether he’d ever worried that someone executed might be innocent. Perry evaded, praising Texas’s capital-punishment process and asserting that those who commit heinous crimes will “face the ultimate justice.” The article contrasts that exchange with two related stories: the long-overdue release of Anthony Graves, who spent 18 years on Texas’s death row before a prosecutor dismissed charges and called him innocent after investigation; and the harrowing 1991 house fire that killed Cameron Todd Willingham’s three children. Willingham’s desperate actions at the blaze and the immediate community response are recounted in vivid detail, followed by the arrival of fire investigators Douglas Fogg and Manuel Vasquez—experienced arson specialists whose confidence in reading fires shaped the original finding of arson. The piece highlights the stakes of prosecutorial and forensic error in death-penalty cases and implies a troubling disconnect between political rhetoric and scientific scrutiny.

At the Oakland premiere of Moneyball, Brad Pitt sought to clarify remarks from a recent Parade interview that many read as a criticism of his ex-wife Jennifer Aniston. He said his comments were misinterpreted and that people “read things into it that just weren't there.” Pitt emphasized to Matt Lauer on TODAY that his intent was to praise Aniston as a good mother to their children and that his remarks had “no reference to the past.” He added it was unfortunate that a kind comment about Angelina Jolie drew Aniston into controversy; he called Aniston “a dear friend” and said he didn’t want negative things said about her. Pitt noted Aniston did not contact him after the Parade quotes appeared.

The wider media reaction included gossip and backlash: reports claimed Aniston’s team “went ballistic,” confronting Pitt’s camp and prompting a quick apology/clarification. Tabloid sources suggested jealousy—specifically that Pitt resented Aniston’s happiness with Justin Theroux—though such motives are speculative. Some commenters called Pitt’s follow-up statements disingenuous; others framed the row as routine Hollywood PR maneuvering. Despite the controversy, Pitt remained focused on Moneyball, describing his immersion in the Oakland baseball world as a privilege and deflecting premature Oscar talk. He also shared a light personal anecdote about his son Maddox’s enthusiasm for baseball. Overall, Pitt attempted to tamp down the feud narrative, reiterating respect for Aniston while promoting his new film.

Israeli police arrested a woman after CCTV showed her allegedly igniting a fuel pump at a Jerusalem gas station following a request for a cigarette that was refused. The incident occurred at the Paz station on Derech Bethlehem. Footage reportedly captures the woman approaching a man who was filling his car, briefly speaking with him, then leaving and returning near the pump. She is accused of producing a lighter and setting the pump handle alight; the blaze quickly spread to the vehicle. The car owner reacted by pulling the burning pump away, which spread the fire further, and fled the scene. His brother, who had been inside the vehicle, was unharmed. Station staff extinguished the flames, and police detained the suspect shortly afterward. She denies the allegations. Authorities have extended her arrest by five days and ordered psychological evaluations as part of the investigation. A police spokesman confirmed the sequence of events and that workers quelled the fire, while the probe continues.

Rainbow Loom bracelets have become a nationwide elementary-school craze—colorful rubber-band bracelets woven on small plastic looms—that’s so popular it’s disrupting some classrooms and sparking bans. Two New York City public schools recently moved to restrict them: P.S. 87 on the Upper West Side prohibited bracelets and kits after administrators said they were causing conflicts and distractions, while Park Slope’s P.S. 107 allowed students to wear finished bracelets but banned looms and related paraphernalia because kids were arriving with bags and tackle boxes full of bands. Parents are divided. Some criticize the bans as overreactions that stifle a cheap, creative, collaborative outlet and even welcome the toy’s cross-gender appeal—boys and girls equally enjoy making complex patterns, building pride and community. Others applaud schools for curbing disruptions, addressing equity issues between children who have kits and those who don’t, and limiting obsessive in-class use. Teachers and principals cited interference with instruction and safety concerns (teachers at one school limited students to one bracelet after children wore many up their arms). The Rainbow Loom phenomenon, invented by Michigan father Cheong‑Choon Ng and popularized via YouTube tutorials, has led to shortages and a booming DIY culture. Observers note the craze may signal a shift in gendered toy preferences, since boys enthusiastically join a traditionally “feminine” crafting activity.

Sébastien Bras, 46, chef of the three-Michelin-starred Le Suquet in Laguiole, central France, has formally asked the Michelin Guide to remove his restaurant from its next edition, citing the relentless pressure that accompanies the accolade. Le Suquet, set on the Aubrac plateau and famed for vegetable-led dishes such as the Gargouillou, has held three stars since 1999. Bras—who took over the family restaurant from his father, Michel Bras, a figure central to modern French cuisine—announced his request in a Facebook video saying he wants “to give a new meaning to my life” and “redefine what is essential.” He said he hopes to cook with “a free spirit and in serenity,” no longer living under the constant possibility that anonymous Michelin inspectors could be dining any night and that any service might be judged.

Bras acknowledged he may lose fame but said he accepts that trade-off to escape the daily tension of maintaining a three-star standard. He also referenced the 2003 suicide of chef Bernard Loiseau—often linked to fears of losing a star—as a reminder of the toll Michelin pressure can take, though he said he was “not in that kind of headspace.” AFP reported Michel Bras supports his son’s decision.

Michelin said this was an unprecedented type of request in France—chefs have previously exited the guide only by changing their restaurant concept or closing—and that the guide is intended for customers, not restaurateurs. Claire Dorland-Clauzel of Michelin’s executive committee said they noted and respected the request but that removal would not be automatic and must be considered; in Michelin’s view, the scrutiny that causes stress is also part of what drives culinary excellence. The move echoes past high-profile departures from star culture—such as Alain Senderens returning stars in 2005 and Olivier Roellinger closing his restaurant—as some chefs seek quieter, less pressured professional lives.

Login credentials for as many as 117 million LinkedIn accounts have surfaced for sale online, reportedly tied to LinkedIn’s 2012 breach. A seller using the handle “peace_of_mind” (or “Peace”) listed a dataset of 167 million accounts for about five bitcoins (~$2,200) on a dark-web marketplace, The Real Deal. Researcher Troy Hunt and the paid breach index LeakedSource examined samples and say roughly 117 million records include both email addresses and passwords hashed with unsalted SHA-1. Unsalted SHA-1 is weak; LeakedSource claims to have cracked about 90% of the passwords within 72 hours. Many recovered passwords are trivially weak or reused—examples include “123456,” “linkedin,” and “password”—highlighting poor user practices and insufficient enforcement of strong passwords. The newly revealed scope suggests the 2012 theft was far larger than the ~6.5 million hashes publicly known then; LinkedIn now confirms the additional data stems from that incident and says it’s invalidating affected passwords and contacting impacted members to reset them. LinkedIn also emphasizes that it has since adopted salted hashing, email challenges, and two-factor authentication. Security experts urge anyone who had a LinkedIn account in 2012—or who reused old passwords on other sites—to change passwords immediately and enable two-step verification to reduce risk.

The Obama administration is expected to include in next month’s budget a yet-undetermined fee on big banks aimed at recouping taxpayer costs from the financial bailout. Officials prefer a levy that can’t be easily passed to customers and would avoid a transaction tax or targeting compensation directly. Options include fees on liabilities or profits; details and who would be covered remain unsettled. The move seeks to soothe public anger over bank bonuses and help repay TARP losses while discouraging risky behavior.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, 85, said she hopes to remain on the Court until at least age 90, noting her senior colleague John Paul Stevens stepped down at 90. Speaking in New York after seeing The Originalist, a play about the late Justice Antonin Scalia, Ginsburg noted she has already hired clerks for at least two more terms. She praised the dynamic she shared with Scalia — likening their exchanges to a “ping-pong game” and saying that writing against him sharpened her arguments. Her appearance came amid heightened attention on the Court after Justice Anthony Kennedy’s retirement and President Trump’s nomination of Brett Kavanaugh, developments seen as threatening long-standing liberal precedents such as Roe v. Wade.

Ginsburg reflected on American politics and institutions, invoking her late spouse’s metaphor of the pendulum to suggest political swings will reverse. She discussed key cases she views as pivotal, naming Obergefell v. Hodges on same-sex marriage, and noted her 2013 dissent criticizing the gutting of the Voting Rights Act helped elevate her as a liberal icon. A self-described “flaming feminist,” Ginsburg also spoke about facing discrimination as a Jewish woman, recounted influences such as conductor Dean Dixon who introduced her to opera, and emphasized that courts follow social change rather than lead it.

A controversy erupted after American hunting show host Larysa Switlyk posted photos from a hunting trip on Islay, Scotland, showing herself and companions posing with dead wild goats. The images sparked widespread social media outrage, with critics calling them “disgraceful” and “sickening” and tagging Scottish officials. First Minister Nicola Sturgeon and Environment Secretary Roseanna Cunningham acknowledged public upset; Sturgeon said the government would review the situation and consider whether legal changes are needed. Cunningham likewise said she would examine the laws.

Defenders of the hunt argued it was legitimate wildlife management: wild goats on Islay lack natural predators and estates offer controlled hunting—like deer culls—to manage herd sizes, prevent overgrazing, and protect the environment. Supporters framed hunting as population control and a traditional rural activity, and some noted country sports tourism contributes significantly to Scotland’s economy—about £155 million annually, per a 2015 industry report.

The episode fed into broader global debates over trophy hunting. High-profile incidents, such as the killing of Cecil the lion in Zimbabwe and subsequent hunts of related animals, have provoked international condemnation and scrutiny of paid big-game hunting. Images of hunters with animal carcasses have led to resignations and public backlash elsewhere, while proponents defend hunting as skilled, bonding, and sometimes conservation-minded. Critics counter that trophy display is anachronistic, morally troubling and potentially harmful to wildlife and ecosystems.

Switlyk responded defiantly on social media, saying she was heading to another hunt and urging critics to “get educated” about hunting and conservation. Her posts, and ensuing threats and counter-arguments, underscored the cultural clash over hunting’s role in modern conservation and tourism policy.

Robin DiMaggio, a 47-year-old professional drummer and former music director for United Nations events and Arsenio Hall’s late-night show, has been charged with felony wire fraud for allegedly stealing $750,000 intended for a charity concert benefiting homeless and displaced children. Prosecutors say DiMaggio told the Bulgaria-based Peace for You Peace for Me Foundation he could secure top artists for a benefit in Sofia and promised the sponsor’s August 2016 wire transfer would be placed into escrow to guarantee future artist payments. Instead, the complaint alleges, DiMaggio deposited the funds into his personal bank account and spent them on cars, credit-card debt, living expenses and other personal uses. Within weeks, prosecutors claim he used $251,370 of the money to buy a Calabasas home for his ex-wife and wired $150,000 to an account for his company, DiMagic Entertainment, Inc. None of the funds were paid to artists or their management for the concert, according to the complaint.

When the sponsor sought the return of the money, DiMaggio allegedly claimed he had already forwarded deposits to artists and later asserted that a third party had used his email to contact the foundation and withdraw funds. The sponsor sued DiMaggio in December 2016; he subsequently filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. A bankruptcy court awarded the sponsor about $1.2 million, though that judgment had not been fully entered in recent filings. DiMaggio was arrested and released on bond with a tracking device; the FBI investigated the case. If convicted of wire fraud, he faces up to 20 years in federal prison. DiMaggio’s long career includes performances with Paul Simon, David Bowie, Dr. Dre, Diana Ross and others.

Andrew Gillum, the progressive mayor of Tallahassee, won the Florida Democratic gubernatorial primary in an upset, becoming the party’s nominee and potentially the state’s first Black governor. Endorsed by Bernie Sanders and buoyed by liberal outside groups, Gillum outpaced better-funded rivals, including Gwen Graham, despite raising the least campaign money and facing questions tied to an FBI probe of Tallahassee city government. He will face Republican Rep. Ron DeSantis, who easily won the GOP primary after securing President Trump’s high-profile endorsement. DeSantis credited Trump for raising his profile and relied on pro-Trump appeals to defeat establishment favorite Adam Putnam. Their November matchup turns Florida into a major battleground with implications for the 2020 presidential map. Other notable outcomes included Gov. Rick Scott winning the GOP Senate primary and competitive House contests in Florida and Arizona shaped by John McCain’s recent death.

Relatives of California Highway Patrol Officer Mark Saylor have sued Toyota, several U.S. Toyota entities and the El Cajon dealership, alleging product liability and negligence after a 2009 Lexus ES350 loaned to Saylor unexpectedly accelerated on Aug. 28, killing Saylor, his wife Cleofe, their daughter Mahala and Cleofe’s brother Chris Lastrella. The complaint, filed in San Diego Superior Court by family members, seeks unspecified damages and faulting the vehicle and dealership for a crash investigators linked to a wrongly sized floor mat that trapped the accelerator. The wreck, which reached more than 120 mph before crashing and bursting into flames, prompted Toyota’s massive recalls to replace floor mats and later fix sticking gas pedals. Family members, including Fe Lastrella, testified before Congress; Toyota declined to comment on pending litigation.

Egypt erupted in violent confrontations as protesters clashed with police and military forces in Tahrir Square and other cities, marking the most serious challenge to the ruling Supreme Council of the Armed Forces since Hosni Mubarak’s ouster. Demonstrations, driven by anger at the military’s refusal to hand power to civilians and at stalled revolutionary promises, left dozens dead (reports varied from 24 to 33) and over a thousand wounded. Security forces used batons, birdshot, tear gas and armored vehicles; protesters hurled stones and reclaimed the square after troops briefly pushed them out. The unrest was sparked by attempts to expand the military’s constitutional role and by the broader frustration over delays in civilian rule, continuing martial law, military trials of civilians and economic decline. Political groups are divided: Islamists like the Muslim Brotherhood criticized the crackdown but largely did not lead the protests, while secular activists and unaffiliated citizens filled the streets. The military pressed ahead with parliamentary elections beginning Nov. 28, despite calls for delay and international appeals for restraint. With the council retaining significant power until a future presidential vote, analysts warn prolonged turmoil, economic deterioration and further protests are likely.

The writer mocks hipster culture by describing a pretend dog with Radiohead taste, American Apparel sweatshirts and ironic Olive Garden eating. They highlight viral sites like Hipster Puppies and Hipster Kitty, which mash cute animals with hipster stereotypes for comedy, likening their rapid spread to other internet fads. Featuring characters like Clara and Bailey, the piece argues simple mashups of beloved trends can create wildly popular blogs.

A single ticket matching the Powerball numbers 6-7-16-23-26 and Powerball 4 won the $758.7 million jackpot, the largest grand prize ever claimed by a single lottery ticket in U.S. history. The winning ticket was sold at the Pride Station & Store in Chicopee, Massachusetts; the store will receive a $50,000 retailer bonus. The winner, identified as 53-year-old Mavis Wanczyk of Chicopee, came forward within hours, claimed the prize at lottery headquarters in Braintree, and said she plans to retire and keep a low profile. Wanczyk, a longtime Mercy Medical Center employee and mother of two, said she discovered the win after comparing numbers with a coworker and described feeling shocked and emotional. The cash option would be substantially lower than the annuity, and taxes would further reduce the payout. Massachusetts Lottery officials initially misreported that the jackpot ticket was sold in Watertown—where a separate $1 million prize ticket was sold—but corrected the error, attributing it to human transcription mistakes during late-night processing. In addition to the grand prize, six tickets won $2 million each and 34 others won $1 million, with Powerball played across 44 states plus D.C., Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

In Portage, Michigan, Democratic state House candidate Rev. John Fisher accused the Michigan Republican Party of crossing an ethical line after GOP-paid campaign mailers this week instructed voters to call him at a phone number that connects directly to his 91-year-old mother’s room at Tendercare Portage. The mailers urged recipients to “Tell him hard-working Michiganders are being hurt by Obamacare,” and listed a number registered to Fisher that, in fact, rings Isabel Kramb’s hospice room, where she is receiving care for congestive heart failure. Fisher’s campaign manager, David Topping, said the family had no problem with earlier mailers that listed Fisher’s personal number, but directing calls to a frail, dying parent is “beyond the pale.” Fisher condemned the tactic as contemptuous of personal privacy and seniors, urging voters to question what the Republican Party stands for ahead of the Nov. 4 election. GOP candidate Brandt Iden, who faces Fisher and Libertarian Michael Stampfler for the 61st House District seat, said the mailer was not produced by his campaign and that he does not condone negative tactics; he did not immediately comment further. The Michigan Republican Party later issued a statement accepting responsibility and apologizing for distress caused, saying it did not intend for calls to reach Fisher’s mother and that it obtained the number from an online directory where it was listed under Fisher’s name. Local news coverage shows multiple callers reached Kramb, who told some she was his mother and that he was not there. Fisher criticized the maneuver as unconscionable and has asked Iden to denounce the state party’s action.

An international team of researchers has traced the origin of the HIV/AIDS pandemic to Kinshasa (then Léopoldville) in the 1920s, using extensive genetic sequencing and historical data to reconstruct the virus’s family tree. By analysing archived HIV genomes and mapping mutational “footprints,” scientists pinpointed HIV-1 group M—the single cross-species jump that became pandemic—as arising and expanding from Kinshasa. Although other simian-to-human transmissions occurred (producing strains such as group O), only group M achieved global spread.

The study links the virus’s emergence to a “perfect storm” of social and infrastructural factors in early 20th-century Belgian Congo: rapid urban population growth, a male-skewed labour influx that fuelled an expanded sex trade, and widespread movement of people via railways and rivers. Colonial transport networks funneled about a million passengers annually through Kinshasa by the 1940s, enabling the virus to reach cities and mining regions—Kisangani, Mbuji-Mayi and Lubumbashi—between the late 1930s and early 1950s. Public health practices, particularly injections with unsterilised needles during campaigns against other diseases, likely amplified transmission. These conditions, persisting for a few decades, allowed the virus to go from confined groups to a generalized epidemic that later spread internationally.

Researchers emphasize that genetics offers the only reliable window into pre-recognition spread; while causality can’t be proven definitively, the timing and location are robustly supported. Experts describe the findings as a compelling and plausible explanation for why one simian-derived virus became a global pandemic—highlighting travel, demographic change, unsafe healthcare interventions and prostitution as key enabling factors.

Reports of forcible sexual assaults on U.S. college campuses rose sharply over the last decade, with Department of Education and NPR analyses finding increases around 49–52% between the early 2000s and 2011–2012. Advocates and officials say the rise partly reflects improved reporting and greater student willingness to come forward after heightened education, activism, and new federal guidance, not necessarily a surge in assaults themselves. Universities like Michigan, which expanded prevention training, bystander education, and revamped investigative practices, saw large jumps in reported cases as students felt safer reporting. High-profile controversies and student pressure have pushed schools to hire investigators and adopt new policies. Federal rules such as the Campus SaVE Act now require more prevention education and stronger responses to campus sexual assault.

An agency nurse accidentally switched off the ventilator of 37-year-old tetraplegic Jamie Merrett at his Wiltshire home in January 2009, leaving him with serious brain damage, footage showed. Merrett—paralysed from the neck down after a 2002 road accident but able to speak, use a wheelchair and operate a voice-activated computer—had installed a bedside camera because he was concerned about the care he was receiving. The recording captured Violetta Aylward turning off the life-support machine; paramedics restarted it after 21 minutes, by which time Merrett had suffered severe brain injury and his cognitive ability reportedly regressed to that of a young child. A leaked Wiltshire social services report concluded the supplying agency, Ambition 24hours, knew it should provide staff trained in ventilator use but lacked adequate systems to check training. The agency is under internal investigation; Aylward has been suspended and is subject to a Nursing and Midwifery Council probe. NHS Wiltshire PCT said it has implemented actions to prevent recurrence; legal action is being considered.

North Korea’s state media announced that Kim Jong Un has assumed “supreme commandership” of the military, after power was reportedly transferred on October 8 at the behest of his late father, Kim Jong Il. The National Defense Commission emphasized that leadership change would not alter Pyongyang’s policies, warning South Korea’s government and “foolish politicians around the world” not to expect any change. The commission angrily criticized Seoul for allowing only select private delegations to visit Pyongyang to mourn Kim Jong Il and for permitting anti-North leaflets near the border, accusing South Korea of creating a “war-like atmosphere” and threatening retaliatory revenge. South Korea’s Unification Ministry expressed regret but reiterated its commitment to easing tensions and dialogue. Regional concern prompted the U.S. to send Assistant Secretary Kurt Campbell to China, South Korea and Japan in early January to discuss developments related to North Korea. The transfer of power and Kim Jong Un’s elevation—despite his inexperience—have left neighbors wary about future relations, denuclearization talks and stability on the Korean peninsula.

Sam’s Club, Walmart’s membership warehouse chain, will close 63 U.S. clubs (plus three in Puerto Rico) as part of a real-estate “right-sizing” to better align locations with growth and strategy, CEO John Furner said in a companywide email. Furner noted some clubs cannibalized others or were built where population growth fell short of expectations. Walmart expects a charge of $0.14 per share related to the closures, primarily hitting fourth-quarter results, and will provide further details with its Feb. 20 earnings release. Furner said the company will try to reassign as many affected associates as possible to nearby roles and provide support and severance where eligible. Analysts expect Sam’s Club to intensify efforts on faster delivery, e-commerce expansion, stronger grocery assortments, private-label marketing and recruiting new members—targeting households with $75,000–$125,000 annual income. Cowen analyst Oliver Chen described the move as preparing for “the next generation of retail warfare,” noting Sam’s Club has underperformed peers like Costco, BJ’s and Boxed despite recent improvements. The announcement includes a detailed list of affected store addresses across numerous states, with Illinois losing six locations and Alaska three, among other statewide impacts.

For more than half a century, Yellville, Arkansas, has staged an annual Turkey Trot festival famous for its controversial “turkey drop,” in which domestic turkeys are released from small planes roughly 500 feet above fields and sometimes thrown from the courthouse roof. Organizers say the drop is a longstanding local tradition tied to the region’s turkey industry; participants chase and claim the birds on landing. Animal welfare groups and rescuers have long condemned the practice. Reports from recent years say that out of a dozen birds dropped in 2016, two died on impact; others were injured and later rescued by groups such as Farm Sanctuary and rehomed to sanctuaries and private farms.

Scientists explain why domesticated turkeys fare poorly when dropped: selective breeding has produced heavy bodies and relatively small wing area, so while turkeys can generate brief bursts of powerful wing flapping (fast-twitch muscle) they lack sustained lift or effective gliding ability. Wild turkeys can fly short distances—enough to roost in trees—but domestic breeds typically cannot. Experts call the drops unethical and dangerous for the animals.

The Federal Aviation Administration investigated after media and activist attention but found no regulatory violations, noting that FAA rules do not explicitly ban dropping live animals from aircraft, though the agency does not endorse the practice. The turkey drop continues to spark debate about tradition versus animal welfare, drawing activists, rescuers, and national scrutiny.

Technology’s benefits are widely touted, yet a deep digital divide leaves millions of Americans—especially seniors—without reliable access. Over 25 percent of Americans lack Internet access; more than half of those over 65 are offline and nearly half don’t own a computer. Despite this, federal agencies have been rapidly phasing out paper-based services—mailing of benefit checks, annual Social Security earnings statements, savings bonds, prescription inserts and other paperwork—pushing recipients to use direct deposit, electronic debit cards, or online portals. These moves disproportionately affect seniors, low-income, disabled and poorly educated Americans who may lack bank accounts, be uncomfortable with electronic systems, or fear privacy and cybersecurity risks. Critics argue the shift disenfranchises vulnerable populations and lacks sufficient congressional oversight.

A major force opposing the government’s paperless push is Consumers for Paper Options, a lobbying group formed and funded by the paper industry (including the Envelope Manufacturers Association and major paper manufacturers). Presenting itself as a consumer coalition defending choice, it argues government digitization ignores those without digital access. The group has had legislative successes—helping secure language in a budget deal requiring the Social Security Administration to plan for restoring mailed earnings statements for some retirees, and persuading lawmakers to retain printed prescription inserts. It conducts polls and research showing strong public opposition to mandatory online-only government interaction, though its industry ties are often not disclosed when its findings are cited.

Paper-industry backers say digitization has slashed demand for paper products, closed mills and cost jobs, so protecting paper services is both consumer advocacy and industry survival. Supporters include some consumer groups uneasy about rapid digitization, while opponents note electronic processing saves government money and efficiency. Lawmakers have introduced measures to require federal agencies to offer paper options alongside electronic services, seeking balance between modernization and protecting access for all.

Google is targeting a massive shift in the productivity software market, aiming to capture up to 90% of Microsoft Office users who rely only on basic functions. Microsoft’s Office suite, together with Windows, has been a core revenue driver, and Microsoft continues to dominate desktop operating systems. However, Google has long pursued Office’s foothold with its web-based productivity tools, gradually winning some enterprise users. Amit Singh, VP and head of Google Enterprise, stated the company’s explicit goal to attract the large segment of users who “don’t need to have the most advanced features of Office.” To that end, Google has steadily improved its Enterprise offerings and is closing feature gaps with Office, while shifting from a free trial model to paid access for Google Apps. The strategy focuses on convenience, cloud-based collaboration, and incremental feature additions to appeal to organizations and individuals whose needs are served by simpler word processing, spreadsheets, and presentation tools. The move is part of broader competitive dynamics among major technology companies—Apple, Amazon, Google, and Facebook—as they encroach on each other’s territories, especially around hardware and search, and as companies like Google pursue acquisitions and product expansion to strengthen user loyalty and revenue streams.

Bai Yun, a 23-year-old giant panda at the San Diego Zoo and mother of six, underwent a dental procedure after keepers noticed a chipped lower tooth. Zoo veterinarians anesthetized her, took X-rays and performed a restorative treatment using dental composite to cover the damaged area. Fortunately the pulp canal had not been compromised, though the chip came close to exposing it; the repair aimed to prevent further chipping or deterioration. The team also cleaned her teeth and took additional X-rays. Pandas are prone to worn and damaged teeth because their diet consists almost entirely of bamboo, which is tough, low in nutrition and requires many hours of chewing—Bai Yun can spend up to 12 hours a day feeding. Bai Yun is part of a U.S.-China research loan program—San Diego is one of four American zoos studying and breeding the critically endangered species, which faces habitat loss and has roughly 1,600 wild individuals remaining.

This collection of posts criticizes the Washington Post for publishing a Sarah Palin op-ed urging President Obama to boycott the Copenhagen climate talks in reaction to the “Climategate” email controversy. Tim Lambert and others argue Palin’s claims—accusing leading climate scientists of destroying data, manipulating records to “hide the decline,” and suppressing critics—are contradicted by the Post’s own reporting and the broader scientific consensus that Earth is warming and humans contribute to it. Media commentators noted the Post’s decision to run an expanded Facebook post as odd; some saw it as providing Palin a platform to capitalize on the controversy. Coverage also traces Palin’s shifting stance: once acknowledging climate impacts in Alaska and forming a state subcabinet, she now frames climate science as politicized and warns that emissions-reduction policies would harm the U.S. economy. The argument concludes that, absent trustworthy science, Americans should be skeptical of Copenhagen outcomes—hence Palin’s call for a presidential boycott.

Huma Abedin, a top Hillary Clinton aide, announced she is separating from husband Anthony Weiner after six tumultuous years of marriage marked by his repeated sexting scandals. Abedin said the decision followed “long and painful consideration” and emphasized their devotion to their son, asking for privacy. The split followed a New York Post expose of new explicit messages and an image of Weiner in underwear beside their child, which friends said was the final catalyst after about a year of estrangement. Though the couple still share an apartment and parenting duties and had made public appearances together, Abedin has been appearing more often without her rings and scaling back routine campaign travel, sometimes acting as an ambassador to donors and celebrities. Clinton and campaign allies rallied to support Abedin, stressing the campaign’s focus on her well-being and generally resisting calls for her to step back, though some privately worried her personal troubles could distract from Clinton’s message. Weiner faced professional fallout—social media disappearance, media gigs suspended—and attacks from Donald Trump alleging security risks, claims allies dismissed as baseless. The campaign hopes the news cycle will move on so Abedin can continue her role.

Clemson food scientist Paul Dawson and his students tested the “five-second rule” and concluded it’s unreliable: bacteria on floors and tabletops can transfer to food immediately, so time alone isn’t a safe guide. Their work, published in the Journal of Applied Microbiology, was part of a creative inquiry program teaching research methods through practical food-safety experiments (including double-dipping and drinking from cartons), emphasizing questioning assumptions. Other studies show mixed results: some researchers found quick contamination possible and recommend a “zero-second” rule for risky surfaces like kitchen or bathroom floors, while Connecticut College students found moist foods picked up bacteria after about one minute and dry foods like candy took longer. Experts agree location and contamination source matter most; risk assessment often comes down to context and personal tolerance.

A newly revealed wartime photograph and newly uncovered diary sections together deepen the historical record of Heinrich Himmler, the SS chief and key architect of the Holocaust. The photograph, unseen until now, was taken by Lance Corporal Guy Adderley of British Intelligence in May 1945 and shows Himmler dead after biting a cyanide capsule, his round glasses still on. Arrested by Army officers and due for interrogation the next day, Himmler’s body was later shown in official propaganda photos, but Adderley kept this grainy image among his mementoes. Adderley’s family plans to sell the photo at Dreweatt’s militaria auction in Bristol on March 29 with an estimate of £2,000–£3,000. Auctioneer Malcolm Claridge emphasized the collection’s importance: Adderley was part of the team that arrested Himmler, and the materials reportedly include photos taken inside the British safe house in Lüneburg where Himmler swallowed the cyanide, plus images of British and Russian officers in the house. Conspiracy theories have swirled around Himmler’s death, intensified by wartime orders that Army personnel sign the Official Secrets Act and by the fact that four British soldiers transported and buried his body in an unmarked grave on Lüneburg Heath, which has never been found. Separately, about 1,000 pages of long-lost sections from Himmler’s wartime diary have been discovered in a Moscow archive, described by the German Historical Institute as “of outstanding historical significance.” The newly found diary material ranges from mundane travel and leisure notes to chilling accounts of him observing mass gassings, underscoring researchers’ portrayals of Himmler as a man of brutal contradictions who committed suicide in May 1945 rather than face justice.

Scottish craft brewer BrewDog has lost a trademark dispute with Elvis Presley’s estate over the name of its popular grapefruit-and-blood-orange IPA, Elvis Juice. Launched in 2015, Elvis Juice became one of BrewDog’s best-selling beers, but the Presley estate objected when BrewDog sought to register “Elvis Juice” and related marks in the U.K., arguing consumers might think the product was endorsed by or associated with Elvis Presley’s estate. In an unusual counter, BrewDog co-founders James Watt and Martin Dickie legally changed their names to Elvis in an attempt to show the name was not exclusive to Presley, but that tactic failed to persuade the Intellectual Property Office. Hearing officer Oliver Morris ruled that Elvis is a relatively uncommon name and that many consumers, including younger ones, would likely conceptualize the name as referring to Elvis Presley, despite his death in 1977. The office found for the Presley estate, ordered BrewDog to pay £1,500 in costs, and required BrewDog either to rename the beer or seek permission from the estate to use the trademark. The decision highlights the strong protections around Elvis Presley’s name and likeness, managed by Elvis Presley Enterprises through licensing. The outcome is notable given BrewDog’s own aggressive trademark enforcement history, having defended its “Punk” and “Lone Wolf” marks in other disputes.

The piece opens with the honest aphorism “Nobody knows anything,” yet the writer argues that, despite uncertainty, signs pointed to a Romney surge. While Hurricane Sandy temporarily focused attention on Obama and exposed infrastructure failures and political disconnects in the tristate area, Romney’s campaign quietly gained momentum. Big, enthusiastic crowds, disciplined advance work, effective closing speeches and ads, and growing warmth toward Romney from former skeptics are cited as evidence. The writer describes a palpable shift among evangelicals, Protestants, Catholics and independents toward Romney and contrasts Republican enthusiasm with perceived Democratic fatigue. Visual cues—yard signs, chants, rope-line fervor—and personal encounters convince the author Romney’s support was real and underestimated by poll-focused observers. Yet many pundits had already predicted a Romney victory; the piece lists numerous high-profile conservatives who forecast his win. Ultimately, the narrative notes Obama’s re-election and Nate Silver’s vindication: Silver’s statistical model accurately tracked the outcome, earning public recognition and challenging gut-driven punditry even as the campaign’s late dynamics offered conflicting impressions.

Saturday Night Live’s recent episode, hosted by Melissa McCarthy, delivered spirited physical comedy but uneven material. McCarthy’s fearless performances—falling in her monologue, drinking from a punch bowl, dancing in a ham-themed sketch, and playing an over-the-top Rutgers coach in “Outside the Lines”—were highlights; that coach parody was named Sketch of the Night. Other decent bits included “Bathroom Businessman,” “Weekend Update” with guests like Peter Dinklage, and a growing-on-you “Pizza Business.” Yet several sketches faltered: a limp “The Voice,” a baffling cold open featuring Bobby Moynihan’s Kim Jong-un and a Dennis Rodman cameo, and the weak “Million Dollar Wheel.” Overall, McCarthy elevated the show, but inconsistent writing left the episode merely good, not great.

A 2014 study published in the Journal of Evolutionary Biology examined links between male facial traits, perceived attractiveness, masculinity, and semen quality. Researchers analyzed semen from 50 Caucasian university students and had diverse raters evaluate facial photographs for attractiveness and long-term mate suitability; they also performed anthropometric measurements of masculine features. Results showed a small but significant negative association between masculine facial characteristics and certain sperm quality measures (notably motility), while overall attractiveness correlated positively with semen quality. The authors note prior work linking high testosterone to reduced sperm production, suggesting a possible trade-off, but they caution that causation and mechanisms remain unproven and that outliers influenced some findings. The study challenges simplistic applications of the phenotype-linked fertility hypothesis in humans—that more ornamented or attractive males always confer hereditary reproductive advantages. Researchers call for larger, diverse samples and further investigation before drawing mate-selection advice, emphasizing that these preliminary results are intriguing but not definitive.

The Beck-Massa affair involved an unlikely meeting between Rep. Eric Massa and conservative host Glenn Beck, both vehemently opposed to the Obama administration’s health-care push but for starkly different reasons. Massa, who initially cited health issues for his resignation and later acknowledged ethics problems, claimed he had been “set up” by Democrats because he opposed the health-care bill. Seeking sympathy, he urged listeners to contact Fox News and appeared on Beck’s show, where their brief rapport quickly soured. Massa favors a government-run single-payer system, a stance Beck derided as socialist. Beck pressed Massa for concrete evidence of Democratic corruption or coercion; Massa supplied none and could not substantiate his allegations. The interview ended with Beck apologizing to viewers for wasting their time, signaling that the unlikely alliance was merely a one-night encounter without substance.

The 2017 Harris Poll Reputation Quotient finds U.S. corporate reputations politically polarized: Republicans rate Chick-fil-A and Hobby Lobby far more favorably, while Democrats prefer Target. Amazon tops the list with the highest RQ in the study’s history; Wells Fargo suffers the largest-ever decline after its fake-accounts scandal. Vision and leadership are increasingly critical to reputation, yet half of Americans view CEOs negatively. Major reputational threats include intentional wrongdoing, dishonesty, and financial misuse. Tesla debuts strongly despite limited consumer access; Takata and Mylan rank poorly after crises.

Engel & Völkers identified the priciest suburbs nearest each of the U.S.’s ten largest metro areas. Highlights include Los Altos Hills and Bel Air (both $3.45M median) near San Jose and Los Angeles, Rancho Santa Fe ($2.119M) by San Diego, Bronxville ($2.325M) near New York, Westlake ($2M) outside Dallas, and Paradise Valley ($1.1M) by Phoenix. Other affluent enclaves listed are Glencoe, Bryn Mawr, Terrell Hills and Southside Place, each noted for high-end homes, celebrity or historic residents, and multimillion-dollar listings.

Following the U.S. raid that killed Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad, U.S. Sen. John Kerry visited Pakistan and announced a joint commitment to cooperate on future actions against “high-value targets,” while defending the U.S. decision not to notify Islamabad beforehand. Kerry framed the raid as a necessary, covert triumph against terrorism and acknowledged Pakistani anger over the unilateral operation, saying secrecy was essential to protect operatives and ensure success. He said Pakistani leaders agreed to explore increased intelligence sharing and joint operations, though specifics were not disclosed. One tangible step: Pakistan agreed to return the intact tail section of a U.S. stealth helicopter disabled during the raid, which U.S. forces had partly destroyed to safeguard technology. Kerry warned that lawmakers will demand concrete Pakistani actions against militant groups if U.S. aid is to continue, noting concerns about alleged Pakistani support for insurgents and groups like Lashkar-i-Taiba. A joint statement reassured Pakistan the U.S. has “no designs” on its nuclear arsenal. The visit aims to “recalibrate” strained ties crucial for Afghanistan logistics and regional stability, even as Pakistan protests sovereignty violations, debates drone strikes, and faces ongoing militant violence including the recent killing of a Saudi diplomat in Karachi.

Early warnings that this would be a severe flu season proved accurate: influenza activity climbed sharply across the United States, with most of the country experiencing high levels of influenza-like illness. The CDC reported outpatient visits for flu symptoms rose to 5.6%, well above last season’s peak, and nearly 30 states (and later 41) reported widespread activity. The predominant strain is H3N2, which often causes more severe seasons. By the end of 2012, at least 2,257 people had been hospitalized and 18 children had died nationwide. Cities and regions from New Jersey and Chicago to Minnesota, Florida and Ohio have seen surges: New Jersey recorded about twice as many flu-related ER visits as the previous year; Chicago-area hospitals temporarily placed some emergency departments on ambulance bypass because they were overwhelmed; Minnesota reported 600 hospitalizations and several deaths. Health systems limited visitors, required hand hygiene, and urged symptomatic people to stay home to limit spread.

Public health officials and physicians repeatedly emphasized vaccination as the best defense—even though vaccine effectiveness can be partial (around 60% effectiveness reported) and some vaccinated people still become ill, vaccinated individuals generally experience milder illness. Antiviral medications like oseltamivir are most useful if started within 48 hours of symptom onset. Authorities urged hand-washing, use of sanitizers, staying home while contagious, and seeking vaccines—reminding the public it is not too late to get a shot, which takes about two weeks to become protective.

Twelve people were killed on Friday as protests across Afghanistan intensified over the desecration of Qurans at NATO’s Bagram base, marking the deadliest day in four days of unrest. The incident, in which Afghan workers found charred Qurans while clearing rubbish, prompted widespread anger, chants of “Death to America,” rock-throwing and attempts to storm foreign compounds. Demonstrations swelled in Kabul—where riot police and army helicopters were deployed—and in provinces including Herat (seven killed), Khost (two), and Baghlan (one). Herat saw an assault on the U.S. consulate; officials said agitators and possible foreign intelligence involvement stoked violence. President Obama apologized to Hamid Karzai; Afghanistan demanded public trials for those responsible. NATO is investigating the burns, and many rescued Qurans remain held at Bagram as evidence. The Taliban urged attacks on foreign forces. Westerners were largely confined to fortified compounds; Germany pulled troops from a northern outpost early over security concerns. The unrest reflects deeper mistrust of foreign troops amid a decade of war.

Clint Eastwood’s Sully, starring Tom Hanks as Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger, is a lean, quietly powerful dramatization of the 2009 “Miracle on the Hudson.” Eastwood’s direction is economical and musical in tone—alternating steady, everyday rhythms with sudden, heart-thudding intensity—most memorably during the film’s recreation of the bird strike and emergency water landing. The landing sequence itself is a masterclass in tension: ambient hums give way to near-silence and then to panicked cries and the repeated command, “Brace, brace! Heads down, stay down!”

Rather than a straightforward exaltation, Sully is a nuanced portrait of a reluctant, classic-style hero. Hanks embodies Sullenberger’s modesty and reserve: a man whose actions saved 155 lives yet who is haunted by nightmares of what might have happened and uncomfortable with fame. The film’s central conflict comes not from physical peril but from an NTSB investigation whose simulations suggest Sully might have been able to return to LaGuardia—raising doubts about his judgment. Eastwood stages these procedural hearings with crisp clarity, juxtaposing bureaucratic scrutiny and algorithmic certainty against human experience and the impossibility of real-time decision-making.

Supporting performances, especially Aaron Eckhart as co-pilot Jeff Skiles and Laura Linney as Sully’s wife, offer warmth and authenticity. The movie’s wintry Manhattan cinematography and evocative touches—moments that recall 9/11’s shadow over the city—lend poignancy without mawkishness. At 95 minutes, Sully is a tight, satisfying ode to competence and quiet courage: respectful to the real events and deeply engrossing, proving that restrained filmmaking can deliver profound emotional impact.

Actress and disability advocate Jamie Brewer made history at New York Fashion Week as the first woman with Down syndrome to walk a major runway, modeling a Carrie Hammer original for the designer’s “Role Models Not Runway Models” campaign. Hammer created the initiative to showcase real clients—accomplished women across fields including business, nonprofits and research—rather than conventional models. The campaign began when Hammer invited a friend who uses a wheelchair to model, drawing strong public response and hundreds of nominations for future shows.
