Katie Driscoll, co-founder of Changing the Face of Beauty, recommended Brewer so her daughter Grace could see a role model with Down syndrome in fashion. Brewer, known for roles on American Horror Story, has a long history of advocacy and leadership on disability boards in Texas. Hammer designed a black A-line dress to reflect Brewer’s “bewitching” onscreen persona and flattering figure, a look Brewer said she felt honored to wear. The show, held at Lightbox in New York, featured bespoke looks for each inspiring participant.

Tiger Woods was arrested early Monday in Jupiter, Florida, after police found him asleep at the wheel of a running 2015 Mercedes-Benz with flat tires and minor vehicle damage. Officers described him as cooperative but confused, with extremely slow, slurred speech. His breath test was .000. He struggled with field sobriety tests but ultimately completed tasks when instructions were repeated. Woods, 41, was booked at 7:18 a.m. and released on his own recognizance at 10:50 a.m.; a court date is set for July 5. In a statement he said prescribed medications—not alcohol—caused an unexpected reaction and apologized, taking responsibility. The arrest comes amid ongoing recovery from back problems and recent spinal fusion surgery; friends like Jack Nicklaus expressed concern and support.

The document recounts the Battle of Takur Ghar during Operation Anaconda in March 2002, focusing on the actions and aftermath involving Navy Chief Petty Officer John Slabinski’s SEAL team and Air Force Staff Sergeant John A. Chapman. Ordered to establish an observation post atop the 10,000-foot peak, the SEALs intended to land near the base and climb stealthily, but delays forced a dawn insertion. Enemy fighters already occupied the summit and struck the insertion helicopter; Petty Officer Neil C. Roberts fell from the aircraft and was later found dead. A second helicopter returned with five SEALs and Sergeant Chapman to attempt a rescue. Under intense fire and amid deep snow, the team killed two fighters but were forced to retreat after Chapman was wounded. Subsequent reinforcements suffered casualties, and tensions rose among units, with accusations that the SEALs’ choice to land directly on the peak violated reconnaissance doctrine.

An Army-led investigation by Lt. Col. Andrew Milani reviewed events, including blurry Predator drone footage that suggested someone in the bunker killed an attacker; Milani offered competing explanations without definitive conclusions. Chapman was posthumously awarded the Air Force Cross; recent Air Force reanalysis—using enhanced imagery, Predator and AC-130 footage fusion, and autopsy review—contends Chapman regained consciousness after being presumed dead, fought alone from a bunker, killed multiple attackers, and later died from machine-gun fire as reinforcements approached. That analysis led Milani to revise his view toward Chapman likely surviving the initial assault. Chief Slabinski, who received a Navy Cross and who struggles with PTSD, expresses mixed reactions: he defends Chapman's valor and questions some technical interpretations of the footage, while grappling with the possibility that another service member may have been left fighting alone. The episode highlights the fog of battle, interservice tensions, and enduring questions about what transpired on Roberts Ridge.

Republican presidential candidate Jon Huntsman announced he will boycott next week’s Nevada debate in protest of Nevada moving its caucus to Jan. 14, a change that challenges the traditional Iowa-New Hampshire primary order. Huntsman told WMUR, "If you are going to boycott something, boycott it," and his campaign said he will instead campaign in New Hampshire, holding a town hall to defend its first-in-the-nation status. He accused Mitt Romney of pushing Nevada’s earlier date to gain an advantage with its sizable Mormon population; Romney’s team denied the charge. Other candidates, including Newt Gingrich, have threatened similar actions over the calendar change, while Michele Bachmann and Rick Santorum weighed responses.

Two Indiana brothers, Noah Batz, 24, and Timothy Batz, 21, were arrested after a chaotic incident at Lighthouse Landings apartments on the city’s south side in January. Neighbors and apartment staff reported finding the pair naked in the complex parking lot, behaving aggressively, damaging vehicles and fighting with one another and other residents. Witnesses described the brothers as yelling, chasing people, and engaging in unusual conduct; one neighbor said they were “completely naked” and on top of each other, and an assistant manager reported seeing them “grab onto each other’s head and passionately begin making out” near a dumpster. According to court documents, Noah chased and punched a woman who had tried to walk away, leaving a knot on her forehead, threatened to kill the assistant manager and damaged her car, and smashed other vehicles in the lot. Officers who arrested them said the brothers told police they had smoked psychedelic mushrooms; Timothy allegedly had also used marijuana. During detention, Timothy resisted and attempted to remove handcuffs, while Noah had to be subdued with a stun gun after approaching an officer with a balled fist. Police later entered Timothy’s apartment, finding signs of a violent disturbance—broken glass, dishes, clothing stains and blood—and a green leafy substance suspected to be marijuana. Initially charged with a variety of offenses including public nudity, resisting law enforcement, criminal mischief and unlawful vehicle entry (Noah also faced a battery charge; Timothy faced possession), both brothers pleaded not guilty and were expected at a May pretrial conference. An update notes that all charges against Noah and Timothy Batz were subsequently dismissed; no further details were provided.

Aides from North and South Korea met at the Panmunjom truce village on Saturday evening and into the early hours of Sunday to discuss resolving a recent crisis that had pushed the rivals toward armed conflict. The talks began after the deadline on a North Korean ultimatum demanding Seoul halt loudspeaker propaganda broadcasts along the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) passed without reported incidents. South Korea’s presidential office said envoys discussed easing tensions and improving ties; the meeting broke before dawn and was set to resume later. South Korean national security and unification officials met Hwang Pyong So, a top military aide to Kim Jong Un, and Kim Yang Gon, a veteran inter-Korean affairs official. Pyongyang’s KCNA unusually referred to the South as the Republic of Korea in announcing the meeting.

The confrontation followed an exchange of artillery fire on Thursday—North Korea fired shells and the South returned fire—with no reported casualties. The dispute stems from Seoul’s loudspeaker broadcasts started after unexplained landmine explosions wounded two South Korean soldiers; Seoul demands North take responsibility. The United States and China urged calm; U.S.-South joint military drills resumed and allied aircraft patrols flew as border villagers sheltered. Analysts say both sides often step back from all-out war and view the high-level meeting as an opportunity to defuse the crisis. Meanwhile, South Korean sources reported an unprecedented sortie rate of North Korean submarines and raised frontline readiness, signaling Pyongyang may be combining military posturing with diplomatic engagement.

Donald Trump’s Aug. 15 national security speech in Youngstown, Ohio, attempted to outline his approach to the Middle East and terrorism but produced a confusing, contradictory set of prescriptions that left observers unsure what his administration would actually do. Much of the speech stitched together familiar conservative complaints: that George W. Bush’s 2003 Iraq invasion destabilized the region, that Barack Obama’s withdrawal created a vacuum exploited by ISIS, and that Hillary Clinton’s support for interventions like Libya’s contributed to weak states that radicals could use as bases. Yet Trump’s critiques are largely retrospective — he previously praised or supported many of the same policies he now denounces — and provide little coherent forward-looking strategy.

Central to his proposals was a mix of non-interventionist rhetoric and hawkish, transactional ideas. He denounced “nation-building and regime change” as failures, aligning intermittently with isolationist strains in the GOP, but also advocated seizing Iraqi oil fields in wartime and profiting from them — a doctrine of “to the victor go the spoils” that contradicts postwar norms the U.S. has historically upheld. He suggested forging an anti-ISIS alliance that would include NATO, Israel, Egypt, Jordan and Russia, though such cooperation already exists in various forms and Russia’s priorities in Syria often diverge from U.S. aims.

On immigration and counter-radicalization, Trump proposed “extreme vetting” and a Cold War–style ideological screening to bar immigrants who allegedly hold “hostile attitudes,” support Sharia supplanting American law, or fail to “believe in the Constitution.” He also proposed a Commission on Radical Islam to expose domestic networks that support radicalization. Critics warned these measures would be legally dubious, logistically impractical, and counterproductive — encouraging concealment of beliefs, fostering alienation, and echoing McCarthy-era tactics that punish thought rather than deed. Many terrorist attacks cited in the U.S. and Europe were carried out by citizens of Western countries who would not be affected by such screening.

Experts across the political spectrum found Trump’s positions inconsistent and incoherent. Some agreed that Obama’s withdrawal from Iraq was a contributing factor to ISIS’s rise, but rejected Trump’s overall foreign-policy framework as a “blathering jumble” lacking guiding principles. Antiwar conservatives noted Trump’s lack of reliable anti-interventionist commitments, pointing out his advocacy for a bigger military and scant interest in diplomacy that might avert conflict.

Implementation challenges loom large: defining “regions with a history of exporting terrorism,” designing an enforceable ideological test, and balancing diplomatic relationships with allies whose citizens might be barred would be legally and practically fraught. Trump’s flirtation with authoritarian leaders and praise for transactional spoils of war mark a departure from decades of bipartisan U.S. foreign-policy norms. In short, the speech offered many criticisms and provocative ideas, but no coherent, actionable Middle East strategy, leaving voters uncertain about what he would actually do as president.

Between late 2016 and late 2017, 24 U.S. diplomatic staff in Havana reported unexplained symptoms—headaches, confusion, hearing loss—and described strange sounds, prompting speculation about directed attacks. Early theories ranged from sonic weapons to, more recently, pulsed microwave attacks. William Broad’s New York Times piece argued microwaves might cause auditory sensations and brain injury via the microwave auditory effect, which produces perceived sounds when microsecond microwave pulses heat tissue slightly and launch internal acoustic waves.

Allan Frey, the scientist who first explained the microwave auditory effect, calls the microwave-weapon explanation implausible. He emphasizes that the effect is a near-threshold hearing phenomenon; the pulses produce acoustic pressures far too weak to cause structural brain damage unless intensities reached levels that would burn tissue. Practical deployment against specific individuals at distance would be technically difficult, detectable, or require huge equipment. Frey notes simpler harassment methods exist and that the medical evidence is equivocal: a University of Pennsylvania study reported widespread network injury in 21 patients, but critics argue findings may be statistical artifacts or influenced by psychological factors.

Recordings released by the Associated Press resemble sounds produced by intermodulation distortion of two ultrasound beams. Researchers showed ultrasound devices—common in sensors and anti-piracy tools—can create audible artifacts and could explain reported sounds, possibly unintentionally or for surveillance. Cuban investigators and neurologists have dismissed microwave weapon claims as science fiction, noting logistical and evidentiary gaps and finding no hard proof of attacks. Historical parallels include low-level Soviet microwave irradiation of the Moscow embassy. Ultimately, facts remain murky; multiple hypotheses persist, and definitive conclusions are lacking.

Both supporters and opponents of same-sex marriage have converged on one point: they want the Supreme Court to resolve whether the Constitution forbids states from defining marriage as between a man and a woman. Recent rapid developments in the federal courts have pushed the issue toward the justices, and a decision to take up the matter could come quickly; a final ruling, however, likely would not arrive before June 2015.

In a burst of activity, federal courts have struck down state bans in multiple circuits. Officials in Indiana, Wisconsin, Oklahoma, Utah and Virginia immediately appealed those adverse rulings to the Supreme Court, filing on an accelerated schedule so the justices could consider them at their upcoming conference. Momentum stems from the 2013 U.S. v. Windsor decision, where Justice Anthony Kennedy’s opinion struck down part of the Defense of Marriage Act and has since been relied on by nearly two dozen judges to invalidate state bans across the country. Only a handful of judges have dissented or upheld bans.

Unusually, winners in many lower-court cases — plaintiffs who typically prefer to keep favorable rulings undisturbed — have urged Supreme Court review, joining the losers in pressing the court to act. Altogether 36 states, representing both pro- and anti-marriage-equality positions, have signaled the court should weigh in. Thirty major companies, including Amazon, eBay, Intel, Nike and Target, have urged nationwide recognition, citing employer and employee uncertainty caused by patchwork state laws.

Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg has suggested the court will not dodge the question if presented properly; historically the court sometimes avoided ruling on marriage issues. Observers note Justice Kennedy’s central role: he authored Windsor and is often the pivotal vote in gay-rights cases, leaving many to speculate his stance will be decisive.

Despite expectations that the Supreme Court might wait for a circuit split — for example, a likely contrary ruling from the Sixth Circuit — the court surprised some by declining to review several appellate rulings, effectively allowing same-sex marriages to proceed immediately in multiple states. The pattern of lower-court victories for marriage equality makes it more costly politically and legally for the Supreme Court to reverse course later, especially if many marriages occur before any eventual ruling. The question of timing now hinges largely on whether and when a conservative circuit will uphold a ban, creating the split that historically prompts Supreme Court review.

The Associated Press fact-check examines recent statements by President Trump and others, finding several misleading or inaccurate claims. Trump’s tweeted photos celebrating the start of border-wall construction actually showed work on a two-mile Calexico project funded in 2017; no new wall construction began after the latest budget law. His attacks on Amazon and the U.S. Postal Service exaggerate facts: package delivery — including Amazon deliveries — has been one of the Postal Service’s few revenue growth areas, and federal regulators found its contract with Amazon profitable; overall USPS losses stem mainly from pension and health-care obligations, not parcel delivery. Claims that Amazon pays no sales tax are overstated since buyers in taxed states generally pay sales tax, though third-party sellers sometimes fail to collect it. The piece also notes Trump floated diverting Pentagon funds to build the wall, which would likely require congressional approval. Other items covered: former VA Secretary David Shulkin’s defense after ethics findings and staff email alterations; a misleading White House and Commerce Department portrayal of the citizenship question’s census history; and a clarification that no party can “hold” the Supreme Court, though confirmations shape its ideology.

Russian President Vladimir Putin made a surprise appearance at a youth music awards show, an outing that struck many as awkward and calculated. Dressed in a polo-neck jumper and sports jacket, Putin stood stiffly amid a crowd of baseball-cap–clad teenagers while security mingled covertly. Taking the stage, he urged young people to avoid drugs and vodka and tried to signal familiarity with "mass youth culture," praising rap—“even urban rap and street rap”—for its social content, calling graffiti a “real art form” and describing breakdancing as “completely unique.” His performance drew mixed reactions: one rapper effusively labeled him a “legend” and hoped for a duet, but many observers and some journalists viewed the appearance as a strained, even desperate, attempt to court Russia’s youth rather than a genuinely successful outreach.

A British-Australian team led by Tim Jarvis successfully reenacted Ernest Shackleton’s famed Antarctic survival journey, completing a perilous mountain crossing to the old Stromness whaling station on South Georgia. Jarvis and mountaineer Barry Gray, using clothing and gear mirroring Shackleton’s 1916 expedition, reached Stromness after a grueling climb of about 900 meters across the island’s mountainous interior. The pair endured a severe blizzard that forced them to hunker down in a tent at Shackleton’s Gap amid whiteout conditions, 45–50 knot winds, sleet and snow. The climb featured numerous crevasse falls—more than 20 incidents—one plunging Gray to his armpits and requiring rescue by their lone support member. The crossing followed a 12-day re-creation of Shackleton’s 800-nautical-mile lifeboat journey from Elephant Island to South Georgia, part of a larger effort to replicate the original voyage as authentically as possible. Several teammates had withdrawn earlier after suffering trench foot during the sea leg, leaving Jarvis and Gray to finish the ascent. Jarvis lauded the endurance of early explorers and said he hoped their achievement would inspire others, reaffirming Shackleton’s place among the great Antarctic explorers.

Apple has been spotted testing unmarked, heavily instrumented vehicles around San Francisco and New York that appear to be leased to the company, fueling speculation about new mapping or autonomous-vehicle efforts. Local blog Claycord published photos of a people carrier outfitted with a roof-mounted array of about a dozen cameras and a spinning LIDAR sensor; CBS affiliate KPIX 5 confirmed the car’s lease to Apple. A similar Dodge minivan with matching equipment was captured on video in New York. Both vehicles also carry wheel sensors like those used previously by Navteq and Microsoft’s Bing mapping vehicles.

LIDAR and multi-camera rigs are long-established tools for creating street-level imagery—Google, Nokia, and others have used them for Street View services—and for autonomous driving systems, where spinning LIDAR assemblies continuously scan surroundings. Apple’s vehicles could therefore be collecting data for several possible projects: a Street View–style layer for Apple Maps, enhanced ground-truthing to improve mapping detail and navigation, or initial tests related to self-driving technology. Apple Maps has been substantially overhauled since replacing Google Maps as iOS’s default app, but it still lacks comprehensive street-level imagery, and matching Google’s global coverage would require a major fleet and investment beyond localized tests in two U.S. cities.

Apple has not commented on the vehicles. The company also does not currently hold permits to test self-driving cars in California, although it could partner with authorized firms. With their secrecy and lack of official explanation, these camera-laden vans remain a mystery, leaving observers to weigh mapping improvements against the possibility of autonomous-vehicle research.

President Trump’s administration has taken aggressive executive actions that critics say will destabilize Obamacare markets, potentially harming women, older Americans and people with preexisting conditions. Six physician groups, including the American Academy of Family Physicians, warned that allowing insurers to sell narrow, low-cost plans would shift costs and reduce options for sicker and older enrollees. Health-policy experts and some insurers echoed that concern: expanding short-term plans—currently exempt from Affordable Care Act (ACA) benefit requirements—could draw younger, healthier people away from ACA exchanges, worsening risk pools and driving up premiums for those who remain.

The administration announced it will cut off cost-sharing reduction (CSR) payments to insurers—about $7 billion this year—arguing there is no appropriation for the subsidies. That decision, coupled with a separate executive order to encourage loosely regulated, cheaper plans, represents a major effort to undermine the ACA without new legislation. The CSR payments help insurers reduce out-of-pocket costs for low- and moderate-income enrollees; ending them could jolt already fragile markets, though some insurers had already priced plans anticipating this risk or left the exchanges.

Administration officials say they can rewrite regulations to exempt more plans from ACA rules without changing the law, and the executive order would also ease rules for association health plans, enabling small businesses to band together across state lines—an aim long promoted by Republicans. Supporters argue this increases options and risk pools; critics say it will create weaker plans that siphon healthier enrollees from the regulated marketplaces.

The White House framed the CSR cutoff as a legal and fiscal correction. Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders cited Department of Justice guidance saying payments lack appropriation. Attorney General Jeff Sessions also argued Congress must fix the issue. Trump suggested cutting payments might press Democrats to negotiate, but congressional Democrats called the move “sabotage” and threatened legal challenges. Several state attorneys general and some insurers have already signaled plans to sue.

Insurers can respond by raising rates, adding surcharges, or exiting markets—actions that require negotiation with state regulators and may vary widely by state. While some Republicans see the move as forcing congressional action, others warned it would increase uninsured rates in their districts. Observers say the immediate effects are uncertain but could significantly disrupt enrollment, premiums, and marketplace stability heading into the 2018 open enrollment.

Funny Or Die released a PSA starring Jimmy McMillan and Billy Eichner as Timmy McMillan joking that "the only thing higher than the rent is Charlie Sheen," warning Sheen could lose his "Two and a Half Men" job and even quipping Sheen might "snort a shoe." Separately, NY gubernatorial loser Carl Paladino delivered a combative concession speech, brandishing an orange bat and ominously declaring he’s not finished.

Uber Technologies Inc. has confidentially filed its S-1 registration for an initial public offering, according to people familiar with the matter, entering a high-profile race with smaller rival Lyft Inc. Both companies are preparing IPOs that could rank among the largest expected in 2019, with Lyft saying it filed its S-1 and targeting a March or April debut. The filings mark a pivotal moment for the ride-hailing sector as the two companies position themselves to be the first to go public. Their near-simultaneous filings reflect intense competition for market attention and investor capital, and they underscore the broader trend of high-profile technology and transportation companies pursuing public offerings. The closeness of the timing suggests both firms are responding to favorable market conditions and investor appetite for disruptive, growth-oriented businesses, setting up a consequential showdown as each company lays out its financials, growth prospects, and path to profitability for prospective public-market investors.

Facing what many see as an escalating threat to reproductive rights under the Trump administration, the international advocacy group Women Help Women has launched a US-facing web portal — Self‑managed Abortion, Safe and Supported (SASS) at abortionpillinfo.org — to offer real‑time counseling and medically informed guidance to people who obtain abortion drugs outside clinical settings. The project responds to evidence that some US residents already self‑administer misoprostol (often bought over the counter in Mexico and elsewhere) because clinic access is limited by cost, distance, legal restrictions and clinic closures. Women Help Women does not ship drugs to the US; instead its counselors, trained by medical professionals, provide step‑by‑step instructions, safety information, signs of complications, and referrals to abortion funds when possible.

The group built legal precautions into SASS: counselors are based abroad, servers are outside the US, and conversations are deleted after seven days, reflecting prosecutions in some states of people who self‑induced abortions. Legal experts say sharing information is generally protected but note the law is complicated and risks can be amplified when communications or purchases leave a paper trail. Medical experts quoted stress that misoprostol is relatively safe and effective when used with accurate information; the main risks are legal rather than medical. Still, clinical concerns remain: determining gestational age, confirming pregnancy by ultrasound, and recognizing complications are harder outside clinics, and regimens differ by pregnancy stage.

The initiative is framed as harm reduction: activists argue silence is riskier given growing search activity and documented cases of desperation—women unable to pay clinic fees, barred by parental consent laws, isolated by clinic closures, or facing travel and legal barriers. SASS aims to support those who have "decided to use the pills" by providing evidence‑based guidance, while acknowledging legal ambiguity and the broader policy drivers pushing people toward self‑management.

Lieutenant Scott Sears, a 27-year-old officer in the 1st Battalion Royal Gurkha Rifles and brother-in-law of tennis star Andy Murray, has completed a solo, unsupported trek to the South Pole, arriving on Christmas Day after more than five weeks on the Antarctic plateau. Pulling a sled with supplies, Sears covered roughly 702 miles from Hercules Inlet, enduring temperatures near -50°C and winds up to 150 mph. He completed the journey in 38 days—about 12 days faster than he had expected—and is believed to be the youngest person to reach the pole solo, though Guinness World Records had not yet confirmed the claim at the time of reporting.

The route from Hercules Inlet is perilous, especially the crevasse-filled initial stretch; traveling alone meant Sears could not be roped to a teammate for safety and instead used skis to negotiate the ice. In his expedition blog he described a severe low point 38 km from the pole on Christmas Eve, when fatigue made each step feel impossible. He revived himself with juice, biltong, chocolate and music, and the next day reached the pole under blue skies, saying he was “absolutely chuffed to pieces.” After nearly six weeks isolated in a tent, he said the experience felt overwhelming and he was eager for a shower and proper food.

Sears, who previously played tennis internationally until age 19 before joining the Army, raised more than £33,500 for the Gurkha Welfare Trust to support rebuilding schools in Nepal after the 2015 earthquake. His achievement earned public congratulations, including from Judy Murray.

Kenneth Starr, a high-profile New York investment adviser to celebrities and wealthy clients, was arrested after agents found him hiding in a closet; prosecutors allege he ran at least a $30 million fraud involving family, political figure Andrew Stein, and other associates. Charged with wire fraud, investment adviser fraud and money laundering, Starr allegedly operated Ponzi-like schemes siphoning client funds for personal use, including buying a $7.5 million apartment. Victims named anonymously in court papers include an elderly heiress (reported as Rachel Mellon), entertainers and industry figures; media reporting and sources identify actress Uma Thurman and a former talent executive among those affected. Co-defendant Stein was released on bail; Starr was detained without bail and faces SEC civil action as well as criminal prosecution.

On October 10, 2017, the United States men’s national team suffered a historic and humiliating defeat, losing 2-1 to already-eliminated Trinidad and Tobago and failing to qualify for the 2018 World Cup—their first absence since 1986. The result erased three decades of momentum in American soccer and exposed failures at nearly every level: player performance, coaching, federation leadership, and systemic youth development.

The U.S. entered the final match in Couva needing only a draw but produced a lifeless first half, conceding an own goal by Omar Gonzalez and a long-range strike by Alvin Jones. Christian Pulisic’s second-half goal proved too little, too late. Across the region, other results conspired against the Americans—Panama beat Costa Rica on a controversial goal and late winner, while Honduras rallied to defeat Mexico—yet commentators argue the U.S. had itself to blame for poor qualifying form (three wins in ten Hex games) and tactical errors. Tim Howard’s performance drew criticism, Gonzalez’s mistakes were costly, and several veterans showed decline while younger prospects beyond Pulisic were scarce.

Accountability extends beyond the pitch. Criticism targeted head coach Bruce Arena for selection and tactical choices, former coach Jurgen Klinsmann for earlier damage to the program, and U.S. Soccer president Sunil Gulati for insufficient investment in youth development and for problematic hires. Analysts point to deeper structural issues: a pay-to-play youth model that limits talent discovery, weak scouting and coaching, and a conspicuous “missing” cohort of players in their early-to-mid 20s.

The consequences are wide-ranging: lost opportunities to grow the sport domestically, financial impact for broadcasters like Fox (which paid heavily for World Cup rights), and an urgent need for rebuild and reform. While some argue that a setback could catalyze necessary change, the immediate reality is stark—U.S. Soccer must overhaul development, leadership, and talent identification to avoid another national embarrassment before 2022.

The Sentinelese of North Sentinel Island are among the world’s most isolated people, likely direct descendants of the first humans to leave Africa and possibly living on the Andaman Islands for up to 60,000 years. Numbering perhaps 50–200, they have fiercely rejected outsiders, defending their shore with bows and arrows and surviving independently on fish, turtles, wild pigs and island resources. Their language and culture are distinct from other Andaman groups; they lack formal chiefs or witchdoctors, count only to two, and practice simple body painting. They cannily salvage metal from wrecks but otherwise retain many pre-Neolithic lifeways.

Contact history has been traumatic. Colonial-era kidnappings and later contact attempts introduced disease and violence; an 1879 abduction led to rapid sickness and deaths among captives while colonial officers demeaned them. Repeated intrusions by salvagers and others in the 1980s and 1990s caused deadly skirmishes. Conversely, intentional contact efforts by Indian anthropologists in the 1960s–1990s gradually reduced hostility through gift-giving, culminating in a largely peaceful encounter in 1991. Still, exposure of other tribes (e.g., Jarawa, Onge, Great Andamanese) to outsiders brought exploitation, alcoholism, sexual abuse and epidemics, sharply reducing their numbers and dependence on state aid.

Incidents continue to underscore the Sentinelese desire for isolation: in 2004 a helicopter found them alive and hostile after the tsunami; in 2006 two illegal fishermen who drifted ashore—likely asleep and intoxicated—were killed by islanders, and recovery attempts were repelled by arrow fire. Rumors of cannibalism are unfounded and conflated with unrelated customs among other tribes. Environmental and indigenous-rights groups, along with many anthropologists, now advocate strict non-interference: the Indian government enforces an exclusion zone and increasingly recognizes the Sentinelese right to self-determination. Debate persists over whether and how eventual contact should occur, but consensus leans toward protecting them from outsiders and preventing the catastrophic consequences earlier contacts inflicted on neighboring tribes.

Classified U.S. military and intelligence documents released by WikiLeaks depict deep, long-standing tensions and troubling ambiguities in the Afghanistan war, especially regarding Pakistan’s role. The files include reports suggesting Pakistani intelligence (ISI) cooperated with or sheltered militant networks, and in some cases may have helped plan attacks or run suicide-bomber networks that struck inside Afghanistan. U.S. officials confronted Pakistani leaders with allegations and lists of suspected ISI operatives working with militants, while Pakistan repeatedly denied culpability and insisted ties had been severed. Former and retired Pakistani figures, notably ex-ISI chief Lt. Gen. Hamid Gul, are repeatedly implicated in reactivating old militant networks and meeting insurgent and alleged Al Qaeda representatives to plan operations. The logs also reveal American frustration at cross-border insurgent movements, Pakistani inaction at border posts, and strained on-the-ground cooperation despite public U.S.-Pakistani partnership rhetoric and continued U.S. aid. Separately, the trove documents thousands of battlefield incidents, including many unreported civilian casualties and controversial coalition operations, and shows NATO concerns that neighboring states may fuel the insurgency. U.S. officials call for Pakistan to shift strategy; lawmakers demand proof of ISI disengagement from militants.

After eight years and about 180,000 bites from a laboratory colony, researchers at Simon Fraser University have identified a chemical combination that reliably lures bedbugs into traps and keeps them there. The multidisciplinary team—biologists Regine and Gerhard Gries, chemist Robert Britton, and students—isolated airborne pheromones from bedbug shed skin and feces and discovered histamine acts as a “safe shelter” signal. In early lab work a pheromone blend attracted bedbugs but failed in infested apartments; further analysis with advanced spectrometry revealed histamine, which causes bedbugs to remain once they contact it. Additional analysis of fecal volatiles revealed three previously unreported compounds; the full lure combines the airborne attractants and histamine placed on filter paper to hold the insects in a simple trap. Field tests in Metro Vancouver apartments were successful, and the team is partnering with Contech Enterprises to produce an affordable commercial trap expected next year; chemical cost per trap is under a dime. The trap aims to detect early infestations and monitor treatment effectiveness—important as bedbugs have resurged globally over the past two decades, infesting homes, shelters and hotels and posing health concerns such as itching, rashes and potential links to diseases like Chagas. The research was published in Angewandte Chemie and funded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada in partnership with Contech. Despite the progress, Regine Gries continues to feed the lab colony weekly to support ongoing work.

Kanye West has been discharged from UCLA Medical Center after more than a week of treatment following what people close to him describe as a mental breakdown. Sources say West left the hospital under the care of his wife, Kim Kardashian, and his personal physician, Dr. Michael Farzam, who had initially called 911 when West was admitted. The hospitalization followed a period of extreme exhaustion and erratic behavior, including an episode at trainer Harley Pasternak’s home where West reportedly showed paranoia and had difficulty distinguishing reality. Insiders tie the decline in his mental state to multiple stressors: the October 3 Paris robbery in which Kardashian was tied up and robbed of millions in jewelry, the nine-year anniversary of the death of West’s mother Donda, relentless touring, and sleeplessness. Those close to the family stress that West is “not out of the woods” and requires ongoing psychological and medical treatment. Kim Kardashian reportedly stayed by his side in the hospital and has been actively nursing him, hoping treatment will help repair strains on their marriage caused by his recent behavior and his demanding work habits. The incident led to the cancellation of the remaining dates of West’s Saint Pablo Tour; Live Nation and other sources indicate all shows are on hold indefinitely while he focuses on recovery, with no firm return date. Financially, West is reportedly covered by insurance for cancelled concerts. Media outlets including TMZ, Us Weekly, X17, and CNN have reported on the events, and friends and insiders provided much of the detail about the couple’s struggles and the hopes that treatment will aid both West’s health and their relationship.

On July 24, the first day New York’s same‑sex marriage law takes effect, Mayor Michael Bloomberg will officiate at the wedding of two of his top aides, consumer affairs commissioner Jonathan Mintz and chief policy adviser John Feinblatt. The couple, together for 14 years and parents of two daughters, will be married at Gracie Mansion. Bloomberg—who has only officiated twice as mayor, including his daughter’s wedding and Rudy Giuliani’s—said Mintz and Feinblatt helped him “see the issue of marriage equality in very clear terms” and called the day one they’d long awaited. The city extended City Clerk hours that Sunday so couples could marry immediately after Gov. Andrew Cuomo signed the bill on June 24; New York became the sixth state to legalize same‑sex marriage and is home to roughly 42,000 same‑sex couples.

Saudi billionaire Prince Alwaleed bin Talal was released from detention at Riyadh’s Ritz-Carlton on Saturday, more than two months after being held in a sweeping anti-corruption crackdown. A senior Saudi official said his release followed a financial settlement approved by the attorney general, though officials declined to disclose terms. Prince Alwaleed told Reuters in an interview hours before his release that he expected to be cleared, maintained his innocence of corruption charges, and anticipated retaining full control of Kingdom Holding Co. He described his confinement as a “misunderstanding,” said he supported Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s reforms, and displayed no sign of mistreatment during a suite tour. Saudi authorities have released dozens of detainees after settlements or dropped charges while still holding others; the attorney general said 90 had been freed and about 95 remained detained. Officials expect settlements to raise as much as $100 billion, though analysts question that target. The prince’s detention had alarmed foreign investors because of his high-profile stakes in companies like Twitter and Citigroup. After release, he said he would remain in Saudi Arabia and resume managing his global investments.

Casey Affleck has withdrawn from presenting the Best Actress award at the Oscars and will not attend the ceremony, citing concerns that his presence could distract from the actresses’ performances. Deadline first reported the decision, which Affleck framed as avoiding a “no-win situation” amid the heightened scrutiny of the #MeToo and Times Up movements. The move follows renewed attention to allegations from 2010 by two women who worked on I’m Still Here, the film Affleck directed. The women filed lawsuits alleging sexual harassment and other inappropriate conduct; the cases were settled out of court. Affleck has denied the claims and previously considered counter-suing; in a 2016 New York Times profile he described the matter as settled and expressed regret over its effects on others. Public reaction included petitions urging the Academy to bar him from presenting; a Care2 petition gathered thousands of signatures. Traditionally, the previous year’s Best Actor presents Best Actress, so Affleck’s absence changes that Oscar convention for 2018. The Academy thanked him for keeping focus on the show and nominees. His withdrawal reflects ongoing industry efforts to avoid spotlighting figures enmeshed in sexual misconduct controversies while the awards attempt to center achievements.

Caitlyn Jenner’s highly publicized transformation and Vanity Fair debut have generated widespread attention and family reactions, as well as new media projects and private family news. In teased excerpts from her Vanity Fair interview, Jenner—formerly Bruce—described how difficult it was to choose a new name. She considered options like Heather and Cathy and even searched for inspiration in unlikely places such as the Miss America pageant. The name Caitlyn became a frontrunner when her assistant Rhonda independently suggested it; Jenner’s enthusiastic response to the coincidence helped seal the decision. She also wrestled with spelling, ultimately choosing to break from the Kardashian family’s familiar “K” naming pattern. Jenner, who was married to Kris Jenner and was a step-parent to the Kardashian siblings, faces the additional challenge of acclimating family members: her 88-year-old mother, Esther Jenner, praised Caitlyn’s Vanity Fair look and said Caitlyn seemed “so much more at ease,” but admitted she still finds it hard to stop calling her child Bruce and expects it will be a struggle to adjust.

Meanwhile, confidential reports surfaced that Kim Kardashian is quietly pregnant with twins after a successful in vitro fertilization procedure that produced two fertilized eggs. According to the unnamed source, Kim has told only a few people—her mother, sisters and husband Kanye West—and is waiting to see whether both embryos will implant and be healthy before making any announcement. Kim’s recent public behavior reflects a desire to let Caitlyn have her spotlight: she’s reportedly lying low about the pregnancy and planning a family outing intended to be “accidentally” photographed by paparazzi to show public support. Kim, who has documented fertility struggles on Keeping Up With the Kardashians, is also dealing with morning sickness and laryngitis while avoiding antibiotics because of the pregnancy.

Caitlyn is set to further share her transition in a new E! documentary, I Am Cait, which promises an intimate look at her life as a transgender woman. Promos show her learning makeup techniques, reflecting on gender pressures, and expressing the relief of living authentically. The series premieres Sunday, July 26, and aims to broaden conversations about identity, acceptance and what Jenner describes as becoming “the new normal.”

Joshua Holt, a 26-year-old American and former Mormon missionary from Utah, has released urgent cellphone videos pleading for help from a Venezuelan prison where he fears for his life amid a violent inmate uprising. Holt, who moved to Caracas in 2016 to marry Thamara Candelo — a woman he met online — has been held at the notorious El Helicoide detention center for about two years after police claimed to have found an AK-47 and a grenade in the couple’s apartment. He remains jailed without formal charges, and has repeatedly sought U.S. government assistance.

In two short Facebook videos and written posts, Holt describes begging his government for two years with no resolution and says he is “not a political pawn” but a human being who wants to live with his wife and children. He warns that guards are at the prison and people are trying to break into his room to kill him. The U.S. embassy in Venezuela expressed concern about his safety, tweeting that Holt and other political prisoners are in danger and that the Venezuelan government is responsible for their safety.

The unrest at El Helicoide unfolded as videos posted by inmates showed they had taken control of parts of the facility, alleging torture, human rights abuses and extortion. Prisoners, including jailed opposition figures, denied government claims that authorities had “normalized” the situation. Venezuela’s Attorney General Tarek William Saab said he sent a commission to negotiate and described the incident as a prisoner protest that had reached a “positive agreement,” while rejecting allegations of torture and minors being detained there. Regional leaders and many countries, including the U.S. and several Latin American nations, condemned President Nicolás Maduro’s government and urged suspension of upcoming presidential elections, calling them illegitimate amid a deep economic and humanitarian crisis. U.S. diplomats acknowledged uncertainty about the situation inside the detention center and called for accountability for detainees’ safety.

David Goldberg, 47, chief executive of online survey company SurveyMonkey and husband of Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg, died suddenly Friday night. The news was shared on Facebook by his brother and amplified by Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Goldberg’s career began in music and media: at 26 he sold his first start-up, Launch Media, to Yahoo for $12 million, later serving as general manager of Yahoo Music and working at Benchmark Capital as entrepreneur in residence. In 1999 he bought a small online survey company and built SurveyMonkey into a billion-dollar business.

Goldberg and Sandberg met in Los Angeles in 1996 while both working there; they remained friends when Sandberg moved to Washington, D.C., and began dating six years later. He praised Sandberg as an invaluable partner, regularly seeking her advice and joking that he often tells his team, “Well Sheryl said.” The couple emphasized family life despite demanding careers, committing to leave work by 5:30 p.m. to be with their children; Goldberg described structured evening time with his kids and acknowledged working later at night when necessary.

As a leader, Goldberg promoted work-life balance, limited formal meetings to three weekly to prevent time waste, and kept an open-door approach for informal conversations. He valued allowing employees to fail as a means of learning and growth, intervening only when failure is repeated. Goldberg framed progress as a long-term endeavor rather than urgent daily wins, reinforcing his belief that giving teams choices and modeling balance mattered as much as business results.

Saudi Arabia stunned the international community by refusing to take up its newly won nonpermanent seat on the U.N. Security Council, protesting what it called the Council’s double standards and failure to resolve major Middle East crises. The Foreign Ministry said Riyadh would refrain from membership until reforms allow the Council to effectively maintain international peace, citing its inability to resolve the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, to halt Syria’s civil war, and to prevent regional proliferation — implicitly criticizing Western inaction and the U.S.–Iran rapprochement after President Obama’s call with Iran’s Hassan Rouhani. The decision reflects deep Saudi frustration with Washington, long its closest ally, over policies since the Arab Spring that Riyadh opposes and over perceived U.S. blocks to action against Israel. The move followed Saudi anger that Syrian President Bashar al-Assad avoided strikes after agreeing to relinquish chemical weapons, and comes amid broader regional strains, including U.S. cuts to Egyptian military aid. The volte-face surprised Saudi elites who had celebrated the seat and had signaled a desire for a more public diplomatic role; analysts say it also fits Saudi reluctance to be constrained by high-profile Security Council politics. Russia criticized the gesture. Diplomats expect the decision to stand; formal notification to the U.N. and timing for selecting a replacement remain unresolved.

Rolling Stone’s August 5, 2010 issue profiles Leonardo DiCaprio amid the success of Inception, revealing a candid, often anxious side behind his public persona. Despite his confident on-screen presence, DiCaprio describes routine, irrational worries—small, arbitrary things that churn his stomach and force him to mentally check items and reassure himself that the stress isn’t worth it. He links this tendency to the way his mind stores and magnifies trivial concerns. The piece also reflects on the aftermath of his 1997 breakthrough in Titanic: a period when he “got to be wild and nuts” and enjoyed Hollywood nightlife without becoming one of its cautionary tales. DiCaprio says he avoided the “tornado of chaos” that engulfed some peers, noting with sadness that two contemporaries he competed with as a young actor—Jonathan Brandis and River Phoenix—died prematurely, one by suicide and one from a heroin overdose. He emphasizes that he never got into hard drugs or the excesses that lead to such outcomes. On romance, DiCaprio admits Titanic complicated his dating life, diminishing the organic interactions he had before fame and introducing stigma about people’s motives for approaching him. The full interview, including more on his career, love life, and nightmares, appears in Rolling Stone’s issue and is available in full to All Access subscribers.

Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas announced he will seek full UN membership for Palestine at the UN General Assembly, asking the Security Council to recommend statehood based on pre-1967 borders (East Jerusalem, West Bank, Gaza). He framed the move as a peaceful, diplomatic bid to secure international recognition that the territories are occupied and to place Palestinians on equal footing for future negotiations over Jerusalem, borders, refugees and prisoners. Abbas said recognition would not end occupation immediately but would strengthen legal and diplomatic avenues and isolate Israeli policies rather than Israel itself. Israel rejected a unilateral UN approach, and Prime Minister Netanyahu warned peace requires direct talks; some Israeli ministers proposed punitive responses. The U.S. has indicated it will veto Security Council admission, arguing statehood must come from negotiations, a stance that risks accusations of double standards amid regional uprisings. Arab states back Abbas, while Hamas dismissed the bid and banned Gaza demonstrations. Admission requires a Security Council recommendation with no veto, then a two-thirds General Assembly vote; the U.S. veto likely blocks immediate success but procedural delays or alternate UN routes remain possible.

A large body of research suggests that optimism and happiness are linked to better cardiovascular health. Multiple analyses, including a broad review of more than 200 studies and a focused examination of over 5,100 adults, found that people with higher levels of optimism and life satisfaction had substantially lower risks of heart disease and stroke. One multi-study review reported happier people had better heart outcomes overall, reinforcing earlier findings that poor mental health (depression, anxiety) worsens cardiac prognosis. The University of Illinois-led analysis of data from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) measured cardiovascular health using the American Heart Association’s Life’s Simple 7 metrics—blood pressure, BMI, fasting glucose, cholesterol, diet, physical activity, and smoking—scored to produce a 0–14 total health score. Participants with the highest optimism were about twice as likely to meet criteria for ideal cardiovascular health and 55–76 percent more likely to fall into intermediate or ideal health ranges, even after adjusting for socio-demographic factors and poor mental health. Optimists showed better blood sugar and cholesterol, healthier BMIs, greater physical activity, and lower smoking rates. While causality remains unclear—optimism might directly protect health through biobehavioral pathways, or healthier people may simply feel more optimistic—some studies found protective associations after controlling for behaviors and socioeconomic status. The researchers argue that boosting psychological well-being could be a viable public-health strategy to improve cardiovascular outcomes at the population level, potentially helping meet AHA goals for reducing heart disease. Further prospective analyses from MESA are planned to examine optimism’s long-term effects.

Disney’s Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales opened at number one domestically but with underwhelming results for a $230 million production. The Johnny Depp-led sequel earned an estimated $62.2 million over the three-day weekend and about $77 million across the four-day holiday, marking the weakest opening for the franchise outside the original. Earlier sequels opened much higher, yet strong international demand—an estimated $208.4 million overseas—buoys its global debut to roughly $270.6 million for the weekend and over $300 million by Monday, keeping the series profitable with over $4 billion worldwide to date. The film features Javier Bardem as Captain Salazar and returns Orlando Bloom and Keira Knightley; directors are Joachim Rønning and Espen Sandberg. Paramount’s Baywatch badly underperformed, earning about $18.1 million three-day ($22 million four-day) against a $60–70 million budget, blamed partly on poor reviews despite positive research testing. Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 continued to perform, nearing $340 million domestically, while Alien: Covenant and Everything, Everything rounded out the top five. Disney’s slate also hit milestones, with several releases boosting studio box-office dominance in 2017.

A heated confrontation threatened between Occupy Wall Street protesters and the NYPD over a planned cleanup of Zuccotti Park, the movement’s 28-day encampment. Brookfield Properties, which owns the privately owned public space, demanded a power wash, calling conditions “unsanitary and unsafe.” The city scheduled cleaning for Friday morning and said demonstrators could return afterward — but Police Commissioner Ray Kelly warned that sleeping bags, tents and other camping gear would be barred. Protesters saw the move as a pretext for eviction, vowed to resist, and called supporters to form human chains at 6 a.m., risking mass arrests. Occupiers have mounted their own sanitation efforts: volunteers swept, hauled trash, rented power washers (which lacked a water source), bought supplies with movement funds, and even planted flowers. Civil liberties lawyers representing the protesters wrote to Brookfield asserting a sanitation crew has been active and offered to meet to resolve the dispute. Local politicians and union figures rallied with the occupiers, criticizing Mayor Bloomberg’s stance and warning against heavy-handed tactics. Some supporters, including Russell Simmons, offered to fund cleaning to avert confrontation. The standoff raised concerns that arrests could boost sympathy and publicity for the movement.

Noel Cintron, who served as Donald Trump’s personal driver for more than two decades, has sued the Trump Organization claiming significant unpaid overtime, inadequate raises and improper benefit changes. Cintron, 59, says he worked as Trump’s driver until the Secret Service assumed that role in 2016 and that he was on call daily from 7 a.m. until Trump, family members, or associates no longer needed him. He alleges he regularly worked long hours—up to about 55 hours per week—and accumulated roughly 3,300 hours of uncompensated overtime in his final six years, which he calculates amounts to about $178,000. Cintron’s complaint details a stagnant pay history: a $62,700 salary in 2003, a $68,000 increase in 2006, and a 2010 raise to $75,000 that he says was contingent on surrendering his health insurance. He alleges that losing benefits effectively clawed back much of that raise, saving the company roughly $17,866 annually. The suit also claims the Trump Organization failed to provide required annual wage notices under New York law. Cintron seeks about $200,000 in damages and is limited to six years of overtime by statute of limitations. The Trump Organization responded that Cintron was “paid generously and in accordance with the law” and expects vindication in court. The case is pending in Manhattan Supreme Court as Cintron v. Trump Organization LLC.

Spanish authorities say remains found on a rural property in northwest Spain are most likely those of Denise Thiem, a 41-year-old American from Arizona who went missing April 5 while walking the Camino de Santiago pilgrimage route. Interior Minister Jorge Fernández Díaz reported that evidence and "well-founded suspicions" link the death to a 39-year-old prime suspect, Miguel Ángel Muñoz, who was arrested Friday in Grandas de Salime, Asturias, after fleeing the area. Officials said Muñoz led investigators to his small farm near the St. James Way, where the remains were recovered and are believed to be Thiem’s. The ministry described the suspect as a reclusive man little-known in his neighborhood. The search mobilized as many as 300 police and military personnel and helicopters, and Fernández Díaz said the FBI cooperated in the investigation. Thiem was last seen in Astorga, on the Camino route, about 10 kilometers east of Santa Catalina de Somoza, near the suspect’s farm. Spanish television aired footage of police taking the bearded suspect from an apartment building; authorities have released few details. The U.S. Embassy in Madrid declined to comment due to privacy rules. Thiem’s disappearance raised safety concerns about the popular 470-mile pilgrimage that draws tens of thousands annually.

Thousands gathered in Soho Monday night to remember the 49 victims of the Pulse nightclub shooting in Orlando. Among those attending were Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and London Mayor Sadiq Khan. LGBT people and supporters stood in silence on Old Compton Street, holding Pride banners and signs reading slogans such as "Not Afraid." After the silence, 49 rainbow-coloured balloons—one for each person killed—were released as the crowd applauded and cheered. The London Gay Men's Chorus joined the vigil, singing Simon & Garfunkel’s "Bridge Over Troubled Water" to an emotional audience. Vigils worldwide have paid tribute in the aftermath.

Rush Limbaugh told the author he rarely directs listeners to call Congress, noting he typically avoids using his massive radio platform for coordinated political activism. He recalled once giving out Capitol switchboard numbers in the 1990s to demonstrate how quickly calls could tie up the lines; the lines were overwhelmed then, and the toll-free numbers he shared recently likewise became unusable. Limbaugh explained he made an exception now because he believes the health care legislation fight is a pivotal moment — "this is ball game" — and that public pressure is the only effective counter because Republicans lack sufficient influence to stop it. He urged listeners to oppose both the bill’s substance and the process, arguing it would transform America into something unlike its founding principles.

A New Jersey couple, Kathryn M. Schurtz, 35, and her fiancé Joseph D. Kearney, died when their car was struck in a fiery chain-reaction crash on westbound Interstate 78 in Windsor Township, Berks County, as they drove to their wedding in Pittsburgh. The crash occurred Wednesday afternoon amid heavy traffic caused by an earlier collision. A tractor-trailer unable to stop struck the couple’s vehicle, pushing it into another tractor-trailer and triggering a chain involving five tractor-trailers; two trucks and the passenger car caught fire. Three other people were injured. State Police closed the westbound lanes for hours for investigation and cleanup; one lane of eastbound traffic reopened around 7 p.m. and westbound lanes reopened early Thursday. The accidents forced long diversions, snarled traffic, and left motorists stranded on alternate routes; local volunteer fire and rescue crews worked through the night. Schurtz, a Jersey City resident who grew up in Fanwood, attended George Washington University and earned an MBA from Notre Dame; she was head of platform partnerships for Oracle Data Cloud. Services and visitations are scheduled at Immaculate Heart of Mary R.C. Church in Scotch Plains; donations are requested to the Kathryn M. Schurtz Scholarship Fund in lieu of flowers.

Eli Manning returned from Disney World to join the New York Giants’ Super Bowl XLVI victory celebration in New York City. The parade began at Battery Place and Washington Street, winding up the Canyon of Heroes and ending at City Hall Plaza, where Mayor Michael Bloomberg presented the team with the Key to the City. All Giants players attended and huge crowds filled the streets. Coverage includes pictures, quotes and videos. Some returning soldiers question honoring troops amid parades, fearing it implies wars are over, while others argue servicemembers shouldn’t wait for wars to end to be recognized.

Attorney General Eric Holder said the Obama administration will soon issue guidance to make it easier for banks to work with state-legal marijuana businesses, aiming to reduce the large amounts of cash these businesses must hold. Holder framed the move as a public-safety measure: heavy cash on premises increases robbery and other risks. The guidance, developed with the Treasury Department, would instruct federal prosecutors and law enforcement about priorities and handling of banking relationships with marijuana-related businesses, but would not change federal law nor provide a legally enforceable safe harbor guaranteeing banks won’t face prosecution.

Banks remain cautious because marijuana is illegal federally and accepting dispensary funds can expose them to regulatory penalties or money-laundering liability. Industry groups say banks need detailed assurances before offering deposits, loans, or payment services. Dispensary operators describe daily cash-management burdens—armored cars, paying bills in cash, moving accounts—and heightened vulnerability. It is unclear whether the forthcoming guidance will apply only to states that legalized recreational use (Colorado and Washington) or also to states allowing medical marijuana. The administration previously signaled it would not aggressively challenge state legalization initiatives, focusing federal enforcement on large-scale trafficking rather than state-compliant businesses.

North Korea fired short-range missiles into the Sea of Japan over consecutive days, Yonhap and South Korean officials reported, after launching three such guided rockets on Saturday and another on Sunday. The ministry said the missiles traveled northeast, away from South Korean waters, and Seoul has increased monitoring and readiness. Short-range guided missiles travel under about 1,000 km; experts note these tests are less alarming than longer-range or satellite launches but still provoke concern because they come from North Korea. Tensions have eased since a period of near-daily threats last month, which followed the North’s December long-range rocket launch and February nuclear test and prompted tougher U.N. sanctions. The incidents contributed to a recent rupture in inter-Korean cooperation, including the Kaesong industrial complex closure.

Israeli forces and Hamas militants exchanged intense strikes across Gaza and southern Israel in a rapid escalation that raised fears of a broader ground invasion and widened regional tensions. Israel’s cabinet approved mobilizing up to 75,000 reservists and the military reported calling 16,000 to active duty as tanks and artillery massed near the Gaza border. Roads leading into Gaza and nearby highways were closed to civilian traffic, and the army warned municipalities to prepare for prolonged fighting. The offensive, dubbed Pillar of Defense, began with Israeli air strikes targeting hundreds of sites in Gaza after months of rocket attacks at southern Israel; Israel said it hit more than 600–700 targets in the initial days.

Hamas and other Gaza militants stepped up rocket fire, firing hundreds of rockets at Israel. Israel reported dozens of impacts and that its Iron Dome intercepted many others; sirens sounded in Tel Aviv and, for the first time since 1970 and the 1991 Gulf War respectively, in Jerusalem. Hamas claimed responsibility for launches toward Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, though Israel said one rocket landed in the occupied West Bank and another fell short of Tel Aviv. Rocket strikes killed at least three Israeli civilians in Kiryat Malachi and wounded others.

Gaza health officials reported rising Palestinian civilian casualties amid heavy bombardment: by various tallies some dozens were reported killed, including many children and women, and scores wounded. Israel said it targeted Hamas commanders and rocket infrastructure, including the Gaza Interior Ministry and Hamas cabinet headquarters. Hamas confirmed the deaths of some field commanders and warned Israel that a ground incursion would have “grave results.”

Egypt’s new Islamist government reacted strongly: Prime Minister Hisham Kandil visited Gaza to show solidarity and offered to mediate a truce, while President Mohamed Morsi decried the strikes and promised support for Gaza without undermining the 1979 peace treaty with Israel. International responses included U.S. backing for Israel’s right to self-defense coupled with calls for restraint and appeals to countries with ties to Hamas to press for an end to rocket fire. Diplomatic efforts were underway—Egyptian and Tunisian delegations planned Gaza visits and the U.N. secretary-general prepared regional trips—but prospects for a ceasefire remained uncertain as both sides continued exchanges and civilians on both sides endured growing fear and disruption.

A Florida woman, Felicia Nevins, says the Pasco County Sheriff’s Office publicized enough information about a private incident that her attempt at artificial insemination became widely known and left her embarrassed. Nevins and her husband have been trying to conceive for three years. While storing sperm and dry ice in a thermos, she forgot to remove a rubber O-ring and feared the container could explode. She called the sheriff’s nonemergency line; a deputy and firefighters responded, took the thermos away, safely opened it and left without discussing the matter with neighbors. 

The agency later posted a brief account on its Facebook page, using a stock photo and no name. Nevins says the post included enough details—her age, location and time—that reporters and the public could identify her through public records; media soon showed up at her door and the post was shared more than 200 times. She was distressed by harsh online comments and by what she sees as unnecessary disclosure of personal and medical information. Nevins asked that the post be removed; the sheriff’s office did not take it down and said it does not delete comments. 

Pasco Sheriff Chris Nocco defended the post as part of the department’s social media strategy to show the variety of calls officers handle and to share safety information. The agency later said it avoids publishing names or identifying details and that any identifying information came from public records obtained and published by media. Critics say the office could have warned about dry-ice dangers without prompting public identification and ridicule; supporters applaud transparency and public safety messaging. Nevins said she will unfollow the department and criticized what she called belittling behavior by the agency.

In late September 2017, several European monitoring networks detected elevated levels of ruthenium-106, a radioactive isotope produced in nuclear fission and used in medicine, prompting an investigation by France’s nuclear safety technical institute IRSN. Measurements across most of Europe showed trace concentrations beginning at the end of September, peaking in early October and steadily declining after October 6; detections in France ceased after October 13. IRSN concluded the release was accidental, large in scale (estimated 100–300 TBq), and most plausibly originated in the area between the Ural Mountains and the Volga River — suggesting a facility in Russia or possibly Kazakhstan — during the last week of September. The institute ruled out a reactor accident, which would have produced other radionuclides, and excluded re-entry of a ruthenium-powered satellite based on IAEA findings. IRSN judged the likely source to be a nuclear fuel treatment installation or a radioactive medicine production site. Although the released quantity would have required local evacuation or sheltering if it had occurred in France, the concentrations measured across Europe posed no health or environmental threat. IRSN also assessed the risk of contaminated food imports (notably mushrooms) from the affected area as extremely low and advised that systematic controls on imported food were unnecessary. Russian authorities reported no known accident; IRSN had not contacted Kazakh authorities.

Soylent, the Silicon Valley–born meal-replacement company, is taking its first step into brick-and-mortar retail with a test rollout at 18 7-Eleven stores across greater Los Angeles starting July 10. Previously sold only through Soylent’s site and Amazon, the ready-to-drink bottles will be offered in three flavors—Cacao, Cafe Coffiest and a new Cafe Chai—positioned alongside energy drinks and iced coffees. 7-Eleven frames Soylent as a differentiated, on-the-go product aimed at millennials, and Soylent’s CEO Rob Rhinehart called the partnership the “first step” in a broader retail distribution plan, though no pricing or expansion details were provided (a 12-pack costs about $39 online). 

Soylent, formally Rosa Labs/Rosa Foods, markets its drinks as nutritionally complete meals providing necessary macronutrients and micronutrients in a convenient format appealing to “hacker” and efficiency-minded consumers. The brand is well funded—having raised $50 million in May to bring total funding to $74.5 million—and has leaned into marketing toward tech-savvy, time-pressed buyers. 

However, Soylent’s move into convenience stores comes amid mixed consumer reactions: the original powder has been criticized for bland, cardboard-like taste, and recent ready-to-drink flavors prompted digestion complaints and were part of multiple product recalls over an 18-month span. Soylent’s website still warns against non-authorized sellers, but 7-Eleven is explicitly exempted as an authorized retail partner for this trial. The limited rollout will indicate whether mainstream convenience-store shoppers will embrace drinkable meals beyond Soylent’s niche online following.

Hillary Clinton’s campaign on Wednesday released a detailed letter from her physician, Dr. Lisa Bardack, addressing last week’s pneumonia diagnosis and updating her medical history to counter concerns after she became ill at a 9/11 memorial. Bardack described Clinton’s illness as a “mild, non-contagious bacterial pneumonia” confirmed by a non-contrast chest CT showing a small right middle-lobe pneumonic focus. Clinton began a 10-day course of the antibiotic Levaquin and has been examined multiple times since the diagnosis; Bardack wrote that Clinton is recovering well, had a normal physical exam, and is “healthy and fit to serve as President.” The letter listed medications (including Coumadin and Armour Thyroid), vaccinations (Prevnar and Pneumovax), normal vital signs and routine lab results, and noted treatment earlier this year for sinus and ear infections that included a myringotomy tube. Doctors who reviewed the release said vitals and labs are reassuring but noted that Levaquin can cause dizziness and that some medications are uncommon choices. The campaign also released a letter declaring vice-presidential nominee Tim Kaine in “overall excellent health,” with only a vitamin D recommendation. Critics had faulted the campaign for delays in disclosing the earlier episode.

In the run-up to Facebook’s $16 billion IPO, underwriter Morgan Stanley’s consumer Internet analyst Scott Devitt and analysts at other lead banks unexpectedly cut revenue forecasts during the company’s roadshow—an unusually timed move that shocked institutional investors. The revisions followed Facebook’s May 9 amended SEC prospectus warning that revenue growth could be hurt by rapid mobile migration, where advertising is less lucrative. Morgan Stanley told some major clients the new estimates—Q2 revenue cuts to roughly $1.11 billion and full-year 2012 down to about $4.85 billion—while it’s unclear how broadly the information was shared. Sources say the selective, verbal dissemination to sophisticated investors likely dampened institutional demand and contributed to Facebook shares plunging more than 18% below the $38 IPO price within days. Critics argue the practice amounts to unfair selective disclosure—privileging big investors with materially negative guidance not available to retail buyers—and possibly violates securities rules. Regulators including the SEC and FINRA have signaled interest and inquiries, and the episode has triggered debate over underwriter conduct, transparency of analyst estimates, and protections for smaller investors in large IPOs.

The documents describe controversies around Florida fundraiser Harry Sargeant III and his associates, linking dubious campaign donations, Pentagon fuel contracts, and alleged bribery. Dozens of California names appeared as $500 donors to Charlie Crist’s 2006 campaign, some claiming they never gave money; many donations were bundled by Sargeant and traced to Middle East-linked intermediaries. The McCain campaign returned $50,000 tied to Sargeant amid questions about straw donors and foreign influence. Sargeant’s company, International Oil Trading Co., won large Iraq fuel contracts but was later accused by Congress and a Pentagon audit of overcharging the military by up to $204 million. A civil suit by ex-partner Mohammad al-Saleh alleges Sargeant and partner Mustafa Abu Naba'a cut him out and paid $9 million to Jordanian intelligence (“Pasha”) to secure shipping rights; Sargeant’s lawyers say the payments were legitimate subcontractor fees. Former CIA official Marty Martin, later hired by Sargeant, is implicated in emails about the transfers and criticized in press reports for ethical lapses. The scandal has prompted probes and reputational fallout for Sargeant and associates.

The New York Times Book Review published a long interview with Alice Walker in which, when asked what was on her nightstand, Walker named David Icke’s And the Truth Shall Set You Free. That casual mention prompted sharp criticism because Icke is a long-established conspiracy theorist whose work traffics in antisemitic tropes—reliance on The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, repeated invocations of “Rothschild,” claims that a Jewish cabal secretly controls world affairs, and other conspiracist and Holocaust-questioning passages. Critics, notably Tablet’s Yair Rosenberg, faulted both Walker for promoting Icke and the Times for reproducing her praise without context or qualification in a high-profile cultural forum.

The piece lays out Icke’s record—his conspiratorial claims, examples of overt antisemitic assertions from his book, and his influence—and details Walker’s long history of engaging with and endorsing his work: praising his books in interviews and blog posts since at least 2013, sharing his lectures and interviews, and promoting his writings repeatedly. Walker has also posted material widely criticized as antisemitic, including a 2017 poem attacking the Talmud and employing classic antisemitic slanders. Critics argue cultural elites have often overlooked or ignored her repeated expressions of antisemitism, sometimes excusing them as political criticism of Israel or conflating anti-Zionism with antisemitism.

The Times responded that the “By the Book” column reflects subjects’ personal tastes and is not an editorial endorsement; editors do not provide background on named books. Detractors counter that uncontextualized citations of clearly antisemitic tracts in major outlets risk amplifying bigotry and that serious cultural platforms should avoid passing on such recommendations without challenge. The controversy spotlights broader tensions about holding prominent cultural figures accountable when their views cross into hateful territory.

Federal agents allege that Brad Harris, founder and CEO of Frisco-based Novus Health Care Services, directed nurses to administer excessive doses of palliative drugs, including morphine, to hasten hospice patients’ deaths and protect company profits. An FBI affidavit obtained by news outlets says Harris — an accountant who started Novus in 2012 — instructed staff to “make this patient go bye-bye,” urged executives at a lunch to “find patients who would die within 24 hours,” and directed one employee to raise a patient’s medication to about four times the allowable maximum. In at least one instance an employee refused to comply; the affidavit does not confirm whether the alleged overdoses caused any deaths. The probe, opened in October 2014, initially targeted claims that Novus enrolled and billed Medicare and Medicaid for patients who did not qualify. The affidavit explains hospices face an “aggregator cap” that can force providers to return payments if average stays run long, creating incentives to enroll short-stay patients or, prosecutors allege, hasten deaths. FBI agents searched Novus in September 2015 and executed a warrant in February 2016 to seize emails and records; Smarsh, a data firm, turned over account data. No charges have been filed, and Harris has not responded to requests for comment.

Herman Cain, campaigning in Nashua, N.H., acknowledged he’s trailing in the first-primary state though remains optimistic about finishing strong. Speaking to roughly 250 supporters in a half-full ballroom, Cain spent much of his 22-minute talk addressing controversies dogging his campaign—sexual harassment allegations and a widely criticized stumble on Libya—and defended his grasp of foreign policy by arguing presidents need leadership and advisers, not encyclopedic knowledge. His day was worsened when he skipped a scheduled meeting with the influential Union Leader after negotiations over C-SPAN and interview length broke down; the paper called his absence a “no-show.” New Hampshire GOP Chairman Wayne MacDonald said such scandals and perceived foreign-policy weaknesses will hurt Cain’s prospects. Polling puts Cain fourth in New Hampshire with about 8 percent, behind Mitt Romney, Ron Paul and Newt Gingrich, even as he remains more competitive nationally and in Iowa.
