Sixteen-year-old New Zealander Lorde (Ella Yelich-O’Connor) is VH1’s You Oughta Know artist for September after her breakout single “Royals” propelled her to international alternative pop success. The song became the first track by a female artist to top Billboard’s Alternative chart in 17 years and was likened to Gotye’s rapid ascent with “Somebody That I Used To Know.” Lorde says the idea came from a National Geographic photo of a baseball player wearing a shirt that read “Royals,” and from her long-standing fascination with historical aristocracy — she likens kings and queens of 500 years ago to modern rock stars and tabloids. VH1 is featuring her all month at Lorde.VH1.com. Separately, San Francisco radio station 96.5 KOIT temporarily removed “Royals” from its playlist after listeners urged the station to stop playing the song until the World Series concludes, cheering the Giants’ matchup against the Kansas City Royals.

President Obama ordered flags at the White House and federal buildings lowered to half-staff through Saturday after bipartisan criticism over a delay in honoring five service members killed July 16 in Chattanooga. The presidential proclamation called the shootings “senseless acts of violence,” honored the victims and first responders, and emphasized national unity against fear and division. The move followed earlier action by House Speaker John Boehner and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, who had directed Capitol flags lowered; the White House had initially left its flags at full-staff, prompting criticism from Republicans and veterans who said lowering flags was a needed sign of respect. White House aides had previously declined to comment on flag status.

Former U.S. Rep. Jesse Jackson Jr. and his wife, former Chicago Ald. Sandi Jackson, were sentenced in federal court after admitting to using campaign funds and filing false tax returns. Jesse Jackson Jr., 48, received 30 months in prison for spending about $750,000 in campaign money on personal items; he also agreed to a $750,000 forfeiture. Sandi Jackson, 49, was sentenced to one year for filing false joint federal tax returns that understated roughly $600,000 in income; the judge ordered $22,000 in restitution for funds she misused. U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson rejected defenses including Jackson Jr.’s bipolar disorder and Sandi’s plea to avoid incarceration for the sake of their two children, saying their conduct was knowing, organized and repetitive and stressing equal application of the law. The judge allowed staggered reporting so the couple can arrange who serves first; Jesse will report around Nov. 1. Both expressed remorse in court amid emotional scenes and pleas for leniency; supporters including Rev. Jesse Jackson attended and later offered public statements. Prosecutors depicted substantial, prolonged personal spending on luxuries and criticized defenses as insufficient. Sentences were below prosecutors’ recommendations but reflected guilty pleas that avoided trial. The outcome marks a dramatic fall for a prominent political couple.

A rat infestation at the Puerto Rico Federal Affairs Administration’s (PRFAA) Kissimmee office left boxes of donated water, food and other supplies contaminated and unsent to Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria. PRFAA Executive Director Carlos Mercader said the regional office, which had collected donations from local organizations and individuals in the hurricane’s aftermath, lacks the budget to pay shipping costs and previous attempts to forward the aid through other groups were unsuccessful. Mercader could not specify how many boxes were affected and said an inventory will be conducted to determine what can be redistributed to Puerto Rican families displaced to Central Florida; some meals already have been donated locally. The Kissimmee site had reported a rodent infestation on August 10, about a month before Maria struck, and Mercader described the building as deteriorated and old, prompting plans to relocate to more appropriate space. The office is currently managed by Mercader following the recent resignation of director Frances Ortiz. Former Kissimmee PRFAA director Juan Hernandez Mayoral called the episode “baffling” and labeled it government negligence, noting staff who repeatedly saw the boxes did nothing while needs on the island persisted. The spoiled donations add to broader criticisms of U.S. aid to Puerto Rico after Maria, including congressional scrutiny of FEMA contracts and failures—such as a $156 million award to a small Atlanta firm that delivered only a fraction of promised emergency meals—prompting calls for accountability.

Newly released deposition videos from the civil suits tied to the June 2013 Fort Worth-area crash paint a fuller picture of Ethan Couch’s privileged, largely unpunished teen life and what his family knew before the wreck that killed four and injured many. Couch, 16 at the time and now 18, admits in the tapes to heavy drinking and drug use — listing Valium, Hydrocodone, marijuana, cocaine, Xanax and ecstasy — and says he often drank at the family’s second home. He recalls almost nothing from the night of the crash, only “waking up handcuffed to the hospital bed,” while police found his BAC about three times the legal limit. 

The deposition also captures the first under-oath statements by parents Tonya and Fred Couch. They acknowledge allowing Ethan unsupervised access to the Burleson house and early driving, but largely deny knowing the extent of his drinking. Tonya says she “sometimes” disciplined him and can’t recall the last time she punished him; Fred disputes the “affluenza” concept the defense raised at trial. The tapes contradict some parental claims: Ethan denies being made to walk to work as punishment for a prior drunk‑involving summons, and Tonya admits he didn’t complete required community service. 

Psychologist G. Dick Miller’s deposition reiterates that the parents “strongly enabled” Ethan and had recommended separating him from them during sentencing. Couch avoided prison in the criminal case, receiving rehab and ten years’ probation — a decision that sparked national outrage. The families ultimately settled the civil suits; survivors and relatives continue to wrestle with grief and the sense the tragedy was preventable.

Amazon is expanding beyond retail into broader logistics, aiming to deliver anything customers want to their doorstep worldwide — but faces significant challenges in that ambition. According to a Wall Street Journal report, Amazon is preparing a new business-to-business delivery service called "Shipping with Amazon" that would pick up packages from merchants and deliver them to customers, directly competing with established carriers like FedEx and UPS. The service is set to launch in Los Angeles within weeks, initially serving third-party sellers on Amazon’s platform, with plans to extend to more cities and eventually to other businesses. Amazon intends to undercut UPS and FedEx on price, a move that rattled markets and drove shares of those carriers sharply lower in pre-market trading. Despite the potential competition, UPS said it remains a partner of Amazon and declined to comment on Amazon’s strategic decisions. The rollout underscores Amazon’s push into logistics as part of its broader strategy to control more of the delivery chain and reduce reliance on traditional carriers — a shift that could reshape shipping economics and put pressure on incumbent delivery companies. The WSJ report highlights the evolving contest between tech-driven logistics and legacy shipping providers.

Two new Pediatrics studies link common plastic-related chemicals to metabolic problems in youth but stop short of proving cause and effect. One study of 766 U.S. adolescents found higher urinary levels of DEHP, a phthalate used in packaging and medical equipment, were associated with greater insulin resistance—a precursor to Type 2 diabetes—even after adjusting for calorie intake and weight. Another study of over 10,000 children reported that those with the highest urinary bisphenol A (BPA) had twice the odds of obesity compared with those with the lowest levels. Researchers caution these associations may reflect greater intake of contaminated foods or increased storage and excretion of the chemicals in fatter tissues rather than direct toxicity. Experts note limitations of using urine to measure biologically active exposure because BPA is rapidly metabolized and blood levels remain low. Regulators view current exposure as low and generally safe, though some jurisdictions have restricted BPA in certain products. Reducing canned and heavily packaged foods can lower DEHP and BPA exposure.

As debt negotiations stall in Washington, the Commerce Department’s annual revision and first estimate for the April–June quarter paint a weaker-than-expected U.S. economy. GDP growth was only 1.3% annualized in Q2, below economists’ 1.8% forecast, and the Q1 figure was sharply revised down to a 0.4% pace from a previously reported 1.9%. Lower-than-expected inventory accumulation, weaker federal and consumer spending, higher gasoline prices, and reduced consumer outlays contributed to the downward adjustments. The revision also deepened the assessment of the 2007–2009 recession: output fell 5.1% from its start to end, a full percentage point worse than prior estimates, making it the worst postwar downturn in six decades. The government also revised 2009 output down to a 3.5% contraction (from 2.5%) and 2008 to a 0.3% decline, while nudging 2010 growth up slightly to 3.0%. The annual revisions incorporate more complete data on consumer and business spending and accompany the GDP estimate for the current quarter.

A 911 call about a shooting at Virginia College in Spartanburg on a Tuesday morning triggered a large, rapid law enforcement response before it was revealed to be an April Fools’ prank by a college employee. Shortly after 10 a.m., deputies converged on the campus after the woman’s daughter called 911 saying her mother had texted that she was hiding in a bathroom and had heard gunshots. While on the call, the daughter received a follow-up message from her mother saying it was a joke. Sheriff Chuck Wright said 15–20 deputies responded “at breakneck speed,” prepared for a mass-casualty event and likening the initial fear to Columbine or Sandy Hook. The woman, identified as 54-year-old Angela Timmons, who reportedly works in Virginia College’s financial aid office, was arrested and faces multiple charges: disturbing schools, aggravated breach of peace, and two counts of unlawful use of a telephone. She was released on personal recognizance bond and called the incident a one-second prank she regrets, claiming no intent to harm. Virginia College expressed disappointment and said it is cooperating with authorities; the school would not comment on Timmons’ employment status. Timmons said she plans to hire an attorney and felt the response was intense, though she accepted responsibility and apologized.

President Donald Trump publicly criticized Attorney General Jeff Sessions after the Justice Department filed indictments against two prominent Republican congressmen shortly before the midterm elections. In tweets, Trump framed the prosecutions as “Obama era investigations” brought forward by Sessions’ DOJ to jeopardize “two easy” Republican wins, saying the timing left insufficient time to salvage the races. His comments underscored a recurring theme: Trump’s expectation that the Justice Department operate with political sensitivity to his interests, a view at odds with the department’s intended independence.

Though Trump did not name the lawmakers, reporting points to Rep. Duncan Hunter (R-CA), indicted on charges including misuse of campaign funds stemming from a probe that began in June 2016, and Rep. Chris Collins (R-NY), charged with insider trading for conduct described in a 2017 indictment; Collins withdrew from his re-election bid while Hunter remains in his race. Both deny wrongdoing. While the seats are still likely to remain GOP-held, the indictments have energized Democrats.

Sessions has resisted political influence, asserting the department will not be improperly guided by politics and indicating he will not resign despite Trump’s repeated public admonitions — including frustration over Sessions’ recusal from the Russia probe. Some Republicans have warned that firing Sessions before the midterms would harm the party, though leaders such as Sen. Lindsey Graham suggest a DOJ leadership change may come after the election.

Israeli forces struck multiple targets in Gaza after a Palestinian sniper killed a 22-year-old Bedouin Israeli civilian, Salah Shukri Abu Latyef, who was working on fence repairs near the northern Gaza border. Israel said the shooter fired as Abu Latyef operated a tractor; he later died at Soroka Medical Center. Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Moshe Ya’alon, vowed a forceful response and held Hamas responsible. The military reported tank and air attacks hit weapon workshops, rocket launchers and other “terror infrastructure” across northern, central and southern Gaza. Hamas sources said one airstrike near an al Qassam camp in central Gaza killed a 4-year-old girl and wounded three relatives; overall Hamas cited 11 injured in the strikes and shelling. Al Qassam and other groups claimed responsibility for attacks, with some disputing whether the slain Israeli was a soldier or civilian. The UN secretary-general expressed concern, condemning the killing of Abu Latyef and deploring Palestinian civilian casualties. Israeli leaders warned Gaza’s authorities to curb attacks or face further action amid heightened tensions and recent cross-border incidents.

Francesco Schettino, captain of the ill-fated Costa Concordia that struck rocks off Giglio in January, apologized in his first full TV interview since the disaster, saying he thinks constantly about the victims and accepts responsibility as the ship’s representative. Schettino, who faces charges including multiple manslaughter, causing a shipwreck and abandoning ship, acknowledged mistakes but argued he was not solely to blame. He said he had been “distracted” and admitted failing to act decisively once the vessel neared the island, though he maintained that another officer was actually handling navigation when the hull was holed. Schettino described the accident as a breakdown in human interaction and decision-making—“a blackout in everyone’s heads and in the instruments”—and said he ordered manual navigation when he reached the deck. Investigators have criticized him for bringing the 290-meter liner too close to shore, delaying evacuation and leaving before all passengers and crew were safe. Schettino denied rumors about showing off to a woman on the bridge and broke down when asked about a five-year-old victim. He was recently released from house arrest but remains confined to his hometown while inquiries continue, which also target other officers and Costa Cruises.

The Internet Archive is conducting crawls to preserve web pages and the pages they reference so that when original links change or disappear, archived versions remain available as replacements or companions to maintain the original context. This “No More 404s” effort seeks to fix broken links across the web.

Separately, at a March 4, 2017 “March 4 Trump” rally at the Minnesota State Capitol, roughly 400 Trump supporters and about 50 counterprotesters clashed. Video and police accounts describe a disturbance in the Capitol rotunda when a group of counterprotesters — some dressed in black and wearing masks — used air horns, whistles, chants and allegedly set off fireworks or a smoke bomb. A black-clad individual was seen throwing a smoke bomb that struck, but did not injure, a 61-year-old woman.

Linwood “Woody” Kaine, 24, son of U.S. Senator and Democratic vice-presidential candidate Tim Kaine, was among five people arrested on suspicion of second-degree riot; a sixth was cited for disorderly conduct. Police say officers chased and ordered the group to stop; Kaine initially resisted, squared off with an officer, and was subdued after chemical spray and a knee strike. The Ramsey County attorney declined to file felony charges due to insufficient evidence but referred the investigation for possible misdemeanor charges; the St. Paul City Attorney’s office is reviewing the case. Local Republicans criticized the decision not to pursue charges and called for federal review, alleging political bias, while county officials denied any preferential treatment and said the investigation remains active.

German police have recovered more than 100 items stolen from John Lennon’s estate, including three leather-bound diaries and personal effects, after identifying the memorabilia at a Berlin auction house. The objects—stolen from Yoko Ono’s New York home in 2006—were put on display at Berlin police headquarters and include two pairs of Lennon’s signature round glasses, a cigarette case, handwritten music scores (including for “Woman” and “Just Like Starting Over”), contract documents related to “I’m the Greatest,” a school exercise book from 1952, and a tape and playlist from a Beatles concert in 1965. One diary contains entries dated the morning of 8 December 1980, hours before Lennon’s murder, referencing the Annie Leibovitz photo session that day.

Authorities say the haul first came to light when a bankruptcy administrator for the Berlin auction house Auctionata discovered the items in storage in July. Police seized them from the auctioneers and later arrested a 58-year-old German businessman of Turkish origin in Berlin on suspicion of handling stolen goods; more items were found hidden in his car. A second suspect, who formerly worked as Ono’s chauffeur and now lives in Turkey, is currently beyond German authorities’ reach and has a prior New York conviction linked to the theft. German prosecutors and police flew to New York to have Ono verify the recovered objects; she identified items from photos and was reportedly emotional at their retrieval. Investigators continue to examine computer files and contracts to determine how the goods reached the auction house and whether auctioneers knowingly handled stolen property. It remains unclear when all items will be returned to Lennon’s estate.

North Korea launched an unidentified projectile from Pyongyang that flew over Japan and splashed into the Pacific, officials said, marking an especially provocative test that will heighten tensions in an already anxious region. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the South Korean and U.S. militaries were analyzing the launch and had not immediately confirmed the projectile’s range. Japanese authorities reported it passed over Hokkaido and caused no damage to ships or other targets; NHK said the missile broke into three parts. The launch follows a series of recent North Korean tests: days earlier it fired what was assessed as three short-range ballistic missiles into the sea, and about a month prior it conducted a second flight test of an intercontinental ballistic missile that analysts warn could eventually reach deep into the U.S. mainland. Pyongyang often stages weapons tests and issues threats in response to U.S.-South Korean military exercises, which it characterizes as invasion rehearsals; Seoul and Washington insist the drills are defensive measures to deter North Korean aggression. Relations are unusually fraught after U.S. President Donald Trump warned of “fire and fury,” and North Korea has even discussed potentially firing missiles toward Guam. North Korea’s U.N. ambassador condemned the exercises as “provocative and aggressive,” saying the peninsula is “like a time bomb.”

Lawmakers in New York are nearing a deal to expand the state DNA database to require samples from all convicted criminals, part of a package also resolving the budget, redistricting and pension reforms. Proponents, including Manhattan D.A. Cyrus Vance Jr., cite cases where minor-conviction DNA collection helped link suspects to dozens of cold-case murders and sexual assaults; prosecutors also say the database can exonerate the wrongly convicted. Defense advocates and innocence groups insist statutory safeguards are needed so defense lawyers can access evidence and run database comparisons, warning that eyewitness misidentification and false confessions drive many wrongful convictions. Parallel negotiations touch on misdemeanor marijuana decriminalization and pension tier changes for new public employees. In Virginia, a statewide DNA audit uncovered dozens of exclusions indicating potential wrongful convictions, but authorities have been slow, secretive and sometimes ineffective in notifying people. Private attorneys and innocence groups have stepped in to locate and inform excluded individuals, criticizing the forensics lab and prosecutors for poor communication, secrecy, and procedures that impede timely exoneration.

The document compiles numerous guest accounts and news coverage about Union Street Guest House in Hudson, NY, revealing a split between some praise for its vintage decor and cleanliness and many serious complaints about service, cleanliness, management, and an unusual policy. Positive comments note tasteful antique furnishings, a roomy Gallery Suite, proximity to Warren Street shops, and reasonable rates. However, the overwhelming voice is negative: guests report noise, thin walls, creaky floors, dog waste, unsanitary bathrooms, moldy odors, poor maintenance, billing errors and withheld refunds, rude staff, and chaotic common areas. Several reviewers describe being charged incorrectly or not receiving promised refunds; others recount management threatening to deduct $500 from a wedding deposit for any negative online review—an intimidation tactic widely condemned and reported by media. The inn’s stance is that the $500 charge will be refunded if the review is removed. Many reviewers urge avoiding the property, citing unethical business practices and recommending alternate Hudson lodgings.

In the final days before the 2016 election, Hillary Clinton and her campaign sharply criticized FBI Director James Comey after he informed congressional leaders that the FBI was reviewing newly discovered emails that could be "pertinent" to its earlier probe of Clinton’s private email server. Speaking to supporters in Daytona Beach, Clinton called Comey’s decision to disclose the review so close to Election Day “unprecedented” and “deeply troubling,” arguing voters deserve “full and complete facts” and urging Comey to promptly “explain everything” and release more information. Her remarks drew boos from the crowd and marked an intensified campaign confrontation with Comey.

Top Clinton aides amplified the rebuke. Campaign chairman John Podesta said Comey should have vetted the material more thoroughly before publicizing the review and accused the director of providing “selective information.” Campaign manager Robby Mook contended the FBI’s action risked wading into political territory and violating the Justice Department practice of avoiding actions that might influence an election, calling the move unfair to both Clinton and voters. Surrogates emphasized that the newly discovered emails, uncovered during the FBI’s investigation into Huma Abedin’s estranged husband Anthony Weiner, might be duplicates and not yield new material.

The development placed Comey at the center of a contentious late-stage political fight; earlier in the year Clinton’s campaign had defended Comey’s professionalism when he recommended no charges. Now the campaign’s criticism echoed concerns voiced by others about the timing and propriety of the disclosure. Republicans, including Donald Trump and supporters like Newt Gingrich, seized on the news—Trump suggested Abedin’s role should be reconsidered and questioned whether she had received any immunity; Gingrich urged the FBI to release emails immediately. Clinton aides stressed she remained composed and focused despite the distraction, with running mate Tim Kaine and other campaign figures calling for greater FBI transparency while vowing to press forward in the campaign’s final days.

Just days after announcing their split, Scarlett Johansson and Ryan Reynolds were seen dining together, smiling and laughing at New York’s Blue Ribbon. Insiders say the meeting was a friendly, civil catch-up rather than a reconciliation—partly arranged to show they can remain amicable despite busy schedules and media speculation. Reports suggest Scarlett orchestrated the outing to manage their public image, while friends insist the pair are not getting back together.

The Gravity blanket is a high-tech weighted duvet launched on Kickstarter that uses “deep pressure touch stimulation” (also called deep touch pressure) to mimic the sensation of being hugged or swaddled. Built with high-density plastic poly pellets distributed in a grid pattern, the blanket is offered in three weights—15, 20 and 25 lbs—equating to roughly 7–12% of a user’s body weight, a guideline the creators promote. Materials include a soft fleece removable cover and a cotton inner shell intended to be breathable, washable and durable. The designers claim the pressure increases serotonin and melatonin while lowering cortisol, heart rate and blood pressure, reducing movement and promoting deeper REM sleep. They suggest potential benefits for insomnia, PTSD, OCD, ADHD and anxiety, citing small studies and historical occupational-therapy observations that deep pressure can be calming.

The product raised millions in crowdfunding but drew scrutiny after promotional language asserting it could “treat” psychiatric conditions was changed or removed following inquiries from reporters and Kickstarter, which bars medical-treatment claims. Critics and sleep experts caution that the evidence is limited—existing studies are small, often uncontrolled or unblinded—and that weighted blankets are not a substitute for medical treatment where underlying disorders exist. Gravity’s creators position the blanket as a premium, design-conscious wellness product shipping in the autumn and priced from about $169, while commentators advise skepticism about broad health claims despite some people reporting subjective calming and improved sleep. The piece also notes other recent travel-friendly cozy innovations, like duvet suits and Slanket-style wearable blankets.

Brent Scowcroft, a Republican national security heavyweight who advised presidents Ford and George H. W. Bush, endorsed Hillary Clinton, praising her international experience and temperament after Donald Trump attacked her credentials. Scowcroft highlighted her work on high-pressure issues like Iran and Israel and said she has the expertise essential for commander-in-chief. His backing followed fellow Republican Richard Armitage’s decision to support Clinton.

The document also examines President Obama’s 2013 decision not to strike Syria after a chemical-weapons “red line,” drawing on reporting that describes his reluctance to deploy troops, misreading of the Arab Spring, and regret over intervening in Libya. Obama’s unilateral cancellation of planned strikes—after consulting only his chief of staff—angered several advisers and allies and was later framed by him as a defining, proud moment of restraint.

Separately, the Associated Press fact-checked a broad June 2016 Trump speech attacking Clinton and other claims. Many of Trump’s assertions were found misleading or false: he overstated Clinton’s responsibility for Middle East instability, misrepresented Libya and Benghazi history and refugee costs, exaggerated a Brunei gift story, and misreported the China trade-deficit change. He also misstated U.S. tax burdens, Clinton’s refugee-screening and immigration positions, and the economic effects of Obamacare and his own tax plans—whose large revenue losses economists warn would balloon deficits.

Forrest Sanco and Donna Grant, both 56 and high-school friends who reconnected and fell in love, vanished during a small-plane trip in the Bahamas after planning to elope in Rum Cay. The couple flew their recently purchased Cessna 150 from Texas through Florida and into Freeport, Grand Bahama, where they cleared customs and spent the night. On Sept. 26 their Instagram shows them enjoying a Bahamian sunrise; later that day they landed in North Eleuthera around 1:30 p.m., purchased 13 gallons of fuel, and departed about 2:30 p.m. for Rum Cay, roughly 121 miles away. Forrest officially closed his flight plan at 4:58 p.m., indicating he was nearing destination, but the pair never arrived and no communication followed. Concerns grew after they failed to return to Fort Worth and missed scheduled commitments; family members realized something was wrong about 10 days later when the couple did not appear and could not be reached.

Search efforts have involved the Royal Bahamas Defence Force (RBDF) leading official operations, with U.S. Coast Guard assistance. Debris and a life raft sighted near Cat Island were later judged unrelated. The family, frustrated by perceived resource limitations and delays, has raised more than $12,000 via GoFundMe to hire private search crews and pilots. Relatives say weather that day included afternoon storms and repairs had been performed on the plane during the trip, complicating possibilities. Despite dozens of leads and private searches, every lead has produced dead ends so far. Family and friends remain devastated but determined, oscillating between hope and realism as they continue to fund and coordinate searches for Forrest and Donna and seek answers about what happened on their final flight.

In her memoir The Secrets of My Life, Caitlyn Jenner reveals she underwent gender confirmation surgery in January 2017, describing it as successful and saying she feels “wonderful” and “liberated.” The former Olympic gold medalist, who publicly came out as a trans woman in 2015 and legally changed her name and gender marker in 2016, frames the operation as a complex, carefully considered decision weighed against health risks. Jenner says she disclosed the surgery to end public speculation and intrusive questions about her body—calling for candor and adding that this will be the first and last time she discusses it. She explains practical reasons for the procedure, including wanting “to have all the right parts” and being tired of tucking. Jenner also recounts earlier procedures: in March 2015 she had breast augmentation and facial feminization surgery, after which she felt she would finally live authentically. The memoir, released April 25, also touches on broader aspects of her life and transition; reports note she received a substantial advance for the book. Jenner emphasizes that, despite complexities and risks, the surgery was a freeing step in her long journey to live as herself.

New laboratory and population studies raise concerns about long-term use of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), common over-the-counter drugs for heartburn and GERD. Researchers at Houston Methodist found that prolonged exposure to PPIs caused human endothelial cells (which line blood vessels) to exhibit features of accelerated biological aging in vitro. Treated cells lost normal anti-adhesive properties and became more prone to trapping blood elements—changes that could promote vascular blockages. The team also observed impaired lysosomal acidification in those cells: lysosomes failed to generate enough acid to clear cellular waste, leading to buildup and faster cellular aging. An H2 antagonist did not produce the same effects. Study authors caution this laboratory work cannot prove PPIs cause these changes in people; clinical trials are needed to confirm in vivo relevance. Limitations include testing only two PPIs (one commercially available, esomeprazole/Nexium) and not detailing the precise mechanism by which PPIs impair lysosomal acid production.

Separately, large Danish observational research linked PPI use to higher ischemic stroke risk: overall stroke risk rose about 21% among PPI users, with dose-dependent increases up to 79% for some drugs at high doses. Prior studies have tied PPIs to kidney disease, infections and dementia. Pharmaceutical makers emphasize labeled safety, while clinicians urge caution. Experts recommend reserving PPIs for short-term, indicated use and considering alternatives—lifestyle modifications, antacids, H2 blockers or, for severe GERD, surgical options. Patients should consult clinicians before starting or stopping therapy, weigh nonpharmacologic measures, and reassess ongoing PPI need.

After the United States defeated Japan 5-2 in the 2015 Women's World Cup final, some US Twitter users turned the victory into a controversial moment by invoking World War II events like the 1941 Pearl Harbor attack and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. “Pearl Harbor” shot into US trending topics, surging from its typical ~500 daily mentions to over 50,000 during the discussion. A hyper-patriotic, possibly parody account set off much of the commentary; its tweet “Hey Japan, that one was for Pearl Harbor” was widely retweeted. Others posted similarly provocative messages implying the soccer win was “revenge,” and a minority made jokes referencing the wartime bombings, prompting further outrage.

Many Twitter users condemned these remarks as inappropriate and insensitive, arguing that jokes about Pearl Harbor, Hiroshima, and Nagasaki are not funny and that the match should not be framed as wartime payback. Supporters of Japanese fans and many neutral observers called the comments “awful,” reminding people this was a sporting event in 2015, not a historical grievance. The episode highlighted how social media can amplify a few provocative voices and turn a sporting celebration into a heated cultural debate.

Harvard appointed Evelynn Hammonds, a scholar in history of science and African-American studies and former senior vice provost for faculty development and diversity, as dean of Harvard College, making her the first Black woman to hold the post. The move followed Harvard’s recent selection of its first female president, Drew Gilpin Faust. Hammonds, a Spelman, Georgia Tech, MIT and Harvard graduate, previously led diversity initiatives and supported faculty-family policies. Her deanship has been marked by accomplishments—new programs and residential reforms—but also controversy over covert searches of resident deans’ e-mail during a major cheating investigation. Facing criticism and publicity from that episode, Hammonds later stepped down, planned a sabbatical, and will lead a race-and-gender-in-science program.

Fifteen former staffers from the 1970s Church Committee — the bipartisan Senate inquiry that exposed widespread illegal activity by U.S. intelligence agencies — have urged President Obama and Attorney General Loretta Lynch to negotiate leniency for NSA whistleblower Edward Snowden so he can return to the United States without facing prolonged imprisonment. Led by former chief counsel Frederick Schwarz Jr. and ex-staff director William Green Miller, the group’s eight-page letter acknowledges Snowden broke the law but argues his intent was to spur reform, which his disclosures demonstrably achieved. They credit Snowden with prompting rare bipartisan changes, including amendments that ended bulk metadata collection and increased scrutiny of overseas surveillance. Drawing on the Church Committee’s own history of uncovering abuses — COINTELPRO, surveillance of civil rights leaders, CIA experiments and more — the signatories say secrecy often enables wrongdoing and that disclosure can prevent greater harm. They point to past cases of leniency for officials who mishandled classified information, such as David Petraeus, to argue comparable mitigation is appropriate for Snowden, who did not conceal his identity and accepted personal risk. While they stop short of seeking a full pardon, the former staffers call for settlement negotiations that weigh public benefits and Snowden’s motives, urging a fair, pragmatic resolution before geopolitical shifts complicate his situation.

A joint investigation by The Atlanta Journal-Constitution and The Associated Press documents systemic leniency toward physicians accused of sexual misconduct. Researchers identified roughly 450 cases from 2016–2017 in which doctors faced disciplinary action or court scrutiny; nearly half remain licensed despite allegations involving patients, staff and minors. Some physicians returned to practice even after criminal convictions. Typical penalties from state medical boards are limited—short suspensions, probation and mandated therapy—treating abusive conduct as an impairment rather than grounds for permanent revocation. High-profile scandals in other fields have spurred accountability, but medicine has shown little change: many hospitals do not report allegations, two-thirds of physicians sanctioned by employers avoided board discipline, and state boards often accept settlements that leave licenses intact.

Cases highlighted include a gynecologist in California who retained his license under probation after exposing himself and sexually inappropriate comments; a Florida doctor convicted of misdemeanor battery who still practices; an Arkansas physician facing multiple rape and assault charges allowed to continue with chaperones; and an Idaho psychiatrist whose license was later reinstated despite findings of sexual misconduct with minors. Critics point to institutional bias—boards composed largely of doctors reluctant to revoke colleagues’ licenses—opaque rehabilitation programs, weak interstate reporting, and inadequate therapeutic models. Experts say mandated treatments emphasize addiction-style remediation but lack evidence and fail to focus on victim restitution or proven sex-offender interventions. Advocates urge stricter reporting, zero-tolerance policies, and permanent revocations for proven sexual abuse to protect patients and restore public trust.

TIME’s 2013 coverage captures a year of dramatic personalities and global shifts, led by its Person of the Year: Pope Francis. In nine months as pope, Francis rewired the papacy’s tone without altering doctrine—prioritizing mercy, humility and outreach over doctrinal enforcement. Living simply, washing prisoners’ feet, embracing the poor and calling the church a “field hospital,” he has energized lapsed Catholics and drawn global attention to poverty, inequality and institutional transparency. Skeptics note entrenched Vatican bureaucracy and unresolved scandals, but Francis’s symbolic gestures, timely messages (like attacking the “idolatry of money”) and media savvy have broadened the church’s influence, especially in the growing Catholic South. He affirms traditional stances on abortion, marriage and male-only priesthood while urging less culture-war bickering and more service.

Also profiled is Edward Snowden in Moscow: the exiled whistleblower who leaked massive NSA programs and, from refuge, watched the world react—diplomatic fallout, legal charges and debates on privacy versus security. Snowden frames his acts as a warning against mass surveillance, distinguishing targeted lawful intelligence from dragnet collection that undermines civil liberties.

TIME examines Bashar al-Assad’s transformation from a hesitant successor into a ruthlessly pragmatic autocrat, surviving civil war and chemical weapons condemnation by calculating concessions that preserved his military strength and international negotiation leverage.

Finally, the magazine flags rising U.S. conservative insurgency embodied by Senator Ted Cruz, whose dramatic push to defund Obamacare and willingness to provoke a government shutdown alienated many yet burnsish his outsider credentials. Cruz rejects establishment politics, betting that being vilified by Washington equals success with a new, direct-access electorate. Together, these profiles trace shifting authority, conscience and the contest between institutions and individual conscience in 2013.

Lena Dunham celebrated body positivity after appearing on Glamour’s February 2017 cover without Photoshop, thanking the magazine in an Instagram post for showing her cellulite. She reflected on a lifetime of being told she was “funny looking” — potbelly, rabbit teeth, knock knees — and described posing as confident while feeling hurt by cruel comments. Dunham emphasized that she never hated her appearance so much as the culture that taught her to, and criticized the way her look has often been framed as brave rather than simply accepted. She argued that no one’s body should be fair game—regardless of size, color, or gender identity—and praised women in Hollywood and on Instagram who normalize varied female bodies. On the cover Dunham posed with her Girls co-stars Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet, and Allison Williams in bold outfits. The piece also includes a wide-ranging reflection on Girls’ cultural impact and an interview styled as an “exit interview” with the cast conducted by executive producer Jenni Konner. The show was noted for depicting women as realistic, imperfect people—awkward sex scenes, cramped apartments, and candid portrayals—and for pushing boundaries with nudity and frank storylines. Cast members discussed satisfactions and frustrations from working on the series: Jemima called her relationship with Dunham both most and least satisfying; Allison enjoyed character evolution but wanted more screen time; Zosia relished playing someone unlike herself but now misses the role; Dunham spoke about learning collaboration and sometimes feeling isolated as creator and showrunner when criticism landed on her. They also recalled a difficult second season and moments of tension, including Jemima briefly considering quitting. Girls’ final season premiered February 12, 2017, and the show’s influence was credited with shaping subsequent female-driven comedies and fostering new women storytellers.

A group calling itself Truckers for the Constitution (also promoted as Truckers Ride for the Constitution/Truckers to Shut Down America) planned to clog the Capital Beltway around Washington, D.C., in a multi-day protest beginning Oct. 11 to draw attention to driver grievances and broader political anger. Organizers cited low pay, high diesel costs, federal regulations (including EPA fuel-efficiency and anti-idling rules), insurance and technology mandates, and perceived erosion of Constitutional protections. Framing their action in Tea Party–style rhetoric, the truckers accused national leaders of lawlessness, named President Obama, Secretary of State John Kerry and Senators John McCain and Lindsey Graham as “domestic enemies,” and threatened to pressure lawmakers to obey the Constitution — even calling for arrests of officials via a so-called citizens’ grand jury. Coordinators said trucks would circulate the 64-mile I-495 beltway “three lanes deep,” keeping one lane open for emergencies, and expressed willingness to escalate if challenged. Plans drew thousands of online RSVPs and controversy over legality and public-safety impacts; organizers later updated that they would not attempt to arrest members of Congress.

A new report by the Syrian Centre for Policy Research (SCPR) paints a harrowing picture of five years of conflict in Syria, estimating 470,000 deaths—nearly double the United Nations’ previous figure of 250,000—because it counts both direct violence (about 400,000) and indirect deaths from collapsed services, disease, hunger and displacement (about 70,000). The SCPR finds 11.5% of Syrians have been killed or injured since 2011, with 1.9 million wounded, life expectancy plunging from 70 (2010) to 55.4 (2015), and aggregate economic losses around $255 billion. The report documents dramatic social and economic collapse: 45% of the population displaced (6.36 million internally, over 4 million abroad), a 21% population shrinkage, 13.8 million losing livelihoods, soaring consumer prices (53% rise in one year), and an 85% jump in poverty in 2015. It attributes continued fragmentation to coercion, black market economics, war profiteering (including oil revenues for armed groups), and international interventions that deepen polarization. The UN halted counting deaths in mid-2014 citing data access problems; SCPR says its rigorous field-based methods provide a more complete toll, including indirect mortality often ignored. Amid continued fighting—particularly around Aleppo, where advances backed by Russian strikes and allied militias threaten to cut the city off—the international diplomatic effort in Munich seeks a ceasefire. Washington demands an immediate halt with full humanitarian access, wary that delayed or staged ceasefires could allow government and Russian forces to crush opposition groups before talks resume.

A large University of Southern California study published in Pediatrics tracked 5,490 Southern California adolescents across cohorts graduating between 1995 and 2014 to examine cigarette and e-cigarette (vaping) use. Traditional cigarette smoking among 12th graders fell from about 19% in 1995 to 9% in 2004 and then plateaued at roughly 8% in 2014. However, when e-cigarette use was included, the combined prevalence of past-30-day cigarette or e-cigarette use among seniors in 2014 rose to about 14%, comparable to smoking levels seen a decade earlier. The pattern held across grades, sexes, and Hispanic and non-Hispanic white groups. Researchers conclude e-cigarettes are not simply replacing cigarettes; instead they appear to be attracting adolescents who otherwise would not have used tobacco, raising overall nicotine exposure among youth.

Follow-up longitudinal analyses found that never-smoking adolescents who vaped were far more likely to begin smoking combustible cigarettes over roughly 16 months: e-cigarette users had more than six times the odds of initiating cigarettes compared with never users, even after adjusting for potential confounders and prior use of other combustible products. The association was strongest among youth who initially reported no intention to smoke.

Experts warn that e-cigarette liquids often contain nicotine (with widely variable concentrations), flavorings appealing to youth, and other inhalation risks; the products were largely unregulated until recently. While some argue many teens vape nicotine-free flavors socially, mounting evidence links adolescent vaping to nicotine addiction risk and subsequent cigarette initiation. The study authors call for more longitudinal research, stronger youth-focused tobacco control, and regulation to prevent a new generation from developing nicotine dependence.

A Blue Angels F/A-18 fighter jet crashed Thursday during a practice near Smyrna, Tennessee, outside Nashville, killing the pilot days before a scheduled weekend air show. A U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, identified the pilot as Marine Capt. Jeff Kuss, who joined the Blue Angels in 2014 and logged more than 1,400 flight hours. Smyrna town manager Harry Gill said the pilot was the only casualty and no civilians on the ground were injured. The Navy reported the crash occurred as the jet was beginning its takeoff during an afternoon practice; five other F/A-18s landed safely moments later. Adm. John Richardson, the Navy’s top officer, expressed condolences and pledged a full investigation to help prevent similar incidents. The crash came the same day as a separate incident involving the Air Force Thunderbirds: a Thunderbird pilot ejected safely after a crash in Colorado following a flyover at the Air Force Academy graduation. Kuss, a Durango, Colorado native, was commissioned in 2006 and had served in Afghanistan before joining the Blue Angels. Local residents who had been watching practice described shock and sorrow. Retired teacher Brenda Lewis said she’d stepped away briefly and then heard a loud boom, later seeing smoke and emergency responders; she said the event left her heartbroken. Phil Dennis, who grew up attending airshows, watched the jet appear to come out of a loop and dive toward trees, followed by a massive fireball; he described feeling shaken and stunned. The report included separate coverage of deadly flooding in Texas: at Fort Hood, three soldiers were killed and six were missing after an Army truck was swept off a flooded crossing; heavy rains have produced widespread flooding in Texas, forcing evacuations and raising rivers to record or near-record levels.

CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta briefly became the subject of online ridicule after he sent a two-word direct message—“F**k you”—to Justin Caporale, a GOP consultant and former Melania Trump aide, following a Twitter exchange about loud music at a Trump rally. Acosta had tweeted from the Missoula, Montana event that the Trump campaign and White House had turned up the music so loudly that press risers were vibrating and live TV was nearly impossible; he also raised a possible security concern for the Secret Service and local law enforcement. Caporale replied mockingly, “Dear Diary…..,” which provoked Acosta’s blunt private response. Caporale posted a screenshot showing Acosta’s message and that Acosta then blocked him; Daily Caller reporter Peter Hasson verified the DM’s authenticity. Conservatives seized on the interaction to mock Acosta, and the incident circulated widely. Early the next morning Acosta apologized on Twitter, saying he had mistaken Caporale for an old campaign friend and expressing regret if he offended him. CNN declined to comment and Acosta did not immediately respond to requests for further comment. The episode follows Acosta’s history of contentious exchanges with the Trump administration, where he has been a frequent target of criticism by the president and his allies.

Dennis Rodman, the former NBA star known for his unconventional diplomacy with North Korea, has recently been involved in two notable developments. On the diplomatic front, Rodman reiterated that he has not spoken with President Donald Trump in some time and criticized the president’s frequent Twitter attacks on North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Rodman—who has visited Pyongyang and met Kim on multiple occasions—said he would welcome a call from Trump to offer perspective on Kim, noting Trump has “never met him” and “never talked with his people.” Rodman suggested that while people may call Kim “crazy,” they should consider what Kim has actually done to the U.S. or others, implying that personal contact and context matter before passing judgment.

Separately, Rodman was arrested for driving under the influence in Newport Beach. Police stopped him around 11 PM for a traffic violation, administered a field sobriety test which he failed, and say he blew over the legal 0.08 blood-alcohol limit on a breathalyzer. He was handcuffed, taken to the station, held for about seven hours, and then released when officers determined he was sober enough to care for himself. Rodman reportedly cooperated with police. His representative told TMZ that alcoholism has been an on-and-off struggle for him over the past 15 years and that he is facing tough personal issues; the rep said they plan to encourage Rodman to return to rehab. This is not his first DUI: he was previously arrested for DUI in 1999.

The USDA and EPA announced the United States’ first national food waste reduction goal: cut food loss and waste 50% by 2030. The federal government will convene a partnership of charitable and faith-based groups, the private sector, and local, state and tribal governments to reduce food losses across the supply chain, improve food security, and conserve natural resources. Food loss and waste now account for roughly 31% of the U.S. food supply—about 133 billion pounds annually—and are a major component of municipal solid waste and methane emissions from landfills. Officials note that even a 15% reduction would free enough food to feed over 25 million Americans annually. The move builds on existing efforts such as the U.S. Food Waste Challenge, launched in 2013, which surpassed its initial participation goals by 2014. USDA has pursued related actions—an app on safe food storage and date labels, guidance to encourage donations of sub-spec or misbranded food, and research into cost-effective technologies—while launching a new consumer education campaign and ChooseMyPlate.gov guidance on reducing household waste. The agencies will press the private sector, including food service companies, retailers and institutions, to set aggressive reduction targets; industry groups like the Consumer Goods Forum have pledged similar goals. Officials framed the initiative as part of broader climate and environmental commitments by the administration.

Federal land managers abruptly halted a weeklong roundup of cattle belonging to Nevada rancher Cliven Bundy, citing serious safety concerns after armed supporters and militia gathered to protest the removals. BLM Director Neil Kornze said contracted wranglers and rangers had gathered about 400 cows—short of a planned 900—but decided to release roughly 300 head back to the range to avoid potential violence as tensions escalated near Bunkerville and along Interstate 15, which was briefly blocked by protesters. The dispute dates to the 1990s, when Bundy stopped paying grazing fees after rule changes meant to protect the desert tortoise; the BLM says he owes about $1 million. Bundy, who asserts state sovereignty and that his family has grazed the land since the 1800s, did not comment after the operation ended. Clashes during the week included a videotaped scuffle involving rangers with Tasers and dogs and protesters who said they were mistreated; federal officials reported assaults and a kicked police dog. Nevada officials, including Gov. Brian Sandoval and Sen. Dean Heller, urged calm and praised safety-focused resolution efforts, while local law enforcement mediated the exit of BLM personnel. The incident remains under federal investigation.

Thae Yong-ho, 55, the No. 2 diplomat at North Korea’s London embassy, has defected to South Korea with his wife and children, Seoul confirmed. A senior and trusted official—whose family had a notable legacy in North Korean history—Thae lived in Britain for about a decade, socializing locally, promoting the regime’s image, and even escorting a brother of Kim Jong-un to a concert. His disappearance from the embassy surprised colleagues; details of how he evaded embassy monitors remain unclear. South Korean officials say Thae expressed disillusionment with Kim Jong-un’s increasingly isolated government, citing disgust with the regime, admiration for South Korea’s democratic system, and concern for his family’s future. He had been pressured in London to rebut criticism of North Korea’s human rights record, and formerly defended the state publicly. South Korea has placed Thae and his family under government protection.

Jeffrey Tambor has reemerged publicly amid a sustained controversy following his February firing from Amazon’s Transparent after accusations of inappropriate and sexually harassing behavior by two transgender colleagues, Van Barnes and Trace Lysette. The dispute exploded in late 2017 after Barnes posted a #MeToo account alleging unwanted advances, crude comments, and exploitation; Lysette later detailed an on-set incident she described as sexual touching during a scene. Tambor has admitted to being “mean,” “difficult,” moody and prone to outbursts, and acknowledges past yelling and temperamental behavior on multiple sets, but he denies the more serious sexual misconduct claims. Amazon conducted a lengthy investigation and opted not to renew his option; Tambor says he was devastated and stunned by the firing, having expected only a reprimand for his temper.

The controversy is complicated by Transparent’s status as a landmark show for transgender representation and by debates over casting a cisgender man in a trans role. Some cast and crew rallied behind Tambor—Jason Bateman, David Cross and others voiced support—while Alia Shawkat and showrunner Jill Soloway publicly expressed sympathy for the accusers and stressed the broader cultural moment. Investigations included many interviews; Tambor says he answered questions with his lawyer present and issued evolving statements that ranged from denial to partial admission of bad behavior. Relationships fractured: Soloway and Tambor have not spoken since she told media she respected Barnes and Lysette; Tambor says he feels abandoned.

Barnes and Lysette have pursued different paths since going public—Lysette remains active in acting and activism, Barnes returned to Missouri—and the Transparent team is planning a final season without Tambor. Tambor, emotionally affected, says he is learning to be more present and patient, spending time with family and continuing to appear in Arrested Development’s new season while the broader reckoning around workplace conduct and accountability continues.

Tyra Banks will host the 12th season of America’s Got Talent, NBC announced, replacing Nick Cannon after his eight-year run. The supermodel, Emmy winner and creator of America’s Next Top Model joins returning judges Simon Cowell, Mel B, Heidi Klum and Howie Mandel. Banks said she’s excited to connect with contestants and plans to get a few to “smize” for the audience. The talent competition, which awards a $1 million prize, showcases a wide variety of acts and will air live this summer from the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles. Separately, the Internet Archive is crawling and preserving web pages—capturing live versions so references won’t break when original pages change or disappear.

The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) confirmed that a Russian-linked hacking group, known as Fancy Bear (also APT28 or Tsar Team), breached its Anti-Doping Administration and Management System (ADAMS) and published confidential medical records of several high-profile U.S. athletes. On Monday the group released documents showing Therapeutic Use Exemptions (TUEs) for tennis players Serena and Venus Williams, gymnastics champion Simone Biles, and basketball star Elena Delle Donne. Fancy Bear framed the disclosures as evidence that American Olympians were using “licenses for doping,” saying it had identified “dozens of American athletes” who tested positive after studying the hacked database and promising further leaks.

WADA and U.S. anti-doping authorities forcefully rejected that characterization. WADA said the cyberattacks were criminal acts aimed at undermining the global anti-doping system and re-establishing trust after its investigations revealed state-sponsored Russian doping. Director General Olivier Niggli emphasized the threat to athletes whose private medical information had been exposed. U.S. Anti-Doping Agency chief Travis Tygart called the hack “cowardly and despicable,” noting each athlete had followed the global rules to obtain TUEs for legitimate medical needs. USA Gymnastics and the U.S. Olympic Committee likewise said the athletes had done nothing wrong and had adhered to medical guidelines.

The leaked files show that Biles had a TUE for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder medication, Serena Williams had permissions for treatments commonly used for muscle injuries, and similar routine exemptions were detailed for others. Specialists and former anti-doping officials said the content looked normal and stressed the core issue was a privacy breach, not newly revealed wrongdoing. The International Olympic Committee condemned the method and affirmed that none of the athletes named violated anti-doping rules at the Rio Games.

WADA said the intrusion was likely accomplished through spear-phishing to harvest passwords; it noted a recent prior breach of the ADAMS account of Yuliya Stepanova, the Russian whistleblower who exposed systematic doping. The incident adds to tensions following WADA’s report that led to bans for many Russian athletes and comes amid broader investigations into Russian hacking activity. Cybersecurity analysts and critics view the leak as retaliation intended to tarnish reputations and erode trust in anti-doping institutions while raising fresh concerns about the security of athlete medical data.

Israel launched a ground offensive into the Gaza Strip after 11 days of intense exchanges with Palestinian militants, sending troops and tanks to target Hamas infrastructure, including cross-border tunnels. The government framed the move as necessary to protect Israeli civilians and "strike a significant blow to Hamas"; military spokespeople warned Gaza residents to evacuate operational zones. Gaza health officials reported at least 24 Palestinians killed and 200 wounded since the ground phase began, including a five-month-old; Gaza sources put total deaths since 8 July at more than 250, most civilians. Israel reported killing militants overnight and suffered its first soldier fatality in the invasion; Israeli civilians and soldiers were also reported killed or injured by rocket and mortar fire. Heavy clashes and bombardment were reported, with damage to homes and hospitals and displacement of thousands. Diplomacy continued in Cairo amid ceasefire efforts; Hamas condemned the invasion and vowed resistance, while Palestinian and regional leaders warned the offensive would escalate bloodshed.

The Republican National Convention’s speaker lineup showcased a pop-culture–heavy, nontraditional roster as the GOP moved to formally nominate Donald Trump. The Tuesday program, themed “Make America Work Again,” aimed to highlight Trump’s business credentials and included a mix of party leaders, former rivals, family members, and celebrities. High-profile congressional figures such as House Speaker Paul Ryan, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and House Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy were scheduled to speak in a display of party unity, even as some Republicans remained visibly uneasy. Former primary opponents Chris Christie and Ben Carson were also on the bill; Christie offered to argue Trump’s readiness for office, despite being passed over for VP.

A number of unconventional surrogates underscored the campaign’s showbiz bent: UFC president Dana White, pro golfer Natalie Gulbis, reality star Willie Robertson, actors Scott Baio and Antonio Sabato Jr., and soap-opera actress Kimberlin Brown — famous for her villainous roles on The Young and The Restless and The Bold and the Beautiful — all took the stage. Brown, who also runs an avocado farm, hosts a design show and operates an online boutique, was given a primetime slot and introduced by Ben Carson. Tiffany Trump made her national-stage debut that night as well.

The convention’s faster-than-usual roll call formally secured Trump’s nomination after Never Trump objections were quelled. The evening sought to fuse celebrity appeal with economic messaging, featuring Trump family members, business associates, and lesser-known local supporters such as restoration-company owner Andy Wist, all intended to present Trump as the candidate best positioned to revive the economy.

Two weeks after Sandra Bland, 28, was found hanging in a Waller County, Texas, jail cell following her arrest for failing to signal a lane change, a viral theory claimed she was already dead in her mugshot. Social media users and some outlets pointed to photo details—background color, shoulder position, hair, and a supposed flatness in her eyes—as evidence. Major outlets like BuzzFeed, Complex, The Independent and USA Today covered the controversy. Leading forensic experts strongly rejected the claim. Dr. Michael Baden, a veteran forensic pathologist who performed a family-requested Michael Brown autopsy, called the idea “ridiculous,” noting a low-resolution headshot cannot establish life or death; only clear signs like marked decomposition would allow determination from a photo. Other pathologists with decades of experience agreed it is impossible to tell from the mugshot alone. Baden emphasized that mugshots are taken at booking and that the conspiracy doesn’t explain why officials would delay announcing a death for days. Separately, questions about the circumstances of Bland’s arrest and death remain: dashcam footage showed an officer threatening her with a stun gun; booking documents contained inconsistencies about medications and prior suicide attempts; and details about how she reportedly hanged herself and evidence handling prompted scrutiny. Prosecutors later released booking video showing Bland walking and posing for her mugshot, which dispelled many, though not all, circulating rumors.

Donald Trump posted and then deleted a Twitter image depicting Hillary Clinton over a pile of $100 bills with a six-point star; critics said the image evoked the Star of David and exploited antisemitic stereotypes. The Trump campaign’s social media director, Dan Scavino, later said the graphic was “lifted from an anti-Hillary Twitter user” and argued the star was a sheriff’s badge available as a Microsoft shape, a defense echoed by supporters who called the controversy overblown. Mic traced the meme’s origins to the alt-right message board 8chan’s /pol/ and to racist Twitter accounts; the image’s file name and watermark suggested ties to white supremacist sources. The Clinton campaign, particularly Sarah Bard, director of Jewish outreach, condemned the post as “blatantly anti-Semitic” and part of a troubling pattern. The Anti-Defamation League’s Jonathan Greenblatt urged Trump to apologize and forcefully reject bigotry, calling the episode another in a series that “perplexing, troubling and wrong.” House Speaker Paul Ryan said anti-Semitic images have no place in a presidential campaign. Some Trump backers dismissed the outcry as political correctness; white nationalists praised the tweet. Trump defended himself on Twitter and on his campaign site, accusing Clinton of deflecting and insisting the star was a sheriff’s badge. The incident occurred amid other campaign controversies and raised questions about the campaign’s sourcing of online content and its relationship to extremist online communities.

President Barack Obama used his weekly radio address to mourn the victims of the mass shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut, and to urge Americans to unite and take “meaningful action” to prevent future tragedies. He expressed deep sorrow for the 26 people killed, including 20 children, and described the nation’s collective grief, urging support for the families and survivors. Obama stopped short of proposing specific gun-control measures, prompting calls from figures like New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg for bolder leadership. The shooting reignited national debate over gun violence amid a strong gun lobby and partisan divides in Washington. In a rare gesture of unity, House Speaker John Boehner canceled the Republican weekend address so Obama could “speak for the entire nation.”

Prince Alireza Pahlavi, the youngest son of Iran’s late Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, was found dead in his Boston South End home on Jan. 4, 2011, from an apparently self-inflicted single gunshot wound, authorities and his family said. He was 44. His older brother Reza announced the death, saying Alireza had struggled for years with sorrow—deepened by exile after the 1979 revolution and by the deaths of their father and their sister Leila, who died in 2001 after a drug overdose. Neighbors described Alireza as reserved and reclusive; he lived in a renovated West Newton Street rowhouse and had studied music at Princeton and ancient Iranian studies at Columbia, with postgraduate work at Harvard, though he was not enrolled there when he died. Family friends and Iranian-American community leaders expressed sorrow and asked for privacy as Reza and their mother planned to travel to Boston. No funeral arrangements had been announced.

Vice President Joe Biden officiated his first-ever wedding, uniting longtime White House staffers Brian Mosteller and Joe Mahshie at the Naval Observatory. Biden’s office said he obtained a temporary District of Columbia certification to preside over the private ceremony, which was attended only by the grooms’ families. Biden posted a photo of the event on Twitter, writing, “Proud to marry Brian and Joe at my house. Couldn't be happier, two longtime White House staffers, two great guys.” His wife Jill Biden also tweeted “Love is love!” Biden had publicly endorsed same-sex marriage in 2012.

Poland summoned the US ambassador and demanded an apology after FBI Director James Comey wrote in a Washington Post piece, adapted from a Holocaust Museum speech, that “murderers and accomplices of Germany, and Poland, and Hungary, and so many, many other places” convinced themselves their actions during World War II were right. Poland’s foreign ministry said Comey’s wording suggested some Poles were accomplices in the Holocaust; officials including President Bronislaw Komorowski and Prime Minister Ewa Kopacz protested, insisting Poland was a victim of Nazi occupation and praising Polish rescuers of Jews. US envoy Stephen Mull attended Warsaw Ghetto commemoration events, clarified that the United States holds Nazi Germany solely responsible for the Holocaust, and apologized profusely, saying he had “a lot of work before me to make things right.” Mull nevertheless noted that Comey’s broader point — that many people aided, or failed to sufficiently resist, atrocities — can apply beyond Europe, including in the US. Comey’s original commentary emphasized Holocaust education and moral lessons: he described the Holocaust as both humanity’s worst inhumanity and a terrifying example of ordinary people’s capacity for moral surrender. He said he requires new FBI agents and analysts to visit the Holocaust Museum to learn about abuses of authority and the dangers of rationalization, arguing that institutions like the rule of law and a free press are necessary checks on power. The dispute prompted critical commentary in the Washington Post and intensified sensitivities about historical responsibility during Nazi occupation.

As kids we played staring contests, daring not to blink and imagining we might miss something big. That childhood memory frames a recent viral stunt by supermodel Gigi Hadid: a four-minute video of her staring straight into the camera, occasionally blinking or smiling. Glamour promoted the clip—slow‑motioned for added eeriness—as “weirdly mesmerizing,” even suggesting it as alternative ambient footage for holiday gatherings. The video accompanies Hadid’s recognition as one of Glamour’s 2017 Women of the Year, highlighting her commercial and editorial success (Victoria’s Secret, Sports Illustrated, Maybelline collaboration, Vogue covers, Tom Ford runway) and her large Instagram following. At 22 she’s noted for both a strong work ethic and outspoken engagement on issues from gun control to human rights; she studied criminal psychology before modeling and says she intends to use her platform to speak on causes she cares about.

Critics, however, see the four‑minute stare as symptomatic of digital media’s awkward shift to video. Some view the clip as little more than repurposed photo‑shoot footage turned into a tongue‑in‑cheek inside joke, or evidence that magazines struggling to adapt to the web are producing hollow content. The piece lampoons the notion that celebrity fame allows someone to “do nothing” and still captivate audiences, questioning whether this kind of minimalist performance art truly entertains or simply reflects how baffled outlets are by new kinds of stardom. In short, the Hadid video is both a showcase of her hypnotic presence and a lightning rod for debate about content, fame, and what counts as meaningful media in the digital age.

Researchers studying the 2013–2016 West African Ebola epidemic report that a substantial fraction of infections may have been asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic, implying the outbreak was broader than case counts suggested and that containment strategies need rethinking. In a serosurvey conducted in Sukudu, a Sierra Leone “hotspot,” investigators tested 187 people who had been quarantined because they had shared housing or latrines with confirmed Ebola cases. Using validated ELISA assays for antibodies to Ebola glycoprotein and nucleoprotein, they identified 14 individuals (7.5% of those tested) with IgG indicating past Zaire-EBOV infection. Of these 14, two recalled only fever during quarantine; the other 12 denied any Ebola-consistent symptoms. Adding these findings to the village’s reported 34 EVD cases yields an estimated 25% contribution from minimally symptomatic infections to the total caseload. 

The study underscores several implications and uncertainties. It confirms that Ebola infections can present along a spectrum from asymptomatic to severe, echoing earlier, smaller studies. If minimally symptomatic infections are common and capable of transmitting virus (a question not yet answered), many transmission events could have gone undetected, complicating contact tracing, survivor definitions, and vaccine trial designs. Limitations include reliance on retrospective symptom recall, possible under- or overestimation from assay cross-reactivity, inability to date infections from IgG alone, and the study’s single-village scope, which limits generalizability. The authors call for broader serosurveys and research into whether asymptomatic individuals can transmit Ebola and whether they experience late clinical sequelae, so public-health responses and survivor support policies can be better informed.

A gunman opened random fire in Belgorod, southwest Russia, on April 22, killing six people — including a 14-year-old girl — and wounding another before fleeing in a BMW X5. Witnesses said he fired in the street and inside a shop; police later found the car and identified 32-year-old Sergey Pomazun, who has a criminal record, as the prime suspect. Authorities mounted a large manhunt involving some 1,200 officers and special forces, issued a reward, and warned residents to stay home; border and regional units were alerted. Conflicting reports about a second suspect and prior psychiatric treatment were not confirmed. Belgorod declared two days of mourning, offered victims’ families financial aid, and sent psychologists to assist grieving relatives. Russian leaders were kept informed as investigations continued.

Pope Francis told reporters aboard the papal plane returning from Armenia that the Catholic Church and Christians should apologize to groups it has marginalized, explicitly including gay people. Echoing the Catechism’s instruction that homosexuals “must not be discriminated against” and deserve pastoral accompaniment and respect, Francis said the Church is holy but its members are sinners and must ask forgiveness for past behavior. He broadened the apology to the poor, exploited women, child labor victims and for having blessed weapons, calling the gesture a necessary act of contrition. His remarks were hailed by LGBT advocates and some clergy—Rev. James Martin called it “groundbreaking,” and Francis DeBernardo of New Ways Ministry called it an “immense blessing of healing”—because no previous pope had apologized to the LGBT community so directly. Francis reiterated his 2013 stance distinguishing orientation from acts and asking “Who are we to judge?” while maintaining traditional doctrine that deems homosexual acts sinful. The press conference also touched on Brexit—urging creativity and renewed forms of unity for the EU—his continued use of the word “genocide” for the Armenian massacres, and the role of Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI, whom Francis described as “the wise grandpa” who prays for him. His comments have drawn praise from progressives and criticism from some conservative Catholics.

A long-term study following more than 400 men from adolescence into their mid-30s found no clear link between chronic adolescent marijuana use and later physical or mental health problems. Using data from the Pittsburgh Youth Study, researchers tracked 506 boys recruited in seventh grade in 1987–88 and followed them through regular interviews into young adulthood; about 408 participated in a final follow-up at age 35. The cohort—roughly half Black and half White—was divided into four marijuana-use trajectories: low/nonusers (46%), adolescent-limited users (11%), late-increasing/adult-onset users (21%), and early-onset chronic users (22%). Chronic users reported the highest frequency, peaking at more than 200 days per year in their early 20s. The investigators compared physical and mental health outcomes across these groups while controlling for confounds such as tobacco use, other drugs, and socioeconomic factors.

Across measures including depression, anxiety, psychotic symptoms, asthma and other respiratory problems, allergies, headaches, and high blood pressure, there were no statistically significant differences among the marijuana trajectory groups in their mid-30s. The authors note these results contrast with some earlier studies that found small associations between long-term marijuana use and disorders such as depression or psychosis, but align with others that did not. They highlight the strength of prospective measurement rather than retrospective recall.

Limitations include the all-male sample, follow-up only into the mid-30s before many chronic disease onsets, reliance on certain self-reported and diagnosable outcomes, and relatively few psychotic cases. The researchers also suggest individual differences—genetic liability or susceptibility—might moderate risk, and that marijuana could accelerate onset in vulnerable people. They caution the findings should be weighed within the broader body of evidence and not taken as a definitive answer on marijuana’s long-term risks or policy implications.

A Mountain View police traffic officer stopped a slow-moving Google self-driving car on El Camino Real near Rengstorff Avenue after noticing traffic backing up behind it. The vehicle was traveling at 24 mph in a 35 mph zone; when the officer approached he realized it was a Google Autonomous Vehicle and contacted the onboard operators to ask how the car selected speeds and to remind them about impeding traffic under California Vehicle Code 22400(a). A passenger, not the car, assumed control and pulled over for the officer. Mountain View police noted the Google vehicles are legally classified as neighborhood electric vehicles under California Vehicle Code 385.5 and are permitted only on roads with posted speed limits of 35 mph or less; El Camino Real meets that criterion, so the car was lawfully on the road. No citation was issued, leaving the humorous question—who would be ticketed, the human or the car—unanswered. Google’s Self-Driving Car Project explained its prototypes are capped at 25 mph for safety and approachability and joked about humans rarely getting pulled over for driving too slowly. Mountain View Police Department said it meets regularly with Google to ensure safe operations and directed media inquiries to policepio@mountainview.gov.

Researchers report that reduced eye contact between 2 and 6 months of age provides the earliest measurable behavioral sign that a child may later develop autism. Using eye-tracking technology, Warren R. Jones and Ami Klin followed 110 infants—59 at high familial risk (siblings with autism) and 51 low-risk—ten times between 2 months and 2 years while they watched videos of caregivers.
