By age 3, 13 children had been diagnosed with autism; detailed analyses focused chiefly on the 11 boys with autism. Infants who later developed autism began to show a steady decline in time spent looking at people’s eyes beginning around two months, continuing through 24 months, whereas typically developing babies increased eye-looking until about nine months and then plateaued. Those with the steepest early decline tended to have more severe symptoms later. Children who developed autism also showed relatively greater attention to mouths, bodies, and objects as they aged. Authors and outside experts emphasize that these differences are subtle and detectable only with specialized equipment and repeated measurement, not by casual parental observation. The finding suggests a developmental window in very early infancy when social engagement diverges and when interventions—if developed and applied extremely early—might alter trajectories. Experts call for replication in larger samples and caution that eye-tracking alone will not identify all forms of autism, given the spectrum’s heterogeneity. Still, the study is hailed as a major advance in pinpointing when autistic social differences emerge and in motivating research into earlier screening tools and preventive or early interventions during infancy.

The document explains that Twitter (or “Tweets”) can include location information—either a general city or a precise location—when posted from the web or third-party apps, and users can delete their Tweet location history. It also states that the content was gathered in a web crawl whose seed list consisted of every host indexed by the Wayback Machine. The crawl was executed at “level 1,” meaning it captured each URL and its embedded resources, plus the URLs and embeds of all outbound links. Finally, it notes that the WARC (web archive) files produced by this crawl are not currently accessible to the general public, and a link or note offers to “Learn more.”

More than 200 people gathered in Crenshaw County, Alabama, for the unveiling of a new Confederate monument dedicated to "Unknown Alabama Confederate Soldiers" at the privately owned Confederate Veterans Memorial Park near Brantley. The modest stone marker, placed among replica cannons, other monuments and flagpoles flying Confederate banners, commemorates unnamed Confederate soldiers from the Civil War, especially those from the county and surrounding area. Organized by David Coggins, who owns the adjacent Dry Creek RV Park and the memorial park, the ceremony featured speeches by Sons of Confederate Veterans leaders, a flag-raising, a roll-call of Confederate veterans, the removal of a red cloth revealing the stone, and blank musket and cannon fire. Attendees included local Sons and Daughters of the Confederacy members, reenactors in period dress, and about ten members or affiliates of the right-wing Three Percenters militia in camouflage and body armor who said they were present “in case anything were to happen.” Organizers insisted the dedication was not in response to the recent violence in Charlottesville, Virginia; they said the event had been planned for months and the monument ordered last year, though they acknowledged scrutiny after the date was posted online shortly after the Charlottesville clashes. Many attendees expressed pride in honoring ancestors and preserving heritage amid growing controversy over Confederate symbols; donations were solicited to fund a future monument to the Confederate Navy. Media access was restricted and only cellphones were allowed for photography.

A viral moment captured 106-year-old Virginia McLaurin joyfully meeting President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama at a White House Black History Month event. In the footage, McLaurin walks in enthusiastically, exclaiming "It's an honor," as the president greets her and Michelle hugs her, saying she wants to be like McLaurin when she grows up. The trio laugh and dance together in the Blue Room. McLaurin, moved by the occasion, says she never thought she'd live to be in the White House and expresses pride at seeing a Black president. The lighthearted encounter delighted viewers and made headlines.

When the Islamic State (IS) swept through northern Iraq, the Yazidis of Sinjar faced particularly dire peril. IS regards the ancient Yazidi community as heretical "devil worshippers," making them targets for slaughter and enslavement. After IS’s swift weekend offensive routed Kurdish peshmerga—who fled in the face of heavier weaponry seized from Iraqi forces—thousands of Yazidis abandoned Sinjar and nearby villages, many seeking refuge on Mount Sinjar. Instead of sanctuary, the mountain became a trap: surrounded by IS fighters, cut off from water, food and medical supplies, and exposed to heat, dehydration and disease. UNICEF and other agencies reported dozens of children dying within days; UNICEF cited some 40 child deaths among displaced Yazidis over a 48-hour period, and local sources reported up to 70 infant and toddler deaths. Estimates of those stranded vary from 10,000 to 40,000, with roughly 150,000 children in the broader district at risk. Airdrops by Iraqi planes reached few of the marooned; U.N. agencies warned that sustained airdrops—many flights’ worth—or safe evacuations are required to avert catastrophe. Reports also describe mass killings and abductions in Sinjar, homes marked with white flags to signal submission, and images circulated of executions. The assault displaced roughly 200,000 people nationwide, flooding Kurdish-region camps and exposing Iraq’s fractured politics: Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki’s contested leadership and paralysis have hampered a unified response. Humanitarian officials and Kurdish factions urged coordinated action to rescue and protect the trapped Yazidis before conditions become irreversible.

A federal judge in California dismissed a $42 million copyright lawsuit filed against Taylor Swift by R&B artist Jessie Braham (who records as Jesse Graham), delivering the ruling with playful references to Swift’s lyrics. Braham claimed Swift’s 2014 hit “Shake It Off” copied a 22-word chorus from his song “Haters Gone Hate” on the album Sexy Ladies, asserting that 92% of Swift’s song derived from his work. His chorus included lines such as “Haters gonna hate/ Players gonna play/ Watch out for them fakers/ They’ll fake you every day,” which resemble Swift’s refrains—“players gonna play… haters gonna hate… fakers gonna fake.” 

U.S. District Judge Gail Standish tossed the complaint for failing to plead sufficient factual detail, finding the allegations speculative and legally deficient. In her opinion she liberally quoted and alluded to Swift’s catalog—citing lyrics and titles including “We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together,” “Blank Space,” and “Bad Blood”—to underscore her reasoning and to inject irony into the dismissal. Standish wrote that Braham’s complaint currently has “a blank space” and that mere “Band-Aid” amendments wouldn’t cure its “bullet holes,” but she allowed him the chance to refile if he can remedy the deficiencies. Concluding with a nod to Swift’s phrasing, the judge observed that, for now, the defendants have “shaken off this lawsuit.” The decision emphasizes the need for detailed factual pleadings in copyright claims.

Neiman Marcus disclosed late last week that customer payment-card data was stolen, but investigators briefed on the case say its network was first penetrated as early as mid‑July and the breach wasn’t fully contained until January 1. The company initially told the public in mid‑December it had detected suspicious activity but did not reveal the intrusion’s scope or timeline; it later said some customers’ cards were used fraudulently and apologized, adding it believed Social Security numbers and birth dates were not compromised. Neiman informed card issuers around Christmas that fraudulent charges tied to cards used at its stores had been occurring, and offered affected customers one year of free credit monitoring. The delay in public disclosure drew criticism, with observers noting the announcement came after the holiday shopping season; Neiman maintained timing was based on forensic confirmation, not sales concerns. Investigators and state attorneys general are probing possible links to the large Target breach; Neiman says it has no knowledge of a connection. Separately, reports on the Target hack describe sophisticated point‑of‑sale malware that harvested card data from system memory during authorization, a technique traced to criminal groups with capabilities in Eastern Europe and elsewhere. Authorities believe both attacks were likely carried out by organized cybercriminal groups overseas, and joint federal and state investigations are ongoing.

Vincent van Gogh’s reputation as a supreme colourist rests on his bold yellows, blues and impastoed surfaces, yet new research shows some of those colours have faded and shifted since he painted them. The Van Gogh Museum’s exhibition Van Gogh at Work presents findings from a major, non‑invasive technical study of his materials and methods. Using microscopes and imaging, curators reveal practical details — Van Gogh painted on varied canvases, sometimes reused panels or painted on the reverse, and exchanged supplies and ideas with contemporaries such as Toulouse‑Lautrec and Gauguin. The show includes intimate artefacts (his smeared palette, paint tubes and a self‑portrait) and allows visitors to inspect paint layers electronically.

A striking scientific discovery concerns the bleaching of certain reds made from red lead (minium, Pb3O4). Conservators have long observed that bright red areas, such as leaves in Wheat Stack under a Cloudy Sky, slowly turn whitish. Belgian researchers led by Koen Janssens used x‑ray powder diffraction tomography on a tiny white globule from that painting to map chemical changes within paint grains. They found a core of altered minium surrounded by an unexpected mineral, plumbonacrite (3PbCO3·Pb(OH)2·PbO), and outer shells of lead carbonates (hydrocerussite and cerussite). Plumbonacrite had not previously been detected in pre‑mid‑20th‑century works and appears to be a photochemical intermediate: light converts red lead into plumbonacrite, which then reacts with CO2 to yield white carbonates. The result informs conservation practice and museum lighting policies, but does not diminish Van Gogh’s genius; rather, it deepens understanding of his working life and the material fragility of his chromatic effects.

Kanye West flew to Almaty, Kazakhstan, to perform a private set — reportedly including "Can't Tell Me Nothing" — at the wedding of a grandson of longtime president Nursultan Nazarbayev. Sources claim West was paid around $3 million for the Royal Tulip Hotel engagement; video and photos of the performance circulated online. The report notes Nazarbayev’s immense wealth and allegations of corruption tied to Kazakhstan’s oil revenues, and that the country ranks poorly on corruption indexes. The wedding is believed to involve Altay Qulybaev, a grandson through Nazarbayev’s daughter Dinara, whose family is tied to Kazakhstan’s elite.

Death Valley recorded an average July temperature of 107.39–107.4°F, making it the hottest month averaged at a single U.S. location in recorded history, the National Weather Service reported. That monthly average, which combines daily highs and lows, included an average daily high of about 119.6°F. Nights were extremely warm too: temperatures never fell below 89°F all month, and three nights stayed above 100°F. The hottest single day in July was 127°F on the 7th; Death Valley reached 127°F on two days in June as well. Weather historian Christopher Burt noted this was the hottest average monthly temperature measured in the U.S. and the Western Hemisphere, though climatologist Brian Brettschneider pointed out the world warm-month record remains King Khaled, Saudi Arabia, in August 2015 at 107.44°F. Death Valley, a park with few permanent residents, is the hottest, driest and lowest U.S. national park; several other Western cities and Miami also saw record-warm months.

A white nylon sample bag flown to the Moon on Apollo 11 and used by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to collect the mission’s first lunar material has become the subject of a federal legal dispute after it was mistakenly sold at a government auction. The bag, described by prosecutors as “a rare artifact, if not a national treasure,” was seized in 2003 from the garage of Max Ary, founder and longtime director of the Kansas Cosmosphere and Space Center, during an investigation that uncovered hundreds of missing space artifacts. Ary was convicted in 2005 of stealing and selling museum pieces, some on loan from NASA, and was sentenced to three years in prison and ordered to pay roughly $132,000 in restitution; he has since denied intent, saying he mixed museum items with his private collection.

Due to a clerical error that merged inventory numbers for two distinct flown lunar sample bags, the Apollo 11 bag was misidentified and not properly flagged to NASA during forfeiture proceedings. As a result, it was auctioned by the government on Feb. 15, 2015, and sold to Nancy Carlson of Inverness, Illinois, for $995. Carlson later sent the bag to NASA’s Johnson Space Center for authentication, at which point NASA learned it had been sold without notice. Federal prosecutors have asked the Kansas judge who oversaw Ary’s case to rescind the forfeiture order, cancel the sale and refund Carlson.

The confusion stems from conflation with a different bag flown on Apollo 17, which Ary had sold at a 2001 auction for over $24,000 and which investigators later recovered. Carlson separately sued NASA in Illinois federal court seeking return of the artifact. The case underscores issues in handling and tracking historic space objects and has prompted officials to attempt to reverse the erroneous sale.

After a boozy night out in Middlesbrough, 33-year-olds Phillip Boyle and Jamie Blyth unexpectedly found themselves on last-minute flights to Pattaya, Thailand — a story that grabbed worldwide attention. What began as a “quiet pint” at The Southern Cross in Marton escalated into heavy drinking, more alcohol at a gas station and, by 11 a.m. the next day, a hungover decision to head to Manchester Airport. With no bookings and only a carrier bag with a few T-shirts and boxer shorts between them, they impulsively purchased tickets and endured two seven‑hour flights with an Abu Dhabi stopover to reach the beach resort.

Despite initial sobriety-induced panic mid-journey, they resolved to make the most of it. Their brief stay was a whirlwind of meals, bar-hopping and little sleep; Phillip admitted he’d fallen behind with work but said the trip was “brilliant fun.” Phillip upgraded his improvised luggage with a backpack and bought trainers while there, though the trainers were stolen, forcing him to wear work shoes. Jamie, who organized the trip and has a new girlfriend, said she was annoyed at first but later amused by the escapade. Friends and former schoolmates were reportedly shocked to see them appear in Thailand.

The pair avoided any major disaster reminiscent of The Hangover films and returned proclaiming the experience worth it, with Phillip recommending such spontaneity to others — with obvious caveats about packing ahead. The story echoes other drunken travel stunts, like a British teenager who once blundered onto a flight to Paris, underscoring the unpredictable, often hilarious consequences of late-night impulsivity.

Maine voters will decide a ballot measure on Nov. 7 to expand Medicaid and extend coverage to roughly 80,000 more residents, a move supporters say would reduce the uninsured rate, improve public health, create an estimated 4,000 health-care jobs, and stabilize struggling rural hospitals. Expansion would add about $525 million per year in federal funds to the state while costing Maine taxpayers an estimated $54 million annually, according to the Legislature’s nonpartisan Office of Program and Fiscal Review; the federal government would cover 90 percent or more of expansion costs. Supporters include hospitals and advocacy groups like Maine Equal Justice Partners, which argue expansion would relieve hospitals of uncompensated care, help workforce recruitment, and shore up facilities at risk of closure.

Opponents are led by Gov. Paul LePage, who has vetoed five legislative attempts to expand Medicaid and calls the measure “pure welfare,” arguing it would burden taxpayers and benefit hospitals’ finances at the public’s expense. LePage claims expansion would cost $500 million over five years—a figure the fiscal office disputes—and has criticized hospital leaders for supporting the referendum. Hospitals and advocates counter that expansion would not divert care from the elderly or disabled and that states can manage Medicaid spending without cutting other services. Turnout uncertainty poses a key challenge for campaigners, who hope residual public attention from national health-care debates and support from figures like Sen. Susan Collins will boost passage.

Tesla has filed an international patent for an automated turn-signal system that uses its Autopilot sensors and onboard processor to detect when a driver intends to change lanes or turn and, if nearby vehicles are sensed, activate the signal automatically. The system would infer intent from steering angle and other data, potentially helping when drivers forget to indicate. While similar warnings already exist, this would physically operate the signal rather than rely on the driver. There’s no timeline for deployment, and Tesla hasn’t commented; many patents also never reach production.

Researchers estimate that indoor tanning causes substantial health and economic burdens in the United States. A study published in the Journal of Cancer Policy found that skin cancers attributable to tanning beds generated about $343 million in direct medical costs in 2015. Using data on tanning prevalence, risks linked to tanning devices, and Medicare treatment costs, the researchers attributed 8,947 melanoma cases, more than 168,000 squamous cell carcinomas, and at least 86,000 basal cell carcinomas to indoor tanning that year. Average treatment costs were calculated at $5,054 per melanoma case and $1,168 for other skin cancers. Beyond direct treatment expenses, the team estimated lost productivity and premature death among those currently diagnosed would amount to over $127 billion across their lifetimes, valuing each year of life lost at $55,266 based on 2015 GDP metrics. The study’s authors noted potential underestimation because they did not capture long-term follow-up care or productivity losses beyond their measures; conversely, some experts suggested the economic impact might be overstated and that natural sun exposure also carries significant risk. Dermatologists emphasize that any unprotected ultraviolet exposure increases skin cancer risk, but that tanning beds—especially when used by young women—significantly raise melanoma risk (women under 30 who tan indoors face markedly higher odds). Policy steps like FDA warnings and a federal excise tax on tanning services aim to curb indoor tanning by highlighting these health and financial costs.

Julian Assange publicly rejected Benedict Cumberbatch’s request to meet while the actor prepared to play him in DreamWorks’ film The Fifth Estate, calling the movie misleading and harmful. In a January letter released later, Assange thanked Cumberbatch and praised him personally but said he could not meet because doing so would legitimize a production Assange views as politically motivated and based on “toxic” books written by adversaries. He accused DreamWorks of basing its script on discredited, vendetta-driven accounts and argued the film would distort events, resurrect false defamatory stories, and aid efforts by U.S. authorities and others seeking to undermine WikiLeaks. Assange warned that feature films shape public perception and said this one would “bury good people doing good work” at a time when his organization faces intense legal and intelligence pressure. He called Cumberbatch a “decent person” but said the actor’s participation would make him a “hired gun” lending authenticity to a falsified history and urged him to reconsider involvement. After calling the film a “geriatric snoozefest,” Assange noted Cumberbatch’s courteous reply acknowledging script concerns. The dispute comes amid Assange’s asylum in Ecuador’s London embassy and ongoing legal battles tied to WikiLeaks’ 2010 disclosures.

Twitter under CEO Dick Costolo is portrayed as a new kind of company—neither purely tech nor media—boldly protecting user privacy and reshaping its culture as it scales. Costolo, who became CEO in 2010 after moving from Chicago, replaced earlier founders in day-to-day control and has steered rapid, sometimes brusque decision-making: ousting staff, pushing off board members, and cutting ties with some third-party apps. Co-founder Jack Dorsey was brought back but with reduced operational authority; he remains influential on strategy. Twitter has defended users against legal demands and emphasizes protecting anonymity. The company is also considering building its own in-house video hosting so users could upload videos directly through Twitter apps. That move would improve consistency, user experience, and ad opportunities but threaten third-party hosting services and is still under internal debate.

The FDA announced it will make Plan B One-Step emergency contraception available over the counter for women ages 15 and older, while younger teens will still need a prescription. Previously, OTC access was limited to those 17 and older. Commissioner Margaret Hamburg cited studies showing women 15+ understand proper use and that the pill does not prevent sexually transmitted infections. The move partially responds to a federal judge’s April ruling that sought removal of all age restrictions; the FDA stopped short of eliminating age limits, ensuring purchasers must show ID and enabling retailers to enforce age verification and security measures. Teva’s amended application, based on label comprehension and actual-use data, supported the agency’s decision; Teva will also educate consumers and may audit age-verification practices. Advocates split: Sen. Patty Murray called it progress toward science-based access, while the Center for Reproductive Rights criticized the continued restrictions and vowed to continue litigation, arguing barriers like ID checks and limited store hours still impede timely access. The FDA said its decision is independent of the court case; the Justice Department is reviewing next steps.

Federal prosecutors in Manhattan disclosed that Michael Cohen, President Trump’s personal lawyer, has been under a criminal investigation for months focused on his business dealings. The Justice Department revealed the probe after agents executed court-authorized raids on Cohen’s home, office, hotel room, safety deposit boxes, two cellphones and multiple email accounts. Prosecutors said their warrant reviews found Cohen did "little to no legal work" and exchanged no emails with Trump. Cohen has not been charged.

Cohen’s lawyers and Trump’s counsel moved to block prosecutors from using some seized materials, arguing attorney-client privilege; prosecutors asked the court to permit a government "taint" or filter team to screen documents first, a standard practice. Prosecutors disputed that much of the material is privileged, noting Cohen told a witness his only client was Trump and that Mueller’s office had referred Cohen’s business matters to New York. The searches sought communications about election-era matters, including the Access Hollywood tape and a $130,000 payment to Stormy Daniels. The judge ordered the parties back to court Monday; Cohen must appear. Public access to parts of the hearing was contested but largely preserved.

A senior North Korean diplomat sharply rebuked US Vice‑President Mike Pence’s recent comments, heightening uncertainty over the planned June 12 summit between Kim Jong Un and President Donald Trump. Choe Son‑hui, a vice foreign minister and seasoned North Korea expert on US affairs, called Pence’s remarks “ignorant,” “stupid” and said Pence was a “political dummy.” She condemned comparisons to Libya—invoked by Pence and other US officials—as a grave insult because North Korea views Libya’s fate after denuclearization (Muammar Gaddafi’s overthrow and death) as a warning. Choe warned Pyongyang would not “beg” for dialogue and threatened a “nuclear‑to‑nuclear showdown” if diplomacy failed, saying whether talks occur depends on US behavior. Though harsh, her statement avoided direct attacks on President Trump, suggesting North Korea may still prefer to keep the summit option open unless Washington pursues “unlawful and outrageous acts.” The exchange follows prior tensions: US National Security Adviser John Bolton referenced a “Libya model,” prompting North Korean anger; Trump later distanced himself from that idea. Despite the rhetoric, both sides continue logistics planning, with reports of officials meeting in Singapore and North Korea proceeding to dismantle its Punggye‑ri nuclear test site as a goodwill gesture. Analysts note the dispute underscores how sensitive messaging is in delicate diplomacy—insults directed at US aides rather than Trump hint Pyongyang’s desire to preserve the summit while pushing back against perceived disrespect.

Police say the early-morning break-in at Sandra Bullock’s home may not have been random. Joshua Corbett, 39, was arrested on suspicion of burglary after reportedly rummaging through Bullock’s belongings; law enforcement tells Today he may have been obsessed with the Oscar-winning actress and might have kept a diary about her. The intrusion occurred hours after Bullock attended the Spike TV Guys’ Choice Awards. Bullock and her 4-year-old son Louis were unharmed.

A Texas Court of Criminal Appeals has stayed the June 21 execution of Robert Roberson III, a 49-year-old death row inmate convicted in 2002 of murdering his 2-year-old daughter, Nikki Curtis, and remanded his case to the Anderson County trial court for review. The reprieve follows his attorneys’ assertion that his conviction relied on “junk science” linking a trio of internal head injuries—brain swelling, subdural bleeding and retinal hemorrhages—to intentional shaking. New legal avenues under a recent Texas law allow inmates to challenge convictions using updated scientific evidence; Roberson’s lawyers argued that modern research shows those injury patterns can also result from short falls, medical conditions (like clotting disorders or latent birth trauma), or other nonviolent causes, and that reliable proof of fatal shaking would require severe neck injuries Nikki did not have. At trial, prosecutors presented experts who testified Nikki died of shaken baby syndrome and initially advanced sexual-abuse allegations, which were later dropped when evidence was inconclusive. Roberson has maintained the child may have suffered a fall from her bed or died after a high fever or undiagnosed illness; defense counsel also cited possible meningitis, an earlier accidental injury, or congenital issues. The Texas attorney general maintains the conviction was proper; one appeals judge dissented from the reprieve, and no timetable for resolving the remand was set.

The Supreme Court’s ruling on the Affordable Care Act produced two competing victories: Chief Justice John Roberts joined the Court’s liberal justices to uphold the individual mandate, but simultaneously endorsed a major curtailment of congressional power under the Commerce Clause. Roberts rejected sustaining the mandate as an exercise of Commerce Clause authority, arguing Congress cannot regulate people for “doing nothing,” and instead upheld the mandate as a tax. That maneuver handed President Obama a 5–4 victory while also undercutting long-standing Commerce Clause precedent that enabled broad federal regulation. The decision surprised many legal scholars who had assumed the mandate clearly fell within Congress’s regulatory power; it reflects a Federalist Society-inspired effort to narrow federal authority that Roberts has long pursued. The ruling preserves Obamacare but opens the door to future limitations on federal regulation, and gives Republicans fresh political ammunition to frame the mandate as a tax burden. Public perception may see Roberts as moderate, but his opinion marks a significant doctrinal rollback.

A woman in Taunton, Massachusetts narrowly escaped moments before her two-story single-family home exploded and burned Sunday afternoon, authorities and neighbors said. Police identified the homeowner as 52-year-old Laurie Beliveau. Officials from the State Fire Marshal’s office and the Taunton Fire Department said Beliveau had been attempting to repair a gas-fueled hot water heater and removed the gas shut-off valve, allowing natural gas to fill the basement. An unknown ignition source then ignited the leak, producing a blast and rapidly spreading fire.

Multiple bystanders called 911 at about 3:53 p.m.; recordings released to ABC News include callers saying they felt the ground shake and saw smoke. Neighbor Paul Saltalamacchia recounted that Beliveau ran to his house screaming for help; he and his son gave her sandals and water before the home became engulfed and windows exploded. Beliveau reportedly told neighbors she had “done something to the furnace” and was distraught about her pet cockatoo believed to be inside. Taunton officials cautioned homeowners against attempting gas-related repairs themselves.

Taunton Deputy Fire Chief Scott Dexter said the blast leveled the house, leaving it a pile of unsalvageable lumber. Investigators from the fire marshal’s office, state police, the Office of Public Utilities, and Columbia Gas of Massachusetts responded; Columbia Gas turned off utilities at the property and reiterated safety advice to evacuate and avoid operating utilities if a gas leak is suspected. An August affidavit indicates the property faced foreclosure proceedings. The investigation remains ongoing.

Less than two hours after U.S. District Judge Derrick Watson in Hawaii issued a nationwide temporary restraining order against President Trump’s revised travel ban, Trump condemned the ruling as “an unprecedented judicial overreach.” Watson’s ruling, handed down a day before the order was to take effect, said a reasonable observer could conclude the ban was intended to disfavor a particular religion. Speaking that night at a Nashville rally, Trump accused the court of political motivation, called the revised order a “watered-down” version of the original that should not have been blocked, and said the decision “makes us look weak.” He reiterated his argument that temporary travel restrictions are needed while an “extreme vetting” process is implemented to protect against terrorism. 

Trump signed the revised executive order on March 6 to replace his January 27 ban, which targeted travelers from seven majority-Muslim countries and had triggered widespread protests and legal challenges; the original was previously halted by a federal judge in Washington state and not stayed by the 9th Circuit. At the rally, Trump said the new order was tailored to address the 9th Circuit’s ruling and vowed to pursue the case through the courts, including the Supreme Court, asserting he would “win” and keep citizens safe. 

Earlier that day, Trump visited the Hermitage in Nashville to mark Andrew Jackson’s 250th birthday, praising Jackson as an inspirational populist whom he admires and linking Jackson’s opposition to elites to his own political identity.

A photograph circulating on social media showed a British Royal Air Force bomb with “LOVE FROM MANCHESTER ❤” scrawled on its side; an RAF spokesperson confirmed the image is genuine. Although details about when or whether the bomb was used remain unclear, the photo prompted strong reactions because it surfaced shortly after the Manchester Arena terrorist attack. Writing such messages on munitions is a long-standing, informal practice among aircrews, but linking a city ravaged by recent loss to an instrument of death struck many as grotesque and disrespectful.

Critics argue the slogan exemplifies a damaging mindset in foreign policy: a punitive “eye for an eye” approach that perpetuates violence rather than fostering healing. Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn addressed the broader context, noting that while foreign policy does not excuse terrorists’ actions, the “war on terror” has not made Britain safer and may contribute to the problem. Historical reference to the Chilcot inquiry and comments by ex-MI5 chief Dame Eliza Manningham-Buller are cited to show how the Iraq invasion increased terrorism threats at home and strained security resources.

A humanitarian worker experienced in Syria, Iraq, Yemen and Palestine emphasized the human cost of airstrikes: civilian casualties, besieged populations deprived of aid, and horrific injuries to children and families. They argued bombing won’t bring back Manchester’s victims, aid healing, or reliably punish ISIS; instead, it inflicts more suffering on vulnerable civilians. Their plea: keep the bombs and stop using the city’s name as justification—don’t drop them in our name.

The Comedy Central Roast of Justin Bieber brought a star-studded panel—Kevin Hart as roastmaster, Jeff Ross, Hannibal Buress, Chris D’Elia, Snoop Dogg, Natasha Leggero, Ludacris, Shaquille O’Neal, Martha Stewart and surprise guest Will Ferrell—to Los Angeles for a night of brutal jokes. While some performers landed strong, sharp bits—Buress’s blunt honesty, Hart’s smooth hosting, Pete Davidson’s risky material and Ferrell’s focused takedown—much of the evening felt like comics using Bieber as a networking prop rather than genuinely skewering him. Several comedians misfired with tasteless or repetitive jabs (notably D’Elia’s controversial routine and some Paul Walker jokes), and many quips aimed more at fellow roasters than the singer. Bieber appeared uncomfortable and subdued during his rebuttal. Overall, the roast was entertaining in parts but often celebrated the comedians more than its youthful target.

German Chancellor Angela Merkel and U.S. President Barack Obama discussed mounting tensions after disclosures by former NSA contractor Edward Snowden that U.S. intelligence allegedly spied on European allies. Merkel said Obama took Germany’s concerns seriously and they agreed to high-level bilateral talks, alongside planned EU–U.S. discussions on intelligence, privacy and data protection beginning as soon as July 8. Germany will send Interior Minister Hans-Peter Friedrich to the U.S., and German leaders debated contacting Snowden in Moscow and possibly granting witness protection. The European Parliament approved an in-depth inquiry into U.S. surveillance programs and called for full disclosure, warning EU data-protection standards must not be undermined by upcoming Transatlantic Trade and Investment Partnership negotiations. France urged a brief delay to trade talks; the European Commission insisted negotiations proceed but stressed trust and transparency are essential. EU offices will be swept for listening devices. Polls showed U.S. trust in Germany fell sharply, underscoring the diplomatic fallout from the revelations.

Sen. John McCain said he would withdraw support for Indiana Senate nominee Richard Mourdock unless Mourdock apologized for comments that pregnancies from rape are "something God intended." Speaking on CNN, McCain said he’d forgive mistakes when candidates own up to them; his spokesman later clarified McCain supported Mourdock after the candidate’s press conference in which he said he regretted being misinterpreted and apologized to Indiana voters. The controversy began after Mourdock’s debate remark that even pregnancies resulting from rape are meant by God; he also said abortion should be allowed only to save the mother’s life. Mitt Romney’s campaign has not withdrawn its endorsement and continues to air an ad featuring Romney backing Mourdock, though campaign spokeswoman Andrea Saul stated Romney disagrees with Mourdock’s views on rape and incest exceptions. President Obama criticized Mourdock on "The Tonight Show," calling rape a crime and arguing politicians—mostly male—should not make decisions about women’s health; he invoked the stakes for Roe v. Wade and Supreme Court appointments. Democrats and the Obama campaign used the episode to pressure Romney to distance himself further, releasing a web video juxtaposing Romney’s pro-Mourdock ad with Mourdock’s remarks. Public debate intensified as Republicans weighed responses.

Brazil faces an international outlier problem: cesarean rates far above WHO guidance. New Brazilian regulations and a public campaign "Childbirth is normal!" aim to curb an “epidemic” of C-sections—over half of births nationally, about 84–90% in private care and roughly 40–45% in public hospitals—compared with ~32% in the U.S. Authorities now require doctors and insurers to provide women with information (including clinicians’ C-section statistics), written justification for operations, consent forms, and full labor records; insurers who withhold data face fines. Advocates stress that informing women about surgical risks will reduce unnecessary operations. Drivers of high rates include maternal convenience and status, scheduling ease for doctors and hospitals, economic incentives, medico-legal fears, scarce maternity beds for spontaneous labor, and cultural beliefs that C-sections are modern and preserve appearance. Critics say doctors’ pressure and loss of skills for vaginal and instrumental births reinforce the trend. Evidence links C-sections to maternal risks and possible long-term child health effects. Research from Quebec highlights similar barriers to guideline implementation—organizational constraints, staffing, legal concerns, training gaps, and women’s preferences—and recommends education, audit-and-feedback, peer-review, opinion leaders, standardized patient information, and local data to promote vaginal delivery where appropriate. Overall, multifaceted strategies addressing systemic incentives, professional practices, patient education and legal fears are needed to shift culture and reduce unnecessary cesarean births.

Early Thursday morning, a house fire on Haggard Street in Plano, Texas, claimed the life of 72-year-old Rex Benson after he went back into the burning home to retrieve a cell phone. The blaze began shortly after 1 a.m.; a roommate alerted Benson and his adult daughter, and all three initially escaped. Because they lacked a phone to call 911, two men went back inside to retrieve one. Benson was unable to get out a second time and was later found dead; the roommate escaped unharmed and the daughter survived. Firefighters arrived about three minutes after the call and found the single-story brick house fully engulfed, forcing crews to fight the fire from outside. Plano Fire and Rescue spokeswoman/Capt. Peggy Harrell stressed the danger of re-entering burning structures, noting that roughly nine out of 10 people who return to a fire do not survive. Neighbors expressed shock and sadness, saying Benson was well known and could have sought help from nearby houses. Authorities say the cause of the blaze remains under investigation, and no foul play is suspected. The incident underscores fire officials’ warnings that possessions—even a cell phone—are not worth risking one’s life.

A manhunt is underway after a deadly early‑morning shooting in Montpelier left 33‑year‑old Markus Austin dead. Vermont State Police have issued an arrest warrant for 29‑year‑old Jayveon Caballero of Barre on a charge of second‑degree murder; bail was set at $500,000. Authorities say Caballero and Austin, who knew each other, were involved in an altercation outside Gusto’s bar in Barre before Caballero allegedly followed Austin to an apartment complex at 191 Barre Street and shot him around 4:30 a.m. Witnesses described seeing Caballero fire, then check on Austin before driving away. Investigators believe Caballero may have boarded a Greyhound bus in White River Junction headed toward New York City, though he could have gotten off at intermediate stops; police have reached out to other states and are asking the public for tips. Caballero’s girlfriend, 22‑year‑old Desiree Cary, was arrested later Sunday in an unrelated ongoing drug investigation; she faces charges of selling crack cocaine and heroin and has pleaded not guilty to drug charges. Montpelier police noted this is the city’s first homicide since the 1920s. Officers executed a search warrant at Caballero’s residence but he was not found, and the search for him continues.

As Hurricane Sandy hit the U.S. East Coast, Apple CEO Tim Cook used the moment to reshuffle senior management, signaling a shift from internal politics to product-focused unity. Scott Forstall, long-time iOS chief, was ousted after tensions with other executives and his refusal to sign an apology over Apple Maps’ flawed launch. Jony Ive gains responsibility for Human Interfaces, while Craig Federighi will lead both OS X and iOS, consolidating software design under leaders known for collaboration and refined user experience. Bob Mansfield returns to head a new Technologies group combining wireless and semiconductor teams, hinting at ambitious hardware and smart-home initiatives. The changes reflect Cook’s aim to eliminate silos and one-man fiefdoms, prioritize honest assessment of product readiness, and leverage Apple’s design-driven retail and platform strengths to explore new product categories. Overall, the reshuffle positions Apple to refocus on producing world-class, cohesive hardware-software experiences.

Pope Francis, born Jorge Mario Bergoglio to Italian immigrants in Argentina, was inaugurated as the 266th pontiff in a Mass that emphasized humility, service and care for the marginalized. The first Latin American and first Jesuit pope addressed about 150,000–200,000 people in St. Peter’s Square on the Feast of St. Joseph, underscoring that authentic power is service and urging protection for the poorest and weakest—the hungry, sick, prisoners, migrants and children. He linked his message to St. Joseph’s guardianship and to St. Francis of Assisi’s legacy of simplicity, charity and love for creation, calling on leaders and all people to be “protectors” of one another and of the environment. Francis received the fisherman’s ring and the pallium, but kept a modest style: plain vestments, black shoes instead of red, a gold-plated silver ring, and continued to live at the Vatican guesthouse rather than moving immediately into the Apostolic Palace. He toured the crowd in an open vehicle, kissed babies and greeted a disabled man, signaling openness and personal contact. Delegations from 132 countries attended, including President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, U.S. Vice President Joe Biden and controversial figures like Robert Mugabe; religious leaders from many faiths were present. Francis phoned his predecessor, Benedict XVI, offering affection and thanks; the Vatican reported a warm, cordial exchange and Benedict’s prayerful closeness. Observers noted Francis’s simpler, pastoral tone contrasted with Benedict’s academic style and suggested his emphasis on personnel and pastoral priorities could lead to substantive changes amid church scandals and internal reform needs.

The Weinstein Company (TWC) filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in Delaware after months of failed attempts to find a buyer or investor amid a growing wave of sexual-misconduct allegations against co-founder Harvey Weinstein. The company listed $500 million to $1 billion in both assets and liabilities and named Lantern Capital Partners’ affiliate as the “stalking horse” bidder to purchase substantially all assets, establishing a floor for a court-supervised auction that may include other suitors such as Lionsgate, Miramax, and Killer Content.

Crucially, TWC announced it will immediately release employees, victims and witnesses from nondisclosure agreements that had reportedly been used to silence accusers—an action long sought by New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman, who called it a watershed moment. Schneiderman had filed a broad lawsuit alleging civil-rights and business-law violations and seeking restitution for victims. The bankruptcy stay pauses pending civil actions, while claimants will be treated as unsecured creditors and assets may be sold “free and clear,” potentially limiting recovery for some plaintiffs.

TWC emphasized the move aims to maximize asset value, preserve jobs, and pursue justice for victims. The filing appoints restructuring officers and signals further creditor scrutiny and possible adversary proceedings to pursue liability against the Weinsteins or others. Harvey Weinstein faces multiple civil accusations and ongoing investigations, including potential criminal matters independent of the bankruptcy.

South Korean media report that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un ordered the public execution of two senior officials at a Pyongyang military academy in early August, using an anti-aircraft gun. The JoongAng Ilbo, citing unnamed sources with “special knowledge,” named the victims as Hwang Min, a former agriculture minister, and Ri Yong-jin, a senior education ministry official who may have held ministerial rank. Hwang was reportedly purged for proposing policies seen as a direct challenge to Kim’s authority; Ri was allegedly arrested after dozing off during a meeting with Kim and later charged with corruption. The report has not been independently verified and was not confirmed by North Korea’s state media; South Korea’s Unification Ministry said it could not immediately confirm the story.

If true, these killings would extend Kim’s pattern of brutal purges since he took power in 2011, which have included the high-profile execution of his uncle Jang Song-thaek in 2013 and other senior military and party figures accused of corruption or disloyalty. Analysts suggest such executions serve to replace the old guard with loyalists and to instill fear, especially amid recent high-level defections, including that of Thae Yong-ho in London. Seoul’s leadership views the defections as signs of internal strain but experts note the regime’s stability depends heavily on continued Chinese support and control over elites.

Robert B. Sherman, who died in London at 86, was half of the famed Sherman Brothers songwriting duo that shaped generations with memorable, multilayered songs for children and adults. With brother Richard, he wrote for Disney classics including Mary Poppins, The Jungle Book, The Aristocats, Chitty Chitty Bang Bang and the endlessly played theme "It's a Small World (After All)." Trained by their father Al Sherman, they won Oscars, Grammys, a National Medal of Arts and a Songwriters Hall of Fame induction. Known for simple, singable, sincere lyrics that work across ages, Robert lived his final years in Britain and is survived by his brother and four children.

President Barack Obama will make a historic trip to Cuba on March 21-22, becoming the first sitting U.S. president to visit the island in 88 years. Announced publicly via Twitter and detailed by White House officials, the visit is part of a broader Latin America trip that includes Argentina. Obama will meet Cuban President Raúl Castro — the pair met previously at the Summit of the Americas — and will also engage with Cuban entrepreneurs, dissidents, and other members of Cuban society. First Lady Michelle Obama will accompany him. 

The trip follows more than a year of rapprochement after secret talks led to a December 2014 announcement to normalize relations. Since then, embassies reopened, commercial air service was agreed upon, and travel restrictions and economic channels have been eased, though the U.S. embargo remains in place pending Congressional action. Administration officials stress the visit aims to press for further reforms and expand opportunities for Cuban people through travel, commerce, and information access, while continuing to raise human rights concerns directly. The announcement drew mixed reactions: Cuban officials welcomed it and urged lifting the embargo, while some U.S. politicians — notably Senators Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz — criticized the engagement as premature given Cuba’s record on dissent.

The document combines two unrelated items: an explanation of an archiving effort and a criminal complaint summary. The archiving project aims to crawl and preserve webpages and the pages they reference at the time content is created, so that when referenced pages change or disappear, links can point to the archived versions. The Internet Archive’s stated goal is to prevent broken links across the web by inserting preserved links or companion links that let readers see what authors originally intended, targeting supported “No More 404” sites.

Separately, the complaint describes a fatal workplace attack on County Road FF near River Falls. Four roofers were replacing shingles when, according to witnesses, Navarro used a circular saw to cut co-worker Valles-Flores. Valles-Flores fell onto a garage roof where Navarro allegedly continued cutting him; two other coworkers reportedly jumped off the roof and hid until police arrived. There was no obvious argument before the attack, though Miguel allegedly claimed in a jail call he had been teased, underpaid, and possibly drugged to work more. Valles-Flores died on the garage roof, suffering multiple sharp-force injuries and transection of the jugular and carotid arteries per a provisional autopsy. Navarro faces first-degree intentional homicide and mayhem charges, with potential life imprisonment and up to 40 years plus fines; he was held on $500,000 cash bond.

Belgian authorities and family members have identified Najim Laachraoui, a 24–25-year-old Belgian, as one of the suicide bombers in the Brussels airport attack and a suspected bomb-maker linked to the November Paris attacks. His brother Mourad, a Belgian taekwondo athlete, described Najim as a “nice, intelligent” youth who showed no warning signs of radicalization before leaving for Syria in 2013 and cutting off contact with family. Mourad said the family alerted police when Najim announced he had gone to Syria; police visited and later searched their home after the Paris attacks. The family and Mourad expressed shock and sorrow, saying they had no idea what drove Najim to extremism and that he had not been seen with suspects like alleged mastermind Abdelhamid Abaaoud. School officials recalled Najim as a model student who never failed a class at a Brussels Catholic school and last attended in 2009. Investigators say Najim traveled under the alias Soufiane Kayal and was documented with suspected Paris attacker Salah Abdeslam driving from Hungary into Austria in September 2015. Belgian prosecutors confirmed Najim’s DNA was found on a suicide belt used at the Bataclan and at several safe houses, and surveillance footage showed him pushing a luggage trolley with a bomb at Brussels airport. Authorities have not officially confirmed his death to the family.

Newly recovered documents from the collapsed Rana Plaza building in Bangladesh suggest Wal‑Mart merchandise was produced there last year, intensifying pressure on U.S. retailers to join a landmark, legally binding safety accord adopted by many European chains after the disaster that killed over 1,100 workers. Photos of orders, including one from Fame Jeans for Wal‑Mart, were found in rubble of the Ether Tex factory; Wal‑Mart and Fame Jeans dispute authorized production at the site and say no evidence shows production at the time of the collapse. Wal‑Mart declined to join the European-led five-year Accord on Fire and Building Safety, saying it prefers its own plan of independent audits, full inspections of 279 Bangladesh factories, public disclosure of results, and immediate suspension of unsafe producers. Unlike the Accord, Wal‑Mart won’t underwrite renovation costs and objects to governance and dispute-resolution provisions that could create legal exposure. Other American retailers, including Gap and Sears, have also resisted the Accord, citing liability concerns; some U.S. firms are developing separate plans. Advocates criticize U.S. firms’ voluntary approaches as unenforceable and insufficient. European signatories and labor groups argue the legally binding Accord, with independent inspections and cost-sharing for safety upgrades, offers stronger, enforceable protections for Bangladeshi garment workers.

This document describes two distinct features related to online content and archival collections. First, it explains that Twitter (Tweets) can include location information: users may add a city or a precise location to their Tweets from the web and through third‑party apps, and they always retain the option to delete their Tweet location history. A brief pointer to additional information is included, indicating users can learn more about how location tagging and history deletion work.

Second, the document outlines a web archive collection focused on labor unions in the New York City metropolitan area, with emphasis on unions whose records are held at the Tamiment Library’s Robert F. Wagner Labor Archives. The Tamiment Library has been designated by the New York City Central Labor Council as the official repository for records of its member unions, and the archive periodically captures and preserves websites from those unions. The collection also includes selected national labor union websites and sites of organizations related to the labor movement: groups that support organized labor’s goals, advocate social and economic justice for working people, or promote democratic practices within unions. A caveat notes that archived websites may not be exact replicas of the originals as they existed at the time of capture due to technical, privacy, or other constraints. Overall, the document communicates both user-facing guidance about Tweet location settings and an overview of a specialized web archiving effort preserving labor‑movement web content for research and historical purposes.

Three women from Sandusky, Ohio—identified as Ashley England, Mary Jordan and Sammie Whaley—were arrested after allegedly assaulting a McDonald’s employee in Bellevue on June 8 because they believed she was serving them and their children too slowly. The attack occurred in the restaurant parking lot; security video led police to identify and arrest the women the next day. Booking photos show two of the suspects smiling. Charges differ: England faces assault, theft and child endangerment; Jordan faces assault and child endangerment; Whaley faces assault. Child endangerment counts were filed because England and Jordan had their children with them and the children reportedly participated in the incident. All three have pleaded not guilty to multiple charges. The local police department reported the suspects traveled with family and friends from Sandusky, and the case drew attention due to the involvement of minors and the demeanor captured in mugshots.

A three-year-old boy fell into the gorilla moat at Cincinnati Zoo’s Gorilla World on May 28, 2016, prompting a fatal zoo response: Harambe, a 17-year-old, 450-pound western lowland gorilla, was shot and killed after grabbing and dragging the child. The boy had climbed through barriers and dropped about 10–15 feet into the shallow moat. Video and witness accounts showed Harambe initially standing over and even appearing to shield the child, then dragging him through the water and across the habitat amid loud, agitated crowds. Fire and zoo reports described Harambe as “violently dragging and throwing” the boy, and the zoo’s Dangerous Animal Response Team—composed of trained keepers, veterinarians, maintenance and security staff—decided a gunshot was necessary because a tranquilizer would act too slowly or could further agitate the animal. The boy was taken to Cincinnati Children’s Hospital and released the same night with non-life-threatening injuries; his family later said he was “doing well” and asked for donations to the zoo in Harambe’s name rather than gifts to them.

The incident sparked intense public debate and outrage. Many criticized the parents for alleged negligence and called for charges; others condemned the zoo for killing an endangered animal. Online petitions and a “Justice for Harambe” movement gathered tens of thousands of supporters, and vigils and protests were held. Animal-rights groups such as PETA argued captivity and insufficient secondary barriers contributed to the tragedy. The zoo defended its safety record—Gorilla World had no prior breaches since 1978—and said it will review procedures while continuing plans for a larger, naturalistic gorilla habitat. Authorities said they were not pursuing charges against the parents.

America Saves’ triannual Personal Savings Index (PSI) found Americans’ interest, effort and effectiveness in personal saving rose sharply from May to September, reaching the highest levels in seven surveys. In September, reported interest climbed from 63% to 75%, effort from 58% to 65%, and effectiveness from 55% to 62%. The survey of 1,000 adults, conducted Sept. 10–13 by ORC International (±3 points), converts 10-point responses on each measure into percentages. Income strongly correlates with greater saving attitudes and behavior: 84% of households earning over $100,000 reported interest in saving (76% effort, 71% effectiveness), versus 68% interest (58% effort, 55% effectiveness) for those under $25,000. America Saves, managed by the Consumer Federation of America, notes the PSI does not yet show multi-year trends and that factors such as perceived personal and national financial conditions may influence results. The campaign uses behavioral economics to encourage low- and moderate-income households to save, reduce debt, and build wealth and promotes pledges and programs nationally and locally.

Pop star Justin Bieber was arrested in Miami Beach in the early morning after police say he participated in a pre-dawn drag race in a rented yellow Lamborghini, resisted officers and admitted to using alcohol, marijuana and prescription drugs. The incident reportedly began around 4:30 a.m. on Pine Tree Drive, a residential street, where members of Bieber’s entourage allegedly blocked traffic to create a drag strip. Police pursued multiple vehicles; Bieber’s car and a red Ferrari driven by rapper Khalil Amir Sharieff (aka Crazy Khalil) were stopped. Officers said Bieber was incoherent, belligerent, cursed at police, refused to follow commands, kept his hands in his pockets and initially declined to exit the vehicle. He failed field sobriety tests; breath tests showed a blood-alcohol reading below .08 but above Florida’s zero-tolerance limit for underage drivers. Bieber was booked on charges including DUI, drag-racing and resisting arrest, and for driving on a suspended license; Sharieff was also charged with DUI. Bieber spent the mandatory post-DUI detention, appeared in bond court via video and was held on $2,500 bail before posting bond and briefly greeting fans. The episode prompted an Opa-locka probe into an allegedly unauthorized police escort and added to Bieber’s string of recent legal troubles, including vandalism and previous complaints about reckless driving.

President Trump asked his lawyers about the possibility of pardoning Paul Manafort and other aides under scrutiny in Robert Mueller’s Russia probe, attorney Rudy Giuliani said. Giuliani said he and Jay Sekulow advised against pardoning anyone tied to the investigation until Mueller finishes, warning that pardons for witnesses might be construed as obstruction of justice. Trump reportedly agreed and did not press the issue. White House officials, including press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders, later said pardons for Manafort were not under active consideration.

Timing of the discussion is unclear; Giuliani initially said it occurred “three to five weeks ago,” later noting it was in June and part of a broader conversation about potential pardons. A senior official said Trump weighed pros and cons “a few weeks ago.” Inside the West Wing, key aides—Chief of Staff John Kelly, White House counsel Don McGahn and attorney Emmet Flood—oppose a Manafort pardon and have tried to steer Trump away from the idea. Critics warn a pardon would not end Mueller’s probe, could spur political backlash, and might increase legal exposure.

Manafort was convicted on multiple tax- and bank-fraud counts; Trump has publicly defended him, calling him “brave” for not cooperating. The article also covers Michael Cohen’s guilty plea to campaign finance violations and tax charges; Trump and his lawyers privately minimized its impact, arguing it doesn’t prove conspiracy with Russia and stressing Cohen’s prior inconsistent statements. The president’s sympathy for Manafort and frustration over perceived heavy-handed treatment motivated consideration of clemency, Giuliani said.

Chicago police charged a second man, Derrick A. Hillard, 37, with first-degree murder and unlawful use of a weapon by a felon in the Oct. 6, 2013, killing of 19-year-old Jamal Harmon. Hillard’s uncle, Andre Davis, 52, was earlier arrested and charged with murder and kidnapping in the same case; prosecutors say Harmon was shot after an argument over a dice game at a party, then moved into a Cadillac trunk and later dumped in a South Side alley. Harmon was found Oct. 26 with multiple gunshot wounds, stab wounds, and cuts to his neck; witnesses report Harmon was still alive after being shot and that Davis admitted to cutting his throat. Hillard is due in bond court.

The report also recounts Andre Davis’s controversial past: convicted in 1981 and again in 1983 for the 1980 rape and murder of 3-year-old Brianna Stickel, he served 32 years before DNA testing prompted his 2012 exoneration and release. Davis’s case drew attention from Northwestern’s Center on Wrongful Convictions; allies later raised questions about the original investigation, forensic evidence, and witness accounts. Now accused in Harmon’s 2013 slaying, Davis faces renewed legal scrutiny and is being held without bond.

A comprehensive CDC and Pew Charitable Trusts analysis of 2010–2011 ambulatory care data found that about 13% of outpatient visits in the United States resulted in an oral antibiotic prescription, and roughly 30% of those prescriptions were likely unnecessary. Using the National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey and National Hospital Ambulatory Medical Care Survey, investigators estimated annual, population-adjusted outpatient antibiotic prescribing rates by age and diagnosis and judged appropriateness using national guidelines and regional prescribing patterns. Across all ages and conditions, an estimated 506 antibiotic prescriptions were written per 1000 population annually, but only about 353 per 1000 were considered appropriate, implying approximately 47 million unnecessary outpatient prescriptions each year. Acute respiratory conditions were the main driver of overprescribing: they accounted for 44% of outpatient antibiotic prescriptions and produced 221 prescriptions per 1000 population annually, of which only 111 per 1000 were estimated appropriate. Sinusitis (56 prescriptions per 1000), suppurative otitis media (47 per 1000), and pharyngitis (43 per 1000) were the top diagnoses associated with antibiotic use. The analysis likely underestimates total inappropriate use because it excludes telephone encounters, urgent care clinics, retail clinics, dentist offices, and prescriptions by some clinicians. The findings underscore the public health threat posed by antibiotic overuse—contributing to the rise of resistant “superbugs” that cause an estimated 2 million infections and 23,000 deaths in the U.S. annually—and support national stewardship efforts. The White House’s National Action Plan aimed to halve inappropriate outpatient antibiotic use by 2020; based on these estimates, achieving that target would require an overall outpatient antibiotic reduction of about 15% (roughly 23 million fewer prescriptions). The report recommends targeted stewardship actions by clinicians, health systems, payers, public health agencies, and professional organizations to reduce unnecessary prescribing and preserve antibiotic effectiveness.

In April, Boko Haram abducted more than 200 schoolgirls from a Chibok boarding school in Nigeria; roughly 60 have escaped while many remain missing amid fears of recapture and ongoing village attacks. Jubilee Campaign USA, a human-rights nonprofit, launched the “Education After Escape” campaign to support ten of the escaped girls by raising $125,000 to place them in specialized boarding schools abroad or in safe locations, covering tuition, travel, and care. The effort seeks to transform trauma into opportunity, protect the girls from further violence or forced marriage, and counter the wider chilling effect Boko Haram’s violence has had on girls’ education in northern Nigeria. Jubilee stresses both humanitarian and spiritual motives, describing the program as a way to ensure the girls’ futures and preserve Chibok’s culture. The group has raised over $20,000 in an initial month and points to prior advocacy work, international partnerships, and formal nonprofit credentials while urging public donations and continued pressure on authorities to find the still-captive students.

Sunni Islamist militants — chiefly the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (ISIS/ISIL) — claimed on multiple social media channels in mid‑June 2014 that they had captured and massacred hundreds of Shiite members of Iraq’s security forces, releasing graphic photographs purportedly showing mass executions in Tikrit. The group’s claim of 1,700 killed could not be independently verified; Iraqi officials, human-rights investigators and media warned the images and numbers remained unconfirmed even as they noted ISIS’s documented brutality and intent to inflame sectarian tensions. Photographs showed masked gunmen and bound young men at apparent execution sites; captions openly taunted Shiites and Prime Minister Nuri al‑Maliki’s government. Local reports said many captured at Camp Speicher and elsewhere were air force cadets; Sunnis among prisoners were reportedly released while Shiites were separated and allegedly killed, with some bodies seen in the Tigris River. Authorities recovered some bodies but disputed the scale of the massacre.

Concurrently ISIS consolidated gains across northern and northwestern Iraq: it seized Mosul earlier and took Tal Afar after heavy fighting, advancing toward Baghdad and prompting mass civilian displacement. Iraqi Shiite cleric Grand Ayatollah Ali al‑Sistani called for restraint even as his previous plea to defend the country accelerated volunteer militia mobilization. Baghdad saw renewed bombings and attacks that killed dozens. The U.S. repositioned naval assets to the Persian Gulf, augmented embassy security and prepared options short of ground troops; Washington engaged regional partners and explored direct talks with Iran to coordinate responses. Analysts warned ISIS sought to provoke sectarian reprisals to deepen civil war and that any external support aligned with Iran risked alienating Sunni populations and regional allies. Iraqi leaders vowed to fight back amid intense international concern about Iraq’s stability and the widening humanitarian and security crisis.

More than 200 bottlenose dolphins were held for a second day in Taiji Cove, Japan, where fishermen separate pods to capture animals for sale to aquariums or for slaughter, U.S. conservationists reported. The Sea Shepherd Conservation Society, which has been livestreaming the operations, said fishermen selected dozens of dolphins judged desirable for captivity— including a rare albino calf—and moved them away, while many others, visibly injured and stressed, remained penned without food or rest. The group warned fishermen would soon slaughter the less marketable animals, often under tarps to hide the killings, and said past drives have turned the water red with blood. Two dolphins reportedly died during captures. Activists cite high mercury levels in dolphin meat and urge people not to support marine parks that buy wild-caught animals. Taiji officials and Wakayama Prefecture defend the hunt as a long-standing, regulated local tradition and have criticized Western coverage as biased. The issue gained global attention after the documentary The Cove and remains a flashpoint between local practice and international animal welfare concerns.

London’s Olympic Park buzzed with drama and triumph as British royals and elite athletes made headlines. Zara Phillips, 31, made her Olympic debut in the dressage phase of eventing, riding High Kingdom to cheers from home crowds and watched by husband Mike Tindall, Prince Philip, Princess Anne, and family. A former European and World champion, Phillips said competing for her country was “incredible” despite a few mistakes; she’ll return for Monday’s dramatic cross-country phase, which features a rugged 3.5-mile course of massive jumps. Cousins Prince William and Kate are expected to attend. 

In athletics, Britain suffered a blow as marathon star Paula Radcliffe withdrew from the London Games with a persistent foot injury. The 38-year-old, still the women’s marathon world record holder, said accepting the end of her Olympic dream “hurts,” but that she had done everything to try to make the start line. Scotland’s Freya Murray is set to replace her, joining Claire Hallissey and Mara Yamauchi. Radcliffe’s storied career includes multiple London and New York wins and a world title in 2005, yet Olympic medals have eluded her. 

Across at the Royal Artillery Barracks, U.S. shooter Kimberly Rhode made history by winning women’s skeet gold, becoming the first American to medal in an individual sport at five consecutive Olympics. Rhode tied the world record and set an Olympic mark with 99 points, sealing a dominant victory.

Following threats from North Korea, Guam’s Office of Civil Defense echoed Ready.gov guidance warning survivors of a nuclear blast not to use hair conditioner during decontamination. Nuclear detonations create fallout—fine, sand-like radioactive dust—that can settle on clothing, skin and hair. Human hair is made of overlapping protein scales; tiny fallout particles can lodge between those scales. Regular washing with soap or shampoo and removing outer clothing can eliminate roughly 85–95% of contamination. By contrast, conditioners contain cationic surfactants, silicones and cationic polymers that are designed to remain on hair and smooth the scales. Those oily, positively charged compounds can pull scales down and bind or trap radioactive particles, making them harder to rinse out and potentially increasing exposure. Cosmetic chemists and radiation-safety experts therefore recommend avoiding conditioners and other oily or sticky personal-care products (lotions, some cosmetics) while decontaminating. After thorough decontamination—once fallout risk is past—normal hair and skin care is acceptable. Authorities emphasize that the best protection is avoiding exposure in the first place: get inside immediately after a blast, seek a fallout shelter or a basement, remove outer clothing, and take a decontamination shower with soap or mild shampoo. Simple, repeated washing typically removes contamination; minimizing additional binding agents like conditioner is a small but sensible precaution.

President Trump threatened to withhold federal funds from the University of California, Berkeley after administrators canceled a scheduled Milo Yiannopoulos speech following violent protests. Trump tweeted that if Berkeley “does not allow free speech and practices violence on innocent people with a different point of view - NO FEDERAL FUNDS.” The event was called off roughly two hours before it was to begin after clashes involving roughly 150 masked agitators, according to UC police: smoke bombs, commercial-grade fireworks, Molotov cocktails, rocks thrown at officers, smashed windows and a bonfire. More than 1,500 protesters gathered; at least six people were injured. Critics called Trump’s threat an abuse of power; UC defended the cancellation as necessary for public safety.

Brittany Williams, a young Texas mother, lost vision in her left eye after contracting a severe bacterial infection following a “Mud Run” in Dallas. Hours after the race she felt intense pain and described her vision turning white; an ER visit that night diagnosed multiple corneal abrasions and what appeared to be a chemical burn. Sent home initially, her condition worsened within 24 hours and she was hospitalized when doctors determined flesh-eating bacteria had invaded a cut on her eye and rapidly destroyed the cornea—Williams says it “completely melted off.” After a week in hospital and ongoing treatment to prevent systemic spread, she is now blind in that eye and may require further antibiotics and surgery; some doctors have refused treatment because she lacks insurance. Working two jobs, Williams had previously opted out of health coverage to save money, saying she rarely used care and feared routine costs. Her family has launched a GoFundMe appeal; about 170 donors have contributed nearly $10,000 so far, while accumulated medical bills exceed $100,000. The case highlights infection risks associated with mud runs and similar obstacle-course events, which have been linked previously to outbreaks of diarrheal illness and gastroenteritis from contaminated mud or water. Despite the traumatic experience and uncertain prognosis, Williams is trying to stay positive, acknowledging a chance she could regain sight with surgery but facing barriers due to cost and insurance coverage. The family seeks financial help and wider awareness of the potential hazards of such events.

A long-term study of nearly 75,000 U.S. nurses suggests rotating night shift work is linked to modestly higher mortality risks. Using 22 years of Nurses’ Health Study data, researchers led by Dr. Eva Schernhammer defined rotating shifts as working at least three nights per month in addition to days or evenings. Women who worked rotating night shifts for five years or more showed an increased risk of death: about an 11% higher all-cause mortality for those with six to 14 years of such work, and elevated fatal cardiovascular disease risk of roughly 19% (six to 14 years) to 23% (15+ years). While overall cancer mortality was not associated with rotating shifts, nurses with 15 or more years of rotating night work had about a 25% higher risk of dying from lung cancer. The observational study cannot prove causation, but the findings add to prior evidence that shift work may harm longevity. Researchers call for further study of duration, intensity, schedule patterns and individual traits (for example, chronotype) to clarify risks and guide practical recommendations for shift workers.

A 17-year-old girl died after a shark attack while surfing with her father near Esperance on Western Australia’s south coast. The attack occurred Monday at Kelp Beds, a popular break at Wylie Bay about 4pm; witnesses say the girl was pulled underwater and lost a leg before being hauled ashore by her father and another teenager. Paramedics treated her on the beach and she was taken to Esperance Hospital in critical condition, where she later died. The girl’s mother and two younger sisters witnessed the incident. Authorities suspect a great white shark; the exact size is unknown. Wylie Bay Beach was closed and the Department of Fisheries advised people to avoid the area for at least 48 hours and planned patrols. The location has a recent history of shark activity, including a 2014 attack at the same spot when surfer Sean Pollard lost both arms.

With NFL officials locked out amid a labor dispute, Shannon Eastin will become the first woman to work as part of an NFL officiating crew, assigned to Thursday’s preseason game between the Green Bay Packers and San Diego Chargers. Eastin, an experienced referee in the Mid-Eastern Athletic Conference and other small-college and high-school leagues, joins replacement officials the NFL is training while talks with the officials’ union continue. Replacement crews, who already worked the Hall of Fame Game, have shown early miscues, such as a mistaken coin-toss announcement, highlighting the challenges of using replacements during the ongoing standoff.

The Guardian’s investigation portrays Private Bradley Manning as mentally fragile long before his 2007 deployment to Iraq, describing frequent outbursts, self-harm, wetting himself, throwing chairs, shouting at officers and repeated psychiatric evaluations. An officer at Fort Leonard Wood called Manning “a mess of a child” who should never have been sent to combat. Despite an adjustment disorder diagnosis and warnings by senior officers, Manning retained clearance and was posted to Forward Operating Base Hammer, where two months in his rifle bolt was removed amid concerns he was dangerous. Eyewitnesses report lax computer security: SIPRNet laptops with passwords on sticky notes and many soldiers accessing sensitive networks, making large-scale leaks plausible. Manning is accused of illegally downloading and passing thousands of military and diplomatic documents to WikiLeaks; he denies the charges and faces up to 55 years if convicted. The Defence Security Service is probing why pre-deployment screening and intelligence access controls failed.

A federal survey of about 13,500 Americans aged 15–44 (2006–2008) reveals notable shifts in sexual behavior. Virginity rose: 29% of females and 27% of males aged 15–24 reported no sexual contact, up from 22% in 2002. Most adults report vaginal intercourse; oral sex is common and may precede vaginal sex for some teens. About 36% of women and 44% of men have had opposite-sex anal sex. Women were more than twice as likely as men to report same-sex experiences (≈12.5% vs. 5.2%) and reported bisexual identity more often. Educational patterns differed by gender. Data were collected via in-person interviews with private computerized responses to sensitive questions. Researchers say findings inform sexual health policy and show fluidity across sexual behavior categories.

Pete Davidson, a Saturday Night Live cast member, told High Times he uses medical marijuana to manage Crohn’s disease, saying conventional treatments failed and cannabis is the only thing that helps him eat and perform. He criticized New York’s medical marijuana program as inadequate and argued cannabis should be legal beyond medical use. Davidson, who joined SNL in 2014, said performing sober “has gone awful” for him and defended his cannabis use as necessary for his work. He also announced he’s been sober from drugs for the first time in eight years, thanked supporters, and praised Kid Cudi for helping him through dark times. Season 42 of SNL premieres October 1; his stand-up special airs October 29.

At a Women for Women International luncheon in New York, Hillary Clinton delivered a pointed assessment of her 2016 campaign and a barbed remark about President Donald Trump.
