While acknowledging personal responsibility for losing the race—“I was the candidate, I was the person who was on the ballot”—Clinton said external events in the campaign’s final days were decisive. She told CNN’s Christiane Amanpour that “if the election had been on October 27, I would be your president,” citing FBI Director James Comey’s letter on October 28 and Russian-linked WikiLeaks disclosures as factors that “raised doubts in the minds of people who were inclined to vote for me and got scared off.” Clinton said she believes those intervening events in the last 10 days cost her the election, even as she reminded the audience that she won the popular vote by more than 3 million ballots. When Amanpour teased that a Trump tweet might follow, Clinton shrugged and welcomed the diversion, saying she was happy to be one since there were “lots of other things to worry about,” and suggesting Trump should focus less on her popular-vote win and more on substantive issues facing the country. The appearance coincided with other New York events Clinton was attending, including a Planned Parenthood dinner.

A 41-year-old Canadian, identified by Peruvian authorities as Sebastian Woodroffe, was lynched in a remote community in Peru’s Ucayali region after locals accused him of involvement in the fatal shooting of 81-year-old Shipibo-Conibo healer and activist Olivia Arévalo. Arévalo, a respected indigenous shaman known for her traditional knowledge and ayahuasca ceremonies and an outspoken defender of indigenous land rights, was shot to death near her home. In the days following, a cellphone video circulated showing a bloodied man—reported to be Woodroffe—being dragged by a rope or hose around his neck in front of thatched houses while villagers watched. Police later exhumed a body buried in a shallow grave about one kilometre from Arévalo’s home; fingerprints identified it as Woodroffe. Forensic reports indicate he died by strangulation and sustained multiple blows.

Authorities say they are pursuing several lines of inquiry into both deaths, including theories involving debts owed by Arévalo’s son and possible gang involvement; officials have not confirmed Woodroffe as the shooter. Woodroffe, from Vancouver Island, had traveled repeatedly to Peru seeking apprenticeship in plant medicine and raised funds online to study traditional healing and use psychedelics therapeutically. Friends describe him as a gentle seeker, making his alleged connection to the killing hard to reconcile. The killings have intensified local outrage and concern: Peru’s human rights ombudsman and Canadian officials called for investigations and condemned the lynching. Shipibo leaders decried the violence yet said distrust in formal justice systems contributed to community members resorting to “traditional” reprisals. The murders come amid other unresolved attacks on indigenous leaders defending ancestral lands.

President Obama urged action in his inaugural address, but a polarized Washington raises doubts about how much of his agenda will pass and how looming budget battles will shape his second term. The panel — including Jim DeMint, Ben Jealous, Bob Woodward, Andrea Mitchell, and Ted Koppel — discussed those challenges and Hillary Clinton’s uncertain future after tough Capitol Hill questioning over Benghazi as she prepares to depart. Separately, Michele Bachmann reiterated she’s running for president, dismissing criticisms and refusing to call gay couples with children “families,” calling the issue “the defining political issue of our time.”

A 22-year-old Davenport woman, Ashley R. Hautzenrader, has been charged with child endangerment after allegedly delivering a baby in a University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics restroom on May 8 and attempting to dispose of the newborn. According to a criminal complaint, Hautzenrader, who said she did not know she was pregnant, gave birth into a toilet about 9:24 p.m., believed the infant was stillborn, tried to flush it, then placed the child in a pillowcase and left it in a trash can after cleaning the bathroom. UIHC employees found the newborn alive shortly after delivery. Hautzenrader admitted to putting the baby in the trash can when confronted by officers. Hospital officials declined to comment on whether she was a patient or the infant’s condition, citing privacy laws, and police say the investigation is ongoing. Hautzenrader was arrested, placed on supervised release after an initial court appearance, and will be represented by a public defender. She faces one count of child endangerment, an aggravated misdemeanor carrying up to two years’ imprisonment. Iowa’s Safe Haven law allows parents to leave newborns at hospitals without prosecution.

Giorgio Armani used his final-day show at Milan Fashion Week to air frustrations about the industry's calendar, its leadership and the direction of Italian fashion. Angry that American Vogue editor Anna Wintour skipped his runway to attend Paris previews, Armani publicly complained that being the lone major designer on the last day leaves him penalized as journalists and buyers decamp to France. He suggested rotating which houses close the calendar so “power people” would stay, criticized the Camera della Moda (National Chamber for Italian Fashion) for letting the day become “empty,” and warned that organizers must do more to protect and promote Italian fashion. The Camera’s president, Mario Boselli, responded that the schedule won’t change but acknowledged the importance of keeping major journalists present and said efforts would be made next season.

On creative grounds, Armani emphasized craftsmanship and wearability over spectacle. His Fall-Winter collection showcased subtle innovations—softened, pleated ankle-length trousers, rounded single-button jackets, gray tones brightened with lime accents, green side stripes for a sporty note, luminous evening grays, strapless sheaths, and a standout wispy gray fur lit by lime. He derided what he sees as excess and fantasy-driven runway shows that may please critics but fail shoppers, urging that fashion must deliver functional, economically viable products if it expects government or market support. He even suggested some domestic labels risk losing credibility by prioritizing pure creativity over commercial relevance, citing copycat retailing of older Armani designs.

By contrast, DSquared2 staged a theatrical, darker show set in a psychiatric-ward tableau: glamorous, distressed minis, beading, fur and silk, and motifs of locks, keys and syringe-like ankle bands—an aesthetic of crazed Hollywood glamour that underscored Milan’s mix of discipline and theatricality during the week.

Actor Shia LaBeouf was arrested after disrupting a performance of Cabaret at Studio 54 in Manhattan. According to police and witnesses, the 28-year-old smoked in the theater, slapped audience members on the buttocks and heads, cursed loudly and was removed at intermission. Officers described him as “incoherent” and “very agitated”; he fell while being approached and was taken to the Midtown-North precinct. At the station he allegedly became belligerent, spat at officers when they refused to remove his handcuffs, was fitted with a spit mask, and hurled profanities and threats, including a homophobic slur and claims he could “ruin” an officer’s career. He was charged with criminal trespass and disorderly conduct (reports also cite harassment). LaBeouf has faced prior erratic incidents and apologized earlier this year for plagiarism in a screenplay. He was released and given a court date.

The government shutdown entered its third day amid sharp partisan disagreement over immigration. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell offered to allow floor debate on immigration in mid- to late February if leaders don’t reach a deal; Democrats doubted his commitment, demanding that protections for Dreamers be included in any funding measure. Trump and House Republicans blamed Democrats for prioritizing undocumented immigrants, while Democrats and moderates sought a short-term funding extension tied to an immigration bill. Negotiations involved offers on wall funding and other concessions, but GOP hard-liners and many Democrats rejected parts of proposals. Weekend effects were limited but with longer shutdown implications—federal workers idle, contractors unpaid, and agencies like the IRS delayed—while both sides jockeyed for leverage.

Veteran cinematographer Vittorio Storaro has defended Bernardo Bertolucci and Marlon Brando amid renewed outrage over Last Tango in Paris’ notorious 1972 “butter” scene, insisting no on-set wrongdoing occurred and criticizing the media backlash as sensationalist. Storaro, a three-time Oscar winner who collaborated with Bertolucci on The Conformist, Last Tango in Paris and later films, told THR he was present throughout the shoot and rejects claims that Maria Schneider — then 19 — was raped or coerced. He says the film set was collaborative and joyful, with a small crew working closely for weeks in the Paris apartment where much of the movie was filmed. According to Storaro, daily discussions between Bertolucci and Brando sometimes produced last-minute adjustments; the director would then explain staging to the crew. He acknowledges Bertolucci may not have mentioned a particular detail to Schneider, but insists she fully understood the nature of the project, was an active performer, and later lamented the film’s end — not its making. Storaro recalled Brando as intelligent, generous and invested in realizing the story, and he called the resurfaced 2013 interview — in which Bertolucci admitted springing the butter element on Schneider — a “ridiculous” controversy amplified by “ignorant” journalists. He emphasized cinematic sex is simulated, and that the sensational headlines misrepresented both the shoot and the filmmakers’ intentions. The dispute reignited after Bertolucci’s earlier remarks circulated online, prompting condemnation from several contemporary actors and renewed debate over consent and responsibility on film sets. Bertolucci has defended that Schneider had read the script and knew about the simulated rape element, claiming only the butter was improvised; Schneider, who died in 2011, had said she “felt a little raped” in later interviews. Storaro maintains the scene was a filmmaking choice, not an act of violence, and regards Last Tango’s power as rooted in its thematic provocation rather than any real-world assault.

President Obama’s Jan. 21 speech proposing strict limits on big banks—banning proprietary trading and investments in hedge and private equity funds—spooked markets and knocked financial stocks sharply lower. The S&P 500 fell 1.9% as major banks like Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Bank of America dropped on investor concern. Analysts say the issue isn’t opposition to regulation itself but the uncertainty legislation creates while debated; political events such as Scott Brown’s Senate victory have heightened perceived political risk and prompted tougher rhetoric from Washington. Some experts expect regulation to be phased in slowly to avoid fire-sale conditions, and note that long-term benefits could strengthen the system’s integrity. Still, markets may react emotionally in the short term, and earnings, economic data, jobless rates and Fed policy will remain the ultimate market drivers.

Candida auris is an emerging fungal pathogen that the CDC identifies as a serious global health threat because of three main concerns: multidrug resistance, difficulty of accurate laboratory identification, and its propensity to cause outbreaks in healthcare settings. Since 1996 Alexa Internet has donated crawl data to the Internet Archive, and those data are added daily to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period; this note appears alongside CDC updates documenting the agency’s evolving guidance on C. auris. Key CDC updates include new and reorganized recommendations for laboratorians and health professionals posted December 21, 2018—covering environmental disinfection, species identification, and screening—plus earlier additions such as patient, laboratory staff, and infection preventionist fact sheets (July 20, 2018). The agency also reported a case count update to 523 on December 21, 2018. The CDC emphasizes that C. auris is often resistant to multiple antifungal drugs commonly used to treat Candida infections, and because standard laboratory methods can misidentify it, many labs need specific technologies to detect it reliably. Misidentification can delay or misdirect patient management and infection control. Because C. auris can spread within healthcare facilities and cause outbreaks, rapid, accurate identification is critical so facilities can implement appropriate precautions to halt transmission. The CDC urges all U.S. laboratory staff who identify C. auris to promptly notify their state or local public health authorities and to alert CDC directly via the dedicated email candidaauris@cdc.gov. The document also references CDC expert commentary and resources intended to support surveillance, laboratory identification, infection control, and clinical response to this emerging threat.

Three days after voters signaled widespread unease about the economy, the government reported that U.S. employers added a strong 214,000 jobs in October, extending the healthiest hiring streak in eight years. Revisions also showed 31,000 more positions added in August and September than previously estimated, marking nine consecutive months of at least 200,000 jobs—the longest run since 1995. The unemployment rate ticked down to 5.8 percent from 5.9 percent, its lowest level since July 2008. Economic growth has accelerated, with a roughly 4.1 percent annualized pace over the last six months, prompting the Federal Reserve to end its bond-buying stimulus. Manufacturing expanded at its fastest pace in three years and services also grew solidly; home sales rose in September at the quickest rate this year. Yet many Americans remain unconvinced: nearly 60 percent of voters in recent elections said the economy was stagnating or worsening. Wage growth has been weak—real average hourly pay rose only 0.3 percent year-over-year through September—and income gains have mainly favored the wealthiest, while most households saw stagnant or lower incomes. Slower global growth and falling exports have trimmed some near-term growth forecasts.

In 2007 Mylan acquired the decades-old EpiPen auto-injector and transformed it into a blockbuster through aggressive marketing, lobbying and public-awareness campaigns. Originally a $200 million product, EpiPen now generates more than $1 billion annually and accounts for roughly 40 percent of Mylan’s operating profits. Mylan expanded markets by pushing federal and state policies to encourage stocking epinephrine in schools and public venues, distributing free devices to tens of thousands of schools, striking deals with organizations like Disney, and increasing advertising spending dramatically. Changes in FDA labeling and 2010 guidance recommending two doses per patient helped Mylan pivot to selling twin-packs rather than single pens, further boosting sales.

While the device’s medicine—epinephrine—costs only a few dollars, wholesale and retail prices climbed steeply after the acquisition. Estimates put the wholesale price rise at about 400–480 percent since 2008–2009; a two-pack often costs insured patients roughly $415 after discounts, and uninsured or high-deductible patients report bills of $500–$1,100. Mylan argues it does not set final retail prices, offers coupons that can eliminate co-pays for many patients, and says investments and product-support justify price changes. Critics, including doctors, patient advocates and some senators, call the increases excessive and say they put life-saving medicine out of reach for many families. Reports of patients foregoing EpiPens because of cost have emerged.

Competition has been limited: Sanofi’s Auvi-Q entered at comparable pricing and initially struggled with coverage, and a Teva generic faced patent settlement timing and regulatory hurdles. Mylan cites strong brand equity—EpiPen is widely prescribed and familiar to doctors and patients—as protection against market erosion. The result: a trusted emergency product whose rising price has sparked public outcry, political scrutiny, and debate over affordability and industry practices.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Carl Paladino faced backlash after sharply criticizing homosexuality in a Brooklyn speech and later sought to soften his remarks on NBC’s Today show. Speaking to Orthodox Jews in Williamsburg, Paladino said he did not want children “brainwashed into thinking that homosexuality is an equally valid and successful option,” and had drafted lines blaming “dysfunctional homosexual[ity]” to parts of his speech he later said were crossed out. He emphasized opposition to same-sex marriage while claiming he is not anti-gay, saying he would “absolutely” recruit gay people for his administration. Paladino also attacked rival Andrew Cuomo for attending a gay pride parade with his daughters, calling such events inappropriate for children and describing some parade behavior as “disgusting.” His campaign manager framed Paladino’s views as aligned with Catholic teaching. Critics, including LGBT advocates and Cuomo’s campaign, condemned the remarks as homophobic and dangerous, calling for an apology and arguing Paladino is out of the mainstream. Polls show majority support for gay marriage in New York, and Cuomo’s lead in the race reportedly widened after the controversy. The report also briefly includes unrelated metadata about a large web crawl dataset offered by the Internet Archive.

This document compiles legal precedent, commentary, and policy material concerning corporal punishment in schools. It centers on the U.S. Supreme Court’s 1977 decision Ingraham v. Wright, which held that the Eighth Amendment’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause does not apply to school disciplinary paddlings because the Amendment historically targets criminal punishments. The Court recognized that corporal punishment implicates Fourteenth Amendment liberty interests—freedom from bodily restraint and appreciable physical pain—but concluded that due process does not require prior notice and hearing where common-law limits and post hoc civil/criminal remedies suffice. The majority emphasized schools’ openness, community supervision, and existing state-law constraints; dissenters argued the Eighth Amendment should cover inhumane school punishments and that minimal pre-punishment procedural safeguards (an informal opportunity to be heard) are necessary to prevent irreversible harm. The compilation then surveys contemporary practice and debate, focusing on Alabama where corporal punishment remains legal and common. Data show substantial use and racial/gender disparities; advocates including medical and psychological associations oppose corporal punishment, urging alternative disciplinary methods and cautioning about its harms. State statutes, local policies, and professional resolutions reflect continuing contention over efficacy, equity, and constitutional protection.

President Trump defended his handling of staffing at the State Department and other agencies during a Fox News interview with Laura Ingraham, arguing vacancies would not derail his agenda. Asked about numerous unfilled senior posts — including roles overseeing Southeast Asia and arms control — Trump insisted he is the ultimate decision-maker and that policy reflects his priorities. He framed limited nominations as a deliberate, businesslike cost-saving choice: “When you don’t need to fill slots, don’t fill them.” He blamed Senate Democrats, particularly Chuck Schumer, for obstructing confirmations and acknowledged he has sent fewer nominations than recent predecessors, citing appointee-tracker data showing he lags behind past presidents in confirmed appointments.

Trump defended Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, saying Tillerson is “working hard,” and noted Tillerson disputed reports of low morale at State. The president also said he’s unhappy with some career officials’ “thinking process,” which has influenced decisions not to appoint certain positions.

The interview ranged widely beyond staffing. Trump criticized the Steele dossier as fabricated and attacked media coverage; called the Justice Department and court processes slow and in need of reform; said DACA and "chain migration" will be part of any immigration deal and that Republicans won’t accept preserving chain migration; and touted economic gains under his administration, including deregulation, judicial confirmations, rising GDP, and companies repatriating or moving operations back to the U.S. He defended the proposed tax plan as a historic middle-class boost.

On foreign policy, Trump previewed an important Asia trip — to China, Japan, South Korea and Vietnam — stressing North Korea as a primary concern and saying China has been helpful on sanctions. He indicated possible talks with Putin and stressed alliances with Japan and security discussions involving Korea and Syria. Overall, he projected confidence in accomplishments while arguing staffing shortfalls are manageable and intentional.

The Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) and the National Association of Theatre Owners (NATO) have formalized a zero-tolerance policy on wearable recording devices in movie theaters. Announced at the ShowEast conference, the rule requires patrons to turn off and stow smart glasses, smartwatches, and similar devices while films are showing. Theater staff will ask anyone who keeps such gear visible to put it away, and persistent noncompliance can result in ejection. If employees suspect someone is recording a movie, they may contact law enforcement. This policy extends existing anti-piracy measures that already apply to phones and other recording equipment; many theaters had similar bans individually, but the MPAA and NATO statement makes it an industrywide stance intended to curb illegal copying. The organizations emphasized they welcome technological advances and acknowledge consumer interest in intelligent devices, but stressed protecting films from in-theater recording takes precedence during screenings. Critics note the practical limits of the rule: a person willing to wear a head-mounted computer might also know more effective ways to pirate films than filming content with devices like Google Glass, so enforcement may deter casual recording but won’t eliminate piracy. Still, the unified policy gives theater owners clearer authority to prevent visible use of wearables during movies and to act if recording is suspected.

Hugh Hefner has publicly disputed claims by his ex-fiancée Crystal Harris that their sex life was unsatisfying. After Harris told Howard Stern she had sex with the 85-year-old Playboy founder only once and that it “lasted like, two seconds,” adding she’d “never seen Hef naked” and wasn’t attracted to him, Hefner responded on Twitter calling her interview “crazy” and suggesting she might be trying to impress a new boyfriend. He denied her account, tweeting that their first night together was “good enough” to keep her for two more nights and accusing her of lying about their relationship. Harris, 24, has been seen socializing with Jordan McGraw, Dr. Phil’s son, though reports say they denied a romance; observers described them relaxed and drinking together at a New York bar. Harris also partied with Heidi Montag around the time of her canceled wedding and later attempted to sell her engagement ring. The exchange has drawn public attention and social media commentary, with both sides publicly sticking to conflicting narratives about their breakup and intimacy.

A large prospective study suggests that repeated cycles of weight loss and regain—commonly called yo-yo dieting or weight cycling—are linked to substantially worse outcomes in people with existing coronary artery disease (CAD). Investigators followed 9,509 men and women with stable CAD, recording body weight about 12 times over a median 4.7–5 years. After adjusting for average body weight and other risk factors, those in the highest fifth for weight variability faced markedly higher risks versus the lowest-variability group: 78% higher risk of new-onset diabetes, 117% higher risk of heart attack, 136% higher risk of stroke, and 124% higher risk of death. Weight fluctuations in the highest group averaged about 3.9 kg (≈8.6 lb) versus about 0.9 kg (≈2 lb) in the lowest group. The study population all had high cholesterol and prior heart problems; roughly half received intensive cholesterol-lowering therapy. Authors note the research is observational and cannot prove causation; they could not determine why individuals’ weights changed, so reverse causation (illness causing weight change) is possible. Nonetheless, given CAD’s prevalence and the large effect sizes, researchers urge attention to maintaining weight loss rather than allowing repeated regain. The findings reinforce earlier studies tying weight cycling to poor cardiovascular outcomes and highlight the need for further research and clinical strategies to help patients sustain healthy weight.

The FDA warned on Sept. 30 that some homeopathic teething tablets and gels may be dangerous to infants and toddlers and is investigating reports of seizures in children given such products. Homeopathic remedies are not evaluated by the FDA for safety or effectiveness under current agency policy, and some products labeled “homeopathic” have been found to contain substantial or inconsistent amounts of active, potentially toxic ingredients. The agency advised parents to seek immediate medical care if a child given these products shows seizures, breathing difficulty, lethargy, excessive sleepiness, muscle weakness, flushing, constipation, urinary difficulty, or agitation.

Homeopathy is an alternative system founded on “like cures like” and extreme dilution; many products are so diluted that no molecules of the original substance remain. Remedies derive from plants, minerals, or animals and are often individualized. Scientific assessments find little reliable evidence that homeopathy is effective for any health condition, and core homeopathic claims conflict with established science. Research is further complicated by individualized prescriptions and variable dilutions.

Past safety concerns include a 2010 FDA alert and recall after teething tablets contained inconsistent amounts of belladonna (deadly nightshade, which contains atropine). The FTC now requires substantiated evidence for health claims by homeopathic products, and the FDA proposed a risk-based enforcement approach targeting products with greatest potential harm, vulnerable populations, and those failing quality standards.

For teething, doctors recommend nonmedicated measures: firm teething rings, hard unsweetened crackers, cold (but not frozen) objects, pacifiers, spoons, or clean wet washcloths. Avoid benzocaine gels in children under 2; topical OTC gels can cause local reactions, overdose seizures, or methemoglobinemia. If needed, parents should use correct dosing for acetaminophen or ibuprofen and consult pediatric guidance.

In Oswego, Illinois, a knife attack at an apartment building on Harbor Drive was halted when neighbor Dave Thomas fetched his AR-15 and ordered the assailant to stop. The confrontation began during an argument in a hallway; witnesses reported blood on the floor and multiple people involved. Thomas said he chose the AR-15 over a handgun because its size provides greater intimidation and because he is trained and comfortable with that firearm for home defense. No shots were fired. The suspect briefly fled but was later apprehended by police. The stabbing victim was transported to a hospital and is expected to recover. Authorities confirmed Thomas holds a valid firearm owner identification card and a concealed carry permit; he also works as a firearms instructor. Thomas called the episode an example of “good guy with an AR-15 stopped a bad guy with a knife,” noting that no lives were lost. The account was reported by WGN 9 and carried by outlets including Breitbart, where the item was framed within Second Amendment commentary.

Apple has expanded its nationwide recycling efforts, offering free recycling of Apple products across the United States and providing state-specific information and guidance for independent recycling professionals on handling batteries and components that need selective treatment. The company highlighted recycling as a major initiative, leveraging partner programs and robotic disassembly systems to keep valuable materials out of landfills. In its annual environmental report, Apple disclosed substantial recovery figures: over 61 million pounds of materials—steel, aluminum, glass, and other components—were reclaimed from returned devices. Notably, Apple recovered 2,204 pounds of gold from old iPhones, computers, and other devices. At the spot gold price cited ($1,229.80 per troy ounce), that amount of gold is worth just under $40 million (about $39.5 million). Fairphone, an electronics supply-chain activist group, estimates the average smartphone contains roughly 30 milligrams of gold, primarily in circuit boards and other internal parts, which helps explain how recycling millions of devices yields significant precious-metal returns. While some recovered gold might originate from luxury items such as gold Apple Watches—speculated to contain over 50 grams of 18-karat gold—it's unlikely many high-end watch owners recycled expensive pieces quickly. Apple’s report includes a full breakdown of recovered materials, underscoring the financial and environmental value of large-scale electronics recycling.

Boat-based whale- and dolphin-watching, long promoted as eco-friendly tourism, may increasingly threaten cetaceans, conservationists warned at the International Marine Conservation Congress in Glasgow. Participation has grown from about 4 million people in 1991 to 13 million in 2008, producing an industry worth roughly US$2.1 billion. Research shows boats do more than cause occasional collisions: they can alter behaviour and raise stress, making animals flee, expend energy, or forgo feeding—effects that might accumulate into serious population impacts. Studies presented include minke whales in Iceland that responded to boats like predators, increasing speed and respiration, and bottlenose dolphins in New Zealand’s Doubtful Sound whose numbers fell (67 to 56 between 1997 and 2005) as tourism pushed them from preferred areas and disrupted feeding. About 70 endangered Irrawaddy dolphins in the Mekong face intense pressure from tourist boats, though fisheries entanglement is also a major threat. Short-term measures—minimum approach distances, speed limits and no-go zones—help but are inconsistently applied and often voluntary; only 38% of guidelines in one study were binding. Observers urge combining short-term behavioural data with long-term population models to identify vulnerable populations and design local protections, but note funding and political will are limited. Speakers agreed that better management, enforcement and public education are needed to prevent “death by 1,000 cuts.”

Two Baylor University management researchers studied how workday breaks affect energy, concentration, motivation, health and job attitudes. Emily Hunter and Cindy Wu asked 95 employees, ages 22–67, to record every non-bathroom break over a five-day workweek, yielding 959 break reports (about two breaks per person per day). Their analysis tested common assumptions about breaks and identified practical features of “better breaks” that aid recovery.

Key findings:
- Timing: The most restorative breaks occur mid-morning. Breaks later in the day were less effective; the longer the elapsed work time before a break, the more depletion and health symptoms reported afterward. An early pause helps replenish cognitive resources before depletion sets in.
- Activity preference: What matters most is that the break activity is preferred by the employee. Contrary to conventional wisdom, non-work activities aren’t inherently superior; enjoyable, self-chosen activities—even brief work-related ones—provide better recovery because they confer autonomy and don’t demand extra resources.
- Frequency and length: More frequent short breaks were associated with higher restored resources. The study could not prescribe an exact optimal length, but frequent short “recharges” are better than waiting until fully depleted.
- Outcomes: Employees who took these “better breaks” reported fewer somatic symptoms (headache, eyestrain, back pain), greater job satisfaction and organizational citizenship behavior, and less emotional exhaustion.

Implication: Encourage mid-morning, self-chosen, frequent short breaks to sustain well-being and performance throughout the workday.

Wynonna Judd says she’d back sister Ashley Judd if the actress-activist runs for the U.S. Senate in 2014, despite their frequent political differences. The country singer, appearing on Dancing With the Stars, emphasized family loyalty over judgment — calling Ashley “one of the first people” she confided in when Ashley and Indy 500 champion Dario Franchitti announced their amicable split after ten years of marriage. Wynonna praised Ashley’s supportive role in her own life, including comforting Wynonna’s husband Cactus Moser after he lost a leg in a motorcycle accident, noting Ashley’s warm, nurturing side. Wynonna insists she’ll offer opinions only when asked and otherwise stands solidly behind her sister.

Meanwhile, Democratic operatives are quietly courting other candidates to challenge Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell in Kentucky. Alison Lundergan Grimes, the 34-year-old secretary of state, has drawn interest because she carries little political baggage and comes from a politically connected family. Bill Clinton privately urged Grimes to consider a bid and reportedly promised support if she ran. Party strategists worry that Ashley Judd’s high-profile liberalism and inexperience could jeopardize down-ballot Democrats by making the race harder to win in conservative Kentucky. Some Democrats fear a messy primary or nominating the wrong candidate could squander their best chance to unseat McConnell in 2014.

Eva Longoria and husband José “Pepe” Bastón welcomed their first child together, son Santiago Enrique Bastón, on June 19 at Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles, weighing 6 lbs., 13 oz. The couple shared a first photo with HOLA! USA, showing Eva cradling the newborn. Longoria, 43, who remained active during pregnancy—working, exercising, supporting Time’s Up, premiering Overboard and receiving a Hollywood Walk of Fame star—will raise Santiago in their Bel Air Crest home. Bastón, 50, already has three children from a previous marriage, and Longoria has said she intends to raise a feminist son surrounded by strong female role models. They described the baby as “a beautiful blessing.”

Russian skicross racer Maria Komissarova, 23, suffered a serious spinal injury during a training crash at the Rosa Khutor Olympic venue and underwent a 6.5-hour emergency operation in Sochi. Doctors reconstructed her T12 vertebra, inserted a metal implant, and stabilized her condition; officials said prognosis will be clearer in several days. She remained in Sochi because her condition was too grave to transfer. President Vladimir Putin visited her in hospital; Komissarova is ruled out of competition. The accident highlights risks in freestyle ski disciplines.

Major central banks coordinated a move to ease growing strains in global finance, prompting a sharp stock-market rally. The Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, Bank of England, Bank of Canada, Bank of Japan and Swiss National Bank announced steps to enhance liquidity support, chiefly by cutting the price of temporary U.S. dollar liquidity swap lines by 50 basis points. The new pricing—U.S. dollar overnight index swap (OIS) rate plus 50 basis points—takes effect December 5, 2011, and the swap authorizations have been extended through February 1, 2013. Several central banks will continue three-month tenders until further notice.

As a contingency, the banks agreed to establish temporary bilateral swap lines enabling liquidity in any participating currency should market conditions require, though for now only dollar facilities are deemed necessary. The measures are intended to reduce funding costs for banks, support interbank lending, and prevent a credit crunch that could tighten credit availability for households and businesses amid worries about Europe’s sovereign-debt troubles. Markets reacted positively: Germany’s DAX and U.S. Dow futures jumped about 4 percent after the announcement. The Fed emphasized its readiness to use tools to backstop liquidity and promote credit extension if conditions worsen.

Dustin Snyder, 19, and his longtime girlfriend Sierra Siverio, 21, accelerated plans to marry after Snyder’s aggressive synovial sarcoma returned and doctors determined he had only weeks to live. The pair first met in middle school in Valrico, Florida, drifted apart when Snyder moved, then reconnected in 2015 when Siverio applied for a job where Snyder was working. Their relationship deepened through Snyder’s cancer fight, which began the day before his 18th birthday when chest pains led to a diagnosis of synovial sarcoma, a rare soft-tissue cancer common in teens and young adults. Surgeons removed a lung and he underwent chemo and radiation; the disease briefly went into remission but later recurred in his bladder and then spread through his abdomen and pelvis, leaving it inoperable. Snyder recently entered hospice care.

When the couple discussed marriage, Snyder wanted to wed as soon as possible to honor Siverio’s support. His sister, Brittany Hails, posted their story on Facebook seeking a ring and tuxedo; the community response was immediate and generous. Donations flooded in: a diamond ring, tuxedos (including a new one from Men’s Warehouse), a donated wedding dress and bridesmaid gowns from a Tampa company, and The Big Red Barn in Plant City offered the venue. A GoFundMe created by Hails raised more than $13,000–$14,000 to cover wedding costs and to help the family with future expenses when Snyder passes. LifePath Hospice and others contributed flowers and services. Surrounded by community generosity and faith, the couple focused on celebrating their love rather than the prognosis. They married on Sunday, Jan. 28, 2018, supported by family, friends and neighbors who rallied to give them a joyful day.

Zynga priced its IPO at $10 a share, the top of its $8.50–$10 range, selling 100 million shares (with a 15 million share overallotment) and listing on Nasdaq as ZNGA. The offering values the social-game maker at roughly $7–8.9 billion depending on count, raising about $1 billion. Zynga, known for FarmVille, CityVille and Mafia Wars, has ~227 million monthly users and reported $828.9 million revenue in the first nine months, with $30.7 million net income. Proceeds will fund general corporate purposes, possible acquisitions and ~$83.6 million in tax-withholding for RSU vesting.

Roberto Unger, a veteran Harvard Law professor who once advised Barack Obama, publicly urged voters to defeat the president in 2012, arguing Obama betrayed progressive principles. In a May YouTube video titled “Beyond Obama,” Unger, a prominent Brazilian politician and two-time presidential candidate, criticized Obama’s record as insufficiently transformative. He charged that Obama prioritized rescuing financial interests with trillions in bailouts while leaving workers and homeowners “to their own devices,” and reduced policy to “financial confidence and food stamps.” Unger faulted the administration for subordinating broad economic and educational opportunity to healthcare reform, describing Obama’s approach as a politics of “hand-holding” that avoids necessary struggle. Though he warned a Mitt Romney victory would entail harmful judicial and administrative appointments, Unger said Republicans would not be dramatically worse on issues like military adventurism; instead, he called for a political reversal to restore a bolder democratic vision. A prolific author and longtime Harvard faculty member (tenured at 29), Unger’s critique reflects a leftward dissatisfaction that has been viewed thousands of times online.

South African forensic scientists analysed residue from 24 clay pipe fragments excavated from William Shakespeare’s Stratford-upon-Avon garden and adjacent areas to identify what was smoked there. Using sensitive gas chromatography–mass spectrometry, researchers detected a variety of plant compounds preserved in pipe bowls and stems dating to the early 17th century. Results showed cannabis residues in eight samples and nicotine in at least one. Importantly, two pipes—though not from Shakespeare’s immediate garden—contained clear chemical evidence of cocaine derived from Peruvian coca leaves. The study confirms that several New World plants, introduced to Europe by figures such as Sir Francis Drake and Sir Walter Raleigh, were being smoked in England in Shakespeare’s era. Authors suggest these botanical findings can inform literary readings: for example, Sonnet 76’s reference to “a noted weed” and “compounds strange” might hint at cannabis use and a wary attitude toward unfamiliar stimulants like coca. The research raises broader questions about whether Elizabethan performance spaces and social gatherings were pervaded by smoke from diverse plant materials and whether such substances influenced writers and audiences. The work, bridging chemistry and literary scholarship, appeared in the South African Journal of Science (July 2015) and was conducted with artefacts loaned by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust.

The piece examines why housework remains predominantly a woman’s responsibility despite greater gender equality in other domestic areas. Drawing on Arlie Hochschild, it argues cleaning is not only physical but emotional labor: an orderly home provides a sense of safety and women worry they’ll be judged first for mess. That social pressure often motivates women to clean more, even when men do similar tasks and receive the same or less credit. Efforts to equalize chores—like explicit negotiation of task splits—feel impractical to many; others recommend using comparative advantage so each partner handles tasks they do relatively better, allowing skill and repetition to improve the partner who takes on new chores. Practical fixes include lowering personal cleanliness standards (where safe) and making cleaning more appealing through gadgets or incentives.

The article contrasts perspectives: Jessica Grose laments persistent housework inequality, while another contributor emphasizes differing cleanliness preferences as a major factor—men often tolerate more mess and thus invest less in cleaning. Personal anecdotes show varied arrangements: one household pays for a weekly cleaner and accepts lower standards; another couples converge at a compromise level of tidiness, with chores divided across visible and unglamorous tasks (e.g., maintenance, trash, childcare duties). The author stresses that not all domestic labor is equivalent—childcare, cooking, finances, and home maintenance differ in stress, time, and reward—and that recognizing these distinctions and tolerating some mess can ease imbalance. Ultimately, the piece suggests a mix of negotiation, economic logic, lowered expectations, and better incentives rather than assuming male exploitation alone explains the divide.

Caitlyn Jenner’s transition from Bruce is portrayed as a long, private struggle finally made public. After decades of secret cross-dressing, hormones in the 1980s, and intermittent surgeries, Jenner pursued facial-feminization and breast augmentation in 2015, emerging as Caitlyn. The piece details her isolation in Malibu, panic during recovery, and determination not to die having never lived authentically. It traces Jenner’s athletic rise—1976 Olympic decathlon gold—marriages, strained relationships with four children from earlier unions, and later family dynamics with the Kardashians. The family is divided over an E! docuseries; some children refuse to participate, fearing spectacle. Despite hurt and controversy, Caitlyn finds purpose advocating for transgender visibility, receiving public support after a Diane Sawyer interview and planning public projects, while seeking to rebuild family ties.

After Hurricane Maria hit Puerto Rico as a Category 4 storm, widespread damage knocked out power and much of the island’s communications infrastructure. In response, Alphabet’s experimental Project Loon partnered with AT&T, Puerto Rican and Pan-American aviation authorities, the FCC, FAA, FEMA and several spectrum and ground-infrastructure providers to launch stratospheric balloons to restore basic internet and texting for LTE-enabled phones in the hardest-hit areas. Project Loon’s balloons, operating around 60,000 feet and powered by solar energy, ride stratospheric winds and use machine-learning algorithms to cluster over the island; this deployment is the first to use those new algorithms and teams are still learning to hold balloons over needed areas amid shifting winds. Two balloons were already providing service and more have been launched from Nevada, with FCC authorization to send up to 30. SES Networks and Liberty Cablevision helped establish ground links; a range of spectrum holders and utilities provided support. Project Loon, which has flown extensive tests since 2013 and previously aided flood zones in Peru, remains experimental and primarily offers daytime coverage. Alphabet and partners plan to continue providing emergency connectivity as long as it is useful and feasible, while other tech firms including Cisco, Facebook and Tesla also contributed aid to restore communications and power.

In response to escalating scandals — Benghazi, the IRS’s targeting of conservative groups, and the Justice Department’s seizure of AP phone records — President Obama and his team launched an aggressive damage-control effort that included releasing 100 pages of Benghazi-related emails and securing the resignation of acting IRS Commissioner Steven Miller at the president’s direction. The moves were intended to demonstrate decisive action and regain control after political pressure threatened Obama’s second-term agenda. Republicans, however, remained critical, demanding further cooperation with Congress, apologies, and continued investigations; they viewed the measures as insufficient and pledged to press at upcoming hearings. Within the White House, aides stressed the need for careful, timely responses — declassifying emails and awaiting inspector general findings before acting — to avoid mistakes that could fuel more controversy. Commentators urged Republicans to investigate vigorously but warned against relying on scandal as an electoral strategy, noting past overreach and the need for substantive policy proposals. Internally, Obama acknowledged limits on what he can accomplish amid a polarized Congress but sought to refocus on achievable goals like immigration reform, budget deals, gun control, climate actions via executive authority, and judicial nominations. Despite frustrations, he and advisers emphasized perspective: scandals are significant, yet lasting legacy may hinge more on economic and policy outcomes than this week’s turmoil.

Justin Bieber surprised fans by posting an Instagram photo of a FaceTime call with Malala Yousafzai, the Pakistani education activist who survived a 2012 assassination attempt by the Taliban. Bieber, 20, praised her “incredible story,” said he looks forward to meeting her, and expressed interest in supporting the Malala Fund. The post gives few details about how the chat came about or any specific collaboration. The gesture contrasts Bieber’s recent negative headlines, including an alleged scuffle with actor Orlando Bloom and controversial Instagram posts involving Miranda Kerr. Yousafzai continues to campaign globally for girls’ education, highlighted by concern over kidnapped Nigerian schoolgirls.

A previously mysterious dimming of star KIC 8462852, which sparked speculation ranging from catastrophic collisions to alien megastructures, now appears most likely explained by a family of comets. The star drew attention after Planet Hunters users flagged unprecedented, irregular drops in brightness recorded by NASA’s Kepler telescope in 2011 and 2013—dips as deep as 22 percent that did not match known planet-transit patterns. Early hypotheses included collisions among planets or asteroids, clouds of dust, and even engineered structures, prompting follow-up observations and SETI radio monitoring that found no artificial signals.

A team led by Massimo Marengo at Iowa State University analyzed infrared data from NASA’s Spitzer Space Telescope taken in January 2015. Violent collisions or massive debris fields would produce warm dust detectable as excess infrared emission; neither Spitzer nor earlier WISE observations revealed significant infrared excess. That absence makes scenarios involving rocky smashups unlikely. Instead, researchers favor a model in which a swarm of cold comets on a long, eccentric orbit produced the transient light-blocking events: a large comet could have caused the 2011 dip, with trailing fragments creating the 2013 dimming. By 2015 those bodies would be distant enough to leave little infrared signature.

The authors caution that more observations are needed to fully settle the case and acknowledge they did not test the alien-structure idea directly. The system remains unusual and intriguing, and further monitoring could reveal the precise dynamics behind its bizarre behavior.

Starbucks appears to be following the whimsical “unicorn” food trend with a limited-time Unicorn Frappuccino, a pink-and-blue specialty drink that surfaced online via social posts and barista chatter. Though the company hadn’t formally announced it, photos and tweets indicated an April launch (reported around April 19–20). Early impressions from baristas and a Snacktaku writer describe a tart, sour raspberry–like flavor layered with a strong sour syrup—some likening it to Tropical Skittles—making the taste a mix of fresh-fruit notes and an overly sour component. Discussion about the drink circulated on Reddit and social media in mid-April, generating curiosity and mixed reactions as fans and critics awaited wider availability and an official Starbucks confirmation.

Sen. John McCain’s announcement that he will oppose the latest GOP ObamaCare repeal bill has cast significant doubt on Republicans’ seven-year effort to dismantle the Affordable Care Act, while leaving both parties cautious about declaring victory. With the Sept. 30 budget-rule deadline the last viable path to pass repeal without a filibuster, some Republicans continue to seek votes, and Vice President Pence said the administration remains “undeterred.” But McCain’s opposition likely sinks the Graham-Cassidy bill, joining skepticism from Sens. Rand Paul and Susan Collins; Republicans can only afford two defections. 

The stalemate has shifted attention toward bipartisan Senate talks led by Sens. Lamar Alexander and Patty Murray, aimed at stabilizing insurance markets—especially by securing cost-sharing reduction payments that insurers say are essential to prevent premium spikes and market disruption. The Trump administration has threatened to halt those payments, and Democrats warn of ongoing “sabotage” via funding cuts for outreach and changes to healthcare.gov during enrollment. Administration officials say scheduled site downtime is routine maintenance. 

Democrats, while relieved, urged restraint: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer commended McCain’s stance but called for renewed bipartisan negotiations rather than celebration. Progressive activists remain mobilized, planning rallies and ad campaigns targeting vulnerable GOP senators. Some Republicans float further strategies—pairing repeal with tax reform under a new budget resolution—but such moves risk derailing tax priorities. 

Experts and advocates warn repeal remains a real threat and that administrative actions could undermine enrollment and exchange stability even without new legislation. For now, the likely outcome is preservation of ObamaCare on the books, continued partisan pressure, and a possible pivot to bipartisan fixes aimed at shoring up the law rather than repealing it outright.

Media outlets obtained thousands of leaked Islamic State (ISIS) documents—centering on a 23-question recruitment form—that reveal detailed personal data on more than 22,000 alleged jihadis from at least 51 countries. The standardized form, stamped with ISIS insignia and used at border entry points into ISIS territory, collects routine biographical information (name, birthdate, education, blood type, address) and militant-specific details such as prior fighting experience, “Sharia level,” level of obedience, special skills, travel history, recommenders, whether the applicant prefers to be a fighter or a suicide attacker, and emergency contact information. Some entries correspond to already known figures (e.g., Londoner Abdel Bary, media chief Junaid Hussain), while many reveal previously unknown recruits across Europe, North America, the Middle East and North Africa. German and British officials say the files appear authentic and represent a potential intelligence “goldmine” for tracking routes taken by foreign fighters, identifying recruiters and prosecuting returnees. The cache reportedly came from a memory stick stolen from an ISIS internal-security official by a defector who now claims disillusionment with ISIS leadership. Analysts say the leak exposes organizational weaknesses, could help disrupt plots and networks, and underscores the need for international information-sharing as ISIS faces increasing military pressure.

The piece chronicles Pizza Hut’s 1994 PizzaNet pilot—an early online pizza-ordering system requiring Mosaic and internet access—highlighting its novelty and limits. Orders routed from PizzaNet’s Wichita server to local restaurants, which phone-verified purchases; payment occurred on delivery. Michael Schrage argues the service was clever but missed the web’s true potential: interactive customization. He proposes on-screen pizza design tools and selling design software, turning ordering into a valuable, engaging experience rather than a commodity transaction. The article then pivots to a Gizmodo-curated list of influential websites, noting PizzaNet’s place as an early e-commerce milestone among 100 significant sites that shaped internet culture, commerce, and community.

About 10 people reported feeling ill after a suspicious package arrived in the mailroom of a large IRS building in downtown Kansas City, Missouri. Symptoms included vomiting and sweating; two people were taken to St. Luke’s Hospital and are in good condition, officials said. The Kansas City Fire Department checked for gases and fumes but had not identified the package’s contents; it was isolated from the public. The building was not evacuated and has resumed business. The investigation was turned over to the IRS and other federal authorities.

After a high-profile car crash and multiple women alleging affairs, Tiger Woods announced an indefinite leave from the PGA Tour, prompting sponsors and media to step back. Golf Digest said it will suspend his bylined instruction articles while he’s away, though it will keep him on the masthead and has no plans to end their long-standing relationship; the magazine pays him roughly $3 million annually. Analysts noted business and advertising pressures drove such decisions. Accenture and Gatorade cut ties, Gillette stopped airing his ads, and AT&T said it was reevaluating. Swiss watchmaker TAG Heuer briefly removed then reposted images, declaring it “stands with Tiger Woods.”

The U.S. Under-23 team was shockingly eliminated from CONCACAF Olympic qualifying after a 3-3 draw with El Salvador in Nashville. Needing a win to advance after a prior upset by Canada, the Americans took an early lead when Brek Shea’s cross found Terrence Boyd inside the first minute. But keeper Bill Hamid injured his ankle in the 31st minute and remained until the 39th; El Salvador scored twice in the 35th and 37th minutes to lead 2-1. Sean Johnson replaced Hamid and the U.S. rallied: Boyd equalized in the 65th and Joe Corona headed a go-ahead goal four minutes later, put through by Freddy Adu’s service. In the fourth minute of stoppage time Jaime Alas struck a bouncing shot that Johnson failed to hold, the ball ricocheting into the net to tie 3-3 and eliminate the U.S. Critics pointed to poor possession, defensive lapses and the decision to delay substituting the injured Hamid. El Salvador advanced to the semifinals, one win from an Olympic berth.

A prospective, multi-institution U.S. study of 386 terminally ill metastatic cancer patients examined whether receiving palliative chemotherapy months before death affected end-of-life care and place of death. At enrollment—median four months before death—56% were receiving chemotherapy. After adjusting with propensity scores for demographic, clinical, and psychosocial factors, chemotherapy recipients had markedly higher rates of intensive interventions in the last week of life (cardiopulmonary resuscitation and/or mechanical ventilation: 14% vs 2%; adjusted risk difference 10.5%), greater use of feeding tubes (11% vs 5%), and more late hospice referrals (within one week of death: 54% vs 37%). They were also more likely to die in an intensive care unit (11% vs 2%; adjusted risk difference 6.1%) and less likely to die at home (47% vs 66%) or in their preferred place (68% vs 80%). There was no significant survival benefit associated with chemotherapy (hazard ratio 1.11). Chemotherapy recipients were younger, better educated, and less likely to acknowledge terminal illness or have discussed end-of-life wishes. The authors conclude that palliative chemotherapy in the final months is associated with more intensive, medicalized deaths without clear survival advantage, and recommend improved advance care planning and exploration of how chemotherapy influences end-of-life outcomes and goal attainment.

U.N. human rights investigators and multiple activist sources describe an escalating and complex Syrian conflict marked by allegations of chemical-weapons use, intensified fighting around military air bases, and cross-border strikes by Israel. Carla Del Ponte, a member of the U.N. independent commission of inquiry on Syria, said investigators have interviewed victims, doctors and field medics in neighboring countries and found "strong, concrete suspicions" — though not conclusive proof — that the nerve agent sarin was used. Del Ponte said the commission’s testimony points to use by opposition forces rather than government troops, although she gave no specifics on location or timing. That inquiry is distinct from a separate U.N. probe of alleged chemical weapons use that has stalled. Both the Syrian government and rebel forces accuse each other of three chemical attacks in recent months; the U.S. has voiced varying degrees of confidence that the Syrian government has used sarin. The wider conflict, which began with protests in March 2011, has killed tens of thousands and displaced large populations.

On the battlefield, rebels have increasingly targeted Syrian military aircraft and bases. Activist groups reported rebels shot down a government helicopter in Deir el-Zour province, killing eight soldiers, and that insurgents occupied parts of the Kweiras (Mannagh) air base in northern Syria after heavy fighting, seizing a tank unit and reportedly killing the base commander. Government warplanes continued strikes against rebel positions there.

Separately, Israel struck sites around Damascus twice within days, reportedly targeting advanced Iranian-made guided missiles destined for Hezbollah. Israeli officials say the strikes aimed to prevent high-tech weapons transfers, not to intentionally weaken the Assad regime, and tried to avoid escalation by not publicly acknowledging the raids. Syria condemned the strikes and warned of possible retaliation. The conflict has now produced more than 70,000 deaths and driven over a million refugees into neighboring states.

Courtney Stodden is pregnant with her first child, confirming to FOX411 after a video showing the 21-year-old with a positive pregnancy test circulated. A source claiming to be a friend sent the clip, which appears to show husband Doug Hutchison, 55, filming in their bathroom. In the footage Stodden displays the test, says "Here's the first [line]," and later, sitting on a toilet, tells Hutchison she feels "a little overwhelmed." Stodden, reportedly about four weeks along per Us Weekly, called the video an "invasion of...privacy" and said she and Hutchison hadn't planned to go public so soon. The source claims it was shared with Stodden's closest friends and family; her estranged mother and former manager Krista Keller said she learned of the pregnancy from media coverage. The announcement comes amid ongoing family turmoil spotlighted on Lifetime’s The Mother/Daughter Experiment: Celebrity Edition. Episodes revealed deeply strained dynamics: Keller admitted telling Hutchison she loved him and even suggested an alleged sexual "fantasy" involving herself and Courtney, which horrified other cast members. The series portrays a fraught history—Courtney married Hutchison at 16 with Keller’s consent, they briefly split in 2013, then reconciled and renewed vows in 2014—and ongoing conflicts about parenting, boundaries, and past behaviors. The situation has provoked public fascination and discomfort as Stodden navigates pregnancy amid intense personal and media scrutiny.

British scientists at Imperial College London report a major advance in understanding genetic influences on human intelligence. While no single “intelligence gene” has been found, Michael Johnson and colleagues describe evidence that two distinct gene networks—labelled M1 and M3—are implicated in cognitive abilities. One network contains roughly 1,000 genes and the other a little over 100. These networks appear to be regulated together, perhaps by a master regulatory system, suggesting coordinated control of many genes that influence aspects of intelligence such as reasoning, memory, processing speed and attention.

The researchers combined diverse data sets, starting with gene-expression profiles from mouse brains and from 122 human brain samples plus 102 postmortem whole human brains, then cross-referencing these signals against genetic and cognitive data from thousands of people. They used the Generation Scotland family health study (6,732 participants) and the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936 (1,003 volunteers), along with genetic information from healthy people who had taken IQ tests and from individuals with autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, and people who had undergone neurosurgery for epilepsy. Massive computational analysis revealed that the same gene groups associated with higher cognitive performance in healthy people are also implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders: mutations in these genes can impair cognition and cause conditions such as epilepsy and intellectual disability. The two networks’ functions do not overlap and their precise roles remain to be clarified.

About 40% of intelligence variation is attributed to inheritance, the researchers note. They suggest that understanding coordinated gene regulation could open paths to intervene—ultimately to help people with learning disabilities or cognitive impairments—although practical applications remain theoretical. The work underlines that intelligence is a composite of multiple cognitive abilities governed by large groups of interacting genes; future research must identify how these genes cooperate, which are the key players, and how such knowledge might lead to treatments for neurodevelopmental diseases.

Sen. Ben Cardin (D-Md.), a Foreign Relations Committee member, told Fox News Sunday that President Trump’s tariff-driven trade policies contributed to General Motors’ decision to close five plants and cut about 15% of its North American salaried workforce, potentially affecting up to 14,000 employees and ending several models’ production. Cardin and Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau linked GM’s restructuring to tariffs on steel and aluminum and urged removing those barriers. Cardin welcomed the 90-day U.S.-China trade truce reached at the G20, which paused planned tariff increases on $200 billion of Chinese goods and opened negotiations on technology transfer, intellectual property and agriculture, but he warned that Trump’s initial tariffs on U.S. allies undermined unity needed to confront China. Sen. Roy Blunt (R-Mo.) called the China pause and the USMCA signing encouraging but sought more specifics. Bipartisan concern about Chinese IP theft was noted, with Sen. Chuck Schumer supporting tough action. The article also includes a separate piece where Dick Cheney responds to critical remarks by the late President George H.W. Bush, calling himself an “iron ass” post-9/11 and describing reconciliatory gestures from Bush.

International Women’s Day on March 8 has become both a moment to celebrate women’s cultural and economic achievements and a magnet for corporate marketing. This year’s wave of brand activations—spurred in part by renewed focus from the #MeToo and Time’s Up movements—ranged from earnest to awkward. Mattel unveiled 17 “role model” Barbies honoring figures like Amelia Earhart, Katherine Johnson, Patty Jenkins and Chloe Kim; the dolls include props and diverse faces but were widely critiqued for retaining the brand’s uniform, rail-thin body type. Nike aired an Oscars ad with Serena Williams asserting “there’s no wrong way to be a woman,” a motivational tone that experts say is welcome but insufficient as calls for concrete action amplify. Facebook rolled out IWD-themed frames and cards; Uber targeted Asian markets with a myth-busting video about female drivers; Google’s interactive Doodle showcased stories from everyday women in over 80 languages; and McDonald’s briefly flipped a California outlet’s golden arches to a “W,” a stunt mocked by some as superficial.

Commentators argue that after #MeToo, brands must move beyond feel-good messaging toward measurable initiatives—Getty Images’ female-focused sports photography internship and Frances McDormand’s call for inclusion riders were highlighted as meaningful examples. Other attempts flopped: Diageo’s “Jane Walker” whisky prompted backlash over condescending messaging despite the company citing women in leadership. Outside corporate promotions, media and civic acts marked the day: French paper Libération charged men more to highlight the 25% wage gap, and The New York Times continued an “Overlooked” obituaries project to correct historical exclusion of notable women. Overall, IWD 2018 showcased real progress and heightened expectations, but also underscored the risks brands face when symbolic gestures outpace substantive change.

Violent clashes in Kiev escalated as protesters occupied central squares opposing President Viktor Yanukovych’s rejection of an EU trade pact and new harsh anti-protest laws. Streets saw burning buses, cobblestones, Molotov cocktails, rubber bullets and stun grenades, leaving scores injured and about 1,500 activists seeking medical help. Opposition leaders condemned violence but faced pressure from radical elements; some activists detained men they accused of being government-hired provocateurs. Opposition figure Vitali Klitschko sought talks with Yanukovych but met aides; hopes for a quick resolution dimmed. Authorities sent threatening mass-text warnings tied to the new law criminalizing violent protest; cellphone firms denied sending them. Russia’s foreign minister Sergey Lavrov blamed the EU and U.S. for encouraging unrest, while Moscow urged restraint and warned the situation was “getting out of control.” Tensions remained high amid fears of a wider crackdown or state of emergency.

A nurse in northern Germany, known under reporting rules as Niels H. (Niels Hoegel), who was jailed for life in 2015 after convictions for two murders and two attempted murders, is now suspected of killing at least 84 more patients; investigators say the true toll may be substantially higher. Hoegel, 40, worked as a nurse at clinics in Oldenburg (1999–2002) and Delmenhorst (2003–2005) and admitted during his 2015 trial to deliberately inducing cardiac crises in around 90 patients at the Delmenhorst intensive-care unit so he could then resuscitate them and win approval. The murders involved overdoses of heart medication that caused heart failure or circulatory collapse.

Relatives had long urged a wider inquiry, and a special police commission formed in 2014 has reviewed hundreds of medical records and exhumed 134 bodies to test for drug residues. Many potential victims were cremated, hampering forensic confirmation, and some records and memories have faded over years, complicating the probe. Oldenburg police chief Johann Kuhme described the findings as beyond imagination and warned the number of victims could still rise; prosecutors expect to file new charges in early 2018.

Authorities have criticized local health officials and some hospital staff for failing to report unusual patterns of deaths and resuscitations seen as early as 2001, allowing Hoegel to transfer and continue working. Criminal proceedings are also being pursued against some former hospital staff. Although more murder charges are expected, Germany’s system does not permit additional prison time to be added onto Hoegel’s existing life sentence, so further convictions would not extend his incarceration. The identities of the newly suspected victims have not been publicly released.

President-elect Donald Trump’s victory opened a clear path for congressional Republicans to pursue repeal of the federal estate tax—the so-called “death tax”—which could deliver large, recurring savings to the very wealthiest Americans. The levy, a 40 percent tax on estates above roughly $5.45 million for individuals ($10.9 million for couples), affects only about 0.2 percent of estates. Republicans view repeal as a longstanding priority; House passage is certain, and Senate reconciliation could eliminate the tax with a simple majority, though the party’s narrow margins leave little room for error. Supporters frame repeal as protecting family farms and small businesses, but data show those make up only a small share of taxable estates. Repeal would disproportionately benefit billionaires and many of Trump’s own picks—estimates suggest Trump’s family could save hundreds of millions to over a billion dollars depending on net-worth assumptions, while other nominees (Wilbur Ross, Richard DeVos, Linda and Vince McMahon, Steven Mnuchin, Gary Cohn) would also gain large windfalls. The estate-tax fight exemplifies the tension between Trump’s populist campaign rhetoric and policies favoring the wealthy; some conservatives warn that up-front high-end cuts could be politically risky and advise emphasizing visible middle-class benefits. Democrats strongly oppose repeal. Public opinion depends on framing: more Americans favor repeal when told it’s a “death tax,” but support drops when informed whom it benefits. The estate-tax debate is likely to be an early, high-stakes test of the new administration’s priorities.

Thom Hartmann argues the Second Amendment was ratified primarily to preserve Southern slave patrol militias, not individual hunting or sport rights. He cites colonial statutes like Georgia’s mid-1700s militia laws and scholars such as Carl Bogus and Sally Haden showing militias enforced slave discipline, suppressed uprisings, and inspected enslaved people. Facing fears that a federal militia power (Article I, Section 8) could subsume state militias or emancipate slaves via military service, Southern delegates including Patrick Henry, George Mason, and others insisted on protections for state-controlled militias. Hartmann recounts Virginia ratifying-convention debates where Henry warned federal control could enable manumission and loss of “property” and peace; Madison responded and adjusted his amendment language—changing “country” to “state”—resulting in the modern Second Amendment wording. Hartmann ties this origin to contemporary debates over gun control, noting political risks for Democrats and arguing the Amendment’s core purpose was guarding a “free State” against centralized power. He concludes that while reform is possible through amendment, historical context complicates modern regulation efforts.

A key Senate procedural vote on the Defense Authorization bill that included repeal of the military’s 17-year-old “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell” (DADT) policy failed 57-40, three votes short of the 60 needed to advance debate, likely blocking repeal during this Congress. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid pressed the motion without a procedural agreement with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who supports repeal but sought clearer terms for amendments and timing; she voted aye but was critical afterward. Moderate Republicans Scott Brown and Lisa Murkowski, and Democrat Joe Manchin, voted no. Supporters warned that congressional inaction could force a rushed, disorderly change if courts strike down DADT; opponents argued repeal during wartime could harm troop effectiveness. Reid blamed Republicans for running out the clock but praised Collins’s negotiation efforts. Collins and independent Sen. Joe Lieberman announced they will introduce a stand-alone repeal bill, with Reid promising support and to bring it up during the lame-duck session; however, such a focused bill faces hurdles, including potential amendment fights. President Obama and advocates condemned the filibuster-like defeat and urged renewed efforts to pass repeal and the broader defense bill.

Secret files obtained by BuzzFeed News and the BBC reveal long-standing, detailed evidence of suspected match‑fixing at the highest levels of men’s tennis. Leaked reports and betting analyses dating back to 2007–08 identify a core group of roughly 16–28 players (many former top‑50 or Grand Slam winners) repeatedly linked to suspicious betting patterns; yet few, if any, have been sanctioned and most continued to compete, including at recent Grand Slams.

The revelations centre on a landmark probe triggered by a highly anomalous Betfair market on a 2007 match between Nikolay Davydenko and Martin Vassallo Arguello. Investigators traced heavy, coordinated betting to gambling syndicates in Russia, northern Italy and Sicily and documented phone, text and betting links suggesting inside information and orchestrated fixes across dozens of matches—including at Wimbledon and Roland‑Garros. For some matches, analysts calculated the odds of observed performances occurring naturally as vanishingly small.

Despite investigators’ formal reports urging disciplinary inquiries and handing over extensive electronic and phone evidence, tennis authorities adopted a new anti‑corruption code in 2009 and, after legal advice, declined to pursue retrospective probes. The Tennis Integrity Unit (TIU) says it treats corruption seriously and investigates credible intelligence, but critics—including former investigators—say the unit is under‑resourced, secretive and reluctant to use betting intelligence and bookmaker records that only they can provide. Bookmakers and police warn that many alerts on repeat offenders were not followed up, hampering prosecutions.

The reporting stops short of naming current players—citing lack of full phone, bank and computer records—but exposes systemic failures in detecting and deterring corruption in a sport uniquely vulnerable to single‑player fixes amid huge online betting volumes. Critics call for stronger, better‑resourced, transparent investigations to restore integrity.

Health officials are investigating a national Cyclospora outbreak that has sickened 397 people across 16 states and hospitalized at least 22. Cyclospora cayetanensis, a protozoan transmitted when fecal contamination enters food or water, causes watery, sometimes explosive diarrhea plus fatigue, cramps, nausea and weight loss; it is treated with antibiotics. Iowa and Nebraska epidemiologists have traced many cases to a particular brand of prepackaged salad mix containing iceberg and romaine lettuce, carrots and red cabbage distributed nationally, but federal agencies and other states have not confirmed a single definitive source. Investigators face challenges: bagged salads have short shelf lives so implicated packages were often discarded before testing; cases in other states show different timelines and exposures, suggesting multiple sources or separate outbreaks; and state laws protecting agricultural producers can limit public disclosure of supplier names, which critics say slows traceback. Public health labs first detected Cyclospora in late June after a parasitologist in Iowa identified the parasite in stool samples; cases peaked with several new reports per day. Officials continue traceback work with the FDA and CDC but say pinpointing the contamination source is complex and ongoing.

Rolling Stone, the iconic music and culture magazine co-founded by Jann Wenner in 1967, is being put up for sale, Wenner confirmed after The New York Times first reported plans for his 51 percent stake. Wenner, 71, said selling is “just the smart thing to do” despite his long attachment to the magazine. Wenner Media issued a statement saying it is exploring “strategic options … to best position the brand for future growth,” and credited Gus Wenner, the company’s president and COO, with helping engineer the planned sale.

Rolling Stone helped shape rock ’n’ roll history and broader cultural discourse, publishing landmark writers like Hunter S. Thompson, Joe Klein, P.J. O’Rourke and Tom Wolfe. But the magazine’s influence and finances have eroded over recent years. A 2014 Rolling Stone investigation, “A Rape on Campus,” was later retracted after the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism criticized it as a major journalistic failure; the fallout produced multiple libel suits and a federal jury awarded a plaintiff $3 million. That episode significantly damaged the publication’s reputation.

Financial strains predate that scandal: Wenner’s prior dealings—selling and later buying stakes in Us Weekly, borrowing heavily, and selling other titles like Us Weekly and Men’s Journal to American Media Inc.—left the company burdened and diminished. Print ad revenue and newsstand sales declined as audiences shifted online, a transition Wenner was often reluctant to embrace. Wenner sold 49 percent of Rolling Stone in 2013 to a digital music startup (BandLab reportedly paid $40 million). The current sale would close a defining chapter in Wenner’s arc from countercultural founder to media mogul, a career that once saw him turn down offers he later suggested would be unattainable today.
