In Connecticut stops Saturday, Donald Trump dismissed suggestions he should tone down his combative campaign style even after his new chief adviser, Paul Manafort, told Republican officials Trump was “projecting an image” and could be more restrained in private. Speaking in Waterbury and Bridgeport to large, energized crowds, Trump framed his brash rhetoric as necessary to energize supporters and said being “presidential” would actually be easier. He reaffirmed policy positions like building a wall on the Southern border and vowed to carry out everything he promises. Trump also revived his longtime questioning of Ted Cruz’s eligibility, deriding him as “Rafael” and joking about Cruz’s Canadian birth, while Cruz campaigned in Pennsylvania and Indiana trying to halt Trump’s march to the 1,237-delegate threshold. Cruz criticized Trump’s comments about transgender bathrooms, saying local governments should decide. On the Democratic side, front-runner Hillary Clinton campaigned in Connecticut, pressing for higher wages, expanded early childhood education and closing the gender pay gap; she called raising the $7.25 federal minimum wage overdue and backed states and cities that set higher floors. Bernie Sanders spoke to a youthful crowd in Baltimore, attacking big banks and “disastrous trade agreements,” contrasting his positions with Clinton’s past support for trade deals. The weekend underscored high stakes in the Northeast primaries as Trump pursues a delegate sweep while rivals on both sides press their distinct appeals to voters.

Marine archaeologists working on the famed Antikythera shipwreck have recovered a bronze right arm and a range of other artifacts and now believe at least seven more large bronze statues remain buried at the site. The wreck, a roughly 50 m (about 130 ft) Roman-era merchant ship that sank circa 1 BC while sailing from Asia Minor to Rome, lies on a boulder-strewn slope off the Greek island of Antikythera. Divers found the arm encrusted and green under about half a metre of sediment; bespoke underwater metal-detection surveys also flagged multiple large metal targets nearby, leading the team to estimate a minimum of seven and possibly nine statues beneath the seabed and boulders.

The international project is led by Greece’s Ephorate of Underwater Antiquities and Lund University, with participation from other institutions. During the 2017 season the team also recovered a patterned slab of red marble, a silver tankard, ship timbers, pottery, nails, lead sheathing fragments and human bone. Earlier work at the site yielded skeletal remains whose DNA has been analyzed (the individual is provisionally nicknamed “Pamphilos”) and produced the remarkable Antikythera mechanism—an ancient geared astronomical device. This season divers also retrieved a bronze disc about the size of a geared wheel; preliminary x-rays show no teeth and depict a bull, so it may be decorative rather than a gear, though specialists say more mechanism parts might still be present.

Many finds are trapped beneath multi-tonne boulders thought to have tumbled onto the wreck after seismic events. Recovering intact bronzes will demand difficult, costly operations—hauling or fracturing rocks, or using controlled charges—and subsequent lengthy conservation and reconstruction. Because ancient bronze was widely recycled, surviving bronzes are rare, making any intact recovery invaluable for understanding whether the cargo represented trade, booty or metal for recycling. The team plans further excavations in spring, hopeful of lifting more statues and other cargo from the ship’s hold.

A Crimson survey of over 1,300 incoming Harvard freshmen (nearly 80% of the class) found significant self-reported academic dishonesty: 10% admitted cheating on exams, 17% on papers/take-homes, and 42% on homework/problem sets. Recruited athletes and men reported higher rates; recruited athletes were roughly twice as likely to admit cheating on some assignments. These rates exceeded those reported by Harvard’s Class of 2013. Harvard officials say the college is addressing cheating through faculty efforts and a joint committee. The survey also detailed academic and extracurricular plans: 84% expect to prioritize academics, 26% anticipate concentrating in economics or government, only 11% plan arts/humanities, 59% plan a secondary field, and many were highly involved in high school activities and athletics.

Comedian Russell Brand was arrested at LAX after allegedly striking several paparazzi who he and fiancée Katy Perry say were trying to take an upskirt photo of her. Brand pushed and hit photographers while passing through Delta security on September 17; a victim performed a citizen’s arrest and Brand was booked on misdemeanor simple battery, later released on $20,000 bail. Perry defended him on Twitter. Though claiming protection of his partner may sway juror sympathy, it isn’t a legal defense to battery.

Former nanny Stephanie Santoro told RadarOnline that Jon Gosselin once told her he planned to kill himself, expressing concern about his mental state during and after his relationship with Hailey Glassman. Santoro said Jon confessed suicidal thoughts to her after he and Hailey broke up, claiming he couldn’t handle the pressure of his life. Hailey has publicly described feeling emotionally abused by Jon, saying she’s put her life on hold and endured public shaming as a “home wrecker.” Jon, speaking to The Insider, acknowledged Hailey’s sacrifices under intense media scrutiny, apologized for any pain he caused, and said he’s committed to making things right with Hailey, Kate, and his children. Santoro hopes Jon isn’t still despondent and suggests counseling, though she worries about his well-being.

Google disclosed, for the first time, how many government requests it received from July 1 to December 31, 2009, to remove content or provide user data across services like Search, YouTube and Blogger. The company launched an online map showing requests by country (excluding China) and included compliance rates for content removals; data-turnover rates will be added later. Google said requests are reviewed by its legal team, narrowed when possible, and complied with only when legally required, and it generally tries to notify affected users. Brazil topped the list for data requests (3,663) and content removals (291); the U.S. was second in data requests. Privacy advocates praised the transparency step, though critics cautioned numbers are imperfect and urged stronger privacy protections following recent controversies such as Buzz and Street View.

North Korea conducted another ballistic missile test Sunday, firing a medium-range Pukguksong-2 from Pukchang that South Korea said traveled about 310 miles and reached some 560 km altitude before landing in the sea. Pyongyang hailed the launch as a success, with state media saying leader Kim Jong Un supervised the test, approved deployment and ordered mass production. North Korean outlets framed the test as an “answer” to U.S. policies and warned of many more launches; they stress missiles and nukes are deterrence against the United States.

The launch was the second in a week and the 10th this year, coming after a May 14 Hwasong-12 flight that analysts see as a major step toward an ICBM capable of threatening the U.S. mainland and Guam. Washington, Seoul and Tokyo condemned the tests. U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson called the testing “disappointing” and “disturbing” but defended the current pressure strategy, saying its effects may still be emerging. The U.S., South Korea and Japan pushed for a closed-door U.N. Security Council meeting to consider tougher sanctions; Washington is pressing China for stronger measures. Experts warn solid-fuel missiles like the Pukguksong-2 are harder to detect and can be launched more rapidly, though some note North Korea still faces technical hurdles before fielding a reliable long-range solid-fuel ICBM.

French authorities intensified their manhunt and security measures after a series of linked attacks that left 17 victims and the three gunmen dead. Prime Minister Manuel Valls said there was “without a doubt” at least one accomplice and vowed the hunt would continue, stressing the threat remained. Defense Minister Jean-Yves Le Drian announced deployment of 10,000 troops to protect sensitive sites, while Interior Minister Bernard Cazeneuve said 4,700 personnel would guard France’s 717 Jewish schools.

Investigators focused on Hayat Boumeddiene, the common‑law wife of Amedy Coulibaly, who is suspected of accompanying or abetting attacks that included the killing of a policewoman and a kosher supermarket siege. Turkish officials said Boumeddiene arrived in Turkey from Madrid on Jan. 2, stayed in Istanbul with a companion identified as Mehdi Sabri Belhoucine, was tracked by Turkish intelligence via her cellphone and CCTV, and crossed into Syria from the border town of Akcakale on Jan. 8. Turkish and French accounts contained some discrepancies about timing and movements. Authorities also sought a Mini Cooper registered to Boumeddiene and warned several terror-cell members might still be at large.

Video surfaced showing Coulibaly pledging allegiance to ISIS; the Kouachi brothers, who attacked Charlie Hebdo, had claimed ties to al-Qaida in Yemen. The attacks prompted a massive solidarity turnout in Paris and worldwide, and Charlie Hebdo prepared an unprecedented print run for a survivors’ issue. The investigation continued with cross-border cooperation as France remained on high alert.

Tabloid claims that Tom Cruise is negotiating a reunion with his estranged daughter Suri are false, according to Katie Holmes’s representative. Star magazine alleged Cruise had “rounded up his lawyers” to arrange visits and that Holmes had agreed in their 2012 divorce to stay silent about Scientology if Cruise didn’t see Suri. The tabloid’s anonymous “insider” said Holmes fears Cruise might try to draw Suri back into the church but is “slowly warming up” after assurances he wouldn’t bring religion into meetings. Gossip Cop and Holmes’ spokesperson debunked the account, noting Star’s repeated history of baseless stories about Cruise and his daughter — including past claims he’d quit Scientology or arranged surprise visits — none of which materialized.

Separately, Brendan Tighe, a former Scientology security member, told Megyn Kelly he’d seen lists of women who “auditioned” to date Cruise and named Scarlett Johansson. Johansson denied the allegation as demeaning and untrue. Actress Erika Christensen discussed being raised Scientologist on Dax Shepard’s podcast, describing Scientology as a practiced upbringing rather than mere belief, recalling childhood courses and parents’ approach to parenting. She defended members’ reluctance to engage with critics and questioned the credibility of sources behind exposés like Going Clear.

Following multiple fires and explosions linked to lithium‑battery “hoverboards,” major retailers and regulators have moved to restrict sales and investigate safety. Amazon has removed many hoverboard listings and told sellers they must provide documentation proving compliance with battery and charger standards (UN 38.3, UL 1642 for batteries and UL 60950‑1 for chargers) and indemnify Amazon against patent claims. Overstock discontinued sales and offered refunds; Walmart pulled items from stores; airlines banned hoverboards from flights. eBay continued selling many listings, though online availability varies by marketplace and country.

The safety concerns center on large rechargeable battery packs used in most mass‑produced, China‑manufactured models and on counterfeit or poorly assembled units whose battery components lack proper testing. U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission reported at least 10 hoverboard fires across nine states and opened a high‑priority investigation; the CPSC and UK trading standards found many imported units failing basic safety checks. UL, which certifies components rather than entire products, indicated no hoverboard brand has fully passed its tests; however, devices with UL‑listed batteries or chargers are considered safer. Consumer advocates and officials urge buyers to purchase from reputable sellers, verify national testing lab certification on parts, and be aware of legal restrictions on public use in some countries (e.g., UK pavements and roads).

The surge in demand amid patent disputes has encouraged many low‑quality imports and knockoffs, raising both safety and intellectual‑property risks. Retailers’ recent crackdowns aim to force manufacturers to prove compliance and limit hazards from defective batteries and chargers.

Luca Guadagnino’s films consistently show nature’s power to reveal our true selves, and Call Me By Your Name is his most vivid expression of that idea. Set in northern Italy in the lazy summer of 1983, the film treats the landscape—the warm skies, gentle breezes, fruit-laden trees, and tree-lined roads—as an active presence that shapes mood and behavior. Guadagnino’s patient pacing invites viewers to inhabit this sensual world: days are filled with reading, piano, art, and harvesting peaches and apricots, creating a perfect backdrop for an unexpected, transformative romance.

Seventeen-year-old Elio (Timothée Chalamet) spends the season at his family’s villa with his cultured parents—his father, a Greco-Roman scholar (Michael Stuhlbarg), and his mother (Amira Casar). Elio is intellectually precocious and linguistically fluid, switching between English, Italian, and French, but still carries adolescent awkwardness that unravels over the summer. The arrival of Oliver (Armie Hammer), an attractive and confident American doctoral intern, ignites a slow-burn attraction. Initially prickly and competitive, their connection soon reveals deep chemistry: flirtatious intellectual sparring, tense poolside conversations, spontaneous bike rides that feel like furtive first dates, and finally an intimate confession about an hour into the film—an earned, breath-catching moment.

James Ivory’s sensitive adaptation of André Aciman’s novel captures the evolving dynamics and emotional truth of their affair. Both leads give layered performances—Chalamet’s arc from guarded teenager to emotionally open young adult, and Hammer’s mix of swagger and vulnerability—making their erotic and heartbreaking love scenes convincing. Guadagnino accentuates impermanence and melancholy through long takes, silences, tactile 35mm cinematography by Sayombhu Mukdeeprom, and a carefully chosen score: John Adams opens, Sufjan Stevens closes with aching sorrow, and the Psychedelic Furs’ “Love My Way” marks pivotal, liberating moments.

The film acknowledges the inevitability of the relationship’s end, but Stuhlbarg’s compassionate monologue as Elio’s father offers consolation. With its sensory richness, emotional precision, and memorable performances, Call Me By Your Name stands out as an exquisitely crafted, deeply affecting film.

Toughie, the last known Rabbs’ fringe-limbed tree frog (Ecnomiohyla rabborum), has died at the Atlanta Botanical Garden, marking the extinction of his species. Collected as an adult in 2005 during an urgent rescue effort as the chytrid fungus surged through central Panama, Toughie became a global symbol of the extinction crisis. His exact age was unknown but he was at least 12. The species itself was described only in 2008, after Toughie’s rescue, underscoring how some species vanish even as scientists are still cataloging them. Field research indicates that chytridiomycosis likely eliminated up to 85 percent of amphibians in Toughie’s small elevational range, and it’s unlikely any wild individuals remain. Toughie’s distinct morphology — superb climbing abilities and extensive toe webbing that allowed gliding between trees — could not save him or his kind from the rapid spread of the fungal pathogen.

Toughie became a public figure: named by the son of Amphibian Foundation head Mark Mandica, he had his own Wikipedia page, his recorded call was captured in 2014, and his image featured in Joel Sartore’s Photo Ark project. Sartore and others hoped Toughie’s story would raise awareness and spur action to combat extinctions; his image was even projected onto St. Peter’s Basilica. Despite attention and admiration, Toughie’s death illustrates a broader pattern—many species are disappearing, sometimes before they are fully known to science—and highlights the growing threat to biodiversity and the ecosystems upon which humans also depend.

Cosmetic foot surgery to fit fashionable shoes is rising, and many foot specialists warn it causes lasting harm. Surgeons and podiatrists report increasing numbers of women seeking procedures—toe shortening or lengthening, bunion corrections, fat-pad augmentations, collagen or stem-cell injections, and other aesthetic fixes—so they can wear high heels or designer footwear. A survey of American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society members found more than half had treated complications from such surgeries; the society and the American Podiatric Medical Association plan statements discouraging medically unnecessary operations.

Critics call the trend dangerous and ethically dubious: feet are complex structures that bear huge forces, and altering them for fashion can destabilize biomechanics and produce chronic pain, nerve damage, and permanent deformity. Some patients, like a woman left with numb toes after collagen injections, now can wear only sneakers. Detractors urge nonoperative measures and footwear changes over surgery.

Proponents and practitioners argue many women view shoes as essential to confidence and identity, and some patients experience real pain that insurers cover. Clinics market procedures with glamorous branding—“Cinderella” operations, “Perfect 10!”—and doctors report booming demand tied to designers like Manolo Blahnik and Christian Louboutin. Patients report regained mobility in fashionable shoes but accept trade-offs; others regret long-term consequences. The debate centers on balancing aesthetic desire, patient autonomy, medical responsibility and long-term function.

Zig Ziglar, the effusive motivational speaker and author who popularized homespun self-help maxims, died Nov. 28 in Plano, Texas, at 86 after a bout of pneumonia. Born Hilary Hinton Ziglar in Alabama in 1926 and raised in Mississippi, he served in the Navy, worked as a door-to-door salesman and rose through sales and training roles before launching a fulltime speaking career in his 40s. Ziglar built Ziglar Inc., toured relentlessly until retiring in 2010, and wrote more than 30 books—including See You at the Top and Confessions of a Happy Christian—while selling seminars, audiotapes and motivational packages to corporations and the public. Known for upbeat, faith-infused slogans (“failure is an event, not a person,” “you can get everything in life you want if you will just help other people get what they want”), he mixed anecdotes, humor and Southern charm to urge positive thinking, goal-setting and moral character. He credited his devout mother and a 1972 religious conversion for his message. Survived by his wife Jean, three children, grandchildren and great‑descendants, Ziglar left a lasting influence on the self-help industry and countless followers.

All Nashua public schools were closed Monday after officials received a specific threat of violence targeting both city high schools. Superintendent Mark Conrad said the threat, delivered to a school administrator, contained troubling detail and was slated for Monday, prompting the district and Nashua Police to err on the side of caution. Police, working with state and federal partners including the FBI, New Hampshire Homeland Security and the State Police, said the investigation into the threat’s credibility was ongoing. A state police bomb squad was dispatched to Nashua High School North as a precaution.

District officials sent thousands of automated calls to parents Sunday evening notifying them of the closure; more than 11,400 students, teachers and staff across the district were affected. All after-school events were canceled, and some nearby private schools also closed for the day. Officials emphasized safety as the top priority and expected schools to reopen Tuesday, though some parents expressed fear and uncertainty about sending children back. Governor Maggie Hassan and state emergency officials stated they were coordinating with local authorities to monitor and investigate the situation, and noted no credible threats had been identified elsewhere in the state at that time.

Several hundred Pacific walruses hauled out on a barrier island near Point Lay on the Chukchi Sea coast in early August — the earliest recorded haulout since walruses began regularly coming ashore in 2007. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service spokeswoman Andrea Medeiros said adult females and young normally rest on sea ice between feeding dives, but this year the sea ice retreated beyond the continental shelf earlier than in past years, forcing them ashore to rest. The haulout formed around August 3; numbers grew from several hundred to about 2,000 within a week. Historically, haulouts on narrow barrier islands have reached tens of thousands, and as many as 40,000 walruses have been observed on such sites in recent years, creating dangerous overcrowding.

Researchers link these shoreings to climate-driven loss of summer and fall sea ice. When ice melts north of the shallow continental shelf into very deep water, walruses cannot reach benthic feeding grounds from the ice and instead travel to land. The National Snow and Ice Data Center reported July 2017 sea ice extent as the fifth-lowest July in the nearly 40-year satellite record, and warned August weather and storms could shape the seasonal minimum.

Local leaders and Fish and Wildlife urge people to stay away from haulouts to avoid frightening the animals; stampedes triggered by aircraft, boats, polar bears or people can crush calves and smaller walruses. Point Lay’s tribal council emphasizes protecting the animals and notes the village lacks infrastructure for tourism. Fish and Wildlife is considering whether to list the Pacific walrus under the Endangered Species Act, with environmental groups warning that ongoing sea ice loss threatens the species’ survival.

Chelsea Manning, the Army private serving a 35-year sentence for leaking U.S. state secrets to WikiLeaks, was found guilty of four disciplinary infractions at the military prison in Fort Leavenworth and has been sentenced to 21 days of restricted recreation. A prison disciplinary board ruled she will be denied access to the gym, library and outdoor time for three weeks. The charges included “disrespect,” “disorderly conduct,” possession of prohibited property and “medicine misuse” after a search found an expired tube of toothpaste. Items confiscated from her cell reportedly included books and magazines such as I Am Malala, A Safe Girl to Love, Out Magazine, Vanity Fair (Caitlyn Jenner issue) and Cosmopolitan, which featured an interview with Manning. Her attorney at the ACLU, Chase Strangio, said legal counsel was barred from the closed four-hour hearing and credited public support—more than 100,000 petition signatures delivered to Congress—for likely preventing indefinite solitary confinement, a possible earlier punishment. Strangio warned the infractions could negatively affect Manning’s parole and clemency prospects and cautioned that punishing reading and advocacy risks chilling her voice on government accountability and trans justice.

Tropical Storm Harvey shut or severely curtailed large portions of U.S. Gulf Coast energy infrastructure, triggering refinery closures, pipeline outages and a government emergency crude release as market participants scrambled to head off shortages ahead of the Labor Day weekend. Motiva Enterprises’ Port Arthur, Texas refinery — the nation’s largest at roughly 603,000 barrels per day — halted operations as floodwaters rose. Sources said the plant may remain offline up to two weeks for assessment and repairs; Motiva said it cannot provide a restart timeline and will begin inspections once local flooding recedes.

Colonial Pipeline, the nation’s biggest refined-products pipeline that carries nearly 40 percent of the U.S. South’s gasoline and large volumes of diesel and jet fuel, suspended major lines after storm-related refinery shutdowns and pumping-point outages reduced available product. Lines serving areas west of Lake Charles were out of service; Colonial estimated some service from Houston could resume following infrastructure checks and a successful startup plan, with an expectation to restore full service from Lake Charles east by Sunday. Colonial stressed other supply routes — trucks, barges and alternative pipelines — can mitigate shortages, but the pause intensified regional supply anxieties.

In response, the U.S. Energy Department authorized a 500,000-barrel emergency release from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, sending crude to Phillips 66’s Lake Charles refinery to help bolster available product and support deliveries, including via Colonial. Officials said the release is aimed at tempering price spikes and easing logistics, and signaled further assistance could follow if needed.

About one-quarter of U.S. refining capacity — roughly 4.4 million barrels per day — was shut amid Harvey, affecting at least 13 Texas refineries and others across the Gulf. The disruptions pushed U.S. retail gasoline averages higher and sent futures sharply upward: U.S. gasoline futures jumped, with front-month contracts reaching multi-year highs, and national pump prices rose by about 10–11 cents over the prior week. Analysts warned refinery restarts could be slow; some expected a portion of the offline capacity to remain shut for months, extending supply strains. Global markets reacted as traders sought cargoes from Europe and Asia to fill the gap, but delivery timing and logistics complicated the response.

Chris Kluwe, former Minnesota Vikings punter for eight years, recounts events from the 2012 season through his release in May 2013, arguing his outspoken support for same-sex marriage contributed to his firing. Cleared by team legal counsel to speak as a private citizen, Kluwe campaigned publicly for marriage equality in Minnesota and wrote a viral letter defending another player’s free speech. He says head coach Leslie Frazier privately told him to stop speaking out; team owner Zygi Wilf later expressed support. Kluwe describes persistent homophobic remarks and hostility from special-teams coach Mike Priefer—comments ranging from belittling gay people to an extreme remark about nuking them—that created a tense work environment. He reports being singled out on performance charts, facing unusual criticism after a weak game, and limited communication from coaches during his knee surgery recovery. Despite reasonable season statistics and compliance with coaching requests to alter punts, the Vikings drafted a punter in the fifth round and later released Kluwe, telling him the move was about competition. Kluwe believes Priefer’s bias, and Frazier’s and GM Rick Spielman’s unwillingness to confront it, cost him his job. He calls for accountability for Priefer, reflects that advocacy likely ended his NFL career, and urges speaking up for change while noting institutional homophobia exists among individuals rather than entrenched league policy.

Oscar Pistorius, the 26-year-old Paralympic star known as the "Blade Runner," faced a sudden and harrowing fall from grace after his girlfriend, model and law graduate Reeva Steenkamp, 29, was shot dead at his home on Valentine’s Day. Authorities charged Pistorius with murder; prosecutors indicated they would pursue a premeditated murder count, which carries an automatic life sentence. During a first court appearance he repeatedly wept, while family members and legal advisers stood by him, insisting he is innocent and claiming the evidence does not support premeditation.

Pistorius’s father, Henke, told The Sunday Telegraph the family has "zero doubt" Oscar mistook Steenkamp for an intruder and shot her in a panic. The family released statements describing Oscar as "numb with shock as well as grief" and vowed to support him "heart and soul." They stressed that the couple had been happy and had plans together, and they denied any motive for harm. An uncle and sister echoed that the state’s own forensic evidence, they believe, undermines allegations of premeditated murder.

Eyewitness and media accounts report chaotic scenes at the gated Pretoria home: neighbours and security guards saw Pistorius carrying Steenkamp downstairs, attempting mouth-to-mouth resuscitation; some said she was still breathing when moved. A close friend, Justin Divaris, recounted receiving a 3:55 a.m. phone call from a distraught Pistorius who said, "There has been a terrible accident, I shot Reeva," and later sobbed, "My baba, I’ve killed my baba." Forensic teams removed the bathroom door; reports suggest she was struck multiple times through it.

Steenkamp, a rising media figure who appeared in the reality show Tropika Island of Treasure, was returned to her hometown for a private funeral. Meanwhile, Pistorius remains in police custody ahead of a bail hearing; his agent canceled his upcoming races and sponsors have so far remained publicly supportive while awaiting legal outcomes. The tragic case has shocked South Africa and drawn intense global attention.

Researchers analyzing footage from April 10 at the Royal Burgers’ Zoo in Arnhem conclude that a chimpanzee named Tushi deliberately planned and executed an attack on a camera drone, demonstrating forward planning and purposeful tool use. While a TV crew used a camera-equipped drone to film the chimp enclosure, several chimpanzees collected willow branches. Two females, Tushi and Raime, climbed scaffolding holding long twigs. As the drone approached, Tushi brandished a roughly six-foot stick and struck at the drone twice; the second blow struck and brought the drone down, eventually breaking it. The camera continued recording as the chimps inspected and played with the disabled device. Authors Jan van Hooff and Bas Lukkenaar, writing in Primates, emphasize that Tushi collected and carried the stick to a vantage point where the drone could be hit, and her facial grimace coincided precisely with the strike. They interpret the grimace as an expression of determined exertion rather than fear, arguing the sequence indicates deliberate, planned action akin to human behavior in comparable situations. The authors place the episode in context of the zoo’s chimpanzees, who have not been formally taught tool use but regularly observe humans and spontaneously employ various implements: sticks to harvest leaves and heavier objects as throwing weapons. The incident supports broader evidence that chimpanzees engage in prospective planning when using tools, choosing implements by size and weight for intended purposes.

A 20-year-old woman’s 911 call from a gated Atlanta-area mansion led police to rescue eight young women and arrest 33-year-old Kenndric Roberts on human trafficking and false imprisonment charges. In the call, the woman said she and seven others were lured to the nearly $1 million, 6,800-square-foot home with promises of modeling or financial help after meeting Roberts online. She described being sent for plastic surgery, forced to work at strip clubs, having IDs and phones confiscated, and being continually threatened—Roberts allegedly carried firearms and warned he would kill women or harm their families if they tried to leave. Officers found an AK-47 and a Glock in the house; Roberts faces multiple counts including false imprisonment, trafficking for labor, and firearm offenses, and is held without bond as federal investigators assist. Investigators say victims ranged from 19 to 22 and some endured extreme threats, including mutilation. Authorities placed the women with families or safe houses and urged other potential victims to come forward. Local advocates noted trafficking can be disguised by glamour and basic needs being met, stressing outreach and services are crucial to help victims escape and rebuild.

After an unusually warm winter with blossoms and 60s temperatures, the Northeast faces a major late-season blizzard starting Monday night into Tuesday. A rapidly intensifying nor’easter — a “bomb” development fueled by cold air from the Great Lakes and subtropical moisture from an unusually warm Gulf Stream — is expected to produce heavy, fast-falling snow, hurricane-force gusts in some spots, and coastal flooding. Blizzard warnings cover a broad swath from Philadelphia to Portland, Maine, including New York City, where forecasts call for 12–18 inches of snow and gusts of 40–50 mph; isolated totals of up to 2 feet are possible across parts of Massachusetts and New England. Washington, D.C., and Boston may sit near a sharp snow/slush cutoff, with Washington likely to receive 6–10 inches. The storm’s intense bands could drop snow at rates up to 2–5 inches per hour for several concentrated hours, creating white-out conditions, widespread travel closures, power outage risk (made worse by budding trees), and significant disruption to schools and services. Officials urged residents to avoid travel and prepare emergency kits. Meteorologists note the pattern resembles some of the region’s most extreme historic storms and fits research suggesting big East Coast snow events are becoming more frequent.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Haslam has allowed a legislative resolution authorizing a lawsuit over the federal refugee resettlement program to become law by returning it without his signature, citing constitutional concerns about one branch of government directing another. Haslam asked state Attorney General Herbert Slatery to clarify whether lawmakers can hire outside counsel to represent the state; sponsors say the Thomas More Law Center has offered pro bono representation if the attorney general declines. The resolution and the push for litigation arise amid post-2015 fears following terrorist attacks in Paris and San Bernardino, with supporters arguing refugees may not be adequately vetted by the Obama administration. Opponents — including immigrant- and refugee-rights groups and civil liberties advocates — contend the measure is discriminatory, constitutionally suspect, and intended to impede or limit Muslim refugee resettlement in Tennessee. The Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition urged stronger moral leadership and continued support for lifesaving resettlement work, while the ACLU of Tennessee called the resolution a “discriminatory” and “fear-driven” attempt that undermines separation of powers and does not enhance safety. Slatery previously advised that states cannot refuse refugees admitted by the federal government without running afoul of the Supremacy Clause, and Alabama and Texas have already sued the federal government over refugee policy. The federal Office of Refugee Resettlement notes that since 1980 more than 3 million refugees from over 70 countries have resettled in the U.S.; Catholic Charities of Tennessee has administered resettlement in the state since Tennessee withdrew from the federal program in 2008.

A March coup in Mali that ousted President Amadou Toumani Touré has produced a dangerous power vacuum, enabling Tuareg rebels to seize the country’s entire northern third, including Gao, Kidal and the UNESCO world heritage city of Timbuktu. The junta, led by Capt. Amadou Sanogo (CNRDRE), overthrew the government purportedly because of poor management of the northern insurgency but has not dispatched forces to halt rebel advances. The main rebel faction, the National Movement for the Liberation of Azawad (MNLA), seeks an independent Azawad; allied Islamist groups such as Ansar Dine aim to impose Sharia while keeping territory within Mali. Their occupation has caused reports of bans on alcohol and Western music and threats to Timbuktu’s unique mud-architecture and ancient manuscript collections. West African leaders, led by Ivory Coast’s Alassane Ouattara and ECOWAS, have imposed sanctions, closed borders and frozen Mali’s regional bank account to pressure the junta to restore civilian rule. Sanctions are already producing fuel shortages and economic strain in landlocked Mali, threatening power and irrigation during the hot season and risking unpaid civil servants. Humanitarian fallout is severe: over 200,000 people displaced since January and 13 million in the Sahel needing food aid. Regional and international support is urgently required to prevent state collapse and wider Sahel destabilization.

Researchers reconstructed 1,112 years of warm-season moisture in central Mongolia using tree rings from long-lived, stress-sensitive Siberian pines, capturing 56% of regional water-balance variability and correlating with steppe productivity. Contrary to prior suggestions that drought fostered Mongol expansion, the record shows the rapid rise of Chinggis (Genghis) Khan and early 13th-century Mongol conquests coincided with an unprecedented 15-year interval of persistently wet, warm conditions—unmatched in the millennium-plus record. That decadal amelioration followed a severe drought in the late 12th century and plausibly boosted grassland productivity, increasing fodder and “horsepower” and thereby facilitating mobilization, consolidation of power, and large-scale military campaigns across Eurasia. The study also combines tree-ring data with gridded temperature reconstructions to show the early 21st-century drought in central Mongolia was the hottest in the 1,112-year record, consistent with regional warming trends. Authors warn that future warming may negate benefits from higher precipitation by producing heat-amplified droughts with damaging effects on semiarid ecosystems and societies. Overall, the findings highlight how decadal-scale climatic anomalies—both unusually wet periods that can spur societal expansion and hot droughts intensified by anthropogenic warming—can strongly affect pastoral landscapes and human history in semiarid regions.

Author J.K. Rowling has launched a legal claim against her former personal assistant, Amanda Donaldson, seeking about £24,000 after alleging the assistant misused funds, spent on personal items with a business credit card and took Harry Potter merchandise without permission. Donaldson, 35, worked for Rowling from February 2014 until her dismissal for gross misconduct in April 2017 and denies the allegations.

Court papers filed at Airdrie Sheriff Court allege Donaldson wrongly benefited by £23,696.32 through unauthorised transactions and removals. The complaint says Donaldson had responsibility for funds, was provided a card for business and personal items only, had to submit monthly statements and receipts, and had access to a safe containing foreign currency. In February last year account reviews revealed numerous personal expenditures, prompting a meeting, suspension and later legal action.

Specific items listed include purchases such as £823 at Bibi Bakery, £1,482 at Jo Malone, £3,629 at Molton Brown, £2,139 at Paper Tiger, and £1,636 at Starbucks. Rowling also alleges Donaldson took a motorised Hogwarts Express (£467.56), Harry Potter Wizard Collection (£2,231.76) and Tales of Beedle the Bard set (£395) without consent. Other claims include buying two cats for £1,200, withdrawing £7,742 in foreign cash from the safe, and taking £400 intended as a restaurant deposit that was reportedly not paid.

Rowling’s spokeswoman confirmed legal action after dismissal for a substantial breach of trust but declined further comment. Donaldson disputes that Rowling suffered loss and says she is not entitled to damages. The case, overseen by Sheriff Derek O’Carroll, is due back in court later this year.

Tens of thousands of protesters — many young and some too young to vote — poured into U.S. streets after Donald Trump’s presidential victory, chanting “not my president” and staging demonstrations in cities from New York and Los Angeles to Portland, Chicago, Seattle, Philadelphia, Boston, Columbus, Minneapolis, Madison and Milwaukee. The protests, which began the night after the election and continued for several nights, were largely spontaneous and youth-driven, with high school and college students walking out of classes and many participants describing shock and fear over the outcome. Large gatherings included an estimated 10,000 outside Trump Tower in New York and thousands in Portland, where police declared a “riot,” saying a minority of “anarchists” smashed cars, threw rocks and Molotov cocktails, spray-painted graffiti and prompted 26 arrests. Oakland police reported dozens of fires and vandalism. In Los Angeles, up to 185 arrests were reported and an effigy of Trump was burned; protesters blocked freeways and targeted Trump-branded buildings. Slogans and hashtags such as #notourpresident proliferated. The movement lacked centralized strategy, but some activists sought to pressure Electoral College electors who meet Dec. 19; Clinton has conceded and urged acceptance of the result. Responses ranged from President Trump’s tweets condemning “professional protesters” to later conciliatory remarks, while allies like Rudy Giuliani dismissed the demonstrators as “spoiled crybabies.” A Change.org petition opposing Trump drew over two million signers in under 24 hours.

A former student allegedly stabbed a faculty member and a current student Friday afternoon at Rutgers Business School’s Livingston Campus in Piscataway. The unprovoked attack occurred near a fifth-floor lounge; witnesses described screams and a woman bleeding as professors applied pressure. The suspect fled but was quickly taken into custody with self-inflicted injuries. All three were taken to Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital. The campus was briefly locked down; the investigation remains ongoing.

A Jefferson Parish magistrate found probable cause Aug. 7 to hold Shantel Parria Wagner on a second-degree murder charge in the June shooting death of her husband, Jefferson Parish Sheriff’s Office Sgt. Troy Smith. Magistrate Commissioner Paul Schneider lowered her bond from $500,000 to $300,000 and ordered GPS-enabled home confinement if she posts bail. Prosecutors say Wagner gave multiple inconsistent statements and that one witness heard her admit to shooting Smith; Assistant District Attorney Kellie Rish emphasized an alleged confession. Investigators contend the physical evidence does not support Wagner’s claim that Smith shot himself. Defense attorneys Leo Palazzo and Wiley Beevers maintain Wagner consistently said Smith, who suffered PTSD, depression, financial and relationship stresses and had texted a suicide threat the day before, took his own life. They also noted Wagner’s DNA was not found on the gun. Dr. Dana Trosclair, the forensic pathologist, testified about entry and exit wounds—entry at the right parietal scalp above the ear, exit at the scalp vertex—with a right-to-left, slightly front-to-back, upward trajectory, but said the autopsy remains inconclusive until toxicology is complete. Crime Lab Chief Deputy Tim Scanlan said reconstruction is preliminary but that the total evidence is inconsistent with a self-inflicted wound. Smith, 44, a former NOPD member and JPSO instructor and negotiator, died June 24 after being found injured in the couple’s Waggaman home on Father’s Day. Defense calls the prosecution politically motivated; prosecutors will proceed.

A nearly 100-year-old Dutch grandmother named Annie had an unusual bucket-list wish: to experience being arrested and spend time in a police cell. With help from family, her niece notified local authorities in Nijmegen-Zuid, and police obliged—handcuffing and booking her for the novelty. Photos posted on the department’s Facebook page show Annie grinning as she is led into custody and testing the handcuffs. The accommodating officers called it a “day to remember,” happily helping the centenarian tick off this memorable and lighthearted item from her list.

A man attempted to jump the north perimeter fence at the White House on Friday, prompting a brief lockdown and street closures, law enforcement said. The 2:45 p.m. incident led police to shut Pennsylvania Avenue (open only to pedestrians) for over an hour while Secret Service and U.S. Park Police agents pulled the man down and took him into custody. Authorities checked a briefcase and declared the situation over; the individual was not immediately identified and no charges had been announced. President Obama was in Michigan at the time.

The 25th annual amfAR Gala Cannes, Cinema Against AIDS, staged May 17, 2018 at Hôtel du Cap-Eden-Roc, delivered a star-studded, high‑earning evening. Performances included Sting and Shaggy, Grace Jones, Ellie Goulding and Jason Derulo, and a fashion show curated by Carine Roitfeld; the runway looks sold as a collection for $1.7 million. Auction highlights included Pierce Brosnan’s Bob Dylan painting, which fetched $1.4 million (the buyer reported to be Ukrainian collector Marina Acton and the sale included a lunch with Brosnan), a restored 1964 S3 Bentley Convertible that sold for over $800,000, and a Joe Bradley painting that brought nearly $1 million. Presented by Bold Films and Chopard and produced by AAB Productions, the black‑tie benefit featured numerous celebrity honorary chairs and raised significant funds for amfAR’s work. Contact details for sponsorship, tickets and press were provided.

Elon Musk’s offhand tweets about founding “The Boring Company” to dig tunnels under Los Angeles have drawn intense attention because when Musk talks, people ask whether he’s serious. Last month he publicly complained about LA traffic and suggested digging tunnels as a solution, then followed up with tweets saying “I am actually going to do this,” updating his bio to include “Tunnels,” and assuring followers he planned to start digging “in a month or so” near SpaceX headquarters by Crenshaw and the 105 Freeway. His stream of commentaries — which also included jokes about “neural lace” and other ambitious projects — left observers unsure if the tunnel idea was earnest, opportunistic, or a prank. Practical hurdles are significant: tunneling is technically possible but expensive and logistically complex, especially in earthquake-prone Southern California. Political and regulatory questions, funding needs, and engineering challenges mirror those that surround Musk’s other large-scale visions like Mars colonies or self-driving cars. Still, past assurances from experts and legislative efforts to expand LA’s subway suggest modern tunneling can be feasible. Musk’s team did not immediately comment, so whether The Boring Company will move from tweet to tunnel remains uncertain.

U.S. birthrates fell sharply in 2017, reaching the fewest newborns since 1987 and deepening a longer-term trend below replacement levels. The CDC reported 3,853,472 births in 2017, a 2 percent drop from 2016, and a general fertility rate of 60.2 births per 1,000 women aged 15–44—a record low and a 3 percent decline from the prior year. The CDC’s total fertility rate, an estimate of lifetime births per 1,000 women, fell to 1,764.5, contrasted with the replacement benchmark of 2,100. The single-year decline from 2016 to 2017 was the largest since 2010, and births are down about 10 years from the 2007 peak of more than 4.3 million.

Declines were broad-based across age groups: teen births plunged 7 percent to 18.8 per 1,000—continuing a long-term fall (down 55 percent since 2007 and 70 percent since 1991 peak). Women aged 20–24 and 25–29 saw 4 percent declines; women in their early 30s experienced a 2 percent drop though they still had the highest age-specific rate (100.3 per 1,000). The only rise was among women aged 40–44 (up 2 percent). Trends reflect broader economic, generational, and demographic forces and align with projections that U.S. population growth will increasingly rely on immigration.

The declines have been most pronounced among minority women: between 2007 and 2016 Hispanic women’s fertility fell over 27 percent, Black women’s about 11 percent, Asian women’s about 5 percent, and White women’s about 4 percent. Health indicators also worsened modestly in 2017: preterm births rose (driven by late preterm births), low birthweight edged above its previous high, and cesarean deliveries nudged up to 32 percent. Social and economic factors—greater career focus among women delaying childbirth into prime career-building years, financial pressures, and changing family plans—are cited as contributing influences on the downward trends.

La Casa Pacifica is an exceptional 5.45-acre oceanfront estate in San Clemente with 450 linear feet of beachfront, extensive coastal gardens, and panoramic ocean and sunset views from a privileged elevation. The fully walled Spanish Colonial Revival compound, restored and modernized from its circa-1927 main residence, has appeared three times in Architectural Digest. The gleaming white buildings, exotic palms, Monterey cypress, emerald lawns, and immaculate seaside landscaping surround roughly 15,000 sq. ft. of structures: a ~9,000 sq. ft. main house, a 3,000 sq. ft. entertaining pavilion with guest wing, a two-bedroom guest house, staff quarters, pool, lighted N/S tennis court, and putting green behind three gated entrances. Once the Western White House for President Richard M. Nixon and a venue for many social and political events, the estate has returned to the market at $63.5 million, down from $75 million three years ago.

Russian state media and the consumer protection agency have turned a global toy trend into a national controversy. Fidget spinners—small hand-held devices that became popular for stress relief and as a novelty—were the focus of multiple segments on state-owned Rossiya24, which suggested the toys could be used by political opponents to manipulate and “zombify” children and young people. Hosts and commentators claimed spinners were being distributed at opposition events, noted the toys’ English-language branding, and argued they might dull critical thinking or make users more impressionable. A psychologist featured on one program said spinners help dexterity in very young children but otherwise “take you to a different world.”

Responding to “anxiety among parents and teachers,” Rospotrebnadzor announced an investigation to study spinners’ effects on children and teenagers’ health and any possible negative impacts, advising parents to supervise usage and buy from trusted sellers. The move follows broader safety concerns elsewhere: spinners have been modified into weapons, and customs officials in Germany seized 35 tons amid fears small parts could be dangerous to young children. Some therapists endorse spinners for attention disorders, while many U.S. schools have banned them as distractions. Independent Russian journalists mocked the TV panic as politically motivated, calling the insistence that spinners are an opposition tool absurd and emblematic of state media’s propensity for sensationalism.

Afghanistan’s president has appointed a delegation to probe UN allegations that detainees in Afghan custody have been routinely tortured, sexually abused, threatened and sometimes killed. The two-week fact-finding team includes advisors from the Interior Ministry and the National Directorate of Security (NDS), both accused in the UN report based on hundreds of interviews across 89 facilities from October 2011–October 2012. The UNAMA report details 14 abusive practices—beatings, electric shocks, ripping fingernails, genital twisting and moving prisoners to hide injuries—and quotes an anonymous NDS operative alleging secret detention sites used for torture. Afghan officials initially denied the findings and questioned UN motives; NDS and presidential spokesmen say access is provided to oversight groups like the Red Cross. Human-rights lawyers, judges and former detainees dispute that openness, recounting coerced confessions, mock trials and abuse, and warn the internal inquiry may be limited by NDS influence.

Families of roughly 800 to 850 victims of the September 11, 2001 attacks have filed a consolidated federal lawsuit in Manhattan seeking to hold the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia accountable for aiding the hijackers and supporting al-Qaida. Brought by aviation law firm Kreindler & Kreindler, the suit alleges multiple forms of Saudi involvement: logistical and financial backing for al-Qaida through a network of charities, direct assistance by Saudi embassy and consular officials in the U.S. and abroad to several hijackers, and government efforts to conceal the money trail. According to the complaint, Saudi officials in embassies—including posts in the U.S. and Germany—helped individual hijackers such as Salem al-Hazmi, Khalid al-Mihdhar and lead hijacker Mohamed Atta secure apartments, learn English, obtain credit cards and cash, and otherwise “blend into” American society in the 18 months before the attacks. The suit points to FBI findings and passport markings said to identify al-Qaida sympathizers, and names charities—including the Al-Haramain Islamic Foundation and others that plaintiffs say were government-supported and served as “alter egos” funneling funds and running training camps linked to Osama bin Laden. Plaintiffs argue Saudi elites knowingly cultivated fundamentalists and allowed or directed funds to flow to terrorists. The litigation follows Congress’s 2016 override of President Obama’s veto to enact JASTA, which carved out an exception to sovereign immunity and opened the door to suits against foreign governments for terrorism. The complaint seeks unspecified damages on behalf of victims’ families, first responders and others; Saudi representatives had not commented, and the cases are being coordinated in federal court. Plaintiffs’ counsel emphasize the families’ determination to pursue accountability.

Marion "Suge" Knight, co-founder of Death Row Records, pleaded no contest to voluntary manslaughter for a 2015 hit-and-run in Compton that killed Terry Carter and severely injured Cle "Bone" Sloan. In the plea, Knight admitted using a "deadly and dangerous weapon"—his pickup truck—and avoided murder and attempted murder charges; related robbery and criminal-threat counts were dismissed. Under California law the no-contest plea is equivalent to guilty. A judge sentenced Knight to 28 years in state prison: an 11-year high term doubled under the three-strikes law, plus additional years for a serious-violent-felony enhancement and a deadly-weapon allegation. The incident followed an argument on a Straight Outta Compton set; security footage shows Knight’s truck striking the men. Knight has a long criminal history and will begin serving his sentence in October.

President Obama announced a comprehensive response to U.S. gun violence in January 2013: 23 executive actions and several legislative proposals aimed at strengthening enforcement, improving data and research, and pushing Congress on broader bans. Executive measures focus on tightening background checks—by improving data sharing among federal agencies and states, clarifying legal barriers (eg, HIPAA), increasing penalties for lying on forms, tracing recovered guns, and guiding dealers on private-sales checks—alongside nominating an ATF director, funding and directing CDC research into gun violence, reviewing safety standards for locks and safes, and promoting safe-ownership campaigns and active-shooter training for schools and first responders. The package also lifts the practical restraints that chilled CDC research since the 1990s and asks Congress for modest funding to resume studies and expand violent-death reporting. Legislative priorities Obama urged Congress to pursue include universal background checks, reinstating and strengthening the 1994 assault-weapons ban, limiting magazines to 10 rounds, banning armor-piercing bullets, cracking down on straw purchases, and boosting school safety and mental-health services. The proposals prompted fierce debate: public opinion showed support for stricter laws, while the NRA and many Republicans vowed strong opposition, framing actions as threats to Second Amendment rights.

Three senior Kandahar officials were killed when members of the governor’s own elite guard opened fire during a high-level security meeting ahead of Afghanistan’s parliamentary elections. Kandahar Police Chief Abdul Raziq, Governor Zalmay Wesa—who later died of his wounds at a hospital—and provincial intelligence chief Abdul Mohmin were all reported dead after the attack at the governor’s residence. Afghan officials said the gunfight began around 3 p.m. and lasted more than an hour, with Afghan forces cordoning off the area and a U.S. military helicopter overhead. NATO confirmed Gen. Scott Miller, commander of U.S. and NATO forces in Afghanistan, was the apparent target but escaped unharmed; three Americans, one service member and two civilian workers, were wounded. The Taliban claimed responsibility and said they targeted Miller. Local reports suggested an Afghan military corps commander also died. Raziq was a powerful, controversial figure and close U.S. ally in Kandahar who had survived several previous attacks. The incident came amid escalating violence ahead of the elections, including a NATO convoy bombing near Bagram that killed two civilians and wounded Czech troops, Taliban attacks that killed a parliamentary candidate in Helmand, and assaults on checkpoints in Baghlan and Maidan Wardak.

The article criticizes conservative media attacks on Michelle Obama’s anti-obesity campaign, highlighting sexist mockery like Rush Limbaugh’s nickname and an offensive Andrew Breitbart cartoon. It then scrutinizes James O’Keefe’s defense after a failed prank on a CNN reporter, noting his claim that a lurid plan was a draft he never intended to use. The author argues O’Keefe’s explanations strain credulity, given his associates and past deceptive stunts, and doubts his stated innocence.

ABC has officially revived American Idol for a shortened return season slated to start March 2018, after a competitive bidding process that included NBC and the show’s original home, Fox. The Disney-owned network framed the move as reclaiming a “pop-culture staple,” saying Idol “left the air too soon” and promising a “bigger, bolder and better-than-ever” version that will join ABC’s reality lineup. Executives suggested the show will be heavily promoted and could benefit from placement alongside high-profile events like the Oscars.

Details remain sparse: judges, format tweaks and episode length haven’t been confirmed, though industry speculation points to a shorter season airing on Sunday nights. FremantleMedia and 19 Entertainment are co-owners involved in the deal. Some insiders and former producers worry the comeback could be premature given Idol’s steep ratings decline late in its 15-season Fox run and high production costs that helped drive its initial cancellation in 2016.

Ryan Seacrest — newly of Live with Kelly & Ryan and a longtime Idol host — is widely reported as the likely returning host, though no formal agreement has been announced. If he signs on, logistical challenges loom: with Live taping in New York, Seacrest would face cross-country travel to participate in live Idol episodes filmed in Los Angeles, potentially requiring multiple overnight round-trips per week. ABC hopes Idol’s established brand and promotion will reignite audiences despite past declines and strong competition in the reality-TV space.

James Debney, chief executive of American Outdoor Brands (formerly Smith & Wesson), addressed his company’s sharply worsened financial results while responding to last month’s Parkland, Florida, school shooting, in which a shooter used an M&P 15 rifle made by the firm. Debney expressed sympathy for the victims and affirmed the company’s support for firearm ownership while saying it would back efforts to improve community safety. He attributed the steep decline in quarterly profit — $4.7 million versus $37.6 million a year earlier — and nearly one-third fall in revenue ($157.4m from $233.5m) to “challenging market conditions.” 

A broader industry slump that began after Donald Trump’s 2016 election, when perceived regulatory threats evaporated, has reduced demand; rivals have faced similar pressures, and Remington filed for bankruptcy. The Parkland massacre intensified scrutiny: major retailers including Dick’s and Walmart stopped selling assault-style rifles and raised minimum purchase ages. Debney warned of flat revenues for the next 12–18 months, cut profit and sales guidance, and described heavy discounting amid excess inventory and falling background-check numbers. He has repositioned the company financially—repaying $75m and extending $75m of notes—and acknowledged uncertainty as politics and grassroots calls for controls continue to affect demand for firearms.

On Aug. 2, Shoukhrat Mitalipov’s Crispr study was published in Nature, after an accidental leak sparked sensational headlines about “designer babies.” Mitalipov, an OHSU researcher, used Crispr to correct a four–base-pair mutation that causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), an inherited heart disease that can kill young, athletic adults. Choosing HCM for its prevalence and severity, his team secured two years of institutional approval to work on viable human embryos because embryo-like stem-cell models don’t replicate embryonic DNA repair behaviors. Crispr makes a targeted cut; repair depends on cellular machinery. Mitalipov co-injected Crispr with sperm during fertilization so the egg’s high-fidelity repair system could copy the healthy maternal strand to fix the paternal defect. Across 163 viable embryos, nearly 50% were corrected, with only one mosaic case and no detected off-target effects—far better than earlier Chinese attempts on nonviable embryos. Independent experts urged caution, noting possible gaps in mosaicism detection and evidence for the repair mechanism. Mitalipov, who previously advanced mitochondrial replacement (“three-parent baby”) approaches, aims for clinical use but stresses success rates must improve. The technique’s complexity makes immediate “designer baby” scenarios unlikely, but unregulated applications pose real risks: mosaicism, off-target changes, and unpredictable harms. The piece also chronicles several families affected by mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes—like baby Russell Cruzan III—underscoring the urgency driving gene-editing research, while emphasizing the need for public debate and robust regulation before clinical deployment.

US Olympic swimmer Ryan Lochte’s parents, Steven and Ileana (Ileane) Lochte, are facing foreclosure on their Florida home after falling behind on a 2007 mortgage. CitiMortgage filed suit in Volusia County, alleging payments stopped in February 2011 and claiming roughly $242,239 plus interest remains owed on the $258,000 loan; the bank seeks to foreclose and could pursue a deficiency if the sale doesn’t cover the debt. Ileana moved to dismiss the case last month; a judge has not ruled. The couple divorced last year and both attended the London Olympics, where Ryan won five medals. Attempts to reach them and their attorneys were unsuccessful.

Emma Coronel Aispuro, wife of Mexican drug lord Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán, spoke in her first-ever televised interview with Telemundo journalist Anabel Hernández, expressing fear for her husband's wellbeing and saying she has not seen him since his recapture on January 8. The interview, part of a Telemundo special produced with UC Berkeley’s Investigative Reporting Program, took place on February 12 in Sinaloa. Coronel, a former beauty queen with dual U.S.-Mexican citizenship whom Guzmán met when she was a teenager and married on her 18th birthday, criticized the conditions at the Altiplano prison and held the Mexican government accountable for his health and treatment. She claimed authorities were punishing Guzmán for his past escapes and questioned whether he was being given basic necessities. Coronel framed Guzmán primarily as her husband rather than the narco-legend portrayed in media, saying people’s accounts are not always true and emphasizing his intelligence despite a lack of formal education.

Coronel discussed family life and the impact of Guzmán’s notoriety on their twin daughters, now four, worrying they might be judged or ostracized as they grow up. She described Guzmán as calm under stress but resentful of losing control over his public image. The couple’s desire to shape his story led to interest in a biopic; actress Kate del Castillo was involved in exploring a film project and later arranged a clandestine meeting between Guzmán and actor Sean Penn. Coronel criticized Del Castillo for allowing a video of Guzmán—intended as context for a movie discussion—to be published, calling it a betrayal, but said she felt no jealousy over Del Castillo’s interactions with her husband.

Actress Angelina Jolie drew cheers at Comic-Con in San Diego while promoting her new action film Salt alongside co-star Liev Schreiber. Jolie, 35, appeared in a leather jacket and pencil skirt and shared onstage anecdotes, including falling on set and initially fearing a concussion until remembering she’d left earplugs in from firing a gun. She described enjoying using many weapons and even experimenting with a fire extinguisher, calling Salt “meaner and harder and darker” than her past action movies and suggesting it’s a superior entry in her action work. Separately, Jolie and partner Brad Pitt quietly resolved false breakup allegations: their lawyers accepted an undisclosed settlement from Britain’s News of the World after the tab’s January story claimed they had consulted a divorce lawyer. The couple sued when the paper refused to retract or apologize, and attorneys said the settlement ends the litigation.

A Honolulu medical examiner determined that 3-year-old Finley Puleo Boyle of Kailua probably died because of sedatives and local anesthetic given during a December dental procedure, ruling the death accidental. Finley lapsed into a coma on Dec. 3 in Dr. Lilly Geyer’s Island Dentistry for Children office during treatment for cavities and root canals and died Jan. 3. The autopsy found no underlying heart condition or allergic reaction; it noted she received five drugs—including Demerol, hydroxyzine, nitrous oxide, and an injected lidocaine with epinephrine—after which she became unresponsive and went into cardiopulmonary arrest. Her parents filed a negligence lawsuit while she was in a coma; attorneys for both sides have largely declined comment. The dental office has closed. Hawaii implemented tighter dental sedation oversight in January, and no criminal charges have been filed.

More than three dozen La Salle University students and three staff on an annual Project Appalachia spring-break trip became lost after a late-afternoon hike near Bad Branch Falls on Pine Mountain in eastern Kentucky. The 40-member group reached a popular overlook called High Rock around 5 p.m., then became disoriented as darkness fell on a wooded, snow- and branch-covered trail. With temperatures dipping into the 20s and few flashlights or proper cold-weather gear, they called 911 about 7 p.m. and stayed together near a campfire while communicating with rescuers by cellphone. Search teams worked through rough terrain; some accounts say they were first located by 11 p.m., and the entire group was brought off the mountain by about 3:30–3:45 a.m. Most were evaluated at Appalachian Regional Hospital in Whitesburg for possible hypothermia, dehydration and exhaustion; one student was admitted for observation (reported stable) and others received warm clothing, food and emotional support. The group planned to return to Philadelphia Saturday.

SmartAsset analyzed the 100 largest U.S. cities to rank the worst places to own a car, using seven factors: annual hours stuck in traffic, cost of time and fuel lost to congestion, commuter stress index, non-driving options (walk/bike/transit scores), motor vehicle thefts per 1,000 residents, repair shops per 10,000 drivers, and parking garages per 10,000 drivers. Coastal cities dominate the list, especially older East Coast metros not designed for cars. Newark tops the ranking for congestion and theft risk; San Francisco, D.C., Oakland, Arlington, Portland, Anaheim, New York, Seattle, and Boston follow for various mixes of time lost, costs, theft, and limited alternatives. Data sources include Texas A&M, WalkScore, FBI, and U.S. Census.

A new, comprehensive study of 188 countries from 1980 to 2013, published in The Lancet by researchers at the University of Washington’s Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, finds global obesity and overweight rates have surged: from 857 million people in 1980 to 2.1 billion in 2013, nearly 30% of the world’s population. The United States contains the largest share of the world’s obese—about 87 million people, or 13% of the global total—despite having roughly 5% of the world’s population. Obesity has risen across rich and poor nations, men and women, and children and adolescents; childhood overweight and obesity increased by about 47% over the study period. No country saw declines in obesity in the past three decades. Regions with especially high rates include the Middle East, North Africa, Central America, Pacific and Caribbean islands; some countries report adult obesity exceeding 50% in particular sexes. Two-thirds of obese people now live in developing countries. Researchers link the trend to greater calorie intake, changes in diet composition, cheaper and more accessible processed foods, reduced physical activity, and possibly shifts in gut microbiota. The World Health Organization has launched a commission to address rising childhood obesity and propose solutions.

January Irene Neatherlin, 32, was sentenced to 21 years and four months in prison after admitting she abandoned and mistreated children at her unlicensed Bend day care, Little Giggles. Neatherlin pleaded guilty to 11 counts of first-degree criminal mistreatment and one count of third-degree assault as part of negotiated pleas from a broader 122-count indictment. Prosecutors had sought 35 years. The sentencing followed emotional, daylong testimony from numerous parents and family members describing lasting physical, emotional and financial harms to their children and households.

Police intervened on March 15, 2017, after surveillance and tips from a former roommate and boyfriend showed Neatherlin repeatedly leaving seven children, ages 6 months to 4 years, unattended while she went to a tanning salon or gym. Officers found children drugged with melatonin—routinely given to make them sleep during “nap time”—and one infant covered in vomit who could have suffocated. Testimony recounted other injuries and neglect over several years: an 11-month-old later treated in Portland for bleeding and swelling in the head consistent with shaken-baby injuries; a child burned when a bottle was overheated in a microwave; chronic sleep disruption in children given melatonin; bruises, broken blood vessels and reports of hitting. Many parents described loss of trust, therapy needs, lost jobs or broken relationships stemming from the case.

Neatherlin apologized in court, saying she loved the children but made “very poor” choices and had “demons” to face. Judge Wells Ashby acknowledged her acceptance of responsibility but cited a pattern of dishonesty and danger, noting prior theft and ID-theft convictions and efforts after arrest to solicit false testimony and promises of offshore funds. The judge emphasized community safety in imposing the lengthy sentence and allowed 30 days for appeal. Parents largely expressed relief and a desire for closure, while some urged even harsher punishment and restrictions to keep her away from children.

Israel expanded a ground offensive into Gaza after 10 days of air and naval strikes failed to halt rocket fire, with no diplomatic breakthrough in sight. The campaign, aimed at destroying Hamas’s tunnel network and weapon stockpiles, entered its 12th day amid intense fighting, repeated rocket barrages into Israel and mounting civilian casualties in Gaza. Israeli forces say they uncovered at least 13 tunnels—some very deep—with multiple openings and destroyed more than 300 Hamas targets including rocket launchers and command centers. The military reported three soldiers killed since the ground incursion began and several wounded in ongoing skirmishes; Hamas said its fighters continued to attack Israeli forces, carrying out cross-border raids through tunnels that killed two Israeli soldiers and attempted abductions. Militants used antitank missiles, machine guns and even a booby-trapped donkey, while firing hundreds of rockets—Israel claims over 1,500 fired during the month, with around 160 since the ground offensive began. Gaza’s Health Ministry said more than 330 Palestinians have been killed, roughly 80 percent civilians and many children, and about 2,200 wounded; UN agencies report tens of thousands sheltering in schools and widespread power and water concerns. Diplomatic ceasefire efforts, including an Egyptian proposal, have stalled—Hamas rejected terms demanding lifting the blockade. International actors, including the UN and France, pressed for a truce; Ban Ki-moon planned to travel to the region. Media coverage saw controversy when NBC briefly withdrew correspondent Ayman Mohyeldin after his report on children killed in Gaza, then reversed the decision. Protests erupted internationally, reflecting deep regional and global divisions as violence and humanitarian distress escalated.

Two years after Jay Z purchased Tidal for $56 million, the struggling streaming service has found a lifeline: Sprint bought a roughly one-third stake (reported by sources at about $200 million) and will make Tidal available to its 45 million customers. The deal leaves Jay Z and about two dozen artist-owners in place, adds Sprint CEO Marcelo Claure to Tidal’s board, and creates a dedicated marketing fund (reported at $75 million annually) for artist exclusives. The partnership aims to bolster Tidal’s finances, reach and exclusive content as it challenges dominant rivals.

With The Day I Met El Chapo: The Kate del Castillo Story set to premiere on Netflix, Sean Penn unsuccessfully sought edits to the three-part series to correct how his October 2015 meeting with Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán is portrayed. Penn’s representatives insist his only goal was accuracy and concern for his safety, not to block the show. Producers and Netflix, however, did not accede to his requests. The series, produced by 25/7 Productions and distributed by Netflix, highlights Mexican actress Kate del Castillo’s role in facilitating contact with the fugitive Sinaloa cartel leader and centers her perspective, which she and the producers say was previously untold.

Penn’s involvement in the episode—he later published a controversial Rolling Stone piece about the meeting—has been a focal point. The documentary reportedly suggests Penn alerted the U.S. Department of Justice about the rendezvous; his camp calls that depiction a “complete fabrication.” Producers deny claiming Penn colluded with the DOJ. Penn’s legal team requested to preview the series; after finally viewing it, Penn asked for changes and raised safety concerns, warning in correspondence that associates of El Chapo could retaliate. Netflix says Penn was repeatedly invited to participate and that the series aims to present del Castillo’s side rather than break new facts about Penn’s role.

The documentary traces del Castillo’s long-standing public fascination with El Chapo, their communications, and the logistics that brought journalists—including Sean Penn—and del Castillo to meet Guzmán in 2015. It includes extensive first-person material, including a detailed Rolling Stone-style account of the trip and Guzmán’s own video responses. The release renews debate over journalistic access, the ethics of engaging with notorious criminals, and how personal narratives shape high-profile crime stories.

A Gold Coast lifeguard, Nick Malcolm, rescued 10-year-old Prince Christian of Denmark after the boy was swept off his feet by a strong current at Mermaid Beach, Queensland. The prince, eldest child of Crown Prince Frederik and Australian-born Princess Mary, was swimming with his family between the flags when a “flash rip” pulled him out to sea. Malcolm, who is based on the Gold Coast while training in surf lifesaving and originally from New Zealand, paddled his rescue board out a short distance, helped the boy back to shore and handed him to his parents. Malcolm did not know who he had saved until a beachgoer informed him; he has declined media comment and returned to patrol duties. His supervisor and colleagues described the rescue as a standard, routine operation—something lifeguards handle frequently—while noting the significance of the outcome. Prince Frederik personally thanked Malcolm. Experts said the incident underscores the danger of powerful, sudden rips and the importance of swimming in patrolled areas; flash rips can form during wave surges even when people are between the flags. Australian beaches record many rip-related drownings each year, making lifeguard presence vital. Malcolm previously helped resuscitate a tourist at the same beach in 2014. The Danish royal family has been holidaying on the Gold Coast and will next visit Tasmania. Malcolm, feeling overwhelmed by attention, remains on duty and has not been restricted by council from speaking to media.

Apple announced the long-delayed white iPhone 4 will be available tomorrow, selling through Apple, Verizon, AT&T and authorized resellers in 16GB ($199) and 32GB ($299) models with two-year contracts. Apple’s Philip Schiller called it “beautiful” and thanked customers who waited through the extended rollout. Meanwhile, Apple addressed concerns about iOS location data collection after researchers found a cache of location-related information. Apple denied tracking customers’ movements, saying it never has and never will track individual iPhones. The company explained the data were part of a crowd-sourced database of Wi‑Fi hotspots and cell towers compiled anonymously and encrypted from millions of devices; entries may reflect the locations of towers or hotspots, not the phone’s past or present location, and can sometimes be far from the device. Apple acknowledged bugs: the cache was stored too long, was backed up, and in some cases updated even with Location Services off. It promised a free iOS update within weeks to reduce cache size, encrypt it, stop backing it up, and delete it when Location Services is disabled. Legal and regulatory scrutiny, including a class-action suit and probes in Europe and South Korea, has followed the disclosure.

A tragedy struck an El Paso church carnival Friday night when a 16-year-old girl was ejected from a spinning amusement ride known as The Sizzler at St. Thomas Aquinas Church’s Dia De Los Niños Fiesta and later died at Del Sol Medical Center.
