Two other female teenagers, ages reported between 15 and 18, were on the ride: one was also ejected and taken to University Medical Center with non-life-threatening injuries, while the third was not ejected and suffered no injuries beyond on-scene treatment. Friends and local reports identified the deceased as Sam Aguilar, a Hanks High School athlete described as sweet and active in softball and track, though authorities had not officially released an identity at the time of some updates. Witness accounts relayed by relatives said the girls told the ride operator that a seat belt would not buckle; the operator allegedly told them the belt was fine. The aunt of the uninjured teen said only two riders were supposed to be on the ride, and her niece survived by hooking her arms over the handlebar. El Paso Police Department Sgt. Enrique Carrillo confirmed the incident is under investigation and said the Crimes Against Persons unit is handling the case. Playtime Amusements Inc. operated the carnival; state statutes require ride inspections, and officials said compliance will be examined. The Sizzler ride model is common nationwide, with roughly 200 in operation per past reporting.

Trevor Noah’s selection as the new host of The Daily Show provoked immediate controversy as journalists and social-media users dug up years-old tweets in which the South African comedian made provocative jokes about Jews, Israelis, women, and other groups. Examples cited include jokes about nearly hitting “a Jewish kid,” quips equating Israel with a lack of peacefulness, a punchline invoking a “BeatsByDreidel” hashtag, repeated “fat chick” jokes, and crude lines about prostitutes and proposals. Some of these posts date from 2009 through 2014.

The backlash intensified after comedian Roseanne Barr publicly criticized Noah on Twitter for what she called sexist and antisemitic humor. BuzzFeed and other outlets highlighted a string of such tweets, framing them as evidence that Noah’s comic sensibility often relied on ethnic or gendered stereotypes. Critics argued that those remarks clashed with The Daily Show’s modern reputation — built under Jon Stewart — as a platform with moral authority that critiques power and inequality. Some commentators acknowledged that Twitter has long served as a testing ground for comedians’ rougher material, and that Stewart’s own tenure included mean-spirited jokes, yet they maintained Noah’s tweets appeared especially off-target or merely stupid rather than sharply satirical.

Comedy Central defended Noah, calling him a boundary-pushing comedian who “spares no one, himself included,” and saying it would be unfair to judge him solely on a handful of jokes. Noah himself initially made a brief, deleted tweet about Twitter’s limitations and later responded more fully: reducing his views to a few jokes “that didn’t land” misrepresents his character and evolution as a comedian. The episode raised questions about the network’s vetting process and whether appointing a relatively unknown comedian with a provocative online past was prudent, given The Daily Show’s high-profile cultural role and audience expectations.

Photos of Pippa Middleton laughing as a male companion in a Paris car produced and pointed a gun at a pursuing photographer sparked an international uproar. The 28-year-old, sister of the Duchess of Cambridge, was photographed in an Audi convertible with three male friends after attending an 18th‑century–themed birthday party for fashion entrepreneur Vicomte Arthur de Soultrait. The image shows her grinning while the driver appears to reach into the glovebox and aim a pistol at a paparazzo. Initial reports raised the prospect of criminal charges and even a French probe; some outlets warned of possible jail terms of up to seven years if the weapon were real. However, subsequent accounts softened the story: the photographer said he knew the gun was fake and never felt threatened, and friends of those in the car said they possessed a toy gun. Vicomte A, de Soultrait’s firm, called it “a stupid joke.” Paris police told ABC News there was no open investigation because no complaint had been filed, though other reports said at least one witness filed a complaint and authorities might still investigate. The episode was an awkward public-relations setback for Middleton, who has previously sought legal measures to curb intrusive paparazzi attention.

California regulators have concluded that Nestlé Waters North America may lack legal rights to divert about three-quarters of the water it bottles from Strawberry Creek in the San Bernardino National Forest for its Arrowhead brand. A nearly two-year investigation by the State Water Resources Control Board examined Nestlé’s claims that it extracted an average of 62.6 million gallons annually from the spring between 1947 and 2015. The board concluded the company may only have rights to roughly 26 acre-feet per year—about 8.5 million gallons—leaving a significant portion of its diversions without a demonstrated legal basis. Regulators have asked Nestlé to apply for permits and to bring all diversions into compliance with California law, giving the company 60 days to submit an interim compliance plan and 90 days for an investigation and monitoring plan.

The probe was prompted by complaints during California’s drought and a 2015 Desert Sun report that highlighted limited statewide oversight of bottled-water operations. Nestlé maintains it holds valid rights to a substantial amount of water and says it monitors spring sites to avoid harm; the Water Board’s report was inconclusive on environmental impacts but found the company could not satisfactorily justify the full volume it withdraws. Activists who sought to halt the withdrawals welcomed the decision. The board noted Nestlé might be able to establish additional valid claims, but until then it must demonstrate lawful rights or reduce take. The record underscores ongoing tension between historic claims, regulatory oversight, and environmental concerns in California water management.

In 2008 Hillary Clinton was widely seen as a consummate policy wonk with deep ties to Democratic policy staff, yet much of the policy establishment preferred Barack Obama because they doubted Clinton would follow expert judgment under political pressure. High-profile moments—most notably Iraq, and smaller episodes like Clinton’s support for a summer federal gas-tax holiday—fed that perception. Economists criticized the gas-tax idea as pandering that worsened policy outcomes, and Clinton’s dismissive “I’m not going to put my lot in with economists” line reinforced concerns about her deference to polls and politics.

The piece argues Clinton was again prioritizing politics over policy in 2015–16. Examples include her opposition to Obamacare’s Cadillac tax despite her prior support for similar reforms and the policy community’s backing of the tax, her late reversal on the Trans-Pacific Partnership despite past praise for it, and her shifting stance on Keystone XL. Some of these moves are credited to tactical aims—securing union backing and blunting left-wing challengers like Bernie Sanders—not principled policy shifts. While Clinton’s intellectual mastery of issues remains respected, her reputation as a policymaker is muddied by decisions seen as interest-group or poll-driven. That pattern weakens her chief asset—the image of a trusted, expert decision-maker willing to make unpopular but sound policy choices.

Christopher “Big Black” Boykin, 45, best known as Rob Dyrdek’s friend and sidekick on MTV’s hit reality series Rob & Big, has died, his representative confirmed. No official cause of death has been released; some sources cited suspected heart attack. The show, which ran from 2006 to 2008, followed Boykin and skateboarder-entrepreneur Dyrdek through humorous stunts and everyday antics—adopting a mini-horse, breaking Guinness records and more—and made Boykin a fan favorite. After leaving the shared home to raise a child, Boykin appeared on Dyrdek’s follow-ups Fantasy Factory and Ridiculousness. A U.S. Navy veteran, he launched a clothing line called “Do work” in 2007. MTV expressed sadness at his passing. Boykin is survived by his nine-year-old daughter, Isis; friends and colleagues, including Chanel West Coast, paid tribute.

The D.C. Council’s Committee on the Judiciary and Public Safety unanimously approved the Youth Vote Amendment Act of 2018, a bill to lower the voting age in the District from 18 to 16, and it will advance to the full Council for final consideration. If enacted and signed by Mayor Muriel Bowser, and after the required 30-day congressional review, D.C. would be the first U.S. municipality to allow 16- and 17-year-olds to vote in all elections, including federal contests such as the presidency. The Office of Planning estimates roughly 10,400 residents would be newly eligible, about 80 percent of whom are youth of color. The bill, introduced by Ward 6 Councilmember Charles Allen and co-introduced by several colleagues, follows renewed interest after student activism around the Parkland shooting and was supported strongly by local youth group Vote16DC, which mobilized testimony and advocacy; about 70 people—mostly young people—testified in favor and none testified against. Proponents argue enfranchising teens who already shoulder responsibilities (jobs, taxes, driving) will boost civic engagement and create lifelong voting habits. Opponents raise concerns about teens’ political maturity and parental influence. The full Council must pass the measure in two votes under D.C. Home Rule; it is scheduled for a Council vote later this month.

Archaeologists working at the Rimrock Draw Rockshelter near Riley in southeast Oregon have uncovered a small orange agate scraper that may predate known human sites west of the Rockies. The tool was found about 12 feet below the surface and approximately 8 inches beneath a layer of Mount St. Helens volcanic ash that has been dated to about 15,800 years ago, suggesting the artifact could be older than that ash. If confirmed, the site would be pre-Clovis—earlier than the roughly 13,000-year-old Clovis culture—and about 1,500 years older than other accepted pre-Clovis sites such as Paisley Cave and Monte Verde.

The excavation, led by University of Oregon archaeologist Patrick O’Grady in partnership with the Bureau of Land Management and volunteers, began in 2011 after BLM archaeologist Scott Thomas first noticed deep sediment and surface artifacts. Surface finds include about 30 stemmed projectile points; excavations have also recovered tooth enamel fragments identified as likely belonging to extinct Camelops and blood-residue on the agate scraper consistent with bovid proteins, probably an ancient bison species. Researchers caution that the claim requires rigorous testing: establishing that the ash layer is undisturbed and that the artifact did not migrate downward is essential before publication and wider acceptance. Further excavations planned this summer aim to gather more evidence and test the tentative, but tantalizing, implication of a very early human presence in the high desert.

An 11-year-old Northern California girl, Paige Warner of Roseville, died after a sudden, severe allergic-type reaction while on a family Thanksgiving trip to Oahu. Paige, who had long-standing food and environmental sensitivities, became distressed roughly 10–15 minutes after swimming at a gathering in Hawaii Kai. She complained that her nose was stinging and her throat began to swell. An EMT guest administered Benadryl and EMT responders and paramedics gave epinephrine en route to Kapiolani Children’s Hospital. Paige suffered cardiac arrest; CPR was performed for about an hour before her heart was restarted. She was intubated with difficulty, placed on life support, treated with therapeutic cooling and admitted to the pediatric ICU in a coma.

Despite initial hopes, subsequent MRIs showed rapidly worsening, widespread brain damage. Tests over several days, including cessation of the ventilator to check for spontaneous breathing, found no neurological recovery. Paige was pronounced medically and legally dead on Dec. 4. Her family—including mother Karin Carpenter, father Hank, sister Violet, and grandparents—spent her final hours with her. On a GoFundMe and in public messages, family and teachers remembered Paige for her art and warmth; donations have helped the family. Carpenter and doctors remain uncertain about the exact trigger: possibilities include airplane travel, new environmental allergens in Hawaii, feral cats in the area, pool chemicals or runoff, or a bronchospasm related to water temperature. A funeral was planned for January, and the family continues to grieve while receiving community support.

This edition of Mendocino County Today (July 23, 2015) covers a range of local news items. Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl, the controversial U.S. soldier exchanged in Afghanistan and later charged with desertion, turned up in Mendocino County while visiting friends at a Redwood Valley property raided by the county drug task force. Bergdahl, on authorized leave and carrying military ID, was not involved in the marijuana operation; authorities notified the Pentagon and an Army escort collected him in Santa Rosa to return him to duty while his Article 32 hearing is pending.

An Anderson Valley couple, Thomas R. Plowright III and Patricia Plowright, must pay $25,000 in penalties after a long-running Regional Water Board enforcement dating to illegal road and bulldozer work from 2010 that discharged sediment into Little Mill Creek, affecting salmonid habitat; cleanup has been completed though monitoring continues. Former reporter and community activist Michael Albert Kisslinger, 60, died July 20; an obituary and memorial details are included.

Other items: library workshops on communication and conflict management were canceled; debate over a proposed Coast trash transfer station was postponed amid Fish and Wildlife opposition; a Fort Bragg burglary arrest of repeat offender John Cooley Jr.; the county jail’s recent booking list; a remembrance piece for Rosie Marie Grover on the 30th anniversary of her 1985 murder and its lasting community impact; local environmental concerns over a proposed 500,000-ton-per-year asphalt plant on Outlet Creek and a Friends of Outlet Creek lawsuit seeking CEQA review; coverage of the Laytonville double homicide and related court actions; debate over a potential statewide bobcat trapping ban to be considered by the Fish and Game Commission; and Mendocino’s first West Nile virus case of 2015, with public-health precautions advised. The issue also features community commentary and light cultural pieces.

Vili Fualaau has filed for legal separation from his wife, former teacher Mary Kay Letourneau, according to Washington State court records dated May 9 and reported by RadarOnline. Fualaau, 33, told Radar the move isn’t an emotional split — he insisted the couple remains in love and that “a piece of paper doesn’t break someone’s feelings.” He framed the filing as a business precaution: he’s pursuing a marijuana distribution license for his “Cigaweed” product and said licensing background checks vet both spouses, noting Letourneau’s criminal history. Letourneau, 55, served over seven years for sexual relations with Fualaau when he was her sixth-grade student; they married in 2005 and have two children together. TMZ later reported Letourneau filed paperwork seeking dismissal of the separation petition, while Vili plans to press forward. Story developing.

The current U.S. flu season remains active and it is too early to tell whether pediatric deaths will exceed typical levels. As of Jan. 13, the CDC had recorded 30 flu-associated pediatric fatalities, though that figure likely understates the true toll because reporting lags and states vary in how quickly they submit data. The agency will release updated pediatric death counts on Jan. 26. Experts caution the total will probably rise as the season continues through May. Pediatric infectious-disease specialist Dr. John Williams noted that historically 100 to 300 child deaths from influenza are reported each year in the U.S., and that number is likely an underestimate; the season may not have peaked. Vaccination remains the primary defense: even imperfect matches can reduce severity and risk. This season’s vaccine is a poor match for one prominent strain, with estimated effectiveness of 10–30 percent against that strain, but it can still lessen symptoms if infection occurs. The vaccine works by exposing the immune system to surface proteins from inactivated virus, so antibodies are ready if exposure happens at least two weeks after vaccination. CDC spokeswoman Kristen Nordlund said 80–85 percent of children who died from flu in past seasons were unvaccinated. There is ample vaccine supply nationally, though providers may need to source different brands or presentations. Clinicians urge parents to seek care for persistent or recurrent fevers, breathing difficulties, or trouble staying awake. The season’s duration and severity remain uncertain; more weeks of data are needed.

The American Friends of the Onion Pulitzer (AFAJP) is campaigning publicly to influence journalism awards, asking supporters to sign a petition and upload videos on afajp.org to show backing for awarding The Onion a Pulitzer. AFAJP President Stephen Forbeck appeared on ABC Nightly News, where the segment treated the topic with less gravity than Forbeck does, but the appearance achieved two clear outcomes for the organization. First, it showcased Forbeck as a composed, determined leader committed to the cause. Second, it demonstrated that awareness of AFAJP is growing: the campaign is reaching viewers and generating attention. The group interprets the media exposure as evidence that public opinion can be mobilized to alter the future of journalism awards. The video posting notes technical issues with interactive transcripts and disabled ratings, but emphasizes momentum and urgency—now is the moment to reshape how awards like the Pulitzer are decided by rallying supporters and increasing visibility through petitions and user-generated video submissions.

This week’s celebrity-value roundup spotlights how moments of publicity can sharply raise someone’s “fame stock.” AshleyMadison, the infidelity dating site, bought visibility by sponsoring Howard Stern’s Miss Mistress pageant and reports a 22% revenue increase and 27% membership jump in the 55 days after the announcement—proof that controversy sells. Conan O’Brien’s Twitter follow of Sarah Killen transformed her life: overnight she gained thousands of followers, wedding gifts (including an iMac and a gown), rings, $2,600 in donations, and publicity that linked vendors like Kelima K to charitable promotion. The tragic death of Corey Haim also boosted Corey Feldman’s profile as he gave high-profile interviews describing Haim’s decline—renewed attention that may benefit Feldman’s media value despite the somber context. Separately, Kanye West’s decision to follow 19-year-old Steve Holmes sent the student’s followers surging and unleashed a media frenzy. Overall, brief, often viral moments continue to convert into tangible commercial and social capital in today’s fame economy.

An autopsy on actress Brittany Murphy has been completed with no signs of foul play or trauma; the body appeared normal and not overly thin. The Los Angeles County Coroner deferred a final cause of death pending toxicology, histopathology and neuropathology results, expected in 4–6 weeks. Murphy, 32, died after sudden cardiac arrest; officials noted internal bleeding and that she had been taking prescription medications.

In 1990 explorers found two carefully arranged oval rings of stalagmite fragments deep inside Bruniquel Cave in southwest France. Initially studied by archaeologist Francois Rouzaud, the site included burnt bear bone carbon-dated to about 47,600 years — a figure suggesting human activity older than known cave art but at the limits of carbon dating. After Rouzaud’s sudden death in 1999 the site languished until stalagmite specialist Sophie Verheyden, on holiday in the region, questioned why the stalagmites themselves weren’t dated. She assembled a team including Jacques Jaubert and Dominique Genty to re-examine the structures using uranium-thorium dating on drilled stalagmite cores. The analyses revealed a clear break between original growth and newer deposited layers, enabling precise dating of when the stalagmites had been broken and rearranged. That date: roughly 176,500 years ago. The rings consist of hundreds of similarly cut, pillar-shaped stalagmites laid in two ovals up to 40 centimeters high and covering areas of 16 and 2.3 square meters. Their position 336 meters inside the cave, traces of fire, and the deliberate cutting and placement argue strongly against natural or animal origins and indicate purposeful human construction. Because modern humans had not yet arrived in Europe, the builders must have been Neanderthals. Researchers suggest the complex behavior — deep-cave use, fire management, cooperative construction and possibly ritual activity — shows Neanderthals were far more socially and cognitively sophisticated than long assumed, though the structures’ precise purpose remains speculative.

Canadian pop star Justin Bieber was asked to leave the seaside Mayan archaeological site of Tulum after reportedly attempting to climb one of the ruins, a National Institute of Anthropology and History official said. Speaking anonymously because they were not authorized to be named, the official said the incident happened Thursday but could not specify which structure was involved. While some pre-Hispanic pyramids in Mexico may be climbable, fragile or unstable ruins are roped off or marked with “no entry” signs to protect them. The brief report noted Bieber has been involved in several incidents in Latin America in recent years.

GQ published a provocative feature listing “21 Books You Don’t Have to Read,” arguing many canonical works have not aged well—are boring, sexist, or racist—and offering contemporary or overlooked replacements. Contributors suggest swapping revered titles like Lonesome Dove, The Catcher in the Rye, The Old Man and the Sea, A Farewell to Arms, Blood Meridian, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, The Lord of the Rings, Gravity’s Rainbow and even the Bible for alternatives ranging from Jean Stafford’s The Mountain Lion and Dorothy Strachey’s Olivia to Tove Jansson’s The Summer Book, Shirley Hazzard’s The Great Fire, Patrick deWitt’s The Sisters Brothers, Ursula K. Le Guin’s Earthsea sequence, and Clarice Lispector’s Near to the Wild Heart. The piece pairs each dismissal with a short rationale—criticizing outdated attitudes, stylistic tedium, or problematic depictions—and recommends books deemed fresher, more humane, or more engaging.

Placing the Bible on the list provoked immediate backlash from Christian commentators and public figures. Fox’s Father Jonathan Morris called the move “foolish and a shame,” and evangelist Franklin Graham urged readers to revisit Scripture’s centrality to Christian faith. Social media responses ranged from angry condemnations to mocking the magazine’s cultural authority. GQ defended the project’s premise in its intro—questioning the unquestioned status of “Great Books”—but had not publicly responded to the specific criticisms at the time of reporting.

Aldabra giant tortoise Abuh, a 35-year-old female roughly one metre long and weighing about 55 kg, was found safe two weeks after escaping Shibukawa Animal Park in Okayama prefecture. The tortoise, allowed to roam freely in the zoo during opening hours, disappeared on August 1. Despite search efforts, keepers had no solid leads and announced a ¥500,000 (about $4,500) reward for her safe return. On August 16 a local family — or, in some accounts, a “sharp-eyed bounty hunter” — spotted Abuh in shrubbery or a nearby forested slope very close to the zoo, with reports varying between about 50 metres and 140 metres from the entrance. The find was promptly reported to zoo staff, who reunited her with the park; she is recovering well and eating pears and watermelon. Staff described Abuh as gentle and popular with children, and said they were relieved at her safe return. Officials noted this was her second disappearance in under a month and said they will implement new measures to prevent repeat escapes, though they did not specify what changes would be made. The episode drew national attention and was featured on NHK.

Researchers from the University of Nottingham and the Finnish National Institute for Health and Welfare sampled frequently touched surfaces and air at Helsinki-Vantaa airport during winter 2016 to assess respiratory virus contamination. Using genetic detection methods, they found viral material on about 10% of surfaces tested. Plastic security screening trays had the highest concentration of viruses; other contaminated sites included shop payment terminals, staircase rails, passport-check counters, children’s play areas and the air. The most commonly detected pathogen was rhinovirus, which causes the common cold, and influenza A was also identified. Toilets surprisingly yielded no respiratory virus detections in this survey. The study, part of the EU-funded PANDHUB project and published in BMC Infectious Diseases, emphasizes that the detection of viral genetic material does not prove the viruses were viable or infectious, though earlier studies indicate many microbes can survive on surfaces for days. Investigators say the findings reinforce public-health advice: frequent hand washing, using hand sanitizer, and covering coughs (into a tissue or sleeve) are simple but effective measures to reduce transmission in crowded transport hubs. The results also inform preparedness planning for future pandemics and suggest practical responses such as more regular cleaning of high-touch items like security trays, provision of hand-sanitizing stations immediately before and after security screening, and potential design improvements in airport facilities to limit spread.

A dispute over roughly 200 historical photographs of the Walmart–Walton family has become a federal copyright battle between the Walton family/Walmart Museum and the widow of a longtime Arkansas studio photographer. Robert A. Huff and his son David of Bob’s Studio of Photography photographed Walton family members, the original Wal‑Mart board and related subjects from about 1950 to 1994. After the photographers’ deaths, David Huff’s widow, Helen Huff, retained negatives, prints and proofs. The Waltons (filing as Crystal Lands, LLC, and Wal‑Mart Stores, Inc.) sued to recover those materials, claiming the images were created as “works for hire” and therefore belong to the family and museum; they seek a declaratory judgment and to block Huff from commercially using or selling the images. Huff counters that the photographers were independent contractors who owned the copyrights: they used their own equipment, controlled shoots, arranged processing, and provided copyright notices. The Professional Photographers of America (PPA) supports Huff, calling the suit a David‑vs‑Goliath attempt by a corporate giant to seize photographers’ rights and citing precedent (Natkin v. Winfrey) where courts sided with photographers absent written work‑for‑hire agreements. Reports say the Waltons offered $2,000 for the materials, which Huff turned down. The case, removed to federal court because it raises copyright issues, proceeded to case management with a trial term set; the court will decide whether the studio or the Waltons hold the copyrights and who may use the historic images.

A self-described British “email prankster” used fake accounts to impersonate several Trump administration figures and trick White House officials into replying, CNN reports. Using aliases including Jared Kushner, Reince Priebus, Jon Huntsman Jr., Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr., the prankster persuaded Homeland Security Adviser Tom Bossert to accept a Kushner invitation and even provide his personal email address. Bossert did not comment; the prankster — who posts as @SINON_REBORN and describes himself as a “lazy anarchist” — told CNN he intended humor rather than harm.

The impersonator also engaged Anthony Scaramucci, then White House communications director, in heated exchanges by posing as Priebus and Huntsman. In those messages Scaramucci argued with the fake Priebus over accusations of hypocrisy and criticized others; he later told the bogus Priebus to “Read Shakespeare. Particularly Othello.” The prankster likewise tricked Huntsman into believing he was Eric Trump, and briefly fooled Eric Trump by posing as his brother before Trump alerted law enforcement, though the prankster said he heard no follow-up.

White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said the administration is treating the incidents seriously and is investigating. Cybersecurity experts told CNN the episodes illustrate officials’ vulnerability to spear-phishing tactics: attackers often gain trust by posing as associates before attempting to elicit sensitive actions. No links were clicked in these exchanges, and the prankster appeared motivated by mischief rather than malicious theft. Nonetheless the incidents underscore persistent risks to high-level government email security.

A new study led by Rutgers’ Bob Kopp reconstructs global sea-level (GSL) change over roughly 3,000 years and finds the 20th-century rise was exceptional. Using 24 regional proxy reconstructions (from marshes, coral atolls, archaeological sites) plus 66 tide gauges, the authors built a spatiotemporal statistical model to separate global signals from regional effects (tectonics, glacial isostatic adjustment, ocean dynamics). Preindustrial GSL varied modestly—about ±7–11 cm—with notable phases: a small rise 0–700 CE, a fall 1000–1400 CE coincident with ∼0.2 °C cooling, and stability until the late 19th century. The 20th century saw about 14 cm of rise (1.4 mm/yr average), and it is “extremely likely” (≥95% probability) this century-scale increase exceeded any of the prior 27 centuries. Semiempirical modeling calibrated to temperature reconstructions indicates that without anthropogenic warming the 20th century would likely have seen between a 3 cm fall and a 7 cm rise—far less than observed—placing a strong human fingerprint on recent sea-level change. Projected 21st-century rises depend on emissions: under strong mitigation (RCP2.6) the study estimates 24–61 cm by 2100; under high emissions (RCP8.5) 52–131 cm, with higher tails possible if ice-sheet processes intensify. The paper and a companion study also link human-driven sea-level rise to thousands of U.S. “nuisance” coastal floods already observed. Authors caution that models calibrated to past drivers may not fully capture future ice-sheet dynamics, particularly potential rapid Antarctic contributions, making high-end outcomes uncertain and potentially larger.

Spencer West, born with sacral agenesis and having both legs amputated below the pelvis in early childhood, defied doctors’ expectations to achieve extraordinary feats. At 31, the Toronto-based motivational speaker and Me to We ambassador climbed Mount Kilimanjaro, taking roughly 20,000 “steps” to the 5,895-meter summit. Over eight days he propelled himself hand over hand for about 80 percent of the trek, sometimes using a custom wheelchair on easier terrain or riding porters when necessary. The expedition—supported by two close friends, a 50-person crew including porters, guides and videographers—traversed varied microclimates from jungle to snowfields and the lunar desert. West and his team trained for a year, building strength and endurance. He undertook the climb to inspire others to “redefine possible” and to raise $750,000 (about $500,000 raised so far) for Free the Children to fund clean-water boreholes, aiding thousands affected by a severe regional drought. Despite cuts, soreness and altitude-related illness among teammates, West reached the summit, calling the moment humbling and transformative, and urging people to tackle their own challenges, big or small.

Records released by the Seminole County Sheriff’s Office show George Zimmerman, under GPS monitoring while free on $1 million bond in the Trayvon Martin case, attempted to obtain a bulletproof vest and an infrared home‑security device. The 57‑page log, active July 6, 2012–July 13 this year, tracked Zimmerman’s ankle‑monitor movements, required twice‑daily check‑ins, and flagged departures outside Seminole County other than court‑approved attorney visits in Orlando. A police‑supply sales representative informed deputies on Aug. 8, 2012, that Zimmerman wanted a vest and an infrared entry sensor; Zimmerman later confirmed he ordered both, saying they were for his protection. The log also records routine issues such as complaints about the ankle monitor’s discomfort, multiple residence moves with his wife Shellie, and a July 14 call reporting new phone numbers after media obtained his wife’s number. Deputies even reviewed security footage after a sporting‑goods visit to ensure he had not entered firearm sales areas. Zimmerman was acquitted last month in the fatal 2012 shooting of 17‑year‑old Trayvon Martin, a case that intensified national debate over race and profiling.

Iowa police have distributed 30,000—and plan another 30,000—colorful thumb bands reading "TXTNG KILLS" to discourage texting while driving as part of the statewide "X the TXT" campaign. The bands are handed out at events like the Iowa State Fair, high-school and college football games, and during traffic stops; law enforcement gets a warning-only period in the first year under the new ban before fines begin. Officers say catching texters is difficult—drivers often warn others—so the bands are a public-awareness tool aimed at teens and families, supported by national efforts such as Allstate’s pledging campaign. Distracted driving remains deadly: nearly 6,000 U.S. deaths in 2008 involved distraction, and Iowa has recorded 16 cellphone-related fatalities since 2001.

A federal government shutdown became increasingly likely as conservative activists and Tea Party-aligned House Republicans pressured Speaker John Boehner to reject a Senate stopgap spending bill that funds government operations and preserves Affordable Care Act (ACA) implementation. Senate Democrats urged the House to accept the Senate-passed continuing resolution, warning that any House changes would risk shutting the government. Conservatives threatened to oust Boehner if he allowed funding that didn’t defund or delay Obamacare, while grassroots campaigns flooded lawmakers’ offices with calls. House Republicans considered amendments — including a one-year delay of the ACA individual mandate, repeal of the medical device tax, ending health benefits for members and staff, or eliminating IPAB — but Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid vowed to block any bill containing ObamaCare riders. Leadership talks produced little progress; aides from both parties said the government looked likely to close Tuesday if no compromise emerged. A shutdown would furlough roughly 40–41% of nondefense federal employees, disrupt passports, visas, gun permits, some court cases and mortgage approvals, and close national parks and museums, though Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid would continue. Lawmakers also face an imminent debt-limit fight by mid-October, raising stakes if short-term funding merely delays conflict.

Max Lomas, a longtime friend and former housemate of Bobbi Kristina Brown, described a life of drugs, partying, fights and pain leading up to finding her unconscious in a bathtub on Jan. 31, 2015. Lomas, who had lived with Brown and her then-boyfriend Nick Gordon in Roswell, Georgia after Whitney Houston’s death, says the group briefly tried to get sober but relapsed. He recalled volatile, jealous fights between Brown and Gordon and alleged instances of abuse Gordon denies. Lomas helped pull Brown from the tub and perform CPR; she later died after months in a coma. Lomas later struggled with addiction and reportedly died of an apparent overdose, found with a syringe nearby. No charges were filed against him; Brown’s family won a wrongful-death civil suit against Gordon.

Pope Francis drew fresh attention to exorcism after images showed him laying hands on a wheelchair-bound Mexican man during Mass in St. Peter’s Square; the man heaved, convulsed and slumped, prompting debate over whether an exorcism occurred. The Vatican said Francis “didn't intend to perform any exorcism” and merely prayed for a suffering person, while several Roman exorcists, including famed Rev. Gabriele Amorth, insisted it was an exorcism or at least a liberation prayer; Amorth later said he performed a separate exorcism and found four demons. Witnesses disagreed on what was said, and TV2000 — which broadcast the footage and cited exorcists — later apologised for mischaracterizing events. Observers note Francis’ frequent references to Satan reflect his background and concern over secularization; the church permits exorcisms only by bishop-authorized priests after ruling out psychological illness.

An American Airlines flight from Dallas/Fort Worth to Chicago (Flight 2332) was delayed after a flight attendant began a disruptive, incoherent PA announcement as the plane taxied for takeoff. Passengers reported she warned of a crash, referenced 9/11 and the airline’s bankruptcy, and appeared to be in a manic or disturbed state; some later said she mentioned bipolar disorder and not taking medication. Other crew and several passengers, including a pilot riding in first class and a group of Sam’s Club colleagues, restrained her and the aircraft returned to the gate. Two flight attendants were injured and taken to local hospitals; no passengers were hurt. FAA described the event as an altercation; the FBI said no federal investigation was needed. American Airlines replaced the cabin crew, said customers were never in danger, and the flight subsequently departed about 80 minutes late.

White House Chief of Staff Rahm Emanuel said on Charlie Rose that he would like to run someday for mayor of Chicago, putting on record an ambition he had earlier tried to play down. Emanuel said he hopes Mayor Richard Daley seeks re-election and would support him, but if Daley does not run Emanuel would pursue the job, noting the mayoralty has long been an aspiration dating to his House years. He described missing direct constituent contact and cited examples—from helping a small business get a loan to drafting the Elderly Justice Act after meeting a constituent—that drew him to local service. Emanuel pledged to serve President Obama through the end of the year (and possibly longer if asked), has moved his family to Washington, and gave up a safe House seat when he became chief of staff. Daley’s camp called Emanuel’s interest “laudable,” acknowledging he’d face competition despite strong fundraising potential.

Federal agents arrested 19-year-old Sergio Morales Soto on April 5 as he attempted to leave the country on a flight to Guatemala, after severe weather delayed the plane. Homeland Security agents tracked the specific aircraft and seat, boarded the flight and apprehended him before takeoff, then transferred him to Caroline County Sheriff's Office custody. Soto was returned to Maryland to face six felony sex assault charges. Officials highlighted the capability to locate and arrest suspects booked on flights throughout Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta Airport, with U.S. Customs and Border Protection's port director noting they arrest more than 20 suspects nationwide daily. Bad actors cannot evade capture by reaching an airport.

The article argues that Wall Street’s influence on U.S. politics remains strong despite public portrayals of growing hostility between Democrats and the financial sector. Using New York politicians as examples, it notes that Democratic lawmakers—Gary Ackerman, Barney Frank, Kirsten Gillibrand and Charles Schumer—continue to receive large contributions from banks, securities and investment firms. Ackerman, despite a high-profile 2009 rebuke of regulators over Bernie Madoff, later defended Wall Street interests. Gillibrand, though a Democrat, has become a reliable advocate for financial services and has attracted major industry donations that dwarfed support for her Republican opponent. Nationally, the financial industry has shifted more money to Republicans and conservative PACs since 2008, but still gives significant sums to Democrats, underscoring bipartisan ties and the sector’s pragmatic support for influential lawmakers.

Hillary Clinton’s selection of Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine as her running mate drew a mix of cautious approval and sharp criticism across the Democratic Party, underscoring tensions between the party’s centrist and progressive wings as delegates prepared to convene in Philadelphia. Many Democrats praised Kaine’s broad experience and steady, governable demeanor—attributes seen as assets for general election voters—while others, particularly supporters of Bernie Sanders, worried he would do little to heal the rift with progressives or energize their base.

Kaine, a former governor, mayor and DNC chair, is viewed as a reliable, experienced choice who could help Clinton in key swing states like Virginia. Supporters highlighted his record on labor, women’s rights and environmental protection, and emphasized his temperament and ability to assume the presidency if needed. Prominent labor leaders and women’s groups, including the AFL-CIO, SEIU, Planned Parenthood and Emily’s List, voiced support, praising his pro-worker positioning and advocacy on issues affecting women and marginalized communities. Clinton’s campaign framed Kaine as a lifelong progressive fighter, pointing to high ratings from groups such as the Human Rights Campaign and the NAACP.

However, progressive activists and many Sanders delegates expressed disappointment. Critics pointed to Kaine’s past votes and positions on trade and banking—most notably his earlier praise for and support of the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) and a bipartisan letter urging caution in Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rulemaking—to argue he is insufficiently populist on economic issues. Groups like the Progressive Change Campaign Committee and Democracy for America warned Kaine’s record could open Democrats to attacks from Republicans and alienate working-class voters in the Rust Belt. Documentary filmmaker Michael Moore and organizations aligned with Sanders suggested the pick risked depressingly low turnout among disaffected progressives and threatened party unity.

Sanders delegates debated protest tactics, with some proposing walkouts during the convention roll call and others awaiting Sanders’ guidance. The Bernie Delegates Network and related groups signaled plans to press for progressive visibility and policy demands at the convention.

Outside progressive criticism, Wall Street lobbyists expressed relief, seeing Kaine as a non-confrontational figure who would not sharply escalate financial-sector battles. Some strategists warned the selection might risk ceding anti-trade populist ground to Donald Trump in key Midwestern states. Latino leaders had mixed reactions after Clinton passed over Hispanic finalists like Julián Castro and Tom Perez; some were disappointed while others noted Kaine’s Spanish fluency and past outreach to Latino communities.

Kaine’s biography—son of a welder, Jesuit-educated, a year spent as a missionary in Honduras that made him fluent in Spanish, and a long record of public service—was presented as a unifying, competent narrative. Yet critics pointed to past controversies over gifts accepted during his time in Virginia and questioned whether his centrist credentials would bridge the party’s growing ideological divide. Overall, Kaine was cast as a steady, conventional pick who may reassure moderate and swing voters but is unlikely to fully placate the progressive base.

Virginia Attorney General Ken Cuccinelli ignited online ridicule after tweeting, "How much would I give to be one of the 72 Virginans Osama is 'hanging out' with since Sunday?" following Osama bin Laden’s death. Cuccinelli later explained he was referencing a circulating joke in which bin Laden is beaten at heaven’s gates by founding Virginians—George Washington, Patrick Henry, Thomas Jefferson, James Madison and others—before an angel remarks, “I told you there would be 72 Virginians waiting for you.” The tweet’s misspelling ("Virginans") and the joke’s obscurity prompted mockery and speculation, including a Huffington Post writer suggesting, sarcastically, that Cuccinelli’s message implied sexual intent or envy of the Navy SEALs credited with the raid. The writer later updated his post after finding the joke. Cuccinelli attempted to clarify the tweet in a follow-up, noting the intended wording, but the episode highlighted social media pitfalls for public officials and drew widespread attention from news outlets and bloggers.

A six-member medical board at Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) has decided to begin multi-stage plastic surgery on Abul Bajandar, the 26-year-old Bangladeshi known as the "Tree Man," in about three weeks. Abul, from Khulna, suffers from massive bark-like warts caused by the exceedingly rare genetic condition epidermodysplasia verruciformis. The growths, which first appeared in his teens and accelerated four years ago, have formed thick root- and trunk-like protrusions on his hands and feet weighing several kilograms and rendering his hands largely nonfunctional. Doctors aim to restore some hand function by surgically removing excess tissue from the thumbs and index fingers, but Abul is presently malnourished and too weak for immediate operation, so preoperative blood tests, biopsies and other examinations will begin immediately. DMCH has formed a surgical team, is waiving treatment costs, and is coordinating with foreign specialists—several international doctors and researchers have contacted the hospital offering help and requesting blood and biopsy samples. Preparations include evaluating risks of nerve damage and other complications; doctors estimate Abul may need to stay in hospital for up to six months. He is currently staying in a DMCH cabin with family members nearby, and hospital security will be increased to control crowds of curious visitors. Abul previously sought local and foreign treatments, including homeopathic remedies and consultations in India, but could not afford surgery there. This is reportedly one of only three known global cases of the disorder.

A viral mix of publicity, satire and genuine concern erupted after Kanye West tweeted in February 2016 that he was $53 million in debt and appealed to tech billionaires for help. West’s dramatic statements — calling himself everything from “the greatest living artist” to “Shakespeare in the flesh” and pleading for financial backing from Mark Zuckerberg and Larry Page to realize his Donda venture — sparked headlines and social-media reactions across entertainment and tech circles. The exact state of his finances was unclear; outlets couldn’t independently verify the $53 million figure, but the tweets did highlight West’s long-running attempts to court Silicon Valley support for business and creative projects.

In response, fans and jokesters launched crowdfunding campaigns on GoFundMe to “help get Kanye out of debt.” Minnesota graphic designer Jeremy Piatt created a high-profile fundraiser modeled on the Medici patronage ideal, arguing that great artists need private backers. Piatt framed the campaign as grassroots support for the arts, though donations were minimal — only a few dozen dollars in early reporting — and GoFundMe restrictions meant funds couldn’t be withdrawn without Kanye’s acknowledgment. Other efforts appeared and faltered, including a Washington, D.C. page that raised nothing and was later canceled.

Coverage linked West’s outreach to his established social ties in tech: appearances at Apple offices, relationships with venture capital figures like Ben Horowitz, and past presentations of his Donda concept to investors. Observers noted the curious cultural crossover: musicians seeking tech credibility and technologists’ fascination with celebrity. West’s public behavior around that period also included the controversial Tidal release of The Life of Pablo, public boasts about other stars, and detours into fashion and startup ambitions — all framing his financial plea as part PR stunt, part real plea, and part performance art. Overall, the episode underscored how celebrity, crowdfunding, and Silicon Valley intersect, and how public appeals for patronage can become spectacles in their own right.

Amazon is extending its mobile push into physical stores with a limited Price Check app promotion. For a short window (9 PM PST Dec. 9 to 11:59 PM PST Dec. 10), users who scan barcodes in-store with the iPhone or Android app, or enter product info manually and enable location services, will receive 5% off an Amazon purchase of that item (capped at $5) within 24 hours. The discount can be used on up to three products per user. Amazon says the move promotes price transparency and smarter holiday shopping; it also lets Amazon track competitors’ pricing and potentially adjust future offers. Critics note the $5 cap limits impact, but the tactic reinforces Amazon’s advantage on price and convenience while blurring lines between online and brick-and-mortar retail during peak shopping season.

Sen. Marco Rubio’s GOP response to President Obama’s State of the Union was overshadowed by a brief, highly memeable moment when he paused to drink from a Poland Spring bottle. Rubio’s prepared remarks ran about five pages — roughly half the length of Obama’s speech — but the thirsty moment at the end prompted a social-media frenzy. Twitter reported roughly 9,200 tweets per minute around 10:43 p.m. ET, with #watergate and Poland Spring briefly trending. Commentators and political figures piled on: Abby Huntsman called the reach “too much awkwardness,” Ana Marie Cox mocked the timing, and Democrat Paul Begala quipped about Rubio being the man “you want to have a desperate gulp of water with.” Some Republicans defended Rubio, arguing the trivial incident would unfairly eclipse his substantive points; strategist Mike Murphy lamented that the gag would dominate attention, and Garrett Jackson blamed staff layout for placing the bottle too far. Rubio himself leaned into the moment, tweeting a photo of the now-empty small water bottle. The viral episode highlighted how a single humanizing hiccup can drown out a formal political message in today’s social-media landscape.

President Trump accepted Attorney General Jeff Sessions’ resignation Wednesday and named Sessions’ chief of staff, Matthew Whitaker, as acting attorney general, immediately placing oversight of Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s Russia probe in the hands of an official who has criticized and suggested limiting the investigation. Sessions, once an early Trump ally who enacted hardline immigration and law-enforcement policies, had long been at odds with the president after recusing himself from matters tied to the 2016 campaign. Democrats and former officials urged that Whitaker recuse himself; they warned against interference with Mueller. Trump framed the change amid mixed midterm results—Republicans held the Senate while Democrats reclaimed the House—and continued to attack detractors and praise loyal candidates. Whitaker pledged to lead a fair Justice Department; lawmakers vowed to seek answers and potential accountability over the removal.

North and South Korea announced plans for a third summit between President Moon Jae-in and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un to be held in Pyongyang in September, following high-level talks at the DMZ. While North Korean envoy Ri Son Gwon said a September date is set but withheld specifics, South Korea’s Cho Myoung-gyon said the exact timing requires further discussion; Moon’s office noted a summit before September 10 would be difficult for logistical reasons. This would be the first South Korean presidential visit to Pyongyang in over a decade and the third in-person meeting between Moon and Kim this year, after the April Panmunjom summit and a May DMZ encounter. The summit follows a broader diplomatic thaw—sparked by the Winter Olympics—that led to the Panmunjom Declaration and the June US–North Korea Singapore meeting between Kim and President Trump, which pledged progress toward denuclearization though critics argue specifics were lacking. Seoul and Pyongyang discussed denuclearization in general terms and emphasized the need to create a positive cycle between inter-Korean and North Korea–US relations. Separately, North Korean media escalated demands that South repatriate 12 defected restaurant workers who left China for the South in 2016, warning delays could undermine family reunions and inter-Korean ties.

Community leaders, clergy and civil-rights activists in Cleveland announced they will file citizens’ affidavits asking a municipal judge to find probable cause and issue arrest warrants for the two officers involved in the November shooting death of 12-year-old Tamir Rice. Using a rarely invoked 1960 Ohio law that lets any person with knowledge submit sworn affidavits to prompt a judge to sign arrest warrants, the group — which includes Rev. Dr. Jawanza Colvin and Case Western Reserve professor Rhonda Williams — said they will seek charges including aggravated murder and manslaughter. They framed the move as a response to perceived inaction by the criminal justice system: “It has been more than six months… and yet the people still have no answers and no one has been held accountable,” Colvin said, describing citizens as compelled to “take matters into their own hands” through democratic tools.

The filing is intended to bypass the ordinary path in this case, in which the Cuyahoga County Prosecutor’s Office is completing an investigation and plans to present evidence to a grand jury — the office’s stated policy for fatal police use-of-force cases. Prosecutor spokesman Joe Frolik said the investigation is not complete and that evidence and analysis will be presented to the grand jury once redactions are made.

The Cleveland Police Patrolmen’s Association criticized the move as “vigilantism,” accusing organizers and lawyers of undermining the justice system and stoking anti-police sentiment. If the citizens’ affidavits lead to warrants, the case would still proceed through the grand jury as guaranteed by Ohio’s constitution. The prosecutor’s office said it will release the investigation’s contents “fairly soon.”

Jonathan Carlyle Merkley, 34, died after being struck by a BMW outside a Staybridge Suites in Mira Mesa shortly after midnight on the night of his birthday. Witnesses said Merkley and several friends, including the woman who drove the BMW, had been drinking. When the woman attempted to leave the hotel, Merkley reportedly lay down in front of her car to stop her. The driver did not stop, ran over him, and drove away. Merkley suffered major chest trauma and died at a hospital about 45 minutes later. San Diego police have identified and located the woman, interviewed her, and impounded a vehicle that may be connected; no arrests have been made. Investigators continue to determine whether the driver knew she had struck him and to evaluate the culpability of other parties. Authorities ask anyone with information to contact the San Diego Police Department or Crime Stoppers at 888-580-8477.

The Last Station, written and directed by Michael Hoffman, is a richly staged period biopic about the final year of Leo Tolstoy’s life, anchored by powerhouse performances from Christopher Plummer as Tolstoy and Helen Mirren as his long-suffering wife, Countess Sofya. Set in 1910 Russia amid revolutionary ferment, the film dramatizes the clash between Tolstoy’s ascetic, egalitarian convictions—supported by disciple Vladimir Chertkov (Paul Giamatti)—and Sofya’s desperate effort to preserve the family’s inheritance and literary legacy. Young secretary Valentin (James McAvoy) is drawn into the conflict; his parallel coming-of-age romance with servant Masha (Kerry Condon) mirrors the older couple’s fraught marriage. Hoffman balances lush visuals, humor and human drama so the story never feels remote or merely reverent; scenes range from intimate seductions to theatrical confrontations. Mirren’s fiery, complex Sofya often dominates, while Plummer gives a magnetic, humane Tolstoy, culminating in a memorable deathbed sequence at a rural railway station. The Last Station is literate, emotionally vivid and highly entertaining—an elegant, compelling portrait of love, ideals and the price of conscience.

Three years ago an anonymous Philadelphia man recounted on Gawker a Halloween night encounter in which an intoxicated Christine O’Donnell showed up at his apartment, persuaded him and a roommate to join her night out, then returned with him and slept in his bed. The narrator, then 25, describes meeting O’Donnell briefly months earlier, her showing up tipsy in a ladybug costume, convincing them to go to South Street, and later getting intimate but not having sex—she reportedly told him she was a virgin. He details awkward morning-after moments, brief follow-up contact, and that she later dated his roommate. Gawker published the first‑person account, paying the source a modest sum and defending publication as newsworthy because it purportedly contrasted O’Donnell’s private behavior with her public image as a Christian conservative. The post sparked swift backlash on Twitter and among journalists, who accused Gawker of misogyny, sleaze and exploiting an anonymous “dudebro” for pageviews; critics argued such items discourage women from running for office and unfairly sensationalize private matters. Gawker’s editors and owner argued editorially that the piece was compelling and properly vetted; O’Donnell’s team issued a response.

Sen. Lindsey Graham, speaking to the Concord City Republican Committee, said his first act as president would be to prevent Congress from leaving town until defense and intelligence budget cuts were restored, adding, “I would literally use the military to keep them in if I had to.” Outlets and commentators seized on the remark, suggesting it implied using the military to compel Congress to pass his agenda — an action critics labeled unconstitutional and akin to a “self-coup.” Analysts noted lawful past practices, like the Senate compelling attendance to reach a quorum, but emphasized those are internal, rule-based measures and do not allow the executive to occupy the Capitol or force votes. Given Graham’s background as an attorney and Air Force JAG, many found the literal reading implausible. His office later clarified the comment was over-the-top humor and “not to be taken literally.”

Fullscreen Media has produced Keeping Score, its first original docuseries, following U.S. women’s soccer stars Hope Solo, Megan Rapinoe and Crystal Dunn as they prepare for, compete in, and cope with the 2016 Rio Olympics. Debuting August 3 exclusively on Fullscreen’s SVOD platforms, the six-episode series uses self-shot footage alongside crew footage to offer an intimate, behind-the-scenes look at the athletes’ lives—home, relationships, sacrifices, upbringing—and their fight for equal pay and recognition amid professional double standards. Fullscreen head of production Ashley Kaplan says the series follows these women as they make history both on the pitch and in their broader campaign for equality. A poignant moment captured in the series shows Solo’s stunned, emotional reaction when informed of a six-month suspension and contract termination by U.S. Soccer after she criticized Sweden following the Americans’ Olympic elimination. The clip, described as difficult to watch, features Solo confronting the possibility that her 17-year national-team career may be over; her episode of Keeping Score airs September 2.

NOAA announced it has likely located the wreck of the Civil War–era sidewheel steamer Planter, the vessel famously seized in a daring 1862 escape by Robert Smalls and other enslaved crewmen. Smalls, then a wheelsman aboard the Confederate transport, organized a covert plan and on May 12, 1862 piloted the Planter out of Charleston Harbor—using the ship’s whistle and a raised white flag to pass Confederate checkpoints—and surrendered it to Union blockaders. The exploit made Smalls a Northern cause célèbre; he served as pilot for the Union, recruited Black soldiers, became the first African-American ship captain in the U.S. military and later served in Congress. After the war the Planter returned to civilian service until it sprang a leak while towing a grounded schooner at Cape Romain in March 1876, was beached and lost in a storm. NOAA’s Maritime Heritage Program reviewed historical accounts and charts, then used magnetometer and probing surveys to detect concentrated iron consistent with a buried hull under 10–15 feet of sand and water off Cape Romain. The site lies within an ecologically sensitive turtle breeding area, so excavation is uncertain; NOAA plans interpretive efforts to highlight the Planter’s legacy.

Jose Flores, one of Pennsylvania’s most accomplished jockeys, died Thursday at 12:42 p.m., three days after a violent racing accident at Parx Racing in Bensalem. The 56-year-old was riding Love Rules, a 14-1 shot he had recently beaten by four lengths, in the ninth race Monday when the horse went down without warning. Flores was thrown and struck the ground headfirst, suffering massive cranial trauma and spinal injuries; he was placed on life support at Aria Frankford Torresdale Hospital before being removed Thursday.

A native of a career that began in 1987, Flores compiled 4,650 victories and his mounts earned more than $64 million across nearly 29,000 starts, making him the top career earner at Parx (formerly Philadelphia Park). Longtime agent Dave Yanuzzi and trainer Scott Lake, who knew Flores for decades, praised him as a consummate professional who loved racing and would likely have reached 5,000 wins if not for several serious injuries in recent years. The Jockeys’ Guild noted Flores as the 157th jockey to die in a racing accident in unofficial records since 1940 and said no prior fatality had been recorded at a Pennsylvania track. Parx canceled the Tuesday card, expressed condolences to his family, and planned to resume racing Saturday. Flores is survived by his wife and three sons.

Former WWE performer Brian Christopher Lawler, known in-ring as Grandmaster Sexay of the Too Cool tag team, died Sunday at 46 after an apparent suicide attempt in a Tennessee jail. Corrections officers found Lawler hanging in his Hardeman County cell on Saturday; they administered CPR until paramedics arrived and he was taken to Regional One Medical Center in Memphis, where he died Sunday afternoon. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation is probing the incident. Lawler had been arrested July 7 on charges including DUI and evading police; bail was set at $40,000. Earlier incidents included an arrest in June over an unpaid hotel bill and an earlier altercation that led to hospitalization. Hardeman County officials said Lawler was placed alone in a cell due to his notoriety and was not on suicide watch because there had been no prior indication he was suicidal.

During WWE’s Attitude Era, Lawler rose to prominence as Grandmaster Sexay alongside Scotty 2 Hotty; the duo, later joined by Rikishi, became famous for hip-hop–inspired post-match dance routines and captured the WWE Tag Team Championship in 2000 by defeating Edge and Christian. After WWE stints (1997–2001), he appeared in TNA and later on the independent circuit, briefly reuniting with Too Cool in 2014.

WWE expressed condolences to Lawler’s family, friends and fans. His death came the same day WWE announced the passing of Hall of Famer Nikolai Volkoff (Josip Peruzovic), 70, and the wrestling community reacted with tributes and remembrances across social media for all three departed performers.

Tesla sales in Hong Kong effectively stalled after the government slashed electric vehicle (EV) tax incentives on April 1. Official transport department data showed zero newly purchased Tesla models were registered in April. The government capped the tax waiver for private EVs at HK$97,500 (about $12,500) and limited it to first-time owners; the change is expected to last until March next year. That regulatory shift triggered a surge of purchases in March—2,939 first-time Tesla registrations, roughly five times February’s level—as buyers rushed to beat the deadline. With the new policy, prices jumped: a Tesla Model S now costs HK$925,500 ($118,400), up from HK$570,000 ($72,900), removing much of its price advantage versus luxury rivals like Mercedes-Benz. While first-time registrations are not identical to sales, they are a close proxy because vehicles must be registered to operate in Hong Kong. Hong Kong had 11,004 EVs in use as of May, including private and public vehicles. Tesla responded that its business does not “rely on” government policy and expects Hong Kong demand to remain strong despite an immediate post-policy dip. As Hong Kong cools, Tesla is focusing on mainland China—where 2016 saw 352,000 new EV registrations and where local manufacturing could avoid import duties up to 50%.

Malcolm Gladwell argued in The New Yorker that social media can’t replace traditional activism, prompting rebuttals from Twitter founders Ev Williams and Biz Stone who said platforms are tools that complement real-world action. The debate gained focus when Gap proposed a new logo and—after harsh criticism across Twitter and Facebook—reversed the change, abandoning crowdsourcing. Critics mocked the minimalist redesign; Gap admitted it mishandled engagement and retreated to the classic blue-box identity. The episode reinforced the view that social media can swiftly amplify public opinion and influence corporate decisions, without claiming that tweeting alone constitutes activism. Observers noted Gladwell was opposing a straw-man position few actually hold.

O.J. Simpson was banned from the Cosmopolitan Hotel in Las Vegas after an incident late Wednesday night that outlets described as involving drunken, disruptive behavior. Multiple reports said Simpson had been at the hotel’s Clique bar around 10:40 p.m.; security removed him after staff alleged he became belligerent, was angry with employees and that glasses were broken. TMZ published audio suggesting staff alerted police about a “drunk and disorderly” guest identified as Simpson, though Las Vegas police treated it as a private-property matter and did not open a criminal investigation. The hotel issued a trespass notice, barring Simpson from returning.

Simpson’s attorney, Malcolm LaVergne, strongly disputed claims that Simpson was intoxicated or belligerent. LaVergne said Simpson is a social drinker who had gone to the Cosmopolitan to eat and left quietly after being told he was trespassed; he also said there is no video showing broken glass or yelling. He noted the hotel has the legal right to ban anyone and challenged anyone with proof of drunken behavior to come forward, adding he will inform Simpson’s parole officer. Simpson, recently released from prison after a 10-year sentence for kidnapping and burglary, is permitted under parole to drink but not to the point of registering a blood-alcohol level above .08. No arrests were reported.

A violent spring storm system swept the Midwest, producing at least 17 reported tornadoes, deadly flooding and widespread damage across Oklahoma, Missouri and Illinois. Oklahoma was hardest hit: Friday’s twisters killed nine people in the Oklahoma City metro (including a mother and child), injured dozens, flooded streets with up to eight inches of rain, knocked out power to tens of thousands, and damaged homes, businesses and Will Rogers World Airport. El Reno and Moore suffered heavy destruction and renewed trauma for residents still recovering from a recent EF5 tornado. Missouri saw significant tornado paths and flooding that drowned three people; in Illinois a gym and dozens of homes were damaged. Emergency crews conducted storm surveys to confirm intensities and assess damage.

Republican nominee Donald Trump made a surprise visit to Mexico City to meet President Enrique Peña Nieto, marking his first foreign trip as the party’s nominee and stirring protests and sharp debate. The closed-door meeting and subsequent joint statements were framed as “open and constructive” by Peña Nieto, who stressed shared interests, trade ties that support millions of jobs on both sides, and urged respect for Mexicans and Mexican-Americans. Peña Nieto challenged Trump’s portrayal of border problems, noting illegal immigration has decreased and highlighting the flow of weapons and cash into Mexico from the U.S. as fueling violence.

Trump tempered his earlier hard-line rhetoric in public remarks, speaking diplomatically about cooperation and declaring each nation’s right to build border barriers while sidestepping his signature campaign pledge that Mexico would pay for a U.S. wall. He said financing “didn’t come up,” calling talks preliminary. The visit preceded a major immigration speech Trump planned in Phoenix, where observers expected him to clarify or possibly soften prior positions such as mass deportations.

Reactions were polarized: some Republicans called the trip a short-term win, while Democrats, including Hillary Clinton, criticized it as inadequate to atone for a year of insults and questioned Trump’s consistency. In Mexico, many rejected the visit—protests erupted and former presidents and public figures condemned it—while Peña Nieto maintained an official posture of constructive engagement despite domestic pressure and prior comparisons of Trump to authoritarian figures.

During the 2016 presidential campaign and after Donald Trump’s victory, a long list of celebrities publicly vowed—half-jokingly or seriously—that they would leave the United States if Trump became president. Outrage, disbelief and satirical hyperbole fueled these declarations, with destinations ranging from Canada and Europe to Africa, Iceland, Jupiter or even another planet.

High-profile entertainers publicly threatening to relocate included Lena Dunham (eyeing Vancouver), Chelsea Handler (Spain), Jon Stewart (joking about leaving the planet), Miley Cyrus, Neve Campbell (returning to Canada), Cher (Jupiter), Samuel L. Jackson (South Africa), Raven-Symoné (already bought a ticket to Canada), Whoopi Goldberg, George Lopez, Amy Schumer (Spain), Bryan Cranston, Spike Lee, Barbra Streisand (Australia or Canada), and Natasha Lyonne. Comedian Jenny Slate and others expressed disbelief with colorful language. Activists and commentators such as Rev. Al Sharpton also said they were “reserving” tickets out of the country if Trump won. Porn publisher Larry Flynt—an outspoken Clinton supporter—said Trump “nauseates” him and that he might move to Canada.

The phenomenon spawned online campaigns and communities encouraging migration: a Cape Breton, Nova Scotia website (cbiftrumpwins.com) drew attention as a suggested refuge, touting affordable housing and scenic life. Trump’s family and supporters derided the threats—Donald Trump Jr. quipped on Fox that he’d buy their airfare, framing departures as endorsements. After Trump’s upset victory, many celebrities expressed dismay on social media; some reiterated relocation threats, while others vented in satirical or rhetorical terms. The episode highlighted celebrity political engagement, performative protest, and the cultural polarization surrounding the 2016 election.

A new drug, nalmefene (Selincro), is now available on the NHS for people who regularly drink at least about half a bottle of wine or three pints a night (roughly 7.5 units a day for men, 5 units for women). Recommended by NICE for use alongside psychosocial support and counselling, nalmefene is intended to help people gradually reduce alcohol intake by lowering the urge to drink; it is not aimed at those who need immediate abstinence for severe dependence. The pill can be taken once daily when needed, costs about £3 per day (roughly £42.42 for a 14-tablet pack), and aims to support people who may not see themselves as alcoholics but drink above low-risk limits. NICE expects up to 35,000 people to receive nalmefene in the first year, based on estimates of those receiving psychosocial interventions, though early Scotland figures suggest actual uptake may be far lower. Experts stress it should follow attempts to cut down and brief counselling; risks begin below the levels for prescription, and the drug is for those with established patterns that make self-control difficult.

Thousands of Arizona voters faced hours-long waits during the March 22 presidential primary after Maricopa County sharply reduced polling places. The county, which had 200 polling sites in 2012 and 400 in 2008, operated just 60 this year, citing budget cuts and an expectation many would vote by mail. The Associated Press obtained Maricopa County records showing 20 of those 60 sites were still processing voters at 10 p.m. or later; five locations remained open past midnight and one site logged its last ballot at 12:58 a.m., meaning some voters waited nearly six hours. Anecdotes included 25-year-old Gustavo Mendez, who waited four hours and left as poll workers brought pizza to those still in line. The long waits occurred at churches, rec centers and other polling places across the Phoenix area, disproportionately concentrated in Phoenix and western suburbs.

The U.S. Department of Justice has opened an inquiry into whether the staffing and site reductions violated voting rights protections, requesting documents about how polling-place numbers were determined and whether impacts on minority voters were considered. Phoenix’s mayor filed a complaint asserting disproportionate effects on minorities. Arizona Secretary of State Michele Reagan certified the statewide primary results—Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump won their parties—while acknowledging problems such as voters incorrectly left off rolls. Certification begins a five-day window for legal challenges; Sanders’ campaign is weighing whether to contest delegate allocations, arguing provisional ballots were improperly discarded. The episode has prompted calls to reevaluate how future elections are run amid reduced federal preclearance requirements.

Sunland Inc., a New Mexico peanut-processing company once linked to a 2012 salmonella outbreak, is at the center of two unfolding bankruptcy-related developments: the destruction of nearly a million jars of peanut butter and an unexpected late bid for its shuttered Portales plant.

Trustee Clarke Coll arranged disposal of about 950,000 jars—roughly 25 tons—of Sunland-branded and contract peanut butter valued at an estimated $2.6 million by hauling them to the Curry County landfill in Clovis at a cost of about $60,000. The product, made with $2.8 million of Valencia peanuts owned by Costco, had been stored since Sunland ceased operations and filed for Chapter 7 liquidation last October. Although court records and Coll state that health and safety testing found no contamination, Costco rejected received shipments as “not merchantable” due to leaky peanut oil and declined offers to take, repurpose, donate, or sell the product to institutional brokers. Roadrunner Food Bank noted its heavy reliance on rescued food but did not comment directly on this case.

Separately, bidding for Sunland’s assets was reopened after Golden Boy Foods of British Columbia made a last-minute $25 million offer—$5 million above the high bid made at a prior auction by Hampton Farms. U.S. Bankruptcy Court Judge David Thuma allowed the reopening, citing the additional funds’ potential to better satisfy Sunland’s creditors, which include about $21 million in secured debt plus significant unsecured claims. Golden Boy had previously expressed interest in Sunland, and both Golden Boy and Hampton Farms say they would restart manufacturing at the Portales facility. The renewed auction and a subsequent hearing will determine final approval of the sale, as creditors and bidders weigh maximizing recoveries against preserving the integrity of judicial auction results.

In 2018 MaineDOT invited the public to submit short, safety-themed messages for the agency’s humorous changeable highway signs through the “My Maine Sign” contest. Launched after the DOT began using witty messages in winter 2016, the signs aim to discourage unsafe behaviors—distracted or impaired driving, speeding, failing to buckle up, and other hazards—by mixing safety reminders with Maine-flavored humor and holiday or event references. The submission period closed March 18 with more than 2,000 entries. DOT staff selected finalists, and the public voted online to pick grand-prize winners in two sign-size categories. Finalists earned transportation-related prizes such as a ride to the Penobscot Narrows Bridge & Observatory, Maine State Ferry tickets, or a state parks vehicle pass; grand-prize winners received a personalized street sign from the state sign shop. The DOT will also archive standout entries for future use on signs, ensuring more community-submitted messages may appear later. Winning messages announced in May included small-sign winners “Put Down UR Cell — Or You May End Up In One,” “Spend Money On Lobstahs — Not Speeding Tickets,” and “Little Known Fact — Snow Is Really Slippery,” plus large-sign winners promoting seatbelts, moose awareness, and Maine accent humor.

Police on Mackinac Island are investigating an alleged barroom assault between aides for Republican presidential contenders Rand Paul and Marco Rubio during the Mackinac Republican Leadership Conference. John Yob, national political director and Michigan strategist for the Paul campaign, posted that Rich Beeson, Rubio’s deputy campaign manager, punched him at Horn’s Bar early Friday. Yob said he has video of the incident and later provided footage to CNN; police and the prosecutor are reviewing that evidence and witness statements. Mackinac Island Police Chief Brett Riccinto said a formal report was forwarded to the county prosecutor, who will decide on criminal charges. The grainy video appears to show a physical altercation, but CNN could not independently confirm the identities involved, and Beeson did not respond to requests for comment.

The Federal Reserve left policy unchanged Wednesday, keeping its benchmark rate near zero and maintaining existing bond-buying programs, but signaled readiness to act if labor market conditions don’t improve. In a firmer-than-before statement, the Fed said recent growth has slowed and is likely to remain moderate, so unemployment is expected to decline only slowly. Officials deferred new measures until at least the mid-September meeting, awaiting incoming data on job growth for July and August. The FOMC vote was 11–1, with Richmond Fed President Jeffrey Lacker dissenting. Markets reacted negatively, with major indexes slipping.
