Economists remain divided: some expect a new asset-purchase program in September if weakness persists, while others caution the Fed’s tools are limited and argue further stimulus may be unnecessary. Chairman Ben Bernanke will outline views at Jackson Hole in late August.

Britain sent an RAF flight to Cyprus carrying one million euros as an emergency contingency to lend to around 3,000 British service personnel and 500 civilian staff if Cypriot banks and ATMs stop dispensing cash amid a controversial bailout levy. The Ministry of Defence is offering to pay March and future salaries into UK accounts and says it will fully compensate any losses to military or government staff caused by the levy. The move follows UK ministers’ assurances and Cabinet backing for full compensation. Cyprus’s proposed bailout—aimed at rescuing troubled banks by levying deposits—sparked domestic and international alarm, fears of capital flight, and warnings it undermines confidence in eurozone banking.

A large community-based study led by UCSF cardiologist Dr. Gregory Marcus found that regular consumption of caffeinated products—specifically coffee, tea and chocolate—was not associated with increased premature heartbeats (premature atrial contractions, PACs, or premature ventricular contractions, PVCs). The analysis included 1,388 participants (mean age 72) drawn from the NHLBI Cardiovascular Health Study; about 60–61% reported daily consumption of at least one caffeinated product. Subjects completed a food-frequency assessment and underwent 24-hour ambulatory electrocardiography. Researchers detected no differences in PACs or PVCs per hour across levels of intake, and more frequent consumption did not correlate with extra heartbeats. The authors caution they cannot define a safe daily amount from these data and did not assess very high-caffeine energy drinks or whether people who felt symptoms had already reduced intake. The findings challenge long-standing clinical guidance that recommends eliminating caffeine to prevent arrhythmias and suggest such advice may unnecessarily discourage items that have been linked to cardiovascular benefits—lower risks of type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, and reduced cardiovascular and all-cause mortality in observational studies. The team notes that acute effects of caffeinated products remain to be studied and reiterates that very high doses of caffeine (e.g., powdered caffeine) can be dangerous and that children should limit intake.

German prosecutors have indicted two nonagenarian former SS guards who served at the Stutthof concentration camp near present-day Gdansk on charges of being accessories to murder. The men—aged 93 and 92 and living in Borken and Wuppertal—were charged last week in the Muenster state court for their roles as guards who oversaw inmates and those taken out to forced labor between 1942 and 1945. Prosecutors say hundreds of killings occurred while the men served at Stutthof, where about 65,000 people died from gassing, shootings, injections and exposure. Evidence cited includes mass killings in gas chambers in 1944, shootings of Jews between June 1944 and April 1945, and lethal injections of phenol and gasoline administered by camp medical staff from 1942 to 1944. The court asserted the defendants must have been aware of the systematic murders and willingly supported them by performing guard duties. Both defendants deny knowledge of killings. The indictments were enabled by evolving German legal reasoning since 2011 that permits prosecuting camp personnel as accomplices even without proof of specific individual murders. The case was advanced with help from Minnesota FBI agents and Stutthof survivor Judith “Judy” Meisel, who identified one defendant from camp-era photos. Meisel, now 88, may join as a co-plaintiff and hopes the prosecution yields answers and justice while also bearing emotional cost.

Police in Italy say they have deciphered a mysterious coded text believed to describe a clandestine oath-taking ritual used by the 'Ndrangheta, the powerful mafia network from Calabria. Discovered during a probe into a high-profile Rome murder in January last year, the three handwritten sheets were found with weapons and ammunition. Investigators say the script was written in a special alphabet devised by the gang and had never before been encountered in Rome. Two police officers with a penchant for crosswords spent weeks cracking the code; the characters reportedly resembled a mix of Arabic, Cyrillic and Chinese-style glyphs. According to Renato Cortese, head of the Rome rapid response team, the document contains the verbal formula a recruit must recite to join the San Luca clan and is rich in symbolism relating to the quasi-mystical initiation ceremony. The translated passages describe how to recognize a mafioso — a “Man of Honour” — by the signs around him. The find underlines that despite its global criminal business and modern trafficking operations, the 'Ndrangheta still uses archaic, ritualized practices. The group is now considered Italy’s most powerful mafia and a major European cocaine trafficker.

A fire aboard an empty Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 787 at London Heathrow forced temporary runway closures and reignited concerns about the Dreamliner’s troubled lithium-ion batteries. The parked jet, “Queen of Sheba,” showed scorching near the fuselage and was doused with fire-retardant foam; no passengers were aboard and the blaze is being treated as unexplained. Heathrow reopened after about 90 minutes; the Air Accidents Investigation Branch and British police are investigating, and Boeing has staff on site. The incident came after a January global grounding of 50 Dreamliners over battery fires; regulators approved redesigned, cooler-running batteries in stainless steel enclosures and flights resumed in April. Boeing shares fell roughly 6–7 percent on the news. Another 787 from Thomson returned to Manchester as a precaution.

On the evening of June 17, 2015, a young white man walked into a Bible study at Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church, a historic Black congregation in downtown Charleston, South Carolina, and opened fire, killing nine people and wounding survivors. The shooter, later identified as 21-year-old Dylann Storm Roof, sat with the group for roughly 40–50 minutes before rising and firing, reportedly making remarks that revealed racial animus. He allowed at least one survivor to live so she could tell what happened; other survivors hid or played dead. Authorities treated the attack as a hate crime and launched a massive, multi-agency manhunt that culminated in Roof’s arrest the next morning in Shelby, North Carolina, after a motorist recognized his car from distributed images. He waived extradition and was returned to Charleston to face charges.

The nine victims ranged in age from 26 to 87 and included clergy and longtime community servants: the church’s primary pastor and state senator, Rev. Clementa Pinckney, 41; Cynthia Hurd, 54, a regional library manager; Sharonda Coleman-Singleton, 45, a pastor and school speech therapist and coach; Tywanza Sanders, 26, an Allen University graduate; Ethel Lance, 70, a retired Gailliard Center employee and church janitor; Susie Jackson, 87, a longtime member and cousin of Lance; DePayne Middleton-Doctor, 49, a retired community development director who had recently become a pastor; Myra Thompson, 59, a pastor; and Daniel Simmons Sr., 74, who died in surgery. The losses devastated the congregation, the Charleston community and the nation.

The massacre reopened painful historical wounds and prompted widespread grief and condemnation. Emanuel AME, founded in the early 19th century and known as “Mother Emanuel,” has a storied past tied to African-American resistance and worship; one early member, Denmark Vesey, led a planned slave rebellion in 1822, and the church was burned and driven underground in the aftermath. Leaders from local activists and city officials to President Barack Obama, Vice President Joe Biden, U.S. Attorney General Loretta Lynch and South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley publicly mourned, called for healing, and emphasized that racially motivated violence has no place in American society.

The shooting intensified national conversations about race, public safety and gun policy. The FBI opened a civil rights investigation alongside local and federal law enforcement, and the attack heightened concerns already inflamed earlier that month by the April 4 killing of Walter Scott, a Black man shot by a white police officer in North Charleston—an incident that was itself under federal review. In Charleston, vigils and prayer gatherings drew hundreds, while other downtown AME sites received bomb threats, adding anxiety to the community’s mourning. Officials vowed to pursue justice and to support healing in a city grappling with history and loss.

Bryshon Nellum, an Olympic silver medalist who survived being shot in the legs in 2008 and was told he might never again be elite, will carry the U.S. flag at Sunday’s London closing ceremony after helping the U.S. men’s 4x400 relay win silver and reaching the 400m semifinals. Chosen by teammates, Nellum was praised as embodying the Olympic spirit.

The United States surged late in track and field to overtake China in the medal standings and is poised to finish atop the overall and gold tallies. Through Friday the U.S. led China 94–81 in total medals and 41–37 in golds, boosted by standout performances including Ashton Eaton and Trey Hardee’s decathlon 1–2, Christian Taylor’s triple jump gold, the women’s 4x100 world-beating relay, and Jordan Burroughs’ wrestling gold. USA Track & Field’s ambitious 30-medal target looks likely to be met or exceeded.

Elsewhere, Britain enjoyed a home boost with its best haul in over a century, while Russia underperformed and South Korea rose impressively. Highlights included Meseret Defar’s 5,000m gold, Renaud Lavillenie’s Olympic pole vault record, Oscar Pistorius’ 4x400 appearance, and varied sailing and BMX winners. The medals race remains unofficial but has dominated coverage.

President Trump’s nominee for Navy secretary, Philip Bilden, withdrew from consideration, saying compliance with federal ethics rules would force “undue disruption and materially adverse divestment” of his family’s private financial interests. Bilden, a former Army Reserve intelligence officer who built HarbourVest’s Hong Kong operations and recently retired after 25 years, informed Defense Secretary Jim Mattis of his decision a month after his nomination. The withdrawal follows a pattern among several of Trump’s preferred candidates who are wealthy businesspeople struggling to separate substantial private holdings from public service; earlier this month Vincent Viola, nominated for Army secretary, similarly stepped aside for difficulty disentangling his business interests. The Pentagon had tried to counter press reports that Bilden might withdraw, and Mattis had expressed confidence in him as a leader to rebuild the Navy and Marine Corps. Bilden said he supports the president’s agenda but declined to pursue confirmation because meeting Office of Government Ethics requirements would require unacceptable personal and family financial sacrifice; he did not provide further detail. Mattis said he will recommend a new nominee to the president in the coming days. The developments underscore ethical and financial hurdles facing business leaders entering high government posts.

A chance meeting in a Memphis Kroger has set off an outpouring of community support for 15–16-year-old Chauncy Jones Black and his disabled mother. Chauncy approached shopper Matt White asking to help carry groceries in exchange for a box of doughnuts. Moved by the teen’s shame, hunger and determination, White took him on a grocery run, learned Chauncy is a straight-A student who wants to work to help his mother, and drove him home. What White found in their house was bleak: an empty refrigerator, almost no possessions beyond a couch and a few lamps, no beds—only sleeping pads on the floor—and no air conditioning. The mother had recently been robbed of most belongings, leaving them with virtually nothing.

White’s Facebook post about the encounter went viral, prompting him to create a GoFundMe initially aimed at raising $250 to buy Chauncy a push mower so he could start mowing lawns and earn income while he gets an ID to apply for regular work. Donations and offers of help snowballed far beyond that modest goal: within days tens of thousands of dollars were raised, and the campaign rapidly expanded to cover immediate needs and longer-term goals. Organizers are collecting clothing (Chauncy: pants size approx. 16–18, small shirts, shoes 8½; mother: pants 12, medium shirts, women’s shoes 8½), bedding, furniture, small household electronics like CD players or speakers, and job or mentoring opportunities. White has been coordinating pickup and delivery of donations and offering to transport Chauncy to work or church; the pair attend Hope Presbyterian. Donors have discussed helping the family move to safer housing and even find a home of their own. What began as a simple act of kindness—donuts for help with groceries—has grown into a broad community effort to restore stability, opportunity and hope to Chauncy and his mother.

Lady Gaga’s Born This Way sold 1.108 million U.S. copies in its first week, including a record 662,000 digital downloads, illustrating how albums remain central marketing anchors even as recorded-music revenue shrinks relative to touring, endorsements and merchandise. Interscope and manager Troy Carter executed a blockbuster-style, six-month campaign timed around televised events and retail tie-ins to make Gaga ubiquitous. However, Amazon’s two-day 99-cent digital sale — intended to promote its Cloud Drive — drove roughly 440,000 downloads, helping the album eclipse a million sales while angering physical retailers and prompting debate about music’s value. Amazon reportedly paid full wholesale to Universal and absorbed a multi-million-dollar loss. Despite the controversy, the campaign’s momentum continues as Gaga leverages the album to fuel broader revenue streams.

Hispanic leaders and immigrant advocates are scrambling to calm widespread fear as federal authorities begin enforcing President Trump’s expanded immigration orders. The high-profile deportation of Arizona resident Guadalupe Garcia de Rayos — a working mother with U.S. citizen children who had previously been exempted under Obama-era priorities — intensified concerns that the administration will pursue broad removals rather than only dangerous criminals. Although Trump campaigned on deporting criminals, his executive orders redefined “criminal alien” to include many misdemeanors and immigration violations and broadened deportation priorities, prompting estimates that millions more could be targeted.

Community groups have mounted know-your-rights trainings, legal hotlines and outreach, but admit they cannot fully reassure mixed-status families who now face raids, workplace and home arrests, and alleged denial of lawyer access. ICE reported large operations in multiple states, saying most arrests involved people with criminal convictions; advocates counter that many detained had no criminal records and that tactics — including daytime actions and alleged checkpoints — are sowing terror and may be retaliatory toward sanctuary jurisdictions.

Legal experts warn that structural incentives within ICE and CBP, fewer immigration judges, and use of expedited removal increase the risk of indiscriminate enforcement and due-process shortcuts. Organizers say aggressive targeting drives immigrants into hiding, undermines trust in law enforcement, disrupts communities and diverts resources from identifying real public-safety threats. Activists are planning protests and legal responses while media and town halls seek to inform terrified families about their rights.

Researchers at the MRC Toxicology Unit (University of Leicester) published a study in Science Translational Medicine showing an orally delivered compound can halt neurodegeneration in mice by blocking a harmful cellular response to misfolded proteins. Many brain diseases—including prion disease, Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s—feature accumulations of misfolded proteins that trigger an overactive protective mechanism, shutting down protein synthesis and leaving neurons unprotected. The compound inhibits the enzyme PERK, restoring protein production, protecting neurons, preventing memory loss and improving behaviour in mice with experimentally induced prion disease. Treated animals also lived longer than untreated controls. Significant side effects were observed—weight loss and mild diabetes from pancreatic damage—so further drug development will be needed to separate neuroprotection from peripheral toxicity. Scientists hailed the result as an important proof of principle and a potential new pathway for treatments that target the cellular response rather than the misfolded proteins themselves, but cautioned human relevance is unproven and translation typically takes decades. Experts recommend replication, testing in models of Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s, and safety optimization before clinical trials can be considered. The work is an encouraging step toward oral therapies for neurodegeneration.

Maple Match is a new dating site created to connect Americans and Canadians who want a romantic route to relocating amid anxiety over Donald Trump’s rise as the likely Republican nominee. Launched earlier in 2016 by CEO Joe Goldman, the site’s slogan, “Making dating great again,” and tongue-in-cheek promise to “save [users] from the unfathomable horror of a Trump presidency” grabbed attention as searches and interest in moving to Canada spiked after Trump’s primary wins. Goldman insists the concept is real and not a political operation—just a response to user frustration with existing dating platforms and genuine demand: the site reportedly had tens of thousands of hits and thousands of signups within days, though it was initially operating with a waiting list and hadn’t made matches yet. Users join by indicating citizenship, preferences and basic details, playfully clicking a “save me from this madness” button. Goldman emphasizes that the service is about building meaningful relationships across the border and believes love can overcome obstacles like immigration. Media coverage framed Maple Match as a novelty grounded in real migration interest, blending humor with earnest plans to launch fully as soon as possible.

A THR analysis reveals extreme pay disparities in Hollywood. Robert Downey Jr. reportedly earned $75 million for Iron Man thanks to a 7% gross stake; he also earns big from endorsements. Leonardo DiCaprio made over $25 million for The Wolf of Wall Street while Jonah Hill took a $60,000 minimum, a 416-fold gap. Jennifer Lawrence earns roughly $35 million versus Jennifer Aniston’s $15 million. Endorsements and TV hosting pay huge sums—Ashton Kutcher reportedly $750,000 per episode, Alex Trebek $10 million annually, Jon Stewart $25–30 million. Extras and most actors earn little; SAG shows average member income around $52,000, with many earning under $1,000 from acting. Unusual payouts include Crystal the monkey’s $108,000 for nine episodes. Reality stars can be outliers, with Kardashians and Duck Dynasty far above typical reality pay.

A Republican amendment from Rep. Ron DeSantis (R‑Fla.) would sharply limit Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s Russia probe by cutting funding 180 days after the amendment’s enactment and barring investigation of “matters occurring before June 2015” (the month Donald Trump announced his presidential campaign). Submitted as one of many amendments to an omnibus spending bill to be considered after congressional recess, the proposal seeks to curtail Mueller’s May appointment to investigate Russian election interference and any ties between Moscow and Trump campaign associates. Its inclusion in the final bill, and survival in the Senate, is uncertain.

Separately, federal investigators working for Mueller are focusing on President Trump’s involvement in drafting the initial public response to The New York Times’ report about a June 2016 Trump Tower meeting attended by Donald Trump Jr., Paul Manafort, and Jared Kushner with Russian lawyer Natalia Veselnitskaya and former Soviet officer Rinat Akhmetshin. Prosecutors want to know what Trump knew about the meeting and whether he sought to conceal its purpose. The White House has acknowledged Trump “weighed in” on the response drafted aboard Air Force One; reports say he may have “dictated” it. The original statement described the meeting as an adoption-related “introductory” discussion, but follow-up emails and statements showed the meeting was arranged to offer damaging information about Hillary Clinton. Mueller’s team is examining whether the president’s public statement was knowingly false; White House attorney Ty Cobb says the statement was not untruthful and that the president’s role was minimal.

The Great Bear Rainforest, a remote Canadian wilderness the size of Switzerland, is home to the rare spirit bear—black bears with a white coat due to a genetic trait—with fewer than 500 believed to remain. The region teems with wildlife, including whales, wolves, eagles and abundant marine life. Conservationists and First Nations, who regard the spirit bear as sacred, are fighting plans for a massive Alberta-to-British Columbia oil pipeline and supertanker traffic that would threaten the coast. To raise awareness, conservation groups recruited the International League of Conservation Photographers—specialized landscape, wildlife and underwater photographers—to document the area’s richness and fragility. Photographers endured long waits and harsh conditions to capture the elusive spirit bears and vibrant ecosystems. Pipeline proponents argue risks are minimal and tout job benefits, but critics point to past spills from the company involved and worry for fisheries and traditional lifeways. Guided by Gitga’at tracker Marven Robinson, the team experienced the forest’s hush, signs of bears and, finally, the haunting sight of a spirit bear slipping back into the trees.

A major international study projects that Antarctica’s roughly 600,000 emperor penguins will decline substantially this century as sea ice—their essential breeding platform—becomes less reliable. Using long-term data from a 50-year study at Terre Adélie and IPCC climate-model projections of sea-ice concentration, researchers modeled trends across all 45 known colonies. They found a continent-wide reduction of at least 19 percent by 2100, with two-thirds of colonies falling by more than half; all colonies are expected to be in decline by century’s end. Short-term increases in some sites may occur by 2050, but these are temporary. The species’ dependence on a “Goldilocks” sea-ice balance is critical: excessive ice forces parents to travel farther to forage, while too little ice reduces krill habitat and leaves colonies vulnerable to wave-driven collapse. The team concludes emperor penguins meet criteria for endangered status due to climate change and urges protections—such as marine reserves in the Ross Sea and East Antarctica—to safeguard refuges and reduce other pressures like fisheries. Authors emphasize that listing could enable conservation measures and management tools, and that focused strategies in likely refuges (notably the Ross Sea) are needed to slow projected declines driven by warming and changing sea-ice dynamics.

Fierce fighting erupted in Malakal, the main town of Upper Nile state, as South Sudan’s conflict entered its second month. The army reported heavy street battles, including tank engagements, while rebels said they had recaptured the town; both sides claimed control. Malakal, a gateway to northern oilfields, has changed hands multiple times since clashes began on December 15 between forces loyal to President Salva Kiir (Dinka) and fighters backing ex-vice president Riek Machar (Nuer). The violence has prompted massive displacement and civilian deaths: UN figures report roughly 350,000–400,000 people displaced, with aid groups and analysts estimating up to 10,000 killed; separate accounts cite more than 1,000 dead early on. A ferry overloaded with fleeing civilians capsized near Malakal, drowning between 200 and 300 people, many women and children. Government forces also say they are advancing on Bor in Jonglei state. Regional mediators from IGAD are hosting talks in Addis Ababa but stalled over key issues such as a formal ceasefire and the release of detained political leaders.

Just weeks after Endemol Shine North America announced plans to develop a television series based on Tejano star Selena’s romance with husband Chris Perez, Selena’s father, Abraham Quintanilla Jr., sued Endemol and Perez in Texas to halt the project. Endemol had signed a deal with Perez earlier this year to adapt his 2012 memoir, To Selena With Love, which recounts their relationship from his perspective. The suit contends Perez breached a 1995 Estate Properties Agreement he signed two months after Selena’s murder, under which Quintanilla Jr. allegedly obtained exclusive, worldwide, perpetual rights to all “Entertainment Properties” — including rights to her name, image, voice, signature, photographs, trademarks, copyrights, publicity, contracts and related income. The complaint asserts Perez agreed to receive 25% of net profits from exploitation of those properties and thus lacks authority to publish materials or license adaptations independently. Because Perez’s book uses Selena’s photo and was published without estate authorization, the estate labels it “unauthorized.” The Quintanilla estate seeks a judicial declaration that Perez and Endemol have no rights to exploit Selena’s likeness or proceed with the television series and asks the court to stop production.

The article criticizes The New York Review of Books’ decision to publish an essay by Jian Ghomeshi and the ensuing fallout that led to Ian Buruma’s departure as editor. It argues the piece should have acknowledged the seriousness and number of allegations against Ghomeshi: after his October 2014 firing from the CBC—following evidence he had physically harmed a woman—more than twenty women accused him of sexual abuse and harassment, including hitting, biting, choking, and verbal abuse. Ghomeshi was charged in November 2014 with sexual assault relating to three women, faced additional counts in January 2015, was acquitted of the courtroom charges in March 2016, and later resolved a separate workplace allegation with a peace bond and apology. Many allegations appeared in respected outlets such as The Toronto Star. Buruma defended publishing Ghomeshi’s first-person piece, claiming it offered a “nuanced” view and that he wanted debate about how to treat accused men not convicted in court, but staff objections and advertiser pressure followed. Critics said the essay was unchallenged, self-serving, poorly fact-checked, and insensitive to the many accusers; social media outrage and threatened university-advertiser boycotts intensified the controversy. Buruma says he resigned under that pressure and denies being fired, while commentators call for greater transparency and for media to prioritize credibility and the perspectives of those disadvantaged by unequal power dynamics. The magazine added an editorial note clarifying details about the allegations and legal history.

In March 2016 Wikipedia outlinks were crawled across all 865 language wikis for the first time since earlier runs focused only on English; duplicate detection was disabled to keep the collection complete because sharing data with pointers to other collections would be complex. These crawl files are not currently publicly accessible.

Separately, a New York Times Book Review piece by historian Douglas Brinkley on Jodi Kantor’s The Obamas drew controversy for a single dismissive phrase—“call it chick nonfiction”—even though the review was largely positive. The phrase prompted criticism that the Times was perpetuating a double standard that diminishes women’s work and the seriousness of books about women, echoed by commentators like Jennifer Weiner, Rebecca Traister and Ezra Klein. Critics argued that labeling Kantor’s reporting as inherently unserious because it centers a woman author and a First Lady subject ignores the political substance: Kantor uncovered tensions involving Michelle Obama’s influence on policy and conflicts with aides over health care and immigration. Defenders noted Brinkley praised Kantor’s reporting skill, vivid prose, and revelatory anecdotes, yet repeatedly undercut that praise with suggestions the book leaned toward tabloid gossip. Traister emphasized Michelle Obama’s rare status as the president’s professional equal—which makes analyzing her role historically significant—and faulted the review for failing to take that dynamic seriously. The controversy highlights broader debates over gendered language in criticism and how coverage treats women authors and women-centered political narratives.

The New York Times reported that President Trump asked then-FBI Director James Comey in February to end the bureau’s investigation into former National Security Advisor Michael Flynn. Comey documented the encounter in a memo quoting Trump: “I hope you can see your way clear to letting this go, to letting Flynn go. He is a good guy. I hope you can let this go.” Comey reportedly has memos chronicling his interactions with Trump; House Oversight Chair Jason Chaffetz has requested them, and Democrats are suggesting the president’s request could amount to obstruction of justice.

Comey’s abrupt firing has become a major political distraction in Washington and is complicating Republicans’ legislative priorities. Senate Republicans began the week focused on overhauling Obamacare and on tax reform, but the controversy over the termination and new questions about the FBI’s probe of possible ties between the Trump campaign and Russia have pushed those issues off the front burner. Because a new FBI director must be confirmed by the Senate, Democrats are leveraging the process: several have said they will not consider a nominee until a special counsel is appointed to independently oversee the Russia investigation. Sen. Mark Warner explicitly advocated delaying confirmation until a special prosecutor is in place.

The firing intensified an already slow Senate calendar, which has been consumed by confirmations and regulatory rollbacks, and offered Democrats opportunities to slow legislative progress. Republicans maintain the episode won’t derail their agenda, arguing Democrats already oppose much of their program and that work on health care and tax reform can continue — some GOP senators insist the fallout won’t impede policy talks. Still, the incident has noticeably diverted attention, forced extra briefings and hearings, and heightened partisan mistrust, making it harder to advance major bills amid heightened scrutiny of the administration’s actions and motives.

Demi Moore has made a public return after a recent hospitalization and rehab stay, attending a Beverly Hills event for the launch of the TV show The Conversation, which she executive produced. Though she has separated from Ashton Kutcher, she has not filed for divorce; she’s back on Twitter using the handle @MrsKutcher and jokingly asked followers for suggestions if she changes her screen name. Moore posted a brief “Testing” tweet and a photo of herself resting in bed, marking her first activity since January 7. Meanwhile, Ashton Kutcher has been linked by reports to former That ’70s Show co-star Mila Kunis; they were seen dining together and reportedly went furniture shopping before returning to his Hollywood Hills home. Kunis will reunite with her old castmates for Fox’s 25th Anniversary Special on April 22.

Enfield police charged dentist Rashmi Patel with criminally negligent homicide and tampering with evidence after the death of 64-year-old patient Judith Gan, who stopped breathing while undergoing extensive dental work under conscious sedation. Patel, 45, surrendered to police on Feb. 17 — exactly one year after Gan died at Baystate Medical Center — posted $25,000 bail and is due in Enfield Superior Court on Feb. 24.

State Department of Public Health inspectors and the Connecticut Dental Commission reviewed the case and filed administrative charges alleging Patel failed to properly respond when Gan’s oxygen saturation and vital signs deteriorated during a full-mouth procedure that included plans to extract 20 teeth and place implants. According to reports, alarms signaled low oxygen repeatedly, Gan made gurgling sounds, and an assistant begged Patel to stop; one assistant reportedly ran to call 911 after the patient “flat-lined.” Gan, who had a significant cardiac history — including a heart attack six months earlier and two strokes within two years — was rushed to the hospital and pronounced dead.

In December, after investigating this death and an earlier December 2013 incident where a patient aspirated a throat pack during extraction, the Dental Commission suspended Patel’s license, permanently banned him from administering conscious sedation, and ordered five years of random monitoring. Inspectors also found at least five expired medications in his office and alleged improper delegation of sedative administration and monitoring to staff.

Patel’s attorney, Paul Knag, contends that the Dental Commission testimony showed Patel followed the standard of care and that the commission chose not to revoke his license; he disputes the criminal charges and urges they be dropped. The victim’s family plans further legal action; the family’s attorney called the tampering-with-evidence allegation particularly serious and said they will cooperate with ongoing investigations. Patel previously faced a malpractice verdict in 2011 that led to a later confidential settlement.

David Letterman returns with a Netflix talk series, My Next Guest Needs No Introduction with David Letterman, debuting Friday, Jan. 12. The hour-long show will stream one new episode per month in 2018 rather than binge-style. The premiere features Barack Obama — his first talk-show interview since leaving the presidency — and Letterman’s lineup also includes George Clooney, Malala Yousafzai, Jay-Z, Tina Fey and Howard Stern. Produced by RadicalMedia and Worldwide Pants, each episode centers on one fascinating guest in intimate, in-depth conversations filmed both inside and outside a studio, plus field segments that take Letterman to locations tied to the guest. Letterman has expressed interest in high-profile, controversial interviews — naming Donald Trump and North Korea’s Kim Jong-un as aspirational subjects — and says the series will blend serious inquiry with moments of levity and unexpected silliness.

Pastor Marrion P’Udongo, often called the “Schindler of Congo,” is a revered humanitarian in northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) whose decades of work saved and aided countless civilians during chronic conflict. He sheltered nearly 100 people during the 2003 Bunia massacre, coaxed child soldiers out of the bush, helped rape survivors obtain medical care, fed and clothed prisoners, and helped run the St. Kizito orphanage for children orphaned by war. Journalists, human-rights workers and public figures like Ben Affleck have praised him as a critical guide, fixer and humanitarian who could reach all sides of a fragmented conflict and whose presence sustained communities amid violence and displacement.

Despite this record, P’Udongo has lately faced a personal crisis: severe kidney failure. He first nearly died in 2011 and received a transplant after a major fundraising effort, but this year his body began rejecting that kidney. He now relies on three-times-weekly dialysis in Kampala, Uganda, lives on a small salary and piecemeal donations, and urgently needs another transplant. A donor match was found and arrangements made for surgery in India, but the procedure and related costs—reported figures range from roughly $35,000 to $76,000 in different accounts—exceed his means. Friends, colleagues and supporters have organized fundraising campaigns, and dozens of donors helped pay for earlier care; his nephew has volunteered as a donor in past efforts.

Supporters emphasize that losing P’Udongo would be a profound blow to the orphans, prisoners and displaced people who depend on him and to reporting on the region. He remains determined to return to his ministry—running the orphanage, reaching child soldiers and aiding communities—and says he still has much to do. Campaigns and appeals continue to raise funds for surgery, anti-rejection medication, follow-up procedures and support for the donor nephew’s education, with donors urged to contribute to the Pastor Marrion Fund to help preserve both his life and the fragile services he provides.

British tabloids and medical commentators have been abuzz following the announcement that the Duchess of Cambridge, Kate Middleton, is hospitalized with hyperemesis gravidarum — a severe form of morning sickness that can cause significant nausea, vomiting, weight loss and dehydration. Medical experts speaking to ABC News noted that while the condition affects roughly 2 percent of pregnant women, it is statistically associated with multiple pregnancies: a study cited by Dr. Ashley Roman of NYU Langone indicated a 7.5 percent higher risk of hyperemesis in women carrying twins. Some studies have also suggested subtle correlations between the condition and the likelihood of a female fetus, though Roman emphasized that hyperemesis itself is not believed to harm the baby and is often interpreted as a sign of a robust pregnancy. Most cases resolve by 16–20 weeks, she said, but a minority of women suffer symptoms throughout gestation. Ohio OB/GYN Dr. Nancy Cossler highlighted the major quality-of-life impact, noting the relentless sickness and vomiting patients endure while the illness runs its course.

Alongside medical commentary, widespread public and media speculation has shifted to the expected baby’s sex and name. UK bookmakers quickly set odds: at Ladbrokes, Elizabeth (8/1), Frances (10/1) and Diana (12/1) led the female list, while John or Charles (10/1) and James (12/1) topped the male list. William Hill put Frances and John at 9/1, with Charles, George and Victoria at 10/1, and maintained even odds for either gender. Pundits and royal-watchers discussed naming traditions: royals typically receive multiple names drawn from family, so Diana — the late Princess of Wales’s name — is widely predicted as a likely middle name for a girl rather than a first name, preserving tribute without bestowing Diana as the baby’s primary name. The coverage combines medical explanation, personal impact, and cultural ritual as the public awaits further updates on the duchess’s health and the new royal’s arrival.

Uganda’s parliament adopted a harsh anti-homosexuality bill that increases penalties—including life imprisonment for repeat offenses—and criminalizes promoting, recruiting for, or publicizing homosexuality. Lawmaker David Bahati, who sponsored the bill, said a death-penalty clause was dropped; the measure now awaits President Yoweri Museveni’s signature. Supporters framed the law as defending “God-fearing” Ugandan values and protecting minors, while critics warn it criminalizes legitimate human-rights work and will fuel fear, persecution, and violence against LGBT people. Activists such as Frank Mugisha described themselves as suddenly “illegal,” and rights groups including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International condemned the legislation as discriminatory and an assault on human rights. The vote followed passage of an anti-pornography and dress-code law restricting “provocative” clothing and banning sexually suggestive media. International leaders, including President Obama, had denounced earlier versions; opponents fear the new law could prompt arrests, intrusive investigations, and potential aid repercussions, deepening hostility faced by Uganda’s LGBT community.

This document compiles a series of federal criminal cases tied to the Special Counsel investigation and related matters, summarizing charges, pleas, and outcomes involving Trump campaign associates, Russian defendants, and others. Michael Cohen pleaded guilty (Nov. 29, 2018) to making false statements to Congress and was sentenced to two months in prison and a $50,000 fine. Paul Manafort faced multiple indictments in D.C. and the Eastern District of Virginia for conspiracy, tax and bank fraud, failure to report foreign accounts, and obstruction-related charges; he pleaded guilty in D.C. to a superseding information (Sept. 14, 2018) and was convicted on several counts in Virginia before admitting remaining charges as part of a plea. Rick Gates pleaded guilty (Feb. 23, 2018) to conspiracy and making false statements. Konstantin Kilimnik was charged with conspiracy to obstruct justice. A 12-defendant indictment charged Russian nationals in computer-hacking and identity-theft conspiracies (July 13, 2018), and the Internet Research Agency and related entities were indicted (Feb. 16, 2018) for election interference, fraud, and identity theft. Alex van der Zwaan pleaded guilty to lying to FBI agents and served 30 days. Richard Pinedo pleaded guilty to identity fraud and received six months imprisonment plus home confinement. Michael Flynn pleaded guilty to making false statements (Dec. 1, 2017).

A substantial portion of the document focuses on George Papadopoulos: he pleaded guilty (Oct. 5, 2017) to making false statements to the FBI about contacts with foreign nationals tied to senior Russian officials and admitted he was told in April 2016 that Russia had “thousands of emails” related to Hillary Clinton. Papadopoulos acknowledged misleading the FBI about the timing and nature of meetings with a professor and a Russian national and said he sought to arrange meetings between the Trump campaign and Russian officials. He cooperated with investigators and received a short sentence (14 days) and community-service/fine penalties. The file notes White House responses distancing the campaign from Papadopoulos and references public controversy over comments by officials about Confederate monuments in an unrelated passage.

The Vacca family released a video message to the unnamed nine-year-old girl involved in the Arizona gun range accident that killed their father and gun instructor, Charles Vacca. In the footage, 11-year-old Christopher and 15-year-old Elizabeth express empathy, urging the girl to move forward, love herself and her family, and not let the tragedy define her. They say they hope to meet and hug her someday. Attorney James Goodnow added the family recognizes the wider national gun debate but wants to emphasize the personal grief experienced by both the Vaccas and the child.

South Korea announced that North and South Korean athletes will march together under the Korean Unification Flag at the Pyeongchang Winter Olympics opening ceremony, and the two sides have agreed to form a joint women’s ice hockey team — a symbolic diplomatic breakthrough after days of talks at the Demilitarized Zone. Seoul’s unification ministry said North Korea will send a large delegation, including about 230 cheerleaders, some 140 artists (including a 140-piece orchestra), and 30 Taekwondo demonstrators; a separate, smaller Paralympic delegation was also announced. The two Koreas will also hold joint cultural events at Mount Kumgang and conduct skiing training together at North Korea’s Masik Pass before the Games. North Korean arrivals are due to begin January 25.

The International Olympic Committee must approve the proposals, and competitive issues like the combined hockey team may be more complicated; the IOC planned talks with both delegations to assess impacts. The rapprochement follows the first Korea-to-Korea talks in over two years, offering a temporary easing of tensions driven by Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programs. International reactions were mixed: some hailed the thaw as significant, while allies including Japan urged caution, calling it a potential “charm offensive” aimed at buying time for weapons development. The U.S. and other countries maintained pressure and moved military assets to the region; scheduled joint U.S.-South Korea drills are suspended only for the Olympics. Analysts warned the moves may be limited in scope and temporary, and North Korea has shown no sign of abandoning its nuclear arsenal. Public opinion in the South was divided, with some athletes and many petitioners opposing a unified hockey roster.

Snoop Dogg has launched Merry Jane, a cannabis-centered lifestyle media platform that blends video and editorial content to serve both beginners and seasoned consumers. Announced at TechCrunch Disrupt, Merry Jane aims to be an authoritative cannabis encyclopedia, offering original shows that cover lifestyle angles like cooking edibles, “Deflowered” (first-time experiences), and exclusive celebrity interviews with contributors “down with the team” such as Seth Rogen and Miley Cyrus. Beyond entertainment, the site will provide in-depth editorial coverage of the cannabis business, legalization developments, policy, and industry growth.

A key feature is a searchable strains database curated by Merry Jane’s editorial team, allowing users to explore products by type—wax, edible, flower—flavor, or symptom, with high-resolution imagery for each listing. The platform connects users to local dispensaries; initially Snoop and cofounder Ted Chung hand-curated participating shops, but dispensaries will eventually manage their own menus and storefronts via a back end. Advertising is part of the business plan, but the primary goal is to give marijuana brands and retailers a definitive online destination; Chung expects rapid user adoption and believes Merry Jane could surpass competitors within six months.

Merry Jane launches in limited beta at Disrupt SF 2015 and will open to the public in the following weeks. The piece also notes a broader trend of celebrities—like Jared Leto, Jessica Alba, Ashton Kutcher, and others—investing in startups and businesses, highlighting how stars increasingly seek revenue and influence beyond entertainment.

During the summit in Singapore, President Donald Trump used a mix of real estate pitch and showmanship as part of his outreach to North Korea’s leader, Kim Jong Un. In a wide-ranging solo press conference after the meeting, Trump repeatedly highlighted North Korea’s “untapped” economic potential, suggesting that if the country opened up it could host “the best hotel in the world” on its coastline. He quipped about North Korea’s beaches while referencing explosions into the ocean, and described showing Kim a video simulation and an iPad presentation depicting potential development projects — flashy incentives framed to encourage denuclearization. Trump said Kim watched the materials and “really enjoyed it,” and even suggested a “smaller version” of the proposals could be pursued. Trump also announced that North Korea had agreed to relinquish its nuclear weapons and signaled optimism about rewriting history toward lasting peace and complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula, though details and verification were sparse in the moment. Separately, as the summit wound down, Trump gave Kim a private, informal glimpse inside the presidential limousine nicknamed “The Beast,” a moment captured as lighthearted and symbolic camaraderie. Trump had earlier said he would know quickly whether a deal was possible; his post-summit tone was upbeat as he prepared to depart Singapore that evening.

Donald Trump’s inauguration as the 45th president took place on January 20, with the ceremony beginning at 11:30 a.m., preceded by musical performances and followed by the traditional inaugural parade at 3 p.m. In Washington, D.C., both ticketed and non-ticketed viewing areas were available; security gates opened at 6 a.m., and many parade sections along Pennsylvania Avenue from the Capitol to the White House were open to the public. Tickets were distributed by members of Congress and the inaugural committee, and major broadcast and cable networks carried the ceremony while POLITICO provided a live stream. The parade passed the Old Post Office near Trump’s hotel, and the inaugural committee expected roughly 800,000 attendees—well below the turnout for President Obama’s first inauguration—though Trump urged supporters to set an “all-time record.”

Attendees included Trump’s family, the Obamas, and several living former presidents and vice presidents: Jimmy Carter and George W. Bush confirmed attendance, as did Dick Cheney, Bill Clinton, and Hillary Clinton; George H.W. Bush did not attend due to health concerns. Prominent faith leaders, such as Cardinal Timothy Dolan and the Reverend Franklin Graham, were also present.

The entertainment lineup featured fewer A-list stars than recent inaugurations, with performers including Jackie Evancho singing the national anthem, the Mormon Tabernacle Choir, the Rockettes, country acts like Toby Keith and Three Doors Down, and various bands. Trump publicly favored a people-centered event over celebrity involvement, and inaugural committee chair Tom Barrack described the ceremony’s tone as having a “soft sensuality” and “poetic cadence.”

Program elements included a call to order by Senator Roy Blunt, readings, invocations, and music from the Missouri State University chorale. Vice President Mike Pence was sworn in by Justice Clarence Thomas, and Trump took the presidential oath administered by Chief Justice John Roberts. After Trump’s inaugural address, the ceremony concluded with readings, a benediction, and the national anthem.

Stephen Miller, who often warmed up Trump rallies, had a major role in drafting the inaugural speech, which aides described as philosophical and focused on priorities such as infrastructure, education, and manufacturing. Presidential scholars advised Trump to balance conciliation—reaching out to groups alienated during the campaign—and reassurance to his base by framing his controversial promises in temperate language. Experts highlighted risks: Trump’s habit of ad-libbing could undermine the occasion, and foreign leaders would be watching for cues on U.S. policy shifts.

The inauguration weekend included other events: a wreath-laying at Arlington on January 19, a public “Make America Great Again! Welcome Celebration” at the Lincoln Memorial, three official inaugural balls that evening, and a national prayer service at Washington National Cathedral on January 21. Many unofficial pro- and anti-Trump events were planned, notably the Women’s March on Washington, which organizers estimated could draw 200,000 participants.

Security closures affected central D.C. streets: the red zone was closed from January 18 to 23, with green zone restrictions beginning January 19; several Metro stations were closed on Inauguration Day though overall transit service ran frequently. The day underscored the ceremonial peaceful transfer of power amid deep national divisions and high international scrutiny of the new president’s tone and policy direction.

Grambling State edged North Carolina Central 10-9 in the Celebration Bowl after Joseph McWilliams blocked a 35-yard extra-point attempt pushed back 15 yards for an excessive-celebration penalty with 2:14 remaining. NCCU’s Quentin Atkinson had hauled in a 39-yard touchdown from Malcolm Bell to bring the Eagles within one, but his helmet-throwing celebration drew the flag that forced the longer kick, which McWilliams swatted away. Martez Carter’s 32-yard touchdown run early in the third gave Grambling the lead, and Jonathan Wallace added a field goal after a forced fumble. Grambling (11-1) completed a SWAC-title season under Broderick Fobbs; NCCU (9-3) won the MEAC under Jerry Mack.

Recent revelations about National Security Agency surveillance have prompted intense public debate and pressure on lawmakers to respond. Senate Intelligence Committee Chairwoman Dianne Feinstein said she is open to holding public hearings on the NSA’s programs — even monthly if necessary — after holding a classified briefing last week attended by 27 senators. Feinstein defended the programs as having helped thwart terrorist plots, citing cases such as David Headley (linked to the 2008 Mumbai attacks) and Najibullah Zazi (the 2009 New York subway plot). She acknowledged, however, that the classified nature of the evidence makes it difficult to publicly explain precisely how the programs have prevented attacks.

Senator John McCain also defended aspects of the surveillance apparatus on Sunday shows, saying he is not bothered by the programs and supports the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISA) system as an appropriate oversight mechanism. McCain argued that collection of call metadata — lengths and calling patterns — is not necessarily wrong and emphasized the court review required for more intrusive measures. His comments reflect a faction in Congress that views the programs as valuable anti-terror tools.

By contrast, civil libertarians and some senators, including Mark Udall and Ron Wyden, have criticized the surveillance initiatives as overreaches into Americans’ privacy. The disclosures, first reported by Guardian journalist Glenn Greenwald, included claims that Verizon was ordered to hand over millions of phone records and that the government collected 97 billion pieces of data in a single month. Greenwald said he has not been contacted by law enforcement and would welcome discussion, stressing First Amendment protections and defending the public’s right to know. He framed his sources’ motives as patriotic: risking careers and liberty to prompt a public debate about a “massive spying apparatus.”

House Intelligence Committee Chairman Mike Rogers sharply criticized Greenwald and his source, saying the reporter “doesn't have a clue” about how the program works and arguing the leaks are dangerous. Rogers and Feinstein suggested that if the leaker is identified, prosecution would be appropriate, contending that selectively disclosed classified information can harm national security. Rogers also argued that concerned insiders should have taken issues to Congress rather than the press.

The controversy has amplified calls for greater transparency and oversight while exposing deep divides between defenders who emphasize security benefits and critics who warn of excessive government intrusion and secrecy. Lawmakers and intelligence officials now face pressure to explain how surveillance is used, what safeguards exist, and whether current authorities strike an appropriate balance between privacy and national security.

Etched on a cross at the Manila American Cemetery is the inscription honoring an unknown World War II servicemember. For Pvt. Arthur “Bud” Kelder’s family, however, that unknown is almost certainly him. Kelder, an Army medic who survived the Bataan Death March but died in Cabanatuan POW camp in November 1942, was buried in communal grave 717 with 13 others. After the war, graves registration identified four of those men, but ten remained unknown and were reinterred as anonymous burials in Manila. Kelder’s relatives, led by his cousin John Eakin, have spent years researching declassified records and dental evidence suggesting one of those unknowns—Manila X-816, interred at A-12-195—is Bud. Two forensic dentists and a former JPAC official backed that conclusion and urged disinterment and DNA testing, but the Joint POW/MIA Accounting Command (JPAC) repeatedly declined, citing insufficient “scientific certainty” to justify disturbing the grave. That refusal prompted a lawsuit; recently the Pentagon reversed course and agreed to exhume X-816 and ten other remains from grave 717.

The Kelder case highlights broader criticisms of JPAC: whistleblowers and family members say modern forensic methods and historical analysis could identify many World War II unknowns, but agency bureaucracy, risk-averse disinterment standards, management failures and backlogs impede progress. Internal reviews and GAO reports have described dysfunction; JPAC missed congressional recovery targets and admitted to staged repatriation ceremonies. Former investigators like Rick Stone claim their work narrowing probable matches—particularly for Tarawa and Punchbowl unknowns—was ignored, while JPAC counters that disinterment decisions require strong circumstantial and anatomical evidence and that practical challenges and limited family DNA samples complicate identifications.

Defense officials say JPAC is expanding disinterment programs and researching thousands of unknowns, and Secretary Chuck Hagel announced a planned overhaul to consolidate the fractured accounting mission. Families, however, remain frustrated that progress often follows litigation and external pressure, and warn reforms are needed to bring hundreds of missing service members home.

First Lady Michelle Obama, “heartbroken” as a Chicagoan and mother, will attend the funeral Saturday for 15-year-old Hadiya Pendleton, a King College Prep honor student and majorette fatally shot near the Obamas’ Kenwood home. Valerie Jarrett and Education Secretary Arne Duncan will accompany her. Pendleton had performed at the presidential inauguration and condemned gun violence; officials hope the Obamas’ presence highlights rising Chicago gun violence.

Charlie Sheen’s Washington stop on his “Violent Torpedo of Truth” tour drew a boisterous, sometimes puzzled crowd to DAR Constitution Hall, where fans cheered his jokey talk of a presidential bid and one-liners about banning country music, legalizing marijuana, disbanding the Fed and sending the IRS “to prison.” He riffed on picking Nicolas Cage as VP, mocked his own court-ordered lateness after losing custody of his twins, and quipped about Moammar Gadhafi marrying his ex-wives. The show mixed stream-of-consciousness rants about drugs, ex-wives and celebrity with a sit-down interview and a guest set by Jeff Ross; audience heckles often outshone Sheen. Reactions ranged from entertained exploitation to journalistic unease. Notable attendees included Tareq and Michaele Salahi. Sheen’s blend of apparent seriousness and irony left it unclear whether his political musings were sincere or provocative performance.

Argentine President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, visiting China to seek investment for her faltering economy, sparked online outrage by posting a tweet that mocked a Chinese accent, replacing r’s with l’s — writing in Spanish, “Are they here only for the lice and petloleum.” The post, shared widely, prompted a follow-up apology noting that the “levels of ridiculousness and absurdity are so high they can only be digested with humor.” The incident came amid a domestic crisis: Fernández’s government has been shaken by the controversial death of prosecutor Alberto Nisman, who had been investigating the 1994 bombing of a Jewish community center and was due to allege that the President covered up Iran’s involvement. Investigators later reported finding a warrant for Fernández’s arrest, signed by Nisman, in trash at his apartment. The document also notes that web crawls aim to archive pages at creation to prevent broken links and preserve original content.

Advocate Sudeep Jaiswal will move the Bombay High Court on Tuesday seeking relief for Kolhapur sisters Renuka Shinde and Seema Gavit, who face imminent execution after President Pranab Mukherjee rejected their mercy petitions. Convicted in 2001 for kidnapping 13 children and killing nine between 1990 and 1996, the sisters were sentenced to death; their mother Anjana Gavit also participated and died in custody, while Renuka’s husband Kiran Shinde turned approver. The sisters have been held at Yerwada Jail, reportedly in solitary confinement with severe weight loss—below 35 kg—and deteriorating health. Jaiswal says he has notified jail authorities in writing and stresses a Supreme Court precedent that convicts in ill health cannot be executed. Authorities note compliance with legal procedures and Supreme Court guidelines; a mandatory minimum 14-day buffer period between communication of mercy petition rejection and execution was observed. That buffer recently expired, prompting the high court filing which will stay execution while considered. Defense argues core evidence relied on approver Kiran’s testimony, claiming their mother was the principal offender and that police altered statements after Anjana’s death. Human rights lawyers and prosecutors highlight the brutal nature of the crimes—children were allegedly starved, struck against hard surfaces, even dismembered—making this a contested “rarest of rare” capital case and one of India’s most notorious criminal sagas.

An annular solar eclipse traced a narrow path across the Pacific from Asia to the western United States, producing a “ring of fire” when the Moon, at its farthest orbital point, failed to cover the Sun completely. Millions witnessed the phenomenon along a 240–300 km-wide track; partial views were visible across much of East Asia and North America. The path began in southern China, passed almost directly over Tokyo—where schools, parks, pleasure boats and even private planes hosted “eclipse tours”—swept below Alaska’s Aleutian Islands, and made landfall in the western US, moving through northern California, southern Oregon, central Nevada, southern Utah, northern Arizona and New Mexico before fading east of Lubbock, Texas. Tokyo enjoyed near-perfect conditions as clouds thinned at peak, with live TV coverage and Panasonic filming from Mount Fuji; Hong Kong observers were largely clouded out. In the US, thousands gathered at viewing parties in Reno, Oakland and at Albuquerque’s Petroglyph National Monument, hailed as an excellent vantage point. Observers described emotional reactions and striking effects—sunlight filtered into crescent shadows through tree leaves. Experts warned against viewing without proper solar filters to avoid eye damage. The Slooh telescope network streamed coverage online. NASA notes the next solar eclipse will occur on 13 November, visible over northern Australia.

Ohio executed Dennis McGuire using a two-drug lethal-injection combination—midazolam (a sedative) and hydromorphone (a painkiller)—never before used in a U.S. execution. McGuire, 53, was condemned for the 1989 rape and murder of Joy Stewart, who was eight months pregnant. The crime went unsolved for months until McGuire, jailed on an unrelated assault, provided information that eventually led to his arrest; DNA later confirmed his guilt and he acknowledged responsibility in a letter to Gov. John Kasich. Ohio adopted the new protocol after supplies of pentobarbital, previously used in executions, became unavailable due to manufacturers’ restrictions. McGuire’s lawyers argued the drug combination risked causing “air hunger,” a terrifying struggle to breathe, and raised his abusive childhood and impaired brain development as mitigating factors; they also sought a stay to pursue organ donation, which Gov. Kasich denied because McGuire could not identify a recipient. Courts, including the U.S. Supreme Court, declined to block the execution; a federal judge allowed it to proceed while ordering the state to photograph and preserve the drug packaging and syringes. Witnesses reported McGuire made snorting or gasping sounds and the execution took more than 15 minutes, making it one of Ohio’s longest since 1999.

NATO moved to end its Libya air mission after the fall of Sirte and the National Transitional Council (NTC) declared the country liberated, marking a key phase toward promised democratic elections in 2013. The collapse of Muammar Gaddafi’s rule followed intense fighting: NTC forces overran Sirte, hoisted the new flag and reported capturing or killing many senior regime figures. Conflicting reports surrounded Gaddafi’s fate; multiple NTC officials and international outlets later said he and his son Mu’tassim were captured wounded and then died—mobile footage showed Gaddafi alive after capture, but graphic images and videos of his corpse circulated and his body was buried secretly to prevent a shrine. Western allies urged investigations into the circumstances of his death and stressed the NTC must uphold human rights and rule of law. Sirte’s fall did not end all fighting; Saif al-Islam remained at large, and concerns persisted about reprisals, regional rivalries and reconstruction. NATO began withdrawing equipment while retaining reconnaissance capacity and the option for strikes. International actors called for reconciliation and legal accountability for crimes committed during the conflict, even as Libya entered a fragile transition.

Rajan Zed, president of the Universal Society of Hinduism, served as guest chaplain and delivered a Hindu invocation in the Idaho Senate chamber on March 3, 2015. Wearing a flowing orange robe, Zed recited a prayer first in Sanskrit and then in English, drawing on ancient Hindu scriptures to urge selfless action, service to the welfare of the world, and peace. Many senators greeted him warmly afterward, shaking his hand or hugging him, and thanked him for coming. Zed said he appreciated the reception and emphasized Hinduism’s inclusiveness and the value of multiple viewpoints.

Three Republican senators — Steve Vick, Sheryl Nuxoll and Lori Den Hartog — stayed outside the chamber during the prayer and returned only after it concluded, citing objections rooted in their Christian beliefs. Nuxoll characterized the United States as a Christian nation and called Hinduism a “false faith,” while Vick had announced plans to protest ahead of time and Den Hartog said attending would have been disingenuous to her faith. A total of nine lawmakers were absent for the invocation, though five were tied up in meetings and one was excused. Senate Pro Tem Brent Hill said guest chaplains commonly fill in when the regular chaplain is unavailable; the chamber has previously welcomed clergy from other faiths, including a rabbi last year.

Anthony Weiner’s mayoral campaign was further destabilized when campaign manager Danny Kedem resigned amid renewed scandal over Weiner’s online conduct. Two campaign insiders, speaking confidentially, said Kedem, 31, informed Weiner of his decision within the previous 24 hours. Weiner confirmed the departure publicly outside a Brooklyn church, praising Kedem’s work. Kedem had been credited with helping lift what was once considered a long-shot candidacy to near the top of the mayoral polls. He had recruited volunteers and donors enthusiastically earlier in the summer and brought prior experience managing the re-election of New Haven Mayor John DeStefano Jr. and working on Hillary Clinton’s 2008 presidential campaign.

Kedem’s exit leaves Weiner’s already thin-staffed operation without a day-to-day leader at a moment of acute crisis. The campaign had been undermanned because of Weiner’s scandal and a reputation inside political circles for being a difficult boss; losing Kedem compounds those challenges. Despite the shake-up, Weiner insisted his campaign still had “an excellent staff” and that volunteers continued to turn out.

The turmoil follows Weiner’s admission the previous week that he had persisted in sending sexually explicit messages and photographs to women online after resigning from Congress in 2011. That revelation contradicted Weiner’s earlier claims of rehabilitation and of having ended such behavior, and it reignited public scrutiny and debate about his suitability for office. Commentators and politicians reacted strongly: David Axelrod, a longtime political counselor to President Obama, said on NBC’s Meet the Press that Weiner should “go away” and stop dominating the mayoral conversation, calling his continued candidacy “absurd.” Republican Rep. Peter King went further on CNN’s State of the Union, urging Weiner to withdraw and asserting the candidate had a “pathological problem,” arguing that Weiner was not psychologically qualified to be mayor and that his polling strength represented a “terrible aberration” driven by celebrity rather than electability.

Kedem’s departure underscores the internal doubts about the viability of Weiner’s bid, even as Weiner vows to press forward with his campaign amid mounting political and personal controversy.

Activists in the Philippines marched on the Chinese embassy in Manila to protest Beijing’s actions around the disputed Scarborough Shoal (Panatag/Huangyan), escalating tensions between the two countries. Hundreds—about 400—carried placards demanding China back off after an April standoff in which Chinese maritime surveillance ships and the PLA Navy prevented a Philippine vessel from arresting Chinese fishermen. The incident has drawn nationalistic response in both countries, with small pro-China protests in Beijing and warnings from Chinese officials urging the Philippines to protect Chinese nationals. China has cautioned its citizens in the Philippines and state entities postponed travel; 1,200 containers of Philippine bananas were held on quarantine grounds amid trade fallout. Philippine organizers say protests aim to alert the international community to Chinese encroachment and insist demonstrations are directed at Chinese government policy, not residents. Civic groups plan further protests at Chinese missions abroad.

A 34-year-old substitute teacher, identified as Lacey Sponsler, was arrested in Pawhuska, Oklahoma, after police allege she exposed herself during a high school choir class. Authorities say the incident occurred last Friday in the junior high choir room at Pawhuska High School, about 50 miles north of Tulsa. According to a probable cause affidavit and police statements, Sponsler, wearing a long dress but no underwear, performed a cartwheel that flipped her dress and exposed her buttocks and genitals. A 17-year-old student who reported the incident told police Sponsler had announced she was not wearing underwear before doing the cartwheel and described seeing Sponsler’s “vagina open and close” as her legs went in the air. The act was recorded on a student’s cell phone; an officer who reviewed the video noted the absence of undergarments. When questioned, Sponsler initially denied performing a cartwheel; after being informed of the Snapchat video, she said she did not remember doing it or exposing herself, later describing her actions as “just dancing with the students” and an attempt to be a “cool teacher.” Police arrested her Tuesday and she is being held on an indecent exposure complaint. Court records show Sponsler has prior convictions and probation-related issues, including past pleas for marijuana and methamphetamine possession and related probation violations. The school and police continue to address the matter.

A new study from Anirban Mukhopadhyay at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology suggests that forcing a smile when you’re unhappy can worsen feelings rather than improve them. Across three experiments involving surveys, reactions to humorous images, and facial-muscle exercises, researchers found that the emotional effect of smiling depends on the motivation behind it. People who naturally smile when they feel happy tend to gain mood benefits from smiling. But for those who don’t habitually smile, grinning as an attempt to mask or induce happiness can backfire: the brain may begin to associate smiling with the prior negative state, making future smiles trigger reminders of unhappiness. Mukhopadhyay argues that smiling itself does not increase wellbeing; instead, believing you were already happy when you smiled is what boosts mood. He recommends waiting for negative emotions to lift organically rather than pressuring someone to smile, and suggests people consider their own beliefs about smiling to decide whether changing their expression is likely to help or harm their emotional state. The study appears in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

Miley Cyrus says she’s “completely clean,” having quit marijuana for weeks while preparing a new, more personal album and promoting its lead single, “Malibu,” out May 11. Living with fiancé Liam Hemsworth on their Malibu compound and leaning into quieter, singer-songwriter and country-tinged sounds, she wrote much of the record herself and worked closely with producer Oren Yoel. Cyrus wants to reach beyond her liberal fan base—reengaging with country audiences via The Voice—and aims to connect compassionately across political divides after activism around the 2016 election and her Happy Hippie nonprofit. She reflects on past controversies, artistic evolution from provocative performances to authenticity, and embracing sobriety and creative focus to shape her next chapter.

Pope Francis made history as the first pontiff to address a joint session of the U.S. Congress, delivering a wide-ranging, often pointed speech that blended moral exhortation, political critique and pastoral appeal. Arriving amid tight security and tens of thousands gathered on the Capitol lawn, he was escorted into the House chamber by bipartisan leaders and greeted with standing ovations; afterward he asked the crowd, in Spanish and English, to pray for him or send good wishes.

The pope pressed lawmakers to adopt a “culture of care,” urging courageous, responsible action on climate change and calling on the United States and Congress to help slow global warming. He appealed for compassion toward immigrants and refugees, invoking his own immigrant roots and Martin Luther King Jr.’s vision, and warned against treating people as disposable. Francis condemned the global arms trade as motivated by profit “drenched in blood,” urged an end to the arms trade and criticized economic systems that make politics a “slave to the economy and finance.”

Consistent with Catholic teaching, he defended the sanctity of life at every stage: he called for abolition of the death penalty and reiterated opposition to abortion while broadly defending the family and expressing concern—obliquely—about challenges to traditional marriage. He cautioned against ideological rigidness and extremism in religion, politics or economics and stressed protecting fundamental freedoms while combating violence done in religion’s name. He also expressed sympathy for indigenous peoples amid early colonial abuses, praised bridge-building between nations, and avoided detailed comment on the Iran nuclear deal or U.S.-Cuba normalization. Throughout, Francis blended moral authority with political appeals, prompting partisan reactions in the chamber but leaving a clear call for lawmakers to pursue justice, care for the vulnerable, and act with hope and common purpose.

A Franklin, Tennessee family is raising awareness for LCHAD, a rare genetic metabolic disorder that prevents the body from breaking down certain long-chain fats for energy. Their son, 2-year-old Owen Torti, was diagnosed via newborn screening at one week old after being born nine weeks premature; his diagnosis followed his mother’s HELLP syndrome during pregnancy. Because Owen cannot access energy from stored fats, he must be fed nearly constantly—hourly during the day and continuously at night—to avoid muscle breakdown and dangerous metabolic crises that can cause breathing problems, seizures, organ damage or death. He has been hospitalized 12 times in 20 months. Owen’s feeding difficulties led to a G-tube at 16 months and dependence on a specialty formula (Lipistart); severe oral aversion means he currently receives all nutrition via tube and requires an intensive multidisciplinary feeding program at Baylor in Dallas. His parents, Kayla and Tyler Torti, are both carriers of the LCHAD gene and face a 25 percent chance of future children inheriting the disorder.

Information and support were scarce when the family sought answers, so they’ve worked to share their story to help others feel less isolated. Community support has grown: two “All in for Owen” teams ran the Ragnar Relay to raise awareness and funds, collecting $15,000 toward medical bills, formulas, and therapy costs. Coworkers, relatives, and strangers have rallied around the family, offering emotional and financial support. The Tortis hope that by publicizing Owen’s experience they can connect other families, raise awareness of this orphan disease—added to newborn screening only six years ago—and provide encouragement and practical help to those newly diagnosed.

A small propeller-driven Rockwell Turbo Commander crashed into two homes on approach to Tweed New Haven Airport in East Haven, Connecticut, killing four people and heavily damaging both houses. Victims included pilot and former Microsoft executive Bill Henningsgaard, his 17-year-old son Maxwell, 13-year-old Sade Brantley and 1-year-old Madisyn Mitchell. The children’s mother, Joann Mitchell, escaped but lost both children; she and the community held a vigil honoring the dead. Authorities performed emergency repairs so recovery crews could work and plan to demolish the two damaged homes this week. The NTSB said the plane struck a house inverted at about a 60-degree angle during its first approach and did not receive any declared emergency from the pilot; investigators found no immediate indication of mechanical problems. Henningsgaard, a noted philanthropist who survived a 2009 ditching in Washington state, was widely mourned by colleagues and community organizations for his civic work. A preliminary NTSB report is expected within about 10 business days.

Bitcoin experienced a dramatic intraday collapse after an extraordinary rally, highlighting the currency’s extreme volatility and the fragile confidence underpinning its recent meteoric rise. Earlier in the day, bitcoin topped roughly $250–$266, then plunged to lows near $105 — a drop of as much as 61% from the peak — before bouncing and trading around $150. The swings that day illustrated both speculative fervor and market instability: within hours the price ranged between about $120 and $266.

The currency’s ascent since January has been steep: from under $15 at the start of the year to triple- and quadruple-digit valuations by spring. That surge attracted heavy media attention, entrepreneurs and venture capital interest, and a flood of retail speculators eager to ride the rally. Some defenders turned to memes (“HOLD!”) and technical-analysis rationales after the crash, but commentators emphasize the core issue: bitcoin’s value rests heavily on confidence and narrative, making it vulnerable to rapid reversals.

Bitcoin’s appeal stems from its architecture: a decentralized, cryptographically authenticated, irreversible-payment system that functions without banks or traditional intermediaries. That permissionless nature lowers barriers for innovators and merchants and enables novel applications — from cheap international transfers to niche marketplaces — yet it also brings practical downsides for mainstream users: limited acceptance, weak consumer protections, clumsy onramps, and operational security risks.
