Exchanges and services have been hacked (notably past thefts at exchanges like Bitfloor), and infrastructure issues (denial-of-service attacks, cash deposit limits) make converting dollars to bitcoins cumbersome, which currently restricts mainstream adoption.

Analysts characterize bitcoin’s market as a classic speculative bubble driven by fixed supply, rising demand, media attention, hoarding, and ease of headline-driven entry. Possible crash triggers include falling demand, security scares, regulatory crackdowns, creation of competing cryptocurrencies, or a sudden shift in sentiment. While some investors celebrate outsized short-term gains and foresee further appreciation if onboarding improves, others warn the environment is unpredictable: prices could rise dramatically or collapse, and many observers advise caution given the risks and structural uncertainties.

Thomas Eric Duncan, the first person in the U.S. diagnosed with Ebola, remained in critical condition at Texas Health Presbyterian Hospital after being admitted Sept. 28. Sedated, on a ventilator and receiving kidney dialysis, Duncan had shown some signs of improvement — normalized temperature and blood pressure and reduced diarrhea — but doctors cautioned he had serious lung and kidney infections and had not yet turned a corner. He received the experimental antiviral brincidofovir; ZMapp doses were no longer available. Hospital officials later announced Duncan’s death.

Duncan, who arrived in Dallas from Liberia on Sept. 20 to reunite with his fiancée Louise Troh and their son, apologized to Troh after learning of his diagnosis, telling her he regretted exposing her and would have preferred to stay in Liberia and die rather than risk her life, a family friend said. His mother, who had not seen him in 12 years, and other relatives traveled to Dallas; they first viewed him via a laptop camera and found the images distressing and painful, so declined further video viewing. Reverend Jesse Jackson joined the family during a vigil. Duncan’s 19-year-old son Karsiah visited his father and asked for prayers.

Public health officials in Dallas monitored 48 people who had contact with Duncan — 10 classified as high risk (three household members and seven healthcare workers) and 38 at lower risk. As of the report, none had developed symptoms; officials emphasized a 21-day maximum incubation period, with many cases appearing within eight to ten days. Authorities monitored contacts twice daily and conducted daily checks of temperature and health.

The case prompted scrutiny of hospital procedures after Duncan was initially sent home from an emergency visit with fever and abdominal pain. Texas health leaders said evaluations would examine that first presentation. Cleaning crews in hazmat suits sanitized Duncan’s apartment, disposing of contaminated items while preserving keepsakes. The event spurred federal discussion about strengthening passenger screening and mobilization of military support to West Africa to build treatment centers and monitor returning service members.

The Pacific sardine, a small but crucial forage fish along the West Coast of North America, is experiencing one of the steepest declines in generations, with a November 2013 estimate of 378,000 tons—well below the 2000 peak of 1.5 million tons and near historical lows. Sardines are a keystone species: they transfer energy from plankton to higher predators and support seabirds, marine mammals, sharks, and commercially valuable fish like salmon and tuna. Their collapse echoes the mid-20th-century crash that decimated California’s sardine industry and triggered an 18-year moratorium. Sardine populations naturally fluctuate on multidecadal cycles tied to ocean conditions such as upwelling and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation, which recently favored other species (e.g., market squid) while disfavoring sardines. Scientists report a 72% drop since the 2006 peak, reduced spawning, and ecological consequences: malnourished sea lion pups, starving seabirds and other predators. The decline also risks shifting fishing pressure onto other forage species (sand lance, saury, lanternfish), which remain largely unregulated and unmonitored. Forage fish globally provide more value left in the water—supporting predators and fisheries—than when caught for industrial feed. In response, conservation groups urge the Pacific Fishery Management Council to set conservative catch limits when sardine numbers are low and to implement its 2013 commitment to prohibit unregulated harvest of other forage species. Federal managers have already cut harvest limits by over two-thirds, though some call for a full halt to fishing until recovery is assured. The underlying causes—climate variability versus fishing impacts—remain debated, complicating recovery predictions and management decisions.

A federal appeals court ruling struck down the FCC’s 2010 Open Internet rules, effectively gutting the regulatory basis for U.S. net neutrality protections and opening the door for broadband providers to discriminate among Internet traffic. The D.C. Circuit concluded the FCC had exceeded its authority by imposing common-carrier-like duties on ISPs after previously classifying them as non-common carriers. That legal mismatch undermined the agency’s attempt to require equal treatment of all online content.

The decision has broad practical consequences. ISPs like Comcast, Verizon, AT&T and others could favor some sites or services—either by speeding their traffic or blocking and throttling competitors—based on commercial arrangements or corporate interests. That raises the prospect of paid prioritization: content providers could be charged tolls to reach consumers at acceptable performance levels, disadvantaging smaller websites and startups that cannot pay for preferential treatment. Entire traffic classes—streaming video or peer-to-peer transfers, for example—could be degraded to protect legacy pay-TV revenues or other ISP priorities.

Critics warn this will entrench large incumbents, harm competition, and worsen service for consumers without necessarily driving network investment. The ruling also makes “sponsored data” models more likely, where companies pay carriers so their services don’t count against users’ data caps—an arrangement that could steer consumers toward big platforms that can afford sponsorship, further skewing the market.

Restoring net neutrality would require either an FCC appeal to the Supreme Court or a regulatory reclassification of broadband providers as common carriers, a politically contentious move that opponents and industry lobbyists resist. The decision highlights tensions between deregulatory precedents and calls for robust protections to preserve an open, non-discriminatory internet, leaving access and competition rules uncertain and potentially reshaping how consumers and content providers pay for and experience online services.

President-elect Donald Trump on Sunday night publicly questioned outgoing CIA Director John Brennan’s credibility, suggesting Brennan might be the source of “fake news” after Brennan criticized Trump’s understanding of the Russia threat. Trump’s tweet quoted a Fox News headline—“CIA's Brennan warns Trump, says he doesn't 'fully understand' Russia threat”—and added that Brennan “couldn’t do … much worse,” citing Syria (the “red line”), Crimea, Ukraine and a Russian nuclear buildup as examples. Trump’s tweets asked rhetorically, “Was this the leaker of Fake News?” and repeated the Fox News summary that Brennan “blasts Pres-Elect Trump on Russia threat.” The exchange follows Trump’s strong reaction last week to intelligence agencies’ report that he had been briefed on an unverified dossier alleging Russia held compromising material on him; Trump has criticized those agencies and their handling of the matter. Brennan responded to Trump’s remarks by saying the president-elect needs to be disciplined about his public statements and rebuked Trump for comparing intelligence community actions to those of the Nazis. The interaction underscores mounting tensions between Trump and elements of the U.S. intelligence establishment as his transition continues, with public accusations and rebuttals played out on social media and in televised commentary.

Scientists at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History have described a new leaf-dwelling praying mantis from Madagascar and named it Ilomantis ginsburgae in honor of Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg for her work on gender equality and her fondness for decorative jabots, which the researchers likened to the insect’s neck plate. The study, published in Insect Systematics & Evolution, is the first formal mantis species description that relies primarily on female genital characters. Lead author Sydney Brannoch, a Case Western Reserve University Ph.D. candidate, and co-author Gavin Svenson examined 30 specimens from three museums, including a 1967 holotype housed in Paris. They analyzed geographic distribution, external morphology, and both male and female genitalia, finding that female genital structures alone could delimit the species; traditional male-based character systems corroborated their conclusions. The findings supported resurrecting Ilomantis as a distinct genus separate from Nilomantis. The newly described mantis is green, leaflike, with a flattened body, conical eyes, and broad wings with leaf-like venation. The authors argue that incorporating female characters improves species identification—important because males and females often differ markedly—and hope this approach prompts taxonomists to more equally consider both sexes and integrate new morphological and genetic evidence for more accurate mantis classification.

New satellite imagery and analysis by the Committee for Human Rights in North Korea (HRNK), working with DigitalGlobe, show significant recent expansion of Camp 25, a political prison camp on North Korea’s northeast coast. Between 2009 and 2010 the camp’s perimeter grew from roughly 3,710 to about 5,100 meters and its area increased by about 72 percent, with new buildings, agricultural fields and nearly two dozen additional guard posts added by 2013. HRNK estimates Camp 25 holds about 5,000 prisoners. Researchers suggest the growth could reflect rising prisoner numbers, consolidation of other camps, or intensified crackdowns on defectors and political opponents after leadership transitions. North Korea operates several large, lifelong political prison camps — Amnesty estimates 150,000–200,000 detainees — and the system remains opaque; few inmates escape to tell their stories. Observers warn any camp reorganization must not be used to hide abuses or eliminate survivors.

Diebold Nixdorf and NCR Corp, two leading ATM manufacturers, have warned U.S. banks and cash machine operators that organized cybercriminals are conducting “jackpotting” attacks—hacking schemes that force ATMs to dispense large volumes of cash. Both firms confirmed they issued client alerts after warnings from U.S. authorities, with Reuters reporting the alerts followed earlier coverage by KrebsOnSecurity indicating the assaults began in Mexico. NCR said the incidents represent the first confirmed jackpotting losses in the United States, though it noted its equipment had not been targeted in recent attacks. Diebold Nixdorf specified that hackers were focusing on its out-of-production Opteva 500 and 700 series machines. A confidential U.S. Secret Service bulletin obtained by KrebsOnSecurity described tactics used by attackers: gaining physical access to stand-alone, front-loading ATMs (often in pharmacies, big-box retailers, and drive-thrus), replacing hard drives or imaging the ATM operating system, and using an industrial endoscope to depress internal reset controls. Attackers then connect a laptop and mobile device to synchronize with the ATM and deploy malware—reportedly the advanced Ploutus.D strain—to enable remote “cash-out” crews to trigger continuous dispensing until the machine is emptied. FireEye and other cybersecurity firms have characterized Ploutus.D as among the most sophisticated ATM malware families, first seen in Mexico in 2013 and noted in attacks across Europe and Asia. The Secret Service cautioned that ATMs running Windows XP are particularly vulnerable and urged operators to upgrade (e.g., to Windows 7) and adopt mitigations. Vendors urged all ATM deployers to treat the warnings as a call to action to harden physical and software defenses as investigations continue.

Chicago endured one of its most violent weekends in recent memory as dozens were shot in a concentrated burst of nightly attacks across the West and South sides. Police reported at least 63 people shot since Friday evening, with 10 killed overall; within a 24-hour stretch from Saturday morning to Sunday morning, authorities documented 34 shootings and five deaths. The worst period came between midnight and 3 a.m., when roughly 30 people were hit and five separate multi-victim shootings wounded 25 people. Victims ranged widely in age, including many teenagers and an 11-year-old boy.

Several large incidents stood out: a drive-by attack at a Lawndale block party left multiple teens wounded and 17-year-old Jahnae Patterson fatally shot; a Gresham courtyard shooting wounded eight people, including four teenage girls; and multiple shootings in Austin and West Garfield Park produced further deaths and dozens of injured. In many cases gunmen targeted groups, opening fire into crowds at gatherings, porches, funerals and block parties. Police say gang conflicts and retaliatory violence appear to be driving much of the carnage.

Chicago Police Chief of Patrol Fred Waller pledged an intensified enforcement focus on illegal guns, gangs and areas at risk of retaliation, stressing officers would not be "defeated" by a small violent element. Hospitals, especially Stroger and Mount Sinai, were overwhelmed by trauma patients and restricted visitation to immediate family. City leaders and community figures called for broader solutions — jobs, anti-violence programs and neighborhood cooperation — while activists criticized government response and funding shortfalls for prevention efforts. Investigations and efforts to prevent retaliatory shootings continued.

Minutes after Sebastian Gorka appeared on Fox & Friends to discuss rising tensions between Washington and Pyongyang, President Donald Trump used Twitter to reiterate harsh warnings to North Korea, prompting a wide-ranging media and administration response. Gorka, a White House adviser, framed Trump’s tweets as a direct, uncompromising message: “don’t test America and don’t test Donald J. Trump.” He characterized the United States not merely as a superpower but as a “hyper-power,” asserting that no nation—especially not North Korea—could match U.S. military capability. Gorka pressed that the ball was in North Korea’s court to “stand down the rhetoric,” called the hermit kingdom a “very insignificant threat in terms of scale,” and urged national unity behind the president during the crisis, drawing a controversial parallel to the Cuban Missile Crisis and saying Americans should support the executive branch “whether you voted for him or not.”

Gorka’s comments came amid broader attempts by the Trump administration to keep pressure on Pyongyang while calming public alarm triggered by the president’s earlier “fire and fury” warning. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson had counseled calm shortly before the tweets, assuring Americans there was no imminent threat from North Korea and saying people should “sleep well at night.” Defense Secretary James Mattis issued a more formal, forceful statement the following day, delivering a stark ultimatum to North Korea: to “cease any consideration of actions that would lead to the end of its regime and destruction of its people.” Mattis emphasized that the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea must stop isolating itself and abandon its pursuit of nuclear weapons, warning that any conflict or arms race initiated by the regime would be “grossly overmatched” by U.S. forces.

Despite his blunt rhetoric, Mattis reiterated his long-stated preference for resolving North Korea’s missile and nuclear challenges through diplomacy and urged Kim Jong Un to heed the United Nations Security Council and the international community, which view the DPRK as a threat to global security and stability. The administration’s mixed messaging—combining aggressive threats, public reassurance, and appeals to diplomacy—prompted criticism from some lawmakers across party lines who condemned the president’s “reckless” and “bombastic” rhetoric. Gorka lamented leaks and public dissent within Washington and called for national solidarity in response to the crisis.

Meanwhile, Pyongyang responded defiantly, declaring that “sound dialogue is not possible” with Trump and reiterating threats to target U.S. territories in the Pacific, including Guam, with intermediate-range missiles. As tensions escalated, administration officials publicly balanced deterrent warnings with assurances intended to temper public fear while urging international cooperation to press North Korea to change course.

President Obama’s 2012 convention acceptance speech in Charlotte was notable for its brevity—38 minutes and 23 seconds—making it the shortest incumbent acceptance speech in 36 years, according to C-SPAN. It was slightly longer than Mitt Romney’s GOP acceptance (37:47), but far shorter than longer modern examples like Bill Clinton’s 1996 address. With the Democratic National Convention over, the campaign entered its final 60 days.

Observers judged Obama’s speech competent but unremarkable: workmanlike rather than inspirational, more akin to a State of the Union than a rousing nomination address. While it energized convention-goers and made appeals to the political center, it lacked the historic resonance of Bill Clinton’s earlier convention performance and didn’t rank among Obama’s own best speeches. Critics argued it failed to explain convincingly how a second term would differ from the first without sounding like an admission of failure; it offered vague goals and nostalgia rather than a clear, new agenda, leaving doubts about why voters should expect greater effectiveness amid likely continued congressional opposition.

The speech contained two main themes. A defensive strand sought to rebut critiques—most notably the “you didn’t build that” controversy—by affirming belief in individual initiative while still emphasizing government’s role. Reviewers saw this as emblematic of a broader progressive instinct to conflate social interdependence with endorsement of existing federal programs, a sign of intellectual exhaustion on the left. The offensive strand focused on attacking Mitt Romney—portraying him as favoring deep cuts and tax breaks for the wealthy and questioning his trustworthiness on foreign policy—arguing that a Romney presidency would erode government protections.

Overall, the convention showcased several standouts—Gabby Giffords’ emotional Pledge recitation, John Kerry’s forceful foreign-policy critique, John Lewis’s stirring defense of voting rights, and strong musical moments from U2 and Foo Fighters—while other speakers fell flat. Analysts concluded both conventions framed the election as a referendum on the other candidate, offering few new policy agendas, which may favor Romney strategically by letting voters blame the incumbent for unmet expectations.

Focus is a glossy caper movie about con artists that ultimately feels like the con itself: promising slick insight into a secret underworld but delivering little truth. Will Smith plays Nicky, a charismatic veteran swindler who runs a wide-ranging operation of pickpockets and grifters; Margot Robbie is Jess, a pretty, quick-study novice who charms her way into Nicky’s tutelage. Directed by Glenn Ficarra and John Requa, the film markets the illusion of an intricate, globe-spanning confidence game—featuring casinos, racetracks, football stadiums and a major Buenos Aires con—but too often the plot is shapeless and self-serving, shifting to accommodate tricks rather than building believable stakes or consequences.

Reviewers praise some pleasures: Smith’s natural charm and easy charisma suit the role, allowing him to relax into the kind of roguish suavity many have missed since his lighter-genre work; Robbie is a magnetic presence, altering her persona with something as simple as hair up or down and bringing a modern, playful sensuality that evokes Hitchcock-era glamour. BD Wong provides a scene-stealing turn as a wealthy gambler whose escalating bets create a tense, odd mixture of menace and playfulness, and Adrian Martinez offers comic relief as a socially awkward member of Nicky’s crew. The movie relishes stylish set pieces and small delights—the hum of race cars outside a track café, an elaborate pocket-picking routine—but these moments don’t cohere into a satisfying emotional core.

Critics find the central relationship between Nicky and Jess unconvincing: the dialogue rings false, the emotional payoffs feel thin, and Smith’s chosen cool, withdrawn romantic style suppresses the warmth that made him a star. Ultimately Focus is enjoyable in fragments—an indulgent, audacious exercise in style and swagger—but it withholds the substance and truth it promises, leaving the viewer entertained but lightly cheated.

New Jersey Governor Chris Christie used a subdued but strategic appearance at CPAC to rebuild rapport with the conservative base amid lingering controversy over aides’ role in a George Washington Bridge lane closure. Welcomed with applause, Christie emphasized gubernatorial achievements over Washington gridlock, praising Republican governors like Scott Walker, John Kasich and Rick Snyder as proof that conservatives can govern effectively in blue or purple states. He framed the GOP as pro-entrepreneurship, pro-market and pro-life, criticized media bias, defended the Koch brothers, and urged Republicans to focus on positive messages—“talk about what we are for, not what we’re against”—to win elections. Christie contrasted hands-on governors with feckless national politicians, warned against nominating candidates too extreme to prevail, and stressed the need for a strong national defense. Speaking off the cuff and noticeably dialed back from past grandstanding, he sought to mend fences after a CPAC snub last year and his widely debated embrace of Obama post–Hurricane Sandy. His reception suggested the frost with grassroots conservatives may be thawing, keeping him relevant for future Republican contests.

Jim VandeHei, Politico co-founder, wrote a Wall Street Journal op-ed proposing a third-party “Innovation Party” and a playbook to disrupt what he calls “fat, lazy” Establishment America. He argues for an outsider presidential candidate who channels the energy of both Bernie Sanders and Donald Trump but avoids their extremes, tapping “Normal America” outside the D.C. bubble. His suggestions mix political marketing, Silicon Valley–style “innovation,” and muscular national-security posturing: stage crusades outside Washington, exploit cable TV, recruit tech leaders for government modernization, and even draft military figures or running mates with “modern-warfare” expertise to exploit public fear of terrorism—advocating explicit promises about when force would be used, including expanded use of drones. Critics find the op-ed alarming and tone-deaf. Slate’s Isaac Chotiner calls it “clueless and despicable,” arguing it blends demagogy with corporate technocracy and flirts with authoritarian impulses. Spoiler Alerts’ critique emphasizes how VandeHei’s prescription repeats bad pundit habits—pandering to Trump’s plain-speaking appeal, overusing “disruption,” and idolizing a military savior. The column’s suggestion of a military nominee invites concern because retired Adm. William McRaven, whom VandeHei’s template would embrace, recently criticized Congress over discipline of a Navy commander accused of whistleblower retaliation, raising alarms about civilian control of the military. Critics stress that fear-mongering and centralizing power—whether through generals, billionaire technocrats, or media-savvy branding—are dangerous responses to political dysfunction. They urge attention instead to restoring public trust in Congress and strengthening democratic institutions rather than seeking magical, top-down fixes.

Nikki Sixx, Mötley Crüe’s bassist, married model Courtney Bingham after more than three years together in a Los Angeles ceremony at Greystone Mansion. About 130 guests attended the gothic-rock–meets–French-countryside themed wedding, where peacocks greeted arrivals. Sixx, 55, proposed in St. Barts two years into their relationship. Bingham, 28, celebrated with a bridal shower at the Hotel Bel Air and made her own flower arrangements; she received playful honeymoon gifts like a candy necklace bikini top. Her aunt, who owns Janene’s Bridal Boutique in Northern California, custom-made her nontraditional gown inspired by red-carpet looks. The couple served Bingham’s favorite triple-berry cake from Sweet Lady Jane. This marks Sixx’s third marriage after unions with Brandi Brandt and Donna D’Errico. The text also references web-archiving efforts to preserve pages and avoid broken links.

The Supreme Court’s mixed ruling on Arizona’s SB 1070 produced immediate partisan backlash, legal analysis and vows of further litigation. The Court struck down three major provisions of the 2010 law but upheld the controversial “show me your papers” provision, which allows state officers to check immigration status of individuals stopped for questioning when there is reasonable suspicion they are in the country illegally. Justice Kennedy wrote the majority opinion emphasizing federal supremacy over immigration policy; dissenting Justice Scalia bitterly criticized the Court and took aim at President Obama’s selective non-enforcement of federal immigration rules.

Arizona officials hailed the partial victory. Gov. Jan Brewer called the decision a vindication of the law’s “heart,” insisted the state would enforce SB 1070 responsibly and denounced federal failures on immigration. Sheriff Joe Arpaio declared he would continue enforcing state laws despite federal pressure and accused Obama of targeting him personally; he also questioned whether federal agencies would cooperate in detaining undocumented immigrants. Republican figures criticized the administration for lacking leadership on immigration and urged federal action.

Civil-rights groups and immigration advocates warned the upheld provision invites racial profiling and pledged continued legal challenges. DOJ Attorney General Eric Holder emphasized the ruling’s federal-preemption rationale and warned against discriminatory enforcement, promising monitoring and civil-rights enforcement. Legal analysts predicted extensive litigation as states grapple with similar statutes and noted the decision leaves many ambiguities about implementation and potential constitutional conflicts. The ruling is likely to fuel political debate and judicial battles nationwide while underscoring calls for comprehensive federal immigration reform.

The government is set to introduce compulsory polygraph screening for around 750 high‑risk sex offenders in England and Wales from January, using powers in the Offender Management Act 2007. MPs will debate secondary legislation to roll out routine lie detector testing for serious offenders released after sentences of at least 12 months, with breaches or deceptive answers potentially triggering recall to prison. The move follows pilots in Midlands and Hertfordshire (2009–11 and 2011) that suggested polygraph sessions made offenders more forthcoming with probation staff and revealed previously undisclosed offending in some cases. Polygraphs monitor heart rate, blood pressure, breathing and sweat to detect evasive responses; proponents claim roughly 85% accuracy, but reliability concerns and risk of misinterpretation mean results remain inadmissible in UK courts. Justice Minister Jeremy Wright argued the tests, alongside the sex offenders register and a new National Probation Service, will strengthen public protection. Critics and policing bodies have cautioned that polygraphs are complex and should be used as an additional tool rather than a standalone solution.

In Chunky, Mississippi, a Halloween hayride turned deadly Monday night when a Ford F-150 rear-ended a flatbed trailer carrying adults and children on U.S. Highway 80. The crash occurred around 7:45 p.m.; investigators have not yet determined a cause and no arrests were reported. Emergency crews — including three helicopters and multiple ambulances — transported numerous injured people to three hospitals. Newton County Coroner Danny Shoemaker confirmed three fatalities: two children and one adult, all related, with two pronounced dead at the scene and a third dying while awaiting air transport. Mississippi Highway Patrol and local officials described chaotic scene conditions and said some victims suffered life-threatening injuries. Authorities have not released the names or ages of the victims or the total number injured. Local officials expressed sorrow for the small community, noting the tragedy’s outsized impact. Investigators remained on scene late into the night; details about who organized the hayride and the exact circumstances leading to the rear-end collision were still under review.

A series of deadly incidents and widespread flooding struck North Texas over the Thanksgiving holiday weekend. In South Dallas around 1:20 p.m., 23-year-old Kelvin Walker, driving a Range Rover at high speed, rear-ended a Honda sedan carrying a family of five. Two children—an approximately 12- or 13-year-old boy and a 13-month-old—were ejected; the boy died at the scene and the infant later died at Children’s Medical Center of Dallas. The parents and another child suffered minor injuries. Walker, with prior theft and burglary convictions, was hospitalized then jailed on a vehicular manslaughter charge; investigators are probing speed, slick roads and possible alcohol involvement.

Separately, flooding and high water claimed at least four lives. In Garland, 29-year-old Benjamin Floyd drowned after his car was swept off Campbell Road. In Johnson County, Jose Vargas, Sandra Jones and a 76-year-old woman identified later as Zenola Jenkins died after vehicles were overtaken by fast water. A 70-year-old driver remained missing in Burleson. A Tarrant County deputy was swept away during a rescue but was recovered; a female motorist in a submerged vehicle was not rescued. Authorities reported hundreds of crashes and dozens of water rescues over the weekend as North Texas experienced record rainfall—making 2015 the wettest year on record for the DFW area—and urged motorists to avoid high water and obey barricades.

Mohammed Abdullah Tawfeeq, a CNN producer and editor and an Iraqi national who has been a U.S. lawful permanent resident since June 2013, has filed a federal lawsuit in Atlanta challenging the implementation of President Trump’s executive order restricting entry from seven predominantly Muslim countries. Tawfeeq says that after returning from Baghdad on January 29, he was detained at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport for additional screening, delaying his re-entry and raising uncertainty about his rights as a green card holder. According to the complaint, a CBP officer scanned his passport and green card, questioned him about his trip, and then told him to wait while officials sought “an e-mail” indicating whether he could enter. When he was finally allowed to leave the airport, he received no explanation, no entry documents, and his passport was not stamped. The suit alleges the executive order’s implementation and his detention violate the Immigration and Nationality Act and the Administrative Procedure Act because lawful permanent residents are entitled to greater procedural protections than nonimmigrants. The filing highlights conflicting public statements after the order: initial State Department guidance appeared to apply the ban broadly, White House Chief of Staff Reince Priebus later said green card holders would not be affected, and DHS said it would enforce presidential orders while indicating permanent residents would generally be exempt absent significant derogatory information. Tawfeeq seeks a declaration that the ban does not apply to legal permanent residents and a mandamus order preventing its application to them. Defendants named include DHS, CBP, the State Department, DHS Secretary John Kelly, and Acting Secretary of State Thomas Shannon.

The uprisings in Tunisia reverberated across the Arab world, energizing populations long frustrated by economic hardship, corruption and repressive, power-preserving regimes. The immediate spark was Mohamed Bouazizi, a 26-year-old fruit vendor whose self-immolation after harassment by police crystallized broad grievances—rising food prices, unemployment and limits on civil liberties—and, relayed by social media, ignited mass protests that toppled President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali after 23 years in power. His flight to Saudi Arabia and the rapid appointment of interim figures—first Prime Minister Mohammed Ghannouchi briefly, then Fouad Mebazaa as president—produced both hope and uncertainty. Authorities declared a state of emergency and set a 60-day timetable for elections, yet the streets descended into violence, looting and chaotic clashes; prison fires, armed attacks on security sites, and fears of regime loyalists fomenting disorder complicated the transition. The army took visible control of key points while police faced public fury. Regional reaction was immediate—solidarity protests, debate over U.S. policy and calls for wider change—yet Tunisia’s upheaval also served as a cautionary tale: dismantling authoritarian rule risks instability, and whether the new government will dismantle the old ruling party’s influence remains uncertain.

Frank Romano is searching for his 6-year-old brindle-and-white Bull Terrier, Ty, after the dog disappeared from Delta’s care at LAX. Romano says Ty was placed in a hard-plastic, metal-doored carrier purchased at PetCo and checked into the aircraft cargo area Friday night. Romano’s family boarded the flight, but a Delta employee later removed Romano and told him Ty had supposedly chewed through the kennel door and escaped an hour earlier—news Romano finds unlikely given the crate’s construction. He also questions why he wasn’t informed immediately, why the kennel never appeared at baggage claim, and why initial leads— including a Tampa cargo contact—turned up nothing. Romano searched LAX and repeatedly contacted Delta without resolution. Delta told LAist it is investigating; an update states early indications suggest procedures were followed and the dog may have compromised the kennel, and that Delta worked with airport teams and the owner to search but was unsuccessful. The case recalls several other high-profile incidents of pets lost, injured, or misrouted under Delta’s care over the past decade, including dogs who were temporarily misplaced, hit by cars after escaping, or never recovered. Critics say these repeated failures show systemic problems in Delta’s pet-transport procedures and demand a thorough internal review to prevent future tragedies.

A Thai surrogate mother, Pattaramon (Pattharamon) Chanbua, has been raising a newborn boy, Gammy, who was born in December with Down syndrome and a congenital heart condition after allegedly being abandoned by his Australian biological parents. Pattaramon, 21, a food vendor and mother of two, says the Australian couple took the healthy twin girl to Western Australia but left Gammy in Thailand. She insists she will not hand Gammy over to the couple and has cared for him since birth; he is currently hospitalized with a serious lung infection and needs heart operations.

The case has provoked strong public interest in Thailand and Australia and prompted major online fundraising: a GoFundMe organized by Australians has raised more than $200,000, now being managed by the charity Hands Across the Water, which plans to meet immediate medical needs and set up a trust for Gammy’s long-term care. The charity’s founder, Peter Baines, has said funds will be distributed responsibly with advice from Down syndrome groups and a subcommittee including the fundraisers.

Conflicting accounts have emerged. Australian media reports and an anonymous police source say the alleged father is a convicted sex offender; Pattaramon said these reports shocked her and made her reconsider earlier willingness to let the twin girl stay with the Australian parents. The Australian couple reportedly deny abandoning Gammy: they say clinic staff told them only about a daughter, that they were not informed of a twin, and that their experience with the surrogacy agency was traumatic. Channel Nine and ABC reported speaking to the couple; they have not spoken publicly. Pattaramon says she did not receive full payment promised for the surrogacy and intends to pursue legal action against the agency. The legality and ethics of international surrogacy remain complex and inconsistent across jurisdictions, and this case has highlighted gaps and disputes when different national laws and practices intersect.

Meghann Foye’s New York Post piece and subsequent novel “Meternity” popularized the idea of a “meternity” leave: a sabbatical-like, socially sanctioned pause for self-reflection and personal recalibration that she envies parents for getting via maternity leave. After a decade in magazine publishing and observing coworkers leave on time to tend children, Foye concluded that parenthood often confers workplace flexibility and a culturally accepted reason to step away. She argues that many childless professionals never receive that enforced break, and that a “meternity” could benefit women—and to a lesser degree men—by reducing burnout, enabling life reassessment, and teaching self-advocacy skills without precluding future maternity leave. Foye took such a leave herself, returned to work with new boundaries, and wrote a novel that explores these themes.

The proposal prompted sharp pushback from mothers, commentators and journalists who say the concept misunderstands maternity leave’s realities. Critics emphasize that maternity leave is not leisure: it’s medical recovery and newborn care, often exhausting and far from restorative “me time.” Many note that becoming a parent typically harms women’s careers—widening the gender pay gap, impeding promotions and adding second-shift domestic labor—rather than conferring perks. Others stress structural problems in U.S. policy: few American workers receive paid parental leave or affordable childcare, so calling maternity leave a professional advantage ignores systemic hardship.

Supporters of broader sabbaticals point to international examples—like Denmark—where career-integrated personal leave fosters family time and creative renewal. The debate crystallizes larger tensions: America’s demanding work culture, lack of family-friendly policies, differing experiences of parents and nonparents, and the need for empathy and flexible workplace norms that recognize both recovery from caregiving and legitimate nonparental needs for time away.

President Donald Trump, under increasing pressure to acknowledge Russian election interference, asserted via tweet that Moscow will be "fighting very hard" to influence the 2018 midterms and predicted Russia would favor Democrats, despite past Russian efforts to help him in 2016. His comment came as lawmakers held a House Oversight hearing on election security, where members from both parties criticized Russian meddling and discussed steps to protect U.S. voting systems.

Homeland Security official Christopher Krebs testified that intelligence agencies have seen "continued malign influence operations" into 2018, though not at the same scale as 2016. Lawmakers referenced a recent indictment charging 12 Russian intelligence officers with hacking Democratic email accounts and attempting to penetrate state election systems; Chairman Trey Gowdy noted the indictment found no evidence vote counts were altered, but added that the Russians tried.

Republicans at the hearing conveyed differing tones: North Carolina Rep. Virginia Foxx directly criticized Trump’s Helsinki summit remarks for not holding Vladimir Putin accountable, while other GOP members sought to distinguish Russian meddling from allegations of presidential collusion. Democrats, led by ranking member Elijah Cummings, argued Republicans must move beyond rhetoric to active oversight, more documents and funding to secure elections.

Congress earlier allocated $380 million for state election-security upgrades, most of which has been distributed; Democrats want continued funding into 2019 but Republicans have been reluctant. State and local election systems’ decentralized nature offers some resilience, yet at least 21 states had systems probed and one experienced a voter-registration breach. DHS has provided remote scanning, onsite cybersecurity reviews and security clearances to state officials. Microsoft also reported suspected phishing attacks on three midterm candidates. In the Senate, two lawmakers introduced bipartisan legislation to impose new sanctions on Russia to deter further interference.

Former President George W. Bush, on the eve of the dedication of the George W. Bush Presidential Center at Southern Methodist University, expressed confidence and comfort with his record—most notably the decision to invade Iraq—while embracing a lower-profile but active post-presidency. In an interview with Diane Sawyer, Bush said the museum lays out the facts, including that Saddam Hussein lacked weapons of mass destruction, and that he is comfortable with the decision-making process that led to Saddam’s removal, believing it served U.S. security and offered Iraqis a chance at freedom. He added that history will ultimately judge him.

The 23-acre center houses the Bush Library and Museum and the Bush Institute, which continues work on issues central to his presidency—global health (including AIDS efforts in Africa), education reform, economic growth, human freedom, veterans’ issues, and empowering women in the Middle East. The museum focuses on pivotal moments of his administration—9/11, the Iraq lead-up, Hurricane Katrina, and the 2008 financial crisis—and features artifacts like a chunk of the Twin Towers, Saddam’s gun, and Bush’s Ground Zero bullhorn. Its “Decision Points Theater” invites visitors to confront presidential choices and understand the pressures leaders face.

Bush said he prefers to avoid daily partisan battles and generally stay out of hot-button debates to avoid undermining the sitting president, though he supports his brother Jeb’s potential 2016 candidacy. He described painting as a life-changing pursuit and celebrated becoming a grandfather. Laura Bush emphasized continued work through the Institute.

Public reassessment of his legacy is underway: a CNN/ORC poll shows 55% now call his presidency a failure (down from 68% in 2009), while 42% call it a success—reflecting sharp partisan, generational, and geographic divides. Overall approval has improved in other surveys as well.

Twitter permanently banned right-wing conspiracy theorist Alex Jones and his Infowars accounts for violating its abusive behavior policy after new reports of tweets and videos, the company said. The action follows a live-streamed confrontation Jones had with CNN journalist Oliver Darcy between two congressional hearings about social media, during which Jones berated Darcy for about ten minutes and lashed out at Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey. Twitter said the videos crossed its rules and noted the accounts’ history of prior violations; Jones and Infowars were also barred from Periscope and prohibited from creating new or takeover accounts. Jones had roughly 900,000 followers and Infowars about 430,000 on Twitter. The ban follows similar moves by other tech companies—Apple, Facebook and YouTube had already removed or suspended Jones’ content—and comes after an earlier weeklong suspension by Twitter. Jones remains active on Facebook for now, where a recent suspension has expired. Associated Press reporting contributed to this account.

A leopard killed and partially consumed a game ranger’s two-and-a-half-year-old son at Mweya Safari Lodge in Queen Elizabeth National Park. The child, Elisha Nabugyere, was seized at about 7:30 p.m. while seated by the doorway of Uganda Wildlife Authority (UWA) staff quarters. According to his father, SSP Francis Manana Nabugyere, the boy had been with a maid at the time; the leopard grabbed and ran off with him. Rescue attempts failed, and searchers recovered the child’s skull and other bones the following day. The mother, who is a park ranger, was at a neighbor’s when the attack occurred. The family buried the remains over the weekend; Nabugyere said UWA provided the coffin and said he expects “something reasonable” in compensation while also urging stronger protections for staff and their children. UWA communications manager Bashir Hangi described the event as unfortunate and confirmed efforts to locate the leopard. Hangi said the authority has arrangements for staff who lose loved ones in the line of duty but did not specify compensation details. He noted the agency is tracking the animal with the aim of removing or relocating it, warning that a leopard that has eaten human flesh poses an increased danger of repeating attacks. Reports indicate the toddler had followed his nanny outdoors toward the staff kitchen; she heard his screams and pursued the animal but could not prevent the abduction. The incident has shocked many because leopard attacks on humans are uncommon in Uganda. It comes amid a series of recent park tragedies, including several lion deaths and a tourist fatality earlier in April, prompting increased concern about wildlife management and staff safety at Queen Elizabeth National Park.

A Mexican vallenato band, Kombo Kolombia, and their road crew—20 people in total—have been missing since leaving a private gig in Hidalgo, north of Monterrey. Family members lost phone contact after the Thursday night performance and found the band’s vehicles abandoned outside the venue. Residents reported hearing gunfire and speeding cars around 4 a.m. Friday; investigators later found spent bullets nearby. Authorities in Nuevo Leon have no leads after two days of searching. While many past attacks targeted narcocorrido performers tied to drug traffickers, Kombo Kolombia plays Colombian-style music without violent or drug-related lyrics. One missing person is a Colombian national with Mexican residency. Fears grow amid Mexico’s wider drug-related violence.

The U.S. is experiencing one of its worst flu seasons in a decade, driven largely by H3N2, a strain that causes higher hospitalization and death rates, especially among older adults. Recent CDC data show a modest decline in doctor visits for flu-like symptoms—down from 7.5% to 6.4%—and a small drop in states reporting high activity (from 43 to 39), suggesting the season may have peaked, though officials caution flu activity could continue into mid‑April. So far this season 97 children have died; most pediatric fatalities occurred in unvaccinated children. Overall vaccine effectiveness this season is estimated at about 36%, but protection is stronger in young children (about 59%). The H3N2 strain’s poor vaccine match—vaccine effectiveness against it is roughly 25%—stems largely from the egg-based manufacturing process: viruses adapt to eggs, acquiring mutations that reduce vaccine-induced immunity. Alternatives exist (cell-based Flucelvax and insect-cell FluBlok), and preliminary data suggest cell-based vaccines might perform better, but evidence is not yet conclusive. Experts stress that even limited vaccine protection can reduce disease severity and hospitalizations. Work is underway on next year’s vaccine strains, FluMist nasal spray has been reinstated for use, and researchers continue pursuing longer-term goals like a universal flu vaccine.

The FDA approved Yescarta (axicabtagene ciloleucel), a CAR-T cell gene therapy, for adult patients with certain relapsed or refractory large B‑cell lymphomas after at least two prior treatments. It is the FDA’s second gene therapy approval and the first for certain non‑Hodgkin lymphomas, including diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and related subtypes, though not for primary central nervous system lymphoma. Yescarta is an individualized therapy: a patient’s T cells are collected, genetically modified to target lymphoma cells, and reinfused. In a multicenter trial of over 100 patients, Yescarta produced a 51% complete remission rate and tumor shrinkage in about 70% of chemotherapy‑resistant cases. Significant risks include cytokine release syndrome and severe neurologic toxicities; Yescarta carries a boxed warning and is being approved with a REMS requiring certified treatment centers and trained staff. A post‑marketing observational study is required. The FDA granted Priority Review, Breakthrough Therapy and Orphan Drug designations; Kite Pharma (now part of Gilead) received approval. The therapy’s complex manufacture and high cost—priced at $373,000 per patient—spark debate, though proponents highlight substantial remissions, manufacturing reliability, and plans to expand CAR‑T approaches to other cancers.

An anonymous driver using the handle AfroDuckProductions claims to have set a new unofficial “lap of Manhattan” record, completing a roughly 26.5‑mile loop around the island in 24 minutes, 7 seconds on August 26, 2013. The dashcam video, filmed from a stock 2006 BMW Z4 (referred to as a Z3 in some reports), shows the run beginning on the FDR at 116th Street, racing under the Williamsburg, Manhattan and Brooklyn bridges, through the Battery Park Tunnel, up the West Side Highway past Midtown, cutting across near the George Washington Bridge, then returning down the East Side to the start. The average speed is about 66 mph, with time gains achieved by aggressive maneuvers: passing on the right, lane weaving and cutting off other drivers, and running several red lights (the driver says he stopped at six). Reaction online is mixed, praising the skill while condemning the recklessness; critics warn of the danger to other road users. The NYPD has signaled interest and noted license‑plate readers could help identify the driver. The stunt revives a history of similar risky record attempts dating back to a 2001 27‑minute run.

Tesla is investigating a rare incident in which a Model S reportedly burst into flames in traffic on Santa Monica Boulevard in West Hollywood. Cellphone video tweeted by actress Mary McCormack—whose husband, director Michael Morris, owned the car—showed flames erupting from the vehicle. McCormack said the fire occurred “out of the blue” with no collision; she later deleted the post but the footage circulated widely. Local officials suggested a battery fault might be to blame, but Tesla characterized the event as “extraordinarily unusual” and said its preliminary review shows the passenger cabin remained unaffected thanks to battery architecture designed to protect occupants. No injuries were reported.

Industry experts noted that while lithium-ion battery fires have appeared in other contexts, electric-vehicle packs are more complex and Tesla says fires are at least ten times less likely in its vehicles than in gasoline cars. Tesla stressed it has not replicated such a spontaneous conflagration in tens of thousands of miles of testing and continues investigating the cause.

The story briefly affected markets: Tesla shares fell in pre-market trading after the report, adding to a string of headline challenges for the company as it races to meet production targets for the Model 3 and manage investor concerns. Separate incidents of Teslas catching fire historically have followed crashes or impacts; investigators emphasized that more analysis is needed before concluding why this West Hollywood blaze began.

TED’s Vancouver conference showcased its usual mix of high production value and wildly eclectic content, though individual talks were uneven. Highlights included Bran Ferren, who compellingly argued that autonomous vehicles could cut pollution, congestion and wasted time, and architect Marc Kushner, who traced architecture’s swing between innovation and comforting symbols and praised digital feedback’s power to align projects with public tastes. Urban planner Amanda Burden described zoning efforts to concentrate housing near subway stations and battles to protect public spaces like the High Line. Lighter and diverse entries ranged from a magician-crossword-creator to a fusion entrepreneur, a font designer, and filmmakers linking civil- and gay-rights histories. The most divisive moment came when Edward Snowden appeared via a remotely controlled robot from an undisclosed Russian location for an extended interview with TED curator Chris Anderson. Snowden argued more NSA revelations remain, urged default web encryption, and framed his actions as defending privacy and rights rather than seeking celebrity. Tim Berners-Lee called him a hero if forced to choose, while the audience largely supported Snowden. The conference closed with Bill and Melinda Gates and a Sting performance, underscoring TED’s blend of ideas, activism and showmanship.

NASA’s New Horizons spacecraft completed a historic flyby of Pluto in July 2015, delivering the first close-up reconnaissance of the distant dwarf planet and its moons after a 9.5-year, roughly 4.8–5.3 billion kilometre (3–3.3 billion mile) journey. The probe’s approach and closest pass — about 12,500 km (7,800 miles) from Pluto — produced a torrent of images and measurements that immediately revised scientists’ understanding of the system and set the stage for many months of analysis: the spacecraft gathered so much data that it will take about 16 months to transmit the full set to Earth.

One of the first significant results from New Horizons was a more precise measurement of Pluto’s diameter at roughly 2,370 km (1,473 miles), making it larger than many earlier estimates and about two-thirds the size of Earth’s Moon. Combined with Pluto’s well-known mass, the new size implies a lower bulk density, meaning Pluto contains more ice and less rock in its interior than previously thought. That has consequences for models of how Pluto and its binary partner Charon formed, and for interpretations of the Kuiper Belt environment where these bodies originated. The mission also settled a debate by reaffirming Pluto as the largest known object in the Kuiper Belt relative to rivals like Eris.

New Horizons’ instruments detected an icy polar cap on Pluto composed of methane and nitrogen ices, confirmed escaping nitrogen in Pluto’s tenuous atmosphere, and revealed a surprisingly complex, varied surface. Early imagery showed an orange-tinted globe with a bright, heart-shaped region and features such as cliffs, craters, chasms deeper and larger than the Grand Canyon, and broad expanses with tightly packed dimple-like patterns reminiscent of features seen on Neptune’s moon Triton. Much of Pluto’s surface appears relatively smooth in places, suggesting recent resurfacing and geological activity; why that resurfacing occurred — whether internal heating, long-lived effects from the Charon-forming impact, or other processes — remains under investigation.

The spacecraft also surveyed Pluto’s moons: Charon’s diameter was confirmed near previous estimates (about 1,208 km), while preliminary sizes for smaller moons Nix and Hydra were put at roughly 35 km and 45 km respectively; Kerberos and Styx are smaller and await better sizing from the flyby data. New Horizons performed a tightly choreographed automated sequence to hit a narrow “keyhole” in space with precise timing and orientation, because its high approach velocity made any collision with even small debris potentially catastrophic. Mission teams accepted a small risk from dust and debris, estimated at about one in 10,000 for a disabling hit.

Beyond characterizing Pluto itself, the mission advances broader planetary science: studying Pluto and Kuiper Belt objects sheds light on early solar system conditions, the distribution of ices and organics, atmospheric behavior in low-gravity environments, and processes that influenced Earth’s formation and volatile inventory. After the Pluto encounter, New Horizons continues outward into the Kuiper Belt and could be retargeted to fly past another object if mission extensions are approved. The flyby marked the completion of the initial robotic reconnaissance of the classical nine planets and opened a new era of detailed study of the outer solar system.

Mitt Romney scored a decisive victory in Florida’s Republican primary, reclaiming front-runner status by winning 47% to Newt Gingrich’s 32%, with Rick Santorum at 13% and Ron Paul 7%. The win delivered all 50 delegates and momentum ahead of Super Tuesday. Florida voters prioritized electability against President Obama; a majority said Romney was best positioned to beat Obama, while Gingrich attracted voters focused on ideological conservatism and strong tea party supporters. Romney’s appeal was broad—he won among women, Hispanics (notably Cuban-Americans), most age and income groups, and many who care about experience—though roughly 40% of voters viewed his positions as insufficiently conservative and very conservative evangelicals leaned to Gingrich. The campaign turned intensely negative, especially in the final week, and women’s concerns about Gingrich’s character likely hurt him; Romney enjoyed far stronger favorable ratings among female voters. Economic issues dominated voter concerns, with 6 in 10 citing the economy as their top issue and many reporting foreclosure impacts or financial strain. With improved organization, heavy ad spending, strong debate performances and early-vote advantages, Romney’s comeback blunted Gingrich’s momentum and positioned him as the likely nominee. The AP/Edison exit poll of 2,739 GOP voters carries a ±3-point margin.

President-elect Donald Trump intensified his public clash with the U.S. intelligence community this week by questioning their conclusions about Russian interference in the 2016 election and mocking planned briefings. On Twitter he suggested an intelligence meeting on alleged Russian hacking had been delayed “perhaps more time needed to build a case,” calling that “very strange.” He also echoed WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange’s claim that a “14-year-old kid could have hacked” John Podesta’s emails and that Russia did not supply the material to WikiLeaks. Assange reiterated his denial of state involvement in a Fox News interview, and Trump tweeted his support.

Intelligence officials and experts, however, maintain that Russia sought to influence the election, with the Obama administration saying the campaign reached the highest levels of the Russian government. U.S. officials disputed Trump’s assertion of a briefing delay: top intelligence leaders—the heads of the NSA, CIA, FBI and the director of national intelligence—were scheduled to brief him later in the week, not on the day he referenced. Trump did receive a Presidential Daily Briefing but not the comprehensive report on the hacks, which CIA Director John Brennan said was in its “final throes.”

The president-elect has repeatedly cast doubt on the intelligence community’s findings, arguing hacking attribution is difficult and asserting he knows things others do not. Critics, including Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and a senior intelligence official, warned Trump’s public antagonism toward career intelligence personnel is troubling. Separately, political news included Rex Tillerson’s commitment to divest Exxon ties if confirmed as secretary of state and Republicans’ reversal of a move to weaken the Office of Congressional Ethics after public backlash.

Reuters Breakingviews columnist defends BP’s decision to raise CEO Bob Dudley’s 2015 pay to about $19.6m, arguing the increase reflects the unusually hard job of running an oil major amid a steep oil-price slump. Dudley inherited the fallout from the 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster and has been judged to have made tangible progress: safety and spill metrics hit five-year lows, cultural reforms reduced risk-taking, and a settlement of up to $18.7bn helped clear the path for balance-sheet repair. By total shareholder return over three years, BP ranks mid‑pack among the six largest oil majors, despite the 2010 catastrophe. Dudley’s base pay remained flat; the headline rise largely came via pension adjustments and deferred share awards, making his package look generous compared with some peers but arguably aligned with the scale and difficulty of his remit.

However, investor sentiment turned sharply against the awards. Proxy advisers including Glass Lewis, ISS and others questioned whether maximum bonuses were earned in a year when BP recorded a $5.2bn loss, announced large job cuts, and slashed spending. At the April AGM, a historic 59% of proxy votes opposed the remuneration report — one of the largest rebukes against a UK company — marking the first time shareholders defeated BP’s pay decisions. The revolt mirrored broader trends of institutional investors taking a harder line on executive pay, bonus clawbacks and long-term incentive structures, especially where payouts seem at odds with company performance and shareholder pain.

BP defended the payouts, noting Dudley met targets tied to safety, cash generation and project delivery and that its remuneration policy had been approved by shareholders in 2014. Chairman Carl‑Henric Svanberg acknowledged shareholder anger, pledged to consult major investors and review pay arrangements, but said the board would not claw back payments already made. The episode underscores growing investor insistence on aligning executive rewards with outcomes and the reputational and governance risks when pay formulas produce contentious results.

The Shin Bet says it foiled an al-Qaida-directed plot after arresting three Palestinians recruited online by an operative in Gaza identified as Ariv Al-Sham. Recruits included Iyad Khalil Abu-Sara from east Jerusalem, Rubin Abu-Nagma, and Ala Anam; they allegedly planned coordinated bombings, shootings, kidnappings and a truck bombing targeting the Jerusalem Convention Center, a bus between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim, the U.S. Embassy in Tel Aviv, and emergency responders. Al-Sham reportedly recruited and trained them via Skype and Facebook, provided bomb-making files, arranged travel to Syria, and intended to send foreign terrorists into Israel with fake passports. Shin Bet sources warned the fast online radicalization and Gaza’s growing role as a base for al-Qaida-affiliated elements, alongside Hamas and Islamic Jihad, pose expanding regional threats.

This fall’s jewelry trend celebrates singlehood, closure, and alternative commitments. Sterling silver Venus-and-Mars rings, often worn on the right ring finger, echo 18th-century gender symbols and signal attraction. Novelty items like the Wedding Ring Coffin—a personalized casket for decommissioned wedding rings—offer symbolic closure after divorce. Retailers market “single” rings in many styles: the Ah Ring (“available and happy”) with diamonds, My Single Ring bands worn by men and women as discreet or bold signals of availability, and gag pieces like the Ms. Taken ring to repel persistent suitors. Specialty designers also serve same-sex couples with tailored commitment bands, such as interlocking white-gold male-symbol rings. A thriving resale market for used engagement rings complements these trends, while many consumers use keepsakes like coffins to bury the past and move forward.

Tancrède Melet, a 32-year-old French stuntman renowned for base-jumping, wingsuit flying, slacklining and other extreme-air pursuits, died while preparing a hot-air-balloon stunt in southeastern France. Melet was a founding member and visible leader of the “Flying Frenchies” (also called the “Skyliners”), a collective famous for pioneering highlining—walking slacklines between distant points such as mountain peaks, cable cars and even between hot-air balloons. The group’s daring videos, including viral clips, helped make them internationally known.

Witnesses say Melet and four crew members were anchored to a balloon on the ground when the balloon unexpectedly lifted. The others released their anchors and descended safely, but Melet became stuck and was left suspended roughly 30 meters (about 100 feet) above ground. Initial reports indicate his anchor later released, and he fell, suffering fatal trauma. French authorities are investigating the circumstances of the accident.

Melet’s trajectory was notable: after working four years as an engineer and growing tired of a conventional 9-to-5 life, he left to pursue flight and aerial acrobatics full time. He was celebrated not only for his technical skill—base-jumping off Mont Blanc’s Italian slopes, tightrope and slackline feats at extreme heights, climbing, kayaking and kiting—but for embodying a free-spirited, working-class inspiration. The Flying Frenchies and fellow Skyliners paid tribute on social media, describing him as a “surprising lover of life” who left “wonderful memories” and a “taste of freedom.” Melet is survived by his partner, Tiphaine Breillot, and their young child.

Conservationists warn that an ongoing outbreak of crown-of-thorns starfish on the Great Barrier Reef risks becoming the worst on record. A WWF‑Australia‑commissioned report estimates the current population at between four and 12 million but projects it could swell to 60 million by 2020, a scale co-author Glen Holmes compared to “a locust plague devastating vegetation.” Over the past 30 years these coral-eating starfish are believed to have caused the loss of roughly 60,000 hectares of live coral. If the outbreak follows historical patterns, coral cover on affected reefs could fall below 10 percent.

Experts say little can be done to halt the present surge, so priority must shift to preventing future plagues. They point to agricultural runoff—specifically nutrient-rich chemical fertilizers—that promotes algal blooms which feed juvenile starfish. Reducing catchment pollution, they argue, would “starve the baby crown-of-thorns starfish” and reduce the likelihood and severity of subsequent outbreaks, giving the reef a chance to recover and rebuild coral cover. Critics say current state and national investments have not met modest pollution-reduction targets and call for increased funding and tougher measures to cut runoff.

Separately, efforts to broaden public engagement with reef ecosystems include new underwater panoramic imagery added to Google Maps through a partnership with the Catlin Seaview Survey and the World Wonders Project. The Street View–style photos, captured with a specialized SVII camera, allow users worldwide to virtually explore reef life—from sea turtles to manta rays—without leaving shore, raising awareness of the reef’s value and vulnerabilities.

The Sesame Street YouTube channel was reportedly hacked, with its content removed or set to private and replaced by a pornographic banner and a 7-minute adult video. The description credited users “MrEdxwx” and “MrSuicider91” for the attack; one named account later denied involvement on his own channel. The explicit clip remained online for about 20 minutes before YouTube removed it and temporarily shut the channel. Most videos have since been restored, and neither PBS, YouTube nor Google issued an immediate comment.

A furious customer went on a destructive rampage inside an Apple Store in Dijon, France, on September 29, 2016, smashing iPhones, MacBooks and iPads with a small steel pétanque ball. Eyewitness video captured him calmly breaking display units while announcing in French that Apple had violated European consumer rights and refused to reimburse him after a refund dispute. He declared, “Give me my money back,” then proceeded to wreck merchandise. A security guard apprehended him and he was later arrested, with local reports noting considerable damage and a failed escape attempt. The incident was widely shared online and covered by outlets including Mashable.

The 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded jointly to Arthur Ashkin (U.S.), Gérard Mourou (France) and Donna Strickland (Canada) for breakthroughs in laser physics. Ashkin received half the prize for inventing “optical tweezers,” a laser-based technique that can trap and manipulate tiny particles—including atoms, viruses, bacteria and living cells—without harming them. That method has become a vital tool for studying biological systems. The other half of the prize was shared by Mourou and Strickland for developing chirped pulse amplification (CPA), which produces extremely short, intense laser pulses by stretching, amplifying and then compressing pulses. CPA enabled a wide range of industrial and medical applications, notably corrective laser eye surgery and high-power laser therapies for cancer. Strickland’s award marks the first time in 55 years that a woman has won the Nobel in Physics; she is the third female laureate after Marie Curie (1903) and Maria Goeppert-Mayer (1963). Laureates and institutions hailed the practical impact of the work, from fundamental studies of life’s machinery to technologies now used worldwide. The prize carries a 9-million-kronor (~$1.01 million) award.

Supermodel Gisele Bündchen told CBS This Morning that her husband, New England Patriots quarterback Tom Brady, “had a concussion last year” and that he “has concussions pretty much every” season, comments that have raised concerns about unreported head injuries and player safety. Bündchen, who champions health and environmental causes and promotes a plant-based lifestyle she says has benefited Brady, expressed worry about the long-term effects of repeated head trauma and said she hopes he stays healthy into old age. The NFL responded that it reviewed reports from unaffiliated neurotrauma consultants, certified athletic trainer spotters, and club injury submissions from the 2016 season and found no records indicating Brady suffered a head injury, concussion symptoms, or complaints; the league said it would coordinate with the NFLPA to gather more information. The Patriots did not immediately comment, and Brady’s agent hadn’t responded to inquiries. Brady, 39, started 12 regular-season games and three playoff games in the 2016 campaign, which culminated in a Super Bowl win; he missed four games earlier that season due to suspension. Brady has publicly said he aims to play into his mid-40s, a prospect that worries Bündchen given her concerns about repeated concussions and their long-term impact on his health.

Seventeen-year-old Johran McCormick was fatally shot early March 13 after being found in a 16-year-old girl’s bedroom in a Spring-area home. Investigators say the girl let Johran in; when her younger brother spotted feet under the bed and fetched their father, the father confronted Johran around 2:30 a.m. According to deputies, the girl denied knowing Johran, an argument followed, and the father — who told authorities Johran reached as if for a weapon — fired a single shot that killed the teen. Johran’s grieving parents, Shawn Curley and Zakia McCormick, and community supporters demand criminal charges. They want the 55-year-old father prosecuted and also urge the district attorney to consider charging the girl with accessory to murder or involuntary manslaughter for allegedly lying and precipitating the confrontation. Law enforcement continues its probe and will forward findings to a grand jury; experts say a self-defense claim could complicate murder charges. Friends and neighbors held a vigil as the family mourned a typical teen with big plans.

Deadpool 2 largely repeats the formula that made the first film a hit, ramping up gore, absurdity and shock humor while keeping the sharp, self-aware voice that defines its antihero. Ryan Reynolds returns as Wade Wilson/Deadpool, a wisecracking, unkillable mutant whose accelerated healing makes cartoonish dismemberment a running gag. The sequel leans hard into meta-commentary, openly mocking comic-book movie tropes, its own “lazy writing,” and pop-culture touchstones—from John Hughes films to The Passion of the Christ—while frequently breaking the fourth wall to taunt the audience.

The plot is deliberately simple yet playfully convoluted: after villains separate Deadpool from his love Vanessa (Morena Baccarin), he briefly spirals into suicidal despair before reassembling a makeshift family. He trains briefly at the X‑Men academy and takes on the role of reluctant mentor to Firefist (Julian Dennison), a troubled, chubby 14-year-old whose flame powers and orphaned backstory make him a target. The pair end up in a Supermax prison, where Cable (Josh Brolin), a time-traveling, Terminator-like soldier, arrives bent on killing Firefist to stop a future catastrophe. Domino (Zazie Beetz), whose power is pure, chaotic luck, joins the ensemble and delivers one of the film’s standout, effortless performances.

Beyond the surface-level action and set pieces—samurai-sword battles, grotesque limb-regrowth gags, and celebrity cameos—Deadpool 2 stages a wider satire. It skewers fandom, questions cinematic solemnity (including the dour tone of some DC movies), and delights in asking audiences whether they should feel guilty for enjoying the spectacle. Emotional beats are sparse—only a couple of genuinely human moments land amid the chaos—but the film’s relentless, raunchy humor and Reynolds’ magnetic, off-kilter charm keep it engaging. For viewers who relish unpredictable, boundary-pushing comedies that both lampoon and revel in superhero conventions, Deadpool 2 is a must-see; for those seeking novelty beyond amplified excess, it often feels like “more of the same.” The closing, absurd subplot about a disfigured cafeteria chef’s bizarre quest underscores the film’s appetite for lowbrow, gleefully subversive silliness.

DineEquity, parent company of Applebee’s and IHOP, announced plans to close up to 160 restaurants as it reshapes its casual-dining portfolio amid shifting consumer preferences toward quick-service chains like Panera and Chipotle. The company said 105–135 Applebee’s and about 20–25 IHOP locations will be shuttered, increases from earlier estimates. Simultaneously, DineEquity expects to open 125 new restaurants globally—revising plans to add 20–30 Applebee’s (mostly abroad) and 80–95 IHOPs (primarily in the U.S.). Executives framed closures as necessary to improve franchisee economics, supply chain efficiency and long-term brand health, calling underperforming sites “well-below average” and harmful to guest experience. The company reported Q2 net income of $20.9 million, down from $26.4 million a year earlier, with Applebee’s comp sales falling 6.2% and IHOP’s down 2.6%. Leadership changes include new CEO Stephen Joyce; the CFO role remains vacant. DineEquity operates over 3,700 restaurants in 19 countries.

A Dartmouth College study has reaffirmed the authenticity of the well-known backyard photograph of Lee Harvey Oswald holding the same type of rifle used to assassinate President John F. Kennedy. Published in the Journal of Digital Forensics, Security and Law, the study addresses longstanding claims that the photograph was a forgery, focusing particularly on assertions that Oswald’s pose in the image is physically implausible. Senior author Hany Farid, a digital forensics expert, led the research, building on his earlier work that had already rebutted claims about inconsistent lighting and shadows in the image.

Farid collaborated with Assistant Professor Emily Whiting and graduate student Srivamshi Pittala to create a physiologically plausible 3-D model of Oswald and to pose it to match the photograph. By assigning realistic mass to body segments and conducting a balance analysis, the team tested whether the stance depicted could be maintained without tipping or unnatural support. Their results show that, although Oswald appears off-balance to some observers, the pose is in fact stable. The study also reaffirmed earlier findings that lighting and shadows in the photograph are physically plausible and demonstrated that the rifle’s length in the image is consistent with the known dimensions of the weapon used in the assassination.

The research counters a set of conspiracy-driven arguments—such as alleged facial mismatches, shadow inconsistencies, and improbable proportions—that have been used to contend the photo was manipulated. Past official inquiries, including the Warren Commission and the House Select Committee on Assassinations, likewise found no evidence of tampering. Farid emphasizes that the detailed 3-D modeling technique used here is a powerful forensic tool that can be adapted to assess pose stability, shadows, and proportions in other images by adjusting the model’s physical parameters, offering a rigorous method to evaluate the physical plausibility of photographic evidence.

Baltimore erupted in violent unrest after Freddie Gray, who died from a spinal injury sustained in police custody, prompting looting, arson, 250+ arrests, 20 officers hurt, and 19 buildings burned. Thousands of police and National Guard enforced a weeklong curfew as officials debated the timing of reinforcements; six officers were suspended and the DOJ opened a civil-rights probe. Separately, a proposal urges Baltimore to invest in six connected regional bike trails—costing less than a highway interchange—to link neighborhoods, boost recreation, tourism, transit, and economic development.

A charter bus operated by OGA Charters rolled over Saturday morning on U.S. Highway 83 about 45–46 miles north of Laredo, Texas, en route to a casino in Eagle Pass, killing eight people and injuring 44. Seven victims died at the scene; an eighth died later at Doctors Hospital in Laredo. The driver survived. The crash occurred just before 11:30 a.m. in rainy conditions, though investigators said it was too early to determine whether weather contributed. No other vehicles were involved, and troopers reported the driver “lost control” before the rollover. Injured passengers were taken to hospitals in Laredo, Carrizo Springs and San Antonio; many were listed in stable condition.

The National Transportation Safety Board sent investigators to Laredo to probe the wreck and planned to assess company operations as part of the inquiry. Subsequent reporting revealed that federal and state inspection records show OGA Charters had been ordered twice in 2015—during Louisiana inspections—to remove a bus from service for brake problems and emergency-exit issues. It was unclear whether the sidelined bus was the one in the crash or what repairs were made. OGA Charters, a small company based in San Juan, Texas, had two buses on file with the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration; inspections since 2014 listed 15 violations, including brake and hours-of-service issues. Safety advocates expressed concern that prior vehicle violations might indicate maintenance lapses.
