Authorities continue investigating causes; names of victims and some details have been released by local media.

President Trump, speaking Friday in Bedminster, New Jersey, declined to rule out military action in two international crises. When asked if the United States would go to war with North Korea after warning of a possible “bad solution,” Trump replied, “I think you know the answer to that.” Flanked by Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and UN Ambassador Nikki Haley, he said his Cabinet is largely unified and stressed the need to stop North Korea’s provocations. Tillerson and Defense Secretary Jim Mattis have emphasized diplomacy, but Trump has repeatedly used bellicose language—at one point promising “big, big trouble” if North Korea targets Guam and earlier threatening “fire and fury.” Trump defended his rhetoric as presidential strength, saying critics would praise identical comments from someone else and that many Americans support his stance.

Trump also would not rule out military intervention in Venezuela amid violent unrest and shortages of food and medicine. He said a military option is possible but declined to discuss details, while the White House refused a request from President Nicolás Maduro for a call until democracy is restored. The administration imposed sanctions after Maduro pushed through a contested constitutional assembly. Latin American governments, including Peru, Mexico and Colombia, condemned Trump’s mention of force as contrary to U.N. principles and warned against foreign intervention. Venezuela’s government dismissed the U.S. statements as hostile, and regional bodies reiterated rejection of force even as Venezuela’s new assembly moved up governors’ elections amid ongoing protests and economic collapse.

On July 23, 2015, a gunman opened fire during a screening of the comedy Trainwreck at the Grand Theatre in Lafayette, Louisiana, killing two women and wounding nine others before fatally shooting himself. Police identified the attacker as 59-year-old John Russell (Russel) Houser, a drifter who had recently been in the Lafayette area after living previously in Phenix City, Alabama. Authorities said Houser fired about 13 times inside the theater; he reportedly sat alone, stood up roughly 20 minutes into the film, and began shooting. Witnesses described hearing loud pops and seeing muzzle flashes; several patrons escaped uninjured but traumatized. Officers arrived quickly, thwarting his apparent attempt to flee—he had parked near an exit—and investigators found wigs and disguises in a motel room they were examining in connection with the case.

Police and court records show Houser had an arrest history dating back a decade or more, including charges such as arson and selling alcohol to a minor, and numerous minor traffic violations in Alabama. In 2008 his wife and family members sought a temporary protective order citing “extreme erratic behavior,” ominous statements, family violence, and mental health concerns including alleged bipolar disorder; his wife said she removed weapons from their home and later filed for divorce.

An extensive electronic trail revealed Houser as an active, outspoken online commenter under names like “Rusty Houser.” He posted frequently on immigration, race, free speech, and apocalyptic views of America’s future, expressing very conservative and Tea Party–aligned positions and praising extremist groups like Greece’s Golden Dawn. His online writings showed distrust of mainstream media, obsession with censorship and free-speech grievances, racialized language, and dark rhetoric implying violent outcomes for large swaths of the population. The shooting prompted federal-level briefings; President Obama was informed while traveling abroad and offered condolences. Authorities continued to investigate motive, links, and the shooter’s recent movements.

Colorado corrections chief Tom Clements, 58, was shot dead outside his Monument home around 8:30 p.m., prompting a manhunt and an investigation that involves the FBI and Colorado Bureau of Investigation. Witnesses reported a dark, boxy car leaving the scene; search dogs and door-to-door inquiries followed. Authorities have not ruled out a connection to Clements’s role as executive director of the Colorado Department of Corrections; he had recently denied a Saudi inmate’s request to serve his sentence abroad. Governor John Hickenlooper, visibly shaken, praised Clements as kind and effective, ordered flags at half-staff, and increased security for state officials. The killing recalled past unsolved or politically charged slayings of public safety officials. Separately, the state’s political landscape has shifted after the Aurora theater massacre: Gov. Hickenlooper, once skeptical about stricter gun laws, pushed through sweeping gun-control measures including expanded background checks and magazine limits. He framed the reforms as pragmatic, data-driven steps intended to reduce violence despite heated opposition.

China warned it will retaliate if the United States imposes new tariffs after reports the Trump administration may raise duties on an additional $200 billion of Chinese goods to 25% (up from a planned 10%). Beijing’s foreign ministry spokesman Geng Shuang urged dialogue but warned unilateral U.S. pressure would be counterproductive and said China would defend its lawful rights, without specifying responses. The dispute follows U.S. 25% tariffs on $34 billion of Chinese goods and matching Chinese tariffs. The Trump administration may also impose duties on another $16 billion of imports imminently. Behind the headlines, U.S. and Chinese officials, including representatives of Treasury Secretary Mnuchin and Vice Premier Liu He, have been holding private talks to restart negotiations, though formats and timetables are unsettled and high-level talks have stalled. Internal U.S. divisions — notably between Mnuchin and harder-line Trade Representative Lighthizer — complicate efforts. The standoff and broader trade tensions have unsettled markets and prompted Chinese policymakers to emphasize growth amid external risks and domestic deleveraging pressures.

The American Psychiatric Association released DSM-5, its fifth major revision, intended as a clinical guidebook and reflecting years of public comment and revision. The manual is organized into three sections: guidance on use; categorical diagnoses with chapters arranged to show relationships among disorders and framed by age, gender, and development; and a third section with self-assessments and conditions needing further research. Notable structural changes include elimination of the multi-axial system and roughly the same number of disorders as DSM-IV. Major diagnostic changes: autism spectrum disorder now unites autism, Asperger’s, childhood disintegrative disorder, and PDD-NOS; disruptive mood dysregulation disorder addresses over-diagnosis of pediatric bipolar disorder; ADHD criteria acknowledge adult persistence (one fewer symptom required for adults, symptom onset by age 12, and stronger cross-situational requirements); removal of the bereavement exclusion for major depression with a detailed footnote guiding distinction from grief; PTSD criteria expanded to four clusters and made developmentally sensitive; dementia is reclassified as Major Neurocognitive Disorder, and Mild Neurocognitive Disorder is newly added. Binge eating, premenstrual dysphoric, and hoarding disorders gained formal recognition. The release prompted debate: NIMH advocates a research-driven RDoC framework aimed at biological bases, critics warn DSM-5 may lower diagnostic thresholds, while APA leaders emphasize its clinical utility and the need for practical guidance now.

A Singapore Airlines Boeing 777-300ER operating flight SQ368 to Milan experienced an engine-related emergency on June 27 after departing Changi Airport in the early hours. About two hours into the flight, the crew announced an engine oil warning and turned the aircraft back to Singapore. Passengers reported hearing unusual vibrations and a faint fuel-like smell before the return. The jet landed at Changi around 6:50 a.m., and shortly afterward the right engine ignited. Fire crews from the Airport Emergency Service arrived quickly and extinguished the blaze within minutes using water and foam; eyewitnesses described flames about a meter high and heat blackening the wing. All 222 passengers and 19 crew disembarked safely with no injuries reported.

Several passengers recounted tense moments as flames rose and some attempted to retrieve carry-on bags; cabin crew repeatedly urged everyone to remain seated and calm while firefighters worked. Dramatic photos and videos of the burning engine and foamy aftermath were shared on social media by passengers. Singapore Airlines confirmed the aircraft was towed away for cleanup and investigation; a replacement flight with a new crew departed for Milan after 10 a.m., and passengers were offered options to reschedule or defer travel. Many continued on the rescheduled service, reporting a largely calm atmosphere in the lounge prior to departure.

Singapore’s Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong and Transport Minister Khaw Boon Wan praised the swift emergency response and said authorities, including the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore and Singapore Airlines, would investigate the cause and review procedures. The incident underscored effective emergency response and crew management, while prompting an inquiry into the engine oil warning and subsequent fire.

During the Olympic 4x400 relay heat, American sprinter Manteo Mitchell broke his left fibula mid-race but nevertheless finished his 200-meter leg, helping the U.S. qualify for the final. Mitchell, running the leadoff leg, felt his fibula snap about 200 meters from the finish yet pushed through intense pain to complete the lap in 46.1 seconds; the team finished the heat in 2:58.87. Initially believing the problem might be a cramp, Mitchell later learned an X-ray showed a complete break of the smaller lower-leg bone. Doctors estimated the fibula would heal in four to six weeks. The fibula is largely non–weight-bearing compared with the tibia, so running on a broken fibula is possible but typically extremely painful and debilitating—Mitchell’s time and resolve were widely noted as impressive under the circumstances. Mitchell reported the fracture stemmed from an earlier misstep on stairs before the Games, though he felt fine warming up before the relay. He maintained good spirits afterward, joking about the phrase “break a leg.” USA Track and Field has not yet announced his replacement; two other relay pool members, Jeremy Wariner and LaShawn Merritt, are sidelined with hamstring injuries, so the team may call on a 400-meter hurdler such as Angelo Taylor or Kerron Clement.

Vice President Joe Biden has not joined President Barack Obama and several Cabinet members in publicly pledging to return a portion of his salary in response to the sequestration cuts, his office said. Biden will consider taking a pay reduction only if his own staff are affected by furloughs; he is committed to "sharing the burden of the sequester with his staff." Obama announced a 5 percent pay cut for 2013 (about $20,000), while others such as Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel and Attorney General Eric Holder said they would give up pay equivalent to 14 days, and Secretary of State John Kerry pledged 5 percent to charity. The $85 billion automatic cuts were intended to force a bipartisan deal, but when lawmakers failed to agree they went into effect March 1, with agency impacts and furloughs still rolling out. Biden’s more modest personal wealth compared with many Cabinet members has been noted as a factor in his decision to wait; his office clarified he has not declined a pay cut but is holding off pending staff impacts.

Google admitted its Street View cars mistakenly collected fragments of payload data from unencrypted Wi‑Fi networks for about three years. Originally saying they only logged SSIDs and MAC addresses to improve location services, Google reexamined its systems after German regulators asked and found legacy code unintentionally captured snippets of network traffic. The company says collection was limited — cars were moving, cycled channels five times per second, and did not gather complete sessions — and that the data was never used in products. Google has grounded the vehicles, isolated the data, plans to delete what was collected, will commission an independent review of the software, and is cooperating with regulators. The incident highlights sloppy engineering and privacy risk; users are urged to password‑protect their Wi‑Fi networks.

Gil Scott-Heron, the influential poet and musician often called a progenitor of hip-hop, died in New York at 62. Born in Chicago in 1949, he grew up in Jackson, Tenn., spent time in The Bronx and at Lincoln University, and eventually settled in Manhattan. His recording career began with 1970’s Small Talk at 125th and Lenox, which included the seminal spoken-word piece "The Revolution Will Not Be Televised"—a satirical, culturally resonant track that made him widely known and has been frequently referenced and parodied. By age twenty-three he had published novels and poetry and recorded several albums. Scott-Heron continued recording through the 1970s and early ’80s, returned briefly in 1994 with Spirits—warning the emerging hip-hop generation to use power responsibly—and after struggles with substance abuse and legal problems in the 2000s resumed performing following his 2007 release and earned acclaim for 2010’s I’m New Here. Known for blending blues, spoken word and political critique—he preferred “bluesologist” to grand titles—Scott-Heron lived modestly in Harlem, beloved by peers and cited as an influence by artists such as Kanye West, who sampled his voice on a major album.

Mitt Romney won the Illinois Republican primary handily, with about 48% to Rick Santorum’s 34%, Ron Paul’s 9% and Newt Gingrich’s 8% with 55% of precincts reporting, positioning Illinois as Romney’s largest big-state victory since Florida. The margin bolstered Romney’s delegate lead and increased pressure on Republicans to bring the protracted primary to a close. Exit polls showed voters prioritized electability over ideological purity, benefiting Romney. His financial edge was decisive: Romney and the Restore Our Future super PAC spent $3.7 million on Illinois advertising versus roughly $532,000 for Santorum and allied groups, particularly dominating costly Chicago media. Santorum, who campaigned in Illinois but also spent time elsewhere including Puerto Rico and Gettysburg, conceded the state but vowed to continue his insurgent campaign, predicting wins in Louisiana and his native Pennsylvania. On the stump in Gettysburg, Santorum delivered a populist, freedom-focused speech attacking big government, Obama, Romney and Gingrich on issues like health care and climate policy, framed his campaign as defending working-class Americans, and insisted he wouldn’t drop out, urging supporters to press on for upcoming contests.

Charlie Gard, an 11-month-old British infant with a rare mitochondrial depletion syndrome that left him brain damaged and unable to breathe unaided, drew global attention as his parents, Connie Yates and Chris Gard, sought experimental treatment abroad. More than £1.3 million was raised via crowdfunding for a U.S. therapy, and GoFundMe donated £10,000; the family announced plans to use donations to establish The Charlie Gard Foundation to support research into mitochondrial and other rare childhood diseases, provide information and advocacy for parents facing similar situations, and clarify parental rights and access to treatment. Despite international offers of help — including public interventions from Pope Francis and President Donald Trump, interest from Italy’s Bambino Gesù hospital, and an offer from NewYork–Presbyterian/Columbia to admit and evaluate Charlie or ship experimental drugs pending legal clearance and FDA approval — British courts and Great Ormond Street Hospital repeatedly ruled the proposed treatment would be futile and risk causing suffering. The European Court of Human Rights declined to intervene, and judges determined decisions should prioritize the child’s best interests over parental wishes. Following exhausted appeals, Charlie’s life support was planned to be withdrawn; the family announced he passed away, asking for privacy and thanking supporters. The case highlighted ethical tensions between parental rights, medical judgment, and limits of medicine even in wealthy nations.

Researchers conducted a large meta-analysis to clarify the long-debated relationship between human brain size and intelligence. They compiled 88 studies (148 mixed-sex samples, over 8,000 participants), using MRI-derived in vivo brain volume measures and IQ scores. The pooled correlation between brain volume and IQ was positive but small (r = .24, R2 = .06), indicating brain volume accounts for roughly 6% of variance in IQ. This modest association generalized across age groups (children and adults), IQ domains (full-scale, performance, verbal), and sexes.

Crucially, the authors identified and corrected for publication and dissemination biases: studies reporting strong positive correlations were disproportionately published, while smaller or null associations were underreported. After adjusting for these biases, the association remained statistically reliable but weaker than often portrayed in the literature, and reported effect sizes have declined over time. The team emphasizes that the observed link is correlational, not causal; brain size should not be treated as an isomorphic proxy for intelligence differences.

The review highlights reasons to prioritize brain structure and integrity over sheer volume. Cross-species comparisons and within-human evidence—such as no sex differences in IQ despite average male-female brain size differences, and conditions like megalencephaly associated with lower IQ—suggest that microstructural and organizational features drive cognitive ability more than absolute size. The authors conclude that while brain volume plays a small compensatory role, structural properties of the brain are more meaningful biological substrates of human intelligence.

Federal and state investigators determined that 13 bald eagles found Feb. 20 on Maryland’s Eastern Shore did not die of natural causes, though officials have not disclosed how they died. The birds, discovered near Federalsburg on farmland and nearby woods, showed no outward trauma, prompting necropsies that also ruled out disease such as avian influenza. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service spokeswoman Catherine Hibbard said details — including information about suspects — are being withheld to avoid compromising the ongoing probe, which is now focused on prosecuting anyone responsible. Maryland Natural Resources Police are assisting federal authorities, and a $25,000 reward has been posted for information leading to a conviction. Killing a protected bald eagle carries substantial fines and potential prison time.

A 36-year-old woman from Florida discovered an unusual souvenir from her honeymoon in Belize: a living human botfly larva embedded in her groin. Two months after returning, she noticed an itchy, pimple-like reddish lesion with a central hole and some pus. Initial treatment by a primary care physician—sulfamethoxazole—reduced redness but did not resolve the lesion. When she sought a second opinion at a wound clinic in Tampa, the treating physician felt a hard, egg-like firmness beneath the skin and consulted a surgeon. The surgeon suspected a parasitic larva; under local anesthesia a 5 mm incision revealed a tapered, spiny maggot later identified by pathology as Dermatobia hominis, the human botfly. After removal the lesion fully resolved within a week.

Human botflies are uncommon in the U.S. but frequent in tropical Central and South America. Females deposit eggs on carrier insects (like mosquitoes); when the carrier bites a human, warmth triggers egg hatching and larvae burrow beneath the skin, where they can live 27–128 days. Larvae maintain a small breathing hole and may be felt moving; their bodies bear rows of spines that complicate extraction. In endemic areas, locals use occlusive home remedies—petroleum jelly, bacon, nail polish, or plant extracts—to suffocate the larva, prompting it to emerge for manual removal. Left untreated, larvae can mature and enlarge the wound. Myiasis from botflies is among the more common skin ailments travelers bring back from developing regions, underscoring the need to consider parasitic causes for persistent, atypical skin lesions after tropical travel.

European leaders and central banks are urgently preparing for the fallout of a possible Greek exit from the euro, as political instability and capital flight intensify contagion risks across the bloc and beyond. Bank of England governor Mervyn King warned the eurozone was “tearing itself apart,” while David Cameron said Europe must quickly choose between deeper integration or facing uncharted danger. Markets increasingly view a Greek departure as possible after inconclusive elections and growing withdrawals—billions left Greek banks in days—raising fears of a disorderly default that could cost about 5% of EU output (roughly $1tn). The ECB, national central banks and rescue funds face large exposures via Greek sovereign bonds, ECB loans to Greek banks and TARGET2 payment imbalances; losses could overwhelm ECB capital and force costly recapitalizations, with Germany and France among the hardest hit. Officials in London, Brussels and Washington debate growth-focused responses versus austerity. Greek Syriza leader Alexis Tsipras rejects austerity, promising renegotiation if his bloc wins the new vote, while interim leaders aim to steady the country before the 17 June election.

President Trump used his Davos World Economic Forum address to promote his “America First” agenda while courting global investors. He touted U.S. economic gains—2.4 million jobs since his election, record stock-market wealth, low unemployment for African- and Hispanic-Americans, and 2.6% GDP growth in Q4 2017—and credited his administration’s tax overhaul and regulatory rollbacks for restoring U.S. competitiveness. Trump highlighted the corporate tax cut from 35% to 21%, employer bonuses, higher household income projections, and large repatriation and investment commitments like Apple’s announced plan to bring profits home. He framed regulation as “stealth taxation,” claiming his team has eliminated far more rules than promised to free businesses and attract capital.

While insisting America will always protect its own interests, Trump said “America first does not mean America alone,” arguing U.S. growth benefits the world. He called for fair, reciprocal trade, criticized intellectual property theft, subsidies and state-led economic distortions, and said the U.S. will enforce trade laws and seek bilateral deals, including with TPP countries. On security, he cited campaigns to denuclearize North Korea, pressure Iran, and defeat ISIS, and urged allies to shoulder more defense costs. He also pushed for immigration reform toward a merit-based system and emphasized workforce investment.

Reactions were mixed: some business leaders welcomed the pro-growth message, while critics called the speech self-centered and tone-deaf. Trump’s attacks on the media and ongoing controversies, including reports he sought to fire Mueller, persisted in the background.

Nathan “Bodie” Barksdale, the notorious 1980s Baltimore drug figure long linked to HBO’s The Wire, has died at 54 in a federal medical prison in North Carolina of natural causes after an illness, officials said. Barksdale ran a violent heroin operation in public-housing complexes including Murphy Homes and Lexington Terrace, survived more than 20 gunshot wounds that led to an amputation, and was implicated in brutal crimes that included a 1985 conviction for torturing three people. He was acquitted in 1982 in the killing of his former mentor, Frank Harper.

Despite efforts later in life to work with Baltimore’s Safe Streets anti-violence program, Barksdale relapsed into heroin addiction and was arrested in a 2014 DEA wiretap probe, pleading guilty to participating in a heroin conspiracy tied to the Black Guerrilla Family and receiving nearly four years in federal prison. He released a low-budget DVD dramatizing his life, The Avon Barksdale Story: Legends of the Unwired, which featured an interview with Wood Harris, who played Avon Barksdale on The Wire.

Series creator David Simon has said Barksdale’s life informed anecdotal elements across multiple characters but was not the direct model for Avon. Barksdale maintained he had done community work and counseled youth, though a judge at sentencing remarked that while he had given back some, he had “taken a lot” and still owed restitution to the community. Attempts to reach his family were unsuccessful.

Investigators arrested 32-year-old Joseph Michael Schreiber in connection with an arson that heavily damaged the Islamic Center of Fort Pierce. The late-night blaze occurred on a major Muslim holiday, Eid al-Adha, and on the 15th anniversary of 9/11. No one was injured, but worshippers were forced to relocate services. Authorities developed Schreiber as a suspect after a tip and surveillance video showing a motorcyclist fleeing the scene; deputies later found a matching motorcycle at his home. After his arrest, Schreiber allegedly confessed, saying he didn’t intend to hurt anyone and was embarrassed. Investigators also found multiple anti-Islamic posts on his social media, including a message declaring “ALL ISLAM IS RADICAL.” The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office is treating the case as a hate crime; under Florida law Schreiber faces arson charges that carry a mandatory minimum of 30 years because he is a prison-release reoffender, and could face life if designated a habitual offender. The FBI is investigating potential federal charges. The mosque had previously received threats and intimidation since being linked to Omar Mateen.

Amal Clooney has joined Yazidi survivor Nadia Murad in an international campaign to document ISIS atrocities and push for prosecutions at the International Criminal Court (ICC) and other tribunals. Visiting refugee camps in northern Greece and a German resettlement program, Clooney met survivors who recounted mass killings, abductions and systematic sexual slavery inflicted by ISIS on Yazidis—a minority whose religion and existence ISIS sought to eradicate. A United Nations inquiry estimates more than 5,000 killed and at least 3,200 still held captive. Murad, who escaped after being raped and enslaved in 2014 and who has lost her mother and six brothers, has become a prominent advocate: testifying before the U.S. Congress, addressing the U.N., founding an organization for survivors, and serving as a U.N. Goodwill Ambassador. Nominated for a Nobel Peace Prize, she insists survivors want “their day in court.”

Clooney and Murad are urging the international community to collect evidence—survivor interviews and exhumations of mass graves—to enable prosecutions. They seek either an Iraqi invitation to the ICC or a U.N. Security Council referral; both Syria and Iraq are not ICC members, complicating jurisdiction. Clooney has lobbied diplomats in New York and plans outreach to Russian and Chinese officials, noting past Security Council resistance to ICC referrals. Describing the crimes as genocide and a “bureaucracy of evil on an industrial scale,” Clooney frames the task as both legal and moral: to hold ISIS leaders accountable and prevent impunity. Survivors’ testimonies—harrowing accounts of rape, murder, child indoctrination and slavery—are already part of the case file. Despite threats and ongoing risks, Murad and Clooney remain steadfast, arguing that achieving justice will restore dignity and hope to the Yazidi community.

Brussels officials say chronic tunnel repairs have been delayed because original construction plans were lost — reportedly eaten by mice. A parliamentary commission investigating the dilapidated 7.1 miles of traffic tunnels heard that plans archived in 1989 inside a pier beneath a viaduct remained there for two decades. When workers relocated them in 2010 after demolition of the viaduct, the documents were allegedly chewed through by rodents. The story provoked amusement and frustration as EU leaders met in the city. Tunnel closures from crumbling concrete have worsened gridlock in the capital of 1.2 million, home to EU and NATO HQs, and repairs are estimated around €1 billion. Former officials said warnings about deterioration and shortages of engineers were issued years earlier, and that authorities had favored emergency fixes over costly, disruptive deep renovations. Critics say the episode underscores broader governance and infrastructure failures in Brussels.

WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange, who sought asylum in Ecuador’s London embassy in 2012 to avoid extradition to Sweden over sexual assault allegations, said he would surrender to British police if a U.N. Working Group on Arbitrary Detention ruled against him. The panel, which had been investigating his claim that his confinement in the embassy amounted to arbitrary detention, informed Britain and Sweden of its findings on Jan. 22 and was due to publish them in early February; Swedish officials indicated the panel had concluded he was arbitrarily detained. The working group’s determinations are not legally binding in the UK, and British authorities and Prime Minister David Cameron’s office reiterated that an outstanding European arrest warrant and alleged rape allegation mean Assange would be subject to arrest if he left the embassy. Assange and his lawyers argued that changes in UK law since 2012 and his inability to exercise asylum rights rendered his continued presence in the embassy unlawful; they urged Sweden to drop the case if the U.N. ruling found in his favor. Sweden said it would reply to the panel and did not accept its conclusions, stressing that its prosecutors would continue court procedures. Assange’s team also demanded assurances from the UK that he would not face U.S. extradition over WikiLeaks publications. While police ended overt 24-hour surveillance of the embassy in 2015, covert measures and arrest plans remained in place.

A Dallas County lawsuit alleges the Boy Scouts of America (BSA) was negligent in the June heat-stroke death of 15-year-old Reid Comita at Buffalo Trail Scout Ranch. The Comita family says Reid, enrolled in an introductory backpacking class intended to be supervised and safe, was instead sent on an advanced, "extremely aggressive" hike in roughly 100-degree heat with a much higher heat index. The petition claims Reid received inadequate training, was accompanied by only two other teenagers rather than the required two adults, and lacked preparation—his parents had chosen the introductory course because he was not an athlete and not ready for advanced treks. Photos of the camp show rugged terrain in Jeff Davis County, Texas, underscoring the hike’s difficulty. The suit also alleges poor communication: the family was not informed of Reid’s death for more than four hours and received unclear answers when calling for information. Reid was completing his final requirement for Eagle Scout; his troop posthumously awarded him the honor. Reid’s parents, John and Copper Comita, express devastation and anger, noting they have not heard from BSA leadership. John, a former Scout, criticizes the organization for failing to live up to its stated principles. The BSA provided a statement expressing sympathy, emphasizing member safety and saying they keep the family in their thoughts and prayers. The family seeks accountability for what they describe as preventable negligence.

Major Japanese stock indexes plunged last week, with the Nikkei 225 ending down more than 10 percent after the March 11 earthquake, tsunami and the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear crisis battered markets. But Warren Buffett called the sell-off a buying opportunity, saying the disaster “will not change the economic future of Japan” and he would not sell Japanese stocks if he owned them. Buffett expects reconstruction to take time but believes Japan will rebound; he noted extraordinary events often create investment opportunities and predicted limited global economic impact. Other investors echoed him, citing overseas buying and potential reconstruction-driven demand for builders and contractors. Estimates for rebuilding range up to roughly $235 billion to $247 billion and could take years. Buffett—who sought acquisitions globally—also expressed continued interest in South Korea despite geopolitical risks.

Newsmax CEO Christopher Ruddy set off a media firestorm Monday by telling PBS’s Judy Woodruff that President Trump was “considering perhaps terminating” Special Counsel Robert Mueller, who is leading the Justice Department’s probe into Russian interference in the 2016 election and possible ties to the Trump campaign. Ruddy later affirmed to other outlets that he believed Trump was in fact contemplating firing Mueller, but a source close to Ruddy and White House officials stressed Ruddy had not personally raised the issue with the president. White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer issued a statement saying Ruddy “never spoke to the President regarding this issue,” and that only the president or his attorneys are authorized to comment on such matters.

Ruddy’s comment appeared to be a reading of public signals and remarks from Trump allies rather than the report of a direct conversation. He referenced remarks by Trump lawyer Jay Sekulow, who on ABC’s This Week declined to rule out the possibility that Trump might fire Mueller. Sekulow framed the matter in constitutional terms, noting the president is “a unitary executive” who would seek advice from counsel both inside and outside the government and that any decision would be discussed if there were a basis for it.

The suggestion that Mueller could be removed triggered immediate scrutiny and drew comment from officials at the Department of Justice. Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein — who appointed Mueller and, unlike Attorney General Jeff Sessions, has the authority to hire and fire the special counsel — told a Senate subcommittee he had “not” seen good cause to remove Mueller. Rosenstein emphasized that Mueller’s removal would require a written justification under federal regulations and said he would not follow any order unless he believed it was lawful and appropriate. He also expressed confidence that Mueller would have sufficient independence to carry out the investigation.

Rosenstein’s appearance came after Attorney General Sessions canceled plans to testify, prompting criticism from Democrats on the panel, including Sen. Patrick Leahy, who said Rosenstein was not the witness they had expected. Sen. Susan Collins pressed Rosenstein on whether he would comply with a presidential order to fire Mueller; Rosenstein reiterated that such action would have to meet the “good cause” standard and be documented.

The episode highlighted tensions in the administration over the Russia investigation and raised questions about norms and oversight. Critics seized on the Ruddy comments as evidence that Trump allies were testing the ground for aggressive steps, while officials and legal experts pointed to the formal protections governing the special counsel’s removal. Ruddy, a Mar-a-Lago member and frequent informal conduit to the president, has a history of publicly discussing potential White House personnel moves, behavior that has fed speculation about internal deliberations even when direct contact with the president is disputed. Meanwhile, archiving efforts noted in the original reporting reflect a separate effort to preserve the online record as pages are updated or removed.

Rare photos from Nirvana’s very first concert in March 1987 have surfaced, shared by Maggie Poukkula, daughter of Tony Poukkula, a member of Seattle band Laytem who grew up with Kurt Cobain and hosted the fledgling band’s debut in his basement. Poukkula, 19, tweeted a three-photo strip showing her father and Cobain playing together, noting she only recently realized the shots were from Nirvana’s inaugural show. At that time the lineup included Cobain, bassist Krist Novoselic and drummer Aaron Burckhard; Tony Poukkula reportedly joined them on guitar for at least two Led Zeppelin covers that night. An incomplete setlist from the Raymond, Washington gig lists covers of Led Zeppelin’s “Heartbreaker” and “How Many More Times,” alongside early versions of songs like “Aero Zeppelin,” “Mexican Seafood,” “Pen Cap Chew,” “Hairspray Queen,” “Spank Thru” and “If You Must.” A “Heartbreaker” jam was later included on the 2004 box set With the Lights Out, and a bootleg of “If You Must” circulates online. The photos arrive amid a flood of rare Cobain and Nirvana material recently publicized, much of it used by Brett Morgen in his documentary Montage of Heck, which drew from Cobain’s notebooks and unreleased audio. Montage of Heck, after festival and HBO runs, returns to theaters beginning August 7.

Gwyneth Paltrow, 43, is widely known today for her wellness-and-lifestyle site Goop.com and for branching into beauty products, including collaborations on makeup with Juice Beauty and a Goop skin-care line. A mother of two living in Los Angeles, she often shares personal beauty and life advice, favoring oils and serums. Paltrow describes herself as “a real oil kind of girl,” dismissing the myth that oil is bad for skin, and says she uses an Instant Facial product with gentle fruit acids and exfoliating beads a bit more often than recommended, followed by day or night cream, oil, and eye cream.

Separately, a disturbing medical report from Spain links a fatality to a controversial alternative therapy that Paltrow has promoted: live bee acupuncture, or bee venom apitherapy, in which patients are intentionally stung. Spanish doctors reported the 2015 death of a 55-year-old woman who had been receiving monthly bee-sting treatments for two years. Immediately after a live sting she developed wheezing, breathing difficulty, and sudden loss of consciousness; she was hospitalized at Ramón y Cajal University Hospital in Madrid and later died of multiple organ failure after suffering a massive watershed stroke and permanent coma attributed to severe anaphylactic shock. The authors of the report note this is the first documented death from live bee acupuncture in a patient without a prior allergy, and suggest that repeated exposure to the allergen can increase the risk of a severe, potentially fatal reaction.

A New Jersey Transit train crashed into Hoboken Terminal early Thursday, plowing through barriers and causing one death and injuries to 108 people, Gov. Chris Christie said. The train struck the station at what witnesses described as a high rate of speed; Christie cautioned officials would not speculate on cause and said the National Transportation Safety Board will lead the investigation. A 34-year-old woman standing on the platform was killed after being struck by debris; the train engineer was injured, briefly hospitalized and cooperating with law enforcement. Christie later said the engineer had been released. The 8:45 a.m. crash left the station in chaos as passengers kicked out emergency windows and exited through doors to escape mangled wreckage. Most of the injured were aboard the train. Witness Alex Wulwick, a longtime commuter, described a sudden jolt, lights going out, a “horrendous” crashing sound and seeing the ceiling demolished with wires hanging; he observed one badly cut man in shock but was otherwise uninjured. Gov. Andrew Cuomo described the impact as devastating and expressed hope there would be no further fatalities. There is no timeline to reopen Hoboken Terminal while its structural integrity is assessed; PATH service was expected to resume later that day. NJ Transit established a Family Reunification Center and hotline for information. The report also notes these crawls help archive web pages to prevent broken links.

Yahoo’s annual meeting, the first under CEO Marissa Mayer, was largely uneventful: shareholders re-elected directors and approved executive pay, while Mayer highlighted user-growth wins from recent mobile and Flickr redesigns — mobile email usage rose 70% since April and Flickr mobile uploads 50% after its overhaul. Mayer emphasized building products that “delight and inspire” to drive traffic, ads and revenue; Yahoo stock traded up over 3% at $24.87. The meeting’s low point was an elderly shareholder’s crude remark toward Mayer and off-topic, trivial questions, which she deftly ignored.

President Obama has taken a cautious, low-profile approach to the Libyan uprising, preferring to work through multilateral and allied leadership rather than lead publicly, advisers say. That posture—meant to reflect humility and to galvanize international action—has drawn criticism from conservatives who call it weak and from interventionists who argue only overt U.S. direction can counter Gaddafi. The administration has pursued private diplomacy, financial sanctions, communications jamming, naval support for humanitarian aid, and NATO planning, while debating but not endorsing a no-fly zone. Intelligence assessments cited at a national security meeting suggested a no-fly zone might not be decisive now.

Meanwhile, France formally recognized the Libyan National Council in Benghazi as the legitimate representative and met its leaders, a move that isolated Gaddafi diplomatically and prompted threats to sever ties. Fighting intensified: government forces reclaimed Zawiyah and attacked Ras Lanuf, with reports of civilian casualties and mass displacement. NATO began 24-hour airspace surveillance and discussed options requiring UN legal backing and regional support. International responses included asset freezes, arms embargoes, humanitarian planning, and calls for coordinated action amid deep uncertainty about Libya’s future.

Reynolds American agreed to acquire Lorillard for about $25 billion (about $27.4 billion including debt), a bold consolidation that would leave the U.S. cigarette market dominated by two firms controlling roughly 90 percent of sales. The deal would give Reynolds Lorillard’s Newport menthols—No. 2 U.S. cigarettes—and combine Reynolds’ Camel and Pall Mall with Newport to challenge Altria’s Marlboro franchise. British American Tobacco will fund $4.7 billion to keep a 42 percent Reynolds stake, while Imperial Tobacco will buy brands including Salem, Kool and Blu e-cigarettes for $7.1 billion to ease antitrust concerns and gain e-cig exposure. Reynolds projects $800 million in cost savings and says the deal will be accretive in year one; combined revenue would exceed $11 billion with about $5 billion operating income. The transaction faces significant regulatory scrutiny from the FTC and investor skepticism; shares of Lorillard and Reynolds fell after the announcement. Executives plan shared R&D on next‑generation products, and leadership continuity was outlined amid months of negotiations.

RadarOnline reports Whitney Houston died with a lethal mix of Valium, Xanax and alcohol in her system after being found partially submerged in a Beverly Hilton bathtub. Sedatives and booze likely suppressed her respiratory system, stopping her heart, though the coroner awaits final toxicology to determine the primary contributor. In her final days she was seen intoxicated after an altercation at Tru Hollywood, reportedly drinking heavily and bleeding from a leg wound. Toxicology results are expected in weeks. The piece also notes controversy over Bobby Brown potentially writing a tell-all, complicated by confidentiality and family concerns.

Transport for London (TfL) has refused to renew Uber’s licence to operate in London, ruling the company is not a “fit and proper” private hire operator. TfL cited failings including inadequate reporting of serious criminal offences, problems verifying medical certificates and driver background checks, and use of software (Greyball) that could obstruct regulators and law enforcement. The decision, supported by Mayor Sadiq Khan and taxi unions, frames Uber’s conduct as a corporate responsibility and public safety concern. Uber’s chief executive Dara Khosrowshahi—hired after earlier scandals—said the company will immediately appeal and acknowledged the “high cost to a bad reputation,” pledging to rebuild trust and urging Londoners and drivers to work with the firm. Uber can continue operating while it pursues legal appeals, with its current licence running until 30 September; the process could take months. Reactions split: many drivers and users condemned the decision as devastating and disruptive to 3.5 million London customers and 40,000 drivers, while employment campaigners and unions hailed it as a corrective for the gig economy and a warning to tech firms over compliance and worker rights.

With just days before a July 20 deadline, nuclear negotiations between Iran and the P5+1 powers were struggling in Vienna despite high-level diplomacy. U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry met repeatedly with Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif amid wider regional crises—Israel-Gaza violence, Syria’s civil war, and instability in Iraq and Afghanistan—that both complicate and occasionally align U.S. and Iranian interests. By the end of the day there was no breakthrough: negotiators acknowledged “huge” gaps on core issues, especially how far Iran may be allowed to enrich uranium.

The current six-month interim deal, in force since January, offered sanctions relief in exchange for curbs on Iran’s nuclear program and set July 20 as the target to conclude a comprehensive agreement. An extension is possible—officials signaled openness to a shorter renewal rather than a full six months—but several delegations sent lower-ranking officials, suggesting they expect talks to spill past the deadline. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned any extension would be limited, while Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei publicly insisted on the need to expand enrichment, undercutting negotiators and raising questions about Tehran’s readiness to accept strict limits.

Beyond uranium levels, disagreements involve inspection regimes, timelines, and verification of military dimensions. Domestic pressures in both countries further complicate compromise: Iranian hardliners resist concessions, and some U.S. lawmakers vow to block any deal perceived as too lenient. Observers note success requires Iran wanting a deal more than its counterparts do—a determination likely to become clear only in the negotiations’ final hours.

Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson reassigned Acting TSA Director Melvin Carraway after an internal Homeland Security Inspector General Red Team assessment found alarming screening failures at dozens of U.S. airports. The covert tests—conducted by teams posing as passengers—succeeded in smuggling mock explosives or banned weapons through checkpoints in 67 of 70 trials, a 95 percent failure rate. In one cited incident, a tester set off the magnetometer and was patted down, yet screeners failed to discover a faux explosive taped to the tester’s back. Johnson announced Carraway’s immediate reassignment to the DHS Office of State and Local Law Enforcement and named Acting Deputy Director Mark Hatfield to lead TSA temporarily. He released a six-point action memo directing immediate revisions to TSA screening standard operating procedures to address specific vulnerabilities revealed by the IG testing, nationwide retraining for TSA officers and supervisors, testing of screening equipment, and expanded random covert testing at checkpoints. Johnson emphasized that while such test results can look bad out of context, they are essential to evolving aviation security and pledged to take the findings seriously. He also urged the Senate to quickly confirm President Obama’s nominee for TSA administrator, Coast Guard Vice Admiral Pete Neffenger.

Images and a video claiming unsanitary conditions at a Golden Corral in Port Orange, Florida, circulated on Reddit and other sites, sparking outrage and renewed scrutiny of restaurant hygiene. A user called GCWhistleblower posted photos showing trash and food spilling from boxes near kitchen garbage; a cook, Brandon Huber, filmed a video alleging the restaurant stored raw and cooked food by the dumpster to avoid poor health inspection results. Golden Corral responded that the incident showed improper food handling, that none of the items were served to customers, and that all affected food was destroyed within an hour with Huber participating in its disposal. The company said the manager responsible was fired for violating food-handling procedures. Huber’s father reportedly tried to sell the video to the company for $5,000, an offer the chain declined. Huber’s employment status is unclear.

Comedian Joan Rivers, 81, remained on life support at Mount Sinai Hospital after going into cardiac and respiratory arrest during a throat procedure last Thursday. Her daughter Melissa Rivers has been at her bedside, issuing brief statements thanking supporters and asking for prayers while surrounded by family and friends. Doctors initially placed Joan in a medically induced coma to evaluate possible brain and organ damage; if she recovers, sources say rehabilitation could take months or years. Reports on her condition conflicted, with some describing small signs of improvement and others urging caution. Fans and celebrities offered widespread public support.

At the first 2016 presidential debate at Hofstra University, Hillary Clinton came across as prepared, focused and disciplined, while Donald Trump appeared rattled, defensive and diminished — a contrast that many observers judged a clear Clinton victory. Early audience groans and the differing moods in the spin room underscored the narrative: Clinton’s team arrived buoyant and energized; Trump’s entourage, subdued and fractious.

Clinton’s strategy was to press on perceived strengths of Trump — his wealth, business record, taxes and treatment of workers — rather than merely expose his weaknesses. She opened with a personal vignette about her middle-class father’s small printing business, then pivoted to question Trump’s “self-made” story and his claims about net worth, job creation and leadership on foreign policy. Her lines were tight and rehearsed; her attacks were aimed where they hurt most: Trump’s ego and credentials. Moderated deftly by Lester Holt, the debate put Trump on the defensive early. Instead of his expected abrasive, dominant persona, he frequently bellowed, interrupted, grunted and ultimately appeared muted and pouty — behavior aides and allies described as a sign he was rattled.

Several key takeaways emerged. First, when put on defense, Trump looked “wimpy” compared with his usual bully-boy image; his tendency to overcompensate and to respond with bluster rather than substance hurt him. Second, Clinton effectively undermined Trump’s business bona fides and highlighted unresolved questions about his tax returns, suggesting he might not be as rich or as charitable as he claims and noting years when he paid little or no federal income tax. His flippant rejoinders — “that makes me smart” and suggesting unpaid contractors were simply unsatisfied with work — reinforced Clinton’s attacks about his treatment of workers, damaging for a campaign pitching itself to working-class voters.

Third, Trump missed or bungled opportunities to press Clinton on the Clinton Foundation and other long-standing critiques; his self-justifications consumed time he could have used to press those angles. Fourth, one of Trump’s durable lines — that Clinton has been in public life for decades without delivering on jobs and trade — landed and will likely be reused. Finally, the debate highlighted preparation versus bombast: Clinton’s preparation and tactical targeting of Trump’s perceived strengths paid off, while Trump’s inexperience in this format showed.

Overall, the first debate reinforced Clinton’s command of message and preparedness and exposed vulnerabilities in Trump’s debate persona and substance — setting the tone for the next encounters.

A US Secret Service agent, 42-year-old Special Agent Noel E. Remagen, died after suffering a stroke while on duty during President Trump’s weekend visit to his Turnberry golf resort in Scotland. Remagen, assigned to protect national security adviser John Bolton on the midnight shift, was found unresponsive Saturday night and was treated by a White House doctor and colleagues before being transported to Queen Elizabeth University Hospital in Glasgow, where he later died. A 19-year veteran of the Service and son of a retired agent, he is survived by his wife and two young children. The Secret Service praised Scottish medical teams, police and White House medics for their care, called him a “dedicated professional of the highest order,” and reported that the President and First Lady visited Remagen’s family. A GoFundMe campaign has been verified to benefit the intended recipients.

President-elect Donald Trump’s recent remarks about nuclear weapons have unsettled experts and prompted mixed messages from his incoming team, raising the possibility of a major shift in longstanding U.S. nonproliferation policy. After tweeting that the U.S. “must greatly strengthen and expand its nuclear capability,” Trump told MSNBC’s Morning Joe off-air, “Let it be an arms race … we will outmatch them at every pass and outlast them all.” The comment appeared to endorse an arms race, but his incoming press secretary Sean Spicer later described the exchange as a private remark and alternately denied an arms race was intended, while other spokespeople suggested Trump meant modernization or enhanced nonproliferation efforts. Senior advisers including Kellyanne Conway and Jason Miller sought to frame the language as rhetorical or focused on deterrent modernization or preventing proliferation to terrorists and rogue states. Still, analysts warned the statements—if acted upon—would contradict decades of bipartisan efforts to reduce nuclear stockpiles and could clash with treaty commitments such as New START. Critics like John Tierney and Joseph Cirincione called the tweets and offhand comments dangerous and unprecedented, stressing nuclear policy requires precise, measured language and international consideration. The controversy coincided with similar rhetoric from Russia: Vladimir Putin urged strengthening Russia’s strategic nuclear forces and praised military gains in Syria, while Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu detailed extensive operations and new procurements, citing NATO activity near Russia’s borders. Moscow insisted it did not seek an arms race even as it readied additional S-400 systems and emphasized arming partners in Asia. The juxtaposition of Trump’s remarks and Russian statements has amplified concern among experts that incendiary public comments could destabilize delicate arms control dynamics.

A 2012 national survey of 534 pediatricians and family physicians, published in Pediatrics, found that most primary care doctors regularly face parental requests to delay vaccines for children under two. Ninety-three percent reported at least one request in a typical month; 21% said more than 10% of families had asked to spread out vaccines. Physicians overwhelmingly believed these requests increased children’s risk of serious diseases (87%) and made vaccinations more painful (84%), yet many acceded—citing relationship-building and retention concerns. About 37% said they often/always agreed to delay, another 37% sometimes did, while only a minority would dismiss families over spreading out the primary series.

Clinicians reported spending substantial visit time on vaccine discussions—10 to 14 minutes or more for hesitant parents, often over half of an average 18-minute appointment—displacing other preventive counseling. Forty percent said vaccine schedule conflicts had reduced their job satisfaction. Doctors use varied strategies to persuade hesitant parents (sharing that they vaccinated their own children, warning about outbreaks), but they judged these methods insufficient and lacking a firm evidence base. Experts cited shifting doctoring norms that emphasize patient partnership, which can lead to acquiescing even when clinicians disagree, and noted a scarcity of proven communication approaches. Recommendations from study authors and commentators included early counseling beginning in pregnancy, dedicated reimbursement for extended vaccine counseling, and broader pro-vaccine public campaigns to normalize immunization. Some physicians respond to outright refusal by dismissing families, but most keep them to maintain opportunities for future persuasion.

Demi Lovato candidly recounted her severe substance abuse and eating-disorder struggles in an Access Hollywood interview. She revealed that at 19 she hit rock bottom despite prior inpatient rehab in 2010, admitting she regularly used cocaine—smuggling it onto airplanes and sneaking into bathrooms to use it—even when accompanied by a sober companion. She described addiction as making her manipulative and secretive, also confessing past alcohol abuse, including traveling with vodka hidden in a soda bottle. Lovato traced her eating-disorder behaviors back to childhood, recounting cycles of bingeing, starvation, and purging. Her mother, Dianna, acknowledged suspecting Demi’s drug use, shared her own history of an eating disorder and depression, and said seeking help brought them closer as a family.

Exploding Kittens is a quirky, strategic card game by Elan Lee, Matthew Inman (The Oatmeal), and Shane Small that riffs on Russian roulette: players draw cards until someone pulls an exploding kitten and loses. The deck includes defensive and sabotaging cards—peek, shuffle, force draws—that let players avoid or redirect explosions. The art features Inman’s signature style and playful kitten antics (they “explode” through mischief, not malice). Launched on Kickstarter, the project rapidly exceeded its $10,000 goal, quickly raising six figures and nearing $1 million, crowdfunding community-driven improvements and production.

The Channel 4 Dispatches investigation revealed that dozens of NHS trusts have been disposing of aborted and miscarried fetal remains by incinerating them as clinical waste, sometimes in hospital “waste-to-energy” furnaces. The programme, presented by Amanda Holden, uncovered trusts that burned thousands of fetuses over recent years without adequately informing parents; examples include Addenbrooke’s (797 below 13 weeks) and a waste‑to‑energy facility linked to Ipswich (1,101 between 2011/12 and 2012/13). Documents and patient accounts suggested some women were told remains would be “incinerated with the day’s waste,” and forms sometimes described disposal as “cremation,” contrary to guidance. The findings prompted health minister Dr Dan Poulter to call the practice “totally unacceptable” and ask NHS medical director Prof Sir Bruce Keogh to tell all trusts to stop. The chief medical officer asked the Human Tissue Authority to clarify guidance; the Care Quality Commission said it may investigate. Sands charity and inspectors emphasised that cremation or burial offers greater dignity and that parents should be informed and consulted. The issue exposed failures in communication and respect around disposal of fetal remains, affecting bereaved families.

More than a week after jolting the 2016 presidential race by announcing the discovery of new emails potentially tied to its probe of Hillary Clinton, FBI Director James Comey told Congress the FBI’s review found nothing that changed the agency’s July conclusion: no recommendation of criminal charges. Comey’s initial October disclosure—sent close to the election and against Justice Department norms—provoked intense backlash from across the political spectrum, with critics accusing him of improperly influencing voters and others praising or condemning his reversal. Twitter erupted with reactions from pundits, politicians and media figures lampooning Comey, speculating about pressure on the bureau, and weighing effects on both campaigns. Democrats argued the new letter should put the controversy to rest, while Republicans continued to assail Clinton and question FBI judgment. Law enforcement officials said agents reviewed thousands of emails quickly—most duplicates or personal material found on a laptop linked to Anthony Weiner—and that intent, not mere classification, remained central to the inquiry. Campaigns scrambled to spin the development: Clinton’s team called it validation; Trump’s camp accused the FBI of being wrong and a “rigged” system. Commentators noted the damage from Comey’s earlier disclosure may be irreversible for Clinton’s momentum, even if the matter is now officially closed.

"Wonder Woman" continued to dominate the US box office in its second weekend, earning an estimated $53–57.2 million Friday through the weekend and pushing its domestic total above $192–205 million and global receipts past $300 million. Patty Jenkins’ female-led DC hit outperformed Universal’s reboot "The Mummy," which debuted weakly with about $30–32.2 million against its $125 million budget, stalling Universal’s planned Dark Universe launch. Fox’s "Captain Underpants" slid to third with a projected $13 million weekend and a two-week $42 million total. "Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales" dropped to fourth, while A24’s low-budget horror "It Comes at Night" opened respectably near $6–6.5 million. Other holdovers included "Guardians Vol. 2," "Baywatch," "Megan Leavey," "Alien: Covenant," and "Everything, Everything."

Researchers Jon Kleinberg and Lars Backstrom analyzed anonymized Facebook data from 1.3 million users (ages 20+, 50–2,000 friends) — about 379 million nodes and 8.6 billion links — to see which network features best identify romantic partners and predict breakups. They found that embeddedness (the number of mutual friends) is a weak predictor. Instead, a measure they call dispersion — how much a person’s mutual friends span otherwise unconnected parts of one’s social neighborhood — is far more informative. A partner often serves as a bridge connecting different social worlds (work, college, family), so high dispersion signals a romantic tie. Using dispersion, the algorithm identified spouses correctly roughly 60% of the time and identified people “in a relationship” about one-third of the time; embeddedness performed much worse. Moreover, among nonmarried couples, low dispersion correlated with higher breakup risk: couples with low dispersion were about 50% more likely to break up within two months. Facebook sees practical uses: better identification of close relationships can help tailor News Feed content and ads. The findings empirically support the intuition that lasting relationships link diverse social circles, and suggest network structure can reveal both partners and relationship health.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov visited Washington and met with Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and President Donald Trump the day after Trump abruptly fired FBI Director James Comey. At a brief State Department appearance with Tillerson, Lavrov reacted sarcastically when asked about Comey’s dismissal—asking, “Was he fired? You’re kidding,” then smiling and leaving—while Tillerson avoided comment and said the visit aimed to continue wide-ranging dialogue begun in Moscow. Lavrov’s Oval Office meeting with Trump was closed to press; afterwards Lavrov told reporters he and Trump did not discuss allegations of Russian election meddling, calling those claims “absurd” and asserting there was no compelling evidence of Russian intervention. The sessions focused instead on Syria—where Russia backs Bashar al-Assad and has proposed “de‑escalation zones” with Turkey and Iran—Ukraine, and other bilateral issues. Russia’s ambassador Sergey Kislyak attended and featured in photos circulated by Russian media; Kislyak’s contacts with incoming national security adviser Michael Flynn are central to U.S. investigations. Lavrov criticized past U.S. expulsions of Russian diplomats and denied Russia is supplying arms to the Taliban in Afghanistan. The timing of the meetings, coming amid intense scrutiny of possible ties between Trump associates and Russia and calls for independent probes after Comey’s firing, prompted warnings from figures like Sen. Lindsey Graham and raised concern about the direction of U.S.–Russia relations. Russian officials, including spokesman Dmitry Peskov and President Vladimir Putin, said Comey’s dismissal should not affect bilateral ties.

A teenage boy was discovered impersonating a doctor at St. Mary’s Medical Center in West Palm Beach, Florida, after staff and security grew suspicious. Police responded on Jan. 13 to reports that a juvenile, wearing a white lab coat embroidered with the St. Mary’s logo and “anesthesiology,” with a stethoscope and mask, had been presenting himself as a physician. Security guards said they had seen him around the hospital for about a month and had observed him accessing secured areas. A patient alerted OB/GYN staff after encountering the youth in an exam room; Dr. Sebastian Kent found the boy there with a patient and called security. Surveillance showed the teen arriving from the parking lot with a lab coat visible in his car. When questioned, the juvenile claimed he had been a doctor “for years” and that his family could vouch for him. His mother told police he is under medical care for an undisclosed illness and had not been taking prescribed medication. The hospital says he never had contact with patients or entered patient-care areas. Authorities and the hospital ultimately declined to press charges.

A 20-year-old mother, identified in court as Ms Jackson, has appealed a Family Court order that bans her from breastfeeding her 11-month-old son after she received a finger and foot tattoo on May 6 without telling the tattooist she was nursing. The boy’s father, Mr Macek, removed the child to live with him and his mother, alleging the mother had mental health and drug issues. In an interim June 5 hearing in Newcastle, Federal Circuit Court Judge Matthew Myers found the mother should have primary care but prohibited breastfeeding, citing potential transmission of blood-borne viruses—HIV, hepatitis B and C—if sterilisation was inadequate. Although Ms Jackson tested negative for HIV, the judge accepted evidence that she was in a “window period” when infections might not show, and he prioritized preventing possible lifelong harm to the child over breastfeeding benefits. The tattoo studio owner said he normally avoids tattooing pregnant or breastfeeding women, but the mother had not disclosed her status. The judge also noted the mother had smoked cannabis while breastfeeding on May 22; both parents provided clean drug screens and were ordered to abstain from illicit drugs within 48 hours of caring for the child. Additional orders require each parent to live with a respective grandmother to ensure a responsible adult, and the mother to follow a mental health plan. An apprehended domestic violence order against the father remains. Breastfeeding advocates, including Dr Karleen Gribble and Australian Breastfeeding Association CEO Rebecca Naylor, have criticized the ruling as unprecedented and worry it may set a dangerous precedent by restricting breastfeeding over speculative risks; they stress that infection risk from reputable tattoo parlours is very low. A full bench of the Family Court in Sydney will hear an urgent appeal against Judge Myers’ orders.

Al Jazeera America (AJA) launched in the U.S. by taking over Current TV’s distribution, debuting in about 45–48 million homes with ambitions to offer substantive, less partisan television news. Backed by Qatar’s funding and Al Jazeera’s global infrastructure of some 70 bureaus, AJA assembled a large operation—roughly 900 employees, including 400 newsroom staff—and set up 12 U.S. bureaus (New York, Washington, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Dallas, Detroit, Chicago, Denver, Miami, Seattle, Nashville and New Orleans). Leadership and on-air talent include experienced U.S. journalists such as John Seigenthaler, Joie Chen, Antonio Mora, Sheila MacVicar and Ali Velshi, and executives like president Kate O’Brian and interim CEO Ehab al-Shihabi. Programming promises a nightly newscast, a newsmagazine, a talk show and business coverage, emphasizing documentary and investigative reporting—AJA is building a 16-person investigative team and plans far fewer commercials (about six minutes an hour) than typical U.S. cable outlets.

AJA’s stated goal is to provide in-depth, less opinionated journalism targeting younger, tech-savvy viewers; early site content covered topics from Egypt to Guantánamo and underreported U.S. issues. Yet the launch faces challenges: cable carriage remains limited, some systems dropped Current upon the sale, and AJA inherits Current’s often high channel placements that hurt discoverability. To gain carriage, AJA agreed to block live Internet streaming of its programming in the U.S., sacrificing an online audience that had grown during events like the Arab Spring. Internally, some Al Jazeera staff voiced concern that AJA’s U.S. orientation—hiring mostly Americans and courting carriers—could dilute the network’s distinctiveness. Executives counter that their aim is bold, public-interest reporting tailored for American tastes and to “win,” while critics caution that brand baggage and distribution hurdles may limit early impact despite significant investment and respected hires.

President Trump told Fox News’ Bill O’Reilly that he respects Vladimir Putin and downplayed accusations that the Russian leader is a killer, saying, “There are a lot of killers. We’ve got a lot of killers. What, do you think our country’s so innocent?” The remark, aired in excerpts before the Super Bowl, placed the U.S. and Russia on a similar moral plane and drew criticism from Republicans including Sen. Marco Rubio and more measured rebukes from Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and Sen. John McCain, who called Putin a “murderer and a thug.” The Kremlin demanded an apology from Fox over O’Reilly’s “unacceptable” comment. Trump reiterated his willingness to improve ties with Moscow, noting possible cooperation against ISIS, and said a summit with Putin has been discussed after a reportedly smooth recent phone call. The interview revisited Trump’s earlier skepticism about claims that Russia’s interference swung the 2016 election in his favor and his long‑repeated, unproven assertion of widespread voter fraud. He also expressed readiness to work with Ukraine and Russia to help restore peace in eastern Ukraine amid renewed shelling.

Hillary Clinton’s announced presidential bid highlights deep tensions in Democratic politics and broader systemic problems in how modern campaigns operate. Her campaign rollout—an airborne, pre-taped video announcement and a planned “listening tour” instead of large public rallies—reflects caution and an effort to appear relatable, yet it risks reinforcing perceptions that she is remote and insulated. Clinton’s longstanding ties to elite circles—paid speaking engagements, Davos, Wall Street—continue to fuel narratives of elitism, making her an easy target for attacks that paint Democrats as out of touch with the struggling middle class.

Leakers and early messaging choices have been damaging: disclosures about a $2.5 billion fundraising target and rehearsed “sit downs” with families make the campaign appear heavy on optics and fundraising and light on substantive policy answers. While Clinton’s top team shows signs of improvement from 2008—John Podesta and pollster Joel Benenson bring competence—persistent leaks and staged messaging suggest a continuing overreliance on consultants, polling, and targeted communications rather than robust policy debate.

Three interconnected structural problems weaken Democrats broadly: dependency on big money and wealthy donors, excessive emphasis on crafted messaging over substantive policy, and a dearth of clear solutions for major economic and social challenges. This system rewards consultants and ad buy strategies, discourages risk-taking on real reforms, and produces a politics of biography and branding rather than meaningful debate. As a result, Democrats often alienate their base by appearing to uphold the status quo.

Electoral fundamentals complicate Clinton’s prospects. Analyses suggest the general election is roughly toss-up territory: Obama’s middling approval, the state of the economy, and narrow Electoral College margins mean outcomes depend heavily on small shifts. Clinton is well known but only break-even in favorability, and fundraising success could be a double-edged sword—necessary for organization yet corrosive if it deepens ties to moneyed interests.

The author argues Democrats need internal renewal: a vigorous primary debate, stronger progressive challengers, and a return to substantive policy work. Without that, Clinton risks being the steward of a dying system—well-positioned to be nominee but vulnerable in a general election if she cannot convincingly offer real answers and reconnect with voters beyond carefully managed events.

During Portsmouth High School’s 2015 graduation, valedictorian Colin Yost turned a typically formal ceremony into a memorable, viral moment by leading a coordinated flash mob to Taylor Swift’s “Shake It Off.” Facing stiff competition for attention in a high-profile commencement season, Yost decided to end his speech — which urged classmates to “embrace your inner nerd” and strive for excellence — with the line “all you have to do is shake it off,” then deliberately began an awkward solo dance. His classmates, who’d rehearsed the routine during five scheduled graduation practices with help from friends who handled choreography and music, gradually joined in. The reaction in the auditorium moved from confusion to laughter and tears as the roughly 235 seniors rose in waves, transforming the sea of maroon and white caps and gowns into a celebratory, synchronized performance.

Yost and fellow organizers worked with school administrators, presenting detailed plans and rehearsal diagrams to secure permission and ensure the music cue would be executed at the right moment. They also created a private instructional video on YouTube so the class could learn the steps. The lighthearted finale was meant to reinforce Yost’s message of self-acceptance and unity, not merely entertain; its positive intent resonated widely. Clips shared on Facebook quickly amassed tens of thousands of views, and an MTV article propelled the footage into the national spotlight, with the YouTube video gaining hundreds of thousands of views. Yost, who will study chemical and biological engineering at Princeton and aspires to be a heart surgeon, said he never expected the flash mob’s reach and is proud of how the class came together.

A North Korean soldier who defected to South Korea in 2017 was found to have anthrax antibodies, indicating prior exposure or vaccination and raising concerns about Pyongyang’s biological-weapons capabilities, South Korean media report. An unnamed intelligence official told Channel A the soldier developed immunity before defecting. The finding adds to suspicions dating to 2015, when materials from the Pyongyang Biological Technology Research Institute—linked to KPA Unit 810—suggested dual-use work that could support biological weapons rather than just pesticide research. Anthrax is highly lethal if untreated, and South Korea’s military — which does not yet have an available anthrax vaccine for troops — expects to develop one by the end of 2019. Reports have also suggested North Korea is exploring ways to militarize anthrax, including experiments to protect spores from the extreme heat and pressure of ICBM re-entry, raising fears about delivery via missiles. A recent White House report likewise warned Pyongyang may be developing chemical and biological agents that could be missile-delivered. Separately, South Korean outlets have reported U.S. military biological detection programs and past imports of live anthrax samples to bases in the South, fueling public concern.

Jennifer Lawrence told Elle magazine she refuses to starve herself for a role and finds Hollywood’s body standards extreme, saying that by industry measures she’s considered “obese.” The Hunger Games star joked she’s “Val Kilmer in that one picture on the beach,” and emphasized that when training to play Katniss Everdeen she worked to look “fit and strong, not thin and underfed.” She framed her approach as deliberately responsible for her young fans, determined to avoid promoting unhealthy dieting or contributing to anorexia rumors.

Lawrence also spoke candidly about her relationship with Nicholas Hoult, whom she met on the set of X‑Men: First Class. She described their life together as unglamorous and relaxed—preferring nights in watching television and snacking on Cheetos to flashy outings—and recounted how they turn into “two perverted Homer Simpsons” joking about people’s appearances. The actress praised Hoult as the person who makes her laugh the most.

Open and blunt, Lawrence admitted she often struggles with Hollywood’s PR expectations, confessing she “never know[s] what’s going to come out of [her] mouth” on the red carpet and finds that difficult. Despite her rising star status and an Oscar nomination for Winter’s Bone, she says she’s not rushing into extravagant living; even after earning millions she’d rather stay in modest housing, noting she has lived in small, imperfect apartments and would find a big mansion alone “very bizarre.”

Bloomingdale’s, the upscale department store owned by Macy’s Inc., came under intense online fire after a holiday catalog ad that many interpreted as endorsing date rape circulated on social media. The ad showed a woman laughing with her head turned while a young man looks her way, accompanied by the tagline, “Spike Your Best Friend’s Eggnog When They’re Not Looking.” Social media analytics firm Networked Insights reported 3,868 comments about the ad within 48 hours, with most responses negative and many users calling the copy “creepy.” The retailer issued an apology, saying the copy was “inappropriate and in poor taste” and acknowledging an “error in judgment.” It is unclear what the ad’s intended message was, but branding experts note that marketers are feeling pressure to capture attention amid a flood of daily advertising, especially during the critical holiday shopping season. Jonah Disend, CEO of Redscout, emphasized that while marketers must work harder to stand out, pushing boundaries raises greater risks. Bloomingdale’s incident illustrates how quickly controversy can escalate in the age of social media; similar flare-ups over Starbucks’ red holiday cups and other seasonal campaigns have shown consumers’ propensity both to complain and to amplify controversies.
