The episode underscores the delicate balance retailers face between creative marketing that attracts attention and content that can provoke public backlash and reputational harm during a pivotal sales period.

In November 2013, Hallie Twomey launched a Facebook project, Scattering CJ, to send her son CJ’s ashes to places he never saw in life. CJ (Christopher John Twomey), who died by suicide at age 20 in April 2010 after an argument with his parents, had been a former U.S. Air Force aircrew member who loved travel, adventure and adrenaline. Hallie, unable to accept the urn sitting on her mantel, asked strangers and friends worldwide to scatter a small amount of his ashes at meaningful or unique locations and to send back photos and a few words. She includes a photo of CJ and a letter asking volunteers to tell him he was loved and that she is sorry.

What began modestly swelled into a global movement: within a year more than 9,000 people offered to participate and over 18,000 people followed the page. Hallie has sent packets selectively to travelers headed to distinctive sites and places not yet represented. The Scattering CJ page displays images from more than 100 countries and all seven continents—ashes have been scattered at Machu Picchu, in Tamil Nadu tea plantations, atop Germany’s Zugspitze, beneath the sea near the Dominican Republic, on Namibian sand dunes, from hot air balloons over Cappadocia, and even in Antarctica. Some envelopes were damaged or lost in transit; Hallie accepts those losses as part of the journey. A small number of packets have been returned when volunteers’ plans changed.

The project has had unexpected benefits: people affected by suicide or suicidal thoughts have reached out saying CJ’s story helped them reconsider. In October, a vial of CJ’s ashes was included in a memorial rocket launch from New Mexico—paid for by Celestis—sending him briefly into space. Hallie plans to keep a portion of the ashes at home and in jewelry; about two-thirds of the planned shares have been sent, with no firm end date. The campaign aims to honor CJ’s memory and ensure he isn’t forgotten while offering Hallie healing through global kindness.

Resting Bitch Face (RBF) — that neutral expression many read as annoyed, judgmental, or bored — has been examined scientifically by Jason Rogers and Abbe Macbeth of Noldus Information Technology. Using FaceReader, a software tool that maps over 500 facial points and classifies expressions into categories including happiness, sadness, anger, surprise, disgust, contempt and neutral, the researchers compared genuinely expressionless faces to those of public figures widely labeled as having RBF (Kristen Stewart, Queen Elizabeth II, Victoria Beckham, Anna Kendrick and Kanye West among them). Baseline “neutral” faces registered about 97 percent neutrality and roughly 3 percent minor emotional blips. Faces commonly identified as RBF, however, showed a roughly doubled share of detectable emotion — about 5.7–6 percent — driven largely by signals the software classifies as contempt. Subtle cues such as a slight tightening around the eyes, one side of the lip pulled back, or a small asymmetrical lift of a lip corner produce that contempt signal, and both machine and human observers seem to interpret those micro-expressions similarly. Importantly, FaceReader found contempt cues equally in male and female faces, suggesting RBF is not a sex-linked physiologic trait; rather, women are more frequently singled out because social norms expect them to smile and appear pleasant more often than men. The authors offered a public-facing follow-up, inviting people to submit neutral-expression photos for analysis on the Noldus site. Macbeth emphasized there’s no need to worry: the study merely explains why some neutral faces are perceived negatively, not a problem that requires correction. The work reframes the meme with objective measurement, highlighting how tiny, unconscious facial cues shape social perception.

Walt Disney CEO Bob Iger disclosed that hackers claiming to have accessed an upcoming Disney film threatened to post it online in segments unless the studio paid a substantial ransom in Bitcoin. Speaking at a town hall with ABC employees, Iger said Disney refused to pay and is coordinating with federal investigators. Though he did not name the title, industry reports identified the film as Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales, due in theaters May 25 and featuring Johnny Depp, Geoffrey Rush, Orlando Bloom and Javier Bardem. According to Iger’s account, the extortionists warned they would first release five minutes and then successive 20-minute chunks until paid. The revelation follows a pattern of recent cyber extortion in entertainment: an anonymous hacker uploaded the fifth season of Orange Is the New Black after Netflix reportedly declined to pay a ransom, and major Hollywood talent agencies including UTA, ICM and WME have been targeted. The incident echoes a high-profile 2014 Sony Pictures attack that disrupted studio operations and sought to derail distribution of The Interview. The disclosure also comes amid a broader surge in ransomware incidents worldwide, including a global cyber-attack that affected British hospitals and organizations across at least 99 countries. Disney’s vast, lucrative slate—extending across its core studio, Marvel and Lucasfilm—makes it an attractive target for such criminal schemes.

U.S. Rep. Trey Radel, a 37-year-old freshman Republican from Fort Myers, was arrested Oct. 29 in Washington, D.C., on misdemeanor cocaine possession charges, Politico and other outlets reported. Authorities say the Drug Enforcement Administration and FBI were involved: a suspected dealer arrested in a separate federal probe identified Radel as a buyer, and Radel allegedly purchased cocaine from an undercover officer in Dupont Circle. He faces up to 180 days in jail and a $1,000 fine and was scheduled to appear in D.C. Superior Court the day after his arrest. Radel, whose legal name is Henry Jude Radel III, acknowledged the arrest in a statement apologizing to his wife, son and constituents, saying he struggles with alcoholism and that the incident was “an extremely irresponsible choice.” He said he intends to seek treatment and counseling and stands ready to face consequences. House Speaker John Boehner’s office said the matter belongs in court and is between Radel, his family and constituents. Radel has missed recent House votes; local and state Republican colleagues expressed surprise, disappointment and hopes he pursues treatment.

Israeli police, working with the FBI and international partners, arrested a 19-year-old dual U.S.-Israeli citizen in southern Israel in connection with a months-long wave of bomb threats against Jewish community centers, schools and other institutions in the United States, Australia, New Zealand and elsewhere. Authorities say the suspect used sophisticated masking and camouflage technologies to hide his tracks; investigators seized multiple computers, antennas and other equipment and are probing a bitcoin account to see if any payments were involved. The arrest follows more than 100 threats in the U.S. alone this year that spanned 33 states and came in several waves, prompting evacuations, heightened security and widespread alarm. Law enforcement has not specified how many incidents are tied to this suspect, and Israeli police continue investigating his motive. The teen’s attorney said he has behavioral issues and was diagnosed with an inoperable brain tumor at 14; his father was detained and questioned. Jewish organizational leaders—while relieved by the arrest—expressed dismay that the alleged perpetrator is reportedly Jewish, and the ADL called the actions anti-Semitic, intended to sow fear. U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions praised the collaboration between U.S. and Israeli authorities. Separate arrests earlier this year accounted for a portion of the threats, but officials say multiple actors were involved across the wider campaign.

A pretrial hearing in Albemarle County brought new details about the investigation into the 2014 disappearance and death of University of Virginia student Hannah Graham and the role of bloodhound tracking in establishing probable cause to search the home and car of the accused, Jesse LeRoy Matthew Jr. Former Louisa County Detective Buck (Stuart) Garner testified that his seven-year-old bloodhound, Shaker, tracked Graham’s scent over several days, from downtown Charlottesville—where surveillance shows Graham walking with Matthew—east to an industrial area and to locations associated with Matthew. Garner said Shaker alerted to a strong scent consistent with fear or adrenaline in a mulch pile at the industrial site and later detected Graham’s scent on the passenger-side door of Matthew’s vehicle, at the entrance to his building, and at his apartment door frame; the dog did not detect scent at other apartments. Those canine findings were included in an affidavit that led to search warrants for Matthew’s apartment and car. Defense attorneys challenged the warrants, arguing inconsistencies between the dog’s tracking, witness statements, and video, and suggested investigators may have misled the magistrate. Judge Cheryl Higgins ruled there was no deliberate falsehood in the affidavit and that multiple other facts—witness reports of Graham and Matthew together and surveillance showing Matthew buying drinks—could establish probable cause. Matthew, charged with capital murder in Graham’s death and linked to another 2009 homicide, faces prosecutors seeking the death penalty; he is also serving a life term for a 2005 attempted murder and sexual assault. A mental health examination has been approved ahead of trial.

A volcanic ash cloud from Iceland’s Eyjafjallajoekull has shut much of Europe’s airspace, disrupting travel for over 6.8 million passengers and prompting emergency EU transport talks. More than 63,000 flights were canceled in four days, costing airlines about $200m (£130m) daily; major hubs including Heathrow, Frankfurt and Schiphol were closed or limited. Airlines such as KLM, Air France-KLM and Lufthansa conducted test flights reporting no visible damage, and KLM submitted results to Dutch authorities, prompting questions about the blanket ban. IATA urged a phased reopening of airspace; Eurocontrol advised caution, noting ash’s patchy but dangerous distribution. Governments considered measures including rerouting stranded passengers via Spain and potential financial support for carriers. The crisis threatens perishable exports—Kenyan flowers and produce face spoilage—and broader economic effects if prolonged. Scientific flights still found hazardous ash concentrations, and officials emphasized safety while seeking flexible, evidence-based reopening.

A disturbing picture emerged after the Tucson shooting that left six dead and 14 wounded, including Rep. Gabrielle Giffords: accused gunman Jared Lee Loughner, 22, kept a macabre shrine in a camouflage tent behind his parents’ home. Photos showed a skull replica atop a pot of shriveled oranges, ceremonial candles and potting soil—elements experts linked to various occult practices—raising questions about additional motivations beyond Loughner’s documented anti-government online rants. Classmates and professors at Pima Community College described him as increasingly strange and unsettling: laughing to himself, asking bizarre questions about mind control and prompting concerns that led to his suspension pending a mental-health clearance. A childhood friend, Bryce Tierney, recounted Loughner’s long-standing grudge against Giffords after an unsatisfying exchange at a town-hall event, his obsession with lucid dreaming and a dream journal that reflected his retreat into an alternate reality. Tierney described Loughner’s drift into nihilistic thinking, fascination with provoking others, and, in recent months, growing interest in guns. Prosecutors charged Loughner with attempted assassination of a member of Congress and related counts; investigators continue probing his motives and mental state.

A Wichita mother and her adult son were found shot to death late Saturday in their home on East Huntington, and friends who were playing online video games with the son say they heard the gunshots. Victims were identified as 62-year-old Huong (Houng) Pham and her 23-year-old son Cody Ha. Several players in a late-night group chat—located across states and even in Canada—recalled hearing loud popping noises through their headsets around 10 p.m. They debated whether the sounds were gunshots, then called Ha’s number and heard it ring repeatedly. One player later heard Ha’s sister panicking when she discovered the bodies and called police. Wichita detectives spoke with the gamers early the next morning to record what they heard.

Neighbors reported frequent, unusual traffic to the house and said different cars came and went more than at nearby homes. Friends told reporters Ha sometimes paused gaming to answer the front door when people came to the house; longtime friend Tommy Ong said Ha had told him strangers came to buy prescription pills, and that Ha earned a share from sales. Ha worked days at the family’s dry-cleaning business and gamed at night; neighbors described him as easygoing.

Court records show Pham previously sought and was involved in reciprocal stalking-related petitions years earlier, but authorities have not linked those disputes to the killings. Police have made no public statement about motive and are asking anyone with information to contact Wichita police or Crime Stoppers. The slayings were among Wichita’s homicides this year as investigators continue to seek tips.

A Bernalillo, New Mexico, middle school math teacher, 63-year-old Benjamin Nagurski, has been arrested and charged after allegedly brandishing a knife and threatening a student during a pop quiz, police said. The incident, reported at Bernalillo Middle School, occurred when some students were talking during the exam. According to a criminal complaint and statements from Bernalillo Police Chief Tom Romero, Nagurski allegedly turned toward the students with a knife in hand, stood about four feet away, and told one student to stop talking. When the student confronted him about the knife, the teacher allegedly replied, "Maybe next time I'll pull a machete on you." Students later interviewed by officers corroborated the account. School officials removed Nagurski from the classroom and the principal told police the teacher had a rounded steak knife and another pointed knife with a wooden handle; Nagurski later told investigators he had only shaken the knife and apologized. He was arrested and initially held on bail; reports listed both $10,000 and a $5,000 cash/surety bond. Nagurski faces felony charges including aggravated assault with a deadly weapon and possession or carrying of an unlawful weapon on school grounds. School district officials did not immediately comment.

A 9-year-old girl, Jordan Landon, survived nearly 48 hours trapped inside an overturned 1995 Chevrolet Monte Carlo after a Friday night crash on Highway 55 in rural Craven County, North Carolina, which killed her father, 39-year-old Douglas Landon. The pair had been returning from a late stop at a nearby Mini-Mart where surveillance captured them minutes earlier. Jordan was pinned by a seatbelt inside the mangled, upside-down vehicle, surviving on Pop-Tarts, water and Gatorade and using a coat to stave off subfreezing overnight temperatures. Rescuers did not find the car until about 5:45 p.m. Sunday, when a passerby spotted it far off the roadway; initial responders believed both occupants were dead until Jordan made a sound. It took three fire and rescue teams over an hour to free her and transport her to Pitt County Memorial Hospital; she suffered non-life-threatening injuries and is expected to recover.

Investigators recovered the speedometer stuck at 110 mph and say speed was a factor; troopers reported Landon was driving over 100 mph. Jordan’s mother, Cissy (Claudette) Leohmann, disputes that claim, suggesting a tire blowout caused the wreck and points to damage on the right rear wheel. Troopers have not found evidence of mechanical failure. Leohmann filed a missing-person report and searched Saturday, during which she herself crashed within 100 feet of the overturned car but was unaware it was there. Friends say Douglas was protecting his daughter during the crash.

ISIS claimed without evidence that the man who drove a rented truck onto a Lower Manhattan bike path, killing eight and injuring more than a dozen, was “a soldier of the caliphate,” saying the attack struck “crusader America.” The claim appeared in ISIS’s al-Naba newsletter rather than its usual Amaq channel and offered inflated casualty figures; authorities say eight were killed and 12 wounded. Suspect Sayfullo Saipov, a 29-year-old Uzbek national, has told investigators he was inspired by ISIS videos and followed the group’s published instructions. Prosecutors charged him with providing material support to ISIS and other offenses; his phone reportedly contained about 90 ISIS videos and thousands of propaganda images. At the scene he allegedly shouted “Allahu Akbar,” left a handwritten note pledging ISIS, and brandished imitation firearms after crashing into pedestrians and a school bus. Officer Ryan Nash shot Saipov in the abdomen, stopping the attack; Saipov survived and did not enter a plea at his first federal court appearance. President Trump called the suspect a “degenerate animal,” urged the death penalty, and said the U.S. military had struck ISIS harder in response. The FBI said it had not found ties to international terrorist networks, suggesting ISIS might be claiming credit opportunistically. New York has begun installing diagonal concrete barriers along the bike path to block vehicles, a measure some cyclists say creates congestion and safety concerns.

A small band of bereaved relatives and an American amateur investigator, Blaine Alan Gibson, have taken the search for Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 into their own hands by scouring remote beaches of Madagascar for debris. Seven relatives, including Chinese son Jiang Hui and campaigner Grace Subathirai Nathan, have been visiting Île Sainte-Marie, Nosy Be and Tamatave to raise local awareness and train fishermen and residents to spot, photograph and preserve possible aircraft fragments. They’ve distributed laminated guides and videos in English, French and Malagasy and enlisted local officials to secure finds until experts can examine them. Jiang found a small white board fragment on Riake beach; Gibson reported a larger cabin-like piece nearby. Families say public beach finds — like flaperon parts previously washed up on Réunion and other items on East African shores — have yielded the clearest clues so far, suggesting the aircraft likely came down rapidly and out of control. Ocean drift modelling explains why debris has reached Madagascar, Mozambique, Tanzania, Reunion and Mauritius despite the believed crash site far to the south. Meanwhile, the official underwater hunt is reaching its likely end: the Dutch vessel Fugro Equator departed Fremantle for a final sweep of a 120,000 sq km Indian Ocean search area, re-examining about 200 small zones with autonomous vehicles. With no “credible new evidence,” Australia, Malaysia and China plan to suspend the seabed search by early 2017, though it could resume if new leads appear. Families, frustrated by perceived delays and omissions in the official effort, warn that many clues may lie undiscovered on coastlines unless locals keep looking. The grieving campaigners hope their grassroots efforts will preserve any remaining evidence and keep MH370’s mystery alive.

President Trump made a secretive, unannounced trip to Dover Air Force Base with daughter Ivanka to honor the remains of Chief Special Warfare Operator William "Ryan" Owens, the Navy SEAL killed in a U.S. raid in Yemen. Owens, 36, was the first known U.S. combat casualty of the Trump administration; several militants and more than a dozen civilians, including an 8-year-old girl linked to a radical cleric, were also killed and three U.S. service members wounded. Trump met privately with Owens’ family during a two-hour visit; the family had requested privacy. The operation, planned during the Obama administration and authorized by Trump, highlighted the human cost of ongoing counterterrorism efforts in hotspots such as Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria and Yemen, where U.S. forces and drone strikes continue to target extremist groups. The raid also touched off debate over tactics after past campaign remarks by Trump about targeting terrorists’ families and White House assurances no Americans would be targeted.

Separately, Melania Trump’s low-profile start as first lady has drawn attention. Two weeks into the administration she has not relocated to the White House and has remained largely absent from official events, choosing to keep son Barron in New York through the school year. Melania has appointed Lindsay Reynolds as her chief of staff and named Stephanie Winston Wolkoff a senior adviser, but many key East Wing roles remain unfilled. Observers note first ladies often start quietly; some view Melania’s approach as a possible redefinition of the role, while critics point to weak approval ratings and past controversies. The White House says she will move to Washington at the end of the school year and is assembling a professional team to manage her agenda. Meanwhile, Ivanka has stepped into ceremonial duties in her stead and has already moved to Washington with her husband Jared Kushner.

Mirror Mirror, directed by Tarsem Singh, is a lavish, visually driven retelling of Snow White that favors spectacle and whimsy over emotional depth. Starring Julia Roberts as a vain, self-amused Queen and Lily Collins as a plucky Snow White, the film modernizes the tale with a girl-power twist: Snow helps shape her own destiny, learns to fence, and rescues a prince rather than awaiting rescue. Armie Hammer plays the buff, slightly foolish Prince Alcott, while Nathan Lane provides scene-stealing comic relief as Brighton, the Queen’s anxious henchman.

Singh’s background in music videos and his taste for high-concept images make the movie a nonstop visual treat—sumptuous production design, striking CGI sequences, and the late Eiko Ishioka’s final, exceptional costume work dominate every frame. The seven “dwarfs” are reimagined as merry outlaw antiheroes and provide much of the film’s heart and humor. Screenplay by Marc Klein and Jason Keller peppers modern jokes and anachronisms throughout, but the dialogue often feels scattershot.

Critics note the movie’s charm and watchability but critique its lack of narrative substance and emotional resonance; its strengths are aesthetics and comic moments rather than character complexity. Overall, Mirror Mirror is a frothy, pretty confection—eye candy that entertains more than it moves.

State Supreme Court Justice Donald Greenwood ordered 30-year-old Michael Rotondo to move out of his parents’ Camillus, N.Y., home after a 30-minute, highly publicized hearing in which Rotondo argued vociferously that he should be allowed more time. Rotondo’s parents, Mark and Christina, had filed for a court order after repeatedly asking him to leave; they say they began giving notices in February 2018 and even offered $1,100 to help him relocate. Their lawyer sought an enforceable eviction order, and Greenwood ultimately directed that such an order be prepared and signed, also asking adult protective services to investigate, citing concern about the family situation.

Rotondo told the judge he deserved six months to find other housing and cited a case he said supported that period. Greenwood, who commended Rotondo’s research but disagreed with his conclusion, produced an appellate decision that undercut Rotondo’s cited authority and told him family members do not receive special treatment absent rare circumstances. The judge repeatedly urged Rotondo to speak directly with his parents during the hearing; Rotondo refused, saying he had made his legal arguments.

The episode drew widespread media attention—local and international outlets covered it, multiple camera crews attended, and Rotondo later addressed media outside court saying he would appeal and calling the eviction “outrageous.” He insisted he wasn’t ready to leave home, claimed to run a website business but declined to explain details, and acknowledged not contributing to household expenses or chores. The parents sat quietly in the gallery while Rotondo sought the spotlight, even asking reporters for interviews after court. No precise vacate deadline was specified in court transcripts; the parents’ attorney said the forthcoming order would allow reasonable time to move. Rotondo left court and returned to the family home.

A Florida appeals court overturned the 2008 second-degree murder-with-a-firearm conviction of former FBI agent John J. Connolly Jr., who had been convicted for his role in the 1982 killing of Boston businessman John Callahan. By a 2-1 decision, the Miami court ruled jurors relied on a flawed charge because Connolly neither carried nor fired the gun that killed Callahan; prosecutors had added the firearm element to avoid Florida’s then-four-year statute of limitations for second-degree murder. The ruling sends the case back to a lower court and raises the possibility that the 73-year-old, long-time handler of mobsters James “Whitey” Bulger and Stephen Flemmi, could be released. Connolly’s lawyers sought immediate release, calling the conviction a “nullity,” while Florida’s attorney general is considering an appeal. Victims’ families reacted with outrage and sorrow; Callahan’s widow and others criticized the decision as a technicality that undermines justice. Dissenting Judge Leslie B. Rothenberg argued the evidence supported conviction, noting juries found Connolly carried his service weapon during meetings that led to the murder and that arranging a hit is equivalent to pulling the trigger. Prosecutors said they will seek rehearing to keep Connolly imprisoned.

Pakistan Railway Minister Ghulam Ahmad Bilour personally offered a $100,000 bounty for the killing of the maker of the anti-Islam film sparking global protests, clarifying he spoke for himself, not the government. At a news conference he said he was “a Muslim first,” and even invited the Taliban and al Qaeda to carry out the assassination. His Awami National Party (ANP) and Prime Minister Raja Pervez Ashraf quickly distanced themselves: an ANP spokesman condemned Bilour’s remarks as unrepresentative, noting the party opposes militancy, and the prime minister’s office said it would raise the issue with the ANP leadership. The U.S. State Department called Bilour’s announcement “inflammatory and inappropriate,” reiterating that offense at the film does not justify violence. The film, widely referred to as Innocence of Muslims, is linked to alleged producer Nakoula Basseley Nakoula, who has gone into hiding in the U.S. Protests over the film have spread across Pakistan and other countries, sometimes deadly, prompting travel warnings and diplomatic actions including French security measures after related tensions.

Olympic gold medallist Ryan Fry and teammates Jamie Koe, Chris Schille and DJ Kidby were ejected from the Red Deer Curling Classic in Alberta after spectators and other teams complained about drunken, abusive behaviour. The foursome forfeited their final match at the World Curling Tour event after a tournament committee intervened following multiple reports that players were "extremely drunk," breaking brooms, swearing and causing damage in locker rooms. Red Deer Curling Centre manager Wade Thurber said complaints and photographic evidence prompted the club to post a notice that the team had been removed from the competition and potentially barred from future events.

Fry, who won Olympic gold with Team Canada in Sochi 2014 and has an extensive national and international record, issued a public apology, called his conduct "disrespectful and embarrassing," and offered to pay for damages. He said he allowed himself to "lose control," promised to strive to become a better person and to contribute positively to the curling community, and expressed a desire to apologize individually to those affected. Koe, though not playing the final game, also apologized on behalf of the team. Brad Jacobs, Fry’s usual skip, condemned the behaviour and said the matter is being handled internally with the team.

The Red Deer Classic counts toward Canadian team rankings and the World Curling Tour has requested a formal complaint from the event committee. Organizers defended their decision to eject the team as necessary to address widespread backlash and to send a stern message that such conduct is unacceptable.

Beijing authorities destroyed over 500 illegal outdoor barbecue grills as part of a three-month emergency push to cut PM2.5 and ease the city’s frequent hazardous smog. State media showed crews cutting up confiscated grills, many run by ethnic Uighur vendors from Xinjiang, drawing online ridicule that officials should target larger pollution sources. The action is one of several emergency measures — including odd-even car restrictions, school closures and factory curbs — aimed at combating smog from factories, heating plants, vehicle emissions and dust from the Gobi Desert.

Ted Cruz’s new memoir, A Time for Truth, has become a political and publicity win amid controversy after The New York Times excluded it from its bestseller list. HarperCollins and Cruz’s campaign say the book sold strongly—Nielsen BookScan reported 11,854 first-week hardcover sales, placing it high on other lists like Nielsen’s and The Wall Street Journal’s—but the Times says its review found the “overwhelming preponderance of evidence” that sales were “strategic bulk purchases,” a practice it excludes to keep the list reflective of authentic demand. Cruz’s team and HarperCollins vehemently deny the accusation, calling the Times’ claim false and demanding the paper publish its evidence or apologize. The dispute has generated major media attention and likely boosted sales, with Cruz advisers noting the controversy is driving readership and giving him useful publicity at a time many 2016 campaigns struggle for attention. Cruz also reported strong fundraising—$51 million across his campaign and allied super PACs—helping him stand out from rivals. The episode echoes past examples where boycotts or disputes increased interest in contested books. Both sides stand by their positions: the Times cites uniform standards and sales-pattern analysis, while Cruz’s camp points to tour signings, queueing readers, and other bestseller lists to challenge the bulk-order claim.

An American Airlines captain died during an overnight flight from Phoenix to Boston after becoming suddenly ill about four hours into Flight 550. The Airbus A320, carrying 147 passengers and five crew, was diverted to Syracuse, where the first officer declared a medical emergency and landed the aircraft safely at about 7:10 a.m. Audio of the crew’s communications captured the first officer reporting the captain “incapacitated” and later that the pilot was “unresponsive, not breathing.” A flight attendant who is a nurse and others attempted to help. American Airlines confirmed the captain’s death and said it was focusing on supporting his family and colleagues; early reports named the pilot as Capt. Michael Johnston, 57, and noted condolences to his wife. The airline did not disclose the cause of death. Passengers said they were not alerted to the fatality while on the diverted flight and described calm, professional handling by the crew and airport authorities; a replacement crew reached Syracuse after about four hours and the flight continued to Boston. Aviation experts and FAA rules note that two qualified pilots are required in the cockpit and that first officers are trained to handle incapacitation, reducing risk to passengers in such emergencies. The incident has been treated as a sudden medical tragedy.

Green Bay’s viral “creepy clown” mystery has ended: local filmmaker Adam Krause has admitted he created “Gags the Clown” as part of a 10-day marketing campaign for his upcoming short film, also titled Gags. Krause revealed on the clown’s Facebook page that the photos circulating online were taken in May 2016 and that no one was endangered during the staged shoots, with safety a priority. The eerie figure—white-face makeup, hollow eyes, black smile, dirty jumpsuit and four black balloons—had prompted dozens of worried calls and nearly 8,000 Facebook shares after being first reported at 2 a.m. Aug. 1. Police noted there was little they could do since the person wasn’t breaking the law.

This article updates readers on celebrities who will be on college campuses in fall 2012. It highlights frequent student James Franco—who’s taken classes at Yale, NYU (where he taught), UCLA, Warren Wilson, Brooklyn College and Columbia—so it’s expected he’ll be studying somewhere again. Emma Watson is returning to the U.S. after a year at Oxford to attend Brown University. The list includes Alex Linz at UC Berkeley (known from Home Alone 3), Olympic gold medalist swimmer Nathan Adrian also at UC Berkeley, and Miranda Cosgrove at the University of Southern California. Other students named are Chet Hanks at Northwestern, Connor Paolo at the Lee Strasberg Theatre Institute, Justin Combs at UCLA, Christy Turlington at Columbia, and Dakota Fanning at New York University. The article corrects an earlier error: Vinny Guadagnino will not attend Cornell. A slideshow with details accompanies the piece.

Amanda Knox, 24, is trying to resume a normal life in Seattle after being cleared in the murder of her former roommate Meredith Kercher. The Mail on Sunday reports Knox is romantically involved with longtime friend James Terrano, a 24-year-old classical guitar student at the University of Washington. The couple were photographed out together in Seattle’s Chinatown—holding hands, sharing ice cream, shopping and spending nights at Terrano’s modest rented flat. Terrano’s brother confirmed the relationship, saying they’ve known each other for years and have been friends since before Knox went to Italy. Knox, who had studied languages at the university and is expected to resume her studies, has moved into the modest apartment they share.

Meanwhile, Knox’s former boyfriend and co-defendant Raffaele Sollecito, 27, has publicly acknowledged that their romantic relationship is over. In his first post-release interview on Italian television, Sollecito described their lives as irreversibly changed by the “cruel injustice” of their convictions and appeals process. He expressed enduring affection for Knox but said the relationship could not continue, wishing her happiness and saying he has tried to reach Meredith Kercher’s family. Both Knox and Sollecito were previously convicted in Kercher’s 2007 killing and later freed after an appeals court raised doubts about the evidence; a third man, Rudy Guede, was separately convicted.

Researchers report discovery of Saccorhytus coronarius, a tiny, 540-million-year-old sea animal interpreted as the most primitive known deuterostome—the broad group whose descendants include vertebrates and ultimately humans. The microfossils, recovered from early Cambrian limestone in Shaanxi, central China, were examined with electron microscopy and CT scanning; preservation was exceptionally detailed despite the specimens appearing as “tiny black grains” to the naked eye.

Saccorhytus was about one millimetre long, roughly sack-shaped with an oversized mouth and bilateral symmetry—a trait inherited by many later animals, including humans. A thin, flexible skin and inferred musculature suggest it moved by wriggling. Conical body structures around its mouth may have allowed swallowed water to exit and could represent precursors to gill slits. Notably, researchers found no evidence of an anus, implying ingestion and egestion used the same opening.

The international team, including scientists from Northwest University (Xi’an), Cambridge and Germany, argue Saccorhytus predates previously known deuterostomes (dated ~510–520 million years) and likely occupied interstitial spaces between sand grains on the seafloor. Its tiny size supports hypotheses that many early animals left scant fossil records, helping reconcile discrepancies between palaeontology and biomolecular “molecular clock” estimates of divergence times. Published in Nature, the study names a new family (Saccorhytidae) and positions Saccorhytus as a plausible model for the primitive ancestor of a wide diversity of later deuterostome lineages.

A Saratov Airlines Antonov An-148 regional jet carrying 71 people crashed near Moscow on Sunday shortly after departing Domodedovo Airport for Orsk, killing everyone aboard. The aircraft disappeared from radar minutes after takeoff and wreckage was found scattered across snowy fields around the Ramenskoye/Argunovo area roughly 40–50 kilometers southeast of the airport. Authorities reported debris and human remains spread over a radius of about a kilometer; initial recovery teams found at least two bodies and one flight recorder. Weather at the time was cold with intermittent snowfall and poor visibility, and some reports said the jet went into a steep descent five minutes after takeoff. State media showed images of wreckage, including an engine, strewn across the snow with no ground casualties reported.

Russian officials — including Transport Minister Maxim Sokolov and the Kremlin — said preliminary indications pointed to no survivors and ordered a special investigative commission. Investigators opened a criminal case and listed multiple possible causes under consideration: weather, human error, technical failure and other factors. Unconfirmed reports cited by media suggested the pilot may have reported a technical malfunction and requested an emergency landing, and some sources mentioned a possible engine explosion. The aircraft was built in 2010, had been stored for some years due to parts shortages, and entered service with Saratov in 2016. President Vladimir Putin postponed other engagements to monitor the inquiry and expressed condolences; DNA testing will be required to identify the victims. The crash follows other recent major Russian aviation disasters and highlights ongoing scrutiny of safety and maintenance practices.

A Louisiana middle school yearbook has attracted attention by including Presley, a 5-year-old golden doodle and service dog, alongside her owner Joseph “Seph” Ware, 14, a seventh-grader at Good Hope Middle School in West Monroe. Seph, diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy at age 3, relies on Presley to assist with tasks his weakening muscles make difficult—picking up dropped items, operating light switches and opening drawers. Presley has been with Seph for four years and is occasionally reunited with her canine sibling Elvis, who works as a service dog for another boy with muscular dystrophy in Wisconsin.

School officials invited Presley to be photographed for picture day, and when asked Seph replied, “Why not.” His mother, Lori Ware, said it took several shots to get Presley to look at the camera, and students have enjoyed Presley’s presence—sometimes sneaking pats in hallways despite rules against petting service animals. The inclusion in the yearbook is especially meaningful to the family because earlier schools were less accepting of the service dog. News coverage and social media have celebrated the gesture, highlighting both Presley’s role in Seph’s life and broader awareness of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a genetic disease that primarily affects boys and leads to progressive muscle, respiratory and cardiac decline.

Salah Abdeslam, the main fugitive sought over the Nov. 13 Paris attacks that killed 130 people, was arrested in Brussels’ Molenbeek on March 18 after a major anti-terror raid. Wounded in a shootout, he was detained alive alongside four others; several suspects are held on charges of sheltering him. The arrest followed fingerprint and DNA links to apartments raided earlier in Brussels, one of which produced a fatal shooting of suspected accomplice Mohamed Belkaid and the discovery of weapons, ammunition and an Islamic State banner. Belgian and French authorities, who plan to seek Abdeslam’s extradition to France, say he likely drove attackers on the night of the massacre and may have worn a suicide belt found afterward. The operation underscored concerns about Molenbeek as a jihadist hub and is expected to yield crucial intelligence on the wider terror cell.

Surgeons at Glenfield Hospital in Leicester have successfully treated a newborn girl, Vanellope Hope Wilkins, born with ectopia cordis — a rare congenital defect in which the heart (and in her case part of the stomach) develops outside the chest. Discovered at a nine-week scan, the condition carries a very poor prognosis (estimated survival under 10 percent) and often leads to pregnancy termination, stillbirth, or death shortly after birth. Despite medical advice suggesting termination, parents Naomi Findlay and Dean Wilkins chose to continue the pregnancy after further testing showed no chromosomal abnormalities.

Vanellope was delivered by Caesarean section on Nov. 22, three weeks early, with around 50 specialists present to reduce infection risk and manage the complex delivery. Immediately after birth she was covered with a sterile plastic bag to keep the exposed heart moist. Within about 50 minutes she underwent the first of three staged operations to relocate her heart into the chest. Over subsequent days and weeks surgeons enlarged her chest cavity to make space, and gravity helped the heart move inward. In the latest procedure surgeons used skin taken from beneath her arms to close the chest and created a protective mesh because she lacks a sternum and ribs. Vanellope remains on a ventilator and faces a prolonged recovery mainly due to infection risk, but clinicians describe her as resilient and doing well so far.

Medical staff note this is believed to be the first surviving UK case of ectopia cordis; only a handful of infant survivors have been reported elsewhere, notably in the United States. Consultants caution long-term outcomes remain uncertain and future protective reconstruction — possibly using growth-accommodating materials or 3D-printed solutions — may be needed. The family named her after a determined Disney character; they hope Vanellope’s survival will offer other families facing similar diagnoses a message of hope and an alternative to termination.

Raffaele Sollecito, recently acquitted on appeal in the Meredith Kercher murder case, has broken his silence in an interview with Italian weekly Oggi. He says he and Amanda Knox speak daily to support one another, "to try and understand what happened" and to rebuild lives after "four years in a circle of hell." Sollecito accepted Knox’s invitation to visit her in Seattle and may travel before Christmas. He emphasized their ongoing emotional bond and the many things they need to discuss after years of suffering. The article revisits disputed forensic evidence—contaminated DNA on a knife and a bra clasp—and notes an independent report criticized the original investigations, which led to their release; prosecutors plan to appeal. Knox, keeping a low profile in Seattle, reportedly faces media interest and alleged offers for televised interviews.

Roger Ebert, the celebrated film critic, died at 70 after a long, influential career that included 46 years at the Chicago Sun-Times, a landmark Pulitzer Prize, and decades co-hosting the iconic television show with Gene Siskel. Known for a writing style that combined scholarship, wit, sarcasm, and vivid enthusiasm, Ebert made moviegoing feel intimately important—his pieces often read like passionate, accessible essays that could make you see films anew. A retrospective of his work highlights ten of his best reviews—spanning classics like Casablanca, Star Wars, and Raging Bull to modern touchstones such as Toy Story, Beauty and the Beast, Fargo, Titanic, Hoop Dreams, Platoon, and E.T.—each showcasing his ability to capture why a film mattered emotionally, culturally, or technically. His praises were as memorable as his scathing takedowns; he produced some of the most blistering and witty critiques in film journalism, from withering one-liners about films like Battlefield Earth and Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen to merciless jibes about lesser comedies and misfires. Beyond reviews, Ebert’s later life and work were marked by resilience: after losing his lower jaw to cancer, he continued to write, blog, and speak to millions via a synthesized voice and social media, earning a Webby award. His memoir Life Itself and interviews reflect candid memories of childhood, friendship with Siskel, devotion to his wife Chaz, and a philosophy of contributing joy despite adversity. Ebert remained active in film festivals and production, insisting he was not courageous—only continuing to do what he loved. He leaves a legacy as America’s most beloved and influential film critic.

Update: initial reports that Henry Cavill earned $14 million for Man of Steel are unconfirmed and likely misleading. The story that Gal Gadot was paid far less than Cavill for their standalone DC debuts sparked discussion about Hollywood’s gender pay gap, but available evidence does not support that specific salary gap.

Early reports claimed Gadot made $300,000 for Wonder Woman while Cavill earned $14 million for Man of Steel. That comparison ignored key distinctions between upfront base pay, bonuses, backend deals and escalators tied to box‑office performance. A source familiar with negotiations told The Hollywood Reporter that Gadot’s upfront pay for Wonder Woman was the same as, or slightly higher than, what Cavill received for Man of Steel; the $14 million figure has been called “ridiculous.” Studios declined to comment.

Industry context shows mid‑six‑figure pay is common for leads with limited track records: Chris Hemsworth reportedly made $150,000 for Thor, Adam Driver around $500,000 for The Force Awakens, and Felicity Jones over $1 million for Rogue One. Box‑office bonuses and renegotiations for sequels can substantially increase earnings; Wonder Woman’s strong performance worldwide (about $574 million to date) makes higher future pay likely for Gadot. Meanwhile, some behind‑the‑scenes players have taken massive sums—producer Jon Peters reportedly earned $80–85 million across Superman projects via long‑standing backend deals. The broader point remains: actors’ compensation varies widely and headline comparisons can be misleading without contract details.

At the Beach to Beacon 10K in Cape Elizabeth, former University of Maine runner Jesse Orach collapsed from heat stroke just shy of the finish while leading the Maine field. Orach, 23, said he felt “it was over” until fellow Maine competitor Robert Gomez, 34, of Windham, helped him to his feet, held him up and pushed him across the line; both were credited with 31:31. Orach later collapsed again and spent about an hour in the medical tent with a recorded core temperature of 107.3°F. The act of assistance surprised and moved spectators and Orach’s family; race officials declined to disqualify either runner. Liam Simpson placed third among Maine men. In the women’s Maine division, Emily Durgin won in 34:43, paced by last year’s champion Michelle Lilienthal, who finished second in 35:11; Tracy Guerrette was third (36:43). The finish-line drama was widely photographed and reported.

Researchers have advanced toward replacing large segments of human bone by growing personalized bone grafts in the lab and using them to repair major jaw defects in pigs. The team, led by Gordana Vunjak‑Novakovic at Columbia University, created custom-shaped scaffolds from decellularized cow bone matched to each pig’s jaw via CT scans. They harvested mesenchymal precursor cells from pig fat, forced the cells and nutrient medium into the porous scaffolds using a snug silicon bioreactor chamber, and cultured the constructs for three weeks so bone matrix began forming before implantation. Fourteen pigs received one of three treatments: six got scaffolds preseeded with their own cells, six received identical scaffolds without cells, and two were left to heal naturally. Over six months all groups showed some regrowth, but the cell-seeded, lab-grown grafts produced more complete regeneration, maintained original bone height, and were the only grafts that matched the mechanical strength of native bone. Unseeded scaffolds tended to shrink, suggesting degradation outpaced new bone formation. The animals recovered quickly and showed no rejection. Experts praise the translation to a large, functional animal model and the bioreactor approach’s potential advantages—provisional bone inside the scaffold may prevent cell loss and help synthesis keep pace with degradation—but note remaining questions. These include optimizing scaffold recipes (for example whether adding bone morphogenetic proteins would help) and proving clear benefits versus other methods such as immediate cell-seeded implantation or current autografts. Vunjak‑Novakovic’s company, EpiBone, aims to pursue further safety evidence and hopes to reach human trials in roughly three years.

A Wealth-X study found Hong Kong overtook New York in 2017 as the city with the largest population of ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNWIs), defined as those worth $30 million or more. Hong Kong’s UHNWI count rose by nearly a third to about 10,000, driven by a booming stock market and deeper financial ties with mainland China. No single mainland Chinese city made the top 10, as China’s wealth is broadly dispersed across the country, though the region has produced many prominent billionaires. Overall global UHNWIs grew 13% to over 250,000 with combined wealth of $31.5 trillion, while the U.S. still hosts nearly a third of ultra-rich individuals. Asia’s UHNWI population rose 20% and may close regional gaps, though China faces economic headwinds in 2018.

President Donald Trump escalated a brewing international trade dispute by threatening to impose retaliatory taxes on European car imports after announcing steep U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum. In a March 3 Twitter post, Trump asserted there is a “big imbalance” between the U.S. and the European Union and warned that if the EU imposed punitive measures on American goods in response to his 25% steel and 10% aluminum tariffs, the U.S. would “simply apply a Tax on their Cars which freely pour into the U.S.” The threat targeted major brands such as Volkswagen and BMW and highlighted that in 2016 the EU exported over 6 million cars worldwide, with more than 1 million going to the United States. U.S. Census figures show the U.S. ran a trade deficit with Europe of more than $151 billion in 2017.

Trump’s move provoked sharp responses from trading partners. Canada’s Prime Minister Justin Trudeau called the tariffs “absolutely unacceptable” and warned of serious market disruption; Canada supplies nearly 90% of the U.S.’s imported steel and accounted for 16% of U.S. steel imports in 2017. Canadian officials signaled readiness to defend their industries. EU leaders, including European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker, threatened retaliatory duties on U.S. items such as Harley-Davidson motorcycles, Kentucky bourbon and blue jeans. EU trade chiefs reportedly considered a broad 25% tax on U.S. imports. Critics, including Germany’s industry head Dieter Kempf, cautioned that such tit-for-tat measures risk a damaging spiral of protectionism that could cost jobs on both sides. The White House reportedly plans global application of the tariffs without exempting allies, intensifying concerns that the initial metal tariffs could ignite a wider trade war.

At a West Hollywood launch party for her new fragrance True Reflection, Kim Kardashian was unexpectedly hit with a bag of flour by a young woman while doing red-carpet interviews. The incident occurred at the London Hotel during a charity event; eyewitnesses say the assailant briefly fled but was detained by Kardashian’s representative and security. The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department filed a non-criminal battery report at Kim’s request, though she declined to press charges and the woman was later released. Firefighters were called to check the powder’s safety and left after confirming it was ordinary flour. Kardashian calmly left to clean up in a private room and returned to the carpet about ten minutes later, laughing off the episode and joking with her makeup artist that she had plenty of “translucent powder.” Family members reacted on social media—Kris Jenner urged security be called if anyone came after her, Khloé tweeted she wished she’d been there, and Kourtney criticized the attack as “classy” given the charitable context and mused the woman wouldn’t have confronted her while pregnant. Media speculation included a possible shout about fur from the assailant, but no clear motive has been confirmed. The incident drew widespread attention and mixed reactions online.

A Chinese animal lover, Yang Xiaoyun, paid about 7,000 yuan (roughly US$1,100) to rescue around 100 dogs from markets in Yulin, a southern city known for an annual dog meat event held on the summer solstice. Photos showed Yang inspecting caged dogs; she plans to rehome them near Tianjin. The Yulin event, dating only from 2009, draws global condemnation from activists and celebrities such as Ricky Gervais and Leona Lewis, who have used social media to campaign against it. Activists say many animals sold there are stolen pets or strays and describe brutal transport, cramped cages, and cruel public slaughter methods. Investigations by groups like Animals Asia and Humane Society International report carcasses, intestines, and live, emaciated dogs being prepared for sale; traders have even used blow-torches on carcasses for shipment. Local authorities insist the city did not officially organize a dog-meat festival and emphasize Yulin’s openness, while also urging adherence to food-safety laws. Eating dog is not illegal in China, but critics point to public health risks—particularly rabies exposure from handling unvaccinated animals—and violations of regulations banning sale of meat from diseased or dead animals. Growing pet ownership and a rising animal-rights movement in China, along with shifting attitudes among younger generations, have intensified calls to end the trade; some regions and businesses have already scaled back or closed dog-meat operations amid mounting domestic and international pressure.

The premiere of Get Hard at the South by Southwest Film Festival provoked unusually blunt criticism that overshadowed the film’s launch and stirred a wider debate about whether the Will Ferrell–Kevin Hart comedy crosses the line into racist or homophobic territory. During a Q&A with director Etan Cohen, an audience member bluntly declared the film “seems racist,” and others questioned whether the movie perpetuated stereotypes. Those comments, amplified by media coverage and early reviews, created negative buzz in the run-up to the wide release.

Get Hard centers on a wealthy hedge-fund manager (Ferrell) sentenced to prison who hires a law-abiding car-wash owner (Hart) to prepare him for life behind bars. Much of the film’s humor plays on the Ferrell character’s exaggerated fear of prison rape, including a joke in which he attempts to solicit oral sex from a gay man in a bathroom stall. Critics singled out scenes like this as examples of “gay-panic” humor; Variety and The Guardian both criticized the film’s treatment of homosexuality, while other reviewers called the jokes ugly or outdated.

In response, the film’s makers and stars have defended the movie as satire rather than endorsement of bigotry. Ferrell argued that R-rated comedies are meant to provoke and hold a mirror to existing attitudes, not endorse them. Hart emphasized that the film portrays two characters who misjudge each other and ultimately grow beyond those misconceptions. Co-writers include Etan Cohen and Key & Peele’s Jay Martel and Ian Roberts; Adam McKay, a producer and longtime Ferrell collaborator, said coverage of the backlash was “lazy journalism” and that the film is intended as a broad, filthy comedy with satirical undertones about income inequality and the insulated views of the one percent.

Some critics and commentators found the film more disappointing than offensive—Vanity Fair’s reviewer said it wasn’t mean-spirited but failed to be very funny—while others defended its aim to lampoon narrow-minded elites. McKay argued that fears of prison assault are realistic and not equivalent to homophobia. The NAACP and GLAAD had not publicly commented. The movie’s commercial prospects may be buffered by Ferrell’s and Hart’s popularity and Ferrell’s high-profile media appearances, but whether the early controversy will affect box office remains uncertain. The producers maintain that the film’s true reception will settle over time.

Romney pollster Neil Newhouse circulated a memo arguing recent convention-driven gains for President Obama are temporary and that the election’s decisive factors are economic: 43 months of 8%+ unemployment, 23 million Americans struggling for work, and 47 million on food stamps. Newhouse urged supporters not to overreact to polling bumps, asserting the “basic structure” of the race remains favorable to Mitt Romney. He said Romney has become more competitive across the map, citing tightening polls in traditional Democratic states like New Jersey and Connecticut, new battlegrounds such as Wisconsin and New Mexico, and eight states where margins are under three points. The memo emphasized Romney’s advantage on economic messaging, fundraising (over $111 million raised in August), and an aggressive grassroots ground game that has eclipsed 2008 door knocks and volunteer contacts. Romney advisers dismissed reports that Ohio was slipping as media spin, noting mixed state polls and confidence in ad buys and turnout operations. Independent poll aggregators show Obama with a modest convention-fueled lead, but Newhouse and allies argued Romney’s organization, cash, and message could still deliver a win.

A baby shower at a Stoughton, Massachusetts social club erupted into a 200-person brawl after a bar-side fight between two men. When a club officer attempted to break up the confrontation, the situation escalated as guests joined in, surrounding officers and throwing bottles and chairs. Police called for backup from neighboring departments, state police and the sheriff’s office; officers deployed Tasers and tased at least one partygoer. Four people—Paulo Depina, Aderito Deandrade, Patrick Lopes and a teenager—were arrested on charges including assault and battery on a police officer. Several attendees and officers suffered non-life-threatening injuries. Club members and organizers expressed shock that a private, Portuguese-community event with many children could turn so violent; the suspects are due in court on Monday.

At the 50th annual Country Music Association Awards at Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena, Garth Brooks won entertainer of the year, defeating Carrie Underwood, Chris Stapleton, Keith Urban and returning champion Luke Bryan. Taylor Swift presented Brooks with the honor as he celebrated country music onstage. The milestone show featured high-profile, sometimes controversial moments, most notably Beyoncé’s first CMA performance of “Daddy Lessons,” joined by the Dixie Chicks. The surprise duet and Dixie Chicks’ return drew enthusiastic responses from many but also backlash on social media from some country fans still critical of the trio after past political remarks.

The night opened with a multi-generational salute—12 artists including Randy Travis, Vince Gill, Charley Pride, Dwight Yoakam and Ben Haggard—celebrating the CMA’s 50th anniversary. Dolly Parton received the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award and was honored by Reba, Carrie Underwood, Martina McBride, Jennifer Nettles and Kacey Musgraves in a stirring “I Will Always Love You.” Chris Stapleton was the evening’s biggest winner with male vocalist and music video of the year. Underwood ended Miranda Lambert’s six-year run by winning female vocalist of the year. Eric Church’s Mr. Misunderstood took album of the year; Maren Morris won new artist; Thomas Rhett’s “Die a Happy Man” was single of the year; Lori McKenna won song of the year for “Humble and Kind.” Other winners included Kenny Chesney (Pinnacle Award), Little Big Town (vocal group), Brothers Osborne (vocal duo) and Dierks Bentley & Elle King (musical event). The three-hour broadcast mixed performances from traditional and contemporary stars and celebrity presenters, under hosts Brad Paisley and Carrie Underwood.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu retracted and clarified remarks after widespread criticism for suggesting that Haj Amin al-Husseini, the former mufti of Jerusalem, inspired Adolf Hitler to implement the Holocaust. In a Facebook post, Netanyahu said he never intended to absolve Hitler or the Nazis of responsibility for the Final Solution, asserting that the decision to move from deportation to systematic extermination was made by the Nazi leadership itself and did not depend on outside influence. He acknowledged the mufti was a collaborator who supported Nazi aims—propagating anti-Jewish lies, recruiting Muslims for the SS, and opposing Jewish emigration—but emphasized that the Nazis “did not need him” to decide on genocide. The clarification followed his Oct. 20 World Zionist Congress speech in which he recounted a disputed 1941 meeting in which he claimed the mufti told Hitler to “burn” the Jews—an account historians called false and potentially enabling Holocaust denial. Netanyahu’s reversal drew rebukes from historians, political figures, and foreign leaders, including German officials who reiterated that responsibility for the Holocaust rests with the Germans.

Seven-year-old Grayson Powell delivered a standout performance at a youth bowling tournament in St. John’s, Newfoundland, rolling a personal best 171 and helping his three-person Riverdale team to what would have been a provincial championship. However, moments before medal presentation provincial director Gordon (Gord) Davis informed Grayson’s parents that he was disqualified because his faded black jeans did not meet the tournament’s dress code requiring black pants. Grayson had warmed up for 15 minutes and bowled three games without comment, and his family and supporters say the disqualification only came after the team had won. Todd Powell, Grayson’s father, accused Davis of scheming to elevate teams from Davis’s own bowling alley in Corner Brook, noting that the second- and third-place teams—both from that alley—were moved up after Riverdale was ejected. Powell demanded a written apology for his son and teammates. Davis and Newfoundland & Labrador Youth Bowl Canada (NL YBC) defended the decision, pointing to a decades-old Provincial A dress code and saying parents were aware of the rule. Davis posted lengthy responses on Facebook explaining that additional executive input was required before action, that he avoided interrupting play to spare embarrassment, and that while the ruling stood the organization later planned a special presentation to recognize the children’s performance. The governing body emphasized moving on and focusing on inclusivity in the sport, though critics say the enforcement timing and alleged conflict of interest marred the event and left Grayson feeling “sad.” The incident sparked debate over strict rule enforcement, fairness, and transparency in youth sports.

The University of Texas at Austin will relocate the Jefferson Davis statue from the South Mall to an exhibit at the Dolph Briscoe Center for American History, President Gregory Fenves announced after a 12-member advisory panel reviewed campus monuments. Fenves said Davis “is in a separate category” because he had few ties to Texas and his role in the Confederacy is best interpreted in an educational setting. The move, expected to begin within days with refurbishment and relocation completed within about 18 months, is intended to allow contextualization rather than honorific commemoration.

Four other statues — of Robert E. Lee, Albert Sidney Johnston, John Reagan and former Texas governor James Hogg — will remain on the South Mall, as they have stronger Texas ties or more complex legacies. Fenves said he will consider explanatory plaques, including possibly on the Littlefield Fountain, to place those figures in historical context. For symmetry, the Woodrow Wilson statue opposite Davis will be moved to another outdoor location.

The panel solicited more than 3,100 public opinions and offered five options; most favored moving some or all statues to a historical center or adding contextual markers. Student leaders who advocated moving Davis welcomed the decision. The announcement follows campus controversies, vandalism and broader national debate over Confederate symbols after racially motivated violence. State legislators urged similar review of Capitol monuments.

Researchers developed targeted error correction sequencing (TEC-Seq), an ultrasensitive blood-based method to detect tumor-derived cell-free DNA (ctDNA) for early cancer detection and monitoring. TEC-Seq targets 58 cancer-related genes (about 81 kb) and uses deep, redundant sequencing (~30,000×), combined endogenous and limited exogenous molecular barcodes, and stringent error filtering to distinguish true somatic mutations from sequencing errors, germline variants, and mutations arising from clonal hematopoiesis. Analytical validation with dilution series showed high sensitivity (97.4% overall; 100% at 0.2% allele fraction) and extremely low false-positive rates (<3.3 × 10−7 per base). In 44 healthy volunteers, TEC-Seq found no driver gene mutations but did detect DNMT3A mutations consistent with clonal hematopoiesis in 16% of individuals. Among 194 cancer patients (breast, colorectal, lung, ovarian), TEC-Seq detected tumor-specific mutations in plasma in 62% overall for stage I–II disease: 71% colorectal, 59% breast, 59% lung, and 68% ovarian. cfDNA concentrations and ctDNA allele fractions were higher in metastatic disease. Comparison with matched tumor tissue (100 patients) showed 72% of assessed plasma alterations were identical to tumor mutations; 82% of patients had at least one concordant alteration. Higher preoperative ctDNA levels in resectable colorectal cancer were associated with recurrence and worse survival. TEC-Seq’s broader gene panel improved detection versus hotspot-only approaches. While promising for noninvasive early-stage cancer detection and patient management, the authors note the need for larger validation studies, improved sensitivity, and careful consideration of clinical implications of detecting indolent lesions.

Firefighters near Grande Prairie, Alta., used specialized large-animal rescue training to save 10 horses that fell through thin, warming ice on a slough about 65 km west of the city. The call came late Sunday afternoon and about 35 firefighters and search-and-rescue members from Hythe, Beaverlodge, La Glace and Grande Prairie responded. Dramatic video shows crews cutting channels in the ice with chainsaws, then using slings and boards to guide horses over mud and melting ice to shore. All 10 animals were out of the water by about 6 p.m.; three later died—two from exhaustion and one from injuries inflicted during the struggle. Seven horses were assessed as likely to recover. Fire Chief Trevor Grant warned that spring temperature shifts can make ice unsafe within hours and urged landowners to monitor animals near sloughs.

Ruth Ann Steinhagen, the Chicago woman whose 1949 near-fatal shooting of former Cubs first baseman Eddie Waitkus inspired Bernard Malamud’s novel The Natural and the 1984 film, died Dec. 29 at 83 after an accidental fall that produced a subdural hematoma. Her death, at Swedish Covenant Hospital, went unreported publicly until discovered by the Chicago Tribune months later. Born Ruth Catherine Steinhagen in Cicero on Dec. 23, 1929, to German immigrant parents, she became obsessed as a teenager with Waitkus, then a Cubs star. After he was traded to the Philadelphia Phillies, her fixation intensified: she created a shrine of his photos, clippings and memorabilia, taught herself Lithuanian and even mimicked his tastes. On June 14, 1949, while the Phillies were in Chicago, the 19-year-old lured Waitkus to a room at the Edgewater Beach Hotel with an unsigned note. When he arrived she shot him below the heart with a pawnshop .22 rifle. Newspapers sensationalized the case and labeled her among the era’s “baseball Annies,” obsessive groupies who pursued players. Steinhagen was declared legally insane and confined to Kankakee State Hospital for nearly three years; doctors later deemed her sane and she was released in 1952. Waitkus, who recovered sufficiently to play the next season and helped the Phillies win the pennant, chose not to press charges at her release, a decision that helped her fade from public view. For decades she lived quietly in a modest Northwest Side home with her sister and parents, rarely speaking about her past; neighbors only belatedly learned of her history. Authors and historians note her case as a striking intersection of obsession, mental illness and baseball lore that reshaped attention to stalking and celebrity fixation.

A vandal sprayed paint on Pablo Picasso’s 1929 "Woman in a Red Armchair" at Houston’s Menil Collection, marking the first such attack on the museum in 25 years. Video—both a bystander's smartphone clip posted to YouTube and the Menil’s surveillance footage—shows a man stenciling a bull and the word “Conquista” on the canvas before fleeing; a photographer seen nearby also left and may be a conspirator. Menil communications director Vance Muse said the painting was quickly taken to chief conservator Brad Epley, who removed the spray paint and reported an “excellent prognosis,” though the work must now rest. Houston police are treating the incident as criminal mischief and are actively investigating; no arrests have been made. The Menil, which acquired the Picasso in 1956, owns several other Picasso works and has reviewed security measures; witnesses are asked to contact authorities with information.

On October 21, a massive distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) assault against DNS provider Dyn disrupted major websites by overwhelming Dyn’s servers in three waves. The attackers leveraged the Mirai malware to hijack poorly secured Internet of Things (IoT) devices—mostly DVRs and IP cameras—turning them into a botnet that flooded Dyn with traffic. Flashpoint’s investigation, which Dyn has supported privately, links the attack to English-language hacking forums such as hackforums.net and suggests the perpetrators were likely non-state “script kiddies” motivated by notoriety rather than politics or profit. Flashpoint found that a video game company, possibly PlayStation Network, may have been the intended target and Dyn was hit incidentally because that company used Dyn’s DNS. The public Mirai source code release by a handle called Anna-Senpai has made attribution harder, since many actors can now repurpose the code. Experts warn the scale of the attack limits the usefulness of any single company’s post-mortem: many IoT devices are unpatchable or poorly maintained, enabling repeat assaults. Policymakers are responding—Senator Mark Warner urged regulators and ISPs to consider restrictions on insecure IoT devices, calling the situation a “tragedy of the commons.” Until manufacturers, ISPs, and device owners improve baseline IoT security, similar large-scale DDoS incidents remain a persistent threat.

Republican front-runner Donald Trump ignited a major controversy when, during an MSNBC interview, he suggested that if abortion were outlawed “there has to be some form of punishment” for those involved. When pressed about whether that would include the woman, he replied, “Yeah, there has to be some form.” The remark provoked swift bipartisan condemnation. Trump later issued a clarification stating that if Congress or states made abortion illegal, the legal responsibility should fall on the doctor or person performing the procedure, not the woman, calling the woman a “victim” and reiterating he is “pro-life with exceptions.”

The fallout was immediate within his own party. Rival Republicans — notably Ted Cruz and John Kasich — condemned any talk of punishing women. Cruz’s campaign emphasized focusing on providers, not patients, and said punishment of women was inappropriate, while Kasich said women “shouldn’t be punished.” Other conservative leaders and pro-life activists also rejected the idea that women should face criminal sanctions; leaders of mainstream pro-life groups said no pro-lifer would advocate punishing women and that outreach for healing is the proper response. Republican strategists warned the comments exacerbated doubts about Trump’s commitment to conservative social views and harmed his already weak standing with female voters, who preferred Hillary Clinton by large margins in polls.

Trump’s remarks compounded a week of controversies — including attacks on reporter Michelle Fields and his campaign manager Corey Lewandowski being charged with misdemeanor battery — and raised fresh worries about party unity. He also drew criticism for saying “we’ll see who [the nominee] is” in reference to pledging support for the eventual GOP nominee, and for lamenting the constraints of the Geneva Conventions. Many Republicans see these episodes as evidence that Trump is unpredictable and could fracture the party ahead of the convention, even as he leads in delegates.

The controversy played out amid a broader debate over GOP positions on abortion. Trump has publicly shifted from earlier pro-choice statements to a pro-life stance, a conversion he likened to Ronald Reagan’s evolution — a comparison fact-checkers and historians say is historically tenuous. Across the Republican field, most candidates favor overturning Roe v. Wade; a significant subset oppose exceptions for rape and incest, positions that polls show are at odds with broad public sentiment. As the Wisconsin primary approached, Trump faced a competitive environment with rivals seeking to capitalize on his missteps while party leaders worried about the long-term consequences of his rhetoric for Republican prospects in the general election.

Coach is acquiring Kate Spade & Co. for $2.4 billion in a deal designed to broaden Coach’s appeal to younger, millennial shoppers and accelerate its multi-brand luxury strategy. Coach will pay $18.50 per Kate Spade share, representing a premium that sent Kate Spade stock up more than 8% and Coach shares up about 5% on the announcement. The transaction is expected to close in Q3 2017 and to be accretive to adjusted earnings in fiscal 2018.

Coach CEO Victor Luis emphasized Kate Spade’s differentiated positioning and millennial awareness. Management said Kate Spade will retain brand independence and key staff. Coach forecasts about $50 million in annual cost synergies over time through combined inventory management and supply-chain efficiencies, which could also reduce Kate Spade’s reliance on frequent online flash sales and lift its luxury positioning.

Analysts characterized the deal as sensible for brand fit and part of Coach’s broader plan to become a global, multi-brand luxury group — following prior purchases such as Stuart Weitzman and reported interest in other acquisitions like Jimmy Choo. Coach’s recent shift away from heavy U.S. discounting has improved its financials, supporting a move from turnaround to growth. As of the announcement, Coach shares were up 12% over the past year, while Kate Spade shares had fallen over the same period.

Investigators uncovered additional human remains Sunday at the 95-acre South Carolina property owned by Todd Kohlhepp, where a woman was found chained inside a metal storage container. Spartanburg County Sheriff Chuck Wright said remains were located at one of two burial sites Kohlhepp identified; officials have not yet identified the remains or determined cause of death, and searches will continue. The probe has expanded to other properties Kohlhepp owns or previously owned, including locations outside South Carolina, with assistance from the FBI and Department of Homeland Security.

Kohlhepp was arrested after the chained woman was discovered; he is charged with her kidnapping and has confessed to a 2003 quadruple slaying at Superbike Motorsports in Chesnee, where investigators say he shot the owner, service manager, mechanic and bookkeeper. He was denied bond during a brief court appearance and did not speak; he lacked an attorney. Authorities suspect he may be responsible for at least three other killings and additional charges are expected.

Families of the 2003 victims expressed mixed emotions—relief, sorrow and a desire for justice—during courthouse appearances. Kohlhepp, a registered sex offender due to a 1987 Arizona conviction for kidnapping and sexual assault as a teenager, was released from prison in 2001 and later obtained a South Carolina real estate license. Investigators continue meticulous work to recover and preserve evidence from the property; one previously recovered body was identified as the boyfriend of the chained woman. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Mitt Romney won the Nevada Republican caucuses decisively, securing a second straight victory after his Florida primary win and extending his lead for the GOP presidential nomination. With returns from most counties showing Romney at about 42 percent, Newt Gingrich around 25 percent, Ron Paul roughly 20 percent and Rick Santorum 13 percent, Romney led comfortably though results from populous Clark County were still pending. Nevada’s contest was low-key compared with Florida—few ads, no debates—and its 28 proportionally awarded delegates required just 3.57 percent to earn delegates. Romney attacked President Obama’s economic record and promoted an assertive American global role. The caucus electorate cited the ability to beat Obama as the top concern; about one-quarter of caucus-goers were Mormon. Gingrich and Paul sought to regroup—Gingrich planning Ohio campaigning, Paul focusing on Minnesota—and Santorum aimed to survive by targeting Gingrich and courting conservative voters. The calendar moves to Minnesota, Colorado and Missouri next, with Michigan and Arizona to follow Feb. 28.

On the night of October 18–19, observers across parts of the Americas and Europe can watch a lunar occultation as the waning gibbous Moon passes in front of Aldebaran, one of the sky’s brightest, orange-hued stars. Lunar occultations occur monthly in the ongoing series of Aldebaran events that began in January 2015 and run through September 2018; after this series ends, the next set won’t start until 2033.
