Depending on location, viewers will witness either a total occultation—Aldebaran disappearing behind the Moon and reappearing up to about 75 minutes later—or a grazing occultation, where the star seems to skim the lunar limb and may vanish and reappear several times due to the Moon’s mountains and valleys. The narrow “graze line” crosses parts of the U.S., including Los Angeles, Denver and near Minneapolis, making those spots ideal for dramatic views. Binoculars or a small telescope are recommended; the star’s disappearance often happens on the Moon’s sunlit side and its reappearance from the dark side. IOTA and Sky & Telescope provide detailed maps, timings and limb profiles for hundreds of locations to help observers time and record the event.

President Trump unveiled a Republican tax-reform framework promising sweeping, pro-growth changes and simpler filing, framing it as a win for the middle class and American businesses. On individual taxes, the plan would condense seven brackets into three—12%, 25% and 35%—while allowing Congress to add a higher fourth bracket if needed. It doubles the standard deduction to $12,000 for singles and $24,000 for couples, increases the child tax credit (amount unspecified), and creates a new $500 credit for non-child dependents. The proposal would eliminate the alternative minimum tax and the estate tax, preserve mortgage interest and charitable deductions, and remove most other itemized deductions—including many state and local tax deductions—while maintaining incentives for education, retirement, R&D, and low-income housing.

On the business side, the corporate tax rate would fall from 35% to 20%, and pass-through businesses would face a new 25% top rate. Republicans also propose moving from a worldwide to a territorial tax system for multinationals, with a yet-to-be-determined repatriation tax and measures to tax foreign profits. The plan would limit interest deductibility while allowing immediate expensing of business investments for five years.

Political and fiscal questions remain: many details are unresolved, safeguards to stop wealthy individuals from exploiting pass-through status are unspecified, and cost estimates vary widely—some analyses projecting multi‑trillion-dollar deficits over a decade despite GOP claims that growth will offset revenues. The White House seeks bipartisan support but has discussed using budget rules to pass the plan with a simple majority. Democrats and some watchdogs criticized the proposal as favoring the wealthy; Trump insisted it benefits everyday Americans and urged voters to pressure lawmakers.

The document highlights the Beloit College Mindset List, a long-running project that catalogs cultural touchstones shaping each incoming college cohort. Created in 1998 by Tom McBride and Ron Nief to help faculty avoid dated references, the list tracks generational norms—technology, media, politics, and everyday life—for classes like 2014 (born 1992) and later cohorts. It emphasizes that these students view digital life as routine: many never wrote in cursive, email is "too slow," smartphones replace watches, and instant online access blurs information and knowledge. Professors are urged to teach research patience and scholarship. The text includes a detailed 75-item mindset list for the Class of 2014 (e.g., Korean cars always common, Nirvana as “oldies,” DNA mapping exists, Russia has not threatened nukes) and notes ongoing Mindset List projects, talks, books, and resources aimed at educators navigating generational communication gaps.

Conservative site RedState and parent Townhall Media abruptly fired several prominent writers and editors, many of whom were known critics of President Trump. Laid-off staff included Caleb Howe, Jay Caruso, Ben Howe, Patrick “Patterico” Frey, Neil Stevens, and Susan Wright. Some discovered their dismissals when accounts were locked; others got an internal memo from Townhall general manager Jonathan Garthwaite saying the outlet could no longer support its full roster. Former editor Erick Erickson and multiple sources told reporters the purge appeared driven by both financial and political motives: higher-paid contract writers were cut, and among lower-paid contributors the anti‑Trump voices were disproportionately targeted. Fired contributors and remaining staff interpreted the moves as signaling an intolerance for criticism of the president and a broader Trump-era shift in conservative media toward loyalty over accountability. Salem Media Group, Townhall’s owner, did not comment. The layoffs highlight deepening splits within the conservative movement and raise questions about editorial independence at influential opinion sites.

Johnny Bobbitt Jr., the homeless Marine veteran who used his last $20 to help stranded motorist Kate McClure, is suing McClure and her boyfriend Mark D’Amico, alleging they committed fraud by misappropriating more than half of over $400,000 raised on a GoFundMe campaign established on his behalf. Attorneys for Bobbitt filed the suit in Burlington County Superior Court, New Jersey, seeking compensatory damages, fees, an accounting of the donations, injunctive relief to prevent dissipation of funds, and appointment of a receiver to hold the money in court. The fundraiser, begun after McClure publicly recounted Bobbitt’s act of kindness in November, drew donations from more than 14,000 people. McClure and D’Amico initially provided Bobbitt with some funds, bought him a camper and supplied clothing and food, and announced plans for trusts, a bank account for daily needs, a modest salary, and a retirement trust. According to the lawsuit, no formal trust was created and the couple have refused to give Bobbitt access to the majority of the funds. Bobbitt’s legal team says the couple treated the donations as a “personal piggy bank” to support a lifestyle they otherwise could not afford. McClure and D’Amico deny wrongdoing, saying they’ve been cautious about giving Bobbitt large sums because of his drug addiction; D’Amico has claimed large portions were spent on drugs, bills, and family support and said more than $150,000 remained. Bobbitt, who relapsed and returned to panhandling after rehab, and his attorneys sought court oversight after repeated requests for a full accounting went unanswered. A hearing on the case was scheduled this week.

Former Toronto mayor Rob Ford listed several personal items on eBay under the username "torontorobford," including the tie he wore when he admitted to smoking crack cocaine, moose-print pajama pants, a size 4XL football jersey, and a novelty poster. The items were presented with brief backstories linking them to Ford’s public persona and time in office—for example, the pajama listing notes they were the patterned pants he wore on a Wal-Mart shopping trip. The auctions appear geared toward collectors of Ford memorabilia, though potential buyers are warned that the seller had a feedback score of zero at the time of listing. The eBay postings included standard purchase and bidding notices—confirmations that a winning bid commits the buyer to purchase, references to the Global Shipping Program and possible import charges, and reminders about automatic bidding, required minimum bids, PayPal requirements, and shipping details. Repeated on-screen bidding prompts and help overlays were shown in the listings, emphasizing customary eBay mechanics like being outbid, increasing a max bid, and checkout estimates. Overall, the sale mixes political notoriety with ordinary online-auction fine print.

The United Nations’ Global Compact for Migration, a non-binding, voluntary agreement adopted Dec. 10, 2018 by 164 of 193 U.N. member states in Marrakech, seeks to improve how migrants are treated worldwide and promote “safe, orderly and regular migration.” Framed as a cooperative pact rather than a new legal right to migrate, it emphasizes international cooperation—using the word “cooperation” repeatedly—and urges measures to fight discrimination and protect migrants’ human rights. The compact responds to the scale of migration, with the IOM estimating about 1 billion migrants globally, and highlights that more than 80% move safely and most flows are South-South rather than toward richer nations. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres stressed the human cost of unregulated migration—more than 60,000 migrant deaths since 2000—and called the pact a response to those dangers and abuses by smugglers and exploitative employers. Supporters, including German Chancellor Angela Merkel, argue migration benefits global economies by replenishing aging workforces and fueling remittances to poorer countries. Opponents—led by the United States, which did not participate in drafting the compact and formally withdrew—contend the pact could impose policies and insufficiently distinguish legal from illegal migration. Several European and other countries (including Hungary, Poland, Italy and others) also voiced objections amid rising anti-immigration sentiment after the 2015 refugee influx. U.N. leaders hope holdouts may still be persuaded despite political headwinds and domestic debates in numerous countries.

Harper Lee, the 87-year-old author of To Kill a Mockingbird, sued in federal court in Manhattan to re-secure the novel’s copyright and seek unspecified damages, alleging exploitation by Samuel Pinkus, the son-in-law of her former literary agent. The complaint says Pinkus took advantage of Lee’s declining hearing and eyesight—she lived in assisted care after a 2007 stroke—to obtain an assignment of the book’s copyright to him and a company he controlled. Although the copyright was reportedly reassigned to Lee last year and Pinkus was discharged as her agent, the suit contends he continued receiving royalties and commissions. The complaint accuses Pinkus of self-dealing and breaching the agent’s duty of loyalty; it also names Leigh Ann Winick, president of Keystone Literary LLC and Pinkus’s wife, and Gerald Posner, who incorporated one of Pinkus’s businesses. McIntosh & Otis, Lee’s longtime agency, previously won an arbitration judgment against Pinkus’s company over diverted commissions. To Kill a Mockingbird, Lee’s only published novel, won the Pulitzer Prize and has sold over 30 million copies worldwide.

Former New York Gov. Eliot Spitzer, who resigned more than five years ago amid a prostitution scandal, has resurfaced as a candidate for New York City comptroller and faced intense scrutiny about his past on MSNBC’s Morning Joe and in interviews with POLITICO. On Morning Joe, asked how he’s changed, Spitzer choked up, saying he had endured “a lot of pain” and that the experience had changed him. Hosts and panelists debated whether his tears were genuine; panelist Nicole Wallace called them authentic, and Mika Brzezinski praised his willingness to face cameras and take responsibility. Spitzer acknowledged his misconduct as “wrong,” attributing it to hubris and failure of judgment, and urged voters to consider the “totality” of his record when judging him.

Politically, Spitzer is pitching himself as an activist comptroller who would leverage New York City’s nearly $140 billion in pension assets to press corporate governance reforms and exert influence over financial institutions. He highlighted priorities like separating CEO and board chairman roles — citing the Jamie Dimon debate at JPMorgan Chase — and said structural checks are important in corporate governance. Spitzer emphasized his prior achievements as attorney general and governor, including high-profile Wall Street actions and progressive stances on issues like same-sex marriage and immigrant drivers’ licenses, asking voters to weigh his record rather than only his scandal.

Journalists and commentators placed Spitzer’s comeback in the broader context of modern politics, noting how sexual scandals no longer necessarily end careers. Observers argued that a coarsened media environment and voters’ pragmatic focus on competence allow politicians to rebound if they demonstrate resilience and effectiveness, a dynamic seen in figures from Bill Clinton to more recent disgraced officials.

Fenway Park, home of the Boston Red Sox for a century, is celebrated as America’s most beloved and oldest major league ballpark. Its distinctive features — the brick entrance on Yawkey Way, the manual scoreboard in left, Pesky’s Pole in right, and the quirky, cramped field with odd angles and minimal foul territory — create an intimate, unpredictable game experience where balls frequently land in the stands and fans hear players’ chatter. Fenway’s character and place in Boston life make it a destination akin to the Freedom Trail; tours run year-round and the park appears across culture, from John Updike’s praise to films like Fever Pitch and Field of Dreams and TV nods in Cheers. Beyond baseball, Fenway has hosted football teams, hockey’s Winter Classic, presidential speeches, and major concerts. Its century of lore includes iconic moments — Babe Ruth’s first pitch, Ted Williams’s last homer, Carlton Fisk’s 1975 World Series blast, Roger Clemens’s 20-strikeout game, and Dave Roberts’s 2004 steal — plus colorful rituals and anecdotes: the Royal Rooters’ “Tessie,” Manny Ramirez’s antics, Pedro Martínez’s tempestuous confrontations, and countless fan memories. Largely unchanged since 1912, Fenway endures as a living monument to baseball history.

Elon Musk announced that he will not take Tesla private, reversing a process he initiated earlier in August. After exploring the possibility with advisors Silver Lake, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley and soliciting feedback from a wide range of shareholders, Musk concluded that remaining a public company is the better path. He emphasized the deep loyalty of Tesla’s investors—many of whom have supported the company since its 2010 IPO when it had no production—and said their views weighed heavily in his decision. Institutional investors pointed to compliance constraints limiting investments in private companies, and retail shareholders generally would lack a clear way to hold shares if Tesla went private. Though Musk believes there was ample funding available to finance a privatization, the consensus from discussions was often “please don’t do this.” He also determined that the process of going private would be more time-consuming and distracting than anticipated, which could divert focus from critical operational priorities—most importantly ramping Model 3 production and achieving profitability. Musk met with Tesla’s board, which agreed to remain public. Going forward, Tesla will concentrate on building desirable sustainable-energy products and demonstrating financial sustainability. Musk thanked investors, customers and employees and expressed enthusiasm for continuing to lead Tesla as a public company.

Belgium is facing its first criminal trial linked to euthanasia since legalization in 2002 after three East Flanders doctors were referred to court over the 2010 death of 38-year-old Tine Nys, who had been diagnosed with Asperger’s two months before she was euthanized. The referral follows a criminal complaint by Nys’s sister alleging procedural irregularities, including fumbling by the physician who administered the lethal injection and requests that family members confirm death. Emails also surfaced in which psychiatrist Dr. Lieve Thienpont, who approved Nys’s request, criticized the family and sought to block investigations. The Chamber of Indictment found sufficient indications to send the case to trial for “poisoning.” The case has revived debate in Belgium—one of the few countries allowing euthanasia for psychiatric suffering—about whether conditions like autism qualify as “unbearable and untreatable” and whether safeguards are adequate.

Controversy also surrounds Thienpont’s broader practice: she has approved a high number of psychiatric euthanasia requests, prompting concern from peers including Dr. Wim Distelmans, head of Belgium’s euthanasia review commission, who stopped accepting referrals from her, citing worries about whether independent consultations and other legal requirements were properly fulfilled. Critics argue Belgium’s vague rules and limited transparency grant too much individual discretion; only one case had previously been referred to prosecutors and review committees release little information. Advocates for psychiatric euthanasia, and some patients who say approval spared them suicide, emphasize autonomy and relief when treatments fail. Meanwhile psychiatrists and relatives call for stricter oversight, clearer guidelines, and ensuring all treatment options are exhausted before granting euthanasia to psychiatric patients. The trial will test legal limits and oversight of euthanasia for mental suffering in Belgium.

On October 27, 2018, a gunman entered the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh during Saturday Sabbath services and opened fire, killing 11 worshippers and wounding six others, including four police officers. The assailant, identified as 46-year-old Robert Gregory Bowers, was armed with a rifle and three handguns, exchanged fire with police, was shot multiple times, and taken into custody. Authorities say Bowers told officers he wanted all Jews to die and claimed Jews were committing genocide against his people; he faces 29 federal counts including murder, weapons offenses and hate crime charges. The FBI is leading the investigation and classifies the incident as a hate crime under federal civil rights statutes.

The massacre is believed to be the deadliest attack on the Jewish community in U.S. history, surpassing a 1985 family murder in Seattle. The Anti-Defamation League (ADL) noted the shooting occurred amid a significant rise in anti-Semitic incidents and online harassment: ADL data showed anti-Jewish incidents jumped nearly 60% in 2017 to 1,986 cases from 1,267 in 2016. FBI statistics for 2016 also recorded Jews as the most frequent religious hate-crime victims and documented increases in overall reported hate crimes, including anti-Muslim incidents.

Religious and civic leaders condemned the attack as an escalation of hate-based violence and warned that emboldened fringe actors, stoked by hateful rhetoric, are increasingly acting on bigotry. The shooting prompted vigils, heightened security at places of worship nationwide, renewed debate over gun access and protection for houses of worship, and promises from prosecutors for swift, severe justice.

Seven-year-old Josh Hardy, a cancer survivor now critically ill at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, will receive the experimental antiviral brincidofovir after his family’s high-profile campaign convinced drugmaker Chimerix and the FDA to allow access through a new study. Josh, who has battled recurring cancers since infancy and recently underwent a bone marrow transplant that left him immunocompromised, developed a systemic adenovirus infection that has sent him into heart and kidney failure. Chimerix initially declined compassionate-use requests, saying individual access could slow drug approval, but following intense media attention and an online grassroots campaign, the company arranged an open-label pilot study of the drug for up to 20 patients, with Josh to be the first recipient. St. Jude expected to receive the medication within 48 hours while cautioning that its safety and efficacy in children remain unproven and that Josh’s condition is complex. Chimerix CEO Kenneth Moch framed the decision as a way to help many patients and said the company and FDA are working toward a pivotal Phase 3 study. Supporters praised the outcome; Josh’s parents and thousands of online advocates called for compassionate intervention throughout the dispute.

Megyn Kelly returned to The Kelly File after a planned 10-day family vacation, but her first broadcast since Aug. 12 quickly drew renewed attacks from Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump. Shortly after the episode — which featured an interview with activist Cornel West — Trump took to Twitter to criticize Kelly’s performance, suggesting she was “off her game,” had been “afraid to confront” West, and had “no clue on immigration.” He also suggested she should take another unscheduled vacation and retweeted a follower who called her a “bimbo.” Kelly did not directly respond to Trump’s tweets.

The timing of Kelly’s vacation prompted speculation that it was prompted by fallout from the first GOP debate, during which she questioned Trump about his past sexist remarks — a line of questioning he later denounced as unfair. Trump hinted that the vacation might be linked to that controversy, but Fox News pushed back, calling the idea a conspiracy and saying the break was a pre-planned, annual summer vacation. A network spokeswoman compared such theories to UFO conspiracies and noted other Fox hosts had also recently taken time off. Fox management emphasized its support for Kelly, highlighting Roger Ailes’s backing and the ratings boost her debate presence generated.

The episode also underscored a pattern: Trump’s frequent refusal to apologize for controversial remarks in numerous prior incidents, and the lack of a public apology in the face of backlash — with rare corrective statements coming from aides rather than Trump himself.

A viral rumor claimed that Neville “Bunny Wailer” Livingston, songwriter of “Electric Boogie” (commonly known as “The Electric Slide”), confessed the song is about a vibrator. The story originated with online outlets and social posts purporting an unnamed source close to Livingston who said he wrote the song after a girlfriend nicknamed her toy the “electric slide.” That interpretation spread rapidly across social media and several news sites, prompting shock, amusement and a flurry of memes about the dance’s supposed sexual meaning.

EDM.com reached out to Livingston and his team to verify the claims. In a direct statement, Livingston firmly denied the vibrator interpretation, saying he “at no time” lent credence to any explanation other than that the song was inspired by Eddie Grant’s “Electric Avenue.” He called claims otherwise a falsehood that offends his legacy and that of singer Marcia Griffiths, and tarnishes the reputation of a song beloved worldwide. Despite the clarification, the internet response—ranging from disbelief to delight—had already transformed the rumor into a widespread cultural joke. Regardless of its disputed meaning, “The Electric Slide” remains a staple at parties and events.

US investigators secretly wiretapped former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort under FISA court orders both before and after the 2016 election, sources told CNN. Surveillance began after Manafort became the subject of an FBI probe dating to 2014, originally tied to his work for Ukraine’s former ruling party and whether U.S. consultants failed to register as foreign agents. The monitoring was paused last year for lack of evidence, then restarted with a new FISA warrant amid growing counterintelligence concerns about contacts between Trump associates and suspected Russian operatives. Some intercepted communications raised concerns that Manafort may have sought Russian help for the campaign, though sources cautioned the evidence was not conclusive. The Special Counsel Robert Mueller team has been given details of the intercepts. The renewed FISA period extended into early this year and included an FBI search of a Manafort storage facility; it also overlapped a period when Manafort reportedly communicated with President Trump. It is unclear whether Trump was ever intercepted. Manafort denies knowingly communicating with Russian intelligence or aiding efforts against U.S. interests. Mueller’s broader probe has subpoenaed several Manafort associates and consulting firms, sought documents from the White House, and pursued grand jury testimony from figures tied to the Trump campaign and Russian contacts, as investigators assemble evidence of potential criminal conduct.

Sophie the Giraffe, a 7.5-inch natural-rubber teething toy made by French firm Vulli since 1961, has become an iconic baby gift in the U.S. over the past decade. Imported by Hélène Dumoulin-Montgomery beginning in 2001, Sophie struggled initially but gained traction after placement in high-end Beverly Hills gift baskets in 2004 and celebrity visibility—then surged further after the 2007 recalls of Chinese-made toys. Priced at about $25 in the U.S., Sophie sells roughly 500,000 units annually there and is now sold in about 75 countries; prices vary widely, cheaper in Europe and more expensive in places like Brazil. Parents praise Sophie’s tactile design, squeezable neck and blank expression that infants seem to love, though not every baby prefers it.

Recently, concerns have surfaced about mold growing inside Sophies. Several parents, including a pediatric dentist who found black mold after cutting a toy open, reported musty smells and visible mold despite following manufacturer cleaning advice to wipe the surface and avoid submerging the toy. Online reviewers posted photos of moldy interiors, prompting discussion about the risks. Experts say mold in toys is most dangerous for those with mold allergies or immune issues; routine, thorough cleaning and complete drying are key to prevention. Good Housekeeping and cleaning experts advise following manufacturers’ care instructions but note practical cleaning methods—dishwasher, boiling, diluted bleach, or vinegar soaks—are effective for other hollow bath or teething toys. Vulli responded that Sophie is made of 100% natural rubber and must not be immersed; they request returned complaints for examination and reiterate their compliance with safety standards.

Ricki Lake announced the death of her ex-husband Christian Evans, revealing he had long struggled with bipolar disorder and died by suicide on Feb. 11 at age 45. In an emotional Instagram message, Lake called Evans her “beloved soulmate” and said he “succumbed to his life long struggle with bipolar disorder,” expressing sympathy for others who have lost someone to mental illness and relief that he is finally at peace. Lake and Evans met in 2010, married after eloping in April 2012, and divorced in 2015 citing irreconcilable differences, though they continued an on-and-off relationship afterward. Lake described Evans as charismatic, loving, and supportive of her sons from a previous marriage, but also haunted by self-esteem issues and “demons.” She witnessed his first manic episode in September 2014, which escalated into delusions—he believed he could fly and cure cancer—leading to hospitalization under a 5150 hold and treatment he resisted. They reunited at times, but his mania returned in September last year and he moved out. Lake learned of his suicide when Evans’ sister emailed a note; his body was found two days later with a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Lake said she plans to honor him by living fully, scatter his ashes in Ibiza, and use his story to raise awareness about recognizing and treating bipolar disorder. Resources and helplines for bipolar disorder and suicide prevention were shared.

In April 2010, for about 18 minutes, Chinese telecommunications infrastructure briefly redirected a large swath of global Internet routing through China, a disruption U.S. officials and cybersecurity firms characterize as a major “IP hijack.” The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission’s report to Congress said erroneous route announcements originated with IDC China and were propagated by China Telecom, causing many global routers to accept paths that steered traffic for roughly 15 percent of Internet routes — including connections to numerous U.S. government and military domains (Senate, DOD branches, NASA, NOAA, Commerce) and major commercial sites (Dell, Yahoo!, Microsoft, IBM). Security researchers at McAfee called it “one of the biggest hijacks” recorded and warned that the episode could have enabled eavesdropping, data manipulation, or diversion to spoofed endpoints. China Telecom denied any hijack. Because the diverted packets were handled and re-routed without obvious disruption, investigators cannot publicly determine whether the data were stored, inspected, or altered while passing through Chinese servers. Analysts note Internet routing uses the trust-based Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), so incorrect route advertisements can rapidly propagate worldwide; similar but smaller incidents have occurred before. Experts also raised concerns about potential attacks on encryption via compromised certification authorities and about China’s long-standing requirements for foreign vendors to disclose sensitive network and cryptographic product details. The incident underscores structural vulnerabilities in global routing and certification systems, highlights limits of attribution, and serves as a wake-up call about how easily traffic can be rerouted for surveillance or exploitation.

Henry Rayhons, a longtime Iowa legislator and farmer, faces a felony charge alleging he raped his wife, Donna Young, at the nursing home where she was a resident. Rayhons, 78, who married Donna in 2007 after both were widowed, has pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors say Donna, who had progressive Alzheimer’s, lacked the mental capacity to consent to sex on May 23 at Concord Care Center in Garner. Donna died of Alzheimer’s complications on Aug. 8; Rayhons was arrested a week later.

The case hinges on whether a sex act occurred and, if so, whether Donna could understand and consent. Nursing-home staff reported concerns: Donna sometimes wandered, forgot routine tasks, and exhibited disinhibition. Two of Donna’s daughters grew worried about visits from Rayhons and, after moving her into a shared room on May 23, their mother’s roommate reported hearing sexual noises. Nursing staff documented an incident; a hallway camera captured Rayhons disposing of Donna’s underwear in a hamper. Donna underwent a sexual-assault exam; lab results found a stain consistent with seminal fluid but no spermatozoa or other DNA beyond Donna’s. The state also cites statements Rayhons made to investigators suggesting he believed intercourse may have occurred. Rayhons’ lawyers dispute the interpretation of his remarks and note the absence of clear forensic evidence.

The story illuminates the fraught legal and ethical dilemmas around sex and dementia. Experts say cognitive tests like the BIMS used by the nursing home indicate dementia but don’t fully measure a person’s capacity to consent to intimacy. Families and facilities often lack guidance on distinguishing consensual affection from abuse when cognition fluctuates. The case also exposes deep family divisions: Rayhons’ children support him, while two of Donna’s daughters instigated the complaint and sought guardianship. Rayhons contends he and Donna were loving partners and he did nothing wrong; prosecutors portray him as exploiting a confused woman. His trial is scheduled for January, and the case raises broader questions about how law, medicine and families should navigate intimacy when a partner has dementia.

Steven Avery, the central figure in Netflix’s Making a Murderer, has filed a broad appeal in Madison seeking release on bond and challenging his 2007 first-degree intentional homicide conviction in the killing of photographer Teresa Halbach. Avery, who previously spent 18 years wrongfully imprisoned for a rape he did not commit, argues in the pro se filing that investigators used an improper, overly broad warrant that tainted evidence as “fruit of the poisonous tree.” He also asserts a juror improperly influenced others, repeatedly alleging the juror declared Avery “is f------ guilty,” and complains that Judge Angela W. Sutkiewicz made misleading statements and that his trial lawyers were ineffective. The appeal bears Avery’s signature, contains numerous spelling and grammar errors, and does not list his newly retained lead attorney, Kathleen Zellner, who recently took over and says the defense has uncovered new evidence that will exonerate him (she has not disclosed details). Manitowoc County Sheriff Robert Hermann said he had not seen the filing but has previously defended the investigation. Filmmakers Laura Ricciardi and Moira Demos, whose series raised public doubts about the handling of Avery’s and his nephew Brendan Dassey’s cases, maintain their work was fair despite criticism from authorities. Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker has publicly said he would not pardon Avery; an appeals panel previously upheld key trial decisions.

South Korea on Thursday approved an $8 million humanitarian aid package for North Korea even as tensions on the Korean Peninsula intensified and rhetoric between Pyongyang and Washington grew increasingly hostile. Seoul plans to channel $4.5 million in nutritional products for children and pregnant women and $3.5 million in vaccines and medical treatments through the World Food Programme and UNICEF; the Unification Ministry said timing and delivery details would be decided later and stressed the government separates humanitarian assistance from politics. The move, the first South-to-North aid since December 2015, drew domestic criticism and dented President Moon Jae-in’s approval rating amid repeated North Korean provocations, though his approval remained relatively high. The decision also unsettled allies Japan and the United States and came after new U.N. sanctions targeting North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs.

At the U.N. General Assembly, U.S. President Donald Trump warned he would “totally destroy” North Korea if it threatened the United States or its allies and dubbed leader Kim Jong Un “Rocket Man.” North Korea’s foreign minister, Ri Yong‑ho, derided Trump’s remarks as “the sound of a dog barking” and “a dog dream,” expressing contempt and pity for Trump’s aides. China urged calm, warning the situation was worsening daily and pressed South Korea to remove the U.S.-deployed THAAD missile defense system. U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson downplayed prospects for substantive talks and noted signs—disputed by some analysts—of fuel shortages in North Korea after recent sanctions. The international community remains sharply divided over how to combine pressure and humanitarian concern as Pyongyang advances its nuclear and missile capabilities.

Loretta E. Lynch, President Obama’s nominee for U.S. attorney general, presented a measured, polished case for confirmation during an all-day Senate Judiciary Committee hearing marked by Republican scrutiny of the Justice Department’s recent policies. Lynch—who would be the first African-American woman to serve as attorney general—stressed her independence as a career federal prosecutor, pledging to be herself rather than a replica of outgoing AG Eric Holder. She repeatedly avoided partisan entanglement, declining to second-guess many high-profile administration decisions while saying she would provide candid legal counsel to the president.

Immigration dominated the session, with Republicans pressing Lynch about the legality of the president’s executive actions. Lynch said she was not involved in those decisions but viewed the administration’s legal rationale as reasonable and emphasized the department’s duty to ensure executive actions are lawful. Critics including Sens. David Vitter, Jeff Sessions and Ted Cruz voiced deep reservations and indicated they planned to oppose her. Lynch also defended prosecutorial discretion and discussed enforcement priorities.

On other issues, she called waterboarding torture and illegal, said she supports the death penalty, does not favor marijuana legalization and believes NSA surveillance programs are constitutional and effective. She emphasized strengthening strained police-community relations and cited her terrorism-prosecution record in New York. Democrats urged colleagues to evaluate her on merit rather than as a referendum on the administration. Lynch drew bipartisan praise for her qualifications, though some Republicans remained unconvinced about her willingness to confront presidential overreach. The committee’s vote is expected in weeks, requiring some GOP support to advance her nomination.

The document mixes two strands: a partisan critique of Washington media and Republican leadership, centered on the Alabama Senate primary upset, and reporting on broader GOP turmoil centered on Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, plus a separate account of U.S. deliberations over funding for the U.N. agency serving Palestinian refugees (UNRWA).

On Alabama: The piece argues mainstream Washington outlets, fond of establishment figures like McConnell and hostile to Trump, are misframing Roy Moore’s primary victory over appointed Sen. Luther Strange as a rebuke of President Trump. Many Moore supporters believed Trump preferred Moore all along and that his endorsement of Strange was merely performative, intended to placate establishment allies while pursuing other priorities like health-care changes. Moore ran explicitly against McConnell’s influence in Washington; McConnell and his super PAC spent heavily to elect Strange, but Moore prevailed handily. The author contends Moore is “the most Trumpian Senate candidate” and that when Trump actively campaigns for Moore in the general election, Moore’s base will accept that as sincere backing. The broader point: media bias and intense anti-Trump sentiment in D.C. distort coverage and protect establishment figures while scapegoating Trump for Strange’s loss.

On McConnell and the GOP: The narrative then details how McConnell suffered multiple setbacks—Strange’s loss, the collapse of the latest GOP effort to repeal and replace Obamacare, and Sen. Bob Corker’s retirement—all constraining McConnell’s agenda and exposing vulnerabilities in GOP leadership. Trump privately denounced McConnell as “weak” for failing to pass health-care legislation and for opposing changes to the filibuster, while publicly and privately criticizing other Republicans such as John McCain. Despite pressure from Trump, Steve Bannon and Moore, McConnell retained the support of his Senate colleagues, who credit him with delivering victories like Neil Gorsuch’s confirmation. Still, the episode underscores tensions between Trump and GOP leaders and uncertainty about future legislative strategy, including tax reform.

On UNRWA funding: Separately, U.S. officials reviewed and temporarily withheld $125 million in aid to the U.N. Relief and Works Agency amid a wider review of U.S. assistance to Palestinians after the Palestinian Authority cut contacts over U.S. recognition of Jerusalem. Administrations reportedly considered deeper cuts up to $180 million. Donors and Israeli security officials warned such reductions could severely harm Palestinian refugees and worsen Gaza’s humanitarian conditions. Israeli leaders, including Netanyahu, privately urged caution—favoring gradual disengagement rather than abrupt cuts—citing Israeli security interests tied to UNRWA’s operations. A final U.S. decision remained pending as deliberations continued.

A Canadian study from the Rotman Research Institute at Baycrest Health Sciences and the University of Toronto, published in Psychology and Aging, shows that time of day significantly affects cognitive performance in older adults. Researchers tested memory and attention in younger adults (19–30) and older adults (60–82) using picture–word association tasks with distracting, irrelevant items while recording brain activity with fMRI. When tested in the afternoon (1:00–5:00 p.m.), older adults were about 10% more likely than younger adults to attend to distractions. fMRI data revealed that older adults tested in the afternoon showed reduced activation in attentional-control regions (rostral prefrontal and superior parietal cortices) and increased activity in the brain’s default mode network—patterns consistent with “idling” and difficulty sustaining focus. By contrast, a separate group of 18 older adults tested in the morning (8:30–10:30 a.m.) performed markedly better: they focused on fewer distracting items, closed the performance gap with younger adults, and activated the same attentional-control brain areas as younger participants. Lead author John Anderson noted older adults are more focused and better at ignoring distraction in the morning. Senior author Lynn Hasher emphasized that testing time aligned with circadian arousal patterns enables older adults to resist distraction and that ignoring time of day can misrepresent age-related differences in brain function. The authors recommend older adults schedule mentally demanding tasks—such as taxes, exams, medical visits, or complex cooking—for morning hours to capitalize on peak cognitive functioning.

Professor Will Brooker, a film and cultural studies academic at Kingston University, is spending a year living through David Bowie’s many personas to better understand the artist’s mind and work. Commissioned to write a monograph titled Forever Stardust, Brooker adopts periods of Bowie’s five-decade career for months at a time, inhabiting the singer’s looks, routines, cultural influences and environments. His method involves deep, performative immersion: he models his hair, makeup and wardrobes on Bowie’s various eras (from Ziggy Stardust and Aladdin Sane to the Thin White Duke and the 1983 comeback look), seeks out bespoke or secondhand period clothing, and consults makeup artists for elaborate looks. Brooker also follows Bowie’s diets and sleep patterns at times—experimenting with red peppers and milk, sleep deprivation and energy drinks to approximate the stimulant-fueled intensity of Bowie’s 1970s lifestyle—while acknowledging he cannot and should not replicate the heavy drug use Bowie endured.

Beyond appearances and habits, Brooker consumes the books, films and music that shaped Bowie: works by William Burroughs, Aleister Crowley, Michael Moorcock and Nietzsche; German music during the Berlin period; and cinema Bowie would likely have watched. He visits places important to Bowie’s life such as Brixton, Bromley, Beckenham and plans to go to Berlin. For the Thin White Duke phase he recreated atmospherics—lighting black candles, painting expressionist works and listening to relevant music—to approximate Bowie’s creative mindset.

Brooker stresses this is a scholarly exercise combining empathetic immersion with critical distance, describing it as a split persona approach to gain fresh insight rather than mimicry. He admits limitations—no one can truly be Bowie or endure everything Bowie did—and worries about how the late artist might view the project. Bowie’s representatives had no comment when contacted.

A 32-year-old woman, Cherie Amoore, was arrested and charged after allegedly abducting 7-week-old Ahsir Simmons from the King of Prussia Mall on the evening of Thursday, March 31, 2016. Authorities say Amoore approached the child’s mother, Malika Hunter, struck up a conversation, followed the family through the mall and into the food court, and — when Hunter briefly tended to other children — took the infant from his stroller and left. Surveillance video captured Amoore carrying the baby out around 5:30 p.m., prompting an extensive law enforcement response including vehicle and bus stops, helicopter support, FBI assistance and an Amber Alert. Ahsir was found safe later that night in a home above a barber shop in Tredyffrin Township; Amoore was taken into custody and reportedly told police, “I took the baby and I am sorry.” She was arraigned and held on $500,000 bail, facing kidnapping, unlawful restraint, false imprisonment, interference with custody and related charges.

Investigators say Amoore told them she gave birth to a son on Feb. 11 who died hours after birth and that she never told anyone; she later described holding Ahsir and feeling like she was “holding my son again,” though police have not confirmed her claimed pregnancy and are checking medical records. Friends had been skeptical that she was pregnant. Amoore reportedly wept in court; her family has asked for privacy. Her mother, Renee Amoore, is a prominent Pennsylvania GOP official.

Hunter described being traumatized and now fearful of taking her children out in public. Mall officials and shoppers expressed shock that the abduction occurred despite heavy security and surveillance. Authorities credited local security and rapid police procedures for the successful recovery. The Amber Alert process faced delays: local notifications went out quickly, but state and national dissemination took additional time as officials gathered images and details.

In late July and early August, Russia moved to seize two U.S. diplomatic properties in Moscow and sharply reduce American diplomatic staffing in the country as retaliation for U.S. sanctions. Moscow ordered the closure of a 2,000-square-meter U.S. warehouse in southern Moscow and blocked access to a recreational dacha complex on the Moskva River used by embassy staff. The Kremlin also demanded Washington cut about 755 diplomatic and locally hired personnel—roughly 60 percent of U.S. mission staff—by September, a decision framed as the toughest demarche since the Cold War. The restrictions followed a U.S. Congress vote that codified existing sanctions on Russia; Russian leaders characterized the measures as retaliatory and politically necessary, with commentators noting Putin may have used the move to bolster nationalist credentials ahead of elections.

U.S. embassy officials said they were denied access to the dacha despite prior notification from Russia that access would be allowed through noon on Aug. 1; embassy convoys with diplomatic plates were reportedly refused entry. Moscow’s foreign ministry, cited by state media, countered that the Americans failed to obtain required permits for activity in the conservation-area property and called accusations of deliberate blocking “a pre-meditated provocation.” The episode echoed earlier tit-for-tat actions: at the end of 2016, the Obama administration expelled 35 Russian diplomats and closed two Russian recreational facilities in the U.S. The U.S. State Department described Russia’s actions as “regrettable and uncalled-for” and said it was assessing the impact and possible responses. The dispute intensified an already fraught bilateral relationship, disrupting embassy operations and underscoring deepening diplomatic tensions.

An Arizona grandfather has been arrested after authorities say he left his five-year-old granddaughter alone in the desert with a loaded, cocked .45-caliber handgun and instructed her to “shoot any bad guys.” Paul Armand Rater, 53 (reports differ on age in local accounts), was booked into the Fourth Avenue Jail in downtown Phoenix on suspicion of two counts of felony child abuse and one count of felony child endangerment following the incident on Sunday. 

According to Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office (MCSO) reports, Rater and the girl left their Buckeye home—about 30 miles west of Phoenix—to drive into nearby washes. The pair were reported missing about four hours after departing. The child was later found in the desert by her mother and an off-duty firefighter riding an ATV; the firefighter heard the girl crying for help. When located, the child was holding the powerful pistol. Sheriff Joe Arpaio quoted the girl as saying she had been left by “papa” and had been told the gun was “to shoot the bad guys,” raising immediate concern about her ability to distinguish “good” from “bad” people given her age. 

Court records indicate Rater later told deputies his vehicle had broken down and that he left the girl under a tree because she complained she could not walk. The sheriff’s office said Rater admitted he left the child with his gun while he went for “a few drinks and a cheeseburger.” Deputies noted he was later found at a store on Miller Road; investigators say he walked for hours to seek help after the truck issue but did not ask anyone for assistance or mention the child. 

The child was returned to her mother, and the Arizona Department of Child Safety was notified. Rater faces criminal charges as authorities continue to investigate the circumstances of the abandonment and the potential dangers posed to the child.

A two-century-old shipwreck has been found about 150 miles off Galveston, lying roughly 3,000–4,300 feet down in the Gulf of Mexico. Discovered by a Shell survey crew, the site is being explored remotely by Texas A&M Galveston, NOAA and partner scientists using robotic submersibles and a vessel from famed explorer Bob Ballard. Live satellite links let researchers onshore guide salvage operations in real time from a campus control room while viewing high-definition imagery of the debris field. Recovered artifacts—muskets, pistols, cannons, navigational instruments, ceramic plates, clothing, anchors and sealed bottles (including one with preserved ginger)—date to about 1800–1830. Copper sheathing preserves the hull’s outline though most wood has decayed; marine life has colonized the wreck. Evidence suggests the ship may have been a warship or arms transporter with Spanish, Mexican and British items aboard, possibly linked to regional conflicts of the era. The haul is en route to Texas A&M for analysis as researchers work to solve the vessel’s origins and fate.

A fast-moving brush fire, named the La Tuna Fire, erupted in La Tuna Canyon north of Burbank on Sept. 1 and quickly expanded, forcing hundreds of mandatory evacuations in Burbank, Glendale and Los Angeles. Driven by triple-digit heat, gusty, erratic winds and canyon terrain, the blaze grew to over 5,000 acres within a day and became the largest fire by acreage in the city’s history. More than 500–1,000 firefighters and dozens of engines and helicopters were deployed; several homes were destroyed and a few people suffered minor injuries. Interstate 210 was closed; authorities warned smoke hazards and kept evacuation orders in place while officials, including Gov. Jerry Brown, declared emergencies to mobilize resources.

Sears’ largest shareholder and longtime CEO Edward Lampert, through his hedge fund ESL Investments, has proposed buying key Sears assets to raise cash and restructure the struggling retailer. In a letter to the Sears board, Lampert said ESL is interested in acquiring the Kenmore appliance brand, the Home Improvement business (SHIP), and Parts Direct, and would also be open to acquiring some Sears real estate and assuming roughly $1.2 billion of property-secured debt. ESL submitted a non-binding indication valuing SHIP and Parts Direct together at an enterprise value of $500 million and said it could close within about 90 days. The proposal followed nearly two years in which Sears tried to market those businesses but reached few acceptable deals beyond the prior sale of the Craftsman brand.

Lampert framed the divestitures as a way to demonstrate the value of Sears’ asset portfolio, provide liquidity, improve the company’s debt profile, and give Sears time to complete a broader transformation. ESL said it would finance the purchases with equity and third‑party debt and might partner with others. The letter also outlined potential exchange and tender offers to address roughly $1.5 billion of unsecured and second‑lien debt, and called for interim contracts—brand licensing and transition services—to preserve operations post-sale.

To avoid conflicts, Lampert and an associate pledged not to participate in Sears’ internal deliberations about any transaction in which ESL might bid, and said any ESL bid would be subject to independent-board approval and a “go shop” process. The announcement briefly lifted Sears shares, reflecting investor interest in monetizing recognizable brands like Kenmore as the company grapples with years of declining sales and store closures.

Senate Democrats delayed action on a major climate-change bill until spring, reflecting fraying political will amid economic anxiety and upcoming midterm elections. Leaders prioritized health care, financial reform, and jobs legislation over cap-and-trade, with Majority Leader Harry Reid saying debate would come "sometime in the spring." Key committee chairs are divided: Barbara Boxer and John Kerry want swift action; Max Baucus, Jay Rockefeller and Blanche Lincoln urge caution to protect coal-state constituents and focus on jobs; Jeff Bingaman seeks a middle path. Concerns include public unfamiliarity with cap-and-trade, potential voter backlash in industrial regions, and economic impacts like higher energy costs. The delay complicates President Obama’s push to show domestic progress ahead of international talks in Copenhagen and negotiations for a post-Kyoto agreement. The White House continues to push climate action as an economic and jobs opportunity while the EPA moves toward greenhouse-gas regulation.

French lawmakers approved a controversial intelligence bill that greatly expands state surveillance powers, passing the National Assembly 438–86 after backing from both the ruling Socialists and the centre-right UMP. The law, prompted by January’s Paris attacks that left 17 dead and amid ongoing jihadist threats, now moves to the Senate in June. Supporters say the measure modernises outdated 1991 wiretapping rules to address mobile and internet-era threats and creates a supervisory body (CNCTR) to oversee intelligence techniques, handle complaints and regulate operations. Provisions include authorization for geo-location monitoring of private residences, interception of mobile communications, bulk metadata collection via internet providers, and installation of “black boxes”—algorithmic tools on servers to flag suspicious online behavior.

Civil liberties groups, internet companies and some political voices have strongly criticised the bill, dubbing it the “French Patriot Act” or “French Big Brother.” La Quadrature du Net warned the law’s scope goes far beyond counterterrorism, potentially permitting surveillance for industrial, scientific espionage and monitoring social movements. Critics argue the measures institutionalise mass metadata collection and mirror broad international surveillance trends, enabling France to compete as an intelligence power despite smaller resources than the US NSA. Polling suggests a majority of French people accept restricting liberties to fight extremism, though opposition is stronger among youth.

Government defenders, including Prime Minister Manuel Valls and MP Jean-Jacques Urvoas, reject comparisons with the US Patriot Act and insist the law targets identified threats rather than enabling widespread predictive monitoring. Nevertheless, opponents fear expansive, lasting encroachments on privacy and democratic checks despite the new oversight mechanisms.

Apple has reversed course on at least one marijuana-related app after previously removing a social network for cannabis users, MassRoots, from its App Store. MassRoots founder Isaac Dietrich said Apple reinstated the app after he agreed to geo-restrict it to jurisdictions where medical cannabis is legal (23 states plus D.C.). MassRoots, which had been in the App Store from July 2013 until its removal last November, hailed the change and pledged to strengthen compliance with state laws and federal enforcement guidelines. The reinstatement followed community support, a public letter, and a petition.

But many cannabis-focused tech companies still face an uncertain, inconsistent relationship with Apple. Dozens of weed tech businesses—ranging from social apps and directories to ad networks and transactional services—have seen apps or social pages blocked or forced to modify features without clear explanations. Developers criticize Apple for arbitrary, unpredictable policies that threaten a rapidly growing legal marijuana market, which expanded by 74% to $2.7 billion last year. Some apps, like Weedmaps, were compelled to alter how they present dispensary information; others, like Whaxy, were approved only after routing restricted functions through external websites. Entrepreneurs and investors argue Apple should allow users to choose cannabis apps and urge clearer, fairer App Store rules for the sector. A petition and industry letters request Apple to ease restrictions while not asking for endorsement of cannabis content.

Sienna Miller and Tom Sturridge quietly welcomed their first child, a baby girl, in London over the weekend, Us Weekly reports. The British actors, dating over a year and engaged as of February when Miller debuted her diamond ring, had kept the pregnancy mostly private. Miller, 30, revealed to British Vogue in April that she was progressing well but stayed tight-lipped about details. The couple celebrated publicly with a May babymoon in Portofino and attended Robert Pattinson’s birthday in London. Separately, Kourtney Kardashian and Scott Disick introduced their daughter Penelope Scotland Disick, born after an all-natural delivery weighing 7 pounds, 14 ounces; both mother and baby are doing well.

Apple and Gilead are emblematic of a broader corporate pattern: massive profits paired with aggressive tax strategies and controversial pricing or capital-return decisions that draw political and public scrutiny. Apple’s cash and investments surpassed $200 billion for the first time, with nearly 90 percent held overseas to avoid the U.S. corporate tax hit on repatriated earnings. Global iPhone demand—particularly in greater China—has helped drive the cash buildup, but it limits Apple’s ability to deploy funds domestically without facing large tax bills. CEO Tim Cook has lobbied for tax-code reform to allow freer repatriation, while investors and activists, including Carl Icahn, press for more returns to shareholders. Apple has increased buybacks and dividends—returning $126 billion so far of a $200 billion program—funded largely by issuing nearly $50 billion in debt and using some domestic cash for taxes. The company also expanded its U.S. lobbying on tax issues.

Gilead Sciences faces related criticism on tax practices and drug pricing. The company’s hepatitis C treatments—Sovaldi, Harvoni and Epclusa—generated explosive revenue and enabled Gilead’s rapid growth, but also triggered accusations of “tax avoidance” via asset transfers to low-tax jurisdictions like Ireland and of keeping billions offshore to avoid U.S. taxes. A report from Americans for Tax Fairness and a Senate Finance Committee investigation allege Gilead prioritized maximizing revenue and shareholder returns over accessibility, setting high price benchmarks and maintaining restrictive payer policies that limited patient access. Internal documents show executives weighed price points up to $115,000, ultimately choosing levels that sparked public backlash. The probe criticized pricing strategy as focused on “value to shareholders” rather than development costs, while Gilead defends its pricing and assistance programs. Together these cases highlight tensions over tax law, profit shifting, corporate influence on policy, and debates about fair pricing and access to essential medicines.

Sherri Papini, a 34-year-old mother from Mountain Gate near Redding, who vanished on Nov. 2 while jogging, was found alive early Thanksgiving morning on the side of Interstate 5 in Yolo County. She flagged down a motorist around 4:30 a.m.; responding officers and CHP reported she was bound with restraints and “heavily battered.” Papini was taken to a Sacramento-area hospital, treated for unspecified injuries, and released. Sheriff Tom Bosenko said she was very emotional when reunited by phone with her husband, Keith, and later reunited in person. Investigators are searching for two Hispanic women armed with a handgun, driving a dark-colored SUV, based on Papini’s description; no motive or further suspect details have been released.

Family members, including Papini’s sister Sheila Koester, expressed immense relief and gratitude, calling it “the most amazing Thanksgiving.” Koester declined to disclose whether Papini has seen her two young children or other specifics about her condition, citing the family’s need for privacy as she recovers. Authorities have conducted interviews, executed about 20 search warrants (some sealed), and examined phone, bank, email, and social media records; detectives also followed out-of-state leads. More than 400 tips had been received during the search. The community, search teams, and the unidentified motorist who stopped to help were publicly thanked. Officials continue to seek information to clarify what happened during Papini’s three-week disappearance.

Belgium reeled Wednesday after coordinated bombings at Brussels Airport and the Maelbeek metro killed at least 34 people and wounded over 270, prompting a nationwide manhunt, heightened security and international responses. Belgian prosecutors identified two suicide bombers as brothers Ibrahim (29) and Khalid El Bakraoui (27); Ibrahim was identified by fingerprint as one of the airport attackers and Khalid detonated himself at the subway. Authorities say a third suspect shown in airport CCTV pushed a heavy bag that later detonated when police handled it; that man remains at large. A taxi driver who recognized a suspect photo led police to an apartment in Schaerbeek where investigators found about 15 kg of TATP explosives, bomb-making chemicals, nails and an Islamic State flag. In a trash-can-recovered laptop near that apartment, Ibrahim left a written “testament” expressing fear of arrest and referencing being sought “everywhere,” possibly alluding to the recent capture of Paris attack suspect Salah Abdeslam.

Turkish officials said Ibrahim El Bakraoui had been detained at the Turkey–Syria border and deported to the Netherlands in July, and that Turkey warned Belgium and the Netherlands he was a “foreign terrorist fighter.” European leaders called for better intelligence-sharing and more investment in security; EU and national officials urged using Europol and easing information exchange. France, Poland and other partners voiced solidarity; the U.S. House unanimously condemned the attacks and Secretary of State John Kerry planned to visit Brussels. Brussels airport stayed closed, disrupting hundreds of flights; Belgium observed moments of silence and three days of national mourning while keeping its terrorism threat at the maximum level amid fears of further attacks.

Ridley Scott’s Alien: Covenant revives the Alien franchise with a taut, visually striking prequel that restores much of the series’ visceral power. Picking up threads from Prometheus, the film follows the colony ship Covenant, carrying 2,000 frozen passengers and 1,140 embryos en route to Origae-6. When a storm damages the vessel and its captain dies, second-in-command Christopher (Billy Crudup) reluctantly takes charge and diverts the mission to investigate a nearby hospitable planet. The apparent Eden, however, harbors deadly life-forms that soon infect and transform crew members in the franchise’s signature body-horror fashion.

Michael Fassbender gives a standout double performance, playing Walter, a calm, updated synthetic with an American accent, and David, the ambiguous, long-haired survivor from Prometheus with a British accent. Their interplay — a contest of ideas and wills — becomes the film’s most compelling element, probing themes of creation and playing God and culminating in a diabolical, tension-filled twist. Katherine Waterston anchors the human drama as Daniels, a terraforming specialist devastated by the captain’s death; Danny McBride offers comic relief as pilot Tennessee; James Franco and Guy Pearce appear briefly to bridge the Prometheus connection.

Writers John Logan and Dante Harper tighten the story’s focus, blending philosophical speculation with suspenseful, often grisly set pieces. The film balances intelligent sci-fi concepts, spectacular production design, and gory franchise staples without excess length or padding. Dariusz Wolski’s cinematography and Jed Kurzel’s score enhance both the planet’s deceptive beauty and its latent horror. Overall, Alien: Covenant is a creative reset that reinvigorates the series, satisfies longtime fans with familiar terrors, and teases future installments with a provocative ending. Rated R, 122 minutes.

President Obama visited flood-ravaged St. John the Baptist Parish, Louisiana, to survey Hurricane Isaac damage, reassure residents of federal recovery aid and praise first responders for preventing any loss of life. Touring Ridgewood in LaPlace, he saw uprooted trees, debris piles and homes flooded after an unexpected levee failure cut off access and trapped some residents who had to be rescued by boat. Obama emphasized rapid recovery priorities: housing and transportation for more than 3,900 evacuees, reopening public facilities and investigating what went wrong with local flood protections. He hailed FEMA’s coordination and the work of law enforcement, National Guard and Coast Guard. The visit came after a Labor Day campaign stop and on the eve of the Democratic National Convention; Obama denied political motives and stressed bipartisan unity in disasters. Accompanying officials included Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal and federal leaders. Isaac left widespread flooding, hundreds of thousands briefly without power, several storm-related deaths and ongoing refinery and infrastructure impacts across the Gulf Coast.

U.S. swimmer Ryan Lochte issued a public apology after his account of an alleged armed robbery in Rio de Janeiro sparked controversy and an official investigation. Lochte said he was sorry “for not being more careful and candid” in describing the early-morning incident, which he initially told reporters involved men with guns and fake police badges stopping his taxi after a gas-station restroom stop. He called the episode “traumatic,” noted the language barrier, accepted responsibility for his role in distracting attention from other athletes, and said he had learned valuable lessons.

Brazilian authorities, however, disputed Lochte’s version. Rio’s civil police said no robbery occurred; instead, investigators allege the four U.S. swimmers — Lochte, Gunnar Bentz, Jack Conger and Jimmy Feigen — vandalized a gas-station bathroom after leaving a party. Police say security confronted the swimmers, brandished a weapon to prevent their departure, and the athletes paid about $55 to cover damages. Witnesses were initially reluctant to speak publicly. Brazilian officials recommended false-reporting charges for Lochte and Feigen, and the IOC opened a disciplinary commission. Lochte, Bentz and Conger have returned to the U.S.; Feigen remained in Brazil briefly while resolving legal conditions tied to his passport. The U.S. Olympic Committee and USA Swimming apologized to Brazil and condemned the athletes’ conduct, saying it did not represent Team USA’s values. The investigation continues.

The Emoji Movie is a shallow, cynical animated feature set inside a teenager’s smartphone that squanders a promising concept on relentless product placement and lazy storytelling. The film follows Gene (T.J. Miller), a “Meh” emoji who’s accidentally capable of many expressions. When his failure to stay on-brand disrupts a live scan, the ever-cheery Smiler (Maya Rudolph) seeks to delete him. Gene teams with the enthusiastic Hi‑5 (James Corden) and hacker Jailbreak (Anna Faris) to escape their messaging app and reach the cloud, pursued by anti‑virus bots. Along the way they pass through branded environments—Candy Crush, Spotify, Instagram, Dropbox and others—turning set pieces into extended ad spots rather than imaginative world‑building.

Critics argue the movie lacks humor, wit, visual originality, compelling performances, or a coherent point of view. Its familiar “be yourself” moral feels tacked on and undermined by a pervasive commercialism that treats apps as characters and marketing tie‑ins as plot. The screenplay’s logic is muddled—why emojis fear a reboot, why they have parents, or how they differ between phones—and dialogue repeatedly misreads teen speech. Stylistically it mimics generic CGI children’s fare, redesigning emojis into rubber‑faced caricatures instead of exploiting their minimalist charm. A few moments of slapstick keep younger viewers engaged, and an accompanying Hotel Transylvania short (“Puppy!”) earns more praise than the feature itself. Overall, The Emoji Movie is widely seen as a brightly colored, 86‑minute exercise in corporate synergy that leaves audiences—especially adults—cold while offering little beyond superficial eye candy for children.

The document is a polemical critique of Muslim responses to the film American Sniper and broader Muslim political behavior in the West. The author opens by sarcastically invoking Islam’s peaceful image and questions how figures like Aboud Rogo and congregants at Masjid Musa could “misunderstand” Islam. The Bush Doctrine’s binary “with us or against us” is invoked to gripe that U.S. leaders presumed Muslim moderates would police radicals—an expectation the writer says failed. The piece accuses Muslim organizations of promoting a “faked hate narrative” and of engaging in “victim jihad”: diverting attention from jihadist violence by claiming Islamophobia whenever jihad or patriotism is discussed. Specific complaints include demands that Clint Eastwood and Bradley Cooper denounce alleged threats supposedly sparked by the film; the author dismisses these as cries for submission and defends free speech. He argues that Muslim groups should instead pressure Muslim authorities and institutions to reject violent, misogynistic, or antisemitic Quranic interpretations. The writer praises American Sniper as a humane, patriotic film and criticizes media and elites for sanitizing jihad and Islam or avoiding the topic. A Reuters note about an Arab-American group asking the filmmakers to denounce anti-Muslim language concludes the piece.

North Korea’s U.N. ambassador So Se Pyong denounced the United States at the Geneva Conference on Disarmament, blaming Washington for creating an “unpredictable” situation on the divided Korean peninsula and for abusing the U.N. Security Council to enforce a hostile policy against Pyongyang. His remarks followed North Korea’s recent long-range rocket launch in December and its third, most powerful underground nuclear test in February, which provoked further U.N. sanctions and international condemnation. So framed the nuclear test and space launches as legitimate self-defence and warned South Korea against “opening Pandora’s boxes.” South Korea urged Pyongyang to abandon its nuclear ambitions, while Ireland’s foreign minister called on North Korea to stop testing and rejoin six-party denuclearization talks. State media and propaganda organs also asserted that the U.S. mainland is “well within” the range of North Korean strategic rockets, a claim viewed with skepticism by many experts despite progress in missile and nuclear testing.

The Wall Street Journal dismissed chief foreign affairs correspondent Jay Solomon after an investigation revealed ethical breaches tied to his involvement with Iranian-born aviation magnate and alleged arms facilitator Farhad Azima. Washington Bureau Chief Paul Beckett informed staff in a sudden meeting that Solomon had been fired; the Journal said Solomon “forfeited” its trust and violated reporting standards. The action followed an Associated Press probe that unearthed tens of thousands of emails and texts — reportedly stolen from Azima’s lawyers — showing lengthy discussions between Azima and Solomon about prospective commercial ventures. Those messages include an October 2014 text from Solomon saying, “Our business opportunities are so promising,” and an April 2015 email in which Azima asked Solomon to convey a $725 million UAE defense-related proposal at a lunch with government representatives. Azima reportedly offered Solomon a 10 percent stake in a company called Denx LLC; AP reporting described Azima as a longtime source for Solomon who has a history of dealing in weapons and contentious international dealings. Solomon, a veteran national-security reporter and author of a book on Iran, told the AP he “clearly made mistakes,” denied entering into business with Azima, and apologized to colleagues, while acknowledging his communications could appear troubling. The Journal is continuing its internal probe, and staffers expect scrutiny of Solomon’s past reporting as the implications of his conduct are assessed.

Ken Taylor, Canada’s ambassador to Iran during the 1979 hostage crisis, and his colleagues at the Canadian Embassy in Tehran played the crucial, often underplayed role in sheltering six American diplomats who escaped the storming of the U.S. Embassy. When militants seized the embassy on Nov. 4, 1979, most hostages were held for over a year. Five Americans initially hid in the residence of Canadian consular official John Sheardown; Taylor took two into his own home and later sheltered a sixth who had been hiding with a Swedish diplomat. Over three tense months, Taylor and staff moved the fugitives, supplied comforts, collected intelligence for Washington, and coordinated with Ottawa and the U.S. State Department on escape options. Several risky exit plans were considered and rejected; ultimately, the Canadians provided passports and documentation while CIA agent Tony Mendez arranged a cinematic cover story to smuggle them out. A nearly fatal administrative error in visa dating was spotted by Farsi‑speaking Canadian Roger Lucey and corrected, averting disaster. On the escape day Taylor organized transport to the airport, ensured the flight departed, and evacuated Canadian personnel before leaving Iran. Taylor later criticized the film Argo for downplaying Canada’s leadership, noting the CIA was a junior partner and much of the vital documentation and logistics came from Ottawa. His actions transformed his life, earned international attention, and remain a model of risky, cooperative diplomacy and moral courage during a chaotic revolution.

Early on March 30, 2015, a dark, unmarked SUV attempted to enter the National Security Agency campus at Fort Meade, Maryland, prompting a deadly confrontation. Two men in the vehicle — later reported to have been dressed as women — arrived after an overnight stay involving three men at a Jessup motel; the SUV’s owner later told police it had been stolen from that motel. Around 9 a.m., the vehicle took a restricted exit and reached an NSA access point. An NSA police officer gave routine instructions for safely exiting the secure campus; the driver allegedly ignored them, barriers were raised, and the SUV accelerated toward an NSA police cruiser. Officers fired at the vehicle; it then crashed into the cruiser. One person in the SUV died at the scene, another was hospitalized, and an NSA officer was also treated for injuries. The FBI’s Baltimore office took the lead on the investigation, processing the scene with an evidence response team and interviewing witnesses; agents said the incident is not believed to be terrorism-related. Officials indicated the episode may have been a mistaken attempt to leave the restricted area after the vehicle was taken, possibly complicated by drugs in the car. The shooting is under federal investigation, and authorities continued to piece together timelines and motives while assuring Fort Meade personnel and surrounding communities remained safe.

British-born Islamic State recruiter Sally Jones, dubbed the “White Widow,” is believed to have been killed in a U.S. drone strike in Syria in June, several British outlets report. U.S. intelligence reportedly told British counterparts that a Predator drone struck near the Syria‑Iraq border as Jones fled Raqqa toward Mayadin. Officials are “confident” but not 100% certain of her death because no ground recovery was possible. Reports also say her 12‑year‑old son, Jojo, may have been killed, though he was not a specific target; his potential death has prompted concern given his age and the absence of on‑site confirmation.

Jones, 50, a former punk singer from Kent, went to Syria in 2013 and married British hacker Junaid Hussain, a senior ISIS cyber operative killed by a U.S. strike in 2015. She became a prolific online propagandist and recruiter for female foreign fighters, using multiple social media aliases and encouraging attacks in the West. Designated a high‑value target and placed on UN sanctions lists, she was accused of publicizing lists of U.S. military personnel and providing bomb‑making guidance. Coalition air and drone campaigns intensified around Raqqa as ISIS lost territory, and Jones’s targeting would be notable as one of the first reported U.S. drone strikes aimed specifically at a woman. British and U.S. officials have declined detailed comment pending further verification.

From the air Baotou’s vast tailings pond looks like a lake, but on the ground it is a thick, black, toxic sludge: a 10 sq km dumping ground for chemical waste from rare-earth processing. Baotou, in Inner Mongolia, processes ore from the Bayan Obo mines and supplies much of the world’s rare earths—elements central to smartphones, flat screens, wind turbines and electric-vehicle motors. China dominates global production (about 90–97% in the period discussed), with Baotou alone accounting for a sizeable share.

Extracting and purifying these elements requires hydro-metallurgical techniques and strong acids, producing vast quantities of poisonous byproducts and radioactive residues such as thorium. Local farmers tell of once-fertile fields ruined over decades: crops fail, livestock die, and soils and groundwater are saturated with toxins. Villages near the refineries have largely been abandoned; populations have plummeted and many remaining residents suffer chronic illnesses. Efforts to pressure authorities have won only partial, problematic compensation and empty relocation towers that villagers cannot afford or fully own.

Factory visits reveal a city physically dominated by industry: sprawling refinery complexes, coal-fired power plants, and endless piping that blurs where city ends and plant begins. Some processing facilities appear strangely quiet, raising questions about production practices and market control. Rare earths like cerium and neodymium, while not geologically rare, become economically viable largely because the hazardous, polluting extraction and refining are undertaken in China at large scale.

Artists and researchers who sampled the lake found elevated radiation and have used the material to highlight the hidden cost of consumer tech. The Baotou case underlines a global dilemma: the essential role of energy-critical and rare-earth elements in modern technology comes at severe local environmental and human cost, prompting international efforts to diversify supply, increase recycling, and find alternatives.

The piece combines Simone De La Rue’s fitness philosophy with PEOPLE’s profile of Sandra Bullock as its 2015 “World’s Most Beautiful Woman.” De La Rue’s Body by Simone (BBS) program is presented not as a crash diet or extreme regimen but as a sustainable lifestyle: consistent effort, sensible workouts, and healthy eating that become habitual rather than punitive. BBS promises long-term gains—better health, happiness, and strength—if participants commit to the tools and time required. In the PEOPLE feature, Bullock, 50, reacts with amused disbelief to the beauty title and emphasizes that true beauty is quiet and rooted in character and kindness.
