She describes motherhood to her 5-year-old son Louis as central to her life—full of everyday routines, rules, humor and touching moments in which he reassures her she’s “not old, just happy.” Bullock credits a balanced diet and working out with Body by Simone four to five times weekly for helping her stay grounded and fit; she recalls the workouts’ intensity but values their whole-body, continuous-movement approach. The full interview appears in PEOPLE’s special issue.

Researchers at the University of New South Wales developed CriSTAL (Criteria for Screening and Triaging to Appropriate aLternative care), a 29-item screening checklist to help identify hospitalized patients aged 65+ who are likely to die within weeks to three months. The tool aggregates objective predictors—age, vital-sign deterioration (eg, hypotension, extreme pulse or respiratory rates, low consciousness), elevated early warning scores, repeat hospital or ICU admissions, emergency admission, and specified advanced comorbidities (advanced cancer, chronic heart, lung, kidney or liver disease, recent stroke or MI). It also includes markers of frailty (weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow gait, reduced activity), cognitive impairment or nursing-home residence, proteinuria and simple bedside tests. CriSTAL was created after a narrative review of 112 studies and 18 existing prognostic instruments; the authors found most prior tools relied on subjective clinical judgment or administrative data and were impractical for ED or rapid-response contexts. The goal is not to withhold care but to prompt earlier, honest conversations with patients and families, reduce futile, intrusive, expensive interventions, and guide consideration of palliative or alternative out-of-hospital care so patients can have dignified end-of-life experiences aligned with their preferences. The checklist is designed for rapid use at ED admission or after rapid response team calls; it will be retrospectively validated (case–control on recent RRT-attended deaths) and then prospectively tested. Developers aim to refine and shorten the tool based on predictive performance (AUROC target >80%). CriSTAL includes communication-training components and emphasizes that decisions remain individualized, ethically guided, and not driven by cost pressures. Early trials in Sydney EDs are planned.

Georgia police identified 22-year-old Kerry Hammond Jr. as the suspect in a bungled GameStop burglary in St. Marys. Surveillance footage showed Hammond wearing clear plastic water-bottle wrap over his head in a failed attempt to conceal his identity; his large stature (6'1", 275 lbs) and a distinctive right-forearm tattoo remained visible. Authorities say he was last seen driving a white 2006 Ford Taurus and already faces two other active felony warrants for burglary and criminal damage to property. Hammond was arrested and booked into Camden County jail on a pair of felony charges and is being held without bond. Police publicized surveillance stills and even joked that the public could help “once you stop laughing.” Separately, the Smoking Gun traced the author of an anonymous Gawker essay about Christine O’Donnell to Dustin Dominiak after linking him through roommate Brad Kurisko; Dominiak’s Facebook was deactivated before the outlet secured a confession.

Wisconsin’s high-stakes recall election pits Republican Gov. Scott Walker against Democratic Milwaukee Mayor Tom Barrett in a contest that has drawn massive national attention and at least $63.5 million. Walker entered Election Day as a slight favorite, and even some Democrats privately viewed a Barrett victory as an upset. The race is widely seen as the second-most influential in 2012 after the presidential contest, with consequences for many political actors.

Scott Walker faces the most immediate risk: a loss would be a major setback for a politician long viewed as a rising conservative star and would complicate any future national ambitions; a win would cement him as a conservative hero and spark talk of possible presidential runs. Organized labor is also deeply invested. Walker’s 2011 law that curtailed public-sector collective bargaining galvanized unions, which helped drive the recall but also backed Barrett’s primary rival—an allocation of resources some Democrats later questioned. If Walker prevails, unions could face diminished political influence.

President Obama and national Democrats have provided financial and organizational help to Barrett—yet the White House stopped short of sending Obama himself, drawing criticism from Republicans who noted his nearby travel. If Walker wins, Democrats worry the result will be read as a warning sign for Obama’s prospects in Wisconsin this fall; if Barrett loses, the president may be criticized for not doing more. Tom Barrett’s political career is on the line: a third gubernatorial defeat would likely end or severely curtail his statewide ambitions. Bill Clinton, who campaigned for Barrett, stands to benefit politically regardless of the outcome—whether as a credited game-changer or as a sympathetic figure who did all he could.

Beyond personalities, the recall has reshaped Wisconsin’s political climate, tightening the state’s competitiveness for the upcoming presidential race. Republicans view a Walker victory as momentum and an opportunity to expand their presidential map; Democrats fear a loss could erode Obama’s 2008 gains among independents. The recall has deepened partisan divisions, vividly illustrated by tense encounters at local events as both campaigns courted voters in a polarized environment.

Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is announced as the official eighth story in the Harry Potter universe and the first original narrative to be staged. Set 19 years after the finale of Deathly Hallows, the play follows an adult Harry — now an overworked Ministry of Magic employee, husband and father of three — and his youngest son, Albus, who struggles under the burden of his family’s legacy. As past and present collide, both father and son confront the revelation that darkness can arise from unexpected places. Written by Jack Thorne in collaboration with J.K. Rowling and directed by Olivier and Tony Award–winner John Tiffany, the production will be presented in two parts because of its “epic nature.” The production will feature a company of over 30 actors; casting details will be released later. Official artwork debuted showing a child hunched in a nest with black wings, sparking fan speculation about Albus’s role, though the identity was not confirmed. Creators say the story was conceived specifically for the live-theatre format and that the team is eager to present this new chapter. Harry Potter and the Cursed Child will open at London’s Palace Theatre in the West End in summer 2016, with priority and general ticketing dates announced.

A widely shared video from Yueyang, China, showing a 2-year-old girl—identified as Tutu—walk ahead of her mother and then struck and crushed by a car has provoked public outrage and renewed concern about “distracted walking.” Chinese prosecutors and social media users implored parents to “put down your phone” after the fatal incident; many castigated the mother for failing to supervise her child. The case is part of a troubling pattern: similar tragedies were reported in Anhui in April and Henan last August, when toddlers were killed after wandering into traffic while caregivers were absorbed in smartphones.

Experts warn that smartphone dependence blurs attention and increases risk. Liu Qinxue, who studies smartphone addiction, said the Yueyang death should serve as a warning about the dangers of overuse and a lack of public awareness. Internationally, authorities have begun addressing related risks: Shanghai police have used high-definition cameras to catch drivers who text or call, and offenders face fines and point penalties; a Hubei lawmaker proposed criminal charges for drivers who use phones. But policy and research have largely focused on distracted driving rather than walking, and pedestrian-crash data have been insufficient to establish firm links to phone use.

Some cities abroad, like Seoul and Hong Kong, post warnings about phone distraction on escalators and sidewalks, but such signage is rare in mainland China. Scholars like MIT’s Sherry Turkle urge reclaiming phone-free spaces—meals, cars, meetings—to restore attention and reduce harm. The incidents have sparked calls among Chinese netizens for parents to prioritize childcare over devices.

Nearly nine years after her abduction, Elizabeth Smart faced her captor, Brian David Mitchell, in a packed Salt Lake City courtroom as he received life sentences for kidnapping and transporting her for sexual abuse. Now 23, Smart calmly addressed Mitchell, saying he took nine months of her life and that he will be held responsible; she affirmed she has a “wonderful life now.” Mitchell, a street preacher who sang hymns and displayed erratic courtroom behavior, did not respond. Smart testified at trial about being forced into a polygamous “marriage,” daily rape, drug use, tethering, threats, and near-rescue when a detective failed to press a veiled encounter. Wanda Barzee, Mitchell’s estranged wife and co-defendant, already serves 15 years. Smart, relieved, plans to work as a child advocate after completing a Mormon mission.

Even as the 2012 election concluded, attention immediately turned to 2016, with both parties already weighing potential contenders and commentators speculating online. For Democrats, the central question remains whether Hillary Clinton will run again. Clinton—having moved from first lady to senator to secretary of state—commands broad name recognition and respect across the party, and her decision could reshape the field. Other Democratic possibilities include Vice President Joe Biden, who hinted he might run and benefits from high name recognition despite occasional gaffes; Maryland Governor Martin O’Malley, popular within the party though not widely known nationally; Los Angeles Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa, who has strong support among Latino voters; Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who could appeal to women—important given that roughly 60 percent of Democratic primary voters are female; and New York Governor Andrew Cuomo, who brings executive experience and access to party networks and funding. Observers also note that an unfamiliar candidate might emerge after the 2012 campaign.

Republicans face a more fractious recovery after Mitt Romney’s loss, likely triggering intra-party battles among establishment conservatives, cultural conservatives, economic conservatives, and populists. Several high-profile GOP names were mentioned as potential 2016 contenders: Jeb Bush, whose family name and resources make him formidable; Paul Ryan, popular with deficit hawks and boosted by his 2012 visibility; Florida Senator Marco Rubio, a rising star useful for Republican appeals to Latino voters; New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, noted for his blunt style and bipartisan visibility during Hurricane Sandy; Rick Santorum and Mike Huckabee, both with social conservative constituencies; Sarah Palin, who retains a base despite challenges; and Rick Perry, who may consider another run. As with the Democrats, the GOP could also see an unexpected entrant rise from the post‑2012 political landscape. International observers and bettors quickly weighed in—some amused, some critical of continuous campaigning and aspects of the U.S. electoral system—but speculation about the 2016 lineup was underway almost immediately.

Silicon Valley entrepreneur Dave Asprey, known for Bulletproof Coffee, has launched FATwater, a bottled beverage that contains tiny emulsified droplets of medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil derived from coconut. Marketed as a disruptive beverage, FATwater (about 20 calories and 2 grams of saturated fat per bottle) is promoted by Asprey as more hydrating than plain water, arguing the fat droplets help water enter cells more effectively and provide a modest energy bump without being stored as body fat. Asprey says the MCTs enhance thermogenesis and suppress appetite, and he plans to expand distribution beyond his Santa Monica coffee shop and select L.A. stores.

The product has drawn skepticism from nutrition experts. Researchers and dietitians note that while MCTs are metabolized differently than long-chain fats and can increase diet-induced thermogenesis at relatively high intakes, the 2 grams in FATwater are far below the grams used in studies (typically 18–60 g) and unlikely to affect fat burning or hydration. Food science experts say MCT emulsions can improve the absorption of fat-soluble nutrients but there’s no evidence they make water more hydrating. Critics also object to labeling water with calories and ingredients; Martin Riese, a water sommelier, called it a “near water product” that should not replace natural water.

Taste tests were mixed to negative: reviewers described berry and lemon flavors as soapy, soaplike, or oddly coated, with some finding it an acquired taste. Asprey acknowledges limited research and says studies on his formulations are in progress. Experts’ bottom line: plain water hydrates adequately—if thirsty, drink water; if hungry, eat food.

Terry Crews publicly thanked Mark Hamill and other celebrities after NBC rescued Brooklyn Nine-Nine days after Fox canceled it. Crews tweeted gratitude to Hamill “for using the power of the force to save Brooklyn Nine-Nine,” and also acknowledged support from stars such as Sean Astin and Lin-Manuel Miranda, who voiced disappointment at the Fox decision. Hamill, a vocal fan with millions of followers, had expressed outrage when Fox pulled the plug, tweeting “Oh NOOOOOOOOO!!!!!!!!!” and vowing long grudges against networks that cancel shows he loves. He shared favorite moments from the series and later celebrated NBC’s pickup of a 13-episode sixth season, joking about forgiving past network cancellations. NBC Entertainment Chairman Robert Greenblatt said the acquisition was driven by business realities — Brooklyn Nine-Nine is produced by an NBCUniversal-owned studio — and that the network had been ready to move quickly. He argued the show fits NBC’s comedy brand better and lamented that, had Andy Samberg been attached earlier, NBC would not have sold it to Fox. The pickup is part of a broader trend of networks reviving canceled comedies; NBC has had success with revivals like Will & Grace and is adding multiple new shows and midseason entries while making schedule adjustments, including winter editions of reality hits and new dramas.

Juan Francisco Lopez-Sanchez (also reported as Francisco Sanchez), an undocumented immigrant with multiple prior deportations, pleaded not guilty to murder in the July 1 shooting death of 32-year-old Kathryn “Kate” Steinle on San Francisco’s Pier 14. At his arraignment he repeatedly answered “no culpable” via a Spanish interpreter; bail was set at $5 million. Prosecutors charged him with murder and a firearms enhancement that could add years if convicted. Investigators say the .40-caliber pistol that struck Steinle had been stolen days earlier from a federal agent in a vehicle burglary, though sources differ on whether it was a service weapon. Sanchez has given inconsistent accounts: in a jailhouse interview he told reporters he found a gun wrapped in a shirt and claimed it discharged after he took sleeping pills; his public defenders argue he may not have understood interview questions and contend the shooting could have been accidental. The case ignited heated debate over San Francisco’s sanctuary policies after Sheriff’s Department officials released Sanchez in April rather than honoring an ICE detainer; federal and local leaders, including Hillary Clinton and Senators Feinstein and Boxer, criticized the decision. The investigation and political fallout continue as Sanchez awaits further proceedings.

Researchers report successful binary brain–computer interface (BCI) communication in four advanced ALS patients, including two in permanent complete locked-in state (CLIS) and two transitioning into CLIS. Conventional neuroelectric BCIs (EEG/ECoG) have repeatedly failed to enable reliable communication in CLIS, likely because these systems require effortful, explicit voluntary attention and often residual motor or eye control. This study used functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to measure frontocentral cortical oxygenation (oxyhemoglobin) changes while patients listened to spoken yes/no questions and mentally answered “yes” or “no.” An implicit, automatic attentional approach focused on overlearned or personally relevant questions to tap automatic cognitive processing rather than volitional motor imagery. Patients completed multiple sessions across weeks (three patients >46 sessions; one patient 20 sessions). A linear support vector machine classifier trained on fNIRS O2Hb features achieved above-chance (>70%) online classification accuracy for personal and open questions, with feedback provided when performance exceeded daily chance thresholds. EEG oscillations (0–30 Hz) and electrooculography (EOG) did not reliably discriminate answers, and lower-frequency EEG power (delta/low-theta) correlated with poorer fNIRS-based performance—suggesting decreased vigilance impairs communication. One patient with very long-standing CLIS showed different EEG correlations, perhaps reflecting altered baseline rhythms. Open-question responses were repeatably consistent, and three patients indicated positive quality-of-life answers. The study used bedside-capable equipment, rigorous session metrics, and public data deposition. While mechanisms producing distinct hemodynamic signatures for yes versus no remain uncertain, these results indicate fNIRS-based BCIs, especially within hybrid EEG–fNIRS systems that monitor vigilance, may provide the first viable channel for restoring basic communication in CLIS due to ALS, pending replication and extension.

Emma Kelty, a 43-year-old British adventurer from Finchley, has been reported missing and is believed to have been murdered while canoeing the Amazon. Kelty, an experienced solo explorer who had skied solo to the South Pole and walked across the United States, began paddling the Amazon in February, aiming to travel from the Peruvian Andes to the Atlantic. In the weeks before her disappearance she posted repeatedly about disturbances and threats after entering Brazil’s Amazonas state: encounters with men wielding machetes, repeated nighttime intrusions near her tent, and boats shadowing her stops. On 10 September she joked about warnings for the stretch of river near Coari; two days later she reported seeing dozens of men in motorboats armed with arrows and rifles. Nearing Coari and camped on Boieiro island opposite Lauro Sodré, she triggered a distress signal and has not been seen since.

Brazilian police have arrested three men — two 17-year-olds and a man named Erinei Ferreira da Silva — on suspicion of her murder and are seeking four more suspects. A 17-year-old told investigators Kelty was approached by two people, then five others arrived, stole her belongings, shot her twice with a sawn-off shotgun and dumped her body in the river. Authorities launched a search involving divers, firefighters and the navy; residents reported sighting her alive after the flare, and searches continue where her body was allegedly disposed.

Locals and officials note river pirates and drug-trafficking gang disputes plague the Solimões stretch, with a history of violent robberies and killings; the area was also where a former police chief disappeared last year. The UK Foreign Office is assisting Kelty’s family, who praised her adventurous spirit and said she will be deeply missed.

President Donald Trump hailed a federal court ruling as a “big legal win” that clears the way for construction of parts of his proposed U.S.-Mexico border wall, despite prior hostility between him and the presiding judge, Gonzalo P. Curiel. On Tuesday Judge Curiel dismissed lawsuits brought by California and several environmental groups that sought to block the administration’s waiver of environmental reviews for certain wall segments. The suits alleged violations of federal environmental statutes and constitutional principles; plaintiffs claimed the waiver process ignored the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act and the Coastal Zone Management Act, and risked harm to sites such as the Tijuana Estuary and to threatened species.

In a detailed 101-page opinion, Curiel—an Obama appointee whom Trump had attacked during the 2016 campaign by calling him “Mexican” and suggesting he could not be impartial—found that judicial intervention was unwarranted. Citing the 1996 law that grants the executive branch authority to construct barriers near San Diego and to waive environmental review “when necessary to ensure expeditious construction,” Curiel concluded that the plaintiffs failed to show the Homeland Security secretary exceeded his authority. He emphasized that the court’s role is not to second-guess political decisions, quoting Chief Justice John Roberts that elected leaders, not judges, bear responsibility for political consequences.

California Attorney General Xavier Becerra and environmental groups signaled continued opposition and intent to evaluate appeals. Meanwhile, the administration has already begun replacing a portion of older barrier in Calexico with new 30-foot bollards and is seeking billions in funding for broader wall construction. Trump also tweeted that sections California wants built “NOW will not be built until the whole Wall is approved,” even though the state opposes the project.

Baltimore police said Thursday they finished the first phase of their investigation into Freddie Gray’s death a day early and delivered the file to State’s Attorney Marilyn Mosby, who urged patience while she determines whether to bring charges. Gray, 25, suffered a severe spinal injury and other trauma after being arrested April 12 and died April 19. Police and city officials stressed the probe remains active even as the department said it had “exhausted every lead” in the current phase. Investigators disclosed a previously unknown stop by the prisoner transport van, captured on private surveillance video, bringing the total stops to four between Gray’s arrest and arrival at the Western District station where he was found unresponsive. Officials said one head wound suggests Gray struck a protruding bolt inside the van. Officers have acknowledged protocol violations — failing to buckle Gray in and not providing timely medical aid — and the six involved officers have been suspended with pay. Mosby, who is conducting an independent review and has been briefed throughout, received the police file but gave no timetable for charging decisions, asking the public to remain peaceful. The case has sparked widespread protests in Baltimore and other cities and intensified scrutiny of police encounters that have resulted in deaths of black men nationwide. The Justice Department is also conducting an independent inquiry, and Maryland’s chief medical examiner said an autopsy report will go to prosecutors shortly. Family lawyers and civil rights groups continue to call for a thorough, unhurried investigation.

Federal authorities have warned state election officials after the FBI uncovered evidence that foreign hackers breached two state voter registration systems this summer. In an August “flash” alert from the FBI’s Cyber Division, obtained by news outlets, the bureau said it was investigating intrusions against two state election websites that included the exfiltration of voter registration data in at least one case. The alert, marked for “need to know” recipients, listed eight IP addresses tied to the attacks and urged states to check their logs for similar inbound and outbound activity without directly probing the suspicious addresses.

Sources say the incidents involved Arizona and Illinois. Illinois officials shut down the state’s voter registration system for ten days in late July after attackers downloaded personal information on up to 200,000 voters, according to Ken Menzel, general counsel for the Illinois Board of Elections. Arizona experienced a more limited intrusion in which malware was introduced but no data theft was confirmed. FBI agents told Illinois officials the perpetrators were believed to be foreign hackers, and the bureau was exploring a possible link to other high-profile political hacks, including the Democratic National Committee intrusion; no attribution had been finalized.

Cybersecurity experts who reviewed the FBI alert noted one of the listed IP addresses has appeared in Russian criminal hacker forums and said the attack techniques resembled those used in suspected Russian state-sponsored operations. Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson had earlier convened state election officials to offer DHS assistance, saying no specific credible threat was known but urging improved protections. Federal officials emphasized the bulletin’s goal of helping systems administrators guard against persistent cyber criminals while investigations continue.

The Paradise Papers leak—some 13m documents from offshore law firm Appleby and other registries shared with the ICIJ and nearly 100 media partners—exposed extensive use of tax havens by billionaires, corporations and celebrities, prompting strong political backlash. Senator Bernie Sanders condemned the revelations as evidence the world is drifting toward an “international oligarchy,” arguing that a tiny number of billionaires and multinationals hide wealth and avoid paying fair taxes through offshore arrangements. He blamed Congress and the Trump administration for tax breaks that benefit corporations and enable cabinet members and the super-rich to shift profits and jobs offshore. Democratic senators including Chuck Schumer and Ron Wyden said the leaks prove Republican tax plans favor the wealthy while burdening the middle class.

Among the disclosures: Wilbur Ross, U.S. commerce secretary and billionaire, maintained business ties with people close to Vladimir Putin through Navigator, his shipping investment linked to Russian gas firm Sibur, prompting calls from Democrats for explanation or resignation. The papers also detail how major firms like Nike and Apple used complex structures to reduce tax bills. Nike routed European revenue through Dutch entities and a Bermuda IP holder and later to a “stateless” CV entity to minimize taxation, lowering its effective global tax rate dramatically and accumulating offshore profits. The OECD and EU measures aim to close such loopholes, including the Dutch “reverse hybrid” CV model.

Lewis Hamilton’s private jet and motorhome arrangements revealed how advisers from Appleby and EY set up leasing structures via the Isle of Man, Guernsey and BVI that allowed reclaiming import VAT and sheltering costs—schemes tax experts described as artificial and potentially abusive, and HMRC opened a review of Isle of Man VAT refunds. Apple, after the EU’s probe into its Irish structures, sought new residency solutions and moved key subsidiaries’ management to Jersey to preserve low taxation; the EU fined Ireland-Apple arrangements and ordered recovery of back taxes, a ruling now under appeal.

The Paradise Papers spotlighted the scale and mechanics of global tax avoidance—legal, complex and often opaque—fueling political debate about closing loopholes, enforcing rules and reforming a system that critics say enables concentrated wealth and evasion at the expense of ordinary taxpayers.

In an extended Fox News interview with Sean Hannity, President Donald Trump defended several early administration actions and vented about mainstream media coverage, national security, immigration, border enforcement, torture, health care, judicial nominations and potential clemency.

Trump repeatedly attacked the press, calling much of it “very hostile,” “very dishonest” and responsible for “fake news.” He said some journalists are honest but complained that reporters publish false stories that cast him as racist, citing the brief controversy over a Time reporter’s mistaken description of a Martin Luther King Jr. bust’s visibility in the Oval Office. Trump and Hannity agreed that journalism has serious problems, with Hannity asserting “journalism is dead” and Trump saying while it isn’t dead, many in the media are dishonest.

On national security and immigration, Trump defended anticipated executive orders to suspend the refugee program and temporarily block visas from several Muslim-majority countries, arguing “we can’t take any chances.” He cited more than 1,000 terrorism investigations and questioned the ability to vet refugees and migrants who lack documentation. A draft order reportedly would pause broader refugee admissions for 120 days and bar citizens of Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen from receiving visas for at least 30 days.

Trump reiterated support for constructing a border wall with Mexico, calling it necessary for protection and likening its logic to Israel’s border defenses. He also addressed torture, saying he believes techniques like waterboarding “work,” but that he would follow Defense Secretary James Mattis’s view, who opposes their use.

On domestic policy, Trump criticized the Affordable Care Act as a “horror show” and predicted it would “explode” this year, arguing Republicans should replace it with a cheaper, better plan. He said he has “pretty much” decided on a Supreme Court nominee (with a formal announcement planned for Feb. 2) and urged Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell to consider the “nuclear option” if Democrats obstruct confirmation.

Finally, Trump said he was reviewing the case of Navy sailor Kristian Saucier, who took photos inside a submarine and was sentenced to prison, suggesting he might consider a pardon and contrasting Saucier’s prosecution with the FBI’s decision not to charge Hillary Clinton over her email use.

An Amtrak passenger train derailed on a bridge over I-5 in DuPont, Washington, during the inaugural run of a new faster route, killing three rail enthusiasts and injuring more than 70 people, some critically. The deceased were identified as Jim Hamre, 61, and Zack Willhoite, 35, both Tacoma-area members of All Aboard Washington, and Benjamin Gran, 40, of Auburn. An early NTSB review using the lead locomotive’s event recorder and cameras captured the engineer warning of an “over speed condition” about six seconds before the crash. The locomotive’s final recorded speed was 78 mph—acceptable for the approach but far above a posted 30 mph curve where the derailment occurred. Brakes were reported to have engaged automatically; positive train control, which can prevent speed-related derailments, was not installed on the train. The recordings showed crew members were not using personal electronic devices. The NTSB’s full investigation could take up to two years.

Scott Walker, the two-term Republican governor of Wisconsin, suspended his 2016 presidential campaign on Monday, Sept. 21, acknowledging that his bid had lost momentum and urging other trailing GOP candidates to consider exiting so a “positive, conservative message” could rise to challenge frontrunner Donald Trump. Walker framed his departure as a leadership choice to “clear the field,” but his exit was driven by a rapid collapse in polls, debate stumbles, messaging missteps and mounting financial strain.

Walker entered the race in July buoyed by a strong showing in Iowa earlier in the year and the backing of powerful conservative donors after his nationally visible fights with public-employee unions. His super PAC, Unintimidated, raised roughly $20 million in the first half of 2015, and he initially rode a perception as a conservative reformer and an appealing next-generation candidate. Yet once he formally launched, his campaign struggled to convert that early promise into sustained momentum. Walker’s debate performances were widely described as lackluster; he spoke little in key forums and failed to generate the breakout moments that helped rivals like Carly Fiorina. That, combined with policy reversals—most notably a string of inconsistent statements on birthright citizenship—and awkward media moments, eroded his outsider appeal.

Polling imploded: a CNN/ORC poll released the weekend before he withdrew placed him under 0.5% nationally, and his Iowa support plunged from stronger single digits to the low single digits in recent weeks. Campaign insiders and strategists said the collapse in Iowa was particularly damaging because the campaign had staked its strategy on the caucus state as a launchpad. Fundraising hardened into a critical problem as donors reacted to poor debate showings; sources reported that hard-dollar fundraising never matched the super PAC haul, leaving the campaign unable to sustain a large paid staff and nationwide operation. Campaign aides described a “death watch” in recent weeks as layoffs and cutbacks loomed.

Walker’s departure intensified jockeying among remaining GOP contenders for his staff, supporters and major donors, including the Ricketts family and others who had bankrolled his super PAC. Rival campaigns quickly reached out to poach operatives and woo backers; Marco Rubio, Jeb Bush, Ted Cruz and others sought to absorb elements of Walker’s Iowa apparatus and donor networks.

Reactions were mixed: Donald Trump tweeted a polite compliment, while establishment figures praised Walker’s record but acknowledged the difficulty of running in an overcrowded, volatile primary. Labor and liberal groups celebrated his exit, pointing to his anti-union record. Walker stressed gratitude to supporters, framed the decision as faith-guided, and said his priority now was to concentrate resources behind the eventual Republican nominee. His suspension reduced the GOP field and underscored the harsh calculus of modern campaigns, where early momentum, debate performances and continuing fundraising quickly determine viability.

A Brenham veterinarian accused of killing a cat with a bow and arrow will not face charges after an Austin County grand jury returned a “no-bill,” finding insufficient evidence to prosecute. The case began when a now-deleted Facebook post showed a woman holding an orange cat with an arrow through its head and boasting about a “bow kill.” The Austin County Sheriff’s Office received an unsworn hearsay report that the woman acted to protect her pets from a potentially rabid stray, and investigators sought to verify the image and location. Their probe could not determine where or when the photo was taken, and subpoenas to Facebook yielded no usable evidence because the account had been deleted before authorities were notified. Without proof the incident occurred in Austin County—or even in Texas—investigators lacked probable cause to obtain search warrants for local properties or to link the image to a specific crime scene. The district attorney also noted uncertainty about whether the death, if connected, amounted to illegal cruelty; veterinary guidelines recognize a bolt to the head as a humane euthanasia method if performed correctly. The veterinarian, identified in news reports as Dr. Kristen Lindsey, was fired from her position at the Washington Animal Clinic after the post went viral; the clinic condemned the conduct and said it had parted ways with her. Protesters outside the courthouse and supporters of the deceased pet, named Tiger, demanded an indictment. Because she has not been charged, local media have withheld the woman’s image in some reports.

When the service works, you’ll receive one email per day only if there are new posts that match your criteria; each email will include a link to the new content. The system informs you whether your notification was saved or if there was a problem. Overall, the feature limits messages to a single daily email and only sends notifications for newly published items that match your saved notification settings.

After a dismal start to the season, Cleveland Browns fans had jokingly organized a "Perfect Season Parade" to mark an 0-16 campaign, raising money to cover parade costs. When the Browns unexpectedly won their first game on Christmas Eve, organizers canceled the satirical event and pledged the funds to the Greater Cleveland Food Bank. The original GoFundMe—intended to pay for security, restrooms and other parade necessities—surpassed its $1,999 goal and collected just over $8,000 after contributions including one from Cleveland Pizza. The Browns then announced they would match the fan donation with an additional $10,000, bringing more support to the food bank. Organizers and the team turned a fan gag into a charitable outcome, redirecting community energy toward feeding those in need.

The National Association of Theatre Owners (NATO) announced it will trial an off-night ticket-discount program later this year, marking a cautious shift for U.S. exhibitors long resistant to reducing posted ticket prices. NATO chief John Fithian said the initiative, already used in Latin America and Canada, could begin as an experiment in a single, unnamed U.S. state for a limited time; studios must approve the plan. Fithian emphasized NATO won’t set discount amounts to avoid antitrust exposure — it would simply designate specific days when theaters could offer reduced admission. The move reflects growing concern about underused theater capacity on weeknights and acknowledges international precedents where discounts have helped attendance. Historically, U.S. exhibitors have resisted price cuts because studios take a fixed share of ticket receipts, so discounts directly reduce theater revenue; past entrants like Groupon and MoviePass had limited, short-lived impact against industry pushback. The announcement came at CinemaCon in Las Vegas, where tensions between exhibitors and studios over shrinking theatrical windows, premium VOD, and pricing have become more pronounced. While box-office revenue keeps rising thanks to higher ticket prices and premium formats, actual ticket sales are flat or declining, prompting some exhibitors to cautiously explore promotional strategies.

Martha Stewart teamed with Triscuit to create a limited-edition Toasted Coconut & Sea Salt cracker, launched in early May. After extensive testing, she picked coconut and sea salt as a savory-sweet, “habit forming” combo. Stewart, who keeps various crackers in her pantry despite not snacking much, suggests upscale toppings like crab and lime, avocado with hot pepper, melted cheese, truffle or even milk chocolate and marshmallow for a luxe s’more. The flavor fits 2015 trends—coconut, avocado, artisanal pairings—and received generally positive taste notes.

Netflix informed customer-service reps a day before announcing a price hike that they should expect angry callers, and added staff to handle a surge of complaints—yet many customers still faced long hold times. Starting in September, Netflix will split its combined streaming-plus-by-mail DVD service: each will cost $7.99 per month, meaning subscribers who want both must pay $15.98 instead of the prior $9.99. The company’s blog filled with around 4,000 mostly negative responses. Netflix spokesman Steve Swasey said the company anticipated backlash, having “tested, researched, [and] analyzed” reactions, and that employees were told to listen to callers and process cancellations if requested. BTIG analyst Rich Greenfield reported long waits (9–15 minutes) in 35 calls and criticized reps for offering no retention incentives, implying Netflix wasn’t concerned about losing subscribers. Despite the uproar, Netflix has renewed a multi-year licensing deal with NBC Universal, adding movies like Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind and shows such as The Office and 30 Rock to Watch Instantly—content additions Netflix says help justify higher fees, though many customers remain unconvinced.

During a Monday preview of the $65 million Broadway musical Spider-Man: Turn Off the Dark, a stunt performer fell from a platform into a stage pit after his harness line apparently snapped. The 31-year-old actor, later identified as Christopher Tierney, was taken to Bellevue Hospital with broken ribs and internal bleeding; Julie Taymor visited him in hospital. Witnesses described a sudden plunge near the show’s end, audience screams, a blackout, and emergency crews outside the Foxwoods Theatre. The production halted and announced performances would be paused; the run had already been delayed until Feb. 7 for creative and safety overhauls. This was the third significant accident during previews: two performers previously suffered broken bones from a slingshot flying technique and actress Natalie Mendoza earlier sustained a concussion. OSHA, Actors’ Equity, and the New York State Department of Labor inspected the show, met with producers, and required immediate additional safety protocols; Actors’ Equity later said performances won’t resume until back-up safety measures are in place. Investigations continue into the equipment failure and human error cited by the union.

A wide-ranging profile of Ted Cruz compiles numerous personal recollections and public criticisms painting him as politically talented but deeply unpopular across Republican circles. The piece recounts long-standing complaints from colleagues dating back to Cruz’s early career on George W. Bush’s 2000 campaign—where aides describe him as arrogant, disruptive, and unwilling to be a team player—through conflicts with prominent GOP figures including Bob Dole, John McCain, George W. Bush, John Boehner, Peter King, and Lindsey Graham. Critics cite episodes like Cruz’s attack on Dole over a U.N. disability treaty, clashes on policy (national security, drones, NSA), and his role in the 2013 government shutdown. Former classmates, clerks, and roommates also recall an abrasive, pompous, and at times creepy young man. Cruz concedes he isn’t everyone’s pal but insists competence matters more than likability. The profile closes with a newly surfaced 18-year-old video of Cruz joking about “world domination,” which his campaign calls evidence of his longtime sense of humor.

Four juniors from Florida A&M University say they were confronted and threatened with a gun by a white man while waiting to enter their friend’s off‑campus apartment building late Saturday night. The incident, captured in part on a roughly 10‑minute video posted to Twitter by student Isaiah Butterfield, shows the man—later identified by social media and local outlets as Don Crandall—telling the group they could not enter without a key, verbally accosting them, and then producing a firearm as the students attempted to get into an elevator. Butterfield’s clip has been widely shared online.

Butterfield, who was joined by classmates Stephen Brooks, Joshua Cosby, and Fitzroy Rhoden, said they were waiting at the garage entrance for another friend, Zavian Flowers, who had just moved into the building and was hosting a party. According to Butterfield, Crandall walked past them, forced the door closed, declared they couldn’t come in without a key, and later returned to continue harassing them. The confrontation escalated until a bystander identified by Butterfield as “Chad” intervened, defended the students, and helped secure their entrance.

Local reporting and social posts linked Crandall to the Baymont Inn & Suites by Wyndham Hotels, where he was listed as a manager. Pax Hotel Group, the inn’s owner, confirmed via Instagram that the general manager was involved in the incident, condemned his conduct, apologized to those affected, and announced that he had been fired. The apartment complex, Stadium Centre—an off‑campus housing option in Tallahassee—stated to residents that Crandall is not a tenant, reiterated that firearms are prohibited on the property, and emphasized its commitment to maintaining an inclusive, diverse residential community.

The students described the episode as racially charged and traumatizing; Butterfield and others expressed disbelief at experiencing such discrimination first‑hand. The matter has drawn significant attention online and prompted swift action by the hotel employer and statements from the apartment management.

Jennifer Herold, a 30-year-old candidate for Ohio’s 7th House District, issued a statement condemning comments by her Republican primary opponent, State Senator Tom Patton, made during a January 18 radio interview. Patton, 62, suggested Herold might be unfit to serve because she is a mother of two young children and noted that representatives must spend three nights a week in Columbus. He contrasted her situation with his own decision to wait until his children were grown before running. Patton also called her “the gal” and used the term “sweetie” on air, prompting Herold to call his remarks “insulting and discriminatory.”

Herold rejected the notion that parenthood is a liability, arguing that raising children is a strength rather than a disqualification. She listed prominent examples of parents—women and men—who have successfully served while raising children, including Sarah Palin, Congresswoman Cathy McMorris Rodgers, Ohio Lt. Gov. Mary Taylor, state Rep. Christina Hagan (who recently brought her infant to testify before a Senate committee), Governor John Kasich and Speaker Paul Ryan. Herold challenged whether Patton’s comments would have been made about fathers and urged local and state Republican organizations to reconsider endorsements that tacitly support his views. She invited supporters to sign a petition, tweet with #ISupportJen, and follow her campaign.

Patton later issued a statement saying his remarks were “misunderstood,” apologizing for a poor choice of words, and noting he did not intend to suggest young mothers couldn’t serve—citing his experience raising five daughters. The GOP primary winner will face Democrat David Thurau in November.

Researchers at Queen Mary University of London demonstrated that bumblebees can learn a novel string-pulling task and transmit that skill socially, challenging assumptions that complex culture needs large brains. Using a clear plastic table hiding blue artificial “flowers” with sucrose wells and attached strings, experimenters found that a few bees spontaneously solved the task but most did not. Through stepwise individual training—moving the flower progressively further under the table—over half of trained bees learned to grasp and pull the string to extract the reward. When naive bees observed trained demonstrators through a transparent chamber, about 60% acquired the ability after a few demonstrations; many learned after roughly five observations and some after only one. In colony-level transmission experiments, a single seeded demonstrator sparked broad diffusion: in three test colonies, dozens of foragers learned to pull the string over successive paired foraging bouts, while control colonies without a demonstrator showed no spread. Network analyses indicated social transmission rather than mere asocial discovery, and the behavior persisted beyond the death of original demonstrators, producing up to four sequential “learning generations.” Detailed video analysis revealed that learning combined local and stimulus enhancement (observers attending to demonstrator location and the string) and trial-and-error perceptual feedback; observers typically learned where and when to try and then refined the pulling action individually. Experienced bees eventually performed without visual feedback. The authors conclude that relatively simple associative mechanisms can support culture-like diffusion of novel behavior in insects, implying that cumulative social transmission need not depend on large brains or human-level cognition.

William Morris Endeavor Entertainment (WME) and technology investor Silver Lake announced an agreement to acquire global sports, events, fashion and media firm IMG Worldwide. WME Co‑CEOs Patrick Whitesell and Ariel Emanuel said IMG’s international reach, management and leadership across sports, fashion and media complement WME’s business, creating a broad global sports and entertainment platform across North America, Europe, Asia, South America and Africa. The combined company will offer an extensive client roster, relationships with sponsors, brands and broadcasters, and marquee assets in sports, events, film, TV and fashion; Whitesell and Emanuel will lead the merged business. Silver Lake’s Egon Durban highlighted IMG’s growth potential and plans to accelerate its digital expansion. Terms were not disclosed and the deal is subject to customary closing conditions; Mubadala Development Company will be a minority investor. Financial advisers to Silver Lake and WME included J.P. Morgan, Barclays, RBC and Deutsche Bank.

A Travis County jury convicted 69-year-old James Miller of criminally negligent homicide for the 2015 stabbing death of 32-year-old musician Daniel Spencer, acquitting him of murder and manslaughter. Miller was sentenced to 10 years’ probation, six months in the Travis County Jail, 100 hours of community service, an alcohol monitor for at least a year, payment of roughly $10,000–$11,000 in fines/restitution and court costs. Prosecutors portrayed Spencer as an upstanding community member whose life was taken for no justifiable reason; his mother described enduring profound grief and the trauma of knowing he suffered alone. The defense argued Miller acted in self-defense after Spencer made a sexual advance during a night of music and drinking at Spencer’s home. Miller—an ex-Austin police officer who played guitar with Spencer—told police soon after the incident, “I think I killed someone… I stabbed him,” and later said Spencer had attempted to kiss him, prompting Miller to stab twice. Jurors accepted a reduced theory of criminal negligence rather than intentional murder. The outcome reignited controversy over the so-called “gay panic” defense, which remains legally available in Texas and most U.S. states despite calls for bans by LGBT advocates and the American Bar Association. Critics say the defense exploits prejudice by treating LGBTQ+ advances as justification for lethal violence and re-victimizes marginalized people; advocates are pursuing legislation in several states to bar its use. Supporters note defense lawyers’ duty to provide zealous representation, but opponents argue the verdict sends a harmful message about the unequal protection of queer people under the law.

A family is urgently seeking help after their dog Jade vanished in Yellowstone National Park following a July 23, 2015 head-on collision caused by a driver who fell asleep. David Sowers sustained multiple injuries and was airlifted from the crash site; his wife Laura Gillice and daughter Angie Sowers have repeatedly returned to the park—despite medical advice and the 550-mile trip from Denver—to search for Jade. Park rangers say Jade bolted when rescuers attempted to remove her from a crushed crate. Multiple sightings, most recently near Canyon Village, suggest Jade is still alive and surviving in the park. Volunteers and park-approved methods, including live traps and scent items, are deployed daily, but capture efforts have so far failed. The family faces mounting medical and travel expenses. Organizers ask for donations, visitors to join search efforts, and help spreading the word to bring Jade safely home to her grieving family. Contact and share information appreciated.

Sources report that Rupert Murdoch surprised wife Wendi Deng by filing for divorce after 14 years of marriage, though the couple had reportedly been living increasingly separate lives. Murdoch, 82, filed in New York, citing an irretrievable breakdown; Wendi, 44, was taken off-guard. Speculation about causes has swirled but no definitive reason is confirmed. Observers note Wendi’s extensive social life and friendships with figures such as Chris DeWolfe, Tony Blair and Eric Schmidt, fueling rumors of affairs—claims denied or unproven—and her ambassadorial role in China-related business and Hollywood circles. Wendi’s visibility rose after she defended Murdoch during a 2011 parliamentary hearing. Media figures, including BBC’s Robert Peston and biographer Michael Wolff, hinted that more sensational revelations might emerge, prompting wide public curiosity. The split follows tensions within the family—Murdoch’s adult children were long uneasy about the marriage—and comes as News Corp. prepares to split into two companies. Both have legal representation; a prenuptial agreement and subsequent post-nups may shape settlement outcomes. The saga has reignited scrutiny of the couple’s private and professional entanglements.

Beginning in 1996, Alexa Internet donated its web crawl data daily to the Internet Archive, where after an embargo the captures are added to the Wayback Machine. These crawls aim to archive pages when created and preserve referenced pages so that as content changes or disappears, links can point to the version live when a page was written. The Archive hopes these preserved references will replace broken links or serve as companion links so readers can see authors’ original intent, contributing to a “No More 404” goal. Scattered biographical snippets appear: Charlie Hunnam (born April 10, 1980, Newcastle) rose via TV roles like Byker Grove and Queer as Folk, later choosing roles for long-term artistic value rather than immediate pay; other fragmented celebrity notes and trivia are intermixed.

U.S. officials say a U.S. contractor working for Development Alternatives Inc. under a USAID democracy program was arrested in Havana on Dec. 5 after distributing cellphones, laptops and other communications gear to Cuban activists. The detainee, who entered on a tourist visa and remains unnamed, is being held in a secure facility; Washington has requested consular access. Cuban charges were not disclosed; authorities can use broad “dangerousness” laws. The arrest risks straining already cautious Obama-era efforts to engage Cuba, which link further openings to concrete human-rights improvements. Critics note past concerns about U.S. democracy programs’ oversight and methods. Observers say the case underscores Cuba’s continued hard-line tactics against dissent and raises questions about U.S. tactics and the pace of reopening relations.

Baltimore County detectives are investigating after 16-month-old Sabriya Towels was found in cardiac arrest inside a black Ford F-150 on McDowell Lane in Lansdowne and later died at the hospital. Neighbors expressed shock and sorrow, noting temperatures near 88°F and the added heat inside a vehicle with leather seats. Police say a relative — not a parent — was supposed to drop Sabriya at the Highland Village Head Start Center but instead went to his home on South Paca Street and fell asleep. About four hours later, when he returned to retrieve the child, he discovered her in the truck. Authorities currently do not believe the incident was intentional; the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner will determine the official cause of death. No charges have been filed and the relative’s name has not been released. Staff at the Head Start Center declined to comment. The report references a similar case in Alexandria, where a mother, Zoraida Magali Conde Hernandez, was charged with felony child neglect after allegedly leaving her 8-month-old in a hot car, underscoring the lethal risk of high temperatures in parked vehicles.

Students, teachers, parents and activists staged nationwide demonstrations on March 4 to protest deep public-education budget cuts, staging rallies, teach-ins, walkouts and marches at campuses from California to Wisconsin, Texas, Illinois and Alabama. While many events were peaceful—large gatherings at UC Berkeley, Sacramento, UCLA and elsewhere—some turned confrontational: arrests at University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee after clashes with police, smashed car windows and blocked gates at UC Santa Cruz, and a freeway shutdown in Oakland that led to more than 150 arrests and injuries. Protesters decried tuition hikes, furloughs and program cuts caused by state budget shortfalls and fading federal stimulus funds, called for restoring funding, and urged alternatives like taxing oil or tobacco. Officials expressed sympathy but warned against violence.

The penny now costs more to produce than it’s worth, prompting calls to abolish it. In 2016 production expenses rose to about 1.5 cents per penny—higher than the coin’s face value—driven largely by rising zinc prices. The U.S. Mint made more than 8.4 billion pennies that year, and combined production and shipping losses on pennies totaled roughly $69 million, the largest loss in nine years. Nickels have long cost more than five cents to produce—about seven cents each—because copper and nickel prices have climbed due to industrial demand and growth in electric vehicles and stainless steel use. Dimes and quarters remain profitable and helped the Mint report $391.5 million in seigniorage last year. Eliminating the penny could reduce costs and simplify transactions, as U.S. bases overseas already use nickels as the lowest denomination.

Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke has recommended altering nearly half of the 27 national monuments reviewed at President Trump’s request, according to a memo reported by The Wall Street Journal and obtained by the Associated Press. Zinke proposes reducing the boundaries of six monuments, including Utah’s Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante, Nevada’s Gold Butte, Oregon’s Cascade-Siskiyou, and two large Pacific marine monuments. He also suggests changes to several other sites—such as New Mexico’s Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks and Rio Grande del Norte, and Maine’s Katahdin Woods and Waters—and reopening extensive ocean areas to commercial fishing. The recommendations follow Trump’s contention that the Antiquities Act has been misused to create oversized monuments that limit energy development, grazing and other uses. Zinke says boundary adjustments would not transfer ownership and would preserve public access for hunting, fishing and grazing, while he emphasizes protecting tribal interests and historical land grants. He declined to specify whether lands would be opened to drilling, mining or logging. Conservationists warn the moves could strip protections from culturally and ecologically important lands and ocean habitats; groups like The Wilderness Society say the administration lacks authority to rescind protections and plan legal challenges if Trump acts on Zinke’s proposals. The White House has not commented.

Auctioneers sold a rare photo album containing informal photographs of Adolf Hitler and members of his inner circle that likely originated from Eva Braun’s possession in the Führer bunker in 1945. Specialist Mr. Tredwen, with more than a decade in military-history items, said the images would have been taken only by someone very close to Hitler because official Nazi photography was tightly controlled to maintain his projected image. The album, lacking signatures to identify its owner or photographer, was reportedly first obtained in April 1945 by British Fleet Street photographer Edward Dean, who is said to have acquired it from a Russian soldier who found the album in a drawer in Braun’s bunker bedroom soon after Hitler and Braun committed suicide. The album’s photographs—mostly from the early to mid-1930s—include candid scenes: Hitler saluting while walking toward the camera at his Berghof headquarters and shots of guards both on duty and at ease. The auction attracted competitive bidding from telephone and online buyers across Britain, the United States, Germany, China, South Africa and elsewhere. Mr. Tredwen emphasized that collectors of Nazi memorabilia he encounters are generally historians rather than sympathizers, driven by an interest in World War II’s historical impact and the grotesque fascination with the Third Reich’s evil. The sale underscores ethical dilemmas around ownership and display of Nazi-related artifacts; institutions and collectors are increasingly urged to investigate provenance and to donate items to memorials. Auschwitz-Birkenau’s director has called for private holders to hand over documents and personal materials to improve historical understanding from victims’ perspectives. The existence and marketability of such artifacts—alongside attractions recreating Hitler’s bunker—highlight persistent public interest and discomfort surrounding this history.

Peaches Geldof, 25, was found dead at her Wrotham, Kent home with her 11-month-old son, Phaedra, playing nearby. Husband Thomas Cohen had been away overnight with their older child, Astala, and asked a friend to check on her when she did not answer her phone. Sources said the family hopes Phaedra, being so young, was unaware of the circumstances; Geldof had practiced attachment parenting and was often with her baby. Her death drew painful echoes of her mother Paula Yates’s 2000 death, when Yates’s infant daughter was also nearby.

Coroners released Geldof’s body so funeral plans can proceed, but an autopsy was inconclusive and the cause of death remains unexplained pending toxicology results that may take weeks. In the weeks before her death, observers noted her dramatic weight loss and risky dieting habits—she publicly discussed prolonged juicing and subsisting on fruit and miso soup. Health experts warned such practices risk electrolyte imbalance, cardiac arrest, muscle wasting and organ damage. Dr. Chris Steele suggested long-term bulimia might have contributed, pointing to knuckle changes and severe weight loss, and noted that underlying heart conditions or enlargement could also cause sudden death in young people. Investigations are ongoing.

Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, and the American Cancer Society (ACS) released a report, "The Global Burden of Cancer in Women," highlighting that the four leading causes of female cancer deaths—breast, colorectal, lung and cervical cancers—are largely preventable or detectable early, when treatments are most effective. The report, the first outcome of a public–private partnership between Merck and ACS, warns that cancer’s impact on women is rising, especially in low- and middle-income countries, driven by global population growth and aging. In 2012, cancer caused 3.5 million female deaths worldwide; by 2030 that figure could reach 5.5 million, a greater-than-57% increase in under two decades. The research emphasizes that increased education, prevention, screening and early-detection programs will be essential to curb this trend and to reduce the substantial societal and economic toll of cancer. A 2009 estimate placed the global economic burden of cancer at about $286 billion, largely due to premature workforce deaths; in the U.S. alone, cancer-related years of productive life lost in 2008 corresponded to $82 billion. The report was presented at the World Cancer Congress and featured panelists from ACS, Merck and global health leaders. The partnership will support expansion of ACS’s All of Me Young Scholars program to train health and civil-society professionals in Brazil, Mexico, Colombia and India to improve prevention and early detection in lower-resource settings. The initiative ties into Merck’s Healthy Women, Healthy Economies effort, which links women’s health to economic growth and promotes policies to increase women’s health and economic participation. The full report is available via the American Cancer Society.

Some big-studio films become costly flops when worldwide grosses fall far short of production budgets. Examples include Cowboys & Aliens, The Lone Ranger, Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within and The Adventures of Pluto Nash. Films can evoke strong emotions and escapism, but mismatched properties, casting, or enormous budgets often leave them unable to attract audiences. Recent box-office results illustrate this contrast: Universal’s The Fate of the Furious dominated, earning $163.6 million domestically in ten days and $908.4 million globally, while family titles like The Boss Baby and Beauty and the Beast posted strong totals. By contrast, Warner Bros.’ thriller Unforgettable opened to a disappointing $4.8 million—Katherine Heigl’s career worst—though its $12 million budget limits losses. Christian Bale’s The Promise fell flat with $4.1 million against a $100 million cost, despite its awareness goals and a $20 million donation to establish a human-rights institute. Other newcomers like Phoenix Forgotten and Free Fire also underperformed.

Researchers at the University of Warwick have produced the first international “normal crying” charts for infants’ first three months, based on a meta-analysis of nearly 8,700 babies from several industrialised countries (including the UK, Canada, Italy, the Netherlands, Denmark, Germany and Japan). The study found a clear, consistent pattern: average daily crying is about two hours in the first two weeks, peaks at roughly two hours 15 minutes around six weeks, and declines to about one hour 10 minutes by week twelve. Individual variation is large — some infants cried as little as 30 minutes per day while others exceeded five hours. Rates of colic (commonly defined as crying more than three hours per day for at least three days a week) also varied markedly by country: the UK, Canada and Italy showed the highest reported colic prevalence at various early ages (e.g., the UK 28% at 1–2 weeks; Canada 34.1% at 3–4 weeks; Italy 20.9% at 8–9 weeks), whereas Denmark and Germany reported much lower rates (e.g., Denmark 5.5% and Germany 6.7% at 3–4 weeks). The authors note that existing standards (the 1950s Wessel criteria) are outdated given changes in family structures and childcare, and argue these new charts can help health professionals reassure parents or identify excessive crying needing support. Lead author Professor Dieter Wolke suggested cultural or parenting differences — and possibly genetic or prenatal factors — may explain lower crying in countries like Denmark and Germany, and warned against anxiety driven by unscientific parenting advice, stressing caregiver wellbeing to better support infants. The study appears in The Journal of Pediatrics.

Stanford researchers challenge the view that early altruism is purely innate, showing that simple reciprocal interactions reliably trigger helping and generosity in young children. Across four studies, 1- and 2-year-olds and preschoolers who experienced brief reciprocal play (e.g., rolling a ball back and forth) subsequently helped an adult far more than children who experienced friendly but nonreciprocal “parallel” play. In Study 1, toddlers in reciprocal play helped on about three of four opportunities versus roughly one in the parallel condition. Study 2 demonstrated transfer: after a single reciprocal warm-up with one adult, toddlers were also more likely to help a new, previously uninvolved person; control and parallel-play groups did not differ, indicating reciprocity increased helping rather than parallel play suppressing it. Study 3 found that even a one-minute reciprocal interaction boosted generosity in four-year-olds in sticker-allocation tasks. Study 4 showed preschoolers who had brief reciprocal play expected others to behave benevolently—choosing the reciprocal partner as the one likely to give a gift, help, or share—suggesting reciprocal interaction fosters an inferred social norm of mutual care. The effects were not explained by simple differences in fun or warmth. The authors argue that subtle social cues—reciprocal responsiveness conveyed during typical warm-up interactions—may acculturate children to expect and enact helping, undermining claims that early helping is unaffected by socialization. Practically, the findings imply caregivers and educators can foster children’s benevolence through simple reciprocal engagement, shaping both altruistic actions and expectations of others’ benevolence.

Vice President Mike Pence spoke at a Capitol ceremony honoring Sen. John McCain, who is lying in state, delivering remarks on behalf of President Trump, who did not attend at McCain’s request. Pence acknowledged disagreements but praised McCain’s lifelong service—from his Navy valor and brutal Vietnam-era captivity after refusing early release, to his decades in Congress—and credited him with advancing limited government, tax reform and a stronger military. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and House Speaker Paul Ryan also paid tribute, calling McCain a national hero and a resolute, authentic fighter. A steady rain accompanied the flag-draped casket’s entry into the Capitol, where officials, family and long lines of Americans filed past to pay respects. The two-day Washington observances will culminate in a funeral at the National Cathedral, with McCain having asked former Presidents Barack Obama and George W. Bush to speak; the procession will pause at the Vietnam Veterans Memorial to honor his POW service. Administration officials present included Defense Secretary Jim Mattis, Chief of Staff John Kelly and others, despite the president’s absence—Trump had been asked not to attend. Earlier services in Arizona featured tributes from figures including Joe Biden, who highlighted McCain’s character and willingness to oppose abuses of power. McCain died last Saturday at 81 after being diagnosed with an aggressive brain cancer; he is survived by his wife, children and mother.

A Moscow court found three members of the punk group Pussy Riot guilty of hooliganism for staging an anti-Putin “punk prayer” in Christ the Saviour Cathedral in February, sentencing them to two years’ imprisonment. Judge Marina Syrova said their actions were motivated by religious hatred and offended Russian Orthodox believers; the women, held in a glass dock, giggled as sentences were read and have already served about five months. The verdict fueled international condemnation from the U.S. and EU as disproportionate and prompted celebrity-backed protests abroad, while domestic polls showed little Russian sympathy. Supporters called the ruling political repression and “Putin’s personal revenge.” The Orthodox Church condemned the stunt but urged mercy, leaving open possible clemency. Lawyers plan to appeal amid broader concerns over tightening restrictions on dissent in Putin’s new term.

Former prosecutor Marcia Clark reacted to reports that a folding Buck knife allegedly recovered from property once owned by O.J. Simpson is being investigated by the LAPD. Clark said she was astonished that someone would hand what could be important evidence to an off-duty officer who then kept it at home, calling the situation unbelievable if true. She urged caution, noting the find might be a hoax or planted, but praised the LAPD for testing the knife. Clark said modern forensic methods can recover DNA from very old items and that if the knife is connected to the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman it could yield information — perhaps even about anyone who helped bury it — though she acknowledged the likelihood of any prosecution stemming from the knife is very slim and stressed her sympathy for the victims’ families.

LAPD Capt. Andrew Neiman confirmed the department is investigating the alleged discovery at the Rockingham property and noted Simpson could not be retried on murder charges due to double jeopardy. Reports say a construction worker found the knife around 2002 and gave it to a retired officer who kept it until asking later to have it engraved; that led another officer to notify detectives and turn it over. The knife reportedly has a 5" blade; Dr. Irwin Golden, the deputy medical examiner from the 1994 case, said such a blade could have inflicted the fatal wounds. Forensics testing for fingerprints, hair and DNA is underway, but experts caution contamination, handling, burial conditions and time could degrade or obscure useful evidence. Even if DNA were found, it would likely be symbolic, since Simpson previously was acquitted and cannot be retried for the murders.

The stock market’s current bull run, which began after the March 9, 2009 closing low of the S&P 500 at 676, is widely counted as eight years old — an uninterrupted, roughly 250% advance that ranks as the second-longest post‑war bull market. By conventional rules a bull begins when a rebound gains 20% and ends only when the index falls at least 20% from a high; that hasn’t happened since 2009. Yet analysts disagree on the true start date: some point to a near‑20% slump in September 2011 as a corrective reset, others to March 2013 when the S&P cleared its 2007 high and some declare February 2016’s broad market washout — severe internally even if the S&P didn’t drop 20% — as a cleansing that renewed the rally. These alternative datings affect labels like “cyclical” versus “secular” bull markets but don’t materially change the market’s lofty valuations and strong past returns.

Despite its longevity, the bull has been “unloved”: household equity ownership fell during the run and volatility has been surprisingly muted, even as world events repeatedly threatened sentiment. The Federal Reserve’s ultra‑easy policy and low interest rates helped sustain equities; corporate profits and money flows also propelled gains. Since the 2009 low the Dow more than tripled, outperforming many global peers and producing outsized winners (Home Depot, Apple, UnitedHealth, Visa) even as some long‑standing Dow names lagged.

Strategists caution that age alone won’t kill the rally — recessions, financial panic or Fed tightening do. Valuations are high (forward P/E around the high teens, other metrics nearer 30), so many expect periodic corrections of 5–10% as healthy “refreshes.” Forecasts hinge on earnings growth, Fed policy and political developments: while some see more upside if tax cuts and deregulation materialize, others warn that elevated valuations plus potential Fed rate hikes, geopolitical risks and investor complacency leave the market vulnerable. In short, the bull is mature and durable so far, but investors should expect bumps and place less weight on the calendar than on fundamentals that might ultimately end the run.

Walmart’s promotion to send rapper Pitbull to whichever store earns the most Facebook “likes” has unexpectedly turned into an online stunt to exile him to remote Kodiak, Alaska. A Boston Phoenix writer and others encouraged people to flood the Kodiak Walmart’s page to make it the top-liked location; by Monday the Kodiak store had amassed over 35,000 likes — more than five times the island’s population — giving it a clear lead in the contest that runs through July 16. Walmart confirmed shoppers can still try to overtake Kodiak but acknowledged the challenge: a Miami location had only 45 likes. Pitbull, currently touring Europe, has taken the campaign in stride, saying in an emailed statement he’ll go “wherever the fans want to have a party,” and joking on Twitter about Kodiak’s bear population and bear repellent while using the trending #ExilePitbull tag. Kodiak Island, about 225 miles southwest of Anchorage, is known for its large Coast Guard base and Kodiak brown bears.

Dr. Fredric Brandt, a pioneering South Florida dermatologist widely known as the “Baron of Botox,” died by suicide at age 65 in his Coconut Grove home. Police found him hanging in his garage after a friend who had been staying with him called authorities concerned about Brandt’s safety. Friends, family and his longtime publicist emphasized he had been under psychiatric care and long struggled with depression; while a recent satirical portrayal on Netflix’s Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt upset him, those close to him say the show did not cause his death, though it compounded his distress.

Brandt built a high-profile career treating celebrities—including Madonna, Kelly Ripa and Stephanie Seymour—developing cosmetic procedures, authoring books on anti-aging, and creating the Dr. Brandt Skin Care line sold internationally and at retailers like Sephora. Trained in multiple medical specialties and with residencies at NYU and Memorial Sloan Kettering, he completed dermatology training at the University of Miami and opened a Coral Gables practice in 1982, later expanding to New York. He ran clinical trials, helped clear injectables with the FDA, taught dermatologists, hosted a SiriusXM show, and released product lines promising cellular-level anti-aging.

Colleagues and clients remembered him as brilliant, generous, and warm—singing show tunes in his office, loving art and his dogs, and adored by patients who once staged a musical tribute for his 60th birthday. Despite his public persona and contributions to aesthetic medicine, those who knew him said his private battle with depression was profound. He is survived by his brother Paul and his dogs.

Former James Bond actor Pierce Brosnan, 62, was stopped by Transportation Security Administration agents at Burlington International Airport, Vermont, after a 10-inch hunting knife was detected in his carry-on luggage. Airport officials confiscated the blade during routine screening; Brosnan was reportedly embarrassed and upset but cooperated with agents. Lieutenant Shawn Burke of the Burlington Police Department said TSA encountered Brosnan at a checkpoint and, after resolving the issue, allowed him to continue his journey. The TSA offered the choice to surrender the knife or place it in checked baggage; Brosnan chose to check it and faced no arrest or citation. Knives (except rounded or plastic butter knives) have been banned from aircraft cabins since the post-9/11 security rules requiring sharp objects be transported in checked luggage. Brosnan’s publicist had not commented publicly.

This document recounts the case of Crystal Mason, a Black woman in Texas whose 2016 provisional ballot led to a conviction and a five-year prison sentence, and situates her story within broader issues of felony disenfranchisement and inconsistent state policies. Mason had been released from a five-year sentence for tax fraud in early 2016 and, unaware that being on supervised release made her ineligible to vote in Texas, cast a provisional ballot at her local church when her name did not appear on the rolls. The provisional ballot was not counted; she later learned of her ineligibility only when meeting her probation officer and was subsequently arrested for voter fraud. In March 2018, State District Judge Ruben Gonzalez convicted and sentenced her to 60 months in prison—an outcome critics characterize as harsh and emblematic of racial disparities in criminal justice. Advocates note contrasting penalties in other cases, such as a white Iowa woman who received probation and a fine for attempting to vote twice, and argue that mass incarceration functions in practice as a form of political suppression akin to the “Three Fifths Compromise,” since felony disenfranchisement disproportionately affects people of color. The case prompted public outcry, an online petition with over 38,000 signatures, and legal interventions including friend-of-the-court briefs from the Texas Civil Rights Project and ACLU asserting that federal law protects the right to cast a provisional ballot when eligibility is disputed. Mason’s motion for a new trial was denied in a 16-page ruling; her attorney plans to appeal to the Second Court of Appeals.
