The document outlines how voting rights for felons vary widely across states—some restore voting on release, after parole, or after completing supervision, while Vermont and Maine never strip voting rights—and highlights the confusion and risk aversion this patchwork causes. Supporters demand that charges be dropped and that officials inform incarcerated and supervised individuals clearly about their voting eligibility to prevent future wrongful prosecutions.

At a high-profile UFO conference in Mexico City, two color slides claimed to show the body of an extraterrestrial recovered in the 1947 Roswell incident were unveiled, sparking immediate controversy and widespread skepticism. Former journalist Adam Dew presented the images, saying Kodak analysis dated the film to the late 1940s; he plans to sell high-resolution scans and a documentary. Organizer Jaime Maussan and some proponents, including former astronaut Edgar Mitchell and UFO researcher Gary Heseltine, defended the pictures as genuine evidence of “little grey” aliens and insisted forensic and photographic experts had validated them. The reveal drew thousands to a paid event and ignited trending ridicule and disbelief on social media, with critics labeling the slides a hoax or publicity stunt.

Skeptics noted parallels to earlier debunked “alien autopsy” material, suspicious financial motives, and historical precedents where mummified human remains—especially infant or intentionally cranially-deformed skeletons—were mistaken for aliens. Experts and journalists pointed out that Kodak dating only proves the film stock is old, not that the subject is extraterrestrial. Observers also highlighted details suggesting the figure might be a mummified child displayed in a case, and noted that cranial deformation and mummification are well-documented in the Americas. Past cases like the “Starchild” skull illustrate how unusual human remains can fuel sensational claims absent rigorous, peer-reviewed science.

Ultimately, the slides are unlikely to settle the long-running Roswell debate: they may be authentic period photographs but, critics argue, are far more plausibly human mummies or staged models than proof of an alien crash. The episode underscores how gaps in provenance, commercial ties, and sensational presentation perpetuate conspiracy narratives rather than producing conclusive scientific evidence.

Madonna has denied reports that she’s applied to adopt two more children from Malawi, saying her visit is to inspect a children’s hospital in Blantyre and support her Raising Malawi charity. Earlier reports — citing a Malawian government spokesman and court sources — said the 58-year-old singer appeared in High Court in Lilongwe seeking adoption orders and would learn the court’s decision within a week. Madonna previously adopted David (2006) and Mercy James (2009) from Malawi; she also has children Lourdes and Rocco from earlier relationships. She founded Raising Malawi in 2006 to aid orphans and underprivileged children, funding schools, scholarships and a pediatric ICU at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital. The story follows broader controversy after Madonna’s Women’s March remarks about “blowing up the White House,” which drew attention from federal authorities; she clarified she does not promote violence. Court officials and local media had reported sightings of children with her after the hearing.

A new high-resolution satellite study has produced the most accurate global lake count to date, finding 117 million lakes worldwide and showing lakes cover about 2 million square miles (5 million km2), roughly 3.7 percent of Earth's ice-free land. Previous estimates, which relied on extrapolation from sampled parcels, over- or under-counted because millions of lakes are small and many medium-to-large lakes had been missing from older databases. About 90 million lakes are tiny (0.2–1 hectare), roughly the size of a large farm pond or two American football fields. Most lakes lie in the Northern Hemisphere between 45° and 75°N—Canada, Russia, Alaska, Northern Europe and the Great Lakes—owing to past glaciation and continental configurations. Eighty-five percent occur below 500 meters elevation. The study excluded the Caspian Sea, Antarctica and Greenland; its authors plan to release the database publicly and to refine counts with Landsat 8. Accurate numbers matter because lakes play complex roles in the carbon cycle, emitting CO2 and methane but sequestering carbon in sediments, and many are changing quickly: permafrost thaw, drought and human use are draining lakes in parts of Russia, Alaska and northern China. Separately, satellite imagery documents the dramatic decline of the Aral Sea since Soviet-era irrigation diverted its rivers. Once a vast inland sea, it fragmented into separate lobes; by the 2000s the eastern lobe dried completely. The retreat has devastated local communities, increased pollution and airborne contaminated dust, and altered regional climate, health and agriculture, becoming a symbol of ecological mismanagement.

A light aircraft made an emergency landing at Humberside Airport after its pilot collapsed mid-flight, and the passenger — an inexperienced flyer identified only as “John” — took control with instruction from two flying instructors contacted by air traffic control. The Cessna 172 had departed Sandtoft Airfield and was returning from Skegness when the pilot fell ill about 18:25 BST. The passenger completed several guided circuits before bringing the plane down at about 19:30. Instructors on the radio talked him through turns and approach; one instructor, Roy Murray, later said without that “talk-down” the outcome could have been fatal. Eyewitnesses reported a rough touchdown with sparks and bumps as the aircraft’s nose hit the runway; two incoming flights were delayed while the plane was removed.

Emergency services, including police, fire and ambulance crews, plus a RAF Sea King helicopter, responded. The pilot — described by a friend as a very experienced and much-liked aviator — later died; police said the death is not being treated as suspicious and a post-mortem will determine the cause and whether a coroner’s file is needed. At the family’s request, authorities are not releasing the pilot’s identity or video footage. Local commentators and acquaintances praised the passenger’s calm and effective handling of the situation, calling his actions “phenomenal” and heroic. Roads around the airport were briefly closed and have since reopened; normal flight operations resumed.

Marcus M. Stanley, a senior economic adviser to Sen. Barbara Boxer, resigned after being arrested Tuesday for attempting to bring marijuana into the Hart Senate Office Building. Capitol Police stopped Stanley at a security screening when he allegedly tried to "remove and conceal" a leafy green substance from his pocket; tests later confirmed it was marijuana. Boxer accepted his resignation, with a spokesman calling his actions "wrong and unacceptable." Stanley, a Capitol Hill staffer since 2007 who earned a six-figure salary and previously worked for the Joint Economic Committee and the Environment and Public Works Committee, is the fourth Hill aide arrested this year. Marijuana possession on Capitol grounds has been recurring since the Visitor Center opened. Boxer opposes California’s Proposition 19 to legalize and tax cannabis.

Hungary’s abrupt sealing of its border with Serbia has shifted the migrant route into Croatia and intensified tensions across Europe over how to handle a growing influx of refugees and migrants. After Hungary declared a state of emergency and erected razor wire along a key crossing near Roszke, hundreds were left stranded on Serbian territory. Clashes erupted at Hungary’s border where riot police used tear gas, pepper spray, water cannons and batons against migrants trying to force their way through; several people were treated for respiratory or minor injuries. Hungary has begun criminal prosecutions for illegal crossings, detaining hundreds and conducting trials of those charged under new laws.

As the Hungarian frontier closed, groups of migrants—many fleeing war in Syria and other conflict zones—altered course, walking through fields into Croatia. Croatian authorities say they are ready to receive or direct migrants onward toward northern Europe, registering arrivals and transporting them to reception centers. Croatian Prime Minister Zoran Milanovic pledged to “accept and direct” people who mainly aim for Germany or Scandinavian countries, and called a National Security Council meeting to coordinate the response. Hundreds crossed into Croatia in a single day, some arriving by bus from southern Serbia; officials warned of practical dangers such as marked minefields from the 1990s war but emphasized orderly processing.

The EU’s border agency reports more than 500,000 migrants have reached EU borders so far this year, compared with 280,000 in 2014, exposing sharp divisions among member states over burden-sharing and border controls. Germany and Austria have tightened their borders; trains and crossings have been disrupted, and migrants continue to trek across the Balkans from Turkey, through Greece, Macedonia and Serbia. International voices—including the UN Secretary-General—criticized hardline responses as inhumane. Meanwhile, private initiatives surfaced: Egyptian businessman Naguib Sawiris proposed using Greek islands to host Syrian refugees, suggesting a joint-stock company to manage donations and facilities, though any plan would require Greek government approval. The situation remains fluid as migrants adapt routes and European countries struggle to agree on collective solutions.

During French President Emmanuel Macron’s state visit to the White House, President Donald Trump made several headline-grabbing, awkward gestures that drew widespread attention and online mockery. Outside the White House, Trump unexpectedly grabbed Macron’s hand and continued holding it while leading him away from reporters, a moment Twitter users found “super weird” and ripe for GIFs. That followed an awkward handshake exchange with First Lady Melania Trump on the South Lawn, where Trump repeatedly reached for her hand—first a pinky touch, then a light shake—before she finally reciprocated. Observers linked these scenes to earlier public displays where Melania appeared reluctant to hold her husband’s hand.

Later in the Oval Office, Trump reached toward Macron and brushed what he described as “a little piece of dandruff” off the French president’s shoulder, telling cameras, “We have to make him perfect — he is perfect.” The gesture prompted reactions calling it a diplomatic “power move,” with many interpreting it as an attempt to belittle Macron. Macron initially seemed surprised but then smiled and laughed. The visit included substantive discussions on Iran, the Paris climate accord, trade, and potential North Korea talks. Social media commentary mixed ridicule and disbelief, comparing the moments to satire and noting how unusual such personal gestures are in meetings between global leaders.

The document is a collage-like compilation of photo captions and brief notes chronicling the public life, appearances and relationships of U.S. Senator Orrin Hatch of Utah over several decades. It highlights Hatch’s long tenure and high-profile roles—senior senator, longtime member and chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee—and shows him alongside presidents, fellow senators, judges and cultural figures. Images and captions record Hatch with presidents Ronald Reagan, George H.W. Bush and Donald Trump; with presidential hopefuls such as Mitt Romney; and with judicial nominees including John Roberts, Samuel Alito and Elena Kagan. The captions show Hatch engaged in partisan and bipartisan moments: greeting Attorney General Janet Reno, co-sponsoring bills with Sen. Edward Kennedy, exchanging light moments with Sen. Dianne Feinstein, and participating in news conferences and committee activities. Local and national events are noted too—Memorial Day speeches in Utah, fundraising receptions, debates with challengers like Scott Howell, and interactions with Utah officials including governors and delegates. Photos capture Hatch with celebrities such as Muhammad Ali and with Utah figures like Sen. Bob Bennett and Gov. Gary Herbert. The collection reflects Hatch’s public visibility, political influence, and longevity, documenting his presence across Capitol Hill proceedings, judicial confirmation processes, campaign events and community occasions over many years.

President Trump criticized Nike’s decision to feature Colin Kaepernick in its 30th anniversary “Just Do It” campaign, calling the move a “terrible message,” but stopped short of condemning the company’s right to make its own business choices. In an Oval Office interview with The Daily Caller, Trump noted Nike is a tenant in one of his properties and said he personally wouldn’t have endorsed Kaepernick, yet acknowledged that freedom to make such decisions is a core American principle. Kaepernick rose to national attention in 2016 by kneeling during the national anthem to protest police brutality and racial inequality; he has since accused NFL owners of colluding to keep him off rosters. Nike’s campaign image, which Kaepernick shared on Twitter with the line “Believe in something. Even if it means sacrificing everything,” prompted immediate reactions: Nike’s stock dipped about 2 percent, critics such as country singer John Rich urged boycotts and posted images of destroyed Nike gear, and the NFL offered a statement affirming that the social justice issues raised by Kaepernick and other players “deserve our attention and action.” The NFL’s communications executive highlighted ongoing league and player efforts to address community and social issues. The episode touches on broader tensions over athlete protests, free expression, corporate endorsements, and political influence: Trump has previously urged punishment for anthem protesters and has been cited by some NFL owners as influencing their stance on demonstrations. The Nike-Kaepernick partnership has provoked debate across politics, business, sports, and public opinion.

The piece is a media roundup that centers on missteps, debates and trends shaping journalism and public discourse. It opens with Denis Finley, executive editor of the Burlington Free Press, whose flippant Twitter responses—including calling Vermont’s move to offer an “X” gender option on driver’s licenses “one step closer to the apocalypse” and equating recognition of trans people with recognizing “pedophiliacs”—provoked local outrage and subscription-cancellation threats. The episode is used to warn newsroom leaders about the perils of impulsive tweeting and the value of traditional editorial processes and restraint. Veteran journalists quoted urge less frequent, more considered public commentary and point out how quick social media blurts can damage both personal and organizational reputations.

The roundup then highlights other media moments: Jake Tapper’s contentious CNN interview with White House aide Stephen Miller, which escalated into mutual cut-offs and Miller’s removal, illustrating the performative nature of cable confrontations. The New York Times’ Golden Globes ad, part of its “The Truth Is Hard” campaign, is praised for intent but critiqued as a TV spot that may have mainly preached to the choir. Pew research showing accelerating declines in local TV news viewership—especially among younger Americans—is noted, along with reflections on media trust and advertising targeting.

Other items include Sarah Stillman’s work documenting deportations that lead to harm, commendation of female studio hosts in English soccer coverage, debate over Mueller’s obstruction inquiry, and reminders about craftsmanship in writing from Robert Graves’ "The Reader Over Your Shoulder." The roundup ends with a note on ESPN’s efforts to market college football to women ahead of the Alabama–Georgia championship. Overall, the collection underscores the evolving responsibilities of journalists, the consequences of social media impulses, and the broader challenges facing news organizations.

A 13-foot, 1,500-pound male great white shark carcass washed ashore Saturday on a rocky Westport, Massachusetts shoreline near the Rhode Island line. State biologist Greg Skomal performed a necropsy but found no clear trauma and officials said determining the cause of death will be difficult, if not impossible. The shark likely washed ashore Friday night and currently lies below the high tide line; authorities hope the tide will carry it back out to sea and have decided to leave the carcass in place because of its size. Nearby Little Compton closed Goosewing and South Shore beaches temporarily; they reopened Sunday and police sent a patrol boat to watch for other sharks. Shark sightings have been rare in that immediate area, though Cape Cod has seen numerous encounters this summer, including a July incident in Truro where a man was bitten. Experts link increased white shark activity to a growing grey seal population—protected since the 1970s—which attracts sharks until they migrate to warmer waters in winter.

A Suncor Energy employee, 36-year-old instrumentation technician Lorna Weafer of Fort McMurray, was killed by a large male black bear at the company’s oil sands base camp about 25 km north of Fort McMurray on May 8. Co-workers witnessed the afternoon attack after she exited a washroom and tried to intervene; she was pronounced dead at the scene. RCMP and Alberta wildlife officers shot the bear and set traps and cameras; another bear was later captured. Officials said the site had no open food and the attack may have been predatory. Suncor and Alberta OHS launched an investigation and urged vigilance as bears emerge from hibernation. Weafer’s family praised her warmth and community work and asked for privacy during their grief.

A completed investigation into the June 8 death of U.S. celebrity chef and television host Anthony Bourdain found no narcotics or toxic substances in his body, French judicial officials said. Bourdain, 61, was found dead by suicide in a hotel room near Strasbourg while filming an episode of his CNN series Parts Unknown. Authorities reported only traces of alcohol and a nonnarcotic medicine at therapeutic levels; no signs of violence or involvement of a third party were detected. Known for candidly discussing past addiction to heroin and cocaine, Bourdain had been clean since entering rehab in the early 1990s, though he acknowledged occasional drinking later in life. He rose from washing dishes in New York to international acclaim, dining with figures such as President Barack Obama and becoming a beloved, opinionated travel-food raconteur. His partner, Italian actress Asia Argento, with whom he had been romantically involved for more than a year, has publicly mourned him, sharing an emotional tribute and describing him as her “love, rock, protector.” Friends and colleagues remembered his fearless spirit and generosity. Resources for those in crisis were reiterated alongside reports.

President Trump’s 90 percent cut to federal advertising and outreach for the 2018 Obamacare open enrollment has pushed many insurers to increase their own outreach spending to reach consumers and counter confusion. With the federal budget trimmed to $10 million for the 39 states on HealthCare.gov (11 states run their own exchanges), insurers and advocacy groups are filling the void: Independence Blue Cross is using a tractor-trailer to bring consultants into Philadelphia neighborhoods; Centene is expanding TV and print ads as it enters three new states; Oscar Health is running multiple commercials; Florida Blue hired 700 temporary staff for enrollment events; and Blue Cross Blue Shield affiliates are shifting resources—some increasing online or grassroots efforts, others cutting marketing and focusing on helping existing customers manage plan changes. The federal cuts, along with truncated six-week enrollment and administration rhetoric, have fueled public uncertainty about whether subsidies and plans will remain, prompting insurers to boost messaging aimed at drawing young, healthy enrollees and clarifying coverage rules. Insurers have also raised premiums—about 20 percent on common “silver” plans—to offset reduced government payments, and some have exited counties. Forecasts vary: the Congressional Budget Office projects 11 million enrollees in 2018 (down from earlier estimates), while groups predict declines of up to 1.6 million. Early data show a surge in first-day sign-ups, but observers caution it may reflect renewals and that final totals remain uncertain.

Three House Republicans—Reps. Matt Gaetz (R-Fla.), Andy Biggs (R-Ariz.) and Louie Gohmert (R-Tex.)—introduced a nonbinding resolution urging special counsel Robert Mueller to resign from the Russia investigation, alleging conflicts of interest tied to his prior role as FBI director. The measure asserts Mueller is compromised by his professional relationship with former FBI director James Comey and by the FBI’s handling of a 2010 bribery probe related to the Uranium One transaction, a sale of a Canadian mining firm with U.S. uranium interests to a Russian company. The lawmakers contend FBI investigators under Mueller gathered evidence of Russian corruption but did not notify Congress or press charges, and that a confidential informant was constrained by a nondisclosure agreement. Gaetz and colleagues argue those events create an appearance of bias rendering Mueller unfit to lead the probe into whether Trump campaign associates colluded with Russia or sought to obstruct justice.

The push comes amid heightened GOP frustration as Mueller’s team revealed its first indictments: charges against former campaign chairman Paul Manafort and aide Rick Gates, and a guilty plea by George Papadopoulos for lying to the FBI. While some conservatives, including Reps. Trent Franks and Ron DeSantis, have publicly criticized Mueller or sought to limit the special counsel’s scope, most Republican leaders have not backed ousting him. Democrats and progressive groups have warned that Republican efforts to discredit Mueller risk undermining the investigation; meanwhile, Senate proposals backed by members of both parties would protect special counsels from undue presidential removal.

A recent case report and accompanying studies highlight potential links between cannabis use and cardiovascular complications, including sudden deaths in young adults. In Germany, toxicology found THC in the blood and brain tissue of two men, aged 23 and 28, who died after sudden collapses. Postmortem investigators ruled out other causes and suggested arrhythmias triggered by smoking cannabis as the likely mechanism, while acknowledging possible underlying predispositions. Experts caution the report is limited—duration of use was unclear—and some critics argue cannabis does not directly paralyze the heart or breathing and that many deaths occur from circumstances surrounding use. Nonetheless, corroborating research raises concern: a French analysis (2006–2010) of nearly 2,000 reported marijuana-related complications identified 35 cardiovascular events (about 2%), including 20 heart attacks and nine deaths; cardiovascular case reports increased over the study period. Authors emphasize that people with pre-existing cardiac vulnerabilities appear especially at risk and recommend clinicians consider cannabis use when evaluating cardiovascular events. Forensic toxicologists urge routine postmortem testing for cannabis to better assess its role in deaths. Overall, while the general population risk is considered low, growing evidence suggests marijuana can, in some individuals, provoke serious or fatal heart-related outcomes, warranting further surveillance and research.

This long profile traces Dinesh D’Souza’s trajectory from an influential conservative intellectual to a provocative filmmaker and partisan figure whose career has blended serious policy work with sensationalism. A former Reagan White House aide and fellow at AEI and the Hoover Institution, D’Souza made his name in campus conservatism and best-selling books attacking liberal policies on race, education, and culture. Early works like Illiberal Education earned mainstream conservative praise, but later books—most notably The End of Racism and The Enemy at Home—provoked sharp criticism for incendiary claims about race and for blaming the cultural left for global anti-American violence. D’Souza moved into documentaries with commercial successes such as 2012’s 2016: Obama’s America and the 2016 film Hillary’s America, which mix historical reenactment with conspiratorial arguments linking Democrats to slavery and the KKK. Personal scandals—including an extramarital affair and a 2014 conviction for campaign-finance violations involving straw donations—led to an eight-month community confinement sentence, probation, and fines; he contended his prosecution was politically motivated. Capitalizing on outrage, he has cultivated a mass audience in conspiracy-oriented conservative media. His pardon by President Trump reignited controversy: D’Souza jeered at the prosecutor who pursued him, while critics argued his work traffics in provocation, racialized rhetoric, and dubious historical claims even as it finds renewed influence in the Trump era.

A 46-year-old British woman, identified as Kay Longstaff, was rescued after spending about 10 hours in the Adriatic Sea following a fall from the aft deck of the Norwegian Star. The incident occurred shortly before midnight as the ship sailed toward Venice, roughly 60 miles off Croatia’s coast. CCTV footage allowed rescuers to determine the time and approximate location of the fall, prompting a search involving the ship, Croatian coastguard vessels, civilian boats and a PC-9 aircraft. She was spotted by a rescue ship at about 09:40 the next morning, around 1.3 km from the fall site, and reached by a rescue swimmer minutes later.

Longstaff, who told Croatian media she practices yoga and sang to stay awake overnight, was exhausted but conscious when found. She was taken to a hospital in Pula for examination and was reported in good overall health, though stressed. Croatian officials and the Norwegian Cruise Line confirmed the rescue; the line said she was in stable condition and would reunite with family. Authorities, including the British embassy in Croatia, are investigating the circumstances. Warm summer sea temperatures may have aided her survival.

This AdAge piece reports that retailers have largely returned to using "Christmas" in holiday marketing, a shift the American Family Association (AFA) sees as a victory in its years-long campaign against generic "holiday" language. AFA director Randy Sharp says use of "Christmas" in ads has risen from 20% to 80% over five years, leaving only a few retailers on its "Companies Against Christmas" list; this season Dick's Sporting Goods was targeted for using "Holiday Shop." Retailers like Target, Walmart, Lowe’s and Gap have reverted to explicitly saying "Christmas" after past boycotts. Industry voices, including the National Retail Federation, note retailers are cautious not to alienate customers and now make strategic C-suite decisions on holiday phrasing. The article includes AFA’s categorized lists of retailers based on their use of "Christmas."

A series of massive multi-vehicle pileups on the Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-276) between Willow Grove and Bensalem closed the highway for most of the day after crashes began around 8:30 a.m. in icy, sun-glare conditions. One eastbound crash involved about 75 cars and several tractor-trailers; another near the Route 1 exit involved roughly 30 cars and a jackknifed tractor-trailer, with at least four vehicles pinned beneath it. Emergency crews ultimately reported about 30 people taken to local hospitals (other accounts cite 27), five classified as serious but none life-threatening. Hospitals treated soft-tissue and blunt-trauma injuries; one closed-head injury was improving. Tow operators collected dozens of vehicles—many totaled—including six tractor-trailers at a single yard. The Turnpike Commission moved a blocking tractor-trailer by midafternoon, allowed limited passage, and reopened the roadway about 7½ hours after the first crash. Investigators blamed slick, icy pavement compounded by sun glare and road spray; drivers said traffic had been moving normally until sudden brake lights and locked wheels triggered the chain reactions.

A rare Vietnamese case in which fraternal twins were found to have different fathers has prompted a wave of anxious calls to Hanoi’s Center for Genetic Analysis and Technologies (CGAT). Director Nguyen Thi Nga said she received many inquiries from fathers worried their twins, who look dissimilar, might not both be biologically theirs. The concern followed media reports that DNA testing at CGAT for a Hoa Binh Province family revealed the father tested was biological parent of only one of the twins while the mother was confirmed to be the parent of both. The phenomenon—heteropaternal superfecundation—occurs when two ova released in one cycle are fertilized by sperm from separate acts of intercourse with different men. Experts stress the occurrence is extremely rare: only about ten confirmed global cases have been reported. Medical authorities, including Vu Ba Quyet of the National Hospital of Obstetrics and Gynecology and former maternal-health official Luu Thi Hong, emphasized that fraternal twins naturally can look very different, like ordinary siblings, and appearance alone is not proof of different paternity. Hong explained that a woman can release two ova in a cycle and the second can be fertilized within the several days it takes the first conceptus to implant. Nga said she often advises families against immediate DNA testing when appearance causes doubt, warning that testing driven by suspicion can devastate family ties given the rarity of heteropaternal twins. The reported Vietnamese case—the first confirmed in the country—remains private to protect identities, but has heightened public attention and concern nationwide.

Hillary Clinton used her closing remarks at the Professional Business Women of California conference in San Francisco to call out everyday "indignities" faced by women, citing recent episodes involving a White House reporter and a Democratic congresswoman. She defended April Ryan after Sean Spicer patronized and cut her off in the press room and condemned Bill O’Reilly’s racially tinged jab at Rep. Maxine Waters’s hair, noting women — especially women of color — too often endure such treatment. Clinton urged Silicon Valley to improve diversity and inclusion through concrete policies like paid parental leave and equal pay, criticizing companies where bias and harassment persist while praising firms such as Salesforce and Gap for meaningful commitments. Referencing Uber’s sexual-harassment controversy, she argued corporate feminism must translate into substantive, systemic solutions rather than performative gestures.

Hawaii faces a contentious clash between conservationists and animal welfare advocates over the state’s large feral cat population and its deadly impact on endangered Hawaiian monk seals. Estimates put hundreds of thousands of free-roaming cats across the islands—about 300,000 on Oahu and 300,000–400,000 on Maui—creating extensive contamination of runoff and sewage with Toxoplasma gondii, a protozoan parasite shed in cat feces. NOAA links toxoplasmosis to at least eight confirmed monk seal deaths since 2001 and suspects additional fatalities, including Hoku, a prominent 10-year-old male who died after symptoms consistent with protozoal meningoencephalitis. With only roughly 1,100–1,300 seals remaining and the population declining by about 4.5% annually, each loss has outsized consequences for recovery goals that require boosting numbers to around 2,900 before downlisting protections.

Researchers warn toxoplasmosis, along with other pathogens like Sarcocystis neurona, Neospora caninum, and leptospirosis, threatens seals via contaminated coastal waters, prey, and in utero transmission. Runoff from urban areas, sewage spills, and improper disposal of cat litter allow resilient T. gondii oocysts to persist in seawater for years. Conservationists urge population control measures—including adoption and humane euthanasia—while animal welfare groups favor trap-neuter-return programs and oppose killing healthy cats. Scientists emphasize major data gaps—tracking infection sources, mapping contamination hotspots, and assessing chemical exposures—and advocate expanded monitoring, treatment capacity (including a proposed monk seal hospital), and public outreach to reduce disease transmission and foster coexistence between people, cats, and seals.

A surge in congenital syphilis has pushed infant cases in the United States to a 20-year high: 918 cases were recorded in 2017, up 46% from 628 in 2016 and more than double the 362 cases in 2013. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported that these infections contributed to 64 stillbirths and 13 infant deaths in 2017. Syphilis is easily cured with penicillin when detected, but failures in prenatal screening, gaps in access to care, and infections acquired after initial testing during pregnancy have driven the rise. Overall syphilis diagnoses also jumped sharply — 30,644 cases in 2017, a 76% increase — and total reported STDs (chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis) reached a record nearly 2.3 million cases, continuing a four-year climb. While gay and bisexual men still represent a large share of syphilis cases, rates among reproductive-age women rose 143% since 2013, increasing the risk to newborns. Cases were reported in 37 states, with the South and West hardest hit; Louisiana had the highest congenital syphilis rate. Contributing factors include reduced STD prevention funding, declining condom use, and the opioid epidemic, which links substance use, risky sex, and reduced prenatal care. Public health leaders call the trend a systemic failure and urge improved testing, timely treatment, targeted outreach, and more resources to prevent avoidable infant deaths.

Aday after NBC News reported that none of Flint’s corroded lead service lines have been removed, Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder acknowledged a “trust issue” with residents but said he has no immediate plans to replace the pipes. Pressed by NBC’s Stephanie Gosk about how trust can be regained while the lead-tainted lines remain in service, Snyder said pipe replacement is not a short-term priority. He emphasized the state’s focus on using phosphates to coat pipes and limit lead leaching and said third-party experts would assess the treatment’s effectiveness and help address public fears. Up to 25,000 lead service lines run between water mains and Flint homes; corrosion after the April 2014 switch to Flint River water caused dangerous lead contamination. The city now relies on bottled and filtered water for many uses.

Flint Mayor Karen Weaver has pushed a contrasting, urgent plan: a proposed $55 million “Fast Start” program to replace about 15,000 lead lines, prioritizing high-risk households (pregnant women, young children, seniors and those with elevated blood-lead levels). Weaver said the project—expected to begin within a month if funding and coordination with state and federal authorities come through—would replace entire service lines from main to meter at no cost to homeowners, install temporary kitchen filters, and deploy up to 32 crews to aim for completion in a year under optimal conditions. Retired Brig. Gen. Michael McDaniel, assisting planning, acknowledged data gaps and assumptions but said the project could move quickly. The crisis has prompted federal investigations, lawsuits, and proposals for major emergency funding; city leaders insist replacement is essential to restore residents’ confidence.

U.S. News & World Report evaluated 41 popular diets and ranked 20 in detail, consulting a panel of 22 experts in nutrition, diabetes and heart disease. Diets were scored across seven categories: short- and long-term weight loss, ease of following, nutritional completeness, and ability to prevent or manage diabetes and heart disease. DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) was named Best Diet Overall and Best Diabetes Diet, beating plans such as Atkins, Jenny Craig and Slim-Fast. The Mediterranean Diet ranked second overall. For weight loss, Weight Watchers placed first, followed by Jenny Craig and the Raw Food Diet. The Ornish Diet was judged best for heart health, with the TLC (Therapeutic Lifestyle Changes) diet second. U.S. News emphasized that no single diet is ideal for everyone and noted that while exercise is important for health, the primary focus of these rankings was dietary patterns. The report comes amid high U.S. overweight and obesity rates, with CDC data showing roughly one third of adults overweight and a similar share obese.

Researchers at Leiden University Medical Center tested whether acute fear from horror movies affects blood clotting, echoing the medieval notion that fear can “curdle” blood. In a crossover trial published in the British Medical Journal, 24 healthy volunteers aged 30 or younger watched the horror film Insidious and the documentary A Year in Champagne in alternating order, with sessions a week apart. Blood samples were taken within 15 minutes before and after each 90-minute viewing and analyzed for coagulation markers: factor VIII, D-dimer, thrombin-antithrombin complexes, and prothrombin fragments 1+2. Participants rated fear on a visual analogue scale; the horror movie scored significantly higher (mean difference 5.4/10).

After excluding three unreliable cases, results from 21 participants showed that watching the horror movie was associated with a mean increase in coagulant factor VIII of 11.1 IU/dL compared with the educational film. Factor VIII rose in 57% of participants during the horror movie but only 14% during the documentary; levels fell in 86% during the documentary versus 43% during the horror film. Other markers (D-dimer, thrombin-antithrombin complexes, prothrombin fragments) showed no significant change, indicating no downstream thrombin formation or fibrin generation. Authors suggest an adrenergic mechanism (epinephrine or related pathways) might raise factor VIII as an evolutionary preparation for bleeding after injury. They note limitations—small sample, non-randomized film order, and an unvalidated fear scale—but conclude that horror films can acutely increase factor VIII in young healthy adults without causing clot formation, playfully reaffirming the literal basis of the term “bloodcurdling.”

The Walt Disney Co. announced it would part ways with Pixar co-founder and longtime creative chief John Lasseter after months of scrutiny over his conduct, ending speculation about his return to leadership at Pixar and Walt Disney Animation. Disney CEO Bob Iger praised Lasseter’s creative influence and achievements but did not acknowledge the specific misconduct that prompted Lasseter’s sabbatical in November. Lasseter had admitted to vague “missteps” and acknowledged giving “hugs,” while others accused him of unsolicited kisses, groping and unwanted physical contact. Disney held a February “day of listening” to address workplace culture concerns after staff reported Lasseter had grown increasingly domineering.

The decision was complicated: supporters argued his return could stabilize Disney’s animation output and keep a celebrated creative leader from joining competitors. Opponents — including employees, advocacy groups and a #LoseLasseter campaign — warned his reinstatement would demoralize staff, especially women, and signal tolerance for misconduct. Pixar has long faced criticism as a boys’ club; only one of its 20 features has a credited female director, and past conflicts included director Brenda Chapman’s removal during Brave’s production after clashing with Lasseter.

Disney plans for Lasseter to serve as a consultant through year’s end while leadership shifts are expected: Frozen director Jennifer Lee is likely to be promoted and Pete Docter to assume greater responsibilities at Pixar. Lasseter said the sabbatical offered time for reflection and that he remains devoted to animation as he prepares for new creative challenges. Women in Animation and other groups welcomed the industry’s increasing intolerance for misconduct and emphasis on workplace safety.

U.S. stocks plunged intraday Wednesday but recovered off their lows as buyers stepped in around the S&P 500’s 1,800 technical level. After sharp early losses—S&P briefly below its October 2014 intraday low—late buying, led by small caps and biotech, halved declines; biotechs reversed a 3% drop to finish up 2.75%. The S&P closed down 1.17% near 1,859, the Dow fell about 250 points, and the Nasdaq ended at its lowest since October 2014. Trading was heavy—about 12.4 billion shares, the busiest session since August—with NYSE and Nasdaq recording their largest single-day counts of new 52-week lows since November 2008. Strategists noted violent short-covering rallies yet warned rebounds may not hold. Veteran investor Mark D. Cook argues the market is in a bear phase driven by oil weakness and China, outlining four psychological stages—denial, high anxiety, fear, and panic—and saying widespread capitulation, historically tied to 20–50% losses, signals ultimate bottoms.

Michael James "Mike" Rogan, 42, of Stratford, Wisconsin, died April 17, 2015, from injuries sustained in a highway collision while driving his pregnant wife and their seven children to the hospital for the birth of their eighth child. A deer struck their van after being thrown into their windshield by another vehicle; Rogan was pronounced dead at Ministry St. Joseph’s Hospital in Marshfield. His wife, Niki, and their children, ages 2 to 15, sustained only minor injuries. Niki gave birth hours later to a healthy son, Blaise, who was baptized days after the crash.

Born March 20, 1973, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, Mike was the son of Ronald and Susan (Rogan) Bornbach. He served honorably in the United States Marine Corps and remained involved with the reserves. He and Niki were married July 11, 1998, and she homeschools their children. For about eight years he owned and operated Arnie’s Farm Care, supplying organic seed and fertilizer and assisting organic farmers across Wisconsin after taking over his father-in-law’s business. A devoted Catholic, he was active at St. Mary’s Roman Catholic Oratory in Wausau, sang in the choir, participated in The Holy Name Society, and helped lead a boys’ group. He enjoyed brewing beer, hunting, and spending time outdoors with his children.

Survivors include his wife Niki; children Anne, Jon, Claire, Ben, Luke, Jacob, Gemma, and Blaise; parents Ron and Sue Bornbach; siblings Beth, Joseph, and Gabriel Bornbach; and mother-in-law Kathleen Richardson. He was predeceased by grandparents John and Sylvia Rogan and several aunts, uncles, and cousins. Funeral Mass was held April 25, 2015, at St. Mary’s Oratory, with burial and military rites at St. Mary’s Catholic Cemetery in Marathon. A memorial fund has been established to support his widow and children; friends and community members organized additional fundraising and donation efforts to cover vehicle, medical, and funeral expenses and to provide for the family’s future needs. Condolences and information were made available through the funeral home and online fundraising pages.

Former Subway spokesman Jared Fogle has filed court papers seeking to withdraw his guilty plea and overturn a “traveling for the purpose of engaging in illicit sex” charge, arguing unequal application of the law by comparing his prosecution to that of disgraced USA Gymnastics doctor Larry Nassar. In documents obtained by The Blast, Fogle contends Nassar, who also committed sexual crimes while traveling with a national team, was not charged under the same travel statute despite similarly unlawful conduct. Fogle says he, by contrast, traveled as a media spokesperson for Subway and was improperly charged, calling the discrepancy “diverging applications of the law.” He further alleges he was pressured into pleading guilty—accusing prosecutors of tweaking charges to coerce a plea and suggesting the risk of bankruptcy and the conduct of his costly defense team influenced his decision. Fogle also cites struggles with alcohol and sex addictions and claims medical treatment later reduced his “overactive libido.” Currently serving a 15-year sentence, he insists the courts have committed “grave error of the law.” The court has not yet ruled on his motion. Critics have derided the comparison to Nassar.

Justin Bieber reportedly upset fellow first-class passengers on an Air New Zealand flight returning from a promotional tour in Australia and New Zealand. According to sources, the 18-year-old singer and his entourage were loudly exchanging profanity in first class on the 12-hour flight, prompting a female passenger — described as a mother of two — to approach Bieber and ask him to stop using such language on the plane because it was inappropriate. Insiders say Bieber was embarrassed, apologized promptly, and even broke into an a cappella rendition of “Boyfriend,” although that last detail may be apocryphal. Separately, actors Kristen Bell and Dax Shepard complained about living near Bieber while promoting their film Hit & Run. Shepard joked that initial “Bieber fever” faded after the star moved in nearby, bringing loud music, parties and paparazzi. Bell added they’re not sure exactly where the noise originates but noted the music has been blaring since Bieber’s arrival.

A California couple walking their dog discovered a buried hoard of rare U.S. gold coins on their rural Northern California property last year; the find has been valued at about $11 million. The coins, minted between 1847 and 1894—most at the San Francisco Mint—were stored in eight cans beneath an old tree and are notable both for their age and their mint-condition state, suggesting they were stashed away shortly after minting. The cache includes four $5 gold pieces, fifty $10 pieces, and 1,373 $20 double eagles, highlighted by an 1866-S No Motto $20 piece appraised at over $1 million. Numismatist Don Kagin, who is marketing the coins, called the discovery the largest such U.S. find; past notable finds include a 1985 Tennessee hoard and silver dollars found in Reno in 1974. One 1874 $20 double eagle—typically worth about $4,250—sold for $15,000 at an auction at the Old San Francisco Mint, and many remaining coins were offered online via Amazon and Kagins.com. The couple wishes to remain anonymous to avoid treasure seekers; they plan to keep some coins, sell others to settle debts and donate to local charities. Proceeds from Tuesday’s auction will aid efforts to convert the Old Mint into a museum. Origins of the burial remain unknown, with various unproven theories circulating.

The United Nations Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 2371 in response to North Korea’s recent intercontinental ballistic missile tests, imposing what U.S. officials called the strongest sanctions in a generation. The measures, agreed 15-0, target major North Korean exports—coal, iron and iron ore, lead and lead ore, and seafood—and restrict other revenue channels including banking ties and foreign joint ventures. The resolution also bans countries from hiring additional North Korean workers, and places nine individuals and four entities, including a major North Korean bank, under asset freezes and travel bans. U.S. officials said the steps would cut more than a third of North Korea’s roughly $3 billion annual export revenue, citing a roughly $1 billion ban on key exports.

The vote reflected diplomatic work between Washington and Beijing, though China opposed tougher measures such as an oil cutoff. Chinese and Russian diplomats supported the resolution while also criticizing U.S. deployment of the THAAD missile defense system in South Korea. China emphasized that sanctions are not an end in themselves and urged a return to negotiations aimed at denuclearization and long-term peninsula stability.

Reactions from experts varied: some argued sanctions would not compel Pyongyang to abandon its nuclear program and that North Korea is prepared to endure hardship to retain weapons capability; others suggested the export and labor restrictions could hurt elites’ foreign-currency incomes and strain Kim Jong Un’s leadership. North Korea’s state media warned of severe retaliation if U.S. hostility continues. U.S. and regional diplomats plan further consultations, and the U.S. urged that future compliance and pressure, including potential additional Chinese steps, will determine next moves.

Researchers studying about 2,000 healthy Australians, including 1,011 cannabis users, report that genetic variants linked to schizophrenia also predict likelihood and heavier use of cannabis, suggesting part of the well-known association between cannabis and schizophrenia may reflect shared genetic predisposition rather than a purely causal effect of cannabis causing the disorder. The study, published in Molecular Psychiatry and led by Robert Power at King’s College London, found that people with higher genetic risk scores for schizophrenia were more prone to use cannabis and to consume greater amounts. Authors and commentators emphasize this does not disprove that cannabis can increase schizophrenia risk—especially in vulnerable individuals—but indicates the relationship is bidirectional and complex, involving many genes and environmental factors. Some experts caution replication is needed and point out conflicting prior results; others note cannabis worsens schizophrenia course and advise at-risk individuals to avoid it. The findings have implications for public-health messaging and policy debates about cannabis legalization, but researchers stress schizophrenia remains rare and the overall population-level impact of reducing cannabis use on schizophrenia incidence is likely modest.

The Senate narrowly approved Republican legislation allowing states to withhold federal Title X family‑planning funds from Planned Parenthood and other abortion providers, with Vice President Mike Pence casting the 51st tie‑breaking vote. The measure, passed after two GOP senators—Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski—joined Democrats in opposition, repeals an Obama‑era rule enacted in January that barred states from denying funds to providers based on factors other than their ability to provide family‑planning services. The House had already approved the resolution, and President Trump was expected to sign it.

Supporters framed the vote as restoring states’ rights to decide where Title X dollars go, enabling redirection of funds to community health centers or other providers that do not offer abortions. Opponents, chiefly Democrats and reproductive‑rights advocates, called the action an attack on women’s health that risks reducing access to contraception, cancer screenings and STD prevention for low‑income people; Title X served about 4 million clients in 2015 with a $286 million budget, many relying on it as their primary care source.

The outcome hinged on Republican Sen. Johnny Isakson, who returned to the Capitol briefly from spine surgery to vote, producing the 50‑50 split Pence broke. Critics noted the vote occurred amid broader GOP efforts to restrict funding for Planned Parenthood following the collapse of the House GOP health overhaul. Advocates warn more efforts to defund reproductive‑health providers may follow, including riders on spending bills. The use of the Congressional Review Act to overturn late‑term regulations was cited as the mechanism for this repeal.

A Danish study of more than 55,000 adults suggests that moderate chocolate consumption is associated with a lower risk of atrial fibrillation (AF), a common irregular heart rhythm that raises stroke and heart-failure risk. Participants, aged 50–64 when recruited between 1993 and 1997, reported their diets including chocolate intake; researchers linked this data to national health registries and followed them for an average of 13.5 years. About 3,346 AF cases occurred. Compared with people who ate chocolate less than once a month, those who consumed about one 1-ounce serving per week had a roughly 17 percent lower AF risk; 2–6 ounces weekly corresponded to about a 20 percent lower risk; and eating more than an ounce daily was associated with a 16 percent lower risk. Sex-specific patterns differed: women showed the largest reduction with one weekly serving, men with two to six weekly servings. Investigators note chocolate—especially dark varieties higher in cocoa—contains flavanols, compounds with anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and blood-vessel–relaxing effects that might protect heart health. But the study cannot prove causation and lacked data on chocolate type, flavanol content, and changes in diet over time. Unmeasured confounders (e.g., kidney disease, sleep apnea, differing activity levels) may influence results; higher chocolate consumers paradoxically had lower BMI, perhaps due to greater physical activity. Editorialists call the findings interesting but emphasize the need for randomized trials with quantified cocoa doses. Overall, moderate chocolate intake within a healthy lifestyle may be a reasonable snack option but is not a substitute for established heart-healthy behaviors.

In recent decades Brazil made remarkable progress cutting Amazon deforestation: annual loss fell from about 27,772 km2 in 2004 to roughly 4,575 km2 in 2012, and land-use carbon emissions dropped substantially. That progress reflected expanded protected and indigenous lands, stricter enforcement, supply-chain and credit interventions, fines and embargoes, and political commitment culminating in Brazil’s Paris climate pledge. But gains have been eroding since 2012: preliminary government satellite data show 7,900 km2 cleared between August 2017 and July 2018, the worst annual total since 2008 and a 13.7% rise year-on-year. Analysts link much of the rise to weakening enforcement, concessions to agribusiness, and an “amnesty” in the 2012 forest code.

The situation could worsen dramatically under president-elect Jair Bolsonaro, who campaigned on dismantling environmental protections: he has proposed shutting the environment ministry or merging it with agriculture, weakening enforcement and licensing, opening indigenous reserves to mining, banning international NGOs, and withdrawing from the Paris accord. Modeling by researchers predicts that removing protections could push annual primary-forest loss to about 25,600 km2—comparable to early-2000s levels and a 268% increase from 2017—with nearly one-fifth occurring inside protected areas. Between 2021–2030 this could emit ~13.12 GtCO2e, undermining Brazil’s Paris commitments and using a significant portion of the remaining carbon budget for 1.5°C.

Beyond carbon, escalating deforestation risks pushing the Amazon toward a climatic and ecological tipping point. Loss and fragmentation reduce the forest’s rainfall recycling, increasing drought susceptibility and fire, and shifting species composition toward drought-tolerant trees. Scientists warn that losing roughly 20–25% of original forest, a threshold the system is nearing, could trigger a rapid transition to savanna-like ecosystems with severe global consequences for biodiversity, regional water cycles, agriculture and climate feedbacks. The authors urge urgent political will and mobilization at all levels to conserve the Amazon and its ecosystem services.

Former President George W. Bush recently appeared on The Ellen DeGeneres Show, where a lighthearted moment about his struggle putting on a poncho at Donald Trump’s inauguration went viral. DeGeneres joked about the “poncho problem,” showing photos of Bush and his mother, Barbara, similarly challenged; Bush accepted an official presidential poncho with instructions and quipped “it’s genetics.” Bush is also promoting his art book Portraits of Courage, featuring paintings of veterans, and praised Michelle Obama, noting their friendly rapport at public events. He said he’d be open to collaborating with the Obamas on veteran and military causes. Separately, sources reported Bush privately described the inauguration as “some weird shit.”

Harold Lyle Hayes, a 21-year-old medic with the 807th Medical Air Evacuation Transport Squadron, survived a 63-day ordeal behind enemy lines after his C-53D transport crashed in Nazi-occupied Albania in November 1943. The plane, carrying 30 people—13 nurses, 13 medics, and a four-man flight crew—became lost in a violent storm over the Adriatic, lost communications and compass bearings, and was attacked by German fighters and antiaircraft fire before crash-landing inland. One crewman was injured; the rest scrambled into rugged, mountainous terrain they barely understood.

Albanian partisans first found and sheltered them, and Albanian villagers repeatedly risked their lives to hide and feed the Americans as they trekked more than 600 miles through brutal terrain, blizzards, and starvation while avoiding German patrols and navigating civil-war–era rivalries among partisan groups. The group endured lice, diarrhea, frostbite, and cultural shocks amid scarce food. They sometimes mistook rescue attempts for liberation and suffered setbacks when German forces overran towns where they sought refuge. British and OSS operatives organized covert rescue efforts; one attempted air extraction was aborted under fire. Ultimately, with British and American help, 27 Americans—10 nurses, 17 medics and fliers—reached the coast and were evacuated on Jan. 9, 1944; three nurses left behind were rescued later.

Upon returning to Allied lines they were ordered to keep their ordeal secret to protect their Albanian helpers and escape routes; revelations could have led to reprisals under Enver Hoxha’s later dictatorship, and at least one partisan contact was later executed. Hayes, who rarely spoke of the ordeal for decades, later recounted his experiences to author Cate Lineberry for her book The Secret Rescue. After the war he became an aeronautical engineer, married, and raised a family. By outliving his comrades, Hayes became the last living link to a dramatic, little-known chapter of wartime bravery and cross-cultural sacrifice.

Eastern Ghouta, a besieged rebel-held enclave near Damascus home to some 400,000 civilians, has been pummeled by a massive regime bombardment that aid groups warn could become the worst atrocity of Syria’s seven-year war. Over two days of “hysterical” airstrikes, barrel bombs, artillery and missile attacks, nearly 200 civilians were reported killed and dozens of medical facilities struck; local monitors say more than 700 people have died in the past three months. Amnesty called the campaign “flagrant war crimes,” while medics and rescue volunteers likened the onslaught to a modern massacre, describing children dug from rubble and hospitals rendered inoperative. The White Helmets reported the death of a volunteer; multiple hospitals and clinics—some repeatedly—were bombed, forcing at least two to suspend services. The UN and humanitarian agencies condemned the targeting of civilians and warned of catastrophic malnutrition and collapsing care under the long siege. Rebels retaliated with shelling on Damascus, killing civilians there, and reports indicated regime forces were preparing a ground assault. The escalation in Ghouta, coupled with shifting fronts elsewhere such as Afrin, underscores the intensifying brutality and the shrinking prospects for a negotiated political solution.

Researchers reported tiny tubes, filaments and squiggle-like structures in ancient rocks from Quebec’s Nuvvuagittuq belt that they interpret as the remains of iron-oxidizing bacteria living at least 3.77 billion years ago—potentially the oldest fossils yet found. The rocks, formed near hydrothermal vents, contain hematite-filled tubes and connected filament pairs, small carbon-rich patches with a biologically suggestive carbon isotope ratio (though not unambiguous), and magnetite-ringed blobs with mixed minerals consistent with reactions between organic matter and vent-derived iron. The morphology resembles modern vent microbes that build iron-oxide tubes, and the assemblage would fit a hydrothermal-vent habitat long proposed as a plausible cradle for life. If validated, the find—together with disputed 3.7-billion-year stromatolite claims from Greenland—would imply diverse microbial ecosystems in different ocean settings by ~3.7 billion years ago and strengthen the case for vents as targets in the search for extraterrestrial life.

However, many specialists remain skeptical. Critics label the structures “dubiofossils,” cautioning that metamorphism and nonbiological mineral processes can produce similar forms. Dating uncertainties for Nuvvuagittuq (minimum ~3.77 Ga, possibly up to ~4.28 Ga) and later high-temperature metamorphism complicate interpretations. Some researchers call the multiple lines of evidence compelling but stress further geological context, age constraints, and alternative abiotic explanations are needed before consensus can be reached.

Investigators arrested 72-year-old Joseph James DeAngelo Tuesday, accusing him of the decades-old reign of terror attributed to the East Area Rapist/Golden State Killer: some 12 homicides, at least 45 rapes and over 100 burglaries in California from the mid-1970s through 1986. The breakthrough came after cold-case detectives used open-source genealogical databases—most importantly GEDmatch—to compare crime-scene DNA to publicly uploaded consumer genetic profiles. Lead investigator Paul Holes and others traced distant matches (third- and fourth-cousins) and built more than 25 family trees—one containing roughly 1,000 people—which narrowed the hunt to DeAngelo. Investigators then confirmed identity through covert surveillance and two discarded items that produced DNA matching the crime-scene profiles, prompting the arrest in Citrus Heights.

The case highlights both the power and privacy concerns of genetic genealogy. Public sites like GEDmatch aggregate consumer DNA uploads from services such as Ancestry and 23andMe; while major firms generally require warrants for law enforcement access, GEDmatch’s volunteer-run, open database lacked such restrictions, enabling familial searches. Experts warn relatives who never tested can be identified when kin upload profiles, and legal protections remain fragmented. Prosecutors are coordinating multi-county charges; some rape prosecutions may be barred by statutes of limitations, while homicide charges in several counties remain possible, and decisions about venue and death-penalty exposure are under consideration. The arrest has prompted renewed attention to how genetic data is shared and used in criminal investigations.

Defense Secretary Ash Carter told the Senate Armed Services Committee that the $500 million program to train and equip “moderate” Syrian rebels had produced only about 60 vetted candidates so far, far short of the administration’s goal of roughly 5,400 fighters in year one. Republicans seized on the low figure as evidence the Obama administration’s approach to defeating ISIL is failing, while Democrats urged patience, noting stringent vetting and operational limits have constrained recruitment. Carter said roughly 7,000 volunteers are being screened but many are excluded by background checks, identity verification, age rules and a U.S. requirement that recruits fight ISIL only—not the Assad regime—which discourages Syrians more hostile to Assad. Senators including John McCain argued recruits need assurance of U.S. commitments such as air cover, resupply and protection from regime attacks, criticisms tied to internal administration debates over Assad’s role. Carter defended progress, citing coalition airstrikes and gradual improvements at training sites in Turkey, Jordan, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, but acknowledged the program and broader campaign remain in early stages and will take time to scale.

H.R. 667, a bill to rename NASA’s Dryden Flight Research Center for Neil A. Armstrong, was taken up by House Republicans at a time when many view Congress as shirking urgent business. Sponsored by Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy, the proposal provided a ceremonial, noncontroversial vehicle for floor time while Republicans pursue a strategy of inaction as automatic sequestration cuts loom. After months of alarm about sequestration, House GOP leaders have embraced allowing the cuts—a 2.5 percent reduction across federal programs—rather than agree to tax increases or another compromise like December’s deal. President Obama has campaigned for replacing the sequester with a mix of tax increases and spending changes, but Speaker John Boehner and others insisted the president already secured tax hikes and should now cut spending. The House’s sporadic schedule—many pro-forma days and planned recesses around the sequester deadline and an upcoming potential shutdown—left little time for substantive work. Floor remarks around the renaming chewed up time, drew criticism from Democrats pointing out impending cuts to NASA and other programs, and highlighted that congressional pay is spared while many federal programs and staff face reductions.

A 95-year-old New York City resident believed to have served as a guard at the Trawniki labor camp in Nazi-occupied Poland has been deported from the United States to Germany, U.S. officials said. The White House identified the man as Jakiw Palij, who allegedly served at Trawniki where roughly 6,000 Jewish men, women and children were massacred on Nov. 3, 1943, and where many other atrocities occurred. Palij, born in territory then part of Poland (now Ukraine), emigrated to the U.S. in 1949, became a citizen in 1957, but concealed his wartime activities, claiming he had worked on a farm and in a factory. U.S. authorities say he later admitted training at the Nazi SS camp in Trawniki and serving as an armed guard who prevented prisoner escapes. A federal court revoked his U.S. citizenship in 2003 and ordered deportation in 2004, but no country accepted him until Germany agreed after talks with Chancellor Angela Merkel’s government. Palij was moved to an elderly care home in Ahlen. German prosecutors have said prosecution may be difficult given his age, health and evidentiary gaps: under German law membership or training alone may not suffice; participation in or facilitation of murder must be shown. Germany’s Central Office for the Investigation of Nazi Crimes is monitoring the case but has not opened proceedings. The deportation follows long U.S. efforts to denaturalize and remove former Trawniki guards; U.S. authorities previously denaturalized 16 such individuals.

California regulators are poised to relax statewide drought rules and let local water agencies tailor conservation targets to their circumstances, a shift prompted by varied regional water conditions after recent storms. The State Water Resources Control Board is considering a proposal that would allow cities and water districts to compare projected supplies against anticipated demand over a potential three-year drought and set conservation goals based on that gap. The regulation, if adopted, would run through January. Supporters like Southern California landscaper Greg Gritters and Irvine Ranch Water District’s Fiona Sanchez argue local officials better understand regional supply realities and can set appropriate measures; some areas could keep strict limits while others might lift mandates. The move follows near‑average rain and snow in Northern California this winter that helped refill key reservoirs, even as Southern California remains deeply dry. Certain restrictions — such as bans on washing sidewalks with a hose and washing cars without a shut‑off nozzle — would become permanent. State water board climate scientist Max Gomberg emphasized that Californians recognize the drought’s seriousness and don’t expect a return to wasteful habits, expressing confidence that conservation behaviors will persist. The proposal aims to balance locally appropriate management with continued vigilance amid an uncertain water future.

A Tennessee musician and a Tennessee diver each set endurance firsts in separate August 2013 feats. Ben Friberg, 35, a Chattanooga guitarist and band leader, became the first person believed to paddleboard the full Florida Straits, traveling about 110–111 miles from Cuba to Key West in roughly 28 hours. Accompanied by a support boat with his father, a medic and a navigator, Friberg stood on a 14-foot board most of the trip, pausing only briefly to eat. He arrived dehydrated and exhausted but in good condition, dressed for sun protection and wearing special socks. Friberg said his crossing promoted peace between Cuba and the U.S. and healthy living; he previously set a 24-hour paddleboard distance record on Canada’s Yukon River. In Tennessee, 49-year-old Jerry Hall set a believed freshwater diving record by remaining submerged in South Holston Lake for six days, one hour and 42 minutes. Monitored constantly with medical staff nearby and surviving on liquids, Hall lost substantial weight, emerged weak but emotional, and said he would retire from further attempts; his time will be submitted to Guinness for certification.

Massachusetts Republicans were left scrambling after several prominent GOP figures declined to run in the special election to fill John Kerry’s Senate seat, leaving the party with only obscure potential contenders. The reluctance of major local Republicans to step forward frustrated state Sen. Robert Hedlund, who likened the situation to a comic scene of volunteers stepping back from a dangerous mission. Among those who said no was Tagg Romney, Mitt Romney’s eldest son, who had been reported as considering a bid after former Sen. Scott Brown decided not to run. Tagg Romney, a private equity founder who campaigned visibly for his father during the presidential race, told the Daily News he declined the invitation due to business and family commitments, and reiterated that the timing was not right for a Senate run. He expressed hope that Massachusetts would elect a senator of integrity, vision and compassion. Meanwhile, William “Mo” Cowan, a former aide to Gov. Deval Patrick, is serving as the interim senator until a special election in June determines Kerry’s long-term replacement.

In April 2012, Anthony Hensley, 37, a father of two from Villa Park who frequently tended mute swans at the Bay Colony condominium complex near Golf Road in unincorporated Maine Township, drowned after being attacked by an aggressive swan. Hensley, who often brought a kayak to feed and care for the birds—kept at the pond to deter geese—was reportedly knocked from his kayak during a swan attack, struggled to swim while the nesting swan continued lunging, and never reached shore. Dive teams recovered him from the roughly 50-foot-deep retention pond; he was pronounced dead at Advocate Lutheran General Hospital. His death was ruled an accident, and OSHA investigated but found no violations related to Knox Swan and Dog, the company that places swans to control geese; OSHA closed the case, noting its jurisdiction requires an employee-employer relationship and the property managers were not part of that probe.

On Tuesday, Hensley’s widow, Amy Hensley, filed a wrongful death lawsuit in Cook County Circuit Court against Bay Colony Properties, Hillcrest Property Management Inc., and the condominium and homeowners associations, seeking at least $50,000 in damages. The complaint alleges negligence, arguing the defendants “should have known the swans are strongly territorial with a dangerous propensity to attack” and thus were liable for “knowingly keeping dangerous animals on the premises.” The lawsuit also asserts Hensley did nothing to provoke the swans. Representatives for the named property management firms did not comment or could not be reached; Knox Swan and Dog is not a defendant.

The story has drawn attention in the community, which lost a regular caretaker of the swans, and highlights tensions around using swans and other wildlife-control methods to deter geese—an approach promoted in various guides that recommend decoys, landscape changes, noise deterrents, repellents, or trained herding dogs to manage goose populations.

DeKalb County firefighter Robert Sutton is being hailed a hero after catching an infant tossed from a second-floor window of a burning apartment building on Glenwood Road in Decatur, Georgia. The baby’s desperate father, trapped by smoke and flames, handed the child out the window; Sutton, among the first on scene, called “Drop him” and caught the infant safely. Contractors renovating the neighboring building filmed the dramatic rescue. Sutton, a 10-year veteran and father of two, deflected praise, crediting training, teamwork and situational awareness. Captain Tom Burrell and other officials emphasized the firefighters’ skill and humility; the family escaped without injuries and the footage circulated widely.

U.S. researchers led by Thomas Kodadek at Scripps Research report a promising new method to detect Alzheimer’s disease by screening blood for disease-specific antibodies. Instead of seeking elusive native antigens, the team used thousands of synthetic peptoid molecules to “lure” antibodies; three peptoids captured markedly higher IgG levels in six Alzheimer’s patients versus healthy and Parkinson’s controls. Additional testing, including mild cognitive impairment samples and 200 elderly non-demented subjects, showed the signal held up and 8% of the latter had elevated antibody levels, suggesting potential early prediction. Kodadek has licensed the approach to OPKO Health to develop diagnostic kits within months. Findings are preliminary, need larger replication, and clinical value depends on future effective treatments.

China’s decision to tightly control nominations for Hong Kong’s 2017 chief executive election sparked vows of civil disobedience and intensified long-running tensions over political reform. On August 31, the National People’s Congress Standing Committee endorsed a framework allowing only two or three vetted candidates—each requiring majority backing from a nominating committee likely dominated by Beijing loyalists—effectively blocking many pro-democracy contenders. The move drew condemnation from activists who called it a denial of genuine universal suffrage and a distortion of the “one country, two systems” principle. Occupy Central leaders, including Benny Tai, Chan Kin-man and Reverend Chu Yiu-ming, formally launched a campaign to paralyze Hong Kong’s Central financial district through peaceful, non-violent occupation, saying dialogue had been exhausted. Hundreds gathered despite rain; police and barricades were deployed around government offices and the PLA barracks. Hong Kong Chief Executive Leung Chun-ying welcomed Beijing’s decision as a historic step forward and urged peaceful expression of views. The U.S. reacted cautiously, urging respect for freedoms of assembly and expression and noting that the chief executive’s legitimacy would be enhanced by genuine voter choice. The NPC framework still requires approval by Hong Kong’s legislature, where democrats could block it; failure would likely return the selection to a pro-Beijing election committee. Meanwhile in Macau, Fernando Chui Sai-on was re-elected unopposed by a 400-member largely pro-Beijing committee amid protests calling for universal suffrage. An unofficial referendum showed strong public support for reform, and activists warned that continued government insincerity would fuel greater political activism. Both cities face growing pressure to reconcile demands for democratic reform with Beijing’s control.

Mass killings were reported after a five-day assault by Syrian government forces and allied militias on the Damascus suburb of Daraya. Opposition activists, watchdogs and video footage showed bloodied bodies in streets, basements, a mosque and a cemetery, with activists saying hundreds — estimates ranged from about 320 to more than 330 — were found dead, many apparently executed, including women and children. The government blamed “terrorists”; opposition blamed troops and shabiha. Independent verification was limited after U.N. monitors left. The UN secretary-general demanded an independent inquiry, and Western governments condemned the reports as a massacre. Fighting continued elsewhere in Damascus, rebels claimed to have downed a helicopter, and calls mounted for humanitarian measures including possible buffer zones to protect civilians.

Belgium has reformed royal finances, ending longstanding exemptions and making most royals taxable for the first time since 1830. The government will limit state allowances to the monarch, the heir and spouse, and the widow/widower of a deceased monarch; an abdicated monarch would also receive support. Other family members will see reduced or eliminated stipends: Crown Prince Philippe’s pay will drop from about €923,000 to a gross €180,000 subject to tax, while siblings Astrid and Laurent will get €90,000. Queen Fabiola’s allowance was sharply cut to roughly €450,000. Tax and VAT exemptions are removed and future siblings of heirs won’t get state support.

A Chicago kayaker fishing near Waukegan Harbor discovered a surprising passenger in Lake Michigan: a roughly 4-foot American alligator with its mouth taped shut. David Castaneda, who had been paddling about four hours, initially thought the floating object was a dead salmon but realized it was an alligator and called 911. Waukegan Animal Control retrieved the animal and transported it to the Lake Forest Wildlife Discovery Center, where curator Rob Carmichael and a veterinarian will assess its condition. Carmichael noted the alligator appeared thin and in poor shape; with lake temperatures falling, its survival beyond a few weeks was uncertain. The city originally described the animal as a caiman but was later informed it was an American alligator. Officials said they will investigate potential abandonment, a criminal offense. Carmichael observed that stricter state permitting has reduced exotic-animal dumping in recent years, though past incidents—like a 2012 Burmese python and a 2010 river alligator—have occurred in the area.

Nigerian authorities reported the liberation of Serah Luka on Thursday, saying she was among 97 women and children freed from Boko Haram in operations in Borno state that also killed 35 militants. The military claimed Luka was one of the schoolgirls taken in the April 2014 Chibok abduction; campaigners and local sources disputed that, saying she had attended the Chibok school briefly but was kidnapped from her home in Madagali, Adamawa. Luka is receiving medical care. Her reported release came two days after Amina Ali Darsha Nkeki — long identified as one of the Chibok girls — was found by a civilian vigilante group on the edge of Sambisa Forest.
