Nkeki, who had a four-month-old baby born in captivity, met President Muhammadu Buhari in Abuja; the president pledged medical, psychological and educational support and vowed to continue searching for the more than 200 remaining Chibok girls. Nkeki reportedly said most of the girls remained in the forest and that six had been killed. Officials said she had been with a man claiming to be her husband, who is suspected to be a Boko Haram fighter and is detained. Critics accused the military of politicizing rescues and mishandling survivors, while the army defended its actions and highlighted broader gains against Boko Haram, noting thousands rescued in recent months even as the fate of many abducted women and girls remains unresolved.

In October 2009, 28-year-old Crissita Cage-Toaster vanished after her car was found abandoned on Detroit’s Belle Isle with her purse, ID and cellphone inside. Her parents, Rosita and Johnny, reported her missing and repeatedly checked with Detroit police for years, emphasizing her distinctive right-shoulder tattoo of a large red rose bearing her parents’ nicknames. Five months after she disappeared, a body was recovered from the Detroit River on March 30, 2010. That body was processed as an unidentified Jane Doe (10-3047), briefly held by the Wayne County Medical Examiner’s Office and ultimately buried in an unmarked grave at Knollwood Cemetery in Canton Township in March 2011. The family learned only this year — after contacting the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System and pressing for attention to the tattoo — that the body had been found and buried years earlier; the tattoo is said to have helped make the match. The parents accuse Detroit police and the medical examiner of negligence and incompetence: the remains were recorded as Caucasian or Hispanic despite Crissita being black, no full autopsy or definitive cause of death was determined (listed as undetermined or drowning), and personal effects reported from her car are now missing or reportedly discarded. Officials say the body’s river exposure affected appearance and that standard identification protocols — fingerprints, dental, DNA, NAMUS entry — were followed; Wayne County will exhume the remains so the family can arrange a proper burial and memorial. The case underscores concerns about thousands of unidentified remains nationwide and procedural lapses that can prolong families’ suffering.

Survivors of one of Australia’s deadliest wildfires have secured nearly A$500 million in the country’s largest class action settlement. The settlement resolves claims arising from the Kilmore East blaze on Black Saturday, February 7, 2009, one of a series of fires across Victoria that killed 173 people in total; the Kilmore East fire alone claimed 119 lives and destroyed more than 1,000 homes. More than 5,000 (reported in some accounts up to about 10,000) plaintiffs sued electricity provider SP AusNet, its contractor Utility Services Corporation Ltd., and the Victorian government, alleging negligent maintenance of power lines that sparked the blaze. A 2009 Royal Commission concluded the fire began when a live conductor contacted a cable stay, producing arcing that ignited vegetation. On Tuesday the defendants agreed to pay about A$494.7–497.4 million, with SP AusNet to contribute roughly A$378.6 million; the settlement still requires final court approval and distribution is expected to take 12–18 months. Plaintiffs’ lawyer Andrew Watson described the payout as a measure of justice and necessary compensation, while lead plaintiff Carol Matthews spoke of enduring pain and a sense of justice. SP AusNet agreed to the settlement without admitting liability, saying the conductor had been damaged by lightning in a way that compromised fail-safety systems.

Bristol Palin and husband Dakota Meyer announced they are expecting a baby in spring, marking Palin’s third child. The couple, who married in June after a rocky period that included a custody dispute and a reconciliation, welcomed daughter Sailor Grace last December. Palin, 26, also shares seven-year-old son Tripp with ex-fiancé Levi Johnston. They told Entertainment Tonight they feel blessed, thankful for “God’s grace and new beginnings,” and eagerly await their expanding family.

A Fresno man released from jail after a jury mistakenly entered a not-guilty verdict was stabbed to death hours later in an apparent confrontation with his sister’s boyfriend, authorities say. Bobby Lee Pearson, 37, had been one of three defendants in a burglary case but was freed after jurors signed a not-guilty form Wednesday; afterward it emerged the panel had actually been deadlocked, with eight jurors believing Pearson was guilty. Judge W. Kent Hamlin had previously instructed jurors that if they could not reach unanimity they should notify the court rather than sign verdict forms, but confusion over the forms and what to do apparently led to the erroneous acquittal. Prosecutors later could not retry Pearson without risking double jeopardy. Pearson was released just before midnight and returned home to collect belongings. Around 1 a.m., police found him lying in the road with two wounds—one consistent with a stab and another possibly a gunshot; witnesses reported a loud pop. Police say the fight was with Willie Gray, the longtime personal rival and boyfriend of Pearson’s sister; Gray was arrested about a mile from the scene after officers served a search warrant and recovered a gun and a minivan believed to be a getaway vehicle. Gray, a landscaper at the Big Fresno Fair who former coworkers described as hardworking, was injured and is being treated at Community Regional Medical Center; he will face murder charges when booked. An autopsy is scheduled and the investigation remains ongoing. Legal analysts note Gray may claim self-defense, but leaving the scene could be used as evidence of consciousness of guilt.

The article explains how the polar vortex’s current strength could produce a mild start to winter but an unstable, colder finish, while also covering broader seasonal forecasting and energy-cost implications. Andrea Lang, an atmospheric scientist at the University at Albany, says the polar vortex—high-altitude, fast-spinning winds around the North Pole that normally contain Arctic air—is stronger than average now and likely to keep cold air locked up through early December. However, weakened and irregular vortices driven partly by Arctic sea-ice retreat have in recent years allowed bitter outbreaks to plunge south. Lang warns that a strong vortex early in winter has a higher chance of becoming unstable later (December–February), potentially breaking into a misshapen pattern that sends late blasts of cold and snow to southern regions. That scenario aligns with long-range forecasts pointing to a warmer winter overall from a strong El Niño, yet leaves room for late-season volatility.

The piece also highlights practical impacts: consumers should face lower heating bills thanks to record-high inventories and low prices for propane, heating oil, and natural gas. New York State projections show notably reduced average bills versus 2013–14, and propane supplies have surged due to increased natural gas production from shale. Separately, seasonal forecaster Judah Cohen, known for using Siberian October snow cover to predict East Coast winters, is confident in forecasting above-normal precipitation and potential for heavy snowfall this season, underscoring the mix of predictable trends and lingering uncertainty in winter weather.

A rare and deadly chain-reaction crash in Florida’s Everglades left three people dead and eight injured after an SUV struck and killed a black bear. The initial collision occurred Sunday night on Snake Road (near mile marker 49 on Alligator Alley) on the Big Cypress Seminole Reservation when a woman driving a Cadillac SUV—possibly an Escalade—hit a roughly 300-pound Florida black bear and became stranded. A second vehicle stopped to assist the SUV’s occupants. As those Good Samaritans exited their car, a third vehicle, reported to be a Mercedes, plowed into the stopped helper vehicle and then struck the three people who had come to help. All three Good Samaritans were killed. In total, 13 people were involved across the three vehicles: eight were injured and two others walked away uninjured, including the SUV driver who reportedly escaped without scratches despite heavy damage to her vehicle. Six injured patients were taken to Broward Health Medical Center and two to Memorial Regional Hospital in Hollywood. Seminole Police spokesman Gary Bitner noted he had never heard of a bear being involved in a traffic accident there, though Florida panthers have been. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Commission confirmed black bears inhabit the Everglades. Authorities have not yet released the victims’ identities.

A series of recent incidents highlights aggressive municipal code enforcement tactics that punish poor and vulnerable residents for minor property violations, often without prior tickets or reasonable procedures. In Cahokia, Illinois, single mother Ebony Conner — who cares for five children — was arrested and briefly jailed for failing to mow her lawn. She was not issued a ticket beforehand; the only explanation given was a vague complaint from the village. Conner’s case echoes other troubling examples: a 70-year-old in Prichard, Alabama, arrested over a property citation for a house she no longer owned, and a 75-year-old in Riesel, Texas, who faced a warrant after being accused of ignoring a court letter about lawn maintenance.

Pagedale, Missouri, is emblematic of a systemic problem. There, municipal revenue has become heavily dependent on fines and fees — nearly 20 percent of the city’s revenue in 2013 — creating profit incentives to issue numerous non-traffic citations. From 2010–2014 non-traffic ticketing rose by 495 percent. Residents describe endless cycles of fines: they lack resources to make mandated repairs, accrue fines they cannot pay, miss court because of work or childcare, and then face arrest warrants and further penalties. The Institute for Justice has filed a class-action lawsuit on behalf of Pagedale residents seeking to end what they call unconstitutional and exploitative practices.

Named plaintiffs illustrate the harm: Vincent Blount owes roughly $2,800 and was threatened with home demolition; his partner Valarie Whitner received vague “house not up to code” tickets and even had Vincent jailed. Elderly resident Mildred Bryant, 84, faces demands she cannot physically or financially meet, including repainting and matching curtains, and risks fines and imprisonment. These cases underscore how punitive enforcement of trivial codes can trap people in debt, threaten housing stability, and criminalize poverty. Separately, media commentary noted Rudy Giuliani’s public campaign undermining the Mueller investigation, describing his role as PR-driven propaganda rather than legal strategy.

The U.S. Air Force Academy disclosed that racial slurs found posted outside the dorm rooms of five black students were written by one of those students, a revelation that reversed initial reactions to the incident. The academy said the cadet candidate admitted responsibility and the finding was validated by an investigation. The individual, whose name was not released, is no longer at the school; officials would not say whether the student withdrew or was expelled, citing privacy laws. The graffiti was discovered in September in a dormitory that houses students in the academy’s prep school, a separate program on the academy grounds that helps prospective cadets meet entrance requirements. The episode prompted Academy Superintendent Lt. Gen. Jay Silveria to deliver a widely viewed and stern speech condemning racism and demanding respect, telling cadets, "If you can't treat someone with dignity and respect, get out." Silveria had cadets record his remarks to ensure the message was heard. He framed the incident against a broader national backdrop that included racial unrest in Charlottesville and protests by NFL players. Silveria, a 1985 academy graduate and veteran fighter pilot who took command in August, has emphasized fostering a climate of dignity and respect. The academy, near Colorado Springs, enrolls about 4,000 students; the prep school typically accepts roughly 240 students.

A 3-year-old girl, Mariah Woods, has been missing since her mother, Kristy Woods, put her to bed Sunday night in their Jacksonville, North Carolina home. Kristy discovered Mariah missing the next morning and called authorities at about 6:45 a.m. The Onslow County Sheriff’s Office, FBI and multiple other agencies launched ground and air searches, issued an AMBER Alert and have been following tips and leads. Mariah is described as about 2 feet 9 inches tall, 30 pounds, with brown hair and blue eyes; she wears leg braces to help her walk. Investigators released surveillance images from a Walmart showing a woman and child Monday morning and are asking the public’s help to identify them and anyone who had contact with the family since Sunday. Authorities have searched the woods behind the home, used K-9 units, drones and helicopters, interviewed Kristy’s mother and her live-in boyfriend, and searched the residence and vehicle. Sheriff Hans Miller emphasized they are using every available resource, expanding search areas and exploring all leads. Mariah’s biological father expressed skepticism about how she could have been taken without anyone hearing. Kristy Woods made an emotional public plea for her daughter’s safe return. Anyone with information is asked to call the Onslow County Sheriff’s Office at 910-989-4070.

Dennis Lee Thian Poh, a 47-year-old Kuala Lumpur businessman and avid trekker, has been missing since April 5 after separating from his group while trekking in Nepal’s Annapurna region. He was last seen between Ghorepani and Ghundrung as the group descended from Khopra Danda toward Bayeli. Lee, who arrived in Kathmandu on March 28 for a hiking trip with eight friends, failed to reach the Bayeli campsite; porters also reported not seeing him. A search began April 7 and his wife, Jennifer (Eileen Peters), flew to Nepal to help coordinate efforts. The family hopes he will be found in time to celebrate their second wedding anniversary.

Rescue efforts, led by SAR Dogs Nepal alongside local police, villagers and Sherpas, have intensified across terrain between Khopra and Bayeli and Dobasto and Tadatani. Teams face thick fog, snow, hail and dangerous, narrow trails above 11,800 feet, hampering visibility and helicopter support. SAR Dogs Nepal is using scent from Lee’s belongings and has identified several potential locations, but steep ravines and poor weather make rappelling necessary; army rappel teams were expected. Family and friends urge experienced volunteers to join and have set up a Find Dennis Facebook page; contact details for tips were provided. Lee carried basic supplies and is fit; rescuers say survival is possible but time and conditions are against them. His wife continues to plead for help and support.

A senior Iranian lawmaker, Hossein Naqvi Hosseini, said Tehran currently does not need more 20 percent-enriched uranium because fuel for the Tehran reactor has been supplied, and Tehran is prepared to convert its 20 percent stockpile into fuel rods to allay concerns about non-peaceful use. His remarks, reported by ICANA, were not an official government statement nor detailed a formal halt to enrichment. The issue is central to talks between Iran and six world powers (U.S., Russia, China, Britain, France, Germany) in Geneva, where the West seeks to stop Iran from producing uranium at the 20 percent level — a threshold that makes further enrichment to weapons-grade significantly easier. Iran has thousands of centrifuges and hundreds of kilograms of higher-enriched uranium; experts say roughly 250 kilograms of 20 percent material could yield one warhead. Negotiations resumed in early November amid signals of progress but also domestic Iranian hardliner resistance and Israeli distrust. Independent analysts warn “breakout” times to weapons-grade have shortened as Iran’s centrifuge and stockpile growth continue, keeping stakes high for any durable, verifiable deal.

Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds are reportedly growing closer, with sources saying their off-screen romance is becoming “more serious.” Though they haven’t confirmed a relationship, insiders say Lively has visited Reynolds twice on film sets—most recently traveling from New York to Boston, where Reynolds is shooting R.I.P.D. After Reynolds allegedly visited Lively on the Gossip Girl set in early October, Lively spent a night at his Back Bay apartment and they were seen dining romantically at Mistral Bistro. Reports note Lively picked up the check and did shopping that could have included gifts for Reynolds. Lively also spent about $5,000 at Chanel’s SoHo boutique. Neither Lively’s spokeswoman nor the actors have publicly commented.

ProPublica reports that the SEC has sued Goldman Sachs for fraud, alleging the bank failed to disclose that a hedge fund helped design and was betting against a collateralized debt obligation (CDO) it sold to investors. Goldman denies the allegations. ProPublica’s reporting shows this pattern was not unique: several major banks—including JPMorgan Chase, Merrill Lynch (now part of Bank of America), Citigroup, Deutsche Bank and UBS—created at least 30 CDOs involving hedge fund Magnetar, totaling roughly $40 billion, with Magnetar both advising on asset selection and taking positions betting the CDOs would fail. Prospectuses and marketing materials for these deals did not reveal Magnetar’s role or contrary interests. The SEC did not sue hedge fund Paulson & Co. in the Abacus matter, instead pursuing Goldman; Magnetar has denied wrongdoing and banks contacted declined to comment. WARC files for the crawl are not publicly available.

At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Alibaba founder Jack Ma argued that globalization has benefited the United States enormously but that the country squandered those gains by failing to distribute wealth broadly. Ma said multinational companies such as IBM, Cisco and Microsoft “made millions and millions” from globalization, yet much of the money was not reinvested domestically. He highlighted that over the past 30 years the U.S. spent about $14.2 trillion on wars instead of on infrastructure or supporting white- and blue-collar workers, fueling domestic economic anxiety. Ma rejected the notion that other countries “steal” U.S. jobs, framing the problem as America’s strategy and distribution choices, and defended outsourcing as a valid outcome of global integration. He urged a more inclusive form of globalization whose benefits reach small businesses and broader segments of society.

Ma also urged patience in judging President-elect Donald Trump’s approach to China, saying Trump is “open minded” and that their recent New York meeting went better than expected; they discussed how Alibaba could help small U.S. firms sell into China and Asia, potentially creating jobs. He warned that a Sino-U.S. trade war would be disastrous and difficult to end. Separately, Ma announced a 12-year Olympic partnership for Alibaba to supply technology, e-commerce and media services, while pledging to intensify efforts against counterfeits on its platforms.

In March 2017 WikiLeaks published “Vault 7,” a massive trove it said came from the CIA’s Center for Cyber Intelligence, releasing 8,761 documents that describe an extensive arsenal of malware, exploit code and operational practices allegedly developed between 2013 and 2016. The files, which WikiLeaks claims were provided by a current or former U.S. government contractor, portray a wide-ranging program to turn everyday devices—smartphones, computers, routers, and even Internet-connected televisions—into surveillance tools and to develop large numbers of “zero-day” exploits that bypass device security. WikiLeaks framed the release as a provocation to public debate about whether the CIA’s hacking capabilities exceed its mandate and how cyberweapons should be governed, arguing that hoarding such vulnerabilities endangers the public because cyberweapons can proliferate once leaked.

The documents detail numerous named projects and toolkits: “Weeping Angel,” which purportedly can put some Samsung smart TVs into a “Fake-Off” mode that records audio while appearing off; mobile-device malware targeting iOS and Android to exfiltrate geolocation, audio, messages and photos; multi-platform suites like HIVE that provide implants and command-and-control infrastructure; and desktop and removable-media tools for Windows, macOS and Linux. The materials show the CIA organized its development into branches and codified operational procedures—Fine Dining questionnaires to tailor attacks, and Improvise for configuring payloads—indicating a sophisticated, production-level hacking capability. WikiLeaks also alleges the CIA used the U.S. consulate in Frankfurt as a covert regional hacking base.

Security experts reacted with alarm but also nuance. Many agreed the documents appear largely authentic and consequential: they expose techniques, code snippets and operational fingerprints that could both enable defenders (antivirus vendors and forensic teams) to detect intrusions and enable adversaries to replicate or find malfunctions in implants. At the same time, experts emphasized that the leaks do not demonstrate that the CIA “broke” modern end-to-end encryption in messaging apps; rather, the agency’s approach was to “hack the endpoint”—compromise devices before or after encryption is applied—making strong crypto irrelevant for targeted victims whose devices are infected. Open Whisper Systems (Signal) and others noted no evidence the cryptographic protocols themselves were broken.

Debate followed on policy and risk. Privacy advocates argued the CIA’s decision to retain rather than disclose pervasive vulnerabilities undermines general cybersecurity, leaving billions exposed; critics noted many referenced vulnerabilities had been patched. Some observers raised alternative sourcing possibilities, suggesting a foreign state—Russia was often mentioned—could have stolen the archive and handed it to WikiLeaks. U.S. intelligence has declined to comment on the files’ authenticity, while investigators sought to determine how a classified development system was compromised.

The release reignited tensions between intelligence secrecy and public safety, highlighting how the creation and stockpiling of cyberweapons can create proliferation and oversight problems. It prompted scrutiny of the CIA’s internal practices, concerns in Silicon Valley, and an intensified discussion about how democratic societies should manage offensive cyber capabilities and the vulnerabilities those capabilities exploit.

The Obama administration says HealthCare.gov is functioning well as the second open-enrollment period begins, a dramatic improvement from last year’s launch problems. HHS Secretary Sylvia Burwell told NBC’s Meet the Press that about 100,000 people submitted new applications over the weekend and roughly 500,000 returning customers were able to log in; call centers handled about 100,000 calls. Around 1 million users “window shopped” plans in the prior week. Burwell expects growth of roughly 2 million enrollments on top of the existing 7 million, while the CBO projects about 13 million for 2015. Though premiums appear stable on average, state-level variation persists, and Washington state reported inaccurate subsidy calculations. The administration is keen to avoid another meltdown under a Republican-controlled Congress.

Mark Herzlich’s presence at Super Bowl XLVI with the New York Giants is a powerful story of survival and perseverance. Diagnosed in 2009 with Ewing’s sarcoma—a rare bone cancer isolated to his left leg—Herzlich faced dire possibilities, including amputation or losing his ability to play. He endured aggressive chemotherapy and radiation, ultimately choosing treatment that preserved his leg and his football dream, though with some risk of recurrence. After missing the 2009 season, he returned to start all 13 games for Boston College in 2010, went undrafted, but kept training and signed with the Giants as a free agent. Two years after being told he might never walk again, he stepped off the plane in Indianapolis and tweeted his gratitude and defiance toward cancer. Herzlich says family was his biggest motivator and football his next, using highlight tapes to get through chemo. His journey has inspired fans—even some Patriots supporters—to root for his recovery and success as he prepares to play on football’s biggest stage.

Prosecutors in Olmsted County have charged 34-year-old Long Vang with third-degree murder, second-degree manslaughter and stalking in connection with the December 16, 2015, suicide of his partner and mother of his children, 28-year-old Jessica Haban. Authorities are not alleging Vang provided a weapon or drugs that directly caused her death; rather, they say a decade of relentless physical and emotional abuse left Haban bereft of hope and led her to take her own life. County Attorney Mark Ostrem said Vang knew of Haban’s fragile emotional state after repeated hospitalizations and continued harassing contact until her death. The charges—an unusual prosecutorial approach in Minnesota—seek to hold an abuser criminally responsible for another person’s suicide, a step Ostrem and others acknowledge is rare and legally challenging.

Court filings recount sustained violence: being knocked unconscious, hair-pulling, being thrown against walls, bruising, a knife held to her throat, and a 2015 punch causing traumatic brain injury. Vang allegedly continued contact despite court orders to stay away and pressured Haban to leave inpatient mental-health treatment, threatening institutionalization and loss of custody; she was discharged on Dec. 13 and died three days later. Advocates note that domestic violence raises suicide risk—researchers found 6–14% of Minnesota women’s suicides from 2009–2011 had documented domestic-violence records—and call for deeper study.

The case has divided legal opinion: some applaud the novel attempt to address coercive control’s lethal effects; others warn of prosecutorial overreach and evidentiary difficulty in proving a defendant consciously disregarded a substantial risk that abuse would lead to suicide. Haban’s family says the charges provide some justice and accountability for her years of suffering.

The Obama Administration announced a broad set of initiatives to help formerly incarcerated people rehabilitate and reintegrate, stressing that reducing barriers to work, housing, education, and services promotes fairness and public safety. At events in Newark, the President highlighted the Federal Interagency Reentry Council’s cross-agency work and urged Congress to pass sentencing and reentry reforms such as the Sentencing Reform and Corrections Act of 2015. Key federal actions announced include: up to $8 million in Department of Education Adult Reentry Education Grants to nine communities; HUD guidance limiting use of arrests and clarifying “one strike” policies in housing decisions; and an OPM directive to delay criminal-history questions (“ban the box”) until later in federal hiring. TechHire expansions will train and place formerly incarcerated people in tech jobs in multiple cities, and a National Clean Slate Clearinghouse (Labor and DOJ) will help legal aid and reentry providers with record-clearing and expungement. HUD and DOJ launched an $8.7 million Pay for Success demonstration to provide permanent supportive housing and reduce homelessness and recidivism. HUD will also fund juvenile record-sealing assistance; the National Bar Association pledged pro bono hours. The announcements build on many prior initiatives—grants for career training, Second Chance Pell pilot, youth employment and reentry grants, veteran reentry tools, reduced prison phone rates, and private-sector commitments to expand employment and education programs—aimed at lowering recidivism and expanding second chances.

With college costs soaring and job prospects uncertain, PayScale analyzed 1.4 million salary reports to evaluate return on investment (ROI) for over 850 colleges. ROI compares the cost of a degree with graduates’ average earnings to show which schools deliver the most economic value. Caltech topped the list with an estimated $1,713,000 ROI, while Shaw University ranked lowest at $15,480. PayScale highlighted the 13 schools with the highest ROIs and offers full public/private breakdowns; BusinessWeek presents a state-by-state best-value slideshow. The findings aim to help prospective students weigh tuition against likely earnings.

The Justice Department has sued California and two top state officials, accusing the state of obstructing federal immigration enforcement by enacting and enforcing laws that impede U.S. operations targeting undocumented immigrants. Filed in federal court in Sacramento, the suit stresses the Constitution’s broad federal authority over immigration and contends that California’s measures block Department of Homeland Security efforts and impose improper obligations on the federal government, potentially endangering communities. The clash intensifies an ongoing feud between the Trump administration and California’s leaders—Gov. Jerry Brown and Attorney General Xavier Becerra—who have opposed the White House on immigration, climate policy and criminal justice. Brown dismissed the lawsuit as a political stunt, echoing President Trump’s blunt rhetoric.

The suit challenges three California laws passed last year: one bans private employers from voluntary cooperation with federal immigration officials and requires businesses to warn workers ahead of federal raids; a second limits state and local law enforcement from sharing release-date information of undocumented detainees and forbids transferring them into federal custody; the third regulates state inspections of facilities holding noncitizens in federal custody. The Justice Department seeks a preliminary injunction against these statutes and cites a 2012 Supreme Court ruling that invalidated parts of Arizona’s immigration law under the Supremacy Clause, asserting federal law preempts conflicting state rules.

Attorney General Jeff Sessions, an opponent of lax immigration policy, will address California law enforcement amid renewed litigation over withholding federal grants from sanctuary jurisdictions. The case will test the administration’s ability to compel local cooperation with deportations and its willingness to override state policies that diverge markedly from federal priorities.

Tens of thousands worldwide held vigils and demonstrations after a deadly gun attack on Charlie Hebdo’s Paris offices that left 12 people dead. In Paris an estimated 35,000 people gathered at Place de la République, leaving candles, pens and copies of the magazine’s covers as tributes; similar gatherings and silent vigils took place across France and around the world, including Trafalgar Square in London, Union Square in New York, Washington’s Newseum, Brussels, Berlin, Madrid, Buenos Aires, Rome, Stockholm and elsewhere. Protesters and online users adopted the slogan “Je Suis Charlie” (“I am Charlie”) to show solidarity and defend free expression. Many held pens aloft as a symbol of press freedom and chanted “We are not afraid” or sang the Marseillaise.

The attack, carried out by masked gunmen who shouted “Allahu akbar,” also killed two police officers and targeted the magazine that had previously received threats for satirizing the Prophet Muhammad and other figures. French authorities identified three suspects—brothers Said and Cherif Kouachi and Hamyd Mourad—while conducting a nationwide manhunt; one suspect reportedly surrendered. France raised its terror alert and deployed thousands of police and troops, with heightened security at media sites and public places. The killings prompted global condemnation, widespread mourning, and reaffirmed public commitment to defend freedom of speech against violent intimidation.

Same Ole Line Dudes (SOLD) is a New York–based professional line-waiting service that aims to save busy clients hours spent queuing for everything from iPhones and Air Jordans to Broadway tickets, sample sales, Cronuts and even Saturday Night Live standby spots. Founder and CEO Robert Samuel launched the business after being laid off in 2012 and beginning by responding to a Craigslist ad request to hold a spot for an iPhone release. Since then SOLD has grown into a niche start-up that treats time as a commodity: Americans reportedly spend about 37 billion hours a year waiting in lines, and many customers—often time-poor rather than cash-poor—are willing to pay to avoid that drain. Samuel charges roughly $25 for the first hour and $10 per additional half-hour, accepts digital payments, and offers a premium “Delivereach” option that includes purchases, delivery and shipping for out-of-state clients. He’s been known to sleep in cots outside stores, once earning $1,000 after 48 hours outside an Apple store for an iPhone launch and coordinating teams to buy limited items—like 18 Cronuts—when per-person limits apply. Clients range from busy parents to wealthy shoppers; some work is done for resellers who export sought-after gadgets overseas, which has created friction with other line-goers. The business is cyclic, so Samuel still works as a security guard to steady income. SOLD faces emerging competition from gig platforms such as TaskRabbit and Agent Anything, and Samuel navigates operational risks—long waits that don’t always yield purchases, tense encounters with professional resellers, and skeptical observers, including his own mother. He has tried to maintain goodwill by offering partial refunds when lines fail to secure promised items, protecting customer relationships and his reputation on platforms like Yelp.

Bexar County Sheriff Javier Salazar called the fatal deputy-involved shooting that killed 6-year-old Kameron Prescott and a suspected car thief a "tragic accident." The incident began shortly after a stolen vehicle report near FM 1518 and Schaefer Road. Deputies searched for 30-year-old Amanda Lene Jones, a wanted felon with numerous past arrests. One deputy found Jones hiding in a closet; she allegedly told him she had a weapon and fled. A multi-deputy pursuit followed through wooded, water-filled terrain into the Pecan Grove Mobile Home Park. Witnesses and deputies reported Jones threatened people and appeared to be armed. She forced entry into a mobile home where an adult, a minor female and Kameron were present, made threats including taking the family's car, and then stepped onto the porch where five deputies confronted her. According to Salazar, Jones again threatened to shoot and was seen holding an object believed to be a weapon. Four deputies—John Aguillon, George Herrera, Jesse Arias and reserve deputy Johnny Longoria—fired; Jones was killed at the scene. A bullet also passed into the home, striking Kameron in the abdomen; he was given first aid but later died at a hospital. Investigators found a dark tubular object with Jones’ blood nearby but have not located a handgun. Bodycam and helicopter footage exist though key moments are obscured; one bodycam captured audio but the view was blocked when an officer raised his rifle. The deputies are on administrative leave and the district attorney is investigating. Kameron’s school and community mourned; donations have been requested to assist his family.

The U.K. has become the first country to allow Pfizer’s erectile dysfunction drug Viagra to be sold over the counter as “Viagra Connect,” offering a pharmacy-only, non-prescription option expected in spring 2018. Adults over 18 can obtain the medication after a pharmacist consultation, which determines suitability. Packs will retail at about £19.99 for four pills and £34.99 for eight. The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) reclassified sildenafil from prescription-only to pharmacy status after a lengthy review and public consultation, aiming to improve access, reduce embarrassment for patients, and curb demand for potentially dangerous counterfeit products; the agency has seized over £50 million of unlicensed erectile dysfunction medicines in five years. Pfizer, which will continue to sell prescription Viagra, pursued OTC status for nearly a decade and previously sought EU approval. Viagra, discovered serendipitously while researching heart treatments and launched in 1998, peaked at over $2 billion in sales in 2012 and earned about $1.6 billion in 2016. With patent expiry already reducing European sales, U.S. generics are due in 2020.

Peter E. Kassig, a 26-year-old former U.S. Army Ranger turned humanitarian, has been identified as a hostage of the Islamic State (ISIS) and appears at the end of a video depicting the apparent beheading of British aid worker Alan Henning. Kassig left the U.S. military after a 2007 deployment to Iraq and later studied at Butler University. In 2012, seeking purpose after struggling with post-service life, he traveled to the Middle East on spring break to learn about and assist victims of the Syrian conflict. He volunteered in Lebanese hospitals and refugee camps, trained as an emergency medical technician, and in 2012 founded Special Emergency Response and Assistance (SERA), a small NGO focused on rapid, grassroots delivery of medical supplies, food, clothing and fuel to Syrians in acute need. Operating from Gaziantep, Turkey, near the Syrian border, SERA ran cross-border aid missions, purchasing stoves, fuel, rice and other essentials to deliver directly to camps such as Qah, despite logistical challenges and dangers. Kassig also worked with TYR Solutions LTD, a British security consultancy, and emphasized SERA’s niche: supplementing larger charities by working closely with affected communities to ensure transparency and responsiveness. His family reports he was detained en route to Deir Ezzor, Syria, on October 1, 2013; they had kept his capture private while quietly trying to secure his release. During captivity, Kassig converted to Islam and adopted the name Abdul-Rahman, a change his family says provided him comfort. Throughout his work he was moved by Syrian resilience, treating both civilians and wounded fighters, and he hoped SERA would grow into a larger international relief organization. His parents have called for prayers for all hostages and for the Henning family. Kassig’s story underscores the personal transition from soldier to humanitarian and the risks aid workers face in Syria’s brutal conflict.

On June 7, coordinated gun-and-bomb attacks struck two of Iran’s most symbolic sites — the national parliament in Tehran and the mausoleum of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini — killing about a dozen people, wounding dozens more, and marking what Islamic State (ISIS) claimed as its first successful strike inside Iran. Attackers, some disguised as women, stormed the Majlis and the shrine, used suicide vests and firearms, and released a video boasting of their presence inside parliament. Iranian security forces killed the known assailants and arrested several suspects; officials also reported foiling another team planning a third attack.

ISIS has long regarded Iran as both a strategic and religious enemy. As a Shiite-majority theocracy, Iran represents a sectarian rival that ISIS and similar Sunni jihadists denounce as apostate. Analysts note that ISIS’s hostility to Iran predates its split from al-Qaeda; early on, al-Qaeda discouraged strikes inside Iran because it maintained covert logistics and detainees there. After the split, ISIS aimed to strike Iran but lacked capability until it built networks and recruited Sunnis from Iran who went to fight in Iraq and Syria. With its territorial losses in Iraq and Syria and diminished recruitment, ISIS has increasingly sought high-profile external attacks — particularly during Ramadan — to demonstrate continued potency, attract followers, and force sectarian polarization.

The choice of targets was symbolic: the parliament represents Iran’s political heart, while Khomeini’s mausoleum is the spiritual core of the 1979 revolution. Striking both political and religious centers was intended to puncture the image of security and resilience. Tehran’s elite security services were surprised by the audacity of the assaults, which will likely prompt tightened protections at religious sites and government buildings.

Iran’s leadership condemned the attacks and vowed retaliation. Hardline elements, including the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, accused regional rival Saudi Arabia of complicity — an allegation Riyadh denied — and blamed broader Western hostility, especially in the fraught context of recent diplomatic rifts in the Gulf and U.S. provocations. Domestically, the attacks are likely to bolster support for hardliners and the IRGC, complicate reformist President Hassan Rouhani’s position, and justify intensified counterterrorism measures. Internationally, the strike underscores ISIS’s shift toward external terrorism as its territorial “caliphate” collapses and heightens tensions across the region as rival states trade accusations and seek to shape the post-ISIS landscape.

Indian officials have paused efforts to recover the body of American missionary John Allen Chau, who is believed to have been killed by the isolated Sentinelese after landing on North Sentinel Island on 17 November to try to convert its inhabitants. Authorities decided the search was too risky and might provoke confrontation or expose the tribe to disease; the island’s residents are legally protected and outsiders are barred from approaching within five nautical miles. Chau, in his mid-20s, reportedly paid local fishermen to take him near the island; eyewitnesses among those fishermen later said they saw the tribespeople dragging what appeared to be his body and burying it. Multiple reconnaissance trips by police using boats and a helicopter kept a distance after tribespeople armed with bows and arrows were seen on the beach. Anthropologists, tribal welfare and rights groups, including Survival International, urged authorities to abandon recovery attempts to avoid deadly epidemics and further violence. Police have registered a murder case and arrested six fishermen and another person for facilitating Chau’s illegal visit; investigators are consulting anthropologists and tribal experts to determine whether and how evidence can be gathered without endangering officials or the Sentinelese. Chau’s family has forgiven those responsible.

Physics students have long been taught that falling through a frictionless tunnel through Earth would take about 42 minutes, assuming Earth has uniform density. Alexander Klotz used seismic-based density profiles (the Preliminary Reference Earth Model) to recalculate the trip and found a more realistic fall time of 38 minutes 11 seconds. The classical uniform-density assumption yields simple harmonic motion and the 42-minute result, but Earth’s real density increases toward the core, altering the gravity profile. Surprisingly, assuming a constant gravitational field equal to surface gravity also gives about 38 minutes; because gravity stays roughly constant down to the outer core, and the falling object traverses the core quickly, the constant-force approximation matches the realistic result well. Klotz’s numerical work also shows straight-line trip times vary with distance and that the time-minimizing (brachistochrone) path digs deeper and is faster than the uniform model predicts.

The Shin Bet and IDF announced they dismantled a large transnational Hamas network planning major attacks against Israelis, arresting over 30 operatives in September after investigations triggered by explosive devices placed in the West Bank on August 31. Raids led by the IDF’s Duvdevan unit recovered two M-16 rifles, ammunition, bomb-making materials and safe houses. Targets included Jerusalem’s Teddy Stadium, the light rail system, Israeli traffic and military sites in the West Bank, Jewish settlements, and plans for car bombings, kidnappings and cross-border assaults from Jordan. The Shin Bet said the network was directed from a Hamas headquarters in Turkey, with operatives recruited while studying in Jordan and trained in Jordan, Turkey, Syria and Gaza — the latter reached via Sinai smuggling tunnels — under oversight from Turkey-based commanders. Training covered weapons handling, explosives, navigation, and clandestine operations. Some members dated back to recruitment in 2012; interrogations implicated senior figures, including Saleh al-Aruri, who leads Hamas’s West Bank efforts from Turkey. Another thwarted August plot led by Ramallah-based commander Riad Nasser had similar external backing and funding. Israeli leaders praised security forces for preventing potentially deadly attacks that Shin Bet claims aimed to provoke a harsh Israeli response and undermine the Palestinian Authority. Palestinian officials acknowledged arrests but framed objectives more narrowly toward West Bank military and settler targets.

WT1190F is a mysterious piece of man-made space debris predicted to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere on Friday, November 13, impacting the Indian Ocean about 65 km south of Sri Lanka around 06:20 UTC. Detected by the Catalina Sky Survey in early October and linked to earlier 2012–2013 sightings, WT1190F follows a highly elliptical orbit reaching twice the Earth–Moon distance. At about 1–2 meters long with low density—possibly hollow—scientists suspect it’s an old rocket stage or paneling from a moon mission, perhaps decades old. Most of it will likely burn up, though experts advise avoiding the predicted splashdown area. The re-entry presents a rare observational opportunity; agencies are coordinating spectral and atmospheric observations, highlighting gaps in systematic tracking and identification of deep-space debris.

The SEC alleges that golfer Phil Mickelson profited $931,000 in 2012 after buying Dean Foods shares on an insider tip from sports gambler Billy Walters and used some of the proceeds to repay a debt to Walters. Mickelson was not criminally charged; instead he was named a relief defendant and has agreed to return all “ill‑gotten gains,” totaling $1.03 million with interest. The SEC said there was no evidence Mickelson knew the illegal origin of the tip. Mickelson issued a statement expressing regret for any appearance of wrongdoing, accepting responsibility for his associations, and declining further comment. 

Walters was arrested and charged with insider trading after authorities alleged he received confidential information from former Dean Foods director Thomas Davis, enabling about $17.1 million in 2012 trades tied to a spin‑off. Davis has pleaded guilty to charges including perjury and obstruction and is cooperating; prosecutors say he received unpaid loans from Walters. Walters faces criminal charges and denies wrongdoing, with counsel promising to contest the allegations. The U.S. Attorney’s office and the SEC are seeking to recoup gains from Walters and Davis. The case is a notable insider‑trading prosecution following recent appellate limits on such prosecutions and signals prosecutors’ intent to pursue high‑profile abuses despite legal hurdles. Sponsors and the PGA Tour have so far offered measured responses.

Lion’s Gate Sanctuary in Agate, Colorado, stunned the community by euthanizing all 11 of its exotic animals — three lions, three tigers and five bears — after county commissioners denied the facility’s request to relocate. Owners Joan Laub and Peter Winney said recurring flooding and property damage made continuing operations at their current site unsafe and that the animals, described as elderly and having special needs, could not survive a move. They blamed Elbert County’s refusal to approve a special-use permit for a new site near Elizabeth for leaving them “backed into a corner,” and initially framed the deaths as victims of the commissioners’ decision.

Elbert County officials, however, say the denial was based on public-safety concerns: the proposed site was closer to a populated, equine-oriented neighborhood and the relocation plan lacked adequate resources and emergency contingencies. Commissioners said they were surprised by the euthanasia because the sanctuary had told them it would continue operating at its longtime location if denied, and because other facilities — notably The Wild Animal Sanctuary in Keenesburg — offered to take the animals. County leaders stressed they had asked owners what would happen if the permit was denied and were reassured the animals would remain.

The episode drew strong public reaction. Colorado Parks and Wildlife called the mass euthanasia unprecedented. The Wild Animal Sanctuary’s director said his 720-acre facility could have taken the animals and doubted age alone prevented relocation. Reporting also highlighted past controversies involving co-owner Peter Winney, including prior charges and a past conviction related to transporting big cats, though he disputes the characterization. Volunteers and supporters describe the euthanasia as a last resort and claim the owners are devastated, while critics question whether other sanctuaries and options were fully pursued. The incident has sparked scrutiny of licensing, relocation logistics, and how authorities and sanctuaries respond when exotic-animal facilities face housing crises.

Walter Thomas, a 91-year-old Woodstock, Illinois resident and longtime car enthusiast who once owned four gas stations and collected antique cars, recently checked an unconventional item off his bucket list: backing a vehicle through a garage door. The stunt was staged with family help and presented as a harmless thrill since the one-car garage—built in 1921—was already slated for demolition. Grandchildren Becky Goers, a driver’s-ed teacher, Andrew Thomas, an accident reconstruction deputy, and Brian Thomas organized the event. Andrew sourced a donated 1998 Isuzu Rodeo from a local shop, and friends Nick and Jamielynn Wedoff, who planned to tear down the garage to build an addition, provided the site. On a Sunday afternoon, with family and friends gathered and his wife Dorothy watching, Walter donned a racing helmet and, with Andrew riding shotgun, floored the gas. The SUV’s tires squealed and the vehicle burst through the wooden garage doors, scattering shattered wood across the driveway. The frame remained intact, though the noise startled one great-granddaughter to tears. Thomas beamed afterward, saying “we really took the door down,” and expressed gratitude to his grandchildren for making the quirky lifelong wish come true. The story corrects an earlier report of his age, confirming he is 91.

A forthcoming paleo baby and toddler cookbook co-authored by celebrity chef Pete Evans, blogger Charlotte Carr and naturopath Helen Padarin has been delayed amid serious public-health concerns. Bubba Yum Yum: The Paleo Way For New Mums, Babies and Toddlers was due for release but Pan Macmillan Australia paused publication after complaints from a consortium of health organisations and queries to the Federal Department of Health. Central controversy surrounds a “DIY baby milk formula” or “Baby Building Broth” made from chicken bones, feet, liver, apple cider vinegar, oils and a probiotic; the book claims it can mimic breast milk and serve as an alternative when breastfeeding is not possible. Public-health experts, including Professor Heather Yeatman and the Australian Breastfeeding Association, say the recipes dangerously contradict national infant-feeding guidelines. They warn the broth formula could expose infants to toxic levels of vitamin A and inadequate amounts of other essential nutrients, and that feeding anything other than breast milk or commercial formula as a primary nutrition source for infants under six months is “extremely dangerous.” The Department of Health is investigating the book’s nutritional claims. Critics also flagged recipes that include runny eggs and added salt, both inappropriate for young babies. Publishers and authors have declined extended comment. The dispute highlights tensions between popular alternative-diet advocates and medical authorities, given Evans’s wide influence and the potential for celebrity endorsement to sway vulnerable new parents.

An administrative law judge, Robert Beltrani, 53, was arraigned in Manhattan Criminal Court on misdemeanor assault, attempted assault and harassment charges stemming from an October 20 altercation in Chelsea in which he allegedly knocked Legal Aid attorney Sam Roberts unconscious. Beltrani, who oversees state parole cases, appeared in court wearing a gray suit and with a visible lump on his forehead; he was released without bail and an order of protection was issued for Roberts. Prosecutors say the incident began after a law‑firm celebration on West 18th Street where Beltrani, reportedly intoxicated, proclaimed “Yeah, I’m the judge. I do justice and I f—ing kill people!” According to complaints and witness accounts, when Roberts turned away, Beltrani struck him, then fell atop him, leaving Roberts unconscious on the sidewalk. Roberts was taken to Bellevue Hospital with a separated shoulder, torn labrum, a black eye and other injuries. Security video and witness statements reportedly captured the episode; one witness said Beltrani fled the scene in his car and was later tracked down after someone recorded his license plate. Beltrani has been placed on administrative leave pending investigation and faces up to a year in jail on the top count. He declined to comment through his attorney, Daniel Ollen, who also did not comment. Roberts, shaken, described the attack as unprovoked and expressed concern that Beltrani “probably needs help.”

A Pembroke Hill school bus overturned Aug. 21 on a ramp from Kansas Highway 7 near K-32 in Bonner Springs, Kansas, after the driver took a turn too fast and the bus slid off the road. Good Samaritans and first responders freed passengers; 22 sixth-grade girls and the driver were injured and taken to hospitals, the driver in serious but stable condition. The field trip was canceled.

Laverne Cox, best known for playing Sophia Burset on Orange Is the New Black, will be the first transgender person immortalized with a Madame Tussauds wax figure. The 31-year-old actress’s likeness will be displayed at the San Francisco museum on Fisherman’s Wharf and unveiled at a June 26 press conference ahead of the city’s 45th annual Pride Celebration & Parade. Cox called the honor “improbable and extraordinary,” hoping it inspires others. Madame Tussauds said the choice aligns with San Francisco Pride’s equality theme and reflects contemporary society. Cox is also the first transgender Emmy acting nominee and a Time cover subject.

A man surnamed Yuan from Changsha, Hunan province, who posed as a successful civil engineering graduate and company employee, was exposed after a car crash brought more than a dozen of his partners together in hospital. Hospital staff contacted his “relatives” following the March 24 accident, and as more women arrived they realized they were all involved with the same man. The women — about 17 in total, aged roughly 20 to 40 — had believed themselves to be his girlfriends or wives; some had been with him for years, and at least one has a child by him. Yuan, who reportedly has only a middle school education, had fabricated a background claiming a degree from Central South University and a role renovating expressways at a large company. After his divorce, he allegedly cheated his ex-wife of 250,000 yuan and later swindled tens of thousands of yuan from multiple partners, with one woman providing financial support for nine years. The women formed a WeChat group in the hospital and compared stories, revealing long-term deception: one said she had planned to marry him and another said she no longer loved him but loved their son. The case is being treated as criminal fraud. Social media responses—more than 6,000 comments—varied from admiration for Yuan’s charm to criticism of the women for not recognizing the deceit earlier. Commentators debated the roles of flattery and false appearances, with some suggesting that his smooth lies and compliments were all some women sought, making them vulnerable to manipulation. The episode has drawn wide attention as a dramatic example of serial romantic deception.

Jeremy Lin’s sudden breakout with the New York Knicks has been spectacular and far-reaching. After coming off the bench to spark a win at Madison Square Garden, he started and scored 28 points with eight assists, then followed with 23 points and 10 assists—capping the week with a 38-point outing that beat the Los Angeles Lakers and Kobe Bryant. Lin, the first U.S.-born NBA player of Taiwanese/Chinese descent and a Harvard grad, has ignited ticket sales, boosted TV ratings, and driven surging social-media interest. Marketers see major endorsement potential: he already has a Nike shoe deal, and agents expect offers from brands targeting Asian-American consumers, a lucrative, educated demographic with strong buying power. Lin’s humble, well-spoken image, academic background, and on-court performance make him an appealing role model and sponsor fit, promising continued commercial and cultural impact if his play endures.

Former live-in housekeeper and nanny Erlinda T. Elemen has filed a lawsuit in Los Angeles Superior Court accusing actress Sharon Stone of racial discrimination, religious harassment and labor-law violations after five years in her employ. Elemen, who is Filipino, alleges Stone forbade her from speaking to Stone’s children because Stone did not want them to “talk like you,” disparaged Filipino people and food, criticized Elemen for attending church, and at one point prohibited her from reading the Bible inside the house. Elemen also says Stone withheld overtime pay; when Elemen raised the issue, she alleges Stone repaid the wages but then accused her of stealing, publicly berated her in front of guests and staff for weeks, and ultimately terminated her employment in February 2011. The suit seeks an unspecified amount in unpaid wages, damages and penalties. Stone’s publicist, Paul Bloch, called the complaint “absurd,” labeled Elemen a disgruntled ex-employee seeking money, and said Stone will be vindicated in court. Last year Stone was ordered to pay $232,000 in an unrelated injury lawsuit.

A student has been taken into custody after 17-year-old Courtlin Arrington was fatally shot inside Huffman High School in east Birmingham during dismissal. Police have not identified the individual; charges await review by the Jefferson County district attorney. Authorities say detectives reviewed evidence, video and statements overnight, and the video footage prompted pursuit of charges. Initial radio reports confused the incident with an active shooter situation, but officials later described it as an accidental shooting unless the investigation indicates otherwise. The shooting occurred around 3:45 p.m.; Arrington received CPR and died after being transported to UAB Hospital. Another 17-year-old boy suffered a self-inflicted leg wound, was treated and released, then held for questioning. A third, non-student person was also injured; their condition is unclear. Huffman uses working metal detectors and has surveillance cameras, though officials would not discuss specifics while the probe continues. School officials closed Huffman the following day for safety sweeps and counseling, and increased security and crisis support were planned when students returned. Community leaders, including the mayor, called for mourning and support as the investigation continues.

A Lake County deputy, Dean Zipes, was fired April 21 following an internal affairs investigation that concluded his conduct posed a serious safety risk to colleagues and the public. The probe was launched after multiple incidents, including one in February in the Minneola sheriff’s office substation parking lot where Zipes allegedly re-enacted a scene from the film Training Day. Witnesses and patrol-car video show Zipes holding his department-issued handgun in one hand and a Taser in the other, rubbing the two devices together and reciting lines from Denzel Washington’s character, a corrupt police officer. A deputy in training, Tammy Peshek, reported being upset that Zipes acted unsafely and in public where civilians could observe him. The report states Zipes told investigators he was “trying to be funny.” The internal review also documented earlier troubling behavior: Zipes had reportedly drawn his firearm twice inside an office setting, pointed a weapon at a breakroom window while saying he “never got to shoot the gun,” voiced racial slurs, and made a motion to draw his gun at a pizza delivery driver while joking that the driver was alleged murderer Markeith Loyd. He allegedly became upset over not receiving free Starbucks coffee. The investigative report lists violations including harassment and on-duty misuse of a firearm, leading to Zipes’s termination for reckless behavior and multiple policy breaches.

Prosecutors in Pierce County say they would consider any credible information Steven Powell might provide about the disappearance of his daughter-in-law, Susan Powell, but they have not offered him a plea deal. Pierce County Prosecutor Mark Lindquist told 97.3 KIRO FM that while no deal has been proposed, his office would "listen" if Powell, his attorney, or Utah law enforcement presented an arrangement tied to information about Susan’s whereabouts. Sheriff’s Office spokesperson Ed Troyer warned against relying on Powell’s cooperation, saying Powell has a history of manipulation and might "jerk everybody around." Powell has been jailed since a September 2011 search of his Puyallup home uncovered thousands of surreptitious images of females, including Susan and minors; his trial is set for March 20. West Valley City Police Chief Buzz Nielson called Powell a "person of interest" but deferred to Pierce County’s prosecution, saying Utah investigators hope to question Powell when he’s ready and seek answers about who might have known or assisted in the case.

A Birmingham church placed a provocative billboard reading “Strip for me,” quoting Hebrews, near a downtown strip club to challenge men to quit wasting money and focus on family and holiness. Pastor Mike McClure Jr. says the sign’s scriptural intent is to encourage men to “strip off” sin, be accountable, and invest in their homes to reduce crime. The church expected controversy; some residents found it inappropriate or confusing, while others praised it as a creative prompt for reflection and better choices. The billboard aims to redirect patrons toward faith and family.

Senate Republicans intensified a high-stakes, closed-door push to produce a bill repealing and replacing large parts of the Affordable Care Act ahead of an informal July 4 deadline set by Majority Leader Mitch McConnell. McConnell wants a quick vote to avoid the debate consuming the legislative calendar and to pursue other GOP priorities, but faces razor-thin math: with 52 Republicans, he can afford only two defections while every Democrat is expected to oppose the measure. Negotiations center on balancing conservative demands to roll back ObamaCare’s regulations and spending with moderates’ insistence on protections for pre-existing conditions, Medicaid expansion funding and Planned Parenthood. Conservatives, led by the House Republican Study Committee and senators including Mike Lee, Ted Cruz and Rand Paul, have warned the Senate not to water down provisions such as phasing out enhanced Medicaid funding, maintaining language defunding Planned Parenthood, and blocking refundable tax credits from funding abortions. Paul opposes refundable credits as a new GOP entitlement; Lee and Cruz press to let states opt out of guaranteed issue and community rating rules. McConnell has proposed phasing out enhanced Medicaid funding in 2023 but faces centrist proposals extending it to 2025–2027. Republicans may use budget reconciliation to avoid a Democratic filibuster, but that constrains what the bill can include. Democrats have launched a public campaign to derail the process, staging floor speeches and a late-night talkathon to protest the secret negotiations and demand more review time. Some GOP senators have also voiced concern about the rushed timeline and limited opportunity to study the bill, even as leaders aim for a vote as soon as next week.

Illinois Republican Rep. Aaron Schock is facing a potential House ethics probe after disclosures about an opulently redecorated Capitol Hill office. Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) filed a complaint alleging Schock may have accepted improper gifts by using outside design services and potentially campaign or taxpayer funds for lavish furnishings. The office, in the Rayburn House Office Building, features bold red walls, crystal chandeliers, gold sconces, pheasant-feather arrangements, a Federal-style mirror, a bust of Lincoln and granite-topped furniture — a scheme reportedly inspired by the “red room” from the PBS drama Downton Abbey. The designer, Annie (Annie) Brahler of Illinois, told reporters she provided design services pro bono and had previously decorated Schock’s former Cannon Building office. House rules define gifts as any item or service with monetary value and generally prohibit members from accepting them; members must personally pay for additional decorations beyond limited House-provided options. Records show Schock has previously spent tens of thousands from his taxpayer-funded office account on renovations, leather furniture, hardwood floors, granite, painting and other items, including transactions in 2009 and later years totaling many thousands of dollars. CREW’s executive director, Anne Weismann, criticized Schock’s pattern of expenditures and image-focused publicity, saying rules require him to pay for renovations himself. The matter drew extra scrutiny because Schock has voted to end federal funding for PBS while his office echoes a PBS show; his spokesman denied Schock is a Downton Abbey fan. Schock did not immediately comment. The complaint could prompt a formal ethics investigation into whether services or items were improperly provided or funded.

Today at 11 a.m. ET De La Soul will offer their entire catalog as free downloads for 25 hours to celebrate the 25th anniversary of 3 Feet High and Rising. The giveaway restores access to music long absent from digital stores because of uncleared samples, label turnover, and cloudy early contracts, issues Posdnuos says have frustrated the group despite honors like inclusion in the Library of Congress. They’ll also post new songs soon and aim to release You're Welcome before summer, plus an EP Preemium Soul on the Rocks (beats by DJ Premier and Pete Rock) and sessions with unreleased J Dilla material. Posdnuos emphasizes renewed momentum and careful self-editing as they prepare to share more music.

Wang Qi, a Chinese former People’s Liberation Army surveyor who accidentally crossed into India in January 1963, has finally been reunited with his family in China after more than five decades. Wang says he lost his way while building roads for the Chinese army, asked for help from a Red Cross vehicle and was handed over to Indian authorities. He spent seven years in various jails before a court ordered his release in 1969. Police then escorted him to Tirodi, a remote village in Madhya Pradesh, where he was not permitted to leave India. Denied citizenship and exit documents for decades, Wang adapted to life in India: he worked at a flour mill, married a local woman, Sushila, in 1975, and raised three children and grandchildren while living in poverty and enduring harassment from local officials. He kept contact with his Chinese family sporadically—letters and rare phone calls—receiving his first reply in the 1980s and speaking with his mother in 2002; she died in 2006 before he could return.

Chinese diplomats and the embassy maintained contact in recent years, helping Wang obtain a Chinese passport in 2013 and providing support. After widespread attention following a BBC report, Chinese officials visited him and coordinated with Indian authorities; the Indian Foreign Ministry issued clearance for his departure and provided passports for accompanying family members. Wang flew from Delhi to Beijing accompanied by his adult children; crowds in Xianyang welcomed him with banners. It remains unclear whether Wang will return to India, where his wife and much of his life remain, but he has expressed longing for both his Chinese roots and his Indian family.

Almost three days after losing a High Court bid to reopen his appeal against a conviction for sending "grossly offensive" letters to bereaved families, Man Haron Monis carried out a 16-hour siege at the Lindt Chocolat Cafe in Martin Place, Sydney, taking 17 people hostage. The High Court had on Friday refused his application to have the constitutional question reheard after a 3–3 split in an earlier decision; Monis’s legal team argued the even split created “special circumstances” but Chief Justice Robert French and Justice Stephen Gageler dismissed the application. Monis, who had once declared “this pen is my gun, and these words are my bullets,” had long fought the letters conviction—which involved abusive communications to families of soldiers killed in Afghanistan and an Austrade official—and had been sentenced in 2013 to 300 hours community service and a two-year good-behaviour bond after pleading guilty.

Monis, an Iranian-born asylum seeker who adopted the title Sheikh Haron, was well known to police and had a history of violent and sexual offences. At the time of the siege he was on bail facing multiple serious charges: more than 40 counts of indecent and sexual assault linked to his self-styled “spiritual healer” practice, and allegations of being an accessory before and after the fact in the murder of his ex-wife, Noleen Hayson Pal. He had also posted extremist material online, announced a conversion from Shia to Sunni Islam, and professed allegiance to the Islamic State’s caliphate, though authorities found no organisational links to IS. Observers and his former lawyer described him as isolated, radicalised, and potentially acting as a lone wolf driven by grievance and marginalisation.

Police were called just before 9:45am on Monday; the siege ended after commandos stormed the cafe shortly after 2:00am Tuesday. Monis and two hostages—cafe manager Tori Johnson, 34, and Sydney lawyer Katrina Dawson, 38—died; four others were injured but survived. Negotiations proceeded for some 16 hours via hostages. The episode prompted urgent questions from Prime Minister Tony Abbott and others about why Monis had not been on terror watch lists and why he had been on bail despite serious charges. Authorities launched investigations into how Monis obtained a firearm and the conduct of the police operation. The attack drew national grief and debate over lone‑actor radicalisation, bail and surveillance priorities, and whether the siege could have been prevented. Widespread public mourning followed, with tributes, floral tributes in Martin Place, and calls for careful review of intelligence and policing responses.

President-elect Donald Trump’s Twitter attack on Rep. John Lewis — calling the civil-rights icon “all talk” and criticizing his Atlanta-area congressional district as “crime-infested” — sparked a broad political backlash and a wave of inauguration boycotts by Democrats. Lewis had called Trump an illegitimate president on NBC’s Meet the Press, citing concerns including possible Russian interference and the late-stage F.B.I. disclosures about Hillary Clinton. Trump responded by disparaging Lewis on Twitter, prompting at least 26 Democratic members of Congress to announce they would not attend the inauguration and instead focus on activism and resistance. Prominent objectors include Rep. John Conyers Jr., who pledged to hold the administration accountable and defend the Constitution; Rep. Barbara Lee, who called for vocal resistance if Trump’s rhetoric becomes policy; and others such as Maxine Waters, Luis Gutierrez, Katherine Clark, and Nydia Velázquez.

The dispute intensified worries among many African-American leaders and voters, given Trump’s weak support in the black community (about 8 percent voted for him) and concerns about appointments like Stephen Bannon to a senior White House role. The Rev. Al Sharpton said Trump’s tweets mobilized more demonstrators. Martin Luther King III met with Trump at Trump Tower and described the meeting as constructive, urging engagement and pressure; his sister Bernice King countered that “God can triumph over Trump.” King defended Lewis’s record, saying Lewis has demonstrated action, not just words.

Locally, the feud led to heated exchanges, including a Gwinnett County commissioner’s social-media invective calling Lewis a “racist pig,” which drew condemnation and calls for apology or resignation. Lewis, for his part, emphasized nonviolence, the sanctity of the vote, and the need to stand up for justice — themes he reinforced during a Martin Luther King Day address where he urged young people to “never give up, never give in.” The controversy also boosted sales of Lewis’s memoir and fed broader debate about Trump’s legitimacy and the tone of the incoming administration.

A risky effort to contain the Gulf’s worst oil spill hit a setback when a diamond-edged saw became stuck while cutting a thick pipe on the blown-out Deepwater Horizon well. Officials aimed to free the saw and finish the cut that day; imperfect cuts could force a looser cap and temporarily raise flow by up to 20 percent. The true fix—a relief well—remains at least two months away. Oil neared Florida’s Panhandle, prompting booms, beach monitoring, and concerns of shoreline impacts between Wednesday and Friday. Storms hampered tracking and response; crews worked from staging centers in Louisiana with floating housing and grounded workers. BP shares plunged, DOJ opened probes, and President Obama urged rolling back oil tax breaks for clean-energy funding. BP apologized for an insensitive remark about wanting “my life back” after the rig explosion that killed 11.

In the wake of the Oregon college shooting, gun policy surged to the forefront of the 2016 campaign. Hillary Clinton unveiled concrete proposals including closing background-check loopholes, revoking licenses of dealers who knowingly enable “straw purchases,” and repealing legal protections for gun manufacturers. Most controversially, she pledged executive action if Congress failed: a regulatory change by the ATF to better define who is “engaged in the business” of selling firearms, thereby requiring background checks for higher-volume private sellers. Experts like Arkadi Gerney say a clearer numerical threshold for sales could be adopted, and even Obama could pursue similar steps now, a challenge implicit in Clinton’s plan.

The piece also highlights political dynamics: Clinton’s move pressures both the Obama administration and rival Democrats—particularly Bernie Sanders, criticized for less aggressive gun reform—and contrasts with Republican candidates’ reluctance to act. Donald Trump emphasized mental illness and suggested more armed security, avoiding policy specifics. Vice President Joe Biden was reported to be leaning toward a presidential run, potentially complicating the Democratic field.

Separately, leaders from 12 Pacific Rim nations reached a Trans-Pacific Partnership deal, setting a major trade fight for the campaign. Sanders continued drawing large crowds, notably 20,000 in Boston, suggesting momentum in some states despite questions about his appeal in diverse electorates.

Obama is actively reviewing executive options, including requiring background checks for buyers from dealers who sell many guns annually, clarifying domestic-violence purchaser prohibitions, and improving federal notification systems. Gun-control advocates press for bolder action, while opponents warn of unintended consequences. Public opinion favors expanded checks, but national debate remains sharply divided, even in affected communities like Roseburg, Ore.

Donald Trump defended his controversial remarks about Mexican immigrants in a wide-ranging NBC interview, insisting he will win the Latino vote if nominated because of his job-creation record. He doubled down on his plan to build an “impenetrable” wall on the U.S.-Mexico border and reiterated he would pressure Mexico to pay for it, arguing Mexico “is making a fortune off the United States.” Trump accused Hillary Clinton of being “weak on immigration” and claimed her policies would allow “killers, criminals, drug dealers” into the country, warning they would raise crime rates. He also labeled Clinton “the worst secretary of state in the history of our nation,” saying “the world blew up around us” under her tenure. Addressing fallout from his remarks, Trump dismissed lost business deals with Macy’s, Serta, NBC Universal and Univision as unimportant and said some companies later apologized. He disputed a report that undocumented workers were on his Washington hotel project, saying his contractor follows strict verification and employment-eligibility rules. During the interview he insulted NBC reporter Katy Tur as “naïve” after a question about immigration and crime.

The House Select Committee’s final GOP-authored Benghazi report, released amid sharp partisan disagreement, spotlights both procedural disputes and substantive accusations about how the Obama administration characterized the September 11–12, 2012 attacks in Benghazi. A central revelation is a two-hour video teleconference the night of the attack, led by White House Chief of Staff Denis McDonough and including Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and senior Defense officials. According to GOP investigators, the call — intended to coordinate potential evacuations — devoted significant time to debating why the attack happened and to discussing an anti-Islam Internet video, which the administration initially cited as a motivating factor. Investigators say roughly half the meeting’s action items were unrelated to evacuation and many involved the video explanation.

Republicans emphasize apparent contradictions between private assessments and public statements. Their supplemental “additional views” timeline juxtaposes officials’ private communications, which often recognized a planned, extremist attack in Benghazi, with public remarks that linked the violence to protests over the video and broader regional unrest. Examples include Clinton’s private notes and emails acknowledging an al-Qaeda–like group and an organized assault, while her public comments — and White House messaging, including remarks by Jay Carney and statements drafted by Ben Rhodes — underscored the video as the proximate cause.
