The timeline cites multiple instances where embassy and intelligence personnel privately concluded the incident was a terrorist attack from the start, yet public messaging continued to reference protests and the video. The GOP report contends that the administration knowingly presented a misleading public narrative.

The report also notes a State Department concern raised during the teleconference about whether Marines should wear uniforms, worried that visible flags might compromise diplomatic relations or security. Commanders reported repeated changes into and out of uniforms while preparing to deploy; however, no military force was sent to Benghazi. State officials have said uniform concerns did not delay any potential military response.

Democrats on the committee, led by Ranking Member Elijah Cummings, denounce the investigation as partisan and obstructive. Cummings called the process one of the lowest points of his congressional career, claiming restricted access to witnesses and transcripts and rejecting GOP conclusions that suggest a deliberate cover-up or “stand-down” order. The committee’s 800-page GOP report criticizes Hillary Clinton for insufficient attention to rising extremism in Libya and for publicly blaming the anti-Muslim video, while Democrats issued a rebuttal aiming to debunk the majority’s findings and to underscore what they describe as persistent partisanship in the probe.

BBC State Department correspondent Kim Ghattas joins Hillary Rodham Clinton aboard a U.S. diplomatic flight, offering behind-the-scenes access to the Secretary of State on a Middle East and Africa trip. Clinton describes the plane as an office with secure communications and a hardworking civilian and military team, acknowledges jet lag and travel strain, and explains her routines—sleeping on flights, drinking water, exercise, and brief walks to recharge. She reflects on the nature of diplomatic travel, meeting presidents and kings because of America’s global reach and her longstanding personal relationships, and the difficulty of engaging with leaders whose values differ from America’s. Clinton emphasizes restoring U.S. global leadership across interconnected challenges—Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and Latin America—rather than focusing narrowly, and stresses supporting democratic and economic progress. She values personal connections, finds the work exhilarating despite fatigue, and plans to return to private life after her term, while remaining committed to advancing human rights and opportunities, especially for women and girls.

Japan, long associated with karoshi—death from overwork—is launching a modest, voluntary measure called “Premium Friday” to nudge workers to reclaim some leisure: employees would leave at 15:00 on the last Friday of each month. The campaign, promoted by the government and business groups and starting in February, aims to reduce overtime, boost consumption, and encourage a healthier work-life balance. The initiative gained urgency after the suicide of a Dentsu employee who logged over 100 hours of monthly overtime; her death was ruled a karoshi case and prompted investigations and executive resignations, highlighting entrenched problems in Japanese workplace culture.

Past government efforts—encouraging use of paid leave, adding public holidays (Japan now has 16), flexible hours, and even office light-offs—have shifted attitudes somewhat but not significantly cut long hours. About 22% of workers put in more than 49 hours weekly, and cultural pressures—guilt about leaving colleagues, small family-run firms’ cost sensitivity, and fear of standing out—will limit uptake. Economists say widescale participation could raise private consumption substantially (estimates suggest up to ¥124 billion per Premium Friday), but full participation is unlikely; many may simply make time up on other days or pursue additional work during freed hours.

Supporters hope that a small, government-backed beginning and changing corporate loyalty among younger workers will gradually drive deeper cultural change, even as skeptics view the plan as a symbolic step rather than a solution.

A Swedish combined heat and power plant in Västerås is converting from oil and coal to become fossil fuel–free by 2020, replacing its remaining coal-fired units with biofuel and waste-burning systems. Operated by Mälardalens Energibolag (Malarenergi), the 54-year-old facility supplies power to roughly 150,000 households and already burns large volumes of municipal refuse and recycled wood. The plant has incinerated some discarded clothing from H&M’s central warehouse—about 15 tons in 2017—alongside roughly 400,000 tons of other trash used for fuel. Malarenergi views unsuitable garments as “burnable material,” while H&M says it only destroys items that are contaminated or fail chemical restrictions, asserting it does not incinerate clothing that is safe to wear.

The story highlights broader tensions in textiles management: while nearly all used clothing and household textiles can be reused or recycled—estimates suggest 45% are re-worn, 30% become industrial wiping cloths, and 20% are processed into new fibers—fast fashion generates massive volumes that strain reuse systems. The textile recycling industry includes collectors, graders, processors and distributors who sort, bale, reprocess and broker materials, with much of the sorted product shipped overseas. Some recycling firms reclaim fibers for insulation, stuffing, soundproofing and other goods. Charities historically handled donations but face overwhelming volumes and public misperceptions about reuse; only a minority of donated items are resold locally. Industry groups urge reframing donations as recycling and expanding convenient disposal options to divert textiles from landfills or incineration as nations grapple with rising clothing consumption and waste.

In late 2016 and early 2017, a fierce national fight over public lands erupted in the American West after President Obama used the Antiquities Act to designate two new national monuments—Bears Ears in Utah (1.35 million acres) and Gold Butte in Nevada (about 300,000 acres)—protecting vast, culturally and ecologically significant landscapes containing ancient Native American sites, fossils and unique habitats. Tribes and conservationists hailed the moves as crucial protections against looting, vandalism and resource extraction; Bears Ears in particular won support from a coalition of five tribes and included an unprecedented tribal advisory commission. Utah and Nevada Republican officials and many rural residents condemned the designations as federal overreach that would restrict energy and mining opportunities and local uses; Utah officials vowed legal challenges.

Shortly after, the incoming Trump administration dramatically reversed course. President Trump issued proclamations cutting Bears Ears by roughly 85% and shrinking Grand Staircase-Escalante by nearly half, splitting both into smaller units—an action defended by Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke as restoring local control and opportunity for development. Critics argued the president lacked authority to rescind or reduce monuments established by predecessors and warned the move endangered archaeological sites, wildlife habitat and outdoor recreation economies. Environmental groups, tribes and businesses like Patagonia launched lawsuits, with Patagonia calling the cuts illegal and describing them as the largest elimination of protected land in U.S. history; the company and others mobilized public protest and litigation.

The clash reflects a long-running West-wide tension between conservation and extractive development, raising legal and political questions about presidential power under the Antiquities Act, congressional authority over federal lands, tribal rights, and who should decide the future of America’s public landscapes. The disputes promised protracted court battles and sustained national debate over stewardship, local economic needs, and historic preservation.

French prosecutors said there was no evidence of foul play in celebrity chef Anthony Bourdain’s death. Bourdain, the 61-year-old host of CNN’s Parts Unknown, died by suicide Friday in his room at the luxury Le Chambard hotel in Kaysersberg, in France’s Alsace region, the prosecutor of Colmar, Christian de Rocquigny, told the Associated Press. Authorities found no signs of violence on his body and saw no indication someone else had entered the room. Investigators said the suicide did not appear highly planned. Toxicology tests, including urine analysis, were being conducted to determine whether medications or drugs played a role and to help his family understand the circumstances. Olivier Nasti, owner of Le Chambard, paid tribute to Bourdain and offered condolences from France’s culinary community.

A nearly 30-minute surveillance video from Cleveland’s Cudell Recreation Center, obtained by the Northeast Ohio Media Group after initial resistance from city officials, shows officers restraining and handcuffing 14-year-old Tamir Rice’s sister moments after her 12-year-old brother was shot by rookie officer Timothy Loehmann. The footage begins with the shooting and, within the first two minutes, captures the girl running toward Tamir as he lay wounded on snowy ground. Officer Frank Garmback is seen forcing her to the ground; Garmback and Loehmann then handcuff her and place her in the back of a patrol car parked less than ten feet from Tamir. The video corroborates the family’s earlier claims that officers delayed aid: no Cleveland officer is shown administering first aid in the critical minutes after the shooting. Instead, an off-duty or nearby FBI agent enters the frame about four minutes later and begins emergency care. Paramedics arrive roughly eight minutes after the shooting, and Tamir is taken away on a stretcher about 13 minutes later. Tamir, who was carrying an airsoft-style pistol, was shot in the abdomen within seconds of officers stopping nearby and died the next day. Family attorney Walter Madison called the officers’ treatment of the girl and perceived indifference to Tamir “shocking and outrageous.” The city has handed the investigation to the Cuyahoga County Sheriff’s Department; evidence will be presented to a grand jury to determine whether criminal charges against Loehmann and Garmback are warranted. The video has intensified scrutiny of Loehmann’s hiring and the officers’ response.

In late March 2012 mutinous soldiers in Bamako stormed the presidential palace and announced they had seized control of Mali, imposing a nationwide curfew, suspending the constitution and dissolving state institutions. Around 20 troops spoke on state television as the “National Committee for the Reestablishment of Democracy and the Restoration of the State” (CNRDR), led publicly by Capt. Amadou Sanogo, vowed not to permanently seize power but to restore unity and territorial integrity before returning authority to an elected government. The coup was driven by army anger over the government’s handling of a growing Tuareg rebellion in the north, fueled by heavily armed fighters returning from Libya; troops complained of insufficient arms and supplies. Gunfire echoed across the capital, the airport closed, ministers were reportedly arrested, and the president’s location was uncertain. Regional bloc ECOWAS and countries worldwide condemned the mutiny, warning it undermined one of West Africa’s few established democracies.

NASA has launched the “Space Poop Challenge,” inviting innovators worldwide to design a hands-free in-suit waste management system that can route and collect urine, feces and menstrual fluid away from an astronaut’s body for up to 144 hours (six days). The contest, hosted on HeroX, offers up to three prizes totaling $30,000 each and requires submissions by Dec. 20. NASA stresses that current short-term solutions—mainly highly absorbent diapers—are inadequate for extended contingencies such as cabin depressurization or long waits in a pressurized launch-and-entry suit. Extended exposure to waste risks diaper rash, infection, sepsis, and other health hazards, so proposed systems must protect crew health, suit integrity and air systems while conserving suit gas and requiring no manual access once sealed.

Designs must function in microgravity, operate within the Modified Advanced Crew Escape Suit (MACES) at 4.3 PSID and 100% oxygen, and be set up by the wearer in five minutes or less. Performance targets include up to 1 L/day urine, ~75 g/day fecal mass (75 mL fecal volume) and up to 80 mL menstrual fluid over six days. Solutions may collect waste inside the suit or route it outside, must work for diverse body sizes, and should tolerate movement, sitting and strapping in. Judges will weigh technical readiness, safety, suit integrity, gas conservation, speed, comfort and ease of incorporation. NASA aims to test winning concepts within a year and implement viable systems within three years to support future deep-space missions.

At a Warsaw press conference, Secretary of State John Kerry was briefly seen nodding off while listening to his translator during a joint event led by President Obama. The conference kicked off Obama's European trip, where he announced a $1 billion plan to boost U.S. military deployments in Europe and addressed rebuilding trust with Russia over the Ukraine crisis. Despite the momentary nap, Kerry remained active in Poland that day.

Suzanne Barr, chief of staff for ICE, has voluntarily placed herself on paid leave while DHS and ICE investigators review allegations that she fostered a “frat-house” workplace and engaged in sexually offensive conduct. Two ICE employees submitted sworn affidavits to support a discrimination and retaliation lawsuit filed by James T. Hayes Jr., a senior ICE official, alleging graphic comments and explicit offers dating to 2009. One affidavit recounts Barr making lewd comments and gestures during a Halloween discussion; another alleges heavy drinking on a Colombia trip, lewd messages from a colleague and Barr offering to perform oral sex. Hayes’ suit, which names DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano as defendant, also accuses ICE adviser Dora Schriro of displacing Hayes due to gender and lacks federal law enforcement experience. ICE referred the allegations to the DHS Office of Inspector General and ICE’s Office of Professional Responsibility; the agency says it will respond vigorously in court.

Daivon Reeder, a 22-year-old Detroit native and soon-to-be graduate of Eastern Michigan University, has gone viral after posting a graduation photo with a pointed caption about his stepfather. Reeder, who majored in Criminal Justice with a minor in Military Science, tweeted that his stepdad once told him attending orientation was pointless and he “wasn’t going to graduate anyway.” Four years later, Reeder wrote, his stepdad is in jail and he is graduating—a quip paired with a laughing emoji that captured contrast between their lives. The tweet drew thousands of shares and congratulations, thrusting Reeder into the social media spotlight overnight.

Reeder’s path to commencement wasn’t easy. He is the first in his family to attend college, arrived on scholarship, lost it, then went to Army basic training and returned determined to reclaim his aid and complete his degree. As the eldest sibling, he has supported his brothers and sisters financially, works two jobs, and navigated life as a Black student at a predominantly white institution. Lacking a steady father figure, he responded constructively by cofounding an organization with nine other students to mentor young boys—embracing a philosophy of “live, learn, teach” to pass on lessons learned through hardship.

On graduation day Reeder will don his cap and gown and receive his diploma, a milestone he frames as proof that negative expectations can be overturned. He urges others to challenge norms and be the change in their families and communities. The broader document also touches on web archiving efforts—ongoing projects to preserve web pages and federal sites—but the central human story remains Reeder’s achievement and newfound online recognition.

Former NSA contractor Reality Winner, charged under the Espionage Act for allegedly leaking a classified NSA report about Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. election, has agreed to a plea deal; details will be disclosed at a scheduled change-of-plea hearing. Her mother said the decision reflected the realities of facing an Espionage Act charge, which she called harsh and limiting of defense options, but expressed continued support and belief in her daughter. Winner had faced up to 10 years in prison and $250,000 in fines; her trial had been set for October.

The leaked top-secret NSA document, authenticated by The Intercept, detailed months-long GRU-directed cyberoperations targeting U.S. election infrastructure: a successful August 2016 compromise of a voting-software vendor (likely VR Systems), followed by October spear-phishing of about 122 local election officials using weaponized Word documents that could have granted persistent access to systems tied to voter registration databases. The NSA attributed the activity unequivocally to Russian military intelligence, though it did not conclude whether the interference affected the election’s outcome and noted many uncertainties.

Cybersecurity experts warn credential theft and remote access could enable wide data exfiltration or manipulation of voter rolls and election-management processes, potentially undermining election integrity. The report prompted concern about decentralized U.S. election administration, limited national oversight, and the need for stronger election-security resources. Winner’s case is the second guilty plea amid an administration push against leaks, contrasting with prior administrations’ more varied outcomes in leak prosecutions.

Comedian Russell Brand was reported to have been ejected from the GQ Men of the Year Awards after-show party at the Royal Opera House following a controversial acceptance speech criticizing sponsor Hugo Boss for its historical ties to the Nazi regime. After receiving an award, Brand referenced earlier jokes by Boris Johnson about Syrian chemical attacks and then accused Hugo Boss of having “made the uniforms for the Nazis,” adding that “they did look f***** fantastic” while “killing people on the basis of their religion and sexuality.” He also mimicked a Hitler moustache and goose-stepped onstage. GQ editor Dylan Jones allegedly told Brand his remarks were offensive to Hugo Boss; Brand tweeted that he replied such actions were offensive to Jews, tagging #nazitailor. Brand was photographed mingling with Noel Gallagher and Rita Ora before leaving with security. The event, hosted by Rob Brydon, featured other contentious moments—Brydon’s joke about Stephen Fry’s suicide attempt and writer Charles Moore’s critique of Brand’s past Sachsgate scandal. Hugo Boss had sponsored the evening with a reported £250,000 contribution. GQ declined to comment on claims of Brand’s ejection.

The New Jersey Supreme Court unanimously ruled that breath-test results from Alcotest devices calibrated by a State Police sergeant are inadmissible, potentially jeopardizing more than 20,000 DWI cases. The decision stems from allegations that Sgt. Marc Dennis, who calibrated devices used in Middlesex, Monmouth, Ocean, Somerset and Union counties between 2008 and 2016, falsified records by omitting a state-required temperature check during calibration. Dennis denies wrongdoing and has pleaded not guilty; his criminal case remains pending.

The court vacated the conviction of Eileen Cassidy, who had pleaded guilty based on one of those breath tests and died while the legal fight continued, and ordered authorities to notify all defendants whose cases involved devices Dennis handled. The justices, agreeing with a special master judge, found that skipping the temperature check raised substantial doubts about the machines’ reliability, despite state claims that the omitted step was one of several redundancies and that New Jersey uniquely requires it.

County prosecutors had been notifying affected defendants since 2016 but had held cases in abeyance pending this ruling. The court’s order requires broader notification so individuals can decide whether to seek vacatur of convictions. Attorney General Gurbir Grewal said his office will issue guidance to prosecutors. It remains unclear how many convictions will be overturned because some defendants were found not guilty at trial or convicted without relying on breath tests, and many may have already served penalties or license suspensions.

Bristol Palin and partner Mark Ballas were eliminated from Dancing with the Stars: All-Stars after failing to secure enough audience votes despite not receiving the judges’ lowest score that week. For the first time, Kirstie Alley and Maks Chmerkovskiy earned the judges’ lowest marks, while Palin and Ballas performed a rock ’n’ roll routine that drew praise for Palin’s improvement. Palin’s mother, former Republican VP candidate Sarah Palin, attended the show. Apolo Ohno and Karina Smirnoff — who had an emotional moment after a fall in a hip-hop number — were also in the bottom three. When host Tom Bergeron announced the bottom contenders, Alley and Chmerkovskiy reportedly giggled. Palin thanked her partner and wished fellow competitors luck as she exited. Ballas later reflected that wardrobe choices and risk-taking can impact longevity in the competition; he noted Palin opted against matching “bunny” costumes he had suggested and acknowledged that stepping outside comfort zones can pay off in an all-star season full of champions and finalists. He defended Palin’s progress given her lack of dance experience and said he was proud of her growth. After elimination he planned to support remaining pairs Shawn Johnson and Derek Hough, and Sabrina Bryan and Louis Van Amstel. Next week contestants will perform team freestyles and individual dances to “guilty pleasure” songs.

The piece critiques media coverage of Mitt Romney’s planned renovation of a La Jolla beach house, arguing a widely circulated claim that he sought to “quadruple” the property’s size was misleading. Publisher Joseph McQuaid reports Romney told him the permit application, filed two years earlier, sought to double living space by converting one story into two; the “quadrupling” figure counted nonliving areas such as a basement and garage. McQuaid says Romney shrugged off issuing a clarification, prompting the publisher’s call for greater accuracy from journalists rather than letting stories fit preconceived notions about wealth and privilege. The columnist recounts a light moment at Manchester’s Red Arrow Diner—where staff wanted a better photo of Romney—and describes Romney as more personable than stereotypes suggest: animated, willing to disagree politely, and persistent with hecklers. The piece stresses that small technical distinctions in reporting matter because they shape perceptions of candidates and influence how presidents are chosen, urging media professionals to prioritize precision over reinforcing assumptions about Romney’s affluence or detachment from ordinary Americans.

Endo Pharmaceuticals set up a donation page for employees to give directly to the American Red Cross to support disaster relief in Huntsville, Alabama, and other communities hit by spring storms, matching all donations made through close of business March 21, 2012. Separately, U.S. mobile users rapidly donated millions for Haiti earthquake relief via text campaigns, giving $10 per text to organizations including the Red Cross, Yele, and the Clinton Foundation. By early Friday, more than $8 million had been pledged via the Red Cross text code 90999, with donations arriving at roughly $200,000 per hour; Verizon reported over $1 million from its users. Mobile giving vastly exceeded earlier records (Katrina, Asian tsunami). Wireless carriers largely waived messaging fees for these donations—Verizon and T‑Mobile confirmed waivers; AT&T and Sprint initially did not, then announced retroactive fee waivers—highlighting mobile giving as a powerful new philanthropy channel.

Ukraine’s defense minister said Kyiv will only resume cease-fire talks with pro-Russian insurgents in the east once the rebels surrender their weapons, reflecting growing confidence after government forces recaptured Slovyansk. President Petro Poroshenko had promised talks, but recent military gains — including routing militants from Slovyansk and forcing many to regroup in Donetsk — appear to have shifted Kiev’s stance. Rebels rejected proposed talks in Svyatogorsk, a government-controlled town, preferring Donetsk, Russia or Belarus. A previous 10-day cease-fire produced little progress; more than 400 people have died and thousands displaced during months of standoff since the government change in February. Russia, which has encouraged the separatists, remained publicly muted after the loss in Slovyansk, wary of provoking further Western sanctions. Ukrainian forces claimed victory in Slovyansk after intense artillery bombardment and improved coordination among regular army, special forces, National Guard units and volunteer battalions. The city is scarred—no running water, intermittent gas and electricity, and many residents displaced—yet not destroyed. Rebels staged a breakout toward Donetsk, where fears of a larger, bloodier siege are rising; many civilians have fled but most have nowhere to go. Insurgents have prepared defenses around Donetsk, destroying bridges and even attempting to restore a museum tank for combat, signaling the conflict’s brutality is far from over.

On the first anniversary of the Boston Marathon bombings, survivors, first responders, families of the victims and civic leaders gathered for solemn ceremonies across the city to remember the three victims killed at the race and MIT police Officer Sean Collier, who died days later. Events included a wreath-laying in Copley Square, a memorial program at the Hynes Convention Center with musical tributes, and a flag-raising and moment of silence at the finish line where two bombs exploded. Survivors, including Patrick Downes and Adrianne Haslet-Davis, recounted losses and resilience; many wounded or bereaved pledged to run or otherwise participate in the upcoming marathon, embodying the “Boston Strong” spirit praised by Vice President Joe Biden and President Obama. Officials and clergy, including Gov. Deval Patrick, Mayor Marty Walsh and Cardinal Sean O’Malley, offered prayers and remarks. Authorities recapped the investigation: brothers Tamerlan and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev were identified as the attackers; Tamerlan died after a shootout and Dzhokhar faces federal charges. Security remained heightened: a late-evening bomb-squad response disrupted two suspicious backpacks near Boylston Street (one a hoax device, one belonging to media), and police discouraged backpacks at the next marathon to reduce risk.

Pope Benedict XVI’s unprecedented decision to resign has sparked intense debate in the Vatican over the role and status of a living former pope. Resigning on Feb. 28, Benedict will surrender the formal powers of the papacy—his ring will be broken and he will no longer appoint bishops or speak ex cathedra—but plans to remain inside Vatican walls, first at Castel Gandolfo and then in the newly renovated Mater Ecclesiae convent. Vatican officials stress he will live a cloistered life of prayer and writing and has pledged not to interfere with his successor. Still, his continued presence raises concerns: he may influence matters such as senior appointments (he was expected to appoint a new Vatican bank chief) and anything he writes or says will be scrutinized against the new pope’s positions. Church lawyers and officials are debating his title, vestments and whether he may grant private audiences. Benedict’s recent public appearances—an Ash Wednesday homily condemning church infighting and an emotional farewell to Roman priests—underscored lingering divisions and scandals that marked his eight-year papacy and shaped the conclave that will elect his successor.

Rachel Park, 39, who had recently spent her first Christmas at home with her prematurely born triplet daughters, has died suddenly at the family home in Bransty, Whitehaven. Police have described her death as "unexplained but not suspicious." Rachel and her husband Steven, 37, welcomed Poppie, Mollie and Evelyn on 11 March after a difficult pregnancy complicated by pre-eclampsia and a severe bleed that required emergency care and an early caesarean. The girls were born at around 26 weeks, weighing just over 5lb 2oz combined, and spent 111 days in neonatal units in Newcastle’s Royal Victoria Infirmary and later West Cumberland Hospital. Each baby faced serious early health scares, requiring incubators, ventilators and extended hospital treatment, but gradually improved and were discharged just in time to be at home for Christmas, a milestone their parents had feared might not come.

Rachel and Steven had tried for years to start a family and achieved pregnancy on a fourth cycle of IVF; the surprise of non-identical triplets followed. Friends and local mums remember Rachel as a supportive presence who helped other triplet mothers. In the wake of her death, community members have launched fundraising appeals to support Steven and the three infants. A GoFundMe and PayPal appeal have raised several thousand pounds toward immediate needs. Tributes describe Rachel’s death as "tragic and heartbreaking," and supporters say they aim to give the family practical and emotional support in the coming months.

Automakers and their trade groups pushed the Obama administration to finalize the EPA’s “Tier 3” rule to cut gasoline sulfur and tighten vehicle emissions standards, meeting with White House OMB officials and EPA staff on March 22. Participants included the Alliance of Automobile Manufacturers, Global Automakers and companies such as Toyota, Chrysler, Honda, Volkswagen and Mercedes. They argued the rule is critically important for public health, harmonizing federal standards with California’s stricter rules, and ensuring fuels compatible with stricter fuel-economy and greenhouse-gas regulations already set by the administration. Automakers said refiners’ cost estimates to achieve lower sulfur have been overstated, noting many refineries already produce ultra-low sulfur fuels in California, Europe and Japan. The EPA planned to announce the nationwide rule, which would cut gasoline sulfur by two-thirds and impose fleet-wide vehicle pollution limits by 2017. The administration estimated the rule would add less than a penny per gallon and yield health benefits comparable to removing 33 million cars, with up to $23 billion in annual benefits by 2030. Oil industry groups countered costs could be much higher—up to 9 cents per gallon or billions in capital upgrades—and lobbied for delay. The rule includes flexibility: a three-year delay for small refiners, early-action incentives and a credit-trading program. Supporters touted large reductions in smog-forming pollutants and fewer respiratory and heart illnesses; critics warned of heavy regulatory burdens on refiners.

Harold “Butch” Knight, 67, is wanted for the January 2015 slaying of his wife, 48-year-old Sara Knight, after authorities say he called 911 and confessed to strangling her. Police found Sara dead in the couple’s Ganges Township, Michigan, home after a call believed to be from Knight on Jan. 13 reporting he had harmed her two days earlier and instructing dispatchers to “do whatever they do with dead bodies.” Knight vanished shortly afterward and has been the subject of a lengthy manhunt that has stretched from Michigan to Maine.

Investigators recovered Sara’s vehicle abandoned in Franklin County, Maine, and surveillance photos later placed Knight in the Rangely area, wearing camouflage clothing with dyed black hair and a mustache. Because Knight previously lived near Rangely and had shown an interest in Amish communities—detectives found books about them in his pole barn—authorities checked local Amish settlements as potential hiding places. Law enforcement agencies, including the FBI and U.S. Marshals, have followed tips nationwide; Knight is considered armed and dangerous.

Sara’s daughter, Roxanne Cameron-Harris, has been leading public efforts for answers and capture. She created a GoFundMe and is selling pink T-shirts reading “No Evil Goes Unpunished – Justice for Sara Lee” to raise reward money and public awareness, and she has organized a vigil for the anniversary of Sara’s death. Roxanne says she believes Knight is playing a calculated game, possibly hiding nearby, and fears someone may be assisting him. Family members reported suspicious activity on Sara’s Facebook account last year, which investigators tried to trace. With months of false leads and few breakthroughs, the family continues to press authorities for leads and urges anyone with information to contact the Allegan County Sheriff’s Office.

Nearly 30 years after he vanished, Edgar Latulip, a man from Kitchener, Ontario, has been found alive and his identity confirmed, bringing a remarkable resolution to a long-running missing-persons case. Latulip disappeared at age 21 from southern Ontario and was believed to have travelled by bus to the Niagara Falls area; he has a developmental delay, which complicated earlier searches. Over the years, investigators received tips placing him in locations such as Hamilton, but they were unable to locate him. Unknown to his family and authorities, Latulip had suffered a head injury shortly after arriving in the Niagara region and effectively forgot who he was, living under an unknown identity in St. Catharines for many years. In January of this year he told a social worker in St. Catharines that he had remembered his name, a disclosure that set official processes in motion. Waterloo Regional Police followed up and, on a recent Friday, a DNA test confirmed the man was indeed Edgar Latulip. Detective Constable Duane Gingerich of Waterloo Regional Police described the case as unique in his experience because of the long interval between disappearance and recovery. Latulip is reported to be doing well, and plans are underway for a reunion with his family; his mother, Silvia Wilson, said she is overwhelmed though she has not yet spoken with him. Police continue to coordinate the reunion and further steps to ensure Latulip’s well-being after nearly three decades apart, offering closure to a case that had long weighed on his family and the community.

Belarus held a presidential election in which long-time authoritarian Alexander Lukashenko was widely expected to claim a fifth term. Lukashenko publicly insisted that any result under about 80% would indicate slipping support; he previously won 79.65% in 2010. Early voting over five days saw the election commission report 36% participation before election day and nearly 75% turnout by mid-afternoon, figures contested by the opposition and international observers who warned early voting and unsecured ballot boxes invite falsification. The opposition largely boycotted, citing a sham process; prominent critics were barred or stayed off the ballot. Lukashenko faced only nominal rivals—two pro-government party leaders and a little-known activist—while key past opponents were jailed after earlier elections. During his 21-year rule he has suppressed dissent, promoted stability and maintained a Soviet-style economy propped by cheap Russian gas and Western loans, which many citizens say still provides for pensioners and factory workers even as others call for change. Recent gestures—pardoning several political prisoners—have aimed at easing Western sanctions. The opposition planned a modest post-election protest expected to be allowed to proceed peacefully.

A June 27, 2011 analysis explains what could happen if Congress fails to raise the $14.3 trillion debt ceiling before federal cash runs out. Updated Treasury data extend the daily outlook through August and detail “layers of defense.” By Aug. 3–4, the government’s cash balances would be nearly exhausted: August obligations total about $306.7 billion while projected revenues from Aug. 3–31 are $172.4 billion, creating roughly a $134 billion shortfall in August alone. The president would face wrenching choices about which obligations to pay—Social Security, military and veterans’ pay, unemployment benefits, student loans, bondholders—and prioritizing bond payments to protect creditworthiness could force cuts to many programs. Failure to raise the limit risks missed Treasury payments, bond-rating downgrades, fewer buyers of Treasuries, sharply higher borrowing costs and widespread economic disruption, including higher mortgage and credit rates.

Ohio state troopers arrested 31-year-old Daniel A. Yates of Eureka, California, after a traffic stop on Interstate 80 in Wood County for following too closely on Nov. 21, 2016. Troopers stopped his rented 2016 Ford Expedition, noticed criminal indicators, and a patrol drug-sniffing dog alerted to the vehicle. A probable-cause search uncovered 10 gift-wrapped boxes in the trunk and back seat containing about 71 pounds of marijuana, 360 THC pills and a pound of hash wax oil. The seizure’s estimated street value was roughly $330,000. Yates was jailed and charged with possession and trafficking in drugs, both second-degree felonies; if convicted he faces up to 16 years in prison and up to a $30,000 fine.

An undercover investigator for Compassion Over Killing filmed graphic footage in May–June at four Tyson-connected broiler breeder facilities in Virginia showing workers punching, kicking, throwing and suffocating chickens, sticking plastic rods into beaks (“boning”), running over birds with forklifts, and leaving injured animals to die. The animal-rights group filed complaints with local authorities; county animal-control officials confirmed investigations. Compassion Over Killing called the abuse systemic and urged accountability. Tyson, which fired 10 employees seen in the video, called the behavior “inexcusable,” said it discontinued beak-modification at the implicated sites, and announced companywide retraining and management briefings on animal-handling policies. Tyson said it is evaluating further steps to ensure humane treatment, while advocates argue the only safeguard is foregoing animal consumption.

Hurricane Irma battered Florida and the Caribbean as one of the largest and most destructive storms in recent U.S. history. Making U.S. landfall first in the lower Keys and later near Marco Island and Naples, Irma produced sustained winds up to 130 mph, widespread storm surge, torrential rainfall and tornadoes. Its nearly 400-mile-wide circulation caused flooding, snapped construction cranes, uprooted trees, ripped roofs off buildings and left millions without power—estimates of outages reached into the several millions, with utilities warning full restoration could take weeks. Officials imposed curfews in many areas to deter looting; arrests were reported. At least several Florida deaths were tied to storm-related crashes and other incidents. Local and federal authorities, including FEMA and the White House, mobilized resources: governors declared emergencies, the president approved disaster declarations, the National Guard and thousands of responders staged for recovery, and shelters housed tens of thousands. Irma’s projected path up Florida’s Gulf coast threatened Tampa Bay and the Big Bend, while forecasts warned of life-threatening storm surge (10–15 feet in places) and massive rainfall totals. The storm also devastated Caribbean islands, prompting international rescue and relief efforts. Officials urged residents to heed evacuation orders and shelter warnings; recovery and damage assessments were to begin once conditions allowed.

Australian Prime Minister Julia Gillard sparked controversy after posing for Australian Women’s Weekly knitting a toy kangaroo as a gift for the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge’s expected baby. She framed the project as a practical hobby—smaller projects fit her busy schedule—and described the shoot as a way to show a different side of herself. The staged photos, showing Gillard in an armchair surrounded by wool with her dog Reuben at her feet, were published alongside an interview covering her legacy, family, republicanism and the looming federal election.

The origins of the shoot became disputed: Gillard’s communications director, John McTernan, pushed the idea to the magazine and described it as a “no-brainer,” while the PM’s office later said the magazine requested the knitting and inclusion of Reuben. Critics in the media and opposition called the images contrived, a PR stunt and at odds with Gillard’s typically non-feminine public persona. Commentators likened the pictures to sentimental or even caricatured portrayals of women; opponents used them to underline perceived disconnection from voters. Supporters noted hostile treatment Gillard has faced, including sexist remarks and personal attacks, and defended her right to present multiple facets of her identity.

Widely reproduced, the photoshoot damaged Gillard’s public standing in some eyes, offering ammunition to opponents as she faces poor polls and a heated election campaign.

This document collects criticism of Sarah Palin’s recent conduct and commentary around journalism, the Gulf oil spill, and her record on energy and environmental matters. Michael Wolff profiles Joe McGinniss, a relentless reporter who moved next door to Palin’s Alaska home; Palin and conservative media figures mobilized followers to harass him, which Wolff frames as abuse of political power and crowd incitement. Separately, Palin’s lengthy op-ed criticizes President Obama’s response to the Gulf spill, accusing his administration of delayed leadership, buck-passing, and insufficient use of authorities in the Oil Pollution Act; she urges continued domestic drilling, rejects a shutdown of Alaska development, and frames oil and gas as a “bridge” to renewables. Her claims prompt pushback: Robert Gibbs disputed her suggestion that campaign donations from oil companies explain Obama’s actions, and fact-checkers note mixed evidence about response timing. Media and Alaska legal experts challenge Palin’s credibility—her account of involvement in Exxon Valdez litigation is labeled inaccurate by lead plaintiffs’ attorneys. Critics argue Palin lacks the standing to lead the argument she’s making, while acknowledging legitimate concerns about the spill response and industry accountability.

A 16-year-old girl will be charged as an adult in the killing of her 7-year-old nephew, Jordan Vong, Denver prosecutors announced. According to a probable cause statement and police, the girl lived in the basement bedroom of the family home in Montbello. On Aug. 6 she was upset after an argument with her girlfriend when Jordan asked to play video games. She told him to leave; after he lay on her bed and would not go, she pushed him off, and he struck his face on the floor. When he began to cry, she covered his mouth and nose while he struggled; he stopped moving. She first slid his body under her bed, later wrapped him in a blanket and hid him in a portable closet. Jordan was reported missing that afternoon, prompting an extensive search involving posters, neighborhood canvassing and the FBI. A search warrant executed two days later led to discovery of his body; the coroner ruled the death a homicide, though the specific cause awaits determination. The girl faces suspicion of first-degree murder and child abuse resulting in death; her identity is withheld because she is a juvenile. Court proceedings have not yet been scheduled.

Far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon opened his 2017 presidential campaign in Lyon using hologram technology to relay his speech simultaneously to a rally in Paris, aiming for a modern, high-tech launch that coincided with rival Marine Le Pen’s event. Mélenchon, in a Nehru-style jacket, sought to present himself as a major opponent to Le Pen; both share skepticism toward the EU and globalization but diverge sharply on migration and other issues. At the rally he criticized Socialist candidate Benoît Hamon, questioning what prevents Hamon from joining calls to abolish the unpopular El Khomri labor law. Polls at the time placed Mélenchon at about 11–11.5 percent support, behind Le Pen, Emmanuel Macron, François Fillon and Hamon.

The campaign unfolded against a backdrop of heightened concerns about misinformation. Facebook announced it had targeted 30,000 fake accounts linked to France ahead of the two-round election scheduled for April 23 and May 7, as part of a broader effort to curb inauthentic activity worldwide. The company reported removing high-traffic sites tied to deceptive content, launching user resources to spot false news in multiple countries, and collaborating with fact-checkers and media to bolster news integrity following criticism over misinformation’s role in the U.S. election.

As voting approached, France’s political landscape was unusually fragmented: four candidates—Fillon, Le Pen, Macron and Mélenchon—were within striking distance of advancing to the second round, according to an Ipsos-Sopra Steria poll. Voter indecision was high, especially among younger citizens, and the weakened Socialist Party under François Hollande’s presidency appeared unlikely to progress beyond the first round. The outcome remained uncertain, with global attention on whether France would follow recent populist trends.

SiriusXM and Reprise will release An American Treasure on September 28: a posthumous Tom Petty box set compiling 60 tracks across four CDs (and special vinyl/2-CD editions). Curated by Petty’s daughter Adria, wife Dana, longtime Heartbreakers Benmont Tench and Mike Campbell, and collaborator Ryan Ulyate, the collection features unreleased studio tracks, alternate versions, deep cuts and historic live performances spanning Petty’s career—from 1974 Mudcrutch material through Wildflowers, Long After Dark, Mojo and 2014’s Hypnotic Eye. The first preview is “Keep a Little Soul,” an unreleased 1982 track. Deluxe packages include extensive booklets, essays, rare photos, lyric reproductions and special artwork by Shepard Fairey. The release follows Petty’s death in October 2017, later ruled an accidental overdose.

Dennis Oland’s defence abruptly closed its case Thursday in the second-degree murder trial over the 2011 bludgeoning death of his father, prominent New Brunswick businessman Richard Oland. Defence lawyer Gary Miller told the Saint John Court of Queen’s Bench there was “no need to call any other evidence” after Dennis had testified on Tuesday and Wednesday, maintaining he did not kill his father and expressing love and grief on the stand. The defence called only two additional witnesses: a bloodstain analyst and a forensic computer expert. Several family members who were expected to testify—mother Connie, sister Jacqueline Walsh, wife Lisa Andrik‑Oland, uncle Jack Connell and friend Mary Beth Watt—were not called.

Richard Oland, 69, was found face down in his uptown Saint John office on July 7, 2011, with dozens of sharp and blunt-force injuries; no weapon was recovered. Dennis, then 47 and the last known person to see his father alive, was the subject of earlier police interviews that contained inconsistencies with his trial testimony. He acknowledged differences—such as how many times he visited the office that night and what jacket he wore—but said shock and grief affected his earlier statements. A brown Hugo Boss jacket seized from his closet bore three small bloodstains matched to Richard’s DNA; Dennis said he had been “mistaken” about the jacket description in his police statement.

Judge John Walsh recessed jurors until Dec. 14 to allow counsel to prepare closing arguments and for the judge to prepare lengthy jury instructions; deliberations could start as early as Dec. 16. Jurors will be sequestered and one of the 13 will be randomly dismissed so 12 will deliberate. The judge warned the jury their task will be “mentally exhausting” and urged them to avoid media coverage during the break. The high‑profile trial, one of New Brunswick’s longest, encompassed nearly 50 witnesses over 47 days and explored potential motives including Dennis’s financial troubles and Richard’s extramarital affair. The verdict now rests with the jury.

Snap Inc., the parent of Snapchat, launched one of the year’s highest-profile tech IPOs amid widespread enthusiasm and notable concerns. The company set an initial price near $17 a share—above an early $14–$16 range—valuing Snap roughly at $20–24 billion and raising about $3.4 billion. The offering was heavily oversubscribed, and Snap sold 200 million shares, though many went to long-term investors under optional one-year “lockup” arrangements intended to stabilize the stock.

Investors’ excitement coexists with skepticism. Snap’s revenue surged—reportedly more than 500% in one year to about $404 million—but losses grew too, and management warned it might never be profitable. Daily active users reached roughly 158 million, a strong base but showing decelerating growth that management partly attributes to competition and Android performance issues. Facebook/Instagram’s replication of key Snapchat features (notably Stories) is a major competitive threat, and observers worry Snap must convert “cool” youth engagement into sustained ad monetization at scale.

Snap’s product and culture differ from typical Silicon Valley peers. CEO Evan Spiegel is seen as secretive and controlling; the company is described as decentralized, with an emphasis on product design, ephemeral communication, and camera-driven mobile experiences. Snapchat’s focus on less intrusive, broadly appealing ads—Lenses, geofilters and short video ads—has attracted direct brand spending but has been slower to win big ad-agency commitments and precise targeting capabilities that drive Facebook’s profits. Snap has begun partnerships (Oracle, Nielsen) to improve ad measurement.

Governance is unusual: public investors receive nonvoting shares, while Spiegel and cofounder Bobby Murphy retain the vast majority of voting power via a multi-class share structure, raising corporate-governance concerns. The IPO will force greater transparency on user and engagement metrics and put pressure on Snap to demonstrate a clear path to sustainable growth and profitability amid stiff competition.

A new Economic Policy Institute (EPI) report finds that chief executives at the 350 largest U.S. firms earned on average 312 times more than typical workers in 2017, driven by a 17.6% jump in CEO pay to about $18.9 million while typical worker compensation rose only 0.3%. The widening gap has been long-term: CEO-to-worker ratios rose from roughly 20:1 in 1965 to peaks around 344:1 in 2000, fell with market downturns, and surged again as stock-linked pay recovered. Stock-related components—realized stock options and stock awards—accounted for nearly all the 2017 increase, with options exercised fueling the bulk of year-over-year growth. EPI shows CEO pay growth far outpaced broader market returns and worker pay: from 1978–2017 CEO compensation rose about 979–1,070% versus 637% for the S&P 500 and just 11.2% for typical workers. High-profile examples illustrate extremes: McDonald’s CEO’s total pay implied a 3,101:1 ratio versus median McDonald’s worker; Walmart’s CEO-to-worker ratio exceeded 1,000:1. The report argues these patterns reflect economic rents and managerial influence over pay, not purely market-for-talent forces, noting CEO pay has grown faster than other top earners. EPI cautions that excessive CEO pay diverts income from broader wage growth and outlines policy options—tax reforms, governance changes, pay caps or penalties—to rein in pay inequality and promote more equitable wage gains.

Yelp Inc., the San Francisco-based consumer review site founded in 2004 by former PayPal engineers Jeremy Stoppelman and Russel Simmons, priced its IPO at $15 a share and debuted strongly, closing up 64% at $24.58, valuing the company around $1.47 billion. The offering raised roughly $106.5–$123 million before expenses and featured a dual-class share structure concentrating voting power with insiders. Yelp, known for more than 25 million reviews and about 66 million monthly unique visitors (5.7 million mobile devices), sells local advertising and daily deals, though it remains unprofitable—posting a $16.7 million loss on $83.3 million revenue in 2011 and carrying about $41.2 million in accumulated deficit. Analysts attribute the exuberant debut partly to momentum in social media IPOs and anticipation of Facebook’s listing; similar earlier debuts include LinkedIn, Groupon and Zillow, though some have since retreated. Yelp faces intense competition from Google (and its Zagat acquisition), Facebook, Foursquare, Groupon and Angie's List. Management emphasizes user trust by separating ads from reviews and filtering unreliable posts, but critics worry about monetization limits, high operating costs and competition siphoning local ad dollars. As a public company, Yelp’s growth and path to sustained profitability will be closely scrutinized.

A massive, unexplained bloom of pyrosomes—tiny, tubular colonial animals nicknamed “unicorns of the sea,” “sea pickles,” or “fire bodies”—has appeared along the U.S. West Coast, stretching from Oregon up to Sitka, Alaska. Pyrosomes are gelatinous tubes formed from many cloned zooids; usually tropical and offshore, they can reach substantial lengths as colonies and sometimes glow. This year’s swarms are unprecedented in density and coastal presence: researchers and fishers report nets and hooks coming up full of the creatures, catches ruined, and beaches littered with washed-up colonies. One research cruise recorded roughly 60,000 pyrosomes in five minutes. The phenomenon has stunned many scientists who had never seen pyrosomes in decades of work. Research teams from institutions including the University of Oregon, NOAA and Oregon State are racing to document and sample live specimens to study feeding, movement, reproduction and ecological effects. Possible causes discussed include warming seas linked to climate change, altered currents, or shifts in prey availability; however, the cause remains unclear. Scientists also worry about potential ecosystem impacts: if large numbers die and sink, their decomposition could deplete oxygen and create localized dead zones, and dense blooms may have economic costs for fisheries. Researchers hope monitoring how long the bloom persists and studying conditions before and after will reveal why these typically tropical organisms have proliferated so close to shore.

Facebook disclosed it has identified an influence operation likely based in Russia that spent about $100,000 on roughly 3,000 U.S. ads over a two-year span through May, promoting divisive social and political messages rather than explicitly advocating for a presidential candidate. The company traced the spending to buyers linked to a known St. Petersburg “troll farm” (the Internet Research Agency) and uncovered 470 “inauthentic” accounts and pages that were suspended for violating authenticity rules. Topics promoted included immigration, race, LGBT issues and gun rights. Facebook also flagged another $50,000 on some 2,200 potentially political ads, some purchased in Russian yet shown to English-speaking users.

Facebook’s security chief Alex Stamos published the findings and briefed congressional intelligence committees and special counsel Robert Mueller’s team; the company said it is cooperating with federal inquiries. While Facebook found no direct link between the ads and any presidential campaign and most ads were national rather than swing-state targeted, the revelations support U.S. intelligence conclusions that Russia sought to shape the 2016 election. The announcement follows criticism that Facebook enabled the spread of false information and demonstrates new challenges beyond traditional spam or hacking—namely coordinated influence operations using fake accounts, targeted data and seeded content. Observers urged Facebook to strengthen detection and transparency, noting foreign spending on election-related advocacy is illegal and that the company’s role in the media landscape carries heightened responsibility.

Bernard Charles, a 42-year-old citizen of Trinidad and Tobago, was arrested at John F. Kennedy International Airport on April 1 after Customs and Border Protection officers discovered nearly two pounds of heroin concealed in his groin. Charles drew attention when he arrived on Caribbean Airlines flight 520 and appeared “visibly nervous,” avoided eye contact, and walked awkwardly while officers inspected his luggage. During a pat-down prompted by his gait, agents found a hard object in his groin area; a private search uncovered two clear plastic packages containing a brown paste-like substance that later tested positive for heroin. Authorities seized a total of 1.79 pounds of the drug, with an estimated street value exceeding $70,000. Charles was detained, ordered held without bail, and transferred to Homeland Security Investigations to face federal narcotics smuggling charges carrying up to 10 years in prison if convicted. New York Field Operations Director Robert Perez praised the officers’ vigilance in preventing illegal drugs from entering the United States.

Former Trump bodyguard and longtime aide Keith Schiller privately told House Intelligence Committee investigators that during Donald Trump’s 2013 trip to Moscow for the Miss Universe pageant he rejected an offer—presented by a Russian accompanying promoter Emin Agalarov—to send five women to Trump’s hotel room. Multiple sources from both parties said Schiller characterized the offer as a joke, relayed it to Trump, and that both men laughed it off. Schiller said he stayed outside Trump’s door for several minutes, his standard security practice, and did not observe anyone enter the room. He could not recall the identity of the individual who made the offer and denied that Agalarov personally extended it; Agalarov’s attorney disputed reports implicating his client.

The committee raised the episode because it echoes lurid claims in the unverified Christopher Steele dossier, which alleged Russia possessed kompromat on Trump and detailed salacious conduct in Moscow. Trump has consistently denied the dossier’s allegations and publicly attacked its origins, noting it derived from opposition research funded by the Clinton campaign and DNC. FBI Director James Comey briefed Trump and Obama on the dossier before the inauguration; Comey later testified Trump denied the allegations to him on multiple occasions. The FBI corroborated some dossier details and used parts to help obtain a surveillance warrant for adviser Carter Page, but investigators have not verified the dossier’s most explosive claims about the Moscow trip.

Schiller also denied knowledge of meetings between Trump associates and Russians and said he was unaware of deliberations around Comey’s firing, claiming he merely delivered the termination letter to the FBI. His lawyer criticized leaks from the committee, calling them misleading and indefensible. White House officials declined to comment.

On what would have been Sen. John McCain’s 82nd birthday, family, friends, veterans and constituents gathered at the Arizona State Capitol for the first of two days of services honoring the longtime Arizona senator who died Saturday of an aggressive brain cancer at 81. A private morning ceremony in the Capitol rotunda, where McCain lay in state with a flag-draped casket, included remarks from Gov. Doug Ducey and former Sen. Jon Kyl, and a benediction by Sen. Jeff Flake. Ducey called McCain “Arizona’s favorite adopted son,” saying imagining Arizona without him was like picturing the state without the Grand Canyon. Kyl praised McCain’s instincts on national security and said he would be missed.

Cindy McCain and McCain’s children attended the private ceremony; Cindy pressed her face to the casket and several family members, including sons in uniform and daughter Meghan McCain, wept as they touched it. Arizona National Guard honor guards carried the casket into the rotunda, which had been draped in black and encircled with U.S. and state flags.

By midmorning, hundreds of people had begun lining up under canopies in the 90-plus-degree heat to view the casket during the public viewing scheduled for the afternoon and evening. Volunteers distributed water and ice. Attendees included longtime supporters across party lines—Democrats who admired McCain’s independence, veterans who praised his advocacy, out-of-state visitors who flew or drove to pay respects, and a high-school student who combined the visit with a class requirement. Freeway electronic signs offered tributes urging “Country First Rest In Peace Senator McCain.”

The schedule called for a public procession through Phoenix to a memorial service Thursday at North Phoenix Baptist Church, a departure from Phoenix Sky Harbor, a viewing at the U.S. Capitol Friday, a memorial at Washington National Cathedral Saturday, and a private burial Sunday at the U.S. Naval Academy in Annapolis. Organizers said public viewings would continue as long as people remained in line.

NASA's Curiosity rover has delivered a major set of findings, summarized in six Science papers, that reshape our understanding of early Mars roughly 3–4 billion years ago. Curiosity confirmed that Gale Crater hosted streams, a long, shallow freshwater lake, and extensive groundwater systems that created fine-grained mudstones with clay minerals—conditions broadly capable of supporting microbial life. The lake may have persisted for tens of thousands to millions of years and could have been ice-covered at times, yet still habitable for hardy microbes such as chemolithoautotrophs that derive energy from rock and mineral chemistry. Curiosity’s Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument has identified up to six organic compounds, though their Martian origin remains uncertain because of destructive chlorine-bearing salts and contamination from a solvent in the instrument. Radiation measurements from the Radiation Assessment Detector reveal that surface radiation levels would likely be fatal to microbes within a few million years, implying that survival today would require deep burial or special niches. Kenneth Farley’s dating of surface exposure (about 80 million years at Yellowknife Bay) suggests strategies for drilling into better-preserved, less-radiation-damaged rocks. While Curiosity hasn’t detected life, its discoveries make ancient habitable environments on Mars far more plausible and guide future sampling.

Nelson Mandela’s name has become shorthand for equality, freedom and revolution, and his death at 95 in Johannesburg prompted an outpouring of tributes across music and world leaders. Musicians from many genres have long honored Mandela through songs that celebrate his struggle and influence. U2’s “Ordinary Love,” written for the biopic Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom, captures the spirit of his life with lines about ordinary love as a guiding ideal. South African jazz great Hugh Masekela’s 1987 “Mandela (Bring Him Back Home)” voiced the hope of seeing Mandela free. The Special A.K.A.’s 1984 upbeat protest “Free Nelson Mandela” demanded his release while celebrating resilience. Senegalese star Youssou N’Dour released an album titled Nelson Mandela in 1986; Public Enemy name-checked him in politically charged “Prophets of Rage.” Santana’s instrumental “Mandela” and Simple Minds’ “Mandela Day” were performed at Mandela’s 70th birthday celebration, as was Tracy Chapman’s protest song “Freedom Now.” Tupac’s poem “Just a Breath of Freedom (4 Nelson Mandela)” and Johnny Clegg’s bilingual “Asimbonanga” (meaning “We have not seen him”) also honored Mandela’s sacrifice; Clegg later performed it with Mandela in 1999. Following Mandela’s death, President Barack Obama eulogized him as a moral giant who “bent the arc of the moral universe toward justice,” ordered flags at half-staff, and praised Mandela’s example of courage, humility and reconciliation. Obama, who was personally inspired by Mandela and visited Robben Island, said Mandela’s legacy now “belongs to the ages” and urged emulation of his commitment to love over hate.

Two Ohio men, Ricky Jackson and Wiley Bridgeman, walked free after nearly four decades behind bars after charges tied to a 1975 Cleveland murder were dropped. Jackson, convicted at 19 largely on the testimony of a 12-year-old witness, Edward Vernon, spent 39 years imprisoned and is believed to be the longest-held U.S. prisoner later exonerated. Vernon recanted last year, saying detectives coerced him and that he lied to protect his parents from arrest; he later told a pastor and the Innocence Project the truth. The Ohio Innocence Project took up the case; prosecutors concluded that without the eyewitness testimony the case “evaporated” and moved to dismiss charges. Ronnie Bridgeman, Wiley’s brother, had been paroled in 2003 and is seeking to clear his record. Jackson, 57, and Wiley Bridgeman, 60, expressed little bitterness, praising Vernon’s courage to recant and thanking advocates and prosecutors who dropped the case. Jackson, originally sentenced to death, had his penalty vacated on a technicality; the Bridgeman brothers remained on death row until Ohio voided capital punishment in 1978. The exoneration followed renewed scrutiny after a 2011 Scene Magazine article questioned the convictions. Cuyahoga County Prosecutor Timothy McGinty declined to pursue charges against Vernon and acknowledged the prosecution could not proceed absent reliable eyewitness evidence. The Ohio Innocence Project has set up a fund for Jackson, and advocates note that state compensation for wrongful imprisonment is not guaranteed for all exonerees.

Investigators probing Prince’s April 21 death have focused on whether an overdose and recent medical prescriptions played a role, law enforcement sources told the Associated Press and other outlets. Authorities are examining whether Prince suffered an opioid overdose aboard his plane during an April 15 emergency landing in Moline, Illinois, where responders reportedly administered Narcan after finding him unconscious. Investigators are seeking to determine what drugs were on that flight and what prescription medications were at Prince’s Paisley Park home, and whether a doctor may have prescribed drugs to him in the weeks before his death.

A Carver County incident report and related court filings indicate the inquiry is being treated as a criminal investigation, though officials caution that criminal charges are only a possibility. The sheriff’s office released a limited timeline showing the 911 call came in at 9:43 a.m.; responders found Prince in an elevator five minutes later, performed CPR, and he was pronounced dead at 10:07 a.m. The cause of death remains “unknown” pending autopsy and toxicology results, expected weeks after testing.

Search warrants executed at Paisley Park the day Prince’s body was found have been sealed by a judge for 180 days or until court proceedings begin, at the request of the county attorney who argued that public disclosure could hamper the investigation and risk harm. Authorities say neither foul play nor suicide is suspected; sources reported finding prescription pills at the compound but have not confirmed if they were prescribed to Prince. The DEA has not been formally involved, officials said, though cooperation could be sought.

Over 75 women have recently accused producer Harvey Weinstein of sexual harassment and assault, recounting similar stories of coercive meetings, requests to undress or give massages, and, in some cases, rape. Three women—actress Alice Evans, actress/photographer Katherine Kendall, and psychologist Tomi-Ann Roberts—joined a Slate conversation to compare experiences spanning the 1980s through the 2000s. Roberts described an early-flier encounter where Weinstein appeared naked in a bathtub and pressured her to remove her top; she later pursued psychology and studies of sexual objectification. Kendall recounted being invited after a Miramax meeting to Weinstein’s apartment, where he demanded a massage, returned naked, and pressed for sexual contact; she resisted, escaped, and felt the episode undermined her confidence in pursuing acting. Evans described a Cannes bar encounter in 2002 where Weinstein attempted to grope her in a bathroom stall and made crude demands; she, too, worried afterward about career repercussions. All three discussed long-standing shame, self-blame, and the difference between a “pass gone awry” and predatory behavior that doesn’t stop when rebuffed. They expressed mixed views on apologies and forgiveness, emphasizing that genuine accountability is rare and that forgiveness is often personal, not public. The conversation highlighted how isolation was relieved by others coming forward, but also how media retellings can retraumatize survivors. Separately, reporting details how Weinstein and a cabal of powerful board members enabled a toxic corporate culture at The Weinstein Company: contracts, governance structures, and secret settlements—including nondisclosure agreements and hidden payouts—protected Weinstein for decades, stifled oversight, and suppressed allegations until explosive press reporting in 2017 forced his removal and sparked broader revelations across industries.

Ohio voters will decide Nov. 3 whether to legalize recreational marijuana via a proposed constitutional amendment from investor group ResponsibleOhio. The group submitted 320,267 valid signatures, surpassing the 305,591 threshold, and plans a well-funded $20 million campaign. Its plan would immediately legalize use for over-21 adults, limit commercial cultivation to 10 named farms—creating an oligopoly—offer 1,150 other business licenses, allow limited home growing, and impose a 15% excise tax (plus sales tax). Opponents include Republican officials, farm groups and grassroots activists who call the plan unfair. Complicating matters, the legislature placed Issue 2 on the ballot to ban monopolies/oligopolies; if both pass, courts will decide.

Western governments accuse Russia’s military intelligence (GRU) of a broad, aggressive cyber-campaign that targeted international institutions, anti-doping bodies, investigative probes and corporate and government entities. Dutch authorities disrupted an April operation in The Hague in which four operatives, traveling on diplomatic passports, were caught near the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) with specialist wifi-hacking equipment, laptops, mobile devices, antennae and large sums of cash. Dutch officials say the team intended to intercept OPCW logins and travel on to the Spiez laboratory in Switzerland, which analysed the Novichok nerve agent used against Sergei Skripal, and that the seized laptop had been used in operations in Brazil, Switzerland and Malaysia, including efforts tied to the MH17 investigation.

The US Department of Justice indicted seven GRU officers, linking them to the Netherlands case and to other intrusions: hacks of the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), breaches affecting FIFA, anti-doping agencies, the Democratic National Committee in 2016, a US nuclear energy company, and attempts to undermine investigations and public trust. Charges include computer hacking, wire fraud, identity theft and money laundering. Britain and the Netherlands publicly named GRU Unit 26165 personnel and called the conduct a threat to international institutions; the US, UK, EU and NATO condemned the actions and discussed further sanctions. Russia rejected the allegations as “stage‑managed propaganda” and “spy mania.”

Western officials framed the operations as part of a GRU “cleanup” effort to discredit inquiries that exposed Russian wrongdoing—doping, chemical weapons use, and responsibility for MH17—and pledged increased cooperation, transparency and countermeasures to hold Moscow accountable.

Chinese movie star Fan Bingbing, once China’s highest-paid actress and an international name after appearing in X-Men: Days of Future Past, has been at the center of a high-profile scandal and public silence. Absent from public since early July and inactive on social media since June, Fan has faced allegations of tax evasion tied to so‑called “yin-yang” dual-contract arrangements, where a lower contract is declared to tax authorities while the real payment is hidden. The controversy began when former CCTV presenter Cui Yongyuan published contracts in May that suggested such practices; Fan’s studio called the posts slander but did not challenge the documents’ authenticity. Subsequent reports said authorities were probing tax practices in Jiangsu province, where Fan has business registrations, and state media signaled a broader crackdown on excessive celebrity pay and tax avoidance.

A Beijing Normal University study evaluating 100 film and TV stars on professional work, charity, and personal integrity gave Fan a 0% score, placing her last and fueling speculation about her legal situation. The report, based on media reports and “web‑scraping,” named only nine stars as passing a 60% threshold; actor Xu Zheng ranked highest. State outlets briefly reported Fan was “under control” and might “accept the legal decision,” though some stories were later taken down. Fan’s disappearance and the report prompted mixed reactions online, with many fans defending her past philanthropy. Amid censorship of related coverage and social posts, Fan remains tied to ongoing industry scrutiny; she is still listed in projects such as the international film 355, but her future public and professional standing is uncertain.

House Republican leadership moved quickly to back Rep. Steve Scalise after reports that he spoke in 2002 to a white supremacist-linked group founded by former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke. The revelation threatened Scalise’s role as House majority whip and forced him to call colleagues to gauge support. Speaker John Boehner and Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy issued near-simultaneous statements saying Scalise has their “full confidence.” Scalise acknowledged speaking to the group while barnstorming his district and called it “a mistake I regret,” insisting he condemns the group’s divisive views and that he did not share their ideology. He and aides said he often spoke to many organizations during that period and may not have known the group’s extremist ties; critics doubt that explanation.

The incident drew bipartisan criticism and prompted national Democrats to pounce, while many Louisiana politicians and some conservatives defended Scalise’s character. Questions remain about what he knew, who invited him, and whether he benefited politically. Conservatives frustrated with establishment Republicans voiced anger at perceived double standards. The controversy landed days before Republicans assumed full congressional control, complicating leadership’s start as other GOP members also faced ethics or legal troubles. Scalise’s fate ultimately depends on rank-and-file reactions when lawmakers reconvene.

A Chinese immigrant who calls himself Danny recounts being carjacked April 18 by Tamerlan and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev days after the Boston Marathon bombings and a campus police killing. Danny says Tamerlan boarded his Mercedes, brandished a gun, boasted about the bombings and the officer’s death, barked orders, questioned his heritage and forbade him speaking Chinese. Dzhokhar rode mostly silently, carried out tasks like ATM runs and asked only about the SUV’s price. The brothers loaded remaining explosives into Danny’s vehicle and spoke of “Manhattan,” suggesting a planned trip to New York. Using a stop for gas, Danny escaped after counting to three and running while Tamerlan tried to grab him; he alerted police. Authorities later found the wounded Dzhokhar and killed Tamerlan after a shootout; Danny’s SUV was heavily damaged.

President Obama used a White House press conference to pick a high-stakes fight with Republicans over ending high-end tax cuts, framing the issue as a moral test of national priorities. He argued that preserving tax breaks for millionaires, billionaires, corporate-jet owners and oil and gas companies forces painful cuts to education, medical research, food safety and Medicare. Repeating “corporate-jet” several times, he highlighted a proposed $3 billion removal of a jet-owner tax perk—deliberately small but politically potent—to cast GOP opposition as defending the wealthy. Obama insisted deficit reduction requires a balanced approach that includes revenue increases, while Democrats will also accept some difficult spending cuts, but warned against shifting Medicare costs onto seniors. Though he stopped short of saying he would reject any final deal lacking high-end tax hikes, he signaled he will relitigate and center the issue politically. Critics accused him of “class warfare” rhetoric and noted he previously accepted extensions of Bush-era tax cuts, suggesting possible inconsistency; some also criticized the absence of a strong pro-growth, business-tax-reform agenda. Supporters praised the strategy of forcing Republicans into the position of protecting wealthy interests. The White House’s message: Republicans can either embrace balance and revenue or be exposed as protecting the rich at the expense of students and seniors.

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) overturned lifetime Olympic bans for 28 Russian athletes accused of doping at the 2014 Sochi Winter Games, ruling evidence was insufficient to prove anti-doping violations in those individual cases. CAS partially upheld appeals for 11 other athletes, finding sufficient evidence of violations but reducing life bans to ineligibility for the 2018 Pyeongchang Games. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) expressed both satisfaction and disappointment: it welcomed confirmation of violations for 11 athletes but criticised CAS for not taking the proven systemic manipulation at Sochi into account for the other 28, warning the decision could harm the fight against doping and that it might appeal to the Swiss Federal Tribunal. The ruling reinstates results and medals for the cleared athletes, potentially restoring Russia to the top of the Sochi medal table and prompting legal moves to seek invitations to Pyeongchang—though the IOC said reinstatement does not guarantee Olympic entry. The decision has provoked strong reactions: Russian officials hailed a triumph of justice and sought further legal steps to let cleared athletes compete; critics, including whistleblower Grigory Rodchenkov’s lawyer and some rival athletes, said the ruling weakens anti-doping enforcement and rewards cheating. The case highlights tensions between evidence standards applied by CAS and the IOC’s broader findings of state-sponsored manipulation documented in the McLaren report, raising questions about future anti-doping strategy and the integrity of Olympic competition.

Badlands National Park’s official Twitter account briefly posted climate-change facts, including that atmospheric carbon dioxide is higher now than at any time in the past 650,000 years.
