The tweets appeared Tuesday but were deleted a few hours later. The National Park Service (NPS) said the posts came from a former employee “not currently authorized to use the park’s account” and that the park removed them after realizing the account had been compromised. NPS added that the park was not instructed to delete the tweets but chose to do so, and reminded social media managers to continue posting public-safety and park information while avoiding content related to national policy issues. This incident is not the first time park accounts have posted material that could conflict with the Trump administration’s preferred presentation of climate science. The deleted messages briefly drew attention to how agency communications are being managed.

"Joe" is a nearly complete baby Parasaurolophus fossil discovered in 2009 by 17-year-old Kevin Terris during a Webb Schools field expedition in Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument, Utah. Terris spotted a sliver of bone; when curator Andrew Farke and students investigated, they found skull fragments and toe bones separated by a boulder, indicating the full skeleton lay between. Excavated under federal permit, airlifted by helicopter, and prepared over thousands of hours, the specimen proved to be the smallest, youngest and most complete Parasaurolophus yet found. Nicknamed "Joe" in honor of Joseph Augustyn, the juvenile measured about 8 feet long in life—roughly a quarter of adult size—and histological sampling of its leg bone showed no annual growth rings, indicating it was less than a year old at death. Remarkably, Joe already bore a small crest bump, challenging prior ideas that lambeosaurine ornamentation developed only at larger sizes; researchers infer Parasaurolophus began crest growth much earlier, producing higher-pitched calls in juveniles ("tweeters") versus adults' low-frequency resonances ("woofers"). The team produced CT scans and a 3-D virtual model available via the DinosaurJoe website; the fossil is on display at the Raymond M. Alf Museum. The discovery is detailed in a PeerJ paper coauthored by Farke, Sarah Werning, students, and others, and underscores both scientific value and the role of student fieldwork in paleontology.

Three months before his planned Facebook internship, Harvard student Aran Khanna created Marauder’s Map, a Chrome extension that scraped Facebook Messenger’s message-associated geolocation data and plotted senders’ locations—accurate to within meters—on a map. Messenger had, since 2011, included location coordinates with messages by default on Android (and with permission on iOS), visible to anyone in a conversation, including group chats with strangers. Khanna built the tool to make the often-invisible accumulation of location data tangible and to test whether users cared enough to demand change.

Khanna announced the extension on May 26, 2015; it quickly went viral via Medium, Reddit, Hacker News and Twitter, was covered by major outlets, and was downloaded more than 85,000 times. Within days Facebook contacted Khanna, asking him to stop publicity and, later, to disable the extension. Facebook then changed its desktop Messenger behavior to stop transmitting location data to browsers—effectively breaking the extension—and, nine days after the post, issued an update making in-chat location sharing opt-in. The update’s announcement did not disclose the previous default settings or the fate of historically collected location data.

Facebook rescinded Khanna’s internship offer, citing violations of its terms for “scraping” data and saying his post did not meet expected ethical standards. Khanna contends the extension only used location information already accessible to any chat participant and that his intent was not malicious. He complied with Facebook’s takedown request and later accepted a different tech internship. Khanna’s study argues that public transparency and media attention prompted Facebook’s change, highlighting how user-unnoticed defaults can accumulate invasive personal data and suggesting external pressure may be necessary to prompt privacy protections.

A new pair of field studies suggests that adopting expansive body postures—spreading limbs and opening the torso—can boost romantic appeal in fast-paced dating contexts. Tanya Vacharkulksemsuk and colleagues analyzed 144 speed-dates and found that participants who sat in expansive postures were judged more attractive; each one-unit increase in coded expansiveness nearly doubled the odds of a “yes” for a follow-up date. Laughing or smiling did not predict success as strongly as taking up space. 

To test causality, the team ran a larger field experiment (~3,000 users) on a popular GPS-based dating app by posting photos of people in open versus closed postures. Overall, expansive images generated about 25% more interest than contractive ones. The effect was stronger for men: although men received fewer total affirmative responses, 87% of their “yeses” came in response to open postures, whereas 53% of women’s affirmative responses were tied to expansiveness. 

Perception data showed that expansive photos were judged more dominant than closed ones. The researchers propose that perceived dominance signals resource abundance and willingness to share—qualities that can matter when strangers make split-second decisions from a single photo or a brief encounter. The findings align with broader evidence that nonverbal cues influence first impressions and mate choice. 

The authors caution, and commentators note, that skepticism is warranted: prior “power-pose” research produced contested hormone findings, and real-world dating involves many variables. Still, in contexts where quick visual judgments rule, literally taking up more space appears to enhance initial attractiveness.

Human Rights Watch’s 102-page report warns that Afghan militias and the U.S.-backed Afghan Local Police (ALP) are committing grave abuses—killings, rape, arbitrary detention, abductions, land grabs and illegal raids—while Afghan authorities fail to provide oversight or accountability. Created in 2010 to bolster village security, the ALP has rapidly expanded with minimal vetting, limited training, and weak command structures; plans could arm up to 30,000 recruits. HRW documented abuses in Kunduz, Baghlan, Herat and Uruzgan, showing patronage links to powerful officials often block investigations. Past auxiliary programs similarly morphed into predatory forces. HRW urges Kabul and Washington to sever ties with abusive militias, halt ALP expansion until safeguards exist, investigate all allegations, fund independent complaints mechanisms, and ensure vetting and accountability. Separate reporting highlights systemic weaknesses in Afghan security forces, persistent U.S. dependence, and controversial backing of strongmen like Brig. Gen. Abdul Raziq, accused of torture, extrajudicial killings and corruption, raising legal and moral concerns about U.S. support.

Barack Obama arrived in Washington with limited foreign-policy experience, having been a part-time lawyer, professor, and state legislator. As a senator beginning in 2005, he deliberately sought to educate himself, reading widely and consulting experts like Anthony Lake, Susan Rice, and Samantha Power, whose influential, interventionist book argued for a “bias toward belief” to prevent genocides. Obama hired Power as a foreign-policy fellow and aimed to build substantive credentials rather than celebrity. His emergence coincided with intense Democratic debates after the Iraq War: some liberals recoiled toward realism, prioritizing national interest over idealism, while others urged preserving humanitarian intervention and democratic promotion despite Iraq’s failures. Over time, observers and critics characterized Obama’s approach—especially in Libya and Iran—as “leading from behind,” a style some see as pragmatic realism acknowledging U.S. relative decline and global resentment, while opponents label it dithering, passive, and tantamount to abdication. Critics argue this posture weakens American leadership and invites domestic political replacement by a more assertive alternative. Supporters counter that cautious, coalition-based action reflects necessary adaptation to complex, constrained global realities.

Jeb Bush’s 2016 campaign began with high expectations: a seasoned two-term Florida governor, vast fundraising (over $100 million via Right to Rise), family name recognition and a wonkish, policy-driven approach. His strategy—“slow and steady”—aimed to leverage organization and detailed plans, but it badly misread the GOP electorate’s mood. Donald Trump’s insurgent, anti-establishment campaign seized voter anger and media attention, and his “low energy” taunt stuck, defining Bush in ways his campaign couldn’t overcome. Bush’s team debated how to respond but fractured over strategy, often choosing to avoid direct confrontation with Trump until it was too late. Other factors compounded his decline: widespread “Bush fatigue” tied to his brother’s unpopular presidency, awkward debate performances and an early Iraq war stumble that raised questions about his preparedness. Heavy reliance on super PAC fundraising left insufficient early efforts to build a distinct, resonant personal brand; massive ad spending failed to translate into enthusiasm. Internal disagreements, loyalist-driven management, and failure to adapt to a year favoring emotion over policy sealed his fate. After weak finishes in early contests and dwindling endorsements, Bush suspended his campaign in South Carolina, ending a campaign that many now view as a mismatch between a technocratic candidate and a radically transformed Republican electorate.

Just in time for cookie season: some vanilla flavoring can come from beaver secretions called castoreum. Castoreum is a brown, musky-smelling goo from castor sacs near a beaver’s tail; because those sacs sit close to anal glands, the material often includes anal gland secretions and urine. The scent—more vanilla-like than foul—comes from the beaver’s diet of leaves and bark, and perfumers and food scientists have used castoreum in fragrances and foods for decades. The FDA lists castoreum as “generally regarded as safe,” and manufacturers may list it under the vague term “natural flavoring” rather than naming it. Harvesting castoreum is difficult and unpleasant: animals must be anesthetized and “milked,” so annual use is tiny—only a few hundred pounds worldwide—making it an uncommon but real source of natural vanilla-like flavor.

Billboard has raised its first-week sales forecast for Taylor Swift’s new album 1989, now predicting it will sell over 1 million copies in its debut week—making Swift the first act in the SoundScan era to achieve three consecutive million-plus opening weeks (Speak Now in 2010, Red in 2012, and now 1989). Despite overall declines in music purchases amid streaming growth, 1989 is on track to be the 19th album since 1991 to crack the million mark and would be the fastest-selling album since Red. Strong performance on iTunes and Target—where an exclusive edition with bonus tracks is sold—helped boost projections after several upward revisions. Final SoundScan figures and the Billboard 200 chart placement were expected to be announced Nov. 5.

Former North York General anesthesiologist Dr. George Doodnaught, 65, was sentenced to 10 years in prison for sexually assaulting 21 sedated female patients during surgeries. Ontario Superior Court Justice David McCombs called the offences “reprehensible in the extreme,” noting Doodnaught exploited patients’ trust and the particular vulnerability of the operating room. The assaults—fondling, kissing, oral sex and masturbation—were committed while patients were semi-conscious and concealed by a surgical drape; most occurred at North York General between 2006 and 2010, with an escalation in the final months before his arrest. Victims, many present in court, described lasting psychological harm: shame, panic attacks, loss of trust, and damaged relationships. Some were manipulated into believing they were responsible. Doodnaught, convicted in November after a 76-day trial, declined to address the court. He remains free on bail pending appeal; a bail hearing at the Court of Appeal is scheduled. His lawyer said he has support from family and colleagues. The hospital has apologized, changed complaint procedures, and suspended his licence; the College of Physicians and Surgeons will hold a disciplinary hearing that could revoke his licence.

Police announced Daniel St. Hubert, 27, as the suspect in the brutal East New York elevator stabbings that left 6-year-old Prince Joshua “P.J.” Avitto dead and 7-year-old Mikayla Capers critically injured. Authorities urged the public to call tips lines and warned that St. Hubert—described as 5'9", 210 pounds with a distinctive forearm tattoo—was armed and dangerous and had a history of violent arrests and recent parole. Forensic evidence and a DNA match linked him to the attack; police also used his cell phone to track and locate him. After a citywide manhunt and a significant reward, detectives arrested St. Hubert in South Ozone Park around 8 p.m., finding a knife on him. Officials noted he may have changed his appearance. Though he’s wanted for the children’s stabbings, investigators said they have not ruled him out in a nearby fatal stabbing days earlier. Community members expressed relief at the arrest while mourning P.J.; leaders urged vigilance and restraint and pledged increased police presence in public housing as the investigation continues.

BP agreed, at the Obama administration’s request, to show video of its planned "top kill" effort to stem the Gulf of Mexico oil leak. The company intends to attempt the delicate procedure as early as dawn Wednesday. The top kill involves pumping heavy drilling mud and cement into the leak to choke off the flow. BP had already begun broadcasting live feeds of the leak after pressure from Washington and lawmakers, who had been told earlier that the top-kill attempt would not be shown. Following discussions with Adm. Thad Allen, the federal official overseeing the response, BP said it will display the video. The company cautioned that the seabed appearance may change significantly during the up-to-two-day operation and such visuals may not reliably indicate overall progress; BP will report results when the attempt is complete. Multiple ROV live streams covering the incident are available, though they may freeze or be unavailable at times.

Australian parents David and Wendy Farnell have publicly disputed accusations that they abandoned one of their twins born via a Thai surrogate, saying they wanted both children but left Thailand with the healthy daughter, Pipah, after the surrogate, Pattaramon (Pattharamon) Chanbua, refused to hand over the boy, Gammy, and threatened to involve police. Gammy, now seven months old, has Down’s syndrome, a congenital heart defect and a lung infection and remains in Thailand in the surrogate’s care. The Farnells said they were told late in the pregnancy about the disability and blamed the surrogacy agency and doctors for failing to detect it earlier; they denied asking the surrogate to have an abortion but acknowledged that, had they known sooner, they probably would have terminated. Chanbua says she refused abortion on Buddhist grounds and has said she feared the Farnells would place Gammy in an institution if they took him. The case ignited international outrage partly because David Farnell has past convictions for sexual offences against young girls from the 1990s; he says he has reformed and poses no risk. The controversy has spotlighted weak regulation of international commercial surrogacy: Thailand has no clear legal framework, commercial surrogacy is barred by its medical council, and draft legislation to outlaw commercial surrogacy is under consideration. An online public appeal has raised significant funds—over A$241,000—pledged for Gammy’s medical care, administered by an Australian charity in Thailand. The Australian government has asked Thai authorities to allow current surrogacy arrangements to conclude before new rules take effect.

Jeff Bezos’s private space company, Blue Origin, achieved a milestone by launching its New Shepard vehicle to the edge of space and successfully landing the booster back on Earth in the company’s first uncrewed reusability test. The mission sent the crew capsule about 100.5 kilometers (roughly 329,839 feet) up at a maximum speed of Mach 3.72. The capsule, designed to eventually carry six passengers on suborbital hops, separated and descended under parachutes, while the booster reignited its engine about 5,000 feet above the pad, deployed landing legs, and touched down gently at about 4.4 mph — landing within 4.5 feet of center. Blue Origin had attempted earlier tests this year but failed to recover the booster due to hydraulic problems.

Bezos framed the achievement as a turning point: reusable rockets could dramatically reduce access-to-space costs by replacing the traditional expendable-rocket approach. “Full reuse is a game changer,” he said, noting the company’s plans to fly suborbital tourists from West Texas and to develop orbital rockets for Florida launches carrying people and cargo. Bezos envisions millions living and working in space, a long-term goal for which repeated reuse is central.

Rival companies, notably Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Richard Branson’s Virgin Galactic, pursue similar aims. Musk congratulated Blue Origin on Twitter for achieving vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) of the booster but stressed the distinction between reaching space and achieving orbit, noting orbital flights require far greater speed and energy. SpaceX has attempted controlled booster recoveries, including ocean landings on a drone ship, with mixed success; Virgin Galactic focuses on air-launched, airplane-like suborbital vehicles. All firms have faced setbacks, yet Blue Origin’s successful booster recovery represents a significant step toward routine, reusable suborbital flight and broader ambitions for lowering the cost of space access.

Filmmaker and writer Miranda July admitted in The New Yorker that she shoplifted frequently from her late teens into adulthood. Her first arrest came as a UC Santa Cruz freshman for concealing Neosporin; she wet herself when caught and was processed by police. Rather than stopping, she developed a practiced, almost ritualized habit of stealing—taking groceries, using a giant purse to hide food, resetting copy counters, cutting alarm tags, and even pilfering from Goodwill while employed there. She describes recruiting friends into schemes, stealing luggage for insurance fraud, and sometimes planting stolen items for others. Getting caught at Goodwill led to her firing, which she framed as another institutional rejection that fed her outsider identity. Over time she phased out theft as relationships and her art life took hold, concluding that creativity could replace criminal rebellion; she also reflects that many adults feel secretly fraudulent.

Voters across six states considered 31 ballot measures, with notable outcomes and contests highlighted in Colorado and Washington. In Colorado, voters ratified a special tax on recreational marijuana—65% in favor—imposing a 15% excise tax to fund school construction and an additional 10% sales tax for marijuana-related law enforcement. The measure was expected to pass, driven by projected revenue: the Colorado Legislative Council estimates nearly $70 million in additional state tax receipts next year. Also in Colorado, 11 northern and northeastern counties faced advisory secession votes proposing a new “North Colorado” state and a Moffat County panhandle for Wyoming. The secession plan has no practical chance—requiring state and congressional approval—but even close county-level support would signal rural conservative frustration with Denver’s liberal policies. Early returns in Weld County showed 58% opposed to secession.

In Washington, Initiative 522 would have required labeling foods with genetically modified ingredients. With more than 800,000 votes counted, about 53% opposed and 47% supported, though the race remained too close to call. The campaign was marked by unprecedented out-of-state spending: opponents raised $22 million, largely from national food-industry groups including the Grocery Manufacturers Association and Monsanto, while proponents also relied heavily on outside donations. Experts warned that large external contributions threaten the initiative process by turning local ballots into national testing grounds for issues like GMO labeling and local minimum-wage proposals. Other noteworthy measures included New Jersey’s bid to raise its minimum wage to $8.25 and New York’s proposal to authorize seven casinos to boost school revenue and potentially reduce property taxes.

Nicole “Snooki” Polizzi and longtime partner Jionni LaValle wed on Saturday, Nov. 29, at The Venetian in Garfield, New Jersey. The Jersey Shore alum and LaValle, parents to son Lorenzo, 2, and daughter Giovanna Marie, 3 months, celebrated with a Great Gatsby–themed reception featuring a cigar and scotch bar and an 18-piece band, Time Machine. Polizzi wore two gowns—an off-white traditional lace dress for the ceremony and a glitzy Gatsby-style reception dress (by Ines DiSanto for the reception, Bridal Reflections for the ceremony)—and her bridesmaids, including BFF Jenni “JWoww” Farley, wore black gowns with bows. Engaged in March 2012 after more than a year together, Polizzi said she stayed calm while planning and embraced the moment. Photos from the wedding were shared on her website.

President Donald Trump publicly supported calls to boycott Harley-Davidson after the company said it will move production of motorcycles sold in Europe to facilities outside the United States. Harley-Davidson attributed the shift to retaliatory tariffs imposed by the European Union in response to U.S. tariffs on a range of EU products, a dispute that the company said could cost it up to $100 million a year. Trump amplified criticism of the move in social media and events: he tweeted that “many” Harley owners plan to boycott the brand if manufacturing moves overseas and called such a move “a really bad move,” adding that it was “great” consumers might pull back. He framed the situation as part of broader trade progress, asserting other companies are moving in the U.S. direction and predicting a soon-to-arrive level playing field. The tweets followed his weekend meeting with roughly 180 “Bikers for Trump” supporters at his Bedminster, New Jersey, golf club. Harley-Davidson declined to comment in the immediate aftermath of the president’s remarks. The controversy highlights tensions between U.S. trade policy and American manufacturers facing retaliatory tariffs, and it raises questions about domestic production, consumer response, and the financial impact of escalating tariff disputes.

Former Winnipeg broadcaster and Red River College journalism instructor Stephen (Steve) Vogelsang, 53, has been charged with two counts of robbery in connection with separate bank robberies in Medicine Hat, Alta., on Oct. 19 and 20. Police say a man passed notes to tellers at a Royal Bank and a Bank of Montreal and fled with an undisclosed amount; no weapons were seen. Vogelsang was arrested at a Medicine Hat hotel without incident and remains in custody awaiting court. A well‑known former CTV Winnipeg (CKY) news director and sports anchor, Vogelsang taught at Red River College from 2002–2011 and part‑time after returning from Nelson, B.C.; the college confirmed he is no longer employed there. Court documents outline financial troubles, foreclosure, a contentious separation and divorce, and allegations by a former student who obtained a protection order in March; Vogelsang disputes those claims. He also has past criminal matters, including a stayed sexual‑assault charge and outstanding charges of disobeying court orders. Former students expressed shock at the developments.

A New York subway attack captured on multiple videos shows attorney Anna Lushchinskaya, 40, launching a profane, racially charged assault on a 24-year-old Asian woman aboard a northbound D train in Brooklyn. Footage shows Lushchinskaya shouting obscenities, pulling back her hair and removing sunglasses before striking the victim with an umbrella and keys, kicking her and spitting while using an anti-Asian slur. A man who intervened—who identifies as Dominican—was also targeted with a racially charged remark and sustained scratches while trying to restrain her. The victim suffered facial lacerations; a good Samaritan who helped held Lushchinskaya until police arrived. The incident, which began after a reported bump-on-the-train, drew widespread attention online and millions of views. Lushchinskaya was arrested at 36th Street, arraigned in Kings County, pleaded not guilty, posted $1,000 cash bond and is due back in January. Bar records show she graduated from New York Law School and was admitted in 2004, though her current registration status is unclear. This episode echoes an earlier 2018 viral rant by another New York lawyer and spotlights potential professional consequences: legal ethics experts note that criminal convictions make bar discipline far more likely, and Lushchinskaya faces multiple misdemeanor and felony-related assault charges tied to the attack.

Choi Eun-hee, one of South Korea’s most celebrated actresses of the 1950s–70s, has died at age 92 after complications from chronic illness; her son Shin Jeong-gyun said she passed during a hospital visit for kidney dialysis. Born in Gwangju, Gyeonggi Province, in 1926, Choi began acting in 1947 and rose to stardom with films such as The Sun Of Night (1948) and A Hometown in Heart (1949). Alongside contemporaries Kim Ji‑mi and Um Aing‑ran, she became a defining screen presence, ultimately appearing in roughly 130 films.

In 1954 she married prominent director Shin Sang-ok; together they founded Shin Film and produced many of the era’s major works, including The Houseguest and My Mother (1961) and Red Scarf (1964). Their marriage ended in divorce in 1978, after which Choi’s career faltered. Later that year she was abducted in Hong Kong by North Korean agents and taken to Pyongyang; Shin was kidnapped a year later while searching for her. Under orders from Kim Jong Il, who prized film as propaganda and professed admiration for Choi, the couple were compelled to make movies for the regime. Their North Korean work included Salt, for which Choi won Best Actress at the 1985 Moscow Film Festival—the first Korean to win at an international festival.

In 1986 Choi and Shin escaped while abroad and sought asylum at the U.S. embassy in Vienna, later living in exile in the United States before returning permanently to South Korea in 1999. Choi served as president of a theater company, produced a stage musical, and in 2007 published her autobiography Confessions (also titled Confessions of Choi Eun‑hee). After Shin’s death in 2006 her health declined; she had been on dialysis three times weekly. She is survived by two sons and two daughters. Her life—and the extraordinary episode of abduction and filmmaking in North Korea—has attracted sustained public attention, inspiring books and the documentary The Lovers and the Despot. Her funeral was scheduled in Seoul.

Former president Jimmy Carter, 92, was treated for dehydration Thursday while volunteering with Habitat for Humanity in Winnipeg. After working in the sun cutting wood for about an hour, he appeared to wobble and was assisted by Secret Service, then taken to St. Boniface Hospital for rehydration; his wife Rosalynn accompanied him. Habitat officials said the hospital visit was precautionary and Carter reported feeling fine, urging volunteers to continue. The Carters were leading a build that’s part of a Canada-wide Habitat blitz to construct 150 homes for Canada 150, including 25 in Manitoba.

Matthew B. Matheny, 40, of Warren, Ohio, was found alive Wednesday on a flank of Mount St. Helens nearly a week after he set out on a day hike and went missing. Search-and-rescue teams located him about three miles from a Subaru Outback he had borrowed and left at the Blue Lake Trailhead. Matheny, who became disoriented on the unfamiliar terrain after starting his hike last Thursday, had not seen another person since that day. He survived the ordeal largely by eating berries—reported as huckleberries or other local berries—and by killing and consuming bees, according to his parents. He ran out of the two liters of water he brought and was without additional water sources for days, leaving him dehydrated; he also sustained scrapes and foot injuries after the sandals he wore broke.

Roughly 30–40 search personnel, assisted by helicopters, tracking dogs and a drone, scoured the area daily. Investigators used cellphone signals and a computer model to narrow the search to a one-square-mile area near Blue Lake Trail, which passes through meadows and firs and provides access to other ridges and views of Mount St. Helens and Mount Adams. A Skamania County-based rescue crew ultimately found him and he was airlifted to a Vancouver, Washington hospital in satisfactory condition. Matheny was alert and talking; he was treated for dehydration and expected to stay overnight as a precaution. Family members, noting his Boy Scout background and resilient humor, thanked rescuers and volunteers who aided in locating him.

Mitt Romney addressed the NAACP convention in Houston attempting to court black voters, drawing boos and jeers when he attacked President Obama’s record and vowed to repeal the Affordable Care Act. He argued his policies—focused on jobs, education as a civil-rights issue, and fiscal restraint—would better serve African-American families, citing a 14.4% black unemployment rate versus 8.2% nationally. Romney acknowledged the GOP’s poor history on race but highlighted his father’s civil‑rights legacy and appealed to shared faith and family values. His repeated opposition to Obamacare and criticism of Obama’s economic stewardship provoked loud negative reactions, though portions of the speech received polite applause. Campaign aides called the appearance courageous outreach; Democrats countered that Romney’s policies would hurt working families and criticized his health-care stance. Biden was slated to speak to the NAACP the following day.

Researchers have documented the rapid origin of a new species of Darwin’s finch on Daphne Major, a small Galápagos island, providing the first direct observation and genetic confirmation of speciation by hybridization in the wild. In 1981 field biologists Peter and B. Rosemary Grant noted an unusual large male finch—later identified by DNA analysis as a large cactus finch (Geospiza conirostris) from Española—among the island’s resident finches. Unable to return home across the roughly 100-km distance, this immigrant mated with local medium ground finches (Geospiza fortis). The hybrid offspring were fertile and, crucially, reproductively isolated from the resident species because they sang different songs and had distinct beak shapes and sizes—key mate-choice cues. Those differences caused the hybrids to mate primarily with one another, forming a closed lineage nicknamed the “Big Bird” population.

Uppsala University genetic analyses of blood samples collected over six generations confirmed the immigrant origin and hybrid ancestry. Natural selection then favored the novel beak morphology, which occupied its own niche in beak-size space and allowed the lineage to exploit different food resources, aiding its ecological competitiveness. Although the lineage suffered severe losses during droughts, it rebounded: after near collapse in 2002–03, inbreeding among survivors produced many offspring, and counts in 2012 found about 23 individuals and multiple breeding pairs. The study demonstrates that hybridization can produce a new, stable, and ecologically competitive lineage in as few as two generations. The authors suggest similar events likely occurred repeatedly in Darwin’s finch evolution; most such lineages may have gone extinct, but some persisted and contributed to present species diversity. The work underscores the value of long-term field studies and expands understanding of speciation mechanisms.

A news roundup covers several stories: Shanyna Isom, featured in 2012, continues to battle a rare condition that causes fingernails to grow through hair follicles, with costly treatment needs threatening her life. Sixteen people with alleged gang ties were arrested in a multi-agency sting tied to drug trafficking, money laundering and violent crimes, Tucson police said. Ohio prison staff were warned of an escape a day before three inmates, including a convicted school killer, briefly fled. Solar eruptions headed toward Earth promise geomagnetic activity. Separately, Orem police arrested Bryan Ford and passenger Christina Schlegel after a Zales employee identified Ford as a ring thief; Schlegel swallowed the stolen ring, later confirmed by hospital X-ray, and both were booked on theft investigations.

Oprah Winfrey is consolidating her media operations in Los Angeles, announcing that Chicago’s Harpo Studios will close production by December, with the 26-year-old facility’s work moving to OWN’s new West Hollywood headquarters. Though Harpo’s lease runs through April 2016, Winfrey and executives plan to end Chicago production earlier; about 200 Harpo employees will be affected, with a small number offered roles in L.A. and others possibly freelancing. Winfrey described the decision as bittersweet, praising Chicago’s role in her career and the West Loop’s revival while stressing the benefits of having the OWN team under one roof as the four-year-old network expands. OWN, co-owned with Discovery, has posted consecutive years of growth and strong ratings among African-American viewers. Winfrey will continue focusing on OWN but will pursue acting, scripted programming and other projects: she’ll recur on Ava DuVernay’s Queen Sugar, produce DuVernay’s pilot, reunite with Lee Daniels for Pryor, and develop Harpo Films projects including Henrietta Lacks. She declined a Broadway revival of ’night, Mother, preferring roles with a happier ending, and plans international speaking engagements. The move marks the end of an era for Chicago’s TV scene and a consolidation of Winfrey’s media future in Hollywood.

Madonna and her 15-year-old son Rocco Ritchie are locked in a public, bitter custody clash that escalated over the holidays. Rocco, who spent part of the year traveling with Madonna on her Rebel Heart tour, ran off during the Stockholm leg after repeated fights with his mother and went to live with his father, director Guy Ritchie, in London. Insiders describe Madonna as a devoted but controlling parent who dictates many aspects of Rocco’s life, including social contacts and religious involvement with Kabbalah—an upbringing that reportedly fueled the teen’s rebellion and desire for stability with his dad.

Sources say Rocco told friends and his father he felt “miserable” on tour, treated more like a trophy than a son, and preferred his dad’s calmer, more settled household. Guy Ritchie is accused of encouraging Rocco’s decision to stay in London, deepening the rift. Madonna responded by seeking legal remedies: a Manhattan judge ordered Rocco to return to New York to face his mother before school resumed in January, and she publicly posted holiday messages about her children while Rocco indicated he would remain in London and briefly made his Instagram private.

The conflict includes cross-jurisdictional legal moves—pending proceedings in the U.K. where Rocco has his own lawyer—and strong feelings on both sides. Friends and sources emphasize a complicated mother-son bond: close but fraught, with shouting matches, tearful confrontations, and accusations that Madonna overshares embarrassing photos of Rocco on social media. The situation remains unresolved as the teen resists the court order and both families prepare for further legal and personal confrontations.

At a United Nations luncheon in New York, President Donald Trump addressed African leaders from countries including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia, Ghana, Guinea, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, Uganda and South Africa, praising Africa’s economic promise and security partnerships while committing U.S. support for health and counterterrorism efforts. Trump highlighted that several of the world’s fastest-growing economies are in Africa and urged increased American trade and investment across sectors such as agriculture, energy, transportation, healthcare and tourism. He noted ongoing U.S. engagement—citing Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and the Millennium Challenge Corporation’s consideration of a multi-hundred-million-dollar investment in Côte d’Ivoire—and encouraged reciprocal investment by African firms in the United States, mentioning Sasol’s $9 billion petrochemical project in Louisiana as an example that will create American jobs.

Trump emphasized health cooperation, praising Uganda’s progress against HIV/AIDS, Guinea and Nigeria’s responses to Ebola, and Namibia’s growing health-system self-sufficiency; he said the U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary will travel to Africa to advance the Global Health Security Agenda. On security, he promised partnership with African nations and regional bodies like the African Union to combat terrorism, help end violence, respond to humanitarian crises, and support African-led peacemaking—singling out conflicts in the Central African Republic, Congo, Libya, Mali, Somalia and South Sudan and naming terrorist threats including ISIS, al-Shabaab, Boko Haram and al-Qaeda. He announced Ambassador Nikki Haley will visit Africa to discuss conflict resolution and prevention, and urged unified implementation of U.N. sanctions on North Korea.

The speech drew viral attention after Trump twice mispronounced “Namibia” as “Nambia,” prompting widespread social-media jokes and debate over whether he meant Namibia, Zambia or The Gambia. Commentators both mocked the gaffe and defended his broader message about economic opportunity and U.S.-Africa cooperation. The president closed by reiterating his belief in democratic governance and expressing eagerness for discussion with the assembled leaders.

Miss World, founded in 1951 as a publicity stunt featuring women in swimwear on the River Thames, is formally ending its swimsuit competition after 63 years. Chairwoman Julia Morley announced the change following the 2014 pageant—won by Rolene Strauss of South Africa—making Strauss the last Miss World crowned in an event that included bikinis. The organization has increasingly emphasized its "Beauty with a Purpose" ethos since 1974, when the service element was introduced; that charity-focused initiative has raised more than $1 billion and shifted attention toward contestants’ community work, interviews, education and advocacy.

Morley has argued the swimsuit round undermines the modern aims of the pageant, saying she wants judges and audiences to listen to contestants rather than appraise bodies. In recent years the bathing suit segment had already become optional, often judged privately and removed from live broadcasts; many contestants chose one-pieces or modest wraps. Going forward, Miss World will replace bikinis with a beachwear-themed fashion round rather than a traditional swimsuit show, and will maintain existing challenge events such as talent, sports, top model, social media, and in-depth interviews.

Supporters and directors praise the move as modernization of an age-old industry, positioning Miss World as a platform for ambassadors and spokespeople rather than a primarily physical appraisal. The decision contrasts with rival Miss Universe, which continues to highlight a swimsuit component.

A Brooklyn family’s birthday celebration turned tragic when Joseph Andrade, 44, and his 22-year-old son Carlos died of a suspected double opioid overdose after stepping outside to smoke, police said. The younger man, not known to use drugs, apparently joined his father—who neighbors said struggled with addiction—in snorting a potent mix of heroin and fentanyl. Carlos was found by his girlfriend, Jasmin Santos, inside the building foyer after 3 a.m., with his face turning purple; Joseph was discovered a short distance away on the street. Distressed relatives called 911 and officers administered Narcan at the scene, but both men later died at Lutheran Medical Center. Carlos had driven from Maryland for the party with his girlfriend and their two young children, ages 1 and 4; relatives emphasized his close relationship with his eldest child and expressed shock that he would take drugs. Neighbors reported rising late-night drinking and disturbance in the building, and said Joseph’s addiction was known in the area. Authorities are investigating and the medical examiner will determine the official cause. The story underscores the broader opioid crisis that claimed many lives nationwide, with thousands of drug fatalities reported in recent years.

In a CNN "State of the Union" interview, Donald Trump said he believes the world would be better off if brutal leaders like Saddam Hussein and Moammar Gadhafi had remained in power. When asked directly, Trump answered "100%," arguing that Iraq and Libya have become fractured and unstable since the removal of those dictators. He acknowledged both men committed atrocities but maintained that their regimes suppressed terrorism more effectively than the post-intervention environments. Trump said Iraq "used to be no terrorists" under Hussein and called contemporary Iraq "the Harvard of terrorism." He described Libya and Iraq as broken, lacking control, and serving as havens or training grounds for extremists after their leaders were ousted—Hussein after the 2003 U.S. invasion and Gadhafi following the 2011 civil uprising and NATO intervention.

Beyond foreign policy remarks, Trump criticized partisan rancor in Washington, calling recent political hearings, including the Benghazi committee’s session with Hillary Clinton, "very partisan" and marked by "unbelievable" hatred between Republicans and Democrats. He argued that such divisiveness harms both parties and prevents effective governance. Presenting himself as a conciliator, Trump said he would unify a divided country, blaming President Barack Obama for fostering division. He pointed to his history of working with both Democrats and Republicans as evidence that he can bridge partisan gaps, framing bi-partisan relationships as business necessity rather than political weakness. Finally, Trump downplayed personal enmity with Clinton, calling her an opponent but not an enemy.

Bob Dylan, the first songwriter to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, has not publicly acknowledged the award and his team removed a recent reference to being a laureate from his website. The Swedish Academy has stopped trying to contact his representatives and cannot confirm whether the 75-year-old, known for shunning honors, will attend the December Nobel banquet in Stockholm. Dylan received the prize for creating “new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition” and previously won a 2008 Pulitzer.

The piece compares Conan O’Brien’s 2010 exit from NBC to the heroic labor drama Norma Rae, arguing the public reaction inflated a routine corporate reshuffle into a symbolic stand against corporate injustice. Conan, a wealthy, Harvard-educated comedian, left The Tonight Show over a schedule move he felt compromised its integrity. The author contends his supporters framed him as a modern everyman victim of corporate greed, though his situation differs greatly from real workplace injustices. Jay Leno appears opportunistic for reclaiming 11:30, while Conan earned sympathy by handling his exit gracefully and humorously. Ratings realities, however, drove NBC’s decisions: Conan struggled to consistently attract key advertising demographics (18–49, 25–54) and even young viewers compared with Leno; younger audiences also fragment across cable, DVRs, gaming, and online clips. The piece concludes that while Conan became an unlikely symbol for aggrieved workers, broader media and generational shifts, not just talent, shaped late-night fortunes.

Chinese tech billionaire Jack Ma has withdrawn his high‑profile pledge to help create one million U.S. jobs, blaming the escalating trade conflict between China and the United States for undermining the plan. Ma made the promise in January 2017 after meeting then‑President‑elect Donald Trump, saying Alibaba would stimulate job growth by enabling more U.S. small businesses and farmers to sell products to Chinese and other Asian consumers through its e‑commerce platforms. Analysts were skeptical from the start because the pledge relied on increased cross‑border trade rather than direct Alibaba investments in U.S. factories or fulfillment centers.

In an interview published by state news agency Xinhua, Ma said the wave of tariffs imposed by both Washington and Beijing has destroyed the cooperative context necessary to fulfill the commitment. An Alibaba spokeswoman confirmed his comments to CNN. Ma emphasized that Alibaba will continue to promote healthy China‑U.S. trade, even as he cautioned that the trade war could persist for as long as 20 years and described the situation as “a mess.” Earlier, Alibaba staged outreach in Detroit to encourage American sellers to use its platforms, but the company has not reported how many U.S. jobs those efforts have generated.

Ma, 54, founded Alibaba nearly two decades ago and announced he will step down as executive chairman next year to be succeeded by CEO Daniel Zhang; Ma has said he plans to return to education. The turnaround on the job pledge underscores how geopolitical tensions can derail private-sector initiatives that depend on stable bilateral relations.

Prepare to have your mind blown. Salon revisits trippy cinema to mark the New York rerelease of Nicolas Roeg’s 1976 sci‑fi puzzler The Man Who Fell to Earth and the ongoing rollout of Terrence Malick’s time‑fracturing The Tree of Life. The piece offers a personal list of great hallucinatory films that mixes acknowledged classics, a feature‑length montage, two experimental‑cinema masterworks, and a recent underrated entry by a surrealist whose name amusingly echoes David Lynch. The author invites readers to contribute their own picks—then playfully dissolves the reader’s agency into a multiverse thought experiment about alternate selves adding identical lists in parallel universes, a wink at the mind‑bending themes these films explore.

A centerpiece of the short excerpt is Disney’s Fantasia, framed as a linked series of short films united by Leopold Stokowski conducting an orchestral concert. Each sequence is presented as a vision occurring in the listener’s “mind’s eye,” but filtered through Walt Disney’s distinctive imagination, producing imagery untethered from conventional narrative. Fantasia operates as experimental cinema beneath a kid‑friendly surface, foregrounding the interaction between music and animation so tightly that the two art forms seem to dance together. Segments like The Sorcerer’s Apprentice, the centaurs, dancing hippos, volcanos, dinosaurs, and the demon shift tone from silly to terrifying, yet remain visually staggering. Uniquely for Disney, Fantasia prompts existential questions—“What am I looking at?” and “What does it mean?”—making it, the author argues, the studio’s most potent cinematic hallucinogen for children.

A South Korean-owned ore carrier, the Stellar Daisy, is missing in the South Atlantic after sending a distress signal Friday saying it was taking on water. The Marshall Islands-flagged very large ore carrier had departed Rio de Janeiro on March 26 bound for China with iron ore. Two Filipino crew members were rescued from a life raft Saturday, but 22 crew remain unaccounted for: eight South Koreans and 14 Filipinos. Additional empty lifeboats and an escape raft were found in the area, and commercial ships discovered the rescued raft. Seoul’s foreign ministry said search-and-rescue operations are ongoing; South Korea has asked Brazil and Uruguay for assistance and Brazil dispatched a C-130 to help. The ship’s operator, Polaris Shipping of Busan, received the crew’s initial emergency text reporting flooding on the port side. The ultimate fate of the 148,000–266,000-ton vessel remains unconfirmed.

Georgia state Representative Jason Spencer is facing widespread condemnation and calls to resign after a shocking appearance on Sacha Baron Cohen’s Showtime series Who Is America?. In the episode Cohen, disguised as Israeli “anti-terrorism expert” Erran Morad, staged a “self-defense” training session with Spencer. Under Cohen’s prompting, Spencer pretended to be a Chinese tourist by shouting racist gibberish, repeatedly yelled the N-word when told it would attract attention during a simulated kidnapping, and rammed his bare buttocks toward Cohen while shouting “America” as an asserted anti-kidnap tactic. He also bit off a prop’s penis in another staged sequence. Spencer later said he had believed the footage was an “educational aid” for officials and claimed producers asked him to shout provocative language he had requested be removed; he said he’s seeking legal counsel. Georgia lawmakers quickly demanded his resignation, though Spencer declined, noting he recently lost his primary and will finish the remaining five months of his term. The segment intensified scrutiny on Spencer—who had previously proposed banning Muslim head coverings—and on Cohen’s methods, which have also reportedly duped other public figures. Critics say the episode both exposed Spencer’s racism and homophobia and demonstrated Cohen’s talent for provoking revealing behavior from his subjects.

Campbell Soup is overhauling parts of its iconic lineup to respond to shifting consumer tastes and stalled soup sales. The company introduced a reformulated chicken-broth product—first appearing in limited-edition Star Wars–themed cans—reducing listed ingredients from 30 to 20 and eliminating several chemical flavor enhancers and other items viewed unfavorably by shoppers. CEO Denise Morrison frames the effort as “closing the gap between the kitchen and our plants,” emphasizing transparency about ingredients, sourcing and environmental impact. The change is part of a broader push under Morrison, who since 2011 has sped up acquisitions and innovation to counter declining unit sales: purchases like Bolthouse (juices, dressings), Plum Organics (children’s foods) and others expanded Campbell’s presence in perimeter categories and new channels. Campbell has also launched new formats—Skillet Sauces, Slow Kettle tubs—and shifted significant ad spend to social and digital media. The company faces meaningful risk when altering beloved recipes; product teams spent months reformulating to maintain flavor without MSG, disodium inosinate/guanylate and other additives, and to preserve affordability. Market forces add urgency: global soup sales peaked in 2012 and are projected to fall, while Campbell lost share in condensed and ready-to-eat soups amid gains by organic and smaller brands. Campbell is testing reforms gradually—clarifying later that classic red-and-white chicken noodle remains untouched for now—while rebranding soup as relevant to modern, diverse families.

NASA senior scientist David Morrison and faith leaders have dismissed a renewed wave of doomsday claims that a mysterious planet called Nibiru (sometimes dubbed “Planet X”) will collide with Earth, despite a viral prediction pinpointing Sept. 23, 2017 as the start of cataclysmic events. The latest forecast, promoted by David Meade and echoed by the evangelical outlet Unsealed in a dramatized YouTube video, blends biblical numerology and astronomical interpretation. Meade emphasizes the number 33—Jesus’ purported age and the frequency of the word Elohim in the Bible—and notes Sept. 23 falls 33 days after the Aug. 21 solar eclipse, which he treats as an omen. He interprets Revelation 12’s image of a “woman clothed with the sun” as the constellation Virgo aligned with the moon, a crown of stars and planets, and Jupiter “giving birth,” signaling that prophecy will begin to play out on that date and unfold over weeks, altering “the world as we know it.”

Scientists and many Christians reject Meade’s claims. Morrison explains simply that if a massive planet or brown dwarf were entering the inner solar system it would be visible to the naked eye, would already have been tracked by astronomers, and would have disrupted planetary orbits long ago—none of which is happening. Conspiracy assertions of a 3,600-year orbit for Nibiru are inconsistent with observed stable orbits of Earth, Mars, Venus and the Moon. Ed Stetzer of Wheaton College criticizes the misuse of biblical numerology, calling “Christian numerologist” a misleading label and urging skepticism toward secret-number interpretations. He and others warn that repeating sensational predictions amounts to fake news that trivializes genuine faith and distracts from responsible discussion about end-times beliefs. Historical doomsday dates—like May 2003 and Dec. 21, 2012—have similarly passed without incident, underscoring the lack of evidence for Nibiru-based apocalypse scenarios.

Four-year-old Eli Waller of Hamilton Township, New Jersey, died in his sleep on Sept. 25 after showing only mild pinkeye, and medical examiners have determined his death was caused by Enterovirus D68 (EV‑D68). Eli, a triplet who had been well enough to attend preschool on Sept. 21 and 22, was kept home by his mother on Sept. 23 because of a slight eye infection. Between that night and the next morning he did not wake. The Mercer County medical examiner and the CDC confirmed EV‑D68 as the cause of death; brain and lymph‑node swelling were attributed to the virus. Local health officials said Eli had no known underlying conditions such as asthma, which has been linked to more severe EV‑D68 cases.

EV‑D68 reemerged in the U.S. in August and by early October had been detected in at least 43 states. This relatively rare enterovirus strain appears to be the dominant type this season and is associated with hundreds of pediatric hospitalizations for respiratory distress and dozens of paralysis cases. The CDC has documented four U.S. deaths where EV‑D68 was detected, though investigations continue into the virus’s role in each. There is no specific treatment or vaccine for EV‑D68; public health advice stresses hand hygiene, covering coughs, and staying home when ill. In memory of Eli, his family announced plans for The First Day of School Foundation to support students in special education.

Little Fockers (2010), directed by Paul Weitz and starring Robert De Niro, Ben Stiller, Owen Wilson, Dustin Hoffman, Barbra Streisand, Blythe Danner, Jessica Alba and Teri Polo, is the third installment in the Focker franchise. The film follows Greg Focker (Stiller) as he vies to be the next “Godfocker” — the patriarch worthy of approval by his paranoid ex-CIA father-in-law Jack Byrnes (De Niro), who subjects Greg to spying and humiliating scrutiny. Returning characters include Pam (Polo), Kevin (Wilson), Dina (Danner), Bernie (Hoffman) and Roz (Streisand); Jessica Alba plays a new drug rep whose flirtation with Greg fuels Jack’s suspicions. The screenplay by John Hamburg and Larry Stuckey and Weitz’s direction aim for broad, sometimes gross-out humor — erectile dysfunction gags, enema jokes, and slapstick set pieces — but critics found the comedy uneven and recycled. Many reviewers lament De Niro’s continued comic persona, seeing it as a fall from his celebrated dramatic work, and complain the film offers little character development, relying on familiar riffs from the earlier films. While intermittently amusing and commercially calculated to reap returns, Little Fockers is widely regarded as a dispiriting, safe crowd-pleaser that squanders high-caliber talent on tired jokes and sitcom-style recycling.

Russian state TV Channel One aired a harrowing eyewitness account claiming Ukrainian troops in Slovyansk had crucified a 3-year-old boy and dragged his mother behind a tank. The witness, Galina Pyshniak, spoke from a refugee camp; the sensational report prompted outrage and widespread skepticism. Opponents and independent journalists quickly challenged the story’s veracity. Prominent opposition figures Alexei Navalny and Boris Nemtsov called the broadcast “dangerously false” and urged Channel One management be held accountable. Novaya Gazeta reporter Yevgeny Feldman went to Slovyansk and found no corroboration; locals he interviewed had never heard of the atrocity. Wall Street Journal reporter Alan Cullison likewise found no mention of such an event among residents. Critics noted factual inconsistencies in Pyshniak’s account—confusion over the name of the city square and discrepancies in her listed hometown—and pointed out the absence of video or other evidence. Some suggested the tale echoed earlier posts by ultranationalist Alexander Dugin. The episode intensified debates over state media manipulation, with opposition activists accusing Channel One of stoking hysteria to boost recruitment for volunteer fighters and to demonize Ukraine, while nationalists defended such narratives as patriotic motivation.

Researchers in Ottawa report that cardiotrophin 1 (CT-1), a naturally occurring protein, can induce a reversible, healthy form of heart muscle growth and stimulate new blood vessel formation, improving cardiac pumping function in animal models. Published in Cell Research, the work by teams from The Ottawa Hospital, University of Ottawa, the Heart Institute and collaborators shows CT-1 promotes organized, elongating growth of cardiomyocytes and angiogenesis, unlike the pathological enlargement triggered by agents such as phenylephrine (PE). CT-1-treated hearts recovered function in two models: left-side damage after myocardial infarction and right-side failure from pulmonary hypertension. Importantly, the CT-1–driven remodeling was reversible when treatment stopped—mirroring physiological adaptations seen with exercise or pregnancy—whereas PE-induced hypertrophy was irreversible and dysfunctional. Mechanistically, both CT-1 and PE engage pathways previously linked to apoptosis, but CT-1 exerts superior control over these signals to drive beneficial remodeling. In animal experiments, short CT-1 treatments produced benefits lasting weeks; delivery used a subcutaneous mini-pump, a method potentially adaptable to humans. The investigators emphasize CT-1’s promise for right heart failure—a condition with limited therapies often requiring transplant—and for left heart failure where current drugs ease symptoms but do not reverse damage. Co-leads Lynn Megeney and Duncan Stewart have patents pending and seek partners for clinical development; they estimate clinical trials in a few years and broader availability possibly within a decade if human studies confirm safety and efficacy. Funders included CIHR, Ontario Research Fund, Heart and Stroke Foundation and industry partners.

On January 5, 2018, someone close to Nikolas Cruz contacted the FBI’s Public Access Line (PAL) with serious concerns: Cruz’s gun ownership, expressed desire to kill people, erratic behavior, disturbing social media posts, and the potential that he might carry out a school shooting. Under FBI protocol, such information should have been treated as a potential threat to life and promptly forwarded to the FBI’s Miami Field Office for appropriate investigative steps. An internal review determined those procedures were not followed in this case: the PAL did not provide the information to the Miami office, and no further investigation occurred at the time. The document notes victims and families have been spoken with and expresses regret for the additional pain caused by this failure. FBI Director Christopher Wray stated the Bureau is still investigating the facts, is committed to getting to the bottom of what happened, and will review processes for responding to public tips. He emphasized the need for vigilance by the public and for the FBI to act properly and quickly when concerns are reported, reaffirming the Bureau’s dedication to public safety and to improving its practices.

Motorists stuck on the M3 at Sunbury, Surrey, faced criticism after some posted callous comments on Twitter while police tried to talk a distressed woman down from a footbridge. The motorway was closed for more than two hours while Surrey Police and emergency teams managed the incident; the woman was eventually helped to safety and detained under the Mental Health Act. During the closure, several Twitter users taunted the woman and urged the force to hurry or take violent measures. One user wrote, “Tell her to get on with it. Bloody ruining everyone’s weekend. Sat in this for an hour and a half now,” while another suggested police use rubber bullets or nets to remove her and clear traffic. Surrey Police responded on social media, explaining the reason for the delay and asking for patience; Chief Constable Lynne Owens personally engaged with a complainant, acknowledging frustrations but stressing there was no better option available. Inspector Julie Hillman condemned the taunting as “completely unacceptable,” urged public understanding that the road closure was necessary to save the woman’s life, and acknowledged the inconvenience but insisted officers acted to ensure her safety. One user later deleted her offensive tweets and issued an apology. The force also reminded anyone in distress that confidential support is available from Samaritans.

Greece’s attempt to form a national unity government collapsed amid deepening economic crisis and party infighting, reviving the possibility that former ECB vice-president Lucas Papademos could lead a caretaker coalition. Prime Minister George Papandreou announced handing over to a non-existent coalition after failing to install veteran Filippos Petsalnikos, as major parties refused to back him and demanded a stronger, independent figure. Papademos insisted both main parties sign written pledges to support a €130 billion bailout with painful austerity, while Europe signaled dwindling patience and lenders warned Greece could run out of cash next month. Bank runs accelerated as citizens withdrew billions in euros amid fears of a return to the drachma. Meanwhile Italy unveiled fiscal reforms—raising pension age to 67 by 2026, privatizing state real estate via funds, forcing local debt cuts, loosening labor rules, and abolishing mandatory tariffs for certain professions—to reassure markets and curb rising yields.

A U.S. official, Raymond Davis, was arrested in Lahore after allegedly shooting dead two men and, indirectly, a bystander struck by an American car. The U.S. claims Davis acted in self-defense against armed robbers and asserts he has diplomatic immunity; Washington has pressured Pakistan for his release. Pakistan’s government faces domestic outrage and diplomatic pressure: relatives and protesters demand justice, while U.S. lawmakers warned aid could be jeopardized. Tensions rose further when Shumaila Kanwal, the wife of one of the slain men, committed suicide by poison, saying she saw no justice and fearing Davis would be freed. Pakistani officials are divided over who decides Davis’s immunity; police call it murder, while U.S. diplomats insist on immunity. The case has inflamed anti-American sentiment and complicated U.S.-Pakistan relations.

The document reports that George Zimmerman’s old Myspace page, “only to be king again,” has resurfaced and contains disparaging comments about Mexicans and references to his 2005 legal troubles and an altercation with an ex-girlfriend. Zimmerman used the name “Joe G.” on the site, posted photos (one matching his 2005 mug shot shirt), and boasted about having felonies reduced to misdemeanors. His attorney, Mark O’Mara, confirmed the page is genuine and said it was abandoned in 2005. The discovery adds to a broader social media battle surrounding the Feb. 26 shooting of Trayvon Martin: Martin’s family used online campaigns to demand charges and raise funds, while O’Mara has embraced social media to raise money, post updates, and rebut rumors. After initial controversial activity, the defense set up a professionally managed site and Facebook page with moderated comments. Critics warn O’Mara’s social media use could taint jurors and possibly violate ABA rules barring improper extrajudicial advocacy. The piece also includes an unrelated primer stressing the importance of estate planning to avoid probate disputes and ensure orderly distribution of assets.

Busy Philipps recounts an alleged violent encounter with James Franco on the Freaks and Geeks set in her forthcoming memoir, This Will Only Hurt a Little, due Oct. 16. In an excerpt published by multiple outlets and confirmed authentic, Philipps says a 1999 scene called for her character to gently push Franco’s character in the chest. She alleges Franco broke character, grabbed her arms, screamed “DON’T EVER TOUCH ME AGAIN!” and threw her flat on her back, leaving her winded. Co-stars and crew reportedly reacted with horror; Linda Cardellini advised Philipps to call her manager. Philipps writes Franco apologized the next day at the director’s and producers’ urging, but was never disciplined.

Philipps has previously spoken about the incident publicly and told The Hollywood Reporter that she and Franco have discussed it over the years and that he apologized. She frames the episode within early-career vulnerability, feeling she had to avoid complaint to remain employable. The revelation arrives amid broader allegations against Franco from multiple women, which he has denied. Philipps’ memoir also addresses other traumatic experiences, including being raped at 14, material she has recently shared publicly. Franco’s representatives had not immediately responded to requests for comment.

Billy Joel surprised guests at his annual July 4th party by marrying Alexis Roderick at his Long Island estate in an intimate ceremony officiated by longtime friend Gov. Andrew Cuomo. The 66-year-old singer wed 33-year-old Roderick, a former Morgan Stanley executive and accomplished equestrian who is pregnant with their first child, a girl due this summer. Joel and Roderick have been together since 2009. Family and close friends attended, including Joel’s daughter Alexa Ray; Christie Brinkley shared congratulations on Instagram. Joel is currently on tour.

Research published in Biology Letters reports a surprising reproductive tactic among male widow spiders: many males copulate with immature females by puncturing their protective exoskeleton to reach internal genitalia and deposit sperm. These immature females have fully developed reproductive organs and sperm storage (spermathecae) before their final molt, but their genitals remain internal and armored. Males use their fangs to cut through the shell a few days before the female molts—timed so the sperm can be stored without apparent injury—and later the female produces offspring once mature. Field collections found that about one-third of immature females had been inseminated this way, indicating the behavior is fairly common in the studied population.

This tactic contrasts with the typical mating system of widow spiders, where adult females often engage in sexual cannibalism, consuming their mates—a behavior thought to enhance species-level reproductive fitness. Male widow spiders are ordinarily monogamous, but by inseminating immature females who cannot consume them, some males gain access to multiple mates and thereby increase their individual reproductive success. The researchers note this behavior is a selfish strategy that shifts male sexual preference toward younger females and could influence the species’ evolutionary path. Whether this behavior will spread or remains a persistent but limited strategy is unclear; sexual cannibalism likely evolved for adaptive reasons, so juvenile insemination may represent a transient or context-dependent tactic. For now, it stands as another extreme and violent facet of widow spider reproductive behavior.

The Obama administration announced waivers for Washington and Wisconsin, bringing to 26 the number of states freed from key requirements of the 10-year-old No Child Left Behind (NCLB) law as Congress remains deadlocked on reauthorization. The waivers lift the rigid 2014 goal that all students reach proficiency in reading and math and give states more flexibility with federal dollars in exchange for commitments to new accountability plans. States accepting waivers must adopt tougher targets for historically underperforming subgroups, link teacher and principal evaluations more closely to student outcomes, and use multiple indicators of school success beyond test scores—such as college enrollment and Advanced Placement participation. Washington’s agreement, for example, requires halving achievement gaps by 2018 relative to 100 percent passage rates and mandates annual identification of the lowest-performing Title I schools for targeted intervention. Supporters say waivers relieve impossible federal mandates and let states focus help on the worst schools; critics argue the administration is sidestepping Congress and still relies heavily on standardized testing, producing only incremental change. Ten states and D.C. still have pending waiver applications.

Since 1996 Alexa Internet has donated crawl data to the Internet Archive, which the Wayback Machine adds after an embargo. The rest critiques Discovery Channel’s Shark Week for sensationalism. Once a forum for marine biology and conservation, Shark Week now often prioritizes shock value—blood, dramatic reenactments, and fictionalized "documentaries" like Megalodon: The Monster Shark Lives—over science. Discovery’s disclaimers and dramatizations mislead viewers by implying real threats from extinct species and by promoting fear of sharks. Critics including Wil Wheaton and scientist Christie Wilcox argue the franchise trades credibility for ratings, mixing legitimate expert interviews with celebrity appearances and contrived segments. Programming frequently leans on horror tropes, recycled great white footage, and sensational titles (e.g., Sharkpocalypse), while neglecting the diversity and fascinating behaviors of many shark species. Viewers miss stories about thresher tails, wobbegongs, cookiecutter bioluminescence, porbeagle play, and complex great white social dynamics and predator-prey shifts involving orcas. The piece calls on Discovery to restore scientific integrity, spotlight real shark biology and conservation, and stop misrepresenting sharks as mindless killers—otherwise Shark Week risks alienating its audience and undermining meaningful conservation messaging.

After a failed presidential bid and a botched petition drive that disqualified him from Michigan’s primary ballot, Rep. Thaddeus McCotter shifted focus to creative pursuits, writing a 42-minute TV pilot titled "Bumper Sticker: Made On Motown." Leaked by a former staffer, the script depicts McCotter as host of a deliberately "train-wreck" variety show populated by caricatures of his congressional aides, brother and public figures. The pilot features crude humor about sex, drinking, race, flatulence and vomiting, and includes a cartoon Oldsmobile smashing through Detroit landmarks. McCotter describes the project as an unfinished, cathartic outlet after the humiliation of his campaign and denies writing on taxpayer time. Some staffers portrayed in the script recently received notable pay increases; the failed ballot petition effort—handled by longtime staff—left 87 percent of signatures invalid and is under investigation by the Michigan attorney general. McCotter, who founded Screaming Lemur Productions, has prior media experience—authoring a 2011 book, songwriting and TV appearances—and says he’s preparing for a post-congressional career. Supporters call him creative and unconventional; critics say the pilot underscores disengagement from his district duties.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak refused to resign, instead delegating most powers to Vice President Omar Suleiman while keeping the presidency, provoking outrage among hundreds of thousands of protesters in Cairo’s Tahrir Square. The half-measure confused observers, enraged opposition leaders like Mohamed ElBaradei, and strained U.S. responses. The army signaled increased involvement. Protesters chanted for resignation and vowed further demonstrations, while regional allies and Western officials worried the situation could grow more volatile and unstable.

A white cockatoo nicknamed "Debbie," pictured bald and clinging among broken branches after Cyclone Debbie struck Queensland, was rescued but found dead in its box two days later and buried in the forest. Photographer Alix Sweeney’s image became a widely shared emblem of the storm; a wildlife carer said the bird had likely been injured during the gale. The cyclone caused heavy rain, widespread flooding, power outages and school closures across Queensland; emergency crews continued rescues. A five-foot bull shark was also found dead in floodwaters near Ayr, prompting warnings to avoid flood zones.

Katharine F. Lemansky, who posts as “Katie Brown” on Facebook, was charged with animal cruelty in North Carolina after she shared a photo showing her chocolate lab-mix with its muzzle taped shut. The image, posted Friday with the caption “This is what happens when you don't shut up!!!,” went viral, generating hundreds of thousands of shares and a flood of calls, messages and emails to multiple police departments, including South Daytona and Cary. Authorities traced the post and learned Lemansky told police the incident occurred in Cary, N.C.; she faces a misdemeanor cruelty charge under North Carolina law.

Cary Police Captain Randall Rhyne called the taping “a terrible decision” and said pressing charges was appropriate. Animal control officers examined both the pictured dog and its littermate and reported they were well cared for—vaccinated, spayed, microchipped, clean, well-nourished and comfortable in their surroundings—with no signs of muzzle injury or hair loss. Because the charge is a misdemeanor, Lemansky was not jailed but must appear in Wake County court.

Investigations involved multiple jurisdictions; Avon, Torrington and South Daytona police clarified Lemansky no longer lived in those towns, and Avon’s animal control continues its inquiry. The viral outrage prompted heated reactions online, including misdirected accusations against unrelated local businesses whose employees had old social-media ties to Lemansky. Advocates note the photo alone lacks context, while callers demanded stronger action. Police said they want to speak with Lemansky and inspect the dog further as the case proceeds.

Small businesses and laid-off workers are feeling the strain as state unemployment insurance systems run dry. Virginia printer Don Miller, who cut staff after a 15% revenue drop, faces a steep rise in employer unemployment taxes—from $95 per worker in 2009 to an estimated $171—making rehiring costlier. Nationwide, 36 states have raised employer unemployment taxes, with increases ranging from modest to dramatic (Hawaii’s average rose to $1,070; Idaho $816; New Jersey $896). Twenty-five states have borrowed over $25 billion from the federal government to keep benefits flowing; nine more may need to borrow soon. Some states are also trimming benefits, disproportionately hurting seniors and low-income families—Virginia capped combined benefits for Social Security recipients, cutting monthly payments for a 70-year-old former worker from roughly $800 to $100. Analysts warn higher payroll taxes during a recession can discourage hiring, undermining the program’s economic stimulus role. Many states had allowed reserves to fall below recommended levels, forcing difficult choices between tax hikes, benefit cuts, and borrowing.

In response to President Obama’s State of the Union plea about unpaid sick and parental leave, D.C. Council members Elissa Silverman and David Grosso introduced the Universal Paid Leave Act of 2015, proposing one of the nation’s most generous paid-leave programs. If enacted, almost every D.C.-based private-sector employee—full- and part-time—would be eligible for up to 16 weeks of paid leave for family or medical reasons, including bonding after birth, adoption or fostering, recovery from illness, care for an ill family member, or recuperation after military deployment. The proposal would make D.C. the most generous U.S. jurisdiction for paid family leave, exceeding existing state programs in California, New Jersey and Rhode Island and far outstripping federal protections that are unpaid or limited to certain employers and workers.

The plan would be funded through a new Family and Medical Leave Fund into which D.C.-based employers would contribute on a sliding scale tied to wages (for example, about 1 percent for employees earning over $150,000). Federal employees living in D.C. and residents working outside the city could opt in by making personal contributions; however, Maryland and Virginia residents employed by the federal government in D.C. would be excluded. Benefits would replace 100 percent of the first $1,000 per week of earnings and 50 percent of additional earnings, capped at $3,000 weekly.

Supporters emphasize the policy’s potential to keep women in the workforce, reduce economic strain on low-income families, and foster employee loyalty and productivity. They cite research funded by a Department of Labor grant that informed the proposal’s design and modeling. Advocates and affected parents recount hardships under the current system, where unpaid or limited leave forces many to choose between income and caregiving.

Business groups, notably the D.C. Chamber of Commerce, express concern about employer costs and competitive impacts, warning that an employer-funded system could drive firms out of the city. Silverman and Grosso argue that pooling risk will lower individual burdens and yield broader social and economic gains. The bill has committee assignment and majority co-sponsors on the Council, positioning it for hearings, CFO cost estimates, and possible passage pending two Council votes and mayoral consideration.

Chris Urmson, director of Google’s self-driving car program, used a July 1 rear-end collision in Mountain View to highlight how distracted human drivers make roads dangerous and underscore why autonomous vehicles could improve safety. A Google Lexus, driving autonomously with safety drivers aboard, had stopped at a green light to avoid blocking an intersection; a trailing car struck it at about 17 mph without braking. Occupants sustained only minor whiplash and no police report was filed, a pattern Urmson notes: many minor crashes go unreported. Since 2009, Google’s fleet has been involved in 14 incidents (mostly rear-end collisions) over roughly 1.9–2 million test miles; in none has the self-driving car been at fault.
