Unnamed military sources told reporters the shot disrupted an ISIS attack on Iraqi security forces and was a precise option that avoided use of a bomb that might have caused civilian casualties. The kill was reportedly corroborated by video and other hard data, including confirmation from a second location with observation equipment, according to sources cited by the press.

JTF2, a highly secretive Canadian special operations unit formed in 1993 and tasked with counterterrorism, sniper operations and hostage rescue, has limited public acknowledgment of its activities. Government statements emphasized that the operation fit within Canada’s stated “advise and assist” mission in Iraq: JTF2 personnel enable and train Iraqi security forces rather than lead ground combat, offering planning advice and using coalition resources to help defeat Daesh. Canadian commandos are not supposed to be routinely engaged in direct combat, though they may go forward on training missions, accompany Kurdish Peshmerga fighters, and designate targets for coalition airstrikes.

The 3,540-metre shot shatters the previous record of 2,475 metres set by British sniper Craig Harrison in 2009 and surpasses earlier Canadian records from the Afghanistan conflict, when Corporal Rob Furlong (2,430 m in 2002) and Master Cpl. Arron Perry (2,310 m) set successive benchmarks. Observers and former snipers praised the skill involved: long-range engagements at these distances demand mastery of ballistics, wind and atmospheric effects, elevation angle, precise ammunition performance, and even accounting for the Earth’s curvature. Snipers operate in two-person teams—a shooter and spotter—carrying heavy equipment to remote positions and applying a methodical firing routine under extreme pressure.

Some commentators urged caution pending full public verification, noting potential measurement issues such as slant range versus true range in elevated shots. Nonetheless, veteran Canadian snipers and military analysts highlighted Canada’s strong sniper training tradition and cross-training practices that produce highly capable, intellectually adept operators. The Canadian mission in Iraq has expanded special forces trainer numbers in recent years even as government messaging emphasizes a non-combat, advisory role; the confirmed long-range shot underlines both the combat capability of JTF2 and the sensitivity around operational disclosures.

In Eagle County, Colorado, 43-year-old Juan Jose Vidrio Bibriesca — already in court for a bond violation on a felony drug charge — landed in deeper legal trouble when a small folded paper containing cocaine fell from his hat while he stood at the podium before Judge Katharine Sullivan. A law enforcement officer in the gallery initially thought someone else dropped the bindle, but courtroom surveillance video reviewed in slow motion showed the packet falling from Bibriesca’s hat as he doffed it. He was promptly taken to the county jail and later appeared before District Court Judge Paul Dunkelman, where prosecutors charged him with narcotics possession and an additional bond violation, both felonies. Bibriesca is reportedly Mexican-born and in the U.S. unlawfully, meaning Immigration and Customs Enforcement may also become involved. Booking records did not indicate whether he has an attorney.

A nationwide class-action lawsuit filed in Cook County, Illinois, accuses Ulta Beauty of routinely repackaging and reselling previously purchased, used, and returned cosmetics and personal-care items. Filed February 8, 2018, by Meghan DeVries (with a similar earlier suit by a California plaintiff), the complaint alleges a corporate practice in which store managers were given quotas limiting how many returned items could be discarded as “damaged.” According to the suit, managers pressured staff not to exceed those quotas and instructed employees to clean or reseal visibly used products—mascara, lipstick, foundation, shampoo and more—so they could be returned to shelves without disclosure. The complaint cites former-employee reports and social-media posts corroborating these practices, including allegations that staff were told to sanitize items with alcohol or cotton swabs before resale.

The plaintiffs emphasize hygiene and safety concerns, citing an undercover investigation that reportedly found used products contaminated with harmful bacteria such as E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, as well as pathogens like Staphylococcus aureus and potentially herpes simplex virus—organisms that can cause infection if applied to lips, eyes, or broken skin. The lawsuit seeks monetary damages for consumers who unknowingly purchased used products and injunctive relief to halt the alleged repackaging practice nationwide.

Ulta spokeswoman Karen Twigg May responded that the company’s policy prohibits resale of used products and that Ulta intends to vigorously defend against the allegations, stressing that guest health and safety are top priorities. The lead plaintiff and attorney are available for media inquiries; a copy of the complaint is obtainable on request.

A crawl of outlinks from Wikipedia began in March 2016; these crawl files aren’t publicly accessible yet. For this renewed collection several key decisions were made: duplicate detection was turned off to preserve completeness because the maintainers may later share the data, and handling references to other collections would complicate sharing. Unlike earlier runs limited to English Wikipedia, this crawl used a seed list compiled from all 865 individual wikis, expanding coverage across languages and projects. Separately, a tabloid report alleges Mel Gibson has intervened to protect his 93-year-old father, Hutton Gibson, from alleged elder abuse by his wife Joye, who reportedly wants to stop his medications to hasten death. Hutton filed for divorce, tensions are high, and legal conflict appears likely.

A German shepherd in Houston waited faithfully at the gate and doorstep of his apartment for more than two weeks, searching daily for his owner who never returned. Neighbors, including Cassandra Eubanks, watched the dog follow cars into the complex and then stand helpless when none belonged to his person. Residents left food and water, but the dog would not approach anyone and seemed confused and distressed. The reason for his vigil became known when it emerged that his owner, 54-year-old convenience store clerk Hatem Abuharbid, had been shot during a robbery at the Kay-B convenience store on Feb. 7. According to police, two men robbed the store and Abuharbid was shot in the thigh; the bullet severed an artery and he later died at the hospital. Of course, the dog could not understand what had happened and only knew that his companion had not come home. After a social media plea for assistance, Good Samaritan Maranda Perez and her own dog went to the complex and spent nearly an hour coaxing the shepherd into trusting them. The frightened animal ran up three flights of stairs before Perez could leash him, and he remained shaken when touched. It was a struggle to get him into her car, but eventually he allowed it and was taken to foster care. Perez said she can care for the dog for a week; Abuharbid’s brother has expressed a desire to adopt him after that. The community’s response—neighbors providing sustenance, a rescuer answering an online appeal, and a family hoping to keep the pet—highlights both the dog’s loyalty and local compassion as authorities continue to investigate Abuharbid’s death.

John Stamos and fiancée Caitlin McHugh are expecting their first child, the actor tells People. At 54, Stamos—best known as Uncle Jesse from Full House and Fuller House—says he and 31-year-old McHugh had discussed starting a family and everything “just fell into place.” McHugh reportedly joked they should have a baby before marrying because “you’re old,” and when she became pregnant Stamos knew he wanted to propose; the couple got engaged Oct. 22 at Disneyland. Both describe excitement and readiness: Stamos says he’s always wanted to be a dad but thought “that ship has sailed,” and now looks forward to fatherhood, calling himself a “fun dad” who’s practiced baby bits on TV. McHugh praises his “biggest, most loving and generous heart,” and expects he’ll be an amazing father, noting qualities—originality, creativity, work ethic and humor—she hopes their child will inherit. The couple are keeping the baby’s sex private. Stamos, who joined a group of older first-time and later-in-life celebrity dads like George Clooney and others, says the pair plan to expand their family further; McHugh also wants more children. The full interview and additional coverage appear in People’s latest issue and on PeopleTV.

Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich insists he will continue his Republican presidential bid despite back-to-back losses to Rick Santorum in Alabama and Mississippi, where he had campaigned heavily. Though Gingrich finished behind Santorum, he placed second in both contests and vows to pursue a revised short-term goal: preventing Mitt Romney from securing the 1,144 delegates needed for the nomination and pushing the fight to a contested convention. Campaign chair Bob Walker says Gingrich aims to block Romney’s inevitability; advisers argue the nomination won’t be decided until the “fourth quarter” and that Gingrich can capitalize on later-state sequencing.

Gingrich’s persistence stems from ambition and financial independence—at age 68 he isn’t under the same economic pressures as younger candidates—and a belief he can be a historic figure. Supporters and allies expect him to continue “as long as there is money in the bank account and gas in the bus.” Critics counter that Gingrich’s Southern dominance has evaporated: his support among very conservative, evangelical, and Tea Party voters dropped markedly from earlier Southern wins, weakening his viability.

Santorum’s twin victories boosted his claim as the conservative alternative to Romney and intensified calls for Gingrich to withdraw so conservatives can consolidate behind Santorum. Romney, meanwhile, increased his delegate haul and remains the statistical frontrunner. With Romney leading in delegates and the GOP calendar favoring him, analysts still see a contested convention as unlikely, though Gingrich and Santorum aim to make it possible.

UPDATED: Rick Santorum faces significant delegate shortfalls in the Ohio Republican primary after failing to file complete delegate slates. Ohio has 66 convention delegates (63 at stake next Tuesday); Santorum’s campaign did not file any district delegates in three congressional districts, eliminating his ability to receive those nine delegates, and submitted incomplete slates in six more districts. As a result he may be ineligible for up to 18 district delegates—more than one-quarter of the state’s total. Ohio awards three district delegates per congressional district; where Santorum submitted fewer names he can only receive the delegates he listed, while any unlisted delegates would remain unallocated until parties or campaigns file petitions. The Ohio GOP can convene a “committee on contests” to resolve disputes, with appeals possible to the RNC. The omission stemmed from Santorum filing only with the secretary of state (which only verifies ballot qualification) and not properly with the state party. Rival campaigns, notably Mitt Romney’s, seized on the organizational lapse as evidence of campaign weakness, while Santorum’s team stressed that votes will count toward at-large delegates.

Astrophysicist Nikolai Kardashev’s 1962 scale for measuring a civilization’s technological power—Type I (planetary), Type II (stellar), and Type III (galactic)—frames a scenario for cosmic dominance: first consume a planet’s resources, then harness your star’s energy, then harvest the stars across your galaxy. A recent preprint by Dan Hooper revisits this idea and adds an urgent twist: because dark energy accelerates cosmic expansion, stars beyond the Local Group will eventually recede beyond the cosmic horizon and become permanently inaccessible. To maximize long-term energy access, any sufficiently advanced civilization would therefore attempt to capture and bring useful stars home before they vanish beyond reach. The proposed method echoes long-standing concepts like Freeman Dyson’s “Dyson spheres”: vast swarms of solar-collecting satellites or “statites” that hover by balancing light pressure, forming a cloud to capture stellar output. These structures could also propel stars by using their energy for acceleration, producing detectable electromagnetic signatures during propulsion. Hooper suggests targeted stars would be in the ~20–100 solar-mass range—too small gives insufficient output, too large risks imminent supernova—and their removal would alter galactic light spectra, shifting peaks to longer wavelengths. Though humans sit around 0.7 on Kardashev’s scale and lack detection sensitivity today, astronomers could seek accelerated stars or galaxies missing their prime stars as indicators of advanced star-harvesting civilizations. The idea blends decades of science fiction and theory in a race against dark energy to secure the universe’s accessible energy.

A Pew Research Center survey of 1,983 U.S. adults (March 21–April 8, 2013) finds 60% say humans and other living things have evolved over time, while 33% assert humans have existed in their present form since the beginning of time. Overall levels are similar to 2009, but partisan differences widened: 67% of Democrats versus 43% of Republicans now accept evolution, a larger gap than four years earlier. Views vary sharply by religion: 64% of white evangelical Protestants and 50% of black Protestants reject evolution, while majorities of white mainline Protestants (78%), the religiously unaffiliated (76%), and white non-Hispanic Catholics (68%) accept it. Among those endorsing evolution, 32% attribute it to natural processes and 24% say a supreme being guided evolution. Beliefs also differ by age, education and gender. The survey’s margin of error is ±3 percentage points.

Eman Ahmed Abd El Aty, a 36-year-old Egyptian woman who has been bedridden for about 25 years and reportedly weighs roughly 500 kg (about 1,100 lb), is being brought to Mumbai for high‑risk bariatric treatment. Confined to her home since early childhood after extreme and progressive swelling—initially attributed by her family to elephantiasis and later thought by her treating surgeon to be obesity‑related lymphedema—Eman’s condition left local doctors unable to help. Her sister contacted renowned Mumbai bariatric surgeon Dr. Muffazal Lakdawala in October. After viewing photos and sparse medical records, Lakdawala, who has extensive experience with massive‑obesity cases and has operated pro bono for this patient, agreed to try to save her life and began raising funds to charter a flight and arrange care. Transport poses major logistical challenges: evacuating her home may require demolition of a wall and a specially equipped aircraft with an accessible entrance. A further hurdle arose when the Indian Embassy in Cairo initially refused a medical visa because Eman could not appear for fingerprinting. Lakdawala appealed directly on Twitter to India’s External Affairs Minister Sushma Swaraj, who intervened from hospital and secured the visa within 24 hours. With visa cleared, Lakdawala is negotiating with airlines and expects to bring Eman to Mumbai within days. He says the surgery is “very high risk,” anticipates she’ll need months of postoperative recovery in Mumbai, foresees at least 200–300 lb initial weight loss, and projects a multi‑year process to reduce her to a healthy weight. The operation will test his team’s skills and resources.

Two pilots in the helium-filled Two Eagles balloon — American Troy Bradley and Russian Leonid Tiukhtyaev — are nearing the end of a record-setting trans-Pacific flight that began from Saga, Japan. By Thursday they had surpassed the long-standing 5,209-mile gas-balloon distance record set in 1981, reaching more than 5,260 miles (about 8,465 km) while tracking near the California coast. Mission control in Albuquerque celebrated the milestone but emphasized focus on safely completing the flight and landing. The team also expected to surpass the 1978 duration record of roughly 137 hours in a traditional gas balloon, a feat anticipated on Friday. Originally aiming for Canada, changing weather — a high-pressure ridge off the U.S. West Coast — forced a southern shift, and the pilots now plan to land on Baja California, Mexico, likely on Saturday. The lightweight carbon-fiber capsule beneath a massive helium envelope carries instruments to document the flight for official certification by the U.S. National Aeronautic Association and the Federation Aeronautique Internationale, which could take weeks or months. Ground chase crews and volunteers are organizing to support a safe landing, with sand dunes and coastal sites considered best options.

In Cristovo de Cea, a town in northwest Spain’s Galicia region, municipal workers accidentally destroyed and effectively sealed a suspected 6,000-year-old Neolithic tomb after mistaking the exposed granite slabs for a broken picnic table. Believed to be an ancient burial chamber with heritage status, the site was unmarked and, apparently, unknown to local officials. Parks and recreation staff poured concrete into the chamber and installed a new picnic table atop it. An environmental group alerted authorities, prompting complaints and an investigation. The town’s mayor, José Luis Valladores, said neither heritage authorities nor the complainants had informed the council; the site wasn’t marked and the team assumed a repair was the logical action. Archaeologist Juan Barceló, who called the incident a “monumental error,” said he was horrified and suggested the lapse in communication may have been exacerbated by summer holidays. He stressed that such accidents are atypical in Spain, where monuments over a century old are legally protected and preservation authorities at various levels generally work effectively. The report places the mistake in a broader context of both accidental and deliberate destruction of ancient sites worldwide: incidents include Nanjing crews destroying burial sites in 2007, a Native American burial ground razed for development in California, workers in Belize dismantling a 2,300-year-old Mayan pyramid for road fill, and well-intentioned but damaging restoration attempts. The Cristovo de Cea case highlights failures in marking, communication, and local awareness that can irreversibly harm archaeological heritage.

Comedy Central marked Newt Gingrich’s exit from the 2012 Republican presidential race with a spoof of the children’s book Goodnight Moon, titled “Goodnight Moon Colony.” The seven-slide image gallery, posted on Comedy Central’s Indecision site, lampoons Gingrich’s signature proposal to direct NASA to build a permanent American lunar base by 2020, followed by trips to Mars. An illustration mimics the 1947 book’s style, showing Gingrich in bed with a moon base visible outside his window. Other slides mock notable campaign lines and controversies, including a jab at his dismissal of Occupy Wall Street protesters and a reference to the defunct Center for Health Transformation, which he founded. Space experts questioned the feasibility and cost of his timeline, and rival Mitt Romney favored stronger NASA-private industry ties and broader coalition planning for U.S. space policy.

Authorities conducted targeted crawls to archive web pages at creation and preserve referenced pages so links remain accessible even if originals change or are removed; the Internet Archive hopes these "No More 404" captures will be used to replace or supplement broken links and preserve authors’ original references.

Separately, police investigating the disappearance of four young men traced cellphone and vehicle movements to properties tied to the DiNardo family. On Saturday, officers tracked a signal from Mr. Finocchiaro’s cellphone to a farm owned by Anthony and Sandra DiNardo in Solebury Township. Early Sunday, a 1996 Nissan Maxima belonging to Tom Meo, 21, was found less than a mile from that farm on another DiNardo-owned property. A Nissan sedan owned by Mark Sturgis, 22, was discovered Sunday at a nearby shopping center. Jimi Taro Patrick, 19, last seen Wednesday, was noted in a family statement as a Newtown resident who had just completed his freshman year at Loyola University on a scholarship.

Investigators focused on Daniel DiNardo early in the inquiry; he was identified as a person of interest and his Bensalem Township home was searched the same day he was arrested on a previously dismissed weapons charge. Court records revealed additional leads: a license plate reader captured a silver Ford truck plate—matching a vehicle DiNardo later said he drove—shortly before also registering Meo’s Maxima two seconds later, about two miles from where Meo’s car was later found. Authorities have also reportedly summoned DiNardo’s parents to a grand jury, though prosecutors declined to confirm.

The Internet Archive is running crawls to capture newly created pages and the pages they reference so that when referenced content changes or disappears, a preserved version corresponding to the citing page remains available. The project aims to reduce broken links by providing archived replacements or companion links so readers can see what authors originally intended. This “No More 404” effort archives supported sites to help keep web citations reliable.

In unrelated public-health news, Iowa’s Alcoholic Beverages Division warned that serving Moscow mules and other acidic drinks in pure copper mugs can be hazardous. Because many cocktails (Moscow mules contain vodka, ginger beer and lime) and other acidic beverages—fruit juices, vinegar, wine—with pH below 6.0 can cause copper to leach into the drink, regular use of unlined copper containers risks copper poisoning. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting and jaundice. The advisory was prompted by the drink’s rising popularity and ensuing safety questions. However, copper-surfaced mugs are still safe if the interior is lined with a nonreactive metal such as nickel or stainless steel; such lined mugs are widely available. The health advisory was reported by Live Science. Finally, a collection of web resources relates to the UCSF Food Industry Documents Archive, which preserves internal company documents (for example from the U.S. sugar industry) that impact public health.

Houston police identified 62-year-old Joseph James Pappas as the suspect in the July 20 fatal shooting of prominent Houston cardiologist Dr. Mark Hausknecht, and said Pappas may have been motivated by a decades-old grudge. Authorities say Pappas’s mother died during an operation performed by Hausknecht about 20 years ago, and investigators believe the killing was premeditated. Surveillance footage shows the suspect riding a 10-speed Schwinn bicycle near the Texas Medical Center during morning rush hour, passing Hausknecht and then turning around two blocks later to fire multiple shots. Hausknecht, a well-known interventional cardiologist who had once treated former President George H.W. Bush, was struck and died at the scene.

Houston Police Chief Art Acevedo called Pappas “dangerous” and “capable,” saying the suspect may be suicidal and should be considered armed. A tipster who recognized images released from surveillance helped break the case. Officers executed a welfare check and later search and arrest warrants at Pappas’s Westbury home; he was not there, but police recovered evidence linking him to the homicide. Investigators also found that the phone number tied to Pappas and his real estate business had been used to post online listings attempting to sell firearms, ammunition, tactical vests and ballistic plates days after the shooting. It is unclear whether any of the weapons advertised were used in the murder.

Pappas worked in Harris County law enforcement for about 30 years, including as a reserve constable until 2013, and had maintained law-enforcement training through 2017. Neighbors and a former acquaintance described him as secretive but outwardly normal; some recalled he regularly rode a 10-speed bicycle. Authorities continued to search for Pappas and urged the public to help locate him. The slaying stunned the Texas Medical Center community and prompted reflections on rare but serious instances of grudge-motivated violence against health-care providers. Hausknecht, 65, is survived by his wife, two sons, his mother and three siblings; a funeral was held at First Presbyterian Church.

A staffing-firm survey from OfficeTeam of more than 600 U.S. office workers and senior managers finds that employees spend roughly a full workday each week on nonwork activities, largely driven by mobile-phone use. On average, office staff report using their phones for 56 minutes per workday—about 4.7 hours weekly—for personal email, social media and other sites. Managers underestimate that behavior, guessing about 39 minutes per day. In addition to phone use, employees spend an average of 42 minutes daily, or 3.5 hours weekly, on personal tasks such as errands. Combined, these behaviors amount to nearly eight hours of lost productivity per employee per week.

Younger workers are the most likely to stray: employees ages 18–34 average 70 minutes a day on mobile devices plus 48 minutes on other personal tasks, totaling just under ten hours per week. The phone also enables bypassing company restrictions—58 percent of workers say they use personal devices to visit websites blocked by corporate IT, while only 39 percent of managers believe that is common. Gender differences were reported for accessing blocked sites, with 68 percent of men and 43 percent of women doing so frequently. OfficeTeam’s district president, Brandi Britton, noted occasional personal use can be understandable but cautioned it can become a major distraction and recommended using breaks to handle nonwork matters.

The Pentagon’s research arm, DARPA, is soliciting ideas for an airborne “mothership” concept that would use existing large aircraft—think B-1s, B-52s or C-130s—to carry, launch and recover Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS). The goal is to extend drone range and mission flexibility by enabling drones to be deployed close to targets and then return to the host aircraft. DARPA stresses this is an early, paper-stage exploration, not a request for prototypes. The idea echoes historical experiments: 1920s rigid airships carried Sparrowhawk biplanes that hooked onto a trapeze, and the CIA’s 1960s D-21 drone launched from a B-52 but faced recovery and reliability problems. Technical challenges—especially midair recovery—remain significant. The concept fits a broader “marsupial” robotics trend, where larger platforms carry smaller systems, and parallels Chinese demonstrations of robot-carrying vehicles. Researchers are also exploring underwater “carriers,” such as submarine-launched drones deployed from missile or torpedo tubes, which recent tests have begun to demonstrate.

Central Arkansas couple Steve and Terri Weaver of Stuttgart won over $1 million in lottery prizes in one weekend. On Saturday Steve bought a $1 million scratch-off and won, leaving him shocked and anxious. The following day Terri purchased a $250,000 “Taxes Paid” scratch-off and won $50,000, bringing their total to $1,050,000. The Weavers admitted feeling nervous about claiming the prizes, joking about lie detector tests, and said they plan to invest the money. Despite the windfall, they intend to keep working and will continue playing the lottery.

Ötzi, the 5,300-year-old Tyrolean Iceman, suffered severe dental disease and provides fresh genetic insights into Neolithic life. Recent 3D CT scans reveal advanced gum disease, deep cavities, and heavy tooth wear from chewing coarse, stone‑contaminated grain and using teeth as a “third hand”; one front tooth shows trauma-induced discoloration and a broken molar likely from a small stone in gruel. The shift toward coarsely ground starches in the late Stone Age likely increased cavity rates. Whole-genome sequencing, published in Nature Communications, shows Ötzi had genetic predisposition to arteriosclerosis despite an active hunter-gatherer lifestyle, suggesting limits to prevention. His Y chromosome places him in rare haplogroup G2A4, linking paternal ancestry to Near Eastern Neolithic migrants; his closest modern genetic matches are small populations in Sardinia, Corsica, and parts of Georgia and Russia. The analysis also identifies brown eyes and hair, type O blood, lactose intolerance, and DNA from Borrelia burgdorferi, marking the oldest known Lyme disease carrier and highlighting long-term pathogen persistence.

Texas politics and national security dominated Sunday morning broadcasts, with several prominent figures weighing in on abortion legislation in Texas and the fallout from NSA surveillance disclosures.

Texas state Sen. Wendy Davis, who became a national figure after filibustering a Texas abortion bill, accused Governor Rick Perry and Lieutenant Governor David Dewhurst of using the 20-week abortion ban to further political ambitions rather than prioritize women’s safety. Speaking on CBS’s Face the Nation, Davis charged that Perry and Dewhurst “are willing to … put women in harm’s way in order to step up on the political ladder.” She said Republicans mishandled the timing and rules in the regular session in an effort to rush the bill through and predicted they would be “smarter” about tactics in the upcoming special session. Still, she argued national attention guarantees accountability: “the eyes of Texas, the eyes of the country are watching.” On Meet the Press, Davis reiterated that the proposal is more than a 20-week ban, calling it a large omnibus bill that would impose many clinic regulations likely to close facilities, and rejected Perry’s suggestion—citing her past as a teenage mother—that her life story should dictate support for restrictions. “My life story is something that belongs to me,” she said, stressing her fight is to ensure all women have choices and opportunities.

On national security, Democrats and former intelligence officials debated Edward Snowden and U.S. surveillance programs. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi defended her criticism of NSA leaker Snowden on Meet the Press, expressing skepticism about the value of what he has disclosed and condemning his threats to share information with Russia and China. Pelosi emphasized legislative safeguards enacted under President Obama—like FISA amendments and oversight mechanisms including inspectors general and the Privacy and Civil Liberties Board—arguing they distinguish current programs from the more expansive surveillance under George W. Bush.

Retired Gen. Michael Hayden, former CIA and NSA director, told Face the Nation that disclosures have done “significant” damage to President Obama and urged the administration to do more to inform the public about surveillance to build consensus and avoid a backlash. Conservative leader Ralph Reed also appeared on Meet the Press to push back against labeling opponents of same-sex marriage as bigots, noting many politicians have changed positions over time.

Rapper T.I. (Clifford Harris) was arrested early Wednesday at about 4:30 a.m. outside his gated community near Atlanta on charges of disorderly conduct, public drunkenness and simple assault after an altercation with a security guard, Henry County officials said. Authorities report T.I. and a friend were taken into custody; both have since posted bail and been released. The incident reportedly began when T.I. lost his key and the guard would not allow him entry. T.I. says the disagreement started because the guard was allegedly asleep in the guard shack as T.I. returned from the studio; he contends he confronted the guard, a “very heated debate” ensued, and the guard called police. T.I. maintains the encounter never turned physical, saying he “may have been hurt by my words” but never laid a hand on the guard. He also characterized the arrest as unjust, telling The Blast he believes he was targeted by “white cops in a very white area” because he is an affluent African‑American celebrity; he noted the guard involved was Black, which he said compounded his frustration. T.I. said he demanded the guard’s name and offered the opportunity to apologize when the guard allegedly refused. He plans legal action against his homeowners association over the guard incident and expects the charges to be dropped once “the truth comes out.” T.I.’s past legal history includes roughly seven months in prison after a 2009 federal gun conviction and about 10–11 months in 2010 for a probation violation following a drug arrest. After his release, he spent time with family and celebrated his son Major’s 10th birthday; his attorney has issued a statement reiterating that T.I. asserts he was wrongly arrested.

Attorney General Eric Holder and other officials strongly condemned an ambush-style shooting that wounded two police officers during a pre-dawn protest outside the Ferguson Police Department. Holder labeled the shooter a “damn punk,” said the attack “turned my stomach,” and warned such violence threatens the nonviolent reform efforts prompted by Michael Brown’s death. Both officers—one from St. Louis County and one from Webster Groves—were shot while standing in a line of about 25 officers; they were treated at Barnes-Jewish Hospital and released, though one still had a bullet lodged near his ear. St. Louis County Police Chief Jon Belmar described the incident as a targeted attack, saying shots came from about 125 yards away and seemed parallel to the ground. No suspects had been identified, but police recovered shell casings and briefly detained three people near a bungalow searched by tactical teams; they were being questioned but not charged. CrimeStoppers and local lawmakers offered rewards totaling at least $13,000 for information. The Missouri Highway Patrol and St. Louis County Police took over protest security that night as tensions in Ferguson remain high since Michael Brown’s killing and the Justice Department’s report finding racial bias in the Ferguson police. Community leaders—including Brown family attorney Benjamin Crump—condemned the violence and urged the public not to let it obscure protesters’ calls for justice. Officials emphasized the need for information from witnesses and pledged federal investigative support as the manhunt continues.

Fifteen years after his 1996 arrest, Ted Kaczynski’s belongings are being auctioned online by the U.S. Marshals to help satisfy a $15 million restitution order to victims of his 1978–1995 bombing campaign. The Unabomber’s handwritten 35,000-word manifesto and his now-iconic ratty hoodie are drawing notable bids—about $17,525 and $20,025 respectively—while his Smith-Corona typewriter is nearing $11,000. Other items, such as a hand-bowed wood saw and letters to his aunt, attract only modest interest. The sale is unlikely to cover the restitution total, especially since his self-built Montana cabin is exhibited at the Newseum. Appraiser Elyse Luray acknowledges the historical value of the manifesto and typewriter while calling many lots collectible mainly to “weird” enthusiasts; she notes hype inflates prices but contrasts such items with enduringly valuable celebrity memorabilia. Crime-memorabilia collector Scott Michaels and criminologist Jeffery Ian Ross offer context: collectors prize physical links to notorious events for their voyeuristic and historical appeal, and this fascination stretches back centuries. Michaels prefers tactile artifacts like the saw, while cautioning buyers not to expect financial gain. In related celebrity auctioning, actor Kellan Lutz is donating luggage for charity via JetBlue and DoSomething.org; and a rare 1917 Charlie Chaplin film reel, initially bought for its tin, may fetch six figures as the sole surviving copy.

A US jury has ordered Facebook, its Oculus unit and executives to pay $500m to video game publisher ZeniMax after finding Oculus breached a contract and infringed some copyrights when launching the Rift VR headset. ZeniMax alleged Oculus and former id Software engineer John Carmack unlawfully used its early virtual reality work; Oculus says the jury rejected theft of trade secrets but found contract and copyright violations. Co-founder Palmer Luckey was found to have violated a non-disclosure agreement. Oculus said it was disappointed and will appeal.

The verdict came as Facebook reported a strong quarter: Q4 net profit more than doubled to about $3.6bn and revenue rose to $8.81bn, driven by mobile advertising—now about 84% of ad revenue—and 53–57% growth in ad sales. Monthly users reached roughly 1.86bn, nearing 2bn. Facebook plans increased spending and video investment, aiming at short-form and episodic content, while pledging to combat fake news with more AI. Management downplayed election-related ad impacts and signaled continued growth despite regulatory and market challenges.

Montana congressman-elect Greg Gianforte pleaded guilty to misdemeanor assault for body-slamming reporter Ben Jacobs the night before a congressional election. Judge Rick West imposed a 180-day deferred sentence, 40 hours of community service, 20 hours of anger management, a $300 fine and an $85 court fee. West initially ordered four days of jail with part to be served through a work program, but replaced that after determining those convicted of assault are ineligible for the program. Under Montana law, misdemeanor assault can carry up to six months in jail and a fine of up to $500. Gianforte apologized to Jacobs and pledged a $50,000 donation to the Committee to Protect Journalists, saying he hoped “some good can come of these events.” The episode drew national attention and sparked criticism after President Trump publicly praised Gianforte at a rally, calling him “a great person” and saying “any guy that can do a body slam, he is my type.” Trump’s comments, made amid broader controversy over media freedom and the killing of Jamal Khashoggi, were condemned by the White House Correspondents’ Association as celebrating violence against a reporter and an attack on the First Amendment. The incident and Trump’s remarks occurred during a politically charged period in Montana, where Trump campaigned against Democratic Senator Jon Tester and weighed in on immigration and other issues. Despite the assault controversy, Gianforte won his special election and later sought reelection. The case highlighted tensions over press freedom, political violence, and partisan reactions in a high-profile, closely watched state contest.

A Cooke Aquaculture net pen near Cypress Island failed Saturday, releasing thousands of farmed Atlantic salmon into Puget Sound waters between Anacortes and the San Juan Islands. The floating pen, which held roughly 305,000 fish and contained about 3 million pounds of fish biomass, suffered anchor and structural failures that left walkways twisted and pens “severely compromised.” Cooke initially attributed the breach to “exceptionally high tides and currents coinciding with this week’s solar eclipse,” saying many fish may still be contained and that full losses won’t be known until harvesting and inventory are complete. Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW) officials have urged recreational and tribal fishers to remove as many escapees as possible—there are no size or bag limits and fish need not be recorded on tickets—while the department and Cooke craft a spill-response plan; penalties are being evaluated.

Local tribal fishers, especially from the Lummi Nation, and environmental groups called the incident devastating and an “environmental nightmare,” worried about competition, disease, parasite amplification, and impacts on endangered chinook and other native salmon. Wild Fish Conservancy noted earlier pen problems at the site and questioned Cooke’s account and preparedness. Critics also challenge the company’s claim that eclipse-driven tides were atypical; NOAA and tidal data show tides and currents that day were not unusually high for the area. Scientists at NOAA and others stress past research indicating escaped, domesticated Atlantic salmon typically fare poorly in the wild and seldom establish or interbreed, but concern remains about short-term ecological interactions and precedent as Cooke seeks expansion permits for other regional operations. The spill has renewed scrutiny of salmon farming practices, enforcement, and preparedness in Washington waters.

Ringing Bells, a Noida startup, has begun shipping its controversially cheap smartphone, the Freedom 251, promising deliveries to start June 30. The device, priced at Rs 251 (about $4), generated massive attention and skepticism after its February launch—claims that prototypes shown to the media were rebadged phones and doubts from experts who said sub-Rs 2,000 manufacturing was impossible led to an FIR and widespread suspicion of a scam. Despite that, founder and CEO Mohit Goel says the company is “ready with nearly two lakh” (200,000) handsets and will ship them first, then reopen registrations for additional buyers. Ringing Bells originally pledged 2.5 million units before June but received over 70 million registrations and saw its payment gateway crash within days. Goel admits the company will lose about Rs 140–150 per unit, yet hopes to profit from volume and from partnerships to preload apps; he frames the venture as fulfilling Digital India and Make in India goals. The phone is a 4-inch, dual-SIM 3G device with a 1.3GHz quad-core processor, 1GB RAM, 8GB storage (expandable to 32GB), 8MP rear camera with flash, 3.2MP front camera, 1,800 mAh battery, and Android 5.1. Ringing Bells says units are manufactured in Haridwar and boot to an Indian tricolour image; IANS was shown only photographs, not devices. The company also plans to launch a “Freedom” 32-inch HD LED TV under Rs 10,000, claiming one lakh units in stock. Skepticism remains widespread, but the startup insists it has delivered a working product and will ramp monthly shipments.

In August 2018, Christopher Watts murdered his pregnant wife, Shanann, and their daughters Bella (4) and Celeste (3) in Frederick, Colorado. Newly released Weld County documents and interview summaries show escalating marital discord in the months before the killings. While Shanann and the girls spent five weeks visiting family in North Carolina, Watts became distant, and investigators later learned he was having an affair with coworker Nichol Kessinger and went on dates during that period. Texts from Shanann reveal hurt and confusion as she confronted Chris about emotional withdrawal, his refusal to hug or be intimate, and his telling her he didn’t want the third child. Shanann canceled a planned gender-reveal party days before the murders.

On Aug. 13 a friend reported Shanann and the children missing. Watts initially denied knowledge, pleaded publicly for their return, and gave inconsistent accounts to police. A polygraph administered Aug. 15 indicated deception on key questions; under sustained questioning and after speaking with his father, Watts admitted to killing Shanann and to placing the girls’ bodies in oil tanks. He later pleaded guilty to multiple counts including first-degree murder, unlawful termination of pregnancy and tampering with bodies, and was sentenced to life without parole plus additional consecutive and concurrent terms.

The released 2,000-plus pages include phone records, texts, interviews with friends, Kessinger’s account, and investigators’ reconstructions: financial stress, in-law tensions, Watts’ lies about his whereabouts, and details of the crime scene. Authorities and family members described Watts as having led a double life before the killings; Shanann’s messages convey mounting fear and desperation in the relationship’s final weeks.

Emmanuel Macron’s decisive victory over far-right candidate Marine Le Pen in France’s presidential run-off elicited broad international congratulations and immediate political challenges at home. Leaders across Europe hailed the result as a relief for the European Union after Brexit and other populist shocks. Germany’s Angela Merkel and EU figures such as Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker and Council President Donald Tusk praised Macron’s pro-European stance, while Britain’s Theresa May and U.S. President Donald Trump offered cordial messages; Trump’s congratulatory tweet came despite prior affinity with Le Pen on security issues. Other world leaders, including Canada’s Justin Trudeau, Brazil’s Michel Temer and Australia’s Malcolm Turnbull, telephoned or tweeted support, signaling readiness for cooperation.

Macron, 39, staged his victory speech at the Louvre—a symbolic choice evoking France’s history and European identity—walking alone to Beethoven’s “Ode to Joy,” the EU anthem, in a deliberate nod to a dignified, somewhat monarchical republican style. He cast himself as a youthful reformer promising a “revolution” in French politics while also aspiring to embody national leadership in a tradition harking back to France’s strong executives. Yet his honeymoon will be short; he assumes office amid economic stagnation, high unemployment, social unrest, a persistent terror threat and overseas military commitments in places like the Sahel.

Key domestic tests loom. Macron plans swift economic reforms—including liberalizing labor laws, reducing public spending, cutting red tape for small businesses and lowering class sizes in deprived areas—potentially via presidential decrees. Those moves risk provoking protests and union resistance, as evidenced by CGT-led marches and warnings from leftist unions about sidelining consultation. Juncker bluntly warned that France’s spending habits are unsustainable, and markets showed caution as the euro eased slightly after Macron’s win.

Politically, Macron’s ability to implement his agenda hinges on June parliamentary elections. His nascent En Marche! movement must secure a majority; otherwise he faces complex coalition-building. Macron’s team has pledged gender balance and a large infusion of political newcomers among its 577 legislative candidates, but the traditional parties are fractured—conservatives and Socialists both weakened—which creates both opportunity and uncertainty. Speculation over his choice of prime minister remains intense as he seeks a figure capable of uniting centrist supporters from left and right.

Internationally, Macron is expected to move quickly to reassure allies, visiting German Chancellor Merkel and French troops abroad. Observers see his triumph as a boost for liberal internationalism and the EU, countering populist momentum seen elsewhere, though analysts caution that populist sentiments remain potent. Macron’s presidency will be judged on his ability to bridge France’s urban-rural divides, deliver tangible economic improvements, and translate his reformist, pro-European rhetoric into effective governance.

On July 26–27, 2017, President Trump announced via tweets that the U.S. government would "not accept or allow" transgender individuals to serve in the military, citing alleged "tremendous medical costs and disruption." His abrupt declaration blindsided Pentagon leaders and created immediate confusion about policy and personnel actions. Gen. Joseph Dunford, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, issued a memo saying there would be no changes to existing policy until Defense Secretary Jim Mattis receives formal direction from the White House and provides implementation guidance. Dunford emphasized treating all personnel with respect and maintaining focus on missions. Mattis was on vacation when the tweets were posted, and the Pentagon said it would work with the White House to provide guidance; officials warned that any guidance could take weeks or months.

Services sought to reassure transgender service members that, for now, they would not be discharged and would continue to receive medical care—most notably the Navy, which told sailors no discharges or changes in care would occur absent further direction. The announcement interrupted a trend toward greater inclusion that included the 2016 lift of the transgender ban under then-Defense Secretary Ash Carter; since October 2016 transgender troops have been allowed medical care and personnel system changes. Estimates of transgender active-duty personnel vary; a RAND study suggested 1,320–6,630 among 1.3 million troops and projected modest annual medical costs (about $8 million), far lower than replacement and recruiting costs. The move drew swift bipartisan reaction: critics like Sen. John McCain opposed forcing capable service members out, while some lawmakers supported the change. Uncertainty persisted over who was consulted before the tweets and how any policy reversal would be implemented.

Alaska State Troopers report that two men skiing in the Rainbow Mountains were involved in an avalanche Saturday afternoon; one man was killed and the other survived after digging himself out and summoning help. The deceased is tentatively identified as 35-year-old Eric Peterson of Delta Junction; troopers say next of kin have been notified but his body has not yet been recovered. The surviving skier is identified as 63-year-old Michael Hopper of Fairbanks, who owns Black Rapids Lodge roughly 20 miles from the avalanche site. Lodge volunteer David Savage said Hopper is experienced in the local mountains and the lodge runs an annual avalanche-safety course, though Savage cautioned that the terrain can be unpredictable. Troopers say the avalanche struck almost directly behind the two skiers. Hopper reported hearing a “whoomp” from about 20 feet above them, was buried, and took two to three hours to dig himself out. After freeing himself he found Peterson’s glove and then dug down to discover Peterson deceased. A motorist driving on the Richardson Highway spotted a headlamp and later found Hopper seeking a ride; Hopper had used another driver’s cellphone to call 911. Responders included Alaska State Troopers, military personnel from Black Rapids, Fort Greely Fire Department, and Rural Delta Fire and Rescue. Troopers warned the area is widely unstable and conditions are worsening with heavy snowfall; recovery of Peterson’s body will be attempted when weather and safety conditions allow. The situation is developing; updates will appear on KTUU.com and Channel 2 newscasts.

A Human Rights Watch report finds that in 2012 only 3 percent of federal drug defendants went to trial, with 97 percent pleading guilty. Author Jamie Fellner attributes this to prosecutors’ powerful leverage created by mandatory-minimum sentencing and charge-stacking: defendants are often given stark choices—accept a plea with a reduced sentence or risk trial and face dramatically longer prison terms. The report’s analysis of U.S. Sentencing Commission data shows defendants who lost at trial received sentences more than three times longer than those who accepted pleas, and on average 11 years longer in another analysis. Most who went to trial—89 percent—lost.

Fellner documents cases where mandatory minimums forced extreme outcomes: one defendant faced a 17-year plea offer but, after prosecutors added charges and she lost at trial, received over 45 years. Judges frequently find their discretion curtailed by statutory penalties, which can turn relatively minor or old offenses into life‑length sentences. Critics say prosecutors favor pleas because they save time, money, and boost conviction statistics; defenders argue the system could not function if most cases went to trial.

Reform efforts are underway: bipartisan bills to reduce mandatory minimums, and DOJ guidance from Attorney General Eric Holder urging prosecutors to avoid harsh mandatory-minimum charges for low-level offenders. The DOJ insists enhancements should target serious traffickers and not coerce pleas. Human Rights Watch urges Congress to restore judicial discretion or eliminate mandatory minimums and calls on the Attorney General to prohibit prosecutors from threatening longer sentences to force guilty pleas.

Researchers from Charles University in Prague report that people can judge men’s intelligence from photographs with accuracy above chance, but cannot do the same for women. In a PLoS One study, 80 photographed students (40 men, 40 women) completed IQ tests; 160 separate raters scored the photos for perceived intelligence and attractiveness. Raters’ perceived intelligence correlated with measured IQ for men—particularly fluid and figural intelligence—but showed no significant link for women. Geometric analyses identified an “intelligence stereotype”: faces judged as intelligent tend to be longer, with wider-set eyes, larger noses, upturned mouth corners, and sharper chins; faces judged less intelligent appear broader, rounder, with closer eyes, shorter noses, downturned mouths, and heavy chins. However, these morphological features did not correlate with actual IQ in either sex. The authors suggest explanations including sexually dimorphic cues, a strong attractiveness halo for women that masks intelligence cues, or evolutionary signaling differences. They conclude people accurately infer some aspects of men’s intelligence from faces, but the visual cues remain unidentified and may reflect cultural stereotypes rather than true morphological markers.

In Sochi 2014, Jamaica’s returning two-man bobsled team inspired a quirky anthem called "The Bobsled Song," written by Sidney Mills and Jon Notar and promoted by the Jamaican Tourist Board. The reggae-flavored track, available at BobsledSong.com and accompanied by an 8-bit animated video, is timed to sync with the Sochi 1,500-meter bobsled course—its 17 turns and 125.5-meter drop—so listeners can press play exactly as pilots Marvin Dixon and Winston Watts begin their run. Jamaica qualified for the event for the first time since 2002 through lower-tier North American races and, while not medal favorites, captured public imagination much like their 1988 Calgary debut.

Alabama running back Derrick Henry, a Heisman finalist, is expected to enter the 2016 NFL Draft, prompting questions about his heavy college workload, style, durability and scheme fit. Former NFL scout Dan Hatman reviewed four games and judged Henry a scheme-dependent back who excels when well-blocked rather than as a small-space, make-you-miss runner. Hatman praised Henry’s balance, vision, patience and power—especially once he reaches full speed—yet noted limited lateral agility. He worries about Henry’s 339 carries this season (rare in NCAA/NFL history) and whether that tread will limit early NFL years. Hatman projects Henry around the fourth round (100–150) given positional value, comparing him to recent backs like Matt Jones and Karlos Williams, and sees fits in teams using power and inside-zone concepts (Oakland, San Francisco, Pittsburgh, Carolina). Henry himself downplays carry concerns, saying he wants the ball and to help his team win.

The Navy has for the first time advanced female candidates into the selection pipeline for its elite special warfare communities: one woman is pursuing SEAL officer selection and at least one is in the Special Warfare Combatant-Craft Crewman (SWCC) pipeline. Officials, citing security, won’t identify them or provide progress updates. The candidates must complete the same rigorous Basic Underwater Demolition/SEAL (BUD/S) and related training as men, with historically high attrition—about 73–75% for enlisted SEALs, 63% for SWCC, and roughly 35% attrition for SEAL officer candidates. Naval leaders say the command has prepared facilities, policies and female staff support for integration, and a transgender service member has also joined SWCC. Despite the milestone, officials caution it may be months or years before a woman graduates, and publicizing identities could harm operational security and careers; expectations are being managed as the deliberate selection process continues.

A campaign in South Korea led by the Society for Textbook Revise (STR) has pushed the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology to allow publishers to remove key examples of evolution—such as the horse lineage and Archaeopteryx—from high-school textbooks. The STR, linked to the Korea Association for Creation Research (KACR), aims to delete what it calls the “error” of evolution; it also targets human evolution and classic case studies like finch-beak adaptation. STR leverages scientific debates (for example, that Archaeopteryx may be one of many feathered dinosaurs rather than a direct bird ancestor) to challenge teaching of evolution, a tactic critics call typical of creationism. Surveys show nearly one-third of South Koreans doubt evolution, with reasons including perceived lack of evidence, religious conflict, or poor understanding. Biology professors say few domestic experts teach evolution—only about five to ten—and many scientists were not consulted about the textbook changes. In response, evolutionary scientists and allied theologians are organizing to strengthen evolution education and counter the removal effort.

Police in Tennessee are investigating whether a January incident in Centerville is connected to the April 13 disappearance of 20-year-old nursing student Holly Bobo from her Parsons home. Heather Sullivan, 31, said a "tall, skinny man" grabbed her arm outside her house around 5:30 a.m., causing her to drop a lamp; her boyfriend frightened the suspect away. Bobo, a cousin of country singer Whitney Duncan, was reportedly taken by a man in camouflage about 7:30 a.m. Both homes border wooded areas. Tennessee Bureau of Investigation director Mark Gwyn said all possibilities are being considered. An $80,000 reward has been posted, including $50,000 from the state. Hundreds of residents have searched nearby woods; a blood sample found has been tested but results have not been released. Bobo’s family continues to hope for her return, with her mother making an emotional public plea for help.

A Nielsen survey of nearly 6,500 women across 21 developed and emerging countries (Feb–Apr 2011) found women worldwide feel stressed and time-pressed, with those in emerging markets reporting the most strain. Indian women ranked highest: 87% felt stressed most of the time and 82% had no time to relax. Mexico (74%) and Russia (69%) followed. Women in emerging economies are more likely to spend extra income on clothes, health and beauty, groceries and their children’s education, while women in developed markets favor vacations, savings and debt repayment. Despite stress, women in emerging markets are optimistic about their daughters’ prospects for financial stability and education. Women are heavier social-network users than men, and more influenced by social recommendations; TV remains a top source for new-product discovery in most countries. Nielsen highlights women’s increasing education, workforce participation and household influence as key drivers of changing consumer behavior and marketing opportunities.

McDonald’s national all-day breakfast has arrived, but offerings vary by location and several popular items are excluded. McGriddles, bagel sandwiches, cinnamon melts and "Big Breakfast" platters are not available all day anywhere. In most markets you can order sausage burritos, Fruit ‘N Yogurt parfaits, Fruit & Maple oatmeal, hash browns, hotcakes and hotcakes with sausage. Where McMuffins are sold, the Egg McMuffin, Sausage McMuffin with Egg and Sausage McMuffin are available, but the Egg White Delight and Steak, Egg & Cheese McMuffin are not. In biscuit markets you can get bacon, egg & cheese biscuits, sausage biscuit with egg and sausage biscuit, but not the southern-style chicken biscuit. Availability depends on location.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev’s body, unclaimed for nearly two weeks after he died April 19 in a shootout following the Boston Marathon bombings, is now in the care of a Worcester funeral home that will arrange a second independent autopsy at his relatives’ request. His death certificate cites gunshot wounds and blunt trauma and lists manner of death as homicide, noting he was shot by police and run over. Locating a burial site in Massachusetts has proven difficult: several cemeteries refused over fear of reprisals, and the family’s parents declined to bring the body to Dagestan. Funeral director Peter Stefan insists everyone deserves burial and may ask the government to find a grave if none is found. Meanwhile, investigations continue into the brothers’ motives and preparations, including explosives residue found in Tamerlan’s Cambridge apartment; Dzhokhar remains hospitalized and detained on charges including using a weapon of mass destruction. Three associates face charges related to disposing of potential evidence.

Thousands joined Occupy Oakland’s general strike, which shut banks, closed streets and ultimately disrupted the Port of Oakland. The day began peacefully at Frank H. Ogawa Plaza with speeches, music, family-friendly contingents and union support; organizers estimated thousands while police gave lower counts. Marches targeted banks—Wells Fargo, Chase and Bank of America—where protesters chanted, taped doors and banged on windows; a small group vandalized a Whole Foods but was confronted by other demonstrators. Teachers, students, labor groups and community activists participated; longshore workers’ attendance was mixed, but by late afternoon port operations were effectively halted as protesters blocked entrances and turned trucks away.

City officials sought a largely hands-off policing approach early on; Mayor Jean Quan, interim Police Chief Howard Jordan and city staff urged peaceful protest while preparing mutual aid. Tensions rose after protesters occupied the foreclosed Travelers Aid building; a police response later that night included tear gas, flash-bangs and dozens of arrests as officers reclaimed the building amid fires and reports of explosives and projectiles. Injuries included people hit by a vehicle during a downtown incident and at least one person treated for a rubber-bullet wound. By early morning the crowd thinned and police lines pulled back. The day combined large-scale peaceful demonstration, some property damage and a late-night confrontation that left the future of the encampment uncertain.

Michael David Elliot, 40, a convicted murderer serving five life terms for four 1993 killings, escaped the Ionia Correctional Facility in Michigan Sunday evening and was captured Monday night in LaPorte County, Indiana. Elliot reportedly slipped out through a sally port and a hole in perimeter fencing between about 6–7 p.m.; his absence wasn’t noticed until a 9 p.m. count. During his roughly 24-hour flight, he carjacked a woman with a box cutter, drove into northern Indiana, and allegedly stole a total of four vehicles. The victim escaped at a gas station in Elkhart County and alerted police. A red Jeep Liberty linked to Elliot was found in Shipshewana early Monday. LaPorte deputies spotted a stolen 2002 Chevrolet Monte Carlo Monday evening, attempted a stop, and deployed Stop Sticks; the driver lost control and slid into a snowbank east of LaPorte. Deputies Slawek Czupryna and Jeffrey Wright pulled Elliot from the wreck and arrested him without injury. He was arraigned in Indiana on auto-theft and resisting charges and is held without bond. Michigan officials praised law enforcement and vowed a thorough review of the escape.

In the New Hampshire contests, several campaigns sought to turn strong showings into momentum for the next phase of the presidential races, and winners on both sides used the state’s attention to define their messages. On the Republican side, Donald Trump declared victory and embraced the front‑runner role, promising sweeping changes and a return to “winning.” With about three‑quarters of GOP votes counted, Trump led with roughly a third of the vote and used his victory speech in Manchester to tout self‑funding, criticize Bernie Sanders’ economic proposals, and reiterate signature promises: rebuilding the military, prioritizing veterans, protecting the Second Amendment, and building a border wall. He cast himself as a dealmaker for ordinary Americans, challenged official unemployment figures, and thanked family and senior campaign staff while gently acknowledging other Republican contenders. Trump’s dominant headline status contrasted with more modest performances by rivals: Ohio Governor John Kasich claimed a respectable second place and presented himself as a compassionate, positive alternative to negative campaigning. Kasich emphasized heart as well as head in leadership, pledged to continue campaigning in South Carolina, and kept his attacks largely focused on Democrats, quipping about Bernie Sanders and urging Hillary Clinton to recalibrate after a poor New Hampshire result. Kasich framed his finish as evidence that decency can prevail amid a toxic race and saw momentum for upcoming contests. On the Democratic side, Bernie Sanders scored an emphatic victory over Hillary Clinton, a win his campaign framed as a repudiation of establishment politics and a mandate for sweeping change. Sanders told jubilant supporters that New Hampshire’s energized electorate signaled potential nationwide gains and urged grassroots fundraising rather than Wall Street fundraisers. With roughly 60 percent to Clinton’s 38 percent in early returns, his team called the margin historic for a contested Democratic primary. Clinton, conceding the state, sought to project resilience and stressed that delegate math favored a protracted fight, highlighting her strengths with diverse electorates and promising to intensify data‑driven efforts in coming contests. Both campaigns acknowledged tougher phases ahead: Sanders warned of intensified attacks, while Clinton planned to refocus on March states and Super Tuesday where she expects demographics and organization to favor her.

President Trump sharply attacked Deborah Ramirez, the second woman to accuse Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh of sexual misconduct, calling the allegations a “con game” by Democrats and dismissing Ramirez’s account as uncertain because she was “totally inebriated” and had “time lapses.” Speaking after a U.N. appearance, Trump said Ramirez “thinks maybe it could have been him, maybe not,” and urged that such claims not disqualify Kavanaugh. His rhetoric came as Republicans rallied behind Kavanaugh while several swing senators remained undecided ahead of Thursday’s highly anticipated Judiciary Committee hearing, when both Kavanaugh and Christine Blasey Ford—who accuses Kavanaugh of sexually assaulting her in high school—are set to testify.

The Judiciary Committee scheduled a possible Friday committee vote with the full Senate vote expected the following week. Senate GOP leaders, including Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, voiced confidence Kavanaugh will be confirmed and decried what they called partisan smears. To avoid the optics of an all-male GOP questioning Ford, Republicans hired Rachel Mitchell, a Maricopa County sex-crimes prosecutor, to question the witnesses. Democrats protested aspects of the process, pressed for an FBI probe, and planned to ask their own questions.

Republicans tried to contact Ramirez’s lawyers but received no new evidence; Ramirez initially expressed uncertainty to The New Yorker but later affirmed her recollection after consulting counsel. Additional potential accusers and calls for further investigation kept the confirmation contested, with several GOP senators saying Ramirez should testify under oath for her claims to be considered.

The NTSB’s preliminary report on the August 9 East Haven plane crash says the aircraft was observed inverted and descending at high speed immediately before impact. At 11:19 a.m., pilot William Henningsgaard, flying aircraft identified as “622,” acknowledged instructions to land on runway 20 at Tweed-New Haven Airport and reported he had the airport in sight. Less than two minutes later, the tower made a truncated call of the plane’s number; no further communications were received. A student pilot driving on I‑95 reported seeing the airplane at the end of a right roll, inverted and nose-first toward the ground near the airport. A neighborhood resident described the aircraft descending right-side down at a steep angle into two homes on Charter Oak Avenue. The twin‑engine plane had departed Teterboro around 10:49 a.m. The last radar target at 11:20 a.m. showed the airplane 0.7 miles north of the runway at about 800 feet. The crash destroyed much of the aircraft and both houses, with fire consuming most wreckage; the cockpit and forward fuselage were found in a basement. Four people died: the pilot, his 17‑year‑old son, and two children inside a struck home. Weather noted shortly after the accident included winds from 170° at 12 knots gusting to 19, 9‑mile visibility, and an overcast ceiling at 900 feet. Environmental cleanup and demolition plans for the damaged homes are underway.

Late-night host Jimmy Kimmel and Sen. Bill Cassidy clashed over the GOP’s Graham-Cassidy Obamacare repeal proposal, and health-policy analysts largely side with Kimmel’s critique. Kimmel, whose infant son required heart surgery, accused Cassidy of breaking promises to protect people with pre-existing conditions after Cassidy co-authored the bill with Sen. Lindsey Graham. In televised monologues Kimmel denounced the bill’s likely effects—deep Medicaid cuts, block-grant funding, and state waivers that could let insurers charge higher premiums or deny coverage—and called Cassidy a liar for assurances given on Kimmel’s show. Cassidy and supporters counter that the bill protects pre-existing conditions and would expand coverage via state flexibility; President Trump publicly praised Cassidy and said the bill offered protections. Graham dismissed Kimmel’s attack as “liberal talking points.”

Independent analysts, advocacy groups, and policy centers warn the legislation cannot guarantee nationwide protections. The bill’s waiver authority and rollback of Medicaid expansion could leave coverage contingent on state decisions, potentially producing higher premiums and reduced benefits. Georgetown’s Center for Children and Families cautioned the plan would “take a fiscal crowbar to Medicaid’s knees,” jeopardizing children with costly conditions. The Commonwealth Fund cited CBO analyses of similar measures predicting millions could lose coverage over time. Some conservatives, like Hoover Institution’s Lanhee Chen, argue state flexibility could expand coverage, though they admit future trade-offs. The CBO said it could not score the bill before a key procedural deadline, complicating debate.

Commentators also debated whether Kimmel, as a comedian, should be a leading voice in policy debates. Critics stress the complexity of health policy and the need for expertise, while supporters note Kimmel’s personal story and broad platform helped spotlight real stakes. The dispute underscores tensions between emotional advocacy and technical policy analysis as Congress weighed a consequential health overhaul.

Former University of Illinois graduate student Brendt Christensen has been indicted on upgraded federal charges alleging he kidnapped and killed visiting Chinese scholar Yingying Zhang in June. The superseding indictment returned Tuesday charges Christensen, 28, with one count of kidnapping resulting in death and two counts of making false statements to FBI agents. The grand jury included a special finding that the offense was committed “in an especially heinous, cruel or depraved manner” involving torture or serious physical abuse and followed “substantial planning and premeditation.” Christensen could face the death penalty if prosecutors seek it; otherwise a conviction would carry mandatory life without parole. The indictment alleges Christensen used a cellphone and vehicle—interstate commerce instruments—in committing the crime. Zhang, 26, disappeared June 9 weeks after arriving at the campus for a research appointment; her body has not been found but authorities believe she is dead. Surveillance footage reportedly shows Zhang entering Christensen’s car after briefly speaking with the driver near a bus stop. Investigators focused on Christensen after identifying his Saturn Astra in the footage. He initially told FBI agents he stayed home playing video games that day but later said he gave a distressed Asian woman a ride and dropped her off after a wrong turn. Court documents allege his car had been cleaned to conceal evidence and that his phone showed visits to a sadomasochism site with kidnapping fantasies. Audio surveillance allegedly captured Christensen describing his “ideal victim,” admitting to kidnapping Zhang, and recounting her resistance. He is held without bond and is tentatively scheduled for trial Feb. 27.

U.S. intelligence officials have concluded the Sept. 11 assault on the U.S. consulate in Benghazi, Libya, that killed Ambassador Christopher Stevens and three other Americans was “deliberate and organized,” the Director of National Intelligence’s office said. The revised assessment marks a shift from early statements that the violence grew out of spontaneous protests against an anti‑Islam video. DNI spokesman Shawn Turner explained the intelligence community’s view evolved as new information emerged, indicating involvement by extremists, some linked to or sympathetic with al‑Qaeda’s North African affiliates, though it remains unclear whether any group exercised overall command of the attack or whether it was premeditated well in advance. The clarification was intended to underscore that early reports are often incomplete and to defend the administration’s changing public accounts. The episode has become politically charged: Republicans allege the White House downplayed terrorist links to avoid exposing security failures before the election, and some have called for accountability for officials such as UN Ambassador Susan Rice. Lawmakers on both sides have sought more details; the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and others are pressing for information as a State Department review proceeds. U.S. investigators, including CIA operatives and federal agents, have been collecting intercepts, informant reports and on‑the‑ground evidence despite compromised crime scenes, while analysts ramp up reporting on Libyan extremist groups to determine the degree of planning behind the attack and whether security lapses occurred.

Sofia Vergara and Joe Manganiello are engaged, Page Six and other outlets confirm. Manganiello proposed on Christmas Day while the couple vacationed with family in Hawaii; witnesses say he popped the question at the St. Regis Princeville Resort in Kauai in front of Vergara’s relatives. Vergara, 42, has been photographed wearing a large, sparkling diamond ring on her left hand as she relaxed at the luxury resort and shared affectionate moments with Manganiello. The pair, who went public in June after being introduced at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner in May, have enjoyed a whirlwind romance. They celebrated Manganiello’s 38th birthday during the trip; Vergara posted a heartfelt birthday message calling him her “love and best friend” and shared a photo of a cake overlooking the sea. Manganiello previously described Vergara as his “dream girl.” Vergara’s ex-fiance Nick Loeb publicly wished them well, saying she “deserves happiness.” Insiders say the newly engaged couple were “very happy and very much in love,” enjoying several celebratory events with family at the resort.

San Diego Mayor Bob Filner, facing a growing sexual harassment scandal, has left an intensive behavioral treatment program earlier than planned and will continue therapy as an outpatient, his lawyers said. Filner, elected last November as the city’s first Democratic mayor in two decades, has been accused by about 14 women of unwanted advances, inappropriate comments, and in some cases kissing or touching. One former aide, Irene McCormack Jackson, has filed a sexual harassment lawsuit. Investigations by the San Diego County Sheriff’s Department and the state attorney general’s office are ongoing.

Political support for Filner collapsed as the San Diego City Council’s nine members unanimously demanded his resignation after two military sexual assault survivors accused Filner of crude advances at a conference for assault survivors. Councilwomen Marti Emerald and Myrtle Cole, the last holdouts, publicly called for him to step down. U.S. Senator Barbara Boxer, a longtime ally, issued a personal open letter urging Filner to resign and seek long-term treatment, saying he’d betrayed trust and hurt many women. City Hall officials also changed the mayor’s office locks while he was away; his chief of staff said it was to protect and preserve potential evidence.

Skye McCole Bartusiak, a Texas-born actress best known for playing Mel Gibson’s young daughter in the 2000 film The Patriot, died at age 21 at her Houston-area home. The cause of death has not been determined; Bartusiak reportedly died in her sleep and had suffered epileptic seizures in recent days, according to her mother. Her boyfriend discovered her sitting up in a garage apartment adjacent to her parents’ home; her mother said she believes Skye suffered a seizure, choked and was alone. Her mother attempted CPR before paramedics arrived, but responders were unable to restore a heartbeat.

Bartusiak began acting as a child at age six, appearing in The Cider House Rules (1999) and later as Michael Douglas’s daughter in Don’t Say a Word (2001). She also had TV roles on shows such as 24, Lost and House M.D. Her final film role was the lead in the low-budget thriller Sick Boy (2012). In recent months she had been preparing to produce and direct her first feature and had produced and starred in several short films. Her mother described her as kind and remembered a life that included photos with prominent figures from Hollywood and politics.

Adventurer Johnny Strange, 23, a Malibu native known for extreme stunts and for completing the “seven summits” by age 17, died Thursday in a wingsuit BASE-jumping crash in the Swiss Alps. Swiss police said Strange crashed a few seconds after launching from Mt. Gitschen around noon; authorities are investigating and noted strong winds had been reported that day. Days earlier, Strange had called into KROQ-FM’s Kevin and Bean show from Switzerland and posted a final YouTube wingsuit video showing him flying over green slopes and rocky peaks before releasing his parachute. His last Instagram image showed him over a tree-topped mountainside. Fellow climbers and fans mourned him: model Gigi Hadid, a Malibu High School classmate, praised his adventurous spirit, saying he “lived more in 23 years than many do their whole life.” Wingsuit BASE jumping—leaping from cliffs or structures while wearing a wingsuit to extend flight—is notoriously dangerous; several recent fatalities, including climbers Dean Potter and Graham Hunt at Yosemite, underscore the risks. Strange had publicly acknowledged the hazards and paid tribute to fallen peers. He first gained fame as a teen for global climbing and later for varied extreme-sports exploits.
