Donald Trump will moderate a Newsmax-hosted presidential debate airing on Ion Television in Des Moines on Dec. 27, a move reflecting his outsized influence with parts of the GOP base. Newsmax CEO Christopher Ruddy praised Trump’s appeal to grassroots conservatives who view him as independent of Washington and mainstream media. Trump’s role, confirmed by adviser Michael Cohen, underscores how candidates have echoed his themes and sought his endorsement; several have met with him privately. The debate, a week before the Iowa caucuses and not limited to a single topic, may pressure candidates to appear despite potential awkwardness. Trump’s celebrity status, media draw, and history of flirting with presidential runs make his moderating role both spectacle and political leverage.

Mexico’s president Enrique Peña Nieto reiterated emphatically that “Mexico will not pay for any wall” after US president Donald Trump signed executive orders to begin building a barrier along the US–Mexico border. In a televised address Peña Nieto said he “regrets and rejects” the decision but stopped short of canceling a planned 31 January White House visit, leaving the trip’s fate to a review by officials in Washington and Mexico City. His stance—refusing to fund the wall while affirming Mexico’s willingness to maintain diplomatic ties—provoked confusion and criticism at home, where many demanded he cancel the meeting.

Political figures across Mexico urged a firmer response. Former presidential hopeful Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas and ex-PRD leader Agustín Basave suggested canceling the visit and re-evaluating cooperation on security and migration. Ex-president Vicente Fox publicly attacked Trump and urged resistance. Analysts note Peña Nieto is politically constrained: his approval ratings are historically low (around 12%), limiting his leverage and capacity to unify the country behind a strong response. Paying for a wall would spark domestic outrage; refusing could antagonize the US administration. Observers call the situation “lose-lose.” Mexican officials have indicated they would impose conditions on any negotiation, including addressing guns smuggled south and cooperation on migration enforcement.

Trump’s executive order directs immediate construction plans for a physical wall and tasks Homeland Security with developing a plan within six months to prevent “all unlawful entries,” an objective many experts consider unachievable. Cost estimates to seal the roughly 2,000-mile border range from $12 billion to $38 billion, plus ongoing maintenance; current fencing and barriers already cost about $7 billion for some 600 miles. Trump suggested Mexico would pay and floated funding ideas like taxing remittances or leveraging NAFTA renegotiation; Mexican leaders publicly reject those notions.

The orders also expand deportation priorities, broaden detention capacity, target sanctuary cities, and seek to accelerate removal processes—moves that can take immediate effect without new legislation. Border agents and researchers note that enhanced surveillance, technology, and resources—not necessarily more wall—are often more effective, and recent trends show more Mexicans returning home than migrating north. The unfolding diplomatic standoff threatens trade and cooperation, with Mexico weighing how to protect its economic ties while responding to a hostile new US administration.

Lady Gaga’s third studio album, Born This Way, debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 1,108,000 first-week sales, according to Nielsen SoundScan — one of only 17 albums to sell a million-plus in a week since 1991 and the biggest week since 2005. It’s Gaga’s first No. 1 album and the largest digital album week in SoundScan history: 662,000 downloads (60% of sales). A promotional 99-cent sale by AmazonMP3 on May 23 and again on May 26 reportedly drove about 440,000 of those downloads; Amazon absorbed the wholesale cost paid to Universal. The feat follows rare million-week successes by artists like 50 Cent and Taylor Swift and highlights how pricing promotions and digital strategies can dramatically affect modern album sales.

Federal agents arrested Ross William Ulbricht, 29, at San Francisco’s Glen Park Branch Library, accusing him of operating Silk Road, an anonymous online black market where users bought and sold illegal drugs using Tor and Bitcoin. Authorities say Ulbricht, who allegedly used the alias “Dread Pirate Roberts” (DPR), ran Silk Road from San Francisco since at least 2011, collecting large commissions as the site connected buyers and sellers without itself stocking drugs. An FBI affidavit and indictments in New York and Maryland charge him with narcotics trafficking, money laundering and solicitation of murder. Investigators reported over 100 undercover purchases across 10 countries and estimated the site generated roughly $1.2–1.6 billion in sales and some $80 million in commissions over several years. Prosecutors allege Ulbricht sought to protect the operation with violence, paying an undercover agent $80,000 to torture and kill a former associate and later offering $150,000 to have a user murdered for allegedly threatening to expose thousands of Silk Road users; no confirmed homicides have been tied to those plots. Ulbricht was identified after early online posts promoting Silk Road were linked to an email address, and his physical movements matched DPR login locations. Authorities also obtained server data and transaction records showing more than a million transactions and nearly a million registered users. Ulbricht, a libertarian and former graduate student, was remanded pending further hearings; his attorney declined comment.

Researchers analyzed 183 hours of Oakland Police body-worn camera transcripts from 981 routine traffic stops (36,738 officer utterances) to measure whether officers spoke differently to Black and white drivers. Using a three-part approach, they first had human raters evaluate 414 sampled officer utterances for respect-related qualities—politeness, friendliness, formality, impartiality—and found utterances directed at Black drivers were rated significantly less respectful across dimensions. Second, they developed computational linguistic models trained on those ratings to predict Respect and Formality from linguistic features (apologies, gratitude, safety reassurance correlated with higher Respect; informal terms like “my man” and disfluencies with lower Respect). The models performed comparably to human raters. Third, applying the models to the full corpus while controlling for officer race, driver age and gender, stop outcome, searches, and offense severity, they found officers consistently used more respectful language with white than Black community members; the disparity persisted across most officers rather than being driven by a few outliers. Respect increased over the course of stops for both groups but rose faster for white drivers, widening the gap. Officer race did not explain differences; Formality did not vary by race. The study demonstrates body-camera footage can be a scalable data source to quantify interaction quality, inform training, and track procedural justice, while acknowledging limits (use of transcripts rather than full audio/video, privacy concerns) and urging broader replication.

On February 27, 1859, Congressman Daniel Sickles fatally shot Philip Barton Key, the U.S. attorney and son of the “Star-Spangled Banner” author, in broad daylight near the White House after discovering Key’s yearlong affair with Sickles’s much younger wife, Teresa. An anonymous letter had supplied Sickles with detailed evidence and an address where Key and Teresa allegedly met; Sickles confirmed sightings and, carrying opera glasses, confronted Key. After firing three shots, Sickles confessed at the attorney general’s office and retrieved Teresa’s wedding ring and earrings. His subsequent trial became a national spectacle. Backed by sympathetic press and political allies, Sickles mounted a dramatic defense that framed adultery as a provocation producing uncontrollable, temporary insanity. His legal team invoked Shakespeare, religious morality and the right of a husband to avenge dishonor; witnesses and theatrical displays of grief swayed public sentiment. The prosecution argued premeditation — Sickles had armed himself and discussed revenge beforehand — but jurors acquitted him after deliberating for only thirty minutes. Initially hailed as justified, Sickles and Teresa later became social pariahs; she retreated to a lonely later life and died young. Sickles’s successful insanity defense established a precedent in American law and remained controversial, attracting critique from figures like Mark Twain and eventually contributing to reform after high-profile later cases (e.g., Hinckley) prompted the Insanity Defense Reform Act of 1984. Sickles went on to a turbulent career—Civil War general (losing a leg at Gettysburg), diplomat, and continued scandal—leaving a legacy of audacity, legal innovation, and moral ambivalence.

After nearly 40 years of violence, Corsica’s main militant separatist group, the National Liberation Front of Corsica (FLNC), has announced it will abandon armed struggle and begin demilitarization, saying it will pursue its goals through conventional political channels. In a communiqué the banned organization declared a unilateral, unconditional exit from clandestine activities and urged intensifying the fight in the public arena. The move follows recent political advances on the island, including an assembly bill restricting property purchases to residents of at least five years to curb speculation and protect local housing. The FLNC, which once numbered over 100 members and has claimed responsibility for thousands of attacks—bombings, robberies, murders and rocket strikes—since 1976, framed demilitarization as a shift from resistance to building Corsican political power. The decision echoes recent decommissioning steps by other European separatists and could mark a historic turning point for the island.

Investigators say twin 29-year-old Australian women entered a suicide pact and shot themselves at a gun range near Denver; one died and the other survived and is now stable. The Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office, citing physical evidence, the survivor’s statement and surveillance video, concluded the incident was suicide and attempted suicide. The sisters had fired small-caliber handguns for about 80–90 minutes before simultaneously collapsing in their rented booth; video captured their falls but not the shots. Visiting on cultural visas, the twins had traveled frequently in North America; one was due to return to Australia the next day. Authorities have not released names while identity is confirmed; no note was found.

Adele’s second album, 21, arrived as an unflinching breakup record built from the wreckage of a single, painful relationship. The singer-songwriter—still only 22 at release—describes the album as “cheap therapy,” a collection of intimate, often raw songs that read like drunken diary entries translating private heartbreak into powerful bluesy ballads. Tracks such as “Someone Like You” and “Rolling in the Deep” showcase her emotive delivery and candid lyricism; some pieces are so personal she admits they may become too painful to perform in the future. Critics and listeners have noted how explicitly the album calls out the ex whose actions inspired the work, joining a long tradition of musical shaming that names wrongs rather than offering vague heartbreak clichés. Beyond the emotional purge, 21 reinforces that Adele’s talent needs no embellishment: her voice and storytelling carry the music. She also reveals a new curiosity about American roots styles—country and bluegrass—which she plans to explore to broaden her craft. Overall, 21 captures a young artist turning personal devastation into resonant, soulful songs that connect with fans dealing with their own love losses, while signaling musical growth and future experimentation.

Kim Cattrall says she was never friends with her Sex and the City co-stars, describing their relationship as professional colleagues rather than personal friends. In a recent ITV interview with Piers Morgan, the 61-year-old reiterated that a clear line between work and private life can be healthy, and criticized the cast—particularly Sarah Jessica Parker—for not reaching out during the recent fallout over a proposed third film. Cattrall denied reports that she made demanding financial or career requests that sank the sequel, calling being labeled a diva “ridiculous,” and insisting she never asked for money or projects. Media outlets and unnamed sources, however, have claimed she made “outrageous demands” and delayed production, prompting Warner Bros. to cancel the project shortly before shooting was due to begin. Cattrall said she had been saying “no” to a third installment for nearly a year and blamed a lack of personal outreach from former co-stars for much of the negative press, calling the situation “toxic.” Separately, she revealed she chose career commitments over motherhood during the show’s run, deciding against IVF because of grueling 19-hour shooting days. Instead, she found fulfillment mentoring younger actresses and acting as a maternal figure off-screen. The full interview airs in the U.K. on Monday night.

LulzSec unexpectedly announced its retirement after a 50-day hacking spree and released a final data dump. The archive contains varied material: a technical AOL network engineering document; an AT&T .rar with internal LTE rollout memos, emails and presentations; account details for over 550,000 Battlefield Heroes users; about 200,000 Hackforums.net user records and roughly 220,000 NATO bookshop logins; an image showing LulzSec graffiti on a US Navy salary list; lists of internal corporate network IPs (including Disney, EMI, Universal); alleged email credentials for private investigators; assorted gaming forum logins; and numerous router IPs using weak passwords like “root” or “admin.” LulzSec framed the retirement as the end of a planned 50-day “cruise,” calling for AntiSec’s continuation by others while hinting the move could be strategic evasion. The group urged mirrors of their releases and expressed hope their actions inspired and provoked thought, leaving open whether the hiatus is permanent.

Sen. Rand Paul is seeking a legislative workaround in Kentucky so he can run simultaneously for re-election to the U.S. Senate and for the Republican presidential nomination in 2016. Kentucky Senate Majority Leader Damon Thayer told The Washington Times he is preparing a bill to clarify ambiguous state law that currently bars candidates from appearing on the ballot for two offices at once—language Paul considers unconstitutional if applied to a dual Senate-presidential bid. Thayer said the measure’s intent is to explicitly allow Paul, or anyone in a similar position, to run for both offices in the same year; he raised the possibility after Paul discussed the matter with the Senate GOP caucus while testifying on restoring felons’ voting rights. If enacted, Paul could pursue the presidency in the primary and still run for Senate in the general: a presidential win would prompt him to vacate the Senate seat, while a presidential loss paired with a Senate win would leave him a second-term senator. The proposal faces uphill battles politically—Kentucky’s Democratic-controlled House may block it, and some Republicans privately doubt it will pass. Thayer said he would decide whether to file the bill before the assembly’s filing deadline; Paul has not formally announced a presidential campaign.

A Tennessee high school junior, Emily Gipson of Lebanon High School, drew national attention after posting a free-verse, anti-bullying video on YouTube criticizing student culture and school responses to bullying and a recent student suicide. Posted Jan. 22 and prompted by a classmate’s October death, the piece—opening with “Welcome to Lebanon High School, where smiles are fake and suicide prevention is something to laugh at”—chastised peers for mocking a school Stop It app and accused administrators of tolerating or dismissing bullying with rationales like “there’s no proof” or “kids will be kids.” The video contains no profanity or explicit calls to violence, yet school officials disciplined Gipson with a two-day in-school suspension. Principal Scott Walters said he could not discuss the punishment’s specifics but objected to the fact the speech was recorded in a classroom without a teacher’s permission and said the video hurt teachers’ feelings; he acknowledged, however, that he could appreciate Gipson’s perspective. Gipson and her family dispute parts of the administration’s account—she says she had permission from two coaches to film—and her grandfather, who is her guardian, said he understands the policy violation but is proud of her message. Gipson followed the first clip with another spoken-word poem, “Have I Made a Difference Yet?,” urging peers to speak up. The videos went viral, drawing hundreds of thousands of views and wide public debate about student free expression, school discipline, and how institutions handle bullying and suicide prevention. Gipson says the attention reinforced that the issue extends beyond her school to a national problem.

Two men living less than 75 miles apart suffered almost identical workplace injuries—each losing part of his left arm in industrial accidents—but received starkly different workers’ compensation outcomes because of state law. Jeremy Lewis, injured in Alabama, got a lump sum of about $45,000 (roughly $33,500 after fees), enough to cover less than a year’s wages and precipitating foreclosure and financial hardship. Josh Potter, hurt a few miles away in Georgia, receives far larger benefits that could total hundreds of thousands over his lifetime and two-thirds of his wages until he returns to work or for life if he cannot. Their divergent fates highlight the “geographic lottery” of U.S. workers’ comp: states set their own scheduled benefits for body-part losses with no federal minimums, producing wide disparities (an arm can be worth $48,840 in Alabama, $193,950 in Ohio, $439,858 in Illinois). Many states have cut benefits in recent decades amid pressure from employers and insurers, shifting costs to families and taxpayers. Critics call the schedules arbitrary and dehumanizing; even Alabama defenders and judges acknowledge the system’s inadequacy but say change is politically fraught.

Wells Fargo employees opened premium checking accounts for Latino immigrants, marketed as allowing free cross-border money transfers, that could be opened with $50 but were supposed to be backed by $25,000 on deposit within three months or incur a $30 monthly fee. Siham El-Dahan, a business banker in the San Fernando Valley who joined Wells in May 2013 and was fired two weeks ago, described a workplace where managers played favorites, denied legally required breaks and regularly pressured staff with sales quotas. She said staff began opening bogus accounts for customers who did not want them “on a daily basis.” Beginning in September she sought help from human resources but was repeatedly referred back to the managers she complained about. Her written complaints to bank directors and a signed letter to CEO John Stumpf drew no response. El-Dahan believes her dismissal was retaliation; the bank cited a customer loan default as the reason, which she denies having any role in approving. Customers reported similar problems. Frank Ahn, a convenience store owner, recounted being repeatedly sold accounts and a credit card he did not request, accruing unwanted accounts and fees despite calls and branch visits to cancel them. After opening two accounts, he felt pressured into a third; later more accounts appeared and, at one point, he had as many as ten. He recovered most but not all improper fees and said switching banks was impractical because many suppliers were tied to the Wells account. Ahn worries especially for immigrants with limited English who would struggle to fight the bank. Wells Fargo declined to comment.

A marine engineer from Jamshedpur, Jharkhand, has faced repeated job rejections—around 40 interviews—because his name, Saddam Hussain, evokes the executed Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein. Despite graduating second in his 2014 class from Noorul Islam University, he remains unemployed while batchmates secured positions. Employers told him his name could raise suspicion and pose operational problems, especially for roles requiring international travel where border and airport authorities flag names. A recruitment executive noted hires whose work involves crossing borders often get delayed or pulled out if red flags appear.

To overcome the barrier, he legally changed his name to Sajid and updated identity documents such as passport, voter ID, and driving licence. However, prospective employers require educational certificates in the new name. His university won’t amend his degree until his Class 10 and 12 certificates are changed. He approached the CBSE for name changes but received no timely response, prompting him to petition the Jharkhand High Court to direct the CBSE. The court, cautious because of potential abuse of name changes, scheduled a detailed hearing for May 5.

He laments paying for his grandfather’s choice of name and describes sleepless nights as peers embark on careers. His case underscores how a notorious namesake can disrupt employment prospects and how bureaucratic hurdles complicate efforts to rectify identity documents. Others named Saddam have faced similar stigma and even violence in Iraq.

Emmis Digital turned intern recruiting into a social-media competition called the "Intern Games," reflecting how hiring has shifted from paper resumes to digital savvy. From over 25 applicants, 10 were interviewed and three finalists—Jake Bouvy, Kelsey Halverson and Katie—spent two weeks competing to drive traffic and engagement for Emmis using hashtags #TeamJake, #TeamKelsey and #TeamKatie. Candidates posted videos, tweets and Facebook appeals to mobilize friends, family and followers; their performance was tracked daily. Bouvy, a marketing major, impressed with a technically polished music-video style entry, while Halverson, a journalism major, generated the most measurable social impact and Facebook likes. Though Halverson emerged as the clear social-media winner, Emmis chose to hire both she and Bouvy as unpaid interns receiving college credit, with Katlyn Hayes noting their complementary strengths would make a "super intern." The stunt was partly designed to create buzz and expand the company’s online reach. The story highlights a broader trend: employers increasingly evaluate candidates by online presence and real-world digital experience, not just resumes. It also underscores debates around unpaid internships and changing hiring practices, where demonstrations of creativity and social-media influence can outweigh traditional application methods.

Three days after Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 vanished en route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing with 239 people aboard, multinational search teams still have no confirmed trace of the Boeing 777. Dozens of ships and nearly 40 aircraft from about ten countries are combing a vastly expanded search area across the Gulf of Thailand, the South China Sea and potentially the Andaman Sea after radar indicated the jet may have turned back toward Malaysia. Authorities reported oil slicks and reported debris sightings but so far laboratory tests and follow-up searches have shown those leads to be false alarms.

Investigators are pursuing every possible explanation — accident, catastrophic failure, pilot error, hijacking or terrorism — but emphasize it is too early to draw conclusions. No distress call or emergency signals were received. Recovery of wreckage and the plane’s black boxes is expected to be crucial, but experts warn that finding debris or flight data recorders at sea is slow and becomes harder with each passing day.

Complicating the probe is the revelation that two passengers boarded using passports stolen from Austria and Italy. Thai and Malaysian authorities say the men who used those documents and the person who bought their one-way tickets are subjects of inquiry. Interpol and U.S. agencies are comparing thumbprints and images to databases; one U.S. intelligence official noted the pattern could reflect human-smuggling activity rather than terrorism. Authorities have not publicly linked the passport misuse to the disappearance.

Families of those onboard face an agonizing wait amid anger and pressure, particularly from China, which has the largest number of passengers. Malaysia has pledged cooperation with international agencies and continues to expand the search, even as criticism grows over response speed and border-screening practices. Until wreckage and flight recorders are recovered, investigators say the cause of MH370’s disappearance will remain unresolved.

For the first time in 146 years, Chicago recorded no days in January or February with at least one inch of snow on the ground, based on 6 a.m. measurements at O’Hare. Small amounts that fell later were not counted. The near snowless start delighted some residents but worried others and sparked debate about climate change—WGN meteorologist Tom Skilling linked it to a warming climate, while other scientists cautioned short-term blips don’t prove long-term trends. Warm winter conditions have ecological and economic effects: earlier bud break risks frost damage to fruit orchards, insects may survive and reproduce more, and bird migration timing can be disrupted; conversely, milder winters cut heating costs and boost outdoor activity. Storms in mid-March, including Winter Storm Stella, finally produced measurable snow.

Queen Elizabeth II used her pre-recorded Christmas message to emphasize the importance of family, friendship and community. Recorded Dec. 9, the broadcast’s theme felt especially poignant as Prince Philip remained hospitalized after a coronary stent procedure; Buckingham Palace said the 90-year-old was recovering and in good spirits. The queen, wearing red in the recording and lavender arriving at church, noted how family can provide strength in hard times and cited Commonwealth ties as an example of family beyond blood. The royal household celebrated Christmas with traditional services at St. Mary Magdelene on the Sandringham estate, attended by senior royals including Princes Charles, William and Harry, the Duchess of Cambridge, Camilla and Princesses Beatrice and Eugenie. After the service children presented flowers; the family lunched together and planned hospital visits to Philip.

Thieves made off with about 300 bottles of fine wine valued at roughly €250,000 from a private apartment cellar near the Jardin du Luxembourg in central Paris after accessing the property through the city’s vast catacombs. Police say the culprits entered the catacombs via one of their many clandestine or sealed entrances, navigated the restricted underground passages and drilled through the cellar wall to seize the vintage bottles before retreating back into the tunnels. Investigators believe the raid required planning and prior reconnaissance, since the attackers targeted that specific wall rather than making a random breach. The Paris criminal investigation department’s 3rd District is handling the probe; authorities have not publicly identified suspects.

The episode highlights risks posed by the catacombs’ extensive off-limits network: only about two kilometres are officially open to tourists, while an estimated 150 miles of dark corridors and ossuaries lie beyond, containing the remains of some six to seven million people. Despite fines and police patrols by a specialist unit sometimes called the “Cataflics,” urban explorers and “cataphiles” occasionally use the tunnels for illicit parties and film screenings, and incidents—such as teenagers getting lost—have occurred. The audacious wine heist underscores both the catacombs’ lure and the security challenges they present.

Alexandria Duval, 37, is fighting extradition from New York to Hawaii after being indicted on a second-degree murder charge in the May death of her identical twin sister, Anastasia. Authorities say the sisters’ SUV plunged about 200 feet off a Maui cliff during a reported struggle over the steering wheel; Alexandria, the driver, was injured and later released from a Hawaii jail after a judge found no probable cause initially. A grand jury later indicted her and Maui police issued a warrant. Duval was located and arrested in Albany on Nov. 11 after investigators traced a possible address; she attempted to flee but was taken into custody and returned to the Albany County Jail. At a Nov. 18 appearance, her public defender, Terry Kindlon, said she is “profoundly distraught,” called the sisters “soul mates,” and maintained the crash was a tragic accident. Duval will not waive an extradition hearing, which is scheduled for Dec. 16; her attorney contends the current paperwork is insufficient to compel extradition.

Prime Minister Theresa May survived a Conservative Party no-confidence vote, but 117 of her MPs—over a third—voted against her, exposing deep party divisions over her proposed Brexit deal. The contest was triggered after she delayed a parliamentary vote on the withdrawal agreement, which critics say keeps the UK too tied to the EU, especially because of the Northern Ireland “backstop.” May appealed to colleagues, pledged to step down before the 2022 election, and warned that ousting her could delay or derail Brexit. Cabinet ministers publicly backed her, while hardline Brexiteers like Jacob Rees-Mogg called for her resignation. The result lets her remain leader for at least a year, but with weakened authority to win parliamentary approval for her deal. Markets briefly reacted with sterling gains. EU leaders, including Angela Merkel, insisted the withdrawal agreement is not reopenable, complicating May’s task of persuading rebels. The episode intensified uncertainty over the UK’s March 29 exit and raised the prospect of a leadership contest and alternative Brexit paths, including no-deal or a second referendum.

The document reports two separate stories. First, the Mo Ibrahim Prize for African Leadership was not awarded this year because no candidate met the foundation’s strict criteria for exceptional, democratically elected leaders who improved living standards and then left office voluntarily. This follows similar decisions in 2009 and 2010. The $5 million prize—paid over ten years with a $200,000 annual lifetime stipend—has been awarded only a few times since its launch: to Botswana’s Festus Mogae, Mozambique’s Joaquim Chissano, and last year to Cape Verde’s Pedro Verona Pires, praised for anti-colonial leadership, introducing multi-party politics, and raising living standards. Mo Ibrahim emphasized that the foundation would not compromise its standards, arguing that maintaining credibility requires awarding only truly exceptional leadership. The foundation also recently gave a special $1 million award to Archbishop Desmond Tutu for speaking truth to power.

Second, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded to Lloyd Shapley and Alvin Roth for their work on the theory of stable allocations and market design. Shapley’s theoretical research on stable matching laid the groundwork for Roth’s practical applications, which improved systems for assigning medical residencies, matching donated kidneys to patients, and placing students in schools—reducing mismatches and better reflecting participants’ preferences. Their combined contributions created a flourishing research field and tangible real-world benefits.

A Texas judge has ruled that Sofya Tsygankova, the estranged wife of acclaimed pianist Vadym Kholodenko, is mentally incompetent to stand trial on charges that she smothered the couple’s two daughters. Tsygankova, 32, who faces two counts of capital murder for the deaths of Nika, 5, and Michaela, 1, has been ordered committed to a state mental health facility for 120 days of treatment aimed at restoring her to a “reasonable degree of rational understanding.” She will remain in Tarrant County jail until a bed is available. Prosecutors did not object to Judge Ruben Gonzalez’s order, signed Monday. Authorities say Kholodenko discovered Tsygankova covered in blood with wrist cuts and the children dead in their beds when he arrived March 17 to pick them up for preschool. Police found an empty bottle of quetiapine, an antipsychotic medication, in the home; reports say Tsygankova had visited a state mental health facility the day before the killings. Kholodenko, 30, who won the 2013 Van Cliburn competition, resumed performing about a month after the tragedy, saying music helped him cope and asking audiences to focus on the music while expressing gratitude for global support.

At Alan Shepard Elementary in Bourbonnais, Illinois, custodian Steve Weidner—known affectionately as “Mr. Steve”—was treated like a local celebrity by students on June 2. As children gathered before school to sign yearbooks, dozens lined up to have him sign theirs; the crowd grew so large someone brought him a chair and the line wound around the playground. Weidner, who has worked at the school for more than 15 years, is widely popular with students and praised by staff for looking out for them. School representatives told News 10 that he was touched and amazed by the display of affection. A photo of the long line and Weidner signing yearbooks was posted to Reddit and quickly climbed to the site’s front page, attracting thousands of upvotes and comments. The anecdote came from a crawl seeded with a list of every host in the Wayback Machine; that crawl included URLs and their embeds as well as outbound links, though the associated WARC files are not publicly available.

Researchers at the University of Texas at Austin released a comprehensive Blueprint for Campus Police to guide responses to sexual assault, emphasizing trauma-informed, victim-centered, science-based policing. Drafted by UT Austin’s Institute on Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault, the report will be used to train nearly 600 officers across the eight-institution UT System. It stresses that survivors often behave differently than victims of other crimes—appearing quiet, passive, or unemotional rather than hysterical—and urges officers to prioritize safety, avoid judgment, and view substance use as increased vulnerability not culpability. The blueprint provides concrete guidance for officers on empathy and interpreting behaviors commonly mistaken as deceit—such as inconsistent recollection—explaining that trauma can cause omissions, exaggerations, or confabulation without negating that an assault occurred. The report also counters common rape myths and addresses victim-blaming, aiming to reshape entrenched misconceptions within diverse campus cultures. Researchers compiled the blueprint from interviews with campus leaders and police and prior survivor data, choosing not to interview survivors directly to avoid retraumatization. Separately, a high-profile legal dispute at UT-Austin illustrates tensions around campus adjudication of sexual misconduct. A 21-year-old male physics student, pseudonymously John Doe, sued to halt a disciplinary hearing and potential expulsion after a nonstudent woman accused him of sexual assault following a night of heavy drinking. No criminal charges were filed; the woman did not file a police report but her father contacted campus officials, prompting a Title IX investigation. Doe alleges denial of due process, gender bias, and overly broad consent definitions; he challenges limits on cross-examination, subpoenas, and witnesses. The case reflects a broader national debate over protecting survivors while ensuring fair procedures for the accused, with numerous similar lawsuits nationwide.

More than 100 former NFL players, including Jamal Anderson, Chris Doleman and O.J. Santiago, have joined over 1,500 others in lawsuits claiming the league hid concussion dangers. Filed in U.S. District Court in Atlanta by attorney Mike McGlamry, the suit alleges the NFL repeatedly denied links between concussions and brain injury, failed to protect players, and misled them about risks. The NFL denies intentional deception, saying player safety is a priority. The filing cites studies connecting repeated head blows to chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative disease only diagnosable postmortem and linked to memory loss and mood changes; 12 CTE cases have been found in deceased NFL players. Boston University researchers, who have frequently found CTE in former players, are seeking Junior Seau’s brain; if confirmed and tied to his suicide, experts say it could change public perception of the sport and prompt more urgent examination of football’s long-term harms. Former players like Dorsey Levens say they were unaware of long-term concussion effects while playing.

A 21-year-old Pleasant Grove woman, Alexandra Nicole Laird, has been indicted and jailed on child endangerment charges after her newborn daughter tested positive for opiates and amphetamines at birth and required a month in intensive care for withdrawal. A Jefferson County grand jury indicted Laird on April 15; she was first arrested May 1, 2015 and remained free on bond until later arrests. Hospital records show the baby was born March 29, 2015 at UAB Medical West and transferred April 6 to Princeton Baptist Medical Center for treatment. Pleasant Grove police say Laird admitted using heroin one to two times weekly for at least five months of the pregnancy. Due to the infant’s severe condition, authorities obtained an enhanced Class B felony chemical endangerment charge. Laird does not have custody of that daughter.

While out on bond, Laird faced an unrelated drug possession incident after a traffic stop turned up 38 hydrocodone pills; neither occupant claimed them. She later missed a court date, tested positive on a court-ordered drug test, and admitted to using heroin three times daily. Authorities confirmed she is now 18–20 weeks pregnant; a judge ordered her jailed without bond until the baby is born to prevent further exposure. Officials emphasize concern for the newborn’s future development and say they will vigorously protect the child. Separately, the federal Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act was signed to improve tracking and support for drug-dependent newborns and their families, though critics note funding shortfalls.

India’s Supreme Court unanimously struck down the colonial-era adultery law (section 497 IPC), ruling it unconstitutional and discriminatory toward women. The five-judge bench held that criminalising a man for having sex with a married woman without her husband’s consent treated wives as property, deprived women of sexual autonomy, and was archaic. Chief Justice Dipak Misra declared “husband is not the master,” and justices emphasized dignity, equality, and that regulating private consensual adult relationships exceeded the state’s remit. The case was brought by Joseph Shine, an Indian businessman in Italy, seeking a gender-neutral reform; the court instead removed the criminal offence while noting adultery may still ground civil remedies like divorce.

Reactions were mixed. Advocates for gender equality and the National Commission for Women welcomed the decolonising move, likening it to the court’s recent decriminalisation of homosexuality. Critics, including some feminists and Delhi’s women commissioner, argued the law provided a deterrent against husbands abandoning families and feared its removal could harm vulnerable women in patriarchal contexts. The government had opposed repeal, citing protection of marital sanctity. Legal commentators noted the ruling targets clear anachronisms but cautioned the court remains unevenly progressive. The judgment also bolsters arguments against the marital rape exception and reflects a broader shift toward protecting sexual autonomy and equality under Indian law.

A north Mississippi school district long used a 30-year-old practice that alternated racial eligibility for certain class offices—one year only white students could run for some positions, the next year only black students. Brandy Springer, mother of mixed-race children, discovered her 12-year-old daughter was barred from running for sixth-grade class reporter because of that rule. The policy, also applied to prom/homecoming selections, drew outrage after Springer contacted mixed-and-happy.com and advocacy groups; the NAACP urged a Justice Department probe. Critics noted the rule erased multiracial, Hispanic and Asian students and taught divisive lessons about race. Facing backlash, Nettleton School District announced it would stop using race in student elections, acknowledging growing ethnic diversity and that the old classifications no longer reflect the student body. Springer moved her family to another district.

President Donald Trump announced on May 8, 2018, that the United States would withdraw from the 2015 Iran nuclear deal, calling the agreement “decaying and rotten” and “defective at its core.” In a televised address, he declared he would reinstate the “highest level” of sanctions on Iran, including primary U.S. sanctions and secondary sanctions targeting foreign entities that do business with Tehran, with enforcement after legally prescribed wind-down periods. The 2015 accord had required Iran to curb its nuclear ambitions and accept international inspections in exchange for relief from crippling international sanctions. The deal was widely regarded as a major foreign policy achievement of the Obama administration, which Trump long criticized as “the worst deal ever.”

Trump framed the withdrawal as necessary to prevent a potential Iranian nuclear weapon and also cited Iran’s missile program, support for militant groups, hostility toward Israel, and cyber-attacks. The decision marked a dramatic U.S. policy reversal and raised concerns about whether Iran might resume prohibited activities or expel inspectors. It also prompted questions about credibility ahead of U.S.-North Korea diplomacy. Reactions were mixed: some Republicans, Saudi Arabia, and Israel praised the move; European leaders like France’s Emmanuel Macron and former President Barack Obama criticized it and warned about damaging nonproliferation norms and U.S. credibility. Iran’s President Hassan Rouhani said Tehran would continue talks with the remaining signatories (Britain, France, Germany, Russia, China) even as Israel’s revelations about Iranian nuclear archives and heightened regional tensions underscored the uncertain fallout.

The Trump transition has ordered an immediate freeze on the Environmental Protection Agency’s grants and contracts, agency staffers and documents reported. Employees were told to suspend all contract and grant awards — including task orders and work assignments — and to refrain from external communication about the directive. The freeze affects a broad array of EPA funding streams that support research, air and water quality monitoring, brownfield redevelopment, environmental justice, state revolving loan funds, and other state, tribal, university and nonprofit programs. EPA routinely awards billions annually in grants and contracts; reports cite past totals of several billion dollars per year, so the pause creates substantial uncertainty for recipients and state programs that rely on EPA funding.

The freeze came as the Trump team, led at EPA transition by Myron Ebell, reviews agency activities while Scott Pruitt awaits Senate confirmation as administrator. Transition officials framed the action as ensuring “nothing happens they don’t want to have happen,” and Ebell likened it to prior administration reviews, though career officials called the scale and communication restrictions unusual and “extreme.” A staff memo circulated agency-wide tightened controls on press releases, social media, blogs, webinars and external speaking engagements pending direction from the incoming “Beach Team.” The agency said it was reviewing grants and contracts and aiming to resolve issues quickly, but the duration and full scope of the freeze remained unclear, prompting concern about impacts on states, tribes and ongoing environmental work.

Former New York governor Eliot Spitzer defended his prosecution record and criticized media attacks in a Slate column, prompting two libel suits seeking $90 million from former Marsh & McLennan executives William Gilman ($60M) and Edward McNenney ($30M). Spitzer argued his cases against AIG, Hank Greenberg, and Marsh were necessary to address fraud, citing AIG settlements, convictions of five defendants, a prosecutor’s label of Greenberg as an unindicted co-conspirator, and a judge’s description of AIG as a “criminal enterprise.” He also noted Marsh’s $850 million settlement and numerous employee convictions, while condemning corporate resistance to regulation. Gilman and McNenney—convicted in 2008 but later cleared when a judge ordered dismissal—say Spitzer’s statements defamed them and made them identifiable despite not being named; they previously sued Marsh claiming they were made “scapegoats.” Slate Group is also named in the suits.

York County authorities arrested three California men after seizing 247 pounds of marijuana—double-wrapped and valued at over $2 million—plus $11,000, a firearm, three duffel bags and a T-shirt linked to the operation. The Dec. 29 stop in West Manheim/Hanover led to charges of delivery, conspiracy to deliver, and possession with intent to deliver marijuana against Christopher Heath, 37; Ryan Falsone, 27; and Tyler Long, 31. Heath is a Yuba County Sheriff’s Department drug task force agent and was carrying his badge and service Glock when arrested. Officials said the bust resulted from a coordinated, intelligence-driven investigation; detectives did not know Heath was an officer beforehand. Authorities expect potential additional and federal charges for interstate drug trafficking. All three were released on bail.

Joe Jackson, the patriarch who launched the Jackson musical dynasty, died at 89 on Wednesday, June 27, after a battle with cancer, family sources confirmed. Born in 1928, he married Katherine in 1949 and fathered 10 surviving children and one infant who died at birth. From Gary, Indiana, Joe shepherded his children into show business: he formed The Jackson Brothers in 1963 and, with the addition of Michael and Marlon, created The Jackson 5 in 1966. Under his early management they signed with Motown and scored an unprecedented run of No. 1 hits in 1970—“I Want You Back,” “ABC,” “The Love You Save” and “I’ll Be There.” The group’s success paved the way for Michael’s solo career as the “King of Pop” and Janet’s international stardom.

Jackson was widely credited for creating the family’s success and was honored by the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as Best Entertainment Manager of All Time in 2002. He was also a controversial figure: his children described his strict, sometimes physically punitive parenting and management. Joe defended his methods as necessary to protect and discipline his children and expressed pride in what they achieved.

In later years he suffered serious health setbacks—a 2015 stroke, a 2017 car-accident hospitalization, heart issues and a pacemaker—and had been in hospice care in Las Vegas. Family members and grandchildren paid tribute on social media, acknowledging his role in making the Jacksons a global phenomenon while reflecting on a complicated legacy.

Sally Jewell was confirmed by the Senate 87-11 to serve as U.S. Interior secretary. A 57-year-old former petroleum engineer, commercial banker and current CEO of Recreational Equipment Inc. (REI), Jewell pledged to balance competing uses of federal lands—recreation, conservation, mining and forestry—when she leads the sprawling department that manages national parks, 500 million acres of onshore mineral lands and extensive offshore resources. Endorsed by environmental groups and seen as sincere by some Republicans, she has also faced questions about prior ties to conservation organizations that opposed fossil-fuel development near public lands. Jewell will replace Ken Salazar, has pledged to resign from REI upon confirmation, and is expected to navigate intense debates over energy, development and protection on federally managed lands.

For decades Easter Island’s history was framed as a cautionary tale: Polynesian settlers arrived, built massive stone moai statues, then collapsed through environmental mismanagement and conflict. A new study in the Journal of Pacific Archaeology challenges that simplified story by analyzing the volcanic basalt tools (toki) used to carve the statues. Excavations of four moai and recovery of roughly 1,600 stone tools allowed researchers to chemically source fragments from 17 toki using mass spectrometry. Basalt from the island’s three quarry complexes carries subtle, distinctive elemental signatures; the analysis showed most of the sampled toki originated from a single quarry complex. That pattern suggests sustained, organized procurement and craft specialization rather than fragmented, competitive scavenging. Lead author Dale Simpson Jr. and co-author Laure Dussubieux interpret the concentrated sourcing as evidence for cooperation among families and craft groups and for sociopolitical complexity—chiefs, priests, and worker guilds—required to produce nearly a thousand moai, some as tall as 70 feet. The findings undercut the narrative of self-inflicted collapse, though researchers note later population decline resulted from colonial contact and slavery. Study leaders caution that exclusive use of one quarry could reflect multiple social arrangements—including coercion—and call for broader mapping and sourcing to confirm patterns. Overall, the chemical tool-sourcing approach opens new lines of evidence that portray Rapa Nui society as more organized and interconnected than long-presumed, while encouraging further work to refine how cooperation, specialization, and social control shaped moai production.

Alan Rickman’s defining screen role was Professor Severus Snape in the Harry Potter films, a character who evolves from brooding antagonist to tragic hero devoted to love and duty. When the early movies were made, J.K. Rowling had not yet revealed Snape’s full arc—many assumed he remained a villain—yet she privately told Rickman that Snape had been a secret agent for Dumbledore. Rickman kept that knowledge close, sometimes even contradicting directors who didn’t know the backstory, as producer David Heyman recalled. That hidden insight informed Rickman’s layered performance: subtle looks, expressions and choices that hinted at deeper loyalties and pain, making his portrayal resonant and emotionally powerful.

Rickman also guarded Rowling’s confidences from journalists. He said he spoke to her once to gain a single, non-plot but crucial piece of information that guided his interpretation of Snape — a detail he vowed never to share. This discretion allowed Rickman to react authentically to the books as they were published; he bought them like everyone else to follow Snape’s unfolding journey. Fans continue to celebrate Rickman’s ability to capture Snape’s complexity—the darkness and the devotion—bringing book nuances vividly to screen. A popular online compilation further emphasizes that emotional arc by assembling Snape’s key moments, from his unrequited love for Lily Potter to the pivotal scene with Dumbledore. Rickman died of cancer at 69, leaving behind an indelible cinematic legacy.

New analyses of large cancer cohorts reinforce that taller people have a slightly higher risk of many cancers, likely because they simply have more cells in which dangerous mutations can arise. Leonard Nunney, an evolutionary biologist, compared observed cancer rates from multiple big studies (including the UK Million Women Study and large US, European and Korean datasets) with predictions based on body cell numbers inferred from height. He found that overall cancer risk rises roughly 10% for every additional 10 cm of height, a result consistent with previous work and with his model (predicted increases ~11–13% vs observed ~9–12% by sex). Most cancer types (18 of 23 examined) showed increased risk with height, notably colon, kidney cancer and lymphoma. Some cancers—stomach, mouth and (in women) cervical—showed no height association, likely because strong environmental drivers (e.g., HPV for cervical cancer) mask any effect of size. Two exceptions stood out: melanoma and thyroid cancer (especially in taller women, with a strong signal driven by Korean data) exceeded predicted associations; reasons are unclear. Nunney and others suggest an additional mechanism: taller people tend to have slightly higher circulating IGF-1, a growth factor that raises cell division and could amplify mutation accumulation in certain tissues. Comparative examples (dwarf Ecuadorian population with low IGF-1 showing little cancer; larger dog breeds having higher cancer rates) support growth-factor influence. Experts emphasize the increased risk is modest and that lifestyle factors—avoiding smoking, healthy diet, exercise, sun protection—remain far more important for reducing cancer risk than stature, though extreme tallness may warrant awareness and vigilance.

Hurricane Harvey stalled over Texas, dumping unprecedented rain and triggering catastrophic flooding across Houston and southeastern Texas, leaving thousands stranded, displacing more than a million people, and prompting massive rescue and relief efforts. Emergency crews and volunteers have pulled thousands from roofs, cars and flooded homes—U.S. Coast Guard and Houston responders reported thousands of rescues and hundreds of emergency calls per hour—while many residents remained trapped, hanging towels from windows to signal for help. Harrowing personal accounts described water seeping through doors and windows, rising past outlets, and families forced onto dump trucks and boats; some evacuees panicked, even attempting to overwhelm or attack rescuers in isolated incidents.

Forecasts warned the storm would linger for days, with the National Weather Service predicting an additional 15 to 25 inches across parts of the upper Texas coast and southwest Louisiana, and isolated totals potentially reaching 40–50 inches—threatening to break state rainfall records. Swollen rivers and ongoing reservoir releases from Addicks, Barker and other dams—done to avoid uncontrolled breaches—were creating controlled but extensive downstream flooding that could persist for weeks as water is drained. Mandatory and voluntary evacuations spread across dozens of communities, including La Grange, Dickinson, parts of Fort Bend and Tyler counties, and many neighborhoods near reservoirs and bayous. Curfews, school closures and large shelter operations were put in place; tens of thousands sought refuge in shelters including large facilities in Houston and Dallas.

State and federal officials mobilized massive resources: the Texas National Guard was activated, FEMA warned recovery would be long-term, and the Pentagon identified military assets for relief. President Trump pledged rapid congressional funding and planned regional visits. The administration requested initial federal disaster aid; Texas officials estimated state recovery needs could top $125 billion. Economic impacts mounted as refinery and port shutdowns removed a large share of U.S. refining capacity, prompting gasoline price spikes and prompting the Energy Department to consider Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases. Insurers and analysts began estimating potentially billions in damages.

Authorities stressed ongoing danger: flooding would be slow to recede, and more rain and repeated storm tracks could worsen already-devastating impacts. Officials appealed for donations, volunteers and community involvement to aid long-term recovery as residents faced the prospect of rebuilding and finding a “new normal.”

Contrary to Hollywood glamor, everyday thieves target common sedans and pickups, not exotic cars. LoJack’s 2013 Vehicle Theft Recovery Report—based on recoveries of LoJack‑equipped cars across 27 states and California—found that the Honda Accord was the most stolen and recovered vehicle for the fifth consecutive year. Across LoJack‑equipped vehicles, $121 million in stolen vehicles were recovered in 2013; the priciest recovery was a 2011 Porsche Panamera valued at $103,400. LoJack’s top‑10 list mirrors a National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB) analysis showing Accords leading theft statistics, with the 1996 Accord cited by NICB as a frequent target. Experts attribute the Accord’s popularity with thieves to its long‑standing sales volume, reliability, and the large number of Accords on the road, which creates strong demand for interchangeable parts across model years—making parts resale lucrative. LoJack’s law enforcement VP noted that more Accords in crashes or needing repairs increases parts demand. Honda emphasizes the Accord’s popularity and durability, notes millions built in Ohio, and says it equips new vehicles with modern anti‑theft systems like immobilizers. LoJack’s most stolen recovered models in 2013: Accord, Civic, Camry, Corolla, Silverado, Integra, Escalade, F350, Altima, Tahoe.

Residents of Wukan, a village in Guangdong province, appear to have reached a tentative compromise with authorities after nearly two weeks of large-scale protests over disputed land seizures and the contentious death of negotiator Xue Jinbo while in police custody. Villagers had planned a march through police barricades but paused after senior provincial official Zhu Mingguo and other officials met village representatives. Authorities agreed to release several detained village leaders, return Xue’s body, withdraw roadblocks, and return land from one development project, with four detainees to be freed in coming days. Police say Xue died of a “sudden illness,” while his family alleges he was beaten. Villagers said some demands were met but warned they would resume protests if promises are not kept. Wukan’s struggle has drawn national attention amid many similar land-grab and labor disputes in southern China.

Nearly a month after hundreds of Broad Run High School students took the May 2 SAT, a sealed box of 236 answer sheets that had been reported missing was found at the school. Loudoun County Public Schools officials initially believed UPS had picked up and transported the exams after video apparently showed a courier carrying a box out of the building, and students were told completed exams never reached the College Board. UPS, however, says the shipment never entered its system. On Monday, school staff discovered the sealed box on the bottom shelf of a cart in the school’s shipping area; an ETS representative was present and will take the materials to an ETS/College Board facility in Princeton for validation. School officials say the tests look likely to be validated so affected students need not retake the exam. The district apologized to UPS and will investigate procedures after acknowledging a mix-up when boxes were moved from the guidance office to shipping.

A study from Colorado College shows that simply believing you slept well can boost cognitive performance—a “placebo sleep” effect. Researchers led by Christina Draganich and Professor Kristi Erdal recruited 164 students and told them a fabricated sleep-measurement technique would assess their prior night’s sleep. Participants received a brief talk on sleep and were shown mock machine readouts and spreadsheets. They were randomly assigned to be told they had either “above average” REM sleep (28.7% of total sleep time) or “below average” REM sleep (16.2%), despite no real measurement. Those informed they had better sleep performed significantly better on the Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test, which gauges attention and information-processing ability. The authors interpret this as a mindset-driven placebo effect, where beliefs about sleep quality alter cognitive states positively or negatively. Published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, the study suggests that perception of sleep—independent of actual sleep—can be a tool for influencing health and cognitive functioning.

On March 10, 2014, photographers Steve Douglass, Dean Muskett and others at Amarillo International Airport spotted three high-altitude, contrail-producing aircraft and photographed them with 300mm lenses. At first the images looked like B-2 bombers, but closer review showed a different trailing-edge shape: slightly curved, almost boomerang-like, lacking the B-2’s distinct “W” rear profile. Douglass noted the “trailing edge is wrong,” prompting inquiries to Whiteman AFB, which ruled out a B-2 flight over Texas that day. Aviation Week’s Bill Sweetman and colleagues examined the photos and concluded they depict a real, unknown aircraft rather than a photographic artifact. The shape loosely resembles Northrop Grumman’s X-47B unmanned combat vehicle but appears larger, and voice signals reportedly picked up by Douglass suggest a piloted platform. Speculation ranges from a stealthy transport or new black project to a deliberate limited reveal—similar to the F-117’s partial exposure decades earlier—to signal capabilities. The sighting has drawn interest because it challenges easy identification and hints at undisclosed advanced aircraft operations, though definitive identification remains unconfirmed.

Cuba’s National Assembly moved through a carefully staged, two-day leadership transition that will for the first time in nearly six decades put someone outside the Castro family into the presidency while keeping Raul Castro as the head of the Communist Party. On Wednesday the assembly selected 57‑year‑old First Vice President Miguel Díaz‑Canel as the sole candidate to succeed the 86‑year‑old president; the secret ballots counted by the National Electoral Commission were due to be announced Thursday. The process, controlled by a government-appointed Candidacy Commission and offering legislators only approval or disapproval, is widely expected to produce overwhelmingly unanimous results consistent with Cuba’s long-standing single‑party system.

Díaz‑Canel, once a low‑profile technocrat who rose as the top party official in Villa Clara and later served as higher education minister, has been positioned in recent months through increased state media visibility. Officials and state commentary framed his elevation as continuity of the revolution — younger leadership to sustain the socialist model amid economic stagnation, demographic aging, and rising discontent among younger Cubans. Observers note Díaz‑Canel has expressed orthodox positions in private party meetings, including support for limiting some independent media, yet he has also defended certain academics and bloggers, prompting debate about whether he might cautiously pursue greater responsiveness.

Raul Castro’s remaining role as Communist Party leader means he will retain ultimate influence even after leaving the presidency, underscoring the symbolic nature of the change. The selection also included nominations for six vice presidents of the Council of State, mostly from a younger generation; only one nominee, Ramiro Valdés, is a surviving revolutionary comrade from the 1950s. State media emphasized that Cuba’s political and economic model will continue despite new faces at the top, urging continuity of the revolutionary project. International and domestic audiences will closely watch Díaz‑Canel’s actions once officially announced, particularly on economic reforms and political openness.

Masafumi Nagasaki spent nearly 30 years living alone on Sotobanari, a tiny, uninhabited island in the Yaeyama archipelago off Okinawa, Japan, becoming one of the world’s longest-serving voluntary castaways. He arrived in 1989, intending perhaps a couple of years away from civilisation, but remained until his removal by authorities in April 2018 at age 82. Sotobanari is remote and harsh—no natural freshwater, dangerous currents, little shelter—and fishermen rarely land there. Nagasaki survived typhoons, insects and isolation, famously choosing to live naked after a storm destroyed his clothes and tent; he described nudity on the island as a “uniform” that fit the environment better than conventional society’s rules.

Before retreating to the island he had worked in a factory in Osaka, briefly as a photographer and reportedly in nightlife businesses; he did not like to discuss his past. His stated motive was to escape pollution and the pressures of urban life. He embraced a highly regimented daily routine—morning exercise, long sessions cleaning the beach with gloves and a rake, preparing simple food like boiled rice cakes, and collecting rainwater for washing and drinking. He made occasional weekly trips by boat to a settlement to buy supplies and collect a small family stipend. He declined to eat meat, often refraining from consuming turtle eggs despite their abundance, moved by seeing hatchlings reach the sea.

Nagasaki articulated a deliberate philosophy: he wanted to choose his place of death and felt Sotobanari was the perfect setting to die “surrounded by nature.” Documentarian Alvaro Cerezo spent five days with him and chronicled his life there; Cerezo later reported Nagasaki was found weak on the island, taken by police, and returned to life in Ishigaki under government housing. Authorities reportedly will not allow him to return to Sotobanari. Nagasaki’s story attracted international attention as a striking example of voluntary isolation, self-reliance and a radical rejection of modern society.

Five more bodies were found near the summit of Mount Ontake on Monday, bringing the presumed death toll to 36 after Saturday’s unexpected eruption, Japanese police said. Rescue work was repeatedly halted because the volcano continued to emit ash and toxic gases, forcing teams off the ash‑blanketed peak as a strong sulfur smell and increased fumes made conditions unsafe. Helicopters airlifted eight bodies earlier and four were recovered Sunday; twelve have been taken down and 24 remain near the summit. Many victims were found near a shrine and in a lodge, some buried under up to 50 centimeters of ash, while others may have been struck by falling rocks. The 3,067‑meter mountain erupted around noon as about 250 hikers—enjoying clear autumn weather—were on the slopes; hundreds were trapped but most descended by nightfall. About 63 people were injured, several seriously; some were rescued by helicopter or stretcher. Authorities said the steam‑driven blast was hard to predict, and officials are reviewing monitoring practices amid Japan’s volatile seismic environment. Families of the missing waited anxiously as bodies were taken to a nearby school for examination.

Three people were wounded in a shooting inside Washington Square Mall on Indianapolis’ far east side Wednesday evening after a dispute between acquaintances turned violent, police said. Officers responded around 6:30 p.m. to reports of shots fired near the mall’s southwest entrance by the Target store. Investigators say a man entered the mall, confronted another man he knew, exchanged words and then shot him. Two other young adults—a 25-year-old man and a 20-year-old woman—were struck by stray or ricochet rounds while nearby. All three victims were taken to area hospitals; one male, 26, was listed in serious condition but expected to survive, while the other two were treated and released. Police emphasized the attack was not random and could have occurred anywhere the parties might meet. No one was in custody immediately after the shooting; police later said they were searching for two male suspects, both about 19–20 years old, and asked that the victims help identify the shooter. Witnesses described a chaotic scene: shoppers fled, hid in dressing rooms and stores, and parents scrambled for children. Mall staff and Indianapolis police responded quickly, and the mall’s property manager said the facility is cooperating with the investigation and prioritizes shopper and employee safety. Authorities confirmed the shooter did not use a long gun and urged anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers. The investigation remains active and the story may be updated.

Bob Tracey, a 62-year-old SEPTA worker from Upper Darby, Pennsylvania, has been awarded $15,200 after finding and turning the money over to police last March. While driving home from his shift on March 7, Tracey saw a Wells Fargo bank bag in the road, opened it, and discovered multiple stacks of cash. He immediately called authorities and surrendered the bag. Upper Darby Police Superintendent Michael Chitwood praised Tracey’s honesty and said the money should rightfully go to him if the true owner did not come forward. The bag also contained drug paraphernalia — a digital scale, a crack-cocaine pipe and an unidentified vial — making it unlikely that a legitimate owner would claim it. Some people did contact police claiming ownership but produced no proof. Under state law, a finder of lost property can claim title against everyone except the true owner, so Tracey petitioned the Delaware County Court of Common Pleas last September after administrative delays. On Monday, Judge Charles Burr II ordered the cash returned to Tracey, closing the prolonged bureaucratic process.

President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un met in Singapore’s Sentosa Island for a historic summit intended to address Pyongyang’s nuclear program. The leaders held a roughly 40–45 minute one-on-one meeting with only interpreters present, then joined larger sessions with aides. The day featured staged cordiality and photo opportunities—handshakes, a stroll, and a working lunch—culminating in a brief joint statement in which both pledged to “work toward complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula” and to pursue new U.S.-North Korean relations and the recovery of Korean War remains. Trump said the process would start quickly and touted what he described as a “fantastic” meeting and an “excellent relationship,” while Kim said they had “decided to leave the past behind.” The statement lacked specifics: it did not define “security guarantees,” what “complete denuclearization” means, or any verification measures. U.S. officials, including Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, emphasized that sanctions would remain until denuclearization occurs and signaled willingness to offer assurances to North Korea, while warning sanctions could increase if diplomacy failed. The summit drew praise and skepticism—supporters urged seizing the diplomatic opportunity and the U.N. offered verification help if requested, while critics argued the summit elevated Kim without concrete concessions and warned of the risks of a private meeting with minimal witnesses. International reactions varied: France and others said they would welcome a deal but cautioned past failures, Iran warned North Korea to be wary given U.S. treaty withdrawals, and analysts predicted any substantive denuclearization would require prolonged negotiation beyond the summit’s symbolism.

Eleven Secret Service agents assigned to an advance team in Cartagena were recalled to Washington after allegedly bringing women—reported to be prostitutes—back to their hotel rooms in the days before President Obama’s arrival for the Summit of the Americas. Rep. Peter King and author Ronald Kessler said the episode involved heavy drinking, at least one payment dispute in a hotel hallway that provoked local police, and reports forwarded to the U.S. Embassy. The agency’s Office of Professional Responsibility opened an investigation; the agents were removed and replaced before Obama arrived. Five U.S. military personnel staying at the same hotel were also implicated for curfew violations and possible misconduct and are under separate military inquiry. White House spokesman Jay Carney said the president retained confidence in the Secret Service, calling the matter a media distraction, while Secret Service officials expressed regret for any distraction. Critics warned the behavior risked embarrassment, ethical breaches, blackmail vulnerabilities, and damage to U.S. reputation, especially given Cartagena’s known sex-tourism trade and the hotel housing press and staff.

Facing mounting criticism for its overwhelmingly older, male, and white membership and growing public outcry about Hollywood’s diversity problems, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has launched a dramatic membership overhaul. In an unprecedented move, the Academy extended 683 invitations to join its ranks—nearly half to women and 41% to people of color—making this its largest and most diverse class of invitees to date. The list reads like a corrective who’s who of notable industry figures who had, for various reasons, previously been overlooked: established Hollywood names, international auteurs, and rising stars.

Directors comprise a major focus of the push, with dozens of filmmakers from across the globe invited, including Catherine Breillat, Park Chan-wook, Lucrecia Martel, Abbas Kiarostami, Hou Hsiao-hsien, Karyn Kusama, Kiyoshi Kurosawa, Lynne Ramsay, the Wachowskis, Apichatpong Weerasethakul, Patty Jenkins, Ryan Coogler, Ramin Bahrani, Nuri Bilge Ceylan, and Ken Loach, among many others—signaling a conscious effort to broaden the Academy’s artistic and geographic representation. The acting invitees likewise mix established and emerging talents: Luis Guzmán, Adam Beach, Kate Beckinsale, Morris Chestnut, Idris Elba, Oscar Isaac, Tessa Thompson, Greta Gerwig, Alicia Vikander, Michael B. Jordan, Regina King, Eva Mendes, Vivica A. Fox, Ice Cube, and three Wayans brothers are included.

This move follows sustained pressure from activists and artists galvanized by the #OscarsSoWhite campaign, created by April Reign after all-white acting nominee lists in 2015 and again in a later year. With public figures like Spike Lee and Jada Pinkett Smith amplifying the criticism, the Academy pledged to double the number of women and people of color in its membership by 2020. The new invitation round represents the organization’s first substantive step toward meeting that commitment.

American journalist James Foley was murdered by Islamic State militants, who publicized his beheading in a graphic video on Aug. 19. Foley had been abducted in Syria on Nov. 22, 2012, and his family, GlobalPost (his employer), authorities and private security consultants had been trying to locate and secure his release for nearly two years. On Aug. 12 Foley’s parents received an email from the captors warning that he would be executed, a message GlobalPost later published with the Foley family’s permission to provide transparency and context about ISIS’s motivations and tactics.

The email framed the killing as retaliation for U.S. airstrikes in Iraq, threatened Americans broadly, and made grandiose, inaccurate claims—such as alleging the Foley family had “many chances to negotiate.” In reality, after more than a year without contact, the captors first demanded an impossible ransom—100 million euros—or prisoner exchanges; experts say the amount indicated they likely never expected payment and may have reserved Foley for symbolic use. The email’s rhetoric emphasized vengeance, promised more blood, and explicitly cited Foley’s execution as the first price to be paid for U.S. military actions.

The execution video featured a masked English-speaking militant widely labeled in British press as “Jihadi John,” identified by a British accent and believed to lead a small group of British guards responsible for foreign hostages. Reports suggest many foreign fighters—particularly from Britain—are heavily represented among ISIS ranks and are often used for brutal acts because of strong ideological motivation. Former hostages described Foley as singled out for harsher treatment, partly after captors found photos linking his brother to the U.S. Air Force. Foley endured mock executions and regular abuse; fellow captives remembered him as compassionate and supportive during imprisonment.

ISIS holds up to 20 Western hostages in Syria, including freelance reporter Steven Sotloff—who was later threatened—and several aid workers. Families of hostages defended their loved ones’ humanitarian motives. The killing prompted global shock and condolences, including a heartfelt 20-minute call from Pope Francis to Foley’s parents, who called their son a compassionate witness who died for his commitment to bearing witness in conflict zones.

Rescuers in northern Thailand continue a high-stakes operation to free 12 boys and their football coach trapped nearly two weeks inside the flooded Tham Luang Nang Non cave. Medical authorities judged Thursday that moving the group then was too dangerous; two boys and the coach show exhaustion from malnutrition. Teams are pumping oxygen into the chamber and have provided food, blankets and medical attention since British divers located the group nine days after they entered. The boys appear in good spirits in recent video, but most cannot swim and lack diving experience.

Water remains the central threat. Hundreds of pumps have removed millions of gallons, clearing roughly 1.5 km of passage to a third chamber, but narrow, murky, winding tunnels still force reliance on diving; reaching the group takes about six hours inward and five hours back. Monsoon rains forecast this weekend heighten urgency: if downpours refill the cave, rescuers may be forced to act quickly or the boys could remain trapped for months. Options under consideration include further draining to allow a walking exit, teaching some boys to dive with full-face masks guided by expert divers along static lines, or finding natural chimneys from above to access the chamber. International teams from Australia, the US, UK, China and other countries support the effort. Authorities emphasize cautious decisions to avoid risking lives in the complex, rapidly changing environment.

The California Supreme Court on Thursday overturned a lower-court ruling that had ordered improved conditions for elephants at the Los Angeles Zoo, delivering a setback to animal advocates who had argued the animals were being mistreated. The dispute began when Los Angeles resident Aaron Leider sued L.A. Zoo Director John Lewis and the City of Los Angeles in August 2007, opposing expansion of the zoo’s elephant exhibit and alleging that keepers subjected elephants to “cruel, abusive and illegal treatment” using chains, drugs, bullhooks and electric shocks.

In a 2012 bench trial, Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge John Segal did not definitively label zoo treatment as inhumane but concluded the city needed to provide better care. Segal ordered the zoo to stop using bullhooks and electric shocks and to ensure regular exercise for the elephants. A divided appeals court later affirmed those directives, and local leaders—including City Councilman Paul Koretz, who called for moving an Asian elephant named Billy to a sanctuary—cited Segal’s findings in urging changes.

Leider’s complaint included allegations that a keeper had shocked Billy and that the elephant’s head-bobbing indicated stress and isolation.
