But the California Supreme Court unanimously reversed the appeals court, rejecting the legal theory underlying Leider’s taxpayer lawsuit. Justice Carol Corrigan wrote that a taxpayer action cannot be used to enforce alleged criminal violations of animal abuse statutes; the trial court’s findings implicated criminal penalties but did not afford the city or defendants a jury trial or the proof-beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard, and the plaintiff had improperly exercised prosecutorial discretion. For those reasons, Corrigan said, the injunction could not stand.

Leider’s attorney, David Casselman, called the decision “extremely disappointing,” said evidence showed premature elephant deaths linked to zoo conditions, and indicated he may seek a jury retrial or pursue legislative solutions. The zoo praised the ruling, asserting it provides the highest level of elephant care in a top-quality, large habitat. The case has been remanded for further proceedings.

A new report from Transportation for America finds at least 66,405 U.S. bridges — about 11% of the national total — are classified as structurally deficient, meaning key elements need significant maintenance, rehabilitation or replacement. Those bridges are used heavily: Americans make roughly 260 million crossings of structurally deficient spans each day. The average age of these bridges is 65, and the Federal Highway Administration estimates repairs would cost about $76 billion, a figure likely to rise as many high-traffic bridges near or pass their design lifespans. Since 2011 fifteen states have seen increases in structurally deficient bridges, and the report projects that in a decade one in four bridges will be 65 or older.

The findings follow the May 23 Interstate 5 Skagit River collapse in Washington, caused by a truck striking the span; that bridge was not on the deficient list. Transportation for America urges Congress to raise dedicated transportation revenues, expand eligibility for new funding to 180,000 bridges, and prioritize bridge and highway repairs. Some experts disagree on the severity: proponents of state-led funding say the overall system is improving and states are better positioned to address needs. Meanwhile, many less-visible overpasses and commuter bridges remain in poor condition, producing potholes, restrictions and lane closures unless investment increases.

J.C.X. Simon, one of four men convicted in the racially motivated "Zebra" slayings that terrorized San Francisco in the early 1970s, was found dead alone in his San Quentin cell Thursday night and pronounced dead at 11:59 p.m., officials said. He was 69. The California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation said Simon was unresponsive and that the cause of death is pending an autopsy. Simon had been serving a life sentence with the possibility of parole after his 1976 convictions for two counts of first-degree murder, conspiracy to commit murder and assault with a deadly weapon. 

Simon and co-defendants Larry Green, Manuel Moore and Jessie Lee Cooks carried out a six-month campaign from October 1973 to April 1974 that left 14 people dead and seven injured, primarily targeting white victims on San Francisco streets. Survivors, including future mayor Art Agnos, helped identify suspects. The investigation, overseen by Mayor Joseph Alioto, involved an intensive manhunt and controversial stops of Black men matching witness descriptions. The four were convicted after testimony by Anthony C. Harris, who said the group was an offshoot called the Death Angels. The remaining three men are serving life terms at separate California prisons.

Kim Kardashian and her family have built a vast consumer brand from their reality-show fame, marketing everything from clothing and jewelry to perfume, skin care and weight-loss products. Despite beginning her public life via a sex tape, Kim remains broadly popular and is tied with Snooki atop Brand Keys’ celebrity loyalty index; sisters Kourtney and Khloé also rank highly. Consumers view Kim as an entrepreneur who listens directly to fans via Twitter and social media—she uses their feedback to shape product choices, from perfume colors to fashion items. Shoppers praise her relatable image—fashionable, curvy, and entrepreneurial—and many see her as representing “the average girl” or a modern, empowered woman. Her product lines tend toward standard Southern California nightlife styles—slinky one-shoulder dresses, leggings and hoop-heavy jewelry with Armenian influences—sold at accessible prices. The family’s marketing strategy deliberately differentiates each sister to appeal to distinct demographics: Khloé to married women, Kourtney to new moms (and viewers who empathize with relationship drama), and Kim to single women, all amplified by Kris Jenner’s savvy management.

A large UK study and an international meta-analysis found that sleeping more than eight hours a day is associated with a higher risk of stroke, particularly in older adults. Researchers from the University of Cambridge followed 9,692 stroke-free participants aged 42–81 in the EPIC-Norfolk cohort for an average of 9.5 years, asking about sleep duration in 1998–2000 and again in 2002–2004. Nearly 70% reported sleeping six to eight hours, about 10% reported over eight hours, and those sleeping under six or over eight hours tended to be older, female, and less active. During follow-up 346 participants experienced a stroke. After adjusting for confounders, long sleepers (>8 hours) had a 46% higher stroke risk (HR 1.46), while short sleepers (<6 hours) showed a non-significant 18% higher risk. Those reporting persistently long sleep at both time points had double the stroke risk compared with persistently average sleepers; participants whose sleep increased from short to long had nearly four times the risk. An updated meta-analysis pooling data from 11 other prospective studies (about 560,000 people across seven countries) produced compatible results: short sleep associated with a 15% increased stroke risk and long sleep with a 45% increased risk. The direction and causes of the association remain unclear — longer sleep could be an early marker, symptom, or contributor to vascular disease. The association persisted after excluding participants with preexisting disease and among those reporting good sleep quality, suggesting independence from typical cardiovascular risk factors. Authors call for further research to clarify underlying mechanisms and suggest clinicians consider unusually long sleep in older patients as a potential warning sign warranting further assessment. The study was funded by the Medical Research Council and Cancer Research UK.

In November 2015, sustained protests over racial incidents at the University of Missouri culminated in the resignation of President Tim Wolfe. The movement was led publicly by graduate student Jonathan Butler, who began a high-profile hunger strike demanding Wolfe’s removal and broader institutional change. Butler and Concerned Student 1950 mobilized after a series of racist episodes and perceived administrative indifference: racial slurs directed at Black students, a swastika drawn in feces in a dorm bathroom, removal of hospital privileges for an abortion provider, and cuts to graduate health subsidies (later reversed). Longstanding patterns of racial hostility on and off campus, recounted by faculty and students, provided historical context for the unrest.

The protests grew rapidly and gained national attention when the university’s black football players announced they would refuse to practice or play until Wolfe resigned, effectively threatening the revenue-driving program and amplifying media coverage. Faculty and student government joined actions—walkouts and teach-ins—and deans and community leaders criticized leadership failures. The Board of Curators convened and the pressure peaked as Butler’s health declined; following Wolfe’s resignation, Butler ended his hunger strike.

In response to the crisis, the Board announced initiatives: hiring a systemwide diversity, inclusion and equity officer; providing more support for those experiencing discrimination; creating a task force to improve diversity and inclusion; and mandating diversity training for all faculty, staff and incoming students. Jonathan Butler framed the campaign as a fight for justice and safer campus climates, connecting it to broader Black Lives Matter activism while underscoring its campus-specific goals. The episode exposed deep-seated racial tensions and forced the university to confront systemic problems it had long failed to resolve.

Lionsgate and AMC have signed a long-term deal with Matthew Weiner, creator and showrunner of Mad Men, guaranteeing he will run the series for two more seasons with an option for a third — potentially taking the show through a seventh season. The deal, reportedly worth about $30 million (roughly $10 million per season), preserves Weiner’s creative control: cast members cannot be cut for financial reasons and will remain unless removed for story reasons. Episodes’ lengths were partially compromised: season openers and finales will stay 47 minutes, while midseason episodes will air at 45 minutes on television to allow more commercial time; Weiner will produce 47-minute “final cut” versions for digital and home video. The fifth season will premiere in early 2012 rather than summer. Weiner, who said the seventh season is likely the last, emphasized the agreement was about maintaining the show’s artistic integrity rather than money, and thanked fans, AMC, and Lionsgate for their support.

The document describes an Internet Archive effort to crawl and preserve web pages as they are created so links remain available even if the original pages change or disappear, with the stated goal of fixing broken links across the web. It then shifts to a detailed report on a deadly April 2018 shooting at a Nashville Waffle House and the manhunt for the suspect, Travis Reinking.

Reinking, 29, allegedly arrived at the restaurant nearly naked, armed with an assault-style rifle, and opened fire in the parking lot before rushing inside. Four people were killed and four injured. Among the dead were employees Taurean Sanderlin, 29, and 20-year-old Joe Perez; inside the restaurant, 21-year-old Belmont student DeEbony Groves and 23-year-old Akilah Dasilva were also fatally wounded. Several victims were treated at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, including Dasilva’s girlfriend Tia Waggoner, who underwent surgery to try to save a leg. A quick-thinking customer, James Shaw Jr., wrestled the gun away, sustaining minor injuries; he has been widely praised but downplayed his role.

A massive manhunt involving over 80 Nashville officers, the FBI, ATF and state troopers sought Reinking, who was believed to be on foot near his apartment’s wooded area and possibly still armed. Authorities warned neighbors to be vigilant and placed him on Tennessee’s Top 10 Most Wanted list. Reports from Illinois painted Reinking as disturbed, with prior incidents including a July detention by Secret Service near the White House, claims of being stalked by Taylor Swift, and other erratic behavior. Illinois authorities had previously seized firearms from him; those guns were later returned to his father, who now acknowledges giving them back, raising questions about how Reinking reacquired weapons. Police recovered three of four previously seized guns and believe he had at least one handgun during the attack. Investigations into motive and how Reinking regained access to firearms continued.

The USS Independence (CVL-22), originally launched as the light cruiser USS Amsterdam (CL-59) in August 1942 and commissioned January 14, 1943, was the first of a class of carriers converted from cruiser hulls. Joining the Pacific Fleet in mid-1943, she saw extensive wartime service: strikes on Marcus and Wake Islands, support for the Bougainville and Gilbert Islands campaigns, pre-landing strikes at Tarawa (where she was torpedoed on November 20, 1943), major operations against Rabaul, sustained duty in the Philippines, and intensive participation in strikes on Luzon, Formosa, Okinawa, and finally raids on Japan. Notably, aircraft from Independence’s task groups helped locate and attack Vice Admiral Kurita’s force in the Sibuyan Sea and took part in the massive carrier strikes during the Battle of Leyte Gulf, contributing to the sinking of the battleship Musashi and the destruction of Japan’s remaining carrier strength—actions that effectively ended the Japanese Navy as a major threat. The carrier pioneered night operations after receiving an additional catapult, supplied night reconnaissance and combat air patrols, and endured the December 1944 typhoon that inflicted heavy losses across the fleet. After Japan’s surrender she performed occupation support and “Magic Carpet” duty, returning veterans home until January 1946.

Postwar, Independence was a target ship in Operation Crossroads at Bikini Atoll, surviving both the Able (air) and Baker (underwater) atomic tests though heavily damaged and contaminated. Decommissioned August 28, 1946, she was later used for further tests and deliberately sunk by torpedoes off the California coast on January 26, 1951. Long believed lost to imagery and sonar, the wreck—lying about 30 miles west of Half Moon Bay and half a mile deep—was revisited in a recent expedition led by famed oceanographer Robert Ballard with NOAA and the Ocean Exploration Trust. Using unmanned submersibles, Ballard’s team captured the first photographs in over six decades: the intact flight deck, a Grumman F6F Hellcat with visible markings, anti-aircraft guns, hatches, ladders and the ship’s name on the hull. The wreck is remarkably well-preserved in deep water, appearing much as it did in 1946 photos. Although records indicate the ship once carried cement-filled barrels of low-level radioactive waste, divers found no trace and experts say remaining radioactivity is negligible after seven decades. Scientists collected sediment and biological samples for testing, while Ballard emphasized non-disturbance of wrecks as deep-sea heritage. The find provides a well-preserved, poignant snapshot of a storied carrier’s wartime service and postwar fate.

An 18-year-old student, Vladislav Roslyakov, carried out a gun-and-bomb attack at Kerch Polytechnic College in Crimea, killing 20 people and wounding dozens before killing himself. The rampage began with a powerful nail-bomb detonated in the cafeteria, showering victims with shrapnel and causing catastrophic injuries; witnesses then described Roslyakov moving through corridors shooting classmates at close range. Investigators found a second explosive device and more munitions; many critically injured were flown to hospitals in Moscow for surgery. Authorities initially called it a terrorist act but later classified it as mass murder. The attack, the deadliest in Crimea since Russia’s 2014 annexation and the worst Russian school attack since Beslan, stunned the city of Kerch, where thousands were expected to attend funerals and a three-day mourning period was declared. Residents left flowers and toys at memorials and mourned publicly. Officials said Roslyakov had few friends, spent much time playing computer games, had recently obtained a shotgun permit and bought large quantities of ammunition. Crimean authorities searched his computer but found deleted material; officials are probing whether he acted alone. Kremlin figures, including President Vladimir Putin and state media, framed the massacre as influenced by “globalization” and foreign examples of school shootings. The tragedy has raised urgent questions about school security, gun licensing and social influences on vulnerable youth.

In Hurricane, Utah, controversy over a large copper bull sculpture atop Barista’s restaurant ended this week when owner Stephen Ward removed the statue’s prominent genitalia. The oversize, cone-shaped feature sparked community outrage after the bull was installed in mid-March, prompting complaints and calls to the city council to revoke the restaurant’s business license. Ward says he removed the piece not because of pressure but because he personally preferred the bull’s appearance without it, insisting the alteration revealed more of the sculpture’s belly and platework.

Tensions between Ward and local residents have run high for years beyond the statue dispute. Customers have accused Ward of poor business practices, high prices and hostility; Ward counters that his food is top-notch and that he’s been unfairly targeted by the community and city officials. A March 14 confrontation between a patron and an employee heightened friction; the patron was cited on several misdemeanors, though Ward criticized how it was handled. City planning officials say the sign was approved but that the installed proportions differed from the plans; Ward disputes some city statements and presented an email showing a planner had viewed the bull and called it beautiful.

The controversy brought widespread attention and a surge of customers to Barista’s, which Ward and his wife say benefited from the publicity. Ward has pursued legal actions related to licensing and a petition against his business, framing the disputes as prolonged harassment by the city and neighbors. The story remains developing.

Dennis Rodman led a team of former NBA players to Pyongyang for an exhibition basketball game and sang “Happy Birthday” to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, dedicating the event to him. About 14,000 spectators attended as Kim, his wife and senior officials watched. Rodman called the visit “historic” and framed it as cultural “basketball diplomacy,” but his trip drew heavy criticism in the U.S. Critics — including members of Congress, the NBA and human rights groups — say his visits are naive and risk legitimizing the regime. Rodman also sparked controversy by implying missionary Kenneth Bae was to blame for his detention; Bae’s family and U.S. officials condemned the remark and urged his release. Former players expressed mixed emotions about the trip.

The detention of U.S. pastor Andrew Brunson has escalated into a major diplomatic and economic standoff between Washington and Ankara. Brunson, a 50-year-old evangelical from North Carolina who ran a small church in Izmir, has been held in Turkey for nearly two years on allegations of ties to outlawed political groups; he denies wrongdoing and is currently under house arrest. His case has prompted sharp U.S. criticism of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s government, with President Donald Trump calling Brunson a "hostage" and demanding his release. The U.S. has responded with financial sanctions and reciprocal tariffs, contributing to Turkey’s economic turmoil and a steep depreciation of the lira.

A senior White House official said the Trump administration rejected Turkish efforts to link Brunson’s freedom to easing pressure on Halkbank, a state bank accused of helping Iran evade U.S. sanctions and facing billions in potential U.S. fines. U.S. Treasury and Justice Department inquiries into Halkbank have advanced—subpoenas were issued and material reviewed—but prosecutors remain unsatisfied and a criminal case is possible. U.S. officials have signaled more sanctions could follow if Brunson is not freed, and have made further negotiations over Halkbank contingent on his release. Analysts view Brunson as both a humanitarian and political issue: freeing him would bolster Trump’s foreign-policy credentials with his evangelical base and reinforce his “strong-arm” posture. Turkish leaders insist they will not yield to U.S. pressure.

A Fort Worth police report and subsequent media accounts detail allegations by Colleen Crowley, who says she is Johnny Manziel’s ex-girlfriend, that Manziel assaulted her in late January in the Dallas–Fort Worth area. Crowley told police Manziel became aggressive in his Hotel ZaZa room after an argument, restrained her, forced her toward a valet area and then drove her to where her car was parked. She alleges he dragged her by the hair, struck her—reportedly hitting her left ear so she couldn’t hear afterward—smashed her phone, and threatened that he would kill them both. Crowley described fearing for her life, fleeing to a neighbor’s door for help and arming herself with a kitchen knife when he returned; she says Manziel fled on foot. She also told officers she thought he appeared to be “on some kind of drugs.” Crowley later grew reluctant to provide details and declined to complete a formal statement; because the alleged assault spanned jurisdictions and she was apprehensive about pressing charges, police completed an “information only” report. Dallas police said their follow-up did not result in criminal charges and the case was closed. Manziel denied the allegations to TMZ Sports, saying he did not strike or threaten to kill anyone and that he was “completely stable.” The NFL confirmed it is aware of the police report and had begun a review when the incident occurred. The Cleveland Browns said they were aware of the report and reiterated earlier comments that Manziel’s repeated off-field incidents undermine team expectations; the team indicated he is unlikely to be with the Browns next season but cannot formally address roster status until league rules permit.

Chelsea Clinton, newly a mother of two, said she finds Donald Trump’s rhetoric — targeting women, minorities, Muslims and immigrants — more disturbing than attacks on her mother, Hillary Clinton. In an NBC Today interview, Chelsea said she can’t imagine raising her children in the world Trump describes and expects to be overwhelmed when introducing her mother at the Democratic National Convention, where Hillary will become the first woman to accept a major-party nomination. Chelsea emphasized that Republicans’ criticism of Hillary pales beside Trump’s insults, but she’s not worried about attacks on her mother because public life taught Hillary how to respond: “She’s tough and she can take whatever people say about her.” Chelsea hopes her speech will convey the real person she knows versus the negative portrayals pushed by opponents and said she loves and admires her mother deeply.

Chelsea acknowledged Democrats still need to win over some Bernie Sanders supporters and praised Sanders for pushing economic and social justice issues. She also noted differences with Ivanka Trump despite their friendship and dismissed Trump’s divisive rhetoric. The convention highlighted Democratic challenges to Trump on issues like his proposed Muslim ban and public safety, featuring voices such as Khizr Khan. Chelsea joked about what her father might be called if he returned to the White House, favoring “first gentleman.”

Since the 2014–2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, which killed over 11,100 and infected nearly 27,000, organizations have responded to treat patients, protect health workers, and rebuild strained health systems. AmeriCares supplied millions of PPE and medicines, staffed and managed treatment units in Liberia, ran mobile clinics, vaccinations, psychosocial support, and is funding an 18-month maternal-newborn project. In Sierra Leone and Guinea it provided PPE, bleach, reunification kits, and training. Partners including WFP, Samaritan’s Purse, International Medical Corps, UNICEF and the Red Cross scaled logistics, food assistance, treatment centers, training and community outreach to control Ebola and strengthen preparedness.

Germany failed to convince Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Poland to accept EU-led migrant relocation and quotas as it grapples with a growing refugee influx. Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier described the situation as “the greatest challenge” the EU has faced, warning that up to 40,000 people might arrive over a single weekend and that Germany now expects about 800,000 migrants this year. Berlin urged a fair distribution of those still en route and backed European Commission president Jean-Claude Juncker’s proposal to allocate 160,000 refugees across member states, but the four Central European governments resisted, citing national sovereignty over immigration decisions. Talks in Prague ahead of a planned meeting of EU interior ministers produced no agreement, and German officials even floated the rare option of moving to majority voting to force a decision.

Domestically, German politicians voiced concern about losing control, and Defence Minister Ursula von der Leyen put 4,000 troops on standby. Hungary’s Prime Minister Viktor Orban defended tougher measures, announcing new laws to arrest illegal border crossers. The UN and aid agencies said Juncker’s plan would help but was insufficient given record Mediterranean crossings. Tensions also flared over incidents like the widely criticized footage of a Hungarian camerawoman tripping migrants; she apologized, was fired and faces criminal charges, underscoring the fraught, emotional atmosphere across the region.

When Fox announced The Mindy Project would end after three seasons, fans erupted online — but Mindy Kaling appeared unfazed. Vacationing in Montana, the 35-year-old posted a twilight video on Instagram showing sweeping scenery before turning to smile and wink at the camera, captioning it, “Hey guys, I’m in Montana, is anything happening in LA? #themindyproject.” Her playful, cryptic post sparked hope that cancellation might not be final. Shortly after, Variety reported Hulu was in talks with Universal TV to pick up the comedy for additional seasons, fueling optimism among viewers. The clip and the streaming talks left fans wondering whether Kaling’s message hinted that the show could be saved.

Scientists have identified a new species of horse-sized tyrannosaur, Timurlengia euotica, from fossils found in Uzbekistan’s Kyzylkum desert that illuminate how Tyrannosaurus rex evolved into an apex predator. Dated to about 90 million years ago, Timurlengia fills a critical 20-million-year gap in the tyrannosaur fossil record and suggests that major sensory and neurological developments preceded the enormous body size seen in late Cretaceous giants like T. rex. Although Timurlengia was modest in size—roughly horse-sized, up to about 200–250 kg—with long legs and blade-like teeth suited to pursuit hunting, CT scans of its braincase show a relatively large brain and inner-ear structures adapted for balance and low-frequency hearing. These traits imply keen senses and cognitive abilities evolved early in the lineage, enabling later tyrannosaurs to exploit ecological opportunities and grow rapidly to multi-tonne sizes roughly 80 million years later. Researchers propose that tyrannosaurs “got smart before they got big,” possibly capitalizing on the disappearance of other large predators such as allosaurs. The discovery was led by the University of Edinburgh with collaborators from Russian and U.S. institutions and is published in PNAS. While partial remains limit knowledge of some features, the find strengthens the idea that evolutionary changes in sensing and behavior set the stage for the later dramatic increase in body size and dominance of tyrannosaurs before the end-Cretaceous extinction.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) has opened a formal investigation into Tesla’s Model S after two U.S. incidents in which road debris pierced the undercarriage and battery compartment, causing fires. Both incidents—one in Washington state and one in Tennessee—allowed occupants to exit safely after the vehicle’s battery monitoring system issued warnings. A third fire in Mexico, resulting from a crash, falls outside NHTSA’s jurisdiction. NHTSA can recommend a recall following its probe; Tesla CEO Elon Musk has said he doesn’t currently believe a recall is warranted.

In response to the incidents and ensuing publicity, Tesla issued immediate and planned actions. The company deployed an over-the-air software update to raise highway-speed ground clearance via the air suspension to reduce the odds of underbody impacts. A further update due in January will let drivers set preferred ride-height transitions. Tesla also amended its warranty to cover fire damage—even if caused by driver error, except deliberate arson—and requested a prompt NHTSA investigation, though the agency says its decision to open the probe was independent.

Musk defended the Model S vigorously, arguing electric vehicles are less prone to fires than gasoline cars. He highlighted statistics claiming zero deaths or serious injuries from Tesla fires worldwide and contrasted that with hundreds of deaths and thousands of injuries from gasoline-vehicle fires in the U.S. since Model S production began. Musk emphasized battery design features (module firewalls and separation from the cabin) and said Tesla would promptly implement any regulator-suggested safety improvements. The announcements and probe affected Tesla’s stock, which dipped on initial news but later recovered some losses.

In mid-July Turkey experienced a violent, disorienting attempted military coup that shook its major cities, killed and wounded hundreds, and accelerated an already bitter political struggle. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan quickly blamed followers of U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gülen — long a onetime ally turned enemy — accusing the “parallel” Gülen Movement of orchestrating the uprising. Ankara demanded Gülen’s extradition from the United States; Washington said it would consider any formal request but had not been presented persuasive evidence and would require proof that withstands scrutiny.

The overnight action saw tanks and attack helicopters rolling through Ankara and Istanbul, fighter jets and artillery fire, a bombed corner of Parliament, and a brief takeover of state television. Civilians heeded Erdoğan’s urgent calls — broadcast notably via smartphone video — and flooded streets, confronting armored vehicles and surrounding tanks. Graphic scenes included protesters pelting and at times assaulting soldiers, followed in moments by gestures of compassion when surrendered servicemen were helped by police. By dawn the coup had largely crumbled: thousands of alleged plotters were detained, hundreds of soldiers surrendered, and loyalist forces reclaimed key sites. Official casualty figures varied but totaled at least into the low hundreds killed and well over a thousand wounded.

The coup’s origins and actors remain contested. Erdoğan and senior officials tied the attempt to the Gülen Movement, prompting a sweeping purge: tens of thousands of arrests and dismissals followed across the military, judiciary, and civil service, and the movement had already been designated a terrorist organization by the Turkish cabinet earlier that year. Critics and analysts, however, advise caution: evidence directly linking Gülen to the coup was not publicly presented, and the military has not been seen as dominated by Gülenists in the way police and parts of the judiciary once were. The U.S. response emphasized support for Turkey’s democratically elected government but underscored the need for legal evidence before acting on extradition requests.

Understanding the coup requires context on Gülen’s rise and fall with Erdoğan. Fethullah Gülen, an influential Turkish imam in exile since 1999, built a global service-oriented movement focused on education, interfaith dialogue, and a moderate interpretation of Islam. Gülen-affiliated institutions operate widely, including more than 100 charter schools in the United States, where they drew scrutiny and investigations for alleged financial and administrative irregularities. In Turkey the movement once allied with Erdoğan and the AKP to weaken secularist establishment rivals; later a power struggle — crystallized by 2013 corruption probes tied to prosecutors perceived as Gülenist and by Erdoğan’s moves to curb Gülen-run prep schools — transformed them into bitter adversaries.

In the coup’s wake Erdoğan framed the failed putsch as an opportunity to “cleanse” the military and other institutions, accelerating consolidation of power. Whether the purge targets are actual conspirators or scapegoats, the result is clear: a sweeping crackdown on perceived Gülenists and a rapid centralization of authority under Erdoğan, with significant consequences for Turkish democracy, institutional independence, and Turkey’s relations abroad. The violent night and its aftermath left the country wounded, politically polarized, and facing deep uncertainty about civil liberties, the rule of law, and its future trajectory.

A short video filmed by an Alaska Bureau of Land Management employee on the Chena River near Fairbanks ignited a wave of online speculation after showing a 12–15-foot segmented, icy object apparently moving in the current. Posted on the agency’s official Facebook page with ominous music and a camcorder overlay, the clip quickly went viral—drawing half a million-plus views and hundreds of comments offering wildly varying theories: everything from giant sturgeon, lost sharks, seals or an enormous salmon to sea monsters, a Nessie-like creature, a “beavegator,” or even moose hide and zombies. The fact the footage came from a government employee rather than an anonymous uploader amplified interest and media pickup, including British tabloids and U.S. outlets.

BLM staff stressed the video itself was unedited apart from speed and minor audio/overlay additions and acknowledged they hadn’t approached the object, which stayed out in the middle of the river. Experts at the Alaska Department of Fish and Game provided the most grounded explanation: the “ice monster” is likely a rope snagged on a bridge pier with frazil ice—loose, slushy ice that forms in cold nights—accumulating on it. That coating of ice would make a stationary rope appear to undulate and “swim” in alternating currents as it floats. Biologist Klaus Wuttig called the footage visually striking but unremarkable in origin, noting no evidence of large sturgeon in the Chena. The BLM embraced the public fascination, posting an update on Halloween that echoed the scientific verdict while celebrating the way such moments spotlight the allure and mystery of the natural world.

Executives of Wheel of Fortune faced backlash after a puzzle answer, “The Fast and The Furious,” aired on about 200 local stations shortly after actor Paul Walker’s fatal car crash. The show said the appearance was an “unfortunate coincidence,” noting the episode had been taped weeks earlier, before Walker’s death. Wheel of Fortune’s verified Twitter expressed condolences to Walker’s family, friends and fans. Host Pat Sajak also apologized for the timing, explaining the taped segment had been distributed long before the tragedy. Walker, 40, and driver Roger Rodas died when their Porsche crashed and ignited.

The USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service issued new guidance urging meat and dairy producers to adopt “Best If Used By” as a uniform date label to reduce consumer confusion and curb food waste. Date labels like “Sell By” and “Use By” are voluntary and often misinterpreted; “Sell By” indicates retail timing, while “Use By” can be wrongly seen as a safety cutoff (and should be reserved for infant formula). FSIS says “Best If Used By” clearly signals quality, not safety, and that food without spoilage may be safe after the date. The USDA cites about 30% of U.S. food lost at retail/consumer levels and hopes consistent labeling—paired with donation-friendly policies—will cut waste. The guidance is voluntary, applies to FSIS-regulated products, and the agency is taking public comments for 60 days.

The two-part document contrasts Hollywood’s modern blockbuster-driven model with the decline of mid-budget, adult-oriented filmmaking and how that shift affects filmmakers and studios alike. First, Disney is highlighted as a corporate success story: strong parks investment (notably Cars Land at California Adventure), robust merchandising, and blockbuster films like The Avengers have fuelled profit growth and elevated stock performance. Disney’s integrated model—studios, parks, TV, merchandise—rewards big franchise films that can spawn rides, shows and toys, making mid-range films harder to justify.

The longer piece documents the broader industry transformation over the past two decades. Mid-budget films (roughly $5–60 million) that supported auteur-driven dramas, comedies and experimental work have largely vanished from major studio slates. Rising production and especially marketing costs, the lure of enormous worldwide returns from tentpoles, and the collapse of DVD and ancillary revenue streams pushed studios to focus on fewer, bigger hits and left a crowded indie sector to absorb many smaller projects. Veteran filmmakers—John Waters, David Lynch, Francis Ford Coppola, Steven Soderbergh and others—find financing scarce; some can self-fund or shift to TV, where episodic prestige and new platforms offer storytelling opportunities and steadier budgets. The piece traces studio slates from 1997 to recent years, showing fewer titles and far more high-budget blockbusters, and argues this model yields profitability but less variety. Observers warn the blockbuster strategy is vulnerable to shifting tastes and market shocks; historically such crises have led to renewals of risk-taking. Meanwhile, many established auteurs have been sidelined or migrated to television, raising concerns about lost films and voices during this transitional period.

A former North Korean soldier, Lee So Yeon, has given detailed testimony about brutal conditions faced by women in the country’s armed forces, corroborated in part by researchers and other defectors. Serving nearly a decade, she described overcrowded concrete barracks, filthy rice-hull mattresses that trapped body odour, and inadequate washing facilities with no hot water—sometimes drawing water from mountain hoses contaminated with frogs and snakes. Malnutrition and stress were so severe that many female recruits stopped menstruating after months of service; sanitary provision was poor, forcing women to wash and reuse traditional cotton pads in secret. Daily routines reinforced gendered roles: women did slightly shorter physical training but were burdened with cooking and cleaning duties denied to men, reflecting entrenched patriarchal attitudes.

Sexual violence, Lee says, was widespread. While she did not report being raped herself, she alleges repeated assaults by commanders on lower-ranking women and recounts a culture of silence that leaves perpetrators unpunished despite official penalties for rape. Independent researchers Juliette Morillot and Jieun Baek note similar accounts from other female soldiers but caution that defector testimonies should be scrutinized and that demand for sensational stories can distort reporting. Still, they and other defectors report common harassment, lack of privacy—rural units often lack private toilets—and vulnerability of women from poor backgrounds housed in informal brigades.

Since 2015 North Korea made seven years’ military service mandatory for women and has announced distribution of premium sanitary and cosmetic products in some units, possibly as morale measures. Many women continue to defect—about 70% of North Korean defectors are female—often fleeing economic hardship and sexual abuse; those repatriated from China face imprisonment and further rights abuses. Lee eventually escaped to South Korea after multiple attempts and now speaks out about systemic violations of women’s dignity in the North Korean military.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has proposed removing the Oregon chub, a small minnow native to Oregon’s Willamette Valley, from Endangered Species Act protections — a milestone that would make it the first fish delisted for recovery. Listed as endangered in 1993 after widespread floodplain loss and predation by nonnative fish left fewer than 1,000 chubs in eight populations, the species benefited from a 1998 recovery plan emphasizing habitat restoration, monitoring, translocations, altered dam flows and partnerships with private landowners. Safe-harbor agreements reassured landowners that hosting chub would not restrict land use. Reclassified as threatened in 2010, the chub now numbers roughly 150,000–180,000 individuals across about 80 sites. The delisting proposal opens a 60-day public comment period and would be followed by nine years of post-delisting monitoring. Officials credit collaborative, locally tailored conservation efforts that were economically compatible with agriculture and development. The chub’s recovery also helped other species, such as salmon, pond turtles and red-legged frogs, recolonize restored habitats.

The first trailer for Peter Jackson’s The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey debuted, revealing several surprises. New, non-book material drawn from Tolkien’s wider works appears throughout, not just in the second film—Galadriel and a Mirkwood side-quest show up in the first. Visually, Middle-earth feels familiar and faithful, with Hobbiton, Bag End and returning actors reassuring fans. The dwarves read as proper dwarves in context, and Gollum’s cave is lit more than in the book to suit 3D. Tolkien-style songs, notably the full “Misty Mountains” lyrics, play a more prominent role.

Justice Clarence Thomas broke a decade-long silence at the Supreme Court by asking questions during oral argument for the first time since Feb. 22, 2006. His intervention came in Voisine v. United States, a challenge to the federal law that bars people convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence from possessing firearms. The case concerns whether convictions based on reckless conduct—rather than intentional acts—qualify as “misdemeanor crime[s] of domestic violence” triggering the lifetime gun prohibition imposed by a 1996 statute.

Thomas surprised courtroom observers when, late in the hour, he pressed the Justice Department attorney Ilana Eisenstein on whether any other misdemeanor violation leads to the suspension of a constitutional right, and how long such a suspension might last. He probed whether the suspension of Second Amendment rights was “directly related to the use of a weapon,” and asked whether the law would be clearer if the underlying offenses had involved guns. Eisenstein responded that the suspension can be indefinite and defended Congress’s intent to cover broadly worded state assault statutes—including those that encompass recklessness—because of the risk domestic abusers pose to family members.

Arguments for the petitioners, Stephen Voisine and William Armstrong III, who entered conditional guilty pleas to reckless domestic-assault charges, focused on whether recklessness meets the common-law battery standard Congress intended. Petitioners’ lawyer Virginia Villa argued that “use” implies intent; several justices, including Sotomayor and Kagan, questioned that narrow reading with hypotheticals illustrating how reckless acts can inflict harm akin to intentional violence.

Thomas’s rare questioning drew attention both because of its substance—probing constitutional implications of limiting gun rights—and because it coincided with the recent death of Justice Antonin Scalia, Thomas’s close friend and erstwhile vocal questioner. Observers noted Thomas has long said he prefers to rely on briefs and deliberations rather than interrupt oral argument, making Monday’s engagement notable amid continuing debate over the statute’s scope.

Flamingo Air, a small Cincinnati-based charter company, has quietly built a niche selling “romantic flights” that let consenting couples attempt to join the mile-high club. Founded after a dare by CEO David MacDonald, the service has operated for more than two decades and has helped thousands of couples book hour-long private flights—typically priced around $425–$495—complete with champagne, chocolates, cushions replacing center seats, and a discreet pilot up front. MacDonald insists the company markets romance rather than sex, avoiding the term “mile-high club” on its site and framing flights as tasteful, memorable experiences. That strategy appears to work: customers tend to be straightlaced, often older couples celebrating anniversaries or bucket-list items, and bookings spike around Valentine’s Day. Flamingo averages about three romantic flights per week and also runs a flight school and other aviation services. Competitor Love Cloud in Las Vegas follows a similar model; despite its brazen marketing, its clientele likewise skews toward real couples seeking a unique romantic adventure rather than hookups. Reports from passengers describe cramped quarters, turbulence, and practical hurdles—yet many value the novelty and the memory, receiving certificates after landing. Occasionally passengers book for nonsexual private time (e.g., parents wanting an hour alone). Flamingo’s success, MacDonald argues, stems from packaging the idea as classy and intimate rather than sleazy, turning what might seem like an illicit thrill into a legitimized, repeatable romantic experience.

Scientists have described Changyuraptor yangi, a 125-million-year-old, feathered, meat-eating dinosaur from Liaoning Province, China, that had unusually long tail feathers—the longest known for any dinosaur—measuring about 30 cm. Roughly 1.2–1.3 meters (about 4 feet) long and weighing near 4 kg (9 pounds), Changyuraptor belonged to the microraptorine group, a collection of “four-winged” theropods with large feathered surfaces on both forelimbs and hindlimbs. Its plumage and limb arrangement gave the appearance of two sets of wings; though not a bird, it was very bird-like and closely related to early avian ancestors such as Archaeopteryx. Bone microstructure shows the specimen was an adult. Researchers suggest Changyuraptor likely could not sustain powered flight like modern birds but could flap and perform primitive aerial locomotion—gliding or controlled descent—with its long tail feathers aiding in reducing descent speed and ensuring safer landings. Feathers may also have served display and species-recognition roles. The fossil adds to growing evidence from Liaoning that many dinosaurs bore feathers and illuminates evolutionary links between non-avian dinosaurs and birds.

A coalition of more than three dozen tech and clean‑energy leaders, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, has urged the California Air Resources Board (CARB) to shift Volkswagen’s post‑scandal obligations away from repairing diesel cars and toward rapidly accelerating Volkswagen’s transition to zero‑emission vehicles (ZEVs). Their argument rests on technical and practical grounds: modern diesel engines are at the limits of physics and cost‑effectiveness for cutting pollutants, making many noncompliant vehicles effectively unfixable without large performance, CO2, or economic tradeoffs. Retrofitting small cars with urea systems is impractical and costly; many vehicles may be scrapped before their useful life ends, wasting vast sums on marginal or counterproductive fixes.

Instead of mandating comprehensive recalls and repairs, the signatories propose a legally enforceable alternative package. Key elements include releasing VW from the obligation to repair cars already in California, requiring VW to dramatically accelerate ZEV rollout to achieve at least a ten‑to‑one reduction in pollutants over five years relative to emissions from the cheating diesel fleet, and directing VW to invest in U.S. manufacturing plants and R&D—particularly in California—to the tune of fines it would otherwise pay. The plan would allow flexibility through ZEV credits and prioritizes building battery factories to overcome supply bottlenecks. The authors argue this approach would yield greater emissions reductions, more California jobs, and a more durable climate benefit than costly diesel fixes, while avoiding ongoing enforcement costs and the risk of future test‑cheating.

A Queensland student, 16-year-old Kyle Thomson, was suspended after a sandwich was thrown at Prime Minister Julia Gillard during a visit to Marsden State High School. Kyle phoned B105 radio during a DisabilityCare announcement to protest his innocence, insisting he was wrongly blamed. He and his mother, Anna Thomson, say Kyle knocked the sandwich out of another student’s hand to stop a second throw and was suspended without full investigation. School officials named him as the lone hurler and imposed a three-week suspension; Kyle and his family argue circumstances were misrepresented and call for further inquiry. Ms Gillard laughed off the incident on air, expressing sympathy but declining to intervene in school disciplinary decisions and urging Kyle to speak with the principal. Radio hosts and social media amplified the story with jokes and conspiracy theories—some claiming a second thrower, debate over whether the sandwich was Vegemite or chicken, and labels like “#sandwichgate.” The episode dominated headlines despite occurring on a day when Queensland and the federal government reached a bipartisan DisabilityCare agreement, leaving unanswered questions about what really happened.

The FBI’s annual Hate Crime Statistics report shows a roughly 17% rise in reported hate crimes in 2017, with law enforcement agencies submitting 7,175 incidents to the Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program, up from 6,121 in 2016. Part of the increase reflects broader participation, with about 1,000 more agencies reporting. Of the 7,106 single-bias incidents, most involved race/ethnicity/ancestry (59.6%), followed by religion (20.6%) and sexual orientation (15.8%); 69 incidents involved multiple biases. Approximately 5,000 incidents were crimes against persons (e.g., intimidation, assault) and about 3,000 were crimes against property (e.g., vandalism, robbery), with some incidents counted in both categories. To improve reporting and identification of bias-motivated crimes, the FBI will provide law enforcement training and the Justice Department launched a dedicated hate crimes webpage. The FBI emphasizes that hate crimes are a top civil rights investigative priority, and better reporting helps communities, researchers, and agencies develop targeted prevention strategies.

At the Malaysian Government’s request, Australia has taken responsibility for the underwater search for Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370, with the Australian Transport Safety Bureau leading operations in the southern Indian Ocean. The Joint Agency Coordination Centre (JACC) issues regular operational updates to report progress, noting searches are methodical and can appear slow. Fugro Equator has been conducting seabed searches using an Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV), completing five missions in the most recent week though operations have been delayed at times by weather affecting AUV recovery and maintenance. Fugro Equator is undertaking its final survey passes and collecting sonar data over previously uncompleted areas; these operations were expected to finish in January 2017. Ministers from Malaysia, Australia and China agreed on 22 July 2016 that if the aircraft is not found within the agreed search area, and no credible new evidence identifies a specific location, the search would be suspended after completing that area—not definitively terminated—pending any new credible information. Separate incidents have hampered the hunt: a towed sonar vehicle (“towfish”) struck a 2,200-meter-high mud volcano, causing its cable to break and the towfish plus 4.5 km of cable to fall to the ocean floor; officials said recovery may be possible and a spare towfish was readied. Another vessel, Havila Harmony, sustained damage to an underwater communications pole and underwent repairs. To date, just over 70% of the internationally agreed 46,000-square-mile search zone has been covered; only one confirmed aircraft piece, a flaperon found on Reunion Island, has been recovered. The search was projected to continue into mid-2017 unless credible new evidence emerges.

The South African government has begun seizing land where negotiations have stalled, targeting two Limpopo game farms after offering owners a fraction of their asking price. Akkerland Boerdery sought 200 million rand but was offered 20 million; a notice ordered an inspection and handover, prompting the owners to obtain a court injunction against eviction while the Department of Rural Development and Land Affairs opposes their application. The move is part of a broader push to speed land reform and to test legal grounds for expropriation without full market compensation under “public interest” provisions, ahead of planned constitutional amendments. The ANC says such measures address past injustices and will create policy certainty to attract investment, while unions and farm groups say due process was denied in some cases. Civil-rights group Afriforum published a purported list of targeted farms and urged owners to seek legal help; the department called the list fake, and critics accused Afriforum of fearmongering. The controversy has unsettled farmers and investors, with some reporting falling land values and canceled sales, amid ongoing national debates over redress, economic risk, and the speed and fairness of land redistribution.

A string of recent school disciplinary actions highlights how strict “zero tolerance” policies can sweep up very young students and lead to lasting consequences. In Colorado, six-year-old Elijah Thurston was suspended from Stratton Meadows Elementary for one day after he reportedly pointed his finger in a “gun shape” at a classmate and said, “You’re dead.” School staff explained the meaning of “dead” to Elijah and told him not to confuse play with reality. Elijah’s father, Austin Thurston, called a one-day suspension excessive for a first grader, suggesting a loss of recess or another mild consequence would have been more appropriate. The Harrison School District 2 defended the suspension as appropriate and said it will remain on Elijah’s permanent record; the district declined further comment citing student privacy. Elijah is writing an apologetic letter to the school—an action his parents said was voluntary—and his family says they have already discussed gun safety and context with him.

A separate Virginia case shows a similar pattern with older students. Parents Bruce and Linda Bays filed suit after their 11-year-old son, identified as RMB, was suspended, expelled for a year, and charged after school staff found leaves and a lighter in his backpack. Field tests later showed the plant was not marijuana. The school nevertheless relied on its zero-tolerance policy, which bans lookalike drugs, and the student was placed in an alternative school under probation. His parents allege the material may have been planted by older students and say the ordeal precipitated emotional problems; they seek his return to the original school and expungement of records.

Both incidents illustrate tension between school safety aims and proportional responses—especially for young children—and raise questions about privacy, due process, and the long-term effects of punitive disciplinary policies on students’ records and wellbeing.

A man who heckled Bristol Palin at a Sunset Strip bar in September 2011 has sued her and Lifetime/A&E for defamation, invasion of privacy and emotional distress. Talent manager Stephen Hanks filed the federal suit in Los Angeles claiming he never consented to being filmed by the reality TV crew and that Palin later blamed him in a magazine interview for her decision to leave Los Angeles and move back to Alaska. Hanks says that claim was false because Palin had already purchased a home in Alaska two months before the bar incident, and that her public statements damaged his reputation and career. Video of the encounter shows Hanks calling Palin’s mother “a whore,” Palin asking if he was gay, and a heated exchange. Hanks also objects to Palin’s public suggestion about his sexuality and to the footage’s use in publicity for her upcoming Lifetime series, Life’s a Tripp, which premieres June 19. Damages sought were unspecified but reported to exceed $75,000.

Bill O’Reilly announced he is taking a preplanned vacation from The O’Reilly Factor and will return April 24, a break he said he booked last fall for spring and Easter. The announcement came amid a wave of advertiser defections after a New York Times report that five women received roughly $13 million in settlements over sexual harassment allegations against him. Kantar Media analysis showed paid advertising time on his show dropped by more than half following the Times story. Despite the boycott, O’Reilly remained a ratings draw: his show averaged about 3.7 million viewers over five nights the previous week, up 12 percent from the week before and up 28 percent year-over-year. For the first quarter of 2017 the program averaged just under 4 million viewers, its best quarter in 20 years.

Speculation swirled that the vacation could function as a de facto suspension. New York magazine’s Gabriel Sherman, citing unnamed network sources, reported internal talk that the episode might be O’Reilly’s last, and said James Murdoch favors removing him while Rupert and Lachlan Murdoch are more hesitant. Fox responded that the vacation was planned and reaffirmed O’Reilly’s return date. Meanwhile, lawyers from Paul, Weiss—who investigated Roger Ailes—were reported to be conducting a deeper review into allegations, including claims from guest Wendy Walsh submitted via Fox’s anonymous hotline. With more than three dozen advertisers having pulled support, some Fox staffers expected O’Reilly’s eventual exit could be arranged during his time off to minimize embarrassment.

A series of small, low‑intensity bombs exploded at and around the Mahabodhi (Bodh Gaya) temple complex in Bihar, India, injuring two people and damaging windows and a door but not the temple or the sacred Bodhi tree. Four of the eight confirmed blasts occurred inside the UNESCO World Heritage site; others struck nearby holy locations. Police called the incidents a terror attack; no group claimed responsibility, though suspicion fell on the Indian Mujahideen, blamed for past bombings. Prime Minister Manmohan Singh condemned the strikes. Attacks on Buddhists are uncommon in India, though regional communal tensions have risen.

A temporary ceasefire between Israel and Gaza militants collapsed as rockets from Gaza — some reaching Tel Aviv and Jerusalem — prompted Israeli air strikes. Negotiations in Cairo to secure a longer truce ended without agreement, with both sides blaming each other: Palestinian negotiators accused Israel of sabotaging talks, while Israel cited renewed rocket fire as undermining the process. The monthlong offensive has killed about 2,016 Palestinians, mostly civilians, and 66–67 Israelis. Key disputes include disarmament demands, lifting Gaza’s blockade, and reconstruction measures.

A new report from the London-based European Leadership Network warns that intensified Russian and NATO military exercises are fueling tensions in Europe and increasing the risk of accidental confrontation. Both sides insist drills are defensive, but the scale, scope and focus of recent maneuvers suggest each is training with the other’s capabilities and likely war plans in mind. Russia staged unannounced snap drills in March involving some 80,000 personnel across the Arctic, Baltic, Black Sea and Pacific theatres, employing strategic bombers, airborne landings, naval missile firings and live-fire ground operations. NATO has responded with sizable exercises—BALTOPS, Saber Strike, Allied Shield and others—bringing thousands of troops, ships, aircraft and high-readiness forces into eastern Europe and the Baltic region. The ELN report cautions that, even without any deliberate intent to go to war, the changed profile of exercises sustains a climate of fear and mistrust and elevates unpredictability, particularly when drills are not pre-notified as has occurred with many Russian exercises. Near-misses, including close encounters between Russian aircraft and civilian airliners, illustrate the dangers of frayed communications. The ELN recommends improved communications and prior notifications between Russia and NATO, limits on exercises near borders, and renewed arms-control dialogue to reduce escalation risk. NATO counters that Russia’s exercises are far larger, sometimes nuclear-capable, and that Moscow avoids transparency; Russia objects to NATO’s eastward posture and cites alliance expansion as a security threat. The dynamic is described as dangerous, and with neither side likely to back down soon, the risk of miscalculation remains elevated.

At the 2015 Emmy Awards, a televised montage celebrating recently ended series sparked widespread viewer anger by including key scenes from finales of shows like Mad Men, Boardwalk Empire, Nurse Jackie and Sons of Anarchy. Many fans took to Twitter to condemn the ceremony for spoiling endings they hadn’t seen, calling the segment “brutal” and criticizing producers’ judgment. Host Andy Samberg acknowledged the backlash onstage, jokingly dubbing the event the “Spoiler Awards” and referencing his pre-recorded bit about locking himself in a bunker to binge shows. Some defended the montage, noting most of the series concluded months earlier and had been widely discussed online, but others maintained they deserved the chance to watch without foreknowledge. The controversy accompanied other highlights of the night, including Jon Hamm’s long-awaited acting win.

President Trump responded to Doug Jones’s upset victory over Republican Roy Moore in Alabama’s special Senate election by saying he had been right to initially back Luther Strange, whom he claimed would have fared better in a general election. Trump noted he had urged Strange early on because “Roy Moore will not be able to win the General Election,” then later endorsed Moore, recording a robocall and holding a rally for him after allegations of sexual misconduct emerged. Moore, a twice-removed former Alabama Supreme Court chief justice, faced accusations of molesting teenage girls decades earlier; he denied them. Jones’s win — the first Democrat elected to the Alabama Senate in 25 years — narrows the GOP Senate majority to 51-49 and prompted Republicans including Sen. Lindsey Graham to suggest Trump’s instincts favored Strange. Critics from across the spectrum credited mobilized women and African-American voters; Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand framed the result as a rebuke of Trump’s tone, while Joe Biden praised Jones and said Senate Republicans likely felt relief at avoiding association with Moore. Media figures like Matt Drudge argued Strange would have won handily, lamenting the “crazy” candidacy that cost the GOP the seat.

German authorities responded to a bomb threat that forced the cancellation of a Germany-Netherlands friendly in Hanover, prompting heavy policing and national debate over transparency and security. Interior Minister Thomas de Maizière faced criticism for withholding details, accused by opposition figures of stoking fear by secrecy. Officials said no explosives were found and no arrests made; state leaders declared no ongoing specific threat to Hanover. Intelligence chief Hans-Georg Maaßen warned Isis views Germany as a target and the overall threat level is high. Measures include stepped-up security at Christmas markets and continued policing at major events; the Bundesliga will proceed with added precautions. Separately, Turkey arrested eight suspects allegedly bound for Germany, and reports suggest Berlin-born rapper-turned-Isis member Denis Cuspert may still be alive despite US claims. Chancellor Merkel praised calm public response and security services.

In late July at the Devil’s Place whisky bar in the Waldhaus am See hotel in St Moritz, a Chinese guest paid about CHF10,000 (roughly $10,000/£7,600) for a small pour reportedly from the last unopened bottle of Macallan 1878. The dram, purchased by bestselling fantasy author Zhang Wei, made headlines as possibly the world’s most expensive poured whisky. Soon after, whisky collectors and experts raised doubts about the bottle’s provenance, citing anomalies in the label wording, the condition and artificial aging of the cork, and historical inconsistencies—such as a non-existent company name linking Macallan and Talisker and details that did not match known Macallan archive records.

The hotel launched an investigation and sent a sample to Rare Whisky 101 (RW101) and other specialists in Scotland. Forensic analysis, including carbon dating by researchers at Oxford’s archaeology lab, indicated with 95% probability that the liquid was distilled between 1970 and 1972, not in the 19th century. Additional lab work by Tatlock & Thomson suggested the spirit was likely a blended Scotch (about 60% malt, 40% grain), disqualifying it as a single malt Macallan 1878. RW101 concluded the bottle was almost worthless as a collector’s item.

Hotel manager Sandro Bernasconi—whose father had acquired the bottle decades earlier—accepted the findings, flew to Beijing, and reimbursed Zhang in full, apologizing and saying the hotel would help publicize the fraud if confirmed. Macallan owner Edrington and RW101 urged buyers to authenticate rare bottles, employ technical testing where feasible, and raise awareness to combat sophisticated counterfeiters circulating fake vintage whiskies.

South Korea and Japan reached a landmark agreement to resolve the decades-long dispute over “comfort women,” the Korean and other Asian women forced into sexual slavery by Japan’s Imperial Army during World War II. Announced after talks between the countries’ foreign ministers in Seoul, the deal includes a formal apology from Japan, expressed by Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and Foreign Minister Fumio Kishida, and a Japanese government-funded payment of about 1 billion yen ($8.3 million) to a South Korean-administered fund for the surviving victims. Both governments described the accord as a “final and irreversible” resolution provided all promises are fulfilled.

The agreement aims to ease a major source of bilateral tension that has hindered security cooperation between two key U.S. allies in East Asia. U.S. and U.N. officials welcomed the pact as a step toward reconciliation and improved trilateral cooperation given regional threats from North Korea. The fund is intended to support healing, restore dignity, and finance projects for survivors; it is not framed as direct government compensation to individuals, a point that left some survivors dissatisfied. Only a few dozen of the original petitioners remain, with an average age near 89, adding urgency to resolving the issue.

The accord also includes mutual commitments to refrain from criticizing each other internationally over the matter and a South Korean pledge to discuss the contentious “comfort women” statue near the Japanese embassy. While seen by leaders as opening a new era of relations, critics and some survivors question whether the measures fully meet demands for formal, direct redress.

Hostess Brands, maker of Twinkies, Wonder Bread and other iconic snacks, told a federal bankruptcy court it will liquidate and close operations after a bakers’ strike over a court-imposed contract. The shutdown affects nearly 18,500 workers, closing 33 bakeries, 565 distribution centers and 570 outlet stores; about 5,000 employees were represented by the Bakery, Confectionery, Tobacco Workers and Grain Millers union. CEO Gregory Rayburn said the company lacked resources to endure an extended strike. Hostess, which filed for bankruptcy in January and is controlled by investment firms including Silver Point Capital and Monarch Alternative Capital, will seek to sell its assets, potentially allowing brands to live on under new owners, though original workers likely will not be rehired. The union blamed management and investors for failures despite workers’ concessions; earlier the Teamsters accepted cuts. Hostess had annual sales around $2.5 billion and produced hundreds of millions of Twinkies and loaves of bread yearly. Remaining in-store products will be sold while production has halted.

About 10,000 people fled across the Thai border after heavy fighting on Monday between Myanmar government forces and a breakaway faction of the Democratic Karen Buddhist Army (DKBA) around the border town of Myawaddy, opposite Mae Sot, Thailand. Myanmar troops reportedly retook the town after reinforcements; at least three people were killed and around ten wounded on both sides, and shells and a stray RPG injured civilians in Thailand. The DKBA split, opposing forced voting and perceived coercion by the junta during Myanmar’s first national election in 20 years, and seized local posts in protest. The vote, widely condemned as neither free nor transparent, drew international criticism and reinforced fears of renewed ethnic conflict and a refugee crisis on Thailand’s border.

A Senate Commerce Committee report and hearings have exposed the extensive, invasive practices of the multibillion-dollar data-broker industry. After probing nine major firms and hearing privacy groups, the Committee found that brokers compile vast consumer profiles and sell deeply personal data — including lists identifying rape victims, people with HIV/AIDS, seniors with dementia, and those with addictions. Companies market highly specific information such as diagnoses, medications, purchases (from soft drinks to yeast infection products), credit scores, travel miles, OB/GYN visits, and even the number of alcoholic drinks consumed. Some brokers, like Equifax, cooperated with the Committee and detailed more than 75,000 data attributes they track; others, including Acxiom, Experian, and Epsilon, refused to disclose sources or buyers, claiming contractual confidentiality. Investigations have linked sold data to alleged identity theft rings and revealed that sensitive or dangerous lists (e.g., police home addresses, domestic violence shelter contacts) are traded. Current federal privacy protections apply mainly to credit, employment, insurance, and housing uses; medical privacy laws don’t cover data gleaned from purchases. Privacy advocates and Sen. Jay Rockefeller urged stronger regulation and transparency, warning that unchecked data sales put vulnerable people at risk.

President Trump, speaking from his Turnberry golf club in Scotland ahead of a high-stakes summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin, described the European Union as one of America’s “foes,” citing trade grievances and what he called unfair economic treatment by EU members. In a CBS interview with Jeff Glor, Trump listed several rivals—China economically, Russia in “certain respects”—but emphasized that “foe” simply meant competitive, not morally bad. He reiterated complaints from the recent NATO summit, where he pressured allied states over defense spending and criticized Germany for the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline with Russia, saying it left Germany paying “billions” to a country the West is supposed to guard against and accusing Germany of effectively “waving a white flag.” German Chancellor Angela Merkel pushed back, asserting Germany makes independent policy choices and recalling her experience under Soviet control.

Trump also attacked the special counsel’s Russia investigation as a “witch hunt” that harms U.S. relationships internationally and expressed frustration about what he called partisan behavior by investigators. He said he had “low expectations” for his meeting with Putin but hoped “maybe some good will come out.” Separately, highlights from a Piers Morgan interview in the Daily Mail covered topics ranging from Roe v. Wade and Brett Kavanaugh to Trump’s meeting with Queen Elizabeth II, his defense of immigration enforcement and family separation policies, and his prolific, hands-on use of Twitter. The visits and remarks have strained ties with close U.S. allies and fueled public protests in the U.K., including the high-profile “Trump Baby” balloon demonstrations.

President Obama warned Afghan President Hamid Karzai that he’s ordered the Pentagon to plan for a complete U.S. troop withdrawal from Afghanistan by year’s end if Afghanistan does not sign a bilateral security agreement (BSA). Obama told Karzai the U.S. is preparing contingency plans because Karzai has delayed signing the pact that would permit a limited post-2014 U.S. mission to train, advise and assist Afghan forces and pursue remaining al-Qaida elements. White House press secretary Jay Carney and Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel confirmed planning for the “zero option,” stressing that without a BSA U.S. troops will not remain beyond Dec. 31. The administration says allied contributions and legal protections for troops hinge on a BSA; domestic lawmakers likewise insist on a signed agreement before supporting any post-2014 presence. Concerns remain about Afghan forces’ long-term sustainment and risks of security vacuums.

U.S. and Canadian fighter jets intercepted multiple Russian military aircraft near North American airspace this week, officials said. Two Alaskan-based F-22s scrambled Wednesday evening intercepted six Russian planes—identified as two IL-78 refueling tankers, two MiG-31 fighters and two Tu-95 “Bear” long-range bombers—about 55 nautical miles off Alaska’s western coast after they entered the Air Defense Identification Zone (ADIZ). The Russian formation looped south and returned to base without incident. More than six hours later, two Canadian CF-18s intercepted two Tu-95 bombers in the Beaufort Sea about 40 nautical miles off Canada’s coastline; those aircraft also had entered the Canadian ADIZ but did not cross into sovereign airspace. NORAD emphasized such intercepts are not uncommon, occurring up to 10 times a year and more than 50 times in the past five years for Russian bombers approaching North America. U.S. officials suggested the activity may have been linked to Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko’s visit and contacts with U.S. and Canadian leaders; the U.S. recently pledged non-lethal aid to Ukraine. Separately, Sweden reported two Russian military aircraft crossed into its airspace near the island of Öland, calling it a “serious violation” and summoning the Russian ambassador.

Pentagon documents and reporting reveal a long-running Office of Net Assessment (ONA) project, called Body Leads, that analyzes leaders’ body movements to infer decision-making styles and predict actions. Using movement pattern analysis—an approach originating with Rudolf Laban and expanded by Warren Lamb that treats an individual’s movement “signature” as revealing cognitive and motivational patterns—the program has examined more than a dozen foreign leaders, including Vladimir Putin in reports from 2008 and 2012. ONA has funded Brenda Connors and outside specialists such as Warren Lamb (paid in 2011), Richard Rende, and Harvard’s Timothy Colton; since 2009 roughly $300,000 a year has gone to contractors working on the effort. Connors and collaborators published on movement analysis and decision-making in Frontiers in Psychology, arguing the method offers a unique window on leaders’ choices. Pentagon spokesmen say the reports reside within ONA and have not driven Defense Department policy; Adm. John Kirby said the studies won’t be released publicly. The work has drawn attention amid the 2014 Crimea crisis as U.S. officials seek any tool to anticipate Putin’s actions. ONA, led for decades by Andrew Marshall, operates with wide latitude on future-focused strategic research.

An Indiana man’s simple selfie with a state trooper has sparked a national conversation about respect and policing after his Facebook post went viral with hundreds of thousands of shares. Greg Barnes Jr. of Muncie was pulled over for speeding on State Road 332. Recognizing he was in the wrong, Barnes cooperated; the trooper issued a warning. After exchanging small talk and discussing their days, the two began a deeper conversation about tense, sometimes deadly, interactions between police and civilians across the country. Moved by the respectful tone of their exchange, Barnes asked Trooper Shawn Cosgrove to take a selfie to show children and others that not all police encounters are negative.

Barnes posted the photo with a message emphasizing mutual respect: neither the officer nor Barnes knew each other beforehand, yet they treated one another with dignity. He wrote that they “thanked each other for our mutual displays of respect” and agreed to the selfie to “help tell our story.” His post urged people to stop viewing one another strictly by race or profession — “not as ‘black man’ and ‘blue police officer,’ but as humans” — and closed with the hashtag #Respect. Cosgrove said he agreed to the photo because of its purpose, calling it a meaningful moment amid nationwide tensions over policing. Both men noted that respect eased the interaction; while it won’t guarantee leniency every time, it can make stops less adversarial. Their encounter and the viral post have been praised as a small but powerful example of how civility and mutual understanding can bridge divides and reshape narratives around law enforcement and community relations.

In January 2014 Elysse and John Eric Mata of Lubbock learned during a routine ultrasound that Elysse was carrying twins — and that the girls were conjoined. The twins, Knatalye Hope and Adeline Faith, were born April 11 at 31 weeks via C-section at Texas Children’s Pavilion for Women, each weighing about 3 pounds, 7 ounces. They were joined at the chest and abdomen and shared multiple structures including portions of the liver, diaphragm, pericardial sac, intestines and some lung tissue. After birth they were cared for in the Level IV NICU at Texas Children’s Hospital, where a multidisciplinary team managed their complex needs while preparing for eventual separation.

Medical teams spent months on detailed planning: extensive prenatal imaging, development of 3‑D organ models, simulations of the separation procedure, and a preparatory operation in December 2014 to place custom tissue expanders in the twins’ chest and abdomen to generate sufficient skin for coverage after separation. Doctors planned the definitive separation when the infants grew bigger and stronger to reduce risk, accepting that the surgery would still carry potential life‑threatening complications.

On Feb. 17, 2015 a large multidisciplinary surgical team performed the separation. The operation lasted about 18 hours to reach official separation, with surgeons working roughly 23 hours on Knatalye and 26 hours on Adeline. Specialists across pediatric surgery, plastic surgery, cardiovascular surgery, urology, liver transplant, orthopedics and pediatric gynecology participated, alongside numerous anesthesiologists and nurses. The team successfully separated the twins — a first for thoraco-omphalo-ischiopagus twins with this organ-sharing configuration — and both girls were transferred to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit for months of recovery. Physicians expect additional reconstructive and corrective surgeries in the future. The Mata family expressed deep gratitude for the surgical team and for the support and prayers received during the ten months of planning, care and recovery.

Sixteen-year-old Oscar nominee Abigail Breslin has released her first music track, “Westfjords,” a twangy indie collaboration with songwriter Teddy Watson and band Stargroves.
