Credited on the 2012 recording, Breslin provides vocals alongside Watson (vocals, banjo guitar), with Enrico de Trizio (keys), Charlie Rauh (electric guitar), Bryan Percivall (bass) and Andrea Belfiore (drums). The song was produced at Threshold Recording Studios by Jeremy Sklarsky and mastered by Fred Kevorkian. Lyrics evoke carnival imagery, highland trolls, and seaside farewells. The release follows a tradition of actors pursuing music: Ryan Gosling’s Dead Man’s Bones, Michael Cera’s Mister Heavenly and Christopher Mintz-Plasse’s Young Rapscallions are cited as similar actor-musician ventures. Links to Stargroves’ site and social pages accompany the track.

In her first network interview since Heath Ledger’s 2007 death, Michelle Williams appears happier and professionally thriving—promoting Blue Valentine and reflecting on work with Ryan Gosling—yet she still cannot find meaning in Ledger’s death. Williams says she’s “found meanings around the circumstance” but not in the actual event, admitting she “can’t find a meaning for it.” She describes a prolonged struggle with how quickly life can change and recalls a period of “magical thinking” when she imagined Ledger might reappear; she even misses that year’s strange possibilities. A comforting book line—“when you’ve truly lost everything, then at least you can become rich in loss”—helped her cope. Gosling praises their creative partnership, joking about perceptions of their relationship.

New research from Spanish scientists, published in Nature, suggests lethal interpersonal violence has deep evolutionary roots but is heavily shaped by social and environmental factors. The team analyzed causes of death across more than 1,000 mammal species (over 4 million individual records) and archaeological and ethnographic data from roughly 600 human populations, including Stone Age remains. They found that closely related species tend to have similar rates of killing their own kind: mammals average about 3 lethal killings per 1,000 deaths, while primate and ape lineages show substantially higher rates. Statistical reconstructions place the ancestor of great apes at roughly 18 deaths per 1,000 from conspecific violence and estimate about 20 per 1,000 (around 2%) for the earliest humans — more than six times the mammalian baseline.

Authors caution that this 2% is not a genetic attribution alone: inherited ecological conditions and social organization also influence violence. The study shows historical fluctuation: prehistoric hunter-gatherers approximate the 2% estimate, violence rose in eras like the Iron Age and parts of the medieval period, and contemporary global rates have fallen below that level — World Health Organization data suggest modern humans average about 13 per 1,000. Prominent scholars reacted divergently: Steven Pinker praised the rigor and argued the findings support his thesis that civilization and institutions reduce innate violent tendencies, while others, like Douglas Fry and Richard Wrangham, warn against overgeneralizing or conflating infant-directed primate killings with adult-targeted human violence.

Overall, the study argues humans inherited a propensity for lethal conflict from a violent primate lineage but emphasizes reversibility: social structures, governance, and cultural choices can significantly raise or lower rates of lethal interpersonal violence, meaning societies can intentionally reduce such deaths.

Yahoo announced it will free up Yahoo IDs that have been inactive for at least 12 months, allowing anyone to claim those email addresses. Beginning mid-July, users can attempt to reserve preferred Yahoo IDs; by mid-August, those who staked claims can see which addresses they received. Yahoo frames the move as an opportunity to give users shorter, more memorable addresses and to reengage dormant accounts, warning users who want to keep an old ID to log into any Yahoo product before July 15.

Security and privacy concerns, however, have been raised. Critics warn releasing inactive addresses could enable account takeovers and social engineering: attackers might claim an unused Yahoo address that was linked to other services (for password resets or account recovery), then use it to access active email, banking, or social accounts. Dormant service registrations—such as old Flickr accounts—could help attackers discover targets. Wired sought comment, and Yahoo responded with a corporate statement expressing confidence that the transition can be made securely while promoting renewed engagement with Yahoo services.

In the third quarter of 2015, Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign raised just over $28 million, narrowly outperforming Bernie Sanders, who pulled in roughly $25–26 million. The close margin highlighted Sanders’ surprising fundraising strength and growing momentum — he overtook Clinton in some New Hampshire and Iowa polls — despite relying largely on small online donations and very few in-person fundraisers. Clinton’s strong institutional operation remains significant: her campaign’s third-quarter haul brought her six-month total to about $75 million after $47.5 million in Q2, and affiliated super PACs such as Priorities USA Action reported substantial sums (about $40 million by mid‑August). Clinton’s team expected a summer dip amid scrutiny over her email practices and fading early-state polls; 93 percent of her Q3 donations were under $100, and her joint fundraising committee with the DNC and state parties raised over $3 million.

Sanders, however, demonstrated remarkable grassroots reach: his campaign announced it exceeded one million individual online contributions in Q3 and reported dramatic single-day receipts, including $2.07 million online on Sept. 30. Sanders’ campaign reported roughly $25 million cash on hand after raising $15 million in Q2. His refusal to use super PACs contrasts with Clinton’s access to big‑donor networks, raising questions about general-election viability but undermining assumptions that he couldn’t muster competitive fundraising. Full disclosure filings for the quarter, to be released soon, will be examined for donor sources and spending patterns.

Hendrix, a six-year-old English Springer Spaniel, was mistakenly loaded onto a United Airlines flight from Newark to Shannon, Ireland instead of Phoenix. The airline discovered the error and arranged for Hendrix to be returned, walking and feeding him while he awaited reunification with his family in Newark before finally arriving in Phoenix Friday night. Owner Meredith Grant and her mother expressed distress and frustration, saying they wanted acknowledgment of the mistake and consequences for those responsible; United apologized and offered a full refund.

Amazon’s new $59.99 AmazonBasics Microwave is a straightforward 700W countertop microwave that also serves as a showcase for Amazon’s Alexa Connection Kit — a small, low-cost module that lets appliance makers add Alexa control to everyday devices. The microwave itself is unremarkable hardware: black, boxy, with a rotating tray, vents, and basic controls. It lacks built-in microphones or a speaker beyond a beep, so it doesn’t function like an Echo device. Instead, it pairs with your existing Alexa system and appears in the Alexa app as “the microwave,” letting you use voice commands through your Echo speakers.

Interaction is centered on a single Alexa button on the unit. Pressing it tells a nearby Echo to listen without the wake word and places your next voice input in the microwave’s context — for example, “stop” will halt cooking. Presets and quick-cook settings are stored in Amazon’s cloud, reducing on-device buttons. A highlighted novelty is the popcorn feature: you can subscribe to have microwave popcorn reordered automatically based on how often you say “Alexa, make popcorn,” and there’s also a popcorn button on the microwave.

The product ships November 14 and is meant less to impress consumers with radical hardware than to demonstrate how simple, secure, and inexpensive Amazon’s module makes adding Alexa to appliances. By offering this plug-and-play solution, Amazon aims to accelerate Alexa integration across many low-cost devices and further entrench itself as the central smart-home hub.

Internal emails from Miss America Organization leaders revealed sustained vulgar, misogynistic and fat-shaming commentary about former Miss Americas, prompting an investigation, suspensions and multiple resignations. The emails—reviewed by HuffPost and later published—showed CEO Sam Haskell, board members Tammy Haddad and Lynn Weidner, and telecast writer Lewis Friedman exchanging crude insults, joking about renaming past winners “cunts,” and privately disparaging titleholders such as Mallory Hagan, Kate Shindle and Gretchen Carlson. Messages included suggestions to ostracize critics, to investigate them, and even to undermine Hagan’s coaching business; sources say some of the actions contributed to lost opportunities for her. Haskell, credited with restoring Miss America to broadcast TV and Atlantic City and earning $500,000 annually, defended himself saying the emails were stolen and mischaracterized; Friedman was later let go. The revelations led Dick Clark Productions to resign its board seats and end its production deal, and triggered a public outcry from former Miss Americas demanding accountability. Haskell was suspended and then resigned; Weidner, president/COO Josh Randle and others also stepped down or offered resignations amid the probe. The organization says it has launched an in-depth investigation and will adopt new communication policies while pledging renewed commitment to empowering young women.

In a New Albany debate, Republican Senate candidate Richard Mourdock stirred controversy by saying pregnancies resulting from rape are "something that God intended to happen," while asserting his belief that "life begins at conception." Mourdock, a Tea Party-backed primary victor over Richard Lugar, opposes abortion except when the mother's life is at risk. Democrats and some Republicans condemned his remarks; challenger Democrat Joe Donnelly, who supports exceptions for rape and incest, called the comment shocking and disrespectful to survivors. Mourdock later attempted to clarify, saying he meant only that "God creates life" and denied believing God preordained rape. The gaffe drew comparisons to earlier GOP misstatements on rape and pregnancy, prompted distancing from Mitt Romney’s campaign, and intensified attention on the closely watched Indiana Senate race ahead of the November election.

A Texas Policy Evaluation Project (TxPEP) report finds that between 100,000 and 240,000 Texas women ages 18–49 have attempted to self-induce abortions, based on a 2014–2015 survey of nearly 800 women. The study estimates 1.7% of respondents said they had tried to self-induce, and 4.1% knew or suspected a close friend had done so. TxPEP’s researchers link these attempts to the dramatic reduction in clinic access since Texas enacted restrictive abortion laws like HB2 in 2013, which forced the closure of more than half the state’s 41 clinics. The researchers and advocates warn the tightening of restrictions appears to be driving a rise in self-induced abortion attempts, echoing prior studies that found increases in self-induction after new limits were imposed.

Two groups showed higher prevalence: Latina women living in counties bordering Mexico—rural regions that have experienced multiple clinic closures—and women who reported difficulty accessing reproductive health care. The report identifies the primary methods women used: home remedies (herbs, teas, vitamins) and medications, chiefly misoprostol procured without prescription in Mexico. While clinicians note that misoprostol alone can cause a complete abortion, women reported widely varying dosing and administration, intense cramping and bleeding, and uncertainty about whether symptoms were normal, raising safety concerns.

Financial barriers, clinic closures, recommendations from friends or family, and fear of stigma were cited as main reasons for self-induction, with poverty commonly compounding these obstacles. Dr. Daniel Grossman, a study co-author, argued that laws like HB2 harm women—especially women of color and low-income women—by increasing risk. Amy Hagstrom Miller of Whole Woman’s Health affirmed the rise in DIY abortions and emphasized the need for safe, accessible care regardless of a woman’s zip code. The study underscores the public-health implications of restricting clinic access and highlights gaps in safe, supervised abortion care.

Hassan Mustafa Osama Nasr, known as Abu Omar, has publicly defended Sabrina De Sousa, a former CIA officer facing extradition from Portugal to Italy over her 2003 role in his abduction in Milan. Abu Omar told the Guardian he views De Sousa and other convicted operatives as scapegoats, arguing that more senior officials who authorized the CIA’s “extraordinary rendition” program enjoy immunity while lower-level participants are punished. De Sousa, a dual US‑Portuguese citizen convicted in absentia in 2009 along with 25 other Americans and some Italians, was detained in Lisbon after traveling to visit family and faces a four‑year sentence. She insists she played only a minor translation role and has long maintained her innocence; she has accused higher‑ups, including former CIA leaders, of approving or exaggerating threats to justify the operation.

Abu Omar, who says he was seized in Milan, flown via Germany to Egypt and subsequently imprisoned and tortured, expressed sympathy for De Sousa’s family and urged Italian president Sergio Mattarella to pardon her, describing her potential imprisonment as unjust and humanitarian. De Sousa has appealed publicly, writing to Pope Francis and seeking to force accountability and a chance to defend herself in Italy; she and supporters say the U.S. government declined to invoke diplomatic immunity or intervene, which she interprets as abandonment. The case underscores tensions between demands for accountability for post‑9/11 counterterror practices and diplomatic pressures: some defendants received pardons, others remain convicted; Washington has largely avoided public involvement. Observers say any pardon would be politically sensitive for Italy amid broader disputes with Egypt and concerns about perceived American unaccountability. Debate continues over who should bear legal responsibility for the rendition program’s abuses.

Barbara and Chad Soper of Rockford, Mich., have three children born on strikingly sequential calendar dates: Chloe on 8-8-08, Cameron on 9-9-09 and Cearra on 10-10-10. None were planned to match those patterns — Chloe’s birth was induced at term, Cameron arrived early after an induction intended to avoid complications from his sister’s delivery, and Cearra was delivered three weeks before her Nov. 4 due date because Barbara developed leg blood clots. Despite seeming extraordinary, statisticians say such alignments aren’t as improbable as they appear; probability estimates vary widely based on assumptions but can be within plausible ranges given many births nationwide. The Sopers say three is their lucky number and they have no further children planned. Observers note risks of closely spaced pregnancies and practical challenges of raising multiple very young children. Congratulations to the family on their unusual dates.

Security researchers are warning Mac users about a new Trojan called OSX/Sabpab that targets machines running Java and Microsoft Word. Discovered by Sophos and Kaspersky Lab, one Sabpab variant exploits the same Java vulnerability used by the Flashback malware; another arrives as a malicious Word attachment titled “10th March Statemnet,” a lure tied to a Dalai Lama statement. If opened on a vulnerable Mac, the boobytrapped document drops a Trojan that installs silently—no username or password prompt—opens a backdoor for data theft or further code, and displays a decoy Word file. Experts urge users to install available patches (Microsoft issued a 2009 Office fix and confirmed its update covers Sabpab) and keep Apple and Java updated. They also recommend running anti-virus software—paid or free—and, if infected, using vendor removal tools such as those from Symantec. Analysts caution this marks an escalation of targeted attacks against Macs.

A 40-year-old man, Jason Luis Rivera, was arrested early Saturday at Miley Cyrus’s Studio City home after jumping her fence and hiding in bushes while armed with scissors. Police, responding to a 911 call from someone at the house, found Rivera at 4:45 a.m.; when he didn’t immediately comply officers used a taser. He claimed to be Cyrus’s husband and said they’d been friends for five years. Cyrus was not home; Rivera faces trespassing and burglary charges and is held on $1,000 bail.

A 1999 photograph by German artist Andreas Gursky, titled "Rhein II," sold at Christie’s in New York for $4.3 million, setting a new auction record for any photograph. The chromogenic color print, face-mounted to acrylic glass, had been estimated at $2.5–$3.5 million; the buyer was not disclosed. The sale surpasses the previous record held by Cindy Sherman’s "Untitled" (1981), which fetched about $3.8–$3.9 million earlier this year. "Rhein II" is a panoramic image of the Rhine and is part of an edition of six, four of which reside in major museums including MoMA in New York and the Tate Modern in London. Gursky, known for large, disorienting landscapes, has described his work as encouraging awareness of our place on a rapidly moving planet. The crawl’s WARC files are not publicly available.

Michigan Attorney General Bill Schuette announced criminal charges July 29, 2016, against six current and former state employees tied to the Flint water crisis, expanding an investigation that already included three earlier defendants. Prosecutors allege coordinated efforts by officials at the Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) and the Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) to alter, bury or conceal reports showing dangerously high lead in Flint’s water and elevated blood-lead levels in children. Those charged include DEQ officials Liane Shekter-Smith (former chief of drinking water), Adam Rosenthal and Patrick Cook, and MDHHS employees Nancy Peeler, Corinne Miller and Robert Scott. Allegations range from misconduct in office, willful neglect of duty and conspiracy to tampering with evidence. Schuette said reports from July 28, 2015—one documenting higher lead in children, another showing elevated water lead—were manipulated or suppressed. Prosecutors described intentional data changes and instructions to delete emails, and accused some employees of minimizing harms and misleading federal regulators. Earlier this year three other workers—Flint’s Michael Glasgow and DEQ employees Stephen Busch and Mike Prysby—were charged; Glasgow has pleaded no contest and is cooperating. Schuette has also filed civil suits against consulting firms Veolia and Lockwood, Andrews & Newnam for alleged negligence and fraud; both deny wrongdoing. The investigation, which has involved hundreds of interviews and been compared to a layered probe “not starting at the top,” could yield further charges. Authorities stressed the goal of delivering accountability and justice to Flint families harmed after the city switched to corrosive Flint River water in 2014 and failed to apply corrosion control, causing lead to leach from pipes.

On April Fools’ Day, pranks on and off the Internet led to embarrassment for both a major news outlet and Republican front-runner Mitt Romney. At Forbes.com, contributor Len Burman published a blog at about 10:40 a.m. headlined “Romney drops out of race, endorses Santorum,” which editors pulled roughly 30 minutes later after the false item spread widely on Twitter and briefly topped Google News. Burman, an economics professor and Forbes blogger, says the piece was intended as transparent satire—he even dated it April 1, 2012—and included implausible faux quotes attributing to Romney comments like having “no chance” in the general election and urging the party to “get our butts kicked now and move on.” Burman framed the satire as commentary on the GOP’s right wing and believed his blog fell within acceptable boundaries; he was surprised when editors removed it and later pulled his explanatory post claiming an unannounced ban on April Fools’ humor. The Forbes editor who removed the posts did not respond to inquiries. Burman has reposted the item on a personal blog and reflected on how headlines travel online while context is lost. Separately in Milwaukee, Romney himself became the butt of a staged prank by aides who led him onto an empty set with canned applause; they shouted “April fools!” after revealing the fake event, then escorted him to a real pancake breakfast with several hundred supporters. Both incidents illustrate how April Fools’ mischief can quickly spill into real-world reputational fallout.

A 12-month pragmatic randomized trial (the SPACE trial) compared opioid versus nonopioid medication strategies for 240 Veterans with moderate to severe chronic back pain or hip/knee osteoarthritis pain despite prior analgesic use. Patients were randomized to a treat-to-target opioid regimen (starting with immediate-release morphine, oxycodone, or hydrocodone/acetaminophen, with possible escalation to long-acting preparations and fentanyl) or a nonopioid regimen (starting with acetaminophen or NSAIDs, then adjuvants like gabapentin, topical agents, duloxetine/pregabalin and tramadol as later options). Medication management was delivered by pharmacists with monthly follow-up until stabilization. The primary outcome was pain-related function (Brief Pain Inventory interference scale); the main secondary outcome was pain intensity (BPI severity). Nearly all randomized patients completed follow-up.

Over 12 months there was no significant difference in pain-related function: mean BPI interference was 3.4 for the opioid group versus 3.3 for the nonopioid group (difference 0.1, 95% CI −0.5 to 0.7; P = .58). A 30% or greater functional improvement occurred in 59% of opioid patients and 61% of nonopioid patients. Pain intensity was slightly better in the nonopioid group (mean BPI severity 3.5 vs 4.0; difference 0.5, P = .03), though the change was smaller than the prespecified clinically important difference. Medication-related adverse symptoms were significantly more frequent with opioids (mean symptom score 1.8 vs 0.9; P = .03). No deaths, diagnosed opioid use disorders, “doctor-shopping,” or diversion events were detected, and serious analgesic-related hospital events were rare.

The trial’s pragmatic design enhances generalizability to primary care, but limitations include unblinded patients and a VA-based sample with few women. Overall, opioids provided no functional advantage and produced more adverse symptoms, supporting guideline recommendations to avoid initiating opioid therapy for these chronic musculoskeletal pains unless alternatives fail and specialist evaluation is considered.

A Le Sueur County judge sentenced 48-year-old Susan Ann Russo to jail time, probation and community service after a distracted driving crash on Oct. 28, 2015, killed 79-year-old New Prague school bus driver Joseph “Joe” Tikalsky. Tikalsky, who drove a school bus for nearly 50 years and was beloved by his family and community, was collecting his morning paper near his mailbox while wearing a reflective jacket when Russo struck him. Russo had told officers she was reading a text and preparing to send one before the crash, but later forensic analysis reportedly found no activity on her phone; she tried to withdraw her plea after that finding, but Judge Mark Vandelist denied the motion, saying Russo should have seen Tikalsky regardless. As part of a plea agreement, Russo will serve four days in county jail split across two anniversaries of the death (two days this year, two days next year), complete 40 hours of community service with Minnesotans for Safe Driving, serve two years’ probation with restrictions on electronic devices in her vehicle and on substance use, and pay a $3,000 fine the family wants used for distracted-driving awareness. In court, there were tearful statements from Tikalsky’s widow Emma Jean, their children and grandchildren, and from Russo, who read a letter apologizing and vowed to spend her life trying to make amends. The Tikalsky family forgave Russo and said they will lobby for tougher distracted-driving laws and penalties in Minnesota to prevent similar tragedies.

A farmer in northwest China has won 520,000 yuan (about $83,000) in compensation after being mauled by a wild giant panda, his lawyer said. The incident occurred on March 1, 2014, when a panda chased by locals wandered into Liziba (Li Baizi) village in Gansu province and was driven onto Guan Quanzhi’s land. The animal bit Guan’s leg and only released him when another villager covered the panda’s head with a coat. The attack required extensive medical treatment—reports variously note seven to eight hours of surgery and multiple follow-up operations—and his right leg may still face amputation. Guan’s son sued local forestry authorities and the Baishuijiang National Nature Reserve, which agreed to the settlement after negotiations. Baishuijiang is home to more than 100 wild pandas. The story underscores the paradox of giant pandas: globally beloved and a major tourism and diplomatic symbol for China, yet wild pandas are bears with powerful jaws and have been known to injure people. Conservation efforts have raised wild panda numbers to about 1,864 by 2013, but habitat loss and low reproductive rates continue to threaten the species.

Vice President Joe Biden asserted unequivocally on Tuesday that Syrian President Bashar al-Assad was responsible for the Aug. 21 chemical attack near Damascus, saying there is "no doubt" the regime carried it out. Speaking at the American Legion convention in Houston, Biden argued the Syrian government alone possessed the weapons, had delivered chemical attacks before, targeted the same areas, and impeded investigations by shelling attack sites and blocking access for five days. He said the U.S. national security team was closely consulting with foreign counterparts and insisted those who use chemical weapons against civilians “should and must be held accountable.” At the White House briefing, spokesman Jay Carney said the United States must respond because allowing large-scale chemical attacks without consequence would threaten U.S. security interests, but emphasized President Barack Obama had not decided on a course of action and that options include nonmilitary measures. Meanwhile, nearly two dozen lawmakers urged that any military action should have prior congressional authorization, warning unilateral strikes without direct U.S. threat would violate the Constitution. Obama noted the alleged use of chemical weapons would factor into his decision.

Mercedes-Benz has unveiled an ultra-luxurious, limited-run Maybach SUV aimed at wealthy buyers who want extreme comfort off-road. The Mercedes-Maybach G650 Landaulet, shown at the Geneva Motor Show, is a V12-powered, long-wheelbase version of the iconic G-Class with a landaulet configuration: a covered front row and a retractable fabric roof over the rear passenger compartment. Priced around $500,000 and limited to 99 units, it will be the world’s most expensive SUV when it goes on sale after September.

Built from high-end components across Mercedes’ range, the G650 features an electric dimmable glass partition between driver and passengers, individual reclining “first-class” rear seats with massage and inflatable support chambers, retractable footrests, folding tables, heated and cooled (thermal) cupholders, premium audio and high-resolution displays. To retain genuine off-road capability it uses portal axles and sits roughly 1.6 feet higher than a standard G-Class, with three locking differentials and low-range gearing. The car exemplifies Daimler’s strategy of selling high-margin, exotic models to fund expensive R&D for electrification, autonomy and ride-sharing, a move that helped Mercedes overtake BMW as the world’s top-selling luxury brand. The G650 continues Mercedes’ tradition of extreme G-Class variants and underscores strong customer appetite for bespoke, opulent off-road machines.

Roger Stone, a longtime GOP operative and Trump confidant, has repeatedly denied colluding with Russia during the 2016 campaign while drawing scrutiny for public claims about backchannel contacts with WikiLeaks and its founder Julian Assange. Stone has asserted on multiple occasions that he communicated with Assange through a mutual friend and predicted that WikiLeaks would release “political dynamite” damaging to Hillary Clinton’s campaign. He publicly suggested in August and September 2016 that Assange possessed deleted Clinton-related emails and predicted regular document “payloads,” including Podesta’s emails, which were later published. Stone also exchanged messages with the persona Guccifer 2.0, whom U.S. intelligence links to Russian intelligence; Stone calls those exchanges “benign.” WikiLeaks later denied having communicated with Stone.

Stone has been asked to preserve documents by the Senate Intelligence Committee and said he assumes he has been under surveillance, though he denies speaking to the FBI. On CBS This Morning he reiterated that he did not collude with Russia and defended the White House’s unproven claim that Obama wiretapped Trump Tower, saying it was “certainly possible” and arguing the intelligence community is politicized. He criticized the FBI and suggested distrust based on past intelligence controversies. Stone has defended other Trump associates such as Paul Manafort and Michael Flynn while declining to vouch for Carter Page. He insists he has been forthright and wants his “day in court” to respond to allegations that ties to WikiLeaks or Russian-linked actors constituted collusion.

Ryan Reynolds was named People’s 2010 “Sexiest Man Alive” the same day the first trailer for his superhero film Green Lantern debuted online. The trailer offers the first official look at Reynolds in the iconic green suit, introduces Blake Lively as fellow test pilot and love interest Carol Ferris, and shows Peter Sarsgaard as villain Hector Hammond; the plot teases Hal Jordan learning new powers and conquering fears to protect the Green Lantern Corps from Parallax. The People feature highlights Reynolds’s humor, physique, and family roots, and notes his playful reaction to the title, while observers debate the choice amid other popular contenders.

Air travel in the U.S. feels paradoxical: passengers overwhelmingly complain it “sucks,” yet industry data and experts say it’s objectively better than ever. The average traveler experiences shrinking seats, extra fees for basics, crowded cabins, and the powerlessness of being controlled by security and crew—conditions that fuel complaints and social rituals of grumbling. Many travelers recount awful individual experiences—lost luggage, cramped middle seats, being stuck on runways—and social outlets like Twitter amplify those stories. Complaining has become communal and performative: it breaks the ice and lets people one-up each other about airplane misery.

But the objective picture tells a different story. Compared with the regulated era before 1978, flying is vastly safer, more punctual (on-time arrivals near 80 percent), and dramatically more affordable. Before deregulation, fares were fixed high—e.g., a 1974 New York–Los Angeles ticket equated to about $1,600 today—so flying was limited to wealthier, often white travelers. Deregulation allowed fare competition, spurring lower prices, unbundling of services (fees for bags, meals, seat assignments), airline consolidation to survive financially, and a focus on filling seats. Adjusted for inflation, domestic airfares have fallen roughly 50 percent since 1978. Premium services still exist for those who want legroom, meals, or first class, often at prices below historical fares.

Cultural factors reinforce the perception that flying is terrible. For decades comedians joked about safety and discomfort—transforming anxiety into laughter—and later shifted to mocking airline quality. Research finds feelings of powerlessness during flights heighten complaint behavior; boredom increases inward focus, amplifying perceived discomfort. Additionally, sheer scale matters: far more people fly today (2016 saw 34 percent more passengers than 2002), making the experience more impersonal.

In short, flying is safer, cheaper, and more accessible than in the past, but social conditioning, increased scale, episodic bad experiences, and the psychological effects of boredom and powerlessness keep passengers complaining. Most flights meet reasonable standards, yet the few negative incidents dominate public perception.

When news broke that Malik “Phife Dawg” Taylor of A Tribe Called Quest had died from complications of diabetes, grief rippled through the music world and beyond. Artists and fans flooded social media with condolences, remembering Phife as a gifted, influential MC whose work helped define a generation of hip hop. Among those mourning were figures like Jill Scott and Chuck D, who praised his lyricism and social commentary.

In Atlanta, WSB-TV traffic reporter Mark Arum responded to the loss with an on-air tribute that wove Phife’s lyrics and Tribe references into his routine. Arum told BuzzFeed he’d grown up with A Tribe Called Quest as the soundtrack to his youth and felt compelled to honor Phife when he heard the news just before going on air. He’s long peppered hip hop lines into his reports, he said, but on this day “decided to let them fly,” mixing a larger number of phrases and callbacks than usual.

Arum’s traffic update included cleverly reworked lines and nods recognizable to fans, such as “more hits than the Braves or the Yankees,” rhetorical flourishes about speed and rhythm, a reference to a DC-20 aircraft, playful repetitions (“do that, do that, do do that that that”), and shout-outs like “tell your mother, tell your father, send a telegram” and “one for the treble, two for the bass.” His tribute highlighted how deeply Phife and Tribe’s music had permeated listeners’ lives and pointed viewers toward the band’s documentary Beats, Rhymes, and Life for further appreciation.

UN chemical weapons inspectors visited sites near Damascus after a deadly suspected chemical attack, even after one vehicle in their convoy was fired on by unidentified snipers. The attack last Wednesday in rebel-held suburbs of eastern Ghouta reportedly killed hundreds — casualty estimates vary from around 300 to as many as 1,300 — and prompted urgent international consultations about possible responses. The UN team collected samples, interviewed survivors and medical staff, and inspected hospitals where thousands showed neurotoxic symptoms, though UN experts are mandated to determine whether chemical agents were used, not to assign blame.

Western leaders reacted strongly. US Secretary of State John Kerry called the attack a “moral obscenity,” and White House officials said there was “very little doubt” the Syrian regime possessed the capability and was culpable, though Kerry acknowledged the UN inspectors could at most confirm use, not responsibility. The US has deployed naval assets and military planners from allied countries met in Jordan to discuss options. British Foreign Secretary William Hague said diplomatic pressure had failed and Britain could act even without unanimous UN Security Council backing, citing humanitarian grounds and international law. Prime Minister David Cameron cut short his holiday to lead National Security Council deliberations; Parliament’s recall was under consideration.

Syria denied responsibility, accused rebels and foreign backers of staging attacks, and warned against foreign intervention. Russia and China urged caution and insisted any action should await UN findings; Russia warned that intervention without Security Council approval would violate international law. Some allies, including France and Turkey, signaled willingness to act outside the UN if necessary; Germany urged caution, though officials said they might support consequences if the inspectors confirm regime use. Analysts warned that limited strikes (e.g., Tomahawk missiles) could punish and deter chemical use but would not end the conflict and risk wider regional repercussions. The urgency reflects Obama’s prior “red line” statement on chemical weapons; US leaders debated calibrated options aimed at deterrence without deepening military involvement.

German authorities are weighing a smartphone-style app nicknamed "Nazi Shazam" to let police instantly identify neo‑Nazi and far‑right music, SPIEGEL and other outlets report. The idea—due for discussion by the interior ministers of Germany’s 16 states—would use audio‑fingerprinting like Shazam to spot indexed or otherwise illegal songs on internet radio, at concerts, clubs, demonstrations or public gatherings, enabling rapid intervention. A Saxony regional police office has prototyped such a system; officials say it would save resources and speed investigations. The move responds to concerns that "rechtsrock" acts as a recruitment gateway to the far‑right: the Federal Review Board for Media Harmful to Minors currently indexes over a thousand far‑right or racist tracks, restricting sales and access for under‑18s. Legal questions remain, notably whether automatic identification in a venue constitutes acoustic surveillance and other privacy or procedural issues. Advocates say it would aid policing and watchdogs, though extremists increasingly use non‑indexed or subtler songs to evade controls.

After an international search that led to the capture of Ethan Couch and his mother Tonya in Puerto Vallarta, the family’s dog, Virgil, remains missing. The Puerto Vallarta SPCA posted a lost-dog notice offering a $1,000 reward for Virgil, described as a half-shepherd, half-wolf (Saarloos wolfdog-type) mix last seen near the Colombia and Argentina streets intersection — where Mexican authorities say the Couches were apprehended Dec. 28. The online post appears to have been made by a relative of Tonya Couch, who declined to comment. Local and U.S. authorities, including the Tarrant County District Attorney’s Office, U.S. Marshals Service, the Jalisco fiscal office, Mexico’s foreign ministry and the U.S. Embassy, say they do not know Virgil’s whereabouts; Jalisco officials say the dog was never in their custody but are looking into the matter.

Tonya Couch waived extradition in Los Angeles and will be returned to Texas; she faces a felony charge of hindering apprehension that carries two to ten years. She has expressed primary concerns for her son and Virgil. Ethan remains in Mexican custody after reportedly avoiding a probation check following a video showing him allegedly drinking; his 2013 sentence was ten years’ probation after a drunk-driving crash that killed four people, a case that drew national attention for the “affluenza” defense. Tarrant County officials say Ethan could face up to 120 days in jail if returned, and prosecutors are seeking to transfer his case from juvenile to adult court.

Harvard College rescinded admission offers from at least ten members of its Class of 2021 after discovering a private Facebook group in which admitted students shared sexually explicit, racist, and otherwise deeply offensive memes. The offshoot chat—originating from a larger Class of 2021 Facebook group used to connect admitted students—was described by participants as a “more R-rated” space; founders reportedly required prospective members to post provocative content in the main group to gain access. Screenshots obtained by The Harvard Crimson showed jokes mocking sexual assault, the Holocaust, and the deaths of children, and included racially targeted punchlines such as a post calling the hypothetical hanging of a Mexican child “piñata time.” Admissions staff asked implicated students in mid‑April to disclose all content they had shared and to submit statements; those under review were told not to attend Visitas. About a week later, at least ten students received letters withdrawing their offers. Harvard’s official Class of 2021 Facebook group warned that the college reserves the right to revoke admission for behavior that calls into question an admitted student’s honesty, maturity, or moral character. Reactions among incoming students were mixed: some supported the rescissions as appropriate accountability, while others argued private speech should not trigger punishment. Critics invoked free‑speech concerns and compared the content’s intent to provocative, irreverent humor like Cards Against Humanity. The episode echoes a similar controversy with the Class of 2020, when offensive messages circulated among admitted students but did not result in disciplinary action. The incident highlights how social media behavior—private or public—can affect college admissions and underscores tensions between accountability, privacy, and free expression on campus.

Comedy Central’s roast of David Hasselhoff mined the star’s much-publicized 2007 “cheeseburger” video and long-running alcohol struggles for relentless, often brutal jokes. Hosted by Seth MacFarlane, the roast opened with repeated references to the viral footage—shirtless, slurring Hasselhoff on the floor—and comedians immediately built on that humiliation. Jeffrey Ross, Lisa Lampanelli, Gilbert Gottfried and others traded savage barbs about his drinking, acting and singing; Ross quipped about Hasselhoff “f--king K.I.T.T.”, while MacFarlane likened his performances to Inception: “no sense of reality.” Pamela Anderson weighed in with cutting, tongue-in-cheek memories from Baywatch. Hasselhoff entered to cheers amid German-themed bits and performed “Hooked On a Feeling,” and the lineup included Hulk Hogan, George Hamilton and Jerry Springer. Though many jokes pushed explicit and personal boundaries, Hasselhoff mostly laughed along and later called the experience therapeutic, saying he’d been waiting for a forum to address the controversy and that the video had been released illegally. The roast, filmed Sunday and set to air August 15, marked the first time Hasselhoff publicly confronted the viral embarrassment and his reported relapses, enduring mockery but exiting claiming victory.

Malaysia Airlines has announced a major restructuring under newly appointed CEO Christoph Mueller that will cut about 6,000 jobs, shrinking its workforce from roughly 20,000 to around 14,000 as the carrier seeks to survive mounting losses. The airline plans to relaunch under a new brand on September 1 and has begun issuing offer letters to about 14,000 staff; management says not all offers may be accepted and a second round of offers will follow. Mueller bluntly described the airline as “technically bankrupt,” saying its decline predated the twin 2014 disasters—MH370’s disappearance in March and MH17’s shootdown in July—which devastated public confidence and precipitated nationalisation. The turnaround blueprint prioritises “stopping the bleeding” in 2015, stabilising in 2016 and resuming growth by 2017. Measures include pulling back from unprofitable long-haul routes in favour of regional focus, renegotiating major contracts, revamping technology and training, and exploring joint ventures. Analysts attribute prolonged losses to poor management, government interference and uncompetitive costs—around 20% higher than rivals. Mueller, noted for past tough restructurings, said core flagship routes such as London–Kuala Lumpur may be retained while the airline seeks rapid operational and financial recovery.

Disney’s Christopher Robin is a gentle, uneven live-action reinvention of A.A. Milne’s world that aims to please both children and parents by blending nostalgia, CG character work and a sentimental adult redemption arc. Directed by Marc Forster (Finding Neverland), the film follows a grown Christopher (Ewan McGregor), a weary World War II veteran and mid-level manager at a London luggage company, who has lost his playful side to work, duty and family pressures. When Winnie the Pooh (voiced by longtime actor Jim Cummings) and the Hundred Acre Wood gang magically reappear—Pooh traverses a tree into London looking for help—the story reintroduces Christopher to the imaginative life he abandoned and forces him to reckon with his neglect of wife Evelyn (Hayley Atwell) and daughter Madeline (Bronte Carmichael).

The movie’s strengths are its earnest performances, especially McGregor’s straightfaced warmth and Cummings’ comforting Pooh; Brad Garrett’s Eeyore also earns laughs and pathos. The character designs consciously echo E.H. Shepard’s illustrations, and the voice ensemble and modern comedic touches keep the animal troupe fresh without overwhelming children. Thematically it’s classic and familiar: an adult reconnecting with his inner child to rediscover priorities and family.

However, Christopher Robin can feel tonally split. The first act’s melancholic meditation on lost childhood and postwar burdens shifts into a more chaotic, child-focused romp late in the film, producing an occasionally discordant experience. Some critics found the CG creatures slightly uncanny and questioned grafting adult darkness onto the tender Hundred Acre Wood. Despite these flaws, the film’s charm, warmth and moments of genuine feeling make it a worthwhile, family-friendly outing—comforting for parents and amusing enough for kids. Overall, Christopher Robin is a nostalgic, if imperfect, reminder of the value of play.

The Obama administration is preparing to restore federal Pell grant eligibility to many state and federal prisoners, ending a 20-year ban and potentially allowing thousands of incarcerated adults to use federal aid for college and job-focused training. Education Secretary Arne Duncan and Attorney General Loretta Lynch planned to announce the initiative during a visit to Goucher College’s Prison Education Partnership at the Maryland Correctional Institution in Jessup. Duncan described restoring Pell access for eligible incarcerated students as part of broader efforts to increase college affordability and expand experimental site programs that can grant limited exemptions to federal financial aid rules. Those experimental sites could make Pell grants available to competency-based credential programs, incarcerated adults seeking productive post-release lives, and adult learners in short-term certificate programs that provide job-ready skills. For the current academic year Pell grants cover up to $5,775. The administration has increased federal student aid overall – adding more than $50 billion to aid and $12 billion in tax benefits – and raised the maximum Pell award by over $1,000, expanding Pell recipients by more than two million students. Lawmakers from both parties, and House Democrats led by Rep. Bobby Scott, have supported reinstating Pell for state and federal prisoners, citing evidence that correctional education reduces recidivism and improves post-release employment prospects. The move aligns with recent juvenile Pell clarifications and broader criminal justice reform efforts championed by President Obama.

A rare, unannounced high-level North Korean delegation visited South Korea for the Asian Games closing ceremony, marking the highest-level contact between the two Koreas in more than five years. The 11-member group was led by Hwang Pyong‑so, widely regarded as Kim Jong Un’s second‑in‑command and the top political officer of the Korean People’s Army, and included Choe Ryong‑hae and Kim Yang‑gon, senior Workers’ Party figures responsible for inter‑Korean affairs. They held a closed lunch with South Korea’s unification minister Ryoo Kihl‑jae and national security adviser Kim Kwan‑jin, and met Prime Minister Chung Hong‑won; a meeting with President Park Geun‑hye did not take place. Both sides agreed to resume formal high‑level talks, with working‑level consultations planned ahead of a follow‑up meeting possibly this month or in November. The visit surprised Seoul and fueled speculation: it could signal a diplomatic thaw or be a staged reassurance amid reports that Kim Jong Un has been absent from public view and is “indisposed.” Analysts noted the trip fits a broader North Korean outreach—global diplomacy and talks with Japan and Russia—but cautioned that details of discussions remain undisclosed.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and other Democrats urged stronger oversight and a special counsel after President Trump fired FBI Director James Comey, saying the Senate should consider withholding confirmation of a new FBI director until the Justice Department appoints one. Schumer told CNN’s State of the Union he’d support such a move and would seek Republican allies. Virginia Sen. Mark Warner also backed public testimony from Comey and said the Senate Intelligence Committee would welcome an open hearing for the former FBI director to tell his side.

Former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper warned the nation’s institutions were “under assault” both from Russian interference and, he said, internally from the president. Clapper emphasized the intelligence community’s assessment that Russia interfered in the 2016 election contained no reporting on political collusion and said he was unaware of any evidence of collusion; he also reiterated his practice of deferring counterintelligence matters to the FBI.

Lawmakers from both parties debated who should lead the FBI next. Some Republicans, including Sen. Lindsey Graham, urged naming an internal career agent or a nonpolitical candidate to restore confidence, while others suggested high-profile options like Merrick Garland. Trump interviewed multiple candidates and indicated a quick decision. Questions persisted about Attorney General Jeff Sessions’s role and possible recusal conflicts, and Democrats requested an inspector general probe into any interference in the Russia investigation. The episode intensified calls for checks and balance actions by Congress.

Suburbicon positions itself as an immaculate 1950s suburban idyll — neat lawns, cookie-cutter homes and happy families — but the town’s pristine surface conceals brutality, hypocrisy and moral rot. George Clooney directs a script rooted in an original Joel and Ethan Coen draft, with additional writing by Clooney and Grant Heslov. The main plot follows Gardner Lodge (Matt Damon), his wheelchair-bound wife and their son Nicky (Noah Jupe). After a violent home invasion leaves Gardner’s wife dead, her twin sister Maggie (Julianne Moore) arrives to help raise Nicky. Strange behaviors and suspicious intimacy between Gardner and Maggie convince young Nicky that adults are hiding terrible secrets, and the domestic unraveling escalates into a convoluted, often violent insurance-fraud caper. Concurrently, the film inserts a heavy-handed subplot about the Meyers family, the first African-American household in Suburbicon, who endure escalating harassment from their white neighbors. That storyline aims to expose mid-century racism but many critics found it blunt, condescending and dramatically disconnected from the central crime narrative — notably rendering Mr. Meyers largely voiceless and sidelining the family’s emotional interior. 

Reviews converge on the film’s tonal confusion: critics describe Suburbicon as a mismatched hybrid that can’t reconcile dark, Coenesque absurdism with sincere social commentary. The result is frequently described as underwritten, awkward, and uneven — too somber to function as broad comedy yet too scattershot to work as pointed drama. Performances earn mixed notes: Oscar Isaac’s brief turn as a shrewd insurance investigator is widely praised for injecting energy and wit, while Noah Jupe supplies genuine pathos as the observant child. Damon and Moore, despite their pedigree, are seen by some as rehashing familiar turns without fresh depth; Moore’s dual roles veer into a “Stepford wife” cliché, and Damon’s guarded everyman feels perfunctory. 

Critics also point to stylistic pastiche — echoes of Pleasantville, Fargo and Far From Heaven — that never coheres into a distinct statement. Production values and moments of dark humor exist, but many reviewers judge Suburbicon a disappointing misfire from strong talent, faulting its inability to balance satire and solemn critique or to own a clear dramatic voice.

Amid a fractious French presidential campaign marked by scandals and a strong far-right presence, a group of disillusioned voters has launched a tongue-in-cheek but pointed petition calling for former U.S. president Barack Obama to run for France’s presidency. The “Obama17” effort — begun by four thirty-something friends in Paris who say they are not political activists — aims to collect one million signatures by March 15; it had gathered roughly 27,000–30,000 supporters within days. Organizers admit the proposal is legally impossible — French law requires presidential candidates to be citizens, and Obama is neither French nor a French speaker — but say the stunt is intended to shock voters into reconsidering the tired political choices on offer. Frustrated by recurring scandals surrounding candidates like François Fillon and the nationalist rhetoric of Marine Le Pen, the petitioners plastered about 500 posters across Paris bearing the slogan “Oui on peut” (“Yes we can”) to evoke the enthusiasm Obama once inspired. They frame the campaign as a critique of France’s insular political class, arguing that competence and global perspective matter more than narrow nationalism. While organizers stress the initiative is largely symbolic and “definitely a joke,” they hope it will provoke debate about renewing French politics rather than endorsing any particular party or candidate.

Tech entrepreneur Scott Jones, founder of ChaCha and credited with inventing practical voicemail, will hold a public estate sale at his expansive Carmel, Indiana, mansion in mid-September. Jones, who has spent recent years living primarily in Hawaii, is liquidating the contents of his 24,000–27,000 square-foot English country–style home at 1150 West 116th St. The sale runs Sept. 14–17, 9 a.m.–4 p.m., and is being managed by Aether Estate Sales Co., which calls it likely one of the best estate sales in Indiana — possibly the country.

Built over seven years at a cost of roughly $20 million, the manor has been featured on HGTV’s Mega Mansions and MTV Cribs and has functioned as a tech incubator. Notable architectural and recreational features include a 33-foot great room, indoor treehouse, circular mahogany slide, a 25-foot saltwater aquarium, indoor basketball court and extensive home automation. Jones has also run a coding school and rented rooms via Airbnb.

The collection up for sale is eclectic and high-end: a T. rex skull cast (offered at about $10,000), a Steinway grand ($100,000), museum-quality antiques, original fine art, custom furniture, an extraordinary clock collection, Kubota tractors, a suit of armor, large-scale models and a massive telescope, plus everyday household items. Everything will be barcoded and sold on-site (not auctioned). The house itself is listed for sale with an asking price near $4.995 million. For details, Aether Estate Sales Co. can be contacted online or by phone.

Missouri Gov. Eric Greitens acknowledged an extramarital affair that took place before his 2016 gubernatorial campaign but strongly denied accusations that he blackmailed the woman involved. The admission came in a joint statement from Greitens and his wife, Sheena, after KMOV-TV published a months-long investigation alleging the governor had a sexual relationship in March 2015 with a St. Louis-area woman who formerly cut his hair. The station aired an anonymous recording provided by the woman’s ex-husband in which the woman described the encounter and said Greitens threatened to publicize a nude photograph to keep her quiet. KMOV reported the woman was unaware she was being recorded; she has not spoken on the record. The ex-husband supplied the recording and later turned over materials to prosecutors and the FBI, according to his attorney. He has called Greitens a “homewrecker” and said the episode contributed to his divorce. Greitens’ lawyer, James Bennett, disputed KMOV’s account, calling it a politically motivated “hit piece,” saying the station refused to provide tape or transcript in advance and asserting there was “no blackmail.” In their joint statement, the Greitenses said Eric took responsibility years ago, that Sheena forgave him, and asked for privacy for their family. The controversy raised questions about Greitens’ character-based political appeal and prompted calls from some Missouri senators for an attorney general investigation.

At the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), President Donald Trump largely abandoned his prepared remarks to deliver a freewheeling, campaign-style address that revived many of his 2016 themes and aimed to energize conservatives for the 2018 midterms and a 2020 re-election bid. Skipping much of the scripted focus on North Korea sanctions and formal tributes, Trump spent more than an hour riffing off-teleprompter about his administration’s achievements—calling his first year “the most successful first year in the history of the presidency”—and touting the tax cut, record judicial confirmations, embassy relocation to Jerusalem and deregulatory actions. He mocked the media, attacked Hillary Clinton (prompting chants of “lock her up!”), and read aloud the lyrics to Johnny Rivers’ “The Snake,” framing it as an immigration allegory.

Trump used the platform to warn against complacency in November, urging Republicans to turn out or risk Democrats reclaiming power, repealing tax cuts, appointing judges he opposed and threatening the Second Amendment. He explicitly asked the crowd whether they valued the tax cuts or gun rights more; applause favored the Second Amendment. Speaking days after the Parkland school shooting, Trump reiterated opposition to gun control that would erode gun rights while endorsing measures such as higher purchase ages, expanded background checks, banning bump stocks and arming “well-trained” teachers—asserting schools should not be soft targets. He paid brief tribute to Billy Graham and, amid the partisan rallying, CPAC served as a venue where Trump comfortably reverted to candidate mode, signaling an aggressive campaign posture for 2018 and beyond even as legal and political challenges swirled around his administration.

Nevada prepared to execute convicted murderer Scott Dozier using an unprecedented three-drug protocol that includes fentanyl, midazolam and the paralytic cisatracurium, raising legal, ethical and practical concerns. Dozier has waived his appeals—“volunteered” to be executed—so the usual prolonged litigation over novel methods has been largely avoided, a fact criticized by death-penalty attorneys who say the state is exploiting his choice to rush a controversial regimen into use. Fentanyl has never been used in a U.S. execution and is central to the ongoing opioid epidemic; it is extremely potent and, in illicit form, has driven thousands of overdose deaths. Midazolam has been implicated in several botched, visibly traumatic executions elsewhere. The combination is thus experimental and, according to civil-rights advocates and legal scholars, risks cruel and unusual punishment.

The Nevada Department of Corrections released only a brief statement and a partially redacted execution manual a week before the scheduled date, citing protocol, prompting ACLU of Nevada litigation demanding records about how the drugs were obtained and will be administered. Court-ordered disclosures revealed the department placed multiple small fentanyl orders over months, sometimes day-to-day, raising questions whether purchases were split to avoid scrutiny. The drugs were supplied by Cardinal Health, a major distributor already facing scrutiny and fines over opioid distribution. Lawyers question whether the department followed DEA licensing rules: the DEA license used belonged to the corrections’ clinic, but the execution site may lack authority to legally administer controlled substances.

Judges and professors emphasize that Dozier’s consent does not relieve the state of its obligation to ensure execution methods are constitutional. Critics warn that amid shortages caused by manufacturers’ refusals to permit lethal-injection use, states are improvising untested protocols—effectively experimenting on human beings—without the usual appellate oversight.

Cory Monteith, the 31-year-old actor best known as Finn Hudson on Fox’s Glee, was found dead in a room at Vancouver’s Fairmont Pacific Rim Hotel on July 13. Hotel staff discovered his body after he missed checkout; police say video shows he left the hotel with friends Friday evening and returned alone early Saturday. Vancouver police have ruled out foul play; an autopsy and toxicology tests were pending to determine the cause of death.

In the days before his death, Monteith appeared to be socializing and reconnecting with friends and mentors. Photos taken July 6 show him at a Vancouver coffeehouse and motorcycle shop, chatting with friends and seated on a bike while others drank beers. Sources described him as friendly and not intoxicated in the photos. Two days before his death he dined at East of Main Café with Maureen Webb, co-founder of the Project Limelight charity he supported, and his manager; Webb said he looked healthy and that no alcohol was consumed at that dinner. Other reports mention unconfirmed nightclub appearances the night before his body was found.

Monteith had a long history of substance-abuse struggles. He entered rehab in March 2013—his second stint, the first occurring at 19—and publicly sought privacy while recovering. His relapse earlier in the year had affected his work on Glee. Co-star and girlfriend Lea Michele was reported devastated by his death; producers and colleagues expressed shock and sorrow, praising him as an exceptional performer and person.

Fans worldwide mourned, with memorials and gatherings, including an impromptu tribute at a Glee fan convention in England. The industry and public awaited toxicology results to clarify the circumstances of Monteith’s sudden passing.

Connor Cummings, 20, of Rockaway, N.J., died after falling from scaffolding at the 52-story Four Seasons Hotel in Midtown Manhattan late Wednesday. Police say Cummings and an 18-year-old friend, identified in some reports as Dimitri Olivares (or Oliveras), had accessed the hotel’s roof to take photographs around 11:15 p.m. Heavy rain had made the scaffolding wet. As Cummings attempted to move through a hatch or walk along a catwalk, he slipped and fell roughly nine stories into an interior shaft, landing on a lower rooftop or catwalk and dying at the scene. His friend descended, sought help and was later questioned by detectives; no charges have been filed. Cummings was a Morris Knolls High School graduate attending the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where he studied psychology and took photography courses; peers and family recall him as passionate about photography and community-minded. Hotel officials said they are cooperating with police and stressed guest and employee safety. The incident remains under investigation as authorities and Cummings’s family seek more details about how the two gained roof access and the circumstances leading to the fatal fall.

Eight people were shot outside City Grill on Main Street in downtown Buffalo; four died and four were wounded. The slain were Danyell Mackin, Tiffany Wilhite, Shawn-Tia McNeil and Willie McCaa III. Wounded victims included Demario Vass (critical), James Robbs Jr. (released), Shamar Davis (stable) and Tillman Ward (good). A parolee, Keith D. Johnson, 25, who had been released about two and a half weeks earlier, was arrested at his home after a SWAT operation and bloody clothing was seized. Authorities initially charged him with the murders, but Erie County DA Frank Sedita III announced he would ask to dismiss charges after new video, photos and witness interviews raised doubts about Johnson’s involvement. Relatives and survivors, including Robbs, insisted Johnson was present at the scene and not the shooter. Police now say Johnson is no longer considered a suspect and are pursuing other leads; no further arrests were imminent as the investigation continues.

The article recounts Edward Snowden’s public revelation that he leaked classified National Security Agency programs he viewed as a severe threat to democracy, and the immediate political, legal and diplomatic fallout. Snowden, a 29-year-old former CIA employee then working for Booz Allen Hamilton in Hawaii, fled to Hong Kong after providing top-secret documents to the Guardian and the Washington Post detailing broad NSA collection of telephone and Internet metadata and the PRISM program that can access online content from major tech firms. He acknowledged expecting prosecution; U.S. authorities began investigating, conducting searches and seeking interviews. Former FBI personnel warned computer forensics would be central to proving criminal elements. The White House welcomed a national debate, with spokesman Jay Carney saying programs are judged necessary by national security teams but open to change if public consensus emerges. Congressional reactions split: some officials denounced Snowden as a traitor or defector and questioned the scope of his access, while others and public figures called him a whistleblower who prompted overdue scrutiny. Julian Assange urged Snowden to seek asylum in Latin America; Snowden reportedly considered Iceland. Hong Kong’s separate legal system and extradition treaty with the U.S., including political-offense exceptions and a Beijing veto for matters affecting national interests, factored into Snowden’s choice to go there. The episode reignited debates over secrecy, oversight, civil liberties and the balance between privacy and security.

Sen. Wendy Davis reveals in her forthcoming memoir, Forgetting to Be Afraid, that she terminated a much-wanted pregnancy in the late 1990s after doctors diagnosed the fetus with a severe brain abnormality. The decision, made with her then-husband Jeff, came after multiple medical opinions and distressing fetal movements Davis describes as the baby “trembl[ing] violently.” Physicians told her the condition would likely be incompatible with life and would leave the child deaf, blind and in a permanent vegetative state. The memoir recounts that the baby, whom they had named Tate Elise, was delivered by cesarean and baptized; Davis and her husband spent time with her, photographed her and said goodbyes before Tate’s lifeless body was taken away. Davis writes of profound grief and lasting change following the loss.

The book also discloses an earlier ectopic pregnancy in 1994 that required termination for medical reasons. Davis notes that Texas law requires such cases be reported as abortions. She considered sharing the Tate story during her nationally noted 2013 Senate filibuster against stricter abortion restrictions but decided it would overshadow that day’s events. The memoir frames these experiences amid a broader life story—financial struggles, family turmoil, community college, Harvard Law School and her political rise. As she runs for governor against Republican Greg Abbott, Davis’ candid disclosure humanizes her stance on abortion and complicates political attacks; commentators and advocacy groups have responded with a mix of sympathy and political positioning. The book is published by Blue Rider Press and is due in bookstores Tuesday.

Ted Frank, a D.C. lawyer, launched ChickenOffset.com to let Chick-fil-A customers "offset" the perceived harm of spending at a company linked to anti–same-sex-marriage positions. For $1 per chicken-meal offset (or $6 for ten), purchasers receive a receipt they can show friends, and Frank pledges to donate the bulk of proceeds to LGBT organizations such as It Gets Better and the Williams Institute. He says offsets will likely channel more money to pro-LGBT groups than a Chick-fil-A purchase funnels to anti-gay causes, and the site will report donation totals. Frank acknowledges donors can give directly to charities to avoid a middleman, and notes modest early sales after launch.

Catalonia’s regional parliament voted on Oct. 27, 2017 to declare an independent Catalan Republic, igniting a constitutional crisis with Madrid. The motion, advanced by the Junts pel Sí coalition and far-left CUP, passed 70-10 with two blanks amid a boycott by most opposition deputies. Celebratory crowds and hundreds of mayors gathered outside and inside the parliament as lawmakers chanted and embraced; regional leaders Carles Puigdemont and Oriol Junqueras exchanged congratulations. The resolution called for drafting new Catalan laws and negotiating “on equal footing” with Spain to establish cooperation, while secessionists hailed the exercise of self-determination.

In Madrid, Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy urged calm and sought Senate approval to invoke Article 155 of the Spanish Constitution to assume direct control of Catalonia’s autonomous institutions. Rajoy told the Senate the measures—intended to restore legality—could include dismissing Puigdemont and his cabinet and calling new regional elections. His Popular Party’s Senate majority virtually guaranteed passage; Rajoy argued the move was necessary to protect rights and Spain’s unity. No foreign government backed Catalan independence.

The session exposed deep divisions: opposition figures ripped up proposals or walked out, denouncing a “coup” against Spanish democracy, while critics warned that unilateral declaration would worsen the situation and trigger punitive national measures. Catalonia, an economic powerhouse representing about a fifth of Spain’s GDP, faces uncertain prospects as both sides prepare for a political and legal showdown.

Two New Mexico State University students reported missing after attending a Feb. 3 concert in El Paso have been located in Idaho and are in good condition, the Las Cruces Police Department (LCPD) said. McKinnah Sinclair, 18, a pre‑social work student and NMSU cheerleader, and her roommate Charlie Daniels, 19, a kinesiology student, were found Thursday morning in Nampa, Idaho, after a Nampa police officer stopped a red Ford Focus traveling well below the interstate speed limit. The two were the only occupants. Officers discovered the vehicle bore a fictitious license plate; investigators say the pair intentionally swapped plates before their multi‑state trip. The Focus is registered to Daniels’ parents. Nampa police determined the vehicle had been reported stolen but—after talking with the women, their families and the agency that reported them missing—did not detain or charge them further; local officials indicated no charges were pursued because of the circumstances and the women’s ages. Nampa officers checked on the pair’s welfare and notified LCPD. Surveillance footage had shown the women at an ATM in Beverly Hills, California, earlier in the week. LCPD believes Sinclair and Daniels traveled to California and Idaho on their own and intentionally kept their whereabouts from family and friends, making calls and social media contact unsuccessful. Families have arranged for the women’s return to New Mexico. Multiple agencies across New Mexico, Texas, Arizona, California, Nevada and Idaho assisted in locating them.

Women have played vital but often under-recognized roles in NASA and STEM. Maia Weinstock, deputy editor of MIT News, has long created LEGO figurines celebrating scientists and engineers to boost visibility for female scientists. Her latest project, “Women of NASA,” highlighting five pioneering women in the U.S. space program, was selected as an official LEGO set after earning 10,000 votes on LEGO Ideas and passing LEGO’s review.

The set features Margaret Hamilton (led Apollo flight software development at MIT), Mae Jemison (first African-American woman in space, 1992), Katherine Johnson (computed and verified Mercury and Apollo trajectories), Sally Ride (first American woman in space, 1983), and Nancy Grace Roman (pioneering NASA astronomer who helped plan the Hubble Space Telescope). Weinstock intentionally chose a diverse group across disciplines, backgrounds, and ages, including representation from both spaceflight and astronomy.

Weinstock started making LEGO likenesses in 2009 and has honored many scientists since, including Carolyn Porco, Jane Goodall, Sylvia Earle, Stephen Hawking, and several MIT faculty. She hopes the new set will educate the public about women’s contributions to STEM and inspire girls and boys alike to see women as normal and expected in science, technology, engineering, and math careers.

Seven-year-old Bana Alabed, who became widely known for tweeting from besieged east Aleppo, has written an open letter to incoming US President Donald Trump pleading for help for Syrian children. Evacuated with her family to Turkey in December, Bana — whose social media account was run with her mother Fatemah’s assistance — recounts losing school and friends to bombing in Aleppo and describes the city as “the city of death.” Now living in Turkey, she says she can play and may attend school, but emphasizes that millions of Syrian children remain suffering “because of adult people.” Addressing Trump directly, she asks him to “do something for the children of Syria because they are like your children and deserve peace,” offering to be his “new friend” if he promises action.

The letter was written before Trump’s inauguration and shared with the BBC by Bana’s mother. Turkey, where the family now lives, supports Syrian opposition forces; Trump’s stance on Syria was then unclear, having alternately expressed admiration for Russia’s Vladimir Putin and suggested both cutting rebel aid and establishing “safe zones.” At the same time, Russia, Iran and Turkey pledged to enforce a ceasefire during peace talks, though its durability remained uncertain without buy-in from Assad’s government and rebel groups. The letter comes amid staggering civilian tolls in Syria’s six-year conflict: estimates exceed 300,000 dead overall, with thousands displaced and many children among the casualties.

The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) reported a sharp rise in Legionnaires’ disease (LD) cases in Genesee County during 2014–2015, prompting urgent surveillance and investigation though no definitive link to the Flint water emergency has been confirmed. From June 2014–March 2015, 45 confirmed cases (seven deaths) occurred; preliminary data through November 2015 added 42 more cases (three deaths) and one Pontiac fever. Overall, at least 87 cases and ten deaths were reported between June 2014 and November 2015, compared with six to 13 cases in prior years. Patients ranged from 26–94 years old. MDHHS emphasized transparency and coordinated with Genesee County Health Department, DEQ, CDC, and EPA to monitor and investigate exposures, noting clinical Legionella isolates from patients—necessary to match environmental strains and identify infection sources—were largely lacking.

Legionella bacteria thrive in warm water found in hot tubs, cooling towers, hot water tanks, potable systems, and decorative fountains; infection occurs via inhalation of contaminated aerosols and cannot spread person-to-person. MDHHS investigations found 47% of early cases used City of Flint water at home; over half had healthcare facility exposures within the two-week incubation window. Ten cases had neither hospital exposure nor Flint water at home. Enhanced surveillance and outreach to clinicians continued into 2016, with hospitals advised on detection, testing, and reporting. High-risk groups include older adults, smokers, people with chronic lung disease, or weakened immune systems.

Independent researchers and local media have highlighted an association between the outbreak and Flint’s water switch and corrosion-control failures; some experts see a strong likelihood of a connection though definitive proof would require strain matching. State and federal responses included returning Flint to Detroit-supplied water, boosting disinfectant and corrosion control, distribution of bottled water and filters, and activation of the National Guard and FEMA assistance. Investigative and academic activity around the outbreak, including contentious studies and critiques of some research groups’ methods and communications, underscored ethical and procedural tensions during the response.

Moore moved to Coronado Circle about eight years ago when the neighborhood was new, fully aware that the adjacent hundreds of acres of dry brush posed a wildfire risk. Still, she was unprepared for how close flames would come to her home. In Southern California, ferocious winds whipped up an explosive wildfire that forced thousands of evacuations and threatened populated areas. The blaze ignited Monday and expanded to more than 15 square miles within hours, consuming vegetation that had not burned in decades, Ventura County Fire Sgt. Eric Buschow said. The winds pushed the fire toward Santa Paula, a city of about 30,000 where most evacuations occurred; officials warned the city of Ventura, 12 miles southwest with about 106,000 residents, might soon be affected. Fire Chief Mark Lorenzen described fire growth as “absolutely exponential,” saying firefighters’ primary options during such high winds are to evacuate residents and protect structures. Thomas Aquinas College, with roughly 350 students, evacuated; students went home or to faculty and staff residences. At least two structures were reported burned, and one person died in a fire-related auto accident, authorities said. Winds exceeded 40 mph with gusts over 60 mph, and thousands of homes lost power. Fire crews and aircraft from Los Angeles and Santa Barbara counties assisted, though aircraft operations were grounded at night because of darkness and unsafe winds.

Honolulu’s City Council has approved a controversial ordinance that would ban pedestrians from looking at or using mobile electronic devices while crossing streets and highways. The measure—passed by a majority vote after several readings—covers phones, tablets, pagers, handheld gaming devices, laptops and digital cameras, though it exempts making 911 calls and emergency responders on duty. Talking on a phone and wearing audio equipment for listening are not prohibited. Reported fines vary across accounts: some say $15–$99 depending on repeat offenses; other versions cite $100 for a first offense and up to $500 by a third citation. Supporters, including the Honolulu Police Department and the bill’s author (who says the idea came from high school students), argue the law will improve safety by holding distracted pedestrians and motorists accountable. Opponents call it intrusive government overreach and say the Council should prioritize other issues. Mayor Kirk Caldwell has not yet decided; his office says he generally favors safety measures but is weighing pros and cons. If he signs the bill it would take effect after a set delay and enforcement could begin as soon as October under some reports.
