This mixed document contains several distinct items related to web archiving, cat rescue postings, and a nonprofit sanctuary’s message. First, it describes an archiving initiative—daily crawls intended to capture newly created web pages and the pages they reference. By saving the versions of referenced pages that existed when an author linked to them, the Internet Archive aims to prevent link rot: when original pages change or disappear, archived copies can be substituted or provided alongside the original link so readers can see what the author intended. The stated ambition is broad—“to fix all broken links on the web”—and these crawls focus on supported “No More 404” sites.

Interwoven with that are multiple cat-rescue items. One is a job posting from God’s Little People Cat Rescue on the Greek island of Syros offering a live-in caretaker role with housing and pay; the Facebook post emphasizes that the offer is genuine and invites verification. Syros is noted geographically as an Aegean island southeast of Athens. Another section promotes RESQCATS, a non-profit cat sanctuary in Santa Barbara, California, dedicated to rescuing, socializing, and adopting abandoned cats and kittens. The RESQCATS message highlights the emotional rewards of cat companionship, the need to assess each cat’s temperament to find the “purrfect” home, and sensitivity to adopters grieving lost pets. It encourages potential adopters to contact the sanctuary, visit the online sanctuary to see facilities and available cats, and offers a personal connection through the president, Jeffyne Telson, with phone and email provided. The text ends with a reflective line—“What matters most is how you see yourself…”—and a copyright credit to Alan Wnuk.

Honda released a two-minute Super Bowl commercial that lovingly resurrects Ferris Bueller’s Day Off to promote the 2012 CR-V. After Jalopnik revealed a teaser, the full spot — created by agency RPA and posted on YouTube — shows Matthew Broderick, as himself, skipping a film shoot to enjoy a day off driving the new CR-V. Broderick effortlessly channels Ferris without tarnishing the original film; the ad is framed as a respectful, fun tribute. RPA confirmed campaign backstory and creative choices, and Honda says the spot contains more than two dozen movie references for fans to spot.

A video from a performance-training session at Zhangze Rural Commercial Bank in Shanxi Province sparked public outrage after showing a trainer physically punishing eight employees with a wooden stick onstage. Filmed by an audience member, the 75-second clip shows the trainer, identified as Jiang Yang from Shanghai’s Hongfeng Leadership Academy, asking why the group ranked last and then striking them across the buttocks multiple times; the victims—four women among them—reacted visibly in pain. Reports say the session, held for roughly 216 staff, included other humiliating measures: 16 employees reportedly had their heads shaved. Jiang later issued a public apology but defended spanking as an effective, if controversial, method to “raise consciousness.” Unnamed sources claimed he charges up to 100,000 yuan per day for such training.

The Shanxi Rural Credit Cooperatives Union, which oversees the bank, confirmed the incident and said two senior managers, including the bank president, were suspended for failing to vet the training. A task force has been launched to investigate, and the bank has halted the program, demanded apologies from the academy and trainer, and is discussing economic compensation for the victims while helping employees seek redress. The footage triggered heated online debate and criticism that the punishment violated employees’ rights.

Jon Stewart’s Rally to Restore Sanity on the National Mall — co-hosted with Stephen Colbert — prompted mixed reactions: some longtime fans worry Stewart is losing his outsider identity by moving toward political activism, while Democrats quietly hope to harness his influence to energize voters. Media analysts frame the event primarily as an entertainer’s publicity play rather than a traditional political mobilization. MSNBC’s Lawrence O’Donnell and others argue Stewart will remain a comedian first, using the rally to extend his brand beyond television and generate “off-the-page” publicity. Critics warn the rally risks two main problems: eroding Stewart’s outsider credibility by positioning him as a mainstream political actor, and alienating moderate viewers who value The Daily Show’s nonpartisan satire.

President Barack Obama’s appearance on The Daily Show shortly before the rally illustrated the blurred line between entertainment and politics. Stewart gently but pointedly challenged the president, accusing him of timidity and asking whether his high 2008 rhetoric had given way to pragmatic caution. Obama defended his record, conceded that change takes time, and used the platform to urge young, disaffected viewers to vote. Their interview showcased mutual respect but limited comic chemistry; it was also a strategic move by the White House to reach Stewart’s desirable demographic.

Commentators emphasize that the rally and the Obama appearance reflect how contemporary politics increasingly intersect with entertainment. While some fear Stewart’s political involvement may damage his image among devoted fans, others see an opportunity for him to galvanize moderate voices and spotlight the toxic polarization he intends to lampoon. Ultimately, the event looks to be a publicity-driven attempt to ridicule extreme media rhetoric while mobilizing a segment of politically disengaged yet influential viewers.

RAF Typhoon and Tornado fighters were scrambled twice in March after suspected hijack or terror threats aboard US airliners passing through UK airspace, BBC defence reporting reveals. On 22 March air-traffic controllers overheard the words "ransom" and "hostage" from a United Airlines flight bound for Frankfurt, and the aircraft made an unusual descent and request to run its auxiliary power unit; Typhoons from Coningsby intercepted the plane as it left UK airspace. On 2 March Typhoons were launched after an American Airlines crew reported a passenger attempting to enter the cockpit; that incident was resolved in flight. Both proved to be false alarms, but triggered established post‑9/11 procedures that can lead, in extremis, to a ministerial decision to shoot down a civilian aircraft. Alerts occur roughly monthly amid three million annual flights; interceptions and Russian aircraft escorts underscore the RAF’s homeland-defence role amid looming defence-budget cuts.

Lamar and Lindsay Austin welcomed their son Cainan at Concord Hospital on Jan. 1, and Lamar — a 30-year-old Army veteran and father of four — chose to be at the birth even though he was a part-time security guard on a 90-day trial with Salerno Protective Services and had been warned to show up for shifts. He missed two shifts while caring for his wife during labor and early delivery; at 1 a.m. on New Year’s Day he received a text saying he was terminated. The company declined detailed comment, citing confidentiality.

The firing drew strong public reaction and sympathy. Because New Hampshire is an “at-will” employment state and federal FMLA protections generally don’t cover very new or part-time hires, legal avenues for Lamar are limited. Readers and local advocates nonetheless rallied: a Hopkinton mother set up a GoFundMe that quickly exceeded its $1,000 goal, and multiple job offers arrived. Labor leaders and legislators — including IBEW business manager Denis Beaudoin and NH AFL-CIO president Glenn Brackett — offered Lamar apprenticeship opportunities in the electrical trades and other employment help. Beaudoin emphasized the apprenticeship is a real career path with pay and benefits, not a handout.

The Austins expressed gratitude for the support and hope their situation will spark broader change. State Sen. Dan Feltes noted a recent bill aiming to provide flexible work arrangements for reasons such as childbirth and family hospitalization, but such protections are limited and not yet law. Advocates say New Hampshire needs stronger parental and medical leave policies to retain younger workers and protect part-time employees. Lamar said he felt at peace with choosing family over a job and is optimistic about new opportunities that allow him to support his family while being present for them.

An EgyptAir Airbus A320 operating flight MS804 from Paris to Cairo vanished from radar over the Mediterranean early Thursday with 66 people aboard (56 passengers, 10 crew). Contact was lost shortly after the jet entered Egyptian airspace; Greek controllers reported normal contact until about 10 miles before handoff, then no response and disappearance around 10,000–15,000 feet after abrupt course changes. International search-and-rescue efforts involving Egyptian, Greek, French, U.S. and other assets scoured the area south of Crete and near Karpathos. Conflicting initial reports about debris surfaced—Greek authorities later said floating objects examined did not belong to the aircraft, and EgyptAir retracted an earlier claim of finding wreckage. Egyptian officials said a terror attack was a likelier cause than technical failure, though U.S. and French officials urged caution; U.S. imagery showed no clear explosion and the FBI/Federal agencies had no confirming evidence of terrorism at that time. Families gathered at crisis centers in Cairo and Paris; national leaders including Egypt’s president and France’s Hollande pledged cooperation in the investigation. Airbus confirmed loss of the A320 (delivered 2003). National investigators from Egypt, France, Greece and Airbus were mobilized to determine the cause.

Early on Oct. 30, 2018, a pickup truck struck four children who were crossing State Road 25 to board a Tippecanoe Valley school bus near Rochester, Indiana. The bus had stopped and its stop-arm was extended when the northbound pickup entered the scene and struck the children as they crossed the southbound lane. Three siblings — 9-year-old Alivia Stahl and 6-year-old twin brothers Xzavier and Mason Ingle, students at Mentone Elementary — were killed at the scene. An 11-year-old boy not related to the siblings, identified as Maverik Lowe, suffered multiple broken bones, was conscious when emergency responders arrived, and was airlifted to a Fort Wayne hospital for surgery in critical condition.

Indiana State Police Sgt. Tony Slocum called the incident an “unspeakable tragedy,” emphasizing that students had the right of way and noting Indiana law requires motorists to stop for buses loading or unloading children. A crash reconstruction team and detectives interviewed witnesses at the rural mobile home community site. The Tippecanoe Valley School Corp. dispatched counselors to support students, staff and families and urged the community to pray for those affected. Gov. Eric Holcomb and his wife expressed mourning and asked residents to keep the families and community in their thoughts.

Later the same day authorities arrested 24-year-old Alyssa Shepherd of Rochester and charged her with three counts of reckless homicide and a misdemeanor for passing a stopped school bus with its arm extended, causing bodily injury; she was held on a $15,000 surety bond. The investigation remained ongoing.

UNESCO on Tuesday published a list of 70 artworks recently stolen from Havana’s National Museum of Fine Arts, condemning the theft as a threat to the integrity of cultural property and warning it risks feeding illicit national and international trafficking. Cuban authorities confirmed the robbery days after investigative reporting brought it to light but initially gave no precise count. The missing pieces, largely canvases from the island’s “Turn of the Century” period (circa 1897–1927), include numerous paintings by Leopoldo Romañach. The theft came to light after several works were offered for sale in Miami; art dealer Ramón Cernuda first flagged the case after purchasing a 20th‑century Cuban painting for $15,000 that proved to be museum‑registered. Cernuda estimated the entire haul could be worth about $1.5 million and alerted U.S. and Cuban authorities; he has handed the painting he bought to the FBI. Cuban investigators reported storage rooms showed no signs of forced entry and that thieves had cut canvases from their frames and then neatly reseated the frames to conceal the loss, making the timing of the theft unclear. Cuba’s National Council of Cultural Heritage has sought help locating the works. In the aftermath, Culture Minister Rafael Bernal was abruptly dismissed, with no official reason given.

Over the past week, identical lists naming alleged campus rapists have repeatedly appeared in women’s bathroom stalls across Columbia buildings—first in Hamilton, then Lerner, Butler and other locations—prompting swift removal by Facilities, which treats the writing as graffiti. Early reports note differences among instances: the initial May 7 Hamilton list featured multiple handwritings and ink colors, suggesting several contributors, while later versions (Lerner, Butler, and another Butler appearance) were largely in the same handwriting and silver marker. Photos and tips have circulated among student media; Bwog published an editorial condemning the tactic as unsafe and potentially illegal, reminding readers that publishing the uncensored list could violate Title IX and FERPA and that vigilante naming is not an appropriate response to sexual violence. Public Safety has closed or taped some bathrooms while crews clean, and officers warn of disciplinary or legal consequences. Jezebel posted photos of flyers and the first descriptions of those named, despite efforts to anonymize the accused. Coverage recalls a similar 1990 episode at Brown. Student outlets urge witnesses to submit tips and photos; campus administrators have been contacted but offered limited comment. The situation continues to evolve as media and officials respond.

A study to be presented at the American Sociological Association’s annual meeting found that people can feel more empathy for abused dogs—both puppies and full-grown—than for abused adult humans, while empathy for abused children and puppies was roughly equal. Researchers Jack Levin and Arnold Arluke surveyed 240 mostly white college students, each reading one version of an otherwise identical fictional news story describing the beating of either a one-year-old child, an adult in his thirties, a puppy, or a six-year-old dog. Respondents then rated their empathy for the victim. Results showed higher empathy for the child, puppy, and dog than for the adult human, leading the authors to conclude that perceived vulnerability and dependence—age—matters more than species in eliciting empathy. Full-grown dogs were viewed similarly to puppies rather than as self-sufficient adults, and women in the sample reported greater empathy than men overall. Levin noted the experimental use of a homogeneous college sample is standard for establishing causality, and he suspects similar patterns would appear for other companion animals like cats, which people often anthropomorphize.

North Korean authorities have rounded up several hundred relatives of Jang Song-thaek, the recently executed uncle and one-time powerbroker of leader Kim Jong-un, in a sweeping purge aimed at erasing his influence. According to a Daily NK source in Pyongyang, Ministry of State Security agents detained "a few hundred people" on the night of Dec. 13 in the Pyongchon district, taking not only close kin but distant relatives, including members of Jang’s father’s lineage. The detentions came a day after Jang’s public denunciation, trial and execution on Dec. 12 on an array of 24 charges ranging from "gnawing at the unity and cohesion of the party" and "dreaming different dreams" to corruption, sexual improprieties, and squandering foreign currency at casinos. North Korean practice often punishes family members of purged officials; in this case, the scale of arrests and threats of political prison camps underline the regime’s determination to obliterate Jang’s legacy. South Korean and U.S. accounts suggest the purge followed a violent clash between forces loyal to Kim and those supporting Jang over control of lucrative exports—coal, clams and crabs—whose profits, largely in Chinese renminbi, sustained elite and military patronage networks. Reports indicate Jang had seized valuable fishing grounds previously controlled by the military, sparking a September–October confrontation that left regular forces routed until a larger government force retook the area. Two of Jang’s senior lieutenants were executed by antiaircraft machine gun before Jang’s own execution. Officials say many of Jang’s associates and relatives face execution or long-term labor camp sentences; some have volunteered for "revolutionisation" through forced labor in mines or farms in hopes of leniency, though observers doubt this will prevent severe punishment. The purge highlights deep fractures within North Korea’s elite over control of foreign currency and power.

Chicago police will begin randomly screening bags on some CTA "L" stations starting the week of Nov. 3 as part of a federally funded counterterrorism initiative. Using a portion of a $3.5 million federal grant, mobile explosive screening teams of four to five officers will set up outside turnstiles at one randomly selected station each day—mostly downtown—during rush hour. Officers will pick riders by a preselected interval (e.g., every 10th entrant), swab the exterior of their bags without opening them, and insert the swab into a machine that detects explosive compounds. The test takes roughly 20–30 seconds (officials say under a minute) and yields a positive or negative readout; a failed result prompts a bag inspection. Officials stress there is no known specific threat and characterize the measure as proactive protection modeled on similar checks used at some Amtrak and East Coast transit facilities.

Police say riders who refuse screening will be ordered to leave that station and may face arrest if they attempt to enter; they may instead go to another station. Screenings will occur several times weekly. Some riders and transportation experts criticized the plan as limited and potentially ineffective—pointing out that random checks are a “needle in a haystack,” that people can opt out or shift stations, and questioning cost and impact on true security. Officials maintain the brief screening time is worth the safety benefit.

Actress Jamie Denbo publicly called out Hollywood ageism after being told at 43 she was “too old” to play the wife of a 57-year-old man in a first marriage with an 18-year-old daughter. Denbo—known for Orange Is the New Black, Crazy Ex-Girlfriend and Veep—tweeted that the casting decision was absurd, noting the timeline meant the character would have had the child at a typical age and that the older actor’s real-life wife is likely about 50. Denbo’s rant criticizes a longstanding industry pattern where older men are paired with much younger female love interests, a complaint echoed by veterans like Helen Mirren and Maggie Gyllenhaal. The episode highlights persistent sexism and ageism in casting and adds momentum to efforts, such as Meryl Streep’s screenwriting lab for women over 40, to create more mature roles for women.

John Carter, Andrew Stanton’s big-screen adaptation of Edgar Rice Burroughs’s A Princess of Mars, is a visually striking yet uneven adventure that divided critics. The film follows a post–Civil War Confederate veteran, John Carter (Taylor Kitsch), who is mysteriously transported to Barsoom (Burroughs’s Mars), where lower gravity lets him perform spectacular leaps and makes him valuable in a complex intercity conflict. Stanton—best known for Pixar hits like Finding Nemo and WALL‑E—brings clear affection for pulpy, old‑school fantasy, populating Barsoom with four‑armed Tharks, scheming immortal Therns, airships that resemble ancient sailing vessels, and a fierce, independent princess, Dejah Thoris (Lynn Collins). Willem Dafoe lends distinctive life to Tars Tarkas, the Thark leader, and Mark Strong delivers a sly turn as the antagonist Matai Shang.

Critics praise the movie’s sense of wonder, production design, and moments of charm (including Woola, a ten‑legged lizard dog), and they note Kitsch’s earnestness. But many fault the film for a convoluted, poorly paced narrative, inconsistent 3D/CGI, and failure to fully capitalize on its technological opportunities—opting for repetitive hand‑to‑hand combat over imaginative gadgetry. Budget backlash and prerelease skepticism compounded its reception. Ultimately, John Carter is a rousing, occasionally clumsy boys’-adventure with rare sparks of genuine wonder, though it never quite achieves the emotional or structural precision of Stanton’s animated work.

U.S. Senator John McCain responded sharply after Syria’s U.N. ambassador lodged a complaint over McCain’s 2013 visit to rebel-held Syrian territory, calling Damascus’s protest both predictable and morally inverted. Bashar Ja’afari asked Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and the U.N. Security Council to act against foreigners who enter Syria without authorization and criticized others, including France’s Bernard Kouchner and former U.S. diplomat Peter Galbraith, for similar visits. McCain said the Assad regime’s focus on his trip rather than its own widespread slaughter — which he cited as exceeding 200,000 men, women and children — exposed the international community’s failure to halt atrocities and was “a stain on our collective moral conscience.” He also boasted on Twitter about what he called a diplomatic “superfecta,” grouping the Syrian complaint with prior incidents in which he angered powerful adversaries: being placed on a Russian sanctions list by Vladimir Putin, being denounced by Fidel Castro (who falsely accused him of helping create ISIS with Mossad), and being labeled ISIS’s “No. 1 enemy.” McCain framed his visit as an act of solidarity with Syrians fighting for freedom and dignity and defended his actions against Damascus’s charges of violating Syrian sovereignty.

Todd Kohlhepp, a South Carolina inmate already serving seven consecutive life sentences plus 60 years for multiple murders, sexual assault and kidnapping, has told investigators he buried two additional victims near Interstate 26 in Spartanburg County. Sheriff Chuck Wright said deputies interviewed Kohlhepp and planned a search after he gave varying accounts to investigators and to a documentary production team. A multi-agency search with cadaver dogs and deputies in the Enoree frontage-road area near Highway 92 and I-26 found no evidence of bodies. Investigators noted Kohlhepp’s statements have been inconsistent—at times describing one burial site, at others two separate locations—and he declined to personally lead officers to any spots. Officials suspended further searches until Kohlhepp provides verifiable specifics, citing concerns he may be seeking attention. Kohlhepp’s crimes came to light in 2016 after police found Kala Brown chained in a storage container and recovered multiple buried bodies on his property. He had previously admitted to four 2003 Superbike Motorsports killings and the 2015 murders of Johnny Joe Coxie and Meagan McCraw-Coxie, among other offenses. A documentary crew from Committee Films is working with authorities on the case.

Anders Behring Breivik, 32, has been charged in Norway’s deadliest peacetime attack since World War II after a car bomb at government headquarters in Oslo and a mass shooting at a Labour Party youth camp on Utoya Island killed at least 92 people and wounded dozens more. Police and officials say Breivik, described as a right‑wing, Christian fundamentalist, posted a 1,500‑page manifesto online hours before the attacks under the name “Andrew Berwick.” The document, titled “2083: A European Declaration of Independence,” denounces liberalism and multiculturalism as “cultural Marxism,” calls for armed resistance to defend Europe from Muslim domination, and recounts months of preparation, including bomb‑making experiments and chemical purchases. It also claims participation in a 2002 meeting to reconstitute the Knights Templar. In a video and online posts Breivik appears in military gear and argued violent revolution was necessary. Witnesses say he posed as a police officer on Utoya, gathering campers before shooting them over about 90 minutes; he surrendered when police arrived. Authorities are probing possible accomplices and whether explosives used ammonium nitrate ordered via a registered farm. The attacks have prompted scrutiny of Norway’s focus on Islamic threats and raised alarms about domestically radicalized right‑wing violence.

Ashley Madison, the infidelity-focused dating service hit by a massive data breach, disputed media claims that most female accounts on its platform were fake. After hackers released the personal data of more than 30 million users and internal documents, several outlets — notably Gizmodo — analyzed the leaked fields and concluded that very few of the site’s female profiles were active, implying many were bogus or male-operated. Company executives countered those conclusions as based on “incorrect assumptions” about the leaked data’s field meanings and pushed back on the narrative that real women were scarce.

Avid Life Media, Ashley Madison’s parent, issued a defensive statement saying the business remained operational and was growing despite the attack. The company claimed it had acquired “hundreds of thousands of new users” in the week after the leak, including 87,596 women, and asserted that women sent more than 2.8 million messages in that same period. The firm did not provide verifiable documentation or clarify how many messages originated from male accounts or automated scripts, leaving room for skepticism about the authenticity of some activity.

Executives are in survival mode: the CEO Noel Biderman left the company by mutual agreement amid the fallout, and Reuters earlier reported the firm had been seeking a buyer before the breach. Because independent verification of the company’s post-breach claims is lacking and because leaked data can be misinterpreted, the true ratio of genuine female users to fake or inactive accounts remains unclear.

Law enforcement officials say the Aurora, Colo., movie-theater massacre displayed a marksmanship and planning level suggesting significant target practice and premeditation. During the midnight screening of The Dark Knight Rises, 24-year-old James E. Holmes allegedly used an AR-15 with a high-capacity magazine, a 12-gauge shotgun and a Glock .40-caliber pistol, killing 12 and wounding 58. Authorities noted an “unusually high” hit rate given the dark, smoke-filled theater, moving targets, weapon recoil and a jammed rifle that forced the shooter to switch weapons. Investigators recovered another Glock in Holmes’ car and found his nearby apartment booby-trapped with explosives and chemicals; police theorize he had contingency plans to retrieve a gun, flee, fight police or kill himself. Investigators are searching for evidence of range visits, receipts, computer searches or calls that could establish training, premeditation and rebut an insanity defense. A local range owner reported Holmes applied for membership in June but never followed through; his answering machine message unnerved the owner.

Holmes had been a neuroscience graduate student at the University of Colorado, admitted to a six-student program and receiving a $26,000 federal stipend. Colleagues and a former Salk Institute researcher described him as an average or socially awkward student, not an exceptional scientist. He failed an oral preliminary exam on June 7 and abruptly left the program June 10. School officials said doctoral students receive stipends and access to campus labs but no psychiatric screening; authorities are checking whether campus materials played a role in the explosives. Holmes appeared in court with orange hair and a dazed demeanor and faces multiple first-degree murder charges.

Fort Lee, N.J., police are handing out $85 tickets to people caught texting while walking after three fatal pedestrian accidents this year. Officers distributed pamphlets in March, then began issuing citations; more than 117 tickets have been given. Officials say texting distracts pedestrians, making them unaware of surroundings. Stony Brook University researchers Eric Lamberg and Lisa Muratori studied how cell phone use affects walking and memory, publishing results in Gait & Posture. Participants walked an eight-foot route while talking or texting; texting caused a 61% increase in lateral deviation, 13% greater distance traveled, reduced walking speed, more navigational errors, and greater interference with working memory than talking. The authors suggest dual-task testing could aid rehabilitation by preparing patients for real-world walking demands, but they do not advocate banning texting while walking—rather, they aim to raise awareness of its disruptive, safety-reducing effects.

Sixteen U.S. Postal Service employees in the Atlanta area were sentenced to federal prison for accepting bribes to deliver kilogram-sized packages of cocaine on their mail routes, authorities announced. The scheme came to light in 2015 during an investigation of a drug trafficking organization; traffickers targeted postal workers believing their official roles reduced the chance of detection. Federal agents used a confidential source who posed as a trafficker and arranged payments while surveillance recorded the handoffs. Defendants negotiated bribes—sometimes as low as $250—and chose to deliver cocaine over marijuana because it fetched higher payments; some recruited coworkers and split fees. Sentences ranged from about three years to nine years, with varying terms of supervised release and orders to pay restitution or forfeiture. Notable sentences included nine years for clerical worker Kawana Rashun Champion and nine years for nonpostal participant Dexter Bernard Frazier; others received between roughly three and eight years. Prosecutors and law enforcement officials emphasized the breach of public trust and the danger posed to communities and innocent postal workers, noting the vast majority of postal employees are honest and that investigators from the FBI, the U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General, and the DeKalb County District Attorney’s Office collaborated on the case. The U.S. Attorney’s Office urged drug-education resources for families and highlighted the case as a deterrent against public-corruption and drug-trafficking schemes.

On Sept. 24 the Texas State Board of Education narrowly approved a 7-6 resolution directing publishers to correct what supporters described as a “pro-Islamic/anti-Christian” bias in future world history textbooks. Backers, primarily social conservatives, said the move aims to ensure more balanced coverage of Christianity and other non-Muslim faiths when new social studies books are reviewed in two years. The resolution cites past texts—not used in Texas since 2003—and alleged examples of disproportionate space given to Islamic beliefs and positive portrayals of Islam. Critics, including Democrats and moderates on the board, called the effort politically motivated, unproven, and a distraction that damages the board’s reputation. Some opponents labeled the language offensive and said the measure is largely symbolic, since it is not legally binding on publishers.

A fierce dispute erupted in the Democratic presidential primary after Bernie Sanders’ campaign accessed and saved portions of Hillary Clinton’s voter files, exploiting a software glitch at vendor NGP VAN. The DNC quickly suspended Sanders’ access to its voter database, crippling his field operation and prompting Sanders to sue the party, alleging favoritism toward Clinton and calling the suspension a breach of contract. Sanders’ team admitted that staffers had inappropriately examined and saved some Clinton data; one aide, data director Josh Uretsky, was fired. Audit logs showed four Sanders accounts conducted 25 searches over about 40 minutes, viewing lists of Clinton’s strongest supporters and weaker supporters across multiple states — valuable targeting information. Sanders called the episode evidence of DNC sabotage, while Clinton’s camp condemned it as theft and demanded an independent audit and disciplinary action. After late-night negotiations and court involvement, the DNC restored Sanders’ access early Saturday after the campaign agreed to provide requested information, submit to an audit by Kroll, and sign an affidavit about staff actions; the Sanders campaign said it would continue its lawsuit. The controversy intensified longstanding suspicions among Sanders backers that the DNC favors Clinton, and became a fundraising and political flashpoint just weeks before early voting in Iowa and New Hampshire. Legal experts noted potential exposure under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act for staff who accessed the data.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet began donating its web crawl data to the Internet Archive; these daily data feeds are incorporated into the Wayback Machine after an embargo. Separately, GQ’s new issue features the young, attractive cast of Glee—Lea Michele, Dianna Agron and Cory Monteith—in a provocative photo shoot by Terry Richardson, prompting cast comments about being scantily clad and surprised at how far they went for the images. The cover story explores the actors’ backgrounds and the show’s devoted “Gleek” fanbase. Michele recalls pressure early in her career to get a nose job and her mother’s refusal, while Monteith warns against romanticizing dropping out of school despite his own past. Creator Ryan Murphy says he aimed for a responsible take on a family show. Michele also describes the surreal experience of performing at the White House Easter Egg Roll.

The Wall Street Journal reports that the NSA’s continued monitoring of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other Israeli leaders may have inadvertently captured private conversations involving U.S. members of Congress. Despite President Obama’s post-Snowden pledge to rein in surveillance of allied leaders, the administration kept certain figures, including Netanyahu, under scrutiny. Initially, the heightened monitoring stemmed from fears Netanyahu might strike Iran unilaterally; by 2013, those concerns waned and attention shifted to the Iran nuclear negotiations. U.S. officials suspected Israel was both spying on the talks and seeking to undermine any agreement by leaking details.

Intercepted communications reportedly confirmed Israeli awareness of the negotiations and intentions to sabotage the deal. When Netanyahu and aides lobbied in Washington—addressing Jewish-American groups and members of Congress—the NSA intercepted related conversations. Senior officials told the Journal these collections raised apprehension that the executive branch could be accused of spying on Congress. Nonetheless, the White House deemed the information potentially valuable to counter Netanyahu’s campaign against the deal. To limit political exposure, the administration delegated decisions about dissemination to the NSA, which removed members’ names and personal attacks before sharing.

The National Security Council declined to comment on the report’s specifics, reiterating that foreign intelligence surveillance has specific, validated national security purposes and asserting that U.S. commitment to Israel’s security is “sacrosanct.” Speaker Paul Ryan’s office said it was investigating; Rep. Devin Nunes and the House Intelligence Committee also sought information to determine legality and procedures followed. Critics, including Sen. Ted Cruz, decried the surveillance as politically directed, while the Israeli Embassy called the allegations “total nonsense.” The report notes prior NSA intercepts showed Netanyahu sought the U.S.’s latest negotiation positions before his congressional address; U.S. officials later used media reports to publicly rebuke him without revealing intelligence sources.

Sir Elton John reignited his long-running feud with Madonna in an interview on Australian TV, calling her a "f***ing fairground stripper" and claiming "her career is over." The 65-year-old blasted Madonna for being cruel to Lady Gaga, who is godmother to his son Zachary, and said Madonna should have stuck to making great pop records rather than dance music. His remarks followed Madonna’s criticism of Gaga’s "Born This Way" and came after Madonna beat Elton for a Golden Globe for Best Original Song, prompting David Furnish to call her "embarrassing" and "desperate." The interview, conducted by friend Molly Meldrum, also covered Elton’s family life, fatherhood, sobriety and upcoming world tour celebrating 40 years of "Rocket Man."

Sleep-deprived New Yorkers have an unusual new caffeine source: caffeinated beef jerky called Perky Jerky. Invented by Tribeca resident Matt Keiser, 38, after spilling Red Bull on jerky while skiing, the product launched online in August and will soon appear in Sports Authority stores. Keiser and cofounder Brian Levin market it as a complementary pairing—like vodka and orange juice—positioned for active, professional adults seeking sustained focus. Perky Jerky sells for $2.99 (1 oz.) and $4.99 (2 oz.), with each ounce providing about 60 mg of caffeine—the equivalent of a small coffee or a can of Red Bull—alongside high protein and low fat. Street reactions were mixed: a barista called the combo “disgusting,” while a gym-goer reported an improved workout jolt without a post-exercise crash. The flavor is described as teriyaki-pepper with a hint of guarana.

Lululemon pulled a shipment of its popular black Luon yoga pants after customers complained the fabric was too sheer, prompting a recall and a roughly $20 million hit to first-quarter sales forecasts. The move sent shares lower and marked what analysts call Lululemon’s fourth quality-control problem in a year, following prior incidents with color bleeding and transparency in swimwear and light-colored pants. Lululemon blamed its Taiwanese supplier, Eclat Textile Co., but Eclat disputed that claim, saying all shipments had passed a certification process Lululemon approved and were manufactured to contractual specifications. The public back-and-forth highlighted concerns about the company’s oversight of a concentrated supplier base—Luon fabric comes from a single supplier—and prompted analysts to question whether Lululemon exercises sufficient supervision in its factories. Lululemon said its sourcing manager is at Eclat’s Taiwan facilities as it investigates the cause. The episode adds pressure on a brand built on premium pricing and scarcity-driven demand, as quality missteps and growing competition threaten customer trust and the company’s recent strong share performance.

Tiger Woods has begun a public romance with Olympic skier Lindsey Vonn, marking his first serious relationship since his 2010 split from Elin Nordegren. Sources say the 37-year-old golfer and the 28-year-old gold medalist began seeing each other in November after meeting through the ski community—Lindsey has been teaching Tiger’s children, Sam and Charlie, to ski. Though both are focused on demanding athletic careers, they’ve made time to connect: Tiger visited Lindsey in Austria during a World Cup event in mid-January and the pair took a romantic trip to Antigua. Friends say they talk frequently by phone, and insiders claim Tiger has been making a stronger commitment and “pulling out all the stops.” Despite the public displays, Lindsey was initially wary because of Tiger’s very public history of infidelity—his 2010 marriage collapse revealed numerous affairs—which has left some of her friends concerned. Reports even suggest Tiger has talked about remarriage and sees Lindsey as a potential partner. Observers are left wondering whether Tiger has really changed or if the pattern will repeat.

American culture often glorifies fame, fortune, and power, yet those advantages can evaporate quickly. 24/7 Wall St. compiled a list of 50 well-known people who recently experienced steep declines in influence, spanning TV personalities, CEOs, financiers, and politicians. Some lost standing through scandal or poor judgment; others fell victim to shifting circumstances or business failures.

Anthony Scaramucci’s tenure as White House Communications Director lasted less than two weeks in July 2017. His brief, tumultuous stint included protocol breaches, public clashes with colleagues, and a profanity-laced New Yorker interview; his marriage suffered as his wife filed for divorce during the episode. New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, once a 2016 presidential contender, ended his term with historically low approval ratings amid lingering damage from the Bridgegate scandal and public perception of opportunism during the Trump transition. FBI Director James Comey became controversial after public actions during the 2016 campaign and was abruptly fired by President Trump in May 2017 amid conflicting White House explanations. At Ford, CEO Mark Fields was ousted after failing to maintain investor confidence despite revenue growth; his push into electric and autonomous vehicles coincided with a nearly 40% share decline. Golf icon Tiger Woods, once dominant with 14 majors, saw his career derailed by personal scandals and health issues, culminating in a DUI-related incident and a steep drop in ranking.

Lady Gaga honored David Bowie at the 2016 Grammys with a multimedia tribute powered by Intel, part of its Experience Amazing campaign and a multiyear partnership with The Recording Academy’s “Next Generation of GRAMMY Moments.” Intel’s technology helped realize Gaga’s vision to “invent the un‑inventable” and reveal “the wizard behind the curtain.” The tribute—one of the night’s largest segments—featured transformative visuals, costume changes, special effects, choreography, hydraulics, and guest guitarist/producer Nile Rodgers. Gaga’s set spanned Bowie classics including “Space Oddity,” “Changes,” “Ziggy Stardust,” “Rebel Rebel,” “Fashion,” “Fame,” “Under Pressure,” “Let’s Dance,” and closed with “Heroes.” Gaga has long cited Bowie’s influence—thankful in liner notes and interviews—and commemorated him publicly at the Grammys, having earlier channeled his Ziggy era on the red carpet and even tattooed his Aladdin Sane likeness. The performance underscored her indebtedness to Bowie and pushed televised production boundaries.

Robin Williams, who died at 63, left a singular imprint on both Hollywood and a generation now in their mid-20s to early 30s. Admired by peers—his emotional acceptance at the Good Will Hunting Oscar underscored that—Williams also pivoted in the 1990s toward children’s entertainment in ways few A-list stars did. After a string of prestige films in the 1980s like Good Morning, Vietnam, Awakenings and Dead Poets Society, he embraced roles that delighted young audiences: Hook showed a renewed playfulness; his virtuoso voice work as the Genie in Aladdin transformed a darker Disney tale into an imaginative classic; Mrs. Doubtfire showcased self-sacrificing physical comedy that felt thrillingly transgressive for kids. Recurrent themes in his family films—men stuck between childhood and adult responsibility (Jumanji, Jack, Flubber)—made him feel like one of them: innocent about adult concerns and eager to meet children on their level. Later attempts at adult dramas met a shrinking market for mid-budget films, but he returned to family fare as Theodore Roosevelt in the Night at the Museum series. Those raised on his movies remember him for bringing joy as much as for dramatic prowess.

The author’s personal encounters—first seeing Williams’ explosive stand-up at the Comedy Store in 1978, shared moments at the Copper Kettle and the AFI event—capture his dazzling improvisational gift and a vulnerability beneath the comic bravura. A whispered, joking “Help me” to a friend amid flashing photographers lingers in the author’s memory, haunting in light of Williams’ death. Renowned as a stand-up and Oscar-winning actor, Williams’ restless intelligence propelled him across comedy and drama; his legacy endures in rewound VHS tapes, classroom recitations and the genuine warmth he brought to projects that mattered to a generation.

Oakleigh Ryan Nance is an 11-month-old infant who has faced serious health challenges since her premature birth at three pounds. Initially nicknamed “Miss Sassy” in the NICU for her feisty responses, she stabilized quickly after birth, breathing room air within days and growing normally for months. Around six months old she developed a high fever and a severe urinary tract infection that likely involved her kidneys. Despite antibiotics, infections recurred, prompting hospitalization and further testing that revealed stage 3 vesicoureteral reflux (kidney reflux) and a dangerous, antibiotic-resistant Pseudomonas infection. Additional cardiac testing uncovered a moderate atrial septal defect (ASD) and pulmonary stenosis—heart problems that are particularly concerning given her kidney infection and overall vulnerability.

Oakleigh’s left kidney is severely affected and now functions at only 22%. Surgeons have scheduled a roughly 4½-hour operation to correct the reflux in that kidney at the end of the month: the procedure will shorten two ureters that are causing reflux (her left kidney is effectively two kidneys with two ureters) and remove an external renal pocket. After recovery, she will see a cardiologist for further heart evaluation. Separately, a news report described an urgent situation in Oklahoma City in which Oakleigh reportedly contracted a “super strain” of E. coli resistant to many antibiotics, leaving her family and doctors racing to find effective treatments; CDC investigators were reportedly involved. Her family emphasizes faith and gratitude, notes their support network, and has launched a GoFundMe to help cover mounting medical expenses as Oakleigh faces a difficult recovery and continued care.

At a South Carolina CNN town hall ahead of the state’s Republican primary, Donald Trump acknowledged that during a 2002 Howard Stern interview he “could have” signaled support for invading Iraq, but insisted that by the time the war began he opposed it. Trump told Anderson Cooper that the Stern exchange occurred early — “probably the first time I was asked that question” — and reiterated his frequent campaign claim that he was against the Iraq invasion before it started, though he conceded he “wasn’t a politician” then and that many private-sector remarks weren’t widely reported. BuzzFeed’s posting of the Stern clip — recorded on the first anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks — showed Trump responding, “Yeah, I guess so,” when asked if he would support an invasion, and later saying, “You know, I wish the first time it was done correctly.” Trump pointed to passages in his 2000 book, The America We Deserve, advocating a tough policy toward “outlaw” states and cited later articles from 2003 and 2004 as evidence of his opposition, despite the lack of contemporaneous public statements showing he opposed the invasion before it began.

Trump’s remarks about Iraq drew a tense moment in the town hall when an audience member confronted him over his assertion that President George W. Bush lied about weapons of mass destruction. Trump replied that “something was going on” but he didn’t know why Bush went in. He framed his position as evolving to strong opposition shortly after the war’s start.

The event also featured Trump responding to criticism from Pope Francis, who had said that a candidate is “not Christian” if he seeks to deport undocumented immigrants and build a border wall. Trump called the pontiff “a wonderful guy,” downplayed the clash as overblown by media and said he would meet the Pope “anytime he wants.” Fellow candidates declined to take sides: John Kasich praised the Pope’s humility, and Jeb Bush, a devout Catholic, said he wouldn’t question anyone’s faith.

Trump continued to attack rival Ted Cruz’s honesty and sided with Marco Rubio after Rubio’s campaign accused Cruz’s team of photoshopping an image — Trump joked the image made Rubio look shorter and called some Cruz campaign tactics “disgusting.” He also discussed his ability to switch between politically correct and blunt tones as circumstances demand and mentioned preferring fast-food chains while on the road.

Separately, John Kasich used his allotted time to reflect on the emotional connections of retail politics, recounting a viral moment where he comforted and hugged a distraught young voter; he spoke about slowing down to listen to people and described how losing his parents shaped him. Jeb Bush defended his momentum, cited endorsements such as Sen. Lindsey Graham’s, and urged more focus on treatment over punishment for drug offenses while recounting personal memories of his wife Columba.

Men in Black 3, arriving 15 years after the original and a decade after its uneven sequel, reunites Agents J (Will Smith) and K (Tommy Lee Jones) in a time-travel caper that generally succeeds where No. 2 failed. The plot: Boris the Animal (Jemaine Clement), a vicious alien imprisoned on the Moon, escapes and goes back to 1969 to kill young Agent K and avert K’s later triumphs — and a protective shield he erected. J follows to save K, leading to encounters with bizarre Rick Baker-designed creatures, period-set set pieces (including a Chrysler Building freefall and a Cape Kennedy finale), and comic oddities like Griffin (Michael Stuhlbarg), who can foresee time-travel outcomes.

Critics praise the film’s surprises: its playful, sometimes tender riff on buddy-movie themes, and especially Josh Brolin’s uncanny, scene-stealing turn as young K — a performance capturing Tommy Lee Jones’s mannerisms better than prosthetics might. Reviews note flaws: creaky dialogue, uneven chemistry between Smith and Jones, 3-D excess, and occasional plot conveniences. Still, the movie delivers imaginative monsters, Hitchcockian locations, nostalgic 1969 moments (Bill Hader as Andy Warhol), and an affecting closing beat that deepens J and K’s relationship, making it an enjoyable, if imperfect, franchise revival.

Attorney General Eric Holder forcefully denied a Justice Department cover-up over Operation Fast and Furious during testimony before the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, calling the investigation politically motivated and insisting he has nothing to hide. Holder repeatedly said he never authorized gunwalking or the tactics used in the botched ATF sting and that when he learned of those methods he ordered them to stop. He acknowledged learning of the operation only in early 2011 and said he did not learn about Border Patrol Agent Brian Terry’s Dec. 2010 killing, where weapons tied to the operation were found, until a day after the death. Holder said internal investigations are underway and promised firings and possible charges against culpable officials within six months, though no one has yet been disciplined. Republicans, led by Chairman Darrell Issa, accused the Justice Department of withholding thousands of subpoenaed documents and threatened contempt proceedings; GOP members pointed to documents suggesting senior officials had greater knowledge than admitted. Democrats on the panel defended Holder, saying no evidence contradicts his testimony. The department has produced many documents and said it will provide more as allowed, while disputing GOP characterizations of certain communications as endorsing gunwalking.

President Trump publicly attacked Nordstrom after the retailer decided not to carry his daughter Ivanka Trump’s fashion line, calling the treatment of her brand “unfair” in a tweet. The dispute began when Nordstrom confirmed it wouldn’t buy the line for the season due to performance. Trump raised the issue publicly after his morning briefing, prompting the official @POTUS account and press secretary Sean Spicer to echo criticism, with Spicer framing Nordstrom’s move as a “direct attack” on administration policy. Instead of hurting the retailer, the episode coincided with a nearly 5 percent rise in Nordstrom’s shares by the close, possibly reflecting investor belief that the controversy would generate free publicity or bolster the chain’s profile in urban markets. T.J. Maxx also dropped the line the same day. The article includes unrelated notes about web archiving and Twitter location settings.

The International Professional Surrogates Association (IPSA), founded in 1973, is a nonprofit and leading authority on Surrogate Partner Therapy. IPSA’s mission is to advance the science, art, availability, training, ethics, and professional standards of surrogate partner therapy worldwide. It supports a community that includes surrogate partners, therapists, and clients by providing training, referrals, research participation, educational services, and fostering professional fellowship. IPSA requires rigorous preparation—surrogates must complete substantial human sexuality study and uphold ethical standards—so therapists can refer clients confidently.

The article profiles Larry Villarin, a 62-year-old California surrogate who has worked for decades helping people overcome sexual dysfunction, trauma, religious inhibition, disability, and lifelong virginity. Paid for therapeutic, guided intimacy sessions, Larry works with clients referred by psychologists to address emotional blocks that manifest physically or socially. Sessions begin conservatively: initial hours focus on history, goals, and non-sexual groundwork. Progression is gradual, often including guided touch, mirror work, blindfold trust exercises, and bodily awareness practices. Techniques range from modeling candid body acceptance to practical exercises—like hip-mobility drills or assisted use of dilators—paired with therapeutic support. Breakthroughs can be profound: clients who never imagined intimacy may learn to kiss, masturbate, or experience orgasm.

Larry stresses boundaries and ethics—avoiding romantic entanglement, keeping a therapeutic frame, and confronting legal gray areas since paying for sexual activity is illegal in the U.S. IPSA skirts explicit recognition of intercourse to distinguish therapy from prostitution. Despite risks and ethical complexities, Larry sees his role as a “gateway” facilitator: he helps clients rebuild trust, body image, and sexual confidence so they can pursue real-life relationships independently. The ultimate measure of success comes when clients leave empowered to continue their growth without him.

Tunisians celebrated the ouster of longtime president Zine El Abidine Ben Ali in January 2011, but much of the public fury targeted his wife Leila Trabelsi and her extended clan, blamed for rampant corruption and economic domination. Once a hairdresser, Leila’s family allegedly ran mafia-style rackets, extracting money from businesses and controlling stakes across banks, airlines, media, car dealerships, telecoms, hotels and retail, discouraging domestic investment and contributing to unemployment. After Ben Ali fled to Saudi Arabia, mobs looted and burned Trabelsi properties; reports said some relatives were attacked and at least one may have died. Authorities arrested dozens of Ben Ali family members and confiscated jewelry; investigations into corrupt enrichment were opened. Tunisia moved to place some assets under central bank control, ministers left the ruling party, and Switzerland froze Ben Ali–linked assets pending formal requests, reflecting efforts to curb illicit transfers.

A renewed wave of Libyan refugees has poured into Tunisia as Col. Muammar Gaddafi’s forces besiege western mountain towns, driving about 30,000 people to border areas like Tataouine. Rather than large camps, most refugees—many with only the clothes they fled in—are being sheltered by Tunisian families, some descendants of earlier Libyan refugees. Aid workers and UNHCR praised Tunisian generosity despite Tunisia’s own post-revolution strains, scarce infrastructure and high unemployment. Local centers coordinate housing, food, medical care and school placements, but authorities worry about long-term pressure. Meanwhile, the Libyan conflict spilled across the frontier at the Dehiba-Wazin crossing, provoking Tunisian outrage after brief clashes and shelling. In Libya, intense fighting and shelling continue, notably around Misrata, with rebels urging NATO action even as international divisions over strikes deepen.

A 41-year-old homeless man, identified by the Secret Service as James Dirk Crudup, was arrested after jumping the White House fence Tuesday evening. Uniformed Secret Service officers, guns drawn, tackled and handcuffed him on the North Lawn; CNN’s live broadcast showed him prone near the metal picket fence. He faces charges of unlawful entry and contempt of court for violating a prior order to stay away from the White House. Authorities did not immediately say whether he posed a security threat; a backpack found nearby is being examined. The area was briefly locked down and an all-clear was issued shortly after 9 p.m. The Secret Service noted similar recent breaches, including a separate incident where a 6-year-old slipped through the fence and was escorted out.

Jurgen Klinsmann’s tenure as coach of the U.S. men’s national soccer team ended abruptly Monday, days after a high-profile European trip and a public defense of his job. Klinsmann, who had been in Berlin Thursday attending a gala with President Obama and Chancellor Angela Merkel, returned home to California amid growing media criticism following two recent losses that significantly damaged the team’s chances of qualifying for the 2018 World Cup. After insisting in a Sunday interview that he was “very comfortable” in his position and not worried about being fired, Klinsmann was nonetheless dismissed following a meeting with senior U.S. Soccer executives Sunil Gulati and Dan Flynn at a Los Angeles-area hotel. The federation announced the decision without immediately naming a permanent successor; Bruce Arena, who previously managed the national team from 1998 to 2006, is expected to take over through the end of the current World Cup qualifying cycle. U.S. Soccer president Gulati said the federation still believes it has quality players capable of reaching the 2018 World Cup but concluded the team’s form and development required a change in direction. Gulati is scheduled to explain the reasoning for Klinsmann’s dismissal during a media conference call.

Advisers to Mitt Romney sharply blamed President Obama for the deadly Middle East protests and the killing of the U.S. ambassador in Libya, arguing such events would not have occurred under a Romney presidency. Senior advisers like Richard Williamson and Eliot Cohen portrayed Obama as weak, risk-averse, and inconsistent about U.S. commitments, criticizing his “lead-from-behind” approach and the administration’s handling of Egypt, Libya, Yemen and Syria. They asserted Romney would have offered clearer, steadier support for pluralism, rule of law and human dignity and would have a firmer strategy to deter threats such as Iran’s nuclear ambitions.

The Romney campaign pushed the foreign-policy debate to the forefront after Romney’s harsh comments were widely criticized; advisers defended the aggressive response as necessary and argued Romney’s repeated candidacies and experience distinguish him from a less seasoned Obama. Romney himself tempered rhetoric on the trail, emphasizing American strength without naming Obama directly.

The Obama campaign countered that the unrest was sparked by an inflammatory video, not U.S. policy, and warned against politicizing the crisis, while White House officials sought to clarify Obama’s comment that Egypt is a “work in progress,” noting that “ally” has legal meaning tied to mutual-defense treaties. The episode intensified scrutiny of both candidates’ foreign-policy approaches, with Romney’s team seeking to force a broader debate on U.S. leadership abroad.

Four bystanders helped prevent an even worse outcome during a Tucson shopping-center shooting that left six dead and 14 wounded, including Rep. Gabrielle Giffords. The shooter, identified as 22-year-old Jared Loughner, fired a semi-automatic Glock at a “Congress on Your Corner” event. Patricia Maisch, Bill Badger, Roger Salzgeber and Joseph Zamudio subdued him as he tried to reload: Maisch grabbed the magazine while Badger and Salzgeber tackled the assailant and Zamudio helped hold him down. Badger, a 74-year-old retired Army colonel, described grappling with Loughner and being grazed by a bullet. Authorities recovered a letter and notes linking Loughner to Giffords and charged him with attempted assassination and related federal counts. Pima County Sheriff Clarence Dupnik criticized inflammatory political rhetoric and Arizona’s permissive gun laws as possible contributors to such violence.

Lexington School District Two clarified that a substitute teacher arrested for appearing intoxicated at Brookland-Cayce High School was not a district employee but worked for Kelly Services, the district’s substitute staffing contractor. The incident occurred Friday, March 10, 2017, when school staff reported the substitute behaving erratically and possibly under the influence. Administrators immediately removed her from the classroom and handed her to the School Resource Officer. The Lexington County Sheriff’s Department arrested 52-year-old Judith Elizabeth Richards-Gartee of Irmo; she was found with an open container of alcohol, charged with disorderly conduct, and released to paramedics who transported her to a hospital. Law enforcement said it will not release further information. The district indicated criminal charges have been filed against the Kelly employee.

James Gandolfini, the acclaimed actor best known as Tony Soprano on HBO’s landmark series The Sopranos, died at 51 of a confirmed heart attack while on vacation in Rome en route to the Taormina Film Festival. Gandolfini reshaped television as the complex New Jersey mob boss across six seasons (1999–2007), earning three Emmys and widespread critical and popular acclaim; the series became a cornerstone of premium TV and one of HBO’s most successful shows. Beyond Tony, he built a diverse career in film, stage and production, appearing in movies such as True Romance, The Taking of Pelham 1 2 3, Zero Dark Thirty and The Incredible Burt Wonderstone, and earning a Tony nomination for God of Carnage. He produced documentaries on veterans and executive produced HBO projects including Hemingway & Gellhorn. At the time of his death he was set to star in HBO’s Criminal Justice and had completed roles in upcoming films including Enough Said and Animal Rescue. Tributes flowed from colleagues and creators like David Chase, who called him “a genius,” and HBO, which mourned the loss of a “gentle and loving” man. He is survived by his wife Deborah Lin, their daughter Liliana, son Michael, and two sisters.

President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un met in Singapore in a historic summit aimed at reducing the nuclear standoff on the Korean Peninsula. The two leaders held nearly four hours of talks, exchanged compliments and handshakes, signed a joint document committing to work toward peace, and shared a public lunch. Trump described the meeting as going “better than expected” and expressed optimism that the summit “could work out very nicely,” while White House officials said discussions had progressed “more quickly than expected.” 

Despite the upbeat optics and a rare, affable public appearance by Kim—who toured Singapore’s waterfront attractions—U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo cautioned that North Korea’s sincerity on denuclearization remained unclear. Pompeo emphasized the summit should establish a framework for the “hard work that will follow,” demanding complete, verifiable and irreversible denuclearization and warning that sanctions would stay in place or increase if diplomacy faltered. 

Analysts remained skeptical that Kim would relinquish nuclear weapons central to his regime’s security, viewing his outreach as aimed at sanctions relief. The summit marked a dramatic shift from the prior year’s hostile rhetoric and opened a diplomatic channel for further negotiations, though observers warned that without a clear, mutual understanding of denuclearization, any process initiated could founder. The meeting was positioned as a first step toward a longer negotiation process rather than a final settlement.

France’s National Assembly approved a controversial bill to legalize same-sex marriage and allow adoption by same-sex couples, voting 329 to 229 with 10 abstentions. The measure, a key pledge of President François Hollande and described by supporters as a major equality advance, now moves to the Senate before becoming law. The debate has been deeply divisive: gay-rights groups and many left-wing lawmakers back the reform, while the Roman Catholic Church, other religious communities, hundreds of mayors and social conservatives strongly oppose it, staging large protests. France would join several countries permitting same-sex marriage; related issues like assisted reproductive technology for lesbians remain deferred.

Christina Grimmie’s family and team expressed deep gratitude for the overwhelming support after her June 10 death. Her parents Bud and Tina and brother Marcus thanked fans, peers and the entertainment community for memorials, donations and tributes, saying Christina’s joyful spirit, voice and faith touched many and will live on. Manager Brian Teefey, grieving and likening Christina to a daughter, set up a GoFundMe to help the family and cover expenses so they can focus on recovery; donations surpassed $100,000. Maroon 5 frontman and Grimmie’s former The Voice coach Adam Levine offered to pay for her funeral and flight, a gesture Marcus publicly acknowledged. Grimmie, 22, was fatally shot by 27-year-old Kevin James Loibl after a post-show meet-and-greet; her brother intervened and Loibl killed himself.

Actor Harrison Ford was injured but expected to recover after the World War II–era single-engine plane he was piloting crash-landed on the Penmar Golf Course in Venice, California, shortly after takeoff on March 5, 2015. Ford, a longtime aviator, reported engine trouble to air traffic control and attempted to return to Santa Monica Airport before the aircraft clipped a tree and went down on the green. Witnesses and two nearby doctors rushed to his aid; paramedics later treated him at the scene and he was transported to a hospital conscious and breathing. Fire and NTSB officials described the emergency landing as skillfully handled, with no other injuries reported. Ford’s publicist and son both said his injuries were non-life-threatening—he was “battered, but OK” and expected to make a full recovery. Aerial footage captured the aftermath, and investigators were working to determine the crash’s cause. Ford has previously spoken about his love of flying and survived earlier aviation incidents.

On November 22, 2013 the FDA issued a warning letter to 23andMe ordering the company to stop marketing its Saliva Collection Kit and Personal Genome Service (PGS) because it lacks required premarket authorization. The agency said PGS functions as a medical device—providing risk reports on hundreds of diseases, carrier status, and drug responses—and many intended uses raise significant health risks if results are inaccurate (e.g., BRCA risk, warfarin dosing). FDA concluded 23andMe failed to provide adequate analytical and clinical validation despite extensive interactions since 2009, submitted 510(k) notifications that were considered withdrawn, and continued to expand marketing without approval. The agency deemed the product adulterated and misbranded under the FD&C Act and demanded written corrective actions within 15 working days or face enforcement such as seizure, injunction, or fines. 23andMe acknowledged receiving the letter and pledged to work with FDA. Observers said the action could clarify regulatory expectations for direct-to-consumer genetic testing, balancing consumer access to genetic information with public health safeguards.

An Egyptian man, Taymour el-Sobky (also reported as el-Sobki), was sentenced to three years in prison with hard labor after claiming on a December television talk show that a large proportion of married Egyptian women are prone to infidelity. State-run Al-Ahram reported he said "thirty percent of women have a readiness for immorality," while other reports cited a figure of about 45 percent. Video clips of the remarks circulated on social media, triggering public outrage, complaints to prosecutors and legal action on grounds of "spreading false news" and harming public peace and interest. Prosecutors pursued the case and a court convicted him; he retains the right to appeal. The verdict sparked debate about free speech and selective law enforcement in Egypt. Rights lawyer Gamal Eid argued el-Sobky’s comments, though offensive to many, did not constitute a crime and compared the prosecution to other recent punitive measures taken against public figures—such as the expulsion of MP Tawfiq Okasha after meeting Israel’s ambassador, and criminal convictions of cultural figures like author Ahmed Naji, TV presenter Islam Behery and writer Fatma Naoot. Critics say these actions reflect a broader pattern under President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi in which the state has intensified crackdowns—initially targeting Islamists and activists and widening to encompass nonpolitical individuals, artists and intellectuals—often driven by public pressure and applied inconsistently, raising concerns about the future of speech and creativity in Egypt.

Rosemont authorities have closed the investigation into 19-year-old Kenneka Jenkins’ death, concluding it was accidental and finding “no evidence that indicates any other conclusion.” Jenkins was found Sept. 10 in a walk-in freezer at the Crowne Plaza Chicago O’Hare Hotel after attending a party the previous night. The Cook County Medical Examiner ruled the cause of death hypothermia, listing alcohol intoxication and the medication topiramate as contributing factors; toxicology and autopsy found no trauma or evidence of drugging.

Rosemont police released extensive records, surveillance video, audio, and numerous postmortem photographs showing Jenkins’ body in the freezer. Police say their probe produced 135 reports, interviews with 44 people (30 confirmed at the party), hours of video review, phone forensics, photo line-ups and warrants. Surveillance shows Jenkins stumbling through halls and entering the hotel kitchen alone; motion sensors indicate no one else entered the freezer area between when she did and when her body was discovered. Investigators also say the hotel room had been booked with a fraudulent credit card and are pursuing suspects tied to that scheme.

Jenkins’ family attorneys criticized the graphic photos shown to them and posted online, calling them disturbing, indecent, and raising unanswered questions—particularly why portions of her clothing were displaced. Experts note “paradoxical undressing” can occur in severe hypothermia, explaining partial disrobing. Police and the medical examiner maintain the accidental-hypothermia conclusion, but the released materials and family objections have left public questions and online speculation unresolved.

A drunk male passenger was offloaded from an IndiGo flight bound for Kolkata on September 24 after attempting to enter the cockpit to charge his mobile phone, authorities and airline officials said. The incident occurred while the aircraft was still on the ground in Mumbai. The captain of flight 6E-395 initiated the passenger’s removal “on grounds of a security violation” and the man, said to be about 35 years old, was handed over to airport police. He was questioned at the police station and subsequently released without charges after officers found no offence to prosecute. The airline reiterated that passengers are prohibited from entering the cockpit.

The report also noted two other recent in-flight safety lapses in India. On September 22 a first-time flyer on a GoAir flight from New Delhi to Patna attempted to open a rear door mid-flight—apparently mistaking it for a lavatory—but was stopped by another passenger and later handed to police after landing; cabin pressure would have prevented the door opening. Separately, more than 30 passengers on a Jaipur-bound flight were hospitalized with nosebleeds, headaches and ear pain after crew reportedly failed to pressurize the cabin. These incidents highlight continuing concerns about passenger behavior and operational safety measures.

The U.S. Olympic Committee has initiated a formal process that could strip USA Gymnastics of its status as the sport’s national governing body after the organization declined a voluntary surrender of recognition. The USOC filed a Section 8 complaint 16 days earlier, citing the organization’s failures in the aftermath of the widespread sexual abuse by former national team doctor Larry Nassar, who pleaded guilty to child pornography and sexual abuse charges and is serving an effective life sentence. More than 350 survivors have come forward, including prominent Olympians.

USA Gymnastics responded to the USOC by refusing to relinquish recognition and instead raised questions about the complaint and hearing procedures. USOC CEO Sarah Hirshland said she will move forward, selecting a three-person panel—chaired by a USOC board member with representatives from the NGB and athlete advisory councils—to hear evidence and legal arguments. The panel will report and recommend action to the USOC board, which will make the final decision; the bylaws set no fixed timeline, and Hirshland estimated the process could take weeks or months.

Until a final decision, USA Gymnastics will continue to operate. If derecognized, the USOC would assume control of elite programs while a new NGB is identified; members and functions would likely migrate to that new body. USA Gymnastics has endured leadership churn, loss of sponsors, survivor mediation, and controversies—most recently revelations about previously undisclosed medical records and the indictment of former CEO Steve Penny for evidence tampering—that the USOC cites as reasons for intervention. The federation maintains it inherited a crisis and is attempting reforms, but the USOC concluded revocation remains the right course.

When a film diverges from its trailers it can disappoint—or delight. Creed, officially Rocky 7, proves to be the latter: a sequel that honors the Rocky legacy while standing on its own. Rather than the brutal boxing melodrama marketing hinted at, Ryan Coogler’s film introduces fresh characters and emotions while leaning into the familiar themes and gambits of classic fight pictures. It unabashedly manipulates the audience—milking tears, piling on hardships, then delivering a wholesome, uplifting finale—but does so with sincerity and charm. The story is straightforward: Adonis Johnson Creed, the out-of-wedlock son of the late heavyweight champion Apollo Creed, grows up shadowboxing and craving his father’s spotlight even though Apollo died in the ring. Adonis, a journeyman fighter hardened by a rough upbringing, wants to rise through the ranks and must protect his fragile soul along the way. Michael B. Jordan, who impressed in Coogler’s Fruitvale Station, brings considerable depth to Adonis, balancing a combative instinct with genuine ambivalence about embracing the sport that claimed his father. Seeking guidance, Adonis travels to Philadelphia to recruit Apollo’s old rival-turned-friend, Rocky Balboa. Sylvester Stallone, now 69, returns in a touching, low-key performance: he’s not the central figure but remains central to the film’s heart. Stallone’s Rocky is an aged, endearing presence—shy smiles, sad eyes, and a shuffling dignity—perfect as mentor and emotional anchor. The chemistry between Stallone and Jordan fuels the training montages and the film’s soul. Tessa Thompson adds depth as Adonis’s demanding, honest girlfriend. Creed unfolds through three pivotal fight sequences—one presented in a nearly uncut barrage—yet it avoids villainy, framing the protagonist’s greatest opponent as himself. The climactic title fight delivers cathartic thrills, but the film’s most stirring moment is a quietly nostalgic image: Rocky and Adonis ascending the Philadelphia Museum of Art steps, a scene that leaves viewers torn between cheering and reaching for a handkerchief. Rating: 3.5/4 stars; PG-13.

Investigators have been piecing together the final movements of the Hart family after a 2003 GMC Yukon plunged off a Mendocino County cliff on March 26, killing parents Jennifer and Sarah Hart and three of their six adopted children, while three other children remain missing and presumed dead. Based on cellphone pings and surveillance footage, authorities say the family was in the Newport, Oregon, area about 8:15 a.m. on March 24 and then drove south along US-101, switching to California’s Highway 1 at Leggett. They reached the Fort Bragg area by about 8 p.m. on March 24 and stayed in that vicinity through the evening of March 25. A grainy Safeway surveillance image from Fort Bragg taken at 8:05 a.m. March 25 appears to show Jennifer Hart buying groceries; investigators are working with the FBI to enhance the footage but have no confirmed sightings of the rest of the family after that time until a German tourist reported the overturned SUV on March 26. 

Authorities believe the vehicle stopped in a pullout near the cliff edge and then accelerated off the road without any skid marks, with the SUV later recovered about 70 feet down the embankment. Data from the vehicle suggest the crash may have been intentional: investigators cite airbag evidence, lack of tire friction at the turnout, and a speedometer pinned at 90 mph (which might have been affected by the crash). 

The three children found dead at the scene were Markis, 19; Jeremiah, 14; and Abigail, 14. The three missing children are Devonte, 15; Hannah, 16; and Sierra, 12. Searches along roughly 20 miles of shoreline from the crash site toward Fort Bragg have been planned. 

The investigation has also examined the family’s background. Neighbors and a former friend reported concerns of food deprivation and abuse dating back to 2013; Child Protective Services had contact but prosecutors said there was insufficient evidence then to act. Sarah Hart had a 2011 Minnesota conviction for domestic assault involving a child. Authorities searched the family’s Woodland, Washington, home and served a warrant while continuing to probe motive and the full timeline leading up to the crash.

Two Chechen-born brothers who had appeared to be living the American immigrant dream became the focus of a massive manhunt after police identified them as suspects in the Boston Marathon bombings. Tamerlan Tsarnaev, 26, a talented heavyweight boxer who aspired to the Olympics, died in a shootout with police. His younger brother, 19-year-old Dzhokhar, a recent Cambridge Rindge & Latin graduate, scholarship recipient and wrestler, was captured after hiding in a boat.
