Neighbors, coaches and classmates described the brothers as quiet, unassuming and, at times, devout Muslims; friends expressed shock and disbelief. Family accounts painted a mixed picture: parents who returned to Dagestan, an uncle condemning them and suggesting they were “radicalized,” and reports of Tamerlan’s increasing religiosity. The FBI revealed it interviewed Tamerlan in early 2011 after a foreign tip alleging he followed radical Islam and planned to travel to join underground groups; investigators then found no terrorism links. Authorities continued probing whether the brothers acted alone or with others and examined travel, internet activity and associations for missed warning signs. The attacks killed three, wounded many, and prompted intense scrutiny of both the family’s background and U.S. intelligence work.

A retrospective cohort study published in BMJ analyzed mortality among 9,889 former Olympic athletes (games 1896–1936) to compare long-term survival across sports varying in cardiovascular intensity, static/dynamic load, bodily collision risk, and physical contact. After adjusting for birth year, sex, and nationality, athletes in high cardiovascular–intensity disciplines (e.g., cycling, rowing) showed no survival advantage over those in low-intensity sports (e.g., golf, cricket); hazard ratios for moderate and high intensity were essentially neutral. By contrast, athletes in sports with high physical contact had a significantly higher mortality risk (about 13–16% increased hazard), and those in disciplines with high risk of bodily collision showed increased mortality in univariate analysis. Authors suggest accumulated microtrauma and repeated injuries—including head blows—may underlie worse long-term outcomes. Findings caution against assuming ever-greater intensity yields greater longevity, highlight harms of contact injuries, and are tempered by historic cohort limits, changes in modern training and care, and potential confounders such as lifetime training duration and post-competitive activity.

Famous Halley’s Comet is producing the Eta Aquarid meteor shower, visible pre-dawn on May 5–6 as Earth passes through Halley’s debris stream. The shower’s radiant rises with Aquarius; viewing is best from about 3 a.m. local time until dawn. Under dark, clear skies away from light pollution observers can expect roughly 10–20 meteors per hour, with May 5 likely offering a slightly stronger display though its precise peak occurs during daylight. The Eta Aquarids are exceptionally fast—around 240,000 km/h (about 148,000 mph)—and can produce persistent “meteor trains,” faint glowing trails that linger seconds to minutes. These trains may result from ionized air recombining or chemiluminescence from vaporized metals; more observations are needed. Online viewing is available via Slooh’s live show.

Last night’s Democratic National Convention featured a surprising moment when Barack Obama appeared to kiss Jill Biden, provoking questions about whether it was intentional or an awkward greeting. The piece riffs on accidental kisses—how they can spark romance with a crush, be laughed off with friends, or be mortifying when involving inappropriate people like bosses or relatives. Media outlets teased Obama’s history of affectionate gestures with prominent women—portrayed humorously as a presidential penchant for smoochey moments—citing playful interactions with Diane Sawyer and Hillary Clinton, and suggesting he once “accidentally” kissed Jill Biden. Coverage also recalls an awkward exchange between Obama and France’s First Lady Carla Bruni at a NATO summit, where an anticipated cheek kiss initially failed, later resolved at dinner. The story mixes satire and gossip with international protocol notes and fashion commentary on Michelle Obama and Bruni’s outfits at the event.

Former Dallas police officer Amber Guyger was indicted on murder charges in the September shooting death of 26-year-old Botham Shem Jean after a grand jury reviewed evidence more than two months after her initial manslaughter arrest. Guyger, who was off-duty but in uniform, says she mistakenly entered Jean’s apartment believing it was her own, confronted him in the dark, issued verbal commands he did not follow, and then shot him once in the torso. Jean died at a hospital. Guyger turned herself in, posted bond, and was later fired by the Dallas Police Department.

Dallas County District Attorney Faith Johnson said prosecutors presented evidence showing the shooting was “knowing,” elevating the charge to murder rather than manslaughter. Guyger’s attorney called the indictment the result of “vindictive emotion” and asserted the shooting was a tragic mistake. Jean’s family and civil-rights groups called the indictment a step toward accountability; his mother described the killing as an unjust violation. The case prompted public protests and scrutiny of police practices. The Dallas Police Department announced efforts to reform training and civilian oversight. Jean’s family has also filed a federal lawsuit alleging excessive force and systemic problems in the department. The case could take more than a year to reach trial.

Coca-Cola has introduced its first alcoholic beverages in Japan: three lemon-flavored fizzy “alcopop” drinks launched to tap a growing market of young drinkers, particularly women. Described by the company as a unique move in its 125‑plus year history, the trio carries alcohol content from 3% to 8% and is modeled on Japan’s popular Chu‑Hi (shochu highball) canned drinks—local mixes of spirit and fruit flavors dominated by firms such as Suntory, Asahi and Kirin. Lemon, a leading citrus flavor in the Chu‑Hi category, is the focus of Coca‑Cola’s entry. The company has kept the recipe private, in line with tradition, and says there are no plans to roll the new range out beyond Japan. The launch drew consumer interest at sampling events, underscoring the appeal of ready‑to‑drink alcoholic sodas. The move mirrors past alcopop booms in Europe and the UK during the 1990s with products like Smirnoff Ice and Bacardi Breezer, which were popular but also controversial for allegedly encouraging underage or increased drinking because of their soft‑drink–like taste.

After two weeks of tense negotiations in Cancún, more than 190 countries adopted the "Cancún Agreements," a compromise package that revived faith in the UN climate process even as critics said it falls short of what scientists deem necessary. The deal — reached amid dramatic late-night exchanges and a lone protest from Bolivia, which denounced the outcome as insufficient and accused the chair of overriding consensus rules — commits all countries to actions to curb greenhouse gas emissions for the first time, while stopping short of a new legally binding treaty. Key elements include recognition of the goal to limit warming to 2°C, strengthened monitoring, reporting and verification of mitigation efforts by both developed and developing nations, and provisions to boost transparency on climate finance. The package establishes a "green fund" and mechanisms for technology transfer and reduced deforestation, aimed at helping vulnerable countries adapt; wealthy nations signaled willingness to consider extending the Kyoto Protocol and to increase mitigation pledges, though specific targets and a global emissions peak date were not set. Supporters called the outcome a crucial step that restores momentum and lays groundwork for a stronger deal in Durban; environmental groups warned the text is vague and risks insufficient ambition. Overall, Cancún delivered modest but tangible progress and bought the multilateral process more time to build a more binding, ambitious framework.

Researchers studying guenon monkeys conclude that the species’ strikingly varied facial patterns evolved to prevent crossbreeding. Guenons — a diverse group of more than 25 (possibly up to 35) forest-dwelling African monkeys — often live, travel and sleep alongside other guenon species, raising the risk of hybrid matings that could produce infertile or unfit offspring. To test the long-standing hypothesis that faces serve as species-recognition signals, teams from New York University, Exeter and the University of Hull photographed 22 species in zoos and a Nigerian sanctuary and analyzed over 150 individuals using human face-recognition algorithms (the eigenface technique). The program showed that facial features are highly consistent within species but more visually distinctive from those species with which they co-occur. The findings, published in Nature Communications, provide strong evidence of visual character displacement: species evolve appearances that maximize distinction from nearby relatives to reinforce reproductive isolation. The researchers plan further work to determine whether divergence reflects current or historical sympatry.

A new ABC News/Washington Post poll shows Mitt Romney and Sarah Palin leading the Republican field in primary preference, but with starkly different general-election prospects. Romney ties Barack Obama nationally (47-47) and leads 49-46 among registered voters, drawing strong support from Republicans, conservatives, Tea Party backers and independents. His standing is aided by appeal to higher-income and college-educated voters, though his 2006 Massachusetts health-care law and Mormon faith remain vulnerabilities with some GOP constituencies. Palin’s primary bounce contrasts with deep negatives: 64% say they “definitely would not” vote for her and 63% deem her unqualified; 42% of Republicans rule her out. Overall voter frustration is high: 89% view the economy negatively, 59% disapprove of Obama’s economic handling, and the ABC Frustration Index mirrors midterm-era anger, especially among independents and conservatives. While Obama retains core Democratic support, economic pessimism leaves his re-election path narrow and sensitive to further economic deterioration.

Sen. Dianne Feinstein, chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, accused the CIA of improperly searching a standalone computer network set up for congressional investigators reviewing the agency’s Bush-era detention and interrogation program. Feinstein said the CIA conducted the search in January, potentially violating an agreement about monitoring committee use of CIA-provided computers housed in a secure facility. She characterized the action as a possible breach of separation of powers, the Fourth Amendment, the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, and an executive order prohibiting domestic CIA searches, and called it an intimidation of investigators. Feinstein has demanded an apology and acknowledgment of wrongdoing but said she received none. The CIA’s inspector general referred the matter to the Justice Department for possible criminal prosecution. CIA Director John Brennan denied the agency spied on the committee, telling NBC News the CIA wasn’t trying to thwart the investigation and respects separation of powers; he supported probing any misconduct. The White House declined to say if laws were broken but affirmed confidence in Brennan. Feinstein noted her panel has obtained more than 6.2 million pages of documents about interrogation policies and emphasized she spoke out to correct inaccurate reports, prompting praise from colleagues including Sen. Patrick Leahy and Majority Leader Harry Reid.

A review of 14 studies analyzed by Cornell’s Food and Brand Lab finds adults eat nearly everything they serve themselves: on average 92% of the food they put on their plates. Lead researcher Brian Wansink and co-author Katherine Abowd Johnson examined 1,179 diners across eight countries (United States, Canada, France, Taiwan, South Korea, Finland and the Netherlands) and found remarkably consistent results across sexes, settings (home or lab), and nations. Eating while distracted slightly reduced consumption (to about 89%), and people consumed a greater share of meals (92.8%) than snacks (76.1%). Healthier choices were eaten at higher rates—about 91.2% of fruits, vegetables, whole grains and lean proteins versus 80.6% of less healthful foods. By contrast, children ate far less of what they served themselves, roughly 59–60%, possibly because they are less certain they will like the food. The researchers focused on portions people serve themselves to fill a gap in understanding how self-served portion size relates to intake, noting that many obesity studies measure either what people take or what they are served. Their preliminary evidence suggests a simple behavioral implication: because people tend to consume almost all they plate, being mindful about how much one dished up can help control intake. Wansink advises reconsidering portion size before serving to support healthier eating.

The Trump administration moved to revive ZTE Corp., China’s second-largest telecommunications equipment maker, by negotiating a deal that would lift a U.S. ban if the company pays a large fine, replaces management, and installs U.S. compliance officers. The ban, imposed in April, had prohibited ZTE from buying U.S. technology for seven years after it violated sanctions by illegally shipping U.S. goods to Iran and North Korea and then breaching a subsequent settlement. The reported arrangement would require ZTE to pay up to $1.3 billion, allow U.S. monitors, and resume purchases from U.S. suppliers such as Qualcomm, steps President Trump described in a tweet. Commerce officials briefed Congress on the proposal, and Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross was expected to announce resolution efforts during talks in China.

The prospect of easing penalties sparked bipartisan backlash on Capitol Hill. Senators including Marco Rubio and Chuck Schumer warned the administration not to reward a firm tied to national security risks; intelligence and law enforcement officials have long expressed concerns that ZTE and similar Chinese vendors could enable spying. Critics also highlighted ZTE’s extensive record of intellectual property disputes, noting dozens of patent suits worldwide and patterns of nonpayment and evasive conduct in licensing arrangements—behavior that undermines U.S. IP interests. Some see the reported deal as part of broader U.S.-China trade negotiations, possibly tied to agricultural or tariff concessions. ZTE has suffered heavy losses since the ban, and U.S. suppliers exposed to ZTE saw share gains on the news of a potential resolution.

A new Islamic State (Isis) media arm called the Zora Foundation has begun distributing guidance aimed specifically at women supporting fighters in Syria and Iraq. Unlike typical Isis propaganda that targets male recruits or showcases violence, Zora focuses on instructing women in roles the group deems appropriate: domestic and supportive tasks. Its Arabic-language material—videos, tweets and posts—carries the slogan “preparing for the honour of jihad” and has gained over 2,000 followers within weeks. Content includes a recipe framed as nourishment for mujahidin “between battles,” and an animated YouTube video promoting “feminine manual labour” such as cooking, nursing, first aid, sewing, and running propaganda workshops (slide-show creation and editing). Charlie Winter of the Quilliam Foundation says Zora is the first media organisation he’s seen providing an organised guideline for women’s roles: preparing others for jihad and sustaining fighters, rather than direct combat. The accounts appear targeted at Arab women, though he notes women from countries like Saudi Arabia also travel to Syria and Iraq. Separately, reporting on Turkey–Syria trade highlights how border chaos has enabled robust commercial flows—legal on Turkish records—where various armed groups extract fees, reinforcing a war economy as goods transit through contested crossings, profiting Turkish traders and entrenching non-state control of cross-border commerce.

McDonald’s has sharply cut the price of its Mighty Wings after disappointing national sales. Originally launched nationally in September 2013 at roughly $1 per wing, the bone-in wings underperformed outside test markets that skewed towards heavier wing demand. This week the chain began a national advertising push for Mighty Wings priced at $3 for a five-piece pack — about 60 cents per wing, a roughly 40% reduction. McDonald’s says its earlier regional tests (notably Atlanta and Chicago) didn’t reflect broader consumer tolerance for the wings’ price or spiciness. The recipe hasn’t changed, but the company now emphasizes that the wings have a noticeable spicy kick. Analysts say the new price likely reduces or eliminates margins on the product; Wedbush’s Nick Setyan estimates operating margins on wings fell by about 10 percentage points and suggests McDonald’s will sell at or near cost until existing inventory is depleted. The chain reportedly held about 10 million pounds of frozen wings after the initial launch. Industry observers note that if the discounted price drives sufficient sales, Mighty Wings could remain on menus, but continued weak demand would probably end further attempts.

Pakistani officials say one of Osama bin Laden’s sons may have disappeared during the U.S. Navy SEAL raid that killed the al-Qaeda leader in Abbottabad. Interrogations of three widows held by Pakistani intelligence reportedly revealed a son had not been seen since the operation; sources speculated it could be Hamza bin Laden, the 19–20‑year‑old dubbed the “Crown Prince of Terror.” Hamza, who appeared in propaganda videos and was alleged to be groomed for leadership and implicated in plots including Benazir Bhutto’s assassination, has uncertain status—initial U.S. accounts presumed him dead but later identified another son, 22‑year‑old Khalid, as killed. Pakistani authorities detained family members and children from the compound and have delayed U.S. access to the widows for questioning. Separately, new details of the raid revealed President Obama insisted on a large task force and backup helicopters and specialist teams to ensure capture or recovery, prepared to fight their way out if necessary.

Researchers mapped water (H2O) and its heavy isotope-bearing form (HDO) across Mars using infrared observations from Keck II, NASA’s Infrared Telescope Facility, and the ESO Very Large Telescope over six years. The global atmospheric maps reveal strong spatial variation in the deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio (D/H). Sublimation from the north polar cap releases water with D/H about seven times that of Earth's ocean (VSMOW), and some basins and depressions show even higher enrichment, while high-altitude regions exhibit much lower values (1–3 VSMOW). These atmospheric measurements imply that polar water ice reservoirs are enriched to at least ~8 VSMOW. Because loss of lighter hydrogen to space preferentially leaves heavier deuterium behind, the elevated D/H indicates massive cumulative water loss from Mars over geological time.

Using the measured enrichment and estimated escape histories, the team infers that early Mars held a global equivalent water layer at least 137 meters deep. In practice, the water likely pooled in a deep northern ocean covering roughly 20% of the planet’s surface—comparable in areal extent to Earth’s Atlantic—and reaching depths of about a mile in places, with a total volume around 20 million cubic kilometers (more than the Arctic Ocean). Much of that water was subsequently lost to space as the atmosphere thinned and the planet cooled, leaving about 13% of the original volume trapped today in polar ice.

These findings strengthen the view that early Mars was warm and wet for extended periods—long enough to support persistent lakes, rivers, deltas, and possibly habitable conditions. While the existence of life remains unproven, the prolonged presence of surface water increases the plausibility that Mars could once have supported life.

Iran’s morality police have intensified enforcement against Barbie dolls, ordering Tehran shopkeepers to conceal or remove the dolls from display as part of a wider campaign to block Western cultural influence deemed harmful to Islamic values. Although Iran declared Barbie un-Islamic in 1996, the doll remained openly sold until a new directive about three weeks ago forced shopkeepers to hide Barbie behind other toys to avoid closure. Attempts to replace Barbie with state-approved dolls—Sara and Dara, introduced in 2002 and dressed in traditional, modest clothes—have failed to win children’s favor, parents and merchants say. Mothers report children prefer Barbie and reject the government alternatives; some stores now display modestly dressed dolls in windows while selling Barbies secretly. The crackdown is framed domestically as part of a long-running effort since the 1979 revolution to purge Western culture—enforcing dress codes and banning Western media. In a related nationalist gesture, Iranian media reported a local company will produce toy models of the U.S. RQ-170 Sentinel drone Iran captured in December. State radio said the company will send a one-eightieth scale model to the U.S. government in response to Washington’s request for return, which Tehran rejected, calling the drone’s presence an invasion; the miniatures will also be sold domestically for roughly $4.

President Barack Obama called Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to congratulate him on his election victory but warned the United States would “reassess” aspects of the U.S.-Israel relationship after Netanyahu’s pre-election rejection of a Palestinian state. The White House said Obama reiterated long-standing U.S. support for a two-state solution and would evaluate options in light of Netanyahu’s campaign statements. Netanyahu later softened his stance in U.S. media, telling MSNBC he still supports “a sustainable, peaceful two-state solution” under conditions he first outlined in 2009: a demilitarized Palestinian state whose leadership recognizes Israel as a Jewish state. He blamed changing realities, including a Palestinian unity pact with Hamas and security threats, for his campaign rhetoric and stressed Palestinian leaders must abandon Hamas and negotiate genuinely. 

U.S. officials signaled they would watch the composition and policy of Netanyahu’s incoming coalition before deciding policy moves; they have also not ruled out supporting a U.N. Security Council resolution defining two-state parameters or other U.N. actions, a shift from longstanding opposition to unilateral moves. White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest criticized Netanyahu’s election-day remark about Arab voters as undermining shared values. Netanyahu emphasized the “unbreakable bond” with the United States and downplayed personal tensions with Obama, while Israeli opposition figures expressed dismay at his inconsistent positions. U.S. officials stressed continued military and security cooperation even as diplomatic stances are reconsidered.

French publisher Seuil has announced the forthcoming publication of a newly discovered sketchbook by post‑Impressionist master Vincent van Gogh, to be released in November under the title Vincent Van Gogh, Le Brouillard d’Arles (The Fog of Arles). Seuil official Bernard Comment described the find as “stunning, dazzling,” and said the sketchbook had been known only to its owners, himself and the publisher. Few details about the sketches’ provenance or how they were discovered have been released; Seuil said more information will be revealed at a world press conference in Paris in mid‑November, on the eve of the book’s international release. The announcement has generated anticipation and curiosity about the previously unseen works.

The Smithsonian’s National Zoo reported that the smaller of two giant panda cubs born August 22 to 17-year-old Mei Xiang died Wednesday after going into respiratory and cardiac arrest. Staff had attempted oxygen, aerosolized antibiotics and mucus-breaking medication and performed brief CPR, but could not revive the tiny cub, which weighed about 3 ounces at birth. A necropsy will seek the cause. Mei Xiang, artificially inseminated in April, gave birth to twins five hours apart; the larger cub, born first at 4.8 ounces, is described as strong, robust and behaving normally. Zoo staff had been rotating the cubs so each could nurse; the smaller had shown regurgitation and was considered high-risk. This follows previous cub losses in 2012 and 2013; Mei Xiang has two surviving offspring from 2013 and 2005.

Algerian special forces ended a four-day siege at the In Amenas gas complex after Islamist militants seized hostages following an attack on buses bringing workers to the remote site. Algerian authorities said 32 attackers were killed; initial reports listed at least 23 hostages dead, but subsequent searches by demining teams uncovered dozens more bodies, raising the death toll to at least 81. Many bodies were badly disfigured, complicating identification; officials cautioned a definitive tally was pending. The attackers, from multiple countries and linked to Mokhtar Belmokhtar’s Masked Brigade, said the operation protested French action in Mali, though planners may have prepared earlier. Algeria rejected foreign military involvement in securing its energy sites and insisted it would bolster domestic protection. Western leaders condemned the assault as terrorism or an “act of war.” Numerous nationals — including Britons, Americans, Filipinos, French, Norwegians, Malaysians and Japanese — were among the dead, injured, missing, or freed.

Vatican circles were rocked when L’Espresso magazine published the full 191-page draft of Pope Francis’ environment encyclical “Laudato Si” three days before its scheduled release, prompting an internal hunt for the leaker and the suspension of veteran Vatican correspondent Sandro Magister’s press credentials. The Vatican insisted the posted text was a draft, but media outlets treated it as authoritative because it echoed themes Francis and advisers had publicly promoted: that global warming is largely human-caused, the burning of fossil fuels must be curtailed, and radical behavioral change is needed to protect the planet and shield the poor from environmental harm. L’Espresso’s editor, not Magister, later claimed responsibility for obtaining and publishing the document; Magister said he only wrote the introduction and had promised to keep the scoop confidential. Commentators speculated the leak aimed to blunt the impact of the official launch—where the Vatican planned a diverse panel including a cardinal, an Orthodox theologian, an atheist scientist and an economist—or to manipulate public reception amid pre-release conservative attacks, particularly from U.S. critics uneasy with the pope addressing scientific matters. Italian media suggested the leak might have originated from conservative Vatican insiders resisting Francis’ reforms. Yet leaks had been likely: drafts circulated for months and translations were prepared in advance. The episode recalled the 2012 “Vatileaks” scandal, which led to criminal code changes in Vatican City imposing penalties—up to two years’ prison and fines—for leaking or publishing Vatican documents. The incident underscored tensions within the curia and the fraught politics surrounding one of Francis’ most consequential initiatives.

Poland has been shaken by leaked recordings that appear to show senior officials discussing political maneuvering with the central bank, prompting controversy over a live-broadcast raid on the offices of news magazine Wprost. The tapes, recorded at a Warsaw restaurant popular with politicians, reportedly capture Interior Minister Bartlomiej Sienkiewicz speaking with National Bank governor Marek Belka, with Belka allegedly suggesting removal of Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski in return for the bank’s support during an economic crisis. Rostowski was replaced four months later, but Prime Minister Donald Tusk denies any link to the tapes. Tusk called the leaks an "attempt at a coup d'etat" and warned that a continuing "crisis in confidence" might force a snap election. A prosecutor, escorted by state security agents, raided Wprost and tried to seize its editor’s laptop on live television; the Justice Minister, Marek Biernacki, later said the raid “should have never taken place,” acknowledging it raised legitimate concerns about breaching journalistic confidentiality. Officials in the Justice Ministry admitted legal errors in the operation. Uncertainty about who made the recordings—speculation ranges from political rivals to foreign agents—has intensified debate during a sensitive period of Polish security decisions and NATO engagement.

Colgate Total® has been promoted for over 20 years as a dentist-recommended toothpaste containing 0.3% triclosan to combat plaque bacteria linked to common oral diseases. Colgate cites more than 90 clinical studies involving over 20,000 people and multiple safety evaluations, and notes regulatory acceptance of triclosan’s use in toothpaste. The brand claims superior efficacy versus regular fluoride toothpaste: 12-hour antibacterial protection, reductions in plaque and gingivitis, and direct anti-inflammatory action. Colgate references a Cochrane Oral Health Group review (1990–2012, 30 studies, 14,835 participants) concluding that triclosan/copolymer fluoride toothpaste delivered meaningful benefits—around 22% reductions in plaque and gingivitis, 41% reduction in plaque severity, and 48% less gum bleeding after six months—without evidence of harm in studies up to three years.

By contrast, the U.S. FDA concluded there is insufficient evidence that over-the-counter antibacterial soaps and body washes (many containing triclosan) are more effective than plain soap and water in preventing illness and raised concerns about long-term safety and potential antibiotic resistance. In 2013–2016 the FDA moved to ban many consumer antibacterial wash products with triclosan and similar ingredients unless manufacturers provide safety and efficacy data; some ingredients remain under review. The FDA and EPA are coordinating triclosan assessments. Consumers are advised to continue washing hands with plain soap and water, which remains effective for preventing spread of infection.

After a man scaled the White House fence Friday and entered through the North Portico doors — carrying a knife before being arrested — Rep. Peter King demanded a full investigation and signaled Congress could hold hearings into the security breach. King, a New York Republican and member of the House Homeland Security Committee, called the incident “absolutely inexcusable” on Fox News Sunday and insisted investigators determine why the intrusion happened and what steps are needed to prevent any recurrence. He emphasized the basic nature of the breach, saying that while complex assassination plots exist, this was a simple failure of routine protective procedures. His committee is likely to convene hearings to examine the lapse in Secret Service performance, particularly alarming in an era of global terror threats such as ISIS. The first family was not at the White House at the time of the incident.

Separately, Sen. Dianne Feinstein used national attention on sports-related domestic violence to urge the National Football League to adopt a zero-tolerance policy after San Francisco 49ers defensive lineman Ray McDonald was arrested on domestic abuse charges yet remained on the team’s active roster for Sunday’s game. Speaking on CBS’ Face the Nation, the California Democrat — and former San Francisco mayor — said she believes she speaks for many women in the Senate in calling for decisive action. Feinstein argued that any player arrested should be suspended and a conviction should end a player’s career in the league. Acknowledging contractual complexities and her own past as a long-time 49ers fan, she nonetheless insisted that the prevalence of violence among players has grown intolerable and teams must set societal examples by enforcing stricter standards. Feinstein framed the NFL as an influential institution that must project clear values about right and wrong by showing strength and accountability in responding to domestic violence allegations.

A California lawyer, Matthew G. McLaughlin, filed a ballot initiative called the “Sodomite Suppression Act” that would mandate execution—“bullets to the head”—of people who have had same-sex relations and impose harsh penalties for advocating gay rights to minors. Though the proposal is flagrantly unconstitutional and could never become law, state law requires the attorney general to prepare a title and summary after the $200 filing fee was paid, allowing signature collection to begin. Legal experts say the measure is unlikely to gather the roughly 365,000 valid signatures needed to reach the ballot, but the filing exposes a gap in California’s initiative process: officials cannot block measures on human-rights grounds. Critics argue this undermines the integrity of the system; some propose a “human rights exception” to prevent initiatives that would strip fundamental rights. Activist Charlotte Laws responded by filing a satirical countermeasure, the “Intolerant Jackass Act,” which would require anyone proposing genocidal ballot measures to attend sensitivity training and donate to pro-LGBT organizations—an attempt to use the same process to mobilize public opposition. Meanwhile, state Senator Ricardo Lara and thousands of petitioners have asked the State Bar to investigate McLaughlin and consider disbarment for advocating murder.

Alfonso Cuarón’s 3-D thriller Gravity blasted to No. 1 at the box office with an estimated $55.6 million opening, far exceeding pre-release expectations and setting the biggest October debut ever. Strong 3-D ticket sales—about 80% of its business—drove the success; overseas it earned $27.4 million across 27 countries. Critics loved it (98% on Rotten Tomatoes) and audiences gave it an A-. Sandra Bullock and George Clooney star. By contrast, Runner Runner opened poorly with $7.6 million and weak reviews, limiting its prospects. Other holdovers included Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs 2 and Prisoners.

British politics faces a period of intense uncertainty after the general election produced a hung Parliament. Prime Minister Theresa May, who retained her seat, said the country “needs a period of stability” and that, if the Conservatives had won the most seats and votes, it would be incumbent on them to provide that stability. The election left no party with the 326 MPs needed for an outright majority: the Conservatives won 318 seats and Labour 262, with other parties making up the balance.

As incumbent, May remains in Number 10 and has the first opportunity to form a government. The most likely immediate outcome is a Conservative minority administration supported on crucial votes by the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) through a “confidence and supply” arrangement. Combined, the Conservatives and DUP would reach 328 seats, narrowly above the 326 majority threshold, allowing them to pass a Queen’s Speech and a Budget if the DUP agrees to back them. Negotiations were reported to be underway between the parties, and May confirmed key cabinet posts would be held by Michael Fallon, David Davis, Amber Rudd, Philip Hammond and Boris Johnson.

If May cannot secure sufficient support, Labour would have the chance to try to form a government, though that would be difficult: Labour’s potential allies are fragmented and several parties, including the Lib Dems and SNP, have ruled out formal coalitions with either main party in some combinations. Jeremy Corbyn hailed Labour’s performance and suggested May should step down, while other parties called for alternatives or reforms.

There is no fixed deadline for forming a government, but political timetables press on: Parliament reconvenes on June 13 and the Queen’s Speech is due June 19, which will test whether any proposed government can command Commons confidence. Brexit negotiations were due to start shortly after the election timetable, complicating matters; the EU warned talks could be affected by the UK’s political uncertainty.

Minority governments have historical precedent but are inherently fragile. If the May government cannot function, a vote of no confidence could trigger either another attempt to form a government or possibly a new election—though that requires specific parliamentary conditions. Meanwhile grassroots movements such as Momentum were credited with energizing Labour’s campaign, mobilizing thousands of volunteers and reaching large online audiences, underlining how ground organisation helped reshape the unexpectedly close result.

Cambria County Coroner Jeff Lees said a 69-year-old woman, Theresa Plummer, may have died after contacting drug paraphernalia while cleaning up following her son’s suspected overdose. Theresa found her 45-year-old son, Ronald, unresponsive in the bathroom on Nov. 5; he was taken to Conemaugh Memorial Medical Center for a suspected overdose. After Ronald was hospitalized, Theresa reportedly returned to clean the bathroom and may have absorbed a potent substance through her skin or suffered a reaction from handling the paraphernalia. She developed shortness of breath, was taken to the same hospital, and died Nov. 6. Ronald Plummer died the following day, Nov. 7. Autopsies have been completed, but toxicology results are pending and expected in six to eight weeks; authorities have not yet identified the drugs involved. Coroner Lees warned the public to exercise extreme caution around unknown powdery substances or drug items and urged families to contact law enforcement or EMS to remove hazardous materials rather than handling them directly. The Cox Media Group National Content Desk contributed to the reporting.

NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) has imaged surface features on Mars consistent with the crash of ESA’s Schiaparelli entry, descent and landing demonstrator. Low-resolution CTX images (6 m/pixel) show a new roughly 15 x 40 m dark patch about 5.4–5.5 km west of the intended touchdown in Meridiani Planum and a bright, roughly 12–15 m feature about 1 km south that is likely the module’s parachute and back shield. These marks were absent in earlier images, and teams from ESA and NASA consider them strong evidence that Schiaparelli impacted the ground at high speed after its descent systems malfunctioned. Telemetry relayed during descent indicates the parachute was jettisoned prematurely and the retrorockets fired only briefly instead of for the planned ~30 seconds, leaving the craft in freefall for an estimated 2–4 km and striking the surface at speeds greater than 300 km/h. The disturbed ground could reflect both kinetic impact and an explosion if fuel tanks were still full. Engineers continue detailed analysis of descent data recorded by the Trace Gas Orbiter, Mars Express and ground arrays to reconstruct the sequence precisely and determine altitudes and timings of events. Higher-resolution HiRISE images from MRO, expected soon, should clarify the scene. Despite the loss, ESA stresses that Schiaparelli returned about 80% of planned descent telemetry, yielding valuable engineering lessons for the ExoMars program and the planned 2021 rover mission.

Teams clearing World War II ordnance in Palau have reopened a sealed cave on Peleliu and found the remains of six people believed to be Japanese soldiers who defended the island in 1944. The cave is one of about 200 sealed field caves on Peleliu, many of which were enlarged, camouflaged and used as fortified positions and tunnels by Japanese forces during the fierce battle with U.S. Marines that began in September 1944. More than 10,000 Japanese troops died on Peleliu and roughly 2,600 remains have never been recovered. The newly opened site sits at a promontory that contained an anti‑tank gun in a concrete bunker; operators believe the bodies were those of the gun crew. Teams also found grenades, projectiles, small-arms ammunition and other explosive remnants, and the site has been resealed after initial investigation. A multinational clearance unit—18 Palauans, two Britons, one South African and one Australian—has been working for six years to make caves safe so Japanese and U.S. anthropologists and archaeologists can enter. The carefully paced, hazardous work involves clearing dense vegetation and unexploded ordnance, checking floors and entrances for booby traps, and using minimal heavy equipment to protect potential graves. The recoveries are timed ahead of an imperial visit by Japan’s Emperor Akihito and Empress Michiko and are part of broader efforts by Palau and Japan to locate and repatriate missing soldiers. Palau remains littered with wartime relics; searches also continue for a long‑lost mass grave and downed aircraft in surrounding reefs.

A 58-year-old Air Force veteran, identified by the Georgia Bureau of Investigation as John Michael Watts with no current address, set himself on fire Tuesday morning outside the Georgia State Capitol in downtown Atlanta to protest the Department of Veterans Affairs, authorities said. Around 10:45 a.m., Watts parked a Nissan Sentra on Washington Street, exited the vehicle and walked toward the Capitol. He was reportedly strapped with homemade incendiary devices and firecrackers, doused himself with a flammable liquid, and ignited the devices, producing several loud explosions. A state trooper quickly extinguished the flames with a fire extinguisher before additional injuries occurred. Watts suffered severe burns—authorities later said about 85 to 90 percent of his body—and was rushed to Grady Memorial Hospital in critical condition; he was coherent enough afterward to say he was disgruntled with the VA and wanted to draw attention to the issue. No other injuries were reported. The incident prompted evacuation of the Capitol and nearby judiciary buildings and the temporary relocation of children from a church-associated day care. Multiple agencies responded, including bomb technicians who cleared and searched the veteran’s vehicle; the area was secured with robots and SWAT support. Roads around the Capitol were closed during the response but were reopened by early evening after officials gave an all-clear. The event occurred during a news conference on a hands-free driving law.

Two young monks from Kirti monastery in Aba prefecture, Sichuan — 18-year-olds Kelsang and Kunchak — set themselves on fire on Monday in protest against Chinese religious controls, exiled Tibetan sources told Reuters. The pair reportedly shouted demands for religious freedom and "Long live the Dalai Lama" as they immolated themselves at 10 a.m.; state media later said both suffered slight burns and were in stable condition while authorities investigated. The incident, following the death by self-immolation of 21-year-old Phuntsog from the same monastery six months earlier and subsequent detentions of about 300 monks, could trigger renewed crackdowns in the already tense, heavily Tibetan region. Eyewitnesses and exile activists say Chinese security removed the monks’ bodies and have detained participants in earlier protests; local officials gave limited comment. Separately, Beijing declared any successor chosen by the Dalai Lama would be "illegal" after the 76-year-old spiritual leader said he and Tibetan religious authorities, not China, would decide whether and how he should be reincarnated. China insists reincarnation must follow state laws and historical conventions, raising the prospect of rival Dalai Lamas recognized by Beijing and the exile community.

A mass shooting at Azana Salon & Spa in Brookfield, Wisconsin, left three women dead and four wounded on Sunday morning. Authorities identified suspect Radcliffe Franklin Haughton, 45, of Brown Deer, and launched a manhunt; later reports said the suspect was found dead. Police believed the attack was linked to a domestic dispute: Haughton had a temporary restraining order issued against him earlier in October and was ordered to surrender weapons. An improvised explosive device was discovered inside the two-story spa, and police and bomb squad teams responded; the surrounding mall, nearby hospital and other buildings were temporarily locked down during the search. Victims included salon employees; among them was 42-year-old stylist Zina Haughton, remembered by clients as warm, hardworking and devoted to her two daughters, who were unharmed. Four wounded women, ages 22, 30, 32 and 40, were treated for extremity injuries at Froedtert Hospital and expected to survive. The incident prompted condolences from state and national leaders and renewed public attention to gun violence after earlier shootings in Wisconsin this year. Investigations into motive and timeline continued.

Alphabet awarded Google CEO Sundar Pichai 273,328 Class C stock units on Feb. 3, a grant valued at about $199 million at the time and now roughly $182 million after share declines. The equity vests quarterly over four years while he remains employed, raising his Alphabet holdings to around $600–650 million—substantial but far below founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin and ex-chairman Eric Schmidt. The award ranks among the largest U.S. corporate grants, comparable to Tim Cook’s 2011 package. Other executives also received large grants: CFO Ruth Porat about $38 million (plus a prior $30 million signing bonus) and cloud head Diane Greene roughly $42.8 million.

Garry Cordell, 47, was sentenced to life without parole for his role in the April murders of Heather Aldrich, 25; Carrie Nelson, 31; and Jody Hutchinson, 42, whose charred bodies were found in a burned Oldsmobile Bravada in Doyle Township. At sentencing family members of the victims implored the court for the harshest penalty; Cordell, who pleaded guilty to two counts of first-degree murder and one count of felony murder, told the court he did what he had to do and expressed no remorse. Prosecutors played a four-minute video of the victims and the burned car, noting research suggesting the time it takes to strangle a person. Judge William Carmody, who said he typically opposes the death penalty, indicated this case might have been an exception in another state.

The case unfolded amid shifting confessions, a jailhouse death and community outrage. Cordell and his girlfriend Marietta Carlson initially implicated Kenneth Brunke, 46, as the mastermind; Brunke was accused of luring Aldrich to his home over stolen drugs and jealousy. Carlson, who later died in custody of an inflamed heart after 47 days jailed, had given statements that could not be used at trial. Cordell, an ex-con and self-described Aryan Brotherhood member, changed his story multiple times — at one point confessing to killing all three with Carlson and later implicating Brunke again. Cordell’s guilty pleas followed after Brunke, who pleaded in October to obstruction of justice and lying to police in exchange for testifying against Cordell, avoided murder charges. Brunke faces sentencing on the reduced felonies and could receive under five years under guidelines.

The plea deal and prosecutorial decisions by Timothy Noble, a relatively inexperienced county prosecutor who handled the case without formal assistance from the state Attorney General’s office, angered victims’ families and fueled suspicion that someone may have escaped full accountability. Allegations surfaced that Brunke paid money to Cordell after Cordell’s exonerating confession, deepening community doubts. A roadside memorial for the victims was later vandalized, and families remain haunted by whether the complete truth and all responsible parties have been held to account.

Researchers using high-resolution micro-CT scanning have revealed that the Oxford Dodo—the best-preserved dodo specimen in the world and the only one retaining soft tissue and viable DNA—was killed by gunshot. Long housed at the Oxford University Museum of Natural History and famously linked to Lewis Carroll’s portrayal in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, the mummified bird’s skull and foot were scanned at the University of Warwick. The scans uncovered 20–30 small, high-density metallic particles embedded in the back of the skull and neck; forensic analysis identified them as lead shot pellets consistent with 17th-century wildfowl ammunition. The pattern indicates the bird was shot from behind, a violent end contrary to prior assumptions that the specimen had died of natural causes or in captivity. Researchers note this evidence is a stark, tangible snapshot of human-driven extinction: dodos were wiped out within about 60 years of European contact through hunting, habitat destruction, and the introduction of invasive species that consumed eggs and young. The team plans chemical analysis of the lead to trace its ore source and possibly determine the country where the shot was manufactured—information that could indicate whether the bird was killed on Mauritius, aboard a ship, or elsewhere. The discovery raises new questions about the specimen’s provenance, including whether it is the same dodo once exhibited in London in the 1630s, and underscores how modern imaging can reopen historical “cold cases.” Beyond scientific curiosity, researchers express sadness: the finding personalizes the dodo’s demise and highlights humanity’s rapid and lasting impact on ecosystems.

Actress Sean Young, 52, was detained by LAPD after an altercation with security outside the Academy Awards’ Governors Ball. According to multiple reports, Young— who did not have a ticket and said she was taking photos for her Facebook page—was asked to leave the party. She left but then returned; when security again asked her to leave, a guard allegedly grabbed her arm. Young says she pulled away and struck the guard. Security placed her under a citizen’s arrest for misdemeanor battery until LAPD arrived and booked her. Young showed bruises and told reporters she was well-behaved and that surveillance footage would clear her. She blamed an Academy attorney for suggesting the citizen’s arrest and demanded a public apology from the Academy’s security. The Academy issued a brief statement acknowledging an incident outside the Governors Ball but said it did not press charges. Video and eyewitness accounts vary slightly: some reports emphasize Young’s interactions with other celebrities earlier in the night—posing with Angelina Jolie, Brad Pitt, and Sandra Bullock—while others focus on the sequence that led to the security confrontation, the citizen’s arrest, and her subsequent release from the Hollywood police station. The dispute remains contested.

Census Director Robert Groves and Commerce Secretary Gary Locke announced 2010 census results showing a national population of 308,745,538, the slowest decade growth since the Great Depression. Regional gains concentrated in the South and West: the South grew 14.3 percent and the West 13.8 percent from 2000 to 2010, while the Midwest rose 3.9 percent and the Northeast 3.2 percent. Nevada led states with 35.1 percent growth; Michigan was the only state to shrink, down 0.6 percent. Locke called the census a success also for its cost performance: final spending was $1.87 billion less than expected—exceeding an earlier $1.6 billion estimate—helped by strong management and a 74 percent mail-back response rate matching 2000.

Millions gathered at Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana Beach Saturday evening for a vigil with Pope Francis, who is visiting for World Youth Day. City and church officials estimated roughly three million people attended, potentially the largest turnout of his trip. Pilgrims from around the world streamed into the city, filling the crescent of sand with sleeping bags, tents and national flags; many camped overnight and organizers asked them to donate bedding afterward to the homeless. Earlier that day Francis urged bishops at the Cathedral of St. Sebastian to leave their parishes and adopt a missionary mindset focused on serving the poor and those on society’s margins, criticizing a church that risks becoming inward-looking as Catholic affiliation declines in Brazil. He delivered his longest speech as pope to outline that vision, and later addressed intellectuals, politicians and business leaders, calling for dialogue, social humility and broader opportunity amid deep inequality and public unrest over corruption and public spending. Francis’ messages resonated with young pilgrims who described the event as a powerful faith experience and an encouragement to live their beliefs concretely. The visit, marked by appeals for outreach and solidarity, culminates with a Mass expected to draw an even larger crowd.

An audio message from Qassim al-Rimi, leader of al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), surfaced days after a Jan. 29 U.S.-led raid in Yemen that killed at least 14 al-Qaida fighters, one U.S. Navy SEAL and several civilians. In the recording, which intelligence sources and media outlets treated as likely authentic, al-Rimi taunted President Donald Trump as the “White House’s new fool,” claimed 25 people died in the raid — including 11 women and children and an 8-year-old girl reported to be the daughter of late U.S.-born cleric Anwar al-Awlaki — and asserted “dozens” of Americans were killed or wounded, a claim sharply at odds with U.S. accounts. U.S. officials reported one Navy SEAL killed (Chief Petty Officer William “Ryan” Owens) and several wounded. The raid, a joint operation with United Arab Emirates forces, was described by U.S. leaders as primarily for intelligence collection and site exploitation; White House and CENTCOM spokesmen denied the operation was intended specifically to capture or kill al-Rimi. NBC and some senior officials, however, said eliminating al-Rimi was a secret objective, noting his high-profile role as a recruiter and his place on U.S. most-wanted lists. The mission involved U.S. Special Operations Command and the CIA, and President Trump approved the high-risk operation. Questions remain about whether al-Rimi was present at the compound or escaped; he remains at large in Yemen and used the recording to publicly mock the raid and U.S. claims of success.

Comedian Roseanne Barr sparked controversy after tweeting a photo of her face—appearing bruised and discolored—alongside a caption joking she’d “got in a tussle w bill cosby.” The 62-year-old later deleted that post after widespread backlash, then reposted the same image clarifying she’d had a chemical peel and had only joked about Cosby. In an interview with the New York Daily News, Barr said she didn’t want legal trouble or retaliation but suggested the mounting number of accusers—“13 to 1”—made Cosby’s situation clear. Barr also called the scandal “the best and the worst thing,” lamenting the ugliness revealed while praising survivors’ ability to be heard. Separately, three more women publicly accused Bill Cosby of sexual assault at a press conference led by attorney Gloria Allred, who urged Cosby to place $100 million into a fund for alleged victims and to allow retired judges to evaluate the claims. Allred proposed Cosby waive the statute of limitations so more women could sue; Cosby’s lawyer Martin Singer criticized recent allegations as “increasingly ridiculous.” The three accusers described encounters in the 1970s–80s: Beth Ferrier alleged Cosby spiked her cappuccino and she awoke disoriented in her car; Helen Hayes accused him of groping her in 1973; and a woman named Chelan said she was given a pill and assaulted in a Las Vegas hotel room in 1986. Cosby has responded minimally, thanking celebrity supporters like Whoopi Goldberg and Jill Scott as the allegations and media scrutiny continue.

A suspicious backpack containing multiple improvised explosive devices was found late Sunday in a trash can near the NJ Transit Elizabeth train station and unintentionally detonated early Monday while bomb technicians were attempting to render it safe, officials said. Two men discovered the bag around 8:30 p.m. Sunday near Morris Avenue and Julian Place—about 300 feet from the door of Willy’s Place, a nearby pub—and after spotting wires and a pipe they reported it to police. Union County bomb technicians and the FBI responded; a bomb-disposal robot was used to examine and attempt to disarm the package. Around 12:40 a.m. Monday the robot’s cutting action set off one of five explosive devices found inside the single backpack, Elizabeth Mayor Christian Bollwage said. The blast was not a controlled detonation. No injuries were reported, but authorities moved press and bystanders back because four other devices were believed to remain live. The FBI’s Newark division described the items as “multiple improvised explosive devices.” Surveillance footage from the restaurant where the bag was first found is being reviewed by the FBI.

The discovery forced evacuations and road closures around the station, and suspended service on NJ Transit’s Northeast Corridor and North Jersey Coast lines and local Amtrak service late Sunday into early Monday. An estimated 2,400 Amtrak passengers were affected and trains were held at New York Penn Station and Trenton before service gradually resumed with delays and some schedule modifications by midmorning. Transit agencies cross‑honored tickets on PATH and bus routes to ease commuter disruptions.

The Elizabeth incident occurred amid a broader weekend of related explosive events and security alerts in the region. On Saturday night an explosion in Manhattan’s Chelsea neighborhood injured 29 people; an unexploded pressure-cooker device was discovered a few blocks away. Earlier Saturday a pipe-bomb-style device detonated in a garbage can in Seaside Park, New Jersey, near the start line of a Marine Corps charity 5K, though that blast injured no one. The FBI detained five people in Brooklyn on Sunday for questioning linked to the Manhattan explosion following a traffic stop on the Verrazano Bridge. At the time authorities said there was no definitive evidence tying all incidents together, but they noted similarities among devices, including use of pressure cookers and cellphone triggers in the New York cases.

New York and New Jersey officials heightened security during the U.N. General Assembly and deployed additional law enforcement around transit hubs, airports and public events. New York Mayor Bill de Blasio and Governor Andrew Cuomo announced increased police presence; Cuomo said 1,000 additional officers would help patrol critical locations. Investigations continued into whether the attacks were the work of a lone actor or part of a broader plot. In the days following the incidents, law enforcement arrested a suspect in connection with the Chelsea and Seaside Park bombings, and federal prosecutors charged him with multiple counts while probing his possible motives and any outside influences. Meanwhile, local officials emphasized caution: Mayor Bollwage said he could not conclude Elizabeth had been specifically targeted and suggested the devices might have been discarded by someone trying to evade detection. The FBI asked anyone with information to call 1-800-CALL-FBI.

Mikhail Kalashnikov, designer of the widely produced AK-47, wrote a heartfelt letter to Russian Orthodox Patriarch Kirill in 2012 expressing deep spiritual anguish over the deaths caused by his rifle. The letter, published by pro-Kremlin daily Izvestia and typed on his personal stationery, asks whether he could be morally to blame for lives taken with the weapon he created. Signed as “a slave of God, the designer Mikhail Kalashnikov,” it says his “spiritual pain is unbearable” and questions why the Lord allowed envy, greed and aggression to drive people to kill. Kalashnikov, who died at 94 in December, had long maintained he was not responsible for the rifle’s misuse, arguing it was meant to defend his country rather than arm terrorists or criminal elements. He told journalists in 2008 that it pained him to see criminals and child soldiers using his weapon. According to Izvestia and family comments, Kalashnikov first entered a church at 91 and was later baptized; his daughter suggested a priest may have helped him compose the letter. The Patriarch’s press secretary said Kirill received the letter and replied, reiterating the Church’s stance that weapons intended to protect the Fatherland and their creators are supported. Kalashnikov was celebrated by Soviet and Russian authorities, received state honors, and made little money from the globally ubiquitous rifle.

Emma Stone and Andrew Garfield turned a paparazzi encounter into a publicity moment for charity, repeating a 2012 stunt in New York by holding up signs naming nonprofits instead of seeking attention. Stone explained they “saw a group of guys with cameras” while eating and decided to promote causes that need visibility. Their cards listed Gilda’s Club NYC, Worldwide Orphans, Youth Mentoring Connection, and the controversial Autism Speaks, with Garfield adding “Here’s to the stuff that matters!” Fans praised their clever, charitable use of fame.

Steven Dishman, 60, who escaped Arkansas prison custody in May 1985, was captured Sunday at a Springdale home after more than 30 years on the run. Arkansas State Police and Springdale officers arrested him following an anonymous tip; the ASP is investigating where Dishman lived and who may have known him under another name. Dishman had been serving a seven-year Washington County sentence for theft of property and burglary, convicted Dec. 20, 1984, with parole eligibility in late 1987. He escaped from the Benton Unit after earlier stints at Cummins and Wrightsville. Dishman is now held at the Varner Unit in Lincoln County; special agents are interviewing associates and the escape file will be forwarded to the Jefferson County prosecutor for possible further action.

Josh Byrne, 30, a Hudson, Massachusetts native, was found dead after being swept away by flash floodwaters in Costa Rica while honeymooning with his wife, Bianca. The newlyweds, married days earlier at a New Hampshire farm, were in Playa Dominicalito when their vehicle attempted to cross a bridge during heavy flooding. Bianca swam to shore; Josh was carried off by the river. After search efforts involving local rescuers, the Byrne family and friends, and assistance from the U.S. Embassy, the Red Cross and others, his remains were recovered Saturday. His father and brother had flown to Costa Rica to join the search. Family and Josh’s employer, SJC Custom Drums, remembered him for his caring demeanor, ability to make friends, and devotion to his wife; a GoFundMe was established to help with recovery and service expenses.

In 2013 a 4.7 Mw earthquake struck Wyoming’s Wind River region that scientists now say was unusually deep for a stable continental area. New research in Earth and Planetary Science Letters indicates the quake occurred at about 75 km depth—well below the local crust, which is 40–50 km thick in the Wyoming Craton—placing the rupture more than 20 km into the upper mantle. That depth would rank the Wind River event among the three deepest earthquakes recorded beneath stable continental lithosphere; only two comparable mantle quakes are noted in the literature (a 1979 event near Randolph, Utah at ~90 km and a 2000 quake beneath the Arafura Sea at ~61 km). Wind River is also notable because the region is normally tectonically quiet: few quakes over magnitude 4 have been recorded there in the past six decades, and the nearest active tectonism—the Yellowstone hotspot—is roughly 200 km away. Deep seismicity often occurs in volcanic areas or from descending slabs, but those scenarios seem unlikely here. The Wind River shock produced characteristics consistent with tectonic faulting rather than magma- or fluid-driven events, implying brittle failure of the mantle beneath the craton. That conclusion challenges current understanding of the stresses and conditions required to fracture mantle material in such cold, stable lithosphere, leaving the precise cause unresolved. The study thus raises intriguing questions about mantle rheology and seismic potential beneath apparently quiescent continental interiors.

The U.S. government, through NOAA Fisheries, proposed reclassifying humpback whales into 14 distinct population segments and removing 10 of those segments from the federal Endangered Species Act (ESA) list. After 45 years of protections—including the IWC whaling bans and U.S. listing in 1970—many humpback populations have rebounded. NOAA’s review, begun in 2010, used morphological, genetic, and biogeographical data showing populations are largely independent, with differing recovery histories. Under the proposal, two populations (Central America and Western North Pacific) would be listed as threatened and two (Arabian Sea and Cape Verde/northwest Africa) would remain endangered; populations delisted from the ESA would still be protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act. NOAA officials framed the change as a conservation success and said managing distinct populations lets resources focus on those most at risk. Scientists who contributed to the review noted varied population sizes—from a few hundred in the Arabian Sea to tens of thousands in places like Hawaii—reflecting uneven impacts of past whaling. Conservationists have cautioned the move could be premature, pointing to ongoing threats such as ship strikes, entanglement, climate change, and ocean acidification that affect prey and survival. NOAA has opened a 90-day public comment period before finalizing the rule.

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump used back-to-back appearances in Las Vegas and Phoenix to amplify his hardline stances on immigration and trade, mixing inflammatory rhetoric with occasional nods of respect for Mexico and its people. At FreedomFest in Las Vegas he charged that Mexico was deliberately sending violent criminals to the United States and blasted U.S. officials as “dumb” on immigration; in Phoenix he briefly said “I love the Mexican people” and “I respect Mexico greatly,” but quickly resumed attacking Mexican leaders for outmaneuvering the U.S. on trade and the border. Trump repeated calls for a border wall and proposed punitive financial charges on Mexico for illegal immigrants, while arguing he could better handle China and Russia and that he could get along with Vladimir Putin.

His speeches were heavy on insults—targeting Univision, NBC, Macy’s, Jeb Bush, Hillary Clinton, the media and President Obama—and light on concrete policy details. He showcased crime victims such as Jamiel Shaw Sr. to underscore his claims about immigrants committing violent crimes. The events included confrontations: protesters were removed amid scuffles and chants, and Trump suggested provocatively that the Mexican government might have “sent them over here.”

Trump’s rhetoric has energized a vocal right-wing segment of the GOP, drawing large, enthusiastic crowds in Phoenix despite mainstream Republican unease. Party leaders worry his approach could damage more electable candidates and the party’s image; some fear he might even run outside the GOP. Critics call for more measured, humane immigration messaging, while Trump’s supporters praise his bluntness as speaking uncomfortable truths. The appearances highlighted tensions within the Republican Party over how to address illegal immigration without alienating broader voters.

Centuries ago, scurvy ravaged seafaring crews who lacked fresh sources of vitamin C; countless sailors died from weakness, bleeding gums, ulcers, and eventual internal hemorrhage. Histories record catastrophic losses—Vasco da Gama, Magellan, and George Anson suffered massive crew deaths—until mid-18th-century findings, notably James Lind’s, showed citrus fruits could prevent and cure scurvy. Earlier remedies and prophylactics (sauerkraut, malt, portable soup) were inconsistently effective, often because vitamin C is destroyed by heat and poor storage. Sailors’ diets, cooking practices, and slow dissemination of medical knowledge prolonged the scourge. Captain Cook’s voyages illustrate both successes and ambiguities: his regimen reduced scurvy deaths on some voyages, yet evidence shows many still suffered; debates persisted about which measures truly worked. Over time, routine inclusion of fresh vegetables and citrus largely eliminated scurvy in developed nations, though it remains a risk where diets lack vitamin C.

Today’s explorers face analogous nutritional challenges in space, where no fresh island stop exists. NASA researchers emphasize that proper nutrition is mission-critical: inadequate intake or menu fatigue, combined with microgravity, increased radiation, altered CO2, and environmental stressors, threaten bone and muscle, cardiovascular and immune function, vision, and more. NASA’s Biochemical Profile project monitors proteins, vitamins, minerals, hormones, and immune markers from blood and urine before, during, and after flights to chart changes and test countermeasures. The Twins Study offers a unique control: astronaut Scott Kelly’s year-long ISS mission is compared to his twin Mark on Earth to isolate spaceflight effects. As missions lengthen toward potential 30-month Mars expeditions, stable, palatable, nutritious, and long-lived food systems are essential. Insights from space nutrition research may also inform treatments for Earthbound patients with limited mobility. While investigations continue, early findings are promising: nutrition, combined with exercise and proper food systems, will be pivotal to sustaining long-duration human exploration.

Authorities say a brunette woman, described as white, in her 20s–30s, about 5'8" and 120–130 pounds, is suspected of robbing six jewelry stores across the Southeast since April, stealing more than $450,000 in merchandise. The most recent robbery occurred Monday at the Jared Vault in Tanger Outlets, Mebane, N.C., where she allegedly displayed a handgun, forced two employees into a back room, zip-tied them and stole jewelry. A Black male accomplice, 30s–40s, about 6' and 250 pounds, appears on surveillance in at least three incidents. All suspects are considered armed and dangerous. Anyone with information should call 1-800-CALL-FBI or local tips lines.

Microsoft’s Surface arrived amid high expectations as a potential hybrid that could finally bridge the gap between touch-first tablets and full productivity machines. Its industrial design largely delivers: a handsome, sturdy magnesium body, a clever integrated kickstand, a vivid 10.6-inch display, USB and microSDXC ports, and innovative keyboard covers (Touch Cover and Type Cover) that magnetically attach and transform the slate into a quasi-laptop. The hardware details—the satisfying hinge, neat fit and finish, and thoughtful ergonomics—make Surface one of the most exciting pieces of hardware in years.

But Surface RT is held back by critical software and usability compromises. It runs Windows RT, an ARM-based cousin of Windows 8 that shares the new touch-centric Metro interface and includes preview versions of Office, yet cannot run legacy x86 Windows applications. Desktop mode exists mostly to host Office, which feels like a cramped compromise rather than a full reimagining for touch. The Windows Store’s sparse app selection and immature third-party offerings further limit the device’s value: popular apps are missing, key clients are buggy, and media workflows (like video importing) are clunky.

The Touch Cover is an impressive engineering feat—ultra-thin, integrated, and battery-free—but its flat, low-travel keys and a small, laggy trackpad make serious, fast typing difficult; the pricier Type Cover improves typing but adds cost and bulk. Performance on RT is occasionally sluggish, and some UI inconsistencies and bugs undermine the experience.

As shipped, Surface RT is an ambitious, beautifully made first step toward a new class of computer but ultimately feels undercooked: a compromise that’s neither a fully capable laptop nor a polished tablet. Given its $499–$599 pricing once covers are added, it’s not recommended as a primary machine today. Future hardware revisions, software updates, and the full Windows 8–based Surface Pro may vindicate Microsoft’s vision, but for now the “future” isn’t quite here.

A retired physicist, Charles D. Goodman, who lives near Oprah Winfrey’s recently purchased parcel above Telluride, Colorado, has filed suit alleging that Winfrey’s Yellow Brick Road company, the property’s former owners and the town of Mountain Village conspired to block long-standing neighborhood access to hiking trails that cross the land. Goodman contends the previous owners, Hoyt and Carol Barnett, requested a correction to the property records shortly before selling the 40-acre site to Winfrey for $10.9 million in March; he says that correction erased easements that had allowed nearby residents to use the trails for decades. The trails in question were established in 1989 after Goodman negotiated with the U.S. Forest Service, which then owned the land.

Mountain Village officials deny any clandestine deal. Chris Hawkins, the town’s community development director, said the record change merely clarified ambiguities and emphasized that both the town and Winfrey’s team intend to maintain trail access. Yellow Brick Road spokeswoman Wendy Luckenbill released a statement saying the company will work with neighbors to ensure “reasonable” access over portions of the property.

Winfrey plans to build a main house and guest home on the site beginning this summer, though formal plans have not yet been submitted. The proposed development will require constructing a bridge over a ski run and removing an estimated 800 to 1,000 trees to meet the town’s wildfire mitigation rules, which could raise additional local concerns. The Denver Post reported that the Barnetts asked for the records correction before the sale; Goodman’s lawsuit argues that action was part of a secret effort to close the trails to the neighborhood. The town and Yellow Brick Road dispute that characterization and express a desire to preserve access, while Goodman presses his claim that established easements were improperly erased. Further legal proceedings will determine whether the easements remain enforceable and what access, if any, neighbors will retain across the newly purchased property.

A public announcement of ties between al-Qaeda in Iraq and Syria’s most effective rebel faction, Jabhat al-Nusra, has raised grave concerns about the Syrian conflict’s trajectory. Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi declared a merger, saying the groups will operate as the “Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham,” though Nusra leader Abu Mohammad al-Golani later said he was not consulted and only pledged allegiance to al-Qaeda’s central leadership. Al-Baghdadi framed earlier secrecy as a way to let Syrians judge Nusra on the battlefield rather than accept negative portrayals. U.S. and regional intelligence corroborate cross-border ties: funding, fighters, training, logistics and weapons flows have linked cells in Iraq and Syria, helping Nusra swell with local and foreign recruits and mount frequent suicide and car-bomb attacks that have increased in tempo. The declaration complicates Western and Gulf efforts to assist moderate opposition forces: arms and materiel intended for the Free Syrian Army have appeared in Nusra videos, prompting European caution and U.S. limits on lethal support. Analysts warn that a strengthened, territorially rooted al-Qaeda affiliate could provide a long-term safe haven and regional reach, undermining hopes for a pluralistic post-Assad Syria and heightening risks for civilians caught between regime, insurgents, and extremist agendas.

Eva Restaurant owner-chef Mark Gold in West Hollywood launched a policy offering diners a 5% discount if they check their phones at the door, aiming to revive conversation and real-world connection at mealtimes. Gold told KPCC’s AirTalk that the idea began locally but went viral after the Associated Press picked it up, producing dozens of media requests and interviews worldwide—from CNN and Good Morning America to stations in Germany, Ireland, and India. His Twitter and email have been flooded with praise from restaurateurs and customers considering copying the approach. Gold says roughly half of patrons accept the offer and no one has objected; he hopes the incentive creates a home-like ambience where guests focus on food and company rather than screens. Despite the publicity, business hasn’t surged yet—he expects more traffic when school resumes—but the policy has sparked debate about “distracted dining” and whether more establishments should curb phone use.

Airlines across Europe and the U.S. suspended flights to Tel Aviv this week amid safety concerns after a Hamas rocket landed about a mile from Ben Gurion Airport. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration imposed a 24-hour ban — later extended — and the European Aviation Safety Agency advised carriers to avoid Tel Aviv, prompting cancellations from Lufthansa (and subsidiaries), Air Berlin, Air France, KLM, Alitalia, SAS, LOT, Air Canada and others. British Airways continued its twice-daily service, saying it judged risks acceptable. Israeli officials and airport authorities insisted Ben Gurion is highly secure and defended its Iron Dome protections; Jerusalem’s mayor and industry voices called the airport among the safest globally. Critics, including Michael Bloomberg, argued bans reward Hamas and harm Israel economically by isolating it and damaging tourism. The disruptions stranded some travelers, raised diplomatic questions over the FAA’s move, and led Israel to open an auxiliary airport as authorities and carriers reassess operations amid ongoing hostilities.

A New Jersey court approved a $325,000 settlement between the New York Jets and their cheerleading squad, the Flight Crew, resolving a class-action wage suit filed in 2014 by a cheerleader identified as Krystal C. The deal, covering the 2012–13 and 2013–14 NFL seasons, awards each of 52 squad members $2,500 for each season they worked during that period; payments will include interest and vary by individual work history. Cheerleaders who participated in photo shoots are eligible for up to $400 per shoot. The suit alleged the women were paid only $150 per game and received no compensation for practices, rehearsals or related obligations; the plaintiffs’ lawyer argued those rates translated to as little as $3.77 per hour, falling below minimum wage once required expenses for hair, makeup and transportation were considered. The Jets denied the claims but agreed to the settlement to avoid litigation costs and distraction. State Sen. Diane Savino praised the outcome and urged the Buffalo Bills and the NFL to adopt uniform rules to ensure fair pay and protections for all cheerleaders. The Jets’ case is part of a broader trend of similar lawsuits: the Buccaneers, Raiders, Bengals and Bills have faced or settled cheerleader wage claims, and the Buffalo Jills recently gained class-action status.

Samuel Forrest, a Kiwi from Auckland, is racing to bring his newborn son Leo back to New Zealand after the baby, born January 21 with Down syndrome in Armenia, was rejected by his mother and their extended family. According to Forrest and a GoFundMe set up to fund their return, hospital staff initially hid the child and warned the family about his condition—reflecting a local practice where children with disabilities are often abandoned or hidden due to stigma.
