When Forrest first met Leo he said he was “beautiful” and resolved to keep him, but his wife issued an ultimatum: keep the baby and she would divorce him. She subsequently left and filed for divorce, and Forrest says he is no longer welcome in his in‑laws’ home.

The fundraiser, titled “Bring Leo Home,” has drawn extraordinary international support after news coverage, jumping from $10,000 to $80,000 within hours and now exceeding $160,000, at one point rising by roughly $1,000 per minute. Forrest says the objective is to raise enough for a year so he can work part‑time while caring for Leo, avoid daycare costs, and establish themselves in New Zealand where they will have family support. He also reports the New Zealand government has fast‑tracked citizenship and a passport for Leo.

Forrest has begun working with disability‑awareness groups to educate parents and combat the stigma that labels children with Down syndrome as less than normal. He emphasizes that these children are “a little different” but are still normal, and he intends to find and nurture Leo’s strengths rather than allow him to be marginalized or placed in an orphanage.

News 6 reports that the public online auction for the Kel-Tec PF-9 pistol George Zimmerman used to kill Trayvon Martin was a sham meant to attract bogus bids, while a real, private auction for pre-qualified bidders was conducted simultaneously. United Gun Group, which hosted the auctions, said its private sale drew at least one verified offer of $120,000, with 22 bidders and 42 total bids. The public-facing listing, however, showed inflated figures—one visible “high bid” approached $140,000 and ended with a $138,900 bid attributed to a “John Smith.” United Gun Group acknowledged running two auctions to “troll the trolls,” and said the tactic worked to expose fake bids. It remains unclear who ultimately won the genuine private auction; Zimmerman must verify the winning bidder and their funds before finalizing any sale, and the buyer’s identity can remain confidential per site rules.

Zimmerman responded to outreach by stipulating conditions for an interview, including four-star hotel accommodations and $1,000 per day. He later released a statement thanking supporters and United Gun Group, saying the auction raised funds for “several worthy causes,” and directing followers to GMZ1776.com for updates. The Trayvon Martin Foundation declined to comment. The firearm, which Zimmerman has described as “a piece of American history,” bears his trial case number in silver marker; Zimmerman says it was recently returned to him by the Department of Justice. Reports vary on the final price, with some inflated public bids misreported as actual sale figures.

The document stitches together several news items and an editorial apology, centering on civility, free expression and corporate responsibility. It opens with an editorial writer’s reflection after the U.S. Supreme Court’s 5–4 Obergefell ruling legalizing same-sex marriage. The writer celebrated colleagues’ relief and joy but sought to curb hateful responses to the ruling on PennLive/The Patriot-News opinion pages. He proposed a policy to “very strictly limit” op-eds and letters opposing same-sex marriage, equating extreme anti-gay speech with racist, sexist or anti-Semitic submissions, while still accepting reasoned critiques of the Court’s legal reasoning. The stance provoked a storm of backlash accusing the paper of trampling the First Amendment. The writer insists the paper supports free expression but will not publish slurs or playground insults, and acknowledges dissenting, good-faith religious or philosophical objections remain welcome. He apologizes to readers offended by his attempt to foster civil discourse and reiterates support for gay and lesbian colleagues granted equal protection under the law.

The document then shifts to lighter media coverage: Seth Meyers and Amy Poehler revived their “Really?” bit to ridicule Sports Illustrated contributor Andy Benoit’s Twitter claim that women’s sports aren’t worth watching, lampooning his Twitter gaffe and mocking his judgment.

Next is a controversy about a Wal-Mart in Slidell, La., that refused to bake a Confederate flag cake but accepted an ISIS-flag cake; the company apologized, saying the ISIS image should not have been made and attributing the Confederate ban to company policy removing Confederate-flag merchandise after the Charleston church shooting.

Finally, the piece reports Takata’s CEO Shigehisa Takada offering a rare public apology amid the massive airbag recall tied to rupturing inflators that have caused deaths and injuries. Takada defended the safety of Takata’s ammonium-nitrate propellant, resisted calls to resign, and described ongoing investigations into manufacturing “alpha” cases and unexplained “beta” cases possibly linked to heat and humidity. The crisis has prompted expanded recalls, litigation, falling share value and intense scrutiny over replacement parts.

Scientists have discovered a large, previously unknown void inside the Great Pyramid of Giza, the first major internal feature located in the monument since the 19th century. The cavity, detected by an international team using muography — a non-invasive imaging method that tracks cosmic-ray-produced muons passing through rock — lies directly above the Grand Gallery, an 47-metre-long, cathedral-like ascending corridor linking the Queen’s and King’s chambers. The newly found space stretches at least about 30 metres and appears to have dimensions comparable to the Grand Gallery, though muon imaging cannot determine whether it is a single chamber or a series of connected cavities, nor whether it is horizontal or inclined. Three independent detection methods (photographic plates and electronic detectors placed inside, and muon telescopes oriented from outside) all registered the same muon excess, confirming a significant low-density region rather than general porosity. Researchers caution that muography provides low-resolution, integrated-density images: it reveals the void’s presence and scale but not shape, contents, or function. Hypotheses range from a structural purpose — relieving weight on the Grand Gallery roof — to an unknown corridor or intentional architectural space; experts disagree on whether its size makes a stress-relief explanation plausible. The ScanPyramids team says they will not drill into the monument; instead they hope to develop tiny flying robots to explore if Egyptian authorities approve further non-invasive probing. Egyptologists and architects are being invited to model possible functions against the muon data. Commentators emphasize the discovery’s significance for understanding pyramid construction while warning against premature speculation about hidden treasures or Khufu’s mummy. The find underscores both the enduring mysteries of the pyramids and the value of modern particle-physics techniques in archaeology.

Denver police pursued a stolen tractor towing an attachment through central Denver Friday night, a chase that began near City Park and ended in the Lower Downtown (LoDo) area. The tractor had been taken from a Denver Water facility in the Lincoln Park neighborhood. Video from witnesses showed the vehicle driving on busy streets and sidewalks, even crossing Park Avenue, while more than a dozen police vehicles and a helicopter followed. The pursuit ended near 15th and Market when a police cruiser rammed the tractor head-on; the impact deployed the cruiser’s airbags. One witness said the officer who drove the ram vehicle then used a Taser to subdue the tractor driver. Two officers were taken to a hospital with injuries but were treated and released by Saturday morning. The suspect, a male, was apprehended and reportedly placed in an ambulance; his identity has not been released as the investigation continues. Authorities said officers did not discharge their firearms. Denver Water confirmed the tractor was stolen and referred additional questions to the Denver Police Department. Further details are pending as the investigation proceeds.

New BYU research finds Oahu’s mountains are being dissolved from within by groundwater more than by surface erosion. Geologist Steve Nelson and colleagues sampled groundwater and stream water, using USGS data to estimate annual mineral mass loss, finding chemical weathering removes more material than physical erosion. Variable rainfall affects weathering rates across Hawaii’s volcanic rock. Tectonic uplift currently outpaces loss, so Oahu may continue growing for about 1.5 million years, after which groundwater-driven dissolution will flatten the island into a low-lying plateau similar to Midway.

A new Gallup poll finds U.S. congressional approval at an all-time low: just 10 percent of Americans approve of Congress’s job performance, the weakest rating in nearly 40 years of Gallup polling. Gallup’s editor-in-chief noted that in the survey’s history only figures like Fidel Castro, Saddam Hussein, Osama bin Laden and Mark Fuhrman have been less popular. The piece highlights surprising things and people that score higher than Congress in various polls. For example, during the 2010 BP Gulf oil spill, 16 percent approved of BP’s response—still more than Congress today. A CBS/New York Times poll found 33 percent view “socialism” positively, triple Congress’s approval. A CNN/ORC poll reported 50 percent of respondents favored allowing waterboarding as an interrogation tactic, higher than congressional approval. On abortion, a July ABC/Washington Post poll found 19 percent support legalization in all cases. Historical comparisons include Richard Nixon at 24 percent approval during Watergate. Other items more popular than Congress: 16 percent of Americans never believed in Santa Claus as children; 21 percent worldwide approved of Greek PM George Papandreou during the debt crisis; 24 percent supported Occupy Wall Street and 27 percent identified with the Tea Party. Even unpopular celebrity Paris Hilton is viewed more favorably than Congress.

Supreme Court argument in Shelby County v. Holder signaled that Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act — the preclearance requirement forcing certain jurisdictions to clear voting changes with federal authorities — is in serious jeopardy. Conservative justices questioned whether historical evidence still justifies singling out nine mostly Southern states and whether those jurisdictions remain subject to a federal “trusteeship.” Chief Justice Roberts, Justice Scalia and others suggested the modern South had moved beyond the conditions that motivated the Act, with Scalia calling the law a “perpetuation of racial entitlement.” Justice Kennedy probed whether Congress’s 2006 reauthorization could rely on decades-old data rather than current evidence. Liberals and defenders of the law, including Justice Breyer, Justice Sotomayor and NAACP lawyer Debo Adegbile, argued Congress reasonably found ongoing discrimination and that the Act responds to a long historical pattern of disenfranchisement. The 2006 renewal overwhelmingly passed Congress, they noted. If Section 5 is struck down, the covered states could more easily enact stricter voter ID rules, relocate polling places, or redistrict without federal oversight. The Court’s conservative majority appears poised to narrow or invalidate Section 5, likely producing a close 5–4 decision and leaving Congress with a politically difficult task to devise a new coverage formula.

The Ig Nobel Prizes are a long-running, tongue-in-cheek awards program that honors research and actions that first make people laugh, then make them think. Organized by the Annals of Improbable Research and presented each September at Harvard’s Sanders Theatre, the ceremony features ten prizes awarded annually since 1991. Genuine Nobel laureates physically hand out the awards onstage amid theatrical antics—paper airplanes, opera singers, and an audience of academics and curious spectators—while winners receive symbolic, often humorous prizes such as a nearly worthless $10 trillion Zimbabwean banknote. The program’s goal is to celebrate imagination, spur interest in science, medicine, and technology, and draw attention to unusual but thought-provoking work; most winning studies are published in peer-reviewed journals.

The 2016 Ig Nobels illustrate the range and rationale of the awards. The Chemistry Prize was wryly given to Volkswagen for cheating emissions tests—“solving” reduced emissions only while cars were being tested—underscoring social critique as well as humor. The Physics Prize went to research showing why white horses attract fewer horseflies and why dragonflies are fatally drawn to polished black gravestones: both phenomena are explained by polarized light signals. The Medicine Prize recognized a study finding that visual input can relieve itch: if you watch a mirror image of scratching, perceived relief occurs even when the actual scratching targets the non-itchy arm. Psychology and related awards highlighted human deception and credulity: a team that surveyed 1,000 self-described liars won for studying how frequently people lie and how well they do it; another group won the Peace Prize for analyzing susceptibility to pseudo-profound but meaningless statements—“pseudo-profound bullshit”—and showing that less reflective individuals and those with lower analytic thinking are more likely to find such gibberish profound.

Other winners in 2016 included a reproduction prize for studies on how different trouser fabrics affect rats’ sexual activity (and parallel human tests), an economics prize for research into perceived “personalities” of rocks, a literature prize for a Swedish author’s multi-volume books on collecting flies, and a perception prize for investigating how bending over and viewing objects between one’s legs alters appearance. The biology prize was shared by two British experimenters—Charles Foster, who has attempted to live as various wild animals, and Thomas Thwaites, who created prosthetic limbs to live briefly as a goat—both projects offering immersive insights into nonhuman perspectives.

Beyond the spectacle, the Ig Nobels host follow-up Informal Lectures where winners get more time to present their work, and maintain an archive of past ceremonies and videos. Nomination and delegation processes, volunteer and sponsorship opportunities, and media coverage reinforce the event’s role as a playful yet serious celebration of curiosity-driven inquiry.

An improvised explosive device partially detonated on a District Line train at Parsons Green during Friday morning rush hour, injuring 29 people, including a young boy. The device, later photographed as a white bucket in a supermarket bag with wires and a small fire, sent a fireball through a carriage but did not fully explode; forensic and security experts suggested the initiator detonated while the main charge failed. Witnesses described panic, crushes on station steps, burns and chemical smells; many victims were treated in London hospitals, with none suffering life-threatening injuries.

Islamic State’s Amaq agency claimed responsibility; police and counter-terror teams are treating the blast as terrorism and are hunting the person or persons who placed the device. CCTV from the Underground and surrounding businesses is being examined; officials believe the device may have been remotely detonated and that the bomber could have left the train beforehand. Prime Minister Theresa May raised the UK terrorism threat level to critical, announced increased armed police and military support at protected sites, and urged calm. Hundreds of detectives and MI5 were involved in the probe, and the public has been asked to submit images and remain vigilant as investigations continue.

Facebook users have mobilized to boycott Spirit Airlines after the carrier refused to refund a dying 76-year-old veteran’s $197 ticket. Jerry Meekins, a former Marine with terminal esophageal cancer, canceled plans to fly from Florida to New Jersey to see his daughter for surgery after his doctor advised against air travel. Outrage exploded on social media: the “Boycott Spirit Airlines” Facebook page, originally created in 2010 over luggage fees, surged from about 700 likes to over 18,000. Much of the backlash has come from active-duty military and veterans, and veterans’ groups including the Veterans of the Vietnam War and the Veterans Coalition have written to Spirit. Commenters called for an apology and vowed never to fly the carrier. Spirit Airlines did not respond to requests for comment. Separately, Spirit is changing its carry-on fee structure effective November 6, raising gate carry-on fees to as much as $100 and increasing online and other purchase fees, with new carry-on ranges of $25–$100.

German police are hunting for a stolen refrigerated trailer loaded with more than 20 tons of chocolate and sweets, including Nutella and Kinder Surprise, taken between Saturday evening and midday Sunday near Neustadt. Authorities estimate the haul’s value at roughly €50,000–€70,000 (about $80,000) and say perpetrators would have needed another truck to tow such heavy cargo. Investigators are unsure if the theft was planned or opportunistic and are probing links to other recent trailer thefts, including an empty trailer taken in Weimar and a separate disappearance of 30 tons of fruit juice in Wittenberg. Officials urge anyone offered large, unusually sourced chocolate to alert police and not to dispose of it. The theft follows other recent confectionery-related crimes in Germany and Europe.

French warplanes and U.N. helicopters searched northern Mali for the wreckage of Air Algerie flight AH5017 after it disappeared en route from Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, to Algiers with 110 passengers and six crew. Nearly half the passengers were French (51), with others from Burkina Faso, Lebanon, Algeria, Luxembourg, Canada, Germany and several other countries. French Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius said the pilot had requested a change of route shortly after takeoff because of a storm, suggesting bad weather might be involved, but he stressed no hypothesis was ruled out. Conflicting reports emerged on the crash location: Mali’s president said wreckage was sighted between Aguelhoc and Kidal near the Algerian border, while Burkina Faso officials and local authorities near Gossi reported remains about 50 km from the Burkina border in southern Mali. French Mirage jets and other search assets initially found no trace. President François Hollande canceled overseas engagements and pledged all available military resources to the search. The operation is hampered by vast, sparsely inhabited desert terrain, limited Malian government presence, and control of parts of the region by Tuareg and Islamist groups. The aircraft, an MD-83 operated by Swiftair for Air Algerie, had a relatively clean operator record; investigators awaited more information as international concern over aviation safety grew.

A Mississippi State University student, 21-year-old John Sanderson of Madison, was fatally shot late Saturday night in Evans Hall, a four-story male residence housing about 300 students. Campus police were alerted around 10 p.m. and arrived within a minute; Sanderson was transported to Oktibbeha County Hospital and died about 30 minutes later. University officials say three black male suspects fled in a blue Crown Victoria and remain at large; no arrests had been made. Mississippi State is operating under advisory conditions, with increased patrols, restricted residence-hall entry, a call center for parents, and frequent text alerts. President Mark Keenum called the shooting unprecedented on campus but characterized it as an isolated incident. Separately, a freshman at Jackson State University, Nolan Ryan Henderson III, 19, was shot and killed early Sunday at an off-campus apartment pool party. State leaders expressed sorrow, pledged assistance in investigations, and reminded campuses have resources and safety measures in place.

In Sutherlin, Oregon, police arrested 37-year-old Jedediah Ezekiel Fulton on March 16 after an incident at a McDonald’s where employees refused his request for 30 double cheeseburgers. Authorities allege Fulton reacted angrily, tore down a banner, and physically damaged the restaurant’s golden arches. He also reportedly grabbed another person’s shirt during the confrontation. A witness, fearing for that person’s safety, drew a gun. Fulton faces multiple charges including second-degree disorderly conduct, second-degree criminal trespass, second-degree criminal mischief and harassment. The News-Review first reported the story; online records do not indicate whether Fulton has an attorney. The incident underscores how an escalated dispute over an order led to criminal charges and property damage.

On May 11, 2015, Antioch police responded around 7:44 p.m. to a reported burglary in the 4900 block of Ridgeview Drive. A homeowner said she saw an intruder enter through an unlocked door while she was inside holding her baby; she fled with the baby but left her four-year-old daughter in the house. Officers found the child at the top of the stairs and directed her outside, where she told her mother the intruder was hiding in the little girl’s bedroom closet. Police located 21-year-old transient Demaria Lopez in that closet. Lopez initially refused commands and briefly struggled with officers but was taken into custody without injury and booked on burglary and resisting arrest charges. Authorities seek tips via Det. McManus or text to CRIMES with keyword ANTIOCH.

President Obama made a surprise, personal 18-minute appearance in the White House briefing room after George Zimmerman’s acquittal in Trayvon Martin’s killing, framing the verdict within America’s long history of racial discrimination. Saying “Trayvon Martin could have been me 35 years ago,” Obama described everyday humiliations African‑American men face—being followed in stores, hearing car doors click shut, or seeing people clutch purses—and explained how those experiences shape the Black community’s response to the case. He urged respect for the jury’s verdict and warned against violence, while calling for “soul‑searching” by Americans about their own biases: “Am I wringing as much bias out of myself as I can?” He noted progress across generations—citing his daughters and their peers—but stressed the nation remains imperfect and must continue improving. Obama proposed concrete steps: training for state and local law enforcement to address racial bias, examining laws like Florida’s “Stand Your Ground” for their potential to encourage deadly confrontations, and pursuing a long‑term effort to support African‑American boys who receive negative reinforcement. His remarks, more expansive on race than most of his presidency, were welcomed by many Black leaders and Trayvon’s parents, though some activists felt he had been slow to speak.

La FDA propuso nuevas reglas para proteger la salud pública al prohibir el uso de lámparas solares y camas de bronceado en interiores por menores de 18 años y reducir riesgos para adultos. La acción responde a la relación comprobada entre bronceado en interiores y cáncer de piel, incluyendo melanoma —el riesgo aumenta 59%— así como quemaduras y daño ocular. Se exigiría a mayores de 18 firmar cada seis meses un reconocimiento de riesgos. También se proponen normas de seguridad más estrictas: advertencias más visibles, botón de apagado de emergencia, requisitos de protección ocular, etiquetado de bombillas de reemplazo y prohibición de modificaciones peligrosas sin recertificación. Hay 90 días para comentar las reglas en regulations.gov; se aplican a fabricantes y operadores de salones.

PBS drew heavy criticism after its live broadcast of the annual A Capitol Fourth concert and fireworks on July 4 mixed footage from prior years into the “live” show. Viewers pointed out inconsistencies—clear-sky fireworks on air contrasted with the actual overcast, foggy conditions in Washington, D.C., and the absence of long-standing scaffolding on the Capitol building in the televised shots. Tweets and Facebook comments accused PBS of airing “fake” footage and questioned the network’s transparency. Producers later acknowledged on social media that the broadcast “showed a combination of the best fireworks from this year and previous years,” calling it “the patriotic thing to do.” A Capitol Fourth representatives told reporters that the decision was made to “make the best television show” because dense cloud cover obscured much of the live display; they said this was the first time they’d had to use such measures. The controversy prompted complaints that viewers should have been informed that portions were pre-recorded. The show’s host, Tom Bergeron, had joked about weather during rehearsals and said rain didn’t worry him, noting the event’s primary draw is the performances, not the fireworks. Separately, the document also included an unrelated piece about a Texas teen severely injured making a homemade fireworks device.

The Metropolitan Police said it is assessing newly received information about the 1997 deaths of Princess Diana and Dodi Al Fayed, examining its relevance and credibility but insisting this is not a re‑investigation. Officers from the specialist crime and operations command will carry out the assessment; the force declined to disclose the source. British newspapers have reported allegations of military involvement and that an Army source passed material to police, but Scotland Yard would not confirm that. A royal spokeswoman said Princes William and Harry and Clarence House would not comment. Dodi’s father, Mohamed Al Fayed, said he had no immediate comment but would be interested in the outcome and trusted the Met to investigate vigorously. The statement underlined that the deaths were thoroughly examined in previous inquiries: the 1999 French probe and Operation Paget, whose 2006 report found no evidence of murder. A 2008 inquest ruled the couple were unlawfully killed due to their driver’s gross negligence, paparazzi pursuit and other factors.

After The Journal News published a searchable map listing names and addresses of pistol permit holders across three New York counties, a backlash erupted: critics called the move invasive and potentially dangerous; supporters cited public-record law. In response, blogger Christopher Fountain and readers crowd-sourced home addresses, photos and contact details for dozens of Journal News employees and executives, uploaded a counter-map and urged advertiser boycotts. The site repeatedly updated names, FOIL requests and correspondence with county clerks, and tracked which Journal staff appeared on pistol-permit lists. The controversy sparked national coverage, threats and defensive statements; the paper later removed its map after a new NYSAFE law allowed permit-holders to request redaction. Observers warn that open data can empower civic debate — or be weaponized for partisan retaliation.

Researchers at Weill Cornell Medical College report evidence that epsilon toxin, produced by certain strains (B and D) of the foodborne bacterium Clostridium perfringens, may trigger multiple sclerosis (MS). In laboratory studies presented at an American Society for Microbiology meeting, the toxin increased blood–brain barrier permeability and killed oligodendrocytes, the myelin-producing cells destroyed in MS lesions; it also bound meningeal cells, suggesting a possible mechanism for meningeal inflammation and cortical lesions seen in MS. Prior work found C. perfringens type B in an MS patient, and testing of banked samples showed MS patients were more likely to have antibodies indicating prior exposure to the epsilon toxin. In a small survey of food, about 13% contained C. perfringens and 2.7% carried the epsilon toxin gene. Experts caution the findings are preliminary; if confirmed, they raise the prospect of vaccines, antibodies, drugs or probiotics to neutralize the toxin and potentially prevent or treat MS.

Eleven-year-old Yonatan Daniel Aguilar was found dead on August 22 in a small Echo Park home, wrapped in a blanket and lying on a hard tile floor inside a cramped bedroom closet. He weighed just 34 pounds, could not stretch his legs in the space, had pressure sores from the tile, and had foam in his nose. Medicinal cups containing pink and red liquid were found near his balding body. Court documents and reporting by the Los Angeles Times indicate Yonatan, who had been diagnosed with autism, was hidden in that closet and repeatedly sedated with liquid sleep medication for about three years to keep him quiet.

Yonatan had stopped attending school around 2012 after being seen with a black eye and hoarding food—behaviors his therapist later linked to earlier deprivation. His mother, Veronica Aguilar, told teachers, counselors and others that he was safe or had been sent to an institution in Mexico; investigators say she successfully misled school staff, medical professionals, coaches and social workers. Although the county Department of Children and Family Services had responded to six reports about the family from 2009 to 2012 and rated Yonatan’s risk as “high” multiple times, social workers ultimately deemed allegations inconclusive or unfounded and did not open a formal case, after which contact ceased.

Investigators say even Yonatan’s stepfather, Jose Pinzon, who lived in the home, was unaware the boy was there until Aguilar led him to the closet and said Yonatan had died. Pinzon immediately called police. Veronica Aguilar, 39, is charged with murder and child abuse causing death and is held on $2 million bail. Authorities continue to probe how the abuse was concealed for years and why protective agencies failed to secure the child’s safety.

Egypt has requested the extradition of Seif al-Din (Seif Eddin) Mustafa, the 58–59-year-old Egyptian who hijacked an EgyptAir flight from Alexandria to Cairo and forced it to land in Larnaca, Cyprus. Cypriot officials described Mustafa as psychologically unstable; he used a fake explosive belt and made incoherent demands, initially asking to see his Cypriot ex-wife who lives in Cyprus. The six-hour standoff ended peacefully after almost all 56 passengers, six crew and a security official were released; seven people remained briefly on board. A crew member escaped through a cockpit window shortly before Mustafa walked calmly from the aircraft and surrendered. He gave a V-sign in court and has been remanded in custody for eight days; possible charges include air piracy, kidnapping and threats.

Cyprus authorities and Egypt’s prosecutors, citing a 1996 bilateral treaty, are coordinating extradition. Officials characterized the act as a family-motivated incident rather than terrorism, though it revived concerns about Egyptian airport security following October’s Metrojet bombing over Sinai. CCTV released by Egypt’s interior ministry shows Mustafa being screened twice and his bag X-rayed at Alexandria’s Borg El Arab airport; authorities say he used ordinary items to simulate an explosive belt. Passengers and crew praised the crew’s calm handling—described as diplomatic and exemplary—which helped secure the passengers’ release. Egyptian media warned the hijacking could harm tourism further, already damaged by the Sinai crash. Investigations continue into Mustafa’s motives and how he bypassed security appearance, while Cyprus proceeds with legal steps and extradition requests.

The U.S. Census Bureau report for July 1, 2013–July 1, 2014 shows Florida has become the nation’s third-most populous state, with nearly 19.9 million residents, surpassing New York’s 19.7 million. Florida added about 293,000 people over the year—an average of roughly 803 new residents per day—while New York’s population grew by only about 51,000. Nationwide, the U.S. population rose 0.75 percent to roughly 318.9 million, with 44 states and the District of Columbia gaining residents; six states—Illinois, West Virginia, Connecticut, New Mexico, Alaska and Vermont—lost population. Puerto Rico experienced the largest proportional decline, losing about 47,000 people (1.3 percent). Growth was concentrated in the South and West, which together accounted for about 2 million of nearly 2.4 million new U.S. residents; the Midwest and Northeast gained about 300,000. North Dakota led in percentage growth at about 2.2 percent, driven by an energy boom. Other fast-growing states included Nevada, Texas, Colorado, Arizona, Utah and Idaho. Texas added the most people overall (451,000). California (38.8 million) and Texas (27 million) remain first and second; Georgia surpassed 10 million for the first time.

A 19-year-old Dutchman forced his way into the NOS broadcaster’s studios in Hilversum on Jan. 29, demanding airtime and threatening bomb attacks, but was quickly arrested without injuries. Wearing a black suit and carrying a pistol with a silencer (later found to be fake), he threatened a security guard and was led to an empty studio where he paced and spoke on camera, claiming to be “hired in by intelligence agencies” and asserting ties to a “hackers’ collective.” He also presented a letter warning of explosives and radioactive material across the Netherlands if not given airtime; authorities could not immediately verify the letter’s authenticity. Police special units swept the building, found no explosives, and detained the suspect—identified as living in Pijnacker—on suspicion of making threats, weapons possession, and taking a hostage. NOS canceled its main evening bulletins, evacuated staff, and resumed broadcasting later from The Hague. Officials said the man appeared to have acted alone and was not on extremist watchlists; there was no immediate link to Islamic extremism. Prosecutors and police were investigating his background, motives, and whether he had accomplices. The incident prompted renewed attention to security at Media Park, which has been tightly guarded since the 2002 murder of politician Pim Fortuyn.

A stolen pickup and a 3-week-old baby were recovered after a passerby mistook a doll in the vehicle for an unresponsive infant and called 911, Lumberton police said. The mother had briefly turned to bring two other small children into a house Monday evening when someone stole her dark gray 2014 Ford F-150; the infant was in a car seat in the back. Police issued an alert and the truck — with the baby still inside — was abandoned about 10 minutes later in a grocery parking lot roughly three miles away. A man walking past noticed a window was down, saw what he thought was an unresponsive baby (actually a doll), and notified authorities. Deputies found the unharmed infant at 9:26 p.m. No arrests have been made; two suspects are being sought. Police credited the caller and deputies and asked anyone with information to contact Detective Deana Locklear.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) at Los Angeles International Airport intercepted 67 live giant African snails in an air cargo shipment from Lagos, Nigeria. The snails arrived in two plastic packages weighing just over 35 pounds and were labeled as Achatina fulica for human consumption, destined for San Dimas, California. CBP agriculture specialists flagged the shipment July 1–7, sent samples to USDA plant protection and quarantine entomologists, and a Washington specialist identified them as giant African snails (Archachatina marginata). Officials said this was the largest such seizure at LAX and that the shipment appeared to be a personal package, not concealed. USDA and CBP described the snails as highly invasive: they can consume more than 500 plant species, damage homes by eating stucco and paint, live up to a decade, and carry parasites dangerous to humans, including one linked to meningitis. Because of their threat to agriculture, ecosystems and public health, the snails were quarantined, transferred to the USDA for final precautions, and ultimately disposed of by incineration. Authorities emphasized the interception as an example of protecting U.S. agriculture from foreign pests.

Tennessee state Sen. Stacey Campfield sparked controversy after posting a blog “joke” about pressure cookers one week after pressure-cooker bombs killed three people at the Boston Marathon. His post, titled “Here comes Feinstein again,” pictured an “Assault Pressure Cooker” with parts labeled mockingly (e.g., “folding stock,” “large-capacity, can cook for hours without reloading”), a jab at Sen. Dianne Feinstein’s efforts to ban certain assault-weapon features. When asked whether the timing was insensitive, Campfield told WVLT “People need to lighten up,” and criticized calls for gun control after tragedies like Sandy Hook as hypocritical. He defended the post in a follow-up blog, accusing the left of a double standard and added a comment about liberals “bitterly clinging to their gun control and secular humanism.” The incident adds to prior controversies involving Campfield, including a withdrawn bill tying student academic performance to family welfare, threats to cut university funding over a “Sex Week,” and past anti-LGBTQ remarks.

Flint’s lead-in-water crisis has extended a potential risk to animals: two dogs in Genesee County recently tested positive for lead toxicity, the first confirmed canine cases in Michigan in five years, state veterinarian Dr. James Averill said. The positive tests were confirmed in October 2015 and January 2016; one dog was a family pet and the other a stray. Officials have not released details about the animals’ locations, ages, weights, symptoms, or blood-lead levels, citing owner confidentiality and the Animal Industry Act. It also has not been publicly confirmed whether the dogs drank Flint tap water.

State officials urged residents to protect pets the same way they would themselves: test household water, install appropriate filters if needed, and give animals only filtered or bottled water. Bathing pets in Flint tap water is considered acceptable, but drinking it is discouraged. Veterinarians are asked to report suspected lead toxicity; if a vet suspects lead exposure, laboratory testing is provided free. Averill noted that most canine lead tests in the area have been negative, and veterinarians are the frontline for detecting potential cases. Symptoms of lead poisoning in animals are varied and often mimic other conditions—vomiting, malaise, behavioral or routine changes, weakness, neurological or blood issues—making veterinary evaluation crucial. Local veterinarians said they hadn’t personally seen recent confirmed cases they attributed to lead but have warned staff to watch for signs and advised owners to seek prompt veterinary care if pets deviate from normal behavior. As an interim measure, vets suggested alternatives like using bottled or filtered water or even melted snow if no safer water is available. Anyone who notices unusual behavior in pets is encouraged to consult a veterinarian.

An international team of researchers has produced the first data-driven global map and estimate of the planet’s groundwater, revealing that only a small fraction is renewed within a human lifetime. Published in Nature Geoscience and led by Tom Gleeson (University of Victoria) with collaborators from several institutions, the study combined nearly a million watershed data points and over 40,000 groundwater models to estimate a total groundwater volume of about 23 million cubic kilometres. Of that, roughly 0.35 million cubic kilometres—between about 1% and less than 6% of groundwater within the upper two kilometres of land—qualifies as “modern” groundwater (younger than 50 years) and thus renewable on human timescales.

Modern groundwater is concentrated in tropical and mountainous regions, notably the Amazon Basin, the Congo, Indonesia, and along western North and South America; arid regions such as the Sahara contain very little. Modern groundwater interacts more readily with the active water and climate cycles and can buffer droughts by sustaining river flows, but it is more vulnerable to contamination and climate change. Much deeper, older groundwater—sometimes saline or containing arsenic or uranium—is often exploited for agriculture and industry and in many cases is effectively non-renewable on human timescales.

The study provides a foundation to assess how long groundwater supplies will last under current depletion rates and to inform sustainable management and policy. The authors plan further global-scale modeling to relate groundwater volumes to extraction and depletion trends, building on earlier work that identified regional groundwater stress hotspots.

Ryder Johnson, a 20–21-year-old man from Lafayette, Colorado, has been missing since Jan. 17 after finishing his shift at Eldora Mountain Resort near Nederland. He was last seen leaving work around 3 p.m.; his vehicle was later found that night parked at the Gross Reservoir/Gross Dam parking area on Flagstaff Road in southwest Boulder County, roughly 20-plus miles from Eldora. Despite extensive searches by law enforcement, rescue teams, volunteers and cadaver dogs across areas including Gross Reservoir, Walker Ranch and 180 acres around Eldora (including eight miles of Nordic trails), investigators have found no sign of Johnson or clear leads. In June, a severed foot in a boot was recovered near the resort; DNA testing by the Boulder County Coroner’s Office ruled the remains did not belong to Johnson. Boulder County Sheriff’s Office has not ruled out foul play but notes the most plausible working theories are that Johnson either intentionally wandered into the mountains and died by his own hand or voluntarily disappeared to start a new life — though the latter seems unlikely given his lack of apparent resources. His parents, frustrated but persistent, have organized searches and, with friends’ donations, have posted a $100,000 reward for information leading to criminal charges, his recovery, or recovery of his belongings; the family set a claim deadline of Jan. 17, 2017 (the one-year anniversary), but say their search will continue. Anyone with information is urged to contact the Boulder County Sheriff’s Office.

Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist Junot Díaz has publicly denied multiple accusations of inappropriate behavior by several women writers, including Zinzi Clemmons’s claim that he “forcibly kissed” her. In his first extended interview since the allegations surfaced, Díaz said he was “distressed,” “confused,” and “panicked,” insisting he had not been sexually inappropriate or abusive. He maintained that some complaints reflect poor relationships or defensiveness rather than predation, drawing a line between being a “bad boyfriend” and predatory behavior. The accusations prompted investigations by MIT and Boston Review; both organizations declined to remove Díaz after reviews concluded the complaints lacked the severity characteristic of the #MeToo cases that led to firings. The situation has split the literary community: some defend Díaz and warn against social-media punishment without due process, while others argue that a range of misogynistic behaviors should be addressed as part of #MeToo. Several women, including Carmen Maria Machado, Monica Byrne, and Alisa Rivera, described encounters they found humiliating, verbally abusive, or invasive; Díaz disputes these accounts. He also faced criticism for a New Yorker essay disclosing his childhood rape, which some saw as preemptive. The controversy prompted resignations at Boston Review and ongoing debate about how institutions should differentiate between types of harmful behavior and what consequences are appropriate. The Pulitzer board’s inquiry continues.

An Alabama truck driver, Keith Maddox, was arrested after posting videos threatening bicyclists that went viral. In clips from May 20–21, 2014, Maddox is shown driving past cyclists while shouting insults and threats—saying he ought to “run him in the ditch,” that he’d “put him in the ditch,” and “I’m gonna hurt one of them one of these days.” He also revved his engine to intimidate riders and mocked them with “That scare you boys?” Cycling groups discovered the footage online and notified the Calhoun County Sheriff’s Office. Authorities charged Maddox with reckless endangerment, a misdemeanor, and released him on $3,000 bond. Following the public outcry, he posted (and later removed) an apology on Facebook, asking forgiveness and claiming he would never intentionally hurt anyone, calling the videos “in very bad taste” and apologizing specifically to the Northeast Alabama Bicycle Association. The case drew attention from cycling advocates and the community; the videos prompted his arrest and widespread condemnation. A compilation of his posted videos circulated online.

A new analysis of Fukushima health-survey data finds markedly elevated rates of thyroid cancer among children who were living near the Fukushima Daiichi plant when it melted down in March 2011. Led by Toshihide Tsuda of Okayama University and published in Epidemiology, the study used results from prefecture-wide ultrasound screening of roughly 298,577 children (initial round) and continued screening into a second round through the end of 2014. Comparing observed cases with expected Japanese incidence and with a reference district inside Fukushima, the authors report prevalence and incidence rate ratios far above normal: up to about 50 times the expected rate using a four-year latency assumption in one district, an overall prevalence of 605 per million examinees (95% CI 302–1,082), and an incidence rate ratio of about 12 in the second round. Tsuda contends these elevations are unlikely to be explained solely by intensive screening (“screening effect”) and suggest a real excess of childhood thyroid cancer in the prefecture within four years of the releases.

The findings have stirred debate. Thyroid cancer in children is a recognized radiation-linked disease from Chernobyl and, while typically treatable, entails lifelong medication and policy consequences for compensation and evacuation. Critics and independent experts caution that the study lacks individual-level radiation dose data and may inappropriately compare screened populations to clinically detected cases, potentially inflating apparent excesses. Authorities such as WHO and UNSCEAR previously predicted no discernible radiation-caused cancer rise; other researchers emphasize the complexities of post-disaster epidemiology and the need for further investigations that link individual exposures, account rigorously for screening intensity, and continue long-term follow-up. Meanwhile, ongoing thyroid screening, mental-health and broader health surveys in Fukushima persist to monitor residents’ health and inform policy.

Vuvuzelas—loud plastic horns ubiquitous at South Africa’s World Cup—have provoked mixed reactions. Players like Cristiano Ronaldo and Patrice Evra complain the 127-decibel noise hampers concentration, communication and sleep; broadcasters and viewers have also criticised its interference with TV commentary. Despite this, FIFA and local organisers insist vuvuzelas are part of South African football culture and will not be banned, though they may be prohibited if used dangerously (thrown onto the pitch) or blown during national anthems and announcements. Supporters and figures such as Jamie Carragher, Sepp Blatter and England’s Supporters’ Band defend the horns as an expression of local rhythm and atmosphere. Organisers continue to monitor use and encourage singing as an alternative.

Philadelphia police are investigating after a 36-year-old woman with intellectual disabilities was found chained to a bed in the basement of a home on the 200 block of Linton Street in Olney. Officers discovered her during a welfare check late Friday after responding to a neighborhood dispute that led to the arrest of 46-year-old Regina Bennett on unrelated charges. During a walkthrough of the residence, police found the victim extremely thin, with sores and a limited vocabulary; chains and zip-ties were removed and she was taken to Albert Einstein Medical Center for evaluation. Neighbors and relatives gave conflicting accounts: some described Bennett as the woman’s caretaker and defended her past care, while others depicted Bennett as volatile, often intoxicated, and fearful to have around the block. Authorities have charged Bennett with multiple offenses, including aggravated assault, unlawful restraint, false imprisonment, terroristic threats, and related counts. The discovery has drawn comparisons to other Philadelphia cases in which disabled people were allegedly held captive for financial gain. Investigators continue to probe the relationship between Bennett and the victim and the full circumstances that led to the woman’s confinement.

Britain’s Duke and Duchess of Cambridge have released a third official portrait of eight-month-old Prince George ahead of their April tour to New Zealand and Australia. Photographed at Kensington Palace by Jason Bell, the image shows the family looking through an open window: Catherine cradles George, who wears a pale blue jumper with his name, while William holds the family dog, Lupo. It is George’s first official picture since his christening last October and will preface the Cambridges’ April 7–25 visit. The itinerary includes Wellington, Christchurch, Dunedin and Auckland in New Zealand, then Canberra, Uluru, Sydney and Adelaide in Australia, with commemorative ANZAC Day events and tributes to war dead. Catherine makes her debut to both countries; William visited previously. It remains undecided which engagements will include George, as the couple will finalize appearances closer to the tour. Their party includes George’s nanny and support staff for the three-week trip.

Historic England has uncovered a medieval holy well, St Anne’s Well, on private farmland in Rainhill after excavation work prompted by its listing on the National Heritage List and a 1983 photograph showing its remnants. Once a focus of pilgrimage, the sandstone well measures almost 2m by 2m and includes three steps leading down to a pool where pilgrims bathed, believing the waters washed away sins and could cure ailments such as eye disease. Holy wells like this were important in medieval Christianity and the cult of St Anne grew in England after the late 14th century, placing the well likely in the late medieval period.

Buried and nearly lost from years of arable ploughing, the site had been on Historic England’s Heritage at Risk Register since 2010. Oxford Archaeology North conducted a careful two-day excavation, revealing the well in reasonable condition. Fallen stones were reset, new wooden edging installed to protect the perimeter from soil collapse and farm machinery, and a management agreement arranged with the farmer to control vegetation. With these measures the well has been removed from the at-risk list.

Though on private land, the farmer allowed visits by Rainhill Civic Society and Merseyside Archaeological Society members, who joined Historic England staff and an Inspector of Ancient Monuments to view the repaired site. Local memory of the well endures—one visitor recalled seeing it as a boy in the 1950s. Historic England emphasizes the find as an example of tangible heritage recovery and community engagement, preserving a once-revered sacred site for the future.

Michael Phelps, the most decorated Olympian in history, heads to his fifth Games in Rio at age 31, a U.S. record among male swimmers. Having won the U.S. trials in the 200m butterfly, 200m individual medley and 100m butterfly, he is likely to add to his 22 Olympic medals (18 gold) and may swim up to three relays. Phelps and fellow veteran Ryan Lochte (turning 32 during Rio) are rare exceptions in a sport dominated by youth; either could become the oldest individual Olympic gold medalist if they win solo gold in Brazil.

Phelps’ Olympic journey began as a 15-year-old in Sydney 2000, where he finished fifth in the 200m butterfly but showed elite potential. In Athens 2004 he exploded onto the scene with six golds and two bronzes across individual and relay events, setting multiple Olympic records. Beijing 2008 became historic: Phelps won eight golds—an all-time single-Games record—setting world records in seven races and cementing his legacy. In London 2012 he secured six medals (four golds), becoming the most decorated Olympian with 22 medals and achieving streaks of three consecutive Olympic titles in the 200m IM and 100m butterfly before a brief retirement.

For Rio, Phelps was also honored as Team USA’s Opening Ceremony flag bearer, chosen by fellow athletes. He said representing the U.S. and his family means more now than medal counts. The Games run Aug. 5–21 in Rio de Janeiro, the first Olympics in South America.

A 27-year-old Bangladeshi immigrant, identified as Akayed Ullah, detonated a crude pipe bomb strapped to his body in a crowded Manhattan subway passage near Times Square on a Monday morning, around 7:20 a.m. The improvised device, affixed with Velcro and zip ties and triggered by a small battery connected to Christmas lights, produced a large puff of smoke and left Ullah wounded with burns and cuts to his hands and abdomen. Three commuters suffered minor injuries — ringing in the ears and headaches — and sought hospital care. Security video captured the moment of the blast and Ullah on the ground; he spoke to investigators immediately and has told authorities he acted alone. Law enforcement officials said Ullah was inspired by Islamic State propaganda and expressed anger at U.S. policy toward Muslim countries. The FBI and NYPD launched an investigation, collected bomb remnants and searched related residences; federal charges were expected. The incident halted morning commutes as authorities secured the area and checked for additional devices. City officials emphasized that quick police response and the device’s poor construction limited harm. Mayor Bill de Blasio called it an attempted terrorist attack; Gov. Andrew Cuomo noted the device was “effectively low-tech.” National figures including President Trump and Attorney General Jeff Sessions seized on the event to criticize immigration policies, while local residents and neighbors expressed shock and concern about potential backlash against immigrant communities. A pro-IS media group later suggested the attack was linked to recent U.S. policy moves, though no formal claim of responsibility was made.

Verizon is rolling out "Share Everything" family plans June 28, replacing per-device data caps with a shared data pool plus per-device access fees and mandatory unlimited voice and text. For families that pay for many devices, the change can be neutral or slightly beneficial on paper, but it often reshuffles costs rather than cutting them. Using a hypothetical seven-device, two-parent-two-kid household, the article compares Verizon’s old family pricing (multiple individual data allotments totaling 11GB for $180) with the new shared option (10GB shared plus device access fees). The shared option costs roughly $290 versus $300 under the old structure—only about $10 savings while actually reducing total data by 1GB; any overage would erase that small difference. The headline benefit is convenience and efficiency: under shared plans light users no longer “waste” unused individual allotments while heavy users can draw from the communal pool, which better matches many families’ real usage patterns.

However, there are important downsides. Individuals and couples who rarely use voice or texts will be forced into paying for unlimited voice and texting they don’t need, plus steep device access fees ($40/month per smartphone, $30 for feature phones, $10 for tablets, $20 for hotspots). That raises monthly bills for many single-line customers and smaller households compared with older, tailored plans. Existing customers can keep grandfathered plans until they upgrade, but upgrades can force loss of unlimited data. Analysts note the strategy increases family “stickiness” to a single carrier by bundling data into households, favoring larger incumbents. Critics argue Verizon’s plan mainly restructures billing and incentives—shifting how average revenue per user is counted—rather than providing broad consumer savings. For families the choice is between simplicity and pooled efficiency versus potential higher per-device costs and loss of flexible, data-only or limited-voice options.

North Dakota’s Republican-led Legislature approved two strict abortion measures Friday that now await Gov. Jack Dalrymple’s signature. If enacted, the bills would create some of the nation’s toughest restrictions: House Bill 1456 would bar abortions after a detectable fetal heartbeat, potentially as early as six weeks, making physicians who knowingly perform such abortions guilty of a Class C felony. HB1305 would ban abortions sought because of the fetus’s sex or genetic abnormalities, treating physicians who comply as committing a Class A misdemeanor (the genetic-abnormality language was debated and the bill was split into parts before passage). Supporters framed the measures as protecting life and preventing discrimination or “eugenics”; sponsors argued heartbeats signal life and compared sex- or genetics-based terminations to unacceptable discrimination. Opponents warned the bills contradict established U.S. Supreme Court precedent protecting abortion until fetal viability (around 22–24 weeks), lack exceptions for rape or incest, and would likely trigger immediate legal challenges by national groups including the ACLU, Planned Parenthood and the Center for Reproductive Rights. Medical ambiguity—whether detection requires transvaginal or abdominal ultrasound—is unresolved in the heartbeat bill, raising concerns doctors could face prosecution. Passage votes were largely partisan, and advocates on both sides predict a costly court battle if the governor signs the measures into law.

Vanity Fair is moving ahead with a major profile of Gwyneth Paltrow despite, and partly because of, her reported attempts to block the magazine. Editor-in-chief Graydon Carter told The Times of London that the magazine “started a story on her,” has “a very good writer,” and will publish it. The piece follows reports that Paltrow emailed celebrity friends asking them not to speak to Vanity Fair and to avoid the magazine in future, after the outlet published probing pieces on Hollywood figures. Carter said her complaints “forced my hand” and defended the magazine’s approach, calling tension with subjects part of the job. He warned that celebrity insulation no longer exists in Los Angeles and dismissed reality-driven fame as fleeting. Paltrow, who has a long history with Vanity Fair including multiple covers, can expect the profile despite her public resistance.

New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg said President Barack Obama would be a "credible, formidable candidate" for reelection, predicting a close contest regardless of the Republican nominee. Speaking on Meet the Press, the independent who has been both a Republican and Democrat said he will "probably not endorse" in 2012 but praised aspects of Republican candidates that have drawn criticism. He defended Texas Gov. Rick Perry’s 2007 HPV vaccine executive order for sixth-grade girls and said Mitt Romney’s Massachusetts health care plan “turned out to be the only health care change that has really worked.” Bloomberg also called New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie “a good governor” and urged him to run if he wishes. Bloomberg criticized President Obama’s use of Warren Buffett as an example for higher taxes on the wealthy, calling it “theatrics,” noting that Buffett’s income mix affects tax rates.

Indiana Gov. Mitch Daniels urged patience with Rick Perry after uneven debate showings, saying it’s too early to write him off and there are many debates left. Daniels also praised Sen. Mark Warner for his work with the bipartisan Gang of Six on deficit reduction.

Republican National Committee Chairman Reince Priebus mocked what he called a new Democratic message — “Hey, it could’ve been worse” — in a joint Face the Nation interview with DNC Chair Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, asserting Democratic talking points failed in a recent New York special House election.

Sen. Mark Warner called the standoff over short-term spending and potential government shutdown “embarrassing,” blaming tea party-aligned House Republicans for insisting on make-or-break positions. Sen. Lamar Alexander countered that Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid had “manufactured a crisis” over disaster aid. On national security, Sen. Lindsey Graham warned the U.S. must keep “all options on the table” with Pakistan after allegations its intelligence service aided terrorists. White House adviser David Plouffe said he doesn’t anticipate major staff or Cabinet changes before the 2012 campaign and reiterated pressure on Pakistan to sever ties to the Haqqani network, saying aid reductions are possible if Pakistan doesn’t act.

U.S. job growth remained resilient despite global headwinds, with employers adding 242,000 nonfarm payrolls in February and revisions boosting January and December gains by 30,000. The unemployment rate held at 4.9% as labor-force participation rose to 62.9%, the highest in a year, with over half a million people entering the labor market. Hiring in construction, retail and health care offset losses in manufacturing and energy, which have shed jobs amid weak global demand and low oil prices. Average hourly earnings rose modestly year-over-year, while weekly hours dipped; the Federal Reserve is watching wages as it weighs future rate moves.

An NBC employee who uploaded a 1994 "Today" show clip—featuring Bryant Gumbel, Katie Couric and Elizabeth Vargas puzzling over "What is the Internet anyway?" and joking about e-mail addresses—was fired, the network confirmed. NBC said the person repeatedly copied and distributed various materials without permission, violating company standards. The humorous clip went viral on Facebook, YouTube and e-mail, was noted by media sites, and was even shown on "Today" again, with Matt Lauer acknowledging how everyone once felt that way.

Former Norwegian prime minister Kjell Magne Bondevik says he was held and questioned for about an hour at Washington Dulles Airport after customs officers noticed a 2014 visit to Iran in his passport. Bondevik, who led Norway from 1997–2000 and 2001–2005 and now heads the Oslo Center for human rights, flew in from Europe to attend the National Prayer Breakfast. He showed ABC7 his diplomatic passport, which identifies him as a former prime minister and U.S. ally, and said he expected that identification to prevent additional scrutiny. Instead, he was put in a room with other travelers from the Middle East and Africa, made to wait roughly 40 minutes, and then questioned for about 20 minutes about the Iran trip, which he said was for a human rights conference in 2014.

Bondevik said he understood concerns about terrorism but found the treatment surprising and troubling for U.S. reputation, especially if other international figures are similarly delayed. He indicated his office had consulted the U.S. Embassy in Oslo before travel and was told his diplomatic passport and ESTA authorization would suffice. U.S. Customs and Border Protection declined to discuss individual admissibility, citing privacy laws, while a CBP source told ABC7 that an hour-long “secondary examination” is not unusual.

Officials at Dulles reportedly attributed the incident not to President Trump’s recent executive order but to a 2015 law signed under President Obama that tightened Visa Waiver Program rules: nationals of participating countries— including Norway—who have traveled to Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria or Yemen since March 2011 may need a visa. DHS notes case-by-case exceptions, such as travel on behalf of international organizations. The Norwegian Embassy in Washington said it was “happy that things were sorted out.”

In Madeira Beach, a Pinellas County small‑claims judge ruled that a black Labrador mix named Elario must be shared between two neighbors who both claim him. Tina Marie Walker, 53, adopted the emaciated, sick 4‑year‑old dog for $5 from a shelter and brought him to live part‑time at fellow resident David Somerville’s apartment after his lung surgery. Somerville, a 68‑year‑old Vietnam veteran recovering from lung cancer who credits Elario with improving his health, cared for the dog daily, walked him and paid veterinary bills. A dispute arose after Walker left Elario with Somerville during a vacation; Somerville later sought sole ownership and asked to have the microchip listed in his name. Judge Lorraine Kelly ordered shared custody with a calendar of pickup times, saying witnesses noted the dog’s affection for both humans. Walker has appealed and moved away; she remains emotionally attached, while arrangements require her to alternate care, dropping Elario off at Somerville’s apartment on scheduled days.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet donated crawl data to the Internet Archive, which are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo. The document then shifts to a collection of user reviews for a restaurant—clearly the Red Hen—reflecting intense controversy and polarized reactions. Many reviewers complain about poor food quality and service: mentions include overcooked steaks, burnt or dry items, underseasoned potatoes, and possible food poisoning or gastric distress. Several diners report unsanitary conditions, citing cockroaches, unclean restrooms, and staff behavior they describe as indifferent or inappropriate. A few reviews claim illegal or illicit activity, with one alleging staff tried to sell drugs. Other reviewers describe rude servers, eye-rolling when accidents occurred, and overall inconsistent service.

Interwoven with quality complaints are strongly political and personal attacks linked to a high-profile incident in which the owner refused service to a Trump administration official. Many posts frame the restaurant as politically biased, using pejorative labels—“liberal,” “hypocrites,” “cuck,” etc.—and urging boycotts. Several reviewers accuse Yelp of deleting negative reviews, alleging censorship or paid suppression. A minority of voices offer positive or neutral notes: one surprised vegetarian found the food decent; another praised a local competitor (JJ’s Meat Shak). Overall, the aggregated feedback paints a picture of a once-ordinary eatery transformed into a flashpoint for partisan outrage, where service and food criticisms mingle with politically charged accusations, review disputes, and claims of sanitary problems—creating polarized, emotionally charged public commentary rather than a focused evaluation of the dining experience.

A grand jury returned a 977-count indictment against Ariel Castro, expanding charges that he held Michelle Knight, Amanda Berry and Gina DeJesus captive in his Cleveland home for about a decade. The new indictment supplements an earlier 329-count one and covers the full period of the alleged abuse. Prosecutors allege Castro repeatedly kidnapped and raped the women, sometimes chaining them and rarely permitting them to leave. The updated charges include 512 counts of kidnapping, 446 counts of rape, seven counts of gross sexual imposition, six counts of felonious assault, three counts of child endangerment, one count of possessing criminal tools and two counts of aggravated murder tied to an alleged forced miscarriage. Cuyahoga County Prosecutor Timothy McGinty did not specify the death penalty in this indictment; a capital review committee is still evaluating whether to seek it, and prosecutors could later add a specification. Defense attorneys welcomed the absence of a death-penalty request, saying they hope to avoid further trauma to the victims and possibly negotiate a plea. The women were freed in May when Berry escaped with her six-year-old daughter; the case remains set for trial, and Castro faces arraignment in mid-July.

A 5,000-pound memorial commemorating a 1969 UFO sighting in Sheffield, Massachusetts, has been ordered moved again after a land survey found it sits on a town right-of-way easement. Installed in 2015 and shifted about 30 feet soon after when it was discovered on town land, the concrete monument, benches and lighting now must be removed by the owner or the town will do so in May, Town Administrator Rhonda LaBombard said. The memorial, funded by community donations and some of the 40 witnesses to the event, marks what supporters call the nation’s first recognized off-world incident. Thom Reed, who was nine at the time and one of the most vocal witnesses, objects to the removal and threatens legal action, saying town officials had helped determine the current placement. Ownership of the monument is unclear; farmer Louis Aragi says it sits on his land. The 6-foot memorial bears a governor’s citation and Massachusetts seal. The 1969 incident—reported by dozens across nearby towns—has been archived by the Great Barrington Historical Society and featured in TV programs and documentaries.

Republican primary calendar changes have created a scramble with significant implications for Mitt Romney’s campaign. Romney benefits from earlier contests because he leads polls; the sooner voting starts, the less time rivals like Rick Perry or Chris Christie have to build momentum. Romney’s team reportedly pushed Nevada to move its caucus from Feb. 18 to Jan. 14, but New Hampshire Secretary of State Bill Gardner has threatened to move the state’s primary to December to preserve first-in-the-nation status under state law. New Hampshire law requires the primary occur on a Tuesday, at least a week before any similar contest, which narrows date options and could produce a December primary (Dec. 6 or 13), isolating New Hampshire from the rest of the calendar and reducing its electoral importance. A December New Hampshire would blunt its role as a buffer for Romney if he stumbled in Iowa, since momentum bounces fade quickly. A simple fix exists: if Nevada shifts its caucus to Jan. 17, New Hampshire could hold its primary on Jan. 10, restoring a more coherent early schedule. Gardner, however, has been unyielding and unresponsive to negotiations, frustrating other state officials and complicating the GOP calendar.

In Other Words, a feminist bookstore and community center in Portland long recognizable to many as the television store “Women and Women First” from IFC’s Portlandia, has formally ended its relationship with the show. After six seasons of filming the bookstore’s on-screen incarnation, the In Other Words community voted to discontinue cooperation following a particularly harmful shoot that left the space disordered, mistreated staff, and forced nearby businesses to close unexpectedly. Repeated attempts to secure accountability from the production were ignored, and the bookstore says the show’s overall impact contradicts its political values and harms the neighborhood and city.

Financially, the small flat fee paid per episode does not compensate for lost revenue from closures required during filming, nor for economic losses suffered by neighboring businesses. Publicity from Portlandia has not translated into meaningful financial or political support; visitors mainly take selfies outside and seldom enter or engage with the organization.

In Other Words criticizes Portlandia for its treatment of gender and race. The bookstore calls the “Women and Women First” sketches trans-antagonistic and trans-misogynist, arguing that jokes relying on men in dresses mock and imperil trans femmes—especially Black trans women who face severe violence. The organization also highlights Portlandia’s lack of Black representation despite filming in a historically Black Northeast Portland neighborhood where In Other Words displays “Black Lives Matter” and hosts local BLM meetings. Producers once requested removal of the BLM sign; the bookstore refused.

The group links Portlandia’s mainstreaming of a sanitized, commodified image of Portland—illustrated by slogans like “put a bird on it”—to gentrification, claiming the show helps realtors market and displace longtime communities. Current board members, staff, and volunteers were not involved in the original decision to allow filming years ago, but they support the recent collective choice to sever ties and back the volunteer who placed a “Fuck Portlandia” sign in the window. The statement ends by asking supporters to donate or volunteer to help the bookstore continue its social-justice work.

An emergency sterilization drive in Chhattisgarh, India, left dozens sick and at least 10 women dead after a single surgeon reportedly performed 83 tubectomy procedures in about six hours using instruments that were not disinfected. Local officials say the doctor violated guidelines that limit surgeons to 30 sterilizations per day; he has been suspended and a criminal probe launched. State authorities and health officers reported that most victims were poor village women under 32 who received a small payment (about 600 rupees, ~$10) to undergo the surgery. Many were sent home the same day and later returned ill; autopsies and investigations cite infections causing septic shock, blood poisoning or hemorrhagic shock as likely causes of death. Ten women died and dozens were hospitalized, with several in critical condition; the state announced compensation payouts to victims’ families.

The incident has renewed scrutiny of India’s long-standing, target-driven sterilization programs and one-day sterilization camps, which critics say encourage high-volume, low-quality care and place disproportionate burdens on women. India has one of the world’s highest female sterilization rates (around 37% of married women), while vasectomy rates remain very low. Activists and rights groups call the tragedy a product of systemic negligence—insufficient accountability, pressure to meet quotas, poor hygiene and the risks inherent in mass sterilization camps—and urge reevaluation of policies and stronger oversight to prevent recurrence.

At its General Convention in Salt Lake City, the Episcopal Church overwhelmingly approved new, gender-neutral marriage rites and revised its marriage canon to allow same-sex religious weddings, joining the Presbyterian Church (USA) and United Church of Christ in formally endorsing same-sex marriage liturgies. The House of Deputies approved the liturgy 184-23 and the canon change 173-27; the House of Bishops had earlier approved the liturgy. The rites—dubbed “The Witnessing and Blessing of a Lifelong Covenant”—and trial same-sex marriage liturgies take effect the first Sunday of Advent (Nov. 29). The measures remove gendered language from church law (e.g., “husband” and “wife” replaced by “the couple”) but preserve conscience protections: clergy may decline to officiate, and diocesan bishops may forbid the services in their dioceses without penalty to dissenting clergy.

Votes followed lengthy debate and years of theological discussion dating back decades, including earlier provisional blessing rites adopted in 2012 and the 2003 election of the first openly gay bishop. Supporters said the changes extend pastoral care and reflect evolving scriptural interpretation; opponents warned of schism and cited traditional biblical views. The move coincided with the U.S. Supreme Court’s nationwide legalization of same-sex marriage and drew concern from the Archbishop of Canterbury about impacts on the wider Anglican Communion.

Idris Elba has grown weary of persistent rumors that he’ll replace Daniel Craig as James Bond. Speaking at London’s British Film Institute, the 42-year-old star said the speculation “is really starting to eat itself” and denied any talks with Bond producers, even blaming Craig for fueling the chatter years ago by praising him. Elba also noted he’d just wrapped season four of Luther and hopes for a spinoff film.

Meanwhile, Anthony Horowitz, author of the new officially commissioned Bond novel Trigger Mortis, stirred controversy by saying Elba is “a bit too ‘street’” to play Bond, insisting his objection is not about race but about suitability and suave. Horowitz suggested Adrian Lester instead, prompting accusations of coded racism. After backlash he apologized and called himself “mortified.” Horowitz’s book revives classic Fleming elements—set after Goldfinger and featuring Pussy Galore—while updating Bond with stronger female characters who challenge him. He praised Daniel Craig’s Casino Royale but criticized later films like Skyfall for showing a vulnerable Bond.

Separately, David Oyelowo was chosen to narrate the Trigger Mortis audiobook, making him, at least in voice, a black James Bond. He defended Elba as an ideal candidate and reflected on past racist reactions he faced in casting debates. The debate over a black Bond continues across media, with the audiobook casting viewed as a modest step forward.

Worldwide, women’s movements have achieved landmark legal victories, from strengthening abortion rights to legalizing same-sex marriage. Marking International Women’s Day’s centenary, the Global Fund for Women highlighted 2010’s top breakthroughs, including expanded employee protections for domestic workers and women’s pivotal roles in the Tunisian and Egyptian uprisings that toppled entrenched leaders. Assessing gender inequality, the UN Development Program’s Gender Inequality Index (0 = equality, 1 = inequality) offers a modern metric across labor participation, empowerment, and reproductive health. In 2008 rankings, Yemen, the Congo, Niger, Mali, and Afghanistan scored worst; the Netherlands scored best. The US scored 0.400, mid-ranked internationally.

After several years of high-profile romances and engagements across Hollywood, multiple celebrity couples made headlines with proposals and wedding plans. Matthew McConaughey and Camila Alves are preparing to marry after four years together and two children. Sources tell Life & Style that Alves, who was born in Brazil, wants a large, family-centered wedding there—she has dreamed about a Brazilian celebration since she and McConaughey began dating in 2007. McConaughey, 42, proposed on Christmas Day and the couple, who live in Austin, Texas, share son Levi, 3, and daughter Vida, nearly 2.

Pop star Britney Spears also generated buzz around her engagement to Jason Trawick, with observers noting a shift in her public demeanor. After a turbulent period in the past decade, some commentators interpreted her social media posts and photos as signs she’s calmer and more mature, sharing excitement about her ring and future. The piece contrasted this stable image with earlier, more chaotic episodes in her life and previous relationships.

Actress Drew Barrymore became engaged to art consultant Will Kopelman while holidaying in Sun Valley, Idaho. The engagement, reported by People, involved a Graff diamond ring; the couple, publicly linked since early last year, spent the holidays together and appeared content. For Barrymore, 36, this will be her third marriage.

Justin Timberlake and Jessica Biel also reportedly got engaged after years together. Insider accounts say Timberlake proposed during a mountain vacation—some reports specify Jackson, Wyoming—choosing a locale Biel loves for snowboarding. Sources describe the couple as happy and ready to take the next step after reconciling following a brief split.
