Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Dianne Feinstein and several congressional leaders debated President Obama’s response to the growing Islamic State (ISIL/ISIS) threat and other international crises. Feinstein said the president is cautious—perhaps too cautious—and endorsed a call by Sens. John McCain and Lindsey Graham for an immediate military plan to confront ISIL, warning the group aims to take Baghdad and threaten the U.S. embassy. She noted Pentagon and State Department planning has been underway and praised Obama for involving Iraq’s new government so it can offer Sunnis alternatives to ISIL rule.

House Intelligence Chair Rep. Mike Rogers argued on Fox that Obama’s “don’t-do-stupid-stuff” approach fails to deter aggression from Russia and China and undercuts allies’ confidence, saying a perceived lack of consistent U.S. resolve invites further pressure. McCain urged sending additional U.S. troops in support roles, expanding airstrikes from Iraq into Syria, and supplying more weapons to Kurdish forces, calling ISIL a direct and possibly unparalleled threat.

Democratic Rep. Dutch Ruppersberger defended the administration’s caution, explaining Syria presents unique risks—air defenses and limited intelligence—and insisting plans are being developed and will be executed when appropriate. Republican Rep. Adam Kinzinger criticized the president’s admission of lacking a Syria strategy, saying the U.S. should have acted sooner. Overall, lawmakers are divided between urging quicker, stronger action and supporting deliberate, coalition-focused planning.

Astringent bacterial infections tied to warm coastal waters have left several people seriously ill, underscoring risks from Vibrio vulnificus. In Texas, Michelle O’Brien’s beach outing turned life-threatening after she stepped on an oyster; despite thick shoes and prompt antibiotics she spent five days hospitalized, largely in ICU, and says early treatment likely saved her foot. In Alabama, Lenny Buck, a diabetic cancer survivor, fell gravely ill after eating raw oysters; he developed fever, blisters and severe leg infection, has undergone multiple surgeries and faces months before he can walk. Florida health officials have issued warnings as V. vulnificus—related to cholera—thrives in warm saltwater (most cases May–October), infecting through open wounds or contaminated shellfish and causing vomiting, diarrhea, skin lesions, sepsis and rapid tissue damage. People with weakened immune systems, chronic disease or diabetes are at much higher risk of severe outcomes or death. Authorities advise avoiding saltwater with open cuts, thoroughly washing after swimming, and cooking shellfish rather than eating it raw. While officials don’t recommend canceling beach plans, they urge caution and prompt medical attention for suspicious symptoms.

A spontaneous sit-in that began in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol has mushroomed into a nationwide movement of “los indignados” protesting high unemployment, austerity and the two-party political system. What started with a few tents and mattresses grew into organised encampments with kitchens, legal and medical centres, and daily assemblies across dozens of cities. Young people—facing roughly 45% youth unemployment—and older activists mix with volunteers supplying food and infrastructure; assemblies use hand-signals and long debates to draft proposals, though a coherent platform remains elusive. Demonstrators demand jobs, electoral reform, punishment for corrupt politicians and protection of public services. Authorities’ bid to enforce an election “day of reflection” failed as police largely stood aside when tens of thousands reoccupied squares. Protesters draw inspiration from the Arab Spring while rejecting comparisons that equate risk levels. The movement has surprised political parties, unions and the media, and may reshape Spanish politics as the Socialist government faces electoral setbacks amid record national unemployment and mounting public anger.

Adam Mayes, 35, has been placed at the top of the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted list as authorities conduct an intense manhunt after he is accused of killing a Tennessee mother and her 14-year-old daughter to abduct the two younger daughters. Mayes is considered armed and dangerous and is believed to be traveling with 12-year-old Alexandria Bain and 8-year-old Kyliyah Bain, who remain missing. Federal charges include unlawful flight to avoid prosecution, giving the FBI jurisdiction; both Adam and his wife, Teresa Mayes, 31, face state charges of first-degree murder and especially aggravated kidnapping. According to affidavits, Teresa told police she witnessed Adam kill JoAnn Bain in the garage and Adrienne Bain inside the home on April 27, then transported the two bodies and the younger girls to the Mayes family property in Mississippi. The bodies were later found buried in that yard. Teresa and Adam’s mother, Mary Mayes, have been arrested—Teresa on kidnapping charges and Mary on conspiracy charges—and both admitted involvement in moving the children and bodies. Investigators found personal items belonging to the girls in a trailer rented by Mayes. Authorities warn Mayes may have altered appearances and are offering about $71,000 in rewards for information leading to his capture and the girls’ recovery.

A viral, edited YouTube montage captured Texas Governor Rick Perry behaving unusually animated during a roughly 25‑minute campaign speech in Manchester, New Hampshire, prompting raised eyebrows and online attention. The clip—assembled to emphasize the giddiest, oddest moments—led some viewers to joke about intoxication, though observers and officials stopped short of that claim. HuffPost noted a reporter attended the speech but only saw the footage later; the montage’s uploader did not respond to inquiries. Perry’s team initially declined comment, then spokesperson Mark Miner defended the governor as “passionate about the issues he talks about.”

A Reuters/Ipsos national tracking poll conducted after Monday night’s first presidential debate found a clear public perception that Democrat Hillary Clinton outperformed Republican Donald Trump, but that perceived victory did not immediately translate into a sustained boost in support among likely voters. Surveying more than 2,000 Americans on Tuesday (including 1,336 likely voters), the online poll found 56 percent of adults said Clinton did a better job in the televised debate versus 26 percent who favored Trump. Party lines were stark: 85 percent of those who said Clinton won were Democrats and 22 percent were Republicans.

The debate drew a record audience of about 84 million viewers and was framed as a high-stakes chance for two unpopular nominees to sway undecided voters. Both campaigns claimed victory afterward—Trump citing online polls and dismissing Clinton’s performance, while Clinton’s team called Trump unprepared and incoherent. Among likely voters, 34 percent reported the debate changed their view of Clinton positively, compared with 19 percent who said the same for Trump. Likewise, 31 percent of likely voters said the debate improved Clinton’s chances of winning the White House versus 16 percent for Trump.

Despite these perceptions, the poll showed little immediate movement in overall support: 42 percent of likely voters backed Clinton and 38 percent backed Trump, a lead for Clinton similar to recent weeks (typically 4–6 points). Among likely voters who actually watched the debate, Clinton led 44 percent to 39 percent. Columbia political scientist Donald Green noted debate effects can take days to fully register, possibly explaining the muted short-term shift.

The Reuters/Ipsos daily tracking poll, conducted in English across all 50 states, reports twice weekly. Its credibility interval is about ±3 percentage points for the full sample and likely voters, and ±4 points for likely voters who watched the debate. Polling methodologies vary nationally—some polls focus on likely voters while others include all registered voters—and aggregators indicate Clinton’s lead over Trump has been narrowing to roughly 2 points this month.

This article reviews the crisis of Panama disease in bananas, focusing on the soil-borne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc), and highlights the emergence and global spread of a single, highly virulent clone known as Tropical Race 4 (TR4). Bananas originated in Southeast Asia and most edible varieties are sterile clones propagated vegetatively; Cavendish clones dominate global trade. That clonality of both the crop and the pathogen underlies extreme vulnerability: monocultures of genetically identical Cavendish plants enable rapid, devastating epidemics. Historically, Panama disease wiped out Gros Michel plantations in the early 20th century; Cavendish replaced it but is now threatened by TR4. Genetic analyses (DArTseq and whole-genome sequencing) of isolates from multiple countries show very low diversity among TR4 strains, consistent with dissemination of a single clone across Southeast Asia, Australia, the Middle East, Africa, and South Asia. TR4 persists long-term in soil, spreads via infected material, contaminated tools, water, or poor sanitation, and currently renders large plantation areas unusable. Management options are limited: exclusion and strict quarantine, rapid molecular diagnostics for surveillance, improved sanitation, and better understanding of epidemiology. Durable solutions require deployment of genetic resistance from diverse wild Musa germplasm through breeding or biotechnology, supported by major R&D investments and recognition of banana as a staple crop. The authors call for urgent global awareness, coordinated containment, and long-term resistance breeding to avert wider catastrophic losses.

For the fourth straight year the 1994 Honda Accord was the most-stolen vehicle in the United States, according to the National Insurance Crime Bureau’s (NICB) Hot Wheels report based on FBI NCIC data. The Accord’s popularity and lack of modern security—Honda didn’t add immobilizers until 1997—help explain its continued appeal to thieves. The 1998 Honda Civic was second, followed by a surprising high-ranking 2006 Ford full-size pickup; other pickups and popular family sedans (1991 Toyota Camry, 1994 Acura Integra, 1994 Nissan Sentra) also made the top ten. NICB warns that thefts of later-model vehicles are rising as criminals illicitly obtain replacement key codes to make keys and steal cars quickly. Still, overall vehicle thefts are declining—FBI figures show the lowest level since 1967. NICB urges a layered prevention approach: common sense, warning devices, immobilizers and tracking.

The Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes Center in Guadalupe, California, is unveiling a remarkable piece of local and film history: the plaster body of a sphinx from Cecil B. DeMille’s 1923 silent epic The Ten Commandments. After spending more than 90 years buried in shifting dunes, a 10½-foot section of one of the 21 sphinxes — nicknamed “Nora” — was excavated, conserved and reassembled for a new permanent exhibit opening June 13, with a 1920s-themed gala unveiling on June 12. The gala, limited to 50 tickets, features jazz, period food and cocktails, an auction of a Steve Thomas “See America” giclée poster, and opportunities to meet archaeologists involved in the digs; a Brunch with the Sphinx event follows Saturday.

DeMille had built an enormous prologue set in the Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes resembling ancient Egypt — including 100-foot gates, pharaoh statues and 21 sphinxes — and left it on site after filming. Over time wind and sand buried the props. Excavations that began in the 1990s revealed fragments and artifacts — tobacco tins, bottles, photographs, even a piece of burnt toast — that hint at the everyday life and levity on the Prohibition-era film camp. Earlier fieldwork in 2012 recovered a sphinx head; the 2014 dig recovered Nora’s torso and hind leg portion, which had partially weathered and fragmented.

Conservators, led by art restorer Amy Higgins, spent months stabilizing and piecing Nora together using reversible materials so she reads as an artifact rather than a full restoration. The exhibit will display Nora, the previously restored head, other artifacts and DeMille-era photographs. The Dunes Center plans further excavation to recover more of Nora and seeks about $85,000 to fund the next phase. The project ties Hollywood spectacle to local history and preserves a uniquely Californian relic of cinematic ambition.

Authorities in Evansville, Indiana, arrested a couple after finding cellphone video showing a one-year-old playing with a handgun. Police discovered the footage while reviewing the phone of 19-year-old Michael Barnes, who had been detained Thursday after attempting to sell a .40-caliber handgun to an undercover officer. In the videos, Barnes and the child’s mother, 22-year-old Toni Wilson, can be heard encouraging the toddler to say “pow” while handling the firearm; at one point the child places the muzzle in their mouth. Police said Barnes made no attempt to stop the child. Investigators determined the gun in the footage appears to be the same weapon recovered when Barnes was arrested; authorities did not say whether it was loaded. Barnes was already wanted on an armed robbery warrant and was charged after the sale attempt with resisting law enforcement with a weapon, carrying a handgun without a permit, and possessing a handgun near a school. Following the discovery of the videos, both Barnes and Wilson were charged with child neglect, criminal recklessness with a deadly weapon, and allowing a child to possess a firearm. Wilson told police the gun was a pellet gun, a claim officials disputed. The one-year-old shown and one-month-old twins in the home were placed in emergency care; Barnes is the twins’ father but not the older child’s. Both suspects remained in custody.

At the April 14, 2013 MTV Movie Awards, actress Aubrey Plaza unexpectedly stormed the stage during Will Ferrell’s acceptance speech for the Comedic Genius Golden Popcorn. While Ferrell was entertaining the audience, Plaza — with the title of her upcoming August film, The To Do List, written across her chest — leapt up and attempted to wrest the trophy from his hand. Though it played like a prank, MTV News confirmed the interruption was not planned: Plaza had not been scripted to join Ferrell, and producers escorted her out of the show shortly afterward. The unscripted moment immediately drew comparisons to Kanye West’s infamous interruption of Taylor Swift at the 2009 MTV Video Music Awards, with many viewers tweeting that Plaza had “tried to pull a Kanye” on Ferrell. Reactions were mixed but leaned toward amused; several fans suggested Plaza and Ferrell should collaborate more. The incident was one of the notable highlights as the broadcast concluded; viewers were encouraged to follow post-show coverage including red-carpet photos, the winners list, and exclusive movie premieres. The report also reminded readers about Twitter’s location feature and how to manage it.

This document stitches together disparate reports about hostage experiences and religious identity under duress and a brief papal comment on contemporary martyrdom. It begins with the 2011 capture of journalist James Foley in Libya: after 45 days in Tripoli jail he was freed following a campaign by college friends, former colleagues and family. A front-page story later quoted Jejoen Bontinck, a 19‑year‑old Belgian who spent three weeks in 2013 in the same cell as Foley, asserting that Foley converted to Islam soon after his capture and took the name Abu Hamza. Bontinck said he recited the Quran with Foley and believed the conversion sincere; three other released hostages and Foley’s former employer reportedly corroborated the claim. The piece notes several Western hostages reportedly converted during captivity—some, according to witnesses, out of duress, others appearing genuinely committed, including Peter Kassig (Abdul‑Rahman) as revealed in a smuggled letter. A few prisoners kept their original faiths; Steven J. Sotloff, a practicing Jew, secretly observed Yom Kippur while detained. Released hostages described differing reactions from captors: Foley’s initial guards from the Nusra Front were suspicious of his professed faith, but subsequent captors eased abuse and allowed greater freedom, while some Syrian prisoners remained harshly treated. The author questions whether Foley’s conversion should be presented as established fact, noting readers’ skepticism. The document closes with an unrelated brief from Vatican City: Pope Francis, reflecting on Gospel martyrdom, warned that persecution of Christians continues today, invoking contemporary martyrs who suffer under authorities “who hate Jesus Christ.”

A comprehensive census of Earth’s biomass finds that plants dominate life by mass, comprising roughly 450 gigatons of carbon (about 80–82% of total biomass), while all life together totals ≈550 Gt C. Bacteria are the next largest group (~70 Gt C), followed by fungi (~12 Gt C), with animals amounting to just ≈2 Gt C. Humans account for only ≈0.06 Gt C—about one ten-thousandth of global biomass—but our influence is immense: human activities have halved plant biomass over the past 10,000 years and reduced wild mammal biomass by about 83–85%. Domesticated livestock now outweigh wild mammals by an order of magnitude (cattle and pigs dominate), and farmed poultry makes up roughly 70% of all birds. The study synthesizes hundreds of sources, using carbon as a standardized measure to avoid variability from water content and deploying remote sensing, genomics, and extrapolation by environmental parameters to scale local samples globally. It highlights that most biomass is terrestrial, a significant portion of microbes live in deep subsurface environments, and marine biomass is much smaller overall. The authors emphasize substantial uncertainties—especially for deep subsurface microbes and poorly sampled groups like terrestrial arthropods—identify major knowledge gaps, and release their data and code publicly. The findings put into perspective humanity’s small mass yet disproportionate ecological footprint and suggest priorities for further sampling and research.

Pete Seeger (1919–2014) was a towering figure in American music and activism whose six-decade career blended song, social conscience and grassroots organizing. Best known for popularizing "This Land Is Your Land" and "We Shall Overcome" and writing "If I Had a Hammer" and "Turn! Turn! Turn!", Seeger insisted he was part of a living folk tradition—often calling himself a "river singer"—and resisted commercialism while using his fame to advance causes. Born to musical parents, he dropped out of Harvard, worked at the Library of Congress archive, teamed with Woody Guthrie, co-founded the Almanac Singers and later the Weavers, whose chart-topping success was derailed by 1950s blacklistings. A former Communist Party member, Seeger was convicted for contempt of Congress in 1955 for refusing to answer HUAC questions; the conviction was overturned in 1961, but he remained blacklisted from television for years.

Seeger was a steadfast activist: he opposed McCarthyism, marched with Martin Luther King Jr., campaigned against the Vietnam War, fought pollution of the Hudson River—founding the sloop Clearwater—and supported Occupy Wall Street. He mentored generations of musicians (Dylan, Baez, Springsteen), influenced the 1960s folk revival, and continued performing into his 90s. Honored with Grammys, a Kennedy Center Award and Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction, Seeger left a legacy of songs and organizing that kept music central to social movements and community life.

President Obama signed an executive order and memorandum on National Equal Pay Day to narrow the gender wage gap by targeting pay secrecy among federal contractors. The measures bar retaliation against workers who discuss wages and require contractors to report compensation data by sex and race. Obama framed the move as restoring opportunity and urged businesses and government to hire more women and expand supports like childcare, college aid and retirement savings. The action affects federal contractors only; advocates call it a meaningful step but say Congress must pass broader laws like the Paycheck Fairness Act or Fair Paycheck Act to cover private-sector workers. Democrats view the initiative as both policy and political mobilization ahead of midterms; Republicans criticize proposed legislation as harmful to workplace flexibility. Experts note pay transparency can reduce gaps and that persisted disparities reflect both discrimination and occupational sorting, with women—and especially Black and Latina women—earning substantially less than white men.

The text explains that Twitter lets users attach location information—like a city or precise coordinates—to their Tweets when posting from the web or through third-party apps. It emphasizes that users retain control over this data by offering the option to delete their Tweet location history. The snippet also mentions an option to learn more about location features, and references Billboard newsletters, which deliver music news to subscribers’ inboxes daily. Finally, it notes that by clicking “Submit” to sign up, users agree to the site’s Terms of Use and Privacy Policy. Overall, the passage highlights location-tagging functionality, user control over stored location history, a prompt to subscribe to music-news emails, and the consent mechanism tied to newsletter signup.

Paul McCartney sued Sony/ATV in New York seeking a declaratory judgment that his termination notices under the 1976 Copyright Act will restore to him the U.S. copyrights in songs he co-wrote with John Lennon between 1962 and 1971. McCartney began serving termination notices in 2008 and expects the reversion to take effect starting Oct. 5, 2018. The catalog at issue includes landmark Beatles compositions such as “Yesterday,” “Hey Jude,” “Let It Be,” “I Want to Hold Your Hand,” and “All You Need Is Love,” many of which were assigned to publishers decades ago and eventually became part of ATV and then Sony/ATV after Michael Jackson bought the catalogue in the 1980s and later entered a joint venture with Sony.

McCartney’s complaint says Sony/ATV has not provided clear assurances it will not contest his terminations and appears to be waiting on the outcome of a related U.K. ruling involving Duran Duran, where an English court held that contract provisions under English law could bar exercise of U.S. termination rights. McCartney’s filing seeks to ensure an American court affirms that U.S. statutory termination rights supersede contrary contractual claims, preventing Sony from using the Duran Duran precedent against him.

Sony/ATV responded that it respects McCartney and values the Lennon–McCartney catalog, calling the suit unnecessary and premature. The parties later reached a confidential settlement and requested dismissal without prejudice, asking the court to retain the ability to enforce the settlement terms if disputes arise.

Mitt Romney has repeatedly insisted his tax plan would preserve progressivity and not reduce taxes for high-income earners, yet admits keeping it deficit-neutral would require raising taxes on people he labels “middle income” while cutting taxes for the wealthy. His proposal—20 percent across-the-board rate cuts—would cost trillions. Romney insists it won’t add to the deficit, won’t raise middle-class taxes, won’t cut taxes for the rich, and won’t eliminate investment tax breaks. The Tax Policy Center dismissed those claims as mathematically impossible given Romney’s refusal to touch capital gains and similar breaks. Some conservative studies, using strained assumptions, suggest revenue neutrality is attainable by limiting deductions for high earners; Martin Feldstein’s Harvard analysis accepts treating households making over $100,000 as not middle class. Even under favorable assumptions, Romney’s plan would raise taxes on households between $100,000 and $250,000 to finance big cuts for those over $250,000. Romney nonetheless keeps promoting optimistic, unsupported claims—asserting his election alone would boost investment and growth—relying on “confidence” rather than concrete policy. Critics argue such faith in a spontaneous turnaround ignores structural problems from the financial crisis and past policy choices, making Romney’s economic case weak and speculative.

A citizen’s criminal complaint accusing Gov. Chris Christie of official misconduct in the 2013 George Washington Bridge “Bridgegate” lane closures was allowed to proceed by a Bergen County municipal judge. Activist William (Bill) Brennan filed the second-degree official misconduct complaint after David Wildstein, a Christie appointee who pleaded guilty and became a key federal witness, testified that Christie was told about the lane shutdowns while they were underway and failed to stop them. The lane closures, ordered at the Port Authority by Wildstein and executed September 9–13, 2013, caused severe traffic jams in Fort Lee, delayed emergency responses, and sparked multiple investigations. Federal prosecutors indicted and tried former Christie aides Bill Baroni and Bridget Kelly on conspiracy, fraud, and civil rights charges; Wildstein testified against them and pleaded guilty. In the federal trial, prosecutors presented extensive email and text evidence suggesting political retaliation against Fort Lee Mayor Mark Sokolich for not endorsing Christie. The municipal judge found probable cause and issued a summons, forwarding the case to the Bergen County Prosecutor’s Office, which may recuse its Christie-appointed prosecutor in favor of a special prosecutor. Christie’s office denounced the complaint as frivolous and said the governor had no knowledge of the closures when they occurred. The Bridgegate scandal damaged Christie’s political standing, led to convictions of his aides, and prompted broad legislative, federal, and internal investigations into abuse of public resources for political ends.

Los Angeles actor Michael Jace, best known for The Shield, was arrested after police say he confessed to shooting his wife, April Jace, multiple times at their Hyde Park home Monday night. April, a respected financial aid worker at Biola University, had returned from picking up their young sons from baseball practice minutes before the shooting; the boys, both under ten, were physically unharmed and are staying with relatives. Neighbors portrayed the family as warm and affectionate—“like the Huxtables on the block”—often seeing Jace walk their German shepherd and children; many were stunned by the violence. Law enforcement believes the motive was domestic violence. The episode renewed attention to past allegations: Jace’s first wife, Jennifer Bitterman, accused him during their 1996–97 divorce of repeated physical abuse, choking, threats to kill, and harsh discipline toward their son; a friend corroborated seeing multiple violent incidents. Jace had also faced financial troubles, filing Chapter 13 bankruptcy in 2011 with substantial debts and later falling behind on payments. Biola’s president called the university “shocked and saddened.” As investigators continue, Michael Jace remains in custody while the medical examiner prepares an autopsy on April.

Former Tesla process technician Martin Tripp has publicly alleged serious quality and safety problems at Tesla’s Nevada Gigafactory, tweeting internal emails, photos, and vehicle identification numbers (VINs) he says show damaged battery cells installed in cars and large volumes of waste stored improperly. Tripp claims these issues reflect dangerous manufacturing shortcuts and environmental hypocrisy, and that Elon Musk was aware. Tesla has repeatedly called Tripp a disgruntled ex-employee and denied his safety claims, saying no punctured cells were used in Model 3 batteries and that identified VINs have safe batteries. Twitter temporarily suspended Tripp’s account after he posted material that reportedly included private email information; his account was later taken down. Tripp is countersuing Tesla after the company sued him in June, accusing him of hacking and transferring confidential information; he denies the hacking charges and says Tesla has harassed and intimidated him for speaking out. Business Insider parallels Tripp’s story with former Tesla engineer Cristina Balan, who says she was pushed out after her team raised quality and waste concerns in 2014. Balan’s arbitration found Tesla underpaid her but did not classify her as a whistleblower; she says Tesla tried to silence her with settlement offers that required gagging. Both cases highlight tensions between rapid production pressures, alleged quality lapses, and the treatment of employees who report problems.

The Supreme Court spent two days hearing high-profile gay marriage cases, and Wednesday’s oral argument focused on Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA), which bars federal recognition of same-sex marriages and withholds more than 1,100 federal benefits tied to marriage. The justices appeared deeply divided but a majority seemed inclined to strike down that key provision. Justice Anthony Kennedy, widely viewed as the pivotal vote, emphasized federalism concerns: DOMA intrudes on states’ traditional authority to define marriage and thus conflicts with state-regulated matters like divorce, custody and other day-to-day legal effects of marriage. Kennedy noted that some states now recognize same-sex marriages, and federal nonrecognition creates real friction.

The court’s liberal justices pushed strongly on the discriminatory impact of DOMA. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg highlighted how federal denial of tax advantages, Social Security survivor benefits and family-leave rights effectively relegates these unions to a lesser status. Justice Elena Kagan challenged defenders of DOMA to explain whether Congress acted out of a legitimate interest in uniformity or from “dislike, fear, animus” toward gay people, citing a House report that explicitly referenced moral disapproval of homosexuality.

Lawyers defending DOMA, including former Solicitor General Paul Clement representing House Republican leaders, argued Congress had authority to define marriage for federal benefits and sought national uniformity in response to early state-level legal developments. The Obama administration, having concluded in 2011 that DOMA is unconstitutional, declined to defend the statute but continued to enforce it pending a Supreme Court ruling. Solicitor General Donald Verrilli, arguing the administration’s view, called Section 3 discriminatory. Chief Justice Roberts pressed whether gay people lacked political power and criticized the administration for continuing enforcement despite its stated constitutional doubts.

Procedural questions loomed large: whether the House’s defenders (BLAG) have standing to defend DOMA, and whether the Court should hear the case at all given the administration’s position—issues Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Scalia sharply questioned. The case stems from Edith Windsor’s suit seeking a $363,000 federal estate tax refund after her legally recognized New York marriage was ignored under DOMA. Lower courts ruled for Windsor. A definitive ruling from the Supreme Court on DOMA could come by June, but procedural hurdles might produce a narrower outcome that leaves parts of DOMA intact pending further litigation.

Hubble spotted an extraordinary object in the asteroid belt, P/2013 P5, that sports six comet-like tails radiating from a single ~240 m (1,400 ft) nucleus. Discovered as a fuzzy blob by Pan-STARRS in August 2013, P5 revealed its multiple dust streamers in Hubble images taken Sept. 10 and Sept. 23; the structure changed noticeably in just 13 days. The behavior is unlike a typical comet or impact aftermath. Lead investigator David Jewitt and colleagues conclude the tails result from repeated, impulsive dust-ejection events over months, not a single collision. Jessica Agarwal’s modelling shows the YORP effect — uneven solar heating that gradually spins asteroids faster — likely spun P5 up until centrifugal forces caused surface material to shed, producing jets that solar radiation stretched into tails. Only about 100–1,000 tons of dust have been lost, a tiny fraction of the body’s mass. Continued observations will test whether the dust departs in the equatorial plane, which would strongly support rotational breakup as the cause and suggest this may be a common asteroid death mechanism.

Lindsay Lohan says she was racially profiled at London’s Heathrow Airport after wearing a headscarf on a trip from Turkey, telling Good Morning Britain an airport worker opened her passport, apologized, then asked her to remove the scarf. The incident made her ponder how other women who feel uncomfortable removing their headscarves would react. Lohan, who met Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan during the visit, said she wore the scarf out of personal respect and has been photographed carrying a Quran; she finds solace studying the Muslim holy book and other religious texts. Separately, Lohan teased a playful Instagram post suggesting she might sing as Ariel in a live-action The Little Mermaid, later shortening the caption.

A Ladue High School mother took legal action after her son—identified as John Doe in court documents—was cut from the varsity soccer team and then barred from returning to the junior varsity (J.V.) squad. The family contends the school’s actions amount to age and sex discrimination because, they say, girls’ team rules differ and permit juniors who miss varsity to continue playing on J.V. The dispute reached federal court, where the mother sought a Temporary Restraining Order (TRO) to allow her son to play J.V. while the case proceeds.

School officials explained their practice: when juniors fail to make varsity, they typically are not allowed back on J.V. so younger students can have developmental opportunities and roster spots. Administrators and the coach told the court the policy’s application depends on the number of players trying out and available team slots rather than a blanket written rule. The coach testified the same criteria are applied to both boys’ and girls’ teams.

The coach also testified about his decision-making around cuts. He said seven juniors were cut from varsity because they were not strong enough to compete at that level or on J.V., and that he framed his feedback to John Doe in supportive language to preserve the player’s self-esteem after the cut. The family appealed the coach’s decision to the superintendent, who reviewed the claim and found it unsubstantiated.

John Doe’s lawyer introduced coach-generated performance ratings that, the attorney argued, indicate John Doe outperformed some players who were selected for varsity—evidence meant to show inconsistency or unfairness in selections. In court, it was revealed Ladue lacks a formal policy banning juniors from playing J.V.; roster decisions are situational. The boy reportedly wants to remain in court and play soccer; his lawyer emphasized the student’s desire to participate.

U.S. District Judge John Ross did not immediately order placement on the J.V. team. He planned to rule on the matter the following Monday. An update later states Judge Ross denied the request for a TRO, meaning the student would not be immediately reinstated to the junior varsity roster.

Greece faced a decisive referendum that could determine both its economic future and its place in the eurozone. The crisis traces back decades of chronic deficits and underreported finances, which culminated in a 2009 revelation of much larger deficits and rising borrowing costs. Europe and the IMF provided bailouts in 2010 and 2012 to avoid defaults that would have heavily harmed foreign banks, but those rescues imposed austerity without substantial debt relief and relied on flawed IMF growth projections. Reforms and spending cuts deepened recession, unemployment soared—especially among youth—and public trust collapsed. In January 2015, the leftist Syriza government under Alexis Tsipras sought to renegotiate terms, demanding eased austerity and partial debt forgiveness. Creditors largely resisted, fearing precedent for other struggling European nations and doubting Greece’s commitment to reforms. Tensions peaked after Greece missed a €1.55bn IMF payment on June 29 and the ECB restricted emergency lending by no longer accepting Greek-government-guaranteed collateral, prompting bank closures, withdrawal limits, and fears among depositors.

Tsipras called a snap July 5–6 referendum asking Greeks to accept or reject creditors’ proposals. Campaigns were emotionally charged and evenly split in polls; most Greeks nonetheless favored staying in the euro. A “No” vote was framed by Tsipras as resistance to “blackmail” and a push for debt relief; European leaders warned it would weaken Greece’s negotiating position and could jeopardize eurozone membership. If Greece defaults fully and loses external funding, it may circulate government IOUs, ration cash, and force steep short-term contraction, with the longer recovery tied to tourism and competitiveness if a new currency were introduced. Analysts argue a structured default or debt relief should have happened in 2010; without it, the crisis remained unresolved and politically explosive.

George Kirby, 103, and Doreen Luckie, 91, married in Eastbourne, southern England, becoming the world’s oldest newlyweds with a combined age of 194 years (and 281 days). The couple, together for 27 years and living as partners since 1988, exchanged vows on Kirby’s 103rd birthday in a ceremony at the Langham Hotel before about 50 guests and a Guinness World Records representative. They surpassed the previous record of 191 years set by a French couple.

Kirby, a former boxer who reportedly won all 60 of his fights in youth and later served 25 years in the Royal Air Force as a physical education instructor, was dressed smartly in a suit and tie and arrived in a wheelchair after a recent fall. Luckie wore a white dress with blue flowers. The pair got engaged on Valentine’s Day earlier this year; Kirby joked he didn’t get down on one knee because he wouldn’t have been able to get back up. Both said they had “no regrets” about not marrying earlier: Luckie noted they “didn’t want to bother about marriage before but eventually we did it.”

They have a large blended family: seven children, 15 grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren between them. Family members organized separate pre-wedding celebrations—a hen party for Luckie and a missed stag lunch for Kirby—and praised the couple’s happiness. Kirby’s son Neil, who runs the hotel where the ceremony took place, said the family had long “adopted Doreen as our mum” and welcomed her becoming a Kirby, though it’s uncertain if she will change her name.

Former EastEnders and Bridget Jones actor Paul Nicholls, 38, was rescued after spending three days trapped at the foot of Khun Si waterfall on Koh Samui, Thailand. Locals alerted police after spotting the rental motorbike he had used; rescue teams hacked through undergrowth to find him semi-conscious in a rock pool with hypothermia and a severely damaged right leg. Nicholls said his phone was lost in the fall and he could not climb out; he told reporters his kneecap was destroyed and would need complete reconstruction. Dramatic footage shows rescuers applying a makeshift tourniquet and hauling him up a steep path; he was drip-attached and taken to International Koh Samui Hospital before being moved due to high fees. Officials and the British Embassy are involved in plans for further treatment or repatriation. Nicholls, who debuted on EastEnders in 1996 and has appeared in shows including Ackley Bridge and Law & Order: UK, is seriously ill but grateful to be alive.

Two federal lawsuits filed against Colorado seek to dismantle the state’s regulated recreational marijuana industry, arguing it violates federal law. Brought Thursday by anti-drug group Safe Streets, three individuals (Phillis Windy Hope Reilly, Michael P. Reilly) and New Vision Hotels Two (owner of a Holiday Inn), the suits name Colorado officials — including Gov. John Hickenlooper and key regulatory directors — as well as numerous marijuana businesses and supporting service providers. Plaintiffs assert state legalization conflicts with the federal Controlled Substances Act and that Colorado’s actions run afoul of the Constitution’s supremacy clause. They also invoke federal racketeering laws, seeking damages for alleged harms such as a licensed dispensary opening near the Reillys’ property and a shop planned close to New Vision’s hotel entrance.

Safe Streets, led by former Reagan DOJ appointee James Wootton, claims the federal government is not enforcing drug laws and seeks court orders to stop licensing and to shut down the industry. Supporters of legalization and Colorado officials call the suits misguided and unlikely to succeed. Rep. Jonathan Singer and other advocates point to strong voter approval of Amendment 64 in 2012, economic gains (an industry valued near $700 million and roughly $60 million in tax revenue for schools), improved employment, lower crime and stable teen use rates as evidence legalization has not produced the dire social effects plaintiffs claim. Opponents, including the anti-legalization group Smart Approaches to Marijuana, praise the litigation as appropriate enforcement of federal statute.

Colorado has already faced a separate interstate suit from Nebraska and Oklahoma in the U.S. Supreme Court alleging cross-border harms. The state Attorney General’s office has pledged to defend Colorado’s laws. Reform advocates argue that regulated markets are preferable to illicit ones and that these legal challenges represent a final push from anti-drug interests rather than a realistic legal remedy.

This document lays out a broad conservative policy agenda centered on immigration, taxes, and Second Amendment protections, framed as ways to “Make America Great Again.” On immigration, it emphasizes three principles: secure borders (including a southern wall), strict law enforcement, and prioritizing American citizens’ jobs, wages, and safety. It portrays prior reform efforts as favoring corporate interests and argues Mexico should pay for a border wall, citing remittances and alleged costs to U.S. taxpayers from undocumented immigrants. The proposal calls for tripling ICE personnel, nationwide E-Verify, mandatory return of criminal aliens, ending catch-and-release, defunding sanctuary cities, harsher penalties for visa overstays, cooperation with local gang task forces, and ending birthright citizenship. It also seeks to reduce new low-wage immigration, require employers to hire U.S. workers first, curb welfare use by immigrants, replace some foreign youth programs with domestic job initiatives, and reprioritize refugee spending toward American children.

The tax plan proposes sweeping simplification: three individual tax brackets (12%, 25%, 33%), a higher standard deduction, repeal of the death tax, expanded childcare deductions and Dependent Care Savings Accounts, repeal of the AMT and certain healthcare investment taxes, and limits on itemized deductions. Business tax reform would cut the corporate rate to 15%, allow a 10% one-time repatriation tax, preserve the R&D credit, and offer special treatment for U.S. manufacturers’ investments.

On guns, the document stresses absolute defense of the Second Amendment, arguing against gun and magazine bans and expansion of federal background checks. It advocates strict prosecution of violent offenders, programs like Project Exile, improved mental health treatment to prevent mass violence, national reciprocity for concealed-carry permits, and arming military on bases and at recruiting centers. Overall, the platform ties strong borders, reduced taxes, and robust gun rights to national renewal and public safety.

The family of 28-year-old Grace Sung Eun Lee, a Manhattan banker with an inoperable brain tumor who is paralyzed from the neck down and sustained by breathing and feeding tubes, released a murky, soundless video they say shows she wants to remain on life support. The footage, recorded hours after Lee reportedly told the Daily News “I want to die,” is inconclusive. Her court-appointed attorney, David A. Smith, says Lee has clearly and repeatedly requested removal of life support, but her devout Korean-born parents — Rev. Manho and Jin-ah Lee — oppose honoring that wish, arguing religious beliefs forbid suicide and that she was too drugged to decide when she first requested withdrawal. A Long Island judge initially allowed the tubes removed, but the parents won a temporary appeals court order keeping support in place while a four-judge panel reviews whether Lee is competent and whether she truly wants to end life support. The hospital is awaiting the appeals decision.

Sesame Workshop has expanded the storyline of Lily, a seven-year-old pink Muppet first introduced in 2011 as food-insecure, to include that her family is experiencing homelessness. Launched through Sesame Street in Communities, the new initiative uses online videos, storybooks, activities and bilingual resources aimed at children ages 2–6 and the professionals who serve them—teachers, social workers, shelter staff and healthcare providers. Materials are research-informed and developed with homelessness experts to help children understand homelessness from a child’s perspective, reduce stigma, and offer coping strategies and comforting routines families can use anywhere. Sample resources show Lily staying with friends, talking with Elmo and Sofia about big feelings, playing games that reinforce support, and later celebrating “survivor’s pride” when her family finds permanent housing. The campaign also includes professional development content and outreach events to raise awareness and better identify and support young children experiencing homelessness. Experts note homelessness among children is widespread and often invisible: estimates range from hundreds of thousands to millions of youth yearly, with more than 2.5 million children homeless nationwide and about 1.2 million under age six. Advocates say portraying homelessness through a relatable character can humanize the issue, build empathy among peers, and help traumatized children feel less alone. The initiative is funded and supported by partners including the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and the Joan Ganz Cooney Fund for Vulnerable Children.

David Blankenhorn, founder of the Institute for American Values and formerly a leading intellectual opponent of same-sex marriage, has publicly reversed his stance and now accepts gay marriage while remaining committed to strengthening marriage as an institution. In a New York Times essay and an NPR discussion, Blankenhorn reiterated his longstanding conviction that marriage’s core social purpose is to unite biological, social, and legal parenthood for children. He still believes same-sex couples cannot replicate that biological bond, but he argued that stigmatizing gay relationships is wrong, and legal recognition of same-sex couples is a matter of fairness and social comity. Blankenhorn had hoped the gay marriage debate would refocus public attention on parenthood and the broader cultural centrality of marriage; instead, it became framed mainly as a civil-rights issue, and opposition often reflected anti-gay animus. Given that shift and an emerging elite and youth consensus for marriage equality, he wants to pivot from opposition toward coalition-building: bringing together gay and straight supporters who wish to reinforce marital norms—encouraging marriage before childbearing, preferring marriage to cohabitation for durability, and debating children’s rights to know biological parents in assisted reproduction. The essay’s author endorses this new strategy but warns it’s harder than resisting legalization because changing cultural practices requires “wide bridges” across fragmented communities—networks and cultural credibility that are unevenly distributed—making diffusion of pro-marriage norms challenging.

SuperNaturals Grafted Vegetables, LLC (creators of the Mighty ‘Mato brand) has introduced Ketchup ‘n’ Fries by TomTato® to American gardeners for the 2015 season, bringing a novelty developed for over 15 years in Europe to North America. First sold as TomTato® in the U.K. in 2014, the grafted tomato–potato plant is now available through Plug Connection in San Diego County, licensed distributors like Log House Plants, and retailers including Territorial Seed Company, GardenAmerica and local garden centers. The TomTato produces cherry tomatoes above ground and white potatoes below, enabling dual harvests from a single plant that can even be grown in a 10‑gallon container—an appealing space-saving option for home gardeners.

Crucially, the TomTato is created by grafting, not genetic engineering: a chosen tomato scion is hand-spliced onto potato rootstock because both are closely related and graft well. Grafted vegetables, long used in fruit trees and common in Asia and Europe, provide stronger root systems that improve water and nutrient uptake, increase disease resistance (including blight and blossom end rot), extend harvests, and boost overall vigor—benefits valuable to commercial growers, organic producers, and backyard gardeners alike. Territorial and other sellers emphasize careful, hand-crafted grafting, hardened transplants shipped in spring with guarantees and shipping guidelines. While some customers later reported uneven potato yields, early reaction to the TomTato’s novelty and practicality was enthusiastic, generating significant buzz and conversation among gardeners and media.

Books and movies have long intertwined, producing both triumphs like The Godfather, Gone With The Wind, and The Silence of the Lambs—and notable flops when adaptations miss the mark, such as certain takes on The Scarlet Letter or clumsy star-driven projects. That history raises the question: are some books truly "unfilmable"? Even notoriously surreal works like Naked Lunch have been adapted, so is any literary work completely untouchable by Hollywood? To explore this, the piece seeks examples of books that seem unsuited to screen translation and invites readers to name novels they think would never work as films or adaptations they hope never materialize. Interleaved with this discussion is a casting news item: Carey Mulligan has been cast as Daisy Buchanan in Baz Luhrmann’s anticipated adaptation of The Great Gatsby, chosen over other contenders including Blake Lively, Natalie Portman, and Amanda Seyfried. Luhrmann confirmed the casting via Deadline, and Mulligan reportedly learned of the role at the CFDA awards in New York.

Bristol Palin continues to promote her 2011 memoir Not Afraid of Life: My Journey So Far, but interest has waned since its poor reviews and her brief celebrity peak after 2008. During a recent D.C. trip with her mother Sarah for CPAC, Bristol resorted to a Craigslist classified to recruit attendees for a book signing at Books-A-Million, offering free autographed copies to the first 100 RSVPs. Critics and the public have largely moved on from her post-vice-presidential spotlight and reality-TV fame, suggesting her moment in the limelight is fading.

Cast and creators of Girls reflect on the emotional end of the series, describing deep bonds formed over years of working together and saying goodbye to characters they've lived with. Lena Dunham calls the cast a close-knit family and finds it emotional to stop creating daily adventures for their characters. Allison Williams hopes audiences feel compassion for Marnie and recognizes the character’s broad relatability, while Jemima Kirke laments losing opportunities to continue refining Jessa. Zosia Mamet explains she’ll miss Shoshanna’s presence in her life more than the act of playing her, since the role felt like a separate entity after so many years. Executive producer Judd Apatow remembers an overall happy, calm set despite external controversy and hopes the show demonstrated varying degrees of personal evolution among its characters. The piece also notes a selection of classic YouTube videos from earlier years.

Mitt Romney, in a Columbus Dispatch editorial-board interview, suggested a shift in his stance on protections for people with pre-existing conditions and defended his plan to repeal the Affordable Care Act by arguing uninsured Americans still receive care. Romney said the nation must help the currently uninsured get coverage, but argued insurers should not be forced to cover people who voluntarily remained uninsured for many years and then seek coverage only after becoming ill. He emphasized that hospitals provide emergency care regardless of insurance status, saying people do not die in their homes for lack of coverage because charity, hospitals or government pay for emergency treatment. 

Those remarks drew criticism from Democrats and health advocates. The Obama campaign disputed Romney’s claim, citing estimates that tens of thousands die prematurely each year due to lack of insurance. Studies vary: a 2009 Harvard analysis estimated about 45,000 annual deaths linked to being uninsured; earlier analyses suggested lower but still significant mortality effects. Experts note EMTALA requires emergency treatment but does not prevent deaths: uninsured people may delay care, lack access to routine management for chronic conditions, face higher mortality risk, and challenge hospitals with uncompensated care costs that are shifted elsewhere.

Romney’s campaign language and his website have previously supported protections only for people with “continuous coverage,” interpreted to favor bans on pre-existing-condition exclusions mainly for those who maintained prior insurance, not for long-term uninsured individuals. He reiterated on national TV and in the debate that people who maintained insurance would be protected. Critics warn repealing Obamacare could leave millions uninsured and increase preventable deaths, while supporters argue state-based reforms and other measures could expand access.

Liliane Cyr has spent nearly four decades searching for her daughter Yohanna, who vanished from their St-Laurent apartment in 1978 at 18 months old. On the day Yohanna disappeared, Cyr left her baby with her then-boyfriend, Aaron Lewis (later Aaron Lewis Guay), before travelling for work. When Cyr called to check on Yohanna, her boyfriend first said the child was bathing, then later claimed the baby was with his mother so he could visit Cyr. After Cyr flew to Boston to retrieve Yohanna, he told her the infant had drowned and that he’d buried her. Cyr immediately searched—asking neighbours, hospitals and police—but found no trace. The taxi driver who had been the only witness died shortly after, evidence and photos she gave police later went missing, and the case cooled. Guay was charged with kidnapping in 1978 but acquitted at a preliminary hearing for lack of evidence; as a U.S. citizen he was deported and vanished. Over the years Cyr followed leads, including a 2005 tip from a U.S. woman who resembled Yohanna; DNA later disproved that link. Cyr has kept the case alive with posters and by sharing age-progressed images; supporters gather annually to mark the loss. In 2016 a Facebook message reignited hope—an American woman reached out asking about a Y-shaped birthmark on Yohanna’s index finger and suggested she might be the missing child, recounting doubts about her birth certificate and hazy childhood memories. Authorities are coordinating DNA testing; results may take weeks or months. Cyr remains torn between hope and fear: she wants to know whether Yohanna is alive or, if not, to finally have closure. Anyone with information is urged to contact the Missing Children’s Network.

Two little-known Dallas attorneys announced Wednesday they’ve been retained to investigate how Irving authorities treated 14-year-old Ahmed Mohamed after he was arrested at school for bringing a homemade digital clock. Attorney Thomas Bowers, joined by Reggie London, said the family hired them Tuesday and that they will seek medical evaluation for Ahmed while probing the city and school district’s actions. Bowers, who has represented high-profile clients before, criticized what he called public comments that “blame the victim” and suggested the lawyers’ involvement should curb further remarks. The attorneys said they were still gathering facts and did not yet know whether the family would take legal action.

Ahmed, a freshman who gained national attention after being handcuffed and briefly detained when a teacher feared his clock looked like a bomb, has reportedly suffered sleep problems since the incident. Irving police said their investigation found no evidence Ahmed intended to create alarm, the hoax-bomb charge was dropped, and the case was closed on Sept. 16. Police also announced that the seized clock has been available for pickup at headquarters on weekdays since they notified a family representative on Sept. 18. Meanwhile, the Mohamed family removed Ahmed and his siblings from the Irving school district, citing “religious persecution,” and said they would homeschool them. City and district officials provided no comment about consulting attorneys.

On Christmas Day 2017, a computer glitch caused gas stations and convenience stores across South Carolina to print tens of thousands of apparently winning Holiday Cash Add-A-Play lottery tickets between 5:51 p.m. and 7:53 p.m. The tic‑tac‑toe style game awards prizes for lining up three tree symbols; due to coding errors by the lottery’s former vendor, Intralot, machines repeatedly printed tickets showing nine tree symbols that were treated as $500 winners. Roughly 71,000 erroneous winning plays were produced, creating the appearance of more than $30 million in prizes and prompting many players to buy multiple tickets and celebrate. The state suspended the game after two hours and later commissioned Gaming Laboratories International for an independent analysis, which confirmed the vendor’s coding and inadequate quality assurance testing caused the error. Under South Carolina law, tickets produced or issued in error cannot yield prizes, so the South Carolina Education Lottery Board of Commissioners voted to reimburse only the original ticket purchase price. Players holding Holiday Cash Add-A-Play tickets showing nine tree symbols and purchased on Dec. 25, 2017 at or after 5:51 p.m. may mail original tickets to the lottery for a $1 refund plus first‑class postage reimbursement, with claims due by Jan. 7, 2019. The mistake cost the lottery about $1.7 million in prizes cashed before the shutdown; honoring all erroneous tickets would have totaled roughly $35 million. The decision has left many disappointed and spurred at least two lawsuits against the lottery and Intralot.

Since reaching a cooperation deal with special counsel Robert Mueller, former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort has become a frequent visitor to Mueller’s Washington office, appearing with his lawyers at least nine times in the past month. Those sessions—often lasting several hours—are part of a flurry of activity by Mueller’s team during a period that publicly looks quiet because of Justice Department guidelines around the midterm elections. Mueller has continued interviewing witnesses, convening a grand jury most Fridays, and pursuing sealed court actions. Prosecutors have reportedly questioned Manafort about his dealings with Russians; details of what he’s provided remain unclear. Manafort’s plea followed his Virginia conviction on eight counts of tax and bank fraud tied to his pre-2016 lobbying for the Ukraine government. He agreed to fully cooperate with Mueller’s probe, and his cooperation is expected to aid potential cases about coordination between the Trump campaign and Russia. Other cooperating figures—Rick Gates, Michael Flynn, and Michael Cohen—have also met with Mueller’s team after guilty pleas. The President’s lawyers are exchanging intensified communications with Mueller’s office in response to written questions about possible collusion and obstruction; the White House team has not settled on whether Trump will be interviewed in person. Court activity has been conspicuous: sealed hearings before Chief Judge Beryl Howell, grand jury business, and subpoenas or testimony orders for witnesses tied to Manafort and associates like Roger Stone’s contacts. Separately, Manafort appeared in a Virginia courtroom in a wheelchair in a prison uniform ahead of a Feb. 8 sentencing on the Virginia convictions; remaining counts were dismissed, removing the option of retrying him on those charges. Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein defended the probe as appropriate and independent, and legal observers expect Mueller’s report and possible further indictments after the election.

Kick-Ass 2 continues the comic-book saga: after Kick-Ass’s headline-making courage spawns a wave of do‑it‑yourself masked vigilantes led by the charismatic Colonel Stars and Stripes, Dave (Kick‑Ass) joins their patrols. Mindy (Hit Girl), trying to live a normal teenage life as graduation nears, is compelled to retire after being caught sneaking out as her assassin persona, forcing her to face high‑school cruelty alone. With Hit Girl sidelined, Dave links with Justice Forever, a team run by a born‑again ex‑mobster, and they start to make an impact—until the world’s first supervillain, The Mother F%&*^r (Red Mist reborn), seeks to annihilate them. Only Hit Girl’s return can prevent slaughter. The sequel, adapted from Mark Millar’s comics, amplifies the violence and consequences familiar from the first film; it delivers broad humor, strong performances (notably Jim Carrey as Colonel Stars and Stripes), and intense action. Carrey later publicly distanced himself from the film after the Sandy Hook tragedy, citing the level of on‑screen violence, prompting a robust defense from creator Mark Millar, who argued the content was always integral to the story and that fictional violence is distinct from real‑world events. The film was scheduled for release on Aug. 16.

Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Scott Pruitt has defended frequent taxpayer-funded premium travel, saying security concerns and unpleasant interactions on commercial flights have required him to fly first class or on government aircraft. Speaking in New Hampshire after a first-class flight to meet the governor and visit toxic-waste sites, Pruitt said decisions about seating and travel mode are made by his security detail, chief of staff and administration, not by him. He cited unspecified “incidents” on flights and said the intensely politicized environment around environmental issues raises threats. Records show Pruitt has taken multiple non-commercial flights costing over $58,000, and spent thousands on premium commercial seats—one trip costing $1,641 for a short D.C.–New York round trip—sparking questions about compliance with federal travel rules. The EPA initially claimed Pruitt had a “blanket waiver” to fly first or business class, but retracted that after POLITICO noted General Services Administration regulations prohibit blanket authorizations; waivers must be approved trip-by-trip unless a traveler has a documented disability. EPA later said waivers are submitted for each Pruitt trip, but the agency’s handling of travel records and exclusions for security reasons have drawn scrutiny. The EPA inspector general is investigating Pruitt’s travel and expects to report by summer. Critics, ethics experts and some former officials argue routine premium travel violates norms designed to prevent waste of taxpayer funds, while some security professionals acknowledge first-class travel can reduce exposure and offer protective advantages if properly justified. Pruitt’s broader travel and spending practices form part of wider scrutiny of Trump cabinet expenses.

With Verizon’s $4.83 billion agreement to buy Yahoo’s core internet business announced, attention shifted to the fate of Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer. Mayer said she plans to stay through the transition and help guide Yahoo into its “next chapter,” but she admitted being “open minded” about the future. Analysts expect she may remain during integration but could leave within a year, possibly replaced by AOL chief Tim Armstrong as leader of the combined AOL-Yahoo entity. Mayer’s tenure has been polarizing: she stabilized Yahoo after joining in 2012, introduced perks, and pursued acquisitions like BrightRoll that were credited as smart moves, but other decisions—most notably the $1.1 billion Tumblr purchase, elimination of remote work, and high-profile hires and deals—failed to produce a turnaround and drew criticism. Mayer has also faced gender-focused scrutiny in coverage. Financially, Mayer stands to receive a substantial payout if forced out — reports estimate between about $57 million to $137 million depending on circumstances, and she has already realized significant compensation. Verizon plans to merge Yahoo with AOL to create a stronger contender against Google and Facebook, while Yahoo will remain a holding company for valuable Asian investments including stakes in Alibaba and Yahoo Japan after the sale closes pending approvals.

Sandy Hook Promise, the nonprofit formed by family members of victims of the 2012 Sandy Hook Elementary School massacre, released a striking PSA as part of its “Know the Signs” campaign that urges people to notice warning signs of potential shooters. The Dec. 2 video follows a teen named Evan who swaps flirtatious messages scratched into a library desk with a mystery classmate; viewers focus on his budding romance. On the last day of school, when Evan’s secret pen pal recognizes his handwriting, a menacing student appears in the background, drops a duffel bag, and cocks an assault rifle as the screen fades to black. The PSA then rewinds to show the same scenes but highlights the other student’s troubling behaviors: reading gun‑enthusiast magazines, watching gun videos, posting pictures with guns, being bullied, and making a threatening gesture after a poor test grade. Text overlays: “While you were watching Evan, another student was showing signs of planning a shooting. But no one noticed.” Sandy Hook Promise stresses that single signs alone don’t prove intent, but cumulative or connected behaviors observed over time can indicate a pathway to violence or self-harm. The organization’s goal is to teach people to recognize at‑risk behaviors and empower interventions, noting that many perpetrators tell someone about plans before acting. By educating communities, Sandy Hook Promise aims to prevent gun violence and save lives.

Alipore Zoo in Kolkata is facing an unexpected problem: Vishal, a 10-year-old white tiger and the zoo’s only male of breeding age, is showing almost no interest in mating with tigress Rupa, aged eight. Despite repeated efforts over the past six months, including health measures such as de-worming and administration of vitamins A, D and E, plus libido enhancers, Vishal has repeatedly spurned Rupa’s advances. Staff report that when Rupa enters oestrus she actively courts him—making mating calls, scratching his back and attempting to initiate contact—but Vishal often retreats instead of responding. Veterinarians and specialists suspect the tiger’s reluctance stems from being bred and raised entirely in captivity; without prior contact with females he may be “shy” and unable to recognize or act on sexual signals. Age may also be a factor: experts say the prime mating period for male tigers is around five to eight years, and fertility beyond ten years becomes uncertain. The breeding program is important to the zoo because its big cats are aging and the last tiger birth there was over a decade ago. Officials have considered introducing Vishal to another, younger tigress, Rani, by moving her closer to his enclosure in hopes she might entice him. Zoo authorities are continuing attempts but remain unsure whether Vishal will mate successfully.

Attorney General Eric Holder visited Ferguson to reassure residents after the fatal police shooting of Michael Brown and to underscore the Justice Department’s intensive, civil-rights–centered response. Speaking to community leaders and students at St. Louis Community College, Holder acknowledged widespread mistrust of law enforcement and drew on his own experiences as a Black man stopped and searched by police, calling those encounters humiliating and influential on his views. He said dialogue alone is insufficient and pledged a fair, independent federal investigation led by the Civil Rights Division and the FBI, noting the department had assigned its most experienced agents and prosecutors and arranged an independent autopsy. Holder met privately with Brown’s parents, promising transparency, and also conferred with federal investigators, Missouri officials and Capt. Ron Johnson of the Highway Patrol. The visit aimed to calm tensions amid nearly two weeks of protests, some of which turned violent, and to demonstrate the administration’s prioritization of civil rights and concrete change. Holder urged local cooperation to improve police-community relations while the grand jury and federal probes proceed.

Starbucks sparked anger in Ireland after tweeting a diamond jubilee prompt—“show us what makes you proud to be British”—to nearly 2,000 followers of its Irish Twitter account. The misdirected message prompted sharp rebukes and calls for an apology, with one user noting the account’s .IE handle. Starbucks Ireland later apologized on Twitter, saying the post was meant for UK followers only, and the company issued a formal apology to Irish customers and followers. The gaffe follows other brands’ missteps in Ireland, such as Nike’s controversial “Black and Tan” St Patrick’s Day shoe that evoked painful historical associations.

Nigerian authorities announced a 50 million naira (about $300,000) reward for information leading to the rescue of more than 200 schoolgirls kidnapped on 14 April from a Chibok boarding school by Boko Haram. The abductions provoked nationwide and international outrage, the viral #BringBackOurGirls campaign, and diplomatic offers of assistance: the US, UK and China dispatched teams or intelligence help. Boko Haram’s leader, claiming responsibility, threatened to sell the girls and denounced Western-style education. Meanwhile the group launched a brutal attack on Gamboru Ngala near the Cameroon border, burning homes and markets and killing scores—locals and officials reported as many as 150–300 dead—with reports of mass burials and survivors fleeing across the border. Security forces and government have been criticized for a slow response; Nigeria said helicopters and troops searched hundreds of locations. International figures including Obama, Kofi Annan and Malala appealed for action and support for the victims.

Russian President Vladimir Putin challenged the US to present UN evidence that the Syrian government used chemical weapons near Damascus on 21 August, calling claims of government culpability "utter nonsense" and warning against giving proponents of intervention a "trump card." The US, citing intelligence it says shows 1,429 killed (including hundreds of children), believes a "limited, narrow" military response—without ground troops—is justified and President Obama asked Congress to authorize force to deter future chemical-weapon use. UN weapons inspectors have left Syria with samples—soil, munitions swabs, blood, hair and other material—and are analyzing them at the OPCW in The Hague; their mandate is to determine whether chemical weapons were used, not who used them. UN spokesmen urged patience, saying lab analysis could take weeks and stressing a political solution. Global reactions are mixed: Russia and China oppose unilateral strikes and have vetoed resolutions; Britain’s parliament earlier rejected action, while France shows ambivalence. Syria denies responsibility, blaming jihadist rebels. Debate in the US is intensifying as Congress prepares hearings and domestic and international opinion remains divided.

Former NFL star Chad Johnson (aka Chad Ochocinco) was jailed for 30 days after a Broward County judge rejected a negotiated sentence for a probation violation in his domestic violence case. Johnson had pleaded no contest to head-butting then-wife Evelyn Lozada and was on probation. Prosecutors and defense had agreed to community service and counseling, but during a hearing Johnson lightly slapped his attorney’s backside when asked if he was satisfied with representation. The courtroom laughed; Judge Kathleen McHugh deemed the act disrespectful, called off the deal, added three months’ probation, and ordered Johnson arrested. He apologized, saying his life was “in shambles.”

On Black Friday in La Crescenta, a man allegedly robbed the Rite Aid pharmacy at The Marketplace Shopping Center, then barricaded himself armed inside a Connect Wireless store. Deputies responded about 4 p.m.; crisis negotiators and the sheriff’s Special Enforcement Bureau (SWAT) spent nearly six hours on the scene. Employees fled and no hostages were taken. Tactical teams entered late Friday and found the suspect deceased, apparently from a self-inflicted wound. No shots were fired by authorities and no deputies or civilians were injured; nearby streets and stores were temporarily evacuated and later reopened.

At her first post-meeting press conference as Federal Reserve chair, Janet Yellen’s attempt to clarify the FOMC’s guidance backfired: pressed on what “a considerable period” meant — the phrase the Fed used to indicate how long it would wait after winding down asset purchases before raising the federal funds rate — she answered “around six months.” Markets seized on that apparent specificity. With the Fed’s taper likely to finish in October or November, six months points to a potential first rate hike in April–May, earlier than many investors had been expecting and somewhat ahead of the Fed’s own dot-plot projections. Stocks fell and bond yields rose on the immediate reaction.

Commentators argued Yellen shouldn’t have moved beyond the statement’s deliberate ambiguity. The Fed intentionally replaced its prior numerical 6.5% unemployment threshold with qualitative guidance, saying policy would depend on a broad set of indicators — labor market measures, inflation pressures and expectations, and financial developments. Yellen repeatedly emphasized those conditions would determine timing, and she cautioned that low inflation could justify keeping rates low longer. Nonetheless, her “six months” remark was interpreted as a tightening signal.

Critics framed the episode as a communications gaffe: seasoned central bankers typically avoid narrowing vague guidance, because markets can treat offhand comments as firm commitments. Observers noted this kind of early misstep isn’t fatal — past chairs erred similarly — but it highlighted the challenges of unwinding extraordinary monetary accommodation while managing market expectations. Going forward, Fed officials may be urged to stick closer to carefully scripted language to avoid spooking markets.

Police and fire officials are warning about the fire risk of sleeping with—or charging—cell phones on beds or under pillows after several incidents where devices overheated and ignited bedding. The NYPD’s 33rd Precinct tweeted a blunt public-safety reminder: don’t put your cellphone under a pillow when sleeping or when charging. The warning echoes a 2015 Hamden, Connecticut, fire in which a teenager’s phone reportedly caught fire, scorching a bed and pillow and prompting firefighters to stress that batteries and chargers generate heat and need ventilation. Fire Chief David Berardesca and local residents described flames that spread on a mattress while the teen slept, thankfully extinguished before crews arrived. Officials advise leaving phones and laptops on hard, flat surfaces so heat can dissipate and never blocking device vents with bedding. They also urge checks of cords and chargers for fraying or damage—faulty cords can spark—and to dispose of damaged equipment. Unplug chargers when not in use, since they still draw power. While there’s no evidence of a widespread uptick in such fires, authorities recommend placing phones on nightstands rather than under pillows as a simple precaution to reduce the risk of burns, melting batteries, or fires.

The writer admires PETA’s work but criticizes them for overreaching, citing a recent letter sent to the founder of the National Buffalo organization as an example. Separately, the Internet Archive is conducting crawls to preserve newly created pages and the pages they reference. By archiving these versions, the Archive aims to replace or supplement broken links with stable snapshots so readers can access the original content authors intended, working toward fixing web link rot.

Health authorities are warning that a novel coronavirus, dubbed MERS-CoV (Middle East respiratory symptom coronavirus), poses a global threat. Since its discovery in September 2012, at least 53 confirmed infections have been reported worldwide, with around 30 deaths; earlier counts noted about half of known cases were fatal. The virus, part of the coronavirus family that includes SARS, causes severe respiratory illness—fever, cough, pneumonia—and can lead to kidney failure and gastrointestinal symptoms. Transmission details remain unclear, complicating prevention: many cases are linked directly or indirectly to the Middle East, but limited local spread has occurred among close contacts in Europe. Recent developments include three first cases in Italy (a man recently returned from Jordan and two close contacts, a woman and a toddler) and fatal cases in France. WHO Director-General Margaret Chan urged international cooperation, calling the outbreak “alarm bells” and stressing urgent joint investigations and resource pooling to understand reservoirs, transmission routes, and to mount an effective response.

Republican nominee Donald Trump launched a broad, angry attack on the news media after several stories portrayed his campaign as struggling and highlighted internal disagreements. In a series of tweets, Trump denounced The New York Times and other outlets as “disgusting,” “dishonest” and “corrupt,” accusing reporters of using anonymous, non-existent sources and of misrepresenting his words and rallies. He insisted the press protects Hillary Clinton and claimed that, if coverage were fair, he would be “beating Hillary by 20%.” Trump complained that media accounts fail to show the “real message” of his events, omit crowd size and enthusiasm, and place false meanings onto his remarks. At a Connecticut rally following the Times piece, he said the newspaper was “going to hell” and suggested revoking reporters’ credentials for writing what he called dishonest stories.

The Times article that set off the outburst quoted anonymous colleagues describing Trump as “exhausted, frustrated and still bewildered by fine points of the political process,” and other reporting raised questions about campaign dysfunction.
