Trump’s campaign chairman Paul Manafort blamed the press for fixating on Trump’s recent controversial comments—such as suggesting that Second Amendment supporters could “do something” about Clinton or falsely saying President Obama “founded” ISIS—rather than his policy proposals. Trump’s running mate, Mike Pence, defended him and previewed upcoming “real specifics” on national security and counterterrorism, while Vice President Joe Biden was set to headline a Clinton rally criticizing Trump as the least prepared nominee in history.

Separately, media scrutiny extended to Manafort, as The New York Times published a probe into his consulting work in Ukraine and alleged ties to networks accused of looting and influencing elections; the piece prompted unusual attention when former Trump campaign manager Corey Lewandowski quickly tweeted a link to it. The episode highlighted tensions within the campaign and the fraught, adversarial relationship between Trump and mainstream news organizations.

WikiLeaks said it has found a new route to bypass the payment blockade imposed by major card companies and could accept donations through a French non-profit, the Fund for the Defense of Net Neutrality. Visa and MasterCard, among several firms that cut off WikiLeaks after it began publishing U.S. diplomatic cables in late 2010, previously blocked other workarounds such as an Icelandic gateway. The group’s founder Julian Assange, holed up in the Ecuadorian Embassy in London and fighting extradition to Sweden, challenged Visa to halt the new plan and said lawyers stand ready. WikiLeaks has criticized the card companies for crippling its funding—reserves fell from €800,000 in December 2010 to under €100,000 by June 2012—and said it could run out of money without increased donations. The blockade drew criticism from free-expression advocates and prompted legal challenges in multiple countries; WikiLeaks recently won a case in Iceland. Details of how French Carte Bleue transactions would be processed remained unclear.

In Kushinagar district, Uttar Pradesh, six newly married women from Khesiya village—Neelam, Kalawati, Shakina (Sakina), Niranjan, Gudiya, and Sita (Seeta)—have returned to their parental homes within weeks of marriage because their husbands’ houses lack toilets. Refusing to go back until proper sanitation is provided, the brides staged a protest that underscores growing awareness among rural women of the health, privacy and safety implications of open defecation. Sulabh International founder Bindeshwar Pathak has pledged to build toilets free of cost in all six households without delay and said the women would be honored for their stand. Pathak framed the protest as evidence of changing mindsets around sanitation and cited previous examples—such as Priyanka Bharti of Maharajganj, who was honored, became a Sulabh motivator and featured in a sanitation advertisement after demanding a toilet at her in-laws’ house. The reports note that nearly half of India’s 1.2 billion people lack toilets at home, a deficit that the World Bank estimates costs India about $54 billion annually in health- and productivity-related losses. Lack of sanitation disproportionately affects rural women, who face indignity, logistical hardship and safety risks; the issue has gained national attention, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi urging action to end open defecation and promote school toilets.

San Francisco City Attorney Dennis Herrera is escalating his probe into Monster Beverage Corp.’s marketing of highly caffeinated energy drinks to minors after the company sued in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles seeking to block his investigation. Monster argues Herrera’s actions would unduly burden interstate commerce and violate commercial speech and other rights, and accuses him of seeking publicity over science. Herrera began investigating Monster in October under California’s unfair competition law over claims that their caffeine levels are “completely safe” and that consumers “can never get too much.” Herrera joined 18 physicians in March urging the FDA to regulate energy-drink caffeine, citing that energy drinks often contain 100–300 mg per 8-oz serving versus FDA soda guidance of about 71 mg per 12-oz serving. Herrera’s office alleges Monster markets to children as young as six via its “Monster Army” site; Monster counters by comparing its caffeine to Starbucks coffee. Herrera vows aggressive litigation to curb what he calls irresponsible, unlawful marketing to youth.

Microsoft’s Windows 8 Consumer Preview is a bold, risky reinvention that clearly signals Microsoft’s push from traditional PCs toward touch-centric mobile devices. The OS splits into two distinct modes: the familiar Desktop for running legacy Windows programs, and the radical Metro interface—tile-based, full‑screen apps inspired by Windows Phone—optimized for touch. Metro is visually striking and introduces helpful ideas like live tiles that surface information without opening apps, edge-swipe gestures for fast app switching, and the ability to display one narrow and one wide app side-by-side. Those features feel modern and, on a tablet, often superior to current tablet competitors.

However, Metro’s dramatic departure from long-established Windows behaviors creates a jarring, schizophrenic experience, especially on large-screen desktops and when using a mouse and keyboard. Some interactions are unintuitive—hover and edge behaviors differ from web conventions, tile rearrangement can be awkward, and many Metro design choices don’t scale well to big monitors where multitasking often requires more than two visible apps. The Consumer Preview still has occasional performance hiccups and missing features: the Windows Store wasn’t active at preview time, and many Metro apps lack full functionality or sharing integration. Microsoft’s choice to restrict Metro apps to the Store and sandboxed access should improve security and installation simplicity but will frustrate longtime Windows users accustomed to freely downloadable software.

Early reviewers found Metro delightful on touch devices and promising even with keyboard and mouse, but warned many users will resist the steep adjustment. Windows 8 shows smart, ambitious decisions and real potential to challenge tablets like the iPad—if Microsoft can smooth out the rough edges and convince users to adopt a dual-interface future.

A recent study by Orsama et al. analyzed daily self-reported morning weights from 80 adults over 15–330 days (4,657 measurements) and found a clear weekly rhythm: body weight typically peaks after the weekend (Sunday–Monday) and reaches its low by Friday. Weekend behavior—larger meals, higher calorie intake, reduced physical activity, and more alcohol—likely drives modest Saturday–Sunday gains, which many people then compensate for during the workweek. Participants were grouped as weight losers (>3% loss), gainers (>1% gain), or maintainers; the largest weekday–weekend swings occurred in successful weight losers, suggesting that allowing occasional weekend indulgences coupled with weekday compensation supports long-term adherence and weight control. The study used semi-parametric spline mixed models to account for individual trajectories and confirmed the weekday–weekend pattern across subgroups, though the gainers showed more variability. Limitations include small subgroup sizes, self-reported data, and retrospective aggregation. Practical takeaways: weigh yourself consistently on the same day/time for comparisons, treat small weekend increases as normal, and focus on compensatory weekday habits—flexible restraint may better sustain long-term weight management than strict forbiddance.

Ashley Taylor Wright, 23, of Pensacola, was arrested after allegedly using her three-month-old daughter as a human shield while trying to flee a shoplifting stop at Dillard’s in the Santa Rosa Mall parking lot. Deputies say Wright left the store with $261 worth of women’s clothing concealed in a stroller. When an Okaloosa County deputy approached her vehicle, she refused to exit, held a baby carrier with the infant between herself and the officer and shouted, “You will have to shoot through the baby to get me!” She then reportedly hurled the 14-pound carrier with the baby inside at the deputy and ran, but fell and was caught after struggling. Two other small children were in the back seat during the incident. The infant was not injured. At the hospital Wright acknowledged drinking a few beers and admitted stealing the items, claiming they were for her children though the items taken were adult clothing. She faces charges including felony child abuse, petty theft, and resisting an officer and is jailed on $7,000 bond.

Researchers continue to uncover dramatic new evidence from the 1564 wreck of the Swedish warship Mars, which exploded and sank during the Northern Seven Years’ War. Discovered in 2011 near Öland and lying 70 metres deep in the well-preserving, low-oxygen Baltic, the wreck has yielded skeletal remains, weaponry, and unique naval equipment that illuminate the violent final moments and broader naval practice of the era. Recent dives and ROV surveys revealed more human bones—including a femur with trauma consistent with a sharp-edged weapon—large cannons, a hand grenade, helmets, swords, and a spectacular grapnel (grappling hook) never before recovered from the period. The ship had been carrying between 800 and 1,000 men—comparable to a medium-sized town—many of whom died in the explosion or as the ship sank; 300–400 Dano-Lübeckian soldiers were aboard after boarding actions shortly before the blast. Historical accounts describe close-quarters combat with hand grenades, lances and spears, and the use of an anti-boarding net on Mars’s deck; the wreck corroborates many written sources while clarifying partisan embellishments. Researchers also document a Swedish tactical shift toward long-range gunnery—Mars carried very large cannons up to 4.8 metres—but close fighting still occurred, evidenced by weapon fragments and bodily trauma. The team used filmed dives to produce detailed 3D models of the site; conservation ethics and the difficulty and cost of deep recovery mean artefacts will remain in situ for now. The multidisciplinary exploration by MARIS, GUE divers, Västervik Museum, Ocean Discovery and others offers a vivid, well-preserved snapshot of 16th-century naval warfare and international conflict.

FBI agent Chase Bishop, 29, who allegedly accidentally discharged his service weapon at a Denver bar in early June, has been booked and charged with one count of second-degree assault, a fourth-degree felony. Video of the June 2 incident at Mile High Spirits shows Bishop, off-duty and visiting Denver for training, performing a backflip while dancing; his firearm fell from its holster, and as he bent to retrieve it the gun fired, striking a bystander in the leg. The victim, identified as Tom Reddington (24), suffered a nonlethal but serious leg wound; his attorney says they are exploring a possible lawsuit against the FBI. Bishop surrendered to Denver authorities after a warrant was issued and was later released to an FBI supervisor. Denver District Attorney Beth McCann said prosecutors filed the charge now because there is sufficient evidence, though additional charges could be added pending blood alcohol content and other test results that remain outstanding. The FBI is conducting an internal investigation, with possible disciplinary outcomes including termination, suspension or reprimand. Bishop is set to be advised of the charge in Denver District Court.

In June–July 2017, the Internet Archive crawled Luxembourg’s .lu domain for the National Library of Luxembourg; the collection also includes other web captures and context such as an article about homelessness in Detroit. The piece profiles Abe Hagenston, who calls himself “Honest Abe” and has been homeless there for roughly seven to ten years, living under the I-75 8 Mile overpass. Abe panhandles in unconventional ways: he accepts credit and debit card donations using a Square card reader attached to his phone and even maintains a website to coordinate help, offer odd jobs, and report suspected fake panhandlers. He describes organizing with other homeless people to panhandle in shifts and says he’s trying to turn his situation into something that benefits others as well as himself. Despite relatively mild winter weather, Abe notes income shortfalls have prevented him from affording new prescription eyeglasses, and he laments the challenges of homelessness without family support. The report situates his story within broader outreach efforts—volunteers and agencies conducting nightly counts and offering supplies and shelter—and notes state and national homelessness statistics and trends, including a recent decline in Michigan and an estimated 578,424 people experiencing homelessness nationwide in 2014.

Occupy encampments in multiple U.S. cities faced looming eviction deadlines with largely peaceful standoffs as authorities weighed enforcement. In Philadelphia, about 100 protesters remained on Dilworth Plaza past Mayor Nutter’s 5 p.m. deadline, sitting, chanting and handing out food as police watched without making arrests. City officials said fencing and renovation work required the plaza, and many campers—some homeless—began dismantling tents; roughly a third of about 300 tents were gone by evening. Philadelphia police stressed cooperation and warned protesters they could not re-establish camps without permits, while supporters urged help finding alternative sites. In Los Angeles, police declared an unlawful assembly around City Hall after a midnight removal deadline but initially focused on clearing streets rather than the park. Officers in riot gear reopened blocked thoroughfares for commuters after a tense confrontation; four people were arrested during a brief scuffle. Hundreds to thousands had gathered overnight, swelling the demonstration. City leaders in both places emphasized restraint and urged protesters to shift tactics from occupying public land to broader political engagement.

Multiple flood advisories and warnings have been issued across western and northern Colorado following heavy rain and unstable conditions. Advisories were posted May 28 for Grand and Jackson counties (until May 29 evening), Rio Blanco, Mesa, Eagle and Larimer counties with varying expiration times May 29, and ongoing alerts for Weld county extending through June 2. Flood warnings remain in effect for Routt County (through May 30) and for Weld County (through May 29). Separately, a massive mudslide struck Grand Mesa near Salt Creek Road (601/2 Road) east of Collbran Sunday evening. Mesa County authorities said the slide may be roughly 2 miles wide, 4 miles long and up to 250 feet deep; three residents from the Collbran/Mesa area are missing. The ridge reportedly had been sliding most of the day; heavy rain likely contributed. The remote site, near Vega State Park, had no reported structural damage and no major road closures, though cellphone service is unavailable. A roadblock on Colorado 330 at Salt Creek Road restricts access and residents are urged to avoid the area as crews assess conditions.

President Donald Trump cut short his first presidential trip to Canada amid sharp disputes with G-7 allies over trade and other policy moves. Arriving in La Malbaie, Quebec, Trump faced overt criticism from leaders including Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and French President Emmanuel Macron for imposing protectionist tariffs on steel and aluminum, withdrawing from the Iran nuclear deal, and retreating from international climate efforts. Those disputes transformed the summit into a confrontation over Trump’s break from decades of U.S. support for freer trade and multilateral agreements.

Tensions escalated on the eve of the summit with public barbs exchanged on Twitter. Trump accused Trudeau and Macron of charging “massive tariffs” on the U.S., highlighted an EU-U.S. trade surplus figure, and warned allies to remove barriers or face matching measures. He also singled out Canada’s dairy protections, alleging a 270 percent tariff on U.S. dairy products and framing his actions as defending American farmers. Trudeau called the tariffs “insulting” and a betrayal of longtime allies who have fought alongside the U.S. in major conflicts. Macron and other leaders signaled willingness to move forward without the U.S. if necessary, framing a possible six-country communiqué as representing enduring shared values and economic weight.

Against this fraught backdrop, the White House announced Trump would depart the G-7 early to travel directly to Singapore for his June 12 summit with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un, skipping sessions on climate, oceans and clean energy and the customary final group photo and joint press events. Analysts warned the standoff could cause lasting damage to U.S.-ally relations and to the rules-based international system that American administrations historically championed. Allies responded with or threatened retaliatory tariffs, and NAFTA renegotiations also stalled after Canada rejected a proposed sunset clause. Observers said the summit was likely to produce “polite acrimony” rather than substantive consensus.

The 70th Cannes Film Festival concluded with Ruben Östlund’s satirical drama The Square winning the Palme d’Or. The film, which skewers contemporary art, commerce and political correctness, stars Claes Bang and Elisabeth Moss and features a notorious scene in which a faux-gorilla disrupts a gala. Jury president Pedro Almodóvar praised the film’s wit and topicality. Sofia Coppola made history as only the second woman to win Best Director, for her Civil War–set The Beguiled, an adaptation starring Nicole Kidman, Kirsten Dunst, Elle Fanning and Colin Farrell; Coppola was absent and released a statement thanking her team and supporters of women-driven films. The Grand Prix went to Robin Campillo’s 120 Beats Per Minute, about ACT UP–era AIDS activism, while Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Loveless received the Jury Prize. Best Actor was Joaquin Phoenix for You Were Never Really Here; Best Actress went to Diane Kruger for In the Fade, who dedicated her award to victims of terror. Best Screenplay was a tie between Yorgos Lanthimos and Efthymis Filippou for The Killing of a Sacred Deer and Lynne Ramsay for You Were Never Really Here. Nicole Kidman received a special prize celebrating Cannes’ 70th anniversary. The festival also sparked debate over Netflix entries and future screening rules.

Federal prosecutors have opened a criminal investigation into the July 19 duck boat sinking on Table Rock Lake near Branson, Missouri, after the U.S. Coast Guard concluded the deaths of 17 passengers “resulted from the misconduct, negligence, or inattention to the duties” of the vessel’s captain, court filings show. The probe names Kenneth Scott McKee, captain of the sunken Stretch Duck 07, and Barry King, captain of nearby Stretch Duck 54, as targets; Ripley Entertainment, the company operating Ride the Ducks Branson, and several of its employees or officers are also identified as targets or subjects. The Coast Guard referred the matter to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Missouri on Aug. 13, citing probable cause for possible federal criminal charges under statutes penalizing negligent vessel operation that causes death. The NTSB is separately investigating the cause of the sinking, and Missouri’s attorney general has opened a criminal inquiry into potential violations of the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act. Cellphone video captured the two boats struggling in a storm that produced winds up to 73 mph and waves over three feet, despite a severe thunderstorm warning and the vessel’s certificate of inspection that forbids water operation in winds above 35 mph or waves over two feet. Survivors and families of victims have filed multiple civil lawsuits against Ripley; prosecutors have asked courts to stay civil discovery until the criminal investigation concludes to prevent interference. Ripley says it is cooperating with federal and state authorities but has limited public comment due to the ongoing NTSB probe.

An archive tracks and publishes public statements deleted by U.S. politicians, letting the public explore tweets and posts officials would rather remove. The project continuously captures deleted content from accounts identified as elected officials or political candidates, creating a searchable repository of retracted statements to improve transparency and accountability. Repeatedly emphasized is guidance for accuracy of tracking: if someone’s account is not an elected official or candidate and they believe they are being monitored in error, they are urged to contact the archive to correct the listing. The resource highlights the importance of preserving public records of officials’ communications, offering citizens, journalists, and researchers a way to review content that politicians tried to erase. By archiving removals, the service seeks to deter misleading deletions and maintain a fuller historical record of public discourse.

What began as a simple holiday potluck invitation at a Utah state office snowballed into a massive email fiasco when the message was accidentally sent to roughly 25,000 state employees. Within minutes on a Friday morning, a torrent of “reply all” messages flooded inboxes: pleas to stop replying, requests to be removed, exasperated caps-locked commands (“STOP REPLYING TO ALL”), and numerous “Sent from my iPhone” responses that only worsened the thread. State public information officer Joe Dougherty shared screenshots of the deluge on Twitter, dubbing it “Replyall-gate 2018,” and urged employees not to reply to all. The cascade clogged phones and computers for several hours, prompting a flurry of social media commentary ranging from bemused (“Is it a white elephant type of swap?”) to anguished (“I … want to die”). Lt. Gov. Spencer Cox weighed in with humor and alarm, calling it “an emergency” and lamenting that a one-department potluck had accidentally reached the entire state workforce. Utah Department of Technology Services staff and communications officials advised prevention measures—such as using BCC for large groups—to avoid future loops. By about 11:10 a.m., Dougherty reported the reply-all storm had largely subsided. The incident follows other high-profile reply-all disasters — including one at Reuters that involved 33,000 employees and hundreds of responses — underscoring how a single misaddressed email can rapidly overwhelm large organizations. Neither the original sender nor their department was publicly identified by day’s end.

San Jose police say data from a Fitbit helped lead to the arrest of 90-year-old Anthony Aiello on suspicion of murdering his 67-year-old stepdaughter, Karen Navarra. Navarra was found dead at her home on Sept. 13 with severe neck and head wounds; a medical examiner concluded she could not have inflicted all injuries on herself and ruled the death a homicide. Police believe the scene had been staged to resemble a suicide.

Aiello, who is married to Navarra’s 92-year-old mother, initially told investigators he visited Navarra on Sept. 8, brought pizza and biscotti, stayed about 15 minutes, and later saw her drive past his house with another person. Surveillance footage contradicted that account: cameras showed Aiello’s car in Navarra’s driveway from 3:12 p.m. to at least 3:33 p.m., and did not corroborate her driving by his home. Navarra wore a Fitbit Alta HR; its data reportedly showed a sharp heart-rate spike at 3:20 p.m. on Sept. 8 followed by a rapid decline and cessation of heart-rate readings at 3:28 p.m. When confronted, Aiello denied being present at the time of death and suggested someone else might have been in the house. Police also found two shirts with blood spatter in his garage; Aiello claimed frequent self-inflicted cuts. He was arrested Sept. 25, is being held without bail, and is scheduled to appear in court for plea proceedings. Fitbit declined to comment. This case follows other investigations that have used wearable-device data as evidence.

Pope Francis expressed shock and deep sorrow after a brutal attack at a home for the elderly in Aden, Yemen, that left 16 people dead, including four nuns from the Missionaries of Charity. The Vatican’s condolence message, delivered by Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin, called the killings “senseless and diabolical” and urged that the “pointless slaughter” awaken consciences, prompt a change of heart, and inspire all parties to lay down their arms and pursue dialogue. The pope assured his prayers for the dead, extended spiritual closeness to their families and everyone affected, and appealed in the name of God for combatants in Yemen’s conflict to renounce violence and renew commitment to civilians, especially those most in need whom the sisters served.

According to officials and witnesses, gunmen entered the retirement home—run by the charity founded by Mother Teresa—moving room to room, handcuffing victims and shooting them in the head. The nuns killed were two Rwandans, one Indian and one Kenyan; they had been serving breakfast to about 80 residents when the attack occurred. One nun in charge managed to hide and escaped unharmed. No group immediately claimed responsibility, though Yemeni officials blamed the Islamic State; both IS and Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula have exploited Yemen’s civil war to gain ground.

Yemen’s conflict, between Iran-backed Houthi rebels in the north and a Saudi-backed government in the south, has killed thousands and displaced millions. The Vatican’s statement concluded with blessings and special sympathy for the Missionaries of Charity and all suffering from the ongoing violence.

Gwyneth Paltrow, 38, posed topless for Vanity Fair’s jewelry supplement, wearing only Louis Vuitton jewelry and fishnet tights, photographed by Mark Seliger. With hair in a French twist, natural makeup and arms crossed modestly, she appeared toned and youthful with no visible stretch marks. The piece highlights her disciplined lifestyle—early-morning yoga, clean eating, GOOP advice—and mentions her family, Glee appearance and fitness and fashion ventures.

A 51-year-old man doused himself with gasoline and set himself on fire Thursday morning in St. Peter’s Square, Vatican City. A Jesuit priest first attempted to smother the flames with his frock and jacket, and two Vatican police officers then used a fire extinguisher to put out the blaze. The man was taken to a nearby hospital and later transferred to a larger facility with serious burns to the upper body; the officers were treated for smoke inhalation and hand injuries. Motives remain unknown; police found a paper with the man’s daughter’s phone number. Vatican police restricted reporter access to the square after the incident. The episode recalled a 2001 self-immolation in the square in protest of Church teaching.

A controversy erupted after emails posted online revealed that Annette G. Beck-Sickinger, a biochemistry professor at Leipzig University, told an Indian student she would not accept male Indian interns because of “the rape problem in India.” The exchange was shared on Quora by a colleague of the student; neither the student nor the colleague identified themselves. Another student later said Beck-Sickinger had rejected his PhD application in 2014 for the same reason. In messages attributed to her, the professor said widespread reports of rape and “multi-rape crimes” from India made her unwilling to host Indian male students and suggested many female professors in Germany had adopted similar stances.

Beck-Sickinger acknowledged the emails and issued an apology on the German Embassy website, calling her actions a mistake and saying she regretted hurting anyone’s feelings. She told Hindustan Times the episode stemmed from an “unpleasant discussion,” that her lab was full, and that she had previously accepted several Indian students. The German ambassador, Michael Steiner, publicly rebuked her, calling her generalisation offensive to Indians and to those working on women’s empowerment, and urging her to learn more about India’s diversity. The affair occurred amid renewed debate in India about violence against women following the banned documentary India’s Daughter, which rekindled discussion of misogyny and safety. Leipzig University, founded in 1409, faced reputational scrutiny as the incident drew attention to discrimination and stereotyping in academia.

A fight over a break-room light at Philadelphia International Airport on Thursday morning escalated into a fatal stabbing involving three cleaning contractors for Worldwide Flight Services, which services Frontier Airlines. Around 11:30 a.m. in a secure Terminal E break room near Gate E6, one worker turned off a light, prompting an argument with another coworker. A third man intervened, and after shoving produced a sharp implement — investigators suspect a box cutter used on the job — and stabbed 28-year-old Aaron Jenkins in the abdomen/thigh area. Jenkins was taken to Penn Presbyterian Trauma Center and later died. The two other employees fled to the departures hall but surrendered when confronted by police. Kevin Emanuel, 35, was charged with murder and possession of an instrument of a crime. The weapon has not been recovered, and the incident did not disrupt airport operations.

In the chaotic aftermath of the Dec. 2 San Bernardino mass shooting at the Inland Regional Center, emergency dispatch recordings and subsequent reporting revealed how confusion, frantic response and evolving evidence unfolded as officers sought suspects and investigators pieced together the attackers’ preparations. An officer on scene relayed co-worker Syed Rizwan Farook’s name to dispatchers after noting he had left a workplace meeting “out of the blue” about 20 minutes before the shooting and matched a gunman’s description. Farook and his wife Tashfeen Malik entered an auditorium rented by the county health department for an annual meeting, where they opened fire, killing 14 people and wounding 21. Survivors described bullets spraying a room decorated for the holidays; many had earlier taken an active-shooter training in the same space but the room offered little protection. Initial gunfire lasted briefly before the shooters reloaded and fired again; witnesses saw two leave, and officers initially reported multiple masked assailants and a possible getaway in a black SUV.

Dispatch audio captures the tense coordination: officers reporting unknown numbers of suspects, possible bombs left behind, and medics seeking treatment areas while bomb squad personnel later deemed a device “out of the norms” and moved to robot-handled disposal. Roughly four hours later a vehicle pursuit ended in a shootout in which officers fired heavily; police say the pair discharged 76 rounds while officers returned 380 rounds. The couple died in that firefight.

Federal probes into radicalization and plotting revealed additional context. U.S. officials told CNN and NBC that Farook may have conspired with another person as early as 2012 to target an attack in California, but earlier plans were reportedly abandoned after terror-related arrests. Investigators also found signs of meticulous preparation: the couple practiced at a local gun range for at least a year, made financial arrangements (including a roughly $28,500 deposit into Farook’s account shortly before the attack), and had left their infant daughter with Farook’s mother the morning of the massacre. Authorities continue examining loans, gun purchases and contacts to determine the full scope of planning and radicalization.

A brutal intimidation campaign and international drug-and-gambling scheme unraveled after a gruesome DVD threat and a lost $2.5 million bankroll tied Owen “O-Dog” Hanson to a cross-continental criminal enterprise. Hanson, a former USC walk-on athlete turned ostentatious gambler and alleged kingpin, was sentenced in San Diego to 21 years and three months after pleading guilty to racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to distribute drugs; prosecutors also seized more than $6.5 million in assets. Hanson’s operation trafficked large quantities of cocaine into Australia and ran illegal sports-betting and money-laundering schemes, including an attempt to launder proceeds through high-roller blackjack play at Sydney’s Star Casino.

The case began to implode after Hanson delivered AU$2.5 million in suitcases to American pro gambler Robert J. “Robin Hood 702” Cipriani in 2011, expecting Cipriani to convert the cash into casino checks. Cipriani, increasingly uneasy that the money was criminal, deliberately lost the full sum by betting maximums—then faced escalating threats from Hanson’s crew: lurking vans, abusive calls, vandalized family graves and, most chillingly, a mailed DVD showing two beheadings with the message that similar violence would follow if Cipriani didn’t repay. Cipriani ultimately became an FBI confidential source (“Jackpot”), prompting a joint FBI–NSW Police probe that led to Hanson’s 2015 arrest and a sweeping takedown of O-Dog Enterprise; about 20 alleged associates have pleaded guilty.

Court materials portray Hanson as a status-obsessed figure who mixed sports-world contacts, illegal bookmaking, and violent intimidation. Cipriani, whose own past and gambling conduct drew scrutiny from the defense, delivered an emotional victim impact statement describing lasting trauma to his wife and himself. Authorities say dismantling Hanson’s ring prevented further distribution of harmful drugs and curtailed a violent, transnational criminal operation.

Archaeologists from the University of Leicester, supported by Hallaton Fieldwork Group volunteers, have uncovered 11 skeletons—radiocarbon-dated to the 14th century—beneath the site of a “lost” medieval chapel, identified as the Chapel of St Morrell near Hallaton, Leicestershire. Among the remains are a striking pair of a man and a woman found holding hands, apparently interred together and of similar age. The team speculates the chapel may have served as a special burial or pilgrimage site, since a perfectly serviceable parish church exists in the village; silver pennies dated between the 12th and 16th centuries and evidence of pilgrim activity support this. Some burials showed stones placed over the bodies, a practice associated with preventing the dead from rising. Notable individual finds include an older male with a lethal head wound consistent with a sharp implement such as a poleaxe, and a young male buried with legs drawn up—possibly indicating disease. Roman remains beneath the chapel indicate the hilltop was a significant place for over 2,000 years, bridging Roman and medieval use. The skeletons have been taken to the university for further study, and researchers hope to fill gaps in the site’s history uncovered through local historian-led geophysical surveys.

In 1925, Philadelphia teen Thomas Curry—sent to Florida’s notorious Arthur G. Dozier School for Boys—was declared dead under vague circumstances: a Florida coroner cited a “wound on the forehead: skull crushed from an unknown cause.” Family members believed his coffin, returned to Philadelphia and buried in an unmarked plot with his great-grandparents at St. Bridget’s, contained his remains for nearly 90 years. After a 2009 investigation revealed systematic abuse, disappearances and a makeshift cemetery at Dozier, University of South Florida forensic anthropologist Dr. Erin Kimmerle led excavations that located dozens more graves than the state had recorded. Her team has exhumed many bodies from the Marianna campus to identify victims and provide answers to families; some remains have been matched by DNA, revealing a history of beatings, exposure, shootings and other violent deaths with no prosecutions.

This summer, Pennsylvania authorities and Kimmerle’s team obtained court approval to exhume Curry’s casket in Philadelphia to resolve conflicting records—Dozier ledgers and an Old Cathedral death certificate variously listed his death as due to being hit by a train or a crushed skull. After carefully uncovering the crate, investigators found no human remains—only layered wood, a small cross, a tattered bow and thumbscrews similar to artifacts recovered in Florida graves. The next nameplate belonged to Curry’s great-grandmother below, confirming the empty coffin had been buried above her. The discovery suggests deception or error in how Dozier handled deaths and returns to families, raising new questions: Was Curry buried at Dozier, shipped back empty, or removed later? With DNA from distant relatives now available, Kimmerle plans to test Florida remains for a match. Though the exhumation yielded no definitive answers about Curry’s fate, it underscored decades of cover-ups and deepened the push to identify and properly bury the many boys who died under Dozier’s troubling legacy.

A federal judge in Los Angeles has ordered a 90-day stay in Stormy Daniels’s civil lawsuit challenging a nondisclosure agreement with President Trump’s former personal lawyer, Michael Cohen, finding it likely Cohen will be indicted in a related criminal investigation. U.S. District Judge S. James Otero granted the stay after Cohen invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination in the lawsuit, citing an ongoing federal probe in New York into his role in suppressing stories about Donald Trump during the 2016 campaign. Cohen’s Manhattan office, home and hotel room were searched by the FBI in April.

Otero concluded the civil dispute overlaps substantially with the criminal inquiry, which he described as “no simple criminal investigation” because it targets the personal attorney of a sitting president and may involve documents subject to attorney‑client privilege. The judge said the unique circumstances and the apparent likelihood of an indictment warranted pausing the civil case to avoid forcing Cohen into testimony or document production that could be incriminating.

Daniels—whose legal name is Stephanie Clifford—contends she had an affair with Trump in 2006 and seeks to void a pre‑election deal under which Cohen paid her $130,000 for her silence, money Cohen says he provided using a home‑equity line of credit and that he “facilitated.” Her suit names Trump and Essential Consultants, an LLC Cohen used for the payment; Cohen was later added as a defendant.

Daniels’s attorney, Michael Avenatti, said he planned to appeal the stay to the Ninth Circuit, calling the postponement unjust. Trump has since acknowledged Cohen represented him in the payment arrangement and defended Cohen’s actions, asserting no campaign funds were used. It is not uncommon for civil proceedings to be paused when related criminal investigations risk forcing self-incriminating disclosures.

Walmart is selling Chased by an Elephant, the children’s book by Janice Barrett Graham, at more than 100 stores in the Intermountain West, prompting concern that the retailer is promoting anti-LGBTQ messages and ex-gay ideology. Janice Graham, wife of Standard of Liberty president Stephen Graham, wrote the book to warn children and parents about what she calls “today’s stampeding sexuality,” addressing gender roles, chastity, and labeling pornography, promiscuity and homosexuality as rising “sexual sins.” The book and its promotion align with Standard of Liberty and S.A. Lifeline Foundation messaging that frames recovery from sexual “deviance” as possible through family support, counseling, repentance and faith. The Grahams also spotlight their son Andrew, an “ex-gay” who authored Captain of My Soul and claims he changed his sexual orientation through counseling and religion. Critics view these publications as endorsing discredited conversion therapy ideas and as harmful to LGBTQ people and youth.

A 7-year-old boy who was accidentally shot in the head Monday after a sibling found a loaded semi-automatic pistol in their mother’s purse has died, Crossville police confirmed. The children—four total—were left unattended in a vehicle outside a Verizon store while their mother and stepfather went inside to pay a bill. Authorities say one child attempted to remove the gun’s magazine, the firearm discharged and struck the boy in the head. Emergency responders transported him by helicopter to a Knoxville-area trauma hospital, where his condition was initially described as serious; police later announced his death about 8:45 p.m. The Cumberland County District Attorney General’s Office and the Tennessee Department of Children’s Services are investigating. The family was visiting from White County; names and ages of the other children were not released. A Verizon spokesperson declined comment.

At Drew Peterson’s murder trial, friends of his third wife, Kathleen Savio, delivered emotional testimony recounting prior threats and attacks by Peterson that prosecutors say show motive and intent. Mary Parks testified that Savio told her Peterson once grabbed her by the neck, showed bruises, and said, “Why don’t you just die?” Parks also said Savio reported Peterson had told her he “could kill her and make her disappear.” Kristen Anderson testified Savio kept a knife under her mattress for protection and described an incident in which Peterson reportedly broke in, donned SWAT gear and held a knife to Savio’s throat. Savio’s 2004 bathtub death was originally ruled accidental; her body was exhumed after Peterson’s fourth wife Stacy vanished in 2007. Judge James Burmila has allowed hearsay testimony under Illinois law, a key development because little physical evidence links Peterson to Savio’s death. The defense disputes the reliability of the witnesses and plans appeals if convicted.

Graphic 911 recordings released by the Fort Bend County Sheriff’s Office recount the final, chaotic minutes before a Katy, Texas mother fatally shot her two daughters and was killed by police. Authorities say 42-year-old Christy Byrd Sheats called a family meeting on June 24, then produced a handgun during an argument. Her husband, 45-year-old Jason Sheats, and daughters Madison, 17, and Taylor, 22, beg her to stop in frantic phone recordings. On one call, Jason pleads, “Please don’t point that gun at us… I promise you, whatever you want…” before the line cuts out. Madison’s call captures shouting and pleas; Taylor’s call contains screams and indistinct cries. A neighbor’s 911 call provides a close-by, second-by-second account: the neighbor witnessed Christy chase her daughters into the street, stand over them and attempt to fire more shots, then return inside to reload and shoot again. Madison was killed at the scene; Taylor, who had been set to marry days later, was mortally wounded and died at a hospital. Officers arrived as Christy fired a final round; a Fulshear police officer shot and killed her after she refused commands to drop the weapon. Investigators reported the couple had marital problems and Sheriff Troy Nehls said Christy sought “to punish her husband.” Friends and acquaintances told media Christy had a history of mental illness and prior hospitalizations. Records show deputies had responded to the family home 14 times over four years for various calls, including multiple suicide attempts. The weapon used was reported to be a family heirloom pistol allegedly unknown to Jason. The tragedy has left friends and relatives planning separate memorials for the sisters and their mother and has prompted renewed attention to the family’s history of mental-health crises.

Early Wednesday near Decatur in Meigs County, Tenn., a confrontation over an allegedly stolen fighting rooster ended in a deadly shootout. Timothy Dewayne Johnson, 52, was found fatally shot in the driveway of a Moore Cemetery Road mobile home after arriving around 2 a.m. to accuse his nephew, 28-year-old Larry Eugene Johnson Jr., of taking the prized gamecock “Bubba.” Larry, found inside the trailer with a serious chest wound, told bystanders his uncle drew a gun and he was shot while trying to grab it; he then returned fire multiple times with a 17-round semi-automatic pistol. Investigators estimate at least 11 shots were fired; Timothy was struck four times and carried a single-action .38 and a loaded .22. The rooster was unharmed and tied to a chair outside. Larry was airlifted to a Knoxville hospital and listed stable. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation assisted local authorities; the district attorney said autopsy, toxicology and a completed investigative file will be presented to the Meigs County grand jury in November.

Seventeen-year-old Kendrick Johnson was found dead in January, wedged face-down in a rolled-up gym mat at Lowndes County High School. State examiners ruled the death accidental, concluding he suffocated while reaching for a sneaker. His parents never accepted that finding and gained a court order to exhume the body for a private autopsy in June. The family’s pathologist, Dr. Bill Anderson, reported that major organs from the pelvis to the skull — brain, heart, lungs, liver and other viscera — were missing when he opened the remains. Newspaper and department-store circulars had been packed into the body cavity and skull before burial. Funeral-home owner Antonio Harrington told the family’s attorney his firm never received the organs, claiming they had been “destroyed through natural process” and discarded by the prosector; the Georgia Bureau of Investigation maintains the organs were returned after the state autopsy. Independent forensic experts called stuffing a body with newsprint inconsistent with standard practice. Anderson also identified a blow to the right side of Kendrick’s neck “consistent with inflicted injury” and concluded death was from apparent non-accidental blunt force trauma. Death-scene photos and video, and questions about evidence handling, led a former FBI agent to suspect foul play. Local law enforcement calls the case closed; the Justice Department declined a civil-rights probe but federal prosecutors in southern Georgia are reviewing material to decide whether to open an investigation. The family insists Kendrick was murdered and continues to press for answers.

Authorities in Reno-Sparks, Nevada, found paranormal investigators Mark and Debby Constantino dead inside their adult daughter’s barricaded apartment after an hours-long standoff. The couple, who had appeared on Travel Channel’s Ghost Adventures and lectured at paranormal conferences, were discovered Tuesday when a SWAT team forced entry into the Sparks apartment near Sparks High School. The incident followed an earlier discovery at 6:30 a.m. of a man dead in a northwest Reno residence where Debby had been living; police say Mark Constantino was a suspect in that death. Officers tracked Debby’s cellphone to the Sparks apartment and, when they approached, heard gunfire and a man yelling threats. Negotiators reported the suspect demanded time to “gather my thoughts” and threatened to kill her. Police used explosives to breach the apartment door; one officer was injured by broken glass and treated at a hospital. Sparks police said no law enforcement fired on the subjects. Officials have not released causes of death or identified the male roommate found earlier. Washoe County court records indicate Debby had recently obtained a restraining order against her estranged husband, and the couple had an ongoing divorce case scheduled for December. Investigations remain active and authorities have not ruled out additional possibilities.

A Texas man suspected of fatally shooting a state trooper during a traffic stop was captured more than 100 miles from the scene, authorities said. The Harris County Sheriff’s Office announced the apprehension on Thursday night in neighboring Waller County. The Texas Department of Public Safety and other agencies identified the suspect as 32-year-old Dabrett Black of Linsdale, Texas. DPS said the trooper was shot with a rifle and killed before 4 p.m. Thursday during a traffic stop on Interstate 45 near Fairfield, about 90 miles south of Dallas; the trooper died at the scene. The trooper’s identity has not been released. After the shooting, the suspect fled. Hours later, Waller County deputies spotted the suspect’s vehicle in Hempstead, roughly 110 miles from the shooting location. The sheriff’s office posted that shots were fired during the encounter but did not specify who fired. Black was taken into custody shortly thereafter. Authorities noted a prior July report by KYTX-TV that Black had been charged previously with evading arrest, reckless driving and aggravated assault on a public servant after a Smith County chase. The trooper’s death prompted reactions from Texas officials: U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz sent prayers to the trooper’s family, and Gov. Greg Abbott condemned the killing as a “heinous crime” and offered his sincere condolences to the family.

Chris Brown has spoken with NYPD detectives about a bar fight that left a gash on his chin; police say he is treated as a witness and victim, not a suspect. His attorney Mark Geragos reportedly gave the NYPD "physical evidence" alleging Drake and Meek Mill were the aggressors, though Drake is said to be cooperating and not currently a suspect. Sources suggest someone in Chris Brown’s entourage may have provoked Drake’s party, and both Brown and Drake had been trash-talking each other earlier. Separately, Rihanna is juggling recording her seventh album, film roles and touring plans, was hospitalized for fatigue after the Met Ball, and says her busy schedule caused weight loss she dislikes.

Jim Carrey is embroiled in a contentious wrongful-death lawsuit brought by the mother and estranged husband of his former girlfriend, Cathriona White, who died by suicide in 2015 shortly after splitting with the actor. Plaintiffs allege Carrey supplied drugs that led to her death and say she became distraught after contracting herpes they claim she received from him. Carrey and his attorney vigorously deny these allegations and have countered with detailed accusations that White attempted to extort him before her death by fabricating evidence that he gave her an STD.

According to court filings and statements from Carrey’s camp, White allegedly texted Carrey in 2013 about bumps on her vagina but those bumps were the result of a poor waxing, not an STD. His lawyers claim White had herpes prior to meeting him and that she and an attorney concocted a scheme using altered medical records. Carrey’s legal team asserts they possess texts in which White asked a friend to obtain medical records from Planned Parenthood and referenced needing to “work on” the layout before presenting them as her own. They say plaintiffs were offered a choice to provide genuine, non-forged medical records or admit White had multiple STDs before meeting Carrey.

Plaintiffs’ attorney Michael Avenatti calls Carrey’s allegations false and warns of possible criminal exposure for Carrey and his advisers, while insisting his clients will continue to pursue the truth. Avenatti also announced Carrey must sit for a sworn deposition in Los Angeles Superior Court, scheduled for Oct. 27, after months of delay; Carrey’s lawyer downplayed the deposition notice but confirmed it will proceed or be formally objected to. The dispute remains highly charged, combining claims of extortion, forged records, and responsibility for White’s death.

A string of brutal attacks on dogs in Los Angeles and Kern counties has shocked rescuers and officials. At least seven dogs — including a young golden retriever named Fergus and several pit bulls — were found with deep, long burns down their backs; investigators now believe a caustic chemical, possibly acid, was poured on the animals. Fergus, discovered in Lancaster with third‑degree injuries, was treated at the Animal Medical Center of Southern California; his nerves were so damaged he felt little pain, and rescuers report he remains affectionate. Other victims, such as “Crissie,” suffered gaping, bleeding wounds; at least two dogs died. The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors approved a $25,000 reward for information leading to arrest and conviction, while PETA and private donors added smaller rewards and a GoFundMe effort raised significant funds for medical care. Sheriff’s detectives and the county Department of Animal Care and Control are investigating and asking the public to report tips to listed contacts or Crime Stoppers. Authorities hope rewards and publicity will prompt witnesses to come forward and stop these cruel, potentially connected attacks.

Nechemya Weberman, a respected counselor in New York’s Satmar ultra-Orthodox community, was convicted of 59 counts of sexual abuse for repeatedly assaulting a girl who had been sent to him for religious guidance. Jurors found Weberman guilty of sustained sexual abuse of a child, endangering the welfare of a child and other charges; he faces up to 25 years on the top count and a combined maximum of 117 years, with sentencing set for Jan. 9. The accuser, who testified for four days and is now 18, said Weberman abused her from ages 12 to 15 behind his locked office door—forcing sexual acts, reenacting pornographic scenes and exploiting his authority. Prosecutors say he intimidated her and betrayed his role as confidant; defense attorneys called the allegations a revenge-driven lie and plan to appeal. The trial highlighted the insularity and strict social codes of the Williamsburg Satmar community, which discourages reporting outside authorities. The victim and supporters said she was shunned and harassed for coming forward; prosecutors charged others with attempting to bribe and intimidate her. Officials hope the verdict encourages other victims to speak out and pressures community leaders to cooperate with authorities.

U.S. officials provided a revised, more detailed account of the raid that killed Osama bin Laden, saying four of the five people shot dead — including bin Laden — were unarmed and never fired at the Navy SEALs. The operation began with a SEAL team taking small-arms fire from a guest house; they returned fire and killed the courier and the courier’s wife, the only time SEALs were actually shot at. As other teams swept the main residence, a man seen standing in the dark with a hand behind his back was shot and killed; he was unarmed. A 19-year-old son of bin Laden was also shot dead while encountered on a staircase and was unarmed. Bin Laden briefly appeared from an upper floor after hearing shots; SEALs fired but missed, he retreated to his bedroom, and commandos stormed the room. One of bin Laden’s wives lunged and was shot in the leg; a commando then fired two fatal shots at bin Laden — who, although weapons were present in the room, was unarmed when killed. The raid was described as a careful, precise clearing operation rather than a prolonged firefight. Most time after the killings was spent exploiting the site for intelligence: seizing computers, hard drives, thumb drives, DVDs and documents. The White House refused to release grisly photos of bin Laden’s body, citing concerns they would be used as propaganda and could incite violence; President Obama and senior aides said the decision was to avoid gloating. Officials said the mission was lawful as an act of self-defense and had been a kill-or-capture operation; SEALs were prepared to take him alive if he surrendered. The operation’s revelations prompted scrutiny of Pakistan’s role and generated debate in Congress over releasing photographic proof, balanced against security risks to U.S. forces.

A Los Angeles lawsuit and multiple recent allegations have intensified scrutiny of Bill Cosby. Attorney Marc Strecker, representing Judy Huth, filed a sworn declaration saying he interviewed two witnesses who corroborate Huth’s account that Cosby sexually abused her at the Playboy Mansion in the mid-1970s when she was 15. Strecker also reviewed photographs showing Huth with Cosby at the mansion. Huth’s suit says she and a 16-year-old friend met Cosby at a film shoot, were given alcohol, then taken to the Playboy Mansion where the abuse occurred. Strecker included a clinical psychologist’s declaration that there is a reasonable basis to believe Huth suffered childhood sexual abuse; that statement does not name Cosby. Los Angeles police are investigating Huth’s allegation. Cosby’s attorney Martin Singer has sought dismissal, called the suit extortion, and questioned Huth’s credibility, noting she allegedly tried to sell her story to a tabloid a decade ago. Separately, Chloe Goins, now 24, told MailOnline she was drugged and sexually assaulted by Cosby at the Playboy Mansion in 2008—an incident she says involved waking naked with Cosby pleasuring himself and licking her toes. Goins plans to contact LAPD; her claim would fall within California’s statute of limitations. More than 20 women have publicly accused Cosby of drugging or sexually assaulting them over decades. Cosby has largely remained silent publicly; his wife defended him, and longtime associate Hugh Hefner said the allegations are saddening. Cosby’s lawyers have denied many accusations.

This document surveys quirky 19th-century death-related inventions and a modern forensic study identifying unique chemicals from human decomposition. Early patents reveal social fears: William Hanlon’s “Beheading Block and Ax” was a stage illusion mimicking a realistic guillotine trick; other inventions aimed to prevent premature burial—coffins with viewing lids, air shafts, head-bumping alert mechanisms, coffin-mounted fluid drains, improved embalming with burning sulfur, and a device to force eyelids closed. Poison bottles shaped like coffins warned users of danger. 

The forensic research, prompted by needs such as cadaver-dog training after California wildfires, tested volatile organic compounds (VOCs) produced by decomposing tissues from six humans and 26 animals in controlled jars over six months using TD-GC/MS. Researchers found 452 VOCs across many chemical classes. Principal component analysis identified eight compounds (including ethyl/propyl propionate, propyl butyrate, ethyl pentanoate, pyridine, diethyl disulfide, methyl(methylthio)ethyl disulfide, and 3‑methylthio‑1‑propanol) that grouped human and pig remains apart from other animals, and five esters that distinguished humans from pigs. Esters arise from fat and muscle breakdown; sulfur- and nitrogen-containing compounds also contributed to separation but were less consistently human-specific. Limitations include jar-based partial tissues, frozen samples, and lab conditions differing from field decomposition. The authors recommend field validation with whole bodies and dog-testing; success could improve cadaver-dog training and lead to electronic detectors for locating human remains.

Autopsy reports released by the Medical Examiner’s Office detail brutal killings of Christina “Tina” Anderson, 44, and her 8‑year‑old son, Ethan, whose bodies were found last month on the property of family friend James DiMaggio in Boulevard. Investigators say DiMaggio killed both victims, abducted Christina’s 16‑year‑old daughter Hannah, then remotely set incendiary devices at his house and detached garage. Christina’s autopsy found blunt‑force trauma to the head with at least 12 impact sites, a nearby crowbar, ankles bound with a plastic cable tie, duct tape around her neck and mouth, abrasions and lacerations on her right arm and left leg, a fractured right arm, and an incision wound on the neck likely inflicted postmortem. Her body and the family dog, which had been shot, were located in the garage; firefighters extinguished that blaze on Aug. 4. Ethan’s remains were recovered from the fully engulfed two‑story house; his body was so badly burned he required DNA identification, using his father Brett Anderson’s DNA. The autopsy states the child most likely died from the fire but notes skeletal fractures and that trauma cannot be ruled out. DiMaggio, 40, was shot and killed by FBI agents in Idaho on Aug. 10 after Hannah was rescued; sheriff’s homicide Lt. Glenn Giannantonio said officials declined further comment and will not release additional investigative information.

Staff Sgt. Robert Bales, a 38-year-old career soldier with multiple combat tours and decorated service, was accused of leaving his outpost in Kandahar on March 11 and killing 16 Afghan civilians, including nine children. He was flown to the U.S. and is held at Fort Leavenworth pending likely charges; he could face the death penalty. Neighbors in Lake Tapps, Washington, described Bales as a quiet, devoted husband and father who played with his young children and was respected as a soldier. His platoon leader praised him as “one of the best soldiers” who saved lives. Bales’s attorney and others have cited prior combat trauma, a past head injury, and PTSD as possible factors; the lawyer also said Bales had witnessed a comrade’s leg being blown off hours before the killings. Court records disclose earlier troubles: a 2002 misdemeanor assault on a girlfriend that led to anger-management, a 2005 reported DUI for which he was not charged, and a 2008 single-vehicle rollover/hit-and-run that was dismissed after fines and restitution. His wife’s blog revealed frustration over a failed promotion and desire to relocate. The massacre has strained U.S.-Afghan relations, prompted Afghan demands for local trial, and sparked debate over combat stress, veteran stigma, leadership, and how the military screens and supports deployed troops.

Authorities in York County, South Carolina, charged Lana Sue Clayton, 52, with murder and malicious tampering after investigators say she confessed to poisoning her husband, 64-year-old Steven Clayton, by putting tetrahydrozoline—found in over-the-counter eye drops—into his water over a three-day period ending July 21. Steven was found dead in their Lake Wylie home; an autopsy and toxicology report revealed high levels of the chemical. Arrest warrants and deputies did not disclose a motive. Lana, who worked as a VA nurse in Charlotte, had no prior local criminal record. She remains jailed without bond; it’s unclear if she has legal representation. Community members expressed shock.

Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, shot in the head less than two weeks earlier, has made remarkable early progress and is leaving Tucson for specialized, intensive rehabilitation in Houston. Doctors say she can stand with assistance, has given her husband a neck massage, and has attempted speech, but warn the coming rehab will be arduous and prolonged. At TIRR Memorial Hermann she will undergo hours daily of speech, occupational and physical therapy to rebuild motor skills, language and other functions affected by the bullet wound through the left side of her brain. Physicians caution recovery timelines are uncertain: while her husband, astronaut Mark Kelly, optimistically predicted she might walk within two months, clinicians say outcomes vary and full recovery may not occur. Risks during rehab include seizures from overstimulation, weight loss, depression and the need for later skull reconstruction after initial decompression surgery. Experts note favorable factors—Giffords’ age, intelligence and strong family support—improve her chances, but emphasize the long, demanding road ahead.

For years, dozens of Midwestern teenage boys endured anonymous torment from Anton Martynenko, a 32-year-old from Eagan, Minn., who used fake social media profiles to coerce and extort nude images and sexual activity from more than 155 mostly 14-to-16-year-old high school athletes. On Tuesday in St. Paul federal court, Martynenko was sentenced to 38 years in prison after pleading guilty in January to charges tied to the largest child-pornography production case ever prosecuted in Minnesota. Victims described long-lasting harm: public shaming when images were posted and shared, threats, intense anxiety, and in at least two cases, subsequent suicides. Several victims who addressed the court recounted being lured by fabricated personas—often posed as attractive young women—or by faux offers of modeling jobs or payment for sex. Martynenko sometimes pressured boys into sexual acts and organized meticulous “target lists” and folders cataloging victims by name, school, age and other details. Prosecutors called him a “tenacious predator” who persisted despite interactions with law enforcement. During sentencing, the judge credited Martynenko with two years for providing investigators with notes from conversations he had as a jail cellmate of Danny Heinrich, the suspect in the Jacob Wetterling case; prosecutors maintain his assistance did not materially solve that case. A forensic psychologist testified Martynenko may benefit from intensive psychosexual treatment, though chat logs show he took pleasure in exposing victims. Martynenko apologized in court, attributing actions to his own depression and addiction, while his mother sought more treatment-focused consequences. Prosecutors and victims stressed the broader lesson about internet safety and the severe, lasting damage sextortion can inflict on young lives.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll found more than half of Americans favor deporting most or all of the estimated 11 million undocumented immigrants, revealing public resistance that complicates current congressional immigration reform efforts. The online survey of 1,443 adults showed 30% favor deporting most with exceptions, 23% want all deported, while only 5% would allow all to stay legally and 31% want most to remain. Views are sharply divided by party: 75% of Republicans versus 40% of Democrats support deporting most or all. Meanwhile, a bipartisan group of eight senators is crafting a major overhaul that would create a path to citizenship contingent on fines, taxes and increased border security. Separately, lawmakers are considering requiring a biometric or high-tech ID for all workers to verify employment eligibility, a proposal raising privacy, cost and civil-liberties concerns. Proponents say it would curb fraud and illegal work; critics warn it could become a de facto national ID and pose large costs and privacy risks.

Jason Garnett, a 23-year-old hotel worker from Harrogate, England, experienced a frightening and painful medical emergency when an erection he woke up with after sex would not subside. What began as a puzzling “morning glory” became a prolonged ordeal: the erection persisted for about 17 hours. Initially unalarmed, Garnett tried home remedies including an ice bath and a jog, but by lunchtime he grew concerned. After eight hours he confided in a flatmate and was taken to the local hospital, where clinicians diagnosed priapism — a rare, non-sexual medical condition in which blood becomes trapped in the penis and cannot drain. Priapism is considered an emergency because prolonged cases can cause permanent damage.

At hospital, doctors drained more than two pints (over 1.1 liters) of blood from Garnett’s penis to relieve pressure. When aspiration alone did not fully resolve the problem, they administered injections directly to restrict blood flow — reportedly 24 injections — until the erection subsided. Garnett described the treatment as excruciating, likening the pain to “10 out of 10” and the experience to a horror film. Following treatment, he said function had returned to normal, though the penis was bruised and “looked like it’s been through a war.” The case highlights priapism’s danger and the need for immediate medical attention to avoid lasting injury.

A suicide bomber on a motorcycle killed Abdul Latif Ashna, deputy governor of Kandahar province, and wounded three bodyguards as Ashna was driven to work, the Interior Ministry said. The Taliban claimed responsibility; a senior intelligence official attributed the attack to the Haqqani network. The killing heightens fears insurgents are renewing a campaign of assassinations that previously terrorized Kandahar, the Taliban’s southern heartland. President Hamid Karzai, U.S. Ambassador Karl Eikenberry and NATO condemned the strike. The attack underscores challenges to recent security gains after a troop surge and special-operations pressure on insurgent leadership, and threatens efforts to stabilize Kandahar and strengthen Afghan governance.

A 30-minute Facebook Live video showing the brutal assault and racial taunting of an 18-year-old man with special needs led to the arrest and charging of four suspects in Chicago. The video depicts the victim tied, gagged, beaten, kicked, and verbally abused while the attackers, who are Black, shout profanities about white people and President-elect Donald Trump; at one point someone cuts his scalp, leaving a bald patch, and police are reviewing another clip that allegedly shows the victim forced to drink toilet water. The victim — from Crystal Lake and described by police as having mental health challenges — had been reported missing after being dropped off at a McDonald’s to meet a friend; investigators say he knew at least one suspect from school. Authorities allege the victim was taken in a stolen van, held for hours, and may have been with the suspects for at least 24 hours; his parents reportedly received texts claiming he was being held captive. Chicago police found the disoriented, bloodied teen wandering a West Side street and later tied the people arrested to the video and scene. Four people — Jordan Hill, Tesfaye Cooper, Brittany Covington and Tanishia Covington — were charged with aggravated kidnapping, hate crime, unlawful restraint and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon; additional burglary, robbery and stolen-vehicle counts were filed against some. Police and prosecutors considered hate-crime charges based on the victim’s vulnerability, the binding, and the racist statements, though officials said they had no definitive evidence the attack was politically motivated. Facebook removed the original livestream, citing policies against glorifying crimes. Community leaders, the victim’s family and national figures condemned the attack; the teen is back home and expected to recover physically while coping with lasting trauma.

Amal Ahmad Abdul Fateh, a 30-year-old widow of Osama bin Laden, has given Pakistani investigators a detailed, if imperfect, account of the family’s movements during the nine years Bin Laden spent hiding in Pakistan after 2001. Her police statement describes marriages and births, repeated relocations, and help from Pakistani hosts. Fateh said she married bin Laden in 2000, joined him in Afghanistan, then fled after Sept. 11. They moved across Pakistan’s north: Karachi, Shangla in Swat (eight–nine months), Haripur (about two years) — where two children were born in a government hospital using false papers — and finally Abbottabad in 2005, where two more children were born. She identified two Pashtun brothers, Ibrahim and Abrar, as hosts; Ibrahim is believed to be the courier known to U.S. intelligence. During the May 2011 U.S. raid on the Abbottabad compound, bin Laden was killed; Fateh was wounded and survived while four others died. The three widows and two adult daughters face Pakistani immigration charges; authorities hold the women under house arrest amid interest from Pakistani and U.S. investigators.

Michael Whalen, a Virginia Beach man who says he shared 15 years with his dog Allie, is facing animal cruelty and related charges after Allie was found partially buried near the Oceanfront in February. Whalen told local news outlets that Allie, diagnosed with Cushing’s disease over a year earlier, had been his close companion and had been managed on medication. He said a veterinarian had offered to euthanize her previously but both weren’t ready. One early morning in February, Allie began having severe, uncontrollable seizures; Whalen says she was at risk of aspirating vomit and could not be helped in time. He told reporters he shot her, believing a handgun would provide a painless, instantaneous end to her suffering, then buried her at the 85th Street beach. A resident discovered the partially buried dog, prompting police involvement. Authorities charged Whalen with animal cruelty and burying trash. Local veterinarians responding to the case said a gunshot is not considered an acceptable or humane method of euthanasia under current guidelines, while Whalen’s attorney argues his client acted out of duty and compassion to end the dog’s suffering. Whalen has pleaded his intent to set the record straight and hopes the pending June court date will highlight euthanasia issues for pet owners. The case has sparked debate about humane euthanasia standards and legal responsibilities when animals are in distress.

Bangladesh’s anti-terror Rapid Action Battalion arrested Farabi Shafiur Rahman, the prime suspect in the machete murder of U.S.-Bangladeshi blogger Avijit Roy in Dhaka. Rahman, detained at a bus stop, previously had ties to Islamist group Hizbut Tahrir and was jailed in 2013 over social media posts endorsing violence against secular bloggers before being released on bail. Authorities say he threatened Roy repeatedly online, urged his killing, and allegedly posted crime-scene photos minutes after the attack. Roy’s wife and fellow blogger Rafida Ahmed were injured. The killing highlights rising threats to critics of religious extremism amid a wider crackdown.

A Japanese woman staying in Kolkata alleges she was lured, abducted and repeatedly raped by a group who posed as guides and held her captive for weeks in eastern India. According to police, she met a man who spoke Japanese on November 20 in Kolkata; he took her to other locations including Digha and then to Gaya in Bihar, where two brothers, Zahir and Shahid, and additional accomplices detained her near Bodh Gaya, a major Buddhist pilgrimage site. While captive she was reportedly gang‑raped multiple times and had about Rs 76,000 taken from her account. She escaped or was released on December 26, reached Varanasi, contacted friends and the Japanese consulate, and then returned to Kolkata to file a complaint. A joint Kolkata–Gaya police operation has arrested between three and five suspects so far, including the two brothers; investigations continue and police seek further suspects. The case has drawn attention amid ongoing national concern over sexual violence in India and past legal reforms meant to strengthen penalties and police accountability.

Manchester police arrested a Windsor husband and wife after a Saturday night fight over crab legs at Royal Buffet, 410 West Middle Turnpike. Authorities say the disagreement escalated around 8 p.m. into a physical altercation in which a 21‑year‑old man was punched, suffering a cut lip and a broken front tooth. The injured man’s mother intervened and used pepper spray on the assailants; police say her actions were self‑defense and she faces no charges. Clifford (Cliff) Knight, 45 or 46, was charged with third‑degree assault and disorderly conduct; his wife, Lataya (Latoya) Knight, 38, was charged with disorderly conduct and threatening. Both were released on non‑surety bonds—Clifford on $5,000 and Lataya on $2,500—and are due in court on April 14. The Manchester Fire Department ventilated the restaurant after pepper spray was deployed, and the Health Department temporarily closed the buffet to assess air quality; the restaurant reported it reopened the following day. An earlier report misidentified the victim’s age; police later confirmed he is a young adult.

Decades-old DNA evidence led to the arrest of two men in connection with the 1973 shotgun slayings of two Northern California girls, authorities announced. Doris Karen Derryberry, 13, and Valerie Janice Lane, 12, were reported missing Nov. 12, 1973, after a shopping trip; their bodies were found hours later alongside a dirt road in a wooded area near Marysville, shot at close range. Semen preserved from Derryberry’s body was retested in 2014 using modern forensic methods, producing DNA profiles that matched cousins William Lloyd Harbour and Larry Don Patterson. Both men, now 65, were 22 at the time of the murders and living in Olivehurst, the small Central Valley town where the victims lived. Harbour, with felony drug convictions, was arrested near his home in Olivehurst after a traffic stop; Patterson, who had a 1976 rape conviction and later failed to register as a sex offender, was located and arrested in Oklahoma after a multi-state search aided by U.S. Marshals. Investigators had conducted more than 60 interviews in the 1970s before the case went cold in 1976; evidence was meticulously preserved and ultimately yielded the DNA matches. Yuba County officials informed the victims’ families, who have asked for privacy after decades of grief. Both men face murder charges; Patterson awaits extradition to California.

India has formally complained to Saudi authorities after a 58-year-old Indian domestic worker, Kasturi (Kasthuri) Munirathinam, was allegedly mutilated by her employer in Riyadh. According to her family and media reports, Munirathinam’s right arm was chopped off when she tried to escape from the household where she had worked for about three months. The family says she had been subjected to prolonged mistreatment—denied proper food, forced to work long hours, barred from phone contact, and not paid—and that her employers became enraged after she complained of the abuse to police. Munirathinam was hospitalized in Riyadh and is reported to be in serious condition; her sister also said her spinal cord was injured. The family learned of the attack on 30 September through the recruitment agents and say they received a mobile video message from Kasturi. New Delhi’s foreign ministry, including Foreign Minister Sushma Swaraj and spokesperson Vikas Swarup, expressed shock, said the embassy in Riyadh is in touch with the victim, and has asked Saudi authorities for a strict, independent probe and prosecution—including seeking a charge of attempted murder and severe punishment for the sponsor if found guilty. The family has requested help paying medical bills and securing Kasturi’s return to India; Tamil Nadu state authorities were also asked for assistance. The case has raised broader concerns about the abuse of migrant domestic workers in the Middle East. Saudi officials had not publicly commented at the time of reports.

A Baltimore man, 30-year-old Mark Ramiro, was arrested and charged with first- and second-degree murder plus weapons violations after fatally shooting 28-year-old Darnell Mitchell during a basem ent stunt to test a bulletproof vest. The incident, recorded on a Cannon E07 camera by a third person, shows Mitchell wearing the vest and boasting he was about to take a “deuce deuce in the chest” — a .22-caliber shot — before Ramiro fired once. The bullet struck Mitchell above the vest; he collapsed and was driven to the University of Maryland Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. Investigators identified Ramiro by clothing and tattoos in the video. Prosecutors sought second-degree charges; a court commissioner also added first-degree murder. Detectives are trying to identify the third person who filmed the shooting.
