During a tense CNN interview, Donald Trump aide Michael Cohen repeatedly challenged host Brianna Keilar when she said Trump’s campaign was “down” in the polls, replying incredulously, “Says who?” The exchange highlighted Cohen’s refusal to acknowledge widespread polling that showed Hillary Clinton leading in key swing states. Keilar responded that “polls — most of them, all of them” showed Trump trailing; Cohen pressed, “OK, which polls?” before pivoting to defend recent staffing changes. The segment followed news of a campaign shake-up that brought Steve Bannon in as CEO and Kellyanne Conway in as campaign manager, moves presented by Cohen as strategic additions rather than an admission of trouble. Cohen also made an awkward comment, saying the Republican nominee knew about the “African American problem” in the US, later clarifying he meant problems within the African American community and insisting Trump is “colourblind.” The exchange sparked the social media hashtag #SaysWho, with users mocking Cohen’s repeated question and flooding his and others’ feeds with the phrase.

An Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) warning follows an incident on February 19 in which a woman traveling from Beijing to Melbourne suffered burns when her battery-powered headphones exploded mid-flight. About two hours into the journey she fell asleep listening to music and woke to a loud explosion and burning on her face. She tore the headphones off as they sparked and produced small flames, then threw them onto the cabin floor. Flight attendants quickly doused the device with water and placed it in a bucket at the rear of the aircraft, but the battery and outer cover had melted and fused to the cabin floor. Photographs released by the ATSB show singed hair and eyebrows and black soot on the passenger; she also reported burns to her hands. Passengers endured the lingering smell of melted plastic, burnt electronics and singed hair and many were coughing and choking for the remainder of the flight.

The ATSB said the most likely cause was the device’s battery catching fire rather than the headphones themselves, but declined to disclose the brand. Authorities highlighted that as more portable devices rely on batteries, the risk of in-flight battery incidents is growing. Lithium-ion batteries, common in phones and portable electronics, contain flammable liquid and can explode if they short-circuit; causes include manufacturing defects, damage, overheating or overcharging. Regulators reiterated safety guidance: stow active battery-powered devices appropriately when not in use; keep spare batteries and power banks in carry-on baggage (not checked luggage); protect battery terminals; and alert cabin crew if a device is trapped in seat mechanisms rather than moving powered seats, which could crush a device and trigger a fire. The event follows past high-profile battery fires, including Galaxy Note 7 recalls and other aircraft incidents involving phones and portable power packs.

Photographer Muhammad Malik encountered the immediate aftermath of a deadly shooting near the Empire State Building while exiting the subway and quickly posted an image of one victim bleeding on the pavement to Instagram, pairing it with a quotation from rapper Nas. He also posted on Facebook with the words “MAN DOWN! SHOTS FIRED!” The provocative posts drew rapid attention: reporters and news organizations began contacting him nationwide for permission to use the image, which Malik initially celebrated online, remarking that callers were “making major deals! #chaching.” When Daily Intel later reached him to ask about licensing or a fee, Malik’s tone shifted; he said he was offering the photo free of charge and that the events of the morning had affected him deeply, making any commercial considerations secondary. He defended his postings against accusations of being offensive. The brief account highlights tensions between sensational social-media sharing, journalistic demand for immediate visual material after traumatic events, and the personal toll on bystanders who capture and distribute disturbing images in real time.

Xavier Jajuan Davis, a Grand Rapids man with prior convictions including a 2012 attempted home invasion and multiple window‑peeping convictions, has been at the center of two separate, high‑profile criminal matters and has filed a federal civil suit alleging serious misconduct by Grand Rapids police. Recently arraigned on three criminal sexual conduct charges—second‑degree for an Oct. 25 incident at DeVos Place and two counts of first‑degree for a Dec. 28 incident on Oak Park Drive—Davis was held on $400,000 bond after tips from a police composite sketch led to his arrest. Details of the alleged assaults were not publicly released, and a probable cause hearing was set for Jan. 30.

Separately, Davis says he was wrongfully arrested and jailed for 129 days in 2018 on sexual assault allegations that were later dropped when DNA, phone and Uber records eliminated him as a suspect. In a 24‑page federal complaint filed against the City of Grand Rapids and three investigators, Davis alleges unlawful imprisonment, malicious prosecution, defamation and intentional infliction of emotional distress. He claims police targeted him based on a sketch that poorly resembled him, pressured victims during identification, and failed to act on exculpatory evidence they possessed by March—evidence that would have demonstrated his innocence. He also contends police obtained his DNA and that investigators coerced victim statements.

While jailed he was assaulted and placed in protective custody; he lost employment at DeVos Place and The B.O.B., was evicted, and spent time in a homeless shelter. Charges tied to the gunpoint December assault and an unrelated sex‑assault charge were ultimately dismissed ahead of trial, with the Kent County prosecutor citing witness issues and lack of DNA match. Davis seeks damages; the city had not been served at the time of reporting. The case raises questions about investigative practices, reliance on victim identifications and the handling of exculpatory evidence.

Mary Jane Lane, 50, of Balch Springs, Texas, was arrested after an April incident in Dallas in which police say she passed out at a red light and then ran over her husband. According to the Dallas Police report, Lane stopped at Northwest Highway and Ferndale while driving west with her husband, Randall, in the passenger seat. When she lost consciousness, Randall exited the SUV, opened the driver’s door and reached in to unbuckle her seat belt. Lane “came to,” accelerated, snagging and dragging him until he fell, suffering head injuries and fractures to both legs. Officers later located Lane a couple of miles away, blocking traffic with the engine off; they reported signs of intoxication. She was initially charged with intoxication assault and leaving the scene, but charges were downgraded to driving while intoxicated. Lane is held in Dallas County Jail on $20,000 bond; her husband’s current condition has not been reported.

Researchers Michael Kasumovic and Jeffrey Kuznekoff analyzed player interactions during 163 matches of Halo 3 to investigate what drives male hostility toward women online. Using prerecorded neutral phrases voiced by either a male or female account, they recorded and transcribed teammate responses, then coded comments as positive, negative, or neutral. They correlated those comments with players’ performance (kills, deaths) and skill level (rank). The core finding: hostility toward a female-voiced teammate was concentrated among lower-skilled, poorer-performing males. When low-status men performed badly relative to peers, they produced more negative, sexist comments directed at the female voice; by contrast, those same men tended to be submissive or conciliatory toward male-voiced teammates. Higher-skilled men, who stood to lose little from a female entrant, were more positive toward the female voice—possibly attempting support or mate attraction. The results support an evolutionary framing: male status and intra-sexual competition shape reactions to women entering a male-dominated arena. The authors argue that lower-status men may use female-directed aggression to try to minimize perceived threats to their rank and mating opportunities, while high-status men have no incentive to act that way. The study leveraged the anonymity and competitive structure of online games—conditions paralleling many real-world online spaces with skewed gender ratios—to capture authentic behavior without social desirability bias. While not prescribing fixes, the researchers suggest interventions like normalizing mixed-gender competition (e.g., through games) to reduce the perceived stigma of losing to women and potentially curb status-driven sexism.

A 14-year-old U.S.-born boy known as "El Ponchis" was arrested at an airport near Cuernavaca, Mexico, while allegedly trying to flee to Tijuana and then San Diego, authorities and media reported. Identified as Edgar, he told prosecutors he was kidnapped at age 11 and forced to work for the Cartel of the South Pacific, a Beltrán Leyva faction, and admitted—he said under threat and while drugged—to participating in at least four decapitations. Arrested with two sisters, one reportedly a 19-year-old accused of helping dump bodies and acting as a decoy, Edgar was found with cell phones containing photos of tortured victims. Reports say gangs paid youths roughly $2,500–$3,000 per killing. The case highlights a growing trend: rising numbers of minors detained for drug-related crimes since Mexico’s 2006 offensive against cartels. Authorities are verifying Edgar’s U.S. and possible Mexican citizenship and have requested federal jurisdiction due to the severity of the alleged crimes. The arrests underscore cartels’ use of increasingly younger recruits amid violent turf battles.

In Luque, a town near Paraguay’s capital Asunción, five bus drivers and one of their wives have staged a prolonged and grisly union protest by nailing their hands to wooden crosses with large nails and lying beside empty coffins. The demonstration began about 20 days ago after the drivers say they were dismissed following demands for overdue benefits — including medical insurance, overtime pay and pension contributions — and they have vowed to remain crucified until all eight fired colleagues are reinstated. Union leader and participant Juan Villalba says roughly 50 drivers for the Vanguardia bus company have long worked without full benefits; he insists the strike will not end unless the eight dismissed drivers regain their jobs with back pay and benefits. Company manager Aufredi Paredes has said five of the drivers will be rehired while the others will receive legal separation payments, but the protesters refuse partial resolutions and insist on collective reinstatement. Several drivers’ wives have taken turns joining the crucifixions; one appealed directly to Paraguay’s president to witness what she called an “inhuman situation.” The extreme tactic highlights deep labor tensions and a standoff between the union and the company over workers’ rights and compensation.

A father, Anthony Powell, 24, pleaded guilty after beating his three-year-old son, Tristan, to death over potty-training accidents; court documents say Powell struck the child multiple times and at one point lifted him like a rag doll after knocking him down. He faces a 60-year prison term. Separately, a tragic accident in Port Arthur claimed the life of 72-year-old James Rogers and his Shih Tzu, “Baby Girl” Leia. Rogers became trapped inside his recently purchased 2007 Corvette in a Waffle House parking lot when an apparent electrical malfunction—possibly an unsecured cable—caused the car to lose power, disabling electronic locks and the horn. Rogers had left his cell phone charging inside the restaurant and was unaware of the Corvette’s manual door-release on the floorboard. Witnesses and first responders found fingerprints on the window and evidence he tried to attract attention; attempts by a bystander and later firefighters to free him were unsuccessful, and both he and the dog are believed to have died of heat exhaustion. An autopsy will determine Rogers’s exact cause of death. He was a Thomas Jefferson High School graduate, a U.S. Army veteran, and is survived by three children and five grandchildren; visitation and funeral arrangements were announced.

On June 25, 2016, Fresno police officers fatally shot 19-year-old Dylan Noble at a Chevron gas station after pulling him over in response to a report of a man with a rifle. Body-camera footage released July 6–7 shows officers approaching Noble with guns drawn, shouting repeated commands to show his hands and get on the ground. Noble exited his pickup with his left hand visible and his right hand behind his back; he moved toward officers and at one point shouted, “I f—ing hate my life.” Two shots from one officer struck him, and he fell to the pavement. While Noble lay on his back and was barely moving, the same officer fired a third shot about 12 seconds later, and a different officer fired a fourth roughly 15 seconds after that. A small clear plastic object later found near his body was identified by reporters as containing malleable clay; the Justice Department is investigating the object. Police initially believed Noble might have had a gun but discovered he was unarmed.

Noble’s parents and attorneys condemned the killing, calling it excessive force and filing a civil claim alleging the officers never had an objectively reasonable basis to shoot and accusing the department of systemic civil-rights abuses. Family members who viewed the footage called for murder charges. Fresno Police Chief Jerry Dyer, who initially delayed public release citing tensions after the recent Dallas ambush of police, said the video was disturbing and that investigators would determine whether each shot was justified and if nonlethal options could have been used. The release of the footage shifted public focus from debates about racial disparities—Noble was white and his vigil briefly featured “White Lives Matter” signs—toward broader concerns about deadly force and police tactics. The incident occurred amid national outrage over other recent fatal police shootings and raised fresh questions about use of force, officers’ decision-making, and accountability in law enforcement.

Over the weekend in St. Johns County, Florida, deputies were summoned after a field marshal riding a golf cart called police on a black father coaching his 15-year-old son at a youth soccer game. Multiple bystanders recorded the encounter and posted videos and commentary to social media, prompting accusations that the marshal — nicknamed “Golfcart Gail” by witnesses — racially profiled the father for simply speaking to his child about obeying the referee. Witness Ginger Williams posted footage titled “Soccer While Black,” and another witness, Maria Morales-Walther, filmed parts of the confrontation; both said the marshal persistently urged police involvement despite the father’s efforts to de-escalate by leaving. In the videos the father repeatedly states he was addressing only his son and following sideline conduct rules; the marshal told deputies she felt threatened and had witnessed other disturbances that day. Ponte Vedra Athletic Association president Gary Easom defended staff actions, saying the call resulted from “a culmination of several immediate prior incidents,” including an earlier parent ejection for verbal abuse and another parent reprimanded for profanity. He stressed staff must protect children and may call law enforcement after warnings are ignored. St. Johns County spokesman Chuck Mulligan noted the department responds to many disturbance calls daily and, after speaking to those present, found no criminal activity and did not detain the father. The episode has been framed by many as part of a broader pattern of white individuals calling police on Black people for routine activities; it follows other viral incidents where bystanders recorded similar confrontations. The athletic association and local clubs have been contacted for comment, and the father says he wants an apology.

On a late July night in Oakland, 18-year-old high school senior Nia Wilson was fatally stabbed and her sister critically injured while boarding a BART train; 27-year-old John Lee Cowell was arrested the next day and charged with murder. The case drew immediate public grief and outrage, especially after local station KTVU broadcast a photo of Nia that appeared to show her holding a gun. The image was actually a cellphone case shaped like a gun handle, and critics said choosing that single picture from nearly 1,000 posts on her social media criminalized and demeaned the victim. Writer and activist Shaun King and many social media users condemned the decision as part of a broader pattern in which media portrayals of slain Black youth emphasize images that suggest culpability, echoing past controversies around Trayvon Martin and Michael Brown. KTVU anchor Frank Somerville issued an on-air and Facebook apology, calling the choice “a huge mistake,” but many rejected this as insufficient and argued structural newsroom change is needed. The evening after the attack, thousands attended a vigil in Oakland; members of the Proud Boys reportedly attempted to disrupt it, intensifying community pain. A GoFundMe for Wilson’s family quickly raised substantial donations as the city mourned and demanded justice.

An airport shooting at Los Angeles International Airport on Nov. 1 left Transportation Security Administration (TSA) Officer Gerardo Hernandez fatally wounded and exposed possible lapses in emergency coordination. Paul Ciancia entered Terminal 3 with an assault rifle and a note saying he wanted to “kill TSA.” He shot Hernandez and others before being shot by airport police four times and taken into custody. Police radioed that Ciancia was in custody five minutes after Hernandez was shot, yet paramedics waited roughly 150 yards away because police had not declared the terminal safe. Hernandez — about 20 feet from an exit — was not removed to an ambulance until 33 minutes after being shot. For all but five of those minutes, officials say there was no threat from the suspected gunman. Surveillance video reportedly shows no officers rendered first aid and an LAPD veteran repeatedly told passing officers “he’s dead.” Hernandez arrived at Harbor-UCLA Medical Center without signs of life and could not be revived. The delay has prompted scrutiny of interagency communication among LAPD, Los Angeles Airport Police and Fire Department, and whether faster entry could have changed outcomes. The incident underscored tensions between active-shooter tactics (prioritizing neutralizing the assailant) and immediate lifesaving care. Ciancia remains hospitalized in fair condition and faces charges that carry a potential death sentence; a public memorial honored Hernandez.

During the murder trial of Markelus Carter for the 2009 shooting death of Kenneth Warrington, a fight erupted in a courthouse holding cell after Carter was mistakenly placed with inmate witness Steven Upham during an afternoon break. Surveillance shows Carter striking first, Upham putting Carter in a headlock and punching, then Carter biting Upham; corrections officers ended the roughly two-minute altercation. Carter returned to court shaken with minor injuries. Defense attorney Jon Paul Rion sought a mistrial, but Judge Jeffrey Reed denied it and allowed the video to be shown to the jury. Upham, a former cellmate at Allen Oakwood, testified Carter confessed details of the murder; on cross-examination Upham admitted seeking early release while incarcerated but denied any deal for his testimony. The state continued presenting evidence, calling lead detective Tim Clark, with testimony to resume Friday.

NBA star Tony Parker has sued SoHo nightclub W.i.P. for $20 million over injuries he says he suffered during the widely reported brawl between entourages of Chris Brown and Drake. Filed in Manhattan Supreme Court, the suit alleges negligent security and management decisions—specifically allowing both rival camps, known to have “bad blood,” into the club and continuing to serve alcohol to visibly intoxicated patrons. Parker claims he was struck by flying glass, sustaining a corneal laceration and other injuries; he’s using a therapeutic contact lens and expects to miss at least a week, potentially affecting his Olympic preparations with France. While neither Brown nor Drake are named as defendants yet, Parker’s lawyer says that could change pending the police investigation and review of surveillance footage. The complaint argues the club effectively “threw gasoline on the flames” by selling bottle service to both sides. W.i.P. has not commented; the incident has already led to the club’s closure.

A girl who vanished at 15 more than two years ago told police she escaped a Washington Park, Illinois, home this week where she says she was held captive, repeatedly beaten and sexually assaulted. Listed as a missing or runaway juvenile by St. Louis police in April 2010, she reported that her captor raped her, impregnated her and that she gave birth after being forced to use a false name on medical records. She said the man pursued and forced her back at gunpoint on several escape attempts. With help from a relative she recently fled and alerted authorities, who deployed a 24-officer tactical team to the house. Officers recovered the infant — reportedly the result of the rape — and carried the toddler from the scene, shielding the child’s identity before transport by ambulance. A 24-year-old man and his mother were taken into custody; police say the mother likely aided the crimes. Officials had not publicly identified or charged them as of the report. Neighbors said they had occasionally seen the girl but did not suspect she was being held.

Detroit Tigers outfielder Delmon Young was arrested early this morning in Manhattan after an allegedly drunken, anti‑Semitic confrontation outside the Hilton New York. Police say the 26‑year‑old shouted a slur at four men who had spoken with a panhandler wearing a yarmulke, then pushed and tackled one man, causing minor arm injuries. Young was taken to Roosevelt Hospital for intoxication before being processed, arraigned later on an aggravated harassment misdemeanor with a hate‑crime element, and released on $5,000 bail. He issued a statement apologizing and saying he will work to “improve myself as a person and player,” while his attorney contesting some allegations and pointing to video evidence. The Tigers declined detailed comment pending legal proceedings; manager Jim Leyland adjusted the lineup for the game. Major League Baseball is unlikely to act until legal matters are resolved, though Young may be directed to the sport’s Employee Assistance Program. Young, a former No. 1 overall pick, has a past suspension for throwing a bat at an umpire in 2006.

Federal agents arrested Hunter Moore, 27, creator of the notorious revenge-porn site isanyoneup.com, and alleged hacker Charles Evens, 25, charging them in a conspiracy to steal private nude photos from email accounts and post them online. The 15-count federal indictment accuses the men of conspiracy, seven counts of unauthorized access to protected computers and seven counts of aggravated identity theft. According to prosecutors, Moore solicited explicit images originally submitted by jilted partners, but to keep the site supplied he allegedly recruited Evens to hack into victims’ email accounts; Evens reportedly was paid via PayPal—about $200 weekly, with requests for specific batches of images documented in email exchanges. The scheme allegedly began in 2011 and continued through May 2012, during which Evens is said to have accessed “hundreds of victims” and Moore posted the photos without consent. If convicted, each faces up to five years on the hacking counts plus a mandatory two-year consecutive sentence for identity theft. The case prompted calls for better online security and highlighted the harms of revenge porn: victims suffered humiliation, harassment and job threats. Prosecutors and advocates stressed stronger passwords, security questions and legal protections to deter similar abuses.

Yoselyn Ortega, the 50-year-old nanny accused of killing 6-year-old Lucia and 2-year-old Leo Krim on the Upper West Side, briefly regained consciousness after surgery and reportedly asked about her own family, sources said. Ortega had been unable to speak following what investigators say was a failed suicide attempt in which she suffered a broken vertebra and a throat wound; police said she remained intubated. Investigators visited her New York hospital bedside seeking a motive, but Ortega, now represented by counsel, declined to answer questions, speaking only with her doctor. A search of her Harlem apartment, which she shares with relatives and her 17-year-old son who recently arrived from the Dominican Republic, yielded no clear motive. The children’s parents, CNBC executive Kevin Krim and Marina Linsley Krim, stayed secluded with their surviving 3½-year-old daughter, Nessie. Marina had been at swimming lessons with Nessie earlier; Ortega collected Lucia and Leo from school but never showed up to meet them later for Lucia’s dance class. The killings prompted nationwide sympathy and numerous social-media tributes to the family.

A mother in central China died after an escalator collapsed beneath her at a shopping mall, sacrificing herself to push her young son to safety. The accident occurred at Anliang Department Store in Jingzhou, Hubei province. Surveillance footage posted on Weibo shows the 30–31-year-old woman, identified by surname Xiang, holding her toddler as they reached the top of the escalator when a metal floor panel adjoining the escalator subsided, creating a void. She thrust her child forward; a nearby shopping assistant caught the boy while others tried to help Xiang. She became trapped as the escalator continued moving and disappeared into the machinery a few seconds later despite a staffer briefly grabbing her arm.

Firefighters took more than four hours to cut into the escalator treads and recover her body; she showed no signs of life. Relatives and local reports said maintenance had recently been performed and an access cover or footplate may not have been resecured—an unnamed source suggested screws were not tightened after work. Netizens and witnesses criticized mall staff for not stopping the escalator immediately or pressing the emergency stop, and accused the mall of attempting to conceal the incident; Chinese media coverage only appeared hours later.

The case provoked widespread public outrage on Sina Weibo, where footage and commentary drew millions of views. The tragedy echoes previous escalator accidents in China and has reignited concerns about safety standards, maintenance lapses and enforcement failures in public facilities. The mall has not issued a formal statement.

Fourteen-year-old Malala Yousafzai, shot in the head by Taliban gunmen after advocating for girls’ education, showed slight improvement as doctors reduced her sedation and she moved her hands and feet, though she remained unconscious and on a ventilator in a military hospital near Islamabad. Military spokesmen said her condition was stable but recovery from the serious head injury would be slow; the next 36–48 hours were critical. A team of specialists provided constant care and contingency plans, including possible transfer abroad, were in place; the UAE offered an air ambulance and hospitals in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. Pakistani authorities offered a reward exceeding $100,000 and reported some arrests, while the two assailants remain at large. The shooting shocked Pakistan and drew global condemnation, sparking prayers, rallies and the largest show of support in Karachi organized by the Muttahida Qaumi Movement. Responses were mixed: some Islamist groups condemned the attack but warned against using it as a pretext for military offensives, and analysts cautioned that entrenched political and religious dynamics may limit a major policy shift. Malala, who gained prominence via a BBC blog about life under Taliban rule in Swat, has become an international symbol for girls’ education; supporters see the attack potentially galvanizing domestic and global efforts to protect and expand educational opportunities for girls.

Peru’s top organized-crime investigator, Eusebio Félix (Felix Murga), was suspended after publicly claiming police had captured a gang of “Pishtacos” who murdered up to 60 people to harvest and sell their fat. Authorities staged a sensational press conference showing bottles purportedly of human fat and grisly images, alleging large profits from cosmetic markets. Regional police later contradicted the account: only one murder was corroborated, and investigators said the case was mishandled. Officials and experts criticized the story as playing on an Andean myth, scaring tourists and damaging police credibility. Medical and forensic specialists dismissed claims of a profitable human-fat trade; the affair has provoked public and political backlash.

Gillian Bennett, an 83–85-year-old Bowen Island woman in the early stages of dementia, chose to end her life publicly to spark debate about assisted suicide and advance directives. Diagnosed three years earlier, Bennett wrote on her blog and a website she prepared, Deadatnoon.com, that she was “nearly lost” to the disease and feared becoming an “empty husk” requiring prolonged institutional care. On a Monday morning she moved a foam mattress to a favorite outdoor spot, took a lethal dose of Nembutal mixed with water and whiskey, and died with her husband of 60 years, Jonathan, holding her hand. Her family—who had been informed and spent a final weekend with her—described the last days as peaceful and lucid; Bennett used the time to say private goodbyes and to assert control over her death.

In her farewell writings she urged reforms: broader public discussion of dying, routine living wills for people over 50 stored securely and accessible to hospitals, and medical protocols to allow physician-administered lethal doses in accordance with patients’ wishes. Bennett argued rising lifespans make prolonged vegetative care costly and undignified, and said she did not want to impose financial or emotional burdens. Her children expressed pain at her loss and frustration that current laws may have prevented safer, assisted options. Bennett is survived by her husband, two children, six grandchildren and two great-grandchildren; she framed her death as a final, deliberate act intended to open a conversation about end-of-life choice.

A Florida driver told Lake Mary police that George Zimmerman threatened to kill him during a road confrontation earlier this week. The driver, later identified in local reporting as 35-year-old Matthew Apperson of Winter Springs, said a Honda Ridgeline pulled up alongside his car, the occupant asked, "Do you know who I am?" and said, "I will kill you" or threatened to "shoot me." Apperson pulled into a Circle K and called police; surveillance showed the Ridgeline left before officers arrived. Two days later Apperson reported seeing the same truck near his workplace; police located Zimmerman, questioned him, briefly took his handgun, then returned it after an eight-minute encounter, and Zimmerman left without arrest. Apperson declined to press charges both times. Zimmerman, acquitted last year of second-degree murder in the fatal shooting of 17-year-old Trayvon Martin, has had multiple post-trial run-ins with police, including past allegations of assault and threats involving a firearm from an ex-girlfriend and disputes with his estranged wife. Those earlier cases produced no convictions after alleged victims did not cooperate or evidence was insufficient.

Esmond Bradley Martin, a 75-year-old American geographer and one of the world’s foremost investigators of the illegal ivory and rhino-horn trades, was found stabbed to death at his home in Langata, Nairobi. His wife discovered his body with a neck wound; police are investigating and have questioned household staff but had not identified attackers. Authorities initially suggested a possible botched robbery, but colleagues and observers note that Bradley Martin’s undercover work—posing as a buyer in China, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and elsewhere to document markets, prices and trafficking networks—had repeatedly put him at personal risk, and some fear his killing could be linked to those investigations.

Bradley Martin spent decades compiling meticulous, hard data that exposed retail ivory and rhino horn markets and helped shape policy responses. He contributed to efforts persuading China to ban legal rhino horn sales in the 1990s and, more recently, to close its domestic ivory market. His reports, many published through Save The Elephants and co-authored with colleagues such as Lucy Vigne, documented rapidly growing retail markets in places like Laos and detailed demand dynamics in Vietnam and Myanmar. His 2017 and 2016 studies informed international bodies including CITES and provided critical evidence used by governments and conservationists.

Colleagues paid tribute on social media and in public statements, describing him as rigorous, brave, and irreplaceable: a sharply dressed, passionate campaigner whose undercover research frequently put him in dangerous settings—Chinese casinos, illegal market hubs and trafficking networks—to record prices and identify actors. His death is widely mourned as a major loss for the international conservation community and a stark reminder of the risks faced by investigators tackling organized wildlife crime.

A small coastal village in north Brittany is living in fear after a disturbing series of attacks in which more than 100 pet rabbits have been killed. The crimes, concentrated in and around Minihy-Tréguier — a picturesque town of about 1,300 people popular with tourists and home to some British expatriates — have unnerved residents and prompted a police investigation. According to the mayor, Jean-Yves Fenvarc’h, the attacker sneaks into gardens, opens hutches, removes rabbits and kills them with a sharp object or by crushing them, sometimes returning later to kill again. Victims are often elderly people who keep rabbits in their gardens alongside chickens or geese; notably, the birds are left unharmed, suggesting the perpetrator is selective. Authorities believe the culprit is human rather than a wild predator and have described the offenses as cold-blooded acts of cruelty. The incidents began in March, paused, recurred in August, lapsed, and resumed recently, totaling around 15 recorded attacks. Police in the Côtes-d’Armor region have appealed for witnesses, warning that the timing and targeting — striking when owners are away and selecting hutches not visible from the road — indicate the attacker knows the area and may be watching properties before striking.

Russian Antarctic researcher Sergey Savitsky has been charged with attempted murder after allegedly stabbing a colleague on October 9 at the remote Russian Bellingshausen research station on King George Island. Interfax reports Savitsky stabbed the unnamed man at least once in the station dining room, intending to kill him. The victim was evacuated to a hospital in Chile, the nearest mainland medical facility. Sources told Interfax the two men had shared cramped living and working conditions for over six months and that Savitsky may have “snapped” from prolonged close confinement. He reportedly surrendered to the station manager without resistance and accepted house arrest at the base; a St. Petersburg court placed him under house arrest until December 8. The Bellingshausen station, established by the Soviet Union in 1968 and named for explorer Fabian von Bellingshausen, lies among several national bases on King George Island. Russian authorities have not publicly commented, and a court date has not been announced.

An on-duty FBI agent conducting surveillance in Canarsie, Brooklyn, was shot in the shoulder Saturday afternoon in an exchange of gunfire with occupants of a BMW. Sources say the agent was inside his vehicle near E. 92nd Street and Avenue N when the BMW drove by and opened fire; the agent returned fire as the suspects fled. One suspect was hit and later sought treatment at Kingsbrook Jewish Medical Center, where he was arrested; another was captured nearby on Remsen Avenue. The wounded agent was taken to Kings County Hospital and underwent surgery; his injuries are not believed to be life-threatening. Authorities have not disclosed what the agent was surveilling or whether the suspects knew his identity. The investigation is ongoing and no suspects remain at large.

Last month Playboy announced it will stop publishing images of fully nude women in its print edition, a dramatic shift confirmed after a meeting in which founder and editor-in-chief Hugh Hefner approved the change. As part of a redesign debuting next March (with the change taking effect in the March issue published in February), the magazine will continue to feature women in provocative poses but no longer full nudity. Executives say the move responds to the internet’s ubiquity of free pornography and changing cultural norms: “That battle has been fought and won,” CEO Scott Flanders told the New York Times. Playboy’s web strategy already removed nudity to access social platforms, quadrupling online traffic, and the company now earns much of its revenue from global licensing of the iconic rabbit logo. Once a powerful cultural platform—publishing notable interviews with figures like Martin Luther King Jr., Malcolm X, Jimmy Carter, and others—Playboy’s print circulation has plunged from 5.6 million in the 1970s to about 800,000 today. Observers note the risk: targeting younger readers by shedding nudity may alienate loyal subscribers while not guaranteeing new audiences who can find comparable content elsewhere for free. Supporters hope the shift will let the magazine foreground its journalism—the famous “Playboy Interview”—while critics say the brand risks losing its identity. The company frames the change as necessary adaptation: times have changed, and a non-nude Playboy is an experiment in preserving relevance in a transformed media landscape.

Judge W. Mitchell Nance, a family court judge in Kentucky’s 43rd Judicial Circuit serving Barren and Metcalfe counties, has announced he will no longer preside over adoption cases involving gay adults, citing a “matter of conscience.” Nance, first assigned to Family Court in 2004 after election as a district court judge in 2000, issued an order disqualifying himself from any adoption proceedings involving “practicing homosexuals,” arguing that his personal beliefs create a bias requiring recusal under judicial ethics rules. He said his decision aims to minimize disruption in litigation and that the other division of the 43rd Circuit, led by Judge John T. Alexander, will handle affected adoption matters so same-sex couples should not face delays.

The move drew polarized reactions. Conservative groups and some supporters praised Nance’s choice as an exercise of conscience and fairness, arguing judges with conflicting beliefs should be allowed to step aside. Critics, including legal ethics experts and LGBT advocates, condemned the blanket recusal as discriminatory and suggested it undermines his oath to uphold laws that protect against sexual-orientation discrimination. Indiana University law professor Charles Geyh warned that refusing to adjudicate cases involving an entire class of litigants raises questions about a judge’s ability to remain impartial. Kentucky law permits adoption by gay couples and the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2015 Obergefell ruling legalized same-sex marriage nationwide. Nance said he would not resign and acknowledged gay litigants might reasonably be reluctant to appear before him; he also said he would decline to perform same-sex marriages if asked.

A 20-year-old man, identified as Chanel Lewis of Brooklyn, was arrested Saturday in the strangling death of 30-year-old Karina Vetrano, who was attacked while jogging near her Queens home on Aug. 2. Vetrano’s father later found her badly beaten body in a secluded marsh. Queens District Attorney Richard Brown said Lewis was expected to be arraigned and faces a murder charge that carries 25 years to life if convicted. Police Chief of Detectives Robert Boyce reported Lewis made “incriminating statements” at arrest, and investigators said DNA evidence linked him to the crime: genetic material recovered from under Vetrano’s fingernails and on her phone and neck produced a DNA profile. At the time of reports, formal charges and attorney information for Lewis were pending.

RevolutionMuslim.com was cited by Roshonara Choudhry in police interviews as one of the sites that radicalised her before she attempted to murder Labour MP Stephen Timms; she was jailed for life. The site praises her as a “mujaahidah” and explicitly lists MPs who voted for the Iraq war, urging Muslims to attack them and even providing details of Timms’s constituency surgery times and a link to buy a similar knife. It includes prayers naming Timms and the judge, and reproduces videos and sermons by extremist clerics such as Anwar al-Awlaki and Abdullah Azzam. The site appears US-hosted (via Enom in Washington), prompting British ministers and the Home Office to press US authorities to remove the content. RevolutionMuslim shows links to British extremists including Anjem Choudary and Abu Izzadeen, promotes events and flags alleged authors including US national Zachary Chesser, arrested for supporting an al-Qaeda-linked group. Critics call the site dangerous; some associated figures deny involvement or refuse to condemn its calls for violence. Authorities warn online jihadist material is difficult to remove when hosted abroad.

George Zimmerman, acquitted seven months earlier of second-degree murder and manslaughter in the fatal shooting of unarmed 17-year-old Trayvon Martin, maintains he was the victim the night of the confrontation. In a CNN interview he said he was “having my head bashed into the concrete” and suffered a broken nose, insisting his actions were self-defense. He acknowledged killing Martin while serving as a neighborhood watchman and said he would have “stayed home” if he could do it over, but is not haunted by memories of the event. Zimmerman attributes his certainty to faith: “I know He’s the only judge I have to answer to.” He expressed plans to continue his education and hopes to become an attorney, believing that would address what he calls a miscarriage of justice. Since the trial he has faced legal and PR troubles — traffic stops, accusations by his wife and girlfriend of threats involving firearms, and selling paintings and signing up for a canceled charity boxing match with rapper DMX. Zimmerman says he receives death threats and feels misunderstood by those who label him racist, noting some of his relatives are black and that personal encounters change people’s perspectives.

In Manchester, Illinois, 43-year-old Rick Odell Smith entered a home about 4:30 a.m. armed with a shotgun, a scoped rifle and a hunting knife and shot multiple residents at close range. Five people were killed: 67-year-old Joanne (JoAnn) Sinclair, 23-year-old Brittany (Brittney) Luark—who was reportedly pregnant—her boyfriend Roy (James Roy) Ralston, 29, and two young boys, ages 1 and 5; a six-year-old girl survived with serious injuries. After the attack Smith carried the bleeding child to a neighbor, fled in a white Chevy, and was later stopped by police; he fired on officers and was fatally wounded in the ensuing shootout. Authorities have not determined a motive; investigators noted Smith and the victims were “acquaintances.” Smith had a criminal record including a DUI-related reckless homicide conviction. The killings stunned the 300-resident rural town, where leaders and neighbors described shock and devastation.

Volusia County deputies are searching for three suspects after a woman was carjacked early Saturday while stopping to help people involved in a crash on westbound I-4 near Daytona Beach. The crash was reported about 5:40 a.m. at mile marker 128. A 34-year-old woman who pulled over to assist was approached by three young men who jumped out of a vehicle involved in the initial collision and stole her car. Deputies say the men loaded an unresponsive, bleeding female—believed to be in her teens or early 20s with short dreadlocks and wearing a red hooded sweatshirt, brown jeans and black shoes—into the stolen vehicle before fleeing westbound. The stolen car is a dark blue 2012 Ford Mustang convertible, Florida tag V83-4QC, with a black vinyl top, a spoiler and no window tint; an image released depicts a similar vehicle. The three suspects are described as Black males in their teens or early 20s: one heavy-set wearing a striped shirt and jeans, and two thin. The initial crash vehicle was also reported stolen. The Volusia County Sheriff’s Office has charged the suspects with carjacking and asks anyone who sees the car or suspects to call 911 and not to approach them; the Florida Highway Patrol is investigating the crash.

Photos obtained by TMZ showing U.S. Marines posing with and burning corpses in Fallujah, Iraq, in 2004 have prompted a formal U.S. military inquiry. TMZ released 9 of 41 images said to depict Marines pouring a flammable liquid on dead bodies, setting them alight, and photographing themselves with the remains; other images reportedly show a Marine rifling through a corpse’s pockets, numerous bodies in various states of decomposition, flies on some, and a dog eating one body. The pictures were reportedly turned over to the Pentagon, and Marine Corps and U.S. Central Command officials reviewed them; the Defense Department has opened an investigation into their authenticity and whether the service members involved can be identified and disciplined. Pentagon spokesmen noted that burning or mishandling remains violates the Uniform Code of Military Justice and can be prosecuted with no statute of limitations, even if the individuals are no longer in service. Military officials condemned the depicted actions as unrepresentative of the service and said they are investigating to determine potential violations and appropriate responses.

Daejona M. Holmes, 15, has been charged as an adult in the April 9 fatal shootings of her parents at their Kansas City home. The Jackson County Prosecutor’s Office filed two counts of second-degree murder, two counts of armed criminal action, and one count of tampering with physical evidence. Authorities responded to a shooting call to the 5000 block of Belmeade Road after Holmes placed a 911 call from a McDonald’s and initially reported a robbery and that her parents had been shot. Officers later found Kinderly Holmes, 37, shot once in the stomach, and Brian Starr, 38, shot three times (twice in the torso and once in the mouth). Holmes’ account changed during interviews: she first said her father shot her mother and that she then shot her father; later she described hearing an initial shot, finding her mother dead, picking up a handgun, and shooting her father as he approached. Investigators obtained a warrant for her phone and found web searches for “scary movies where kids kill parents,” rap lyrics expressing a wish for her father’s death, a video of Holmes dancing with a handgun, and a backpack drawing depicting stick figures labeled “me” shooting “dad.” Police also found the firearm across the street in a puddle. Records show Holmes made nine calls on her mother’s phone after the shooting and waited about an hour before calling 911; a friend met her and persuaded her to call police. Prosecutors have requested $150,000 bond.

A Danish inventor, Peter Madsen, charged with murdering Swedish journalist Kim Wall, had violent video footage on a computer in his workshop showing women being strangled and decapitated, a Copenhagen court heard. Prosecutor Jakob Buch-Jepsen said material “presumed to be real” was found on a hard drive in Madsen’s lab and that new post-mortem findings show Wall suffered 15 stab wounds to her ribcage and genitals inflicted around or shortly after death. DNA matching Wall was recovered under Madsen’s nails, and traces consistent with a saw blade were found, suggesting dismemberment after death; Wall’s headless torso was discovered washed ashore in August. Madsen, who denies murder and a mutilation charge, appeared calm at a pre-trial hearing via video link wearing a green boilersuit and said the searched computer belonged to the shared “space laboratory” and was not solely his. He has previously claimed Wall died accidentally when a heavy hatch fell on her, and that he tried to sink her body and his submarine in panic. The court extended his detention for four weeks as investigations continue; he will next appear on October 31.

A 30-year-old man who had been a fugitive since 2013 was arrested after flagging down a Louisiana deputy for a ride, authorities said. Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Office identified the suspect as Jansen Simon, who allegedly struck another man in the head with a hammer during a bar fight in Cut Off on August 3, 2013, an attack that left the victim with a fractured skull. Two contempt-of-court warrants from that period were also active. In the early hours of July 16, Simon was walking alongside Highway 182 in Raceland and stopped an off-duty deputy in a marked patrol car, saying friends had left him by the roadside. The deputy followed protocol by verifying his identity and arrested him; it is unclear whether Simon realized the vehicle was a police car. Simon was booked into the Lafourche Parish Detention Center on one count of aggravated second-degree battery and two counts of contempt of court and is being held without bond.

Christian Jose Gomez, 23, was arrested and charged with first-degree murder after allegedly decapitating his 48-year-old mother, Maria Suarez-Cassagne, on New Year’s Eve at the Oldsmar home she shared with her two sons. Deputies say the attack occurred around 7:30 p.m.; Gomez allegedly used an ax to sever her head in the garage, placed the head in a trash can outside, and attempted but failed to move the rest of her body. His older brother, Mario Gomez, who had been in a bedroom, called 911 and met officers at the scene. Neighbors described the victim as very kind and said the older son was visibly traumatized. Christian Gomez fled but was spotted riding a bicycle several blocks away; a short pursuit ended in his arrest. According to Sheriff Bob Gualtieri, Gomez admitted to the killing, saying he was upset that his mother had asked him to put boxes away, and had allegedly planned the murder for two days. Authorities noted Gomez has a history of mental illness and prior minor arrests. He is being held without bond in the Pinellas County Jail.

Orange County authorities and the FBI are seeking the public’s help to identify a bank robber dubbed the “Keep Smiling Bandit” after two recent Citibank hold-ups in Costa Mesa and Tustin. In both incidents the man—described as a white male in his early 30s, about 5'7"–5'9" and 140–150 pounds—passed handwritten notes to tellers demanding cash, verbally instructing victims to “keep smiling.” Although he appeared nervous and wore eyeglasses and a baseball cap in each robbery, no weapon was seen. One note delivered at the Tustin branch warned, “Keep your hands away from the alarm or I’ll shoot,” conveying a clear threat. The robber may be linked to an Oct. 12 robbery at a Costa Mesa Citibank and a subsequent incident at a Tustin Citibank on Irvine Boulevard. The FBI and the Orange County Sheriff’s Department Bank Robbery Apprehension Team asked anyone with information to call 911 or, in the Los Angeles area, contact the FBI at (310) 477-6565. The agencies are pursuing leads to identify and apprehend the suspect.

Deven Davis, the 39-year-old estranged wife of Korn frontman Jonathan Davis, has died, sources confirm. The family released a statement saying they are “brokenhearted” and request privacy as they mourn. The cause of death has not been disclosed. Deven, a former model and adult performer, and Jonathan married in 2004 and had two children together: Pirate (born 2005) and Zeppelin (born 2007). Jonathan, 47, filed for divorce in October 2016. On August 17, 2018, he sought and was granted a temporary domestic violence restraining order that barred Deven from child custody or visitation and prohibited contact with the family dog, Chaos. Court documents obtained by TMZ allege Deven struggled with substance abuse for over 20 years, including dependence on prescription and illegal narcotics. Jonathan’s filing claimed she had been to rehab multiple times, relapsed after a stint in a sober living home, and was “constantly under the influence” of substances such as nitrous oxide, cocaine and Norco. He also alleged incidents of neglect and that Deven associated with dangerous individuals while caring for their children. At this time, official details about her death remain unconfirmed, and resources for substance abuse help were noted for those in need.

On the day Baltimore’s police academy celebrated a new class of officers, the department confronted a viral video showing one of its officers repeatedly punching and then pinning a man, identified by his lawyer as 26-year-old Dashawn McGrier. The confrontation, captured by a bystander, begins with officers approaching McGrier during a crime-suppression detail; police say one officer knew McGrier and the encounter escalated after McGrier refused to provide identification. Video shows an officer shove McGrier, then strike him with a series of punches, force him down rowhouse steps, and press an arm across his neck as blood pools on the sidewalk. A second officer is seen nearby but does little to intervene; he has been placed on administrative duty while investigators probe the incident.

Interim Police Commissioner Gary Tuggle called the footage “deeply disturbing,” suspended the punching officer immediately and ordered a review, including body-cam footage. The next day the department announced it had accepted the officer’s resignation; the agency has not publicly named him. McGrier was hospitalized with suspected fractures to his jaw, nose and ribs; he was not charged for the Saturday incident. His attorney plans to seek charges and a civil suit, calling the attack personal brutality, not police work.

The incident intensifies scrutiny of a department already under a federal consent decree stemming from a Justice Department finding of unconstitutional policing and discrimination. Observers — including the mayor and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund — have demanded accountability. The independent team monitoring Baltimore’s compliance with reform measures is reviewing the video and will monitor how the department conducts its investigation. Critics note concerns about training and oversight after reports that many recent academy graduates lack a firm grasp of constitutional policing.

The execution of Jang Song Thaek, once North Korea’s No. 2 and known for close ties with Beijing, has shocked China and worsened bilateral relations. A graphic account published in Beijing-controlled Wen Wei Po described Jang and five aides stripped naked, confined in a cage, and ripped apart by 120 starved dogs while Kim Jong Un and 300 officials watched — a report that signalled Chinese outrage and a willingness to publicly embarrass Pyongyang. The Global Times followed with an editorial condemning North Korea’s backwardness and urging China not to coddle the regime. Official charges against Jang accused him of underselling resources to China, selling land in the Rason zone to foreigners to pay debts, and disposing of precious metals—allegations that implicated China and highlighted Jang’s role aiding Chinese businessmen. Analysts see the purge as rooted in a deep North Korean distrust of China stretching back to Kim Il Sung’s postwar purges of pro-Beijing factions and continued under Kim Jong Il, who reportedly hinted nuclear threats toward China. With Kim Jong Un’s purge of a pro-China figure, Beijing faces heightened security concerns, diminished influence over Pyongyang, and the collapse of hopes for gradual reform via economic opening. Chinese officials sought urgent consultations with Russia, signalling recognition that Beijing can no longer reliably control or moderate the Kim regime.

Seventeen-year-old John David LaDue allegedly planned a three-part massacre targeting his family and Waseca Junior/Senior High School, intending to die in a shootout with police, according to Waseca County charging documents. Authorities say LaDue plotted for about 10 months, refining explosive mixtures and testing devices at local sites — including an elementary school playground, a church and athletic fields. He recorded detailed plans, supply lists and procurement efforts in a notebook found in a locked guitar case in his bedroom. His scheme reportedly involved killing his parents and sister quietly with a .22-caliber rifle, setting a diversionary fire to occupy first responders, then detonating pressure-cooker and pipe bombs in the high school cafeteria and shooting fleeing students and staff; he had originally considered April 20, the Columbine anniversary, but postponed because it fell on Easter. Police recovered an arsenal from his home and a rented storage unit: seven firearms (including an SKS and a 9mm handgun), hundreds of rounds of ammunition, at least six completed bombs, ball bearings, pressure cookers, bomb-making chemicals such as red iron oxide and potassium perchlorate, trip wire, a scale, and other materials. Investigators say a neighbor, Chelsie Schellhas, grew suspicious after seeing LaDue enter a storage unit on foot and alerted police; officers found him inside and took him into custody. LaDue faces multiple attempted murder and explosives charges. Officials declined to discuss how he obtained weapons. The community, shaken and grief-stricken at the narrowly averted attack, has scheduled a school meeting to discuss next steps and express gratitude to the caller whose tip likely prevented mass casualties.

Owen Labrie, a 20-year-old St. Paul’s School graduate convicted last year of sexually assaulting a 15-year-old freshman as part of the so-called “Senior Salute,” will be released on bail again while his lawyers pursue an appeal. After serving two months in jail following a March revocation of his initial bail for multiple curfew violations, a Merrimack County judge ordered Labrie freed once fitted with an electronic GPS monitor; officials expect release between Wednesday and Friday. Labrie had originally been released on $15,000 bail after his October conviction on misdemeanor sexual assault, child endangerment and unlawful computer use charges, under conditions that included living at his mother’s Tunbridge, Vermont, home and a 5 p.m.–8 a.m. curfew. Those conditions were breached at least a dozen times after a reporter tweeted a March sighting of Labrie on a Cambridge train visiting his girlfriend at Harvard, prompting the earlier bail revocation. At Monday’s hearing, defense attorney Jaye Rancourt argued Labrie’s two months in jail were “life-changing” and pledged compliance with stricter conditions; prosecutors emphasized community safety concerns, noting Labrie has not completed a psycho-sexual assessment and contending his primary objection is simply to incarceration. Victim-advocacy groups criticized the decision as undermining accountability. Labrie, who had planned to attend Harvard before his arrest, maintains aspects of his case justify appeal and seeks a new trial, while prosecutors and the judge stressed monitoring will be used to verify his compliance.

A brutal clash between rival drug gangs in western Mexico left dozens dead, displaced hundreds and highlighted the growing lawlessness in several states. In Nayarit, authorities found 29 bodies in fake military uniforms scattered among 14 bullet-riddled vehicles after a highway ambush; military gear, grenades and thousands of rounds were recovered. Officials gave conflicting casualty reports and named the Sinaloa cartel and the Zetas as likely combatants. Separately in Michoacán, three days of fierce fighting among La Familia factions (including the splinter “Knights Templar”) forced about 800 people into shelters, prompted deployment of hundreds of marines and soldiers, and saw a federal police helicopter shot at. The violence has led to mass graves in other states, displacement of tens of thousands nationally, erosion of local governance, and calls for unified political and security responses as cartels increasingly contest territory and exercise de facto control.

Donald Trump repeatedly claimed the Obama administration planned to admit 200,000 Syrian refugees, warning they could include ISIS members and calling the inflow a “Trojan Horse.” He voiced versions of this claim at rallies and on TV in late 2015. Fact-checkers found no support for the 200,000 figure as Syrians specifically. Secretary of State John Kerry had discussed raising the total U.S. refugee ceiling—from 70,000 in 2016 to 85,000, and possibly 100,000 in 2017—totaling 185,000 across two years, but that would be the cap for all refugees, not Syrians. The Obama administration had pledged to admit at least 10,000 Syrian refugees in the coming year, a significant increase from 2015 but far short of Trump’s repeated number. Fact-checkers determined Trump’s repetition of 200,000 for Syrians was misleading and assigned Four Pinocchios. Commentary highlighted Trump’s broader pattern of false and inflammatory claims—about refugees, Muslims, and crime statistics—arguing these appeals to fear and prejudice mirror historic demagoguery. Critics urged journalists and political leaders to challenge such fabrications rather than ignore them, warning that unchecked lies can normalize intolerance and empower bullying rhetoric. The consensus: the 200,000 claim is inaccurate, and persistent fact-checking and public accountability are necessary.

Former LAPD officer Christopher Dorner, 33, is the focus of a massive Southern California manhunt after allegedly killing multiple people and threatening others in an online manifesto. Authorities believe Dorner, a Navy reservist and trained marksman fired from the LAPD in 2008 after internal complaints and a disputed misconduct report, killed at least three people, including the daughter and fiancé of a retired LAPD captain, and shot multiple officers. His manifesto accuses the department of racism and conspiracy, names at least a dozen targets, and promises "deadly consequences" for those he blames.

Law enforcement fears Dorner is heavily armed — possibly with a .50-caliber rifle and other powerful weapons — and skilled in police tactics learned during his LAPD service, which could help him evade capture. His burned pickup was found on Big Bear Mountain with tracks in the snow that went cold; a separate aborted yacht hijacking and the discovery of his wallet and badge in San Diego were also reported. Hundreds of officers, SWAT teams and aircraft have searched cabins, roads and forests, imposing lockdowns in resort towns. Search efforts have been hampered by snow and weather, and authorities caution the public as the manhunt continues.

Mary Anne Forster, an assistant principal from Williamstown north of Adelaide, was seriously injured after a koala attacked while she was walking her two dogs. Two weeks ago the dogs pulled her toward a koala at the base of a tree; the animal, apparently feeling threatened, latched onto Forster’s leg with its jaws and bit deeply. After a prolonged struggle during which the koala would not release, Forster forced her fingers into its mouth to pry the jaws open and free her leg. She then hobbled more than two kilometres home and was later admitted to hospital, where she required 12 stitches. The wound became infected and painful, necessitating antibiotics and a four-day hospital stay. Despite the severity of her injuries, Forster does not blame the koala. Environmental experts warn people to give koalas space in the wild and to prevent dogs from approaching them. Dr Deb Kelly from the Environment Department stressed koalas can fight back with large claws and teeth. Authorities note that while dog attacks kill many koalas each year, human-koala attacks are rare, though they can cause deep, dirty bites that require medical treatment.

Mikhail Popkov, a former Siberian police officer nicknamed the “Werewolf,” has confessed to 59 additional murders, bringing his total admissions to 81 — far surpassing Soviet-era killers Andrei Chikatilo and Alexander Pichushkin. Previously convicted in January 2015 for 22 murders in Angarsk, Popkov targeted mainly young women aged about 17–38 between 1992 and 2010. He often offered nighttime lifts—sometimes in a police car—took victims to remote locations, raped them, and killed them with axes, knives or screwdrivers, leaving bodies in woods or by roads. Detained in 2012 after tire tracks and DNA evidence linked him to killings, he initially confessed to a few murders; investigators later confirmed many more as he guided them to burial sites and matched biological traces. Irkutsk investigators say 47 of the 59 newly confessed killings have been charged, with a dozen more under imminent investigation. Popkov’s motives included a self-styled campaign to “cleanse” the streets of prostitutes and personal grievances. Authorities continue painstaking forensic work to corroborate his confessions; if courts confirm 81 murders, Popkov will rank among the world’s most prolific serial killers.

A south Arkansas crash left a 25-year-old mother dead and her two small sons—ages 3 and 1—alone and surviving on their own for up to four days, authorities say. Ouachita County detectives learned Monday morning when a 911 caller reported a small boy walking alone along a rural stretch of Highway 24 near Camden. Deputies found the 3-year-old covered in cuts and scrapes, visibly traumatized and having been outside for an extended period. After officials bathed him, fed him and changed his clothes, a family member informed deputies that the boys’ mother had not been seen since she went grocery shopping on Thursday and suggested the infant brother was likely nearby.

When investigators located the wrecked vehicle, they found the mother deceased near the car and the 1-year-old still secured in his car seat, positioned partially upside down. The older boy, identified by family as Kylen, had escaped his car seat and climbed out—reportedly through a sunroof—and up a small hill of brush, where he tried to wake his mother. Both boys suffered dehydration; the infant was taken to Arkansas Children’s Hospital and is expected to survive. Family members described the survival as nothing short of a miracle and expressed devastating grief: the maternal grandfather, James Holliman, lamented losing his daughter, and hospital staff revealed the mother had been about four weeks pregnant, meaning the family lost two. Detectives said the children endured “pure hell” and that the cause of the single-vehicle crash remains under investigation. Authorities continue to care for the boys while probing the circumstances of the wreck.

Two daycare workers in Chicago have been arrested after surveillance video allegedly showed one of them burning five toddlers with a hot glue gun while the other watched and laughed. Authorities say the incident occurred Dec. 1 at the Children’s Learning Place in Logan Square. Lizandra Cosme, 32, was arrested and faces five felony counts of aggravated battery to a child; prosecutors say she applied hot glue to the hands and arms of five 2-year-olds — three girls and two boys — who winced and whined in response. Cosme was denied bail and is due back in court Dec. 26. Susana Gonzalez, 27, was charged with five misdemeanor counts of causing the circumstances of child endangerment. Prosecutors say Cosme brought the glue gun from home to use on a Christmas project and had 16 children in her care at the time; an assistant allegedly stood nearby laughing as the burns occurred. Officials say Cosme later attempted to treat one child with Neosporin and reportedly asked a father if an injury had happened at home. The injuries’ extent is unclear. The daycare, which serves children 6 weeks to 6 years, terminated both employees and notified the Department of Children and Family Services, which is investigating. Cosme’s attorney said she “screwed up” but did not act maliciously; both women could not be reached for comment.

RadarOnline.com reports that adult film performer and escort Devon James is claiming Tiger Woods fathered her secret son. James, 29, says she gave birth in early 2001—before Woods’ marriage to Elin Nordegren—and alleges a two-and-a-half-year affair that included a paid “two-girl party” where unprotected sex occurred. According to the site, James confronted Woods in 2006 during a later encounter and insisted he was the child’s father; RadarOnline says it has photos of the boy, who reportedly resembles Woods. No paternity test has been taken or requested, and there’s no evidence Woods paid James. Separately, a Channel 4 documentary and journalist Neal Boulton revive long-running rumors of a Tiger love child, citing sources who claim DNA evidence exists and predicting further revelations.

Oklahoma State Sen. Ralph Shortey, a Republican from Oklahoma City, was charged with three felonies after police found him with a 17-year-old boy in a Moore motel on March 9. Authorities allege Shortey offered the teen money for sex, transported him for prostitution, and engaged in prostitution within 1,000 feet of a church. The teenager, treated as a victim and identified by initials, had an online, explicit conversation with Shortey found on the teen’s Kindle in which Shortey (using the name “Jamie Tilley”) discussed sex and marijuana, called the youth “baby boy,” and used other graphic language. Police say they discovered an open condom box in Shortey’s backpack and lotion in the teen’s. A green container labeled “Colorado Retail Marijuana” with residue was later seized; prosecutors did not pursue marijuana charges primarily due to evidence issues.

Shortey, 35, who surrendered to authorities and posted $100,000 bail, has been a state senator since 2010 and had publicly presented himself as a family man and former missionary-in-training who later worked in oil, gas and political consulting. In response to the allegations, Gov. Mary Fallin, Lt. Gov. Todd Lamb, Senate leaders and others called for his resignation. The state Senate previously voted unanimously to punish Shortey for “disorderly behavior,” stripping him of most Capitol privileges, including his office and parking. If convicted on the charges, Shortey faces up to 25 years in prison. The teen was not charged; he reportedly has a history of soliciting on Craigslist and drug problems.

Former IMF chief Dominique Strauss-Kahn and hotel housekeeper Nafissatou Diallo have reached a tentative settlement to resolve her civil lawsuit accusing him of sexual assault during a May 2011 encounter at a Manhattan hotel. Prosecutors had dropped related criminal charges in August 2011 after raising concerns about Diallo’s credibility, though DNA confirmed sexual contact. Details of the settlement are undisclosed and likely subject to confidentiality; French reports of a $6 million payment were denied by Strauss-Kahn’s lawyer. The agreement, facilitated by Bronx Justice Douglas McKeon and paired with a deal to end Diallo’s suit against the New York Post, has not been signed publicly but a court appearance is scheduled. The matter ends a high-profile legal saga that cost Strauss-Kahn his IMF post and further tarnished his political standing amid other allegations in France.

A 40-year-old DreamWorks animator, identified as Young Song of Pasadena, pleaded not guilty to felony animal cruelty after surveillance video allegedly captured him climbing a neighbor’s fence on April 20, shooting a muzzled German shepherd with a pellet gun, then returning with a hammer and repeatedly striking the dog until it lay motionless. The muzzled, approximately 16-month-old shepherd is now missing and presumed dead; Song also faces a theft charge related to the animal. Industry sources list Song as a “surfacer” with credits on family films such as Kung Fu Panda, Shark Tale, Bee Movie and Madagascar 2. Pasadena Humane Society officials described the footage as among the worst abuse they have seen, saying officers were deeply shaken. Authorities are investigating the incident as possibly stemming from an ongoing neighbor dispute; if convicted, Song could face several years in state prison.

Police in Jalisco discovered 18 dismembered bodies, many beheaded, inside two vans on a dirt access road near Lake Chapala, a tourist and retiree area outside Guadalajara. Jalisco state Prosecutor Tomás Coronado said police were alerted by a phone call and found 15 severed heads in the vans initially, with three more heads and other body parts confirmed later. Handwritten messages were left in the vehicles; authorities said they were clearly communications between rival criminal groups. The scene fits a pattern of cartel violence in which gangs mutilate victims and leave messages. Investigators linked the killings to an earlier abduction of 12 people in the same area; a woman detained as a guard for those captives told police the kidnappings were “a repercussion of what happened in Tamaulipas.” That likely refers to the recent discovery of two dozen slain people in Nuevo Laredo, where tit-for-tat battles among the Zetas, Sinaloa, Gulf cartel and allied groups have escalated into mass killings.

For nearly six months Michigan assistant attorney general Andrew Shirvell has run a vitriolic blog targeting Chris Armstrong, the openly gay student assembly president at the University of Michigan. Writing under the name "Concerned Michigan Alumnus," Shirvell’s posts—begun in late April—label Armstrong a "RADICAL HOMOSEXUAL ACTIVIST, RACIST, ELITIST, & LIAR" and level numerous accusations: breaking promises to minority students, engaging in sexual promiscuity with another male student official, seducing a conservative student into supporting gay causes, hosting a 2009 "gay orgy" in a dorm, and recruiting freshmen into a "homosexual 'lifestyle.'" Shirvell admitted protesting at Armstrong’s home and called him "Satan's representative on the student assembly," while defending his actions as exercising his First Amendment rights and saying he has "no problem" with Armstrong being gay but objects to what he calls a radical agenda. The blog includes a doctored photo of Armstrong marked "Resign" with a swastika over a pride flag. Michigan Attorney General Mike Cox disavowed Shirvell’s views as personal and criticized his immaturity. Armstrong has hired an attorney and may pursue legal action; CNN’s legal analyst suggested harassment charges could be possible.

A Pennsylvania man, Ryan Collins of Lancaster, has agreed to plead guilty to a federal charge of unauthorized access to a protected computer for stealing private information from more than 100 online accounts, many belonging to women and several celebrities. Between November 2012 and September 2014, prosecutors say Collins used phishing emails that impersonated Apple or Google to trick victims into revealing usernames and passwords. He then accessed email and cloud accounts, sometimes downloading nude photos and full iCloud backups. The investigation into a 2014 breach that exposed nude photos of celebrities including Jennifer Lawrence and Kate Upton led to the charges; Collins is not suspected of posting or otherwise publicly releasing the photos, and prosecutors say they have no evidence he was involved in leaking them. Collins has agreed to plead guilty to one count under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, a charge carrying up to five years in prison, though prosecutors will recommend an 18-month sentence. At least 50 iCloud and 72 Gmail accounts were compromised. Authorities stressed the emotional harm to victims and urged stronger passwords and caution about email requests for personal information. His case will transfer to Harrisburg, Pennsylvania.

Arizona Rep. Gabrielle Giffords was critically wounded by a close-range gunshot to the head and underwent surgery at the University of Arizona Hospital; doctors said the bullet entered at her temple and exited through her forehead. Medical experts caution that gunshot wounds to the head are usually fatal, but survival is possible and depends chiefly on the bullet’s path and the brain structures affected. Larger or fragmenting bullets cause more tissue destruction; wounds that cross both hemispheres or reach the brainstem and base of the skull are likeliest to be lethal because they disrupt breathing, circulation and other vital functions. If the injury is limited to one hemisphere or only grazes a lobe, patients can survive and potentially recover with significant rehabilitation, though lasting deficits—memory, motor skills or personality changes—are common. Statistics cited put survival rates very low: roughly 5 percent overall, with many survivors left with neurological impairments. Immediate postoperative management focuses on controlling bleeding and brain swelling; the first three to four days are most critical, and recovery may take years.

A 15-year-old Richmond High School sophomore was brutally raped, beaten and robbed on school grounds after leaving her homecoming dance Oct. 24; police say the assault lasted more than two hours and may have involved as many as 7–10 attackers, ages 15 to mid‑20s. Officers found her semiconscious and naked from the waist down near a picnic table; she remains hospitalized with non‑life‑threatening injuries. Two suspects are jailed—a 19‑year‑old former student, Manuel Ortega, and a 15‑year‑old student—and police say more arrests are expected. Disturbingly, up to two dozen people reportedly witnessed the crime without intervening or calling authorities; investigators are probing whether bystanders recorded it. Authorities called the attack “barbaric,” offered a $20,000 reward, served warrants, and face scrutiny over campus security and nonworking surveillance cameras. Community shock prompted some students to withdraw from the school.

A man walked into Brigham and Women’s Hospital’s Shapiro Cardiovascular Center just after 11 a.m. and asked to see Dr. Michael J. Davidson. When Davidson, a 44-year-old director of endovascular cardiac surgery and Harvard Medical School assistant professor, stepped into an exam room, the assailant fired two shots, striking him. The shooter, identified as 55-year-old Stephen Pasceri of Millbury, was later found dead in the room from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot; police recovered a .40-caliber pistol and believe three shots were fired in total. Davidson was rushed into surgery but died that evening. He left a wife and three children; colleagues and hospital leaders described him as an inspiring surgeon who devoted his career to saving lives and advancing cardiac care.
