Preliminary investigation suggested Pasceri targeted Davidson over dissatisfaction with prior medical treatment of his mother, Marguerite E. Pasceri, who died on Nov. 15 and had been treated by Davidson. Pasceri, described by neighbors as a family and church-oriented man who worked for Waters Corp., had no known prior incidents; his family expressed profound remorse and offered prayers for Davidson’s family.

The hospital briefly locked down; staff, patients, and visitors were told to barricade or shelter as police conducted a room-to-room search. Brigham officials praised the rapid, trained response developed with Boston police, noting active-shooter training and protocols (run, hide, fight) that helped manage the chaotic scene. Boston leaders called the killing a senseless act of violence and urged privacy for the grieving family.

An 18-year-old college student, Connor Golden of Fairfax, Va., lost part of his left leg after stepping on a homemade explosive in Central Park on the morning of July 3. Golden, a University of Miami student visiting New York with two high-school friends—Thomas Hinds, 20, and Matthew Stabile, 18—had been climbing on rocks near East 60th–68th Street and Fifth Avenue when an object in a brown bag detonated around 11 a.m. Witnesses described a loud blast; Hinds said he turned to find Golden “lying there, his foot completely gone,” moaning for help. Bystanders applied a tourniquet and kept him conscious until EMS arrived; Golden was taken to Bellevue Hospital and underwent surgery, with doctors amputating below the knee.

The NYPD bomb squad investigated and concluded the blast resulted from “explosive experimentation”—homemade fireworks likely assembled by an enthusiast rather than a device intended to maim. Investigators found evidence suggesting the device had been left for more than a day and that wet matches nearby indicated earlier failed ignition, perhaps due to rain; the bagged device did not appear pressure-sensitive and was not believed to be meant to detonate underfoot. Authorities do not suspect terrorism and have said the victim and his friends were not involved in constructing the device. The area was cordoned off and searched, including by bomb-sniffing dogs.

Friends and family described Golden as an Eagle Scout, musician, and honor student who loved the outdoors and had planned an upstate camping trip; relatives said he planned to continue at the University of Miami despite the injury. Officials cautioned that amateur fireworks experimentation spikes around July Fourth and urged people to leave fireworks to professionals, while asking the public to provide any information about who left the explosive.

Former Oklahoma City police officer Daniel Holtzclaw was sentenced to 263 years in prison after a jury convicted him on 18 counts, including first-degree rape, forced oral sodomy and sexual battery, for crimes committed while on duty. Prosecutors said Holtzclaw targeted African-American women in one of the city’s poorest neighborhoods between June 2014 and early 2015, selecting victims with drug or prostitution histories whom he assumed would be less likely to be believed. Thirteen women, ranging from a 17-year-old to a 57-year-old grandmother, testified that he coerced or forced them to perform sexual acts during traffic stops, arrests or while they were handcuffed in hospital beds. The case began to unravel after victim Jannie Ligons reported an assault; her complaint led investigators to other victims and ultimately to Holtzclaw’s arrest and firing. Defense attorneys have filed motions for a new trial and appeals alleging discovery violations, which were denied at sentencing. Civil lawsuits by victims against Holtzclaw and the city are pending. Civil-rights attorney Benjamin Crump praised the verdict as significant for survivors of sexual violence.

Actress Daniele Watts, known for roles in Django Unchained and the FX show Partners, was involved in a widely publicized confrontation with Los Angeles police after an incident outside the CBS lot in Studio City. Watts posted on Facebook saying she was handcuffed and detained by officers while “fully clothed” and accused them of harassment and racial bias for intervening as she and her white boyfriend, Brian James Lucas, were affectionate in public. She alleged the officers treated her disrespectfully and that her wrists were injured during the encounter.

Local law enforcement and other sources offer a sharply different account. Sgt. Jim Parker of the LAPD denies Watts’ version, calling her statements “malicious and false,” and says he recorded the interaction from the moment he arrived. According to Parker and witnesses at a nearby office, the couple were engaged in explicit sexual activity in their car—Watts reportedly straddling Lucas with her shirt pulled up and breasts exposed, and others watching from the Art Directors Guild office. A bystander reportedly called police to complain of public nudity and indecent exposure; at least one witness is said to have photographed the scene.

Parker says officers did not initially intend to arrest the couple but asked for identification after the situation escalated. The TMZ-released audio includes Watts asserting racial bias and saying she was being accused of prostitution; officers respond that she was interfering and not simply resisting. LAPD sources affirm the recording’s authenticity. The department has launched an internal investigation amid the case’s publicity. Parker asserts that the recordings protect the officers and that, without them, the officers involved might have faced immediate suspension. Watts’ representatives had not commented publicly at the time of reporting.

A violent clash erupted at Pearson Park in Anaheim, California, when six Ku Klux Klan members staged a small “White Lives Matter”/anti-immigration rally and were met by several dozen counter-protesters. The confrontation began shortly after the Klansmen arrived in an SUV wearing black garb and Confederate flag patches; witnesses said protesters had been peacefully gathered for hours before the Klan’s arrival. Video and eyewitness accounts show objects thrown, a smashed vehicle window, and a chaotic brawl in which one KKK member used a knife and another stabbed a counter-protester with the decorative eagle finial of a flag pole. Three people were stabbed—one critically—and several others assaulted; a nearby fire hydrant was splattered with blood. By the end of the melee, 13 people were arrested. Five Klan members were initially booked for assault with a deadly weapon but were released after police reviewed photos, video and interviews and concluded they had acted in self-defense. Seven counter-protesters remain in custody, facing charges including assault with a deadly weapon and elder abuse for allegedly beating and stomping an older Klansman. Police said officers were aware of the planned rally and had deployed personnel, but critics faulted the response amid the disorder. Brian Levin, director of CSUSB’s Center for the Study of Hate and Extremism, said he intervened to protect Klansmen from an enraged crowd and feared they would have been “torn limb from limb” without police. The injured man who was critical is now stable. The incident revived historical memory: Anaheim was briefly dominated by the Klan in 1924 before voters ousted Klansmen from city council. Today the KKK is a fraction of its former size, but experts note membership pockets persist and some groups claim renewed boldness amid national political currents; a Klan organizer said Donald Trump’s rise has opened “a door to conversation” for white nationalists, a claim Trump has publicly distanced himself from while saying he would “have to do more research” about white supremacist figures. Prosecutors will review the Anaheim case to determine whether charges will be filed.

Suffolk, Va., police responded around 10:45 a.m. Thursday after a reported shooting in the 300 block of East Washington Street that began with an argument. Witnesses said two men inside a barbershop argued about whether Halle Berry played or should play Aretha Franklin in a film. The dispute turned physical and 44-year-old Michael Jermell Hatton produced a firearm and shot 47-year-old Tony Jonathan Lundy at least once outside the shop. Both men received emergency care from Suffolk Fire & Rescue and were taken to hospitals; Lundy is in critical condition at Sentara Norfolk General Hospital. Hatton was treated, released, then arrested, taken to the Magistrate’s Office and is held without bond at Western Tidewater Regional Jail. A nearby business heard 4–5 gunshots. The investigation is ongoing.

Seattle investigator Chris Halsne (KIRO-TV) returned from El Salvador after interviewing a U.S. government subcontractor who says he observed about a dozen Secret Service agents and some U.S. military specialists drinking heavily and hiring escorts at a San Salvador strip club in March 2011, days before President Obama’s visit. The eyewitness described widespread intoxication, visits to the club’s VIP area for paid sexual favors, and at least two agents allegedly having escorts check into hotel rooms. Halsne also interviewed the club owner, who confirmed a large U.S. presence for several nights and said his venue is known for privacy and routinely serves U.S. embassy, FBI and DEA visitors; he denied on-premises prostitution and said performers are adults. KIRO-TV says it has names and records supporting the account and planned broadcast coverage. The report echoes recent Secret Service misconduct revelations in Cartagena and prompted calls from lawmakers, including Rep. Darrell Issa and Sen. Chuck Grassley, for independent investigations. The Secret Service said it will follow up on credible information; DHS Secretary Napolitano maintained there was no evidence of additional misconduct.

A Michigan woman, 25-year-old Kimberly Pappas of Wyandotte, has been ordered to stand trial on multiple murder-related charges after allegedly delivering a baby in a workplace bathroom and then hiding the newborn’s body in a desk drawer. The incidents occurred March 31 at CEVA Logistics in Redford. Co-workers discovered blood in the bathroom and called 911; firefighters later found the male infant, the placenta, and other remains inside plastic bags in a tote within Pappas’s desk drawer. The Wayne County Medical Examiner determined the child was born alive and died of asphyxiation within “several minutes,” citing bruising on the back of the head and facial petechiae consistent with suffocation. Pappas initially told responders she was ill after her period and later said she had delivered a child. She has denied telling family she was pregnant, though a detective reported she claimed to have known since Christmas. Her defense has said Pappas suffers serious mental health issues and sought treatment; competency and criminal responsibility evaluations found her fit to stand trial in July. Prosecutors charged her with first-degree premeditated murder, felony murder, and first-degree child abuse; her attorneys sought lesser manslaughter charges arguing intent could not be proven. 17th District Judge Karen Khalil called the case “very difficult” but bound Pappas over to Wayne County Circuit Court, where she will be arraigned Aug. 31 and faces up to life in prison if convicted.

A recent weekend in Washington highlighted the mainstreaming of alt-right figures and the troubling presence of public personalities who espouse extremist views. Tila Tequila — once an MTV reality star and now a vocal proponent of conspiracy theories and white-nationalist talking points — attended a National Policy Institute (NPI) conference and was photographed giving a Nazi-style salute while tweeting “Seig heil!” In a phone interview, she defended such gestures as trolling and free speech, reiterated conspiratorial claims about Jewish control of media, downplayed comparisons between Trump-era policies and Nazi actions, expressed enthusiasm for immigration pauses, and said she might serve in a Trump administration. She also voiced flat-Earth beliefs and flippant, provocative remarks throughout the exchange.

The NPI group held a private dinner at Maggiano’s Little Italy in Friendship Heights, prompting protests the following day that led the restaurant to close temporarily. Maggiano’s issued apologies, saying the booking had been made under a different name and pledging to donate $10,000 (Friday’s profits) to the Anti-Defamation League after an attendee’s pro-Hitler salute was shared online. Coverage noted the irony of a restaurant’s initial clumsy social post and underscored broader concerns: the blending of reality-TV fame, online trolling, and organized white-nationalist activity has moved extremist rhetoric into visible public spaces, provoking community backlash and renewed debate about platforming and accountability.

Video recorded by a passerby appears to show the moment two Bexar County Sheriff’s deputies shot and killed 41-year-old Gilbert Flores outside his northwest San Antonio home after responding to a domestic disturbance call. Deputies arrived around 11:30 a.m. and found a woman with a head wound and a baby who appeared injured. Officials say Flores was armed and resisted arrest; deputies tried non-lethal options, including a Taser and a shield, during a roughly 20-minute struggle that they say failed to subdue him. The confrontation ended in the driveway of a suburban home, where one witness video aired by KSAT shows a shirtless Flores standing near a sheriff’s SUV with his hands raised while two deputies, positioned about 10 yards away, take aim. Flores then doubles over and collapses; he died shortly afterward. It is unclear from the recording what was said immediately before the shots.

Sheriff Susan Pamerleau acknowledged the video is “a cause for concern” and urged patience while investigators review all evidence. Bexar County District Attorney Nicholas LaHood described the footage as “definitely... troubling” after viewing multiple recordings, including at least one with a closer view. He said he could not comment on investigative details, noting other sources such as 911 calls and witness statements are being examined. Deputies Greg Vasquez and Robert Sanchez, both with more than a decade of service, have been placed on paid administrative leave pending the outcome of the investigation. Flores’ criminal history includes prior convictions such as an aggravated robbery charge in 2003 and a trespass charge in 1999. The shooting is being reviewed by the sheriff’s office and the district attorney; investigators are analyzing two witness videos and other evidence to determine the circumstances that led to the deputies’ use of deadly force. The case adds to a broader local record of officer-involved deaths in Bexar County that has drawn public attention.

A Southern California man, Alex Donald Jackson, 29, has been charged with murder after a pack of pit bulls fatally mauled 63-year-old Pamela Devitt during a morning jog in Littlerock on May 9. Passing motorists called 911; deputies and paramedics found Devitt alive but she died en route to the hospital. An autopsy attributed her death to blood loss from sharp-force trauma, with approximately 150–200 puncture wounds. One dog was still attacking when the first deputy arrived; after it charged the officer twice, the deputy fired two shots. Deputies and animal-control officers later searched Jackson’s home—about a block away—and seized eight fully grown dogs (six pit bulls and two mixed breeds). Detectives found Devitt’s blood on the muzzles and coats of four dogs.

Prosecutors say Jackson had been the subject of at least three prior reports since January of his dogs attacking people, and neighbors described a low 3–4-foot fence that allowed animals to roam and said Jackson encouraged attacks or threw rocks at attempts to stop them. Jackson, who is accused of running a marijuana operation at his home, faces additional charges including cultivation and possession for sale, and assault with a deadly weapon; bail is over $1 million. Animal control currently holds the dogs and they will likely be euthanized. Murder prosecutions in dog-mauling deaths are rare; success typically hinges on proving the owner knew the animals posed a lethal danger and ignored prior warnings.

Thousands of Native Americans and allies staged what organizers called the largest-ever protest against the Washington Redskins’ name outside the University of Minnesota’s TCF Bank Stadium on Nov. 2, where the Redskins played the Minnesota Vikings. The demonstration, estimated by police at 3,500–4,000 and by organizers at 5,000, was peaceful but vocal: chants of “Who are we? Not your mascots!” rang out as protesters drummed, sang and held signs such as “RACIST,” “Change the Name Now” and “Stop Racism in the NFL.” More than two dozen speakers, including Rep. Betty McCollum, criticized the team name as a racial slur and urged the NFL to act; they highlighted Minnesota’s 11 tribal nations and the state’s painful Native history. Many Redskins fans passed through the plaza—some covering their logos or ignoring protesters—and exchanges were sometimes tense and profane but nonviolent. The University of Minnesota had asked the Redskins to wear throwback jerseys without the team name or logo, to refrain from selling Washington apparel on site, and to avoid speaking the name over the public-address system; the Vikings, leasing the stadium while their new venue is built, said they lacked authority to force a name change but were sympathetic. The protest followed growing national debate over the moniker, with polling showing a majority of Americans opposed to change, even as Native activists and tribes press for removal. On game morning two buses carrying the Redskins were involved in a minor collision on a highway ramp en route to the stadium; no serious injuries were reported and the game proceeded as scheduled.

In April, rapper Andre Johnson, known as Christ Bearer of the Wu-Tang-affiliated group Northstar, survived a dramatic and widely reported self-injury: he severed his own penis and jumped from the second-story balcony of a North Hollywood building. Speaking publicly for the first time with E! News and the New York Daily News, Johnson said the act occurred during a bout of PCP use but maintained he was “in complete control.” He described the decision as rooted in a personal, quasi-spiritual conviction—believing sex was “for mortals” while he considered himself a god—and said he viewed excising his genitals as a solution to problems he associated with sexual activity. Johnson denied suicide intent, noting he wasn’t conscious of height when he jumped and felt fortunate to have survived the fall and early hospitalization at Cedars-Sinai.

Contrary to some media assertions, Johnson said doctors did not reattach the amputated organ, though he insisted he “definitely have some penis left” and still experiences sexual arousal. He framed the outcome as a “blessing,” reaffirming his belief in his spiritual stance. Since the April incident he has welcomed a newborn daughter, Kennedy, joining two older daughters, and expressed optimism about the future. Johnson said he is continuing to write music, hopes to sign with an agent, and plans to explore stand-up comedy. He emphasized a message of peace, harmony and love, and indicated enthusiasm for returning to work and being present in his children’s lives. The story highlights issues of substance use, mental state, and the public aftermath of a highly unusual, self-inflicted injury by a public figure.

A midday shootout on Ellis Avenue in Irvington, N.J., left 15-month-old Sania Cunningham dead after a stray bullet tore through the second-floor apartment where she had been bouncing on a bed. The family had moved into the home just two days earlier to live with relatives. Witnesses described a chaotic exchange involving two men firing at a group of three men in black hooded sweatshirts; dozens of rounds struck nearby homes, a parked Lexus and an air conditioner. One bullet penetrated the wall of Sania’s apartment, striking her in the torso shortly after 4:30 p.m.; she was rushed to Newark Beth Israel Medical Center and pronounced dead about half an hour later.

Neighbors reported longstanding violence on the block—broken windows and memorial balloons are common sights—and expressed shock that the shooting occurred in broad daylight. Residents recounted bullets hitting walls and window frames inches from beds, and called the pattern of drug- and gang-related incidents a downward spiral. Community members and leaders, including Newark minister Thomas Ellis of the Enough is Enough Coalition, rallied at the scene to comfort the family and urge perpetrators to turn themselves in. Irvington’s mayor offered condolences and noted recent funding to hire more police.

Essex County investigators recovered ballistic evidence, reviewed surveillance footage and were interviewing witnesses. Authorities believe the Cunninghams were not the intended target and are searching for three suspects. The Essex County Sheriff’s Crime Stoppers is offering a $10,000 reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction; tips can be submitted at (973) 877-TIPS. The county prosecutor planned a press conference to discuss the case.

This report examines conflicting accounts and evidence in the killing of 17-year-old Trayvon Martin by neighborhood watch volunteer George Zimmerman. Zimmerman says he shot Martin in self-defense after a violent fight; his defense depends on that claim. New reporting includes statements from Richard Kurtz, the funeral director who prepared Martin’s body. Kurtz said Martin had a gunshot wound in the chest but showed no other visible injuries—no bruises or knuckle marks—that would indicate a scuffle or beating. He noted that the funeral home would have covered up such marks if they existed.

Surveillance video from about 40 minutes after the shooting shows Zimmerman being led in handcuffs by police and, according to observers and Martin’s family attorney Ben Crump, appearing without obvious injuries. Crump and others argue the footage undermines Zimmerman’s account that Martin beat him and broke his nose. Police reports, however, documented Zimmerman as “bleeding from the nose and the back of the head,” and Zimmerman’s father, Robert Zimmerman, has publicly maintained Trayvon attacked George, saying his son was punched, knocked to the ground, and struck repeatedly. Robert Zimmerman asserted his son fired a 9mm in self-defense after being beaten for more than a minute.

Some family members and supporters contend the initial police response suggested reluctance to arrest Zimmerman; others, including a witness cited here, say the lead investigator told them they did not believe the shooting was self-defense and that they needed to prove it. The decision whether to charge Zimmerman rests with a special prosecutor. The case remains contested, with starkly different narratives about the moments before the fatal shot.

The Happytime Murders, directed by Brian Henson, is an R-rated, adult-oriented puppet noir that imagines a Los Angeles where puppets coexist with humans but are treated as second-class citizens. The plot follows Phil Phillips (voiced and puppeteered by Bill Barretta), a blue-skinned former puppet cop turned private eye, and his human ex-partner, Detective Connie Edwards (Melissa McCarthy), who are reluctantly reunited to investigate a string of grisly murders targeting the stars of the once-popular puppet sitcom The Happytime Gang. The murders coincide with syndication negotiations, raising motives of greed and revenge. Along the way the duo navigates a sleazy puppet underworld—strip clubs, poker games with puppet drug use, and other gross-out set pieces—while encountering Phil’s loyal secretary Bubbles (Maya Rudolph), an exotic dancer played by Elizabeth Banks, and a cast of human characters who often feel cartoonishly hostile.

Critics agree the film showcases strong, skilled puppetry and occasional sharp performances—Rudolph’s comic timing and McCarthy’s one-liners are noted—but say the novelty wears off quickly. Reviewers criticize the film’s reliance on shock value, crude sexual and bodily-humor gags, and scattershot attempts at social allegory about puppet marginalization. Many draw unfavorable comparisons to Who Framed Roger Rabbit, Sausage Party and Team America, arguing that Henson’s movie lacks their wit, storycraft or committed satire. At about 75–90 minutes, the film feels overlong for its thin noir framework and repetitive raunch, leaving most critics to call it tired, unfunny, and a squandered premise despite competent puppeteering and a capable cast.

A widely circulated bystander video showing North Charleston patrolman Michael T. Slager shooting Walter Lamer Scott eight times in the back as he ran away has led to Slager’s firing and a murder charge. The footage, shot after a traffic stop for a broken taillight, contradicted the officer’s initial account that he fired in self-defense after Scott grabbed his Taser. The video shows Slager dropping what appears to be a stun gun, drawing his handgun, firing as Scott fled, then handcuffing the motionless man and returning the device near Scott’s body. Charleston County Coroner confirmed all five fatal wounds entered Scott from behind. Slager, a five-year department veteran, was denied bond and faces 30 years to life if convicted; his original attorney withdrew after the video surfaced.

The shooting ignited local protests—about 200 people rallied—and intensified scrutiny of North Charleston policing. Mayor Keith Summey and Police Chief Eddie Driggers condemned the act, fired Slager, and pledged reforms including outfitting every uniformed officer with body cameras (the city purchased 150 cameras to supplement 101 state-funded units). The FBI and the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division joined state investigators; prosecutors plan to seek an indictment. Scott’s family, represented by L. Chris Stewart, intends to sue; they emphasized that without the bystander video the case likely would not have moved so quickly.

Community leaders and activists said the episode reopened longstanding mistrust between residents and police, citing a history of aggressive patrols and racial tension. Officials vowed public discussions on policy and accountability, but many warned restoring trust will be difficult.

A violent riot erupted at the Cascavel penitentiary in southern Brazil on Sunday, leaving four inmates dead—two decapitated and two thrown from a roof—and several others injured. The uprising began during breakfast when prisoners overpowered wardens; as many as 700–1,000 inmates participated according to varying reports, with later statements putting active rioters at roughly 800, or 80% of the facility’s population. Footage showed inmates on rooftops, beating men with ropes around their necks and holding at least two guards hostage. Authorities and union lawyers reported that rioters used a severed head to psychologically torture a hostage. Negotiations resumed Monday, led by Parana state security officials, and an agreement was signed to end the stand-off; transfers of prisoners to other jails were underway and the hostages were to be freed once police secured the site. Officials have yet to recover all bodies or identify the victims. The riot is attributed both to grievances over poor conditions—food, hygiene, visiting rights, scarce legal assistance—and to gang rivalries exploiting the chaos. Brazil’s prison system is severely overcrowded and under-resourced, housing about 548,000 inmates in facilities built for far fewer, a situation human-rights observers say fuels recurrent, deadly disturbances.

A 3-year-old girl in Lorain, Ohio, remains in critical condition after being shot in the head Sunday morning by her 4-year-old brother, police say. The children were alone in a bedroom around 10 a.m. when the boy found a loaded .40-caliber handgun in a dresser, accidentally pulled the trigger and struck his sister. Responding officers found the father holding the wounded child; the boy was crying and repeatedly told an officer he was sorry. Investigators interviewed three other people who had been in the house and recovered the firearm at the scene. The girl was airlifted to Rainbow Babies & Children’s Hospital and listed in critical condition as of Monday. Lorain Police described the shooting as accidental and said the case will be turned over to the Lorain County prosecutor’s office to decide whether criminal charges will be filed. The incident highlights concerns about unsecured firearms in homes with young children.

Courtney Cash, the great-niece and granddaughter of Tommy Cash (and grandniece of Johnny Cash), was found stabbed to death and stuffed inside a large wooden chest in her home near Cookeville, Tennessee. Putnam County Sheriff David Andrews said her body was discovered just inside the front door Wednesday morning after a second 911 call led deputies to the Rice Road residence. Courtney lived in the home with her boyfriend, William Austin Johnson, who suffered multiple stab wounds but escaped with their 20-month-old daughter and drove to a hospital; his information helped point investigators to a suspect. Authorities arrested 27-year-old Wayne Gary Masciarella, a friend who had been invited over, and charged him with first-degree murder; he is held without bond and is due in court April 21. Officials described a struggle at the scene and said the assailant may have attempted to hide the body. Deputies have not confirmed a motive but indicated the stabbings may be drug-related. The Cash family has asked for privacy and prayers.

Two bombs exploded near the Boston Marathon finish line Monday, killing three people and injuring many others, leaving the city reeling and mobilized for recovery. Among the dead was 8-year-old Martin Richard of Dorchester, who was at the race to watch his father, a community leader. Martin’s mother Denise suffered a head injury and his 7-year-old sister has a serious leg injury; both were hospitalized. Hundreds gathered at a vigil in Garvey Park and left flowers and messages of peace outside the family home. Martin, a former student at Pope John Paul II Catholic Academy, was remembered as kind and eager to learn. The second identified victim was 29-year-old Krystle Campbell of Medford, a restaurant manager who had gone to cheer for a friend; her family endured the additional trauma of a hospital mix-up that first led them to believe she had survived. The third victim was later identified as a Boston University graduate student from China; the consulate and family asked that the student not be publicly named. In the immediate aftermath, authorities increased security across transit hubs and pledged an exhaustive investigation; the FBI said there were no known additional threats. Mayor Thomas Menino and other officials called for unity and resilience as the city sought to heal. Aid efforts included Salvation Army mobile kitchens and a staging center for displaced runners. National and international leaders, including President Obama and Pope Francis, offered condolences and praised first responders.

Kristopher Oswald, a 30-year-old overnight stocking employee at Walmart in Hartland, Michigan, was fired after intervening to help a woman who appeared to be assaulted in the store parking lot around 2:30 a.m. While on his lunch break in his car, Oswald heard screams and saw a man clinging to the woman’s hood. When he approached and asked if she needed help, the attacker allegedly struck Oswald and threatened his life. Oswald subdued the man briefly before two others joined and assaulted him; sheriff’s deputies later arrived and stopped the fight. Walmart gave Oswald termination paperwork citing a violation of company policy during his break and ended his temporary assignment; he had worked there about seven weeks and was still in a 180-day probationary period. Oswald says company policies bar employee violence or tackling shoplifters but offer no clear allowance for defending civilians in imminent danger. Walmart initially did not respond to Action News; a spokeswoman later said the company understood his intent but concluded his actions violated policy.

The article explores how biological abnormalities—specifically polycephaly, or multiple heads—may have inspired multi-headed monsters like the Lernaean Hydra in Greek myth. It opens with the Heracles tale, where the hero and his nephew Iolaus battle a regenerating many-headed serpent; the story’s shock value, the author suggests, could stem from real-world encounters with two- and even three-headed animals. Scientists and historical reports document such cases across taxa: fish, sharks, dolphins, turtles, snakes, kittens and salamanders, plus fossilized two-headed embryos. Early embryology experiments by Hans Spemann showed how manipulating fertilized eggs can produce two-headed salamanders, illustrating how developmental processes can be altered to yield polycephaly.

Developmental biologist Arkhat Abzhanov describes genetic and embryonic mechanisms behind these anomalies. The hedgehog (HH) gene family—especially Sonic Hedgehog (SHH)—helps shape facial width; reduced SHH can produce cyclopia, while increased signalling can widen facial structures, producing two-faced phenotypes. Separate head formation can arise when an organizer cell group that triggers head development is duplicated or transplanted, sometimes accidentally during embryonic manipulation. Environmental factors such as elevated temperature also correlate with higher abnormality rates in eggs and embryos.

Most polycephalic animals have poor survival prospects; many die before or shortly after birth, as illustrated by a two-headed salamander that fared poorly after metamorphosis. Abzhanov also notes non-mutational visual cues—like mating balls of snakes—that could have looked like many-headed beasts to ancient observers. The article argues that cultural fear and fascination with abnormal forms likely amplified rare natural occurrences into enduring mythic monsters. While biology continues to uncover causes of polycephaly, its rarity means it will remain an occasional curiosity rather than a common trait.

Stormy Daniels’ attorney Michael Avenatti released a memo alleging that Michael Cohen, President Trump’s personal lawyer, received about $4.4 million through an Essential Consultants account between October 2016 and January 2018 — including roughly $500,000 from Columbus Nova, a U.S. firm tied in filings to Russian oligarch Viktor Vekselberg. Avenatti said eight wire transfers from January–August 2017, totaling about $500,000, came from Columbus Nova; he also flagged payments from Novartis, AT&T and Korea Aerospace Industries. NBC, AP and CNN reviewed documents that appear to corroborate many of the transfers, though Avenatti did not disclose his sources and Cohen disputed the accounting as “inaccurate.” Columbus Nova and its counsel denied that Vekselberg controlled or funded the payments, saying the firm is American-owned and had retained Cohen post‑inauguration as a business consultant. Novartis and AT&T confirmed limited engagements with Essential Consultants; KAI’s status was less clear. The transactions drew interest from investigators: Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s team and Manhattan federal prosecutors have examined Vekselberg and Columbus Nova, questioned Vekselberg when he traveled to New York, and reviewed campaign and inaugural donations by Columbus Nova CEO Andrew Intrater, who contributed large sums to Trump-related committees. Cohen’s finances and his use of Essential Consultants (the same entity used to pay Daniels $130,000) are under scrutiny following FBI raids on his properties. While none of the companies or individuals cited has been charged, the payments raise questions about access, influence and possible ties linking Cohen to foreign actors during the post‑election transition.

Actress and Harvey Weinstein accuser Rose McGowan is facing a criminal charge after airport authorities said narcotics were detected in personal items she left at Washington Dulles International Airport earlier this year. The belongings in question were left behind on a flight arriving from Los Angeles on Jan. 20; testing by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority Police Department reportedly returned positive for narcotics. Police have issued a bench warrant for McGowan, entered it into a national law enforcement database, and say they have attempted to contact her so she may appear in Loudoun County, Virginia court to respond to the charge. A department spokesman described the charge as a felony.

McGowan, long a public accuser of Weinstein—alleging he raped her in 1997 and that one of his associates offered her $1 million to stay silent—reacted angrily on social media to news of the warrant, tweeting, “Are they trying to silence me? What a load of horseshit.” She has framed her refusal of alleged hush money as a broader stand, tweeting “Refusing Weinstein’s hush money, Rose McGowan calls out Hollywood,” and asserting solidarity with victims by adding, “We are an army of thorns.”

Her social-media posts also referenced recent allegations against other prominent men in Hollywood, including Kevin Spacey, posting a cryptic line invoking Spacey and others. Authorities provided limited comment beyond the narcotics finding and the bench warrant; specifics about the substance detected, the quantity, or any planned arraignment were not detailed in initial statements. The development adds a legal complication to McGowan’s high-profile role in exposing sexual misconduct in the entertainment industry.

West Virginia state Senate candidate Richard Ojeda was violently assaulted at a campaign cookout on Sunday, May 8, 2016, just days before his Democratic primary. Witnesses and Ojeda say Jonathan Porter, 41, asked for a campaign bumper sticker, then attacked Ojeda while he knelt to apply it. According to multiple reports, Ojeda was struck repeatedly — witnesses stated with brass knuckles — rendering him unconscious and leaving him with extensive injuries: multiple facial fractures (reports cite eight bone fractures), three lacerations, severe head swelling and a concussion. Ojeda awoke with his head on a tree stump and blood on his face. He was transported to CAMC General Hospital in Charleston for treatment and later underwent or was scheduled for facial surgery; he intended to delay surgery briefly to try to participate in the primary.

Porter fled the scene in his pickup; bystanders tried to intervene and block his escape with ATVs, which Porter allegedly rammed and drove over while fleeing. After hiding for several hours, Porter turned himself in and was arrested on multiple felony charges, including malicious assault, attempted malicious assault and felony destruction of property. Authorities have not confirmed use of brass knuckles; Porter reportedly denied using them and largely declined to speak to police. Troopers said no clear motive had been established, and investigators found no evidence of co-conspirators.

Ojeda, a military veteran who has campaigned against local corruption and nepotism, said the assault felt politically motivated and vowed it would not silence him. He reported prior threats during his campaign, including violent warnings. His primary opponent, incumbent state Sen. Art Kirkendoll, condemned the violence and wished Ojeda a speedy recovery. Local officials characterized the incident as isolated and did not plan added security at polling places.

Diane Sylvia, a 58-year-old licensed clinical social worker from Linwood, N.J., was arrested after allegedly attempting to hire what she believed was a hit man to assault a Massachusetts man she accused of years-long financial extortion. According to a federal criminal complaint unsealed in Camden, Sylvia recruited an undercover FBI agent — introduced to her by a patient who had past ties to an unspecified organized criminal gang — and repeatedly discussed violent specifics, including breaking an arm and disfiguring the victim’s face without using acid. In her office meetings, prosecutors say, she described wanting the victim’s “pretty little face bashed in” and suggested injuring him so he “can’t do push-ups” or work out. Sylvia told the undercover agent the target had obtained information she feared would be reported to her licensing board and cost her her job.

Over nearly a month of communications, she took steps investigators say showed premeditation: purchasing a prepaid cellphone for covert communication, supplying the alleged hit man with the victim’s license plate, and ultimately paying $5,000 to the undercover agent. During an audio- and video-recorded Halloween meeting in her office, she even discussed disposing of the prepaid phone off a bridge after the assault.

Sylvia was charged in federal court with one count of solicitation to commit a crime of violence, released on $50,000 bail, and faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine if convicted. Her professional profile on Psychology Today emphasized the power of words and the therapeutic relationship; investigators and prosecutors declined or did not provide comment beyond the complaint. Her attorney was not immediately available for comment. The arrest followed an FBI sting that prevented the planned attack.

A manhunt intensified in southeastern Ohio after a deadly attack at a house trailer near Decatur left four people dead and a fifth critically injured. Authorities say three adults were found shot to death Wednesday evening in the trailer; a fourth adult who discovered the scene after work was stabbed but escaped to get help and was airlifted to a West Virginia hospital and is reported doing well. A 7-year-old boy, Devin Holston, initially reported missing, was later found shot and concealed inside the trailer. Warrants were issued for 23-year-old Arron (also reported as Aaron) Lawson of Pedro on three counts of murder and one count of aggravated murder; additional charges may follow. Deputies briefly pursued Lawson early Thursday after spotting him in a blue Chevrolet truck; he crashed, fled on foot into a large, rugged, wooded strip-mine area with caves and has not been captured. Investigators from the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation assisted in a methodical search of the trailer; officials say they recovered a suspected murder weapon. Sheriff Jeff Lawless noted Lawson was related to some victims and lived nearby. Rock Hill and several local schools closed and community fundraisers were organized to help the grieving families as the search continued.

Midwest City police announced a major break in the 1997 disappearance of 8-year-old Kirsten Hatfield after charging 56-year-old Anthony Joseph Palma with kidnapping and first-degree murder. Kirsten was taken from her bedroom window on May 14, 1997. Investigators originally recovered physical evidence at the scene—partially ripped, blood-stained underwear, blood on the bedroom windowsill, cigarettes, a syringe and a beer bottle—but many items were never DNA-tested or produced inconclusive results with the technology available at the time.

The case was reassigned in June 2015 to Detective Darrell Miller, who reviewed the cold-case evidence and requested updated laboratory analysis. In July 2015 the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation matched DNA from the 1997 evidence to Palma; court documents and officials describe the statistical certainty as astronomically high. Palma, who has lived near the victim’s family home since 1991 and has a prior conviction from the 1980s, was arrested at his Midwest City residence and held without bond in Oklahoma County Jail. Police say evidence suggests Palma may have targeted Kirsten for sexual assault and that he likely killed her shortly after abduction; her body has not been located.

Family members, including Kirsten’s mother Shannon and stepfather Chris Hazen, expressed exhaustion mixed with hope. Authorities stress the investigation is ongoing, that additional suspects remain possible, and that considerable follow-up work continues.

On October 24, 2014, freshman Jaylen Fryberg opened fire in the Marysville-Pilchuck High School cafeteria, fatally wounding a female student before fatally shooting himself. Four others, all under 18, were critically or seriously wounded and hospitalized—two girls at Providence Regional Medical Center and two boys at Harborview. Witnesses said Fryberg targeted friends at a table, firing multiple rounds; students described chaos, blood, and frantic escapes. The weapon, a Beretta .40-caliber handgun traced to the shooter’s father, was reportedly high-capacity. Fryberg, a popular student recently named freshman homecoming prince and a Tulalip tribe member, had posted anguished messages on social media. Authorities treated the scene as an active investigation, searched the family home, interviewed witnesses, and closed the school while counseling and crisis services were mobilized.

On the night of February 14, Paralympic star Oscar Pistorius shot and killed his girlfriend, model Reeva Steenkamp, at his Silver Woods home in Pretoria. Veteran detective Hilton Botha arrived minutes after a 4 A.M. call and found Steenkamp’s body at the bottom of the stairs; the bathroom cubicle door was riddled with bullet holes. Botha, who had previously arrested Pistorius on an assault allegation in 2009, concluded quickly that the evidence pointed to murder rather than a tragic mistake: bullet trajectories, casing locations, the locked toilet cubicle and the improbability of a burglar hiding there led him to believe Pistorius fired at close range—likely standing and wearing prosthetic legs—contradicting the athlete’s claim that he shot through the door believing an intruder threatened him and Reeva. Botha’s insistence that the killing was intentional cost him his place on the investigation and eventually his police career; facing internal reprisals and revived charges from an earlier case, he resigned but remains a key, contested witness.

The article sketches Pistorius’s rise from double amputation to international fame—the “Blade Runner” who ran in the 2012 Olympics—and presents accounts of a man whose celebrity may have magnified arrogance, aggression, heavy gun ownership and troubling incidents: a boating crash, threats, altercations and accusations of controlling behavior toward women. Reeva Steenkamp is portrayed as ambitious, compassionate about violence-against-women advocacy, and newly ascendant in modeling and TV. Her family and friends denounce Pistorius and mourn her vividly.

The trial became a national spectacle exposing South Africa’s intimate-femicide crisis, deep social anxieties about crime and race, and the media’s role in shaping public perception. Supporters and detractors rallied—women’s groups demanded justice, while Pistorius’s family and prominent friends defended him. The piece leaves open whether Pistorius genuinely mistook Reeva for an intruder, but underscores that the case forced a reckoning over fame, violence, and accountability in South Africa.

A University of Utah student, 21-year-old track athlete Lauren McCluskey, was shot and killed on campus after being extorted and stalked by her ex-boyfriend, 37-year-old convicted sex offender Melvin Rowland. McCluskey broke off their month-long relationship on Oct. 9 after learning Rowland had lied about his age and was a registered sex offender. Days later she received messages and a demand for $1,000 to prevent compromising photos from being posted online; she paid and reported the extortion to campus police on Oct. 13. Investigators now believe numerous emails and messages sent to lure her to locations were from Rowland, whom police describe as a “master manipulator.” Surveillance placed Rowland on campus for days; he spent hours socializing in McCluskey’s dorm before confronting her in a parking lot, dragging her into his car and shooting her multiple times. He later died by an apparent self-inflicted gunshot in a church as police closed in.

Rowland had been paroled in April after serving nearly a decade for forcible sexual abuse and enticing a minor and had prior parole violations. Authorities knew he was a registered sex offender but say they were not aware he was on parole; parole officers were not notified of McCluskey’s complaint. University Police Chief Dale Brophy acknowledged the extortion investigation formally began six days after the report due to workload, and said early information did not indicate a threat of physical violence. The university announced independent reviews of campus safety and police response; state officials also approved investigations into parole handling. University president Ruth Watkins and others expressed support for reviews and condolences; McCluskey was posthumously awarded her degree. Public reactions included tributes from community and sports figures.

A gunman attacked the Reina nightclub in Istanbul on New Year’s Eve, killing at least 39 people—mostly foreigners—and wounding dozens before fleeing. Islamic State claimed responsibility, calling the attacker a “soldier of the caliphate.” Witnesses described rapid, indiscriminate machine-gun fire; police said about 120 rounds were fired and the incident lasted under ten minutes. The gunman shot a policeman and a civilian outside before entering and continued firing inside, even targeting people already on the floor. Authorities detained eight people and were seeking the shooter, recovering fingerprints from the scene. Victims included citizens of Canada, India, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia and several other countries; notable dead included Bollywood producer Abis Rizvi. Survivors recounted playing dead to survive—35-year-old American William (Jake) Raak of Greenville, Delaware, was shot in the hip and knee and said remaining motionless saved him; seven of his nine companions were also shot. The attack shocked Istanbul’s Ortaköy district, and families and governments arranged to repatriate remains.

Chicago prosecutors have charged 22-year-old Dwright Boone-Doty with the November execution-style killing of 9-year-old Tyshawn Lee, alleging the boy was lured from Dawes Park into an alley and shot in the head because of his father’s alleged gang ties. Authorities say Boone-Doty, a reputed Bang Bang Gang member, and accomplices targeted rivals in a violent feud with the Killaward faction of the Gangster Disciples after the October killing of Tracey Morgan. Prosecutors contend Boone-Doty initially planned to torture Tyshawn, even cutting off his fingers and ears and killing the boy’s grandmother, but instead shot Tyshawn multiple times; part of the child’s thumb was reportedly shot off as he raised a hand to block shots. An inmate informant, secretly recording Boone-Doty in jail, captured him bragging about the murder and composing a rap that referenced it. Boone-Doty is also charged in the October 18 shooting that killed 19-year-old Brianna Jenkins and wounded Dashari Bowens; ballistics link one recovered gun to that killing. He was held without bail and faces further charges alongside co-defendants including Corey Morgan and an outstanding suspect, Kevin Edwards (also named Kevin Williams in reports). The case sparked outrage: Interim Superintendent John Escalante and State’s Attorney Anita Alvarez called the slaying exceptionally savage, highlighting how gang vendettas in Chicago increasingly ensnare innocent victims. Community members voiced fear and sorrow, as the neighborhood grapples with the loss of a child.

Molly Wei, a 19-year-old former Rutgers freshman, has admitted her role in viewing a secretly streamed webcam recording of roommate Tyler Clementi’s sexual encounter and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors. Wei waived grand jury presentation and entered a three-year pretrial intervention (PTI) program that, if completed—along with 300 hours of community service and counseling on cyberbullying and alternate lifestyles—will lead to dismissal of two invasion-of-privacy charges. She has also agreed to testify against classmate Dharun Ravi, who is accused of placing a camera in the dorm room and streaming the encounter from his own laptop. Ravi faces a 15-count indictment including invasion of privacy, bias intimidation, tampering with evidence and witness tampering; he could face up to 10 years in prison and is due to be arraigned May 23. Clementi, 18, jumped from the George Washington Bridge days after the Sept. 2010 incident and later died, galvanizing advocacy over bullying, LGBT bias and online privacy violations. Clementi’s parents, consulted by prosecutors, indicated Wei’s actions differed in nature and extent from Ravi’s and expressed the need for accountability.

Three people, including two young children, died in Delhi after their throats were slit by glass- or metal-coated kite strings (manja) used during Independence Day kite-flying. Three-year-old Saanchi Goyal and four-year-old Harry were fatally injured while looking through sunroofs, and 22-year-old Zafar Khan died after his neck was cut while riding a motorbike. Sharpened manja routinely causes human injuries and kills birds; Delhi hospitals admitted hundreds of injured birds over recent days. Following public outcry and a PETA petition, Delhi has banned production, sale and storage of coated manja, imposing fines and potential jail terms.

An 18-year-old in England who presented with abdominal pain, fever and loss of appetite was initially diagnosed with appendicitis but was found during emergency surgery to have a lacerated, bleeding liver. Treated at North Middlesex University Hospital, the unidentified patient required "repacking" — placement of a special pad and overnight pressure — to control hepatic bleeding; the liver was repacked a second time the following day before bleeding stopped. Only after surgery did clinicians learn the patient had played paintball two days earlier and had been hit twice on his lower right abdomen. The treating team reported this case in BMJ Case Reports as the first documented instance of paintball-related blunt liver injury and only the fourth reported paintball-associated solid-organ injury (previous reports involved kidney and genital trauma). The patient had no external bruising near the liver, underscoring that seemingly minor impacts can cause serious internal damage. He recovered well: discharged after bleeding had ceased, later imaging showed pooled blood being reabsorbed and normal liver function, and no underlying bleeding disorder was found. The authors note paintball pellets, traveling at muzzle velocities of roughly 100–300 ft/s (30–90 m/s), can harm ocular and intra-abdominal structures. They advise participants and clinicians to be aware of potential dangers from this recreational sport.

A weeklong multistate manhunt ended when siblings Lee Grace Dougherty, 29, Ryan Edward Dougherty, 21, and half-brother Dylan Dougherty Stanley, 26, were captured after a high-speed chase and crash on Interstate 25 in Colorado. Affidavits released after their arrests say Lee Grace admitted pointing a machine pistol at Walsenburg Police Chief James Chamberlain; he fired first, wounding her in the right upper thigh. She told agents, "I deserved to get shot," and said she let go of the gun immediately. Authorities recovered two AK-47s, a MAC-11 submachine gun and a handgun at the scene. During the chase, which reached speeds up to 120 mph, Dylan reportedly fired an AK-47 at pursuing officers, while Ryan drove; Lee Grace claimed they "weren't trying to hurt anyone" but felt they were being shot at. Colorado troopers noted no officers fired at the vehicle and suggested the suspects may have mistaken stop-stick sounds for gunfire. The siblings are accused of firing about 20 rounds at a Florida officer on Aug. 2 and of robbing a Valdosta, Ga., bank the same day, where one fired into the ceiling. Each faces multiple charges, including attempted murder and assault on officers, and bond was set at $1.25 million apiece. Their next hearing is Aug. 15; jurisdiction for prosecution remains to be determined.

A 16-year-old girl in Madhya Pradesh, India, was allegedly raped and then set on fire at her home in Jujharpur/Jhujharpura village, dying from her burn injuries. Police say the attack took place when the girl was home alone after her cousin informed the accused, named in reports as 28-year-old Ravi Chadhar (also reported as a 28-year-old man arrested with the cousin). Authorities arrested the suspect and the cousin; the post-mortem confirmed death by burns while forensic steps are being taken to confirm whether rape occurred. This incident is the third similar attack reported in India within a week, intensifying public outrage over sexual violence. Earlier in the week, a 17-year-old in Jharkhand was critically injured after being set on fire by a man who allegedly wanted to marry her and was rejected. Another case involved a 16-year-old who was burned to death after her parents reported her rape to village elders; the accused had been ordered to do sit-ups and pay a fine, then allegedly beat the girl’s parents and killed her. The spate of brutal assaults has reignited national anger over rape and its use as a tool to intimidate the powerless, following high-profile cases since 2012 and recent controversies involving political figures.

A Groupon Super Bowl commercial mocking the political situation in Tibet sparked offense in both the U.S. and China and could hurt the company’s plans to expand into China. The ad, narrated by Timothy Hutton, opens like a PSA about Tibetans being “in trouble” before revealing it promotes a Groupon deal for Tibetan food in Chicago. Reports—unconfirmed by Groupon or Tencent—had suggested Groupon was preparing to enter China via a partnership with Tencent and major hiring. Using Tibet as comedic fodder risks alienating Chinese officials whose approval Groupon would need to operate there; Chinese viewers on social networks criticized the spot as mixing politics with business. The ad was one of three parody PSA spots Groupon ran; the company’s blog framed the campaign as poking fun at celebrity-narrated appeals and pledged to match donations to the charities singled out, including the Tibet Fund. A subtitled version briefly appeared on a Chinese video site and drew backlash. Beyond controversy, Groupon would face strong local competition in China’s burgeoning group-buying market, where startups and millions of users already exist. Groupon’s PR firm later clarified the ads intended to spotlight causes like Greenpeace, The Tibet Fund and Rainforest Action Network, and to reflect Groupon’s roots in collective action and philanthropy. The backlash highlights how humor about sensitive political issues can complicate global expansion.

Stephen Port, a 41-year-old London chef, has been sentenced to spend the rest of his life in prison after being convicted of murdering four young men he met on gay dating apps. Over a 15-month period from June 2014 to September 2015, Port drugged the victims with fatal doses of GHB, raped them while they were unconscious, then dumped their bodies near his Barking flat. The victims were Anthony Walgate, 23; Gabriel Kovari, 22; Daniel Whitworth, 21; and Jack Taylor, 25. The judge imposed a whole-life order, concluding Port intended to cause really serious harm and must have foreseen the high risk of death after the first killing. The court heard that Port planned and executed his crimes with significant premeditation, using fake online profiles to target “twinks,” obtaining drugs in advance, and attempting elaborate cover-ups including planting fabricated suicide notes to mislead investigators.

Port was convicted on 22 offences against 11 men, including drugging and sexual offences against seven survivors. Families delivered powerful victim impact statements describing enduring grief and lives shattered; courtroom reaction included cheers when the whole-life term was announced. Police investigators and senior officers acknowledged missed opportunities to link the deaths, and the Metropolitan Police now face scrutiny: 17 officers are under investigation by the Independent Police Complaints Commission for possible misconduct and whether discrimination played a part. The force is re-examining 58 unexplained GHB-related deaths across London. Port’s family maintain his innocence; his lawyer argued he had become consumed by a sexual compulsion rather than intent to kill. Detectives called Port among the most dangerous individuals they had encountered and said a full-life term was the only appropriate punishment. Authorities have urged other potential victims to come forward.

A judge declared a mistrial in the second trial of Quinton Tellis, 29, who has been charged with the 2014 killing of 19-year-old Jessica Chambers, who was found burned alive in her car in Courtland, Mississippi. This marks the second time a jury has failed to reach a unanimous verdict in the case; a 2017 trial also ended in a hung jury. The second jury began deliberations on a Sunday but could not agree to convict or acquit. District Attorney John Champion said prosecutors will need to assess next steps; he did not announce whether they will seek a third trial, noting logistical constraints including time limits on other matters in Louisiana where Tellis faces separate homicide charges.

Chambers was found on December 6, 2014, alive but with severe second- and third-degree burns; she later died and reportedly told medical personnel “Eric did this to me.” The case attracted national attention and intense online scrutiny. With no immediate suspects, the investigation expanded to involve the FBI, U.S. Marshals, and the ATF; officials posted billboards across three states and offered a $54,000 reward. Investigators later cited “technological data,” including cell phone records obtained via subpoenas, as the basis for an arrest and indictment in February 2016. Champion said those records helped key elements fall into place.

Chambers’ father said at the time that his daughter “is at peace now” and noted Chambers had not named Tellis to the family. Legal observers told media a third trial appears unlikely because the defense would have an advantage from knowing more of the prosecution’s case. Tellis is expected to be returned to Louisiana to face charges in the 2016 murder of University of Louisiana Monroe student Ming-Chen Hsiao; timing for that trial remains unclear. Authorities and media describe this as a developing story.

A Broward Community Charter School teacher, 58-year-old Jennifer King Forshey, was arrested and charged with felony battery of a child after police say she ordered a 10-year-old student to unclog a urinal with his bare hands. According to a Coral Springs police report, Forshey accused the boy of clogging the urinal with paper towels and directed him to remove the soggy wad using his hands and a dry paper towel. The child told investigators the paper and urinal were wet enough that his hands became saturated with what smelled like urine, and the bathroom reportedly had no soap. Forshey admitted to making the student clean the fixture but reportedly told police she only thinks what she did was wrong because she is in trouble and otherwise did not see an issue. She was booked, released on $1,000 bond, and reprimanded by the school. The victim’s family is seeking to learn whether other children were treated similarly, while some parents and colleagues expressed shock and conflicting views about Forshey’s character.

Twin car bombs struck intelligence and security buildings in Damascus on Saturday, killing at least 27 people and wounding nearly 100, state media reported, with officials warning the toll could rise. Explosions hit the aviation intelligence and criminal security departments around 7:30 a.m.; state TV and SANA aired graphic images of charred corpses and widespread damage and said most victims were civilians. A third blast was reported later near a military bus in the Yarmouk refugee camp. No group claimed responsibility. The government blamed "terrorists" and accused foreign backers; opposition figures denied involvement and suggested the regime might be orchestrating attacks to discredit the uprising. U.S. officials have indicated al-Qaida in Iraq could be exploiting the turmoil, an allegation that worries minorities and complicates foreign responses. The bombings follow a string of recent large attacks on security sites and come amid a year-long crackdown on the anti-Assad uprising that the U.N. says has killed over 8,000 people. International condemnation followed, and clashes and killings were reported elsewhere in Syria the same day.

A gruesome attack on the MacArthur Causeway left 65-year-old Ronald Poppo clinging to life with massive facial trauma and identified his assailant as 31-year-old Rudy Eugene, who was shot dead by police at the scene. Poppo remains in critical condition at Ryder Trauma Center with much of his face torn away; photos of the scene spread rapidly online. Witnesses described Eugene as frenzied, naked, growling and biting pieces of the victim’s flesh; officers shot him after he ignored commands and continued the assault. Security video and multiple eyewitness accounts captured the horrific episode, which sparked intense public interest and speculation about causes, including possible drug-induced psychosis (bath salts or “cocaine psychosis”), though investigators have not confirmed a definitive motive. Eugene, once a North Miami-area high school football player, had a history of arrests for mostly misdemeanors and a brief, troubled marriage that ended in 2007. Court records show minimal assets at one point. Locals and homeless people who frequented the area said Eugene had appeared confused in recent times. Authorities continue to seek witnesses and information as they probe what led to the savage attack and whether substance use or other factors precipitated it.

CBC dismissed acclaimed Q host Jian Ghomeshi after receiving unspecified “information” the broadcaster said made continuing his employment impossible. The decision followed The Star’s interviews with three women who allege Ghomeshi physically assaulted them during dates or sexual encounters: hitting with an open hand or closed fist, biting, choking until near unconsciousness, covering nose and mouth to impede breathing, and verbal abuse during and after sex. A fourth former CBC employee accused him of workplace sexual harassment, saying he cupped her from behind in the studio and made a crude sexual remark; her complaint to a union rep prompted little action and she later left the broadcaster.

Ghomeshi has denied any non-consensual conduct. In a Facebook statement he said he engaged in adventurous sexual role-play, dominance and submission, always with consent and safe words, and blamed an unnamed ex-girlfriend for orchestrating a smear campaign. He said he had been open with CBC and provided evidence that interactions were consensual; CBC disputes that and placed him on leave earlier in the week before terminating him. Ghomeshi’s lawyers announced a planned $50-million lawsuit against CBC for breach of confidence and bad faith and said he would file a grievance for reinstatement. His legal team and crisis consultants were retained; CBC executives reportedly held closed-door meetings to protect the broadcaster’s brand.

The Star’s reporting, developed over months through repeated, detailed off-the-record interviews, notes none of the alleged victims filed police reports, citing fears of lawsuits, online retaliation, and that messages or prior role-play discussions could be used to claim consent. The accounts describe initial flattering behavior, followed by escalating aggression and unwanted sexual acts; one woman says she was struck and choked upon entering his home. Ghomeshi’s firing cost him planned public roles and sparked intense public debate over celebrity, consent, workplace complaints, and online backlash against accusers.

A two-year-old black Labrador named Bear, one of only a handful of dogs in the U.S. trained to detect electronic storage devices by scent, played a pivotal role in the investigation and arrest of former Subway pitchman Jared Fogle on child-pornography and related charges. Trained by Todd Jordan, Bear located a thumb drive that human investigators had missed during a July search of Fogle’s Indiana home; that device contributed to evidence used in the case. Bear has participated in at least five investigations, including the recent arrest of gymnastics coach Marvin Sharp, and will soon be transferred to the Seattle Police Department after the Fogle raid. Jordan demonstrated Bear’s abilities by hiding devices around a room; Bear found a memory card, flash drive, and iPad in under ten minutes. Jordan explained the training parallels that of narcotics or explosives dogs: the animal is conditioned to recognize the odor associated with electronic devices and is rewarded—Bear’s reward is food—when he indicates a find. Prosecutor Steven DeBrota, initially skeptical, called Bear “a key part of the team.” Jordan said he sometimes sells fully trained dogs to law enforcement and described it as bittersweet to part with Bear, praising the dog’s temperament. Jordan is currently training two more electronic-sniffing dogs to meet growing investigative demand.

An international law enforcement operation led by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, called Operation Sunflower, resulted in 245 arrests and the identification of 123 victims of child sexual exploitation. Conducted in November and December, the probe uncovered victims as young as under 3 and spanning ages up to 17; 70 were female and 53 male, and 24 identified victims are now adults who were abused as children. Investigators removed 44 children from alleged abusers; the remaining cases involved exploitation by non-household perpetrators or historical abuse. Most arrests occurred in the United States (222), with others made across six countries; California accounted for the largest single-state share, including Bay Area and Fresno arrests and rescues. Some suspects are registered sex offenders; one high-profile arrest involved a man detained on child sex tourism allegations. ICE emphasized the critical role of forensic analysis and international cooperation in tracing and prosecuting offenders and urged the public to provide tips on unsolved cases, including one involving images believed to show abuse in the Los Angeles/San Fernando Valley area about 11 years ago.

Jeffrey Sandusky, son of former Penn State assistant coach Jerry Sandusky, pleaded guilty to all 14 criminal counts Friday in a case alleging he pressured teenage girls into sexual acts and explicit images. The guilty pleas, entered a week before his scheduled trial and nearly six years after his father’s highly publicized arrest, address allegations involving two girls — one from 2013 and another from 2016. Charges included solicitation of statutory sexual assault, solicitation of involuntary deviate sexual intercourse, soliciting sex from a child under 16, and soliciting child pornography. Prosecutors say he pressured one teenage girl to send naked photographs and asked her teenage sister to perform oral sex. As part of the plea agreement, the 41-year-old Sandusky faces up to six years in state prison, although a judge could impose a sentence of as much as eight years. Following the plea, Sandusky will be designated a Tier III sex offender, the highest classification under Pennsylvania law, which brings stringent registration and monitoring requirements. The Centre County district attorney’s office announced the pleas; a request for comment to Sandusky’s attorney was not immediately returned. The case continues to unfold within the broader, long-running legal and public scrutiny tied to the Sandusky family and the original child molestation scandal that deeply affected Penn State and remains active in criminal and civil courts.

Chinese authorities arrested 10 people in Yanjin County, Yunnan province, on suspicion of killing a wild female giant panda, then butchering and selling its meat and parts, state media reported. Forest police seized the panda’s skin, bones, an internal organ and about 22–35 kilograms (reports vary) of meat during a December raid. Two brothers told police they had been hunting an animal that had killed their sheep; after shooting at a creature in a tree, they discovered it was a giant panda and shot it again when it fled, the Yunnan Forestry Bureau and CCTV said. DNA tests confirmed the carcass was an adult female. Xinhua reported the brothers sold meat and four paws for about 4,800 yuan (~$800), and parts were then resold. The case provoked public outrage on social media, though some commenters noted demand drives such crimes. China has about 1,864 wild pandas, and while poaching has declined, experts warn habitat loss from development remains a major threat. If convicted, the suspects could face years in prison as authorities intensify crackdowns on wildlife crimes.

Fabio Sementilli, a 49-year-old internationally known hairdresser and vice president of education for Wella (now part of Coty Inc.), was found beaten and fatally stabbed at his gated Woodland Hills home on Monday evening, Jan. 23, 2017. Paramedics discovered him bleeding profusely on the back patio; he had multiple stab wounds to the face, neck and upper torso and was pronounced dead at the scene. His wife and daughters discovered the body. Detectives believe two men broke into the residence and fled in Sementilli’s black 2008 Porsche 911 Carrera with paper plates, which was missing when police arrived. Homicide investigators are reviewing neighborhood security camera footage—residents reported officers collecting video and creating a timeline—and have appealed to the public for information. Neighbors described a normally quiet, upscale street unsettled by the violent crime and noted a rise in local break-ins. Sementilli, Canadian-born and a decorated competition stylist, had been with Wella since 2007, becoming creative director for North America and later VP of education. Colleagues and industry figures mourned him as a mentor, visionary and beloved educator whose generosity and leadership touched thousands across the hairdressing community. The LAPD Homicide Bureau continues its investigation.

Show Dogs, a family comedy about a Rottweiler police dog who goes undercover at a dog show, was re-cut after parents and advocacy groups said two scenes sent the wrong message about sexual abuse. Global Road Entertainment announced it would remove two sequences and release a revised version nationwide that weekend. The contested scenes depict the main character, Max (voiced by Ludacris), undergoing genital inspection by dog-show judges — a routine part of real dog shows — during which he is instructed to go to a “zen place” and tolerate the handling in order to advance. Parents and groups argued that portraying a character being coached to dissociate and accept unwanted touching resembles grooming tactics used by sexual predators and could confuse children about bodily autonomy and consent.

An Arizona mother’s viral essay framed the scenes as particularly troubling, and the National Center on Sexual Exploitation (NCOSE) demanded distribution be halted until changes were made. NCOSE’s executive director said children’s films should teach the ability to say “no” and respect for bodily boundaries, not normalize unwanted genital touching for reward. Global Road defended the scenes as accurate depictions of dog-show protocol and apologized to anyone who found the portrayal inappropriate, calling the moment a comedic element with no ulterior intent.

Writer Max Botkin praised the decision to recut the film and clarified he did not write the disputed scenes, saying his original script was heavily rewritten by many others. The studio’s edits aimed to address audience concerns while keeping the movie’s family rating intact.

A newborn boy survived after being discarded in a trash can in Greenville, South Carolina, on April 21 and was later released from the hospital into foster care, officials said. The infant was discovered wrapped in a pink blanket and a plastic grocery bag inside a backyard trash can after a neighbor followed a trail of blood and a rental-home owner noticed blood outside the can during maintenance. Emergency responders treated the near-death baby at the scene; by Monday night he was stable and then released to the Department of Social Services. Police arrested 28-year-old Sharon Lenise Ferguson, who according to warrants told investigators she gave birth around April 21, placed the newborn in a bag and blanket, and willfully abandoned him. She was found walking nearby, booked, and held in Greenville County jail on $125,000 cash bond; she faces attempted murder and child endangerment/unlawful neglect charges. A family spokesperson said Ferguson is homeless and has a diagnosed mental illness, and relatives were unaware of the pregnancy. Neighbors described her as displaying unusual behavior but said they did not believe she intended to harm anyone.

Six students at St. Michael’s College School in Toronto were arrested and charged after a video showing an alleged sexual assault circulated online, touching off a wider investigation into hazing and abusive behaviour at the elite all-boys Catholic school. The teens, all aged 14 or 15, face charges including assault, gang sexual assault and sexual assault with a weapon. Five turned themselves in and one was arrested on his way to school; all appeared in court and were released on bail with conditions barring contact with the complainant, attendance at the school and unsupervised social media use.

Police said the criminal charges stem from a short locker-room video that appears to show a boy held down and sexually assaulted with what looks like a broom handle. A second washroom video shows another boy placed in a sink, splashed and slapped. Investigators are probing at least three other incidents on campus; there are “a minimum of four victims,” and multiple videos are reportedly circulating. Police warned that anyone in possession of the footage should delete it immediately because it can constitute child pornography.

St. Michael’s has expelled eight students and suspended one in relation to at least two video-recorded incidents. Principal Greg Reeves acknowledged a serious cultural problem at the school, apologized for failures to protect students, and said the school is cooperating with police, hiring a full-time social worker and providing crisis counseling. The school announced an independent “Respect and Culture Review” to examine traditions, rituals and student practices, led by an outside three-member committee with a report due by summer and recommendations to be implemented before the 2019–20 school year.

Questions arose about the timing of police notification; officials said the school did not immediately report the locker-room video and police first learned of it through media. The episode prompted condemnation from city leaders and renewed scrutiny of institutional cultures that enable hazing and abuse.
