A video circulated by Mexican media appears to show a soldier executing a handcuffed or detained man face down in the street during a May 3 clash in Palmarito, Puebla, prompting condemnation and demands for investigation. The grainy security-camera footage, first published by Diario Cambio and reviewed by authorities, shows a silver car riddled with bullet holes stopping on a darkened street. People exit the vehicle and are forced to the ground; soldiers arrive minutes later. One man lies face down for several minutes while soldiers stand nearby; a soldier then steps into frame and there is a flash from a gun above the prone man’s head. The man’s body jerks and a dark stain spreads from his head. What preceded those minutes and what followed immediately after the shot are not shown, and the Associated Press could not independently verify the video’s authenticity. Mexico’s defense ministry urged federal prosecutors to “comprehensively clear up” whether the video depicts a detained man being shot and pledged cooperation with investigators, saying conduct contrary to law and human rights cannot be justified. The National Human Rights Commission also demanded a swift, thorough probe and said it holds copies of the footage. Officials link the incident to confrontations between soldiers and suspected fuel-pipeline thieves—part of a violent nationwide clampdown on fuel theft that government estimates costs hundreds of millions annually. The army has faced previous accusations of extrajudicial killings, most notably at Tlatlaya in 2014, intensifying public scrutiny of military conduct amid Mexico’s broader violence and impunity concerns.

Aslan Usoyan, 75, a leading figure of the post‑Soviet underworld known as “Grandpa Hassan,” was killed by a sniper in central Moscow as he left the Karetny Dvor restaurant. Shot once in the head, he was rushed to hospital but died en route. A female bystander — reported to be a waitress escorting him — was also gravely wounded. Investigators found evidence pointing to a professional, concealed shooter firing a silenced weapon from a stairwell opposite the restaurant; cartridges and other items were recovered, though authorities say some scene elements might have been staged. Usoyan, an ethnic Kurdish Yezidi who rose to “thief in law” status after early convictions in Soviet Georgia, survived earlier assassination attempts in 1998 and 2010. Police believe his killing is linked to organized‑crime rivalries; a murder and illegal arms probe has been opened amid fears his death could trigger violent turf wars across Russia and former Soviet states.

A brutal, apparently random attack in east Anchorage left an elderly couple dead and their 2-year-old great-granddaughter sexually assaulted, authorities say. Touch Chea, 73, and Sorn Sreap, 71, were found Saturday night with severe blunt-force injuries. Police say both Sreap and the toddler were raped; the child underwent surgery and was treated at a hospital. Family members who had taken their 4-year-old to a movie returned before 8 p.m., found the apartment door chained, broke in through a window and discovered the bodies and an unclothed man in a bedroom. A struggle ensued with the suspect as the family tried to stop him; he escaped but was arrested a block away wearing boxer shorts. The suspect, identified as 24-year-old registered sex offender Jerry Andrew Active, was charged with first- and second-degree murder, sexual assault, sexual abuse of a minor and burglary and arraigned with $1.5 million bail. Detectives said the victims likely did not know the attacker and described the crime as unusually violent and random. Investigators are probing Active’s whereabouts and substance use before the attack; autopsies and further inquiries continue.

Leigh Anne Arthur, a longtime teacher at Union County Career & Technology Center in South Carolina, resigned after a nude photograph of her was copied from her phone and circulated by a student. The district says a student obtained her phone while she briefly left the classroom on hall duty, photographed an existing nude image on her device, and shared it via text and social media. The incident came to the district’s attention on a Monday; Arthur resigned the following Tuesday. Arthur maintains the photo was a private image taken for her husband and was on her phone gallery. She says the student accessed her unlocked phone within minutes, took pictures of the image with his own phone, boasted “your day of reckoning is coming,” and then distributed the image to classmates. Arthur reports that the student later admitted his actions to the principal and that witnesses corroborated his admission; she and the student’s parents initially sought to resolve the matter, and the parents were reportedly supportive. The district, represented by interim superintendent David Eubanks, said Arthur bore some responsibility for leaving her phone accessible and faulted her for making the image available to students; Eubanks indicated potential concerns about contributing to delinquency of a minor. The Union County Sheriff’s Office is investigating and now holds the student’s phone; potential charges have not been announced. In response, students and community members launched a petition seeking Arthur’s reinstatement, which drew thousands of signatures. Arthur has said she filed a lawsuit alleging false accusations and procedural failures by the school district and its superintendent. She has also stated she intends to pursue legal action against the student.

Shasta County authorities and Sherri Papini’s husband, Keith, have provided new details about her condition after she was found alive on Thanksgiving, three weeks after disappearing while jogging on Nov. 2. Investigators say Papini, 34, was located bound by restraints about 150 miles from her California home after apparently flagging down help. Sheriff Tom Bosenko confirmed police are treating the case as a kidnapping and are actively investigating; they have interviewed Papini multiple times since her return and are searching for two Hispanic women driving an SUV based on her description. Bosenko said there is no known motive yet and it remains unclear whether Papini was specifically targeted or taken at random.

Keith Papini, speaking to Good Morning America, described his wife’s injuries and appealed for privacy amid intense public scrutiny and online speculation that the abduction might be a hoax. He said Sherri’s face was “covered in bruises ranging from yellow to black” from repeated beatings, her nose bridge was broken, she weighed about 87 pounds after being found, and her long blond hair had been chopped off. He also recounted additional injuries including multicolored bruises, burns, chain markings and branding, and said she had been thrown from a vehicle with a chain attached to her wrists and waist. Keith thanked the many supporters, law enforcement agencies and volunteers who aided the search, condemned malicious online rumors, and emphasized the family’s need for privacy as Sherri begins a long recovery. ABC News contributed to the reporting.

Two Steubenville, Ohio, high school football players, 17-year-old Trent Mays and 16-year-old Ma’Lik Richmond, stood accused in a juvenile court trial of digitally raping a 16-year-old West Virginia girl after an alcohol-fueled party last August. Prosecutors alleged the intoxicated girl was taken advantage of—first in a car and later in a basement—left naked and photographed; Mays also faced a charge of illegal use of a minor in nudity-oriented material. If found delinquent (the juvenile equivalent of guilty), both could be held in juvenile detention until they turn 21.

The accuser testified she remembers drinking at the party, leaving around midnight with the two players, then waking up the next morning naked in a stranger’s basement with no memory of how she arrived there. Her phone, underwear, shoes and earrings were missing. Over subsequent days, friends showed her a circulated photo of her naked and a YouTube video in which students joked about the episode, prompting her to piece together what likely happened. She testified that Mays later sent frantic texts begging her not to report the incident; in one he admitted taking the basement photo and described semen on her, claiming the encounter had been consensual.

Defense attorneys denied the charges and sought to undermine her credibility, calling former friends who testified she had a reputation for lying and heavy drinking. An expert witness suggested she drank enough for a memory lapse but not to be fully incapacitated, implying possible consent. Several teenage boys granted immunity testified that they saw the defendants digitally penetrate the girl. The case divided the community, raising questions about the football team’s influence and whether more students should have been charged.

Researchers from the University of Portsmouth conducted a six-month investigation of Tor hidden services and found that most user traffic appeared concentrated on child sexual abuse sites. Presented by Gareth Owen at the Chaos Computer Congress, the study ran 40 Tor relays from March to September, catalogued roughly 45,000–80,000 hidden services, and used a crawler to classify site content and count visits. While drug markets and contraband forums made up the largest single category of hidden services by number, visits to a relatively small set of pedophilia sites dominated measured traffic: after excluding automated botnet-related traffic, 83–75 percent of observed visits went to child-abuse destinations. Many of those sites were explicitly labeled, and the crawler fetched only text to avoid illegal image possession.

The authors also observed that a large share of traffic to hidden services originated from botnet-infected machines polling now-defunct command-and-control servers; the top 40 destinations were mostly such malware control points. Most hidden services were short-lived—less than one in six persisted throughout the study—so a small number of long-lived abuse sites could account for disproportionate hits. Tor developers and others cautioned that the measurements are difficult to interpret: law enforcement, anti-abuse crawlers, denial-of-service attacks, or automated clients can all inflate visit counts, and Tor hidden services represent a small fraction of total Tor traffic. Roger Dingledine emphasized legitimate uses of hidden services for privacy and activism and noted methodological limits in inferring human intent from fetch counts.

Owen acknowledged uncertainty about how many hits were human-driven and presented, but did not advocate intervention; he outlined a theoretical mechanism to block specific hidden services by altering Tor’s distributed hash table but emphasized its controversial nature. The study spotlights troubling darker uses of anonymizing infrastructure, raises questions about prioritizing law enforcement efforts, and underscores tensions between privacy tools and criminal abuse.

Trojan has launched a high-profile advertising campaign for Tri-Phoria, a new vibrating “personal massager,” using euphemistic language and infomercial-style humor to navigate broadcast restrictions. The spot, produced by Sullivan Productions, avoids the word “vibrator” while implying sexual pleasure through lines about “screams of ecstasy” and “intense waves of pleasure.” Historian Rachel Maines notes this echoes early 20th-century marketing that masked such devices as relaxation aids; she says the ad nearly admits its purpose while retaining a thin “fig leaf.” Some cable networks, including Comedy Central and VH1, cleared the ad for daytime slots, while MTV limited it to overnight hours because of its younger audience. Trojan is spending millions on the campaign—the company’s biggest vibrator push—and expects wider retailer distribution in 2011. Trojan-funded studies cite substantial vibrator use among adults and notable partner usage. Critics worry about sexualized advertising reaching younger viewers; industry and public-health voices urge caution and time-slot limits for explicit product ads.

A Pakistani court sentenced four men to death for the brutal May murder of 25-year-old Farzana Parveen, who was beaten to death outside Lahore High Court after marrying Muhammad Iqbal against her family’s wishes. Her father, brother and two cousins were convicted; another cousin received 10 years for abetting. The case, captured in daylight and linked to so-called honor killings, provoked international outrage and political comment. Defense counsel called the verdict politically motivated; prosecutors said DNA and forensic evidence proved guilt. Rights groups report thousands of honor-killing victims in Pakistan since 2008; appeals are expected.

A Liberty, Missouri couple and their 16-year-old son were violently robbed and shot Wednesday evening after responding to a Craigslist ad to buy a 2007 Hyundai Sonata, police say. The father, 53, and son test-drove the car with a man who identified himself as “AJ.” After returning, two other men approached, produced black handguns and demanded money. When the suspects pointed guns at the mother, 55, the father stepped in front of her; the assailants opened fire. The father was shot four times in the chest, stomach and legs and required surgery. One bullet shattered the mother’s right upper arm. Their son was uninjured but witnessed the attack. The suspects grabbed the woman’s purse containing $3,000 and fled in the Hyundai, which was later found abandoned nearby; some reports said the robbers also stole the family’s vehicle. Earlier Wednesday afternoon, police believe the same three armed men robbed a man selling an Xbox after answering a Craigslist ad; both crimes occurred within two miles and involved three gunmen. Detectives are questioning four people as persons of interest. Ferrellgas donated $5,000 to boost the Crime Stoppers reward to $7,000 for information. Authorities urge caution when meeting online buyers or sellers: meet in public, avoid carrying cash, and consider using a police station or crowded location. Tips: 816-474-TIPS.

A 62-year-old man, identified as Régis Levasseur, died after being gored by a stag while taking part in a hunt in the Compiègne forest northeast of Paris. The incident occurred around 10am as Levasseur, acting as a beater helping to drive game, was charged and pierced by the deer's antlers; he was not carrying a rifle and died of internal bleeding before emergency services arrived. Police called such a death “uncommon.” Guy Harlé, president of the local hunters’ federation, said the animal unusually charged instead of fleeing and warned the accident underscored the inherent dangers of working with wild animals. Levasseur, who was due to be married, was described by Harlé as someone for whom hunting was life. The fatal goring came a week after public outrage over hunters and hounds cornering and shooting a stag in a nearby town, prompting criticism from France’s environment minister and animal rights protests. The article notes that hunting accidents in France—often involving weapons mishandling or misidentification of targets—have killed 18 people in the past year and 351 since 2001, mostly among participants.

Gossip rags report PDA and cheating scandals among Kardashian circle. After a Jay-Z/Kanye West concert, witnesses say Kanye was very affectionate with Kim Kardashian, sparking rumors they were more than friends. Kendall Jenner landed a Teen Prom cover and says she ignores online negativity. Rooney Mara criticized an early Law & Order: SVU role but later discussed merkin craft. Taylor Armstrong filmed a reaction to abuse footage to raise awareness. Giuliana Rancic is recovering well from a double mastectomy. Amber Rose tells Star magazine Kim helped break up her relationship with Kanye—claiming Kim and Kanye exchanged flirtatious messages and photos while Kim was with Reggie Bush—labeling Kim a “homewrecker,” though Amber credits the fallout with leading her to current boyfriend Wiz Khalifa.

The December 2012 gang rape and death of a 23-year-old student in New Delhi ignited nationwide outrage, sustained protests and intense debate about women's safety and social attitudes. The brutal attack on a bus—by six men who beat her companion, inflicted fatal injuries and dumped the pair—shocked India and spurred candlelight vigils, street demonstrations and media focus. Authorities responded with tougher laws: longer minimum sentences, criminalizing stalking, voyeurism and sexual harassment, and creating fast-track courts. Convictions followed relatively quickly, with four men sentenced to death and others punished. Reporting of sexual crimes rose sharply—Delhi’s reported rapes nearly doubled in early 2013—and activists say publicity has encouraged more women to speak up. Critics caution that legal change alone isn’t enough: conviction rates have fallen nationally and many say societal mindsets still favor men. Voices from politicians to human-rights scholars stress that sustained social change, improved policing and consistent justice are needed to ensure the victim’s death brings real progress.

Sureshbhai Patel, a 57-year-old recent immigrant from India, arrived in Madison, Alabama, to help his son and daughter-in-law care for their 17-month-old grandson. Less than a week after his arrival, a neighbor called police reporting a “suspicious” man walking in the neighborhood. On the morning of February 6, officers Eric Parker (a field trainer) and trainee Andrew Slaughter approached Patel on a sidewalk. Patel spoke no English and could not understand officers’ questions. Dashcam audio shows repeated attempts to obtain ID and address, mounting confusion, and warnings from officers that Patel should not “jerk away.” At one point Parker yanked Patel’s arm and forcefully slammed him to the ground; Patel could not break his fall. He was taken to hospital and underwent cervical fusion surgery the next day. He initially had no feeling in his arms or legs and remains partially paralyzed, slowly regaining some sensation in an arm and one leg; doctors warn of a long recovery. Patel had no insurance.

Following release of the video, Madison Police Chief Larry Muncey said Parker’s actions “did not meet the high standards” of the department, recommended Parker’s termination, and apologized to Patel and the community. Parker surrendered to Limestone County authorities and faces third-degree assault charges; he was released on $1,000 bond. The FBI opened a parallel civil-rights inquiry that could lead to DOJ review. The Patel family has retained attorney Hank Sherrod and filed a federal lawsuit alleging excessive force and an unlawful stop and search. Local Indian community members and Indian Consul Anil Kumar attended a press conference, decrying the treatment. Support and donations have poured in: a GoFundMe set a $25,000 goal and raised over $13,000 to help cover mounting medical bills, and local groups are discussing cultural-sensitivity and communication training for police.

Japanese authorities are investigating the discovery of eight badly decomposed bodies aboard a roughly 7m wooden boat that washed ashore near Oga city in Akita prefecture. Found on Sunday and inspected on Monday, the vessel lacked a rotor blade and navigational equipment; some remains were reduced to bones. The coast guard and police suspect the boat originated from North Korea, noting parallels with recent incidents: two skeletal male bodies were recovered over the weekend on Sado Island alongside North Korean-brand cigarettes and life jackets with Korean lettering, and eight men claiming to be North Korean fishermen washed ashore earlier last week in Yurihonjo city in reasonably good health. Such crew-less or corpse-laden vessels—dubbed “ghost ships”—frequently arrive on Japan’s western coast facing the Korean peninsula. Authorities and experts link the phenomenon to North Korea’s pressured fishing quotas and worsening food shortages, which push fishermen onto aging, poorly equipped boats that range far out to sea and lack distress capabilities. Seasonal rough weather in late autumn further raises the danger. So far this year about 44 wooden ships believed to be from the Korean peninsula have drifted to or been found near Japan, versus 66 for all of 2016, highlighting a worrying and continuing pattern of maritime tragedies.

Dallas priest Rev. Edmundo Paredes, who served 27 years at St. Cecilia Catholic Church in Oak Cliff, is missing after being accused of molesting teen boys and stealing at least $60,000 from his parish. The Diocese of Dallas said Paredes was suspended in June 2017 after admitting to financial misconduct. In February, separate allegations surfaced that he had sexually abused three teenage boys more than a decade earlier; those claims were deemed credible and were reported immediately to law enforcement. Bishop Edward Burns notified parishioners recently that Paredes can no longer administer sacraments or present himself as a priest and that the diocese has hired private investigators to locate him. Parishioners say Paredes may have returned to the Philippines, his homeland, where he frequently vacationed.

The timing of the public disclosure — months after the sexual allegations were reported to the diocese — drew criticism, particularly in the wake of a damning Pennsylvania grand jury report detailing abuse by hundreds of priests. Survivors Network leaders and abuse survivors questioned why parishioners and the public weren’t informed earlier, suggesting the diocese may have delayed to avoid scandal. Diocese officials say they withheld public notice to protect the police investigation and victims’ anonymity, and that Burns only went public after consulting the Diocesan Review Board and in light of national revelations about clergy abuse. The case remains under criminal investigation.

Elrey “Bud” Runion, 69, and his wife June, 66, a charitable Marietta couple, were found shot to death after vanishing while on a trip to southern Georgia to buy a classic car. Bud had posted a Craigslist ad seeking a 1966 Ford Mustang convertible on Jan. 19; three days later the couple drove to meet a purported seller and disappeared. Their daughters reported them missing when they failed to arrive to babysit grandchildren. Authorities located the couple’s SUV in a lake near McRae, Telfair County, and discovered two bodies in nearby woods; both victims had been shot in the head with a small-caliber handgun. Investigators traced the last known cellphone contact to 28-year-old Ronnie Adrian “Jay” Towns of McRae, who was arrested after turning himself in with family present. Towns initially faced charges of making false statements and attempted theft by deception; prosecutors later charged him with malice murder, armed robbery and related counts. At a magistrate hearing, bond was denied and Towns was taken to jail; he has pleaded not guilty. Sheriff Chris Steverson said robbery appears to be the motive and described investigators as having a “mountain of evidence,” though he declined to detail what led to Towns. The killings shocked both the Runions’ Marietta community—where the couple was known for running “Bud’s Bicycles” and other charitable efforts—and small-town McRae. Towns’ family protested his innocence, while the Runions’ relatives and neighbors mourned and remembered their decades of generosity.

The piece criticizes Tony Dungy for saying he would not have drafted Michael Sam, the NFL’s first openly gay draftee, claiming he “wouldn’t want to deal with all of it” and that “it’s not going to be totally smooth.” The author frames Dungy’s remark as cowardly and inconsistent with the progress that allowed African-Americans to gain opportunities despite expected discomfort from bigots. The argument praises past leaders who set aside prejudice to let talent prevail, enabling figures like Dungy himself to rise from high school in Jackson, Mich., to the NFL, a bestselling author, and prominent NBC analyst.

Dungy’s reputation as a moral authority and compassionate mentor—someone who supported controversial second chances, such as Michael Vick’s—makes his comment more disappointing, the writer contends. The piece argues that, unlike an openly stated faith-based objection which would at least be candid (if hypocritical), Dungy offered a cop-out: he would deny opportunity not out of principle but to avoid dealing with others’ discomfort. The article also recounts media reaction, including a Rush Limbaugh excerpt, emphasizing how Sam’s presence will create intense scrutiny no team can easily avoid. Limbaugh defends Dungy’s status yet acknowledges the situation’s complexity for teams and the league, noting potential accusations if Sam is cut or given limited chances. Overall, the author condemns Dungy’s stance as lacking courage and betraying the idea that the best person should be allowed to win regardless of the discomfort their presence may provoke.

Papa John’s has released its first new advertisement since founder John Schnatter was removed as chairman, directly confronting customer outrage over Schnatter’s comments blaming NFL protests for weak sales and his admitted use of the N-word. The social-media ad displays real customer Tweets condemning racism and demanding change, accompanied by messages from the company: “You expected better from Papa John’s. So did we,” and a pledge to “review our culture from top to bottom” and earn trust through action. The campaign echoes crisis-response ads from Facebook, Uber and Wells Fargo and signals a concerted effort to distance the brand from Schnatter—removing his image from marketing, revoking his office privileges and opposing his attempts to regain influence. Schnatter’s spokesman criticized the video as misleading and said some fans want his return.

Papa John’s announced mandatory bias training beginning in October for corporate and corporate-owned stores (about 20% of U.S. restaurants); leadership has already completed training. The program covers unconscious bias, racial and cultural sensitivity, and bias management. CEO Steve Ritchie outlined an internal audit of diversity and inclusion, a minority-owned franchise support program, a community-focused foundation, and a listening tour to guide reforms. The company has also hired Bank of America and Lazard to stabilize the business. Ritchie emphasized a commitment to add diversity to leadership and called the initiatives the start of broader change.

Muhammad Iqbal, whose pregnant second wife Farzana Parveen was lynched by about 20 male relatives outside Lahore High Court, has admitted he previously strangled his first wife six years ago so he could marry Parveen. Iqbal, 45, said he killed his first wife “because of love” for Parveen; police confirm he was arrested then released after his family used Islamic legal provisions that allowed the victim’s kin to forgive him, averting a lengthier prison term. Iqbal’s admission and claim that Parveen’s family had earlier killed another daughter have intensified scrutiny of so-called “honour” killings in Pakistan. Parveen, three months pregnant, was reportedly battered with bricks and had a noose tightened around her neck as she arrived to testify against her family’s allegation that she had been abducted and coerced into marriage. Her father, among those accused and so far arrested, reportedly said the killing occurred because she had “dishonoured” the family; he has shown no regret, according to police. The brutal public murder prompted national and international condemnation. Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif ordered an urgent report and directed Punjab’s chief minister to act, while UN human rights chief Navi Pillay called for strong measures to end honour killings and criticized the state’s failure to protect an at-risk woman. Human rights groups note many such crimes go unreported and cite legal provisions—like Diyat and financial settlements—that let perpetrators evade punishment when victims’ families forgive them. The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan and activists warn the official toll understates the problem, with media and public responses varying from outrage to ambivalence in a society where such violence persists.

On Aug. 9 in Ferguson, Missouri, 18-year-old Michael Brown was fatally shot by a Ferguson police officer, sparking protests, unrest and a federal civil rights and FBI inquiry. Accounts of the shooting sharply contrast. Witnesses, including Brown’s friend Dorian Johnson and nearby residents, say Brown and Johnson were walking when a white officer confronted them, attempted to open his car door aggressively, grabbed Brown by the neck, and then fired. According to these witnesses, Brown fled with his hands raised and was shot multiple times while trying to surrender; they insist Brown was unarmed. Some bystanders tried to record the encounter, and reports variably describe five to ten shots. Brown’s family and community members portrayed him as a recent high-school graduate, about to begin trade-school classes, a “gentle giant” with plans and no history of violence.

Authorities, led by St. Louis County Police Chief Jon Belmar, offered a different narrative. Belmar said preliminary investigation indicated a physical confrontation began when the Ferguson officer tried to exit his vehicle, Brown pushed him back in, assaulted the officer and struggled for the officer’s weapon; a shot was fired inside the car and Brown was later shot roughly 35 feet from the vehicle. Shell casings recovered were from the officer’s gun. The identity of the officer—on paid administrative leave and treated for a reported swollen face—was initially withheld; officials said he will undergo psychological evaluations before returning to duty.

The shooting ignited deep frustration in Ferguson, a predominantly black community with a history of distrust toward a largely white police force. Protests ranged from peaceful vigils and calls for nonviolent action by the NAACP to nights of looting, fires, and clashes with police who used tear gas. Brown’s family retained attorney Benjamin Crump, urged calm, and demanded a fair, thorough investigation. Authorities emphasized the need for time to reconcile conflicting accounts as federal and local investigators pursue answers.

Police released fresh surveillance footage and a sketch as part of the ongoing investigation into the Aug. 2 murder of 30-year-old Karina Vetrano, who vanished during an afternoon run in Howard Beach’s Spring Creek Park and was later found sexually assaulted and strangled in a marshy area off the trail. The newly publicized video shows Vetrano jogging near the park—hair in a ponytail, wearing earbuds—moments before she disappeared; authorities hope it will prompt new leads. Investigators have obtained DNA from three sources (her neck, phone and fingernails), with fingernail DNA strongest, and all samples pointing to a single individual, but no match has appeared in local or national databases. Police also circulated a sketch of a man in a woven wool cap spotted nearby; officials say he is someone they need to speak with, not necessarily a suspect. The reward for information exceeds $300,000. Authorities urge anyone with tips to contact NYPD Crime Stoppers at 1-800-577-TIPS.

A fresh wave of violence erupted in Cairo’s Tahrir Square ahead of parliamentary elections set for November 28, as riot police clashed with thousands protesting military rule. Security forces used tear gas, rubber bullets and pellet cartridges; officials reported at least one to two deaths and more than 600–676 wounded, many with serious head injuries. Protesters had camped after a large rally demanding the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces (Scaf) restore civilian rule; police tore down tents, sparking running battles as demonstrators retook the square, set vehicles ablaze, built barricades and drew in ultras and Islamist groups. Demonstrators denounced Field Marshal Mohamed Hussein Tantawi and accused the military and interior ministry of brutality and seeking to entrench power through the election and a contested draft constitution that shields the army. Solidarity protests spread to Alexandria and Suez. Prominent figures, including Mohamed ElBaradei, proposed postponing elections and shifting control from the military while a new constitution is written; the generals have not responded.

John Bieniewicz, a 44-year-old longtime soccer referee and pediatric dialysis technician from Westland, Michigan, died after being punched during an adult recreational match in Livonia on Sunday. Witnesses and police say Bieniewicz was about to eject a 36-year-old player, identified as Baseel Abdul-Amir Saad of Dearborn, when Saad struck him in the head; Bieniewicz fell unconscious and never regained consciousness, dying at Detroit Receiving Hospital on Tuesday. Saad surrendered to police and was arraigned on a charge of assault with intent to do great bodily harm; bond was set at $500,000 and a probable-cause hearing scheduled. The Wayne County prosecutor’s office said charges would be reviewed and possibly amended now that Bieniewicz has died. Friends and colleagues remembered Bieniewicz as a devoted family man, an avid soccer official who refereed at professional, collegiate, high-school and recreational levels, and a popular medical assistant at C.S. Mott Children’s Hospital who worked with pediatric dialysis patients. A memorial fund and GoFundMe were created to support funeral costs and Bieniewicz’s two sons. The incident revived concerns about violence against sports officials; the National Association of Sports Officials says assault issues have grown and discourage new referees. Medical experts noted a single unexpected blow can produce catastrophic brain injury by rapid acceleration-deceleration and swelling, explaining how one punch proved fatal.

A New York City police sergeant, Michael Iscenko, 54, has been suspended after an alleged incident in January in which he reportedly threw semen onto the leg of a female administrative aide he “liked.” According to police sources cited by local outlets, Iscenko approached the woman from behind while they walked down a hallway, and she felt a substance on her leg, asked him, “What are you doing?” and he walked away without answering. The aide immediately reported the incident to supervisors; testing confirmed the substance was semen. DNA testing to link the sample to Iscenko is pending. Iscenko, a divorced Long Island resident assigned to the Organized Crime Control Bureau, has not been criminally charged. Colleagues described him as appearing professional in uniform, and sources noted he does not fit a “creepy” stereotype, underscoring the unusual nature of the allegation. Separately, the Internet Archive’s web crawls are mentioned as part of an effort to preserve web pages and their references to prevent broken links, ensuring archived versions remain available as originals change or disappear.

A gunman opened fire at Umpqua Community College at 10:38 a.m. Thursday, killing multiple people and wounding others in a chaotic campus rampage. Officials later confirmed 10 dead and nine wounded; three of the injured were in critical condition, and one later died at Mercy Medical Center. Mercy received ten patients and performed four surgeries; most treated there were expected to survive. Some reports varied during the unfolding incident, with early counts ranging higher and the shooter ultimately described as “neutralized,” with unconfirmed reports he had been shot or shot himself.

Witnesses described sudden, terrifying scenes: students heard a noise like a yardstick or a thud, then rapid gunfire. One student, Kortney Moore, recounted shots through a classroom window and seeing her teacher shot; she said the shooter demanded people state their religion before firing. Others fled screaming, some swimming across a creek. Dozens sheltered in locked rooms or were locked down in the cafeteria. Students’ phones were confiscated during evacuations; individuals were marched out building by building, hands raised, patted down, and bused to the Douglas County Fairgrounds where Red Cross and grief counselors awaited about 200 relatives and friends.

Local, state and federal law enforcement, including the FBI’s Portland Division, responded. Authorities cleared campus buildings amid ongoing investigations, and officials including Rep. Peter DeFazio expressed condolences and pledged to pursue preventative measures. Timelines issued during the day recorded evolving casualty figures and ongoing scene management as responders worked to care for victims and identify the shooter and deceased.

A Madison, Wisconsin man’s plan to secretly record “upskirt” videos was thwarted not by law enforcement but by a malfunctioning device and his own conscience. The unidentified 32-year-old bought a camera designed to attach to a shoe with the intent of recording under women’s skirts. While testing it at home, the camera’s battery exploded, causing minor burns to his foot. He sought medical attention and later confessed the incident to a clergyman, who urged him to turn himself in and accompanied him to the West Police District. At about 5:30 p.m., the man admitted his intentions to officers, was counseled and released because no illicit recordings had been made; police said the investigation remains ongoing.

The incident was included in the Madison Police Department’s daily log covering numerous calls for service, which also listed other crimes that day, including assaults, armed robberies, a stolen vehicle, traffic crashes, and sexual-assault reports. The report noted that upskirting is illegal in many places, including Wisconsin, where a 2015 law makes knowingly using a device to record beneath another person’s outer clothing a felony. The log underscored that while ubiquitous recording devices have led to increased upskirting reports nationwide, enforcement and legal clarity vary by jurisdiction.

Mark Williams, a Sacramento-based conservative talk host and prominent spokesman for Tea Party Express, called President Obama “our half white, racist president” in a September email obtained by TPMmuckraker. Writing in response to what he called a false CNN allegation that he’d labeled Obama a “Nazi,” Williams defended his civil-rights record, saying he marched against violent resistance to desegregation. He also has previously described Obama as “an Indonesian Muslim turned welfare thug and a racist in chief,” and admitted on CNN to referring to the president with a derogatory name on his website. Tea Party Express, created by a GOP consulting firm, has been criticized as “astroturf,” and some Tea Party figures, like Robin Stublen of Tea Party Patriots, have publicly disavowed Williams’s style and role. Williams declined further comment.

Opening statements began Tuesday in the trial of 43-year-old Stephen Allwine in Stillwater, accused of killing his wife, Amy Allwine, in November 2016. Prosecutors say Allwine spent months plotting her murder rather than divorcing her to protect his standing as a church elder. Initially charged with second-degree murder, a grand jury upgraded the indictment to first-degree premeditated murder. Authorities say Cottage Grove police found Amy dead of a gunshot wound to the head after Stephen placed a 911 call; a medical exam also detected excessive scopolamine, a nausea drug for which she had no prescription.

Prosecutor Jamie Kreuser told jurors that Allwine, who counseled married couples and wrote sermons at his church, had affairs with women he met on Ashley Madison and turned to the dark web to hire someone to kill his wife. Investigators allege a dark-web user called “dogdaygod” sought to hire killers on Besa Mafia, posted Amy’s description and whereabouts, and later inquired about buying scopolamine. A bitcoin code found in a phone backup on Allwine’s computer matched a code posted by “dogdaygod,” prosecutors say. Kreuser described an alleged plan to drug Amy, shoot her, stage the scene as suicide, and manipulate their son’s presence to bolster that appearance. Detectives found a wiped bloodstain in a hallway and the family 9mm near Amy’s body.

Defense attorney Kevin Devore challenged the timeline and evidence, calling affairs “red herrings” and accusing police of contaminating the scene—specifically removing and then replacing the gun—and relying on speculative computer forensics. He noted neighbors saw Amy outside the home and heard vehicles racing away the night she died, and said an unknown user accessed Stephen’s computer the day of the death. The trial is ongoing.

The USGA and Fox Sports apologized after offensive, violent sexual language between two spectators was inadvertently broadcast during FS1’s live coverage of Round 2 of the 2018 U.S. Open at Shinnecock Hills. The exchange, picked up by one of more than 200 on-course microphones intended to bring ambient sound to viewers, included a man graphically describing rough sex and admitting to head-butting an ex. The USGA called the remarks “inappropriate” and said it regretted the sentiment being heard on the broadcast and is working with Fox to address the issue. Fox spokeswoman Anne Pennington also issued a sincere apology, confirming the audio came from the gallery rather than a radio feed. The incident was first highlighted by Awful Announcing and discussed widely after Joe Buck’s broadcast temporarily shifted back to on-air commentary as if nothing had happened; an earlier eight-minute audio outage had already disrupted coverage. Critics note that while on-course mics enhance atmosphere, they also capture crude spectator behavior that can undermine the event’s presentation. Observers suggested responsibility lies partly with the USGA for allowing pervasive mic placement and with venue spectators whose loud, sometimes drunken antics have increasingly intruded on televised major-championship coverage. The organizations’ responses and any changes to mic use will be watched over the remainder of the tournament.

In Irving, Texas, the anti-Islam group Bureau of American Islamic Relations (BAIR) publicly posted names and addresses of more than 60 Muslims and “Muslim sympathizers” on Facebook, targeting people who opposed a city council vote in March that backed a state bill seen as limiting Muslim influence. The list, copied from a public city document of sign-ups to speak at the council meeting, included critics of the bill as well as some who supported the council — generating alarm among those named and advocacy groups. BAIR’s spokesman, David Wright III, who helped organize an armed protest outside the Islamic Center of Irving, defended the action and has posted pro-gun messages on social media. The armed demonstration, in which participants carried rifles and displayed anti-Islam signs, heightened local unease; critics called it intimidation at a place of worship.

CAIR’s Dallas/Fort Worth director Alia Salem said the publication and the open display of names were unusually menacing and signaled a dangerous shift to more public, targeted Islamophobia. Concerned residents reported the list to police and CAIR said it planned to contact federal authorities. Facebook initially left the post up despite policy against content that creates a genuine risk of physical harm; subsequent reporting indicates the list was removed after complaints. The episode intensified support for the mosque — with rallies and volunteers offering protection — and stoked broader debates over anti-Muslim sentiment in the wake of recent terrorist attacks, echoing earlier controversies in Irving, including the widely publicized arrest of Ahmed Mohamed over a homemade clock. City officials distanced themselves from BAIR while condemning weapons at the protest and noting the publication’s intimidating effect.

New York’s highest court will decide whether a suburban Albany strip club, Nite Moves, can claim a state sales-tax exemption for “live dramatic or musical arts performances” for its nude dances. The club, audited in 2005, was billed more than $124,000 (and the audit initially claimed roughly $400,000) for unpaid sales tax on cover charges and short private “couch” or lap dances. Nite Moves argues the dances are choreographed artistic performances and submitted anthropologist Judith Hanna’s testimony describing choreographic patterns and numerous moves per routine. An administrative law judge sided with the club, but the Tax Appeals Tribunal and an appellate court found the club failed to prove the dances were choreographed performances and noted dancers need no formal training and private-room dances weren’t observed. The state’s attorney general contends some dancers lack training and patrons sometimes pay merely to converse, so the exemption shouldn’t apply. The Court of Appeals will hear arguments; a decision is expected in about a month and could influence similar taxation fights nationwide.

A bomb exploded on a St. Petersburg subway train on April 3, 2017, killing at least 11–14 people and injuring dozens, while a second shrapnel-packed device was found and defused at a busy transfer station hours later. The midafternoon blast occurred between stations on a north–south line; the driver continued to the Technological Institute station, where passengers were evacuated onto a smoky platform strewn with wounded. Amateur video showed the chaotic aftermath. Authorities closed the entire metro system and then partially resumed service after about six hours; security was tightened nationwide at transport hubs.

Initial reports described multiple suspects, but investigators later focused on a suspected suicide bomber, 22–23-year-old Akbarzhon Jalilov, who was identified on security footage leaving a rented apartment and is alleged to have carried an explosive in a rucksack. Jalilov, born in Kyrgyzstan and holding a Russian passport, had recently returned from Osh in the Fergana Valley, a region with a history of Islamist radicalization and recruitment to ISIS. Police raided and sealed his apartment, removing bags and containers reportedly containing powder; his parents traveled to St. Petersburg amid heavy security. Authorities detained several Central Asian-origin suspects on recruitment charges, though no direct link to the bombing had been confirmed publicly.

President Putin, visiting the city, expressed condolences and pledged investigations; international leaders condemned the attack. The incident revived concerns about Islamist-inspired terrorism in Russia and its possible ties to Moscow’s military role in Syria.

An anonymous group of anti-NSA pranksters has been covertly planting miniature tape recorders under benches and tables across New York City for about a year, retrieving the devices and posting selected audio clips on a new website, WeAreAlwaysListening.com. The clips capture ordinary, private conversations—ranging from a woman at a gym discussing rent to a man at a restaurant describing a lover’s sexual fetish—and are presented by the group as a political provocation against mass surveillance. The activists claim, provocatively, to be “contractors” doing a pro bono pilot for the NSA to demonstrate how mundane talk can reveal personal patterns and that many citizens have complacently accepted monitoring because they believe they have “nothing to hide.” Their site links to an ACLU petition urging Congress to allow certain Patriot Act provisions, especially Section 215 bulk data collection, to lapse. The group removed obvious sensitive details (bank account numbers, passwords) and avoids publishing individuals’ names, but photos and exact recording locations could still make identification possible. Their devices were even labeled “PROPERTY OF NSA,” and the activists sent WIRED a recorder and a planting video; they declined to reveal identities, citing operational security. Legal experts note the operation likely violates New York’s two-party consent rules for recordings, and the effort raises ethical questions about using invasive methods to protest invasive surveillance. The stunt has reignited debate over privacy, consent, and effective tactics for opposing mass government snooping.

A gunman, identified as Christopher Sean Harper-Mercer, opened fire at Umpqua Community College in Roseburg, Oregon, killing nine people and wounding several others before killing himself as officers arrived. Relatives of students in the classroom recounted harrowing details: Harper-Mercer ordered some students to crawl to the center of the room before shooting them, asked victims about their religion and allegedly shot some who identified as Christian, and told at least one victim he would spare them if they begged — then shot that person anyway. Multiple survivors described being told that one student was “the lucky one” and handed a package or envelope to deliver to police; authorities later said they had recovered a multi-page manifesto left at the scene but did not disclose its contents. Witnesses said Harper-Mercer carried multiple weapons, wore a flak jacket and had several ammunition magazines; Oregon’s top federal prosecutor said a handgun was used when the shooting began. Police arrived six minutes after the first 911 call and exchanged gunfire with the shooter two minutes later. Victims ranged in age from 18 to 67. Hospitals treated seven victims, with two remaining hospitalized in critical and fair condition; community blood drives followed as locals rallied. Harper-Mercer’s family, shocked and saddened, released a statement mourning the dead; his father called for tighter gun laws. Investigators have not yet established a clear motive.

Paula Deen has faced a wave of corporate severances after acknowledging past use of a racial slur and related allegations in a discrimination lawsuit. QVC announced it would “pause” its relationship, removing her from broadcasts and phasing out her products while encouraging Deen to address the allegations; Deen apologized and said she would step back to “set things right.” Other major partners have cut ties: Food Network didn’t renew her contract, Ballantine Books canceled a five-book deal including an upcoming cookbook, and retailers Sears, Kmart, Target, Wal‑Mart and Caesars Entertainment withdrew her products or relationships. Novo Nordisk also suspended activities with her. Some engagements remain: Hoffman Media hasn’t commented on her magazine, her fan cruises are adding dates, and several cooking-show appearances are still scheduled as organizers cite forgiveness and second chances.

Staff Sgt. Luis Walker, an Air Force training instructor at Lackland Air Force Base, was convicted on all 28 counts in a sweeping sexual-misconduct scandal and faces sentencing after a court-martial. Jurors found him guilty of rape, aggravated sexual contact and multiple counts of aggravated sexual assault for offenses prosecutors say occurred from 2010–2011 involving at least 10 female recruits. Victims testified Walker gained trust, isolated trainees in offices or dorms, and forced them into kissing, touching or intercourse, sometimes threatening their careers to silence them. The case is part of a larger probe into misconduct by 12 instructors allegedly victimizing at least 31 trainees; other instructors face charges or have pleaded guilty. The scandal prompted broader Air Force reviews, tip lines for recruits and policy changes at the Pentagon to improve handling of sexual-assault complaints. Defense lawyers highlighted inconsistencies and lack of physical evidence; prosecutors portrayed Walker as a predator who abused his authority over vulnerable trainees.

U.S. Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, recovering from a gunshot wound to the head sustained in the Jan. 8 Tucson shooting that killed six and wounded 13, is showing encouraging signs in rehab at TIRR Memorial Hermann in Houston, her rabbi said. Rabbi Stephanie Aaron of Congregation Chaverim, who has visited Giffords, reported that the congresswoman sang along to “American Pie,” knew all the words, and joined in a prayer. Giffords, shot in the left forehead with the bullet passing through the left side of her brain, is engaged in speech and cognitive exercises—medical staff encourage mouthing song lyrics to help rebuild brain function. Aaron described moments of recognition and emotional response: when presented with a poster and T-shirt from students at Emily Gray Junior High, Giffords touched the picture showing her with husband Mark Kelly and held the T-shirt close to her heart. Friends also noted earlier signs of speech, including asking for toast and mouthing “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.” Experts note this is a positive sign, but recovery from traumatic brain injury remains long and uncertain.

Separately, internal memos reveal that veteran Tucson firefighter Mark Ekstrum refused to respond to the Jan. 8 shooting call, citing “political bantering” and saying he was too distraught to perform. Ekstrum, who retired two days later amid pending discipline, later stated he was distracted and regretted leaving, saying he had previously supported Giffords. His captain recommended a 20-day suspension; the department considered termination before Ekstrum’s resignation. Officials later indicated they would have first evaluated his fitness for duty. Ekstrum had a long, mostly exemplary 28-year record, including volunteer work in Haiti.

Double-amputee Olympian Oscar Pistorius became emotional in court as graphic images from the night his girlfriend, model and law graduate Reeva Steenkamp, was shot were shown during his murder trial. Pistorius, 27, admits firing the shots that killed Steenkamp on Feb. 14, 2013, at his Pretoria home but maintains he mistook her for an intruder when he shot through a bathroom door. He has been charged with premeditated murder.

During the proceedings the defense called pathologist Prof. Jan Botha, who disputed aspects of the prosecution’s reconstruction—most notably challenging claims that Steenkamp must have eaten about two hours before her death at around 3 a.m., which would contradict Pistorius’s account that they went to bed at 10 p.m. Botha testified that “death ensued fairly quickly after sustaining the head injury.” Prosecutors aggressively cross-examined him, foreshadowing the intensity Pistorius may face on the stand.

Pistorius himself has already taken the witness stand. He delivered a tearful apology to Steenkamp’s family, saying he thinks of them constantly, prays for them daily, and has been haunted by nightmares and the smell of blood since the shooting. He described long-term psychological effects—taking antidepressants and sleeping pills, waking in terror, and relying on his Christian faith for solace. The courtroom was shown close-up images of Steenkamp’s wounds and the bloodied toilet; Pistorius covered his face, retched, and appeared tormented as the evidence was presented. The hearing adjourned with the trial ongoing and further testimony expected.

A Newaygo County jury found Glenna Duram guilty of first-degree murder and a felony firearm charge for the May 2015 killing of her husband, Martin Duram, in their Ensley Township/Sand Lake-area home. Prosecutors say Martin, 46, was shot five times and found dead; Glenna survived a gunshot wound to the head in what prosecutors described as a suicide attempt. Rescuers discovered the couple on May 13, 2015. The jury deliberated more than eight hours before returning the verdict; Glenna, now in her late 40s, was charged a year after the incident following her recovery. Investigators had noted possible financial stress and a foreclosure on the couple’s home as potential contributing factors. The family’s African grey parrot, Bud, allegedly mimicked an argument including the phrase “Don’t f—ing shoot,” and was considered but not used as evidence at trial. Sentencing is scheduled for Aug. 28.

Organizers officially launched a recall campaign Monday to remove Santa Clara County Superior Court Judge Aaron Persky, who drew national outrage after giving former Stanford swimmer Brock Turner a six-month jail term (of which he served three months) for sexually assaulting an unconscious, intoxicated woman in 2015. About 35 people filed a notice of intent with the county registrar of voters and submitted a 198‑word statement branding Persky an apologist for rapists; if approved it will appear on petitions that campaigners plan to circulate starting in August. Led by Stanford law professor Michele Dauber, a friend of the victim’s family and longtime campus‑sexual‑assault activist, proponents must collect 58,634 valid signatures within 160 days to place the recall before voters on the June 2018 ballot. Dauber said supporters have already raised $450,000 and hired a petition firm. Fifty officials, professors and activists signed the statement accusing Persky of routinely giving lenient sentences to athletes and privileged defendants; supporters include elected officials and women’s‑rights leaders. Opponents argue the recall over a single sentencing decision—one that followed the probation department’s recommendation—sets a dangerous precedent that threatens judicial independence. The state Commission on Judicial Performance closed an investigation without discipline, finding insufficient evidence of bias or misconduct. Persky has moved from criminal to civil court and recused himself from a child pornography case. If the recall qualifies and Persky is removed, voters would also immediately choose his replacement, who would serve the remainder of his term to 2022.

Celia Barquín Arozamena, a 22-year-old Spanish golfer and Iowa State standout, was found murdered on 17 September at Coldwater Golf Links in Ames, Iowa. Barquín, the 2018 Big 12 champion, Iowa State Female Athlete of the Year and recent European Ladies’ Amateur champion, had several stab wounds to her head, neck and upper torso, police said. Authorities arrested 22-year-old Collin Daniel Richards, who was living in a nearby homeless encampment, and charged him with first-degree murder; bond was set at $5 million. Investigators say a police dog tracked Barquín’s scent to the encampment. Witnesses told police Richards had recently spoken about an “urge to rape and kill a woman.” Officers found him with fresh scratches and a concealed laceration; police also recovered two pairs of blood-stained shorts and a knife that Richards allegedly handed to others after the attack. Authorities described the killing as a likely random act of violence and said there is no known relationship between victim and suspect. Barquín, from Puente San Miguel, Spain, was completing a civil engineering degree and had earned numerous collegiate and international honors; her European Amateur victory had qualified her for major professional championships. Iowa State and the international golf community expressed deep sorrow; the university honored her memory and her team withdrew from competition to grieve. Funeral arrangements were pending.

Danish commercial station Radio24syv provoked international outrage after hosts killed and ate a young rabbit live on air to dramatize what they called the hypocrisy of meat-eating consumers. The rabbit, named Allan (or Alan in some reports), was struck repeatedly with an iron bicycle pump by presenter Asger Juhl, who said he had been advised by a zookeeper that the method mimicked how zoo staff dispatch rabbits to feed predators. Juhl described fracturing the cervical vertebrae and later skinned the animal in his garden with his children present; he and co-host Kristoffer Eriksen ate the rabbit as stew. The stunt followed a studio segment about animal treatment in Danish agriculture and the presenters framed the killing as an attempt to force listeners to confront that eating meat entails killing animals — a fact most people outsource and rarely witness directly.

Radio24syv defended the action in a lengthy Facebook post, saying the episode met its goal of exposing hypocrisy: many who decry cruelty still buy meat from systems that subject animals to cramped conditions, long transports and high mortality, the station argued. The post cited disturbing industry figures — for example, intensive chicken stocking rates and tens of thousands of piglet deaths daily tied to breeding practices. The station’s defenders framed the act as an illustrative demonstration of everyday slaughter practices that normally provoke less public reaction because they are removed behind supermarket counters and industrial processes.

The broadcast ignited fierce backlash, boycotts and threats against Juhl and his family, and drew comparisons to previous Danish controversies such as the Copenhagen Zoo’s killing of a giraffe. Reality star and animal-rights advocate Linse Kessler, brought onto the show, tried to stop the killing and later said she understood the intended message but condemned killing Allan on air. Juhl said he had expected debate but not the level of threats received; he maintained the killing was humane and said his station backed him, while adding he did not plan to repeat the stunt. The incident raised ethical and legal questions about media provocations, animal welfare and how best to spotlight factory-farming practices.

Danish inventor Peter Madsen was sentenced to life in prison after being found guilty of the premeditated murder, aggravated sexual assault and desecration of the corpse of Swedish journalist Kim Wall. The Copenhagen City Court judge, Anette Burkø, and two jurors concluded Wall’s death was murder, rejecting Madsen’s shifting account that she died accidentally aboard his private submarine. Wall, 30, vanished after boarding Madsen’s homemade Nautilus submarine on Aug. 10 for what was to be a two-hour trip; the vessel sank the following day. Madsen initially gave multiple conflicting stories — claiming at first to have put her safely ashore, later saying she died accidentally and finally admitting he had dismembered her body and discarded parts at sea. Divers recovered Wall’s head, legs and clothing in Køge Bay in the weeks after her disappearance.

Prosecutors presented evidence they say shows the killing was planned and sexually motivated: Madsen allegedly brought tools to bind, cut and stab, heavy objects to weigh down remains, and deleted text messages recovered by investigators in which he described tying up and torturing a woman and spoke of planning a “perfect murder.” A court-ordered psychiatric report described Madsen as narcissistic with psychopathic traits but not psychotic. Madsen admitted only to mistreating the corpse; his defense argued there was no clear proof of murder and that the cause of death could not be established. The court, however, found the prosecution’s version credible, calling the assault “cynical and pre-planned.” Madsen appeared crushed at the verdict and said he would appeal; he was also ordered to pay damages to Wall’s boyfriend. The case drew intense international attention and widespread condemnation.

A Las Vegas judge dismissed the case against Kirstin Blaise Lobato, ending nearly 17 years of incarceration after prosecutors declined to pursue a third trial in the 2001 slaying and mutilation of homeless man Duran Bailey. Chief Judge Elizabeth Gonzalez ordered Lobato’s immediate release after the district attorney’s office, citing exhausted resources and the lengthy time Lobato has already served, elected not to retry her despite previous convictions by two juries. Lobato, who was 18 at the time of the killing, was twice convicted and served more than 15 years in prison; the Innocence Project and pro bono counsel later took up her case.

The dismissal followed a prior ruling granting Lobato a new trial after Judge Stefany Miley found her trial counsel ineffective for failing to present scientific evidence that could have supported her alibi. Forensic entomologists and a forensic pathologist testified at an evidentiary hearing that blowfly activity and rigor mortis patterns indicated Bailey likely died close to when his body was discovered around 10 p.m. on July 8, 2001—by then Lobato was documented to be in her hometown of Panaca, three hours from Las Vegas. At trial, the prosecution relied on a medical examiner’s broader estimate of time of death and a recorded statement by Lobato about an earlier, unrelated assault as a confession; there was no physical or forensic evidence tying her to Bailey.

Advocates, including Innocence Project attorneys Vanessa Potkin, Adnan Sultan and Jane Pucher, said the scientific testimony undermined the state’s timeline and that Lobato’s conviction resulted from investigative tunnel vision and ineffective defense. Lobato also carried an additional 2007 conviction for sexual conduct in prison, which her attorneys say they will challenge. Supporters worked to secure Lobato’s prompt release and reintegration; she will live with an advocate while rebuilding her life after wrongful incarceration.

Algeria’s defense and emergency officials reported a deadly crash of an Ilyushin Il-76 military transport that went down shortly after taking off from the Boufarik air base, about 30 km southwest of Algiers, en route to Bechar with a planned stop in Tindouf. Early reports and state outlets initially put the toll at more than 100 dead; civil protection later gave a provisional figure of 181 fatalities, with some survivors rescued who suffered deep burns after the fuselage caught fire. Over 300 emergency workers were at the agricultural crash site, where images showed thick black smoke and body bags on the ground. The cause remains unclear and a military investigation has been opened; the Defense Ministry offered condolences but gave no immediate death toll.

A 16-year-old student, identified as Alex Hribal, carried out a brief but violent stabbing spree at Franklin Regional High School in Murrysville, Pennsylvania, on the morning of April 9, 2014. Armed with two kitchen knives roughly 8–10 inches long, Hribal ran down a crowded hallway and into classrooms, attacking students and a security guard in an incident that lasted about five minutes before Assistant Principal Sam King tackled and disarmed him. A school resource officer then handcuffed Hribal; he was treated for a minor hand wound and later arraigned as an adult on multiple charges including four counts of attempted homicide, 21 counts of aggravated assault, and possession of a weapon on school grounds. Authorities said he would be held without bail.

Twenty-one students and a security officer were stabbed or slashed; several victims sustained deep abdominal wounds, and at least four were in critical condition, including one described in court as “eviscerated.” Local hospitals treated numerous teenagers—some unaware immediately that they had been stabbed—and doctors and staff credited quick actions by teachers, students and first responders with preventing further fatalities. Teachers used students’ hoodies as tourniquets; a female student applied pressure to a victim’s wounds, likely saving his life. The assistant principal who tackled Hribal was treated at a hospital but reportedly not stabbed.

The attack shocked the suburban, upper-middle-class community of about 20,000 and underscored that school emergency planning, often focused on shootings, must also consider other threats. Investigators, including the FBI, searched Hribal’s home and seized electronic devices; police said they were exploring reports of a threatening phone call the night before. Officials provided few details on motive, though prosecutors said Hribal made statements after being subdued that he wanted to die. Classmates described him as shy and mostly reserved, not an obvious outcast or troublemaker. The district closed the high school for several days, offered counseling, and praised students and staff for their composure and bravery during the ordeal.

Terry Crews testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee to advocate for the Sexual Assault Survivors’ Bill of Rights, recounting his alleged groping by a WME agent and reflecting on toxic masculinity and personal history. Crews described how the agent’s actions conveyed control and how others minimized the assault as a joke; although the agent was demoted, he was not fired. Crews’ testimony underscored the bill’s goals—nationwide implementation giving survivors access to subsidized rape kits, police reports, results, and counseling—and positioned his story alongside other survivors like Amanda Nguyen, who helped champion the legislation.

That same day rapper 50 Cent posted a now-deleted Instagram meme mocking Crews’ account, using shirtless photos with captions implying Crews couldn’t be assaulted because of his size. The post, which garnered likes and criticism (including a laugh-reaction from Russell Simmons), drew heavy backlash online; commenters called it “disgusting,” “garbage,” and harmful to other male survivors who fear speaking out. TMZ reached Crews, who declined to retaliate, saying he still listens to 50 Cent and noting, “I prove that size doesn’t matter when it comes to sexual assault.” The incident sparked renewed conversation about public responses to survivors and the stigma that keeps many from reporting abuse.

Adult-film performer Kacey Jordan told ABC’s Good Morning America she attended a raucous all-night party at Charlie Sheen’s Los Angeles home the night before he was hospitalized for severe abdominal pain. Jordan said Sheen arrived disheveled, wearing a stained white shirt, appearing heavily intoxicated and “squinty,” and consuming large amounts of alcohol and cocaine. She described a late-night delivery that dumped “tennis ball–size” chunks of cocaine on a table and said Sheen repeatedly smoked the drug from a pipe, hitting it every few minutes. Jordan said she had been offered $5,000 to attend and ultimately received a $30,000 check made out to cash. She claims Sheen proposed creating a 24-hour party mansion, complete with a $250,000-a-month rental agreement, offered her a car, and even asked if she could babysit his children. Jordan said she feared he was on a “suicide binge” and left him naked and still using drugs hours before he was stretchered out. Sheen is now in an undisclosed rehab facility and production on Two and a Half Men is paused. Representatives say he is seeking treatment and accused “opportunistic women” of exploiting his situation. Ex-wife Denise Richards reacted angrily, barring Sheen from being alone with their daughters until he completes rehab. Jordan says she won’t pursue legal action and is glad he sought help.

A video released by Islamic State’s Furqan media outlet purportedly shows the execution of 19-year-old Mohammad (Mohamed/Musallam/Said Ismail) Musallam, an Israeli Arab from East Jerusalem whom the group accused of being a Mossad spy. In the footage, Musallam wears an orange jumpsuit, repeats claims that he was recruited and trained by Israeli intelligence, and is then escorted to a field where a child in uniform fires a pistol at his head and then at his body while chanting. The film includes an older, French-speaking militant delivering a verdict and a warning to Jews; French media and supporters identified that militant as Sabri Essid. Reuters, Israeli officials and others could not immediately verify the video’s authenticity. Musallam’s family and Israeli security sources deny he was a spy: his father says he left for Turkey and was recruited online by IS, later becoming disillusioned and attempting to return home. The family contends militants forced a false confession and executed him to intimidate others. The broader reporting situates this killing among IS propaganda practices that have used mock executions and child executioners; separate coverage mentions the notorious executioner “Jihadi John” (Mohammed Emwazi) as an example of IS’s media-driven killings. The case highlights concerns over online recruitment, coerced confessions, and IS’s use of children and media for terror messaging.

After the Orlando nightclub massacre, Donald Trump said the United States should "seriously" consider racial and religious profiling as a counterterrorism tool. In a CBS Face the Nation interview, the presumptive Republican nominee—while calling profiling distasteful—argued it is necessary and effective in other countries such as Israel, and urged the nation to use "common sense" rather than "political correctness." His comments followed the June 12 attack that killed 49 people and renewed his call for a temporary ban on Muslims entering the U.S., which he said might have prevented the shooting despite the fact that the attacker, Omar Mateen, was U.S.-born. Trump also urged members of Muslim communities to report suspicious behavior, citing San Bernardino as an example where people allegedly saw warning signs. He described Mateen as having clear "red flags" in his past. On gun policy, Trump said he is working with the NRA on a proposal to bar people on the no-fly or terror watch lists from buying firearms, while acknowledging concerns about mistaken listings. He dismissed recent GOP criticism of his stances, telling Republican leaders to focus on governing—budgets and military funding—rather than talking about him.

Rutgers dismissed five football players—defensive backs Nadir Barnwell, Dre Boggs, Ruhann Peele, Delon Stephenson and fullback Razohnn Gross—shortly before the Scarlet Knights’ season opener after their arrests earlier in the week. Prosecutors charged Peele, Barnwell, Gross and Stephenson with aggravated assault, riot and conspiracy related to an April street attack in New Brunswick that left a 19-year-old student with a broken jaw; Boggs was charged in two home-invasion robberies in April and May. Authorities say the assault involved players surrounding and attacking a group of people after spring camp. Investigators were reportedly given video evidence of the April 25 incident and, with a court order, confiscated some team members’ cell phones at the Hale Center on Aug. 28. The arrests and dismissals followed interim suspensions; the situation also intersects with an earlier inquiry about coach Kyle Flood contacting a teacher regarding Barnwell’s grade. The removals significantly thin Rutgers’ secondary.

Lifetime announced several new unscripted series, led by the provocative Born in the Wild, which will document women choosing unassisted outdoor births. The network pitches the show as capturing couples deliberately opting for “wild” birthing experiences after unsatisfying hospital deliveries. Production says it will screen participants (excluding first-time mothers), require medical clearance, have trained emergency personnel on site, and stay within a set distance of a hospital. Lifetimes’s nonfiction head emphasizes precautions and personal connection to nonhospital birth practices. The concept grew out of viral footage of a forest birth and aims to document an existing—if niche—trend rather than sensationalize dangerous behavior.

Medical experts push back strongly. A maternal-fetal medicine specialist stresses that historical maternal mortality was high before modern obstetrics and that home or wilderness births remain riskier even today. He argues that, despite safeguards, unpredictable complications will occur and that real-world outcomes won’t always reflect the controlled environment of a television production. He fears the show could indirectly encourage riskier, unsupported attempts by those without the producers’ safety net, though Lifetime counters that participants are a specific subset unlikely to enter lightly.

Lifetime’s slate also includes Girlfriend Intervention, a makeover series starring four African American women helping white participants regain confidence; Threads, a teen fashion-design competition; and Kosher Soul, following an African-American man converting to Judaism for his fiancée. Some of the announced concepts have already drawn criticism for cultural stereotyping, while others—like Threads—garner interest for showcasing young designers.

A catastrophic fire tore through the Kiss nightclub in Santa Maria, southern Brazil, early Sunday, killing at least 233 people (later reports put the toll higher) and leaving many more injured after pyrotechnics used by a performing band ignited ceiling soundproofing. Toxic smoke filled the packed venue within seconds; most victims suffocated, while others were crushed in a frantic stampede. Survivors described instant panic, confusion about exits and locked doors; at least one exit reportedly was locked and security initially blocked fleeing patrons, thinking they were dodging bar tabs. Firefighters found bodies piled at exits and had to breach walls to reach victims. The club may have been overcrowded, and investigators cited safety violations. Authorities, including President Dilma Rousseff, who flew to the scene, mourned with grieving families as the tragedy drew comparisons to other deadly nightclub fires and raised questions about enforcement of safety codes ahead of Brazil’s looming global events.

The MPAA’s film ratings have come under renewed criticism after Ira Sachs’s Love Is Strange, a quiet drama about a long-term gay couple (John Lithgow and Alfred Molina) facing homelessness, was given an R rating for “strong language” despite containing no nudity, explicit sex or violence. Critics argue the rating unjustly groups this mild, mainstream portrayal of gay life with violent, sexually explicit fare opening the same weekend—Sin City: A Dame to Kill For and Jersey Shore Massacre—both R-rated and featuring graphic gore, nudity, prostitution and torture. Commentators including Stephen Whitty and J. Bryan Lowder have accused the MPAA of inconsistency and potential homophobia, noting comparable heterosexual portrayals would likely receive milder ratings. The MPAA maintains the R label is due to language and claims to apply standards regardless of subject matter, but the organization’s history of stricter treatment of LGBT-themed films and its perceived leniency toward violence has heightened scrutiny. Love Is Strange received lower ratings in the UK and Canada, intensifying questions about the MPAA’s judgment and transparency in assigning ratings.

A PBS NewsHour investigation and interviews with 34 current and former U.S. Forest Service women reveal a persistent, nationwide culture of sexual harassment, assault, gender discrimination and retaliation that stretches back decades. The report centers on multiple personal accounts: Michaela Myers, 22, says a supervisor repeatedly groped her during her first season and that her formal complaint to USDA investigators resulted in a closed investigation finding no misconduct. Others describe rape, repeated groping at after-hours gatherings, blunt misogyny, hostile work environments on male-dominated hotshot and firefighting crews, and a pervasive fear of reporting because of likely retaliation.

Women who did report faced a range of reprisals — anonymous threatening notes, demotions, negative reviews, removal of duties, isolation, and stalled careers. Several described management indifference or procedural failures: long, opaque EEO processes, unreliable hotlines, slow FOIA responses and investigations that conclude without clear accountability. A USDA inspector general survey of nearly 2,000 Forest Service employees in California found many knew of a “zero tolerance” policy but did not trust reporting channels or feared consequences, so most incidents went unreported.
