The problem has deep roots: legal and congressional actions since the 1970s and consent decrees sought to boost hiring and reform practices, yet many women say the “boys’ club” culture endures. High-profile developments followed the NewsHour series: Chief Tony Tooke stepped down amid an independent USDA investigation into allegations he had relationships with subordinates before his appointment. The Forest Service has introduced a national hotline and updated policies and training, and reports some findings and corrective actions — but many women remain skeptical the measures will meaningfully change culture or protect complainants. Despite harms, many women still love the work and hope exposure, social media networks and the #MeToo movement will finally force sustained accountability and change.

Molly Shattuck, 47, a former Baltimore Ravens cheerleader and ex-wife of former Constellation Energy CEO Mayo Shattuck III, has been indicted in Delaware on nine counts alleging a sexual relationship with a 15-year-old boy. Delaware State Police say the relationship began after Shattuck initiated contact via Instagram in late May and progressed through months of private messages, lunches and meetings in her Cadillac Escalade at locations including a movie theater and parking lots. Court records and an affidavit allege that over Labor Day weekend at a rented Bethany Beach house she provided alcohol to the teen and at least two other minors, engaged in oral sex with the boy outdoors, and later fondled him in her bedroom; the boy told police she offered intercourse but he left. The McDonogh School reported the matter to police in late September and barred the parent involved from campus. Shattuck was arrested, arraigned in Sussex County Superior Court, pleaded not guilty, and released on $84,000 bail with restrictions including no contact with the alleged victim or other minors and surrender of her passport. Investigators executed a search warrant seizing her phone, computers, storage devices and clothing items. Shattuck’s lawyers declined further comment; she maintains her innocence.

Actor Charlie Sheen has sued adult film actress Capri Anderson for extortion, alleging she demanded $1 million to keep quiet about the night Sheen trashed a room at New York’s Plaza Hotel and that she stole a $165,000 watch. Anderson, who was found in Sheen’s suite when police responded to a disturbance call, filed a separate complaint with the NYPD accusing Sheen of harassment in the second degree. In interviews with ABC’s Good Morning America and Nightline, Anderson said she was hired for $3,500 to accompany Sheen to dinner and later to escort him to his hotel room. She described escalating violence: Sheen grew increasingly intense and intoxicated, allegedly snorting a white powder, hurling racial slurs, putting his hands around her neck, throwing a lamp and other objects, and threatening to kill her. She said she feared for her life and was never paid the promised fee. Anderson also alleges Sheen texted her afterward offering $20,000 for silence. Sheen’s attorney, Yale Galanter, denied wrongdoing, called the claims false and an attempt to cash in on Sheen’s celebrity, and vowed to vigorously defend the suit. A civil suit in Los Angeles was also expected.

The Gulnare Free Will Baptist Church in Pike County, Ky., voted 9–6 to bar interracial couples from membership and participation after a white member’s daughter brought her Black fiancé to sing at a service. The decision sparked local outrage and condemnation from nearby churches. New pastor Stacy Stepp sought help from the Sandy Valley Conference, which ruled the vote invalid under Robert’s Rules because bylaws weren’t properly changed. Stepp plans to rescind the ban and restore inclusivity.

Walter Samuel Radford, 33, allegedly killed attorney Antonio Benjamin Mari hours after his divorce from Cindy Radford was finalized in Bartow County, Ga. Radford did not respond to the divorce petition or hire counsel and failed to appear for the final hearing; the divorce was granted at 12:04 p.m., awarding Cindy Radford custody of their two children and the family home. Less than two hours later, police say Radford fatally shot 41-year-old Mari — a former Cass High School history teacher who had practiced law for nearly 18 years — in Mari’s Cartersville office. Mari, who had told colleagues he feared Radford, was found dead of multiple gunshot wounds shortly before 2 p.m. Radford then called his ex-wife to say he had killed Mari, broke into her Willow Bend Drive home and shot himself; his body was found at about 2:40 p.m. Authorities have not disclosed a motive. Mari is survived by his wife, and his death prompted tributes from Cass High and the Bartow County school system. Colleagues highlighted concerns about security at small law firms and the limits of self-defense when an assailant appears intent on suicide.

A controversial H&M product shot showing five‑year‑old Swedish model Liam Mango wearing a green hoodie labeled “Coolest Monkey in the Jungle” sparked international outrage, with celebrities such as The Weeknd, Diddy and LeBron James condemning the image as racially insensitive. H&M initially removed the image from some channels and apologized for “offending people,” then issued a stronger, fuller apology acknowledging the mistake, removing the garment globally, recycling remaining stock, and pledging to investigate and prevent similar incidents. The company said it had “got this wrong,” recognized the need to be attuned to racial and cultural sensitivities, and committed to taking action.

Liam’s parents, Terry Mango and Frank Odhiambo, have publicly defended that neither they nor Liam saw the image as racist, saying the boy had been contracted via an agency and that the family members who accompany him to shoots did not recall the specific hoodie until the photo went viral. Terry Mango wrote on Facebook that critics should “get over it,” later appearing on ITV’s This Morning and the BBC to explain that while she understands and has personally experienced racism, she did not perceive the jumper as carrying racist intent in the context of her son modeling clothing. She also said she respects differing opinions on racism. The family says Liam is unaware of the controversy and thinks of himself as a “superstar.”

The incident led to protests in some countries—most notably angry demonstrations and vandalism at H&M stores in South Africa—and prompted heightened security concerns for the Mango family; they reported temporarily moving house for safety. The situation highlighted wider conversations about corporate apologies, cultural sensitivity in global marketing, and the responsibilities of brands to prevent unconscious bias in imagery and product promotion.

Michael Cohen, long-time personal lawyer to President Donald Trump, informed a federal court in Los Angeles that he will invoke his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination in a civil lawsuit brought by adult-film actor Stormy Daniels (Stephanie Clifford). In a declaration filed Wednesday, Cohen said he would assert the privilege in all proceedings in the case "based upon the advice of counsel" because of an ongoing criminal investigation by the FBI and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York. He cited recent FBI raids on his home, office and hotel room and the seizure of electronic devices and documents as the basis for his decision.

Cohen’s filing was submitted as part of an effort to pause Daniels’s defamation suit, which challenges Cohen’s public statement that Daniels lied about an alleged affair with Trump. The judge handling the case had said he needed to hear from Cohen directly before deciding the request to stay proceedings. Daniels’s attorney, Michael Avenatti, called the invocation of the Fifth by the President’s personal lawyer "stunning," noting it is unprecedented for an attorney for a sitting President to plead the Fifth in matters connected to the President. Cohen previously arranged and paid Daniels $130,000 under a nondisclosure agreement shortly before the 2016 election, a payment at the center of both the civil suit and the related criminal investigation.

Just after Soundgarden’s May 17 concert at Detroit’s Fox Theatre, frontman Chris Cornell returned to his MGM Grand hotel room and spoke on the phone with his wife, Vicky. She became alarmed when he sounded groggy, slurred his words and repeatedly said, “I’m just tired.” Vicky told the band’s bodyguard to check on him. According to a Detroit Police Gaming Unit report obtained by The Detroit News, bodyguard Martin Kirsten went to Cornell’s suite, where he and hotel security found locked doors; Kirsten kicked them open and discovered Cornell on the bathroom floor with blood coming from his mouth and a red exercise band around his neck. Hotel medic Dawn Jones untied the band and began CPR; emergency responders continued efforts but Cornell, 52, was pronounced dead by 1:30 a.m. The Wayne County medical examiner later ruled the death a suicide by hanging, a finding disputed by Cornell’s family. The family says he was a recovered addict and believes toxicology results are needed to determine whether drugs or other substances affected him; Vicky said Chris told her he may have taken an extra Ativan or two. Police reported Kirsten had given Cornell two Ativan pills earlier while helping with the singer’s computer. Band members declined comment; tributes poured in, including from Tom Morello. Investigators and homicide detectives began an inquiry as the family awaited toxicology results.

Thai authorities will test human faeces found at a campsite in Thungyai Naresuan wildlife sanctuary to try to link construction magnate Premchai Karnasuta to an alleged poaching incident. Premchai, president of Italian-Thai Development Company, and three companions were arrested earlier this month after park rangers found their camp in the western sanctuary, along with firearms and the carcasses of protected animals: a black leopard, a Kalij pheasant and a red muntjac (barking deer). Chaiwat Limlikitaksorn, head of a special task force at the Department of National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Conservation, said the excrement’s proximity to spent bullet casings and the location where the panther was skinned makes it a potentially important piece of evidence. He argued Premchai would not have wandered far into the woods to relieve himself, and that DNA testing could place him at the scene, undermining denials that he was involved. Premchai has denied the poaching charges; he and his companions have been granted bail while the investigation continues. The case has drawn attention in Thailand, where wealthy and influential figures are often perceived as avoiding accountability, and comes amid broader political scrutiny of the ruling junta over separate scandals involving senior officials. The sanctuary is in Kanchanaburi province, a popular tourist area, and the alleged killings involve species protected under Thai conservation law.

Wade Michael Page, identified by federal officials as the gunman who killed six people and wounded three at a Sikh temple in Oak Creek, Wis., emerged from a background that combined military service, music and white-supremacist activity. Page, 40, served in the Army from 1992 to 1998 and was trained as a psychological-operations specialist. His record shows he was demoted from sergeant to specialist and received an administrative discharge that was not honorable; officials would not disclose reasons. Colleagues recall him voicing overtly racist views, calling non-whites “dirt people,” and bearing tattoos referencing the white-power “14 words.” After the Army he drifted into the racist skinhead music scene, fronting bands such as End Apathy and Definite Hate; photos and festival appearances tied him to white-power circles. Neighbors and acquaintances described him as a solitary, often strange presence—quiet, making little eye contact, blasting loud aggressive music, and occasionally acting hostile. He held various jobs, including at a Harley-Davidson dealership and as a truck driver, but lost positions and housing over the years; a VA-backed home he purchased was foreclosed. Friends and his stepmother remembered a once-ordinary, music-loving boy whose trajectory into extremism remains puzzling to them. Mental-health experts note warning signs in his history and question what precipitated his descent into lethal violence, especially given his likely awareness that his attack would end in his own death.

On Friday at Los Angeles International Airport, 23-year-old Paul Anthony Ciancia walked into Terminal 3, produced a .223-caliber semiautomatic rifle from a bag and opened fire at a security checkpoint. The attack killed 39-year-old Transportation Security Administration behavioral detection officer Gerardo I. Hernandez — the first TSA officer killed in the agency’s 12-year history — and wounded several others. Ciancia, who was carrying anti-government written material reportedly critical of the federal government and the TSA and who had texted his brother that morning about suicidal thoughts, was shot in the chest by law enforcement and taken into custody in critical condition. Witnesses described chaotic scenes as travelers dove for cover and others were evacuated onto the tarmac; roughly 746 flights were affected and 46 diverted. Authorities found Ciancia had more than 100 rounds; his motive remains under investigation. His family in New Jersey alerted police after receiving his troubling text, and investigators are probing his background as airport terminals reopened while Terminal 3 remained closed for the ongoing investigation.

President Obama condemned the violence in Bahrain, urging King Hamad by phone to show restraint, hold those responsible accountable, and respect citizens’ universal rights while embracing meaningful reform. His comments followed reports of security forces using tear gas, armored vehicles and live ammunition against protesters, wounding dozens during mass demonstrations at Manama’s Pearl Roundabout. After an especially violent crackdown, the king appointed Crown Prince Salman to open dialogue with mostly Shiite opposition leaders; the crown prince ordered a military withdrawal and called for sincere talks. Opposition parties remain divided, and the uprising’s outcome and short-term outlook are uncertain.

A rare white tiger mauled 40-year-old zookeeper Akira Furusho to death at Hirakawa Zoological Park in Kagoshima, Japan. Furusho was found collapsed and bleeding from the neck in the tiger display cage after the zoo had closed; he was pronounced dead at hospital. The 5-year-old male white tiger, Riku — about 1.8 meters long and 170 kg — was sedated with a tranquiliser by a veterinarian and, at the family’s request, will be kept alive. The zoo’s rules require keepers not to enter the display cage until animals are moved to sleeping chambers; police and labor authorities are investigating safety practices and possible legal violations in the care of the park’s four white tigers.

A UPS driver in Robertsville, Missouri, alerted authorities after noticing “call 911” written on a package, leading to the rescue of a woman allegedly held captive and sexually assaulted in her own home. The driver encountered the woman while making a scheduled pickup Tuesday morning and contacted police; a Franklin County Sheriff’s Department spokesperson called him “a huge help.” Deputies responding to the Willow Ford Road residence discovered a cooperative woman who reported that her 33-year-old husband, James Tyler Jordan, had refused to let her leave, physically assaulted her, forced her to strip, and sexually assaulted her while holding a gun to her head and threatening to kill her and himself. Court documents state Jordan allegedly made the woman speak with the driver while he stood behind her with a firearm; she had managed to scrawl the plea for help on the package. A toddler also lived in the house; deputies say Jordan locked the 3-year-old in a room for several hours, prompting child endangerment charges. Jordan, who reportedly has prior arrests including assault, was taken into custody without incident after initially refusing to cooperate; a SWAT team had been activated due to concerns he was armed and a child was present. He faces multiple charges and bond was set at $100,000 cash only.

A gunman, Jeffrey T. Johnson, a disgruntled former employee, fatally shot ex-colleague Steven Ercolino outside the Empire State Building, then was confronted and killed by two NYPD officers who fired 16 rounds. Police Commissioner Ray Kelly said none of the nine wounded bystanders were struck directly by the suspect; they were hit by bullets, fragments or shrapnel after officers’ rounds struck surrounding objects. Three passersby sustained direct gunshot wounds; six suffered fragment injuries. Victims included a Bronx mother and a tour guide. Witnesses described a chaotic, split-second encounter captured on surveillance video. Experts note officers face extreme split-second decisions and training limits. The shooting raised questions about urban policing and risk to civilians; officials said the officers were justified, while victims and commentators urged greater care to avoid endangering bystanders during such confrontations.

Twenty years after Matthew Shepard’s 1998 abduction, brutal beating and death, advocates say progress for LGBTQ equality exists but significant challenges remain. Shepard, a 21-year-old college student, was tied to a fence, beaten with a pistol butt and left to die; he was found nearly 18 hours later and died five days after the attack. His murder spurred protests and activism that helped bring about the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, expanding federal hate-crime protections to include gender and sexual orientation. His attackers received life sentences, and his friends and family founded the Matthew Shepard Foundation to carry forward his legacy.

Advocates note major gains — for example, same-sex marriage is now legal nationwide — but warn of continuing gaps: many states still allow employers to fire people for sexual orientation or gender identity, cyberbullying poses new threats to LGBTQ youth, and hate crimes rose 12% in the nation’s 10 largest cities in 2017. Anti-LGBT incidents were among the most frequent hate crimes in several major cities, and 15 states lack hate-crime statutes that explicitly include LGBTQ people; a few states still have no hate-crime law at all. Currently, 18 states plus Washington, D.C. include sexual orientation and gender identity in hate-crime statutes.

Voices from the community express mixed feelings: some, like Carl Siciliano of the Ali Forney Center, feel safer than in the 1990s but stress persistent violence against transgender people and rising homelessness among LGBTQ youth. Shepard’s parents continue advocacy but fear worsening hateful rhetoric in recent years. Leaders urge both legislative action and cultural change: personal accountability, confronting hateful speech gently, and fostering acceptance are presented as immediate, everyday ways to reduce hate and protect vulnerable people.

A 17-year-old Texas teenager, Huma Hanif, died on March 31 after a Takata airbag inflator ruptured in her 2002 Honda Civic during a low-speed rear-end crash in Fort Bend County. Deputies and the county sheriff said the crash damage was minor and Hanif would likely have survived if not for the airbag. An investigation determined a metal fragment from the inflator severed her jugular vein and carotid artery, killing her within seconds. Sheriff Troy Nehls said the jagged metal fired at point-blank range from less than two feet. Hanif, a senior at George Ranch High School who hoped to become a nurse, was mourned by family and classmates; her brother urged anyone with vehicles under airbag recall to get repairs completed. Witnesses who tried to help described the shock of a relatively minor collision producing a catastrophic neck wound.

Hanif is the tenth U.S. fatality and the 11th worldwide linked to Takata inflator failures, which can explode with excessive force and send shrapnel into vehicle occupants. More than 100 injuries have been reported. The defect prompted the largest automotive recall in history: at least 29 million vehicles globally and 24 million in the U.S. from about 14 automakers, including Honda, Toyota, BMW, Ford, GM, Nissan and others. About 7.1 million inflators have been replaced in the U.S., but many owners remain unserved; some receive notices but face long waits for parts. Honda said multiple recall notices were mailed for Hanif’s vehicle but the repair was never completed.

Authorities and safety agencies urge owners to check recall status via NHTSA’s VIN lookup, sign up for alerts, and get repairs immediately. With a heavy backlog, drivers may consider temporary measures—asking dealers for loaners, discussing disabling an airbag with a mechanic (while using seatbelts), or seeking alternatives—though manufacturers are being pressed to speed notifications and replacements.

Newly released police and medical documents in the killing of 17-year-old Trayvon Martin provide further detail and conflicting accounts of the Feb. 26 encounter with neighborhood-watch volunteer George Zimmerman. Two officers who arrived after the shooting reported Zimmerman had a bloody, possibly broken nose, abrasions to his forehead and a laceration to the back of his head; his clothing was wet with grass. Multiple redacted witness statements described a man wearing a hoodie straddling another and throwing punches, hearing a “pop” and then seeing the hooded person laid out on the grass, consistent with Zimmerman's claim that Martin attacked him and he shot in self-defense. Zimmerman’s 911 call and other recordings include frantic yelling; investigators noted Zimmerman can be heard calling for help. Martin’s autopsy listed a gunshot wound to the chest from intermediate range, a small abrasion on his finger suggesting a struggle, and traces of THC in blood. Authorities criticized Zimmerman’s decision to leave his vehicle and follow Martin, calling the encounter avoidable if he had stayed or identified himself. The case, which ignited national debate over racial profiling, gun laws and “Stand Your Ground,” led to Zimmerman's second-degree murder charge; trial date remains unset.

Memories Pizza, a small family-run pizzeria in Walkerton, Indiana, became a local flashpoint during the controversy over Indiana’s Religious Freedom Restoration Act. The O’Connor family, owners of the shop for nine years, publicly stated they would refuse to cater a gay wedding, citing Christian beliefs and support for the law. They insisted they wouldn’t deny service to customers who dine in, but would not provide wedding catering for couples whose unions they oppose. The stance prompted intense national attention: supporters praised their religious freedom and some charitable donors reportedly raised large sums for the family, while critics and many online reviewers accused the business of discrimination and launched harsh attacks.

Online customer feedback about Memories Pizza’s food and service was deeply mixed and often polarized along ideological lines. Several patrons described excellent, friendly service and tasty, nostalgic pizza and baked goods, praising the small-town atmosphere. Conversely, multiple reviewers—some admitting they’d never visited—called the pizza low quality, greasy, undercooked, or making them ill. The situation escalated into vitriolic commentary from both sides, including extreme religious denunciations and accusations of coordinated negative reviews. Ultimately, the publicity and backlash contributed to the restaurant’s closure, leaving a divided record of community support and condemnation.

A 51-year-old waterfowl hunter, Robert Meilhammer of Crapo in Dorchester County, was rendered unconscious and seriously injured Thursday when a dead goose fell from the sky and struck him while he hunted with a group near the Miles River. Around 5 p.m., a flock of geese flew overhead and members of the hunting party fired at the birds. One goose fell and hit Meilhammer; Maryland Natural Resources Police spokeswoman Candy Thomson said one of the hunters had shot and killed the bird, though it is unclear which person fired the fatal shot. Meilhammer sustained head and facial injuries and was airlifted to Maryland Shock Trauma for treatment. The article also includes unrelated captions about an Orthodox Saturday morning service before Pascha and a State of Downtown Baltimore breakfast attended by business and civic leaders, and lists contact and Twitter information for the reporter (trichman@baltsun.com; twitter.com/TaliRichman).

A wedding reception in Bhopal ended in tragedy when 26-year-old bride Dr. Jayshree Namdeo was shot dead on stage by her cousin, Anurag Namdeo (also reported as Anurag Singh), after she refused his marriage proposal. The attack occurred late Thursday at Sundervan Marriage Garden as the newlyweds posed for photographs. Anurag, who had developed an obsession with Jayshree years earlier while they attended the same coaching institute, had warned the family previously and reportedly threatened them after seeing the couple’s engagement photo on Facebook. He bought a country-made pistol a day before the murder and had changed his social media cover to “JUST WAIT AND WATCH.” Masked, he entered the hall through the rear, climbed the dais and fired one shot that struck Jayshree below the throat. He then attempted to shoot the groom; the groom deflected the weapon and Anurag appears to have tried to shoot himself before being overpowered and severely beaten by guests. Jayshree was pronounced dead at hospital; another guest was injured. Anurag was hospitalized after the assault and faces legal action. Jayshree’s father, who had once sheltered Anurag and later excluded his family from the wedding due to his opposition, expressed shock that someone he had treated like a son could commit such violence.

A Saturday morning shooting at Melbourne Square Mall’s food court left two dead — the apparent gunman, Jose Garcia‑Rodriguez, 57, and restaurant owner Leonardo Coppola, 36 — and one injured, Garcia‑Rodriguez’s 33‑year‑old wife, who worked in the food court and is recovering in good condition. About 100 people were inside when shots rang out around 9:30 a.m.; witnesses reported multiple shots and panicked evacuations. Police say Garcia‑Rodriguez shot his wife and Coppola, who tried to shield her, then shot himself. Investigators recovered three handguns and ammunition and believe the attack stemmed from a domestic dispute. Multiple agencies, including the FBI, assisted the response.

Heavy fighting erupted in Juba, South Sudan, in early July as clashes between forces loyal to President Salva Kiir and those backing First Vice President Riek Machar reignited fears of a return to full-scale civil war. Intense gunfire, mortars and grenade explosions around the presidential palace displaced tens of thousands—estimates put those who fled at around 30,000 in the immediate outbreak, with many more already sheltering at U.N.-run Protection of Civilian sites—and left hundreds dead. Reports vary, but one count cited 272 fatalities. Humanitarian facilities, including a maternity ward inside a Protection of Civilian site, were shelled; aid workers were injured and international staff evacuated when the airport briefly reopened. Humanitarian agencies warn the crisis worsens already dire conditions: before the clashes, about 3.9 million South Sudanese were food insecure and one in five people displaced. The 2016 humanitarian appeal was far from fully funded, increasing the urgency for donor support.

Aid organizations like World Vision and the International Medical Corps are stretched, prioritizing lifesaving assistance—food distributions (high-energy biscuits), water, trauma care, rape kits and antibiotics—while programs such as education for displaced children risk suspension. Medical staff face overwhelming caseloads of severe trauma victims, sexual violence survivors and people sickened by poor conditions; limited supplies sometimes must be rationed among multiple patients.

Accounts of how the fighting began conflict. A disputed Facebook post and accusations by a South Sudanese ambassador blamed a spokesman for incitement; others point to deep structural causes: divided command and powerful commanders like SPLA chief of general staff Paul Malong, whose militia forces and influence are widely seen as major drivers of violence. Observers argue both Kiir and Machar lack full control over forces, implementation of the 2015 peace deal faltered, and international actors failed to enforce security arrangements—factors that allowed tensions to erupt. Calls for ceasefire compliance, donor funding, unhindered humanitarian access and possible international peacekeeping or sanctions followed amid urgent appeals to protect civilians and prevent further escalation.

On Oct. 22, 2014, a masked gunman shot and killed Cpl. Nathan Cirillo, a 24-year-old reservist on guard at Ottawa’s National War Memorial, then stormed Parliament’s Centre Block, where dozens of shots were fired. The attacker was shot dead inside Parliament by House of Commons Sergeant-at-Arms Kevin Vickers and RCMP officers. Prime Minister Stephen Harper called the incident a “brutal and violent attack,” vowed Canada would not be intimidated, and offered condolences to Cirillo’s family and to the family of Warrant Officer Patrice Vincent, who was killed two days earlier in a separate, reportedly ISIL-inspired attack in Quebec. The suspect was identified as Michael Zehaf-Bibeau, a Canadian born in 1982 with prior criminal convictions in Quebec and British Columbia; authorities said he was not on the government’s high-risk travellers list. Ottawa and Parliament Hill were locked down for hours; hundreds, including daycare children, were eventually evacuated. Several people sustained minor injuries and were treated. RCMP described the situation as dynamic and said they had no forewarning. Officials raised security at government sites nationwide, cautioned military personnel about wearing uniforms in public, and coordinated with allies; President Obama and NATO expressed solidarity. Investigations into motives and possible accomplices continued.

Illinois is confronting a growing outbreak of severe bleeding and multiple deaths tied to synthetic cannabinoids (sold as K2, Spice, fake weed, etc.). Initially reported clusters expanded rapidly: officials have linked at least 153 illnesses and four deaths across 13 counties to contaminated products. Patients have been hospitalized with spontaneous, internal and external bleeding—coughing up blood, blood in urine or stool, bleeding gums, noses and eyes—often requiring intensive care. Toxicology and public-health investigations found brodifacoum, a powerful long-acting anticoagulant used in rat poison, in some samples; it blocks vitamin K–dependent clotting and can necessitate prolonged, high-dose vitamin K therapy and transfusions. Treatment may require daily vitamin K pills for months and is costly. Authorities warn synthetic cannabinoids are human-made, unregulated chemicals far more potent and unpredictable than marijuana; marketing that equates them with cannabis is misleading and dangerous. Health departments urge anyone who purchased or used these products to stop, seek immediate emergency care for unexplained bleeding, and notify providers about possible synthetic cannabinoid exposure. Donations of nearly 800,000 vitamin K tablets have been made to help treatment efforts.

A 34-year-old Anchorage man, Justin Schneider, pleaded guilty to a second-degree felony assault in connection with a violent August 15, 2017 attack in which a woman says he strangled her until she lost consciousness and then sexually assaulted her. The victim, who did not know Schneider, told police she accepted a ride from him at a gas station while trying to get to her boyfriend’s home. Instead of driving to her destination, Schneider diverted to a different area, stopped the vehicle and, according to the criminal complaint, tackled the woman, pinned her to the ground and choked her while threatening to kill her if she screamed. The victim said she lost consciousness and believed she was going to die. Upon waking, she reported Schneider was zipping his pants and told her he had faked the threat of death to become sexually fulfilled. The victim retrieved the license plate as Schneider drove away and called police; a construction worker later identified seeing the SUV at the scene.

Schneider had originally faced four felony counts, including kidnapping and assault. Under a plea deal he admitted to one count of second-degree assault and was sentenced to two years with one year suspended, plus three years of probation. He received credit for time already served while on an ankle monitor and living at home with his wife and two children. Prosecutor Andrew Grannik noted Schneider lost his federal air traffic controller job as a result of the case, calling that loss a “life sentence.” Judge Michael Corey, who called the outcome “breathtaking,” accepted the plea citing rehabilitation prospects and warned Schneider, “This can never happen again.” The victim did not attend the hearing; prosecutors said they attempted to notify her but could not reach her.

Secretly recorded phone conversations alleged to feature disgraced former Subway spokesman Jared Fogle were aired on Dr. Phil, with the tapes containing explicit admissions of sexual interest in minors. Fogle, who agreed to plead guilty in September to child pornography and paying for sex with minors, faces sentencing next month of five to 12½ years. Dr. Phil’s producers obtained the recordings from Rochelle Herman‑Walrond, a former Florida radio host who says she secretly taped Fogle over five years after growing suspicious of him; she also claims to have provided the tapes to the FBI prior to a July raid of Fogle’s Indiana home. The FBI has acknowledged receiving recordings but hasn’t confirmed Herman‑Walrond’s role as an informant.

In the excerpts broadcast, the speaker identified as Fogle repeatedly expresses attraction to boys and girls “of all ages,” describes techniques he allegedly used to groom children—waiting for a “glance,” sharing stories to get “a little closer” until sexual contact occurs—and discusses targeting vulnerable children, including one “from a broken home.” In one exchange he suggests involving underage guests at a supposed party and urges Herman‑Walrond to wear revealing clothing to “get the children ‘sexed up.’” Another clip references traveling to Thailand to facilitate contact with young children and asks about her children’s 7‑ and 8‑year‑old friends, seeking those “most promising.” Herman‑Walrond broke down on the show, describing lasting emotional trauma and nightmares. Subway said it received a complaint via its website in 2011 but found nothing implying sexual criminality at the time and later regretted inadequate escalation. Dr. Phil indicated additional audio would air in a subsequent episode.

Reality star Heidi Montag is promoting her debut pop album Superficial, a project she says took three years to make and aims to be empowering club music despite provocative lyrics like the chorus of "I'll Do It"—“come eat my panties off of me.” Montag told Ryan Seacrest she’s focusing on her music career for now, putting thoughts of children with husband Spencer Pratt “kind of on hold,” and suggested Pratt may not feel the same urgency. She calls the album title a double entendre about Hollywood’s surface-level culture versus inner reality. Montag also says she and Pratt have embraced yoga, which has helped calm his high energy.

Frank Ancona, 51, who led a small Missouri Ku Klux Klan faction and called himself an “imperial wizard,” was shot in the head in his Leadwood home between 2 and 3 a.m. Thursday and later found dumped near the Big River, St. Francois County prosecutors said. Authorities charged his wife, Malissa Ann Ancona, 44, and her son, Paul Edward Jinkerson Jr., 24, with first-degree murder, armed criminal action, tampering with physical evidence and abandonment of a corpse. Prosecutor Jarrod Mahurin said the killing “may have been a marital issue”; investigators say Frank had told his wife he planned to file for divorce.

According to a sheriff’s detective affidavit, Jinkerson shot the sleeping victim in the master bedroom. The body was transported in Jinkerson’s vehicle and left near Belgrade. When police later searched the home they found extensive blood in the master bedroom, a broken safe, missing guns and signs of cleanup. Malissa Ancona allegedly told police Jinkerson shot her husband, that she assisted in cleaning up and helped dispose of the body. The couple’s abandoned car was apparently wiped down and burned clothing was found nearby. Both suspects were jailed without bail and could be arraigned imminently. Jinkerson also faces unrelated probation-violation and property-related charges; his lawyer has expressed disbelief at the murder allegation.

Frank Ancona’s Klan activities included small robed gatherings and leafletting that drew local attention; observers describe his group as tiny and fractious. The Southern Poverty Law Center and ACLU attorneys characterized the chapter as marginal and Ancona as a complicated figure involved in disputes with other Klan leaders. Neighbors described domestic tension at the home. The Washington County coroner reported the fatal wound was from a shotgun-type firearm fired at close range. Local authorities have not provided additional comment.

Eric W. Deaton, a 42-year-old Constitution Party candidate from New Lebanon running for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by Sen. George Voinovich, was indicted Aug. 31 by a Montgomery County grand jury on one count of unlawful sexual conduct with a minor, a third-degree felony. Prosecutors allege Deaton engaged in sexual conduct with a girl aged 13 to 15 between March 20, 2006, and March 25, 2007; if convicted he faces up to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine. Perry Township police say Deaton met the girl through his church, tutored her, invited her to his home, paid her for odd jobs, and that hotel receipts and surveillance video support the case. Deaton, who is married with three children and a Cub Scout leader per his campaign, denies the allegations, calls the indictment politically motivated, and vows to remain in the Senate race. His attorney says evidence and a four-hour polygraph help prove his innocence; Deaton is to be arraigned Sept. 14.

A three-year-old boy fell about 15–16 feet into the jaguar exhibit at the Little Rock Zoo on the morning of October 10, 2014. Witnesses—including the child’s father and grandfather—reported seeing his feet go over the railing; the father threw objects to distract the cats. A primate keeper who rushed to the scene said she saw a jaguar with its mouth around the child’s neck. Zoo staff and arriving workers used fire extinguishers to hold the animals back while another staffer lowered a ladder and climbed into the enclosure to retrieve the conscious, responsive child. One jaguar reportedly ran off while another bit the boy on the back of the neck before releasing him. An ambulance stationed at the zoo transported the child to Arkansas Children’s Hospital within minutes. He was treated for extensive scalp lacerations, a depressed skull fracture and minor puncture wounds; doctors said the injuries were not life-threatening and described his condition as stable and expected to improve. The zoo, accredited by the AZA, and city officials said procedures were followed and an investigation is underway.

Michael Briggs, 38, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and attempted burglary for killing 82-year-old former nun Mary Greco in late December 2012. Greco, a longtime St. Luke’s parishioner and volunteer who lived alone in Schenectady, was found dead on New Year’s Day 2013. Briggs admitted strangling and stabbing her, then stealing her car, which was later recovered in a church lot. Surveillance showed Briggs leaving his home with a snow shovel and walking toward Greco’s after he had shoveled her car days earlier; a neighbor’s call placed him there. Investigators also matched Briggs’ fingerprints from a toilet seat, kitchen items and Greco’s car, and found his DNA on the blanket draped over her body. Briggs was on parole at the time, having been released in 2007 after serving 10 years of a 15-year sentence for a prior violent robbery and sexual assault. He faces sentencing in June to 30 years to life.

Leslie Rasmussen, a 20-year-old drummer in the band Good English and a childhood friend of former Stanford swimmer Brock Turner, sparked national outrage after a character letter she wrote in Turner’s defense was read in court. Turner had been convicted on three felony counts for sexually assaulting an unconscious 23-year-old woman behind a campus dumpster in January 2015. Rasmussen’s letter called the episode “a huge misunderstanding,” argued Turner was “not a monster,” suggested alcohol played the central role, and questioned whether it was fair to “base the fate of the next ten + years of his life on the decision of a girl who doesn’t remember anything.” She also criticized what she called excessive political correctness and implied that campus sexual assaults were not always committed by “rapists.” A judge, Aaron Persky, cited letters like hers when imposing a six-month county jail sentence—far below the two-year statutory minimum—sparking intense criticism and a campaign to recall him.

Public backlash against Rasmussen’s letter led to immediate professional consequences: venues and festivals canceled the band’s appearances, and their PR firm dropped them. Rasmussen initially defended her intent, saying she sought only to highlight alcohol’s role and Turner’s character, and that her private letter had been misrepresented in a social-media firestorm. She later issued two apologies acknowledging the victim’s “enormous pain,” recognizing Turner had been “rightfully convicted,” and saying she had not adequately acknowledged the severity of his crime.

Court and sentencing documents paint a pattern of aggressive, alcohol-fueled behavior by Turner at multiple parties, including unwanted kissing, touching, and persistent advances. Evidence from his phone and photos suggested drug and alcohol use, contrary to statements he made to probation. The victim’s searing public statement on the assault further intensified scrutiny. Legally, Turner was convicted of sexual assault and related offenses involving an unconscious and intoxicated person; under California law, those convictions do not carry the statutory label of “rape” in this case, though he is a registered sex offender for life. The judge has not commented while an appeal is pending.

Tulane University physical anthropologist John Verano has joined excavations at a Peruvian coastal site that has revealed an extraordinary ritual sacrifice of children and young llamas dating to roughly 600 years ago. First discovered by Peruvian archaeologist Gabriel Prieto in 2011 at Huanchaquito—a sandy ridge about 100 yards from the beach and once part of the Chimú state—initial finds included the remains of 42 children and 76 llamas. This summer Prieto and Verano expanded the dig, uncovering numerous additional victims and completing analysis of the 2011 child burials with support from the National Geographic Society and Tulane’s Stone Center for Latin American Studies. The burials are notable and unusual for coastal Peru: many of the child skeletons show evidence that their hearts were torn out and replaced with fabric, and the inclusion of so many young llamas alongside children is unprecedented in the region, making interpretation challenging. Researchers hypothesize the mass sacrifice may have been an offering to the sea or a ritual response to catastrophic flooding associated with an El Niño event; the llamas may have been intended symbolically to carry the children to the afterlife. The site came to light as erosion and local construction exposed bones in the dune, prompting villagers to report them. Multiple laboratories are now analyzing bones and teeth to determine age, origin, health, and details of the deaths, which will permit a more precise reconstruction of the event. Verano cautions that the full meaning remains uncertain, but calls the discovery both unusual and exciting and says further study will provide more answers.

Judy Shalom Nir-Mozes, a prominent Israeli media figure and wife of Interior Minister Silvan Shalom, sparked international outrage after tweeting a racist joke about U.S. President Barack Obama: “Do u know what Obama coffee is? Black and weak.” The post, seen by tens of thousands of followers, drew hundreds of angry responses calling it racist, arrogant and disgraceful, and many noted its insensitivity coming days after the racially motivated massacre of nine African American churchgoers in Charleston. Nir-Mozes deleted the tweet quickly, but screenshots circulated. She issued multiple apologies, first calling it “a stupid joke somebody told me,” then directly apologizing to President Obama and insisting she was not racist, and later tweeting a lighter remark about hoping her husband would not divorce her over the incident. The controversy revived scrutiny of her past social-media missteps, including a deleted tweet when Obama launched his @POTUS account and earlier comments that led to her resignation from a UNICEF Israel role after inflammatory posts about Palestinians.

In eastern China, officials abruptly canceled the centuries-old Jinhua Hutou Dog Meat Festival after a large online outcry led by animal-rights activists and pet owners. The three-day temple fair in Wucheng district, Zhejiang Province, historically featured a dog market and in recent years involved thousands of live dogs being brought in, slaughtered on-site and sold; local journalists estimated at least 5,000 dogs were killed. Graphic photos and eyewitness accounts of brutal handling and public slaughter circulated on microblogs like Sina Weibo, galvanizing public sentiment against the festival. The campaign — amplified by celebrities, editorials and grassroots rescues of dogs from transport trucks — framed the event as cruel and out of step with rising pet ownership and growing animal-rights awareness in China. Officials said the cancellation was made “in full respect of the public’s opinion,” though some villagers defended the custom, which folklore links to a 14th-century wartime episode and which proponents compare to other traditional food practices. The decision reflects shifting attitudes about animals, the influence of social media, and tensions between preserving tradition and responding to modern ethical concerns.

Islamic State released a 10–11 minute execution video showing five orange‑jumpsuited men shot in the head after purportedly confessing to spying for the UK. A masked English‑speaking militant, mocking Prime Minister David Cameron and threatening British soil, delivers a propaganda rant similar to that of the slain London‑born IS propagandist Mohammed “Jihadi John.” The film, unverified by independent sources, includes claims that some victims provided information about IS figures and positions, and features detainees who say they come from Raqqa and Benghazi; none confess to being British. Observers, including the BBC, say the men appear to speak under “extraordinary duress” and may be innocent. The video concludes with a young boy, about four to seven, in military clothing and reportedly speaking with a British accent, pointing and vowing to kill “kafir” (unbelievers). UK authorities and intelligence services are examining the footage and seeking to identify the masked speaker, seen as a potential successor to Emwazi. Analysts suggest the release may aim to distract from IS battlefield setbacks, shock Western audiences, reinforce the group’s brand, and intimidate potential informers or recruits amid the coalition air campaign in Syria and Iraq.

Swedish DJ Tim “Avicii” Bergling, 28, was found dead April 20 in Oman; his family later indicated he died by suicide after long struggles with mental and physical health, including heavy drinking and stress from intense touring. Sources told media he inflicted fatal cuts with broken glass, though reports vary on the exact wound. Avicii rose to global fame with hits like “Levels,” toured widely, and earned substantial wealth, yet gave millions to charity and highlighted social issues in his work. He quit touring in 2016 seeking balance and peace.

Tricia Fraser sued anti-abortion ad firm Heroic Media (Majella Cares) and Life Always after her then-4-year-old daughter Anissa’s photo was used on a controversial billboard near the Holland Tunnel reading, “The most dangerous place for an African American is in the womb.” Fraser says she responded to a casting call for family photos and only signed a release for stock use; the image was licensed from Getty Images with restrictions against “unflattering or unduly controversial” uses. She alleges the defendants violated the contract and New York law by deploying the image in a racially charged campaign without consent, causing international media attention, emotional distress for Anissa and damage to her budding modeling career. Fraser contends the ad falsely implied mother and child approved the message and seeks punitive damages, disgorgement of profits, and an injunction barring further use. Heroic Media, Life Always and Pastor Stephen Broden did not immediately comment.

The document chronicles several episodes highlighting Donald Trump’s brash public persona, unusually large media presence, and mixed business record. It opens with an exchange during a QVC-style segment in which NBC reporter Peter Alexander asked what parents should tell their children about Trump’s language. Trump mocked the premise, deriding political correctness and belittling the reporter rather than addressing concerns about his history of crude remarks. That moment followed a lengthy, 45-minute prime-time press conference on cable news during which CNN, Fox, and MSNBC continued to air Trump while other candidates—Hillary Clinton, Bernie Sanders, and John Kasich—were speaking elsewhere. Critics argued the networks’ choice to prioritize Trump’s rambling appearance over airing rival speeches provided the campaign the equivalent of massive free media exposure and raised questions about news judgment and fairness. Media commentators noted the decision validated Trump’s strategy of staging long, president-like events that attract viewers; defenders of the networks countered that Trump’s unpredictable remarks have higher “news value” and that changing away from his event risked losing audience. The piece then reviews Trump’s history of business flops often cited by opponents and rivals, including Trump University, Trump Airlines, Trump Vodka, Trump Magazine, Trump Mortgage, and the infamous Trump Steaks. The latter—sold through QVC and Sharper Image—was lampooned through archived customer reviews, many of which were scathing: complaints of grease, shrinkage, poor flavor, and low quality appeared alongside a few positive reports. The narrative recounts legal and reputational troubles: lawsuits over Trump University, mixed Better Business Bureau ratings, countersuits, and accusations from rivals such as Mitt Romney and Marco Rubio who labeled Trump’s business record uneven. Overall, the document juxtaposes Trump’s media dominance and provocative style with a record of commercial missteps, suggesting his capacity to captivate television audiences often outweighs substantive scrutiny of his language or business practices.

Police identified a body found bound to a cinder block and wrapped in a tarp off Brooklyn as 35-year-old Carmine Carini, the son of a Colombo crime family associate. Carini’s body was discovered Saturday near East 58th Street and Avenue U, close to his Mill Basin home; investigators believe he had been in the water since Friday night. His legs were tied to a cinder block with an electrical cord, his body wrapped in a blue tarp sealed with duct tape, and a five-pound bag of drywall compound was also attached. Authorities said he died of blunt-force trauma to the head and had also been stabbed; identification was made through fingerprints. NYPD Chief of Detectives Robert Boyce described Carini as a “reputed mobster’s son,” noting his father’s organized crime ties and that detectives are actively investigating who was in Carini’s life at the time. Carmine Carini Sr., an associate of the Colombo family, served lengthy prison terms dating to a 1983 killing, later freed in a plea deal, then returned to prison for posing as a cop in robberies; he was released from federal custody in July. The younger Carini had his own criminal record, including multiple robbery arrests and a five-year sentence for a series of 2003 muggings. Authorities continue to probe motives and suspects in the killing.

Spanish riot police and Civil Guard officers used force to try to stop a disputed Catalan independence referendum on Sunday, breaking into polling stations across Catalonia, firing rubber bullets and clashing with protesters. Authorities said several people were injured; Catalan officials reported 38 treated for mostly minor wounds. In Barcelona, officers fired rubber projectiles while trying to clear crowds who attempted to stop National Police vehicles leaving after ballot boxes were seized. Witnesses described police smashing doors, using batons and dragging out would-be voters; at one Girona-area sports center officers used a hammer and lock cutter to gain entry and at least one woman was stretchered away.

Catalan President Carles Puigdemont condemned the crackdown, calling it an enduring shame for the Spanish state, while Madrid’s regional representative, Enric Millo, defended the actions as professional enforcement of court orders and said any claim the day constituted a valid referendum was doomed. Spain’s Constitutional Court had suspended the vote, and the national government had instructed police to prevent voting, saying the referendum was illegal. Still, Catalan authorities pressed ahead, urging 5.3 million eligible voters to participate, allowing ballots printed at home and permitting voting at any location after courts and police seized millions of ballots and dismantled voting technology. Polling stations were occupied by activists, parents and children who cheered when plastic-sealed ballot boxes were placed on tables, but many centers were sealed off or subject to forced entry and arrests in the run-up to the controversial vote.

The Utah Legislature passed HB277, eliminating the civil statute of limitations for child sexual abuse suits, sending the bill to Gov. Gary Herbert. The change removes the current four-year limit after a victim’s 18th birthday, instead granting victims a four-year window to file civil claims from the time they discover or remember the abuse. Supporters, including Rep. Ken Ivory (R-West Jordan) and Sen. Aaron Osmond (R-South Jordan), argued the law acknowledges that many survivors only process abuse decades later; Osmond cited estimates that one in six boys and one in four girls in Utah experience sexual abuse and that many don’t confront it until after age 40. Deondra Brown, co-founder of the Foundation for Survivors of Abuse and sister in the 5 Browns piano quintet, watched the vote from the Senate gallery and praised the change as giving survivors time to heal and hold abusers accountable; her family’s father was criminally convicted in 2011. Opponents raised concerns about unreliable recovered memories and reasons statutes exist; Sen. Scott Jenkins and Sen. Gene Davis opposed the bill. The Senate approved HB277 24-2. Separately, a retired Rich High School teacher, Michael Layne Williamson, 60, was sentenced after pleading guilty to aggravated sexual abuse of a child for assaults 22 years earlier. Judge Thomas Willmore rejected a lenient pre-sentence recommendation and sentenced Williamson to one to 15 years plus up to five concurrent years, requiring completion of a sex-offender course. The victim, now 35, delivered emotional testimony about long-term trauma and its impact on her life and children; Williamson apologized and sought forgiveness.

Ohio Gov. John Kasich postponed Ronald Phillips’ execution, rescheduling it for July 2, 2014, to allow medical tests to determine whether Phillips—condemned in 1993 for raping and killing a 3-year-old—could donate nonvital organs to his ailing mother or others. The delay came less than a day before Phillips, 40, was to be executed under a newly adopted two-drug lethal-injection combination (midazolam and hydromorphone) prompted by a pentobarbital shortage. Phillips and his attorney say the donation request is a sincere final gesture, not a stalling tactic; he’s willing to donate to others if he can’t help relatives. Ohio’s Department of Rehabilitation and Correction will conduct compatibility testing and, if feasible, arrange surgery at Ohio State’s Wexner Medical Center before returning Phillips to death row. Prison policy requires transplant costs be covered by Phillips or recipients. Officials note this is unprecedented in Ohio and possibly the first U.S. execution postponement to permit organ harvesting; similar donations occurred elsewhere.

A Manhattan double homicide investigation led to the arrest of Isaac Duran (also reported as Isaac Duran Infante), a former student and the father of 4-year-old Miguel, after the bodies of Miguel and his mother, 36-year-old Felicia Barahona, were discovered in Barahona’s Hamilton Heights apartment. The superintendent alerted police to a strong odor; both victims appeared to have been dead for several days when found Monday. Barahona was discovered on the living-room floor with an electrical cord around her neck; the medical examiner ruled her death ligature strangulation. Miguel was found unresponsive in a bathtub and died of asphyxia from neck compression. Law-enforcement sources say Duran, 22–23, confessed during questioning and cited dissatisfaction with how the child was being raised — including anger over the boy’s clothing — as a motive; surveillance footage placed him at the building in the days before the discovery. Duran had been involved with Barahona beginning when he was her student at DeWitt Clinton High School; their relationship, which produced Miguel, became public in 2012 and led to Barahona’s dismissal. Relatives on both sides expressed shock and grief: Barahona’s family remembered her as rebuilding her life, studying forensic science and serving in the Coast Guard Reserve, while some of Duran’s relatives insisted on his innocence. Detectives continued to investigate timelines and Duran’s recent movements as homicide charges were brought. The case drew intense media attention because of the prior illicit teacher-student relationship.

On Father’s Day in New Smyrna Beach, 46-year-old Eugene Blackwell Sr. shot his 18-year-old son, Eugene Blackwell Jr., multiple times during a domestic dispute, police said. The confrontation began when Blackwell Sr. and his wife argued after she mentioned divorce; she told officers he grabbed her by the throat. Blackwell Jr., a recent New Smyrna Beach High graduate and standout weightlifter, intervened to protect his mother. According to investigators, the father fired four shots at his son inside their Edward Street home; the teen fled bleeding—wounded in the abdomen/chest area, hip, thigh and right arm—and collapsed in a neighbor’s driveway, screaming that his father had shot him. Neighbors called 911, helped the injured teen, and one followed Blackwell Sr. after he drove off; the truck was later abandoned. Blackwell Jr. was airlifted to Halifax Health Medical Center in Daytona Beach; surgeons reported one bullet struck multiple organs, another remains lodged in his hip, and his condition was later listed as satisfactory. Blackwell Sr. was arrested and charged with attempted first-degree murder and battery, held without bail after being denied bond. The mother reported a long history of domestic abuse during their 23-year relationship.

What was meant to be a Halloween night out at Nashville Nightmare turned into a genuine emergency when a supposed attraction actor handed a guest a real knife and instructed her to stab a friend. Four friends were visiting the Madison haunted attraction Friday night, where costumed performers interact with patrons and run carnival-style games. According to police and interviews, a thin man in character approached the group, asked if one friend was "fucking around with her," and, when the woman answered yes, handed her a knife and said, "Well, here, stab him." Believing the knife to be a prop and playing along, 29-year-old Tawnya Greenfield plunged it into her friend James Yochim’s left arm. She initially thought it was a joke, even saying "ha, ha gotcha," but when she pulled the blade back she saw blood on the knife, a hole in his shirt, and blood squirting from his arm. Medics on site transported Yochim to Skyline Hospital, where he was treated and released. Two other friends in the group corroborated Greenfield’s account. The man who handed over the knife fled; Nashville Nightmare believes the individual may have been an employee and has placed him on leave pending investigation. The attraction emphasized its safety protocols—metal detectors, onsite medical and security staff—and said it will review procedures and cooperate with authorities. The group involved is considering legal action, and Metro Police are investigating the incident.

A 25-year-old Israeli woman reported she was gang-raped after accepting a lift in the early hours near Manali, a popular Himalayan resort in Himachal Pradesh. Seeking transport to Kaza in Spiti Valley and later to Keylong to join friends, she flagged down a vehicle without license plates that carried six men. She says two of the occupants attacked and raped her at an unknown location before abandoning her in Manali around 3 a.m. The woman and a friend reached the police station about 10 a.m.; she has undergone a medical examination that was sent to Mandi for expert analysis and is being transferred to a larger hospital for further tests. Authorities registered a complaint, collected evidence and reviewed CCTV, including night-vision footage, as much of the town is under high-definition surveillance. Police later reported arrests: two local men were detained and the vehicle allegedly used was recovered; search operations continue for the remaining suspects. The Israeli embassy has been informed; Indian investigators said they are pursuing video leads and expect progress. The case echoes earlier assaults on foreign women in the Kullu district—a 2013 gang rape of an American tourist and a 2012 rape of an Australian—highlighting persistent risks despite legal reforms that increased penalties for sexual violence after the high-profile 2012 Delhi case. Police say investigations are "headed in the right direction" as they work to identify and apprehend all involved.

Prosecutors from six California counties announced they will combine their cases against Joseph James DeAngelo Jr., the suspect long linked to the “Golden State Killer” crimes, into a single prosecution to be tried in Sacramento. DeAngelo, a 72-year-old former police officer arrested in April, faces an amended complaint alleging 13 counts of murder along with multiple kidnapping and weapons charges spanning six jurisdictions across northern, central and southern California. He remains in custody in Sacramento County and will be arraigned on the amended complaint; he has not yet entered a plea.

Authorities described the unified trial as an effort to bring long-sought justice to victims and families after decades without an arrest in a string of murders, rapes and home burglaries from the 1970s and 1980s. Investigators had preserved DNA from several crime scenes — notably the 1980 murders of Lyman and Charlene Smith — and reviewed rape kit samples across jurisdictions. This year they used genetic genealogy: investigators uploaded crime-scene DNA to a public genealogy database, built family trees from matches, and narrowed suspects by age and location to DeAngelo. Surveillance and retrieval of his discarded tissue produced DNA that matched evidence from multiple scenes, prompting the charges and consolidation of prosecutions in Sacramento.

Harris County deputy Darren Goforth, 47, was fatally shot Friday night at a northwest Houston gas station; prosecutors say the shooter, Shannon Jaruay Miles, 30, emptied a .40-caliber pistol into Goforth—14 rounds from the magazine plus one in the chamber—for a total of 15 shots. Miles was arrested Saturday and appeared in court Monday on capital murder charges; a judge found probable cause and held him without bail. Ballistics matched a loaded .40 Smith & Wesson found at Miles’ home to shell casings at the scene, and a witness identified him in a video lineup. Surveillance footage reportedly captured the attack. Investigators say motive remains unclear; Sheriff Ron Hickman said officials suspect Goforth may have been targeted because he wore a uniform. Miles has a lengthy history of run-ins with police, including arrests for assault, resisting arrest, unlawful firearm discharge and a 2012 aggravated assault case in which he was declared incompetent and hospitalized for four months before later being returned to competency and having the charge dismissed. The community has rallied for Goforth’s family—more than 1,000 attended vigils and donations have exceeded $150,000. Funeral services are scheduled Friday.

Toronto Mayor Rob Ford remained defiant amid escalating fallout from revelations about his drug use, even as public and political pressure mounted. At a veterans’ ceremony he was met with shouts of “shame” and one World War II veteran refused to shake his hand, calling him a “druggie.” Ford brushed off the protests, declaring, “I’m not going anywhere.” The next day he appeared at City Hall to sign and sell “Robbie Bobbie” bobblehead dolls—up to 300 people queued for the $20 figures—with proceeds going to charity. The line included both supporters and critics, and Ford autographed many dolls himself.

The controversy centers on reports that police obtained a video showing Ford apparently smoking from a crack pipe; Ford later admitted to smoking crack last year while drunk, apologized, and denied being addicted. The scandal has eroded his ability to lead: Toronto’s mayor holds limited formal powers and depends on consensus-building as the sole citywide-elected councilor, a role many say he can no longer fulfill. City Council members, including former ally Denzil Minnan-Wong, argue Ford has lost the moral authority to set the agenda. Councilors are pursuing motions to isolate him—one would ask Ford to take a leave, apologize, and cooperate with police, and, if he refuses, urge the provincial government to legislate his removal; another would strip or curtail his appointment and agenda-setting powers.

Most councilors are reluctant to request provincial intervention, fearing precedent, so motions to reduce Ford’s powers or to “build a box around the mayor” aim to let the council govern despite him. Meanwhile his base—“Ford Nation”—remains loyal, and his brother Doug Ford vowed to defend him as councilors prepare for contentious proceedings. The scandal has already disrupted council work on major issues like transit and budget decisions.

Hours after being crowned Miss Teen USA at The Venetian Resort and Casino in Las Vegas, 18-year-old Karlie Hay of Tomball, Texas, confronted online criticism over past offensive tweets that surfaced immediately after her victory. Many social media users posted screenshots alleging Hay used profanity, threats and racial slurs, including the N-word, on her now-protected Twitter account. The discovery led to swift public backlash rather than the expected congratulatory response.

Early Sunday, Hay addressed the controversy on Twitter. She acknowledged that several years ago she “had many personal struggles” and used public language she is not proud of, adding there is “no excuse” for it. While she did not offer an explicit apology in the tweets quoted, Hay emphasized personal growth: through “hard work, education and thanks in large part to the sisterhood that I have come to know through pageants,” she stated she is “today a better person.” She pledged to use her Miss Teen USA platform to promote values shared by the Miss Universe Organization and her own, focusing on confidence, beauty and perseverance for all women.

The Miss Universe Organization responded with a statement saying the language Hay used is unacceptable and does not reflect the organization’s values, but noted she was “in a different place in her life,” regrets her actions, and has learned lessons that reshaped her values. The organization said it will support her continued growth and confirmed she will keep her crown.

Former Miss Teen USA Kamie Crawford publicly criticized Hay’s apparent lack of preparation to manage her social media presence after winning. Hay has said she plans to apply to Texas A&M after graduating and hopes to advocate for people affected by drug and alcohol abuse while pursuing a business career.

Lincoln police say Charlie Rogers, a 33-year-old former University of Nebraska basketball player who identifies as lesbian, staged a reported July 22 hate attack on herself and has been charged with filing a false police report. Rogers initially told officers masked intruders stripped, tied, carved homophobic slurs and a cross into her body, and tried to set her home ablaze. The account triggered vigils, national attention, and a local outpouring of support. Investigators, however, found “numerous inconsistencies” between her story and physical evidence: no signs of a struggle or blood on the bedspread, DNA from Rogers inside gloves found at the scene with no male DNA, deleted texts, prior purchase of gloves, zip ties and a box cutter, and a forensic pathologist’s opinion that wounds appeared self-inflicted. Police also highlighted a pre-incident social media post in which Rogers wrote about being a “catalyst.” Rogers pleaded not guilty and was released on personal recognizance; her attorney says she maintains her innocence and will fight the charge. Local LGBT groups praised the police inquiry while urging continued community support against hate.

Customs officers at Graz airport in Austria were surprised when a 35-year-old Moroccan woman arriving from Marrakesh was found to be carrying a four-inch piece of human intestine in her checked luggage. The tissue, carefully preserved—apparently in formaldehyde, triple-wrapped and placed in thick plastic containers—was discovered during a routine random baggage check on Sept. 8. The woman, who has not been publicly identified, told officials the sample was from her 40-year-old husband, who had died and whom she suspected had been poisoned. Her lawyer, Anton Karner, said she had acted on the advice of a Moroccan doctor who removed the intestinal piece and recommended it be tested in Europe. Austrian pathology chief Gerald Höfler described the packaging as professionally done and compliant with EU standards; the sample was sent to his Graz institute for analysis, with results expected the following week. Local police and customs reviewed the case and determined the woman had not broken Austrian law by bringing the specimen into the country, so no charges were filed. Karner added that the couple had lived in Graz for eight years and that tensions with the husband’s relatives—who had opposed the marriage—had prompted the poisoning suspicions.

Houston police charged 39-year-old Jason Griffin of Rosenberg with manslaughter, unlawful possession of a firearm and felon in possession of a gun after a man wearing a bulletproof vest was shot and killed at a Heights garage apartment early Sunday. The victim, identified in court records as Daniel Barber, was shot in the chest at a party in the 300 block of West 23rd Street and was pronounced dead at the scene. Investigators are probing whether the shooting resulted from a dare and have not yet determined if the bullet penetrated the vest or struck an unprotected area. Police say Griffin and another witness initially fled the scene; Griffin was later arrested while receiving treatment at a local hospital for what officers described as a “medical issue.” Court records show Griffin was previously charged with aggravated robbery in 2001. According to a witness quoted by ABC13, Griffin did not intend to kill Barber and believed the gun was unloaded; she described Griffin saying the victim had challenged him and then collapsed after being shot. The witness also said Griffin became suicidal after the incident and required treatment for seizures before being taken into custody. Homicide investigators continue their inquiry.

Shannon Egeland, a 43-year-old Oregon mortgage fraud convict, was sentenced to an additional three years and 10 months after admitting he orchestrated a staged shooting in which his then-17-year-old son shot him in the legs. The July 31, 2014 incident, arranged a day before Egeland was to begin a 10-year federal prison term for a high-profile mortgage-fraud scheme, was intended both to delay his incarceration and to support a bogus disability insurance claim he had filed a week earlier. The shotgun shot severed Egeland’s left leg; he now stood before U.S. District Judge Anna J. Brown on a prosthetic. He pleaded guilty in May to conspiracy to commit wire fraud in the insurance scheme and to interstate failure to pay child support; the new sentence is consecutive to the decade he already faces for the Desert Sun housing scandal, in which he and associates raised millions through falsified loan applications and phony business plans.

Prosecutors portrayed Egeland as a “menace to society” and an opportunistic, narcissistic manipulator who inflicted long-term psychological harm on his son. They sought a five-year term for the insurance fraud; defense counsel urged a shorter, consecutive sentence, noting Egeland’s medical, mental-health struggles, and substantial existing sentence. Egeland told the court he has reflected while jailed, is taking mental-health medications, and is haunted by the pain inflicted on his son. The judge also ordered payment of $90,011 in overdue child support and urged continued mental-health treatment and evaluation during and after incarceration. The attempted fraud did not financially harm the insurer, which detected the deception quickly.

Beginning in 1996, Alexa Internet began donating its web crawl data to the Internet Archive; those daily data streams are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo. Separately, a tabloid-style piece reports ongoing fallout from Michelle “Bombshell” McGee’s alleged affair with Jesse James and the effect on Sandra Bullock. The article claims McGee initially sold her story to InTouch for $30,000 and is now seeking up to $100,000 for additional “Kiss & Tell: Part 2” material, including explicit photos, more text messages, and intimate details about James. A magazine insider and the author express disdain for paying McGee further and call for her to stop publicizing the scandal. The writer’s outlet, Naughty But Nice, states it will not pay for such content and defends Bullock, portraying her as the innocent party being repeatedly embarrassed. The tone is clearly tabloid, focused on sensational details and criticism of McGee’s pursuit of money through further disclosures.

Montreal and Ottawa police launched a Canada-wide manhunt for 29-year-old Luka Rocco Magnotta, also known as Eric Clinton Newman and Vladimir Romanov, after grisly human remains were found in both cities. A headless torso was discovered behind a Montreal apartment building; authorities believe it may be linked to a partially decomposed foot mailed to the Conservative Party headquarters in Ottawa and a hand intercepted at a Canada Post facility, with at least one package reportedly addressed to the Liberal Party. Investigators say the victim and suspect knew one another and that forensic tests are pending to confirm whether all parts came from the same person. Graphic video allegedly showing a stabbing, dismemberment and postmortem abuse was found online and is under police review. Magnotta, a former low-budget porn performer with a large and disturbing online presence and prior fraud convictions, had rented the Montreal unit for months; neighbours described foul odours, bloodstained sheets and an alarming scene inside. Authorities urged public help in locating Magnotta and intend to charge him with murder when arrested.

The 23-year-old New Delhi gang-rape victim remains in extremely critical condition at Mount Elizabeth Hospital in Singapore, suffering significant brain injury, lung and abdominal infections, and having experienced a prior cardiac arrest. Doctors removed large portions of her gangrenous intestines after three surgeries in Delhi; a multidisciplinary team is working to stabilise her. Security at the hospital has been tightened and the Indian High Commission is assisting the family, who rely on interpreters. The case has ignited nationwide outrage over treatment of sexual assault victims and calls for stronger protections. Separate incidents in Punjab and Chhattisgarh led to suspension or firing of police officers accused of ignoring rape complaints; in one Punjab case an 18-year-old woman later died by suicide. Politicians have faced criticism for insensitive remarks, and leaders urged swift justice for the perpetrators.

Between Aug. 29 and Aug. 31, 2015, Arizona Department of Public Safety investigators probed four separate shootings targeting vehicles along an eight-mile stretch of Interstate 10 through central Phoenix. The first two incidents occurred eastbound and westbound around 11:03 a.m. and 11:09 a.m. on Aug. 29; a sport utility vehicle’s windshield was struck and a 13-year-old female front-seat passenger suffered a cut to her right ear, treated at the scene, and a passenger-type bus was also struck while only the driver was aboard and unharmed. Later that night, about 10:15 p.m., a motorist noted bullet holes on the passenger side of her vehicle after hearing a loud bang but waiting to inspect the car until the next day. On Aug. 31 at about 4:25 a.m., a work truck sustained damage consistent with a bullet strike to the front headlamp after its driver heard a bang and at first thought a rock had hit the vehicle. DPS Director Frank Milstead warned the shootings could end in tragedy and said the attacks appeared random; detectives are investigating and asking anyone with information to contact DPS or Silent Witness and to submit tips online. Photos related to the cases were released.

Just days after a video surfaced of Donald Trump boasting about groping women, Melania Trump arrived at the Oct. 9 presidential debate wearing a fuchsia Gucci “pussy-bow” blouse and matching pants — a choice that instantly drew attention and social-media commentary.
