The pussy-bow, a women’s blouse with a tied neck bow, has a long fashion history: popularized mid-20th century by designers like Chanel and Yves Saint Laurent, adopted as a signature of Margaret Thatcher, and recently revived by Gucci. The garment’s name and appearance prompted widespread reaction because it echoed the vulgar phrase Trump used on a 2005 Access Hollywood tape — “grab them by the pussy” — which had ignited a major scandal, costing endorsements and alienating many voters. The Trump campaign and Melania’s spokespeople insisted the outfit was an aesthetic choice with no intent to reference the tape; Melania herself called her husband’s remarks “unacceptable and offensive” while accepting his apology. Nevertheless, critics and commentators read the blouse as an unfortunate, ironic, or tone-deaf sartorial statement that kept the groping controversy front and center during the debate.

A van drove onto the central pedestrian promenade of Las Ramblas in Barcelona on the afternoon of Aug. 17, 2017, veering and zigzagging to mow down tourists and residents. The attack killed 13 people and injured about 100 more, with at least 15 seriously hurt. Witnesses described chaotic scenes of bodies, blood, shattered limbs and panicked families fleeing into shops. Catalan police called it a clear terrorist act; the Islamic State’s Aamaq news agency claimed responsibility. Hours later, police in the seaside resort of Cambrils shot and killed five suspects after they drove into pedestrians and officers; those assailants wore fake explosive belts and carried an ax and knives. Authorities were investigating a related explosion at a house in Alcanar, believed to have contained butane canisters and to have been a planning site for larger attacks; investigators think the blast forced the group to carry out more rudimentary operations. Multiple arrests were made and several suspects remained at large; identities and connections were being clarified. Victims came from many countries, prompting international condolences and three days of national mourning in Spain. The attack echoed a recent European pattern of vehicle-ramming incidents and was Spain’s deadliest since the 2004 Madrid train bombings. Authorities increased searches, held a public minute of silence, and vowed to pursue those responsible.

An 18-year-old man who had both legs severed by a freight train at a Taree level crossing on December 21 has died in hospital, police confirmed. The teenager was asleep on the tracks at about 4:30am while celebrating his birthday and was struck, losing both legs above the knee. He was taken to John Hunter Hospital in Newcastle in critical condition and died on Christmas Eve, three days after the collision. The train driver stopped shortly after the impact and called emergency services; he and two officers were later struck by rocks thrown by some party-goers at the scene. Police say the driver and officers initially sought refuge in the cab until reinforcements arrived. Paramedics reported being blocked, pushed, verbally abused and having an ambulance windscreen smashed while trying to treat the trapped, semi-conscious victim. Taree police are preparing a coronial report and continuing to investigate how the teenager came to be on the tracks and the conduct of those who impeded emergency workers. Authorities warn criminal charges could be laid against people who attacked or obstructed responders. Taree’s mayor described the death and subsequent behavior as very upsetting and unacceptable.

Two former Hooters managers, Paul “PJ” Cagnina and Scott Peterson, have filed a lawsuit in Los Angeles Superior Court alleging years of sexual harassment, hostile conduct and retaliation by a male supervisor, identified in the complaint as Rick Leukert. The suit, brought Tuesday and represented by attorney Jason Oliver, seeks unspecified damages and a court order requiring Hooters to prevent sexual harassment and retaliation at its franchised locations.

According to the complaint, both men worked as managers across several Southern California Hooters, including Hollywood, downtown Los Angeles and Costa Mesa. The suit accuses Leukert of repeated humiliating and sexually charged conduct intended to undermine the plaintiffs. Allegations include an incident after a Costa Mesa bikini contest in which Leukert reportedly threw Cagnina to the parking-lot ground and simulated sodomy in front of others; repeated inappropriate touching of male employees’ buttocks; urging Cagnina to go skinny-dipping with subordinate female employees; and taking and viewing intimate photos from a female manager’s cellphone. The complaint also details frequent derogatory and sexual comments — for example, altering Cagnina’s award name to “PGay,” nicknaming him “cagina,” asking if he had “been impregnating any Hooters’ girls,” and suggesting paternal ties to an expectant employee’s baby. Peterson alleges repeated improper touching, sexualized commentary in manager meetings, and receipt of sexualized photos and stories from Leukert.

Both men say they complained and the company investigated Leukert; he was later fired without explanation. Peterson alleges he was then terminated in retaliation. Hooters of America issued a brief statement noting the matter involves a franchised location and that it has no independent knowledge of the facts. The plaintiffs no longer work for Hooters and say the suit aims not just for compensation but to prevent such conduct in the future.

A coroner’s inquest in Billings, Montana found that Police Officer Grant Morrison was justified in fatally shooting 38-year-old Richard Ramirez during an April traffic stop. Morrison, a five-year department veteran who had been cleared in a separate 2013 fatal shooting, testified that he feared for his life because Ramirez, who was unarmed, appeared to reach for his waistband. Morrison said he repeatedly ordered Ramirez and other vehicle occupants to raise their hands and believed Ramirez “started to jiggle” his left hand out of view before Morrison fired three times into the car. Morrison told jurors he acted on the belief Ramirez had a gun and said, “I wanted to see my son grow up.”

Video presented at the inquest shows Morrison shouting commands and then firing; other footage released this week captures him breaking down immediately afterward—breathing heavily, sobbing and saying, “I thought he was gonna pull a gun on me,” as colleagues comfort him. An autopsy and toxicology showed Ramirez had a potentially lethal level of methamphetamine in his system, and investigators later found a small amount of methamphetamine and a syringe near his seat. Ramirez also had two outstanding warrants.

The seven-person jury deliberated about an hour before finding the shooting justified. Yellowstone County Attorney Scott Twito said he does not expect criminal charges. Ramirez’s family expressed disappointment and plans to file a civil suit alleging excessive force and racial profiling, criticizing the inquest as one-sided because most witnesses were law enforcement. Billings Police Chief Rich St. John noted this was the fifth officer-involved shooting during his tenure, all ruled justified.

Every other Sunday Luis Lopez Gallegos and his wife, Perla Avina, shopped for ingredients so she could make posole for the family during Raiders games. That routine ended in tragedy when, returning from Supermercado Mi Tierra in East Oakland, an angry motorist opened fire into their black 1998 Toyota Camry. A bullet struck 30-year-old Avina in the head while she sat in the front passenger seat. Gallegos drove a few blocks to their Brookfield Village home to call for help; neighbors and family tried CPR but Avina was pronounced dead in the driveway. She was a medical receptionist and mother of four children, ages 1 to 14, and had been with Gallegos since high school. The shooting occurred around 12:30 p.m. on 98th Avenue; police characterize it as road rage and are seeking the shooter and a suspect vehicle. Oakland police and CrimeStoppers are offering up to $30,000 for information leading to an arrest and urge residents to check surveillance footage from the 400–600 blocks of 98th Avenue. Family, friends and coworkers mourn Avina’s death, calling it senseless; a GoFundMe has been set up to assist with funeral expenses. Authorities continue to investigate.

On July 3, at about 3:15 p.m., 14-year-old Stephen J. Brumby was fatally shot at High Noon Gun Range in Sarasota. According to the Sarasota County Sheriff’s Office, Stephen was accidentally struck when his father, 64-year-old William C. Brumby, discharged a handgun in the last shooting lane. A spent shell casing had deflected off a wall and fallen into the back of William Brumby’s shirt; while attempting to remove it with the hand that was holding the firearm, he inadvertently pointed the gun behind him and it discharged, striking his son. Witness statements and interior video led detectives to classify the shooting as accidental. Stephen, a homeschooled boy and one of seven children, was taken to Sarasota Memorial Hospital and later died of his injuries. William Brumby was at the range with two other children, ages 24 and 12, who were not injured. No charges have been filed and the investigation remains ongoing. A GoFundMe memorial fund has been established to help the family with expenses. The incident is the second fatality at an area gun range in the past year; an unrelated suicide occurred last August at a different local range.

Jelinajane Bedrijo Almario, arrested in May 2016 in Hanford, California, was sentenced to 13 years in prison Monday after being tried as an adult for organizing a prostitution and human trafficking ring that exploited 14- and 15-year-old girls. Almario, who turned 18 two days before sentencing, faced charges including human trafficking of a minor, sending threatening communications to a victim’s family member, and making terrorist threats. Prosecutors say the scheme lasted several weeks in the spring and involved at least four girls; Almario allegedly recruited them through friends, acquaintances and social media, posted their photos on prostitution websites, and transported them to motels off Highway 99 in Tulare County to meet clients. Hanford Police Detective Richard Pontecorvo described Almario as the ring’s primary suspect and stressed how traffickers prey on youths with low self-esteem, initially befriending them before coercing them into prostitution. During the criminal activity, Almario reportedly sent threatening messages to a mother searching for her missing daughter. Police recovered the girls and arranged for them to receive help. The case surprised local authorities because the suspected pimp was herself a juvenile, an eye-opener that prompted swift action; detectives emphasized the lasting harm pimps inflict on vulnerable children and expressed relief that the victims were removed from the situation and connected with support services.

A Los Angeles street artist who works under the name XVALA plans to include hacked nude images of Jennifer Lawrence and Kate Upton in an upcoming show called “No Delete” at The Cory Allen Contemporary Art Showroom in St. Petersburg, Florida. The images will be reproduced life‑size on canvas and added to a larger body of work XVALA has assembled over seven years under a “Fear Google” theme that critiques privacy erosion and the permanence of digital footprints. Cory Allen, the gallery publicist, and XVALA frame the inclusion as part of a dialogue about invasion of privacy and say the works are art rather than simple reposted photos; Allen emphasized the gallery is not posting the images online and portrays the pieces as commentary. Representatives for Lawrence and Upton have vowed legal action against anyone who disseminates the stolen photos, and the images are evidence in an ongoing federal criminal investigation. Observers note XVALA chose Florida for the exhibit rather than California, where laws prohibit posting nude photos without consent with intent to cause distress. XVALA has used controversial celebrity material before, including plastering Scarlett Johansson’s leaked images in Los Angeles. The plan has sparked debate over whether using these illegally obtained images as art is a legitimate critique of privacy or an exploitative act that profits from victims’ abuse.

Renowned 104-year-old Australian botanist and ecologist David Goodall ended his life in a medically assisted suicide at the Life Circle clinic in Basel, Switzerland, after administering a lethal drug under doctor supervision. Not terminally ill, Goodall—who campaigned for legal assisted dying—traveled from Perth with donations and family support because euthanasia remains banned in Australia. He said declining abilities and loss of independence led to his decision, and he hoped his act would help free the elderly to choose death with dignity without traveling abroad. He died listening to Beethoven’s "Ode to Joy."

Actress Nastassja Kinski has publicly praised her half-sister Pola for bravely coming forward with allegations that their late father, acclaimed German actor Klaus Kinski, sexually abused her from around age five until 19. Pola detailed the abuse in an interview with Stern magazine timed to her new autobiography, Kindermund, saying their father normalized the abuse and treated her as his “little sex object.” Nastassja, who has starred in films such as Tess and Paris, Texas, told Bild she was “deeply shocked” but proud of Pola for freeing herself from the burden of the secret, calling her a “heroine” and saying the disclosure could help other victims. Klaus Kinski, who died in 1991, was revered for intense performances in films by Werner Herzog—Aguirre, Nosferatu, Fitzcarraldo—and notorious for volatile behavior and many adult affairs. Commentators and a biographer note rumors about his troubling conduct had circulated for years; some argue the revelations retroactively darken appreciation of his art. Werner Herzog’s documentary My Best Fiend captured Kinski’s extremes—rages and tenderness—prompting debate over whether admiring such a figure makes audiences complicit. Pola’s testimony challenges the persistent adulation of a man whose cinematic genius may now be inseparable from alleged criminality.

Five days before convicted murderers Richard Matt, 48, and David Sweat, 34, cut their way out of Clinton Correctional Facility, a violent June 1yard brawl between two inmate factions—some identified as Muslim and others suspected Bloods gang members—erupted. Correction officers in two towers quelled the melee by firing chemical-agent canisters; the fight lasted under a minute but left one inmate with a broken leg. The next day part of the prison was locked down and searches of the yard and two cellblocks uncovered five weapons, but the roughly 3,000-inmate facility was not fully searched. Some officers allege DOCCS headquarters rebuffed requests for a full lockdown; DOCCS declined to comment while investigations continue.

Matt and Sweat, both serving long sentences for murder, escaped from an honor-block tier using tools including a small electric saw powered by spliced extension cords and a 20-pound sledgehammer. They cut adjoining cell walls into an internal utility corridor, spliced power from a light fixture to run the saw, and then breached a 24-inch steam pipe that led to a sewer and outside the prison. The men concealed their activity by piling items under bedding to look asleep and had stored tools in a guitar case. Manhole covers are typically locked from the inside, but the escapees appear to have broken a cover locking mechanism with the sledgehammer. They emerged around midnight and were found missing at a 5:30 a.m. head count; witnesses later reported seeing two men near a house with a guitar case just after midnight.

Investigators are probing whether tools, a cellphone, or other assistance were smuggled in, possibly by a female civilian employee who worked in the tailor shop with the inmates and who developed a relationship with Matt; authorities have visited her home. Employees are not required to pass metal detectors, and bag-size limits are rarely enforced, officials said. The FBI and state police continue a massive manhunt in dense terrain surrounding the prison; authorities believe the fugitives might remain within five to ten miles. A $100,000 reward has been offered, and police warn the public the men are very dangerous. Family members, including Matt’s son Nicholas Harris, expressed shock and concern, recalling Matt’s past escapes and violent history while hoping for a safe resolution.

Michael Doherty, a 40-year-old, 16-year veteran Boston police officer, was arrested after a violent, racially charged altercation with an Uber driver in South Boston early yesterday, authorities said. According to the Suffolk County prosecutor and police reports, Doherty became agitated while in the Uber because he believed the driver had stopped in the wrong place. At about 2:45 a.m., Doherty allegedly shouted, “You think I’m stupid, you [expletive] [racial slur],” then began assaulting the driver when the vehicle stopped near East 2nd and M streets. The driver exited and was chased around the car; a good Samaritan stopped to help, at which point Doherty briefly commandeered the Uber vehicle and drove off. The driver and the helper pursued, and Doherty later stopped on East 1st Street and Farragut Road, reportedly directed an additional racial slur at the helper (who is Black), and struck both men. The victims chased him until police arrived; Doherty fled but turned himself in that morning. He faces two counts of assault and battery with a racial slur and a charge of using a motor vehicle without authority. He was released on his previously posted $500 bail with conditions including sobriety monitoring, drug testing, evaluation, no contact with the victims, and a ban on using Uber. Doherty is on paid administrative leave while the department’s Anti‑Corruption Unit investigates. His attorney contends Doherty was the real victim, citing his injuries; Uber has barred him from its platform and has offered cooperation to investigators.

An overturned oil tanker on a national highway near Bahawalpur, Pakistan, burst into flames on June 25 after villagers and residents rushed to collect leaking fuel, killing at least 153 people and injuring many more, officials said. The tanker, en route from Karachi to Lahore, crashed when a tire burst. A mosque loudspeaker alerted people to the spill and hundreds arrived with jerry cans and on motorcycles; police warned of the danger but could not stop the crowd. Witnesses and officials said a spark — possibly from someone lighting a cigarette — ignited the spill, triggering a massive blaze that consumed people, motorcycles and cars within moments. Rescue teams, ambulances and army helicopters evacuated the critically burned; hospitals declared emergencies as dozens with severe burns—many over 80 percent of their bodies—were treated and some airlifted to Lahore and Multan. Many victims were burned beyond recognition and DNA testing will likely be needed. The disaster struck on the eve of Eid al-Fitr. Pakistan’s prime minister cut short a trip abroad and returned to respond to the catastrophe as authorities warned the death toll could still rise.

Shortly after Afghan and NATO forces cleared a 15-story, unfinished building overlooking the U.S. Embassy and NATO headquarters, officials said the last of six attackers was killed Wednesday morning, ending a nearly 21-hour siege that exposed weaknesses in Kabul’s security. The assault began around 1:30 p.m. Tuesday when at least three suicide bombers detonated explosives elsewhere in the city while gunmen and rocket teams took positions in the unoccupied high-rise, firing rockets and rifles at heavily fortified diplomatic and military compounds. Authorities found burqas in the van used to move weapons, and officials said attackers likely disguised themselves to smuggle arms into the building. NATO reported six coalition personnel wounded; Afghan officials say at least seven civilians were killed and 17 injured. The Taliban claimed responsibility, and U.S. Ambassador Ryan Crocker and others suggested the Haqqani network may have been involved. Afghan forces led the clearing operation with NATO helicopters providing backup, but the prolonged fight—during which diplomats and residents sheltered in bunkers—raised questions about intelligence and checkpoint effectiveness amid the planned handover of security to Afghan forces and the U.S. troop drawdown. The attack, one of several high-profile strikes this year, highlighted persistent insurgent capability and public anxiety about the country’s stability.

A mass shooting at the First Baptist Church in Sutherland Springs, Texas, devastated the tiny community on Sunday, leaving at least 26 people dead and about 20 wounded, authorities said. The suspected shooter was identified as 26-year-old Devin Patrick Kelley of New Braunfels; he was later found dead in his vehicle after fleeing the scene. Witnesses described chaos inside the small wooden sanctuary as Kelley, wearing tactical gear and armed with an AR-style rifle purchased in 2016, opened fire during Sunday service. A local resident engaged the attacker with their own rifle and, along with another man, pursued him until he was located by law enforcement. Authorities said multiple weapons were recovered from the suspect’s vehicle. Victims ranged in age from 5 to 72; among the dead was 14-year-old Annabelle Pomeroy, daughter of the church’s pastor, Frank Pomeroy. The shooting struck a close-knit rural town where the church served as a central hub for worship and community aid—bread baskets, free meals and outreach drew many residents. Survivors and relatives described shattered families, including an expectant mother and several children killed, with others critically injured. Vigils, candlelight prayers and 26 crosses were placed near the church as the town mourned. State and federal investigators, including the FBI and ATF, responded while officials urged prayers and called the attack an unspeakable tragedy.

Pittsfield police arrested two men in mid-November after a months‑long probe into a citywide prostitution ring that allegedly exploited multiple women — some of whom may have been minors — by using drugs, threats and coercion. Joseph E. Van Wert, 65, of Becket, and Randy W. Lambach, 45, of Pittsfield, face charges including human trafficking; Van Wert is also charged with conspiracy, deriving support from prostitution, maintaining a house of prostitution and sexual conduct for a fee. Authorities began investigating in spring 2017 after complaints about increased prostitution concentrated around First, Adam, North, Linden and Wahconah streets. Witnesses and victims say a man known as “Randy” recruited women with drug addictions, photographed them, posted ads (including on backpage.com) and arranged dates with clients. Lambach is accused of transporting women in a blue station wagon, negotiating fees (typically $80 for 30 minutes or $160–$200 for an hour), keeping 50–90 percent of proceeds or paying women in heroin, crack or pills, and sometimes threatening them or warning police wouldn’t believe addicts. He allegedly recruited about 10 women, drove them across town and out of state, and may have prostituted former foster children; one witness estimated a victim could have been about 15. Van Wert allegedly allowed meetings at his third‑floor apartment in exchange for cash and drugs. Both men pleaded not guilty; a dangerousness hearing was set to consider bail and the investigation continues with local and state detectives. Anyone with information is asked to contact Pittsfield Police.

Police charged 23-year-old Reco Latur Dawkins Jr. with attempted murder, felony breaking and entering and conspiracy after he allegedly shot Army National Guard medic Semantha Bunce during a violent home invasion in east Charlotte. Dawkins surrendered to the violent-crimes unit Sunday; police say he and at least one other person kicked in the Matlea Court home’s front door just before 10 a.m. Tuesday. Bunce, 21, was feeding her infant when the intruders arrived; she retrieved a firearm, met them in a stairwell/bedroom area and exchanged gunfire. She was struck multiple times — reportedly in the stomach and arm — and was hospitalized at Carolinas Medical Center in critical condition but showing signs of improvement. Her infant was unharmed. Family, friends and neighbors described Bunce, a combat medic with the 105th Engineer Battalion, as calm and trained under pressure; loved ones credit her training with helping her respond. The incident, believed to be random, drew national attention and prompted community concern on Matlea Court, where residents report recent break-ins and an armed robbery. Dawkins has prior convictions dating to his teens, including a 2010 breaking-and-entering conviction and several arrests over the past three years. Community members and coworkers have organized fundraising pages to assist the Bunce family with medical bills, childcare and other expenses while she recovers. Police continue investigating and have not detailed whether additional suspects remain at large.

A Cincinnati father accidentally shot and killed his 14-year-old son early Tuesday morning after mistaking him for an intruder at their East Price Hill home. The father, who had recently dropped the boy, identified as Georta Mack, at the bus stop, returned home and, hearing a noise in the basement, armed himself to investigate. Startled when the teen appeared, the father fired, striking him in the neck. In a distraught 911 call the father begged for help and tried to stem the bleeding; Georta was taken to Cincinnati Children’s Hospital and pronounced dead shortly after 8:15 a.m. Police say the father has been cooperative and is being interviewed; officers are consulting the Hamilton County prosecutor’s office and have not released names or said whether charges will be filed. Neighbors described Georta as a helpful, well-liked boy; city officials called the incident a “terrible, terrible tragedy.”

Toya Graham, the Baltimore mother captured on video dragging and repeatedly striking her masked teenage son amid the city’s protests and rioting, told CBS News she acted to protect him and to prevent him from becoming another Freddie Gray. Graham, a single mother of six, said she spotted her 16-year-old Michael in a hoodie among demonstrators and “lost it,” confronting him immediately. She described herself as “no-tolerant,” saying everyone who knows her understands she doesn’t play when it comes to her children; her son admitted his instinct was to run when he saw her. After bringing him home they watched news coverage together, and Graham hopes the episode will be a teachable moment so he grasps the seriousness of the unrest.

Graham condemned the vandalism and violence against officers, saying rioting is not the way to seek justice for Gray. Her intervention drew public attention and many supportive comments on her son’s social media. Baltimore Police Commissioner Anthony Batts praised her actions and lamented a lack of parental supervision, noting many rioters were area high school students who left school and engaged in throwing rocks and cinder blocks at police. The disturbances injured at least 20 officers and critically hurt one person in a fire; police made 235 arrests, including 34 juveniles. With the National Guard deployed, calmer streets were reported Tuesday and a 10 p.m.–5 a.m. curfew remained in effect. Graham acknowledged constraints some parents face—many must work—but stressed the need for follow-through to keep children safe.

Samuel Shaffer, 34, a self‑proclaimed prophet and co‑leader of the doomsday sect called the Knights of the Crystal Blade, has been sentenced to lengthy prison terms after admitting to sex crimes involving children. Shaffer pleaded guilty to felony child sodomy in Sanpete County and was given a sentence of 15 years to life; Utah State Courts say his overall time to be served will amount to a minimum of 26 years behind bars. That Sanpete County sentence runs concurrent with an earlier Iron County sentence: Shaffer was previously sentenced there to 25 years to life for first‑degree rape of a child and a second‑degree child abuse conviction.

The charges and investigation stem from events in December 2017, when police began probing the group after John Coltharp’s ex‑wife reported he had taken their four children. Authorities discovered two girls in 50‑gallon water barrels and two others in an abandoned single‑wide trailer; the children were found in poor condition, one pair having spent about 24 hours in subfreezing temperatures without adequate clothing, food or water, and others showing dehydration and lethargy. According to affidavits and prosecutors, Shaffer told detectives he had married an 8‑year‑old — the daughter of fellow cult member John Coltharp — while Coltharp said he had been married to Shaffer’s 7‑year‑old daughter. Coltharp pleaded guilty on June 13 to child sodomy and child bigamy; his sentencing is set for August 8. Additional charges against Shaffer in Sanpete County were dismissed. Another alleged follower of the group was charged on June 8 with child sexual abuse. Shaffer’s attorney has not commented publicly about any appeal.

On Feb. 11, the day Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak resigned, CBS chief foreign correspondent Lara Logan was covering celebrations in Cairo’s Tahrir Square for 60 Minutes when she and her team became separated from security and were surrounded by a mob of more than 200 people. In the crush she was subjected to a brutal, sustained sexual assault and beating before a group of women and about 20 Egyptian soldiers intervened and rescued her. Logan rejoined her crew, returned to the United States the next day and is recovering in a U.S. hospital. CBS and Logan’s family have asked for privacy and declined further comment. The assault was one of many attacks on journalists during the unrest; other reporters were injured and at least one Egyptian journalist was killed.

Otto Warmbier’s parents, Fred and Cindy, described in their first television interview since their 22-year-old son’s death the horrific condition in which North Korea returned him in June, and they called on the U.S. to relist Pyongyang as a state sponsor of terrorism. Warmbier, a University of Virginia student detained in North Korea in January 2016 after a tourist visit, was convicted in a 2016 “sham trial” and sentenced to 15 years of hard labor. The family received little information after March 2016 and were told only in June that Otto had been in a coma for more than a year. When the plane arrived in Ohio, the Warmbiers say they heard “inhuman howling” and found Otto on a stretcher with a shaved head, a feeding tube, mangled lower teeth, jerking violently, and apparently blind and deaf. Doctors at the University of Cincinnati Medical Center later reported extensive brain tissue loss consistent with cardiopulmonary arrest; they could not identify a clear cause and saw no obvious fractures. Otto died on June 19, days after his return. North Korea has denied torturing him, claiming he fell into a coma from botulism and a sleeping pill and calling his death a “mystery.” The Warmbiers vehemently reject that account, calling North Korea “terrorists” who kidnapped, tortured, and intentionally injured their son. They urge the U.S. to reclassify North Korea as a state sponsor of terror; the State Department says it is reviewing intelligence and will act if evidence supports such a designation. President Trump praised the parents’ interview on social media.

State investigators shuttered an unlicensed home day care on San Antonio’s far northwest side after a 4-month-old infant was allegedly bitten 27 times by another child while in care. Child Care Licensing ordered the operator to cease operations after discovering the unlicensed program had been running for eight years at a home on Bentwood View and that eight children were present when investigators arrived.

The infant was rushed to a hospital on Friday with pronounced bite marks over much of his body — including his eyes, cheeks, legs, stomach and back. The baby’s parents said the operator waited about four hours to notify them and only called when the injuries failed to subside; the operator told reporters she called the parents within minutes of finding the marks and said she did not know a license was required. The I-Team is not naming the operator because no criminal charges have been filed.

San Antonio Police Department confirmed the case is under investigation by its sex crimes unit; officials said the assignment does not imply a sexual crime but that the unit handles potential crimes against children. The operator could face charges such as child neglect or injury to a child by omission if investigators determine she failed to prevent the infant’s injuries. Child Protective Services said the operator has expressed interest in obtaining a license and would have to complete steps including background checks and CPR training before reopening.

Neighbors and some parents offered contrasting perspectives: one neighbor said he had safely used the home care for a year, and another parent who used the service for several years called the incident “blown out of proportion.” The story underscores warnings from child-care experts to check licensing status, staff-to-child ratios, caregiver qualifications and reporting practices when choosing care for infants, and to be vigilant about unlicensed operations.

Adriana, 39, and Leandro, 37, a Brazilian couple who have been together for seven years and share a six-year-old daughter, discovered in a single moment on live radio that the woman they had each spent their lives searching for was the same person — their birth mother, Maria. Both had been abandoned as infants: Adriana was left at age one and raised by her father, while Leandro learned at eight that the woman he’d known as his mother was a stepmother. Adriana, still haunted by the absence of her mother, contacted Rádio Globo’s reunion programme “A Hora é Agora” (The Time Is Now) to find Maria. During the on-air reunion, Maria mentioned she had another child, Leandro. Hearing this, Adriana broke down when she realized her husband was the son Maria named. The presenters verified surnames and parentage, confirming the traumatic coincidence: without knowing, the pair had married their biological sibling. Adriana had previously noticed an inconsistency—one of Leandro’s two birth certificates listed Maria as his mother—but had dismissed it as coincidence. The couple never formalized their union legally or religiously, so under Brazilian law the marriage has no official validity; nonetheless, they held a family meeting and decided to remain together, insisting their love and plans won’t be undone. The case highlights phenomena like genetic sexual attraction, where estranged relatives meeting as adults can misinterpret intimacy, and underscores the emotional, legal and ethical complications that can follow late family reunions. The couple says only death will part them.

Thirty years after 14-year-old Claire Hough was found brutally murdered on Torrey Pines State Beach on Aug. 24, 1984, San Diego homicide investigators say DNA evidence identified two suspects in her killing. Hough, who had been staying with her grandparents near the beach, was beaten, strangled, stabbed, had sand forced into her mouth and one breast severed. Cold-case detectives uncovered DNA links in November 2012 that pointed to two men: Ronald Clyde Tatro and Kevin Charles Brown.

Tatro, who died in a Tennessee boating accident in 2011 at age 67, was identified as a suspect in August 2014. The second man, Kevin Brown, was a civilian criminalist who worked in the San Diego Police Department laboratory from 1982 until his retirement in 2002. Investigators say Brown never worked on the Hough case or processed any of its evidence; he was described as a generalist whose duties included narcotics analysis and other lab work. Detectives spent about two years building a prosecutable case after the DNA breakthrough. Preparations were underway to arrest Brown, who had been informed he was under investigation, when he was found dead in Cuyamaca State Park in October; his death was initially ruled a suicide.

Homicide Lt. Paul Rorrison emphasized that the DNA testing—technology unavailable in 1984—was the crucial link. Investigators declined to say whether the suspects knew Hough or whether they had been earlier suspects. Police noted a similar 1978 Torrey Pines murder of 15-year-old Barbara Nantais, who was also beaten, strangled and had a breast severed, but said there is no direct evidence connecting the cases and they are not being treated as related. Authorities continue to ask anyone with information to contact the San Diego Police Homicide Unit or Crime Stoppers.

Juneau police defended their handling of the investigation into the death of newly elected Mayor Stephen “Greg” Fisk, 70, after his bruised and bloodied body was found in his home. Initial uncertainty and the department’s refusal to immediately rule out foul play fueled intense speculation and widespread media attention. Police spokeswoman Erann Kalwara and Chief Bryce Johnson said authorities had to consider all possibilities until autopsy results were available. A preliminary autopsy later indicated Fisk died of natural causes and that his injuries were consistent with a fall or stumbling into objects; Fisk had a history of heart problems and likely experienced a cardiac event before falling. No signs of forced entry, gunshot, drugs or suicide were found. Fisk’s son discovered him after the mayor missed appointments; Deputy Mayor Mary Becker was named acting mayor as the family grieves privately.

An Ontario judge has acquitted Toronto animal activist Anita Krajnc of mischief for giving water to pigs being transported to a slaughterhouse in Burlington in June 2015. Justice David Harris found Krajnc did not interfere with the animals’ owner’s lawful use of property, noting the pigs still reached the abattoir and there was no evidence she gave them anything other than water. Krajnc, founder of Toronto Pig Save, admitted pouring liquid through trailer slats but said she acted out of compassion; courtroom applause followed the verdict. Defence lawyers argued compassion and public-good motives, even likening her actions to historic human-rights activists, but Harris rejected those comparisons—calling some, including equating the act to people giving water to Jews during the Holocaust, offensive—and said such arguments seemed aimed at generating social-media attention. Farmers’ groups expressed disappointment, warning the action risked food safety and could encourage confrontations, while Krajnc’s lawyers hailed the decision as affirming that “compassion is not a crime” and lamented taxpayer expense on the prosecution. The case drew international attention, inspired allied groups and celebrity support, and Krajnc said she hoped it would further animal-rights advocacy; she still faces a separate charge of obstructing police from a later incident.

Eighteen-year-old Mary Kristene “Krissy” Chapa, shot in the head Saturday alongside her girlfriend, 19-year-old Mollie Judith Olgin—who died— is making an “amazing” recovery, her brother Hilario Chapa told NBCLatino. Doctors are impressed: Krissy can communicate using sign language she learned in high school and has regained movement on her right side, though her left remains unresponsive. She remains in intensive care with no timeline for discharge, and investigators, including the Texas Rangers, have not determined a suspect or motive. Portland police say there’s no evidence so far the attack was a hate crime, though they aren’t ruling it out. The Mexican-American Chapa family of Sinton, Texas is coping with the trauma; Krissy’s parents are at the hospital continually and the family has set up a WePay fund to help with medical bills. Mollie’s family, grieving, has been comforted by nationwide support and expects justice. Both families plan to meet when ready. A candlelight vigil and memorials have mobilized community support and calls to find the shooter and prevent similar violence.

The document is a long, opinionated collage of pieces. The first and largest section is a personal essay by a mother of a gender-nonconforming son who confronts cultural confusion and prejudice about boys who prefer feminine toys and behaviors. She rebukes playground moms, reparative-therapy advocates, and confusing media figures like Dr. Phil who say gender expression predicts sexual orientation yet also advise policing children’s play. She stresses that kids aren’t “confused,” that parents aren’t to blame for identity, and that societal ridicule—bullying, shaming, and institutional pressures—harms feminine boys. The essay calls out organizations and therapists who push “preventing” homosexuality and urges readers to stop blaming Barbies and start challenging bullies.

The remainder is a grab-bag of blog excerpts from a conservative local site: snarky commentary about a Virginia congressional candidate’s scandal, and many hyper-partisan posts about Manassas politics, local elections, crime, and culture-war topics, often criticizing Democrats and local officials. Overall the document juxtaposes a plea for acceptance with abrasive political blogging.

David Crosby, 73, struck a jogger near his Santa Ynez Valley home while driving his 2015 Tesla at the posted speed limit of 55 mph, according to multiple reports. The pedestrian, 46-year-old Jose Jimenez, was jogging with his 14-year-old son when Crosby’s vehicle made contact with him on the right front end. Emergency responders airlifted Jimenez to a hospital with multiple fractures, abrasions and lacerations; his injuries are not believed to be life-threatening. Crosby told authorities he had been blinded by the sun at the time and stopped immediately after the collision. A police report indicates no drugs or alcohol were involved; an investigation is ongoing. Crosby’s representative said the musician is “very upset” by the accident and relieved the injuries were not fatal, wishing Jimenez a speedy recovery. The incident occurred amid recent public attention on Crosby for other reasons: last year he confirmed that Crosby, Stills & Nash would not tour again with Neil Young, following a feud sparked by Crosby’s controversial comments about Young and Young’s partner. Crosby also released a solo album, Croz, in January, after focusing on work outside the group. Authorities continue to investigate the crash to determine further details.

Dr. Christopher Driskill, a 42-year-old obstetrician-gynecologist from Hobbs, New Mexico and president-elect of the New Mexico Medical Society, has been suspended by the New Mexico Medical Board amid a serious investigation into professional misconduct. The board’s report, detailed in the Albuquerque Journal, alleges multiple violations that the board found constituted a “clear and immediate danger to the public.” Central accusations include that Driskill drank alcohol at work—keeping a stash of liquor in his office—and practiced while under the influence. He is also accused of repeatedly abandoning patients in labor, including an instance in which a woman required an emergency C-section that was delayed because he was late to work, and another where he allegedly left a patient to give birth unattended because he was engaged in sexual activity with a different patient. The report further alleges Driskill had sexual relationships with multiple patients and some former staff members, wrote lewd personal notes in certain medical charts, and casually prescribed medication to a girlfriend without appropriate records. In August he was fired from Premier Health in Hobbs; Premier notified his other employer, Lea Regional Medical Center, ten days later. Driskill had requested a temporary leave of absence and has not returned to work; he did not inform the medical board of his termination and leave as required. His medical license is suspended pending review and possible revocation; he has the right to a hearing but has not yet requested one and has not publicly responded to the allegations. The New Mexico Medical Society declined to comment until after the hearing.

On July 23, 1992, 19-year-old Morrad Ghonim raced from Creek Park in La Mirada with his wife Vicki fatally shot beside him and their 6-month-old son in the back seat. Initially, Ghonim told police they’d been victims of a botched carjacking after catcalling and confrontation in the park; he said he never saw the shooter. The case went cold for years until a renewed effort by the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, using grant-funded genetic testing, matched DNA on clothing found in nearby bushes to Leon Martinez, then serving time for burglary. Martinez eventually admitted to being the shooter but said he had been hired by Ghonim to stage a robbery and kill Vicki for $10,000 (he later claimed he received $5,000). Martinez testified he approached the Honda high on cocaine, demanded money, and shot Vicki repeatedly as she begged him not to harm her baby; after the killing he accepted cash from Ghonim over the victim’s body.

Martinez’s shifting accounts and recorded jail calls in which he suggested fabricating testimony drew defense criticism, as did questions about motive and limited physical evidence tying Ghonim to the payment. A witness, Deanna Woody, testified Martinez had confessed to her in 1998 and recalled seeing him with a Middle Eastern man days before the murder, though she failed to identify Ghonim in a lineup. Ghonim was arrested years later in Antigua and extradited to California. In 2016 a judge found sufficient evidence to proceed; in a later trial a jury convicted Ghonim of first-degree murder and special circumstances—solicitation, lying in wait, financial gain and use of a handgun. He faces sentencing and potential life or death penalties; prosecutors have not yet decided whether to seek the death penalty.

Michael Cohen, 42, a part-time accountant and British citizen living in Cape Town, was severely mauled by a great white shark while swimming at Fish Hoek beach at lunchtime. Witnesses and authorities said he was about 50 yards (roughly 50 meters) from shore when the shark attacked, repeatedly biting both legs. Friends and shark spotters pulled him from the water; one leg was bitten off above the knee and the other badly mangled or severed below the knee. Paramedics stabilized him on the beach, sedated him, and he was airlifted to Constantiaberg Medi-Clinic in critical condition where he underwent surgery. His father was at his bedside.

Shark warning flags had been flying and spotters had seen great whites in the area about 90 minutes earlier; the beach had been closed, and spotters attempted to warn and recover him after noticing someone had entered the water. A siren that normally alerts swimmers did not sound due to a power cut. Locals said Cohen was a regular swimmer who had been repeatedly warned about sharks but often ignored warnings. An amateur video showed a shark still in the bay after the rescue. Authorities closed Fish Hoek and nearby beaches as a precaution and continued to monitor the shark.

A public online clash erupted between former Alaska governor Sarah Palin and rapper Azealia Banks after Banks reacted angrily to a satirical Newslo piece that falsely attributed racist comments to Palin. Believing the fake interview, Banks launched a graphic, now-deleted Twitter rant in which she said Palin should be gang-raped by black men and filmed — remarks that were captured by other outlets before deletion. Banks later posted a halting apology via Tumblr, calling her tweets a crude joke and insisting they referred to consensual group sex “NOT” rape, while also taking shots at Palin’s family. Palin responded publicly, calling Banks’ rants “bizarre” and accusing her of being duped by a fake article. Palin urged Banks to use her platform for good, warned she would review her daughter’s music exposure, and said she would not let the incident go. Palin told People she would sue Banks “on behalf of all reasonable women,” framing the lawsuit as retaliation against repeated threats and attacks and alleging double standards that allow provocative celebrities to profit from divisive tactics. Banks fired back with further insults, making the dispute unlikely to end soon. The episode revived attention to Banks’ history of public controversies and to Palin’s readiness to pursue legal action; specific lawsuit details remained unspecified.

A Palestinian teenager, Muhammad (Mohammed) Abu Khdeir, was abducted near his Shuafat home in East Jerusalem in the early hours of Wednesday and later found burned to death in a forest on the outskirts of the city, a killing widely reported as retaliatory for the recent abduction and murder of three Israeli teenagers. Muhammad, 16 or 17 in reports, was reportedly taken around 4 a.m. as he headed to dawn prayers during Ramadan; surveillance footage and family testimony point to two assailants forcing him into a vehicle. His badly burned body required DNA to confirm identity, and an extended post-mortem delayed his funeral. His father and other residents said police responded slowly and distrusted Israeli authorities, accusing them of bias toward Jewish settlers. Tensions escalated quickly: earlier that night roughly 200 Jewish extremists marched through Jerusalem chanting “Death to the Arabs” and attacking Arab Israelis; after Muhammad’s body was discovered, clashes erupted between Palestinian youths and Israeli riot police—stones, slingshots and Molotovs met foam-tipped bullets, sound grenades and tear gas, leaving many wounded. The murder drew international condemnation, including from the Obama administration and European officials. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called the killing “despicable” and ordered an urgent investigation; relatives of one of the murdered Israeli teens denounced revenge violence. Palestinian leaders blamed Israeli policies, with President Mahmoud Abbas accusing settlers and threatening legal action at the U.N., while some Palestinians viewed the earlier disappearance of the three Israelis as a pretext for cracking down on Palestinian political reconciliations. Separately, Israeli airstrikes on Gaza followed rocket and mortar fire from militant groups, deepening fears of wider escalation amid mutual recriminations and communal distrust.

Suspected militants stormed the American University of Afghanistan (AUAF) in Kabul on the evening of Aug. 24, 2016, triggering explosions and sustained gunfire that trapped foreign staff and students inside the walled campus. Witnesses described chaos as attackers detonated a car bomb at the main gate, fired into buildings and tossed grenades, prompting some students to jump from second-floor windows to escape; several suffered broken legs, head injuries and other wounds. Afghan special forces, supported by a small number of U.S. advisers, surrounded and then entered the compound, conducting a prolonged clearance operation that officials later said ended with two attackers killed. Casualty reports varied: hospital officials initially cited at least one dead and 14 wounded, while police later reported 12 killed — including students, policemen and guards — and numerous injured. No group immediately claimed responsibility; the assault follows recent kidnappings of two AUAF teachers and occurs amid intensified Taliban and Islamic State attacks aimed at destabilizing the Kabul government. The university, founded in 2006 and seen as a symbol of Afghan‑U.S. cooperation, has about 1,700 students and suspended operations after the earlier abductions.

A violent mass brawl erupted at Moscow’s Khovanskoye cemetery on May 14, leaving multiple dead and scores injured after fighting between rival groups over control of burial-related services. Reports vary, but between 200 and 400 people took part, many armed with bats, shovels, metal bars and reportedly some firearms, including assault rifles and handguns. Police and National Guard units intervened; officers fired warning shots and detained dozens—estimates range from more than 50 to around 100 arrests. Authorities and news outlets reported at least two to three fatalities: several victims were struck and killed by a car trying to flee the scene, and authorities said one victim included a police officer. Nearly 30 people were hospitalized, some critically. Eyewitnesses described prolonged shooting, bullet-riddled cars and a cemetery littered with debris and casings. Investigations suggest the clash stemmed from a turf war: an organized group allegedly sought to extort or impose “taxes” on cemetery workers and seize lucrative service contracts, prompting armed resistance from workers, many identified as migrants from Central Asia, and attackers reportedly from the North Caucasus. Moscow dismissed the cemetery director and pledged action against the private security firm judged to have failed in providing protection.
